### Series Title Page

*Complete Course of the Fathers, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, diligently corrected by comparison with one another and with several manuscript codices; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever any Father has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the individual texts of each biblical book and in which passages of their works they did so. An extremely accurate edition, easily preferable to all others when one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the whole work, the low price, and especially this collection, the first unified, systematic, and chronological gathering of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but assembled for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.*

**SECOND SERIES**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# In the Year of Our Lord 700: Sergius I, Roman Pontiff

[Col. 0009]

## Historical Notice on Pope Sergius

*(From the Book of the Pontiffs, various editions.)*

### [Col. 0009A] Editorial Note

**Sergius, etc.** When Conon, after completing a pontificate of eleven months, died on 21 September 687 [Col. 0009B], an interregnum of two months and twenty-three days preceded the ordination of his successor, as all the codices teach except the Mazarin Codex, which adds one day; the third and fifth Colbertine catalogues and the Veronese catalogue agree with it. Yet all agree in a remarkably strange way: if the day of death is excluded, there are twenty-three days; if it is included, twenty-four days, in addition to the two months of the interregnum.

Accordingly, Sergius, Conon’s successor, after the ambition of his rival, the archdeacon, together with the crime connected with it, had been frustrated—as I discussed in the notice on Conon—was ordained pontiff on 15 December of the aforementioned year, 687, as the letter *F* with the dominical letter shows. He administered the apostolic see longer than his predecessors, closed the seventh century, and, in the first year of the eighth century then unfolding, died on 8 September, the sixth day before the Ides of September, in the fifteenth indiction, as the common, Freherian, and Cavensis codices correctly state. This indiction corresponds to the year 701, the year of Sergius’s death.

The other codices I use give the fourteenth indiction [Col. 0009C], which indicates September of the preceding year, 700. But since all these codices agree with the others in assigning Sergius’s pontificate a duration of thirteen years, eight months, and twenty-three days, it is plainly evident that those codices which give the fourteenth indiction are erroneous. This follows both from the correctly established dates of his predecessors and from a monument which Antonio Pagi reports as derived from Bede and which confirms the beginning of Sergius’s pontificate (Pagi, p. 689, no. 5).

It is the epitaph of King Cædwalla, ending as follows: “On the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, in the second indiction, while the apostolic man, Lord Pope Sergius, was pontiff in the second year.” If in April of the year 689 Sergius was in his second year, there can be no doubt that the beginning of his see is correctly reckoned from the year 687, namely from the final month of that year, December, as I stated above.

Moreover, Sergius’s death cannot be brought back by a whole year on the authority of any codices or catalogues whatsoever. The Bergomate catalogue, the only one supporting this view, gives twelve years instead of thirteen; but because it agrees with the others in determining the reigns of the successors by fixed chronological markers, as I shall show [Col. 0010A], it does not provide support for the others but rather harms itself [Col. 0010B], revealing a new error from which it suffers.

The first, second, and third Colbertine codices, as well as the Palatine-Vatican, Lucan, and Farfense codices, suffer from a lesser fault: they omit a month. The Veronese also began at this point to be less careful, no longer recording the days on which pontiffs died. In the case of Sergius, however, it is not merely careless but plainly erroneous, adding a whole year to his pontificate contrary to the testimony of all the others.

Regarding the addition of one day found in all the Colbertine catalogues except the second and fifth, and scattered among other catalogues, I repeat what I said about the interregnum: every difference is removed by either including or excluding the day of death.

Thus, drawing my conclusion from beginning to end, I state that Sergius, ordained on 15 December 687, sat for thirteen years, eight months, and twenty-three days, and exchanged life for death on 8 September 701.

**CENNUS.**

**Sergius.** According to Molanus, in his *Index of the Saints of Belgium*, Saint Hubert, bishop of Liège and most worthy successor of Saint Lambert the martyr, was consecrated by this pontiff. Hubert was noble by birth. In order to keep his subjects firmly and perpetually established in observance of the Catholic faith and obedience to the holy Roman Church—from which they had received the holy Gospel—and to bind their descendants by the same bond, he gave them the public seal of Saint Lambert the martyr, engraved with the saint’s image and marked with this inscription: “Holy Liège, daughter of the Roman Church.” [Col. 0010C]

**BIN. and LABB.**

**Sergius.** Son of the merchant Tiberius, a native of Antioch, he came to Rome during the pontificate of Pope Adeodatus and was enrolled in the Roman clergy. Soon afterward he became a regular canon and then a cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna at the Two Houses, appointed by Pope Leo II. He acquired such renown that, when Conon died, he was substituted in his place. He was elected on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January and consecrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, at the beginning of the year 687.

**CIACONIUS.**

Sergius, Syrian by nation, from the region of Antioch, born to a father named Tiberius at Panormus in Sicily, sat for thirteen years, eight months, and twenty-three days. [Col. 0010A]

### Editorial Note

Lucan Codex: fourteen.

He came to Rome during the pontificate of the blessed Adeodatus and was enrolled among the clergy of the Roman Church. Since he was diligent and capable in the office of singing, he was entrusted to the senior singers for instruction in chant; he was made an acolyte and, advancing through the ranks, was ordained priest by the blessed pontiff Leo in the title of Saint Susanna, which is called “at the Two Houses.”

### Editorial Note

Lucan Codex: *piorum*; other manuscripts: *priori*. Lucan Codex: *qui*; Labbe: *quae*; other manuscripts: *qui et*.

### [Col. 0010C] Editorial Note

**Here, during his presbyterate, he diligently celebrated the solemn rites of Mass in various cemeteries.** In the cemeteries there were oratories or altars at which stations and gatherings of Christians took place for the purpose of prayer, and Masses were celebrated. Anastasius, in his notice of Gregory III, writes: “He also instituted an annual station to be held in the cemetery of Saint Petronilla.”

Hence, in the time of Decius, Christians were forbidden to set foot in cemeteries. Pontius the deacon, in his *Life of Cyprian*, in Surius, 14 September, writes: “They also ordered that no assemblies be held in any places and that they should not enter cemeteries.” [Col. 0011B]

Socrates relates that the people of Alexandria, so as not to communicate with George the pseudo-bishop, withdrew to a cemetery for the purpose of prayer, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 23:

> Τῇ ἑβδομάδι μετὰ τὴν ἁγίαν πεντηκοστὴν ὁ λαὸς νηστεύσας ἐξῆλθε παρὰ τὸ κοιμητήριον εὔξασθαι.

> In the week after holy Pentecost, the people, having fasted, went out to the cemetery to pray.

For in the week after holy Pentecost, the people, having fasted, went back to the cemetery for the purpose of prayer.

Theodoret likewise, book II, chapter 14.

**ALTASERRA.**

Here, during his presbyterate, he diligently celebrated the solemn rites of Mass in various cemeteries.

After seven years, the blessed Conon, bishop of the apostolic see, died. As usually happens [Col. 0010A], the Roman people of the city were divided into two parties. One party chose Theodore the archpriest; the other chose Paschal the archdeacon.

### Editorial Note

The Lucan Codex reads: “the people of the city of Rome [chose] Theodore the archpriest and Paschal the archdeacon.”

The point which we noted above concerning Boniface III—that he had decreed in a synod of seventy-two bishops that no one, while the pontiff was alive or while a city’s bishop was alive, should presume to speak of his successor or form parties for himself before the third day after his deposition—appears still more clearly in the election of Sergius. There the reason and necessity for issuing that decree, to prevent the evils arising from the ambition of candidates, are plainly discernible.

According to Anastasius in his *Life of Conon*, Conon had bequeathed a fixed sum of gold for distribution to the clergy as a *roga*, or *presbyterium*, as it was called. The archdeacon generally supervised its distribution. Therefore Paschal the archdeacon, while Conon was ill, did not distribute that gold at all but promised it to John the exarch, provided that John would assist him in the election. [Col. 0011C]

From this arose the schism between Paschal the archdeacon and Theodore the archpriest.

For the authority of the archdeacon in governing the clergy, see Agnellus in his *Life of Theodore of Ravenna*. Speaking of an extreme shortage of grain, he says:

> When the priests could not find anything with which to buy it, they went to him and begged him to provide assistance. He summoned the archdeacon, named Theodore … and said to them: “Tell the priests of the Church and the entire clergy: ‘Why are you being consumed by the poverty of hunger? If you surrender the entire fourth-part belonging to the Church and receive only a gift for the fourth-part throughout the course of the year, according to the pontiff’s provision, I shall now relieve your poverty.’” They were long chastised, and as the famine grew worse they consented. From that time the fourth-part was taken away from the clergy of that Church down to the present day.

> He also abolished the custom of the Church, which had been written in separate volumes for each office, and consumed it by fire. All these things had been entrusted to the custody of the archdeacon of Ravenna.

**BENCINUS.**

Paschal the archdeacon.

Theodore the archpriest, arriving with the people who supported him, occupied the inner part of the patriarchate. Paschal occupied the outer part, from the oratory of Saint Sylvester, and the basilica of the Julian House, which looks out over the Campus.

### Editorial Notes

The Lucan Codex reads: “the basilica.”

While neither yielded the place to the other, but both persisted fiercely in order that one might overcome the other, the leading judges and the army of the Roman military, together with a large part of the clergy—especially the priests—and a multitude of citizens [Col. 0011B], took counsel.

The Lucan Codex reads: “others”; another reading is “unanimously.”

Another reading is: “or the seditious clergy”; another: “or the greater part of the clergy, if that is what is intended.”

### [Col. 0011C] Editorial Note

They went to the Sacred Palace. The Sacred Palace, to which the greater part of the clergy and the leaders of the army went from the Lateran in order to deliberate on ending the schism between Theodore the archpriest and Paschal the archdeacon [Col. 0012B], was situated not on the Palatine, where the ancient imperial residences had stood, but not far from the title of Saint Sixtus, at the place where the Appian Way branches off from the Latina.

There stood very spacious buildings called the Sacred Palace. They were used either by the pontiff or by the emperor, whenever it happened that he was present at Rome. Within the Sacred Palace an oratory or church of Saint Caesarius had been built. Both several ancient monuments and the acts of the sacred Council of Trent testify that it had been honored under the title of Saint Caesarius in the Palace; in the latter, Christophorus Cardinal Madrucius is subscribed as priest of Saint Caesarius in the Palace.

Sixtus V removed this church from the list of titles because, having collapsed through excessive age, it was completely inaccessible in his time. It was nevertheless rebuilt not long afterward, during the pontificate of Clement VIII. Clement also ensured that the church’s former dignity would remain intact for posterity by again entering it among the titles.

I record these observations from the most learned Baronius, under the year 603, no. 2.

**MAFEUS.**

They went to the Sacred Palace and, after deliberating at length about what ought to be done and how the dispute between the two rival electors might be calmed, with God’s assent they reached agreement on the person of the then-designated Sergius, a venerable priest.

### Editorial Notes

The Lucan Codex and others read: “the intention.”

Another reading is: “then the priests came.”

They took him from the midst of the people and brought him into the oratory of the blessed Caesarius, martyr of Christ, which is within the aforementioned Sacred Palace. From there they led him to the Lateran episcopate with acclamations of praise.

### Editorial Notes

Another reading is: “which is within the Palace, they introduced him.”

The Lucan Codex reads: “with acclamations.”

Although the inner doors of the patriarchate were fortified and closed, the party that had elected the aforementioned venerable man prevailed because it was stronger, and entered.

When he had entered, one of the two elected men—namely Theodore the archpriest—immediately withdrew and humbled himself.

### [Col. 0012D] Editorial Note

He entered, greeted, and kissed the aforementioned most holy elect.

When Theodore and Paschal had been elected in opposition and Sergius had been elected to dissolve the schism, Theodore, one of the two elected in the schism, approached Sergius by prostration and a kiss.

Cardinals and bishops are admitted to kiss as brothers, and even exempt abbots are admitted to kiss the feet of the supreme pontiff (*Cap. Cum olim*, *De Privilegiis*). Bishops are also admitted to kiss the feet of a prince out of reverence for their order.

Ambrose, Letter 27, concerning his embassy to the tyrant Maximus, seated at Trier, writes:

> When he sat in the council chamber, I entered; he rose so that he might give me a kiss.

Hilary of Poitiers, *Against Constantius*:

> You receive priests with the kiss by which Christ also was betrayed.

Laymen kiss the feet of the Roman pontiff at his ordination. Anastasius, in his notice of Valentinus, writes:

> Then, amid fitting praises of glory and greatness of honor, he was led by them to the Lateran patriarchate and placed upon the pontifical throne; and all the Roman senate kissed his feet with rejoicing, and so forth.

Cardinals also, at the pontiff’s ordination, bow down to kiss his feet. Radevicus, *Deeds of Frederick*, book II, chapter 66 [Col. 0013B]:

> Then, as is customary, the Lord cardinals and the Roman clergy—all who were present and those who later gathered—and the greater part of the Roman people kissed his feet.

Peter Damian, cardinal and bishop of Ostia, when consulted about Cadalo, the antipope, and Alexander II, as to which should be judged the true pontiff, says in book III, letter 4:

> I give my hands, I kiss his soles, and I call not only the apostolic man but even an apostle himself, if you command me.

Even emperors kiss the feet of the pontiff. Justinian II kissed the feet of Pope Constantine, as Anastasius relates in his notice of Constantine:

> On the day when they saw each other, the most Christian Augustus prostrated himself with the crown upon his head and kissed the pontiff’s feet.

Siginolfus, prince of the Beneventans, received a blessing from Sergius II after first kissing the pontiff’s feet. Anastasius, in his notice of Sergius II, writes:

> After the bishop had received him, Siginolfus prostrated himself on the ground, humbly kissed the pontiff’s precious feet, received his blessing, and departed from his presence.

Finally, at the election of the Roman pontiff, it was an ancient custom to kiss the feet of the elected man. The same author, in his notice of Leo IV:

> Preserving the ancient custom, they all kissed his feet.

The same author, in his notice of Benedict III:

> And going forward, they began to kiss his footprints.

**ALTASERRA.**

He entered, greeted, and kissed the aforementioned most holy elect.

But Paschal’s hardness of heart in no way permitted him to do this.

### Editorial Note

Another reading is: “because of the hardness of his heart.”

At last, compelled and disgraced, willing or unwilling, he entered and greeted his lord and elect.

Even then Paschal secretly did not cease sending messengers of his own to Ravenna. By promises of money or various other gifts, he persuaded John the patrician and exarch, surnamed Platyn, to come secretly to Rome with his judges, without anyone knowing.

He came so secretly that neither the standards nor the military banners, together with the soldiers of the Roman army, met him at the proper place according to custom, except near the Roman city. When he arrived and found that everyone had agreed on Sergius, he could not support Paschal.

Nevertheless, through the misery of that same Paschal, the exarch inflicted expense and damage upon the church of the blessed apostle Peter. [Col. 0013B]

### Editorial Note

The Lucan Codex reads: “because.”

This was the amount that had been promised to the aforementioned exarch by Paschal: one hundred pounds of gold, demanded from the Church’s resources. The most holy elect Sergius protested that he had neither promised to give it nor possessed the ability to give it. To move the hearts of those who saw this to contrition, he ordered the chalices and crowns that had hung from ancient times before the sacred altar and the confession of the blessed apostle Peter to be taken down and

### [Col. 0013C] Editorial Note

given as pledges.

In public necessities of the Church, bishops gave sacred vessels as pledges, and even pledged persons who were attached to the service of the Church. Thus, when those who remained in Sicily to administer the patrimony of Saint Peter were held as pledges by the military, Conon arranged for their redemption. Hence Anastasius writes in his *Life of Conon*:

> He sent another order that the household of the aforementioned patrimony and of Sicily, which was being held in pledge by the military, should be restored.

Likewise, when Pope Agapetus had pledged sacred vessels to the royal treasurers in order to undertake a journey to “Colim.” [reading uncertain] for the needs of the Church, once the matter became known, the senator ordered them to be restored, as Cassiodorus relates, book XII, letter 20, p. 197:

> Therefore, warned by our command and made secure by the royal order, return the sacred vessels, together with the written obligation, to the agents of the blessed apostle Peter without any delay, so that, when profitably returned, they may quickly appear to have obtained what was requested; let the desired things be reported to all the ministers of the Church, to be proclaimed throughout the world; let what was originally his be restored, since he rightly received it through generosity.

James II, king of Aragon, abolished the pledging of persons in 1269:

> We do not wish any person to be pledged, or to be seized or detained on account of any pledge for another’s debt in our land … for when a neighbor is pledged on behalf of a neighbor, it is sufficient that property, not a person, be pledged.

**BENCINUS.**

to be given as a pledge.

But even this did not soften the exarch’s hardness, until he received the one hundred pounds of gold, as stated.

### Editorial Note

Another reading is: “pounds.”

And although, as has been said, the wretched Paschal inflicted this expense and damage upon the Church of Christ,

### Editorial Note

Another reading is: “has inflicted” (*infixerit*).

nevertheless, with Christ’s favor, Sergius, priest and elect, was ordained pontiff in the see of the blessed apostle Peter.

### Editorial Note

He was ordained pontiff.

Paschal, a deacon of the Roman Church, sent letters to John, the new exarch of Ravenna, so that he might more easily obtain the pontificate after Conon’s death. He offered him the amount of gold that Pope Benedict had left and that Conon had ordered distributed both to the clergy and to the monasteries, provided that John would secure his election to the pontificate.

Seven days after the death of the blessed Conon, proceedings concerning the election of his successor began, as was customary. When the people were divided into two factions, a schism arose. One party supported Theodore the archpriest, and the other Paschal the archdeacon. One elected Theodore, the other Paschal.

Theodore, with the people who supported him, occupied the inner part of the patriarchate; Paschal occupied the outer part, from the oratory of Saint Sylvester and the basilica of the Julian House, which looks out over the Campus.

When neither would yield the place to the other, the leading judges, the Roman army, the greater part of the clergy, and especially the priests went to the Sacred Palace. After deliberating at length about what should be done, with God’s assent they unanimously elected a third man: Sergius, a priest of the Holy Roman Church, Syrian by nation, a native of Antioch, son of Tiberius, raised at Panormus in Sicily, whom Pope Adeodatus had adopted into the Roman clergy and whom Leo II had ordained priest.

They took him from the midst of the people and brought him into the oratory of the blessed Caesarius, martyr of Christ, which is within the Palace; from there they led him to the Lateran episcopate with acclamations of praise.

Theodore voluntarily yielded to Sergius, the legitimate pontiff. Paschal, obstinate in schism, was compelled to greet him; but, after sending men of his faction to Ravenna, he summoned to Rome the aforementioned exarch John, surnamed Platyn, so that he might assert Paschal’s pontifical name and dignity.

When the exarch saw that Sergius had been lawfully placed upon the see of Saint Peter by the votes and common consent of all, he could not support Paschal. He nevertheless demanded from Sergius one hundred pounds of gold, which Paschal had promised him.

When Sergius protested that he had neither promised them nor possessed sufficient resources for the Church to pay them, he ordered the chalices and crowns that had hung from ancient times before the sacred altar and the confession of the blessed Peter to be taken down and given as a pledge in order to bend the exarch. The money-loving man was no more moved by this and did not cease troubling the Church until he had received the one hundred pounds of gold.

Not long afterward, Paschal was convicted of magic and, by the pontiff’s judgment, deprived of the office of archdeacon and confined in a monastery, where he died unrepentant after five years.

These facts are established by Anastasius.

**PAGIUS.**

He was ordained pontiff.

### Editorial Note

The aforementioned Paschal, not long afterward, was deprived of the office of archdeacon on account of certain incantations and sacred groves that he worshiped, or the divinations that he practiced with other *respectores*.

Paschal, archdeacon of the Roman Church, was deposed on account of certain incantations and the worship of groves that he practiced with other *respectores*, that is, worshipers. There were people who made vows and prayers at trees or springs.

The Synod of Auxerre, canon 3, says:

> It is not permitted to fulfill vows among thickets or sacred trees, or at springs.

*Respectare* is a frequentative verb meaning the same as *colere*, “to worship” or “to regard with reverence.” Velleius Paterculus, book II, writes:

> Having obtained permission to touch his hand, he returned to the little boat and, gazing without end at Caesar, was brought to the bank where his own people were.

Hence *respectores*.

**ALTASERRA.**

The aforementioned Paschal, not long afterward, was deprived of the office of archdeacon on account of certain incantations,

The Lucan Codex and others read: “and little groves.”

and of the sacred groves that he worshiped, or of the divinations that he practiced with other

### Editorial Note

The Lucan Codex reads: *respectatoribus*; another reading is *inspectoribus*.

*respectores*. With the judgment of God and of the blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, intervening, he was deprived of office and confined in a monastery. After five years, unrepentant because of the hardness of his heart, he died.

[Note: [Col. 0015B] Therefore, during his pontificate, Emperor Justinian ordered a council to be held in the imperial city, at which legates of the Apostolic See were also present. The subscriptions of these legates are not extant, unless perhaps the following subscription of Basil, bishop of Gortyna, the metropolitan see of Crete, is to be understood in this way: “I, Basil, bishop of the Gortynians, metropolitan of the Christ-loving island of Crete, and representing the whole synod of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed by defining.” (Quinisext Council.) Accordingly, one must say with Peter de Marca that, when Anastasius calls them legates, he means an apocrisiarius, or representative, [Col. 0015C] who was accustomed, at the pontiff’s command, to remain at the imperial court in Constantinople, conducting the affairs of the Holy See and whatever other matters arose; nevertheless, he had no jurisdiction, so that he could not decide matters, especially important ones, without a special mandate. His sole authority was to report them and await the pontiff’s commands. Emperor Justinian II subscribed first to the council’s decrees; but at the head of the catalogue of all the Fathers, a place was left for Sergius’s subscription, with these words written: “Place of the most holy Roman pope.” The rest is made sufficiently clear by Anastasius, both in this section and in the following one. SOMMIER.]

Therefore, during his pontificate, Emperor Justinian ordered a council to be held in the imperial city. [Note: [Col. 0015C] Emperor Justinian ordered a council to be held in the imperial city. This assembly was held in the same Trullo of the Church at Constantinople in order to supplement the Fifth and Sixth Synods, since they had issued no canons concerning discipline. The bishops of the pseudo-synod testify in their preface to Justinian the Younger that it was held in the Trullo of the imperial Church, where the Sixth Ecumenical Synod had been convened ten years earlier. [Col. 0015D] For this reason it is called by Theodore Balsamon, the patron of the schismatics, the “Quinisext Synod” (σύνοδος πενθέκτη), that is, the Fifth-Sixth Synod. Our author says that legates of the Apostolic See attended it and were deceived into subscribing to it. This should not be understood to mean that Sergius sent legates who expressed his own authority to this assembly, which he condemned. Rather, the meaning is that a representative of the Apostolic See was present, one who had resided at Constantinople since the time of Justinian I and administered matters of faith and discipline, but who could undertake no jurisdiction without an instruction. Basil, archbishop of Gortyna in Crete, alone performed this legation at that time, and subscribed to the pseudo-synod in the name of the Roman Church. Besides him, Balsamon argues that, in order to confer ecumenical authority upon this wandering synod—for that is what the ancients called it—a bishop representing the Roman synod, together with the bishops of Thessalonica, Sardinia, Heraclea, and Corinth, who were then papal legates, also subscribed, as is written in the ancient single-canons. But, leaving aside the papal legation—for the bishop of Heraclea was never invested with it—the very acts of the Trullan assembly that survive today expose Balsamon’s falsehood. The ordinary legate of the Apostolic See, the bishop of Corinth, as well as the bishops of Ravenna, Heraclea, and Sardinia, were absent from it; a blank sheet was left for them so that they might subscribe their names after the synod had been dissolved: “Place of the bishop of Heraclea, of Sardinia, of Ravenna, and of Corinth” (Τόπος τοῦ Ἡρακλείας, τοῦ Σαρδινίας, τοῦ Ῥαβέννης, τοῦ Κορίνθου). Likewise, in the place above, the pseudo-synod left a blank sheet for Pope Sergius, as head of all priests: “Place of the most holy pope of Rome” (Τόπος τοῦ ἁγιωτάτου πάπα Ῥώμης). Sergius rejected it, however, for among the more than one hundred canons it contains, although some are highly commendable, others are very objectionable. In canon 3—not to discuss each one individually—the eighty-five Canons of the Apostles are decreed to be received, although Gelasius had solemnly placed all of them among the apocrypha in a decree accepted throughout the world. Canon 13 attacks the law of ecclesiastical celibacy and censures the most chaste discipline of the Roman Church, by which ministers of sacred things are forbidden the use of marriage. Canon 55 condemns the Saturday fast, a venerable custom of the Roman Church. Canon 67 prescribes abstinence from blood and from what has been strangled, under penalty of deposition for clerics and excommunication for laypeople, as though we ought always to nourish ourselves with milk, which we first began to suck as infants. Whoever wishes to know more about this synod should consult the father of ecclesiastical annals (under the year 692). MAFEUS.]

Emperor Justinian [Note: [Col. 0016C] ordered a council to be held in the imperial city. Since no canons had been issued at the Fifth and Sixth General Synods for the restoration of discipline and the reform of morals, Emperor Justinian convened the Trullan Synod to supplement the Fifth and Sixth Synods. The bishops who assembled there indicate the reason for the synod in their address to the emperor: “Since the two holy and universal synods—namely, the Fifth and Sixth—did not at all formulate sacred canons, as did the other four universal synods . . . therefore, at the command of your piety, we have assembled in this God-guarded and imperial city and have written sacred canons.” Hence this synod was called Quinisext, because it was made as a supplement to both; others also called it the “wandering” synod. It was also called Trullan, because it was held in the Trullo of the great palace, according to Balsamon. Concerning the Trullo, see what is said under Agatho. But how did the Greeks come to believe that an ecumenical synod could not be celebrated without issuing canons, when, as Pope Leo teaches, such synods are held to extinguish heresy and confirm the Catholic faith? There are three opinions concerning the year in which this synod was celebrated. Some, with Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople during the Seventh General Synod, maintain that it was held four or five years after the Sixth Ecumenical Synod, and therefore in the year 686. But this opinion cannot be sustained. For canon 3 says that it was held during the fifth indiction, whereas in the year 685 the fourteenth indiction was in progress. Moreover, what follows will make it clear that its date must be placed during the pontificate of Sergius, who was ordained pope only in December of the year 687. Finally, it is clear that Tarasius was deceived, since he also asserts that those who subscribed under Constantine Pogonatus to the Sixth Synod subscribed to the present synod under Justinian. At this synod Paul subscribed as bishop of Constantinople, whereas George did so at the Sixth Synod. Peter subscribed as bishop of Alexandria, whereas at the Sixth Synod the same Peter was still a presbyter and vicar of the Alexandrian patriarch. Anastasius subscribed as bishop of Jerusalem, whereas at the Sixth Synod George subscribed in the name of the Church of Jerusalem. Finally, to say nothing of the others, George subscribed to this synod as bishop of Antioch, whereas Macarius, patriarch of that Church, attended the Sixth Synod and pronounced the sentence of deposition. The second opinion is that of Theophanes, who writes that this synod was held in the year 699 from the Incarnation according to the Alexandrian reckoning—a year beginning on the Kalends of September in the year 706 of our era. For that reason he also thinks that the synod began in that year, and adds that twenty-seven years elapsed between the Sixth Synod and the Trullan Synod; he ridicules those who assert in their writings that the capitular forms of the Sixth Council were published four full years later. Here he is referring to Tarasius and deriding his opinion. But the date he proposes is far less probable, since Paul, bishop of Constantinople, who presided over this synod, died in the year 693 and left the see vacant for Callinicus, as Theophanes himself records. Secondly, after the author of the synodical booklet has spoken of the Trullan Synod, he says: “When Leontius had seized the empire and had exiled Justinian to Cherson after cutting off his nose, Artemius, who is also called Anastasius, succeeded Leontius.” Therefore the Trullan Synod was convened not in the year 707 but before the year 695, when Justinian was deposed by Leontius. The third opinion is stated explicitly by Anastasius: this synod was convened while Sergius I was administering the Roman Church. He ought to be trusted safely. In his Life of Sergius he recounts so carefully what happened at Rome while Justinian Augustus was reigning for the first time—when Sergius was compelled to subscribe to the decrees of the Quinisext Synod—that he plainly knew the date of this synod well. Moreover, Bede, who lived in that age, in his book On the Six Ages, and Paul the Deacon, who flourished in the following century, in book VI of On the Deeds of the Lombards, chapter 11, both earlier authorities than Theophanes, support Anastasius. Since, then, canon 3 of the Trullan Synod says that it was celebrated in the year of the world 6109, and defenders of both opinions admit that this passage is corrupt and should be corrected from Theophanes under the year 677 from the Incarnation according to the Alexandrian reckoning, so that it should read “the year 6199,” and since that year of the world, according to the Constantinopolitan era, ended with August of the year 691, the Trullan Synod was likewise convened in that year. For on the Kalends of September of that year the year 6200 and the fifth indiction began; the synod was held while these were current, and the aforementioned canon was composed before the beginning of February in the year 692. For more on this matter, see the author of the Critique of Baronius, who, in the dissertation on the Greco-Roman Era prefixed to volume I, explains at length that Constantinopolitan era of the world and the other Greek eras, both those of the world and those of the Incarnation. Matthew Blastares, in the preface of his Nomocanon concerning the Trullan Synod, writes: “The principal figures of that synod were celebrated as Paul of Constantinople, Paul—read Peter—of Alexandria, George of Antioch, Anastasius of Jerusalem, John of New Justinianopolis, and Basil of the metropolitan see of Gortyna on the island of Crete, acting in place of the whole synod of the holy Roman Church. Thus, after the emperor’s subscription, each of the patriarchs and metropolitans signed his own name and dignity in the ancient books.” Nevertheless, Anastasius the Librarian, in his preface to Pope John VIII concerning the Seventh Synod, asserts that the patriarchs were not present even through legates. The author of the synodical booklet writes that 240 bishops attended this synod; Balsamon and Zonaras give the number as 217. In the copies existing today, however, only 211 are found subscribed, among whom were men whom integrity, learning, and holiness made commendable. Baronius and Binius, and even the recent anonymous author of Selection of the Acts of the Universal Church, or New Summary of the Councils, write that Callinicus, successor of Paul as patriarch of Constantinople, was the author and president of this synod. But this contradicts the manifest evidence of the subscriptions, the cited testimony of Balsamon, and Nicephorus in his Chronicle, as well as Theophanes, who connect Paul’s death with the year 693 and Callinicus’s accession. Lupus nevertheless followed Baronius’s opinion in his dissertation On the Cause and Date of the Trullan Synod, where he adds: “I think that his name—that is, Callinicus’s—as a man of disrepute was erased by later supporters of the synod and that Paul’s name was inserted in its place.” But none of the ancients accuses Callinicus of any crime, and it is gratuitously asserted that Paul’s name was substituted for Callinicus’s. Callinicus will be discussed below. Anastasius explicitly testifies that a legation of the Apostolic See attended this synod. In the Life of Pope Sergius he writes: “During the pontificate of this man, Emperor Justinian ordered a council to be held in the imperial city, at which legates of the Apostolic See also assembled and, having been deceived, subscribed.” Recent historians explain this legation in various ways; among them, de Marca, book V of On Concord, chapter 18, seems to have presented the matter most precisely. He observes that Roman pontiffs were accustomed to send legates to Christian emperors to conduct the affairs of the universal Church. These legates, called apocrisiarii and representatives, were permanent members of the prince’s retinue. They pursued before him the particular causes of the Roman Church and pleaded matters of faith and discipline; nevertheless, they exercised no jurisdiction unless by special delegation. This precaution was not useless for avoiding the machinations of the patriarchs of Constantinople. Always intent on enlarging their see, they could, through the emperor’s terror and threats, have extorted a legate’s assent to the establishment of innovations, so that the alteration might at least not appear wholly without color, being supported to some degree by the authority of the Apostolic See. Yet by their prudence the Roman pontiffs could not prevent themselves from falling into the very snares against which they had so carefully guarded. For at this Trullan Synod, so that some appearance of legitimacy might be sought for the new decrees established there, it assumed the title of ecumenical on the grounds that the authority of the Roman See had been employed. The legates—that is, the apocrisiarii or representatives of the Apostolic See who served as advisers before Emperor Justinian—were present at this synod. Certainly Pope Sergius had not sent legates equipped with his instructions to that assembly, for he condemned it as unlawful, as will soon be seen. Basil, bishop and metropolitan of Gortyna in the province of Crete, alone performed that legation at the time. Hence, at the end of the synod’s canons, he describes himself as representing the whole synod of the Roman Church, following the example of the three legates of Agatho and the Western Synod, who had assumed this title at the Sixth Synod. One hundred and two canons were issued at this synod, as Saint Tarasius testifies in the Seventh Synod’s refutation of the iconoclast assembly, as does Photius in his Nomocanon and the author of the synodical booklet. Many of them are excellent and largely breathe the ancient discipline of the Church. Therefore, although many are rightly praised and deserve praise, not all were rejected by the Roman Church, but only five: canon 2, which orders the eighty-five Canons and Constitutions of the Apostles to be admitted; canon 13, which attacks the law of ecclesiastical celibacy and censures the most chaste discipline of the Roman Church, by which sacred ministers are forbidden the use of marriage. Indeed, this canon anathematizes those who forbid presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons association and intercourse with their lawful wives. Canon 55 was also not approved, since it condemns the Saturday fast, most venerable in the Roman Church. Nor was canon 67 approved, which forbids clerics, under penalty of deposition, and laypeople, under penalty of excommunication, to eat blood or what has been strangled, imposing this abstinence as though it were still binding by divine Scripture. Canon 82 was not approved in every respect either, since it prohibits Christ the Savior from being depicted in the image of a lamb, as he was shown to the Fathers symbolically, and requires him to be depicted in human form, by which all the figures were finally fulfilled. The other canons which we rightly called praiseworthy, as anyone can see from reading and examining them, were not rejected by the Roman Church. To speak only of the first and last: the first teaches that the faith confirmed by the six Ecumenical Councils and handed down by the Apostles must be preserved inviolably. The last contains outstanding laws and prescriptions for hearing confession and for how prudently a priest should act toward penitents. He must consider the nature of the sin, the sinner’s burning desire for conversion, and the medicine appropriate to the illness. He must examine whether the evil arises from habit, weakness, or a corrupt affection. Finally, it belongs to his pastoral office to bring back the wandering sheep; therefore he must neither drive the sinner over the precipices of despair nor loosen the reins so far as to permit dissolution and contempt of life. On all the canons of the Trullan Synod, both those approved and those rejected, Lupus should be read, in his notes and scholia on the canons of the Council of Trullo. PAGIUS.]

At which legates of the Apostolic See also assembled and, having been deceived, subscribed. [Note: [Col. 0018D] “Legates of the Apostolic See.” Understand this to mean those Greek bishops who had been appointed in the East as vicars of the Roman pontiff. BIN. and LABB.]

He himself was also compelled to subscribe, [Note: [Col. 0017A] Codex Luc., “the pope himself.”] but he did not consent in any way, because certain chapters had been appended to it that were outside ecclesiastical practice. [Col. 0018A] [Note: [Col. 0019D] “Which were also defined, as it were, synodally.” This passage may also be added to the proofs brought forward by the most learned bishop Ciampinus (in Examination of the Pontifical Book, section 6) to establish that Anastasius the Librarian was not the author of all the Lives of the Pontiffs written in the same Pontifical Book and published in print under his name. For the author of this Life of Sergius I writes in this section things that directly contradict what Anastasius reports in the prefaces to the synods, both the Seventh, addressed to John VIII, and the Eighth, addressed to Adrian II. It will be better to place Anastasius’s words concerning this passage below, so that anyone may see at a glance whether both the statements about the more than one hundred canons of the wandering synod found here and those made about them in the two prefaces could have proceeded from the same pen. In the first preface Anastasius says: “The rules which the Greeks claim were issued by the Sixth Synod are admitted by the principal see in such a way that none of them is received if it is found contrary to the earlier canons or decrees of the holy pontiffs of this see, or to good morals, although until now all of them remain wholly unknown to the Latins, since they have not been translated. Nor are they found in the archives of the other patriarchal sees, although they use the Greek language, evidently because none of them, when these rules were issued, was found either to have promulgated them, to have consented to them, or even to have been present. Although the Greeks claim that the same Fathers who were present at the Sixth Synod promulgated them, they can prove this by no certain evidence.” In the other preface he says: “The Greeks also produce numerous and sufficiently presumptuous chapters of rules, almost all of them very contrary to ancient tradition, which they claim were promulgated by the Sixth Synod, although the Sixth Synod issued nothing except the rule of faith. But the rules which they assert to be its rules are known to have been drawn up among them privately and individually long after the Sixth Synod.” MAFEUS.]

Which were also defined, as it were, synodally, and written out in six volumes and subscribed by three patriarchs—that is, the Alexandrian, Constantinopolitan, and Antiochian patriarchs—or by the other [Note: [Col. 0019A] Others: Constantinopolitan and Alexandrian.] prelates who had assembled there at that time, and confirmed by the imperial hand. [Note: [Col. 0019A] Codex Luc. and others: “by the prelates.”] [Note: [Col. 0019A] Codex Luc.: “at that time.”] These volumes, sent to Lucellum, which is called “the carnal barn,” [Note: [Col. 0020C] “Sent to the place called the carnal barn, in this Roman city, for confirmation.” Scebrum means a granary; hence Ingulfus should be corrected in his Chronicle of Croyland: “The Lord granting it, he began to abound in all good things, so that in treasures and scebra, as well as in lands and tenements, twice as much was afterward restored to him for what he had first lost.” For scauris, read scebris or scearis. ALTASERRA.] were sent to this city for confirmation, or to be subscribed above by Pope Sergius, as head of all priests. [Note: [Col. 0020A] Codex Luc.: “chartale”; the passage is corrupt; others: “is called the carnal barn.”] The emperor sent them to the city [Col. 0020A] so that Sergius might confirm them, or subscribe above, as head of all priests. But that most blessed pontiff, as has been said, gave no assent at all to the same Emperor Justinian Augustus; nor did he allow the same volumes to be accepted or opened for reading. [Note: [Col. 0020C] He rejected them as invalid. What chiefly moved the pontiff to reject that council was the rashness of the Eastern bishops. Acting against the celibacy of presbyters and deacons and intending to overthrow it, they defined as follows: “Since we have learned that it has been handed down as a canon of the Roman Church that those promoted to the diaconate or presbyterate must profess that they will no longer associate with their wives, we, preserving the ancient canon of apostolic perfection and order, decree that the lawful marriages of those in sacred orders shall henceforth remain firm and stable. We in no way dissolve their union with their wives or deprive them of their mutual intercourse at the proper time. Therefore, if anyone is found worthy to be ordained subdeacon, deacon, or presbyter, he must not be prevented from being admitted to such a rank if he lives with a lawful wife. Nor, at the time of ordination, shall he be required to profess that he will abstain from lawful intercourse with his wife . . . . Therefore, if anyone, moved contrary to the apostolic canons, dares to deprive any of those in sacred orders—presbyters, deacons, or subdeacons—of union and intercourse with a lawful wife, let him be deposed. Likewise, if any presbyter or deacon dismisses his wife under the pretext of piety, let him be excluded; and if he persists, let him be deposed” (canon 13). Moreover, this council contained other canons that must not be received: it ordered the admission of the eighty-five canons bearing the name of the Apostles; prohibited the Saturday fasts of Lent, or the practice of the Roman Church; ordered clerics to abstain from what had been strangled and from blood, under penalty of deposition, and laypeople under penalty of excommunication; and finally forbade the Lord Jesus Christ to be depicted under the figure of the lamb indicated by John the Forerunner, since the Savior was to be represented only in human form, through which he fulfilled all the other figures (canons 2, 55, 67, 82). SOMMIER.]

Moreover, he rejected them as invalid, [Col. 0021A] and declared that he would choose to die rather than consent to the errors of innovations. The emperor, [Note: [Col. 0021B] “The emperor sent Sergius the magistrianus to Rome in contempt of the aforementioned pontiff.” Magistriani were agentes in rebus, so called because they served among the palace offices under the authority of the master of offices. Ambrose, On Duties, book II, chapter 29: “The form of a rescript was being read; the ordinances of the master of offices; an agens in rebus was pressing.” ALTASERRA.] sending Sergius the magistrianus to Rome in contempt of the aforementioned pontiff, together with John, beloved of God, bishop of Porto, or [Note: [Col. 0021C] “Boniface the counselor.” Among the Roman clergy and the pontiff, the dignity of counselor of the Apostolic See was among the more distinguished. The man who held this office stood beside the pontiff and clergy as an assessor in more serious and public controversies; and, when the see was vacant, he governed the Church together with the others. Gregory the Great discusses this office in book II, letter 54. In the controversy over the privileges of the Church of Ravenna, the more important investigation was entrusted to the counselor of the Apostolic See. Indeed, when Copronymus complained in a letter to Charlemagne about Christopher, counselor of the Apostolic See, Pope Paul I wrote an apologetic letter to Charlemagne on his behalf, preserved, and so forth, in the Codex Carolinus, volume III of Duchesne’s Writers of Frankish History. Among other things he says: “For they state in their very letters that our beloved son Christopher, primicerius and counselor, without our authority, as though we were unaware, sent those suggestions and, having read one set of messages, sent others in their place; and we call God as witness and judge that this was in no way so. For that counselor never acted or presumed to act outside our will, since he was the sincere and most proven faithful servant both of our predecessor and brother, the lord Pope Stephen, and of us; he is so in all things, and we are satisfied with his unblemished faith and steadfastness of heart.” From this it is clear that the counselor assisted the pontiffs by his learning and judgment in disputes concerning faith and discipline. Therefore this Boniface was chosen to refute Macarius of Antioch, whom the Sixth Synod had condemned to exile, as we read in act 1 of the Seventh Synod, page 63: “For Macarius the heretic, sent into exile by the Sixth Synod, was in exile at Rome; and our father, Pope Benedict of holy memory, gave him a period of forty days and sent Boniface the counselor to him every day. Through admonitory words he taught him from divine Scripture, but he never wished to be corrected. He did this in order to persuade and correct him.” Emperor Justinian, then, perceiving that Sergius had denied confirmation of the Trullan canons at the prompting, as it seemed, of Boniface the counselor, wished to bring both of them to Constantinople so that they might give an account of what had been done. BENCINUS.] Boniface, counselor of the Apostolic See, he took with him to the imperial city.

[Note: [Col. 0022B] “Then Zacharias, and so forth.” Anastasius writes that Emperor Justinian sent all the acts of the synod to the city of Rome for confirmation, or for Sergius the pontiff, as head of all priests, to subscribe above. When Justinian sent the proceedings of this synod, contained in six volumes, subscribed by the bishops and confirmed by the imperial hand, to Pope Sergius, a blank sheet was left in the Code of the Council before the other patriarchs, after the emperor Justinian, for him to fill with his subscription. In exactly the same way [Col. 0022C] a blank sheet was left for the absent bishops of Thessalonica, Ravenna, Sardinia, and Heraclea, so that they might at least subscribe to the acts after the synod had been dissolved; the Code records this in the same words: “Place of the bishop of Thessalonica, place of the bishop of Ravenna,” and of the others. But Sergius refused to confirm the acts. “He himself was also compelled,” Anastasius says, “to subscribe, but he did not consent in any way, because certain chapters had been appended to it that were outside ecclesiastical practice, and which had also been defined, as it were, synodally and written in six volumes,” and so forth. “That most blessed pontiff gave no assent at all to the same Emperor Justinian Augustus, nor did he allow the same volumes to be accepted or opened for reading. Moreover, he rejected and repudiated them as invalid, choosing rather to die than to consent to the errors of innovations.” These canons will be discussed again under John VII. Since Sergius, in no way broken by the entreaties of Emperor Justinian, had rejected the canons of the Quinisext Synod, the emperor sent his protospatarius Zacharias to Rome to transport the pontiff to Constantinople. But the army of Ravenna and the neighboring regions, scorning the emperor’s wicked commands, did not allow them to be carried out. When troops assembled from every side, the protospatarius Zacharias, brought into fear for his own safety, immediately withdrew to the pontiff, prostrated himself at his feet, humbly begged forgiveness, and pleaded with him not to surrender him to the fury of the soldiers. The pontiff ordered him to take courage. He then went out to calm the army, sat before the basilica of Pope Theodore with the doors opened, and, when the soldiers and people had been pacified, thanked them for taking up arms so eagerly for his safety. The soldiers nevertheless refused to leave the city until they had driven Zacharias out, burdened with insults and terrified by fear. These events are established by Anastasius in the Life of Sergius, Bede in his book On the Six Ages, and Paul the Deacon in book VI of On the Deeds of the Lombards, chapter 11. PAGIUS.]

Then he sent his fierce protospatarius Zacharias with orders to transport the aforementioned pontiff likewise to the imperial city. But, by the mercy of God going before him, and with the blessed Apostle Peter, prince of the Apostles, assisting and preserving his Church unharmed, [Col. 0022A] the heart of the army of Ravenna, together with that of the Pentapolitan duchy and the surrounding regions, was stirred [Note: [Col. 0022D] “The strength of the army of Ravenna.” When Zacharias, the imperial protospatarius, attempted to seize Pope Sergius in order to send him captive to the emperor, the Italian army stood in defense of the pontiff and did not withdraw from Sergius until the unjust imperial officer had departed. This force was stationed chiefly in those cities that were under the dominion of the bishop of Ravenna, which Agnellus lists in his Pontifical Book, part 2, especially since various disputes subsequently broke out between the pontiffs and the bishops of Ravenna. BENCINUS.]

not to permit the pontiff of the Apostolic See to go to the imperial city. When a multitude of soldiers assembled from every side, Zacharias the spatharius, terrified and trembling lest he be killed by the crowd of soldiers, asked that the city gates be closed and held. [Note: [Col. 0021A] Codex Luc.: “so that they would not permit it.”] He himself fled trembling into the pontiff’s bedchamber, tearfully begging that the pontiff take pity on him and not permit anyone to harm his life.

The army of Ravenna entered through the gate of the blessed Apostle Peter and came with arms and a crowd [Note: [Col. 0023B] Others: “a trumpet”; Codex Luc.: “a considerable crowd.”] to the Lateran episcopal residence, burning to see the pontiff. They had learned from common report that he had been taken away during the night and put aboard a ship. [Note: [Col. 0023B] Codex Luc.: “they had heard.”] When both the lower and upper doors of the patriarchal residence were closed, they threatened to throw them to the ground unless they were opened more quickly. In the extremity of his fear and despair of life, Zacharias the spatharius entered beneath the pontiff’s bed [Note: [Col. 0023B] Codex Luc. and others: “beneath the bed.”] and hid himself, so that he lost consciousness and his senses. The most blessed pope comforted him, telling him not to be afraid in any way.

The same most blessed pontiff then went outside the basilica of the lord Pope Theodore. With the doors opened, he sat in the seat commonly called “under the Apostles” [Note: [Col. 0023B] Codex Luc.: “sitting in the seat”; others: “into the seat, under the Apostle, the general assembly.”] and honorably received the entire body of soldiers and people who had come to meet him. Giving them an appropriate and gracious reply, he soothed their hearts. Although, moved by zeal for the love and reverence owed both to the Church of God and to the most holy pontiff, they did not withdraw from guarding the patriarchal residence [Col. 0024A] [Note: [Col. 0024B] Codex Luc.: “withdrew from the guard”; Labbé and Mans.: “they withdrew from the guard.”] until they had driven the aforementioned spatharius from the Roman city with injuries and insults. [Note: [Col. 0023C] “For the one who had sent him also, and so forth.” Leontius, the prefect, having received the empire from the Greeks, exiled Justinian to Cherson after cutting off his nose in the year of Christ 694, the tenth year of Justinian’s reign. Cedrenus, Theophanes, Zonaras, and other Greek annalists describe the circumstances of the event. By a just judgment of God, the impious Justinian deservedly suffered this punishment. After, at the urging of Callinicus the patriarch, he had enacted new canons and utterly disfigured the Eastern Church by them, he labored with all his strength either to inflict the same disgrace upon the Roman Church or, at least, if the supreme pontiff resisted the emperor’s command, to have the pontiff forcibly carried from Rome to the imperial city. BIN. and LABB.]

For the one who had sent him was also, at that very time, deprived of his kingdom by the Lord’s retribution. Thus, with Christ favoring it, the Church of God was preserved undisturbed together with its bishop.

This most blessed man, by God’s revelation, found in the sacristy of the blessed apostle Peter, in a very dark corner, a silver casket lying there [Note: [Col. 0024B] Another reading: “he found it lying.”], which, blackened by the age it had passed through, did not even appear to be silver. [Note: [Col. 0023D] After making a prayer, he removed the seal’s impression and opened the little compartment. Inside he found a covering of silk, laid over it, called *stauracis*. The silver casket, which contained a portion of the wood of the Lord’s cross, had been sealed. Reliquary chests were customarily sealed. Gregory of Tours, *On the Miracles of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 33: “When the abbot came, having removed the seal from the cabinet, he found the casket locked.” A silk covering had been placed over the wood of the cross. A *plumacium* was a veil of silk cloth woven in the manner of birds’ feathers. Ambrose, Letter 27: “When I was conferring with his companions, lest they should suffer the old man to be driven out without clothing, without a covering.” This was what they called *opus plumarium* or *plumatile*. Plautus, in *Epidicus*: “Quilted or feather-patterned.”

*Plumatum* in Petronius, *Satyricon*: “Clad in a golden Babylonian feather-patterned garment.” Gregory of Tours, *On the Miracles of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 97: “There stands a table covered with snow-white cloths, adorned with feather-patterned work.” Hence *plumarii* are craftsmen who weave this kind of garment, *Codex Justinianus*, book X, title 64, law 2. Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis*, book III, chapter 10: “Linen-workers or embroiderers.” The same author, chapter 13 of that book: “They will produce linen-workers, or feather-patterned weavers of tunics.” This kind of garment was extremely precious. Vopiscus, in *Carinus*: “Why should I speak of linens brought from Egypt, or of those from Tyre and Sidon, so translucent in their fineness, glittering with purple, and renowned for the difficulty of their feather-patterned work?” Not only garments, but even cuirasses were customarily woven with scales or iron plates arranged like feathers. Virgil, *Aeneid* XI:

> Whom a hide, sewn together with bronze scales arranged like feathers and with gold, covered.

Veils woven in feather-patterned work were also customarily placed before the doors of buildings. Anastasius, in his account of Gregory IV, at the end: “And one linen veil of feather-patterned work before the doors.” He says that it was made of silk called *stauracis*. Veils of *stauracis* are veils of silk or purple interwoven with various flowers or figures, which were imported from Tyre; hence they were also called Tyrian. Anastasius, on *stauracis* or Tyrian cloth. —Altasèrra.]

After making a prayer, he removed the seal’s impression and opened the little compartment, in which he found inside a silk covering laid over it, called *stauracis* [Note: [Col. 0024B] Another reading: “he found it placed inside.”] Having removed this, he saw beneath it a cross richly adorned with various precious stones, [Note: [Col. 0024C] “From which, after four petals had been drawn out, in which the gems were enclosed.” *Petalum*, from the Greek πέταλον, is a golden crown worn by priests or by those descended from priests, such as the apostle John and James, the Lord’s brother. Concerning John, Eusebius, book III, chapter 25: “Having become a priest, he wore the *petalon*.” Concerning James, Epiphanius, *Panarion*, heresy 29: “And he was also permitted to wear the *petalon* around his head” [read περὶ, “around,” for ἐστι].]

from which, after four petals had been drawn out, in which gems of extraordinary size were enclosed, [Note: [Col. 0024D] “And he found an ineffable portion of the saving wood of the Lord’s cross, which from that time, for the salvation of the human race, is kissed and worshiped by all the Christian people on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross in the basilica of the Savior, which is called Constantiniana.” On the feast of the Exaltation of the Lord’s cross, solemn veneration of the cross by kissing was instituted in the Lateran basilica. Pagans also used to kiss images of the gods; hence images of the gods appeared worn down by kisses. Lucretius, book I:

> Then beside the bronze gates  
> The images show their right hands, worn thin  
> By the touch of those who greet them and pass by.

—Altasèrra.]

and he found an ineffable portion of the saving wood of the Lord’s cross. From that day onward, for the salvation of the human race, it has been kissed and worshiped by all the Christian people on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross in the basilica of the Savior, which is called Constantiniana.

He made an image of the blessed apostle Peter [Note: [Col. 0025A] Another reading: “a golden image.”], which is in the women’s section. [Note: [Col. 0025B] “Here he made a censer.” Cardinal Bona shows, in book I, chapter 25, no. 9 of *Liturgical Matters*, that the use of these or similar vessels, in which incense and various fragrances are burned during the solemn offering, arose from apostolic tradition and the example of the Mosaic law. It was customary for every nation, however barbarous and inexperienced in true religion, to believe that no sacrifice could properly be performed without incense, or at least some fragrant fumigation. The Magi venerated and confessed Christ as God with frankincense; similarly, the poets thought that the offering of incense was inseparable from the declaration of divinity. Ovid says:

> I shall erect temples for you; I shall render you the honor of incense.

Constantine the Great, according to the same author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* in his account of Sylvester, offered two censers of the purest gold. Ambrose indicates that the use of perfuming altars during the solemn divine office is very ancient when, commenting on Luke 1, he says: “Would that an angel might also stand beside us as we perfume the altars and bring forward the sacrifice!” Bona, cited above, discusses this matter more fully.

Anastasius relates with what ornaments he adorned the basilicas of Saints Peter and Paul and other churches of the city. He also writes that he established that litanies should be recited annually from Saint Hadrian’s on the feasts of the Annunciation of the Lord, the Nativity and Dormition of the holy Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, and Saint Simeon, which the Greeks call the *Hypapante* and the Latins the Purification. Albinus Flaccus says the same in his book *On the Divine Office*: he moved a portion of the Lord’s cross, hidden in a silver casket in a more secluded place, to a more honorable and celebrated location.

He appointed ninety-seven bishops in various provinces. He held two ordinations during the month of March, ordaining eighteen priests and four deacons.

These words of Anastasius refute the opinion of those who assert that the feast of the Dormition, or Assumption, of the blessed Virgin Mary began to be celebrated only in the eighth century. For, as Francis Maria Florentius observes in his notes on the Hieronymian Martyrology, under 18 January, the feast of the Assumption was celebrated before the time of the emperor Maurice, and therefore before the end of the sixth century, specifically on 18 January. He proves this both from the same Martyrology attributed to Saint Jerome and published by him, and from other sources that he cites.

He discusses at length the institution of this feast and supposes that it was transferred from 18 January to 15 August by the emperor Maurice. John Mabillon adds, in book II of the *Gallican Liturgy*, p. 118, two calendars: namely, the Corbie calendar, which he says was written scarcely more than a century after Maurice, in which under 18 January is found “the burial of the holy Virgin Mary”; and another very ancient calendar from Fleury, in which that burial is recorded on the same day.

Florentius, cited above, proves that this feast was transferred by the emperor Maurice to 15 August from Nicephorus Callistus, book XVII, chapter 28, where he writes:

> The same emperor—that is, Justinian—then first established that the festival of the Savior’s *Reception*—that is, the Encounter, or *Hypapante*, which we call the Purification of the Virgin—should be honored throughout the whole world, just as Justin had done for the holy Nativity of Christ. Not long afterward, Maurice ordered that the Dormition of the all-holy Mother of God should be celebrated on the fifteenth day of August.

From these words Florentius reports that, since Nicephorus, in his accounts of the enactments of Justinian and Justin, added nothing concerning the date established, but in the constitution of Maurice precisely designated 15 August for the feast of the Dormition, he clearly indicates that this feast was transferred to that day of August rather than newly instituted.

Yet, if Nicephorus’s account of Maurice is correct, it nevertheless seems to me that he is mistaken when he says that the emperor Justin established that the feast of the Nativity of Christ should be celebrated throughout the whole world. For under Pope Julius I demonstrated that long before Justin the feast of Christ’s Nativity was solemnly observed both in the West and in the East, either on 25 December or on 6 January. It was Justinian, not Justin, who in the year 551 enacted a law that it should be celebrated on 25 December. Earlier he had likewise prescribed this concerning the feast of the Purification, which he fixed on 2 February, as is evident from the following words of Theophanes, book XVI of the *History*, and Landulfus Sagax, in his *Life of Justinian*:

> In the fifteenth year of Justinian’s reign, in the month of October, a plague occurred at Byzantium; and in that same year the *Hypapante* began, so that it would be celebrated at Byzantium on 2 February.

I have found no other account anywhere of Justin’s constitution. If it is genuine, one might say that it was renewed by the emperor Justinian because it had not been observed.

For the feast of the Purification, see Baronius’s *Critical Notes* under the year 542; for both feasts, see the same Mabillon and Edmund Martene, volume IV of *On the Ancient Discipline of the Church in the Celebration of Divine Offices*. Finally, concerning the feast of the Nativity of the blessed Virgin Mary, see what will be said under Innocent IV. —Pagi.]

Here he made a large golden censer with columns and a lid, which he suspended before three golden images of the blessed apostle Peter. In it, on feast days, while the solemn rites of Mass are being celebrated, incense and the fragrance of sweet odor are offered more abundantly to almighty God.

Here he arranged in the apse of the aforementioned basilica, above the seat, a silver *apallareum* [Note: [Col. 0025A] Codex Luceranus: *appellariam*.] weighing 120 pounds.

Here he made six silver lamps in the aforementioned basilica [Note: [Col. 0025A] Another reading: “weighing 120 pounds.”], each weighing thirty pounds, which are above the beams at the entrance to the confessio. [Col. 0026A]

Here, around the altar of the aforementioned basilica, he made eight *tetravila*, four of white cloth [Note: [Col. 0025A] Codex Luceranus: “four of them white.”] and four of scarlet [Note: [Col. 0025A] Codex Luceranus: “four scarlet ones.”].

Here he diligently renewed and repaired the roof and the chambers surrounding the same basilica, which over a long period had been damaged by dripping water and fallen debris [Note: [Col. 0026A] Codex Luceranus: “had been destroyed.”]. He renewed the mosaic that had been partly ruined on the façade of the atrium of the same basilica. Likewise, he renewed the mirrors of the same church, [Note: [Col. 0026A] Another reading: “both those of the church and those above the seat or the larger silver royal doors.”] which are above the seat or above the larger royal arches.

[Note: [Col. 0026D] “Here [he transferred] the body of the blessed Leo, a most distinguished Father and pontiff.” The body of Saint Leo the Great is said to have been the first of the bodies of confessor-pontiffs to be brought into the Vatican basilica in honor, and it was deposited in the vestibule of that basilica. After Saint Leo, so many pontiffs were buried there that his tomb became hidden beneath the tombs of the others. When Pope Sergius I was divinely admonished, the body of the holy pontiff was transferred from a more obscure place to a more fitting one—namely, to an oratory on the right side of the major apse, near the altar of Saint Peter, as the author of *Subterranean Rome* bears witness.

This was the first translation of Saint Leo’s body—for others took place in subsequent centuries—reported by Anastasius. It is confirmed by an ancient epitaph, found among other inscriptions in the basilica of Saint Peter and published by the distinguished Mabillon in volume III of his *Analecta*. The text, corrected against the Oxford manuscript, is as follows:

> This body of the apostolic man was first buried here,  
> For he was worthy of a tomb in Peter’s citadel.  
> Hence the company of prophets and nobles whom you see present,  
> Their limbs are covered beneath this splendid house.  
> But since long ago the great shepherd Leo,  
> Guarding the flock and fold of Christ’s people, was doorkeeper of the citadel,  
> From the tomb he warns of what he did while alive,  
> Lest the lurking wolf ravage God’s sheepfold.  
> The books sent forth in defense of the true doctrine bear witness,  
> Books cherished by devout hearts and feared by the wicked crowd.  
> He roared, and the frightened hearts of the beasts were stunned;  
> The sheep obey the commands of their shepherd.  
> Yet here he lay beneath the temple’s final marble,  
> Whom many tombs of pontiffs now cover.  
> The bishop Sergius, moved by divine love,  
> Transferred him from there to the front of the sacred house,  
> Adorning the gleaming tomb with precious marble,  
> In which those who ask see heavenly wonders.  
> And because he once excelled in wondrous virtues,  
> The pontiff’s final glory will be greater.

At the foot of this epitaph, Mabillon records the following chronological addition: “He sat in the episcopate for twenty-one years, one month, and thirteen days. He was buried on the third day before the Ides of …” [supply “April”], “and was transferred here again by the blessed Sergius on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in the … indiction.” The Bollandists, in volume II for the month of April, p. 21, present an account of the elevation and translation of the body from a manuscript catalogue of the church of Saint Peter; consult it if you desire further information about the translations of Saint Leo. See also the notes of the most distinguished prelate Bianchini, volume III, p. 159 of this edition. —Maffeius.]

Here he reinterred the body of the blessed Leo, a most distinguished Father and pontiff, which had been placed in a hidden lower chamber of the secretarium of the aforementioned basilica [Note: [Col. 0026A] Codex Luceranus: “in the hidden lower chambers”; another reading: “in the hidden lower chamber.”], and, after carefully constructing a tomb, placed it in a public location in the aforementioned basilica ([Note: [Col. 0027A] Labbé: “where it had been revealed to him”]), and adorned the place itself.

Here he made a large golden paten bearing white gems around it [Note: [Col. 0027A] Another reading: “bearing gems around its rim”; Codex Luceranus: “white gems.”], and in the center a cross of hyacinth and emerald, weighing twenty pounds.

Here he diligently renewed and repaired the roof and all the chambers surrounding the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul, which had been worn out by age over a long period. Likewise, he had beams brought from Calabria and renewed those he found to be extremely old in the same basilica.

Here he replaced the very ancient image of the apostles [Note: [Col. 0027D] “A very ancient image of the apostles.” This shows the antiquity of the use of sacred images and of their placement in churches. On this subject Ciampini should be consulted in his work *On Mosaics*. —Bencinus.], which was above the doors of the same basilica [Note: [Col. 0027A] Another reading: “the very ancient images …”].

Here he made an ambo and a ciborium [Note: [Col. 0027A] Codex Luceranus: “a ciborium.”] in the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian, where he also offered many gifts.

[Note: [Col. 0028B] “He also covered and fortified the dome of the same church with cast lead sheets.” A *trulla* is a hollow wine vessel. Marcus Tullius, *Against Verres* 6: “There was also a wine vessel made from one very large gem.” Apicius, *On Cookery*, book IV: “As many sheets of pastry as you place, fill the same number of *trullae* also, and pour wine over them.” Hence *detrullare* shortly above means “to pour out from a *trulla*”: “And it is proper to pour out from the *trulla* into the dish by turns.” A *trulla* was a hollow vessel with a golden handle. Hence *trullus* could have come to mean the vault or chamber of a church, because it was shaped like a *trulla*; and from this came *Trullus*, the name of the imperial palace at Constantinople. The church roof was made of sheets—that is, lead plates. Anastasius, in his account of Gregory III: “Likewise, in the basilica of the holy Mother of God called *Ad Martyres*, he had the roof, ruined through long neglect, thoroughly cleaned and restored anew with abundant lime or lead sheets.” —Altasèrra.]

He also covered and fortified the dome of the same church with cast lead sheets.

Here he made the ciborium of the basilica of Saint Susanna, which had previously been wooden, out of marble. He also donated there various golden and silver treasures and immovable properties [Note: [Col. 0028A] Codex Luceranus: “to them.”].

Here he covered and renovated the basilica of Saint Euphemia, which had remained roofless for a long time.

Here he covered and diligently renovated the basilica of Saint Aurea at Ostia [Note: [Col. 0028B] “The basilica of Saint Aurea at Ostia.” This is the basilica of Saint Aurea, virgin and martyr, at the mouth of the Tiber. *Roman Martyrology*, 24 August: “At Ostia on the Tiber, Saint Aurea, virgin and martyr.” From this a corrupt passage in Anastasius, in his account of Leo III, should be corrected: “He entirely repaired anew the roof of the church of the blessed Aurea, situated at Ostia.” Read “Aurea.” This correction is supported by Leo IV, canon *Igitur*, 23, q. 8: “The supreme pontiff celebrated Mass in the church of the blessed Aurea.” The name Aurea was given to Petronilla, daughter of the apostle Peter. Sigebert reports that her monument bore the inscription “Aurea Petronilla,” in his *Chronicle* under the year 758. —Altasèrra.], which had likewise been left uncovered or damaged [Note: [Col. 0028A] Another reading: “he covered and renovated it, since it had been stripped of its roof.”], and restored it through his own efforts.

Here he rebuilt from the foundations the oratory of the apostle Saint Andrew, which stands on the Lavican Way [Note: [Col. 0028A] Another reading: “which was situated”; Codex Luceranus: “which is situated on the road.”].

[Note: [Col. 0028C] He established that, at the breaking of the Lord’s body, “Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us” should be sung by clergy and people. Pope Sergius is said by Anastasius to have been the author of this institution, so that the Agnus Dei might be sung during the celebration of Mass. Alcuin mentions this institution in *On the Divine Office*, chapter 40.
