Others, however, hold that the institution was made at the Council of Nicaea, which they prove from the Arabic version of the Council of Nicaea. In the year 1183, the abbot Robert of Mont-Saint-Michel relates in the *Supplement to Sigebert* that the Virgin Mary appeared to a woodworker and handed him a seal engraved with an image of herself and the newborn Christ, bearing this inscription: “Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, grant us peace.” ALTASERRA.]

He established that, at the breaking of the Lord’s body, “Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us,” should be sung by clergy and people, says the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs*. Sergius did indeed institute that “have mercy on us” should be said three times; but, as Innocent III says in book VI, chapter 6, *On the Mysteries of the Mass*, after many adversities had later overtaken the Church—or, as others write, in order to remove the schism—it was decreed that on the third repetition one should say “grant us peace.” This rite was received everywhere except in the Lateran Basilica, where the ancient custom is still observed of saying “have mercy on us” three times, because, as John the Deacon observes in chapter 6 of *On the Lateran Church*, this church represents the type of the heavenly Church:

“In it,” he says, “at Mass there is not sung, ‘Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, grant us peace,’ since there the highest peace of the righteous will itself be Christ.”

Cardinal Bona confesses that he nowhere read which pope made this change, namely, the singing of “grant us peace,” in book II, chapter 16, number 5, of *Liturgical Matters*. “But if he is truthful,” Bona says, “Robert, abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel, in the *Supplement to the Chronicle of Sigebert*, brought this petition for peace from heaven through the blessed Virgin. For, as Robert relates, in the year 1183 she appeared to a certain woodworker who was working in a forest, and gave him a seal bearing an image of herself and of her Son, with this inscription: ‘Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, grant us peace.’ She ordered him to carry it to the bishop and tell him that those who desired peace for the Church should make such seals and carry them as a sign of peace.” PAGIUS.

He established that, at the breaking of the Lord’s [Col. 0029A] body, “Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us,” should be sung by clergy and people.

[Note: [Col. 0029B] He also decreed that on the days of the Annunciation of the Lord, the Nativity and Dormition of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, and of Saint Simeon—which the Greeks call Hypapante—a litany should go forth, and the people should proceed to Saint Mary. *Hypante* or *Hypapante* in Greek means “the feast of the Meeting,” which among the Latins is called the feast of the Purification, because of Simeon’s meeting with the Lord. Paul the Deacon, book XVI, on Justinian: “In that same year the Hypapante of the Lord began to be celebrated at Byzantium on the second day of February.” Siffrid, priest of Meissen, *Epitome*, book II, under the year 551: “Under Pope Pelagius and the emperor Justinian, it began at Constantinople to be solemnly celebrated as the Hypapante of the Lord, that is, the Purification of the blessed Virgin Mary.” Anastasius likewise, in his *History*: “In the fifteenth year of Justinian’s reign the Hypapante of the Lord began, to be celebrated at Byzantium on the second day of February.” ALTASERRA.]

He also decreed that on the days of the Annunciation of the Lord, and of the Nativity [Col. 0030A] and Dormition of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, and of Saint Simeon,

[Note: [Col. 0029C] which they call the Hypapante. From *ὑπαντή* or *ὑπαπαντή* or *ὑπαπάντησις*, that is, “meeting” or “encounter,” because of the meeting that the aged Simeon and the widow Anna had with the Lord when the child Jesus was brought into the temple by his parents Mary and Joseph, the feast of the Purification of the blessed Virgin Mary is called by the Greeks *Hypante* or *Hypapante*. Some call it the Hypante of the Lord, others the Hypante of Simeon and Anna; Theophylact Simocatta, however, calls it, in round numbers, Τεσσαρακοστὴ ἡμέρα τῆς γενεθλιακῆς πανηγύρεως τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ Ἰησοῦ, that is, [Col. 0029D] “the fortieth day of the birthday festival of the great God Jesus.”

For by the command of the old Law, a woman who had given birth to a male child was purified after forty days had elapsed, first in the tabernacle and later, after the temple raised by Solomon, in the temple, with the sacrifices prescribed by the Law. Therefore the most blessed Virgin, who conceived from the Holy Spirit, after forty days had been completed from her saving childbirth, wished to conform herself to other women who had given birth, although, as the most pure *Theotokos*—“God-bearer”—she had absolutely no need of purification. I have shown this in the notes to Sigonius’s *Hebrew Commonwealth*, which appear in volume IV of the *Milan Collection* (p. 224, annotations 58 and 59).

Among ecclesiastical historians it is sufficiently agreed that the feast of the Hypapante was instituted among the Greeks earlier than among the Latins. Cedrenus, under the ninth year of Justin the Great, reports that it was instituted when Antioch collapsed after being shaken by a tremendous earthquake. Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, following Theophanes, assigns it to the time of Justinian:

“In the fifteenth year of Justinian,” he says, [Col. 0030A] “in the month of October, a pestilence occurred at Byzantium, and in that same year the Hypapante began, to be celebrated at Byzantium on the second day of February.”

Landulf the Wise, in the *Life of Justinian*, Sigebert in his *Chronicle* under the year 542, and Usuard’s *Martyrology* say the same. In the latter, under the second day of February, one reads:

“Hypante of the Lord, and the Purification of the blessed Virgin: this feast began in the time of the emperor Justinian at Byzantium, or Constantinople.”

Those who assign greater antiquity to this feast wish it to be remembered by Saint Methodius, first bishop of Olympus and Patara, coastal cities of Lycia, and afterward of Tyre in Phoenicia, who gained the crown of martyrdom at the beginning of the fourth century. Father Combefis reprinted in his *Amphilochius* a homily preached on this feast by Saint Methodius, prefaced by the following title:

Μεθοδίου ἐπισκόπου Πατάρων, καὶ μάρτυρος, εἰς τὸν Συμεῶνα, καὶ εἰς τὴν Ἄνναν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ὑπαπαντῆς, καὶ εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν Θεοτόκον.

“By Methodius, bishop and martyr of Patara, on Simeon and Anna on the day of the Hypapante, and on the holy Mother of God.”

They further add Saint Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, likewise a fourth-century writer and a great interpreter of the Church’s rites, who spoke about the ceremony, including that of candles, employed on this feast; and several other Eastern Fathers who lived before Justinian, whose catalogue may be seen in the Bollandists, volume I for February.

For this reason the authors of this opinion assert either that Justinian instituted this new feast at Constantinople, when the city was being drained by continual funerals, while other Churches, especially that of Jerusalem, already possessed it as an ancient feast; or that he restored by a new decree what was sacred, just as Sixtus V, by a new constitution, did not so much institute a new feast of the Presentation of Mary—made famous by many discourses of the Greek Fathers and not unknown to the Latins—as restore an old one, when he ordered it thereafter to be observed more solemnly in the Church.

On this feast processions are held from ancient custom with burning candles. Saint Ildefonsus, who flourished in the year 644 (*Sermon on the Purification*), and Saint Eligius, bishop of Noviomagus in Gaul, who died in the year 665 (*Homily 2 on the Purification*), write that the use of candles arose from the superstition of the abolished rites of Februus—that is, Pluto—having been transformed into true religion. For, in order to obtain rest for the dead, the Romans in the month of February appeased the spirits around the tombs with expiatory rites and sacrifices, with candles and torches lit, as Macrobius testifies (book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 13).

Cardinal Baronius, in his notes on the *Martyrology*, believes that Gelasius opened the way for the ceremony of lights when he abolished the Lupercalia, which were celebrated at Rome in the month of February. His conjecture appears to have little solidity, since in Gelasius’s defense against the senator Andromachus—in which he attacks at length the games of the Luperci as no less superstitious than licentious—not a word concerning the rite of lights is found.

The author of this procession was Pope Sergius, says the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* at this point, and the Roman *Ordo* agrees with him. But since, before Sergius, the custom of carrying lights on the day of the Purification existed both in Spain and in Gaul, as is clear from the homilies of Saints Ildefonsus and Eligius, who preceded Sergius’s pontificate, it follows that Sergius either first introduced this custom into the Roman Church or, perhaps more probably, determined the route for the procession of that day from the church of Saint Hadrian to Saint Mary Major. In this procession the clergy and the entire populace carried burning candles given by the pontiff, as Bede reports (*On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 10). MAFEUS.]

which the Greeks call the Hypapante, let a litany go forth from Saint Hadrian, [Col. 0031A] and let the people proceed to Saint Mary.

Here he made four silver arches in the basilica of Saint Lawrence the martyr, which is called the title of Lucina.

[Note: [Col. 0031A] During his time, the Aquileian Church, etc. Paul the Deacon writes the same in book V, chapter 14. BIN. and LABB.

During his time the Aquileian Church… Around the year 698, while Tiberius Apsimarus was emperor and Sergius was seated at Rome as pope, the schism of the Aquileian Church concerning the Three Chapters came to an end. For after Paul the Deacon, in book V, chapter 14 of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, had related that Tiberius had seized the empire—which occurred in the year 698—he writes:

“At this time a synod was held at Aquileia. Because of ignorance of the faith, it hesitated to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council, until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of the blessed Pope Sergius, it too agreed to assent to it together with the other Churches of Christ.”

The author of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, wrongly attributed to Anastasius, has nearly the same words in his account of Sergius, although he was living at precisely this time. Paul the Deacon lived not long after this period.

Cardinal Norisius, in his dissertation on the Fifth Synod, chapter 9, section 1, contends from a passage of Bede, in his *Book on the Six Ages*, that this Aquileian synod was the synod convened by Paulinus of Aquileia against the Fifth Synod in the preceding century:

“Bede says, ‘A synod was held at Aquileia. Because of ignorance of the faith, it hesitated to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council, until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of the blessed Pope Sergius, it too agreed to assent to it together with the other Churches of Christ.’ From the adverb ‘until,’ the very learned cardinal says it may plainly be inferred that Bede is speaking of a council assembled before Sergius.”

But apart from the fact that it is unlikely that Paul the Deacon failed to understand Bede’s meaning, even if this were granted, it would not follow that the schism of the Aquileian Church had been completely extinguished before Sergius, since Bede says there that, instructed by the salutary admonitions of the blessed Pope Sergius, that Church agreed to assent to the Fifth Council together with the other Churches of Christ.

I answered the same cardinal’s arguments in my discussion of the pontificate of Saint Gregory.

The acts of Saint Aldhelm, abbot of Malmesbury in England, which are preserved by Surius under 25 May, report that Pope Sergius suffered the calumny of being accused of sexual misconduct, namely, of being the father of a recently born child. When Aldhelm, who was then at Rome, was baptizing the child, Sergius ordered him, in the presence of those standing by, to say whether the child’s father was the man whom the people commonly named. The child, however, answered that he had not been begotten by the man whom the foolish populace falsely identified in this matter, and thus the pontiff was freed from the disgrace.

But Baronius rightly calls this story into doubt. It is not in fact found in the *Life of Saint Aldhelm* composed by William of Malmesbury, although it is read in another *Life of Saint Aldhelm*, written by an anonymous monk of Malmesbury who lived shortly before William of Malmesbury, as Henschenius demonstrated when he published it under 25 May.

Mabillon recites the *Life of Aldhelm* written by William of Malmesbury in part I of the fourth century of the Benedictine order. PAGIUS.]

During his time,

[Note: [Col. 0031D] Aquileian… Synod. Anastasius, as in several other matters, copied this from Bede, who says in his *Book on the Six Ages*:

“A synod was held at Aquileia. Because of ignorance of the faith, it hesitated to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council, until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of the blessed Pope Sergius, it too agreed to assent to it together with the other Churches of Christ.”

Paul the Deacon likewise, in book VI, chapter 14, after relating that Tiberius seized the empire in the year 698, writes:

“At this time a synod was held at Aquileia, because of ignorance of the faith, etc.”

What follows is almost identical with what we have reported from Bede. BENCINUS.

The archbishop of the Aquileian Church and the synod that was convened by him. The Aquileian Church, together with the bishops of Venetia and Istria, long fought against the Fifth Ecumenical Synod, denying that the Three Chapters—which, they said, had not been proscribed by the Fathers of Chalcedon—could be proscribed by anyone.

Paulinus of Aquileia, usurper of the see and instigator of disturbances, held at Aquileia, with his schismatic bishops, a council against the Fifth Synod, at which an anathema had been pronounced against the Three Chapters, around the year 557, while Vigilius occupied the Roman See.

While Sergius was also seated at Rome, another pseudo-synod was held concerning the same matter, that is, around the year 698. Our author testifies here that, finally instructed by Sergius, the Aquileians accepted the venerable Fifth Synod and returned to the unity of the Catholic Church after renouncing the schism.

Cardinal Norisius, in his dissertation on the Fifth Synod (chapter 9, paragraph p.), thinks that no new council was convened under Sergius, contrary to what Anastasius relates. He interprets Bede as agreeing with our author—for in his *Chronicle of the Six Ages*, under the seventh year of the reign of Tiberius Apsimarus, when Sergius governed the Roman Church, Bede says:

“A synod was held at Aquileia. Because of ignorance of the faith, it hesitated to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council, until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of the blessed Pope Sergius, it too agreed to assent to it together with the other Churches of Christ.”

Norisius interprets this to mean that Bede is referring to the council held by Paulinus against the Fifth Synod, whose error and perverse judgment concerning the Fifth Synod long prevailed, until, instructed by the admonitions of Sergius, the Aquileians, having abandoned their error, accepted it together with the other Churches.

The very learned cardinal proves this from the fact that Maximus, bishop of Aquileia, is recorded as having signed the Lateran Synod held in 649; and that under Pope Saint Agatho, who preceded Sergius’s pontificate by only five years, the other suffragans of the Aquileian metropolitan were present at the Roman Synod with Agatho and signed its letter. From this it is inferred that they had accepted the Fifth Synod.

But there are two reasons why I do not agree with the learned Norisius, and why I believe that two pseudo-synods were convened at Aquileia: one in 557 by Paulinus, and the other in 698 by Peter, who at that time held the Aquileian see.

First, the synod convened by Paulinus was held to judge the Fifth General Synod, which he rejected as undermining the Council of Chalcedon through its condemnation of the Three Chapters. This is clear from the fragments of letters of Pelagius I first brought out of darkness by Lucas Holstenius. In the third of them we read:

“It was never permitted, nor will it ever be permitted, for a particular synod to be convened to judge a general synod.”

The synod mentioned by Bede, however, hesitated merely because of ignorance of the faith to receive the Fifth General Synod. For it is one thing to reject an Ecumenical Council, and another not to accept it because of ignorance. The first is to despise an Ecumenical Council through contumacy; the second is to hesitate through ignorance about accepting it.

The second point is confirmed by the clear testimony of Paul, a writer from the province of Aquileia and a deacon of the Aquileian Church, who died in the eighth century. If Bede had been mistaken in indicating this synod, Paul would certainly have corrected him rather than copying his words.

Paul therefore, in book VI, chapter 14 of his *History of the Lombards*, asserts that a synod was convened at Aquileia while Sergius was seated at Rome. [Col. 0033A] After relating that Tiberius Apsimarus had seized the empire, he adds:

“At this time a synod was held at Aquileia. Because of ignorance of the faith, it hesitated to accept the Fifth Ecumenical [Col. 0033B] Council, until, instructed by the admonitions of the blessed Pope Sergius, it too agreed to assent to it together with the other Churches of Christ.”

I had already made these observations concerning the second Aquileian pseudo-synod against the Fifth Ecumenical Council when the very learned dissertation on the schism of the Aquileian Church by the distinguished Father Bernardo Maria de Rubeis came into my hands. In it (chapter 5, section 19) he shows that Bede means a synod different from the one of Paulinus.

To the contrary argument drawn both from Maximus of Aquileia’s signature at the Lateran Synod and from the synodical letter of the Roman Synod under Saint Agatho, which Agatho of Aquileia signed with his suffragans, the same most learned writer replies that Maximus and Agatho belonged not to the Aquileian Church but to the Gradensian Church.

Nor is it surprising that they signed as Aquileians, for they were the Catholic metropolitans of that Church, though ordained on the island of Grado. At that time the Aquileian metropolis had not yet been divided in two; this was later done by the authority of Gregory II.

“There was one metropolis,” says the author cited above, “which was torn by schism: one body with two heads, one schismatic and the other Catholic; healthy members adhered to one, diseased members to the other. The Catholic metropolitan was called Gradensian because he was elected on the island of Grado; the schismatic was called Aquileian because John, opposed to the Catholic Candianus, had been ordained in the old Aquileia. Each acted as Aquileian and claimed rights over the entire metropolis. The schismatic enjoyed the favor of the Lombards; the Roman pontiffs, exarchs, and the most Christian republic of the Venetians favored the Catholic.”

Whoever wishes to know more about the history of this schism should read the same dissertation, which casts much light upon the Aquileian schism. MAFEUS.]

the archbishop of the Aquileian Church and the synod that was convened under him—those who had hesitated, as erring men, to accept the holy Fifth Ecumenical Council—were instructed by the admonitions and teachings of that same most blessed pope and were converted; and they accepted the venerable council with satisfaction.

Those who had previously been held in the fault of error, enlightened by the teaching of the Apostolic See, having harmoniously embraced the truth in peace, were released and returned to their own places.

Here he made numerous coverings, or vessels, of gold and silver [Col. 0033A] for various churches, for the use and adornment of the churches of Christ.

Here he ordained Damian archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna, [Note: [Col. 0033A] Another reading: Ravenna. Here he ordained Bertoald archbishop, and Clement among the people of the Frisians. Here he ordained, throughout various…] and Clement [Note: [Col. 0034A] Codex Luc., “of the Frisians.”] among the Frisians.

Here he ordained Berechyald [Note: [Col. 0034A] Codex Luc., “Berectualdus.”] archbishop of Britain.

Here he ordained ninety-seven bishops throughout the various provinces.

He also held two ordinations in the month of March: eighteen priests and four deacons. He too was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0034A] Codex Luc., “on the fifth.”] on the sixth day before the Ides of September, in the fifteenth indiction, under Tiberius Augustus; and the episcopate remained vacant for one month and twenty days.

[Col. 0033]

LETTER OF POPE SERGIUS I TO CEOLFRID, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF THE HOLY PETER AND PAUL, WHICH IS AT WIRIMUNDA AND INGERVUM, CONCERNING SENDING THE VENERABLE BEDE TO ROME.

(*Mansi, Collection of Councils*, volume XII.)

[Col. 0033C] Sergius, bishop and servant of the servants of God, sends greetings to Ceolfrid, the religious abbot.

By what words and in what manner can we express the mercy of our God and his ineffable providence, or offer worthy thanks for his immense benefits toward us—he who brings those placed in darkness and the shadow of death into the light of knowledge? And below.

Meanwhile, know that we have willingly and gladly received the grace of blessing which your devoted religious community sent to us through the present bearer, just as it was dispatched by you. Therefore, warmly supporting with the closest devotion the petitions of your solicitude, which are timely and worthy of embrace, we exhort the goodness of your religious devotion, beloved of God, that, since certain matters of ecclesiastical affairs have arisen which require examination and will become more widely known, we need men trained in literary skill for consultation, as befits a devoted helper of God and an obedient servant of the holy universal Mother Church.

Do not cease to lend obedient devotion to this our exhortation, but without any delay send the religious servant of God Bede, priest of your venerable monastery, to the threshold of the apostles, my lords Peter and Paul, whom you love and who protect you, so that he may appear before our humble self. With God’s favor, do not doubt that, through your holy prayers, he will return safely to you after, with God’s help, accomplishing the desired solemn conclusion of the matters mentioned above. For, as we trust, whatever is brought to light for the benefit of the universal Church through his excellence will also profit all those entrusted to you.

[Col. 0035]

PRIVILEGE GRANTED BY POPE SERGIUS I TO HERON, PRELATE OF LANGRES.

[Col. 0035A] Sergius, by the grace of God Roman pontiff, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Heron, prelate of Langres.

We must take the greatest care, dearest brother, that the malignant enemy not disturb Christ’s flock on any pretext. For a complaint has reached us from the monks of Dijon who, under the leadership of Abbot Wlfechran, devoutly serve the martyr Saint Benignus: the clerics of the aforesaid fortress are attempting to transfer [something unspecified] to themselves and to their cemetery.

Because this contradicts the decrees of my predecessor John, the successor of Benedict, it is prohibited by the authority of blessed Peter and by ours under threat of anathema. For just as your predecessor Gregory, formerly the builder of that monastery, at the urging of the aforesaid martyr, decreed while both men were still alive that the one cemetery where the saint lies should be held jointly, so our letters of authority have judged that this arrangement must be confirmed.

Whoever, moreover, dares to remove from the village or cloister anything from the stream that divides the two villages—except the abbot or monks—must know that he has been condemned by a similar sentence.

Farewell in the Lord.

Given through the hands of John, librarian of the holy Apostolic See, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Sergius, universal pope, at the most sacred seat of blessed Peter the Apostle, in the eleventh indiction.

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 705: JOHN VI, ROMAN PONTIFF.

[Col. 0035]

HISTORICAL NOTICE ON POPE JOHN VI

(*Book of the Pontiffs*, from various editions.)

[Col. 0035B] **[Note: John VI.]** He collected the deeds of the pontiffs from Sergius to Gregory III. Besides being uneducated in letters, as Ciampinus knows ( *Examination of the Pontifical Book*, section 3), he so utterly neglected chronological order that he long and greatly troubled modern chronologers. Moreover, the manuscripts and catalogues, sometimes by their silence and sometimes by their disagreement, have drawn different writers into different opinions. Two pontiffs in particular, John VI and Sisinnius, appear, according to the chronology of the *Pontifical Book*, to have been ordained outside a Sunday; and that this was so Antonius Pagius demonstrated—although elsewhere we have seen him deceived on this point, and therefore it will not be surprising to expose further mistakes of his. Since each pontiff must be discussed in his proper place, here I shall speak of John and later discuss Sisinnius in the notes concerning him.

Pagius’s teaching concerning papal ordinations must first be heard. He teaches that, after Constantine had conquered Maxentius and peace had been restored to the Church, these began to be performed either on Sundays or on more solemn days (*ad ann. 68*, no. 20). Hence he often censures Baronius for holding the contrary view, beginning with the very ordination of Sylvester—namely, in the very year peace was restored, 314—which he moves back to the last day of January from the Kalends of February, to which Baronius had assigned it.

The first part of this doctrine, namely, that pontiffs were ordained on Sundays, was taught by other learned men before Pagius, and many followed it afterward. Above all, Blanchinus, whose footsteps I follow, maintains that not only Roman pontiffs but also other bishops were ordained on Sundays (Supplement, vol. II, p. 25). Affirming that this is confirmed by historical monuments, he gives an example from the *Pontifical Book* itself: the bishop of Terni was ordained by Zacharias on a Sunday. Moreover, something that strengthens Blanchinus’s opinion deserves notice. In recounting Zacharias’s itinerary, the same *Pontifical Book*, sections 209 and following, lists the individual days by number; but when it comes to Sunday, it does not name it at all, just as though the day were recognized by the bishop’s ordination. Then, passing to other matters, it continues: “On that same Sunday,” etc.

Whether all the other bishops were ordained on Sundays is neither for this place nor for my purpose to investigate; I return, therefore, to papal ordinations. Among the more solemn days mentioned by Pagius, on which he supposes that the consecrations of pontiffs were performed, there certainly belong the Nativity of the Lord, the Annunciation of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the Nativity of Christ’s Forerunner. Yet the fact that Sundays were preferred to those days is plainly shown by Boniface V, John IV, and Stephen III, whom I name especially because I propose to consider the pontiffs of this fourth volume: Sundays were preferred to those days, either by anticipating the ordination when they came before them, or by passing them over when they followed.

Boniface V, who was ordained without the emperor’s command, for the reasons mentioned on p. 26 under the year 619, was ordained on 24 December—that is, on the day before the Lord’s Nativity—in accordance with the custom already established. Similarly, John IV was consecrated in 640 two days before the same solemnity, namely on 23 December, when that date coincided with a Sunday. If those two pontiffs plainly show that even the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity was not considered suitable for celebrating ordinations, and consequently that they were ordained before that solemnity on the day proper for ordination, Stephen III shows that when a more solemn day occurred it had to be passed over so that the approaching Sunday might be awaited.

For in 752, after Zacharias died on 15 March and a certain Stephen was chosen as pontiff but died on the fourth day after his election, another Stephen was immediately elected. Although the Annunciation of the Lord’s Incarnation occurred on the Saturday—which would have preceded the ordination, since the emperor’s command no longer delayed it—nevertheless the ordination was postponed until the following day, 26 March, so that it might be carried out on the proper day.

I have already said that I shall refrain from other examples, some of which will be available to us in the fifth volume. Since this is so, I wish it to be held firm and certain that, after peace had been restored to the Church, Roman pontiffs were customarily ordained only on Sundays. This is taught by the ancient Roman *Ordo* preserved by Mabillon, as Mabillon himself testifies; accordingly, Cencio was rightly rejected by Felix Contelorius, for Cencio should be regarded merely as the writer of an ancient Ritual.

The words of the *Ordo*, no. 81, are as follows:

> After this, on the following Sunday, the elected man goes with all the orders of the sacred palace and with the Roman nobles to the church of blessed Peter, where, at the high altar, as the *Ordo* prescribes, he is consecrated by the bishop of Ostia in particular and by the other bishops of the curia.

Accordingly, Pagius’s opinion collapses: he maintains that John VI was ordained on 28 October, the sacred feast of the blessed apostles Simon the Cananaean and Thaddeus, which in the year 701 fell on a Friday; and that he was consecrated on the following Sunday, 30 October, is shown with the utmost clarity by the interregnum after his death, as I shall demonstrate below.

Meanwhile, I examine the vacancy of the see after Sergius. After Sergius’s death, all the manuscripts and catalogues unanimously affirm that the see was vacant for fifty days, or, as part of them has it, for one month and twenty days, with no other difference whatever appearing. Thus, if fifty days are counted from the day of Sergius’s death, fixed by Anastasius as 8 September, one scarcely reaches 29 October. Therefore either Anastasius put the day of burial in place of the day of death, as Baronius and Aringhius think, reading the fifth day before the Ides—that is, 9 September—or, what seems more probable to me and does not conflict with the Martyrologies, Sergius died during the night preceding the ninth day, so that it remained uncertain whether twenty-three or twenty-four days, in addition to the years and months, should be assigned to his see. There was no uncertainty, however, about assigning 9 September as the day of burial. In this way the fifty days of the interregnum are correctly completed, and one arrives at Sunday, 30 October, on which John was certainly consecrated, the final day being excluded in the customary manner.

John occupied the see for three years, two months, and twelve—or thirteen—days, as the Bergomensis catalogue and the first and third Ambrosian manuscripts have it, while all the others agree in an astonishing manner. I therefore assign his death to 11 January 705, to which I am led by a correct reckoning of the duration of his pontificate, although most manuscripts unusually omit the year and all preserve the day. The Farnesian, Royal, Mazarin, and Thuanean manuscripts, together with three Ambrosian manuscripts, give “in the third indiction, while Tiberius Augustus was reigning,” which most certainly indicates the year 705.

As for the day of his death, I hold it to have been the eleventh, whereas Pagius holds it to have been the ninth, because of the two-day discrepancy arising from the placement of his ordination. Which of us has proceeded more carefully and correctly will become clear in the following note.

**PAGIUS.**

**John.** In the year of the Lord 701, on 28 October, after an interregnum of one month and twenty days, John, sixth pontiff of that name, was elected.

**BIN. AND LABB.**

[Col. 0038B] **John VI.** He was Greek by country and birth, the son of Paternius, also called Petronius. Under the emperor Tiberius Absimarus Augustus, he occupied the pontificate for three years, two months, and twelve days. He was elected on the fourth day before the Kalends and consecrated on the third day before the Kalends of November. He died at Rome on the seventh day before the Ides of January in the year 705. The see was vacant for one month and eighteen days. Some say that he suffered martyrdom, but it is not known by whom; nor is it clear that he was buried at the catacombs of Saint Sebastian on the Appian Way, as some assert.

**CIACONIUS.** John VI, a Greek by nation, occupied the see for three years, two months, and twelve days.

**[Note: [Col. 0035]** “He was in the times of Tiberius Augustus” is absent from another manuscript.]

He was in the times of Tiberius Augustus.

**[Note: [Col. 0038B]** “He was in the times of Tiberius.” When Justinian returned from exile, entered the city secretly by way of the aqueduct, and, after inflicting many humiliations upon him, deprived him at once of life and empire, this appears to have happened by the just judgment of God. For Tiberius had risen against the Roman pontiff through his chamberlain and exarch Theophylactus, as Anastasius describes above; Justinian, for the persecution of Pope Sergius, had his nose cut off and, for the same reason, was deprived of imperial dignity, and thus suffered the same deprivation of life and empire.

It likewise appears to have happened by God’s judgment that Callinicus, patriarch of Constantinople, who, relying greatly on the number of bishops, had polluted the Eastern Church with the canons of the aforesaid council and had risen against the Roman Church, was bound by the same emperor, deprived of his eyes, and sent into exile at Rome. He who had raised his head so arrogantly against the Roman pontiff was thus humbled and received a livelihood from that same pontiff. These matters are taken from the annals of Theophanes and Cedrenus.

**BIN. AND LABB.**

**Tiberius Augustus. In his time:**

[Col. 0038C] **“The chamberlain Theophylactus came, etc.”** John VI illuminated the beginnings of his pontificate by performing two acts with kindness and generosity, which won him great esteem and glory. The first was his protection of Theophylactus, the exarch, who had come to Rome at the command of the emperor Tiberius, for a reason unknown, since history is silent. It may easily be conjectured, however, that he had not come to serve the interests of the Holy See or of the pontiff. For when the armies of Italy learned this, they immediately hastened there and would have imposed much hardship upon the exarch had the pontiff not intervened and settled the disturbance. The second act is related by Anastasius in the following section.

**SOMMIER.**

[Col. 0038C] The chamberlain Theophylactus, a patrician and exarch of Italy from the region of Sicily, came into the city of Rome. When the militia of all Italy learned of his arrival,

**[Note: [Col. 0038D]** “The militia of all Italy.” Theophylactus, exarch of Italy and hostile to the pontiff, attempted to attack his person, but in vain, since the Italian militia resisted him. Its zeal and constancy in defending the faith and the pontiffs had often shone forth. It consisted of the people of Ravenna, the Pentapolis, and Venetia, who from that time had adopted the salutary plan of rescuing Italy from the yoke of the Lombards and from the tyranny of the exarchs. Agnellus reports that they were sometimes summoned as auxiliaries against Aistulf.

[Col. 0038A] The militia of all Italy assembled tumultuously at this Roman city, wishing to harass the aforesaid exarch.

**[Note: [Col. 0038D]** “He sent priests to the camp where they had assembled.” Pope John sent priests to restrain the tumult of the soldiers who were at the camp—that is, in the military quarters beside the city. *Fossata* means a military camp, because it was fortified with a rampart or ditch. Anastasius below, in the same work, says: “And he had made a camp as far as the place called the granaries.” Likewise, in his account of Stephen III: “But the Franks themselves, entering the fortified places, removed the entire camp of the Lombards after completing the slaughter.” Again, in his account of Gregory IV, concerning the fortification of Ostia: “And from outside, not far from the same walls, he surrounded the city itself with a higher ditch.” Hence fortifications arranged along the frontier were called camps, because they originated in military camps.

The *Frankish Annals*, under the year 801, say: “Another Saracen from Africa, an envoy of the admiral Abraham, was stationed on the frontier of Africa in the camp.” The praetorian cohorts likewise established camps beside the city walls. Tacitus, *Annals* VI, concerning Sejanus, prefect of the praetorian guard, says: “Previously he increased the limited power of the prefecture by bringing the cohorts dispersed throughout the city into one camp.” Hence praetorian soldiers, although serving within the city, are regarded as absent on public business; see the laws *Limites* and *Qui mittuntur*, *Digest*, “Concerning causes of greater importance.”

Camillus Peregrinus, in his *History of the Lombard Princes*, reprinted in volume II of *Italian Historical Matters*, reproaches Paul the Deacon and Anastasius on p. 324 for relating this incursion of Gisulphus under John VI, whereas Peregrinus wishes it to have occurred under John V. Yet the testimony of both Paul and Anastasius stands firm, as the distinguished Joseph Antonius Saxi clearly proves in his notes on Sigonius’s *History of Italy*. There, after discussing the chronology of the dukes of Benevento under the years 695 and 704, he shows that the devastation carried out by Gisulphus belongs to the time of John VI, although he admits that it is uncertain whether it occurred in 702, as Baronius writes, or in 704, as Sigonius relates, since no documents are available by which the stronger opinion may be determined.

Aimoinus, continuation, *Book V*, chapter 22: “The Saracens, coming out from Baira and following Louis’s army from behind.” The same author, chapter 28 of the same book: “From there he sent as large an army as he could with Carloman.” William of Tyre, *Book IX*, chapter 3: “Meanwhile he claimed that he could remain in the kingdom with his armies.” Ivo of Chartres, letter 28: “Nor ought I to send excommunicated persons into the army.” Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, *Book II*, chapter 32: “In those days many Roman nobles were killed because of greed; the rest were divided among the armies, and became tributaries, paying the Lombards a third part of their crops.”

Here he newly made an ambo in the basilica of the blessed apostle Andrew, which stands below the church of the blessed prince of the apostles, Peter. On the altar of the church of Saint Mark he made a covering, and in the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul, between the columns of the altar, on the right and left, white curtains.

**[Col. 0040D] [Note: “White curtains.”]** Among the furnishings of churches there were curtains of various colors and considerable value. They were hung especially over altars and over the tombs of martyrs, in order to increase veneration. We read that the tribunals of judges and emperors were formerly covered with curtains.

Concerning the chamber of the eastern emperor, Cyril of Scythopolis, in Cotelerius, *Monuments*, vol. III, p. 299, relates that Saint Sabas came to the emperor and was brought before him, saying: “While he was within the curtain, he saw the emperor, with a certain angelic form preceding him.”

The use of curtains in sacred rites was extremely common among the nations. During sacrifices and solemn festivals, curtains were drawn away from altars and images. Hence Apuleius, recounting how he entered the temple to offer vows to Isis, says: “And while the shining curtains were drawn apart in opposite directions, we prayed for a reverent sight of the goddess.” *Metamorphoses*, book XI, p. 383.

Likewise, after being consecrated through Isiac initiation, when he was about to perform priestly offices before a large crowd, he stood within a curtain, as he says on p. 398:

> Thus adorned in the likeness of the sun and set up in place of an image, when suddenly the curtains were drawn apart, I gazed upon the sight of the people. And from this I celebrated a most joyful birthday, with savory dishes and auspicious banquets.

The Hebrews also had extremely precious curtains, with which the Tabernacle was covered, as were the doors of the Holy of Holies; these were kept in the treasury, hanging from a silver beam. Josephus discusses them in *Antiquities*, book XIV, chapter 13:

> The priest Eleazar, keeper of the treasury, handed this beam over to him—not with an evil intention, since he was just and good, but because the custody of the temple curtains had been entrusted to him. These curtains, hanging in that city, shone with extraordinary beauty and with the most precious workmanship.

The same curtains were widely used in the basilicas and buildings of Christians, with ornaments and figures representing various images of the saints or historical scenes, as we very frequently see noted in these papal biographies. The altar, which generally had four columns and a ciborium, was adorned with curtains hung between the columns. Anastasius repeatedly reports here and elsewhere that these were white and embellished with the addition of precious woven work.

Curtains were also very commonly used as adornments of the tombs in which martyrs or other saints rested, to shade the place for the sake of veneration. Gregory of Tours writes about the tomb of Saint Martin, *Book IV*, chapter 1:

> I approached the place of the tomb without presumption, threw myself upon the ground, and poured out a prayer; then, more privately, beneath the hanging curtains, I drew a sign of the cross with a thread inserted beneath the cloth for this purpose.

And in chapter 2:

> I approached the tomb again to seek healing, and when I touched the hanging curtains, the beating of my vein immediately ceased.

Therefore the curtains sent by the faithful to be hung before the altar were received with solemn and festive ritual, as Saint Gregory the Great teaches, *Book IX*, letter 38, p. 342, where he discusses the curtains offered and their reception:

> You sent them—the curtains—to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, from a most pure and sincere heart. They were received in the presence of all the clergy and hung there. For my son, the venerable lord Symmachus, who had delayed giving me your letter because I was ill with the pain of gout, gave it to me long after the curtains had been received. Later, in the letter of Your Excellency, we found that they ought to have been carried with a litany to the church of blessed Peter.

Gregory immediately adds concerning the use of curtains:

> In whose mercy I also trust: because you covered his body on earth, may his intercession protect you from all sins in heaven.

Much earlier, Tertullian had spoken of their variety, workmanship, and cost in his book *On the Dress of Women*:

> Walls also make use, instead of paintings, of Tyrian and hyacinthine hangings, or those royal curtains which you laboriously unravel and transform.

Concerning white curtains used in the fourth Christian century at the tombs of martyrs, Paulinus says in *Nativity* 3:

> Now golden thresholds are adorned with snowy curtains.

And in *Nativity* 6:

> Come, let others bring precious gifts, lest in the expense of service they surpass what is beautiful for covering the doors: curtains brilliant with pure linen, or dyed and woven with colored figures.

But the curtains that represented sacred histories became especially prevalent from the fourth century onward. Whoever wishes to learn more about this should consult the distinguished Mabillon, *On Diplomatic Matters*, book VI, p. 462.

**BENCINUS.**

[Col. 0040A] He made

**[Note: [Col. 0040A]** Another manuscript reads: “one ordination of nine priests and two deacons.”]

one ordination of presbyters or deacons—that is, nine presbyters and two deacons. He also appointed fifteen bishops in various places,

**[Note: [Col. 0041A]** Another manuscript reads: “twelve.”]

he was also buried at Saint Peter the Apostle; and the episcopal see remained vacant for one month and eighteen days.

**THE WILFRIDIAN CASE**

*(From Mansi, Collection of Councils, vol. XII.)*

[Col. 0041] **OBSERVATIONS OF ANTONIUS PAGIUS**

[Col. 0041D] While John VI was seated at Rome as pope, the case of Saint Wilfrid began to be examined again by the bishops. He had been exiled from his see of York since the year 692, and Pope Sergius had long before decreed that he should be restored. But Aldfrith, king of Northumbria, and Brithwald, archbishop of Canterbury, had delayed the execution of the pontiff’s commands by continually putting matters off.

Now, under the pretext of piety, they convened a council of bishops. They summoned Wilfrid to it and attempted either, by flattery, to bend to their wishes the man whom they had expelled by force, or, if he did not consent, to crush him.

Eddius narrates the event in his *Life* of Wilfrid, chapter 44:

> A synod was assembled in the field called Onestrefelda—today Nestrefeld, a place five miles north of Ripon—under King Aldfrith, with Saint Berthwald the archbishop and nearly all the bishops of Britain. Then, after envoys had been sent to the presence of Saint Wilfrid the bishop, humbly asking that he deign to appear before them, they promised through their messengers that they would give an account of the ancient fraud according to the canonical statutes, if he did not refuse to come to their assembly, etc.

But after he had arrived at the place where the synodal debate was to take place, matters did not proceed as had been promised him. Instead, many serious questions of dispute arose among them, especially from those pontiffs of the churches of which Wilfrid had been deprived. It is beyond doubt that they had done this with the consent of King Aldfrith and of certain abbots. Driven by avarice, they had no desire whatsoever to preserve peace among the churches, and they brought forward many false charges which they could not prove by any argument of truth. Moreover, they declared that our pontiff was to be judged according to the statutes and commands of Archbishop Theodore, etc.

[Col. 0042D] Wilfrid then rebuked their stubborn obstinacy in many harsh speeches, because for twenty-two years they had not feared to resist the apostolic authority contentiously and to exercise their opposition. From this we learn the date at which the synod of Onestrefeld was held.

At the end of 679, the British bishops, assembled in synod under Egefrith, king of Northumbria, began to show themselves disobedient to the commands of the Apostolic See concerning Wilfrid’s case. “After they had heard,” says Eddius, chapter 32, “certain difficult things, contrary to themselves and their will, read aloud, they rejected them insolently,” etc. Thus the twenty-second year of this contentious obstinacy was completed toward the end of 701, and this synod was indeed held in that year, or at least in the latter part of it.

It is no objection that Wilfrid said at this synod: “Shall I not, without some accusation of guilt, become an occasion of suspicion to all who hear the public declaration of my name, by which I have been called a bishop—although unworthy—for nearly forty years?” For not only someone who has spent thirty-eight years in the episcopate, but also one who has spent thirty-five or thirty-six years in it, may be said to have been a bishop for nearly forty years. This expression indicates no definite year.

[Col. 0042B] Eddius continues his account of the deeds of this synod:

> One of the king’s attendants, greatly devoted to our pontiff, whom he had nourished from the cradle of his earliest infancy, secretly burst out from the king’s tent, saying: “By this deceit they are entirely plotting to trick you, so that first you may confirm in your own handwriting only their judgment … so that, once you have been bound by this bond of restriction, you will thereafter be utterly unable to alter it. Their judgment will be disclosed in this way: whatever you once appeared to possess in the land of the Northumbrians, whether in the episcopate, in monasteries, or in anything else, you must surrender in its entirety. And if you acquired anything in the kingdom of the Mercians under King Æthelred, you must leave all of it behind by surrendering it to the archbishop, who will give it to whomever he wishes. Finally, by degrading yourself through your own subscription, you will strip yourself of your sacred dignity …”
>
> At last, when they could no longer conceal the matter from the knowledge of many, they first said—the enemies of Wilfrid, that is—that they wished to strip the holy servant of God of all his possessions, so that he would have not even the smallest portion of a single house either in the kingdom of the Northumbrians or in the kingdom of the Mercians. But when the archbishop and the king had determined this harsh judgment, even the enemies themselves recoiled from it, saying that it was impious to deprive so famous a man of all his possessions throughout the surrounding nations without any capital crime. Finally, after considering something more humane, they decided that they would restore to him only the monastery which he had built at Ripon and which, long before, he had commended by giving it, together with everything belonging to it, to Saint Peter, having obtained a privilege from Pope Saint Agatho and delivered it to the abbot and the community living there. Yet they inserted this condition: he was to attest firmly in his own handwriting that he would remain there quietly, would not cross the precincts of the monastery without the king’s permission, and would undertake no priestly office. They compelled him, moreover—and this was dreadful to say—to cast aside his rank of honor from himself, under the witness of a written confirmation.

[Col. 0043D] When Saint Wilfrid our bishop heard this, he spoke steadfastly and in a fearless, raised voice:

> For what reason are you compelling me to turn against myself, in the misery of so grievous a calamity, the sword of dreadful execution—that is, a subscription to my own condemnation? … But concerning this newly arisen question, by which you have attempted to violate the dignity of my holiness, I confidently appeal to the Apostolic See …

When the archbishop and the king heard this, they said:

> Let him now be marked and condemned by us as guilty, because he chooses their judgment—that is, the judgment of the Romans—rather than ours, etc.

After these speeches, Eddius says in chapter 45, the useless council was dissolved on both sides. “But our holy pontiff,” he continues, “went on and came to King Æthelred, announcing to him the whole grievous persecution expressed in words which the bishops had inflicted contrary to his command.” The king promised that he would send his own envoys or letters to Rome.

Meanwhile, the enemies of Saint Wilfrid announced that he and his companions had been separated from the company of the faithful, and they ordered the vessels of God from which they ate to be washed first, as though polluted by filth, before they were touched by them, says Eddius, chapter 46. In the following chapter he adds that Wilfrid and his companions boarded a ship and came to the Apostolic See, evidently in early spring, when the sea was open, as may be conjectured.

[Col. 0044A] In the year of Christ 704, the case of Saint Wilfrid was examined before Pope John, the charges were investigated, and he was declared innocent. Baronius assigns Wilfrid’s Roman protection and absolution to the following year, when John VII governed the Roman Church. But William of Malmesbury correctly observes, *Book III of the Deeds of the English Pontiffs*, p. 266, that Wilfrid crossed the sea and entered the City when he was already about seventy years old. Therefore this must have occurred either in this year or in the preceding one, since, according to Eadmer in his *Life* of Wilfrid—and this may also be gathered from Eddius—Wilfrid was born in 634.

Eddius says in his *Life*, chapter 50:

> After many periods of days and months, our holy and praiseworthy pontiff appeared to have been purely and completely cleared of every sinful offense from which he was accused and degraded. For through four months and seventy councils of the most holy See, having been examined—or being about to be examined—as in a furnace of fire, he emerged purified, with the apostolic authority thus assisting him, so to speak. A brief account was recited, because on Holy Easter, on the third day, the synod of the most blessed Agatho against the perversities of heretics was convened with 125 orthodox bishops; each of them confessed the true faith for his own province and city and confirmed it by his subscription … He who had exercised the office of bishop for more than forty or fifty years … and therefore deserved to pay the penalty, being imprisoned in the deepest confinement of the prison until the end of his life—these were his accusers, as some said.

From these words some have incorrectly inferred that it is certain that the Roman synod under John VI was completed in this year. But the expression “forty and more years” can designate not only the forty-first year then in progress but also the forty-second or forty-third. We shall soon offer other considerations by which it will become clear that this synod must necessarily be assigned to this year.

[Col. 0044C] Finally, in chapter 50, Eddius reports the sentence of Wilfrid’s absolution pronounced by John VI:

> Blessed Wilfrid, the bishop beloved by God, in whom, after examining him with such diligence through so many councils, we found no charge of any crime, is released from hidden offenses by the authority of blessed Peter the apostle and prince of the apostles, who possesses the power of binding and loosing.

Then, in chapter 51, he produces the letter—or decree—of Pope John to Æthelred, king of the Mercians, and to Aldfrith, king of the Deirans and Bernicians, that is, king of Northumbria. In it John informs them that Wilfrid had been absolved, at least provisionally, until, as John says, “the principal persons themselves, on whose account the dispute arose, should be present”—that is, at Rome. They had to come and sit together so that the dispute might reach an end.

John therefore admonishes Berthwald, prelate of the holy Church of Canterbury,

[Col. 0044D] whom, by the authority of the prince of the apostles, “we confirmed there as most reverend archbishop,” to convene a synod together with Bishop Wilfrid. When the council had been regularly assembled, he was to cause Bishops Bosa of York and John of Hexham to come to the synod, hear the statements of both parties, and bring the case to a synodal conclusion. “If this cannot be done,” he continues, “let them come together to this Apostolic See, so that it may be demanded and decided by a larger council,” etc.

In place of *flagitetur* (“be demanded”), however, *agitetur* (“be discussed”) appears to be the proper reading. Since Pope John wrote to King Æthelred concerning Wilfrid’s absolution and the matters that still remained to be done, and since Æthelred abdicated his kingdom in the year of Christ 704, as is clear both from Bede and from the English authors cited above, it is certain not only that Wilfrid’s case was discussed while John VI presided over the Roman Church, but also that the synod convened to decide it reached its conclusion in this year.

Bede, book V, chapter 20, relates in a single continuous account what occurred in the case of Saint Wilfrid. But because he narrates the matter briefly and summarily, it is not surprising that Baronius, deprived of the resources with which we now abound, was unable to determine whether the Roman synod at which Wilfrid was acquitted was held during the pontificate of John VI or John VII, or in what year it was celebrated. He therefore suspected that the synod dealt with the canons added to the Sixth General Council at the Quinisext Council. Yet it is certain that, in the Roman synod held in 704, certain passages from the Roman council convened by Pope Agatho against the Monothelites were indeed read—but only those relevant to Wilfrid’s case, not those concerning the condemnation of the Monothelites.

[Col. 0045]

CONTEMPORARY DOCUMENTS.

[Col. 0045]

I. Council held under Alfrid, king of the Northumbrians, and Berthwald, archbishop of Canterbury, during the pontificate of Pope John VI, in the year of Christ 701, in which new schemes were devised against Wilfrid, archbishop of York. He appealed once more to Pope John and overcame his enemies.

[Col. 0045B]

Egfrid had already fallen in battle against the Picts, and Theodore was already approaching death. Troubled in conscience by the sin committed against Wilfrid, Theodore summoned Wilfrid and Bishop Erkenwald to London. He confessed all his sins to them and said that he was especially troubled by the fact that he had sinned against a saint, having allowed him to be stripped of his possessions either by overt pressure or by concealed acquiescence.

“And because,” he said, “my end awaits me in the coming year, as I have learned through God’s foretelling, and as frequent illness [Al., ‘illness warns me’] reminds me, I ask you, most holy bishop, kindly to forgive me the wrong I committed and to assume my archbishopric—for you are the most skilled of all the English in Roman law. With God’s help I shall strive to erase my former offenses through the recent diligence of my service, making the kings my friends both by my authority and by my prayers.”

Wilfrid answered him calmly and as befitted a holy man. But he did not consent [Al., “consented”] to accept the archbishopric without a ruling from a greater council.

Theodore therefore exerted all his strength to secure Wilfrid’s restoration to the episcopate. He sent envoys and letters to Alfrid, king of the Northumbrians, who had succeeded Egfrid, and to his sister Elfleda, abbess of Streneshalh, urging them, once their hostilities had been set aside, to embrace his friendship without delay. To make the ardor of his effort clear, I shall insert here the letter he sent to Ethelred, king of the Mercians.

II.

To the most glorious and excellent king of the Mercians, Theodore, archbishop by the grace of God, sends perpetual greeting in the Lord.

Let your wondrous holiness, dearest son, know that I am at peace with the venerable Bishop Wilfrid. Therefore, beloved, I admonish you and charge you in the love of Christ to extend to his holy devotion, as far as your strength permits and as long as you live, the protection you have always given him, because for a long time, deprived of his own possessions, he has labored greatly in the Lord among the pagans.

For this reason I, Theodore, a humble and aged bishop, make this appeal to your blessedness. The apostolic authority, as you know, commends this; and that most holy man, in his patience, possessed his soul. Gentle and humble amid the injuries inflicted upon him, following his Head, he awaited healing. If I have found favor in your sight, then, even if the distance of the journey seems burdensome to you, let my eyes behold your gracious face, and let my soul bless you before I die.

Act, therefore, my son, toward that most holy man in the manner I have begged of you. If you obey your father, who is not far from departing this world, it will contribute greatly to your salvation.

[Col. 0046B]

Farewell.

When Wilfrid arrived before the kings with the archbishop’s letters, he was greeted and favor was granted him. Alfrid, who had once known him well, voluntarily invited him to himself and first generously restored to him the monastery of Heugh, then, by decree of the council, the episcopate of York and the monastery at Ripon.

This friendship between them lasted scarcely five years, until poisonous counsels, hatched within the territories of certain men, burst into public view. Influenced by these, King Alfrid began to mutilate the monastery at Ripon of its possessions and contemplated establishing an episcopate there. He asserted that the decrees of Archbishop Theodore should not be obeyed according to those issued at the beginning and end of his tenure, but according to those promulgated in the intervening years, which were known to have been agitated by discord.

Wilfrid, angered by this, withdrew to his friend Ethelred, king of the Mercians. After spending a considerable time under his protection, and after Sexwulf, bishop of Lichfield, had died, Wilfrid governed that episcopate. He was loved and revered by all the provincials alike, while King Alfrid and Berthwald, the archbishop who had succeeded Theodore, devised and pursued many schemes against him.

At last they settled upon this plan: they would summon him to a council under the pretense of peace and there either bend him to their will by flattery or, if he refused, crush him. Unaware of the plot and judging others by the uprightness of his own heart, he went to the council; but he experienced something far different from what he had hoped.

For after they had wearied him for a long time with insults and false accusations of crimes, they finally asked whether he was willing to obey the decrees of Archbishop Theodore. Perceiving their wickedness, he frustrated them with a shrewd reply, saying that he would gladly obey those decisions of Theodore which were consonant with the sacred canons.

Then, after a long debate in which he attacked them sharply and truthfully, he fell silent. He reproached them for disregarding, for twenty-two years, the commands of three apostles—Agatho, Benedict, and Sergius—and for preferring the decrees of Archbishop Theodore, enacted through dissension.

At this Alfrid’s pride rose so high that he said to the archbishop: “If you command it, father, I shall crush him by force.”

When even his enemies disapproved of this—thinking it improper that so eminent a man, who had come to the council because he trusted them, should suffer the injustice of oppression—they decided that another course should be taken. Thus, as though offering peaceful advice, they began to urge him that, since dissensions in the Church of God so frequently arose because of him, he should voluntarily surrender his possessions and episcopate and confirm this renunciation in writing. They said that this would commend his reputation and increase his glory: it would be better for him, as a private man, to live quietly than to stir up storms of sedition, either personally or through others, on behalf of his episcopate.

The father perceived that the matter was entangled in these threats [Al., “excessively”], and replied that nothing contributed so greatly to a man’s disgrace as condemning himself by his own words.

He had been the first to teach the true Easter in Northumbria after expelling the Scots; the first to establish ecclesiastical singing antiphonally; and the first to require the monks to observe the rule of the most holy Benedict. Yet now, as an old bishop of nearly seventy years, they expected him in this office to be compelled to condemn himself in writing.

They should therefore understand that he would not do what would be a disgrace to himself, a calamity to his subjects, and an injury to everyone. Rather, he would appeal to the apostolic see, and if any of them presumed to engage him in ecclesiastical conflict, he would recall the matter to that see.

Now nearly seventy years old, he again undertook the hardships of travel and once more planned to go to Rome. He did not delay long before crossing the sea, traversing the road, and entering the City. He waited there for several days for his accusers to arrive. When they came, he presented his case in letters, while he himself made the following defense concerning the matters that pertained to him.

III.

To the most blessed lord, universal Pope John, Wilfrid, a suppliant and humble servant of the servants of God, bishop.

Let your holiness know that, owing to the disturbances recently arising in Britain on the part of those who, contrary to the decrees of the most blessed Pope Agatho and of his venerable successors, were usurping for themselves my episcopate, monasteries, lands, and all my possessions, I was compelled to appeal to this most holy apostolic see. I adjured them by the almighty Lord and by the blessed apostle Peter that, if anyone had any accusation against me, he should come into your presence, just as the writings of your most blessed predecessor Sergius had decreed.

Therefore I have taken care that the petition of my humility be presented to your glorious presence, so that you may deign, through the abundant benevolence of your mercy, to confirm what your most blessed predecessors decreed concerning my insignificance. If any accuser should appear against me, let him be brought forward by your command and make whatever charge he wishes. If I do not convincingly refute even the smallest part of it, I am prepared to undergo the severity of the canons.

I further ask to obtain letters of recommendation from your eminence to Ethelred, king of the Mercians, so that all my monasteries located in his province may enjoy peace. I also ask for a letter to Alfrid [Al., “Alfrith”], king of the Northumbrians, so that he may restore everything belonging to me.

If he should find it burdensome for me to retain the episcopate of York, let the apostolic see provide for who is to be bishop there. I shall nevertheless not lose the two monasteries situated in that province, Ripon and Hexham, which I founded.

Finally, I promise to obey all the decrees of Archbishop Brethwald [Berthwald] that are not directed against the firmly established decrees of your predecessors concerning my insignificance.

When the accusers sent by Archbishop Berthwald were ordered to reply to this, they first said that it was a capital offense that Wilfrid had stubbornly declared, in the council assembled in Britain, that he would not obey the decrees of Archbishop Britowald.

The bishop, standing in the midst of them, cleared himself of this charge by saying that he had not answered so unconditionally, but had promised to obey only those decrees which were not contrary to the canons. It was contrary to the rules, however, that he should condemn himself without any charge being brought against him.

When this highly reasonable and straightforward answer had aroused joyful applause among the Romans, the accusers were ordered to return home. The bishops told them that, although the canons provided that an accuser who failed on the first count of an accusation should not rise again to attempt another, nevertheless, out of reverence for Archbishop Berthwald, they would not fail to examine everything in order.

The result was that, over four months, seventy sessions were convened, either for this sole reason or chiefly because of it. They ended gloriously for Wilfrid and shamefully for his accusers. The Romans watched with the greatest attention, marveling at the accusers’ impudence and at Wilfrid’s eloquence: whatever accusations they brought against him, he needed no contrived answer, but, supported by the aid of God and truth, scattered and overthrew them at the first movement of his lips like spiders’ webs.

The bishops were even more amazed at the audacity of these advocates: how could men exempt from ecclesiastical rank—except that one of them was a deacon—presume to accuse a venerable bishop, a pontiff of seventy years, a torrent of eloquence? Thus, after conferring among themselves at length in Greek, they finally turned to our language. They condemned the envoys as worthy of prison, censured the man who had sent them for his folly, and declared Wilfrid free from every charge.

Here I would insert how much benefit the reading of Pope Agatho’s synod brought to Wilfrid’s case, and also how, when he was returning home and was overcome by illness at the city of Meaux in France, east of Paris, he was healed by an angelic vision—if the historian Bede the Venerable, whose moderation of speech deserves belief, had not forestalled my account.

We insert very briefly what he omitted from the written record. Although the bishop had won his case, he nevertheless desired to remain in Rome, pouring out his aged spirit at the feet of the apostolic lords. Pope John’s prudent judgment resisted this pious wish: he said that Wilfrid was necessary to England, and therefore ordered him to spend the remainder of his life not in foreign ears [Al., “mouths”], but in the service of his homeland, and so forth.

IV. Letter of Pope John VII to Ethelred, king.

[Col. 0049A]

(See below.)

V. Letter of Pope John VII to the archbishops, priests, deacons, and all the clergy established throughout the land of the English.

(See below.)

VI. Letter of Saint Aldhelm, bishop of Sherborne, to Wilfrid’s clergy.

(See below.)

VII. Letter of Saint Aldhelm, bishop of Sherborne, to Wilfrid.

(See below.)

VIII. Roman Council convened by the authority of Pope John VII, at the request of the emperor Justinian, to confirm or reject the canons of the Sixth Synod, in the year of the Redeemer 705, during the pontificate of John VII.

[Col. 0049B]

Anastasius indicates above, in the Life of John VII, on what occasion this synod was convened at Rome: namely, because the emperor Justinian had requested by letters and an embassy that Pope John, having assembled a council, examine the canons enacted at Constantinople and approve and confirm those he found to agree with Catholic discipline, rejecting the rest.

The pope granted nothing to this improper request, and rightly so. For it is inappropriate and highly unbecoming to approve even the smallest part of what was established in a pseudo-council. See what I said above in the Life of John, under the heading “Council.”

At this same synod, Wilfrid, bishop of York, who had previously been unjustly accused once under Pope Agatho and acquitted at the Roman council held under that same Agatho, was accused a second time by King Aldfrid and acquitted a second time by a synodal judgment at Rome.

According to Bede, these events occurred four years before Wilfrid’s death and therefore in the year of Christ 705, during the pontificate of Pope John VII. Since Bede testifies that Wilfrid lived four years after this synod, and that in the year of our Redeemer 709, four years after the death of King Osred, he died in the forty-fifth year of his episcopate, it cannot be denied that this synod was held at the time stated.

Bede writes in book V, chapter 20, that Wilfrid held the episcopate for forty-five years. Again, in book III, chapter 26, he states that the first year of his episcopate coincided with the year of the Lord 664. It necessarily follows that the final year of Wilfrid’s episcopate fell in the year of the Lord 709, which was the fifth year after the conclusion of that synod at which, as Bede reports in book V, chapter 20, he was acquitted of the accusations of his adversaries, in these words:

“After five years,” he says, “he was again accused by that same king, namely Aldfrid, and by very many bishops, and was driven from his episcopate. Coming to Rome, when, in the presence of his accusers, he was given the opportunity to defend himself, while several bishops were seated with the apostolic Pope John, it was established by the judgment of all that his accusers had devised certain false accusations against him. The aforesaid pope wrote to the kings of the English, Ethelred and Aldfrid, that they should restore him to his episcopate, since he had been unjustly condemned.

“The reading of the synod of the blessed Pope Agatho greatly assisted his acquittal. That synod had once been held in the City while Agatho himself was present and seated among the bishops in the same council, as we have said. When, therefore, because the case required it, that synod was read for several days before the nobles and a great gathering of people, at the command of the apostolic pope, they came to the passage where it was written: ‘Wilfrid, the beloved of God, bishop of the city of York, appealing to the apostolic see concerning his case and acquitted by that authority in matters certain and uncertain,’ and so forth, as we have quoted above.

“When this had been read, astonishment seized the hearers. While the reader was silent, they began to ask one another who that Bishop Wilfrid was. Then Boniface, counselor to the apostolic pope, and many others who had seen him there in the time of Pope Agatho, said that he was the very bishop who had recently come to Rome, accused by his own people and awaiting judgment from the apostolic see.

“‘When he came here some time ago, likewise under accusation,’ they said, ‘his case and the controversy between the two parties were immediately heard and judged, and Pope Agatho, of blessed memory, established that he had been driven from his episcopate contrary to law. He was held in such honor by him that, in the council he had convened, he ordered him to sit among the bishops as a man of incorrupt faith and upright character.’

“When they heard this, everyone, together with the pontiff himself, said that a man of such authority, who had held the episcopate for nearly forty years, ought by no means to be condemned, but should return to his homeland with honor, acquitted in full of the charges brought against him.”

IX. [Note: [Col. 0049C] Council.] After obtaining his acquittal, Wilfrid departed from Rome and, upon reaching Gaul, fell into a very serious illness. He was miraculously delivered through an apparition and healing by Saint Michael, and in that same year came to England.

When he was honorably received by the archbishop after the apostolic letters had been read, but was despised by Alfrid, the king who had accused him, the king suddenly died. Then, says Bede in book V, chapter 20, after his son Osred had become king, a synod was immediately held beside the River Nidd. After some time spent in conflict between the two parties, all eventually favoring him, Wilfrid was restored to the episcopate of his own Church. Thus he lived in peace for four years, that is, until the day of his death.

This is Bede’s account in the passage cited above. Binius.—Eddius, in the Life of Saint Wilfrid, chapter 57, speaking of this council, at which peace was restored, says:

“In the first year of King Osred, Berthwald, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury and almost the whole of Britain, came from the south. By command of the apostolic see, he carefully invited the northern king, together with all his bishops, abbots, and the leading men of his entire kingdom, to a synodal place to discuss the case of the blessed Bishop Wilfrid—and so it was done.

“For the king—namely Osred—assembled with his nobles in one place east of the River Nidd, together with his three bishops, namely Bosa of York, John of Hexham, and Eadfrid of Lindisfarne, and with the abbots. The blessed abbess Aelfleda of the monastery of Streaneshalch, daughter of Oswiu, king of Northumbria, was also present, always the comforter and excellent conciliator of the entire province. Archbishop Berthwald and Bishop Wilfrid likewise arrived together on the same day.

“Then, when the king and bishops were seated with their nobles in the synodal place, the two books were read from beginning to end. The archbishop said that the apostolic authority had judged that the bishops of the Churches of that province should be reconciled with the blessed Wilfrid. The resisting bishops said that no one could alter what had already been done.

“But because Abbess Aelfleda and the nobleman Berechtfrid strongly favored Wilfrid and said much in the synod on behalf of the bishop, as may be seen in Eddius, the bishops withdrew from one another and began to deliberate separately. Sometimes the archbishop deliberated with them, and sometimes the most wise virgin Aelfleda.

“The outcome of this holy council was that all the bishops and the king with his nobles entered into an agreement of pure peace with Saint Wilfrid the bishop, which they preserved among themselves until the end of their lives, restoring to him the two chief monasteries at Ripon and Hexham, together with all their revenues.” Pagius.

A council held beside the River Nidd in Northumbria by Osred, then king there, and Berthwald, archbishop of Canterbury, at the urging of Pope John VII in the year of Christ 705. At this council, after the letter of Pope John had been received, Wilfrid was finally confirmed in his York archiepiscopate.

[Col. 0051A]

After Malmesbury had completed his account of the council held under King Alfrid and Archbishop Berthwald in the year of grace 701, he proceeded to this council at Nidd and began as follows:

“Wilfrid therefore returned and brought the apostolic letters to Ethelred, king of the Mercians, who had by then become a monk. He humbly and on bended knee received the favor of the apostolic greeting, and, after the letters had been read, readily obtained from Kenred, the son of Wulfhere’s brother, whom Ethelred had appointed king in his place, the fulfillment of what their tenor commanded.

“For Kenred too was full of the fear of God, as he later proved to the world by his voluntary renunciation of the kingdom four years afterward. Nor did Archbishop Berthwald, who was eager to pursue peace, disdain to hasten toward the unity of fraternal concord. Terrified by the threats of the apostolic see, he is said to have done so, while the envoys he sent heaped his condemnation upon him in weighty complaints, although Wilfrid had already rescued them from the sentence imposed upon them.

“Only Alfrid, king of the Northumbrians, persisted, pursuing a more obstinate judgment [Al., ‘path’]. Envoys sent to him on Wilfrid’s behalf initially brought back a gracious reply. But, corrupted—as is believed—by the counsels of malicious men whom he indulged beyond what befitted his dignity, he saddened them when they returned on the appointed day with the following decision:

“Although, he said, he would honor the envoys as parents, since they were both weighty in character and honorable in appearance, he absolutely rejected the embassy’s request, because it was unreasonable to associate with a man who had already twice been condemned by the entire council of the English, regardless of any apostolic letters.
