“Nor did he himself remain long in this life afterward. As soon as the envoys departed, he was seized by a grievous illness and brought near to death. The bitterness of his suffering drew forth the reason that had once lain dormant in his royal mind; and, according to the prophet, ‘affliction gave understanding to his hearing’ [Isaiah 40].

“Understanding that he had been punished deservedly for his disobedience, he promised that he would make every possible amends to Wilfrid if he could be brought to him while he was still alive. He did not cease promising this for as long as he could speak before his voice failed, and he adjured his heir to make the same promise if he himself could not fulfill his vow.

“He died soon afterward, and too late regretted that he had despised the apostolic letters, whose threats he had not been permitted to escape. Since I have mentioned them so often, I am inclined to set them down here in abbreviated form, so that it may be clear what misery overwhelms mortals when those men whom antiquity celebrates as most holy—Theodore, Berthwald, John, Bosa, and also Abbess Hilda—attacked Wilfrid with a hatred fit for combat, although, as what has already been said proves, he was exceedingly acceptable to God.”

Heddius, in the Life of Saint Wilfrid, chapter 58, whom Malmesbury follows, gives a fuller account of the proceedings of this synod. It seems fitting to add it here.

“In the first year of King Osred, Berthwald, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury and almost the whole of Britain, came from the south. By command of the apostolic see, he carefully invited the northern king, together with all his bishops and abbots and the leading men of his entire kingdom, to a synodal place to discuss the case of the blessed Bishop Wilfrid—and so it was done.

“For they assembled in one place east of the River Nidd: the king with his men, his three bishops with the abbots, and the blessed Abbess Aelfleda, always the comforter of the entire province and its excellent counselor. Archbishop Berthwald and Bishop Wilfrid likewise arrived together on the same day.

“Then, when the king and bishops were seated with their nobles in the synodal place, the archbishop began to speak in this manner:

“‘Let us pray to our Lord God that he may grant the harmony of peace in our hearts through the Holy Spirit. For I and the blessed Bishop Wilfrid have received writings from the apostolic see addressed to my unworthiness through messengers, and likewise brought by the pope himself. We humbly ask that they be read in the presence of your reverence.’

“The venerable lords granted permission. In the presence of the synod, while everyone listened, both books were read from beginning to end.

“After the reading, while everyone was silent, Berechtfrid, second among the king’s nobles, said to the archbishop: ‘We who require interpretation are eager to hear what the apostolic authority says.’

“The archbishop answered him:

“‘The judgments of the apostolic see, though expressed through a long circuit and verbal circumlocutions, reveal one and the same meaning in both books. I shall explain their sense in a brief statement.

“‘The apostolic authority—which was first granted to the apostle Peter, prince of the apostles, for binding and loosing—has decreed concerning the blessed Wilfrid that, in my presence, unworthy though I am, and in the presence of this entire assembly, the bishops of the Churches of this province must abandon their ancient hostility for the salvation of their souls and be reconciled in goodness with the blessed Bishop Wilfrid.

“‘For these my fellow bishops are given a choice between two judgments of the apostolic see. Let them choose whichever they wish: either they shall enter into clear and complete peace with Bishop Wilfrid and restore to him, according to the judgment that they and I deem wise, the portions of the Churches that he formerly governed; or, if they do not wish to accept this best course, they shall all proceed together to the apostolic see, where the matter shall be judged by a greater council.

“‘If anyone, however, despising this—God forbid—should refuse to fulfill either of these two alternatives, let him know that, if he is a king or layman, he is excommunicated from the body and blood of Christ; but if he is a bishop or priest—which is more execrable and terrible to say—he is to be degraded from every rank of ecclesiastical dignity. These are the judgments of the apostolic see, set forth in brief.’

“The resisting bishops replied:

“‘What our predecessors, Archbishop Theodore, sent by the apostolic see, and King Ecgfrid once decreed; and what we, together with nearly all the bishops of Britain, judged in the field called Austerfield, in the most distinguished presence of our archbishop and with King Alfrid—how can anyone alter it?’

“Meanwhile, the most blessed Abbess Aelfleda said with her gracious voice:

“‘In Christ I speak the truth: this was the testament of King Alfrid during the illness in which he ended his life. He made a vow to God and to Saint Peter, saying: “If I live, I shall fulfill all the judgments of the apostolic see concerning the blessed Bishop Wilfrid, which I previously refused even to hear. But if I die, nevertheless tell my heir in the name of the Lord to fulfill the apostolic judgment concerning Bishop Wilfrid, as a remedy for my soul.”’

“When she had spoken, Berechtfrid, the king’s prefect and chief noble, answered:

“‘This is the will of the king and of his nobles: that we obey in everything the commands of the apostolic see and the instructions of King Alfrid.

“‘For when we were besieged in the city called Bamburgh, surrounded on every side and confined amid hostile forces and the narrowness of a rocky stronghold, we took counsel among ourselves. We promised God that, if he granted our royal boy the kingdom of his father, we would fulfill what the holy apostolic authority had commanded concerning Saint Wilfrid the bishop.

“‘Immediately after our vows, the minds of our enemies were changed. They all hastened toward friendship with us under oath, the gates were opened, we were freed from our confinement, our enemies were put to flight, and we received the kingdom.’

“After these words had ended, the bishops withdrew from one another and began to deliberate separately. Sometimes the archbishop deliberated with them, and sometimes the most wise virgin Aelfleda.

“The outcome of this holy council was that all the bishops and the king with his nobles entered into an agreement of pure peace with Saint Wilfrid the bishop, which they preserved among themselves until the end of their lives, restoring to him the two excellent monasteries at Ripon and Hexham, together with all their revenues.

“On that day all the bishops kissed and embraced one another, broke bread, and received communion. Giving thanks to God for all this blessedness, they returned peacefully to their own places in the peace of Christ.”

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 707. JOHN VII, ROMAN PONTIFF.

[Col. 0053]

NOTICE CONCERNING POPE JOHN VII.

(Liber Pontificalis.)

[Col. 0053A] [Note: [Col. 0053A] John VII. The catalogs and manuscripts agree almost unanimously that the vacancy of the Apostolic See after the death of John VI lasted one month and eighteen days, except for the Veronese catalog, which counts one day fewer because it excludes the endpoints, and the third Colbertine manuscript, which is plainly corrupt, since it counts thirty days altogether.

“Therefore, once we have correctly established the date of the predecessor’s death as 11 January, the date of John VII’s ordination is self-evident. For, counting one month and eighteen days from 11 January 705 through the interpontificate, one arrives at the Kalends of March. In that same year, 705, they fell on a Sunday, as the dominical letter D confirms.

“Pagius too was compelled to assign the Kalends of March to John’s ordination because no feast day presented itself that would accord with his chronology. But what of it? Just as he moved the ordination and deposition of John’s predecessor back by two days, so now he places them two days away from those same Kalends of March.

“To recover that interval, he employs a plainly singular device, which I think should be presented in his own words so that it may be clearer to the reader: ‘In the interpontificate,’ he says, ‘instead of eighteen days one should read nineteen, excluding also the day of death both from the pontificate of John VI and from the interpontificate; and this error, it seems, should be attributed to Anastasius.’

“Here the most learned man is wrong in two respects, and especially because he removes the ordination from Sunday. He charges the entire series of catalogs and manuscripts with error and extracts one day from their testimony in order, if possible, to fill the gap. Since one day is still lacking, he orders the day of John VI’s death to disappear.

“If he truly ordered that day to disappear after Sergius, he ought not to have opposed the agreement of the manuscripts and catalogs. For, counting fifty days from 9 September, he would end at 29 October, the final day of the interpontificate, which preceded the ordination of John VI—yet only by excluding the very day of death, or deposition, from the interpontificate and joining it to the pontificate of Sergius.

“If the agreement of all the manuscripts compelled Pagius to establish the date of the ordination correctly at the Kalends of March, their equal consistency in defining the day of death as 18 October proves that John’s death cannot be moved from that date, whatever the remarkable disagreement concerning the duration of the pontificate may suggest otherwise.

“And indeed, all the manuscripts and catalogs I have seen assign John VII a pontificate of two years. As for the months and days, however, they differ greatly among themselves. The Veronese catalog and the sixth Colbertine assign eight months; the Bergomese, Lucchese, and Farfense catalogs, the fourth, fifth, and seventh Colbertine manuscripts, together with the common manuscript, both Freherian manuscripts, the second Thuane manuscript, the Cavense, and the Farnesian assign seven months; the Palatine-Vatican, the second and third Colbertine manuscripts, together with the Royal, Mazarin, first Thuane, and first Ambrosian manuscripts, supported by Liudprand, assign six months.

“Of these various opinions, the preferable one is undoubtedly that which assigns John seven months. Likewise, among the different opinions concerning the number of days, the one counting seventeen should be chosen.

“For John VII, ordained in the year 705 on the Kalends of March, after sitting two years, seven months, and seventeen days, was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November—that is, 18 October—in the sixth indiction, or the year 707, as Anastasius reports.”

Cennus. John VII obtained the pontificate in the year of Christ 705, on the first day of March. It was almost miraculous that, though a Greek, he was placed in the Apostolic See through the efforts of Greeks from the ranks of the other cardinals and inherited the apostolic spirit and by no means assented when the heretical emperor requested confirmation of the Constantinopolitan conciliabulum mentioned above.

Bin and Labb. John VII, born to Plato Janidega, originated from Rossano in Magna Graecia, called Calabria. The fourteenth pope who was a native of the realm, he was a cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New and sat for two years, seven months, and twelve days. He was elected and consecrated on a Sunday, the Kalends of March.

Ciaconius.]

John VII, Greek by nationality, son of Plato, sat for two years, seven months, and seventeen days. [Note: [Col. 0053A] Another manuscript omits: “He lived during the reigns of the emperors Tiberius Augustus and Justinian.”]

He lived during the reigns of the emperors Tiberius Augustus and Justinian. He was a highly learned man and eloquent in speech. He built an oratory of the holy Mother of God inside the church of the blessed apostle Peter, whose walls he decorated with mosaic paintings. He spent a great quantity of gold and silver there and set up images of the venerable Fathers on the right and left.

He restored the basilica of Saint Eugenia, which for a long time had been uncovered and broken apart [Al., “unroofed”]. He also labored on the cemeteries of the blessed martyrs Marcellinus and Mark, and of the holy pontiff Damasus.

[Note: [Col. 0054C] He also made images in various churches. Whoever wishes to know them will find his face depicted in them. Statues and images of emperors were worshiped and were commonly placed in temples and in the forum. Ambrose, Hexameron, book VI, chapter 9: “Only the heads of princes cast in bronze, and faces fashioned from bronze or marble, are worshiped by men.” The same author, On the Interpellations, chapter 9: “See how in cities the images of good princes endure, while the images of tyrants are destroyed.” Corippus, On the Praises of Justinian, book III:

“. . . . . Justinian was painted everywhere;

the painting pleased the lords, …”]

And they rejoiced when they saw the likeness of their progenitor.

**ALTASERRA.** He also made images in various churches; whoever wishes to know them will find his likeness depicted in them.

[Note: “His likeness depicted in them.” When the pontiff ordered various images to be painted in the churches in mosaic work, he took care to have his own image added as well. Ciampinus observes this practice in his work on mosaics, and Agnellus mentions it more than once when he records images of this kind commissioned by the archbishops of Ravenna. Those who were depicted while alive were customarily represented in the likeness of one praying. **BENCINUS.**]

He likewise adorned with paintings the basilica of the holy Mother of God, which is called the Ancient Basilica; there he newly made an ambo, and above that same church he preferred to establish an episcopal residence for himself. There he completed the term of his pontificate.

[Note: Codex Luc., “he wished to construct.”]

[Note: Another reading: “he completed his life.”]

He made a particularly fine golden chalice weighing twenty pounds, and adorned it with precious gems.

[Note: During his reign, Aripert, king of the Lombards, restored by his own right to the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which for a long time had been taken away from the Church’s legal possession and was being destroyed by that same people, having had the donation inscribed in golden letters. A royal donation written in golden letters for the Church is mentioned. Pachymeres reports that imperial documents were sealed with a golden bull in *Palaeologus*, book V, chapter 20:

“Immediately the emperor gives the order, and a document is issued, sealed with a golden bull.”

That is: “A diploma issued immediately by order of the emperor, secured with a golden bull.”

The same author says in *Andronicus*, book I, chapter 2:

“For the guarantees given through documents bearing golden bulls.”

That is: “For the pledge given in diplomas secured with a golden bull.” **ALTASERRA.**]

During his reign, Aripert, king of the Lombards, restored by his own right to the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which for a long time had been deprived of the Church’s legal ownership and was being held by that same people, having the donation written in golden letters.

This passage of the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, or rather of Paul the Deacon, from whom Anastasius—or whoever else was its author or interpolator—easily copied it into the *Book of the Pontiffs*, represents an illustrious proof of the most ancient possession of temporal dominion in favor of the holy Roman see. Anyone who is not excessively hostile to it will readily acknowledge this with me.

This donation—or restoration—of the Cottian Alps is said to have been made in the year 704, during the pontificate of John VII, not long after the time of Paul the Deacon, who narrates the event and who flourished until about the year 770. He not only asserts that the grant was committed to writing, but that it was written in golden letters—something he himself could have observed with his own eyes.

This was not the donation of some estate, farm, garden, or olive grove, of the kind of which innumerable examples are presented to us by marble inscriptions and church titles, as the most illustrious bishop and most experienced scholar of ecclesiastical affairs, Francesco Bianchini, very properly observed in his preface to Anastasius (*vol.* I, no. 43 and following). The loss of the papers which he was unable to illustrate with his notes to the very end is understood and lamented in them, to the great loss of readers.

Rather, it was the donation of an enormous tract of land extending from the Gallic frontier through the Allobroges and Segusium as far as Bobbio, a region formerly reduced by Nero to the status of a Roman province, as Suetonius states in his *Life of Nero*: “He likewise converted the kingdom of the Alps, after the death of Cottius, into the form of a province.”

It is also noteworthy that these lands are not called simply “the Alps,” but “the patrimony of the Alps.” In ancient documents this expression is used indiscriminately both for property dedicated to blessed Peter through the piety of the faithful and for property bound by royal rights.

The registers of Anastasius, composed as this century was ending, greatly illuminate and confirm this distinguished monument of the rights of the Roman Church: they record donations, restitutions, and recoveries of lands and patrimonies made by the Lombard and Frankish kings to the holy Roman Church.

It is useful to cite one or two examples in advance, in confirmation of the argument. Under the year 714, in the *Life of Gregory II* preserved by Anastasius—who perhaps copied it from Paul the Deacon as well—we read of the unlawful seizure of the same Cottian Alps and, shortly afterward, of their just restoration by Liutprand.

“At that time,” Anastasius says, “King Liutprand confirmed the restoration of the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which King Aripert had made and which he had recovered, returning it at the exhortation—or rebuke—of so great a man, Gregory II.”

Here again one sees the repeated expression “patrimony.” This was not accidental, but was plainly employed by deliberate design to declare the transfer of property from royal rights to the rights of the holy see.

In the year 715 the Lombards seized the fortress of Cuma by treachery; it unquestionably belonged to the dominion of the Roman Church. The pontiff demanded back the possession unjustly taken from him. When he had tried in vain to recover it by entreaties, he used the allied forces of the ruler of Naples and bought it back by paying him money.

“At that time,” Anastasius says in the *Life of Gregory II*, “the fortress of Cuma had been seized by the Lombards through a treacherous breach of the peace. When this was heard, everyone was filled with sorrow. The most holy pontiff exhorted and admonished the Lombards to restore it; if they would not comply, he denounced in writing that they would fall under divine wrath because of the treachery they had committed. He also wished to give them many gifts if they would restore it. But they, with arrogant minds, would neither heed the admonitions nor permit its restoration.

“Therefore the same holy pontiff grieved exceedingly and entrusted himself to divine hope. He called upon the duke of Naples and the people, and by writing to him daily he made known how they should proceed. Obeying his command, they took counsel together and entered the walls of the fortress by force in the silence of night. John the duke, together with Theodimus the subdeacon, the governor, and the army, killed nearly three hundred Lombards, along with their castald, and captured more than five hundred alive, leading them as prisoners to Naples. Thus they were able to recover the fortress. For its redemption the most holy pope himself, as he had previously promised, gave seventy pounds of gold.”

From this testimony, which I have wished to present in full, it is clearly established that during those times the Roman Church possessed by undisputed right lands and fortresses. To retain them, or to recover what had been lost, the holy pontiffs spared no effort, using at one time prayers and threats, and at another even arms and money.

You have seen, reader, how Baronius constructs his commentary on the passage of Anastasius just quoted. He shows that this holy pontiff, like Gregory the Great, who was received into the number of the saints, did not in the least disregard ecclesiastical property seized by enemies or cease trying to recover it, however nearly impossible the conquest of the place might appear. Rather, what he could not accomplish with his own forces, he arranged to recover through the arms of others, and he was ready to assist with every kind of effort—counsel, aid, and money. He even made use of a subdeacon of the Roman Church.

But observe the order in which he proceeded: first, he acted through paternal admonitions; then he terrified the contemptuous with ecclesiastical censures; finally, he took up arms against those who despised all these measures and arranged for the fortress to be conquered.

Thus God wished a pontiff distinguished both by learning and holiness to undertake so great an enterprise, and by his example to establish a discipline by which his successors, instructed by him, would vindicate ecclesiastical property taken by unjust possessors, even by arms if the other remedies were despised.

But I shall discuss this matter more fully and more suitably when the subject of Hadrian I arises.

**BALDINUS.**

**Aripertus.** Anastasius copied this from Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapter 28:

“At this time Aripert, king of the Lombards, restored the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which had once belonged to the right of the apostolic see but had long been taken away by the Lombards; and he sent this donation, written in golden letters, to Rome.”

With regard to the pontificate of John and the year in which this donation occurred, Hermannus Contractus noted the following in his *Chronicle*, edited by Canisius:

“Year 707. At this time Aribert, king of the Lombards, handed over to blessed Peter and Pope John the possession of the Cottian Alps, which had long before been seized and held by the Lombards, by means of a charter written in golden letters.”

**BENCINUS.** During the reign of Aripert. While John VII was seated in the papal chair, Aribert—or Aripert—the second king of that name among the Lombards, restored the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which had belonged to the rights of the Roman Church but had long been taken away by the Lombards. He sent this donation, written in golden letters, to Rome, as Paul the Deacon testifies in book VI of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 28. In chapter 43 of the same book he also writes that Liutprand, son and successor of Ansprand, confirmed that restoration made to the Roman Church.

Anastasius says that this occurred while John VI was seated; but Hermannus Contractus, in the Canisian edition of his *Chronicle*, connects the donation with the year 707, when John VII was still seated. Under that year he writes:

“Year 707. At this time Aribert, king of the Lombards, restored to blessed Peter and Pope John the possession of the Cottian Alps, which had long before been seized and held by the Lombards, by means of a privilege written in golden letters.”

The Cottian Alps, so called after King Cottius, who subdued them, begin, according to Ammianus Marcellinus, book XV, chapter 10, at the town of Segusium. In the Bordeaux Itinerary, however, their beginning is placed at the town of Ebredunum in the present-day Dauphiné. For thus it reads:

“Station at Hebredunum, sixteen miles. From there the Cottian Alps begin.”

And below:

“City of Secussio, sixteen miles. From there Italy begins.”

But the Paul the Deacon cited above, in book II, chapter 16, while enumerating the provinces of Italy, writes that the Cottian Alps—so called after King Cottius, who lived in the time of Nero—extend eastward from Liguria as far as the Tyrrhenian Sea, while on the western side they adjoin the borders of Gaul. In that province, which he counts as the fifth of Italy, he says that there are Dertona and the monastery of Bobbio, as well as the cities of Genoa and Savona.

But Paul the Deacon is mistaken concerning King Cottius when he says that he lived in Nero’s time. Ammianus, in the passage cited, asserts that Cottius was received into the friendship of Octavian, namely Augustus.

Paul the Deacon then says, in chapter 18, that the ninth province of Italy was the Apennine Alps. They begin where the Cottian Alps end, and he concludes:

“There are some who say that the Cottian and Apennine Alps constitute one province; but the history of Victorinus refutes them, for it calls the Cottian Alps a province in their own right.”

**PAGIUS.** Arivertus, king of the Lombards, restored the donation of the patrimony.

After the Lombards obtained Italy, the Cottian Alps also came under their rule—that region lying between Sedunum and Ebredunum, on the far side of these mountains in Cisalpine Gaul.

These lands had once belonged to the holy see and formed part of its patrimony. Since the Lombards had retained them for a very long time, usurping them without any right, their king Aripert restored them to Saint Peter and his successor John VII, and sent him the donation, authenticated in golden letters, as Paul the Deacon testifies (*De Gestis Langobardorum*, book VI, chapter 28):

“At this time Aripert, king of the Lombards, restored the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which had once belonged to the right of the apostolic see but had long been taken away by the Lombards; and he sent this donation, written in golden letters, to Rome.”

**SOMMIER.** During the reign of Aripert, king of the Lombards, he restored by the lawful right of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which for a long time had been deprived of the Church’s legal ownership and was being held by that same people, having the donation written in golden letters.

[Note: Codex Luc., “of the Cottian Alps”; another reading, “of the Corcian Alps.”]

During the reign of Justinian—

[Note: Justinian. This passage too is taken from Paul, chapter 31. Justinian, having lost the imperial power and living in exile in Pontus, recovered the kingdom with the aid of Trebellius, king of the Bulgars. He killed the patricians who had expelled him. He also captured Leo and Tiberius, who had usurped his position, and had them slaughtered in the middle of the circus before the entire people. He sent Gallinicus, patriarch of Constantinople, to Rome with his eyes torn out, and appointed Cyrus, the abbot who had supported him in exile in Pontus, bishop in Gallinicus’s place. For Justinian’s restoration to the imperial power at Constantinople, and for his savagery and ferocity, consult the author of the *Miscella*, page 142. For what the emperor did against the people of Ravenna whom he discovered to be supporters of the conspiracy, Agnellus treats at length in the *Life of Felix of Ravenna*, chapter 2, page 160. **BENCINUS.**]

The emperor Justinian, coming from the regions of Khazaria through Bulgaria with the aid of Trebellius, king of the Bulgars, reached the imperial city and recovered his own kingdom, from which he had been expelled.

[Note: Codex Luc. and others, “of Gazaria.”]

He captured Leo—

[Note: Codex Luc., “Leontius and.”]

—and Tiberius, who had usurped his position, and had them slaughtered in the middle of the circus before the entire people. He recovered the imperial power from which he had previously been violently driven out. As soon as he entered the palace and regained his own imperial authority, he sent the *tomos*—

[Note: Another reading, “the *protomos*.”]

—which he had previously sent to Rome under Pope Sergius, of apostolic memory, and in which various chapters contrary to the Roman Church had been written, through two metropolitan bishops. Through them he also sent a sacred letter, by which he adjured and exhorted the pope named above to assemble a council of the apostolic Church, to confirm whatever seemed right to him, and to exclude by rejection whatever was contrary.

[Note: *Tomos.* Understand this as the canons of that Constantinopolitan assembly, mentioned above under Sergius. **BIN. and LABB.** The *tomos* previously sent under Lord Sergius. The canons of the Trullan, or Quinisext, Council were sent to John VII by the younger Justinian, so that he might reject whichever of them he wished and approve the remainder; and the pope was ordered to bring them intact to Constantinople. The *Bibliothecarius* narrates this quite clearly.

What must be observed is that some accuse the pontiff on this occasion of weakness and timidity, while others say that nothing improper would have resulted from separating the many useful provisions from the much smaller number of useless ones (Christophorus Lupus, notes and scholia on the Trullan canons).

For the rest, if the matter is brought before a fair judgment, the pontiff could not have acted with greater prudence than by approving absolutely nothing that had been produced by an assembly arrogating to itself the name of an ecumenical council, while the Roman pontiff was entirely unaware of its convocation and celebration—especially since a spirit of pride and envy toward the apostolic see prevailed in it.

Does not the same holy see daily reject and condemn entire books because a few bad propositions are mixed among many good ones, without nevertheless preparing a detailed catalogue of everything that ought to have been rejected and condemned?

**SOMMIER.** “The *tomos* which he had previously sent,” etc. Here the author, speaking of Justinian’s restoration to imperial power, which, as was just said, occurred about the end of the same year, 705, writes: “As soon as he entered the palace and regained his own imperial power, he entrusted to two metropolitan bishops the *tomos* which he had previously sent to Rome under Pope Sergius of apostolic memory, containing various chapters written contrary to the Roman Church; through them he also sent a sacred letter, by which he adjured and exhorted Pope John VII to convene a council of the apostolic Church, to establish what seemed good to him, and, by rejecting it, to exclude what was adverse.”

Justinian therefore not only sought from Pope Sergius, as stated above, confirmation of the Quinisext Synod and received a refusal, but also sought it from John VII. As Anastasius adds, John, timid through human weakness, did not amend these *tomos* at all, but sent them back to the emperor through the aforesaid metropolitans; after this he did not remain long in this life.

Anastasius therefore reproves John VII because he was unwilling to sift the canons of the Quinisext Synod and separate the wheat from the chaff. Nor without reason, says Lupus in his notes and scholia on the canons of the Trullan Council; for the synodical booklet truly says of this synod: “It issued the canons omitted at the Fifth and Sixth Synods, and cleansed the Churches of every Greek—that is, pagan—and Jewish, indeed even heretical, tradition.” This synod has good things mixed with bad, and the useful is not corrupted by the useless; therefore, says the same Lupus, they could have been separated.]

The *tomos* which he had previously sent to Rome under Pope Sergius, of apostolic memory, and in which various chapters contrary to the Roman Church had been written, he entrusted to two metropolitan bishops. Through them he sent a sacred letter, by which he adjured and exhorted the pope named above to assemble a council of the apostolic Church, to confirm whatever seemed right to him, and to exclude by rejection whatever was contrary.

[Note: But John, timid through human weakness. The younger Justinian, restored to the empire through Trebellius, king of the Bulgars, ordered Tiberius Apsimar to be beheaded; and, after securing his position through the death of many, he sent two metropolitan bishops to John VII, so that the canons of the errant synod might be submitted to the supreme judgment of the apostolic see. He requested that the pontiff himself should confirm whatever in them seemed praiseworthy to him and correct whatever required amendment. But although this request of the emperor seemed fair, the pontiff nevertheless judged that it concerned the majesty of Peter’s chair not to approve what had been decreed by that conventicle, and returned the same canons to the emperor through the said metropolitans, without confirming them even in part. This is why our author censures John here for human weakness: lest he do something unwelcome to the emperor, he feared to separate the wheat from the chaff. **MAFEUS.**]

[Note: Another reading: “he ceased.”]

But this man, timid because of human weakness, did not correct these *tomoi*; through the aforementioned metropolitans he sent them to the emperor, after which he did not remain long in this life.

[Note: Another reading omits “these *tomoi*.”]

**MAFEUS.**

During his pontificate he appointed eighteen bishops in various places.

[Note: Another reading omits: “He was also buried … while governing.”]

He too was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle, before the altar of the oratory of the holy Mother of God, which he himself had built, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the sixth indiction, while Justinian governed the Roman state. The episcopal see was vacant for three months.

[Column 0059]

## LETTER OF POPE JOHN VII TO ETHELRED, KING OF THE MERCIANS, AND ALFRID, KING OF THE DEIRANS, ETC.

He admonishes Berthwald, archbishop of Canterbury, to convene a synod, and either to bring Wilfrid and his adversaries together or to have them hasten to Rome.

*(Mansi, Collection of Councils, vol. XII.)* (C, S)*

[Column 0059C]

John the pope to the most eminent lords Ethelred, king of the Mercians, and Alfrid, king of the Deirans and Bernicians.

By the cooperation of God’s grace, we rejoice in the advances of your religion, seeing in you the fervor of faith which you received through the preaching of the prince of the apostles, while God enlightened your minds, and which you hold firmly and effectively. Would that the growth of better things enlarge our joy.

The irreconcilable disagreement of certain people troubles our minds. It must be corrected, lest you be found transgressors of the apostolic commandments rather than their guardians.

Long ago, under Pope Agatho, of apostolic memory, when Bishop Wilfrid had appealed to this see on behalf of his case, and when the accusers sent by Theodore, archbishop of the holy Church of the Cantuarians, and those sent by Hilda, the abbess of religious memory, had come here, the bishops then assembled from various regions examined and decided the matter according to canonical procedure. The successors of that pontiff, our predecessors, maintained the same judgment.

Nor is Archbishop Theodore known to have opposed it, since afterward he never brought any accusation against him.

Now, too, we arranged for the accusations of those who came here from Britain against Bishop Wilfrid, and his defenses, to be presented for several days before the most reverend bishops who were found here. These included both earlier and recent letters, as well as what the parties brought forward orally. But the principal persons from whom the entire dispute arose were not present here; they must come so that the dispute may reach an end.

For this reason we admonish our brother Berthwald, archbishop, to convene a synod together with Wilfrid, and to cause Bosa and John to meet in synod. Let him hear the statements of the parties and consider what each side can establish against the other.

If he is able to settle the matter at that synod, it will be welcome to us. But if not, let him urge them to hasten to the apostolic see, so that what has hitherto been impossible to resolve may be decided by a greater council.

Let him know that whoever refuses to come submits himself to deposition and is no longer to be received as a bishop either here or there. Therefore let your royal sublimity bring about their meeting, so that what, with Christ’s help, we have discerned may come to fulfillment.

But whoever, through the bold rashness of any person, refuses to comply will not go unpunished by God and will not escape without being bound by a heavenly penalty.

[The events narrated below are added by Mansi to John’s letter.]

After Alfrid’s death, a certain Eadwulf, plotting tyranny, also vented the fury of his deranged mind against Wilfrid, as though he had sworn allegiance to Alfrid’s madness.

For when the pontiff, remembering that he had once been his friend, judged it not unwise to visit him, Eadwulf became so violently foolish that he immediately ordered him to leave his kingdom; indeed, he wished to expel him dishonorably after stripping him of all his possessions.

But after two months he was deprived of life and kingdom. Dying with the diadem captive, he struck the ground, while the nobles of the kingdom restored Alfrid’s son Osred to the throne.

Berhtfrith, the greatest of them in faith and authority, urged by Archbishop Berthwald, agreed that a council should be held in Northumbria, so that at last Wilfrid’s just cause might receive a peaceful conclusion.

There, according to the apostolic commands, the bishops were given the choice either of yielding to Wilfrid in his episcopal see or of traveling to Rome to defend their case. Whoever thought it right to resist these provisions was to be excluded from communion.

While the bishops resisted in their usual manner, the most blessed virgin Ælfflæd, Alfrid’s sister and abbess, who had succeeded Hilda of Streaneshalch, fixed an end to the dispute, saying:

“Without further evasions, I produce the testament of my brother, at whose presence I was. It is known that he promised, if he recovered, to carry out without hesitation the commands of the apostolic see, and that what he could not do because death intervened he transmitted to his heir to accomplish.”

Then Berhtfrith, joining his own words to those of the virgin, said:

“I believe that the pope’s commands must be obeyed, especially since the command of our king and the pledge of our necessity add strength to them. For when, after his death, we were shut up in Bebbanburh, pressed by our enemies, in the narrow confines of the siege and in danger of our lives, we vowed to God that we would fulfill the pope’s command if we could escape.

“We had scarcely finished our vow—and I confess this to you, most sacred archbishop—when obedience immediately began to prevail and the entire province hastened to our agreement. The royal boy was raised to the kingship, the enemy was driven away, and the tyrant was destroyed.

“It is therefore the king’s will that Bishop Wilfrid be restored.”

At these words the clouds of dissension were dispersed and the calm of peace poured in. The episcopal dignity hastened into an embrace, and with united minds he spent whatever remained of his life.

Wilfrid was given two monasteries, Ripon and Hexham. Enjoying unshaken peace, after four years, as the archangel Michael had foretold, he was tested by the same illness that he had once suffered at Meaux, so severely that he suddenly lost both sensation and speech.

But when his companions prayed that he might at least be granted speech for the division of his property, he recovered it openly, so that he immediately spoke again. After several days, when health and strength had returned, he visited all his possessions.

Then, because of his frequent illnesses and having no doubt that death was near, he made up whatever he seemed previously to have done too half-heartedly in certain matters. He appointed superiors over all his monasteries and divided his treasures into four portions.

One portion, and the best, he assigned to the Roman Church, by whose authority he had always been freed from every injury and restored to his honors. Although, weighed down by years, he was planning to carry this out personally, iron sleep overtook him before he could do so.

The second portion he assigned to the poor. The third he entrusted to the superiors of the monasteries, so that they might purchase the friendship of the powerful and repel the assaults of their opponents. The fourth he gave to those who, as inseparable companions of his labors, had not yet received lands by which they could support themselves.

Having received permission from the people of Ripon, whom he had always loved with particular affection, and from the other Northumbrians, he set out to meet King Æthelred of Mercia, who had invited him. At the same time he wished to secure the peace of his monasteries, of which he had founded very many in that region through the generosity of the kings.

After he had visited and enlarged all these places, and after a year and a half had passed since he had been warned a second time of his approaching death, he was staying on the island of Oundle when illness suddenly attacked him. He sensed that his final day had arrived.

After addressing his sons briefly, as far as his strength allowed, and imparting the sacred blessing, he appeared entirely free from distress and came to his end. The monks had already recited the Psalter up to the verse: “Send forth your spirit, and they shall be created” (Psalm 103), and so forth.

He died in the seventy-sixth year of his age and the forty-sixth of his episcopate: a man who, because of his merit in the cause of justice, was exposed to many dangers; who, even in his exiles, was not devoted to idleness but was industrious in founding monasteries and bishoprics; who was exceptionally fitted to win the favor of the rulers among whom he lived in exile, yet because of the rigor of justice was hated by the kings of his own people.

He left as many monasteries as no one else had done, monasteries which he alone had brought together, distributing them among many heirs. His body was carried to Ripon and buried with great reverence.

Thus far Malmesbury.

[Column 0063]

## LETTER OF POPE JOHN VII TO THE BISHOPS OF BRITAIN

[Note: I am uncertain whether this letter, which I present from Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. V, p. 478, belongs to John VII or rather to John VI, since the Englishmen gathered at Rome seem to have been none other than those whom Saint Wilfrid had brought there with him to defend his case. If this conjecture is correct, it should rather be referred to John VI. **MANSI.**]

*(Mansi, Collection of Councils, vol. XII.)* (C, S)

[Column 0063A]

John the bishop to the archbishops, priests, deacons, and all the clergy established throughout the country of the English.

After all the nobles of the English who were then staying at blessed Peter the apostle had assembled, and after appropriate arguments had been presented by both sides, the judgment of the apostolic see prevailed to such an extent that all the English clerics voluntarily, during the very vigils of Saint Gregory, laid aside their secular and flowing dress, as well as their entire secular habit, and put on ankle-length tunics according to Roman custom.

For this reason, since we embrace you in the same way as our own members within the body of our holy Church, we admonish you by apostolic authority to lay aside secular garments and assume clerical vestments according to the custom of the Roman Church.

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 709. SAINT ALDHELM, BISHOP OF SHERBORNE

*(From the edition recently published in London by Doctor J. A. Giles.)*

[Column 0063]

## LIFE OF SAINT ALDHELM, BY FARICIUS

“This work,” says Doctor Giles, “which was published among the *Acta Sanctorum*, I have compared anew with the manuscript preserved in the British Museum (Faust. B. IV). In this manuscript the chapters are shorter than in the printed edition.”

## PROLOGUE

[Column 0063C]

Recalling attentively the pious contests of the holy Fathers, we judge that there were three reasons why their writers, serving the benefit of those who came afterward, committed them with the greatest care to writing.

The first, and more excellent than the others, was that God—who endures in the bodies of the faithful the punishments inflicted on them in any manner for his sake, and who grants strength to those who suffer—might be praised in his majesty.

The second was that the saints, who voluntarily endured so many labors, fasts, vigils, insults, and hardships, whether from themselves or from enemies, might be magnificently celebrated by later worshipers of the true faith.

The third follows so that we, their sluggish and weak successors, by reading or hearing of their most victorious deeds, may raise the eyes of our minds and follow their unharmed footsteps.

Therefore we fragile and ignorant men, who by no means perform the works of monks but merely bear the name unworthily, undertake faithfully, however inadequately, to describe the origin and life, miracles and teaching of the most holy bishop Aldhelm.

Nevertheless, we recount not only the great things which, with the supreme Creator granting them, we ourselves have seen through him, but also those which, by careful investigation, we found recorded on many pages in barbarian languages and in Latin. Some of these records are still attested in our own time by Roman privileges and by grants of various kings, inscribed under the testimony of many bishops and abbots.

We also include what we have often heard from truthful people who live according to the regular monastic order, or from others who practice the Catholic faith according to a different way of life: namely, what was accomplished through the merits of his servant. These people either saw such things with their bodily eyes or repeatedly heard them from their elders, who now rejoice in heavenly joy before the presence of divine mercy.

They said that they had read a volume written in a clear style about his virtues, but that they had lost it during the time of the Danes, when they were still persecuting the Church of Christ. Everything dedicated to our God, whom they did not know, they either trampled underfoot, burned with fire when anger overcame reason, or destroyed in whatever way they could.

Our older Fathers also saw many accounts of his deeds, assigned by the first Fathers to silver plates for the memory of later generations, in a chest made not long after his death, where his blessed bones were kept.

Because this chest had already been almost consumed by negligence and age, a certain bishop, together with other servants of God, transferred the same accounts to another chest for the sake of their preservation and the memory of successors. They can still be seen there.

After the holy man’s original foundations, there were also many devoted lovers of his place, such as Archbishop Dunstan, whose sanctity is beyond doubt, and many other bishops, whose sacred bones rest in the same basilica.

If they had not believed these things to be true on the report of their predecessors, they would certainly not have left them unharmed down to our own memory.

We have deliberately omitted many matters concerning them, and from those that seemed worthy of report we have selected a portion, in accordance with the authority of those who reported them. For the things that we ourselves have often seen in the present provide true credibility for events of the past.

In this matter we see no reason why anyone should accuse us, since we observe that blessed Gregory did the same in his books of the *Dialogues*. And, as he himself reported, Luke the physician—whose praise is in the Gospel throughout all the churches, as the Teacher of the Nations says—and Mark, patriarch of Alexandria and disciple of Peter, did not write what they had seen, but only what they had heard, in the volumes of the Gospels.

Far be it from us to claim that we are in any way equal to them, or that we attempt in our minds to make our informants resemble theirs. Nevertheless, we faithfully believe that what was permitted to our superiors in so great a work was also permitted to us, their lowliest and least capable followers, in this small work, provided that we remain faithful.

We find that many others did the same thing in the divine books and Scriptures. But in this matter we wish, according to our ability, though walking far behind them, to imitate the three whom we mentioned above: Catholics of complete faith, most holy in conduct and action.

## CHAPTER ONE

### The Royal Family, Studies, Monastic Life, and the Office of Abbot
Turning, then, our talent to the genealogy of Saint Aldhelm, let us explain, so far as God has granted us ability, from what lineage he arose. He descended from royal stock, born of illustrious parents and of parents who were unceasingly devoted to the true practice of orthodox religion. In faith he was brighter and in the work of divine worship more precious than they, as the rose is more precious than the thorns from which it springs, and the lily’s flower than the soil from which it rises.

The beginning, so far as royal sublimity is concerned, of this renowned offspring was Ina, the wisest king of the English, radiant in life and character, most vigorous in war [Col. 0065D] and illustrious in virtues. We have often heard, reading through an interpreter from very ancient documents in the English language, that Primatis—an especially distinguished man—had as his second son Kenten, a good man, richly endowed with holiness and magnificent in uprightness. Seeking to fulfill the apostle Paul’s precepts, and fearing God above all with no little virtue, he lived in union with a chaste wife.

He did not enter his wife’s chamber for the purpose of indulging the desire of the flesh, as is customary with some, but so that, like Hannah with Samuel, he might beget a son who, as Scripture teaches, would love the Lord with all the strength of his soul. At last God, looking down from above upon his vows—as it is written concerning the revered parents of the most blessed Nicholas—gave him a son such as the purpose of this little work will show you. At the proper time, according to the custom of the faithful, he devoutly offered the child to God in the church through the hands of priests and asked that he be made a catechumen. Not without divine direction did he give him the name Aldhelm. For *Ald*, they say, means “old” in the barbarous language, and hence *Aldhelm* is as if to say “venerable old man.” Indeed, although young in body, he lived with an old man’s mind and in commendable works.

After this, as the years passed, the boy was weaned and entrusted by his most Christian father to the study of the sacred writings. In this matter God, who knew the future, opened his understanding so greatly that the teacher himself often marveled at the boy, because he grasped so easily and retained so sharply in memory what was shown to him [Col. 0066B] each day. His mind, watered with heavenly dew, was the cause of this; for the grace of God was with him—that grace of the one who said through prophetic speech (Ps. 80:11): “Open your mouth, and I will fill it with my teaching.”

Through mastery of three languages, this most holy man proved skilled not only in ordinary knowledge but also in the learning of letters. In a wondrous manner, by the grace of eloquence, he knew every language and, as though Greek by nationality, pronounced it in writing and speech. This was not astonishing, since the grace of the Holy Spirit had made its dwelling in him, and since the illustrious King Ina, whom we mentioned above, had brought from Athens two teachers thoroughly skilled in that language, to strengthen his literary knowledge.

He was also deeply steeped in the streams of Latin learning, and after Virgil no one used the particular forms of its parts better than he—so it is read in the ancient books of his language. He knew well, in Hebrew letters, the examples of the prophets, David’s psalms, Solomon’s three books, and the Mosaic Law. He also retained in memory and used daily all the instruments of musical art that can be made with strings, pipes, or other varieties of melody. To compress many great matters into a few small words, lest what we say become wearisome and cheap through prolixity: as a man learned in every field, he was filled with knowledge of all things.

But why linger over lesser matters? Let us turn our style toward higher things, so that we may show how this holy man lived from childhood [Col. 0066D], and, insofar as our small talent permits, demonstrate how he lived among men in the monastic habit, imitating Paul and Antony, the first of the hermits.

Having become a monk in the church at Maldon, which the perfect man Eleutherius governed through his own zeal, he lived among the other servants of God in such a way that, although he made use of human company, he was always present in spirit among the citizens of the angels. Transcending the requirements of the Rule, this most religious man conducted his life in the present age according to such a standard that he despised with a most chaste heart all things pleasing to the eye and sweet to the ear, as though they were worthless scraps of hay destined to perish.

He imitated the most righteous Fathers of the Old Testament, following each in a holy virtue of the soul: Abraham, in his revered zeal for hospitality and in perseverance in obedience, which is believed to be the perfection of good works; Jeremiah, dwelling in solitary pits and commendably withdrawing from the sight of men; and Job, a man worthy of praise for supreme virtue, whom he unceasingly followed in the fervor of patience, lest in him—God forbid—what is read somewhere come to pass: “Every virtue is widowed unless strong patience strengthens it.”

In the fervor of charity he imitated David, the typological victor over the warrior Goliath, as Scripture relates, and followed him in overcoming the vice of envy. In the chastity of both substances—body and spirit—he imitated John, the apostle beloved of Christ, whom he had learned to have pleased that same Lord more than others in this devotion also.

But in his purpose of true compassion, whom did this most holy man follow except the very maker of all things, who for the sin of the whole human race tasted the cup of bitter death for a time? We have passed over these matters briefly, not to weary anyone but for edification, because, with the help of the Holy Spirit, we intend to proceed to the narration of many other deeds of the same man.

This man, wholly devoted to Christ, voluntarily imposed upon himself, together with his other practices, a martyrdom by which he might win an immense triumph over the most wicked enemy. Whenever he felt the incitements of burning lust, armed over his whole body with the unconquerable breastplate of faith and crowned with the helmet of righteousness, kindling hope through the fervor of heavenly glory, he imposed such shame upon the spirit that administered carnal wickedness.

He made a virgin, exceedingly beautiful according to the impurity of perishing flesh, lie beside him on his most chaste bed until, with his spirit fixed upon heaven, he had recited the entire Psalter in order. Even then the evil spirit could not resist him in any way. O man worthy of praise beyond measure, who, although he stood at the edge of the burning abyss, felt none of its gaping maw!

He is that honorable tree of which Solomon’s words testify: planted beside streams of water, it put forth an unfailing root for the moisture of the Holy Spirit—namely, the virginity that shared the citizenship of the angels. He did not fear the outward heat inflicted by his enemy, because inwardly he had been fully watered by divine dew.

He is also that magnificent man of whom [Col. 0067D] Scripture says: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful.” Following the divine commandments, he girded his loins with exceptional chastity, holding burning lamps in his hands, ready to enter with the Bridegroom into spiritual and heavenly marriage.

Eleutherius, a bishop commendable in life and character, whom the venerable priest Bede mentions in his *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, considering him worthy of the priestly office, promoted him to that high order, both by personally requesting it and by urging other men of Catholic faith. After the man of God had lived for some time in that office irreproachably, the same bishop deserved to establish him as father of the monks in the aforesaid monastery at Maldon.

Placed over them against his own inclination, whatever he continually taught with powerful eloquence he brought entirely into effect through appropriate action, like a good shepherd, earnestly desiring to return a profit on the talent entrusted to him by God.

At that time the people of the region were perverse in conduct, although subject to our faith. They did not attend church and paid little heed to the authority of priests. This gentle man admonished them in soft words, often unfolding the divine utterances when the occasion permitted, and, having modestly summoned the worldly people to church, enriched them with saving commandments. In this he imitated the Teacher of the Nations, who first gave milk to the inexperienced and afterward fed the strong with solid food.

On one day of the week a very large crowd of merchants from various regions gathered in the same town. This father, an imitator of the apostles, went out to meet them beyond the town and, standing on the bridge, supplied them with divine nourishment for as long as was necessary. By the work of his servant and through the grace of God, some of them left aside for a time the commercial dealings for which they had come and willingly followed him to the holy folds of the saints. Remaining in the church, they reverently listened to the holy offices; afterward, once the business for which they had come had been completed, they returned home, their souls first fattened by the divine service.

## CHAPTER II. His deeds at Rome; the books written by Aldhelm.

While he persevered in such steadfastness of good works, the supreme pontiff of the apostolic see, Sergius, a man of great holiness, had summoned him. Although vast stretches of land, rocky mountains, rugged valleys, and seas separated them, he had often heard of the matters we have mentioned, and of many others that the pen, having lost them from memory, will not record.

As soon as the Saint heard the admonitions of so great a father and of the Roman curia, he set out on his journey, arduous though it was, filled with immense joy because he had obtained the long-desired opportunity to see the thresholds of the princes of the Apostles. Yet he grieved that, even for a time, he was leaving behind so great a company of brothers in bodily distance.

When this most precious man came to Rome, rejoicing in the obedience he had fulfilled—for without obedience it is impossible for anyone’s soul ever to be saved—he was honorably received into conversation by the apostolic man and, as he wished, enjoyed his companionship in all things because of the grace of God dwelling in him. He was adorned by God, to whom he had devoutly given himself, with a benefit unheard of in our times, so that he might be revered still more by so great a pontiff and by all the people.

This commendable man carried priestly vestments with him wherever he went, in order to fulfill the duties entrusted to him. When he had put them on in the Lateran presbytery to offer the sacraments, the following miracle was displayed before everyone. After he had rightly and devoutly completed the office of the Mass, and while he was handing the chasuble to his ministers, the power of the divine majesty, unquestionably present there, caused it to hang so firmly and steadily from a ray of sunlight as though it were supported by some solid material. It is still preserved in the church at Maldon with the great reverence due to holiness.

O truly new prodigy of the great Elijah! Before his disciple’s eyes, a fiery chariot raised Elijah to heaven; before the astonished eyes of many, a ray of sunlight served this man in the city of Rome. Elijah was carried by bright light into a distant region of heaven; this priest’s vestments hung upon a similar element.

But far be it from us to equate him with holy Elijah! That magnificent prophet still lives, so that he may fight against the son of iniquity; indeed, by dying and rising again he will precede the divine judgment. This holy confessor, however, rejoices most happily before God’s tribunal in the reward he has received, where by his piety he intercedes for all the faithful. Nevertheless, although their merits are unequal, if it is permissible to speak the truth, both were greatly pleasing to God.

After the holy man had remained for a long time with the aforementioned pope, the Spirit of God prompted the pope to ask him to baptize a certain child. The identity of the child’s father was sufficiently doubtful among the people, without any evident cause, because, as is customary among nearly all nations, the rumor-loving populace thought that the apostolic man had fathered him.

The ignorant people falsely held this opinion of so great a bishop, for by the merit of his life the apostolic man is declared to be an apostolic man in his own records and in other passages of Scripture. Obeying this father’s wishes, Saint Aldhelm, after the child had been catechized in the church according to the custom of the faithful—he was said to have been only nine days old—commanded him, before the assembled crowds, to declare whether the man commonly named was his father.

Immediately the infant, although extremely young, removing by an unnatural power the obstructions of his tongue, did what that most holy abbot had commanded. By speech divinely granted to him, and sufficiently intelligible, he showed everyone that he had not been begotten by the man whom the foolish populace falsely named.

This is not at all astonishing, since it lacks novelty: the same one who made the dumbness of an ass skilled in human speech made this infant’s tongue learned in response to the command of the most religious man. O man worthy of great praise, filled with surpassing holiness! By employing such prudent discernment, he both freed the father from a sin unknown to him and revealed to the people of so great a city what sort of merit he possessed before God.

This man, supremely learned in literary knowledge and among the foremost in learning, was one day entering the church of the Apostles in the queen of cities. In praise of them he composed these memorable verses:

> [Here, etc. See Poem X below.]

Having Aldhelm, the model of monks, kindly enjoyed the companionship of so great a man, the ruler of the highest see, and having been well instructed through their conversation with one another, as is customary among the holy Fathers, he decided to return home and resume his former purpose.

Then he asked the holy pope for the sacred gifts written below, for the benefit of his successors, so that they might celebrate the due services of God without disturbance. He did not ask for weights of gold, silver, or any metal, since, secure about the morrow, he sought help from no one but God.

He therefore requested an edict sanctioned by the authority of the Supreme Father, by which the monasteries he governed with attentive care by God’s favor—namely, Maldon, where he had been enthroned, founded by Maldon of holy memory, from whose stock this saint descended, and another monastery subject to it, founded in honor of Saint John beside the river called From—would be made free from every secular service, from episcopal sees, from ecclesiastical order, commands, and synods.

If at any time they needed someone in any ecclesiastical order, or even a priest, they were to have him ordained by whomever they wished, provided that the bishop was Catholic. If a religious abbot should die and the election of another became necessary, the man whom the religious congregation of God’s servants chose by common agreement was to be promoted immediately.

For even then the ambition of monks had begun to take root: already the hireling sought to enter not through the door as a shepherd, but from elsewhere as a thief. Therefore this steward of divine things requested these provisions.

Yet all these things seem to have been changed through the vices of the inhabitants and the ambition of certain people. For, religion having been almost reduced to nothing, and the exhortations of the Apostles contained in that very privilege having been despised, not only in that place but also in many places throughout England, those who served dishonesty and shameful profits lost, by the just judgment of God, their freedom and the freedom of their possessions.

For, as the apostolic man himself says in the context of his prayer, such freedom is owed and granted to holy men endowed with every uprightness. If so great an opportunity for freedom were granted to those who served their own will and thirsted after earthly advantages, the beauty of life and the appearance of holiness would be seriously disfigured.

The saint brought these written grants of freedom to the aforesaid monasteries and showed them to the two kings then ruling in England: namely, to his uncle Ina, king of the Saxons, and to Ethelred, king of the Mercians. These most vigorous kings, filled with zeal for God, also confirmed them by their authority, since they recognized that they had been secured by the uncorrupted authority of the Apostolic See.

They decreed that, whatever disturbance of expedition or war might arise between neighboring peoples, the places belonging to the aforesaid Father, revered for his holiness and knowledge, should be free from every service. They also left written instructions, impressed by their own hands, that their successors should likewise preserve these rights.

But an opportunity for disregarding them arose. Since they did not find the decrees of such great Fathers marked with wax seals, they lost them, claiming that they were not to be observed—as though the impression of perishable wax had greater probative force than an institution established by apostolic or royal law and deserving to be preserved.

For at that time the cunning of certain men, carried across the sea in Liburnian ships, had not yet arrived, nor had avarice, though destined to pass throughout the world, yet raged so fiercely. The integrity of faith still reigned in the minds of many; human greed had not yet, to such an extent, devoted itself to itself rather than to God.

After some time had passed, while the holy man enjoyed both temporal peace and the consolation of angels in the church at Maldon, Osred being king of the English, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 706, certain bishops of the Britons were heretically disputing, at least in name, about the date of Easter and many other institutions of ecclesiastical orthodoxy.

Therefore the holy synod of the eastern region of the Saxons asked the venerable abbot Aldhelm—still only a priest, for he had not yet been placed among the bishops in holiness of life and character—to compose an excellent book by which the wicked heresy of the Britons, then flourishing beyond measure, might be destroyed.

The Saint, being polished in speech, rich in wisdom, distinguished in holiness, full of arguments and equipped with syllogisms, exceptionally learned in the liberal arts and in ecclesiastical authorities, and, as Bede relates, prudent in all things, filled with the teachings of the Israelites and with those of the Egyptians, sent the work to the aforesaid heretics through certain members of his household, faithful servants sufficiently suited to this task. He also drew upon many inventions, authentic traditions of the holy Fathers, the poem delivered by angels to Abbot Pachomius, and the clearly expressed teaching of other religious men.

He himself, alone and afflicted, prayed continually that God would deign to free their minds from the entanglement of so great a heresy. In this way he recalled both the bishops and an innumerable multitude of the people to the rule of the true faith of the Lord.

Here we can contemplate the great merciful kindness of almighty God, who fully justifies his saints wherever, whenever, and however he wishes, so that through them—even when absent in body—he may perform such remarkable works of virtue.

This holy man had certainly not traveled there on foot; rather, through an excellent handbook he admonished them and, through diligent prayer, strengthened them, leading them back to the path of truth. Filled with the grace of God, he clearly imitated the Apostle in this deed also: through his Epistles the Apostle recalled the Corinthians, Galatians, and Colossians, who had been misled by false apostles, to the state of true faith.

In this matter too the apostle and father Aldhelm proved himself an apostle, because, just as Peter and the others, prompted by the Holy Spirit, set Paul and Barnabas apart for the work of God, so the holy synod advanced this man to the aforesaid task by choosing him.

He therefore wrote the *Enigmas*, and composed an outstanding book *On the Praise of Virgins* in a twofold work, in prose and in verse. He also composed a sevenfold little book, woven from flowers of the New and Old Testaments and from the Sevenfold Calculation, drawn from the disciplines of the philosophers and relating to the sevenfold gift of the Holy Spirit.

He also wrote one volume *On the Admonition of Fraternal Charity*. He composed another on the nature of insensible things, which are represented as speaking metaphorically. He wrote on the rules of feet, metaplasm, synaloepha, the scanning of verses, and the omission of syllables; on the metrical alternation of question and answer, distinguished by two letters.

He wrote several other works as well, being learned in every field—for he was polished in speech and, as we have said, remarkably learned in the Scriptures, both liberal and ecclesiastical. We have considered it worthwhile to place these matters in the volume of this little work, taken from a very ancient codex discovered in the library of the same church.

## CHAPTER III. Miracles performed; the episcopate; death and burial.

While the most holy man was building a certain monastery at Maldon in honor of the Mother of God, a marvelous deed, performed by the Virgin-born Son, was revealed for his praise, for the honor of his Mother, and for the man’s renown.

When great beams of various kinds were being raised by machines to the lofty heights of this temple, one of them was found by the axe-men to be too small, although the workmen had carefully cut it to match the length of the others. Almighty God shortened it because it pleased him to do so, in order also through this event to make his servant’s merit known to men.

The craftsmen were exceedingly distressed, because this beam was supposed to take second place in the construction, and, uncertain what to do, they hurried to the counsel of this holy Father. Although he was inwardly anxious, he addressed them kindly, trusting in God’s mercy:

> “Come, brothers. If it has been measured against the dimensions of the other beams, learn from this and devoutly trust in the help of the blessed Mother of God. She who, though a virgin, nourished the God-man with milk can easily fulfill our desire in this labor.”

Then he boldly went to the timber and urged the people to pull the beam upward with all their strength, without hesitating over its length. Immediately the people, supported by the help of so great a Father and calling upon the Lord with devout hearts, raised the beam as the Father had commanded.

Then, by divine mercy cooperating for the service of his servant, they supported it, and it was now longer than the others, to whose measure it had previously been cut.

In this deed he imitated blessed Donatus, bishop of the city of Reate, who restored by prayer alone a glass cup shattered by the violence of pagans; and also our father Benedict, an abbot and a man of wondrous holiness, who, while certain brothers were striving to establish a monastery, by devout prayer removed a massive stone from the place.

In the same way the Creator of things lengthened this beam, though the type was different, as he caused the rod of the bishop of the Israelite people to bud and bear fruit. The former prefigured the birth of the untouched Virgin; this one plainly foretold to the assembled church the immense growth of the holiness of so great a man. The former bore fruit and leaves; this one showed what the future works of Father Aldhelm would be.

For now, let this suffice concerning that matter, since my mind desires to pass on to other deeds of the same man.

After not much time had passed, Father Berthwald, archbishop of Canterbury, a man reverend in life and character and highly learned in literary and ecclesiastical knowledge, desired, because of the greatness of this man’s holiness and virtues and because of his study and knowledge of liberal and divine letters, to have him frequently with him if he could. He sent envoys asking him to come for consultation about ecclesiastical affairs.

The Saint, being gentle, willingly obeyed him, came to him, and stayed as long as he wished. When he had properly completed the business for which he had come, he decided to go to the fortress of Canterbury. God arranged this so that the merits of this saint’s virtues might be revealed even in distant parts of the world.

As he was traveling on horseback beside the harbor, seated near the road, some merchants wished to bring a ship to the seashore. But they could not do so until this remarkable man gave the command, although they attempted it three times with a great exertion of strength.

Beforehand, however, he courteously asked whether they were carrying anything useful for the daily needs of the church. They despised him in the manner of the proud because he was clothed in a cheap covering, and they did not even deign to look at him.

But God, for whose love he had made himself so lowly in dress, exalted him in their presence, as he always exalts his own. After they had repeatedly made many futile efforts, they stood sad and fearful, their strength exhausted in vain.

Then one of the sailors addressed his companions through tears:

> “I hope and firmly believe that the man whom you see on the shore is a most Christian man. In our pride we did not even speak a word to him. Thus our pride is blunted by his humility, and our stubbornness is crushed by his goodness. I do not know what we should now do except to implore his mercy with pure hearts, so that God, appeased by his devout prayers, may grant us the harbor and the shore.”

They immediately took counsel and humbly begged the holy man, with troubled hearts, not to delay coming to them and helping them by his prayers, and not to refuse to inspect their small boat and, if he found anything useful, to accept it in the exercise of his office.

The servant of God, not enticed by the gift they promised but compelled by charity to help them, went aboard the little skiff and immediately approached them without disdain. As soon as that holy man placed the weight of his body upon the boat, the sea, previously disturbed, presented itself as calm for sailing.

Thus the company of sailors entered the harbor with joy, praising God in his servant.

They immediately offered the saint a volume bound together from the Old and New Testaments. The saint did not reject the offering, but gave them greater gifts from his own possessions, although they were unwilling to accept them, so that—God forbid—anyone might understand that he had acted for payment, because of the great devotion they had shown him.

When they saw this, they fell at his feet and asked him to commend them to God in his prayers. O man filled with charity and full of piety! Following in the footsteps of blessed Nicholas, he both delivered sailors from danger and declared to foreigners what God continued to accomplish through his faithful servants living in the flesh.

He brought the book, acquired through an act of goodness, to the monastery at Maldon. The brothers still preserve it there, in due reverence for so great a man. At its beginning we saw an anathema written forbidding anyone to remove it from that place.

Thus this man, filled with God, lived as an outstanding abbot in that place until, through the laying on of Berthwald’s hands, he was canonically advanced to the office of bishop. This took place in the following manner and for the following reason.

In the time of Osred, the illustrious king of the English, Hedda, a most holy bishop whose commendable life the venerable priest Bede recounts in his *Ecclesiastical History*, died and departed to heavenly glory.

Because his diocese was too extensive to be governed by one man, it was divided in two by the counsel of the ecclesiastical fathers and the kings. One part was governed by Daniel, a man vigorous in many respects. To govern the other diocese, the primates, clergy, and a great multitude of the people, agreeing as though with one voice and following the ancient commandments of the canons, chose this holy man Aldhelm.

What contributed most strongly to his election was that he refused when called and resisted as much as he could when drawn forward. This father, beloved of God, was neither drawn by ambition nor ultimately withdrawn by disobedience; in both matters he preserved moderation without abandoning any goodness.

In him was fulfilled what the Apostle of the Gentiles had said to Timothy in his Epistle: “It is necessary that a bishop be irreproachable” (1 Tim. 3:2). In that one command given by the Apostle all the subsequent requirements are contained, although they are not individually named for purposes of explanation.

As Saint Gregory says of good prelates, just as this man presided at the summit of honor, so he surpassed his subjects in the breadth of every virtue. Whatever he preached with his mouth, he first demonstrated by his deeds, without the swelling of pride.

After he had governed the episcopate with the greatest vigor for four years, he wished to place fathers over the monasteries that, through God’s merciful providence, he had governed before receiving that office. But the devout multitude of the congregations, living happily under their devout father, refused, while he lived, to have any patron other than him.

Then the holy man, considering their most kindly wish and fearing, by appointing another, to disturb the stability of the order, remained their abbot as he had been before. With King Ina’s consent and his fellow bishop Daniel’s testimony, he enacted a privilege with an anathema, forbidding anyone of ecclesiastical dignity or exalted secular power to appoint an abbot other than the one chosen by the devout assembly of the brothers.

He later deposited this privilege, which he himself had caused to be approved by the synod of all England, in the library of the church at Maldon. It remains there to this day.
