Yet, as was said above, because sins impeded it and the sluggishness of prelates prevailed, it is known to have been rendered ineffective for us for a time.

In truth, hindered by secular affairs in the episcopate, he was afterward not so powerful in virtues as he had previously been, as is customary with all men—just as it is written concerning blessed Martin, bishop of Tours. Nevertheless, he is rightly called most holy, although he did not abound in his customary virtues, since whoever devoutly fulfills in all things the office entrusted to him by the Lord is holy. This the most righteous father did.

Having related these matters, let us now turn to his glorious death.

After completing four years in the episcopate, weighed down by bodily illness, he summoned the flock of monks, the Catholic clergy, and nearly the entire people. Preaching the unity of peace and the bond of charity, without which no Church is pleasing to God, he commended his sheep to the Lord like a good shepherd.

Afterward he asked those close to him and faithful members of his household that his little body be buried in the monastery at Maldon, which he had loved above all others. Having thus made a prayer worthy of God and armed with the divine sacraments, he departed gloriously from the world. Michael received him with the company of angels [Col. 0075A].

He died in the village of Dunting, to which he had gone for the salvation of those whom he governed under God’s protection, visiting his diocese like a devoted shepherd. At first the two congregations of the faithful began a modest dispute among themselves over which should carry the body of so great a patron to burial.

But that side prevailed whose claim rested upon the fact that he himself had commanded that he be carried there for burial. In that same village, at the very place where he had ended his life, a wooden chapel had been built. After his death, a religious monk from Glastonbury constructed there, from cut stone, a small oratory.

When he caused it to be dedicated in the saint’s honor, an old woman who had long been deprived of the light of her own eyes received her sight and began to see like a young woman.

At that time Saint Egwin, bishop of the Church of Worcester, himself a man highly approved in learning and conduct, was traveling to Rome for the sake of prayer, bound with the chain of fetters. Divinely instructed, as one may rightly believe, by a voice, he came as a bishop to Maldon to render the due service to the dead pontiff.

When the latter had been buried as was fitting, that most holy bishop completed the journey he had begun, and at Rome the binding of his chains was loosed by divine power, as is related in the book of his Life.

This man, exalted upon the heavenly throne as the advocate before God of all who invoke him, governs by continual prayers the flock of the aforesaid place, which is devoutly subject to him. Through him many benefits are bestowed there, to the praise of him to whom are honor and glory throughout infinite ages of ages. [Col. 0075C] Amen.

## CHAPTER IV. The body of Saint Aldhelm raised and placed by Saint Dunstan in a stone tomb; the Danish persecution; miracles performed.

Having now briefly, though in rustic fashion and not without fidelity to the facts, passed over the life of the most holy Father Aldhelm, illustrious confessor and orthodox bishop, according to the smallness of our talent, let us turn to the miracles that the Lord deigned to perform through him in the same monastery after his death.

He was buried in the church of Saint Michael the Archangel, adjoining the church that the father had built, and lay there until the time of Edwy, brother of King Edgar. Before Edgar, Edwy had wandered through every byway in the slothfulness of his youth, enjoying the counsel of no upright man. By dissipating the kingdom, he divided it and distributed the goods of the churches to internal plunderers.

He also removed religious monastics of both sexes from the Lord’s folds and installed in the church clerics of both kinds who were wanton, devoted to the enticements of gluttony, and greedily pursuing the profits of avarice—not men who cherished canonical conduct for its adornment, but men who shamefully and brazenly desired secular ambitions.

Yet almighty God took pity on the monastery at Maldon. He did not wish his lamp to remain hidden for long under a bushel, but wished it to be raised upon a lampstand so that it might shine for everyone. Through the clerics then living there, who were unlike those mentioned above, he caused so great a treasure—namely, the body of that man, adorned with such great virtues—to be raised from the sarcophagus and honorably placed in a silver reliquary.

There, too, certain of his deeds—those concerning the book, the beam, the boy, and the chasuble—still appear engraved on gilded plates.

The most holy bones of that man rested in the aforementioned bier for some time, until Saint Dunstan, by the favor of divine mercy, assumed the archiepiscopal mitre of Canterbury, and the savagery of the Danes began to rage against the English. When he heard of the works of so great a man and observed his frequent miracles, he began to cherish that monastery above all the others, except his own, in which he had been enthroned. He placed there many things suitable for ecclesiastical service from his own possessions, several of which are still preserved in the monastery to this day. Among them, his anathemas are also seen inscribed in verse, lest anyone should dare to remove them to the detriment of the Church. On the organs, which the archbishop had given in honor of so great a father, these verses were written in bronze letters:

> Dunstan, archbishop, gives these organs to holy Aldhelm;  
> May he lose his eternal kingdom who wishes to remove them from here.

On the small water-vessel which the archbishop had ordered to be made so that it might pour water for the ministers of the altar, we saw these verses written:

> This small vessel for pouring water Dunstan, the archbishop, had made,  
> So that it might serve holy Aldhelm in the temple.

On the little bell, which, gilded, hangs above the principal table in the refectory, we saw this stamped in gold figures:

> May he never reach the heavenly hall of Elysium  
> Who carries this bell away from the seat of blessed Aldhelm.

There were also other objects there, which had been purchased by blessed Dunstan for forty pounds. He gave many other things as well, but we leave them untouched for this reason: lest they produce weariness in those who hear of them.

Later, during the time of this revered bishop, the treacherous nation of the Danes, still ignorant of the true God, invaded the island of Britain with a multitude of fleets. The English people, greatly terrified by their ferocity, as frightened people are accustomed to do, continually offered hymnody to the most holy Trinity with devout mind, asking that those whom He had redeemed and who persevered in the Catholic faith might be saved from the barbarians’ excessive cruelty, and that He might preserve immovable in their places the blessed bodies of the saints. Through their prayers, the faithful people, subject to His authority, might be aided and escape the burden of the calamity inflicted by their savage enemies.

Then the aforementioned bishop, recognizing the perversity of the wicked enemies and considering their filthy greed for precious metal, feared that, enticed by love of the gold or silver present in the bier, they might touch the relics of so great a father with polluted hands and, after handling them disgracefully, leave them in a worse condition—or, God forbid, if they carried off the church’s ornaments, might throw such a treasure away somewhere. He therefore reverently removed the most holy body from the bier and placed it in a stone tomb, wrapped in silken cloths.

He performed this translation—or, more truly, this faithful concealment of the holy body—on 5 May, as many Martyrologies testify. Nevertheless, God, protector of the faithful, brought a reproach upon this sinful nation through the merit of His servant, blessed Aldhelm. When the army of the wicked was ranging here and there throughout the whole of England, it finally reached the monastery at Malmesbury, where it had heard that the native people, trusting in the protection of so great a bishop, had brought together a large quantity of gold.

Like a roaring lion ranging through the desert and fearing no beast’s attack, blinded by the heat of hunger and seeking only what it might devour, it burst into the church and madly advanced as far as the Holy of Holies. As soon as one of them, having learned the secret, wished to pull precious stones from the bier, he immediately lost his sight through divine vengeance and fell to the pavement.

Then the other maddened enemies, although unwillingly, left behind everything that was in the monastery—except what the wandering populace had already taken in the workshops—and eagerly fled along the road. Thus God freed that place from the rage of the plunderers through the prayer of His servant. For this saint stands in great favor with God, and, as we have said, rescued the people dear to him from fear of so great a danger.

Let us therefore also entreat him with pure heart and submissive voices, so that through his prayers he may render us, unworthy in life and character, cleansed from sins and exalted in mind before God, worthy that after this life we may enjoy heavenly things with him, seeing the One who was born seated at the right hand of the Father. To Him be power, honor, and glory with the Holy Spirit throughout endless ages.

[Col. 0077C]

After these events, the Danish host—hateful to God because of the enormity of its crimes and its abandonment of the Christian faith—after various turns of war in different places, after the destruction of castles and the overthrow of many cities, while the entire region everywhere had been devastated beyond measure, held the kingdom for a time under its perverse rule, God permitting it.

As a result, the worshipers of orthodoxy were exhausted, afflicted by poverty of resources and by many bodily tribulations. Churches were no longer frequented by the customary gatherings of the faithful, nor did companies of faithful monks or nuns take part in the nocturnal or daily synaxes. It therefore happened that the body of the saint remained for a long time in the tomb where it had been placed by Saint Dunstan, a bishop renowned for his accumulation of virtues. Although it lay hidden beneath a lowly covering, almighty God adorned it with great powers.

Often, and at different times, he freed many men and women afflicted with various illnesses. These, when opportunity allows and their memory grows, will be described individually and more systematically in their proper places: namely, those things that God performed through him after the savagery of the Danes had been destroyed by preachers and after their hated audacity had been overcome by warriors.

The memory of antiquity preserved none of these things, even though the deeds he performed while the Danes’ perfidy still survived were great. For at that time there was a great scarcity of good men and, because sins demanded it, an innumerable abundance of wicked ones. The same thing happened to many martyrs and even to certain disciples whom the supreme Shepherd and Lord sent ahead through the cities before the arrival of His preaching, because the heat of so great a persecution had burst upon them, and none of them had been able to commit the subsequent course of their deeds to writing.

Nevertheless, their merit before God and their authority among human beings are no less, because people frequently see the far from insignificant deeds that God deigns to display through them. For these reasons, what was not previously written is retained in faithful hearts and transmitted without uncertainty.

Since we must now come to the deeds of this saint—certainly no less significant than those mentioned above—even though they were revealed by God only after the passage of many years, let what has been said here for the present suffice.

Long afterward, when the most savage kings of the Danes and Norwegians had devastated Britain, they carried away, as barbarian enemies customarily do, some of the more beautiful young women. Among them was a certain very noble woman named Helphildis. While she was being led away captive, she greatly pleased one of the leading men because of her beauty. He abandoned the lawful marriage he had previously contracted according to the custom of his people and, while perhaps using her as a concubine, died when death overtook him.

She, deprived of his protection, remained amid foreigners. The Danish archimandrite, wishing to accomplish what follows—for he had no children, although his wife was still alive—entered her chamber for one night only and fathered a son.

When this became known, the king was moved by pity, since she was a foreigner, and was attracted by the affection for the child he had begotten in her. Wishing to preserve her and provide her with necessities, but cautiously fearing his wife’s anger, he entrusted her to a certain God-fearing bishop. The bishop, desiring to receive a reward from the Lord and wishing to retain his lord’s goodwill, had her generously guarded until the child was weaned.

When the infant had been weaned, that king died. She, however, taking her son by night, sought a hiding-place in flight, fearing the danger of encountering the queen, who was still alive.

After seven years had passed, many heard that she was living not far away in a distant region. The Danes then sent for her, so that she might bring back her son and he might enjoy his father’s throne. This was done. Yet that young king, after a year and a half at the summit of power, died from this life.

Then Helphildis, seeing herself bereft through the death of her child, and turning over in her heart both the misery of the past and the great distress of the future, resolved, if she could, to return to her homeland. There, through the merits of the saints dear to God, she might already regard earthly things as nothing and acquire heavenly glory.

She therefore came to her native soil, Britain, and purchased the grant of three villages from the revenue that she had brought with her. She lived for a very long time in the quiet of this peace, continually maintaining the fear of God and reverence for the saints in the secret of her heart.

Nevertheless, struck by a divine scourge—the sort by which He sometimes knows how to afflict His servants so that they may advance toward better things, as with the most patient Job, whom He wished to set before later generations as an example, so that each person might recognize what he himself was—she suffered for three years from paralysis, the weakening of the limbs that is called *paralysis* in Greek.

She said that the beginning of this affliction had happened to her in the following way. Before returning from Denmark, she had vowed that she would never eat food of flesh, and she had kept this vow unblemished for a long time. Later, however, at the earnest urging of certain priests of good conduct, when several of them were dining with her, she reluctantly yielded to their requests that she taste it just once. Immediately divine vengeance struck her with the aforementioned sting of paralysis.

In a wondrous manner, almighty God binds people who sin with different intentions of mind under different penalties, and in all His deeds shows Himself to be a just judge and a merciful Lord. Ananias and Sapphira, because they fell through the envious intention of their hearts, He did not delay striking with an irrevocable sentence. But because she sinned unwillingly and under a certain appearance of charity, He wished to correct her for a time.

By these examples everyone ought to take care either not to vow or, after making a vow, to fulfill what was promised, and not afterward to break what one offered to God, whatever the intention and difficulty involved.

Thus, clothed in the habit of a nun, she had herself carried about in a cart by her attendants to the shrines of the saints, so that through their holy intercession her deadened limbs might revive. Yet it was not because almighty God, who always glorifies His own, rejected the prayer of His faithful; rather, He mercifully kept her in danger from her illness for so long so that, by repeatedly displaying miracles, He might make the fame of His servant Aldhelm more exalted, until she came to the monastery at Malmesbury as she had determined.

Finally, when she lay there on the vigil of this saint’s feast, awaiting God’s consolation through the merit of His servant with devout mind, prostrate because she could not stand, and when the devout company of monks, after the solemn Matins, was singing according to custom a hymn in honor of Saint Mary, Mother of our Redeemer, she was immediately touched by a divine medicine. She felt her previously withered limbs revive, rose up quickly in good health, and reached without a guide the place where the most holy body had been.

From that very day she gave to his healing church whatever she was able to possess, and there, having died in the flesh, she rested in peace.

## Chapter V. A Possessed Man, a Cripple, and a Blind Man Healed. The Revelation of the Body

[Col. 0079D]

Afterward, when they were celebrating the sacred vigils there on the night of the Ascension of the Lord, a highly remarkable event occurred.

A certain peasant of that parish had been seized by a demon, because his sins demanded it. His relatives, seeing him driven by madness, spitting blasphemies against God and His faithful from his foaming mouth, and seizing stones, fire, weapons—in short, whatever his insane fury supplied—against them and their neighbors, bound him with iron chains. Under careful supervision, insofar as their lack of refinement allowed, they kept him in this condition for some time, day and night.

Then, after taking counsel with those whom they knew to be wiser, they hastened to lead him, still bound, around to the places where they had heard that the bodies of certain saints rested. But the Creator of all things, who daily according to His custom exalts the humble and casts down the proudly swollen, reserved this glory for His servant, the most humble Father Aldhelm.

When they came with the madman to his monastery at Malmesbury, they addressed the monks living there in brotherly charity with humble speech, asking them to pray for God’s mercy, so that through the merit of His servant Aldhelm He might display His customary miracles upon this possessed man.

The monks gave them this salutary answer:

> “Today is the vigil of the Ascension of the Redeemer of all, on which He carried into heaven the flesh received from the undefiled Virgin and glorified through the suffering of death. There God and man, one Christ, seated at the right hand of God, judges and heals the illnesses of souls and bodies. Therefore, dearest brothers, remain overnight in the church, celebrate the sacred vigils with attentive heart, and believe without hesitation that the One who exalted him so greatly as to make him rejoice with Him in heaven will Himself, through him, display what you seek.”

While they stood before the icon of our Redeemer for the nocturnal office, divine mercy touched the sick man for the merit of His servant. He expelled the possessor of His own workmanship with the fitting disgrace due to him, restoring the sick man to health as though no affliction from that foul guest had ever touched him.

When this was seen, all who were present, together with those who had arrived upon hearing the joyful cries, praised the mighty works of the eternal King with the devotion of their hearts and the sound of their voices, while the bells rang.

At another time a certain sick man, whose feet and hips were joined to his legs, could scarcely cover the little distance he had to travel by crawling along the ground with his hands. At last, exhausted by continual effort, he carefully pondered within himself whom he should ask for God’s mercy and whose saintly assistance he should seek.

Finally, as the report spread throughout the entire province, he learned that in an oratory called in English *Christ’s Church* almighty God was performing His customary wonders: namely, that, as the merciful restorer of the human race, He was granting countless healings to those oppressed by the burden of various illnesses.

He therefore began somehow to direct his steps there, almost without leaving a trace, so that, just as he had possessed faith, he might become a participant in health. After several days had passed, although the journey was short, he scarcely reached the monastery at Malmesbury, since it lay along his route.

As soon as the same old man entered the monastery, he felt that some remedy, as it were a gentle easing, was present within him against the torpor of his limbs. He therefore spent the night there, intending to depart the next morning, which his purpose compelled him to do—unless God, through the merit of His holy confessor, deigned to offer him the assistance of His mercy.

It was Saturday at Vespers and within the octave of the aforementioned Father’s feast. When morning had come, the heat of the sun had grown strong, and the congregation of the brothers had sung the first hour of the day in the place where they were staying, the procession was being prepared to enter the choir. The sick man came with the others who wished to proceed, following as best he could.

There he lay in prayer for so long that the congregation of the brothers completed its customary passage through the cloister and the workshops and returned from where it had gone. While the company of monks was singing and a multitude of laypeople stood by, divine mercy immediately touched the cripple. Struck with great astonishment and almost beside himself, he leapt up healthy from the place where he had been lying, as though he had never felt any impairment of his body, and ran to the tomb of the most holy body, so that he might offer God whatever thanks he could through His servant.

When this was seen, all who were present praised the mighty works of almighty God, who had done such things through the prayer of His saint.

The man who had thus obtained the remedy of health remained in that monastery for many years in praise of the same saint. Many still live there in monastic habit who knew him well both before and afterward. Through their testimony we have written these things about him, to the glory of our Redeemer and the laudable memory of His saint.

Among the many other revered deeds that almighty God revealed through the merits of His servant, a miracle remarkable to relate was displayed there, as follows.

In the time of William I, the most vigorous king of the English, while Abbot Warinus governed the same church with regular discipline, a certain fisherman lived on an island called in English *Wichland*. Compelled by the poverty of his needs, he labored every day by fishing the waters, repeatedly exposing himself to the dangers of the sea and seeking his livelihood by hand and skill.

One day, while he was wandering upon the sea, a fog suddenly rushed in from the opposite direction. On that occasion he lost the sight of his eyes, perhaps because his sins demanded such a punishment. After wandering for a long time through the trackless waters, tossed here and there by the alternating waves, he was finally assisted by his companions, who were in other small boats, and reached the shore. Relying on the help of a guide, he returned to his accustomed little lodging.

Then the report of this blindness flew here and there through the province. A crowd of friends, whose ears it had reached, hastened to visit him and asked how this unexpected misfortune of blindness had happened to him. Beginning in a mournful voice, he declared everything that had happened to him in order.

Afterward he began to ask them what he should do and with which saint they hoped he might find mercy. The sorrowful gathering of his relatives is said to have answered him:

> “Brother, we know no better counsel to give you in this matter than that you hasten as quickly as possible to the threshold of Christ’s Church in the western region, where divine miracles frequently occur. For, as popular report says, there the various kinds of illness are driven away. In that place, implore almighty God’s mercy with devout prayers, earnestly promise satisfaction for your past sins, and redeem your evil deeds through whatever almsgiving you can offer, until the abundant mercy of divine power restores you safe and sound to your former health.”

Often encouraged by these words from his friends—although they were peasants, they were wise—he went to the monastery where various disabled people had gathered. He remained there for three years, suffering from his illness.

But the merciful and compassionate Father, who accomplishes whatever He wills in an instant, did not wish to fulfill his desire during so long a period, working mercifully within him. Since He knew what would happen and for whom He was reserving the glory of His praise, by delaying in this way He was first making the gift of health arise from misfortune.

At last, one night, as he lay prostrate on his bed, he was warned in a dream that he should direct his steps to the church at Malmesbury, where the body of His servant Aldhelm rested. There, with God’s help and at the insistence of His saint’s prayer, he would recover the sight he had lost for so long.

After this revelation, forewarned by God, he was brought on the following day to the church at Malmesbury, with a companion leading him. There for seven consecutive days he entreated God’s mercy through vigils and prayers, together with the intercession of His saints, asking that He who had come to save sinners might deign to restore him to the condition of his former sight. In the meantime he was sustained by the alms of the brothers, for he so earnestly desired the Lord’s grace.

On the seventh Sunday, when our Redeemer wished to grant him mercy and also to make known the fame of His faithful servant in this matter—for that saying is true: “If you ask anything of the Father in my name, it will be done for you” [John 14:13]—he recovered, through the prayers of this saint and the intercession of the other saints resting there, the sight that he had lost.

On Sunday, while the monks were proceeding through the monastery cloisters to the procession according to custom and had returned singing to the entrance of the church, he lay in prayer in the middle of the church before the crucifix. Then so great a grace of the Holy Spirit descended upon him that, while everyone watched, blood flowed drop by drop from his eyes. As scales fell away, he cried out that he could now see.

Immediately rising, he who previously could not walk without a guide hastened alone to the saint’s tomb. After lying there for a long time, weeping for joy, he finally rose and returned to the place from which he had come.

All who were present, seeing these things, devoutly offered praises to God, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0082D]

Earlier in the course of this narrative we reported that, because of the treachery of the Danes, the most sacred bones of our Father Aldhelm had been honorably placed by the revered bishop Dunstan of Canterbury beneath a marble tomb, in silken coverings and wooden cases. We now wish to relate how much time elapsed between the deaths of the two bishops, how long the bones lay after Dunstan’s death, and how and by whom they were raised.

This man had been appointed abbot at Malmesbury, in the church of the apostles Peter and Paul, by blessed Eleutherius, the fourth bishop of the Saxons, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation approximately 666. He became bishop in the year 705 from the birth in the flesh into the world of the same true Savior, under Blithwald, successor to Theodore and archbishop of Canterbury, a man powerful in ecclesiastical matters and greatly endowed with honorable character.

He died in the year 709. According to this reckoning, the two offices were joined for forty-three years, four of which he lived irreproachably as bishop, as stated above. During the remaining years he was master in the order of abbot—not of one abbey only, but of many.

The death of this archbishop of Christ, Dunstan, came 279 years after Aldhelm’s. His revered relics rested in the place where they had been deposited by Dunstan for ninety-two years after the death of that archbishop. At last, we saw them raised in the following manner.

The abbot Warinus presided over the same monastery. He was learned in many matters and endowed with the teaching of monastic religion. He governed the flock entrusted to him, a flock distinguished in life and conduct, according to monastic traditions.

Being somewhat uncertain about the most holy body, he ordered the faithful congregation to observe a three-day fast, to sing psalms devoutly at the appropriate places, and to humble themselves in every way before the sight of divine mercy, so that through almighty God’s mercy they might discover the relics of so great a bishop.

The religious congregation of Gloucester, joined to this one by the bond of charity, did the same fast at the command of Father Serlo, a man revered for his monastic religion, during the days preceding the holy day of Pentecost.

On the third day of the aforementioned solemnity, after the morning office had been performed with reverence, both abbots, filled with fear, came to the tomb of the holy body. Two brothers came with them to assist in lifting the stone. One of them was named Hubertus, a man also of remarkable patience. As he often related to us, he had been burdened by the weight of a certain illness. As soon as he sensed the fragrance of the holy relics, he fixed his knees upon the ground with the others and praised almighty God’s mercy, which had so glorified His saints that their bodies were honored both in heaven by their fellow angelic spirits and among mortals.

After prolonged prayer, when he rose, he felt himself completely healed, as he often told us; and we ourselves, together with many others who had previously known him to be very ill, bear witness to this.

The abbots opened the sarcophagus and then left it untouched until the eighth day, on which his feast was to be celebrated.

On the day of his feast, the abbot of that place summoned Osmund, the orthodox bishop of the diocese, a man worthy of honor and praise for his humility, wisdom, and holiness, as well as the aforementioned religious abbot of Gloucester. With a multitude of clergy and a great crowd of people, a throng of princes, and companies of soldiers, his second revelation took place: he was raised from the tomb in which he had been placed by Archbishop Dunstan and honorably deposited by the servants of God in a gilded bier.

On that day and afterward, through his benefits and through the merits of the other saints resting there, gifts of healing were granted to many, to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns throughout all ages. Amen.

[Col. 0083]

# Another Life of Saint Aldhelm

## From Capgrave’s *New Legends of England*

[Col. 0083C]

Blessed Aldhelm was born of the most illustrious stock of the English, and even descended from royal ancestors. His father, named Kenten, a man devoted to God, was the full brother of King Ine of the West Saxons.

This Kenten, then, fathered by his wife a son named Aldhelm. For *Aldhelm* means in English “old helmet,” because, protected in his head by the helmet of salvation, he carried an excellent victory from the enemy into heaven.

After his childhood years had passed, he was given over to the liberal studies. There he flourished so greatly in a short time that he was judged preferable even to the teachers he had, both Greek and Latin.

Finally, in the monastery at Malmesbury, now called Malmesbury, he was first made a monk, then a priest and abbot. Abstaining from food and drink, he devoted himself to vigils and prayers. His fame, illuminated by many praises, had already crossed the sea, passed beyond the Alps, and penetrated to Rome.

Moved by this report, Pope Sergius summoned him by letter and received him honorably. One day, after celebrating Mass in the Lateran church, Aldhelm took off his chasuble and held it behind him, thinking that he was handing it to one of the attendants. But when the attendants failed to act, divine providence immediately intervened. For at once a ray of sunlight entered through the window, caught the chasuble, and held it up for a long time.

That chasuble, in memory of the miracle, has continued to adorn the church at Malmesbury to this day.

At about the same time, it happened in Rome that a boy born of an incestuous mother and an incestuous father damaged the pope’s reputation, because, as commonly happens, popular opinion believed that he had been fathered by the pope.

Aldhelm was distressed that the bishop bound to him by great friendship should be linked to such infamy. He therefore ordered the nine-day-old child to be brought before him and commanded him, by the power and in the name of Jesus Christ, to say whether Sergius was considered guilty of incest.

The infant answered in perfectly clear speech that the bishop was not implicated in the crime and had nothing in common with the second sex. Thus Aldhelm both removed the disgrace from his friend the pope and increased his own favor.

When he was constructing the church of Saint Mary in his monastery, one of the lower beams needed for the building was found to be shorter than the others. Aldhelm therefore poured out a prayer to God and immediately found that the beam had been lengthened according to his petition.

At that time Archbishop Berthwald summoned him to a meeting. As he was traveling near the seashore, certain sailors did not hesitate to despise and mock him because his clothing was dirty.

And behold, when the wind blew against them, the sea rose, winter raged, and the storm grew stronger. The sailors, therefore, in danger and expecting death, confessed their guilt with tears and loudly implored the assistance of Saint Aldhelm.

He boarded a small boat to bring help, and as soon as the saint placed his body upon the vessel, the sea made itself ready for complete calm and brought the sailors and their ship safely to land.

This holy man wrote many books, for he was learned in every field. Among them he composed a book *On the Praise of Virgins*, *On the Battle of the Seven Principal Vices*, *On the Disciplines of the Philosophers*, *On the Admonition of Brotherly Charity*, and many other books.

He also founded a monastery beside the river called the Frome, where a church constructed in honor of Saint John the Baptist still stands. He built a third monastery at Bradeford. But those monasteries were later destroyed and laid waste by the Danes.

He never went out from the monastery unless compelled by great necessity. He was not at all greedy for money, but spent everything given to him on useful purposes and on the poor.

To subdue his fragile flesh, he immersed himself up to the shoulders in the spring nearest the monastery, which is called Saint Aldhelm’s Spring. There, without caring about the icy cold, he remained through the nights, singing the entire Psalter.

He did not avoid the company of women. Rather, whether seated or lying down, he would keep one of them there until, when the flesh’s slippery heat had cooled, he departed with calm and unmoved mind.

The devil saw that he was being mocked, observing a woman clinging to him while the man, with his mind withdrawn elsewhere, persevered in singing the Psalter. The saint then dismissed the woman without compromising modesty or violating chastity.

On one occasion Saint Aldhelm brought with him from Rome an altar of white marble, six feet thick, four feet long, and three palms wide.

A camel carried this stone with him as far as the Alps. There, because of the steepness of the road, the animal fell, was crushed by the collapse, and broke the marble into two pieces.

When Aldhelm saw this, he poured out a prayer to God and gave a blessing. He restored the animal’s strength and health, while the fracture in the stone—which had not split in a straight line but had cracked apart in a certain winding course—immediately joined itself into a solid whole.

Nevertheless, in memory of the miracle, the scar of the split is still visible: healed by a miracle, yet still plainly discernible to a curious eye.

That stone is now said to be in a certain priory of canons called Britons, in the county of Somerset.

In the course of time, the West Saxon region was divided into two bishoprics. Daniel was appointed to Winchester, and Aldhelm was installed at Sherborne, after Bishop Hedda, who had presided over both provinces.

Aldhelm, in a good old age and full of virtues and holiness, departed to the Lord on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, and was buried with great honor in his monastery at Malmesbury.

Saint Egwin, divinely foreknowing his death, wrote as follows in one of his writings:

> “After two years Aldhelm, a religious bishop, departed to the Lord. Learning this through a revelation, I summoned the brothers and disclosed to them the passing of the venerable father. With swift steps I reached the place where his sacred body lay, situated nearly fifty miles beyond the monastery at Malmesbury. I brought it to burial and buried it honorably, ordering that wherever the sacred body had rested during its transport, markers of the holy cross should be erected.
>
> “All the crosses remain to this day, and none of them has suffered the injuries of age. One of them can still be seen in the monks’ cloister.
>
> “When, during his lifetime, he was going through a certain valley to preach and was delivering a sermon to the people, he happened to fix in the ground the ash staff he was using. It is said that, through God’s wondrous power, it grew to an immense size, animated by sap, clothed in bark, and putting forth the beauty of leaves and branches.
>
> “He died in the year of the Lord 709, in the thirty-fourth year from the time he became abbot and in the fifth year of his episcopate.
>
> “Two hundred forty years after his death, namely in the year of the Lord 949, his sacred body was raised from the ground and placed with great honor in a shrine.”

For Bede narrates in Book Five, Chapter Eighteen, that Aldhelm, nobly instructed in ecclesiastical matters and in the knowledge of Scripture, wrote, at the command of the synod of his people, an excellent book against the error of the Britons. They either celebrated Easter at the wrong time or practiced many other things contrary to ecclesiastical purity and peace. Through the reading of this book he brought many of them to the Catholic celebration of the Lord’s Easter.

He also wrote an outstanding book *On Virginity*, which, following the example of Sedulius, he composed in a twofold work, both in hexameter verse and in prose. He wrote several other works as well, for he was learned in every field. As I have said, he was polished in speech and remarkable for his learning in both liberal and ecclesiastical studies.

[Col. 0086D]

This is Bede.

[Col. 0085]

# Extracts on Saint Aldhelm

## From Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History*, V.18

[Col. 0085D]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 705, Alfrid, king of the Northumbrians, died, not yet having completed the twentieth year of his reign. His son Osred, a boy of about eight years, succeeded him in power and reigned for eleven years.

At the beginning of this reign, Hedda, bishop of the East Saxons, migrated to the heavenly life. He was a good and just man, and he practiced the episcopal life and teaching, formed more by an inborn love of virtue than by lessons.

The most revered bishop Pechtelmus, of whom we must speak in his proper place below, had for a long time been a deacon or monk together with Aldhelm, Hedda’s successor. He was accustomed to report that, in the place where Hedda died, many miracles of healing were performed because of the merit of his holiness.

The people of that province were accustomed to put soil taken from that place into water for the sick. The drinking or sprinkling of this water brought healing to many sick people and animals. For this reason, because the sacred soil was frequently removed, a considerable pit was formed there.

When he died, the episcopate of that province was divided into two parishes: one was given to Daniel, who governs it to this day; the other to Aldhelm, over which he presided with the greatest vigor for four years. Both were sufficiently instructed in ecclesiastical matters and in knowledge of the Scriptures. Finally, while he was still a priest and abbot of the monastery which they call the town of Mailduf, Aldhelm wrote, at the command of the synod of his people, an excellent book against the error of the Britons, who either celebrate Easter at the wrong time [Col. 0087B] or carry out many other practices contrary to ecclesiastical purity and peace. By reading this work he brought many of the Britons subject to the West Saxons to the Catholic [Col. 0088A] celebration of the Lord’s Easter. He also wrote an outstanding book *On Virginity*, which, following the example of Sedulius, he composed as a double work, in both hexameter verse and prose. He wrote several other works as well, being a man learned in every respect; for he was polished in speech and, as I have said, remarkably learned in both liberal and ecclesiastical letters. After his death, Forthere assumed the pontificate in his place; he still survives, a man himself greatly learned in the Holy Scriptures.

### From William of Malmesbury, *On the Kings*

He founded two monasteries: one for himself, the other for his sister. His sister’s monastery is called Barking, situated eight miles from London on its side. There, she, named Ethelberga, had as her companions in holiness and piety Hildelid, who succeeded her in due course. To Hildelid the book of the blessed Aldhelm in praise of virgins was sent.

[Col. 0087]

## THE LETTERS OF SAINT ALDHELM, BISHOP OF SHERBORNE, OR THE FIRST PART OF HIS WORKS. (C, S)

### LETTER I. ALDHELM TO GERUNTIUS

[Note: [Col. 0087C] This letter is found among the letters of Boniface the Martyr; from there it has been transferred here. GILES.]

[Col. 0087C]

To the most glorious lord Geruntius, king, governing the scepters of the western kingdom, whom I embrace with brotherly charity, as the Searcher of hearts and Witness of all things knows; and likewise to all the priests of God dwelling throughout Domnonia: Aldhelm, performing the office of abbot without any precedence of merit, sends the desired salvation that is in the Lord.

Recently, when I was at a council of bishops, an innumerable throng of God’s priests gathered from almost the whole of Britain. They had assembled especially so that, out of concern for the churches and the salvation of souls, the canonical decrees and the statutes of the Fathers might be examined by all and, with Christ’s protection, preserved in common. After these matters had duly been prayed over, the entire priestly council compelled my insignificant self, by a common command and a similar judgment, to send written letters to the presence of Your Piety and to communicate in writing their paternal request and salutary exhortation—namely, concerning the unity of the Catholic Church and the harmony of the Christian religion, without which one’s labor grows idle in torpor and the future reward withers away.

For what benefit are the profits of good works if they are performed outside the Catholic Church, even if someone diligently observes the actual rule of a strict way of life under the discipline of a monastery, or, avoiding the company of all mortals, lives a contemplative and eremitical life in a desolate solitude? Therefore, so that your sagacity may more certainly perceive the reasons for which my mediocrity has sent this writing, I shall explain them briefly and concisely.

We have heard, and learned through reports conveyed by various rumors, that your priests are by no means in agreement according to the rule of the Catholic faith and the commandment of Scripture, and that through their rivalries and verbal disputes a grievous schism and cruel scandal arise in the Church of Christ. The Psalmist’s saying bears witness to this when he declares: “Great peace belongs to those who love your name, and there is no scandal in them.” Pious concord unites the peace of religion, just as bitter contention defiles charity.

The Psalmist exhorts the followers of the true faith to the unity of brotherhood, saying: “God, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house.” This house, according to allegory, is understood as the Church spread throughout all the quarters of the world. Heretics and schismatics, strangers to the fellowship of the Church, spring up throughout the world through contentious arguments and, like dreadful seeds of weeds sown amid a fertile crop, stain the Lord’s harvest.

But the apostolic trumpet restrains the disgrace of such quarrelling: “If anyone wishes to be contentious,” he says, “we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God,” which “has neither spot nor wrinkle.” The evangelical oracles proclaim that peace is the mother of Catholics and the mother who gives birth to the children of God: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.”

Therefore, when our Lord and Savior descended from the highest summit of heaven in order to erase the bond written against the first-created man and reconcile the world through peace, the angelic melody sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.” And the Psalmist says: “Let peace be within your strength, and abundance within your towers.”

Finally, a report contrary to the faith of the Church has spread far and wide: that in your province there are certain priests and clerics who stubbornly reject the tonsure of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, and obstinately defend themselves by such an apology, claiming that they imitate the tonsure of their founders and predecessors. They assert in grandiloquent declarations that these men were illumined by divine grace. Yet, if they are carefully asked who first originated this shaving and tonsure, they fall completely silent, either through ignorance of the truth or through concealment of falsehood.

We, however, according to the opinion of many, have learned that Simon, the inventor of magic, was the originator of this tonsure. The contest of the apostles and the ten books of Clement bear witness to what sort and how great a deception of necromancy he fraudulently contrived against blessed Peter.

We, I say, bearing witness to the truth concerning our tonsure according to the most sacred authority of Scripture, assert that the apostle Peter first adopted this practice for various reasons: first, so that he might carry upon his head the form and likeness of Christ, when Christ was about to undergo the gallows of the cross for our redemption and was cruelly crowned by the impious Jewish people with sharp points of thorns; next, so that the priests of the Old and New Testaments might be distinguished by tonsure and dress; finally, so that the apostle himself, his successors, and their followers might carry among the Roman people the ridiculous mockery of derisive laughter, since their barons were accustomed to sell enemies defeated in battle beneath a crown.

Moreover, in the Old Testament the sign of tonsure, from the Nazirite—if I am not mistaken, that is, from the holy—took its beginning. It is an indication of royal and priestly lineage. For among the ancients the tiara was placed upon the heads of priests. It was round, made of twisted linen like half a sphere; this is signified in the shaved part of the head. The crown, however, is the golden breadth of a circle that encircles the heads of kings.

Thus both signs are expressed on the heads of clerics, as Peter says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood.” By this practice of cutting and shaving, the cutting away of vices is signified, and we are stripped of the hairs of our flesh as though of our crimes.

There is, however, another and more grievous destruction of souls: that, in the most sacred solemnity of Easter, they do not follow the rule of the 318 Fathers, who at the Council of Nicaea wisely established the nineteen-year cycle of the calendar, proceeding by the eight-year and eleven-year periods in a straight course to the end of the world. They handed down the sequence of computation from the fourteenth moon to the twenty-first, and the limit of the paschal calculation; they judged it unlawful, contrary to right and justice, to anticipate or exceed it.

These men, however, according to the ten- and nine-year computation of Anatolius—or rather according to the rule of Sulpicius Severus, who described a course of eighty-four years—celebrate the paschal sacrament with the Jews on the fourteenth moon, although neither of these systems is followed by the pontiffs of the Roman Church in the perfect calculation of the cycle. Nor did they decree that later generations should follow the course of Victor’s paschal calendar, which is contained within a cycle of 532 years.

There was, in fact, a certain kind of heretics among the Easterners called *tessareskaidekatitai*, that is, “fourteenth-day people,” because they celebrate the solemnity of Easter on the fourteenth moon with the Jews, who blaspheme Christ and trample the pearls of the Gospel underfoot like swine. For this reason they are alien from the blessed fellowship of the orthodox and are unhappily reckoned among the assemblies of schismatics. I remember that blessed Augustine mentioned them in his book written concerning the ninety heresies.

But how greatly this differs from the Catholic faith and conflicts with evangelical tradition is shown by the fact that, beyond the channel of the River Severn, the priests of the Demetae, boasting of the purity of their own private conduct, greatly abominate our communion. They will neither celebrate with us the offices of prayer in church nor partake together with us of dishes at the table as an act of charity. Indeed, they throw the fragments of dishes and the remains of meals to be devoured by the jaws of gluttonous dogs and unclean swine.

They also command that their vessels and bowls be purified and cleansed either with gritty sand and gravel or with yellow ashes of embers. No peaceful greeting is offered, no kiss of pious brotherhood is given, although the Apostle says: “Greet one another with a holy kiss.” Nor is water for washing the hands, or water with a towel, provided; nor is a basin placed for washing the feet, although the Savior, girded with a linen cloth, washed the feet of his disciples and gave us a rule to imitate when he said: “As I have done, so do you also to others.”

But if anyone from our people—that is, from among the Catholics—goes to them for the purpose of dwelling there, they do not deign to admit him to the fellowship of their association until they compel him to spend forty days in penance. In this too they unhappily imitate the heretics who wished to be called *Katharoi*, that is, “the pure.”

Alas, alas, because of so many errors! Rather than “Evax! Evax!” I think one ought mournfully to repeat with tearful voices and complaining sobs. They are known to do all this contrary to the commandments of the Gospel, following the empty traditions of the Pharisees, with Christ truly confirming it (Matthew 23): “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who cleanse what is outside the cup and the dish.”

For the Lord is described as celebrating banquets with tax collectors and sinners, so that, as the true physician, he might prepare the medicines of divine mercy and the poultice of heavenly clemency for the festering wounds of souls. Therefore he did not, after the manner of the Pharisees, disdain the company of sinners. Rather, he mercifully restored that sinful woman, who mournfully lamented the offenses of her polluted life, moistened the Lord’s feet with showers of tears, and wiped them with the loosened and flowing locks of her hair, saying (Luke 7:47): “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much.”

Since these things are so, for the sake of our common share in the heavenly homeland and our fellowship with the angels, with prayers supported and knees bent we earnestly beseech and implore your brotherhood: do not henceforth abominate the teaching and decrees of blessed Peter with the stubborn brow and arrogant heart of contumacy, and do not, relying on tyrannical obstinacy, presumptuously reject the tradition of the Roman Church because of the ancient statutes of your predecessors.

For Peter confessed the Son of God with blessed voice and deserved to hear (Matthew 16): “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

If, then, the keys of the heavenly kingdom were bestowed by Christ upon Peter, of whom the poet says:

> Heavenly key-bearer, who opens the gate in heaven;

who, while scorning the chief statutes of his Church and despising the commands of his teaching, enters joyfully through the gate of heavenly paradise? And if he deserved, by a happy lot and singular privilege, to receive in heaven and on earth the power of binding and the sovereignty of loosing, who, rejecting the rule of the Easter festival and the rite of the Roman tonsure, would not judge that he must rather be bound inseparably by tight bonds than be mercifully released?

But perhaps some crafty reader of books and shrewd examiner of Scriptures may defend himself with such a shield of excuse and protect himself with such a defense:

“I venerate with sincere faith the commandments of both Testaments; with believing heart I confess one essence and one substance of the Holy Trinity, and a threefold substance of persons. With free voice I shall proclaim among the people the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation, the gallows of his Passion, and the trophy of his Resurrection. I shall diligently announce the final judgment of the living and the dead, when unequal recompense according to each person’s merits shall be weighed on the most equitable scales of judgment. By the privilege of this faith I shall be gathered into the company of Catholics and counted among them without any obstacle of misfortune.”

But I shall strive to shatter and break to the ground, with the ballista of apostolic correction, the fortress of this excuse beneath which they trust themselves hidden. For James, the son of the Lord’s maternal aunt, says: “You believe that there is one God”—and because he was speaking ironically to the twelve tribes scattered among the nations, he immediately added: “You do well; even the demons believe and tremble,” because faith without works is dead.

Catholic faith and the concord of brotherly charity move inseparably along the same path, as the outstanding preacher and chosen vessel elegantly testifies (1 Corinthians 13): “If I know all prophecy and all mysteries, if I have faith so as to move mountains, and if I deliver my body to be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing.”

To conclude everything within the enclosure of a brief statement: he boasts vainly and uselessly of the Catholic faith who does not follow the doctrine and rule of Saint Peter. For the foundation of the Church and the foundation of faith, established principally in Christ and subsequently in Peter, will by no means waver or totter when the whirlwinds of storms assail it, as the Apostle declares (1 Corinthians 3:11): “No one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.” But to Peter the Truth granted this privilege of the Church (Matthew 16): “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.”

### LETTER II. ALDHELM TO HIS SISTER OSGITHA

[Note: [Col. 0092B] This letter, like the preceding one, is found among the letters of Boniface the Martyr; from there it has been transferred here. GILES.]

To my most beloved and dearest sister, venerable to me with sincere affection of charity: Aldhelm, your suppliant, performing the unworthy office of abbot, sends greetings in the Lord.

Let Your Benevolence know that I asked the bishop about the baptism of the sister; he gave permission for that nun to be baptized, but only secretly and privately.

I greet you carefully, Osgitha, from the innermost chamber of my heart, earnestly beseeching you not to cease occupying your mind with continual meditation on the Scriptures, so that you may fulfill the Psalmist’s saying (1:2): “He shall meditate on his law day and night.” The same Psalmist also bears witness to this when he says (119:103): “How sweet are your words to my palate!” and so forth.

Earnestly ask through Christ that all the sisters remember me in their prayers, for the Apostle says (James 5:16): “The continual prayer of a righteous person has great power.”

Farewell, most beloved—ten times; indeed, a hundred and a thousand times. May God grant you health.

### LETTER III. ALDHELM TO EAHFRID, RETURNED TO HIS HOMELAND FROM IRELAND

[Note: [Col. 0092C] It is extant in Usserius’s *Collection of Irish Letters* and in Wharton’s supplement to Usserius’s *History of Dogma*, p. 350, quarto, London, 1690. I found nothing in the London manuscript codex that seemed worth reporting here. GILES.]

[Col. 0092D]

To Eahfrid, worthy to be proclaimed a venerable lord and greatly honored for the merits of the saints: Aldhelm, insignificant, sends eternal salvation in the Lord.

First, let us hymn—especially by the pious and paternal privilege of the chiefs and rulers of all—let us proclaim everywhere in prose beneath the heavens a panegyric and poems, tuning them with the shrill harmony of voices and the song of melody and chant, especially because at last he deigned to send to earth the offspring of the gracious mother, destined to erase the ancient written record of sins, the insoluble guilt of the first parents. He thrust into Tartarus the one who, with his three-forked tongue, vomited foul and poisonous venom through the ages, amid the dread torments of dark punishment. [Col. 0093A]

And where formerly the young serpents and little snakes of that same wicked serpent were worshiped in profane shrines with crude stupidity, now, by a reversal of fortune, the dwellings of the disciples—indeed, the gracious houses of prayer—are skillfully built through the architect’s art.

I confess, as a client of brotherly fellowship and a citizen of your lofty municipality, that after we learned through rumor-bearing messengers that you, returning here, had safely reached the border of British territory from the wintry, northwesterly climates of Ireland’s island—where for approximately eighteen years you had been suckled on the abundant nourishment of wisdom—we immediately, as flaming and ardent love demanded, offered ineffable thanks to the Most High, rejoicing with hands outstretched on high.

This was especially because the gracious Judge deigned to bring you back in exile to visit the ancient rural household of your father, across the blue-grey sea, over its enormous shingle banks and the foam-bearing surges of the water [the text’s wording is corrupt in part], while the rejoicing helmsman’s curved keel cut through the stormy deep. Thus, where long ago, born from the cradle of infancy, you had grown from rough childhood to the mature age of puberty, now, by a reversal of fortune, richly supported by heavenly aid, you return from dwelling in a foreign land and, having obtained and assumed the title of teacher, fulfill its duties with confidence.

I do not conceal from Your Blessedness, but openly reveal it from the innermost recesses of my heart, as an increase of joy, and, as I think, for the glory of the name of the Lord: that a report beyond measure has grown among those dwelling in Scottish territory, whose fellowship you have enjoyed for a little while. It reaches our hearing like a certain thunderous roar, a stormy crash emerging from the clouds; and throughout so many and such great stages of the earth the reputation of your learning, spread through villages and provinces, continually increases. [Col. 0093C]

For there is such frequent traffic—this way and that, hither and thither—across the navigable channels of the sea, as though there were a kindred brotherhood of bees skillfully making nectar. Just as, by turns, when the returning mist of night has withdrawn, the honey-bearing swarm, with the sun rising as far as the heavens, carries its gathered yellow burdens from the blossoming tops of the linden trees to the slender hives, so, if I am not mistaken, the mass of gluttonous readers—“dunning tac fridh” [corrupt phrase as printed; meaning uncertain]—and the remaining discerning throng of students eagerly pluck from the flower-bearing fields of hagiography not only the grammatical and geometrical arts and the sixfold apparatuses of natural philosophy, but indeed also the more important, twofold oracles of allegorical and tropological exposition, sweetened in the heavenly obscurities of enigmatic problems. [Col. 0093D]

They take these thirstily and hide them away, storing them in the beehives of wisdom, to be preserved there by continual meditation. From their company, your diligence is said to have proceeded, laden with spoils and overflowing with the torrent of the sacred stream, as your surpassing fame has spread.

Therefore, bending down and supported on my knees, with prayers I earnestly implore your gracious discipleship not to let this escape your obliterating memory: that Pacificus, endowed with heavenly ambrosia—having succeeded his father by hereditary right and having ruled the Israelite people for eight periods of five years—spoke when enriched by gracious inspiration:

> Drink water from your own cistern,  
> and flowing water from your own well;  
> let your springs flow out,  
> and divide your waters in the streets;  
> let them belong to you alone,  
> and let no strangers share them with you.

Therefore, imbued with these sacred shoots, open the torrent of orthography through continual effort and water the thirsty fields of minds, so that the seed of heavenly ecstasy, sown in the living and fertile furrows of the orthodox by the sweat of the sower, may sprout and grow without any obstacle of burning drought, and that at last, by God’s aid, the dense harvest may ripen abundantly.

For this reason, I, a suppliant, appear to have offered this prayer so earnestly: that some people are known to be endowed with heavenly wisdom and extraordinarily filled with hidden light. Yet what they have received through the free generosity of heaven and God’s lavish gift—without any labor of personal merit—they do not fully proclaim, once the treasury of knowledge has been unlocked, but distribute it piecemeal to gluttons. [Col. 0094B]

For, according to the experience of evangelical authority, a burning lamp is not hidden secretly in the dark hiding-place of a gloomy vessel; rather, it ought to shine for all with clear light from the top of a lampstand. Nor are the profits of a talent uselessly hidden beneath underground heaps of sand; they ought to be entrusted to the money-changers for the increase of many coins. Otherwise, the servant who received the talent and lies idle in sluggishness may be cast down into the lowest squalor of the prison; rather, he ought to deserve to enter the rejoicing of “evax” and “euge” from the gracious Creator.

Hence the prophetic Psalmist, expiating for this reason the offense of his own conscience, began with a sacred prediction and said: “I have not hidden your righteousness,” and so forth.

But as I, a wretched little man, revolved these matters while dictating, I was immediately troubled by a twofold scruple: “Why,” I asked, “is Ireland exalted with some ineffable privilege, as though teachers of Argive or Roman Quirites could not be found there, on Britain’s fertile soil, who might be able to unravel the problems of the gloomy heavenly library and open them to the little students who inquire?”

For although the aforesaid land of Ireland is rich and flourishing in learners, possessing, so to speak, a pasture-like multitude of readers, just as the poles of heaven are adorned with the shimmering flashes of glittering stars, nevertheless Britain, situated in the farthest west, almost at the edge of the world—so to speak—enjoys the fiery sun and the bright display of the moon: namely, Theodore, performing the office of bishop, mature in the flower of philosophical art from the very apprenticeship of his rudiments, and also his associate Hadrian, endowed with ineffable urbanity and clarity. [Col. 0094D]

And boldly proclaiming this openly, disregarding the frivolous deceit of falsehood and discerning by the balanced judgment of truth, I shall declare: even if Theodore, of blessed memory, holding the reins of the highest priesthood, is surrounded by a throng of Irish disciples—like a savage boar enclosed by a snarling kennel of Molossian hounds—he swiftly scatters the rebellious ranks with his polished grammatical tooth, suffering no loss or expense.

Like a warrior standing in the middle of the field, surrounded by the dense phalanxes of opposing legions, he soon bends his powerful arms into a taut bow and draws arrows from his quiver—that is, the dark and sharp syllogisms of chronology. Then the troop swollen with the arrogance of raised eyebrows, abandoning the tortoise-shell formation of its shields and turning its back, hastens toward the dark hiding places of caves, while the victor triumphs. [Col. 0095A]

Yet let no one suppose that by philosophizing in this way I am mocking the Scottish little students, whose sagacity has for a while drawn upon the jeweled honeycomb of your teachings. When I labored to fashion and kindly weave a proclamation of our own people, I was not laughing derisively and spreading rumors of mockery about yours; rather, in the manner of a jesting buffoon and clown, I was bantering those who speak with reckless wit under the pretext of brotherly irony.

But if, through the assistance of ignorance, the loquacious page is shown to have uttered something rash, as the word-spinner says:

> May the fugitive “gurgo” be worthy, speaking with a babbling tongue [the opening nonce-like wording is uncertain];  
> let the writer not fear to pluck at the frightening sheets,  
> as a shaggy goat gnaws grapes with its tooth;  
> yet let him not correct the stumbling poet’s *gramma* (metrical or lettered line).

### LETTER IV. ALDHELM TO HEDDA, BISHOP

[Note: [Col. 0095B] It is found among the letters of Boniface, from which it migrated here; the text has been somewhat improved by comparison with the same letter preserved by William of Malmesbury. GILES.]

To the most reverend lord, venerable for every effort of virtue, and, after God, my special patron: your humble dependent sends greetings in the Lord.

I confess, most blessed bishop, that I had long resolved, if circumstances and the flying changes of time allowed it, to celebrate with dancing the approaching solemnity of the desired Nativity of the Lord there, in the company of the brothers, and afterward, with life as my companion, to enjoy the approachable presence of your charity. But because, delayed by various obstacles of hindrances, we could not accomplish this—as the bearer of this letter will explain more fully in person—I therefore ask you to grant pardon for the difficulty.

For no small intervals of time must be prolonged in this study of reading by anyone who, inflamed by the keen desire to read, searches deeply into the laws of Roman jurisprudence, examines all the secrets of the legal experts from the innermost recesses of his heart, and—what is much more intricate and perplexing than these matters—distinguishes a hundred kinds of meters by a pedestrian rule and investigates the measures mingled with song along the proper sequence of syllables.

For students devoted to this subject, obscurity presents itself as all the more inextricable the rarer is the multitude of teachers. But the narrowness of a letter does not allow me to discuss these matters at length: how the hidden instruments of the metrical art itself are combined from letters, syllables, feet, poetic figures, verses, tones, and times; how the discipline of the sevenfold division of poetry varies—that is, the acephalous, the lagaric, the protilic, and the rest; which verses are measured as monoschematic, which as pentoschematic, and which as decaschematic, according to a fixed measure of feet; and by what reasoning catalectic, brachycatalectic, and hypercatalectic verses may be recognized. [Col. 0096A]

These matters, I think, and others like them, cannot possibly be grasped in a brief interval of time or in a momentary stroke.

And what should be said about the method of calculation, when so great a despair arising from computation has oppressed the necks of my mind that I have considered all my former labor in reading of little value, although I had believed that I knew its secret chambers? To use the saying of blessed Jerome, I who had previously seemed to myself a little learned began again to be a student, when the opportunity presented itself. Thus at last, relying on heavenly grace, through persistence in reading I discovered the most difficult arguments of things and the calculations of computation, which are called the parts of number.

Moreover, I think I ought to remain silent about the method of the zodiac and of the twelve signs that revolve in the turning of heaven, lest an obscure and profound subject, which requires a lengthy explanation, be disgraced and cheapened if it is revealed in a poor sequence of interpretation—especially since expertise in the astrological art and the perplexing calculation of the horoscope require the labor of a more learned investigation. [Col. 0096B]

These matters, dearest Father, I have touched upon briefly and step by step, not enticed by the noisy chatter of loquacity, but so that you may know that such great secrets of things cannot be understood unless frequent and prolonged meditation is applied.

Greet in Christ all the company of my associates, from the least to the greatest. I beseech and adjure them, through the clemency of Christ, to pour out prayers to the Lord for me, oppressed by the weight of sins and the burden of crimes.

### LETTER V. OF A CERTAIN ANONYMOUS SCOT TO ALDHELM, ABBOT OF MALMESBURY

[Note: [Col. 0096C] Let the reader consider whether this anonymous Scot is the same as Cellanus, whose letter appears below. GILES.]

To the holy, most wise, and truly beloved of Christ Aldhelm: an unnamed Scot sends greetings in the eternal God.

Since I know you to be outstanding in talent, in Roman eloquence, and in the varied flower of letters—even after the manner of the Greeks—I prefer to learn from your mouth, the purest fountain of knowledge, rather than drink from anyone else, especially from a muddied teacher. [Col. 0096D]

Know this beforehand: for this reason I earnestly and confidently beseech you to receive and teach me, because—as has been said—the radiance of wisdom shines in you beyond that of many readers, and you understand the minds of foreigners who desire to learn wisdom. You were a newcomer at Rome, and, moreover, you were nurtured by a certain holy man of our race.

These brief remarks may suffice for the sake of concision, because, if you are willing to attend humbly through charity, you will perceive as much through a few words as through very many speeches. I also explain this to you sincerely.

You have a certain little book, no larger, I think, than an *acceptorium* of two weeks [the object denoted by *acceptorium* is uncertain], which I desire to copy. I mention this short period not because I need more time, but lest this request create weariness in your mind. I think I shall also obtain a servant and horses. During this season of harvest I shall hope for a joyful answer from you.

May divine grace deign to guard Your Blessedness, who prays for us:

> Powerful Christ, creator of returning time,  
> voice and mind of the Most High God, whom the Father poured forth  
> from his lofty mind and granted a share in so great a kingdom.  
> You subdued the impious crimes of our life,  
> suffering to be clothed in bodily form,  
> openly to address the peoples and confess yourself human.  
> You whom Mary enclosed in her womb, at whose divinity’s appearing  
> the virgin’s breasts then swelled,  
> the unmarried mother marveled that her secret womb  
> was filled by a wondrous birth,  
> about to bear her own Creator. Mortal hearts  
> enclosed the Maker of heaven; the discoverer of the world  
> became part of the human race and lay hidden beneath one  
> breast, he who embraces the whole world far and wide.  
> And he whom neither the spaces of earth, nor the waves of the sea,  
> nor heaven can contain gathered himself into tiny limbs.  
> You even underwent the name and bonds of punishment,  
> so that you might snatch us from death and drive death away  
> by your own death. Soon you were carried up into the heavenly breezes,  
> returning in purified light to your joyful Father,  
> so that you may cherish the august man,  
> that on festal days he may often celebrate the annual fasts of the pure sacred rite.

### LETTER VI. ETHELWALD TO ALDHELM

[Note: [Col. 0097C] It is found among the letters of Boniface; yet it undoubtedly rightly claims a place for itself in this edition …, since the name of Aldhelm is prefixed to the verses appended to this letter … GILES.]

[Col. 0097C]

To the most sacred abbot Aldhelm, bound to me, as his merits require, by the intricate knots of fiery charity: Ethelwald, the humble pupil of your pious fatherhood, sends perpetual health in the Lord.

During the course of summer, when this most wretched homeland was being grievously ravaged by the destructive force of envy through the immense expeditions of savage encounters everywhere, I lingered in your company, occupied with the pursuit of reading. Then your sacred sagacity, which, as I believe, had been most fully imbued with the writings of almost all the volumes edited in the panegyrics of secular literary eloquence and in the works elaborated in the style of ecclesiastical doctrine, revealed to me the hidden studies of the liberal arts—studies obscure to ignorant minds only because of the veiled secrets of their mysteries—by swiftly tearing away the veil of dense stupidity and displaying them with perfect clarity.

After I had eagerly consumed these abundant feasts of your overflowing intellect with the thirsty mouths of my understanding, they continually refreshed my still pallid emaciation of dullness with the monthly allowance (*epimenia*) of your most generous and gracious promise, assuring me that you would willingly instruct and imbue me with every instrument of the reading I desired, especially those in which you had recognized the industry of my mediocrity as sufficiently eager.

Therefore, my most beloved teacher of pure instruction, so that you may readily place faith in my words, supported by the affection that accompanies them, we think it worthwhile, prompted by such oracles of Sacred Scripture as these (Prov. 6:1): “My son, if you have become surety for your friend, you have pledged your hand to a stranger; you have been ensnared by the words of your mouth.” And I say now: even if you do not remember having become entangled and ensnared by any restraints binding a promise you have uttered, nevertheless, since from the very tender cradle of my infancy you fostered me, loved me, and gradually restored me with the more delicate foods of skill until you brought me to vigorous adolescence, everyone judges it fitting that, once the nourishment of my tender intellect has been strengthened, you should also provide the more solid foods of deeper wisdom.

Yet if the most humble urgency of my submissive devotion, persistently and importunately seeking abundant nourishment, asks you to supply such feasts, do not refuse to provide them; and although you may regard me as a person of no account, do not decline, for a time, to enrich your adopted offspring from the entire wealthy treasury of paternal prudence. Otherwise, when the hateful bands of audacious rivals are found rejoicing and exulting with the mocking laughter of their desired condemnation, they may congratulate themselves if they discover that the offspring of an affluent paternal philosophy has been disinherited and made acquainted with the deadly poverty of folly.

And not inappropriately might that Rehoboam be mournfully compared with me: born from the illustrious stock of the most famous king Solomon, whose wisdom was extraordinarily excellent and whose material resources were abundant, yet poured forth in an unfortunate birth and deprived of almost all his father’s felicity.

Finally, now fulfill my vows and hasten to complete the benefaction of your generous instruction, knowing without doubt that you will thereby gain the greater glory of everlasting reward, with the Lord bearing witness, because (Matt. 10) “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

To this letter of our littleness we have appended three songs in measured composition, arranged in two kinds. The first, in the dactylic hexameter of heroic poetry and, as I suppose, in the rule of prose, has been refined and weighed, and—by a circumstance that so occurred, or, more truly, under the direction of heavenly providence—divided into formulas corresponding to seventy verses. The third, not elaborated according to the measure of feet, but composed of eight syllables in each verse and fitted to one and the same letter through equal lines, I have rapidly engraved with the pen and dedicated to you, most discerning sower. The middle one, composed in lines of verses and syllables likewise similar to one another, I have presented to my client and yours, Winfrid, concerning his pilgrimage on a transmarine journey.

For this reason I judged that these works ought to be presented to the venerable sight of your blessedness: it seemed worthy, in my judgment, that I should first disclose and publish to you, as my father, this little edition of my writings, so that, once approved by the favorable judgment of your exalted reason and brought into conformity with the rule of equity, it might thereafter prove acceptable to all the multitude of readers.

Farewell in Christ.

## EPISTLE VII. ALDHELM TO ADRIAN

Most reverend Father and venerable teacher of my uncultivated infancy, to Adrian: Aldhelmus, a native servant of Christ’s household and a suppliant fosterling of your piety, sends greetings, and so forth.

I confess, my most beloved one, whom I embrace with the grace of pure affection, that after I withdrew from your companionship approximately three years ago and was separated from Kent, my littleness has continually burned with ardent desire for association with you.
