I would long ago have considered how to fulfill and accomplish this desire, as I wish, if circumstances and the changing course of time had permitted it, and if various obstacles had not held me back—especially if I had not been prevented by the bodily weakness that consumed my limbs to the marrow. It was on account of this weakness that, once, when I was again with you after my first elementary studies, I was compelled to return home.

## EPISTLE VIII. CELLAN TO ALDHELM

To Aldhelmus, the archimandrite of the Saxons, enriched by learned studies and adorned with honey-flowing little works, remarkably discovering on his shores what some scarcely earn through labor and sweat in foreign lands: Cellanus, born on the island of Ireland, an exile hiding in a remote corner at the edge of the Franks, the last and most worthless slave of Christ’s famous colony, sends greetings in the complete and secure Trinity.

As though on winged flight, a panegyric rumor of your Latin eloquence reached the ears of our poverty—a rumor whose agile readers do not fear to hear without mockery or the dregs of deceit, renowned for the beauty of Rome’s [uncertain reading: *Alburnum dictricis*; perhaps *almum ductricis*, “nourishing guide”]. And although we have not deserved to hear you in person, we have nevertheless read your chronicles, carefully composed and painted with the delights of various flowers.

But if you refresh the sad little heart of an exile, send a few little utterances from that most beautiful mouth of yours, from whose purest spring many minds may be refreshed, to the place where the lord Fursey rests in a holy and incorrupt body.

## EPISTLE IX. ALDHELM’S LETTER TO CELLAN [Fragment]

I marvel that the industry of your *franite* [perhaps *Francicae*, “Frankish”] fraternity addresses me—a tiny little man, born of Saxon stock and cradled from tender infancy beneath the northern sky—from the famous and flower-bearing countryside of the Franks.

## EPISTLE X. ALDHELM TO ETHELWALD

To my most beloved son and at the same time my disciple, Ethelwald: Aldhelmus, the least of the servants of God, sends greetings.

Just as I have taken care several times to admonish you by word of mouth concerning various matters, so now I do not hesitate to exhort you in writing while you are absent, relying upon paternal authority according to God. For we do this because, as the Apostle says, the love of Christ urges us.

Therefore, my dearest son, although you are young in age, do not subject yourself excessively to the most vain amusements of this world—whether by shamefully exceeding all measure in frequent and prolonged daily drinking and banquets, or by culpable wandering on horseback, or by any of the detestable pleasures of bodily delight.

Always remember what is written: “Youth and pleasure are vanity.” I have also admonished you not to serve beyond measure the excessive pursuit of money and every boastful display of worldly glory, which is always hateful to God, remembering that saying: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? For the Son of Man will come in his glory and that of the holy angels, and he will repay each according to his works.”

But much more, my dearest one, devote yourself constantly either to divine reading or to sacred prayers. If you strive to know anything further of secular literature, do so only for this reason: since in the divine law all, or almost all, the texture of the words rests entirely upon the principles of grammatical art, you will understand the deepest and most sacred meanings of that divine eloquence more easily in reading, the more fully you have learned the very different rules of the system by which it is woven. [The manuscript or printed text is lacunose here.]

Do not fail to keep this letter continually among the other books you read, so that by its frequent reading you may be reminded in my place to fulfill the matters written in it.

Farewell.

## EPISTLE XI. ALDHELM TO THE CLERGY OF BISHOP WILFRID

Recently, as you have learned by experience, the furious disturbance of the storm shook the foundations of the Church as though by some immense earthquake; its roar resounded far and wide through the various regions of the earth like the crash of thunder. Therefore I earnestly ask you, my kinsmen in the faith, bowing the knees of your legs and supporting my request with prayer, not to be scandalized by the stratagem of this disturbance, lest any of you grow sluggish in faith through torpor of mind—even if necessity should demand that you be driven from your ancestral land together with your own bishop, deprived of the dignity of the episcopate, and that someone should have to undertake the transmarine fields of distant kingdoms.

Who, I ask, could be so harsh or cruel a hardship as to separate you from that bishop and keep you away from him? From the very apprenticeship of your first rudiments and the earliest infancy of your tender age, he advanced you through nurturing, teaching, and correction to the flower of mature youth. Like a nurse or foster-mother refreshing her beloved children with arms spread wide, he embraced you mercifully, cherishing you in the bosom of charity.

Consider, I ask, the order of created things and the nature divinely implanted in them, so that, by comparing the smallest things, you may receive, with Christ’s help, a pliable pattern of compassion. Consider how swarms of bees, when the heavenly heat has grown warm, emerge at once from their nectar-scented hives in competing throngs; and when their leader departs, leaving behind the winter shelters of their dwellings, a host of dense caves gathers swiftly in flight toward the heavens, except only for the keepers of the ancient seats, who remain for the propagation of future offspring.

Their king, more wonderfully—as it is remarkable to say—surrounded by dense ranks of his companions, leaves the winter camp with the swarm and examines the hollow trunks. If he is delayed by a dusty sprinkling of sand that obstructs him, or by sudden rains, when the cataract of Olympus drips down in drops, and if he returns to his beloved lattice and former dwelling, the entire army immediately breaks through the accustomed vestibules and enters joyfully into the ancient enclosures of the cells. [The text contains a lacuna.]

If, then, a creature without reason, which life and implanted nature govern without written laws, obeys the command of its leader through the recurring succession of the seasons, answer me, I ask: are those not to be branded with the disgrace of a dreadful abomination who, endowed with the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, break the reins of devoted submission in the manner of madmen?

But why should I run through the calculations of various things, gathering them together with a screeching pen to stir the innermost parts of your hearts? Listen.

Behold: if secular people, deprived of divine knowledge, should abandon a devoted lord whom they loved in prosperity when the abundance of good fortune ceased and the adversity of calamity arose, preferring the secure sweet leisure of their rejoicing homeland to the oppression of their lord, would they not be regarded by everyone as objects of execrable laughter and the noisy mockery of derision?

What, then, will be said of you if you leave alone in exile the bishop who nourished and raised you? And so forth.

## EPISTLE XII. ALDHELM TO WINBERT

To the most beloved Winbert in the Lord of lords: Aldhelmus, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings. He is the cornerstone of the two Testaments, cut from the summits of the mountains, who crushed the statue fashioned from four kinds of metal, signifying the four kingdoms of the peoples down to its legs, with its golden head.

We have sent Cerulus, the bearer of this letter, to your piety’s presence; he will explain more fully by word of mouth the matter of our pressing need: namely, the land which the venerable patrician Baldred offered to us for possession in exchange for an agreed price, especially since it lies in a suitable and convenient place for catching fish.

Therefore, while it appears to have been granted and conveyed into the power of our king, we earnestly beseech you that, through the protection of your charity, we may be able firmly to obtain and retain that same portion of land, lest, deprived of the possession by violence—for the rights of justice often totter—we be defrauded of it, and so forth.

## EPISTLE XIII. ALDHELM TO WILFRID

To the venerably beloved and delightfully revered lord Wilfrid: Aldhelmus, a native servant and suppliant in Christ, sends everlasting greetings.

I have learned, through the reports of rumor-bearers, of the industry of your charity: that, with the Lord as your guide, you have determined to undertake a transmarine journey, inflamed by the zeal of reading.

Therefore, once you have reached the desired harbor of Ireland, if life accompanies you, read especially the sacred prophecies, rejecting the fictions of philosophers. For I consider it absurd, after rejecting the inextricable rule of the primitive and ancient Instrument, to travel through the slippery byways of thorny country—or rather through the difficult winding passages of philosophers.

Rather, you ought thirstily to drink the clear waters of glasslike springs rather than the muddy waters of marshes and filthy pools, in which a black host of toads teems in crowds and the chattering croaking of frogs resounds.

What benefit, I ask, does it bring to the sacrament of orthodox faith to grow deaf through laborious reading and investigation of the story of the polluted incest of filthy Proserpina—a subject I shrink from uttering—or to venerate in the proclamation of reading the wanton Hermione, offspring of Menelaus and Helen, who, as ancient works report, was once betrothed to Orestes by right of dowry but later, when the decision was changed, married Neoptolemus? Or to engrave in heroic style the history of the priests of the frenzied Luperci, parasites celebrating Priapus in the manner of revelers—stories that, when the snake was once raised on the summit of the scepter and presented to the eyes of Hebrew caution, that is, when the nourishing death of death was fastened to the trunk of the gallows, collapsed to the ground and vanished?

Furthermore, compelled by a foul report, I beseech your discipleship, as though kneeling with bowed knees and bent hocks, that it may by no means, through seductive luxury, go to the brothel-prostitutes—trifles in which puffed-up harlots lurk—who are adorned, like courtly women, with gleaming gold ankle-rings and smooth armlets as though with phalerae; but rather, rejecting the lofty magnificence of the court possessed by patricians and praetors, may your brotherhood happily enjoy the humble lodging of a hut.

And, in opposition to the cold blasts of winter rising long ago from the northern region, may it use, as Christ’s discipline teaches, a light cloak and the unadorned covering of a shaggy garment rather than dyed purple.

## EPISTLE XIV. OF THE BLESSED ALDHELM, BISHOP, GRANTED TO ALL THE COMMUNITIES ESTABLISHED UNDER HIS GOVERNANCE

[Extracted from the register of the monastery of Malmesbury. See Alf., *Annales Ecclesiastici Anglicani*, II, 451.]

### On the Freedom of One’s Own Election

Nothing in this age enjoys prolonged happiness; nothing possesses lasting dominion; nothing appears not to be hastening with swift course toward the fated end of life. Therefore we must enjoy the patrimonies of worldly things in such a way that we are never deprived of the benefits of our eternal homeland.

For this reason I, Aldhelmus, after divine grace had enthroned me—though unworthy and approved by no merits deserving such honor—in the seat of pontifical office, resolved in the secret affection of my mind that my monasteries, Maildunesburg, Frome, and Bradanford, over which, having long ago been established as abbot, I had regularly presided with the Lord’s support, should establish, by canonical creation and regular sanction, a religious abbot whom the voluntary choice of my communities had elected with unanimous voice.

My monks stubbornly resisted these voluntary proposals of mine. When I had repeatedly and diligently related this in the assembly of my brothers, no one offered the most welcome assent to my wishes. They said:

“As long as you are sustained by the breath of life and remain devoted with us to the concerns of the present life, we do not disdain humbly to submit our necks always to the yoke of your rule. But we beg you by this humble and common petition to strengthen, by the testimony of Sacred Scripture and the clear agreement of favorable men, the provision that after your death neither royal audacity nor pontifical authority, nor any man of ecclesiastical or secular rank, may claim authority over us without the decision of our will.”

I most willingly consented to this rightful petition of my monks, especially of the servants of God. In the monastery situated beside the river called Wenburnia, over which Cuthberga, sister of our venerable king, presides, with the desirable consent of the famous King Ine and the devout approval of my most reverend brother and fellow bishop Daniel, I confirmed by the sign of the holy cross the most proper petition of the servants of the Lord that had been presented.

The same venerable king and the aforementioned bishop likewise subscribed with equal devotion. Not long afterward, in the most sacred council known to have been assembled beside the river called Wodor, the authority of all the archimandrites of the Saxon people, with the assent of royal power and the approval of pontifical authority, likewise consented.

But if anyone attempts to act against the decrees of such illustrious persons and presumes to violate the sacred decisions of this present document, let him know that before the terrible throne of the divine Majesty he will be struck by the mournful judgment of condemnation together with the transgressors of the Lord’s commandments.

This charter of confirmation was written in the year 705 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the third indiction.

+ Sign of the hand of Daniel, bishop.  
+ Sign of King Ine.  
+ Sign of the hand of the patrician Ethelred.

# THE TREATISES OF SAINT ALDHELM, BISHOP OF SHERBORNE, OR THE SECOND PART OF HIS WORKS

## ON THE PRAISE OF VIRGINITY, OR ON THE VIRGINITY OF THE SAINTS

[Note: I collated the prose work *On Virginity* first with the manuscript of Gonville and Caius College; after the text had already been printed, I collated it again with the Bodleian manuscript (97). — Giles.]

### I

To the most reverend virgins of Christ, venerated with every devoted affection of sisterhood, celebrated not only—as is the case with many—for the praise of bodily chastity but also—as is the case with few—glorified by the grace of spiritual purity: Hildelith, teacher of regular discipline and monastic conduct; likewise Justina and Cutberga, and also Osburga, joined to me by the bonds of kindred relationship; Aldgida and Scholastica; Hidburga and Burngida [Bodleian manuscript: Berengida]; Eulalia and Thecla, who unanimously adorn the Church by the report of their holiness—to these Aldhelmus, a sluggish pilgrim of Christ’s cross and a suppliant servant of the Church, sends the desired blessing of perpetual prosperity.

### II

When I was recently setting out for a pontifical council, accompanied by bands of brotherly companions, I gladly received the writings of your kindness that had been brought to my mediocrity. Raising my palms toward heaven, I took care to offer immense thanks to Christ with joyful gratitude for your well-being. In those writings not only did the ecclesiastical bonds of the promises and vows that you had pledged with faithful assurance shine forth abundantly, but also the studies of the honey-flowing divine Scriptures were revealed in a most discerning sequence of words.

As I read aloud each text of your letters, examining them with the swift sight of my eyes and contemplating them with a certain natural curiosity concerning hidden matters—which, as I am told, has been implanted in me—and as I greatly admired the abundant eloquence of your words and the virginal *desertitudo* (“artlessness” or “unpolishedness”) of your expression [Bodleian manuscript: *disertitudo*, “eloquence”], behold, I say, the ruler of Olympus above and governor of heaven rejoices with ineffable delight when he sees Catholic servants of Christ—indeed, daughters of the regenerating grace adopted by him—born from the fruitful womb of ecclesiastical conception through the seed of the spiritual word, instructed in divine teachings by maternal care, and exercised in the gymnasium under the disciplines of the wrestling-ground and athletic arts, like discerning gymnosophists under a highly skilled trainer.

By these labors they earnestly obtain the crown of strenuous combat and the triumph of the Olympic contest through the most difficult exertions of their own practice.

One of them, therefore, diligently strives to exercise the vigorous struggles of athletes with a rival, sweating as he bends his sides in sinuous movements, drenched in the middle of the wrestling-ground with the fragrant nard of slippery oil.

Another, drawing the bolts of catapults and the darts of arrows from the hidden recesses of a quiver, does not release them freely through the air at the passive gaze of the eyes, but, in order to show definite sights to the pupils (*demonstraret*; Bodleian manuscript: *demonstrat*), directs them unfailingly toward their appointed place with a resounding bow and a shrieking bowstring.

Another trusts in the swift feet of runners panting in the stadium. Concerning them the distinguished combatant and teacher of divine speech says: “All run, but one receives the prize.” Surpassing the troops participating in the contest and the companions in labor, the fortunate victor happily enjoys the palm of victory.

Another rides with a crowd of kinsmen upon an ornamented horse, whose sides, bloodied by spurs and beaten with whips, are adorned with golden trappings. Of it the witty poet wrote:

> With four-footed speed the hoof beats the crumbling field,  
> swiftly intertwining circles with circles, and measuring the spaces of the earth.

Another, surrounded by cohorts of sailors and enclosed by dense ranks of rowers, drives a swift ship or light boat through the glassy gulfs of Ocean, urged on continually by the helmsman and propelled by the foaming, seaweed-laden strokes of the oars, while the boatswain’s signal sounds [Bodleian manuscript: “the helmsman’s signal”].

### III

All these activities that we have brought forward as exercises of the gymnosophists are indeed performed, among the scholarly disciplines of secular learning, through the diligence of your discipleship—not by movements of the exterior person, but by the actions of the inner person.

For I do not think it has escaped your discerning skill that the microcosm, that is, the lesser world, consists of a twofold and dual substance of matter. Rather, just as the nature of the exterior person, who was visibly formed in the open and is visibly perceived, can readily be discerned, so I believe that the quality of the inner person—who, according to the account in Genesis, is believed to have been inspired by a heavenly breath—has been subtly investigated by your prudence limb by limb and part by part.

Indeed, that most renowned bearer of Christ’s name set forth athletic competition as an example for Christian warfare, saying: “They do it to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible”; and elsewhere: “Not as one beating the air.”

Although the examples of athletes, who by bodily agility obtain the spectacles of theatrical crowds and the praises of the circus, properly correspond as comparisons to those who run through the broad stadiums of Scripture and, through constant application to reading, exercise the most discerning diligence of mind and the quality of a lively intellect—

### IV

Nevertheless, abundant experience clearly shows that the industry of the most diligent bee can be fitted to the foregoing patterns of example. When the dewy twilight has departed and the radiance of the clearest sun has risen, dense armies of dancing swarms immediately spread in groups across the open fields.

At one moment they settle upon the honey-bearing leaves of the caltha or the purple flowers of the mallows, plucking drop by drop with their mouths the sweet trickles of nectar, and, like slowly thickened boiled-down must prepared for royal dishes, striving eagerly to fill the receptacles of their entrails.

At another, they surround the yellow willow branches (*saliculas*; Bodleian manuscript: *saliculos*) and the saffron-colored tops of the broom, carrying fertile booty on their numerous legs and the burdens of their thighs, with which they construct their waxen camps.

At another, pressing together the rounded clusters of ivy and the very light shoots of flowering lime trees, they build a multiform structure of honeycombs with angular, covered cells.

The distinguished poet, relying on metrical eloquence, is believed to have sung of this labor in a catalectic verse when he said:

> The honeycombs grow yellow in gem-studded baskets;

and, in a shorter catalectic verse, or conclusion:

> And the golden vessels shine with their own honeycombs.

For just as a swarm, having streamed forth in troops through the narrow openings of the windows and the confined vestibules of the hive, ravages the pleasant meadows of the fields, so, unless I am mistaken, your memorial intellect wanders widely through the flower-filled fields of Scripture, running onward with thirsty curiosity.

Now it investigates with strenuous attention the divine oracles of the ancient prophets, which long ago foretold the coming of the Savior with sure assurances.

Now it carefully scrutinizes the mysteries of the ancient laws, wonderfully arranged by him who is described as having cruelly struck the Egyptian kingdoms with ten successive afflictions, and as having separated the swelling gulfs of the Red Sea and the returning waves of the foaming sea from one another by the holy touch of the staff, recently transformed from a serpent into the image of a wall, and afterward, following a heavenly conversation, as having driven away the unbelieving crowd with a horned face.

Now it diligently investigates the sayings of the evangelical account in four ways (*quadrifariam*; Bodleian manuscript: *quadrifaria*), expounded in the mystical commentaries of the Catholic Fathers and spiritually clarified to the very marrow, and arranged according to the fourfold rules of ecclesiastical tradition: historically, allegorically, tropologically, and anagogically.

Now it properly examines the ancient tales of historians and the sequence of chroniclers who handed down the accidental changes of past times in the enduring fabric of memory.

Now it insightfully investigates the rules of grammarians and the disciplines of orthographers, weighed according to tones and tenses, compacted in poetic feet, and divided by cola and commas—that is, by penthemimeres and hepthemimeres—indeed separated individually into hundreds of kinds of meter.

### V

The bee, I say, because of the privilege of its particular chastity, is affirmed by the unquestionable authority of Scripture to prefigure the type of most chaste virginity and the form of the Church. Ravaging the flowering turf of the forests with ineffable booty, it produces the sweet pledges of its offspring, knowing no marriage, through a fertile concentration of the most delightful juice.

The Church, however, piercing the living hearts of human beings with the two-edged sword of the Testaments, makes the hereditary offspring of legitimate eternity fruitful through the chaste seed of the word.

### VI

I also think that something should be recalled about the harmonious fellowship of bees, something wondrous, as though in a theatrical spectacle: namely, the voluntary inclination toward willing servitude that they are known to exercise in service to their rulers.

Does not all the discipline of monastic conduct and the regular institutions of monasteries become clear through a very similar comparison?

For as long as the one who performs the office of ruler among the others decides to inhabit their ancient seats [the text has *illa*; Bodleian manuscript: *ille*], and care for their small dwellings woven from slender branches or stitched together from hollowed bark, none of the immense multitude wanders through the air in flight or roams about as a fugitive.

But if, for definite reasons and under the compulsion of the necessity of travel, the one to whom the rule of the others has been entrusted in place of a consul prefers to seek foreign kingdoms, nowhere among mortals would you see an exile, driven from his own homeland, accompanied by armies so dense and cohorts of legions so closely packed together.

They proceed abroad much more willingly out of reverence for their ruler than they remain in their cells, accustomed to domestic delights and content with native peace [Bodleian manuscript: *incolatum … proficiscantur*, “they proceed into residence abroad”].

What, I ask, can be seen in the nature of visible things that obeys the command of its creator [Bodleian manuscript: *quod* for *quid*] with such great zeal and strives to fulfill the order of its king?

Thus, deservedly, because of the type of untouched virginity and the service of spontaneous devoted submission by which it offers an example of obedience to mortals dwelling in the valley of tears, it prepares a nectarous food before all other creatures and stores nourishment of honeyed sweetness in its yellow waxen hut.

This nourishment not only surpasses all dishes of delight and all peppered abundance of food, and overcomes every incense of fragrant ambrosia and every scent of breathing nard; it also—as the discourse passes from the particular to the general—surpasses the sweetness of every worldly pleasure, exceeds the refined delights of opulent luxury, and despises the drinking of boiled-down wine.

### VII

Therefore, if the glory of holy virginity is believed to be akin to angelic blessedness, and if the beautiful fellowship of the citizens above is rightly praised for its chastity, it must be exalted with fitting praises, since it is recognized as governing among the other insignia of virtues the scepters of supreme authority and the monarchy of rule.

For just as every pleasant and delightful thing introduced to the human throat and mortal palate incomparably surpasses all other tastes with the sweetness of honey, so divine Majesty—which I shall nevertheless say with the peace and reverence due to the saints who were once joined by marital bonds—has placed the special privilege of virginity above all the degrees of the general virtues enumerated in the catalogue of spiritual gifts.

A sufficiently clear indication of this is found in the fact that, when the venerable offspring of God descended from the highest summit of heaven to redeem the wandering sheep and seek the lost drachma, he entered the womb of one endowed with undefiled virgin childbirth without endangering perpetual purity or diminishing chastity.

For this reason also, I believe, the sacred one who reclined upon the Lord’s breast and was the fourth stream of paradise—the one who chiefly watered the seven churches of Asia with inexhaustible showers of doctrine—earned, before the other apostolic heralds, a special prerogative of divine love and a private generosity of affection.

He had voluntarily offered the pleasing libations of virginity to Christ, who is a desirous lover of chastity and a jealous teacher of holiness.

Therefore, while the true physician considered the wounds of crimes and the scars of sins by which the souls of the sick were laid low in cruel destruction, he prepared a most salutary remedy and gave the antidote of heavenly medicine as a life-giving drink to the fibers fatally infected by the poisonous draught of spiritual wickedness.

Then, climbing the summit of the gallows and suffering on the sixth day of the Sabbath, that is, on Parasceve, remembering the honor due to his mother, he mercifully commanded the disciple, who awaited the outcome amid the dangers of treacherous soldiers, to care for his mother.

Thus it may appropriately be said in a rhythmic poem:

> Christ, suffering upon the gallows,  
> and in the joyful hiding-place,  
> entrusted the Virgin to the Virgin  
> for the Virgin’s protection.

Later, when the cycles of time had passed, Domitian—who at that time, relying upon imperial scepters, inflicted savage tortures and punishments upon the worshipers of orthodox faith—banished him as an exile to Patmos. There he deserved to hear, carried away into the vision of ecstasy, and to behold with chaste eyes one hundred and fifty-four thousand virgins [Bodleian manuscript: one hundred and seventy thousand], singing an unpractised song in sweet-sounding melodic harmony.

Of them it is said: “For they are virgins, and they follow the Lamb wherever he goes.” The other faithful will hear these songs; these saints will sing them and walk together with the Lamb through the narrow glory of the heavenly kingdom [Bodleian manuscript: *Isti sancta* for *Ista sancti*].

### VIII

Nevertheless, although we heap immense praises upon the glory of virginal chastity and stir the minds of those who strive for Christ by proposing it as an example of strict conduct and an arduous purpose, we do not consider the undefiled fellowship of marriage or the lawful union of the legal marriage-bed to be despised, as the ravings of schismatics babble.

Far be this from the Catholic faith of the Churches, especially since we know for certain that in ancient times the patriarchs, while observing the divine decrees and the bonds of marriage, were pleasing to the heavenly Majesty and, filled with the charism of the Holy Spirit, foretold in prophetic words of anticipation the cradle of the future Incarnation.

Such is the saying: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent; and he will be the expectation of the nations,” and so forth. This can be clearly proved and confirmed by an accumulation of thousands of testimonies.

Yet when the dark shadow of the Old Instrument has passed away and the grace of the Gospel shines clearly (*clare*; Bodleian manuscript: *clara*, “bright”), we say that the distance between the flowers of virginity and the customs of marriage is as great as the distance between east and west.

Hence, one of the Catholic writers, explaining the flourishing glory of virginity as arising from the stock of marriage, elegantly began under the figure of a trope:

> “I read gold from the earth, a rose from the thorn, and a pearl from the shell.”

## IX.

For the bright appearance of pure silver is not disgracefully disfigured merely because the metal of glowing gold is preferred; nor does the beauty of white marble suffer any loss of loveliness when the more beautiful splendor of a reddening gem is praised. Nor do the woolen threads unwound from a skein and from little pieces of cloth become contemptibly cheap through neglect, even if a silken purple robe and the imperial garment of silk shine more splendidly.

Are pomegranates, filled with their red cells and grains and covered with the simple binding of their books, thought to endure nature’s contemptible reproach, although we believe the honey-sweet dates of the palm groves and the honey-wine of nectar, *Nicolaum* [reading uncertain], to surpass them incomparably? [Col. 0109B] Certainly the usefulness of the rough anvil, the rigid hardness of the striking hammer, or the tenacity of the rust-covered tongs and shears is not despised merely because a bossed belt, a royal diadem, and the various splendor of ornaments fashioned and wrought from those same iron instruments are preferred.

Nor does the smooth circular disk of the lunar sphere suffer any loss of its own beauty, although the brilliant radiance of the clearest sun is believed to illuminate the world’s three-cornered wheel more brightly. Do we think the deep water of a well, or the cold water of a cistern, which we draw out with a water-lifting device—that is, an *anthlia*, or the whole drawing apparatus [Bodl.: “wheel”]—should be held cheap, although the alternating overflow of the purest spring seems to surpass it, and the unceasing course of aqueducts, raised aloft in an elevated channel through frequent and lofty arched vaults, with devouring cascades, seems to excel it? [Col. 0109C]

For the dark form of the voracious diver-bird is not confused, nor is the black creation of its body despised, merely because the many-colored glory of the peacock excels it in the smooth roundness of its circles. The beauty of the peacock’s feathers now yellows with a saffron hue, now reddens with purple loveliness, now gleams with the green brilliance of a blue-gray color, or shines with the appearance of yellow gold. The dignity of its beauty, not without reason compared with the virginal form, despises the remaining toys of the world and considers the ornamentation of the adorned age of little worth.

For blessed Augustine testifies in the book *The City of God* that by experiment he proved the flesh of the peacock to be naturally incorruptible. For is the nature of wild trees, or the barren greenness of leaves, or the moist little stalk of earthly plants, despised when purple and crimson flowers, arising from the very branches of the trees or produced from the little plants of the spring meadow, redden more beautifully and emit a sweeter fragrance by the force of their scent? Yet it is evident that from flowers the benefits of coming fruits wonderfully ripen with abundant return and manifold gain, while the leafy foliage of shoots and the thick tendrils of vines, once the sap has ceased to flow, miserably wither and, when the burning heat of autumn approaches, fall in masses like the densest carpet. [Col. 0109D]

“No,” I say, “does the sublimity of praiseworthy virginity shine like a lofty beacon set upon a high rocky promontory in such a way that the strict continence of marriage, which is the second rank, becomes altogether despised and worthless below it, or that the fruitfulness of lawful marriage, undertaken for the succession of children, is notably diminished.” I do not see that such a good is dishonored by comparison; rather, I judge that what is better should be praised more earnestly.

## X.

And yet, most often—alas!—when the orders have been altered, the reverse commonly occurs: the lower degree of life, gradually advancing in every way, overtakes the higher one while it lies sluggish and torpid. Stirred by the spur of the sharpest contrition, the one who had earlier been superior and had achieved the victory of his vow is surpassed, while the one who had been considered later because of the negligence of his former way of life thereafter becomes the foremost, inflamed by the fire of divine love and remembering the evangelical saying: “To whom much is forgiven, he loves much.”

The one who, scorning the blandishments of the world as refuse and rejecting the allurements of carnal luxury, had become a successor in the holy vocation, now courageously undertaking the apprenticeship of a chaste life, trembling at the dreadful abyss of Gehenna and burning with desire for eternal life, supported by Christ’s free grace, becomes an antecedent through the labor of his sweat. I judge that this should be mourned with lamentable sobs and tearful groans by those of either sex who, with weeping struggles and deep sighs from the heart, must grieve over it.

Those who are puffed up with the swollen brow of pride boast only of the integrity of their flesh, while others, having escaped the perilous shipwreck of the world and the raging whirlwind of the dreadful storm, hasten toward the harbor of monastic life like sailors navigating between Sicily’s Scylla and the abyss of the chasm, and, although the joints of their little boat have been somewhat shaken, arrive safely under Christ’s guidance. [Col. 0110B]

But these others, seeking the habit of holy conduct with the ships of their souls intact and the boat of their undefiled bodies safe, without encountering the reefs, are all the less eager to devote themselves to lamentation and to wet their faces with showers of tears because they trust that they have not been disfigured by any stain or befouled by any mark of worldly dross.

The former never cease to moisten their sorrowful faces with the dewy springs of their eyes and dripping eyelids, all the more because they remember that they committed certain forbidden acts, prohibited by the severity of the law, amid the company of the world. But the latter, because they consider themselves celibate, chaste, and entirely free from every sewer of impurity, swell arrogantly, puffed up by confidence in their virginity, and do not avoid by the circle of humility the most savage whale of pride, which devours all the other virtues. [Col. 0110D]

## XI.

For in the conflict against the eight principal vices, although pride is placed last, it is recognized as usurping for itself, more than the others, the command of tyrannical power and the monarchy of domination, like a savage queen. Without any doubtful hesitation, one must truly believe that Lucifer, surrounded by the companions of his parasitism and gathered together with the satellites of apostasy, first fell headlong into the deep abyss of pride and the dark Tartarus of swollen arrogance before the first-created man, inhabitant of the newly planted paradise and possessor of the whole earthly creation—which the smooth revolving vault of heaven whirls around like a rotating sling—fell cruelly into the gulf of gluttony by tasting the forbidden food with his broad, ravenous mouth and greedy lips. [Col. 0111A]

If the lofty company of the heavenly citizens was deprived of blessed fellowship with the others and of participation in the divine contemplation merely because it swelled with the brow of arrogance, how much more will the exceedingly frail weakness of mortals be unhappily excluded from the banqueting hall of the heavenly Bridegroom if it swells like an inflated bladder over the profits of its own merits and begins, with the gums of *kenodoxia*—vainglory—to chew the little morsels of virginal chastity as though it were a special sanctity?

Therefore Christ’s virgins and the Church’s recruits must fight with sinewy strength against the dreadful beast of pride and at the same time against these seven poisonous beasts of the vices. With ravenous molars and venomous teeth they strive savagely to tear apart the defenseless, those stripped of the armor of virginity and deprived of the shield of chastity. We must contend vigorously, as against the fiercest legions of barbarians, with the darts of spiritual armor and the iron-tipped spears of the virtues. Those barbarian forces never cease, troop by troop, to shake Christ’s recruits’ testudo with the ballistae of twisted deceit. Let us not, like timid soldiers who womanishly fear the horror of war and the blast of the trumpet, sluggishly offer the backs of our shoulders to the fiercest enemies in place of shield-bosses. [Col. 0111B]

Rather, let the champions of monastic warfare boldly present to the ranks of their adversaries the front armed with the standard of the cross. Let them carry steadfastly the weapons of war that the outstanding warrior enumerates: the sword of the divine word and the unbreakable breastplate of faith. Protected by the secure shield, let them persist against the thousand arts of harm employed by spiritual wickedness. Then, having received from Christ our rewarder the triumph due to victory, we shall rejoice and celebrate happily in the heavenly dwellings and celestial glory—if now, like the Lord’s soldiers, we fight bravely at the front of the battle against the principalities of Leviathan, the powers of darkness, and the rulers of the world, obstinately resisting obstinate foes.

## XII.

First, as I have said, let us strive, relying on divine assistance, to overcome the leaders of the eight principal vices, to whom the Cherethites of crimes and the Pelethites of wicked deeds are enslaved with a dreadful apparatus of war. They never cease to fight tirelessly against the ranks of Christ’s recruits and the warlike cohorts of virgins with the enemy’s savage armies, with innumerable fire-darts of deceit and dense missiles of deception, although often, when Christ grants protection and encourages the phalanxes of his soldiers with the palm of predestined victory, they shamefully turn their fleeing backs.

But, alas, the prosperity of the peace we have gained is not secure, nor is the happiness of acquired triumphs safe, nor is the trophy of deceptive fortune inflexible and lasting. For the enemies who were thought to have been brutally slaughtered to the point of annihilation in a final massacre, and who had been happily defeated by the desired success of events, again, in reverse, summon the victors to an unwelcome battle, take up bloody arms, renew the dreadful war, and prepare revived conflicts for those who have obtained their wish. [Col. 0112A]

Therefore let the unwelcome dragon of gluttony be driven away first by abstinence from food. This is the dragon that lethally vomited the poisonous virus of transgression from its venomous throat upon the first inhabitants of the flower-filled earth. Finally, let the savage serpent of pride—the one that sorrowfully disturbed the blessed household of heaven and the citizens of the gracious city—be expelled from the hidden recesses of our soul and the secret hiding places of our hearts, and be thrust far away under divine terror [Bodl.: “driven on”].

Just as the Hebrew phalanx, advancing in twelve times fifty thousand expeditionary troops and infantry formations, handed over to the jaws of the abyss of hell the seven nations of the Canaanites—which typologically shadow the seven divisions of the vices—after Pharaoh’s eager army had been submerged in the waters of the Red Sea and suffocated in the deep waves of the ocean, through which gluttony is represented; and just as Israel, so long as it did not resist the sanctions of the Decalogue, happily inhabited the promised land, divided by lot among the twelve tribes, and thus left the lineage of its ancestral race to its grandchildren and great-grandchildren as a perpetual possession by the lawful right of inheritance— [Col. 0112B]

## XIII.

But if the vigilant concern of your discernment eagerly desires to know how many troops of legions serve the aforesaid leaders of spiritual wickedness and the dark princes of darkness; how many tyrannical fellow-soldiers of the military ranks follow, intending harm to human nature; how many satellites of the wicked conspire to attack our battle line and gather together in companies to overthrow the bulwarks of faith; and how, by the specific properties of their names, the various members of that same impious army are individually called—both the camp-followers and dependents, belonging to the lower rank together with the bands of servants, and the satraps and nobles who claim for themselves the disgraceful tribunate of those same spirits—

if you desire to observe these matters more fully, they are plainly disclosed not only by the ten Conferences composed by Cassian, archimandrite of the district of Marseille, endowed with a special eloquence for dictation, but also by Gregory, bishop of the apostolic see, from whom we received the beginnings of faith and the sacraments of baptism, who clarified them allegorically, more brightly than daylight, in the thirty books of the *Moralia*. [Col. 0113A]

These are the profane armies of the Philistines, formed into hundreds and thousands, which urge on the Israelites gathered at the summit of Mount Gilboa to battle: namely, the dreadful unseen armies of the vices, which, with their appointed leaders, strive to rush in groups against the Catholic parish of the Church. With the poisonous darts of their crimes and the terrible sword of their wicked deeds, they wound not only the sluggish but sometimes also lay low the veteran soldiers of Christ with the deadly wound of chastity—[Bodl.: “and with a deadly arrow”]—so that the intellectual David, who is the flower of the shoot descending from the root of Jesse, may not undeservedly compose, with compassionate feeling, a funeral song and lamentation—called an *epithrenion* and an *epitaphion*—over the peoples of the Church falling in heaps beneath the slaughter of the vices.

I say, if your curious and diligent concern has preferred to observe these matters more fully, we have been compelled to debate and discuss the roots of the eight shameful vices above all for this reason: certain people, raised to the summit of virginity and exalted upon the strongholds of public [Bodl.: “chaste”] conduct, consider the second degree of chastity contemptible and far beneath themselves, and trust that they surpass incomparably the praises of the others, somehow blotting out and putting behind them the saying: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” [Col. 0113B]

For although the undefiled virginity of Mary gave birth to the incarnate Word of God through a heavenly childbirth, nevertheless, after the course of one week had passed, Anna, the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, proclaimed the same Redeemer under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Therefore both degrees shine as consecrated to virgins and widows at the beginning of the divine birth, so that the one enriched by the abundance of a hundredfold fruit may in no way presume arrogantly to consider of little worth the one enriched by sixtyfold bundles. Otherwise the wound of bodily virginity may generate pride in the mind, or the remedy of health may nourish the fuel of destruction.

For calamity must be mourned if the gracious substance of humility, by which the growth of the remaining virtues is healthfully preserved, fastens to holy virginity a restraint or snare of pride [Bodl.: “a net … a snare”], and if the antidotes and remedies that ordinarily remove deadly poison, their order being changed, become sources of harm rather than salvation. [Col. 0113C]

## XIV.

On the other hand, certain imitators of the blessed life, who from the very beginning of their infancy never cease to persevere tirelessly in the highest resolve of virginity and strive happily to preserve the unbroken barriers of chastity to the end without any offense against purity, are nevertheless so pierced by the spur of divine love and inflamed by the spark of heavenly ardor that every day they eagerly desire to depart from the world’s misery and emigrate from the prison of the body, revealing through the frugality of their restraint how quickly they wish to hasten to the heavenly homeland of paradise.

They cannot conceal their burning desire of mind with furtive songs of psalmody and counterfeit springs of tears; through frequent sighs of contrition, uttered from the deepest recesses of their hearts, they groan heavily. Thus they are sweetly satisfied with the delight of the contemplative life and fattened on the nectar-like food of contemplative sweetness, so that no one in the practice of the active life—which we call practical conduct—can equal them, even while washing away his offenses with tears.

To such people, who are known to increase the glory of virginity through this supplement of virtues and holiness of conduct, every lofty greatness of the continent yields, and every sublime eminence of the married yields. [Col. 0113D]

## XV.

Therefore let no one trust that this single privilege of purity is sufficient for the complete attainment of perfection without the assistance of the other virtues, as though, having preserved only this, he might remain at leisure and secure without struggling against the remaining vices.

Rather, lest the noble distinction of singular virginity become shabby because it lacks adornment, let it be supported by the remaining aid of the legal precepts and suitably adorned by the manifold variety of the commandments. Thus, according to the Psalmist’s saying, it may shine like a queen at the right hand of the divine Majesty in a golden garment, gleaming with a variety of merits, and accompanied continually by heavenly cohorts may deserve to stand in attendance and happily enjoy the inseparable fellowship of the angels.

Otherwise, the unadorned diligence of virginity, without the support of the remaining virtues, will not be enriched with the abundant harvest of the ecclesiastical field and with a hundredfold sheaves of merits; rather, withering in fruitless and barren sterility, it will be punished with the foolish virgins carrying extinguished lamps.

For the weaving of curtains or coverings, unless little pieces of cloth dyed purple—or rather with a variety of different colors—run back and forth among the dense threads and unless the art of embroidery adorns the whole woven work with various figured panels, will plainly seem neither pleasing to the eyes nor beautiful in the loveliest elegance of ornament if it has been made piece by piece in a uniform color.

The curtain of the ancient sanctuary, too, is not said to have shone with a simple and single kind of dye. Rather, it is described as gleaming with gold, hyacinth, purple, scarlet twice-dyed or vermilion, together with twisted byssus, and with varied sea-purple. [Col. 0114C]

But why do we devise subtle thoughts about dyes and sea-purple? Even a sheet of pure gold—the gold that surpasses the other metals of silver, electrum, and tin—will somehow appear cheap without topaz, carbuncle, and the red glory of gems, or the amber-colored dragon-stone.

Examine these distinct varieties of colors and kinds of metals, assumed for the increase and enlargement of the merits of chastity, according to the rule of allegory; search them out through the mystical explanations of the Fathers by the typological scrutiny of tropology.

## XVI.

Therefore let the true, not frivolous, glory of tender virginity be protected by the true, not false, vigilance of humility. Let the wantonness of noble and tender youth be restrained, as it were, by the hard discipline of a tutor, because the mind is lifted up in vain over chastity alone when it is wounded by the dart of pride; and the spirit rejoices over the grace of integrity to no purpose if it is pierced by the dart of swelling arrogance.

Indeed, as we have learned by experience, the consciousness of chastity is often struck by the *kenodoxia* of pride. From the very thing by which it considers itself superior to the other faithful in the Church through the merit of the holiness it has attained, it will be deprived of the deserved reward and robbed of the palm of its laborious contest.

For the evangelical word did not promise that all the companies of ten virgins would be received into the bridal chamber of the heavenly Bridegroom and rejoice together with equal celebration in heavenly glory. It promised this only to those who, preserving the marriage decrees with the shining lamps of purity and the torches burning with the oil of chastity, will deserve happily to meet the returning Bridegroom from above. [Col. 0115A]

Therefore it seems worthwhile first to uproot completely the weeds of wickedness and the growths of pride, and to make the most fruitful plantings of the fruit-bearing tree fertile with flourishing foliage. Thus, once the fuel of the vices has been eradicated and the roots of the passions torn out, we may be able to cultivate fruitful shoots of the virtues, with Christ planting them.

Thus bodily integrity is in no way approved unless spiritual chastity accompanies it as a partner. Hence the Chosen Vessel says: “That she may be holy in body and spirit.” Behold, the apostolic words make clear that immunity from bodily impurity alone cannot open the gates of the heavenly kingdom, nor can it by itself unlock the gate of paradise, which the conclusion of Genesis originally declares to have been closed by the cherub with a revolving and flaming sword, unless a twofold holiness shines harmoniously on both sides.

Hence the same Apostle says: “I discipline my body and bring it into servitude”—namely, lest the flesh grow insolently against the spirit with tyrannical power and, swelling with the arrogant pride of liberty, disdain to bend its neck to the yoke of lawful servitude.

Therefore the pure and undefiled perseverance of virginity is devoted to God through unwearied diligence of thought; conversely, the freedom of unrestrained marriage becomes the captive poverty of secure immunity.

## XVII.

The outstanding preacher distinguishes this twofold quality of life in the following manner: “There is a difference between the wife and the virgin: the unmarried woman thinks about the things of the Lord, how she may please God; but the married woman thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband.”

There is indeed a great interval and a broad difference of spacious separation between the generosity of divine love and the diligence of lowly affection. The one rejoices that she will be the companion of angelic chastity; the other delights in being the fuel of marital sensuality.

The one longs to adorn her neck with crescents, her arms with bracelets, and her fingers with jeweled rings; the other desires to shine in the loveliest splendor of radiant chastity, to gleam with the golden necklaces of the virtues, and at the same time to be adorned with the white pearls of merits.

The one carefully arranges herself delicately with curled locks, crimped by the curling iron, and strives to paint her cheeks and jaws in rows with red cosmetic; the other, with the unadorned cutting of her hair and a carelessly roughened head of hair, will bring forth upon her head a crown of glory with the palm of virginity.

The one, fruitless amid foolish displays of ornaments, arranged like that woman whom the Apocalypse describes as sitting upon the beast and offering in a golden cup the deadly draught of prostitution, presents to those who look upon her a spectacle both beautiful and destructive. The other never ceases to display to those who desire to imitate them the examples of chaste conduct and of the citizens above. [Col. 0115D]

## XVIII.

Therefore the future exaltation of angelic life is already, in a certain manner, violently anticipated by the men and women who follow undefiled virginity and carry a treasure pleasing to God in an earthen vessel, although it is voluntarily anticipated by spontaneous affection, because “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.”

It is clear, indeed, that the condition of affairs is exceedingly difficult and demanding: a human being, whom maternal fertility has brought forth into the world from the genuine womb of birth, must reject the laws of nature and become an undivided companion of angelic chastity. Before the supreme glory of the resurrection casts the dominion of dreadful death into dark Tartarus and “this incorruptible” [Bodl.: “corruptible”] puts on incorruption, earthly celibates are compelled, in a wondrous manner, to become heavenly citizens.

Therefore our Lord, refuting and rejecting the factional accusation of the Pharisaic temptation with the argument of his true answer, says: “In the resurrection they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but they will be like the angels in heaven.”

O splendid grace of virginity, which, like a rose arising from thorny shoots, reddens with its purple flower and never withers through the failure of dreadful mortality! Although the weary frailty of dying flesh grows weak, and, as the end of fate approaches, ages with stooping and bent old age, virginity alone continually grows green and constantly grows young like joyful youth.

“Concerning virgins,” says the Apostle, “I have no command of the Lord,” so that the gift of the greater merit may be what is offered by the free choice of spontaneous will rather than what is ordered to be fulfilled by the strict authority of a compulsory command.

Formerly, when the earth’s three-cornered breadth had not yet been filled with the lineage of fruitful offspring, divine decrees were issued in this manner: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth.” Now, however, the decrees of the same King are changed according to the quality of the times, and he is thought to promulgate the law differently: “Whoever can receive it, let him receive it.” [Bodl.: “they are thought to promulgate it.”] [Col. 0116C]

He, knowing human frailty, seems to urge this not by the stern goad of a command but by the gentle counsel of a merciful suggestion, so that each person, devoted to the free examination of the will and endowed with the judgment of choice, may test the capacity of his strength and, investigating the quality of his own virtue, strive to endure the long labor of patience. The blessed possession of this gift is obtained from Christ by the special diligence of one’s own virtue through persistent prayers, as he himself bears witness: “Not all receive this word, but those to whom it has been given.”

Therefore human diligence agrees with divine indulgence; and in that which we earnestly ask for in faithful prayer, let us also cooperate with fitting effects of our works.

Thereafter, let us confidently await from the true trainer of the contest, who watches the course of the struggle, the palm of patience [Bodl.: “awaiting”]. At the end of the contest, the one who now appears never to grow weary in preserving virginity will undoubtedly deserve to receive it, so that, when the enemies have been defeated, he may proclaim the sweet melody to be sung by the hymnist and joyfully chant the triumphal song with apostolic exultation:

“I have fought the good fight, I have completed the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the righteous Judge, the Lord, will award me on that day.”

## XIX.

Moreover, the Catholic Church, worshiper of orthodox faith, receives the threefold distinction of the human race, as it is related in a certain volume through an angelic account: virginity, chastity, and marriage differ separately in three degrees. Just as they are individually separated by a threefold diversity of unequal life, so they are distinguished in three ways by distinct orders of merit, as the angel alternately distinguishes them in this manner:

Virginity is gold; chastity, silver; marriage, bronze.

Virginity is wealth; chastity, moderate means; marriage, poverty.

Virginity is peace; chastity, redemption; marriage, captivity.

Virginity is the sun; chastity, the moon; marriage, darkness.

Virginity is day; chastity, dawn; marriage, night.

Virginity is queen; chastity, mistress; marriage, handmaid.

Virginity is the homeland; chastity, the harbor; marriage, the open sea.

Virginity is a human being; chastity, one half-alive; marriage, a body.

Virginity is purple; chastity, renewed color; marriage, wool.

All these are not outside the king’s palace. Yet in one manner the dignity of prefecture sits in a carriage, in another manner the lowliness of mule-drivers, and in another manner the person who restrains the mules on foot; nevertheless, all are known to serve under one emperor, and so forth. [Col. 0117B]

From the argument of this distinction it may be inferred and gathered that virginity is the state of one who remains chaste, undefiled by all carnal impurity, through the spontaneous desire of celibacy; chastity is the state of one who, having entered into marriage through betrothal agreements, has renounced marital relations for the sake of the heavenly kingdom; and marriage is the state of one who is bound by lawful marital bonds for the propagation of posterity and the begetting of children.

To these three orders of degree, by which the multitude of believers flourishing in the Catholic Church is distinguished, the evangelical paradigm promised a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit according to the commerce of their merits. Some, however, customarily assign the sheaves of hundredfold fruit, flourishing abundantly in the evangelical fields and producing the husks of grain-bearing ears, to the martyrs’ sacred blood shed for the confession of Christianity.

But lest the verbose chatter—or chattering verbosity—of my own argument, lacking the firm support of the Scriptures, be censured by anyone, with Christ’s favor I shall strive to weave the fairest crown of virginity by plucking the purple flowers of chastity from the meadow of the sacred books.

## XX.

The prophet Elijah, adorned with the grace of virginity and inspired by the prophetic spirit, opened the gates of heaven and the barriers of the clouds through prayer. He destroyed two captains of fifty soldiers, blazing with the lightning of heavenly fire and consumed by a cruel flame, to burn in the fires above. Thereafter, as the poet relates in heroic hexameter,

> Carried upward to the stars in golden, flame-bearing chariots,

he entered the starry path in a flashing chariot. Raised into heaven below the limit of human life, he is recognized as having escaped the general debt of death for a long time, dwelling vitally in a certain hidden region of the climate, while all who are bound by the violent laws of nature and fettered by the bonds of the first transgression are compelled to pay death as an unavoidable tax and fiscal tribute.

Elisha, however, endowed with twice Elijah’s spirit and furnished with a double grace—in whose coming a golden quadruped is described as having resounded at Gilgal with a braying voice, signifying that the fall of idolatry and the ceremonies of images must be rejected—did he not, relying on the virginal fillet of chastity and on his master’s mantle, divide the enormous current of the Jordan? Did he not hand over young men who mocked the prophet with the derision of their jeering to the ravenous jaws of ursine ferocity? And, having himself been lulled to sleep by death, did he not restore living breath even to a corpse suffocated in the jaws of icy death? [Col. 0118A]

Behold, holy Jeremiah appears openly before us as an example of the virginal state. Before he was brought forth in his mother’s childbirth, he is said to have been set apart for the Lord by blessed predestination, and from the very tender beginning of his crude cradle to have been consecrated to virginity. Concerning him the divine decree proclaims: “Before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you”—a beautiful omen, plainly, of virginity. How could anyone, relying on the polished eloquence of urbane speech, adequately recount how brilliantly, splendidly, and gloriously the grace of prophetic dignity shone in him?

## XXI.

Daniel, whose prophetic name means “judgment of God,” and who, because he investigated the mysteries of hidden things, was often called by the archangel “a man of desires,” is remembered as having offered voluntarily, like the fragrant incense of *thymiama*, the most pleasing gift of spontaneous virginity to the Father of spirits until the final limit of his fleeting life. [Bodl.: “as incense to the Father.”]

Although the evangelical trumpet had not yet sounded, “Whoever can receive it, let him receive it,” he is nevertheless clearly shown to have been most chaste, free from every carnal impurity and secure from the enticement of temptations. In return for his chastity, hidden things were disclosed to him above other mortals, and what had been closed beneath the mystical coverings of the sacraments was opened from heaven.

For which of the prophets who foretold the future, whose minds the gratuitous grace of the Holy Spirit inspired and abundantly enriched with prophetic gifts of virtue, is known to have woven a fuller and clearer sequence of oracles concerning the divine Incarnation? For in ten times seven weeks of years—by the reckoning of which 490 years are counted—the birth of the saving heavenly Leader is prefigured. [Bodl.: “seven times seven weeks.”]

He also explains, by suitable interpretation, the statue fashioned from four kinds of metal, signifying the ages of four kingdoms, struck and shattered by the cornerstone of the two Testaments, cut from the summit of the mountain without a man’s palm—that is, without marital union—into fragments and pieces.

He likewise interpreted the tree growing with thick branches of shoots and flourishing with fruitful twigs, whose immense height rises upward as far as the sky. Beneath the lofty cone of its summit it abundantly fed winged flocks of birds, penetrating the barriers of the clouds in swift flight, and at the same time many kinds of beasts roaming throughout the earth on four-footed courses, with rich nourishment of food—until, shaken by the heavenly will, it cruelly fell, and, cut down sorrowfully by the instrument of heavenly power, collapsed. He related prophetically that for seven cycles of years [Bodl.: “eight”] it was deprived of the luxuriant greenness of its leaves and the leafy shoots of its fruit-bearing branches. [Col. 0119A]

He is also remembered as having wisely explained, beneath a threefold meaning of the words, the terrifying letters traced with bent strokes upon the square surface of the wall, foretelling the ruin of tyrannical power and the peril of royal monarchy: **Mene, Techel, Phares**—which, when interpreted, means: “numbered, weighed, divided.”

Even at that time, we read that the three youths, descended from the ancient stock of the Hebrews and carried away to the Chaldeans in the Babylonian captivity, in no way devoted themselves to the pleasures of sexual intercourse, but remained steadfast in the strict resolve of voluntary virginity. Yet the importunate chatter of the Jews fabricates frivolous fictions, asserting that they were not pubescent men, nor the aforementioned companion of their foreign exile, voluntarily celibates devoted to chastity, but unwilling eunuchs—those whom evangelical testimony assigns to the second rank of eunuchs.

These men, finally, are described as having observed so faithfully the rule of their ancestral tradition and the judgment of divine sanction that, in order to obtain the glory of integrity and continence, they despised, in the tenderest years of puberty, the sumptuous delicacies of royal dishes and the food of the imperial table. Content to sustain life only on humble vegetables, they restrained the wanton impetuosity of youth.

Therefore, when the enormous image of the Chaldean ruler—which surpassed the height of the Colossus, stretched aloft to a height of one hundred and seven feet, by a stature of twice thirty cubits—was set up, although the terrifying blast of trumpets had sounded, and the musical harmony of sambucas had rung out in lively performance, and at the same time the fires of the flame-vomiting furnace had been kindled dreadfully with the fuel of naphtha and bundles of wood, they refused to bow their knees and look upon it. In their inflexible steadfastness of rigid mind, supported by angelic aid, they overcame by unconquered faith the scorched, clattering mechanisms and the roaring globes of the furnace.

## XXII.

But why, among the men of ancient times—men to whom the license of the old Law mercifully permitted the marital unions of the bridal chamber for the propagation of grandchildren and the offspring of later generations—should we, while seeking the treasure of virginity according to the rule, weave bonds of delay and waste the leisure of time, like bees joining together, with tenacious glue, the structures of yellow honey from the various flowers of the meadows?

For even among the new and inexperienced followers of the Catholic faith, after the hidden recesses of the former Instrument had utterly vanished and the clear lights of the succeeding Testament, illuminating the dense darkness of night through the grace of evangelical preaching, had spread more widely throughout the four-cornered circuit of the earth, countless examples of blessed virginity abound and overflow abundantly. From these we have gathered, piecemeal and hastily, the few that came to mind, so that it may more readily become plainly clear to all who seek the votive gift of integrity by whose examples the lofty stature of chastity was brought forth. Like the most excellent beacon of all virtues—or like the globe of a rounded obelisk set upon a square base—it rose aloft to such a summit of perfection and height of divine contemplation that it is rightly believed to attain the sixth step of evangelical blessedness, concerning which the figurative evangelist, like the liquid flowing from a flourishing paradise, which Ezekiel presents with a human face, fittingly bears witness:

> Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.

O how brightly the pupil of virginal chastity flashes! O how splendidly the keen vision of devout purity shines—those eyes which neither the darkness of carnal enticement dims nor the glaucoma of thorny obscenity stains! By that glaucoma, alas—sad is the saying! [Bodl., *dictu!*]—even the eyelids of the perfect often grow heavily thick, and those thought to be endowed with chastity are deceived, since human judgment is frequently mistaken, just as the eyes of people suffering from scotoma are closed by gloomy darkness.

Those who perfectly possess the glorious palm of genuine purity are believed truly to be free from this foul sewer of impurity, which mournfully drowns the little ships of souls. While carrying the victorious standards of the chaste battalion, they will joyfully march in groups through the gates of the heavenly Jerusalem, bearing the trophy of virginal triumph and the uninjured banners of chastity before the angelic assembly of the heavenly theater and the terrible tribunal of the Judge, who weighs the deeds of each person in the just balance of discernment.

## XXIII.

Holy John, not yet born from his mother’s womb, the boundary-marker of the Old Instrument, and, when grace first ruled in its rough beginnings, the voice smoothing the rugged windings of the Word with the harsh file of repentance; the herald proclaiming far and wide the saving advent of Christ the King; the paranymph of the heavenly offspring; the one administering the beginnings of the primitive Church—was he not, on account of the integrity of his chastity, described as having baptized the Author of all chastity, with a voice resounding through the open heavens, while the Spirit descended in the likeness of a winged creature: the Pure One in the stream of the Jordan, and a virgin the Virgin?

Burning with the torrid fire of chastity, he restrained the forbidden marriage of the royal bed and rebuked polluted unions of shameful marriages with the severity of the harshest denunciation. For this reason, gladly prepared to endure the foul squalor of prison, he foretold by mystical signs the sacred passion of the Redeemer, when the purple blood of his flesh ran down in red streams from the fibers of his body.

John, the writer of the four-part history and the truthful tetrarch of evangelical testimony, whom the Savior—the sole redemption of the world and the gracious prefiguration of chastity to be preserved—particularly loved among all others with devoted affection on account of the glory of virginal purity, became famous throughout the whole world through wondrous signs of virtue.

Indeed, he changed wild branches brought from leafy forests into the refined metal of shining gold. He also very easily transformed, contrary to the order of creation and relying upon heavenly power, the smooth gravel of cliffs and the rounded little stones of crags, brought from the sandy shores, into red heaps of gems. He restored to their original state even scattered fragments of gemstones, which the deceived simplicity of the Germans, following the advice of a most foolish sophist, had rubbed into tiny pieces for public display.

He also raised from the deadly sleep of death a matron whom the supreme lot had punished with a double lot of death, at the prayerful request of crowds of poor people, whom she had supported with the costly nourishment of alms she had distributed. When, moreover, in the savage fury of pagans, he was cruelly forced to drink a deadly draught in which there was a poisonous juice of dreadful herbs, together with the savage venom of snakes and asps—poisons to which the pestilential concoction of the four-footed toad and the *spalangium* was considered injurious to human nature—he did not tremble at the poisonous harm of dragons, nor, pale with fear, shrink from the dreadful dangers of death. Having first displayed the banner of Christ, he was protected and armed with Christ’s standard.

He also restored to their former state of life the twin corpses of two dead men whom deadly poison had swiftly struck down in a cruel end. Thus, flourishing in chastity, he happily remained until the swan-white hoariness of old age.

Some, however, maintain that he did not die a general death but lies alive in a sarcophagus, lulled by a special sleep, because the Savior said:

> “I wish him to remain thus until I come,”

especially since dust is said to bubble up from the tomb and, as though with the alternating breath of one who breathes, to well up slowly upon the surface of the cavern.

Didymus, once an unbelieving denier of the Lord’s resurrection but, after seeing the scars of the wounds, a believing preacher, who illuminated the three provinces of Eastern India with the serene light of evangelical preaching and utterly emptied the accursed purifications of shrines and the foolish priestly offices of the pagan flamens, spoke of the praises of virginity while instructing chaste married partners:

> “You possess integrity, which is the queen of all virtues, and the fruit of perpetual virginity. Virginity is the sister of angels and the possession of all good things; virginity is victory over lust, the trophy of faith, victory over enemies, and security of eternal life.”

Behold the trumpet-blast of the apostles, resounding like a thunderous crash, exhorting devoted virginal minds to the practice of integrity while celebrating it with immense praises.

## XXIV.

Paul, formerly Saul, the vessel of election, the figurative Benjamin devouring prey at twilight and dividing spoils in the evening—he compelled a pythoness, who prophesied frivolous falsehoods through the spirit of necromancy and thereby abundantly accumulated the costly wealth of the powerful and richly increased her delightful treasures of profit, to place the barrier of mute silence before her shameless lips under the threat of a terrifying command.

He also—wondrous to say—passed safely through twenty-four hours in the depths of the sea, and received five times forty lashes, less one, under the sharpest torment of cruelty.

Was it not on account of the privilege of pure integrity, while traversing the third heaven, that he contemplated the secrets of the heavenly citizens with chaste eyes and examined the hidden things of the celestial army in an ineffable account of realities? Yet the *Revelation* that they call Paul’s babbles that he visited the delights of the flourishing paradise in a golden ship.

But divine law forbids the followers of the Catholic faith to believe anything more than the judgment of canonical truth proclaims. The orthodox Fathers, in their decretal writings, have decreed that the remaining ravings of the apocrypha must be utterly rejected and driven far away like terrible thunderclaps of resounding words.

Luke, designated by Ezekiel through the prophetic symbol of the calf and the third historian of evangelical preaching, while proclaiming a medicinal poultice at Antioch, first healed the purulent illnesses of bodies and the diseased fibers of the inner organs, and then the spiritual ailments of souls, with the burning cautery of doctrine or the phlebotomy of the divine word. He is remembered to have remained the most chaste companion of unblemished chastity until the seventy-fourth year of his life.

Therefore, when he had paid the general debt owed by mortal nature [Bodl., “mature nature”] at the final lot of death, while Constantine governed the empire of the world, his bones are read to have been transferred to Constantinople for the protection of the Roman realm.

## XXV.

Clement, first successor of the heavenly key-bearer and second administrator of the Roman Church—although some needlessly place Linus and Cletus before him in the government of the pontificate—reveals in his own written words how deeply he loved the chastity of celibacy even before he was immersed in the baptistery of the saving bath and cleansed from original sin. He says:

> “I, Clement, born in the city of Rome, practiced devotion to chastity from my earliest age.”

If, then, while still unregenerate, he so highly valued and embraced something acknowledged to be most excellent among all the grades of virtue and exceedingly difficult for mortal nature, how much more should we rightly believe that, after receiving the beginnings of faith and rejecting the rites of the pagans, he preserved it more fully and perfectly while following Peter through the provinces as Peter sowed the seeds of the divine word, planted shoots of the evangelical vine in the trenches of believers, and uprooted the deadly tendrils of Simonian necromancy.

Afterward he polished, more clearly than daylight, the itinerary of Peter arranged in ten volumes, when Rufinus translated it from the Greek libraries into Latin.

Sylvester, who assumed the priesthood of the pontifical chair at Rome, became renowned throughout all the provinces of Europe and the parishes of flourishing Ausonia, encircled by the icy Alpine passes and the precipitous crags of the mountains. Relying upon uncontaminated bodily chastity and endowed with the frugality of constant abstinence, he is said to have descended inward through a hundred steps of hiding places to the deadly dragon of Rome, which lay concealed in a secret cavern. With its venomous jaws and pestilential breath it corrupted the air and cruelly afflicted the wretched people.

He permanently punished that beast of marvelous size, to which the deceived pagan gentiles burned the filth of fanatical purification in order to calm its mad fury, binding it with an unbreakable collar and subjecting it to perpetual retribution. He also corrected Rome, a worshiper of deceptive idolatry, by evangelical declarations and equally resplendent signs, turning it away from the fatal ritual of sacrifices.

Nor should I omit what displays a particularly important proof of preserved chastity: the fact that the emperor Constantine’s prolonged illness and elephantine bodily affliction, after he received the sacrament of baptism, were immediately healed by that saint; and that both the disposition of the inner man and the fever of the outer man were healed by a heavenly poultice through a double medicine, without hindrance or confusion.

Moreover, I thought it absurd that so celebrated a spectacle, spread throughout all the quarters of the world, should grow worthless by being sealed in the silence of silence and remain hidden untouched by our written words.
