In it the victory of the triumphant Christ and the chastity of Sylvester as a combatant resound with a double proclamation of praise.

For while Constantine governed the world and crowds of people flocked together to a synodal council, Sylvester, relying upon the divine shield, refuted twelve Jewish teachers and Pharisaic rabbis who were cruelly hurling the dreadful darts of disputation against the novice of Christ.

The same bishop also wisely disclosed, with marvelous discernment, Constantine’s dream, which foretold the hidden future. When the emperor had surrendered his limbs to sleep in the city called Byzantium and paid nature’s debt, an old woman appeared to him in a nocturnal vision, greatly decrepit and almost dead. While Sylvester was pope, Constantine was commanded to raise her by prayer.

As Constantine prayed, the old woman rose and became a most beautiful young woman, as though covered with the ruddy bloom of graceful youth. When she pleased the royal eyes by her chaste appearance, he clothed her in his cloak and placed upon her head a diadem adorned with refined gold and purple gems. His mother Helena said to him:

> “This woman will be yours, and she will not die until the end of the world.”

The emperor awoke, fiercely troubled by ignorance of future events. After an interval of one full week, while his body had grown lean through frugal restraint, he again sank into sleep. On the seventh day of his fast, the venerable man Sylvester appeared to him, saying once more in a vision:

> “The decrepit old woman—that is, the city in which you dwell, called Byzantium—whose walls have now been consumed by age and almost all whose fortifications have collapsed. Mount that horse of yours on which, baptized and clothed in white, you sat in the city of Rome and went around the thresholds of the apostles and martyrs. Sitting upon it, hold your standard, the labarum painted with the sign of Christ in gold and gems.
>
> “Holding this labarum in your right hand, release the horse’s bridle, so that it may go wherever the angel of God leads it. You, however, drag the fixed spear-point of the labarum through the earth, so that it makes a path as it passes; along that path you shall build walls. Thus you will raise this ancient and almost dead city as a young woman and name it with your own name, so that you may make it queen of all cities.
>
> “For the name of the Lord Jesus Christ will be magnificent in it, and temples of God will be built there in honor of all the saints. Your sons after you, and the sons of your sons, will reign in it.”

When Constantine awoke, he immediately went to the church. He told the holy bishop of the city, Sisinnius, the dream he had previously seen, offered gifts to God, and received communion in the Lord’s sacrament. Then he mounted his horse and went where the angel of the Lord led him, and along the paths the foundations rose through the labarum.

The city was called Constantine’s City, which in the Greek language is interpreted as Constantinople, and it remains so called to this day.

Thus Sylvester, having completed the office of his pontificate and finished the course of his life, climbed Jacob’s ladder with the palm of virginity and was joined to the companies of angels, happily enjoying the blessed fellowship of those above.

## XXVI.

Nor will I allow Ambrose, fragrant with the ambrosia of heavenly nectar, to remain hidden beneath the veil of silence. The beautiful signs that preceded him foretold the honeyed sweetness of his doctrines and the privilege of pure virginity.

When he was still an infant and lay on his back in his cradle, a swarm of bees suddenly filled his mouth and lips without harming the sleeping child. They repeatedly went in and out through the tender lips of the little boy, taking turns among themselves. At last, while Ambrose’s father awaited the outcome and ordered the nurse who had cared for the infant not to drive them away, they flew off in a swarm through the air toward the heights of heaven, disappearing from mortal sight.

How great and how glorious that same patriarch was in virtue and in signs of miracles, I do not think anyone experienced unless he learned of his deeds and manner of life as recorded by the venerable Paulinus.

Nor should Christ's celibates, who restrain the wanton impetuosity of nature by the strict laws of chastity and curb bodily motions of titillation like unruly draft animals with iron bits, be ashamed to recall the bishop of Tours. Before the womb of regenerating grace gave birth to him [Bodl., “before he was born through it”] and he learned the beginnings of holy baptism, while still among the catechumens and in the condition of those preparing for baptism, he gave alms to the poor and distributed charitable gifts to the needy. When he had surrendered his limbs to nightly rest, a heavenly oracle blessed him.

He is remembered to have shone with marvelous signs of virtue because of the crown of integrity he had gained and the auspicious diadem of virginity, which he strove to preserve with tireless strength to the end, like a royal diadem and jewel-encrusted crescents of ornaments.

Indeed, he raised to the light of life from the gate of death a catechumen’s corpse whom, as they say, the savage violence of cruel fortune and the murderous ferocity of the Fates, sparing no one—indeed, the mercilessness of cold death—had swiftly crushed, deprived of the sacrament of regenerating grace.

He also brought back to the upper world, in fulfillment of his prayer, two others whom the cruel boundary of death had struck down and robbed of the desired spoils of life, rescuing them from the hidden abyss of death and the torment of savage Tartarus.

He fearlessly watched a tall, leafy pine trunk dedicated to the forbidden ceremonies of the pagans, although repeated double axes of the inhabitants were cutting it down in competition as it leaned in a slanting curve [Bodl., “were trying to cut it down”]. He despised, with resounding contempt, the deceptive tricks of the crafty Anatolius, a swindler, which a fraudulent faction of envious rivals, armed with a thousand arts of harm, boldly thrust forward by displaying the illusion of a false veil.

By the surpassing grace of his merits he caused these tricks to fail utterly and vanish far away like a ridiculous phantom. Distrusting mortal assistance and relying upon the aid of angels—for armed and shield-bearing servants are read to have come to protect the servant of God—he shook, overturned, and destroyed to the ground the ancient pagan shrines, built by a mason with the most finely fitted stones and roofed with red tiles.

## XXVII.

Gregory, governor of the Church of Nazianzus, incomparably more learned than the others at Athens—where at that time the loudly celebrated reputation of grammarians and the hidden sophistry of Academic disputation held sway—and Basil’s fellow student in philosophical doctrines, as the eleventh book of Ecclesiastical History makes clear, was, from the tenderness of his earliest infancy, a despiser of bodily temptation and a zealous lover of chastity.

When he was overcome by sleep, a vision of beauty gently consoled him. Because of his resolve of virginal modesty and his athletic devotion to philosophy, chastity and wisdom are described as having appeared to him in sleep under the double image of the female sex.

In this manner they addressed the saint, urging him toward the crown of integrity:

> “One of us is called Wisdom, the other Chastity; and we have been sent by the Lord to dwell with you, because you have prepared in your heart a pleasant and very pure dwelling for us.”

From the interpretation of this dream, it is permissible to infer and to recognize from these arguments that he was endowed with such generosity of merits and guarded the crown of uninjured purity with tireless strength all the way to the end of his lot, especially since this was sung about him:

> “Neither in life can anything more deserving and holier be found, nor in eloquence anything clearer and more illustrious, nor in faith anything purer and more upright, nor in knowledge anything fuller and more perfect.”

Rufinus, endowed with marvelous elegance of language, explained this more fully in his apologetic preface.

Bishop Basil, the celebrated Cappadocian, likewise trained at Athens in rhetorical disciplines and sophistical arts, clearly and completely set out the rule of monastic conduct by responding to repeated written inquiries through an alternating exchange of letters. He also published, relying upon marvelous eloquence, the *ἔργα τὰ Ἑξαμέρων*, that is, the “Works of the Six Days,” which are read to have been translated into Latin.

I draw the inference that he flourished bodily incorrupt through the grace of integrity from his own eulogy, which continues:

> “And I do not know a woman, and I am not a virgin.”

For it is said to be an old custom of experienced preachers who stand elevated before the platform and address the crowds: in the wedge of a different speech and with a different gender, they sometimes speak both in their own person and in that of another, opening the secrets of their minds and unlocking the hidden chambers of their hearts with the key of eloquent speech before astonished hearers and ignorant listeners.

By this kind of preaching the aforementioned bishop is believed to have spoken. He did not think that merely external freedom from carnal impurity was sufficient to earn the insignia of vigorous integrity unless the chastity of the spirit as well restrained, by its command, the unruly wantonness of bodily lust—just as a domestic servant is subjected to the nods of a matron so that she may not grow insolently rebellious and may remain inwardly attached to her in harmonious companionship.

There was a certain man adorned with pontifical dignity, rightly named Felix. When he was tortured by executioners for the constancy of his faith and martyred in the agonies of dreadful torturers, he is said to have cried out:

> “I give you thanks, Christ: for fifty-six years in the world I have guarded my virginity.”

## XXVIII.

Anthony, holder of the handle of the heavenly plow and sower of the evangelical word, from whom first throughout Egypt the fertile crop of monasteries and the fruitful seed-bed of communal life sprang up in grain-bearing ears—whence afterward the land of Memphis, watered by the Nile’s alternating currents, produced thousands of sheaves of souls sprouting in the fruitful new fields of the Church, which angelic reapers will carry in groups into the inexhaustible granaries of the heavenly kingdom, when the form of the world has vanished in an instant and atom and the vast elements of creation have shone forth transformed for the better, after the bundles of weeds have been separated—did he not, endowed with ineffable grace of virtues because of the outstanding chastity of his soul, become famous by report as far as the farthest quarters of the earth?

Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, disclosed his virtue and miracles more fully in a single volume, translated into Latin by Evagrius.

Likewise Paul, illustrious and most celebrated among the Fathers, betrayed and exposed contrary to the laws of nature by a deceitful son-in-law deceived by the blind greed of avarice, penetrated, from the beginning of his youthful training, the deserted wastes of the Memphitic wilderness, where the blandishments of carnal impurity decay and the sorrows of the world become worthless [Bodl., *luxus*, “luxury”].

Relying upon the defense of burning faith, he fearlessly despised the dreadful bellowing of beasts and the savage growls of lions. Wearing only woven palm leaves and sustaining his wretched little body on the sweet nourishment of dates, he paid the debt owed to nature.

Did he not, because the chastity of his flourishing purity had been preserved by an unbreakable barrier to the very end, after twelve five-year periods of time—that is, an interval of sixty years—deserve, until decrepit old age, to receive with thankful joy half a little cake, which a winged bird had brought in its gaping beak through tireless service and repeated flights?

## XXIX.

Hilarion, the most renowned inhabitant of the Palestinian wilderness, born of pagan parents devoted to the worship of idols, flourished like a red rose blooming among the thorns commonly growing in the wild. He became famous at the time when the aforementioned Anthony was being widely celebrated throughout Egypt.

Jerome, the distinguished cultivator of the heavenly library and the foremost of all interpreters, elevates his life with such great tales of reputation that he says even Homer, if he rose from the underworld, would either envy the material or succumb to it.

To preserve the integrity of chastity, Hilarion avoided the company of mortals. At the beginning of puberty, he entered the desolation of the squalid desert to explore it and, contrary to ordinary practice, undertook a contemplative life before a practical one as an inexperienced inhabitant, cruelly chastising the wanton impetuosity of youth by the hungry frugality of a starving life.

> “I shall make you a donkey,” he said, “so that you do not kick. I shall not feed you barley, but shall wear you down with straw and hunger.”

Therefore, shining with countless marvels of miracles, he was compared with the ancient patriarchs.

Near the municipality of Epidaurum in Dalmatia, he extinguished by the weapons of prayer a dreadful dragon with a scaly body, called a *boa*, because it is of such enormous size that it regularly slaughtered oxen with the poisonous teeth of its jaws and greedily swallowed them in the gluttonous fullness of its belly. It not only dragged herds and sheep toward itself, but also absorbed farmers, oxherds, and swineherds by the force of its breath.

O heavenly powers, turn such a monster away from the earth!

He did this as follows: he ordered the basilisk of astonishing size to climb, before the watching populace, a pyre built high from piled logs and set ablaze with flaming splinters. By a terrifying command he forced it upward, drew its scaly rib-cage and rigid curve of spine over the burning coals, and cruelly consumed it amid the glowing balls of the logs, rescuing the people from the beast’s deadly breath.

Moreover, when the waves of the boiling Ocean and the blue waters of the foaming flood passed beyond their proper bounds, threatening, as though by the judgment of divine power, an outbreak of deluge, or as though everything were being forced to return to ancient chaos, the inhabitants of Epidaurum, driven by inexperienced terror, set this servant of God against the roaring waves and the salt masses of the whirlpools.

As he traced the three signs of the cross upon the gravelly shores of the sandy beach, it is marvelous to say how the swelling sea rose into a heap and to what height, so that it stood before him like an icy wall.

O how great is the power of chastity, which subdued the fury of a raging beast by the humblest prayer and suppressed the swelling madness of the sea by the authority granted to it, matching the deed of the prophet Daniel against the dragon and imitating the lawgiver Moses upon the waters.

John, the hermit of the Nilotic wilderness, while Theodosius governed the empire of the world, labored for forty years in the practice of active life—prefigured by Martha, Lazarus’s sister, who offered Christ the desired service of hospitality—and displayed an extraordinary fervor of devotion. Finally, after hiding for fifty years in a remote hut, he passed his life in the contemplative practice of anachoresis.

From this it is clear that he preserved the gift of pure virginity unblemished until the decrepit old age of ninety. When a chiliarch, that is, a military tribune, earnestly begged him to allow him to visit him in order to seek advice about his wife’s illness, he is said to have replied with firm resolve that it had never been his custom to see women, especially since he had shut himself within the monastery of that rock.

Because of the cloak of integrity he had acquired, which he welcomed as a domestic companion in the fabric of angelic purity [Bodl., “by which he was clothed as a companion”], he experienced, under the breath of a prophetic spirit, future oracles of divination that had remained hidden from other mortals.

## XXX.

I think that Benedict of blessed memory must not be passed over. From the very cradle of infancy, a fortunate omen in his name so nourished him that he could not live in the purpose of divine religion in any way other than the dignity of his own name and the privilege of heavenly εὐλογία—“blessing”—allowed.

For when the boy grew strong through the free generosity of heavenly liberality and became widely renowned throughout the august kingdom of Hesperia through the favorable successes of his merits, he did not share without reason the blessed privilege of the name with our Advocate and Redeemer.

Of him, those rejoicing and singing with harmonious evangelical voices sang together:

> “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

Our own mediocrity, supported by the authoritative tradition of the ancients, also celebrates this rule in the sacred solemnity of palms, resounding with a melodious voice in two choirs and leaping in twin harmonies of “Hosanna.”

Thus prophetic signs followed the aforementioned soldier of Christ, protected by the guardianship of the Holy Trinity because of the incorruptible and ever-shining garlands of unfading chastity, and heavenly miracles accompanied him from above.

After the shrines of idols had been destroyed and the ceremonies of fanatical paganism scattered—paganism which, according to the astrological doctrine of the mathematicians, supposes that a life devoid of truth is governed by fate, fortune, and birth [Bodl., “folly,” for “fate”; “to govern,” for “is governed”]—he is said to have built twelve monasteries. In them, abundant profits of holy conduct and rich gains of souls, acquired through orthodox doctrines, accrued abundantly to Christ.

As a knowledgeable cultivator of the Lord’s vineyard, he cut these clusters of ripening shoots and red bunches of branches with the evangelical pruning-hook and carried them in filled sacks and loaded baskets to be trodden in the winepress and regularly pressed in the Church’s vats. Thus he happily delivered the sweet wine of refined nectar to be stored in heavenly storerooms and entrusted to angelic keepers, so that the banquets of those above might be glorified joyfully by such gifts brought from the earthly marketplace.

## XXXI.

Great, therefore, is the privilege of purity. Whoever is forcibly compelled to lose it, if for that reason he hates human society and voluntarily withdraws from common life, will rejoice gloriously in the heavenly fellowship of the hundred and forty-four thousand who sing the virginal song.

Eusebius, the Greek historian, testifies that this was done by virgins devoted to God who, in order to preserve the modesty of their integrity, plunged themselves headlong into the channel of a rushing torrent. Hence one of the Fathers said:

> “It is not permitted to perish by one’s own hand, except where chastity is endangered.”

O astonishing matter and decree almost impossible to investigate! In other crimes and disgraceful acts, which disturb the order of the world mournfully, when someone is compelled against his will to become a slave and, deprived of the freedom of choice, is forced to commit the guilt of crime, if under the pretext of avoiding harm and shunning sin he cruelly inflicts death upon himself by any form of destruction, he will on that account be regarded as an outsider from the fellowship of the Church and counted among the *biothanati*, those who kill themselves.

From this one may infer how precious the nobility of chastity is to the citizens above. Not even that can abolish or obliterate it by any means which is capable of mocking the merits of the perfect and emptying every kind of virtue.

Thus, when Malchus was being forced into sexual union by the violence of his father’s severity and his mother’s strictness—both of whom were concerned for the posterity that would follow—he resolved to despise it for the sake of chastity and the kingdom of heaven.

But when, through concern for his kindred, he had begun gradually to grow lukewarm from the fervor of the religious life he had embraced, and was slowly cooling from the burning rigor of coenobitic life as he prepared to depart at the prompting of the wily enemy, he was captured by Saracen robbers and Ishmaelite marauders who were savagely laying waste everything in their path.

He was ordered to serve as a household slave—a very just judgment, so that he who sought to recover a forbidden return to his former status might serve as a worthless slave. Since he had not feared the loss of the woman who perished among the Sodomites, he was to feel cruelly the harm of prolonged slavery and the hated service of a master.

While he carelessly guided the plow-handle, looking back behind him, he wasted the acre’s harrow in folly, breaking apart the clods of the furrows. When he was then compelled, by a drawn sword, to surrender the emblems of the chastity he had preserved in his native soil, he preferred to perish cruelly, pierced by the blade, rather than defend his life by violating the laws of purity. He did not fear the danger to his soul if the condition of unbroken virginity could be preserved through the shedding of blood.

[Textual apparatus omitted above: in the phrase “uninjured banners of chastity,” the text reads *illaesa*, while Bodl. reads *illaesae*; for John the Baptist's “harsh file,” the text reads *asperrima*, Bodl. *asperrimae*. For the iron bits, the text reads *salivaribus*, Bodl. *salinaribus*. In the angelic-aid clause, the text reads *quia* (“because”), Bodl. *qui* (“who”). In the notice on Gregory, the text reads *cantum* (“a song”), Bodl. *cautum*; and the text's *fruniscantur persona* is read by Bodl. as *fruriscantur personae*. In the Martha clause, the text reads *Christi* (“of Christ”), Bodl. *Christo* (“to Christ”); in the tribune's request it reads *ut se*, Bodl. *se illum*; and in the cloak clause it reads *quam … asciscebat*, Bodl. *qua … adsciscebatur*. In Benedict's acclamation, the text reads *vicis*, Bodl. *vocis*; and Bodl. omits the *et* after “cutting … with the evangelical pruning-hook.”]

### XXXII

Moreover, I shall not allow Narcissus, of blessed memory, endowed both with the privilege of virginal chastity and with the authority of the pontifical insignia, to lie hidden under the shelter of silence. His life shone so brightly with signs and wonders of miracles that, contrary to the nature of things, relying on the armor of prayer he changed into another kind the quality of liquid matter, which God alone can alter. For during the Paschal vigils, when the Lord’s Resurrection was celebrated with the customary festival joy at the recurring cycle of the years, it happened by chance that the church lacked a sufficient supply of the rich oil needed for lamps and lanterns.

Then the man devoted to God exorcised the liquid waters of the springs and, making them fruitful through the abundance of sacred blessing, caused them to grow thick in a wondrous display of power—so much so that the water poured into the hanging lamp-holders was swiftly changed into the consistency of oil, and the papyrus placed at the center shone more brightly than usual, as though soaked in fat or tallow [Bodl., *assungia*, “lard,” instead of “fat or tallow”].

Yet the ancient persecutor of the human race was inflamed with oblique zeal of envy at so great a distinction of renown [Col. 0130A], by which the praises of Catholics were multiplied, and sought to destroy the man of God’s favorable reputation by shifting it through false grounds for suspicion [Bodl., *tam*, “so,” instead of *tamen*, “nevertheless”]. For the deceitful craftsmen of stratagems contrived a sufficiently shameful deed and unheard-of crime against him: seated in the chair of pestilence, they fabricated it in a council through the false perjury of three witnesses, as the Psalmist records in writing:

> “Unjust witnesses rose up against me,  
> and iniquity lied to itself.”

One of them testified that he was speaking truthfully so that he would not be scorched by the crackling fire. Another, so that he would not be ravaged by the poisonous affliction of royal plague. The third, so that he would not be deprived of sight in both eyes.

Thus Narcissus, trusting in God, did not seek an apologetic defense, as the guilty and innocent commonly do, but on this occasion, leaving the height of the pontifical chair, sought the hidden wilderness and concealed himself, fleeing the frivolous contrivances of his rivals and their fabricated factions.

But the avenging judgment of divine power cruelly struck the deceitful persons of the witnesses—who imitated the elders muttering against Susanna—with the very disasters to which they had condemned themselves by their perjury [Bodl., *devotabant*, “were condemning,” instead of *devoverant*, “had condemned”]. The first of them is said to have burned together with all the dependents of his household and the kinsmen of his close family, consumed by avenging balls of flame within the beamwork of his own house.

The second, swelling from the crown of his triple-branched head to the soles of his feet with jaundice, breathed out a foul breath, just as he had earlier madly, shamelessly, and insolently invoked.

The third, observing the unhappy fortune of his companions, openly disclosed before all who listened, in late repentance, the whole guilt of the crime they had fabricated. Weeping bitterly, he lamented with such sobs of mourning and such hoarse complaints of tears that he was utterly deprived of the light of both pupils. Hence it is ordained:

> “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,”  
> says the Lord.

What shall I say of Athanasius, of holy memory? Although the far-spreading fame of his merits and the praises of his flower-bearing chastity shone especially throughout Alexandria and Egypt, they nevertheless spread far and wide through all the regions of the world wherever the Catholic faith flourishes with fruitful branches. His nourisher and teacher in doctrine, the blessed Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, is remembered to have instructed him from the tenderest softness of infancy, courteously teaching him both the characters of scribes and the periods of grammarians, distinctly separated by colon and comma.

This Alexander, after Arius the schismatic’s bowels had shamefully poured down into the hidden channel of a latrine, was raised up in the Church’s triumphant trophy. But what wonder if Athanasius possessed divine grace of spiritual gifts at the highest summit of rank, when even his tenderest infancy was not without a prophetic portent of character, and the gestures of a child’s games foreshadowed the authority of the future bishop?

For after the mysteries of the Mass had been completed, Alexander saw troops of unvested boys on the pebbly shores of the sea [Col. 0131A] offering Athanasius the reverence due to a priest. He also saw certain catechumens and candidates for baptism regenerated by him through the mystical office of baptism. What had been performed as a theatrical joke of children’s play was seriously confirmed by synodal decrees.

Therefore, after Alexander’s death, Athanasius assumed the episcopate of the Church. How many plots of heretics he experienced and how many fraudulent tricks of schismatics he endured—tricks which they contrived by a treacherous faction against an innocent man—is confirmed by the tenth book of ecclesiastical history, composed by Rufinus.

Indeed, they showed Constantius Augustus, who governed the scepter of the Eastern Empire, an arm torn from a corpse and carried in a sarcophagus. They falsely claimed that Athanasius had removed it by magical necromancy from the body of Arsenius [Col. 0131B]. Therefore the emperor, enticed by the flattering inventions of the heretics and deceived by their shameful faction, rashly ordered the bishop to be condemned in council.

But Arsenius, who had once served as a reader at the lectern, exposed the entire scene of the fabricated crime and declared that the sacred priest was free from such disgraceful deeds. Oh, how great was the pallor that accused certain hard-faced men, trembling at the discovery of their guilt; and, conversely, how the purple redness of the cheeks of others painted their faces as though with rouge, when in the council they saw alive and unharmed the man whom they had confessed to be maimed and disabled by the severing of his sinews!

Yet, defeated by this holy victory, they devised another kind of accusation. They contrived that a fallen harlot should brazenly charge the most chaste man with the disgrace of prostitution—a defilement from which he had kept his body wholly pure since puberty [Col. 0131C; Bodl., *prostituta*, “prostituted,” instead of *prostrata*, “fallen”]. After she had vomited forth from the recesses of her false heart the whole incestuous filth of her false chatter, like the nauseating stench of melancholy, he was immediately defended by the presbyter Timothy. The shameless woman had seized him with her abominable embracing arms, but he defended Athanasius with the truthful apology of his words, as though protected by a fixed tortoise-formation of shields.

Nevertheless, yielding to the madness of his rivals, who were tortured by rancid envy of hatred while showing zeal against the man of God, Athanasius went far away into exile. For six years he hid in the dry recess of a cistern and did not enjoy the clear ray of the sun. Yet his mind, devoted to God, harder than a whetstone, stronger than iron, and more rigid than adamant, endured with steadfast heart all the persecutions of misfortune that the secret conspiracy of the envious inflicted with hostility.

### XXXIII

What shall I say of the blessed Babylas? He guarded the watch-posts and folds of the Lord’s flock, the churches, against the savage fury of tyrants, as against the ferocity of wild wolves—not in the manner of a hired servant, but with pastoral skill—since he was endowed with the insignia of the highest pontificate.

He did not permit Numerian Augustus, stained with the blood of those he had killed, to profane the sanctuary of the basilica by entering it with polluted feet. Rather, by the judgment of the sternest correction, he barred the entrance of the deadly king from the sacred lights of the Church. He did not fear the loss of possessions, nor did he tremble pale with terror at the danger to his life [Col. 0132A].

Then he was led to the palace at Zetas and to the entrance of the imperial hippodrome, so that he might dispute and argue with the wicked king in repeated conflicts and alternating exchanges. But neither the ferocity of threats bent the mind dedicated to God, nor did the gentleness of flatteries soothe it into turning from the balance of the Catholic faith toward the crooked ceremonies of idols.

At once, by order of the Augustus, and to the accusation of the bishop and the disgrace of the clergy, they fastened a collar around his neck and shackles around his legs. Moreover, with elaborate instruments of punishment, they cruelly tore apart the most sacred limbs of the living sacrifice. They also brought before the king three young brothers whom Babylas had received to be properly instructed under his disciplinary guardianship.

When the emperor could not deceive them, fortified as they were by marvelous steadfastness of faith, through arguments of words, he ordered them to be beaten with bloody blows of rods [Col. 0132B]. Seeing the boys’ unconquerable constancy, the furious prince asked the venerable bishop whether they were truly his sons. He is said to have replied:

> “They truly are my sons according to God;  
> but I have not known a woman before my God since I was born.”

Then the holy Babylas received the sentence of decapitation and was beheaded together with his three pupils, being consecrated by the red streams of their veins.

### XXXIV

I also consider it worthwhile not to separate Cosmas and Damian, the celebrated warriors of spiritual warfare and chief physicians of heavenly medicine, from the historical account of the virgins, as though we should set them apart as unworthy of the company of the others. We confidently believe that they were predestined for the heavenly citizenship of Jerusalem, enrolled in the register of celestial writing, and destined to rejoice there with the comrades mentioned above.

For in the time of Diocletian and Maximian, in the 267th Olympiad, when by cruel edicts the worshipers of the Catholic faith—whom they called Christ-worshipers and cross-worshipers—were forced to offer incense to the little images of the pagans, those unwilling to apostatize, that is, to return to the mire of apostasy, were compelled to undergo a capital sentence.

At that time the devout mother of the aforesaid young soldiers of Christ gave birth to twins. Little by little, at the beginning of puberty, they were instructed in medical instruments and, through a heavenly poultice, cured both the illnesses of the dropsical, the melancholies of the viscera, and the afflictions of souls [Col. 0132D].

They gave sight to the blind and applied a poultice to the one-eyed; they opened the gate of silence for the mute; they restored the harmonies of things to the ears of the deaf; they granted correctness of speech to the stammerers and lispers; they restored the lame and maimed to their former soundness; they refreshed the possessed and those suffering from vertigo by the grace of their merits; and they even restored to life those crushed by the accidents of fortune.

Yet, endowed with such generosity of powers, they bestowed the desired health upon the sick not through a commercial love of money but through free generosity, in agreement with the evangelical pronouncement:

> “You received without payment; give without payment.”

Meanwhile, during the persecution of the aforesaid persecutors, when the holy martyrs were slaughtered like sheep for slaughter by the bloody swords of executioners, and the athletes of the Church, not terrified at all, wrestled as though in the wrestling-ground of the gymnasia, who could adequately recount how greatly and in what ways the aforesaid confessors were tortured by instruments of punishment while Lisias sat in judgment?

Their arms were bound and the joints of their legs fastened together; they were sunk into the deep waters of the sea. But, supported by angelic aid, they were restored unharmed to the shores, for the savage violence of the waves did not dare touch them.

Again the savage governor, confused and confounded by so great a triumph of the holy young soldiers, ordered them to be thrust brutally into a furnace heated with abundant fuel for sacred rites and crackling with various brands of wood. But like salamanders, which naturally cannot be roasted or burned by torrents of glowing coals [Col. 0133B; Bodl., *cremare*, “burned,” instead of *cremate*, “roasted”], they were not consumed by the fires of the blazing furnace.

Afterward, when they had been tormented on the rack, hung upon the gallows, and further overwhelmed by dreadful blows of arrows, angelic protection guarded them. At last, having received the sentence of decapitation, they struggled on with the palm of virginity and the triumph of martyrdom.

### XXXV

Nor should we be reluctant to remember the renowned soldier of Christ, Chrysanthus, whom his father, departing from Alexandria, entrusted at Rome to gymnosophists and rhetoricians so that he might be educated in every liberal study of letters.

For, as is said, he possessed such ardent intelligence and retentive memory that whatever he investigated with particular effort through reading and inquiry clung prematurely within his youthful heart like something glued with birdlime [Col. 0133C] and remained rooted within the chamber of his keen mind.

Therefore, after completing the studies of grammarians and the disciplines of philosophers, which are divided into seven branches—namely grammar, rhetoric, dialectic, arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy [Al., arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy, astrology, mechanics, medicine]—when he came to the most sacred passages of the Gospels, he quickly saw through all the arguments of the Stoics and Aristotle’s *Categories*, which are distinguished into ten kinds of predicaments [Bodl., *despexerit*, “will have despised,” instead of *dispexit*, “saw through”].

He carefully recognized how much the doctrine of heavenly philosophy surpassed the disciplines of the world and the inventions of mortals. Conceived in the womb of regenerating grace and brought forth from the fruitful births of the baptistery, he was nourished in the venerable cradle of the Church. Immediately after the rudiments of faith, as a neophyte disciple he became a distinguished teacher of doctrine, publicly proclaiming Christ, the Son of God, without fearing the threats of the faithless.

When his father learned of this through reports from relatives and household companions, he confined his son in the hidden recesses of a prison, contrary to the laws of nature, and weakened him with hunger and fasting. He also greatly feared the proscription of his possessions and the loss of his patrimony, as well as the danger of execution, lest the emperors confiscate his wealth entirely, together with the loss of his life.

Thus, when he observed that Christians were willing to endure the harshness of punishments, he tried to bend his son to his own desires not by the torment of tortures but by the seduction of flatteries. He removed him from the filthy prison and dressed him in garments of fine silk and cloth of sea-silk, then sent him into a dining room where very beautiful maidens, adorned with costly robes, prepared delicate delicacies of spiced wine and sumptuous banquets. They mingled uncontrolled peals of laughter and playful embraces, so that the young man’s iron heart might soften amid such flatteries.

But the man devoted to God was overcome neither by the honeyed nourishment of feasts nor turned from the firmness of his purpose by the beauty of the maidens. He avoided the soft lips of the girls as one avoids the harmful venom of vipers, paying little regard to the marriage song in which it was sung:

> “Then honeyed lips cling to rose-colored lips.” [Col. 0134A]

Afterward some of the family’s kinsmen urged the father that his son should be bound by the gentle ties of marriage and overcome by the enticement of wedlock. Thus Daria, a sufficiently beautiful Vestal virgin of elegant appearance, radiant with gems and gold, was to approach Chrysanthus boldly, so that both the urbane eloquence of her words and the ornamented trinkets around her neck might incline the soldier of Christ toward the union of the marriage chamber.

But things turned out otherwise than they had thought. A rather prolonged contest of words and reciprocal disputation of opinions arose between them, since Daria was said to have been trained in dialectical arts and equipped with the deceptive conclusions of syllogisms. Indeed, the most eloquent orators feared to test the virgin’s keen intelligence in alternating conflict.

What more need be said? At last the venerable man, gaining the palm of victory in their reciprocal contests—not by an argument of deceit but by a demonstration of reason—received Daria, who now believed in the sacraments of the Catholic faith. He lived with her under the pretense of marriage until she herself was cleansed in the water of the saving bath.

Soon, abandoning the disciplines of dialectic, in which she had earlier exercised herself diligently in the schools [Bodl., *gymnasii*, “of the school,” instead of *gymnasiis*, “in the schools”], she was instructed in the canonical Scriptures and spiritual writings. It is utterly impossible to enumerate on a tablet or calculate with an abacus how great a multitude of both sexes flocked in groups from the superstition of fanatical shrines to the Catholic faith under their teaching.

For this reason the blessed Chrysanthus, by order of the tribune Claudius, was handed over to seventy soldiers to be tortured by various kinds of punishment unless he consented to offer incense, according to pagan custom, at the shrine of the Amphitryoniad—that is, Hercules.

Then the soldiers cruelly bound him with wet and raw cords of sinews, so that, as the cords gradually dried in the scorching heat of the sun, he would be unable to withstand the force of their tightening. But in an instant, by heavenly will, the dreadful bonds were loosened.

Next they fastened the man of God’s shins and calves in the enclosure of a knotted stock. Immediately the hardness of the rigid stock, crushed by invisible power, was reduced to nothing. But the soldiers, thinking that this had been done by magical tricks, drenched him in the foulest odors of urine, by which they supposed all the phantoms of Chaldaeans and hierophants, as well as the devices of soothsayers and Marsi, would vanish [Col. 0134D–0135A].

Yet the purification of the stinking urine was changed into fragrant ambrosia and transformed into the scent of rose-colored nectar.

Then they ordered a young calf to be flayed, so that the martyr’s naked limbs might be enclosed in the rawness of its fresh hide and he might be cruelly roasted under the fiercest heat of the sun, in the green freshness of the hide. But, relying on Christ’s aid, he escaped unharmed and free from danger.

Soon they bound his neck, arms, and calves together with iron chains and threw him into the black recess of a prison. But the tightly fastened bonds quickly broke like strands of flax, and the gloomy darkness split apart like a clear lamp burning in a lantern.

Finally, when the bloody savagery of the executioners beat him with rods and knotted branches, the scepter-like rods, which had previously been rigid in their knotted hardness, became softer than feathers and lighter than papyrus [Col. 0135B].

Seeing these great wonders, the tribune Claudius was astonished. Struck in heart, he believed, together with the seventy soldiers, his entire household, his native dependents, his parasites, and his companions, in Christ, the Son of God who saves the ages.

Immediately all of them, regenerated by the water of baptism, received the purple crowns of paradise, happily pouring out their blood. Their holy corpses lie buried together in an underground passage and will rise to glory at the final judgment.

After these had migrated to heaven, the survivors, Chrysanthus and Daria, were separately confined in reciprocal tortures. He was sent, bound in irons, into a hidden recess of the stone quarry, where the foulness of sewer tunnels had deposited the stench of excrement.

But the stench and darkness were driven away by clear light and nectarous fragrances [Col. 0135C]. She was thrust into the brothels and the company of prostitutes and harlots. There, by God’s command, a lion was sent from the bars of the amphitheater to protect the consecrated virgin, so that if some insolent defiler and lustful fornicator, wandering with wanton gestures, preferred to enter the brothel, he would be mauled by the beast’s jaws [Bodl., *vagabundis*, “with wandering men,” instead of *vagabundus*, “wandering”].

But sometimes an abundance of virtues produces a poverty of words. Overcome by the immense mass of miracles, I pass over many things for the sake of brevity.

After this, by decree of Numerian Augustus, they died as martyrs together in one crypt, destined to receive together in the company of the saints the rewards of their merits, just as they had together shared their torments.

### XXXVI

Nor will I allow the virginal glory of the martyr Julian to lie hidden under the secret shelter of silence [Col. 0135D]. He was born of noble lineage in the time of Diocletian and Maximian. When his parents had made him flourish in the first beginnings of childhood, having mastery both of the art of dialectic and of the art of rhetoric [Bodl., *partis*, “of a part,” instead of *artis*, “of the art”], and had entrusted him to tutors and teachers to be instructed in the various disciplines of philosophers, they observed that he had already grown into the tender beginnings of puberty.

When they discovered that he was a lover of the Catholic faith, attached to the sacred thresholds of the Church, and frequently visiting the prisons of confessors, they were greatly afraid that, if their only pledge were taken from their line because of his devotion to religion and his habit of holy conduct, they themselves—as the patriarch says when uttering a tearful complaint—would go down to the underworld leading their gray hairs in sorrow, utterly deprived of the heirs of the desired offspring and of future generations of grandchildren.

Therefore they tried with earnest prayers and unheard-of exhortations of flattery to bend the young man, so that they might incline the iron affections of the youth—indeed, harder than adamant—toward the torches of the marriage chamber and the companionship of wedlock.

They even employed apostolic pronouncements as arguments for their persuasion, in which it is said:

> “I want young women to marry, to manage households, to bear children, giving no occasion to the adversary.”

He is said to have replied:

> “It is neither the time of my will nor of my age for me to do what you urge.”

When they persisted stubbornly in their entreaties, he said:

> “I have neither the power to promise nor the authority to refuse; what you urge I entrust to the power of my God,” and so forth.

Nevertheless, he asked his parents for a delay of one week, so that he might test the will of the heavenly Majesty by evident signs. When the interval had passed, overcome by sleep and weighed down by slumber, he saw Christ in a dream saying:

> “Arise; do not fear, nor dread the persuasions of words or the will of your parents. For you will receive a wife who will not separate you from me by defiling you, but through you she will remain a virgin; and many young men and women below will ascend to the heavenly army through your teaching or your life.”

Therefore a blessed virgin named Basilissa was taken from the marriage chamber, a name foretold by its meaning: “queen,” beautiful in the appearance of her forehead, but more beautiful in the chastity of her heart. Beautiful, I say, in the bodily features of her limbs, but still more beautiful inwardly, adorned in spiritual robes [Col. 0136C].

Oh, how great a multitude of believers of both sexes, trampling the foul sewers of crimes and abhorring the putrid wallows of vices, converted to the Catholic faith under their teaching and struggled triumphantly with the trophy of martyrdom!

For, with Christ’s help, they built many monasteries in the celebrated city of Alexandria, which is the metropolis of Egypt. In them approximately ten thousand soldiers of Christ, living under Julian’s strict governance, followed the rule and did not deviate to the right or left by the crooked turns of the path of holy religion.

Basilissa, devoted to God, harvested a thousand sheaves of the holy harvest with the sickle of evangelical preaching and carried them into the threshing floor of the executioner to be threshed and into the heavenly granaries to be stored [Col. 0136D].

Finally, when the savage rage of the persecutors attacked the sacred young soldiers of the Church with murderous edicts and fierce tortures, and sought utterly to overthrow the bulwark of the Catholic faith, shaken by the ballista of worldly argument and undermined by the rams of atrocious engines, who could adequately express in the majestic fabric of a lofty style how much Julian endured in martyrdom together with his other comrades and companions of the same purpose?

While Marcian the governor was speaking from the high summit of the tribunal or from the theater’s platform, Julian was flogged with knotted clubs and bloody whips, without regard for mercy, but could not be bent away from the worship of Christ. Indeed, he restored unharmed the eye of the executioner who had cruelly inflicted the welts of the scourge upon him, although he himself was drenched with foul urine as though he were a magician [Col. 0137A].

Moreover, he cast down, shattered, and overturned to the ground more than five hundred abominable images of idols, which the priests of the shrines used to incense with offerings in the manner of Bacchants.

Julian was also thrust into the depths of a prison together with the governor’s young son, a goatish youth, who was a neophyte and had recently been converted to the faith. There, where the foul corpses of the condemned had long produced horrid swarms of worms, he endured the nausea of filth.

But divine mercy, which always remembers its soldiers, in exchange for the stinking dung-heap graciously granted clear light and the fragrance of ambrosia and nectar to those enduring the prison’s filth and darkness [Col. 0137B].

Seeing these great wonders, the soldiers assigned to guard the confessors abandoned the worship of fanatical superstition and joined the ranks of the orthodox.

Meanwhile, at the governor’s demand, Julian raised a dead body, wrapped in long coils of bandages and not yet buried in the sarcophagus, after pouring out prayers toward heaven. Rising from the depths of Tartarus before the astonished spectators, the dead man revealed the whole tragedy of his departure from this world and the mercy of his return.

Therefore, when the emperors’ decree pressed upon them, the holy martyrs were enclosed in thirty vessels in the spectacle of the circus. Inside, these were stuffed with black pitch, bituminous fuel, and the stench of sulfur; outside, they were kindled with the blazing logs of a crackling pyre and torches of brushwood [Col. 0137C].

The summits of the flaming pyre rose in a cone thirty cubits above the threatening height of an obelisk and the rounded peak of a sphere. Yet when the heavenly power restrained the torrent of fire, the triumphant men came forth into public view before the crowd of the circus, like gleaming refined gold.

Then the repeated ferocity of the wicked executioner, which always feeds on the punishments of the innocent and fattens itself on spilled blood, added the sacrificial offerings of martyrdom to the merits of the athletes and champions of Christ.

They wrapped the joints of their fingers and the thumbs of their hands with cords smeared with the liquid of oil, and likewise cruelly bound the toes of their feet. But when the threads of the cords had been burned by the flame, divine protection kept the athletes of God—struggling in the wrestling-ground of the world in the manner of an athletic contest—safe from the smoking balls of fire [Col. 0137D].

But, defeated by this victory of Christ’s confessors, the bloody executioner ordered the saints to be led into the amphitheater, bound with iron collars, so that, when the doors of the caverns had been opened and the barriers of the cages removed, they might be torn by the teeth of bears and gnawed by the jaws of lions.

Thus the governor’s foolish heart nourished an empty hope hateful to God, while the furious rage of the beasts and the greedy appetite of the animals, restrained by heavenly command and not daring to devour the prey offered to them, closed the gaping throats of their gullets, as the poet says of the prophet:

> “And the savage lions learned to spare their prey.”

At last the blessed Julian, struck cruelly with a drawn sword together with his fellow soldiers and bathed in a red stream of blood, happily died [Col. 0138A]. When ten lepers came to their venerable sarcophagi—men whose limbs had been spotted not in separate patches but throughout their bodies by the rough thickening of the dreadful skin that disfigured them with elephantine corruption—they were immediately regenerated in the baptistery by the grace of a second birth. Carried in sheets and shrouds, the sick departed in health through the merits of the saints, having obtained what they had prayed for [Bodl., *illico et s.*, “immediately also,” instead of *illico*, “immediately”].

### XXXVII

Amos was the first famous inhabitant of Nitria. Although his parents unwillingly forced him into marriage, and although, despite being unwilling, he was in no way deprived of the palm of chastity, he resisted the marriage lot imposed upon him more and more intensely, as though it were the contagion of filthy mud or the bite of a poisonous asp.

This Amos was born of noble lineage. Through the overwhelming abundance of his wealth and the sumptuous opulence of his patrimony, he was renowned throughout Egypt [Col. 0138B; Bodl., *habebantur*, “they were renowned,” instead of *habebatur*, “he was renowned”].

When his parents discovered that their beloved offspring had grown up and was already reaching puberty in the years of youth, they invited him—although he strongly resisted—to the unions of the nuptial chamber, as though they were providing for posterity to come.

Unable to frustrate their stubborn persistence by refusing, he reluctantly received a little virgin, betrothed to him by a marriage ring, but in the hidden chamber of the marriage bed he persuaded her through secret words and exhortations to seek the rewards of chastity. Obeying his prayers and admonitions, she aspired to the highest summit of virginity.

They are said to have lived together for a long interval of time in chastity, with God alone as witness, and to have prospered continually in the strict purpose of holy conduct through the increase of their virtues. Under their instruction, a great multitude of both sexes flocked to faith in Christ and contempt for the world.

When he grew strong in practical virtue through the favorable progress of his merits, he undertook the terrifying vastness of the wilderness and practiced the theoretical life of anchoritic solitude. He was endowed by the true rewarder of virtues with countless miracles.

For a certain young man, driven mad and bound in chains, was brought to him in the jaws of a rabid mastiff and was immediately restored to his former soundness. But this was first stipulated: the goods stolen and stripped from a poor little woman had to be returned to her.

When they recognized that the stratagem committed in secret had been exposed by prophetic power, they voluntarily restored what they had taken by fraud [Col. 0138C].

This too should be recalled briefly and summarily: two men promised that they would transport a jar for the man of God. One of them, having broken his promise, lost the camel that was carrying the load as it departed; the other, fulfilling what he had promised, continued to enjoy the safety of his little donkey.

How great the virtue of chastity is will become still clearer from this: while the man of God was trying to cross the waters of the Nile’s channel, he was ashamed to strip off his sheepskin cloak and other garments, lest the shameful nakedness and indecent exposure of his body offend chaste eyes. At once, by divine power, he was transported to the nearer bank of the riverbed.

And lest this seem incredible, remember how Habakkuk, the reaper’s carrier, carried the food of the reapers from Judea to the Chaldaeans by angelic service, swiftly transporting it in an instant across such great distances of land, and abundantly fed and nourished the hungry prophet of God in the lions’ den.

Thus, when the hermit Antony saw the spirit of this Amos being released from the chains of the prison of the flesh, he saw it being carried by a troop of the heavenly army into the starry ranks of heaven [Col. 0139A].

### XXXVIII

During the time of the most wicked Julian, who had abandoned the ecclesiastical rank of the clergy and, straying from the straight path of religion through wandering twists and turns, had begun mournfully to apostatize [Bodl., *apostatare*] according to the rite of the pagans, there was in the Thebaid a certain man of venerable life named Apollonius. It is said that in the fifteenth year of his age he entered the secluded places of a vast wilderness, avoiding the company of mortals, and remained hidden not far from an ancient shrine. Our Redeemer entered that shrine, and the offspring of the wicked Antipater was pursuing him; there he cast down to the ground, face-first, all the busts of the idols together, in accordance with Isaiah’s prophetic prediction:

> Behold, the Lord sits upon a light cloud, and he will come into Egypt; and the manufactured things of the Egyptians will be shaken before his face, and they will fall to the ground.

He says that the “light cloud” prefigures the most chaste womb of the virgin Mary, free from the defilements of human corruption and from the embrace of a man.

Finally, the aforesaid servant of God, enduring the horror of the desert for eight periods of time—that is, for the course of forty years—not with flagging but with tireless strength, had become abbot and ruler of approximately five hundred monks. Because of the outstanding glory of his virginity, shining with many signs and wonders, he is said to have bent his knees a hundred times during the daytime hours and as many times during the night, calling upon God. His *colobium*, which he began to weave from the fiber—or rather the husk—of flax, without any elaborate variety of little pieces of cloth, was made into a linen garment from a smooth mass of spun and twisted threads, with the rays of the loom creaking and the comb beating. Although he remained hidden for a considerable time in the deserts, throughout all those long periods the garment was never at all undone by age.

His food—or rather, his frugality—was said to have been so austere that he ate chiefly bundles of green herbs and fresh little vegetables from the gardens, as though he were enjoying a dish seasoned by the kitchen, although he rejected food that had been prepared by boiling or roasting over hearth fires.

On one occasion, when Julian—who had seized tyranny and apostasy alike—was forcing not only those established in the clerical order but also those committed to the monastic profession into military service, Apollonius was thrust by a centurion into the hiding place of a prison. But in the silence of the dead of night an angel, shining with an exceptionally clear ray of light, unlocked the prison bolts before the trembling guards and rescued the man of God from the filthy squalor of the stone prison.

One day, as Apollonius was traveling, he found bands of pagans raging everywhere around an idol. By the bonds of his prayers he caused them to remain fixed as though rooted to the ground, beneath the open sky and the burning heat of the sun, motionless, unable to proceed anywhere or in any other direction [Bodl., *nec*, “nor”]. When they discovered that this had been done through the man of God, they immediately sent envoys and promised that, if they were given permission to depart, they would reject all observance of religious rites, embrace the Catholic faith, and break the frivolous image of the idol into pieces or burn it into ashes and cinders. The outcome of events proved that this was indeed done.

On one occasion a nearly sufficiently bloody quarrel was being waged between two populous estates, one of believers and the other of unbelievers. By a chance occurrence the aforesaid man of God came upon armed bands, protected by a tortoise formation of shields, who were already about to cut one another’s throats with drawn swords. As he earnestly tried to calm the confused hostility of both crowds with peaceful words and attempted to restrain the cruelty that had arisen among the furious band, a certain warlike instigator, supporter of the conflict and standard-bearer of the intensifying battle, is said to have resisted with frenzied and furious uproar, saying that, with peace rejected, he would fight to the death.

Then the saint said:

> May the fortune you desire come to you according to your words. While the others reconcile the broken treaty in harmony, you alone shall pay the avenging penalty of bloody death. Moreover, no sarcophagus of a tomb shall receive your accursed corpse as it receives other mortals; rather, torn by the beaks of birds and gnawed by the jaws of beasts, you shall be deprived of common burial.

And so the bloody fate occurred just as the prophetic word had foretold.

At a certain time, when the most sacred solemnity of Easter was being celebrated within a cave, and many were crowding eagerly to the cave of the man of God to observe the feast, like a swarm to a beehive, the celebration was completed and they were nourished with the customary frugal fare: dry and scanty crusts of bread and bundles of vegetables sprinkled with salt. Then, having poured out prayers toward heaven, he faithfully implored God’s protection. Before long, at the entrance outside the vestibule, Christ in his accustomed compassion bestowed such an abundance of delicacies upon his hungry people, carried by bearers whom they had never known, that they were daily fed abundantly, until Pentecost—which is reckoned as the course of seven weeks, just as a jubilee is calculated by seven-year periods—with the divinely supplied provision of banquets.

That this was a gift of heavenly munificence rather than a present of human generosity is gathered from the clearest proofs. The fruitful little gift of blessing, brought to the unknown guests, was divinely supplied at the wrong season—that is, in spring, not autumn: pomegranates, which are also called “granate apples,” together with the dates of the palm, which they call *nicolaos*, honeycombs, grapes, and *palatae*, that is, masses of dried figs. Yet we know that the shoots of vines and the offshoots of palms put forth leaves and flowers in spring, while in autumn they ripen and mature, swollen with clusters and yellowing with bunches.

On one occasion, while a disastrous famine was cruelly raging indiscriminately among the people of Egypt, many crowds came to him for provisions. But he blessed three baskets filled with crusts and little cakes, provisions sufficient to feed the brothers for only one day, and presented them to the hungry crowds of the people. Those baskets, by a fruitful blessing, supplied the people’s need for bread for four months, refreshing them and protecting them from the famine and danger that threatened. He is also remembered to have done the same with fine wheat flour and meal, together with the thick richness of oil.

In the first miracle he resembles the Gospel baskets and baskets of provisions. In the second he equals the jar of oil and the handful of flour made abundant by the prophet Elijah’s fruitful blessing.

### XL

Having now completed, although only in summary, the examples of the male sex—men who supported the structure of chaste conduct upon the unwavering foundation of integrity—let us likewise proceed step by step in our discourse to the illustrious persons of the second sex, who persevered in holy virginity with the unbending firmness of mind and remained steadfast throughout, striving happily to pluck from them the most beautiful flowers of chastity.

Thus, with him graciously providing the aid of his protection—he who is born a virgin from a virgin’s womb, expiated the guilt of the first-created man, and blessed the condition of the whole world after overthrowing the rulers of darkness—let us ornament our account with an inextricable thread. Just as earlier we gathered from both Testaments examples of this principal sex suitable to chastity, whose virginal purpose opened above all other gifts of virtue the courts of paradise and the vestibules of the heavenly kingdom, so let us now strive carefully to unfold, within the lineage of the female sex, the richest proofs of chastity, as we shall support with examples below.

First, as we related above, there was blessed Mary: perpetual virgin, enclosed garden, sealed fountain, little branch of the root, bearer of the flower, dawn of the sun, daughter-in-law of the Father, mother and sister of the Son at once, and also his bride and blessed handmaid; mother-in-law of holy souls, queen of the citizens above, a dove among sixty queens and eighty concubines. Because of the perpetual privilege of her purity, she deserved happily to receive within her womb the hostage of the age, the monarch of the world, the ruler of heaven, the redeemer of earth—announced by the archangel, overshadowed by the Paraclete, and welcomed with a rejoicing heart.

Yet, as I was carefully writing about Mary’s perpetual virginity—who was a favorable virgin before receiving the sacred Word and remained an even more favorable virgin after the proclamation of her heavenly childbirth—the memory of the most holy virgin Cecilia suddenly came to mind. Rejecting, for the sake of chastity, the marriage allotted to her and the betrothal arranged by her suitor, she despised, scorned, and rejected them with the praiseworthy fervor of her spirit, as though they were filthy refuse from latrines.

Although an instrumental harmony resounded with one hundred and fifteen notes, as though the deadly melodies of sirens had enticed the inexperienced toward the dangers of life, she listened to them with deaf ears under the pretext of preserving her integrity. Therefore, turning her own suitor—and, if virginity’s fortune permitted it, her future brother-in-law—from the superstitious worship of shrines, she caused those reborn in the baptismal font visibly to enjoy the sight of angels. A heavenly citizen, sent from the stars, offered them garlands woven of white and purple flowers, saying:

> Guard these crowns with an immaculate and pure body, because I have brought them to you from the paradise of God.

### XLI

The celebrated report of the virgin Agatha also spread widely at that time, when the emperor Diocletian, governing the monarchy of imperial power, inflicted savage edicts of torture upon the worshipers of the orthodox faith. It penetrated throughout the whole province of Trinacria. Neither the cruel mutilation of her limbs, nor the dreadful harassment of the lictors, nor sharp fragments of pottery, nor the blazing fires of coals could in any way restrain, impede, break, or overcome the chastity of her integrity. Rather, like an adamantine rock, she grew harder than iron against the tortures inflicted by the executioners.

A native of Sicily and a citizen of the town of Catana unanimously bear witness to these events and to the signs of their undisguised truth. When the fires of Mount Etna boiled, its ashes glittering widely, and rivers of molten torrents, rushing headlong in sulphurous globes of flame, crackled, they set the sacred sarcophagus in which the virgin’s little body was enclosed against the descending rain of fire like a tower in its way and a bulwark of a wall. Immediately, with the virgin’s intercession, they quieted the terrible heat of the furnaces, which would have burned everything in their path, and the heaps of rocks melted by the flames, which would have been swallowed up.

### XLII

It also seems worthwhile to me that the praises of the most chaste virgin Lucia should follow the reports concerning holy Agatha. Our teacher and guide Gregory is known to have joined them together in the daily canon when the solemnities of the Mass are celebrated, placing them in the catalogue of martyrs in this manner: “Felicity, Anastasia, Agatha, Lucia,” so that those born among the same neighboring people in Sicily, who rejoice together in heavenly glory, should not be separated by the sequence of letters.

For just as the municipality of Catana is happily crowned above the other cities of Trinacria by Agatha’s martyrdom, so the town of Syracuse in Sicily is exalted by the prosperous successes granted through the privilege of the most famous young soldier of Christ, Lucia. When her mother, exhausted by a prolonged illness and healed of a flow of blood through Agatha’s merits, was conversing with her, Lucia addressed her in alternating prayer:

> By her herself, I beg you, who saved you, do not name a husband for me, nor seek from my posterity the fruit of mortality. Instead, give me, as I go to the author of my integrity, our Lord Jesus Christ, everything that you were about to give me, as I went to a mortal man, the author of my corruption.

When her mother consented, a sudden redistribution of possessions took place: the chests were unlocked and the purses of the poor were filled; wedding ornaments were distributed, and banqueting halls in heaven were purchased. While the carnal inheritance was uprooted, a spiritual commerce was carried on.

But the bridegroom was inflamed with the torches of anger over this affair. The consul Pascasius, relying on tribunician authority, was afflicted with bitter anguish because the young soldier of Christ could not be bent from her firm purpose of virginity, neither corrected by the severity of words nor handed over to the deceitful seduction of procurers, although they attempted to drag or drive her, bound with ropes [Bodl., *restibus*], to a detestable brothel and hated house of prostitution.

But the protection of Christ guarded the saint unharmed from every device of magicians and uncontaminated by the superstition of diviners. At last the furious consul handed her over to be roasted on fire-breathing grates, so that lumps of black pitch and resinous fuel, together with glittering oil, might heap up the fires of the pyres. But these were quickly quenched by a shower of divine power.

Thus blessed Lucia the virgin, with the seal of her modesty preserved and the course of her life completed, deserved the glorious triumph of martyrdom. Pierced by the sword, she preferred to pour out her purple blood rather than lose her precious chastity. Yet the bloody executioner did not look upon the dying virgin with rejoicing. Instead, bound by chains and rejected by the whole of Trinacria as a barbarian marauder or cruel pirate chief, he was led toward the city of Romulus weighed down by rigid collars. Having received a capital sentence from the Roman senate, he provided a mournful spectacle.

### XLIII

Finally, Justina, a servant of justice and a virgin not to be despised by the orthodox, endured at Antioch, during the unhappy reign of Diocletian, such suffering and such things for the preservation of her virginity that who, relying on only moderate ability, could claim to explain them—unless he had carefully learned all the deeds of signs and wonders that are read uncertainly in the written records?

Neither could her suitor drive her from the stronghold of her integrity, nor could the magical necromancy of sorcerers overcome her in any way. Every stage of magical illusion that deceitful rogues had fashioned through cunning phantasms disappeared like vanishing smoke, withered like melting wax, and dissolved in an instant like a fading shadow.

When Cyprian, who at that same time is remembered as the most celebrated of diviners and, after Zoroaster and Simon, the most eminent of magicians, could not bend her to marital union and the companionship of marriage by employing leviathan-like arguments and deceitful traps of deception, he prudently understood, although still a pagan, the unconquered trophy and irresistible prize of Christ through the most chaste virginity of Justina, by which she had destroyed and expelled every device of opposing powers.

Accordingly, he was soon instructed by the ecclesiastical exorcism and reborn in baptism, in the womb of the grace that was giving birth, where twelve or six steps are arranged. He was admitted into the assemblies of Catholics, so that he who had utterly overturned and destroyed the machinations of magicians might, in turn, learn the mysteries of heaven from above and become a fearless preacher. He who had been an obstinate opponent of the faith thus gradually advanced through the seven degrees of the Church and happily reached the highest summit of the pontificate.

Justina, however, not only remained favorably endowed with the glory of integrity to the end, but also, to receive the palm of passion, did not yield when tortured by various torments, harder than diamond. She had not placed the foundations of her unconquered mind upon the sandy gravel, wavering this way and that, but, like the wise man described by the Gospel oracle, she set the lofty structure of her house upon the most solid rock.

While she was savagely beaten with harsh whips upon her sinews and repeatedly struck with slaps, she was finally ordered to climb into an iron frying pan crackling with tallow and pitch, so that the tender virgin might be roasted amid such torment. But Christ, in his customary mercy, by which he takes care of the humble and willingly shows pity to the brokenhearted, restrained the power of the blazing fire and powerfully protected the virgin’s limbs from the approaching destruction of the frying pan, for the illustrious glory of his name.

Finally, when Claudius Caesar was torturing the willing martyrs of God in the squalor of prisons and compelling them by cruel edicts to observe the rites of the shrines, Justina received the sentence of decapitation. Together with Cyprian—no longer relying on necromancy but endowed with the pontificate—she was made purple with the sacred crimson of her blood.

### XLIV

What, then, shall I say of blessed Eugenia, crowned with garlands of perpetual chastity and armed with the banner of flowering virginity? After being trained in the liberal arts, she had learned perfectly, according to the disciplines of sophistry, all the syllogisms of the philosophers, the sects of Epicurus, and the arguments of Aristotle, together with the fivefold silence of the Stoics.

When summoned by her father Philip and sought in marriage by a suitor born of noble ancestry, she rejected marriage for the sake of the greater glory of virginity as though it were filthy dung; she despised it as discarded refuse [Bodl. omits *projecta*, “discarded”]; she recoiled from it as from the ink of black soot in a foul chamber pot. Rejecting the conveyance of a litter and leaving behind the attendants of her parasites, she went to the maternal bosom of holy Church accompanied by only two eunuchs.

There, intending to receive the sacrament of baptism and to seek the novitiate of monastic service—not in a womanly fashion—she joined the assemblies of the saints under the tonsure of the male sex, after cutting the curls of her hair contrary to the laws of nature. She was admitted into the ranks of Christ’s soldiers without a scar upon her chastity, with the seal of her modesty preserved.

Her entire family’s pious affection and the domestic concern of her household clients believed that she had been taken away by accidental circumstances and mourned her sadly with tearful sobs, like Proserpina, whom the fictions of poets claim was carried off by Pluto. Immediately she sought foolish advice from soothsayers and diviners, who chattered empty ravings of falsehood and vainly applauded themselves as possessing, above other mortals, knowledge of hidden things.

But while they invented frivolous matters that caused anxiety and lacked the truth of prophecy, the customary mercy of the Savior did not allow a city set upon a mountain or a lamp shining beneath a bushel to remain hidden for long. Thus, amid the savage and infamous reproach of slander, the praise of her concealed chastity was revealed.

Although the author of her integrity had decided to hide the gift of her virginity in secret places and had endeavored that it should be known only to the knowledge of the divine majesty, to which the hidden mysteries of secrets are disclosed, the following occurred. Melantia, a virgin whose name itself suggested darkness, forgetting the chastity proper to a matron and driven by the mockeries of wanton obscenity and the incentives of the flesh with seductive goads, attempted deceitfully to bring against Eugenia the false disgrace of prostitution and the sinful pollution of a brothel.

But Eugenia, striking back like a shield of iron in an apologetic defense, turned against those who had directed them the deceitful accusations launched from the quiver of falsehood. The text of Eugenia’s little book explains this more fully. It recounts how, in ancient times, when the fabricators of falsehood, rather than elders of the people—whom the spur of adulterous desire had bloodied with the crime of incest—were attempting falsely to accuse Susanna with discordant insolence of speech, they were overwhelmed by a dense and dreadful shower of stones and provided a cruel spectacle of death.

Thus the Psalmist’s judgment seems rightly to correspond and agree historically with the prosperous outcomes of both women’s lives, although it is believed to have been prophesied allegorically concerning the Redeemer:

> Unjust witnesses rose up against me, and iniquity lied to itself.

And as though an appropriate requital followed for this insult of slanders, which the innocent suffer from the deceitful, the Psalmist declares:

> I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.

### XLV

It also seems worthwhile that the glorious example of the illustrious Agnes should not remain unknown to celibate imitators of integrity and despisers of carnal impurity. Indeed, it should become known to those who share the same virginal purpose and belong to the fellowship of chastity.

For the preservation of her integrity, she rejected all the glory of ornaments offered by the son of the prefect, who sought to obtain the proposed marriage. It is said that, despising them like the filthy wallowing of a stinking sewer, she gave this reply:

> Depart from me, kindling of sin, nourishment of crime, food of death, because I have already been anticipated by another lover, who has betrothed me with the ring of his faith. He has surrounded me with fresh and glittering gems [Bodl., “precious gems”]; he has clothed me in a robe woven with gold. His father knows no woman; his mother is a virgin; angels serve him; the sun and moon admire his beauty.

Although for this reason she was stripped of her own clothing and thrust, to the infamous disgrace of her birth, into the hated brothel of prostitution, where the detestable obscenity of harlots rages [Bodl., “rages wildly”] and the brazen shamelessness of adulteresses is disgracefully violated, she nevertheless, surrounded by the radiant splendor of immense light, enjoyed the sight of angels and was given the Lord’s garments.

Oh, how great is the ferocity of raging lust, and, by contrast, how great is the mercy of restored modesty! For when the aforesaid lover of obscenity, inflamed by carnal fires, entered the brothel with his companions in crime, intending to inflict upon the most sacred virgin the filthy mockeries of seduction with shameless lips, he was swiftly struck down by the sword of heavenly wrath and fell dead.

Like Uzzah, who did not fear to touch with profane hands the ark of the covenant, in which were stored the flowering priestly staff, the golden urn filled with a heavenly gift, and the tablets engraved with the letters of the Decalogue, he immediately paid the penalty of premature death.
