But then, for the greater glory of God, so that the attackers of the Catholic faith—who devised a plan but could not establish it—might be silenced with stammering lips, and so that the pagan tumult, raging against the untouched chastity of the Church, might cease to growl fiercely with foaming teeth, God restored that man, revived and strengthened, from the abyss of hell to the light of life. Then she, bathed in the rose-red color of purple blood, was martyred, offering Christ the immaculate victim of virginity.

Her tomb, placed in the cemetery, restored the virgin Constantina—whose grave illness we shall record below—to her former health, as though she had been nourished by heavenly medicine.

### XLVI

I also considered it inappropriate to pass over the glorious persons of the distinguished girls Thecla and Eulalia, whose examples correspond to the pattern of virginal material.

Thecla, a devoted young girl of Christ, had been betrothed and was reaching maturity in the first years of her life. She had not yet been reborn in the baptismal font and was growing up in the chaste practices of modesty. When she heard the teaching of an excellent teacher expounding the gift of integrity, she was not swayed by her mother’s entreaties nor compelled by the pleas of her suitor to turn toward the companionship of the marriage bed and the banqueting halls of marriage.

She was brought before the bars of the theater into the bloody hands of executioners, who earnestly tried to deprive her of the reward of chastity. Nevertheless, with Christ granting his protection, she preserved inviolate, amid the torn ornaments of chastity, the precious robe of virginity amid the stern roars of lions and the fierce jaws of ravenous bears.

She also safely and happily escaped the crackling grates of enormous pyres and the half-burned brands of funeral fires, which had been extinguished by the fountains of heavenly mercy.

Eulalia, endowed with a double triumph and adorned with a twin trophy, is recorded in the heavenly register as one who would complete her course and preserve her faith. After the glory of her loudly proclaimed virginity, through which she recoiled from the filth of the carnal sewer and rejected the companionship of the marriage bond, she happily reached the glorious palm of martyrdom.

### XLVII

Moreover, Scholastica, Christina, and Dorothea, born at Caesarea in the province of Cappadocia, although separated by a differing sequence of ages, were nevertheless crowned by Christ with the same diadem of integrity.

The first, under the title of confession, although the occasion of a bloody passion was lacking, lived honorably among the Catholic community and shone at such a lofty height of purity that, when her only brother—whom she had opportunely requested in earnest prayers for the interval of one night—stubbornly refused to comply, she immediately changed the serenity of the sky into storms by pouring out fountains of tears, stirred up thunder with terrible crashing to frighten the trembling world, and at the same time brought forth fiery flashes of lightning, presenting the world with a marvelous spectacle.

The second is remembered to have been so inflamed by the torches of divine love even before she received the beginnings of baptism that, from the age of eleven, she is said to have been a despiser of fanatical superstition [Bodl., “profane superstition”] and a worshiper of heavenly decrees.

Her father, serving in the palace as master of the soldiers, instructed this daughter in the liberal disciplines of sophistry. He erected for her a tower, raised high with threatening height and constructed with a strong framework of masonry. In it, together with twelve girls, she was compelled by her father, devoted to the worship of shrines, according to the custom of invocations, to burn incense to the gods and offer sacrifices.

But when he discovered that he had rightly been rejected by his only daughter, and saw the gilded images of the idols—Jupiter and Apollo, as well as Venus, the lover of adulteries—broken into tiny pieces, the bloody executioner and savage parricide, rather than a pious father, immediately devised various kinds of torture to torment the same daughter.

Nevertheless, her mind devoted to God feared neither the foul squalor of prisons nor the rock fastened around her neck and submerged in the depths of the sea. It did not soften before stakes cruelly beating her tender limbs, nor did the disfigurement of her beautiful head—although her blond hair was shaved and she was dragged bald through the streets—bend the firmness of her heart.

She was not astonished by the blazing fires of the furnace, comparable to the devices of the Chaldean ruler, nor did the frightened girl fear the poisonous jaws of asps, which the Marsi provoked with their incantatory spells. Rather, with Christ granting his protection, she happily overcame all these things while preserving the treasure of her modesty.

Finally, wounded by twin blows of a spear and drenched in purple blood, she was martyred for Christ.

When the bloody executioner Sapricius could not compel the third—not only to marry but also to observe the wicked worship of idols and the foolish rites of the pagans—he immediately exercised the cruelty of the racks, displayed livid bruises from blows of the palms, and applied the blazing flames of torches.

He also handed her over to two women who had recently suffered shipwreck in the faith and apostatized from the companionship of Christ, so that they might corrupt her. But the opposite occurred: she so healthfully healed the disgraceful scars of those apostates with the medicine of repentance that, in reverse order, they immediately preceded their own teacher to the palm of martyrdom.

As she was leaving the cruel tribunal, Theophilus mockingly and laughingly asked her to send him pleasant little gifts of fruit from the paradise of her heavenly bridegroom, toward whom she confessed that she was hastening. Although this was spoken with the muttering of slander, it was fulfilled in truth. For it is recorded that, on the day before she suffered and was handed over to be cut down by bloody swords, she sent the same Theophilus three apples together with an equal number of purple roses. Through this event he obtained the occasion of his own salvation and was crowned with the red garlands of martyrdom.

### XLVIII

Constantina, a virgin of completely unblemished virtue and daughter of the emperor Constantine, who is known to have governed the monarchy of the threefold world with prosperous success at that time—did she not, once the report of her famous virginity became known, encourage nearly all the daughters of the Roman prefects, and almost the entire noble offspring and beautiful young growth of the female sex, to practice the Christian religion and seek the crown of chastity? By conversation she urged them, by her words she persuaded them, and by her example she stirred them.

Thus, rejecting the marriage chamber and the commerce of marital luxury, each one was led to confess with frequent sighs that she earnestly desired the embrace of the heavenly bridegroom and hastened among the wise virgins with clear-burning lamps. This is more fully revealed by the writings and brief works that transmit her conduct and teachings. Attica and Artemia provide sufficiently clear evidence of this matter through their unstained virginity and flourishing chastity.

Their father, Gallicanus, was converted to the Catholic faith after pagan worship had been uprooted from its foundations. At that time, while Constantine, the son of Constantius and born from the concubine Helena, held the imperial scepters in Britain, no one in the Roman monarchy was more distinguished. Constantine alone judged him, above all persons of tribunician power and all magistrates of the nobles, worthy of receiving Constantina, born of royal lineage, in a marriage dowry because of the favorable outcomes of his wars and the prosperous successes of his triumphs, and of betrothing her to him for marital union, if circumstances allowed.

He was believed to have been the only man at that time capable of withstanding the attack of the Scythian people, who, setting out from the northwest with an immeasurable apparatus of war, were ravaging the provinces of Thrace like enemies.

### XLIX

After these bands of virgins have been mentioned, let not the little report of the virtues of Eustochium and Demetrias, spreading everywhere through Europe, fail to be received in our sheets of writing and little painted letters.

The first, the favored daughter of Paula and sister of blessed Blesilla, was so distinguished in the Western empire, endowed with an assiduous talent for books, that in the libraries of the orthodox, where Jerome’s most discerning commentaries are read, her opinion also is circulated through frequent and constant reading. Indeed, six times three—or three times six—volumes on Isaiah’s prophecy are said to have been written for that same virgin in an extensive succession of discourse.

It would also be tedious to mention individually all the remaining little commentaries on the canonical Scriptures, upon which the aforesaid interpreter of the divine law labored, compelled by both his mother’s diligence and the virgin’s industry. I believe that they cannot remain hidden from the philosophy of your intelligence as it hastens through the open fields of books. He also produced for her a distinguished little work of exhortation concerning the preservation of virginity.

The second, born from a noble lineage, was so exalted by the wandering praises of rumor that, even instructed by transmarine writings, she ascended through the degrees of virginal merits to the highest beacon of virtue.

At the request of her mother, a volume arranged in a lengthy and elegant sequence of discourse was sent across the sea to the aforesaid young soldier of Christ. In it, the beginnings of her life are described as follows:

> It must therefore be written to Demetrias, a virgin of Christ, a noble virgin, a wealthy virgin, and—greater than these things—a virgin ennobled by the ardor of faith and trampling upon riches.

And below:

> Born in the highest rank, raised amid the greatest wealth and the greatest pleasures, she suddenly burst free from the many and varied allurements of this life, which had entangled her as though with extremely tenacious bonds, and transformed all her possessions at once through the virtue of her spirit.

And shortly afterward:

> For she remembers what riches and glory of the world she rejected, what allurements of the present life she finally despised, and what pleasures she renounced.

Again, near the end of the volume, when he was elegantly setting forth the example of the final judgment and the terror of the Judge, who will weigh the deeds of each person on the equal scales of discernment, he began as follows:

> It is a recent event, which you yourself witnessed, when, at the sound of the shrill trumpet and the blare of the Goths, the mistress of the world, Rome, oppressed by grief, trembled with fear.

And below:

> If, he says, we fear mortal enemies and the human hand in this way, what shall we do when the blast begins and the terrible trumpet resounds from heaven, and the whole world echoes together at that voice of the archangel, clearer than every trumpet? Then you, accompanied by the choirs of the righteous and the holy virgins, will fly upward to meet the bridegroom, and so forth.

Textual variants otherwise omitted above: XL: *nasciturus prot.* (Bodl.; incomplete: “about to be born, first-created …”) for “is born … [and] expiated the guilt of the first-created man”; *monarchum* (Bodl., masculine “monarch”) for *monarcham*. XLII: *auctorem* (Bodl., singular “author”) for *auctorum*. XLIII: *omnium contrariarum virtutum* (Bodl., “of all contrary virtues”) for “every device of opposing powers”; *et ad* (Bold., “and for”) before “the illustrious glory of his name”; *sacrosancti* (Bodl., genitive “of sacred blood”) for *sacrosancto*. XLIV: *caruerint* (Bodl., “have lacked”) for *carerent* (“lacked”). XLVII: *profanaticae* (Bodl., “profane-fanatical”) for *fanaticae*; Bodl. omits *eidem* (“for her”); *vexaturas* (Bodl., feminine plural) for *vexaturus* (“about to torment”). XLIX: *virginitatis* (Bodl., “of virginity”) for *virgineis* (“virginal”); *metu* (Bold., “with fear”) for *metuit* (“feared”).

### L.

Likewise, we shall sketch, at least in the rough strokes of our pages, the glorious passions of the three sisters Chionia, Irene, and Agape, who triumphed with equal rejoicing under the title of confession and the proclamation of holy virginity. As reports celebrating them grew widely and abundantly, Diocletian, who at that time unhappily wielded the imperial scepters, ordered that the aforesaid foot soldiers of Christ be summoned. If they would apostatize from the practice of the Christian religion and, straying from the straight path of faith, be shipwrecked in the whirlpools of impious paganism, he promised them courtly insignia and offered them wealthy inheritances, if they preferred marriages [Bodl. adds: “of the world”].

Since they refused, with unanimous judgment, the world’s wealth and the allurements of the present life that entice like a procuress, immediately, under the pressure of the impious persecutor’s command, cruel torturers thrust these followers of the holy Church into the hidden chambers of the stone quarries. Blessed Anastasia, so that they might not fail from the frugality of hunger, supplied them with an allowance of food and a ration of provisions, and willingly remained at the entrance of the quarry.

Thereafter the aforesaid sisters were handed over to Dulcitius, Diocletian’s satrap, to be tortured unless they burned incense to the gods. When the insolent governor gazed upon the beauty of their faces—beauty not fashioned with cosmetics or acquired by curling their locks with a curling iron, but innate through their natural complexion—he was immediately captivated by the enticement of their eyes and slid into lust, as wax melts before a hearth. He was seized by such a blind fire and inflamed by such secret goads that, in the silence of the untimely night, he did not fear violently breaking into the cell where the aforesaid virgins were celebrating the chant of the psalms. There all the kitchen equipment and numerous utensils of the cooks were kept.

Soon seized by the furies of madness, he began, like a raving or frenzied man, to embrace blackened kettles and pots darker than soot, and to kiss foul frying pans. After raging for a long time under the prompting of his twisted desire and being mocked in ridiculous derision, he withdrew. His intention had not been fulfilled but exhausted; he emerged as pot-black in body as he was stained by illness of mind. Darkened as though by Ethiopian blackness, he was not recognized by his own parasites and household dependents.

Indeed, the dark image of his forehead was hidden from his own eyes, which alone were open to him, but was visible to all his companions and lictors. When, blackened like a kettle, he struggled to break into the palace vestibule so that he might make a lamentable complaint to the emperor, in tearful sobs, about the insult inflicted by the household servants, some beat him with flexible rods, others struck him with open hands and fists, and some, blowing in his face as though he were the black phantom of a scoundrel, drove him far away.

Thus he was led to his own house by the hands of his servants and was mournfully received amid the noise of his lamenting dependents. He supposed, in vain, that he had been mocked by the magical deception of necromancy practiced by Christ’s young recruits. Like a crushed serpent hissing with its forked tongue, he again climbed the high tribunal, so that he might gaze upon the holy virgins after they had been stripped of their cyclades, inflamed by the filth of obscene desire and kindled by the torches of insolent wantonness.

But when the little coverings of their garments were pulled away piece by piece by criminal hands, they could not in any way be stripped from the holy limbs. Finally, since Governor Dulcitius was frustrated in all the devices he had begun and whatever he planned to contrive against Christ’s young virgins was rendered useless [Bodl.: “was rendered useless”], Diocletian ordered the companion Sisinnius to receive the aforesaid servants of God for punishment with sufficiently savage cruelty.

They were to be tortured unless, by performing foul rites in the shrines, celebrating the Lupercalia and Compitalia, carrying out the Portumnalia, offering sacrifice in the suovetaurilia, or observing the Floralia and Nictelia, they reconciled the maddened gods and restored the gods’ favor. Since they obstinately refused to fulfill this execrable command, two of them were thrust into the blazing fire of a crackling pyre, while one was wounded by the points of arrows. They were destined to possess the rewards of paradise with the palm of virginity and the crown of martyrdom, and, together with the 144,000, to sing the virginal melody; thus they departed together to Christ.  
[Col. 0150D]

### LI.

Moreover, when the Augusti Valerian and Gallienus were ruling, and the heat of the burning persecution and the ardor of cruelty had grown fiercer, the soldiers of the heavenly army—who, for confessing the faith, did not shun the arena of combat like fearful wrestlers—were being killed by the bloody blades of executioners.

At that time two virgin sisters, named Ruffina and Secunda, born of noble parents, briefly avoiding the fury of the persecutors, were hastening in a covered wagon toward their little estate in the regions of Tuscia. Immediately, when their betrothed betrayed them—men who had recently returned to the sewer of apostasy like mastiffs to their vomit—they were brought back to Rome by a chiliarch pursuing them with a cavalry troop. They were to be confined in the foul hiding place of decaying prisons and endure the mockery of jeering ridicule.

After Ruffina had been beaten with the most savage blows and her flesh had been bloodied by the blue welts of the lashes while she was being scourged before the raging satrap, Secunda said steadfastly:

“Apply fires, stones, swords, whips, clubs, and rods. As many punishments as you inflict, so many glories will I count; as many acts of violence as you commit, so many palms of martyrdom will I reckon.”

Soon the holy virgins were again shut in the hidden depths of a prison, which was loathsome with the smoky stench of fetid dung. But the dark gloom was driven away by heavenly splendor, and the foul filth smelled like incense and the fragrance of pure nard.

Again they were ordered to be thrown into the burning vapors of baths heated mercilessly over a pile of coals, but they are said to have emerged from the baths unharmed and safe in the beauty of their limbs. Yet the bloody severity of the torturers, repeatedly shattered and weakened by successive reversals, knew neither how to relent nor how to pity.

For he ordered the servants of God, bound to the mass of a huge rock, to be sunk without mercy in the middle of the bed of the Tiber. But the whirlpools of the waters, giving to God the glory denied by the unbelievers, restored the holy virgins unharmed to the riverbanks. Therefore the satrap, astonished at such great marvels, is reported to have said:

“Either these women surpass us by magical art, or the holiness of virginity reigns in them.”

Finally, having received the sentence of death, they ascended to the stars of heaven, borne aloft by angelic companies, with the banner of virginity.  
[Col. 0151B]

### LII.

Nor, I think, should the praises of the holy virgins Anatolia and Victoria be passed over. Their reports and the privileges of their miracles spread far and wide through all the quarters of the world, whenever, as the circle of the year turns, their birthdays are celebrated by Catholics in the church and recited from the written pages.

Thus, when Decius was ruling and the unbridled ferocity of torturers had cruelly blazed against Christ’s soldiers, no fury of persecutors and no severity of punishments could drive the aforesaid virgins from the stronghold of integrity. Instead, with lavish generosity, they bestowed their entire patrimony and the glory of their ornaments as alms on the maimed and the matricularii (those enrolled for church support): both the headbands and leg bracelets, and the little scent-boxes of nard, and the pendants hanging at the neck with jewel-studded crescents.

When this became known, the hearts of their suitors were inflamed by the frenzied torches of madness. While all the income of their resources and the abundant proceeds of their wealth were being given to the poor beggars for an agape, Eugenius and Aurelius, who were believed to be destined to become their husbands, obtained by fraudulent counsel and concealed dealings imperial documents authorizing them to be taken from the city of Rome to their own estates. They feared that, if they publicly denounced them on the charge of Christian religion, their possessions and the estates of their lands might be proscribed under the authority of the treasury.

Blessed Victoria—whose prophetic name truly signified Christ’s victory—was therefore taken to the territory of Tribulanum, so that there she might be distressed by the abundance of hunger and the scarcity of food. At that time it happened that all the townspeople whose citizenship had been in the municipality of Tribulanum, unable to endure the venom and breath of a scaly dragon, abandoned the town and scattered everywhere along wandering paths.

Holy Victoria promised them voluntarily that, if they turned to God, abandoned the little images of the gods, and renounced the Lupercal rites of the shrines, she would drive far away the poisonous openings of the foaming basilisk and restore the city to its former safety. For because of the poisonous blasts of the dreadful chelydrus, the unfortunate populace was being slaughtered in great numbers and ranks; parents, seeing the premature funerals of their children in an inverted order, were cruelly confined by the lamentations of bereavement.

Then the patron of the city promised, speaking generally on behalf of people of both sexes, that all would open their trusting hearts to the girl’s oracles, provided that the savage cruelty of the *gipsa* [reading uncertain], which was bringing a deadly plague upon the pitiable citizens, were kept farther away.

Then the holy virgin, supported by angelic assistance, was led with the crowds of the populous city, who flocked together in companies to witness the spectacle, to the dragon’s cavern. The applause of its young had already begun to crackle, and the cockcrow was sounding. She addressed the lurking beast without trembling in fearful gestures or wavering with frightened pallor:

“In the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, come out from here, most wicked dragon, and give honor to God. Go where human beings do not dwell.”

The dragon obeyed her words and fled away at the swiftest pace. She, entering the beast’s hiding place, urged the people, now freed from danger, to build an oratory for her in that same cave and to provide young girls for the support of her religious life. At the command of their parents, seventy young virgins were subjected to divine service; sweetly singing hymns in harmonious melody and gently resounding with the chant of psalms, they remained devoted to the examples and teachings of Victoria.

After three years had passed, her suitor Eugenius earnestly begged the flamen of the Capitol to compel Victoria, once Diana’s image had been brought in, to burn incense to it according to the rites of apostasy. She abhorred the impious crime and detested the bearer of the image, and was killed by a sword-stroke.

Yet the bloody executioner did not gain victory over Victoria. Rather, crippled, with a withered hand, and festering with the thickened skin of elephantiasis and swarming with worms, he breathed out a foul spirit.

Anatolia, meanwhile, having been thrust into exile and becoming renowned through the miracles of her signs, equaled her aforesaid companion in deeds of power. Indeed, she quickly healed the consul’s demoniac son, who was bound with rigid chains, by driving out the inhabitant. As this report grew famous, she restored to their former health both the possessed, the epileptics, and the other sick.

She also swiftly rescued Marsus, who by magical incantations was provoking poisonous snakes to injure the holy virgin, as the poet says:

> In the meadows, by chanting, the cold snake bursts apart,

and she rapidly freed him from coils wound in dreadful spirals. Then blessed Anatolia, while standing in prayer with her hands raised to the stars and her prayers poured out toward heaven, received, with the triumph of virginity, the red garlands of martyrdom, when a drawn sword was driven hilt-deep through both her sides.  
[Col. 0153A]

### LIII.

But what is surprising, when grace shines forth in its simplicity, after a virgin has borne a virgin through holy childbirth, of whom it is said that the principate rests upon his shoulders, if the Church should thus abound in virgins, just as heaven gleams with stars?

Even the most chaste Joseph is celebrated by the ancient legal books with immense praises. Divine protection guarded him unharmed from the danger of the many calamities that threatened him—not only the conspiracy of his envious brothers, who did not shrink from fraternal murder, but also the obscene schemes of a deceiving mistress who had forgotten marital modesty, so long as he remained the companion of pure virginity and the despiser of the seductive brothel.

God filled him with the secrets of future wonders and miraculously instructed him, through a kind of prophetic inspiration, with foreknowledge of signs and portents hidden from other mortals. Thus, not without reason, while he slept, he seemed to be worshiped and revered by the clearest lights of the sun and moon, by the remaining stars of heaven, and at the same time by the fruitful bundles of sheaves.

While flourishing in the most beautiful grace of youth and in the beauty of his handsome face, relying on a still more beautiful virginity, he treated lightly the twisted snare of female boldness and avoided the trap of crafty deception. Likewise, he rejected the fraudulent enticements of feminine teasing and the alluring provocations of flattering speech, which, like the pleasures of thickening nectar-wine or of a honeyed mead-like drink, pour in the black poison of venom and brutally drive to Tartarus all who are found unguarded, without the armor of faith and the military equipment of virtue.

He despised them, conquered them, and fled away with the palm of virginity. Although he suffered the narrow, filthy hiding places of the prison and the foul squalor of the dark dungeon because of his outstanding purity of chastity, God, who knew his secret chastity, to whom hidden things lie open and from whom concealed matters are not hidden, entrusted to him the government of the Egyptian people and committed to him the administration of a flourishing empire.

David too, the most renowned of kings, while still undergoing the apprenticeship of youth and endowed with undefiled virginity, before he was bound by the union of marriage and the ties of wedlock, did he not soothe the frenzied man with the well-tuned strings of his harp and cure the madman through the abundant grace of healing, driving far away the dreadful madness of foul spirits?

He is also described as a tender youth who, though weak in his arms [Bodl.: “strong in his arms”], tore apart the jaws of roaring lions and broke the fierce mouths of bears limb from limb. Relying only on smooth stones and a sling, he alone engaged and beheaded the enormous giant of the Philistines, clad in a helmet’s crest and breastplate, armed with [lacuna] and protected by the bronze boss of a shield.

Therefore, although his life had remained worthy of approval to the end of his death—since he alone, by the privilege of his own merit, could have wiped away the offenses of his grandchildren and great-grandchildren, as is often carefully prescribed in the Book of Kings concerning kings who violated the ancient law: “I will not extinguish the lamp of David”—nevertheless, after abandoning the state of virginity, the innocent Uriah was killed, Bathsheba was joined to him in an illegitimate marital bond, and, to expiate this rashness, the firstborn child was struck by the sword of heavenly wrath.

Although, I say, both patriarchs were most pleasing to the heavenly majesty as long as they lived on ethereal air and the breath of life [Bodl.: “as long as they lived”], nevertheless, after the fellowship of carnal union [Bodl.: “after the union of the fellowship”], lesser praises of virtue grow around both of them.

That Nazarite Samson, sacred to the Lord from the very frail infancy of his cradle by his seven locks, before he was captured by the deceitful embraces of Delilah and was weakened by the disgraceful deception of adultery, being bound in the seductive chains of enticement—before the curls of his hair were cut away by the iron—is reported to have shone throughout the whole age, until that time, with how many signs of miracles and reports of virtues previously unknown [Bodl.: “is proclaimed”].  
[Col. 0154B]

### LIV.

Therefore, just as we stated above, through Jeremiah, Daniel, and the other companions of the same purpose and associates of flourishing chastity, the future virginity of the incarnate Word was represented by mystical veils of the sacraments, so through innocent Abel were prefigured gentle innocence and passion, while through Melchizedek were prefigured the priesthood of heavenly power and the dignity of the celestial office.

The former, to explain the matter by returning further to its origin, on account of the worthy palm of innocence and the title of original patience, was the first of mortals to deserve to offer holocausts acceptable and pleasing in the divine sight, while rejecting his brother’s sacrifice. For this reason, cruelly bloodied by his impious and wicked brother, who broke the unbreakable bond of brotherhood contrary to divine justice and human right, he prefigured the future passion of our merciful Redeemer at the end of the ages by the purple-red dye of his precious blood.

But Melchizedek, flourishing at the beginning of the third age of the world, the first supported by the dignity of the highest priesthood and endowed with the illustrious summit of pontifical office, encountered the patriarch at the time when the kings’ rivalry had arisen. The patriarch was returning with 318 household servants after winning a famous trophy and, after the enormous slaughter of the armies, bringing back abundant spoils from Sodom together with his cousin.

Did Melchizedek not offer, on account of the holiness of his way of life, the typical offerings of bread and wine, thereby typologically prefiguring the person of the Redeemer, who would offer a twofold sacrifice? Hence David’s prophetic utterances rightly compose praises concerning the priesthood of Christ, in which he offered a double victim:

> You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

His paternal lineage and the descent of his maternal generation are hidden from the ages, as is the nature of his genuine birth. The Apostle likewise testifies:

> Without father, without mother, without genealogy.

Although the widespread tradition of the Hebrews supposes that he was Shem, Noah’s firstborn, the great-great-grandfather of Abraham, Nahor, and Haran, there is nevertheless a great difference between the uncertain traditions of the Pharisees and the carefully elaborated definition of sacred Scripture. For the Catholic Church in no way accepts the laments of apocryphal writings or the uncertain fables of trivial storytellers.  
[Col. 0155A]

### LV.

But I shall return to the subject. Let the integrity of blessed virginity be adorned, I say, not by the beautiful grace of the outer person but by the religious chastity of the inner person.

For if the outer person boasts in worldly fashion of the costly adornment of clothing, the inner person gives thanks in vain and emptily for its own beauty, since the Chosen Vessel, by a general judgment, seems to oppose this as though it were a particular matter, saying:

> Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of the Lord.

Why, then, is the splendid vanity of the world admitted into the Catholic basilica of Christ, on account of which the virgins of Christ, living in the service of the monastery, strive to be decorated with delicate garments?

Did not Achan, son of Acharmi, who, from what had been devoted to destruction in the town surrounded by seven circuits of walls, secretly stole a scarlet cloak and a bar of gold for himself against the commander’s decree, provide a dreadful spectacle of death to the ranks of the Hebrews when he was buried beneath a rain of stones, together with all his relatives and the household companions of his dependents?

By allegory, the decrees of the ancient Fathers established that the town of Jericho, with its sevenfold barrier of walls, signified the world with its seven thousand ages. Therefore the forbidden ornaments of the world—colored with the costly purple dye of sea-snails—cannot properly and regularly be fitting for the pupils of the monastery, the virgins of Christ, contrary to apostolic statutes and legal ordinances.

For the shepherd of the Lord’s flock and the doorkeeper of the heavenly court, of whom the poet says:

> The heavenly key-bearer who opens the gate in the sky,

proclaims with principal authority and authentic pontifical office:

> Let a woman’s adornment not be outward—the decoration of gold or clothing—but the adornment of the heart.

Hence Gregory, our ever-watchful shepherd and teacher—our teacher, I say, who removed from our parents the error of gloomy paganism and handed down the rule of regenerating grace—when explaining the Gospel saying, “Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses,” added:

> “Let no one therefore suppose that there is no sin in the pursuit of clothing. For if this were not a fault, the Apostle Peter would never have restrained women, in his letter, from desiring costly garments, saying: ‘Not in costly clothing.’ If this were not a fault, the Lord would in no way have praised John for the roughness of his garment. Consider what a fault it is for men also to desire that from which the pastor of the Church took care to prohibit women.”

[Col. 0155D]

### LVI.

For it seems evident to me that an inexcusable disgrace of arrogance and a sign of ostentation is revealed by the fact that no one desires to be clothed in costly and colored garments where no one is able to see him. Hence blessed Cyprian, speaking of virgins, says:

> “Why does she go out adorned and carefully dressed, as though she either had or were seeking a husband?”

And below he added:

> “For it is not lawful for a virgin to adorn herself for the display of her beauty or to glory in the flesh and its beauty, since the Apostle says: ‘But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.’ Let them have no struggle greater than that against the flesh, and no stubborn contest greater than that of conquering and subduing the body. The emblems of ornaments and clothing, and the enticements of beauty, belong only to prostitutes and immodest women; and scarcely any women have more costly adornment than those whose modesty is cheap. In the Apocalypse that woman was clothed in a purple and scarlet mantle. Let chaste and modest virgins flee the dress of adulteresses, the attire of the immodest, the insignia of whores, and the ornaments of prostitutes.”

And elsewhere:

> “Moreover, if you arrange your hair more extravagantly at your own expense and walk conspicuously in public, attracting the eyes of young men to yourself, drawing the sighs of adolescents after you, nourishing the desire to lust and kindling fuel for hope, so that, even if you yourself do not perish, you nevertheless destroy others, and present yourself to those who see you like a sword and poison, you cannot be excused on the grounds that your mind is chaste and modest. Your disgraceful dress and immodest adornment convict you, and she can no longer be counted among Christ’s virgins who lives in such a way that she can be loved.”

Thus far Cyprian.

Could God, the author and creator of all things, not have dyed the rough wool of yearling sheep and the bristly fleece of rams with the red blood of the shellfish or with the bloody juice of berries, or indeed naturally colored them with the purple dye of sea-snails, if through his careful foreknowledge he had seen that this would be useful and beneficial for our needs? Then what the poet ironically and happily sang would truly be fulfilled:

> Nor will wool learn to counterfeit varied colors;

> but the ram himself, now with softly glowing  
> purple dye, now with saffron-colored mud,  
> has changed his fleeces;

> of its own accord, scarlet will clothe the grazing lambs.

And as though he who is said to have “created all things at once,” living forever, had been unable to create the world originally, he now strives to add to it and enlarge it through the foolish and superfluous inventions of human industry.

Hence the illustrious Cyprian, bishop of the Punic people, likewise says:

> “For God did not make scarlet or purple sheep, nor did he teach them to dye and color wool with the juices of herbs and shellfish. The rule of Catholic faith rejects the notion that the Almighty left anything necessary in the fashioning of visible things unfinished and imperfect. But what wonder if the sayings of the apostles and the ordinances of jurists abominate the aforesaid trivial fables, when even pagans are read to have reproached pagans and gentiles, as a ridiculous insult of jeering mockery, in this way—laughing and scoffing with the infamous proverb:

> ‘For you there is clothing painted with saffron and shining with purple dye,

> and tunics with sleeves and bands around the mitre.’”

### LVII.

Judith, daughter of Merari, after Manasse’s death, taking up the garment of widowhood and rejecting the bridal veil, despised the flattering enticements of suitors. Before the trumpet blasts of the Apostle’s horn had resounded—“I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as they are”—she lived chastely in the upper room of the dining chamber, flowering like a glowing lily in devout chastity and hiding from public view.

When she planned, accompanied by Abra, to circumvent the dreadful prince of the Assyrians, who had terrified the trembling world as innumerable thousands of infantry and cavalry gathered around him, she believed that he could be deceived in no other way and judged that he could be beheaded only if she were captured not merely by the natural beauty of her face but also by bodily ornaments. Concerning her it is written among the Seventy translators:

> “She put on the garment of her joy and placed on herself leg bracelets, bracelets for the arms, rings, and all her ornaments, and she arranged herself exceedingly, for the capture of men.”

Behold: not by our assertions but by the testimony of Scripture, women’s adornment is called “the capture of men.”

But because she is remembered to have done this during the severe siege of Bethulia out of compassionate grief for her fellow citizens, not from any failure of chastity, she returned, with the respect due to modesty preserved, a celebrated trophy to the fearful townspeople and a renowned triumph to the trembling inhabitants, bearing the tyrant’s head and the canopy.

Likewise, in Proverbs that bold and obstinate woman, veiling the figure of the Synagogue, promises that her husband will return at the full moon. She is described as having seduced a foolish young man with the attire of a prostitute and the luxury of seductive display, and as having sorrowfully lured him out after deceiving him with the pleasure of fraudulent words. Thus, like an ox led to sacrifice, seized by the insolence of blind desire, he does not fear entering the infamous brothel of the prostitute, unaware that he is being dragged toward chains, until an arrow pierces his liver, just as a bird hastens swiftly toward a snare.  
[Col. 0157C]

### LVIII.

It would be embarrassing to recount the shameless arrogance of certain people and the carefully adorned insolence of their stupidity, which are found assumed in both sexes—not only among nuns living under the rule of a monastery, but also among ecclesiastics living in the clergy under pontifical authority—in opposition to the decrees of the canons and the norm of regular life. Their sole purpose is that the bodily form, adorned with forbidden cosmetics and embellished beauty, should be dressed and decorated limb by limb and part by part.

For the attire of both sexes of this kind consists of a linen or hyacinth-colored undergarment; the scarlet tunic’s collar and sleeves are surrounded by silk bands and red-dyed shoes [Bodl.: “banded shoes”] and skins [Bodl.: “surround”]; the locks at the forehead and temples are curled with a curling iron [Bodl.: “combed”]; dark head coverings give way to white and colored cloaks, sewn together with bands and hanging down excessively to the ankles; the fingernails are sharpened like those of falcons and hawks, or even like those of owls, which their naturally implanted need to eat urges to advance cruelly against birds and mice with the hooked fork of their feet and the predatory talons of their claws.

But lest, because of the publicized insolence of the arrogant and the exposed arrogance of the undisciplined—who prefer to be carelessly ignored rather than mercifully reproved—we be accused through oblique envy or be disparaged by the mockery of twisted slander, this discussion will not be prolonged any further but will be ended promptly with a suitable conclusion.

Otherwise, while we seek a medicinal poultice for the festering wounds of the arrogant, we may experience at the hands of rivals the rigid lashes of insults and the poisonous blows of harsh attack violently inflicted upon us. Yet I am not greatly troubled, however much they may grow livid against the champion of truth and groan heavily against the reprover of swelling self-display.

For:

> Better are the wounds of a lover than the kisses of a hater;

the livid stripe of a devoted friend is easier to bear than the false flattery of an enemy. Hence the proverb says:

> The flattering tongue aggravates the sinner’s vice,

> and binds the delighted man to his crime with praise.

And below, it says:

> Rather let the voice of a correcting friend be free,

> and let it not allow blind poisons to creep through books.

Therefore I think that forgiveness and pardon can easily be obtained from everyone in general, since the severity of these words has aggravated no one in particular by chastising him. For the generality of many people taken collectively ought not rightly to be wounded where the particular character of individuals cannot be blamed. Indeed, genus and species—that is, generality and particularity—differ greatly from one another.

But since we have decided to speak of the glory of untouched virginity, it is almost superfluous to discourse rhetorically about coverings, when we have resolved to philosophize only about the proclamation of chastity, setting aside for a little while the concerns of other matters, as the free grace of God supplies the means.

For the entire privilege of pure virginity is preserved rather in the protection of a free mind alone than contained in the narrow enclosure of the flesh. It is more healthfully guarded by the inflexible judgment of a voluntary will than utterly destroyed by the compelled servitude of the body.

Hence Augustine the African, bishop of Hippo, proclaims in an elegant prose statement:

> “The holiness of the body is not lost when the holiness of the mind remains, even when the body is violated; just as the holiness of the body is lost when the purity of the mind has been violated, even when the body remains untouched.”

Prosper impressed the same point through cola and commata in honey-sweet poetic epigrams, saying:

> An uninjured mind loses nothing when the body is violated;  
> the wounds of the flesh do not stain one who does not consent.  
>   
> The will, not joined to the deed, does not incur the crime;  
> it harms one more to desire the crime than to endure it.

> Thus all things return to the inmost chambers of the heart,  
> so that often the mind is guilty without the flesh,  
> when it alone conceives within  
> what has been removed from an untouched body  
> and carries it out through hidden movements.

Finally, the aforesaid bishop of the Punic people says:

> “Virginity of the flesh is an untouched body.  
> Virginity of the soul is incorrupt faith.”

Prosper likewise says:

> Virginity of the flesh is possessed in an untouched body;  
> virginity of the soul is undefiled faith;  
> without it, concern for bodily modesty benefits nothing,  
> but devotion of mind increases both goods.

Therefore, having completed the little book on the most beautiful virginity, though written with only moderate urbanity, my pen now demands an end, and the course of dictation must be concluded, because the illustrious preacher says:

> “There is a time for speaking and a time for keeping silence.”

For I did not believe that any other little gift would be more acceptable and pleasing to Christ’s virgins than that the rewards of chastity should be earned by the chaste and the gifts of purity sent to the pure.  
[Col. 0159A]

### LIX.

But I confess to your charity that I could not complete and send this little work to you as quickly as you urged me to dictate it, although it is small, because I was burdened by the load of pastoral care and oppressed by the weights of earthly affairs. Careful concern for ecclesiastical governance denied me the space of secure rest and the prolonged interval required for dictation, while the tumultuous noise of secular affairs disturbed me.

For leisure, secret quiet, and the solitude of seclusion provide abundant material for writing to those who dictate. Conversely, the wordy loquacity of chatterers and the hostile secular business which the Apostle commands to be administered by those held contemptible in the Church violently take it away.

We did not presume, like Origen, the illustrious teacher of the Greeks, who, at the beginning of his third five-year period of life, had almost completely mastered all the disciplines of the philosophers—that is, arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy, astrology, and mechanics—at the beginning of puberty, to take up the course of dictation while notaries recorded it and copyists transcribed it.

For these reasons, the proper return owed to your letters was delayed, as though by an obstacle of postponement. They proved that the repayment of my vows had so far remained unfinished [Bodl.: “unfinished,” singular], especially, as I said, because the neck of my weary mind was pressed down by the heavy bundle of distractions from various affairs.

This slow delay caused the promised reply of the little booklet to be postponed for a very long time, across so great an interval. For the leaky boat of my fragile intellect, shaken by the whirlwind of a dreadful storm, reached the desired harbor of silence only late, though the oars of my arms were laboring.

Nevertheless, the pledge of our rusticity, relying on the heavenly protection of Christ, confidently trusts that the sails of our masts, filled by favorable blasts of wind, have happily crossed between the Scylla of solecism and the chasm of barbarism on unbroken ropes, and that they have not feared the rocky collisions of lautacism [a grammatical fault] or the whirlpools of moytacism, which violently thrust the unwary—those found without the guidance of grammarians—toward the shipwrecks of error.

LX. Furthermore, just as I endeavored to honor the glory of inviolate virginity with the favorable testimony of rhetoric [Col. 0159D], so likewise, if this bodily prison of the soul does not perish before its appointed end, as they say, amid the cruelties of advancing fate, and if the hard repose of the Fates and the iron sleep of death does not entangle the folding of my eyelids, I shall endeavor, with Christ’s help, subtly to adorn the praise of that same chastity in heroic hexameter verses. And, as though I had already laid rhetorical foundations and built prose walls, I shall confidently rely on heavenly aid to place upon them a firm roof, with trochaic tiles and the dactylic shingles of meter.

Nevertheless, remember that I promised the little gift of the following eulogy only on condition that you deign to spur on, with as many repeated letters as before, the sluggish talent of my mediocrity—which, like a hearth covered with the yellow ashes of embers, grows cold in wintry weather unless kindled by the fuel of inquiry or writing [Col. 0160A]—since you had confidently sought to obtain the preceding text of the little book, not at all arranged with the pleasing eloquence of urbanity [Bodl., *nequaquam*, “not at all”]. For I shall strive in vain to weary myself with the laborious burden of the following little work unless I discover that the style of the preceding writing is pleasing to your discernment, especially since the elegance of metrical charm and the eloquence of rhetorical exposition differ from one another as much as sweet must differs from heady unmixed wine.

Thus far, meanwhile, I have depicted the appearance of beautiful virginity and composed the lovely countenance of chastity with various colors [Col. 0160B] of virtues, like flowers of pigment. So noble craftsmen of images and painters of royal persons commonly adorn cuirasses with gilded petals [Bodl., *thoraciclas*] and embellish the most beautiful outlines of the limbs with artfully fashioned faces. Yet these same artisans are often physically deformed and contemptible by nature, and the royal portrait, painted with a carefully adorned crest, is praised more than the painter’s despicable person is revered. For this reason I suppose that the prelate of the apostolic see said:

> “I have painted a handsome man, though I am a foul painter; I direct others toward the shore of perfection, while I myself still wander amid the waves of sins.”

Come, then, young women of Christ: may the fitting recompense for this present little work be the frequent return of your prayers, and may the support of my labor and sweat be the assistance of your intercession [Col. 0160C] [Bodl. ends here]. I seem to tremble, waver, and totter, both because of the quality of my own merits and because of the fragility of my faith; may I therefore, relying on the most steadfast pillar of your patronage, deserve to be supported happily and firmly. May the powerful assistance of your merits, in kindly compassion, mercifully sustain me, whom the heavy burden of crimes and disgrace weighs down beneath the sorrowful load of guilt. Thus, when in the holy assembly the entire company of the venerable monastic order has offered, with bent knees and in concord, to the Creator the marrow of its prayers as holocausts, may it deign to remember my contemptible person, in accordance with what your devout vows have promised. And may our prayer for you who beseech us be directed, according to the Psalmist’s saying, like incense is burned before the divine Majesty: it is compared with the raising up of outstretched hands and made equal to the evening sacrifice.

Therefore the sacred offspring of the Lord’s maternal aunt, the first bishop of Aelia, when the splendor of the Gospel was beginning to dawn and the radiance of eternal light was shining, said:

> “Pray for one another, so that you may be saved.”

And immediately afterward he added:

> “The continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful.”

Indeed, exceedingly frequent prayer is believed to be like a lofty fortress and an impenetrable bulwark against the poisoned snares of rivals. May the nourishing Trinity, one in the substance of its Godhead and threefold in the subsistence of its persons, which governs the monarchy of the whole world, deign continually to protect your blessedness from the heights of heaven [Col. 0161A].

Farewell, flowers of the Church, monastic sisters, scholarly fosterlings, pearls of Christ [Col. 0162A], gems of paradise, and participants in the heavenly homeland. Amen.

[Col. 0161]

# LETTER TO ACIRCIUS, OR THE BOOK ON THE NUMBER SEVEN, AND ON METERS, RIDDLES, AND THE RULES OF FEET

[Note: [Col. 0161A] “This is Aldhelm’s treatise, about which so many critics have written so much. The *Riddles* were formerly published by Delrio and later reprinted in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. But the *Riddles* are only one part of the entire work. Maius published the other part in volume V of the *Classici Auctores*. At last this work is now being published complete [Col. 0162A]. In correcting the *Riddles*, I used seven Paris manuscripts, one of which, perhaps from the tenth century—a circumstance sufficiently rare—contains the entire work, both *On Meters* and the *Riddles*. GILES.”] (C, S)

[Col. 0161B] To the most distinguished lord, glorious above all ranks of dignity, and long ago bound to me by the chains of spiritual clientship, the illustrious Acircius, ruler of the scepters of the northern empire and dispenser of the governance of an illustrious royal kingdom: Aldhelm, a native son of the catholic Church, sends unfading health unto eternity.

I do not doubt, most reverend son; rather, loosening the reins of profound trust, I am confident that your prudent heart remembers that, two pairs of five-year cycles ago, we entered into the pledge of an inseparably joined covenant and united ourselves in the fellowship of devoted charity. For formerly, in the time of our youth, when your accomplished nature was being adorned beneath the hand of a venerable bishop with the sevenfold abundance of spiritual gifts [Col. 0161C], I remember that I acquired the name of father, while you received the titles of adoptive dignity together with the prerogative of heavenly grace.

This fruit of spiritual growth is indicated by prophetic speech, which explains it through allegorical riddles: a shoot, representing the blessed and incorrupt Mother of God, sprang from the root of Jesse with fruitful branches; and the purple flower of its young shoots, brought forth under mystical overshadowings, prefigured the Redeemer of the world, who mercifully annulled the handwriting of the first parents and caused the sevenfold wisdom of understanding, together with the Spirit of the remaining virtues, to germinate. That same sevenfold number of mysteries is most frequently attested by the holy miracles of the Testaments [Par., *oraculis*, “oracles” rather than “miracles”].

As I turn over the mystery of this number through repeated recurrence, I shall endeavor to gather, from the most delightful paradise of the Scriptures, a collection of field-stalks and spring flowers, as it were, and weave them into a single crown, so that it may become more plainly evident and shine more clearly than light for all who investigate it with scrutiny, from how many advances and through how many sacred orders the beginnings of our relationship and the still immature training of our apprenticeship originally proceeded, sprang forth, and flourished [Col. 0162B].

This, I say, sacred number of sevenfold units existed from the very beginning of the world’s creation. For it is related that not only the entire universe of creation, encompassed by the turning and swift motion of the heavens and by the two hemispheres, was fashioned in the manifold form of a single seven-day week—although the living Eternal created everything simultaneously in an instant and atom—but also that the longed-for rest of the future promises and the blessed happiness of everlasting life, which will be repaid to each person according to the reward of his merits, will be granted to the innocent, those free from the guilt of sin, only after the condemned multitude has been separated by a thousand-year number divided into seven stages of time.

The mysteries of the same calculation also became clear if I unfold matters by recalling their ancient origins. When the dreadful eruption of the Flood, restraining the crimes of mortals and washing away in avenging waters the stubbornness of their heavenly life, killed to destruction all creatures that were nourished by the reciprocal breath of bodily life—except those left for the propagation of future offspring—and cruelly filled the dire maw of Stygian Pluto with the bloodless souls of the wretched, the clean animals are read to have entered the ark in groups of seven, with its three levels or, as another translation has it, its two chambers [Col. 0162C].

Likewise, the sevenfold lineage of Job’s children is described at the beginning of the book in prose, and afterward, according to the Hebrews, is said to scan in dactyl and spondee; and the total of seven sheep is related [Col. 0162D]. Again, at the end of the book, the same number of two-toothed animals is restored twofold as a reward for the palm of his illustrious patience, and is shown to have prefigured the mysteries mentioned above.

Finally, Isaiah, by no means the last among the prophets, testifies that seven women, under the figure of the seven Churches, seized one man—namely Christ, reconciler of heavenly and earthly things. When Elijah lamented the crimes of a cruel people and complained of the mournful slaughter of the prophets, it was said to him by divine oracles:

> “I have left to myself seven thousand men who have not bent their knees before Baal.”

When Elisha raised the child of the bereaved Shunammite woman, who had been put to sleep by the cruel lot of death, joining limb to limb and member to member seven times, he signified the Redeemer, who gives life to the human race through the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, awakening it from the sleep of crimes and the stain of sin.

The noble pledges of brotherhood among the Maccabees, who under the tyrannical rule of Antiochus rejected the flesh of swine and, for the sake of the ceremonies of the divine laws and the rites of ancestral tradition, refused the foul practices of the pagans and the profane nation’s sacrificial foods, are likewise recognized, not without reason, to have prefigured the sevenfold form of the universal Church.

And what of that hall of Proverbs, whose architect and pontiff is said, according to Solomon, to have been Wisdom? Is it not supported by the strengthening of seven columns, when we read:

> “Wisdom built herself a house; she hewed out her seven columns”?

Are not the curtains of the tabernacle, darkened with the purple colors of shell-fish dye and scarlet, and sewn together with various interlacings of loops, extended in length by the fourfold calculation of seven—that is, twenty-eight cubits? [Col. 0163B]

That the number seven sometimes prefigured the grace of the Paraclete Spirit, but at other times represented the image of the ancient Law, we learn from sacred authority, as in the saying:

> “Give a portion to these seven.”

Likewise, Eleazar, wearing the insignia of the high priesthood, is read to have sprinkled the tabernacle seven times with the blood of a red heifer, which had been burned as a holocaust according to the ceremonial rites [Col. 0163C]. Heavenly oracles promised that the remains of its ashes would benefit the expiation of the people of Israel.

The most glorious of the kings, who before knowing the cradle of his first birth figuratively bore, in the very title of his name, omens of pious peace, is described as having celebrated for seven days, with the entire multitude of the children of Israel, the solemn feast of the sanctuary, from the entrance of Hamath to the Brook of Egypt, where the Memphis kingdoms wield imperial sovereignty. Thus the brief epitome of the Old Testament, namely the *Chronicles*, testifies.

But lest I use only the formula of the ancient Law and merely search out and examine the examples of past ages, behold, many things lying openly before us and corresponding by harmonious reasoning support what I believe is properly marked by a recapitulation of Deuteronomy [Col. 0163D]. For when the dark hiding places of the shadows have ceased and the nocturnal retreats of darkness have faded, at dawn the clear, golden radiance of the most limpid sun is poured over all the regions of the earth.

For the holy guest reclining on the Lord’s breast, and the fourth river of the heavenly paradise—from which abundant streams of living water flow in an everlasting, dew-bearing flood—is said to have written a sevenfold series of discourses to the Churches of Smyrna, Pergamum, and Philadelphia and to the other Churches throughout Asia.

In that same vision of the Apocalypse, he also deserved to see, with the keenest eyes of a purified heart, seven seals of the sealed book, containing the mystery of a past prefiguration [Col. 0164A]. Only the lion from the tribe of Judah, the strongest of beasts, fearing no encounter, who according to the patriarch’s prophecy is remembered to have gone up to the prey and lain down in repose, was able to open them. By right he had surpassed the power of heavenly, earthly, and infernal things through the prerogative of his birth and passion. For he is said to possess the key of David:

> “He opens and no one shuts; he shuts and no one opens.”

Indeed, unless someone has broken into pieces the reins of obstinate and wicked unbelief and believed with the marrow of his mind that he has loosed the seals of the preachers’ signs, he will contemplate the mysteries of the Law and the obscurities of the prophets with the circles of his pupils closed and blind and the sight of his eyelids dulled, like an epileptic or one afflicted with visual darkness [Col. 0164B].

[Mai adds here: “Nevertheless, when the seventh seal of that book had been opened, after a heavenly silence among the citizens above and an interval of half an hour, he testifies that he saw seven angels, with seven trumpets and the terrible martial blasts of instruments resounding throughout the whole world.”]

In that same ecstasy of revelation, he beholds seven golden lampstands and an equal number of golden stars, and the feet of the one holding them in his right hand, like burnished bronze resembling Lebanon; from his mouth proceeded a two-edged sword.

I also believe that the famous lampstand of Exodus, whose shaft, fashioned from beaten gold with its branches, cups, and little spheres, was adorned with cultivated ornaments like a leafy yew or branching plane tree, does not differ at all from the aforementioned mystery of the lampstands [Col. 0164C]. Its seven lamps, gleaming with flame-spouting lights—from which the lanterns of all the Churches are illuminated with bright radiance—were joined together by golden bonds.

Thus the illustrious vessel of election, the wise architect, and the typological Benjamin, bearer of the name of Christ, “eating the prey in the morning and dividing the spoils in the evening,” abundantly drenches the seven newly planted fields of the Churches with the dew-bearing rains of sacred teachings.

Likewise Zechariah, eleventh in the order of the prophets, carried away in the vision of revelation and raised to the summit of divine contemplation, deserved to see with spiritual and mysterious insight of the heart and with pure eyes the famous spectacle of the illustrious stone, which is described as mystically adorned with seven eyes [Par., “in the face,” instead of “mystically”] [Col. 0164D].

The foundations of the glorious city of God, which the Psalmist recalls as built upon holy mountains, abundantly satisfied the dry and thirsty hearts of the nascent Church with the canonical streams of seven letters. Like dark water in the clouds of the air or drops falling from above, they moistened and watered the gaping throats of the faithful [Par., “to be satisfied” and “to be watered”]. Those men, as I believe, imbued with divine teaching and instructed by the example of the commandments, may rightly be said to have chewed over and belched forth for succeeding posterity what they had deserved to receive for chewing and belching forth from the nurse of their tender and unformed infancy, through freely preceding grace.

For the supreme author of ecclesiastical administration and instructor of the primitive and illustrious family, whom the seventy-seventh Psalm, as is appropriate to the present aid for explaining these matters, figuratively calls “the bread of heaven” and “the bread of angels,” is read, according to the text of the Gospels, to have fed and abundantly satisfied four thousand men, apart from the multitude of the second sex, with seven loaves. The fragments that remained were lifted up, the crumbs were collected and broken into pieces, and seven baskets or hampers were filled, to the amazement of all who witnessed the spectacle [Col. 0165A].

Nor should that famous legal festival of the Jubilee be omitted. It was celebrated after seven weeks of years had passed, when agriculture rested in a sabbatical year, the dusty shaking of mattocks and rakes ceased, and, as the circle of the seventh month revolved, the trumpets resounded with noisy blasts. It is declared to have figuratively announced by allegory the future mysteries [Col. 0165B].

Moreover, does not the most holy solemnity of Pentecost, recurring through the repeated cycle of seven weeks, suitably attest this kind of calculation? The Paraclete, sent from the highest citadel of heaven after an interval of ten days and rightly called the pledge of the promised inheritance, made the hearts of the apostles fruitful with the grace of heavenly gifts and inspired speech in seventy languages.

The ten-times-seven descendants of the warlike Jerubbaal—that is, Gideon—were prefigured as having been cruelly killed on the summits of the rocks, in a dreadful slaughter unheard of in earlier ages, by Abimelech, who, upheld by tyrannical rather than lawful royal power, broke the rights of kindred and the bonds of devoted brotherhood in frenzied fashion.

Because of the terrible guilt of parricide and the abominable crimes of his deeds, the thorny shoot of the bramble, under the type of the foul and wicked Antichrist, is not without reason compared with him in the example taken by Jotham. The flowering fig tree, together with the leafy branches of the vine and the olive grove with its gray-green foliage, rejected the scepter of empire and refused to assume it. This also bent the shadowed antiquity of the Law and withdrew its foul entrails of cattle and the stinking fibers of holocausts.

And when the ray of the rudiments of the New Testament flashed forth, our Redeemer, the heavenly key-bearer, concerning whom the poet says:

> “The heavenly key-bearer who opens the gate in the heavens,”

answered the question of how often the bonds of offenses should be loosed for sinners: not merely “up to seven times,” but “up to seventy times seven”—that is, fifty times nine and five times eight, which together are reckoned as four hundred and ninety [Col. 0165D].

Likewise, the lineage of eleven generations of seven, linked from the beginning of the world’s creation in a fertile succession, after the shapeless matter had originally received formed appearances through the alternating progression of days, is recognized to correspond with this mystery, extending even to the revered cradle of the heavenly birth.

The physician of Antioch, endowed with the chastity of incorrupt virginity, began weaving this genealogy from the revered offspring of God. He proceeded step by step through the descendants of grandsons and great-grandsons, counting the generations of grandfathers and great-grandfathers, and then recapitulating the order of the genealogy individually through great-great-grandfathers and ancestors. After completing the total of seventy-seven generations, he set down the endpoint of the first-created man [Col. 0166A].

This had formerly been prefigured by the historical account of sacred Genesis, which says:

> “Sevenfold vengeance shall be taken for Cain, but for Lamech seventy-sevenfold.”

The avenging punishments that punish the intelligible Lamech—that is, the guilt of the whole world—after an equal number of generational cycles were shattered, broken, extinguished, and driven into Tartarus by the long-desired and foretold birth of our Redeemer, which overthrew the dominion of dreadful death.

What, I ask, of that famous grandson of the principal patriarch, returning from his uncle in Mesopotamia of Syria with a double sixfold lineage of children, after two ten-year periods had already elapsed? After the arena of his angelic wrestling, he acquired the name of the Israelite race. When the furious madness of his brother came against him with four hundred armed men, and almost trampled underfoot all the rights of kinship, did he not bend himself seven times in repeated acts of prostration, stooping down to appease the rancor of that shaggy brawler and the rage of ancient jealousy? [Col. 0166B]

For the authoritative decrees of the Fathers have established that the sevenfold calculation signifies mystical allegory not only through a simple or sevenfold progression, but also through a tenfold series of recapitulation.

Thus the illustrious man of desires, from the very beginnings of his apprenticeship, although dedicated to divine worship in the midst of a barbarian nation and inspired by the prophetic spirit while Gabriel unlocked the secret things of the world with hidden keys, declares that, in seventy weeks, extending as far as the birth of the Bethlehem ruler, the people of Israel and the nations would be ruled with an iron rod. This means that ninety-eight cycles of five years were completed and extended, beginning from the twentieth year of the reign of Artaxerxes, who held the reins of the Persian empire [Col. 0166C].

At that time, during the eighty-fourth Olympiad and continuing to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when the awaited redemption of the nations is said to have arrived, four hundred and seventy-five solar years are counted. According to the lunar reckoning of the Hebrews, this amounts to four hundred and ninety, with quarters and intercalary additions included, as Julius Africanus, the writer of chronology, is shown to have arranged it [Par. omits “four hundred and seventy-five … reckoning”] [Col. 0166D].

Likewise, the ruler of the Syrians, whom the foul pollution of leprosy had covered limb by limb, rather than merely in separate parts, with elephantine corruption, approached the most famous prophet at the urging of his foreign servant. He bent his terrifying bodily stature seven times, leaning and bowing down into the channel of the Jordan, and most clearly manifested the form of regenerating grace and the prerogative of a second birth, which is bestowed upon the faithful from the womb of the holy Church, from her fruitful entrails, through the sacrament of baptism.

Thus, does not the sixth text of the volume of the Heptateuch declare the sevenfold calculation mentioned above—which is depicted with the mystical flowers of the sacred canons [Mai omits “which … is depicted”] [Col. 0167A]—through the celebrated spectacle of triumphs and through events whose success had until then been unknown?

When the chosen race, the royal priesthood, and the people of possession, sprung from the stock of the patriarchs, with a great phalanx of troops, surveyed for the course of a single week the famous city hated by the powers above, sounding seven priestly trumpets—that is, seven horns—with the broken blasts of the Jubilee resounding through the war-trumpets, they overthrew and utterly destroyed it to the ground.

This figure of future events, according to the anagogical interpretation, is clearly understood to portend, after the completion of seven cycles of ages, the dreadful end of the world about to collapse and the final closure of fleeting life.

The ornaments of the universal Church, according to the decrees of the ancients, are contained in the seven grades of sacred offices [Col. 0167B]. These, distinguished by name from the first order of the sacraments, receive their growth in virtues through exorcists and acolytes and gradually reach the governance of the supreme pontificate and the spiritual insignia of priests.

Therefore the *Praxapostolon*, that is, the Acts of the Apostles, proves that an equal number of men served as deacons and administrators of the primitive Church. Concerning them Arator, relying on poetic eloquence, writes:

> “The laws of ministry suited to the sacred altars  
> they established in seven men.”

But, alas, immediately at the first threshold of the young religion, against the rule of orthodox faith, the wicked Nicolaitans arose from that same group with the jaws of canine barking.

How they sprang from the most destructive roots of error and grew with the poisonous foliage of heretical perversity, the Apocalypse revealed and exposed in angelic fashion. This is clearer in the fifth chapter concerning the heretics; but I shall return to my subject [Col. 0167C].

For the double and ambiguous dream of the ruler of the Nile, portending omens of future things, in which he saw seven ears ripening at the top of fertile stalks, together with an equal number of well-fed cows of massive bulk cropping the pleasant green banks, is found to be entirely consistent with the forms of number mentioned above.

The other tablet of the Testament was likewise read to contain seven commandments in writing. The intercession of the Lord’s Prayer, a helper and a medicine refreshing the ulcerated wounds of souls, is composed in a series of seven petitions.

Indeed, the intervals of day and night, during which we continually perform the duties of prayer, as though paying some public levy and fiscal tribute, revolve in the completed interval of a sevenfold assembly [Col. 0167D]. Hence I believe that the Psalmist sang (Psalm 118:164):

> “Seven times a day I have praised you.”

Elsewhere, the sacred oracles of the same Psalmist also uttered a judgment consonant with the calculation mentioned above, when they are known to have fitted together, by a very similar comparison, the sayings of the Lord, which are chaste sayings, with the purest silver, which is said to be refined sevenfold in the furnace of blazing fire, after the foul rust of dross has been removed.

The secular and foreign disciplines of the philosophers are likewise seen to be reckoned in the same number of parts: arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy, astrology, mechanics, and medicine [Col. 0168A].

And does not the annual recurrence of the seasons, which the Psalmist calls the “crown of goodness,” enriched by the abundance of divine blessing, continually revolve through two and fifty weeks and through the reciprocal turning of its cycles?

Nor is the heavenly and celestial creation itself known to lack this kind of numerical scheme, since the bodily and visible structure of the world is enclosed by seven circles of heaven, descending headlong with the swift motion of the flying sphere, although surrounded by the retrograde courses of the planets in thirtyfold circuits [Mai, “three hundred”].

Moreover, the roundness of the lunar globe, which grows through twice six monthly replenishments of moments by three successive rotations of five days until it reaches the complete circle of the full moon [Col. 0168B], and declines through an equal succession of days as the beauty of its lovely face fades, is varied by seven forms: namely, the two-horned, the divided, and the remaining forms which, according to the decrees of the Fathers, signify the sevenfold form of the Church.

Nor, I think, should the constellations of the Pleiades or Arcturus be passed over. Concerning them divine oracles addressed a man oppressed by a terrible illness through the whirlwind, saying:

> “Can you bind together the shining stars of the Pleiades, or can you loosen the circle of Arcturus?”

For Arcturus, carried through the Rhipaean mountains and revolving at the northern pivot of the sky, where the barbarians inhabit the kingdom of Scythia, is marked by the sevenfold star of the pole and the wagon. Since it never sets and is always joined to the wintry Circius because of its nearness to the axis, it not without reason prefigures, through allegorical riddles, the stern austerity of the ancient Law [Col. 0168C].

Why should I mention the stars called Atlantids by a patronymic name, which Greek tradition named Pleiades because of their multitude, while Latin tradition called them Vergiliae, from springtime, or a cluster (*botrus*), from a wine-heavy bunch of vine shoots?

As they emerge through oblique breaks in their lines from the eastern region, where the golden radiance of the sun rises and pours over the earth, they complete the circuit’s course and beautifully prefigure, through the brightness of an equal number of stars, the sevenfold distribution of the charisms of the universal Church.

The position of the stars which in the language of the Argives are called the Hyades, concerning which the Mantuan poet is read to have sung:

> “Arcturus, and the rainy Hyades, and the twin Bears,”

and which the ancient Roman Latin tradition called the Little Swine, is shown to be sevenfold. It is placed before the forehead of the heavenly bull, which is contained among the twelve signs of the zodiac [Col. 0168D].

Hence mathematicians, with ridiculous foolishness, think that they can divine and foreknow fate, fortune, birth, or the final threads of the Fates, concerning which Maro writes in the *Bucolics*:

> “Such ages,” they said, “run with their own spindles,  
> harmonious Parcae, by the steadfast power of fate.”

Likewise, the differing revolutions of the planets, which—as we have said—regulate the headlong turning of heaven by diverse courses of lines, revolve through seven courses of stars, although in an unequal crown of years.

The dark hiding places of nocturnal blindness, of which it is sung, “He made darkness his hiding place” [Col. 0169A], and which are said to be generated beneath the grim shelter of the earth, are divided into seven separate parts: namely, the time of silence, the dead of night, dawn, and so forth.

The rhythmic rule of musicians declares that the lyre, sounding with the harmony of concordant modulation, consists of seven strings, as Virgil says:

> “Seven … distinctions of voices.”

In the same way, the Catholic monuments of our predecessors demonstrate, more brightly than light, seven formulas of the spiritual library and seven rules of divine Law.

But for me, as the poet says:

> “Before the day, evening will enclose Olympus in darkness,”

and elsewhere:

> “Before I have traversed the boundaries of both worlds in exile,  
> either the Parthian will drink from the Arar, or Germany from the Tigris,”

I shall not be able to pluck all the flowers of the laws that display examples in the sacred number seven [Col. 0169B].
