Perhaps, however, some scrupulous person, secretly examining my rusticity in the thoughts of his heart, may ask and inquire why the calculation of the number seven—which, compelled by the need to explain matters, I had gathered from both canons of the Testaments—is repeated again and again through a sevenfold and sevenfold perplexed recurrence.

Moved by such concern, let him recall and remember that, at the beginning of the letter which I had prolonged at such length for the sake of example, I took the root of my future discourse from my own mediocrity, after offering the subject of this calculation. From it the shoots of my frail and slender talent and the wavering twigs of my words grew up, spreading through open branches [Col. 0169C].

Since, then, charity is bound by so many and such great bonds of mysteries and by such sacred interlacings of numbers through the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, charity of which the outstanding preacher who searched the secrets of the third heaven wrote to the Romans in a linked arrangement—the Greek grammarians gave this arrangement the name *climax*—beginning as follows:

> “Patience produces proven character; proven character, hope; and hope does not disappoint, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us,”

it seems worthwhile that spiritual and unbounded kinship should be preferred to bodily and corruptible relationship. For the instruments of the Gospel relate that the incarnate Word of God—of whom it is written, “My heart has uttered a good word,” and whom the Psalmist likewise sang as begotten from the womb before the Morning Star—seemed in some manner to disregard, contrary to the law and custom of nature, the closeness of human kinship and the affection owed to an undefiled mother [Col. 0169D].

And although the Catholic Fathers, extracting the marrow of the discourse and searching out the hidden meaning in the letters, allegorically referred this to the type of the Synagogue, they are nevertheless known, on the basis of the historical account, in no way to deny that the person of the most holy mother was present.

For this reason we have expressed these matters through such extensive verbal circumlocutions: so that the affection of our former brotherhood, which we are known to have reconciled and joined together through the completed cycles of past years, might in some way be recovered and warmed by fresh remembrance, lest it grow numb through the turning of prolonged time [Col. 0170A] or cool through the long distance between our places.

For truly, the bond of unbroken charity neither withers through the number of years nor fades through the vast interval of lands. Rather, the hearts of perfect charity are sometimes stirred more by absence than nourished by presence.

As the famous trainer of the spiritual contest, in which the competitors will receive the prize of the heavenly palm, said graciously:

> “Although I am absent in body, I am present in spirit.”

Therefore this affinity, strengthened by right hands, must not be despised or considered of little worth, since the aforementioned preacher joyfully relates that he and Barnabas gave the right hand of fellowship to the unshaken pillars of the Churches—that is, Peter, James, and John.

Hail, most distinguished and beloved son! Remembering our ancient brotherhood, may the unbreakable bond of true affection be tied ever more tightly and earnestly, through the successive ages of the world, with unbroken cords “for the remainder of eternity,” in proportion as it is clear that the same intertwined web of affection grows more adhesive through the sacred and sevenfold number of mysteries [Col. 0170B].

Therefore, addressing your venerable greatness with this little preface in a friendly manner, I have appended a few small gifts of verse. Relying on the confidence of domestic familiarity, and especially prompted by the authority of the ancients, I have briefly and summarily culled examples from the various qualities of things, sometimes heavenly and sometimes earthly, finding materials of one kind now grand, now slender, and considering the nature of created things.

For Symposius, a poet skilled in versification and endowed with [Col. 0170C] expertise in the art of meter, is said to have sung obscure riddling propositions, drawn from slight material, in playful lines, and to have ended each individual formulation with three verses. Aristotle also, the keenest of philosophers, argues intricate riddles through the eloquence of prose. Therefore, stimulated by the examples of these men and spurred toward invention by their compositions, the diligence of our exercise strove to compose ten times ten—that is, one hundred—riddle propositions [the printed explanation adds *quinas*, “five,” inconsistently], and, wishing to exercise the first rudiments of our little talent in a kind of gymnasium so that it might later advance to more excellent subject matter—provided, however, that these modest works first lacked none of the rules of metrical definition and properly observed the threefold distinction of syllables according to the exact standard of scansion.

Finally, the aforementioned chapters of riddles were first arranged in lines of four little verses; the following ones, however, according to the opportunity presented by the subjects being composed, are set in five, six, or even seven metrical verses and more. In these I took care continually to attach, in accordance with the discipline of poetic tradition, cola, or commata, or penthemimeres and hepthemimeres, after every two or three feet; otherwise they would waver with slippery syllabic steps, deprived of the proper balance of the rules of the dactylic hexameter. Moreover, the fact that the mute and insensible nature of things, from which an enigma or concealed proposition is composed, is represented as though it speaks and converses is also found inserted in the sacred writings. For sometimes a rational creature uses the gestures and persons of irrational beings, and conversely an irrational creature lacking intellectual vitality makes use of the gestures and voice of intellectual beings.

Thus, in the Book of Judges, various kinds of trees are reported to have sought a monarch, speaking with articulated human voice: “The trees went,” it says, “to anoint a king over themselves.” There, individually, as we have already said above, the fig tree, the vine, and likewise the olive, and finally the bramble, which with its own fire and devouring flames was to consume the cedars of Lebanon, are said to speak in the manner of human speech.

The figure of this trope is also found in the Fourth Book of Kings, where Joash, having gained control of the Israelite people, cruelly compares Amasias, resplendent with the scepters of royal authority, through the mad mockery of derisive banter and the insulting expression of jeering contempt:

> “The thistle,” he says, “which is in Lebanon sent to the cedar which is in Lebanon, saying: Give your daughter to my son as wife,” and so forth.

The Psalmist likewise metaphorically transferred from the animate to the inanimate when he reported that all the trees of the forests had rejoiced, that the rivers had played with the clapping of their hands, and that the fields had appeared to celebrate. He also used that poetic expression:

> “A mother begot me, and soon she is begotten from me.”

And as arguments of rational thought are sought even from mute and brutish creatures, the wisest of all former kings and of those who were to be born thereafter frequently uses the persons of the most foolish in Ecclesiastes, saying:

> “What more does a human being have than a beast, or a wise person than a fool?”

—and other similar expressions.

We have said this so that no one might perhaps think that we have sung the aforementioned riddles by means of a new and unusual mode of expression, as though it had been trodden by the footsteps of none of our predecessors. And, so that the rationale of these matters might become clearer, we appended the legitimate twenty-eight metrical feet with which not only all the principal eight kinds proceed, but also the species that spring from the same stock and are woven into branches of a hundredfold metrical growth. For the sake of a clearer indication, we collected and accumulated for each individual foot as great a supply of examples from different parts of speech as we believed sufficient for the standard of this little work.

What the most celebrated predecessors are known to have made public by the example of a uniform name, we, investigating their footsteps with greater diligence, have worked out in a fuller series of examples. For in so dense a forest of the whole Latin language and in the wooded thickets of syllables, where ancient tradition declares that multiple branches of rules have sprung from the individual roots of words, the matter is not easily grasped by the untrained, especially by those lacking discipline in the metrical art. Nor is it easy for them to distinguish intelligently how, or by what method, long and short syllables—and also common syllables, which are suitable in either position and which the Greeks call δίχρονα (*dichrona*, “of two durations”)—are to be discriminated.

Indeed, from this threefold definition of syllables, rather than from the fountain or mountain of the Muses, about which Persius Flaccus says:

> “Nor have I,” he says, “moistened my lips at the Caballine fountain,”

> “Nor do I remember having dreamed upon two-peaked Parnassus,”

the whole theory of meters is demonstrated, as is which verses are called *monoschemi*, which *pentaschemi*, and which *decaschemi*, with twenty-four time-units, except when they end in a trochee.

[Col. 0172A] On this threefold little outline of the description [*descriptionis*; Maius: *discretionis*, “distinction”], all versification of the heroic hexameter, or principally the scansion of its caesuras, is based, although synaloepha, a kind of joining together, and the additional effects of collision that are elided are frequently inserted among lyric and satiric poets by metrical necessity. These arise chiefly from vowel letters or from syllables ending in a semivowel.

Junius Juvenal, in the fifth book of his *Satires*, elided both of these at once in the course of a single verse, saying:

> “Omenta, ut video, nullum discrimen habendum est.”

> “As I see, no distinction must be made concerning the entrails.”

“It must be scanned as follows: *omen* is a spondee; *tut vide* is a dactyl through synaloepha; *o nul* is a spondee; *lum dis* is a spondee; *crimen ha* is a dactyl; *bend est* is a spondee through synaloepha.”

Again, the same lyric poet, Book IV:

> “The watch-posts of wars, fixed upon trophy-trunks.”

It is scanned thus: *Bello, rex cubi* through synaloepha, then *ae trun, cis af, fixa trop, aeis*.

Thus Annaeus Lucan, the poet of Corduba, twice elided in a single verse of Book VIII, saying:

> “Come, then, companions, let us hasten toward the eastern world.”

Again, the same poet says in Book X:

> “From behind, the infantry assail them; there is no road to safety.”

And elsewhere:

> “At the world’s farthest edge we shall seek the banquets and tables.”

Hence Paulus the Quaestor elided the letter *m* in this way:

> “The new bride follows her husband to the Tartarean abode.”

Prosper too, poet and rhetorician, in the book he entitled *Epigrams*, is known to have elided the same letter twice, saying:

> “Nothing begun or increased, nothing here is changeable.”

Likewise, below:

> “Striving toward the heavenly homeland, recognize the one who calls.”

This same synaloepha is contained in verses of the poetess Sibyl, who says:

> “Then he, the fairest form of the eternal kingdom.”

Phocas the grammarian also elided synaloepha in his first verse, saying:

> “My art belongs to many whom the ancient ages brought forth.”

Isidore elided vowels in this way:

> “Sharp-minded among the waters and musical breezes.”

Virgil likewise, Book XI:

> “Meanwhile, rising Dawn left the Ocean.”

The same poet, in Book VII of the *Aeneid*, included two synaloephas and an eclipsis in a single verse:

> “Now I return: Anchises left behind the secrets of fate.”

For it is scanned thus: *Nunc repet, Anchi, ses fa, torar, cana re, liquit.*

But ambiguity in scansion often confuses these two metaplasms; the following distinction resolves them. If the preceding vowel is elided, it is synaloepha; if the following vowel is elided, it is eclipsis. Thus, in the final verse of the Book of Kings, we read:

> “Greater than the purple tyrants in the seat of the Persians.”

Virgil the Grammarian likewise, in the book he entitled *The Pedagogue*, whose beginning is:

> “If, with you as judge, the songs should be worthy of approval,”

> “the title and purple brilliance will be restored.”

> “If not, you may wrap summer sardines in them,

> “or cover either pepper or peeled nuts with them.”

He elided a syllable, saying:

> “A hard road and the great labor of life.”

Arator the subdeacon likewise elided the final syllable of a genitive in his first verse, saying:

> “Seeing the fires of war amid the wave-tossed walls.”

And below he added in an elegiac verse:

> “And we are carried upon your shoulders, while you lift us with devoted care.”

And Andreas the orator says:

> “The Son of Man himself, who is the God of man.”

For this reason I have attempted to investigate and explain these two kinds of metaplasm from the number twenty-four, because they are inserted very frequently throughout the whole body of poetic books; and unless they are recognized beforehand with discerning subtlety, they regularly create various obstacles for those scanning [Maius adds: “as though traveling along a road”]. Therefore we have collected in groups various metrical verses corresponding to the metaplasm of synaloepha, so that, once these have been examined, no hidden disorder of elided collision, no obscure abyss of broken synaloepha, may thereafter confuse the light of the person scanning or blunt the reader’s perception.

Therefore, so that the threefold measures of the heroic hexameter may be known with greater certainty, I shall attempt to explain them briefly and summarily, as ancient authority is remembered to have handed them down. I believe that I can make this clearer [Col. 0173C] and more intelligible if the style varies slightly through question and answer in alternating turns, just as the blessed Augustine did throughout several bodies of books—namely, the *Soliloquies*, *On Free Will*, and the work he entitled *On the Teacher*, as well as the six books he is known to have written *On Music*—or as Isidore did in the two volumes entitled *Synonyms* or *Polyonyms*.

I think that this mode of writing was transferred from the eleventh species of appellative nouns. Junilius likewise used it in the systematic instruction that he had learned from Paul, who had been diligently trained in the schools of the Syrians, when writing to Primasius, pontiff of the apostolic see:

> “So that no confusion might arise through the negligence of copyists, as commonly happens, I set the Greek letter M for the teacher and D for the students, so that, through foreign characters and those which Latin writing does not use, every error might be entirely removed. For by this method, as by certain whetstones, the powers of the mind are sharpened better and more keenly.”

Therefore, setting aside the remaining kinds of meter, which are divided into a hundred species of variation, let us disclose the most excellent rules of the dactylic hexameter, since it possesses the citadel and insignia of all the others, by placing the aforementioned letter-characters alternately and in turn.

**Question.** How many kinds of verse are there in dactylic meter?

**Answer.** Five.

**Question.** What is dactylic meter?

**Answer.** That which consists of dactyl and spondee.

**Question.** Does not the final foot usually end in a trochee?

[Col. 0174A] **Answer.** Some who are endowed with expertise in the metrical art judged that this foot should be excluded from the verse, because every syllable in the final verse is *adiaphoros*, that is, it is accepted indifferently, and it makes no difference whether it is shortened or lengthened. Hence some consider a verse defective if it admits a trochee. For reason requires that a complete verse contain twenty-four time-units; if a trochee is admitted, the number of time-units is reduced, and there will be twenty-three, which is a *colophos* verse.

**Question.** Above you said that there are five kinds of verse in the dactylic hexameter. Name them.

**Answer.** Hexameter, pentameter, tetrameter, trimeter, and dimeter.

**Question.** Is *hexameter* more correct, or *hexametrus*?

**Answer.** Both, just as *Evander* and *Evandrus*: one comes from Greek, the other from Latin.

**Question.** How many feet does the hexameter, whether *hexameter* or *hexametrus*, contain?

**Answer.** Six, with dactyls and spondees placed throughout it or varied by alternating insertion.

**Question.** How many kinds of hexameter verse are there?

**Answer.** Three.

**Question.** Which?

**Answer.** Dactylic hexameter, heroic hexameter, and iambic hexameter, which is also called senarius. It consists of six simple feet and is likewise a trimeter made of double feet.

**Question.** If a hexameter verse consists of six spondees, can it be called dactylic?

**Answer.** It is indeed called a *spondiazon* verse, but its meter is dactylic; for such a composition belongs only to dactylic meter.

**Question.** What are dactylic hexameter verses?

**Answer.** Those that consist solely of six dactylic feet and contain something other than the wars and deeds of heroes—for example, the *Bucolics*, the *Georgics*, and other works of this sort.

**Question.** What are heroic hexameters?

**Answer.** Those that embrace wars and the deeds of heroes, such as Homer’s *Iliad*, Virgil’s *Aeneid*, or Lucan’s poem celebrating the battles of Caesar and Pompey.

**Question.** What is the fifth foot?

**Answer.** A dactyl.

**Question.** Why does the fifth place belong to the dactyl?

**Answer.** Because in a verse it always properly occupies the fifth position, apart from the other places where it is variously placed. A verse is less smooth if it has a spondee in the fifth place, and it is called a *spondiazon*, as in:

> “Or they draw light greaves with pliant silver.”

Therefore a dactyl ought not to be placed at the end, nor a spondee in the fifth place. For this reason some call the spondee the lowest foot, because it claims the sixth position for itself.

**Question.** What is the syllabic range in a dactylic heroic hexameter?

**Answer.** Every dactylic or heroic hexameter grows from twelve syllables up to seventeen; for the shortest has no fewer than twelve syllables.

**Question.** Do we not often find a verse of eighteen, nineteen, or even twenty syllables, such as these?

> “But to retrace his steps and escape to the upper air.”

Likewise:

> “A laurel stood in the middle of the roof, in the innermost chambers.”

Likewise:

> “Or they receive the burdens of those arriving, with the column formed.”

Likewise:

> “Dear to me before all others, and so forth, up to Diana.”

**Answer.** There are indeed many of eighteen syllables, or of nineteen; those of twenty are rarely, scarcely, or not at all found. But it must be understood that in metrical reckoning those syllables are never counted which, as we said above, are removed by the metaplasm of synaloepha. Thus all those verses that seem to exceed the stated number of syllables, once their synaloephas have been subtracted, are reduced to seventeen, sixteen, or even fifteen, as in the examples you gave above. Hence it must be understood that no dactylic hexameter can be found that appears to exceed seventeen syllables. Thus every dactylic hexameter ends below this number, down to twelve syllables.

**Question.** Please explain and unravel this more lucidly.

**Answer.** A dactylic hexameter consisting only of spondees has twelve syllables. If it has one dactyl, it has thirteen; if two, fourteen; if three, fifteen; if four, sixteen; if five, seventeen. Thus one syllable is added each time a dactyl is added.

**Question.** Into how many species is the dactylic hexameter verse divided?

**Answer.** As metrical theory declares, it has thirty-two schemes.

**Question.** Explain these species of schemes more clearly and in order.

**Answer.** In a verse of twelve syllables there is one species. This is the verse that we said above is called *monoschemus*. It contains spondees throughout, without any variation, and for this reason is called a *spondiazon*, as in:

> “Here the Minturnian envoys are led forth.”

This kind of versification is so harsh and rough that Albinus, in the book he wrote on meters, forbids ending the entire verse with spondees. But when a dactyl is added in the fifth position, it is more clearly adorned.

**Question.** How many schemes are there in a verse of thirteen syllables?

**Answer.** Five, without any hesitation.

**Question.** How and by what method?

**Answer.** A single dactyl is admitted among the spondees and freely runs through all five positions.

**Question.** To investigate the thirty-two dactylic metrical labyrinths, are minds more easily bent by examples brought forth in formulas that illuminate the foolishly concealed hiding-place of ignorance than by the naked chatter of loquacious words?

**Answer.** A verse of thirteen syllables, consisting of one dactyl and four spondees, claims for itself five species, as we said. The dactyl is placed in the first position as follows:

> “Fastened to the cross, Christ saved the world.”

In the second position:

> “Christ, Son of the Eternal, saved the world.”

In the third position:

> “Christ through the wood of the cross removes the world’s guilt.”

In the fourth position:

> “Climbing upon the wood, Christ gave the pledge of life.”

In the fifth position:

> “Hanging, Christ removed the world’s sins.”

**Question.** How many schemes does a verse of fourteen syllables have?

**Answer.** By the most certain definition, it consists of ten schemes.

**Question.** Give the account of these species in order.

**Answer.** Either the dactyl is placed in the first and second positions, or in the first and third, or in the first and fourth, or in the first and fifth, or in the second and third, or in the second and fourth, or in the second and fifth, or in the third and fourth, or in the third and fifth, or in the fourth and fifth. In this way the tenfold species of schemes is counted by alternating insertion.

**Question.** Prove this with examples.

**Answer.** Juvencus the Spaniard reveals knowledge of this matter in the first verse of his prologue:

> “Nothing immortal is held within the world’s structure.”

It is scanned thus: *immor, tale ni, hil mun, di com, page te, netur.*

And below:

> “The poets heap up their fame and praises.”

Sedulius likewise, in the metrical preface that proceeds in a hexameter and a catalectic pentameter, composed the first verse as a *decaschemus*:

> “Whoever seeks the Paschal feast as a guest.”

Juvenal, Book V of the *Satires*:

> “Great indeed are the precepts that he gives in sacred books.”

For it is scanned: *magna qui, dem sa, cris quae, dat prae, cepta li, bellis.*

Likewise below:

> “What day so festive, or what day fails to expose the thief?”

Lucan, Book X:

> “The fortunate plunderer lies dead, with the earth having become his avenger.”

**Question.** In the verses you seemed to offer as examples, all ten rules of the schemes were by no means clearly revealed. Only three formulas appeared: a dactyl in the first and fifth positions, likewise in the second and fifth, and likewise in the third and fifth. The remaining schemes still lie concealed, since they have not yet been produced. Therefore I think it worthwhile for you now to do what you had not completely made public in the generality of a broad definition, and, by recapitulating the schemes in order, to strive to unravel it completely in precise and fully developed particularity.

**Answer.** A heroic hexameter of fourteen syllables receives a dactyl in the first and second positions as follows:

> “The almighty arbiter of the world removed its sins.”

A dactyl in the first and third positions:

> “On the wood, God took away every stain of the world.”

In the first and fourth positions:

> “God shook the gloomy scepters of dreadful Tartarus.”

In the first and fifth positions:

> “Hanging on the wood, Christ crushed the world’s evils.”

In the second and third positions:

> “Christ bore the world’s sins from the harsh cross.”

In the second and fourth positions:

> “Christ from the cross crushed all the world’s evils.”

In the third and fourth positions:

> “Christ cleansed the stains of the human race.”

In the third and fifth positions:

> “Christ saved the human race by the sacred cross.”

In the fourth and fifth positions:

> “May Christ preserve us, now releasing all our crimes.”

**Question.** How many schemes does a verse of fifteen syllables contain?

**Answer.** According to what the authorities of the ancients have disclosed, [Col. 0177A] it is composed of ten schemes, like the preceding one. For just as in the verse of fourteen syllables the dactyl is varied ten times, so in this one the spondee is inverted as many times.

**Question.** I wish to be taught examples of these matters in verses belonging to this species.

**Answer.** Lucan explains it in Book VIII, saying:

> “For lofty faith requires strong years.”

And likewise in Book V:

> “He is borne toward the level waters and threw himself into the waves.”

It is scanned thus: *fertur ad, aequore, as ac, se pro, jecit in, undas.*

Virgil, in the *Georgics*:

> “I sing the Ascraean song through the Roman towns.”

And Paulus the Quaestor says:

> “Arbiter of the winds, who rules the dark waves.”

Therefore verses of this kind are called *decaschemi*.

**Question.** I do not think I have been satisfied by the argument of this response unless the things excerpted piecemeal in verses are universally supported by a tenfold accumulation.

**Answer.** A hexameter of fifteen syllables, consisting of three dactyls, contains ten schemes, as we said, in the following manner:

A dactyl in the first, second, and third positions:

> “Now the venerable offspring of God has saved the world.”

In the first, second, and fourth:

> “Now the renowned offspring of God preserves the ages by the cross.”

In the first, second, and fifth:

> “Behold, the venerable offspring of God saves the world by the cross.”

In the first, third, and fourth:

> “Hanging on the cross, he saves the world without guilt.”

In the first, third, and fifth:

> “On the wood he grants everyone hope of salvation.”

In the first, fourth, and fifth:

> “Fastened to the cross, he has renewed the ancient ages.”

In the second, third, and fourth:

> “Now the venerable offspring of God has saved the world.”

In the second, third, and fifth:

> “Let honor be celebrated to Christ, who governs the ages.”

In the second, fourth, and fifth:

> “Let the world celebrate the due praises of Christ.”

In the third, fourth, and fifth:

> “Purchased by Christ, O world, celebrate him and sing songs.”

**Question.** How many schemes are contained in a verse of sixteen syllables?

**Answer.** It has as many species as we have just disclosed in the verse of thirteen syllables, namely five.

[Col. 0177D] **Question.** Give examples of these schemes drawn from the books of authors.

**Answer.** Lucan, Book III:

> “By the sudden ruin of the shattered ships they perished.”

For it is scanned: *fracta, rum subi, ta rati, um peri, ere ru, ina.*

It should be noted that this verse and other similar ones are praised by metricians because no complete part of speech is ever found divided in the scansion, as frequently occurs in the other orders of schemes.

Paulus the Quaestor says in his thanksgiving:

> “Leaving and revisiting the Ocean with swift chariots.”

Virgil, in the *Bucolics*:

> “Go on, Pierian Muses, Chromis and Mnasilus in the cave.”

Persius Flaccus says in two joined verses:

> “Surely I am not working at this, so that, amid plundered trifles,”

> “the page may be wiped clean and given weight fit for smoke.”

Thus, just as in the verse of thirteen syllables the dactyl is inverted in five positions, so in this verse of sixteen syllables the spondee is known to alternate in those same positions; and these verses are called *pentaschemi* because of the five schemes mentioned above.

**Question.** I do not think it absurd that the species of these schemes, which have been presented in reverse order in poetic verses, should correspond properly, five times five, in their sequence.

**Answer.** A heroic verse of sixteen syllables, consisting of four dactyls, contains five species, as follows:

A dactyl in the first, second, third, and fourth positions:

> “Now the venerable offspring of God saves the world by the cross.”

In the first, second, third, and fifth:

> “Now the venerable offspring of God saves the world by the cross.”

In the first, second, fourth, and fifth:

> “Behold, the venerable offspring of God shines through the ages by the cross.”

In the first, third, fourth, and fifth:

> “Now the immense piety of God has blessed all things by the cross.”

In the second, third, fourth, and fifth:

> “Now the venerable offspring of God saves the world by the cross.”

**Question.** What, then, do you suppose should be counted as the number of schemes in a verse of seventeen syllables?

**Answer.** Likewise, as in the case of twelve syllables, I affirm that it contains one scheme.

**Question.** How, or by what method, can the shortest and longest verse proceed according to the same law of schemes, when they differ so greatly in the number of syllables?

**Answer.** Because in the former the spondee is present in five positions; here, however, the dactyl is inserted in the same number of positions, except in the final foot, which necessarily has to be disyllabic so that the greater number of syllables does not increase further.

[Col. 0178C] **Question.** I open my credulous heart to the opinions of the dogmatist and the sayings of the teacher, but nevertheless I wish to test this more certainly from the ancient poems of the old authors.

**Answer.** The chronicles of Eusebius report that Virgil, under the approaching threat of death, composed the epigram called an epitaph for the final funeral rites, saying:

> “Mantua gave me birth; the Calabrians seized me; now [it] holds me.”

It is scanned thus: *Mantua, me genu, it Cala, bri rapu, ere te, net nunc.*

Lucan, imitating him, reproduced it in these words:

> “Corduba gave me birth, Nero seized me; I sang of battles.”

The same poet, Book VI:

> “On every side the sea is driven back by cliffs rushing steeply.”

It is scanned thus: *undique, praecipi, ti scopu, lis remo, ventibus, aequor.*

But the aforementioned Mantuan poet elsewhere says:

> “But the trumpet, with its brazen sound, raises a terrible noise far away.”

Sedulius also, among other things, speaks of the *monoschemus* verse in this way:

> “He praises and offers his vows to the splendid spoil.”

Prosper likewise sang in the *Epigrams*, saying:

> “The mind wishing what is right, wise, and a lover of honesty.”

**Question.** Is a dactyl, then, never placed at the end?

**Answer.** It can be, as Virgil holds, but not in a verse that has all its other feet as dactyls. Thus, in the *Georgics*:

> “Or they mix the foam of silver and living sulfur.”

Some, inverting the order, read:

> “[lacuna] and living sulfur.”

Again, the same poet, Book VI of the *Aeneid*:

> “Twice the hands of the fatherland fell, unless immediately everything…”

Some exclude this by synaloepha, not understanding that synaloepha occurs when vowels collide with one another, whether alone, as in Virgil, Book IV:

> “What city, sister, will you see here, and what kingdoms rising?”

and Lucan, Book V:

> “Savage rest upon the sea and sluggishness in the mournful deep”;

or with a consonant interposed, as in:

> “I shall move farther away and unfold the secrets of fate.”

But this cannot at all be asserted in the aforementioned book, since *omnia* is a complete foot, as in the *Bucolics*:

> “Time carries all things away.”

> “Love conquers all things.”

Thus a verse could also consist of six dactyls, if metricians in modern times did not reject this, as in the verse:

> “Meanwhile, let my little heifer graze on tender grass.”

And elsewhere:

> “But the trumpet, dreadful, raises a terrible sound from afar.”

**Question.** What term have metricians given to these verses that end in a dactyl?

**Answer.** Among metricians verses of this sort are called *catalectic*, as in:

> [Col. 0179B] “The pale stars flee, terrified by the torch of light,”

and likewise the two verses above.

**[Maius omits:] Question.** Having enumerated the thirty-two orders of schemes, I earnestly request that you explain in a fully worked-out series of examples how many species can be found in the poems of Virgil, Lucan, Persius Flaccus, or Terence of Africa.

**Answer.** Of the thirty-two species mentioned above, I was able to investigate no more than seventeen in the poems of the authors named, except for Terence. Since, following Menander, he composed the books of his comedies not in heroic verse, their prologue, when it was attacked by the canine tooth of his rivals, was offered in his own defence, like an *Apologeticus* (a defense), in six-foot verses.

**Question.** I desire to know these seventeen species more certainly.

**Answer.** In the verse of thirteen syllables, two schemes are found to have been adopted by Virgil: the second and the fifth. In the second position only two dactyls are found [sic], as in:

> “Or they draw light greaves with pliant silver.”

Or in the fifth:

> “The two chosen men who with iron cut the rampart.”

And below:

> “The leaders of the Teucrians, the first and chosen youth.”

**Question.** How many species were adopted from the verse of fourteen syllables?

**Answer.** Only seven [*probably three*]. For the dactyl is inserted either in the first and fifth positions, as in:

> “His son in reply, who turns the stars of the world.”

Or in the second and fifth, as in:

> “And black night, borne along by twin chariots, held the pole.”

Or in the fourth and fifth, as in:

> “Hissing, the opening of the pierced skull remained fixed.”

**Question.** Of how many schemes did he make use in the verse of fifteen syllables?

**Answer.** Although this kind of verse is called a *decaschemus*, he nevertheless adopted six [*probably five*] species from it. For a spondee is found either in the first and second positions, as in:

> “The cloud splits and clears a way open into the ether.”

Or in the first and third:

> “Winter shut them in and terrified the travelers.”

Or in the first and fourth:

> “With tears and prayers he bore it; I call the stars to witness.”

Or in the second and fourth:

> “And now farewell! Moist night twists the middle courses.”

Or in the third and fourth:

> “Ascanius, never forgetful of so great a service.”

**Question.** How many species is he found to have claimed for himself from the verse of sixteen syllables?

**Answer.** Although the Greeks called this verse *pentaschemus*, the poet mentioned above nevertheless adopted four species from it, because a spondee is found either in the first position, as in:

> “May Carthage oppress Ausonia; nothing from there belongs to the cities.”

And elsewhere in two verses:

> “May he see me, half-dead, snatching bloody arms for myself,”

> “and may dying eyes bear away Turnus as victor.”

[Supplement: “Or in the second,”] as in:

> “Gnashing with his teeth in a groan, he walks across the sea.”

Or in the second and third [*probably read: in the third*]:

> “And we left the homes of the Greeks and the suspect fields.”

Or in the fourth and fifth [*probably read: in the fourth*]:

> “Take him as a companion in counsel and join him to yourself, since he is willing.”

Likewise:

> “Ascanius threw his helmet before his feet into the river.”

**Question.** Finally, how many species did he adopt from the verse of seventeen syllables?

**Answer.** He rejoices in the allotment of only one scheme, without which he is known to be completely without the species of the other schemes. This is called in Greek a *monoschemus* verse, when all the feet except the last are dactylic in scansion, as in:

> “Far away from there, trembling, we celebrate our flight after our recovery.”

Likewise, the first verse of Book XII:

> “Meanwhile the house of almighty Olympus is opened.”

And in Book XII:

> “Then the stone itself of the man, rolled through the empty void.”

And in the *Georgics*:

> “He flies, at once sweeping the fields in flight, at once the seas.”

[Col. 0180C] **Question.** What is a heroic catalectic verse?

**Answer.** Virgil supplies an example, saying:

> “And the sleeves of the tunic, and they have the ribbons of the cap.”

It is scanned thus: *et tuni, cae mani, cas et hab, ent redi, micula, mitrae.*

The same poet, Book XI:

> “He had made [the cloth] and had distinguished the threads with fine gold.”

And in the Book of Judges:

> “He had previously cut off the bodies of seventy kings.”

And Lucan, Book III:

> “He was the first to add glory to the Caesarean arms upon the sea.”

**Question.** What is a hypercatalectic hexameter?

**Answer.** One in which a single syllable is added to the established number of six feet.

**Question.** Produce a verse composed in this way.

**Answer.**

> “Nourishing Venus enters Paphos; may a rose shine from the inner sanctuaries.”

And elsewhere:

> “To break the bolts by hand and give companions from the icy cliffs.”

A hypercatalectic verse is likewise admitted in the dactylic pentameter, as in:

> “O almighty God, grant a way to prayers.”

And elsewhere:

> [Col. 0181A] “The beautiful girl encircles her hair for herself with branches.”

**Question.** How many species are there in the caesura of a hexameter verse?

**Answer.** Four.

**Question.** Name the terms of these caesuras.

**Answer.** *Districtus* (“drawn apart”), *divisus* (“divided”), *mistus* (“mixed”), and *Priapeius* (“Priapeian”).

**Question.** What is a *districtus* verse?

**Answer.** One in which, in the scansion of the feet, no complete part of speech is ever accommodated.

**Question.** I am instructed more effectively by examples than by bare verbosity.

**Answer.** Arator supplies an example:

> “And let the mortal origin propose this purpose for itself.”

It is scanned thus: *Morta, lisque si, bi studi, um pro, ponat o, rigo.*

Behold: no complete expression is found in any foot. The same poet elsewhere:

> “To grant the aid of the Savior, and the number of days.”

Prosper likewise, in the *Epigrams*:

> “Deceitful people are always tormented by bitter cares.”

Virgil:

> “Unutterable queen, you command me to renew the grief.”

The poet Symposius produced a *districtus* verse, saying:

> “Sweet is the scent of the grove; I am wearied by flame and smoke.”

**Question.** What is a *divisus* verse?

**Answer.** One that has separated parts of speech in its scansion, so that, as it has feet, it has an equal number of expressions; for example:

> “Tell me, Clio, who first fashioned verses.”

But modern usage in dactylic hexameter does not readily admit a verse of this kind if it lacks a penthemimeral or hepthemimeral caesura.

**Question.** What is a *mistus* verse?

**Answer.** One that contains both within itself—that is, part of a *districtus* verse and part of a *divisus* verse.

**Question.** I will be persuaded more easily by an explanation if you prove it by an example.

**Answer.** Virgil, Book IV:

> “But the queen, long since wounded by heavy concern.”

And below:

> “She feeds the wound in her veins and is consumed by hidden fire.”

The prophetess Sibyl says:

> “The conscious avenger silently counts so many crimes.”

And elsewhere the poet says:

> “Peter, who presides over the heights of the apostolic citadel.”

It is scanned thus: *Petrus ap, ostoli, cae qui*—behold, the *districtus* part—*culmina, praesidet, arcis*—behold, the *divisus* part.

**Question.** What is a verse of Priapeian caesura?

**Answer.** One found assigned to the Priapeian meter.

**Question.** What is the Priapeian meter?

**Answer.** It is a hexameter verse in which the first three feet are joined together and divided and separated from the remaining three feet that follow.

**Question.** I wish to be taught examples of these matters through authoritative verses.

**Answer.** Virgil, in the *Bucolics*:

> “When the whole chorus of Phoebus rose up for the boy.”

Likewise, a Sibylline verse declares the same:

> “May the good man live eternally, and may the evil man burn in fire.”

Likewise Symposius:

> “I am not shameless in mouth, nor is my tongue reckless.”

Virgil:

> “Either the Parthian will drink the Arar or Germany the Tigris.”

**Question.** Why is it called the Priapeian meter?

**Answer.** Because many poems of this kind were written in honor of Priapus. For this reason many wish this kind of composition to be more appropriate to bucolic poetry.

**Question.** What is the Pythian meter?

**Answer.** The same as the hexameter.

**Question.** Why is it called Pythian?

**Answer.** Some think it is because oracles were first delivered to Apollo in this kind of meter. After he killed Python, he was called Pythian; for, as the story goes, when he pursued the serpent Python on Parnassus with arrows in revenge for his mother, the inhabitants of Delphi exalted him in this verse and in the lofty style of eloquence (literally, its “tragic buskin”).

**Question.** How many πάθη (*pathē*, “passions”) do you affirm are inserted in the dactylic hexameter? Or what are *pathē*?

**Answer.** *Pathē* are called *passiones* in Latin, “passions.” [Col. 0182B] There are six in number: *acephalon*, *procephalon*, *lagaron*, *procylon*, *dulicheron*, and *miuron* or *spicode*.

**Question.** What is *acephalon*?

**Answer.** A verse without a head, when the first syllable is shortened contrary to its nature.

**Question.** Give an example established by an author’s authority.

**Answer.** Virgil placed an *acephalon* in the second verse of the *Aeneid*, saying:

> “To Italy, an exile by fate.”

For, by a barbarism, he admitted a tribrach in place of a dactyl. Likewise, the other passions are inserted either in the middle or at the end.

D. Since it would take too long to elucidate in order the question and solution of each of these matters, let at least the final point be disclosed. What are *miuron* or *sphicodium*?—M. Μῦς (*mys*) is rendered in Latin by *mus* (“mouse”) or *sorex* (“shrew”). From the same initial formation is derived *miurus*, or *miurinus*, or *soricinus* (“shrew-like”).

D. What do you assert *sphicodin* to be?—M. Σφήξ (*sphēx*) is Greek for *crabro* (“hornet”); from it is derived *sphicodis*. Nevertheless, *miurus* and *sphicodis* are understood to belong to one rule of meaning, because both animals terminate in a thin and slender extremity of the limbs. The same applies to a verse that closes with a pyrrhichius.

D. What is the caesura *penthemimeres*, and how is it interpreted?—M. In Latin *penthemimeres* is called *semiquinaria* (“half-fivefold”); for ἥμισυ (*hēmisy*) means “half.” Thus *hemisphaerium* is understood in Latin as “half-sphere,” that is, half of the pole above or below the earth, balanced in equal scales. A *penthemimeres* in heroic verse occurs when, after two feet, a syllable follows that completes a part of the sentence, as in:

> The earth covers the trunk; waters lie hidden in the turf.

Likewise Prosper, in his riddles on the Lord’s Prayer:

> When with prayer he poured bloody drops from his body.

D. What is *hepthemimeres*?—M. In Latin this caesura is called *semiseptenaria* (“half-sevenfold”), when, after three feet, a syllable follows that completes a part of the sentence, as in:

> Muse, recount to me the causes.

And elsewhere:

> Nor do they seek the rays of the robe.

Likewise Phocas:

> Seeking distant lands, the traveler carries a companion for himself.

D. What is the caesura of the *trititrochaic*, or *tritustrochaeus*?—M. It occurs when the third place is ended by a dactyl, as the poet promised when he said:

[Col. 0183A]

> This I desire: let my first syllable not be read as short.

And elsewhere:

> Nor am I now called earth, although earth is produced from me.

Prosper’s epigram likewise produced a *tritontrochaeon*:

> Yet the good things that are truly good are not held even at the end.

D. What is the definition of the caesura of the *tetartitrochaic*, which some call *tetartebucolicon*?—M. It occurs when, in the fourth place or division, a part of the sentence ends with a dactyl.

D. I ask that this be made clearer through evident examples.—M. Virgil, in the first eclogue, begins:

> We are leaving the boundaries of our homeland and its pleasant fields.

And below:

> Often the tender lamb will stain them from our sheepfolds.

Paulinus likewise, in his first verse:

> Yearly vows return to you, and likewise the yearly tongue.

[Col. 0183B]

It must be noted that the rule of bucolic verse requires the fourth foot always to be closed by a dactyl, a requirement that Virgil neglected, overcome by the difficulty of the work.

D. Now that you have explained the uncertain difficulty of the art of meter with light brighter than day, the time and order of the subject require that you disclose in verses of brilliant elegance the promised problems of the riddles, and thereafter regularly impress upon us the account of each individual foot, except for the needless confusion of the *synzugiae*.—M. I would have tried to do this long ago, had your painstaking questions, anticipating my haste, not forestalled it by a kind of force.

# BOOK OF RIDDLES

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0183C]

> Ruler, who continually wieldest the scepter by heavenly dominion,  
> And likewise arrangest the light-bearing royal tribunal of heaven,  
> Governing it by eternal laws,  
> For thou didst punish the dreadful limbs of Behemoth,  
> When once he fell headlong from the lofty citadel,  
> Ruler who presidest over one dictating clear metrical songs,  
> Grant gifts now, that in my ignorance I may unfold  
> Through verses the riddles hidden by fate.  
> Thus, God, I repay thy freely given gifts to the unworthy.  
> I do not call upon the Castalian nymphs with such songs,  
> Nor did she scatter nectar for me into my mouth.  
> Thus I never traverse the peaks of Cynthus, but neither  
> Did I lie prostrate on Parnassus, nor did I see dreams there.  
> For God will be able to add to me a poet’s song,  
> Breathing into my foolish mind pious gifts freely given.  
> If he touches the mind, the heart soon returns praise.  
> Metrical songs declare that Moses, the prophet,  
> Sang long ago the celebrated standards of the ancient triumph,  
> Renowned throughout the peoples, wherever the shining sun  
> Surveys the world, now raising its head from the ocean’s flood;  
> And the Psalmist, singing metrical songs with his voice,  
> Proclaims the divine Word born through divine generation,  
> Born first in heaven, before the morning star of the world  
> Had poured forth splendid lights upon the formed ages.  
> But if these riddles shall prove good, their verses  
> Having been wholly purged of blemishes and rusticity,  
> Correctly traversed in dactylic form, and if error  
> Has not led the mind astray through the empty appearance of its designs,  
> I shall begin with weightier matters: may God, who once gave strength to his warlike servant Job,  
> Fill his inward parts with a draught of everlasting dew.  
> For you led streams from dry rocks,  
> When the wedge passed through the Red Sea  
> And entered the desert—a deed David celebrated in song.  
> Father of the heavenly citadel, who preservest all the ages,  
> Deign now to release the offenses of wicked sins.

## I. FOUR-LINE RIDDLES

### 1. On the earth

> I am called the nourisher of all things that the world bears  
> In its sphere, and rightly so; for never do wicked offspring  
> Tear their mother’s breasts so savagely with their teeth.  
> Green with offspring in summer, I waste away in winter.

### 2. On the wind

> No one can see me, nor seize me in his hands;  
> I quickly reveal throughout the world the sharp crack of my voice.  
> With my terrible, resounding powers I can shatter oaks;  
> For I strike the heavenly poles and traverse the countryside.

### 3. On the cloud

> Multicolored, I flee and leave behind both heaven and earth:  
> I have no place on earth, nor anywhere in the regions of the poles.  
> No one now fears an exile so cruel;  
> Yet with my dripping drops I shall make the world grow leafy.

### 4. On nature

> Believe me: nothing remains without my governance.  
> No light will see my forehead and face.  
> Who does not know that, under my dominion, the vaults  
> Of the lofty pole, the sun’s radiance, and the moon’s courses revolve?

### 5. On the rainbow, or celestial bow

> I am fashioned as the offspring of Thaumas, according to ancient speech;  
> But I shall disclose the first beginnings of my kind.  
> Born red from the sun, I arose from the birth of a watery cloud;  
> I traverse the heavens everywhere, but do not ascend through the southern regions.

### 6. On the moon

> Now I keep company with the sea under a common fate,  
> Rolling the months through recurring cycles;  
> As the glory of my light-bearing form diminishes,  
> So the water loses its increase in its swelling flood.

### 7. On fate, or generation

> It is agreed that an eloquent poet once sang:  
> “Where God calls, and where harsh Fortune calls, let us follow.”  
> The ancients falsely used to call me their mistress,  
> Ruling the scepters of the world, while Christ’s grace reigns.

### 8. On salt

> Long ago I was water overflowing with scaly fish;  
> But nature yielded to a new distinction of fate,  
> While I endured scorching torments amid burning fires.  
> For my appearance shines like ash and snow.  
> [Variant: *constant*, “remains constant.”]

### 9. On heliotropia, or the sun-follower

> I am born of my own accord, blooming from fertile turf;  
> My shining summits grow yellow from a saffron-colored flower.  
> I am closed when the sun sets, and so I open when it rises.  
> Hence the learned Greeks gave me my name.

### 10. On a woman who has given birth to twins

[Col. 0185A]

> I have six eyes, and likewise I stand with as many ears;  
> But on my body I carry sixty fingers.  
> Of these, behold, when forty have been torn away from the flesh,  
> I see only twenty remain.

### 11. On the diamond

> Behold, I do not fear the harsh dangers of iron,  
> Nor the burning heat of flames; but through the blood of a goat  
> The hard strength of my unconquered rigidity grows soft.  
> Thus blood overcomes what the iron mass fears.  
> [Variant: *quod*, “which,” rather than *quem*, “what.”]

### 12. On the Molossian hound

> Long ago the venerable power of things made me such  
> That I should pursue the savage enemies of my master,  
> Carrying weapons in my jaws and performing the battles of war;  
> Yet soon, fleeing the blows of infants, I avoid them.

### 13. On the *Poliades*, that is, the bellows of smiths

> I feed upon alternating blasts together with my twin brother.  
> I have no life, although I possess the openings of life.  
> My art has given ornaments to jeweled metals;  
> No honor is granted to me, but another receives the glory.  
> [Variant: *vexor*, “I am harassed,” rather than *vescor*, “I feed.”]

### 14. On silkworms

> When the yearly seasons for weaving webs return,  
> Their yellow insides are filled with bristling threads;  
> Soon I climb the leafy tops of broom plants,  
> Making little globes, until I rest according to fate.

### 15. On the *barbitus*, or organ

> Although trumpets of hollow bronze sound martial signals,  
> And citharas rattle, while the noise of the trumpet provides melody,  
> My entrails nevertheless belch forth a hundred songs;  
> When I resound, the musical strings are immediately astonished.  
> [Variant: *Me praesente*, “when I am present,” rather than *me strepente*, “when I resound.”]

### 16. On the peacock

> Beautiful and outstanding, wondrous in appearance throughout the world,  
> Made from bones, sinews, and red blood,  
> While life is my companion, nothing shines more  
> Than my golden beauty; and when I die, my flesh never rots.

### 17. On the salamander

> Living amid fires, I do not feel the flames,  
> But I make the destruction of the funeral pyre wholly a mockery.  
> Neither in the crackling hearth nor in the sparkling ember  
> Do I burn; rather, the blazing heat grows warm through me.

### 18. On the squid

[Col. 0185D]

> Now the spectacles of our life are pleasing to behold:  
> With the fish-filled shoal I search the sea’s waters with my scales;  
> With the flock of birds I also climb through the air on wings;  
> Yet I cannot live on air from the sky.

### 19. On the *perna*

> I am born with twin shells in the blue waters of the Propontis [variant: *ponti*, “sea”],  
> Producing golden fleece from my bristling body.  
> Behold, I provide a cloak, a fold of clothing, and food for the flesh;  
> Thus I discharge a double tribute to fate.

## II. FIVE-LINE RIDDLES

### 1. On the Pleiades

> Our predecessors, in their foolishness, said that we were sown by Atlas;  
> For there is a company of seven, but scarcely one is visible.  
> We move through the citadel of the pole, and also beneath Tartarus;  
> We are seen amid the earth’s dark shadows and conceal ourselves in the light,  
> Deriving our ancient names from the season of spring.

### 2. On the ant-lion

> I bear a name formed from two figures joined together:  
> “Lion” and “ant” are what I am called in the language of the Greeks.  
> By my double name I signify a figurative double omen;  
> Yet I cannot withstand the beaks of birds [variant: *rescindere rostra*, “to tear apart beaks,” rather than *resistere rostro*, “withstand the beak”].  
> Let the wise man investigate why I am fashioned with a twofold name.

### 3. On the bee

> Formed in wondrous ways, created without seed,  
> I load my inner chambers with sweet spoils from flowers.  
> Through my art the dishes of kings grow saffron-yellow.  
> I always carry sharp, cruel weapons of war,  
> And, lacking hands, I overcome metals worked by smiths.

### 4. On the file

> With a furrowed body and bluish rust,  
> I am formed to rub shapeless metal into grooves.  
> Accustomed to polish the materials and masses of gold,  
> I remain level in surface, yet am the roughest of things.  
> I chatter, though without a voice, hissing with a hoarse murmur.  
> [Variant: *plana superficie*, “with a flat surface,” rather than *plano superficiem*, “I make the surface flat.”]

### 5. On the nightingale

> My beautiful voice varies in different forms;  
> With a hoarse beak I shall never sing melodies.  
> Though despised for my color, I am not despised for singing.  
> Thus I do not cease to sing, though fearful fate approaches;  
> For winter drives me away, but I shall return soon in summer.

### 6. On the balance, called *Momentana*

[Col. 0186C]

> Nature once gave birth to us as twin sisters,  
> Whom the judgment of a straight law continually governs.  
> We are accustomed to observe times, persons, and law.  
> The age of mortals would become happy on earth  
> If they observed the norm of justice according to our sisters’ custom.

### 7. On the water-snake

> I am said to have been born from the head of a dreadful dragon;  
> I enlarge the brilliance of gems with purple dyes.  
> But power will not be granted to me through rigid strength  
> If the water-snake should first fall with its scaly body,  
> Before I am stripped of the red ornament from the crown of my head.

### 8. On the iron-bearing magnet

> Nature’s power gave me—or rather, the creator of Olympus gave me—  
> What all the wonders of the ancient world lack.  
> For I suspend the cold metals of steel through the air.  
> Thus, overcoming iron destiny by a certain force, I reverse it.  
> Soon, when the diamond of Cyprus is present, I am deprived of my power.

### 9. On the cock

> I used to be called a chatterer in the darkness, singing  
> The red rays and lights of the majestic brightness of Phoebus.  
> As a feathered creature I bear the name known among peoples;  
> Carrying weapons on my feet, I create the dangers of war,  
> Bearing serrated crests upon the crown of my head.

### 10. On the whetstone

> Cold, brought forth from the frozen womb of the earth,  
> I polish the hardness of iron with my square face.  
> I never fear the dangers of old age,  
> Unless Mulcifer (Vulcan), by fire, diminishes the number of my years.  
> Soon my rigid appearance softens in black fires.

### 11. On the Minotaur

> I am difficult in face and two-formed in limbs;  
> I am armed with horns, while the rest of my dreadful  
> Limbs resemble those of a man, famous throughout the Cnossian fields.  
> Born in Crete from an uncertain adulterous father,  
> I am called by a name belonging both to man and beast.

### 12. On the cauldron, or basin

> Dreadful, curved, rapacious, fashioned from broad plates of metal,  
> I hang suspended, touching neither heaven nor deep earth.  
> I blaze with fires and also boil with a flood;  
> Thus I endure two battles of different kinds,  
> While I contain both watery liquids and fierce flames.

### 13. On the thousand-leaved plant

> In the language of the Greeks and likewise in Latin  
> I am called “thousand-leaf,” born from green turf.  
> Therefore I shall bear a name of ten times a hundred,  
> Since I flourish with little stalks, and no other plant  
> Grows through the countless furrows of the earth in such a way.

### 14. On the book chest

> Now my entrails are filled with divine words,  
> And my whole inner chamber bears sacred books.  
> Yet I cannot understand anything from them,  
> Unhappy, deprived by fate of such a gift,  
> For the dreadful Fates take away the books’ lights.

### 15. On the nettle

[Note: [Col. 0187B] [The final verse of this five-line riddle is missing in the printed editions; consequently it has a place among the four-line riddles. GILES.]]

> I torment those who torment me, but I torment no one willingly.  
> I do not wish to harm anyone unless he himself first  
> Contracts guilt and tries to pluck my green stalk:  
> Soon the limbs of the offending man swell hotly;  
> Thus I avenge the injury and punish it with sharp stings.

## III. SIX-LINE RIDDLES

### 1. On water

> Who would not be astonished at the spectacle of my fate,  
> When by my power I carry a thousand tree trunks?  
> Yet a slender needle breaks such great burdens,  
> For the birds of heaven and the fish swimming through the sea  
> Once received from me the beginnings of life.  
> By right, a third part of the world belongs to me to hold.

### 2. On the crab, called *Nepa*

> The ancient Latins called me *Nepa* by name.  
> I range along the wet shores of the foaming sea,  
> Crossing the Ocean backward with reversed steps.  
> Yet through me the heavenly Olympus is adorned,  
> While I climb in the sky, red and twelvefold in stars,  
> Which oysters fear, terrified by dreadful rocks.

### 3. On the crane fly

> I proceed over water, supported by four feet,  
> Yet I do not fear being plunged into watery pools.  
> On foot I tread alike upon land and rivers.  
> Nature does not permit me to swim swiftly through streams,  
> Nor to cross fierce rivers by bridges or rafts;  
> Rather, I walk with dry feet upon the waters.

### 4. On the lion

> In the forests I crush bristling boars armed with teeth,  
> And horned stags, although they bellow with their mouths;  
> I crush them, and, sparing no bears, I shatter their strength.  
> Carrying bloodstained jaws, I do not fear  
> The bites and gaping mouths of wolves,  
> Relying on royal majesty.  
> For I sleep with wide-open eyes, not closing their jewel-like lids.

### 5. On pepper

> I am black on the outside, covered with wrinkled bark,  
> Yet within I bear a gleaming white kernel.  
> I store in the kitchen delicacies, royal banquets,  
> Luxuries of food, sauces, and pounded meats.  
> But you will not see me supported by any strength  
> Unless my inner parts have been shaken with shining kernels.

### 6. On the cushion

> I do not wish you to break faith, although my words may be thought vain;  
> Rather, open your believing heart to my words.  
> I can swell higher toward the heavenly clouds  
> If my head is removed together with my whole body;  
> But if I am burdened by the weight of my head,  
> Seeking the lowest place, I shall always appear to grow smaller below.

### 7. On the ostrich

> Great limbs become feathered upon my dense body;  
> My color is like that of the hawk, but my reason for flying is different.  
> I do not pass through the upper air on small wings,  
> But rather range on foot through barren fields,  
> Providing smooth eggshells for drinking vessels.  
> The land of Africa among the Carthaginians is said to produce me.

### 8. On the leech

> I roam through muddy marshes amid murky waters,  
> For bloody fortune composed my name.  
> While I feed on red blood with thirsty cheeks,  
> I lack bones and feet, as well as paired arms;  
> Yet I bite bodies with dreadful, three-pronged wounds,  
> And thus I provide care with healing lips.

### 9. On the dove

> When God was already punishing the unspeakable sins of the sea  
> And at the same time washing away the contagion of crimes with water,  
> I was the first to fulfill the commands of the parent,  
> Signifying by my fruit that salvation would come to the earth.  
> Therefore I always bear a gentle heart,  
> And, a fortunate winged creature, I shall remain without black gall.  
> [Variant: *jussa parentis*, “the parent’s commands,” rather than *jura parenti*, “the duties owed to the parent.”]

### 10. On the fish

> The gracious Ruler had deprived me of feet and hands alike  
> When at the beginning he was setting the immense world in place.  
> I am supported neither by flying on the swift wing of a bird;  
> Nor does breath enliven my body with alternating currents,  
> Although I see the lofty summits of the heavenly vaults;  
> Nevertheless, I do not disdain the watery marble of the sea.

### 11. On the ox, or young bull

> Dissolving the dry fields with foaming jaws  
> [Variant: *arva*, “fields,” rather than *ora*, “mouths”],  
> I drink from four fountains.  
> While living, by the force of vigorous effort,  
> I break up fertile clods of earth together with their deepest roots;  
> But when the breath leaves my cold limbs,  
> I can bind men with dreadful chains.

### 12. One born blind

> Now I shall tell you in words what you could scarcely believe,  
> Although it is established as true, and empty things do not deceive the mind.  
> Long ago I had given my offspring delightful little gifts,  
> Gifts that no one else could ever give me,  
> While God from above deprived me of the bright light  
> In which the hearts of all things rejoice as a gift.

### 13. The shield

> I am made from the trunk of a willow and from the scraped hide of an animal,  
> Enduring the harsh dangers of battle.  
> I shall always preserve the body of the bearer  
> With my own body, lest Orcus take the man’s life.  
> What soldier in war, however savage, undergoes so many disasters,  
> Or receives so many wounds of death?

## IV. SEVEN-LINE RIDDLES

### 1. On the elements, or the alphabet

> We are seventeen sisters born without a voice;  
> We do not count six others as illegitimate.  
> We are born from iron and die again through iron,  
> And likewise from the feather of a bird flying through the air.  
> Three brothers created us, with an uncertain mother.  
> Whoever thirstily desires to hear the teachers,  
> We quickly give the words requested in silence.

### 2. On the stork

> Shining in white beauty, yet also darkening into brown,  
> Such am I when I am composed in the various image of my feathers.  
> Lacking a voice, I make rattling sounds with my trembling beak.  
> Although I tear apart scaly serpents with ferocity,  
> My limbs do not swell with deadly poisons.  
> Thus I am accustomed to nourish tender chicks and offspring  
> With the poisoned flesh and grim blood of dragons.  
> [Variant: *nam faxo crepacula*, “for I shall make rattling sounds,” rather than *voce carens tremulo faxo crepitacula rostro*, “lacking a voice, I make rattling sounds with my trembling beak.”]

### 3. On the breastplate

> The dewy earth gave birth to me from its cold womb.  
> I was not made from the woolly fleece of a bristling animal;  
> No threads draw me out, nor do chattering fibers resound;  
> Nor do Serian worms weave me with saffron-colored down;  
> I am not cut by rays, nor struck by a hard comb;  
> Yet behold, in the speech of the common people I shall be called a garment.  
> I do not fear arrows drawn from long quivers.

### 4. On the locust

> Although I am not a welcome guest to farmers,  
> I harvest in swarms the fruits of the fields  
> From the green turf of the countryside, gnawing leaves from the stalk.  
> My heart is beneath my knees, for it is enclosed in a prison.  
> My breast is placed beneath my knees in the manner of a toad.  
> Long ago I was famous for despoiling the Egyptian kingdom,  
> When the ten plagues were inflicted upon the filthy people.

### 5. On the night-heron

> Art properly doubles my name by means of two figures,  
> For one part belongs to darkness and one part to birds.  
> Rarely will anyone see me beneath a clear daylight;  
> Rather, at night I cherish the star-bearing shadows.  
> Accustomed to rattle through the middle air with a hoarse voice,  
> I am written in Roman books, but with a Greek voice,  
> Since by my name I always preserve the darkness of night.

### 6. On the *Cinyphus*

> I have a slender body and am armed with sharp stings.  
> Flying in swarms, I climb on wings over lofty places,  
> Taking bloody spoils with a bloodstained point.  
> I spare no four-footed creature, but thrust my stings  
> Into the wounds of bristling animal flesh.  
> Once I was notorious for ravaging the fields of Memphis,  
> For I penetrate the muscles of bulls and feed on their blood.

### 7. On spindles

[Note: [Col. 0190A] [In other manuscripts the verses that compose this riddle are found in another order; this single notice may suffice for the other riddles as well. GILES.]]

> I am born in the forest, growing green with leafy branches;  
> But nature changed my destiny in due order,  
> While I carry a whorl through the smooth distaff by its turning motion.  
> From me is made the royal spread of a robe.  
> No hero is girded by so long a belt;  
> Through me the Fates are said to determine the destinies of men.  
> Harsh cold would lay men low unless I happened to resist.

### 8. On the double vessel

> Who could believe that the harmony of such great things  
> Is governed, and that fate controls fates contrary to custom?  
> Behold, I carry a hearth and also water within my belly,  
> Yet the flames do not overcome the surging waters,  
> Nor are the streams of the spring dried by grim fires;  
> Rather, there is a treaty of peace between flames and waves.  
> A hammer and an anvil first formed me.  
> [Variant: “Who could believe that spectacles arising from such causes are governed?”]

### 9. On Hesperus, or Vesper

> My name attached itself to me at the first time of night.  
> I embrace the western regions of the world,  
> When Titan has dipped his nourishing body into the Ocean  
> And the pole, descending, rolls through the blue-green waters.  
> Then I follow, hiding my lights in glassy fields,  
> And suddenly, fortunate, I am lifted from the sky,  
> So that I may drive away the dark shadows of night.

### 10. On the dagger, or *spatha*

> The earth’s womb first fashioned me by its art;  
> My remaining material came from savage bulls,  
> Or rather, it is said to have been made from stinking goats.  
> A sheath was constructed for me from cut hide,  
> And also from boards split from a scraped trunk.  
> Through me the eyes of many are closed in death,  
> While I, naked and gleaming, strive to defend my master’s life.  
> [Variant: “I was first fashioned from the wombs of the earth,” rather than “the earth’s womb fashioned me.”]

### 11. On the water bubble

> I am born from drops falling from the moist, dewy air,  
> Swollen, gathering together through the flowing movement of liquid;  
> Yet no hand can touch me as I swim in the wet flood  
> Without my inner parts immediately bursting at the touch  
> And my fragile, thin breath departing into the air.  
> Before this, in swarms, I lead companies through the waters,  
> While many companions born together enjoy the same place.  
> [Variant: *spatiuntur*, “walk about,” rather than *potiuntur*, “enjoy.”]

### 12. On the millstone

[Note: [Col. 0190D] [The two final verses of this seven-line riddle, indeed many others that we now publish for the first time, are missing from the printed editions. GILES.]]

> We are equal sisters under a common destiny,  
> Who provide food for all from our own labor.  
> The labor of both is equal, but the fortune of the two is different;  
> For one runs, which the other has never done,  
> Yet we are not driven by the bitter goads of envy.  
> Whatever one chews, whatever she ruminates with open mouth,  
> She returns, breaking it up and serving it without malicious deceit.

### 13. On spelt, or the little shield

> I rise from the earth, spelt with a shining body,  
> Fertile with snow, growing hard in Vulcan’s furnace,  
> More precious by far than the other shields of battle;  
> Yet no iron boss stands in the middle of the shield.  
> Without me, what use is the shield of savage warriors?  
> Their limbs and souls would scarcely be free from the path of death  
> If I did not resist Orcus with powerful strength.  
> [Title variant: *Pelta*, “small shield,” rather than *Spelta*, “spelt.”]

### 14. On a spring

> Through the hollow caves of the earth I creep secretly and very swiftly,  
> Winding circles through the twisting bends of the veins.  
> Though I lack life and am wholly without sensation,  
> What number could contain, or what calculation equal,  
> The thousands of living beings whom I generate by giving birth?  
> Neither the stars of the shining celestial sphere  
> Nor the wave-bearing sands of the sea can be compared with them.

### 15. On the apple tree, or cultivated apple tree

> I was a favorable origin at the beginning of the newly born world,  
> Until the one overthrown by the evil one succumbed to his art.  
> From me then came the cause of the ancient ruin,  
> The sweet apples that I offered to the inexperienced inhabitants.  
> Behold, I testify again that salvation has returned to the world,  
> When the Ruler of the world hung upon an outstretched trunk  
> And the venerable offspring of the Thunderer paid the penalty.

### 16. On the fig tree

> Who first brought forth clothing in the world?  
> Or who mercifully protected the unfortunate poor man?  
> I shall not report empty things in words or invent futilities:  
> I first produced upon the earth a garment from my own body,  
> As the story goes, from lofty leaves.  
> The Carian fig bends me with its masses, while the diligent farmer provides  
> food which he eats in the season of winter.

### 17. On hellebore

[Col. 0191C]

> In the field I sprang up, bearing shells amid bristling leaves,  
> Like a shell dyed with cooked red murex.  
> Purple blood drips in drops from my summit.  
> I do not wish to take away the life of one who eats me,  
> Nor will gentle poisons strip him entirely of his mind;  
> Yet madness troubles the insane heart,  
> While he whirls his limbs in a circular frenzy.

### 18. On the camel

> Once I was a Roman consul, a soldier, a horseman,  
> While I ruled the scepters of the kingdom as judge by authority.  
> Now humped bodies carry a dreadful burden,  
> And a savage load of immense weight presses upon me.  
> Now I terrify the swift ranks of horn-footed horses,  
> Which soon flee in trembling, four-footed motion,  
> When they see the immense limbs of my savage body.

### 19. On the asp or basilisk

[Note: [Col. 0191D] [The entire riddle is missing from the printed editions. GILES.]]

[Col. 0191D]

> More cunning than all creatures that feed upon the air of heaven,  
> I scatter the seeds of death widely throughout the world,  
> From which a dreadful crop grew with sinister ears of grain.  
> The fornicator reaps it for his crimes with an evil sickle.  
> I greatly fear the battles of the horned stag,  
> For I shall be stripped of my old, aging skin  
> And, relying once more on a new youth, shall remain.

## V. EIGHT-LINE RIDDLES

### 1. On a candle, or wick

> I was shaped by open hands from two kinds of material;  
> My inner parts grow white with flax,  
> Or, certainly, shine when stripped of slender rushes.  
> But now my outer bodies grow yellow with a flower  
> And pour forth smoking flames and hearth fires.  
> Again and again wet tears drip from my foreheads;  
> Yet in this way I extinguish the dreadful hiding places of night,  
> Soon my twisted inner parts leave remnants of ashes.

### 2. On the eagle

> The armor-bearer of unlucky Jove and the ravisher of Ganymede,  
> Although deceitful poets have sung in verse,  
> I was not the winged creature concerning which the Dardan race is reported—the supplied wording is elliptical;  
> Rather, at the heights I shall drive away fleeing swans  
> And burning cranes beneath the vault of heaven.  
> While old age corrupts bodies weary from years,  
> My limbs are immersed and made wet in clear springs;  
> After this I am restored by the splendid light of Phoebus.

### 3. On a writing feather

[Col. 0192B]

> Long ago a shining white onocrotalus produced me,  
> The bird that swallows waters from the flood with open throat.  
> I proceed in a straight path across white fields  
> And leave blue tracks along a gleaming road,  
> Darkening bright fields with blackened winding furrows.  
> Nor is it enough to open a single path across the fields;  
> Rather, the track stretches through a thousand pathways,  
> Which carries those who do not stray toward the summit of heaven.

### 4. On the trumpet

> I am hollow, because by the clamor of warriors I rouse their hearts,  
> Stirring companies into battle with dreadful sounds.  
> Therefore I resound with such a great cry,  
> Because nothing within restrains my voice;  
> Rather, blasts of breath rule throughout my entire body.  
> A chattering cicada can never surpass me,  
> Nor a melodious nightingale singing among the groves—  
> The bird whom the Greeks call by her own name *Acalanthis*.

### 5. On the yew

> I always have green hair upon my leafy body;  
> At no time am I deprived of my thick covering,  
> Although the Circius, the North Wind, and the blasts of the Caurus  
> Strive with dreadful strength to overthrow my leaves.  
> But fate made me poisonous for the condemned,  
> And when a venomous trunk grows from my body,  
> The ravenous gluttons who gnaw it with their jaws  
> Soon die, many corpses lying dead after eating it.

### 6. On the colossus

> The maker of the body fashioned all my limbs,  
> Yet I received none of the functions of my limbs from the same source.  
> I cannot proceed with my feet, nor see with my eyes.  
> Although open windows stand beneath my forehead,  
> No breath proceeds from my breathing inner parts.  
> Nor do I strive to hurl arrows with my two arms.  
> Alas, in vain the maker fastened together this enormous body,  
> Since within I am deprived of all the senses of my limbs.

### 7. On the weasel

> I bend my multicolored limbs into curved caves,  
> Practicing battles against the dreadful race of dragons.  
> I do not swell with the beloved offspring of a husband;  
> Nor did a fertile womb produce offspring for a male,  
> So that the remaining mothers might receive the seeds of birth,  
> But rather my inner parts are made pregnant by a breath from the air.  
> If the offspring suffers the dangers of death,  
> I am said to possess a rough remedy, composing it by art.  
> [Variant: *quin magis*, “but rather,” instead of *cum magis*, “since rather.”]

### 8. On the ram

> I am armed and dreadful with wrinkled horns,  
> I pluck green grasses of the fields with my mouth,  
> Yet as I proceed I am surrounded by a star-bearing company  
> Whose groups climb the lofty summits of heaven.  
> With a battle of my head I shake turreted cities,  
> Overthrowing towns and their walls with lofty fortifications.  
> I clothe mortals with a robe of twisted thread;  
> The fifteenth letter makes me a part of the house in which I stand.

### 9. On writing tablets

> My first origin came from honey-bearing bees,  
> But the rest of my outer part grew in the forests.  
> Hard hides supplied me with footwear.  
> Now the goad of iron plows up my beautiful face  
> And makes slanting furrows in the likeness of a plow.  
> But nourishing seed is brought from heaven to the field,  
> Which produces a thousand sheaves in a rich harvest.  
> Alas, such a holy crop is destroyed by dreadful weapons.

### 10. On fire

> Father and mother begot me in icy blackness,  
> When my first beginnings soon grew strong among dry kindling.  
> By their own strength I can overcome fortune,  
> Since nothing can overcome my fate in liquids.  
> I shall utterly crush forests, rocks, ponds, and metals of iron,  
> And dissolve the laws of nature.  
> When life nourishes me, I resemble a shining star;  
> After this, overcome by fate, I become blacker than pitch.  
> [Variant: *fontibus*, “from springs,” rather than *fomitibus*, “from kindling.”]

## VI. NINE-LINE RIDDLES

### 1. On the swallow

> For many months I languished without food,  
> But sleep and slumber endured the long fasts.  
> When the fields grow pale and the purple meadows flourish,  
> Soon my chattering throat resounds with red songs.  
> After my tender young and the offspring of my kind have grown,  
> I voluntarily flee and seek shadowy hiding places.  
> But if anyone harms the eyes of my chicks,  
> I bring a tested healing poultice as a remedy,  
> Seeking a field flower named after me.

### 2. On the turning of the pole

> Thus the gracious creator of nature formed me:  
> I traverse the whole rounded world through spacious cycles,  
> Carrying broad lands in my bosom with their weight.  
> Thus I enclose the surging masses and blue waters of the sea.  
> For nothing in the order of nature would be so swift  
> That it could proceed on foot or cross the air on wings,  
> Nor would any inhabitant of the sea fly through the blue waters with scales,  
> Nor could a wheel run in a circle, driven by a machine of water,  
> Unless seven stars were set in motion.

### 3. On Arcturus

> I am surrounded by starry troops at the summit of the world.  
> I bear a wagon under the famous name used by the common people.  
> Turning continually in a circle, I do not descend,  
> While the other lights of heaven hasten toward the sea.
