> I am enriched by this privilege because I am near the axis  
> That wanders through the broad Riphaean mountains of Scythia,  
> Matching the Pleiades in number at the pole’s citadel;  
> Its lower part is said to sink into the Stygian and Lethean marsh  
> And to lie beneath the black bottom of hell.

### 4. On the *Crismale*, or *Crismarus*

> I reverence a gracious house full of divine bounty;  
> Yet no one opens its doors or throws open its thresholds,  
> Unless its summits have been raised beneath four halls.  
> Although gems shine externally from its body,  
> And a golden boss gleams yellow with tawny metal,  
> Its inner parts are nevertheless enriched more abundantly,  
> Where the most beautiful appearance of Christ burns within.  
> Thus the white glory of holy things flourishes;  
> Neither beams rise in the temple, nor are they touched by columns.

### 5. On the beaver, called *fiber* in Latin

> A creature dwelling as a guest on the edge of steep banks,  
> I am not sluggish, but warlike in the weapons of my mouth.  
> Rather, I sustain life through hard labor,  
> Soon felling thick trees with hooked axes.  
> I swim in the watery depths where the fish swims,  
> Often plunging my own head beneath the flood.  
> I heal wounds of the limbs, as well as yellow members afflicted with corruption,  
> And dissolve the plague and deadly disease.  
> I feed on gnawed inner bark (*liber*) and bitter bark.

### 6. On the cat, or *muricipes*, or *pilax*

> A sufficiently faithful guardian, preserving the house while ever watchful,  
> I shall patrol blind darkness during the black nights,  
> Not losing the light of my eyes in the caves of the air.  
> For hated thieves who ravage heaps of grain  
> I silently arrange traps of death,  
> And as a wandering huntress I search the lairs of beasts.  
> I do not wish to drive fleeing bands together with dogs,  
> Who, barking at me, will stir up cruel battles.  
> A hated people gave me the name I bear.

### 7. On the sieve

> I pour forth dry frost through frequent windows,  
> And cast gleaming snow from my dark summit.  
> Everyone loves me, although I am cold with a denser cloud  
> And am widely scattered through the chamber of mist.  
> Through me mortals rush toward the funeral of death,  
> And through me the delayed ones despise the thresholds of Dis.  
> Thus souls perish together while life withers away.  
> This snow melts in embers that never burn,  
> But, wondrous to say, grows harder in fire.

### 8. On the sling

[Col. 0194D]

> The gray crop of flax blooming from the field  
> And hide supplied me with the beginnings of my fate.  
> I have two arms made of twisted leather,  
> With which I once slaughtered an immense tyrant in bulk,  
> When the ranks of a people wished to rage.  
> I prefer to wage war with a smooth stone  
> Rather than fight with a hard spear armed with iron.  
> Three fingers turn my whole body above the heights;  
> I whirl my head around and am stretched into the thin air.

### 9. On a glass cup

> I flowed slowly from cracks in stones,  
> When flames broke open the hard entrails of rocks  
> And the furnace’s heat burned with loosened reins.  
> Now I shine in a capacious form, very like ice.  
> Indeed, many wish to break my neck with the right hand  
> And grasp my slippery body beautifully with their fingers.  
> But I change minds when I offer kisses to lips,  
> Bestowing sweet embraces upon compressed cheeks  
> And laying low the staggering steps of feet [the printed reading *sterno ruma* is unclear].

### 10. On a pregnant sow

> Now I have twelve eyes in a single body.  
> I have a twice-threefold head, which governs the remaining limbs.  
> For I walk supported by twenty-four feet,  
> And my body has ninety-six hooves.  
> I shall represent an equal number of walking *synzugiae*:  
> The poplar and the yew, and the willow also with its green foliage.

### Printed Paris variants

The supplied text marks the following *Par.* readings. The source forms and their English distinctions are retained here where English wording alone cannot show the variant.

- Prologue: *celebris* (“renowned”) for *prisci* (“ancient”) in “trophies.”
- Nature: *non ulla manent sine me moderante* (“nothing remains without my governing”) for *res nulla manet* (“no thing remains”).
- Rainbow: *ruber* (“red”) for *rubens* (“reddening/red”).
- Salt: *constant* (“remain constant”) for *fulget* (“shines”).
- Adamant: *quod* (“which”) for *quem* (“whom”).
- Bellows: *vexor* (“I am buffeted”) for *vescor* (“I feed”).
- Organ: *salpinctae* (“female trumpets”) for *salpinctis* (“with trumpets”); *me praesente* (“with me present”) for *meque strepente* (“while I resound”).
- *Perna*: *Proponti* (“of the Propontis”) for *ponti* (“of the sea”).
- Myrmecoleon: *rescindere rostra* (“to cut apart beaks”) for *resistere rostro* (“to resist a beak”).
- File: *plana superficie* (“with a flat surface”) for *plano superficiem* (“I make the surface flat”).
- Water: *arcus at* (“but bows”) for *ast acus* (“but a needle”).
- Crane fly: *laticum* (“of waters”; a grammatical form) for *latices* (“waters”).
- Dove: *jussa parentis* (“the parent’s commands”) for *jura parenti* (“duties to the parent”).
- Ox: *arva* (“fields”) for *ora* (“mouth/face”).
- Stork: *nam faxo crepacula* (“for I make little rattles”) for *faxo crepitacula* (“I make rattlings”).
- Cinyphean gnat: *dum* (“while”) for *sed* (“but”).
- Double kettle: title *De cocuma duplici* (“On the double kettle”) for *De cucuma*; *tantis spectacula causis* (“spectacles of such causes”) for *tantarum foedera rerum* (“bonds/compacts of such great things”).
- Dagger: *De ter. gremiis formabar* (“I was fashioned from the earth’s wombs”) for *me terrae gremius formabat* (“the earth’s womb fashioned me”).
- Water bubble: *spatiuntur* (“move about”) for *potiuntur* (“possess/enjoy”).
- Spelt: title *Pelta* (“small shield”) for *Spelta* (“spelt”).
- Trumpet: *retundant* (“beat back”) for *retrudant* (“drive/push back”).
- Weasel: *quin* (“rather”) for *cum* (“when”).
- Fire: *fontibus e siccis* (“from dry springs”; corrupted/uncertain in the supplied reading) for *fomitibus siccis* (“from dry kindling”).
- Chrismal: *intus* (“within”) for *potis* (“ample/abundant”; contextually uncertain).

Source/review notes: The supplied section ends after the fragment ‘And below:’; no continuation has been invented. Latin metrical forms are retained with adjacent English glosses because their spelling, inflection, and quantity are the subject of the text.

I hate them, but I love the hooked beeches with their acorns,

and likewise the fruit-bearing oaks with their flourishing crowns;

so too the many-branched holm oak is not despised.

### 11. On the Dwarf Elder

[Col. 0195B]

While the decaying elder reddens with foliage in the forest,

I am its equal in leaves, for I grow as a shoot in the fields,

bearing black clusters of berries upon my crown.

When, green across the countryside, physicians are said often to have sought it,

whenever the scabies of disease had invaded afflicted flesh,

to cleanse the body’s surface—

while dreadful sores torment the inward parts with corruption—

I can help prevent the leprosy’s poison from spreading,

thus restoring the foul-smelling tissues of human beings by my growth.

## VII. TEN-LINE RIDDLES

### 1. On the Raven

While savage floods were destroying the human race,

and new seas were punishing all mortals,

except the few who produce the seed of the generations,

[Col. 0195C] I was the first of living creatures to violate the bonds of duty,

scorning to submit my neck to my father’s command.

Hence, I think, the poet once said in verse:

“Whatever he had polluted on land, he washed away in the waters”—

for I shall never satisfy my offspring with food,

unless I first see feathers grow black upon their flesh.

Let the letter be removed; thereafter I shall remain without offspring.

### 2. On the Wine Cup

Behold, I pour out many cups, intoxicating with Bacchus,

which the winegrower pressed from yellowing grapes;

the vine-leaf produced them from the green shoot,

filling the tavern of the wine-merchant with nectar from the vine.

Thus my inward parts swell to fullness with must;

yet drunkenness does not distress my inflated body,

although it has drunk this nectar from a hundred jars.

[Col. 0195D]

I am a child of the earth, growing in the high forests.

The countryman splits my substance with wedges,

overturning tall pines and oaks with iron.

### 3. On Lucifer

I always precede the bright light with my own clear radiance,

the standard-bearer of Phoebus, who brightly illuminates the world;

as I travel through heaven, I turn along an oblique path:

from the eastern regions I shall proceed thence toward the central light. [Paris: *admodum* (“very greatly”) in place of *ad medium* (“toward the middle”).]

Those who first behold the lights at the borders of India—

O happy one, once preserved under the law of the Thunderer!

Alas, afterward I fell, proud in my insolent mind;

therefore vengeance struck the doomed enemy.

Thus six companions climb with me above the ether,

[Col. 0196A]

whose names the learned reader will be able to unfold through books.

### 4. On the Lighthouse

On lofty cliffs, where the blue waters beat against the rocks

and the surging waves of the salt sea swell—[Paris: *undantis … ponti*, “of the heaving sea.”]

a structure built me broad upon the highest masses of stone,

a guide to display the navigable routes to fleets.

I did not scour the sea’s watery plains with an oarsman,

nor cleave the sea by a winding course in ships;

yet I mark those driven along by immense waves

and lead them toward the shores from lofty towers,

setting flame-bearing torches upon the high towers,

while the fiery stars hide the wintry clouds.

## VIII. ELEVEN-LINE RIDDLES

### 1. On the Palm Tree, Which Grows Leafy When Fertilized by the Date

[Col. 0196B]

The almighty ruler, who created all things by his command,

gave me a name to be held victorious in the world.

For by my name the glory of things flourishes;

when the martyrs conquer the battles of the world,

they seize the heavenly rewards of life;

the host of warriors is covered with leafy crowns,

and the soldier with a green branch after victory in combat.

At the crown of my head a fleece thickens,

from which coverings for many garments are twisted.

Thus too I nourish people with the honey-sweet richness of foods,

granting to peoples the sustenance of food through nectar.

### 2. On the Monoceros, or Unicorn

On lofty hills are the dangers of savage war,

although the hunter, with his barking Molossian hound, vainly cries out,

[Col. 0196C] skillfully hurling iron darts at the wild beast,

I fear nothing; trusting in my great strength,

I attack the lofty elephants in battle and lay them low with wounds.

Alas, savage Fortune, which deceived me in this way!

While I slaughter the great, I am defeated by an unarmed maiden;

for as she opens her lap, the beautiful woman in childbirth soon seizes me,

and, having achieved her wish, leads me down to the high city.

The Greek language gave me my name from the horn.

The Latins likewise called me by their own word.

### 3. On the Sun and Moon

The most filthy offspring of Saturn did not beget us—

Jupiter, whom the poets’ songs imagine as immense—

nor was mother Latona our creator on Delos.

I am not called Cynthia, nor is my brother called Apollo.

[Col. 0196D]

Rather, the ruler of highest Olympus begot us,

he who now presides over the lofty citadel in heaven.

We divide the square-shaped world under a common law;

we govern the nocturnal courses and the reins of the days.

If sister and brother did not rightly govern the wandering ages,

alas, immense chaos would darken everything with hiding places,

and the black Tartarus of Erebus would now reign everywhere.

### 4. On the Spark

What thing on earth is armed with such mighty strength,

or dares attempt to perform with equal powers?

My beginnings in life are small,

but, slender as I am, I habitually bring down great things to death—

things whose own inner chambers carry death.

For I scatter beneath the sky the dense thickets of forests,

the shrublands alike,

[Col. 0197A] and the pine-bearing mountains together with their lofty masses;

savage, rapacious, and fierce.

And I am smaller in body than the slender *sciniph*;

while the cold mother was giving birth from her harsh womb,

at first bringing forth the offspring of her race from the uterus.

## IX. TWELVE-LINE RIDDLE: ON THE HORNET

Through the clear air I now row with two wings,

bristling, and I produce the murmurs of a coarse voice;

in a hollow tree-trunk I turn about among dense swarms,

making sweet food for my own companies.

Yet these foods are dreadful to human mouths.

But whoever wishes, breaking the bonds of peace,

to defile a house beneath an oak roof,

I summon my allied cohorts to war as an example.

[Col. 0197B] While they hiss in swarms and thrust their stingers,

the ranks flee, terrified by the dreadful darts.

Thus, against the guilty enemy, the innocent twist many weapons—

weapons steeped in hideous poisons.

## XI. THIRTEEN-LINE RIDDLE: ON THE SEA-SCYLLA

Behold, fate has given me the name of the Molossians.

Thus the language of the Argolic people declares it in speech,

from the time when the songs of dreadful Circe deceived me;

she stained the clear waters of the spring with her spells,

and cruelly removed my legs with their hips,

and my calves (*pulpas*; Paris: *suras*, “calves”) with both knees.

Now frightened sailors report how the offspring howl,

while they propel their fleets with oars and cleave the blue,

[Col. 0197C]

vast waves as the storm advances.

A little palm, spread over the waters, comes to the aid of the oars;

from afar they hear the loins barking all around.

Thus the daughter of the Titan once beguiled me,

so that deservedly I live as an exile in the salt waves.

## XII. FIFTEEN-LINE RIDDLE: ON THE ELEPHANT

Iron battle-lines and dense troops,

whom the empty desire for war spurs on,

while they strive to stain the pious treaties of the kingdom with weapons,

the trumpet drinks in the air through its windy blasts,

and the savage war horns resound with clashing noise—

I learned, without fear, to behold the grim murmurs of Mars.

Although my creator made me ugly at birth,

when I emerged from the womb and received the gifts of life,

[Col. 0197D]

behold, the glory of my form succeeded death,

while the deadly end spreads through my exposed fibers.

A gold leaf, precious for its shining metals,

although decorated with the lights of gems,

will never be able to surpass the flowers of my trappings.

Nature denied me the ability to bend my knees when weary

and, with my knee-joints bent, surrender my eyes to sleep.

Rather, I am compelled to live standing.

## XIII. SIXTEEN-LINE RIDDLE: ON THE NIGHT

The flower-bearing earth gave birth to me, black in body,

and I produce nothing fertile from my barren womb;

although poets, recounting the Eumenids in song,

assert that the Tartarean realm gives birth to offspring,

[Col. 0198A]

I possess no substance of any definite birth.

But at times I embrace the blue, square-shaped world.

While Phoebus’ Titanian lamp surveys the ages,

it is hostile to me, though it is friendly to all.

Savage robbers always used to love me,

and I protect them, hidden in my dark womb.

It is established that Virgil sang of a dear sister [Paris: *fateor*, “I admit,” in place of *constat*, “it is established”]:

“A dreadful, huge monster, beneath whose body are as many feathers

as there are watchful eyes—wondrous to say—

as many tongues, as many mouths resound, and as many ears she raises.

She flies through the middle of heaven by night,

enters the earth, and hides her head among the clouds.”

## XIV. POLYSTICHIC RIDDLE: ON THE CREATURE

[Col. 0198B]

The Creator, who shone through the ages on everlasting pillars,

the ruler of kingdoms, restraining thunderbolts by law,

while the hanging heights of the spacious world revolve,

made me various when at first he founded the universe.

Ever-watchful at my posts, I ought never to sleep,

yet immediately my eyes are closed in sleep.

For just as God governs the world under his own authority,

so I embrace everything beneath the vault of heaven.

No one is more sluggish, since a little mask frightens me,

yet against the bristly boar I stand more boldly.

No one surpasses me in desire for the banners of triumph,

except the supreme God who reigns in the heavenly citadel.

Breathing forth, I am more fragrant than scented frankincense,

smelling of ambrosia and of the earth’s growing produce.

[Col. 0198C]

I can surpass lilies joined with purple roses,

full of the sweetness of fragrant nard;

now I putrefy, foul with the filth of stinking mud.

Whatever things are beneath the sky and under its axis are governed,

while the father who bears the bow has granted me the right to rule.

I grasp the coarse and delicate forms of things;

higher than heaven, I search out the secrets of the Thunderer,

yet lower than earth, I behold gloomy Tartarus.

For I preceded the ancient ages of the world [Paris: *mundi*, “of the world,” for *mundo*, “than the world”];

yet, behold, I was born from my mother’s womb this year [Paris: *generabor*, “I shall be born,” for *generabar*, “I was born”].

More beautiful while a golden clasp gleams with bosses;

more hideous than brambles, and baser than rejected seaweed.

Behold, I stand broader than the open reaches of the earth,

[Col. 0198D]

yet I am enclosed within the middle of a fist.

Colder than winter frosts and gleaming hoarfrost,

although I burn with Vulcan’s blazing fires.

Sweeter on the palate than a draught of sluggish nectar,

and again more bitter than the green wormwoods of the field.

I chew food and devour it like the Cyclopes,

although I can live happily forever without nourishment.

Faster than eagles, swifter than the wings of Zephyrus,

and quicker even than the hastening hawk—yet dreadful—

the worm, the snail, the sluggish marsh tortoise,

and the black dung-beetle, offspring of foul excrement,

surpass me in the race, quicker than speech can say.

Thus I wield the weight of rocks, heavier than lead;

I am lighter than the feather to which a water-gnat yields.

[Col. 0199A]

For, since (*quia*; Paris: *quae*) it pours dense flames from the inward parts of flint,

I am harder than iron, but softer than roasted entrails.

[Here the Paris manuscript inserts the following seven verses, from “Behold, at the aged man’s wounds …” to “… vibrates in the atom.” GILES.]

For I wear no locks of hair upon the crown of my head,

to adorn my brow and temples with ornaments and bristles;

whereas my curly tresses fly from the crown of my head,

and adorn themselves more than hair treated with a curling iron.

I grow much fatter than the lard of swine,

when they once again display their bodies beneath acorn-bearing beeches,

and swineherds rejoice in their fattened flesh.

But cruel hunger will torture me, poor and emaciated,

while I am continually filled with rich food.

I am clear—indeed, brighter than the orb of the shining Titan,

[Col. 0199B]

whiter than snow when a cloud snows with its fleece;

yet darker than the black shadows of a prison,

and than the hidden places that Tartarus surrounds with darkness.

I am fashioned smooth and round like the sphere of the stars,

like a little ball or sphere, and likewise like crystal in form;

and, by reversal, I am stretched out like silk threads,

extended into a slender cloth like the warp-threads of a garment.

Behold, where the world’s farther side is laid open by the wounds of age,

I extend much farther—wondrous to say;

beneath me or above me nothing exists through the ages,

except the parent of things, who restrains the world by his word.

I am greater in the blue waves than the dark whale,

and smaller than the tiny worm that plows through bodies,

or than the small atom that vibrates in Phoebus’ rays.

I walk across the fields with a hundred feet,

[Col. 0199C]

yet I never proceed on foot entirely across the earth.

Thus my Wisdom surpasses the wisdom of the wise,

although rich learning in books did not teach it to me,

nor have I ever been able to know what constitutes a syllable.

Drier than the summer heat of the sun,

yet again wetter with dew than a moist stream from a spring,

saltier by far than the marble surfaces of the swollen sea,

and I am more tasteless than the earth’s icy waters.

Adorned with the manifold appearance of all colors,

from which the structure of the present world is decorated,

now I am deprived of all color and have become lurid.

Believers, listen to the utterance of my word;

a learned teacher will scarcely be able to explain it,

yet the reader who disbelieves will not suppose it trivial.

I ask the inflated wise men by what name I should be called.

[Col. 0199D]

(The Paris manuscript adds what follows. GILES.)

While a virgin consecrated to Christ twists golden threads with a slender needle in her pale hand,

then I paint hairy pages with tears by means of a bronze reed.

The poor poet does not know the caves of the Muses as I do.

The blessed Cross shines, consecrated by Christ’s blood.

D. Now that the propositions of the riddles have been set forth and the melody of the metres arranged, the promised order of subjects demands that you should not refuse to disclose the manifold rules of feet, drawn from the different parts of speech—especially those which grammarians are known to claim as their own.

—M. In general, the catalogue of all feet consists of three times forty plus four, that is, 124. But from this intricate multitude twenty-eight feet are set apart, which the eloquence of poets employs in verse and which do not exceed the measure of four syllables.

[Col. 0200A]

D. I am pleased to hear this explained more plainly and clearly.

—M. From the nature of two syllables four feet arise; from three syllables eight proceed; from four, sixteen. These are the grammarians’ specifically legitimate feet, from which the discipline of a hundred metres has sprung.

D. How many are the feet of orators, which are governed by the rule of rhetoric and assigned to the elegance of prose?

—M. Three times thirty and three times two, that is, ninety-six, which Greek eloquence called *syzygies* [paired feet]. For thirty-two feet are formed from five syllables, and sixty-four syzygies arise from the reciprocal variation of six syllables.

[Col. 0200B]

D. How many properties of feet are there?

—M. Seven: arsis and thesis, the number of syllables, time, resolution, figure, and metre.

D. Give the difference between arsis and thesis.

—M. *Arsis* means raising, *thesis* placing; but arsis is to be placed in the first part of a noun or verb, thesis in the second. For these divisions are said to have been devised for distinguishing the times of feet. For example, in *polus*, *po* is arsis and *lus* thesis. So also *crocus*, *thronus*, *torus*, *aetas*, *aestas*, and every noun or verb which the formula of examples below will require us to attach under a pyrrhic or a spondee, are legitimately subject to this rule.

[Col. 0200C]

D. How many kinds of division occur in feet, especially those known to belong to grammarians?

—M. As the authority of our predecessors is remembered to have handed down, a threefold condition of division is defined: some feet have equal division, some double division, and others sesquialteral division. Antiquity established that the first is called dactylic, the second iambic, and the third paeonic.

D. I ask that you explain this threefold rule of divisions more fully.

—M. Ten feet receive equal division and are weighed, as it were, in an equal balance of times; arsis and thesis govern them with an equal scale of distinction: pyrrhic, spondee,

[Col. 0200D]

dactyl, anapaest, proceleusmatic, dispondee, double iamb, double trochee, antispast, and choriamb.

D. How many feet are divided according to the double ratio?

—M. Six: iamb, trochee, molossus, tribrach, lesser Ionic, and greater Ionic. Arsis and thesis now incline one way, now another, on an unequal balance of times.

D. What is sesquialteral division, why is it so called, and how many feet serve that division?

—M. It is called sesquialteral, as though half-double, because one part exceeds the other not twice over but by half of a double. Therefore, outweighing equal division of time by an increment, as it were, of a momentary sixth, it is sesquialteral; although double division, armed with twice the time, surpasses that same sesquialteral division.

[Col. 0201A]

Finally, the following seven feet belong to the sesquialteral class: bacchius, palimbacchius, amphimacer, and the four paeons.

D. By what reasoning or signs can one determine whether more times are assigned to arsis or to thesis?

—M. All syllables, whether of nouns, verbs, or any other part of speech, are counted from the end, not from the beginning. Accordingly, the times in arsis and thesis are distinguished by accents, which are confined to three positions: final, penultimate, and antepenultimate. The antepenult receives an acute and is never circumflexed. More times are reckoned in the arsis; but if the penult is pronounced with an acute or circumflex accent, thesis will claim the fuller reckoning of times.

[Col. 0201B]

D. I am now eager to hear formulas of examples belonging to the pyrrhic foot, especially examples gathered from the principal parts of speech, noun and verb.

—M. These are nouns commonly known to have sprung from the diverse root of the five declensions: *Deus, decus, pius, genus, pecus, bonus, modus, domus, lupus, lepus, latus, chorus, crocus, torus, thronus, dolus, nemus, novus, scelus, opus, locus, equus, cibus, reus, comes, Ceres, seges, acus, manus*. *Malus*, when it appears to mean “wicked,” consists of two short syllables and is pyrrhic, as also in:

> That wicked serpent, wandering in the Calabrian woods.

And in the *Bucolics*:

> What a wicked error carried me away!

[Col. 0201C]

But if *malus* is a mast, to which the canvas and ropes of the yards are attached, it is reduced to the rule of the trochee, long plus short, as Virgil says in book V of the *Aeneid*:

> From the lofty mast there hung a yard, to which it was attached.

Likewise, *malus*, if it is the fruit-bearing tree called *melarius*, of feminine gender, belongs to the trochee, as in the *Georgics*:

> And barren plane trees bore strong apple trees.

*Apis, lapis, avis, navis, canis, famis, sitis, chelys, chlamys, cutis, polus, globus, homo, leo, caro, Maro, ovis, scrobis.* Likewise this aforesaid foot ends in the letter *r*, though it is not produced from one and the same declension: *pater, puer, piper, niger, siler, socer, gener, aper, caper, tener, miser, celer, iter, scaber, sacer, ruber*,

[Col. 0201D]

*amor, glomer, jubar, cruor, honor, sator, soror, labor.* But if it is the deponent verb, *la* is lengthened, as in:

> The misshapen glory of a feeble flame glides away.

*Jecur, ebur, ager, timor.* *Liquor*, if it is a noun of the third declension, is pyrrhic, as in Arator:

> … foods from dew, liquids from the rock.

And below:

> And the liquid of bronze hardened into solid food.

But if *liquor* is a verb of the third conjugation, or third order as Valerius the grammarian preferred to call it, it is a trochee, as Virgil in the *Georgics*:

> … when moisture melts from the mountains,

> and the rotten clod dissolves in the west wind.

*Rosa, faba, aqua, mora, rota, coma, via, toga, gula*,

[Col. 0202A]

*schola.* *Plaga*, if it denotes the cardinal regions, is pyrrhic, as Ambrose, bishop of Milan, expressed it in hexameter:

> And the azure region of the coloured world glows red.

And Sedulius:

> Then it gathers together the four regions of the square world.

But if *plaga* is punitive vengeance, it is reduced to the trochaic rule, as that same poet reports in the prophetic utterance of evangelical verse:

> He who covers it and fears to uncover the wound for the healer.

It should also be noted that certain monosyllabic nouns produce a pyrrhic in the oblique cases, that is, in the genitive and ablative: *crux crucis, nux nucis, grex gregis, pes pedis, lar laris, sal salis, mas maris, nix nivis, nex necis, pix picis, prex precis, grus gruis*,

[Col. 0202B]

*trabs trabis, bos bovis, dux ducis, trux trucis.*

D. Thus the rules for nouns which support the laws of the first foot have been set out briefly and summarily.

—M. Verbs of both the first conjugation and shortened third conjugation likewise concur under the same condition: *voco, veto, levo, seco, neco, puto, cavo, lito, voro, nego, amo, frico, plico; dico dicas dicat*, with a shortened penult, as the poet says:

> Virgin Mary, for you Sixtus dedicated new temples,

which is of the first conjugation. But *dico dicis dicit*, of the third, has a lengthened penult:

> You say that a rough [one] is coming to the farmers and sailors.

*Paro, aro, crepo, sono, tono, novo, cibo, cubo, ligo, mico, creo, meo, beo, rigo, lito, labo, loco, rogo, jugo, fugo, labo*—for it differs from *labo* meaning “I totter”; *lavo* is active and *labo* neuter—*roto, pio, hio*, whose frequentative or iterative is *hieto hietas hietat*, and whose inchoative is *hisco hiscis hiscit*; *domo, nato, gravo, probo, jugo, gelo*, whence *congelasco*; *volo*. *Volo*, whether denoting a flying or a willing person, is declared to belong to the pyrrhic, as in:

[Col. 0202C]

> the world flying through the ages;

and:

> and he ceased to say more, though wishing to do so.

*Capo, cado, fremo, gemo, fero, gero, tero, sero, sino, ago, meto, peto, tego, colo, bibo, rego, lego, traho, fio, scio*, whence *exscire*. *Vomo, pluo, spuo,* and *monuo* [so written], *juvo, meo, creo, beo, queo, fluo, luo, ruo, strio, loquor, precor, sequor, queror, reor, fruor, moror.* Similar defective verbs are joined to this rule: *libet, placet, piget, pudet, juvat, decet, liquet*,

[Col. 0202D]

*licet.*

D. Then will the aforementioned verbs of mixed conjugation which end in the letter *o* always belong to the pyrrhic?

—M. Whenever the final syllable is shortened, a pyrrhic is unquestionably produced, as in:

> I prefer to remain black; I shall fear final fates less.

And:

> Nor do I carry out great things at once, but heap up many in turn.

And again:

> I do not wish to endure tombs; I know that earth buries me.

But if the same syllable is lengthened, an iamb is certainly produced, as in Virgil:

> And I sing an Ascraean song through Roman towns.

For it is scanned: *Ascrae, umque ca, no Ro, mana per, oppida, carmen.*

[Col. 0203A]

D. Can a pyrrhic or iamb be inserted in heroic hexameter, since you have produced examples in hexameter verses?

—M. If the aforesaid verbs of the conjugations are uttered without the context of parts of speech and without metrical versification, they are subject to the rules of pyrrhic or iamb. But if, in dactylic verse, the method of scansion and the division of caesuras by cola and commata compel them to be separated, they are subject only to the laws of spondees or dactyls. This can very easily be proved by thousands of examples, produced without the frivolity of deception or falsehood.

D. With what accent or prosody is the very numerous collection of nouns and verbs recognized as belonging to the pyrrhic pronounced?

—M. In disyllables where both syllables are short, the penult is pronounced with an acute accent.

**THE DISCUSSION OF THE PYRRHIC ENDS.**

**The discussion of the spondee begins.**

D. I now set forth the rules of the spondee, gathered as examples from different parts of speech.

—M. These are examples of the second foot derived from nouns: *felix, pernix, perdex, index, illex, cortex, remex, cornix, bombix, cervix, audax, forfex, forceps, anceps, auceps, princeps, praeceps, virtus, tellus, aetas, aestas, pumex, judex, rumex, vertex, caudex, codex, mordax, fornax, fallax, pollex, murex, ilex, carex*—that is, a very rough grass, as Virgil:

[Col. 0203B]

> … fed on sharp sedge.

For *carica* is the fruit called a fig; hence masses of *caricae* are made from fresh figs.

[Col. 0203C]

Hence it is inappropriately reported by some that the famous hermit, living a solitary life under strict laws of frugality on the border between Syrians and Saracens, sustained and nourished the exhausted vital parts of his limbs and the withered entrails of his breast, contrary to the nature of things, with five *caricae*. For it is human nature to be nourished by *caricae* that ripen after the large figs, whereas oxen, tragelaphs, and ibexes are reared and feed on *caricae*.

*Simplex, duplex, triplex, vervex, fornix, radix, matrix, lodix, victrix, natrix, vivax, verax, pellax, edax, radix, mendax, imbrex*—so called because it keeps off rains; *auspex*, one who attends to the omens of birds, while *auceps* is one who practises bird-catching; *complex, duplex, triplex, elix*. *Elices* are the larger furrows drawn to drain fields; *velox*,

[Col. 0203D]

*atrox, Pollux, conjux*. Concerning *conjux*, I recall that in book VI of *On the Noun* I discussed the addition of the letter *n* in the nominative and vocative, though it wholly fails in the oblique cases. Examples also come from monosyllables when they are inflected in the nominative and accusative plural: *flos flores, mos mores, ros rores, pons pontes, fons fontes, rex reges, lex leges, lanx lances, glans glandes, plus plures, mus mures, cors cortes, cos cotes, sors sortes, dos dotes, ars artes, pars partes, calx calces, merx merces, sol soles*, when it refers to days, as:

> Those forty suns were in order;

*vox voces, nox noctes, lis lites, dis dites, glis glires, puls pultes.*

D. Give examples from conjugations.

[Col. 0204A]

—M. The first and second conjugations: several agree in the second and third persons, as *libo libas libant, sedo sedas sedant, sudo sudas sudant*. Likewise *caneo canes canent, polleo polles pollent, frondeo frondes frondent*. In the fourth conjugation, however, only the second person: *hinnio hinnis, tinnio tinnis, grunnio grunnis, grundio grundis, trinnio trinnis, grincio grincis.* There are also verbs of the second conjugation which in the first person of the indicative perfect produce a spondee. Likewise, in the second person singular of the present imperative: *jubeo jussi jube, fulgeo fulsi fulge, rideo risi ride, mulgeo mulsi mulge.*

[Col. 0204B]

There are others of the same conjugation which agree in the perfect, but in the aforesaid imperative person produce an iamb, not a spondee: *faveo favi fave*, as:

> Christ, favour our prayers.

*moveo movi move, maneo mansi mane, paveo pavi pave*, as:

> Once even the ravens were afraid to serve Elijah.

And much further below:

> the unarmed host was afraid.

*Sedeo sedi sede, video vidi vide*, and the rest of the same kind. From the third conjugation too, when it turns to the first person of the perfect, a spondee is formed: *scribo scripsi, scalpo scalpsi, sculpo sculpsi, repo repsi, mergo mersi, serpo serpsi, cudo cudi, rumpo rupi, cedo cessi, sepio sepsi, plaudo plausi, farcio farsi, haurio hausi, sarcio sarsi, flecto flexi, rego rexi, veho vexi, figo fixi, vivo vixi, meio minxi, tingo tinxi*,

[Col. 0204C]

*cingo cinxi, sugo suxi, uro ussi, trudo trusi, coquo coxi, duco duxi.* Examples of this foot are also taken from adverbs of quality and quantity: *sancte, caste, docte, care, late, longe.* But if these are nouns in the vocative, they are reduced to the trochee, not the spondee. Very many present participles also do not resist, but support, the laws of the spondee: *dicens, ducens, vivens, turgens, trudens, sternens, stertens, scandens.*

D. With what accent should the parts of speech subject to the spondee be pronounced?

—M. All syllables long either by position or by nature are regularly given an acute.

**The discussion of the iamb begins.**

D. Do not shrink from first gathering examples of the iambic foot derived from nouns.

[Col. 0204D]

—M. The nouns known to concur under the iambic laws are: *silex, senex, culix* [F. *salix*], *calex, apex, latex, tenax, rapax, fugax, sagax, procax, minax, edax, emax, varix*—whence one deformed by *varices*, that is, tortuous convolutions of veins in the knee and calves, is called *varicosus*—*trilex, triplex, salex, culex*. Commentaries state that Virgil made the following distich:

> Little gnat, guardian of the herds, to you who deserve it,
>
> he renders this funeral rite in return for the gift of life.

It is scanned thus: *parve cu, lex pecu, dum cus, tos tibi, taleme, renti*; and this verse is called bucolic. *Ferox, ferax, sequax, loquax, procax, parens, frequens, recens, cliens, fides, dies, salus.* If *palus paludis* is of the third declension, it undoubtedly belongs to the iamb, as Virgil, book VI:

[Col. 0205A]

> the sewn boat groaned beneath the weight
>
> and, leaky, took in much marsh-water.

But if, in the second declension, its genitive ends in *i*, it is properly subject to trochaic laws, as that versifier is remembered to have sung elegantly in the seventh book of the divine law concerning Samson’s deceitful concubine, who by her treacherous seduction prefigured the synagogue:

> Hanging, she entwines with her right hand and, bending back, the stakes.

And below:

> Leaping out, he throws back the stakes and ties up his hair again.

Certain verbs of both the first and second conjugation likewise suit the iamb in the second person singular, indicative and imperative: *amas ama, putas puta, paras para, aras ara, secas seca, necas neca, vocas voca, locas loca.* Likewise there are as many from the second

[Col. 0205B]

conjugation: *doces doce, moves move, viges vige, riges rige, pates pate*, whence the inchoative form *patesce*; *tenes tene, times time, cares care, caves cave, studes stude, manes mane, lates late.* But when it receives the spoken formation, *a* is altered: *lateo lates latet, delitesco delitescis delitescit*; and in the perfect we say *delituit*, not *delatuit*, as the poet:

> gleaming beneath the cloud,
>
> he hid himself.

From the third conjugation, in the present infinitive of both passive and deponent verbs, I judge the iamb to be formed: *geri, teri, seri, tegi, legi, regi, trahi, vehi, mori.* From the aforementioned monosyllables, which we set out for the sake of explaining the pyrrhic, the sure rule of metre declares that iambic feet are derived when they are declined in the singular dative or plural nominative: *crux cruci cruces*, as Prosper confirms:

[Col. 0205C]

> Not even the harshness of the cross could frighten one willing to do so.

*Fax faci faces, trux truci truces, nux nuci nuces, dux duci duces.* So *grues, sues*, and the rest of the same kind. Iambic feet are also taken from participles only of those verbs which we set out above in the pyrrhic: *rigans, litans*, as the poet proves:

> which offer sacrifice to the stars driven away by light.

It is scanned: *lisque li*, a dactyl; *secans, necans, negans, vorans, volans, curvans, lavans, ligans, micans.* They come no less from the second conjugation, when a tribrach is changed into an iamb, that is, when the meanings of active and neuter verbs are converted into present participles: *doceo docens, careo carens, rigeo rigens, faveo favens, sileo silens, caleo calens, rubeo rubens*, as Juvencus:

[Col. 0205D]

> If the red evening star advances in the star-bearing sky.

And Virgil:

> … golden Phoebe is always red in the wind.

Nor do I think that participles coming from the shortened third conjugation produce an iamb; from the fourth I have nowhere found them—for example, *gero gerens, gemo gemens, tero terens, sero serens, ruo ruens, struo struens, alo alens, colo colens, emo emens, lego legens, premo premens, cano canens.* Therefore the legitimate rule of grammarians advises that all the aforementioned nouns, verbs, and participles belonging to the iamb be pronounced with an acute accent.

**On the trochee.**

[Col. 0206A]

D. Give examples suitable to the trochaic law.

—M. First, the nouns which appear to agree with the trochee are: *almus, sanctus, nympha, lympha, abba, offa, occa, sapa*—that is, boiled-down must—*ostrum, rostrum, rastrum, sceptrum, scalprum*, from which diminutively *scalpellum*; *labrum*, whence *labellum*; *bulla; bucca, gibbus, cippus, burrus, barrus, floccus, soccus, muscus, luscus, fuscus, tuscus.* But enough of syllables long by position, which lie everywhere publicly and openly and are most easily detected by metrical writers. I shall now briefly add those which enjoy natural length and which especially need the support of poetic examples: *musa, meta, seta, creta, theta, feta, spina, Roma, ruma, rima, lima, bruma, fama*,

[Col. 0206B]

*mirus, dirus, funus, munus, fumus, prunus, pirus, pinus, taxus, malus, flavus, canus, sanus, fatus, nanus*—that is, a dwarf—*crinis, finis, funis, clunis*, whence *clunaculum*. Thus Julius Solinus in his *Collection of Memorable Things*: “And the weary,” he says, “take turns supporting their heads upon their buttocks.” *Nudus, udus, ludus, mutus, nutus, tutus, fotus, lotus, totus, motus, notus, nodus, nisus, risus, visus, fretus, spretus, cretus, fulmen, famen, flamen*—that is, a priest of a shrine—*numen, lumen, rumen, plemen, limen, crimen, vimen, gramen, stamen.* Hence Lucan says of Orpheus:

> Now the Fates set down their full distaffs and threads,
>
> and many ages clung to the brought-down strands.

Trochaic feet are also formed from pronouns long by position: *ille, iste, ipse, noster, vester, quisquam, quisnam, isdem.* They also arise from verbs lengthened by the laws of position: *prendo, scando, necto, pecto, cerno, pingo, ningo, mingo, fingo, pinso, hisco, quasso, lasso, laxo, taxo, faxo*—which is anomalous—*sperno, texo, vexo, mando, pando, linquo, vinco, subdo, abdo, condo, pango, cingo, tingo, pungo*, whose perfect is *pupugi*.

[Col. 0206C]

D. What verbs has the authority of the ancients decreed are lengthened by the rules of nature?

—M. Without the obstacle of any difficulty, these are believed to be: *rado, fumo, dico, duco, giro, promo, prodo, cudo, lego, legas*; but *lego legis* is shortened; *subdo, sedo, udo, cogo, dedo, trudo*, as in the *Georgics*:

> The root of the olive is thrust from dry wood.

*Credo, nolo, malo*, as:

[Col. 0206D]

> I prefer to remain black; I shall fear final fates less.

*Pono, laudo, laedo, oro, clamo, duro, edo, fido, libo, privo, vivo, quaero quaesivi*; for *queror quaestus sum* is pyrrhic; *ludo, sumo, suo, plaudo, demo, dego.* Passive, common, and deponent verbs likewise agree with this rule when long by either position or nature: *promor, prodor, scrutor, vador, praedor, laetor, bacchor, nascor, ructor, tutor, venor, fungor.* If *nitor* is a deponent verb, it will be a trochee, as:

> … I strive to reach certain branches.

### English glosses for the metrical word registers, columns 0201B–0206D

The Latin forms remain above because their endings and quantities are the evidence under discussion. The following glosses give their readings in the same groupings and preserve the stated case, person, tense, or participial contrasts.

**Pyrrhic nouns (0201B–0202B).** *Deus* “God”; *decus* “honor”; *pius* “dutiful/pious”; *genus* “kind/race”; *pecus* “livestock”; *bonus* “good”; *modus* “measure/manner”; *domus* “house”; *lupus* “wolf”; *lepus* “hare”; *latus* “side”; *chorus* “chorus”; *crocus* “saffron”; *torus* “couch”; *thronus* “throne”; *dolus* “deceit”; *nemus* “grove”; *novus* “new”; *scelus* “crime”; *opus* “work”; *locus* “place”; *equus* “horse”; *cibus* “food”; *reus* “accused/guilty person”; *comes* “companion”; *Ceres* “Ceres”; *seges* “crop”; *acus* “needle”; *manus* “hand.” The distinct quantities of *malus* mean “wicked,” “mast,” and “apple tree,” as the author explains with the verses above. *Apis* “bee”; *lapis* “stone”; *avis* “bird”; *navis* “ship”; *canis* “dog”; *famis* “hunger”; *sitis* “thirst”; *chelys* “lyre/tortoise-shell”; *chlamys* “military cloak”; *cutis* “skin”; *polus* “pole/heaven”; *globus* “sphere”; *homo* “human being”; *leo* “lion”; *caro* “flesh”; *Maro* “Virgil”; *ovis* “sheep”; *scrobis* “ditch.”

The forms ending in *r* are: *pater* “father”; *puer* “boy”; *piper* “pepper”; *niger* “black”; *siler* “willow”; *socer* “father-in-law”; *gener* “son-in-law”; *aper* “boar”; *caper* “goat”; *tener* “tender”; *miser* “wretched”; *celer* “swift”; *iter* “journey”; *scaber* “rough”; *sacer* “sacred”; *ruber* “red”; *amor* “love”; *glomer* “ball”; *jubar* “radiance”; *cruor* “gore”; *honor* “honor”; *sator* “sower”; *soror* “sister”; *labor* “labor.” *Jecur* is “liver,” *ebur* “ivory,” *ager* “field,” *timor* “fear,” and the noun *liquor* “fluid,” distinguished above from *liquitur*, “it melts.” *Rosa* “rose”; *faba* “bean”; *aqua* “water”; *mora* “delay/mulberry”; *rota* “wheel”; *coma* “hair”; *via* “way”; *toga* “toga”; *gula* “throat”; *schola* “school.” *Plaga* means “region” in the pyrrhic example and “blow/wound” in the trochaic example.

The oblique pairs explicitly mean: *crux/crucis* “cross/of a cross”; *nux/nucis* “nut/of a nut”; *grex/gregis* “flock/of a flock”; *pes/pedis* “foot/of a foot”; *lar/laris* “household god/of a household god”; *sal/salis* “salt/of salt”; *mas/maris* “male/of a male”; *nix/nivis* “snow/of snow”; *nex/necis* “death/of death”; *pix/picis* “pitch/of pitch”; *prex/precis* “prayer/of a prayer”; *grus/gruis* “crane/of a crane”; *trabs/trabis* “beam/of a beam”; *bos/bovis* “ox/of an ox”; *dux/ducis* “leader/of a leader”; *trux/trucis* “savage/of a savage one.”

**Pyrrhic verbs (0202B–0202D).** *Voco* “I call”; *veto* “I forbid”; *levo* “I lift”; *seco* “I cut”; *neco* “I kill”; *puto* “I think/prune”; *cavo* “I hollow”; *lito* “I sacrifice/appease”; *voro* “I devour”; *nego* “I deny”; *amo* “I love”; *frico* “I rub”; *plico* “I fold.” The first-conjugation *dico, dicas, dicat* means “I dedicate, you dedicate, he dedicates,” whereas *dico, dicis, dicit* means “I say, you say, he says.” *Paro* “prepare”; *aro* “plow”; *crepo* “crackle”; *sono* “sound”; *tono* “thunder”; *novo* “renew”; *cibo* “feed”; *cubo* “lie down”; *ligo* “bind”; *mico* “flash”; *creo* “create”; *meo* “pass”; *beo* “bless”; *rigo* “water”; *labo* “fall/glide”; *loco* “place”; *rogo* “ask”; *jugo* “yoke”; *fugo* “put to flight”; the other *labo* “totter”; *lavo* “wash”; *roto* “turn”; *pio* “expiate”; *hio* “gape,” with frequentative *hieto, hietas, hietat* “gape repeatedly” and inchoative *hisco, hiscis, hiscit* “begin to gape”; *domo* “tame”; *nato* “swim”; *gravo* “burden”; *probo* “approve”; *gelo* “freeze,” whence *congelasco* “begin to freeze”; *volo* “fly” or “wish.”

The following first-person forms mean: *capo* “seize”; *cado* “fall”; *fremo* “roar”; *gemo* “groan”; *fero* “bear”; *gero* “carry”; *tero* “wear away”; *sero* “sow”; *sino* “allow”; *ago* “do/drive”; *meto* “reap”; *peto* “seek”; *tego* “cover”; *colo* “cultivate”; *bibo* “drink”; *rego* “rule”; *lego* “read/gather”; *traho* “drag”; *fio* “become”; *scio* “know,” whence *exscire* “find out”; *vomo* “vomit”; *pluo* “rain”; *spuo* “spit”; *monuo* [as printed] “warn”; *juvo* “help”; *queo* “be able”; *fluo* “flow”; *luo* “pay/atone”; *ruo* “rush/fall”; *strio* “creak”; *loquor* “speak”; *precor* “pray”; *sequor* “follow”; *queror* “complain”; *reor* “think”; *fruor* “enjoy”; *moror* “delay.” Repeated *meo, creo,* and *beo* retain the readings above. The defective forms *libet, placet, piget, pudet, juvat, decet, liquet,* and *licet* mean respectively “it pleases, is agreeable, irks, causes shame, helps, befits, is clear,” and “is permitted.”

**Spondaic nouns and plurals (0203B–0203D).** *Felix* “happy”; *pernix* “nimble”; *perdex* “partridge”; *index* “informer/index”; *illex* “enticer”; *cortex* “bark”; *remex* “rower”; *cornix* “crow”; *bombix* “silkworm/silk”; *cervix* “neck”; *audax* “bold”; *forfex* “shears”; *forceps* “tongs”; *anceps* “two-edged/doubtful”; *auceps* “bird-catcher”; *princeps* “chief”; *praeceps* “headlong”; *virtus* “virtue”; *tellus* “earth”; *aetas* “age”; *aestas* “summer”; *pumex* “pumice”; *judex* “judge”; *rumex* “sorrel”; *vertex* “crown/summit”; *caudex* “tree-trunk”; *codex* “book/block”; *mordax* “biting”; *fornax* “furnace”; *fallax* “deceitful”; *pollex* “thumb”; *murex* “purple-shell”; *ilex* “holm-oak”; *carex* “sedge.”

*Simplex* “single”; *duplex* “double”; *triplex* “triple”; *vervex* “wether”; *fornix* “arch”; *radix* “root”; *matrix* “womb/source”; *lodix* “blanket”; *victrix* “victorious woman”; *natrix* “water-snake”; *vivax* “long-lived”; *verax* “truthful”; *pellax* “enticing”; *edax* “voracious”; repeated *radix* “root”; *mendax* “lying”; *imbrex* “roof-tile”; *auspex* “augur”; *auceps* “bird-catcher”; *complex* “entwined”; repeated *duplex/triplex* “double/triple”; *elix* “boiled”; *velox* “swift”; *atrox* “savage”; *Pollux* “Pollux”; *conjux* “spouse.” The plural pairs are *flos/flores* “flower/flowers”; *mos/mores* “custom/customs”; *ros/rores* “dew/dews”; *pons/pontes* “bridge/bridges”; *fons/fontes* “spring/springs”; *rex/reges* “king/kings”; *lex/leges* “law/laws”; *lanx/lances* “dish/dishes”; *glans/glandes* “acorn/acorns”; *plus/plures* “more/more persons”; *mus/mures* “mouse/mice”; *cors/cortes* “enclosure/enclosures”; *cos/cotes* “whetstone/whetstones”; *sors/sortes* “lot/lots”; *dos/dotes* “dowry/dowries”; *ars/artes* “art/arts”; *pars/partes* “part/parts”; *calx/calces* “heel/heels”; *merx/merces* “merchandise/wares”; *sol/soles* “sun/day, suns/days”; *vox/voces* “voice/voices”; *nox/noctes* “night/nights”; *lis/lites* “lawsuit/lawsuits”; *dis/dites* “rich person/rich persons”; *glis/glires* “dormouse/dormice”; *puls/pultes* “porridge/portions of porridge.”

**Spondaic verbs, adverbs, and participles (0204A–0204C).** *Libo/libas/libant* “I pour—you pour—they pour”; *sedo/sedas/sedant* “settle”; *sudo/sudas/sudant* “sweat”; *caneo/canes/canent* “be gray”; *polleo/polles/pollent* “be powerful”; *frondeo/frondes/frondent* “put forth leaves.” The fourth-conjugation pairs are *hinnio/hinnis* “neigh”; *tinnio/tinnis* “ring”; *grunnio/grunnis* and *grundio/grundis* “grunt”; *trinnio/trinnis* “trill”; *grincio/grincis* “snarl.” The perfect-and-imperative sets are *jubeo/jussi/jube* “order/ordered/order!”; *fulgeo/fulsi/fulge* “shine/shone/shine!”; *rideo/risi/ride* “laugh/laughed/laugh!”; *mulgeo/mulsi/mulge* “milk/milked/milk!”; then *faveo/favi/fave* “favor/favored/favor!”; *moveo/movi/move* “move/moved/move!”; *maneo/mansi/mane* “remain/remained/remain!”; *paveo/pavi/pave* “fear/feared/fear!”; *sedeo/sedi/sede* “sit/sat/sit!”; *video/vidi/vide* “see/saw/see!”

The third-conjugation present/perfect pairs are *scribo/scripsi* “write/wrote”; *scalpo/scalpsi* “scratch/scratched”; *sculpo/sculpsi* “carve/carved”; *repo/repsi* “crawl/crawled”; *mergo/mersi* “immerse/immersed”; *serpo/serpsi* “creep/crept”; *cudo/cudi* “hammer/hammered”; *rumpo/rupi* “break/broke”; *cedo/cessi* “yield/yielded”; *sepio/sepsi* “hedge/hedged”; *plaudo/plausi* “applaud/applauded”; *farcio/farsi* “stuff/stuffed”; *haurio/hausi* “draw/drew”; *sarcio/sarsi* “mend/mended”; *flecto/flexi* “bend/bent”; *rego/rexi* “rule/ruled”; *veho/vexi* “carry/carried”; *figo/fixi* “fix/fixed”; *vivo/vixi* “live/lived”; *meio/minxi* “urinate/urinated”; *tingo/tinxi* “dye/dyed”; *cingo/cinxi* “gird/girded”; *sugo/suxi* “suck/sucked”; *uro/ussi* “burn/burned”; *trudo/trusi* “thrust/thrust”; *coquo/coxi* “cook/cooked”; *duco/duxi* “lead/led.” The adverbs *sancte, caste, docte, care, late, longe* mean “holily, chastely, learnedly, dearly, widely, far.” The present participles *dicens, ducens, vivens, turgens, trudens, sternens, stertens, scandens* mean “saying, leading, living, swelling, thrusting, spreading, snoring,” and “climbing.”

**Iambic nouns and case forms (0204D–0205C).** *Silex* “flint”; *senex* “old man”; *culix/culex* “gnat” [suggested *salix*, “willow”]; *calex* “pebble”; *apex* “summit”; *latex* “liquid”; *tenax* “tenacious”; *rapax* “rapacious”; *fugax* “fleeing”; *sagax* “keen”; *procax* “bold/shameless”; *minax* “threatening”; *edax* “voracious”; *emax* “eager to buy”; *varix* “varicose vein”; *trilex* “triple-threaded”; *triplex* “triple”; *salex* “willow.” *Ferox* “fierce”; *ferax* “fertile”; *sequax* “following”; *loquax* “talkative”; repeated *procax* “shameless”; *parens* “parent”; *frequens* “frequent/crowded”; *recens* “fresh”; *cliens* “client”; *fides* “faith”; *dies* “day”; *salus* “health/salvation.” *Palus/paludis* means “marsh/of a marsh” in the third declension, but second-declension *palus/pali* means “stake/of a stake.” The dative-and-plural sets mean: *crux/cruci/cruces* “cross/to a cross/crosses”; *fax/faci/faces* “torch/to a torch/torches”; *trux/truci/truces* “savage/to a savage/savage ones”; *nux/nuci/nuces* “nut/to a nut/nuts”; *dux/duci/duces* “leader/to a leader/leaders”; similarly *grues* “cranes” and *sues* “swine.”

**Iambic verbs and participles (0205B–0205D).** *Amas/ama* “you love/love!”; *putas/puta* “you think/think!”; *paras/para* “you prepare/prepare!”; *aras/ara* “you plow/plow!”; *secas/seca* “you cut/cut!”; *necas/neca* “you kill/kill!”; *vocas/voca* “you call/call!”; *locas/loca* “you place/place!” Then *doces/doce* “teach”; *moves/move* “move”; *viges/vige* “thrive”; *riges/rige* “be stiff”; *pates/pate* “lie open,” whence *patesce* “begin to open”; *tenes/tene* “hold”; *times/time* “fear”; *cares/care* “lack”; *caves/cave* “beware”; *studes/stude* “be eager”; *manes/mane* “remain”; *lates/late* “lie hidden.” *Lateo/lates/latet* means “I/you/he lies hidden”; *delitesco/delitescis/delitescit* “I/you/he goes into hiding”; its perfect is *delituit* “lay hidden,” not *delatuit*.

The passive/deponent infinitives *geri, teri, seri, tegi, legi, regi, trahi, vehi, mori* mean “to be carried, worn away, sown, covered, read/gathered, ruled, dragged, conveyed,” and “to die.” The participles *rigans, litans, secans, necans, negans, vorans, volans, curvans, lavans, ligans, micans* mean “watering, sacrificing, cutting, killing, denying, devouring, flying, bending, washing, binding,” and “flashing.” The active/neuter present pairs are *doceo/docens* “teach/teaching”; *careo/carens* “lack/lacking”; *rigeo/rigens* “be stiff/stiffening”; *faveo/favens* “favor/favoring”; *sileo/silens* “be silent/silent”; *caleo/calens* “be hot/hot”; *rubeo/rubens* “be red/red.”

**Trochaic nouns and pronouns (0206A–0206C).** *Almus* “nourishing”; *sanctus* “holy”; *nympha* “nymph”; *lympha* “water”; *abba* “abbot”; *offa* “morsel”; *occa* “harrow”; *sapa* “boiled-down must”; *ostrum* “purple”; *rostrum* “beak”; *rastrum* “rake”; *sceptrum* “scepter”; *scalprum* “chisel,” diminutive *scalpellum* “little knife”; *labrum* “lip/basin,” whence *labellum* “little lip”; *bulla* “bubble”; *bucca* “cheek”; *gibbus* “hump”; *cippus* “stake”; *burrus* “red”; *barrus* “elephant”; *floccus* “tuft”; *soccus* “slipper”; *muscus* “moss”; *luscus* “one-eyed”; *fuscus* “dark”; *tuscus* “Etruscan.”

The naturally long nouns are *musa* “Muse”; *meta* “turning-post”; *seta* “bristle”; *creta* “chalk”; *theta* “theta”; *feta* “pregnant”; *spina* “thorn”; *Roma* “Rome”; *ruma* “teat”; *rima* “crack”; *lima* “file”; *bruma* “midwinter”; *fama* “fame”; *mirus* “wonderful”; *dirus* “dreadful”; *funus* “funeral”; *munus* “gift/duty”; *fumus* “smoke”; *prunus* “plum tree”; *pirus* “pear tree”; *pinus* “pine”; *taxus* “yew”; *malus* “apple tree”; *flavus* “golden”; *canus* “white-haired”; *sanus* “healthy”; *fatus* “spoken/fated”; *nanus* “dwarf”; *crinis* “hair”; *finis* “end”; *funis* “rope”; *clunis* “buttock,” whence *clunaculum* “rump-covering”; *nudus* “naked”; *udus* “wet”; *ludus* “game/school”; *mutus* “mute”; *nutus* “nod”; *tutus* “safe”; *fotus* “warmed”; *lotus* “washed”; *totus* “whole”; *motus* “movement/moved”; *notus* “known”; *nodus* “knot”; *nisus* “effort”; *risus* “laughter”; *visus* “sight/seen”; *fretus* “relying”; *spretus* “scorned”; *cretus* “born”; *fulmen* “lightning”; *famen* “utterance”; *flamen* “priest of a shrine”; *numen* “divine power”; *lumen* “light”; *rumen* “cud”; *plemen* “fullness”; *limen* “threshold”; *crimen* “charge”; *vimen* “pliant twig”; *gramen* “grass”; *stamen* “warp/thread.” The pronouns *ille, iste, ipse, noster, vester, quisquam, quisnam, isdem* mean “that one, this one, self, ours, yours, anyone, who then?” and “the same.”

**Trochaic verbs (0206C–0206D).** The positionally long forms are *prendo* “seize”; *scando* “climb”; *necto* “bind”; *pecto* “comb”; *cerno* “discern”; *pingo* “paint”; *ningo* “snow”; *mingo* “urinate”; *fingo* “shape”; *pinso* “pound”; *hisco* “gape”; *quasso* “shake”; *lasso* “weary”; *laxo* “loosen”; *taxo* “assess”; anomalous *faxo* “I shall do”; *sperno* “scorn”; *texo* “weave”; *vexo* “harass”; *mando* “entrust/chew”; *pando* “spread”; *linquo* “leave”; *vinco* “conquer”; *subdo* “subject”; *abdo* “hide”; *condo* “found/store”; *pango* “fasten”; *cingo* “gird”; *tingo* “dye”; *pungo* “prick,” perfect *pupugi* “I pricked.”

The naturally long forms are *rado* “scrape”; *fumo* “smoke”; *dico* “say”; *duco* “lead”; *giro* “turn”; *promo* “bring forth”; *prodo* “betray/publish”; *cudo* “hammer”; *lego/legas* “bequeath/you bequeath,” distinguished from shortened *lego/legis* “I read/you read”; *subdo* “subject”; *sedo* “settle”; *udo* “moisten”; *cogo* “compel”; *dedo* “surrender”; *trudo* “thrust”; *credo* “believe”; *nolo* “be unwilling”; *malo* “prefer”; *pono* “place”; *laudo* “praise”; *laedo* “harm”; *oro* “pray”; *clamo* “shout”; *duro* “harden/endure”; *edo* “eat/publish”; *fido* “trust”; *libo* “pour/taste”; *privo* “deprive”; *vivo* “live”; *quaero/quaesivi* “seek/sought,” whereas pyrrhic *queror/quaestus sum* means “complain/having complained”; *ludo* “play”; *sumo* “take”; *suo* “sew”; *plaudo* “applaud”; *demo* “remove”; *dego* “spend/pass.” Finally, *promor* “am brought forth”; *prodor* “am betrayed/published”; *scrutor* “search”; *vador* “go/pledge”; *praedor* “plunder”; *laetor* “rejoice”; *bacchor* “revel”; *nascor* “be born”; *ructor* “belch”; *tutor* “protect”; *venor* “hunt”; *fungor* “perform”; and deponent *nitor* “strive/rely.”

And below:

He strives either to touch the thread of the averted Christ. But if *nitor* is a noun, it will be a pyrrhic, as the same poet says:

> Who was that radiance of Mary?

And Virgil, in the book entitled *The Pedagogue*:

> The title and the purple radiance will be restored.

But this verse must not be scanned like a heroic line, because the *colophon* is retained in the middle and at the end. The following also belong here: *labor, liquor, vescor, causor, tristor, testor, mercor, rimor, piscor, metor, grator, ringor, miror, frustror, grassor*.

Participles of the past tense likewise sometimes conform to the trochaic foot, such as *dictus, lectus, captus, raptus, scriptus, tensus, mersus, flexus, vexus,* and *nexus*. For I have not found present- or future-tense participles belonging to the trochee, unless I am mistaken.

**D. In what manner, and with what accents, are trochaic feet to be pronounced? Or by what pattern of division are their arsis and thesis separated, and on what temporal scales are they weighed?**

**M.** If a trochee is present, it is pronounced with an acute accent, as in *lappa, mappa, napta, cirrus, birrus, burrus, barrus, poples,* and *cespes*. But if the vowel is lengthened by nature, metrical law has ordained that it be pronounced with a circumflex accent. The arsis receives two morae and the thesis one, as in *fanum, frenum, granum, bubo, bufo, tufus, tubus, limes, stipes,* and *remes*.

## On the tribrach

**D.** Having set forth the rules of disyllabic feet, the exposition now demands that, in accordance with the promise of the prologue, you disclose the trisyllabic feet.

**M.** These are tribrachs, named in Greek from three short syllables. From the first declension come: *anima, aquila, pedica, palea, tonina, macula, famula, patera, hedera, ulula, galea, lacryma, Asia,* and *Libya*.

Likewise, from the second declension, both masculine and neuter nouns belonging to the tribrach are: *dominus, radius, catulus, capulus, querulus, licinus, puteus, pavidus, patulus, Zephyrus, socius, medius, medicus, numerus, rutilus, placidus, titulus, loculus, modulus, modicus, bibulus, gerulus, gemitus, fremitus, humerus, platanus, tumidus, thalamus, fluvius, uterus, oculus, cumulus, solidus, stolidus, stupidus, rigidus, calidus, validus, varius, monitus, sonitus, gelidus, trepidus, timidus, laqueus, tremulus, vetulus, olidus, cuneus, pelagus, geminus, cupidus, nitidus,* and *digitus*.

Likewise, neuters of the same declension and the same foot are *meritum, pretium, gremium, stabulum, studium, barathrum, proprium, lolium, jugulum, jaculum, spolium, bivium, trivium, spatium, corium, vitium,* and *speculum*. From the third declension likewise come *facilis, gracilis, viridis,* and *facinus, tenuis*.

Verbs similarly derived from the three conjugations conform to the tribrach. From the first are: *numero, rogito, maculo, propero, dubito, habito, vacuo, temero, ululo, socio, gemino, saturo, satio, tolero, tenuo, onero, brevio, resero, violo, revoco, timeo, cumulo, glomero, radio, rutilo, titulo, titubo, solido, vario, trepido, jugulo, spolio, vitio, numero, rogito, maculo, propero, memoro, vigilo, supero, educo*—which means “I nourish”—*remeo, stimulo, similo, simulo, lapido, crepito, volito, crucio, itero, glacio, macero, lacero, lanio, genero,* and *agito*.

From the second conjugation come *jubeo, doceo, soleo, studeo, stupeo, video, rigeo, tepeo, noceo, tabeo, rubeo, taceo, habeo, vigeo, egeo, caleo, doleo,* and *oleo*, as the poet says:

> [Col. 0208A] … and accustomed to live in foul-smelling mud.

Also: *careo, jaceo, caveo, maneo, tumeo, teneo, valeo, niteo, lateo, pateo, cieo, voveo, vireo, moneo, paveo, foveo,* and *moveo*.

From the third: *fodio, quatio, redimo, venio, facio, rapio, capio, fugio, cupio, metuo, tribuo, statuo, polio, jacio, ferio,* and *nequeo*.

Passive, common, and deponent verbs ending in *-r* in the first person likewise conform to the tribrach: *numeror, temeror, operor, imitor, veneror, dominor, modulor, famulor, jaculor, stabulor, comitor, stipulor, medicor,* and *medeor*, which poets show to belong both to the first and second conjugations. Sedulius says:

> Nor is your salvation small, Mary, when the Lord is healing you.

Prosper likewise:

> And let the care of the healer descend into the decaying fibers.

Also: *populor, jaculor, epulor, comitor, spatior, speculor, moderor, medicor, mereor, fateor, vereor, tueor, gradior, patior, potior,* and *morior*.

I do not recall that a tribrach has ever been derived from pronouns or participles of any tense, although I remember it being frequently inserted in other parts of speech in poems, as in *igitur, quoniam, etenim,* and similar words.

**D.** With what accent are the examples of the forms mentioned above pronounced?

**M.** Almost all are stressed with an acute accent; and since the antepenultimate syllable bears the accent, I think that two morae in the tribrach belong to the arsis and one to the thesis.

## On the molossus

**D.** Give an account of the nouns and verbs belonging to the molossian foot.

**M.** I shall first arrange the nouns briefly and summarily, collecting both singular and plural forms: *majestas, libertas, tempestas, paupertas, ubertas, sermones, mangones, lenones, praedones, musmones, caupones, perones, sutores, praecones, lurcones, doctores, lectores, tortores, crabrones,* and *rumores*. Prosper says:

> Let ears not easily lie open to savage rumors.

Also: *Romani, humani, divini, formosi, frontosi, setosi, muscosi, dumosi, obscoeni, cancelli, rostrati, nervosi, herbosi, hirsuti,* and *rugosi*.

The molossus also arises from verbs in the perfect past tense, such as *dixisti, vexisti, prompsisti, sepsisti, repsisti, scalpsisti, sculpsisti, serpsisti,* and so forth.

The molossus is likewise recognized as arising from both present- and future-tense participles, such as *dicentes dicturi, viventes victuri, mergentes mersuri, scindentes scissuri, prandentes pransuri,* and *pingentes picturi, tondentes tonsuri*.

This foot therefore divides according to a twofold rule of division, is pronounced with an acute accent, and, since the penultimate syllable is stressed, I think it has four morae in the arsis and two in the thesis.

## On the anapest

**D.** What examples are assigned and subject to anapestic rules?

**M.** These are nouns supporting and conforming by consistent rule to the anapest: *deitas, pietas, bonitas, novitas, brevitas, levitas, gravitas, probitas, feritas, species, sanies, macies, glacies, rabies, scabies, series, facies,* and *acies*, along with the rest of the same kind.

But these few examples conforming to the anapest will suffice, because an anapest is legitimately generated from the nouns listed above, which we collected under the tribrach: in the singular genitive, dative, and ablative, and in the plural nominative, accusative, vocative, and ablative, if they are masculine or feminine nouns of the first and second declensions, as *anima, aquila, pedica,* and *hedera*, and likewise *dominus, radius,* and *catulus*. Neuter nouns, in the singular, conform to the anapest in the same cases, but in the plural they differ except in the dative and ablative.

The fourth declension, however, differs in its cases, as in *sonitus, fremitus, gemitus, rugitus, reditus,* and *ruditus*.

Verbs of both the first and third conjugations that we presented under the tribrach, when converted into participial meanings, will properly obey the laws of the anapest through resolution of the final syllable into *-ans* or *-ens*, as *numerans, rogitans, maculans, properans,* and *dubitans*. From the third conjugation come *veniens*, as in:

> Virtue, coming in a beautiful body;

and *faciens, rapiens, capiens, fugiens,* and *metuens*, as in the *Georgics*:

> Fearing this, observe the months of heaven and the stars.

But I judge that the verbs of the second conjugation that we mentioned under the tribrach, when attached to participial meanings, belong not to the anapest but to the iamb, since, having lost the form of trisyllabic feet, they are reduced to the rule of disyllabic feet, as *jubeo jubens, doceo docens, caleo calens, madeo madens,* and *oleo olens*.

**D.** By what pattern of division is the anapest divided, and with what accent is it pronounced?

**M.** The anapest has an equal division, because the arsis claims as many morae as are contained in the thesis. It is pronounced with an acute accent on the antepenultimate syllable, while the penultimate is naturally short.

## On the dactyl

**D.** From where did the dactyl derive its name according to the meaning of the word?

**M.** Greek interpretation has called the dactyl a finger, which is formed from three joints; accordingly, the same foot consists of three syllables.

**D.** Give examples of the dactylic foot that regularly conform to it.

**M.** The nouns should first be given briefly: *fibula, fabula,* and *alea*—hence *aliter*, “otherwise,” and *calculus*, “a small stone,” as well as dice-playing by means of *alea*. Also: *area, ardea, simia, vernula, garrula, tippula, tessera, fistula, castula, calculus, luridus, squalidus, horridus, frigidus, humidus, aridus, carbasus, Caucasus, Moenalus, frivolus, cernuus, culleus, caerulus,* and *annulus*, as in that epithalamic line:

> Let the ring be removed from the soft fingers, rough though it is.

Some of these are primary and original forms, such as *Allia, tessera,* and *Caucasus*. Others are epithets joined to nouns, such as *garrulus, squalidus,* and *luridus*.

Likewise, *populus*, when it refers to the tree, is a dactyl, as in:

> The poplar most pleasing to Alcides, the vine to Bacchus.

And in the fourth book of the *Georgics*:

> As the mourning nightingale beneath the poplar’s shade.

But if *populus* means “the people,” it will be a tribrach, as in:

> I shall speak of customs, pursuits, peoples, and battles.

Likewise the neuters are *vinculum, simpulum, serpulum, symbolum, cymbalum, tympanum, sarculum, nabulum, lilium, spiculum, crustulum, Tusculum, plusculum, clanculum, ferculum,* and *succinum*. Hence Junius Juvenal the satirist, in Book Three:

> For whom you send the green parasol, for whom the amber?

On this subject Pliny the Elder, explaining the natural history of things with keen intelligence in Book Thirty, says:

> “Among the rustic women of Transpadana, wearing amber in place of necklaces.”

And below:

> “Amber,” he says, “is stained; moreover, when it has received the warmth of heat through the rubbing of the fingers, it draws straws and dry leaves to itself, as a magnet draws iron,”

and so forth.

A dactyl also commonly arises from nouns of a compound formation, when they are compounded from the meanings of *gero* and *fero*: *setiger, squamiger, turriger, naviger, flammiger, belliger, floriger, fumifer, somnifer, pinnifer, aliger, ferriger, furcifer, fatifer, corniger, crinifer, armiger, pomifer, astrifer, ostrifer, umbrifer, grandifer, buxifer, spumifer, lotifer,* and *lanifer*, as in:

> Wool-bearing sheep and the warlike offspring of horses.

**D.** Can the fourfold distinctions of the conjugations regularly conform to the dactylic foot?

**M.** Every fourfold class of conjugations can properly be assigned to the dactyl, as *verbero, strangulo, postulo, castigo, mastico, bassio, pastino, milito, exsulo, pectino,* and *navigo*. As in:

> An enemy people sails the Tyrrhenian sea against me.

Also: *commeo, recreo, remigo, praeparo, advolo, compulo, dedico,* and *confrico*. Virgil says:

> And with his foot he drives the earth forward and rubs his flanks against a tree.

**D.** Give examples from the second conjugation that supply the dactyl.

**M.** *Mordeo, torqueo, haereo, debeo, misereo, arceo, splendeo, turgeo, luceo, algeo, palleo, urgeo, censeo, horreo, torpeo, polleo, torreo, squaleo, floreo,* and *caneo*. As in the *Georgics*:

> … and the willow groves, gray with foliage.

Also: *mulgeo, luceo, fulgeo, rideo, impleo, repleo, tondeo, spondeo, terreo,* and *arceo*.

**D.** Give the formulas from the third conjugation.

**M.** These are verbs belonging to the third conjugation: *desero, dissero, assero, insero, consero, degero, ingero, suggero, aggero, astruo, destruo, instruo, alluo, confluo, induo, exuo, imbuo, diruo, eruo, obruo, contero, protero, impeto, competo, ingemo, perstrepo, excolo, describo, dirigo, conveho, adveho, contraho,* and *retraho*.

**D.** Give those of the fourth.

**M.** *Fulcio, farcio, sarcio, audio, punio, mugio, sopio, sancio, prurio, garrio, finio, servio, munio, exeo, hinnio, mollio, sepio, accio, saevio, ambio, tinnio, bullio, gestio, nutrio, vestio, dormio, condio, haurio, vincio,* and *sentio*.

Likewise, verbs ending in *-r*: *criminor, demoror, suspicor, auspicor, cornicor, aemulor, arbitror, praelior, ordior, osculor, nundinor, glorior, gratulor, muneror, molior, machinor, praestolor, partior, sortior, largior, blandior,* and *mentior*.

Likewise the passive forms *sopior, sepior, fulcior, accior, ambior,* and the rest.

I have not been able to find participles conforming to the dactyl anywhere, except in the past tense: *deditus, editus, traditus,* and *inditus, additus*. For the past tense of the participle contains a threefold rule: ending in *-tus*, as *scriptus, sopitus, fultus, accitus,* and *septus*; or in *-sus*, as *occisus, visus, mersus, tersus, sparsus,* and *missus*; or in *-xus*, as *crucifixus, complexus,* and *adnexus*.

Future participles of any meaning, if their penultimate syllable is naturally long, are pronounced with a circumflex accent, as *scripturus* and *lecturus*. But if they are long by position, they receive an acute accent, as *audiendus* and *sarciendus*; and neither type will support the dactyl. For the arsis and thesis are separated according to equal rules of division, with two morae apiece.

## On the amphibrach

**D.** Why is it called an amphibrach?

**M.** Because it is surrounded on both sides by short syllables, just as an *amphitapete* is said to be a type of garment shaggy and hairy on both sides; and an *amphitheatrum* is a place where, on either side, the theatrical games and the comic inventions of actors are performed, while, under the presiding *agonotheta*, the displays of theatrical pancratiasts take place in the wrestling arena. Thus *ἀμφί* means “on both sides,” and *βραχύς* means “short.”

**D.** Give examples belonging to the amphibrach.

**M.** These are nouns of the first declension that support the same rule of the foot: *corona, carina, lacerna, acerva, acerra, arena, arista, papilla, mamilla, capella, catena, popina, culina, amurca, tabella, querela, locusta, marisca, rubeta, pharetra, camina, sagitta, loquela, medulla, medella, taberna, caverna, caterva, latebra,* and *tenebra*.

The masculine forms are likewise *camelus, caminus, caninus, egenus, opimus, alumnus, eburnus, cothurnus, togatus, anhelus, libellus, amicus, iniquus, propinquus, profanus, ocellus, avitus, subulcus, bubulcus, cinaedus, Quirinus, tumultus, tyrannus, severus, honestus, triumphus, cachinnus, capillus, lapillus, Latinus, amarus, amoenus, agellus, asellus, magister, minister, equester, pedester, sequester,* and *sinister*.

Likewise the neuters are *macellum, metallum, cylindrum, aratrum, sacellum, tropaeum, talentum, fritillum, lupercal, tribunal, quadrantal,* and *minutal*. Hence Juvenal, in Book Fourteen:

> To preserve yesterday’s *minutal* in the middle of the month;

and *canistrum*, “basket,” for September.

**D.** Please also gather examples of verbs arranged according to the qualities of the conjugations—which the Greeks call *syzygies*—so that you do not shrink from the task.

**M.** *Saluto, sagitto,* and *sagino*, as the poet says:

> I take no small quantity of fat.

And below:

> From high above, expect green fattening food.

Orosius, in historical prose, says:

> “They fed the misshapen monster on the lights of Greece,”

that is, the Cretan Minotaur.

Likewise: *honoro, coloro, laboro, adoro, requiro, anhelo, refuto, corusco, cachinno, inesco, inundo, redundo, capesso, lacesso, quiesco, cruento, secundo, propago, recuso, gelasco, recondo,* and *saburro*. Solinus says of cranes:

> “After lifting little stones, they ballast themselves to a moderate weight.”

Virgil says:

> Often they lift little stones,

> just as unstable boats, when the wave tosses them, lift ballast.

Also *fatigo*, as in:

> They weary the night and the day.

The same foot also arises from first-conjugation verbs that we previously collected under the pyrrhic, in these persons: *vocamus, vocatis, vocabam, vocabat; vetamus, vetatis, vetabam, vetabat; litamus, litatis, litabam,* and *litabat*.

Hence Persius Flaccus:

> I shall approach the temples and make offering with meal.

From the passive: *litamur, litantur, litabar,* and the future *litabor*. Prosper says:

> And with the gift of virtues he performs the sacred rite.

Virgil says:

> With blood the return must be sought, and sacrifice must be made with life.

The second conjugation likewise joins the amphibrach through the same paths of forms, from the series of words that we previously amassed under the tribrach: *docemus, docebis, docebam,* and *docebat*. From the passive: *docemur, docentur, docebar,* and the future *docebor*. Thus *foveo, voveo, jubeo, moveo,* and *moneo* are declined.

Inchoative verbs of the third conjugation, likewise sprouting from roots of the second conjugation, properly generate an amphibrach: *rigeo, rigesco; tepeo, tepesco; stupeo, stupesco; tabeo, tabesco; madeo, madesco; rubeo, rubesco; caleo, calesco; tumeo, tumesco; niteo, nitesco; aceo, acesco; vireo,* and *viresco*.

**D.** Can the amphibrach, arising from participial meanings, be subjected to these rules?

**M.** I do not think that the past and future tenses of the participle resist this rule: *amatus amandus, litatus litandus, necatus necandus,* and *cavatus cavandus*. Likewise *docendus, movendus,* and *fovendus*; and likewise *tegendus, terendus, gerundus,* and *serendus*.

**D.** With what accent is the amphibrach pronounced?

**M.** If the penultimate syllable is long by position, it receives an acute accent, as *marisca, noverca, madasca,* and *ladasca*. But if the penultimate is lengthened naturally, it is pronounced with a circumflex accent, as *carina, catena, camera,* and *rubeta*.

**D.** By what pattern of division does it operate?

**M.** It does not observe the same rule of division as the feet mentioned above; rather, a threefold increase of the condition contends against a single temporal loss, since the arsis contains one mora and the thesis three.

## On the amphimacer

**D.** Give a clear example and evident indication appropriate to the amphimacer.

**M.** *Almitas, trinitas, unitas, charitas, castitas, veritas, orbitas, sanctitas, dignitas, claritas, qualitas, quantitas, densitas, lenitas, caecitas, siccitas, civitas, vilitas, largitas, vastitas, suavitas,* and *torvitas*.

Solinus, in the *Collection of Remarkable Things*, says of the panther:

> “It is terrified by nothing except the grimness of its face.”

Also: *aequitas, falsitas, sanitas, firmitas, vanitas, paucitas,* and *raritas*.

The same forms are found in the plural: *margines, cardines, furfures, fomites, cespides, cuspides, termites, stipites, poplites, remites, murices, sandices,* and similar words.

Likewise, in the singular: *pontifex, artifex, carnifex, aurifex,* and *exstipex*, which is also *aruspex*. *Opifex*, however, belongs to the anapest.

I was unable to find examples of the amphimacer among verbs in the first person, unless perhaps the final syllable is found lengthened in the authoritative examples of illustrious poets. Virgil says:

> Horrible and, in the telling, I see a pitiful monster.

And elsewhere:

> I entrust the Trojan household gods

> to my companions.

But this rests on authority rather than on reason. For in the other inflections of persons the amphimacer is frequently inserted, as *conglobas conglobant, ambulas ambulant, cursitas cursitant, somnias somniant,* and *basias basiant*. Ovid says:

> You gave sweet, tender kisses to one who was resting.

Also *expias expiant*.

It also arises from the third conjugation, lengthened in the third-person plural, as *farciunt, sarciunt, tinniunt, hinniunt, sopiunt, sepiunt, sanciunt, bulliunt,* and *acciunt*.

From present-tense participles it is likewise generated: *territans, basians, amplians, expians, imbuens, induens, exuens, ambiens, garriens,* and *pruriens*.

**D.** From where did the amphimacer derive its name?

**M.** Because a short syllable is enclosed by long syllables on both sides; for *μακρά* means “long,” and *macrologia* means a long statement.

**D.** By what type of division is this same foot separated?

**M.** We divide the amphimacer by a sesquialteral division, because the arsis and thesis are separated by intervals of two and three morae.

## On the bacchius

**D.** Give examples belonging to the pedestrian rule of the bacchius.

**M.** *Voluntas, voluptas, facultas, potestas, honestas, juventus,* and *senectus*—and nearly all the nouns of the first or second declension that we previously piled up in a crowd under the amphibrach—will, when their cases are otherwise inflected, form a bacchius, except in the singular nominative, accusative, and vocative, and in the plural genitive.
