Thus: *popinae, culinae, rubetae; popinas, culinas, rubetas; popinis, culinis,* and *rubetis*.

Likewise the masculine forms: *cothurni, triumphi, tyranni,* and the rest.

The following likewise conform to the bacchius: *Kalendae, cathedrae, cicutae, cicadae, tiarae, tabellae, polentae, patellae, olivae, lagenae, fenestrae, saginae, Sibyllae, supinae, columbae, palumbae, columnae, podagrae, Minervae, modestae, molestae,* and *farinae*.

Likewise the masculine forms *benigni, maligni,* and *saligni*. Virgil says:

> Willow wickerwork

> for the bosses.

Also: *papyri, phaselli, lacerti, cruenti, suelli, miselli, tribuni, gulosi, pusilli, pupilli, lupini, mariti, silari, juvenci, caballi,* and *coculli*.

Likewise the neuters: *theatri, sepulcri, flagelli, labelli, tigilli, fritilli, sacelli,* and *macelli*. These correspond to the preceding forms in the singular genitive, but differ in the plural nominative, accusative, and vocative, because in those cases they are known to return again to the amphibrach.

**D.** From where was the bacchius named?

**M.** From Bacchus, who was also called Dionysus and Liber Pater. Hence antiquity, lacking true religion, decreed that the rites offered to Liber by the Bacchants should be called *Liberalia, Bacchanalia,* and also *Orgia*. Virgil says:

> Like a Thyiad aroused by the stirred sacred rites,

> when, upon hearing Bacchus, the triennial rites spur her on.

> Orgia.

The same poet, in Book Six:

> She, pretending to lead the chorus, the rites of Evanthes.

These are called *Nychthelia* in Greek, that is, “nocturnal rites.” Hence Virgil says:

> And nocturnal Cithaeron calls out with a shout.

A *nycticorax* is called a nocturnal raven. This foot, therefore, has a sesquialteral division.

## On the palimbacchius

**D.** For what reason is it called the antibacchius or palimbacchius?

**M.** The antibacchius is contrary to the bacchius, just as *antitheta* are opposed things and Antichrist is contrary to Christ. The palimbacchius, however, is recognized as being called “bacchius again” because, in reciprocal reversal, a syllable is changed.

**D.** Give examples derived from nouns and conforming to the palimbacchius.

**M.** *Natura, fortuna, pressura, tonsura, bascauda,* and *Aurora*, as in:

> Yellow Aurora shone in her rose-colored chariot.

Also: *captura, fetura, matura, rasura, strictura, basterna, persona, fixura, pictura, factura, scriptura, censura, caesura, farrago, Carthago, sartago, aerugo, salsugo, ferrugo, lanugo, prurigo, uligo, caligo, formido, fiscella, tessella, umbella, lanterna, regina, Europa, urina, formica, testudo, aulaeum, portentum, sarmentum, electrum, antiquus, argutus,* and *cristatus*—although the latter is a participle without a verbal origin—as in:

> Crested Achilles,

that is, “equipped with a crest and the cone of a helmet”; also *vittatus, versutus, cornutus, nervosus, frontosus, squamosus, exosus, barbatus, larvatus,* and *cerritus*.

Hence Jerome says:

> “Despising images and the shadows of ghosts, whose nature, it is said, is to frighten little children and chatter in dark corners.”

Likewise *pauxillus, tantillus, taxillus,* and *cultellus*, whose primitives are *Paulus, palus, talus, tantus,* and *culter*.

**D.** Give the rules for verbs that likewise support the laws of the palimbacchius.

**M.** *Conclamo, desquamo, reclamo, jejuno, insulto, exsulto, obsecro, adjuro, conrado, conjuro,* and *perjuro*, as in:

> And the winds, sworn together, come to the trumpet-call.

Also: *commendo, desudo, defendo, extendo, impingo, depromo, exantlo*—that is, “I drain out”; for the water-wheel used for draining a well is called an *antlia*—*consterno, emungo, invergo, desterno, convecto, compello, detrudo, compungo, contundo, impendo, ulciscor, percontor, contemplor, irascor, perfungor, amplector, nanciscor, indignor, infirmor,* and *commentor*.

Likewise the inchoatives *squalesco, algesco, haeresco, frondesco, fulgesco, ignesco, turgesco, raresco, torresco, torpesco, canesco, floresco,* and *lentesco*. Valerius attests that *lentesco* arose from the first conjugation, from *lento, lentas, lentat*; this occurs rarely, as in *amasco, lavasco,* and *gelasco*.

We have drawn these examples piecemeal from the first and third conjugations, since in the first-person indicative of the second conjugation an antibacchius is not easily found, although it is admitted in the other inflections of moods and tenses.

From fourth-conjugation verbs that we previously connected with the dactyl, a palimbacchius appears in the infinitive: *sopire, sancire, accire, bullire, hinnire, farcire, sarcire, haurire, gestire, sepire, ambire,* and the rest.

Future participles likewise do not refuse the service of the aforesaid foot: *recturus, mersurus, sumpturus, missurus, lecturus, acturus,* and *visurus*. Likewise in the passive sense: *mergendus, sumendus,* and *mittendus*. But *regendus, legendus, agendus,* and *vivendus* are assigned to the amphibrach.

Some past participles supply the palimbacchius: *compactus, infectus, mactatus, gestatus, detrusus, retortus, perpessus, depressus, adnexus, complexus, defixus, contritus,* and *consultus*.

But *attritus* and *consultus* are both nouns and participles. When they function according to the rule of participles, Virgil makes this clear, saying:

> And the plowshare, worn down by the furrow, begins to shine.

And again the same poet:

> The unconsulted Sibyls depart and hate their dwelling.

It is a noun when it is said:

> “It was decreed by the resolution of the entire senate.”

And Pliny the natural philosopher says:

> “Moreover, when it has received the warmth of heat through the rubbing of the fingers,”

and so forth.

**D.** With what accent is the palimbacchius pronounced?

**M.** If the penultimate syllable is lengthened by position, it has an acute accent, as *devexus* and *congestus*. But if it is lengthened by the decree of nature, it is marked with a circumflex prosody, as *indutus, exutus, imbutus, obrutus, explosus, complosus,* and *corrosus*.

## On the proceleusmatic

**D.** Having clarified the rules of trisyllabic feet, I think it worthwhile to arrange carefully the tetrasyllabic feet, as the order of the preface promised.

**M.** I think that the examples of the following feet should be disclosed rapidly and piecemeal, since the tetrasyllabic feet mentioned above are composed through reversed and reciprocal variations from the disyllabic feet whose examples we have arranged with a modest degree of explanation.

In short, these are nouns belonging to the proceleusmatic, which, as a doubled alternation of the pyrrhic, uniquely contains a twofold function of revolution and a sequence of recapitulation: *crocotula, animula, miseria, memoria, Italia*—although it is lengthened by ectasis—*apicula, canicula, avicula, fidicula, cuticula, crucicula, benevola, malevola, lapideus, equuleus, aculeus, itinera, facinora,* and *pelagicus*.

Also *puerulus* and *manipulus*. The latter noun does not fit intact into a dactylic hexameter, and therefore poets very often remove the vowel *u* by syncope. Sedulius says:

> Carrying sheaves as our Christ comes.

Virgil says:

> They remembered to toss the sheaves

> with unrestrained mouth, the filthy swine.

Also: *geniculum, latibulum,* and *patibulum*.

The proceleusmatic also sometimes arises from the third declension through the oblique cases, the dative and ablative: *nemoribus, operibus, oneribus, lateribus, comitibus, segetibus, cineribus, sceleribus, pecoribus, leporibus, generibus, gracilibus, facilibus, agilibus, teretibus, veteribus,* and *proceribus*.

Verbs of various classes are likewise known to comply with the rules of the proceleusmatic by harmonious agreement: *misereor, opitulor, arieto, humilio, aperio, operio, reperio,* and *sepelio*. Hence Prosper, in an elegiac line, produced a not-unsuitable rule of syllables, saying:

> And a new one is made in life.

The perfect past subjunctive also supports the proceleusmatic, but only from the second or third conjugation: *docuerim, timuerim, viguerim, habuerim,* and *stupuerim*. As in:

> Thus the dry marble was astonished by foreign feet.

*Nas stupu* is scanned as a dactyl. Also *patuerim, latuerim,* and *statuerim*, as in:

> For the father of things established it;

and *rapuerim, tribuerim, metuerim,* and *nequiverim*. For in the penultimate syllable of the perfect past subjunctive the *e* is always shortened, as the authority of Priscian confirms.

**D.** Give the character of its division and partition.

**M.** The proceleusmatic is divided by an equal pattern of separation. Therefore the arsis and thesis are weighed equally, with an equal balance of syllables and an equal measure of morae—that is, two and two.

**D.** In what manner is the proceleusmatic pronounced?

**M.** It is always stressed with an unbroken and unwavering firmness of accent.

## On the dispondaeus

**D.** What nouns properly conform to the dispondaeus?

**M.** *Servatores, praeceptores, bellatores, oratores, pastorales, aeternales, immortales, infelices, scrutatores, dictatores, mercatores, piscatores, regnatores, curatores, luctatores, rimatores, auditores, nutritores, venatores,* and *vespellones*—that is, grave-diggers who bury corpses. Hence Orosius says:

> “It was dragged into the Tiber by grave-diggers.”

Verbs of both past and future tense likewise support these rules: *mulcaverunt, sulcaverunt, stipaverunt, sudaverunt, illexerunt,* and *perrexerunt*. Likewise future forms: *conquassabunt, humectabunt, exantlabunt, resultabunt,* and the rest.

There are likewise feminine verbal nouns ending in *-trix*, just as masculine nouns end in *-tor*. But the feminine forms belong to the dispondaeus, while the masculine forms do not refuse to bear the yoke of the fourth epitrite through shortening of the final syllable: *indagator indagatrix, collaudator collaudatrix, declamator declamatrix, suffragator suffragatrix, exaltator exaltatrix, commendator commendatrix,* and *commentator commentatrix*. The latter derives from *commentor, commentaris, commentatur*, and hence also *commentum* and *commentarium*.

Also *inflammatrix, insultatrix, dispensatrix,* and *assentatrix*. Hence Prosper, speaking of the crime of flattery, added:

> The flattering tongue piles up the sinner’s fault.

The rule of this foot also arises from participial meanings: *contorquentes, impingentes, suffragantes, allegantes, retrudentes, jejunantes, exsudantes, emungentes,* and *fecundantes*. Likewise future forms: *truncaturi, sulcaturi, surrecturi, porrecturi, submersuri, possessuri,* and *concessuri*.

**D.** Give the rule of the accent.

**M.** The dispondaeus is always pronounced with an acute accent, while the arsis and thesis are separated by an equal distribution of morae—that is, four and four.

## On the diiambus

**D.** What examples of nouns belong to the diiambus?

**M.** I shall not be too weary to produce these examples promptly: *paternitas, enormitas, iniquitas, propinquitas, fidelitas, profunditas, severitas, ferocitas, atrocitas, acerbitas, Latinitas, procacitas, benignitas, cupiditas,* and *inanitas*.

These nouns of the third declension are known to be pentaptote in the singular according to the rule of their case-forms, and triptote in the plural. Likewise: *imagines, origines, hirundines, harundines, propagines,* and *voragines*.

Verbs are similarly subject to these rules in the pluperfect tense: *amaverant, ligaverant, necaverant, putaverant, litaverant, rigaverant, negaverant,* and so forth.

**D.** What prosodic pattern of pronunciation is established for the diiambus?

**M.** Nouns and verbs assigned to the diiambus are indeed accented like the dispondaeus, but they differ in this respect: the dispondaeus has its acute accent on the penultimate syllable, whereas the diiambus has it on the antepenultimate, and the remaining syllables will be unaccented.

## On the ditrochee

**D.** Give formulas of examples by which the rule of the ditrochee may be suitably clarified.

**M.** *Cartilago, cantilena, celsitudo, altitudo, gippitudo, lippitudo, longitudo, latitudo, fortitudo, magnitudo, crassitudo, spissitudo, aegritudo, pulchritudo, turpitudo,* and *fortitudo, rectitudo*. All these are pentaptotes. *Cantilena* is excepted, since it is a triptote noun.

Likewise from the second declension: *publicanus, Tusculanus, passerinus, anserinus, oppidanus, rusticanus, Claudianus, Adrianus, masculinus, feminïnus, Gaditanus, Gallicanus, Formicinus,* and *Maximinus*.

Also *bombycinus*, an epithet derived from *bombyces*, that is, worms commonly called *seri*; from them a light silk garment is woven from the strands of its threads.

Also: *ludibundus, iracundus, fraudulentus, pompulentus, corpulentus, vinolentus, merulentus, principatus,* and *paludatus*, that is, “clothed in a *paludamentum*,” just as *togatus* means “dressed in a toga.”

The ditrochee is also found in the moods and personal inflections of verbs: *castigamus, lectitamus, irrogamus, subrogamus, clamitamus, fascinamus, pastinamus,* and *ruminamus*, as in:

> Beneath the dark ilex it chews pale grasses.

Also *expiamus, sauciamus, confricamus, strangulamus, sciscitamur, machinamur,* and *praestolamur*.

Likewise in the infinitive: *fascinare, pastinare,* and *remigrare*.

Passive and deponent forms of the same type are excepted: *sciscitari, machinari,* and *strangulari*, which are known to pass into the rule of the second epitrite.

Sometimes the standard of the trochaic rule arises from participial meanings: *verberandus, masticandus, calculandus, calcitrandus, dedicandus, ventilandus,* and *vellicandus*. From the third or fourth conjugation likewise: *imbuendus, obruendus, exprimendus, sopiendus, sarciendus, sepiendus, sanciendus,* and *fulciendus*.

**D.** Give the rule of division.

**M.** The ditrochee is weighed by an equal balance, while the arsis and thesis are made equal by measures of three morae each.

**D.** With what accent is the ditrochee formed?

**M.** If the penultimate syllable is lengthened by position, it is marked with an acute accent, as *aggregandus, digerendus,* and *basiandus*. But if the penultimate is naturally long, it is unambiguously marked with a circumflex, as *passerinus, vulturinus, anserinus,* and the other derivatives that we collected above from their primitives.

## On the antespast

[Col. 0218A]

D. Let examples of an antepastus be brought forth, please.  
M. Arenosus, “sandy”; lacertosus, “muscular”; querelosus, “complaining”; lapillosus, “full of pebbles”; latebrosus, “full of hiding places”; cavernosus, “cavernous”; tenebrosus, “dark”; coronatus, “crowned”; capillatus or capillosus, “haired”; likewise venenosus, “poisonous”; papillatus, “having nipples”; paludatus, that is, “clothed in a paludamentum”; catenatus, “chained”; pharetratus, “equipped with a quiver”; palumbinus, “of a wood-pigeon”; columbinus, “of a dove.”

D. To what inflectional form will these nouns or participles be adapted?  
M. The authority of the ancients declares that all are *pentaptota* (“five-case forms”).

D. Give examples agreeing with the antepastus from the persons of verbs.  
M. Amabam, amabatis; amaremus, amaretis; litabamus, litabatis; litarem, litaretis; necabamus, necabatis; necaremus, necaretis; likewise negabamus, negabatis; favebamus, favebatis; emebamus, emebatis; [Col. 0218B] serebamus, serebatis; agebamus, agebatis. Thus, too, in the other tenses and moods and in the inflections of the persons, the formula of this same foot is frequently inserted; I am reluctant to unfold and explain it individually and universally. For the antepastus is sought out differently in the inflections of participles: in the present tense, from the inchoative form through the singular genitive, as nitescens, nitescentis; rubescens, rubescentis; virescens, virescentis; madescens, madescentis; rigescens, rigescentis. Likewise, in the past and future tense, through the plural genitive: amati, amatorum; necati, necatorum; litati, litatorum; amandi, amandorum; necandi, necandorum; litandi, litandorum; likewise docendorum, legendorum, regendorum, gerendorum.

D. With what accent is the antepastus pronounced?  
M. It is sometimes given an acute accent, as in tepescentis, tabescentis, acescentis. At other times it is circumflexed, as in paludatus, palumbinus, columbinus. The position or nature of the accent makes perfectly clear whether such words are to be pronounced with an acute or a circumflex. Here it is divided according to the form of equal division, since arsis and thesis correspond under equal temporal laws, that is, in groups of three and three.

## On the choriamb

D. From where did the choriambus receive its name?  
M. Because it consists of a choraeus and an iambus, doubled into a twofold structure of feet; for the choraeus is also called a trochee.

D. Please do not refuse to gather examples corresponding to the choriambus.  
M. Omnipotens, “almighty”; ignipotens, “fire-powerful”; pinnipotens, “wing-powerful”; armipotens, “weapon-powerful”; arcitenens, “bow-bearing”; caesaries, “hair”; canities, “whiteness of hair”; progenies, “offspring”; esuries, “hunger”; planities, “plain”; luxuries, “luxury,” as in the *Georgics*:

> Luxuriem segetum tenera depascit in herba.  
> “It grazes on the luxuriance of the crops in tender grass.”

Temperies, “temperateness”; segnities, “sluggishness”; calvities, “baldness”; ingluvies, “gluttony”; illuvies, “filth”; sinceritas, “sincerity”; posteritas, “posterity,” as in the following:

> Et sit priscorum nescia posteritas.  
> “And may there be a posterity ignorant of the ancients.”

Crudelitas, “cruelty”; sedulitas, “assiduity”; ebrietas, “drunkenness”; sobrietas, “sobriety”; simplicitas, “simplicity”; duplicitas, “duplicity”; impietas, “impiety”; nobilitas, “nobility”; utilitas, “usefulness”; calliditas, “cleverness”; asperitas, “harshness”; virginitas, “virginity.” As Prosper says in the *Epigrams*:

> Nec crucis asperitas potuit terrere volentem.  
> “Nor could the harshness of the cross terrify one who was willing.”

Those among these that belong to the third declension are most certainly pentaptota; those belonging to the fifth declension, however, are reduced to the tetraptote formula. Likewise, feminine nouns lacking a singular number and belonging to the choriambus are exuviae, “spoils”; deliciae, “delights”; divitiae, “riches”; inferiae, “funeral offerings”; blanditiae, “blandishments”; primitiae, “first fruits”; insidiae, “ambush”; exsequiae, “funeral rites”; reliquiae, “remains”; excubiae, “watch.” These are *tetraptota* (“four-case forms”).

We shall also attempt, compelled by the necessity of explaining the matter, to place beneath the rules of the first paeon certain nouns of the first and second declensions; through the other cases of both numbers they will properly belong to the choriambus, except in the singular nominative, accusative, and vocative, and in the plural genitive, if they are masculine or feminine. Neuters, however, differ in certain cases. Examples are justitia, “justice”; laetitia, “joy”; spurcitia, “filthiness”; moestitia, “sadness”; tristitia, “sorrow”; munditia, “cleanliness”; likewise purpureus, “purple”; caeruleus, “blue”; discipulus, “disciple”; egregius, “excellent”; legitimus, “legitimate”; likewise auxilium, “aid”; augurium, “augury”; dissidium, “dissension”; concilium, “council.”

The choriambus also arises from the nouns mentioned above, which we previously brought forward when attempting to devise the dactylus—namely, that dactylus formed from *gero* or *fero* through the oblique cases, as we stated shortly before: setiger, setigeri, “bristle-bearing”; ros, roris, “dew”; squamiger, squamigeri, “scale-bearing”; likewise laniger, “wool-bearing”; corniger, “horn-bearing”; lucifer, “light-bearing”; umbrifer, “shade-bearing”; furcifer, “fork-bearing.”

D. By what forms of division do we divide this foot?  
M. By equal measures of time.

D. Give an example separated from the persons of verbs.  
M. The second person singular and the third person plural display it properly, as conglomeras, conglomerant; ingeminas, ingeminant; praetitulas, praetitulant; acceleras, accelerant; commemoras, commemorant. Likewise the present-tense participles conglomerans, ingeminans, praetitulans, and so forth.

## On the minor Ionic

[Col. 0219C]

D. What nouns or verbs belong to the minor Ionic?  
M. These few examples may suffice for the minor Ionic: rapientes, “seizing”; populares, “fellow citizens”; seniores, “elders”; furibundi, “raging”; rubicundi, “ruddy”; verecundi, “modest”; moribundi, “dying”; rudibundi, that is, “braying and bellowing”—for *ruditus* properly belongs to asses and donkeys, as the poet says:

> Linguaque rudenti edidit pecuale loquelas.  
> “And with its braying tongue it uttered beastly speech.”

Since an appropriate opportunity for discussing voice has presented itself—not only because of the structure of feet and the principles of meter, but also because of differences among voices and distinctions of sounds—I think it not absurd to distinguish carefully the voices of four-footed animals, birds, and reptiles, both with respect to the generality of the plural and the specificity of the singular. For the authority of philosophers and grammarians alike has made known that voice is fourfold in quality: articulate, inarticulate, literate, and illiterate. Some, however, attest that there are two kinds of voice, namely articulate and confused. Articulate voice belongs only to human beings, because it can be comprehended in writing through letters; confused voice is that which cannot be written.

D. Set forth examples of confused voice gathered from different kinds of things.  
M. These are the species of confused voice, as the authority of our predecessors has handed them down. Bees ambizant or bombizant, “hum”; eagles clangunt, “scream”; geese crinciunt or trinsiunt, “cackle”; birds minuriunt, vernant, or vernicant; hawks pipant or pipilant, “chirp”; ducks teretissant; rams trissitant or blaterant, “bleat”; asses oncant or rudiunt, “bray”; boars frendunt, “grunt”; weapons crepant, “rattle”; bronze tinnit, “rings”; a poured-out amphora bilibit; oxen mugiunt or reboant, “low”; crows butant; swans desistant; cicadas fretinniunt; storks gratulant, glottorant, or critalant; ravens crocitant or croccant; goats mucciunt; dogs baubantur, latrant, or ganniunt; puppies glattilant; deer rugiunt; lyres sonant; a hunting dog cusnitit; elephants barriunt or stridunt; horses hinniunt; wild animals mussitant; cranes gruddant, gruunt, or grugulant; hens cacillant; roosters cantant or cucurriunt; yellowhammers fringilliunt; jays griciunt; swallows trutissant or trissant; hyenas hirriunt; kids balant or belant.

Jupiter thunders—so the fables imagine; infants wail; lions roar; lynxes hircant; hares vagitant; wolves ululant; shores murmurant; kites lugiunt, vigilant, or luriunt; blackbirds zinzitant; weasels dindrant; mice mintriunt or muniunt; owls cucubiunt; swans drensitant; sheep balant; wild asses vagillant; wood-pigeons raucitant; sparrows titiant; parri tinnipant; peacocks paululant; partridges cacant; chicks and children pipant; panthers chauriunt; leopards feliunt; piglets grunniunt; pigs grundiunt; frogs coaxant; starlings parsitant; shrew-mice denticant; snakes sibilant; forests strepunt; thrushes soccitant or faccilant; tigresses raccant; trumpets clangiunt; bulls mugiunt; vultures pionpant; winds flant, tremunt, or sibilant; bears urgant or saeviunt; foxes ejulant; boars quiritant.

Human beings speak; country people shout for joy; and there are other similar examples. These kinds of voices do not belong to the Ionic, but have been introduced for the sake of distinction.

[Col. 0220C]

D. Give examples of verbs subject to the minor Ionic.  
M. They are taken from verbs of the first conjugation which we presented under the tribrach, in the future tense: numerabunt, “they will count”; rogitabunt, “they will ask”; glomerabunt, “they will gather”; sociabunt, “they will join”; temerabunt, “they will violate”; maculabunt, “they will stain”; dubitabunt, “they will doubt.” Likewise, in the present infinitive passive: numerari, “to be counted”; rogitari, “to be asked”; glomerari, “to be gathered”; sociari, “to be joined.” From the third conjugation they occur in the imperfect past: veniebant, “they were coming”; capiebant, “they were taking”; rapiebant, “they were seizing”; poliebant, “they were polishing”; metuebant, “they were fearing”; tribuebant, “they were granting.” Likewise from present participles: numerantes, glomerantes, titulantes, polientes, statuentes, jaculantes, modulantes, spatiantes, speculantes, and the rest.

D. What division does the minor Ionic serve?  
M. It belongs to the rule of double division.

D. Say, then, whether arsis or thesis will carry off the palm of victory in the distribution of times.  
M. Thesis unquestionably governs four temporal units, and arsis two.

D. How does this come about?  
M. Because the final syllable bears an acute accent and the antepenultimate a grave accent, as in populantes, maculantes, glomerantes, numerantes, venerantes, and almost all the verbs of the first conjugation that we gathered under the tribrach when they are converted into the meanings of participles; they are subjected to the laws of the minor Ionic.

## On the major Ionic

D. Give rules properly corresponding to the major Ionic.  
M. Clementia, “clemency”; sententia, “opinion”; concordia, “harmony”; discordia, “discord”; prudentia, “prudence”; vecordia, “folly”; vesania, “madness”; dementia, “insanity”; Germania, “Germany”; Saxonia, “Saxony”; contentio, “struggle”; conventio, “assembly”; possessio, “possession”; confessio, “confession”; insania, “madness”; infamia, “infamy”; [Col. 0221A] confectio, “completion”; defectio, “defection”; refectio, “refreshment”; protectio, “protection”; virguncula, “little maiden”; fornacula, “little furnace”; cunabula, “cradle”; paupercula, “little poor woman”; matertera, “aunt”; matercula, “little mother”; majuscula, “somewhat larger”; cervicula, “little hind”; vulpecula, “little fox”; veprecula, “little thornbush”; nubecula, “little cloud”; mercedula, “little wage”; ficedula, “fig-pecker.”

In five of these nouns the *e* is lengthened, as Priscian remarked in Book III. Of these, the nouns of the first declension are triptota in the singular and tetraptota in the plural. Those that we selected from the third declension for the rule of the major Ionic are pentaptota in the singular and triptota in the plural. Likewise, masculine or common nouns are triptota in both numbers, as mirabilis, “wonderful”; laudabilis, “praiseworthy”; affabilis, “approachable”; effabilis, “expressible.” Virgil writes:

> Nec visu facilis nec dictu effabilis.  
> “Neither easy to see nor expressible in speech.”

Spectabilis, “visible”; triplabilis, “capable of being tripled.” Sedulius writes:

> Quod simplex triplicet, quodque est triplabile simplex.  
> “What is simple, let it triple; what is capable of being tripled, let it be simple.”

Ramusculus, “little branch”; rumusculus, “little rumor,” a diminutive of *rumor*; fraterculus, “little brother”; laterculus, “little brick.” Paterculus, “little father,” is recognized as a second paeon. Also majusculus, complusculus, latrunculus, furunculus, carbunculus, lenunculus, authenticus, pauxillulus, tirunculus, ranunculus, arnotinus, hornotinus. Their primitive forms are *major*, “greater”; *plus*, “more”; *latro*, “robber”; *fur*, “thief”; *carbo*, “coal”; *leno*, “pimp”; *paulus*, “little”; *tiro*, “recruit”; *rana*, “frog”; *arnus*, “arbutus”; *horno*, “of this year.”

Diminutives of diminutives are also found, as paulus, paululus; pauxillus, pauxillulus; likewise agnus, agniculus, agnicellus, agnicellulus; and *mons*, “mountain,” and the rest. These are pentaptota in the singular and tetraptota in the plural.

Likewise neuters are fastidium, “disgust”; ludibrium, “mockery.” Virgil writes:

> rapidis ludibria ventis;  
> “to the swift winds, a plaything.”

Plumarium, “featherwork”; aerarium, “treasury”; proscenium, “stage.” Virgil writes:

> ineunt proscenia ludi;  
> “the plays enter upon the stage.”

Collarium, “neckband”; plantarium, “plantation”; palmarium, “of the palm,” that is, “of the praise of victory”; convivium, “banquet”; colludium, “joint play”; corpusculum, “little body”; turpisculum, “somewhat ugly”; spiraculum, “breathing place”; solatium, “consolation”; coenaculum, “upper room”; venabulum, “hunting spear”; spectaculum, “spectacle”; mastigium, “whip”; miraculum, “miracle”; connubium, “marriage.” These neuters are *triptota* (“three-case forms”) in both numbers.

D. Give rules for verbs that do not conflict with this foot.  
M. Elimino, “I eliminate”; ingurgito, “I gulp down”; procrastino, “I postpone”; eradico, “I eradicate”; insignio, “I mark”; lascivio, “I behave wantonly”; exhaurio, “I drain”; emollio, “I soften”; obstetrico, “I act as midwife,” as in Exodus:

> Ut quando obstetricabitis Hebraeas;  
> “When you act as midwives for the Hebrew women.”

Enuntio, “I declare”; annuntio, “I announce”; congaudeo, “I rejoice with”; enucleo, “I extract the kernel”; assentio, “I assent”; consentio, “I agree”; irretio, “I entangle”; praesagio, “I foresee”; insanio, “I rage”; custodio, “I guard”; discrimino, “I distinguish”; determino, “I determine”; fastidio, “I disdain”; contorqueo, “I twist”; resplendeo, “I shine brightly”; arrideo, “I smile upon.”

Likewise, the future tense of the indicative of this same kind admits two persons: gaudebimus, gaudebitis; [Col. 0221D] mulcabimus, -tis; sculcabimus, -tis; truncabimus, -tis; lentabimus, -tis. Virgil writes:

> Ante Trinacria lentandus remus in unda;  
> “Before Trinacria, the oar must be bent in the wave.”

Quassabimus, -tis, “we shall shake, you shall shake.” Likewise from the third conjugation with a shortened vowel, but in the present tense: compescimus, compescitis; infindimus, infinditis; annectimus, annectitis; rescindimus, rescinditis; depectimus, depectitis. As in the *Georgics*:

> Velleraque ut foliis depectant tenuia Seres.  
> “As the Seres comb the delicate fleeces from the leaves.”

Likewise in the infinitive: compescere, “to restrain”; infindere, “to cleave”; annectere, “to attach”; rescindere, “to cut off”; depectere, “to comb down”; excludere, “to exclude”; detrudere, “to thrust down”; corradere, “to scrape together”; corrodere, “to gnaw away”; illidere, “to dash against”; depromere, “to draw forth”; colludere, “to play together”; emergere, “to emerge”; lentescere, “to become sluggish”; canescere, “to grow white”; haerescere, “to cling,” as in the epithalamium:

> Mellea tunc roseis haerescunt labia labris.  
> “Then honeyed lips cling to rosy lips.”

D. How and in what manner do arsis and thesis divide the temporal units of the syllables in the major Ionic?  
M. Arsis contains eight half-units of time, and thesis four half-units; that is, arsis takes a doubled increase of time, while thesis governs a single measure, because the relation is four against two.

D. Give the rule of accents.  
M. In every part of speech the major Ionic is marked by an acute accent on the antepenultimate; therefore arsis, as we have said, will be crowned with the doubled trophy of triumph.

## On the first paeon

D. The epitrites and paeons remain, whose examples you have not yet made known in your discussion.  
M. As I gradually explain the formulas of the first paeon, I shall not delay at all; I shall strive to gather its examples briefly: ecclesia, “church”; justitia, “justice”; laetitia, “joy”; duritia, “hardness”; luxuria, “luxury”; spurcitia, “filthiness”; navicula, “little ship”; clavicula, “little key”; lenticula, “little lens”; particula, “particle”; [Col. 0222B] dulcicula, “little sweet thing”; assecula, “little follower”; coticula, “little whetstone”; graticula, “little grate”; Ausonia; Arcadia; harmonia, “harmony”; ambrosia, “ambrosia.”

I think fidicula, “little lyre,” belongs to the proceleusmaticus; its primitive is *fidis*, “string,” as in:

> fretus cithara fidibusque canoris;  
> “trusting in the lyre and ringing strings.”

Likewise cuticula, “little skin.” All these diminutives shorten both the penultimate and antepenultimate syllables, although cuticula lengthens the antepenultimate. Juvenal says in the *Satires*:

> Cum bibet aestivum contracta cuticula solem;  
> “When the contracted skin drinks in the summer sun.”

Metre compelled him to do this; for a word having four short syllables could not otherwise be placed in heroic verse. Virgil, however, is accustomed to use proceleusmatic feet in such nouns—that is, in those having four short syllables—as in:

> Labat ariete crebro;  
> “It wavers under repeated blows of the battering ram.”

And:

> Depectunt tenuia Seres;  
> “The Seres comb out the delicate [fleeces].”

And:

> Genua labant.  
> “The knees give way.”

Likewise masculine nouns belonging to the first paeon are ponticulus, “little bridge”; folliculus, “little pouch”; panniculus, “little cloth,” from *pannus*, “cloth”; panucula, “little cloth,” from *panus*, although the diminutive differs from its primitive; fonticulus, “little spring”; marticulus, “little hammer”; igniculus, “little flame”; testiculus, “little testicle”; funiculus, “little rope”; criniculus, “little lock of hair”; pisciculus, “little fish”; curriculus, “little course”; and *curriculum*, “course,” which is neuter; versiculus, “little verse”; flucticulus, “little wave”; articulus, “little joint”; ridiculus, “laughable”; aniculus, “little old woman”; vermiculus, “little worm”; agniculus, “little lamb”; fasciculus, “little bundle”; ensiculus, “little sword”; cuniculus, “little rabbit”; ventriculus, “little stomach.”

Juvenal writes in Book I:

> Infra ventriculum tenui distantia rima.  
> “Below the stomach, a narrow cleft lies at a distance.”

These diminutives arise either from monosyllables, as *pons*, *ponticulus*; or from disyllables, as *ensis*, *ensiculus*; *dulcis*, *dulciculus*.

Likewise mobile adjectives are purpureus, “purple”; caeruleus, “blue”; marmoreus, “marble”; aequoreus, “of the sea”; funerus, “funereal”; Herculeus, “of Hercules,” as Juvenal writes:

> Audiet Herculeo stridentem gurgite solem.  
> “He will hear the sun hissing in the whirlpool of Hercules.”

Tartareus, “of Tartarus”; carbaseus, “of canvas”; pampineus, “of vine leaves”; puniceus, “scarlet,” as Virgil writes:

> Tota  
> Puniceo stabis suras evincta cothurno;  
> “You will stand wholly girded about the shins with a scarlet buskin.”

Sanguineus, “blood-red”; sidereus, “starry”; corporeus, “bodily”; femineus, “feminine”; virgineus, “maidenly”; populeus, “of poplar”; aetherius, “heavenly”; Elysius, “Elysian”; Gorgoneus, “of the Gorgon.” Virgil writes:

> Ex in Gorgoneis Allecto insecta venenis;  
> “Then Allecto, steeped in Gorgon’s poisons.”

Egregius, “excellent”; exiguus, “small”; praecipuus, “outstanding”; assiduus, “constant”; irriguus, “watered”; rorifluus, “dew-flowing”; horrisonus, “dread-sounding”; raucisonus, “hoarsely sounding”; grandisonus, “loud-sounding,” as the poet says:

> Grandisonis pompare modis tragicoque boatu,  
> “To parade in grand-sounding rhythms and tragic bellowing,”

Ridiculove Geta. [Col. 0223A] This verse is interpreted quite disgracefully by the unskilled and ignorant of the art of meter, relying on dull-minded cleverness: they construe *vegeta* as though it were under one part of the sentence, with the sense depending on the preceding neuter noun, namely *figmenta*. But neither the method of scansion nor the rule of syllables agrees with this. For *ve* is a disjunctive conjunction, whereas *Geta* is a principal and primitive noun. Thus Terence the African says in the *Phormio*:

> Amicus summus meus et popularis Geta  
> Heri ad me venit;  
> “My closest friend and fellow citizen Geta came to me yesterday.”

And below:

> Geta, provinciam cepisti duram.  
> “Geta, you have undertaken a difficult task.”

If *vegeta* were a neuter noun in the plural accusative, the rule of heroic verse would waver, since neuters in the plural always shorten *a* in the nominative, accusative, and vocative, as in:

> Arma virumque cano  
> “I sing of arms and the man,”

and:

> Arma Amyclaeumque canem Cressamque pharetram.  
> “Arms, the Amyclaean hound, and the Cretan quiver.”

Therefore *vegeta* is not a plural accusative, but *Geta* is a singular ablative; in the first declension, *a* is always long in every gender, as in proreta, “pilot”; agonotheta, “judge of contests”; lanista, “trainer of gladiators”; archinirata [reading uncertain]; pirata, “pirate”; satrapa, “satrap”; rabula, “pettifogger”; athleta, “athlete”; psalmista, “psalmist”; exorcista, “exorcist”; Baptista, “Baptist”; Agrippa.

Likewise feminine nouns are sica, “dagger”; amica, “female friend”; pica, “magpie”; rima, “crack”; lima, “file”; mima, “mime actress”; ruga, “wrinkle”; bibliotheca, “library”; umbella, “little shade”; libella, “small balance”; serula, “little saw”; columella, “little column”; tympanistria, “female tambourine player,” as in:

> In medio juvencularum tympanistriarum;  
> “Among the young women playing tambourines.”

Common-gender nouns include advena, “newcomer”; verna, “slave born in the household,” whence *vernaculus*, “native-born.” The authority of the ancient orthographers testifies that this is better written with *v* than with digamma, because *ver*, from which *vernum*, “spring,” is derived, is written with *v*.

[Col. 0223C] We have brought forward these nouns, not because they belong to the first paeon, but to demonstrate the ending of the ablative of the first declension, in which *a* is always long, as in *Geta*. It is scanned thus: *ridicu, lo ve Ge, ta seu, qualibet, arte ca, nendi*—or, by whatever art of scansion. Otherwise *ta seu* would not be a spondee but an iambus, which the rule of the heroic hexameter rejects.

Likewise neuters of the first paeon are concilium, “council”; augurium, “augury”; supplicium, “punishment”; discidium, “separation”; principium, “beginning”; servitium, “servitude”; vestibulum, “vestibule”; thuribulum, “censer”; conjugium, “marriage”; auxilium, “aid”; eloquium, “utterance”; colloquium, “conversation”; consilium, “counsel”; peniculum, “sponge.” Hence the poet, composing a poem about the Savior’s gallows, says:

> Peniculo infusum calamo porrexit acetum;  
> “He offered vinegar poured into a sponge on a reed.”

Ingenium, “intelligence”; judicium, “judgment”; arbitrium, “decision”; imperium, “power”; solsititium, “solstice”; hospitium, “hospitality.”

Likewise coelicola, “heaven-dweller”; agricola, “farmer”; Christicola, “worshiper of Christ”; ruricola, “country-dweller”; Phoebigena, “born of Phoebus”; Trojugena, “born of Troy”; Graiugena, “Greek-born”; folligena, “born of bellows”; nubigena, “cloud-born,” that is, “a Centaur,” as Lucan writes:

> Ixionidas Centauros  
> Feta Pelithroniis nubes effundet in arvis.  
> “The cloud, pregnant in the Pelithronian fields, will pour forth the Centaurs, sons of Ixion.”

D. Give rules for verbs.  
M. Sanctifico, “I sanctify”; aedifico, “I build”; vivifico, “I give life”; clarifico, “I glorify”; glorifico, “I glorify”; magnifico, “I magnify”; mellifico, “I make honey”; mirifico, “I make wonderful”; laetifico, “I gladden”; testificor, “I testify”; ludificor, “I mock”; polliceor, “I promise”; confiteor, “I confess”; auxilior, “I assist”; progredior, “I advance”; astipulor, “I support”; appretior, “I estimate”; intueor, “I behold”; contueor, “I gaze upon”; irradio, “I radiate”; discrucio, “I torment”; invigilo, “I keep watch”; conglomero, “I gather together”; inficio, “I infect”; perficio, “I complete”; efficio, “I accomplish”; afficio, “I affect”; sufficio, “I suffice”; officio, “I hinder”; conficio, “I complete”; cio, “I summon”; interimo, “I destroy”; comperio, “I discover”; advenio, “I arrive”; invenio, “I find”; deripio, “I tear away”; eripio, “I rescue”; invideo, “I envy”; admoneo, “I warn”; contineo, “I contain”; commoneo, “I remind”; edoceo, “I teach thoroughly”; confugio, “I flee for refuge”; effugio, “I escape”; ingemino, “I double”; dilapido, “I squander”; dispolio, “I strip”; evacuo, “I empty”; annumero, “I count”; exsupero, “I surpass”; assimulo, “I imitate”; commemoro, “I commemorate”; exacuo, “I sharpen”; retribuo, “I repay”; constituo, “I establish”; instituo, “I institute”; restituo, “I restore”; oncupio, “I desire”; decipio, “I deceive”; excorio, “I flay”; febricito, “I have a fever”; effodio, “I dig out”; delacero, “I tear apart”; delanio, “I tear to pieces”; esurio, “I hunger”; mellifico, “I make honey.” Thus Virgil writes in the theatrical tetrastich:

> Sic vos non vobis mellificatis apes;  
> “Thus you bees make honey, not for yourselves.”

Degenero, “I degenerate”; abbrevio, “I shorten”; suppedito, “I supply”; quadripedo, “I go on four feet.” Virgil writes:

> Quadrupedante putrem cursu quatit ungula campum.  
> “With four-footed course, the hoof beats the yielding plain.”

D. By what method or in what manner is the first paeon divided?  
M. It is separated by a sescuple division, since it follows neither the equal rule of division nor the double nor the triple.

D. How many temporal units do arsis and thesis govern?  
M. Arsis governs three temporal units, thesis two, because the antepenultimate is pronounced with an acute accent.

## On the second paeon

D. Give the nouns belonging to the second paeon.  
M. Potentia, “power”; frequentia, “frequency”; colonia, “colony”; crepacula, “rattle”; novacula, “razor”; sororcula, “little sister”; diecula, “little day”; domuncula, “little house”; laguncula, “little flask”; puellula, “little girl”; [Col. 0224B] bonoria [reading uncertain]; puerpera, “woman in childbirth”; pecuscula, “little flock.” As Juvencus writes:

> Foveam si forte pecuscula vestra  
> Inciderit;  
> “If perchance your little flock should fall into a pit.”

Likewise lepusculus, “little hare”; pedunculus, “little foot”; homunculus, “little man”; or homuncio, “little man”; or homullulus, “little man”; or homullus, “little man,” as Cicero says:

> Homullus ex argilla et luto fictus.  
> “A little man fashioned from clay and mud.”

Homullus belongs to the amphibrach. The second paeon is also commonly derived from superlative forms when the letters *r* or *l* are doubled, as *acer*, *acerrimus*; *vetus*, *veterrimus*. Virgil writes:

> Veterrima laurus,  
> Religione patrum multos servata per annos:  
> “The very ancient laurel, preserved for many years by the religious devotion of the fathers.”

Although analogy requires adjectives ending in *r* to form their superlative with a doubled *r*, as *teter*, *teterrimus*; *creber*, *creberrimus*. Hence the most ancient writers used not *vetus* but *veter*, as Ennius writes:

> Cum veter occubuit Priamus sub Marte Pelasgo;  
> “When old Priam fell beneath Pelasgian Mars.”

[Col. 0224C] Niger, *nigerrimus*; miser, *miserrimus*; celer, *celerrimus*; piger, *pigerrimus*; tener, *tenerrimus*, as it is established in the *Basilion*:

> Quasi vermiculus ligni tenerrimus.  
> “Like the most delicate little worm of wood.”

Pauper, *pauperrimus*, “poor, poorest,” and pulcher, *pulcherrimus*, “beautiful, most beautiful,” are assigned to the major Ionic. The anomalous forms *sinistimus* and *dextimus* are excepted; their primitives are *sinister* and *dexter*. Thus the historian Sallust writes in the *Jugurthine*:

> Sylla, inquit, cum equitatu apud dextimos, in sinistra parte Mallius cum fundatoribus.  
> “Sulla,” he says, “was on the right with the cavalry, while Mallius with the slingers was on the left.”

According to analogy one would say *sinisterrimus* and *dexterrimus*. Likewise facillimus, “easiest”; gracillimus, “slenderest”; humillimus, “humblest”; simillimus, “most similar”; agillimus, “most agile.”

Neuters too are brought under this rule: opusculum, “little work”; majusculum, “somewhat larger”; holusculum, “little vegetable”; crepusculum, “twilight”; pecusculum, “little animal,” whose plural we have already given; piaculum, “expiatory offering”; periculum, “danger”; silentium, “silence.”

The same paeon is also found in the moods, persons, and tense-inflections of verbs, from the first conjugation, which we arranged under the pyrrhic, and from the second, in the future tense, which we arranged under the tribrach: amabimus, amabitis; beabimus, beabitis; meabimus, meabitis; creabimus, creabitis; cavabimus, cavabitis; secabimus, secabitis. From the second conjugation, active and neuter forms include docebimus, docebitis; stupebimus, stupebitis; fovebimus, fovebitis; ciebimus, ciebitis; rigebimus, rigebitis.

Passive, common, and deponent forms agree in both numbers: doceberis, docebitur, docebimur; medeberis, medebitur, medebimur; fateberis, fatebitur, fatebimur; vereberis, verebitur, verebimur. Likewise from the inchoative form, but in the present tense: virescimus, virescitis; rigescimus, rigescitis; tumescimus, tumescitis; madescimus, madescitis; rubescimus, rubescitis, as the poet writes:

> Quem magis offendit quisquis superando tepescit.  
> “Whoever grows lukewarm through surpassing others offends him all the more.”

Participles likewise appear to correspond to the second paeon in the plural nominative and dative of the neuter gender: videntia, videntibus; vigentia, vigentibus; olentia, olentibus; nitentia, nitentibus—these signify shining, not striving; litantia, litantibus; micantia, micantibus; luentia, luentibus; fruentia, fruentibus; euntia, euntibus.

D. Give the law of division in the second paeon.  
M. It is divided by a sescuple distinction, just as its predecessor was; arsis, thesis, and accent follow the same temporal rule that we stated for the earlier paeon.

## On the third paeon

[Col. 0225B]

D. Let examples of the third paeon be brought forth.  
M. Nemorosus, that is, “full of groves”; likewise decorosus, “beautiful”; speciosus, “handsome”; rabiosus, “rabid”; varicosus, “full of varices”; scabiosus, “scabby”; generosus, “noble”; macilentus, “lean”; truculentus, “savage”; gracilentus, “slender”; feculentus, “muddy”; opulentus, “rich”; oriundus, “sprung from”; moribundus, “dying”; rudibundus, “braying”; Palinurus; paliurus; as in the following:

> Carduus et spinis surgat Paliurus acutis;  
> “Let the paliurus rise, and the thistle, with sharp thorns.”

Alienus, “foreign”; sceleratus, “wicked”; galeatus, “helmeted”; tunicatus, “tunic-clad”; trabeatus, “clad in the trabea”; cuneatus, “wedge-shaped”; equitatus, “mounted”; peditatus, “on foot”; comitatus, “accompanied”; capitalis, “capital”; glacialis, “icy”; specialis, “special”; generalis, “general”; lateralis, “lateral”; Cerealis, “of Ceres,” as in:

> Cereale papaver  
> Tempus humo tegere;  
> “It is time to cover the cereal poppy with earth.”

Operosus, “laborious”; maculosus, “spotted”; numerosus, “numerous”; onerosus, “burdensome”; animosus, “spirited”; populosus, “populous”; spatiosus, “spacious”; oculosus, “full of eyes”; and oculatus, “eyed,” as in the Apocalypse:

> Animalia intrinsecus oculata.  
> “The creatures were eyed within.”

D. Give the distinction among the nouns just mentioned.  
M. All are mobile and are called epithets, except *paliurus* and *Palinurus*, and those that we introduced as derived from *eques*, “horseman,” *pedes*, “foot soldier,” and *comes*, “companion,” because *eques* and *equetus* are one and the same. Thus *pedes* and *pedester*; *equitatus* and *peditatus*, however, refer to the number of horsemen and foot soldiers.

D. To what inflectional form are the examples of the nouns just given assigned?  
M. All nouns of the second declension ending in *-us* are pentaptota in the singular and tetraptota in the plural.

D. What examples of verbs correspond to the third paeon?  
M. They are taken from the first and third conjugations, in the present and future tense of the indicative, especially from the verbs that we fitted together above when discussing the tribrach: glomeramus, glomeratis; glomerabo, glomerabis, glomerabit; properamus, properatis; properabo, properabis, properabit; geminamus, geminatis; geminabo, geminabis, geminabit; rogitamus, rogitatis; rogitabo, rogitabis, rogitabit; rapiemus, rapietis; capiemus, capietis; poliemus, polietis; veniemus, venietis. Virgil writes in the *Eclogues*:

> Rapidum Creta veniemus Oaxen.  
> “From Crete we shall come to swift Oaxes.”

Passive, common, and deponent forms do not correspond throughout the same persons, but occur in this fashion: jugulamur, “we are slaughtered”; jugulentur, “let them be slaughtered”; jugulabor, “I shall be slaughtered”; veneramur, “we revere”; venerantur, “they revere”; venerabor, “I shall revere”; stipulamur, “we stipulate”; stipulantur, “they stipulate”; stipulabor, “I shall stipulate”; stomachamur, “we are indignant”; stomachantur, “they are indignant”; stomachabor, “I shall be indignant.”

The infinitive mood also belongs to the third paeon in active and neuter verbs, in the present and past tenses: stipulare, “to stipulate”; stipulasse, “to have stipulated”; titulare, “to title”; titulasse, “to have titled”; ululare, “to howl”; ululasse, “to have howled”; spoliare, “to strip”; spoliasse, “to have stripped”; temerare, “to violate”; temerasse, “to have violated.”

Hence Proba, most distinguished among poets, at the beginning of her Virgilian cento—although it contains the frivolities of the Apocrypha under a prophetic guise, yet preserves the legitimate rule of the hexameter—elegantly wrote:

> Jam dudum temerasse duces pia foedera pacis.  
> “Long ago the leaders had violated the sacred treaties of peace.”

It is scanned thus: *Jam du, dum temer, asse du, ces pia, foedera pacis.*

D. Give examples approved by the meanings of participles.  
M. Participles of the past and future tense proceeding from passive, common, and deponent forms do not reject the third paeon: glomeratus, glomerandus; veneratus, venerandus; jaculatus, jaculandus; [Col. 0226B] imitatus, imitandus, as in:

> Demens perpetui qui non imitanda parentis  
> Jura caducorum gradibus simulavit honorum.  
> “The madman who fashioned, through the steps of fleeting honors, the laws of an everlasting father—laws that ought not to be imitated.”

Likewise from active and neuter verbs: fugiturus, “about to flee”; ruiturus, “about to rush”; trahiturus, “about to drag”; doliturus, “about to grieve”; domiturus, “about to tame,” as in the *Georgics*:

> . . . . . Et durum Bacchi domitura saporem,  
> “And about to tame the harsh flavor of Bacchus,”

petiturus, “about to seek”; periturus, “about to perish.”

D. By what distinction is the third paeon separated?  
M. It is divided by a sescuple division, but arsis and thesis conflict with the first and second paeons, since arsis takes two temporal units and thesis three.

D. I ask, then, from where does this difference—and this seemingly discordant dissonance—arise, when in the ten feet mentioned above the melody of an ordered modulation is held together by such a harmonious concord of times, balanced by an equal measure of division?  
M. Because the third paeon always lengthens the penultimate with an acute accent, as in *calamistrum*, “curling iron,” from which the epithet *calamistratus* is derived; or with a circumflex, as in *medicina*, “medicine.” The laws of the first and second paeons, however, always compel the accent to be acute before the penultimate.

## On the fourth paeon

D. Bring forth at last the regular formulas of examples of the fourth paeon.  
M. I shall explain this foot somewhat more briefly, since abundant examples are not supplied in great number: humilitas, “humility”; saturitas, “fullness”; satietas, “satiety”; varietas, “variety”; temeritas, “rashness”; agilitas, “agility”; facilitas, “ease”; gracilitas, “slenderness”; celeritas, “swiftness”; viriditas, “greenness”; tenuitas, “thinness”; cupiditas, “desire”; stabilitas, “steadfastness,” as Prosper says in the *Epigrams*:

> Lex aeterna Dei stabili regit omnia nutu.  
> “The eternal law of God governs all things with steadfast command.”

Likewise stoliditas, “stupidity”; proceritas, “height.” Moreover, those nouns that we previously gathered in the rectus case under the proceleusmaticus will be regularly adapted to this foot through the genitive: fidicula, fidiculae; miseria, miseriae; crucicola, crucicolae; apicula, apiculae; avicula, aviculae; crucicula, cruciculae. Juvenal’s authority, however, varied this, as we reported above.

Coticula, “little whetstone,” whose primitive is *cos*, “whetstone,” belongs to the first paeon; it is used in a poem about the water of contradiction:

> . . . . Rumpuntur cotibus amnes.  
> “The rivers are broken by the rocks.”

Thus, in the fourth paeon: latibulum, latibuli; patibulum, patibuli; manipulus, manipuli; puerulus, pueruli. But those forms which we grouped under the proceleusmaticus by accumulating the genitive and ablative through the oblique cases do not at all contribute to the evidence for the fourth paeon.

The verbs of both the indicative and subjunctive moods that we introduced under the proceleusmaticus also agree properly with this rule, but only in the third person: humilio, humiliant; arieto, arietant; likewise operiunt. In the subjunctive mood: docuerim, docuerint; tumuerim, tumuerint; statuerint; patuerint.

Observe, please, the intricate subtlety of the metrical art. *Patuerunt* is indicative, in the perfect past tense, where *e* is always lengthened, as in:

> Pervia divisi patuerunt caerula ponti.  
> “The open blue waters of the divided sea lay exposed.”

It is scanned: *pervia, divisi, patuerunt*. And below:

> Et jejuna novum vomuerunt marmora potum.  
> “And the thirsty marble poured forth a new drink.”

It is scanned: *et jejuna, novum, vomuerunt*. But *patuerunt* and *vomuerunt* in the subjunctive mood, perfect past tense, always shorten *e* by a fixed rule.

D. Give an example from participles.  
M. I have been able to find no participles, except those of the present tense, suited to the fourth paeon from the verbal forms mentioned above: arietans, “butting”; humilians, “humbling”; sepeliens, “burying”; operiens, “covering”; aperiens, “opening.” Those that we placed in the subjunctive mood differ from the participial rule here; they either belong to the iambus, as docens, “teaching”; vigens, “flourishing”; stupens, “being astonished”; or properly form an anapest, as statuens, “establishing”; metuens, “fearing”; tribuens, “granting”; poliens, “polishing.”

D. Give the rule of accents.  
M. The fourth paeon is always pronounced with an acute accent on the antepenultimate. Moreover, arsis contains two temporal units and thesis three; balanced by a sescuple division, they are weighed on a scale of distinction that is rather unequal than equal.

## On the first epitrite

D. Now that the rules of the paeons have been set forth clearly and purged of obscurity, let examples of the first epitrite be published.  
M. Facultates, “abilities”; potestates, “powers”; honestates, “honourable qualities”; voluntates, “wills”; voluptates, “pleasures”; sacerdotes, “priests”; puellares, “of girls”; novercales, “of stepmothers”; maritales, “marital”; theatrales, “theatrical”; loquelares, “of speech”; Quirinales, “Quirinal”; Palatini, “Palatine”; Numantini, “of Numantia”; palumbini, “of wood-pigeons”; columbini, “of doves”; tiarati, “wearing a tiara”; capistrati, “bridled”; medullati, “marrow-filled,” as the Psalmist says:

> Holocausta medullata offeram tibi;  
> “I will offer you sacrifices filled with marrow.”

Capillati, “haired”; papillati, “having nipples”; pharetrati, “equipped with a quiver”; lapillosi, “full of little stones”; paludosi, “marshy”; lacertosi, “muscular”; and almost all nouns, whether derivatives or those which we introduced in the guise of participles in the singular number under the antepastus—these same forms in the plural are plainly assigned to the rule of the first epitrite.

In the same way, verbal forms agree in the perfect past tense: namely, only active and neuter forms of the first conjugation, which we presented under the pyrrhic, and which end their perfect tense in the syllables *-avi*. These same forms in the plural produce the first epitrite: amavi, amaverunt; rogavi, rogaverunt; dicavi, dicaverunt; piavi, piaverunt—whence *expiavi*, “I expiated,” is compounded; volavi, volaverunt; meavi, meaverunt; beavi, beaverunt, as in:

> Famamque beavit  
> Gurgitis;  
> “And he blessed the fame of the whirlpool.”

Rotavi, rotaverunt; plicavi, plicaverunt; and plicui, plicuerunt—both forms are used. Hence the compounds *explicavi* and *explicui*; as in:

> Et cum complicuisset librum.  
> “And when he had folded up the book.”

Those whose past tense ends in *-ui* reject this pattern: crepo, crepui; tono, tonui; mico, micui; frico, fricui; domo, domui. For *crepuerunt*, *tonuerunt*, *micuerunt*, *fricuerunt*, *domuerunt* do not take the first epitrite but the minor Ionic.

[Col. 0228A] It should also be noted that the grammarian Phocas gave *frico, fricui* as the past tense; Gregory, however, in the third book of the *Dialogues*, reported not *fricuit* but *fricavit*, saying:

> Faciem defuncti fricavit.  
> “He rubbed the face of the dead man.”

And below:

> Cumque diutius fricaretur, etc.  
> “And when he had been rubbed for a longer time,” etc.

D. Can participles of this kind be subjected to the definitions of the first epitrite?  
M. Just as we have already stated that the meanings of participles proceeding from inchoative forms become evident through the genitive according to the laws of the antepastus, so we affirm that they support this epitrite through the dative: nitescens, nitescenti; rubescens, rubescenti; tepescens, tepescenti; likewise tumescenti, fatiscenti, tremescenti, calescenti, acescenti.

Likewise, future-tense participles derived from the perfect form of the first conjugation, which were arranged under the pyrrhic, serve the first epitrite through all their cases, except the singular nominative, accusative, and vocative, and the plural genitive: litaturi, litaturo, litaturis, litaturos. Likewise amaturi, “about to love”; crepaturi, “about to crack”; beaturi, “about to bless”; meaturi, “about to pass”; ligaturi, “about to bind”; fricaturi, “about to rub”; plicaturi, “about to fold”; necaturi, “about to kill”; negaturi, “about to deny”; araturi, “about to plow.”

D. Give the rule of division and the quality of the prosody.  
M. The epitrites are not at all governed by the laws of the divisions mentioned above. Since the penultimate syllable of the first epitrite is acute, three temporal units are unquestionably gathered in arsis and four in thesis.

## On the second epitrite

D. Let the parts of speech that properly obey the structures of the second epitrite be submitted without delay.  
M. Vinitores, “winegrowers”; proditores, “traitors”; debitores, “debtors”; creditores, “creditors”; traditores, “surrenderers”; venditores, “sellers”; portitores, “carriers”; limitores, “boundary-setters”; [Col. 0228C] funditores, that is, those who engage in single combat with slings. Likewise saeculares, “worldly”; corporales, “bodily”; carcerales, “of prison”; cardinales, “principal”; temporales, “temporal”; criminosi, “criminal”; calculosi, “stony”; ponderosi, “heavy”; ulcerosi, “ulcerous”; cancerosi, “cancerous”; vultuosi, “expressive of countenance.”

Likewise feminine nouns: dignitates, “dignities”; qualitates, “qualities”; quantitates, “quantities”; vastitates, “devastations”; vanitates, “vanities”; almitates, “nourishing qualities”; sanitates, “healths”; summitates, “summits”; caecitates, “blindnesses”; densitates, “densities.” Thus also the other forms that we confined to the amphimacer in the singular will be joined to this epitrite in the plural.

Active or neuter verbs of the first conjugation, which produce a dactyl in the first person, are likewise admitted to these rules in the future tense and plural number: verbero, verberabunt; pignero, pignerabunt; fenero, fenerabunt; exsulo, exsulabunt; expio, expiabunt; irrigo, irrigabunt; reprobo, reprobabunt; fascino, fascinabunt, as in:

> Quis teneros mihi fascinet agros.  
> “Who will bewitch my tender fields?”

Likewise with the other conjugations. But in the perfect past tense, if they belong to the second conjugation, examples are palleo, palluerunt; censeo, censuerunt; caneo, canuerunt; torpeo, torpuerunt; horruerunt; terruerunt; floruerunt; arcuerunt; marcuerunt; languerunt.

But if one says in the subjunctive mood *censuerint*, *palluerint*, *canuerint*, they are unquestionably joined not to the epitrite but to the choriamb. From the third conjugation, examples support the pattern both in the perfect and imperfect past tenses: eruebant, eruerunt; diluebant, diluerunt; obruebant, obruerunt; diruebant, diruerunt; afferebant, attulerunt; conferebant, contulerunt.

Participles from all three tenses, proceeding only from active and common forms, likewise do not differ, [Col. 0229A] as dedicati, dedicandi; strangulati, strangulandi, strangulantes; pastinati, pastinandi, pastinantes; osculati, osculandi, osculantes. Likewise from the third or fourth conjugation, without the past tense: conterentes, conterendi; inserentes, inserendi; diluentes, diluendi. Arsis and thesis are known to divide the temporal units of the second epitrite in no other way than those of the first.

## On the third epitrite

### Glossary for the catalogue of confused sounds

The following preserves every sound-verb form in the supplied catalogue. Glosses marked “uncertain” are deliberately cautious where the rare form is not securely recoverable from the supplied context.

- *ambizant, bombizant*: hum/buzz; *crinciunt, trinsiunt*: cackle/hiss; *minuriunt, vernant, vernicant*: birds chirp or warble (rare forms; exact distinction uncertain); *pipant, pipilant*: chirp; *teretissant*: quack (uncertain); *trissitant, blaterant*: bleat.
- *oncant, rudiunt*: bray; *frendunt*: grunt; *crepant*: rattle; *tinnit*: ring; *bilibit*: gurgle/bubble; *mugiunt, reboant*: low/bellow; *butant*: caw (uncertain); *desistant*: sing/cry (uncertain); *fretinniunt*: chirr.
- *gratulant, glottorant, critalant*: clatter or rattle (stork calls; individual distinctions uncertain); *crocitant, croccant*: croak; *mucciunt*: bleat or low; *baubantur, latrant, ganniunt*: bark, bark, yelp; *glattilant*: yelp; *rugiunt*: roar/bellow; *sonant*: sound; *cusnitit*: whines (hunting dog).
- *barriunt, stridunt*: trumpet/squeal; *hinniunt*: neigh; *mussitant*: mutter/growl; *gruddant, gruunt, grugulant*: crane-call, cry, or croon; *cacillant*: cackle; *cantant, cucurriunt*: sing/crow; *fringilliunt*: chirp; *griciunt*: chatter (jay); *trutissant, trissant*: twitter.
- *hirriunt*: snarl; *balant, belant*: bleat; *vagiunt*: wail; *hircant*: cry like a goat (uncertain); *vagitant*: squeal; *ululant*: howl; *murmurant*: murmur; *lugiunt, vigilant, luriunt*: cry, call, or lament (kite calls; rare forms uncertain).
- *zinzitant*: chirp; *dindrant*: squeak; *mintriunt, muniunt*: squeak (mouse calls); *cucubiunt*: hoot; *drensitant*: cry/sing (swan); *vagillant*: bray; *raucitant*: coo hoarsely; *titiant*: chirp; *tinnipant*: ring/chirp; *paululant*: cry.
- *cacabant*: cackle; *chauriunt*: roar/growl; *feliunt*: cry like a cat; *grunniunt, grundiunt*: grunt; *coaxant*: croak; *parsitant*: chatter; *denticant*: squeak/nibble; *sibilant*: hiss; *strepunt*: rustle/roar; *soccitant, faccilant*: chirp (thrush calls; rare distinction uncertain); *raccant*: roar; *clangiunt*: sound a trumpet; *pionpant*: cry; *flant, tremunt, sibilant*: blow, roar/tremble, hiss; *urgant, saeviunt*: growl/rage; *ejulant*: howl; *quiritant*: squeal.

### Lexical and source-anchor notes

*Authenticus* means “authoritative/genuine”; *arnotinus*, “of this year”; *hornotinus*, “of last year.” The bare comparative examples are likewise semantic pairs: *acer/acerrimus* “sharp/sharpest,” *vetus/veterrimus* “old/oldest,” *niger/nigerrimus* “black/blackest,” *miser/miserrimus* “wretched/most wretched,” *celer/celerrimus* “swift/swiftest,” *piger/pigerrimus* “lazy/laziest,” and *tener/tenerrimus* “tender/tenderest.”

For source-boundary reference, the supplied transitions run through Col. 0218B, 0218C, 0218D, 0219A, 0219B, 0219C, 0219D, 0220A, 0220B, 0220C, 0220D, 0221A, 0221B, 0221C, 0221D, 0222A, 0222B, 0222C, 0222D, 0223A, 0223B, 0223C, 0223D, 0224A, 0224B, 0224C, 0224D, 0225A, 0225B, 0225C, 0225D, 0226A, 0226B, 0226C, 0226D, 0227A, 0227B, 0227C, 0227D, 0228A, 0228B, 0228C, and 0228D.

Examples of nouns that regularly serve the third epitrite should, I ask, by no means remain hidden but be brought openly to light.—M. *Divinitas* (divinity), *vicinitas* (nearness), *aequalitas* (equality), *finalitas* (finality), *felicitas* (happiness), *maturitas* (ripeness), *aeternitas* (eternity), *impunitas* (impunity). Eusebius, in the *Chronicles*: “Because of the impunity afforded by the asylum, a great multitude joined Romulus”; *crudelitas* (cruelty), *audacitas* (boldness), *immanitas* (savagery), *humanitas* (humanity), *obscenitas* (obscenity), *obscuritas* (obscurity), [Col. 0229B] *moralitas* (morality), *antiquitas* (antiquity), *velocitas* (speed), *infirmitas* (weakness), *deformitas* (deformity), *fecunditas* (fertility), *urbanitas* (urbanity), *affinitas* (affinity), *pluralitas* (plurality), *vivacitas* (vigor), *fraternitas* (brotherhood), *germanitas* (kinship). There are also plural nouns serving the forms of this epitrite, such as *fuligines* (soots), *prurigines* (itchings), *sartagines* (frying pans), *caligines* (mists), *ferrugines* (rusts), *testudines* (tortoises), *uligines* (marshes). Yet these and the preceding nouns follow the pentaptote rule in the singular and the triptote rule in the plural.

**D.** Can these examples be found in the conjugations of verbs, or not?

**M.** I judge that the third epitrite is derived from the subjunctive and optative moods of the third conjugation, as in *emungerent* (they would blow out), *excuterent* (they would shake out), *retruderent* (they would thrust back), *rarescerent* (they would become thin), *vilescerent* (they would become cheap), *lentescerent* (they would become pliant), *squalescerent* (they would become rough), *ignoscerent* (they would forgive), *depromerent* (they would draw forth), *depecterent* (they would comb out), *connecterent* (they would join).

**D.** Why do the first and second conjugations not at all correspond to this third epitrite in the persons of the subjunctive mood? [Col. 0229C]

**M.** Because the verbs of both conjugations in the aforesaid mood and in the imperfect tense are lengthened in the penultimate position, as in *macerarent*, *lacerarent*; likewise *maderent*, *vigerent*, *squalerent*. For the imperative lengthens both conjugations, and this in no way permits the penultimate syllables of the verbs mentioned above to be shortened.

**D.** By what distinctions do arsis and thesis alternately separate the portions of the tenses?

**M.** Sometimes arsis triumphs over the tenses as a trophy, while it governs eight and a half; thesis, in turn, employs six and a half. And arsis, which earlier in the preceding epitrites had been victorious by subjugating them, now finally succumbs in the succeeding epitrites by servilely enslaving and feebly yielding. [Col. 0229D]

**D.** It is worthwhile, for the clarification of these matters, that you repeat from what source this is believed to be established.

**M.** Clearly, this usually happens for prosodic reasons, because this epitrite, about which we are presently attempting to devise a brief account, is pronounced with an acute accent on the antepenultimate syllable, just as its predecessor is on the penultimate.

## On the fourth epitrite

**D.** Draw out as quickly as possible the rules from the parts of speech that conform to the laws of the epitrites.

**M.** *Constantinus* (Constantine), *Marcellinus* (Marcellinus), *Saturninus* (Saturninus), *cancellatus* (grated), *fortunatus* (fortunate), *contignatus* (joined with beams), *aerumnosus* (wretched), *libertinus* (freedman’s), *collibertus* (fellow freedman), *Augustinus* (Augustine), *Coelestinus* (Celestine), *crystallinus* (crystalline), *smaragdinus* (emerald-colored). These, both proper and common nouns, are pentaptotes in the singular; common nouns, however, are tetraptotes in the plural. Neuter nouns in both numbers are triptotes, such as *fundamentum* (foundation), *sacramentum* (sacrament), *juramentum* (oath), *spiramentum* (breath). Virgil, in Book Eight:

> He tore apart the breath of life with a deadly wound;

* salsamentum* (salted food), *atramentum* (ink), *purgamentum* (purging substance), *firmamentum* (support), *nutrimentum* (nourishment), *fulcimentum* (prop), *ornamentum* (ornament), *ostimentum* (display), *armamentum* (equipment). The place of storage where equipment is kept is called an *armamentarium*, which belongs to shipmasters and helmsmen. For the arms of one soldier there is *armatura* (armor), or for a whole expedition; *armentum* is what an *armentarius*, or herdsman, tends.

**D.** With the richest array of evidence, I ask you plainly to explain what the distinguished commentator on grammatical art means when he says: “Prepositions either corrupt verbs or are themselves corrupted.” [Col. 0230B]

**M.** This statement is recognized as containing three rules, which nevertheless are gathered according to a fourfold arrangement of forms.

**D.** In my judgment, this answer has not plainly untied the knot of the question, but has rather wrapped it up like a little cloth.

**M.** The threefold definition of prepositions, as we said, is gathered according to the following distinctions: either the prepositions themselves are corrupted, as in *accedo*, *succedo*, *oppono*, *appono*; or they corrupt the other parts of speech to which they have been prefixed while remaining themselves uncorrupted, as in *quaero*, *exquiro*, *inquiro*, *requiro*, and *frango*, *confringo*, *infringo*, *spargo*, *dispergo*, *sparsi*, *dispersi*; or else they are corrupted reciprocally, that is, both the preposition and the other parts of speech that follow, compounded with the prepositions according to the form of the construction, as in *corripio*, *coerceo*, *corrigo*, *sinciput*, *occiput*. [Col. 0230C]

**D.** Give examples of prepositions that corrupt the other parts, and of those that are themselves corrupted when joined to the remaining parts.

**M.** *Ex, ad, ob, in, sub, trans, con, circum, ante.* The preposition *ex* sometimes changes the letter *x* into *f*, as in *effringo*, *effugio*, *effluo*, *effundo*, *effatur*, *effabilis*, *ferus–efferus*, *frenatus–effrenatus*, *facio–efficio*, *factus–effectus*, *efficax*; or it remains intact when joined. It is corrupted in *aestimo–existimo*, *carpo–excerpo*, *quaero–exquiro*, *arceo–exerceo*, *cado–excido*, *effodio*, *effodis*, *effossus*. Or it loses the same letter altogether, as in *evenio*, *evenit*, *egero*, *egessi*, *egredior*, *egressus*, *emano*, *emanavi*, *elicio*, *elicui*, *elimino*, *eliminavi*, *elido*, *elisi*, *enarro*, *enarravi*, *enucleo*, *enucleavi*.

The preposition *ad* often changes its final *d* into the same letter with which the following part of speech begins, as in *cedo–accedo–accessi*, not *adcessi*; *accommodo*, *accolo*, *accipio*, *accepto*, *accingo*, *accumulo*, as in:

> The poets heap up their fame and praises;

*accubo*, *accubitus*, as in: “While the king was reclining at table, my nard gave its fragrance.” The word *cantus*, after receiving the preposition *ad*, is corrupted on both sides, as in *accentus*, which is called *prosodia* in Greek. Thus the same *d* is changed into *t*, as Lucius Annaeus Seneca says in the sixth book, in a tetrameter brachycatalectic:

> And the house raises twin Argos with doubled towers.

And below:

> With uncertain neck she sways; servants, raise up—

*attuli*, *attero*, *altrivi*, *attritus*. Virgil, in the *Georgics*:

> Often also, wandering over the hard rocks, they wore away their wings.

It sometimes passes into *p*, as in *appono*, *apposui*, *appareo*, *approbo*, *appello*, *applico*. Sometimes it changes into *l*: *laedo–allido–allisi*, *ligo–alligo–alligavi*, *allicio*, *allecto*, *allegatio*. It is also resolved into *r*, as in *arripio*, *arripui*, whose simple form is *rapio*; but after receiving the preposition *ad*, neither part suffers corruption: *arreptus*, *arrepticius*, *arrigo*, *arrexi*, *arrogo*, *arrogans*, *arrogantia*. It also passes into *n*, as in *annuo*, as is noted in proverbs concerning the gaze of the fickle and slippery man: “He nods with his eyes and strikes the ground with his foot.” Virgil, in Book Ten:

> He nodded and made all Olympus tremble at his nod.

Nevertheless it changes into the semivowel *f*: *afflatus*, *effectus*, *affixus*, *affabilis*, *afflatus*, as in:

> The little she-ass, shaken by angelic threats, speaks.

[Col. 0231B]

It is resolved into the mute *g*, as in *aggrego*, *aggredior*, *aggressus*, *aggero*, *aggestus*. Hence etymology explains the words *aggerem*, “embankment,” and *aggestis*, “with earth brought from the ditch and stones collected into a heap,” just as *congeries* comes from *congerendo*. It sometimes changes into *m*, as in *ammoneo*, *ammonitus*, *amminiculor*, *amminiculabor*, *amminiculum*.

The preposition *sub*, sometimes losing the letter *b* in either case, changes it into the letter with which the following noun or verb begins; or it composes a part of speech from a corrupted and an intact element, as in *suffulcio*, *suffultus*, *suffodio*, *suppono*, *suppositura*, *suggestio*, *suggero*, *suggessi*. Virgil, in Book Ten:

> Bring me weapons;

*suffero*, *suffert*, as in: “Blessed is the man who endures temptations.” [Col. 0231C] *Suffusio*, as in: “For one who has a dimming or suffusion of the eyes, which the Greeks call *glaucoma*.” *Summoveo*, *summotus*; *succubo*, *succubui*; *successus*, *succedo*, *successi*. Virgil:

> Burning Mezentius advances to the battle.

*Succurro*, *succedo*, *succingo*, *succresco*, *succrevi*; *plico–supplico*, *puto–supputo*, *peto–suppeto*. Or else the form is made from two corrupted elements, as in *supprimo*, *sustineo*, *sufficio*, *suscipio*, whose primitive forms are intact: *sub* and *premo*, *facio*, *capio*. But in the composition of the forms, *b*, *e*, and *a* are changed into other letter-shapes. Nevertheless, in the perfect and pluperfect tenses these verbs are formed from corrupted and intact elements, as in *suppressi*, *suppresseram*; *sustinui*, *sustinueram*; *suffeci*, [Col. 0231D] *suffeceram*; *suscepi*, *susceperam*.

The preposition *ob*, usually governing the accusative, changes *b* into the letter with which the following part of speech begins, as in *peto–oppeto*, as in:

> Beneath Troy’s lofty walls  
> it happened that he met death;

*oppono*, *opposui*; *occumbo*, *occubui*; *cado–occido*, which may refer both to one who suffers and to one who acts, as does *ruo*; *ommutesco*, *ommutui*; *officio*, *offeci* (that is, “I harmed”); *offero*, *obtuli*, the original form being restored; *offulcio*, *offulsi*; *offusco*, *offuscavi*; *offuit*, *offendit*, *occurrit*, *occalluit*.

The preposition *in* sometimes changes *n* into *m*, as in *pius–pietas*, *impius–impietas*, *improbus–improbitas*, *imploro*. Cicero, in Book Fifteen: “I implore and beseech everyone”; *immunis*, *immunitas*, *immanis*, *immanitas*, *impunitas*. Augustine the African: “Nothing is more wretched than the happiness of sinners, by which punitive impunity is nourished.” *Imbuo*, *imbutus*, *immortalis*. Or, when the preposition itself remains intact, the attached forms are corrupted, as in *salsus–insulsus*, *sapiens–insipiens*, *aptus–ineptus*, *castus–incestus*. Virgil:

> To dare to violate the marriage chambers of his stepmother;

*facio–inficio*, *capio–incipio*, *amicus–inimicus*, *aequus–iniquus*, *quaero–inquiro*, *partior–impertior*, *armatus–inermis*, *barbatus–imberbis*, *damnatus–indemnis*.

The preposition *con* is either itself corrupted in composition, as in *commoveo*, *commercium*, *meo–commeo*, *meatus–commeatus*, *corroboro*, *corruo*, *corrumpo*, *colloquor*, *colloquium*, *collega*, *collegium*, *collectio*, *collectanea*, *colludium*; [Col. 0232B] or it corrupts the parts of speech that are joined to it while remaining intact: *fateor–confiteor–confessus*, *gradior–congredior–congressus*, *cantus–concentus*, *scando–conscendo*, *statuo–constituo*, *cano–concino*, *jacio–conjicio*, as in:

> Turnus hurled the blazing torch;

*cado–concido*, as in: “Why has your face fallen?”; *taceo–conticeo*, as in:

> All fell silent and, intent, held their faces;

hence the inchoative *conticesco*; with Samuel’s mother prophesying: “And the wicked shall fall silent in darkness”; *teneo–contineo*, *tango–contingo*, *calco–conculco*, *facio–conficio*, *capio–concipio*, *quaero–conquiro*, *quaestio–conquisitio*. For *queror*, a deponent verb, is shortened. From it are derived *querela* and *querimonia*, just as it is recorded in ecclesiastical history: “He ordered all the books of complaints to be burned.” [Col. 0232C]

Or both are corrupted, namely both the preposition and the following part, as in *rapio–corripio*, *mando–commendo*, *plector–complector*. Cicero, Book Thirteen: “In no way can I attain it either in memory or encompass it in speech”; *laedo–collido–collisio*. Hence the poet:

> Yet scarcely did I escape, crushed through all my marrow.

*Rego–corrigo*, *lego–colligo*. Sometimes, however, the same preposition *con* does not corrupt the letter *n* but loses it altogether if the following part begins with a vowel, as in *aeternus–coaeternus*, *coaevus*, *coetaneus*, *coepiscopus*, *coacervo*, *coarcto*: “And the angel of the Lord hemming them in”; Lactantius, *To Demetrianus*: “And with a light, not constricted, spirit, he produces speech whenever we wish”; *occipio*. Terence, in the *Adelphi*:

> Quite right, by Pollux, I hope so; only now do the pains begin in my passage.

*Caput–occiput–sinciput*, formed from two corrupted elements, namely half a head.

The preposition *in* corrupts verbs, as in *facio–inficio*, *capio–incipio*, *gradior–congredior*, *partior–impertior*. As Tullius Cicero says, and Lucan in Book Ten:

> And the maker of things restrains them under a fixed law;

*cohibeo*, *coaequo*, *coalesco* or *inolesco*. Virgil:

> And they teach it to grow in the moist bark.

*Ago*, through synaloepha, becomes *cogo*, as *nolo* becomes *malo*, which is clearer in the perfect *coegi*.

The preposition *re* either corrupts the parts of speech attached to it while suffering no loss itself, as in *salio–resilio*. Prosper, in the *Epigrams*:

> If he recoils, he dwells in wretched exile;

*capio–recipio*, *captio–receptio*, *captus–receptus*, *sapio–resipio–resipisco*, *facio–reficio*, *factus–refectus*, *cano–recino*, *gradior–regredior*, *statuo–restituo*, *statutus–restitutus*, *quaero–requiro*, *teneo–retineo*, *taceo–reticeo*, *premo–reprimo*, *spargo–respargo*.

Or the same preposition *re*, when joined to verbs beginning with vowels, frequently assumes the letter *d*, as in *emo–redimo*, *emptio–redemptio*, *emptus–redemptus*, *arguo–redarguo*, *ago–redigo*, *actus–redactus*, *undo–redundo*, as in: “All rivers run into the sea, and the sea is not filled.” *Eo–redeo*, *reditus*, *euntes–redeuntes*, *iturus–rediturus*, *redintegro*, *redhibeo*, *redhibito*, *oleo–redoleo*, *olere–redolere*, *redolentes*. Virgil:

> and the fragrant Medes  
> refresh their faces with it;
