[Col. 0233B] but if verbs begin with a digamma, that is, with *u* placed in the position of a consonant, the aforementioned preposition rejects the letter *d*, as in *revertor*, *revolvo*, *revinco*.

The preposition *trans* sometimes loses *n* and *s*, as in *traductus*, *traducit*, as in: “He did not wish to lead her across.” Augustine, Book Twenty of *The City of God*: “Even if, he says, they could not by these means lead them across to their own side,” and so forth; *trajectus*, *trajecit*. Virgil, in Book Ten:

> Then Pallas pierced Rhaeteus, fleeing in his two-horse chariot;

*Trano*, *tranas*, *tranat*, whose simple forms are the monosyllables *trans* and *no*, *nas*, *nat*. Virgil:

> Beneath the dark clouds  
> the Strymonian cranes give their signals and cross the air.

Solinus likewise, in the *Collection of Things*, concerning stags: “If, he says, they cross the seas, they seek the shores not by sight but by smell.” [Col. 0233C]

The preposition *circum* sometimes loses *cum*, as in *circuitus*. Likewise the preposition *ante* changes *e* into *i*, as in *anticipo*, with the Psalmist agreeing, as in: “My eyes anticipated the watches.”

The preposition *dis* sometimes loses the letter *s* in composition, as in *diluto*, *dilusus*, *dilanio*, *diluo*, *dilabor*, *dilapsus*, as in:

> having fallen into a dark pit;

*dilancino*, *dilancinatus*. The same Solinus says of the beast called the *leontophon*: “They refrain indeed from biting, but they kill those they have torn apart by the force of their feet.” But if the letter *s* is placed at the beginning of the verb, the same preposition does not lose its *s*, as in *disspolio*, *dissolvo*, *dissero*. Sometimes *s* changes into *f*, as in *fido–diffido–diffidentia*, *fero–differo*, *differentia*, *fundo–diffundo*. Virgil, in Book Ten:

> And he pours out his soul into his weapons with streaming blood.

[Col. 0233D] Hence Julius Solinus, in the *Collection of Remarkable Things*, says: “And they estimated that it extended for one hundred and twenty thousand paces, reckoning the reports of travelers.”

*Facultas–difficultas*, as the same Solinus says: “Exhausted by many difficulties, he attaches himself to the Rhipaean mountains.” *Facilis–difficilis*, with both the preposition and the noun corrupted. But when followed by *c*, *p*, or *t*, the preposition *dis* remains intact, as in *cerno–discerno–discerniculum*, *crepo–discrepo*, *curro–discurro*, *calcio–discalcio*, *credo–discredo*, *cingo–discingo*; *placeo–displiceo*, *placuit–displicuit*, with the corrupted *a* changed into *i*; *puto–disputo*, *perdo–disperdo*, *pono–dispono*, *tendo–distendo*, *tribuo–distribuo*, *traho–distraho*, *tingo–distingo*, *pecto–dispecto* (that is, “comb”), *pendo–dispendo*.

[Col. 0234A]

There are other prepositions that similarly corrupt the parts of speech attached to them in the composition of forms, such as *per, prae, pro, de, re*: *perficio*, *praecipio*, *proficio*, *decipio*, *deripio*. Virgil:

> They tear the hides from the ribs;

*paro–separo*, *cerno–secerno*, *pono–repono*, *cedo–secedo*, *cubo–secubo*, *duco–reduco*, *cado–decido*, as in: “Its leaf does not fall”; and elsewhere: “The hay withers and the flower falls.” *Patior–perpetior*, *passus–perpessus*, and other similar forms.

**D.** You have lucidly illustrated the threefold rule of the preposition, together with the fourfold composition of forms, as though it were a chaos of black darkness illuminated by lamps of evidence. It remains, once the matter of prepositions and composition has been set aside, that you explain regularly the times of position and elevation corresponding to the fourth epitrite. [Col. 0234B]

**M.** The epitrites are not subject to divisions, although in the fourth epitrite arsis anticipates four times and thesis three.

**D.** Let the law of prosody be proclaimed.

**M.** The fourth epitrite, if its penultimate position is long, is pronounced with an acute accent, as in *hostimentum*, that is, “equalization,” or the weighing of a balance. But if the penultimate syllable is lengthened according to the laws of nature, it is pronounced with a circumflex accent, without any troublesome ambiguity, as in *contignatus*, *fortunatus*.

## On prosody

Prosody is a sign of speech that makes the path straight for the reader. There are ten prosodic signs: acute, grave, circumflex, long, short, *daseia*, *psile*, apostrophe, hyphen, and hypodiastole. These are divided [Col. 0234C] into four classes: tones, quantities, breathings, and affects.

A tone is either drawn out, drawn back, or the middle of a syllable possessing a proper sound. There are three tones: acute, grave, and circumflex. The acute tone is a mark rising obliquely toward the right, as in *pax*, *pix*, *nux*. The grave descends from above toward the right, as in *homo*, *bonus*, *parvus*. The circumflex is a mark formed from the acute and the grave, as in *môeta*, *mûsa*, *côepi*.

Quantity signifies extension or contraction and distinguishes what is invisible. There are two quantities, long and short. A long quantity signifies a lengthened vowel, as in:

> I sing of arms and the man, who first came from the shores of Troy.

A short quantity signifies a shortened vowel, as in:

> The great and acute songs sing our verses.

[Col. 0234D]

A breathing is the production of a sound that is uttered from the mouth either with aspiration or smoothly. There are two breathings, *daseia* and *psile*. *Daseia* is the quality of a syllable according to the sound of one breathing, as in *homo*, *habitans*, *habens*. *Psile* is the quality of a syllable uttered near the edge of the lips, as in *orator*, *adiit*, *orare*.

An affect is a sound joined and united, distinguishing things that can be divided. There are three affects: apostrophe, hyphen, and hypodiastole. An apostrophe is the sign of the removal of one or two vowels, which the Latins do not have but the Greeks do. A hyphen is the joining of a word composed from two complete or incomplete words, as in *lucifer*, *unigenitus*, *primogenitus*. A hypodiastole is the division of compounded letters to avoid ambiguity, as in:

[Col. 0235A]

> and a boar is seen on the green shore,

so that the reader does not err by reading *ursus* (“bear”) instead.

The acute has three positions, as the Greeks say, but the Latins have two: the penultimate and the antepenultimate. A penultimate word has the accent one syllable from the end, as *árma*, *órna*, *hónus*. An antepenultimate word has the accent two syllables from the end, as *Basílius*, *Gregórius*, *Bobátius*.

The circumflex, as the Greeks say, has two positions, but among the Latins one. A circumflex word has the accent one syllable from the end, as *coelum*, *coelorum*. Quantities are placed on vowel letters where they are lengthened or shortened, as in *nihil*, *amnis*, *flamina*, *munus*. A breathing is placed at the beginning of vowel letters, more rarely in the middle, as in *hujus*, *traho*, *inruho*. [Col. 0235B]

The apostrophe is placed above, as we have said; the Latins do not use it, but the Greeks do. The hyphen is placed below toward the right, as in *suburbanus*. The hypodiastole is placed below, opposite the hyphen, as in *Constantinopolis*.

Now that the rules of the grammarians and the feet of the meters have been explained—feet which, as we have already declared, are completed seven times in a fourfold measure—I think it worthwhile that, compelled by the goad of haste, we strive to pass over the various alternating repetitions of *synzygiae* that are subject to rhetorical disciplines. Their names are known to be these: *proxilius*, *diprolius*, *diopros*, *trampus*, *cribussus*, *namprossimalus*, *phymarus*, *atrorbus*, *rivatus*, *pranulus*, *linuatus*, *machaus*, *matrimus*, *phynulus*, *febrinus*.

These are properly the feet of rhetors, which, exceeding the measure of four syllables, are rejected and despised by metricians. For *proxilius*, consisting of three long and three short syllables, is composed according to a figure of this kind: [figure not legible in the supplied text]. *Dipodius*, by contrast, consists of three short and three long syllables, in the following figure: [figure not legible in the supplied text]. *Diopros* and *trampus* vary by the reciprocal alternation of two syllables, namely [figure not legible in the supplied text], and again [figure not legible in the supplied text]. Thus the other feet of the *synzygiae* are also understood to alternate in such reversed orders of interchange.

Moreover, the noun *synzygia*, denoting a compounded form, is found in the plural genitive to contain nine syllables and twenty letters: thus, if one says *pontifex Constantinopolitanus* (“a Constantinopolitan bishop”), the genitive plural is *pontificum Constantinopolitanorum* (“of Constantinopolitan bishops”).

As the end of my writing now approaches, most reverend son, I earnestly implore you with the prayers appended below, humbly as though on bent knees, to deign to protect this little work—which most plainly declares that I do not grow envious through your keen learning or waste away through your vigorous instruction—against all the catapults of rivals and the poisoned arrows of chatterers, which they usually hurl from the quiver of crooked envy, with the impenetrable shield of meters and the buckler of grammarians.

And if the highest ruler of Olympus makes me attain my desire, I ask that, showing the affection of a devoted mind, you admire and honor the industry of my labor all the more earnestly and abundantly, so that this may be a suitable portion of recompense for my wearied mind and an offered exchange of reward. For no one born from the lineage of our stock and nurtured in the cradles of the Germanic people is known to have labored so greatly before my mediocrity at such a task or to have transmitted the arguments of his own intelligence according to the discipline of the metrical art and the text of letters—especially one placed amid so many and such great tumultuous noises of secular affairs and weighed down by the anxieties of ecclesiastical pastoral care, by which a fearful and scrupulous mind is confined as though by a very tight barrier of chains. [Col. 0236A]

For I do not think that, by putting this forward, I should be wounded by the terrible arrows of raised eyebrows; nor do I shudder at being pierced by the most savage fire-dart of swollen pride if, trusting for a little while in the free grace of the divine gift—which is bestowed on each person not by the privilege of preceding merits but by the generosity of heavenly favor—I glory in the Lord.

Indeed, that distinguished man who said:

> I shall be the first, if life remains, to bring the Muses  
> home with me, returning from the Aonian peak;  
> I shall be the first to bring Idumaean palms to you, Mantua;

and the same poet continues somewhat farther below:

> It is pleasing to go over ridges where none of my predecessors  
> has turned aside toward Castalia by a gentle slope;

this poet, I say, wished to signify that no Latin before him had written the *Georgics* for the Romans, although Hesiod and Homer and the other Greeks, relying on the eloquence of their speech and endowed with the privilege of Argolic refinement, had set forth the fourfold cultivation of the land in their language. [Col. 0236C]

Finally, before the final speech is brought to an end by an appropriate reckoning, compelled by paternal concern, which is accustomed to look after the welfare of children, I admonish you not to disdain or contemptuously reject the things that I had written down by dictation with the most difficult exertion of sweat and labor, as though oppressed by a heavy burden, but to examine and review them without shrinking from sweat and labor. Nor should you allow the grace of the skillful intelligence divinely granted to you above your fellow pupils and contemporaries to grow rough through the sluggishness of idle leisure.

For I consider it absurd if you have become weary of kindly investigating, examining, and traversing what did not weary me to compose with difficulty, accumulate, and arrange; if, I say, you are reluctant, like one grown haughty and delicate, gradually to chew and ruminate what did not weary me—acting, as I did, in the office of a baker who kneads—to grind and lift.

Although, therefore, wearied by the cares of worldly administration, as by rocks resisting the blows of seaweed, and by the whirlpools of waves barking all around, you govern by directing the reins of the peoples entrusted to you, nevertheless do not, because of this, regard the honey-sweet study of the divine Scriptures as something to be neglected or undervalued under the pretext of such an occasion.

For that illustrious Theodosius, as the ancient little works of the past reveal, who governed almost the whole world’s monarchy and enjoyed the royal scepters of a flourishing empire for eleven circuits of passing years, obtained the daily nourishment of expenses and the food of bodily sustenance, on which mortal vitality feeds, at the exalted summit of power through the commerce of an antiquarian scribe. He preferred to acquire, through the exertion of labor, nourishment for bodily life by the profit of the Scriptures and letters rather than, wasting away in the torpor of inert idleness, to be fattened on free banquets of delicacies.

Thus, when he was copying out the eighteen books of the grammarian Priscian—who was called the light of Roman eloquence—fully arranged to the very end, he proclaimed a judgment unheard by his predecessors and untried by emperors of former ages, leaving, as I believe, an example of industry for posterity. “I,” he says, “Theodosius, emperor of the whole world, copied this volume with my own hand amid the cares of the palace,” and so forth.

Therefore the trumpet blast of the heavenly trumpet and the martial horns of the upper [Note: [Col. 0237] “Perhaps *salpicis* should be read, from *salpix, salpicis*, instead of *salpinx, salpingis*.” EDIT.] realm resounded, saying: “Let not the book of the law depart from your mouth, and you shall meditate on it day and night.” [Col. 0238A] Therefore, in all your works, remember your last things, and you will never sin.

For what is the prosperity of the passing world, or the happiness of deceptive life? Is it not, by a very similar comparison, that it vanishes like a dream, fades like smoke, and withers like foam? “If riches are present,” says the Psalmist, “do not set your heart upon them.” Would that the possession of present things were not the repayment of future things! Would that abundance of perishable goods were not the want of things to come! Would that the pleasures of the world that entices us did not produce losses of eternal blessedness! Rather, when the interval of fragile life has passed, may perpetual rewards of merits follow, with Christ’s support!

May he himself deign to grant this, he who hung for us upon the gallows, living and reigning with the eternal Father and with the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# Poems of Saint Aldhelm, Bishop of Sherborne, or the Third Part of His Works

[Col. 0237]

## On the Praises of Virgins

[Note: [Col. 0237] These two poems—this one and the following, on the Eight Principal Vices—which in certain manuscripts form a single work, I collated word for word, first with the Paris manuscripts and afterward with the Bodleian manuscript. They are very corrupt in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, nor are they now entirely free from errors. GILES.]

## Preface to the Abbess Maxima

[Col. 0237C]

Now let the beginners bring forth metrical songs with chaste intent,  
and let the Virgin receive praise in a measured poem.  
May the triune God in the citadel, mighty, who created the ages,  
the ruler of the world, reigning in lofty seats,  
deign to grant me, unworthy as I am, in heaven  
rest with the saints whom I praise in these verses.  
The high-throned judge, who preserves the heavenly scepters,  
gave them the means to ascend through the sky,  
among the ranks of the saints, who rightly glorify forever  
the one who governs the kingdoms with thunderous power,  
the all-holding Lord, maker and author of the world.  
Grant certain help to us poor ones,  
and do not permit us to be thrust here to our enemies;  
rather, defending the insignificant, may your right hand touch us,  
lest the deceitful robber be able to close the gate of heaven,  
or deceive the saints by the spectacle of their sins;  
lest the crafty thief thrust into darkness those  
whom Christ the Creator preserves from the highest heaven.

Shepherd guarding the flock, lest the ravager  
be able to devastate the royal folds—[the following words are corrupt: *bis dicere puppup*]—  
may the guardian now defend all the sheepfolds,  
you who bear the foremost name by divine power.  
Mother, deign by your prayer to add protection,  
for you have brought forth the everlasting Light from Light,  
the Titan whom the sacred prophet calls by his inspired breath,  
whose radiance shines throughout the world from its lofty axis,  
and fills the heavens alike with flashing lightning.  
Called king of kings and prince of peoples from eternity,  
great from the Great One, ruler of things under righteous authority,  
neither earth nor heaven can contain him,  
nor the sea-bearing ocean with its foaming flood,  
nor the zones of the world that surround the lofty sky.

With God’s help I shall undertake, in holy devotion,  
to proclaim the lives of the renowned saints,  
if, poor as I am, I can worthily bring forth such rewards.  
Since no one can explain all things openly in words,  
[The following sequence is corrupt in the supplied text: “Sotsac animract Namorp Cnunsenorita cirteM.”]

## The Book Begins

[Col. 0239A]

Almighty Father, governing the world by your dominion,  
you who build the shining heights of the star-bearing sky,  
and by your word establish the forms and foundations of the earth,  
you who paint the pale green fields with purple flowers,  
so also restrain the blue waters of the wave-tossed sea,  
lest they be able to engulf the shores of the earth with their floods,  
but let the barriers of the rocks break the swelling waves.  
You who water the cultivation of the fields with icy springs  
and increase the husks of the crops with rain-bearing showers,  
you who bring down the world’s concealments with a doubled star—  
the Titan attends the day and Cynthia the night—  
you who adorn the sea’s plains with rich fish,  
forming scaly shoals in the green-blue flood,  
thus filling the clear air with winged flocks,  
which chirp ringing songs with their beaks,  
and confess the Creator with varied voices,  
give pious and merciful aid, so that in song I may be able  
to compose the illustrious deeds of the holy forebears;  
so that, as prose once praised the chaste,  
poems may, if only they support heroic praise, do the same.

As I remember saying earlier in the sequence of the *Fasti*,  
and as the little book long ago brought forth with a vow as guarantor,  
I do not ask for rustic verses or the Muses’ periods,  
nor do I seek the songs of the metrical Castalian nymphs,  
whom they say guard Helicon as their lofty mountain;  
nor do I pray that Phoebus, whom the creative Latona bore on Delos,  
grant me a loquacious tongue in speech.

For never do I deem it fitting to speak in unspeakable verses,  
as the witty poet is once said to have spoken:

> Climb Helicon now, goddesses, and stir up your songs.

Rather, I shall strive by prayers to call upon the Thunderer,  
who grants us the oracles of tranquil speech.  
“Word from the Word,” I ask—this the Psalmist sang—  
the Word begotten from the Father’s heart, which is the only Son,  
through whom the almighty Father created all things throughout the world.  
Thus may the gracious Spirit of the Father and the Son  
mercifully grant aid to his frail servant.

For there is one simple substance abiding in the Godhead,  
and in the Godhead there also remains a threefold subsistence.  
Therefore let property be understood under a threefold name,  
but let majesty be spoken of under a single name.  
For faith compels us to believe three persons.  
But the nature of God, the splendid creator of heaven,  
governs all ages in its simplicity.

Now let the promised songs be written in a new verse;  
let the talkative page bring forth praises of virgins;  
let lines and periods proceed in groups of three feet,  
with the dactyl running through the meters except at the end;  
let the fifth foot reject the spondee;  
thus let the final letter of the trochee conclude the verse,  
the last syllable always delighting to be held at the end.  
Thus let the epigrams hasten in three feet of meter.  
I do not think anything at all is difficult for you,  
who often relax the laws of nature,  
since the monuments of ancient books testify to us beginners  
that a she-ass once spoke with human voices,  
the one that formerly brayed with a loud throat  
when the prophet wished to go forward and curse the people,  
and to strike the innocent with the weapons of words.

You can therefore, I confess, contribute more to me;  
indeed, you deign to shape my earthly form  
and breathe a living breath into my brutish breast;  
you adorn hearts with intelligence and lips with speech,  
so that no one uselessly loosens the plectra of speech,  
but tunes songs to Christ on the strings of the lyre.

But if anyone rejects the songs of the strings  
and desires better things than those he strikes with the plectrum,  
let him hear the pious Psalmist, who once sang in melodies,  
and who longs for his mind to be nourished by a great harmony,  
and refuses to be content with the delicate song alone,  
listening to the greatest organs with their thousand bellows;  
let such a one soothe his hearing with wind-filled bellows,  
however much the other instruments gleam in gilded cases.

Who will be able worthily to know the mysteries of things,  
or with an informed understanding to recognize the hidden things of God?  
Unless a burning coal from the altar, taken up with tongs,  
or a glowing ember cleanses his filthy lips,  
with which the cherub once purified the prophet’s lips,  
so that thereafter, rightly blazing with heavenly speech,  
the outstanding teacher may unlock the little chambers of the Word,  
and burn away the people’s offenses with the torches of Scripture,  
so that by doctrine he may convert many to Christ,  
changing rustic ranks into the kingdoms of heaven.

The human race is said to have a threefold distinction,  
which now dwells throughout the world on a three-cornered axis,  
and strives on earth to purchase the kingdoms of the Thunderer.

Finally, some receive the married life,  
who live rightly under the permitted law of marriage,  
and strive with all the effort of their minds  
to preserve God’s commandments while remaining under the law of the bridal chamber.

After these follows another degree of the chaste, a second order:  
the married who now reject marriage,  
and tear apart the bonds of luxury granted to them,  
leaving behind the foul companionship of polluted flesh,  
so that they may preserve their age in chaste conduct,  
while breaking the bonds of the bridal chambers formerly joined.

The third life shines with virginal lamps,  
whose dignity surpasses the rites mentioned above.  
Virginity, trampling the false mockeries of worldly luxury,  
flourishes at the highest summit of virtues,  
since it is established as the most chaste sister of angelic life.  
In it the deceptive wantonness of the age does not reign,  
but rather the spirit struggles to restrain rebellious flesh,  
so that it may suppress earthly offenses  
and overcome the enormity of crimes,  
which often customarily conquer iron-clad minds,  
however hard they may be, like a whetstone.

By these degrees, therefore, the ruler of Olympus opens  
the doors and thresholds of the heavenly palace of life,  
which we have already said above to number three.  
To these also he generously grants crops with fertile seed,  
which the pious glory of the everlasting kingdom foretold  
would grow in the plowed furrows of the rough countryside.

One hundred sheaves of merit, by right, He promised to the saints,

and continually promised to virgins a fruitful allotment,

who despise the world’s false splendors in their hearts,

[Col. 0241A] trampling underfoot the foul contagions of filthy flesh.

But Christ, the glory of heaven, brought forth sixtyfold fruits from the soil of the field,

which the chaste themselves gather as sheaves from the field:

those who now break apart the bonds of marriage,

and remove their own hiding places with devoted minds,

despising the permitted pleasures of worldly display.

Thus at last, he who reaps ten sheaves from the field

will receive threefold [i.e. thirty], he who binds the nuptial bonds,

who does not entirely trample upon the intercourse of permitted life,

but rather wishes to beget offspring and grandchildren in the world,

and gladly desires to bring forth the descendants of his stock.

Therefore, all of you whom concern for chastity inflames,

and whose hearts are pierced by love of integrity,

let spirit and chaste flesh join their covenant,

[Col. 0241B] while divine teaching declares life to be twofold.

For the gracious soul is preferred to bodily actions;

therefore let the monarchy of the mind rule continually,

so that the phantoms of the flesh may not insult the soul,

nor may the servant overcome her mistress by a foolish servile gesture,

nor ever may the handmaid rule over her mistress in proud contempt.

Now therefore let songs pluck rare flowers,

from which they may fashion virginal crowns.

What pleases the heavenly ones more in our struggle

than the love of integrity reigning in a pure heart?

For the praises of chastity nourish the heavenly beings.

Although on earth it is permitted for the generations of a family to arise,

nevertheless chastity climbs the summits of the virtues in heaven.

Virginity, preserving chaste flesh without sin,

surpasses all other praises of the virtues in glory.

[Col. 0241C] The gracious Spirit of the Most High claims it as his temple.

If the will thus burns, free from stain, in the heart,

as the holy apostolic utterance sang:

“Do you not know that you are the temples of God?”

The Spirit of the Thunderer now dwells in you by right.

To violate this is sacrilege, and to defile it is a crime.

Virginity shines like a jewel of the crown

that encircles the head of the eternal king with its diadem.

It tramples beneath its feet the associations of filthy life,

rooting out entirely the pleasures of wanton flesh.

The material of gold, and the refined metal,

from which the structure of the present world is adorned,

the filthy earth brings forth from its bosom as gravel.

So chaste integrity, the image of shining gold,

[Col. 0241D] is born from the filthy flesh of an earthly parent.

As the rose, dyed with crimson purple,

surpasses all tinctures and likewise all scarlet colors,

and as pale gravel produces purple gems,

which the dusty clod of the filthy countryside conceals,

and as a yellow flower climbs from the bark of the cornel tree

in springtime, when the earth brings forth its shoots,

so you, sweet date, are thrust forth from the leafy crown of the palm,

and from its dry trunk produce offspring.

As a pearl, shining from a shell filthy with the sea,

is born and surpasses its mother in its own honor,

and as, beneath the neglected turf of the barren countryside,

a yellow leaf draws forth threads of metal.

To conclude my examples in a twelve-line verse: thus sacred virginity is pleasing to the inhabitants of heaven.

[Col. 0242A] It takes the beginning of its life from an impure body.

As the glory of a fruitful vineyard stands in productive fields,

while the vine produces immense clusters from its branch,

and the vinedresser strips the leafy shoots with his sickles,

and as the stars yield to the brilliant light of the sun,

when the Titan surveys the earth by his slanting course,

surpassing all the stars of the heavenly spheres,

so virginity, which illustriously accompanies the saints,

surpasses all the rewards of the saints in supplication.

Integrity, too, is called queen of the virtues,

when it is joined, by chaste desire, to angelic companies.

This virtue, I say, endowed with heavenly grace,

provides golden ornaments with flame-bearing gems.

Virginity shines like the red purple of kings,

which rulers wear by right in their robes.

[Col. 0242B] The integrity of the soul reigning in a chaste body

is a virginal flower that knows no losses of old age,

nor falls to the ground as privet leaves wither.

See how lilies bloom in fertile furrows,

and how the rose reddens among the bushes with blood-red blossom.

From these the one who wins, adorned with strength in the gymnasium,

receives wreaths in the circus as victor of the contest.

In the same way integrity, having conquered rebellious flesh

and laid low the hosts of the impious,

will bear beautiful crowns when Christ reigns.

Although integrity is adorned with the praise of verse,

and the life of the chaste grows celebrated through the ages,

nevertheless those who cultivate the permitted unions of lawful life

are not deprived of Christ’s eternal gift.

The despised little silver coin does not therefore become tarnished—

[Col. 0242C] the equal ounce which the balance weighs in twelve parts—

even though a clasp with golden bosses surpasses it,

or even though golden petals shine more brightly.

Nor should the glass lamp seem worthless to you, Virgin,

whether made with scraped hide and joined willow wood,

or fashioned with the thin covering of membranes.

Even if a bronze lamp should perhaps surpass it,

or a lamp illuminating dark hiding places with its light,

the pale lights of the moon at night are not to be despised,

while night darkens the ages with its black shadows.

Though the Titan may pour forth more rays from his center

when the clouds flee and the torrid ether burns,

nor do we consider the water of a deep well contemptible,

which a pump habitually draws upward from cisterns,

[Col. 0242D] even though the chief rivers surpass the spring

whose gravel produces cold water in icy streams.

Nor is the diver entirely despised for its black wings,

though it fills the belly’s greed with scaly fish.

Nor is the chattering black jackdaw worthless,

which strives to ravage the husks of the grain and the fertile fields,

plucking sheaves from the harvest,

although the peacock’s many-colored feather may gleam yellow,

and the smooth circles of its plumage shine more brightly with red purple,

whose beautiful appearance and golden loveliness

surpass all the works of craftsmen.

So, wondrously, flesh does not know how to putrefy,

as the teachings of the men of old report to us.

This is the sign and appearance of beloved virginity,

which, with devoted mind, habitually tramples the wicked impurities of the world,

[Col. 0243A] despising the corruption of the flesh.

Nor are round pomegranates despised for their kernels,

whose rind encloses them with a single covering,

although the sweet fruits of the palm surpass them,

imitating in taste the flavors of nectar and honey.

Thus, I say, let integrity be honored in fame throughout the ages,

yet let the page not seek to tear with a twisted grin

at the chosen who bind themselves in marriage,

and who live justly according to the law of chaste wedlock.

Especially since the ancient letter of the Law tells

that the fathers of old led illustrious lives,

who by the Holy Spirit proclaimed beforehand

the gifts of salvation to come, while Christ blessed the ages.

The prophet Elijah, whom the dreadful books of Kings

remember as distinguished and held fast by the slender bonds of virtue,

[Col. 0243B] was known through the ages as a holy virgin.

For this reason he performed miracles upon the earth,

and brought forth the secret oracles of God in words,

as the sequence of the book proclaims in clear speech.

Once, relying on the lightning of heaven,

he ordered two captains of fifty [*Pentecotarchos*] to bear the flames of the fires,

and had a hundred men driven to their death,

as they likewise fulfilled the tyrant’s commands.

And when forty-two months had passed,

he closed the star-bearing heaven with a fourfold bolt,

so that the dry ether might not be sprinkled by any clouds,

and waters might be denied to the dying grasses,

nor might the thirsty meadow receive nourishment from the water.

Then, again, at the nod of the clouds, he broke their barriers,

so that abundant rains might flow from the dark ether,

[Col. 0243C] and the earth might again swell with fruitful growth,

bringing dense food to the fields blooming everywhere.

The eternal Judge ordered the prophet to ascend in a chariot,

penetrating the golden heights of heaven.

Safe, he never experienced the dangers of death,

as the rest of the crowd of ancestors lived throughout the world,

and as the crowd of descendants yet to come will live;

but the hero remains to this day in the temples of paradise.

Enoch keeps Elijah company in the heavenly dwellings—

him whom the divine power of heaven once snatched away,

so that he would not suffer the foul injuries of the wicked world.

Therefore together they carry the Thunderer’s standards

into the fierce battles against the Antichrist.

All bodies will rise from the black tombs;

the closed tombs throughout the fields will open of their own accord,

while the trumpet resounds and the clear voice of the horns rings out,

as God approaches, who assigns rewards to all—

whether the pious to the perfected, or savage punishments to the profane.

So too the prophet Elisha, burning with virginal purity,

adorned the ages with famous signs.

Golden rods marked this prophet at his birth [*bombis*: uncertain], because he destroyed the sacred things of the gods.

The gracious Spirit enriched him with a double gift,

lavishly bestowing the offices of heavenly things,

and heaped individual graces upon holy minds.

He raises a corpse bound fast in dreadful death,

although it had already been sunk in the sleep appointed by death.

But to foolish boys who sought to mock the holy prophet

and tear him apart while shouting in a loud voice,

[Col. 0244A] he freely handed them over to the jaws of bears,

because they spoke of the baldness of his head in the manner of jesters.

Thus God avenges the saints with terrifying anger,

and deservedly punishes sinners with a savage blow.

Jeremiah was renowned for possessing a double gift.

Although that illustrious hero was exceedingly rich

in the countless gifts of virtue that Christ’s grace bestows,

nevertheless, as I have said, two great gifts were especially his:

holy virginity adorned him with the flower of chastity,

as he preserved his whole life under unbroken laws,

and the heavenly foreknowledge of God filled the prophet with riches,

so that he might know things hidden in secret places

and be able by understanding to open the innermost chambers of heaven.

God consecrated him pure from his mother’s womb

before he had seen the light of the present life,

[Col. 0244B] so that he might abundantly utter the prophet’s oracles.

Concerning him the heavenly judgment of the Father declares

that long before he was born from his mother’s womb,

the virgin was sanctified by an outstanding gift.

Meanwhile the prophet was sent forth to prophesy,

so that, relying on the power of the Thunderer,

he might overthrow in the world the kingdom of the demon

and likewise the scepters of the tyrant,

and, once the malign deception had been destroyed,

build the kingdom of heaven and restore the scepters of the heavens.

He sees two rods blossoming at the height of spring [Bodl.: “with twigs”],

which perhaps signify the appearance of two peoples.

He also sees two baskets in due order.

Yet the interpretation, making them equal,

extends two peoples through the mysteries of antiquity [Bodl.: “foretells two ancient peoples through the mysteries”].

The clear monuments of the ancient writings testify

that Daniel, gracious, always flourished as a virgin.

He infused us with the rule of consecrated virginity

and showed his disciples a mirror of life.

Therefore, with prophetic voice, he announces more certainly

the times of Christ than all the ancient prophets,

explaining the number of years in right order.

He announces in the world the cradle of our king,

for he writes that four hundred and ninety years had passed

before Christ the ruler came forth into the world.

Moreover, in truthful speech he discussed future things:

that four kingdoms would arise in the world as scepters.

[Col. 0244D] First, while lying upon his bed, he saw the towering image

foretelling things through metals of various kinds.

Finally, he saw a ruler, relying on the strength of a leafy trunk,

growing from the ground with imperial power.

Its lofty crown touched the clouds,

and beneath it flocks of birds and every kind of beast

plucked sweet food from its branches.

The lofty tree was rightly marked as a tyrant.

Then the prophet understood with his prophetic heart

whose heavenly power had crushed its scepters,

until seven periods had tormented the proud one,

so that deservedly, fleeing, he might wander through thorny thickets.

And when he had despised the lashes of the terrifying Thunderer,

the filthy, shaggy tyrant sought the myrtle groves of wolves,

having become the mindless companion of four-footed beasts.

[Col. 0245A] Here too he destroyed the temples of the impious Bel,

after the priests had suffered the dangers of death for their crimes,

and he punished with bloody death the priests

who, through the deceit of the shrine, were misleading the people.

At another time, overcoming the dragon by his virtue,

he hurled a black morsel into its dreadful jaws.

When the cruel beast swallowed the pitch-black mass,

at once the creature’s punished entrails burst apart.

God always protects him from dreadful anger,

however much he may endure the torments of evils.

Finally, relying on heavenly arms,

he does not tremble before the savage assaults of beasts and the bites of lions,

although the outstanding prophet was shut up in a dark pit

among savage torturers.

Thus virginity always preserves its chaste friend,

[Col. 0245B] despising dreadful losses amid a thousand dangers.

So too, once, three boys fragrant with virginal flowers

alike preserved the laws of chastity,

despising together the golden images of the foolish tyrant.

The tyrant commands all the crowds of the people

to worship the deaf and mute metal under his terrifying authority,

when the trumpet resounds loudly with hoarse cries,

when the pipe, answering with lyres, strikes the air,

and the sambuca replies in music to the frequent trumpet calls.

Thus the people, with knees bent and legs bowed,

were to pray to the king’s golden idols throughout the fields.

But the Hebrew youth, despising the impious mockeries,

does not bend his neck in worship before the detestable images.

Therefore the impious man threatens to roast them in a furnace,

so that the fire may impose worship upon the chaste boys,

[Col. 0245C] while furious bonds encircle the arms of the pious.

At once the flames burned through the fierce bonds,

but could not consume the sacred limbs of the saints.

O wondrous thing to tell! The flame of the furnace

cooked the boys beneath the dreadful prison

with harmless fires.

But virginity despised the torments of the pyres,

while their hearts burned with sparkling faith.

For a holy angel, fiery-winged, descends from the stars,

quelling the scorching flames with cooling breezes

and extinguishing the globes of coal with heavenly rain.

But why should the page disclose only the ancient fathers,

whom the clear monuments of the books of old celebrate,

when the new grace surpasses the ancient Law,

through which the merciful Savior blessed all the ages?

[Col. 0245D] Then the prophet, filled with the sacred Spirit, first set forth John as an example to virgins,

who, while still enclosed in his mother’s womb,

recognized the Lord, with Mary bearing the pledge of heaven on earth.

In the wilderness he ate the wild food of honey

and the small bodies of locusts as his frugal fare,

and despised all other dishes of nectarous luxury.

Holy Gabriel had foretold him earlier to his father,

uttering oracles to the prophet at the right side of the altar,

when he was carrying the censer by lot in the gilded sanctuary.

But when the blessed forerunner had grown to maturity,

and was already ripening into prophetic age,

the herald proclaimed Christ’s coming throughout the world,

turning many crowds through his sacred speech.

[Col. 0246A] For the pure John the Baptist washed the world’s saving Thunderer,

plunging him into the waters of the sea.

From that point the water immediately received the sacred gifts of salvation,

which now are scattered throughout the four-cornered world,

while peoples everywhere receive the gifts of baptism.

Thus the blessed John the Baptist, a virgin, shone,

and was called the Lord’s messenger and forerunner forever.

A venerable offspring, born late, produced him for his father,

although his mother’s fruitful body had been without fruit,

and her womb had long grown cold in barren pregnancy.

No one born from a woman’s womb was greater,

except the world’s physician, the offspring begotten by the Thunderer.

Therefore the pure one washed the world, free from the stain of sin,

and baptized Christ beneath the flowing water,

sanctifying the watery blue expanse of the sea with its wandering waves,

[Col. 0246B] and granting the gifts of birth through glass-clear springs,

while the old return again to the cradles of life.

Then, as God left the green marble waters of the streams

and traversed the riverbanks with holy steps,

the high barriers of the heavenly realms opened.

While the ruler of Olympus thundered from the lofty ether,

addressing his offspring with a word carried through the air:

“This is, behold, my beloved Son,” he says,

“whom it has pleased me to reign over the whole world.”

The gracious Spirit descended from heaven upon Christ,

coming swiftly in the likeness of a dove.

For this reason the bird is associated with the sacred Spirit:

alone, it lacks the cruel gall of poison,

whereas the rest of the feathered host growl in anger.

But that swift bird bears a gentle whiteness.

[Col. 0246C] The prophet, suffering very many torments for Christ,

endured the filth of prison and the dark places without light,

condemning the marriage of the savage king,

who had broken the covenant of his brother’s blood,

and had unlawfully violated his kinsman’s marriage bed.

Therefore he restrained the tyrant sharply with his voice,

not fearing the raging torments of an impious death.

Immediately the platters grew red with poured-out blood,

when they carried the severed head to the people’s banquet.

The fierce queen had demanded it through her daughter’s deceit,

the theatrical virgin displaying her spectacle in a dance.

Thus he marked Christ with the purple of blood,

the dreadful wound healing the wound of the world,

when the violence of criminals compelled the innocent one

to bear punishments while hanging upon the exposed wood of the cross.

[Col. 0246D] Nevertheless the ages experienced the desired salvation,

when God descended to the wandering shades of Erebus,

to break the iron thresholds of the gate-bearing doors

and shatter the bronze barriers of the dreadful gates,

as the Psalmist had earlier sung with prophetic voice,

proclaiming at the end that the Thunderer would suffer for the world.

Now I shall strive to bring forth the sacred John in speech,

who reclined most beloved beside gracious Christ,

and drank rivers from the sacred breast of the teacher,

filling his belly with eternal rains while thirsting.

He preserved the flowering years of a chaste life,

shuddering utterly at intercourse with false flesh.

Therefore, as he spread abroad very many seeds of fame,

the report of his virtues grew throughout the wide world.

[Col. 0247A] The discourse does not therefore rehearse his appearance in every detail,

but the page explains his kind in a rugged verse.

Meanwhile he raises corpses sunk in the sleep of death,

which the cold bonds of death had tightly fastened.

He restored sight by touching the eyes of the blind,

and immediately ordered the lame to go upon strengthened feet.

The deaf received harmonious sound through their ears,

and the mute likewise released their lips into speech.

He granted life to crippled hands once they were healed.

He did not feel the black harms of dark poisons,

although he drank deadly draughts with his throat.

Thus we read that Saul was made famous in ancient times,

the man who despised Christ’s teachings at the command of rulers,

tormenting the gracious limbs of blessed men,

while he wished the obscurities of the ancient Law to reign,

[Col. 0247B] and to set the ancestral rites of the elders above Christ.

Meanwhile, with his name changed, the holy Paul

earned the praises of apostolic fame.

A sacred diadem of virginal chastity accompanies him,

although long before he had condemned in a dreadful prison

the bodies of the crowds who kept the covenants of Christ.

Thus the exalted God, who changes the hearts of the guilty,

dragged the excellent sheep from the savage jaws of wolves.

He often turns black crows, dark with dreadful blackness,

into white doves without bluish gall,

while mercifully loosening the crimes of sinners

and granting the bright gifts of sacred virtues.

When the Father twice called him aloud from the high citadel,

Paul fell face-first with bent knee,

surrounded by darkness and deprived of the sight of bright light,

[Col. 0247C] although, blinded, he felt the injuries to his pupil.

Nevertheless, from heaven he saw the Sun shining,

the one who would always illuminate hearts with serene light.

He was an outstanding teacher and master of the world,

turning barbarian hosts through sacred teachings.

Luke, formed in the likeness of a four-footed calf,

wrote the bright teachings in a divine book.

He wrote the names of the seventy-seven fathers,

from whom Christ, the almighty glory of kingdoms,

was begotten and took the cradle of our flesh.

Sacred wreaths of virginal flowers adorned him,

when he had lived forty-seven years,

relating the Lord’s lineage from its first origin,

while hidden chaos and sluggish confusion of things

had covered the ages with dreadful hiding places.

[Col. 0247D] He opened the Father’s heavenly treasures with a key,

until the all-powerful creator of the four-cornered world

had formed the flowering ages beneath the heavenly clouds.

This man, once a physician, healed wounds of the flesh,

tending putrid ulcers in the fibers with nourishing care.

Thereafter, as Paul’s disciple, he removed from the doctrine of Scripture

the sins of guilty souls and the crimes of wickedness

that inflict wounds upon the mind.

Finally, after death, he adorns with his sacred bones

the seat of the Augusti, where now the monarchy of the world,

after the empire of Rome, reigns beneath the vault of heaven.

Rome produced the priest Clement in ancient times,

to whom clemency rightly gives his name.

God enriched him freely with heavenly grace,

[Col. 0248A] while he preserved himself pure through the gift of virginity.

The heavenly seed of the Word brought forth this pledge, and Peter, who presides over the summit of the apostolic church, granted him the sacred beginnings of baptism.

For the disciple, devotedly following faithful footsteps,

equals the sacred teacher who continually teaches doctrine

and frequently sows the heavenly commands of God.

Thus it happened that he visited his aged parents

and likewise his own brothers, his blood relations,

whom Peter, the famous fisherman of Christ throughout the world,

snatched from the sea of the world in angelic nets

and carried with himself, blessed, to the stars of heaven.

At the time when the illustrious ruler shone throughout the world,

the age called him Constantine,

Sylvester lived in Rome as bishop,

[Col. 0248B] the holy man who ruled the heights of the apostolic seat.

This priest performed very many signs of virtue,

which are now read throughout the world, inserted in writings.

Finally, by his virtue, he bound a scaly dragon,

fastening its strength with iron chains.

Previously, breathing forth a deadly spirit from a crypt,

it had troubled the hosts of the Roman kingdom by right,

while they had despised serving Christ alone,

thinking instead to offer worship to the cult of the dreadful serpent.

But when he had bound the beast with tight collars,

restraining the diseased breaths of the poisonous dragon,

joy immediately arose among the happy citizens.

The beast hid itself, although previously it had been accustomed to rage.

Therefore, at once, the shining grace of baptism

illuminated the Roman citadels from heaven like the sun.

[Col. 0248C] He healed Constantine’s diseased limbs,

driving away the horrible scaly ulcers of leprosy,

when he baptized the ruler beneath the water.

Therefore Rome shattered the shrines of its sanctuary,

despising the ancient temples of the impious gods,

and pursued the higher heights of the new temple,

marked by the blood of the Savior and shining brightly,

proclaiming the perpetual triumphs of God throughout the ages.

Thus it adorned the vast world with its own customs,

when it corrected the king of Rome with the doctrine of Christ.

Moreover, that same teacher fought a contest

against twelve masters contending with skill.

They denied the pledge of the world with deceitful speech,

while they despised the gifts of the Mediator who calls,

the one who opens the bright gates of perpetual life.

Therefore, relying on heavenly arms,

he immediately overcame them all, obtaining the victory he desired.

Like a soldier confronting snarling mastiffs,

which vainly fill the upper air with their barking,

he directed the iron arrows of Scripture,

while all the others, terrified, soon turned their backs—

except Zambri, who then, relying on necromancy,

deceived the ignorant people with a fraudulent trick.

While the magician deceitfully whispered without a voice into the bull,

the four-footed beast collapsed to the ground, abandoning its breath,

while the immense shouting of the crowd struck the cloudy heavens.

But the fearless Sylvester worships the Lord,

so that the people whom Christ, through the purple of his precious blood,

had made free from guilt, after the malign deceit had been removed,

[Col. 0249A] would not be deceived by the dreadful apparition of false Zambri.

Then he raises the bull’s corpse, struck down by death,

loosening the bonds of its tightened knots,

and caused the gentle bull to return to the herd.

Then the people everywhere cried out to the Thunderer,

and, praising the Lord, began to give thanks.

This man, as the story goes, obtained the companionship of integrity,

and remained so until he closed his final life.

Once King Constantine, examining reliable prophecies

and investigating dreams of future things,

while preparing the emperor’s limbs upon a feathered couch,

saw in an ecstatic vision the figure of a wrinkled matron

with an aged and misshapen brow,

walking with bowed head and trembling arms.

Moreover, the bitter lot of death already punished her.

[Col. 0249B] The illustrious priest Sylvester commands the king in speech

to restore the old woman’s decrepit body,

so that she might again return to life in health.

Then, at the king’s prayers, a beautiful young woman rose,

whom the grim appearance of old age had previously disfigured.

Although earlier she had lain stiff as a corpse in death,

she immediately became a beautiful young mother in appearance.

The king, rejoicing, gazes upon her, accompanied by her diadem.

He encircles her temples and crowns them with shining gold,

and adorns her with the cloak of a chlamys and with cyclades,

so that, as queen, she might wear red ornaments upon her neck.

Such was the appearance of the beautiful and gracious virgin.

Then Helena, teaching the king future things in speech,

said thus to Augustus, revealing everything in the dream:

[Col. 0249C] “This woman will always be yours, for she will lack the stroke of death,

unless the final ages burn in dreadful flames.”

When Augustus was terrified upon his lofty bed,

he awoke pale, seized by fear of the dream.

He gathered into an assembly eloquent sophists skilled in their art,

who boast of empty doctrines with puffed-up folly.

He asked them to unravel for him the hidden fates of things,

the future mysteries that had been marked earlier in the bedchamber.

But when they reported nothing in their foolish speech,

and had fabricated many trifles with false words,

then the king chastened his frugal limbs by fasting,

and abstained from sumptuous food for seven days,

asking Christ the Lord to reveal the oracles.

Night fell and enclosed the world in a dreadful veil,

and likewise embraced the earth with dark wings,

while sleep occupied the royal limbs upon the bed.

To him Sylvester spoke, revealing the mysteries of things:

“The woman whom you saw grow old beneath a grim light,

who greatly horrified you with her squalid old age,

is the city commonly called Byzantium.

After this it will be called Constantinople forever;

indeed, it bears your name’s triumphs throughout the ages.

In it, once, the lofty summits of the walls—

now thrown down upon the ground as the crumbling citadel collapses—

grow old; the walls decay and the fortifications totter,

shaken by rot and broken by exhausted age.

But I shall command you to preserve my instructions.

Riding upon a horse’s back,

remember to furrow the ground with the point of a standard.

[Col. 0250A] Thus, riding, drive the standards across the land with your right hand,

cutting four furrows along a straight path.

Through these, with the high towers of the camps raised,

restore the walls with red tiles,

and in them a son and the sons of sons will reign,

as the numerous offspring of the fathers reigned,

whose descendants and ancestors are gathered together.”

Once Ambrose was a priest famous for the praise of Hesperia,

fulfilling the gracious commands of Christ.

He preserved the covenant of spirit and chaste flesh,

and bore a name derived from the nectar of ambrosia.

Once, when he was still a little child in his cradle,

he displayed great portents of future events.

For a swarm of bees, in a numerous cluster,

covered the child’s face—a wondrous thing to tell.

[Col. 0250B] Although they surrounded his lips with a dreadful company,

the child’s body nevertheless felt no danger.

Again and again they filled the mouth of the one lying there,

and then strove to return in a swarm.

Afterward, returning in a mass to the heavenly clouds,

they struggled to withdraw beyond human sight.

Ambrose’s father was astonished to see these marvels,

and from this the illustrious child received his name.

For this swarm, with which the saint’s lips overflowed,

foretold the sweet words of honeyed favor,

from which the hearts of the people would grow abundantly sweet.

The venerable teacher arranged bright little works,

revealing with devout reasoning from the beginning

how the wisdom of the highest Father

made this present world through twice three days,

ordering the ages by his eternal will.

[Col. 0250C] This, I say, the priest taught in frequent speech,

leading many ranks to the kingdoms of heaven.

Now let the loquacious page reveal the praise of Martin,

whom the whole world beneath the fourfold sphere celebrates.

The almighty Father blessed him with heavenly praise at night,

when he had not yet been washed in baptism

or anointed with the sacred chrism of balsams,

while he carried alms to the crippled and a cloak to the needy,

already devoted to Christ as a catechumen.

Who, relying on eloquent speech,

would attempt to describe in writings all the signs of his virtues,

and how many gifts God bestowed upon his devoted servant?

Often he corrected the villages with saving doctrine,

so that they might wish more fully to uproot impious rites

[Col. 0250D] and believe in Christ the reigning Creator.

For he destroyed the profane shrines of the pagans,

overthrowing by right the temples of guilty tyrants.

Then, having broken the deceit of the ancient sanctuary,

the venerable priest built temples for the Most High.

So too he cut down the famous pine with its leafy trunk,

which foolish nobles once used to burn incense before,

when—alas, the crime!—they roasted the entrails of two-year-old sheep upon spits,

so that error in worship would not deceive the people.

Three times he caused dead corpses to rise from death,

breaking apart the dreadful realms of terrifying death,

and likewise bestowing the gifts of life upon the sick.

He tended the diseased limbs of feeble men.

Although he had never experienced wounds from iron,

nor, as a martyr, dripped red with blood,

nor burned in dreadful fires,

[Col. 0251A] nevertheless he earned the glorious palm of confession,

since his mind had been prepared to endure the dangers of death.

This bishop remained continually an everlasting virgin

until, as a soldier, he departed into the heavenly court,

carried by angelic hosts to the vaults of heaven.

In ancient times Greece produced venerable fathers,

among whose number the blessed Gregory stands most famous,

renowned in fame above the ether.

God taught him to preserve bodily purity

and to join it to the covenant of a chaste mind.

For once, seeing two women in a dream,

he saw girls shining with virginal flowers.

When he looked upon them, he recoiled with severe eyes,

because he did not wish to gaze upon female faces.

[Col. 0251B] Then both addressed the holy man with gentle voices:

“Do not harshly reject, young man, the maidens devoted to you,

nor, in anger, despise the face of your sisters,

since we are joined to you by the perpetual love of a brother.

For you have given us a pure sanctuary in your heart,

where, rejoicing, we shall both always be nourished.

Brother, you will never be deprived of our friendship.

One of us is called Virginity, with fruitful flower;

the other will bear the name of diligent Wisdom.

We have been sent here from angelic dwellings

so that our companionship in life may remain with you.”

Once Basil, the greatest authority among teachers,

established an excellent law through divine doctrine.

From it proceeded the rule of a balanced life,

which bends toward no side beneath a cruel burden.

It weighs the chosen with a just measure of the little book,

and in alternating turns [Bodl.: “with alternating voices”] gives oracles to the saints,

teaching how the true harmony of brothers may be adorned

and how the covenants of a just mind may continually shine.

He also arranged a book in eloquent speech,

revealing the first beginnings of created things:

how the eternal ruler fashioned the ages,

and by what power he founded the four-cornered world,

distinguishing the world’s matter in right order,

while forming the golden stars of the inclined heaven.

Hence for us arises the origin of the world at its birth,

when the highest prince of things forged its works.

[Col. 0251D] Here he declares that he preserved virginal chastity,

affirming thus in perfected speech, the bishop:

“Never did I know female bodies in reckless fashion,

nor did I shamefully touch women’s limbs.

Nevertheless I shall not be called by the name ‘virgin.’”

The land of Memphis produced illustrious fathers,

purchasing the bright gifts of perpetual life.

Among their number, by blessed fortune, there flourished

the famous and fortunate teacher named Antony,

seeking the highest kingdoms of the heavens.

He first taught holy devotees in an ordered community [Bold.: *accola*, “dweller”]

to seek the barren countryside through desolate wildernesses,

so that in them they might pluck contemplative fruits

and continually serve the exalted Lord.

[Col. 0252A] This man, I say, instructed those who desired the kingdoms of heaven

to despise delicacies and abandon the treasures of the world,

to pursue difficult paths and avoid the downward slopes.

For two roads extend by different courses:

one through the fields of heaven toward the heavenly heights,

the other thus surveys the depths of Erebus without end.

Whoever wishes to learn of his glorious life,

by what signs the gracious man shone in the world,

and in what manner he healed filthy bodily diseases,

restoring dreadful ulcers by saving care,

how, as a physician resisting the diseases of peoples,

he renewed diseased inward parts with healed tissues—

let him by no means hesitate to examine the sequence of the little book

in which his extensive virtues are written.

In no different way Paul, renowned for signs above the ether,

[Col. 0252B] and throughout all the kingdoms that the lights of Phoebus survey,

was more excellent than any other in the desert,

and, a blessed soldier, journeyed toward eternal dwellings.

His treacherous son-in-law preferred to deceive this innocent man

with a crooked gesture, breaking the bonds of peace.

Therefore, fleeing, he sought hiding places beneath a rock,

until the torments of the savage torturer should cease,

and the world should again rejoice in peaceful times.

A date palm nourished him in a narrow cavern,

and he enjoyed its leaves instead of a sunny covering.

The water of a spring removed the heat of his thirst.

As soon as it had been produced, the bluish gravel of the earth

had again poured its waters obliquely into the cave.

A winged creature, rushing down, fed him with a slender supply of grain

in the cave beneath the lofty palm leaves.

[Col. 0252C] Lions, though they had rejected savagery, served him,

and he ordered wolves to soften their savage jaws.

He lived on earth, relying on a heavenly gift,

for one hundred and thirteen fortunate years.

Then at last, accompanied by heavenly hosts as was his due,

the chaste man went to the fellowship of the eternal kingdom,

about to receive new joys as a victor on high.

Likewise, relying on the outstanding grace of his virtues,

the blessed Hilarion, known by his famous name,

performed many wondrous signs in the desert.

The present world often celebrates him in its report,

while he eagerly strives to equal the rule of his teacher

and to imitate the measure of his own father.

He restrained his wanton body under a strict law,

[Col. 0252D] extinguishing the burning fires of lascivious flesh.

He despised the first beginnings of tickling luxury,

severely trampling upon the games of early youth.

He became renowned in Egypt, as I set forth in strict verse.

For he burned the gypsum which had long ago swallowed

the wretched natives in its dark jaws,

destroying it in flames,

while a pyre blazing with an immense supply of wood

consumed in the furnace the creeping *chelydrus* amid the embers [the source’s *gipsum … chelydrum* is materially uncertain].

Finally, when once the waters of the sea boiled

with mountainous waves across the glassy fields,

and the swelling sea no longer knew its ancient shores,

but the deep blue waters ruled over the wandering masses,
While they spurned their own shores amid the foaming waves,

then all together, massing in a dense formation,

they stood against the swollen breakers before the holy old man,

[Col. 0253A] and duly entreated their trembling and faithful patron

to bring aid unbidden to the afflicted citizens.

He traced the signs of the cross, and at once the dreadful heap

of salt waters, rising higher and higher toward the stars of heaven,

grew solid; then he restrained the raging blue waters of the savage sea.

Thus Christ’s soldier curbed the marble waters of the deep,

so that, deservedly, the holy man’s fame should never perish.

So too, it is said, John journeyed in Egypt,

dwelling in the desert and leading a blameless life.

He bound his own years with tight bonds,

overcoming the fleshly prison of a wanton mind,

preserving a double burden with just moderation,

while divine teaching instructs that life is twofold,

which the ruler must distinguish with a just balance,

[Col. 0253B] and must understand how the movement of the flesh is to be governed.

Famous grace filled this unlearned prophet,

so that he could unlock the hidden recesses of things,

revealing secret mysteries with a virginal key.

For once, in a dream, a woman perceived

how richly he had been endowed with the gift of virtues,

when she received the healing she desired in the flesh,

although previously she had carried whatever complaint she had groaning in her heart.

When Rome, flourishing, held sovereignty over the world

and governed the scepters of kingdoms throughout the earth,

in those same times blessed Benedict shone forth,

whom the merciful Creator had granted to Ausonia,

so that he might lead the people of the Lord, traveling along the straight path,

to the footsteps of the eternal ruler of the kingdom:

[Col. 0253C] whom error, previously hidden in savage winding paths,

had dragged to the black depths of the infernal torrent.

He often shattered the temples of former tyrants,

who denied the Lord of light with darkened hearts.

Then, planting there the victorious standards of salvation,

Christ’s soldier triumphs over the defeated enemy,

restoring a basilica to the Lord in a renewed building.

What method, number, or reckoning could possibly explain

his mighty virtues,

which exceed measure and number in proportion to the magnitude of his deeds?

For he restored light to dead bodies,

which the power of cold death had deprived of life.

He gave hearing to the deaf and adorned the lame with steps.

He revived the sick, increasing the strength of their limbs.

[Col. 0253D] Driving away the weapons of the demon and likewise breaking its darts,

he restored wounded hearts after the enemies had been expelled.

For he renewed a sieve broken by a fragment of its cracks,

when the nurse poured forth rivers of tears.

He shattered by the signs of salvation, with his outstretched right hand,

the deadly cup that held the draughts of death.

So too, he ordered the Goth’s steel implement, which had fallen into the whirlpool,

to return again to its owner’s arms.

He was the first to establish the disciplines of our life,

and taught how monasteries should keep their desired rule,

and by what straight path the holy man should hasten,

as a worshiper climbing to the heights, the summits of heaven—

whose illustrious life, revealing it from its beginning,

Bishop Gregory once set down in writing,

until the blessed man migrated to the heavenly citadel—

[Col. 0254A] among the number of whose disciples we joyfully gather

those whom fruitful Britain bears as citizens in her bosom;

from him the grace of baptism has already flowed to us,

and the venerable company of teachers has run forth.

Why should I mention the two brothers joined by fraternal bond,

who gave their souls to the stars and their bodies to the earth?

Revering Christ, who suffered in purple blood,

they became martyrs and reddened with bloody flesh;

and they give back to the Lord what the Psalmist sang:

“Behold, the cup of salvation through the draughts of death”—

together they receive it, proceeding along Christ’s path.

The holy Ambrose found them together, Saint Paul revealing them to him,

their bodies lying buried;

a square-hewn stone tomb covers them in its excavated chambers.

[Col. 0254B] Holy virginity adorned them with a heavenly flower,

virginity that is always dear to the angelic hosts.

One was Gervasius, the other Protasius;

they bear names assigned to them by the authority of the ancients.

There was once a bishop, perhaps named Narcissus,

fragrant with the merits of his virtues and flourishing in name,

whom the summit of the episcopate adorned together

with the honor of virginity, shining with a double gift.

Therefore he became famous throughout the world,

while his teaching was supported by the merits of his life.

For he made the waters of a spring grow rich with oil,

and changed liquid streams into thick drops.

Finally, when the season suited to the Paschal feasts arrived,

and he renewed throughout the world the annual vows of Christ’s worshipers—

the season in which Christians usually celebrate Christ’s triumphs

more abundantly than the other solemn festivals of the year—

[Col. 0254C] then the oil ran out in the empty glass lamp,

and the smoking wick grew numb beneath dark shadows,

while the hanging lamp gave no light at all.

At once Narcissus ordered the fountain’s liquid waters,

trusting in the Lord, to be drawn by the sacred ministers

and to fill the hollow glass with its greenish stream.

Meanwhile the water poured through all the lamps;

thus, exorcising the lamps, he blessed them although filled with water.

Now the shining liquid was feeding the devouring flames,

and papyrus glowed with light at its very center,

brighter by far than the rich fuel of olive oil,

or than the swine’s fat shining in glass.

Then the crowd, seeing the miracles,

[Col. 0254D] repeatedly offered common thanks and praise to God.

The assailant could not bear this blessed fame to grow—

he who strives to destroy [Bodl., “mock”] the human race by deceptions.

He gathered [Bodl., “they gathered”] an evil council with three witnesses,

who contrived [Bodl., “he contrived”] a dreadful crime through a false accusation,

so that they might attack the bishop’s reputation with a serpent’s tooth

and maliciously slander the holy man with poisoned deceit.

One of their number came forward first;

although he swore an oath, he spoke deceitfully by treacherous fraud:

“May I burn utterly in black fires and flames stuffed with fuel

if I invent a frivolous falsehood.”

Another followed, bringing a deceitful complaint;

[Col. 0255A] thus he addressed the crowds in an insolent voice:

“May my body not perish from the royal disease, though the sworn declaration utters true words.”

But the third witness brought forth his complaint from his heart,

and, foolishly, tried to bind the knots of his oath

with false words chained together:

“May my eyes not grow black in gloomy darkness,

nor glaucoma completely cloud my diseased eyes,

if I, the truthful accuser, invent false words.”

Therefore the priest chose to endure exile,

turning aside from injustice and fleeing the stain of envy.

Thus, it is said, the father lived withdrawn in the wilderness,

gathering contemplative bands beneath the mountain,

while he alone desired to serve Christ alone,

trampling the slippery joys of the deceiving world.

[Col. 0255B] Then punishment immediately chastised the witnesses mentioned above,

who contrived frivolous falsehoods by means of false oaths

and attempted to accuse the innocent prophet of a crime.

Behold, the wicked witness burns in a torrid dwelling,

the first who twisted weapons from his impious lips,

so that evil words might darken the bishop’s life.

The lofty roof crackled, scorched by fiery embers,

and the heat burned the surrounding crowds.

So too, the punishment grew savage against the second,

afflicting his jaundiced limbs with the royal disease,

until a rotting breath issued from his chest.

The third was deprived of the two windows beneath his brow,

while the clear lights of his eyes were closed in dreadful darkness.

Then, trembling, he observed the torments of the others,

how the Most High punished their deceitful tricks,

[Col. 0255C] and revealed the obscure scene of their horrible crime.

The plot was exposed, and its blind contrivances were confounded;

and the guilty man poured forth such rivers of tears,

irrigating his face with the salty springs of his eyes,

until his pupils were deprived of the light of their little eyes.

Thus the Thunderer’s threefold vengeance punished the guilty,

until bitter death raged in the flight of life.

While the eternal Judge punished the crimes of the guilty,

he displayed the glorious praises of the holy priest.

Meanwhile the Memphite land was no less astonished

by the renowned reports of the fathers beneath the vault of heaven,

among whom the blessed Athanasius had once arisen,

whose most holy nurturer was Alexander.

By him Arius, who taught the savage schism, was defeated,

when the ill-fated man shamefully expelled the foul contents of his belly,

his intestines torn from the anal passages,

which filled the hollow chambers of the latrine vaults.

[Col. 0255D] When the sacred offerings of the Mass were being celebrated

and the libations of the holy table were being performed,

Saint Alexander saw crowds of children along the shore,

imitating the divine mysteries in a wondrous game.

For he saw from afar that Athanasius was thus

immersing those children in the waters of baptism,

as though he were a bishop ordained according to sacred custom.

Such signs foretold that he would become a holy man,

as the favorable outcome of events clearly declared.

But the seriousness behind this game was confirmed by its alphabetic signs,

when gracious Alexander closed his life in death.

After this, Athanasius succeeded him, flourishing in his age:

[Col. 0256A] as a shepherd he guards the watches of the flock and the sheepfold

against the jaws and deceits of wild beasts and wolves,

which habitually scour the sheep-pens and enclosures of the two-year-old sheep.

This bishop, therefore, courageously endured the foolish doctrines

of the schismatics, fierce and dangerous even in their honeyed words.

The same schismatics, deceiving with their dense crowd,

attempted to disgrace him by inventing frivolous falsehoods,

while they displayed to the emperor an arm torn from the flesh

and carried a mutilated body in a coffin for public spectacle—

something which the foolish claimed had been produced by magical phantoms—

saying shamefully that Arsenius was mutilated in body,

although he had once been a reader along the path of the books.

Then Augustus Constantius ordered the gracious prophet

to be driven away [Bodl., “summoned”] immediately from that region.

[Col. 0256B] But matters turned out differently from what the crooked scheme expected,

when the aforesaid reader exposed the black fraud.

Then the pious bishop, after the malicious fraud had been revealed [Bodl., “of the malicious one”]:

“Behold,” he said, “look upon the reader’s sound right hand,

and all of you observe his strong left hand as well.”

Then a new triumph grew through innocent praise,

when they recognized that the priest was holy and without guilt.

The adversary was stunned when the fraud was exposed.

O what a boxwood pallor covered the helpless men—

or, rather, what men were marked by the redness of a shameful brow!

Thus, with God’s support, the guilty fabrications collapsed.

But the viper, crushed beneath the wheels, raised its head

and again vomited foul poison from its throat.

For they tried to deceive the holy man by another fraud.

[Col. 0256C] A shameless woman, equipped with wicked tricks,

attempted to accuse the prophet of the crime of adultery.

But more quickly than words, the presbyter blunted the darts of speech with his shield,

overcoming the adulteress by his stratagem,

whom the hooked hand of one who raises it sharply and disgracefully seizes.

Nevertheless, the bishop, relying on Christ’s shield,

avoided the inventions of his savage enemies.

He concealed himself for the course of years,

descending into the deep hiding place of a cistern,

which, empty of water, offered the shelter of a little roof:

there, they say, he lay hidden as the years revolved,

so that nowhere might he see Phoebus shining with light.

Yet he never ceased to behold with the eyes of his heart

the sun of justice of the sevenfold heaven,

which sacred Scripture described in its splendid books.

[Col. 0256D] Now let the talkative little page of Babylas bring forth the palm of victory,

revealing many praises of the illustrious bishop,

who had been trained by written doctrine of the books

to guard the watches of the flock and the folds of the sheep

against the dreadful bites and jaws of wolves.

The prince who had bound together the vast power of Rome—

indeed, the square-shaped world within its measured boundaries—

when, with no hesitation in his step, he fiercely wished to approach

the threshold of the holy gate, goaded on by malicious deceit,

then the pious bishop rebuked the proud Augustus with his voice,

scolding him while disregarding the emperor’s rank,

and defending by his speech the entrance hall of the sacred temple.

Boldly he ordered the emperor, stained with bloody slaughter,

not to touch the church’s apse with his impure hands.

[Col. 0257A] Therefore the bishop was led to a narrow court,

so that the crooked man might speak with the emperor in place of words.

At once the impious ruler began to compel the venerable Christian

with punishments, binding him in tight chains,

so that he might supplicate the ancient images of the gods

and, making sacrificial offerings of holocausts to the statues in the shrines [Bodl., “in the shrine”];

but the blessed priest rejected these filthy poisons,

and did not bend his neck to the shrine’s flatteries.

Then the Augustus ordered three infants, united by brotherly bond,

whom the pious bishop had instructed in the doctrine of Scripture,

to be tormented with slow lashes,

so that their hearts, which had previously resisted obedience

to the wicked king, might yield beneath the blows.

Yet the bodies of the children did not yield to the punishments;

[Col. 0257B] rather, their hearts overcame the dreadful rods,

although the blows poured out streams of blood

and raw wounds sprinkled their tender flesh.

At last the priest, having endured a capital punishment,

sought the blue heavens, borne aloft and triumphing in death;

and likewise, as their master ascended on high, the ephebes—that is, the youths whom red garlands of roses

adorned—entered together the summit of heaven in triumph,

joined to the angelic hosts as they penetrated the heights.

Who, urbane in polished speech, could utter

the clear praises of the saints beneath the vault of heaven,

where Titan pours his golden rays throughout the world

while he traverses the broad earth on his returning course?

Yet the babbling page, bringing forth these excellent men

in rough verse, will now begin to celebrate

[Col. 0257C] those whom one mother, bearing twins together,

brought forth into the world, endowed with two names.

One was called Cosmas, the other Damianus.

She imparted to them alike the healing arts of the world,

and divine grace also freely bestowed its gifts,

so that they could drive out putrid diseases from the body

and apply healing care to illnesses,

expelling dreadful afflictions from the body by their arts.

The mute, the maimed, the lame, and the deaf;

the one-eyed and the cross-eyed, who enjoy distorted light;

the stammerers and stutterers, who corrupt their words

while speaking with savage utterance;

and whatever else is considered weak—

they restored by heavenly means, Christ granting salvation.

Thus by medicine they drove away the corruption of the diseased flesh.
