Yet, though rich in the exceptional gift of virtues,

[Col. 0257D] they did not carry purses stuffed with deceptive gold;

they trampled the money-boxes of coin as though they were foul poisons,

giving everything freely in exchange for heavenly reward.

Meanwhile the ruler of the world, who held the scepters,

cruelly punished the martyrs by savage edicts.

Then he plunged the two brothers mentioned above into the sea,

while they trusted in the power of the Thunderer;

but the icy waters grew gentle in their glassy waves,

and, at the word’s command, carried the holy men swiftly to the shore.

Thus the sacred power of salt water, restrained by virtue,

quieted the swelling blue waters across the wave-tossed plain,

while the Father’s right hand opened a harbor in the waters.

Therefore, when the impious man saw the banners of victory,

he devised another disaster through Gorgon-like poisons.

[Col. 0258A] For the savage tyrant heated the cruel fuel of flames

and filled the furnace of the sacred rites with fuel.

He ordered the holy men to be thrust into the blazing furnace,

so that the fire might burn the innocent limbs with the heat of its embers—

limbs which the swelling sea had previously been unable

to submerge beneath its black waves of water.

Thus the furnace’s torch grew cold despite the fuel,

so that Christ’s soldier, disregarding the storm of flame,

might offer immense thanks for his life preserved,

like the salamander that habitually leaps through the fires of pyres,

although a heap of pyres may be gathered together.

Then they forced them to climb upon the exposed timber

and to endure the dense arrows of the quivers.

At once the eternal Creator, who rightly grants triumph to the saints,

broke the dreadful arrows of the guilty torturers.

[Col. 0258B] Thereafter they received bloody garlands of martyrdom,

migrating to the lofty, vaulted heights of heaven.

Nor do I delay to recall the brilliant praises of Chrysanthus,

whom the world deservedly celebrates with famous praise.

His father, when he was flourishing in his earliest years,

handed him over as a boy to teachers of rhetoric,

so that the beardless boy might learn the arts of books—

arts which worldly wisdom foolishly cultivates.

He was, they say, endowed with an acute mind,

burning with intelligence and mature in prudent judgment.

Afterward, when the illustrious reader had absorbed

with his ears the sacred volumes written in heavenly script,

he immediately scorned the doctrines of the ancient sect,

trampled the empty falsehoods of the old laws,

and, having quickly acquired the rudiments of faith,

[Col. 0258C] learned through the water of baptism to wash away the foulness of sin.

Then he openly preached Christ to the pagans,

freely disregarding the dreadful tortures of their proud threats.

His father, therefore, overturning the laws of nature,

thrust his son into the darkness of a sealed prison,

greatly fearing the decrees of the wicked treasury

and, trembling, dreading the capital punishment as well.

But when the young man’s mind willingly endured the torments,

his father soon contrived another scene:

he brought seductive worldly pleasures before him,

offering silken garments in purple robes,

which the worm produces from its dying, stinking womb,

and clothed the excellent youth, shining in precious attire.

Then, at his father’s command, girls brought lavish banquets,

as well as delights, food, and the luxuries of the kitchen,

[Col. 0258D] adorned in various garments and lovely in face,

so that the bold soldier might be softened by such spectacles—

spectacles before which men’s iron hearts often yield.

Yet the young man, armed with Christ’s shield,

scorned slippery kisses from virginal lips

and did not permit the darts of fornication to pierce his breast;

instead, he cast far away the arrows hurled by deceit.

Not as the poet sang in a nuptial song,

“When soft lips cling to rose-red lips,”

but Christ’s sweet lips grew languid upon those lips.

At last the grown virgin came to the contest,

Daria, a Vestal, blushing with a beautiful face,

whom a golden crescent accompanied with pale-blue gems.

She tried to bind the young man in Venus’s bond,

so as to bend his mind toward the marriage rites of the bridal chamber.

[Col. 0259A] She was adorned and relied upon eloquent speech.

Indeed, the eloquent teachers were astonished

at the girl’s intelligence, cultivated by the language of the books [Par., “supported”].

She had been tenacious of writing and swift at reading.

But the dark course of fortune turned out otherwise,

when the pious man opposed contrary fate to fate.

Daria, who had previously served the divinity of Vesta,

was converted by Chrysanthus’ eloquent words

and believed in the Most High, who governs the scepters of heaven.

Then they pretended to share a marriage bed,

but both lived harmoniously in chaste conduct,

so that they might wholly avoid the foul stain in their hearts

and flee from their hearts the dark blemish of Venus.

[Col. 0259B] After this she was washed in the sacred waters of baptism,

so that she might strip old things from her mind

and take up a new garment from the flowing water.

Then the virgin rejected the teachings of the ancient books

and followed the doctrines of Christ in the sacred Scriptures.

Who could count the great crowds of the people

whom they compelled by their examples to believe in Christ?

Therefore he was handed over to be tortured by bitter punishments.

Seventy men guarded him in a dense troop,

in the temple of Hercules, unless perhaps he should offer incense.

Then the savage soldiery began to torment the one who refused,

the athlete of the Lord, trusting in heavenly power,

constricting him with wet and raw bonds of sinew,

while he was to endure the scorching heat of the blazing sun.

But more quickly than a moment, the ropes were loosened from his arms,

[Col. 0259C] when almighty God dissolved the wicked cords.

Again the fetters of stocks closed around his shins,

and they bound his swollen legs with rigid pieces of wood.

Immediately the ruler of Olympus split the stock,

although the foolish men, blinded in mind, had fastened him in it.

Then the cruel lictor ordered urine to be sprinkled,

wetting the sacred limbs with its putrid stench.

They say that this liquid drove away the black phantom,

while necromancy hoped to overcome the servant of the Lord;

but the stench smelled like ambrosia, sweet as nectar.

After this the torturers ordered a heifer’s hide to be stripped,

so that the martyr’s limbs might be bound in the raw skin

and forced to endure the burning sun’s heat.

But scorching Titan, roaring, restrained his burning rays,

so that no fire should carry its heat into the innocent limbs.

[Col. 0259D] Then they shut the holy man in alternating prisons,

binding his arms with the tight bonds of chains,

and fastening his neck together with his two legs.

Behold, suddenly the pious Judge rescued his knotted limbs

and soon broke the tight bonds of iron.

Moreover, when the unlucky soldier struck the holy man

with a twisted rod, delighting in red blood,

strange to say, the blessed martyr did not feel

the painful blows of the rods;

rather, the rods grew soft for the holy man like feathers,

gentle, as green papyrus grows pliant in a stream.

Claudius, pierced by these signs, willingly believed,

converting the seventy men by his clear teaching,

and caused those who had been plunged into it to be cleansed

in the waters of baptism.

[Col. 0260A] Therefore the soldier, blessed, led those stained

with the red purple of blood to heavenly Olympus.

Together a blessed cave enclosed them, buried there,

where they would see the shining rewards of everlasting life.

While they deservedly traversed the lofty vaults of heaven,

Daria endured torments together with the harsh Chrysanthus.

But he, unwearied and bound by an iron device,

was thrust into the darkness to endure the blackness of prison,

where foul excrement flowed along rotten channels [Par., “crypts”];

but the stench yielded to nectar, as though light filled the hiding place.

Meanwhile Daria was handed over to a wicked prostitute:

she entered the savage adulteress’s brothel without guilt.

But a roaring lion was sent from its cramped confinement

to guard the virgin’s limbs unharmed,

[Col. 0260B] should anyone desire to violate her holy modesty,

touching her honorable body with obscene gestures.

As once the shameful Uzzah touched the ark,

so the insolent offender would immediately die,

confounded in face,

and, his jaws gnawed by the tooth of the raging lion,

would experience avenging punishment in a beast’s death.

At last, under the Augustus who ruled Rome,

they received red crowns through death by decree,

and together were buried in a cave covered with sand.

They whom bloody punishment had tormented together in life—

we believe that, rightly gathered into blessed companies,

when the earth willingly opens from the embrace of the tomb

and the human race rises from its dark graves,

he will raise them to rest while he loosens the world’s reins.

After time had passed, savage persecution

[Col. 0260C] bloodied Christ’s holy Church with pagan weapons,

heaping up a thousand dangers of death for the sacred martyrs,

torturing the innocent without any guilt,

so that Christ’s soldier might be slain by the drawn sword

while enduring the impious scourges of evil torturers.

Among these there was a certain martyr named Julianus,

who endured dreadful contests amid bloody punishments.

His father, when he was first growing into youth,

sent him to school so that he might learn in books

the dialectical doctrines of things

and at the same time the rhetorical arts of the books.

Then the young man, though handsome and growing to maturity

in the tender season of youth,

wrote out the ancient teachings of the books

with clear scholarly skill.

When his father saw that his child had grown into a mature adult,

he tried to bend him, born of illustrious ancestry,

[Col. 0260D] with entreaties, so that he might take up the rights of marriage,

in order that a line of descendants might afterward succeed him,

if he preferred to marry a wealthy bride.

He asked for a delay of seven days,

so that during this interval he might entreat the Thunderer aloud,

petitioning the divine oracles with supported prayers,

so that he might more surely learn Christ’s will.

Finally, when the allotted time had passed,

after the venerable young man had surrendered his limbs to sleep

on his bed,

he saw a heavenly vision during the night

and happily heard these words:

“Soldier, hasten to rise from your bed. Do not fear, young man, to take a girl as your allotted bride,

nor, in your rigidity, break the sweet decrees of your parents.

[Col. 0261A] Yet remember to preserve this holy companion,

who will be joined to you as a virgin with an undefiled body,

for she will remain an unfailing companion of chastity.

Many thousands of peoples will serve me,

those who believe your words concerning the scepters of heaven.”

Meanwhile the young man carried out his father’s commands,

promising his mother the pretended marriage of the bridal bed,

and accepted the girl adorned with gems and gold.

Nevertheless the Most High, creator of the square-shaped world,

protects the chaste agreements of bridegroom and virgin,

so that their limbs might never be darkened by crime,

as they restrained the lust of the flesh in their noble loins,

especially when Christ, pricking their pious hearts,

warned them in sleep to preserve chaste modesty.

For they saw the sequence of the books which the King of Olympus had directed,

[Col. 0261B] written in golden script in the bridal chamber,

in which holy virginity is commanded to be preserved.

After this they established monasteries for Christ’s servants,

who observe the rule of justice along the written path.

They also founded small cells for virgins,

whom the order of the lower sex may distinguish,

but whom no inferior rank separates from the pivot of virtues.

Among them ten thousand nuns flourished,

with continual songs and frequent psalmody.

Thus they served continually, by night and by day,

with unbroken strength knocking at the courts of heaven,

while by their prayers they traversed the threshold of star-bearing Olympus.

Meanwhile the black poisons of the ancient dragon

were vomited from its throat, tormenting Christ’s holy companies.

Then Christ’s soldier endured the scourges of a knotted staff,

[Col. 0261C] bound undeservedly in tight chains.

The lashes leapt with a crack amid bloody slaughter,

until streams were sprinkled with purple blood.

Thus the servant followed the Lord with devoted mind,

striving by a narrow path toward the heavenly citadels,

just as his master had previously advanced along the narrow way,

purifying the world’s sins with purple blood,

when, in his piety, he deigned to climb upon the exposed wood.

Then the one-eyed torturer felt the loss of his eye,

struck by the martyr’s scourges and by the blows of the staff.

Soon the martyr restored the one-eyed man’s sight,

although the priests, having suffered the mockery of their shrine,

could not restore the light torn away from its stock.

Moreover, a lofty shrine, strongly built,

[Col. 0261D] contained fifty images standing together, made of metal.

He overthrew it to its foundations, laying its ancient structures low.

Mars, the wounding god, who scatters the seeds of war,

breathing rancid poison into hearts through Gorgon-like venom,

could not aid the statues of the shrine with his shields;

nor could Venus, nor Venus’s most foul offspring [protes, uncertain], help.

The golden images of Minerva were thrown down to the foundations,

she whom the foolish called a powerful goddess by their art.

Nor could Bacchus, for whom vines leaf with tendrils,

as the false inventions of ancient books relate,

support the temple’s columns as they trembled under the god’s power.

But the temple’s marbles wavered in their trembling crusts,

and the structure collapsed headlong as its blocks broke apart.

Neptune, famed as the ruler of the waters,

who governs the empire of the sea with swelling waves,

[Col. 0262A] could not then sustain the false images of the ancient gods—

images carved in blue-green marble

or adorned with golden or yellow petals upon the brow.

Alcides is said to have been the mighty victor over the Centaur,

he who crushed the fiery blasts of the robber Cacus,

although Cacus belched smoke in his smoky breath

and wielded a club in Hercules’ cave with his right hand.

Yet he did not prevail by rigid strength in the temple,

where Christ’s servant poured forth humble prayers.

The crafty Vulcan, whom they imagine powerful with fire,

controlling scorching thunderbolts with fiery reins,

fell utterly, deprived of the heat of its pyres.

Thus the shattered structure collapsed with its images fallen,

as the truthful history of past events [Par., “kings”] relates.

[Col. 0262B] When the priest saw the two sons sinning together,

yet no paternal severity restrained them,

nor did growing vengeance punish the guilty sons,

the Thunderer’s vengeance flared up fiercely in that place,

so that, after the dreadful slaughter, the ark of God,

carried through Azotus, might overthrow the lofty image.

Then Dagon fell upon his face with his knee broken,

and had left his shameful head and limbs behind;

the citizens saw the head torn from its shoulders on the threshold.

When dawn shone in its yellow chariot,

and the saffron radiance gilded the square-shaped world,

and poured rosy rays over the open fields,

only the trunk remained with part of the limbs.

So too, against the gods whose power had been nullified,

the ruler of Olympus raged as they fell to the foundations;

[Col. 0262C] so that no one might be free from the dreadful danger,

as the sequence of the stylus reveals in its present writing,

Phoebus likewise turned his back when his divinity was abolished.

Jupiter, the savage son of ill-fated Saturn whom the poets’ songs extol,

seized his father’s power—which, as ancient little books relate,

after his father, made a eunuch against nature, had been driven out.

Then Saturn, wretched in Latium, an exile deprived of his genitals,

hid himself, avoiding the danger posed by his son.

Nor does Pluto help, who ruled Tartarus with dreadful scepters

and governed in the dark hall of the underworld.

He carried Ceres’ offspring to the black shadows.

But Proserpina, the queen, is said to have refused

to follow her mother, according to the ancient books falsified in writing.

Nor did Pan of Arcadia, whom the people worship

by offering their inner organs,

[Col. 0262D] while roasting much entrail meat upon spits over the flames,

bring aid when the temple’s foundation was shattered.

The lofty structure tottered while its broken heights collapsed.

Neither pliant glue fastens the walls of the masonry,

nor does the hard rock become squared by a bond of limestone.

Thus, when the power of the ancient gods had been utterly exhausted,

the avenging judgment of the Thunderer shook the august shrine

and destroyed it into ashes,

when the martyr, humbly praying, asked aloud

that the pagans might be able to believe in the Most High,

who reigns in a splendid citadel, through glorious signs.

Then the prefect’s only child willingly believed God,

and with pious, fruitful words opened his heart.

The young man embraced the martyr’s blessed oracles.

[Col. 0263A] Then both were thrust into the dark hiding places of the prison,

where a decaying corpse of the condemned,

boiling foully within, seethed with black worms.

Yet the nostrils of the innocent men were filled with nectar,

breathing the heavenly fragrance of ambrosia.

Nor did the prison cease to possess rays of light;

rather, the clear lights kept the murky darkness away.

Thus God triumphs in his saints by gracious power.

Then the guard, seeing such great miracles,

believed in the Most High, the king who saves the ages.

Having received baptism, he was joined by the dense band

that had previously guarded the dark prison.

Meanwhile he ordered the corpse sentenced to death

to rise from its black hiding place, its soul returning,

the body previously wrapped and bound with a bandage:

[Col. 0263B] the dead man awoke, bursting through the dreadful realms of Tartarus!

Then the crowd, with prayers, resounded in a great tumult

and urged the young man to reveal in true speech

how the lifeless man had been able to enter

the dark vestibules of the gloomy gate

and the black hiding places of the underworld,

and, restored to life, to see the shining sun again.

Poshumus, restored to life, immediately revealed the ordinances of death,

disclosing the angels’ assistance to the crowd.

Behold again, through the dragon’s deceitful prompting,

the martyrs were plunged into jars stuffed with fuel,

in which a black mass of pitch had burned fiercely,

and fires belched forth sulfurous flames,

burning the fuel of the rural branches,

until the flame burst into the regions of heaven.

Yet Christ’s aid protected the innocent.

Then they bound oil-soaked threads around their fingers;

soon the devouring fire burned them with harsh flames,

but it did not consume the saints’ arms with its heat.

[Col. 0263C] Behold again the serpent [gypsus, perhaps an OCR corruption], twisting in malicious coils,

raised its blue neck with poisonous venom.

The martyrs were dragged to the theater, bound with a rope,

so that lions might gnaw the limbs of the saints,

and the punishment of the torturers might force the innocent arms

to endure the bloody jaws of bears.

But victory’s palm turned out differently for the saints:

the beast licked the saints’ footprints with its lips,

offering service and forgetting its recent prey.

Thus, when God changed them, the hearts of wild beasts grew gentle,

although the hearts of foolish men remained numb.

As once the poet set it forth in verse with its clause,

the savage lions learned to guard their prey.

After this they won bloody garlands of martyrdom,

climbing the shining summits of star-bearing heaven.

After the cold funerals of death, lepers later came

to their tombs with hardened bodies.

When they were plunged together into the sacred waters of baptism,

they received healing of spirit and flesh within their hearts.

In ancient times there was a certain man famous,

legitimately serving the lofty Christ as a servant,

whom the Nile-land brought forth illustrious into the world,

seeking the sacred rewards of chaste men.

Egypt calls him Amos in its frequent reports.

Here this priest performed many signs of virtues,

while he dwelt among the leafy thickets of Nitria,

[Col. 0264A] cultivating the rough fields of the desert countryside.

This place derives the name Nitria from nitre.

It is sometimes believed that names are generated by the ages.

It is the cause of fortune—if it is permitted to trust such things—

if chance, or fate, or some constellation has any power;

if the Fates, sparing no one, guide their threads

and threaten mortal life, spinning it around,

carrying its burden upon a smooth neck in whirling motion.

But I rather think that Nitria cleansed the sins of the guilty

just as little bodies, cleansed of foul dirt by nitre,

shine after being washed.

Once, at the time of the swelling Nile,

he encountered that river,

which waters the fertile Memphite kingdoms with its waves.

For, wishing to cross, he had no desired boat.

But modesty of face forbade him to strip his body,

[Col. 0264B] lest, naked in body, he violate the laws of modesty.

Then, more quickly than speech, he was carried across

the foaming waters of the shore, like a winged bird borne through the air,

as long before the fish-bearing prophet, in a moment of time,

had traversed the Chaldean kingdoms by angelic rapture,

so that they might nourish the Lord’s servant with little cakes of meal.

Behold, a certain boy, torn by the tooth of a mastiff

and suffering wounds from its poisonous jaws,

was turned to madness, deprived of his discerning mind.

Iron chains bound him tightly,

for he raged like a madman with wandering steps.

Therefore the parents mourned the fate of their child

and, weeping, sought the holy man’s venerable oracles,

so that he might heal the wretched boy’s calamity and grievous wound.

They say that, consulted, he gave this answer:

[Col. 0264C] “Now return to the widow the young ox stolen by fraud,

and your healthy child will accompany you, beloved.”

They marveled that he knew the secret thefts,

which they had previously believed were carried out

in hidden places.

Then the father, rejoicing over his son’s recovery,

immediately restored [Par., “they restored”] what had been taken in savage plunder.

Thus it happened, as he had promised with truthful speech.

Later he asked them to bring a jar,

which two men had vowed to provide, but one deceived his vow.

Therefore a camel, bound by icy death,

lost the hump by which it had been spared carrying the vessels.

But the truthful one enjoyed the service of a healthy little donkey,

with which the kindly man fulfilled his promise to the old man.

The blessed Antony once saw him carried away,

when the excellent soldier had released the bonds of his flesh,

borne by angelic hosts to the stars of heaven

and entering the beautiful gates of everlasting life.

In ancient times there was also the gracious Apollonius.

The Nile-land brought him forth famous for his signs.

He was widely celebrated throughout the four-cornered world,

providing an equal example to five hundred brothers,

and he sought the desert in the time of his youth.

For three times five years he voluntarily fled from mortals.

There he spent eight periods of five years in residence.

Almost a hundred times he prayed in the night’s hiding places,

and as many times, it is said, he performed such deeds by day.

So that, with knees bent and knee bowed, he might pray, bowed before the Father,

Trusting in the piety of the Thunderer.

[Col. 0265A] His covering garments were woven of tow (coarse flax),

Never to wear out so long as he lived.

For this reason he shone, sparkling in celebrated renown.

For far away there remained the pagan worship of the populace,

Where a shrine stood dedicated according to ancient custom:

From there the priests, repeatedly carrying the images together,

Wandered in long winding processions, in the manner of Bacchants.

When he happened to see such mad companies

Carrying the abominable statue of the shrine around in a circle,

Then, bending his knees, he struck the Thunderer with his voice:

And at once he made the Bacchants’ marching bands stand still,

So completely that no one could proceed anywhere on foot;

But all together, like bronze statues, they stood rigid,

Enduring the scorching rays of the blazing sun,

While Titan burned more fiercely in the summer season.

[Col. 0265B] Meanwhile, when they learned from where the calamity had come,

Their credulous hearts promised obedience to the teaching in words,

Receiving the mystical gifts of the heavenly bath,

If the priest, rivaling them in prayer, should break their bonds,

So that a path might open through the countryside for hurried steps,

And they might proceed along the accustomed road.

He broke the delay, pouring prayers upward,

While repeatedly striking the lofty heaven.

Thus the high-throned Creator dissolved the closed roads,

So completely that the band, having obtained what it had prayed for,

Purified of its stains in the sacred flood of baptism,

Rubbed against the shattered idols and soon reduced them to fragments.

Once, growing fierce, strife broke the honorable peace

Between believers who confessed Christ in their hearts

And unbelievers who rejected Christ deceitfully.

[Col. 0265C] For savage Bellona infected their hearts with poisons,

Bearing bloody weapons, she disturbed the treaties of peace.

The battle lines advanced, with a dense multitude pressing around them;

Horrible Mars rejoiced in the cruel conflict.

The hoarse horns sounded, and the trumpet blared,

While the phalanxes urged on death with their booming voices.

Then the priest mentioned above quickly arrived,

And, striving to calm the savage struggles of war,

Attempted to extinguish the flame kindled by deceit

And to quiet the senseless tumult of dreadful slaughter.

But a certain instigator raged with a wicked mind,

Who had been the leader, chief, and grim standard-bearer of the battle,

Saying that he would never want pledges of peace

Until he had accomplished death through a foul funeral.

Then he boldly spoke, revealing the fate that lay ahead:

[Col. 0265D] “May such a bloody fortune of death befall you,

As you desire in your words, as you fall beneath a cruel heel.

You alone, dying, shall behold bitter death,

While the rest, safe, live rejoicing [printed *funguntur*, “live”; Par., *fruantur*, “may enjoy life”].

But after your death [Par., *finem*, “end”], the earth will not provide you a grave;

Rather, a savage beast will tear you apart with swift jaws [Par., *discerpat*, “may tear you apart”],

And the beaks of birds will likewise attack your mangled limbs.”

It happened as the priest had truthfully foretold in his speech:

After the funeral, the body, covered with sand,

They saw again in the morning, when the light broke through the dawn,

The body dug out by beasts from its accursed lair,

[Col. 0266A] And the beaks of birds had torn its wicked limbs.

Then everywhere the people believed that he was a prophet,

Since the swift fulfillment of events disclosed the spectacle.

All those who vied in offering incense at the shrines

Abandoned together the pale images of their ancient worship,

Following the clear gifts of the cleansing bath.

Here the illustrious Father, celebrating the solemnities of Easter,

Ordered the companies of the desert to assemble from every side

And to gather the faithful band into a multitude.

After this, when the chants of the Mass had been completed, all,

While they sought the customary dishes of the poor table,

Ate together dry nourishment of grain,

And also the little bundles which the garden in springtime

Brings forth from its bosom, when the earth swells with grass.

Then the pious man addressed the companies in these words:

[Col. 0266B] “If, brothers, we truly bear believing hearts,

Let us now together strike the Lord of heaven with prayers,

Who reigns in his citadel and rules the government of the world

While he guides the scepters, seeking worthy comforts.

So that the Judge may provide nourishment for the wretched—

For on a festival day the reins of severity are loosened.

Look! Before the entrance of the cave they see splendid foods

And abundant gifts of nourishment, a wondrous sight.

These are carried by bearers whom no one had ever seen,

Although he had traversed the fields of Egypt on foot.

They see pomegranates, filled with seeds and citrons,

Grapes and figs, and many round cakes arranged in order.

Here too is seen the date of the tall palm,

And honey growing viscous, enclosed in a structure of wax,

And the golden nectar of the honeycombs, dripping in a stream,

[Col. 0266C] And, at the same time, abundant white colostrum of milk.”

After these things, the bearers hurried away again.

But those men began to give thanks to Christ,

Who, generous with food, had filled the dishes with rich fare,

Until the day of Pentecost (the verse divides its name into *penti* and *costen*).

Thus almighty God, who knows all hidden things,

Was feeding his own disciples with such great delicacies.

Now famine had punished the companies of Egypt with disaster.

Look! They came in dense battalions, company by company,

So that the wretched might together seek food for nourishment.

Then he apportioned three baskets filled with bread,

Which, after first praying, his blessed hand had consecrated.

Thereafter he nourished them all for twice four months,

So that he never entirely failed to provide fragments of grain,

Nor did the little basket cease to supply crusts, though they were not exhausted.

[Col. 0266D] Thus too he made the supply of rich olive oil abundant,

As the prophet Elijah is read once to have made it abundant,

Making fruitful by his word the thick liquid in the little vessel.

Now, while my mention of the holy man strikes the innermost places of the heart,

I shall unfold the praises of the generous priest,

Whose fame, four-square, grows throughout the world,

And whose wisdom shines to the furthest boundaries.

He was both interpreter and virgin guardian of modesty,

Translating the Hebrew oracles into Roman words.

For he laid open the abyss of the rough and ancient Law,

Revealing the seventy-two books in the pages [Al., *bargina*] of the Bible,

Which writing now records on sacred sheets.

Moreover, by his skill he brought forth astonishing treatises,

[Col. 0267A] And, through reliable commentaries on the prophets,

He unraveled hidden sayings, revealing the mysteries of events.

This renowned teacher is attested in writings throughout the ages,

Which are now properly written throughout the world in fourfold form.

And although the illustrious company of readers throughout the world,

Born from the father Eusebius, as that same author related,

Enumerates the published volumes of the ancient Fathers—

From the time when the Savior took upon himself

The cradle of our flesh on earth, cleansing the sins of the world,

When he mounted the gibbet of the cross with his sacred body,

And, having endured wounds, purified the human race,

Polluted by the deceit of the Evil One, with red blood—

Who ever strives with such devotion to examine the twin teachings of the Law,

Or to search them out so diligently,

As that same learned teacher had practiced,

[Col. 0267B] So that, as the Psalmist sings, he might study the books night and day?

Therefore his rival, polluted by the plague of envy,

Tore at that same prophet with dreadful jaws.

Thus glory is gnawed by the black jaws of envy,

And the praise of the excellent is blunted by the deceit of the wicked.

For dogs repeatedly surround the boar with their barking,

Enclosing him everywhere in a dense encircling ring.

But he scatters the hostile mastiffs with his teeth,

And, having obtained his desire, reigned in the lofty woodland.

Now that the praises of excellent men have been set forth,

Who granted that shining virginity, beloved by the inhabitants of Paradise,

Should have its praises celebrated by the vast world

Until the ages are dissolved in the final flames?

While the hills flow like wax and the woods gape open?

Indeed, after the world has passed away and the cycle of heaven is complete,

[Col. 0267C] Their garlands will shine more brightly before the throne of the saints.

The time has come to make sacred maidens renowned in verse,

To show how integrity has given shining crowns

To virgins who have attained the summit of virtues.

They despise the impure delights of the age in their hearts,

Leaving behind the foul joys of sinful spectacles,

So that they may follow the Lord of light with devoted minds.

The Lamb, when a company of virgins surrounds him

In dense ranks at the heavenly summit of the sky,

And the white flock rejoices with its pious Shepherd,

Where the fields flourish with purple flowers—

There the wolf does not snarl savagely with dreadful teeth,

Nor do they know the ravages of the cruel robber in the pastures;

Rather, perpetual harmony in peace reigns forever.

Now, therefore, I venerate Mary with chaste praise.

[Col. 0267D] In excellent verses I strive to praise the maiden,

Whom the entire world rightly celebrates with praises.

She was of the clear stock of the people of Israel,

A virgin, a fruitful mother, betrothed to a suitor.

But almighty God, creator of the four-square world,

From whom the structure of the present world proceeded,

To whom all hidden things are open from his lofty summit,

And who searches out dark secrets with his own light,

Seeing the pure and undefiled heart of the virgin,

Preferred that a virgin should give birth to a heavenly offspring,

Who, coming into the world, would remove its filthy sins,

While she gave Christ temples and shrines of chastity.

Soon she gave birth to the true Light from the Father’s Light,

So that Christ might strip the world of its dark gloom,

[Col. 0268A] In which the human race lay inert in a grim world,

Until the lights of the radiant sun shone forth—

The one of whom the prophets had long ago sung in their words.

This virgin, I say, pregnant with a heavenly pledge,

Brought forth from her womb the King who saves the ages,

Who alone by right governs the empire of the world,

As the maiden learned earlier from the angelic message,

When the Father enthroned on high sent Gabriel from the stars.

This was the distinguished one whom the prophet foretold in his song,

He who once reigned wealthy in the fields of Jerusalem:

“A garden enclosed,” flourishing with a flowering crown;

“A fountain sealed,” powerful with a heavenly flood;

And also “the trembling turtledove,” to whom the angel, knowing beforehand, said:

“Behold, virgin, you shall bear an everlasting offspring,

And, being a mother, you shall give birth to the child you are to bear.

[Col. 0268B] Let him be called forever the blessed Son of the One enthroned on high.

The holiest Spirit will come from heaven upon you,

And power will provide a shadow over your heart.

The lofty power of the Father will overshadow you, virgin.”

At these words the mother’s womb swelled with the fetus,

Who, once born, released the world from its pitiable stain,

And, crucified, removed its criminal sins.

Moreover, what page of verse could worthily preserve

The living praise of Cecilia?

She converted her own bridegroom through holy teaching,

Despising the honeyed amusements of carnal luxury.

For she preferred to love Christ’s sweet kisses,

Embracing his shining neck with beautiful arms,

Although organs resounded with many harmonies,

And musical songs echoed in Pierian melody.

[Col. 0268C] Yet the deceptive pomp of the profane,

Which weaves nets for the holy lest the soldier hasten

Toward the joys of Paradise,

Did not entice her treacherous heart.

Meanwhile she spoke in this way,

While they sought the private chambers granted by the law of marriage.

“Behold,” she said, “an angel has crossed over from the heavenly stars.

Here, as my protector, he strengthens me through a heavenly covenant,

So that I cannot love anything carnal at all.

For he continually preserves my body forever,

So that no one, inflamed by filthy love,

May touch my limbs with shameful crime.

Rather, he immediately avenges and defends me with angelic weapons—

Those who strive to seize me with polluted hands.”

Thus the woman devoted to God converted her bridegroom,

And also freed her brother-in-law from his ancient error,

Until both received the gifts of baptism,

Became citizens in the highest citadels,

And, having become martyrs, paid the price in torments of the flesh.

[Col. 0268D] Sicily, the land enclosed by the blue sea,

Which the raging salt waves strike throughout the ages,

Gave birth to Agatha, suited to the service of Christ,

Whom the Sicilian inhabitant frequently celebrates with famous praise.

She willingly subjected herself to divine worship.

For she flourished for Christ in the season of puberty,

Trampling in her mind the fleeting riches of the world,

Soon abandoning all the ornaments of the ages,

And, as a young girl devoted to Christ, following the Lord.

But who could recount in words the bitter punishments,

Or describe the dark calamities of death,

[Col. 0269A] Which the young maiden then endured in her tender limbs?

She suffered the dreadful dangers of the wound-inflicting iron,

Which lacerated her chaste body with a bloody blade.

Her beautiful breasts were deprived of their maidenly nipples,

And purple blood flowed, dripping from her flesh.

Thus also the executioners roasted the girl in fire,

Cooking her virgin limbs over black flames.

But sooner than words can say, the flame lost its strength,

Burning the girl’s limbs with harmless fires.

Nor was the punishment merely a simple torment of the flesh;

Rather, a threefold constriction tortured her limbs.

Then the burning pyre, fragments of red pottery,

And the cutting of the cruel, rigid iron

Bloodied her limbs, though she was guilty of no foul crime.

Then almighty God, nourisher of the devoted virgin,

[Col. 0269B] Fixed his eyes from the heavenly citadels upon the earth,

Rejoicing to see the triumph of a woman’s character.

Soon the merciful hearer [Par., defender] of the needy gave help,

So that she might become stronger against those savagely torturing her.

After this she purchased the crown of martyrdom with blood,

Receiving from her flesh the everlasting crowns of the kingdom.

Finally, after her death, she was not without signs,

Although her bones rested in the tomb of the burial place

And her holy spirit rejoiced in the star-bearing citadel.

For at a certain time, when Etna was seething with fires,

It thrust burning sulfur through streams issuing flame.

Then it rushed headlong, abandoning its scorched summits—

A mass of stones and the melted entrails of the mountain.

Then the Sicilian worshiper, seeing the thunderbolts of flame,

[Col. 0269C] Set the holy woman’s tomb, together with her body, against the fires,

And in less time than words can tell put the ravages of the flames to sleep.

For this reason the land of Trinacria rejoices forever.

When foolish rulers, who governed the kingdoms of the world,

Killed martyrs, unjustly punished in their flesh,

Or rather adorned the saints with their shed blood,

A certain young girl was present among those about to suffer:

Lucia, who diligently loved the Lord Christ.

She was born from a good stock and illustrious ancestry,

And some young men desired to take her into their marriage chambers.

But, consecrated to God, she abandoned her marriage engagement,

For the sake of chaste conduct and the winning of the heavenly kingdoms.

She advised her mother, exhausted by a bloody illness,

To touch the tomb in which the blessed virgin’s body,

[Col. 0269D] Agatha, rested beneath a peaceful death—

As once a woman afflicted by a flow of blood

Secretly touched Christ, and the fringe of his garment

Cured her, bringing healing because the Lord granted salvation.

Thus the holy mother, trusting in the power of the tomb,

Immediately closed her open tissues,

So that the little stream of her veins would flow no further,

And in less time than words can tell dried up the flood of blood.

Then the daughter began to tell her mother in words

That she wished to serve Christ chastely forever,

And that, as a virgin, she preferred to reject a bridegroom’s bed,

Leaving behind the golden trinkets of jeweled pomp,

And giving the adornments to foreign suitors—

Bestowing alms and gifts upon the poor and the maimed—

So that she might store her treasures beneath heaven’s citadel.

[Col. 0270A] Soon the daughter corrected her mother with friendly speech,

As she opened her trusting heart in maidenly words,

So that together they might offer their rich inheritance to Christ.

When this became known and spread through popular report,

And ears were wearied by the sacred rumors,

The bridegroom’s gloomy heart soon boiled with bile,

Polluted by Gorgon-like evils because the virgin had been taken from him—

The bride whom the Savior had joined to himself as a grown woman,

Seeking the girl as a blood-bought pledge with her dowry.

The frenzied people’s hearts blazed,

And the consul Paschasius gnashed his teeth in dreadful anger,

While the cruel tyrant argued aloud,

Striving to take the beautiful bride from Christ.

She yielded neither to the goads of harsh speeches

Nor could she be bent by the flattering deceit of pimps,

[Col. 0270B] However much she might be dragged by a foul rope to a brothel,

And although oxen together dragged the blessed girl with ropes [Par., *trusirent*, “might drag”],

Even though the torturers brought the tender girl to fire,

In which black pitch and rich olive oil

Roared in streams over the terrifying heat of the pyres,

So that the blessed virgin might feel greater horror,

While the people increased the fuel for the flames.

But quickly the machinery of the torment that harassed her gave way.

The coals cooked her limbs in harmless embers,

While God defended her and drove away the flames of the pyres.

Then, tortured by the bitter disease of his mind,

The judge did not endure the insult inflicted by the virgin,

But violated her bright entrails with rigid iron.

Purple blood immediately flowed from her flesh,

[Col. 0270C] Yet the savage tyrant did not rejoice in her death.

Nor did he celebrate triumphantly over the slain virgin of Christ.

But just as they were binding the necks of the condemned with chains,

Rightly fastening their arms in knotted bonds,

So the guilty consul arrived at the city of Rome,

So that severe vengeance might punish his enormous crime,

While the blood of the innocent, together with the blood of the guilty that had been shed,

Was worthily avenging such deeds.

Thus also I shall sing verses about the chaste Justina,

Who won the golden kingdoms through maidenly modesty,

And broke the earthly bonds of married union,

Trampling the flower-filled commerce of worldly life.

An illustrious suitor, inflamed by depraved love,

Never ceased weaving webs of words for her in vain,

So that the virgin might perhaps be his in marriage forever

And descendants might come from her as grandchildren.

But since the wicked man harbored such a crime in his mind,

And could neither corrupt the innocent woman by deceit

[Col. 0270D] Nor set the virgin’s limbs ablaze with hidden flames,

He attempted to defile the excellent woman with magical poisons.

At that time the famous Cyprianus was skilled in deceitful fraud,

Learned in the dreadful art of criminal magicians.

He promised to bring much help to the one who sought it,

Devising many schemes against the sacred mind,

So greatly that he contended with the weapons of the dreadful demon.

The magician, ever full of tricks, sent these things repeatedly against the blessed woman,

So that they might strike her devout heart with goads of lust.

But when God’s virgin had rejected the trifles of the flesh,

Breaking the pale weapons of the monstrous robbers,

[Col. 0271A] He believed in Christ, the One enthroned on high, who saves the ages,

And, faithful, turned toward the Lord with his whole mind.

At last the magician repented, abandoning his filthy idols,

Having learned what danger the virgin could withstand—

She who could never be overcome by a thousand arts of harm—

And he fled the uncertain crime of wickedness.

After this, when Claudius ruled the world by imperial authority,

Impious, harassing the saints with cruel edicts,

Alas, what a crime!—that they should deny Christ in a condemned man’s voice.

But those unwilling to follow the tyrant’s decrees—

O how harshly they paid the dreadful torments of death!

Then, Justina, you did not fear to submit your neck to the sword,

Nor to let streams of blood flow from your flesh.

Thus the fortunate virgin was adorned with twin triumphs,

And, as a martyr, reddened gloriously with rose-colored crowns.

[Col. 0271B] The white woman flourished in maidenly garlands,

Together with whom Cyprianus, the fierce athlete of God,

Earned the bloody standards of martyrdom through shed blood.

Thus the saints together ascended the stars of heaven,

Since together they endured the foretold torments of death.

As for Eugenia, born of illustrious ancestry,

A red jewel gleaming in a maidenly diadem—

What unlearned rustic could ever worthily explain her

In the verses of metrical song?

The world beneath the heavens joyfully celebrates her praises everywhere,

And the heavenly court echoes them in its harmonies.

Finally, before yet beholding the sacred cradle of baptism,

She venerated Christ with wondrous love,

So greatly that the woman cut away her own hair,

Rejecting her tresses and taking the marks of Christ,

[Col. 0271C] And, pretending to be a man, could hide her true identity

By means of a manly tonsure.

For the woman, carrying the Lord’s cross with sincere devotion,

Joyfully left the empty litter behind,

While she went on with the youths, whose tricks she thwarted by her skill,

So that, as a prudent virgin, she might return by byways.

With hurried steps she visited the thresholds of the saints,

Seeking the bishop and obtaining the blessings of baptism.

At once she came to the abandoned litter.

When her parents saw the rejected litter return empty,

Their weakened hearts stiffened with iron cares.

Then the entire company of relatives,

Driven by the accidents of fortune, uttered many complaints from the heart,

Pouring salty streams from their eyelids,

[Col. 0271D] Wetting their sorrowful faces with rain-bringing tears.

Then the woman was accompanied by two eunuchs,

So that no suspicion might give rise to any accusation.

God, the pious helper of the innocent and needy,

Protected this defenseless woman with the shield of his merciful right hand,

As the famous poet once sang in verse:

“For her tongue had lied with deceitful speeches,

Striving to condemn the girl on charges of fornication.”

But almighty God, who knows all hidden things,

Wished to display the triumphs of the untouched virgin,

Convicting the author of the crime before the people.

Just as a married woman, driven on by the goads of the Evil One,

Strives with shameless speech to deform

The illustrious servant-woman of Christ, violating the laws of nature,

So again the unfortunate woman, while a crowd surrounded her,

[Col. 0272A] Suffered the great mockery of laughing voices,

And deservedly punishment struck her face with confusion,

So that the nations would never say: “Where is the God of these people?”

A certain young woman of Christ flourished in the world,

Whom her ancient parents named Agnes.

She was illustrious, fragrant with the virtue of modesty.

Her thirteenth year of age had passed on earth, as her first youth began to flourish.

She despised in her heart the foul mire of the world.

But a distinguished suitor, the prefect’s son, sought Agnes—

A man who was famous and arrayed in royal insignia—

Striving to take her into marriage with earnest prayers,

Offered golden trinkets in red cloth,

And, promising many talents of silver,

Attempted to deceive the untouched girl with the sticky bait of gifts,

[Col. 0272B] Just as a fowler entangles a bird in knotted nets.

But the young girl immediately perceived the deadly disaster:

If she were to listen more frequently to filthy words with her mouth,

Or if the virgin were to be assailed by shameless lips,

Fearing the trap, she rejected the insolent speech.

For she promised instead that she would be Christ’s bride,

Always preserving her body in a maidenly covenant,

He who had properly pledged himself to her with the dowry of faith,

And whose ring had consecrated the girl’s limbs.

Therefore, enduring many dangers, the virgin,

Though innocent, suffered dreadful imprisonment on earth.

But the pious Judge, looking upon the girl’s struggle,

Dispersed the horrible shadows of the prison,

And poured forth heaven’s bright light from Light,

So that the virgin’s eyes might not endure the dark shadows.

[Col. 0272C] The chaste girl was handed over to a foul brothel,

So that the virgin might be darkened by an uncertain crime,

And her blessed life marked by shameful words—

Words that sought to disgrace the names of Christ’s servants,

As barking mastiffs habitually tear with their jaws.

Then the suitor arrived with a dense crowd accompanying him,

Hurling darts with chattering, word-filled lips,

Because she despised his marriage proposals with chaste vows.

But God, who always justly triumphs through the innocent,

Punished his guilt with the sword of heavenly anger.

For, sooner than words can tell, in a cruel death

He had abandoned life and touched the Tartarus of dreadful Dis,

He who had wished to injure the holy woman with a polluted gesture.

Then, by her prayers, she broke the bonds of death,

[Col. 0272D] Restoring the pale limbs to their purple color,

Those limbs which earlier, punished, had lain numb in death’s cold,

So that from the place where there had previously been mockery through filthy words

There might thereafter be praises of Christ.

For the tomb of burial, and the sarcophagus in which the maiden’s limbs rest, healed Constantina.

Thus the king’s daughter could rightly give magnificent thanks

For her restored life to the eternal King of kings,

Who reigns in heaven.

A virgin dedicated to God wept in ancient times.

Her parents of old called her Thecla by name.

She was converted through Paul’s sacred teaching

And followed Christ, abandoning her promised marriage.

The love of virginity, burning in the girl’s heart,

Despised the sweet fellowship of worldly life,

[Col. 0273A] In which heavenly grace had founded her mind—

A mind that the ages could never soften completely—

So that she would be harder than iron against bloody torments.

Her father and mother together strove,

Through a marriage contract, to give her in marriage for the continuance of their line.

Thus her mind, burning hot with maidenly flames,

Could not grow tepid when drenched in the flood of the world.

Although her parents sprinkled her with a rain of words,

As drops fell from the sky amid storm clouds,

For this reason the hearth and blazing fire were kindled;

Vulcan boiled far and wide over black fires,

So that the blessed virgin might endure the torment of pyres,

Which would consume her holy flesh, though she was guilty of no crime.

By such a device the wicked strive to torture the woman’s body,

So that, limb by limb, they might empty her bones of their marrow,

[Col. 0273B] If it could be done.

Thus God defended the girl from his eternal citadel,

So that, having obtained her desire, she escaped the flames of the fire.

The virgin was handed over to the jaws of lions to be torn apart,

So that they might gnaw her womanly limbs with dreadful bites.

But the beast did not dare to tear the sacred body,

For God defended the limbs of the devoted girl,

While it spared the tender flesh nowhere of its own accord;

Thus the Creator, when his chosen contend in the arena of the world,

Grants the golden rewards of the heavenly kingdom.

She adorned the final moments of her life in this way,

Saturating her sacred flesh with purple blood,

While, as a martyr, she ascended the thresholds of everlasting heaven.

Eulalia, once made famous by the praises of prose,

Let metrical songs now strive to venerate as a holy woman—

[Col. 0273C] She who loved nothing mortal with vain affection,

Nor sought to place anything in the world above the Thunderer,

But despised all the rich pomp of the world alike,

So that, having utterly rejected the delights of wealth,

As though they were foul, squalid mud, she might freely follow Christ.

She despised the luxury of marriage beds and the pleasing joys of chambers,

And the allotment of fleeting honors,

So that the almighty Judge, lover of chaste virtue in heaven,

Might bestow the rewards of life,

He who is accustomed to adorn the chaste with continual triumphs

And to open the gate through heaven for his soldiers,

While the saints conquer the rewards of the deceiving world

And carry their standards in crowned battalions.

In the time of the Goths there was a certain young woman

[Col. 0273D] Who took the name Scholastica from her school.

God richly endowed her with a heavenly gift,

As she won golden rewards through her maidenly vow.

Concerning her, this distinguished report of her holy life

Is accustomed to spread throughout the world wherever it extends:

That she eagerly urged her brother, joined to her by natural kinship,

With earnest prayers,

So that they might receive at night the sweet courses of sacred books

And the banquets of the holy word,

From which the hearts of the people are abundantly satisfied

And the hearts of holy men are nourished.

But her faithful brother was not moved by any prayers;

Indeed, he despised his holy sister in words.

Then the virgin struck Christ with a gracious voice,

So that he might deign to heal the wound of her grief.

[Col. 0274A] At once the whole sky grew dark with a stormy whirlwind,

And the vaults of heaven blackened with gloomy air.

Vast rumblings sounded mingled with flashing flames,

And the trembling earth shook with a great roar.

Moist fleeces were soaked by showers of rain,

And the air watered the earth with dark rains.

The valleys were filled, and abundant streams overflowed.

Then he remained unwillingly who earlier had freely refused

What his sister, anxiously lamenting her cares, had requested.

Thus God listens to those who ask with a devoted mind,

Even if they receive words of comfort from no one.

In Rome there lived a noble and most beautiful virgin,

Constantina, offering a spectacle of a new life

To all who desired to live in integrity,

Leaving behind the filthy contamination of the former life.

[Col. 0274B] This virgin, I say, relying upon a heavenly protector,

Happily despised the world while it flourished in bloom,

Like dry chaff thrown away, filthy and worthless.

And, to make you wonder still more, listen to the report of her parents:

For her father, Augustus, governing the scepters of kingdoms,

Ruled the empire of the world while Christ reigned,

He who bears the name Constantine forever.

He loved his holy offspring with wondrous affection,

While praises of her virtue ran far and wide.

The supreme father had promised her, untouched, as a dowry,

When she was already growing into maidenly years.

For she had been betrothed, with a marriage pledge,

To a suitor than whom no other was superior—

Except the kings who rightly govern the world.

But God, striving to preserve the girl intact,

[Col. 0274C] Pierced the satrap’s mind with sharp goads,

So that he might utterly despise the rich pomp of the age

And prefer, free from worldly bonds, to serve the lofty King,

Rather than live richly amid the world’s abundant pleasures.

For him the wonderful beginning of salvation came about in this way:

At a certain time, a Scythian army arriving with dreadful weapons,

With a dense multitude pressing around it,

Was devastating defenseless Thrace with countless enemies.

Then the son-in-law of Augustus, surrounded by a small force,

Shut inside the walls, soon climbed the defenses,

Having lost confidence in his weapons while savage tumult raged,

So that the dreadful image of death might grow fierce

And the despairing army might lie numbed within the city.

Then the consul Paul, with John also urging him,

Quickly promised devoted vows to the Most High,

[Col. 0274D] That he would serve the Savior for the rest of his life,

Famous as a worshiper of Christ and abandoning the ancient shrines,

If Christ’s customary mercy would immediately remove

The slaughter of the people and the savage dangers of war,

Restoring peace after the storm of battle had been dispersed.

When these words had been spoken in the voice of the one making the vow,

The commander immediately felt the consolations of Christ,

As the heavenly citizens soon defended the city,

While the opposing battalions everywhere turned their backs,

And peace surrounded the people with saving crowns.

Finally, when he returned to the city having obtained his desire,

The prince, having received the decorated standards of triumph,

Brought back famous trophies from the enemy,

And the hero freed five hundred times ten servants.

[Col. 0275A] That is, five thousand enslaved attendants,

Making them all participants in Roman citizenship.

Nor did he ask Augustus to return the bride promised to him,

Freely rejecting the celebrated marriage altogether.

He rejected the bonds of wealth and abandoned the reins of the world,

So that, as a poor soldier, he might follow needy Christ,

Now fulfilling through his deeds the words taught by Scripture:

“Make vows to God, paying what has been promised.”

Thus almighty God protected the devoted servant,

Who struck at the realms of the Thunderer with continual prayers,

So that the Creator, lover of integrity, might preserve her,

As she abandoned the filthy intrigues of savage luxury.

For she converted many companies to Christ through her teaching,

Shining at the same time by her example and celebrated renown.

The twin sisters, Attica and Artemia,

[Col. 0275B] Born from the blood of a prefect whom ancient ages called Gallicanus,

Open the matter more fully.

The queen admonished these daughters of the aforementioned man

To preserve their maidenly life through chaste behavior.

Together they earned the flower-filled trophies of modesty,

While they abandoned the world after the time of life had passed

And happily hastened toward the starry course of heaven.

Meanwhile, no less in Rome, the young woman of Christ

Eustochium flourished, the venerable daughter of Paula.

A chaste headband adorned her shining youth,

As she observed the laws of the angels and the rules of modesty.

Although worldly fortune bound her sister Blaisilla

To the union of marriage and the bridal torches,

Subjecting her to the pleasant bonds of elegant marriage beds,

Nevertheless, the bride mourned the modesty that had been taken from her,

When her husband had closed his eyes at the boundary of worldly life,

As a married woman ordinarily laments a husband laid before her,

Anxiously grieving her husband’s funeral with sobs.

[Col. 0275C] But Eustochium, the virgin, did not feel with bitter tears

These laments which the fate of the world brings about,

And which deadly disease attacks with a cruel heel.

She despised the honeyed contagions of worldly luxury.

As she rejected the kiss of the asp upon her lips,

She pressed Christ’s sweet lips against her own,

And, while she fixed her pure kisses upon the heavenly Bridegroom,

She did as the prince once sang in his famous poem—

He who raised the scepter of the kingdom in the fields of Jerusalem,

Taking the role of Christ in a bridal drama.

Thus, I say, the young woman lived having obtained her vow,

So that her fame deservedly might be celebrated for the rest of time.

The sacred interpreter wrote many little works for her,

[Col. 0275D] He who organized the sayings of the rough and ancient Law,

Translating the Hebrew oracles into the language of Romulus,

And also the Greek expressions into the speech of Italy.

That same translator, rich in shadowed books,

Transferred foreign volumes into Latin, bringing their contents to light,

And likewise brought forth into the light of day

The treasures of Pelasgian books which the page had enclosed in darkness,

Unlocking with Ausonian keys the locks of the word.

Moreover, that same teacher wrote a polished volume

For the servant of Christ in refined language,

In which the praises of a chaste life are painted,

And the garlands by which spotless integrity is adorned,

Preserving undefiled limbs without the stain of wantonness.

[Col. 0276A] Thus the most excellent virgin, Paula’s daughter, lived,

Until the ages had closed the final limit!

Then her spirit swiftly entered the golden kingdoms of heaven,

As her soul returned to the heavenly hosts.

Here too, throughout the world, let the honor

Of the consecrated virgin Demetrias resound in metrical praise.

Although she was born of fortunate European ancestry,

And many dense companies celebrated her,

Nevertheless the Punic scepters marvel at her sacred praises,

Wondering everywhere at the maiden’s extraordinary fame.

For just as a lamp is not hidden by the shadows of a bushel,

But rather is placed shining upon a lofty stand,

So that it may radiate with clear, sparkling light for everyone,

So the young woman, consecrated to God in chaste womanhood,

Lived on earth relying upon a heavenly protector.

[Col. 0276B] She had been illustrious through the noble stock of her parents,

Receiving the cradle of life amid noble titles.

Yet before God she stood far nobler still,

Gleaming with the merits of her virtues like a crown-jewel,

Beautiful in her hair, graceful in her curls, and bright in face.

The frugal virgin of the Thunderer shone with a lovely brow.

A wealthy company of suitors eagerly sought to take her

Into marriage because of her beauty,

While she possessed many prosperous estates of rich wealth,

Gold and shining gems,

And the woman gleamed in a garment decorated with embroidery.

But unmarried, she wished to abandon the pomp of dowries

And rather to grow languid upon the lips of her heavenly Bridegroom,

Offering sweet kisses with pressed lips.

For recently I read in an eloquent book

[Col. 0276C] An account written in measured form of the virgin’s excellent life,

As the holy mother requested with earnest prayers,

When, devout, she appealed across the sea to a certain teacher,

That he might properly write the heavenly instruction of her daughter—

How she might store it in the treasury of her heart,

Preserving maidenly modesty without the lot of fornication.

At the time when the harsh torments of a savage tyrant

Compelled Christ’s athletes to endure bloody suffering,

Three illustrious sisters together drew the lot,

Wearing splendid garlands woven with purple crowns,

While shining integrity and red passion together

Heaped double rewards upon Christ’s virgins.

Their names I previously described in prose.

The impious Augustus who ruled Rome with his scepters

[Col. 0276D] Desired to take these handmaids of Christ in marriage [Par., *supremi fallere*, “to deceive the Most High”],

Promising many gifts to the consecrated girls,

If they all preferred to become the companions of noble suitors,

Enjoying the beauty and dowry of husbands.

But if they were unwilling to fulfill the marriage rite,

He immediately ordered the holy girls to endure torments,

Destined to suffer filthy imprisonment in tight cells,

Where they would receive only meager nourishment of crusts.

Yet the fortunate Anastasia did not cease feeding

These innocent maidservants, providing nourishment for the wretched,

And giving them both alms from her earnings and wealth from her estates,
He compares her with the martyrs who endured the perils of death:

For this reason the ages proclaim her fame,

And the perpetual rumor of her praise grows ever louder,

[Col. 0277A] She who, despising her own patrimony, rejected the marriage of a husband,

And follows the Lord, having renounced the lot of wedlock.

For this reason the matron endured bloody punishments,

Which the order of the biblical books now arranges in writing,

And her blessed passion is read in recorded pages,

As the annual seasons return for the celebration of the feasts.

Finally, the sisters mentioned above, united in spirit,

The cruel torturers lead from the dark prison.

When the savage prefect Dulcitius sees them together, with their beautiful faces,

He is inflamed by a filthy fire,

Seized by blind desire through the goads of lust.

Then the crafty man promised the girls many gifts,

If they would willingly fulfill his unspoken wicked desire.

But the shield of modesty protected the maidservants of Christ,

As they rejected the profane darts of lust in their hearts.

[Col. 0277B] But when nocturnal rest takes possession of weary limbs,

While the maidservants had sung sweet songs to Christ,

Striking the doors of heaven with the psalms,

The savage man, inflamed by filthy desire,

Dares to burst into the holy women’s cell with foolish steps.

But, by God’s providence, the wicked man is blinded in his mind:

While the fool offered kisses to blackened pots,

Thus he became black upon the pots, and foul upon the dark frying pan.

Throughout the night the prefect is mocked in his madness,

While God defends and protects the sacred maidens.

At last the unhappy man leaves the little hut,

But his companions in crime cannot recognize him by his face.

They withdraw far away amid a great resounding uproar,

Leaving him behind, they took him for a mask, a dark phantom.

For the unjust protector had blinded their own eyes,

So that the adulterer alone did not recognize the trick,

Which the others could see without malicious deceit.

Then the madman seeks the support of Augustus,

Asking that he avenge the guilty crimes of the maidservants.

When the nobles saw him, with a dense crowd surrounding him,

They beat him with blows and with a flexible willow switch,

So that he might flee far away, his wicked face disguised.

He is led to his own palace, accompanied by servants,

And soon the halls resound with the sobs of his household,

As they see their master painted with pitch-black soot.

He declares that, relying in vain upon the power of magicians,

This filthy illusion had been carried out against him by the holy women.

Therefore he ordered the blessed women to be deprived of their garments,

So that their naked bodies might feed the obscene gaze

[Col. 0277D] Of those whom the phantom of deceit had previously fooled in hiding.

Thus God from on high, who rightly triumphs through the saints,

Defended the unarmed maidservants with his strong hand,

So that no one could strip the garments from their bodies.

At last the savage prince Sisinnius comes,

To kill the maidservants of Christ with a cruel death

If they refused to offer incense,

Or to perform the profane rites of the shrines.

But no one was able to separate the holy women from the worship of Christ by threats of terror,

Although the savage man inflicted a hundred blows upon them.

Then he orders the two sisters to be burned in crackling flames.

But as they prayed rather than suffered their punishments,

They ascend to the stars of heaven in angelic arms.

The third, however, follows, about to behold the heavenly assembly,

[Col. 0278A] Advancing by a different path toward the rewards of life.

While she suffers the darts drawn from long quivers,

The wounded virgin falls beneath repeated injuries,

And purple blood flows from her tender flesh.

Moreover, fame proclaims two sisters,

Who received the beginnings of their life at Rome.

The first is called the blessed Rufina by name;

The other, Victoria, was younger in age and flourishing.

Their father was Austerius, and Aurelia their mother.

They arrange for these noble girls splendid marriages with suitors.

Yet the illustrious women reject the laws of betrothal,

And despise all the patrimonies of the deceiving world,

So that they may be joined forever to the bridal chamber of the Bridegroom who reigns in heaven,

Where beautiful youth flourishes,

And old age, furrowed with wrinkles, never approaches.

[Col. 0278B] Their suitors, therefore, abandoning the path of Christ,

Follow the winding roads of error along a rugged way,

Although earlier they had carried pure faith in their hearts.

Therefore the brides, rejecting the claims of their suitors,

Leave the lofty heights of the city of Rome,

So that they might not know, with tranquil minds, the storm

Which the guilty speeches of their wicked suitors were preparing.

For together they make for the well-known estates in litters,

Which they held far away in a fortunate region of Tuscany.

But when both women are betrayed by their suitors, they are brought back to Rome,

And, soldiers having been sent, they are quickly led back to the city,

To endure together the foul squalors of prison.

Then Rufina, the sister, refused to obey the wicked commands,

That she might offer forbidden honor to the shrines.

For this reason, it is believed, the woman was beaten with pliant whips,

[Col. 0278C] So that her sister, seeing her, might soften in spirit

When she saw the holy limbs endure cruel blows.

But the result was otherwise than the savage torturer expected,

For the virgin did not speak with faltering words.

Rather, she firmly said, never trembling:

“Bring all the bloody torments upon us together:

Fires, swords, and red rods marked with stripes,

Ropes, forks, and stones hard as hail,

Bluish hooks tearing wounds with streams of blood—

Whatever kinds of punishment you cruelly inflict,

I shall bear as splendid trophies over my defeated torturer.

As many cruel dangers of death as you devise,

So many crowns shall we count in the heavenly citadel.”

Then once again he shuts them in a prison deprived of the light of lamps,

[Col. 0278D] To suffer punishment amid notorious filth.

But the splendor of radiant light from the vault of the heavens

Extinguishes the dark shadows of the hidden prison,

And the stench of dung breathes forth like the fragrance of incense.

Afterward they thrust both women, relying on divine power,

Into baths heated by a fire-burning furnace.

Yet the heavenly power immediately extinguished

The crackling flames in the baths with nourishing dew.

Thus the shield of modesty covered their virgin limbs,

So that no flesh innocent of harm was injured by the ashes.

The torch, the fuel, and the coal, their strength removed,

Grew warm in vain, burning beside the extinguished furnace.

Then the savage torturer orders the consecrated maidservants

To have their necks bound with a stone’s weight,

So that the bed of the Tiber might swallow them in its green whirlpool.

[Col. 0279A] Yet the furnaces that had previously been heated did not dare to burn them,

But the blue waters carried the maidservants of Christ upon their waves.

The cold rivers, with their glasslike currents, were astonished,

As the body of the virgin floated like a level ship,

Returning safely once more to the banks.

Then, by the cruel command of the stern prince,

The limbs of the holy women are likewise reddened with purple blood.

Both, purchasing martyrdom by a bloody lot,

Rightly receive the triumphs of virginity.

Leaving the countryside, they take possession of the kingdoms of heaven,

Although the earth covers their bones and a tomb encloses

Their limbs, which suffered death for Christ,

Until the flashing coal consumes the ages.

Nevertheless, they ascend to heavenly dwellings,

Bearing banners amid dense throngs, without tumult.

[Col. 0279B] When they surround the heavenly tribunal in great companies.

When Decius ruled the threefold world,

Inflicting the dangers of death upon Christ’s soldiers,

The fame of two sisters arose in Rome,

Striking ears with extraordinary reports.

No torturer could conquer them by torments,

However much he punished the innocent women with bloody slaughter,

So that they might deny the author of life with minds turned away.

One of the twins was called the blessed Anatolia;

The other bore the true name Victoria.

Their suitors, born of distinguished families,

Strive to join them as wives to their offspring.

But the minds of both women, burning with virginal flames,

Burned the straw of lust in the furnace of modesty,

Despising in their hearts the fleeting impurities of the world.

[Col. 0279C] They scatter their riches, giving away their patrimonies as well,

And trample golden trinkets set with purple gems.

They immediately sell all their ornaments to the poor and wretched,

Keeping nothing for themselves, in exchange for heavenly alms.

A winged messenger glides down from heaven above,

Fiery in appearance, flashing with snowy brightness.

In his gracious right hand he carried a scepter-like branch.

He addressed both girls in these words:

“Now drive the pallor far away from your faces,

And do not let fear shake your hearts or strike your ribs,

While a bridal chamber in paradise is prepared for you,

In which the fellowship of the eternal Bridegroom

Will never wholly fail, but lasting joys will remain,

If steadfast virginity protects you as your companion.”

[Col. 0279D] Then both preserve the fellowship of a chaste life,

As the angel had given the commands of holy modesty,

Until the flight of life, when death howls at the threshold,

Destroying the withered breasts with its life-consuming breath.

When these deeds had been accomplished, the cruel hearts of their suitors

Are stained with the deadly poison of jealousy,

As they see the brides spend their abundant wealth.

Meanwhile the virgin Victoria leaves Rome,

And, exiled into exile, is led before the tribunal of the city.

There a deadly dragon belched the blasts of its belly,

Corrupting the clear air with poisonous fumes,

So that the citizens, amid a vast resounding uproar,

[Col. 0280A] Now preferred to leave the city polluted by its breath,

Hating the hiding place where the dreadful beast lay concealed.

To these wretched people the virgin Victoria promises

That, if they open their hearts in faith to the Lord Christ,

Abandoning their pale idols and their pestilential worship,

She will drive the savage dragon from the people at once—

The dragon that slaughtered the crowds of common people—

If they preferred to believe in Christ.

When the crowds promised this with one accord,

The virgin immediately drives away the scaly serpent,

And orders it to crawl far off into empty wastes.

Then the cruel dragon, crushed by the force of her words,

Leaves its dark, scaly den.

Thus the blessed virgin, relying upon an aerial triumph,

By holy power explodes the enormous serpent,

[Col. 0280B] So that never again might the serpent enter the cavern.

Instead, withdrawing far away, it lives in exile in uncultivated fields,

Just as she had ordered the dragon to depart by her terrifying word,

Granting the citizens, once the snake had been expelled, the palm of victory.

Then the blessed native maidservant of Christ asks the citizens

Whether they would kindly build a cell for her together

In the crypt from which the wicked serpent had fled.

As soon as the venerable virgin of God had humbly requested this,

They also joined sixty maidens to her,

Who would praise the Thunderer aloud with frequent prayers,

Chanting the Davidic songs in sacred verse.

Then the suitor Eugenius, relying on the priest of the shrine,

Orders incense to be burned and an offering to be made to Diana.

But the gracious woman refused to carry out the wicked command.

Therefore the cruel torturer brandished a sword with drawn point,

[Col. 0280C] Pouring forth bloody streams,

And consecrated the virgin limbs with red blood.

Soon the executioner felt the danger to his hand,

As his right arm withered dry and became numb.

Moreover, after leprosy had attacked his hardened body,

He died, covered with worms, breathing out his spirit into the air.

Thus the blessed Anatolia also became renowned through famous signs,

After enduring the exile imposed by the savage tyrant.

Behold, she restores to sound mind the consul’s offspring, bound in tight fetters

And wandering with a brutish mind, deprived of understanding.

At the report of this, they gather together the sick,

Afflicted by various diseases, crowding around the holy woman in a throng.

The virgin restored to them the health they desired.

She also immediately healed the bite which, by a dark spell, provoked the grim dragon,

So that the cruel beast might gnaw the holy limbs

With dreadful teeth and open jaws.

She broke apart the serpent’s bonds at once,

The serpent that had earlier gathered an inert bite within its coil.

For this reason the man hastens to believe in Christ,

Recognizing his own salvation through such great power.

Moreover, he increased his merit with the purple of blood,

To receive rewards among the blessed assemblies of heaven.

Afterward the white martyr follows, with two garlands.

Virginity, bright, and passion, red,

Together feathered a crown, slaughtered through courage.

[Col. 0281]

## ON THE EIGHT PRINCIPAL VICES

[Note: [Col. 0281A] See the note prefixed to the preceding work.]

[Col. 0281A] Thus, when the noble praises of the saints have been set forth—

Those whose fame blazes beneath the vault of heaven—

It remains to bring forth great songs concerning the battles

That proceed from vices and from virtues,

Which will deny the virgins of Christ the kingdoms of heaven,

Closing the thresholds of the flower-filled, light-bearing gate,

Unless, driven far away and destroyed by the power of God,

They flee into dark shadows, driven by Christ.

Behold, in companies, phalanxes mass for battle:

The companions of justice and the holy ranks of virtues.

Against them stand the wicked camps of vices,

Which hurl dense darts of unspeakable evils,

As one army of two peoples fights its rival,

While they carry standards and the trumpet sounds,

[Col. 0281B] And the horns of the legions spur Mars with their music.

Against these, I say, many virtues advance in a dense formation,

Carrying the signs of war against the vices:

A helmet, a breastplate, and the shield of battle,

And the sword of the word, which kills the monsters of sin.

Together they carry themselves into the battles of the world.

The virtues also, protected by the shell of their shields,

Crush the savage weapons of the profane spearmen.

Therefore virginity, which tramples the crimes of fornication,

Which no savage scar of sin disfigures,

Must strive to fight against the opposing ranks,

The eight leaders to whom the savage [Par.: holy] armies cling.

The virgin must strive to conquer them with armed strength.
