For it is not enough to overthrow the recruits of fornication

[Col. 0281C] And to scourge one’s own flesh with a cruel wound [Par.: stripe],

Unless the seven remaining crimes of the vices

Are also laid low by weapons advancing toward dreadful death.

When the people of the Lord left the Egyptian scepters,

Crossing the watery blue sea on dry feet,

They completed a period of forty years—

That is, the spacious cycles of eight five-year periods—

Until they took possession of the kingdom of the promised land.

But the Egyptian people, drowned beneath the red whirlpool,

Which the watery waves destroyed in dense ranks,

Can rightly signify gluttony.

Therefore, as the virgin conquers the wicked cohorts,

Let her first defeat this dreadful plague in battle,

Which is followed by the criminal phalanx, luxury of food,

[Col. 0281D] Drunkenness as well, and gluttony of the heart,

Which constantly feeds gluttony with rich banquets.

But gluttony, which earns sweet dishes of food [Par.: greedily devours],

And desires to fill the inner chambers of its belly,

And strives to stuff its stomach with overly fat entrails,

Is overthrown by the strong weapons of fasting.

For the first-created man, whom the King of Olympus formed,

And whom he shaped as a rustic primitive with gracious hands,

Filling his breast with the heavenly breath of life,

Long ago fell prostrate through the deceit of gluttony,

[Col. 0282A] When Adam plucked the forbidden apple from the tree,

From which the pestilential seed increased throughout the world,

And from which a dense crop of unclean ears grew.

Drunkenness customarily weakens the courage of men.

For the sower and ruler of the world, after the flood,

When the waters punished the human race with their waves,

Planted a vine in trenches with leafy shoots,

And, drinking its nectar, exposed his shameful nakedness.

So that his offspring might foolishly mock him with insolent speech,

A disgrace which the brothers wished to conceal from their father,

The first and third covered him beneath a garment.

If drunkenness was able to compel the venerable prophet

To curse his offspring and the whole race of descendants,

Saying, “Let Canaan be a servant, cursed forever!”

[Col. 0282B] Now the virgin fears the cups of boiled wine,

Lest, victorious, she should perhaps abandon her heavenly crown.

The drunken man does not know how to pursue the path of life.

Lot too, who had lived generously among the wicked,

Offering shelter beneath his roof to his guests,

And generously granting everyone the comforts of food,

When the fornicators and soft, filthy catamites

Who practiced the unspeakable crime of Sodom

Were burned by blue rivers of sulfurous flames,

Did not the father, drunk, know his grown daughters,

Wandering unknowingly in the marriage bed?

He would never have committed that unspeakable crime,

Had he not, soaked in wine, been unaware of the laws of marriage.

Why should I mention Nabal, drunk on the nectar of boiled wine?

[Col. 0282C] He, an exile from his lineage and from his ancestral name,

Drunkenly reproached it, laughing with foolish speech.

And if his prudent wife had not known, with watchful understanding,

That future harm was approaching her husband,

Alas, how many and what great heaps of slaughter

Would the madman, slow to act, have suffered in the palace of the rejected king!

So that no wall might know a man urinating,

Before Dawn spread her red light across the fields,

Therefore let the heroine strive to overcome this beast,

Lest the voracious whale [Par.: Bellona] burst open the gates of Olympus,

And the spirit be unable to ascend to the scepter of paradise.

The virtues constantly wage harsh battles,

Against gluttony, which conquers iron hearts.

[Col. 0282D] Yet virginity resists with the strength of fasting,

Lest the fortifications of the mind be broken by food.

Therefore the virgin despises the cups of honeyed nectar,

And flees rich dishes for Christ,

So that blessed virginity may be able to serve the Thunderer.

Next comes the second battle, the battle against fornication,

Which raises its bland wars against those who chastely serve Christ on high.

But chaste virginity tramples underfoot the brothel of prostitutes,

Like stinking filth.

From this monster arise the most shameful words,

As well as buffoonery and wanton gestures,

Frivolous and deceitful love, and luxurious insolence.

[Col. 0283A] How many men, and what sort of men, renowned for praise,

Has this savage Bellona thrust beneath gloomy Tartarus,

Madly, through her deceitful trickery, destroying the triumph of virginity!

Yet beauty was not able to compel the excellent Joseph

To lose the noble palm of virtue.

He rejected the mistress who cast the nets of luxury,

And, fleeing fornication, left behind the coverings of his garment.

For this reason he deserved the Egyptian scepter,

And the whole world proclaims his fame.

Why should I mention Judith, born of a noble family,

Who despised the king’s brothel with a pure heart,

And trampled the profane crime of fornication in her heart?

For this reason, while her fellow citizens endured the dangers of death,

She carried the bloodied trophy before the people [Par.: the tawny trophy],

Preserving her chastity with devoted mind.

[Col. 0283B] Thus chastity, in a holy triumph,

Despises the vice of the flesh, foul with harmful defilement [Par.: of the reborn],

Driving away the wars of its rival with virginal arrows,

Lest the pale poison of the brothel creep

Into fragile fibers, with the marrow burned in the furnace.

After this, the third battle is produced by philargyria,

A vice whose name is interpreted as covetousness, or love of money.

This leader of the battle is surrounded by a dense soldiery.

She does not walk alone on public roads,

Carrying bloody weapons and darts smeared [Par.: spread] with poison.

She gathers into a wedge her wicked companions—

That is, a thousand lies,

Frauds and thieves, frivolous deeds founded on falsehood,

[Col. 0283C] The shameful appetite for profit, and foolish perjuries,

And gains stained by the crime of robbery—

Burning together with false witnesses.

As the Psalmist sings, lamenting the crimes of the guilty,

Of those who always wish to serve the coins of avarice:

“He hoards up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it.”

Paul, the teacher who proclaimed the apostolic doctrine,

Declares this to be the cause of all evils.

Therefore let the virgin strive to break this vice,

When the avaricious keeper of the purse had committed

A vast crime through dark deceit against the Lord of light.

He secretly steals the entrusted purses with greedy hands,

And covetously defrauds the needy of their alms.

Therefore vengeance with a deadly heel

Avenges the offense and punishes the thief with cruel blows—

The madman who, blinded by the gift of silver,

Sold the King of heaven, who redeemed the ages with blood.

Nor did the avaricious ruler of the Hebrew people escape,

The man from whom Naboth’s flower-bearing vineyard was stolen,

When his cruel wife wrote a wicked document.

The avenger, looking down from the heights above,

Punishes the crime committed by both through deceit.

For the bloody dogs fashioned streams

Where long ago the innocent prince fell beneath a vast hail of stones,

A prince who had harmed no one with weapons.

But Jezebel, who wrote the letter to the city [“Tomum” in the transmitted text],

And cruelly condemned the Lord’s upright prophets,

Was savagely torn apart by the teeth of dreadful mastiffs.

[Col. 0284A] Her limbs fell, drenched in purple gore.

Thus the prince too, battered beneath the walls of the city,

Lost his life through profits of golden metal.

Such was the death of the wretched dependents,

Whom the crowd crushed together at the mountain of stones,

When the people of the Lord surrounded the seven wall-towers

With a dense wedge of shining weapons.

The trumpet’s clangor, and likewise the war horns,

Struck dreadful fear into the hearts of the men.

Soon the heights of the shattered city collapsed,

The city that had formerly stood broad upon seven towers.

Thus the greedy man, piling up golden trinkets through profit,

Constantly stuffs his needy sack with yellow coin,

Yet his inflamed rage is never permitted to be satisfied.

As the flames of a burning household crackle more fiercely,

[Col. 0284B] And the more the piles of wood increase,

The more they thirst, so that the logs may blaze with fuel,

So greed, hell, and fire

Can be compared according to a threefold likeness.

But savage anger gathers the fourth troop,

Which, always raging, desires the hazards of war,

And discord incites the minds of brothers to battle,

While, once joined, it tears apart the bonds of holy peace.

From this arise killings with unspeakable slaughter,

The shouting of voices, and growling indignation.

But let measured patience carry a shield against it [Par.: a firm … earth],

And the breaking of a bloodied brain with iron

Quells the enormous noise of raging anger,

Lest the greatest of the Furies be able to conquer minds,

[Col. 0284C] Although, stained with Gorgon’s blood,

She hisses while biting with venomous serpents.

When the daughter of black Night raises her head from Erebus,

Emerging into the world from Stygian hiding places,

Allecto rouses savage minds to scandals.

She is accustomed to lead iron-shod spears to war,

Which will inflict dreadful wounds upon holy souls,

Unless the Lord defends our unarmed minds.

The fifth battle, advancing in the tumult of sadness,

Breaks the walls and defenses of the virtues,

And harasses God’s recruits with cruel weapons.

And savage despair of a faint heart

Oppresses the unwary mind under the cloak of bitter resentment.

But the warrior of Christ soon blunts it with his shield,

Along with the deeds of sadness and every kind of sword,

[Col. 0284D] Which usually goad the mind, lest it perhaps give way [Par.: resist].

The joys of the heart heal this sickness of the sick,

And the spirit moderates the breast with cheerful conduct,

So that neither rigidity nor resentment may disturb the inner chambers of the mind,

So that the soldier of Christ may live securely.

Rather, let gloomy despair immediately be broken,

Lest the structure of the wavering mind fall headlong,

If it lacks the firm foundation of our Christ,

Who always protects the trembling with free grace,

And permits no one to slip through a deadly wound,

Lest the desperate sick man reject the healer.

This name is believed to divide itself into two parts,

And the causes are separated by a twofold path:

[Col. 0285A] One, salutary, tending toward the thresholds of light;

The other, deadly, penetrating into gloomy Tartarus.

May God deign to save us from the latter from his citadel.

From here torpid Acedia leads the sixth battle line,

Acedia, which cherishes idleness and seeks sluggish sleep,

Together with the untimely frivolity of guilty words,

The unstable movements of mind and actions of body,

And restlessness, accompanied by a dense soldiery.

Wakeful steadfastness of mind tramples this plague,

For it desires to defend life with Christ’s shield,

And, after driving away its enemies, enjoys secure peace.

That wandering spirit desires the mind to seek idleness.

Let drowsiness seize the senses and occupy them,

But let diligent reading strike the anxious breast,

And let the eyes of the watchful not travel along the path of Scripture [Par.: let it travel].

[Col. 0285B] Seventh follows with an army in dense armor.

The Greeks of old call this plague kenodoxia,

A name translated into Latin as “empty glory” or “vain glory.”

It seduced the first-created farmer through deceit,

With the wicked supporter of evils persuading him to a dreadful crime,

While he uttered these words from his dark breast:

“On whatever day you wish to pluck the fruit,

Your eyes will immediately be opened,

And divine honors will also accompany you.”

O how many false trifles the lying robber promised,

So that the unformed man might darken the gifts of life granted to him!

Would it not have been enough for the world, with its four-sided hinge,

Which the turning of the heavens surrounds in long circuits,

To serve human uses properly throughout the ages,

Unless a heavenly diadem adorned earthly pupils?

Alas for the crime, alas for the deed born among wretched mortals [Par.: alas for the wretched age]!

And especially relying upon this vain glory,

The prince, surrounded by empty hope, did not fear.

From this arise calamities nourished by the fuel of vices:

First, the headlong contention of the deadly word;

Then heresy grows, and boastfulness increases.

Presumption of novelties also joins battle with these.

But the recruit of Christ, protected by an unbroken tortoise formation,

Thrusts down the dreadful darts of the wounding iron.

Savage pride completes the eighth troop,

Tormenting Christ’s soldiers with the spears of sin.

It strives, through windy deceit, to gather companies,

[Col. 0285D] And always advances accompanied by malicious arrogance,

While it deceitfully proceeds on foot through the crimes of the world.

But it shakes its crested head beneath the dark clouds.

For it often attempts to overthrow the upright with their own weapons,

And creates slaughter with the arms of others.

From this root grows a dark, leafy shrub,

And a shady grove rises from its dreadful seed.

First comes contempt for the commands of noble teachers,

While the swelling of the mind rises in a windy breast.

From it also is born the plague of envy,

Which is accustomed to despise equals with swollen arrogance,

And to reign proudly after scorning its attendants.

For through envy deadly scepters flourished,

When the crafty robber and lover of dreadful death

Enticed the author of the race with empty deceit,

Lest the multitude of descendants ascend to the heights above.

Thus too, corrupted by the enormous poison of jealousy,

The brother, corrupted by the enormous poison of envy, shattered the splendid bond with his brother—

With Abel, who had first burned the rich entrails of the two-year-old sheep—

While God despised the cruel offerings of Cain.

From this a wicked crop thickens with bitter dormice (*gliribus*) [reading uncertain],

While the savage man stains the fields with purple blood.

From this arise the murmurs of arrogant voices,

And the crime of a heart refusing to obey a command in speech,

And the savage tongue’s slander, which tears human beings apart.

The other seven armies which we previously counted

Are born among mortals from earthly stock.

But the monster about which this page now speaks

Took its beginning upon the lofty heights of heaven:

The angelic prince, Lucifer, the first light of heaven,

[Col. 0286B] When he desired to raise his throne from the North

And deceitfully promised to make himself like the Lord.

Already adorned with the beautiful form of nine stones,

He began vainly to swell against the Creator,

While he revolved a dreadful crime beneath his foul breast,

Daring to make himself equal to the Lord in power.

Therefore Lucifer, abandoning the region of heaven,

Filled black Tartarus, surrounded by his followers.

This beast overthrew the proud inhabitants of heaven,

Who had previously shone radiant in angelic light,

And flourished in the heavenly seats by a blessed lot.

When a third portion of the stars fell headlong,

Only twice that number of shining stars remained above.

Finally, if the poisonous serpent, spewing venom from its throat,

Could punish the companies of heaven,

Let the earthly cultivator of the worldly field

Fear all the more to tear apart proud arrogance.

A humble follower can overcome such monsters,

One who does not swell with the mind’s inflated pride,

And tramples the crimes of proud behavior.

Chastity seeks in vain the praises that proclaim its reputation,

If a moth gnawing the garment of the heart furrows it;

If windy pride fills the bosom of the mind,

Virginity vainly seeks praise from rumors.

The humble virgin can climb lofty heights,

If she follows Christ, who provides the model for his pupils,

And who cleansed the stains of the world with his shed blood.

But lest the mass of material, like a great burden,

Press down so that the page cannot contain all the crowns

[Col. 0286D] Of virgins, much remains for others to complete:

Those who prefer to know the unpolished meaning,

And do not wish to let the whetstone of their intellect grow dull,

Do not lose the edge of their heart to rough rust,

Nor leave their own mind to be blunted by idleness.

Rather, they turn sacred books within their breasts,

Frequently examining the prescribed volumes of the laws,

Which surpass honey and sweet mead in sweetness of taste,

And the yellow comb, as the poet sang in verse.

Thus the diligent reader and knowledgeable lover

Strives to gather the chosen fruits of Scripture,

As cattle pluck grasses from a country meadow,

Which, lying down at night, they chew again.

But the pig, suited to the filthy muck of a wallow,

Cannot ruminate in its coarse throat,

[Col. 0287A] While the fat swine rests lying upon beds

Of reeds and straw, and also bundles of ferns.

The blazing days of July, I say, or even August,

Though they should prolong their course over the earth,

Would fail before I could unfold the whole renown

Of the chaste virgins and sing the praises of their glory.

Nor can a babbling page, in a hoarse-sounding verse,

Fully encompass their immeasurable chastity,

Even though thousands of mouths should praise it,

As organs breathe through bellows,

And musical instruments and lyres resound with cut-off notes.

A small vineyard has produced yellow grapes for me,

Although its vine flourished in a slender field.

Therefore, gathering clusters of chastity from the vine,

I quickly pressed a little must of verses.

[Col. 0287B] Yet I do not suppose that it will become entirely sour with age,

Or that the teeth of those drinking it will perhaps grate,

Unless a deceitful wine-seller pours in watery tricks,

Who sometimes deceives merchants with water,

While he strives to spoil the nectar of boiled wine in his cups.

Thus, supporting the young clusters from the vine,

From which the grape is crushed by feet in the press,

The time now compels me to close my running verses,

As I compose rustic songs for magnificent saints.

When the boundary of the meter comes at the watery edge,

As a sailor crosses the foaming waves of the sea,

Measuring the vast waters with a little skiff,

He reaches the desired shore, weary from the deep,

Lowering the swollen sails from the windy masts,

And at the same time loosening the yards from their ropes.

[Col. 0287C] Now let the metrical anchor hold the wave-tossed boat,

So that at least in harbor the sailor, shaken by the waves,

May, as he moves toward rest, enjoy his desired lot.

Therefore, poor and suppliant, I beseech these patrons,

Who adorn their age with virginal deeds,

And I, miserable, shall appeal in prayer to the maidservants of the Lord,

Who by their chastity deserve the kingdoms of Christ,

As they climb the clear heights of the star-bearing heaven.

May they strike the Lord the Thunderer with a loud voice,

The Lord who is accustomed to pity the unworthy servants freely,

And, when the guilty are converted, to loosen the bonds of their offenses.

May it be granted that, before the day which closes the lights of life,

And also before the day which opens the thresholds of death,

All the deeds of my sins may be released,

And whatever evil wanton youth has done,

May Christ, the eternal glory of heaven, erase it,

Mercifully granting pardon and forgiving sins,

Whether committed by deeds, words, or merely harmful thought.

Thus may the supreme power of the saints deign

In turn to bring devoted protection to me in my misery—

The saints whom I have described in virginal verse,

So that the garlands of the chaste may not remain hidden throughout the world,

And so that it may be known how they deserved crowns from their own flesh.

But you, whom the diadem accompanies with virginal garlands,

Defend this work against querulous buffoons,

Closing the lips of those who speak reproachfully.

Yet I do not fear the words of buffoons who read,

Who prefer to tear apart the pages of singing poets,

While they seek dark places of the word in the light,

[Col. 0288A] And investigate smooth ground for twisted roughness,

If a letter stumbles, or perhaps a syllable falters,

If gender, number, or case departs from its order,

If the threefold person remains, and the double form,

And the five tenses of verbs run properly.

Yet they do not correct the poet’s faltering grammar;

They always desire to gnaw the pages of writers,

As a shaggy goat gnaws clusters with its teeth,

Emptying the vines of their flowers from the leafy shoot—

The goat that once carried the people’s sin into the wilderness,

As the sacred ordinances of the ancient scroll commanded.

But let the timid man fear such weapons of words,

Who never trusts in his own fighting arms,

Nor has learned to place the helmet of meter upon his head,

Nor knows how to defend the breastplate of prose with its thorn.

[Col. 0288B] Rather, let him arm his right hand with a sword hilt,

And his left with a shield;

Let his legs not lack greaves, nor his thighs armor,

And let the writer not fear the playful tongue of terror.

A phantom frightens the trembling in nocturnal hiding places,

One that is accustomed always to chatter in dark shadows.

Thus too the crested face of masks causes fear,

When the brave soldier does not dread mask or disguise,

Who, relying upon his own resources, presumes to trust himself.

Since both sexes of the saints have been set forth—

Those who climb the lofty fields of the heavenly poles—

And the eightfold reckoning of dark sin

Has likewise been explained openly with a slender key of words,

May God drive it from the cavern of our breast,

And make it depart far away from the light into dark shadows.

Now at the end I pray that all who read prose and meter

[Col. 0288C] May examine this work with a kindly mind,

While they survey the text through open windows beneath their brow.

The work consists, perhaps, of two separate books,

So that they may loosen the bonds of sin for me through their prayers,

And pay the price of the book with repeated supplication.

May he who preserves the heavenly kingdom by his rule—

Without beginning or end, and outside time,

Whom the long antiquity of the world has neither given nor taken anything—

Now pity me forever as eternal judge.

The saints will rejoice upon the heights of heaven,

And in companies praise the Thunderer with their voices.

First come the patriarchs, who begot the origins of the holy race,

And the unformed offspring and stock of descendants.

They proceed together in a dense procession through their ranks,

[Col. 0288D] And surround the exalted tribunal of the ruler.

There too the foremost company of prophets rejoices,

Those who once sang of the beginnings of our Christ,

When the Redeemer restored the failing ages,

Mercifully cleansing the records of ancient evils.

There eternal life flourishes for the martyrs,

Who sought rewards through wounds and slaughter,

Purchasing the open kingdom with purple blood.

There the holy companies of confessors will rejoice,

Although they were strangers to shed blood;

Nevertheless confession earned them the distinguished palm.

There glory of the kingdom is granted to the virgins,

Who leave behind the foul earthly pleasures of the flesh,

While one hundred and forty-four thousand chant songs to Christ,

[Col. 0289A] Following the Lamb who once, with red blood,

Cleansed the filthy curses of the sinful age.

With these are the inhabitants of heaven who enjoy a blessed lot,

And who, crowned, carry the standards of victory.

[Col. 0290A] And who, in dense companies of thousands,

Surrounded the heavenly tribunal in a circle above among the stars,
Last, may I, trusting in the divine gift, be led into rest,

Under Christ’s reign through the ether.

[Col. 0289]

## ON THE BASILICA BUILT BY BUGGA, DAUGHTER OF THE KING OF THE ENGLISH

[Note: [Col. 0289A] I have compared these two poems—this one and the following one, “On the Altars”—with MS Paris, Bibliothèque Royale 8318, where they form a single poem without distinction, the former being inserted after the first section of the latter. The first appears among A. Mai’s *Classici Auctores* [Col. 0289B] (8vo, Rome), vol. V; the second among the works of Rabanus Maurus and Alcuin, to whom they have been falsely attributed. GILES.]

Bugga, noble daughter of King Centwine,

Erected this temple, built with beautiful workmanship—

He who had previously governed the Saxons’ realm in due order,

Until, scorning the heights of the present kingdom,

He abandoned the world’s riches and the reins of its affairs,

Spending extensive estates on new basilicas,

Where Christ’s worshippers now observe monastic discipline.

Thereafter he went in search of a consecrated life,

While abandoning his own kingdom for Christ’s name;

Yet before that he had engaged in three battles

And likewise completed three wars with three triumphs.

Thus he ruled the kingdom happily for many years,

[Col. 0289C] Until, converted, he moved into a blessed cell;

Thence, led to heaven’s heights by angelic hosts,

He sought the upper citadels with shining merits

And, joined to the heavenly inhabitants, rejoices in the lot above.

After him succeeded the war-renowned and battle-tested

King Cadwalla, mighty possessor and heir of the kingdom.

But soon abandoning worldly power and the royal scepter,

He plowed the swollen blue waters with curved ships

And traversed the sea’s watery plains by ship.

The cold sails crackled beneath the windy blasts,

Until the boat struck the shore with its rough prow.

Thereafter he crossed the cloud-covered Alps,

Fenced about by snowbound ridges and the mountain’s summit.

At his arrival Rome’s clemency rejoiced,

And likewise the clergy of the city rejoiced,

[Col. 0289D] While he deservedly was plunged into the baptismal flood.

Then, after the white-robed season, seized by illness, he departed,

Until he closed the breathing passages of mortal life,

Seeking the lofty kingdoms of the heavenly spheres,

And ascending the bright summit of star-bearing Olympus.

But when these princes had entered high heaven—

I have already described their two names—

A third received the rich ruler’s scepter,

Whom the peoples call by the established name Ini,

Who now governs the Saxons’ kingdom by right.

Under his reign Bugga, Christ’s humble servant,

Built a new chapel with lofty structure,

In which sacred altars shine under a twice-sixfold name;

Moreover, she consecrated an apse to the Virgin’s altar.

[Col. 0290A] Therefore let us all celebrate the present day with rejoicing,

And let us sing responsive songs to God and Christ.

The months revolve in alternation with the festivals,

[Col. 0290B] And at appointed intervals the lustrums of the years will roll around.

Let antiphons strike the ears with sweet accents,

And let the hymn resound in two choirs of psalms;

Let the articulated voice of the hymn-singers echo frequently,

And shake the lofty roof with a clamorous song.

Brothers, let us praise the Thunderer with harmonious voice,

And let the company of sisters loudly acclaim him with repeated songs.

At the festivals, let us bring forth suitable hymns,

Psalms, and responsories beneath the temple’s vaulted roof,

Speaking the melody of the psaltery in frequent modulation,

And striving to stretch the lyre with ten strings,

As the Psalmist urges us to sing with ten strings.

Let each person adorn the new chapel with his voice,

And let the male or female reader unfold the sacred books.

[Col. 0290C] Indeed, the Virgin Mary consecrated this day,

On which the temple’s festivals shine,

By her Nativity;

The season of August continually renews it [Absent in the editions],

While the sixth month is divided at its midpoint,

Which restores our joy of heart once more,

As Mary’s solemn festivals return in their appointed seasons,

And the venerable altars glow with pious gifts.

This house within shines with serene light,

Which the sun perhaps illuminates through glass windows,

Spreading clear beams throughout the square temple.

There are many ornaments in the newly built basilica:

Golden hangings gleam with twisted threads,

Beautiful coverings for the sacred altar.

A golden chalice also gleams, covered with gems,

[Col. 0290D] As the sky is fitted with blazing stars;

So the broad paten stands fashioned from silver,

Carrying the remedies of our divine life,

For we are nourished by Christ’s sacred body and blood.

Here a sheet of shining yellow gold gleams from the cross,

And at the same time the silver metal is adorned with gems.

Here too a thurible, enclosed on every side by little capitals,

Hangs from above, opening smoky apertures.

From these Sabaean incense will breathe ambrosial fragrance

When priests are commanded to offer Masses.

Now let clear glory be spoken to the unbegotten Father,

And no less let glory be proclaimed to the begotten Son;

Let the Holy Spirit also share in praise with his consort.

[Col. 0291]

## POEM ON THE ALTARS DEDICATED TO BLESSED MARY AND THE TWELVE APOSTLES

[Col. 0291A] I.

This hall of the Lord is guarded by Mary’s protection,

For whom the venerable, newly built heights of the temple are consecrated,

And new standards rise in sacred triumphs.

In this hall the honor of the holy Mother is celebrated,

She who gave birth to the true Light from the Father’s Light,

Whom the poets call Titan, with its nourishing breath.

Most powerful woman and sacred virgin who has borne a child,

Hear mercifully the vows of peoples who pray,

Who moisten their withered faces with streaming rains,

And beat the ground with their knees bent,

While they earn pardon by pouring forth a fountain of tears,

And erase the sins of life with frequent prayers.

This virgin, I say, pregnant with a heavenly pledge,

Brought forth from her womb the King who saves the ages,

[Col. 0291B] Who alone governs the world’s dominion by right,

As the maiden learned long ago from the angelic utterance,

When the Father enthroned on high sent Gabriel from the stars.

This was the distinguished woman whom the poet proclaims in his song,

He who once ruled richly over the fields of Jerusalem:

“A garden enclosed,” flourishing at its blooming summit,

And also “a sealed fountain,” strong with heavenly waters,

And likewise a trembling turtledove. To her the foreknowing

Angel said: “Behold, virgin, you shall bear everlasting offspring,

And, destined to give birth, you shall bring forth a child;

Let the blessed Son of the Most High be called so forever.

The most holy Spirit will come upon you from heaven;

Behold, power will cast its shadow over your heart.

The lofty power of the Father will overshadow you, virgin.”

At these words the mother’s womb swelled with its offspring,

[Col. 0291C] Who, once born, released the world from its pitiable stain,

And, crucified, wiped away its polluted sins.

### II.

Peter crowns this apse with the lot of the saints,

The heavenly key-bearer who opens the gate in the ether,

The doorkeeper who unlocks the lights of eternal life.

Here he set forth a twofold doctrine throughout the world,

Properly written in two books,

Which those with open hearts receive as Christ’s commands,

Just as he previously and rightly captured the watery multitudes,

Extending a line and casting nets among the scaly throngs.

Thus he leads bands of men, snatched from the world’s abyss,

To the eternal kingdom with a heavenly oarsman,

As the Savior promised you in truthful words,

When he called you, fishing, from the open boat.

[Col. 0291D] He trod with his feet upon the green-blue sea,

But the sea did not swallow him as he sank into the swelling waves;

When Christ’s right hand pressed the surging marble waters,

Whose shadow offered healing to the dead,

So that the healthy returned again to the light of life,

Although previously they had traversed the threshold of black death.

[Col. 0292A] Here too, relying on the Thunderer’s power,

He restores the lame man in both knees and feet,

And quickly commands the healed feet to proceed—

The man whom his relatives had previously carried to the temple.

Here also he punished two wicked men with death,

Who fraudulently concealed the price of a field.

Moreover, utterly emptying the false magical apparition of Simon,

He drove it down into the dark shadows,

Freeing the Roman people from their ancient error.

He who climbed the lofty heights of a newly built tower,

And, crowned with laurel foliage, flew upward,

But soon, bringing down his fruit-bearing airs from heaven,

Headfirst, with both bones shattered,

Fell to the ground, and victory in the battle passed to Peter.

He who was fastened to the cross and gladly endured torments,

Destined to suffer the horrible wounds of cruel iron,

God, the almighty Judge, adorned with eternal triumphs,

Carried to the heights of heaven.

### III.

Saurus, who imprisoned holy crowds,

Is made a believer, changing his name to Paul;

Scattering abundant seeds through fruitful words,

From him the sacred harvest of the world grew in the field.

God called him, while he was faithless, from heaven’s citadel:

“Why do you persecute me, resisting with a hard heel?”

Therefore, plunged beneath the abyss of the sea day and night,

He earned the great spectacles of heavenly things.

Caught up to the third height of heaven, he ascended,

And saw, in spirit, the princes of heaven in their companies,

When the insolent Pythoness called out in an arrogant voice.

[Col. 0292C] The spirit departed from the girl when Paul purified her,

And, fleeing far away, vanished into empty air.

He raises up a young man who was traversing death’s Tartarus,

By entering into the innermost parts of his soul.

Was it not deserved that he deprived him of the use of both eyes,

So that she would never see Phoebus shining with light?

He restores the sick lame man in his legs and shins,

Whom fortune had previously deprived of the ability to walk.

Thus also he helped the father of the people,

Whom panting fever tormented,

While torrid heat and wintry cold consumed him.

He also cured many shameful ailments,

The Lord granting healing quickly,

While Paul had first gathered branches for the fire,

To drive away the cold amid wintry clouds.

[Col. 0292D] A dreadful viper bit his hand with a lethal tooth,

But Paul did not feel the icy poison in the wound,

Nor could the cruel venom harm the holy man.

Finally, he threw the scaly, skin-covered water-snake

Straight into the black flames to be burned.

After he completed the span of his passing life,

[Col. 0293A] He sought the sacred martyrdom in red blood,

And purple gore flowed from the fountain of his veins.

Although the earth now covers his bones with the bulk of a tomb,

His spirit nevertheless ascended to the lofty heights,

Led through the cloudy ether among angelic companies.

### IV.

Here Andrew too will guard the altar of the temple,

Peter’s brother, who once endured the horrible death

Of hanging in consecrated flesh.

God summoned him from heaven while he was vainly traversing the Ocean in a little boat,

Walking along the shores of the sea.

At once Andrew, pierced by the Thunderer’s voice,

Believed in the eternal King who saves the ages,

Abandoning the hanging nets of the rejected catch,

And, quicker than speech, carried out Christ’s commands.

[Col. 0293B] Who can count the towns crowded with populous throngs,

Which, through his eloquence, rubbed away their profane shrines,

Opening their believing hearts to Christ the King?

Indeed, he repaid his debt to the Lord with a bloody heel,

While, as a martyr suspended on the exposed trunk of the cross,

He closed the final breath of mortal life,

Receiving purple crowns while Christ reigned.

### V.

Here James too, born of an ancient father,

Defends the lofty shrine beneath a holy covering;

When pious Christ called from the shore of the sea,

He was leaving his own father in the open boat.

He first converted the Spanish peoples through doctrine,

Turning barbarian multitudes through divine words—

[Col. 0293C] Those who, deceived by the fraud of a dreadful demon,

Had long worshiped ancient rites and ghastly shrines.

Thus, as a wondrous bishop, he performed many signs,

Which are now rightly written on square pages.

Cruel Herod, the tyrant tetrarch of the kingdom,

Struck and killed him with a savage sword.

But the exalted Father, who rightly triumphs over the saints,

Carried him, radiant with merits, to the heavenly heights.

### VI.

Meanwhile, the virgin John is not daunted by threats,

Whom brotherly fellowship likewise joined to Christ,

When he left his old father in the open boat,

Closing watery prey in nets amid the sea’s marble waters.

Previously he swept the blue waters with algae-covered oars,

Laying snares for fish beneath the sea’s abyss;

But when God called from the shore of the struggling waters,

He left the net-bearing ship with his dear brother,

And followed the Lord who reigns in heaven’s citadel.

He was the distinguished disciple of reigning Christ,

Foremost among all, beloved with great affection.

The king who ruled Rome and its kingdoms,

Having him carried across the blue waters in a small boat,

Thrust him into exile.

There, placed in exile, he witnessed many things,

And grew in ecstasy, sustained by heavenly power.

The things now read throughout the world written on parchment—

The bishop, after making his preface with an exhausted body [Paris: “in Ephesus”]—

Rests, awaiting his reward when the trumpet sounds,

When the final ages slip away into the ancient centuries.

[Col. 0294A] ### VII.

Here Thomas Didymus, who received an Achaean name,

Guards the consecrated temple beneath its sound vault;

When he touched the wounds inflicted by the cruel spear,

He immediately believed in the Monarch who saves the ages.

Although previously he had been unbelieving toward his gracious companions,

And bore faith, uncertain, in a doubtful heart,

While the Redeemer, rising from death, was leaving the infernal chaos,

The hidden place, accompanied by a vast throng,

Soon the red scar converted his doubt,

When the disciple touched the little wounds of the savage iron,

While Christ the Savior, the bringer of peace, entered the hall

Through closed doors, where the trembling company was hiding.

Therefore the venerable offspring of the Thunderer sent him

To convert the nations of the East with gracious books,

Performing many signs through magnificent triumphs.

India, instructed in the foolish doctrines of its ancestors,

Then worshiped idols with impious rites;

But, confessing the faith and winning salvation through Thomas,

It believed in Christ, who governs the scepters of heaven.

Finally, when the period of his present life was completed,

Thomas immediately traversed heavenly Olympus.

The priest and worshiper of the ancient shrine

Pierced him through with a rigid sword, dripping with blood.

He will receive his rewards when the earth gapes open of its own accord

And all bodies rise from their ancient tombs.

### VIII.

James too, born as the kinsman of Christ’s mother,

And relying on the fortunate name of cousin,

Guards this house of the Lord from lofty Olympus.

[Col. 0294C] The Jewish people, while savage tumult raged,

Killed him, driven from the parapet of the temple with a fuller’s club,

Because, ascending the temple heights, he repeatedly preached

About Christ to the peoples, as a priest.

On his knees, calloused skin is reported,

While he prayed frequently to the Thunderer,

With bent knees beating the pavement of the chapel.

He rejected woolen coverings of shaggy cloth,

Taking linen towels amid the wintry blasts.

Likewise, scorning fragrant nard burning upon his body,

He utterly disregarded the pomp of baths.

He did not remove the curls of his head with an iron forceps,

Nor did a knife shave his cheeks of their covering of hair.

Such are the great praises of his virtues,

That the vengeance for his death, which he suffered by a dreadful death,

[Col. 0294D] Became the destruction of Jerusalem and the ruin of its people,

When Caesar Titus, accompanied by a dense throng,

Born in the Roman citadels together with his father,

Besieged the great city with iron-bearing multitudes,

Until dreadful famine consumed the crowds,

Confined by blocked walls and enclosed in the prison of the ramparts.

At that time a woman killed her tender child,

Then pierced him with sharp spits so that he might be roasted,

And, once cooked over the hearth, the cruel mother ate him,

Utterly dissolving the laws of human nature.

I shudder to recount the bitter death of the child.

Thus the vengeance of the cross punished the wicked with disaster;

Thus also James’s suffering punished the guilty.

Eleven times a hundred thousand are said to have fallen

[Col. 0295A] Throughout the wretched city, among its dying citizens.

Moreover, a hundred thousand are sold everywhere,

Those whom the neglected sword’s rigid blade had spared;

And the dead perished through the meager provision of famine [Paris: “fled”].

### IX.

Here too the metrical line commemorates Philip,

Whom pious Christ enriched with heavenly grace.

He taught barbarian multitudes through sacred doctrines

To believe throughout Scythia in Christ, who saves the ages—

Those who had long lain inert in the foul shadow of death,

Denying the author of light with darkened heart,

And serving creation in an inverted order.

Until they drank in apostolic speech with their ears,

Seeing the clear lights of everlasting Phoebus,

They all eagerly plunged into the sacred flood,

Cleansing the guilt of sin in the fountain of washing.

[Col. 0295B] Thence he hastened to convert Asia with holy books—

Asia, which had long worshiped idols, deceived by fraud—

But which quickly opened its heart in faith to Christ,

As it received the splendid words spoken by the disciple.

Thus by his doctrine he converted the fortunate kingdom of Asia,

In which, after his death, he rests by fateful destiny.

Its consecrated altar will guard this temple.

### X.

India, preeminent at the ends of the earth, is constituted,

And the written books divide it into three parts;

It was devoted to pagan rites and worshiped idols.

But Bartholomew destroyed the ghastly shrines,

Rightly shattering the images of the ancient gods.

Hebrew speech calls him “the son of him who suspends the waters

In black clouds,” while the heavens drip with rainy drops,

Marking the gifts of the heavenly depths of the mighty—

As the poet once sang in the song of the psalms:

“Behold, liquid falls like dew from the dark clouds of the air.”

[Col. 0295C] After this he purchases the blood-red garlands of martyrdom,

And follows the Lord, marked with Christ’s stigma.

This temple’s venerable altar will guard him.

### XI.

Matthew, describing the distinguished doctrine of salvation,

Set forth Hebrew words in a single book,

Narrating many miracles for the sanctified ages,

Which his four-sided writings now spread throughout the world.

The river Pishon, overflowing from the fountain of paradise,

Reveals figurative mysteries of things [Paris: “wonders”].

It rightly represents the figure of the Savior,

From whom four rivers flow in four channels.

Just as, at the beginning of the newly born age,

Clear rivers flowed throughout the broad world,

And watered red flowers and meadows green with soil

With pure currents and blue-green dew,

So God’s teaching flowed from the fourfold fountain,

Sprinkling dry hearts with divine streams.

Matthew, the truthful writer, once expressed this;

Him the prophet of God, full of the Holy Spirit,

Once saw marked out in human form—

Because he was to number Christ’s fathers

And the ancestors of his ancestors,

From whom our Savior mercifully took

The cradle of his sacred life in the world,

To cleanse its sinful offenses.

[Col. 0296A] ### XII.

Simon Zelotes, also called the Cananaean,

Who likewise bore the name Peter among the apostles,

Taught the gentiles the heavenly doctrine,

So that they might seek the lofty kingdom by a heavenly path.

His altar will be kept sacred in this hall,

When heaven and earth and the sea’s currents fail,

Until the ages sparkle in the final ashes,

And the mass of the world, its mountains and hills, melts,

And creation’s structure, like wax flowing,

Collapses beneath a fire crackling throughout the world.

### XIII.

Thaddeus shall close the noble number at the end,

Whose famous surname was formerly Libbeus.

They say that he carried a letter from Christ

To Abgarus, who once ruled with the scepters of the kingdom,

After he had condemned the Tartarean tyrant to death

And joyfully emerged from the foul caverns of Erebus.

Thereafter Christ ascended starry Olympus.

He is also said to be called Judas by the common name,

Whose praises are celebrated in this hall;

He gave us a twofold book in eloquent speech,

Proclaiming ancient sayings with his mouth,

Which the ancient prophet Enoch described

Before the ravenous sea punished the world with its waters,

Saying: “Behold, the Lord comes with gracious thousands

To pass judgment on all who inhabit the world.”

He calls them clouds lacking dripping waters,

Which cold winds scatter with rapid blasts;

And he compares them also to trees born from sterile trunks,

[Col. 0296C] Which lose their fruit at the season of autumn.

Thus too he compares them to the foaming waves of the waters,

Calling the guilty wandering stars of heaven,

For whom punishment remains preserved in dark storms.

Judas had indeed bent savage nations and the barbarian kingdoms of the sea

Toward the Lord through his gracious teachings.

His body, laid to rest in Armenia by death,

Rests until it will rise at the fated end.

Yet his spirit has traversed the heavenly heights.

### XIV.

The holy Matthias guards this gracious shrine,

He who is said to have been one of the seventy

Disciples of the Lord who taught the sacred doctrine.

God marked him out as chosen by heavenly lot,

When Judas Iscariot, deceived by wicked trickery,

[Col. 0296D] Lost the lofty honor of the apostolic office

And poured out his foul innards together with his stinking entrails,

When, suspended high by a noose, he burst apart,

He who, greedy to seize the yellow coin,

Sold the Lord who redeemed the ages with his blood.

Therefore Matthias, rejecting the abominable robber,

Relying on the Lord, completed the same number,

And rightly rejoices, joined to the apostles’ triumphs.

Now I have set forth the twelve names of the fathers together,

From whom the world, converted, believed in the Most High.

I ask that these men, with frequent prayers and a devoted heart,

May mercifully lighten the burdens of my sins for me,

And, granting pardon, dissolve my committed offenses,

So that, trusting in divine grace,

I, the last, may enter into rest

With Christ reigning through the ether.

[Col. 0297]

## VERSES WRITTEN IN HONOR OF THE APOSTLES WHEN THE AUTHOR ENTERED THEIR CHURCH IN ROME

[Note: [Col. 0297] Preserved in Faricius’s little book *On the Life of Aldhelm*. GILES.] (C, S)

[Col. 0297A] Here the glory of the temple, worthy of celebration, blossoms,

A clear sign of the standards of sacred triumph.

Here Peter and Paul, lights of the darkened world,

The foremost Fathers of the people who govern its reins,

Are revered in the gracious hall with frequent songs.

Heavenly key-bearer, who opens the gate in the ether,

Unlocking the bright kingdoms of the heavens of the Thunderer,

Hear mercifully the vows of the peoples who pray,

Who moisten their withered faces with streaming rains.

Receive the sobs of those lamenting their committed offenses,

Who, with fragrant prayer, wash away the sins of life.

[Col. 0298A] Here is the greatest teacher, Paul, called from heaven,

Saul, who, after the change of name, was called Paul.

When you desired to place the ancient rites before Christ,

You began, after darkness, to see the clear light.

Now open kindly your ears to the voices of those praying,

And, as protector, extend your right hand together with Peter

To those who frequent and traverse the thresholds of the hall,

So that lasting indulgence for sins may be granted here,

Flowing from abundant mercy and a heavenly fountain,

Which never grows cold toward worthy peoples forever.

[Col. 0297]

## FRAGMENT ON THE DAY OF JUDGMENT, AS IT SEEMS. NOW FIRST PUBLISHED, BUT VERY CORRUPT

[Note: [Col. 0297] It is in Codex Parisinus 8318; I leave the elucidation of its text and meaning to others. GILES.] (C)*

[Col. 0297B] Why should it not be possible for a recognizable form

To be fashioned from something,

Which had once been the figure of one who had lived before,

And for it to be ordered to rise again in a form like its own,

Since all things belong to God? For the sea will restore everything.

The earth, commanded, will disgorge whatever it once held together.

If perhaps fire dissolved something on quiet funeral pyres,

Or the sea swallowed someone in its vast waves,

If fish had devoured the flesh of someone through hunger,

Or wild beasts had fixed cruel deaths upon the limbs,

If blood from the stolen body had lain scattered among birds,

The final funerals will deny no one to the Lord;

It is necessary that everyone appear alive before God from death,

And that human beings stand again in their own forms.

Thus seeds cast upon dry lands are believed

To waste away, dead, beneath the pressed furrows;

[Col. 0297C] Then the stalk is revived with restored ears of grain.

Behold, again the strong grains grow alive in living grain,

And the harvests come together … with varied increase.

All the stars fall; renewed, they shine again,

And day dies with its light in dense night.

The sun falls, and heaven returns beneath the light;

Its rising will shine again in the completed radiant sphere.

Light perishes when evening comes, casting the world into shadow,

And returns, renewing joys throughout the whole age.

Thus the phoenix, renewed, lives from its own death,

And, by its example, the bird rises again for its offspring in the nest;

The tree, stripped of leaves in its season, bears fruit,

And again the branches bend beneath their apples.

Therefore, when the trembling world hears the divine voice,

[Col. 0298B] And the powers of the lofty ether have been utterly shaken,

Then there will be an inborn crash and the greatest rumblings of heaven,

As God advances, coming as judge of the world.

Immediately innumerable ministers hasten to come together,

And surround God with heavenly majesty.

Broad angelic companies descend upon the earth,

All God’s messengers, to whom divine power belongs—

All spirits of outstanding form and strength.

They possess fiery vigor and most noble bodies;

Divine power moves from heaven,

And resounds throughout the entire ether.

Here the whole earth, trembling deeply, roars,

Giving birth to the human beings whom it will be commanded to restore.

The companions marvel; finally the clouds are troubled;

The stars, astonished by the power from above, suddenly melt,

And, bending before the Lord, descend from heaven,

[Col. 0298C] At God’s command, readily, with a mighty voice.

Immediately, when the tombs have been broken open throughout every kingdom,

Every soil pours out bones through its joyful openings,

And the sand belches forth living … peoples.

Limbs cling to hair, bones are joined to marrow,

And nerves, woven together, govern breathing bodies;

Veins, filled with blood, begin to move,

And souls, released, are returned through their hollow openings.

All the organs regain their proper places as everything rises.

Oh, wondrous rest! Here every generation springs forth.

The ancient earth springs forth from the dust of the dead.

Mothers and men rise in restored light,

Brave young men, children, and unmarried girls.

The dead old men stand among the living souls,

[Col. 0299A] And the world, lamenting its misfortune, resounds with cries.

Then various peoples come from their lowest dwelling places:

Peasant and soldier; kings with their diadems laid aside;

Rich, mingled with the poor in an equal procession.

Everywhere a profound trembling now groans through the world in prayers,

And the peoples, stretching out their hands, delay with their cries.

The Lord himself sits, standing out, bright with light,

And all-powerful fire flashes in every virtue.

He shines from a heavenly seat upon an exalted throne,

Surrounded by martyrs, a radiant multitude of men.

He stands accompanied by his beloved prophets,

Whose temples shine with bright white ribbons.

Now the priests too are present in shining garments,

Wearing gleaming reward-bearing bands and crowns,

And all, with bowed knees, … worship.

“Holy, holy, holy God” is the one voice of all;

Eternal day and unchanging time;

There clear light shines, a healthier breeze breathes,

And a region most rich in fields, hidden with God,

And an exceedingly blessed seat beneath a serene pole,

Shines, destined always to live and always to remain in light,

While the wind breathes with life-giving air,

And the earth, rich in every kind of produce, … .

Purple blazes through flower-filled meadows shaken by the breeze.

Here the seeds of the rose-colored countryside vary the snowy land,

Or the breeze is ruffled with snowy flowers of rose color.

No one knows with what the more beautiful grass becomes sweet,

Or from what the gentler breeze of the ether breathes,

Or what is more beautiful in appearance or surpasses it in honor.

Never do similar flowers arise in flower-bearing gardens;

[Col. 0299C] No lilies have bloomed like these in our fields,

Nor does the white rose immediately redden when it opens,

Nor is purple so steeped in Tyrian redness.

A gem gleams beautifully among colored stones:

The green stone shines on one side, the carbuncle blazes on the other,

And the emerald pours forth flashing lights.

Here cinnamon too is born on fragrant branches,

And the green beauty blazes with delightful joy.

Here gold lies, radiant with immense light,

And, holding lofty groves, heaven occupies a flowering summit.

There is no night to defend its gloomy darkness,

And anger, treachery [or: fear], and cares are driven from the threshold.

[Col. 0300A] Here the wicked man is bound as an exile on the farthest shores,

And he who feared labor dwells at the borders of the blessed.

There ancient faith, chosen, rests in its seat;

Justice, rejoicing, lives in an eternal covenant,

And secure salvation is relaxed in pleasing fields.

Here whoever is good … and a cultivator of the good,

And whoever fears God with an innocent, trembling mind,

And honors his parents with sacred devotion,

Or whenever he has comforted a needy friend with resources,

And has always cultivated a holy life without crime,

And has helped anyone laboring in distress—

The helper of the poor, or one accustomed to cherish orphans,

Who has rescued the condemned and aided those oppressed by crime,

And has given guests gifts from his table,

Who has harmed no one and coveted nothing belonging to another—

[Col. 0300B] For them all, rejoicing, sing divine praises,

And, praying, raise their voices to the stars;

Singing psalms to the Lord, they celebrate praises in their joy.

They will go to the blessed life accompanied by messengers.

After the Lord has bestowed these happy gifts,

And sent the righteous ahead to eternal rewards,

Behold, the pitiable crowd comes, mourning its sins,

And all groan with burning tears,

Testifying to their deeds with repeated howls.

Flaming weapons tremble according to their merits [the transmitted reading *infantia* is uncertain].

The angels seize them now, now, and forbid them to pray;

They forbid them to pour forth belated words in repentance.

Now, when the flame approaches, pardon for prayers is denied.

O wretched ones! How often divine power

Made itself known to you! How often you learned the majesty of truth!

[Col. 0300C] You heard the crashes, you saw the flashes of heaven;

You experienced the constant rains, the blasts of winds, and the fury of hail.

How often serene nights and days

Gave you the gifts of seasons fertile with abundance!

Spring generously provided roses, and summer did not lack crops;

Autumn had supplied varied and mellow fruits;

Winter, icy, had always broken the joyful olives.

God’s goodness bestowed everything; it was never lacking.

Yet through so many things the human race did not recognize God.

The earth feared God; the sea depended upon God’s command.

The river, pressed by dry sands, flowed back,

And every fruitful thing joyfully confessed God throughout all things.

[Col. 0299]

## LETTER OF AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR TO AN ANONYMOUS SISTER

(C)

[Col. 0299D] To you, adorned with the splendid chastity of flourishing virginity,

Watered from heaven by the honey-sweet water of the heavenly stream,

A virgin distinguished not only by the noble lineage of bodily birth,

But also—and this is more excellent—beautifully adorned with the spiritual honor of dignity;

To the governess of Christ’s maidservants who bear the easy yoke of God,

Who unfailingly offers to the flock entrusted to her

The rule of monastic conduct, in due order,

According to the authoritative formulas of the ancient Fathers;

And likewise to the distinguished character of noble youth,

Equally adorned with the white garment of uncorrupted integrity,

Quenched by the water of the heavenly flood,

Which flows broadly, living and ever-abundant;

Illustrated not only by outward study of letters,

But also by the inward light of divine knowledge;

To N., who, without the assistance of preceding merits, N.,

Exercises the generosity of spiritual service,

I offer desirable salvation in the Cornerstone, namely Christ.

I confess to your charity that, after I had fled and abandoned

The illustrious scepters of the land of Britain,

As I believe, touched by the wholesome admonition of divine piety,

And had left behind the most fertile island of my native country,

Which the blue-green waters of the foaming sea surround everywhere

With rocky shores,

Conscious of my weakness and, at that time, recalling to some extent my sins,

I rejoiced to have reached the shore of this region,

Carried across the surging masses of the raging sea,

With Christ’s favor, together with almost the whole company of my kindred.

Having attained my vows, I danced for joy,

And endeavored to present myself at the thresholds of the blessed apostles

In order to diminish the innumerable burdens of my sins through prayer.

There, with nearly all my relatives sunk in a long sleep of rest,

I alone remained bereft amid the misery of this exile

—and I deserved it.

I must say that I remained sad and grieving.

Yet I did not escape this illness in the former health of my body

Or in the strong joints of my limbs;

Rather—thanks and praise to the merciful Chastiser—

With all the joints of my limbs shaken and crushed,

I remain panting and exhausted.

This is something both new and familiar to me:

I solemnly declare that I have found no woman among the inhabitants there

More faithful in every respect,

Not from a motive of flattery, but with the firmness of truth.

When, for nearly five times five months,

A panting fever had afflicted my whole body,

Boiling me with cold and heat,

I remember that I was received with the kindly humanity of charity.

This, in accordance with the Lord’s command, I recognize that you did then

[Col. 0301C] For the sick and infirm,

For the sake of the reward of eternal recompense.

And I understand that, until now,

You have continued to observe and fulfill that same love

With a not-sluggish affection of sisterhood,

Under the prompting of divine love.

Therefore, having found a wholly fitting subject for writing to you,

By which I might address your beloved spiritual bond of sisterhood

In a carefully composed work,

When Christ, the giver of all good things,

Going before me in his mercy,

Made me somewhat a participant in his heavenly grace

Through one who shared in it,

I long held fixed in my mind, and cherished in my heart,

The intention of sending you verses composed according to metrical art.

For I know no readers to whom I would more gladly send them,

Since I know for certain that no suspicion of dreadful deceit

Will gnaw at the mind of the recipient,

Nor tear apart the writer with hostile criticism,

Even if a faulty page or rough sheet should be found.

This knowledge of metrical art I had recently learned

Under the instruction of our venerable bishop Boniface,

Who is general lord of all and my particular lord.

Through him, after the heavenly Illuminator,

To whom the secrets of hearts lie open

And from whom hidden and concealed things are not hidden,

The sight of my mind is opened,

And my dry breast is daily watered

By the heavenly rain of supernal nectar.

You will find these verses composed in the manner of a word-game (*jocista*),

If you do not disdain carefully to examine the heads of the letters:

That is, the other verses placed in the middle

Are enclosed as if within a surrounding frame by four verses.

These verses, which I have specifically entitled with your name,

As with that of a spiritual mother,

Begin regularly at the beginning

And run continuously to the end.

But my female disciple’s verses begin from the end of yours,

Not inappropriately,

Because a disciple ought to follow her teacher,

Just as a maidservant ought to follow her mistress.

Source/review notes: Several verses are corrupt or syntactically disordered in the supplied Latin; the translation retains them as fragments or marks genuine uncertainty rather than supplying missing syntax.

Be … [lacuna] … mindful of the Lord reigning in the sanctuary; thus they begin concerning the faith … [lacuna] … in heaven’s citadel. If you find anything in this work insufficiently suitable or polished, or inserted contrary to the rule of grammatical art, remember to smooth it by planing, taking a file from the grammarians’ workshop. I also ask with earnest prayer, by that unfading bond of spiritual friendship, that you show this work to no one without my consent or disclose its author without my permission, lest a dreadful crop of envy grow where the concord of true peace ought to sprout. [Col. 0302C] Rather, remain forever mindful of the covenant and united brotherhood pledged between us by the firmest joining of hands; and I humbly ask that you deign to aid the sweat of my labor with the pure prayers of your devotions.

Asc. berc. can. dour. ehu. feli. gip. ha. gal. is. ker. lagu. man. not. os. pert. quirun. rat. suigil. tac. ur. ilc. ian. zar.

R R R: *Rex Romanorum ruit*—the king of the Romans falls.  
P P P: *Pater patriae profectus est*—the father of the fatherland has departed.  
F F F: *Ferro, frigore, fame*—by iron, cold, and famine.  
M M M: *Monitum, monumentum, mortuus est*—a warning, a monument, he is dead.  
V V V: *Victor, vitalis, veniet*—victorious, living, he will come.  
A A A: *Aurum a nobis aufert*—he takes gold away from us.

## Poem

*The transmitted verse is often corrupt or syntactically disordered. The translation below follows its surviving lines and leaves broken constructions fragmentary rather than supplying a continuous narrative.*

[Col. 0301]

Reader, bulwark of the catholic faith,  
and champion hostage,  
moved by your prayers,  
I, the hymn writer, have sung a song,  
as I promised long ago,  
as far as dreadful Domnonia.

Upon flowered turf  
the monstrous elements  
are shaken beneath the sky,  
while the fabric of the world trembles.

Behold, in the night,  
a tempest shaking the earth,  
when the compact of the winds was broken  
and their restraint burst.  
Then, their liberty established,  
dense blasts at once—  
those winds with twice-six names.  
Their ruler, raging savagely  
with his breath—  
hence Titan’s burning heat …

With the winds’ victory  
the troubled earth was trembling.  
They fell together with their crowns,  
roots torn out at once.  
The drops did not flow gently  
but menacingly;  
sprinkling the wheel of the world,  
they drenched it with showers.  
With overpowering rain  
the whirlwind ravaged the earth  
with its rounded courses,  
so that the rivers were full.  
Things crowded down from heaven;  
the storm ranged violently.  
Even the heights of heaven  
thickened with black clouds,  
whose beautiful expanse  
was without the darkness of night.

[Col. 0302]

Until, beneath raincloud and clouds—  
for they grow dark in the whirlwind—  
the kindred lights of Phoebus,  
clear as ice,  
were covered by savage darkness.  
The flame bearer did not blaze  
as he very often does,  
but was blinded by gloom,  
the order of things disrupted.  
The splendid lights,  
and Lucifer, leader of the days,  
did not show their courses;  
the golden star did not rise  
as it diligently keeps its course,  
but lay hidden as if by black soot.

The chariot’s exceedingly beautiful course  
did not appear.  
Seven lamps concealed  
the Pleiades’ beautiful union.  
From Aquilo and Circius,  
these ascend through the sky.  
With as many torrents  
the balance then stood level and clear.  
To those earnestly asking,  
I returned answers.  
The zodiac with the other signs,  
which we find called Mazaroth of old,  
when I had set out  
through barren Cornwall,  
with its twice-six stars  
shining through Olympus,  
and through fertile grasses  
and shapeless works—  
the transmitted construction remains unfinished.

[Col. 0303]

The vaulted chamber of heaven  
lay beneath the monarchy of the winds.  
When the winter whirlwind arose,  
devastation brought confusion;  
the winds raged in the sky.  
The transmitted *desae virent* is obscure.  
With servitude lulled to sleep,  
they lead armies of war.  
The volumes supplied names;  
their ruler, fiercely sweeping fame away,  
came from the quarter of the sky.  
The heavenly lights fell.  
The winds did not rage without glory;  
oaks were uprooted,  
their roots torn up together.

Sirius did not shine red  
as he was accustomed;  
the blackest cloud  
hid the poles beneath coverings  
spread across heaven’s heights.  
Yet lightning flashed;  
the high places vomited flame.  
When the hanging mass grew pale,  
it advanced amid collisions;  
the nature of the clouds  
was heaped upon the gravel.

The blue sea also—  
the onslaught of the winds—  
foamed with salt water  
where the irruption rushed  
along the sea’s paths.  
A wave-whirled vortex,  
with bubbles and winter storms,  
and with dreadful surges,  
the Ocean with its masses,  
with victory assisting,  
struck the headlands.  
Thus the sea swelled under cruel winds,  
against rocky shores,  
driving the rivers onward.

What shall I say of the mighty works  
of the One enthroned on high,  
which no one could count  
on a reckoning stone?  
Behold, many now appear openly  
as a wonder:  
Christ’s bright mercy  
in these recent events.

When welcome cockcrow,  
as at the fourth watch,  
roused the sleepy with its sounds,  
then, standing in two choirs,  
we celebrated in harmony  
the morning melody  
and the psalmody of the congregation.

Behold, at once the supports, shaken by the gale,  
tottered from their foundations;  
all the timbers and beams  
trembled under enormous blows  
to every part of the hall.  
In such tempests  
our hearts were afraid  
at the whirlwinds before dawn,  
when eyes beheld  
so many monstrous prodigies:  
roofs and panelled ceilings  
shaken with dreadful crashes,  
leaving thresholds broken.

At length the company, running,  
sought the harbor of the basilica,  
escaping the ravaging destruction.  
Thus dangers are driven away  
through the help of the Mother  
from the offspring of Atlas.

Some greatly feared the peril  
on the steep and slippery sides  
of hilly country;  
they avoided it by leaps.  
They heard a shattered hut crack.  
The shelters too would have failed.  
But when the foul darkness,  
its covering collapsing,  
was split—blind gloom torn apart—  
and the daylight’s radiance rose,  
then one looking from the church  
saw an image as of death.

“Behold,” I said, “the fearful night:  
fragments of rafters lie scattered.  
Behold the tops of huts  
that once appeared most splendid.  
Behold the sunny broom bushes:  
their leafy coverings  
are driven from the walls  
as by the battering rams of workmen.  
Alas, the protection of roofs  
is cast down in the street.  
Behold, lattices fall from the ridge,  
collapsing without defense.”

[Col. 0304]

The breaths of the savage gale  
made this mockery.  
Had the feast of Saint Paul  
not protected trembling hearts,  
we perhaps would have been struck  
from the shattered roof and by lightning.  
The Gospel sayings disclose  
how cruelly,  
about eighteen times,  
the tower’s fragments broke,  
together with an immense wall—  
the utterances of the triune Thunderer.

Therefore, delivered from peril,  
let us together give sweet thanks to Christ,  
who remains immortal.  
Glory to God unbegotten,  
and likewise to the begotten Son,  
together with the Holy Spirit above,  
the breath that governs the ages.

## Another poem begins

Recently, concerning the things that descended—  
without delay, my … yours …  
as with honey-making …  
once an illustrious poet,  
with the screeching reed of his pen,  
inscribed in sacred pages  
the world, unfolded in its turning courses,  
through two seasons of winter,  
soon completed as they declined,  
in heroic verses.

A native of the city of Rome,  
writing with tireless care,  
learned Sedulius  
told how, by the threefold utterance,  
the mass of the world in its rotations  
was driven swiftly onward,  
stretched through the open spaces,  
and made known through the sky.  
Virtue crowned them—  
and the transmitted *Paetanamque per fabricam*  
remains obscure—  
with the triple strands of faith.  
Thus the forces of tyranny are thrust down.

[Col. 0305]

Upon these it rushed horribly,  
warlike in the contest.  
Confounded—what does truth …?—  
beneath the heights of Christ’s cross,  
which fleeing Orcus … with horrors.  
The syntax of these lines is broken.

But you, renowned for strength,  
conquered the savage foe with a trophy.  
Neither relatives and homelands,  
nor the turf of an unknown land  
to which you came in sudden chance,  
nor raging, wave-roaring whirlpools,  
nor the swollen land of Dis,  
terrible in its warfare,  
nor robbers who gather spoils  
with the native enticements  
of death-bearing lust,  
nor beasts with ravening jaws  
and snapping beaks,  
nor wanderers along pathless roads  
at the boundaries of bushy country,  
could restrain the purpose  
of Christ’s exalted soldiers  
or the course of their endeavor.

Then for the sake of divine love,  
advancing toward the heights  
in their desire to see him,  
they sought Peter’s aid.  
They obtained from God  
the favor that all these might be joined  
in the Lord with firm cement.

At last they ran swiftly down  
and came to the nurturing shrine,  
frequenting it for pardon,  
where Peter’s little body  
lies hidden, buried in the earth.  
Then at the altar, with blessed brothers,  
by Peter’s helping word,  
the flesh, secretly torn from prison,  
clung to heaven’s fortress.  
Raised there among blossoms,  
joined to the exalted ones,  
it reigns there throughout the ages.

The key bearer of the royal realm—  
the intervening obstacles …  
standing but little and unsteadily.  
The surviving construction is fragmentary.

Two by two, for the age,  
the men without delay,  
through the moisture of brotherhood  
to the heights of highest Olympus,  
along the boundary of a very long road  
that they had sought as homeland—  
the text passes again into broken praise:  
a crested crown encircles them;  
the living breast of the heavenly Lord;  
they circle the shoulders of the cuirass.

You, eloquent one of the recruit—  
a shower falls as though upon you.  
Against Christ’s battle line  
the dark standard raised indicates …  
We bear banners upon our brows;  
it fears showers of missiles.  
Brave men sweating in the struggle  
defeat the enemy in heavenly war.

Two by two among the blessed,  
green as little flowers,  
they seek the flowering homelands of Paradise  
by the paths of merit,  
having once despised with swift feet  
the refuse of the world.  
They do not seek what luxury makes fleeting,  
but gifts of grace,  
what is borne in no small measure  
through the flowery regions of souls,  
where dry land is enriched  
by numerous hosts.

Behold, they carried volumes  
elaborated according to many and mystical rules.  
Their author is known to be inspired from heaven:  
the oracles of learned speech,  
which prophets and apostles,  
under the nurturing breath of inspiration,  
set down on parchment.  
No utterances disclose …  
They carried them quickly.

Now they also carried coverings of garments  
as an extraordinary and wondrous gift.  
[Col. 0306] They draw out their origins,  
derived from the beginning:  
certain offspring, marvelous indeed,  
were at first the smallest worms.  
The one who knows them feeds on leaves;  
the creature arises through winter’s passage.  
When its offspring advances,  
it arises from the womb of eggs.  
It did not issue as seed  
from the creatures that produced it;  
the same worm grew warm again  
from the deepest principle of nature—  
a thing hopeless to the world.  
What is more marvelous:  
the warmed eggs of male and female  
bring forth living offspring,  
clothed in fleece.

Purple wool comes forth  
when it becomes a little worm.  
Like a dense spider  
it weaves a fly-like web.  
From the barking—or rough workings—of the wool,  
the filaments are greatly spread in flight;  
it is twisted into threads like bristles.  
From it silks are taken.

The things they carried together  
shone in beautiful appearance:  
purple with roses of Paradise,  
and linen lilies among ivory forms.  
Thus indeed the silken insignia, blood-red,  
beautifully painted on snow-white,  
saffron-colored, green, tawny, and flowery;  
dyed and woolen cloths  
like the mantles of robes  
upon the turf of Paradise.

They brought the relics of so many saints  
in extraordinary quantity,  
and the prayers those relics bestow;  
and still another small gift:  
images with golden ornaments  
protecting the breastplate.  
With many noble things  
they brought gifts to Christ’s mother,  
the Church,  
the rich mother of those who believe in Christ.

Farewell amid blessings,  
both theirs and everyone’s.  
They display beautiful ornaments,  
the outstanding works of some persons;  
another, dedicated vigorously by command,  
adds the faithful prayers of those who pray;  
another adds a most beautiful gift,  
turning the eyes toward the heads  
of Christ’s mother.  
They bore all these gifts,  
before closing life beneath their heels.

## Another poem begins

The highest Sower, who sits  
in the citadels of lofty Olympus,  
surrounded by threatening powers,  
seeing all from the summit,  
in heaven’s highest light,  
the heights of the pole and the bounds  
of the broad earth—  
whose immense gifts and works of death  
I am altogether unable to sing in harmony  
before ravening jaws seize and gnaw them,  
drawing breath from the body  
in the stiff numbness of fate.

I therefore ask him with abundant tears,  
amid the harsh strains of lofty praise.  
Gladly striking myself down to the ground,  
bending my neck and the crown of my head,  
I ask that he grant sacred consolation  
to one who totters,  
through sublime and nurturing help,  
supporting him strongly with his hand.

[Col. 0307]

May he remove the missiles of enemies  
with which the hostile assail  
the strong helmets of Christ’s recruits;  
may they carry cuirasses on their shoulders  
while deadly showers blow upon them  
amid foul, murderous crashes  
and flashing missiles.  
May the Almighty drive those enemies  
into eternal darkness,  
where most dreadful Typho  
twists in the coiled bosoms  
of whirlpools,  
under the avenging weapons of black fire.  
Behold, the transmitted *pilarum acerrima*—  
“the sharpest of balls” or “missiles”—is uncertain.  
May his shield repel their points  
from savage enemies  
as they contend in combat.

O heavenly one, who formed all things  
in the beginning  
by the divine power of the Word alone,  
lord of the world,  
pour out eloquent words for me,  
who by your signs make new things for me  
amid the play of letters,  
so that in the poem begun  
I may fit songs to their uses  
and approach a man renowned for virtue,  
an ancient helmet in name …  
[lacuna]

The stars of Olympus, with fiery light,  
bring forth a light-flowing radiance;  
their threatening mass upon the world,  
and dark smoke in the cold.  
The brightness of heaven from its summit—  
Titan trembles beneath torrents.  
Throughout the margins of the world,  
Phoebe too, with blazing torches  
shining far to heaven’s boundary,  
scatters black night with clouds.  
Both spread their breath;  
one brother assists the other with his heat.  
The light shines with little horns.

The lights of ethereal fire  
do not harm with their brilliance;  
beside a stream in the watered countryside,  
upon wooded turf,  
with dewy moisture  
continually watering the earth.  
But the muddy ground with liquid—  
the transmitted relation is broken.  
The stars were dry with fiery heat;  
the seeds of the clods grow,  
the trees in a dewy place,  
and take on the savor of their juices.

That ancient helmet through the heights,  
glorious among the hosts,  
crowned with shining light—  
the stars of vaulted Olympus.  
[Col. 0307] For Aldhelm, most exalted,  
powerful in heavenly things,  
with our people’s lofty name:  
thus indeed amid sublime things,  
as upon the heights of heaven,  
protecting those faithful to Christ  
in all things with reeds—  
the wording *protegens arundinibus* is transmitted without a clear construction.

I would undertake, with wavering songs,  
to proclaim in lofty speech  
one shining in heaven,  
adorned as with light,  
giving life to the steep world.  
The fiery axis and its citadels shine;  
hearths fill them with heat  
and pour forth saffron lightning.

The ancients disclose resplendent,  
gem-bearing utterances,  
clear as refined gold.  
They shine upon the green world,  
white and most bright,  
called by name and by divine power,  
powerful and sufficiently adorned  
with earthly rites.  
They glow through rising lightning.

I call him equal in deeds.  
Whatever may be said sublimely—  
the very length of the rising discourse …  
May salvation remain yours  
immortally through the ages.  
I detest the monstrosity of this song;  
its disorder resists me.  
Safe from every stain,  
may you prosper happily to the end.

## Another poem begins

Farewell, farewell, most faithful Phile,  
dearest of Christ,  
whom I bind in the chamber of my heart  
with the bond of love.  
I offer suppliant greetings:  
“Hail, highest Hova,”  
together with the words of Ethelwald.

You, lord in all things,  
made him illustrious in deeds,  
manly in form and appearance,  
an elder in deed and word.  
No winged creature can,
