by deep investigation of mind,  
carefully conjecture and behold  
your first offspring  
beneath the clouds of highest heaven.

[Col. 0308]

Nevertheless, having undertaken with joy,  
we shall speak with some trembling.  
Born as the noble offspring  
of the highest Sower,  
nobly brought forth,  
released from your mother,  
remarkable in stature,  
agile in build and form;  
your head gleaming with hair,  
your hair surrounding it with shining locks.

Lights shine beneath your forehead,  
like the hot, bright heavens;  
stars of clear radiance  
upon broad heights.  
The twin cheeks gather in rounded masses,  
slowly purple,  
painted in dye and snow-white,  
like roses bright with red blossoms.

The ears listen to all things.  
The countless words of the kindly mouth  
cannot tell its gifts—  
bright, abundant speech is present,  
wisdom and everything luminous.  
Hands, wondrous hands;  
feet most pleasing,  
shins smooth in running,  
yet strong as a warhorse.  
They often follow in their courses,  
leaping with winged speed.

Even if someone should shout a hundred times,  
and call out among the timbers,  
roaring with an iron voice  
and making a great crash with his mouth,  
no one in this age can truly express by an oracle  
how wonderful you are to the world.  
Nor can anyone with sounding words  
express your lofty intellect.

For that reason I offer no more.  
May the Lord who rules all things  
keep you safe from every stain,  
cover you entirely with protection,  
drive away the enemy’s point,  
and rightly grant you refuge  
through mighty aid.

May he place you in the heavenly realm,  
in the bosom of the celestial scepter,  
where companionship with the heavenly ones  
is always without end. [Col. 0309]

[Lacuna.]

Though a mortal cry out in harmonious songs,  
he cannot explain it;  
nor can I recount it with any praise.  
Its boundaries shine clear to all.  
May you enjoy the company of angels  
and live your life upon those fields.

[Col. 0309]

# SOME CHARTERS OF SAINT ALDHELM, BISHOP OF SHERBORNE, OR THE FOURTH PART OF HIS WORKS

## I. Excerpt from the Book of the Antiquities of the Monastery of Maldulph, transcribed word for word

[W. Dugdale is cited in *Monasticon Anglicanum*, from Leland’s manuscript *Collectanea* in the Bodleian Library, vol. III, p. 266.]

[Col. 0309A]

Meldulph, leading the eremitical life beneath the castle of Bladow, which in Saxon is called Ingelborne Castle, lived there. It had been built by a certain British king named Dumwallo Molvicius. A city had once stood there, but it was utterly destroyed by foreigners. The castle kept itself fortified and guarded; for a long time it stood without a nearby settlement.

The royal residence, and its manor, both of pagans and of Christians, was not far from the castle, at Kairdurberg, which in Saxon is called Brohambergh, [Col. 0309B] but is now called Brokenberg. The aforesaid hermit asked the castle-dwellers to build him a hut beneath the castle, and he obtained his request; for there was not a large gathering of people there.

When he lacked the necessities of life, he gathered scholars around himself for instruction, so that by their generosity he might improve the scantiness of his food. In a short time the scholars grew together into a small community. Through their companionship and example Saint Aldhelm was fully instructed and added the art of dialectic to his education.

From there he departed to the feet of the philosopher Adrian, abbot of Saint Augustine’s at Canterbury, and studied for some time. Once sufficiently instructed, he returned to Maldulph’s monastery. Later, with his companions, he was tonsured under the monk Maildulph; Maildulph lived fourteen years after his tonsure.

The aforementioned castle was then under the authority of Eleutherius, bishop of Winchester, who ruled throughout Wessex. After Maildulph’s death, the aforesaid bishop gave the site of Malmesbury to Saint Aldhelm.

## II. Charter by which Eleutherius gives Maildulph’s monastery to Aldhelm

[See William of Malmesbury, *De Regibus*.]

I, Leutherius [sic], by divine grace bishop, governing the reins of the episcopate of Saxony, have been asked by the abbots who are known to preside, with pastoral concern, over the monastic company of monks subject to the jurisdiction of our parish, to deign to confer and give to Aldhelm the priest, for the regular conduct of his life, that land called Maildulfesburch.

In that place, from the earliest age of infancy and from the very beginning of his training, he was educated in the studies of the liberal arts and nurtured in the bosom of holy mother Church, and there he lived. For this reason above all, brotherly love seems to have suggested this petition.

Therefore, consenting to the prayers of the aforesaid abbots, compelled by their fraternal petition, I freely grant the place both to him and to his successors who follow the rule of holy discipline with diligent devotion.

Publicly enacted beside the river Bladon, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 675.

## III. How Eleutherius, bishop of Winchester, granted in perpetual gift to Aldhelm the priest and the monastery of Maldulph the land of Maeldumesberg

[From the cartulary of the monastery of Malmesbury in the Bodleian Library, fol. 10b.]

[Col. 0310B]

It commonly happens that, when the burning heat of autumn has departed, the winter blasts of raging winds succeed one another in alternating courses. By them the stormy blue of the sea and the vast whirlpools of Ocean are shaken here and there, so that, when the ship wanders, no sailor crosses without danger, while the furious wind tears the sails.

So, clearly, the fallen splendor of the world, and its end already approaching, seems by evident experience to show that the storms of the fluctuating age are pressing upon us, so that, truly and without any doubtful hesitation, those prophecies of the Lord are at last proved to be fulfilled in our own times, by which He spoke these heavenly oracles: “See the fig tree,” and so forth.

Moreover, amid these turbulent storms of the age, the rudders of Scripture must be steered, and the equipment and instruments of the entire ship must be prepared, so that, once the chattering song of the Sirens has been rejected, the vessel may be brought safely by a straight course to the harbor of its homeland.

Therefore I, Eleutherius, by the grace of God bishop, governing the reins of the Saxon episcopate, have been asked by the abbots who are known to preside, with pastoral concern, over the monastic company of monks subject to the jurisdiction of our parish, to deign to confer and give to Aldhelm the priest, for the regular conduct of his life, that land called Maldumesburga. In that place, from the earliest age of infancy and from the very beginning of his training, he was educated in the studies of the liberal arts, nurtured in the bosom of holy mother Church, and lived.

For this reason above all, brotherly love seems to have suggested this petition. Therefore, consenting to the prayers of the aforesaid abbots, compelled by their fraternal petition, I freely grant the place mentioned above both to him and to his successors who follow the rule of holy discipline with diligent devotion, so that in future generations, with every conflict of impending disputes removed, they may serve God in continual quiet and perpetual peace [Col. 0311B] without hindrance.

But, lest an occasion for contention should afterward arise, I strengthen and confirm this grant by inserting this condition: no bishop or king who succeeds us may, relying on tyrannical power, violently invade this charter of our donation, asserting stubbornly that it appears to have been taken away and separated from the lawful authority of the episcopate. Therefore it must be known and proclaimed against opponents that I have added much more benefit and increase to the episcopal Church than I have taken away by force.

Finally, so that the generosity of the aforesaid donation may remain continually firm, we ordered the aforesaid abbots to subscribe with their own hands. If anyone attempts to invalidate these writings and decrees of our decision, let him know that he will render an account before the tribunal [Col. 0311C] of Christ.

Publicly enacted beside the river Bladum, on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, in the year of Christ’s Incarnation 680.

+ I, Eleutherius, although unworthy as bishop, asked by the brothers, have subscribed this charter of donation.  
+ I, Cunebert, abbot, have subscribed.  
+ I, Hedde, abbot, have subscribed.  
+ I, Wynebert, priest, have subscribed.  
+ I, Hiddi, priest, have subscribed.  
+ I, Hedda, have subscribed.

## IV. How King Ethelred granted Newentune and Cherletone near Tetteburi to Aldhelm the abbot and the monastery of Maldulph

[Ibid., fol. 13b.]

[Col. 0311D]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior.

As the apostolic oracle testifies, “We brought nothing into this world, nor can we take anything away.” Therefore earthly and perishable things must be exchanged for eternal and lasting things.

Accordingly I, Ethelred, king of the Mercians, at the request of my patrician and kinsman Coenfrid, for the remedy of my soul and for the prayers of the brothers serving God at Meldunesburg, have willingly granted thirty cassates on the western side of the public road and, not far away, in another place, fifteen near the monastery of Tettan, to Aldhelm the abbot and his successors, in perpetual freedom from earthly services.

I have confirmed this donation with the sign of the holy cross and with my own [Col. 0312A] hand, and strengthened it by the clear consent of favorable men, so that after our death no royal audacity or secular dignity might attempt to break our decree.

If anyone wishes to increase and enlarge this donation, may God increase his portion in the book of life. But if anyone, relying on tyrannical power, attempts to diminish or take it away, let him know that he will render an account before Christ and the nine orders of angels.

This charter was written in the year 681 from the Incarnation of Christ, indiction 9.

Sign of the hand of Ethelred, king of the Mercians.  
Sign of the hand of Coenfrid, earl.  
I, Theodore, archbishop by the grace of God, have confirmed [it].  
[Col. 0312B] + I, Saxwulf, bishop, have subscribed.  
+ I, Bosel, bishop, have subscribed.

## V. How the same king gave fifteen cassates near Tetteburi to the same Church

[Ibid., fol. 14b.]

In the name, and so forth, up to “serving God at Meldunesburg”: I have willingly granted fifteen cassates near the monastery of Tettan to Aldhelm the abbot.

If anyone wishes to increase and enlarge this donation, may God increase his portion in the book of life. But if anyone, relying on tyrannical power, attempts to diminish or take it away, let him know that before Christ and the nine orders of angels, at the dread judgment, he will render an account. [Col. 0312C]

This charter was written in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 680, indiction 9.

+ I, Theodore, archbishop by the grace of God, have confirmed [it].  
+ I, Saxwulf, bishop, likewise.  
+ I, Bosel, bishop, have subscribed.  
+ Sign of the hand of Ethelred, king of the Mercians.  
+ Sign of the hand of Cenfrid, earl.

## VI. Concerning Kemela, which King Ceadwalla gave to the same Church

[Ibid., fol. 15.]

All things that are seen are temporal, and those that are not seen are eternal. Therefore invisible things are to be preferred to visible things, and heavenly things to perishable things.

For this reason I, Ceadwalla, king by the reign of the Lord, have decided to bestow some benefit upon the Church: namely, land on both sides of the wood called Kemele, amounting to 132 cassates.

Let this donation remain so fixed and immovable that no one may presume to break or invalidate this decree. But if anyone, swollen with proud tyranny, attempts to violate or transgress this donation, let him know that at the dread judgment of all, before the judge of the living and the dead, he will render an account.

This charter was written in indiction 1, in August, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 682.

+ Sign of the hand of King Cadwalla.  
+ I, Hedde, bishop, have consented.  
+ Sign of the hand of Cisi.  
+ I, Wynbert, have subscribed.

## VII. Charter of Berthwald concerning Sumerford, situated beside the river called the Thames, which he granted by royal munificence to Aldhelm, abbot of the Church of Maldulph, and to his successors in perpetual inheritance

[From the cartulary of the monastery of Malmesbury in the Bodleian Library, fol. 10b.]

[Col. 0313A]

Things established with religious devotion according to the fear and love of the Lord, although speech alone would suffice to proclaim them, must nevertheless, because of the uncertain condition of future times, be confirmed by public writings and records of documents.

Therefore I, Berthwald, king by the reign of the Lord, for the remedy of my soul and the forgiveness of my committed sins, have decided to confer and grant some land to Aldhelm the abbot: namely, forty cassates on the eastern side of the river called Temys, beside the ford whose name [Col. 0313B] is Summerforde.

The condition is that every portion of that land shall be perpetually free from the service of secular powers, for the needs of the monks serving God in the monastery called Malmesburge.

And so that this donation of mine may be strengthened more firmly and securely, we have called the most excellent monarch, King Ethelred, as witness; with his consent and confirmation this munificence has been enacted.

If anyone attempts to oppose this donation, or, relying on tyrannical power, invades it, let him know that at the dread judgment of all, before Christ, he will render an account.

Publicly enacted in the synod beside the ford of Bregforde, in July, on the thirtieth day of that month; indiction 13, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 686.

[Col. 0313C]

+ Theodore, archbishop.  
+ Ethelred, king of the Mercians.  
+ Berthwald, sub-king.  
+ Kenfrith, patrician.  
+ Sexwulf of Lichfield, bishop.  
+ Bosel, bishop of Worcester.

## VIII. Charter of liberty which King Ina granted to Bishop Aldhelm and to the Churches established under his governance

In the name of our Lord God the Savior.

I, Ina, king by the reign of the Lord, with the counsel and decree of our bishop Aldhelm, and likewise at the urging of all God’s priests and the petition of the monks who live in the parish of the Saxons, grant this liberty to the Churches and confer this dignity of privilege upon the monasteries: that, without hindrance from secular affairs and without tribute from fiscal obligations, they may serve God alone with free minds, and, with Christ’s help, practice the monastic discipline of the community according to the rule.

For the condition and prosperity of our kingdom, and for the forgiveness of our committed sins, may they deign to pour out prayers before the sight of the divine majesty, and, frequenting the duties of prayer, strive to intercede in the churches for our frailty.

But if anyone attempts to oppose the charter of this decree, let him know that before Christ and the nine orders of angels, at the dread judgment, he will render an account.

We decree that this decree, willingly granted by us, be confirmed and observed in such a way that, while divine favor accompanies us and we govern the reins of the kingdom, it may be firmly strengthened by an inextricable law. [Col. 0314B]

For a still fuller testimony of its firmness, we have caused princes and senators, judges and patricians to subscribe; their names are written below.

Publicly enacted and confirmed at the place called Eburleaugh, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, indiction 2, in the year of Christ’s Incarnation 704, successfully.

+ Sign of the hand of King Ina, who confirmed all this with his own hand.  
+ I, Aldhelm, servant of the servants of God, have strengthened this decree with my own hand.  
+ I, Hagona, abbot, consenting, have subscribed.  
+ I, Heagha, abbot, consenting, have subscribed.  
+ I, Wedre, abbot, consenting, have subscribed.  
[Col. 0314C] + I, Wilgar, abbot, consenting, have subscribed.  
+ I, Froda, abbot, consenting, have subscribed.  
+ Sign of the hand of Beoban.  
+ Sign of the hand of Ceonberth.  
+ Sign of the hand of Ethelfrid.  
+ Sign of the hand of Deduce.  
+ Sign of the hand of Bealdhum.  
+ Edbert, abbot, consenting, have subscribed.  
+ I, Wintra, abbot, consenting, have subscribed.  
+ I, Beorwald, abbot.  
+ I, Beawulf, abbot, consenting, have subscribed.  
+ I, Witta, abbot, consenting, have subscribed.  
+ Sign of the hand of Camberth.  
+ Sign of the hand of Coen.  
+ Sign of the hand of Easwald.  
[Col. 0314D] + Sign of the hand of Ticceau.

# In the Year of the Lord 715. Constantine, Roman Pontiff

[Col. 0315]

# Historical Notice Concerning Pope Constantine

(*Liber Pontificalis*, from various editions.)

[Col. 0315A] [Note: 1. Constantine. Although the less careful reckoning of dates and the uncertain testimony of the manuscripts compel even the most distinguished chronologists to conjecture, nevertheless the support of an ancient document sometimes confirms matters that had seemed either dubiously asserted or rashly preferred over another opinion. Such is the case with the beginnings of Pope Constantine. Since the two difficulties just mentioned made the chronology of the preceding three pontificates extremely laborious, and continue to do so in establishing the dates of the pontificates of this pope and Gregory II, an ancient document elsewhere demonstrates which opinion ought to be followed. It teaches that the depositions in the commonly circulated Codex of Anastasius [Col. 0315B] are to be preferred to those found in manuscript codices. The document is preserved in the frequently cited Veronese catalogue, contemporary with those times, which says as follows: “In the first year of his pontificate [Constantine’s], the 150th year of the repeated cycle of Victorius is completed, in the 7th indiction, the first year, while Tiberius was emperor together with his father Justinian.” Three things become known from this valuable document—especially since the Victorian period had not yet fallen out of use among the Italians—which I shall briefly pursue because they concern my purpose.

That document is distinguished by three chronological markers: the cycle, or Victorian period; the indiction; and the emperor. The 150th year of the repeated Victorian period begins with the Kalends of January of the Dionysian year 709. For, as the learned Cardinal Noris demonstrates against Scaliger (*On the Paschal Cycle of Ravenna*, chapter 2), the beginning of that period must be taken from the leap year 28 of the Passion of Jesus Christ, whose Kalends of January fell on a Thursday, Easter on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, and the lunar cycle on 16; after the entire revolution had been completed, the year 569 arrived, whose Kalends of January fell on a Wednesday, Easter on the Ides of April, and the lunar cycle on 9. Therefore, in the following year, 560, a new revolution began, and its 150th year began to run with the Dionysian year 709, in which, according to the document cited, the first year of Pope Constantine was in progress.

The 7th indiction, however, since it began in September of the year 708, unquestionably coincides with the 150th year of the Victorian period and the Dionysian year 709. As for the emperor, the document does not count the years, but it bears witness to the otherwise neglected sovereignty of Tiberius, Justinian’s son, who had been admitted as co-emperor. Baronius records this in the year 703 from the Greek annals of Theophanes and Cedrenus. Indeed, Baronius also states there that Justinian, immediately upon recovering the empire, adorned his wife Theodora with the imperial crown alongside Tiberius. Concerning Tiberius, Paul the Deacon (*History of the Lombards*, book VI, chapter 32) had conveyed the matter in these words: “Justinian ruled together with his son Tiberius on this second occasion for six years.” From this the year of each emperor [Col. 0316A] can easily be recognized. Since it is clear from Anastasius that the pope returned from Constantinople to Rome in the year 711, on the twenty-fourth day of October, and that the slaughter of Justinian, whose empire Philippicus had usurped, was announced at Rome three months later, there is no doubt that Justinian was killed in December of that same year, 711. Consequently, he began to reign again with his son Tiberius in December of the year 705—a point Pagius also correctly observes, against the opinion of the learned cardinal, who adds two years to the empire.

Accordingly, in the 150th year of the repeated Victorian period and the Dionysian year 709, the fourth year of both emperors was in progress. Let these observations be accepted as contributing to a fuller understanding of the ancient document.

Now, relying on its testimony, I shall pursue what concerns the pontificate of Constantine. I rightly wondered, as is evident, that some learned men thought Constantine’s pontificate had to begin in December of the year 707, for in that case his first year could by no means be counted together with the year 709. To establish the matter correctly in the following year, 708, the interval between pontificates after Sisinnius must be considered.

When that pontiff died a sudden death and was buried at Saint Peter’s on 7 February of the year 708, the apostolic see was vacant for one month, as all the codices and catalogues unanimously state, and eighteen days, as is read in the Lucchese catalogue and four Colbertine manuscripts; or nineteen days, as the first Colbertine and the Royal, Mazarin, Thuane, and the first and third Ambrosian codices have it. The authority of the other manuscripts, which add ten days, must be rejected, as is shown by the date of Constantine’s death. Therefore, after an interregnum of one month and eighteen days—excluding the day of Sisinnius’s death—or nineteen days, including it—the date 25 March is reached, which coincided that year with a Sunday, in a leap year. It is consequently clear that this date must be assigned to the pope’s ordination.

After sitting for seven years and fifteen days, by the agreement of all the catalogues and codices, with only a difference of a few days in some of them, he died on the fifth day before the Ides of April, that is, on 9 April, in the 13th indiction, which indicates the year 715. This is correctly stated by the common text of Anastasius and by the second Freherian, Cavensis, and Farnesian codices. The Lucchese catalogue supports them, clearly distinguishing the day of death from the day of burial, when it assigns Constantine’s death to 7 April. Thus the same number of years is reckoned from the day of his ordination, 25 March 708, to the day of his death, or deposition, 9 April 715.

A careful chronologist will observe that the manifest contradiction of the other codices—which persist in the error once begun and extend the pope’s death by many months—must be attributed to the stupidity of the copyists. I shall not take care to wrap the opinions of others once more in the same labyrinth from which they have at last been drawn. Enough concerning Constantine. Cennus.]

**2. Constantine.** In the year 708, 1 March. In his time Spain, through the treachery of Count Julian and with a lamentable outcome, was entirely subjected to the rule of the Saracens—clearly by the permission of God, the avenger who was punishing the lust of Roderic and the defection of King Witiza from the apostolic see. See Baronius, year 713. Bin. and Labb.

**3. Constantine.** Son of John, a Syrian; under the emperors Justinian the Younger and Philippicus Bardanes Augustus, he sat for eight years, one month, and twenty days. He was created on the tenth day before the Kalends of January and consecrated on the eighth day before the Kalends, on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, at the beginning of the year 708; during his pontificate there was a great famine. Ciaconius.]

Constantine, Syrian by nation, son of John, [Note: [Col. 0316D] He sat for seven years. Baronius correctly proves that Constantine held the apostolic see for six years, one month, and one day. Bin. and Labb.] sat for seven years, [Note: [Col. 0315A] Lucchese Codex 40: six.] fifteen days. [Note: [Col. 0316A] Other copies omit “There were … Augusti.”] He lived during the reigns of the Augusti Justinian, Philippicus, and Anastasius. He was a very gentle man. During his pontificate a great famine occurred in the city of Rome for three years. Afterward there was such abundance that the plentiful harvest caused the poverty of the former scarcity to be forgotten.

[Note: [Col. 0317B] 1. Felix. Here Anastasius records the wrongs inflicted upon the people of Ravenna because they had dared to do certain things without consultation and rashly. He is silent, however, about the rebellion against Justinian, which Agnellus recounts at length, since on that account Archbishop Felix had his eyes torn out and lived for some time in exile in Pontus. The caution which was to be delivered by the same man was similar, or perhaps more extensive, to that found in the Roman *Diurnus*, which the elected metropolitans used to make. More extensive, I say, was that of the bishops of Ravenna, since it had to include those clauses which, according to Agnellus in the *Life of Theodore of Ravenna*, chapter 4, page 153, had been agreed upon under Leo II. See Bacchinius, *Observations on the Life of Felix of Ravenna*. Bencinus.

2. Here he ordained Felix. At the very beginning of the pontificate of Pope Constantine, after Damian, bishop of Ravenna, had died, Felix was substituted in his place. He came to Rome, though reluctantly, according to custom, in order to receive consecration from the pope, and issued a profession of faith and a pledge of obedience. But when he returned to Ravenna, he violated it at the instigation of the citizens and again separated himself from the apostolic see by schism. For this reason the emperor Justinian, enraged against him, sent the patrician Theodore with an army to Ravenna. After capturing the city, Theodore stripped the rebels of their property and sent them in chains to Constantinople, where they were put to death; Archbishop Felix himself was deprived of his eyes and deported into exile in Pontus.

Thus Anastasius relates the matter. He adds, however, in the Life of Pope Constantine, that after Justinian was killed Felix was released from exile and, although blind, restored to his church after rendering the usual obedience to the Roman pontiff. Jerome Rubeus, in his *History of Ravenna*, even testifies that Felix shone with distinguished holiness and miracles. From that time the bishops of that city displayed complete obedience to the Roman pontiffs until the beginning of the eleventh century, as we shall see under Paschal II. Pagius.

3. Here he ordained Felix, archbishop of Ravenna. The archbishops of Ravenna had long been plotting to withdraw themselves from the jurisdiction of the Roman pontiffs, at least in what concerned their ordination and the rights of the Roman Church as patriarchal Church of the West. In this matter they undoubtedly imitated the archbishops of Constantinople, who had finally emerged as patriarchs because their city had become the imperial residence. Following their example, the people of Ravenna became convinced that they too might obtain something similar, since the exarch resided in their city.

For this reason Archbishop Felix, who had been displeased at being ordained by Pope Constantine, carried the crime of attempted independence farther than any of his predecessors. No sooner had he been ordained at Rome than he returned to Ravenna, shook off the yoke of the holy see, and drew the leading citizens into his schism. But alas for his unhappy audacity! The emperor, especially offended by it, decided to punish him rather than encourage him. Accordingly, he sent an army to Ravenna, a city that had prepared in vain to resist. After capturing the archbishop and his followers, he ordered the latter to be killed and condemned the former, deprived of his eyes, to exile. Sommier.]

Here he ordained Felix, archbishop of Ravenna, who, contrary to the customary cautions of his predecessors in the archives, [Note: [Col. 0318B] “He did not wish to make the customary cautions in the archives.” Among medieval writers, a man was said “to make cautions in the archives” when he deposited in the records office a written statement of his faithfulness and obedience. Hence the term *caution*, which Felix, following the custom of the archbishops of Ravenna, did not wish to provide. It does not here signify a financial guarantee for money to be sent to Rome, as some have wrongly written, but a sincere profession of faith expressed in fixed formulas. A newly ordained bishop of Ravenna swore by it that he wished to be subject to the Roman pontiff—not merely with the common reverence by which all bishops are subject to him, but with the special subjection by which the metropolitans of Ravenna were subject to the Roman pontiff as patriarch of the West.

Anastasius adds: “But because of the power of the judges he set it forth as he preferred”; that is, Felix, relying on the power of the judges of the exarchate, or even on those judges who administered justice at Rome in the emperor’s name, set it forth according to his own decision, insofar as he favored the freedom of the Church of Ravenna.

I am convinced that Felix did not wish, at his ordination, to provide Pope Constantine with the same cautions that the bishops of Ravenna supplied after the schism had been extinguished—cautions that removed every pretext for autocephaly and resembled those found in the *Diurnus*. Rather, he either added something to them or, more probably, wished to remove from them certain elements that expressed the patriarchal right of the Roman Church over the metropolitan church of Ravenna.

This caution, however, after being placed by the pope in the confession of blessed Peter the apostle, was found many days later black and as though scorched by fire, as Anastasius relates here. The matter entrusted to God by the pontiff and commended to the patronage of the prince of the apostles was made manifest by a divinely produced sign, as a sure indication of the divine will: Felix’s ungrateful profession was displeasing to God, because it did not express that the Church founded by blessed Apollinaris at Peter’s command was subject to the Roman Church insofar as the latter is the patriarchal Church of the West. Mafeus.]

did not wish to make the customary cautions in the archives, [Note: [Col. 0318D] “He did not wish to make cautions.” It was then customary for bishops, before being consecrated, to make a profession of their faith and obedience and deposit it in the papal archives; this they called making cautions in the archives. Ciaconius.] but, through the power of the judges, set it forth [Col. 0318A] as [Note: [Col. 0317A] Lucchese Codex: “wished”; others: “was able”; Labbé and Mansi: “preferred.”] he preferred.

His caution, after being placed by the pope in the most sacred confession of blessed Peter the apostle, was found after not many days [Note: [Col. 0318A] Other copies omit “black.”] black and as though burned by fire. For the citizens of Ravenna, swollen with pride, were punished with a penalty worthy of vengeance.

The emperor Justinian, sending the patrician Theodore and [Note: [Col. 0318A] Lucchese Codex: “chief officer”; others: “first officer.”] the commander of the army of the island of Sicily with a fleet of ships, captured the city of Ravenna. He held the aforementioned arrogant archbishop bound in a ship and fettered all the rebels whom he found there; he seized their wealth and sent them to Constantinople.

By God’s judgment and by the sentence of the prince of the apostles, Peter, those who had been disobedient to the apostolic [Note: [Col. 0319A] Lucchese Codex: “see.”] see were put to a bitter death, [Col. 0320A] and that same archbishop, [Note: [Col. 0319A] “Deprived of his sight.” After looking into a concave bronze vessel heated until glowing, for from it an ignited ray emerges that easily strikes and blinds the surface of the eyes. Ciaconius.] deprived of his sight, received a punishment worthy of his deeds and was sent into exile in the region of Pontus. [Note: [Col. 0320A] Others: “the island and region.”]

[Note: [Col. 0319A] “At the same time he sent, etc.” What Pope Constantine did at Constantinople is concealed by the scarcity and silence of the sources. Baronius nevertheless infers that a controversy concerning the canons of the Trullan Synod was being debated there at that time, from the fact that, since no other question was then being disputed between Easterners and Westerners, Anastasius nonetheless writes in the Life of Gregory II:

“Gregory, then a deacon of the Roman Church, went with the holy man Pope Constantine to the imperial city. When questioned by the emperor Justinian about certain chapters, he resolved each question with an excellent answer.”

It is regrettable that this answer has either remained hidden or perished.

Christian Lupus, in his scholia and notes on the Trullan canons, page 1078, gathers from the words of Anastasius cited above that Constantine was the first of the Roman pontiffs to approve the canons of the Trullan Synod as not contrary to the decrees of the Roman Church. He also concludes that Justinian obtained from Constantine what he had requested from John VII, and therefore confirmed by new edicts all the privileges of the Roman Church. For earlier, as I said in the second note, he had restored the Roman Church against the renewed autocephaly and rebellion of the archbishops of Ravenna.

This apostolic confirmation of the Trullan canons supplied Pope Adrian I of Rome and Saint Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople, with an illustrious basis for bearing witness to those canons. Adrian I approved only those canons of the Trullan Synod that had been lawfully and orthodoxly promulgated, says the same Lupus. He adds that those are gravely mistaken who believe the confirmation of these canons made by the Seventh Synod in its first canon to be authentic, since the Roman Church never confirmed all the canons of the Seventh Synod.

Thus the confirmation of the Trullan canons by Pope Constantine remained unknown not only to the Roman Church but also to the other patriarchal Churches, except Constantinople. For this reason it had to be renewed by John VIII, as we shall see in his Life. Pagius.]

At that time the aforementioned emperor sent a letter to Pope Constantine, by which he ordered him [Note: [Col. 0319D] “To go up to the imperial city.” Anastasius recounts at length the pope’s journey and the deeds of his companions. Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapter 31, writes the following about Justinian:

“He ordered Pope Constantine to come to him, received him honorably, and sent him back. He asked him, prostrate on the ground, to intercede for his sins, and renewed all the privileges of his Church. When he sent an army into Pontus to capture Philippicus, whom he had exiled there, the same venerable pope strongly advised him not to do so, but he could not prevent it.

“If this is compared with Agnellus’s account, who reports that Justinian was extremely hostile to the people of Ravenna and had inflicted many injuries upon the city and its leading men, whom he knew to be responsible for his deposition from the empire, we may perhaps conjecture the reason for the journey undertaken by the pontiff to Constantinople. Pope Constantine, it seems, had complained about Felix of Ravenna’s refusal to provide the caution and had therefore been summoned by Justinian for an examination of the matter in his presence. Among the privileges granted to the apostolic see, Justinian confirmed Constantine Pogonatus’s decrees concerning the subjection of the Church of Ravenna to Rome.

“As for Paul’s assertion that Justinian was warned by the pope not to send his soldiers and forces against Philippicus because he suspected treachery, the outcome itself confirmed it and showed that the warning had been wisely given.” Bencinus.]

to go up to the imperial city. [Note: [Col. 0320B] “This most holy man, obeying the imperial commands.” After prayers had been offered and every possible security had been provided by letter, Justinian the Younger, now restored to a better disposition, summoned Pope Constantine to the imperial city. Orders were issued that wherever the pontiff stopped, he should be received by the magistrates as though the emperor himself were present.

Anastasius recounts the sequence of events. Since Sigonius describes it elegantly from Anastasius in his *History of the Kingdom of Italy*, under the year 711, I do not hesitate to transfer his words here:

“Constantine, departing from Otranto at the beginning of spring, was honored with every kind of generosity in all the Greek towns through which he passed. When he then approached Constantinople, Tiberius, Justinian’s son, and Cyrus the patriarch, together with the patricians and all the citizens, came out to meet him seven miles from the city. Celebrating a feast day, they escorted him into the city on richly adorned horses with their retinue. He was dressed, according to custom, in the papal cloak and was lodged in the house of Placidia, where quarters had been prepared.

“When Justinian learned of the pontiff’s arrival, he sent him another letter from Bithynia, giving thanks and asking him not to consider it burdensome to come to Nicomedia, since he himself would proceed there from Nicaea. Constantine therefore went to Nicomedia, where he was received with great honor by that city as well. Not long afterward Justinian arrived. A meeting between pope and emperor such as no one in human memory had witnessed in those places stirred all the neighboring peoples to view so rare a spectacle.

“Thus, surrounded by a very great crowd of every kind, the emperor entered the city and approached the pontiff, who was waiting according to the agreed arrangement. Crowned according to custom, he fell at the pope’s feet and kissed them. After they embraced one another ceremonially, he addressed him with particular kindness and generosity, while everyone present expressed immense applause out of joy; and our people rejoiced no less because of the notable concord between the rulers and their Churches.

“Then each withdrew to his own lodging, and the following days were spent in various discussions concerning the ordering of the Church and the empire. When the emperor said that he wished to send a fleet and an army against Philippicus, the pontiff strongly dissuaded him from doing so, but all his speech was in vain.

“Afterward both agreed that the pontiff should celebrate the divine service on Sunday. When the ceremony had been completed with the greatest splendor, the emperor, having first been absolved from his sins, received the Lord’s body from him and confirmed all the ancient privileges of the Roman Church. He then sent him back to Rome.”

Thus far Sigonius. But for what principal reason the emperor summoned the pontiff to Constantinople is not certainly known, owing to the scarcity of the sources. Nevertheless, from what Anastasius relates in the following Life of Saint Gregory II, it may be inferred that a controversy had long been troubling Latins and Greeks concerning the canons added to the Fifth and Sixth Ecumenical Synods, and that the pope’s presence was intended finally to put an end to it. Anastasius writes there:

“He went with the holy pontiff Constantine to the imperial city, and when questioned by the emperor Justinian about certain chapters, he resolved each question with an excellent answer.” Mafeus.]

This most holy man, obeying the imperial commands, immediately had ships prepared so that he might undertake the sea voyage. He departed from the Roman port on 5 October, in the 9th indiction.

He was accompanied by Nicetas, bishop of Silva Candida; George, bishop of Portus; [Note: [Col. 0321B] Lucchese Codex: Michael.] Michael; Paul; George [Note: [Col. 0321B] Others: priests.], the priest; George the deacon; George the *secundicerius*; John the chief defender; [Note: [Col. 0321B] Lucchese Codex: Cosmas.] [Note: [Col. 0321C] Cosmas the *sacellarius*, Sisinnius the *nomenclator*. The *sacellarius* and *nomenclator* are counted among the offices of the Roman Church. The *sacellarius* is the keeper of the church treasury. Anastasius, in the Life of Constantine: “He was made subdeacon and *sacellarius*.” Likewise, in the Life of Gregory II: “He was made subdeacon and *sacellarius* under the holy-memory Lord Pope Sergius.” Likewise, in the Life of Stephen IV: “Together with Sergius, then *sacellarius*.” Likewise, in the Life of Leo III: “Likewise Campulus the *sacellarius*.” Likewise, in the Life of Adrian II: “There he was greeted by Paul, keeper of the books; Joseph, keeper of the vessels; and Basil the *sacellarius*, all dressed in ecclesiastical vestments.” The *sacellarius* is distinguished from the *arcarius*: Anastasius mentions “Paul the deacon and *vicedominus*, Peter the *arcarius*.” The *nomenclator* is an attendant who informs the pontiff of the name of those approaching the Roman pontiff. Concerning both offices, see Anastasius in the Life of Agatho, where I discussed them. A *sacellarius* of the treasury is an administrator or prefect of the treasury. Baldric, in his letter to the Emperor Henry III: “Just as your generosity has a *sacellarius* who provides daily expenses when matters arise, so I too am their *sacellarius,” etc. John the Deacon, book II, chapter 23: “The same Gregory, according to his custom, ordered the *sacellarius* to invite twelve pilgrims to dinner.” And shortly afterward: “After summoning the *sacellarius*, he asked why he had presumed to invite a thirteenth person contrary to his command.” Altaserra.] Cosmas the *sacellarius*; Sisinnius the *nomenclator*; Sergius the record-keeper; Dorotheus and Julian, subdeacons; and a few clerics from the remaining orders of the Church. [Note: [Col. 0321B] Lucchese Codex: “not a few.”]

Thus, when he came to Naples, he found there John the patrician and exarch, surnamed Rizocopus. When John came to Rome, he slaughtered [Note: [Col. 0321B] Lucchese Codex: Paul; others: Saul.] Saul the deacon and *vicedominus*, Peter the *arcarius*, [Note: [Col. 0317D] Sergius the priest-abbot and Sergius the *ordinator*. “Priest-abbot” is specified because at the beginning each monastery had a single priest, its abbot, from whom the monks received the sacraments and heard Mass. Augustine, in the letter numbered 81, wrote to the abbot and fellow priest of the monks of the island of Capraria. Likewise, in *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, book I, chapter 33: “I myself saw at Milan residences of holy men, housing not a few people, over whom one priest presided, a most excellent and learned man.” John, bishop of Jerusalem, in the letter numbered 60, writes that he ordained Paulinianus priest of the Bethlehem monastery because blessed Jerome, superior of that monastery, through humility did not endure administering the sacraments to the brothers. Anastasius, below, in the Life of Stephen III: “Fulrad the abbot and priest.” An *ordinator* is the master of the order of Mass, or the instructor of those being ordained. Instruction of those to be ordained precedes ordination, and after ordination the ordinators give the newly ordained an official booklet containing the order—that is, the arrangement—of the ecclesiastical office. Council of Toledo IV, canon 25; canon *Quando*, distinction 38. Altaserra.] Sergius the priest-abbot and Sergius the *ordinator*. Proceeding to Ravenna because of his unspeakable crimes, John there met a most disgraceful death by God’s judgment.

George the priest was left at Naples. The pontiff and his companions continued to Sicily, where the patrician Theodore, [Note: [Col. 0321B] Lucchese Codex: “and military governor”; others: “commander”; others: “exarch.”] the *extraticus*, met the pontiff while suffering from an illness. He greeted and received him with great reverence and immediately obtained a cure.

Leaving there, the pontiff passed through Rhegium and Cortona and crossed the sea to Gallipoli, where Nicetas the bishop died. While he was delayed at Hydruntum, because it was winter, [Note: [Col. 0322C] “There he received the imperial seal through Theophanes the *regionarius*.” The imperial seal here is an imperial command secured with a seal; elsewhere the *sigillum iconiae*, or seal of the image of blessed Mary, is an inscription on an image. Robert of Mont-Saint-Michel, in the supplement to Sigebert, under the year 1183: “In the preceding year Our Lady, the mother of mercy, holy Mary, appeared to a certain carpenter while he was working in a forest and offered him an image of herself and of her Son, our Savior, whose inscription was: ‘Lamb of God,’ etc. Altaserra.] there he received an imperial seal through Theophanes the *regionarius*, containing the following order: wherever the pontiff might happen to arrive, all the judges were to receive him with such honor as though they were seeing the emperor himself in person.

Thus, after leaving and reaching the regions of Greece, at the island called Caea [Note: [Col. 0322C] The patrician Theophilus, *extraticus* of the *caravisians*, met him and received him with the highest honor. *Extraticus*—read *strategus*—of the *caravisians*, that is, commander of a cavalry unit. The term derives from the Latin barbarism *scara*, which means the same as a cavalry unit. Aimoin, book IV, chapter 26: “In the tenth year Dagobert assembled from the warriors of Francia a *scara*, which we may call a troop or wedge.” Hincmar of Reims, to the bishops of his diocese, chapter 3: “Lines of warriors, which in the vernacular we call *scarae*.” In William the Breton, *Philippid*, book X, *scala* is wrongly read for *scara*: “They cling beside the king in the king’s *scala*.” Hence *scaritae*, soldiers enrolled in a *scara*. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, chapter 37: “And there Theodoric approached with ten thousand *scaritae*.” It is a reasonable conjecture that the *caravisians*, or *scarite* soldiers, mentioned here were Frankish soldiers who served in *scarae* for Greek pay, since we know from Cedrenus, in the Life of Constantine Monomachus, that Franks served the Greeks in the East; indeed, Byzantine emperors used Franks and Germans as their bodyguards, armed with double axes, as Nicephorus relates in the Life of Alexius Comnenus. Altaserra.] Theophilus the patrician, [Note: [Col. 0322B] See note 6 above.] *extraticus* [Note: [Col. 0322B] Lucchese Codex: of the *curavisians*.] of the *caravisians*, met him and received him with the highest honor. Embracing him, as the imperial order prescribed, he completed the journey he had begun.

From that place they sailed [Col. 0323A] [Note: [Col. 0323B] “They came to Constantinople.” In the year of Christ 710, the third year of Constantine’s pontificate. What he did there is hidden by the scarcity of the sources, although it can plainly be inferred from the Life of Gregory II that at this time he discussed with the emperor the authority of the canons of the Sixth Synod, which were then disputed between Easterners and Westerners. Bin. and Labb.] and came to Constantinople, at the seventh milestone. There Tiberius, the emperor and son of Justinian Augustus, came out with the patricians and [Note: [Col. 0323B] Lucchese Codex: “the senate,” instead of “all the illustrious men.”] all the illustrious men, [Note: [Col. 0323C] “Illustrious men.” Understand senators. Bin. and Labb.] and Cyrus the patriarch [Note: [Col. 0323C] “Cyrus the patriarch.” Justinian appointed him in place of Callinicus, after having deprived the latter of his eyes and exiled him to Rome, because Callinicus had foretold that Justinian would be restored to the empire. Theophanes, in the *Annals*. Bin. and Labb.] with the clergy and a multitude of the people. All rejoiced and celebrated the day as a feast.

The pontiff, however, and his chief officials entered the city with imperial saddlecloths, gilded saddles and bridles, and *mappulae*. [Note: [Col. 0323C] “The pontiff and his chief officials entered with imperial saddlecloths, gilded saddles and bridles, and *mappulae*. Here *sellare* is distinguished from *sella*. *Sellare* appears to be a cloak spread over the saddle and placed upon it as an ornament, a saddlecloth. Anastasius, in the Life of Stephen III: “And he hastened with the *vicestrator* as far as a certain place beside his saddlecloth.” Anastasius likewise calls the garment a cloak in the Life of Conon: “He also granted him permission to use a cloak for riding.” The pontiff and the cardinals used gilded bridles and saddles. Bernard of Clairvaux makes the same observation concerning the bishops of his age, in Letter 42 to William of Sens:

“Tell me, pontiffs, what is gold doing on a bridle?”

The Lateran Council under Innocent III, chapter *Clerici*, concerning the life and conduct of clerics, forbids clerics to use gilded bridles, saddles, breastplates, or spurs. The pontiff and cardinals, riding in solemn procession, used *mappulae*. *Mappulae* are small white linen cloths, concerning which Gregory writes in the *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 19:

“One day he sent someone according to his custom; but the monk who had been sent, after being admonished by the holy women, accepted *mappulae* from them and hid them in his bosom.” And below: “He said to him: ‘Was I not present there when you received the *mappulae* from the handmaids of God?’ At once he fell at his feet, repented that he had acted foolishly, and threw away the *mappulae* he had hidden in his bosom.”

The use of *mappulae* was common to the bishops and deacons of the Roman Church. Gregory, book II, letter 54. Hence the canon *Illud*, distinction 93, was taken. Altaserra.]

The apostolic pontiff, with his [Note: [Col. 0323B] Lucchese Codex and others: *camelauco*.] camelaucum, as he was accustomed to proceed at Rome, left the palace and hurried as far as Placidia, where [Note: [Col. 0323B] Lucchese Codex: “where he was going to lodge.”] he was lodging.

[Note: [Col. 0324D] “The apostolic pontiff, with his camelaucum, as he was accustomed to proceed at Rome, left the palace and hurried as far as Placidia, where he was lodging.” A *camelaucum*, or *camelaugum*, is a cap worn by the pontiff. The term derives from the Greek καῦμα, “heat,” because it serves to ward off heat. Suidas: Καμηλαύκιον, παρὰ τὸ καῦμα ἐλαύνειν, “*Camelaukion*, because it drives away the heat.” The Etymologicum Magnum: Καύσια εἴρηται μὲν καμελαύκιον, παρὰ τὸ ἐλαύνειν τὸ καῦμα, “The *causia* is called *camelaucum* because it drives away the heat.” Achmes, *Oneirocritica*, chapter 219: Τὸ καμηλαύκιον ἐπὶ βασίλεως εἰς τὴν Αὐγούσταν, καὶ εἰς τέκνον κρίνεται, “The camelaucum of a king is interpreted as referring to the Augusta and to his child.” The camelaucum was a head covering common to kings and private persons, differing in color. In time, however, it came about that among the Romans *camelaucum* properly meant the pontiff’s cap. Papias: “Camelaucus: the pope’s garment.” Altaserra.]

The lord Emperor Justinian, hearing of his arrival and filled with great joy, sent a letter from Nicaea in Bithynia [Note: [Col. 0324B] Lucchese Codex: “a letter.”] full of thanksgiving. The pontiff ought to have gone to meet him at Nicomedia, and he himself was to come from Nicaea, and this was done.

On the day when they saw one another, the most Christian Augustus, with the imperial crown on his head, prostrated himself and kissed the pontiff’s feet. Then they fell into one another’s arms, [Note: [Col. 0324B] Lucchese Codex: “mutually.”] and great joy arose among the people, everyone looking upon the humility of the good ruler.

On Sunday he celebrated Mass for the emperor. The ruler received communion from his hands and asked the pontiff to pray for his sins. He renewed all the privileges of the Church and then released the most holy pope to return to his own country.

After leaving the city of Nicomedia, the pontiff, worn down by frequent illnesses, at last recovered his health by God’s gift and reached the port of Gaeta safely. There he found priests and a very large crowd of the Roman people. On the twenty-fourth day of October, in the tenth indiction, he entered Rome, and all the people rejoiced and exulted.

He ordained twelve bishops as he traveled out and returned through various places. After three months, a mournful report resounded: Justinian, the most Christian and orthodox emperor, had been slain [Col. 0324B].

[Note: [Col. 0324C] Justinian was murdered. The author of the *Miscella* and Theophanes relate the unfortunate fate of Justinian, caused by Philippicus’s tyranny and the treachery of his own army. Agnellus, in the same *Life of Felix of Ravenna*, reports the matter but attributes its cause to what the emperor had done against the people of Ravenna, with Joannicius as the instigator of the revolt. Shortly beforehand, Joannicius had said to assassins and traitors: “Tomorrow, at this same hour as now, you will kill your emperor, and he will be with me before the most just Judge” [lacuna]. On the following day, at the hour he had foretold, they rushed upon the emperor and, unable to endure the wickedness of his people, killed him. Agnellus also adds the manner of his death and the insult inflicted upon the emperor, whose head was carried throughout all Italy. But here, as elsewhere, the unskilled historian describes a shallow popular tradition.]

[Note: [Col. 0324D] And Philippicus the heretic. Anastasius copies what Paul says, chapter 32: “The army that had been sent against Philippicus went over to Philippicus’s side and made him emperor. When he came to Constantinople against Justinian, he fought him at the tenth milestone from the city, defeated and killed him, and obtained his kingdom.” Justinian’s excessive cruelty moved the people to revolt, as Paul observes there; in chapter 33 he adds: “But Philippicus, who was also called Bardanis, ordered Cyrus [lacuna], expelled from the episcopate, to return to Pontus to govern his monastery. This Philippicus sent Constantine the pope a letter containing an evil doctrine, which he rejected with the counsel of the Apostolic See. For this reason he caused paintings to be made in the portico of Saint Peter, depicting the proceedings of the six holy universal councils. For when such paintings were displayed in the imperial city, Philippicus had ordered them removed; and the Roman people decreed that they would accept neither the name of a heretical emperor, nor his documents, nor the image of his solidus.” BENCINUS.]

Philippicus the heretic was raised to the imperial citadel [Col. 0325A] [Note: [Col. 0325A] Another reading: *archem*.] [Note: [Col. 0325B] Constantine also received his letter, with its writing of an evil doctrine, but rejected it with the counsel of the Apostolic See. Before three months had scarcely passed, Constantine had returned to Rome, from which he had been absent for a year, when he learned that an Armenian named Bardanis had been proclaimed emperor and called Philippicus, and that by his order the emperors Justinian and Tiberius had been killed. Since this usurper, as Agatho the Deacon says (*Collection of the Councils*, p. 1405), had from early youth been a disciple of Stephen the abbot, himself a disciple of Macarius, he immediately used the authority and imperial power he possessed to order the image of that holy council—the Sixth General Council—which had been placed many years earlier in the vestibule of the imperial palace, to be cast down [lacuna]. And to strengthen his crime still further against the Sixth Council, he arranged, as Theophanes says in his *Chronicle*, for “an insane conciliabulum” to be held against the holy ecumenical council. John, patriarch of Constantinople; Andrew, metropolitan of Crete; and Germanus, metropolitan of Cyzicus, openly subscribed to it and, together with all their colleagues, condemned by anathema the aforementioned holy ecumenical synod held against the Monothelites. But the tyrant did not long enjoy the fruits of his impiety and revolt. His wasted life and negligence in administering the empire earned him the hatred and contempt of the officers of the praetorian guard; they therefore expelled him from the palace and stirred up a general revolt against him. Then, with the consent of all the orders, they elected Philarthemius, who wished to be called by the name Anastasius, a man of high reputation and, above all, a Catholic; Philippicus, deprived of his eyes, was driven into exile. SOMMIER.]

Constantine also received his letter, together with its writing of an evil doctrine, but rejected it with the counsel of the Apostolic See.

[Note: [Col. 0325C] For this reason, moved by zeal for the faith, the entire assembly of the city of Rome erected in the church of blessed Peter an image—which the Greeks call a *votarea*, or, as others read, a *pancarea*—containing the six holy and universal councils. An image of the six universal councils, which the Greeks call a *votarea* or *pancarea*, erected by the Roman people in the church of blessed Peter. This image, removed by the heretical emperor Philippicus, was restored at Constantinople by Theodosius. Anastasius, in his account of Gregory II: “As soon as Theodosius entered the imperial city, he restored to its former place that venerable image on which the six holy synods had been depicted and which Philippicus, without even mentioning it, had removed.” ALTASERRA.]

For this reason, moved by zeal for the faith, the entire assembly of the city of Rome erected in the church of blessed Peter an image—which the Greeks call a *votarea* [Note: [Col. 0325A] Codex Luc., *pancaream*; another reading, *botaream*.]—containing the six holy and universal councils.

He restored the golden paten, weighing twelve pounds.

At the same time Felix, archbishop of Ravenna, was brought back from exile. Moved to repentance, although deprived of the light of his eyes, he nevertheless returned to his own see. He too confessed the customary declarations made by everyone in the bishops’ archive, as well as the exposition of the faith; thus he deserved to receive absolution and reconciliation.

[Note: [Col. 0325D] In his time there were two kings, etc. The pontificate of Pope Constantine was rendered especially illustrious by the abdication of Coenred, king of the Mercians, and Offa, king of the East Saxons. In the year 709 they went to Rome, having abandoned their kingdoms for Christ, and there assumed the monastic habit. When they came to the threshold of the Apostles, Pope Constantine received them with the greatest kindness, rejoicing that, having renounced earthly kingdoms, they wished to serve Peter the fisherman. This is confirmed by Bede both in his *Epitome* and in his *History*, book V, chapter 20. In the *Epitome* he writes: “In the year 709, Coenred, king of the Mercians, after reigning for five years, went to Rome.” In the *History*: “In the year of Osred’s reign”—which ends in 709—“Coenred, who had governed the kingdom of the Mercians for some time with great distinction, relinquished the royal scepter with still greater distinction. For he came to Rome, where, under the pontificate of Constantine, he was tonsured and became a monk; and at the threshold of the Apostles he remained in prayers, fasts, and almsgiving until his final day. Ceolred, son of Æthelred, succeeded him in the kingdom; Ceolred had held that same kingdom before Coenred. With him came Offa, son of Sighere, king of the East Saxons, a young man of exceptional age and beauty and greatly desired by his whole people to retain and preserve the royal scepter. Led by an equal devotion of mind, he abandoned his wife, lands, relatives, and homeland for Christ and for the Gospel, so that in this life he might receive a hundredfold and in the age to come eternal life. When they reached Rome and the holy places, he too was tonsured and, completing his life in the monastic habit, attained the long-desired vision of the blessed Apostles in heaven.” PAGIUS.]

In his time two kings of the Saxons came to Rome to pray at the tombs of the Apostles with many others, and speedily ended their lives, as they desired [Note: [Col. 0326A] Codex Luc., “with speed.”]. Benedict, archbishop of Milan, also came with a vow of prayer, in order to present himself to his own pontiff.

[Note: [Col. 0326D] He also disputed on behalf of the Church of Ticinum. Two examples, whose memory still survives, clearly demonstrate that the ordination of the bishop of Ticinum had from ancient times belonged to the metropolitan of Milan. Thus Sigonius writes incorrectly (*On the Kingdom of Italy*, under the year 715) that Benedict, archbishop of Milan, wished to transfer to himself the consecration of the bishop of Ticinum in order to establish a new right, but, opposed by all the precedents of antiquity, withdrew defeated. The first example is taken from the action of Saint Crispinus, bishop of Ticinum. Knowing, broken by age, that the day of his dissolution was approaching, he brought Saint Epiphanius to the bishop of Milan and asked him, after he had departed this life, to place Epiphanius over the priesthood of Ticinum. The Milanese bishop did so immediately after Crispinus had migrated to heaven, as Saint Ennodius, himself also bishop of Ticinum, testifies in the *Life of Saint Epiphanius*. The second example is found in the *Life of Saint Ambrose*, written in the same period by the presbyter Paulinus, where we read: “After being ordained priest of the Church of Ticinum, he fell ill.” But in the Roman synod under Constantine, Benedict, archbishop of Milan, lost the case, because, as our author says, “from ancient times the bishop of that same Church of Ticinum belonged and belongs to the Apostolic See for consecration.” These ancient times cannot be traced further back than to the period when the kings of the Lombards established the see at Ticinum. For when the Lombards invaded Italy, Honoratus, bishop of Milan, terrified by the ferocity of the new people, withdrew to Genoa with most of the clergy and leading men. After him, several archbishops of Milan are said to have been elected there, until Saint John the Good, not fearing the monstrous domination of the Lombards, returned to his own see and nearly brought the Ligurian secession to an end after the lapse of a century. When Benedict brought a suit before the Roman council to recover the ancient right of consecration of the bishop of Ticinum, a century and a half had passed since the departure of Honoratus. For this reason our author asserts that from ancient times it had belonged to the Roman pontiff to consecrate the bishops who were to preside over Ticinum, the royal city; hence Benedict, defeated by the judgment of the Roman synod, withdrew. Paul the Deacon also writes that this was the outcome of the controversy (*Book VI*, chapter 29), adding that the venerable Benedict, archbishop, was a man of outstanding holiness, whose good reputation spread throughout all Italy. Such was the holiness of this archbishop that his name was entered in the registers of the saints, and the Ambrosian Church celebrates his memory each year with solemn rites on the fifth Ides of March. Indeed, in the table of the archbishops of the Church of Milan published by decree of the provincial council, which appears in the fourth part of the *Acts* under Saint Charles, Saint Benedict is said to have belonged to the Crispi family. This is not accepted by the learned Papebrochius (*May*, volume VII, in the *Exegesis on the Bishops of Milan*), because at the time when Saint Benedict lived—that is, the eighth century—the use of hereditary surnames was not known; it became common only after the eleventh century. Hence, following Puricello, he believes that Peter Galesinius was the first to add the surnames of noble families to the ancient names of bishops. Yet long before Galesinius, who lived in the sixteenth century, certain archbishops who flourished before the eleventh century are found written with family surnames in manuscript catalogs of bishops. This is especially true of the manuscript catalog of Filippo da Castelseprio, which he brought down to his own time, namely the year 1331; when I was in Milan, I read its copy in the library of the distinguished monastery of Saint Ambrose. Galesinius, therefore, was not the first to append individual episcopal surnames to catalogs. I do not mean by this, however, that surnames were in use before the eleventh century, especially among the bishops of the Churches, since I hold only that the origins of the ancient bishops in the noble families of Milan—something Puricello also attests in the *Life of Saint Lawrence of Litta*—could have been preserved by a continuous tradition of ancestors, so firmly that, supported as though by a domestic history, each person could rightly assign to himself a namesake line of descent after surnames had been added. The Crispi family could have done this more easily than the others, since Saint Benedict illumined the see of Milan for many years—specifically for forty-seven years—with such holiness of life that, as Paul, whom we have just cited, testifies, his fame spread throughout all Italy. SOMMIER.]

He also disputed on behalf of the Church of Ticinum, but was defeated [Col. 0327A], because from ancient times the bishop of that same Church of Ticinum belonged and belongs to the Apostolic See for consecration.

In those same times, when the Roman people had resolved in no way to accept the name of the heretical emperor, or his documents, or the image of his solidus—hence neither was his likeness brought into the church, nor did they proclaim his name at the solemn celebrations of Mass [Note: [Col. 0327A] Codex Luc., “of the emperor Philippicus.”] [Note: [Col. 0328A] Codex Luc., “was proclaimed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0328B] It happened that a certain Peter sent an order to Ravenna concerning the duchy of the city of Rome [lacuna]. And it came to pass while Christopher, who was duke, [lacuna]. The first person whom Anastasius mentions is Christopher, who is plainly designated under the title “duke of the city of Rome.” I would gladly investigate what this new title of duke signified, what dignity and jurisdiction it involved, what functions it entailed, what the order and succession of the dukes were, what the boundaries of the Roman duchy were, and what cities belonged to it, if there were anywhere hope of discovering and establishing something certain, by which the *Liber Pontificalis* might properly be elucidated. But everything is buried in darkness, unstable, and uncertain, so that one cannot safely rely upon it: contemporary authorities are silent on the matter, while later writers lack the support of ancient records. I shall attempt to see whether Anastasius can be illuminated from Anastasius.

All Italy obeyed the emperors before barbarian nations invaded it and laid everything waste with sword and fire. The last people to occupy most of Italy were the Lombards. Having seized the principal Italian provinces, they left the Greek emperors nothing except the tract extending from the Po to the Adriatic Sea, between the Apennines, the Pentapolis, and the sea. Longinus gave this territory the name of the Exarchate of Ravenna, after the model of the Exarchate of Africa. He had been appointed by the emperor Justin as Narses’ successor in the year 567. They also retained that part of Italy washed by the upper sea as far as Sicily, except for the duchy of Benevento, which the Lombards likewise held.

The exarch resided at Ravenna. From there he sent both the emperor’s sacred commands and his own officials—who were designated by various titles, such as *magistri militum*, *sacellarii*, and *chartularii*—to the other lands subject to the emperor in the East.

For those times, down to approximately the year 711, the *Liber Pontificalis* is completely silent about a duke and a duchy of Rome. If there is any mention of Roman magistrates, they are designated either by the title “judges,” or as the Roman army, as in the case of Theodore, no. 125: “the clergy, people, and army of the Roman city”; or as “the judges and commanders of the army,” as in Conon, no. 156; or as “the commanders of the judges and army of the Roman soldiery,” as in Sergius, no. 158.

Accordingly, while Constantine was pope, Christopher is first called duke on the following occasion. When the heretical emperor Philippicus, a hater of the holy images, sent a certain Peter to obtain the Roman duchy, the Roman people—who, as Anastasius says, had resolved in no way to accept the name of the heretical emperor, or his documents, or the image of his solidus, so that neither was his likeness brought into the church nor was his name proclaimed at the solemn celebrations of Mass—were inflamed with zeal for the faith. They refused to receive that Peter and presented themselves armed before Duke Christopher, so that under his leadership they might fight against Peter and prevent him from entering the city and exercising the magistracy.

The battle was fought on the Sacred Way. When many on both sides were falling wounded, the pope sent priests with the Gospels and the crosses of the Lord to calm the factions. Peter’s party had already been pressed into such straits that it had no hope of survival, when, at the pope’s command, the other party, which was called the Christian party, withdrew.

From this I learn that military affairs and the entire administration of military matters belonged to the duke. I infer that he also administered urban affairs from the fact that, when Pope Zacharias departed from Rome, he left the city to Duke Stephen to govern (Anastasius, *Life of Zacharias*, no. 213). I likewise believe that, while the see was vacant, he took great care that disturbances should not arise in the city and protected the election of the new pope by the authority of his office and the support of arms. For in the *Life of Hadrian*, no. 292, I read that Hadrian, on the very day on which he was elected, caused the judges of this Roman city—both clergy and soldiers—who had been sent into exile by Paul the chamberlain, surnamed Afiarta, during the passage of Pope Stephen, to be recalled. After Stephen’s death, Afiarta had been placed in charge of governing the city during the interregnum and had sent the leading citizens into exile.

Christopher, therefore, was the first duke of the city of Rome, when the Roman people refused any longer to obey the heretical emperor, as I have reported above from Anastasius. Following his example, the other peoples of Italy, according to the same Anastasius, no. 184, everywhere elected dukes for themselves.

I present the succession of the Roman dukes from Anastasius:

- Christopher, duke, from the year 711 (Anastasius, *Life of Constantine*, near the end);
- Peter, duke, from the year 713 (Anastasius, *Life of Constantine*, near the end);
- Basil, duke, from the year 717 (Anastasius, *Life of Gregory II*, near the end);
- Marinus, *spatharius* and duke, from the year 718 (Anastasius, *Life of Gregory II*, midway);
- Peter, duke, from the year 720 (Anastasius, *Life of Gregory II*, midway);
- Stephen, duke, from the year 740 (Anastasius, *Life of Zacharias*).

Besides those mentioned, a certain Gratiosus is also named—at that time a *chartularius*, later duke—in *Stephen IV*, nos. 269 and 288; and John, duke and brother of Pope Stephen, in *Hadrian*, no. 297. But the following consideration persuades me either that they were not dukes with the ordinary ducal power possessed by their predecessors, or that one of them was elected during a disturbance raised by factious citizens, while the other, supported by his kinship with the pope, usurped the title of duke: from the time of Stephen III onward, the authority of the dukes ceased with the establishment of the Roman patriciate.

I have no doubt, therefore, that the dukes were abolished when Pippin was first anointed king of the Franks and was elected patrician of Rome by Stephen III, on account of his outstanding services to the Roman Church, especially the donation made to it of the Exarchate of Ravenna. Anastasius affirms that authentic documents of this donation still existed in the Roman archive in his time, no. 253.

For in a letter sent by Stephen III to Pippin before Pippin again descended into Italy to take the Exarchate of Ravenna from Aistulf, king of the Lombards—who had seized it—and to hand it over to the pope, Stephen recalls the donation of the Exarchate made by Pippin to blessed Peter. He both justly demands that it be fulfilled and earnestly begs for its execution. Thus he says in Letter 3:

“Let it grieve you on behalf of the holy Church of God and of blessed Peter, and you ought to hand over to him for possession what you promised would be offered to blessed Peter by the donation. Remember, and always hold firmly in your hearts, what you promised to that same doorkeeper of heaven [lacuna]. See that you hasten to hand over everything that you promised him and pledged by donation [lacuna]. Know that, just as a written bond, your donation, the prince of the apostles firmly holds, so it is necessary that you fulfill that written bond.”

T. VIII of Labbe’s *General Councils*, p. 381, Venetian edition.

Meanwhile, while the dukes ruled in Rome, supreme authority over the city of Rome and the Roman duchy lay with the pope. Anastasius makes this clear; in this note I use the testimony of Anastasius alone.

Anastasius reports in the *Life of Sisinnius*, no. 169, that Sisinnius ordered lime to be burned for the restoration of the city walls, but was unable to accomplish anything because death overtook him. In the *Life of Gregory II*, no. 177, he says:

“At the beginning of his pontificate, he ordered lime to be burned and, beginning at the Gate of Saint Lawrence, had decided to restore the walls of this city. After completing part of the work, he was hindered by the occurrence of unsuitable and various disturbances.”

What clearer proof could there be of supreme authority over the city than fortifying it and constructing walls around its circuit?

The same Gregory comforted the exarch, who was staying in Rome frightened and disturbed because certain cities had defected to Tiberius the usurper, and sent leading members of the Church and of the army to his aid, no. 187.

Gregory III had the ruined walls of the city of Centumcellae rebuilt with great strength, almost from their foundations, no. 204.

When Zacharias was about to leave Rome and go to Luitprand, king of the Lombards, for the safety of Ravenna, he left the Roman city to Stephen, patrician and duke, to govern, no. 213.

From these facts it plainly appears that supreme authority over the city and duchy rested with the popes, although the dukes administered justice.

I have not been able to determine with complete certainty from Anastasius which cities and fortresses constituted the Roman duchy. I understand that Centumcellae belonged to the Roman duchy from the construction of its walls ordered by Gregory III. Likewise, the fortress of Gallese, recovered under the same Gregory, belonged to it; for, says Anastasius, no. 203, “the Roman duchy was daily attacked by the duchy of Spoleto” on its account.

Similarly, four cities—Ameria, Horta, Polimartium, and Blera—were taken from the Roman duchy by the same king, as Anastasius says in *Zacharias*, no. 207:

“From the Roman duchy the king took four cities, namely Ameria, Horta, Polimartium, and Blera.”

I do not pronounce so confidently about the other places. Anastasius does say in *Zacharias*, no. 210:

“For he also restored to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, by a deed of donation, the Sabine patrimony, which had been taken away for nearly thirty years, and likewise the Narnian, Auximan, and Anconitan possessions, as well as Numanum and the valley called Magna, situated in the territory of Sutri; and that king confirmed peace with the Roman duchy for twenty years.”

But this passage shows that Anastasius did not intend to enumerate places properly belonging to the Roman duchy, since he includes Ancona, Auximum, and the Sabine patrimony, all of which are clearly outside the duchy.

Sigonius (*On the Kingdom of Italy*) asserts that the Roman duchy comprised the Roman city, Portus, Centumcellae, Caere, Blera, Maturanum, Sutrium, Nepi, the fortress of Gallese, Horta, Polimartium, Ameria, Todi, Perugia, Narnia, Otricoli, Signia, Anagni, Ferentinum, Alatrium, Patrica, Frusino, and Tibur. In my opinion, he took this enumeration from the charter of confirmation issued by Louis the Pious to Paschal in 817; yet Anastasius says nothing about it in the *Life of Paschal*. BALDINUS.]

it happened that a certain Peter sent an order to Ravenna concerning the duchy of the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 0330D] “Concerning the Duchy of the City of Rome.” From this it is clear that in those times the Roman commonwealth was ordinarily governed by dukes sent by the emperors. BIN. and LABB.] and received an order concerning this matter.

When it became known that Peter himself had obtained his advancement under the name of the heretical emperor [Note: [Col. 0330A] Codex Luc., “in that name”—], [Note: [Col. 0330A] Codex Luc., “the same”—] [Note: [Col. 0330A] Another reading, “had been sought”—] a large part of the Roman people, inflamed with zeal for the faith, resolved in no way to receive him as duke.

And it came to pass that, while Christopher, who was duke, was contending over this matter with Agatho and his men, civil war broke out, so that they engaged one another on the Sacred Way before the palace [Note: [Col. 0331B] “More than twenty-five on both sides were wounded and died. *Plagare* means ‘to inflict a wound.’ Augustine, *City of God*, Book XXI, chapter 11: ‘He provoked or wounded the Lord.’ ALTASERRA.], and more than twenty-five from both sides were wounded and died [Note: [Col. 0331A] Another reading, “more than thirty were scourged”—]

until the pope sent priests with the Gospels and the crosses of the Lord, and thus the factions were calmed.

[Note: [Col. 0331B] “Until the pope sent priests with the Gospels and the crosses of the Lord, and thus the factions were calmed. Litanies, or processions, were conducted with the Gospels and crosses carried before them. It was customary for a bishop to be met with the Gospel. Ekkehard the Younger, *On the Fortunes of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, chapter 1: ‘He immediately prepares the basilica and altar, prepares carpets and a hanging canopy, and orders the bishop and some priests who were present to be received with the Gospel.’ And below: ‘Not long afterward, it happened that Peter of Verona, returning from the palace, unexpectedly came to the same place by a similar act of courtesy; but the brothers, receiving him, offered him the Gospel, which was the best thing they had.’ The same work, chapter 9: ‘For receiving a bishop with the Gospel, all agree that they should meet him together, even if he is not a professed brother.’ The bishop is received; Victor offered him the Gospel, and when he kissed it, Victor returned.
