In litanies it is a custom of the greatest antiquity for crosses to be carried before the procession. Novel 123 of Justinian, chapter 32, forbids litanies to be held without crosses. In litanies it was customary for the golden cross given by Charlemagne to be carried before the pope; see Anastasius in *Leo IV*. The clergy solemnly went out to meet princes and rulers with crosses. Gregory of Tours, Book X, chapter 9: ‘Ebraccharius approached the city as far as Venice; for the bishop had sent his royal clerics to meet him with crosses and singing, and they escorted them as far as the city.’ The emperor Lothair was met with crosses and standards, that is, banners. Anastasius, in *Sergius II*: ‘His Holiness sent sacred crosses and also standards to meet him, and had him received with great honor, as is customary in receiving an emperor or king.’ ALTASERRA.]

For Peter’s party was so hard-pressed that it had no hope of survival. But at the pope’s command the other party, which was also called the Christian party, withdrew.

[Note: [Col. 0331A] Codex Luc., “And thus the party of Peter’s heretical defenders did not prevail but, crushed, withdrew.”]

And thus the party of Peter, the defender of the heretic, prevailed, as though the other party, having been crushed, had withdrawn.

Not many days afterward, letters arrived from the island of Sicily, which [Note: [Col. 0331C] “Announced that Philippicus the heretic had been expelled from the imperial throne. Bardanes Philippicus, advanced through the agency of the devil and of a certain magician who was later blinded, was acclaimed emperor. Having obtained the empire through a rebellion stirred up against Justinian, he deposed Cyrus, patriarch of Constantinople, and replaced him with a certain John, a Monothelite. He fulfilled what he had promised under oath to the pseudo-monk, namely, that the holy sixth ecumenical synod would be condemned, trusting that by this means he would retain the empire for a long time. But shamefully deceived by the magician, he lost confidence; for when he had scarcely reached the second year of his reign, he was blinded and dragged into exile by Anastasius, suffering the same punishment that he had inflicted on others. Such is the account of Theophanes and Cedrenus. BIN. and LABB.—

‘They announced that Philippicus the heretic had been expelled from the imperial throne.’ Bardanes, called Philippicus, obtained the empire through a rebellion stirred up against Justinian with the aid of the Chersonites. After ejecting Cyrus, patriarch of Constantinople, and replacing him with John the deacon and *chartularius* of the *oeconomium*, he carried out what he had sworn to the pseudo-monk and magician who had foretold the empire for him: namely, the abolition of the sixth universal council.

It was not difficult to drive Bardanes into this crime, since from childhood he had heard Stephen, an abbot and Monothelite disciple of Macarius, teaching, and had imbibed the heresy deeply in his mind through that corrupt instruction. After a conciliabulum had been convened, he impiously pronounced an anathema against the Sixth Synod and ordered its image—which had been painted in the vestibule of the palace between the fifth and sixth scholae—to be erased before he entered the city, as is read in the *Peroration of Agatho the Deacon* in Combefis, *History of the Monothelites*.

From this Bardanes expected that he would possess the empire for a long reign, as the demoniac had foretold to him. But shamefully deceived by the magician, he was blinded somewhat more than a year after his accession, by Rufus, prefect of the Opsicians, and then was driven into exile by Artemius, who, after becoming emperor, was called Anastasius.’ MAFEUS.]

announced that Philippicus the heretic had been expelled from the imperial throne, and [Note: [Col. 0332C] “Anastasius the Orthodox, Augustus. In the year 713, the impious Bardanes, or Philippicus, after holding the empire for one year and six months, as Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book VI, chapter 33, and Bede, *Book on the Six Ages*, report, was expelled and overthrown on the third day of June. Philartemius, changing his name and being called Anastasius—a pious and orthodox man—was installed and crowned in his place the following day, on the feast of Pentecost. He sent a profession of his faith to Pope Constantine through Scholasticus, chamberlain and patrician, whom he dispatched to Italy as exarch, as Anastasius relates in *Constantine*. When Pope Constantine heard that a Catholic emperor was reigning in the East and had received through the exarch a profession of orthodox faith from him, he wished him, received into Catholic communion, to be entered in the register of orthodox emperors, so that the whole Church might pray for him. He also sent to him, as was customary, Michael the priest, *apocrisiarius*, to obtain ecclesiastical responses, as Theophanes reports.

Such an embassy seemed entirely necessary, so that there might be someone in Constantinople who, by the authority of the Apostolic See, could reconcile to the Catholic Church the bishops who had fallen during Philippicus’s persecution and now repented. Since many had consented to the condemnation of the Sixth Synod only because they were shaken by fear, their repentance was very easy; and Constantine the pope, through his *apocrisiarius*, hastened to extend a hand to those shipwrecked men and rescue them as quickly as possible. For John, bishop of Constantinople, had asked this of Constantine himself, as head of the Christian priesthood, in the letter mentioned below. PAGIUS.] Anastasius the Orthodox Augustus assumed the royal scepters and began to govern.

Then there was great rejoicing among the orthodox, while a day of darkness spread over all the heretics. After some time [Note: [Col. 0332A] Codex Luc., “a period of time”—] the chamberlain Scholasticus, patrician, and [Note: [Col. 0332D] “The exarch, coming to Rome, brought with him the sacred letter of the emperor Anastasius. As soon as Anastasius ascended the imperial throne, he sent a letter to Constantine in which he openly professed the Catholic faith and declared that he adhered to the Sixth Synod. Moreover, he thought that, since the patriarch of Constantinople was sending his synodical letter to the Roman pontiff, he should attach to it an account of what had been done against religion during the tyrant’s reign. When this had been decided and approved, a letter of defense was written by John, the most holy pontiff of this city, to Constantine, the most holy and blessed pope of Old Rome. It was sent, as customary, together with the synodical letter. It properly informed him of everything previously written (Agatho the Deacon, epilogue).

The notable beginning of this letter of the patriarch John presents a comparison from which everything that the pope is in the Church is clearly recognized:

‘He himself, the Creator of our nature, when in his workmanship he had arranged for the head to be placed over the whole body, and had located in it the principal instruments of the senses, caused all movement and perfection of the remaining members to arise from it and be preserved there. If any one of them should happen to be injured or afflicted by some inconvenience, he determined that he should care for them attentively, and, through the ministry of the hands and under the direction of the eyes, he naturally tends even the extremities, which are suffering, with affection and sympathy.

We can compare your apostolic pontificate to this, O most holy head of the Christian priesthood. We regard you canonically as the head, and rightly seek through you a remedy for the sickness that has befallen our ecclesiastical body, and consolation from the pestilential and destructive power of the tyrant over our souls. For you too, as befits the head, will certainly not despise us who suffer unwillingly, nor will you cast us away from the natural and firmly established union [lacuna], especially since the illness did not arise from any fault of the body but was caused from outside by a violent and unforeseen calamity.’ (John of Constantinople, letter to Pope Constantine.)

He then explains the pernicious plans of the tyrant and his adherents, which had advanced to the abolition of the Council of Chalcedon, while they had condemned the Sixth Ecumenical Council, which confirmed and upheld it. He leaves no stone unturned in excusing those who, adapting themselves to the necessity of the times, seemed in some measure to have complied with him, since, if they had acted otherwise, he could by force of arms have brought matters to an even more lamentable end.

He relies upon the examples of several holy Fathers and calls God himself as witness both to his own intention and to that of his brethren. He adds:

‘Among the people there is the religious *apocrisiarius* of your most holy see who resides here. In the present urgent crisis, we have satisfied him by an oath, openly revealing to him the pure devotion to the orthodox faith that existed in us.’ (Ibid.)

He continues his defense of himself and his followers:

‘We judged that we ought for a little while to yield to the movement, so that in what is most important the confession of the faith might remain inviolate—not in words, perhaps, but in meaning [lacuna]. We say this not as wishing to overturn the words already defined synodically and confessed by the entire Church of God for so long a time: namely, that in the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation, according to the devout understanding known from the holy Fathers, there are two natural wills and two natural operations [lacuna]. To say that Christ in one nature possesses the power of willing and acting is nothing other than to understand two natural wills and two natural operations.’ (Ibid.)

He proceeds to praise the happiness of the Church, which had obtained a Catholic emperor ardently zealous for the good cause. Then, turning to the holy pontiff, he says:

‘Therefore, O sacred head, extending to us the hand of a kindly appeal, protect us through the contact of reciprocal letters and, according to ecclesiastical custom—namely, that of the anti-synodical apostles—apply the medicine of charity [lacuna]. For since you are disciples and successors of him who heard from the Lord, “I have prayed for you also, etc.,” you ought diligently to introduce what supports and strengthens correction, and even more readily to grant what belongs to a merciful and compassionate spirit.’ (Ibid.)

He supports such prayers by the example of Aaron, who was rebuked by his brother:

‘For Aaron, when he had yielded to the pressure of the ancient people and had assisted them in fashioning the idol, was indeed rebuked by his brother. But when he defended himself by asserting that he had done this under compulsion, he received no rebuke from God and was not deprived of the dignity of the priesthood.’ (Ibid.)

The pope felt such joy at the election of the excellent emperor that he immediately sent Michael the priest, *apocrisiarius*, or resident at the court, with authority to reconcile to the Church all the bishops and other repentant ecclesiastics whom fear of the tyrant Bardanes had compelled to subscribe to the condemnation of the Sixth Council, as Baronius teaches from Theophanes, under the year 713:

‘Constantine the pope wished to have Anastasius, received into Catholic communion, entered in the register of orthodox emperors, so that the whole Church might pray for him. He also sent to him, as customary, Michael the cardinal priest and *apocrisiarius* to obtain ecclesiastical responses.’ SOMMIER.]

the exarch of Italy came to Rome and brought with him the sacred letter of the emperor Anastasius, in which he declared himself before everyone to be a preacher of the true orthodox faith and a confessor of the holy Sixth Council. He presented it to the pope and then proceeded to Ravenna.

While these things were taking place, Peter obtained the duchy [Note: [Col. 0333A] Codex Luc., “the duchy of the City”—], promising [Note: [Col. 0333A] Codex Luc., “that he would in no way continue [in opposition] to Rome”; another reading, “that he would in no way retain opposition”—] that he would strive to oppose no one.

He conducted one ordination: ten priests, two deacons, and sixty-four bishops in various places.

[Note: [Col. 0334A] In another copy: “He too [lacuna] ceased”; everything else is lacking.]

He was also buried at blessed Peter the apostle on the fifth day before the Ides of April, in the thirteenth indiction, during the reign of Augustus Anastasius, and the episcopate remained vacant for forty days.

[Col. 0335]

[Note: [Col. 0335D] At the end of this Life, the following note is found in Codex Luc.: “Up to this point there are 129 years and 7 months since the Lombards came.” These words are written in the same ancient hand as the rest, but in rubricated characters.]

## LETTERS OF CONSTANTINE, ROMAN PONTIFF

*(Mansi, Collection of Councils, vol. XII.)*

### FIRST LETTER. OF POPE CONSTANTINE TO BRITHWALD, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

Concerning Egwin’s vision, the council to be held, and the establishment of a monastery.

[Col. 0335A]

Constantine, bishop and servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Brithwald, primate of the Church of the Britons.

The venerable man Egwin, bishop, whom your Fraternity sent twice to the Apostolic See, we now send back to you a second time, laden with the sheaves of justice. We admonish you to pursue and assist his undertakings in such a way as you have recognized that he began them from God and ran in the way of God.

Moreover, concerning that vision—or rather, that open manifestation—in which the blessed virgin Mary revealed herself to him, we hold it to be equally certain, just as we do not doubt the goodness of the man. Finally, we admonish your vigilance to summon, in those parts where the manifestation is reported to have occurred, a council of all England [Leg. “summon the kings”], and to arrange for bishops and religious persons of the sacred order to assemble there. Command the nobles of the kingdom to attend with their leading men.

When they have been gathered in the name of the Lord, we announce to them that the two kings of England, Kenred and Offa, with whom the aforesaid bishop came to the threshold of the apostles, have, at the place where the vision was manifested, transferred many possessions from their royal resources in our presence, and have confirmed them by apostolic authority, so that a congregation of monks may be established there according to the Rule of the aforesaid Father Benedict—a rule not yet sufficiently observed in those regions—and may serve Christ without ceasing.

The aforesaid kings specifically determined those donations and possessions in their charter, and caused them to be confirmed by us.

Therefore, beloved brother, however Christ is proclaimed, seek Christ’s profit and perform Christ’s work. After the judgments of all sides have been published in the council—those of the vision shown by God, of apostolic authority, of royal liberty and donation, and of your own assent and that of the clergy and people—establish for Christ the sheepfold divinely revealed, supported by apostolic authority, endowed by royal liberty, and confirmed by the blessing of the clergy and people.

To you and your successors, with the consent of the aforesaid Bishop Egwin, we specially entrust the care of the souls belonging to that church, so that, if—God forbid—any invader or tyrant should presume, at the devil’s prompting, to attack the sacred place, he may not dare to carry out his purpose, struck by the sentence of the power granted to you by God and by the blow of anathema.

If anything belonging to a hostile party is discovered to have arisen there, let it be brought to the ears of the supreme pontiff rather than allowing the holy place to be unjustly corrupted by anyone’s secret judgment.

Accordingly, the place itself, which royal power has bestowed upon royal liberty, and which we, by the authority of God, of the holy apostles, and of ourselves, also bestow, is to remain such that no person of any order may presume to corrupt or diminish what we have established. Whoever destroys or wickedly contaminates it shall be accursed; whoever preserves and enlarges it shall be filled with blessings.

## CHARTER OF KENRED AND OFFA, KINGS

Concerning the lands on which the blessed virgin Mary is said to have appeared to Bishop Egwin, together with many other possessions transferred to the monastery of Evesham in the Lateran Church, with Pope Constantine confirming everything.

[Col. 0336B]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

Since the changeability of the passing world daily diminishes as the course of time increases, and grows less as it expands, and since, as the sudden ruins caused by incursions increase, it is evident that the end of all things is near, heavenly rewards that will endure must be purchased through things empty and transitory.

Therefore I, Kenred, by the gift of God king of the Mercians, and I, Offa, by divine permission ruler of the East Angles [Another reading: Saxons], for the redemption of our souls and for the salvation of our predecessors and successors, give and grant, at the place where the blessed Mary revealed herself to the venerable Bishop Egwin at Homme—and by this present document confirm it—in honor and reverence of that same Mother of God, sixty-six hides on the two sides of the river called Avon:

three, namely, those which are at Homme; one at Leuchwic; one at Nortona; seven at Offeham; one at Litlintona; thirteen at Adintona; one at Baddeseia; six and a half at Bretfortona; twelve at Hombure; two and a half at Willereseia; seven at Wikwane; three at Benigrith; and nine at Hampton.

And out of pure generosity, as is fitting, we grant the aforementioned hides—where the manifestation is reported to have occurred—together with the other portions assigned above, to royal liberty, and grant them forever free to almighty God and his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, so that a congregation of monks may be established there according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and may serve Christ without ceasing.

For the greater security of our donation, we wish it to be known to those present and to those who will succeed them in the future within what boundaries the sacred place, which we have bestowed upon God and granted to royal liberty, is enclosed and surrounded.

First, from Twyford on the southern side as far as Cronchomme, the boundary of the place extends along the course of the river. From there it proceeds along the water as far as the division of the land of Fledenburgh, which is called Merdic; then straight along the slope of the hill, through the middle of Caldegaran, to Ealdanswinhagan; from Ealdanswinhagan to Beolagasete; from Beolagasete to Nordevol; from there through Leuchdune as far as the divisions of the lands of Leuch; and from Hervertona to Wenemecumbe.

From there it proceeds through Fulanbroc to Harmeville; from Harmeville to Carkeforde; then to Calkeville; from there along the length of the stream to Smalemorsihee; then to the Avon; from there to Offepol; from Offepol to Pickereshomme; from Pickereshomme to Burchlinches; from Lincheon to Oldendune; from Oldendune to Ealdemixam; from there to Buggildestrete; from Buggildestrete to Semassond; from there to Chirchluge, to Flirendegaren, and then to Blakenpyte.

On the eastern side, not far from Blakenpyte, it proceeds to Merchirnan; from Merchirnan to Humburnan; from there through Northamuere to Easthammor; then around the meadow of Poddeho; afterward to Poddehommore; then to Herianchale; again to Humburnam; along the stream as far as Siamthanford; again to Buggildestrete toward Scenendune; from there to Meadebroc; from Meadebroc to Merdich; then to Winburnan; from Wainburna to Leallesthorn; from Leallesthorn to Laverkbeorh; from Laverkbeorh to Poddesthomme; from Poddesthomme to Polthorn; from Polthorn to Merebroc; and then to Stamthanhillessiche.

From Siche to Burghwillon; from Burghwillone to Burhwalles; from there to Ealdegare, which the natives call Navemannessond, beside Buggildestrete; from there, on the western side, as far as Beorges.

From Beorges to Pichestan; from Pichestan to Cademynster; from Cademynster to Blechemere; from Blechemere to Bracedestan; from Bracedestan to Ealdegaran; in Willeriseie; from Willeriseie to Sandbroc; from there to Hegweye; then to Northomme; from Northomme to Brerthirnam.

From there to Hecauhege; from Hecauhege to Badeswillo; from Willein to Litlethyrnan; from Thyrnan through Piccedesho to Prestmeade; from there to Merethorn; from Merethorn to Brudmere; from Brademere to Estmereslewe; from there to Pottycote; from Pottycote to Thrittiacre; then to Riggewere; from Riggewere to Meredic; through Meredic to Wadberge; from the hill to Lithmeade.

Again through Meredic to Esanburnam; from Esanburnam again to Meredic. Then to Wrethmeade; then to Merebroc; through Merebroc as far as Dominpol; from there to Allesbeorg; from Allesbeorg to Merwillon; and from Merwillone again to the Avon.

Moreover, in the name of the Lord, we wish and decree that the land of five hides called Morton shall enjoy the same liberty forever. I, Kenred, king of the Mercians, granted this land to him in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 709, when I was preparing, together with the venerable man Egwin, to visit the threshold of the apostles, among certain other gifts for the construction of a monastery at Homme; and I confirmed it in writing under the testimony of many of my powerful men.

Therefore, in the name of the Lord, we decree and command, by the power of almighty God, both to those now living and to those who by the Lord’s predestination will succeed us in the future, that no one dare in any way invalidate the provisions of this donation. But if anyone should attempt to corrupt or diminish this gift of our munificence, let his name be erased from the book of life. These things were enacted in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation

[Note: [Col. 0337D] Although there seems no reason to doubt that the years of the Incarnation were used by English kings in charters and public acts throughout the preceding century, no example shows that the Roman pontiffs used this era in the preceding or the current century; therefore these subscriptions are additions. Indeed, Warthon, in his preface to *Anglia Sacra*, infers that the whole privilege is spurious from the fact that in the original document still preserved in England, [Col. 0338D] Coenred and Offa, who had renounced royal dignity and assumed the monastic habit, call themselves kings—something wholly contrary to probability. This argument may be reinforced by the fact that the original is said to be written in Saxon characters, entirely unknown at Rome and in the chancery of the Roman pontiffs (Pagius, on the year of Christ 709, no. 7).]

709, in the church of the Savior at the Lateran, with Constantine, pontiff of the Roman see, confirming it, while the kings of England, Kenred and Offa, stood present, at the request of the venerable man Egwin, bishop, together with many archbishops and bishops, princes, and nobles of different provinces, all crying out and saying: “We praise this will and royal generosity; we consent to the donations and the liberty.”

### Subscriptions

I, Constantine, bishop of the Roman see, have confirmed these donations and this liberty by this sign of the holy cross. I, Egwin, humble bishop, have confirmed them. I, King Kenred, have ratified them. I, King Offa, have consented.

## Letter II. Pope Constantine to Brithwald, Archbishop of Canterbury

He places the monastery founded by Ecgwin under his authority, while nevertheless asserting certain rights for it.

Constantine, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Brithwald, primate of the Britons: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Promoted by divine dispensation for the purpose of devoting ourselves, by apostolic authority, to the peace of the churches, we announce to your fraternity that you should protect, by your own authority and that of the holy apostles, the churches established throughout Britain, lest any invader of whatever rank overthrow the privileges established by God and by us. Among these, we place especially under your jurisdiction the church recently established by the venerable man Ecgwin through our authority and that of the king, so that, by the power divinely granted to you and your successors, you may render it forever free from every attack by its adversaries.

For it seems just to us that, since the same venerable Ecgwin, following the example of the Lord, humbled himself and became abbot there, this church should, according to what it requests through its legate Aetelwald, obtain from our see a greater dignity on account of his merit. Therefore, in the name of the Lord, we decree that the same place, under the rule of its own abbot, shall be free from every tyrannical exaction, and that no person of whatever rank dare impose any burden upon it.

When the abbot dies, however, an abbot shall be chosen by the brothers of that place, according to canonical authority, either from the monastery itself or from the diocese of the Hwiccians. He shall be consecrated freely and canonically in that same church, without any exaction, and, out of reverence for the venerable Ecgwin, shall use the ring only in the celebration of Mass; and by our authority he shall perpetually hold the first place after the bishop of the Hwiccians.

Therefore, if anyone should wish to violate this privilege, or should attempt to introduce clerics into the place of the monks, let him be anathema forever before God and his angels. But if anyone preserves this authority of ours, may God preserve him forever.

This letter was written in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 713, while Pope Constantine presided over the apostolic see, and he himself made this + sign of the holy cross with his own hand.

This letter was written in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 709 in the church of the Savior at the Lateran, with Constantine, bishop of the apostolic see, commanding and confirming it, while the kings of England, Kenred and Offa, stood present and confirmed it, at the request of the venerable man Ecgwin, bishop, before many archbishops and bishops, princes, and nobles of different provinces, all crying out and saying: “Whatever your holiness does in this constitution, we praise, grant, and confirm.”

+ I, Constantine, bishop of the Roman see, have confirmed these donations and this liberty by the sign of the holy cross. [Col. 0339D] I, Ecgwin, humble bishop, have confirmed them. I, King Kenred, have ratified them. I, King Offa, have consented a.

[Note: [Col. 0339D] This letter is written in the year of grace 709, and when the place had been consecrated by Saint Wilfrid, bishop, Wilfrid and Ecgwin themselves spoke before everyone as follows:

“Lord God, who dwell in heaven and created all things, preserve him who shall pacify and preserve this place. We too command, in the name of almighty God and of all the heavenly powers, that neither king, prince, nor person of any rank diminish this holy place; but let it be, as we desire, a well-ordered wall for the flocks and pastors of God, under the authority of its own abbot, according to the rule of God and Saint Benedict. But if anyone, God forbid, seized by a spirit of avarice, should wish to alter it, let him be judged before the tribunal of God and never come into the remembrance of Christ; rather, let his name be erased forever from the book of the living, and let him be bound in hell by the knots of eternal punishments, unless he repents and makes amends in this life. The dedication of this church took place in the year of grace 714. Capgravius.”]

## Charter of Bishop Egwin of Worcester

He speaks of his visions and of the founding and endowment of his monastery at Evesham in the territory of Worcester.

I, Egwin, humble bishop of the Hwiccians, wish to make known to all the faithful of Christ how, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and through the labor of many great visions, it was shown to me that I ought first to build a place for the praise and glory of almighty God and of holy Mary and of all Christ’s elect, and also for eternal [Col. 0340B] recompense.

When, therefore, I was flourishing especially in the days of King Ethelred, I asked him for the place called Ethomme. In that place the holy and perpetual virgin Mary appeared first to a certain shepherd of flocks named Eoves, and afterward also to me, holding a book in her hands with two virgins. I therefore cleansed the place and, with the help of God’s grace, brought the work I had begun to completion.

I therefore wish to show to every future generation what possessions I acquired for the aforesaid place, and how I freed those lands from every exaction by every authority; and I caused that exemption to be confirmed by attached authorities and privileges, as well as by royal edicts, so that the brothers serving God there according to the rule of Saint Benedict might live without disturbance.

I also wish to make known the names of the villages, all of which I offered to God and holy Mary as free possessions lawfully acquired. Thus, from King Ethelred I obtained a monastery called Flendaburch, which I afterward exchanged for another monastery called Streatford. Afterward, from Osward I acquired twenty hides at a place called Tuiford. Then, when Kenred succeeded to the kingdom, he too granted me eighty-four hides on both sides of the river called the Avon. A certain young man named Atheric granted me eight hides, and the venerable priest Walter donated another eight hides to me.

Thus, by God’s favor, in a short time I acquired 120 hides for the aforesaid church of Christ, as is written and confirmed in the charters [Col. 0340D] of the church; and in the book written by Archbishop Brithwald, and dictated by order of the Roman pontiff with the consent of the princes of all England, the land and its boundaries are made known.

These, then, are the names of the villages which, as stated above, I acquired: Lovesham, Benjucgurthe, Hautun, Baddescye, Wicque, Humburne, Brotsortun, Willersey, Witheleia, Samburne, Kiveuvarton, Greater and Lesser Saltford, Ambresloy, Ulbeorge, Mortun, Buchtun, Meleigaresbyri, Titlestrop, Greater Suella, Mayeldesbeordi, and Sildesuicoque. I acquired all these lands, as I have said, free from every claim, and offered them to the holy Church of God.

[Col. 0341A] Therefore, whoever should presume to corrupt, diminish, or defile the place which apostolic dignity and royal power have endowed with royal liberty, and which we grant by the authority of God and the holy apostles, let him be judged before the tribunal of Christ and never come into the remembrance of Christ, unless he repents and makes amends in this life. But whoever preserves and increases it, let him be filled with blessings. Fiat. Amen.

This charter was written in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 714.

### Subscriptions

I, Egwin, have confirmed it by the sign of the holy cross. I, King Kenred, have subscribed. I, Offa, have confirmed it by the sign of the cross. I, Brithwald, archbishop, have subscribed. [Col. 0341B] I, Osward, the king’s brother, have confirmed it.

## Letter III. Apologetic Letter of John, Most Holy Archbishop of Constantinople, to Constantine, Most Holy Pope of Rome

Concerning the matters stirred up against the holy and ecumenical Sixth Synod during the tyranny of Barda [or Bardanes].

To the most holy and blessed brother and fellow minister, the lord Constantine, John, an unworthy bishop, sends greetings in the Lord.

God, who has constructed the magnificence of visible things as an indication of his divinity and power, has especially displayed his glory and wisdom in the most precious of created sensible beings—in what I mean, our human form. For this reason the prophet exclaimed that divine knowledge itself had been made wondrous (Psalm 128).

The creator of our nature, having arranged through his artistry that the head should be placed over the whole body, and having stationed in it the principal instruments of the senses, caused all movement and perfection of the remaining limbs to arise and be preserved from it. If any of them should be injured or afflicted by some trouble, he determined that he himself should take no slight care of them; indeed, displaying natural affection and sympathy even toward the extremities, he treats through the service of the hands, guided by the eyes, whatever is suffering.

We can compare your apostolic pontificate to this, O most holy head of the Christian priesthood. Since we canonically regard you as the head, we rightly seek through you consolation for the sickness that has befallen our ecclesiastical body through a pestilential and destructive tyranny over minds. Surely you too, as is proper to a head, will not despise us who suffer unwillingly, nor send us away from the bond of natural and united connection. Rather, grieving over our wounds—for when one member suffers, all the members likewise suffer, as is fitting according to the apostolic voice—you will rightly rejoice now at our recovery of health, especially since the disease did not arise from any fault of the body but was caused externally by a violent and unexpected calamity.

To inform you more fully about this, we have necessarily sent this letter, opening and indicating to you through it, as it were, the gravity of the wound. For this reason we have until now been prevented from sending you the customary synodal letter, since we were being held under tyranny. Otherwise, we were not permitted to write to you, setting forth the doctrines of piety clearly and without confusion.

When this city, guarded by God, had been seized by external force—for I should not truly call it an empire, since he brought a wound upon us like a brigand and as though from ambush, by methods known to the Providence that governs all things; for it is not ours to scrutinize the depths of divine judgments—he cast down, even before his entry, the image of the holy Sixth Synod that had been placed in the halls of the palace, laying force rather than laws as the foundation of his power.

But when he wished to place in the pontifical see a man who was not from our ecclesiastical community [Col. 0342B] but shared his perverse opinion, he was nevertheless compelled, by the persistence and opposition of our clergy, to advance us to the dignity and rank of the pontificate, although we did not expect it, did not wish it, and endured it not without grief, reluctantly and with distress.

For who, wholly inexperienced in navigation, would board a ship and dare to cross the straits? It is still more serious when someone is about to travel abroad across the sea and the helm of a merchant ship is entrusted to him alone, so that he may undertake the task of steering both himself and the crew.

Anyone who observes this in our case—for we have never aspired to the splendor of ecclesiastical dignities that belongs among pontiffs, but have devoted ourselves solely to the ministry of the mysteries—will not regard what we say as incredible. That this was not done by our will is proved by the testimony of our own conscience, which the divine apostle defined through his glorying (1 Corinthians 1), while God brings it forth in us to prove the truth of what is said.

This man, therefore, who regarded his own honor as the dishonor and disgrace of the Church, was giving birth and striving to produce the basilisk of impiety, the offspring of the serpent, author of evils, so that the holy Sixth Synod and the elders of your apostolic and venerable see who had held the venerable doctrine of piety might be publicly subjected to anathema in the Church and in the confessions of the bishops.

We were also being compelled to make a common confession in absurd expressions having no kinship with the notions that signify the perfection of the mystery that exists in Christ. The mystery of the Word’s assumption of humanity would be kept far away. Indeed, some were already murmuring that the holy Council of Chalcedon itself ought to be abolished, since, in matters concerning the agreement of doctrines, it depended upon that council and, so to speak, had its root and confirmation in the holy Sixth Synod.

I say nothing of how many genuine difficulties he presented to us in directing letters to your fraternal blessedness in accordance with the aim of his madness. As for how and with what plan we acted, so as to repel his tyrannical and insolent force while bringing his arrogance down to something somewhat more moderate—knowing that, in evils, indifference should not be rejected altogether when it is impossible to obtain the good in the first place—the power itself that observes the counsels of hearts will bear witness for us.

Moreover, so will the religious apocrisiarius of your most holy see who is active here, to whom, when this tempest pressed us most urgently, we satisfied by an oath, revealing to him the pure affection we held for the orthodox faith.

For you also know, as those who have learned this plainly through experience, O most holy ones, that to behave too harshly and obstinately against the necessity imposed by power in such matters, without some skill and ingenuity, was in no way easy. The prophet Nathan, for example, did not openly rebuke David for the adultery and murder he had committed (2 Samuel 12); rather, after presenting the matter in a plausible story, he pronounced judgment upon him from David’s own verdict, although David himself was also endowed with the prophetic spirit.

For this reason we too, as the great Basil says, judged that we ought to yield somewhat to the character of the men, so that in matters of primary importance the confession of faith might remain inviolate, if not in words, then in meaning. “Truth is not in words but in realities,” cries Gregory the Theologian.

[Note: [Col. 0343D] Read *salvation* (σωτηρία, *sōtēria*), not *truth* (ἀλήθεια, *alētheia*), in Oration 20, *On Basil*. Harduinus.]

Again, he declares that it is exceedingly absurd and shameful to argue minutely about the sound of a voice. The apostolic Dionysius the Areopagite likewise pronounces it irrational and foolish to disregard the force of the purpose and subject while attending to expressions. He says that this is not characteristic of those who wish to perceive divine understanding, but of those who admit only sounds, contain them externally because they cannot let them penetrate farther than the ears, and do not wish to know what a given expression signifies or how it ought to be explained through other expressions that have the same force and express the matter more clearly.

We say this not because we wish to overthrow the expressions already defined synodically and confessed by the whole Church of God for so long. We mean, rather, the statement that in the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation there are, according to the pious understanding received from the holy Fathers, two natural wills and two natural operations.

We observed that this was directed solely at the tyrant’s persuasion, as the apostle calls it (Galatians 5), and that through clever contrivance it was being turned into its opposite, lest alien doctrines be openly introduced into the Church and the established decrees of piety concerning the matter be utterly shaken. At the same time, we considered it a great advantage if even the enemies of the named holy synod should, by their own confession, admit its doctrine, so that it might plainly appear to confirm rather than overthrow it—at least to those who know how to consider these matters with a sound and unbending eye.

For to say that Christ possesses the power of willing and operating in the other nature is nothing other than to understand two natural wills and two natural operations. The synod assembled in your great city of Rome under the venerable Martin, who presided over your Church, had already expressly decreed that these expressions should be understood in this sense, as God’s wisdom arranged through us also, sinners and the least of men: “He catches the wise in their craftiness” (Psalm 111).

Gregory the Theologian places this saying in his funeral oration for the great Basil, where he represents Basil as having followed David’s counsel by managing his words in judgment: he passed over in silence the principal expression concerning the Holy Spirit but strengthened the pious proclamation of the faith with other expressions of equivalent force.

Although how great the difference is between the two matters—between what concerns faith and the confession of divinity and what concerns the divine Incarnation—as the holy Gregory the Theologian says, the reflections that subtle contemplation necessarily investigates in order to indicate the perfection [Note: [Col. 0343D] Read: “In each nature, I think no one is unaware ...,” where he speaks of the divine nature, or the life-giving Trinity, etc. Harduinus.] of both natures or of the life-giving Trinity possess excellence and distinction.

The same is evident in what the wise theologian says in his oration on theology against the Eunomians. There he says:

“Philosophize about the world, about matter, about the soul, about rational natures, both more excellent and inferior, about the resurrection, judgment, recompense, and Christ’s sufferings. In these matters, it is not useless to attain the truth, nor dangerous to err. For the teacher did not set them forth simply and absolutely, but in comparison with the matters spoken and decided concerning the divine Trinity.”

Believing, therefore, O most holy ones, that the rest of what was done proceeded according to this dispensation and plan, do not on that account impose upon us a fault that cannot be forgiven. Even if anyone should think that we did not attain what is exact and perfect, let us be acquitted of fault and every condemnation by comparison with those who acted economically in accordance with the holy Fathers.

For the most wise Cyril likewise does not expressly command that Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, be repudiated, deliberately showing consideration toward those who were still more weakly disposed toward him, although he knew him to be the author and father of the opinion of the perverse Nestorius. This is indicated by what he himself wrote concerning him to Saint Proclus, who presided over our most holy Church.

The tyrant of the faith mentioned above, having his conscience seared, as the most holy Paul says (1 Timothy 4), dared to burn the volumes of the Acts of the aforesaid holy Sixth Synod that had been deposited in the palace, thinking that he would thereby also destroy the word of truth.

But we allowed him to be deceived by his own opinion and to glory in his disgrace as though in some splendid deed. We carefully preserved among ourselves the volumes of the Acts of the aforesaid holy Sixth Synod, in which the subscriptions of all the bishops who assembled at this holy Sixth Synod are contained, together with the imperial subscription, in the decree issued by them.

Moreover, in our own time special care was taken that the Acts of that same holy synod should be preserved and not perish. For a book written in his own hand by Paul of holy memory, who was bishop of our most holy Church, was kept by God’s grace among us. While he was secretary, he served at this holy synod.

Thus, through this book, provision has also been made for posterity by God and the Church, so that no one may dare, through any act of malice—for time often renews many things among human beings—to adulterate what, as was said earlier, was continuously enacted by the holy Sixth Synod, or to transmit it perversely to others. For the genuine and uncircumscribed truth will be shown more clearly to all from this book.

Our true ruler and Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, did not endure to remain asleep any longer amid these things. Rising through his goodness and power, he has now rebuked the wave—not of water, but of an impious endeavor—and has calmed the storm of the churches’ tempest.

He has granted us great tranquillity in public affairs, together with a pious emperor endowed with virtue in every respect. He possesses a zeal for orthodox faith corresponding to imperial majesty, uprightness and moderation of character, and, in accordance with his name—Anastasius—has caused ecclesiastical peace and concord to rise again.

We also trust in him who granted this to us, because he is beginning, in accordance with the meaning of his name, the restoration [Note: [Col. 0345D] Read *erection* or *restoration*. Harduinus.] of the commonwealth as well.

[Col. 0345C] Therefore, O sacred head, extending to us the hand of a gracious appeal through the most discerning virtue of the Spirit that is in you, and applying the medicine of charity through the gentle exchange of letters according to ecclesiastical custom [Note: [Col. 0345D] Read *antisynodical letters*—that is, an exchange of synodical letters—in the sense of a reciprocal sending. [Col. 0346D] Harduinus.], namely, the letters of the apostles, strive to heal what is troubled and throbbing within us.

For our relaxation will never come, nor will sleep rise to our eyes, nor rest settle upon our temples and drowsiness upon our eyelids, until we see the whole Church of God once again preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

Since you are disciples and successors of the one who heard from the Lord: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, that he might sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22), you ought carefully to introduce what supports and establishes correction, and more readily to grant what belongs to a merciful and compassionate spirit.

For the Lord himself exhorts the foremost of the apostles, on the basis of what happened to him, to recognize the weakness of the flesh; but those who have fallen through the assault of external circumstances, as happened also to him at the time of the saving Passion, should not be prevented from being restored through correction to their former freedom from suffering.

Let this also not escape the memory of your sacrosanctity: certain men who had deposed the impious Eutyches in the time of Flavian of holy memory later, in the synod held at Ephesus by Dioscorus, pronounced just the man who had rightly been condemned and most unjustly condemned the blessed Flavian. Nevertheless, at the holy Council of Chalcedon, the profession of a holy confession was sufficient for them to be completely cleared of the accusation; they required no great labor or many words concerning it.

Fraternal love knows that kindness and clemency toward one’s neighbor should not be long delayed. For Leo, that most illustrious light of your apostolic see—and indeed of the whole world—wrote the following to the holy Fathers assembled at Chalcedon:

“But since many things often occur that can lead to repentance, and God’s mercy overcomes the sins of sinners, punishment is therefore suspended so that correction may have a place” (*Letter* 47).

Moreover, when writing to Pulcheria in the letter beginning, “The pious care of your kindness, which continually watches over the Catholic faith,” the most excellent mind of Leo of blessed memory says:

“For, as I have written very frequently from the beginning of this matter, I wish this moderation to be maintained between dissenting minds and carnal minds: nothing may be added to or contributed toward the perfection of the faith; but to those who return to unity and peace, the remedy of pardon should be offered, since the works of the devil are destroyed more powerfully when they recall human hearts to love of God and neighbor” (*Letter* 51).

Cyril, too, most skilled in divine matters, is found to have done this long before, during the attack and dispute of the eastern bishops against him. They wished to absolve Nestorius from condemnation and sought to weaken the judgment pronounced against him; in doing so, they dared to commit not merely something intolerable but the greatest offense. For they anathematized the blessed Cyril himself and his synod.

But he too applied a swift and uncomplicated remedy: namely, that they should consent to what had been established and piously defined synodically, and approve the condemnation of the impious man. Afterward, with the divine Father himself crying out those words full of joy, one might suspect that they were spoken as though he himself had received pardon for his own fall rather than had pardoned the fallen man:

“Let the heavens rejoice,” he says, “and let the earth exult; the wall of the fence has been broken down, and every cause of dissension has been removed, since Christ our Savior has reconciled peace to his Churches.”

You therefore possess, O divinely inspired men, a strong and legitimate defense of the offense committed through another’s force and injury, and a pure and free confession of the orthodox faith that can in no way be overturned or weakened.

Do not, therefore, O blessed ones, be sluggish or slow toward what is joined and indivisible with you in spiritual fellowship and concord. Do not, by attending to what was done by force, expel us, upon whom force was inflicted, from your charity; nor regard us as enemies, as the divine apostle says, but console us as brothers (2 Thessalonians 3), showing imitation of God.

For you will surely consider, O most holy ones, from the scriptural history of Aaron the holy one of the Lord, as the divine Spirit called him, that what is done by force and not from inward malice of soul is followed by a just pardon—except in the case of a complete denial of the Word and a leading away into perfect impiety.

When that Aaron yielded to the pressure of the ancient people and assisted them in making an idol, he was indeed rebuked by his brother. But when he asserted in his defense that he had done this under compulsion, he received no rebuke from God and was not deprived of the dignity of the high priesthood (Exodus 32). The one who formed our hearts individually, as the great David says (Psalm 72), looks wholly to inward and genuine worship of God, not to external recklessness.

[Col. 0348A] Having therefore shown the soundness and agreement of our judgment concerning the true Word, since we are ready, contrary to custom, to condemn what was absurdly done but to approve and confirm the doctrines of piety of the holy Sixth Synod, embrace us, venerable brothers.

“For each one must bear the other’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ,” the divine apostle cries to us in a loud voice (Galatians 2), so that with one mind and in one spirit we may glorify God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

### Subscription

Strong in the Lord, pray for us, most holy and blessed brother.

## Letter IV. Complaint of Benedict, Archbishop of Milan, in the Synod Concerning Pope Constantine

[Col. 0348B]

See below among the writings of Benedict.

## In the Year of the Lord 709. Ceolfrid, Anglo-Saxon Priest

[Col. 0347]

### Historical Notice on Ceolfrid

(*Fabricius, Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*)

[Col. 0347C] Ceolfrid, also called Geolfrid, priest and, after Benedict Biscop, abbot of the monasteries of Saints Peter and Paul, of the Benedictine order, at Wearmouth and Jarrow in England for thirty-five years, died at Lingon in Gaul Narbonensis in the year 716, on the seventh day before the Kalends of October, at the age of seventy-four. Bede, whom he instructed in learning, celebrated him with worthy praises.

[Note: [Col. 0347D] See Leland, chapter 81.]

When King Naiton of the Picts consulted him about the lawful observance of Easter and the tonsure of clerics, he wrote a useful letter through which he satisfied the king, and the king brought his people back to harmony with the Church.

Bede preserved this letter in book 5, chapter 22, of his *Ecclesiastical History*. Spelman took it from there, page 200, volume 1 of the *Councils of Britain*. The other editors of the councils included it under the year 714, although Norisius concludes that it was written around the year 709.

[Note: [Col. 0348D] *Dissertation 3 on the Paschal Cycle of Ravenna*, p. 158; Oudinus, volume 1, p. 1665.]

[Col. 0348C] In his edition of the councils, Harduinus followed Petrus Franciscus Chifletius, who revised Bede’s *History* in *Bede and Fredegarius Scholasticus in Concord*, Paris, 1681–1684.

As for other works by Ceolfrid, which Balaeus, century 1, chapter 93, and from him Pitsius, p. 123, mention—solemn homilies, letters to his monks, a testament to Hunebert, and *On His Pilgrimage*—I do not know whether anyone has actually seen them.

A life written by Wicbert, his successor and a martyr in the year 730, is mentioned by the same Pitsius, p. 124; but where it reads “while Ceolfrid was reigning in Northumbria,” one should read “Ceolwulf,” about whom more will be said shortly.

Cangius, too, should be corrected where he makes Ceolfrid, abbot of Saints Peter and Paul, different from the abbot of Wearmouth.

[Col. 0349]

## Letter of Ceolfrid, Anglo-Saxon Priest, to Naiton, King of the Picts, Concerning Catholic Easter and the Roman Tonsure

*(Mansi, Collection of Councils, volume 12)*

### Bede’s Preface

[Col. 0349A]

At that time Naiton, king of the Picts, who inhabit the northern regions of Britain, having been admonished through frequent meditation on the ecclesiastical Scriptures, renounced the error by which he and his people had until then been held in the observance of Easter, and brought himself and all his people to the catholic observance of celebrating the time of the Lord’s resurrection.

To accomplish this more easily and with greater authority, he sought assistance from the English, whom he had long since learned to have established their religion according to the example of the holy Roman and apostolic Church.

Accordingly, he sent envoys to the venerable man Ceolfrid, abbot of the monastery of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, which is at the mouth of the river Wear and beside the river Tyne, at a place called Ingrivum, where Ceolfrid presided most gloriously after Benedict, whom we mentioned above.

He requested that Ceolfrid send him an exhortatory letter by which he might more powerfully refute those who presumed to observe Easter at the wrong time, and also address the manner or method of the tonsure by which clerics ought to be marked. He himself, moreover, had already been instructed to a considerable degree in these matters.

He also asked that architects be sent to him who, according to Roman custom, might build for him a great church of stone, promising to dedicate it in honor of the blessed prince of the apostles, and promising that he himself, together with all his people, would always imitate the custom of the holy Roman and apostolic Church, insofar as those so far removed from the speech and nation of the Romans could learn it.

The most reverend abbot Ceolfrid, favoring these religious vows and prayers, sent the architects whom he had requested, together with a letter written as follows.

### Letter of Abbot Ceolfrid

To the most excellent and glorious lord King Naiton, Ceolfrid, abbot, sends greetings in the Lord.

The Catholic observance of holy Easter, which you, king, have devoutly and zealously sought from us, we strive most readily and gladly to make known according to what we have learned from the apostolic see, in accordance with your desire. For we know that the truth of the holy Church—truth to be learned, taught, and guarded concerning the Lord’s affairs—is bestowed from heaven whenever people devote themselves to it. Indeed, one of the secular writers truly said that the world would be governed in the happiest condition if either kings became philosophers or philosophers became kings. But if, concerning the philosophy of this world, he could rightly understand the condition of this world and love this world, [Col. 0349D] how much more ought the citizens of the heavenly homeland, while journeying in this world, to desire and implore with all the powers of their soul that, the more each person possesses power in the world, the more earnestly he should strive to obey the commands of him who is judge above all, and instruct by both example and authority those entrusted to him to observe them as well.

There are therefore three rules established in the sacred Scriptures by which the time for celebrating Easter is prescribed for us and may not be changed by any human authority whatsoever. Two of these were divinely established in the Law of Moses; the third was added in the Gospel through the effect of the Lord’s passion and resurrection. For the Law commanded that Passover should be celebrated in the first month of the year and in the third week of that month—that is, from the fifteenth day through the twenty-first. [Col. 0350B] Through apostolic institution, something was added from the Gospel: in that third week we are to await the Lord’s Day and observe in it the beginning of the paschal season. Whoever properly observes this threefold rule will never err in determining the feast of Easter.

But if you wish to hear more clearly and at greater length about each of these matters, it is written in Exodus that, when the people of Israel were to be delivered from Egypt, they were first commanded to celebrate the Passover, because the Lord said to Moses and Aaron:

“This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year. Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel and say to them: On the tenth day of this month each man shall take a lamb for his families and houses” (Exod. 12).

And shortly afterward:

“You shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month. Then the whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it toward evening” (ibid.).

From these words it is most clearly evident that, although the fourteenth day is mentioned in the observance of Passover, Passover is not commanded to be celebrated on the fourteenth day itself. Rather, when the evening of the fourteenth day arrives—that is, when the fifteenth moon, which begins the third week, appears in the face of heaven—the lamb is to be sacrificed.

That this is the night of the fifteenth moon, on which, after the Egyptians had been struck down, Israel was redeemed from long servitude, is shown by the words:

“For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread” (ibid.).

By these words again the entire third week of the same first month is decreed to be solemn. Yet, lest we think that those seven days are to be counted from the fourteenth through the twentieth, he immediately added:

“On the first day there shall be no leaven in your houses. Whoever eats anything leavened in your houses, that soul shall perish from Israel, from the first day through the seventh day” (Exod. 12),

and so forth, until he says:

“For on that same day I shall bring your army out of the land of Egypt” (ibid.).

He therefore calls the first day of unleavened bread the day on which he was to lead their army out of Egypt. It is clear, however, that they were led out of Egypt not on the fourteenth day—on whose evening the lamb was sacrificed and which is properly called Passover or *phase*—but on the fifteenth, as is stated most plainly in the Book of Numbers:

“So they departed from Rameses on the fifteenth day of the first month. On the following day the children of Israel kept the Passover with uplifted hand” (Num. 33).

The seven days of unleavened bread, on the first of which the Lord’s people were led out of Egypt, must therefore be counted from the beginning, as we have said, of the third week—that is, from the fifteenth day of the first month through the completed twenty-first day of that same month. [Col. 0351B] The fourteenth day, moreover, is set apart outside this number and marked under the title of Passover, as the continuation of Exodus plainly teaches. For after it had been said:

“For on that same day I shall bring your army out of the land of Egypt,”

it immediately adds:

“And you shall keep this day throughout your generations as a perpetual observance. In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, you shall eat unleavened bread until the twenty-first day of the same month at evening. For seven days no leaven shall be found in your houses” (Exod. 12).

Who does not see that from the fourteenth through the twenty-first there are not merely seven days but rather eight, if the fourteenth itself is counted? [Col. 0351C] But if, as the truth of Scripture more carefully examined teaches, we count from the evening of the fourteenth day through the evening of the twenty-first, we shall certainly see that the fourteenth day extends its evening as the beginning of the paschal feast, so that the entire sacred solemnity comprises no more than seven nights together with seven days. Hence our definition is proved true: the paschal season is to be celebrated in the first month of the year and in its third week. For the third week truly begins at the evening of the fourteenth day and is completed at the evening of the twenty-first.

After Christ, our Passover, had been sacrificed, and after he had made the Lord’s Day—which among the ancients is called the first or one of the Sabbaths or of the Sabbaths—a solemn day for us through the joy of his resurrection, apostolic tradition inserted it into the paschal feasts in such a way that it decreed that nothing whatsoever should be anticipated or diminished in the time of the legal Passover. Rather, it established that the first month of the year should be awaited according to the command of the Law; that its fourteenth day should be awaited; and that the evening of that day should be awaited. If that day should happen to fall on the Sabbath, each person was to take a lamb for his families and houses and sacrifice it toward evening (ibid.). That is, all the churches throughout the world, which constitute one catholic Church, were to prepare bread and wine as the mystery of the body and blood of the immaculate Lamb who took away the sins of the world; and, with the fitting solemnity of paschal readings, prayers, [Col. 0352A] and ceremonies preceding it, they were to offer these things to the Lord in hope of their future redemption.

For this is the very night on which the Israelite people were rescued from Egypt through the blood of the lamb; this is the night on which, through Christ’s resurrection, all God’s people were delivered from eternal death. When morning dawned on the Lord’s Day, they were to celebrate the first day of the paschal feast. For this is the day on which the Lord revealed to his disciples the glory of his resurrection through the joy of manifold holy revelations. This is the first day of unleavened bread, about which it is written very distinctly in Leviticus:

“In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, toward evening, is the Lord’s Passover; and on the fifteenth day of this month is the solemnity of the Lord’s unleavened bread. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread; the first day shall be most celebrated and holy.”

If, therefore, it were possible for the Lord’s Day always to fall on the fifteenth day of the first month—that is, on the fifteenth moon—we could always celebrate Easter at one and the same time with the ancient people of God, although distinguished from them in the kind of our sacraments, just as we are united with them in one and the same faith. But because the days of the week do not proceed in equal course with the moon, apostolic tradition—which was preached at Rome by the blessed Peter and confirmed at Alexandria by Mark the evangelist and his interpreter—decreed that, when the first month arrives and the evening of its fourteenth day arrives, the Lord’s Day should also be awaited from the fifteenth through the twenty-first day of that same month. For on whichever of these days it is found, Easter is rightly celebrated on that day, since it belongs to the number of those seven days on which the Law commands unleavened bread to be celebrated.

Thus it happens that our Easter never departs in either direction from the third week of the first month. It either includes the whole of it—that is, all seven of the legal days of unleavened bread—or at least some of them. Even if it includes only one of them, namely the seventh itself, which Scripture commends so especially:

“The seventh day shall be more celebrated and holier, and no servile work shall be done on it” (ibid.),

no one will be able to accuse us of failing to celebrate correctly the Lord’s Easter day, which we received from the Gospel, in the very third week of the first month established by the Law.

[Col. 0352D] Once the catholic reason for this observance has been made clear, the irrational error of those who, without any compelling necessity, presume either to anticipate or to exceed the limits fixed in the Law becomes clear by contrast. Those anticipate the time prescribed in the Law without any necessary reason who think that the Lord’s Easter day must be observed from the fourteenth day of the first month through the twentieth moon. For when they begin celebrating vigils of the holy night from the evening of the thirteenth day, it is clear that they establish as the beginning of their Easter that day of which they find no mention whatsoever in the decree of the Law. And when they refuse to celebrate the Lord’s Easter on the twenty-first day of the month, it is plainly evident that they entirely exclude from their solemnity that day which the Law repeatedly commends as memorable through a greater festival than the others. Thus, by a perverse ordering of the Easter day, they sometimes complete the whole feast in the second week and never place it on the seventh day of the third week.

Again, those who maintain that Easter should be celebrated from the sixteenth day of the aforesaid month through the twenty-second day depart from the straight path of truth through no lesser an error, although on the other side. Like those fleeing the shipwrecks of Scylla, they fall into the whirlpool of Charybdis, where they are swallowed up. For when they teach that Easter must begin at the rising of the sixteenth moon of the first month—that is, from the evening of the fifteenth day—it is plainly evident that they entirely exclude from its solemnity the fourteenth day of that same month, which the Law originally and especially commended. Thus they scarcely touch the evening of the fifteenth day, on which God’s people were redeemed from Egyptian servitude, on which the Lord liberated the world from the darkness of sins by his own blood, and on which, after being buried, he granted us hope of blessed rest after death. Receiving the punishment of their error upon themselves, when they establish the Lord’s Easter day on the twenty-second day of the month, they openly violate the lawful limits of Easter, since they begin Easter from the evening of that day on which the Law decreed that it should be completed and brought to an end. They assign as the first day of Easter a day of which no mention is found anywhere in the Law—namely, the first day of the fourth week.

Both groups err not only in defining and calculating the moon’s age but sometimes also in determining the first month. This discussion is greater than can or ought to be contained in this letter.

I shall say only this: through the spring equinox it can always be determined with certainty which month, according to the reckoning of the moon, ought to be the first month of the year and which ought to be the last. According to the opinion of all the Easterners, and especially of the Egyptians, who surpass other teachers in the art of calculation, the equinox customarily occurs on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April; we ourselves have also proved this by observing the clock. Therefore, whatever full moon occurs before the equinox—whether it is the fourteenth or the fifteenth—belongs to the last month of the preceding year and is consequently unsuitable for celebrating Easter. But whatever moon has its full moon after the equinox or on the equinox itself must, without any doubt, be recognized as belonging to the first month; the ancients used to celebrate Easter in it, and we too must celebrate Easter in it when the Lord’s Day arrives.

This ought to happen for the following compelling reason: it is written in Genesis that God made two great lights, “the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night” (Gen. 1). Or, as another edition reads, “the greater light for the beginning of the day, and the lesser light for the beginning of the night.” Therefore, just as the sun first fixed the spring equinox by its rising from the midpoint of the East, and afterward the moon alone, at evening, followed from the midpoint of the East and was itself full, so in every year the first month of the moon must necessarily be preserved in the same order. It must have its full moon not before the equinox, but either on the very day of the equinox—as happened in the beginning—or after the equinox has passed. If the full moon precedes the time of the equinox by even one day, the reasoning already stated proves that this moon is not to be assigned to the first month of the new year but rather to the last month of the preceding year and is therefore unsuitable for the paschal feasts.

If you are also pleased to hear the mystical meaning of these matters, we are commanded to celebrate Easter in the first month of the year, which is also called the month of new things, because, with the spirit of our mind renewed for love of heavenly things, we ought to celebrate the mysteries of the Lord’s resurrection and our deliverance. We are commanded to celebrate it in the third week of that month, because Christ, who was promised before the Law and under the Law, came with grace in the third age of the world to be sacrificed as our Passover. On the third day after the sacrifice of his passion he rose from the dead, wished that this day should be called the Lord’s Day, and commanded us to celebrate each year on it the paschal feasts of his resurrection. For we too celebrate his solemnity truthfully only if, through faith and charity, we strive to pass over with him from this world to the Father—that is, to celebrate Passover as our passage.

We are commanded to observe the full moon of the paschal month after the spring equinox so that first the sun may make the day longer than the night, and afterward the moon may display to the world the full circle of its light. For first the Sun of righteousness, in whose wings there is healing—that is, the Lord Jesus—overcame all the darkness of death through the triumph of his resurrection. Then, ascending into heaven and sending the Spirit from above, he filled his Church, which is often signified by the name of the moon, with the light of inward grace. The prophet contemplated this order of our salvation when he said:

“The sun was raised, and the moon stood in its order” (Mal. 4).

Whoever therefore maintains that the fullness of the paschal moon can occur before the equinox disagrees in the celebration of the greatest mysteries with the teaching of the holy Scriptures, but agrees with those who trust that they can be saved without Christ’s preceding grace. Although the true light never overcame the darkness of the world by dying and rising again, they presume to dogmatize that they can possess perfect righteousness.

Accordingly, after the equinoctial rising of the sun and, following it in due order, the full moon of the first month—that is, after the completion of the fourteenth day of that same month—we still await, as the Gospel instructs, in that third week the time of the Lord’s Day. Having received all these matters from the Law as things to be observed, Only then do we celebrate the desired feasts of our Easter. In this way we show that we do not venerate the shaking off of the Egyptian yoke of servitude together with the ancients, but rather honor with devout faith and love the redemption of the whole world, which was prefigured in the liberation of God’s ancient people and completed in Christ’s resurrection. We thereby show that we rejoice with the most certain hope of our own resurrection, which we believe will take place on that same Lord’s Day.

[Col. 0355A] This method of calculating Easter, which we show you ought to be followed, is contained in a nineteen-year cycle. It began to be observed in the Church long ago—that is, in the very time of the apostles—especially at Rome and in Egypt, as we have already said. But through the diligence of Eusebius, who bears the surname derived from the blessed martyr Pamphilus, it was arranged more distinctly and systematically, so that what until then the bishop of Alexandria had been accustomed to communicate each year to all the churches could thereafter easily be known by everyone through the lunar sequence of the fourteenth day, arranged in order. The Alexandrian bishop Theophilus composed a paschal calculation covering one hundred years for the emperor Theodosius. His successor Cyril likewise contained a sequence of ninety-five years in five nineteen-year cycles. After him, Dionysius the Little appended another equal number in the same arrangement; these extended up to our own times.

As the end of these approaches, there is now such an abundance of calculators that even in our churches throughout Britain there are many who, committing to memory those ancient Egyptian methods, can very easily extend paschal cycles over any number of periods, even if they wish to extend them to five hundred and thirty-two years. Once these are completed, everything relating to the succession of the sun and moon, the month and the week, recurs in the same order as before. For this reason we have refrained from sending you the cycles of the coming periods, since you sought instruction only concerning the calculation of the paschal season and have shown that you possess an abundance of the catholic cycles of Easter.

But after recalling these matters concerning Easter briefly and concisely, as you requested, I also urge you to take care to have the tonsure that is ecclesiastical and fitting for the Christian faith, about which you likewise wished letters to be written to you. We know, indeed, that not all the apostles were tonsured in one and the same manner; nor does the catholic Church now, although united in one faith, hope, and love of God, possess throughout the world one uniform and indistinguishable form of tonsure.

Finally, if we look back to earlier times, namely those of the patriarchs, Job, the model of patience, when the crisis of his tribulations came upon him, shaved his head. This proves that in a time of prosperity he had been accustomed to grow his hair. Joseph, however, himself an outstanding practitioner and teacher of chastity, humility, piety, and the other virtues, is said to have been shorn when he was to be released from servitude. It is plainly evident that in the time of his servitude he had customarily remained in prison with unshorn hair. Behold: each man of God outwardly displayed a different appearance from the other, yet inwardly their consciences agreed in an equal grace of virtues.

If we may freely express our view, the difference in tonsure does not harm those whose faith in God is pure and whose charity toward their neighbor is sincere, especially since we never read that the catholic fathers engaged in controversy over a difference of tonsure as they did over differences concerning Easter or the faith. Nevertheless, among all the tonsures that we find in the Church or among the human race, I would rightly say that none is more worthy of being followed and embraced than the one worn on his head by him to whom the Lord said, when he confessed him:

“You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, and I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XXVI).

But among all the tonsures I believe that none deserves to be more abhorred and detested by all the faithful than the one worn by the man to whom Peter said, when he sought to purchase the grace of the Holy Spirit:

“May your money be with you for destruction, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money. You have neither part nor lot in this word” (Acts 8).

We are not shorn into a crown merely because Peter was shorn in that way. Rather, because Peter was shorn in memory of the Lord’s passion, we too, who desire to be saved through that same passion, carry with him on our crown—that is, on the highest part of our body—the sign of that passion.

Just as the whole Church, which became the Church through the death of its giver of life, is accustomed to carry the sign of his holy cross on its forehead, so that it may often be defended from the attacks of evil spirits by the protection of this standard and frequently be taught by its reminder that it too must crucify its flesh with its vices and desires, so also those who either have taken the monastic vow or hold the rank of cleric, and who must necessarily bind themselves more strictly for the Lord with the restraints of continence, ought to bear this sign.

They should likewise wear on their heads, through their tonsure, the form of the crown that he himself wore in his passion—a crown of thorns, by which he bore, that is, carried away and removed from us, the thorns and thistles of our sins. Thus, even by the appearance of their forehead, they may show that they willingly and readily endure mockery and reproach for him; that they always await the crown of eternal life which God promised to those who love him; and that, in order to receive it, they despise both the adversities and the prosperity of the world.

As for the tonsure that they say the great Simon possessed, I ask: what faithful person would not immediately detest and rightly reject it together with the magic itself? In appearance, on the surface of the forehead, it seems to display the form of a crown; but when, on examining it, you reach the neck, you will find that the crown you thought you saw has been cut short. You may therefore rightly recognize that such an appearance is suitable to simoniacs rather than to Christians: in the present life they were thought by deceived men worthy of the crown of perpetual glory, but in the life that follows this one they are not only deprived of every hope of a crown but also condemned to eternal punishment.

Nor should you think that I have pursued this matter as though I judged that those who possess this tonsure must be condemned if they support the unity of the catholic faith by faith and works. On the contrary, I confidently declare that many of them have been holy and worthy of God. Among them was Adamnanus, the distinguished abbot and priest of the Columban people. When he had been sent as ambassador of his people to King Alfrid and wished also to visit our monastery, he displayed remarkable prudence, humility, and piety in his conduct and speech. In conversation I said to him, among other things:
