“I beg you, holy brother: since you believe that you are striving toward the crown of life that knows no end, why do you carry on your head an image of a crown terminated by a form contrary to your faith? And if you seek fellowship with the blessed Peter, why do you imitate the appearance of the tonsure of the man whom he anathematized, rather than show that you now cherish, as far as you can, the appearance of the one with whom you desire to live blessed forever?”

He replied:

“Know for certain, my beloved brother, that although I have Simon’s tonsure by the custom of my homeland, I nevertheless detest and reject Simon’s impiety with my whole mind. As far as my smallness permits, I desire to follow the footsteps of the most blessed prince of the apostles.”

But I said:

“I truly believe that this is so. Yet let it be an indication that you embrace in the secret of your heart the things that belong to the apostle Peter if you also keep on your face those things that you know belong to him. For I think your prudence can very easily judge that it is far more fitting to separate from your face the appearance of the one whom you abominate with your whole heart and whose dreadful face you refuse to see, and, on the other hand, that just as you desire to follow the deeds and teachings of the one whom you seek as your patron with God the Father, so it is proper that you imitate his manner of appearance.

“This is what I said to Adamnanus. How much he had profited from seeing the statutes of our churches he demonstrated when, after returning to Scotland, he later corrected many crowds of his people through his preaching and brought them to the catholic observance of the paschal season. Nevertheless, he was not yet able to lead back to the path of the better rule the monks who lived on the island of Iona and over whom he presided by the special right of a superior. He would also have remembered to correct their tonsure, if he had possessed sufficient authority to do so.

“But now, king, I admonish your prudence to strive, together with the people over whom the King of kings and Lord of lords has set you, to observe in all things whatever agrees with the unity of the catholic and apostolic Church. In this way it will come about that, after you have received the power of a temporal kingdom, the most blessed prince of the apostles himself will gladly open for you and yours, together with the other elect, the entrance to the heavenly kingdom.

“May the grace of the eternal King preserve you, most beloved son in Christ, safe and reigning for a long time, for the peace of us all.”

## Decree of King Naiton Concerning Catholic Easter and the Roman Tonsure

When this letter had been read in the presence of King Naiton and many learned men, and had been carefully translated into his own language by those who were able to understand it, he is said to have rejoiced greatly at its exhortation. He rose from the midst of his nobles’ assembly, bent his knees to the ground, and gave thanks to God that he had been deemed worthy to receive such a little gift from the land of the English.

“Indeed,” he said, “I already knew that this was the true celebration of Easter; but only now do I understand so clearly the method by which this time ought to be observed that I seem to have understood almost nothing about these matters before. Therefore I openly profess, and declare before you who are seated here as leaders, that I wish to observe this time of Easter perpetually with all my people. I decree that all the clerics in my kingdom ought to receive this tonsure, which we have heard is fully rational.”

Without delay he fulfilled what he had said by royal authority. At once, by public order, nineteen-year paschal cycles were sent throughout all the provinces of the Picts to be copied, learned, and observed, while the erroneous eighty-four-year cycles were entirely abolished. All the ministers of the altar and monks were shorn into a crown, and the corrected people rejoiced as though they had submitted themselves to a new discipleship under the most blessed prince of the apostles Peter and had placed themselves under his protection.

## In the Year of the Lord 717: Felix, Bishop of Ravenna

[Col. 0357]

## Historical Notice Concerning Felix

*(Ughelli, Italian Sacred History, vol. II.)*

[Col. 0357D] Felix [Note: Concerning him, see more in Ciacconius, latest edition, vol. I, p. 499.] was made archbishop of Ravenna in the year 707 [Note: From Anastasius we learn that Felix was consecrated by Pope Constantine, who was not elected until the year 708, on the fourth or seventh day of March. Felix therefore could not have been consecrated before that year. Since Agnellus says in his *Pontifical* that Felix occupied the see for eight years, seven months, and nineteen days, and died on 25 September, his ordination, if dated from 25 November, would fall on 6 April. Since this is incompatible with the episcopal ordinations of the year 708, it follows that “nineteen days” should be written “twenty-one,” and his ordination should be moved back to 4 April of the year 708. Felix would consequently have died on 25 November 716. Once the age at which Felix occupied and left the see has been established, the preceding facts become clearer. Agnellus says that Damian occupied the see for sixteen years, two months, and sixteen days, and died on 13 May—or rather March, as Rubeus correctly believes. Thus Damian died on 12 March 708; he had been ordained sixteen years, two months, and sixteen days earlier, on 27 December 691. Yet in that year the solar cycle was 28, the dominical letter A, and the feast of the Nativity fell both on Saturday and on the Lord’s Day. I think an error also entered here in the number of days, and that nineteen days should be substituted for sixteen; consequently the ordination should be moved back to the twenty-fourth. Theodore, Damian’s predecessor, had died at the beginning of the year, namely on 18 January, after completing thirteen years, three months, and twenty days in the episcopate, as Agnellus records. Counting backward by the stated years, months, and days, his ordination falls on 29 September 677. But since the solar cycle in that year was 14 and the dominical letter D, two days must be added to the number of days, and twenty-two written instead of twenty; thus the ordination falls on the twenty-seventh. Reparatus had therefore died on 30 July of that same year, after holding the episcopate for five years and nine months; Rubeus adds that twenty-six days were omitted by the copyist from our Agnellian manuscript. He had therefore been ordained on 4 October, a Saturday, in the year 671. The day of Maurus’s death is not recorded. Considering, however, the circumstances of those times, when, according to the privileges obtained from the emperor through Maurus, the new bishop was required to put on the pallium at the emperor’s command, I believe that at least three months elapsed between Maurus’s death and the schismatic ordination of Reparatus; during that time someone was sent to Constantinople to request the pallium and, I suppose, returned. I therefore think that Maurus died around July of that same year, 671. This is also suggested by calculating the date of his ordination from Agnellus’s record and subtracting the twenty-eight years, ten months, and eighteen days during which he held the see from the year 671: we arrive at September 642. We must exclude from Maurus’s tenure 25 August, which Agnellus records as the day of death of his predecessor Bonus. From this it may be inferred that Bonus held the see from the year 630 until August 642. — Bacchinius.] and was consecrated at Rome.

But, having little regard for the faith that he had professed at his consecration, he returned to Ravenna and compelled the citizens to shake off Caesar’s yoke, while he compelled the clergy to rebel against the Roman pontiff. When the exarch Theodore, equipped with a powerful army, captured Felix, the leader of the sedition, and subdued Ravenna, he sent the instigator of the revolt, together with others, to the emperor Justinian at Constantinople. After Justinian had blinded him with red-hot bronze, he banished him to Pontus, where Felix, now unhappy, could mourn his rashness.

Felix endured exile for six years. Then, taught by misery, he renounced his error and, having been restored to himself, returned in moderation to the see from which he had fallen, in the year 715. Thereafter he lived so holily and devoutly that he became renowned for miracles. He enriched his church with various gifts. Before the light of his eyes was taken from him, he wrote a commentary on Matthew; but, because his blindness prevented him from either completing or polishing it, when death drew near he ordered it to be burned.

He gathered the golden sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus into one volume. He possessed eloquence worthy of praise and addressed the people with great zeal for piety. After displaying in life clear signs of holiness, he fell asleep in the Lord on 25 November 717 and was buried near the church of Saint Apollinaris, beside the altar of Saint Felicula, where these words are read:

> THIS TOMB PRESERVES THE ENCLOSED BODY OF THE MOST HOLY AND THRICE MOST BLESSED LORD FELIX, ARCHBISHOP.

[Col. 0359]

## Prologue of Felix, Bishop of Ravenna, to the Sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus

*(Oudin, Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers, vol. I.) (S)*

[Col. 0359D] The divine gifts of grace, brought forth from the heavenly treasury, when they have filled devout hearts most abundantly with the rich mysteries of virtues, distribute the sweetness of the Holy Spirit through fragrant narration, so that they may be revealed in manifest praises and become ornaments of salvation, according to the Lord’s voice resounding in the sacred pages of the Gospel:

> “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly”;

and again:

> “Open the door, and I shall fill it”;

and Solomon:

> “The Spirit shall give wisdom to those who seek him, and he makes the tongues of teachers eloquent.”

For this reason the venerable and blessed pontiff Peter, the radiant glory of the Church of Ravenna and the foremost teacher of catholic truth, kindled by the warmth of heavenly love and watered by the irrigation of perpetual grace, filled everyone’s ears and hearts with delightful sweetness by completing, in worthy adornment of speech, little works of flourishing readings on each of the parables of the Gospels in polished language.

Therefore, beloved ones, let us read with attentive and anxious minds the writings of so great a shepherd, and embrace them with ardent desire and spiritual arms, so that, storing the fruit of his labor in the granaries of our minds, we may rejoice together with him in the glory of magnificent praise and receive the rewards of the eternal gift.

This humble bishop Felix, from the treasury of his poor heart, has offered this small gift to those who read the sermons.

## In the Year of the Lord 725: Saint Benedict Crispus, Bishop of Milan

[Col. 0361]

## Historical Notice Concerning Saint Benedict Crispus

*(Ughelli, Italian Sacred History, vol. IV.)*
[Col. 0361A] Saint Benedict Crispus [Note: [Col. 0361B] Concerning him, see the *Acta Sanctorum*, March, vol. II, p. 84; some hold that he originated from Aquila among the Samnites.] Distinguished both for learning and holiness, he was promoted to the see of his fatherland after Mansuetus. A serious dispute before the Roman pontiff tested him as a most vigorous defender of his jurisdiction. For when he maintained that the bishop of Pavia ought to be subject to the Milanese see, while the latter resisted, claiming on the contrary that by ancient right he was immediately subject to the judgment of the Roman pontiff, the more favorable outcome of the litigation went to the bishop of Pavia.

But when Benedict had lost his case, he returned to Milan, where he built the monastery of Saint Benedict, which at the present time serves as a residence and enclosure of modesty for penitent women. Benedict’s fame spread throughout all Italy, since he was considered renowned not only for learning but also for holiness, as Paul the Deacon relates. Benedict himself composed the epitaph of Cadoald, king of the Anglo-Saxons, who, having renounced idolatry, had converted to Christ and had been washed in the sacred font by Pope Sergius; after his death shortly afterward, he had been buried at Saint Peter’s with such an epitaph.

Benedict, moreover, was taken from the living in the forty-third year of his pontificate [Note: [Col. 0361B] According to the Catalogue, Benedict sat for 47 years and died on the fifth day before the Ides of March; he was buried at Saint Ambrose’s. He is now commemorated on 6 September, because the rite of the Milanese Church admits no feast of the saints to be celebrated during Lent. That his death cannot be postponed beyond the year 725 is clear from the suitable succession of the bishops who followed, unless four or three years are added to them and consequently must be added to Benedict, who cannot have been introduced into the episcopate before 681 because of Mansuetus, whom, as we have seen, was present at Rome in 680. I therefore assign Benedict only forty-four years in the see: for IV could easily have been read and written as VII, and thus he would have lived until 725. PAPEBROCHIUS.], or, as others hold, the forty-seventh, on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the year 735 (725); and he was buried in the Ambrosian basilica and enrolled among the saints. Concerning him, see the Roman Martyrology, Baronius, and others.

His fame was especially celebrated in the time of the emperor Justinian and of the Lombard king Aripert the Younger [Note: [Col. 0362B] Some hold that Benedict originated from Aquila among the Samnites, but Toppius, in the *Bibliotheca Neapolitana*, says that he was born at Amiternum. Because of the dispute by which he had long been harassed, as Ughellus mentions above, he is honored as the principal protector and advocate of those who are harassed in any way by lawsuits and other troubles, as appears from his Life, printed at Naples by Benedict Lentinus through Franciscus Mollo. SGAMBATELLUS.].

[Col. 0361]

## Complaint of Saint Benedict Crispus, Archbishop of Milan, in the Synod, concerning Pope Constantine

(Mansi, *Collection of Councils*, vol. XII.) (C,S)*

### The Blessed Benedict’s Complaint in the Synod, because Pope Constantine had deprived that archbishop of the consecration of the bishop of Pavia, contrary to ancient custom

[Col. 0361C]

To the supreme founder of the heavens, the maker of all lands, the author of all nations, the creator of all creatures, the firm support of heaven and earth, of angels and human beings, the one support of the Catholic faith and of the Apostolic See, the solid support of orphans and widows and of all the churches, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, I return immense thanks, because in his ineffable goodness he has mercifully determined to choose and mercifully ordain such a man as pontiff for the holy Apostolic See.

Therefore let the entire chorus of bishops and the college of priests diligently remember that he graciously and mercifully provides for the human race, since in his supreme compassion he has determined that such a discerning, illustrious, orthodox man should preside over and be set over this holy see in advance: a man who does not cease to strengthen the world entrusted to him by good works and holy admonitions, and to teach those who wander.

Concerning him the Truth says: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers.”

For this reason, venerable Father, assisted by the presence and strengthened by the mercy of God, of you, and of this holy council, I, Benedict, archbishop of Milan, have resolved to present myself before your presence and this holy assembly, and to disclose and lay open, with such voice as I possess, though worn down by long old age, the cause of our church—which, by God’s dispositions and through the teachings and miracles of the blessed apostle Barnabas, has blossomed again, and which now shines adorned with the disciplines and honored by the virtues of the most glorious confessor Ambrose.

Accordingly, the Church of Milan, the Church of God, exalted by the deeds and virtues of the blessed Ambrose and elevated by many bishops through many preceding ages, now humbly and devoutly complains to you that it has been unjustly deprived of the consecration of the church of Pavia. Among the other suffragans of our church, and through the merits of the blessed Syrus, it has until now maintained with utmost force the prerogative of primacy as evidence for our claim.

But now, ambitious for the dignities of the Roman See and the honors of our ancestors, having unlawfully abandoned and unjustly deserted its own proper metropolitan, it approached the Roman pontiff in order to receive the consecration secretly—a consecration which our Church had possessed for many preceding years, through a long succession of time, from the era of the blessed apostle Barnabas down to my own presence, I who have occupied the Milanese see for forty years, and which, with God’s help, it had humbly and charitably maintained there by consecrating Bishop Gregory.

Therefore, with your mercy coming to our aid and the holy canons praising the cause, we faithfully and devoutly entreat that our church may be able to regain what it unjustly lost.

May your wisdom, preferable to every discipline, benefit us. For he who presides over all ought, with due paternal care, to benefit all, harm no one, and envy no one; he should not usurp the honor or prerogative of dignity belonging to any church. As a discerning judge, he weighs all things in the balance of supreme justice, condemning those who inflict injuries unjustly, while mercifully supporting those who suffer unlawful wrongs, defending them by the right hand and ceremonies of the law.

But the judge of iniquity, overturning all affairs for a price, obscures what belongs to the law and criminally exalts what gives temporal pleasure; from such things the lover of justice daily guards himself, protected by God’s right hand.

Let us learn justice. Thus the prophet Isaiah, filled with the Holy Spirit, says: “Learn justice, you who dwell upon the earth.”

Venerable Father, let divine reason overcome the power of the Roman throne. Hence Saint Ambrose says: “It is fitting that reason should overcome power.”

Judge the judgment of the cases in our complaint justly. For the Lord speaks through Zechariah, saying: “Judge a just and peaceful judgment, and do not retain the malice of your brother in your hearts.” And David says: “From your countenance let my judgment proceed; let my eyes see equity.”

But so that I may unfold more clearly and most truthfully the truth of our Church and of our complaint, kindly recognize, with your customary piety, the privileges of ten Roman pontiffs concerning the consecration of the church of Pavia, privileges that assert our claim and strictly prohibit all bishops, under the edge of anathema, from acting otherwise.

Moreover, carefully recognize how our city, from its very beginnings, was cultivated and exalted by the diligent care of our ancestors through the Roman emperors and the consuls and patricians who dwelt in that city, when the world was governed under a single empire.

As I have discovered from the description of its site, the Roman kings and princes later exalted it still more greatly, after expelling the Senonian peoples, and enlarged it through magnificent works. In accordance with ancestral custom, they established there an imperial palace worthy of the dignity of the Augusti, a theater, aqueducts, baths, a pleasant garden delightful with diverse flowers and varied fragrances, and an arena marvelous for its stones and workmanship, in which all the citizens of Italy could sit together and appropriately listen to a single orator addressing the assembly.

For this reason it began to be very frequently visited, inhabited, and honored by those same Augusti above all the cities of Italy, especially because it possessed the most suitable climate of healthful air and a site wholly prepared for domestic uses.

Then, venerable Father, when holy Christianity appeared to the whole world, it believed in God immediately upon hearing of it, after the holy apostle Barnabas had been sent there by the Holy Spirit and faithfully preached the orthodox faith. From him, from the very beginnings of our Church, it has held Milan as the head of Italy through the metropolitan see, by God’s merciful dispensation, and by God’s gift it will hold it forever.

Therefore the Milanese chair, appropriately exalted and suitably raised up by that apostle, flourished again by God’s right hand and through the aid of the blessed Peter.

For we find this stated most truthfully in our annals, in the account of his arrival, and in the Life of Saint Anatalon. One of the Lord’s disciples speaks with the greatest faithfulness and certainty, saying that the aforesaid city, Milan, was already at that time considered the most famous city after the Roman citadel, since, elevated by equal authority and, as I have said, second after Rome, it held the imperial insignia of the Augusti of the Western Empire.

Thus the holy apostle Barnabas, by God’s merciful dispensation, decreed that Milan—whose elevation above all the cities of Italy he knew the emperors had established—should forever be regarded as the principal seat of ecclesiastical authority, and the metropolitan of the other churches in that province, since he himself had first founded it through holy preaching.

Indeed, as I found in the Life of Saint Anatalon, whom Barnabas had consecrated there before proceeding from Jerusalem, Saint Anatalon knew that his master had granted that city such a gift of privilege that, just as among the other cities of the Italian provinces—namely, those extending from the boundaries of Italy all the way to its western edge—the chief cities appeared after the Roman citadel, conspicuous under an eminent throne and amid the most frequent gathering of peoples, so, in the prerogative of ecclesiastical authority, it should surpass all others after the Roman See.

In the same manner that aforesaid bishop, differing in nothing from his founder, established that the same metropolitan chair should remain for future generations among the faithful of Christ, so that the metropolitan bishop of the Milanese see ought to be a kind of head and distinguished ornament, after the Roman pontiff, for all the peoples who would in future belong to the holy mother Church throughout the aforesaid provinces: Venetia, Liguria, Emilia, Raetia, and Alpes Cottiae.

Thus the Church of Milan, supported and adorned by these and many other aids, reached almost to my own time, through God’s mercy and the merits of Saint Ambrose, devotedly retaining all these honors.

But, since the cause of our complaint is fittingly fortified and suitably defended by many considerations, hear the testimony of certain holy bishops of Pavia, Crispinus and Epiphanius.

For when Saint Crispinus saw that he was hastening toward death, as is recorded in the Life of Saint Epiphanius, he brought Saint Epiphanius to Milan and said to Bishop Protasius and to the orders whom he found there:

“Behold, sons, my age has now completed the course of my life. I commend the city; I commend the church; I commend this man, to whose labor and grace I owe the fact that I have lived to this time, aged and weak, whose bodily well-being and strength of soul have carried my weakness without weariness.”

Again, in the same work:

“Blessed Epiphanius was led to Milan while still reluctant, promising great gifts if he were released; yet, in order that he might become bishop, he refused to promise even the smallest thing. He was consecrated by the blessed Protasius, predecessor of Saint Ambrose and the Church’s most steadfast champion, with the utmost devotion and amid the celebration of all.”

Furthermore, venerable Father, accept a most certain testimony, which the holy Fathers have decreed it dangerous and criminal either to doubt or to oppose. For in the Life of Saint Ambrose, our patron and the protector of all the churches, we read:

“After he had been ordained priest of the church of Pavia, he fell ill.”

Therefore, venerable Father, as Saint Fabian the pope asserts in his decree, your concern must be directed toward ensuring that what has been ordained by the apostles and their successors and established by the grace of the Holy Spirit can be neglected neither through dissimulation nor disturbed by any presumption.

But just as what Roman necessity demanded had to be defined, so, once defined, it ought not to be violated. Therefore, venerable Father, with charitable entreaty I appeal especially to the reverence of your Paternity and to the reciprocal charity of this holy council; and on behalf of God and Saint Ambrose I earnestly insist that no bishop of our Church, especially this bishop of Pavia concerning whom I complain to the mercy of this holy council, presume to retain or ordain a suffragan of our Church, thereby disturbing your fraternity.

If this should occur, the ordination of the one who receives and of the one who ordains shall be forever invalid and void.

Hence Saint Sixtus the pope, divinely instructed in his decree, says:

“No bishop shall presume to retain, ordain, or judge another’s parishioner without that person’s consent. For just as his ordination will be invalid, so also will his judgment. For he who could not ordain him will in no way be able to judge him.”

Venerable Father, each metropolitan see continues even now to possess in due order its boundaries, established by the holy Fathers and granted by the Apostolic See, which surpasses all in dignity. Concerning these, Pope Callistus says in his decree:

“Let no one presumptuously and unlawfully usurp another’s boundaries.” Hence the Lord says: “Do not transgress the ancient boundaries that your fathers established.”

Therefore every church that desires to preserve faithfully the faith of its holy ancestors and strives to honor the decrees of the saints should, faithfully and charitably, take heed of our complaint for its own protection, lest it suffer similar things.

## Muratori’s Censure of the Preceding Oration

[Col. 0366B]

I wish to explain my opinion concerning the author of this oration. I believe that it was not composed by Benedict, but devised by the historian Landulf himself. It was customary for him, after the manner of other historians, to introduce men as speakers and to attribute speeches to them which they might plausibly have delivered or might already have delivered.

Thus in his work one may see the speeches of the archdeacon Wibert, the deacon Ambrose, and the decanus-priest Andrew against Saint Ariald, as well as the speech of the latter against them and many other examples; their uniformly similar style suggests that they are all the offspring of one Landulf.

Moreover, Benedict would not have said that he had sat in the Milanese chair for forty years. For since it is established that this case was debated under Pope Constantine, and Benedict was raised to the archiepiscopal dignity only in the year 687, his fortieth year in the archbishopric would have extended far beyond Constantine’s time. The blame for this error must therefore be assigned to Landulf, the author of the oration.

Another most conclusive argument proves the point. Three decretal letters are cited in this oration, namely those of the Roman pontiffs Fabian, Sixtus, and Callistus. Although, as all learned men now admit, these letters were falsely attributed and fabricated under the names of such great pontiffs, for many centuries they were nevertheless regarded as their genuine offspring and obtained exceptional credence from all Catholics, no less in earlier times than in our own.

Isidore—or Mercator, or Peccator—as the distinguished and eminent Cardinal de Aguirre, the greatest ornament of Spain and of the purple senate, proves after Archbishop de Marca in his lucid *Collection of the Councils of the Spaniards*, vol. I, dissertation 4, either collected or composed this material in such a way that even very learned men were deceived and believed it to be the work of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville.

The letters themselves reveal when this collection appeared, since among them are some bearing the names of Gregory II and Gregory III and of Zachary, the supreme pontiffs. Since these pontiffs occupied the see in the eighth century, down to the year 751 of Christ, we recognize that this Isidore wrote after those times.

But these decretals did not immediately become public. Riculphus, bishop of Mainz, was the first of all to bring them from Spain, where they had originated, into Gaul. Hincmar of Reims says the following in his *Opusculum*, chapter 24:

“Concerning the book of collected letters by Isidore, which Bishop Riculphus of Mainz obtained after it had been brought from Spain, and by means of which he caused these regions to be filled.”

This Riculphus governed the Church of Mainz from the year 787 of Christ until 814. It must therefore be affirmed absolutely that those letters began to circulate among learned men only toward the end of the eighth century.

If this is true—as it most certainly is—how could Archbishop Benedict, who is said to have pleaded in Rome in the year 711 of Christ, have used them?

It remains, therefore, that we must admit either that the oration was composed by Landulf himself, or by someone else who lived many years after Benedict.

As I should also explain, the style appears to differ somewhat from Landulf’s usual style, so that, what is more, we may suspect that this oration existed even before Landulf. In any case, I have shown clearly, if I am not mistaken, what the strongest arguments were that the bishop of Milan could bring against the bishop of Pavia.

Now we must see in what words this history is presented by Sigonius, a man of great name. In book III of his *History of the Kingdom of Italy*, under the year 715 of Christ, he says:

“A dispute arose between the archbishop of Milan and the bishop of Pavia. In order to obtain a new right, the archbishop wished to transfer to himself the consecration of the bishop. When the bishop maintained that this right did not belong to him, the matter was referred to Rome by common agreement. There the case was argued on both sides before the pontiff, and the archbishop, opposed by every precedent of antiquity, withdrew defeated.”

But Sigonius is staging a tragedy. No new right was being prepared for Benedict, nor were all the precedents of antiquity opposed to him. A prescription extending over many years caused judgment to be given in favor of the bishop of Pavia.

Sigonius also failed in assigning the year of this dispute. For in 715, the year in which he thinks the matter was settled, Gregory II occupied the Roman See, not Constantine. Constantine had died the previous year, and Gregory had been elected supreme pontiff in that preceding year, as the distinguished father of the *Annals*, guided by the reliable testimonies of Anastasius the Librarian, Theophanes, Sigeifred, and others, clearly demonstrates.

Since this dispute was settled only under Constantine, it is evident that the year assigned to it must be either 711, with Baronius, or 712, with others.

Furthermore, I could demonstrate through many authorities how far the other writers on this matter depart from Sigonius’s view, but it will be sufficient, as representative of them all, to produce Benvenutus. I believe him to have been from Imola, an ancient writer who wrote more than three hundred years ago and beyond, and whose manuscript chronicle exists in the Ambrosian Library.

In chapter 137, concerning the city of Pavia, he says:

“The bishop of this city is said to have been a suffragan of the archbishop of Milan. This is clear from the fact that the blessed Protasius, archbishop of Milan, consecrated the blessed Epiphanius as bishop of Pavia, the successor of Saint Crispinus.

But because, during the time of the Lombards, who were unbelievers, the archbishops of Milan resided at Genoa out of fear of them, as is recorded concerning Honoratus, the bishops of Pavia began to be consecrated by the pope.

Therefore, when Benedict, archbishop of Milan, summoned the bishop of Pavia, his ancient suffragan, to the Roman court, he was defeated. Hence even today the bishops of Pavia, Piacenza, and Ferrara are immediately subject to the lord pope.”

Let us examine what follows.

After these matters had been settled, for a long time the bishops of Pavia ignored the metropolitan of Milan and, depending upon a single Roman pontiff, were also enhanced by the dignity of the pallium.

We dare not determine precisely when this honor was conferred upon them. Nevertheless, I consider it necessary to affirm without hesitation that Ughellus departs from the truth when, without documents or witnesses, he asserts the following concerning the church of Pavia:

“To it Pope Hormisdas”—he held the Roman See from 514 to 523—“granted the use of the pallium, and extended that gracious indulgence to his successors.”

For during that period the use of the pallium was granted by the supreme pontiffs either to very few or to no one. Later, in the age of Saint Gregory, as the very learned de Marca observes in book VI, chapter 7, no. 3, of *On the Concord of Sacred and Imperial Power*, it became customary for the Roman pontiff to adorn with the pallium the principal metropolitans who belonged to his consecration, or those to whom he entrusted his authority in the provinces.

If, therefore, the pontiff did not adorn all metropolitans with the use of the pallium, but only the principal ones, and if this practice began to be employed only in the age of Gregory the Great, how much less could the pallium have been granted to Pavia in the age of Hormisdas, when Pavia was counted not among metropolitan sees but merely among ordinary bishoprics?

I will add no more on this matter, both lest I deprive you of this harvest and in order to spare the ears of learned men, who expect more abundant fruits from you.

I would nevertheless have you weigh carefully whether the beginnings of this prerogative should be referred to Pope John VIII. For that pontiff had nothing more at heart than to raise up the see of Pavia, so as to blunt the excessively vigorous—and perhaps too forceful—spirit of the bishop of Milan, who at that time refused to render prompt obedience to the Roman Church.

Certainly this supreme pontiff issued a letter, numbered 139 among his works, in which he established that the metropolitans of Milan and Ravenna could be summoned to a synod by the bishop of Pavia. Unless that letter is to be counted among the apocrypha, this seems so astonishing that Baronius did not hesitate to declare under the year 878 of Christ:

“I would not believe it, had I not read it.”

For my part, I readily follow this conjecture, though I shall abandon it as soon as you, as I hope, produce better arguments.

[POEMS.]

[Col. 0367]

## Mai’s Preliminary Observations on the Following Poems

[Col. 0367D]

Paul the Deacon adorns Benedict, surnamed Crispus, archbishop of Milan from 681 to 725, who through the holiness of his life attained heavenly honors in his own Church, with this testimony in *History of the Lombards* VI.29:

“Then also, in the year 689, Benedict, archbishop of Milan, came to Rome and pleaded the case of the Church of Pavia; but he was defeated because from ancient times the bishops of Pavia had been consecrated by the Roman Church. This same venerable Benedict was an archbishop and a man of outstanding holiness, whose reputation for goodness burned throughout all Italy.”

Ludovicus Muratori gave a lengthy account of the Pavia controversy—which is not relevant to our present purpose—in his *Latin Anecdotes*, vol. I. He also maintained that the oration of Benedict delivered at Rome in defense of his case, which is read in the same Muratori, in the cited place, and in *Scriptores Rerum Italicarum*, vol. IV, p. 76, should be considered not so much the work of this archbishop as that of the historian Landulf or of some other person.

Whatever the truth of the matter, either certain tradition or, rather, the stone excavated at Saint Peter’s in the fifteenth century bears witness that Benedict, while residing in Rome, wrote the epitaph of Ceduvalla, king of the English, who died shortly after receiving baptism. John de Deis, a man of that same age, relates this in a little book entitled *The Successors of Saint Barnabas*.

That stone, as I think, is nowhere now to be seen in Rome; but the epitaph itself had long since been quoted by Bede, *History* II, book V, chapter 7, and by Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards* VI.15.

Up to this point, therefore, Benedict’s writings that had become known were the oration delivered at Rome and the written epitaph. Nevertheless, the aforesaid John de Deis says that Benedict composed some commentaries worthy of praise.

In fact, I am now publishing a short medical work that I observed in two Vatican Library manuscripts. In one manuscript it is called a *commentary*, and in the other a *medical booklet*.

I will say nothing further about it except that it was a youthful work, written while Benedict was still a deacon and, as de Deis says, was illustrious and renowned in the schools of the liberal arts, and counted Maurus among his pupils; it was to Maurus that he wrote this little poem.

Otherwise, I have seen this medical composition mentioned neither by Muratori, nor by Argelati, nor by Saxius, the three men who wrote most carefully about Benedict; for it appears actually to have survived only in the Vatican manuscripts.

[Col. 0369]

## The Medical Poem of Saint Benedict Crispus, Archbishop of Milan, Written during His Diaconate

(Mai, *Classical Authors*, vol. V, from a Vatican manuscript.) (C,S)*

### Crispus, Deacon of Milan, to Maurus, Provost of Mantua [Note: [Col. 0369D] Concerning the man, see what we said in the preface.]

### Preface to the Medical Booklet [Note: [Col. 0369D] In the seventh and indeed also the eighth century, the episcopal see had not yet been established at Mantua; and it is clear from Ughellus, *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 858, that this church was subject sometimes to the Milanese chair and sometimes to others.]

[Col. 0369B]

Because I have educated you, dearest son Maurus, almost from your very cradle, and enriched you with the liberality of sevenfold eloquence, there is one thing still lacking which, though you remain in the flower of youth, you have always wished to regard as unpleasant: namely, you have utterly despised the knowledge of useful medicine and declared that you retain no share or participation in the liberal disciplines.

But now, since an abnormality of various illnesses frequently dominates you, you compel me to enlarge that very knowledge of the arts which you were not previously ashamed to call wicked and most disgraceful.

You therefore demand that I make you a countryman, teach you the properties of medicinal herbs, show them individually at their appointed times, and, according to the various kinds of illnesses, provide without hesitation the forms of treatment.

I have willingly accepted your request and, striving for brevity in this little work, desire to feed you with heroic honey, so that I may gradually lead you toward a love of the art. For if, at the beginning, I were to unfold too much by thrusting it into your mouth, abundance would produce disgust, and disgust would remove desire.

Therefore I have touched upon what I consider most thoroughly tested in a concise account, so that when you have proved these things true through the clearest experience, you may pursue the many matters that remain with greater ardor and diligence.

### I. Concerning the Head

If the sick head is shaken by countless throbbings,

And is troubled by some burden bent around it,

[Col. 0369D] Immediately take care to crown it with a wreath of ivy.

Thus also mix frankincense with harsh vinegar.

Myrrh likewise is joined with liquid olive oil,

And celebrated savin with cephalota and salt.

[Col. 0370B] But if some part is violently shaken by the illness itself,

Catch a live mole and let it be cooked whole in oil,

Then anoint the head and face with the salve from which [Note: [Col. 0370D] Thus below, chapter 24; the verse ends with *quo*.]

### II. Concerning Toothache

But if the teeth of a great eater are shaken by turmoil,

Press potent symphoniaca against the tooth with your thumb:

Immediately every raging pain will depart from it.

Yet I warn you not to swallow it, because the treacherous poison,

Once taken, snatches away the senses and assumes the likeness of death.

But if a mad, chilling [reading uncertain: *quatit/quater*] seizes and shakes the throat,

A drink will be the remedy, and an ointment a health-giving medicine.

### III. Concerning Frenzy

But if immense pain should penetrate the meninges,

And a raging, accursed frenzy corrupt the brain,

[Col. 0370C] Deer’s lung, taken from the animal’s flesh, will be agreeable,

Prepared with *cephalo*, or the power of coriander drunk as a potion,

Or radish skin softened in harsh vinegar:

Taken by itself it is excessively sharp, but certainly an ancient remedy.

### IV. Concerning the Eyes

A swift weakness undoubtedly quickly damages the rapid orbs,

And fortune, disturbed in various ways, presses hard:

For it harms, but the loving one cures at the appointed time.

Come, then, immediately prepare boiled horehound,

Join it with betony, and also with moist wool:

It quickly removes every evil and restores the beloved eyes.

If the eyes suffer pain made red by an inflamed humor,

Then powerful vervain should be drunk in gentle water.

### V. Concerning a Spot in the Eye

If you retain a spot in your eyes while it turns inward,

Look, as you proceed through the fields, for a red snail,

And carefully apply to the eye a *modius* of what it exudes [syntax uncertain; Note: [Col. 0370D] Thus both manuscripts read. I would prefer *findens*, “splitting,”].

### VI. Concerning Throat Angina

But if angina should truly spread through the broad throat,

[Col. 0371A] And, obstructing it with swollen leaves, should fill it,

Arsenic is ground together with pepper and bole clay,

Then, placed thus, it is blown through the throat by means of a feather.

### VII. Concerning the Throat’s Uvula

When the swollen uvula happens not to keep its proper measure,

And drips heavy and putrid drops within the body,

And foully pierces the delicate wings of the lung,

It is quickly dried by a similar powder as it rages.

### VIII. Concerning Treating the Lung

Often the very strength of a man’s chest is shaken,

And is seen to stretch toward harsh death for many.

If therefore you wish to restore the sick man’s chest through treatment,

Do not hesitate to examine the various remedies of herbs.

Wool soaked in oil, and also the juice of Greek hay—

These restore the stomach, as does a drink of tamarisk;

A large cabbage is joined to celebrated betony,

Radish with honey-water, and also the juice of horehound should be given.

The celebrated herb *lelisphagus* is also suitably taken;

Thus the final remedy, that of the great cedar, will be given [Note: [Col. 0371D] Both manuscripts read *pigrae*. I wrote *cedri*, referring to Pliny, *Natural History* XXIV.1.]

### IX. Concerning Pain of the Heart

When mad pain strikes the side and the region before the heart,

And harsh pain greatly torments the fibers of the heart,

Dreadful fluids help when joined with the power of coral.

Then light pimpernel is joined to a decoction of fennel.

Sizaduar is taken, and also vigorous tansy,

Which both calms fevers and drives away poisons from the heart.

### X. Concerning the Treatment of Pleurisy

But if by chance an immense illness should strike the gentle side,

And life be troubled by a twofold danger,

Take care to procure a wolf’s skin and place it hot upon the body,

And you will be able to use deer’s marrow with goat’s salve.

Immediately let them be placed in a cauldron and boiled over a slow fire;

Let pitch, *britia*, likewise be added and boiled,

Together with lupin meal itself, and saffron as well.

Thus let the soothing poultice be applied to the bitter illness,

So that rest may be granted to the man suffering excessive torment.

And the celebrated medicine of the Thunderer drives away the disease [Note: [Col. 0371D] This is said for Jupiter. For below an herb called “Jupiter’s beard” is mentioned.]

### XI. Concerning Treatment of the Spleen

When a swollen spleen happens to trouble a man [with *plaustum*, reading uncertain; Note: [Col. 0371D] Thus the manuscripts],

Boil betony and add the cleansed product of a dove [reading uncertain];

When these two are joined together, they require that cephalota

And rose oil also be joined to them; thus, with care, you combine them while moist.

Short savory is taken, and lupins are also joined to it;

They are given repeatedly, and deer’s tongue is also drunk,

[Col. 0371D] By whose power the face perishes, but is gently wrinkled.

It grows low among the rocks, but is great and friendly

To the spleen and to man, though not suited to laughter.

As many members as a man has, so many diseases are in the body.

But powerful medicine restrains many of them by its gift.

When the liver is diseased and scyrosis grows in the usual way,

Bitter costus is drunk, and also great rhubarb.

When crushed together with salt, they suppress the swelling.

Lupin fibre is effective and helps when drunk by the sufferer,

[Col. 0372A] When the liver is afflicted on the right and the spleen itself on the left.

Thus the treatment of both is joined together equally for the two.

### XII. Concerning Pains of the Stomach and Intestine

The innermost entrails are shaken by torments of many kinds,

And the sick man is wholly racked by threatening weakness;

No hope of life remains when the breath itself

Seeks the depths and departs as a stranger, abandoning every good thing.

This is called “the twisted thing,” because it twists the heavy entrails,

And again and again soothes them; the entire

Dear nature is corrupted, which the fervent fluid restores.

Thus let the sluggish limbs be warmed by that very liquid,

And let everything cold be bathed in warm streams.

Afterward let goose fat be melted and poured out,

And let the power of Greek hay, joined with it, appear.

Nor is its own power cooked any less in liquid streams.

[Col. 0372B] Immediately a fearful clyster is poured into the anus,

By whose power the wretched man will be able to restore the pain

Which *squibala* (hard feces) cause when there is no health-giving treatment,

And cholera closes the sufferer’s narrow passages.

White ivory is scraped and immediately drunk;

This drink quickly straightens the twisted condition.

The tender entrails of a blind puppy are taken, as it is said;

Thus its soft little limbs should be applied to delicate fibers.

And all pain passes from the *habra* [Codd., *habre*] into the split entrails.

Pliny [Note: [Col. 0372D] Pliny, Val., book II, chapter 18: “A two-day-old puppy, given to an unsuspecting sick person in food and vinegar, is helpful.” Our author said “a blind puppy,” that is, one whose eyes had not yet opened.] records this; we know that he spoke the truth.

### XIII. Concerning the Treatment of Dropsy

From splenic scyrosis there arises a deadly humor,

And it separates the skin of the wretched man from his wretched entrails,

And so great is the force of the disease that the thirsty man is not satisfied.

[Col. 0372C] Ashes from a tall ash tree are taken;

From these, by lye, hard barley is broken down.

After boiling them together twice, prepare them faithfully for the sufferer.

The best radish is eaten with sweet honey,

And from its leaves the very poultice is applied.

Sulfur preparations are drunk hot with old wine:

Nor less apply a poultice made from these to the swelling.

These remedies dissolve splenic scirrhus and also dry up the fluids.

## XIV. ON RINGWORM

If putrid wounds worsen with bloody diseases,

it will be suitable to drink warm goat’s milk [Note: [Col. 0372D] *Lacte* is neuter, in the accusative case, as also occurs in the nominative.],

and no less does milk from a she-ass dissolve the dreadful abscess.

The ashes of the Aminean vine are poured into olive oil:

this drink is worthy, through many ages, for many putrid wounds.

But celery and fig together, and also laurel berry,

[Col. 0372D] iris, great Illyrian centaury, and rue—

these will quickly cleanse away the purulent filth

and restore the man to renewed health in happier days.

## XV. ON THE WORM OF THE EAR

It is proper for the heedless to take heedful precautions,

lest their bodies be disturbed by an unaccustomed sensation.

When immense sleep has overcome a man’s limbs,

then an animal commonly enters the unworthy ears.

Take it quickly with onion or with mouse vinegar,

[Col. 0373A] and make no delay: thus you will be able to drive out the worm.

## XVI. ON DEAFNESS

But if you suffer deafness, gather red worms

from an ancient tree, and mix them thus with pure olive oil;

pour it into the ears, and restore to yourself the health you desire.

Goose fat is beneficial, as is that of the black vulture.

The juice of onions helps the ears and brings good,

when fluid commonly penetrates the ears of the heedless.

## XVII. ON DYSENTERY

Often an excessive discharge of the belly runs on,

little by little dissolving the tender flesh of many,

which prudent medicine of God knows how to restrain.

Asian gall is beneficial, as is also the long fruit of the cherry;

cheese will be suitable together with the sweet gift of honey,

and warm suet torn from the entrails of a he-goat will also be beneficial,

[Col. 0373B] applied to the belly—the treatment is well known.

But if, by chance, it lowers its own nail from the very place,

it quickly signifies that the desired life is already being lost.

## XVIII. ON HARDNESS OF THE BELLY

But if the belly is troubled by an immense weight,

look for where *pallas* grows from a shoot found by searching;

this maiden is said to be friendly to all and favorable to health;

take it at once, and its good power will flourish for the belly.

Hellebore is taken, crushed, and drunk with mulled wine;

it has always been effective for this disease, and likewise *chamaeactis*,

diluted and immediately to be drunk with old wine.

A taste of mare’s milk, taken without delay, will also help.

Eupator, *prasion*, and hermodactyl itself,

as the books report, are always friends of the belly.

## XIX. ON THE BLADDER

[Col. 0373C]

Many things help many people because they are contrary to diseases;

the disease is overcome by the antidote of the high divinity [Note: [Col. 0373D] Codex 1: *numine summi*; 2: *numine summi*.].

There is a kind of illness, an enemy and plague to many,

when the mad, burning stone of the bladder rages,

producing stones by which the urine is delayed.

The suffering man cannot release the kindly showers.

High ivy will give berries from its lofty summit;

take its juice with warm wine,

and without delay *plantago glandis* is crushed; it too is taken and drunk, together with the wholesome *olusatrum*.

*Saxifrica*, *petro*, and *selino* remove the stones.

Supported by these remedies, you will be secure; and you will pray to the Lord.

## XX. ON EXCESSIVE FLOW OF URINE

But if, contrariwise, a flowing discharge drenches you with excessive showers,

[Col. 0373D] immediately restrain the flow with the brain of a hare.

Take old wines, with the brain itself;

it is indeed cheap as a drink, but not cheap as medicine.

## XXI. ON NOSEBLEED

When a stream of blood pours forth,

one must tell all about the hemorrhoidal nostril, and what certain hope of health there is.

Rue, crushed, will provide a drink and likewise an odor;

low-growing cumin from the fields, crushed, is beneficial,

and, combined with *hypporis*, stops the blood at the nostril.

With the powder of a boletus, which they say is lupine,

you should also associate the humble herb mint for the nostrils.

## XXI. ON HEMORRHOIDS

But if a shameful disease attacks the anus,

[Col. 0374A] seek *maurella*, powerful and hostile to the mole;

and also henbane, whose treatment is beneficial.

These, drunk together, immediately stop the blood.

Burnt lead is harmful when combined with moist olive oil.

Together these two [Codd.: *justus*] stop the stream of blood.

## XXIII. ON THE FIRE

A fierce fire rages, always burning the entrails;

the savage flame continually wanders beneath the skin,

leaping forth again and swelling under the appearance of a spring.

Let the mind of the man always be on guard against its inward deceptions;

it helps to smear on the herb of celandine.

The white inner part of a snowy egg is joined to it;

rue helps and drives away the disease, and also contracts the flame,

[Col. 0374B] if it is mixed at the same time with warm, pure olive oil.

Do not think that I speak falsely in this, when Truth itself commands me to speak the truth:

bring out the dung of a sheep for the disease,

and apply it warm, as many report in verse.

## XXIV. ON CARBUNCLE

A hostile force is vigorous when the immense disease rages;

the terrifying carbuncle destroys the languishing entrails.

For this, the juice of Jupiter’s beard and of *benigna*, which is likewise its enemy, together with crushed savin, are drunk with a broth made from the dung of a shining dove.

If, once taken, these remain in the trembling body’s belly,

health and life are thus promised to the frightened patient.

But if the exhausted patient seems to reject the drink,

believe me: he seems to be opening the way to swift death.

[Col. 0374C] Quintus Serenus asserted, with sound reasoning, that this dreadful disease is also driven out by the seed of turnips [Note: [Col. 0374D] “For treating carbuncle.”].

Cauteries impressed upon the severe disease are also beneficial;

quicklime is likewise immediately sprinkled on it.

When, by God’s command, the scar has become red,

then, undaunted, set in order your timid treatment,

so that the poisonous plague may be able to drain away its toxins.

Yet I testify to this: know that you must avoid sleep,

lest the terrible disease, returning, be able to recover its strength.

## XXV. ON SCIATIC ARTHRITIS

If sciatica has robbed someone of his very ability to walk,

and the fluid, raging as it passes through the bones, has grown,

take polypody, which they call *filicula*,

to which crushed black clove is well added,

and pliant pepper, and cinnamon pleasing to all.

[Col. 0374D] Prepare it thus as a drink; but give it not without honey.

Learn to seek the bark of the elm tree,

mix madder with it, and drink it together.

When you see nettle in the countryside, do not despise the larger one,

which, drunk for a long time, knows how to burn away the plague.

Hold this as certain, firm, and true, my son.

## XXVI. ON CURING GOUT

Many report many things, whose written testimony is health-giving;

yet they assert that sluggish gout is without a remedy,

if one is able to say so. If you wish to aid the disease,

begin what I advise: cut up the welcome *lactes*.

Thus the immense pain knows how to overcome pain.

An ointment of *felix*, applied, gives rest to the feet,

[Col. 0375A] and powerful tamarisk, together with the living little beard of Jupiter,

are pounded together and bound onto the feet;

they are continually plucked, providing a drink to the lame man.

Do you wish to entrust yourself now with marvelous health?

Take little fish called *ruccae* of the spine.

Place them on the side and add them to burning coals,

then apply them hot to the afflicted feet with certainty;

they repress every evil, and thus the hard disease is driven away.

[Col. 0376A] Here ends the work of Crispus, deacon of Milan, addressed to Macer, provost of Mantua. But in truth this Crispus is neither a poet nor a good versifier; for he composed his verses not according to the law of meter but to the sound of his own ears—that is, merely rhythm.

**THE END.**

Peter Cenninus wrote this at Florence, 13 Kalends of November, 1468.

[Col. 0375]

# EPITAPH OF CEADUAL, KING OF THE ANGLO-SAXONS, COMPOSED BY BENEDICT, ARCHBISHOP

[Note: [Col. 0375C] Concerning this epitaph, John de Deis records the following in his booklet published at Rome in 1589, entitled *Successors of Saint Barnabas*, p. 23b: “When Benedict the archbishop was living at Rome, Ceadual, a pagan king of the Anglo-Saxons who had been converted to Christ, was baptized in the basilica of Saint Peter by Pope Sergius and given the name Peter. Having died there, he was buried there. Benedict composed his epitaph; because it had long lain buried with the sarcophagus on which it was carved, and in past years was found by the excavators of the fabric of Saint Peter’s basilica, I have wished to transcribe it here, so that his learning and piety might be more clearly attested.” We possess three ancient copies of this epitaph: in Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 7; in Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, VI, 15; and on the Roman stone quoted by de Deis. Several other variants are recorded by Muratori, *Scriptores rerum Italicarum*, vol. I, p. 495. With these aids I have supplied a sufficiently corrected epitaph; for John de Deis, if he himself copied the stone—which I scarcely believe—acted with extreme carelessness and infidelity.]

(From Mai, *Classical Authors*, vol. V, from the Vatican manuscript.) (C, S)*

[Col. 0375B]

The heights, wealth, offspring, powerful kingdoms, triumphs,

spoils, nobles, walls, camps, and household gods—

all that the valour of his fathers, and that Ceadual mighty in arms [Note: [Col. 0375D] Bede: *Ceadval armipotens*; Paul: *Cedoald armipotens*.], had amassed—

he left for love of God,

so that the king, as a guest, might behold Peter and Peter’s see [Note: [Col. 0375D] Thus Bede and Paul; John de Deis, against the metre, reads *Petrique sedem* (“and Peter’s seat”).],

from whose font, made white [Note: [Col. 0375D] Bede and Paul read *almus* (“nourishing” or “blessed”).], he might receive sacred waters [Note: [Col. 0375D] Bede and Paul read *meras* (“pure”).].

And that, with a radiant draught, he might partake of the splendid beam [Note: [Col. 0375D] De Deis absurdly reads *basta*.],

from which life-giving radiance flows everywhere [Note: [Col. 0376C] Paul reads *fuit* (“was”).].

Eagerly perceiving the rewards of renewed life [Note: [Col. 0376C] John de Deis wrongly reads *perspiciensque*.],

converted, he joyfully changed his barbarian fierceness,

and thereafter his own name;

and Bishop Sergius, himself Father,

commanded that he be called Peter.

[Col. 0376B]

Christ’s grace cleansing him as he was reborn from the font [Note: [Col. 0376C] Thus the Lindisfarne manuscript in Muratori, *S. R. I. T.*, I, p. 495: *renascentis*; all the others read *renascentis*.],

immediately bore him, made white [Note: [Col. 0376C] Thus Paul; John de Deis reads *ablutum* (“washed”), Bede *ablatum* (“carried away”).], into heaven’s heights [Note: [Col. 0376C] Thus the Lindisfarne manuscript; all the others read *arce* (“citadel”).].

Wonderful is the king’s faith, greatest Christ’s mercy,

whose counsel no one can attain!

For, coming safe from the farthest British world [Note: [Col. 0376C] Lindisfarne: *suprema ex urbe* (“from the highest city”). Bede, Paul, and John de Deis: *Britanni*; the editor prefers *Britanno*, and would also prefer *extremo* to *supremo*.],

through diverse peoples, across straits and along roads,

he saw the city of Romulus and beheld

the venerable temple of Peter, bearing mystical gifts [Note: [Col. 0376C] Bede and Paul read *gerens* (“bearing”).].

White, he will go among Christ’s companionable sheep;

for in body he occupies a tomb, but in mind the things above.

You would more readily believe that he exchanged the insignia of sceptres,

when you see that he earned Christ’s kingdom [Note: [Col. 0376C] Besides this poetic epitaph, Bede adds the following prose one: “Here lies Ceadvalla, also Peter, king of the Saxons, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, in the second indiction. He lived approximately thirty years, while the most pious lord Justinian was emperor, in the fourth year of his consulship, and while the apostolic man Lord Sergius was pope, in the second year of his pontificate.” It is deeply regrettable that this distinguished trophy of the Christian religion—the tomb of the neophyte king Ceduvalla, set up and inscribed at the command of Pope Sergius, as Bede says—has been removed and destroyed from the Vatican basilica, together with innumerable and almost all the monuments of ancient art and piety, through the calamity of the ages, the greed of workmen, and the negligence of officials! Recall what I said about such losses in the preface to the Christian inscriptions.].

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 729. SAINT EGBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK.

[Col. 0377]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE ON SAINT EGBERT

(*Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latinitatis*.)

[Col. 0377A] Ecbertus, Eckbertus, Egbertus, or Eckebertus, archbishop of York from 732 to 767, is the person to whom Bede wrote, not long before his death, a letter on the duties of a Christian prelate, as I said in volume I. After the Dublin edition of 1644 in octavo by James Ware, his *Dialogue on Ecclesiastical Institution* was reprinted by Henry Wharton at London in 1693 in quarto, together with some short works of Bede. It is also found in the editions of the Councils by Labbe, Hardouin, and Coleti of Venice, under the year 747. In those same editions of the Councils, as also in the royal edition, excerpts from his *Ecclesiastical Constitutions* are printed [Note: [Col. 0377B] Add Oudinus, vol. I, p. 1794 and following], which Leland, chapter 85, and Pits, p. 154, attest were carefully reduced to an abridgment by Hucarius, deacon of the shrine of Germanus in Corinia. One hundred and forty-five chapters drawn from the sayings and canons of the holy Fathers; thirty-five chapters from Ecbert’s *Penitential*, a work divided into four books and preserved in manuscript in various English libraries, as Cave noted. Both works were first published by Henry Spelman in volume I of the *Councils of England*, London, 1639, folio, pp. 258 and 276. John Morin also included the first in his collection of ancient penitentials, at the end of his work *On Penance*, after the first Paris edition of 1651, reprinted at Brussels in 1685 [Col. 0378A] and at Venice in 1702, folio. In the same Spelman, p. 278, there follow the titles of ninety-seven chapters on priestly law. There are also fifteen chapters on the remedy for sins, printed there on pp. 281 and 288 under Bede’s name [Note: Above, vol. I], and also in Antonio Agustín’s collection of penitential booklets, Tarragona, 1582, quarto, and Venice, 1584, quarto, as well as among Bede’s works, vol. VIII, p. 961, and in the volumes of the Councils. These may seem attributable to this Ecbert, whom Alcuin [Note: In his letter to Charlemagne, quoted by William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the English Bishops*, book III, p. 269] declares to have been his teacher. See, if you wish, the notes in volume XI of the *Bibliotheca Graeca*, p. 74 and following. I omit the homilies mentioned by Bale II, 15, and Pits, p. 154; the readings for instructing disciples; the instructions to the pastors of his province; the letter to Pope Zacharias requesting the pallium, which he received in 735—see Wharton, [Col. 0378B] volume I of *Anglia Sacra*, p. 697; the letters to his brother, King Egbert, to Alcuin, and others. Besides Spelman and the others, Wilkins most recently reprinted Ecbert’s excerpts in his collection of the Councils of Britain, checked against manuscript codices, and added sixteen others from an Oxford manuscript that had not previously been published anywhere. See volume I, p. 111 of that work.

[Col. 0377]

# EXCERPTS OF SAINT EGBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK, COMPOSED FROM THE SAYINGS AND CANONS OF THE HOLY FATHERS AND CONTRIBUTING TO THE ESTABLISHMENT OF ECCLESIASTICAL GOVERNMENT

(Mansi, *Collection of the Councils*, vol. XII.) (S)

# JOHN DOMINIC MANSI’S PREFACE TO THE CANONICAL COLLECTIONS OF EGBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK

[Col. 0377D] Ecgbert, who held the see of York from 735 until approximately 771, although he commended himself to the English by other deeds, made a celebrated name for himself among them through his written works. He is praised for an extensive work on priestly law, a portion of which, still unpublished, the Ballerini consider to be these excerpts, in the dissertation prefixed to the Old Canonical Collection among the works of Saint Leo the Great, volume III, part IV, chapter 6, no. 2; and for a booklet on remedies for sins, published indeed under Bede’s name but headed in most manuscripts with the title of Ecgbert, archbishop. Rhabanus Maurus, a contemporary of Ecgbert, also quotes in his letter to Heribald, chapter 18, from Ecgbert, bishop of the English, the words of chapter 9 of that work on remedies for sins.

Another booklet is published under his name, entitled *Excerpts of Ecgbert, Archbishop of York*, and so forth. This is the title it bears in the Cottonian Codex, as Wilkins presents it; but, according to Ware, other British codices offer the same work under this title: *Excerpts from the priestly law of Ecgbert, archbishop of York, by Huncarius the levite*, and so forth. From this it may rightly be inferred that these excerpts are an epitome of the more extensive work mentioned above. From these excerpts Spelman, and Labbe after him, published 145 chapters; Wilkins supplemented them from the Cottonian Codex [Col. 0379A] up to chapter 163, and they are reproduced here from that edition. From chapter 158 of those additions we learn of a peculiar custom of the English Church: namely, that chrism was administered by presbyters to infants in danger. I suppose this practice originated with Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, a Greek. Some additions probably belong to Huncarius, since they do not fit the age of Ecgbert, as in book I, chapter 7: “Let all priests pray continually for the life and reign of the lord emperor and for the safety of his sons and daughters.” Ecgbert could not have expressed himself in this way in Britain, writing for Britons, at a time when the Britons obeyed their own kings, not an emperor. Moreover, chapter 131 is copied word for word from chapter 38 of book II of the *Life of Saint Gregory the Great*, written by John the Deacon after Ecgbert’s time.

The third work presented here is Ecgbert’s *Penitential*, published by Wilkins from an Oxford manuscript. From book II of Ecgbert’s *Penitential*, Spelman had printed thirty-five canons, which Labbe incorporated into his collection. The Ballerini state that they found the same canons in book II of a certain manuscript collection in Vatican Codex 1352, divided into four books; they also say that they encountered them in another Vatican Codex, numbered 1357, but testify that Ecgbert’s name appears in neither. They add that in the same manuscripts there is a preface that may plainly be considered foreign to Ecgbert, as these words show: “You have asked and commanded, dearest ruler, that for correcting and instructing the conduct of your subjects,” and so forth. I therefore consider it certain that the Oxford Codex, which Spelman testifies he himself never saw, presents another collection entirely different from Ecgbert’s *Penitential*. Nevertheless, whoever its author may ultimately be, I have judged that these canons should be retained here, preserving the title they bear in Labbe. I also insert Ecgbert’s *Penitential*, but only in Latin, omitting the Anglo-Saxon. It is an ancient Latin version from the Saxon; although Ecgbert himself translated this Saxon work from another Latin *Penitential* of Isidore of Seville, as we understand from the title and from other indications throughout the work. Wilkins demonstrates that the same is true of the Latin version made from the Anglo-Saxon by several expressions in that version formed according to the character of the Saxon language rather than Latin—for example, “nights” are used here for “days,” “winters” to signify years, and likewise “days of the sun” for Sunday. Whether the work is genuinely Ecgberti could indeed be questioned on the basis of the conjecture that a different measure of penance is imposed for *interlectores* [reading uncertain] than in chapter 3 of the booklet on remedies for sins, which I defended above as Ecgbert’s. In my note to that chapter of the booklet I indicated a way of reconciling this difference; if scholars accept it, the authenticity of both works will be established.

Finally, I have thought it appropriate to retain here Ecgbert’s dialogue, published by Labbe in his collection from Ware’s edition. Although I have encountered no one who has doubted that this is Ecgbert’s work, I would nevertheless remain somewhat doubtful, since I have noticed something contrary to what is transmitted in the *Penitential*. For in book I, chapter 17 of the latter, it is stated: “If a man has been baptized by an adulterous presbyter, let him immediately be rebaptized.” In the dialogue, question 5, however, it is decreed that those baptized by a wicked presbyter condemned for a crime are not to be immersed again. It then adds: “This cannot properly be understood of baptism, which must not be repeated.” These statements conflict with one another; the position of the *Penitential* also conflicts with Catholic doctrine. Perhaps, however, baptism administered by a wicked priest was ordered to be repeated because it could reasonably be doubted whether the wicked priest had deliberately omitted something necessary for conferring the sacrament. In any case, it is clear that this opinion concerning repeated baptism was then widespread among the English, from the anonymous *Penitential* published by Martène in *Anecdota*, volume IV. It was composed for the use of the English Church and, as I am convinced, was readily attributable to Bede; it will be given below under Bede’s name. The words of this *Penitential* are: “One baptized by an unbaptized presbyter ought to be baptized again.” Nor would it be unreasonable to suppose that that untutored people considered the repeated administration of baptism to be a doctrine not of faith but of discipline, which varies among different Churches; or at least something that could be debated in either direction without endangering the faith, as the same *Penitential* of Ecgbert suggests in book I, chapter 7: “Any presbyter who knows that he is not baptized should be baptized, and all those whom he had previously baptized also.” Yet the Roman pope established that if the minister of the Mass is corrupt or pagan, the service of the Holy Spirit is nevertheless present in the gift of baptism, not in any human being. It is well known that before Charlemagne such deep darkness prevailed among the common people concerning many matters, especially those relating to baptism, that this pious emperor compelled the learned men of his age to write about baptism. Hence the many letters and treatises on baptism produced toward the end of the eighth century and at the beginning of the ninth. Indeed, even among the Greeks, from whom many things were brought into England by Theodore, a Greek and bishop of Canterbury, the doctrine that baptism must never be repeated does not seem to have been fully known. Read the prolegomena of the Fathers of Saint-Maur to the new Paris edition of the works of Saint Cyril of Jerusalem. I have judged that these matters should be explained at somewhat greater length, so that they might serve in place of the notes needed by Ecgbert’s collections.

# PREFACE

[Col. 0379C]

We call “canons” the rules established by the holy Fathers, in which it is written how those who are canonical—that is, regular clerics—ought to live.

[Col. 0380C] Augustine, bishop of Aurelia, says: “So that none of the priests may be permitted to be ignorant of his canons, or to do anything contrary to the rules of the Fathers; and so that no excuse may arise from ignorance, or anything be neglected through forgetfulness, let them frequently look in this booklet, as in a mirror, at what has been defined by the rules of the canons. Nevertheless, not all clerics ought to assume or read the judgments of canonical constitutions, but only presbyters. For just as no one except bishops and presbyters ought to offer the sacrifice, so no one else ought to assume these judgments.”

# THE EXCERPTS BEGIN

[Note: [Col. 0381D] In the Oxford manuscript, these first twenty-one excerpts are inserted before Ecgbert’s *Penitential*, under the title: “These are the rights of priests, which they ought to observe.”]

## I. Priestly Law

Each priest shall build his church with every care and shall preserve the relics of the saints with the greatest diligence, through night watches and divine offices.

## II. Likewise

All priests shall have the bells of their churches rung at the proper hours of day and night, then celebrate the sacred offices to God and instruct the people concerning how, and at which hours, God is to be worshiped.

## III. Likewise

On all feast days and Sundays, each priest shall preach the Gospel of Christ to the people.

## IV. Likewise

Each priest shall instruct all those subject to him, so that they may know how to offer to the churches of God the tithes of their entire property in the proper manner.

## V. Likewise

The priests themselves shall receive tithes from the people, keep written names of all who have given, and, according to canonical authority, divide them before those who fear [Col. 0381C]. They shall assign the first part to the adornment of the church; the second they shall mercifully distribute through their hands, with all humility, for the use of the poor and strangers; the third the priests themselves shall retain.

## VI. Likewise

Each priest shall carefully teach the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed to the people entrusted to him, and shall display to their minds the whole discipline of religion and the observance of Christianity.

## VII. Likewise

All priests shall pray continually for the life and reign of the lord emperor and for the safety of his sons and daughters.

## VIII. Likewise

Each priest shall attend the daily prayers for the bishop under whose governance he is ruled.

## IX. Likewise

No priest shall dare to celebrate Mass in houses or other places, except in consecrated churches.

## X. Likewise

All priests shall observe with the greatest care the law and proper time of baptism, at suitable seasons and according to canonical institution.

## XI. Likewise

All priests shall administer baptism with the greatest diligence, at whatever hours, to all who need it because of illness.

## XII. Likewise

No presbyter shall presume to sell the sacred office, the sacrament of baptism, or any spiritual gift for a price, lest he imitate those who sell and buy doves in the Temple; nor shall they desire earthly prices for what they have obtained through divine grace, but shall strive to receive only the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

## XIII. Likewise

No presbyter shall leave the proper seat of the holy church under whose title he was ordained and go to another church for the sake of admonition, but shall remain there devotedly until the end of his life.

## XIV. Likewise

[Col. 0382B]

No one among the priests shall cultivate the vice of drunkenness, nor compel others by his command to become drunk.

## XV. Likewise

No priest shall maintain intimacy with strange women, nor ever permit any woman to live in the house where he himself resides.

## XVI. Likewise

No priest shall be permitted to act as a surety, nor, abandoning his own law, presume to go to secular courts.

## XVII. Likewise

No priest shall ever carry weapons belonging to fighting men,

[Col. 0382C] nor stir up any quarrel against his neighbor.

## XVIII. Likewise

No presbyter shall enter taverns for the sake of eating or drinking.

## XIX. Likewise

No priest shall swear an oath with an oath, but shall speak everything simply, with purity and truth.

## XX. Likewise

All priests shall prescribe fitting penance, with the greatest vigilance, to all who confess their sins, and shall mercifully give all the sick, before the end of life, the viaticum and communion of the body of Christ.

## XXI. Likewise

[Col. 0382D]

According to the definition of the holy Fathers, if anyone falls ill, he shall be carefully anointed by priests with sanctified oil and prayers.

## XXII. Likewise

A presbyter shall always have the Eucharist prepared for the sick, so that they may not die without communion.

## XXIII. Likewise

Without the authority or consent of the bishops, presbyters shall neither be appointed nor expelled in any churches.

## XXIV. Likewise

Churches established in ancient times shall not be deprived either of tithes

[Col. 0383A] or of any other possession, so that these may be assigned to new oratories.

## XXV. Priestly Law

To each church one complete *mansus* shall be assigned without any other service. The presbyters established in them shall perform no service from the tithes, the offerings of the faithful, the houses, the courtyards or gardens situated beside the church, or the aforesaid *mansus*, except ecclesiastical service; and if they possess anything additional, they shall render from it the service owed to their superiors according to the custom of the country.

## XXVI. Likewise

Bishops and presbyters shall have a small lodging not far from the church.

## XXVII. Likewise

[Col. 0383B]

In the church, the bishop shall sit in the higher seat with the consent of the presbyters; but within the house he shall recognize himself as a colleague of the presbyters.

## XXVIII. Likewise

Each bishop shall carefully see to it in his diocese that the churches of God are well constructed, restored, and adorned—in their services, lights, and every other restoration—and that the servants of God live according to rule, each according to the rank of his order. The bishop shall take the greatest care, and shall also ensure that they celebrate the canonical hours together at the appointed time.

The holy Fathers therefore established that seven assemblies of worship should be sung. The clergy ought to sing them each day at their respective hours: the first is the nocturnal assembly; the second is the First Hour of the day; the third is the hour itself that we call Terce; the fourth is the Sixth Hour; the fifth is the Ninth Hour; the sixth assembly is at the hour of Vespers; and the seventh assembly we call Compline. These seven assemblies we ought diligently to render to God every day, for ourselves and for all the Christian people, as the Psalmist testifies, saying: “Seven times a day I have praised you because of the judgments of your righteousness” (Psalm 118). Moreover, we must not omit the Masses, as did the holy Fathers whom we call confessors—that is, the bishops and presbyters who served God in chastity.

## XXIX. Concerning Bishops: Paul Says
