For a bishop must be blameless in all things, as God’s steward—not arrogant, not angry, not addicted to wine, not violent, not greedy for dishonest gain, but hospitable, kind, sober, holy (1 Timothy 3), and so forth.

## XXX. The Apostle Likewise

Therefore a bishop ought to have a good testimony from those outside, so that he may order the teaching of our God in all things (ibid.).

## XXXI. Concerning the Great Synod; Concerning Women Living in Close Association; From the Council of Nicaea

The great synod absolutely forbids [the text reads: *indicit*, “commands”] a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all who belongs to the clergy to have a woman living in close association with him.

## XXXII. And Likewise

The canons also teach that if anyone has taken a widow or a divorced woman, or has married twice, he shall never become a deacon and never a priest.

## XXXIII. Likewise

A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has been caught in fornication, perjury, theft, or murder shall be deposed.

## XXXIV. Institutions of the Holy Fathers

It must therefore be observed by bishops that, rooted and founded in charity, they maintain true peace and complete harmony among themselves, so that in all things there may be, as it were, one heart and one soul, and that the complete teaching of the true faith may be in the mouth of all.

[Note: [Col. 0383] I do not know what is missing here in the manuscript codex; we have nevertheless added the numbers as though nothing were lacking.]

[lacuna]

## XXXV

Nothing ought to be placed in a church except what pertains to ecclesiastical ministry. It is written in Deuteronomy: “You shall not plant a grove or set up an image beside the sanctuary of the Lord” (Deuteronomy 26).

## XXXVI. On the Sabbath Begins

God, the creator of all things, created man on the sixth day, and on the Sabbath rested from his works and sanctified the Sabbath because of its future signification of Christ’s Passion and his rest in the tomb. He did not rest because he was tired—he who made all things without labor, whose omnipotence cannot grow weary—and he rested from his works in such a way that afterward he made no creatures different from those he had made before. He did not make other creatures afterward, but all those he made he continues to make each year until the end of the age. He creates human beings in souls and bodies, and animals and beasts without souls; every human soul is given by God, and he renews his creatures, as Christ says in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5).

Christ suffered for us in the sixth age of the world, on the sixth day; through his Passion he restored fallen humanity, and, having worked his miracles, rested in the tomb on the Sabbath and sanctified the Lord’s Day by his resurrection. For the Lord’s Day is the first day of the age, the day of Christ’s resurrection, and the day of Pentecost, and therefore it is holy. We ourselves ought spiritually to be a Sabbath keeping Sabbath—that is, abstaining from the works of servitude, namely sins—because “whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (1 John 3). But because we cannot be without sins, let us beware as far as we can, and amend whatever we have sinned. Let us give good examples to those subject to us, correct ourselves and our subjects, and continually exhort them to better things. Amen.

## XXXVII. Likewise, From the Holy Fathers

All should generally strive to celebrate Easter at the appointed times, that is, after the fourteenth moon of the first month.

## XXXVIII. Synod of Agde

Laymen who do not receive communion at Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost are not to be considered Catholics.

## XXXIX. African Canon

[Note: [Col. 0385D] See the *Chapters of Theodore of Canterbury*, volume IX of the *Spicilegium*, p. 42, chapter 12. Hardouin.]

According to the canons, penitents ought not to receive communion before the completion of their penance; but, through the mercy of the merciful God, we grant some permission after one, two, or three years.

## XL. Likewise, From the Holy Fathers

Presbyters shall administer the sacraments of baptism indiscriminately to those in need, and shall come to the aid of those seeking penance with the greatest speed, demanding no payment for it, unless their parents or those giving alms voluntarily offer something.

But if anyone attempts to oppose these institutions, he shall either suffer the penalty of excommunication or endure the misery of imprisonment for a long time.

## XLI. Canon of the Fathers

It has been decided concerning infants that, whenever completely certain witnesses cannot be found to testify that they were baptized, and the infants themselves, because of their age, are not able to answer concerning the sacraments entrusted to them, they are to be baptized without any scruple, lest this hesitation cause them to be deprived of the cleansing of the sacraments.

## XLII. Likewise

There are some who mix wine with baptismal water, improperly; Christ did not command baptism with wine but with water.

[Note: [Col. 0385D] This canon is inserted as XLIII in Wilkins; thereafter the numbering differs from his by one.]

## XLIII. Council of Chalcedon

[Col. 0385C]

No presbyter shall depart without chrism.

### XLIII. Canon of the Apostles

If any bishop, priest, or deacon has obtained this dignity through money, let both he and his ordainer be deposed and altogether cut off from communion, like Simon Magus by Peter.

### XLIV. African Canon

A bishop shall not ordain clerics without the council of the priests.

### XLV. Canon

A bishop shall hear no one’s case without the presence of his clerics, except in the case of confession.

### XLVI. Carthaginian Canon

[Col. 0385D] Let no ruler do anything without the counsel of his brothers; for it is written: “Do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not repent” (Ecclesiasticus XXXII, 24).

### XLVII. Canon

A decree cannot be firm if it is not found to have had the consent of many.

### XLVIII. Roman Canon

If questions arise in any province, let them be referred to the greater see or synod, or even to the apostolic see at Rome.

### XLIX. Canon of the Bishops

Let a bishop not rashly deprive anyone of communion, [Col. 0386A] lest he do so contrary to just judgment; and let no other bishop receive one whom another bishop has expelled from the Church, whether cleric or layman.

### L. Nicene Canon

Let no one take away someone who belongs to another and ordain him in his own church without the consent of the one to whom he belongs.

### LI. Chalcedonian Canon

Let no one be ordained absolutely and without designation of the place to which he is to be ordained.

Altars shall not be consecrated unless they are of stone, with the anointing of chrism.

### LII. Epaon Canon

It is not proper for bishops or priests to celebrate offerings in undedicated houses.

### LIII. Canon of the Saints

[Col. 0386B]

In prayers, let no one name either the Father in place of the Son or the Son in place of the Father; but whenever one stands at the altar, prayer must always be directed to the Father.

### LIV. Canon. Likewise.

It is sufficient for a priest to celebrate one Mass in one day, because Christ suffered once and redeemed the whole world; likewise, it is written in Leviticus that Aaron ought not continually to enter the inner sanctuary.

### LV. Aurelian Canon

Let a bishop provide food and clothing, insofar as his means permit, for the poor and sick who, because of disability, are unable to work with their own hands.

### LVI. Theodore says

[Col. 0386C] It has been established that priests shall neither be appointed to nor expelled from any churches without the authority or consent of the bishops; and if anyone attempts to do this, let him be punished by synodal judgment.

### LVII. Canon of the Bishops

Bishops must in no way be subject to secular affairs more than to the service of God—which God forbid—but must devote themselves above all to the care of souls, so that, in accordance with the Apostle, they may rightly correct God’s people by their example and instruct them also with the words of sound doctrine.

### LVIII. Canon

Let clerics, subject to their bishops in complete submission, render them the obedience owed to them, and let them not exalt themselves through any desire for self-display.

### LIX. Chalcedonian Canon

[Col. 0386D]

If any clerics or monks are found swearing oaths together, conspiring, or laying ambushes for bishops, let them be utterly removed from their proper rank.

### LX. Nicene Canon

If anyone receives a cleric or monk belonging to another bishop without that bishop’s consent, let him be judged sacrilegious and suspended from communion until he restores the cleric or monk to his own bishop. [Note: [Col. 0386D] Read: “And even if the cleric . . . should not wish.” Harduin.] But if the contumacious cleric should be unwilling to return, let him be anathema.

### LXI. Irish Canon

[Col. 0387A]

Whoever raises his hand with a spear or sword to strike someone in the presence of a bishop shall ransom his hand, or lose it. If he has wounded the person, he shall have his head and beard shorn and shall serve God, but first he must make satisfaction to the bishop and to the person whom he injured. If anyone wounds a cleric or harms anyone belonging to the ecclesiastical order, let him make sevenfold compensation according to the rank of the injured person, and let him do penance according to that person’s dignity; otherwise let him be expelled and live in exile from his own homeland. For the Lord says through the prophet: “Do not touch my anointed ones” (Psalm CIV); and so forth.

### LXII. Aurelian Canon

Let abbots, out of religious humility, remain under the authority of bishops; and if they do anything outside the rule, let them be corrected by the bishops. Once a year, after being summoned, they shall assemble at the place chosen by the bishop. Monks, for their part, shall submit themselves to abbots with complete devotion to obedience. If anyone proves disobedient through contumacy, or presumes to wander about from place to place, or to possess anything privately, let everything he has acquired be taken from him by the abbots for the benefit of the monastery according to the rule. [Note: [Col. 0387D] Read: “for the future benefit.” Hard.] Those who have wandered away shall be brought back under guard, with the bishop’s assistance, as fugitives; and let the abbot know that he will be held guilty if he has not restrained such persons by regular discipline, or if he has received another’s monk.

### LXIII. Aurelian Canon

If any abbot is not cautious in governance, humble, chaste, sober, compassionate, and discerning, and does not demonstrate the divine commandments in word and example, let him be deprived of his office by the bishop in whose territory he resides, together with the neighboring abbots and the other persons who fear the Lord, even if the entire congregation, consenting to his vices, wishes to have him as abbot.

### LXIV. Canon of the Apostles

If an abbot proves himself a transgressor of the divine commands and a despiser of the holy rule, let him be deprived of the honor of abbot by the bishop of the city, with the consent of the abbots and of the other monks who fear God. For it is fitting that the bishop of the city should exercise proper supervision over the monasteries, as the holy and great Synod of Chalcedon decreed.

### LXV. Pope Leo says

[Col. 0387D] A monk’s profession cannot be abandoned in any way; for what one has vowed to God, one must render. The Psalmist says: “Vow and pay to the Lord your God” (Psalm LXXV).

### LXVI. Theodore says

Monks shall not move from place to place, but shall remain in the obedience which they promised at the time of their conversion.

### LXVII. Fructuosus says

A monk who violates or despises the holy rule, or who pursues little boys or adolescents in an incestuous manner, shall be publicly flogged, shall lose the tonsure he wears, and, disgracefully shaved, shall endure reproach; or, bound in iron chains, he shall be worn down in the confinement of prison.

### LXVIII. Agathensian Canon

If any monk commits adultery or theft—which can more properly be called sacrilege—we decree that, after being beaten with rods as guilty of so great a crime, he shall never assume clerical office. If he is already a cleric when he is caught in such a deed, let him be deprived of the dignity of his status.

### LXIX. [Note: [Col. 0387D] Read “Aurelius.” Harduin.] Bishop Aurelius says

Monks shall never eat meat; but chickens and all poultry shall not be served in the congregation. They shall be provided only for the sick, and they may receive them. [Col. 0388B]

### LXX. Bishop Isidore says

[Printed: “Insid.”; read “Isidore.”] An abbot or monk may not make a monastery’s servant free. It is impious for one who has made no contribution to the Church’s property to inflict loss.

### LXXI. Canon

If any bishop, priest, or minister takes anything from the goods of the Church that the faithful bestow in whatever places, let him restore what he has wrongly seized with shame and undergo a sentence of excommunication for one year.

### LXXII. Irish Canon

Money stolen or seized from the Church shall be repaid fourfold; secular property, twofold.

### LXXIII. Likewise, Irish Canon

[Col. 0388C] If anyone steals money from a church, let lots be cast so that either his hand is cut off or he is put in prison, fasting and mourning for a long time; and let him restore in full what he took, or let him be cast out as an exile and restore double. If he remains in his homeland, let him restore fourfold and do penance perpetually.

### LXXIV. Toletan Canon

If a cleric is caught demolishing tombs, let him be removed from the clerical order for sacrilege. If anyone violates a tomb, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water.

### LXXV. Irish Canon

[Printed: “Hibritanensis”; read “Hibernensis,” Irish.] Those who have fled for refuge to a church ought not to be dragged away; rather, their masters should persuade them by a promised intervention. [Col. 0388D] If the master inflicts anything punitive on those leaving the church, let him be regarded as an enemy of the Church and excommunicated. [Note: [Col. 0387D] The following appears in Wilkins under a new title [Col. 0388D] and as a new canon. The title is: “Irish Canon: If anyone …” Mansi.] If anyone harms another in any way while the latter is under ecclesiastical refuge or under the protection of any sign of sanctity, let him make sevenfold compensation, pay and restore what is owed, and remain in severe penance for seven years. Otherwise he is to be excommunicated from the whole Catholic Church.

### LXXVI. Jerome says

The Church defends those whom she has received into her bosom, like a hen that nourishes and protects her own chicks and those of others; [Col. 0389A] so the Church must defend all who flee to her.

### LXXVII. Irish Canon

Whoever kills a man within the precincts of a monastery shall go into exile under condemnation; or, after laying down his arms and having his head and beard shaved, he shall serve God for the rest of his life, first making satisfaction to God and to the victim’s relatives.

### LXXVIII. Jerome says

Those who sin in a holy place must also be killed in that same place. In the camp, Phinehas killed the man and the prostitute; Mattathias killed the Jew who was sacrificing to an image. For whoever defiles what is holy will not be protected by holy things. Christ restrained evildoers in the Temple with whips.

### LXXIX. Jerome says

[Col. 0389B]

Whoever strikes the wicked because they are wicked is the Lord’s minister.

### LXXX. Jerome likewise says

To punish murderers and sacrilegious persons is not the shedding of blood but the mystery of the laws [Harduin: “ministry of the laws”]. Therefore, the person who spares the wicked harms the good.

### LXXXI. Arausian Canon

Whatever things belong to mercy are to be given to the insane.

### LXXXII. Carthaginian Canon

Every day exorcists shall lay hands upon the possessed.

### LXXXIII. Arausican Canon

Those who have at any time been publicly possessed shall not only not be admitted to any clerical order, but, [Col. 0389C] if some have already been ordained, they shall be removed from the office imposed upon them.

### LXXXIV. Carthaginian Canon

When a priest is delivering a sermon in church, anyone who leaves the audience shall be excommunicated.

### LXXXV. Carthaginian Canon

A layman shall not dare to teach in the presence of clerics, unless called upon by them.

### LXXXVI. Isidore says

No worldly wise man, however wise he may be, shall judge the judgments of the Church.

### LXXXVII. Carthaginian Canon

A woman, however learned and holy she may be, shall not dare to teach men in an assembly.

### LXXXVIII. Carthaginian Canon

[Col. 0389D]

When a bridegroom and bride are to be blessed by a priest, they shall be presented by their parents or by the bridal attendants; after receiving the blessing, they shall remain virgins that same night out of reverence for the blessing.

### LXXXIX. The Canon says

A priest ought not to attend a banquet celebrating a second marriage, especially since he is asked to impose penance for second marriages.

### XC. Pope Gelasius

A sacred veil shall not be imposed on virgins or widows devoted to God except at Epiphany, during the Easter season when the white garments are worn, or on the feasts of the apostles; unless, perhaps, as has been said concerning baptism, it is not refused to those afflicted by serious illness who request it, lest they depart from the world without receiving this gift. [Col. 0390A]

### XCI. Carthaginian Canon

It has been determined that before the age of twenty-five neither a deacon shall be ordained nor virgins consecrated, unless reasonable necessity compels it.

### XCII. Of Bishop Basil

Children ought to be received with the will and consent of their parents—or rather, presented by the parents themselves—in the testimony of many.

### XCIII. Of Isidore

Whoever has been dedicated by his own parents to a monastery should know that he will remain there perpetually. For Hannah offered the boy Samuel, after his birth and weaning, to God, and he remained in the service of the Temple.

### XCIV. Canon of the Romans and Franks

[Col. 0390B]

A child up to the age of fifteen shall be punished for an offense by corporal discipline; after that age, whatever he does wrong, even if he steals, let him make restitution or pay the legal penalty.

### XCV. Neocaesarean Canon

No priest shall be ordained before his thirtieth year, unless reasonable necessity compels it, because the Lord Jesus did not preach before the age of thirty.

### XCVI. Nicene Canon

A bishop should, if possible, be ordained by all the bishops of the province; if this is difficult, certainly by no fewer than three. Bishops’ ordinations ought to take place on Sundays, not in fields or small villages, but [Col. 0390C] in the principal cities, in keeping with the dignity of so great a title.

### XCVII

Priests and deacons, however, shall be ordained on the Saturdays of the four Ember seasons, so that, while this ordination is carried out before the people, the opinion of those elected and ordained may be examined through the testimony of everyone.

### XCVIII

The priests of God must always carefully ensure that the bread, wine, and water, without which Masses cannot at all be celebrated, are pure and clean. For if it is done otherwise, they will be punished together with those who offered the Lord vinegar mixed with gall, unless true repentance comes to their aid.

### XCIX. Concerning Tithes

It is written in the law of the Lord: “You shall not delay offering tithes and firstfruits” (Exodus XXII). And in Leviticus: “All the tithes of the land, whether of grain or of the fruits of trees, belong to the Lord; oxen, sheep, and goats, whatever passes beneath the shepherd’s rod—whatever comes tenth shall be sanctified to the Lord” (Leviticus XXVII). Neither good nor bad is selected, and one shall not exchange the other. [Harduin: “the other” rather than “one.”]

### C. Augustine says

Tithes, therefore, are the tribute owed to churches and to needy souls. O man, the Lord demands tithes from that by which you live. From military service, trade, and craftsmanship, pay tithes; for our Lord is not in need and does not seek rewards, but honor.

### CI. Likewise

When you reap the crop of your land, you shall not cut it down to the very surface of the earth, nor gather the remaining ears, nor collect the clusters and fallen grapes in your vineyard; instead, you shall leave them to be gleaned by the poor and by strangers (Leviticus XIX). [Col. 0391A]

### CII. And in the law

If you enter the grainfield of your friend, break off ears and rub them in your hand, but do not reap with a sickle (ibid.). The Savior’s disciples also did this, rubbing ears with their hands and eating them on the Sabbaths, as the Gospel says.

### CIII. Likewise in the law

When you enter your neighbor’s vineyard, you may eat as many grapes as you wish, but you shall not carry any away with you (ibid.).

### CIV. Instruction of the Fathers

[Col. 0391B] On Sunday nothing else should be done except to devote oneself to God in hymns, psalms, and spiritual songs; all the days of Easter week must likewise be observed with equal religious devotion.

### CV. Aurelian Canon

Out of consideration for mercy, we have also judged it right to preserve this provision: those who are assigned to prison for whatever offenses shall be visited by the archdeacon or by the church’s provost every Sunday, so that the needs of the prisoners may be mercifully relieved according to the divine commandment, and that suitable food may be supplied to them by the bishop from the Church’s household.

### CVI. Likewise

Whoever marries on Sunday night shall do penance for seven days.

Whoever marries on Wednesday or Friday shall do penance for three days.

[Col. 0391C] Whoever marries during Lent before Easter shall do penance for one year.

### CVII. Likewise

Let no one presume to violate or break the fasts that have been proclaimed, lest he incur God’s anger.

### CVIII. From the Council of Bra… [Read: of Braga]

Religious persons ought not to take food before the third hour of the day, nor hold banquets; nor should clerics ever eat bread unless a hymn has been recited, and … after the meals they should give thanks to the Creator.

### CIX. Canon of the Saints

Those who are married shall abstain for three nights before they receive communion, and for one night afterward. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not defraud one another, except by mutual consent, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer for a time.”

### CX. Gregory says

[Col. 0391D]

If someone uses his wife, insofar as possible, not out of the desire of lust but solely for the procreation of children, he should certainly be left to his own judgment both concerning entering the church and concerning receiving the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood. We ought not to prohibit him, since, according to the previously established judgment, he is also permitted to enter the church. Nevertheless, because this lawful union with one’s wife cannot take place without the desire of the flesh, one must sometimes abstain from entering a holy place, since that desire itself can in no way be without fault.

### CXI. Concerning Marriage, It Is Written in the Law

“If anyone seduces a virgin who is not yet betrothed and sleeps with her, he shall provide her dowry and take her as his wife” (Exodus XXI). [Col. 0392A]

### CXII. Augustine says

Whoever wishes to take a wife, just as he desires to find her a virgin, should himself also preserve his virginity until marriage.

### CXIII. The Roman Synod says

When sons reach the age of puberty, they must either take wives or profess continence; likewise, daughters at the same age must observe the same law.

### CXIV. The Apostle Paul says

“Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband” (1 Corinthians VII). Let no one presume to dissolve a legitimate marriage: “Therefore what God has joined, let no human being separate.”

### CXV. Paul says

[Col. 0392B]

“A woman does not have authority over her own body, but her husband does; likewise, a man does not have authority over his own body, but his wife does” (1 Corinthians XVII).

### CXVI. The Synod says

After a woman’s death, a man may take another wife after one month; after a year, however, a woman may take another husband.

### CXVII. The Apostle Paul says

“A woman is bound by the law as long as her husband lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. Yet she will be happier if she remains as she is” (1 Corinthians VII).

### CXVIII. Likewise, African Canon

A legitimate marriage may not be dissolved without the consent of both parties. One may, however, with the counsel of the bishop, grant the other permission to enter the service of God. Some also say that if a man or woman has entered religious life with the consent of the other, the other may contract a new marriage—but with a girl or boy, if unable to remain continent. I do not approve this. But if a married person wishes to convert to monastic life, he or she must not be received unless first released by the spouse who has professed chastity. For if, while the spouse is alive, that person marries another through lack of self-control, the person will undoubtedly be an adulterer; and the one who dismissed the spouse will share in that person’s sin.

### CXIX. Likewise, Concerning Legitimate Marriage

No one should presume to dissolve a legitimate marriage except by the consent of both parties, and for the love of Christ, who says: “Whoever has left his wife,” and so forth, “will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matthew XIX). No one should dismiss his wife for any other reason than fornication, because the Pharisees, testing the Lord Jesus Christ, asked him whether it was lawful for a man to dismiss his wife for any cause. Jesus answered and said to them:

“Have you not read that the one who made them from the beginning made them male and female? And he said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.’ Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh. What God, therefore, has joined, let no human being separate.”

They said to him: “Why then did Moses command that a writ of divorce be given and the wife dismissed?” He said to them: “Although Moses permitted you to dismiss your wives because of the hardness of your heart, it was not so from the beginning. But I say to you that whoever dismisses his wife, [Col. 0393A] except on account of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery” (ibid.).

Hence the Apostle also says: “I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not leave her husband” (1 Corinthians VII); and again: “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife” (ibid.).

Elsewhere it is written concerning adultery or fornication: “Whoever keeps an adulteress is foolish and impious” (Proverbs XVIII). Concerning the expulsion of the children of adulteresses with their mothers, Ezekiel likewise says: “Cast out the fornication-mother and the children of fornication,” and so forth.

Augustine also says: “If a woman has committed fornication, she must be abandoned, but while she is alive another woman must not be taken.” Wherever, therefore, there is fornication or a true suspicion of fornication, a wife may freely be dismissed. Otherwise, even if she is barren, deformed, foul-smelling, drunk, angry, of bad character, lustful, foolish, gluttonous, wandering, frivolous, or abusive, she must be retained, whether one wishes it or not, and she must be kept as she was taken. For the Apostle says: “When you were free, you voluntarily subjected yourself to slavery” (2 Corinthians IX).

### CXX. African Canon

According to evangelical discipline, neither may a wife dismissed by her husband take another husband while her own husband is alive, nor may a husband take another wife while his former wife is alive; instead, they must remain as they are or be reconciled to one another.

### CXXI. Augustine says

If a woman has committed fornication, she must be abandoned, but while she is alive another woman must not be taken.

### CXXII. The Canon says

[Col. 0393C] If a woman leaves her husband, despising him, and refuses to return and be reconciled with her husband after five or seven years, then, with the bishop’s consent, he may take another wife if he is unable to remain continent, and he shall do penance for three years—or even for as long as he lives—because according to the Lord’s judgment he is proved to be an adulterer.

### CXXIII. Likewise

If someone’s wife has been taken captive and cannot be ransomed, he may take another wife after seven years. If afterward his own wife—that is, the former wife—returns from captivity, he shall receive her and dismiss the later wife. Likewise, if such things happen to the husband, the wife shall act as we have stated above.

### CXXIV. Concerning the Marriage of Slaves

If a master joins a male slave and a female slave in marriage, and afterward the male or female slave is freed, then, if the one who remains in slavery cannot be ransomed, the free person may join in marriage with a freeborn person, as some hold; nevertheless, according to the Lord’s judgment, the person is proved to be an adulterer. Whoever acts in this way—that is, abandons human servitude because of the first wife and afterward takes a free woman as wife—shall do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water; and for as long as he lives, he shall always do some penance. The woman likewise shall do penance if she acts in this way.

If a free man takes in marriage a female slave, whether his own or another’s, he does not have permission to dismiss her if they were previously joined with the consent of both. But if he dismisses her and takes another wife, whether slave or free, he shall do penance as written above.

### CXXV. Concerning Concubines

Augustine says: What is it that many men are not ashamed to take concubines before marriage, only to dismiss them after several years and then take legitimate wives? Therefore, before the Lord and his angels I testify and declare that God has always forbidden such unions and has never been pleased with them; and especially in Christian times, it has never been lawful, is not lawful, and never will be lawful to have concubines.

### CXXVI. Likewise in the Law

No one shall defile himself through incestuous unions, because it is written in Leviticus: “No man shall approach his nearest blood relation to uncover her nakedness.” And again: “The soul that does any of these things shall perish from the midst of its people” (Leviticus XVIII). Those to whom an unlawful union is forbidden shall certainly have the freedom to enter into a better marriage.

### CXXVII. The Synod says

Those who have been joined in an unlawful marriage ought not, after penance, to live in one household, lest they unite with one another because of love.

### CXXVIII. Likewise, the Synod Concerning the Bed of a Deceased Brother

Hear the decrees of the synod: A surviving brother shall not ascend to the bed of his deceased brother, since the Lord says: “The two shall be one flesh” (Genesis II). Therefore, your brother’s wife is your sister.

### CXXIX. Gregory says

[Col. 0394C] If anyone takes as wife a nun, or a spiritual godmother, or his brother’s wife, or a niece, or a stepmother, or a cousin, or a woman from his own kinship, or one whom his kinsman had as a wife, let him be anathema.

### CXXX. Likewise, Concerning Blood Relatives: Gregory’s Response to Augustine’s Questions

[Note: [Col. 0393D] In *Responses to Questions*, question 6. Harduin.]

A certain earthly law in the Roman republic permits a brother and sister, or the son and daughter of two full brothers or of two sisters, to enter into union. But experience has taught us that offspring cannot grow from such a marriage, and the sacred Mosaic law prohibits uncovering the shame of kinship. Therefore it is necessary that, from the third or fourth generation onward, the faithful should be permitted to unite; for the second degree, as we have stated, must abstain from one another in every way. [Col. 0394D]

### CXXXI. Likewise, Concerning a Reasonable Cause

After a considerable time, Gregory was asked by Felix, bishop of Messana in Sicily, whether he had written to Augustine that marriages contracted within the fourth degree among the English should by no means be dissolved. The humble father gave, among other things, the following explanation:

You should understand that what I wrote to Augustine, bishop of the English nation and our pupil, concerning a union between blood relatives, I wrote specifically to him and to the English nation, which had recently come to the faith, and not generally to the rest of the faithful: namely, that they should not abandon the good they had begun out of fear of excessive severity.

The whole city of Rome is therefore my witness, and I did not give them these instructions with the intention that, after they had become firmly rooted and established in the faith, they should not separate if they were found within their own blood relationship, nor that they should unite within the line of affinity—that is, as far as the seventh generation. Rather, while they were still neophytes, it was necessary first to teach them what was unlawful, instruct them by word and example, and thereafter reasonably and faithfully exclude them from such conduct. For, according to the Apostle, who says, “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Corinthians III), we permitted them to observe these things for the present, not for later times, as has been established, lest the good that had been planted with a still-weak root be burned up [read: uprooted], but so that it might be strengthened somewhat and preserved unto perfection.

### CXXXII. Roman Canon

[Col. 0395B] A layman who defiles himself with a servant of God, or with a spiritual godmother, or with a female relative, or perhaps with a woman whom his kinsman previously had, shall first be anathematized and afterward do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water. The woman likewise shall do penance, because the Christian religion condemns fornication equally in both sexes.

### CXXXIII. Likewise

Pope Gregory, seated in synod before the body of the most blessed Peter, said: If anyone takes a priestess in marriage, let him be anathema.

### CXXXIV. Likewise

If anyone takes in marriage a nun, whom they call a servant of God, let him be anathema.

### CXXXV. Likewise

[Col. 0395C] If anyone takes as wife a woman from his own kinship, or one whom his kinsman had, let him be anathema. And all who responded said: Amen.

### CXXXVI. Likewise

If anyone commits fornication with two female relatives, let him first be anathematized and then do penance for seven or ten years.

### CXXXVII. Likewise, Gregory to Bishop Felix

We decree that everyone shall preserve his lineage through the seventh generation; and as long as they recognize themselves as close by affinity, no Christian is permitted or ever will be permitted to take them in marriage. We do not wish to be reproved by you or by the other faithful in this matter, because in the case of the English nation we granted this concession [Col. 0395D] not as a rule, but acted out of consideration, lest they abandon unfinished the good of Christianity that they had begun (Register, book XII, indiction 7, letter 32).

### CXXXIII. Concerning Genealogical Diagrams

[Read: “stemmatibus,” genealogical diagrams.]

Genealogical diagrams are called little branches in general, when they indicate the degrees of kinship—for example, this one is a son, that one a father, another a grandfather, another a kinsman, and so forth; their forms appear below. As this blood relationship gradually separates itself through the ordered branches of descent until it withdraws to the final degree and ceases to be close kinship, the law of marriage again takes it up through the bond of matrimony and, in a certain sense, calls back what was fleeing.

Kinship was therefore established through the sixth degree, so that, just as the generation and condition of the human race are completed through the six ages of the world, the kinship of a family might likewise end after so many degrees. Among these degrees of relationship, no one ought to approach another for conjugal union. Nor is any Christian permitted or ever will be permitted to take as wife a woman whom someone from his own blood relationship had as a spouse, because such incestuous intercourse is abominable to God. We read that the holy Fathers established long ago that incestuous persons are not to be counted under the name of marriage at all.

### CXXXIX. Pope Vigilius

If the altar is moved, the church shall be consecrated again. If only the walls are altered and not the altar, it shall be purified with salt and water. If it has been violated by homicide or adultery, it shall be cleansed with the greatest care and consecrated again.

### CXL. Pope Vigilius. From the Council of Carthage; Gregory

[Col. 0396B] When a cleric comes to judgment, if he wishes and it is necessary, let the delays established by the Fathers be granted without hindrance to him who requests them, and let chosen judges be granted, … if [Wilkins: “Let judges chosen by himself be appointed by the Father. If …”] he fears any violence from a rash multitude there, let him choose a suitable place where, without fear, he may have his own witnesses if necessary and may conclude his canonical judgment without impediment. For many things commonly occur through surreptitious action.

Do not merely refuse to uphold the judgment of a brother that conceals mercy; refuse even to hear it, because mercy is more excellent than all burnt offerings. Ecclesiastical affairs must not be conducted in the same way as secular affairs. In secular matters, before the person compelled by the laws has come, pleaded, and given an answer, he cannot withdraw before the case has been completed. In ecclesiastical matters, however, once the case has been stated, it is permissible to withdraw if necessary or if one sees that one is being overburdened.

### CXLI. In the Nicene Synod

It was established that no others should be judges in a synod except those whom the accused himself has chosen, or whom his primates have appointed with his consent and by the authority of this holy see. For it is unworthy that one who ought to have provincial judges chosen by himself should be judged by outsiders.

A bishop’s gift, sale, or exchange of ecclesiastical property shall be invalid without the approval and subscription of the clerics.

### CXLII. Roman Council

[Col. 0396D] In the time of the emperor Constantine Augustus, Pope Sylvester convened a synod at Rome with seventy-three bishops. With their consent and superscription it was established:

No layman shall dare to give testimony against any cleric; therefore, laymen shall not be admitted as witnesses against a cleric. Accusers who are blood relatives, household members, or persons coming from the same household shall not give testimony against outsiders; neither accusers nor suspect witnesses shall be admitted, because the affection of kinship, domination, and familiarity commonly obstructs the truth. But if they are unwilling to do otherwise and the relatives agree among themselves, let them testify, but not against others; for carnal love, fear, and bitterness commonly blunt human judgment and distort opinions.

### CXLIII

[Col. 0397A] No monk shall presume to judge, nor shall he dare to accept a secular accusation against a cleric. If anyone is proved to admit such an accusation, let him understand that, as an “exauctor of fury” [read: “an exactor of interest/usury”] or as a possessor of usurious gains, he is to be degraded according to the statutes of the Fathers. When someone is burdened by grave sins of his own, he does not cleanse away the sins of others.

### CXLIV. Concerning Ancient Marriage

It is therefore sufficiently clear that, at the beginning of the world, the sons of Adam could not have taken wives except their own sisters or close female relatives. From the beginning, however, it was always unlawful to violate the wife or concubine of one’s father.

Hence the patriarch Jacob said to his son Reuben: “You have been poured out like water; you shall not increase, because you went up to your father’s bed [Col. 0397B] and defiled his couch” (Genesis XXIV). The Apostle Paul, teacher of the nations, also wrote concerning such sacrilege, saying: “It is reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as does not occur even among the nations, so that someone has his father’s wife; and you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that the one who has done this deed might be removed from your midst” (1 Corinthians V).

Behold, the Apostle judged that the man who presumed to violate his stepmother should be removed from the midst of Christians, saying: “Not even among the nations”—that is, among the pagans—is such a crime committed.

It is therefore true, and abundantly evident, that almighty God prohibited in the law of Moses the taking of one’s father’s wife, brother’s wife, or close relative, or sleeping with her. But what is written in Deuteronomy—that a brother should take the wife of his deceased brother and raise up offspring for his brother (Deuteronomy [Col. 0397C] XXV)—is not to be understood carnally but observed spiritually.

A teacher is exceedingly blind who does not know the distinction between the Old Testament and the New, but still wanders blinded by the shadow of ancient darkness, not knowing the truth of Christ’s grace. He does not know that the law and the prophets prophesied until John the Baptist. For the Lord himself says: “The law and the prophets were until John; from the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Mark XI).

And whoever, blinded in heart, still follows only the letter with the Jews, persists without the life-giving Spirit and the grace of Christ, eating the crusts of bread and not the inner crumbs.

A great difference exists between the letter that kills and the life-giving Spirit; and a very ignorant, cowardly, [Col. 0397D] and foolish teacher is one who, after so many years and after so many interpreters, inspired by God, who have expounded books on the law of Moses, still wishes to Judaize, despising Christ and all the holy teachers. For in Deuteronomy we read:

> When brothers dwell together and one of them dies without children, the wife of the deceased shall not marry another, but his brother shall take her and raise up offspring for his brother; and he shall call the firstborn son born from her by his name, so that his name may not be blotted out from Israel. But if he does not wish to take his brother’s wife, who is owed to him by law, the woman shall go to the city gate, appeal to the elders, and say: “My husband’s brother refuses to raise up his brother’s name in Israel and to take me in marriage.” [Col. 0398A] Immediately they shall summon him and question him. If he answers, “I do not wish to take her as my wife,” the woman shall approach him before the elders, remove his sandal from his foot, spit in his face, and say: “So shall it be done to the man who does not build up his brother’s house”; and his name shall be called in Israel, “The House of the Unsandaled Man” (Deut. XXV).

For what is written in Deuteronomy, and in the Gospel, namely that a brother took his deceased brother’s wife in order to raise up offspring for his brother, is not to be observed carnally by Christians, but spiritually. Christ says in the Gospel: “But you are all brothers, and you have one Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. XIII). And when spiritual brothers dwell together, and that brother who presides over the Church of God has passed from this world to Christ, then his brother should take over the governance of the Church [Col. 0398B] of God and raise up spiritual children for God, lest, when one mortal teacher dies, the bride of Christ—which is the mother of us all—become barren. And if some teacher does not wish to govern the Church after the death of another teacher, caring not for the salvation of others but for his own, then he shall be “unsandaled,” contrary to what Paul said: “And having your feet shod in preparation for proclaiming the good news” (Rom. VI, 10). If he does not wish to sow the word of God, although he is able, but hides Christ’s talent in a napkin—that is, in the torpor of his sloth—he shall be spat upon by the Church in the face, deemed worthy of disgrace, and cast into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. VIII). But each teacher should always succeed another in governing the Church of God until the end of the age, so that [Col. 0398C] spiritual children may be raised up for Christ from his virgin bride, as he himself established; for “whoever does not wish to labor for God is not worthy of a reward.”

## CXLV. Canon of Laodicea

Let no Christian dare to Judaize, nor participate in their feasts.

[Here the excerpts of Ecgbert end in Labbe; the following material is added by Wilkins from the Cotton manuscript Nero A, fol. 131 verso, where it is given in continuous sequence with the preceding material. I have preserved the same chapter numbering used by Wilkins, which differs by two units from Labbe’s numbering.]

## CXLVIII. Likewise

Let no Christian pay heed to pagan superstitions, but let him utterly reject every pollution of the heathen.

## CXLIX. Canon of Braga

[Col. 0398D]

If anyone, following the custom of the pagans, brings diviners and sorcerers into his house, as though to drive out evil, discover spells, or serve pagan purification rites, let him do penance for five years.

## CL. Canon of the Saints

If any Christian sells a Christian person into the hands of Jews or heathens, let him be anathema; for it is written in Deuteronomy: “If a man is found soliciting someone from the people of Israel, and, after selling him, receives payment, he shall be put to death.”

## CLI. Likewise, canon of the saints

It is therefore unlawful that those whom Christ redeemed by the shedding of his blood should be entangled in the bonds of Jews or heathens.

## CLII. On the Tonsure

[Col. 0399A]

The origin of the tonsure began with the Nazirites, who, after preserving their hair throughout a life of great continence, shaved their heads in order to consecrate their devotion to the Lord. We also find written in the canons of the holy Fathers: If any Catholic cuts his hair in the manner of barbarians, he shall be regarded as alien to the Church of God and excluded from the table of all Christians until he makes amends for his offense.

## CLIII. On Peter’s Tonsure

The apostle Peter was therefore the first to use the clerical tonsure, bearing on his head the image of Christ’s crown of thorns. Hence the African canon commands that a cleric neither grow his hair nor his beard.

## CLIV. From a Roman Canon

Whoever is seen in church as a cleric without a tunic (*colobium*) or cloak, and who has not cut his hair and beard in the Roman manner, shall be excommunicated. A cleric must not dress in monastic clothing or use laymen’s garments; and if a man wears women’s clothing, he shall be excommunicated, or a woman, if she wears men’s dress.

## CLV. Likewise

A cleric must not use weapons or go to war, because the canons teach that any cleric who dies in war or in a quarrel is not to be prayed for or commemorated in the offering, although he is not to be deprived of burial. The Apostle also says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs”; hence he is not free from the snares of the devil who wishes to involve himself in worldly military service. Therefore it must be stated emphatically to presbyters and deacons that they carry no weapons, but rely more on God’s protection than on arms.

## CLVI. Likewise

Clerics must also beware of serving as judges in the condemnation of a person.

## CLVII. Likewise

The authority of the canons forbids any bishop or cleric to give consent to the death of anyone, whether a thief, robber, or murderer.

## CLVIII. Likewise

It has been decreed that presbyters are not to be sent indiscriminately to different places, either by bishops, other prelates, or laymen, lest through their absence dangers to souls arise—especially the deaths of infants without chrism—and lest the duties of the churches in which they have been appointed be neglected.

## CLIX. African Canon

All clerics who are physically able to work should learn both crafts and letters.

## CLX. Caesarean Canon

There are therefore two kinds of clerics: one consisting of ecclesiastics under episcopal governance, the other of Acephali, that is, “headless” men, concerning whom Gregory says: If there are ordinary clerics outside the sacred orders—that is, neither presbyters nor deacons—who cannot remain continent, they ought to take wives and receive their stipends externally. Priests, however, must by no means take wives, but should love the Church, use no weapons of war, and undertake spiritual warfare.

## CLXI. Likewise, on Military Service

Brothers, know that secular authority and spiritual authority are distinct. It is fitting that those devoted to secular affairs be defenders of the Church and champions of Christ’s flock; those devoted to spiritual things, however, should be intercessors for all God’s people. A soldier of Christ ought not to use human weapons, as many testimonies make clear.

Let us begin our testimony with God and our Lord Jesus Christ. When he wished to undergo the suffering of the cross for the human race and was seized by soldiers, he forbade Peter to fight with a sword. If Peter was not permitted to fight in defense of the insult inflicted upon his Lord, what is more proper for us than to imitate his example? Understand, therefore, that God saves not by spear and sword alone, but rather through constant prayers and the other divine services.

The confessor of Christ, Martin, likewise, when ordered by the apostate Julian to assume military clothing, said that he was a soldier of Christ and therefore could not fight. We also have a useful example from the Book of Exodus: while Joshua fought against Amalek, Moses did not fight with weapons, but prayed to God with his hands extended toward heaven, and the Israelite people prevailed; whenever he lowered his hands, Amalek grew stronger. These and many other examples show that a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or monk must carry no weapons in battle [Col. 0400C] except those of which it is written: “Taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one, and taking the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” It is therefore wholly contrary to ecclesiastical regulations to return to secular military service after ordination.

## CLXII. On Homicide, an Ordinance of the Saints

If a presbyter or deacon commits homicide, he shall be degraded and do penance until the end of his life.

## CLIII. Likewise

If any cleric commits homicide, let him do penance in exile for ten years, three of them on bread and water; afterward let him be received back into his homeland. If he has performed his penance well, as attested by the bishop, priest, or person to whom he was entrusted, and if he makes satisfaction to the relatives of the man he killed, he may be restored. But if he does not satisfy that man’s relatives, he shall never be received back into his homeland; rather, like Cain, he shall be a fugitive and wanderer upon the earth.

If he committed the homicide accidentally—that is, without intending it—let him do penance for five years, three of them on bread and water. If he consented to a homicide and it was carried out, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water. If he intended it but did not accomplish it, let him do penance for one year. If anyone strikes another and draws blood, let him do penance on bread and water for forty days; if he is a deacon, six months; if a presbyter, one year. If a layman kills a layman, let him abstain from church for forty days and fast on bread and water; afterward let him do penance according to the priest’s judgment.

[Col. 0401]

# The Penitential of Saint Ecgbert, Archbishop of York

[Note: Wilkins cites this in volume I of the *Councils of Britain*. In both the printed editions and the manuscripts, these words appear under the title: “Here begin the chapters of the book which we call the Penitential”; and below: “Ecgberht, archbishop of York, translated these chapters from Latin into English so that the unlearned might easily understand them.”]

*(Mansi, Collection of Councils, vol. XII.)* (C)*

## Preface

[Col. 0401A]

When someone comes to do penance, let him prostrate himself before God with the greatest fear of God and humility; and let him pray in a voice broken by weeping that God may teach him to do penance for all the offenses he has committed against God’s will. Let him confess his misdeeds to the priest, so that the priest may know what penance ought to be imposed upon him.

Then the priest should ask him what faith he has in God, exhort him in various ways concerning the needs of his soul, admonish him, and say:

“Do you believe in almighty God, and in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit? Do you believe that all people will rise from the dead on the day of judgment? Do you repent of everything evil that you have done, said, and thought? Are you willing to forgive all those who have ever sinned against you?”

If he says, “I am willing,” then the priest should say to him:

“May almighty God have mercy on you and grant me what I ought to have.”

Fast every day during this Lenten season until None, and abstain from white food; beware of the eight capital vices, so that you do not commit them. They are homicide, theft, perjury, avarice, unlawful intercourse, lust, detraction, and false testimony. Observe the twelve days of Lent that occur each year, and beware of barbarous sacrifice, sorcery, intercourse with a virgin, double-tongued speech, pride, and coveting the possessions of other people.

Beware of all these things, and love your Lord with all your soul, with every virtue and all your strength, and firmly with the whole depth of your heart. Be kind toward the poor, gentle, distributing alms, diligently visiting the church, and diligently giving tithes to the Church of God and to the poor. Then God will be favorable, beneficent, and merciful toward you, and you will reign with him forever and ever [Col. 0402B] without end, if you do these things.

And I ask you to tell me everything evil that you have ever done, because it is better for you to be ashamed now here before me, a miserable man, than later before God at the great judgment, when the inhabitants of heaven, earth, and the underworld will all be gathered together.”

# First Part of the First Book

[Col. 0401]

## Chapter I. On the Prudence of a Presbyter

It is fitting for every priest, when he imposes a fast as penance upon someone, to know who that person is: whether healthy or sick, rich or poor, young or old, ordained or lay, and what sort of penance he is performing; whether celibate or married. Discretion is fitting in dealing with all people, even if they have not deliberately committed adultery. The rich are to be judged more severely than the poor, according to canon law.

## Chapter II. The Law Concerning Various Sins

The holy and pious bishop Theodore established the following instruction as an example and teaching for all those who wish to amend their offenses before God, and he said:

“We read in the *Penitential* that penance should be performed for capital crimes for one, two, or three years on bread and water, and for lesser crimes for a week or a month, all in the same manner. But for some people this is harsh and difficult. Therefore we shall teach by what means someone who cannot keep his fast ought to redeem it: namely, by performing penance through psalmody and almsgiving over a long period.

If he can fulfill everything written in this book, that is very good and properly ordered. If he cannot, let him sing fifty psalms in order, in church or in another private place. Whoever fasts for one week on bread and water should sing three hundred psalms on bended knees, or three hundred and twenty without kneeling, as stated above.

If someone must do penance for a month on bread and water, let him sing twelve hundred psalms on bended knees, or one thousand six hundred and eighty without kneeling. Thereafter, every day except Wednesday and Friday, let him take food at midday; on those days he should fast until None, abstain from meat and wine—that is, from every kind of drink by which one can become drunk—and, after singing, eat whatever other foods God has given him.

If he knows neither the psalms nor how to fast, let him distribute an obol, or its value, to the poor every day. Each week let him fast one day until None and another until Vespers, and use what he has, as stated above.

If someone must do penance for an entire year, let him distribute twenty-six shillings as alms and fast two days each week, as stated above. During the three Lents, let him consider what his food has been and distribute half of it as alms.

In the second year, penance is to begin from the Nativity of the Lord to Epiphany, and from Easter to Pentecost. A person who cannot do penance for his sins in the manner described above should distribute twenty-six shillings as alms in the first year, twenty in the second, and eighteen in the third, making sixty-four shillings.

Let the rich person know that God has entrusted him with many riches and possessions of this life, so that he may know how to amend his capital crimes. Let him take up the Gospel and read there how Zacchaeus spoke with the Lord when he received him into his house for a meal. Then he called upon him, saying:

‘Lord, I give half of all my goods to the poor; and if I have taken anything from anyone through unjust fraud, I restore it fourfold.’

Then he deserved to hear from the Lord:

‘Today salvation has come to this house’—that is, the forgiveness of all sins.

To increase these good works of which we have spoken above, let him free and ransom those who are in captivity. From the day on which he abandons his injustice, let him not renew it thereafter, lest he be like the dog that devours what it previously vomited.

Nor should what the Apostle said be neglected: ‘Whoever sins through his body should make compensation through his body’; that is, through fasting, vigils, prayers, supplications to God, contrition of heart, and the shedding of tears.”

The first abstinence is the baptism of fire; the second is love of God; the third is the desire to give alms; the fourth is the shedding of tears in true penance; the fifth is confession of offenses; the sixth is affliction of heart and body through fasting; the seventh is the correction of one’s conduct before God; the eighth is holy prayer for those offenses; the ninth is mercy and good faith; the tenth is leading others away from offenses toward God’s will; the eleventh is God’s forgiveness, by which God forgives that person’s sins; the twelfth is martyrdom, as occurred in the passion of Christ.

## Chapter III. On a Bishop’s Adultery

If a bishop commits adultery, according to canon law he shall fast for twelve winters, give abundant alms, and implore God’s honor with the shedding of tears. Some wish him thereafter to deprive himself of his orders.

## Chapter IV. On a Presbyter’s Adultery

When a presbyter has fornicated, let him fast for three winters and observe three fasts each week, fasting on two days until Vespers. If he has fornicated with a nun, let his fast be greatly increased, namely to seven years.

## Chapter V. On a Priest Who Pollutes Himself with Impure Speech or Other Vices

A priest who speaks impurely, or pollutes himself through looking at or seeing a woman, and does not cleanse himself, shall fast for twenty days. Whoever has polluted himself deliberately to a great extent shall fast for one hundred days.

If he has been polluted involuntarily in sleep, let him rise and sing a psalm from the Psalter, and on the following day bow his face to the ground thirty times. If he has been polluted involuntarily, or if he has willingly committed adultery in sleep, let him sing twenty-four psalms.

If someone discharges his semen while sleeping in church, let him rise and sing the Psalter. If a priest kisses a woman lustfully, let him do penance for twenty days. If a priest is polluted by touching a woman, let him fast forty days; some prescribe thirty.

If a priest is polluted by the will of his thoughts, let him fast one week; if by the touch of his hand, let him fast three weeks. If anyone commits fornication frequently, the canon judges that he should fast ten winters; some prescribe one year, and, with discretion, three.

## Chapter VI. On a Presbyter Who Refuses to Baptize Because of the Necessity of His Journey

[Col. 0404B]

Any priest who travels in his own province or in another, and who is asked to perform a baptism along the way but refuses, shall be detained on his journey; and if a pagan infant dies, he shall be stripped of his rank.

## Chapter VII. On an Unbaptized Presbyter and Those Whom He Baptizes

Any presbyter who discovers that he has not been baptized shall be baptized, as shall all those whom he previously baptized. Nevertheless, the Roman pope decreed that if the minister of the Mass is defective or pagan, the service of the Holy Spirit is present in the gift of baptism, though not in any human being.

## Chapter VIII. On a Bishop or Presbyter Who Loses His Rank

[Col. 0404C]

If anyone loses his rank, whether presbyter or bishop, let him do penance until death, so that his soul may live. If a priest kills a person or commits fornication, he shall be stripped of his rank; if he wounds someone, let him fast one hundred days.

## Chapter IX. What a Priest Should Wear When Celebrating Mass

When a priest celebrates Mass, he should not wear a hooded *caracalla*; but when he reads the Gospel, he should place it over his shoulder.

## Chapter X. On a Priest Who Spills the Chalice, and on Food Before the Eucharist

If a priest spills the chalice after celebrating Mass, let him fast thirty days. If he eats before going to the Eucharist, and after receiving the Eucharist, let him fast seven days.

## Chapter XI. On a Presbyter Who Takes Something of Great Value

If a presbyter commits theft involving something of great value, let him fast five winters, or according to what the bishop assigns him.

## Chapter XII. On a Deacon and Monk Who Fornicate

If a deacon fornicates, let him fast three winters, and likewise a monk. If he begets a child, let him fast more, according to what the bishop or the laws assign him. An unordained man who is not a monk, if he fornicates, shall fast twelve months; if he begets a child, let him fast three winters; if he kills the child, let him fast seven winters.

## Chapter XIII. On Monks and Nuns Who Fornicate

If a monk or consecrated woman fornicates, let them fast seven winters; some prescribe three. A wife must not be given to a young man if he has previously formed the intention of entering the monastic order.

## Chapter XIV. On Laymen Who Fornicate

A layman who has a wife, if he violates another man’s woman or a virgin, shall fast one winter; if he has a child, let him fast three winters. But if he is unmarried, let him fast seven winters; some prescribe ten.

If anyone has intercourse with his mother, sister, or daughter, let him fast twelve winters, though the priest must nevertheless determine what his status is. Anyone who has intercourse with an animal shall fast ten winters, or seven; some prescribe three winters, some one, and some one hundred days. Let the priest consider what sort of person and what sort of animal is involved. In all matters prudence is fitting for a priest, as we said earlier.

Whoever discharges semen into a mouth shall fast seven winters. Any man who fornicates with his female servant shall fast one winter; if she bears a child, let him redeem the child and nevertheless fast one winter.

## Chapter XV. On the Unlawful Acts of the Young

If a small boy is overpowered in intercourse by an older person, let him fast five nights; if he submits to it, let him fast twenty nights. If he steals or eats an animal that died of itself, and knows that it died of itself, let him fast seven days. If he is twenty years old and commits such an act, let him fast twenty days.

If he pollutes himself with his own hand, let him fast twenty days. If this occurs in mature manhood, let him fast forty days; some prescribe one hundred.

## Chapter XVI. On Fornication During Menstruation and Other Unlawful Fornication

Any man who has intercourse with his wife during her menstrual period shall fast forty days. Anyone who drinks his own blood or a man’s semen shall fast five winters.

Anyone who fornicates in a church shall be judged according to what seems right to the bishop and punished accordingly. If anyone has intercourse with an animal or with a male, let him fast ten winters. If boys commit fornication with one another, let them be hanged.

If an animal has been violated by a male, it shall be killed and given to the dogs; if there is doubt, it may be allowed to live.

## Chapter XVII. On the Fornication of Heathens; on One Who Was Baptized Twice Without Knowing It; on One Baptized by a Presbyter Who Fornicates Unlawfully; and on One Baptized Twice Voluntarily

Concerning the fornication of heathens, one who has been baptized twice involuntarily, one who has been baptized by a presbyter who fornicates unlawfully, and one who has voluntarily been baptized twice:

After baptism, every heathen should leave his heathen wife under his authority, whether he himself has baptism or not; likewise, whether either of them is a heathen or baptized. A heathen should depart from a baptized person, as the Apostle said: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart.”

One who has been baptized twice without knowing it should not be assigned any fast, unless he is to be consecrated according to canon law, even if he conceals his situation. If a man has been baptized by an adulterous presbyter, he should immediately be rebaptized.

Anyone who knowingly baptizes someone a second time acts as though he were crucifying Christ; let him fast seven winters, two days of fasting each week, and three days of a full fast.

## Chapter XVIII. On a Man’s Receiving a Woman at Baptism and a Woman’s Receiving a Man

A male should receive a female at baptism, and a female a male. The baptized person [Read: the baptizer] should not eat in the same house with those who have been baptized, nor kiss them, especially since this is not permitted among the heathen.

## Chapter XIX. On the Promises of Men and Women

If a man or woman vows to remain celibate and thereafter the man enters a lawful marriage, this must not be disregarded: he shall fast three winters, because a foolish and impossible vow has been violated.

If a certain man’s wife commits adultery, the husband may leave her and take another wife if she was his first wife. But if she was his second or third wife, he may not take another. If a wife wishes to commit offenses within five years, she ought to marry another man.

If the husband is dead, the wife may take another within one year. Any husband who abandons his wife and joins himself to an unlawful marriage shall fast seven [Col. 0406C] winters with a severe fast, or fifteen with lighter fasts.

Anyone who has committed many evils—homicide, killing a person, and unlawful intercourse with animals and with women—should go to a monastery and fast continually until the end of his life if he has committed very many offenses.

## Chapter XX. On the Impropriety of a Man’s Seeing His Wife Naked, and on His Inability to Have Intercourse with Her

A man ought not to see his wife naked. When a man and woman have been joined in marriage, and the man is unable to have intercourse with her, the woman may leave him and marry another if this condition in the man is manifest.

Parents ought to give women who are to be married to men; except that if the woman wholly objects, saying that she does not want him, then, if he wishes, she may omit the marriage and choose entry into a monastery.

If a woman does not wish to live with the man to whom she was previously married, the money he gave for her shall be returned to him, together with a third part of her inheritance. If he does not wish this, he shall lose the money, and the woman may go to a monastery or preserve her chastity elsewhere.

## Chapter XXI. On Unlawful Fornication

If a husband has intercourse with his wife in the manner of a dog, let him fast forty days; if he has intercourse with her with her entrails, let him fast ten winters. Anyone who has intercourse on Sunday, whether by day or night, shall fast three days.

A husband must not have intercourse with his wife for forty days before Easter, nor for seven days before Pentecost, nor for fourteen days before the Nativity of the Lord.

## Chapter XXII. On Various Homicides

[Col. 0407A]

If anyone kills another in homicide, in anger and secretly, let him fast three years; some prescribe seven. Whoever consents to homicide and then commits it shall fast five winters; some prescribe seven, and he shall not enter a church for forty days.

Whoever kills his own servant shall fast one year. Whoever causes another impotence in the genitals or inflicts a wound upon him shall compensate him for that wound, perform his work until the wound is healed, pay the physician’s fee, and fast two or three fasts. If he does not know how to make compensation, let him fast twelve months.

Whoever kills someone shall fast three winters. But if he wishes to compensate the victim’s relatives, let him fast one and a half years. If anyone wounds another, let him fast forty days for the shedding of blood.

## Chapter XXIII. On the Killing of a Bishop, Presbyter, or Monk

If anyone kills a bishop or presbyter, the matter belongs to the jurisdiction of the king or bishop. Whoever kills a presbyter or monk shall be subject to episcopal jurisdiction as to whether he should lay down his arms and go to a monastery, or fast seven winters.

## Chapter XXIV. On Various Homicides

If anyone kills another in a public fight, or out of necessity while recovering his lord’s property, let him fast forty days. If anyone kills another without it being homicide, let him fast twelve months.

If anyone kills his father, mother, sister, brother, son, or daughter, the matter belongs to episcopal jurisdiction. Some prescribe that he do penance in a foreign land for ten winters. A man who hates his brother is a murderer, as the evangelist John says.

## Chapter XXV. On How Brothers May Take Kinswomen as Wives, and on Various Other Matters

Two brothers may marry two sisters, and a father and son may marry a mother and daughter.

If a male slave and a female slave join together by mutual consent, and afterward one of them is manumitted but cannot redeem the female slave, she must gain her freedom in whatever way he is free. Any free man who takes a female slave as his wife must not afterward abandon her if she had previously been a slave by mutual consent.

Whoever frees his pregnant wife, however, the child is nevertheless a slave. A man who is in a lawful marriage must not have intercourse for three days before the Lenten fast, nor for the entire forty days until the ninth day after Easter.

Whoever has a husband or wife, even unlawfully, must nevertheless buy food for that person in whatever way he can, because the prophet says: “The earth is the Lord’s.”

If a man and woman are joined in marriage, and one wishes to be God’s servant while the other does not, or if either of them is an unbeliever or is healthy, they may separate by mutual consent if they wish.

## Chapter XXVI. On a Man’s Washing after Intercourse

[Col. 0408A]

If a husband has intercourse with his own wife, let him wash before going to church.

If a woman rejects her husband and afterward does not wish to repent and make peace with him within five years, the husband, with the bishop’s consent, may take another wife.

If a husband is taken captive, let his wife wait six years; and a man should do the same for his wife if she is taken captive. If the husband takes another wife and the captive returns after five years, he shall leave the later wife and take back the captive woman whom he had previously married in the same manner.

When a man has been joined in adultery to a woman belonging to his wife’s household, after his wife’s death he may be lawfully joined to that woman as his wife.

## Chapter XXVII. On Young Men and Girls, and the Age at Which They Can Govern Themselves

[Col. 0408B]

A girl of fourteen years may have authority over her own body. When a young man is fifteen years old, he shall be under his own authority; thereafter he may become a monk if he wishes, but not before.

A female shall remain under the authority of her parents until she is thirteen or fourteen years old; after that age her master may take her with her consent.

If a father is very poor, he may give his son into service until seven years have passed; nevertheless, he must not do so without his son’s consent.

If an enemy deprives a man of his wife and he cannot recover her, let him take another, since this is better than committing the offense of adultery.

## Chapter XXVIII. On the Intercourse of Kinsmen, and How Long a Pregnant Woman Must Abstain from Her Husband

People may marry in the fifth degree; and in the fourth degree, if such a case occurs, they should not be separated; in the third degree they should be separated.

A woman must abstain from her husband for seven months before he has intercourse with her, and for forty days after her childbirth. Any husband who has intercourse with his wife during that period shall fast twenty or forty days.

A woman during her menstrual period must not enter the church or approach the Eucharist, whether she is a nun or a laywoman. If any have done these things, let them fast twenty days.

## Chapter XXIX. On a Wife Who Practices Magic

[Col. 0408D]

If a woman practices magic, enchantment, sorcery, or anything similar, let her fast twelve months, or three fasts, or forty days; let her recognize how great the offense is. If she has intercourse with a sorcerer, let her fast seven winters.

A woman who enters the church before cleansing herself from her blood shall fast forty days. If a woman mixes a man’s semen with her food and does this so that she may be dearer to men, let her fast three years.

## Chapter XXX. On a Woman Who Kills Her Newborn Child by Magic

If a woman induces an abortion by killing what has been conceived from her in the womb [Col. 0409A], and the thing conceived from the seed is killed within forty days, before it has been animated, let her fast three years as for homicide, and each week two days until Vespers and three days of the legal fast. If she miscarries, let her fast one year, or observe three legal fasts.

## Chapter XXXI. On a Woman Who Kills Her Child, and on the Eucharist and the Consumption of Blood

If a mother kills her child, let her fast fifteen winters without interruption, except on Sundays. If she is poor, let her fast seven years; if she fornicates with others, let her fast ten years.

If a woman assists her intercourse by any device, as she herself knows, let her fast two years, because the pollution is hers. One fast is appropriate for widows and women. A greater one is appropriate for a wife who has a husband if she commits adultery.

A wife must not leave her husband, even if she commits adultery. A wife may approach the Eucharist before giving birth, when it is especially necessary for her.

A woman who gives her husband’s blood as some kind of medicine shall fast forty days.

## Chapter XXXII. On the Sacrifice of Enemies, and on Enchantment Where Grain Is Burned

If anyone sacrifices even a great offering to devils, let him fast for one year. If he sacrifices something great, let him fast ten winters.

Whoever sacrifices food assigned to enemies, and afterward confesses to the priest, let the priest consider what sort of person he is, what his age is, and how knowledgeable he is; then let him judge according to what seems most just to him.

Whoever burns grain [Note: [Col. 0409D] “In the house” should be supplied. WIKLINS.] in the place where someone died, for the health of the living and of the male, shall fast five winters.

## Chapter XXXIII. On a Woman’s Enchantment, and on Whether She Commits Fornication, and on Her Vow after Her Husband’s Death
If a woman places her daughter upon a house or an oven, intending thereby to cure her fever, let her fast for seven years. If she is involved in an illicit adultery and her husband does not wish to live with her, let her go to a monastery, if she wishes; if she does not wish to do so, let her take a quarter of the inheritance. If any woman commits an unlawful adultery, let her punishment be at the discretion of her husband. A wife who has one husband, if she promises God that after her husband’s death she will not want another, and nevertheless takes another [Col. 0409D], let her then do penance because she did not fulfill her promise; thereafter let her wish to make amends around the eleventh year, after she has come under her husband’s authority—that is, whether she fulfills this promise or whether she must live with the man with whom she is out of necessity. If anyone makes a promise without the consent of the bishop, let the promise be at the bishop’s discretion—that is, whether he changes it or not.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Perjury

If anyone commits perjury in a church, or upon the book of Christ, or over holy relics, let him fast for four winters. If anyone commits perjury in the hand of a bishop [Col. 0410A], priest, or deacon, or at the consecrated cross of Christ, let him fast for one year. If anyone is brought to an oath and knows no other law than this, yet swears along with others and is thus deceived, and afterward learns that it was false, let him perform three canonical fasts. Whoever knowingly commits perjury of his own accord, and afterward recognizes that he is perjured, let him fast for three or two winters. If anyone swears upon the hands of a layman, whether with deceit or not, let him fast according to canon law before approaching the Eucharist, before he has established his fast. Some wish him to approach immediately after about twelve months, or about seven months; some wish him to approach when he has completed his fast.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On Unlawful Works on Sunday

[Col. 0410B]
