The Greeks first threaten with words anyone who works on Sunday; if he does it afterward, then at least something of his work is taken away from him; on the third occasion he is suspended, or they order him to fast for seven days. The Greeks wish both laymen and priests to approach the Eucharist every Sunday; and whoever does not approach the Eucharist on three Sundays is excommunicated according to canon law. Thus the Roman goes to the Eucharist, except that he excommunicates those who cannot. Deacons must not break consecrated bread with the Greeks, nor read the collects, nor say, “The Lord be with you.” On one and the same altar you must celebrate two Masses each day. Whoever is not present at the first Mass must not approach for the kiss before the Eucharist. Whoever does not wish to approach the Eucharist must not afterward approach the priest for bread, or for the Eucharist, or for the kiss. No one should approach the priest for the Eucharist’s grace if he cannot, according to custom, fulfill the consecration or the reading.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Celebration of Mass for a Monk and a Layman

For a deceased monk, Mass must immediately be sung on the third day, and according to what the abbot wishes. For a devout layman, Mass must be sung on the third day or around the seventh day; for a penitent, Mass must be celebrated around the thirtieth or around the seventh day, if his relatives and friends vouch for him and do at least something beneficial for his soul at the altar. Among the Romans [Col. 0410D] it is customary for the body of the deceased man and husband to be buried in the church, for his body to be anointed with chrism, for Mass to be celebrated over him, and for him to be carried with singing to the grave; when he has been placed in the grave, earth is to be thrown over him, and then Mass is to be sung for him on the first, third, ninth, and thirtieth days, and afterward as each person wishes.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On a Woman’s Reception of the Holy Eucharist

Women are to approach the Eucharist under the rules of Bruno, as Basil taught. Among the Greeks, wives were obliged to offer sacrifice, as among the Romans. There are three canonical fasts each year: one for the whole people, namely forty days before Easter; then when we pay the annual tenth obol, forty days before the Nativity of the Lord; at that time all are to pray for the army and read prayers; and forty days after Pentecost.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On Foxes, Birds, Horses, and Wild Animals That Are to Be Eaten

Fish may be purchased even if they are found dead, because they are of another species. Horseflesh is not prohibited, although many families do not wish to buy it. Birds and other animals that have been suffocated in nets are not to be eaten; nor are those pecked by a hawk, if they are found dead, to be eaten, because this is what is enjoined in the Acts of the Apostles: “Abstain from fornication, from what has been suffocated, from blood, and from idolatry.” Halices (small fish) may be eaten and are good for fever and diarrhea when boiled in water; their gall may be mixed with pepper to heal sores of the mouth.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On Bees That Sting People and on Various Matters

If bees kill a person, let them be killed before they reach the honey, and at least before they remain there overnight; and let the honey they made be eaten. If a piglet falls into water and is brought out alive, let consecrated water be sprinkled over that water, let it be fumigated with incense, and let that water be sold. If it is then dead and the water cannot be sold, let it be poured away. If anyone touches with impure hands an animal of any kind, whether a dog, cat, mouse, or any clean or unclean animal, Theodorus said that nothing harmful comes to him. If a mouse or weasel falls into a small quantity of water [Col. 0411C] and dies there, let it be sprinkled with consecrated water, and let the water be sold. Whoever sells an unclean animal out of necessity incurs no harm. Sick people are permitted to take food at any time and whenever they wish. If anyone is confirmed twice and knows this, let him fast for seven winters; if he does not know it, let him fast for three winters.

## CHAPTER XL. On Defiled Swine and Other Unclean Animals

[Col. 0412A]

If a sow eats dead flesh or swallows human blood, we nevertheless permit it not to be discarded, although it must not be eaten until it is clean. If a hen drinks human blood, it may be put to use after three months, although we have no ancient testimony concerning this. If anyone knowingly eats something bloody, mixed into half-cooked food, let him fast for seven days; if he does not know it, let him fast for three days or sing the Psalter. Whoever unknowingly swallows his own blood in saliva suffers no harm from this. Whoever eats something that a dog or mouse has eaten, or beside which a weasel has lain, and knows this, let him sing one hundred and ten psalms. Whoever sells to another water in which a mouse [Col. 0412B] or weasel has been drowned, if he is a rustic, let him fast for three days; if he is a religious person, let him sing three hundred psalms; if he had not known beforehand and learns it afterward, let him sing the Psalter.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the Sayings of Saint Dionysius and Saint Augustine

Dionysius the Areopagite said that singing was hateful to God if anyone celebrated Mass for evil people; but Augustine said that Mass ought to be celebrated for all people, whether this is done for the benefit of the dead, or for those who pray and generously offer the sacrifice. Whoever fasts for a dead person should take this as consolation for himself if he has not helped the dead person. God alone knows what the dead person has done.

Saint Sylvester said: “Let an acolyte not defame any subdeacon, nor an exorcist defame any acolyte [Col. 0412C], nor a doorkeeper defame any lector under any pretext; and we do not wish a subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, doorkeeper, or lector to be expelled, even if they have children, provided they rightly proclaim the law of marriage and of Christ. Unless, however, everything is not most certainly pure, let him speak in seven languages; and no deacon may be expelled unless there are thirty-six witnesses, nor a priest unless there are forty-four.”

# SECOND PART OF THE FIRST BOOK

[Col. 0411]

## CHAPTER I. Here Begins the First Chapter: How One Ought to Take Precautions According to the Nature of Sins

It is fitting for a priest to consider the correction of sins according to episcopal law, and not to regard the rich or the poor when prescribing for them, but to prescribe as the book directs him; for the Savior says that if a priest does not prescribe the correction of a sinner’s sins for the sinner, he will afterward demand that soul from him.

## CHAPTER II. On One Who Wishes to Turn to Penance on the Last Day of His Life, So That This May Not Be Denied Him

Saint Isidore says that it was the opinion that a man’s true confession and conversion would be acceptable to God on his final day [Col. 0412D], because the Savior says: “On whatever day a person returns to a devout life, he shall live and shall not die.” Therefore true repentance is not to be rejected, whenever it occurs; for a priest has no reason to deny true confession to such people, since God observes the inner thoughts of every person and knows the secrets of all human hearts.

## CHAPTER III. On One Who Desires to Do Penance and Receive Viaticum, That Is, the Body of Christ, Through Fear of Death; and on One Who Has Lost His Speech before the Confessor Arrived

It is necessary for a priest to console a man in this condition, hear his confession, and [Col. 0413A] at least not deny him the Eucharist; and although he has been so weakened by that illness that he cannot speak as he could before, nevertheless, if he has the testimony of the people who are with him that he made confession and received the Eucharist, then the priest should grant him remission and make his judgment concerning him.

## CHAPTER IV. On One Who Considers Confessing His Sins

[Col. 0413A] Many people would wish to undertake penance, but afterward doubt because of the multitude of their sins, despairing that they can bear what their confessor prescribes for them, and abandon it. Then this despair is considered a graver sin than the sins they had intended to confess and now neglect. But whoever [Col. 0413B] wishes to confess his sins with contrition is to be received by the priest, who is to assign him a penance suited to the purpose, so that the wounded soul, bound and wounded by sins, may reach the true remedy, that is, the forgiveness of God.

## CHAPTER V. On the Need to Abstain from Many Things Desired in Life If One Wishes to Correct One’s Sins

One thing is for a righteous person to repent of everything in which he sins against God; another is to refrain, out of love for eternal life, from those things most dear to his body. For the Apostle Paul says: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial to me.” This is the desire of the world, which benefits nothing those who [Col. 0413C] wholly surrender themselves to it; for it is exceedingly necessary for all people not to neglect confessing or correcting their sins, since it is better for everyone to correct his sins here than to remain in eternal darkness.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Prohibition against a Penitent Engaging in Any Commerce

Saint Isidore, who composed this book, speaks of one who begins penance for capital crimes and who has been expelled from the land for a time. He says that such a person is not permitted to conduct any commerce in a marketplace or to occupy himself with worldly business before he has completed what his confessor prescribed for him.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Penitent’s Not Returning to Worldly Affairs after the Contrition of His Penance

[Col. 0413D]

Holy Scripture says that it is unbecoming for a penitent, after he has made amends as his confessor prescribed, to attach himself in any way to worldly matters or ever again think of the penance for which he previously repented, because Saint Paul says: “Whoever wishes to serve God ought not to be occupied with worldly business.”

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Penitent’s Not Observing What His Confessor Prescribes for Him

Saint Peter the Apostle says that whoever, after penance for his sins, turns back to the vanity of this world is [Col. 0414A] altogether like a dog that vomits and then devours it. These are the vanities of this world: first, pride, wickedness, envy, hardness of heart, theft, drunkenness, anger, adultery, pagan sacrifice, greed, plunder, sorcery, murder, and many others like them. Certainly a person who commits these things is not worthy of any fellowship with honorable people; and although he may go to church with others, he must not presume to approach God’s altar or receive Christ’s body before he has turned to penance; afterward, let him act as his confessor prescribes and shows him.

## CHAPTER IX. On Not Granting Remission to a Penitent through the Bishop’s Intercession

[Col. 0414B]

It is not fitting for a bishop or priest to deny confession to those who desire it, even if they are deeply involved in sinful matters; for God’s mercy is so great that no person is unable to attain it. The prophet said through the Holy Spirit: “When a sinner turns from his sins to penance, then he will be healthy,” and he further says: “Confess your iniquity, so that you may be justified.” The Psalmist says that, since the Lord’s mercy is immeasurable, bishop and priest ought to judge the sinner mercifully, for no one is without faults.

## CHAPTER X. On One Who Desires the Sacrament at the End of Life, and on the Evil That Arises from This

[Col. 0414C]

It is said in the teaching of the holy apostles: “If a person desires to receive Christ’s body on his final day, it must not be denied him,” provided that he has previously been in contrition, even if he has not completely made amends; for this is his viaticum and that of all who attain the kingdom of God. And if afterward he returns to this life so that he may observe what he promised to God and to his confessor, let him enjoy his good portion and dwell with well-mannered people.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Priest’s Not Receiving a Penitent without the Bishop’s Permission, Except When He Cannot Approach the Bishop

It is especially fitting for a priest to consider carefully the need of the soul of one who seeks to do penance [Col. 0414D]: how he may prepare him most justly for God’s will and for the benefit of his soul. He should always prescribe penance for him according to the nature of his offense. If the offense is so capital that it must be prescribed by a bishop, let him be brought there; for Saint Augustine says elsewhere that if someone is bound by capital crimes, he should be brought before episcopal jurisdiction, and if he cannot reach the bishop, the priest should act in those matters as the bishop’s deputy.

## CHAPTER XII. On Penitents and the Times at Which Remission Should Be Granted Them

These customs are observed by Christians across the sea: namely, that every bishop be in his episcopal seat [Col. 0415A] on Wednesday, which we call the beginning of the fast before Lent. Then everyone in that province who is polluted by capital crimes must approach him on that day, confess his sins to him, and he prescribes for each person the correction of his sins according to the nature of the offense. Thus, with his permission, the person returns home. Then, on the Thursday before Easter, he gathers them all together at the same place; the bishop sings over them and grants them remission, and they return home with the bishop’s blessing. This is to be observed by all Christians, and the priest must carefully consider whether the penitent has corrected, with some contrition and a certain degree of completeness, what had been prescribed to him; and thus he should grant him remission according to it.

## CHAPTER XIII. On One Who Has Been Forbidden the Eucharist and Dies under This Interdict

[Col. 0415B]

If the Eucharist has been denied to someone and he dies in the meantime, we can issue no other judgment concerning these matters except what belongs to God’s judgment, since it was in God’s power that he died without the Eucharist.

## CHAPTER XIV. On One Who Wishes to Turn to Penance for His Various Sins with Complete Contrition

[Col. 0416A]

Whoever is bound by various sins and wishes to confess them to his confessor with a contrite mind and out of love for eternal life, and to correct them as he prescribes, we permit to receive forgiveness from God.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Epistle of Saint James the Apostle, in Which He Says How One Should Pray for a Sick Person and How He Is to Be Anointed with Oil

Here Saint James notes that if someone becomes ill, he should summon his priest and other ministers of God, so that they may admonish him; the sick person should make his need known to them, and they should anoint him in God’s name with holy oil [Col. 0416B]. He may be preserved through the prayers of the faithful and through the anointing, and the Lord raises him up; and if he is full of sins, they will be forgiven him. Every believer, if able, ought to obtain this anointing for himself and the regulations pertaining to it, for it is written that whoever has observed this discipline will have a soul after death as pure as that of an infant who dies immediately after baptism.

# THE SECOND BOOK

[Col. 0415]

## CHAPTER I. On One Who Voluntarily Kills a Person

[Col. 0415B]

[Col. 0415C] A layman who kills someone without fault shall fast for seven years: three on bread and water, and four as his confessor prescribes. After seven years of penance, he must always diligently regret his offenses as far as he can, if he wishes to receive forgiveness from God, since it is unknown to him how acceptable his penance will be to God. If he did this unwillingly, let him fast for five years. Whoever wishes to kill another but cannot carry out his intention shall fast for three years: one year on bread and water, and two as his confessor prescribes. If a layman kills someone unwillingly, let him fast for three years: one year on bread and water, and two as his confessor prescribes. If he is a subdeacon, let him fast for five years; if a deacon, seven years [Col. 0415D]; if a priest, ten years; if a bishop, twelve years. If anyone unwillingly kills his own child, let him fast for five years: three on bread and water, and two as his confessor prescribes. If a bishop or priest kills a person, let him lose his order.

## CHAPTER II. On a Woman Who Fornicates and Then Kills Her Child Out of Fear

If a woman kills her child by means of a potion or various other things while it is still within her, or kills it after it has been born, let her fast for ten years: three on bread and water, and seven as her confessor mercifully wishes to prescribe to her.

## CHAPTER III. On One Who Kills His Slave on Account of Theft without the Testimony of His Hundred

[Col. 0416B]

[Col. 0416C] If anyone kills a person belonging to his property and has no testimony concerning what was committed, but killed him in anger and through negligence, let him fast for two years.

## CHAPTER IV. On a Woman Who Kills Her Female Slave Out of Resentment

If a wife, in some slight fit of anger, hangs her female slave and she dies by hanging, while being innocent, let the mistress fast for seven years. But if she has witnesses that the slave was guilty, let her nevertheless fast for three years.

## CHAPTER V. On One Who Kills Himself through Some Negligence, and on One Who Is Punished for His Sins

If anyone kills himself with weapons or by various other means [Col. 0416D], at the instigation of the devil, it is not permitted that Mass be sung for such a person or that his body be committed to the earth with any psalmody. The same law is to be applied to one who loses his life through punishment for his offenses.

## CHAPTER VI. On One Who Commits Unseemly Fornication, That Is, with Animals, or Defiles Himself with Young Men, or a Male with a Male

A man who defiles himself with an animal, or a male with a male in indiscriminate acts, if he is twenty years old and able to understand that he has committed a shameful and unseemly act, must repent, confess, and fast for fifteen years. If he has a wife and commits such a thing, let him repent and fast as long as he lives, and let him not presume to receive the Lord’s body before the end of his days [Col. 0417A]. Young and thoughtless persons who have committed such a thing are to be entirely suspended.

## CHAPTER VII. On One Who Commits or Has Committed Adultery

Whoever commits adultery shall fast for seven years, three days each week on bread and water; and if a woman has a man other than her true lord, let her be worthy of the same.

## CHAPTER VIII. On a Husband Who Abandons His Wife, and on a Wife Who Abandons Her Husband and Chooses Another

A man who abandons his true wife and takes another is an adulterer. The priest must not give him the Eucharist or any of the rights proper to Christians; and if he happens to die, he must not be buried [Col. 0417B] with Christians. If a wife abandons her true husband and chooses another, let her be subject to the same law, as stated above; and let the relatives who are involved in this lose the same right, unless they first wish to turn to penance as their confessor prescribes for them.

## CHAPTER IX. On a Husband Who Has a Wife and a Concubine

To a man who has both a legitimate wife and a concubine, no priest is to give the Eucharist or any of the rights granted to Christians, unless he turns to penance. If he has a concubine and not a legitimate wife, let him do what seems appropriate to him, but let him know that he is bound to one of them, whether she is a concubine or a wife.

## CHAPTER X. On One Who Has a Legitimate Wife and Attaches Himself to Foreign Women

[Col. 0417C]

If a man has intercourse with another man’s legitimate wife, or a wife with another man’s true consort, let him fast for seven years: three on bread and water, and four as his confessor teaches him.

## CHAPTER XI. On a Man Who Marries Two Sisters, or on a Woman Who Takes One Brother after Another

If a wife takes two brothers, one after the other, as her partners, let them be subject to judgment and remain in penance as long as they live, as their confessor prescribes for them. After their death, let the priest apply to them the law applicable to Christians [Col. 0417D], if they promise that, should they live longer, they will make amends. If anyone remains in some abominable offense until his end, we cannot prescribe any penance for him except what pertains to God’s judgment.

## CHAPTER XII. On a Betrothed Woman, Whom No Other Man Is Ever Permitted to Despoil

If a woman is betrothed, it is not permitted that any other man despoil her. If anyone does this, let him be excommunicated.

## CHAPTER XIII. On a Man Who Takes a Wife or Girl by Unlawful Means

If anyone by fraud forces a wife or an unwilling slave girl [Col. 0418A] into unlawful intercourse, let him be excommunicated.

## CHAPTER XIV. On a Man Who Entices Another Man’s Female Servant into Unlawful Intercourse

If anyone by trickery entices another man’s maidservant away from him for fornication and has intercourse with her against her will, if he is an ordained man, let him lose his order; if he is a layman, let him be excommunicated.

## CHAPTER XV. On a Betrothed Girl Whom Another Man Violates against Her Will

If a girl is betrothed and in the meantime is violated or carried off by some circumstance, let her belong to the man to whom she was betrothed; and if it then happens that they become near relations, let them be joined [Col. 0418B] with permission, since she had been separated from him against her will.

## CHAPTER XVI. On a Consecrated Girl Who Is Enticed into Fornication; and on an Unconsecrated Girl Who Is Enticed into Unlawful Intercourse

If a woman is ordained according to the common rite and afterward despises the bridegroom to whom she had previously been betrothed—that is, Christ—and returns to worldly vanities, takes up a household, and considers how to appease, through her possessions and the goods of the world, the anger of God that she has aroused, she nevertheless cannot do anything worthy of a devout body, nor can any priest require confession from her before she has abandoned her sin and returned to Christ [Col. 0418C], and thereafter lives the life her confessor prescribes for her.

If a girl lives in the company of ordained women and is aspiring to the same order, but in the meantime is incited to fornication by the devil’s temptation, she is not innocent before God, although she is not ordained, because she had previously intended to become the bride of God. It is therefore especially necessary for her to confess her sins and make amends as her confessor teaches her.

## CHAPTER XVII. On a Man Who Takes a Kinswoman as His Wife

If anyone takes as his wife a near kinswoman, his father’s or brother’s widow, or his uterine mother, let him be excommunicated by all Christians. If he turns to penance as he must, let him continually make compensation and repent for as long as he lives, according to episcopal law [Col. 0418D].

## CHAPTER XVIII. On What Saint Gregory Says about Unlawful Intercourse

If anyone takes a nun, who is called the bride of God, as his wife, let him be excommunicated from the communion of all the faithful. The sacred books say that he is liable before Christ in the same way as a king’s minister who has intercourse with the king’s consort. And if this happens anywhere—if, that is, someone has fallen into it through the devil’s temptation—let them be separated, and let each of them continually do penance and pray for as long as he or she lives, according to episcopal law.

## CHAPTER XIX. On a Man Who Commits Frequent Intercourse

[Col. 0419A]

It is not permitted for any Christian to contract marriage more than twice, because Saint Paul forbids this in his teaching and instructs all people how they ought to conduct themselves in this matter. That is, if a man’s first wife has died, he may, with permission, take another wife; and if she later survives him, he must thereafter live without a wife.

## CHAPTER XX. The Earlier and Later Judgment Are the Same, Although They Appear Divided in This Way

Likewise, if a woman has buried her first husband after his death, let her take another with permission, if she wishes to choose this; and if she then survives him, let her afterward remain permanently in the order of widows as long as she lives [Col. 0419B]. If any man or woman violates this, let them not despair of God’s mercy, but let them turn back and make amends as their confessor prescribes and shows them.

## CHAPTER XXI. On How Married Couples Ought to Conduct Themselves before God

The sacred books note what every believer must do when he has first brought his legitimate wife home: namely, according to the prescription of the book, they are to preserve their chastity for the first three days and nights; then, on the third day, their Mass is to be held and received without the Eucharist; afterward they are to maintain their marriage before God and before the world as is necessary for them [Col. 0419C]. It is also fitting for all households to preserve their chastity for forty days and nights before Easter and throughout Holy Week. Thereafter, on the nights preceding Sunday, Wednesday, and Friday, every wife is likewise to preserve her purity for three months before childbirth and for sixty days and nights after childbirth, whether the infant is male or female.

## CHAPTER XXII. On One Who Commits a Deceptive Act

If anyone vows or offers something at a stream, a stone, a tree, or any other creature, instead of at the church of God in God’s name, let him fast for three years on bread and water. Even if he presumes to eat or drink in such a place and offers no sacrifice, let him nevertheless fast for one year on bread and water [Col. 0419D].

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Prohibition against Practicing Vain Divination

Certainly Christians are not permitted to practice vain divinations, as the pagans do: that is, to believe in the sun, the moon, and the course of the stars, and to establish divinations of the times for arranging their affairs. No gathering is to take place with any incantation, except with the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed, or with prayers pertaining to God. If anyone commits this vain act, let him repent and confess, and let him fast for forty days; and if afterward he again joins himself to that vanity, let him fast for three Lents.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Perjury and How It Should Be Corrected

[Col. 0420A]

If a layman commits perjury and knows that he is perjured, let him fast for four years; if he is a man of ordinary status, let him fast for five years; a subdeacon, six years; a deacon, seven; a priest, ten; a bishop, twelve. If anyone is compelled to swear falsely, or does not know what he is doing, let him fast for three years: one on bread and water, and two as his confessor prescribes. If he is not ordained, let him restore someone to freedom out of love of God. If anyone commits perjury out of fear or love of someone, or for some interest, let him distribute his property to the poor, go to a monastery, and make amends as his confessor notes for him; and let him do penance for as long as he lives.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Theft

[Col. 0420B]

If anyone steals a valuable object, let him fast as follows: if he is a layman, five years; a subdeacon, six; a deacon, seven; a priest, ten; a bishop, twelve. If anyone takes an object of moderate value, let him return the stolen property to the person who possessed it and fast for one year on bread and water. If he has no means by which to return the stolen property, let him fast for three years on bread and water.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On False Testimony

If anyone is found in false testimony, he is not permitted to receive the Eucharist until he confesses and makes amends as his confessor prescribes for him [Col. 0420C].

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Discord with One’s Neighbor

Certainly no Christian is permitted to offer a gift to God in God’s church while he has envy, anger, or any discord in his heart toward his neighbor, because his gift is not acceptable to God until he reconciles himself and makes amends with his neighbor. For the Savior says in his Gospel: “If you offer a gift at God’s altar and there remember that your brother”—that is, any Christian—“holds enmity against you, leave your gift there, go to your brother, be reconciled with him, and then come to the altar and offer God an acceptable gift.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Anger

[Col. 0420D]

If anyone is so furious and hard-hearted that he does not wish to return to any worldly justice or peace with the person who has offended him, let him be excommunicated.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On One Who Swears That He Will Not Be Reconciled with His Neighbor

Whoever becomes the enemy of his neighbor because of some disagreement and is so unyielding that he swears he will not return to friendship with the person who offended him, let him be excommunicated. If he then wishes to turn back and be reconciled, let him fast for one year because of the oath, and three Lents on bread and water; and during that year let him also fast as his confessor prescribes for him.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Prohibition against Lending One’s Money at Unjust Interest

[Col. 0421A]

Every believer is forbidden to lend his money or property at unjust interest—that is, to offer to repay more than he had previously borrowed. Rather, out of love and because of necessity, each person should lend his money and property to others as he would wish it to be done to him [Col. 0422A]. If anyone does this out of some greed, the sacred books prescribe for him a three-year fast: one year with bread and water, and two as his confessor prescribes for him.

# THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0421]

## CHAPTER I. Here Begins the First Chapter on the Marriage of Ordained Men

[Col. 0421A]

If a priest or deacon takes a wife, let him lose his order; and if, after they have been ordained, they commit fornication [Col. 0421B], let them also fast for seven years according to episcopal law.

## CHAPTER II. On Those Who Desire to Observe the Priestly Order Properly

If a priest has been accused of capital crimes before he was ordained, and previously confessed and corrected them as his confessor prescribed for him, but then, after he has been ordained, commits the same vices, he must not perform any service at God’s altar; instead, let him remain among people of ordinary status. If he wishes to return, let him make amends as the bishop prescribes for him.

## CHAPTER III. Then, on Priests

[Col. 0421C]

If a priest or deacon kills a person or commits perjury, let him lose his order; and if he wishes to turn to penance, let him make amends according to episcopal law.

## CHAPTER IV. Then, on the Ministers of God

The priests of God, deacons, and other ministers of God, who ought to serve God in God’s temple and handle the sanctuary and the sacred books with their hands, must always preserve their chastity. But if anyone of this kind falls into fornication, let him confess to his confessor and make amends as he prescribes for him, because the Savior says: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God and your Lord, am holy.”

## CHAPTER V. On How a Priest and Deacon Ought to Conduct Themselves

[Col. 0421D]

Priests, deacons, and ministers of God who neither wish nor are able to preserve before God the chastity enjoined upon them are to be removed from their ministry, which pure men render to God in God’s house. If afterward they wish to return and confess, let them make amends as their confessor prescribes for them.

## CHAPTER VI. On Bishops and Other Ministers of God
[Col. 0422A] It is certainly forbidden in all the sacred books for any bishop, abbot, or priest to keep another man’s wife with him; likewise, every minister of God who ought to serve God in chastity is forbidden to keep either his kinswoman or any other woman indoors with him on account of any business, lest perhaps through the devil’s temptation they sin with them.

### CHAPTER VII. Concerning ordained men who lend out their property at interest.

[Col. 0422B] If a bishop, abbot, priest, or similar minister of God lends his money at an unjust rate of interest and does not remember what the Savior says through David the psalmist: “Then you ought to use his wealth who does not hand over his money at any unjust interest,” whoever acts against this is not worthy to receive the Eucharist until he has corrected it, as was said above—that is, through a three-year fast.

### CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the occupations of ordained men.

No priest or deacon is permitted to be a prefect or steward, or to be occupied with worldly business, except with those matters to which he has been appointed.

### CHAPTER IX. Concerning an ordained man who takes pleasure with a woman.

[Col. 0422C]

It is not fitting for a true minister of God, who is occupied with God’s service, to go from place to place or from house to house desiring his neighbor’s wife, without his teacher’s permission. But if anyone has this habit, let him repent and make satisfaction as his confessor prescribes.

### CHAPTER X. Concerning the same matter.

It is not fitting for a monk who has vowed himself to God and accepted the holy rules to desire any worldly honor or to violate what he has vowed to God. If he does so, let him repent and make satisfaction as the bishop prescribes to him.

### CHAPTER XI. Concerning the offenses of monks and nuns.

If a monk and a nun, who have consecrated themselves to God and vowed their vow to God, violate this through the devil’s temptation, let them be separated from all ordained men. If they wish to return to God, let them first confess with tears and make satisfaction for as long as they live, as the bishop of the province prescribes to them.

### CHAPTER XII. Concerning women’s ministry at the altar, which does not belong to them.

We often read in the sacred books that it is not right for any impure laywoman to handle the divine mysteries at [Col. 0423A] Christ’s altar, nor the sacred books, nor the sanctuary, which consecrated men ought to handle with their hands, since Saint Paul strictly prohibited this.

### CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the duty of every priest to know his statutes.

Every priest ought to know the teaching belonging to his holy order, to teach it to the people, and to prepare them for God’s judgment and for the benefit of their souls.

### CHAPTER XIV. Concerning Saint Augustine’s sending to Saint Gregory at Rome, and Saint Gregory’s sending him a reply.

As soon as Saint Augustine had introduced baptism among the English people and established and ordained servants of God everywhere, [Col. 0423B] he sent a letter to Rome to Saint Gregory, who was pope there, and asked him to send him by letter what should be done concerning nocturnal pollution, which often happens to men in sleep: whether on the following day he could go to the Eucharist or, if he were a priest, consecrate the Eucharist.

He sent him a wise reply and said that every minister of God should carefully inquire from what causes nocturnal pollution arises, since it originates in the sleeping mind from three causes. Sometimes it arises from natural infirmity and weakness; sometimes from an excess of food and drink; and sometimes when someone thinks about and meditates on vain and forbidden things during the day—things which, when he thinks about them while awake by day, come to him at night while asleep.

Therefore, when someone is polluted in [Col. 0423C] sleep through carnal weakness, this was not within his control. Let him earnestly pray to God and ask forgiveness from God. If it arises from excess food or drink, let him be liable to penance; nevertheless, the Eucharist should not be denied him, nor the celebration of Mass if he is a priest, especially if it is necessary and no other priest is present to perform this ministry. But if another is present who can perform this ministry, it is better for him to omit it that day and diligently [Col. 0424A] seek remission through psalmody and almsgiving.

But if it happens in the third manner—when a man sees, thinks about, or meditates on a forbidden thing by day, and a guilty love and burning desire arise, and through this, or through the devil’s deception, he is polluted in sleep—he is not permitted to receive the Eucharist on the following day after this has happened to him. Rather, he must confess it and make satisfaction as his confessor prescribes.

### CHAPTER XV. Concerning the fact that it benefits a priest nothing to be just if he does not wish to lead the unjust away from their injustice.

Here it is said, as Saint Paul teaches, that every priest appointed to teach God’s people should spare none of them out of fear of any man [Col. 0424B] or for any money, but should preach to all people what they must do and what they must avoid, if he himself wishes to be saved on the day of judgment before God himself.

### CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the conduct of priests.

Every priest should be what he has been called to be. “Priest” is a Greek word and in Latin signifies “one who gives what is sacred” (*sacrum dans*). He himself ought to give what is sacred to the people over whom he has been appointed teacher and shepherd—that is, he should show them holy conduct and examples.

Let him warn them lest the terrible word be said of them which the Savior spoke concerning the shepherds of the people of Israel:

“Woe to you shepherds, who consume the milk of the flock, clothe yourselves in their wool, and, when they have grown fat, slaughter them; when they are weak, you do not strengthen them; when they are sick, you do not heal them; when they are broken, you do not restore them; when they are scattered, you do not gather them; and you do not seek the scattered. Now all my flock is rebellious, because they have no shepherd, and they have become food for all wild beasts.”

All this is said concerning bishops and priests, who must lead God’s people to judgment on the day of judgment, each person to the portion that had previously been assigned to him in life.

## BOOK FOUR

It should be known why this fourth book is not divided into chapters, although the preceding books are divided into chapters: namely, because this fourth book has been extracted from three others. If anyone cannot quickly find something in the three books, it is found in the fourth, concerning both greater and lesser matters, more clearly and more quickly.

[Col. 0423]

[Col. 0423D] If any bishop kills a man, let him lose his order and fast for twelve years: seven on bread and water, and for five years three days each week, while using his ordinary food on the remaining days.

If a priest or monk kills a man, let him lose his order and fast for ten years: five with bread and water, and for the other five years on three days each week, while using his ordinary food on the remaining days.

If a deacon kills a man, let him lose his order and fast for seven years: four with bread and water, and for three years let him fast on three days each week, while using his ordinary food on the remaining days.

[Col. 0424D] If a cleric kills a man, let him fast for six years: three with bread and water, and for three years let him fast on three days each week, while using his ordinary food on the remaining days.

If a layman kills someone, let him fast for five years: three on bread and water, and for two years on three days each week, while using his ordinary food on the remaining days.

If anyone kills an ordained man or his kinsman, let him leave his country and his property, go to Rome to the pope, and afterward do as the pope prescribes to him.

If any bishop commits fornication or adultery, let him fast for twelve years; a priest or monk for ten years, a deacon for seven, [Col. 0425A] a cleric for six, and a layman for five, according to what is written above concerning homicide.

If any bishop, priest, monk, or deacon had a partner before he was ordained, and abandoned her out of love for God and received ordination, and afterward they joined together again through fornication, let each fast according to his order, as written above concerning homicide.

If anyone fornicates with a nun who has been betrothed to God as her bridegroom, if he is a bishop, let him fast for twelve years: seven with bread and water, and for five years three days each week on bread and water, while using his ordinary food on the remaining days, except meat alone. Let each person fast according to his order, likewise as has been said above concerning homicide. And [Col. 0425B] let the nun fast for ten years, entirely as has been written above concerning priests.

If anyone wishes to fornicate with a nun and she does not consent, let him fast for one year on bread and water for that unjust desire.

If anyone wishes to fornicate with another man’s lawful wife and she does not consent, let him fast for three Lents for his unjust desire: the first at midsummer, the second at the autumn equinox, and the third at the Nativity of the Lord.

If anyone wishes to fornicate with a woman and she does not consent, let him fast for forty days and forty nights on bread and water.

If anyone deprives another of his daughter, let him make compensation among the friends, and let each of them fast for one year [Col. 0425C] on bread and water; on the remaining days let them use their ordinary food except meat. Thereafter let him take her as his wife, if the friends consent.

If the devil so besets anyone that he mates with mute beasts, let him confess to his confessor and fast for fifteen years: seven on bread and water, and in each of the seven years let him fast three Lents on bread and water—one Lent before Easter, the second after Pentecost, and the third before the Nativity of the Lord—and let him always fast on Wednesdays and Fridays for as long as he lives.

If anyone has the habit of polluting himself voluntarily, let him fast for three years: in each of those years three Lents on bread and water, and on the remaining days let him abstain from meat every day except Sundays [Col. 0425D] .

If anyone destroys another by incantations, let him fast for seven years: four on bread and water, and for three years on three days each week on bread and water.

If anyone strikes someone with a club, let him fast for three years on bread and water, and for two years let him fast on three days each week on bread and water. If the man dies from the blows, let him fast for seven years, entirely as written above.

If anyone uses incantations to win someone’s love for himself, and gives him something in food or drink, or by any kind of incantation, so that his love for him may thereby increase, if a layman does this, let him fast for half a year on Wednesdays and Fridays on bread and [Col. 0426A] water, and on the other days let him use his ordinary food except meat alone. If he is a cleric, let him fast for one year on bread and water for two days each week and abstain from meat on the remaining days. If he is a priest, let him fast for five years: one on bread and water, and for four years every Friday on bread and water, while abstaining from meat on every other day.

If anyone practices sorcery or divination, or keeps vigils beside a stream or any other creature rather than in God’s church, let him fast for three years: one on bread and water, and on Wednesdays and Fridays on bread and water; on the remaining days let him use his ordinary food except meat alone.

A wife is likewise liable if, through any incantations, she brings forth a child, or drags it to [Col. 0426B] crossroads and along the ground; all this is great paganism.

If a wife voluntarily causes her infant to perish within her by means of her drink, or corrupts it by some other means, let her fast for seven years: three on bread and water, and on the remaining days let her use her ordinary food except meat alone.

If a layman wounds another, let him compensate him for the wound and pay for the medicines, and let him fast one Lent before the Nativity of the Lord on bread and water.

If anyone wounds a cleric, let him fast two Lents—one before midsummer and the other before the Nativity of the Lord—on bread and water every other day.

If anyone breaks into God’s church for the sake of theft, let him return what was stolen and fast for seven years, as is written above concerning homicide.

[Col. 0426C] If anyone steals food or clothing, and hunger and nakedness have compelled him to do so, let him fast for three weeks on bread and water. But if he is able to return the theft, he is not to be compelled to fast; rather, for the love of God, let remission be granted him.

If any Christian sells his own child or his neighbor’s for a price, let him have no fellowship with Christians until he has redeemed the child from servitude. If he cannot obtain him, let him give as much money as he had previously received for him, and redeem and free him from servitude, and let him fast seven weeks on bread and water. If he lacks the means to redeem him, let him fast twenty-eight weeks on bread and water.

If anyone eats blood or dead flesh, and does not do this from necessity, let him fast for twelve weeks, every other day on bread and water.

If anyone strikes a wild animal with an arrow, and it nevertheless escapes, and is found dead after the third day, and a dog, wolf, fox, bear, or wild animal of another kind has attacked it, no Christian is to touch it.

If a wolf of any kind tears apart someone’s livestock, and the animal then dies, no Christian is to touch it. If anyone does so, let him fast four weeks on bread and water. If it survives and is then killed, let them eat it with permission.

If a wild animal is suffocated in a net, no one is permitted to use it. If anyone uses it, let him fast four weeks, every other day on bread and water.

[Col. 0427A] If anyone finds a dead fish in a fishpond and eats it, let him fast four weeks on Wednesdays and Fridays on bread and water, and on the remaining days abstain from meat. If anyone finds a dead fish in a river, it may be eaten.

If an ordained man goes hunting, if he is a cleric, let him abstain from meat for twelve months; a deacon for two years, a priest for three, and a bishop for seven.

If any bishop or ordained man repeatedly and deliberately becomes drunk, let him either abstain from this or lose his order. If a monk vomits from excessive drunkenness, let him fast for thirty days.

If a priest or deacon vomits from drunkenness, let him fast for forty days. If a layman vomits from drunkenness with permission, let him fast for forty days. If he makes another drunk [Col. 0427B] by deceit, let him fast for forty days.

If a mouse falls into water, let it be removed, and let the water be sprinkled with consecrated water. If it is alive, let the water be sold; but if it has died in it, let the water be poured out and the vessel washed.

It is also said elsewhere that if a large amount of food has been collected there, let it be sprinkled with consecrated water, and let the food be sold if necessary and if someone greatly needs it.

The faithful may marry in the fifth generation; and if they are found to be related in the fourth, they are not to be separated; in the third generation they are to be separated.

A woman during her menstrual period is not to enter a church or receive the Eucharist, whether she is a nun or a laywoman. If she does so, let her fast for twenty days.

If anyone sells something which a dog, mouse, or [Col. 0427C] weasel has damaged or begun to eat, and he knows this, let him chant one hundred psalms; if he does not know it, let him chant fifty psalms.

If anyone loses the Eucharist through his own carelessness, let him fast three Lents, every Friday on bread and water; on the remaining days let him use his ordinary food except meat.

If an unconsecrated particle falls to the ground through carelessness, let him chant fifty psalms.

If anyone neglects consecrated Eucharist so that it is kept too long and some impurity is in it, or it no longer has its proper form, let him fast forty days.

If anyone vomits the host through drunkenness or lust, let him fast forty days.

If anyone vomits the Eucharist because of illness, let him fast seven days or chant two Psalters.

If anyone throws a host into fire or into a river so that it may decay and be eaten, let him chant one hundred psalms.

If a dog devours someone’s vomit, let the person who vomited fast one hundred days; if he did not know this would happen, let him fast forty days.

If a host is impure or too old, let it be burned.

If a mouse eats a host through the negligence of the person who was responsible for preserving it, let that person fast forty days; whoever loses any part of a host shall fast twenty days.

Whoever loses his chrism in the presence of the people and afterward does not find it, let him fast three Lents or one year.

[Col. 0428A] Whoever spills the chalice during his Mass shall fast thirty days.

Whoever eats before going to the Eucharist and afterward receives the Eucharist shall fast seven days.

If a husband and wife are joined in marriage, and one of them wishes to become a minister of God while the other does not, or one of them is ill and the other healthy, they may nevertheless separate by mutual consent if they wish, and this must take place with the testimony of the bishop.

A minister of God who has been polluted in sleep shall rise, chant seven psalms, and bend his knee to the ground at the end of each verse, and fast the next day on bread and water; or let him chant thirty of the psalms that seem best to him, bending his knees to the ground at the end of each verse.

[Col. 0428B] If a pig, hen, or animal of any kind eats from a human body or drinks his blood, let the animal be killed and given to the dogs.

If anyone burns another person’s house, let him fast for three years, every other day on bread and water; on the remaining days let him fast in the opposite manner and abstain from meat.

If an animal of any kind falls into a water pit and is found dead there, let the pit be cleansed and consecrated water sprinkled in it. If anyone tastes from it before the pit has been consecrated, let him fast one week on bread and water; if he did not know, let him fast one day on bread and water.

If anyone cannot endure, because of illness or softness, this fasting and severity which his confessor prescribes, he is permitted to redeem his fast with piety and worldly means. Thus, if someone is rich, let him give thirty solidi for a twelve-month fast; if he is not so rich, let him pay twenty solidi; if he is not even that wealthy, let him give ten solidi. If he is poor and does not even have ten, let him give three solidi, since a rich man can more easily give thirty solidi than a poor man can give three. A true solidus shall always consist of twelve obols.

Almsgiving of this kind is to be divided into three parts: one is to be placed on God’s altar; another is for redeeming people from servitude; and the third is to be kept for distribution to ecclesiastical needs.

A one-day fast can be redeemed by one obol, or by two hundred psalms, or in another way: let him chant “Have mercy on me, O God” twelve times and twelve Our Fathers, and at the end of each verse prostrate himself on the ground before God’s altar. If someone does not know psalmody, then for a one-day fast let him chant fifty Our Fathers and prostrate himself the same number of times.

A seven-year fast may be redeemed within twelve months if someone chants a Psalter each day, another at night, and fifty psalms in the evening.

A seven-day fast can be redeemed with one Mass; a four-month fast with ten Masses; a seven-month fast with twenty Masses; and a twelve-month fast with thirty Masses.

If anyone wishes to intercede for himself through true love of God, it is said in the sacred Scriptures that almighty [Col. 0429A] God grants human beings remission of sins in twelve ways.

The first remission of sins is through the washing of baptism.

The second remission is through love of God and of human beings: that one love God with one’s whole heart, and then one’s neighbor—that is, every Christian—as oneself.

The third remission is through the distribution of alms, since it is written that just as fire is extinguished with water, so almsgiving erases human sins.

The fourth remission is through psalmody and the shedding of tears: that one repent and weep for one’s sins as one does because of the death of a friend.

The fifth remission is through confession of sins: that one confess one’s sins to one’s confessor, reveal one’s secrets to him, and afterward make compensation as he has prescribed.

The sixth remission is that, out of love for God and for the salvation of one’s soul, one overcome the unjust desires of one’s body and subdue oneself so completely through fasting and other virtues that the inner man—that is, the soul—may be regarded as pious.

The seventh remission is that one abandon one’s property, children, and homeland out of love for God, go to a foreign land, and end one’s life there.

The eighth remission occurs when someone departs this life through punishment; his friends, while he is alive, can redeem him and obtain remission for him before God through pious services and their worldly possessions.

The ninth remission is mercy and good faith.

The tenth remission is when we turn someone from his sins to the will of God.

The eleventh remission is that, out of love for God, one forgive the offenses of those who have offended against him, since the Savior says in his Gospel: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.”

The twelfth remission is martyrdom, as happened to the thief before the Lord’s Passion, when the Savior said to him: “Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in my Father’s kingdom.”

These are the divine commandments which we must observe: first, true love of God and human beings, chastity, fasting, steadfastness; let us be humble, moderate, kind, patient, gentle, hospitable, full of almsgiving and holy vigils; let us be merciful and peaceable.

Let us abandon these things: pride, greed, envy, vainglory, [Col. 0429D] theft, robbery, fornication, gluttony, homicide, perjury, lying, cursing, and strife.

The season for acts of service comes each year, so that everyone may speak with his confessor, begin his fast with his confessor’s permission, and confess to God and to his confessor the offenses he has committed—whether homicide, killing a man, fornication, or any of the things by which we can sin against God.

Then, O man, have true faith toward God and pray diligently during this devout season, since you know what you have done: with your fasts, your almsgiving, and your prayers, in the best way you know. Come to church every Sunday [Col. 0430A] and pray there diligently for yourself, for all baptized people, and for your confessor; then you will have prayed for us all.

My beloved, I ask you to consider how you were born into this world; how and what you give back to this world in return; how your body and soul will be separated; afterward, in what place of habitation your soul must await the day of judgment; and also the time when your soul and body will be reunited and then led to God’s judgment.

Then you and every human being will justly receive recompense according to your works and will receive judgment from that tribunal. Thereafter, with soul and body, you will obtain either eternal life or eternal death, according to how you have previously sinned—both eternal life and boundless punishment.

Then, when you first rise in the morning, sign yourself most diligently and pray to God. When you go to bed, do the same, asking that through God your sins may be forgiven and that after death he may grant you eternal rest and his mercy.

Come, my beloved, consider what our parents once were and what we now are; or who among those who were covered by the dust of the earth one hundred years ago now appears. Such shall we soon be when the soul has departed from the body.

Come, my dear one: since God grants us time, let us beware of sins and of those vices which the devil suggests to us. All anger comes from the devil, and all strife, and all misfortune. Let us therefore resist him, calm our spirit, and implore God’s mercy [Col. 0430C] and his help, so that we may be able to observe his commandments.

Let us attend our churches on Sundays and feast days, and often between these times—the more often, the better. Let us beware of envy, anger, useless words, gluttony, blasphemy, double-talk, false testimony, homicide, perjury, frequent fornications, and every impurity of our bodies.

Let us also consider how we ought to prepare our soul and body, since God grants us the opportunity to be occupied with this, so that at least after this world we may have rest through God’s mercy.

My Lord, I ask you, who say in your Gospel to all the truly faithful, “Ask, and it will be given to you”: my Lord, I humbly ask you to grant me what I beg, if it pleases you, and may the salvation of my soul endure forever together with the blessing of my worldly life.

If anyone swears an oath in the hands of a bishop, priest, or deacon, or at the altar, or upon Christ’s consecrated cross, and commits perjury, let him fast three years. If anyone commits perjury upon an unconsecrated cross of Christ, let him fast one year; whoever commits perjuries shall fast three years.

If anyone fornicates with a woman, let him fast three years, or two [years] fully. If anyone commits adultery with another man’s wife, let him fast four years: two complete years, and the other two in three Lents, with three days each week.

Whoever has intercourse with a delicate man, or with another male, or with a beast, let him fast ten [Col. 0431A] years. It is said elsewhere that whoever has intercourse with a beast shall fast fifteen winters, and sodomites shall fast seven years.

If a delicate man has intercourse with a delicate man, let them do penance for ten years. If a delicate man has committed fornication once through carelessness, let him fast four years. If it is habitual, as Basil said, if he is not ordained, fifteen years—one year entirely as a woman. If he is a boy, two years the first time; if he does it again, let him fast four years. If he did it during the daytime, one year or three Lents. If he pollutes himself, let him fast four days without meat. If he desires to fornicate but cannot, let him fast forty days or twenty. If he is a boy and does this often, let him either be hanged or fast twenty days.

If a wife fornicates, let her do penance for three years [Col. 0431B]. If she imitates the same manner of fornication with herself, let her do penance for one year. The same penance applies to widows; and a woman who has a husband deserves a greater penalty if she fornicates.

Whoever places semen in the mouth shall fast seven years. Some have judged this to be the worst [crime], so that they should do penance until the end of their lives.

Whoever has intercourse with his mother shall fast fifteen years and never cease except on Sundays and the feasts of the saints; he shall also go to a foreign land and fast there for seven years.

Whoever has intercourse with his sister shall fast seven years. Some canons say twelve years, because [Col. 0432A] “their mother encountered those things which oppose these”—a materially uncertain reading. [Note: [Col. 0431B] “I would prefer to read: ‘because it is fitting for their mother to oppose herself to this woman.’ WILKINS.]

Whoever fornicates frequently: the first canon judges that he should do penance for ten years; the second canon judges seven years; if it occurs because of someone’s weakness, some say three years.

If a brother has intercourse with his brother through bodily union, let him fast fifteen years without meat.

If a mother has intercourse with her little son, let her fast three years, so that she does not taste meat for one day each week until evening.

Whoever pollutes himself with impure thoughts shall do penance until the thought has passed.

Whoever loves women in his mind shall ask God’s forgiveness. If he seeks their friendship—that is, love—and does not obtain it, let him fast seven days.

If anyone kills a man in revenge for his kinsman, let him act as a homicide for seven or ten years; [Col. 0432B] if he pays compensation, let him fast for half that period.

If anyone kills a man in revenge for his mother, let him fast three or ten years; a homicide [shall fast] ten or seven.

If anyone kills a monk or cleric, let him lay aside his weapons and serve God, or fast ten years; and this shall be under episcopal jurisdiction.

Whoever kills a bishop or priest shall be subject to royal jurisdiction.

Whoever kills a man at the command of his lord shall fast forty days. If he does it in anger, let him do penance for three years; if he does it without cause, let him fast one year; if he kills a man through drunkenness or some lack of skill, let him fast three years; if he kills a man in a pointless quarrel, let him fast ten years.

## FROM THE SECOND BOOK OF THE PENITENTIAL OF THE SAME ECBERHT, IN THE BODLEIAN LIBRARY AT OXFORD, UNDER THE TITLE [Note: [Col. 0431] “For these canons, see above my Preface to Ecgberht’s Canonical Collections.” MANSI.]

### HERE FOLLOW VARIOUS JUDGMENTS CONCERNING VARIOUS OFFENSES

[Col. 0431]

[Col. 0431C] I. If anyone performs the duty of prayer too late or too lukewarmly, let him redeem it with tears, sorrow, and prayers.

II. If anyone falls asleep while prostrate in prayer, let him cleanse this fault by threefold prayers, together with a threefold chanting of Psalm 50, while prostrate on the ground.

III. If anyone presumes to play or occupy himself with stories during prayer—which is a most wicked thing—let him atone for it through vigils, tears, and prayers. If he makes a habit of it, let him atone through a greater penance.

IV. If anyone stumbles even slightly while chanting a psalm, let him prostrate himself on the floor of prayer and ask the Lord’s forgiveness.

V. If any cleric or monk, being in bodily health, is absent from vigils and daily offices, let him lose communion.

VI. If any cleric is absent from vigils without bodily incapacity, let him be deprived of his stipend and excommunicated.

VII. If any cleric, after the signal has been given, does not immediately hurry to the church [Col. 0432C], he shall be subject to correction.

VIII. If anyone during prayer and the psalms runs here and there because of restlessness and weariness, or lets his wandering eyes stray during the office itself, let him do penance according to the prior’s judgment.

IX. We decree that a cleric who is found to have been drunk, as the order permits, shall be removed from communion for thirty days, or handed over to corporal punishment.

X. If any cleric or monk is a drunkard, let him do penance for three months on bread and water.

XI. If any cleric is wanton, insolent, mocking, foul-mouthed, given to jesting, fickle, angry, fearful, or obstinate, let him do penance for three days according to the prior’s judgment.

[Col. 0432D] XII. If any cleric swears by created things, let him be rebuked most severely. If he persists in the vice, let him be excommunicated.

XIII. If any cleric, without the command of his prior, makes useless journeys through the streets of the city, let him do penance.

[Col. 0433A] XIV. A cleric is not to walk through streets and passageways [Note: [Col. 0433D] That is, places where the people gather], unless compelled by a definite and very important duty of his office.

XV. If any cleric presumes to speak alone with a woman alone without two or three witnesses, which the ancient statutes of the canons prohibit, let him be severely corrected and perform public penance according to the measure of his sin. The holy Fathers Augustine, Jerome, Basil, Gregory, and very many others prohibited this in their decrees.

XVI. If anyone thinks of something that is according to the Lord’s commandment but does not do it, he will be condemned by the Lord as a liar and a despiser, unless he does penance for this in the present life.

XVII. If anyone determines to do things that do not please the Lord, let him do penance according to the measure of his sin, [Col. 0433B] and let what he rashly and unjustly determined be revoked as invalid.

XVIII. If anyone does not provide guests and pilgrims, with joy and eagerness and according to his ability, the necessary services, if he is a layman, let him do penance at the priest’s discretion and thereafter amend his conduct, lest he hear from the Lord: “I was a stranger, and you did not receive me” (Matthew 25).

But if he has been appointed to some ecclesiastical rank, let him perform greater penance, with tears and prayers, according to the dignity of his consecration, and afterward amend his conduct.

XIX. If anyone turns over evil and useless thoughts in his heart, let him immediately reveal them to his priest and, according to the priest’s counsel, seek divine help through fasts, almsgiving, tears, and [Col. 0433C] prayers, until this passion departs.

XX. If anyone in the clergy inflicts damage, however small, upon someone, let him return what belongs to another and do penance for three days; a layman for two days.

XXI. If anyone sins against another person by word, and, remembering it immediately, is inclined to ask forgiveness, let him receive pardon from the person whom he is known to have wronged. But whoever either does not ask or does not ask sincerely shall undergo appropriate penance according to the extent of the injury.

XXII. If anyone does not consent to make satisfaction when he has inflicted an injury, let him be admonished to offer satisfaction to the injured person. But if he does not listen, “let him be to us as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matthew 18).

XXIII. If anyone, being grieved, refuses reconciliation when the person who caused the grief makes satisfaction, let him be severely afflicted by the harshest fasts until he willingly accepts the satisfaction.

XXIV. Those who exchange insults with one another, if they recognize that these ought quickly to be forgiven mutually, are not to be judged by another, since they hasten to grant each other pardon—provided, however, that they do not presume to exceed the bounds against one another too frequently.

XXV. If any cleric presumes to become proud, let him be excommunicated from his customary food more often [Note: [Col. 0433D] See below, chapter 32]. Likewise, the wanton shall be subject to a similar sentence.

[Col. 0434A] XXVI. If anyone consecrated in any ecclesiastical rank becomes a striker—which ought not to happen—let him be corrected most severely by ecclesiastical satisfactions. If he does not amend, let him undergo penance for three months with the utmost devotion to weeping, taking only bread and water.

XXVII. If any presbyter, deacon, or monk loves idleness, foolish talk, buffoonery, loquacity, sleep, laziness, torpor, and things of this kind, let him do penance for three days.

XXVIII. If any monk violates the rule’s ordinance and, contrary to the custom of the elders, presumes to eat meat, let him be subject to confinement and penance for a period of six months.

XXIX. Whoever slanders, or willingly listens to one who slanders, [Col. 0434B] shall do penance for three days; but if the slander concerns a superior, he shall do penance for seven days.

XXX. Whoever slanders a brother, or listens to a slanderer and tolerates it, ought to be excommunicated. If the slander concerns one who presides, he shall be excommunicated even more severely.

XXXI. If anyone refuses to be reconciled to his brother whom he hates, let him do penance on bread and water until he is reconciled to him.

XXXII. If anyone is awakened and becomes distressed and angry against the person who awakened him for prayer [Note: [Col. 0434D] Alternatively: let him be excommunicated from his customary food, as above, chapter 25], he ought to be excommunicated and not eat until, moved to contrition, he acknowledges his folly and, thus converted, receives pardon.

XXXIII. If any Christian is found to be a liar—which ought not to happen, since Christ our Lord, [Col. 0434C] from whom he has received his name, is truth—let him do penance according to the character and extent of the lie. For it is written: “You will destroy all who speak lies. And every lie is from the devil” (Psalm V).

XXXIV. If any Christian devotes himself to idle tales, foolish talk, joking words, and things that provoke laughter—which, according to the Lord’s teaching and that of his holy apostle Paul, is recognized as sin—let him disclose it to his priest and do penance according to the priest’s judgment and the measure of the offense.

Let no Christian consider lightly or neglect even his smallest sins, which are commonly committed in vain and empty thoughts, in excessive and idle speech, and in deeds performed without necessity, such as craving food, immoderate laughter, excessive sleep, and countless things of this kind. Rather, let him fear to stand before the tribunal of the strict Judge to give an account of them. For it is written: “For every idle word that people have spoken, they will give account to God on the day of judgment” (Matthew I). Scripture likewise says: “God will leave nothing unpunished.” Therefore, let him do penance for these and other sins.

XXXV. If anyone is contentious or contradicts holy commands, or is a liar or disobedient, or loud in speech, or angry, or a mocker, or more devoted to joking than is proper, or answers harshly, or—quite generally—does anything contrary to the authority of the sacred Scriptures, let him do penance according to the measure [Col. 0436A] and deed of the sin, at the priest’s discretion.

[Col. 0435]

# DIALOGUE OF SAINT EGBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK, ON THE INSTITUTION OF THE CATHOLIC [Note: [Col. 0435] First published at Dublin in 1664 through the work of Sir John Waraeus.]

(Mansi, *Collection of Councils*, vol. XII.)

[Col. 0435B] At the very beginning of this page, we ask your venerable holiness to receive with grateful affection those matters which, attested by sacred writings and directed by us to pontifical foresight, have been sent to you—for “love builds up”—and, if any of them appear worthy of acceptance, to confirm them by the signature of your brotherhood. If, however, anything is recognized as less suitably expressed, may you, as the most discerning interpreter, not disdain to insert what is more useful. After you have provided an account in writing of what has been sent to you, we wish your blessedness to make your counsels known to us in written letters, so that, as the pages pass back and forth, we may, bound together by the bonds of love, hold one and the same understanding. But so that your brotherhood may judge more certainly concerning the matters mentioned above, we set forth both together, namely, the questions [Col. 0435C] and the answers.

## I. QUESTION

If necessity compels it, to what extent is the oath of a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or monk valid?

### ANSWER

The ranks mentioned above shall have the authority to give testimony according to the level of their advancement: a presbyter according to the number of 120 tributaries, a deacon according to the number of 60 tenants, and a monk according to the number of 30 tributaries. This applies in a criminal case.

But if a dispute arises concerning the boundaries of fields, a presbyter may, by the testimony of his oath, transfer to the Church in a legal action land equivalent to one tributary. The same is granted to two deacons. The testimony of three monks shall likewise suffice.

## II. QUESTION

May a presbyter or deacon become a witness to the final words spoken by dying persons concerning their possessions?

### ANSWER

Let him also take one or two with him, so that “every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses,” lest the relatives of the deceased, under the pretext of greed, contradict what is said by ecclesiastical persons when only a presbyter or deacon bears witness.

## III. QUESTION

[Col. 0436B]

If a presbyter, deacon, or monk is accused of unspeakable crimes, with no evident proof, by what means may he be cleared if he is innocent?

### ANSWER

Since it is established that faithful testimony rests on the mouth of two or three witnesses, and since we do not wish, through an overly narrow judgment, to appear to oppress one who is without sin, so that innocence may be overwhelmed by the difficulty of producing witnesses, let any accused person established under the rule, from any of these three ranks—namely, presbyter, deacon, or monk—be permitted to produce witnesses to purify himself. It is entirely sufficient that he bring with him two or three whom he can obtain in his defense.

But if he lacks defenders, [Col. 0436C] or because of the terror of his accusers, let he himself alone suffice in the defense of his innocence; neither the testimony of witnesses nor children begotten by him exposes him as guilty. For it is dishonorable either that iniquity should increase through the negligence of priests or that purity should be oppressed through lack of rights [Possibly: “strength”]. Therefore we decree that the person against whom the crime is charged shall place the Lord’s cross upon his head and testify by the One who lives forever, whose gallows is the cross, that he is free from such a sin; and thus everything is to be left to the judgment of God.

## IV. QUESTION

If a presbyter or deacon is found, after examination, to have been corrupted, with what vigilance must the shepherds take care that, even after removal from office, he does not attempt to minister in another diocese, thereby causing some people to be scandalized?

### ANSWER

If a presbyter or deacon, expelled by his own bishop when his faults have become clear, attempts to minister in another church, as soon as this becomes known he shall be expelled by the bishop of that diocese. Thus, throughout all the sees of the Churches, he shall never be settled but always wander as an exile and fugitive, until, humbled by prolonged affliction, he returns to undertake ecclesiastical obligations.

## V. QUESTION

What are we to hold concerning the sacred ministries that a corrupted presbyter performed before his condemnation, or that he rashly usurped after being condemned?

### ANSWER

As for the ministries that he performed under the assumed name of priest, though he had not been ordained and the people were unaware, we by no means believe that they should be rejected; for, while ministering good things wickedly, he himself became guilty but did not harm others.

But in the case of one who knows that the causes have not been expiated and yet has become a participant with the condemned man, how can a perfection be attributed to him which was not in the giver [Note: [Col. 0437D] Something appears to be missing. HARDUINUS]? The ensuing wording is defective: he who, through what he had, gave by wrongful offices, is to receive condemnation, so that his participant may incur a like sentence of excommunication.

But this may not rightly be understood of baptism, since baptism must not be repeated. The remaining ministries conferred by an unworthy person, however, appear less secure.

## VI. QUESTION

May a presbyter or deacon who, without the consent of his superior, transfers to another diocese minister there?

### ANSWER

We forbid the deserter of his own Church to minister in another. The person ministering in this way is to be removed from his office by his own superior until he is reconciled to his Church.

## VII. QUESTION

If anyone, of whatever dignity, in wrongful boldness presumes to retain under himself a fugitive cleric or monk, what do you decree concerning such persons, dearest brothers?

### ANSWER

Whoever among the brothers, contrary to the prohibitions of the venerable canons, receives a fugitive cleric or monk without letters of peace, and, when summoned, persists in this obstinacy, shall pay what has been established: thirty shekels, fifteen to the bishop of the place and fifteen to the abbot whose monk he received without the consent of his superior. He shall release the fugitive; otherwise, being further excommunicated, he shall suffer the consequences.

But if any layperson who is known to preside over monasteries receives in this manner someone who does not belong to him, he shall pay the prescribed due: ten shekels to the king and ten to the abbot whose dependent he received without the consent of the Church. He shall release the deserter; otherwise, he shall pay again as much money as he is known previously to have paid.

After this, let him be excommunicated until satisfaction is made, so that obstinate persons who, fearing God not at all, utterly despise the censure of excommunication may at least, being partially punished by the loss of their possessions, not presume to act contrary to the regulations. This decree shall also apply to monasteries of virgins that are shown to be under a rule.

## VIII. QUESTION

If one of the monks has become involved in a sacrilegious pollution, is the punishment of the crime to be pursued now by the laypeople who are their relatives? [Note: [Col. 0437D] That is, whether it pertains to them.]

### ANSWER

In the case of those who commit grave or minor offenses within the Church, no punishment belongs to those who are outside, especially since the Apostle says that all cases of the Church ought to be judged before priests.

But if ecclesiastical persons commit some crime among laypeople—committing homicide, fornication, or theft—it has been resolved that these persons are to be seized in every way by the secular authorities against whom they have sinned, unless the Church is willing to make satisfaction for such persons.

As for laypeople who become involved in sacrilegious pollution with veiled women, the law has not judged that they should be punished in the same way as public fornicators, but by a doubled payment of thirty shekels. That is, we wish adulterers to pay sixty pieces of silver to the Church, because serious cases require more serious and harsher remedies.

## IX. QUESTION

Should presbyters, whether foreigners or of our own people, be permitted to minister indiscriminately without the knowledge of the bishop of the place in whose diocese they are again staying, especially under laypeople, being nowhere settled and established beforehand either by place or by pontifical authority?

### ANSWER

We do not allow foreign presbyters, or those ordained without a title, to travel through the provinces and minister anywhere or administer the sacraments without the knowledge of the bishop of the place. We have decided that they may administer what is necessary; but we do not wish such men admitted to sacred ministries without great discernment.

## X. QUESTION

If a brother or sister does not reclaim something belonging to them, as they suppose, in such a way that it may be peacefully restored to them by the bishops judging the Churches, but, having contempt for their own bishop, irrationally [Note: [Col. 0438D] Something appears to be missing here.
