HARD.] hastens to obtain [Col. 0438C] what they claim as theirs, whether justly or unjustly, what do you say concerning this?

### ANSWER

Whoever—brother or sister—does not reclaim something belonging to them, as they suppose, through the judgment of the priests of the Churches, but obtains it by force through external authorities, shall completely lose even what he or she violently seized, or shall be expelled from the Church.

Nor do we thereby impose prejudice upon that person’s Church. After the death of the anathematized person, with everything intact and remaining in its proper condition, and with the parties placed before the court, let careful inquiry be made into what antiquity or truth establishes; then the matter is to be left to the judgment of the bishops.

## XI. QUESTION

What do we say concerning this, since some people, possessing monasteries of their own, arrange them so thoughtlessly that after their death two persons of either sex together possess one monastery or divide it equally [Note: [Col. 0438D] Read: “if among themselves.” HARD.], if they have not agreed to remain together?

### ANSWER

Let the venerable community choose one of the two whom it wishes to preside over it, and let this person, with the counsel of the bishop of the place, be appointed abbot.

When the person who presides has died, let the second, who was counted at the beginning as heir, assume the governance of the entire monastery, which he had previously been glad to possess not wholly but only in part—provided that he is found worthy, as his bishop judges.

[Col. 0439A] If anything else is done, let such a testament be judged ineffective and invalid; and let the person who makes it, consents to it, or accepts it be anathema.

## XII. QUESTION

If a layperson kills a cleric or monk, should the price of blood be paid to his relatives according to the law of the birth-status of his parents, or should satisfaction be made to his superiors with a greater sum? Let your unanimity decree this.

### ANSWER

If any layperson kills a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or monk, let him do penance according to the established degrees of penance, and let him pay the price to the bishop of his Church [Note: [Col. 0439D] Read: “according to the decree of the universal [council].” HARD.] according to the universal council: for a presbyter, eight hundred shekels; [Col. 0439B] for a deacon, six hundred; and for a monk, four hundred pieces of silver—unless the dignity of his birth or the nobility of his lineage demands a higher price.

For it is not just that the service of holy profession should lose in the higher rank what the outward life under lay dress is known to have possessed by right of parents. But if he lacks the means to redeem himself from the homicide he has committed, he is to be handed over to the king for punishment, lest the killers of God’s servants think that they can sin with impunity.

This punishment which we have determined for the homicides of presbyters shall also apply to abbots who are without ordination, unless a synodal college, after higher deliberation, judges one of them to be subject to a higher or lower penalty.

## XIII. QUESTION

If, by the mutual agreement of both parties, a lawful marriage is dissolved because of the infirmity of the husband or wife, may the healthy but incontinent partner enter a second marriage, with the infirm partner’s consent and promise to observe continence forever? What does your holiness judge concerning this?

### ANSWER

No one acts against the Gospel or against the Apostle without punishment; therefore we do not at all give consent to adulterers.

Nevertheless, we impose on no one burdens that cannot be carried without danger; but the commandments of God we proclaim confidently. As for the person whom infirmity prevents from fulfilling them, we leave the matter to the judgment of God alone.

Therefore, lest we appear by silence to encourage adulterers, or lest the devil, who deceives adulterers, rejoice over adulterers, hear [the wording is uncertain: *ultoribus*]: “What God has joined, let no human being separate”; and likewise, “Let the one who can accept it accept it.” For often, through changes in circumstances, necessity breaks the law. What did David do when he was hungry? Yet he is without sin. Therefore, in doubtful matters no sentence should be pronounced.

But counsels must be risked for the salvation of others, on this condition: that the person who has devoted himself to continence must in no way enter a second marriage while the first partner is alive.

## XIV. QUESTION

What are we to say if a layperson declares that a cleric or monk is liable on account of certain offenses committed long ago under lay status but not yet resolved—whether because he did not prevail, or because he previously concealed the matter by silence until now—and now presses the Church with trouble and importunity?

### ANSWER

Whoever among the secular people desires to undertake the service of holy profession must, when questioned, answer that he is not bound by servile status, that he has not openly committed an unamended homicide, and that he does not presently hold under himself property belonging to another, except that he is God’s servant because of the offense of sin.

But if he has deceived the Church of God and fraudulently concealed his crime, it has been decided that the Church shall have the power either to dismiss him or, if it wishes, to make satisfaction on his behalf.

As for those found to be such persons, [Col. 0440B] we wish them to be forcibly removed from the threshold of the Church. From the day of the summons, no time is thereafter to be granted to the Church for concealing the guilty; rather, out of reverence for God, they are to be let go without any injury—and more properly so—because the Church is a house of propitiation, not a den of thieves. Read the dedication of Solomon’s temple.

Whatever possessions he had offered to the Church, the priest shall return to him, so that he may have the means by which to redeem himself.

## XV. QUESTION

For what crimes may no one be made a priest, or for what crimes is someone already ordained deposed?

### ANSWER

The ordination of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon shall then be considered valid if he is not proved to be contaminated by any grave crime; if he has not had a second wife, nor one abandoned by her husband; if he has not performed public penance; if no part of his body appears mutilated; if he is not burdened by servile status or by his origin; if he is shown to be released from the bonds of civic office; and if he has acquired literacy. We have chosen such a person to be promoted to the priesthood.

But no one may be ordained on account of these crimes, and we declare that all who have been promoted while guilty of them are to be deposed: namely, those who worship idols; those who surrender themselves as captives to the devil through diviners, seers, and enchanters; those who attack their faith with false testimony; those contaminated by homicides or fornications; those who commit thefts; and those who violate the sacred name of truth through the recklessness of perjury.

Such persons, however, ought not to be admitted to obtain the grace of communion except through public penance—and not in order to recover the honor of their former dignity. For it is foreign to the Church that penitents should administer the holy things, since they were once vessels of vices.

## XVI. QUESTION CONCERNING THE FAST OF THE FOUR SEASONS

The customary fasts of the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth months: are they to be celebrated at the beginning of those months or otherwise? And by whose authority, in what manner, or for what reasons were they instituted? A harmonious judgment explains that they should be celebrated uniformly by everyone throughout all the sees of your love and the Churches of the English [Note: [Col. 0440D] Read: “or uniformly.” HARD.].

### ANSWER

Since the world is contained by four regions—the East, West, South, and North; since the human being consists of four elements, namely fire, air, water, and earth; since the inner sense is contained by four virtues—prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice; since the four rivers of Paradise flow to irrigate the whole earth as a type of the four Gospels; since the year turns through four seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter; and since the square number is recognized as perfect in every respect—the ancient Fathers therefore instituted the fasts of the four seasons according to the law of God, and now, in the New Testament, holy men and apostolic teachers have done likewise.

### I. Concerning the first month

The Lord says to Moses: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year” (Exodus XII, 2). And again the Lord says to Moses: “Observe the month of new grain, when you came out of the land of Egypt, as a statute throughout your generations” (Deuteronomy XI, 1).

The holy Fathers established this fast in the first week of the first month, on Wednesday and Friday and Saturday, except during the days of Lent. In the Church of the English, however, we observe this same fast of the first month indiscriminately during the first week of Lent, as our teacher, blessed Gregory, transmitted and prescribed it through our instructor, blessed Augustine, in his antiphonary and missal.

### II. Concerning the second fast

The fast of the fourth month arose from the old law, when the law was given to Moses on Mount Sinai. The Lord commanded that the people should be prepared to hear his voice on the third day and should not approach their wives.

And again the Lord says to Moses: “You shall take the first fruits of all your produce and offer them to the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy XXVI, 2).

This was also established in the New Testament, in accordance with what the Lord says: “The children of the bridegroom cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them” (Matthew XIX, 15), and so forth.

In accordance with the succession of the seasons, after the Lord’s ascension into heaven, when his bodily presence had been withdrawn, the fast of the fourth month was then proclaimed, on the second Saturday. Blessed Gregory, through the aforesaid legate, directed that this fast be celebrated in the Church of the English during the full week after Pentecost, in his antiphonary and missal.

Not only do our antiphonaries attest this, but also those which we ourselves saw, together with their missals, at the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0441D] ### III. Concerning the third fast

The fast of the seventh month is commanded by the Lord through Moses, who says: “Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: The tenth day of the seventh month shall be called holy; you shall humble your souls in fasting. Every soul that is not afflicted on that day shall perish from its people” (Leviticus XXIII, 7).

This fast is celebrated in the Church according to ancient custom, both because the days grow shorter and the night grows longer, and because the approaching death by which our life fails is shown through the decline of the sun and the increase of the night. That death will be restored to life in the judgment of God and in the resurrection.

If the end of our life is expressed by the shortening of the days, and the arrival of death by the increase of the night, we have judged it necessary, in memory and remembrance of so great a mystery, to humble our souls every year—as we read that the children of Israel did at this time—in fasting and affliction, not only from food but from every contagion of vice. We heed the Gospel saying: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you; but the night will come when no one can work” (John XII, 35).

The Church of the English customarily celebrates this fast during the full week before the equinox, disregarding the reckoning of the third week.

### IV. Concerning the fourth fast

The fourth fast was observed by the ancients in November, according to the Lord’s command to Jeremiah, which says: “Take the scroll of the book and write in it all the words that I have spoken against Israel and Judah. And it came to pass that in the ninth month they proclaimed a fast in the sight of the Lord for all the people in Jerusalem” (Jeremiah LVI, 2).

Therefore, by the authority of the divine Scriptures, the Catholic Church maintains the custom and celebrates the fast and observance of the tenth month on the fourth Saturday, on account of the approaching venerable solemnity of our Lord Jesus Christ. Several days beforehand, abstinence from flesh and fasting are to be practiced, so that each believer may prepare himself to receive the communion of Christ’s body and blood with devotion.

The English Church has likewise always been accustomed to observe this during the full week before the Nativity of the Lord—not only on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, but also for twelve continuous days in fasts, vigils, prayers, and generous almsgiving. In monasteries and in parishes, this has reportedly been practiced before the Nativity of the Lord as a customary fast.

For this custom arose in the Church of the English, thanks be to God, from the time of Pope Vitalian and Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, and was held almost as a lawful observance: not only clerics in monasteries but also laypeople, with their wives and households, would come to their confessors and, through weeping and generous almsgiving, cleanse themselves during these twelve days from participation in carnal desire, so that they might receive the Lord’s communion at the Nativity in greater purity.

Besides these appointed fasts, many also fasted on Wednesday and Friday because of Christ’s passion, and on Saturday because on that day he lay in the tomb.

[Col. 0443]

[Note: [Col. 0443C] I restored this title from what I observed above in the Preliminary Notice to Ecgbert’s Canonical Works, since in all the preceding editions of Labbe this little book appeared under the other title: “The Canons of the Venerable Priest Bede,” etc. I explained there, on the basis of the Ballerinis, that it forms part of a larger work composed by Ecgbert. MANSI.]

# THE CANONS OF SAINT EGBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK, ON REMEDIES FOR SINS (C)*

## PREFACE

[Col. 0443A]

We have excerpted the following very brief statements concerning remedies for sins from the records of earlier writers. In all of them, however, we have relied not on the authority of a censor but rather on the counsel of one who shares compassion. We earnestly admonish every learned priest of Christ that, in everything he finds noted here, he carefully discern the sex, age, condition, status, and person of each individual who wishes to do penance, as well as the penitent’s own heart; and that, according to these considerations and as it seems appropriate to him, he judge each matter separately.

Some must correct their errors by abstaining from food [Note: [Col. 0443D] *Penitential*: “by giving alms to others.”], some by bending their knees more often, some by standing in the form of a cross, or by doing something else of this kind that contributes to the purification of sins [Note: [Col. 0443D] *Penitential*: “to the salvation of the soul.”], while many must do all these things. All of these matters must be weighed in the examination of a discerning judge.

## I. Excerpt from the canons of the Catholic Fathers, or penance as a remedy for souls, of Lord Ecgbert, archbishop

That holy institution which was practiced in the days of our fathers never abandoned the right paths. They established for penitents and mourners remedies for their sufferings that lead to true salvation, because diversity of faults produces a diversity of remedies for penitents—just as physicians of the body ordinarily prepare different medicines or potions for different illnesses, and just as judges of secular cases do.

Therefore, good and upright judges weigh and handle different judgments, considering how they may judge rightly between the wretched and the rich, and between one case and another. How much more, then, priests of God, ought you to weigh and administer different remedies for souls invisible to human eyes, lest, through a foolish physician, wounds of the soul [Note: [Col. 0443D] *Penitential*: “fester and become worse,” etc.] become worse, as the Prophet says: “My scars have become putrid and worsened because of my folly.”

O foolish physician, do not deceive your own soul, lest you receive a double punishment for that person—whether sevenfold or a thousandfold [Note: [Col. 0443D] *Penitential*: “or sevenfold or a thousandfold.”]. Hear Christ saying: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit.” If you do not consider my judgment, another person neither hears nor sees who will judge me. O, do you not understand that God, the just and mighty Judge, sees and hears, brings hidden things into the open, and repays according to deeds?

And indeed there are some blind men, running like dogs toward the corpses of the dead or like ravens flying toward them, who are carried into the priesthood, being eager not for the Lord but rather for earthly honor, blind to [Note: [Col. 0444C] *Penitential*: “divine power.”] divine wisdom.

Gregory of Nazianzus said concerning such men: “I fear this: that dogs pursue the pastoral office, especially when they have prepared no pastoral discipline within themselves.”

Ezekiel says: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and not the flock: they drank the milk, clothed themselves with their wool, and ate what was fat; what was broken they did not bind up” (Hosea IV), and so forth.

Ezekiel likewise says: “Woe to the priests who eat the sins of my people,” that is, taking their offerings for themselves and not praying for them—consuming the sacrifices and not correcting them. When they hear that people are about to die, they rejoice and prepare themselves for plunder, like ravens for the corpses of the dead.

Now, therefore, brothers, whoever wishes to receive [Note: [Col. 0444C] *Penitential*: “to bear the name of priest.”] priestly authority should first consider God and prepare his weapons before the bishop’s hand touches his head: namely, the psalter, lectionary, antiphonary, missal, baptistery [Note: [Col. 0444D] *Penitential*: “the computus, the penitential canon.”], [Col. 0444D] martyrology, the annual cycle for preaching with good works, and the computus with its cycle [Note: [Col. 0444D] *Penitential*: “then prayers for the commendation of souls, and homilies to be preached to the people throughout the annual cycle on Sundays and each feast day.”]—that is, the law of priests.

Afterward, he should have his penitential, which is arranged in this order according to the authority of the canons, so that it may first investigate the distinctions among all cases, without which a right judgment cannot stand. For it is written: “In no matter should you appear undiscerning; distinguish what, where, how long, when, and how you ought to do it.”

Therefore, not everyone is to be weighed on one and the same scale, even if they are bound by the same vice. There must be discernment among each of them: between rich and poor; free and slave; infant, child, young man, adolescent, old man; dull and knowledgeable; layperson, cleric, monk, bishop, presbyter, deacon, subdeacon, and lector; those in a rank and those without one; those married and those unmarried; foreigner [Note: [Col. 0444D] *Penitential*: “native.”], virgin, woman, [Note: [Col. 0444D] *Penitential*: “widow.”] canoness, or religious woman [Note: [Col. 0444D] *Penitential*: “nun.”]; [Col. 0445A] weak, sick, and healthy.

According to the condition of beasts or human beings; whether continent or incontinent; whether by will [Note: [Col. 0445D] *Penitential*: “by will, necessity, or chance.”] or by chance; publicly or secretly; whether he amends in compunction through necessity or through will—the holy apostles established the places and times of conferences.

After them came the holy Fathers and Saint Paphnutius [Note: [Col. 0445D] *Penitential*: “Paphnutius.”]; then the canons of the holy Fathers; then others, including Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, and Theodore.

From the words and judgments of all these we have faithfully written these things, so that all may be saved and not become fainthearted, since “the powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wisdom VI).

Likewise, in Jesus son of Sirach: “In judging, be merciful to the insignificant as a father, and on behalf of a man to his mother” (Ecclesiasticus IV).

Saint James also said: “Judgment without mercy will be for the one who has not shown mercy; but mercy exalts itself over judgment” (James II), so that he himself may obtain the same, as Saint Benedict [apparently says]: that is, for those who truly do penance.

That is, those who truly do penance in fasting and weeping, in almsgiving and prayers, and do not do again what they have committed; and if they do, nevertheless do not persist in it. For God said: “You conceived evil; I forgave. You spoke evil; I forgave. You did evil; I forgave. You wish to persist in evil; I do not forgive.”

Therefore, do not forgive those who persist in evil, but judge them with strict judgment according to the canons, so that others may have fear.

## II. Concerning fornication
[Note: [Col. 0445D] Many provisions from the canons of this and the following chapters can be found in Burchard, Ivo, Anselm, Gratian, the *Panormia*, and similar compilers of canon law, as the distinguished Antonius Augustinus observed in his notes on this penitential.]

If a young man sins with a virgin, let him do penance for one year. If it happened once and accidentally, let the penance be mitigated, but still continue for a full year. If a young girl under twenty years of age sins, let her do three forty-day periods of penance and the appointed fasts. If, because of this sin, they have been assigned to human servitude, forty days; if there was only an attempt and no pollution, let the penance be twenty days.

If a widow has been violated, let her do penance for the whole year, together with the fasting days in the alternate year. If this continued until a child was conceived, let her do two full years and two further years with a lighter penance. If they also killed the child, three years, followed by four further years with a lighter penance.

If a monk sins with a laywoman, let him do penance for three years; let her do two years and the appointed fasts. If a layman sins with a nun, let him do penance for two years and the appointed fasts; let her do three years. If this continued until a child was conceived, four years; if they also killed the child, let them do penance for seven years.

If an unmarried man violates another man’s wife, let him do penance for two years. If a married man violates a virgin, likewise, so that in the first of these years he abstains from his own wife if she consented; otherwise, an additional measure of penance is to be imposed.

If a married man violates another man’s wife, let him do penance for three years; during the first of these years he shall abstain from his own wife, if she consents. If a married man violates his female slave, let him do penance for one year, three forty-day periods, and the appointed fasts during the first three months, and let him abstain from his wife. If she suffered unwillingly, let her do penance for forty days; if she consented, three forty-day periods and the appointed fasts.

If a young man sins with his sister, let him do penance for seven years; with his mother, seven years, and, for as long as he lives, never without penance. If with male partners, seven years; if it was habitual, seven years; or, if he is a monk, seven years.

Whoever sins with an animal shall do penance for one year; if he is a monk, two years. Laymen who repeatedly fornicate with laywomen shall do penance for three years; and the more frequently or carelessly they have done so, the more the period and severity of the penance shall be increased.

Whoever has long been devoted to fornication, perjury, theft, and other vices shall do penance for seven years. Whoever is polluted by an alluring embrace of a woman or by a kiss shall do penance for thirty days. Whoever is polluted through immodest physical contact with her shall do penance for three months.

A boy who voluntarily pollutes himself shall do penance for thirty days; a young man, forty days. Whoever is polluted through neglect in obscene speech shall do penance for seven days. Whoever is unwillingly defiled through an assault of thought and nature shall recite fifty psalms for four successive days and fast on Wednesday and Friday until the ninth hour or evening.

Those who marry in a consecrated church: Whoever is polluted in a church through a dream shall do penance for three days. A married man shall abstain for forty days of the year before Easter and Christmas, and every Sunday, Wednesday, and Friday from the time the conception is made known until after the child is born. The husband shall abstain from his wife for three months.

After giving birth, a wife shall abstain from the church: thirty days if the child is a boy, forty if it is a girl. But during the time of menstrual blood: for whoever then [Note: [Col. 0446D] *Poenit.*, “has married or joined himself”] has intercourse shall do penance for thirty days; whoever [the surviving text is incomplete] for seven days.

A parent whose child dies because of neglect without being baptized shall do penance for one year, and never be without some form of penance. If the priest responsible, having been summoned, neglected to come, he shall be disciplined by the judgment of his bishop because of the destruction of the soul.

Nevertheless, in every case it is permitted to the faithful—indeed, it is commanded—when they happen to find unbaptized persons near death, to rescue their souls from the devil through baptism: that is, to baptize them with simple blessed water in the name of the Lord, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Water is then poured over the person who has been immersed. Therefore those who are able—especially faithful monks who possess knowledge of baptizing—ought, whenever they go farther afield, always to carry the Eucharist with them.

[Note: [Col. 0446D] Perhaps “chrism,” says Antonius Augustinus.]

### III. On Killing

[Note: [Col. 0446D] Some things here do not agree with the *Penitential*; perhaps Ecgbert is writing here according to his own understanding, whereas in the *Penitential* he speaks in the words of Isidore. MANSI.]

Whoever kills a monk or cleric shall lay down his weapons and serve God, or do penance for seven years. Whoever kills a layman out of hatred or in order to possess his inheritance shall do penance for four years. Whoever kills in revenge for a brother shall do penance for one year, and thereafter two years, three forty-day periods, and the appointed fasts.

Whoever kills in sudden anger and quarrel shall do penance for three years. Whoever kills accidentally, one year. Whoever kills in a public war, forty days. A slave who kills at the command of his master, forty days. A free man who kills an innocent person at the command of his superior shall do penance for one year, followed by two further periods of three forty-days and the appointed fasts.

Whoever, in a quarrel, renders a man crippled or deformed by a blow shall repay the medical expenses, the compensation for the scar, and the value of his labor until he is healed, and shall do penance for half a year. If he has no means to make this restitution, he shall do penance for a full year.

Whoever rises to strike a man, intending to kill him, shall do penance for two weeks. If he was a cleric, seven months. If he also wounded him, forty days; if he was a cleric, a full year. He shall also give the injured man money according to the severity of the wound, although the law does not [Note: [Col. 0447D] *Poenit.*, “command or order this”] require it, so that the injured man may not [Note: [Col. 0447D] *Poenit.*, “be scandalized”] cause scandal.

A woman who voluntarily loses her child before forty days shall do penance for one year. If after forty days, three years. If after it has been born, she is to be treated as a murderer. Yet it makes a great difference whether a poor woman acts because of the difficulty of raising the child [Note: [Col. 0447D] *Poenit.*, “because of the difficulty”] or, as a fornicator, in order to conceal her crime.

Whoever knowingly commits perjury under compulsion from his master shall do three forty-day periods of penance and the appointed fasts. Whoever knowingly understands the force of an oath or perjury and commits perjury by the hand of a bishop or priest, or at an altar, or upon a consecrated cross, shall do penance for three years. If upon a non-consecrated cross, one year. If by the hand of a man, among the Greeks—[Note: [Col. 0447D] “Greeks,” *Graecos*; the note says that “pagans,” *paganos*, seems to mean *Ἕλληνες*]—it counts for nothing.

Whoever, having been led into perjury while ignorant [the reading is corrupt], afterward recognizes his perjury, shall do penance for one year [Note: [Col. 0447D] *Poenit.*, “if, having been deceived and unknowingly, he commits perjury and afterward…”].

### IV. On Unclean Meat

Whoever eats unclean meat or meat torn apart by beasts shall do penance for forty days. If compelled by the necessity of hunger, the penance shall be much lighter.

If a mouse falls into a liquid, it shall be removed and the liquid sprinkled with blessed water. If it is dead, the entire liquid shall be discarded and not consumed by people, whether it is milk, beer, or anything similar. If the mouse or weasel has died after falling into the liquid, the liquid shall be purified and sprinkled with holy water, and may be consumed if necessity requires it.

If a bird defecates into any liquid, the dung shall be removed, the food cleansed with blessed water, and it may be consumed. Whoever unknowingly swallows blood with saliva shall not be harmed. Whoever unknowingly pollutes himself while eating shall not be harmed. But if he knows, let him do penance according to the degree of the pollution.

### V. On Capital Sins

[Col. 0447D]

Now, therefore, I shall explain the capital sins according to the canons. The first are pride, envy, fornication, vainglory, long-lasting anger, worldly sorrow, avarice, and gluttony of the belly. Augustine added sacrilege—that is, theft of sacred things, which is the greatest theft—or serving idols, that is, through auspices and similar practices. Then there are adultery, false testimony, theft, robbery, habitual drunkenness, and idolatry; the effeminate, sodomites, slanderers, and perjurers. These, therefore, are the capital sins.

[Note: [Col. 0447D] The seven capital sins are commonly designated by this expression: S. A. L. I. G. I. A. The ancients vary. See Cassian, Theodulf, Burchard, and the penitential books.]

Saint Paul, Augustine, and other saints reckoned that for these sins abundant almsgiving should be made and a long period of fasting observed. That is, as others judge, for capital sins—namely, adulterers, murderers, perjurers, fornicators, and their like—a layman shall do penance for four years, a cleric for five, a subdeacon for six, a deacon for eight, a priest for ten, and a bishop for twelve, if the practice was habitual.

### VI. On Lesser Sins

That is, theft, false testimony, and similar offenses. Laymen shall do penance for one year, clerics for two, subdeacons for three, deacons for four, priests for five, and bishops for seven years.

Likewise, if sodomy was habitual, a bishop shall do penance for fourteen years, a priest for twelve, a deacon for ten, a subdeacon for eight, a cleric for seven, and a layman for five.

If a monk fornicates with a female servant of God, he shall do penance for four years; if with a girl, seven years. Regarding parricides and fratricides, some prescribe seven years, others fourteen and seven.

### VII. On Greed and Other Vices

Likewise, a covetous, avaricious, drunken, proud, envious, rapacious, long-angry, slanderous person, or one guilty of similar things [Note: [Col. 0448D] *Poenit.*, “one who does these things”], which would take too long to enumerate, shall do penance for three years.

Likewise, if a cleric fornicates with a quadruped, he shall do penance for two years; a subdeacon, three; a deacon, five; a priest, seven; and a bishop, ten years.

Whoever fornicates with his mother shall do penance for fifteen years. With his daughter or sister, twelve years. Whoever fornicates with his natural brother through sexual intercourse shall abstain from all flesh and do penance for fifteen years.

If a cleric practices hunting, he shall do penance for one year; a deacon, two; a priest, three. If a priest, deacon, or monk takes a wife, he shall be deposed in the sight of the people. If he commits adultery with her and this becomes publicly known, he shall be expelled from the Church and do penance among the laity for as long as he lives.

Whoever dismisses his wife for another husband shall do penance for seven years.

If a cleric commits homicide and kills his neighbor, he shall do penance for ten years; if he is exiled, he shall do penance for seven, if the killing arose from hatred.

If a layman commits homicide in fury and with premeditation, he shall do penance for four, five, or seven years. If in a quarrel, four years.

Likewise, whoever sacrifices to demons in major matters, if the practice is habitual, shall do penance for ten years; in minor matters, one year. For auguries and divinations, five years. Weather-makers shall do penance for seven years.

Let penance always be observed in this order, beginning with one year and proceeding thereafter for any sin: in each week, three days without wine, mead, or meat; let the penitent fast until evening and eat dry food. Let there also be three periods of forty days on dry food, and let him fast three days until the ninth hour and three until evening.

On Sundays, at Christmas four days, at Epiphany, at Easter until the white-robed days, at the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, the feast of Saint Michael, Saint Mary, Saint John the Baptist, the twelve apostles, Saint Martin, and the feast of whatever saint is celebrated in that province, let him show charity on these appointed days [Note: [Col. 0449D] That is, let him use the same food and drink as his peers], whether clerics or laymen. In all things let them beware of drunkenness and distension of the belly.

Let them do what the Apostle says: “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10). Then penance is worthy, if this is fulfilled.

### VIII. On the Penance of Clerics

Likewise, the canon of the apostles [Note: [Col. 0449D] *Poenit.*, judged under XXV] states that a bishop, priest, or deacon who has been caught in fornication, perjury, or theft is to be deposed, but not deprived of communion, because God does not judge twice for the same offense (Nahum, according to the Septuagint).

If any bishop commits fornication and judges it natural [the text is corrupt], he shall do penance for twelve years and seek pardon from the Lord through many tears and almsgiving; after three or four years, the penance may be lighter.

A priest who sins with a girl, without the monastic vow, shall do penance for three or four years, with three forty-day periods and dry-food fasts every Wednesday and Friday. If with a female servant of God or with a male, more shall be added—namely, seven years—if it was habitual.

Likewise, deacons, if they are not monks, shall do penance for two or three years. So also a monk without a rank, if with a girl, three years. If they are deacons or monks, they shall do penance for five or seven years. If monks without a vow sin with a girl, they shall do penance for nine or ten years.

A cleric without a monastic vow who commits fornication shall do penance for one year. If repeatedly, two years. If with a canoness, two years; if repeatedly, three. If he has fathered a child, he shall do more penance—namely, four or five years; others say seven, with exile.

Likewise, a consecrated virgin with laymen without rank: if the cleric is one of the canons, one year; if repeatedly, two. If in an ecclesiastical rank, like a monk, three years.

Theodorus said: A monk who commits fornication and is not discovered shall do penance for one and a half years. Likewise, a monk who sins with a girl shall do penance for six years.

A layman who pollutes himself with a female servant of God shall do penance for two years. If he fathers a child by her, three years. If they are unmarried, three forty-day periods; some judge forty days, according to the customary rule.

Likewise, regarding sodomites: some prescribe ten years—that is, for one who has done it repeatedly—or, if the person is in an ecclesiastical rank, some prescribe seven years, some one year; for an effeminate person, some prescribe one hundred days, as for boys; for adult men, [a term of] years; for boys, two years.

Whoever sins with an animal or beast of burden shall do penance for ten years; some prescribe seven, some three, some one, and some one hundred days, as for boys. There ought to be discernment according to the kind of animal and the age of the persons, as we said above.

Likewise, if a bishop fornicates with a quadruped, he shall do penance for eight years; if habitual, ten; a priest, five; a deacon, three; a cleric, two.

### IX. On Oaths

Whoever swears an oath in a church, or upon the Gospel, or upon the relics of the saints, shall do penance for seven years. Others judge twelve years.

If he swears by the hand of a bishop, priest, or deacon, or upon a consecrated cross, he shall do penance for one year. Others judge three or four years. Upon a non-consecrated cross, one year, or seven months, according to others.

Whoever, having been deceived and ignorant, later recognizes the matter shall do penance for one year, or three forty-day periods, or forty days.

If someone is compelled for any reason of necessity, three forty-day periods; others prescribe three years or one year, with some of that time on bread and water, according to other judgments.

Perjurers shall do penance for three years. Whoever suspects something before the animal is led away, yet swears with consent, shall do penance for two years. If someone swears by the hand of a layman, among the Greeks it counts for nothing.

### X. On Women’s Abstinence

A woman shall abstain from her husband when she has conceived, until she gives birth, and for forty days after childbirth. Whoever has intercourse during these days shall do penance for ten, thirty, or twenty days.

Those who are married shall abstain for three forty-day periods and do penance [the sentence is incomplete]. Those who are married shall abstain for three forty-day periods, and on Sunday night, Saturday, Wednesday, and Tuesday, as is lawful; they shall abstain for three nights before receiving communion.

If, during Lent before Easter, a man has intercourse with his wife and refuses to abstain, he shall do penance for one year, or give its value to the church, or distribute it to the poor, or pay twenty-six solidi. If he approaches her through drunkenness or for some other reason, without habitual practice, he shall do penance for forty days.

If a woman practices divination or diabolical incantations, she shall do penance for one year, or three forty-day periods, or forty days, according to the nature of the offense.

If a woman kills someone by imitating her own magical practices—that is, through a potion or some form of sorcery—she shall do penance for four years. If she is a poor woman, four years. If a woman kills her own son by homicide, she shall do penance for eleven years.

### XI. On Auguries and Divinations

Auguries or lots—called false “saints”—or observing divinations, or promising the future through inspection of any writings, or making a vow [Note: [Col. 0450D] *Poenit.*, “or fulfilling it to a tree, stone, or any object”] to a tree or any object other than a church: if a cleric does this, or a layman, they shall be excommunicated from the church; alternatively, the cleric shall do penance for three years, and laymen for two or one and a half.

If a woman places her son upon a roof or in a furnace for the healing of fevers, she shall do penance for five years.

Do not practice such things when the moon is eclipsed, trusting that through cries and magical rites of sacrilegious custom you can defend yourselves.

Caragios and divining enchanters [Note: [Col. 0451D] *Poenit.*, “and if he attempts to employ or impose upon another or himself diabolical phylacteries, diabolical characters, herbs, or juices”]: laymen shall do penance for three days without beer, wine, or meat; others, twelve days.

If a faithful layman, out of wickedness, gets another drunk, he shall do penance for forty days. If he vomits because of illness, he is without guilt.

### XII. On Drunkenness

If through drunkenness or gluttony someone vomits the Eucharist, a cleric who is a monk shall do penance for forty days, a deacon sixty, a priest seventy, and a bishop one hundred ten [Note: [Col. 0451D] Ninety. The error may easily have arisen from XC being read as CX].

If it occurred because of illness, each person shall do penance for seven days. If not because of illness, on the day of the sacrifice, four days; some prescribe the Psalter, some twice the Psalter [Note: [Col. 0451D] Antonius Augustinus emends this as follows: “if he cast his own sacrifice…”]. If he threw his sacrifice into a fire or river, let him recite one hundred psalms.

If dogs eat such vomit, he shall do penance for one hundred days if he knew; if he did not know, forty.

Those who become drunk against the Lord’s command—if they have a vow of holiness—shall do penance according to the following measure. Drunkenness is when the state of the mind changes, the tongue stammers, the eyes become confused, dizziness occurs, and distension and pain of the belly follow. If he is a cleric, four days; a monk, fourteen; a deacon, four weeks; a priest, four; a bishop, five; superiors, three days, without wine or meat.

### XIII. On the Eucharist

If someone loses the Eucharist through negligence, he shall do penance for one year, three forty-day periods, or forty days.

If the sacrifice falls upon the ground through negligence, he shall recite fifty psalms. Whoever neglects the sacrifice so that worms appear in it and it has neither color nor taste shall do penance for twenty, thirty, or forty days, and [Note: [Col. 0451D] *Poenit.*, “the worm shall be burned”] it shall be kindled in the fire; its ashes shall be hidden beneath the altar.

If it falls all the way to the ground, he shall do penance for one day. If a star has burned, [or] the altar has fallen [the transmitted text is corrupt; Note: [Col. 0451D] *Poenit.*, “if it drips and falls in the altar”], he shall do penance for thirty days.

Whoever loses a small portion in the church and does not find it shall do penance for twenty days, reciting forty psalms each day.

Whoever loses his chrismal among the people [Note: [Col. 0451D] *Poenit.*, “among the people”] and does not find it shall do penance for forty days or three forty-day periods.

Whoever spills something from the chalice at the end of the solemnity shall do penance for thirty days [Note: [Col. 0452D] *Poenit.*, “something upon the altar from the chalice while the solemnity of the Mass is being celebrated”].

### XIV. On Various Matters

[Col. 0451D]

Whoever loses a creature, *ithus* [reading uncertain; Note: [Col. 0452D] Antonius Augustinus: *crateram*, “a bowl”], tablets, or his writing tablet, blessed salt, newly consecrated bread, or anything similar shall do penance for four days.

Whoever unknowingly eats carrion shall do penance for forty days; knowingly, one hundred days.

Whoever eats something obtained by fraud [Note: [Col. 0452D] Antonius Augustinus: “obtained by theft or fraud”], and is poor or feeble-minded, shall do penance for four days. The healthy and the sick, if they know, shall do penance for forty days. Those who do this repeatedly shall do three forty-day periods or one year.

Whoever eats or drinks something contaminated by a domestic animal—that is, a dog or cat—and knows it, shall recite one hundred psalms or fast for one day.

If someone gives another person a liquid in which a dead mouse or weasel is found, if he is a layman, he shall do penance for four days; in monasteries, he shall recite three hundred psalms.

Whoever later learns that he drank such a beverage shall recite the Psalter [Note: [Col. 0452D] *Poenit.*, “one hundred fifty psalms”].

If someone unknowingly eats something half-cooked, he shall do penance for three days or recite the Psalter. If knowingly, four days.

For a small theft, he shall do penance for thirty days over twenty years. Children of ten years who commit a theft shall do penance for four days.

If someone dips his hand into some food with an unsuitable hand, he shall make amends with one hundred blows of the palm [Note: [Col. 0452D] *Poenit.*, “blows with the palm”].

If a dead mouse or weasel is found in flour, dry food, porridge, or curdled milk, whatever remains around it shall be thrown outside; what is left may be eaten.

Furthermore, whoever is able to fulfill what is written in the penitential has done well. Whoever cannot, we offer this counsel through the mercy of God: first, for one day, on bread and water, let him recite fifty psalms while kneeling [Note: [Col. 0452D] *Poenit.*, “on bended knees in the church”], or seventy psalms without kneeling, within the church or in one place, in order.

For one day, two hundred genuflections are equivalent; or one denarius [Note: [Col. 0452D] *Poenit.*, “if he is poor; if rich, three denarii”] is equivalent for a day. Three almsgivings to three poor people are equivalent. Some say that fifty blows [Note: [Col. 0452D] *Poenit.*, “strokes”] or fifty psalms are equivalent to one day.

That is: in winter, autumn, and spring, one hundred blows or psalms; in summer, one hundred fifty psalms or blows.

Likewise, for one month during which he ought to do penance on bread and water, let him recite psalms kneeling or without kneeling—namely, six hundred eighty—and afterward let him take food on all days at the sixth hour, except that on Wednesday and Friday he shall fast until the ninth hour.

Let him abstain from meat [Note: [Col. 0452D] *Poenit.*, “and animal fat”] and wine; after reciting the psalms, he may eat other food.

In the second year the penance shall be lighter, from Christmas to Epiphany, and on the days mentioned above that are not counted as days of penance.

Likewise, whoever cannot do penance in the manner described above shall, in the first year, distribute twenty-three solidi in alms; for one year on bread and water, he shall give twenty-two solidi in alms; each week he shall fast one day until the ninth hour and another until evening; and three forty-day periods [the text is abbreviated: “3 quadr. in 2…”]. For one year, twenty solidi; for three years, eighteen solidi, making sixty-four solidi.

Powerful men shall do the following for criminal offenses, as Zacchaeus says: “Lord, I give half of all my goods to the poor, and if I have taken anything unjustly from anyone, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19). Let him also free his slaves, redeem captives, and, from the day on which he ceases to sin, not cease to receive communion.

[Note: [Col. 0453B] This is not in the letters of Saint Paul, any more than the popular saying: “By what things one sins, by those things he is punished.”]

As the Apostle says: “Whoever sins through the body should make amends through the body”—that is, through fasts, vigils, and prayers to the Lord.

Whoever has turned back and committed every evil—in shedding blood, theft, fornication, lying, oath-taking, and all other evils—and afterward wishes to serve God to the end shall do penance for three and two years, or according to the priest’s judgment.

Let the priest himself, however, consider the medicine of souls: how he may preserve his own soul and theirs by instructing them, teaching sound doctrine. Whoever ministers well acquires a good standing for himself before him who is God, blessed above all, for ever and ever. Amen.

### XV. Also on the Value of a Year or a Day

[Note: [Col. 0454B] *Poenit.*, “some permitted, for one year…”]

In the first year some prescribed four periods of three days, with one night intervening. Others say twelve periods of three days; that is, some said that once each month there should be a three-day fast. Some prescribed four days occupied with scourging or vigils; others prescribed this, others that.

The value of a day is an *agape* [Note: [Col. 0454B] Read *agape*], given to two or three poor people. Others prescribe the entire Psalter—that is, in summer—and in winter, spring, or autumn, fifty psalms. Some prescribe twelve wounds or blows, more or fewer, according to the seasons.

Some prescribe another’s labor, or bending [the text is obscure]: forty [times] twice, forty [times] three times, 120 [times] six times; and ten is to be added at the second stage, twenty at the higher, thirty above that, if there is no labor.

**In the Year of Our Lord 731. Saint Gregory II, Roman Pontiff.**

[Col. 0453]

## Historical Notice on Saint Gregory II, Pope

(*Book of the Pontiffs, from various editions*)

[Col. 0453B] **[Note: [Col. 0453D] 1. Gregory.]** The order of events now leads us to the time of Saint Gregory II, who, if all his deeds had survived, could rightly be compared with Saint Gregory the Great, with whom I began, as Bollandus, that most learned father of the Annals, asserts (Preliminary Commentary on the Life of Gregory II, 13 February). Antonius Pagius and other recent writers establish the certain dates of this pontiff’s life against the opinion of Panvinio and Baronius; Papebrochius had done so before them, although, by anticipating the ordination, he customarily separates the death from the deposition by several days.

It will soon become clear that we must not depart from their view. For of the three matters considered in determining the age of any pontiff, two—the interval between pontificates and the end, or day of death—are certain by the unanimous agreement of all; the matter considered second, namely the length of the pontificate, is enclosed between them and therefore becomes evident of itself. Nevertheless, before presenting these three matters for consideration, I shall, for the sake of scholarly instruction, resolve the remarkable disagreement found in the catalogues and manuscripts concerning the years, months, and days. [Col. 0454D]

The catalogues and manuscripts, divided into two groups, give Gregory fifteen or sixteen years. Eleven of them stand for fifteen years, while thirteen, supported by Luitprand, give sixteen. The Bergomian and Colbertine catalogues, five manuscripts, two Freherian manuscripts, one Thuanus manuscript, the Farnesian manuscript, and one Ambrosian manuscript have fifteen years. All the remaining catalogues—four of ours and two Colbertine—as well as four of our manuscripts and three Ambrosian manuscripts have sixteen years.

There is a similar disagreement concerning the number of months, for seven, eight, and nine months are assigned inconsistently to Gregory’s pontificate. Finally, the discrepancy concerning the days is still greater, since ten, eleven, twenty-two, twenty-four, and twenty-nine are found recorded in various places. These differences would certainly make the chronology of this holy pontiff extremely laborious; but since, as I said shortly before, the beginning and end of his pontificate are clear, [Col. 0455A] it is easy to determine the intervening period.

The matter therefore stands as follows. After the death of Constantine on 9 April, as we saw above, correctly recorded in the manuscripts, the same manuscripts, together with the catalogues, unanimously give an interval of forty days between pontificates. Counting these from the aforesaid day brings us to 19 May; the dominical letter F shows that in the year of Constantine’s death this was a Sunday. Consequently, the beginning of Saint Gregory II must be assigned to the very day of his ordination, 19 May 715.

The end, or death, of this pontiff is likewise consistently reported by all the manuscripts as 11 February, in the fourteenth indiction, which unquestionably indicates the year 731. [Col. 0455B] This is so because the same fourteenth indiction, which was current in the second year of Gregory’s pontificate, is mentioned by Anastasius in connection with the celebrated lunar eclipse, after which there was a great flooding of the Tiber in the fifteenth indiction; and especially because Gregory II vigorously defended the sacred images against Leo the Isaurian and the other Iconoclasts. I shall shortly establish the epoch of that madness and of the sacrilegious audacity of the Easterners.

Thus Saint Gregory governed the apostolic see with great holiness for the entire period lying between these two extremes, from 19 May 715 to 11 February 731—namely, fifteen years, eight months, and twenty-four days—as correctly stated by four Colbertine catalogues, one of the Thuanus manuscripts, two Freherian manuscripts, and the Farnesian manuscript, together with the authorities cited by Pagius. This count includes both the day of ordination and the day of death; nor do the Martyrologies in the least disturb this age as certain, although they commemorate the pontiff’s passing on the following day, or after two days. On these matters, see Bollandus under 13 [Col. 0455C] February, in the preliminary commentary on his Life.

Having completed what concerns Gregory’s age, I shall touch, in accordance with my purpose, on several matters that confirm it. These are the war against the sacred images initiated by the impious Leo, which Baronius discusses at length under the year 726, and two letters of Gregory II written on that occasion to the emperor, which clearly reveal the pontiff’s chronology.

Baronius correctly teaches, against Theophanes and despite the opposition of certain recent scholars who seek to defend Theophanes’ view, that Leo was elevated to the empire in the year 716, on 25 March, while the fourteenth indiction was still current. For the first of Gregory’s letters supports Baronius’s opinion:

> “While you were reigning in the fourteenth indiction, we carefully preserve in the holy Church, at the threshold of the confession of the holy, glorious, and foremost of the apostles, Peter, your letters received in the fourteenth, fifteenth, first, second, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth indictions” (Baronius, under the year 726).

Pagius uses the same evidence to support both his own and the recent writers’ [Col. 0455D] opinion, saying that Leo, who was proclaimed emperor in 717, wrote the letter in the fourteenth indiction, which was current in that year. And lest the error be attributed to the copyist, he adds below: “Gregory mentioned letters written to him by the emperor in the fourteenth indiction, namely in the first year of his reign.”

I confess that I was astonished at the learned writer’s negligence. Having noticed only late that Gregory’s letters had not been assigned to their proper year, he failed to see that in 717 the fourteenth indiction continued only until the September Kalends; and, if Leo’s letters were written one in each indiction, as Gregory states, there would be not eleven but ten letters, with the ninth indiction counted among them.

Moreover, under the year 741, no. 4, because the lengthy reign of Copronymus, correctly arranged by Theophanes over a series of years, conflicts with his own opinion, he completely throws it into confusion and declares Theophanes’ *Chronicle* corrupt, failing to see that an enormous sequence of events reported both by Theophanes and by the author of the *Miscellany* is thereby overturned. Therefore, [Col. 0456A] for everything to proceed consistently, the beginnings of both the Isaurian and Copronymian periods must be moved back by one year, with the corrupt indication of the indictions rejected.

Since I have arranged these matters in the *Caesarean-Pontifical Chronology*, I shall pursue the remaining points concerning Gregory II that I promised.

Leo the Isaurian, therefore, after the tenth year of his reign, as we read in the Life of Saint Stephen the Monk and Martyr, began his criminal course by throwing down the image of the Savior that had been placed above the bronze gate. But he did not promulgate public edicts for the destruction of all images everywhere until the fourteenth year of his reign, A.D. 730.

Anastasius is an advocate of this opinion. He relates [Col. 0456B] the invasion of the Lombards, followed by the donation of the Castle of Surrientes to Saint Peter in 728; and in the following year, 729, the appearance of a comet in the western sky, which Bede also reports in that same year, saying that another was seen in the east. Anastasius then writes:

> “After these events, the wickedness of that same emperor became manifest, on account of which he persecuted the pontiff, so that he compelled all the inhabitants of Constantinople, by force as well as by persuasion, to remove wherever they were found the images both of the Savior and of his holy Mother and of all the saints, and—what is cruel to say—to burn them in the middle of the city, and to whitewash all the churches that had been painted.”

The abdication of Saint Germanus also most certainly confirms this epoch, since he intervened unsuccessfully against the emperor’s audacity and impiety; Pagius discusses it learnedly under the year 730, beginning with no. 1. Accordingly, we would more correctly place the beginning of the war against the images in 730 rather than 726.

Nevertheless, since the ancient writers teach us that this war began as soon as Leo’s monstrous [Col. 0456C] crime emerged, we place the beginning of the persecution in 726 and maintain that it was publicly promulgated four years later, namely in 730.

Perhaps I shall be ridiculed for so frequently opposing Pagius. He teaches that the edict for the public destruction of the images was promulgated in 726:

> “Just as, therefore, the pagan emperors in their decennial years used to promulgate edicts against the Christians, so Leo the Isaurian, in the tenth year of his reign, raised a persecution against the Orthodox and declared war on the sacred images; and this before the September Kalends, when the tenth indiction began” (*Annals*, 726, no. 1).

But, with due respect, the Isaurian, who according to Pagius himself began to reign on 25 March 717, was, on the September Kalends of 726, in the fifth month of the tenth year of his reign. For that reason he could not have promulgated an edict, like the pagans, in a year dedicated to his decennial celebration, since decennial vows were proclaimed after the decade had been completed and a new decade had begun. Examples of this may be seen [Col. 0456D] in Cardinal Noris (*Chronological Dissertation on the Decennial Vows*). I shall not prolong the discussion beyond what is relevant.

It is true that, according to Baronius’s chronology, which I follow, Leo was in his eleventh year, which would have been especially suitable for celebrating the decennial vows. But since I have shown that the promulgation of the edict belongs to the year 730, all the learning concerning the decennials collapses.

[Col. 0457A] Once these matters are understood, the date of the two letters of Saint Gregory also becomes clear. Pagius discusses them learnedly under the years 726 and 730, against the opinion of Cardinal Baronius, who wants them to have been written before the events about which they speak had occurred.

They were therefore written after Saint Gregory had received the synodical letter of Anastasius, whom the emperor had intruded into the patriarchal see after expelling Saint Germanus—namely, in the fourteenth indiction, which began with the September Kalends of the year 730. For it is clear from Anastasius that the holy pontiff first wrote to him and afterward to the emperor.

Pagius the nephew, Antonius’s copyist, and Sommier discuss these matters explicitly; [Col. 0457B] their notes should be consulted below, sections 184 and 188.

As for why Leo appears not to have written to Gregory after 726, the reason is plain. When the holy pontiff counts, year by year, the emperor’s letters, he understands them to have been Catholic. But after the ninth indiction—that is, after 726, when the persecution of the images began—they were no longer Catholic. Therefore, if Leo sent any letters—as certainly he did, when he recognized Italy as allied against him and wished a council to be summoned—there was no reason for them to have been preserved. Gregory detested him as a most wicked heretic, as is confirmed by the council held at Rome, a fragment of which survives, and by the two aforementioned letters written a few months before Gregory’s death. Read the sequence of events in the historical annotators.

**CENNUS.**

**2. Gregory.** After the apostolic see had been vacant for forty-two days following the death of Pope Constantine, Gregory, the second of that name, was created supreme pontiff by the unanimous agreement of the entire clergy and [Col. 0457C] people on 22 May 714, contrary to Panvinio in the *Fasti*, during the reign of the emperor Anastasius.

This is proved above all by the statement of Anastasius the Librarian, who, when he reckons sixteen years, eight months, and ten days for Gregory’s pontificate and says that he died on 11 February, necessarily requires us to affirm that he began to sit in the year 714. The same is confirmed when Anastasius writes that John, bishop of Constantinople, sent letters to Gregory. If this is true, it must plainly be conceded that Gregory held the pontificate at the aforesaid time. For Theophanes makes it clear that the aforementioned John was removed from his episcopate by the emperor Anastasius in the second year of that emperor’s reign, which is A.D. 714.

This pontiff is wrongly surnamed “Dialogus” by the earlier Greeks and by certain later Latins, since that title properly belongs only to Gregory I, on account of the books of dialogues he wrote. Gennadius, in his exposition for the Council of Florence, chapter 5, section 16, and chapter 3, sections 5 and 6, either [Col. 0457D] fails to distinguish between the two pontiffs named Gregory or wrongly thinks that both should be called by this name. For in chapter 5 he calls Gregory II “the Dialogist,” while in chapter 3 he gives that title to Gregory I. See Baronius, under the year 726, no. 31.

**BIN. and LABB.**

**3. Gregory II.** The younger Roman, son of Marcellus, a monk of Saint Benedict, was made cardinal deacon of the Roman Church by Pope Constantine. Under the emperors Flavius Anastasius, Artemius, Theodosius of Adramyttium, and Leo the Isaurian, all Augusti, he sat for fourteen years, ten months, and twenty-one days. He was elected on the twelfth day before the Kalends and consecrated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. Initiated into holy orders under Pope Sergius, he was in charge of the chapels and the library.

**CIACONIUS.**

**Gregory** **[Note: [Col. 0453C] Another copy omits “II.”]** II, a Roman by birth, son of Marcellus, [Col. 0453C] sat **[Note: [Col. 0453C] Another copy: fifteen years, eight months, and twenty-two days; Codex Luc. 490: nine months and eleven days.]** for sixteen years, eight months, and twenty days. **[Note: [Col. 0453C] In another copy the whole passage beginning “He was” and ending “Augusti” is absent.]** He lived during the reigns of the emperors Anastasius, Theodosius, Leo, and Constantine.

From childhood he was brought up in the [Col. 0454B] patriarchal residence **[Note: [Col. 0454C] In another copy, the words beginning “under the…” and ending “pope” are absent.]** under the lord [Col. 0454C] Pope Sergius of holy memory. He was made subdeacon and treasurer **[Note: [Col. 0454C] In another copy, the words beginning “treasurer…” and ending “thereafter” are absent.]**, and the care of the library was entrusted to him **[Note: [Col. 0454C] Codex Luc.: “he assumed its administration.”]**. Thereafter he was promoted to the order of deacons.

When he set out [Col. 0455A] with the holy man Pope Constantine for the imperial city **[Note: [Col. 0455A] In another copy, the words beginning “and…” and ending “For he was” are absent.]**, he was questioned by the emperor Justinian **[Note: [Col. 0456D] Concerning certain chapters. Gregory accompanied Pope Constantine on his journey to Constantinople and was questioned by Justinian about certain chapters, which appear to have been none other than the Trullan canons, toward the promulgation of which the emperor had already devoted prolonged effort, as we read in the Life of Sergius, p. 151. Some think that on this occasion several of the Trullan canons were approved and confirmed by the Roman pontiff. We do not wish to decide the matter without certain evidence. BENCINUS.]** about certain chapters, and answered every [Col. 0456A] question with an excellent reply.

For he was a chaste man, learned in divine Scripture, eloquent in speech, steadfast in spirit, a defender of ecclesiastical affairs, and **[Note: [Col. 0456A] Codex Luc.: “of opposing things.”]** a most resolute assailant of *contrariis* (“opponents”; Codex Luc. reads *contrariorum*, “of adversaries”). **[Col. 0457A] [Note: In another copy, the passage beginning “This man…” and ending “was hindered” is absent.]**

At the beginning of his pontificate he ordered lime to be burned **[Note: [Col. 0457D] He ordered lime kilns to be fired. This was because of fear of the Lombards, who were lying in wait for the city. See Baronius, under the year 715, no. 2. BIN. and LABB.]**, and, beginning at the gate of Saint Lawrence **[Note: [Col. 0457A] Codex Luc.: “from the portico.”]**, he resolved to restore the walls of this city. After completing a portion of the work, he was [Col. 0458A] hindered by the emergence of various unfitting and diverse disturbances.

[Note: [Col. 0457D] 1. “In his time, John of Constantinople, etc.” When Gregory’s elevation became known in the East, John, bishop of Constantinople, sent him a synodal letter according to custom, as Anastasius himself records, saying: “During his pontificate John, bishop of Constantinople, sent him a synodical letter, and the pontiff likewise made use of written replies to him.” Some, with Baronius, think that Gregory rejected John’s synodal letter and regarded him as a heretic; consequently, after receiving Pope Gregory’s letters, the emperor Anastasius brought John to order but deposed him from his throne, and Theophanes remembered his deposition. Yet not only Theophanes but also Anastasius, in his Ecclesiastical History, or in Theophanes’ translation, expressly state that John the patriarch died after three years in office. Since only Zonaras mentions this John’s deposition, much greater credence should be given to Theophanes. From what we said concerning Pope Constantine, however, it is clear that John was not a Monothelite, and therefore that his synodal letter was not rejected by Gregory II. As soon as the tyrant Philippicus was overthrown, John explained his administration to Pope Constantine, apologized for it, and had not a few associates in it, among them Germanus, his successor in the see of Constantinople, and Andrew of Crete, men of great virtue. It is not surprising that this escaped Baronius, who had not seen John’s letter to Constantine, published by Combefis.

“Moreover, this John, according to the cited Theophanes and Anastasius, and also according to Nicephorus in his Chronicle, died after occupying the see for three years. Therefore, in the year 715, and in that same year, on the eleventh day of August, Saint Germanus, metropolitan of Cyzicus, was transferred to the administration of the Church of Constantinople, as Theophanes writes under the Alexandrian year of the Incarnation 707, which begins on the Kalends of September in the Dionysian year of Christ 714; on that same day the emperor’s regnal years also begin. ‘In the second year,’ he says, ‘of the reign of Artemius, also called Anastasius, in the thirteenth indiction, on the eleventh day of August, Germanus was transferred from the metropolitan see of Cyzicus to Constantinople.’ We shall have occasion to speak of him more than once below, because he resisted the emperor in defense of the holy images and was sent into exile.” PAGIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 0458D] 2. “In his time, John, bishop of Constantinople, etc.” As soon as it was heard at Constantinople that Gregory II had been raised to the highest dignity, John the patriarch wrote him a synodal letter, to which the supreme pontiff likewise sent his synodal reply. Some more recent writers, who neither saw nor properly considered the patriarch’s defense, of which we have reproduced part in our discussion of Constantine, believed John to have been a Monothelite on the authority of Zonaras. They therefore held that Gregory rejected his synodal letter and that the emperor Anastasius subsequently drove him from his see. But apart from the fact that John’s defensive letter makes this opinion wholly improbable, other very distinguished authorities, and men more knowledgeable about the matter than Zonaras, expressly state that the patriarch John died after holding office for three years and that Germanus, bishop of Cyzicus, was given as his successor (Theophanes, Anastasius in his translation, and Nicephorus in his Chronicle). SOMMIER.]

In his time, [Note: [Col. 0458D] John of Constantinople. He had presided over the Constantinopolitan assembly held under Philippicus and had subscribed to those decrees which, as we have noted, were promulgated in an encyclical and accepted by many. This excerpt from Anastasius belongs to the Life of Constantine, to whom John wrote his synodal letter. Accordingly, after the words in the Acts of Constantine, p. 163, line 1—“Thus he proceeded to Ravenna”—the following should be added; they have been wrongly inserted into the Life of Gregory: “In his time, John, bishop of Constantinople, sent him a synodal letter, and the pontiff likewise made use of written replies to him.” For John could not have written a synodal letter during the pontificate of Gregory II, since he died before Gregory was raised to the papacy. Constantine died in 715, whereas John of Constantinople died in 714 and was succeeded by Germanus. Theophanes writes of this in his Chronicle, p. 322: “In the second year of the reign of Artemius, also called Anastasius, in the thirteenth indiction, on the eleventh day of August, Germanus was transferred from the metropolitan see of Cyzicus to Constantinople, and a decree concerning this transfer was promulgated …” Agatho the deacon, a contemporary writer as well, makes this completely clear. After recounting Anastasius’ accession to the empire, he adds: “Thus, shortly afterward, when it had seemed right to him and he had consented, a letter of defense was composed by John, the most holy pontiff of this city, to Constantine, the most holy and blessed pope of Old Rome. This letter was sent, as customary, together with the synodal letters. It made him duly informed about everything that had previously been written.” From this we learn more fully about the Roman synod mentioned above: Constantine had sent John a threatening letter, reproaching him for what had been done in the predatory Constantinopolitan synod. John, in addition to the customary synodal letter, sent Constantine a defense, so that whatever he had done wrongly might be attributed to the most salutary remedy of ecclesiastical administration. Agatho also implies that John wrote to the pontiff because, as was proper, he ought to answer the Roman synodal letter, lest he appear contumacious. John’s letter is in volume III of Hardouin’s Councils, p. 1838, with this heading: “The apologetic letter of John, the most holy archbishop of Constantinople, to Constantine, the most holy Roman pope, concerning what was stirred up against the holy and ecumenical Sixth Synod during the tyranny of Bardas.” BENCINUS.]

John, bishop of Constantinople, sent him a synodal letter, [Note: [Col. 0458A] In another copy, “to him” is absent.] and the pontiff likewise made use of written replies to him. He [Note: [Col. 0459A] Another copy reads: “He replaced the beams of the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul, which had been weakened by age, covered the greater part of the basilica that had collapsed, and rebuilt the altar.”] covered the greater part of the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul, which had collapsed, with beams brought from Calabria; he rebuilt the altar and covered the silver ciborium, which had been damaged by the collapse [Note: [Col. 0460A] Codex Lucullanus adds: “he covered it.”].

He likewise repaired the church of Saint Lawrence situated outside the walls, which, with its beams broken, was already close to collapse, and after a long interval brought water back into the same church through joined pipes. He renewed various churches lying in ruins, which it would take too long to list individually. [Note: [Col. 0459C] 1. “Here in Germany he preached the word of salvation through Bishop Boniface and converted that people, sitting in darkness, to the doctrine of light and to Christ.” Boniface, consecrated bishop by Gregory II and sent to Germany for the conversion of its people, was the first bishop of Mainz. The ordering and sending of bishops for the conversion of unbelievers belongs to the Roman pontiff. By this authority Boniface was sent to Germany by Gregory II. Sergius ordained Willibrord, called Clement, and sent him to convert the Frisians; he became the first bishop of Utrecht. Anastasius speaks of him in the Life of Sergius; so do Bede, Book V, chapter 12, and Sigebert in his Chronicle under the year 697. Gregory I sent Augustine to England with great success for the conversion of the English; Gregory himself discusses him in Book V, Letter 53 and following, and Bede in Book IV, chapter 23 and following. ALTASERRA.

2. “Here in Germany through Boniface.” Concerning the deeds splendidly accomplished by Saint Boniface, father, apostle, and martyr of Germany, the venerable and most learned Nicholas Serarius, Jesuit theologian, has written much in his History of Mainz, Book III. BIN. AND LABB.

3. “Here in Germany, etc.” In the year 718 Saint Boniface, who had crossed from England into Frisia, went to Rome to the threshold of the apostles. On the thirtieth day of November, sacred to Saint Andrew the Apostle, Pope Gregory orally granted him authority to announce the Gospel to the peoples of Germany and declared him his legate. Consequently both Willibald, in his Life of Boniface, and Othlonus, who also wrote a Life of Boniface—both works being reproduced by Mabillon in the third century of the Benedictines, part II—date the beginning of his episcopate from that day, because they use “episcopate” improperly for the office of preaching and call him a bishop whom Gregory II created preacher of the faith and legate of the apostolic see throughout Germany.

“Thus Boniface, after receiving the apostolic letters of his legation, dated on the fifteenth day of May in the year 719, came to Thuringia. From there he sailed to Frisia, where, sowing the seeds of the divine word, he drew many away from the error of idolatry,” as Othlonus says in Book I, chapter 10, of his Life. He remained there for three years, and thereafter preached in Hesse and Thuringia with the greatest success.

“Later, he informed Pope Gregory through one of his companions of the favorable outcome of the preaching he had undertaken. He was immediately summoned to Rome by apostolic letters and hastened there by long journeys. There, on the day before the Kalends of December, he was ordained bishop by that same pope, in the year 723, as is clear from a letter of Pope Gregory written on the day after Boniface’s ordination and addressed to all the Christians living in Germany; Willibald reproduces it.

“Gregory therefore consecrated Boniface bishop, though attached to no particular see, so that he might be strengthened by the authority of the apostolic dignity and might be more acceptable to all in the office of preaching. Gregory required Boniface to swear a solemn oath to preserve the integrity of the faith and the unity of the Church and to render perpetual and singular obedience to the pontiffs of the apostolic see. After being confirmed by his own subscription, he deposited this oath, according to custom, above the body of Saint Peter, as the cited Othlonus reports in chapter 14.

“I have said that Boniface was consecrated bishop but attached to no see. To understand this, one should observe with Serarius, note 25 on the Life of Saint Boniface, that two kinds of bishops and archbishops must be distinguished: ‘For some,’ he says, ‘there is a definite see, a definite place, and a fixed location, from which they are called bishops or archbishops. For others, however, the see is uncertain and there is no definite or fixed place. This latter kind is usually found among those peoples and in those provinces which have only recently begun to be gathered into the faith of Christ. Since those who announce the Gospel to them must run here and there and do not yet possess a flock gathered into one territory or city, they receive from the apostolic see the episcopal power of ordaining presbyters and placing them in various locations, or even the archiepiscopal power of creating bishops; meanwhile they wander among uncertain sees and gather, from every direction and wherever they can, sheep for Christ Jesus, the true and supreme Shepherd of souls. These men are called, strictly and simply, bishops, or, more generally, bishops and archbishops of the region in which they labor and seek out the Lord’s flock.’ Thus Serarius.

“That Saint Boniface was a bishop of the latter kind is clear from the two authors of his Life. Gregory sent Boniface back, equipped with various letters of recommendation to Charles, duke and mayor of the palace of the Frankish kingdom; to bishops and other clergy and laity of every rank; to the clergy, nobles, and entire people of the Thuringians and Saxons, so that he might continue to discharge the apostolic office he had begun.
