“From a letter of Gregory himself to the clergy and people, which Othlonus includes with five others in Book I, it is clear that the pontiff instructed Boniface not to presume to perform illicit ordinations; not to admit to sacred orders a bigamist, a man who had not married a virgin, an illiterate man, anyone mutilated in any part of his body, anyone formerly subjected to public penance, a civil magistrate, anyone bound to any servile condition, or anyone marked by any stigma of infamy; not to lay hands indiscriminately upon Africans; to celebrate ordinations only outside the Ember Saturdays—or, more precisely, not outside the Ember seasons; not to confer baptism outside Easter and Pentecost except upon those in danger of death; to strive to increase the Church’s ministries, ornaments, and patrimony, never diminishing them; and to distribute ecclesiastical revenues and offerings into four portions.

“These commands appear to have been taken from Letter 9 of Pope Gelasius I, addressed to the bishops established throughout Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily, written in 494. We discussed it in the same place; Cointius demonstrates the details under the year 723, no. 17 and following, in his Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks. Yet when Gregory speaks of avoiding illicit ordinations, he mentions Africans, about whom Gelasius is silent, and Gregory gives this reason: some of them had been shown to be Manichaeans and some repeatedly rebaptized. Before the Saracens crossed into Spain, they occupied Africa, and the African exiles who poured into Europe began to seek their livelihood from ecclesiastical orders. But because most of them were recognized as either Manichaeans or Donatists, a universal law was enacted—as Baronius writes under the same year 723—that no African should in any way be ordained by any bishop. There is no doubt that by ‘Africans’ Gregory means Donatists, because they existed in great numbers in Africa and stubbornly defended Anabaptism.

“In the year 726, Gregory, consulted by Boniface about various matters, answered each point in a letter beginning ‘Desirable to me,’ said to have been given on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, while the most pious lord Augustus Leo, crowned by God, was emperor, in the tenth year of his reign, and while Constantine the Great was emperor, in the seventh year of his reign, in the tenth indiction. Since the current tenth indiction coincides with November of the year 726 and with Leo’s tenth imperial year, it is evident that Leo’s reign was correctly dated from 717.

“For many centuries this practice of the Church and monasteries prevailed: boys, or infants, offered by their parents were bound permanently to the monastic life, and were not permitted to renounce that state of life either before or after the years of puberty. Numerous examples of this practice exist among the Franks on both sides of the Rhine. When Boniface consulted Gregory about it, Gregory replied in these words:

“‘You also added’—namely, in the seventh consultation—‘that if a father or mother should hand over a son or daughter, during the years of infancy, within the enclosure of a monastery and under regular discipline, may they, after completing the years of puberty, leave and marry? We altogether reject this, because it is wicked that the reins of pleasure should be loosened for children offered to God by their parents.’

“What Gregory permits in his second response—that if a woman, stricken by illness, is unable to render the marital debt, the husband, if he cannot remain continent, may marry—must be understood as referring to a permanent impediment that was unknown when the marriage was contracted. Natalis Alexander reports Gregory’s responses to Boniface’s other consultations in the eighth century. Gratian wrongly attributed this letter to Gregory III. The remaining matters concerning Saint Boniface’s apostolate will be examined under Gregory III and Zachary. PAGIUS.

4. “Here in Germany through Bishop Boniface, etc.” In the age of Gregory II, the more celebrated herald of the Gospel was undoubtedly the Englishman Wilfrid. After him Boniface is honored, and he is regarded as the apostle of the Germans. He had become a monk; afterward, preferring the ministry of a preacher of the Gospel to the dignity of abbot that had been offered to him, he fled to Gregory’s feet to obtain permission to announce the Gospel to the nations.

“Moved by the testimony of the bishop of Winchester, to whom Boniface was subject, and by Boniface’s own merits, discovered during frequent conversations, the pontiff granted him an apostolic diploma by which he gave him authority to preach the faith to idolaters and instructed him to baptize those who were converted according to the rite of the Roman Church and to inform the Holy See of everything that appeared necessary for completing the work he had undertaken.

“‘Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to Boniface, a religious presbyter. The evident intention of your religious purpose, burning with piety in Christ, and the report brought to us of your most sincere and approved faith, require that we employ you as a fellow-worker in the administration of the divine word, whose care we bear by the grace of God,’ etc. (Gregory II, Letter 1, to Boniface).

“And indeed, when he had carried out his ministry with very great success in Frisia, Hesse, and Thuringia, he informed the pontiff, who wished him to come to Rome so that he might give an oral account of his work. He therefore came and afterward returned as a bishop, carrying Gregory’s letters of recommendation to Charles Martel, mayor of the palace of the Franks; to bishops; to ecclesiastics of the second rank; to nobles; to magistrates; and finally to the peoples of the provinces I have just mentioned (Gregory II, Letters 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7).

“Gregory afterward sent him a letter (Letter 8), beginning ‘Moved by the anxiety of the entrusted watch and also by evangelical instruction, etc.,’ in order to support him in his apostolic ministry and encourage him to persevere.

“In a decretal letter addressed to him, in which he answers several questions of discipline, Gregory first commends him for consulting the see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and of the episcopate, concerning matters belonging to the Church. He then says that he is not making the decision on his own authority but by the inspiration of him who gave speech to many and made even children eloquent:

“‘You appended to your letter,’ he says (Letter 13), ‘certain chapters, asking how this holy apostolic Roman Church holds or teaches these matters. It is entirely fitting, since the blessed apostle Peter was the beginning both of the apostolate and of the episcopate. To you, who consult us concerning the state of the Church, we say—not from ourselves, but by the grace of him who opens the mouths of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent—how the doctrines of apostolic vigor ought to be held: first, etc.’

“In this decretal Gregory restricts the impediment of marriage to the fourth degree of consanguinity. He permits a man who has a wife unfit for marital relations to take another, provided that he also supplies support to the first. He permits presbyters to clear themselves by oath of crimes of which they had been lightly accused and for which there were no certain witnesses. He prohibits repeating the sacrament of confirmation, consecrating a second chalice in the sacrifice of the Mass, eating what has been offered to idols, permitting marriage to children whom their parents have devoted to God, and rebaptizing those already baptized with the legitimate form by presbyters, even unworthy ones. He nevertheless wishes children taken from their parents to be baptized, unless it is clear that they had already been baptized after the abduction. He does not wish the Eucharist to be denied to lepers on the pretext that eating with them is forbidden. He says that it is foolish to withdraw from monasteries or churches infected by contagion, as though God’s hand could thereby be evaded. He teaches that one should not avoid the custom and table of ecclesiastics and illustrious men who abound in vices, since such association often contributes more to recalling them to their duty than correction and reproach. SOMMIER.]

Here in Germany, through Bishop Boniface, he preached the word of salvation and converted that people, sitting in darkness, [Note: [Col. 0461A] Another copy adds: “to Christ, and he washed the greater part of that same people in the waters of holy baptism. The most holy pope also renewed the monasteries,” etc.] to Christ.

He renewed the monasteries that stood near the basilica of Saint Paul, after they had been reduced to solitude, and, having appointed servants of God as monks, established a community there after a long interval, so that [Note: [Col. 0461A] Another copy reads: “so that three times during the day and at night they might sing matins [Col. 0462A] and hymns.”] they might render praises to God there by day and by night.

He made into a monastery the gerocomium [Note: [Col. 0462A] Codex Lucullanus: “gerontocomium,” an institution for the aged.] situated behind the apse of Saint Mary, Mother of God, at the Crib [Note: [Col. 0462A] Another copy reads: “beside the church of the holy Mother of God at the Crib, and the monastery placed next to it, belonging to Saint Andrew the Apostle, etc.”].

He also restored the monastery of the apostle Saint Andrew, called Barbara, which had been reduced to extreme abandonment, [Note: [Col. 0463B] Codex Lucullanus and another copy: “in which.”] and in which not even a single monk [Note: [Col. 0436B] Codex Lucullanus: “dwelt.”] remained. [Note: [Col. 0463B] Another copy reads: “Restoring it, appointing monks, he ordered that on the third, sixth, and ninth days they should conduct the morning offices in the same church of the holy Mother of God, on each successive day, and his pious arrangement remains to this day.”] Having brought in monks, he ordered that both monasteries should sing praises to God every day and every night in honor of the holy Mother of God.

At that time [Note: [Col. 0463C] 1. “Luitprand.” Our author excerpted this from Paul the Deacon, Book VI, chapter 43: “At that time King Luitprand confirmed the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps to the Roman Church.” BENCINUS.

2. “At that time Luitprand.” The same account is given by Bede, Paul the Deacon, and Oldradus in his letter to Charlemagne, where he states that these things were done by Luitprand himself in the first year of his reign. BIN. AND LABB.

3. “At that time Luitprand, etc.” During the pontificate of this holy man, many supreme rulers demonstrated exceptional reverence toward the Holy See. For Theodo II, duke of Bavaria, whom Saint Rupert, bishop of Salzburg, had converted to the Catholic faith, was the first of all the German princes to come to Rome out of piety, to visit Saint Peter and his successor, the supreme pontiff.

“Yet King Ina of the English deserves precedence over Theodo in piety. Not only did he come to Rome to visit the tombs of the apostles, as Bede relates (Ecclesiastical History of the English, Book V, chapter 7), after he had ruled that people for thirty-seven years; it is also said that, before departing from the city, he decreed that a penny should be given to blessed Peter from each household of his kingdom. This was long called Romescot by the English, and in Latin Peter’s penny (Ranulf of Chester, Book, chapter 24).

“While he was in Rome, Ina also obtained permission from the pontiff to build a house called the School of the English. ‘To this house,’ says Matthew of Westminster, ‘the kings of England and the royal family, together with bishops, presbyters, and clerics, were to come to be instructed in Catholic doctrine and faith, lest anything erroneous or contrary to Catholic truth should be taught in the English Church; thus strengthened in the faith, they might return to their own country.’

“He also built a church, which the English clergy would serve and in which the English who died in Rome would be buried. ‘And so that all these things might obtain the strength of perpetual stability,’ he continues, ‘it was established by a general decree throughout the kingdom of the West Saxons, in which the aforesaid Ina reigned, that each year one penny from every household should be sent to blessed Peter and the Roman Church, so that the English dwelling there might derive from it the means of sustaining life.’ SOMMIER.

“Concerning Eudo, duke of Aquitaine, who sought the aid of the apostolic see against the Saracens; concerning his astonishing victory after the pontifical blessing; concerning Luitprand, king of the Lombards, restoring to the apostolic see the Cottian Alps, which had recently been invaded again; and finally concerning the usurpations of the Lombards at Benevento, etc., Anastasius speaks at length. The most illustrious Archbishop Sommier renders him in French, so as to relate together the services rendered by the princes to the Holy See. BLANCHINUS.]

King Luitprand confirmed the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which King Aripert had made and this king had recovered, having returned it at the admonition or rebuke of so great a man. [Note: [Col. 0464B] Copy A: “At that time, in the fourteenth indiction, a sign appeared in the moon,” etc.]

During his pontificate a sign appeared in the moon in the fourteenth indiction, and it was seen to be blood-red until midnight.

At that time [Note: [Col. 0464B] Codex Lucullanus: “Theodo.”] Theodo, duke of the nation of the Bavarians, [Note: [Col. 0464B] Codex Lucullanus: “of the Bavarians.”] was the first of that people to come to the threshold of the blessed apostle Peter, fulfilling a vow of prayer. [Note: [Col. 0464B] Another copy adds: “together with others of his people.”]

During his pontificate [Note: [Col. 0464C] “The emperor Anastasius.” Paul narrated this, preserving the chronological order, before the confirmation of the donation mentioned above, in chapter 36, as follows: “At that time the emperor Anastasius sent a fleet to Alexandria against the Saracens. When his army, turning to another plan, returned from the middle of its journey to Constantinople, it sought Theodosius the Orthodox, elected him emperor, and forced him to assume and confirm the imperial throne. Theodosius defeated Anastasius in a serious battle near the city of Area [reading uncertain]. After obtaining an oath from Anastasius, he made him a cleric and had him ordained presbyter. As soon as he received the kingdom, he immediately restored in the imperial city the venerable image depicting the holy synod, which Philippicus had removed, to its former place.

“In those days the river Tiber flooded so greatly that, overflowing its channel, it inflicted much destruction on the Roman city. It rose in the broad street to a height of one and a half human figures, and the waters spread and joined together from the Gate of Saint Peter to the Milvian Bridge.” PAGIUS.]

the emperor Anastasius sent a prepared fleet of ships toward the region of Alexandria against the Hagarenes, whom God had destined for destruction. They, turning to another plan before reaching their appointed destination, returned from the middle of their journey to the imperial city, sought out Theodosius the Orthodox, elected him emperor, and forced him to assume and confirm the imperial throne.

Anastasius therefore went with the citizens and with as many of the army as he could gather to the fortified city of Nicaea. There he fought with the fleet in which Theodosius had been made emperor, and nearly seven thousand of the army were killed. The defeated party of Anastasius then sought a declaration of amnesty. [Note: [Col. 0464B] Another copy: “obtained.”] After giving him an oath, they made him a cleric and had him ordained presbyter.

As soon as the aforesaid Theodosius entered the imperial city, [Note: [Col. 0464D] 1. “The venerable image.” Both Paul and his copyist Anastasius attribute the restoration of the image of the Sixth Synod to Theodosius. Agatho, however, who was involved in the events, openly attributes this work to Anastasius. Therefore both historians must be corrected, and in place of Theodosius the passage should read: “As soon as the aforesaid Anastasius entered,” together with the other matters that likewise belong to the Acts of Constantine.

“For after describing Anastasius’ election, Agatho continues in the frequently cited passage: ‘Since, after the removal of the image of the synod mentioned above, the impious and mad criminal Bardanes, who had ordered it to be wickedly removed, commanded that the five holy and ecumenical synods alone be depicted in what is called the arch of Melios, setting himself and Sergius upright in its center, it was entirely necessary and most appropriate that, after these two persons had been removed from it, a representation of the same holy and ecumenical Sixth Synod, together with the other five, should be made on the column. A common feast and joy, and spiritual exultation in the Lord, arose throughout the whole assembly of the God-loving Church, because of the restoration and peace of the most holy Churches.’ BENCINUS.

2. “The venerable image.” When Artemius, later called Anastasius, had been crowned emperor on the fourth day of June in the year 713, as we said above, and had held the empire for two years and eight months, the soldiers revolted and chose another emperor named Theodosius. Artemius was therefore deposed and thrust into a monastery, and Theodosius was proclaimed emperor around the beginning of 716. Since he was Catholic, Theodosius considered nothing more urgent than restoring the noble monument that Emperor Philippicus had destroyed, on which the six ecumenical synods had been depicted. By doing this he so silenced the mouths of the heretics that every controversy concerning the faith ceased in that city.

“Thus Baronius relates the matter from Anastasius in his account of Gregory II. Yet I am firmly convinced that Anastasius was deceived in this matter. It was the emperor Anastasius, not Theodosius, who restored the image of the Sixth Synod that Philippicus had erased from the imperial palace. Agatho the deacon expressly asserts this in the oft-cited peroration, both in his account of Agatho and in that of Conon. As an eyewitness, he deserves greater credence than Anastasius.

“After saying there that Anastasius, a pious and Orthodox man, was proclaimed emperor, and that with his approval and consent John the patriarch wrote to Constantine the pope, Agatho adds: ‘But because, after the previously declared destruction of the complete image of the synods, with the image of the Sixth Synod erased, the wretched and insane Bardanes, who had wickedly ordered its destruction, had commanded himself, together with Sergius, to be painted standing upright in its center in the chamber called that of Melios, with only the five ecumenical synods left there, it was wholly necessary and most fitting that, after such persons had been driven out, that same holy and ecumenical Sixth Synod should again be depicted there together with the other five. The entire God-loving assembly of the holy Church celebrated with common rejoicing and joy, and with spiritual exultation in Christ, because tranquility and peace had been granted to the most holy Churches.’

“See what was said concerning this act of Bardanes, or Emperor Philippicus, in the account of Pope Constantine. There, with Baronius, we also observed from Theophanes that Constantine sent Michael, a presbyter of the Roman Church and apocrisiarius, to the emperor Anastasius; yet Baronius here says that he was sent by Gregory II. PAGIUS.] he restored that venerable image, in which the six holy synods had been depicted and which Philippicus had removed—an act not to be spoken of—, [Note: [Col. 0465B] Codex Lucullanus: “He restored it to its former place and inscription.”] to its former place, [Note: [Col. 0465B] Another copy: “to its former inscription and place,”] so that, through the fervor of his faith, every controversy ceased in the Church.

At that time, the river called the Tiber, having burst from its channel, spread across the plains. It also swelled through a great inundation of waters and entered through the gate called Flaminia [Note: [Col. 0465B] Codex Lucullanus: “having burst forth.”]. Meanwhile, in some places it rose above even the walls of the city and extended through the streets beyond the basilica of Saint Mark. Thus, in the broad street, the water of that river rose to a height of one and a half human figures; and the waters spread from the Gate of the blessed apostle Peter as far as the Milvian Bridge; when they subsided, [Note: [Col. 0465B] Codex Lucullanus: “the waters of that river spread into the channel.”] they returned to the channel of the river itself.

It overturned houses and devastated fields, uprooting shrubs and crops. Indeed, at that time most of the Romans could not even sow. Great distress threatened on account of this. For seven days the waters held Rome in their grip. [Col. 0466A] Therefore litanies were repeatedly performed by the lord pope. While he persisted in prayer and litanies, on the eighth day God took pity and removed the water, and the river returned to its own channel in the fifteenth indiction. [Note: [Col. 0466B] Another copy omits: “in the fifteenth indiction.”]

[Note: [Col. 0466C] The fortress of Cumae as well. We have said that Pope Sisinnius had seriously considered restoring the walls of the city of Rome and had therefore ordered lime-kilns to be fired; Anastasius asserts that Gregory II likewise attempted this at the beginning of his pontificate, but was prevented by various disturbances that arose. What those disturbances were by which he was diverted from his purpose, the same author reports: namely, that the Lombards seized and carried off a fortress belonging to the Roman Church under the pretext of peace; and when they could be induced to restore it neither by fear of divine vengeance nor by gifts offered by Pope Gregory, Gregory recovered it with the assistance of the duke and people of Naples, paying seventy pounds of gold for its redemption, as he had promised. Paul the Deacon gives the same account in book VI, chapter 40, of his History of the Lombards, and informs us that this fortress, which Anastasius does not name, was the fortress of Cumae, which the Lombard duke of Benevento had taken from the Church. The same Paul the Deacon, in the cited work, chapter 42, also reports that at this time Luitprand, king of the Lombards, confirmed the restitution of the Cottian Alps already made to the Church while John VII was seated [on the papal throne], as was said there. Bede adds, in his book On the Six Ages, that Luitprand demanded the Cottian Alps back from the Roman pontiff, but, admonished by the venerable Pope Gregory, confirmed Aripert’s restitution. PAGIUS.]

At that very time the fortress of Cumae had also been seized by the Lombards through the treachery of a pretended peace. When this was heard, everyone was overcome with sadness [Note: [Col. 0466B] Another reading: “sad at the surrender of the fortress.”]. The most holy pontiff also exhorted and admonished the Lombards to return it; and if they did not comply, he declared in his writings that they would incur divine wrath because of the treachery they had committed [Note: [Col. 0466B] Codex Lucullanus and others: “he protested.”]. He even wished to give them many gifts in order that they might restore it. But they, stubborn in mind, would neither heed his admonitions nor permit its return.

Therefore the same holy pontiff was exceedingly distressed, and committed himself to divine hope; relying on the fortification of the duke of Naples and the people, he daily informed him by letter how they should proceed [Col. 0466B] [Note: [Col. 0466B] Codex Lucullanus: “he supplied [the plan].”]. Obeying his command, they took counsel together and entered the walls of the fortress by force in the silence of night [Note: [Col. 0466B] Codex Lucullanus: “craftily.”] [Col. 0467A]. The duke John, namely [Note: [Col. 0467B] Together with the subdeacon Theodimus and the administrator. Theodimus was a regional subdeacon and administrator, in the name of the Apostolic See, of the deaconry of Saint Andrew in Naples. In those places where the Roman Church possessed estates, deaconries had been established, in which alms were distributed by a subdeacon who administered the patrimony. For, as many letters of Saint Gregory the Great teach us, it was the duty of subdeacons to care for the poor of the deaconry. This Theodimus was buried at Naples in that same church of Saint Andrew, called “at the Nest”; concerning him the following funerary inscription exists on a marble tablet before the altar:

“Joyfully embrace the rotting bones, worn away by decay, of one who flees to your aid, holy apostle, who, out of longing for the desire of your merit, caused the walls of your palace to shine with wondrous beauty.

“By your assistance, when the bonds of hell have been broken, may miserable flesh rise again from here, and on the day of judgment, when criminal sins have been trampled down, receive divine joys, with you interceding, martyr Andrew.

“Here in peace lie the limbs of Theodimus, subdeacon, regional administrator and administrator of the Holy Apostolic See, and steward of this deaconry of blessed Andrew.

“If anyone should presume to violate this tomb, he shall be bound by the bond of anathema.”

MAFEUS.]—with the subdeacon and administrator Theodimus, and with the army [Note: [Col. 0467C] “And they killed nearly three hundred Lombards together with their castaldus.” A castaldus, or gastaldus, among the Lombards was the governor of a city or fortress. Paul Warnefrid, On the Origin and Deeds of the Lombards, book V, chapter 29: “And he ordered that Alzoron himself, after his title had been changed, should be called a castaldus instead of a duke.” Rainerius the gastaldus of the city of Sora is mentioned by Leo of Ostia, Chronicle of Monte Cassino, book II, chapter 32; Tacipertus the castaldus and Ramingus the castaldus of Tuscany by Anastasius in his Life of Zacharias. Sometimes gastaldus means an administrator. Urban II, in canon Salvator, distinction 1, question 33: “In the name of defender, he appointed for himself an advocate, castaldus, and judge.” A gastaldus named Pandulphus is mentioned in the inscription of John VIII, letter 215; he is likewise called judge of Capua in letter 217 of the same pope. ALTASERRA.]—killed nearly three hundred Lombards together with their [Note: [Col. 0467A] Codex Lucullanus: “castaldus.”] castaldio (*castaldione*), and captured more than five hundred alive, leading them as prisoners to Naples. Thus they were able to recover the fortress. For its redemption the most holy pope himself gave seventy pounds of gold, as he had previously promised.

Here he covered and restored the holy church of Jerusalem, which had long stood exposed [Note: [Col. 0467A] Another reading: “disfigured,” or “laid bare.”], and repaired the surrounding porticoes, damaged by age, by laying beams over them. He also made a marble ambon in the same church [Col. 0468A] and enriched it with various linens and ecclesiastical furnishings.

[Note: [Col. 0467D] At the same time the impious nation of the Hagarenes. From the words of Anastasius in the Life of Gregory, where he asserts that the Saracens fought with Eudo, duke of Aquitaine, and from what Paul the Deacon writes in book VI, chapter 46, of his History of the Lombards concerning the Saracens’ entry into Aquitaine, when these accounts are compared, the author of Baronio’s Critical History rightly concludes that the battle took place in the year 725 and that the victory was won by Eudo with the aid of the sponge sent to him by Gregory II. Anastasius adds, speaking of Eudo’s letter written to the pontiff: “In the preceding year, three sponges were sent to them as a blessing by the aforesaid man, sponges which are placed for the use of the pontiff’s table. At the hour when the battle was joined, Eudo, prince of Aquitaine, distributed them to his people in small portions for them to take; and not one of those who partook of them was wounded or killed.” Here Anastasius is speaking of the sponge with which the pontiff’s table was wiped, sent to Eudo and distributed as a blessing to the army. Frodoard also speaks of the victory won through the aid of the sponge in his book On the Roman Pontiffs, in his Life of Gregory II.

“Victories abroad too, blessed by the sponge,  
the sponge celebrates the Franks victorious for the pope,  
while, returning, it protects them from the Hagarenes’ arms,  
so that those who shared the iron were neither wounded  
nor harmed, when the few were struck down without such protection.”

Frodoard’s words clearly establish that this battle between the Hagarenes, or Saracens, and the Franks under Gregory II was different from the battle fought under Gregory III in the year 732. On sponges, consult the Thesaurus of the Latin Language and Calepinus, under the word “Sponge,” where one will find that the ancients prized sponges as luxuries and used them in place of scrapers and cloths for rubbing and cleansing their bodies. Martial, book XIV, epigram 149, states that it was customary to wipe tables with them:

“This sponge is given to you by lot, useful for wiping tables.” PAGIUS.]

At the same time [Note: [Col. 0468C] “The impious Hagarenes.” With some alterations, this section was transcribed in full from Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapters 46–47. BENCINUS.] the impious nation of the Hagarenes [Note: [Col. 0467A] Another reading: “the nation, crossing over to the place called Septem, entered Spain; they devastated most of it with their king, subjected all the rest together with their property, and thus possessed that province for ten years.” [Col. 0468A] “In the eleventh year a general movement of the Franks was made against the Saracens, and, surrounding them, they killed them. Three hundred …”]—after they had held the province of Spain under occupation for ten years—attempted in the eleventh year to cross the river Rhône in order to seize Francia, where Eudo was in command. He, having caused a general mobilization of the Franks against the Saracens [Note: [Col. 0468A] Codex Lucullanus: “summons”], surrounded and killed them. For 375,000 were killed in a single day, as was stated in the letter of that same Eudo, duke of the Franks, sent to the pontiff. They said that only 1,500 of the Franks had died in that battle [Note: [Col. 0468A] Codex Lucullanus: “the little book stated.”]. He added that [Note: [Col. 0468D] “In the aforesaid year three sponges were sent to them as a blessing by the aforesaid man, sponges which are placed for the use of the pontiff’s table.” Before the year in which the Saracens, under their king Addiramen, invaded Gaul, Gregory II sent three sponges to the duke of Aquitaine, Eudo, as a blessing. These were among those used to wipe the pontiff’s table. After being cut into pieces and distributed among the soldiers, all who received a share of them emerged safe and unharmed from the battle in which Charles Martel and Eudo, joining their forces, destroyed the Saracens. Sponges were used for wiping tables, as is proved by this passage, which Martial illustrates in book XIV, epigram 144:

“This useful sponge is given to you by lot for wiping tables.”

They were also used for wiping floors. See the Digest, book XXXIII, title 7, law 27, section “Item pertica,” concerning legacies of equipment. Marcus Tullius Cicero, For Sextius: “You remember, judges, how the Tiber was filled with the bodies of citizens, the sewers repaired, and the blood wiped from the forum with sponges.” Hence the Egyptian virgin who, pretending to be foolish, humbly served the others was called ἐπόγγος τῆς συνοδίας, “the sponge of the monastery.” Palladius, Lausiac History, chapter 40. ALTASERRA.] in the preceding year, three sponges were sent to them as a blessing by the aforesaid man [Note: [Col. 0469A] Codex Lucullanus: “sent”], sponges which are placed for the use of the pontiff’s table [Note: [Col. 0469B] 1. “Three sponges were sent in the preceding year, which are placed for the use of the pontiff’s table.” After being cut into pieces and distributed to individual soldiers, the three sponges sent to him by Pope Gregory II—sponges which are placed for the use of the pontiff’s table, or, as other manuscripts read, “which the pontiffs used for the use of the table”—enabled Eudo, duke of Aquitaine, to destroy 375,000 Saracens, with none of his own men who had received a share of such a sponge being lost. What should be understood by these sponges used by the pontiff at his table must, I think, be explained.

Franciscus Pagius, in his Brief History of the Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs, in the Life of Gregory II, says that Anastasius is here speaking of the sponge with which the pontiff’s table was wiped, sent to Eudo and distributed as a blessing to the army. He adds this commentary: “On sponges, one should consult the Thesaurus of the Latin Language and Calepinus, under the word ‘Sponge,’ where one will find that the ancients prized sponges as luxuries and used them in place of scrapers and cloths for rubbing and cleansing their bodies.” It was very well done, then, that the holy pontiff Gregory II sent Eudo, in place of a blessing, sponges which he had valued as luxuries and used, instead of a scraper, for rubbing and cleansing his body.

No less successfully did Joseph Maria Suaresius, bishop of Vaison, a man otherwise of extensive and distinguished learning, explain this rather obscure passage of Anastasius in his booklet On the Annual Washing of the High Altar of the Basilica of Saint Peter. There he says that writing was erased with a sponge, as Suetonius reports in chapter 20 of his Life of Gaius Caesar Caligula; hence Augustus replied to his friends, according to the same Suetonius, chapter 85, that Ajax had lain upon his sponge. Those three sponges therefore foretold that the Hagarenes would be destroyed to the last man, and the piety of the duke and soldiers preserved them safe and unharmed. That is, it would have been Eudo’s soldiers whose destruction was foretold, since portions of the sponges were distributed among them, not the Hagarenes, whom the sponge did not touch at all.

I believe the distinguished bishop Giovanni Cristoforo Battelli touched the matter with precision in a book published at Rome in 1702, in which he explains and illustrates the rite of the annual washing of the high altar of the Vatican Basilica on Maundy Thursday. After recounting the sacred and secular uses of sponges and mentioning the deed of Eudo, as described by Eudo himself in a letter sent to Gregory II, he continues:

“What the ancient use of sponges at the pontiff’s table may have been has so far remained unknown to us. This, however, we know with certainty: in our own times such sponges are accustomed to be placed neither on the pontiff’s spiritual table nor on his bodily table. Nevertheless, we believe it probable that sponges of this kind were customarily used when the pontiff celebrated solemn Mass, for wiping the vessels of the sacred table, which are now wiped with purificatory linens and cloths. Such indeed was, and still is, the use of sponges among the Greeks, both in solemn Mass and in the washing of the holy table on Maundy Thursday, as we have shown above. Indeed, the patriarch is accustomed to distribute to the people, as a blessing, sponges used in the washing of the sacred table, since they are believed to have drawn holiness and divine power from contact with the altar, as Goar explains in his notes on that rite, no. 13. Anastasius records that Gregory II did the same when he says that he sent sponges from the pontiff’s table as a blessing to the duke of the Franks.” [Col. 0470A]

If I may add something to Battelli’s explanation, I would not think it improper to understand the sponges sent by the pontiff—and which Anastasius notes, in that circumstance, as having been used by the pontiff at his table—as sponges of the kind the pontiff had used in the solemn washing of the altar on which he himself celebrated Mass. It is a very ancient rite of the Vatican Basilica, which that same basilica still religiously retains and observes: on Maundy Thursday, the high altar is washed with wine, swept with sprinklers, and finally carefully wiped first with sponges and then with small cloths.

The ancient collectors of rites mention this ceremony: Isidore of Seville, book I On Divine, or Ecclesiastical, Offices; Alcuin, book On Divine Offices; Amalarius, book On Ecclesiastical Offices; and Rabanus Maurus, book II On the Instruction of Clerics—men who flourished from the sixth through the eighth and ninth centuries. This high altar of the Vatican Basilica stands above what is called the Confession of Saint Peter, that is, the lower chapel in which the sacred relics of Saints Peter and Paul are venerated. Apart from the supreme pontiff, no one may celebrate Mass upon it unless the supreme pontiff has granted him permission, preceded by a special bull which must be affixed near the altar, as prescribed by the Roman Ordinal, no. 15, in Mabillon, Italian Museum, volume II, page 455, by Peter Amelius, section 17, under the title “On the Circumcision of the Lord”:

“This Mass the Roman pontiffs have always been accustomed to celebrate … Also note: if the pope is in the city on this day and does not celebrate, but has a Mass said by some cardinal in the Church of Saint Peter, before the cardinal vests, the bull must be presented by which the pope dispenses him so that he may celebrate upon the altar of Saint Peter; and throughout the whole day it hangs before the royal doors. The same applies to all other Masses celebrated upon that altar.”

What wonder, then, if this altar is properly called the pontiff’s altar? But is the altar the same thing as the table? Both terms are used interchangeably. Anastasius, in the Life of Stephen IV, no. 294, says:

“He decreed that every Sunday the solemn Mass should be celebrated upon the altar of blessed Peter by the seven cardinal bishops who serve by turns in the church of the Savior.”

There was also in the Lateran church a wooden table, held in great honor, formerly consecrated to blessed Peter by frequent liturgies. The Roman Ordinal, numbered 10, in the aforementioned Mabillon, volume II of the Italian Museum, page 99, says:

“If the pontiff is at the Lateran, after the Creed ‘in one God’ has been sung, and before he enters to celebrate the sacrifice, the deacons lift the table from the altar—here one is distinguished from the other—with the coverings folded over it, and with reverence and complete devotion carry it back to the chapel of Saint Pancratius beside the canons’ cloister, because that is the place of reservation; and it is guarded there with every precaution until Saturday.”

We therefore have the sponges, the pontiff’s table, and the sacred use of sponges in wiping that table. What more do we seek for a fuller understanding of Anastasius’s text?

That the sponges could have been sent by the pontiff to the pious duke of the Franks, Eudo, as something sacred or like holy relics, having been in some manner consecrated by contact with the altar placed above the tomb of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, is taught by many similar examples from that period: cloths brought onto the body of blessed Peter, and keys taken from the body of Saint Peter, of which there is more than one mention in several letters of Gregory the Great sent to distinguished men; and golden keys, concerning which Gregory of Tours writes in book I On the Glory of the Martyrs:

“Many also make golden keys for the venerable grilles of the holy tomb; those who carry them receive them first as a blessing, and by them they heal the sickness of the afflicted.”

BALDINUS.

2. “Three sponges were sent.” Paul omitted what our author says here about the sponges. Among the ancients the use of sponges was common. They were frequently used at tables, indeed they were also employed in sacred contexts, and certainly for polishing the lamps situated before the altar, as the facts recorded below in the Life of Paschal make clear. They were kept in silver vessels intended for the service of the altar; for we read how, among the things dedicated by Paschal, a silver basin for holding a sponge was established for the nocturnal services. I believe that these particular sponges were sent because they had been soaked in oil used in the service of the martyrs’ tombs. BENCINUS.]

At the hour when the battle was joined, Eudo, prince of Aquitaine, distributed them to his people in small portions for them to take [Note: [Col. 0469A] Another reading: “within which.”] [Col. 0470A] [Note: [Col. 0470A] Codex Lucullanus: “from them.”], and not one of those who partook of them was wounded or killed.

[Note: [Col. 0470A] In another manuscript: “At that time also …” The following words are absent.] At that same time, in the regions of Campania, burnt wheat, barley, or legumes fell from heaven like rain in a certain place [Col. 0471A].

[Note: [Col. 0471A] “At this time he instituted that during Lent, on Thursday, fasting and the celebration of Mass should take place in the churches, which had not previously been done. The apostles also instituted a perpetual relaxation of the fast during Lent in honor of the Lord’s Resurrection. Gregory, Homilies on the Gospels, homily 16: ‘Although something else may still be understood concerning the season of Lent: from the present day until the joys of the Easter solemnity there are six weeks, making forty-two days; when the six Sundays are subtracted from these, only thirty-six days remain in abstinence.’ Besides Sundays, Thursday too was traditionally exempt from the Lenten fast; but Gregory the Younger restored fasting on Thursday as well as the celebration of Mass—that is, of the offices—during Lent. Anastasius bears witness here, as does the Micrologus, On Ecclesiastical Observances, chapter 50. ALTASERRA.

“At this time he instituted that, during Lent, fasting and the celebration of Mass should take place in the churches on Thursday, which had not previously been done.” What Walafrid Strabo, a contemporary of Anastasius, reports in his book On Ecclesiastical Matters, chapter 120, may shed light on this passage of Anastasius, although in some respect the two seem to conflict. Anastasius says that Gregory II instituted fasting and the celebration of Mass on Thursday, which had not previously been customary; Strabo, however, asserts that Gregory II instituted a proper Mass, since previously the Mass of the preceding Sunday was repeated on Thursday. Strabo’s words are:

“Because Melchiades, the thirty-third bishop of Rome in succession, decreed that no Christian should in any way fast on Sunday or Thursday—for the pagans frequently observed quasi-fasts on those days—therefore blessed Gregory, in arranging the offices of the year, left Thursday free during Lent, so that, because it was festive like Sunday, it might also be celebrated with the office of Sunday. But because that Thursday later began, like the other days, to be assigned to fasting, Gregory the Younger, namely Gregory II, decreed that it should be solemnized with Masses and prayers; that is, that it should have its own proper Masses, as the other weekdays of Lent have, and he enlarged its offices by gathering material from everywhere.”

The Micrologus, who wished to conceal himself under a humble name, almost transcribed Strabo’s words, adding in chapter 50: “Most especially, passages from the Sunday Gospels are still found assigned to Thursdays.” Cardinal Bona, in On Liturgical Matters, book I, chapter 18, no. 12, reconciles Anastasius with Strabo in this way. He holds that Anastasius means that Thursday had been observed without any special honor until Gregory II decreed that during Lent fasting and Mass, as on the other appointed weekdays, should be observed. Strabo, however, means that outside Lent Thursday long remained without its own solemn office, and that if anyone wished to celebrate the sacrifice privately on that weekday, he used the Mass of the preceding Sunday.

But if anyone finds Strabo’s explanation less satisfactory—namely, that Saint Gregory I left Thursday free when arranging the offices because pagans frequently observed quasi-fasts on those days—although his assertion can be supported by canon 15 of the Council of Narbonne, held in 589, where it is decreed, against certain persons who superstitiously celebrated the day called Thursday, that unless some feast occurred, the day was to pass without any religious rite, let him read Grimold’s preface to the Book of Sacraments published by Pamelius, volume II of the Liturgies. Grimold gives a much clearer reason why certain days in the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory the Great lack an office. “As we have learned from the report of some,” Grimold says, “the apostolic lord is entirely free from stations on those days, because, having been wearied by observing stations on the other weekdays, he rests on those days, so that, free from the tumult of the crowds, he may more freely distribute alms to the poor and attend to external affairs.”

The Book of Sacraments of Saint Gregory, in the same Pamelius, confirms Grimold’s statement: wherever certain days are marked as free, these words are added: “The lord pope gives alms.”

Christian Lupus, in his notes on the Trullan canons, canon 52, believes that Strabo is mistaken when he says of Saint Gregory I that, in arranging the offices, he left Thursday during Lent free; and he holds that on all the days of Lent, except Good Friday and Holy Saturday, the Latin Church celebrated the full sacrifice of the Mass. To support his view, the distinguished author adduces two arguments.

The first is chapter 4 of the letter of Innocent I to Decentius of Gubbio, where it is said: “The tradition of the Church holds that on these two days the sacraments of the Church are not celebrated at all.” But I do not see what can be established from this passage of Innocent, since the sole purpose of the holy pontiff there is to show that one must fast not only on Friday but also on Saturday, not to enumerate the days without liturgy on which the Roman Church lacked Masses.

The second argument is that Masses assigned to Thursdays are found in the Sacramentary of blessed Gregory the Great. But the most learned man did not notice that Grimold warns that all those things in Gregory’s Sacramentary that are marked with strokes were added after the age of blessed Gregory, as were the Masses assigned to Thursdays. Indeed, it is certain that in the ancient books of the Sacraments, as also in Lectionaries and Calendars, no Mass or Gospel is found assigned to Thursday, either during Lent or outside Lent, throughout the entire year, except after Saint Gregory II: during Lent alone and in the octave of Easter. This can also be seen in the Calendar published by Fronto; consult him in the notes cited above, paragraph 6. MAFEUS.]

At this time he instituted that during Lent, on Thursday, fasting and the celebration of Mass should take place in the churches, which had not previously been done [Note: [Col. 0471A] In another manuscript, “fasting and” is absent.].

He also rebuilt from the foundations the oratory in the patriarchal residence, in the name of the blessed apostle Peter [Note: [Col. 0471A] Another reading: “of Hosanna.”], richly adorned with various metals [Col. 0472A] [Note: [Col. 0471A] Another reading: “and in various ways.”], and he silver-plated the walls surrounding the altar and painted the twelve apostles; these furnishings weighed 180 pounds [Note: [Col. 0472A] In another manuscript: “he made it.”].

[Col. 0473A] [Note: [Col. 0473B] 1. “In the meantime, Constantinople.” Constantinople was besieged for two years—or three—by the Saracens and liberated through the aid of the Virgin Mother of God. After Bede and Paul the Deacon, Theophanes gives a fuller account. Saint Gregory also mentions it in his letter to Saint Germanus, bishop of Constantinople. BIN and LABB.

2. “In the meantime, Constantinople for two years.” Besides Latin authors, Theophanes and Nicephorus among the Greeks remember this famous siege, during which Masalmas, the Saracen commander, blockaded Constantinople with land forces, while Suliman the caliph blockaded it with his fleet. In the first year of the siege, after the death of the caliph on October 2, Omar II, the twelfth caliph according to Langlet’s chronological tables, was installed in the caliphate, as Elmacinus writes in his Saracenic History. The Greek historians testify that the imperial city was liberated through the special protection of the Mother of God.

The city dedicated to the Mother of God venerated her with intense devotion in many places, but most frequently at Blachernae, where a magnificent church had been dedicated in her name. The Greek Church commemorates the city’s liberation annually on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September in the Menaion; in the Menologion of Basil Porphyrogenitus, first printed at Urbino in elegant type, it is expressed as follows in Latin translation:

“Under the emperor Leo the Isaurian, a great army of Saracens came and surrounded Constantinople by land and sea, intending to crush that city under siege. When they observed that the emperor was being driven by the extremity of necessity and supposed that he was prepared to come to terms with them, they even thought of imposing a garrison upon the city. But the Lord, who resists the proud, made their plan useless. For when the ruler of that people discovered that he was accomplishing nothing, he asked that he might at least be permitted to enter through the Bosphorus Gate on horseback. While others entered without hindrance, his horse alone, rearing up, could not enter. Then he raised his eyes and, seeing above the gate an image of the Mother of God, understood that this had happened because he had uttered blasphemies against her. Thus they withdrew without accomplishing their purpose; and when they reached the Aegean Sea with their ships, they perished, struck by a storm of fiery hail.”

The Greeks recall this favor in an annual celebration called τῆς ἀκαθίστου, “of the Unseated One”; that is, they stand throughout the entire night, singing psalms, hymns, and songs without sitting. See Codinus, On the Offices of the Court of Constantinople, chapter XII, no. 10, and note 13 on it in the royal edition. See also the most learned Father Combefis, in the second volume of the Supplement to the Library of the Holy Fathers, where he published a historical oration on the liberation of Constantinople, from which further relevant material may be obtained. MAFEUS.]

In the meantime Constantinople was besieged for two years by the Hagarenes, whose names ought neither to be given nor spoken [Note: [Col. 0473A] Codex Lucullanus: “not to be named.”]. But since God was against them, and the greater part of them there had been destroyed by hunger and war, they withdrew in confusion [Note: [Col. 0473D] “Under the emperor Leo.” Leo seized the empire after deposing Theodosius; and when the soldiers, after expelling Anastasius, acclaimed Theodosius emperor, Leo alone resisted, according to the author of the Miscellany, book XX, page 116:

“When Leo was commander of the eastern forces, because he was supporting Artemius, he was not subject to Theodosius.”

Such depositions of emperors were very frequent. As Nicephorus observes in his Chronicle, after narrating the deposition of Theodosius:

“While conspiracies against the emperors were continually occurring in this manner, and while, as tyranny grew stronger, the condition of the empire and the state was neglected and gradually slid into decline, the study of letters likewise began to be extinguished and perish, and military discipline was no less ruined. Thus the Roman empire came to be attacked with impunity by wars, indiscriminate massacres and abductions of people occurred everywhere, and cities were destroyed. To the sum of these evils was added the incursion of the Saracens, who, making a land expedition against the imperial city, gathered countless infantry and cavalry from the peoples subject to them. At the same time they moved a huge fleet of approximately 1,800 ships, under a commander named Musulman—for that is how they called him in their own language.

“When these events became known, both the military commanders and the civil magistrates, observing Theodosius’s incompetence and knowing that he was unequal to resisting such powerful enemies, began to press and urge him to abdicate the empire and to allow himself to be safely compelled to return to private rank. He did not reject the condition; but, while the year of his reign was still in progress—717—he voluntarily abdicated. They then took counsel concerning the choice of a successor, and at that moment Leo Patricius happened to be proposed, then commander of the eastern forces. Accordingly, as emperors are accustomed to do, he was received with solemn ceremony, entered Byzantium through the Golden Gate, and received the imperial crown in the great church.” BENCINUS.] under the emperor Leo.

For it was also said that 300,000 people of that same city, of different sexes and ages, were destroyed by the necessity of the plague [Note: [Col. 0473A] Another reading: “of different ages.”].

Formerly cups were placed on tables in silver baskets. Servius, in that passage of Book I of the Aeneid …]

Who load the tables with dishes and place the cups: among the ancients, cups were not handed to people, but were placed on tables; and today, among many peoples, cups are placed in silver baskets, which are called *siccaria*. **ALTASERRA.** He also bestowed ten baskets, each weighing twelve pounds, and many other gifts.

At that time the fortress of Narnia was seized by the Lombards. But the king of the Lombards, Luitprand, having made a general mobilization, advanced toward Ravenna and besieged it for several days. Having overrun the fortress, he carried away several captured ships and plundered immeasurable wealth.

Marinus, the imperial *spatharius*, who held the duchy of Rome and had been sent from the royal city by order of the emperor, approved their plan. But they could not find an opportunity, for he was dissolved and crippled by God’s judgment, and so withdrew from Rome.

[Note: [Col. 0475A] The Luc. Codex reads, “stirred.”]

Basil, however, became a monk and ended his life confined in a certain place.

Paul the exarch, by order of the emperor, attempted to kill that same pope; he hindered him from imposing the tax in the province, and was considering stripping the churches of their resources, as had been done elsewhere, and appointing another in his place.

After him another *spatharius* was sent with imperial commands, so that the pope might be removed from his see.

Again Paul the patrician, to carry out such a crime, sent those whom he could seduce from Ravenna, together with his associate, and some men from the fortresses.

[Note: [Col. 0476A] The Luc. Codex reads, “from among the people of Ravenna.”]

But the Romans were aroused, and Lombards from every quarter came to defend the pope at the Salarian Bridge; and from both sides Lombard dukes surrounded the Roman territory. Thus they prevented the attempt.

[Note: [Col. 0475C] “With commands.” Concerning these edicts promulgated by Leo the Isaurian, Paul gives the same account, book VI, chapter 49. In copying Paul, Anastasius confuses the emperor’s heretical edicts, making no distinction between the earlier and later ones. Leo therefore promulgated two decrees. In the first, issued in the year 716, he had forbidden the veneration of images. The words of Stephen the deacon of Constantinople in the *Life of Saint Stephen the Younger* are to be understood of this decree. There we read:

“After the tenth year of his reign, that new Balthazar breathed into the Church the Manichaean heresy and, so to speak, one scarcely unlike that of the Aphthartodocetists. Calling together the people subject to him, that inhuman beast, roaring before them in Leonine fashion, and bearing the celebrated name of Leo, with an angry heart, as though from Mount Etna, spewed forth and uttered fire, sulphur, and that pitiable proclamation: ‘Since the making of images is an idolatrous art, they ought not to be worshiped.’”

The sources from which Leo derived his error are reported more fully by Theophanes under that year and by the author of the *Miscella*, page 150.

That he began by forbidding the veneration of images, before proceeding to decree their destruction by fire, Theophanes clearly demonstrates, page 340:

“That impious man was not merely involved in error concerning the relative veneration of images worthy of worship; the most criminal of men also abominated the intercessions of the most holy Mother of God and of all the saints, and their relics, in the manner of his Arab teachers. From that time, therefore, he foolishly began hostilities against the blessed patriarch Germanus of Constantinople. Condemning all his imperial predecessors, the bishops, and the Christian peoples as idolaters because of their veneration of the holy and venerable images, he was unable, through excessive unbelief and boorishness, to comprehend or discuss the relative honor paid to them.”

**BENCINUS.**

2. “Afterward, therefore, when commands had been sent, the emperor had decreed that no image—”

The learned archbishop Sommier gives a lengthy account of the history of the Iconoclasts, which I shall provide in full below, section 188, in Pagii’s notes. For the present I shall summarize it from the same archbishop’s *Dogmatic History*, book VIII, chapter 24.

The law and institution of the Iconoclasts was to reject the worship of images of Christ and the saints, and to accuse their invocation and relics of superstition.

Leo the Isaurian is commonly regarded as a heresiarch. Constantine Manasses says of him:

“The accursed emperor was giving birth to those absurd and novel designs against Christ; but he could in no way bring forth the offspring of his wickedness, since his timid spirit drew him back from his purpose.”

Indeed, before bringing forth the crime he had conceived, in the very year in which he was made emperor, and thereafter every year, he always sent Gregory orthodox letters. Gregory himself testifies to this in his first letter to the emperor:

“We carefully preserve in the holy Church, at the entrance of the confession of the holy, glorious, and chief of the apostles, Peter, the letters that we have received from you for eleven indictions, as well as the letters of your predecessors who, as lovers of Christ, ruled piously.”

In those letters he had promised the pope that he would never depart from the principles of the orthodox faith. But after the tenth year of his reign, that new Balthazar … uttered and proclaimed that pitiable statement:

“Since the making of images is an idolatrous art, they ought not to be worshiped.”

(Jacob Loppin, *Analecta*, vol. I, *Life of Saint Stephen, Monk and Martyr*.)

For some time, however, the emperor remained silent because of the disturbances that had arisen in Constantinople over this matter, while the holy patriarch Germanus was chiefly working to avert the impious deed.

At last, however, he revealed his mind in the senate and dared to persuade the pope to remove the sacred images, if he wished to enjoy the emperor’s favor. Believing that his majesty had been injured by the pope’s paternal admonition, he repeatedly sent men to Rome to kill him.

He expelled Saint Germanus from the patriarchate, cast down the image of Christ erected by Constantine the Great in the vestibule of the palace, and sent commands everywhere to his subjects, especially those living in Italy, that they should consume the sacred images by fire—horrible to say—and kill the pope if he resisted.

Then Saint Gregory necessarily confirmed the Catholics everywhere in the faith by his letters against the heresy. By God’s special favor it happened that he heard that all had bound themselves by oath to defend the faith and the life of the pope.

The Lombards also, whom the impious emperor was trying to draw over to his side, nobly rejected his gifts and made a treaty with the Italians to defend the righteous cause.

King Luitprand, indeed, enticed by the hope of obtaining the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento and by the assistance promised by the exarch—an outcome he in fact achieved—made a treaty with that same exarch, and in turn assisted him in attacking the city of Rome.

But when the king surrounded Rome with his forces, and the pope was deprived of every human means of aid—for the forces of the allied Italians were insufficient—God protected him, since by private and public fasts and prayers he had made God favorable to him.

Trusting in God, he went out from the besieged city to the hostile king and so softened him by gentle speech that the king, overcome, fell at the pope’s feet and promised that he would harm no one. Thereafter, filled with obedience and reverence, he did everything that the *Liber Pontificalis* recounts with sufficient clarity.

**SOMMIER.**

Afterward, therefore, when commands had been sent, the emperor had decreed that no image of any saint, martyr, or angel, wherever it might be found, should remain.

[Note: [Col. 0476B] The Luc. Codex reads, “Leo the emperor.”]

[Note: [Col. 0476B] The Luc. Codex reads, “but he ordered all of them to be taken down and burned.”]

Therefore the pious man, looking upon the profane command of the prince, armed himself against the emperor as against an enemy, rejecting his heresy and writing everywhere to warn the Christians, because such impiety had arisen.

the wretched plot did not remain hidden. The evil plan became clear to everyone: they were attempting to violate the churches of Christ, destroy everyone, and plunder the possessions of all.

[Note: [Col. 0478C] The Luc. Codex reads, “all the places.”]

When he sent his own man to Rome with letters in which it was stated that the pope and the leading men of Rome were to be killed, the Romans, having recognized the most savage command,

[Note: [Col. 0478C] The Luc. Codex reads, “the Romans immediately wished to kill the messenger of that patrician.”]

immediately wished to kill that patrician’s messenger, had not the pope’s great protection prevented them.

Nevertheless, they anathematized Eutychius the exarch, binding themselves, great and small alike, by oath never to permit the pope, a champion of the Christian faith and defender of the churches, to be harmed or removed, but declaring that all were prepared to die for his safety.

[Note: [Col. 0478C] Another manuscript reads, “but binding themselves, great and small alike, by oaths,” and so forth.]

The patrician then sent messages here and there to the Lombard dukes and king, promising many gifts and urging them to abandon their assistance to the pope.

[Note: [Col. 0478C] The Luc. Codex reads, “promising.”]

They replied, scorning the man’s detestable treachery.

[Note: [Col. 0479C] The Luc. Codex reads, “from his letters”; Mansi reads, “from the replies.”]

Romans and Lombards bound themselves together as brothers by one chain of faith, all desiring to endure a glorious death in defense of the pope. They would never allow him to suffer harm, fighting for the true faith and the salvation of the Christians.

[Note: [Col. 0479C] The Luc. Codex reads, “fighting”; Mansi reads, “fighting for him.”]

In these circumstances that father chose the greater defense: with a most generous hand he distributed to the poor whatever he found, devoted himself to prayers, fasts, and litanies, and daily besought God.

[Note: [Col. 0479C] The Luc. Codex reads, “the pope.”]

Thus he always remained supported by hope beyond that which human beings could provide. Nevertheless, he gave thanks to the people for their willing resolve and urged everyone in gentle speech to advance in good works toward God and to persevere in the faith.

He also admonished them not to abandon their love for, or faith in, the Roman Empire. Thus he softened the hearts of all and mitigated their continual sorrows.

At that same time, in the eleventh indiction,

[Note: [Col. 0479C] Another manuscript omits “eleventh.”]

the fortress of Suerium was seized by the Lombards.

[Note: [Col. 0479C] Another manuscript reads, “the fortress of Sutrium.”]

It remained in the possession of those same Lombards for one hundred and forty days.

[Note: [Col. 0479C] The Luc. Codex reads, “forty days.”]

But after many continuous letters and admonitions from the pope had been sent to the king, and although many gifts had been given,

[Note: [Col. 0479C] The Luc. Codex adds, “nevertheless.”]

the king of the Lombards at least restored and donated the fortress, stripped of all its resources, by sending the aforesaid deed of donation to the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Note: [Col. 0479C] Another manuscript adds: “After some time, the same king, having made a general mobilization in order to subject the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento, and having received oaths and hostages from those dukes, joined his entire army in Nero’s Field. To him …”]

At that time, in the twelfth indiction, in the month of January, for ten days and more, a star called *Antifer* appeared in the sky with rays in the west. Its rays faced toward the northern regions and extended to the middle of the sky.

[Note: [Col. 0479C] The Luc. Codex reads, “aurifer”; perhaps “Lucifer.”]

[Note: [Col. 0479C] The Luc. Codex reads, “in the west.”]

At that time the often-mentioned patrician Eutychius and King Luitprand formed a wicked plan: after gathering their armies, the king was to subject the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento, while the exarch was to attack Rome and carry out what had previously been commanded concerning the person of the pope.

The king, coming to Spoleto and receiving oaths and hostages from both dukes, withdrew with his entire retinue to Nero’s Field.

[Note: [Col. 0480C] The Luc. Codex reads, “with his entire army.”]

The pope went out to meet him and, having been brought before him, did all he could to soften the king’s mind through pious communion, so that the king prostrated himself at the pope’s feet and promised that he would inflict harm on no one. Thus, moved by pious exhortations to such deep remorse,

[Note: [Col. 0480C] Another manuscript reads, “so that he removed what he had been wearing.”]

he removed what he had been wearing,

[Note: [Col. 0479C] “And he placed before the apostle’s body his cloak, *armilausa*, belt, sword, and gilded blade, as well as a golden crown and a silver cross.” Luitprand, king of the Lombards, overcome by the pope’s prayers, laid down his royal garments and ornaments before the altar of Saint Peter: his cloak, *armilausa*, belt, and sword. The *mantum* is a short little cloak that covers the shoulders and reaches only to the hands. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XIX, chapter 24: “The Spaniards call it *mantum*, because it covers only the hands; for it is a short covering.” Here *mantum* is placed among royal ornaments; among pontifical ornaments Radevicus places it, *De Gestis Friderici*, book II, chapter 62: “Many of our men say that they saw the chancellor leave the city on the eleventh day without a cloak, without a stole, without a white horse, and without any protection of dress, wearing skins covered by a royal mantle and a black hood reaching to the cistern.” The *armilausa* is placed among royal garments. It is military clothing that covers the arms—that is, the shoulders—and extends to the knees, so as to allow greater freedom of movement. Paulinus, letter 7, to Severus: “Let him keep his *armilausa*, his leggings, and his shoes.” The same author, letter 13, to the same person: “Moreover, he blushed in his face no less than in his *armilausa*.” Isidore explains the etymology of *armilausa* from arms, *Etymologies*, book XIX, chapter 22: “Commonly called *armilausa*, because it is divided and open in front and behind, but closed only around the shoulders, as though *ARMI CLAUSA*—‘closed around the arms’—with the *c* removed.” Suidas: “*Armilausion*, from *harma*, ‘the part above the weapons.’”

The belt is joined to the *armilausa*. It is a military girdle. Paulinus, letter 7, to Severus: “They are girded not with a belt but with a rope.” It was an ancient custom to place a belt upon the altar as an offering. Gregory of Tours, *On the Miracles of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 61: “At a certain time a devout man placed upon the altar of that basilica a belt of the purest gold, most carefully fashioned with all its adornment, praying that the power of the martyr might deign to assist him in his affairs.”

He says “a silver cross.” Emperors wore a golden cross around the neck. Of Charlemagne, Ditmarus testifies, book IV: “Taking the golden cross that had hung around his neck, together with part of his clothing, still undecayed, he placed the rest away with great reverence.”

**ALTASERRA.**]

and placed before the apostle’s body his cloak, *armilausa*, belt, sword, gilded blade, golden crown, and silver cross.

[Note: [Col. 0480C] In another manuscript: “cloak …”; the words following are absent.]

[Note: [Col. 0480C] The Luc. Codex reads, “armlets, or an *armillaria*.”]

After prayer had been offered, he begged the pope to deign to receive the aforementioned exarch into reconciliation and peace, as was done. Thus he departed, while the king turned away from the evil plans he had formed with the exarch.

[Note: [Col. 0480C] Another manuscript adds: “After prayer had been offered, he departed. For he had united many men against Rome so that he might carry out, with the exarch, what the emperor had commanded. But having been warned by the pope’s most gentle persuasion that this was not expedient, he then turned toward the cause of salvation and did what he had been instructed to do. He did not consent to the wicked counsels, and he departed gentle who had come savage. Thus the malice of the adversaries was suppressed, when the king turned away from the evil plans he had formed, on account of which he was persecuting the pope, so that he compelled …”]

Therefore, while the exarch remained at Rome, a certain seducer came into the territory of Tuscany, to the fortress of Manturium.

[Note: [Col. 0480C] The Luc. Codex reads, “the Mantuan fortress”; another manuscript, “the Maturan fortress.”]

[Note: [Col. 0480D] “Named Tiberius.” If Anastasius’s account is accurate, two tyrants must be distinguished: one who seized power in Sicily at the beginning of Leo’s reign, and another who, around the year 728 or 729, made himself emperor in Tuscany and was also called Tiberius. The first is discussed by the author of the *Miscella*, page 150, under the year 718, where, in the second year of Leo’s reign, we read:

“Sergius the *protospatarius* and governor of Sicily, having heard that the Saracens were besieging the imperial city, crowned there as emperor a certain Constantinopolitan, one of his own men, the son of Gregory Onomagulus. He changed his name and called him Tiberius, who made appointments and installed his own officials, following the counsel of the aforesaid Sergius.

“But the emperor, having heard this, sent Paul, his own *chartularius*. Having appointed him patrician and governor of Sicily, he gave him two *spatharii* as auxiliaries and very few men for his service, together with commands to the princes of the West and sacred documents to be read to the people.

“When they had entered by night into a swift *dromon*, they sailed to the region of Cyzicus. After traveling from place to place by land and sea, they suddenly came to Sicily. When they entered Syracuse, Sergius heard of it and was stunned. Reflecting on his transgression, he fled to his neighboring Lombards in Calabria.

“The people gathered, and, after the sacred documents had been read, became certain that the empire still stood and that the city was more ready to resist the nations. When those men also recounted what had happened concerning the two *stolae* [“stoles”; reading uncertain], they praised the emperor Leo and handed over Basil Onomagulus and the officials who had come from him, bound, to the governor.

“He beheaded Basil himself together with his special governor, and sent their heads, preserved in brine, to the emperor through the *spatharii*. As for the others, he sent some into exile after flogging or tonsuring them, and others after cutting off their noses.

“Thus it came about that a great restoration of order was established in the western regions. Sergius, after receiving and requesting a promise of pardon from the governor, went out to meet him, and so all the regions of the West obtained peace.”

The other tyrant, in the territory of Tuscany, likewise called Tiberius and mentioned here by Anastasius, was surnamed Petasius. He induced Etruria to revolt, although he was suppressed by the Roman army with the cooperation of Pope Gregory. **BENCINUS.**]

His name was Tiberius and his surname was Petasius. He was attempting to usurp for himself the rule of the Roman Empire.

He also deceived lesser men, so that the people of Manturium, Luna, and Blera had sworn allegiance to him.

[Note: [Col. 0481A] The Luc. Codex reads, “Blerans.”]

When the exarch heard this, he was disturbed. The most holy pope encouraged him, and, sending with him the leaders of the Church and the armies, they set out.

When they arrived at the fortress of Manturium, Petasius was killed there. His severed head was sent to the prince in Constantinople. Yet even then the emperor did not grant the Romans his full favor.

[Note: [Col. 0481C] 1. For after this the emperor’s wickedness became manifest. Natalis Alexander, in Dissertation 1 on the Ecclesiastical History of the Eighth Century, vol. V, p. 733, denies that Gregory II withdrew the peoples of Italy from obedience to the emperor Leo the Isaurian because of the abolition of the veneration of sacred images, or that he prohibited them from paying tribute any longer. He relies on the authority of [Col. 0481D] Paul the Deacon, *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, book VI, chapter 49, who says:

“All the armies of Ravenna and of Venetia, with one mind, resisted such commands, and, unless the pontiff had restrained them, they would have undertaken to appoint an emperor over themselves”;

and on Anastasius, who says in §184:

“When the emperor’s wickedness became known, all Italy took counsel to choose an emperor for itself and bring him to Constantinople. But the pontiff restrained this plan, hoping for the prince’s conversion”;

and in §185:

“He urged them all, with gentle speech, to advance in good works toward God and to persevere in the faith; but he admonished them not to abandon their love or their fidelity to the Roman Empire.”

He also quotes letters sent by Gregory himself to Leo, in which the pontiff does not threaten to turn the peoples away from loyalty to the emperor or to obstruct the payment of tribute, but declares himself unarmed and destitute, saying that he would withdraw into nearby Campania if an attack were made, and would call upon Christ that what had happened to the incestuous Corinthian through blessed Paul might also happen to the emperor. “Yet,” he adds, “it was wholly unfitting that the most holy bishop, learned in the divine Scriptures, should involve himself in popular disturbances, urge the people toward revolt, and withdraw them from the obedience owed even to an heretical emperor.”

Franciscus Pagius agrees with Natalis in his *Life of Gregory II*, where he says:

“So far was Gregory from urging the Italians and Romans to revolt, or from preventing them from paying their taxes, that he kept the armies of Ravenna [Col. 0482B] and Venetia, although prepared for rebellion, at their posts in obedience.”

He then quotes the same testimonies used by Natalis.

I willingly grant that matters stood thus before the emperor’s wickedness became manifest, as Anastasius says. The most holy pontiff wished to endure patiently the injuries inflicted upon him by the impious emperor, even at the risk of his life, and to try every remedy of gentleness and kindness, so that he might win the emperor’s goodwill and recall him from the fury with which he raged against the sacred images. He also kept the peoples of Italy, subject to the Eastern Empire, who were contemplating revolt, in their allegiance; he restrained them from appointing a new emperor whom they would bring to Constantinople; and he commended to Urso, duke of Venetia, the exarch of Ravenna, who had been expelled by the Lombards and was staying in Venetia, sending a letter to Urso so that the latter might support him and restore the city of Ravenna to its former condition. He wrote two letters to Leo in order to break his obstinate spirit [Col. 0482C] and lead him to better counsels.

Leo had threatened to send someone to Rome who would shatter the image of Saint Peter and carry Gregory away from there in chains. Gregory replied that the pontiffs sat in Rome for the sake of making peace, like an entirely sound wall and a dividing barrier between East and West, and as arbiters and moderators of peace:

“But if you send anyone,” he says, “to overthrow the image of Saint Peter, know—and we protest this to you—that we are innocent of the blood which they will shed; rather, that blood will fall upon your neck and upon your head.”

The holy pontiff had foreseen what would happen if the emperor dared to attempt anything by force of arms. For, as Anastasius relates, the people of the Pentapolis and the armies of Venetia, prepared to resist the emperor’s commands, had chosen leaders for themselves; and, concerned for the immunity of the pontiff and of themselves, Romans and Lombards had bound themselves together as brothers by a single chain of faith. All desired to suffer a glorious death in defense of the pontiff, never permitting him to endure harm while he fought for the true faith and for the salvation of Christians—or, as others read, while they fought for salvation.

And to whom could the Roman people more properly entrust their safety and faith than to the Roman pontiff, whose deepest concern was to relieve the poverty of the needy with the most generous hand; to open the granaries of the Church to the poor when famine threatened; to embrace everyone with gentle speech; to enlarge the city with churches and monasteries; and to adorn the churches with gifts of gold and silver?

Gregory had applied himself to restoring the walls of the city; he had reunited with the Church’s patrimony the Cottian Alps, which had been severed from it; and he had recovered for the Roman duchy the forts seized by the Lombards—sometimes by force, sometimes by prayers, and sometimes by gifts. It is therefore no wonder that, once the authority of Leo, the heretic who threatened ancient Rome with the same things he had accomplished in the new Rome, had been rejected, the Romans entrusted themselves, their lives, and their possessions to their most holy bishop.

These events occurred toward the end of the pontificate of Gregory II.
