But the matters that Natalis Alexander reports from his sources [Col. 0483A] belong to the period before the emperor’s wickedness had been revealed to the whole world. Leo seized the empire in the year 716, and Gregory wrote to Leo about the year 727:

“For ten years,” he says in his letter to Leo, “you walked rightly by the kindness of God and made no mention of sacred images; but now you say that they occupy the place of idols.”

Thus, in the year 726, Leo openly began to rage against the sacred images and to commit those monstrous acts of brutality and folly which Gregory reproaches him for in the said letter. For this reason the peoples of Italy began to shake off the yoke of Greek imperial rule, trample upon the emperor’s laureate images, and seize the cities subject to him. From the year 727 onward the emperor’s wickedness became still more conspicuous: he tore the sacred images from the churches and burned them in the fire; he put to death eminent citizens who were hostile to his impiety; and he afflicted holy bishops with exile and death.

Therefore, in the year 730, toward the end of Gregory’s pontificate, the events occurred that are also recorded by the Greek historians Cedrenus, Zonaras, and Theophanes. The pontiff subjected Leo, as a public heretic, to anathema. All the peoples of Italy, by a just use of arms, defended themselves against the emperor’s tyranny, and Gregory aided them by his counsel, authority, and protection.

Natalis, who was generally hostile to the authority of the Roman See, either did not attend to this chronological distinction or did not wish to attend to it; Pagius followed him, carried away by an excessive zeal for criticism. Let the most diligent reckoner of years, Baronius, be heard under the year 730. He writes:

“Until this time Gregory had often held back the reins of the rebellious people, lest they rebel completely against the emperor, so long as there remained some hope that, frequently admonished, he might revoke the edict he had published concerning his impiety; nor did Gregory care that on this account he was repeatedly brought into danger of his life. But when he could neither recall him from his undertaking by words or letters, nor restrain him by benefits from slipping into worse conduct, he judged that the time had now come for the axe to be applied to the root of the unhappy tree. By apostolic authority he cries: ‘Cut it down.’ Awakened by this thunderclap, the faithful of the West immediately break entirely away from Leo’s empire and cling to the apostolic pontiff. Thus Gregory left to posterity a worthy example, so that heretical rulers should not be permitted to reign in the Church of Christ if, after repeated admonition, they were found to persist stubbornly in error. For then occurred what all the Greek historians affirm, and Theophanes himself says: in the fourteenth year of the emperor Leo, Leo himself was deprived by Gregory of the collection of tribute in Italy. Cedrenus and others bear witness to this. Zonaras reports that these things were done at Rome—something we may reasonably believe—in a synodal manner, and that in the same council the emperor himself was punished with the penalty of anathema.”

BALDINUS. 2.—“For after this the emperor’s wickedness became manifest.” Most of what Anastasius records here is taken word for word from Paul the Deacon, at the end of chapter 49. Accordingly, in the year 730 the emperor promulgated a second edict, ordering that the venerable images throughout the empire should be removed and burned. Theophanes reserved the place, time, and circumstances for the year mentioned above:

“Moreover, on the seventh day of the month of January, in the thirteenth indiction, the irreligious Leo held a session against the sacred and venerable images in the tribunal of the nineteen couches. He had summoned Germanus, the most holy patriarch, believing that he could persuade him at last to subscribe to his decree for the abolition of the sacred images. But that brave servant of Christ, in no way yielding to Leo’s abominable plan, but rather rightly distributing the word of truth, resigned the episcopate . . . . On the seventh day of the same month of January, they substituted in his place Anastasius, a man of false name, the disciple and chancellor of blessed Germanus. Moved by ambition for secular power, he assented to Leo’s impiety and was created a false bishop of Constantinople. Meanwhile Gregory, the sacred bishop of Rome . . . . deposed Anastasius together with his writings, and rebuked Leo himself in letters as an irreligious man. He also stirred up Rome with all Italy to revolt against Leo’s empire. As a result, the tyrant, daily driven to greater fury, launched persecutions against the holy images, so that many clergy, monks, and devout laymen, endangered because of their sound judgments concerning the faith, were crowned with martyrdom.”

Stephen gives a fuller account of the persecution raised against Catholics in the *Life of Stephen the Younger*. [Col. 0484B] Meanwhile, while the Lombard princes Luitprand and afterward Aistulf were attempting to invade the whole of Italy, which was embroiled in such disputes, and were seizing more and more territories belonging to Roman rule, Gregory secretly entered into an alliance with Charles Martel. Later pontiffs did the same, as we shall note in its proper place.

BENCINUS. 3.—“For after this the emperor’s wickedness became manifest.” Leo began to think more intensely about abolishing the sacred images and sent the pontiff a letter concerning the matter. Gregory replied to him, in a manner befitting the dignity of the See, that the sacred images were venerated in the Church according to the ancient practice of Catholics, and that it was neither lawful for him, at his own discretion, nor proper to his office, to abolish their veneration. He also warned him repeatedly to consider carefully both what he was doing and how far he was proceeding. For it was not the emperor’s role to establish anything new concerning the faith, but rather to defend by every means whatever had been decreed from ancient times by the Fathers.

CIACONIUS. 4.—“After this the emperor’s wickedness became manifest.” Leo the Isaurian, the impious Iconoclast, raged so wildly—burning or defacing the images of the saints here and there—that he rashly wrote to Saint Gregory II, the supreme pontiff, who was attempting to recall him from his error, saying that he too, as Baronius reports under the year 726, would send someone to Rome to shatter the bronze image of the most holy apostle Peter, which stood prominently there.

This statue of the prince of the apostles, considered by the judgment of the most authoritative writers to be of great antiquity, is rightly believed to have been cast from the metal of the statue of Jupiter Capitolinus, by order of Saint Leo the Great, after Rome, in the year 452 of the Christian era, had been delivered from the imminent scourge of Attila, king of the Huns, through the patronage of that same most holy apostle, and had come to rest.

Nevertheless, it was moved from the very ancient oratory of Saint Martin, built near the Vatican basilica through the work of that same Saint Leo, where it had first been placed, to another church of the holy martyrs Processus and Martinianus—as Matthew Vegius says, who flourished under the pontificate of Martin V—and from there, under Paul III, to the front portico of the same basilica, as the contemporary writer Tiberius Alpharanus records. Finally, under Paul V, it was moved to the place where it is now seen.

This celebrated statue likewise enjoyed an ancient cult, especially through the kissing of its foot, which is visibly smooth and worn from the continual contact of innumerable lips. Indeed, Cardinal Caesar Baronius, whenever he visited the basilica of the prince of the apostles, venerated the statue by kissing it twice: first, when he approached the confession of the apostles, saying these words as he kissed it: “I believe in one, holy, catholic, and apostolic Church”; then, when he departed from the confession, saying these others: “Peace and obedience.”

We have also thought it necessary not to pass over the remarkable miracle of an instantaneous healing which God, through the intercession of the prince of the apostles, brought about by a kiss impressed with living faith upon this statue at the time when this Anastasian Codex was being printed. In the Jubilee Year 1725, on the fifth day before the Ides of June, under Benedict XIII, the supreme pontiff, John Kouvalschi, a soldier from the province of Silesia who had fought in the Turkish war, was grievously wounded during the assault on Belgrade. He fell from a certain cliff into a deep pit, so that his vertebrae were dislocated by the fall and contusion. He could no longer walk or stand, for his shins and hips, almost dried up by contracted paralysis, had become useless to him.

The unfortunate man moved himself—or rather dragged himself as best he could—using certain little wooden supports fitted to his hands, for about eight years. At last, a light shone in the chamber of his mind, and he seemed to see that he should be taken to Rome to be healed of his infirmities. He therefore made a vow and, not without the special providence of God, eventually reached Rome. He fasted for three days and, after receiving sacramental absolution from the Reverend Father Alexander Morichoni of the Society of Jesus, penitentiary for the Polish language, was refreshed by Holy Communion in the Vatican basilica.

Then he approached the statue of the prince of the apostles, prayed for a while, and wished to kiss the sacred foot, but could not. He therefore asked several pilgrims who were standing nearby for assistance. With their help he kissed the foot of the statue with living faith, asking to be restored to health through the intercession of Saint Peter.

Wonderful power of faith! Immediately his legs and feet were strengthened, and he began to walk and praise God, just as did the lame man from his mother’s womb who sat begging for alms at the Beautiful Gate of the temple and was healed by blessed Peter, as can be seen in the Acts of the Apostles.

The marvel of this instantaneous healing was spread far and wide. Our most reverend chapter of the Most Holy Vatican Basilica ordered it to be published in the Vatican press on the basis of authentic proofs and documents preserved in our archive, through the care and diligence of the most learned man Dominic Baptisti, a beneficiary priest. His Eminence Annibal, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Albanus by title of Saint Clement, archpriest of the same basilica, ordered an image of the statue to be engraved in copper with this inscription:

“THE BRONZE STATUE OF THE PRINCE OF THE APOSTLES, PLACED IN THE VATICAN BASILICA AND FREQUENTED WITH THE MOST ANCIENT WORSHIP OF THE CHRISTIAN PEOPLE, AT WHICH, IN THE JUBILEE YEAR 1725, DURING THE PONTIFICATE OF BENEDICT XIII, GOD GLORIFIED THE MERITS OF HIS APOSTLE BY THE DISTINGUISHED MIRACLE OF RESTORING HEALTH TO A PARALYTIC WHO HAD IMPLORED THE AID OF BLESSED PETER. ANNIBAL, CARDINAL OF SAINT CLEMENT OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH, CAMERLENGO AND ARCHPRIEST OF THIS MOST HOLY BASILICA, CAUSED THIS TO BE REPRESENTED ON A COPPER PLATE, ENGRAVED IN ORDER TO INCREASE THE GLORY OF THE APOSTOLIC PATRONAGE AND THE RELIGION OF THE FAITHFUL OF CHRIST, IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1727.”

We too, who through the favor and generosity of that same most eminent archpriest had been admitted—although unworthy—to the order of beneficiary clergy in the same basilica of the prince of the apostles, saw that young man walking and glorifying the Lord. We therefore faithfully bear witness to the truth.

Lest the memory of this most illustrious deed perish with the passage of time, we decided that it should be inserted in this Anastasian Codex, for the greater glory of the Most High, whom we proclaim wonderful in his apostle Peter.

THOMAS ACETA. 5.—“After this the emperor’s wickedness became manifest,” etc. In the earliest times after the rise of the Christian religion, while pagan fury still raged against it and the superstition of idols still lay hidden in human minds, the use of sacred images was not so frequent. Dionysius Petavius observes this in book XV of his *Theological Dogmas*, *On the Incarnation*, chapter 13.

Since images belong to the category of things that are not absolutely necessary for salvation and do not pertain to the very substance of religion, it lies within the Church’s authority either to employ them or to set them aside, according to what she judges more advantageous. Such things are commonly said to belong to positive law.

From this arose the reproach of unbelievers expressed in these words of Minucius Felix, p. 25:

“Why do they have no altars, no temples, no recognized images?”

Octavius replies, p. 95:

“Do you suppose that we conceal what we worship because we have no shrines and altars? What image could I fashion for God, when, if you judge rightly, man himself is God’s image? What temple could I build for him, when this whole world, fashioned by his work, cannot contain him? And though I occupy a greater space, shall I enclose the power of such majesty within a single little building? Is it not better that he be dedicated in our mind, indeed consecrated in our breast?”

Thus some then thought that it was not lawful to build temples for God, because this practice had not yet been established among the Christian people, and because it was not yet permitted under pagan rulers, who considered it impious and unlawful. Many seem likewise to have held a similar view concerning sacred images, which differed greatly from idols.

Christians gradually abandoned both opinions after experience and reason as their teachers showed them that neither practice ought to be condemned, but that both could contribute to piety.

Accordingly, they did not hesitate to build basilicas—or, as they eventually came to be called, churches—and altars in honor and worship of God, indeed magnificently and expensively, once peace and freedom had been restored. They were not deterred from doing so either by the former practice and ancient custom or by the authority of great men. At the same time the Church began to employ images of Christ and the saints, whose use had not previously become widespread, since there was no longer any danger of idolatry. Images appeared useful for propagating the memory of Christ, the martyrs, and the other saints, and for encouraging the faithful, through their example, to steadfastness in piety.

It is by no means established that this was done everywhere according to the same practice and at the same time. In some places it happened earlier, in others later, according to the capacity and character of the peoples and the judgment of those who ruled them.

This point must be observed all the more carefully because it applies to the interpretation of many examples and testimonies from antiquity that Protestants misuse to attack the Church’s practice. Catholic theologians who oppose them are sometimes excessively disturbed, whereas, when it is established that images were rejected and condemned by the Orthodox, this should be appropriately explained according to the circumstances of place and time.

Therefore, in the controversy concerning images, greater weight ought to be given to the examples and practices of the later Church than to those of the earlier Church. For while pagan superstition was still spreading with full force, it seemed preferable in those first centuries of the Church to suppress or omit many practices that were either not in themselves harmful or might even have been useful, because there was a danger that the outward appearance of certain rites would cause offense by its very resemblance to pagan ceremonies. This was done lest the uneducated and inexperienced should take images of Christ and the saints for the idols to which they had been accustomed, and so that their minds might be drawn farther away from the memory and practice of empty images.

It is therefore credible that images were used only sparingly by Christians during approximately the first four centuries, throughout which the abominable worship of demons in idols and the most savage persecution of the Christian name continued their course. Only in the fifth century, after the Church had attained freedom and had begun, so to speak, to stretch out her limbs, did images begin to be displayed openly in most places and placed in churches and oratories. Until then, although they were in some use, they had not been employed indiscriminately and frequently.

These and many other observations concerning the use of images in the ancient Church are made by the Petavius cited above. Natalis Alexander demonstrates at length that this use and veneration of images of Christ and the saints not only does not conflict with God’s law, but is also consistent with religion and useful for arousing the piety of the faithful, in his sixth dissertation on the eighth century.

At the beginning of that same eighth century, a horrible monster arose in the East: the heresy of the Iconoclasts, which declared war on venerable images. The seventh synod, in its first and fifth sessions, testifies that its precursors were pagans, Jews, Marcionites, Manichaeans, and Theopaschites.

The Jews began this impious war in the year 723 of Christ. At the command of Jezid, the Arab caliph, they cast down the images of Christ and the saints from the Christian churches throughout the borders of his entire kingdom, as Baronius reports for that year from Theophanes and from the account of John the monk, vicar of the Eastern bishops, in the fifth session of the same seventh synod. From the fourth session it is clear that this impiety passed from the Hebrews to the Christians, through the agency of Constantine, bishop of Nacolia in Phrygia Salutaris. Expelled by his own diocesans, he insinuated himself into the court of the emperor Leo the Isaurian and inflamed him against the holy images.

The Jews had also bound Leo the Isaurian by an oath that, once he had risen to imperial power, he would grant them whatever they requested, which they themselves had foretold. They therefore incited him to abolish the holy images and their veneration as remnants of idolatry, as the Greek historians Cedrenus, Zonaras, and Constantine Manasses testify.

Just as pagan emperors on other occasions promulgated edicts against Christians at the beginning of their decennial years, so Leo the Isaurian, having begun the tenth year of his tyranny, as Zonaras puts it, raised a persecution against the Orthodox in the year 726 of Christ and declared war on the sacred images.

After the tenth year of his reign—that is, after it had begun, as Stephen the Deacon of the Church of Constantinople says in the *Life of Saint Stephen the Younger, Monk and Martyr*, written about the year 808 and published in Greek and Latin in volume I of the *Greek Analecta* by the Benedictine monk Jacobus Loppinus—“that new Belshazzar, Leo the Isaurian, breathed into the Church the Manichaean heresy and one perhaps not altogether unlike the heresy of the Aphthartodocetae, if I may put it so.

“Thus, after summoning the people subject to him, this inhuman beast, distinguished by the name of Leo, roared like a lion before them all. From his angry heart, as from Mount Etna fire and sulfur, he belched forth and uttered this pitiable cry: ‘Since the making of images is an idolatrous art, they ought not to be worshiped.’”

That this occurred only after the tenth year of Leo’s reign had begun, not after it had ended, as Stephen the Deacon appears to suggest, is also evident from an anonymous author published by Combefisius among the writers of Byzantine history who wrote after Theophanes. In an invective composed to refute those who oppose the sound faith and the teaching of the holy and Orthodox Fathers, this author testifies that Leo began to resist the truth in the ninth indiction, which coincides, until the Kalends of September, with the tenth year of his reign and the year 726. This anonymous author was still alive in the year 760.

The monk Theosterictus, a disciple of Saint Nicetas, abbot of Medicion in Bithynia, who was most renowned for his defense of the sacred images and died in exile in the year 824, observes that this heresy was most bitter at its very beginning. He wrote the saint’s life within the first five years after his death; it was quoted by Bollandus under April 3. In it he says:

“Consider also this point: other heresies arose from bishops and lower-ranking priests, but this one proceeded from the emperors themselves—and you know how great is the difference between kings and priests. Other heresies grew through teaching and dispute and gradually gained strength; this one was extraordinarily powerful from the beginning because of imperial authority.”

Nevertheless, a great tumult was raised by the people as soon as the emperor Leo’s decree for abolishing the images was issued. Fearing for himself, the emperor concealed his sacrilegious plan. “My opinion,” he said, “does not aim at their complete destruction. I merely say that they should be placed higher up, so that no one may touch them with his mouth and thus in some way insult objects worthy of honor.”

By such devices he intended to abolish all veneration of images.

In the same year, 726, Leo Augustus wrote to Pope Gregory that, if Gregory wished to retain the imperial favor, he should remove the images of the saints; and Gregory II in turn wrote back to the emperor. Paul the Deacon, book VI of *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 49; Anastasius; and Theophanes testify to this. But those letters have perished.

Afterward, when the emperor could obtain nothing from Gregory, he repeatedly plotted against the life of the holy pontiff through his exarchs, dukes, and other ministers. But Romans and Lombards, piously allied for Gregory’s defense, preserved him unharmed from their treachery and attacks by their united strength:

“Romans and Lombards bound themselves together as brothers by a single chain of faith, all desiring to suffer a glorious death in defense of the pontiff and never permitting him to endure harm, while fighting for the true faith and the salvation of Christians,” says Anastasius.

The pontiff, as the same author adds, thanked the people for their good will and, according to his purpose, urged everyone with gentle speech to advance in good works toward God and to persevere in the faith. He also admonished them not to abandon their love and loyalty to the Roman Empire.

The emperor was hostile to Gregory II not only because of the new opinions that Gregory rejected, but also because Gregory would not permit a new census to be imposed in the Roman province. For this reason the emperor arranged to have him killed first through Marinus, the *spatharius* and duke of the Romans, and afterward through Paul, the patrician and exarch.

“Paul the exarch,” says Anastasius, “by the emperor’s command, attempted to kill the same pontiff because he prevented the imposition of a census in the province.”

That census was a form of head tax similar to the one imposed upon Sicily and Calabria, of which Theophanes speaks.

Saint Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, resisted the impiety of Leo the Isaurian with all possible steadfastness. Through one of the chief ministers of the Church he informed Leo that images had been made from the beginning, after Christ’s assumption into heaven; that he would gladly die for them; and that whoever dishonored the image of Christ inflicted the insult upon the one whom it represented.

He therefore set before Leo the tradition and practice of the holy Church, and the veneration of images approved by councils. He recalled the solemn promises Leo had made, when he was inaugurated as emperor, not to overturn the rites of the Church. He entreated him by all that is sacred not to permit the destruction of the sacred images during his reign, adding that whoever perpetrated such a crime would be a precursor of Antichrist. At last he left no stone unturned in attempting to recall Leo from the impiety he had conceived.

These facts are established by another *Life of Saint Stephen the Younger, Monk and Martyr*, which Baronius and others wrongly attribute to Saint John Damascene because John Billius appended it to the works of that saint. In fact, it is the genuine product of Metaphrastes, as Allatius teaches in his *Dissertation on the Simeons*, p. 126.

But the holy patriarch accomplished nothing. Indeed, in the year 730, on the seventh day of January, in the thirteenth indiction and on the third weekday, the irreligious Leo, as Theophanes says under that year of Christ, held a session—that is, an assembly of nobles convened by imperial command to deliberate on matters of state—against the sacred and venerable images in the tribunal of the nineteen couches. He had summoned Germanus, the most holy patriarch, believing that he could persuade him at last to subscribe to his decree for abolishing the sacred images.

But that brave servant of Christ, in no way yielding to Leo’s abominable plan, but rather rightly distributing the word of truth, resigned the episcopate. Then [Col. 0489B] the emperor sent satraps to the patriarchal residence and ordered them, as Stephen the Deacon says in the aforementioned *Life of Saint Stephen the Younger*, to drive the holy man from it with blows and insults.

Germanus withdrew to the Platanium, a hereditary residence, intending to live a private life. But shortly afterward, by Leo’s command, he was carried from his home to a monastery far away and was strangled when he was nearly a hundred years old, Stephen the Deacon adds.

After he had been expelled and had become a participant in monastic life, one could see the whole city, deprived of the father’s honey-sweet teaching, giving vent to abundant weeping and lamentation. That day was not a day but darkness and weeping upon weeping, and woe upon woe, as the prophet says.

In those same miserable days, the impious Anastasius—the disciple and fellow chamberlain of Saint Germanus—seized the pontificate with the hand of impiety. Anastasius and the author of the *Miscella* write that he was ordained on the twenty-second day of the same month of January, through military force and not by the suffrage of divine piety. He handed over everything belonging to the Church to the emperor’s buildings.

Saint Germanus was then ninety-five years old, as is read in a letter written by Pope Gregory to Leo in that same year. He wrote various works, most of which remain unpublished. He is commemorated in the Greek *Menaea* on May 12.

Then the tyrant, the same author continues, having received unrestricted authority to proclaim the heresy, immediately attempted to cast down and consign to the fire the holy and lordly image of Christ our God which, placed above the imperial entrance, was called the Holy Bronze because of its form. He accomplished this.

Meanwhile, as the image was being removed, honorable women, strengthened by divine zeal, rushed forward courageously. Seizing the ladder, they threw to the ground the *spatharius* who was removing the image and, after tearing him apart, put him to death.

After this they hurried immediately to the patriarchal residence and pelted the impious Anastasius with stones, saying:

“Most impure head and enemy of the truth, did you invade the priesthood for this reason—to destroy the holy and sacred votive offerings?”

Unable to endure this victory over himself, the profane man fled from the sight of the pious women and took refuge with the tyrant, persuading him to put those holy women to death by the sword. This was done, and they, having entered into combat for the image of Christ, received from Christ himself the reward of victory, rejoicing with all the victorious saints in the kingdom of heaven.

The martyrdom of these pious women and men is commemorated in the *Menaea* on August 9.

That image was kept in the church dedicated to the Mother of God, called Chalcopratia, after the district of the city in which it had been established. Hence it is sometimes called Chalcopratina, sometimes Aerea or Aenea, and sometimes Antiphonetes, as though one were to say “sponsor” or “surety.”

Combefisius published, in his *History of the Monothelite Heresy*, p. 613, a pious account of the Lord’s image at Chalcoprateia. It explains the origin of the devotion shown toward that image and reveals why it is called Antiphonetes.

There Combefisius conjectures that women were permitted to enter the Holy of Holies and the altar area in that church, whereas in other churches throughout the East only ministers entered there, along with the emperor when he was about to make an offering, or monks when they were being consecrated to God. He conjectures, I say, that under Leo the pious women claimed entry for themselves in order to deter his sacrilegious minister from his impious attempt, wisely judging that what in one circumstance served religion should not be preserved as though it were itself a religious rule when it worked against religion.

Accordingly, as a reward for that zeal, the women of that church were granted free access to the altar area, because they had forestalled so great a crime and pulled away the ladder.

Meanwhile the emperor Leo, having sent an edict by which he ordered the images to be cast down, promised Gregory II his favor if he subscribed to the impious decree; otherwise he threatened that Gregory would speedily be expelled from his rank.

Gregory immediately prepared himself against the hostile disposition of the prince and warned the armies of the Pentapolis and Venetia to guard against that impiety:

“Therefore,” says Anastasius, “the armies of the Pentapolis and Venetia, moved by these events, resisted the emperor’s command and declared that they would never submit to the murder of that pontiff; rather, they would fight manfully for his defense.”

The minds of all were inclined to protect the pontiff, and they withdrew from obedience to the exarch. Each, by his own choice, appointed leaders for himself, as the same Anastasius testifies:

“They subjected Paul the exarch, or those who had directed him, and his accomplices, to anathema. Rejecting his appointment, they all chose dukes for themselves everywhere in Italy, and thus they were all concerned for the immunity of the pontiff and of themselves.”

From that time the Roman province, like the other provinces, had a duke chosen at its own discretion—that is, by the selection of the leading men—who exercised the same authority in administering the commonwealth as the dukes sent by the emperor.

The Italians wished to break out into open revolt and create a new ruler, but the pontiff intervened, and through the urging of Luitprand of the Lombards...

The king returned to friendship with the exarch Eutychius and, according to Anastasius, restored his authority in the city of Rome:

> “When all Italy learned of the emperor’s wickedness, it resolved to choose an emperor for itself and bring him to Constantinople. But the pope restrained this plan, hoping for the ruler’s conversion.”

And below:

> “He urged the Romans not to cease from their love or loyalty toward the Roman Empire.”

From this it is clear that Theophanes, and the Greek authors Zonaras and Cedrenus who followed him—men generally poorly informed about events in the West—wrote erroneously that Pope Gregory had led Rome, Italy, and the other Western provinces away from obedience to and rule by Leo. For, besides what we have quoted from Anastasius, Paul the Deacon also writes in Book VI, chapter 49, of *The History of the Lombards*, that Gregory “kept the peoples in their duty and in the loyalty owed to the Empire”; more on this shortly.

—In the same year, 730, Gregory, having been informed by Saint Germanus the patriarch about Leo’s heresy, replied to him in a letter inserted in the fourth session of the Seventh Synod. After receiving Leo’s letters, he wrote him two dogmatic letters worthy of the supreme pontiff. Theophanes refers to them, writing that Gregory openly rebuked the same Leo in letters “known to many.” Baronius reproduces these letters under the year 726, the year in which he believes they were written; but, as will clearly appear from what follows, they were sent in the year 730.

When Leo saw that the Romans, Campanians, Ravennates, and Pentapolitans had already defected from him and that there was talk of stripping him of the Empire, he wrote again to the same pontiff and requested that a general council be convoked. Gregory had broken off all correspondence with him because Leo had attempted to deprive him of life. Nevertheless, he replied to his letter and mocked him for insolently insulting and threatening him.

> “You wrote,” Gregory says in his earlier letter, “that a universal council should be convened, and this seemed useless to us. You are a persecutor of images, an insulting enemy, and a destroyer. Cease, and grant us this favor: be silent. Then the world will enjoy peace, and scandals will cease. . . . Do you not perceive that this undertaking of yours, by which you rose up against the images, is a turbulent, insolent, and arrogant deed? While the churches of God were enjoying profound peace, you began conflicts and stirred up hatred and scandals. Cease and be quiet; then there will be no need for a synod. Write to all those regions of the world where you have caused offense that Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, and Gregory, pope of Rome, have prayed concerning the images; and we shall keep you free from this affair, so that no sin or transgression may be yours, since we have received from God the power to loose both heavenly and earthly things.”

Before this he had prescribed the limits of papal and imperial authority:

> “You know, Emperor, that the doctrines of the holy Church do not belong to emperors but to pontiffs, who customarily transmit the doctrines securely. For this reason pontiffs, abstaining from the affairs of the state, have been placed over the churches; and therefore emperors too should abstain from ecclesiastical matters and attend to what has been entrusted to them.”

—It is certain, moreover, that Gregory’s dogmatic letters to Leo were sent in the year 730. In the first he says:

> “You stripped the churches of God, which the holy Fathers had clothed and adorned; you despoiled and denuded them, although you had such a pontiff—namely, our lord Germanus, our brother and fellow minister. You ought to have obeyed his counsels as those of a father, teacher, and elder, endowed with great experience both in ecclesiastical and in civil affairs. For that man is now completing his ninety-fifth year, having served each of the patriarchs and emperors.”

Therefore, when that letter was written to the emperor, Germanus was no longer in Constantinople and had abdicated the patriarchate, which, as Baronius himself admits, he abdicated only in the year 730.

Moreover, in that letter Gregory mentions the image of the Savior called *Antiphonetes* and the killing of the *spatharius* sent by the emperor to remove it, after he had struck the face of the Savior’s image three times with an axe. He also mentions the martyrdom of those holy women who, unable to endure that wicked deed, killed the *spatharius*. This occurred after Anastasius had occupied Saint Germanus’s see, as will shortly be demonstrated from the *Acts of Saint Stephen the Younger*. Therefore [*ideo jue*; the text is uncertain], in January of the year 730, the aforementioned letters of Gregory II were written, after the beginning of September, when the fourteenth indiction had begun.

—Not content with this, Pope Gregory held a synod at Rome. There, sitting and presiding together with the neighboring bishops, he condemned the heresy of the Iconoclasts and confirmed the Catholic faith concerning the holy images. Only one fragment of this synod survives, quoted by Adrian I, Roman pontiff, in his first letter to Charlemagne.

Cedrenus and Zonaras also remembered this synod. From them Baronius concludes that Gregory, seeing that the emperor was thoroughly heretical, cursed him with an anathema at this synod; that he then caused the Romans and Italians to withdraw from the emperor’s obedience; and that he prohibited them from paying tribute to him. Bellarmine likewise writes this in Book V, chapter 8, of *On the Roman Pontiff*, as do Sigonius in Book III of *On the Kingdom of Italy* and several others.

**PACIUS.** For after these events the wickedness of that same emperor became evident. Because of it he persecuted the pontiff, to such an extent that he compelled all the inhabitants of Constantinople, both by force [Note: *Codex Luc., Vi*] and by blandishments, to remove wherever they were found the images both of the Savior and of his holy Mother, as well as those of all the saints, and—what is cruel to say—to burn them in the middle of the city and whitewash all the churches that had been painted.

Because many of the people of that city hindered such a crime from being committed, some were beheaded, while others suffered punishment by having parts of their bodies cut off. [Note: *Codex Luc., In aliqua parte*—“in some part.”]

[Note: At that time, according to another version, the patriarch Germanus was expelled from his own see by the emperor’s wickedness, and so forth.]

For this reason that same emperor also deprived Germanus, bishop of the holy Church of Constantinople, of his patriarchate, because he had refused to give his consent to him, [Note: *Codex Luc., Idem*—“the same,”] and installed in his place the presbyter Anastasius, his accomplice. When Anastasius sent a synodal letter to Rome and Gregory found him consenting to such a heresy, the holy man did not judge him worthy to be called “brother” or “fellow priest,” as was customary, but—

[Note: **SOMMIER.** In admonitory rescripts, unless he should convert to the Catholic faith, etc. When Leo learned that the Italian provinces belonging to the Western Empire had defected and had all chosen dukes for themselves, threatening to elect a new Augustus and take him to Constantinople, he sent letters to the Roman pontiff requesting that an ecumenical council be summoned. But the pontiff, scorning the emperor’s proposal, said: “You wrote that a universal council should be convened, and this seemed useless to us. . . . You are a persecutor of images, an insulting enemy, and a destroyer; cease, and grant us this favor: be silent. Then the world will enjoy peace, and scandals will cease. . . . Suppose that we had obeyed you and that pontiffs from the whole world had assembled, and that the senate and council had taken their seats: where is the lover of Christ and pious emperor who, as custom requires, ought to sit in the senate, reward those who speak rightly, and banish those who babble things alien to the truth, when you, Emperor, are wavering and imitate barbarians?” (Gregory II, Letter 1 to Leo.)

Meanwhile, the pontiff resolved that a synod should be held at Rome. There, after defending the veneration of sacred images and the invocation of the saints both by the authority of Sacred Scripture and the Fathers and by the custom introduced into the Church through the piety of the faithful, he condemned the contrary teaching as a mad opinion and a most pernicious heresy. “The lord Pope Gregory II the younger, in his sacred council, with that same most high and most blessed former Lord Pope Gregory presiding there, likewise himself said: . . . Since we see that very many, with minds disturbed, are troubling the ordinances of the Church, we desire, in order to restrain the madness of error, to say something further from the ancient testimonies,” etc. (Fragment of the Third Roman Council, in Adrian I’s letter to Charlemagne.) Only a fragment of this council survives in Adrian I’s letter to Charlemagne.

Nevertheless, contemporary Greek authors—Theophanes, Cedrenus, and Zonaras—whom most modern writers follow, report that Leo was excommunicated in that council and that the Italians were released from their oath of loyalty to that ruler. “Gregory,” Zonaras says, “who then governed the Church of Old Rome, having rejected communion with the ruler of New Rome, that is, the Emperor Leo, and with those who followed him, bound them together with the emperor by a synodal anathema, prohibited the payment of the taxes that had until then been rendered from there, and made an alliance with the Franks.”

Other modern writers, however, hold otherwise. They teach that Leo was neither excommunicated nor deposed in that synod. They say that he was not separated from communion because Paul the Deacon and Anastasius the Librarian, Latin writers and better informed than the Greeks about events occurring at Rome, are silent on this matter. Nor, they maintain—for this is the view of the latter—was he deposed; and this seems more probable. For the same Latin authors state in express terms that Pope Gregory always opposed the desire of the Italian peoples and forces to raise a new Augustus in Leo’s place, since he had conceived the hope that the emperor might at some time be converted. “The whole army of Ravenna,” says the Deacon (Book VI, chapter 49), “and of Venetia resisted such commands with one mind; and, had the pontiff not forbidden them, they would have undertaken to set an emperor over themselves.” And Anastasius (section 184): “All Italy resolved to choose an emperor for itself and take him to Constantinople; but the pontiff restrained this plan, hoping for the ruler’s conversion.” What we know with certainty about the same matter is clear from Gregory’s often-cited first letter: “We invoke Christ, the Prince of the army of every creature, seated in heaven, who is above all the armies of the heavenly powers, that he may send you a demon, as the Apostle says, ‘to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved.’” From this, it seemed that nothing other than excommunication could be understood.

As for Gregory’s dogmatic letters, in the first he reminds the emperor why God forbade the Israelites the worship of images: namely, to turn their minds from idolatry, on account of which he was sending the peoples of the land of promise to be exterminated. He says that the Lord did not grant Moses, when he asked to behold him under a perceptible image, this favor. But in the fullness of time the Son of God, clothed in human flesh, made himself visible in all the mysteries which he had wrought for our redemption. Those who had seen Jesus Christ portrayed him in the same likeness in which they had known him. Likewise, the likenesses of the holy James, Stephen, and the other martyrs were made by those who had seen them.

Yet the worship of Catholics is not confined to such images, nor do they place their hope in them. Rather, on looking at the image of Jesus Christ, they turn to Jesus Christ himself, saying: “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, help us; save us.” Looking upon the image of the most blessed Virgin, they say: “Holy Mary, virgin Mother of God, intercede for us with the Lord, that he may save us”; and so with the images of the other saints. He says that Leo had brought upon himself universal hatred and even the contempt of little children learning the catechism by declaring war on sacred images. As Roman pontiff, he had wished to use the power and authority which he had received from Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, to punish him; “but,” he says, “since you have brought the curse upon yourself, keep it for yourself with the counselors whom you embrace. . . . Write that Gregory, pope of Rome, has entreated you concerning images; and we shall keep you free from this concern, so that no sin or transgression may be yours, since we have received from God the power to loose both heavenly and earthly things.”

He continues that bishops, not Augusti, determine doctrine, and declares himself absolved before God and men concerning the veneration of images, from the alleged charge of idolatry which the emperor attributed to it. He says that he and his successors, the Roman pontiffs, will always be arbiters and mediators of peace between East and West, whatever evils Leo may threaten; and that, if Leo should send to Rome, as he boasted, persons to cast down the image of Saint Peter, he does not disclose to him what will happen. He nevertheless declares that he will be innocent of the bloodshed to come, for which the emperor alone will be blameworthy.

In the second dogmatic letter, he testifies to Leo how great was the pain he suffered because Leo persisted in error; then he sets before his eyes the examples of Leo’s predecessors, who had arranged for councils to be held together with the pontiffs. He says that emperors do not define the doctrines of faith, but pontiffs do; and that, just as the pontiff does not meddle in the affairs and offices of the imperial household, so the emperor ought not to meddle in ecclesiastical affairs: to elect or consecrate ministers of the altar, celebrate the sacred mysteries, or finally partake of them without the ministry of priests. In civil affairs, princes of the world punish crimes by confiscation of property and by death or exile. In the Church, however, after confession of crimes, people are punished by fasts, vigils, and prayers; after these they are admitted to communion of the precious body and blood of Jesus Christ and fully reconciled with the Lord. Augusti distinguished by religion and piety had willingly been subject to such laws like other human beings; but Leo, on the contrary, after rebellion and crimes, uses force and arms to afflict the chief pontiff and lays snares for his life. Finally, since he has always rejected the pontiff’s salutary admonitions and counsels and is certainly addicted to the damnable teaching of the perverse, he will without doubt have his portion with them, unless merciful God calls him to repentance. **SOMMIER.**]

—in admonitory rescripts, ordered that he should be removed even from priestly office unless he converted to the Catholic faith. [Note: Advising the emperor for his salvation. Gregory II issued several letters concerning the holy images. Only two are now extant, and they are read at the beginning of the Seventh Synod. Indeed, Anastasius noted above that after Leo’s earlier decrees the pontiff issued an encyclical to the entire Catholic world, in which he declared the emperor a heretic; from this the first disturbances among the Italian forces arose. Theophanes also suggests that the same letter was circulated throughout the East, when he says that John of Damascus pronounced an anathema against Leo: “Gregory, in letters sent to him, which everyone knows, was angered against him; and finally John [of Damascus], together with the bishops of the entire East, bound the impious Leo with an anathema.” **BENCINUS.**]

He also exhorted the emperor in writing, offering salutary advice so that he might turn away from such an execrable misery.

He made a particularly splendid golden chalice, adorned with various precious stones, weighing 30 pounds; likewise, a golden paten weighing 28½ pounds. He left to all the clergy, monasteries, deaconries, and mansionarii 2,160 solidi, and to the lamps of blessed Peter the Apostle 1,000 solidi. He carried out five ordinations, four in the month of September and one in June: thirty-five priests, four deacons, and 150 bishops in various places. He too was buried at blessed Peter the Apostle on the third day before the Ides of February, in the fourteenth indiction, under the emperors Leo and Constantine. And the episcopate was vacant for five days and one month.

[Note: In some copies, “under Leo and Constantine” is absent.]

[Note: While Saint Gregory was in office, a son, Constantine, was born to the emperor Leo in the year 718; he was later called, and additionally given the title, Copronymus, because he polluted the sacred font when he was immersed as an infant. Saint John of Damascus, that noble defender of the sacred images, calls him *Cabalinus* in his *Demonstrative Oration on the Sacred and Venerable Images*, from horse dung (*equino stercore*), because this utterly impure man delighted in its smell and touch. In the year 720, in the third indiction, on Easter Day itself, as Theophanes writes, the emperor Leo made him his associate in the empire. Consequently, his years are reckoned [Col. 0494D] from 21 March, the day on which Easter fell in that year.]

## FABRICIUS’S NOTICE ON POPE SAINT GREGORY II

Gregory II, son of Marcellus, was pope from being prefect of the papal library and a deacon, beginning on 28 April 715, until 13 February 731. Among others, Gregory Polydorus, an Augustinian from Pistoia, discusses him in his *Gregorian*, or book on the fourteen Gregories—Roman pontiffs, thirteen bishops, and one priest—Florence, 1598, and in the *Acta Sanctorum*, volume II for February, page 692. “If his writings had survived,” says Baronius under the year 731, no. 1, “and if the deeds accomplished by him had been more carefully committed to writing, you would judge him no less worthy than Gregory the Great.” Besides letters and other works, he is said to have written one book of *Responses* to the emperor Leo the Isaurian and another to John, bishop of Constantinople.

By this Gregory, Saint Corbinian and Saint Boniface were sent into Germany to spread the teaching of Christ. According to Bede, in his preface to King Ceolwulf, Nothelm, a priest of the Church of London, with Gregory’s permission searched through the archives of the holy Roman Church and brought to England the letters of Gregory I and other pontiffs, to be incorporated into its history.

Through an error, this Gregory is called “Gregory the Dialogist” by the Greeks, as by Cedrenus, and in the heading of the two letters to Leo the Isaurian written in defense of the veneration of images, printed by Baronius under the year 726, no. 27 and following. That title belongs to Gregory I, and the surname was assigned to him because of the famous *Dialogue* mentioned above, composed by him on page 84. In the same way, John is customarily called “Climacus” by the Greeks because of the book entitled *Climax*, or *The Ladder of Paradise*, which he composed.

Besides Baronius, Binius and other editors of the councils print those two letters to Leo in Greek and Latin before the acts of the Seventh Synod, and in the fourth session of that same synod, the letter to Germanus of Constantinople. Moreover, the same collectors of the councils offer in Latin—the language in which Gregory wrote—twelve letters of this Gregory, except that only two to Boniface survive in Hardouin. They append to them a capitulary issued by the same Gregory to Martinianus the bishop, George the priest, and Dorotheus the subdeacon, sent as legates to Bavaria to visit the churches.

Some attribute several of these letters to Gregory III, whom we shall discuss shortly. The same is true of the letter to Austrobert, archbishop of Vienne, which Louis Jacob, on page 89, records as having been published by John Bosco in the Floriacensis Library and by John Lievreus in the *Antiquities of Vienne*, page 181.

Likewise, some do not hesitate to attribute to Gregory II the liturgy, or Mass, which I listed among the writings of Gregory I, as does the distinguished Cave. [Note: Concerning the antiphons, see above, volume I, page 272.]

The *Responses* of Gregory, by which he is said to have resolved the questions of the emperor Justinian concerning certain chapters, are now lost. I hesitantly attributed to this Gregory II certain penitential canons that I found in a manuscript of Lucca, clearly different from the canons of Gregory III, and published them in the *Supplement to the Councils*, volume I, page 538. From Wilkins’s *Concilia Britannica*, volume I, page 81, I added Gregory’s letter to the bishops of England, in which first rank is asserted for the bishop of Canterbury among all the bishops of England.

## LETTERS AND CANONS OF SAINT GREGORY II, ROMAN PONTIFF

*(Mansi, Collection of the Councils, volume XII.)*

## FIRST LETTER OF POPE GREGORY II TO BONIFACE THE PRIEST

He grants him authority to announce the mystery of the faith to unbelieving peoples.

### Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to Boniface, his religious priest

The intention of your religious purpose, which has been made known to us and burns piously in Christ, and the report brought to us concerning your most sincere faith, which we have approved, require that we employ you as a fellow minister in the administration of the divine word, whose care we undertake by the grace of God.

Accordingly, since we have learned that from childhood you have studied the sacred writings, and that, by the insight of divine love, you have extended the natural capacity of your gifts toward increasing the talent entrusted to you from heaven—namely, that you have devoted the grace of knowledge of the heavenly oracle to the labor of saving proclamation, so that the mystery of the faith may become known to unbelieving peoples—we rejoice in your faith and desire to become helpers of the grace bestowed upon you.

Therefore, since you have brought the pious impulse of your undertaking, as stated above, to the modest notice of the apostolic see, it has seemed fitting that, just as a member seeks the head from its own body, you should demonstrate the movement of your mind, humbly submit yourself to the judgment of the head, hasten along the right path under its direction, and become established as the fullness of the bond.

For this reason, in the name of the indivisible Trinity, by the unshaken authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose teaching and administration we exercise and whose sacred see we govern, we establish the modesty of your religious office and command that, in the word of God, by which you appear to strive with the saving fire that the Lord came to cast upon the earth, you may, with God’s assent, hasten to whatever peoples are held fast by the error of unbelief. By proclaiming the name of Christ the Lord, our God, with a persuasion grounded in truth, you shall make known the mystery of the kingdom of God, and through the spirit of power [Roman Edition: truth], love, and self-control, you shall pour the preaching of both Testaments into unlearned minds by an appropriate method.

Finally, concerning the discipline of the sacrament, which, with God guiding you, you strive to maintain for those who are to be initiated into the faith, we wish you to observe the form of the offices of our holy apostolic see, as previously outlined for your instruction. Whatever you perceive to be lacking in the action you have undertaken, you shall take care to report to us as you wish [variant: whenever you are able].

Farewell. Given on the Ides of May, while our most pious lord Leo, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the third year of his reign, in the eleventh indiction [second].

### Summary of the oath that Boniface made at Rome when he was ordained bishop, and presented in his own hand

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ. While our lord Leo, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the sixth year, after his sixth consulship [Note: “Leo’s sixth year.” So it appears in the Rheims Codex and the Pithoean Codex, but incorrectly in the printed editions as “the seventh year.” For Leo the Isaurian entered upon the empire on 25 March, and soon afterward, as is conjectured, entered the consulship on the following Kalends, in the year of Christ 717, the fifteenth indiction. Boniface, moreover, as the history of his life shows, was consecrated on the day before the Kalends of December, in the sixth indiction. Thus it was Leo’s sixth imperial and consular year, not the seventh, and the year of Christ 722, not, as some prefer, 723; for then the seventh indiction would have fallen in November. Sirmond.]

—and also in the fourth year of Constantine, his son, the great emperor, in the sixth indiction—I, Boniface, by the grace of God a bishop, promise to you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to your vicar, blessed Pope Gregory, and to his successors, by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the inseparable Trinity, and by this most sacred body of yours, that I shall show every faithfulness and purity of the holy Catholic faith and, with God working, persevere in the unity of that same faith, in which the salvation of all Christians is unquestionably found.

I shall in no way consent, at anyone’s persuasion, to act against the unity of the common and universal Church. Rather, as I have said, I shall show my faith, purity, and cooperation in every respect toward you and toward the interests of your Church, to which power of binding and loosing has been given by the Lord God, and toward your aforesaid vicar and his successors.

Moreover, if I learn that bishops are conducting themselves contrary to the ancient institutions of the holy Fathers, I shall have no communion or association with them. Rather, if I am able to prevent them, I shall prevent them; if not, I shall immediately report the matter faithfully to my lord the apostolic bishop.

But if—which God forbid—I should in any way, by any device or occasion, attempt to do anything contrary to the terms of this promise of mine, I shall be found guilty at the eternal judgment and incur the punishment of Ananias and Sapphira, who presumed to defraud you even of their own property or to speak falsely.

I, Boniface, an unworthy bishop, have written this summary of the oath with my own hand. Placing it upon the most sacred body of blessed Peter, I have rendered the oath as prescribed, with God as witness and judge, and I promise to keep it.

[Note: At first Charles, duke of the Franks, showed himself less approachable toward Boniface, as Saint Ludger indicates in the *Life of Saint Gregory of Utrecht* in Serarius. But when he had read these papal letters and had seen Boniface, returning from Rome, entrust himself to Charles’s faith, dominion, and protection, he immediately received him with great kindness. By the authority of those letters, he wished him to be safe and secure throughout all the regions of Germany and the entire Frankish kingdom. These letters, found by the Reverend Father Fronton Ducaeus in a codex of the Church of Verdun, are preserved in Baronius under the year 724, no. 2, and in Serarius’s *History of Mainz*, note 18.]

## SECOND LETTER OF POPE GREGORY II TO CHARLES, DUKE AND MAYOR OF THE PALACE OF THE FRANKS

He commends Boniface so that Charles may support him in the ministry he has undertaken.

### Pope Gregory to the glorious son Charles, duke

[Note: “To Charles the duke.” Thus he addresses Charles Martel, who at that time was mayor of the palace of King Theuderic II. Among the old charters of Saint Gall there is a subscription of this kind: “I made [this] in the month of June, on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, in the fifteenth year, while our lord King Theuderic reigned over Charles, the mayor of the palace.”

After the death of King Theuderic, Charles alone ruled without a king for nine years, as I found in the Tilian Codex, or seven, according to another Rheims codex—an important fact not observed by our writers. During that time, since there was no king, public documents dated the year elapsed since the death of King Theuderic, as can be seen in Charles’s documents at Saint-Denis, by which he granted the estate of Clichy to the monastery of Saint-Denis: “Enacted at the estate of Cariciacum, in the palace, on the seventeenth day of September, in the fifth year after King Theuderic’s death. The mark of the illustrious Charles, mayor of the palace, who ordered this charter of donation to be made.” Sirmond.

The first person who, so far as I have seen or learned, explicitly remembered that interregnum—which seems especially necessary for understanding our national history—was the Reverend Father James Sirmond, whom we have just cited. After him came the Reverend Father Denis Petau, in book VIII, part I, of the *Rationarium temporum*; Aubert Miraeus, in the *Notice of the Churches of Belgium* and in his *Chronicle*; Andrew Duchesne, in his genealogical chart of the kings of France; and others. But they departed from the path of truth in subtracting two years from Theuderic II, assigning his death to the year 735 of the Christian era, and extending the limits of the interregnum no farther than the death of Charles Martel.

To aid the faltering chronology of the Frankish kings, for several years now we have brought forward, partly in our biographical notices, partly in our historical miscellanies, and in both of our chronicles, certain venerable antiquarian treasures (*κειμήλια*) which we shall now undertake to display together, to the considerable benefit of readers who are candidates for deeper chronological knowledge.

First of all, it must be proved that Theuderic II, commonly called “of Chelles,” did not end his life before the year 737. This is first demonstrated by the ancient genealogies of the Frankish kings, which Duchesne, on page 781 of volume I of the *History of France’s Contemporary Historians*, and others have published, and which still lie hidden in manuscript codices. For in them not merely fifteen years but seventeen altogether are assigned to this Theuderic—the number reckoned from the end of the year 720, or the beginning of 721, to the year 737.

The anonymous author whose treatise on the ecclesiastical computation we possess, written on parchment several centuries ago, proves the same point clearly: “From the birth of the Lord,” he says, “to the present year, in which Theuderic, king of the Franks, died, 737: in that year, in the fifth indiction, epact 15, concurrent 1, lunar cycle 13, 14, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April; Easter on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, moon 17, 24, according to the 532-year cycle of the Greeks.” Thus he writes.

Fredegarius the scholastic, or whoever else was the author of the appendix added to Gregory of Tours’s *History*, also contributes to this conclusion. When, in chapter or section 107, he said, “After his death they established King Theuderic on the royal throne, who now occupied the royal seat,” together with the years of life either expected, or—as I have advised that the text be corrected—extended, he expressed his meaning clearly enough: when he first brought his chronicle to an end at the beginning of the year 736, he showed that King Theuderic was still alive.

That the year 736 mentioned above is intended is plainly suggested by the same author in chapter 109 of the appendix, in these words, on page 771 of volume I of Duchesne’s edition:

“Victor returned in peace, with Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords, giving aid. The courses of the years are found as follows: from Adam, or the beginning of the age, to the Flood, 2,242 years; from the Flood to Abraham, 942 years; from Abraham to Moses, 505 years; from Moses to Solomon, 489 years; from Solomon to the rebuilding of the Temple in the time of Darius, king of the Persians, 512 years; from the restoration of the Temple to the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, 548 years. Certainly, from the beginning of the world to the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, 4,538 years; from the Passion of the Lord to this present year, in Victor’s cycle 177, on the Kalends of January, a Sunday, 735—according to the Gallic reckoning, for according to Roman custom the year began on those Kalends in the year 736 from Christ’s birth—and, for this millennium to be completed, 265 years remain” [Duchesne says in the margin of the cited page, “122,” but incorrectly].

The anonymous continuator of Aimoin has nearly the same words, chapter 54 of book IV in the edition of Jacobus Breulius. One point, however, must not be omitted: he asserts that the present year, 735, was the nineteenth year of Charles’s rule, reckoned from the year 717, when Charles defeated and routed Raganfred at Vincy in a memorable battle, for all posterity to remember.

After Theuderic’s death, Charles Martel, for as long as he lived, appointed no king. Thus began the interregnum in Francia, which, beginning in 737, ended at the beginning of 743, after at least six or seven years had begun.

That interregnum is expressly remembered first by the very brief chronicle extending from King Theuderic I to Childeric, whom Pippin succeeded. Sirmond copied it from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Remi at Rheims, and Duchesne published it on page 781 of volume I of the *History of France’s Contemporary Historians*: “Theuderic reigned seventeen years; for seven years meanwhile no other king reigned; King Childeric reigned nine years.” All of this fits perfectly and corresponds with our calculations, so that nothing more suitable to our purpose could be devised.

It is also remembered by another, considerably longer chronicle, extending from King Chlothar II to Pippin’s death, which Duchesne presents on the same page from the Tilian manuscript. In that chronicle, however, one point must unquestionably be corrected: it assigns nine years to Charles Tudites (*Carolo Tuditi*, reading uncertain) after Theuderic’s death. I therefore think it should read: “Theuderic reigned seventeen years; Charles ruled without another king for four or five years; Childeric reigned nine years; Pippin reigned sixteen and a half years.”

The same meaning was expressed by Erchambert in the fragment surviving from his *Brief History of the Frankish Kings and Mayors of the Palace*, which appears on the same page of Duchesne’s first volume, though it is badly damaged at the end and terribly distorted by faulty punctuation. I restore it as follows:

“The Franks established Theuderic, son of the younger Dagobert, as their king. He had been raised in the monastery of Chelles. Charles was mayor and prince for four years—not six, as that printed fragment reads—and, already governing both kingdoms with manly strength, continually engaged in battle everywhere with kings and dukes, until by conquering all those who seemed likely to oppose him, he was clearly recognized as the victor.”

These words most plainly declare that Erchambert wrote his brief history either at the end of 740 or during 741, before Charles Martel died in the autumn.

This most powerful prince and sub-king of the Franks, shortly before his death, donated the estate of Clichy to the royal monastery of Saint-Denis, where he was later buried. The following subscription strongly confirms and almost illuminates our conclusion in letters of gold:

“Enacted at the estate of Cariciacum, in the palace, on 17 September, in the fifth year after King Theuderic’s death. The mark of the illustrious Charles, mayor of the palace, who ordered this charter of donation to be made. The mark of the illustrious matron Sunechildis, consenting. The mark of Griso, her son, consenting. Audoenus, chaplain, subscribed. I, Theuderic, subscribed. Crothgangus, ordered to do so, examined this charter of donation.”

The documents of Robert, count of Hasbain, son of Lambert, had almost slipped from memory. In them he makes extensive grants to the abbey of Saint-Trond in Hasbain. Aubert Miraeus quotes them in chapter 16 of the *Notice of the Churches of Belgium*, but incorrectly assigns them to the year 745, although it would have been easy for him to recognize that error from what he had copied from Sirmond on page 21 of the same *Notice*, as we have noted elsewhere:

“I, Robert, in the fifth year after the death of King Theuderic, on the seventh day after the Kalends of April, by lawful transfer, gave and assigned something from my allod to the basilica of Saint-Trond, which is built in the estate called Sarcinium, etc.”

Perhaps more evidence will arise in the future that can easily be added to these materials, although these are more than sufficient to establish the point for fair-minded judges of the facts.

As for the end of the interregnum and the inauguration of King Childeric III, lest the reader who loves chronological precision justly complain that anything is lacking from this annotation, I believe I have observed that Francia was administered by the brothers Pippin and Carloman for at least one full year, and several additional months, after the death of their father Martel, without any king. Toward the end of 743 they raised one to the royal throne of their ancestors.

It is therefore necessary to admit that nearly all chronologers up to the present have erred in deriving the beginning of Childeric’s reign from 741 or 742. There exists, in Peter Balleuraeus’s *Antiquities of the City of Mâcon*, by Saint Julian, dean of Chalon, and also in James Severtius’s work on Domnolus, bishop of Mâcon, a diploma of unquestionable reliability. From it even those who have not yet been washed in the air (*aere lavantur*, an uncertain expression) can easily conclude that at the beginning of the year 743 the kingdom had not yet been granted to the Franks:

“The mark of Pippin, mayor of the palace. I, Rodalgus, wrote at his command. Enacted on the Kalends of January, in the second year of that same Pippin’s principate, in the city of Metz, in the royal palace.”

Arguments drawn from several councils held during that period may perhaps seem even more certain. The first is the so-called Germanic Council, whose location is uncertain, but whose preface does not permit ignorance of the year in which it was held:

“I, Carloman, duke and prince of the Franks, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 742, namely on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, gathered the bishops who are in my kingdom—that is, in the part of the kingdom entrusted to me—together with the priests, into a council and synod for fear of Christ. Boniface the archbishop, Burchard, and others.”

The second was convened at Liptines, in a royal estate of the district of Cambrai, and begins as follows:

“Now, in this synodal assembly, which was gathered on the Kalends of March—that is, in the year 743 of the Christian era, according to Roman reckoning—at the place called Liptines, all the venerable priests of God, counts, and officials, agreeing with the decrees of the earlier synod, confirmed them.”

The third remains, namely the Council of Soissons, which is correctly assigned to the year 744 in the collections of the councils. It begins:

“In the name of God and of the Trinity, in the year 744 from the Incarnation of Christ, on the sixth day—or rather the fifth, as other manuscript codices read—before the Nones of March, and on the fourteenth day of the moon, in the second year of Childeric, king of the Franks, I, Pippin, duke and prince of the Franks, held a synod at the city of Soissons, etc.”

Until greater light shines from elsewhere, I believe this much to be entirely established and clear: Childeric was elevated to royal dignity not before the Kalends of March 743—since the collectors of the councils assign the Council of Liptines to Childeric’s first year freely and on the basis of mere conjecture, although no mention of that king is found in its acts—but after the Kalends of that same month, on the first or second day, in the year 743. Thus an ancient writer most truthfully wrote: “Meanwhile, for seven years there was no king in Gaul,” provided that “seven years” is understood to mean years begun, not completed.

No one, therefore, should find this annotation too long or disagreeable, since its subject is of great importance in chronological matters and has not hitherto been treated with the accuracy it requires—especially anyone who has long and carefully considered that golden saying of the graceful poet:

> “If you happen to discover anything,  
> remember to support it carefully with several indications.”

—Pope Gregory to Charles the duke.

Since we have learned that you, most beloved in Christ, possess a religious disposition of mind in many circumstances, after extending the requisite greeting of salvation, we make known to your God-beloved dignity that we are sending to preach to the peoples of the German nation, and to those dwelling in various places on the eastern side of the Rhine, held fast by pagan error or still obstructed by the darkness of ignorance, our present brother Boniface, a bishop consecrated and approved by us in faith and conduct, and instructed in the ordinances of the holy apostolic see over which, by God’s authority, we preside, with the Church’s universal concern.

For this reason we commend him entirely to your glorious benevolence, so that you may assist him in all necessities and most earnestly defend him against any adversaries over whom you prevail in the Lord. Be absolutely certain that whatever favor you promptly extend to him, you offer to God, who declared that, when his holy apostles were sent to be a light to the nations, he himself would be received by those who received them. The bishop mentioned above, instructed through us, proceeds into the lot of preaching according to their teaching.

## THIRD LETTER OF POPE GREGORY II TO BISHOPS AND OTHERS OF EVERY ORDER, BOTH CLERGY AND LAITY

He commends the same Boniface and explains for what purposes he has been sent.

### Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to all most reverend and holy brother bishops, religious priests and deacons, illustrious dukes, distinguished officials, counts, and all Christians who fear God

Because of the charge entrusted to us, we are deeply concerned after learning that certain peoples in the regions of Germany, or on the eastern side of the Rhine, are wandering in the shadow of death at the persuasion of the ancient enemy and, as though under the guise of Christian religion, are serving the worship of idols. Others possess no knowledge of God and have not been washed in the water of holy baptism; as pagans, more like brute animals, they do not recognize their Maker.

We have therefore judged it necessary, for the illumination of both groups, to send to those regions the bearer of this letter, Boniface, our most reverend brother and co-bishop, to preach the word of the true faith. By preaching the word of salvation, he may provide them with eternal life; and if he should perhaps discover anyone anywhere [Roman Edition: or anywhere] who has strayed from the path of the true faith, or whom he finds deceived by diabolical cunning into error, he may correct them, restore them to the harbor of salvation by calling them back, instruct them according to the teaching of this apostolic see, and establish them in perseverance in the same Catholic faith.

We exhort you, moreover, for the love of our Lord Jesus Christ and in reverence for his apostles, to provide him every assistance [variant: you ought to assist him with all your efforts], and receive him in the name of Jesus Christ, as it is written concerning his disciples: “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matthew 10). Provide also the necessities of his journey, assign him companions, and furnish food and drink, or whatever else he may need, so that, with God’s favor, the work entrusted to him and the task of salvation may be completed through a single labor and shared goodwill. Thus you may deserve to receive the rewards of your labor, and a recompense for the conversion of the erring may be credited to you in heaven.

If, therefore, anyone offers assistance or cooperation to this servant of God, sent by this apostolic and Catholic Church of God for the illumination of the nations, may he deserve, at the intercession of the princes of the apostles, the fellowship of the holy martyrs of Christ Jesus.

But if anyone—which we do not desire—attempts to obstruct his labors by opposing them [variant: attempts, by turning away, to hinder his labor], or proves hostile to the ministry entrusted to him or to those who enter upon the same labor after him, let him be struck, by divine judgment, with the bond of anathema and subjected to eternal condemnation.

Given on the Kalends of December, while our most pious lord Leo, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the seventh year of his reign, and also in the fourth year of Constantine, his son, the emperor, in the sixth indiction.

## FOURTH LETTER OF POPE GREGORY II TO THE CLERGY, ORDER, AND PEOPLE FOR WHOM BONIFACE HAD BEEN ORDAINED BISHOP

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to the clergy, order, and people residing in Thuringia, his most beloved sons in the Lord: greeting.

[Note: “To your reasonable desires.” This is a general formula customarily written to the city for which a bishop had been ordained. It is read in exactly the same words among the ancient formulas of the Roman Church and is entitled “The synodal letter received by a bishop.” Sirmond.]

Not delaying to respond to your reasonable desires, we have ordained our brother and co-bishop Boniface as your priest. We instructed him never to presume to carry out illicit ordinations; never to permit a bigamist, a man who has not married a virgin, an illiterate person, anyone physically maimed in any part of the body, a penitent, a person attached to the curia or to any other condition, or anyone under legal censure to approach the sacred orders. If he should happen to find anyone of this kind, he must not dare to promote him.

He must in no way admit Africans who present themselves as proceeding to ecclesiastical orders, because some of them have been proven to be Manichaeans and others to have been repeatedly rebaptized.

He must take care not to diminish the ministries and furnishings [ornaments] of the church, or anything belonging to its patrimony, but rather to increase them.

As for the church’s revenues and the offerings of the faithful, he must make four portions: one he shall retain for himself; a second he shall distribute to the clergy in proportion to their diligent service; a third he shall assign to the poor and strangers; and a fourth he shall reserve for ecclesiastical buildings, for all of which he will have to render an account at the divine judgment.

He must know that the ordinations of priests and deacons are to be celebrated only during the fasts of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months, as well as at the beginning and middle of Lent, on Saturday evening.

The sacrament of holy baptism, moreover, must be administered only at the feast of Easter and at Pentecost, except for those whom the urgency of danger at the point of death requires to be assisted by such remedies, lest they perish eternally.

You ought therefore to obey with devoted hearts this man who observes the commands of our see, so that the body of the Church may be irreproachable and pleasing, through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the almighty Father, through [Roman Edition: and the Holy Spirit, through] all ages of ages. May God keep you safe and unharmed, beloved.

Given on the Kalends of December, while our lord Leo, most pious Augustus, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the seventh year, and also in the fourth year of Constantine, his son, the great emperor, in the sixth indiction.

## FIFTH LETTER OF POPE GREGORY II TO THE NOBLES OF THURINGIA

He praises their steadfastness in the faith of Christ and urges them to obey Boniface, their bishop.
