### Pope Gregory to the magnificent men and sons Asulf, Goddaw, Willeric, Gunthar, and Albold [Roman Edition: Asuleus, Guodelanus, Mutereus, Gunthareus, Alualdus], and to all the faithful Christians of Thuringia beloved by God

Recognizing the steadfastness of your magnificent faith in Christ, which has been reported to us—namely, that when pagans compelled you to worship idols, you answered with complete faith that you would rather die happily than in any way violate the faith once received in Christ—we are filled with immense joy and offer due thanks to our God and Redeemer, the giver of every good thing.

With his grace accompanying you, we hope that you may advance toward better and higher things, cling with religious minds to the holy apostolic see in order to strengthen your purpose of faith, and, whenever the need of sacred religion demands it, seek spiritual assistance from that holy apostolic see, the spiritual mother of all the faithful, as sons who are co-heirs of the kingdom properly seek it from their royal parent.

Through the ministry of our present most beloved brother Boniface, whom we have sent to you as a bishop consecrated for the lot of preaching and instructed in the apostolic ordinances for the teaching of your faith, we wish and exhort you in all things to agree obediently with him, for the completion of your salvation in the Lord.

## SIXTH LETTER OF POPE GREGORY II TO THE ENTIRE PEOPLE OF THURINGIA

They are to obey Boniface, their bishop, in everything and build episcopal residences and churches.

### Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to the entire people of Thuringia

The Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God and true God, descended from heaven, became man, consented to suffer and be crucified for us, was buried, rose from the dead on the third day, and ascended into heaven. He also said to his holy disciples [Roman Edition: apostles]: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” To those who believe in him he promised eternal life.

Therefore, desiring that you may rejoice with us forever, where the joy has no end and there is neither tribulation nor any bitterness, but everlasting glory, we have sent our most holy brother Boniface the bishop to you, so that he may baptize you, teach you the faith of Christ, and lead you from error to the way of salvation, so that you may have salvation and eternal life.

You must therefore obey him in everything, honor him as your father, and incline your hearts to his teaching. We did not send him to you to seek any temporal profit, but we sent him to you for the profit of your souls.

Love the Lord, therefore, and receive baptism in his name, because the Lord our God has prepared for those who love him what the human eye has never seen and what has never entered the human heart.

Now turn away from evil works and do what is good. Do not worship idols or sacrifice meat, because God does not accept such things. Rather, in everything, observe and do according to what our brother Boniface teaches you, and you will be saved, both you and your children, forever.

Therefore build a house where this father of yours, the bishop, may live, and churches where you may pray, so that God may forgive your sins and grant you eternal life.

## LETTER VII. OF POPE GREGORY II TO THE ENTIRE PEOPLE OF THE OLD SAXONS

[Note: [Col. 0503D] The Old Saxons. That part of Germany from which the later Saxony in England arose is called Old Saxony. For around the year of the Lord 409, when the Saxons had been summoned to provide assistance against enemies, the Britons also gave them a place to live among them; little by little they retained and enlarged it by force. Hence the New Saxons [Col. 0504D], or Anglo-Saxons, in England; whereas the Saxons simply, or Old Saxons, that is, the ancient Saxons, are in Germany. Bede, *History*, Book I, chapters 10, 11, 12, and 15, and Book V, chapters 10, 11, and 12. Serarius made fine observations on this subject, *History of Mainz*, Book III, note 1.]

He confirms them in the faith of Christ, which they had embraced after abandoning the worship of idols.

[Col. 0504C]

Gregory, pope, to the entire people of the province of the Old Saxons [Edit. Rom., Saxons].

I am a debtor to the wise and to the foolish, dearest brothers, wishing you to know what concern I have for you and for those who have received the word of exhortation concerning the faith of Jesus Christ our Lord, and for those who are still to receive it, so that your hearts, instructed in charity, may be comforted and enriched with every wealth of understanding, for the knowledge of the mystery of God the Father of Jesus Christ, as the outstanding Apostle says: “In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” [Col. 0504D] (Colossians II).

I say this because the kingdom of God is near (Luke XXI), and so that no one [that no one] may deceive you any longer with lofty speech, so that [or: “or in”] you may seek your salvation in any metal, worshiping manufactured idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, or made from any other material. These, under a deceitful name, were called gods by the ancient pagans. Demons are known to dwell in them, since “all the gods of the nations are demons,” as Scripture says; “but our Lord made the heavens” [Col. 0505A] (Psalm XCV).

Therefore, whoever among you has received Christ Jesus our Lord must walk in him, rooted and built up and strengthened in faith, abounding in thanksgiving. See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit (Colossians II). For the children of darkness are more cunning than the children of light.

Depart, children, from the worship of idols; approach and worship the Lord God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything that is in them; and your faces will not be ashamed. For there is one Lord of human beings, birds, four-footed animals, and fish, who is blessed forever and ever.

Therefore strip off the old man and put on the new Christ, laying aside all malice, anger, indignation, and blasphemy. Do not bring shameful speech [Col. 0505B] forth from your mouths, and withdraw from the worship of idols.

Already the day of the world is growing dark, and the time of darkness is approaching. Therefore do not be idle, but rather work the good work, so that Christ may dwell in you. Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God the Father through him (Colossians III), rejecting the sect of paganism and knowing that you have the Lord in heaven.

Persevering in prayer, lift your hearts to that Lord, because our Lord God is great, exceedingly worthy of praise, and terrible above all gods (Psalm XCV), who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (I Timothy II).

I admonish you concerning this, brothers: whoever among you wishes to turn to Christ, do not in any way prevent him, nor use force against him to make him worship images, because Christ the Lord himself lives with God the almighty Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

Dearest brothers, our brother and fellow bishop Boniface is a faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that he may learn what concerns you and comfort your hearts with a word of exhortation in Christ Jesus our Lord, so that, having been freed from the devil’s deception, you may be counted among the children of adoption and, having been freed from eternal condemnation, may possess eternal life.

[Alternative text: “I have sent to you Boniface, a faithful minister and fellow servant, my brother and fellow bishop, for this very purpose: that he may learn what concerns you and comfort your hearts with a word of exhortation in Christ Jesus our Lord …”]

## LETTER VIII. GENERAL LETTER OF CHARLES, MAYOR OF THE PALACE

Concerning Bishop Boniface, received under protection and defense.

[Col. 0505D]

To the holy and apostolic lords, fathers in Christ, bishops, dukes, counts, deputies, household officers, or all our young agents, or traveling messengers, and to our friends: the illustrious Charles, mayor of the palace, wishing you well.

Know how the apostolic man, our father in Christ, Bishop Boniface, came to us and represented to us that we ought to receive him under our *mundeburd* or protection. Know that we did so with a willing heart.

Therefore we have seen fit to give him this document, strengthened by our own hand, so that wherever [Col. 0506A] he may be seen traveling, he is to remain secure and protected with our favor, or under our *mundeburd* and protection, on the condition that he render justice, administer justice, and receive justice.

And if any accusation or necessity should arise for him that cannot be determined by law, he is to remain secure and protected before us, both he himself and those who appear to bring their claims and hopes through him. Let no one presume to inflict upon him any opposition or penalty against him; rather, at all times he is to remain secure and protected under our *mundeburd* or defense.

And so that this may be believed with greater certainty, we have signed it below with our own hand and sealed it with our ring.

## LETTER IX. OF POPE GREGORY II TO BISHOP BONIFACE

He congratulates him on the conversion of unbelievers and urges him to persevere steadfastly in the ministry of the word he has begun.

[Col. 0506B]

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop.

Moved by the concern of the entrusted watch, and also by the evangelical instruction in which Christ says, “Entreat the Lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest” (Matthew IX), we have therefore determined to direct your reverend brotherhood, in imitation of the apostles—who, at the Lord’s command, were instructed, “Go and preach the gospel of the kingdom” [Mark XVI], and, “You have received freely; give freely” [Matthew X]—into the regions of the West [of the Hessians], for the illumination of the Germanic people sitting in the shadow of death, so that you might bring profit from there [Col. 0506C], like that servant who dealt with the talent, whom Scripture declares to have proved faithful to his future master (Matthew XXV; Luke XIX).

Since we see that, through the gift of obedience, the ministry of the word is flourishing, and since we have heard—as you have reported—that the unbelieving people has been converted through the proclamation of preaching, we give thanks to the power of the Lord. We wish that he himself, from whom good proceeds and who wills all to come to the knowledge of the truth, may cooperate with you and, through the inspiration of his power, lead that people from darkness to light.

For this reason we believe that a rich reward is being credited to you in heaven by almighty God. If you persevere, you will be able to say with the Apostle: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith” (II Timothy IV).

But persist in your labor so that you may receive the crown; [Col. 0506D] for God promises salvation to those who persevere to the end. Let neither threats terrify you nor terrors cast you down; holding firm confidence in God, proclaim the word of truth.

For, through divine assistance, there will be protection [Edit. Rom., perfection], provided that the work is good in the will. Accordingly, we have learned from the reckoning of your syllables how many you have converted from error; rejoicing, we exult and give abundant thanks to God for the profit of souls.

Moreover, concerning that bishop who until now, through a certain indolence, had neglected to spread the word of preaching among the same people, and who now claims for himself a portion of it, as though it were a parish, we have written to our excellent son Charles, the patrician [“patrician” is absent], persuading him to restrain him; and we believe [Col. 0507A] that he will order this to be avoided [or: forbidden]. But you, at a convenient and inconvenient time alike, must not cease preaching the things that belong to salvation.

Accordingly, we have not failed to write to the Thuringians and the people of Germany about the matters that concern the benefit and salvation of the soul, admonishing them, among other things, to build bishoprics and churches. For he who does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live (Ezekiel XVIII), will grant increase to all.

May God preserve you safe and sound.

Given on the day before the Nones of December, while the most pious lord Augustus Leo, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the eighth year; in the eighth year after his consulship; and also while his son Constantine the Great was reigning, in his fifth year, in the eighth indiction.

## LETTER X. OF THE MOST HOLY POPE GREGORY THE ROMAN TO THE MOST HOLY GERMANUS, WHO HAD BEEN PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE

[Col. 0507B]

What kind of delight, and what delight, knows how to make my soul rejoice in this way, like the welcome message concerning your name—which is truly reverend to me and rightly worthy of honor—O sanctified one and divinely inspired?

For now also, informed by your honorable letter, I rejoiced, and through excessive joy was gladdened in spirit. Then, raising my eyes toward heaven, I offered acts of thanksgiving to God, the ruler of all, who has now likewise willed to cooperate with you to the very end and to bring all your affairs into the light.

This is what I must pray for night and day, and, trusting in Christ, I shall declare that this desire must never at any time be abandoned.

My statement is also confirmed, O most praiseworthy and beloved of God, by my recollection at every hour of your goodwill. Since I have it dwelling upon my lips and cannot bear the pain of the matter, I hastened immediately to address you by letter.

It is my duty—and more distinguished than all duties—to greet and address you as my brother and defender of the Church, and to praise together the causes of your struggles.

Even if someone should say, and with great appropriateness cry out, that he was rather the forerunner of impiety, who has now suffered, in order to exchange an evil deed for a good deed through your good fortune. For he thought that, following him who fell from above, he would at once rage and prevail against piety; but he was hindered from heaven, deprived of his hope.

He heard from the Church the things that Pharaoh, the Egyptian tyrant, had previously heard when Moses sang concerning him: “The enemy said, ‘I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoils, I will fill my soul’” (Exodus XV).

But he also heard what the devil himself heard, when the prophetic curse was announced to him: “Therefore God will destroy you forever; he will tear you away and uproot you from your dwelling, and your root from the land of the living” (Psalm LI).

Thus he perished, frustrated beyond hope in his attempts, which had been founded upon hope. Through your heavenly struggle and strength, the apostate’s attack against God was weakened, brought low, and almost driven to its final destruction by the ferocity of the one who fought against Christ. Thus Scripture was truly fulfilled concerning him: “The bow of the mighty has been broken, and the weak have been girded with strength” [Col. 0508A] (I Samuel II).

For there is no strength, against the weak God, in the abomination of those who fight against God; and [it is written that] he asserts the world’s struggle for God against the senseless.

How, then, could you not be moved, O most holy one, fighting with God against those who are without God and against God? They find the one who is invisibly opposed to them—or, to speak more truly, who himself fights alongside you—and who puts the enemies to flight (Wisdom V), precisely where you began the battle, as God himself showed you.

He commanded the glorious and truly distinguished standard to stand at the head in the camps of Christ’s kingdom—namely, the life-giving cross, the great trophy of his greatness against death—in which he circumscribed the world’s fourfold bounds, marking them out with lines.

Then also [he commanded you to honor] the holy image of the Lady of all and true Mother of God, whose face the wealthy of the people will entreat.

For she is holy, as the Fathers believe, and, being piously honored in this way by you, she grants corresponding benefits. “The honor shown to the image passes to the prototype,” according to Basil the Great.

And the matter of the venerable images is full of piety, as Chrysostom says: “I too loved a painting covered with wax, filled with piety; for I saw in an image an angel pursuing the battalions of barbarians, and David speaking the truth: ‘In your city, Lord, you will reduce their image to nothing’” (Psalm LXXII).

The Church did not err at all, although it was judged to have done so. May God forgive us; nor is this tradition, heaven forbid, in accordance with pagan practice. Rather, the intention of the matter is proved in a certain respect, while what is accomplished is not at all taken into consideration.

For in the city of Paneas, the pious memorial of the woman with the issue of blood, on account of the miracle that had happened to her, was not rejected: a plant had grown around the feet of the statue which she had erected in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ; it was of a foreign and unknown appearance and, through the condescension and goodness of God and our Savior, was set forth as a remedy for various illnesses.

Indeed, if we may put it so, this kind of erection is lawful before God, although grace and truth are to be preferred to figures, and the latter are more clearly marked by representations [Greek: “more expressively represented by figures”].

Therefore, by God’s counsel, the assembly of the saints handed down this greatest cause of salvation: that, in the faces of all people and through the working of colors, we should raise up the venerable and holy likeness according to the humanity of him who takes away the sin of the world [Col. 0508D].

Through him, considering the exaltation of the humility of God the Word, we are led, as it were by the hand, to the remembrance of his life in the flesh—both his passion and saving death, and the redemption accomplished through these things for the world. There is nothing here contrary to divine teaching.

For if the prophetic predictions had not reached their fulfillment—if events were not to be written down as evidence of things that had not yet happened; that is, if the Lord had not become incarnate—then his holy image according to the flesh should not be formed.

If he was not born in Bethlehem (Matthew II) from the glorious virgin, the Mother of God, neither did the Magi offer gifts, nor did the angel stand above the shepherds, nor did the multitude of the heavenly host offer a hymn at his birth (Luke II). If he was not carried as an infant in his mother’s arms, he who carries all things, and did not receive nourishment from milk, he who gives food to every creature, then neither should this be represented.

If he was not looked upon by the old man who holds authority over life and death, and through whom the Lord of all was at once recognized, proclaimed, and asked to grant release; if he did not go to Egypt for the sake of the divine dispensation, upon a light cloud—the mother made radiant by every light and strengthened by holiness—he who sits on high; and if he did not return from Egypt and dwell in Nazareth, then let these things not be represented in colors.

If he did not raise the dead, restore the paralytics, provide cleansing for lepers, and illuminate the blind; if he did not also give articulate speech to the mute, strengthen the feet of the lame, and drive out demons; if he did not open the ears of the deaf, perform every glorious deed, and accomplish signs in God, then let these things not be painted.

And if he did not willingly undergo passion, despoil hell, rise, and ascend into heaven—he who is to come to judge the living and the dead—then let neither the Scriptures nor the histories that recount these things depict them, whether in letters or in colors [Greek: “neither written nor represented”].

But if all these things happened, and if “the mystery of piety” is great, would that heaven and earth and sea, and all living creatures and plants, and whatever else exists, could proclaim them through voices, writings, and paintings.

For the representation of things that do not exist is called idolatrous painting. It is also the invention of pagan fable, which foolishly asserted as a real creation the production of things that never existed [Col. 0509C].

Certainly there is no accommodation between the Church of Christ and idols—far from it. We have not worshiped calves, nor cast a calf at Horeb, nor judged a creature to be God. Nor again have we fallen before a graven image and been initiated into Baal-peor; nor have we been killers or sacrificers of children, nor celebrated secret rites; nor have we ever sacrificed our sons and daughters to demons, so that the things said by Solomon against worshipers of idols might be applied to us.

Was it by us that the earth was stained with blood, or did we make an image in the temple, an idol having four forms, and worship it (I Kings XI)? Did we paint upon the wall of the temple the abomination of reptiles and animals [Col. 0509D]?

Or again, did Ezekiel see us mourning Adonis and offering incense to the Sun (Ezekiel VIII), concerning whom the Apostle says: “They served the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans I)?

Do you suppose that we set up images of the two prostitutes in Egypt—Oholah, that is, and Oholibah—and worshiped them (Ezekiel XXXIII)? Or again, were sacrifices offered by us to Bel in Babylon (Daniel XIV) and to Dagon in Palestine (Judges XVI)? Or did we fall before other gods of the nations?

These things are not so; they are not so. Let no one bring accusations, because, among none of the things that exist and have been made, has the people of Christ, down to the present day, honored or served any name that is above every name, except the holy life-giving Trinity [Greek: “worshiped with latria”]. Far from it.

For the manner of idolatry is manifest. But among Christians, worshipers of God, the ruler of all is to be worshiped.

Moreover, if someone, stirred to accusation in the Jewish manner, should spread abroad the things once said against worshipers of idols and should charge our Church with idolatry because of the godly and wondrous guidance of the venerable images toward better things, we should judge nothing else than that a dog is barking, and that, thrown far away in a sling, he hears like a Jew:

“Would that Israel had also been seen by God offering worship through visible things, and had remembered the Creator through types, rather than retaining the calf and the flies upon the tablets of the covenant!

Would that he had desired the holy altar more, and not the calves of Samaria! Would that he had attended to Aaron’s staff, and not to Astarte!

For it would have been both good and just for him to honor the rock of salvation, which gave rain by divine power, and not Baal.

Would that he had looked more attentively upon Moses’ staff, and the golden urn, the ark, the mercy seat, the frontlet, the ephod, the table, the inner and outer tabernacle—all of which, although made by hand, were produced for the glory of God and were nevertheless called holy among holy things—and then also the sculpted cherubim, concerning whose memory the Apostle says: ‘The cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat’ (Hebrews V), and by which Scripture teaches us that the divine glory was carried!

If he had attended to these things, he certainly would not have fallen before idols.”

For every work that is done in the name of the Lord is precious and holy.

And why should I prolong the letter? Especially to a man pleasing to God, a vessel chosen by God, who has received the grace of the Spirit and is capable of contemplating the depths of divine doctrines and, with God as guide, considering the highest summit of knowledge.

Let us therefore return to our subject: to the praises of your defender, O most holy one and lord of all Christians, and to our admiration of how you yourself have been shown to be directed and saved by her in all things and strengthened against your enemies.

Those who for a long time have raged against her found her resistance as great as the contradiction they encountered.

And this is not surprising. For if Bethulia was saved by the hand of Judith, an Israelite woman, whose deed was the killing of Holofernes (Judith XIII), and those who lived in Israel at that time proclaimed her their savior, how much more ought your most exalted holiness, using such a defender, to attack the enemies of the faith and crown with victory those who have been subdued? [Col. 0510D]

But may our God, powerful in battle, strong and long-suffering, through the supplications of that same woman and of all the saints, preserve you, O most holy one, for many years: doing good to the entire Christian community, teaching and urging all to obey the sacred canon, and guarding the deposit that we received from the Fathers; converting those who, in some small matter, have not understood—O our perpetual joy, and the common benefit and refreshment, most holy one and beloved of all Christians.

Tarasius, the most holy patriarch, said: [Note: [Col. 0511C] Gregory’s. Pope Adrian, in his letter to Constantine, the son of Irene, testifies that Gregory II and his successor Gregory III wrote to Leo the Isaurian concerning the images. This letter is found in the second act of the Second Council of Nicaea, among whose words are these: “For this reason both Gregorys, the most holy Roman pontiffs of those times, were cast into great tribulation; they also repeatedly warned the grandfather of your serenity not to permit the venerable images to be thrown down from their position.  

“But the events narrated by the pontiff in their own historical setting persuade us to believe that this letter belongs rather to the second than to the third Gregory. Among other things, it mentions Ravenna being occupied by the Lombards, and it calls this author of the *Dialogues* by that title; Cedrenus likewise gives that title to the second Gregory in the tenth year of Leo.

“In Rome, however, Gregory, the apostolic man and associate of Peter, chief of the Apostles, who acquired the title ‘of the Dialogues’ because of his learned writings, defected from Leo because of his impiety, refused tribute to Leo after making an agreement with the Franks, struck Anastasius and his associates with an anathema, and openly rebuked the emperor in many letters, many of which were read.

“And Theophanes, falsely entitled Paul the Deacon, says in Book XXI: ‘In the ninth year of his reign the impious emperor Leo began to speak against the [Col. 0512C] holy and venerable images. When Pope Gregory of Rome learned this, he prohibited the tribute of the city of Rome and of Italy, writing a doctrinal letter to Leo that an emperor ought not to speak about faith or violate, through novelty, the ancient doctrines of the Catholic Church proclaimed by the holy Fathers.’

“We read the same in the *Pontifical Book*, from which Trithemius, in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, reports that this Gregory, a learned and most holy man, wrote certain little works full of learning:

*Responses to the Questions of Justinian*, Book I; *Against Leo Augustus*, Book I; *To John, Bishop of Constantinople*, Book I; *Letters to Various Persons*, Book I.

[Col. 0512D] He died in the year of the Lord 731, in the fourteenth indiction, on the third day before the Ides of February.

“It is therefore less surprising if a Greek—whether translator or copyist—who transcribed this letter added the title ‘of the Dialogues’ to Gregory, since Cedrenus himself, through a lapse of memory, did the same.

“That this title belongs among the Greeks to that great Gregory, whose *Dialogues* Pope Zachary translated into Greek, is evident from Greek sources: from John of Damascus, in his *Oration on the Faithful Departed*; from Euthymius; from the Greek *Euchologion*, chapter 96; and from the Latin Sigebert, under the year of Christ 605—clearly so that he might be distinguished from Gregory Thaumaturgus, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa.

“I certainly judge that the incompetence of the same translator is responsible for the fact that many things here are *anakóloutha* (ἀνακόλουθα), that is, syntactically irregular and insufficiently coherent.

“Whatever the nature of this little work, we publish it in the interest of preserving antiquity, from a copy of the library of the most illustrious Cardinal Charles of Lorraine, Archbishop of Reims, transcribed in the year 1590 from the manuscript preserved in the monastery of Saint Remigius at Reims.”]

[Col. 0511A] Imitating the divine Apostle Peter, this blessed Father also sounded the trumpet of truth for us from Rome.

Theodorus [Greek: Theodosius], the most reverend monk and notary, read this.

## LETTER XI. OF POPE GREGORY II TO URSUS, DUKE OF VENICE, FOR THE DEFENSE OF RAVENNA AGAINST THE LOMBARDS

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Ursus, duke of Venice.

Because, through the agency of sin, the city of Ravenna, which stands as the head of all, has been captured by the Lombards, a people whose name should not even be spoken, and because our distinguished son, the lord exarch, is staying at Venice, as we have learned, your nobility ought to support him and fight alongside him in our place, so that the city of Ravenna may be restored to its former condition, in the service of the holy commonwealth and of our lords and sons, the great emperors Leo and Constantine.

Thus, through zeal and love for our holy faith, may we be able, with the Lord’s cooperation, to remain firm in the condition of the commonwealth and in imperial service.

May God preserve you safe and sound, dearest son.

## LETTER XII. [Note: [Col. 0511C] Pagius argues at length that these two letters of Pope Gregory II were written in the year of Christ 730, under the year of Christ 726, paragraph 3 and following. Labbe, however, judges that they belong to Gregory III, in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. The first was brought to light by Father Fronto Ducaeus, of the Society of Jesus, from the manuscript of Cardinal Charles of Lorraine, Archbishop of Reims. He warned beforehand that many things here were insufficiently coherent. Cardinal Baronius published the same letter with notes, under the year 726, paragraph 28. HARD.]

OF POPE GREGORY II TO THE EMPEROR LEO THE ISAURIAN

Concerning the sacred images.

We have received the letters of your Majesty, guarded by God, and of your brotherhood, sent through the imperial spatharocandidatus, during your reign in the fourteenth indiction. We also carefully preserve your letters from the fourteenth and fifteenth, and from the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth indictions, deposited in the holy church at the threshold of the confession of the holy, glorious, and chief of the apostles, Peter, where there are also the letters of your predecessors, lovers of Christ, who ruled piously. And in ten syllables you promised that, rightly and piously, and as befits an emperor of the Christians, you would observe and preserve intact all the admonitions of our holy fathers and teachers. Most important of all was this: your letters were indeed your own, not another’s, carefully sealed with the imperial seals, and inside they bore carefully executed subscriptions in cinnabar, written in your own hand, as emperors customarily subscribe. You also rightly and most piously set forth a confession of our blameless and orthodox faith, and you wrote that he who loosens and dissolves [rescinds and destroys] the boundaries established by the Fathers must be accursed.

When we had received these things, we offered hymns of thanksgiving to God, because your empire had plainly been granted to you by God. But while you were running rightly, who sounded in your ears and perverted your heart like a crooked bow (Psalm XVII), so that you looked back at the things behind you? For ten years, by God’s kindness, you walked rightly and made no mention of the sacred images; but now you say that they occupy the place of idols, and that those who venerate them are idolaters. You have turned wholly to overturning and utterly destroying them, nor have you feared God’s judgment, when scandals were rushing into the hearts of human beings—not only of the faithful but also of unbelievers.

Yet Christ warns you not to scandalize even one of the little ones, and says that for a small scandal one will be cast into eternal fire (Luke XVII). But you have scandalized the whole world. What will you do, since you do not wish to undergo death and render an unhappy account?

You wrote that things made by human hands are not to be venerated, nor any likeness fashioned according to a model, as God said (Exodus XX), whether in heaven or on earth. Show me who handed down that things made by human hands are to be venerated and adored, and I will then acknowledge that it is God’s command. Why, then, as emperor and head of the Christians, did you not consult wise men, experienced people from whom you could have learned for what reason God spoke of these manufactured things, before confusing, mingling, and disturbing the humble peoples?

Nevertheless, you rejected and repudiated our holy fathers and teachers and sent them away, although by your own hand and in your writings you had promised to obey and follow them. Our Scripture, our light and salvation, is our holy and God-filled fathers and teachers; and the six synods in Christ have handed this down to us, yet you do not accept their testimonies.

We are forced to write to you in crude and unlearned language, since you are crude and unlearned; nevertheless, they truly contain within themselves the power and truth of God. We beseech you by God to lay aside the arrogance and pride with which you are overflowing, and to lend us your ears sincerely, with great humility. May God bend your mind toward the truth by the efficacy of his words.

For God was speaking because of the idolaters who occupied the promised land. They worshipped golden, silver, and wooden animals, and every created thing, as well as all flying birds, and said: “These are our gods, and there is no other God.” Because of these harmful and execrable works made by the devil, God said that we must not worship them.

For there are certain things made by human hands for the service and glory of God. When he wished to introduce his consecrated people, the Hebrews, just as God had formerly promised Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob that he would give them the promised land, make them possessors and heirs of the possessions of the idolaters, and cut off and utterly destroy those nations because they had polluted the land and air by their iniquity, God foretold these things and warned his people in advance, lest they fall into the worship of those nations.

Among the Israelite people God chose two men, blessed them, and consecrated them so that works made by human hands might be fashioned—not for any other purpose, but for the glory and service of God, as a memorial for their generations (Exodus XXXI): namely, Bezalel and Eliab [Oholiab] [Note: From the first tribe, Dan. There is an error here, perhaps to be corrected as follows: τῆς πρώτης φυλῆς καὶ τῆς τοῦ Δᾶν, “from the first tribe and from Dan,” rather than “from the first tribe of Dan.” For we read in Exodus XXXI that Bezalel was from the tribe of Judah, which may here be called “first” because authority was conferred upon him; and Oholiab—called Eliab by the Greek Septuagint—was from the tribe of Dan. The scriptural passages that follow are cited not so much verbatim as according to their sense.]

God said to Moses: “Cut out two stone tablets” (Exodus XXXIV), “and bring them to me.” When he had cut them out, he brought them, and God wrote upon them with his own finger ten living and immortal words. Then God said: “Make cherubim and seraphim, and make a table; gild it inside and outside; and make an ark of incorruptible wood, and place your testimonies in the ark as a memorial for your generations” (Exodus XXV)—that is, the tablets, the urn, the rod, and the manna.

Are these figures and images made by human hands, or are they not? Yet they are for the glory and service of God.

That great Moses, seized with fear when he wished to look upon the figure and image, lest he should err, prayed to God, saying: “Show me yourself openly, so that I may see you” (Exodus XXXII). God answered: “If you see me, you will die; but climb up through the opening in the rock, and you will see my back.” God showed him in a vision the mystery hidden from the ages and from generations. But in the age of our generations, in the last times, he perfectly showed us himself, both his back and his front.

When God saw that the human race would perish forever, he had mercy on his creature and sent his Son, begotten before the ages. Descending from heaven, he entered the womb of the virgin Mary, and when the true light shone in her womb, light became flesh in place of seed. He was baptized in the river Jordan, and he also baptized us. He began to give us tokens of the signs, lest we be deceived. Entering Jerusalem, in the upper room of holy and glorious Zion, at the mystical supper he set before us his sacred body and gave us drink of his precious blood. There he also washed our feet; with him we drank and ate; our hands touched him; and he became our familiar companion. The truth was revealed to us, and the error and darkness with which we had been surrounded fled and vanished from our midst. “Their sound went out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

People from every part of the world began to come to Jerusalem, flying like eagles, just as the Lord said in the Gospels: “Where the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matthew XXIV). Christ is the corpse; the eagles flying on high are religious people and lovers of Christ.

When they had seen the Lord, they painted him as they had seen him, setting him forth for contemplation. When they had seen James, the brother of the Lord, they painted him as they had seen him, setting him forth for contemplation. When they had seen Stephen, the protomartyr, they painted him as they had seen him, setting him forth for contemplation. And, to put it in a single word, when they had seen the faces of the martyrs who had shed their blood for Christ, they painted them. Thereafter, on seeing these images, people throughout the whole world abandoned the worship of the devil and displayed these images—not with latria, but with relationship.

[Note: Not with *latria*, but with relationship. Our Turrianus translates the passage from Nicephorus of Constantinople, cited from his *Orthodox*, in this way in Book I of the *Pro Apostolic Canons*, chapter 25: “When Christ was first preached, the preaching of his image was joined to that preaching σχετικῶς, that is, relationally; and just as the image is not worshipped for its own sake but on account of the prototype, so it must not be said to be worshipped absolutely, but σχετικῶς, that is, relatively. And just as purple and the emperor clothed in it constitute one thing by association, so the image and its prototype constitute one thing σχέσει, that is, by relationship.” Likewise, in the opinions of the Fathers on images published in Paris by G. Morel in 1562, p. 10: Ἐπὶ τοῦ Χριστοῦ λατρευτικὴ προσκύνησις, καὶ φυσικὴ, ἐπὶ δὲ τῆς εἰκόνος τοῦ Χριστοῦ σχετικὴ ἡ προσκύνησις, καὶ ὁμωνυμική—“In Christ himself there is worship of latria and natural worship; but in the image of Christ the worship is relative and equivocal.” See also Francisco Suárez, *On the Third Part of St Thomas*, disputation 44, section 4.]

Does it seem right to you, emperor, to venerate these images, or do you consider it a diabolical error?

When Christ was staying in Jerusalem, Augarus, who at that time ruled and was king of the city of Edessa, having heard of Christ’s miracles, wrote a letter to Christ; and Christ sent him a written reply in his own hand, together with his sacred and glorious face. Go, then, and see that image not made by human hands: crowds of peoples of the East gather there and pray. There are also many other such manufactured images, preserved by assemblies of lovers of Christ who travel to them and gather for spectacles of this kind—images that you daily venerate and look upon [F. “you venerated and despised”? according to the Greek].

Why, then, do we not place before our eyes and paint the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ? Because we do not know what he is, and God’s nature cannot be presented for viewing or painted. If we had looked upon and known him as we know his Son, we could likewise have set him forth for contemplation and painted him, so that you might call his image an idol as well.

We beseech you as brothers in Christ: return again to the truth from which you have departed; shake off your elevated thoughts and remove your stubbornness; and write in every direction to all those whom you have offended, raising up those whom you have blinded, although in your excessive stupidity you consider this nothing.

Christ’s love knows that whenever we enter the temple of the holy chief of the apostles, Peter, and contemplate the painted image of the saint, we are struck with compunction, and our tears pour forth like rain from a rain-filled sky.

Christ restored sight to the blind; you have blinded those who saw correctly and placed an obstacle before them, although you consider this nothing. You have made people ignorant, interrupted the right course of human beings, deprived them of prayers, and, instead of vigil, constant attendance, and devotion toward God, you have cast and driven the humble peoples into sleep, drowsiness, and negligence [and beheaded them].

You say that we worship stones, walls, and panels. It is not so, emperor, as you say. Rather, our memory is aroused, and our dull, ignorant, and sluggish mind is lifted up and carried on high through those whose names and titles these are, and whose images these are—not as though they were gods, as you say; far from it, for we do not place our hope in them.

[Note: If indeed it is an image. Similar is the passage in the same opinions on images, p. 16: Καὶ εἰ μέν ἐστιν εἰκὼν τοῦ Κυρίου, λέγομεν, Ἰησοῦ Χριστὲ etc.—“And if it is an image of the Lord, we say, ‘Jesus Christ,’ etc.” Moreover, the words of Leo that follow contain, with empty arrogance, a notable mnemonic error. It was not King Uzziah who broke the bronze serpent, but his grandson Hezekiah, as stated in 2 Kings XVIII:4—unless Uzziah had learned elsewhere to remove the bronze serpent from the temple and Hezekiah to break it. The same is true of what he adds about David introducing it into the temple or tabernacle, according to Gregory; as I think, this is not established by the sacred writings. Furthermore, eight hundred years had not yet elapsed from the beginning of the evangelical law. For, as Cedrenus, the Greek historian, notes, Leo’s son Constantine began to reign in the year 6236 of the world, A.D. 739 [more accurately, A.D. 741].]

If it is indeed the image of the Lord, we say: “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, help and save us.” If it is that of his holy mother, we say: “Holy Mother of God, Mother of the Lord, intercede with your Son, our true God, that he may save our souls.” If it is that of a martyr: “Holy Stephen, who shed your blood for Christ, and who, as protomartyr, possess confidence in speaking, intercede for us.” And of any martyr who has suffered martyrdom we speak in this way; through them we offer such prayers. It is not, as you say, emperor, as though we called the martyrs gods.

Turn away from your evil thoughts, I beseech you, and free your soul from the scandals and curses with which you are assailed by the whole world, since even little children mock you. Go into the schools of those who are learning their letters and say: “I am the overturner and persecutor of images.” At once they will throw their writing tablets at your head, and what you could not be taught by the wise, you will be taught by the foolish.

You wrote to us as follows: “King Uzziah of the Jews, after eight hundred years, removed the bronze serpent from the temple” (2 Kings XVIII) [Note: This appears to be an error caused by a lapse of memory.] “but I, after eight hundred years, removed the idols from the churches.” Truly Uzziah was your brother and possessed the same stubbornness as you; he also used force against the priests of that time, as you do.

That serpent had been brought into the temple by the consecrated David together with the holy ark (2 Chronicles XXVI:16–18). What was it, then, if not bronze consecrated by God for the sake of those who at that time were sick and had been injured by serpents? It was so that it might be shown to the peoples that the one who had first suggested sin to Adam and Eve, God’s original creation, had himself been appointed for the healing of sinners.

But you, as you boast, after eight hundred years finally expelled blessing from the churches, and the sanctification of the martyrs. And just as at the beginning you rightly confessed, deliberately and not out of any necessity, so finally, by subscribing with your own hand, you turned their curse back upon your own head.

We too wished, since we possess the ability, power, and authority from holy Peter, chief of the apostles, to inflict punishment upon you. But because you have brought the curse upon yourself, keep it for yourself and for your counselors, whom you embrace.

What an edification and progress of those who were running rightly have you interrupted? Christ’s love knows. Whenever we ourselves enter the church and contemplate paintings of the miracles of the Lord Jesus Christ, and of his holy mother nursing the Lord, our God, in her arms, with angels standing around and singing the thrice-holy hymn, we do not depart without compunction.

For who is not moved and does not likewise grieve when contemplating the vessels of the laver, the priests standing around in a circle, the mystical supper, the illumination of the blind, the raising of Lazarus, the healing of the leper and the paralytic, the people reclining on the grass, the baskets, the hampers and the remnants, the transfiguration on Mount Tabor, the crucifixion of Christ, his burial and resurrection, his holy ascension, and the descent of the Holy Spirit?

Who, seeing the painting of Abraham and the sword hanging over the child’s neck, is not moved and moved to tears? And who is not moved by all the sufferings of the Lord?

It would be better for you, emperor, if, when the alternatives were put before you, you were called a heretic rather than the persecutor and destroyer of the histories, paintings, images, and sufferings of the Lord.

Yet it is bad and by no means advantageous for you to be called a heretic; nevertheless, I shall explain to you why. A heretic is called known when he is known to a few and not to many; when the stumbling blocks are difficult and the opinions tangled, and cannot easily be judged; likewise, those who spread doctrine and are not endowed with humility immediately fall through their ignorance and blindness. They are not guilty of so great a crime as you are, worthy as you are of condemnation.

You openly attacked things that were known and visible like the light, and you stripped the churches of God. The holy Fathers had clothed and adorned them; you robbed and stripped them, although you had such a pontiff—our brother, I mean, the lord Germanus, and our fellow minister.

You ought to have obeyed his counsels as those of a father and teacher, and as those of an elder endowed with great experience in both ecclesiastical and civil affairs. For that man is now in his ninety-fifth year, having served every patriarch and emperor, and he has been continually occupied because he was wonderfully useful and capable in managing both kinds of affairs.

You therefore listened to that lawless Ephesian, the son of Apsimar, and to his like, while setting aside the man who stood at your side.

[Note: That wicked Ephesian. In the manuscript it read τοῦ παρανόμου μωροῦ Ἐφέσου, which, if μωροῦ is read, would mean “the wicked and foolish Ephesian.” But it is more probable that a name is missing here: τοῦ Θεοδοσίου τοῦ Ἐφέσου, “Theodosius of Ephesus,” the bishop who advised Constantine Copronymus and, as is clear from this passage, also his father Leo. Cedrenus, under the thirteenth year of Copronymus, writes: Κατὰ τῶν ἁγίων εἰκόνων παράνομον συνέδριον τλή ἐπισκόπων συνέλεξεν, ὧν ἐξῆρχε Θεοδόσιος ὁ υἱὸς Ἀψιμάρου ὁ Ἐφέσιος, καὶ Παστηλᾶς ὁ Πέργης—“Against the holy images he assembled an unlawful council of thirty-eight bishops, of whom the leaders were Theodosius of Ephesus, son of Apsimar, and Pastillas of Perge.” In Theophanes—whom they say was Paul the Deacon—the passage is rendered into Latin by Anastasius the librarian as follows: “Against the holy images he assembled an unjust council of thirty-eight bishops [Cedrenus has three hundred and thirty-eight], whose leaders were the Ephesian, son of Apsimar, and Pastillas of Perge.” “Theodosius of Ephesus” should be added; for in the Seventh Synod, act 1, in the confession of Basil of Ancyra, it is likewise said that a false council was assembled, presided over by Theodosius, bishop of Ephesus, together with Sisinnius of Perge, surnamed Pastillas. Zonaras also bears witness to the same.]

When the lord Germanus and the lord George, who was patriarch at that time, had advised and persuaded Constantine, son of Constans and father of Justinian, to write to us at Rome, he wrote to us after taking an oath and dealt with us as follows: we were to send useful men for the convocation of a universal synod. “I shall not sit with them,” he said, “as an emperor, nor speak imperiously, but as one of them. Whatever the pontiffs decide, I shall carry out. We shall admit those who speak rightly, and expel and banish those who speak wrongly. If my father has distorted anything from the undefiled and pure faith, I shall be the first to anathematize him.”

Then, God willing, we sent them, and the Sixth Synod was celebrated in peace.

You know, emperor, that the dogmas of the holy Church do not belong to emperors but to pontiffs, and must be promulgated securely by them. For this reason pontiffs, who abstain from the affairs of the state, have been placed over the churches. Therefore emperors likewise should abstain from ecclesiastical affairs and undertake what has been entrusted to them.

The unity of purpose of Christ-loving emperors and pious pontiffs is a virtue, when affairs are administered in peace and charity.

You wrote that a universal council should be convened, and this seemed to us useless. You are the persecutor of images, their insulting enemy and destroyer. Stop; grant us this favor by keeping silent. Then the world will enjoy peace, and scandals will cease.

Suppose that we had listened to you and that pontiffs from the whole world had assembled, and that the senate and council had sat: where is the Christ-loving and pious emperor who by custom ought to sit in the senate, reward those who speak rightly, and dismiss those who babble things alien to the truth, when you, emperor, waver and imitate barbarians?

Do you not perceive that this undertaking of yours, by which you rose up against the images, is a turbulent, unprecedented, and arrogant deed? While the churches of God were enjoying profound peace, you stirred up battles, hatreds, and scandals. Stop and be quiet; then there will be no need for a synod.

Write to everyone and to every region of the world whom you have offended, that Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, and Gregory, pope of Rome, sinned concerning the images. We shall then give you rest from this concern, so that you may have no sin or lapse, since we have received from God the authority to loose both heavenly and earthly things.

God is witness that whatever letters you sent to us, we presented to the ears and hearts of the kings of the West, reconciling their peace and goodwill toward you, praising you and exalting you greatly, as we observed you conducting yourself formerly.

[Note: Therefore also the *laurata*. We have retained the Greek word, together with the old translator of the Seventh Synod, as cited by Francisco Balduinus in Book III of Optatus, near the end: “The peoples go out to meet the laurata and the icons that are sent to cities or regions, with candles and incense, honoring not a panel covered with wax but the emperor.” I believe these words were cited by Pope Adrian in his letter to Constantine, in act 2 of the Seventh Synod, from a sermon for the fifth day of Easter; and again in act 4, from an address concerning the basin, as follows in Gregory, Book XI of the *Register*, letter 1: “When the icon of Phocas and Leontia arrived, acclamation was made for them, and Gregory ordered the icon to be placed in the oratory of Saint Caesarius.” There is also the law of Theodosius, Book XV, title 5, of the *Theodosian Code*, concerning imperial images.]

For this reason they also received your *laurata*, as it is fitting that kings should be honored by kings, and they did so before they had heard of this undertaking and attempt of yours, by which you rose up against the images. But when they learned of it and became fully informed—

[Note: Jovinus the spatharocandidatus. The same event is related by Paul the Deacon, Book XXI of the *Miscellany*—although this work is inscribed as belonging to Theophanes the true author—where he says that certain imperial men were killed while removing the icon of God, which was seen to be placed above the great bronze gate. It is also related in the *Life of Saint Stephen the Younger*, recently published by the very learned Billius together with the works of John of Damascus. Cedrenus, moreover, shows that a *spatharius* was a Roman bodyguard, p. 139: Σπαθάριος ὁ σωματοφύλαξ, “a spatharius, the bodyguard”; and in the same author, *protospatharius*. Sergius is called chief of the spatharii in the first year of Leo and is numbered by the Curopalates among the officials of the imperial court. He also writes that the chief, closely related by birth, carried the emperor’s σπάθα, that is, sword. Paul the Deacon, whose work is inscribed as belonging to Theophanes, also mentions, in Book XXII, among the names of certain officials, Theophylactus the candidatus, in the twenty-fifth year of Constantine Copronymus. Liutprand of Cremona, Book VI, chapter 5, writes: “After these comes an immense crowd of protospatharii, spatharii, candidati, and clients of that kind.” This office of spatharocandidatus perhaps arose from the union of the two types.]

For this reason you sent Jovinus the spatharocandidatus to the Chalcoprateia to overturn and break the Savior called Antiphonetes, where many miracles also take place. There they found women inflamed with zeal, imitators of those who carried ointments, and the women begged the spatharocandidatus: “Do not do this, we beseech you; do not do it,” they said. But he did not heed their prayers. He climbed up a ladder, and when he had struck the face of the image of the Savior three times with an axe, the women, seeing this and unable to endure the wicked deed, pulled down the ladder and killed him there, cutting him to pieces with clubs.

Then you, an imitator of evil, sent soldiers and killed there I do not know how many women, while useful Roman men stood by, together with men from Francia, the Vandals, Mauretania, Gothia, and, to speak generally, the entire interior West.

When they arrived and each had recounted your youthful and childish deeds in his own region, they threw down and trampled your *laurata*, and battered your face. Then, after a levy had been made, the Lombards and Sarmatians, and the other peoples who dwell in the North, ravaged unhappy Decapolis with their incursions. They occupied Ravenna itself, the metropolis, expelled your officials, and established their own. They also resolved to treat the neighboring royal seats belonging to us, and Rome itself, in the same way, since you are entirely unable to defend us.

And all this you endured through imprudence and stupidity.

But you frighten them, you say, declaring: “I will go to Rome and break the image of Saint Peter. I will also have Gregory, the pontiff there, brought back in chains, just as Constantine [Constantius, Constans] ordered Martin to be brought back.”

[Note: Just as Constantine did to Martin. Paul the Deacon writes that Constans, grandson of Heraclius, in Book XVIII, in the eighth indiction and the ninth year of his reign, exiled Saint Martin and Maximus to Cherson and other regions because they did not favor the errors of the Monothelites. Cedrenus places the event in his sixteenth year. Here Gregory calls him Constantine, as does Ado of Vienne in his *Chronicle*, under the year 641, and the Greek catalogue of the emperors of the East; others call him Constans. Authors also vary in giving the name of his killer. Zonaras and Cedrenus call him Μιζίζιον Ἀρμένιον, “Mizizius the Armenian”; the translator of Theophanes, said to be Paul the Deacon, calls him Mitius; Constantine Manasses, in his history written in political verse, calls him Mixizius: καὶ τυραννεῖ Μιξίζιος ἀνὴρ ἐκ Σικελίας, “and Mixizius, a man from Sicily, acts as tyrant.” Gregory here calls him Nezeuxius. Perhaps the barbarous name was altered through the fault of copyists or of the Greek translator, who may also have written τὸ ἱερὸν, “the temple,” instead of “the bath.” For all the others assert that Constans was killed in a bath, not in a temple, or else the matter was reported differently at Rome.]

You must know and be certain that the pontiffs who have existed at Rome in their respective times sit, for the sake of establishing peace, like an unbroken wall and a dividing barrier between East and West, as arbiters and moderators of peace. The emperors who came before them labored intensely in this struggle to establish peace.

If you insolently insult us and threaten us, we need not enter into combat with you. The Roman pontiff will withdraw twenty-four stadia into the region of Campania; then you may go—

[Note: “Pursue the winds.” This alludes to Ecclesiasticus XXXIV:2: Ὡς δραξόμενος σκιᾶς, καὶ διώκων ἀνέμους, “Like one who grasps at a shadow and pursues the winds, so is he who attends to dreams.” There is a similar expression from secular writers: Ἀνέμους γεωργεῖς, “you cultivate the winds,” said of those who gain no fruit from their labors. It is cited from Clement of Alexandria’s *Stromata*, where it corresponds to Proverbs XVI:4: “He who relies on lies feeds the winds”; the same passage continues, “and pursues flying birds.”]

Pursue the winds.

Our predecessor, Pope Martin, sat exhorting peace. Therefore that wicked Constantine [Constantius, Constans], holding an evil opinion concerning the faith of the Holy Trinity and supporting the heretical pontiffs whom he had proscribed—Sergius, Paul, and Pyrrhus—sent soldiers, seized Martin, and carried him away to Byzantium by tyrannical force, then, after surrounding him with many evils, sent him into exile. He also inflicted many evils upon Maximus the monk and his disciple Anastasius, and sent them into exile in Lazica.

But Constantine [Constantius], who had exiled them, was killed and died in his sin. For Nezeuxius, who was then his officer of attendants, having been informed by the bishops of Sicily that he was a heretic, slaughtered him inside the temple, and he perished in his sin.

The city of Cherson, to which Martin was exiled, bears witness that Martin is blessed, as do the Bosphorus, the whole North, and the inhabitants of the North, who hasten to his tomb and receive healings.

Would that it might be granted us by God’s favor to walk in Martin’s path, although for the benefit of the people we wish to live and survive, since the entire West turns its eyes toward our humility. Although we are not such men, they nevertheless place the greatest confidence in us and in him whose image you declare that you will overturn and destroy—namely, Saint Peter, whom all the kingdoms of the West regard as an earthly god.

If you wish to test this, the Westerners are fully prepared to avenge even the Easterners whom you have injured.

Nevertheless, we beseech you by the Lord: turn away from youthful and childish deeds. You know that Rome cannot avenge itself upon your empire, except perhaps the city alone, because of the sea beside it and its ships. For, as we said before, if the pope withdraws twenty-four stadia from Rome, he fears none of your threats.

There is one thing that troubles us: the rustic and barbarian peoples are becoming gentle, while you, though gentle, are on the contrary becoming rustic and savage.

The entire West offers the fruit of its faith to the holy chief of the apostles. If you send anyone to overturn the image of Saint Peter, beware: we declare to you that we are innocent of the blood they will shed. Rather, these things will fall back upon your neck and upon your head.

Recently we received a request from the interior West from the one whom they call Septetus, who desires, by God’s grace, to see our face, so that we may go there to impart holy baptism to him. And lest an account of our sluggishness and negligence be required of us, we are preparing for the journey.

May God place his fear in your heart and turn you toward the truth, away from the things that you have wrongly introduced into the world. May I receive your letters as soon as possible, announcing your conversion to us.

May the God who descended from heaven and, for our salvation, entered the womb of the sacred virgin, the Mother of God, dwell in your heart, and quickly drive out those who inhabit you and introduce scandals. May he grant peace to the churches of all Christians forever and ever. Amen.

EPISTLE XIII. OF POPE GREGORY II TO EMPEROR LEO THE ISAURIAN. Second [Note: Published from the same manuscript by Fr. Fronton du Duc, and by Cardinal Baronius under the year 526. HARD.] letter concerning the sacred images.

[Col. 0521B]

We have received the letter of your God-preserved imperial authority and of your brotherhood in Christ, delivered by your envoy Rufinus. I have been utterly wearied with life because you do not change your opinion but persist in the same evils, and do not understand the things that are Christ’s, so as to follow and imitate our holy and renowned Fathers and teachers, who worked miracles. I do not simply cite foreign teachers, but only those who came from your own city and region. Are they wiser than Gregory the miracle-worker, Gregory of Nyssa, Gregory the Theologian, Basil of Cappadocia, and John Chrysostom? I will not even mention the countless thousands of holy, God-filled Fathers and teachers like them who are ours.

But you have followed your obstinate mind and domestic disturbances, and have written: “I am emperor and priest.” Indeed, the emperors who preceded you demonstrated this by their deeds and words: they founded and cared for churches, together with the pontiffs, inflamed by zeal and desire, and searching out the truth of the orthodox faith—Constantine the Great, Theodosius the Great, Valentinian the Great, and Constantine, the father of Justinian, who attended the Sixth Synod. These emperors ruled religiously; together with the pontiffs, and in one counsel and judgment, they convened synods, sought the truth of doctrine, and established and adorned the holy churches.

These are priests and emperors, who demonstrated this by their deeds. But you, ever since you seized the imperial power, have not preserved the definitions of the Fathers; rather, when you found the holy churches clothed and variegated with fringed golden vestments, you stripped them of their adornment and laid them waste. For what are our churches? Are they not things made by human hands—stones, wood, straw, mud, and lime? Yet they are adorned with paintings and with histories of the miracles performed by the saints, of the sufferings of Christ, of his holy and glorious Mother, and of the holy apostles. People spend their resources on these histories and paintings. Men and women holding newly baptized infants in their arms, as well as young people in the flower of their age and people who have come from various nations, point out these histories to them with their fingers; they edify them and lift their minds and hearts upward to God. But you have occupied the humble peoples, whom you ordered to abstain from these things, with idle talk, trifles, lyres, rattles, pipes, and futilities; and instead of thanksgiving and celebration, you have led them over to fables. May you have your inheritance with them, and with those who tell useless tales and babble foolishness.

Hear our humility, emperor: cease, and follow the holy Church as you found and received it. These are not the doctrines of emperors but of pontiffs, for we possess the mind of Christ (II Cor. 2). The institution of ecclesiastical constitutions is one thing, and the understanding of secular affairs another. In the administration of worldly matters you possess a military, inept, and crude understanding; you cannot apply it to the spiritual administration of doctrine.

And here I set before you the distinction between the palace and the churches, between emperors and pontiffs. Recognize it and be saved; do not be contentious. If someone were to take from you your royal garments, your purple, your head-diadema, your robe, and the ranks of your attendants, you would be regarded by men as disgraceful, deformed, and despised. Such is the condition to which you have reduced the churches: because you yourself do not possess these things, you have stripped the holy churches of their adornments and made them deformed.

For just as a pontiff has no authority to inspect the palace or to confer royal dignities, so neither does an emperor have authority to inspect the churches, conduct elections among the clergy, consecrate, administer the symbols of the holy sacraments [Hardouin: mysteries], or even receive communion without the ministry of a priest. Rather, each of us must remain in the calling in which God called him (I Cor. 7).

Do you see, emperor, the distinction between pontiffs and emperors? If someone offends you, you confiscate and strip his house, leaving him only his life; finally, you either kill him by hanging, behead him, or exile him, banishing him far from his children and all his relatives and friends. Pontiffs do not act in this way. When someone sins and confesses, instead of hanging or beheading him, they place the Gospel and the cross around his neck; they cast him, as though into a prison, into the secretariat and the treasury of the sacred vessels; they send him away to the church’s diaconicon and catechumenium; they impose fasting upon his entrails, vigils upon his eyes, and praise upon his mouth.

When they have punished him thoroughly [Hardouin: excellently] and afflicted him sufficiently with hunger, they then give him the precious body of the Lord and make him drink the holy blood. After restoring him as a vessel of election and making him free from sin, they send him pure and innocent to the Lord.

Do you see, emperor, the distinction between churches and empires? Emperors who lived piously and in Christ did not refuse to obey the pontiffs of the churches, nor did they harass them. But you, emperor, after transgressing, becoming perverse, and signing with your own hand—thereby subjecting yourself—and after confessing that the one who removes the boundaries established by the Fathers is accursed, have been condemned by this very judgment of your own, and have alienated the Holy Spirit from yourself.

You persecute us and tyrannically harass us with a military and carnal hand. We, unarmed and naked, who possess no earthly or carnal armies, invoke the commander of every created host who sits in the heavens, Christ, who is above all the armies of the heavenly powers, asking him to send a demon against you, as the Apostle says: “To hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved” (I Cor. 5).

Do you see to what shamelessness and inhumanity you have brought yourself, emperor? You have driven your soul headlong into abysses and precipitous places because you have refused to humble yourself and submit your stiff neck. For when pontiffs, after offering excellent admonition and instruction, present emperors to God as irreproachable and cleansed of sins and offenses, they obtain great praise and glory from him at the great holy resurrection, when he will bring our hidden matters and deeds into the light, to our shame before his angels.

Then we humble men will be ashamed that, because of your disobedience, we did not win you over, whereas the pontiffs who preceded us presented to God the emperors who ruled in their own times. This will bring shame upon us humble men, if we do not present the emperor of our time as glorious and renowned, but as disgraceful and infamous [Hardouin: marked with dishonor].

Even now, therefore, we exhort you: do penance, turn back, and enter upon the truth. Preserve it as you found and received it. Honor and glorify our holy and glorious Fathers and teachers, who, according to God, drove blindness from our hearts and eyes and restored our sight.

But you have written: “How is it that nothing was said about images in the six councils?” Indeed, emperor, not even anything was said about bread and water—whether they should be eaten or not eaten, drunk or not drunk—since these things were handed down from ancient times and from the beginning for the preservation of human life. In the same way, images had been handed down, and the pontiffs themselves brought images to the councils. No one among Christ-loving and religious people, when traveling, undertook a pilgrimage without images, since such people were endowed with virtue and upright before God.

We exhort you to be both pontiff and emperor, as you previously wrote. But if you are ashamed to attribute this to yourself as emperor, write to all the regions in which you have become a scandal that Gregory, the Roman pope, is wrong concerning images, and likewise Germanus, the patriarch of Constantinople. We will accept the blame for the sin, since we have received from the Lord the power and authority to loose and bind earthly and heavenly things. We will relieve you of this concern.

You neither wished nor wish to do so. We, who must render an account to Christ the Lord, have given you admonitions and instructions as we were taught by the Lord. But you refused and declined to obey us humble men, as well as Germanus the prelate and our holy and glorious Fathers, workers of miracles and teachers. Instead, you followed perverse and wicked teachers of doctrine who have strayed from the truth. Have your portion with them.

As we wrote to you previously, through God’s kindness we are setting out toward the farthest regions of the West, toward those who are requesting holy baptism. For when we sent bishops and clergy of our holy Church there, their rulers had not yet been persuaded to bow their heads and be baptized, although they desire this, wishing me to be their sponsor. For this reason, through God’s kindness, we are preparing for the journey, lest we should have to render an account for condemnation and negligence.

May God grant you prudence and repentance, so that you may turn back to the truth from which you have departed. May he restore the humble peoples once more to one shepherd, Christ, and to one fold of orthodox churches and prelates. May the Lord our God grant peace to the whole world, now and always, and for ever and ever. Amen.

## LETTER XIV. OF POPE GREGORY II TO BONIFACE, BISHOP

He responds to various questions and inquiries of his.

To the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop, Gregory, servant of the servants of God.

[Col. 0524C] **[Note: “Desiderabilem mihi.” Gratian attributes this letter to Gregory III whenever he uses its testimony, as in *Decretum* 2, question 5, “Presbyter”; 32, question 7, “Quod proposuisti”; *De Consecratione*, distinction 4, “Parvulos”; and distinction 5, “De homine.” Hincmar also appears to hold the same view in Letter 7, chapters 15 and 18, as does Ivo in Part VII, chapter 78, when they attribute it to the younger Gregory. By this name they were accustomed to mean Gregory III. But the year ten of Leo and indiction 10 in the subscription to the letter oppose its attribution to him; these correspond to the year of Christ 726, when Gregory II was pope, whereas Gregory III did not occupy the see before the year 731. Therefore it must be assigned to Gregory II. Sirmond.]**

The religious priest Denval, sent by you, brought me welcome news: he reported that you were safe and announced that, by God’s favor, you were making progress in the ministry for which you had been sent. He also delivered letters sent by you, in which you indicated that the Lord’s field, lying uncultivated and stiff with the thorns of unbelief, had received the seed of the word when plowed by the plowshare of your teaching and had produced a fertile harvest of faithfulness.

In the same letters you appended certain chapters, asking how this holy apostolic Roman Church holds or teaches these matters. You know well that the blessed apostle Peter was the beginning both of the apostolate [Roman edition omits “and the apostolate”] and of the episcopate. In response to your inquiry concerning the condition of the Church, we say—not from ourselves as though from ourselves, but by the grace of him who opens the mouths of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent—how you ought to maintain the doctrine of apostolic authority.

### I

First, you asked in which degree of relationship marriage may be contracted. We say that, so long as the parties recognize that they are related by kinship, they ought not to enter into this union. But because moderation is preferable to strict severity, especially among so barbarous a people, it should be permitted that they marry after the fourth generation.

### II

You asked [Roman edition: “you stated”] what a husband should do if his wife, overcome by illness, is unable to render the marital debt. It would be good if he remained in this state and devoted himself to abstinence. But because this is a matter for the spiritually strong, let the man who cannot contain himself marry instead. Nevertheless, he must not withdraw assistance from the woman whom illness hinders, since she is excluded not by detestable guilt. (*Decretum* 32, question 2, “Quod proposuisti.”)

### III

Concerning a presbyter: if any priest is accused by the people, and there are no certain witnesses who can establish the truth of the charge brought against him, an oath shall be required, and he shall offer as witness to the purity of his innocence the one to whom all things are naked and open. Thus he shall remain in his own rank. (*Decretum* 2, question 5, “Presbyter vel quilibet”; Hincmar of Reims, *Epistle 7.*)

### IV

Concerning a person who has been confirmed by a pontiff: such a repetition of confirmation must be prohibited for him. (*De Consecratione*, distinction 5, “De homine qui.”)

### V

In the solemn celebration of the Mass, what our Lord Jesus Christ gave to his holy disciples must be observed. For he took the cup, saying: “This is the cup of the New Testament in my blood” (Luke 22); “Do this whenever you receive it” [Roman edition: “whenever you receive it”] (I Cor. 11). Therefore it is not appropriate to place two or three cups upon the altar when the solemn celebration of Mass is being performed.

### VI

You consulted us concerning sacrificial foods: if the sign of the life-giving cross has been traced over them by the faithful, may they be eaten or not? It is sufficient to answer what the blessed apostle Paul says: “If anyone says, ‘This has been offered in sacrifice,’ do not eat it, for the sake of the one who indicated this and for the sake of conscience” (I Cor. 10).

### VII

You added that, if a father or mother entrusts a son or daughter, while still an infant, within the enclosure of a monastery to the regular discipline, may they leave after reaching the years of puberty and marry? We entirely reject this, because it is impious that children offered to God by their parents should later be allowed to loosen the reins of pleasure. (*Decretum* 20, question 1, “Addidistis.”)

### VIII

You acknowledged that certain people had been baptized by adulterous and unworthy priests without being questioned concerning the Creed. In these cases, let your affection maintain the ancient custom of the Church: whoever has been baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit may in no way be rebaptized. The gift of this grace is received not in the name of the one baptizing but in the name of the Trinity. And they must hold to what the Apostle says: “One God, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4). We charge you to impart spiritual instruction to such people with particular care.

### IX

Concerning infants who have been taken away from their parents, and concerning whom it is unknown whether they have been baptized, since you asked whether you ought to baptize them: according to the tradition of the Fathers, reason requires that you do so if there is no one to testify otherwise. (*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, “Parvulos qui.”)

### X

If lepers are faithful Christians, they are to be given participation in the Lord’s body and blood. They must, however, be prohibited [Roman edition: “excluded”] from dining with the healthy.

### XI

You also added that, if a pestilential disease or mortality breaks out in a church or monastery, should those whom it has not yet touched flee from the place in order to avoid the danger? This seems exceedingly foolish, for no one can escape the hands of God.

### XII

At the end, the letter stated that there are certain presbyters or bishops entangled in many vices, whose lives stain the priesthood in themselves, and you asked whether you might eat or speak with them unless they had been restrained. We say that, by apostolic authority, you should rebuke and admonish them and restore them to the purity of ecclesiastical discipline.

If they obey, they will save their souls, and you will have gained a reward. Nevertheless, do not refuse conversation and a common table with them. It often happens that those whom disciplinary correction makes slow to receive the rule of truth are led to the way of justice by persistent fellowship at table and gentle admonition. You must observe the same practice with those leading men who provide you assistance.

Let these words, therefore, dearest brother, written from the authority of the apostolic see, suffice.
