For the rest, we implore the mercy of God, that he who caused you, by apostolic authority and in our place, to go to those regions, and predestined the lights of truth to shine through your mouth in a dark forest, may grant you the most merciful increase of his assistance, so that you may yourself be able to receive rewards for the fruit of your work and find forgiveness of sins.

May God keep you safe, most reverend brother.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, while our most pious lord Augustus Leo, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the tenth year of his reign; and while Constantine, the great emperor, was also reigning, in the seventh year of his reign, indiction 10.

## LETTER XV. OF POPE GREGORY II TO SERENUS, BISHOP OF FORUM JULII

On not invading the Church of Grado.

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Serenus.

Each person is enriched by so great a gift as, when placed in eminence, he humbly thinks of himself in accordance with the command of the Lord Redeemer; for pastoral dignity is singularly adorned by humility. Apostolic teaching indeed rebukes the proud as worthy of contempt: “What have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. 4).

For, when, at the prayers of our most excellent son the king, we were moved to send you the pallium, greatly urged by the Church on account of the soundness of faith through which we learned that you and your Church embraced us, we forbade and, among other things, prohibited you ever to invade another’s rights or to usurp anyone’s jurisdiction by a rash venture, but to be content with what you had possessed up to that point. **[Note: The passage is corrupt. Mansi.]**

But now, as we have learned, you are striving to invade the rights of the patriarch of Grado and to usurp everything that he has possessed. Therefore, lest you prove a transgressor in any respect, we command by apostolic authority that you in no way approach the boundaries he has possessed [perhaps: exceed them], but retain what you have possessed until now. Nor presume to extend your steps farther than the boundaries located within the territory of the Lombards, lest by your presumption you show that you have unjustly received the grace of the pallium bestowed upon you and, if proved disobedient to the force of apostolic counsel, be judged worthy of punishment.

## LETTER XVI. OF POPE GREGORY II TO DONATUS, PATRIARCH OF GRADO, AND HIS SUBJECTS

He announces that the bishop of Forum Julii has been forbidden to invade other provinces.

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Donatus, patriarch, and the bishops, and Marcellus, duke, and the people of Venetia and Istria.

Although, by virtue of the ministry which we exercise through divine mercy, it is fitting that whatever has been prudently decided should be carried out without obstacle, nevertheless, lest we should seem to have rendered judgment in vain, we desire to pursue those measures that look not to anyone’s injury but rather to security, and to strive for those things from which rewards, rather than punishments through the power granted us, may be hoped for. For it is fitting that, while we comply with one party’s wishes, another’s rights should not be defrauded.

Accordingly, because, in a report sent to us, your community preserved by God requested action against the bishop of Forum Julii, who wished to invade the jurisdiction of the patriarch of Grado, we have forbidden him by apostolic authority to attempt any attack upon that Church at present, and have ordered him never to exceed its boundary or invade another’s rights, but to be content with what he has possessed up to now. Know, dearest ones, that he has assented to this condition, and that we have commanded him not to presume to exceed it.

Therefore, lest their people, by some injury or dissension, treacherously invade the place, as is their custom, keep careful watch. Rather, after divine protection, be solicitous for your own safety, because this is not done opportunely; but where they can, let them strive to obey their power, God not opposing them. We desire that henceforth you may flourish in the love of our Lord Jesus Christ and remain free from every adversity. Farewell.

## LETTER XVII. OF POPE GREGORY II TO THE BISHOPS OF ENGLAND

He recognizes Tatwin, archbishop of Canterbury, as primate of all England and commands that he be recognized.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the bishops of England: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We praise together the greatness of the immense mercy of almighty God, who has deigned so to extend the glory of his majesty that now the sound of his preachers has gone forth into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world. By the grace of his ineffable mercy, as we are known to have been begotten, so we have also been adopted, bearing the mystery of holy regeneration in hope of the glory of the children of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Therefore, dearest brothers, rejoicing with your dedicated fellowship, we exhort your reverence that you may be found steadfast in faith and effective in work, outdoing one another in honor and bearing one another’s burdens, because so you will fulfill the law of Christ; maintaining unbroken charity in love of God and neighbor, without which it is impossible to please God.

The arrival of our brother Tatwin, who has succeeded to the episcopal chair of your preacher Augustine of blessed memory, greatly gladdened us, because during the time that he remained with us we came to know him as a man of religion and great probity. Accordingly, having heard his petitions, we caused the rights of dignity of his predecessors to be sought in the sacred archive; and, finding that he had asked justly, we gave him by apostolic authority the sacred pallium with the venerable use of the dalmatic, also confirming all the rights of dignity which his predecessors are known to have possessed from the time of Augustine of blessed memory.

Therefore, just as the decree of our holy Father Gregory, Roman pontiff, subjected all the bishops of England to the aforesaid Augustine, his *syncellus* and your preacher, so we, with God as author and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, though unworthy to exercise his office, subject to you, Tatwin, archbishop of the city of Canterbury, and to your legitimate successors, all the Churches of Britain and their rulers. By apostolic authority we command that every person throughout the whole English region obey your canonical commands and know you to be the watchman and primate of the whole island, to whom we have entrusted the exercise of our office in every respect in that region.

We hold your Church, established at Canterbury, as the special object of the protection of our hand, as the proper and first offspring of your region in Christ. We desire it to flourish in the tranquility of peace and religion, and that its rights and privileges of dignity be preserved unimpaired forever, because it is the first and mother of all the others, first established in your region in honor of the holy Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ. For it is written: “There is none holy as the Lord”; and where the head is flourishing, the remaining members flourish more strongly.

Therefore, brothers, hear and receive these commands of apostolic authority with eagerness and the reverence of submission, and labor with the aforesaid brother, your archbishop, in God’s harvest, knowing that you will thereby receive a good reward. But if anyone should wish to disturb these things or strive to tear down and violate the ordinances of our definition, let him know that he strives against the Savior of the world himself and the authority of blessed Peter; and therefore, unless he repents, he will incur the sentence of eternal damnation. May God keep you safe, dearest brothers.

## LETTER XVIII. OF POPE GREGORY II TO STEPHEN, PRESBYTER

Gregory to Stephen, presbyter, and to two successive persons.

Whenever things that unquestionably accord with reason are hoped to be granted by us, it is fitting that we grant them with a willing mind and afford a suitable favor to the desires of petitioners. Accordingly, because you asked us to grant you, by an issued command, possession of the Campanian estate with its house and vineyard, situated on the Via Flaminia about fourteen miles from this city of Rome, which was held by our presbyter and *vestararius* Sergius by leasehold improvement, and which estate belonged to the body of the Tuscan patrimony under the right of the holy Roman Church that, with God as author, we serve: we, yielding to your prayers, grant you by the tenor of this command the aforesaid estate with house, vineyard, and all appurtenances, entire, for you to hold during your lifetime from the present eighth indiction.

Provided, however, that you pay, without delay, three gold solidi each indiction as rent to the ecclesiastical accounts, and that you undertake without doubt and without distinction every improvement and defense required by the aforesaid estate, vineyard, and house. Nor shall any delay thereafter arise from you in paying the annual rent; rather, from the aforesaid time it shall be paid voluntarily to the agents of our holy Church. But if, which God forbid, the matter should proceed otherwise concerning the aforesaid improvement, defense, and annual rent, we decree that this command of ours shall be invalid. After your death, the aforesaid estate shall return entire to the right of our holy Church, whose property it is. Given on the Ides of April, indiction 8.

## LETTER XIX, OR PRIVILEGE, OF POPE GREGORY II TO BASINUS, ABBOT

Pope Gregory II, at the request of Abbot Basinus, grants immunity and other privileges to the monastery of Saint Maximin of Trier, in the year 729.

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to Basinus, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist and of the most holy confessor of Christ, Maximin, whose body rests there: greetings and apostolic blessing.

If those things which accord with pious desires are always to be granted, then what is requested for the worship of God must be granted and carried out all the more readily, with cheerful devotion, benevolent intention, and every obstacle removed.

You therefore asked us to grant to your monastery—which is known to have been built in the suburb of Trier in honor of Saint John the Evangelist, where the aforesaid confessor of Christ rests—a privilege of our holy apostolic Church, which by God’s authority we serve, in order to confirm for the brothers serving God there the rule of monastic tranquility.

We have accordingly endeavored to assent to your pious petition, decreeing by a command of apostolic authority that the congregation religiously serving God there shall henceforth possess free power to choose from among themselves as abbot whomever they select according to God’s will, just as in earlier times kings granted this to the same monastery. No person of any rank may presume to arrange or rashly undertake anything within the aforesaid monastery according to his own will unless summoned by you or by another abbot who succeeds you.

Furthermore, by our apostolic authority we absolutely prohibit that it ever be subjected to any church or see by exchange or by any other device, but that it enjoy, without disturbance and perpetually, such liberty and immunity as other royal establishments possess.

Let the monastery itself remain under the protection of the kings, and let it never be open to any person for exploitation or seizure as a benefice. Rather, let it remain peaceful for the use and tranquility of the monks who serve God there under the Rule of Saint Benedict.

We also establish and, from this paternal affection, grant to you and your successors that, at the sacred mysteries on the principal feast days, you may use the mitre, dalmatic, and sandals. We admonish your fraternity that, as your honor increases, the power of divine love may also increase in you.

We prohibit and absolutely forbid, by the authority of blessed Peter, whose place we occupy, though unworthy, in this apostolic see, that any duke, count, or any ecclesiastical or secular person whatsoever presume to seize a mountain or crag in the possession or allod of Saint Maximin, or to build any fortification there—unless perhaps the abbot of that monastery should, because of fear of the pagans or an incursion of wicked men, fortify himself and his people there temporarily, until the tranquility of peace returns.

For the further increase and strengthening of monastic tranquility, we add that no person of any rank may presume to alienate or diminish anything, great or small, from the property of the Church—whether from what has now been granted to the same monastery by you or by others, or from what other faithful people may hereafter contribute for the remedy of their souls.

If anyone, which God forbid, should wickedly presume to infringe or in any way violate what we have established for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid venerable monastery, let him know that, under the testimony of divine judgment and through the intercession of the blessed apostle Peter, he is inextricably bound by the bond of anathema, excluded from the kingdom of God, and destined to burn with the devil and his followers in the most terrible punishments.

But whoever, with pious regard and reverence for the fear of God, observes this apostolic command of ours shall deserve to obtain from the Lord the grace of eternal blessing.

Given … …

Written by the hand of Benedict, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of January, indiction 12, in the name of God.

## PENITENTIAL CANONS

I am uncertain whether these decrees or penitential canons, which I publish here before all others, should be attributed to Gregory II. The age certainly permitted the issuing of such canons by him. At that time, nearly all pontiffs, bishops, and even certain private persons issued penitential canons. Gregory III issued his, as did Theodore, bishop of London; Saint Boniface of Mainz issued his; and finally Bede, a presbyter, though of private authority, issued his.

They therefore do not conflict with an attribution to Pope Gregory II, to whom the author of the manuscript codex of the library of the canons of Saint Martin of Lucca appears to attribute them, and from which I obtained this material. In the preface that the writer of the codex placed before these and several other canons, he states that he will provide the decrees of Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, Gelasius, Anastasius, Symmachus, Hormisdas, and the younger Gregory—that is, Gregory II—and immediately adds the decrees published here. He then proceeds in order to the decrees of Siricius and the others, and no other decree of Gregory II appears anywhere in the entire book.

These points support Gregory. But, on the other hand, I am prevented from attributing them to him by decrees of Gregory III, his successor, concerning perjurers, in which certain provisions are laid down that plainly agree with these canons. Gregory III says that he is prescribing these provisions according to an ancient definition. Therefore his predecessor Gregory II did not establish them. Perhaps, then, the decrees I publish are those very ancient decrees that Gregory III mentions in his excerpts, canon 7.

If anyone swears an oath, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water, and let him never swear again.

If anyone commits perjury under compulsion—that is, by force, because of some necessity, or unknowingly—let him do penance for three years on bread and water.

If a layman commits perjury out of greed, let him give all his possessions to the poor, be beaten, and serve in a monastery for the days of his life.

If anyone leads another, who is ignorant, into perjury, let him do penance for seven years. But whoever realizes that he is being led into perjury and nevertheless swears, let him do penance for five years.

## CAPITULARY GIVEN BY POPE GREGORY II TO MARTINIANUS, BISHOP, GEORGE, PRESBYTER, AND OTHERS, SENT TO BAVARIA

In the name of the Lord begins the capitulary given at Rome by Pope Gregory to our most reverend brother Martinianus, bishop, or [read: and] George, presbyter of the holy apostolic see, and Dorotheus, subdeacon of the aforesaid see, as they go, with the Lord’s help, to Bavaria.

**[Note: Martianus, bishop of Gabii or Sabina, and George, presbyter of the Roman Church with the title of Saints John and Paul, subscribed the Roman Council of 721. Ciaconius, in *The Lives of the Pontiffs*, under the year 735, lists George as a cardinal-presbyter with the title of Saints John and Paul, under the title of Pammachius.]**

### I

When our written instructions have been given, deliberate with the duke of the province so that an assembly may be convened of the priests, judges, and all the leading men of that people. From among the priests and ministers who have been carefully examined, and whose canonical promotion you have approved, as well as their holding or receiving of the orthodox faith, grant these men authority to celebrate the sacrifice, minister, and also sing the psalms according to the form and tradition of the holy apostolic and Roman Church [read: grant them authority according to the order of the form and tradition of the holy apostolic Roman Church].

But those whose soundness in the faith or the approved validity of their canonical ordination has not become clear must be entirely prohibited from exercising ministry, so that canonically approved successors may be appointed in their place.

### II

Providing for the places of the individual churches [read: providing for the place of each church], determine how each priest or minister ought to maintain his church, and how he should carefully observe the solemn celebration of Mass, the other offices of the day and night hours, and also the reading of the sacred New and Old Testaments, according to the established order handed down by the antiquity of the apostolic see [read: according to the order handed down by the antiquity of the apostolic see]. You shall arrange these matters [read: arrange them].

### III.

That, after considering the distances between places, you should arrange the bishoprics according to the jurisdiction of each duke, and define the territories subject to each see. And if three, or four, or a greater number of sees appear to have been established, reserving the place of the principal see for the archbishop to occupy, and having convened three bishops who are reliable in faith, of good reputation, and learned in sound doctrine, you shall ordain suitable men as bishops by the authority of blessed Peter the apostle, assigning them to the places entrusted to them according to the dispensation handed down in the succeeding order.

### IV.

That, having provided a place for the archbishop, if you can find a man of such character as can instruct the priests subject to him through saving doctrine and examples of good works, govern the clergy and people with the greatest prudence, and suitably enlarge the flock entrusted to him, you should either send him to us with your letters or have him come to us. But if you certainly cannot find such a man, you should make this known either in person or by your letters, so that, providing for this previously mentioned holy see, we may, with God’s help, send a suitable man.

### V.

That, once the bishops have been ordained, you should give each of them this as a model of our ordination [Note: See above, the letter to the Thuringians, where the reading is “of our ordination”], charging them that he never presume to perform unlawful ordinations; that he permit no bigamist, nor one who has not taken a virgin as wife, nor an unlearned man, nor one deformed in any part of his body, nor a penitent, nor anyone subject to any condition and marked as such, to approach the sacred orders. But if he should happen to find persons of this sort, he must not dare to promote them. Let him in no way admit Africans presenting themselves for ecclesiastical orders, because most of them have been proven to be Manichaeans and frequently rebaptized.

Let him strive not to diminish the ministries and adornment of the church, or whatever is or shall be part of its patrimony, but to increase them. From the church’s income and from the offerings of the faithful, let him make four portions: one he shall retain for himself; a second he shall distribute to the clergy in accordance with their diligent performance of their offices; a third shall be for the poor and pilgrims; and a fourth he shall understand to be reserved for ecclesiastical buildings, for which he will have to render an account at the divine judgment.

He shall understand that the ordinations of priests and deacons are to be celebrated only during the fasts of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months, and at the beginning of Lent and on the evening of Saturday. But the sacrament of holy baptism is to be administered only at the festival of Easter and at Pentecost, except in the case of those for whom, when the danger of death presses, such remedies must be provided lest they perish eternally.

For the rest, the whole body of religion is subject to the one who observes the precepts of the previously mentioned Roman see, and the entire community of peoples marked with the renewed sign of the Christian name is to be admonished to obey with a most willing heart, so that the body of the Church may become an irreproachable offering through Christ our Lord.

### VI.

That you should establish, by apostolic authority, an order for those who are marrying or intend to marry, so that neither intercourse within marriage may be judged condemnable by those who plead continence, nor the permission to marry be presumed to offer an occasion for fornication. But just as God commanded male and female to be joined at the very beginning of the world, “so that the two may be one flesh” (Genesis II), so, in accordance with apostolic teaching, “Let each man have his own wife” (I Corinthians VII).

And let it not be permitted for husband and wife to defraud one another, except by mutual consent for a time, so that they may devote themselves to prayer, as the Apostle says on this very subject: “You are bound to a wife; do not seek release” (ibid.). That is: while one’s spouse is alive, one must not wish to pass to intercourse with another desired woman, because, as the same teacher of the Gentiles affirms, “He who commits fornication sins against his own body” (I Corinthians VI)—that is, against his own wife, with whom he is one body—and by defrauding her through illicit embraces he binds himself under the charge of sin.

Therefore a marriage that has exceeded the number two is not to be rightly regarded as marriage, since the yoke is not borne except by two. The marriage of one man and one woman is likewise to be taught to be wholly impermissible within close blood relationship: no one may dare to join in marriage, or unite in adultery, with his father’s wife, his paternal uncle’s wife, or his brother’s wife; with his own sister; with his father’s or mother’s sister; with his sister’s daughter; or with the daughter of his father’s sister or of his mother’s sister.

But if anyone, whether through marital intercourse or through the rashness of committing adultery, should dare to perpetrate such an act, let him know that he is subject to the pollution of incestuous crime and that, for this reason, he is made unworthy of the sacred communion of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, without receiving which no one can be saved.

The integrity of faithful virgins and of those who practice continence is also taught to be preferable to marriage itself.

### VII.

That nothing in the consumption of foods is to be judged unclean except what has been sacrificed to idols, because, as is taught by apostolic instruction, “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving” (I Timothy IV).

### VIII.

That dreams and omens, since according to the divine oracles they are vain, are to be taught to deserve no attention whatsoever.

### IX.

That incantations and *fastidiationes* [perhaps *fatidictiones*, “prophetic utterances”], or the various observances of the days of the Kalends, which pagan error has handed down, are to be prohibited, as are magical practices and the tricks of magicians, as well as lots and the abominable observances of diviners.

### X.

That on Sundays it is not permitted to fast at all, because of the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection; nor on the Lord’s festivals of the Nativity, the Apparition, or the Ascension.

[Note: This means the Epiphany and the Ascension. —Harduinus.]

### XI.

In all things, therefore, let the charity of Christ be maintained, so that, in accordance with the statutes of the sacred canons, the offerings of those who are at variance may in no way be received in the church before they have been reconciled.

### XII.

That no one should think himself not in need of the remedies of penance for the daily transgressions of human weakness, without which we cannot exist in this life.

### XIII.

That they should be instructed concerning hope in the future resurrection in such a way that they do not doubt that all human beings will rise in the same order and form in which the Lord himself rose from the dead, in the same body in which we are and live—not changing our nature or sex, but laying aside only our frailty and vices.

Satan himself, together with his angels and his worshipers, is to be consumed by eternal fire, and is not, according to the sacrilegious argument of certain people, to be restored to his former—that is, angelic—dignity, from which he fell. This agrees with what the Lord foretold in the Gospel that he would say to the condemned standing at his left hand in the future judgment: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew XXV).

Farewell. Given on the Ides of March, while the lord Augustus Anastasius, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the third year of his pontificate, etc.

[Editorial correction: “in the first year, or in the second year of his empire, or of his patriciate.” Gregory customarily records not years of pontificate but years of empire.]

## In the Year of Our Lord 739

### Saint Willibrord, Bishop of Utrecht

## Historical Notices Concerning Saint Willibrord

### I

*(From the Catalogue of the Bishops of Utrecht by Hadrianus Barlandus)*

Willibrord, by nationality a Saxon Briton, was the first bishop of Utrecht; when he attained that dignity, he assumed the name Clement. His childhood was spent among men distinguished for their piety. Through their constant association he became, as a young man, an excellent person, and in the study of the liberal arts he progressed so greatly within a few years that he surpassed his peers by an immeasurable distance in knowledge.

Afterward, having been initiated into the sacred ministry, he set out for Germany in the thirtieth year of his age. There, through his preaching, he drew many people to the worship of the one God; and, traveling through other regions as well, he spread Christian doctrine far and wide. Through these and other works of piety he was placed over the Church of Utrecht and, by implanting the name of Christ in the hearts of his people, proved a most excellent bishop.

He consecrated the famous church of Saint Martin that now stands in that city, and he held the episcopal dignity for nearly forty years.

### II

*(From the Catalogue of the Bishops of Utrecht by Gerard of Noyon)*

In the year 690 from the Nativity of our Savior, Lord and God Jesus Christ, Willibrord, a priest from the very famous island of Britain—which in that century the Angles and Saxons, after conquering the Britons, had made subject to their own authority and name—came to Lower Germany, which was still called Francia. At Rome he was ordained archbishop of Utrecht by Sergius, the Roman pontiff, at the request of the most pious Frankish prince Pippin, on the feast day of Saint Cecilia, and received the name Clement.

Returning from there to Utrecht, the fortress of the Eastern Franks, he received from Pippin the site of the episcopal see and built a church of moderate size in honor of the Holy Cross. In it he also consecrated the first font of Christian baptism.

Later, at the place where the church of the apostle Saint Thomas had been destroyed by the Danes and Normans, not far from the fortress of Wiltaburg—which Bede testifies was called Utrecht in French—he arranged for another church to be built. He gathered one hundred monks of blameless life so that they might devote themselves assiduously to divine worship, and he wished this church to be the first and chief church of his diocese.

Finally, after governing the Church of Utrecht for forty years with great holiness of life, he died and was enrolled among the saints.

# Charters Granted to Saint Willibrord or Issued by Him

### I. Charter by which Hedenus, an illustrious man, grants gifts to Bishop Willibrord

[Note: Martenius published it from the charter collection of Echternach, *Amplissima collectio*, volume I, column 13; Eckart, *Francia orientalis*, volume I, page 311; Bertholet, *History of Luxembourg*, volume II, page 24; and Hontheim, *Diplomatic History of Trier*, volume II, page 99, reprinted it. All used Martenius except Bertholet, who used the Echternach cartulary. Eckart notes that Hedenus was also called Hetanus and was the son of Gozbert, duke of Thuringia. On page 312 and elsewhere he establishes this with several arguments useful for clarifying the document, but it is not our purpose to dwell on them here, nor do the limits imposed on our notes permit it. We shall present another charter of Hedenus below, under the year 716, page 308.]

*(Year 704)*

In the name of Christ. While each person appears to live in the present life, and with watchful mind perceives that this fleeting life must be ended by death, he ought to consider how, while he is alive, he may seek for his soul a reward and refreshment with God in the future.

Therefore I, Hedenus, an illustrious man, together with my most illustrious wife Theodrada, have decided to give something from our possessions, for the love of Christ, the remission of our sins, and the future reward, to God and to our lord and father in Christ, Bishop Willibrord—and so we have done. That is, I hand over and transfer entirely into your power, venerable lord Father, our estate at a place called Arnestali, on the river Huitteius, with all its integrity: houses, farmyards, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, slaves and beasts of burden, cowherds, shepherds, swineherds, and whatever appears to belong to it from this present day onward, so that you may have, hold, and possess it, and give it in God’s name to whomever you wish.

And at the castle of Mulenberge we give you three farmsteads with their slaves, together with all their private property, and one hundred daylands—that is, *jugera*—of arable land, for drawing water and timber.

And at another estate of ours called Monhore, we give you seven *hubae*, seven farmsteads, and three hundred daylands of land; one-third of the woodland belonging to the same estate; meadows sufficient to cut fifty wagonloads of hay; two swineherds with fifty pigs; and two cowherds with twelve cows.

These farmsteads, remaining there with all their property and labor, whatever they have or are known to have, I hand over to you in their entirety. All the possessions listed above we give to you, our lord and father in Christ, and we wish them to be given permanently, so that you may have them and leave them to your own people to possess, or may have entirely free and secure power to do whatever you wish with them.

If anyone—and I do not believe this will happen—whether we ourselves, God forbid, or any of our heirs or descendants, should attempt to act against this charter of our donation, seek to invalidate it, or try to take anything from these possessions from you as though by hereditary right, may he first incur the anger of almighty God and of the holy angels, be excluded from the thresholds of God’s Church and from the communion of the saints, and suffer the leprosy of Gehazi or the punishment of Ananias and Sapphira. May he share the portion of Judas Iscariot, who betrayed the Lord, and moreover pay to you, together with the enforcing treasury, five pounds of gold and fifteen *ponda* of silver. Even then may he be unable to claim what he seeks; rather, his attempt being frustrated, may this charter remain firm and immovable forever, supported by formal stipulation.

Executed publicly at the castle of Virteburh, on the Kalends of May, in the tenth year of the reign of our lord Childebert, the glorious king.

I, Laurentius, an unworthy priest, at the command of lord Hedenus, duke and illustrious man, wrote this charter of donation and signed it in God’s name.

I, Hedenus, have confirmed with my own hand and subscribed this charter of donation, made by me and read before me, together with Theodrada.

I, Thuringus, son of Hedenus, have confirmed my father’s donation.

Rocchus. Doda.

### II. Charter by which Irmina, abbess, grants to Bishop Willibrord whatever she possesses in the estate of Stancheim

[Note: Martenius published it from the Echternach cartulary, *Amplissima collectio*, volume I, column 12; Hontheim reprinted it in *Diplomatic History of Trier*, volume I, page 101. We have spoken elsewhere of Irmina the abbess and Willibrord, bishop of Utrecht. In Irmina’s charter, which we presented above on page 250, Basinus and Leodowinus subscribe, both with the title of bishop; and indeed both attained the episcopate of Trier, as we have already noted, and were distinguished by the episcopal title at the same time, although Basinus had handed over the government of the church to Leodoinus. Here Basinus, the bishop, subscribes, and Leodoinus, the priest. Is this Leodoinus the same as Leodowinus, who subscribed other charters of Irmina under the title of bishop? We by no means think so, since his name lies indiscriminately among the names of other witnesses subscribing without any title of rank.]

*(Year 704)*

To the holy lord and apostolic father in Christ, Bishop Willibrord, Irmina, an abbess consecrated to God in Christ, donor.

Whatever each person, of his own possessions, freely gives to places of the saints and servants of God, he believes that he will receive from God in the future the reward of recompense for it. Therefore I, Irmina, give to you, for your monastery at Echternach—which we have newly built, situated on the river Sûre, in honor of the Holy Trinity and the saints—and I wish it to be given permanently for possession, namely, whatever from this present day is my possession or gift in the estate of Stancheim, situated on the river Sûre, both houses and buildings, homesteads, slaves, vineyards, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses.

This is granted on the condition that from this present day you or the monastery’s community may have entirely free and secure power to do whatever you wish with it, and that you need fear no claim from anyone on this account.

If anyone—and we do not believe this will happen—whether I myself, or any of my heirs or co-heirs, or any opposing person, should attempt to act against this charter of our donation or seek to violate it, may he first incur the anger of almighty God and moreover pay to the treasury one pound of gold and two *ponda* of silver. Even then may he in no way be able to establish the claim he makes, while the validity of the donation nevertheless remains.

Executed at Trier, on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the tenth year of King Childebert.

I, Huncio, priest, in the name of Christ, at the request of the lady Irmina, abbess, wrote out this charter of donation, and she herself confirmed it below with her own hand together with the witnesses.

I, Irmina, have reread and subscribed.

Basinus, bishop.  
Radobertus.  
Dagoinus.  
Leodoinus, priest.  
Gaucebertus.  
Caribertus.  
Magnobertus.  
Quitario.  
Trasebertus.  
Waltarius, deacon.  
Bobo.

[Note: We publish this according to the fidelity of a copy from the Echternach cartulary in our archives.]

### III. Charter by which Aengilbaldus grants to Bishop Willibrord whatever belongs to him in the estate of Waderlo

[Note: Martenius published it from the Echternach cartulary, *Amplissima collectio*, volume I, column 14; Hontheim reprinted it in *Diplomatic History of Trier*, volume I, page 102, from Martenius. We have nothing to note concerning this charter except that Martenius, carelessly, in the index of contents to the first volume of his extensive collection, confused Aengilbaldus with Aengelbertus. The two are entirely different: this Aengilbaldus is said to be the son of Hildiboldus, whereas Aengelbertus, according to Martenius himself above, column 19, is the son of Gaboertus. The similarity of the names, and the fact that both granted gifts to the same Bishop Willibrord at approximately the same time, provided an opportunity for the error.]

*(Year 704)*

To the truly holy and apostolic father in Christ, Bishop Willibrord, Aengilbaldus, son of the late Hildiboldus, donor, greetings in the Lord.

While each person appears to live in the present age, it is necessary for him to consider how he ought to free his soul from sin and eternal punishment. Therefore I, Aengilbaldus, for the salvation of my soul and everlasting rest, hand over to you, Bishop Willibrord, land at a place or estate called Waderlo, on the river Dutmala, together with everything that I appear lawfully to possess there by hereditary right or through labor. From this present day I hand over and transfer the whole into your power: arable lands with fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, and the woodland belonging to the same place; eight farmsteads with their inhabitants and slaves, and all their property.

All these things I give to you from this present day, and I wish them to be given permanently, so that you may have, hold, and possess them, leave them to your own people to possess, and have entirely free and secure power to do whatever you wish with them.

If anyone—and I do not believe this will happen—whether one of my heirs or descendants, or any opposing person, should attempt to act against this charter of donation and seek to invalidate it, may he first incur the anger of almighty God and of the holy angels, be alienated from the thresholds of the Church, share the portion of Judas, suffer the vengeance of Ananias and Sapphira, or be struck with the leprosy of Gehazi. May he pay to the rights of the treasury one pound of gold and ten *ponda* of silver. Even then may he be unable to establish the claim he makes; rather, may this donation, supported by stipulation, remain firm and immovable forever.

Executed publicly at Bittinum, before witnesses, in the tenth year of the reign of our most glorious lord King Childebert, on the Kalends of October.

I, Aengilbaldus, have reread and confirmed this charter.

Onsbaldus.  
Eburumes.  
Edilhardes.  
Robertes.  
Tolebaldes.  
Etrele.  
Eutlinde.  
Bertlinde.  
They subscribed.

I, Elduynus, priest, at the request of Aengilbaldus, an illustrious man, wrote and subscribed this charter and affixed the sign of the cross +.

### IV. Charter by which Pippin and Plectrudis, his wife, grant to the monastery of Echternach one-half of Echternach itself

[Note: Browerus published a fragment of this charter from an Echternach manuscript, *Annales Trevirenses*, volume I, page 360; Cointius, *Annales*, volume IV, page 446, and Foppens, supplement to Miraeus’s diplomatic works, volume II, page 805, reprinted it. Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, volume I, proofs, column 84; Bertholet, *History of Luxembourg*, volume II, proofs, page 25; and Hontheim, *Diplomatic History of Trier*, volume I, page 103, published the complete charter from the Echternach archive. The name of Plectrudis’s father was unknown before this document appeared, as Eckart notes, *Francia orientalis*, book XVI, no. 25. The other half of Echternach had been granted to Willibrord by Irmina in 698; we presented that charter of donation above, page 250.]

*(Year 706)*

I, in God’s name, Pippin, an illustrious man, son of the late Ansgisilus, and my illustrious wife Plectrudis, daughter of the late Hugobertus, considering the uncertainty of human frailty and how we may wash away our sins and, through the Lord’s gift, attain eternal joys, therefore, for the honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, give and wish to have given permanently to the monastery situated in honor of the most holy Trinity, the apostles Peter and Paul, and Saint John the Baptist, at the place called Echternach, in the district of Bedgau, on the river Sûre, built on our own property.

There we appoint the energetic man and apostolic worshiper of God, lord Bishop Willibrord, together with a company of monks under his community, to live and conduct themselves in holy and regular life. We give one-half of Echternach itself, which the late Duke Theotarius formerly held there, and which afterward his son, the late Theodardus, transferred to us, except for the portion that Ermina held at Echternach; namely, whatever in our half of Echternach from the present day appears to be our possession or donation, with lands, houses, buildings, resident dependents, slaves, *liti*, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, mills, and animals of both sexes, whatever at the present time we possess in that half at Echternach.

With its entire integrity, by our right and donation, we hand over and assign it permanently in God’s name for possession to the right and donation of the aforesaid monastery, to its rectors and successors, and to the entire community residing there, so that in time it may prosper there in increase for our reward. This is on the condition that the monastery shall thereafter always remain under the donation or protection of us or our heirs.

It also pleased us to insert the following: if any of our heirs or relatives, or any foreign or opposing person, should attempt to act against this donation—which we have requested to be made and confirmed as a full and complete donation for the remedy of our souls—and if this charter should be shown to him for rereading, but he should not restrain himself thereafter, may he first incur the anger of God and be made an outsider from the thresholds of the saints. May he pay to the parties of the monastery itself, or to anyone against whom he has brought a lawsuit, twice the value that the property itself shall have attained through improvements at that time. Moreover, together with the associated treasury, may he be compelled to pay ten pounds of gold and twenty *ponda* of silver. May he be unable to establish the claim he makes; rather, may the present donation, like a testament and supported by stipulation, gain firm stability at all times.

Executed publicly at Gaimundas, on the third day before the Ides of May, in the twelfth year of the reign of our lord Childebert, the most glorious king.

[Note: Gaimundae, at the confluence of the Saar and Blies, according to Hontheim; today Gemünd, in German Saargemünd, for us Sarreguemines. Hontheim conjectures that Pippin held here a council of bishops who subscribed this donation.]

Pippin and his wife Plectrudis.  
Drogo.  
Cuchobertus, bishop.  
Garebaldus, bishop.  
Bernarius, bishop.  
Constantinus, bishop.  
Josephus.  
Wintharius, bishop.  
Chariganto.  
Agione.  
Grodobaldus.  
Cardimus.  
Remedius.  
Raimingus, ordered by Pippin and Plectrudis, wrote this, and [signed] for Harduinus.

### V. Charter by which Pippin, son of Ansgisilus, takes the monastery of Echternach under his protection and grants the brothers assembled there permission to appoint an abbot from among themselves after Willibrord’s death

[Note: On the same day on which Pippin granted the Echternach monastery the charter immediately preceding this one, he issued this second charter, which Martenius took from the Echternach cartulary, *Amplissima collectio*, volume I, page 15. Hontheim, *Diplomatic History of Trier*, volume I, page 104, and the collectors of the *Writers of Frankish History*, volume IV, page 683, reprinted it. We publish it more accurately according to a transcript made from the same cartulary, volume II, folio 30 verso and following, called the Golden Book. It was carefully collated in 1784 by D. Colloz, subprior of Saint Agericus of Verdun, and deposited in our archives by D. Tabouillot of the congregation of Saint Vanne. It is fortified by the same subscriptions as the other charter of the same day. Among others, Drogo subscribes; in the cartulary his name is abbreviated as Drgo, but in the printed editions it is incorrectly given as Drodo. Concerning Gaimundas, see note I above.]

*(Year 706)*

Human frailty must always consider unavoidable misfortunes, so that whenever sudden change comes upon us, it may not find in us something to punish but something to crown, according to the Lord’s command: “Give, and it will be given to you”; and: “Give alms, and everything is clean for you.”

Therefore I, in God’s name, Pippin, an illustrious man, son of the late Ansgisilus, and my illustrious wife Plectrudis, daughter of the late Hugobertus, considering the uncertainty of human frailty and how we might wash away our sins and, by God’s gift, reach eternal joys, grant to our lord and father in Christ, the apostolic man Bishop Willibrord, the monastery of Echternach, situated in the district of Bedgau on the river Sûre, which he, by God’s gift, built on our property, and concerning which blessed Willibrord confirmed a testament, so that we might hold it under our protection and that of our heirs.

Therefore it pleased us to confirm this monastery to our apostolic father Willibrord. This we have done in such a way that the brothers there may gather pilgrims and other God-fearing men, so that they may live and conduct themselves there according to holy order.

It likewise pleased us to insert that, when blessed Willibrord has departed from this life, the brothers themselves shall appoint as abbot the person whom they choose from among themselves, on the condition that he appear faithful in all things to our heirs, live there according to holy order, and remain under our protection and defense.

And if anyone who fears God, whether from our party or from among other people, should decide to donate and confirm any of his possessions to this monastery, or whatever, through God’s inspiration, should come to it from donated goods, may it, by God’s favor, prosper for their increase.

If anyone—and we have no belief that this will happen—whether one of our heirs or relatives, or any foreign or opposing person, should wish to act against or violate this confirmation of ours, which we have requested to be made and confirmed out of regard for God or for the remedy of our souls, and if this charter is shown to him for rereading but he refuses to restrain himself thereafter, may he first incur the anger and offense of almighty God, be made an outsider from the thresholds of the saints, and moreover pay to the parties of that place and to the brothers serving there at that time, or to anyone against whom he has brought a lawsuit, twice the value that the property itself shall have attained at that time.

Moreover, together with the associated treasury, may he be compelled to pay ten pounds of gold and twenty *ponda* of silver. May he be unable to establish the claim he makes; rather, may the present confirmation, like a testament and supported by stipulation, acquire firm stability at all times.

Executed publicly at Gaimundas, on the third day before the Ides of May, in the twelfth year of the reign of our lord Childebert, the glorious king.

Pippin and Plectrudis.  
Drgo.  
Chugobertus, Gerbaldus, Bernarius, Constantinus, and Josephus, bishops.  
Winitharius.  
Agione.  
Remedius.  
Ramingus, ordered by Pippin and Plectrudis, wrote this, and [signed] for Harduinus.

### VI. Charter by which Aengelbertus grants gifts to Willibrord in Alfheim, a place in Toxandria

[Note: Martenius published it from the Echternach cartulary, *Amplissima collectio*, volume I, column 16; Foppens, supplement to Miraeus’s diplomatic works, volume III, page 285, and Hontheim, *Diplomatic History of Trier*, volume I, page 105, reprinted it from Martenius. We publish it according to Martenius. This charter is addressed to Willibrord, bishop of Utrecht and abbot of Echternach, as is clear from Willibrord’s own testament, which we shall present in its proper place on page 349, where he mentions the estate of Alfeim in the district of Toxandria as having been donated to him by Engelbertus.]

*(Year 709)*

In the name of Christ, to the most holy and beloved father, lord Bishop W., Aengelbertus, son of the late Gaobertus, donor.

Since laws and rights permit, and it is customary among the Franks, that each person should have free power to do whatever he wishes with his possessions, and since it is necessary for everyone, in view of the uncertain end of this life, to entrust something of his possessions to God’s cause, so that by this he may receive forgiveness for his sins, therefore I, Aengelbertus, for the remedy of my soul and eternal recompense, decided to give something of my possessions to you, lord Father and bishop W., and so I have done.

That is, in the district of Toxandria, at a place called Alfheim, which came to me lawfully by hereditary right from my father: eleven farmsteads, with my hall and farmyard, which I appear at present to possess, together with their slaves and all their property.

All these things, with their complete integrity and appurtenances, I hand over and transfer to you from this present day: houses, farmyards, woods, lands, meadows, pastures, arable land, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, rights of exit and entry, and a *watrischafo*.

[Note: Hontheim interprets *watrischafo* as a fishpond or water reservoir; see note 3, page 284.]

I give all these things to you and wish them to be given permanently, so that you may have, hold, and possess them, leave them to your own people for possession, and have entirely free and secure power to do whatever you wish with them.

If anyone—and I do not believe this will happen—whether I myself, or any of our heirs or relatives, or any foreign or opposing person, should wish to act against or violate this confirmation of ours, which we have requested to be made or confirmed out of regard for God or for the remedy of our souls, and if this charter is shown to him for rereading but he refuses to restrain himself thereafter, may he first incur the anger and offense of almighty God, be made an outsider from the thresholds of the saints, and pay to you, together with the enforcing treasury, five pounds of gold and ten *ponda* of silver. Even then may he be unable to establish the claim he makes; rather, may this donation, supported by stipulation, remain firm and immovable.

Executed publicly at Tilliburgis, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, in the fifteenth year of Childebert, the most glorious king.

And I give you, in the district of Testeventi, on the Meuse, at the place called Birni, one farmstead together with all its property.

I, Virgilius, priest, wrote this.

Aengelbertus.  
Werengatto, his brother.  
Paulus, priest.  
Aldrao.  
Alduino.  
Nargaoto.  
Egisgaro.  
Nanduiano.

## VII. Charter by which Bertilendis, consecrated to God, donates to Bishop Willibrord whatever she possesses from her maternal inheritance in Toxandria

[Note: Martenius published it in *Amplissima collectio*, vol. I, col. 17, from the Echternach cartulary; Hontheim reprinted it in *Historia Trevirensis diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 106. Bertilendis donates her maternal inheritance to Bishop Willibrord, who was at the same time abbot of Echternach. He had already received gifts from Aengilbert, whose charter we published above, p. 280; Aengilbert himself subscribes to Bertilendis’s donation. She was a nun of Cala, as may be inferred from the fact that the charter was issued at Cala. Before 1789, Cala was a famous monastery of virgins not far from Paris. That Bertilendis came from a noble family is clear from the text of the charter itself; in the subscription she is distinguished by the title “illustrious woman.” Although she is called a virgin consecrated to God, she possessed substantial property, part of which she assigns to pious uses. Do not confuse her with Bertilana, first abbess of Cala: the latter had already died eight years before the charter presented here was issued.] (A.D. 710).

In the name of Christ. To the most holy and venerable lord father W., bishop, Bertilendis, daughter of Wigibaldus, consecrated to God, donor.

Whoever wishes to give or assign something of his possessions to God’s cause or to the places of the saints should have this confirmed by a solemn document, so that, through the sequence of its provisions, the faith may be celebrated as valid and approved. Therefore, judging that this ought to be done, and considering the uncertain and fragile condition of this life, I have decided to give you, lord father and bishop, something of my possessions for the remedy of my soul and for the unfading fruit of your prayers; and so I have done. In the county of Texandria, at the place called Hoccascaute, on the river Dudmala, I give you what my mother Oadrada lawfully left me by hereditary right: namely, five holdings, with a hall [Note: By this word, which had not yet occurred in the documents of this collection, everyone undoubtedly understands a house. Hence Eccard, in his commentary on the Salic Law, p. 107, asserts that the *terra salica* discussed in that law—Eccard, 61; Fenerbach, 59; Schilter, 92; Herold, 62—is nothing other than land belonging to the hall, or principal house, of the estate. Although the distinguished Montesquieu approved this opinion, I cannot agree with it. But this is not the place to discuss the matter.] and my farmyard, which I appear presently to possess, together with five dependent persons, and their wives and children.

From this day I give all these things to you, for the increase of my reward, and transfer them from my authority into yours, together with all their property, namely, houses, farmyards, woods, lands, meadows, pastures, and arable land, waters and watercourses, mills, movable and immovable property, with right of entry and exit, and a *watriscafo* [Note: See what was said about this word above, p. 280, note 2. It appears to derive from the Saxon *water* and *scaff*, and, as Hontheim writes, to signify a fishpond or water reservoir.], and six vassals with three girls, and a wood at the place called Hulislaum, and whatever lawfully comes to me there.

At another place called Heopurdum, I give you lands and woods and whatever I appear to possess there from my mother; and I wish this to be given permanently for all time.

If anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself or any of our heirs or relatives, or any outsider or opposing person, should wish to act against or violate this confirmation of ours, which we have requested to be made and confirmed for the sake of divine consideration or the remedy of our souls, and if this charter is shown to him for rereading, and he does not restrain himself thereafter, may he first incur the displeasure of almighty God’s anger, be made an outsider from the thresholds of the saints, and pay you, together with the enforcing fisc, five pounds of gold and ten pounds of silver. Even then may he not be able to vindicate what he claims; rather, may this donation of ours remain firm and unshaken, supported by formal stipulation.

Publicly enacted at Cala, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, in the sixteenth year of the reign of our lord Childebert, most glorious king, with Ansbaldus, Folebaldus, Aengelbertus, Robertus, Adlefus, Werengatus, Nanduino, and Wigbertus as witnesses.

I, Laurentius, priest, at the request of Bertilendis, an illustrious woman and virgin consecrated to God, wrote and subscribed this.

## VIII. Charter by which Ansbaldus, a monk, bestows gifts on Bishop W. (Willibrord)

[Note: Martenius extracted it from the Echternach cartulary, *Amplissima collectio*, vol. I, col. 18; Hontheim reprinted it, on Martenius’s authority, in *Historia Trevirensis diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 107. Ansbaldus appears to have been the brother of Bertilendis, the nun whose charter we reprinted above, p. 284, daughter of Vigibaldus, who is here called Ansbaldus’s father. We shall present another charter of the same Ansbaldus below, p. 291, by which he bestows new gifts on the same Willibrord. These documents confirm that at that time it was customary for persons consecrated to God to enjoy their ancestral property and that they were permitted to give it away.] (A.D. 711).

In the name of Christ. To the most beloved and holy father W., bishop, Ansbaldus, monk, son of the late Wigibaldus, donor.

The laws and rights permit, and it is customary among secular persons, that each individual should have free power over his own possessions to do whatever he wishes, and that this should be confirmed by a solemn document in accordance with the passage of time. Since this is so, I, Ansbaldus, weighing in my mind the frailty of the present life, have considered giving and assigning to you something of my possessions for the remedy of my soul and as the profit of your prayers; and so I do.

This is what I give you in the place called Haeslaos, in the county of Texandria, on the river Dudmala: everything in its entirety that my late father Wigibaldus left me by hereditary right, or whatever I appear to have lawfully cultivated there; namely, houses, farmyards, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, with a *watriscapo* [Note: The same as *watrischafo*; see note 2, p. 280.], arable land, movable and immovable property, together with the dependents residing there, ten servants, *gafergarias* [Note: Hontheim, in the passage cited above, interprets *gafergarias* as orchards; *hochofinnas* perhaps means high tree-groves, or perhaps marshes.], and *hochofinnas*, with right of entry and exit, with all appurtenances.

From this day I give all these things to you, and wish them to be given permanently for all time. Have, hold, possess, and defend them, and leave them to your successors to possess; and whatever you wish to do with them, may you have free power in every respect.

If anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself or any of our heirs or relatives, or any outsider or opposing person, should wish to act against or violate this confirmation of ours, which we have requested to be made and confirmed for the sake of divine consideration or the remedy of our souls, and if this charter is shown to him for rereading, and he does not restrain himself thereafter, may he first incur the displeasure of almighty God’s anger, be made an outsider from the thresholds of the saints, and pay you, together with the enforcing fisc, five pounds of gold and ten pounds of silver. Even then may he not be able to vindicate what he claims; rather, may this donation of ours remain firm and unshaken, supported by formal stipulation.

Publicly enacted at the monastery of Suestra, in the first year of King Dagobert, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November. [Note: By the unanimous agreement of the chroniclers, the death of Childebert, succeeded by Dagobert, is assigned to the year 711, as Longuerue notes, *Annales Francici*, at the end of vol. III of the *Collectio scriptorum rerum Francicarum*, p. 697. The day is supplied by the Chronicle of Saint-Médard, in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 783: namely, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, 14 April.]

I, Laurentius, an unworthy priest, wrote this at the request of Ansbaldus, servant of God.

## IX. Charter by which Ansbaldus the monk bestows new gifts on Bishop Willibrord in the county of Toxandria

[Note: In the opening formula Ansbaldus is named, but in the body of the charter he is called Ansbertus, son of Willibaldus. The reading should certainly be Ansbaldus, son of Wigibaldus, brother of Bertilendis, daughter of Wigibaldus. Martenius, *Amplissima collectio*, vol. I, col. 19, correctly prefixed this charter with Ansbaldus’s genuine name. He extracted it from the monastery of Echternach.] (A.D. 712).

In the name of Christ, to the most holy and blessed father Willibrord, Ansbaldus, servant of the servants of God.

While each person appears to live in the present world, he ought to consider how he may acquire here the consolation of his soul through almsgiving to holy places or through the assistance of prayers, as the Lord says: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.” And again: “Just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin.”

Therefore I, Ansbertus, son of the late Willibaldus, give, for the remedy of my soul and in return for eternal salvation and for your prayers, to you, lord father and bishop, something of my own possessions in the county of Texandria, at the place called Diesne: six holdings with a hall, and my farmyard with six dependent persons and their children. I transfer these to you with all their property and in their entirety: houses, farmyards, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, and arable land, movable and immovable property, with right of exit and entry, and a *vatriscafo* [Note: Hontheim interprets *watriscafum*, *Historia Trevirensis*, vol. I, p. 107, note, as a fishpond or water reservoir. See pp. 280 and 289, note 2.].

Likewise, in the county of Texandria, at the place called Levetlaus, on the river Dutmala, I give you seven holdings with a hall and my farmyard, with eight dependent persons and their wives and children, together with houses, farmyards, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, and arable land, movable and immovable property, with right of entry and exit.

But if anyone … [Note: Martenius notes that what is missing there should be supplied from the preceding charters. See the charter of the same Ansbaldus, p. 289.]

Publicly enacted at Waderloe, on the Kalends of June, in the second year of King Dagobert.

I, Ansbaldus the monk [Note: Whether Ansbaldus was truly a monk is uncertain. In the preceding charter, while calling himself a monk, he says that he uses the rights of secular persons. The word *monk* was sometimes used for a cleric. Hence our note appended to the preceding charter may perhaps need correction. In my opinion, the distinguished scholar does not resolve the question more successfully in his prolegomena, part III, section 1, chapter 2, § 3.], reread this charter made by me and subscribed it with my own hand.

## X. Charter by which Aengelbertus donates to W. (Bishop Willibrord) what he possessed in the county of Texandria, at Eresloch and at Osne

[Note: Martenius published it, *Amplissima collectio*, vol. I, col. 19, from the Echternach cartulary; Hontheim reprinted it, *Historia Trevirensis diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 168. See another charter of the same Aengelbertus, which we presented above, p. 280, by which other gifts are bestowed on the same Willibrord; see also the notes appended to it. We follow Martenius’s reading, from whom Hontheim borrowed the charter. Hontheim appears, through a typographical error, to write Aegelbertus for Aengelbertus. A double donation by Aengelbertus is remembered in Willibrord’s testament, to be published below, p. 349, though the place-names are somewhat corrupt, as we shall note in connection with that testament.] (A.D. 713).

In the name of Christ, to the most holy and beloved father W., bishop, Aengelbertus, son of the late Gaobertus, donor.

Since the laws and rights permit, and it is customary among the Franks, that everyone should have free power over his possessions to do whatever he wishes, and since it is necessary that anyone, in view of the uncertain outcome of this life, should entrust something of his possessions to God’s cause, so that through this he may receive pardon for his sins, therefore I, Aengelbertus, with the counsel and permission of my brother Verengaotus, have decided to give you, lord father and bishop, something of my possessions for the remedy of his soul and in return for eternal reward; and so I have done.

This is what I give: in the county of Texandria, at Eresloch, what has lawfully come to me by paternal right, namely, three holdings, with a hall and my farmyard, which I appear presently to possess; three dependent persons with their wives and children; and, at Osne, one holding and one dependent person, with his wife and children.

From this day I hand over and transfer all these things to you, together with all their property, entirety, and appurtenances, namely, houses, farmyards, woods, lands, meadows, pastures and arable land, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, right of exit and entry, and a *watriscafo*. I give all these things to you and wish them to remain given permanently for all time.

If anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself or any of our heirs or relatives, or any outsider or opposing person, should wish to act against or violate this confirmation of ours, which we have requested to be made and confirmed for the sake of divine consideration or the remedy of our souls, and if this charter is shown to him for rereading, and he does not restrain himself thereafter, may he first incur the displeasure of almighty God’s anger, be made an outsider from the thresholds of the saints, and pay you, together with the enforcing fisc, five pounds of gold and ten pounds of silver. Even then may he not be able to vindicate what he claims; rather, may this donation of ours remain firm and unshaken, supported by formal stipulation.

Publicly enacted at Osne, on the Kalends of March, in the second year of the reign of our lord Dagobert, most glorious king.

I, Aengelbertus, reread this charter made by me and confirmed it with my own hand, in the presence of the witnesses: my brother Verengaotus, Volebaldus, Framundus, Aeumlaus, Adlefus, and Nandinus.

I, Docfa, priest, at the request of the illustrious man Aengelbertus, wrote and subscribed this charter.

## XI. Charter by which Duke Pippin, with his wife Plectrude, donates the monastery of Suestra to Bishop Willibrord

[Note: This instrument, taken from the Echternach archives, has often been published: by Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica*, vol. III, p. 286; Martenius, *Amplissima collectio*, vol. I, col. 20; Hontheim, *Historia Trevirensis diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 109; Calmet, *Historia Lotharingica*, vol. II, proofs, p. 89; Bertholet, *Historia Luxembur gensis*, vol. II, proofs, p. 27; and in the *Collectio scriptorum rerum Francicarum*, vol. IV, p. 689. Browerus mentions it, *Historia Trevirensis*, vol. I, p. 361, and testifies that he read it in the monastery of Echternach. We reprint it from a copy preserved in our archive and carefully collated with the Echternach cartulary called the Golden Book, fol. 36 verso, written at the end of the twelfth century. This charter shows that Pippin of Herstal, after dismissing Alpais, had shortly before his death been reconciled with his wife Plectrude, or Blictrude. See above, pp. 213 and 246. Pippin died toward the end of 714, the year in which this charter itself was issued. The monastery on the little river Suestra had already been founded for several years, whence it was called Suestrense; above, p. 289, we published the charter of a certain Ansbaldus, said to have been issued in the first year of Dagobert at the monastery of Suestra. This monastery, situated in the duchy of Jülich, was later converted into a collegiate house of noble canonesses; see the *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. III, p. 996. The negligence of the cartulary scribe should be noted: he sometimes calls Pippin’s wife Blictrude or Blittrude, and sometimes, more correctly, Plectrude.] (A.D. 714).

I, Pippin, in the name of God, an illustrious man, son of the late Ansgisilus, and my illustrious wife Blictrudis, daughter of Hugobertus, considering, out of reverence for the fear of God and for the remedy of our souls, that we ought to build anew an oratory and cell in honor of the Savior, the saints Peter and Paul, the other apostles, and the relics of the saints, at the little estate of Suestra, situated in the county of the Mosarians on the little river Suestra—which Blictrudis purchased for a price from Albericus and Hadericus—we have done so, and have assigned that estate itself to the cell.

It pleased us to hand over that basilica to the apostolic father, Bishop Willibrord; and so we have done, on the condition that he should gather there foreign brothers and others who fear God.

We also wished this to be inserted: when Willibrord himself has departed from this light, the brothers shall choose from among themselves whomever they wish and appoint him abbot, on the condition that he appear faithful in every respect to us, to our son Grimoaldus and his sons, and to the sons of Drogo, our grandsons; that he live there according to the rule of holiness; and that he remain under the protection of our *mundeburdium*, of Grimoaldus and his sons, and of the sons of Drogo, our grandsons.

If any person who fears God, whether from our side or from among other people, should give them something of his possessions, may it, by God’s favor, contribute to their increase.

If anyone—which we scarcely believe will happen—whether one of our heirs or successors, or any opposing person, should attempt to act against this charter of donation and try to violate it, may he first incur the anger of almighty God and of the holy angels, be excluded from the thresholds of the Church, share the lot of Judas and the punishment of Ananias and Sapphira, or be struck with the leprosy of Gehazi. Moreover, may he be compelled to pay to the rights of the fisc one pound of gold and ten pounds of silver. Even then may he not be able to vindicate what he claims; rather, may this donation remain firm and stable for all time.

Publicly enacted at the village of Bagoloso, on the second day of March, in the fourth year of the reign of our lord Dagobert, king.

Since, because of illness, we could not write in the charter itself, we requested our wife Blittrudis and gave her authority to confirm it in our place; and she did so. We also requested those who would subscribe or sign it in the present matter.

Blittrudis.  
Blendumen, abbess.  
Helmoinus.  
Remigius.  
Chrodoaldus.  
Geraldus and Adalbertus, abbots.  
Chammingo, count.  
Crodegerus.

I, Adricharius, at the command of my lords Pippin and Plectrude, wrote and subscribed this donation.

## XII. Charter by which Duke Hedenus bestows gifts on Willibrord, an apostolic man

[Note: It appears in Martenius, *Amplissima collectio*, vol. I, col. 22, and in Bertholet, *Historia Luxembur gensis*, vol. II, proofs, p. 28, from the Echternach cartulary; also in Eckard, *Francia orientalis*, vol. I, p. 323; Calmet, *Historia Lotharingica*, vol. II, proofs, p. 110; and Hontheim, from Martenius. We reprint it on Martenius’s authority; Bertholet’s variant readings in *Historia Trevirensis diplomatica*, vol. II, p. 111, are supplied in brackets. On Hedenus, see what we said in our notes to another charter of his, p. 263, by which he gave other gifts to the same Willibrord in A.D. 704.] (A.D. 716).

I, Hedenus, in the name of God, an illustrious man and duke, give from this day, for fear of God and the increase of my reward, and wish this to be given permanently, to the lord and father in Christ Willibrord, in the district belonging to Hamulo Castle, where I also intend [main text: *et*; Bertholet: *etiam*], by God’s mercy and through the counsel of that apostolic man, to build a monastery, on the western side, on the river Sala, in the county of Salvense: fields as well as meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, the very possessions which my father and mother [Bertholet: *mea*, “my”] left to me, together with eight male and female servants, as much as I appear to possess there. I hand over and transfer everything in its entirety, so that he may have free power in every respect to do whatever he wishes with it.

If anyone—which I do not believe will happen—etc.

Publicly enacted at Hamulo Castle, in the first year of King Chilperic, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May.

Cato, count.  
Sigericus, count.

I, Hedenus, an illustrious man and duke, wished the donation [Bertholet: “this donation”] to be made and subscribed it, together with my wife Theodrada.

Ado, Hedenus’s foster-father, and Tiringus, Hedenus’s son [these four words are absent in Bertholet].  
Adogoto [Bertholet: Adagelo].  
Herericus.

I, Richisus [Richarius], a cleric, having been asked, wrote and subscribed this.

## XIII. Charter by which Duke Arnulfus, son of Duke Drogo, donates to the monastery of Echternach whatever came to him from his father in the village of Bollane

[Note: Published by Martenius, *Amplissima collectio*, vol. I, col. 21, and Bertholet, *Historia Luxembur gensis*, vol. II, proofs, p. 27, from the Echternach archive; by Calmet, *Historia Lotharingica*, vol. II, proofs, col. 89; and by Hontheim, *Historia Trevirensis diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 110, from Martenius. We reprint it according to Martenius’s reading, supplying in parentheses the differences found in Bertholet. Duke Arnulfus, who was the son of Duke Drogo and brother of the priest Hugo, is mentioned in a charter of that same Hugo, which we published above, p. 301, and which we condemned with Cointius as false. We also presented Arnulfus’s own charter for the year 706, p. 275, which we judged to be of no better quality. But there is no indication of falsity in the charter now presented that would permit us to declare it spurious. Indeed, this charter agrees with another, which we publish next, issued by Charles, son of Pippin and grandson of Drogo. In that charter Charles donates to the monastery of Echternach the portion of the same village of Bollana that had come to him by hereditary right; Arnulfus, his paternal uncle, grants his portion to the same church in the instrument under discussion. The first year of the reign of Chilperic III extends from June of A.D. 715 to June of A.D. 716.] (A.D. 716).

In the name of the Lord our God Jesus Christ. I, Arnulfus, duke, son of the late Duke Drogo, for the remedy of my soul and eternal reward, give by this charter of testament to the monastery of Echternach [Bertholet: Epternach], which is built in honor of the saints Peter and Paul on the river Sura, where W. [Bertholet: Willibrord] appears to preside as bishop, in the village of Bollane, namely houses, homesteads, fields, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses, and the dependent persons residing there, as much as legally came to me in the village [Bertholet: that very village] of Bollane. I give and hand over my portion in its entirety, so that from this day the monks may possess the property [Bertholet: have, hold, and possess it] and leave it to their successors to possess.

(If anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether we or any of our heirs, or any opposing person, should attempt to act against this testament or wish to alter it, may he first be excommunicated by Saints Peter and Paul, and moreover pay the fisc two pounds of gold and a weight of silver and bronze (*argenti pondus aeris*; the wording is materially uncertain); and may he not be able to vindicate what he claims [Note: The words enclosed in parentheses are absent in Bertholet].)

And so that this testament [Bertholet: “my testament”] may remain firm and stable at the holy place, we subscribe it with our own hand and have requested the witnesses who would subscribe or sign it in the present matter, with formal stipulation.

Publicly enacted at the castle of Bedense [Bertholet: Bedeese], in the first year of King Chilperic [Bertholet: of our lord King Chilperic].

## XIV. Charter by which Charles, son of Pippin, grants to the monastery of Echternach whatever he possesses at Bollumvilla

[Note: We publish this previously unpublished charter from a copy made by Dom Colloz from the Echternach cartulary called the Golden Book and deposited in our archive. The year is not stated, but the copyist prefixed A.D. 717, perhaps on the authority of that cartulary. Certainly the charter can be connected with this year quite suitably: Charles, son of Pippin, had already been deprived of his father when he issued it; Pippin died in 714. In 715 Charles was, by divine assistance, released from the custody into which his stepmother had thrown him, and not long afterward he seized her treasures. It may therefore be conjectured with sufficient probability that at the beginning of 717 Charles granted to the church of Saints Peter and Paul—that is, to Echternach—the part of his ancestral inheritance that had come to him at Bollumvilla. This place appears to be the same as Bollana, whose other part had passed from the paternal inheritance to Arnulfus, Charles’s paternal uncle, namely Pippin’s brother, and which we have seen him grant to the same church above, p. 310. [The learned man appears to have fallen into error: Arnulfus was not Charles’s uncle; rather, Charles was Arnulfus’s uncle, namely the brother of Drogo, whose son Arnulfus was. This Arnulfus was not Pippin of Herstal’s brother, but his grandson.]] (A.D. 717).

In the name of God, Charles.

For divine consideration, for eternal reward, and for the remedy of my soul, I give to the churches of Saint Peter and Saint Paul and their companions the villa called Bollumvilla or Bolluntorf, as much as came to me there from my father Pippin, which I received *contra allodiones meos* (“against my allodial lands/holders”; the phrase is materially uncertain). I give and transfer everything in its entirety: lands, woods, fields, meadows, dependent persons, churches, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, everything in its entirety, as much as came to me there.

This is on the condition that from this day the church shall have, hold, and possess the property, or whatever it wishes to do with it, and shall have free and most secure power in every respect. If I myself, or any of my heirs or successors, or any opposing person, should attempt to act against this donation or testament, or wish to alter it, may he first be excommunicated by Saint Peter and Saint Paul and their companions, and incur the anger of God. Moreover, may he be compelled to pay those churches and the fisc one pound of gold and two pounds of silver, and may he not vindicate what he claims; rather, may this donation remain firm and inviolate at all times, supported by formal stipulation.

Publicly enacted at the villa called Fidiacus, on the twenty-third day of February.
