## XV. Charter by which Charles, mayor of the palace, bestows gifts on the monastery built within the walls of the fortress of Traiectum

[Note: Published by William Heda, *Historia Ultrajectina*, p. 28; reprinted on his authority by Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 491; Cointius, *Annales*, vol. IV, pp. 683 ff.; and the collectors of the *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. IV, p. 697. Mabillon notes it, *Annales*, vol. II, p. 69. Charles, in royal fashion, claimed the title “illustrious man,” though with the order of the words reversed: here he is called *illuster vir*, and later mayors of the palace are described in the same way. The authors of the *Nouvelle Diplomatique*, vol. IV, p. 616, thought this worth observing. Certainly Pippin, while mayor of the palace, was called *illuster vir*; when he assumed the title of king, he was called *vir illuster*. Cointius observes, in the passage cited above, that Ebroin repeats his chronological formulas not from the years of his mayorship but from the years of King Theuderic. The church mentioned in this charter, as Cointius notes above, p. 335, is the church of Traiectum itself, which Willibrord founded in A.D. 697.] (A.D. 722).

I, Charles, in the name of God, an illustrious man and mayor of the palace, son of the late Pippin, considering the fall of human frailty and how I may wash away my sins and, with God’s gift, attain eternal joys, therefore from this day, by this page of testament, we give and wish to be given permanently the following:

To the monastery situated within the walls of the fortress of Traiectum, built there, where the apostolic man D., our father in Christ, Willibrord, archbishop, appears to preside as guardian under the coenobitic rule of holy conduct, we give every property under the jurisdiction of the fisc—whatever appears presently to belong to the fisc in that fortress of Traiectum, both within the walls and outside them—with all its appurtenances and dependencies, including the pasture called Graveningo, and everything else belonging there to the fisc, all and in every respect, in its entirety, with every acquired and investigated right.

Likewise, the villa or fortress called Fethna, situated in the county of Insterlaco, with all its right and legal integrity, and all its appurtenances and dependencies—whatever appears to belong or pertain either to that villa and fortress of Fethna or, as we have said, to the aforesaid fortress of Traiectum—with all their entirety and whatever can be said or named: namely, homesteads, lands, houses, dwellings, buildings, resident inhabitants, *luiti* [Note: The same people who in other documents are called *liti* or *lidi*; see note 2, p. 273.], dependent persons, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, herds with shepherds of both kinds and sexes, movable and immovable property, all and in its entirety, as we have said.

From this day we hand over and assign everything to that monastery and to that house of God, permanently, in God’s name, for possession, so that it may at all times contribute there to our reward and increase.

Whatever the fathers or rectors of the aforesaid monastery decide to do with it for their needs, may they have free and most secure power in every respect.

If anyone—which we do not believe will happen—whether we ourselves, or any of our heirs or successors, or any opposing or foreign person, should attempt to act against or violate this donation, which we have decided should be made and confirmed in the manner of a testament for divine consideration and the remedy of our souls, may he first incur the anger of heavenly God and be made an outsider from the thresholds of the saints and from the fellowship of Christians. Moreover, may he be compelled to pay, together with our associate fisc, five pounds of gold and ten pounds of silver; and may he not be able to vindicate what he claims. Rather, may this donation, made by me in the manner of a testament, remain firm and stable at all times, supported by formal stipulation.

Publicly enacted at Heristall, a royal villa, on the Kalends of January, in the second year of the reign of the glorious lord King Theuderic.

The sign of the illustrious man Charles, mayor of the palace, who requested that this donation be made and confirmed.  
The sign of Charles’s son, Carloman.  
The sign of Gariao.  
The sign of Odo.  
The sign of Baldric.  
The sign of Abbo.  
The sign of Engilbald.

## XVI. Charter by which Charles, mayor of the palace, donates the villa of Eliste to Bishop Willibrord and the basilica of Saint Savior at Utrecht

[Note: Published by William Heda, *Historia episcopatus Ultrajectini*, p. 30; reprinted by Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 492; Cointius, *Annales*, vol. IV, p. 741; and the collectors of the *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. IV, p. 705, all from Heda. Cointius observes that in this instrument Charles neither claims the title “prince of the Franks” nor reckons the chronological formulas from the years of his mayorship, but from the years of the reign of Theuderic IV. Add that Charles is called *inluster vir*, not *vir inluster*, as was customary with the kings of the Franks; since we have already noted this above, p. 334, it is permissible to think that it did not happen accidentally.] (A.D. 726).

I, Charles, in the name of God, an illustrious man and mayor of the palace, son of the late Pippin, considering the fall of human frailty and how I may wash away my sins and, with God’s gift, attain eternal joys, therefore from this day I hand over by this page of testament [Note: Regarding this word, see the charter of testament that I wrote above, p. 329], for the redemption of my soul, and wish it to be given permanently, at the place called Marithaime, where there was a fortress, to the basilica built in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and of blessed Mary, Mother of God, and also of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, of all the apostles, and of Saint John the Baptist and the other saints—which is known to have been built in the county of Batavia—the villa of our right called Eliste, at that same place of Marithaime.

This is as much as Everhardus had or possessed there when he appeared faithless to the king, joined the enemies of the king of the Franks in exile from his country, and, because of this, all his property was transferred into the royal fisc. The glorious King Childebert granted these possessions from his fisc and as a gift of his generosity to our father Pippin; and my father Pippin granted the aforementioned villa Eliste to me as hereditary property.

This villa, also called Marithaime, includes everything that the aforesaid Everhardus possessed there, together with homesteads, lands, houses, dwellings, woods, fields, dependent persons of both sexes, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, and movable and immovable property—in its entirety.

All these things we hand over to the aforesaid church, together with whatever Everhardus had or possessed in Batavia, on the condition that lord Bishop Willibrord receive the aforesaid possessions into his right and dominion and that of his successors, in God’s name, for possession, so that they may at all times contribute there to increase for the remedy of my soul.

If anyone—which I do not believe will happen—should wish to make any unjust claim against this charter of transfer, may he first incur the anger of almighty God, be made an outsider from the thresholds of God’s holy Church, and be anathematized and accursed with the same curse that descended upon Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive. May he not be able to vindicate what he claims; rather, may this present transfer, made by us in the manner of a testament, remain firm and stable at all times, supported by formal stipulation.

Acted at the public castle of Tulpiac, in the month of July, on the ninth day, in the sixth year of the reign of the glorious king of the Franks, Theuderic. The mark of Charles, illustrious man, who made this conveyance and requested that it be confirmed. The mark of Count Salecon. The mark of Count Folcar. The mark of Count Bergetesio. The mark of Count Maginharius. The mark of Luidolf. The mark of Odo. The mark of Agilo. The mark of Count Heriger. The mark of Count Erkenfrid, who was the bishop’s advocate and who, together with his lord, received this conveyance in his own hand.

[Note: Up to this point I have found no charter of donation in which mention is made of acceptance by the recipient.]

Aldo, cleric, ordered by my lord Charles, wrote and subscribed this charter of testament, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

## XVII. Charter by which Rohingus and his wife Bebelina donate to Bishop Willibrord the church of Saints Peter and Paul at Antwerp

[Note: Miraeus published this in *Opera diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 10, from the archive of Echternach; from Miraeus it was reproduced by Cointius, *Annales*, vol. IV, p. 742. Hontheimius, *Historia Trevirensis diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 114, and Bertholetus, *Historia Luxembourgensis*, vol. II, proofs, p. 32, reprinted it, omitting the curse against violators. Rohingus is also written Rauchingus, as Miraeus observes; that is how it is read in Hontheimius. The church of Saints Peter and Paul, which is at issue here, is situated, according to Miraeus, in the old town or borough of Antwerp, not far from the bank of the Scheldt. The gift bestowed upon Willibrord by this charter is mentioned in Willibrord’s testament, which we shall publish immediately below, p. 349.]

*(A.D. 726.)*

We believe that we shall acquire the rewards of merit if, for the redemption of our sins, we confer something from our possessions upon the priests of God. Therefore I, Rohingus, in the name of God, and my wife Bebelina, give to the apostolic lord and our father, Bishop Willibrord, and wish this gift to remain permanent forever: namely, the church that has been built within the fortress of Antwerp, on the river Scheldt, which Bishop Amandus built in honor of Saints Peter and Paul, the chief apostles, and of the other saints.

In exchange for this church, and for whatever appears to belong to it, we gave to the venerable man Firminus, abbot of the monastery of Quorcolodora, our little estate called Tumme. And from the present day onward we give and convey to the aforesaid lord Willibrord the aforesaid church, together with its lands, houses, buildings, residents, male and female slaves, holdings, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, appurtenances and dependencies belonging to it there, mills, flocks with their shepherds, movable and immovable property, acquired and unacquired property—in its entirety, everything that can be said or named, whether from the dowry or from what was purchased, or from any property known to have come to us.

We also granted and donated to him in full that toll which had come there to our share, namely, the entire third part, on the condition that incense or lamps should be provided there and that the priests who serve there should entreat the Lord’s mercy for our sins. And so that the aforesaid lord Willibrord may have, hold, and possess that church, whatever appears to belong to it there, and that toll, he shall have in all matters free and most secure power to give it, exchange it, or do with it whatever he wishes.

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether one of my heirs or those claiming through my heirs, or any opposing person, should attempt to come against this charter of donation and endeavor to invalidate it, let him first incur the wrath of almighty God and of the holy angels; let him be excluded from the thresholds of the Church; let him share the lot of Judas; and let him be struck with the punishment of Ananias and Sapphira or with the leprosy of Gehazi. Moreover, let him pay to the treasury two pounds of gold and five pounds of silver; nor, if he makes any claim, let him be able to establish it. Rather, let this donation remain firm and unaltered for everlasting ages, confirmed by formal stipulation.

This was publicly enacted at Weimodo, a royal estate, when October had completed twenty days, in the sixth year of the reign of King Theuderic.

[Note: The royal estate of Weidomus, where this charter is said to have been issued, is known only from this document, as D. Germain admits in his treatise on royal estates, which may be consulted in Mabillon’s often-cited work *De re diplomatica*, at the end of Book IV, p. 342.]

## XVIII. Testament of Bishop Willibrord, by which he bestows many gifts upon the monastery of Echternach

[Note: Miraeus published this in *Opera diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 11, from the Echternach archive. It was reprinted by Cointius, *Annales*, vol. IV, p. 743; Bertholetus, *Historia Luxembourgensis*, vol. II, proofs, p. 33; Calmetus, *Historia Lotharingiae*, vol. II, proofs, col. 92; and Hontheimius, *Historia Trevirensis diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 115, who asserts that the original of this charter is still preserved at Echternach. In this document several charters recording gifts bestowed upon Willibrord are mentioned. We have given some of them above: that of Pippin, p. 298; of Rohingus, pp. 348 and 349; of Ansbaldus, pp. 289 and 291; of Engelbertus, pp. 280 and 293; and of Hedenus, pp. 263 and 308; of Angilbaldus, p. 265; of Bertilenda, p. 284; of Charles Martel, pp. 334 and 347. The documents of the others do not survive.]

[Col. 0554D]

In the name of Christ. Christians ought to recognize the way of truth, by which they may serve their Creator worthily through their good works, so that the offering of their alms and their devotion may lead to salvation, since he himself, the Most High, says: “Give, and it will be given to you,” and: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.”

Therefore I, Clemens Willibrordus, bishop, in the name of God, considering the frailty of the human condition, how I may wash away my sins, and, with the Lord’s gift, attain everlasting joys, give from the present day onward, and wish this gift to remain forever: namely, to the monastery of Echternach, which has been built over the river Sûre, in the district of Bedgau, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and of Saints Peter and Paul the apostles, and of Saint John the Baptist and the other saints, where I myself, Clemens Willibrordus, appear to preside as guardian and governor, and, if it pleases Christ, where my body is to rest.

This is what I give and convey to that holy place, Echternach: every possession, estate, or slave that freeborn Franks have handed over or donated to me out of their love and for their salvation. Likewise, those possessions that my lord Pippin donated or assigned to me, or his wife, the lady Plectrude, or his son, our lord Charles, mayor of the palace; possessions which the lord Charles and his father Pippin donated for their reward, both while I am alive and when I depart this life.

I also specify some of the other possessions, and the persons who handed them over or assigned them to me, so that this document may solemnly confirm them for the course of time. These are the persons named:

Rohingus donated or conveyed to me a church built in the fortress of Antwerp, on the river Scheldt, in the district of the Rhine-dwellers, together with its dependencies; estates called by these names: Bacwalde, Vinnelincheime, and Furgalare; and in the fortress of Antwerp itself, a third part of that toll.

Heribaldus, cleric, donated and conveyed to me another church in the district of Marsum, where the Meuse enters the sea, with its dependencies, and a marsh from which sheep are born.

Angilbaldus donated or conveyed to me an estate called Wadradoch, in the district of Taxandria, on the river Dutmala.

Ansbaldus donated or conveyed to me his entire portion in the estate called Busloth, in the district of Taxandria.

Berethinda, a woman consecrated to God, donated or conveyed to me her entire portion in the estate of Bobanschot, in the district of Taxandria.

Henricus donated to me property in the estate called Pieplo.

Engelbertus once donated or conveyed to me his entire portion in the estate called Hinesloten, in the district of Taxandria.

Likewise, Engelbertus donated or conveyed to me the estate called Alpheim, in that same district of Taxandria.

Likewise, Ansbaldus, cleric, donated or conveyed to me the estate called Diosna, in the district of Taxandria, on the river Digena.

Thietbaldus donated or conveyed to me a church situated in the estate of Montnahim, which is called Araride, together with its dependencies.

The illustrious man Hedenus donated or conveyed to me his entire portion in the estate called Aimistadi, on the river Wielheo, in the district of the Thuringians.

I, Clemens Willibrordus, hand over and transfer the possessions named and written above to the house of God named above, Echternach, and to the holy congregation of brothers serving God there, on the condition that they shall have full power in every respect to do whatever they decide concerning the aforesaid possessions, so that they may continually increase there for our reward, for that of our lord Charles, mayor of the palace, and for that of the men who handed their possessions over to me.

We also deemed it proper to insert this provision: if any one of my heirs or those claiming through my heirs, or any opposing or foreign person, or any judicial authority, should come against this testament or donation which I, Clemens Willibrordus, bishop, ordered to be made with sound mind, full counsel, and complete devotion; or should wish to bring an action against it or to invalidate it; and if, when this charter has been shown and presented to him for rereading, he should refuse to restrain himself thereafter, let him first incur the wrath of almighty God and of the holy angels; let him be made an outsider from all churches and from the fellowship of Christians; let him share the lot of Judas, who betrayed the Lord, and of Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive. Moreover, let him be compelled to pay with the public treasury ten pounds of gold and fifty pounds of silver, and let him be unable to establish any claim that he makes.

Enacted in the sixth year of the reign of King Theuderic.

[Note: The surname Clemens was bestowed upon Willibrord by Pope Sergius I when he ordained him archbishop and sent him to the Frisian people, as Mabillon reports in *Acta sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, vol. III, p. 565.]

## A.D. 741. Saint Gregory III, Roman pontiff

[Col. 0557]

## Historical Notice on Saint Pope Gregory III

*(From the *Liber Pontificalis*, according to various editions.)*

[Col. 0557A]

[Note 1: Gregory. Gregory III was elected on 16 February 731. He was an excellent pontiff, whom Saint Boniface, the apostle of the Germans, consulted once through legates and once by his own journey to Rome concerning the propagation of the faith among pagans and heretics. — Binius and Labbe.]

[Note 2: Gregory. After 11 February, when, as we have consistently seen, the death of the holy pontiff Gregory II was assigned, the see was vacant for thirty-five days, according to the three Colbertine and Veronese catalogues and all the codices, both ours and the Ambrosian, except the fourth, which, together with the printed editions, the second Freherian copy, and the Cavensis manuscript, gives one month and five days. Pagius wants these witnesses to agree with the others, but he did not observe that, when the month is counted—namely, two days of March plus five days—the sixteenth of that month falls on the consecration, which is unsuitable because it fell on a Friday. On the other hand, because February lacks two days, if thirty-seven days are counted, one arrives at 18 March, namely the Sunday indicated by the letter G, on which Gregory III was ordained; and this occurred in the year of his predecessor’s death, 731.

“Since I saw that thirteen days had to be removed either from the interregnum or from the period during which Gregory sat, I long hesitated whether, following the fifth and seventh catalogues, I should make the interregnum twenty-two days and say that Gregory was ordained on 4 March—for the period of the pontificate, which most codices and catalogues give as ten years, eight months, and twenty-four days, is wonderfully completed on 28 November 741, the day of his death—or whether, with Pagius, following the catalogue of Regino, I should count eleven days as belonging to the see, out of the twenty-four days.

“But when I saw that no historical record was opposed to removing those thirteen days wherever they might be removed, and moreover observed that they were counted inconsistently—for one finds them variously given as nine, twelve, twenty, twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-four, and twenty-five—I therefore judged that Regino, together with Pagius, should be preferred. It is also relevant that Regino flourished at the beginning of the tenth century, whereas the copyists of the catalogues lived in the twelfth and fourteenth centuries; the seventh catalogue is generally found to be corrupt, while the fifth plainly shows that its copyist did not understand the symbols of the exemplar. For although an interregnum of thirty-five days like this one occurs, one again finds twenty-two days.”

“Since this is so, Gregory III was therefore, on account of the restoration of the churches of Rome and his continued defense of the sacred images, no less memorable than his predecessor. While he was attending his predecessor’s funeral as an act of service, he was elected, as Anastasius says, by all who were moved by divine inspiration. He was ordained on 18 March, after an interregnum of thirty-five days, in the year 731. He governed the Church in the most turbulent times until the fourth day before the Kalends of December, that is, 28 November, when, as the martyrologies record, he died in the year 741, after having held the see for ten years, eight months, and eleven days. His death was preceded by one month by Charles, mayor of the palace of France. ‘His sons,’ says the Pithoean annalist, ‘Carloman and Pippin, under the pretext of the mayoralty, assume the kingdom of all France and divide it between themselves.’ I gladly establish my chronological point here on account of the outstanding services of the Frankish kings toward the apostolic see, which originated with Pippin, the son of Charles. For the rest concerning Gregory, read the following note on Zacharias. — Cennus.

“Gregory III, son of John, a Syrian, cardinal priest of the Roman Church, reigned under the emperor Leo III the Isaurian for ten years, eight months, and twenty-four days. He was elected on the third day before the Nones of March and consecrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the year 731; by universal consent he entered upon the pontificate. — Ciaconius.”]

Gregory III, a Syrian by nationality and the son of John, sat for ten years, eight months, and twenty days.

[Note: He sat for ten years, eight months, and twenty days. He died in the year 741, on the fourth day before the Kalends of December. Baronius correctly writes in the aforesaid an[...] that he had sat for ten years, nineteen months, and twelve days. — Binius and Labbe.]

[Note: The Lucerne Codex has nine months and twelve days; another copy has twenty-five days; another, eight months and twenty-four days.]

He was a very gentle and exceedingly wise man, adequately instructed in the divine Scriptures, learned in the Greek and Latin languages, retaining all the psalms in order by heart and refined in their meanings through the most subtle practice. His speech, too, was polished in reading; he exhorted all to every good work; he proclaimed salutary teachings to the people with great eloquence; he was an unwavering guardian of the Catholic and apostolic faith;

[Note: Another copy reads “with immutability.”]

continually strengthening the hearts of the faithful by his admonitions. He was a zealous adherent and a most vigorous defender of orthodox faith; a lover of poverty; and, in caring for the needy, solicitous not only through the compassion of his mind but also through the labor of his efforts;

[Note: The Lucerne Codex reads “in providing for the poor.”]

he was also a redeemer of captives, a benefactor of orphans and widows, supplying what was necessary; a lover of religious observance according to Christian discipline; and a lover of those who wished to live religiously and of those who held the fear of God in their hearts.

[Note: The Lucerne Codex adds “and of Christian discipline.”]

[Note: The Lucerne Codex reads “and of those who have” the fear of God.]

[Note: The Lucerne Codex reads “a guide.”]

With God’s favor, he attained the sacred order of the priesthood. The Roman men—

[Note: The Lucerne Codex reads “all the people.”]

—or rather, all the people, from the greatest to the least, moved by divine inspiration, suddenly, when his predecessor had departed from this world,

[Note: “While he was before the bier,” etc. Gregory’s knowledge of Greek and Latin, his learning in the divine Scriptures, his understanding of the psalms, which he embraced in memory, his eloquence, his devotion to preserving the faith, his courage and constancy, his exceptional wisdom and gentleness, his love of poverty, his pious concern for redeeming captives and relieving orphans, widows, the poor, and all the needy, and his inclination toward religious men made him so worthy of the supreme pontificate that, as Anastasius testifies, the Roman men—or rather, all the people, from the greatest to the least—moved by divine inspiration, suddenly seized him by force and elected him to the pontificate when his predecessor had departed from this world, while Gregory was occupied in paying his respects to his predecessor. Frodoardus says the same in his *Fragment on the Roman Pontiffs*.

“While attending his father’s funeral, he was snatched from the bier

“and summoned to the highest rule.”

Although Gregory III was elected immediately after Gregory II died, his ordination was nevertheless postponed until 18 March, the thirty-fifth day after his predecessor’s death, because confirmation had to be sought from the exarch of Ravenna. The Roman Church was freed from this servitude after the death of Gregory III, as will be seen in the pontificate of his successor Zacharias.

“From these words of Anastasius and Frodoardus, I also believe that I can reconstruct the form of the letters which the Roman clergy, after electing a pontiff, wrote to the exarch, the judges, the archbishop, and the apocrisiarius of Ravenna. In these letters they reported the election that had taken place and requested its confirmation. The form preserved in chapter 2 of the *Liber Diurnus of the Roman Pontiffs* was not written after the death of Gregory II, for the purpose of requesting confirmation of Gregory III, because Gregory III was elected immediately after his predecessor’s death, while he was occupied in paying his respects to his predecessor, as Anastasius says, or while he was attending his predecessor’s funeral, as Frodoardus writes. The person whose confirmation was requested in those letters, however, had been elected only three days after his predecessor’s death, as the same letters state.

“Moreover, at the time of Gregory’s election, while the see was vacant, the government of the Church was in the hands of the elected pontiff, not in those of the archpriest, archdeacon, and chief of the notaries, as we proved in the case of Benedict II. I therefore believe it likely that this formula—which Papebrochius, in his *Chronological-Historical Attempt*, appended to his dissertation on the pontificate of Gregory II, believing that it had not yet seen the light, reproduces in full—was written long before Gregory III. — Pagius.”]

While he was before the bier, occupied in paying his respects to his predecessor,

[Note: The Lucerne Codex reads “while he had been found there.”]

they seized him by force and elected him to the pontificate.

He lived in the time of the emperors Leo and Constantine, during the persecution which they themselves initiated for the deposition and destruction of the sacred images of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the holy Mother of God, of the holy apostles, and of all the saints and confessors. On behalf of these images, that most holy man, so that they might recover from this and withdraw from their error,

[Note: The Lucerne Codex reads “the same.”]

sent written admonitions,

[Note: “Written admonitions.” At the beginning of his pontificate Gregory considered it his duty to defend the veneration of the sacred images, which was being attacked by the emperors Leo and Constantine. He therefore immediately wrote letters to them, exhorting them to abandon such a perverse opinion. The priest Gregory, who carried the letters, did not dare to deliver them because of fear of the persecution in which the emperor Leo, during that period, drove many bishops, patricians, and people of every kind into exile or handed them over to death. He returned to Rome without accomplishing his mission and brought the letters back intact to the pontiff. For this reason the pontiff received him with the greatest severity and would even have deposed him in a synod held at Rome on the matter, had not the intervention of the fathers of that synod mitigated the pontiff’s anger. He did so, however, on the condition that the same priest Gregory should again go to Constantinople with the same letters. But the emperor ordered him to be detained in Sicily, the writings to be taken away, and him to be sent into exile. Anastasius records all these events. — Pagius.]

established by the authority of the apostolic see, just as his predecessor of holy memory had also sent them, through the priest Gregory.

[Note: The Lucerne Codex reads “according to the force and institution of the apostolic see.”]

Moved by human fear, Gregory did not present the same writings to the emperor. On his return, bringing them with him back to the city of Rome, he disclosed the matter to the most holy pontiff himself, confessing that he had made himself guilty of the offense. The pontiff himself wished, with a severe threat, to deprive him of the priestly order.

[Note: The Lucerne Codex reads “while he was presiding in council”; another copy, “while he resisted.”]

When a council had assembled, however, both the council and the nobles entreated that he not be deposed, but that the same priest rather be subjected to penance. A suitable penance was imposed upon him, and he was sent a second time with the same written letters to the imperial city.

But the wickedly increased policy of those same emperors caused the venerable writings to be detained on the island of Sicily and did not permit them to pass to the imperial city.

[Note: The Lucerne Codex reads “their policy, having been wickedly strengthened.”]

The same bearer was kept in exile for almost an entire year.

Therefore, moved by an even greater ardor for the faith, the pontiff issued a synodal decree while he and the assembly of priests were seated before the most sacred confession of the most holy body of the blessed apostle Peter, together with the same supreme and venerable pope and the archbishops—namely, Antonius, archbishop of Grado,

[Note: Another copy reads “Antoninus.”]

John, bishop of Ravenna,

[Note: Another copy reads “archbishop.”]

together with the other bishops of this part of Hesperia, ninety-three in number,

[Note: One copy lacks “ninety-three.”]

and the priests of this holy apostolic see, with the deacons standing by, together with the entire clergy, the noble consuls, and the rest of the Christian people standing by.

He decreed that if henceforth anyone, despising the faithful practice held by ancient custom and by the apostolic Church, should act against the same veneration of the sacred images—namely, of God, of our Lord Jesus Christ, of his ever-virgin, immaculate, and glorious Mother Mary, of the blessed apostles, and of all the saints—as one who removes, destroys, profanes, or blasphemes them, he should be banished from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and from the unity and structure of the whole Church. All solemnly confirmed this by their subscriptions.

[Note: “Among the other enactments.” Anastasius asserts that the famous encyclical issued by the Roman synod was attached to the other papal decretals. He therefore presupposes the existence of a codex in which the decretal letters of the pontiffs were inserted as evidence, and which was reverently and carefully preserved in the apostolic archives. Indeed, in the age of Pope Gregory I, such a codex was sought in the provinces in order to preserve the strength of faith and discipline. The monk and recluse Secundinus had requested from Gregory the Great a copy of the papal decrees. In replying to him, Gregory says in Book VII, Letter 54, p. 255: “Regarding the ordinations of the pontiffs of the apostolic see, your Charity asks whether anything was added after the blessed man Hormisdas; but know that the ordinations of the bishops were set forth up to the time of Pope Vigilius.” Therefore, whenever more solemn decrees were promulgated by the pontiffs, they were attached, together with the assent and confirmation of whatever synods happened to be held, to the same body or codex of decretals. This is what the present synod decreed. Another example of the same practice is recorded in the *Acts of Leo IV*, where we read: “He also ordered these chapters to be written after the other decrees of the pontiffs in the holy canons, so that in the future they might be preserved inviolate by all.” — Bencinus.]

And among the other enactments they decreed that it should be attached to those of the orthodox pontiffs, their reputable predecessors.

After this aforementioned synodal decree had been completed, he again sent other written admonitions for the raising of the sacred images through Constantine the defender; these were detained in the same way as the earlier ones.

[Note: “He sent other writings,” etc. Adrianus says the same in his letter to the emperor Constantine: “Both Gregories, the Roman pontiffs, were cast into great tribulation during their holy pontificates. They repeatedly admonished your serenity’s grandfather not to permit the venerable images to be thrown down from their position, but their salutary prayers did not move his mind in the least.” — Binius and Labbe.]

They also confined their bearer under the strictest guard for almost an entire year. Later, forcibly taking the writings away from him and threatening him, after such a lengthy period of confinement they sent him back with insults.

For the entire body of this province of Italy likewise unanimously sent petitions to those same rulers for the raising of the images;

[Note: The Lucerne Codex reads “writings of supplication.”]

these too were taken away, like the earlier writings, by Sergius, the patrician and exarch of that island of Sicily.

[Note: The Lucerne Codex adds “and strategos.”]

After being detained for nearly eight months, their bearers were sent back, likewise with insulting abuse.

And once again the lord pope, composing exhortatory letters for the raising of the sacred images mentioned above and for the steadfastness of the orthodox faith, sent them through Peter the defender to the imperial city, both to Anastasius, the usurper of the see of Constantinople, and to the rulers Leo and Constantine.

[Note: The Lucerne Codex reads “to” instead of “who was at.”]

[Note: [Col. 0561D] 1. Here he set up the columns granted to him. He had defended the use of sacred images against Leo in writing, and also confirmed it by deed when he erected in the church of blessed Peter images of great value depicting the Savior, the Mother of God, the apostles, and the holy virgins. BIN. and LABB. 2. Here he confirmed, etc. The most holy pontiff Gregory opposed the emperor’s impiety not only in writing but also by his actions, in the worship of sacred [Col. 0562B] images and the veneration of holy relics. Anastasius adds to what was said above that he magnificently erected images of the Savior and the apostles on one side, and of the Mother of God and the holy virgins on the other, in the basilica of Saint Peter. In the same place he built an oratory, in which he honorably deposited sacred relics gathered from every quarter for veneration, and established that the saints’ feasts should be celebrated daily with sacred offices and Masses by monks serving the Lord there from three monasteries. Finally, he ordered the priest celebrating Mass in that oratory to say the following clause in the canon, after the words “and all your saints”: “Whose solemnity is celebrated today in the presence of your majesty, Lord our God, throughout the whole world.” He had this institution inscribed on stone tablets in the same oratory. But Gregory instituted this specifically for that oratory, and therefore, as Walfridus notes in chapter 22, it is not recorded in the canon that is recited generally. Cardinal Bona, *Liturgical Matters*, book III [Col. 0562D], chapter 11, no. 2, testifies that among the great number of manuscript Missals he examined, he found only one in which these words had been added; it is preserved in the Barberini Library, Codex 1858. Edmund Martene, book I of *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, chapter 4, article 8, no. 16, observes that the Colbert Codex no. 2585, formerly belonging to the monastery of Saint-Denis in France, contains a similar clause. It reads: “And also of those martyrs whose solemn triumph is celebrated today in the presence of your glory.” Moreover, when questioned on this matter by William, abbot of Saint Albans, Innocent III by no means disapproved such or similar additions, as Matthew Paris writes in *The Lives of the Abbots of Saint Albans*. On the canon of the Mass, see what is said under Gelasius. PAGIUS.]

Here he brought six movable onyx columns granted to him by Eutychius the exarch into the church of the blessed apostle Peter. He placed them around the presbytery, before the confession: three on the right and three on the left, beside six other ancient columns matching in *filio* [uncertain technical term]. [Note: [Col. 0561B] Others: *filo*; Codex Luc.: *lithoparias*; others: *philopareas*.] Upon them he placed beams and covered them with the purest silver. [Note: [Col. 0562B] Codex Luc. has: “in which.”] On one side were represented images of the Savior and the apostles, and on the other side those of the Mother of God and the holy virgins. He placed lilies and silver lamps above them, weighing altogether [Note: [Col. 0562B] Codex Luc. has “seven hundred.”] seventy pounds.

[Note: [Col. 0562D] Here he made an oratory. In this oratory the same pontiff honorably placed the relics of all the saints that he could gather throughout the Christian world, [Col. 0563A] because the relics of the saints were being despised by Leo the Iconoclast. BIN. and LABB.]

Here he made an oratory within the same basilica. The more cruelly the impious emperor Leo the Isaurian raged in the East against sacred images and their defenders, the more earnestly Saint Gregory III sought in the West to establish the Catholic doctrine concerning the veneration of the saints by writings and deeds. Once and again, through his envoys, he sent threatening letters to Leo, in order to recall him from heresy and impiety. After convening a synod of ninety-three bishops in the basilica of Saint Peter, he struck the iconomachists with the sword of anathema. On one side of the same basilica he placed images of the Savior and the apostles, and on the other an image of the Mother of God and of the holy virgins, executed with magnificent workmanship. In the same place he built an oratory, in which he honorably deposited relics of the saints gathered from throughout the world for the sake of religious veneration. Among them was the body of blessed Gabinus the presbyter, for whom an altar was established; Sardinia and Corsica sent an annual tribute to it. There was also an altar of blessed Mary ever-virgin, together with her image embracing her Son.

These altars remained in Gregory’s oratory until the time of Pope Eugene III, as attested by a Roman canon who was present when, at Eugene’s command, the ancient altars were demolished and a new one was erected there from its foundations. Since he wished this oratory to be enriched more and more each day by heaven’s assistance, Gregory also decreed that the anniversaries of these saints should be celebrated daily with solemn sacred offices by monks serving God in the Vatican basilica from three monasteries. A priest celebrating the sacred rite in the same oratory was to recite, after the words of the canon “and all your saints,” the following: “Whose solemnity is celebrated today in the presence of your majesty, Lord our God, throughout the whole world.” Anastasius writes this at this point; Walfridus Strabo, a writer of the same period, agrees entirely. In chapter 22 he says that Gregory III, having built an oratory in the basilica of blessed Peter in honor of all the saints, and having established that daily offices and Masses should be celebrated there in their veneration, ordered the priest to say in the canon: “Whose solemnity is celebrated today in the presence of your majesty, Lord our God, throughout the whole world.” Since this belonged specifically to that celebration, it was not entered into the canon that is recited generally.

For since the words instituted by Saint Gregory III were to be said only in the aforesaid oratory by the priest performing the divine service, it plainly follows that nothing was added to or altered in the canon after Saint Gregory the Great. That canon consists of the very words of the Lord, apostolic traditions, and the institutions of the holy pontiffs, as the most illustrious archbishop of Ravenna, Hieronymus Crispi, observes with equal dignity and learning in the second edition of his *Golden Dissertation on the Mysteries of Evangelical Law*, p. 110. This work, first composed for the advancement of that clergy, was twice printed at Rome for the common good. MAFEUS.]

Here he made an oratory within the same basilica, beside the principal arch, on the men’s side, in which [Note: [Col. 0562B] Codex Luc. has “on the side.”] he deposited, in honor of the Savior and his holy Mother, the relics of the holy apostles, all the holy martyrs and confessors, and the perfect righteous who rest throughout the whole world. Their feasts, with vigils, were celebrated daily in due order by the monks serving there [Note: [Col. 0563A] Codex Luc. has “who were present”; others, “who were serving.”] and he established that the Masses of their anniversaries [Note: [Col. 0564A] “Masses of anniversaries.” Masses of anniversaries, or birthdays, are the Masses of the solemn day of their final struggle, because on that day they were born to Christ. Anastasius, under Gregory III: “On the day of their anniversaries,” that is, of the holy apostles and martyrs. The same under Hadrian: “On the anniversary of the pontiff.” Ambrose, sermon 72: “As they say, with the vintage approaching, we prepare the anniversary of his martyrdom.” Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 3: “We make offerings for the dead, for their anniversaries, on the annual day.” ALTASERRA.] should be celebrated in the same place [Note: [Col. 0563A] Codex Luc. has “he established.”], [Note: [Col. 0563A] Codex Luc. omits “in the canon.”] and in the canon of the Mass [Col. 0564A] he added this, to be said by the priest: “Whose solemnity is celebrated today in the presence of your majesty, Lord our God, throughout the whole world.”

[Note: [Col. 0564C] He had this institution inscribed on stone tablets in the same oratory. There he made a *pergula* and bestowed gifts of various kinds. Pope Gregory founded an oratory beside the basilica of blessed Peter, and in it constructed a *pergula*, where he displayed various gifts offered by him. In churches, votive gifts are displayed on a *pergula*. Anastasius below at this point: “And above the same apse three silver crosses, and the other things arranged as ornaments of the *pergula* or for the altar coverings.” Tertullian alludes to this in *Against Valentinus*, chapter 7: “With various *pergulae* built one above another, and each god assigned by as many stairways.” A *pergula* is a place or appendage of a building from which one looks out into the public way. Fulvius, during the Second Punic War, was punished by prolonged imprisonment because he was seen looking from a *pergula* into the forum with a wreath of roses. Pliny, book XXI, chapter 3: “Lucius Fulvius, during the Second Punic War, was said to have looked out from his *pergula* into the forum during the day with a wreath of roses; by authority of the senate he was brought to prison and was not released before the end of the war.” The same author, book XXXV, chapter 10, writes that Apelles displayed painted panels in a *pergula* and hid behind the paintings so that he could hear the judgments of passers-by: “After completing works, he displayed them in a *pergula* for passers-by, and, hiding behind the panel itself, listened for defects that were noticed.” Slaves were also put up for sale in a *pergula*. Plautus, in *Pseudolus*:

“Tomorrow I shall have you yourself carried off in a sack to the *pergula*.”]

He had this institution inscribed on stone tablets in the same oratory. There he made a *pergula* and bestowed gifts of various kinds, namely [Note: [Col. 0564D] Two golden *gabathae*, and five others called *saxicae*. *Gabathae* are hollow dishes of gold, silver, or bronze, in which oil was burned. Anastasius, under Honorius: “He also made four golden *gabathae*, each weighing one pound.” Papias explains the name: “*Gabatha*: a dish, a vessel, as though hollowed out.” Hence Phocas was mocked by the Greens as though, in his madness, he used a *gabatha* instead of a cup. Anastasius, in the *History*: “Phocas held a circus spectacle, and the Greens dared to assail him with insults, shouting: ‘You drank from a *gabatha*; you have lost your senses again.’” There is a certain kind of *gabathae* called *saxicae* or *saxisc ae*. Anastasius, under Benedict III: “One *saxisca* *gabatha* of the purest silver, weighing three pounds.” Perhaps they were called *Saxonicae* because they were found in Saxony, a province of Germany, just as *Saxonicia* is a kind of garment named from the Saxon people. The author of *Questions on Both Testaments*, chapter 127: “Is not the ordinary tunic of a common man, although clean, nevertheless filthy and unlawful for an emperor, and likewise a *Saxonicia* for a senator?” Or because they were sold and made at Rome in the Street of the Saxons. Rome had such a Street of the Saxons, mentioned by Anastasius under Leo IV: “At the very beginning of his pontificate a powerful fire seized the Street of the Saxons.”

Other *gabathae* are called *interrasiles*. Anastasius, under Leo III: “Nine *interrasiles gabathae*, weighing eleven pounds.” They were called *interrasiles* because they were as if scraped smooth, that is, pure and simple, without engraving. The same under Gregory IV: “Five *interrasiles gabathae with their feet.” Thus *interrasile* gold is as though scraped and leveled. Pliny, book XII, chapter 19: “The emperor Vespasian Augustus was the first of all to dedicate in the temples of the Capitol and Peace crowns enclosed in cinnamon and *interrasile* gold.” The same author supports this interpretation in book XVII, chapter 23: “The bark being scraped until it is covered over; hence they also use *rasilem* for something pressed down into a furrow.”

*Gabathae* were made in the form of lions or other beasts. The same author in the same work: “He also has a *saxisca gabatha* in the form of a lion.” Griffins and other beasts were engraved on *gabathae*. Anastasius, under Leo III: “Silver *gabathae* bearing gilded griffins”; and in the same place: “A *saxisca gabatha* in the form of a lion.” *Gabathae* hung in the *pergula* before the altar. Anastasius, under Leo III: “He also made fifteen *gabathae* of the purest gold, set with gems, hanging in the *pergula* before the altar.” The *gabatha* was a kind of dish known to the ancients. Martial, book VII, epigram 47:

“Dishes race past, and platters fly.”]

two golden *gabathae*, five others [Note: [Col. 0564A] Others: *axiscas*.] *saxicae*, and four hanging crosses [Note: [Col. 0564A] Others: “four silver crosses,” etc.]. Likewise [Col. 0565A] ten crosses [Note: [Col. 0565A] Codex Luc. has “similar.”], [Note: [Col. 0565C] Two pairs of gilded *amulae* hanging. Five *fibulatoria*. The subject of arms or *amulae* was treated above. *Fibulatoria* are ecclesiastical garments, such as dalmatics and similar garments fastened with brooches. Anastasius, under Leo IV: “Five larger and smaller *fibulatoria*.” Trebellius Pollio, under Claudius: “Brooched cloaks.” A *fibula* is a fastening made of gold, silver, or bronze, by which garments are secured. In this sense Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*, says that a connective device is applied like a brooch to join parts of speech: “For art has also been applied to the connection of speech like a connecting brooch.” Hence *fibula* came to mean the garment itself fastened with a brooch. Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle of Cassino*, book I, chapter 28: “Also bowls, *humuli*, *boci*, and brooches of the purest gold.” Virgil, *Aeneid* IV:

“A golden brooch fastens beneath the purple garment.”

Valerius Flaccus, *Argonautica* I:

“But now the brooch releases the garments you had gathered.”

Related to these are *campestria*, or *succinctoria*, with which young men girded themselves when exercising in the Campus Martius; hence the name *campestria*. Augustine, *City of God*, book XIV, chapter 16: “And they made for themselves *campestria*, that is, coverings for the genitals; moreover, *campestria* is indeed a Latin word, but it was so called because young men who exercised naked in the field covered their private parts with them. Thus the common people call those who are so girded *campestrati*.” Hence *campestrati* means those wearing *succinctoria*. Liutprand, book VI, chapter 4: “Two boys were brought in naked but *campestrati*, that is, wearing *succinctoria*.] two pairs of gilded *amulae* hanging, five *fibulatoria*, a golden crown with a hanging cross, decorated with gems, above the altar, a golden paten and chalice, a single pair set with gems [Note: [Col. 0565A] Codex Luc. has “prepared.”], [Note: [Col. 0566B] One silver *aquamanile*. An *aquamanile* is a vessel from which water is poured for washing the hands. Anastasius, under Sixtus III: “Silver *aquamaniles*, each weighing eight pounds.” Paul, in the Digest, book III, *On Legacies of Household Goods*: “Water vessels, basins, *aquamanilia*.” Varro, *On the Life of the Roman People*, book II: “We call a little water-pitcher an *aquamanile*, because water is poured from it into a basin.” *Aquamanus*, in Anastasius below, under Leo III: “Two pairs of gilded gold hand-washing vessels.”] one silver *aquamanile*. And an image of the holy Mother of God wearing a golden diadem with gems, [Note: [Col. 0566C] “And a golden necklace with hanging gems.” A *collare* is a necklace of gems, an ornament for women’s necks. Virgil, *Aeneid* I:

“...and around her neck a beaded necklace.”

Ammianus, book XX: “He was ordered to produce a diadem; when he denied ever having possessed one belonging to his wife’s neck or head, he was pressed further.”] and a golden necklace with hanging gems, having six hyacinth earrings [Note: [Col. 0565A] “Six” is absent in another manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0566C] And he covered the front of the altar and the confession with silver strips. *Regulae* are rods of gold, silver, bronze, or iron, from which curtains are drawn before an altar or sacred images. Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book III, chapter 6: “On the journey they deceived many through their trade, selling bronze strips which, colored in some unknown way, imitated the appearance of tested and assayed gold.” In other places Anastasius calls them *regulares*, under Stephen IV: “He also made three silver *regulares* above the curtains through which one enters the altar, where images have been placed on the front.” The same under Hadrian: “At the entrance to the presbytery of the church, where he also made a *regularis* covered with silver, and placed the aforesaid three images above that same *regularis*.” “On the upper curtain, that is, in the middle of the presbytery, he made another *regularis* covered with silver.” The same under Leo III: “Four small silk curtains of *stauracium*, hanging from the *regularis* before the images.” And below: “He also made six silver columns and two *regulares* of the purest silver, weighing together eighty pounds.” The same under Paschal: “He also made before the entrance to the altar a *regularis* covered with silver plates.”]

And he covered the front of the altar and the confession with silver strips, and on three sides of the altar he placed three silver crosses, weighing altogether [Note: [Col. 0565A] Others: twenty-six.] thirty-six pounds. Two silver baskets [Note: [Col. 0566A] Others: six.]. A daily-use silver chalice.

[Note: [Col. 0566D] Five small silver crowns. The golden or silver crowns, or small crowns, were votive gifts frequently offered by the faithful, as below at this point: “And also a small golden crown with a cross hanging above the altar.” *Coronula* is a diminutive of *corona*; the further diminutive of *coronula* is *cornula*. Matthew Paris, under the year 1247: “And a golden *cornula*, commonly called a garland.” From this came the vernacular *cornette*.]

Five small silver crowns, and one silver chalice [Note: [Col. 0566A] Others: golden.] hanging in the apse of that oratory; and above the same apse three silver crosses, and the other things arranged as ornaments of the *pergula* [Note: [Col. 0566A] Others: “or for the covering.”] or for the altar coverings [Note: [Col. 0566A] Mansi: “arranged.”].

[Col. 0567A] [Note: [Col. 0567C] Here, in the church of the holy Mother of God at the Manger, he made around the circuit of the building, above the columns, a *regularis* of lamps, after the model of the church of the blessed apostle Peter. A *regularis* of lamps is a line or row of lamps arranged in order. ALTASERRA.]

Here, in the church of the holy Mother of God at the Manger, he made around the circuit of the building, above the columns, a *regularis* [Note: [Col. 0567B] Codex Luc. has “of lamps.”] of lamps after the model of the church of the blessed apostle Peter. He also made there, in the holy oratory called the Manger, a golden image of the Mother of God embracing the Lord our Savior, [Note: [Col. 0567B] Codex Luc. has “adorned with.”] adorned with various gems and weighing five pounds.

Here he renewed the roof of Saint Chrysogonus the martyr and the vault, or the paintings on the walls; and the silver ciborium, or five arches, weighed altogether [Note: [Col. 0567B] Others: 220.] 220 pounds. There he offered four silver crowns, two *pharacanthara*, one silver paten, one silver chalice, and also altar coverings, as well as [Note: [Col. 0567C] White silk curtains decorated with *blatta*, that is, with a purple border. *Blatta* is the same as purple. Trebellius Pollio, under Claudius: “When his wife asked him to use a single silk cloak of purple, he replied: ‘Far be it that gold threads should be weighed; for at that time a pound of gold was the price of a pound of silk.’ Gregory of Tours, *History*, book II, chapter 38: “Thus he received from the emperor Anastasius the document of the consulship, and in the basilica of blessed Martin he was dressed in a purple tunic and cloak.” ALTASERRA.] white silk curtains decorated with purple, hanging all around.

[Col. 0567B] [Note: [Col. 0567C] He also built beside the same titular church a monastery of the holy martyrs Stephen, Lawrence, and Chrysogonus. There he appointed an abbot and a community of monks, organized to offer praises to God in that titular church by day and by night, after the model of the offices of the church of the blessed apostle Peter. The basilica of Saint Chrysogonus the martyr is a titular cardinal church. In it Gregory III founded a monastery and appointed an abbot and a community of monks to celebrate the divine office day and night, after the example of the church of blessed Peter. From the church of blessed Peter the custom spread to all other secular and regular churches of celebrating the divine offices at their appointed hours, by day and night. These are called the canonical Hours, because the divine offices are recited at fixed times, namely at morning, first, third, sixth, ninth hour, and vespers. Anastasius, under Hadrian: “And in the basilica of blessed Eugenia he newly built from the foundations a monastery of women, and established that they should continually sing praises to God there, namely at first, third, sixth, ninth hour, vespers, and morning.” Augustine, *On Time*, sermon 55: “And therefore I ask you, dearest brothers, rise early for the vigils; above all, gather for terce, sext, and none.” The same, sermon 78, *On Time*: “Yet I ask and admonish you more earnestly, brothers, to strive to rise early for the vigils; come gladly to terce, sext, and none.” Gregory III is likewise remembered below as having restored a monastery beside the Lateran basilica, so that offices might be celebrated there by day and night, after the model of the offices of the church of blessed Peter. Hadrian also established that the canonical Hours should be celebrated in the monastery of Pope Honorius, as in the Lateran Church. Anastasius, under Hadrian: “And he appointed them to celebrate offices in the basilica of the Savior, also called Constantinian, situated beside the Lateran patriarchate, namely the morning hour, first, third, sixth, and also ninth and vespers.” The same is said below to have been established in the monastery of Saint Lawrence. ALTASERRA.]

He also built beside the same titular church a monastery of the holy martyrs Stephen, Lawrence, and Chrysogonus, appointing there an abbot and a community of monks organized to offer praises to God in that titular church by day and by night [Note: [Col. 0567B] Codex Luc. has “after the model of.”] according to the model of the offices of the church of the blessed apostle Peter, [Note: [Col. 0568C] That is, separated from the jurisdictional authority of the presbyter of the aforesaid titular church. Gregory III founded a monastery in the church of Saint Chrysogonus the martyr, which is a titular cardinal church, but exempted it from the jurisdiction of the cardinal presbyter of that title, since the general custom in Rome is that no monastery should be subject to a cardinal title. *Dilectus*, in the *Extra*, “Concerning Monastic Chapels.” ALTASERRA.] specifically separated from the jurisdictional authority [Note: [Col. 0567B] Others: “of the presbytery.”] of the presbyter of the aforesaid titular church. In that monastery this same most holy man bestowed estates, gifts, and dependents for its support. [Col. 0568A] Many other faithful people and lovers of our Lord Jesus Christ likewise devotedly bestowed estates and gifts on the same monastery of Saints Stephen, Lawrence, and Chrysogonus.

In a similar manner he restored the monastery of Saints John the Evangelist, John the Baptist, and Saint Pancratius beside the church of the Savior, which had been founded in ancient times [Note: [Col. 0568B] Codex Luc. has “built.”] but had been left entirely [Note: [Col. 0568B] Codex Luc. has “from the monastic order.”] without a monastic community through extreme neglect. He contributed estates and gifts to it, and restored to the same place, after paying their price, whatever he found alienated from that monastery. There he appointed a community of monks and an abbot to perform daily the sacred offices of divine praise in the basilica of the Savior our Lord Jesus Christ, which is called Constantinian and is situated beside the Lateran, at the appointed hours of day and night [Note: [Col. 0568B] Others: “hours,”] according to the model of the offices of the church of the blessed apostle Peter.

He also re-silvered the ancient image of the holy Mother of God and covered it with the purest silver, weighing fifty pounds. He also made a large golden paten with various stones, weighing twenty-six pounds. Likewise, a chalice with gems, weighing [Note: [Col. 0568B] Others: twenty-nine.] thirty-four pounds. Likewise, a golden Gospel-book with gems, weighing fifteen pounds.

[Note: [Col. 0568D] He also newly made the roof and vault of Saint Andrew the apostle at Saint Peter the apostle and painted it. It is an ancient custom for churches to be painted. Anastasius below at this point: “Here also he rebuilt almost from the foundations the basilica of Saint Calixtus, pontiff and martyr, with new construction and a roof, and painted the whole of it.” And below: “Likewise, the basilica of the holy Mother of God, called in Aquiro, in which previously there had been a deaconry and a small oratory, he built from the foundations longer and wider and painted.” I have discussed this more fully in Gregory of Tours, book II, chapter 17. ALTASERRA.]

He also newly made the roof and vault of Saint Andrew the apostle at Saint Peter the apostle and painted it. He made in the same basilica a golden image of the blessed apostle Andrew set with gems, weighing eight pounds [Note: [Col. 0569B] Others: “and an entrance.”], and he lined the interior of the confession with silver, which he gilded with the purest gold.

Here also he rebuilt almost from the foundations, with new construction and a roof, the basilica of Saint Calixtus, pontiff and martyr, and painted the whole of it. There he bestowed a silver paten together with a chalice and an altar covering [Note: [Col. 0569B] Codex Luc. has “coverings.”].

He newly built the roof of the basilica of Saints Processus and Martinianus, placing beneath it, behind the venerable bodies of those same saints, a pier of exceptionally strong masonry to support the walls of the holy basilica. In the church of blessed Genesius the martyr he newly restored the roof, and there erected an altar in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior. On it he bestowed a silver paten and chalice, as well as a silver crown with six dolphins, and also a small golden crown with a cross hanging above the altar.

In the basilica of the holy Mother of God called “at the Martyrs,” he had the roof, which had collapsed through ancient neglect, thoroughly cleared and restored anew with an abundance of lime and lead coverings; whatever around the perimeter of that roof had been damaged [Note: [Col. 0569B] Others: “of the exposed roof.”] he rebuilt with new splendor.

He also built from the foundations, longer and wider, the basilica of the holy Mother of God called in Aquiro, in which previously there had been a deaconry and a small oratory, and he painted it. He also enlarged from the foundations, with more spacious construction, the deaconry of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, situated at Saint Peter the apostle, where previously there had been a small oratory. He granted all the possessions belonging to the use of the deaconry and established that they should serve in perpetuity for the support of the poor through the ministry of the deaconry.

Also, he instituted that an annual station be held in the cemetery of Saint Petronilla, where he offered a golden crown, a silver chalice and paten, and various other things pertaining to the adornment of the church. Also [Note: [Col. 0569B] The Lucca manuscript has *accubitus qui*; others, *ad accubita*.] [Note: [Col. 0569C] Also, he restored anew from the foundations and decorated the *accubita* located at Saint Peter’s, which had been placed in ruins. Properly speaking, an *accubitum* is a dining couch on which people recline for a meal. Lampridius, in *Heliogabalus*: “He did not readily recline on couches unless they had hare’s fur or the under-feathers of partridges. Frequently changing the mattresses, he spread leather cushions instead of couches for his less distinguished friends.” Sometimes *accubitum* denoted a dining hall in which couches were arranged. Anastasius, in his life of Leo III: “He also made in the Lateran patriarchium a dining hall of extraordinary size, in which place he arranged couches.” And below, in the same work: “He also made a house of the atrium, in which he likewise placed couches.” The same author, in his life of Leo IV: “For the dining couch which Pope Leo III, of blessed memory, had built from the foundations, and all the ornaments which he had prepared there, were destroyed through excessive age and the neglect of his pontifical predecessors; and on the feast of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh, neither Lord Gregory nor Lord Sergius, of holy memory, celebrated a meal there.” [Col. 0569D] “But the same most blessed and supreme bishop Leo IV repaired anew, with joy and the greatest delight, all the ornaments and provisions that had been destroyed there, and magnificently restored the place to its former use.” Hence the corrupt passage in Gregory IV should be emended: “He also made beside the *acoliti* a small lodging for the pontiff’s repose, where, after the morning prayers or the offices of Mass, his limbs might sleep.” Read: “beside the *accubita*,” namely those that were at the basilica of Saint Peter. ALTASERRA.] Also, he restored anew from the foundations and decorated the *accubita* located at Saint Peter’s, which had been placed in ruins.

Also, he rebuilt from the beginning the roof of the basilica of Saint Mark, situated outside the walls of this city on the Roman Appian Way. [Col. 0570B] Also, in the church of the blessed apostle Paul, he replaced five beams and repaired and restored the entire roof of that basilica, from the arch of the altar to the royal doors. He likewise replaced five beams in Saint Mary, the Mother of God, at the Manger.

He built anew the church of Saints Marcellinus and Peter beside the Lateran, as well as the cemetery of the blessed martyrs Januarius, Urban, Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus, [Note: [Col. 0570B] The Lucca manuscript has “the roofs placed in ruins”; Mansi has “the roof of them.”] and he completed anew their roof, which had been left in ruins. [Note: [Col. 0570B] The Lucca manuscript has “rebuilt”; Mansi has “having rebuilt it.”]

[Note: [Col. 0569D] 1. “During his pontificate,” etc. In the year 740, Luitprand, king of the Lombards, surrounded Rome with a siege, because Thrasamund, duke of Spoleto, and Godescalc, duke of Benevento, hostile to him, were in friendship with the Roman pontiff. Therefore, in the year 741, Gregory sent a double embassy to Charles Martel, mayor of the palace of the Frankish kingdom, with the keys of Saint Peter and fragments of the chains, and wrote him a double letter, with the intention—as Anastasius says—of freeing them from such great oppression by the Lombards. Anastasius, however, mentions only one embassy, undertaken by Anastasius the bishop and Sergius the presbyter.

But we learn that Gregory sent a double embassy to Charles from the Continuator of Fredegar, who, in chapter 110, writes that Gregory sought Charles’s aid not only against the Lombards but also against the emperor, who, as Baronius says, had stirred up the Lombard king against the Roman Church:

“At that time,” says the Continuator, “the blessed Pope Gregory sent twice from Rome to the aforesaid prince”—namely Charles—“the keys of the venerable tomb, together with the chains of Saint Peter and great and countless gifts, an embassy such as had never before been heard of or seen in any age.”

The same Anonymous gives this explanation of the double embassy: “This was done so that he might withdraw to the emperor’s side and confirm the Roman consulship—or patriciate—for the aforesaid prince Charles.”

That Gregory requested aid from Charles not only against the Lombards but also against the emperor is expressly stated in the *Metz Annals*, preserved in Duchesne’s collection of Frankish historians:

“In the year 741, Prince Charles, having subdued the peoples situated all around him, while he was arranging within the boundaries of his rule the matters pertaining to peace, received twice in that same year an embassy of the most blessed Pope Gregory, sent from the apostolic see. Those who came offered him the keys of the venerable tomb of the prince of the apostles Peter, together with his precious chains and great gifts; something that no Roman bishop had previously sent to any Frankish prince. The aforesaid bishop Gregory had also sent him a letter, by decree of the Romans, stating that the Roman people, abandoning the emperor’s rule, wished to turn to Charles’s protection and unconquered clemency.” [Col. 0571A]

From this it is also clear that the double embassy belonged to the year 741, and that Gregory asked Charles to withdraw from the emperor’s side. What Charles replied to Gregory III’s embassies and letters no ancient author has recorded. But that they were most welcome to Charles is made known to us by the Continuator of Fredegar, who writes in his Appendix:

“He himself received the embassy with extraordinary and magnificent honor, presented precious gifts, and, together with great rewards, sent Grimo, abbot of the monastery of Corbie, and Sygobert, a recluse of the basilica of the martyr Saint Dionysius, with his own envoys to Rome, to the thresholds of Saint Peter and Saint Paul.”

Since this embassy was most welcome to Charles, there is no doubt that through his envoys he threatened King Luitprand with war unless he immediately withdrew from Roman territory. Deterred by these threats from his undertaking, Luitprand returned to Pavia, from which he had come, although, as Anastasius relates, he retained the four towns he had occupied. These were later restored under Zacharias, Gregory’s successor, as we shall say in that place.

There is likewise no room for doubt that Charles promised aid to the pontiff; but since he died in that same year, 741, he was unable to provide it. Moreover, from the words of the Continuator of Fredegar and of the Annalist of Metz it follows that Gregory III offered Charles the consulship—or, as the author of the *Critique of Baronius* explains at length, the patriciate—since the latter says that the Roman people, abandoning the emperor’s rule, called Charles to their defense.

The dignity of patrician was conferred upon those who were chosen to defend churches and the poor against the violence of the powerful, as is clear from the formula reported by Paul the Deacon in a Vatican manuscript in his *History of the Lombards*, by which the prince proclaimed someone a patrician:

“We grant you this honor so that you may establish law for the churches of God and for the poor, and thereafter render an account before the Most High Judge.” Then the emperor should clothe him with a mantle, place a ring on the index finger of his right hand, and give him a piece of cotton written in his own hand: “Be a merciful and just Patrician.” Then he should place a golden circlet on his head and dismiss him.

The patriciate entailed a certain extraordinary right of protection, as Marca explains in book I, chapter 12, number 1, of *On Concord*: namely, the protection that those who otherwise are not bound by their office to provide it customarily extend to churches not subject to them, against the public or private violence of the powerful. Although princes are obliged by office to protect the churches established in their kingdoms, that ordinary right of protection depends upon jurisdiction.

That extraordinary right of protection was granted to distinguished men called patrons, defenders, protectors, and advocates, who provided particular churches with special protection and defense beyond what was expected from kings in accordance with the order of public discipline.

But the patriciate of the Roman Church, or the title “patrician of the Romans,” included two things: jurisdiction, by which the Frankish kings, with the consent of the pontiff and the Roman people, exercised power in the City; and protection, or defense, which they had promised to the Roman Church. That defense was established by agreements made with the Roman pontiffs.

Marca traces the beginning of those agreements concerning protection with the Roman Church to the time when Gregory III entrusted himself and his Church to the guardianship of Charles, duke of the Franks. He writes that this protection was later strengthened by new laws enacted by Pippin, king of the Franks, and Stephen II, Roman pontiff, who assigned the dignity of patrician to Pippin and his sons.

In these exceedingly difficult times, Charles Martel was called patrician of the Romans and defender of the Church. This is clearly suggested, besides the Continuator of Fredegar already mentioned, by the emperors Charles the Great and Louis the Pious. The former, in the division of his kingdom among his sons in the year 806, says:

“Above all, we command that these three brothers jointly undertake the care and defense of the Church of Saint Peter, just as formerly it was undertaken by our grandfather Charles and by our father, King Pippin, of blessed memory, and afterward by us; and that, with God’s help, they strive to defend it against its enemies, and ensure that it receive its justice insofar as it pertains to them and as reason requires.”

Louis the Pious says the same in the division of his kingdom, which Goldastus places in volume II of the *Imperial Constitutions*, and Baluzius in volume I of the *Capitularies*, in the year 837. The author of the *Critique of Baronius*, however, more correctly considers it to have been made in 835:

“Above all, we command and charge that these three brothers jointly undertake the care and defense of the Church of Saint Peter, just as formerly it was undertaken by our great-grandfather Charles, our grandfather Pippin, by our father, the emperor Charles, of blessed memory, and afterward by us.”

From these things it must be concluded that Charles Martel was the first of all Frankish princes—or of any other nation—to undertake the patronage of the City and of the Roman Church. Whoever wishes to learn more about this matter should consult the aforementioned Marca and the *Critique of Baronius* at the year 740.

The origin of apostolic envoys in Francia seems to have arisen from that embassy of Gregory III to Charles Martel, in whose hands the entire administration of Francia then lay. At that time the *apocrisarii* of the Roman see were first seen in Francia; they dealt twice with Charles Martel so that he might provide the Romans with aid and counsel.

“Those who held the Roman pontificate after Gregory III,” says Cointius in the *Ecclesiastical Annals of Francia* at the year 740, number 7, “sent envoys to Francia more frequently, and matters reached the point that, besides the legates sent from Rome for newly arising causes, an *apocrisarius* of the apostolic see remained continually in the king’s entourage. Nor was it unusual for that office to be conferred by the Roman pontiff upon the man whom the king had appointed archchaplain of his palace.” PAGIUS.]

[Col. 0572C] 2. “During his pontificate,” etc. Leo was contemplating vengeance against Italy and especially against the pontiff, whom he regarded as the supporter of Italy’s defection. He therefore placed Manes, one of his more powerful commanders, in charge of the fleet he had equipped.

“But the emperor,” says Theophanes in his account of Leo, “was raging against the Pope and against the secession of Rome and Italy; and he sent against him a large fleet, appointing Manes, the governor of the Cybrrhaeots, as its commander.”

Meanwhile the pontiff had taken precautions for his affairs by preparing an embassy to Charles Martel, prince of the Franks, from whom he sought aid both for the holy see and for the Roman people, who rejected Leo’s rule.

The *Annals of Metz* speak of this embassy above all others (in Duchesne’s *Collection of Frankish Historians*), where the following is read:

“In the year 741, Prince Charles received twice in that same year an embassy of the most blessed Pope Gregory, sent from the apostolic see . . . The aforesaid bishop Gregory had also sent him a letter, by decree of the Roman princes, stating that the Roman people, abandoning the emperor’s rule, wished to turn to Charles’s protection and unconquered clemency.” [Col. 0572D]

He had also requested aid from that same Charles against the Lombards, who were oppressing Italy and inflicting many hardships upon the holy see (Letters 5 and 6). But God, without the intervention of human assistance, wondrously protected the holy see against Leo’s wrath. For a violent storm struck his fleet between the Empire and Italy; it scattered part of it upon the rocks and buried part in the deep waves.

Yet Leo did not thereby return to a better course. Rather, “then,” says Theophanes in the cited passage, “the enemy of God, raging still more fiercely, since he was held by an Arabizing disposition against the images, imposed capital taxes upon a third part of Sicily, that is, Calabria. He also ordered that the estates of the holy princes, the apostles, which formerly paid the public treasury half a gold piece and three talents of silver to the churches, should make payment; and he ordered that male children be counted and registered, just as Pharaoh once did with those who were of Hebrew descent.” [Col. 0573B]

Therefore, while this new Pharaoh ruled, the Empire suffered plagues no less terrible than those with which Egypt was once afflicted under the ancient Pharaoh. The Saracens invaded it and devastated its provinces. Famine and pestilence subsequently completed their desolation. As the calamity increased, a dreadful earthquake overthrew its principal cities and crushed most of their inhabitants beneath the ruins.

But the worst of all the evils that this emperor, the agent of divine wrath, inflicted upon his subjects was that he left them his son Constantine Copronymus as successor, who far surpassed his father in impiety and every kind of crime. SOMMIER.]

During his pontificate, a very large part of the walls of this Roman city was restored. He also supplied from his own resources the provisions for the craftsmen [Col. 0572A] and the money for purchasing lime.

[Col. 0573A] [Note: [Col. 0573C] During his pontificate, the fortress of Gallienus was recovered. On its account the Roman duchy was daily attacked by the duchy of Spoleto, while it paid considerable sums of money. In the time of the Lombards, Italy was divided into duchies; individual provinces were called duchies, such as the Roman duchy, the duchy of Spoleto, and the duchy of Friuli. Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book IV, chapter 52: “About this time, after Grasulf, duke of Friuli, had died at Forum Julii, Hago undertook the government of the duchy. At Spoleto also, after Atto had died, Theudelapius became ruler of that city.” During this period the Roman territory suffered much from Luitprand, king of the Lombards, because of Thrasamund, duke of Spoleto, who had fled to Rome while pursued by the king.
