Four cities were taken from the Roman duchy by siege: Ameria, Hortas, Polimartium, and Blera, concerning which see Anastasius in his life of Zacharias. ALTASERRA.]

During his pontificate, the fortress of Gallienus was recovered. On its account the Roman duchy was daily attacked by the duchy of Spoleto, while it paid considerable sums of money to Thrasamund, their duke, so that they might cease their wars and disputes; [Note: [Col. 0573B] Others: “and he was able to settle the case.”] he was able to settle the matter and ordered that it be joined to the fabric of the holy commonwealth and to the body of the Roman army beloved by Christ.

Here he made vestments for the altars in the churches of the Savior, of the Mother of God, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of Andrew, [Note: [Col. 0573B] The Lucca manuscript has: “for the altars in the churches of Saint Savior”; others: “for the altar in the church of the holy Mother of God, of the saints.”] [Note: [Col. 0573B] Others have: “and so forth in various churches.”] and of the others in various churches.

For in the city of Centumcellae he also had the ruined walls, almost from their foundations, constructed with great strength. [Note: [Col. 0573D] “He also decreed that, in accordance with the decree made by the college of priests before the sacred body of Saint Peter, for the celebration of the solemn vigils and Masses of our Lord Jesus Christ and of his holy Mother, of the holy apostles, of all the holy martyrs and confessors, and of the perfected righteous resting throughout the whole world, vigils should be celebrated by monks in the oratory dedicated to their name within the church of the blessed apostle Peter, beneath the principal arch, and the solemn Masses by the weekly priests. This decree contains two provisions. One is that the vigils of the holy apostles, martyrs, and confessors resting throughout the world should be celebrated by the weekly priests. In the church of Saint Peter there were weekly priests who celebrated Masses by turns; concerning them, see Anastasius in his life of Hilary, where I have discussed them.” ALTASERRA.]

He also decreed [Note: [Col. 0574B] Others have: “so that, the decree having been preserved, according to which,” etc.] that, in accordance with the decree made by the college of priests [Note: [Col. 0574B] Others have: “before the sacred body,” etc.] before the sacred body of Saint Peter, for the celebration of the solemn vigils and Masses of Christ our Lord Jesus Christ, of his holy Mother, of the holy apostles, and of all the holy martyrs, confessors, and perfected righteous resting throughout the whole world, vigils should be celebrated by monks in the oratory dedicated to their name within the church of the blessed apostle Peter, beneath the principal arch, and the solemn Masses by the weekly priests.

[Note: [Col. 0574B] By these same decrees he arranged that, in the cemeteries situated all around Rome, on the anniversaries of their births into glory, lamps should be carried for the celebration of vigils and offerings from the Patriarchium should be brought by the *oblationarius* for the celebration of Masses, through the priest whom the pontiff then in office should appoint. Gregory III decreed that on the anniversaries of the apostles and martyrs, lamps should be carried to the cemeteries for the celebration of vigils, and offerings—that is, bread and wine—for the celebration of Masses should be brought from the Lateran Patriarchium by the *oblationarius*—as had previously been decreed by John III, as observed from Anastasius in his life of John III. The *oblationarius* is a subdeacon who received the offerings—that is, the bread and wine intended for the sacrifice of the Mass—from the pontiff’s hand and then handed them to the archdeacon. The Roman *Order of the Mass*: “The subdeacon receives the offerings from the Pontiff and places them in the linen cloth carried behind him by two acolytes.” And below: “Then the archdeacon receives two offerings from the *oblationarius* and gives them to the Pontiff,” etc. ALTASERRA.]

By these same enactments he arranged that, in the cemeteries situated all around Rome, on the anniversaries of their births into glory, lamps should be carried for the celebration of vigils and offerings from the Patriarchium should be brought by the *oblationarius* for the celebration of Masses, through the priest whom the pontiff then in office should appoint. [Note: [Col. 0574B] Others have “priests”; the remainder is absent, and the life of Zacharias follows immediately.]

He held three ordinations during the month of December: twenty-four presbyters, three deacons, [Note: [Col. 0574C] “Bishops in various places,” etc. Boniface, the bishop formerly sent for the conversion of Germany, had reported to the pontiff by letter the circumstances that had occurred there. Therefore, as a mark of gratitude and esteem, the pontiff conferred upon him the dignity of archbishop and sent him the pallium, explaining when he should use it:

“We have sent you the gift of the sacred pallium. Receiving it by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter, you shall put it on; and, by God’s authority, we command that you be reckoned one among the archbishops. But learn, instructed by apostolic mandate, how you are to use it. Thus, when you celebrate the solemnities of Mass, or when it happens that you consecrate a bishop, use it only at that time” (Gregory III, Letter 1, to Boniface).

Moreover, he granted him the power to create bishops in accordance with the laws of the sacred canons:

“We command that, in accordance with the statutes of the sacred canons, wherever the multitude of the faithful has increased, you should, by the authority of the apostolic see, ordain bishops—yet with prudent consideration, so that the dignity of the episcopate may not be cheapened” (same letter).

He teaches that those whom pagans have baptized in another manner ought to be baptized in the name of the most holy Trinity. He orders him to prohibit Christians from eating horseflesh and to impose a severe penalty upon transgressors. The dead are to be prayed for, and the priests are to mention them in the sacrifice of the Mass. Counsel is to be given that no one marry more than once and again. He prescribes lifelong penance for parricide, and orders that communion be given to such persons only at the point of death. Those who sell slaves to pagans for sacrifice are to be treated like murderers. The consecration of a bishop is always to be performed in the presence of two other bishops. He admonishes him concerning all these matters.

Afterward, when Boniface himself had come to Rome, Gregory gave him three letters as he was departing. The first was addressed to all the bishops, presbyters, and abbots whom he might meet on the journey; he urged them not to detain or delay any of the ecclesiastics under their jurisdiction who might wish to depart with Boniface for the conversion of unbelievers. The second was addressed to the nobles and people of the recently converted provinces; he asked them to support Boniface’s ministry with their own authority and to banish from their territories all the superstitions and remnants of idolatry that paganism had left there. The third was addressed to the bishops of Bavaria and Germany; in it he stated that he had appointed Boniface his apostolic vicar in their dioceses, had given him power to convene synods wherever he judged it useful, and had authorized him to report to the holy see whatever was done in them.

Boniface returned to his mission and visited Bavaria, where he found every kind of corruption among the clergy because of the scarcity of bishops: only one bishop governed that vast province, and he had neither a cathedral city nor a territory. Therefore Boniface established three others there with the consent of the duke and nobles, and founded four cathedral sees—Salzburg, Freising, Regensburg, and Passau—and reported all this to the pontiff.

The pontiff, disapproving of none of it, replied:

“Because you reported that you had gone to the people of Bavaria and found them living outside ecclesiastical order, since they had no bishops in the province except one named Vivilo, whom we ordained previously; and because, with the consent of their duke Orilo and of the nobles of that province, you ordained three bishops and divided that province into four parts, that is, into four dioceses, so that each bishop might have his own diocese, you have acted well and very wisely, brother, since you fulfilled the apostolic command in our place, and acted just as we commanded you” (his Letter 7 to the same, Willibald, *Life of Saint Boniface*, chapter 31).

When Gregory appointed Boniface archbishop, he established no metropolitan see in those provinces, since he did not wish Boniface to be bound to any particular episcopate, but rather to assume general care of them all. SOMMIER.]

He ordained eighty bishops in various places, and [Col. 0575A] also, by giving him the pallium, appointed the venerable Vulcarius archbishop in the parts of Francia, in the city of Vienne. [Note: [Col. 0576B] Others: “He appointed Vulcarius archbishop in the parts of Francia, in Vienne, by giving him the pallium.” An archbishop is said to be appointed by the gift of the pallium because through the pallium the fullness of pontifical office is conferred; see chapter *Nisi* on the authority and use of the pallium. ALTASERRA.]

He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on the fourth day before the Kalends of December. His episcopate was vacant for four days.

THE EXTANT WRITINGS OF SAINT GREGORY III, ROMAN PONTIFF

[Col. 0575]

LETTERS

(Mansi, *Collection of Councils*, volume XII)

LETTER ONE. OF POPE GREGORY III TO BONIFACE, ARCHBISHOP. He sends him the archiepiscopal pallium and teaches him how he should use it. He grants him power to establish new bishoprics. He replies concerning a certain presbyter and answers his various questions.

[Col. 0575C]

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop, sent from this apostolic see for the enlightenment of the German people and of the peoples dwelling round about in the shadow of death and established in error. [Editio Romana: “of the Church of God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0575D] “He received great joy from us.” Gratian, in the same way, attributes this passage to Gregory the Younger in distinction 16, question 1, *We Command*. Although they sometimes used that designation for Gregory III, as I have said, it is nevertheless clear that Gratian does not understand Gregory III here, because he explicitly attributes the same letter to Gregory II in question 2, *For the Departed*, and in *On Consecration*, distinction 4, *Those from the Pagans*. Gratian is supported by the fact that in certain manuscripts the following is read at the end of this letter: “Up to this point, Gregory from the first; from here, Gregory the Younger from the second,” that is, the third. By these words it is plainly attributed to Gregory II. Nevertheless, the mention of the pallium sent to Boniface shows that the letter belongs to Gregory III. The author of Boniface’s *Life*, book I, chapter 31, indeed says that it was sent by Gregory III. It is therefore more correctly attributed to him in that same *Life*, and also by Ivo, part X, chapter 179. SIRMOND.]

We were filled with great joy when we read the letters of your most holy fraternity, because, after rereading their contents, we found that by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ you had converted very many people from paganism and error to the knowledge of the true faith. Since divine instruction teaches us in the parables that the one to whom five talents were entrusted gained five others (Matthew 25), we rejoice together with the whole Church in the profit of such an exchange.

For this reason we have rightly sent you the gift of the sacred pallium. Receiving it by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter, you shall put it on, and, by God’s authority, we command that you be reckoned one among the archbishops. Learn, instructed by apostolic mandate, how you are to use it. [Editio Romana: “you will learn.”] Thus, when you celebrate the solemnities of Mass, or when it happens that you consecrate a bishop, use it only at that time.

But since you affirm that, by the Lord’s grace, crowds in those same regions have been converted to the right faith, and therefore you cannot attend to everyone or provide and proclaim the things that lead to salvation, since the grace of Christ and his faith have already spread far and wide in those regions [Editio Romana: “have spread throughout those regions,”] we command (16, q. 1) that, in accordance with the statutes of the sacred canons, wherever the multitude of the faithful has increased, you should, by the authority of the apostolic see, ordain bishops—yet with prudent consideration, so that the dignity of the episcopate may not be cheapened.

As for the presbyter whom you stated had come to us in the previous year and, by our judgment, had been absolved from his wicked deeds, you should understand that he made no confession to us and that he was not absolved by us so that he might fulfill his desires. But if you find him devoted to error, we command you, by the authority of the apostolic see, to correct and amend him according to the judgment of the holy canons; and likewise if you happen to find others of that sort. For when he came he said, “I am a presbyter,” and asked for letters of recommendation to our son Charles. We granted him no other permission. We wish him, if he conducts himself wickedly, to be avoided along with the others.

I. Those whom you stated to have been baptized by pagans, if this is indeed the case, we command you to baptize again in the name of the holy Trinity. (*On Consecration*, distinction 4.)

II. Among other matters, you added that some of them eat wild horse, and many also domestic horse. Most holy brother, do not allow this to happen henceforth, but, by whatever means you can with Christ’s help, restrain them in every way and impose an appropriate penance upon them; for it is unclean and detestable.

III. You also consulted us concerning the departed, asking whether it is permissible to offer [Editio Romana: “to offer offerings.”] (*13, q. 2*). The holy Church holds that each person should offer offerings for his truly Christian dead, and that the presbyter should make mention of them. Although we are all subject to sins, it is nevertheless fitting that the priest make remembrance of and intercede only for catholic dead. For it is not permissible to do such a thing for the impious, even if they were Christians.

IV. [Note: [Col. 0577D] In the Roman edition this canon reads: “For we also command that those who are uncertain whether they were baptized or not, or who associate with a presbyter sacrificing to Jupiter and eating sacrificial meats, should be baptized.” [Col. 0578D]] We also command that those who are uncertain whether they were baptized, or who were baptized by a presbyter sacrificing to Jupiter and eating sacrificial meats, be rebaptized. [Col. 0577D]

V. We have also decreed that each person observe his own lineage up to the seventh generation.

VI. And if you are able, teach that it must be avoided lest, when someone’s wife has died, he marry more than two women. [Note: [Col. 0578D] The Roman edition has: “Avoid this, lest a man whose wives have died be joined to more than two.”]

VII. Concerning those who have killed their father, mother, brother, or sister, we decree that they not receive the Lord’s Body throughout the whole of their life, except as viaticum at their death. They must also abstain from eating meat and drinking wine for as long as they live; they should fast on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, so that by mourning they may be able to wash away the crime they have committed. (Ivo, part X, 179.)

[Col. 0578A] VIII. You have also reported that among other crimes committed in those regions, some of the faithful sell their slaves to pagans for sacrifice. We urge you, brother, to correct this with the greatest diligence, and do not allow it to happen again; for it is a crime and impiety. Therefore, impose upon those who have committed such acts the penance appropriate to a murderer.

IX. Whenever you consecrate a bishop, let two or three bishops assemble with you, so that what is done may be pleasing to God; and when they have assembled and are present, consecrate him. We wish you, dearest brother, to observe these things diligently and to carry out with devoted piety the work of salvation that you have begun, so that you may receive from the Lord our God a reward in eternal recompense for the gain you have brought him.

As for the privilege, we have prepared it according to your request and sent it enclosed with this letter, hoping that, under the protection of the Lord our God, you may bring Christ the Lord a very abundant harvest from the conversion of those who have gone astray. [Editio Romana: “an abundant and complete harvest.”] May God preserve you safe and sound, most reverend brother.

LETTER TWO. OF POPE GREGORY III TO ALL BISHOPS, PRESBYTERS, AND ABBOTS. He commends Boniface, returning to Germany, to their support and asks them not to prevent anyone who wishes to join him.

Gregory, [Editio Romana adds: “bishop,”] servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops beloved by us, to the venerable presbyters, the religious abbots, and all the provinces.

[Col. 0578C] With the Lord cooperating and confirming the word, the most holy man Boniface, our brother and fellow bishop, who had been sent by our predecessor Gregory, bishop of holy memory, to the regions of Germany to preach the word of truth, has now, after a long time, come to the sacred thresholds of the blessed apostles with an eager desire for prayer and wished to present himself to us. After completing his prayer, he was dismissed by us to his undertaking, with the angel of the Lord going before him. [Editio Romana: “with the angel of the Lord going before him, he was released by us.”]

I ask that all your love, reverence, and devotion deign to offer him assistance for the love of Christ, when you recall what our Lord Jesus Christ promised, saying: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward” (Matthew 10).

And if perhaps any of your ministers should wish to join this most holy man in the ministry of exhorting people to the holy and catholic faith, do not prohibit them in any way, dearest brothers. Rather, offer them your support and provide helpers from your flock who, by God’s grace, may adequately minister the word of preaching to the nations, so that they may win souls for almighty God, and so that your community may share in the good work and they may deserve to hear the Lord’s saying: “You who have left everything and followed me will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matthew 19).

Farewell.

LETTER THREE. OF POPE GREGORY III TO THE NOBLES AND PEOPLE OF THE PROVINCES OF GERMANY. As Boniface returns to them, he urges them to obey him and to cast far away all pagan rites.

Gregory the pope to all the leading men and people of the provinces of Germany, Thuringians and [Note: [Col. 0579D] In the Roman edition these names are given as follows: Thesis, Bortharis and Nistresis, Unedredis and Lognais, Sudnodis and Graffeldis, etc.] Hessians, Botharians and Nistresians, Wedrinians and Lognians, Suduodians and Graveldians, and all those established in the eastern region.

Since our predecessor, Gregory, a bishop of holy memory, moved by divine prompting to make a people perfect for God, ordained and sent to you the bearer of this letter, Boniface, our most reverend brother and fellow bishop, instructing him in the rule and norm of the apostolic and catholic faith of the Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve; and after a period of time he presented himself at the thresholds of the blessed apostles for the sake of prayer and asked us to be instructed in matters pertaining to the salvation of souls: we, instructing him, with God’s favor, as Holy Scripture teaches, have released him to return to you, dearest ones. We exhort you in the Lord to receive worthily from him the word of exhortation, and to admit into the Church’s ministry the bishops or presbyters whom he ordains by the apostolic authority granted to him.

And if he should find any who have strayed from the path of the true faith or from canonical teaching, and should prohibit them, let no one among you in any way obstruct him; let them accept obediently, for God’s sake, whatever has been imposed upon them. For whoever proves reckless in refusing obedience acquires condemnation for himself.

But you, dearest ones, who have been baptized in the name of Christ and have put on Christ, abstain and restrain yourselves from every pagan observance—not merely correcting yourselves, but also your subjects. Reject and cast away entirely diviners and sorcerers, sacrifices for the dead, omens from groves or springs, amulets, enchanters, poisoners and malefactors, and sacrilegious practices that used to be carried out within your borders. Turn with your whole mind to God, fear him, adore him, and honor him, “sharing in the memorials of the saints” (Romans XII), as the Apostle says.

For if your faith, according to the words of our Lord (Matthew XVII), is like a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, “Move,” and it will be moved [Roman edition: “Pass from here”]. For our Lord and Savior himself teaches in his sacred utterance: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Matthew XXII). And again: “Whoever acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew X). Elsewhere also he promises, saying: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name will be done for you” (John XIV); and: “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Luke I).

And you, dearest ones, produce worthy fruits, so that on the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ you may deserve to attain the heavenly mansions. Farewell.

## LETTER IV. OF POPE GREGORY III TO THE BISHOPS OF BAVARIA AND ALAMANNIA

That they should fittingly receive Boniface, acting as the representative of the Apostolic See, and assemble for the councils that he convokes.

To our most beloved bishops established in the province of the Bavarians and in Alamannia, [Note: [Col. 0580D] In the Roman edition these names are given as follows: Iuggo, Luidoni, Ridolfo, Phipilo, and Savada.] Wigo, Luidon, [Col. 0580B] Rodulf, Wivilo or Adda: Gregory the pope.

The authority of the holy Fathers of the Catholic Church commands that synods be celebrated twice each year for the salvation of the Christian people and for the exhortation connected with the adoption of sons, and that examination of canonical cases take place, so that each person may be assisted by a pious judgment according to the necessity of each case.

Therefore, following the Apostle’s teaching, I admonish and exhort you, dearest ones, through the mercy of God, to walk worthily according to the calling with which you were called (Ephesians IV), so that your ministry may be perfect before the Lord. It is fitting that you should know to receive our brother and fellow bishop Boniface, who is present as our representative, with the honor due to him and appropriate for Christ’s name; and that you should willingly receive and maintain from him the ecclesiastical ministry, with the Catholic faith, according to the custom and norm of God’s holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, over which, through God’s preceding mercy, we seem to preside, just as he was sent by us with apostolic authority.

Reject and prohibit the rites and teaching of paganism, whether those of the Britons who come among you, or of false priests and heretics, or of people of whatever origin. Teach the people entrusted to you by God through pious admonitions, and abstain entirely from sacrifices for the dead. According to what you have been taught by our aforesaid fellow priest, hold to the Catholic and apostolic teaching and strive to please the Lord God and our Savior.

Wherever he commands you to assemble for the celebration of councils—whether near the Danube, or in the city of Augsburg, or wherever he shall judge—let you be found ready for Christ’s name, so that through his command we may learn of your assembly and so that, on the day of Christ Jesus’ coming, you may deserve to stand before his tribunal with the fruit of good works, saying: “Behold, we and the children whom you have given us, Lord” (Isaiah VIII); and so that you may deserve to hear the Lord’s voice saying: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew LV). Farewell.

## LETTER V. OF POPE GREGORY III TO CHARLES MARTEL, MAYOR OF THE PALACE OF THE KINGDOM OF THE FRANKS

For undertaking the defense of the holy Roman Church against the kings of the Lombards, who were harassing it with their arms.

[Note: [Col. 0581A] All learned men know well the Carolingian Codex, in which Charles the Great collected the letters of the Roman pontiffs addressed to Charles Martel, to Pippin, and to himself. Labbe included some of these in his collection; of others he supplied only a summary, and some he omitted altogether. I am entirely unaware of his reason for doing this. I do not understand why some should have been published, others merely indicated, and still others suppressed, unless perhaps he intended to follow the example of Baronius, who included only selected letters in his Annals, merely mentioned others, and left others unpraised. Whatever the case may be, I have judged that the entire Codex should be reproduced here, so that nothing concerning the letters of the individual pontiffs might be lacking. I use Muratori’s edition, *Rerum Italicarum*, volume III, part II, as the most accurate of all. If, however, I encountered among the letters of the individual pontiffs anything reported by Labbe, I retained his reading unchanged, while marking variants of greater importance. I also thought that Muratori’s notes should be preserved in full, especially those that contribute to the restoration of the text. Furthermore, Muratori presents the text of the Gretser edition and records variants from the extremely rare edition of Lamnecius. I have done the same here, at least in those letters that I have introduced here first from the same Muratori. It remains only to add the heading prefixed to that collection, which Gretser published from a venerably ancient parchment codex, as he himself says. MANSI.]]

[Col. 0581A]

To the most excellent lord, his son [Note: [Col. 0581D] “To Charles, the sub-king.” It was published together with what follows by our Gretser in the *Codex of Pontifical Letters*. In both passages the pontiff calls him “sub-king,” whereas his predecessor, another Gregory, called him “duke” in Letter 3 and “patrician” in Letter 8—namely Charles Martel, prefect of the palace, or mayor of the royal palace [Col. 0582D]. In the next letter to Boniface he will again be called “prince of the Franks”; we do not recall that Charles Martel used this title. The acts of the synods of Liptina and Soissons show that it was used by Carloman and Pippin, the sons of Martel. SIRMOND.] Charles, the sub-king: Gregory the pope.

We are tossed by excessive tribulation, and tears do not cease from our eyes by day or by night, when we see daily and everywhere that the holy Church of God is being abandoned by her own sons, in whom there was hope that she would be defended. Therefore, constrained by grief, we remain in groaning and mourning, while we see that what remained last year, however little, for the support and nourishment of Christ’s poor and for the furnishing of lamps in the territory of Ravenna, is now all being consumed by sword and fire by Luitprand and Hilprand, kings of the Lombards.

But in these Roman territories, they too sent several armies and did and continue to do similar things to us; they destroyed all the steps [Gretser: “halls”] of Saint Peter and carried off the possessions that remained. Until now no consolation has reached us from you, most excellent son, although we have made you our refuge. But, as we see, while permission has been granted by you to those same kings to make incursions, their false insinuation has found more acceptance with you than our truth. We fear that this may be reckoned to you as sin, since now, wherever those kings are staying, they utter these words to our reproach: “Let Charles come, in whom you have placed your refuge, and the army of the Franks; if they are able, let them help you and rescue you from our hand.”

O what an incurable pain these reproaches retain in our breast, while such and so great sons do not attempt to defend their spiritual mother, the holy Church of God, and her special people! The prince of the apostles himself is powerful, because God has granted him authority, to defend his house and his special people and to take vengeance on their enemies; but he tests the minds of faithful sons.

Do not believe, son, the deceitful insinuations and persuasive arguments of those same kings. For they falsely insinuate everything to you, writing about alleged conspiracies, as though their commanders had committed some fault against them [Lambecius: “against them, their commanders”], namely the commanders of Spoleto and Benevento. But it is all lies. For they persecute those commanders for no other crime—let the truth satisfy you, son—than that last year they refused to invade us from their own territories, destroy the possessions of the holy apostles as those others had done, and plunder the special people.

Those commanders themselves spoke as follows: “Because we do not make war against the holy Church of God and her special people, since we have a pact with them and have received the faith from that very Church, their sword therefore rages against us.” Indeed, the aforesaid commanders were and are ready to obey them according to the ancient custom. But those others, retaining their anger because of what we have said above, sought by a contrived pretext to destroy and invade both them and us. Thus, by persecuting both sides, they report falsehoods to your goodness, so that they may degrade those most noble commanders, appoint their own wicked commanders there, and attack the Church of God with still greater force every day and from every direction, dissipate the possessions of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and take captive his special people.

Nevertheless, so that the truth of the matter may be fully disclosed to you, most Christian son, order your most faithful envoy to be sent here after those kings’ return to their own lands. Let him be one who cannot be corrupted by rewards, so that with his own eyes he may see our persecution, the humiliation of God’s Church, the desolation of her possessions, and the tears of strangers, and may report everything to your devotion.

But we exhort your goodness before the Lord and his terrible judgment, most Christian son, that for God’s sake and for the salvation of your soul you assist the Church of Saint Peter and his special people; that you swiftly repel those same kings, drive them away from us, and order them to return to their own lands.

Do not despise my prayer, nor close your ears to my request, lest the prince of the apostles close the heavenly kingdoms to you. I adjure you by the living and true God, and by the most sacred keys of the confession of blessed Peter, which we sent to you for the kingdom, not to place the friendship of the Lombards above love for the prince of the apostles. Rather, let us swiftly and with the utmost haste experience, after God, your consolation for our defense, so that your faith and good name may be proclaimed among all peoples, and so that we, with the prophet, may deserve to say:

“May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation;
may the name of the God of Jacob protect you” (Psalm XIX).

The bearer of this letter, Anchardus, your faithful servant, will relate orally to your gracious excellence everything that he has seen with his own eyes and that we have entrusted to him. We ask your goodness, with God as witness and judge, to ease our pains with the greatest haste and quickly send us joyful news, so that, gladdened in spirit, we may day and night pour out prayers for you and your faithful before the sacred confessions of the holy princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul.

## LETTER VI. OF POPE GREGORY III TO CHARLES MARTEL, MAYOR OF THE PALACE OF THE KINGDOM OF THE FRANKS

Likewise, for the defense of the Roman Church.

[Col. 0583B]

To the most excellent lord, his son Charles, the sub-king: Gregory the pope.

Because of the excessive grief of our heart and our tears, we have judged it necessary to write again to your excellence, trusting that you are a loving son of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of us; and that, out of reverence for him, you will obey our commands to defend the Church of God and his special people, who can no longer endure the persecution and oppression of the Lombard nation.

For they have carried off all the lamps dedicated to the honor of that prince of the apostles, as well as the offerings given by your parents or by you. And because, after God, we flee to you for refuge, the Lombards therefore hold us up to reproach and oppress us. Thus the Church of Saint Peter has been stripped bare and reduced to extreme desolation.

Nevertheless, we have placed all our griefs more fully in the mouth of your faithful bearer presently before us, who must report them to your excellence. But you, son, may have with that prince of the apostles, both in this life and in the life to come, before our almighty God, the reward corresponding to how swiftly you have resolved and struggled for the Church and for our defense. Then all nations may recognize your faith and purity, and the love that you have for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and for us and his special people, whom you zealously protect and defend. From this you will be able to acquire immortal and eternal life.

## LETTER VII. OF POPE GREGORY III TO BONIFACE, ARCHBISHOP

He approves that Boniface divided Bavaria into four bishoprics; answers several of his questions; and orders that a council be held beside the bank of the Danube.

[Col. 0583D]

To the most reverend and most holy brother Boniface: Gregory, servant of the servants of God.

[Col. 0584A] It is the voice of the eminent teacher of the nations, the blessed apostle Paul, saying: “All things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans VIII).

Therefore, recognizing from the words of your brotherly letter what you have already reported concerning the peoples of Germany, whom our God in his mercy has freed from the power of the pagans and, through your efforts and those of Charles, prince of the Franks, has deigned to gather nearly one hundred thousand souls into the bosom of Mother Church; and recognizing also what you have accomplished in the province of the Bavarians, we raised our hands toward heaven and gave thanks to the Lord our God, giver of all good things. He opened the door of mercy and piety in those western regions, an entrance to the knowledge of the way of salvation, and sent his angel, who prepared your way before you. To him be glory forever and ever.

Since, therefore, you reported that you had gone to the Bavarian people and found them living outside ecclesiastical order, because they had no bishops in the province except one named Wivilo, whom we ordained some time ago; and since, with the consent of their duke Otilo and of the leading men of that province, you ordained three other bishops and divided that province into four parts, that is, into four dioceses, so that each bishop might have his own diocese—you acted well and with sound prudence, brother, since you fulfilled an apostolic command in our place and acted just as we instructed you.

Therefore, most reverend brother, do not cease teaching them the holy Catholic and apostolic tradition of the Roman See, so that the unlearned may be enlightened and hold to the way of salvation by which they may reach eternal rewards.

[Note: [Col. 0583D] “The presbyters, however.” On this passage the Centuriators attack Gregory III, but with great injustice; for here he commands nothing other than that those ordained by bishops who were not genuine or whose status was doubtful should be consecrated again. Bellarmine, Book IV *On the Roman Pontiff*, chapter 12. BIN.]

As for the presbyters (Distinction 68) whom you found there, if the men by whom they were ordained are unknown, and it is uncertain whether those who ordained them were bishops or not; if those presbyters are men of good conduct and Catholic, and are instructed and competent in the ministry of Christ and in every holy law, let them receive from their bishop the blessing of the presbyterate and be consecrated, and thus perform the sacred ministry.

[Note: [Col. 0584D] “Those, however, who have been baptized.” In this passage Pope Gregory explicitly teaches that the baptism of those baptized by the ministry and in the language of pagans in the name of the most holy Trinity is not to be repeated; rather, they are to be received as Christians through the laying on of hands and anointing with chrism. Therefore the true interpretation of the letter is that he commands those baptized by pagans without an explicit invocation of the Trinity to be baptized again in the name of the most holy Trinity. See the letter of Pope Zachary beginning, “At the sacred thresholds” [Col. 0585D], in which, in a reply sent to Boniface, he responds, following the example of his predecessor Gregory, that those not baptized lawfully through an explicit invocation of the most holy Trinity must be baptized again according to the legitimate form. BIN.]

Those, however, who have been baptized through the diversity and deviation of pagan languages, yet have been baptized in the name of the * Trinity (Ivo, Book I, chapter 149), must be confirmed through the laying on of hands and the anointing with sacred chrism.

For Wivilo was ordained bishop by us. If he exceeds anything beyond the canonical rule, teach and correct him according to the tradition of the Roman Church that you received from us.

With regard to the council, we command your fraternity, by apostolic authority, to present yourself there, so that you may celebrate it on our behalf beside the bank of the Danube. And insofar as the Lord gives you strength, do not cease preaching the word of salvation, so that the Christian religion may grow and multiply in the name of the Lord.

For, brother, you will not have permission to remain in one place in return for the labor you have undertaken. Rather, after strengthening the hearts of the brothers and of all the faithful who are unlearned in those western regions, do not cease preaching the word of salvation wherever the Lord opens a way for you. Wherever you find a necessary place, ordain bishops according to the canonical rule on our behalf, and teach them to hold to the apostolic and Catholic tradition.

By this you will prepare for yourself a great reward, since you will make a perfect people for our almighty God. Do not be reluctant, most beloved brother, to travel rough and varied roads, so that the Christian faith may be extended far and wide through your efforts.

For it is written: “Narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life” (Matthew VII). Work, therefore, brother, at the good work that you have begun, so that on the day of Christ our God, standing among the company of approved holy Fathers, you may deserve to say: “Behold, I and the children whom you have given me; I have lost none of them” (Isaiah VIII).

And again: “Lord, you entrusted five talents to me; behold, I have gained five others” (Matthew XXV). And afterward may you deserve to hear the Lord’s voice saying: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Since you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (ibid.).

May God keep you safe, most reverend brother.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, during the reign of the most pious lord Augustus Leo, in the twenty-third year of his reign, and also during the twentieth year of Constantine the Great, his son and emperor, in the eighth indiction.

## LETTER VIII. OF POPE GREGORY III TO THE BISHOPS OF TUSCIA

Gregory to all the bishops in Lombard Tuscia.

Your fraternal holiness remembers that, at the time of your ordination, you promised blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, by written pledge and the bond of an oath, that when difficulties arose for his holy Church you would labor with all your strength.

Therefore, since we have sent our faithful men, Anastasius, our beloved son and presbyter, and Adeodatus, a regional subdeacon, to plead and, with God’s favor, obtain the restoration of the four fortresses that were taken from blessed Peter last year, and to beseech our sons Luitprand and Hilprand that they be restored, behold, dearest brothers, this is an acceptable time for you, in accordance with your written pledge, to bring the fruit of good works to blessed Peter.

By his authority we exhort you in the Lord to hasten with the aforesaid sons of ours to those kings, so that, inspired by God, they may restore those fortresses to their protectors, the blessed princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul.

For if—which we do not believe—you delay undertaking the journey for God’s sake, I, although I am weak because of bodily illness, shall undertake the arduous journey myself, and I shall see to it that your negligence does not become an obligation upon you through the bond of your agreement.

Given on the Ides of October, in the ninth indiction.

## LETTER OF POPE GREGORY III TO ANTONY OF GRADO

That he should come to Rome for the council.

Gregory III, pontiff, to his beloved brother Antony, archbishop of Grado, or to our most beloved bishops belonging to his ordination or council.

Amid the various persistent miseries that surround and overwhelm us in this world, a vain and pernicious calamity has arisen, which, as though through certain stormy winds, continually disturbs the Church with grave violence, though undertaken without effect.

For there is, as we believe you know, an unhappy impiety at the royal city and throughout the various provinces: the holy images are being cast out of all the churches of the Lord and our Redeemer Jesus Christ, they are being torn apart, and—an ominous evil and intolerable ruin—the churches of God themselves are being turned into dwellings for men and even for vile herds, so that no praise to God should be sung in them.

Therefore, with the prophet, we must say in a lamentable voice: “Who will give water to my head and fountains of tears to my eyes, so that we may weep over so great a ruin?” (Jeremiah IX, 1).

Accordingly, dearest brother and most beloved rectors of God’s Churches, we exhort your love that, for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, following the apostolic voice, you must earnestly admonish and instruct all the Churches subject to you:

“Pay attention,” I say, “dearest brothers, to yourselves and to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his blood,” so that, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers and the venerable antiquity, all may defend the true faith and, if necessary, lay down their holy bodies and shed their blood. For behold, the acceptable day has come; behold, now is the day of salvation.

You know, dearest ones, that the saints through faith conquered kingdoms. Let this be your admonition, brothers, to the whole people of Christ, so that, while defending the Christian king, they may be able through steadfastness of faith to contribute to their own salvation.

But you all, dearest ones, who diligently govern the houses of the Lord, assemble at this apostolic see on the Kalends of November of the coming fifteenth indiction, setting negligence aside, in order that, through common assembly and deliberation, a judgment may be promulgated and established by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, concerning this matter: how we may anticipate the fury of our adversaries and secure the salvation of our souls and of those subject to us; and how we may deserve, for the sake of the saints, to become companions of our predecessors, whose radiant teaching sustains us after the protection of Christ.

May God keep you safe, our most beloved ones.

[Note: [Col. 0587A] The matters relating to this same council include what Muratori published in the epitome of the *Chronicles of Monte Cassino* under the false name of Anastasius the Librarian, *Rerum Italicarum*, volume II. I by no means make myself guarantor of the truth of what is reported there. That writer says as follows:]

Gregory III, moved by zeal for holy religion, decreed in synod with the assembly of priests before the most sacred confession of the most sacred body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Seated with the same supreme and venerable pope were Antony, archbishop of Grado, and John, archbishop of Ravenna, together with ninety-three other bishops or presbyters of the holy Apostolic See [Col. 0588A]; deacons, the entire clergy, the most noble consuls, and all the Roman people were also standing by. It was decreed:

If the people of Arles and Le Mans should disdain to return the holy relics that they had retained until then, they were to be excluded from the body and blood of Christ and from the unity and structure of the whole Church.

After this decree had been issued, he sent written admonitions demanding the return of the most sacred relics, which were likewise despised, as those of his other predecessors had been.

[Note: [Col. 0588A] The matter here concerns the restoration of the sacred relics of Saint Benedict and Scholastica, which, as this historian had related above, had been carried off to Gaul.]

## EXCERPT CONCERNING VARIOUS CRIMES AND THEIR REMEDIES

From the sayings of the Fathers and the judgments of the canons.

## PREFACE

[Col. 0587B]

We observe in the Church something that greatly troubles us: the judgments concerning penitents in the small works of our presbyters have become so confused, so varied and mutually discordant, and so unsupported by any authority, that they can scarcely be distinguished because of their disagreement.

As a result, those who come seeking the remedy of penance cannot be helped at all, both because of the confusion of the books and because of the slowness of their understanding. Therefore, from the many flowers of allegory, from the treatises and published sermons of great men, from the sayings of the Fathers and the judgments of the canons—namely, those of Isidore, Augustine, Gregory, Bede, Gelasius, Innocent, Theodore, Cassian, Egbert, and others—we have taken care to excerpt and gather together this penitential little book for the use of our fellow priests.

It is rightly called penitential because it is suited to penance. “Penance” (*poenitentia*) is so called from *poenitere*, “to repent,” since a person should repent in his heart and blush before God at having sinned. For, with God granting it, the devil can accomplish nothing against us through his wickedness if we desire to perform pure penance—that is, if we do not add wounds to wounds and injure what has been healed, because later wounds are worse than the earlier ones.

This too must be observed: if bodily physicians prescribe various medicines against diseases of the body, how much more ought the priests of God to provide innumerable healing remedies against the unlawful fruits of the works of the flesh?

We say with great fear that some of those like us are so oppressed by the sluggishness of great dullness that they cannot fully bring either their own errors or those of their subjects to light, nor do they know how to comfort those who have fallen by means of the medicine of penance. As we think, Scripture was written concerning such men: “Mute dogs, unable to bark” (Isaiah LVI).

And if the unlearned are advanced to the priesthood, one must consider what becomes of the flocks, when wolves become shepherds. There are also some who seek the priestly burden not for God but—what is wicked to say—rather for earthly profit. Blind men regarding divine wisdom! Concerning such men a certain truthful teacher says: “I fear,” he says, “that dogs are attaining pastoral office.”

After this, we judged it necessary to publish in this penitential little book distinctions of persons, faults, and lengths of time, so that we might carefully agree about how and in what manner and for how long each person should be judged.

Above all, care must be taken that the Lord’s mercy be applied to each sinner, because it is written: “My son, in judging be merciful” (Tobit IV). Hence the Apostle says: “Judgment without mercy will be for the one who has shown no mercy” (James II).

For this reason, the canons do not establish the period of time to be spent in penance for each crime with sufficient precision; rather, they determine that it should be left to the discretion of the bishop or presbyters, because of mercy. For with God the measure of time does not count as much as the measure of sorrow, nor abstinence from food alone as much as the mortification of vices. Therefore they command that the periods of penance be shortened through the faith and conversion of penitents.

We have compressed this letter into a concise style, so that its brevity may remove from the reader the harmful weariness of excessive length and lighten and open the profitable understanding of his heart. A short reading is read more eagerly, understood more quickly, more easily entrusted to memory, and more firmly retained.

It is therefore necessary that faithful priests frequently read this medicinal excerpt and recite it wisely, constantly, and humbly, because in it the health of the heart is found and medicine for the soul is discovered.

For this little book contains great consolation for mourners, blessed hope for the righteous, health for the sick, and strength and refuge for those in danger. Thus the penitent heart is pierced, and a fruitful rain of tears is poured out from it. Forgiveness of sins is promised in it, and refreshment with everlasting glory is happily prepared for those who labor.

For in it is hidden a treasure of wisdom and knowledge, which grants eternal life to faithful penitents and remains perpetually open for those who mourn without ceasing.

We do not wish, brothers, to place the lamp kindled within us under a bushel, but to set it upon a lofty lampstand, so that it may shine for all the brothers who are in the house of God.

May the grace of him who undertook this labor and work come upon us—he who joined himself as a third companion on the road to the two disciples who were traveling and opened their minds so that they might understand the holy Scriptures.

May the Paraclete Spirit, with every virtue and perfect teaching together with knowledge of charity, enlighten our hearts, most gracious brothers.

Lord God, heavenly King, who willed that we, your unworthy servants, should be placed over the holy Church so that we might console penitents and mourners with suitable medicine, mercifully grant that we may enjoy lasting health of body and soul here, and again happily share in the rewards of the heavenly kingdom. May the people continually rejoice through the salutary remedies handed down by our predecessors, and may the entire choir of heaven, together with us, joyfully sing eternal praises to the one whom it serves.

Let this letter be despised by no one; let everyone know that it has been gathered by our elders from the judgments of the saints and excerpted by us, lest its excessive length produce weariness in negligent readers.

## HERE BEGIN THE APPROPRIATE JUDGMENTS FOR PENITENTS

### I.

[Note: [Col. 0589D] This excerpt is from Cassian, *Collection* 20, chapter 8, and from others. HARD.]

The first is the remission by which we are baptized in water; the second, the effect of charity; the third, the fruit of almsgiving; the fourth, the pouring forth of tears; the fifth, affliction of heart and body; the sixth, amendment of conduct, that is, renunciation of vices; the seventh, the intercession of the saints; the eighth, the merit of mercy and faith; the ninth, the conversion and salvation of others; the tenth, our indulgence and remission; the eleventh, the suffering of martyrdom, the sole hope of salvation, when the forgiving God replied to the crucified thief, saying: “Truly I say to you: today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII).

[Note: [Col. 0589D] I have emended this reading from the *Penitential* that I attributed above to Bede, since the older reading, “the indulgence of salvation,” was less suitable in the Lord’s reply to the bloody thief: “Amen,” and so forth. MANSI.]

## II.

Sacrilege—that is, the theft of sacred things—is the greatest sin. A sacrilegious person is one who violates sacred things or steals them. According to the more lenient definition, it was decreed that those who fall into this vice should do penance as follows: if he is a bishop, twelve years; a presbyter, ten; a deacon, seven; a subdeacon, five; clerics and laypeople, four. Yet it must be considered very carefully, and the Lord’s mercy must be applied, as blessed Gregory himself added. For the character of the thief must be taken into account, so that one may judge how he can be corrected. Some have resources and commit theft; others offend in this matter from poverty. Therefore some must be corrected by restitution, others by beatings, some more strictly, as has been judged, and others more lightly. When the correction is somewhat stricter, it must be carried out from charity, not in anger, because this is done for the one being corrected, lest he be handed over to the fires of Gehenna.

## III.

Whoever kills a bishop, presbyter, or deacon is to be handed over to the king for judgment. Whoever kills a cleric of a lower order is to be judged by the bishop’s court, so that he may lay aside arms and serve God in a monastery, or do penance for seven years with mourning. If a cleric commits homicide, he shall do penance for ten years, and for seven of those years he shall live in exile. Whoever kills his father or mother, sister or brother, shall, according to the more lenient definition, do penance for fourteen years, and for seven of those years shall live in exile.

If a layman kills another layman, he shall abstain from the church for forty days and, according to the ancient definition, do penance for five years; if it was conceived in hatred, four; if in anger, three; for vengeance on behalf of a brother, two; if by accident, one. The one who kills in battle, and so forth.

If a woman, inflamed by jealous anger, beats her maidservant with whips so that she gives up her life in torment within three days, she shall do penance for seven years if she did it intentionally, five if by accident. But if she falls ill during the appointed period, she shall receive communion.

## IV.

Adultery is committed when someone violates another man’s wife or a nun. An adulterer is called the violator of marital chastity, because he defiles another man’s marriage-bed. If a bishop commits adultery, he shall do penance for twelve years; a presbyter, ten; a deacon, seven; a subdeacon, five; clerics and laypeople, three.

But if the matter becomes known to the people, they are to be expelled from the church and do penance among laypeople as long as they live. If a woman commits adultery with the knowledge of her husband, and he consents to live with her, it was decreed that communion should not be given to them even at the end of their lives. But if he abandons her, she may receive communion after the fifth year.

If a man, or a woman, remains adulterous until the end of his or her life with another woman, or she with another man, it was decreed that communion should not be received even at the end of life.

## V.

If a bishop commits fornication, he shall, according to the more lenient definition, do penance for seven years; a presbyter, five; a deacon, four; a subdeacon, three; clerics and laypeople, two.

If they understand that they have committed adultery with a nun, then, according to the ancient ordinance, additional fasting is to be imposed: a bishop shall do penance for ten years; a presbyter, seven; a deacon, five; a subdeacon, four; clerics and laypeople, three.

Those who frequently commit fornication, whether clerics, laypeople, or women, were judged by the first canon to do penance for seven years. But if they obey, the more lenient authorities have determined that their penance should last three years.

## VI.

The following is found in the canon of Neocaesarea:

“It was decreed that if anyone lusts after a woman, even if his lust includes desire, but the effects do not follow, it is clear that he has been delivered by divine grace. It is ridiculous that someone should be found condemned for touching, kissing, or embracing women.”

## VII.

If anyone commits perjury at an altar where relics are kept, or on the Gospel, he shall, according to the ancient definition, do penance for seven years. Whoever leads another who is ignorant into perjury shall likewise do penance for seven years. Whoever was led into it in ignorance and afterward recognizes what happened shall do penance for two years. Whoever suspects that he is being led into perjury but nevertheless swears by his consent shall likewise do penance for two years.

If anyone is compelled by necessity to swear on account of any fault, he shall do penance for three years. If anyone swears upon the hand of a bishop or presbyter, or upon a consecrated cross, he shall, according to the ancient definition, do penance for three years. The more lenient authorities have defined one year.

## VIII.

According to the ancient definition, it was decreed that if a bishop, presbyter, or deacon habitually suffers from the vice of drunkenness, he must either desist or be deposed. The more lenient authorities, however, have determined that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who vomits because of drunkenness shall do penance for forty days, and clerics and laypeople who do so for seven days.

If a presbyter or deacon, because of illness or because he has abstained for a long time, though it is not his custom to eat and drink much, has done this from joy at the Nativity of the Lord or Easter, or at least in commemoration of some saint, and has nevertheless taken no more than the elders decreed, it has done him no harm.

Absolutely anyone who becomes so drunk that his state of mind is altered, his tongue stammers, his eyes are clouded, and pain follows from the distension of his stomach, and who then vomits the Eucharist, shall do penance as follows: a bishop, ninety days; a presbyter, seventy; a deacon, forty; a subdeacon, twenty; clerics and laypeople, ten.

If dogs eat such vomit, they shall do penance for one hundred days; if they did not know what it was, forty. If illness compelled him to do this, the matter is to be left to the Lord’s judgment.

Whoever compels someone to become drunk under the pretext of human kindness shall do penance as a drunkard. If he did so out of hatred or some wickedness, he shall do penance according to the priest’s judgment, namely, forty days.

## IX.

If anyone commits major theft—that is, steals gold, silver, or four-footed animals, or breaks into houses—then, if he can return what he unjustly took, his penance is greatly shortened; otherwise, he shall do penance for five years. If he has done this repeatedly, he shall do penance for seven years. The more lenient authorities have defined three years.

If a boy over ten years old commits theft, he shall do penance for forty or twenty days, according to his age and the quality of his instruction. For a small theft, he shall do penance for twenty days. A ten-year-old boy who commits some theft shall do penance for seven days.

## X.

It was decreed that when landowners receive their accounts, they must not record as received anything that has been given to an idol. If they do so after the prohibition, they are to be excluded from communion for a period of five years.

## XI.

Those who perpetrate an illicit sexual union are called incestuous. They are called incestuous as though “unchaste” (*incasti*). Such persons are called incestuous if a son has intercourse with his mother; a brother with his sister; someone marries his stepmother or a female relative; a male cousin with his female cousin or with his sister’s daughter; someone has intercourse with his uncle’s or paternal uncle’s widow; someone defiles himself by intercourse with his stepdaughter; or a man has two sisters, or a woman two brothers.

If a son commits so dreadful and unnatural a vice [more precisely, “so abominable a vice”] with his mother, then, according to the ancient definition, he shall do penance for fifteen years, unarmed, with weeping and mourning; he shall never take a wife; for seven of those years he shall live in exile beyond the borders of that land; and he shall not receive communion except when the danger of death is imminent.

If he commits it with his daughter or sister, he shall be subject to a similar sentence. If he commits it with his niece, mother, or any of those named above, then, according to the paternal definition, he shall submit to twelve years of penance [possibly: “do penance for twelve years”], never take a wife, and, as a man, lay aside arms and go into exile. He shall not receive communion except when the danger of death is imminent.

If a woman has two brothers, or a man two sisters, they are to abstain from communion until death; at the point of death, however, communion is to be given to them out of mercy. If they survive after receiving communion and recover from their illness, they are to perform full penance for the period established in the same council.

If, after his wife’s death, a man marries her sister, and she is a believer, it was decreed that he should abstain from communion for five years, unless perhaps the necessity of illness compels peace to be granted sooner.

## XII.

An informer is so called because he uncovers what was hidden. If a believing informer causes someone, through his denunciation, to be proscribed [read: *proscriptus*] or killed, it was decreed that he should not receive communion even at the end of his life. If the case was a lesser one, he could receive communion within five years. The more lenient authorities, however, have determined that communion may be received after three years.

## XIII.

A false witness shall be excluded from communion according to the gravity of his crime. If the charge he brings is not a capital one, but he is unable to prove the crime he has alleged, he shall be excluded for two years. If he proves it, then, after consulting the clergy, it was decreed that he should be excluded for five years.

## XIV.

If anyone attacks a bishop, presbyter, or deacon with false accusations and cannot prove them, we have judged that communion should not be given to him even at the end of his life.

## XV.

Peace drives out hatred. Whoever hates his brother must be reconciled with him. Let each person know that, for as long as he keeps hatred in his heart, he must submit to penance on bread and water for the same length of time. For “if a man harbors anger against another man, he cannot seek healing from God” (Ecclesiasticus 28:3). The Lord says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Luke 6).

## XVI.

[Note: [Col. 0591] Bede, *On Remedies for Sins*, title “On Auguries.” Burchard, book X, chapter 9. HARD.]

Augurs are those who pay attention to the flights or cries of birds. Diviners (*harioli*) are those who sacrifice around the altars of idols. Auspices are the signs observed by travelers.

If anyone practices auguries, auspices, or divinations; or makes a vow outside the church; or practices divination in incantations—which is wholly diabolical—let them do penance for three years. The more lenient authorities have defined two years, one year, or half a year according to the character of the sinners.

## XVII.

If a woman commits fornication and kills the child born from it; if she attempts to cause an abortion and kill what has been conceived; or if she takes measures not to conceive, whether from adultery or from a lawful marriage, earlier canons decreed that such women should receive communion only at death. We, however, out of mercy, judge that such women, and those who are aware of their crimes, should perform penance for ten years.

If a poor woman kills her own child [Note: [Col. 0593D] This confused reading is corrected by the anonymous *Penitential*. MANSI.—See this *Penitential* among the works of St. Egbert. EDIT.], the canon says that her penance should last seven years.

A woman who conceives and kills a son or daughter in the womb before forty days shall do penance as a homicide. If the child died without baptism through her fault, she shall do penance for three years; without fault, for three periods of forty days.

Those women who negligently suffocate their children shall do penance as murderers; otherwise, the matter shall depend upon the priest’s judgment.

## XVIII.

If anyone corrupts a virgin and afterward does not take her as his wife, or attempts such an outrage upon another man’s betrothed, he shall, according to the ancient definition, do penance for five years. The more lenient authorities, however, have defined three years.

[Note: [Col. 0593D] A remedy for this corrupt reading is supplied by the Isidorian canon 24 of Ancyra, whose words are these: “If someone, having a betrothed woman, perhaps uses violence against her sister and clings to her as though she were his own; but after deceiving her, he takes the betrothed woman as his wife; while the woman who suffered the outrage,” etc. Gregory took the canon from the *Penitential* which I have attributed to Bede. In it, because the words “but after deceiving her” are incorrectly rendered as “but after deceiving this woman,” Gregory likewise retained the same error. MANSI.]

If anyone perhaps commits an offence [the text is defective] against the sister of another man’s betrothed [Note: [Col. 0594D] This is how it appears in the earlier Royal edition and in the Labbe edition. Perhaps it should read: “and has committed fornication with her sister,” etc. HARD.], and clings to her as though she were his own, and joins her to himself as one to be sought for himself, but afterward takes the betrothed woman as his wife, while this woman has been deceived [the transmitted wording is corrupt]; and if the woman who suffered the outrage perhaps takes her own life, all who were aware of this deed shall do penance for ten years according to the institution of the canons. Some, however, have defined seven years.

## XIX.

Concerning those who, in apostasy, have been rebaptized without any necessity: it was decreed that the provisions established at Nicaea should be observed concerning them—that is, that they should remain seven years among the catechumens and two among the laypeople, and afterward, through the moderation and clemency shown to the faithful, share in the offering and the Eucharist.

## XX.

If any cleric or layperson is caught demolishing tombs, because this crime is called a bloody one under the public laws on account of its sacrilegious character, the person exposed in such wickedness must be removed from the clerical order and assigned three years of penance.

## XXI.

If anyone ordained to sacred office is defiled by the Sodomite crime—a vice described as so abominable before God that even the cities of such people are said to have been overturned by fire and sulfur—he shall, according to the ancient ordinance, do penance for ten years. Some have defined seven years more leniently.

Those who do not know the force of this disgrace have prescribed three years of penance. Boys who know how to practice it must hasten to amend their ways: they shall do penance for fifty days and in addition be beaten, because it is necessary to cut down the crop that grows up wickedly.

## XXII.

If a man over twenty years old who has a wife falls into this most foul vice, and has intercourse with a heifer, he shall do penance for ten years. Its milk must not be consumed, nor its flesh eaten, but both are to be given to dogs.

With other animals, according to the more lenient definition, younger and less capable persons shall do penance for seven years, or three, or one.

## XXIII.

[Note: [Col. 0594D] See Burchard, book X, chapter 14.]

Maleficia are evil practices which, whether performed or believed in, torment their authors and drag them down to the depths unless they repent.

If a male or female practitioner of magic places his or her son or daughter on a roof or in a furnace to cure fevers; or, when the moon is eclipsed, trusts that he or she can defend himself or herself by cries or by magical practices of sacrilegious use; or presumes, according to pagan custom, to render honour in connexion with Jupiter, Bel, or Janus [the preceding word is corrupt: *frater*, perhaps *fertur*], it was decreed according to the ancient ordinance that the person should do penance for six years. The more lenient authorities have judged three years.

## XXIV.

If anyone is violently defiled through an assault upon the mind, he shall do penance for seven days, or until the thought is overcome.

Whoever is polluted willingly in sleep shall rise and sing seven penitential psalms while kneeling, namely, “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger,” and the others; and in the morning he shall sing thirty psalms.

If someone wishes to sin in sleep but is polluted without willing it, he shall sing twelve psalms. One who sins but is not polluted shall sing thirteen psalms. One who sins in sleep and is polluted as a result of a thought shall sing twenty-two psalms; if he sins in sleep without a thought, he shall sing twelve psalms.

If he emits semen while sleeping in a church, he shall sing the Psalter, or do penance for three days. If he voluntarily emits semen in a church through an evil thought, then, if he is a cleric, he shall do penance for fourteen days; a deacon, twenty-two; a presbyter, forty; a bishop, fifty.

But in the same illusion there is a very necessary distinction, which must be carefully considered. For this happens to the sleeping mind sometimes from gluttony, sometimes from an excess of nature, sometimes from necessity, and sometimes from illness. In every case this illusion is not to be feared, because the mind endured it without knowing.

## XXV.

A man should not approach a woman during her menstrual period; if he does so, he shall do penance for forty days.

Women should not enter a church during their menstrual period. If they presume to do so, some Fathers have determined that they should do penance for three weeks.

But a woman who suffers from her customary menstrual flow should not be forbidden to enter the church, because the excess of nature cannot rightly be counted as her fault, and it is not just that she be deprived of entry into the church because of what she suffers unwillingly.

For we know that the woman who suffered from a flow of blood came humbly behind the Lord, touched the fringe of his garment, and was immediately freed from her illness. If, therefore, a woman suffering from a flow of blood could rightly touch the Lord’s garments, why should a woman who suffers from menstrual blood not be permitted to enter the Lord’s church?

If, then, the woman who touched the Lord’s garment while afflicted by illness rightly presumed to do so, why should what is granted to one person because of illness not be granted to all women who suffer from the weakness of their nature?

Women should not be forbidden to receive the mystery of holy communion during those same days. If, out of great reverence, a woman does not presume to receive it, she is to be praised; but if she does receive it, she is not to be condemned. For menstruation is not any fault in women, since it occurs naturally.

## XXVI.

Whoever sacrifices to demons in minor matters—that is, at springs or trees—shall do penance for one year. Whoever sacrifices to demons in magical devices shall, according to canonical ordinance, do penance for ten years. The more lenient authorities have defined seven years.

In my opinion, to sacrifice to demons in magical devices means to believe in their most shameful imaginings, or to profess knowledge of divination through certain things falsely called “the lots of the saints,” whether in incantations, characters, or objects of any kind that are hung up or bound. In all these things the art of demons arises from a certain deadly alliance between human beings and evil angels. Therefore Christians must avoid them and utterly reject and condemn them with every form of abhorrence.

## XXVII.

If a believing man who has a wife commits adultery with a Jewish or pagan woman, he shall be excluded from communion. If someone else exposes him, then after five years, once he has completed lawful penance, he may be admitted to the Lord’s communion.

## XXVIII.

[Note: [Col. 0595D] Among the Chapters of Theodore of Canterbury, chapter 57. HARD.]

If anyone loses the Eucharist—that is, the sacrifice—through negligence, he shall do penance for one year or for three periods of forty days. If it falls to the ground through negligence, he shall sing fifty psalms.

Whoever neglects the sacrifice so that worms are found in it, or it has lost its color and taste, shall do penance for thirty or twenty days, and it shall be burned.

Whoever spills the chalice at the end of the solemn Mass shall do penance for forty days. If the chalice drips upon the altar, the minister shall suck up the drop and do penance for three days. The linens touched by the drop shall be washed three times, with the chalice placed beneath them, and the water used for the washing shall be cast into the fire.

## XXIX.

We call something “suffocated” when it is killed without the shedding of blood, or when it is strangled in a snare. If anyone finds an animal suffocated by a wolf, dog, or snare, it must not be eaten under any circumstances. No one should presume to eat or drink the blood of any animal. If anyone does so, he shall do penance for forty days.

## XXX.

If anyone, though not ordained, presumptuously baptizes, he is to be rejected both from the Church and from ordination, and he must never be ordained.

If a bishop or presbyter denies penance or baptism, he will be guilty concerning souls, for the Lord says: “On whatever day the sinner turns, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezekiel 33).

If necessary, each person may make his confession privately to God alone.

If anyone renounces the world and afterward returns to secular life, he shall, according to the ancient definition, do penance for seven years.

If anyone contemptuously disregards an appointed fast contrary to the decrees of the elders, he shall do penance for forty days; if he does so during Lent, for a full year.

If anyone disregards the Council of Nicaea and celebrates Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon, he shall be expelled from the whole Church until his death unless he performs penance.

If anyone fasts on the Lord’s Day through negligence, he must abstain for the entire week. If he repeats this, he shall do penance for forty days.

If a woman has intercourse with another woman, she shall do penance for four periods of forty days. Effeminate men shall do penance for one year.

If a man has intercourse with his wife from behind, he must be admonished not to do so and must do penance for himself.

If a woman enters the church before the blood has been cleansed, because this is not customary, she shall do penance for forty days.

If she marries during these periods, she shall do penance for twenty days.

Whoever marries on the Lord’s Day shall ask God’s forgiveness and do penance for one or three days.

Whoever disparages his brother out of envy, or willingly listens to one who disparages him, shall do penance for seven days.

If a cleric practices hunting, he shall do penance for one year; a deacon, two; a presbyter, three.

If anyone strikes or injures another in anger, he shall do penance for forty days.

If anyone intentionally burns another person’s field or house with fire, he shall, according to the ancient definition, do penance for three years.

If anyone intentionally cuts off another person’s limb, he shall do penance for three years. The more lenient authorities have defined one year.

Whoever eats carrion unknowingly shall do penance for twenty days; knowingly, forty.

Whoever eats stolen food, knowing it to be stolen, shall, if he is poor or mentally deficient, do penance for seven days; healthy persons who know what they are doing, forty days; those who do this repeatedly, three periods of forty days.

Whoever eats or drinks something soiled by a dog or mouse shall sing fifty psalms; a layperson shall do penance for three days.

Whoever gives someone a liquid in which a dead mouse or weasel is found shall do penance for seven days. Whoever later discovers that he has drunk such a beverage shall sing the Psalter; a layperson shall do penance for three days.

If a dead mouse or weasel is found in flour, in any dry food, in honey, oil, or curdled milk, whatever is around its body shall be thrown away. After the remainder has been sprinkled with holy water, it may be consumed with a sound mind.

If a dead fish is found in a fishpond, it must not be eaten under any circumstances; and if anyone eats it, he shall do penance for seven days (Burchard, XIX, 106).

## XXXI.

If, by accident, while the priest invited to him is on his way, a man is overcome by illness and loses the power of speech, or is found in a state of delirium, those who heard him are to testify, and he is then to receive penance. If he is immediately believed to be dying, the Eucharist is to be poured into his mouth, and the matter left to the Lord’s judgment.

If he survives, the witnesses mentioned above are to inform him that his request has been fulfilled, and he is to be subjected to the period of penance (Burchard, XVIII, 10).

## XXXII.

It was likewise decreed that no commemoration at the offering is to be made for those who inflict death upon themselves, whether by sword, poison, jumping from a height, hanging, or any other form of violence; nor are their bodies to be carried to burial with psalms. For many have arrogated this to themselves through ignorance. The same was decreed concerning those who are punished for their crimes.

## XXXIII.

If a bishop, presbyter, or deacon has been unjustly expelled from his rank and is found innocent at a second synod, he cannot remain as he was unless he receives back the rank he lost.
