If he was a bishop, he is to receive before the altar, from the hands of the bishops, the stole and chasuble. If a deacon, the stole and alb; a subdeacon, the paten and chalice. Likewise, the remaining ranks are to receive, for their restoration, the things they received when they were ordained.

[Note: [Col. 0597A] We have appended, as especially appropriate to this place, the little penitential book compiled from the holy Fathers and the canons of ancient councils by the Venerable Bede, as they maintain, under the judgments of Pope Gregory III. But since a royal compiler attached it to the excerpts of Egbert, archbishop of York, in the Luparea edition, we did not wish to disturb its order, contenting ourselves with this advance notice. We have also added in the margins of the pages several items selected from the annotations of Antonius Augustinus, archbishop of Tarragona. We likewise added Egbert’s brief dialogue on ecclesiastical discipline, in the form of questions and answers, published in Dublin in 1664 together with two letters of Bede by Sir John Ware. LABBE.—We provide the penitential books to which the preceding annotator alludes: one among the works of St. Egbert in this same volume, and the other among the works of the Venerable Bede contained in the following volumes. EDIT.]

# In the Year of Our Lord 747: Saint Boniface, Bishop of Mainz and Martyr

[Col. 0597]

## Historical Notice on Saint Boniface

*(Fabricius, Library of the Middle and Later Ages.)*

[Col. 0597C] Saint Boniface, Winfridus, an Englishman from Devon, of the Benedictine order, archbishop of Mainz from 745 to 754, and apostle of the Germans. For whatever others accomplished before him, the chief glory for defending and restoring the Christian religion throughout Germany belongs to the emperor Charlemagne and Boniface.

Boniface certainly taught the Christian faith to all the peoples between the Rhine and the Weser, especially the Frisians. Those who had already accepted the Christian rites he strengthened, and he established ecclesiastical discipline and laws for them.

This is truly what Hermann Conring says in volume II of his works, page 701. The illustrious Hermann von Bünau should be added, in volume II of his *History of the German Empire*, published in German, page 295. On page 300, in a note, he also says that this Boniface first anointed Pepin, king of the Franks, in the year 752; Pope Stephen III anointed him again in 754, after the Franks had been absolved from the obligation of homage owed to Childeric III.

Concerning this Boniface, see above all the *Acta Sanctorum*, 5 June, volume I, pages 452ff. There, besides the Life written by Willibald, one finds on page 477 another written by a presbyter of Saint Martin of Utrecht, and on page 481 one written by a certain monk of Münster.

Othlonus’s work, in which he presented Willibald’s account in a more accessible style and divided it into two books, is also found in Surius, 5 June.

See also Nicolaus Serarius, book III of his *History of Mainz*, together with the notes of Georg Christian Joannis upon it. See also the Life of Saint Sturm by Surius, 17 December; that of Saint Lebuin, 12 November; and that of Saint Willibrord, 7 November, as well as the authors whom I cited in my book *On the Propagation of the Light of the Gospel*, chapter 19.

The 151 letters of Saint Boniface, written to him or by him, were published with notes by Nicolaus Serarius, Mainz, 1605, in quarto, and in the Paris and Cologne collections of the Fathers, supplement, volume II, page 48, and volume VIII, and in the Lyon collection, volume XIII.

A letter to Pope Zacharias, in the year 745, concerning the case of Adelbert the Gaul and Clement the Scot, is found in Usher’s *Irish Letters*, page 44, together with Zacharias’s letters to Boniface.

Thirty-six statutes from an ancient canonical collection in the manuscript of the monastery of Corbie are found in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, volume IX, page 63, and in the new edition, volume I, pages 507 and 509.

I shall shortly speak below of the Life of Saint Livinus, whom Mabillon considers one hundred years older than Boniface.

A letter to Erchebald, king of England, is found in Werner Rolevinck, book I of *On the Customs and Situation of Westphalia*, chapter 7.

Oudinus, volume I, page 1789, mentions six sermons copied by Mabillon from a codex belonging to Queen Christina.

[Note: [Col. 0597] Add Mabillon, *Analecta*, page 207 of the new folio edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0599] He made fifteen of Boniface’s sermons public in P. Martène, *Ancient Monuments*, volume IX, page 187, and elsewhere. From these, however, the fifteenth sermon might easily be thought to be entirely identical with the fifth, since the same matters recur in both in the same order and often in the same words, although some other material is interspersed in one that is not found in the other. Since the individual letters of Saint Boniface bear erroneous dates in the printed editions, I investigated the matter in a written dissertation. It is found in the *Supplement to the Councils*, volume I, page 551. MANSI.]

[Col. 0599]

## Preliminary Observations on the Following Two Lives of Saint Boniface

*(Mabillon, Benedictine Acts of the Saints, century III, part 2.)*

### 1.

The man whom the Anglo-Saxons called Winfrid or Winfreth in their native language, and whom the Latins later called Bonefacius or Bonifacius, with a softer pronunciation, has been commended by various writers.

The first to appear is Willibald, his disciple, who was himself, as it seems, the first bishop of Eichstätt and who composed his teacher’s deeds in a separate book.

Next, the monk Ruthard, sent from Fulda to Hirsau, wrote the passion of the holy martyr in two books in heroic verse, as Trithemius reports in the *Chronicle of Hirsau*.

Ruthard flourished during the reign of Louis Augustus. When Louis wished to appoint Ruthard bishop of the Church of Halberstadt in place of Bishop Haimo after Haimo’s death, Ruthard refused to consent, uttering this memorable statement:

“Give the bishopric to someone suitable. I have judged the quiet of the regular life and the study of the Scriptures incomparably preferable to all the riches and honors of the world.”

The third author of a Life of Boniface is Othlonus, a monk. The fourth is a certain anonymous writer, apparently a monk of the monastery of Fulda.

Here we present two accounts of Saint Boniface, namely those of Willibald and Othlonus, because both seem necessary for a complete knowledge of his deeds.

In addition, the following authors discuss Saint Boniface: Lupus, in the *Acts of Saint Wigbert the Abbot*; Lieudger, in the *Life of Saint Gregory, Abbot and Rector of the Church of Utrecht*; Ratbod, bishop of that same church, according to Trithemius in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; John Gerbrand, John of Beka, and Willem Heda in their histories. Rabanus Maurus is to be preferred to these, for he composed a poem about Saint Boniface.

Among the Lutherans, too, John Lezner published and illustrated the Acts of the same holy martyr in German.

A few preliminary remarks must be made here about Willibald, Othlonus, and the anonymous author.

### 2.

Willibald, the principal author of the Life of Boniface, indicates his period in the preface that he dedicates to Megingoz, bishop of Würzburg, and Lullus, bishop of Mainz, disciples of Boniface. There he calls himself a presbyter.

This gives rise to the question whether this Willibald is the same as Willibald, the first bishop of Eichstätt and likewise a disciple of Boniface, especially since the author of this Life, when discussing the episcopal ordination of Willibald and Burchard, calls them “men of good industry,” perhaps speaking more modestly of himself if he himself had been that Willibald.

Christoph Brower, in his observations on the Acts of Saint Gregory, rector of Utrecht, introduces other arguments into this question, though they are of less importance.

Nevertheless, I believe that Willibald, bishop of Eichstätt, was the author of this work. After spending only a few years with Boniface, he says in the preface that he reports things received from others rather than things he himself witnessed.

Nor is there any objection in the fact that he uses only the name “presbyter,” for Notker likewise attributes only that title to him in his *Martyrology* on the Nones of June.

Nor does he exceed the bounds of modesty when he calls both himself and Burchard “men of good industry,” since he used this praise more to commend Boniface, who ordained them, and Burchard, than to commend himself.

Finally, at the end of the Life he wrote, he himself added this clause: “I, Willibald, bishop,” and so forth.

### 3.

Othlonus belonged to a later period. He performed valuable work in illuminating the deeds of Saint Boniface, collecting and reporting letters of Boniface himself and of others that seemed relevant to the matter.

The name Othlonus, which had long been hidden, was discovered by Henricus Canisius in the manuscript codex of the monastery of Rebdorf, in these words:

“Here begins the prologue of the venerable presbyter Othlonus and M. S. of the monastery of Boniface concerning his Life”—that is, as Canisius conjectured, “of the monk of the monastery of Saint Boniface.”

That Othlonus was a monk is sufficiently clear from the preface, since he not only calls the monks of Fulda “brothers,” but also says that he and they were made lowly and became a spectacle to the world.

He was German by nation, as is clear from book I, chapter 38: “I speak of what Boniface wrote for the salvation of our fathers, namely the Germans.”

He does not, however, seem to have been a monk of Fulda, since, addressing the monks of Fulda in the preface, he calls it “your monastery.” Nevertheless, he came from some monastery of Saint Boniface, whom he calls “our Patron.”

Othlonus lived around the beginning of the twelfth century, according to the prologue of the Life, which he divided into two books.

### 4.

Leaving Ruthard aside, whose two books have not yet appeared in print, a few remarks must be made about the anonymous author. His work, in the manuscript codex of Compiègne, begins with these words:

“After the illustrious nation of the English, through the teachings of Saint Gregory, pontiff of the city of Rome, …”

It did not seem worthwhile to reproduce that work in full, both because it is deficient in many respects and because it is riddled with certain errors.

For it describes Boniface’s single journey from Britain into Frisia, omitting his return to his homeland. It also postpones Boniface’s first journey to Rome until after he had labored with Saint Willibrord.

Nevertheless, we cite certain passages from that author in the notes and in the appendix to the first Life.

### 5.

The writers of the ancient calendars—Wandalbert, Usuard, Rabanus, Ado, and Notker—praise the holiness of Boniface.

These are Wandalbert’s words for the Nones of June:

> On the Nones, Boniface the bishop shines forth, born  
> Among the English, who drew the children of Ocean to Christ,
Submitting the necks of the Frisians to the pure laver.

6. That Boniface was an Anglo-Saxon, not a Scot born in Ireland, as Marianus and Trithemius maintain, [Col. 0601A] is established both by the words of Wandalbert quoted above and by Boniface’s own Acts and letters. His letter is read in Othlonus, book II, chapter 1, in which Boniface writes as follows:

“The synod and Church in which I was born and brought up—that is, in transmarine Saxony, or West Saxony—whose bishop was Daniel, from whom he received letters of recommendation to the Roman pontiff.”

Therefore Boniface was born in western Saxony, specifically in the present county of Devon, in the town of Crediton, called Cridiantum, Crediton, or Kirton. It was once an episcopal see and lies about six miles from Exeter. William Camden and John Speed affirm this, on the basis of local tradition and living memory, in their description of Devon.

7. It is not worth the trouble—and certainly not proper—to investigate by empty conjectures the parents of Boniface, whom the silence of the ancients has left unknown to us. Those who assign him royal ancestry and call him a kinsman of Saints Willibald and Winebald rely on no legitimate evidence. What is established is the report of the anonymous author of his Life: Boniface was born of noble lineage and was related by kinship to the nun Leobgitha. Thus Leobgitha writes in a certain letter to Boniface, numbered 36 among the Bonifacian letters:

“I ask your kindness to remember the former friendship which long ago you formed with my father, whose name is Tinne in the western regions and who was taken from this life eight years ago. Do not refuse to offer prayers to God for his soul. I also commend to you the memory of my mother, called Ebbe, who, as you know well, is related to you by ties of blood; she is still living with difficulty and has long been grievously afflicted by illness. I am the only daughter of both my parents.”

This is Leobgitha, also called Lioba, who, summoned into Germany by Saint Boniface and placed over the nunnery at Bischofsheim, flourished in holiness of life, as we shall see in her Acts under the year 767.

8. Willibald and Othlonus deny that Boniface was an abbot in his homeland. Yet the nun Egburga addresses Letter 101 to the holy abbot and true friend Winfred. If this is correct, it is clear that he held the dignity of abbot for a short time before crossing a second time into Frisia. After he had already settled in the lands across the sea and had been ordained archbishop without a fixed see, King Sigebald of the West Saxons wrote him Letter 49 in these words:

“First, with suppliant prayers—as though prostrating myself and bending my knees—I beg you to grant my request, which I asked of you through your priest named Eobo: namely, that you be my bishop together with my bishop Daniel.”

Nevertheless, he refused this dignity, lest he fail in the conversion of the pagans.

9. Boniface appears to have been ordained bishop by Gregory II, Roman pontiff, without a fixed see. Yet Willibald repeatedly mentions the diocese and churches entrusted to Boniface before the holy man was attached to the see of Mainz. After receiving [Col. 0601D] his archiepiscopal ordination, and after his fruitful work among the Hessi and Bavarians, Boniface is said, in chapter 8, to have gone to the brothers of his diocese, and, in chapter 9, to have returned to his own churches and cared for the people entrusted to him. This certainly cannot be said of the see of Utrecht, which Saint Willibrord, still alive at that time, occupied. It seems more correctly interpreted of the Hessi, Thuringians, and neighboring regions, to which Boniface had been sent especially.

Indeed, from a letter of Zacharias reported by Othlonus in book II, chapter 14, we learn that up to this point—that is, shortly before the year 751—Boniface had claimed no cathedral see for himself. Hincmar also confirms this in Letter, or booklet, 44, chapter 20:

“Gregory II, and also Gregory III, sent Winfrid, surnamed Boniface, legate of the Apostolic See, first ordained priest and afterward bishop, to reform the Christian religion. For twenty-five years he labored in the same preaching without a cardinal see. His successor, Pope Zacharias, among other things, wrote and confirmed in the privilege addressed to him that he should have a place: Mainz, namely, whose see he obtained after Gewilieb had been deposed.”

Yet there is one difficulty: after Boniface had become archbishop of the Church of Mainz, he is said to have ordained Gregory at Utrecht, both by Othlonus, book I, chapter 38, and by Saint Liudger in the Life of Gregory himself. For, according to Liudger’s words, Boniface is said to have succeeded Willibrord, and Gregory Boniface, in the governance of the Church of Utrecht:

“When Saint Willibrord departed from this life to the Lord, Saint Boniface succeeded him, and the devout Gregory succeeded him.”

Greater weight, however, seems due to the contemporary Willibald, who in chapter 10 makes no mention of Gregory’s promotion, and in chapter 11 speaks of Saint Eoban, companion in martyrdom, whom Boniface, to assist the weakness of his old age, appointed bishop among the Frisians in the city called Utrecht. Eoban therefore truly governed the Church of Utrecht, although only for a short time, after the death of Saint Willibrord, when it was subject to Boniface’s care; and he had as his successor Saint Gregory—not as bishop, but as abbot and rector of the Church of Utrecht, as we shall say in his Acts under the year 772. Boniface addresses Letter 27 to Eoban, and King Sigebald of the West Saxons calls him a priest in Letter 49.

10. The Germans acknowledge Boniface as their apostle. On this subject one should read Adam, canon of Bremen, in chapter 8 of his history. The preface prefixed to this age should also be read. For Boniface preached the word of God not only to the Frisians but also to the eastern Franks, Thuringians, Hessi, and Saxons, indeed also to the Bavarians, both personally and through his followers.

Pope Gregory II, in a certain letter, additionally names the Borthari, Nistresi, Wedrevi, and Lognai, the Sudvodi, Ingevones, and Graveldi, peoples belonging to the provinces mentioned above. The Borthari seem to be the Bructeri, or Busactores, settled between the rivers Lippe and Ems. The Nistresi are the western Frisians inhabiting West-Rachia. The Wedrevi, or Wederavi, occupied the district called Wederavia along the river Werra near Mainz. The Lognai were inhabitants of Wederavia along the river Logana. The Sudvodi were Austrasian peoples. The Ingevones are thought to be the inland and interior Germans. The Graveldi, or Grapfeldi, were the clearers of the Buchonian forest, in which the monastery of Fulda was built, situated among four peoples whom Boniface brought to the faith.

11. Boniface cared for monastic affairs only slightly less than for Christian affairs, since he knew that the former were both an aid and an ornament to the latter. Therefore, when he sent to his native province and homeland, he caused many religious women and men, instructed in various kinds of knowledge, to come from there, and divided among them the burden of his labor, says Othlonus in book I, chapter 25. He entrusted monasteries of monks to the men and convents of virgins to the women, so that they might govern their subjects according to the precepts of the Benedictine Rule. That Boniface had observed this Rule from his earliest age is clear from Willibald, chapter 2. Hence Marianus Scotus, following the author of the Annals of Fulda, says that monasteries of both sexes were first established in Germany by Boniface, although Willibrord had already built some.

12. Boniface wrote many letters, edited and elucidated by Nicholas Serarius; they are serious and pious. Pope Zacharias praises his book On the Unity of the Catholic Faith in Othlonus, book II, chapter 9. It is likely that this book is nothing other than certain synodal decrees, such as Acherius recently published in volume IX of the *Spicilegium*. Boniface is said to have committed to writing the Life of Saint Livinus, bishop and martyr; we proved this to be entirely suspect in the preceding century, under the year 656. Arnoldus Wion wrongly attributes to Boniface the Life of Saint Libuinus written by Hucbald.

Walafrid Strabo reports a saying of Boniface in his book *On Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 24, in these words:

“When Boniface, martyr and [Col. 0603A] bishop, was asked whether it was permissible to celebrate the sacraments in wooden vessels, he replied: ‘Formerly golden priests used wooden chalices; now, on the contrary, wooden priests use golden chalices.’”

[Col. 0603]

# LIFE OF SAINT BONIFACE, by WILLIBALD, his disciple

[Col. 0603]

## AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

[Col. 0603A]

To the holy lords and truly beloved in Christ, the fellow bishops Lullus and Megingozus [Note: [Col. 0603D] We shall discuss Saint Lullus, bishop of Mainz and successor of Boniface, under the year 786. Concerning Megingozus, or Mengozus, bishop of Würzburg, we have said more above in the Life of Saint Burkhard, bishop of that same see, under the year 751.]—Willibald, though unworthy, priest in the Lord.

Having perceived both the affection and the wish of your pious fatherhood, I willingly obeyed—not trusting in the literary knowledge of my own merit, but offering your holiness the due service of obedience—and began with my small strength the difficult work you proposed, bringing it at last to the goal of completion. But I ask you, if anything has turned out otherwise than your will desired, to bear with equanimity both the weakness of my infirmity and the greatness of the work imposed, since it is a most evident sign of reverence on my part that, under the command of your eminence, I do not refuse the service of obedience.

If I have produced anything worthy and useful to our own times, it must certainly be ascribed to the divine gift and to the desire of your command, since the pious will of one who desires sometimes imitates the hand of the press, and by the force of its impression prepares even the smallest sweetness of the knowledge desired and refreshes the hungry by imparting it. For your holiness has resolved to place the ignorant beside the learned and the less capable beside the prudent, and to impose upon me, as though I were uninformed, what you could reveal without any effort of ours in prudent speech.

But I beg that he whom the press of your command weighs down may be refreshed by the pouring forth of continual prayer, and that the will of your spontaneous affection may awaken from sleep the mind dulled by the darkness of idleness, so that it may be restored with a more tenacious and lively narration of words to those matters to which, under your compulsion, it has been summoned.

2. You compelled me to insert into writing, following the model of those works in which holy Fathers have undoubtedly transmitted the chastity of life or holiness of conduct of exemplary men through an elegant weaving of words, a preface, middle, and conclusion of the Life of Saint Boniface the martyr, with as much investigation as I could, at the request of religious and Catholic men among whom the fame of Saint Boniface and the radiance of his miracles resound in the regions of Tuscany, the borders of Gaul, the approaches to Germany, and even the confines of Britain, as I have learned from his disciples who lived with him for a long time and from you yourselves.

Just as Egesippus, who is said to have come to Rome under Anacletus, after the document of the first transgression had been dissolved and the ray of true light had shone forth, is reported to have published five books of ecclesiastical deeds for the benefit of readers; and as Eusebius of Caesarea, the most renowned of historians, together with the martyr Pamphilus, his assistant, and those who preceded them, wove histories of their own times and earlier ages with extraordinary eloquence and produced countless volumes in writing; and as Gregory, a man of blessed memory, highly learned in literary studies, seated upon the glorious summit of the Apostolic See, wrote the lives of blessed confessors, displayed the dialectical art with remarkable discipline, and composed four books of logical reasoning, which to this day, inserted in the libraries of the churches, bring to posterity the dignity of carefully worked-out knowledge—so you command me to display the life of this blessed man, his lofty virtues, his devotion, and the strength of his abstinence to the present age and to the ages yet to come.

Although I recognize that I am a small and insignificant author for setting forth the account of such great matters, nevertheless, compelled by the will of your benevolence, I shall undertake what you have entrusted to me at your command, relying not upon the insolence of personal presumption but upon the testimony of Catholic men. I seek no proclamation of personal praise from the pen of my smallness; rather, through the account of so great a matter, I offer readers an example that will benefit them, while each person is instructed by these models and led to better things through the perfection of his progress.

# THE LIFE BEGINS

## CHAPTER I — How he began the service of God in infancy

3. We shall therefore endeavor to weave together the illustrious and truly blessed life of Saint Boniface, supreme pontiff, and his character, consecrated above all by imitation of the saints, threading it through the fabric of this brief work, though impeded by the obscurity of our knowledge, and covering it with the simple garment of history, just as we learned it from religious men who, constantly present at his daily conversations and religious conduct, transmitted to posterity as examples what they had heard or seen.

By gathering a variety of words and weaving them together, we strive to unravel these matters and, from beginning to end, to reveal as fully as we can the holiness of his divine contemplation. When, in the first bloom of childhood, he had been weaned and nourished—as is customary—under the great care of his mother’s solicitude, he was loved by his father with extraordinary affection, more than the other children. But he had already subjected all passing things to his mind and resolved to think more about eternal things than about the present. When he was about four or five years old, he strove to submit himself to God’s service, continually laboring with great effort of mind in monastic life and daily yearning for it with the exertions of his spirit.

Whenever certain priests or clerics, as was customary in those regions, visited the people or laity for the purpose of preaching and came to the farm and house of the aforesaid head of household, the child’s weakness, insofar as its capacity permitted in those years, immediately began to discuss heavenly matters with them and to ask what might benefit him and his weakness in the future.

4. As he continued for a long time to think about heavenly matters in prolonged meditation of mind, extending his whole self toward the future and raising it to higher things, he eventually revealed to his father what he was carrying in his heart and asked him to heed his desire. When the father learned this, he was astonished and, with great insistence in reproving him, partly forbade him by threats to abandon him, and partly encouraged him by soothing words to attend to secular business. He wanted to bind him to the temporary profit of a passing inheritance and, when he himself died, to leave him as guardian—or rather heir—of his earthly property.

Using many words and the deceitful cunning of human cleverness, he tried to turn the boy’s tender mind away from completing the purpose he had begun. By repeated flattering speeches he maintained that an active life devoted to this world would be more tolerable for his childhood than the contemplative life of monastic service, hoping in this way to restrain him from striving toward his purpose and to encourage him toward the softness of worldly luxury.

But the man, already filled with God in childhood, the more strongly he was forbidden by his father, the more eagerly he yearned, with the strength of mind he had acquired, to gain a heavenly treasure and join himself to the study of sacred letters. And, in a wondrous manner, as divine mercy always acts, God foresaw and granted to His soldier of feeble age both assistance in the undertaking he had begun and an increase of his anxious desire, as well as a sudden change in his resisting father’s mind.

Thus, in one and the same succession of events, a sudden illness stealthily overtook the father as death was already near, while the boy’s pious desire, long hindered, quickly grew; and, with the Lord God’s help, by growing it was fulfilled and brought to perfection.

[Col. 0605D] 5. For after, by the wondrous dispensation of God’s judgment, a great sickness had seized the holy man’s fleshly father, he immediately laid aside his former obstinacy. After summoning the relatives, he voluntarily sent the boy, now overcome by the Lord, to the monastery known by the ancient name Adestancastre [Note: [Col. 0605D] It is also called Adescancastre and *ad Escam castrum*. Edward Maihew, in the *Anglo-Benedictine Martyrology*, not implausibly interprets it as Exeter, commonly called Excester, the principal city of Devon on the river Exe, which may have been called Adescancastrum, as though “the fortress at the Exe,” although no monument records that there was then a monastery at Exeter. Bede, in book III, chapter 22, mentions Ytancestir, a city of the East Saxons, which he places on the bank of the river Pante, where Saint Cedd the bishop was accustomed to establish his see. Itancester in Essex, a town, is today called Saint Peter at the Wall, commonly Saint Peters. But this passage should be interpreted as referring to a monastery of the West Saxons, as we proved above.]

He entrusted him through faithful messengers of his mission to the faithful man Wolfhard, who was also abbot of that monastery. While still a child, the boy wisely addressed the friends standing around him and, presenting a reasonable petition, explained that he had long desired to subject himself to the monastic Rule, just as he had previously been taught by his parents.

The father of the monastery immediately consulted the brothers and, having received their blessing—as the order of regular life required—gave his consent and brought the matter to completion. Thus the man of God, deprived of his earthly father, followed the adoptive Father of our redemption; renouncing the profits of the world, he thereafter strove to acquire the commerce of an eternal inheritance, so that, in accordance with the truthful word of Truth, by leaving father and mother, fields, and other things belonging to this world, he might receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life (Matthew 19).

## CHAPTER II — How he first broke the incentives of adolescence and adhered to every good thing

6. Having completed, though only in outline, the preliminary order of our account, we have briefly shown how and with what kind of holiness he submitted himself at the beginning of his dedicated life, so that, after laying the foundation of the structure, its lofty edifice might gradually rise higher toward the summit.

After seven years of infancy had passed, when the beauty of childhood arrived, an extraordinary strength of learning also prevailed in him. Enriched, through the inspiration of heavenly grace, with great and ineffable seriousness of mind, as the subsequent evidence of this work makes clear, and adorned with the chastity of many virtues, he was subjected, instructed, and distinguished according to the example displayed by the saints and the institutions of venerable Fathers who had gone before.

He burned so intensely with divine intelligence and devoted himself so thoroughly to the exercise of reading that, with each passing period, moment, hour, and course of years, the heavenly assistance and divine increase of the gifts of his protector also grew in him. And the more he advanced under the instruction of pastoral teaching, the more his daily studies, through constant literary meditation and unceasing praise, urged him day and night toward the progress of eternal blessedness—as faithful companions of his household certainly testified—while they also wonderfully protected him against the assaults of diabolical suggestion, which often obscure the tender flower of youth among mortals with a kind of cloudy darkness of blindness.

Thus, because of his unremitting care and long examination of the sacred laws, the enticing impulses of adolescence and the attacks of carnal desires, which at first assailed him, were, with the help of the Lord God, largely quieted in him. More and more they advanced him toward the common instruction of the peoples, which, after not much time had passed, [Col. 0607A] he began, expanded, and completed according to the decree of ecclesiastical judgment concerning the episcopate.

For, despising the fading ornaments of this world, he rightly observed the norm of monastic life in his infancy for many years under the measured governance of the aforesaid Father. Then, when the wantonness of childhood was fading [Al.: “departing”] and adolescence was beginning with puberty, the more ardent inclination of his youthful intellect inflamed him to go even to neighboring monasteries, summoned by the lack of instruction in reading, with the consent and counsel of his faithful fellow servants and the monastery’s Father.

7. As he continually asked with great insistence of prayer that the support of the Almighty be present to him in both his vow and his intention, at last, through the heavenly inspiration of divine grace, he reached the monastery that to this day is called Nutscelle [Al.: Nuiscelle]. Drawn by the spiritual diligence in letters of Winbercht [Al.: Wibert], abbot of blessed memory, who reverently governed the aforesaid monastery under regular discipline, he chose his instruction and the fellowship of the brothers living with him in the Lord.

Thus, joined to the company of God’s servants, he offered the Lord God devoted service, laborious vigilance, and attention to divine reading with immense diligence of meditation. In the end he was so imbued with knowledge of the Scriptures—both with the eloquence of grammatical art and the modulation of metrically wrought eloquence, as well as with the simple exposition of history and the interpretation of the threefold spiritual understanding—and he so commendably shone in the skill of dictation, that he eventually became for others a teacher of the traditions of the Fathers and an authoritative master, although he had previously not refused to be a disciple of those set over him.

[Note: [Col. 0607] Pope Gregory II affirms in a letter numbered 118 among the Bonifacian letters that Boniface learned the sacred writings from infancy.]

8. It is a custom of sacred conduct that he who has refused to be subject to others fears to place himself above the rest, since he will not be able to offer the service of proper obedience to those subject to him, which he will not justly show to his superiors under the heavenly dispensation.

He offered this obedience to all who lived together in common, and especially to his abbot, to whom he was monastically subject under regular discipline, in such a way that he constantly persisted in daily manual labor and the disciplined administration of duties according to the established form of the blessed Father Benedict’s right constitution. Presenting himself to all as an example of good living—in word and conduct, in faith and chastity—he ensured that all might receive fruit from him and that he himself might receive a share in everyone’s eternal reward.

Only God, who knows hidden things, knew the excellence of his humility and charity, by the intimate scrutiny of His inspection. Through these virtues Boniface had carefully attached all his fellow soldiers to himself, so that they might hold him in both fear and love. Since they had him as a companion in divine reading, they would anticipate one another in honoring him as a father with apostolic admonition.

Such a greatness of affability toward the brothers and of heavenly teaching grew in him that, as the report of his holy exhortation spread, his fame became openly renowned through many monasteries of both men [Col. 0608A] and virgins of Christ. Very many of the former, strengthened by the vigor of the male sex and encouraged by diligence in reading, flocked to him. Drinking from the fountain of wholesome knowledge, they reviewed numerous volumes of Scripture by reading them.

Those who possessed the weakness of the frailer sex and were denied the constant ability to travel caused such a man of wisdom to be brought to them, through the love of God breathed into them by the divine Spirit. Passing through the sequence of pages, they clung earnestly to heavenly scrutiny and continually meditated on the hidden things of the sacraments and mysteries.

He was so lifted up by heavenly grace that, following the example of the outstanding preacher and teacher of the nations, he carefully presented himself to God as an approved and unashamed worker, bearing the pattern of sound words in faith and love in Jesus Christ and rightly handling the word of truth (1 Timothy 2).

## CHAPTER III — That he offered the word of teaching to all, and that he had not seized it beforehand by his own will

9. Our discourse now turns for a while to the general pattern of his daily contemplation and his long observance of frugality, so that, following one ascent after another with a concise economy of words, we may more eagerly trace the lofty works of this holy man and pursue, with subtler investigation, the whole course of the venerable Boniface’s life.

Thus, with balanced moderation, he may become for us an example of eternity and a powerful rule of apostolic instruction. Climbing successfully, through the examples of the saints, the difficult path of heavenly understanding, and offering the peoples a guide who went before them, he himself entered and opened the gate of the Lord our God, through which the righteous shall enter.

From infancy to the decrepit old age of his life, he imitated to no small degree the wisdom of the Fathers who had gone before him. He continually committed to memory the words of the prophets and apostles, written in a style of holiness, and the glorious passion of the martyrs, inserted—as was fitting—in the letters of books. He also daily entrusted to memory the evangelical teaching of the Lord our God.

And, according to the Apostle (1 Corinthians 10), whether he ate, drank, or did anything else, he always offered God, both in mind and mouth, a proclamation of praise and the height of devoted rejoicing, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm 33).

He burned with such desire for the Scriptures that he joined himself with all his attention to their imitation and hearing. What had been written for the instruction of the peoples, he himself effectively unfolded in preaching, with marvelous eloquence and very careful exposition of parables.

He possessed such a balanced discretion that gentleness was not lacking from the force of correction, nor the force of preaching from gentleness. But the zeal that inflamed him to firmness was tempered by the gentleness of love.

To rich and powerful, free and enslaved, he offered an equal discipline of holy exhortation: he neither caressed the rich by flattery nor burdened servants or free people with excessive severity. Rather, according to the Apostle, he became all things to all people, so that he might win all (1 Corinthians 9).

He did not prematurely assume the teaching of heaven by his own will, nor did he acquire it by usurping it through the violence of obstinacy. Instead, through the progress of holy humility, when he was thirty years old or more, he received it according to the rule of canonical constitution, elevated by the choice of his teachers and companions, and entered the rank of priestly office [Note: [Col. 0609D] When Boniface had been ordained priest, he performed the sacred rites only once each day, as Walafrid Strabo testifies in *On Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 22; for, according to the same author, others sometimes performed them three times.] enriched with various gifts.

Thus, insofar as he prevailed under the strictness of regular and monastic life, he devoted himself wholly in deed and will to almsgiving and works of mercy. He also anticipated every hour with nocturnal vigils and exercised himself with more earnest labor in prayer. Neither anger stole away his patience, nor fury disturbed his long-suffering, nor lust conquered his continence, nor gluttony violated his abstinence.

He subjected himself so completely to the frugality of fasting that, drinking wine and strong drink, he imitated the Fathers of both Testaments and, with the outstanding teacher of the nations, said: “I discipline my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected” (1 Corinthians 9).

## CHAPTER IV — That he was sent to Kent by all the leading men, and that he reached Frisia

10. Having gathered above, in scattered form, the lofty virtues of this holy man, we do not think that what follows should be passed over in silence. We learned these matters from the report of faithful men and strive to expose them through the clear disclosure of written testimony: namely, with what perseverance of his strength he clung to good beginnings and hastened eagerly toward other undertakings, spurring his mind onward.

As he had long disciplined his mind through the virtues listed above and advanced from day to day toward higher examples of goodness under the aforesaid priestly rank, while Ina, [Note: [Col. 0609D] We gave above, under the year 730, the encomium of Ina, or Ine, the most devout king of the West Saxons.] the king of the West Saxons, was reigning, a sudden necessity arose from a new kind of disturbance. Immediately a synodal council was held by the leading men of the churches, with the counsel of the aforesaid king and the servants of God.

When everyone had assembled together, a salutary question concerning this recent dissension arose prudently among the priestly ranks of the ecclesiastical order. After wiser deliberation, they decided that faithful envoys in the Lord should be sent to Berctwald, archbishop of the city of Canterbury, lest anything be ascribed to their presumption or rashness if they acted without the counsel of so great a pontiff.

[Col. 0610A] When the entire council and the whole order of clerics agreed after such prudent discussion, the king immediately addressed all the servants of Christ and asked to whom they should entrust the message of this embassy.

Then suddenly the supreme archimandrite in Christ, Winberch, who presided over the aforesaid monastery; Wintra, who governed the monastery called Disselburg; and Beerwald, who by divine governance ruled the monastery called by the ancient name Glestingaburg [Note: [Col. 0609D] That is, Glastonbury. Thus it is read in volume I of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, page 13: “Hemgiflus, abbot [Col. 0610D] (of Glastonbury), having fulfilled his fate, received rest for his body in the ancient church; Berwald succeeded him in the year of grace 705.” In a charter of a donation made by Ina, King Kentwin is said to have been accustomed to call Glastonbury “the mother of the saints.” He declared it exempt from every secular and ecclesiastical service and granted the brothers the privilege of electing an abbot according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. See the letter of the priest Wiethbert, Letter 53 among the Bonifacian letters, to the brothers of the monastery of Glestingaburg.]—together with many other Fathers of this holy purpose, brought this holy man, summoned, before the king.

The king entrusted him with the message and the knowledge of the embassy and, providing him with companions, sent him forth in peace. Having received the message, in accordance with the command [Col. 0610B] of his elders, he reached Kent by a prosperous journey. To the archbishop, adorned with the insignia of the highest pontificate, he wisely disclosed everything in order, just as he had been instructed by the king.

Having received the voluntary response, he returned to his homeland after not many days. In the presence of the aforesaid king and the aforementioned servants of God who stood with him, he knowingly delivered the voluntary response of the venerable archbishop. He brought great joy to everyone. From then onward, through the wondrous dispensation of God’s benevolence, his name became widely known and celebrated among all, both in secular dignities and in the ranks of ecclesiastical office. Thus, advancing from that time forward, he very often took part in their synodal proceedings.

11. But because a mind dedicated to God is not elated by human favors [Col. 0610C] nor lifted up by praise, he had begun to hasten more attentively toward many other concerns, to avoid the company of his parents and relatives, and to desire foreign lands rather than the territories of his paternal inheritance. But after deliberating very carefully with himself over a long interval of time about abandoning his homeland and parents, at last, having received the counsel of the aforesaid Father of blessed memory, he openly revealed all the secrets of his heart that he had previously hidden within his conscience, and with great insistence in prayer urged the holy man to consent to his will. The latter, initially struck with great astonishment, for a time firmly opposed the journey desired by the petitioner and suppliant, so as to restrain the zeal of his undertaking. But finally, as [Col. 0610D] the providence of almighty God grew stronger, the petitioner’s words also prevailed; and the journey he had undertaken through the devotion of the abbot and his brothers, who lived with him under regular discipline, he completed by God’s dispensation. They even willingly supplied him with the necessities of human expense [Col. 0611A] and, with great agitation of heart, poured out streams of tears for a long while and offered prayers and supplications to the Lord on his behalf.

Thus, strengthened with spiritual armor and elevated by worldly provision, lacking neither the resources of one life nor of the other, he set out with two or three brothers whose bodily and spiritual support he needed. After traversing immense stretches of land, rejoicing in the prosperous company of his brothers, he reached the place where there was a market for merchandise [Note: [Col. 0611D] Bede, in Book II, chapter 3 of his History, calls London an emporium of many peoples arriving by land and sea; this is the city meant here. The same author calls London the metropolis of the East Saxons, who, he says, are separated from Kent by the River Thames and themselves border the eastern sea.], and which to this day is called Lundenwic in the ancient language of the Angles and Saxons. Not long afterward, as a returning stranger, he courageously approached a ship as a new passenger (*epibata*) of the sailors, with the agreement of the shipmaster; and, having paid the fare, he reached Dorstat [Col. 0611B] with a favorable wind [Note: [Col. 0611D] Dorestat, or Dorestad, commonly Wijk-Duurstede in Frisia, more than once occupied by the Northmen, lies on the River Laka, or Lek, somewhat above lower Utrecht, here called Trech or Trecht by Willibald, and now Utrecht.]. There he remained for some time and rendered to the Lord God the tribute of praise day and night.

But when a hostile conflict arising amid a severe onslaught of the pagans disturbed the peoples on both sides—between Charles, the glorious prince and duke of the Franks, and Radbod, king of the Frisians—and when most of the Churches of Christ that had previously been subject to Frankish rule in Frisia had been devastated and destroyed under Radbod’s persecution and the expulsion of God’s servants, while the worship of idols had also been mournfully renewed through the construction of shrines for the gods, then the man of God, having perceived the wickedness of this perversity, reached Trech. After waiting there for several days, he addressed King Radbod when he arrived, in order to inquire, after surveying and examining many of the surrounding regions, whether anywhere there might be an opening for preaching in the future [Col. 0611C]. He proposed in his heart that, if an entrance should be opened in any part of this people through which the Gospel might shine forth, he would sow the seeds of God’s word. Many years afterward, the glorious testimony of martyrdom confirmed this.

12. But because the distinctive task of holy men is holiness, when they perceive that their labor for a time bears no fruit from the green shoot of spiritual growth, they migrate to entirely different places where labor is fruitful; for a place is inhabited in vain if the fruit of holiness is absent. While the holy man had dwelt for some time in the barren land of the Frisians, and a little of the summer and autumn had passed, he had already left those fields dry of the dew of heavenly fertility and migrated with the companions mentioned above from his native soil [Col. 0612A]. Seeking the seclusion of his monastery, he spent the winter of the second year there as well, welcomed with joy by the loving brothers [Note: [Col. 0612D] “He left,” and below, “he spent.” We have already observed similar modes of expression in Alcuin’s Life of Saint Willibrord, where pluperfect forms are more than once used as simple past tenses.], so that he might imitate the apostolic voice of the teacher who said: “For there I have decided to winter” (Titus 3).

CHAPTER V.—How, after his abbot had died, he remained for some time with the brothers, and afterward reached Rome with letters of recommendation from his bishop.

13. Having now passed over, in part, the virtues of the holy man, we openly set forth what follows concerning him, as we have learned from the reports of those who told the story, so that, for those who strive after the standard of his holy conduct, the path of his life and character may forever be more clearly evident. After he had endured the great dangers of pilgrimage, escaped the perils of the sea, returned once more to the company of his brothers, and spent many days thereafter in their fellowship, he was finally seized by deep sorrow of mind and oppressed by fresh grief of spirit. He saw the aged limbs of his master growing weak; and, as the severity of his illness increased, he perceived the day of his death approaching, while he trembled and struggled for breath in the presence of the assembled monks, and at last saw him, after laying aside the prison of the body, breathe out his final spirit beneath the sorrowful gaze of his grieving brothers [Note: [Col. 0612D] The seventeenth letter of Saint Boniface concerning the death of Wigbert, undoubtedly the abbot of Fritzlar, does not refer to the death of Winberht, abbot of Nurscell or Nutscell; Wigbert died in Boniface’s absence, as the letter itself states, whereas the man discussed here breathed his last in Boniface’s presence.].

For in the hearts of holy men the special mercy of compassion frequently shines forth as fellow-suffering, through which they customarily grieve for a time with those who suffer; but, adhering to the apostolic command, they are continually consoled in the Lord. He now began gently to address the brothers and, mindful of their father’s tradition, exhorted them in spiritual conversations to preserve in all things the form of the regular constitution and the norm of ecclesiastical ordinance. He instructed them also to submit themselves to the authority of some spiritual father.

Then they all unanimously urged him with harmonious voices, and all entreated this holy man—who at that time was called Winfrid—to undertake the pastoral authority of an abbot over them. But he immediately rejected the resources of his homeland and renounced the primacy of governance. Ready and prepared for the destination already appointed, he excused himself with careful diligence and, by renouncing it, refused the whole substance of his heirs [Al., “of his prospective heirs”].

[Col. 0612D] 14. When winter had passed and the heat of summer was growing white-hot, and the former purpose of the passing year had been renewed, he undertook with every concern to renew the interrupted journey by setting out again. Having also received letters of recommendation from Daniel of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0613D] This is Daniel, bishop of the West Saxons, who, according to Bede in Book V, chapter 19, succeeded Bishop Pecthelm together with Aldhelm in the year 705 and was still alive in 731, when Bede completed his history.], the guardian of God’s people, he attempted to come to Rome, to the threshold of the apostles.

Yet the need of the orphaned brothers, left without their Father, held him back for some time, and the love and compassion of those who lamented and grieved on both sides temporarily resisted his departure. Thus he was oppressed by great anguish of mind and did not know which way to turn. He feared that the flock entrusted to its master, now without the guardianship of an attentive shepherd, would, after his departure, lie exposed to the bites of wolves; and he was also afraid that the autumn season suitable for setting out abroad would fail him.

But when the Almighty, mindful of his customary mercy, wished to rescue his servant, disturbed by such pressure of mind, from his anxious grief and to provide the flock with a pleasing shepherd, the aforesaid bishop’s inward deliberation concerning the brothers had already taken shape. He caused a man of good character named Stephen to preside over this Church, and directed the holy man, who desired to travel by the long roads of pilgrimage, safely toward his appointed destinations [Col. 0613B].

He immediately took leave of the brothers and departed. He reached, after long stretches of land, the place already mentioned, called Lundenwic, having fulfilled his desire; and, quickly climbing aboard a small vessel, he began to attempt the unknown routes of the sea. As the sailors rejoiced, the sails rose high when the immense Corus wind blew; and with full wind and a favorable course they soon saw the mouth of the river called Cuent, now entirely free from danger of shipwreck [Col. 0613C]. They reached the dry land safely. They also made camp at Cuentawic until [Col. 0613C] the multitude of his companions who were arriving had gathered together.

When all had assembled, they set out day by day as winter’s cold threatened. They visited many churches of the saints in prayer, so that, with the help of the Most High, they might cross the Alpine ridges of the mountains more safely, experience more gently the kindness of the Lombards toward them, and more easily escape the malicious arrogance and ferocity of the soldiers. With the patronage of the saints assisting them and God the Lord directing all things, the entire company of companions who adhered to the fellowship of this holy man successfully approached the threshold of the blessed Apostle Peter. They immediately offered immense thanks to Christ for their safety. Entering the church of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, with great joy, they asked for the remission of their sins; and many of them brought various gifts [Col. 0613D].

After not many days had passed, this holy man addressed Gregory, the venerable pope of the apostolic see, of blessed memory—Gregory the Second, though first in succession and earlier in time, who in the common Roman language is called “the Younger”—and disclosed to him in order the whole reason for his journey and arrival [Col. 0614A]. He also revealed with what anxious longing he had labored for so long.

The holy pope, therefore, suddenly looked upon him with a cheerful face and smiling eyes and asked whether he had brought letters of recommendation from his bishop. The other, immediately removing his cloak, brought forth a document wrapped according to custom [Note: [Col. 0613D] Boniface had received two letters from Daniel: one wrapped, that is, sealed, for Pope Gregory; the other circular and open, addressed to all Christians. The former has been lost; the latter is preserved among the Bonifacian letters as number 33. Boniface himself also wrote three letters to Daniel; Serarius likewise cites Daniel’s letter in his notes on Letter 3.], and handed the letter to the man of holy memory. He immediately accepted it and signaled to him to leave.

But after the apostolic pope had read the letter and reviewed the written document of recommendation, he thereafter maintained with him a diligent daily conversation of discussion, until the summer season for setting out and returning drew near.

CHAPTER VI.—Concerning his return from Rome at the pope’s command, and what he accomplished by preaching in Thuringia, Francia, and Frisia; and concerning his deeds with Bishop Willibrord.

[Col. 0614B]

15. When the month of Nisan, which is April, was passing, and Jair, which is May, was already opening its gates, he then also sought and received a blessing and letters from the most blessed pope [Note: [Col. 0614D] These letters survive, dated on the Ides of May in the third year of the reign of Leo Augustus, indiction 2; these chronological indications correspond to the year of Christ 719.]. He was sent to examine the most savage peoples of Germany, to determine whether they might be willing to receive the seed of preaching after their uncultivated hearts had been plowed by the Gospel’s plowshare.

Thus, immediately gathering a large number of relics, he reached the borders of Italy on the return journey of his fellow servants. He addressed the excellent king of the Lombards, Liutprand [Al., Liodbrand], greeting him with peaceful gifts. Received honorably by him, he rested his journey-weary limbs; then, having been rewarded, he traversed the difficult and level expanses of the fields [Col. 0614C], crossed the precipitous Alpine ridges, and, entering the unknown territories of the Bavarians and the regions bordering Germany, proceeded into Thuringia in accordance with the command of the apostolic see.

He did so like a most prudent bee, which flies about the fields of the countryside, softly rustling with its winged wings among the abundant, fragrant plants, testing with its harvesting beak the honey-bearing substances where the sweetness of nectar lies hidden; rejecting entirely the bitterness of every poisonous juice, it carries the sweetness into its hives. In accordance with a certain likeness drawn from the language of apostolic reasoning, he tested everything and held fast to what was good.

16. Thus the holy man of God, in Thuringia and according to the apostolic pontiff’s command implanted in him, addressed the senators and, finally, the leaders of all the people with spiritual words. He called them back to the way of true knowledge and the light of understanding, which they had once lost after being led astray, for the most part, by wicked teachers.

He also corrected, admonished, and instructed the priests and presbyters, as far as he could, by evangelical discourse, leading them away from the perversity of evil toward the rectitude of canonical constitution. Some of them had been inflamed by the religious worship of almighty God; others, contaminated by fornication, had lost the continence of chastity, which they ought to have preserved as servants at the sacred altars.

Then he entered Francia with the brothers traveling with him. As soon as he heard of the death of Radbod [Note: [Col. 0615C] The death of Radbod, duke of the Frisians, occurred in the same year as Boniface’s return from Rome, namely in the year of Christ 719, as is clear from the chronology just noted. Bugga, or Eadburga, abbess, congratulates Boniface the priest on Radbod’s death in Letter 35 among the Bonifacian letters; there she mentions a revelation made to Boniface concerning his future harvest among the Germans, and the book on the Passions of the Martyrs, which Boniface, himself destined to become a martyr, had asked to be sent to him.], king of the Frisians, he ascended the river by boat with great joy, hoping that Frisia too might receive the word of God, and reached its uncultivated lands with heavenly preaching.

Now that the savage persecution of King Radbod had ceased, he sowed the seeds of heavenly teaching and, having driven away the famine of God’s word, refreshed the hungry multitude of pagan superstition with the food of eternal preaching. When the desired effect of his work suddenly followed the longing of his mind, and, by God’s dispensation, the wished-for light of the appointed teaching began to shine, and the authority of the glorious Duke Charles over the Frisians had been strengthened, the trumpet of the heavenly word sounded, and, with the fertility of the heavenly dew arriving, the voice of God thundered through the preachers. The word was also spread through Willibrord, the venerable man, and his coworkers.

But because he saw that the harvest was indeed great while the laborers were very few, this holy servant of God also became a coworker of Archbishop Willibrord for three years [Note: [Col. 0615D] Saint Liudger, in the Life of Saint Gregory, abbot of Utrecht; Hucbald, in the Life of Saint Lebuin; John of Beka, in his Chronicle; and others, if there are any, write “thirteen years.” But both Othlonus, Book I of the Life of Saint Boniface, chapter 11, and the pontificate of Pope Gregory II persuade us that “three years” alone should be read. From what follows it is clear that Saint Boniface was ordained by Pope Gregory in 723, that is, four years after he had been sent into Germany by the same pope.]. Laboring greatly in Christ, he acquired for the Lord no small people, with the aforesaid pontiff assisting him, after destroying the shrines of the gods and constructing churches and oratories.

[Col. 0615C] 17. When this highest pontiff had grown old and was burdened by many years of age, he decided, at the urging of the assembled disciples, to provide support for his decrepit old age in so great a ministry and to choose from the small congregation a faithful man who could preside over so great a people. Summoning this servant, he admonished him with salutary instruction to accept the rank of bishop and assist him in governing God’s people.

But he immediately and humbly rejected the proposal, declaring that he was entirely unworthy of the episcopal rank. He begged that the summit of so great a dignity not be imposed upon him while he was still in the years of youth [Note: [Col. 0615D] From this it is clear that those who believe Boniface was born in the year of Christ 670 are mistaken, since otherwise he could not be said to have been in the years of youth in 720, when he began to labor in evangelical preaching with Saint Willibrord. Nevertheless, he had already reached manhood, since he had previously been ordained a priest in his thirtieth year.]. And because he had not yet fully reached the age of fifty [Note: [Col. 0616D] No ecclesiastical laws forbid the ordination of a bishop before the fiftieth year of age; indeed, it may occur well before the thirtieth. Boniface seems to have had in mind Numbers 8:24–26: “This is the law of the Levites. From twenty-five years of age and upward they shall enter to serve in the tabernacle of the covenant. When they have completed the fiftieth year of age, they shall cease to serve, and shall be ministers of their brothers in the tabernacle of the covenant, to guard what has been entrusted to them.” Certainly Gregory the Great, Book II of the Dialogues, chapter 2, had this passage in mind when he says that Moses had commanded in Exodus—read “Numbers”—that Levites should serve from twenty-five years of age and upward, but from the fiftieth year should become guardians of the vessels; he applies this to pastors. A passage in the Life of Pope Sylvester can also be adapted to explain this verse.], according to the norm of canonical rectitude, he testified that he should avoid the eminence of this rank by every possible excuse and evasive argument.

The aforementioned pontiff of so holy a proclamation rebuked him in gentle words and urged him with careful attention toward undertaking this office. He emphatically proclaimed the extreme poverty of the people subject to him. But when, even after this rebuke, he did not consent to accept the rank of such eminence, and a spiritual dispute had already arisen between them through the long delays of their arguments, a disagreement consonant with beautiful discretion came about.

The one, overcome by great humility, refused so great an honor; the other, ensnared by the most pious desire for gain, desired the salvation of souls. After they had exchanged various words in their discussion, this holy servant of God, as though placed in some spiritual arena, calmly put forward his words of excuse and said:

“O pontiff of supreme holiness, O spiritual helmsman of the struggle: I received from the blessed Pope Gregory, of holy memory, a commission to the Germanic peoples. Serving as legate of the apostolic see, I voluntarily entrusted myself to the authority of your governance in the western regions of the barbarians, and by my own will joined myself, without the knowledge of the exalted rulers, to whom I remain bound to this day by a pledge of service and subjection. Therefore, without the counsel of the apostolic see and the mandate of an authoritative command, I do not dare to accept the office of so illustrious an eminence” [Col. 0616C].

He also offered other words in a reasonable and humble petition, saying:

“I therefore beg you to send me, bound by the chains of my own pledge, back to those lands to which I was first sent by the apostolic see.”

Immediately, when the man of God had heard the reason for such a declaration, he gave him his blessing and permission to depart. Setting out at once, he reached the place called Amanaburch, nourished, in accordance with the Apostle, by words of faith and good teaching which he had attained.

CHAPTER VII.—How he converted the peoples of the Saxons and Hessians, sent a messenger to Rome concerning his deeds, and was soon afterward summoned there to confer with the pope.

[Col. 0617A]

18. In successive stages, from the beginning, we have briefly traced the holy man’s evidence of virtue and steadfastness in labor for the Lord, so that we may now recall more carefully, gathered together in memory, the subsequent examples of his goodness. When he was acquiring a great people for the Lord among the Frisians, and many, instructed by him in spiritual teaching, reached knowledge of the truth as the rays of the true light shone upon them, he then, with the Lord’s protection, entered other regions of Germany for the purpose of preaching.

With the Lord’s help he obtained the aforementioned place, whose rulers were two brothers, Detdic and Dierolf. He recalled them from the sacrilegious worship of idols, which they had wickedly practiced under a certain name of Christianity, and, by rightly revealing the path of understanding, he led a very large crowd of people away from the evil superstition of paganism after they had laid aside the horror of their errors. He also constructed a monastic cell by gathering a congregation of God’s servants.

Likewise, near the borders of the Saxons, he freed the people of the Hessians, who were still wandering in pagan rites, from captivity to demons by preaching the evangelical commandments; and, after the pagan antiquity had been cleansed, he baptized many thousands of people.

19. He sent to Rome a suitable messenger and faithful bearer of his letters, named Binnan. Through the silent medium of writing, he disclosed in order to the venerable Father, the pontiff of the apostolic see, everything that had been accomplished around him by God’s gift [Col. 0617C]. He also reported that a great multitude of people, enlightened by the divine Spirit, were receiving the sacrament of regeneration.

He wrote at greater length by asking the advice of the apostolic see concerning matters that related to the daily needs of the Church of God and the welfare of the people. When this messenger had remained for several days in the place mentioned above, and the time of his return was already approaching, he also received from the aforesaid pontiff of the apostolic see the reciprocal response to his mission. Returning immediately, he brought the written document of the apostolic see to his master after not much time had passed.

20. When the holy man had read the letters brought to him, he understood that he had been summoned to Rome by an abbreviated invitation and hastened to fulfill the highest degree of obedience. Immediately surrounded by a crowd of attendants and encircled by a troop of brothers, he crossed the boundaries of the Franks, Burgundians, and Italy, having already traversed the Alpine hills and the military frontiers. When he saw the walls of the Roman city, he suddenly offered the Most High worthy praises of thanksgiving. Soon reaching the church of blessed Peter, he fortified himself with diligent prayer.

When his wearied limbs had rested for a little while, word was brought to the blessed Gregory, pontiff of the apostolic see, that this servant of God had arrived. He was received favorably and led to a hospice. When the proper day for their conversation arrived, and the glorious pontiff of the apostolic see was approaching the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter, this servant of God was immediately summoned.

After they had exchanged a few peaceful words of greeting, the apostolic pontiff questioned him about the Creed and the tradition of ecclesiastical faith. The man of God immediately answered him humbly:

“Lord Apostolic, as a stranger I know that I am now unskilled in the language of your familiarity; but I ask you to grant me leisure and time to write out my faith, so that silent writing alone may rationally disclose my faith to you” [Col. 0618B].

He immediately granted this and ordered him to bring the writing quickly. After some time had passed, Boniface brought him a written statement of the faith of the Holy Trinity, composed with polished eloquence, and presented it to the pontiff.

He nevertheless waited several days longer. Then he was summoned again and led into the Lateran. After humbly seeking the requested blessing with bowed face, he fell at the feet of the apostolic pontiff. The latter immediately raised him from the ground and returned to this servant of God the document in which the truth of the faith had appeared whole and incorrupt. He made him sit beside him and instructed him with salutary teaching, so that he might preserve this undefiled bulwark of faith without interruption and preach it diligently to others according to the capacity of his strength.

He also raised many other questions concerning religious observance and the truth of the faith, so that they spent almost the whole day conversing together in turn. Finally, he asked how peoples who had previously wandered through the byways of crimes were receiving the lessons of the faith through Boniface’s preaching.

21. When he had learned for certain that Boniface was bringing a very great multitude of people from the sacrilegious worship of demons into fellowship with the holy Church, he informed him that he wished to impose upon him the rank of bishop [Al., “was willing to impose”], so that he might place him before peoples who had previously been deprived of pastoral care and who, according to the saying of our Lord God, lay like sheep without a shepherd.

But because he did not dare to oppose so great a pontiff, the prelate of the apostolic see, he consented and obeyed. Thus the supreme pontiff of holy authority appointed the day of his ordination, namely the day before the Kalends of December [Note: [Col. 0617D] This was in the seventh year of the emperor Leo and the fourth year of his son Constantine, indiction 6, as is confirmed both by Saint Boniface’s profession of faith and by the letters of Pope Gregory cited below by Othlonus; therefore it was the year of Christ 723. It is consequently clear that Boniface did not collaborate with Saint Willibrord for thirteen years but only for three, and that he was ordained by Gregory II, not Gregory III; the following section, no. 25, also establishes this.].

When the holy solemn day, the feast of Andrew, and the appointed day of ordination dawned, the sacred pontiff of the apostolic see conferred upon him the dignity of the episcopate and the name Boniface [Note: [Col. 0618D] Winfrid already bore the name Boniface before his ordination, as is established by a letter of Pope Gregory II reported by Othlonus in Book I, chapter 9. It was dated on the Ides of May in the third year of Leo’s reign, indiction 2—that is, in the year 719—yet it was addressed to Boniface, a religious priest. There is also another letter sent in the same year by Bugga, abbess, to Boniface, or Winfred, a most worthy priest of God; this is Letter 35 among the Bonifacian letters.], and supplied him with a booklet in which the most sacred laws of ecclesiastical constitution had been recorded for episcopal councils. He ordered that henceforth this episcopal discipline and order of instruction should remain unshaken among them and that the subject people should be formed by these examples.

He also granted from that time forward familiarity with the holy apostolic see both to himself and to all subject to him. By his most sacred letters he placed this holy man, now endowed with episcopal rank, under the protection of the glorious Duke Charles, entrusting him to the defense and devotion of the kingdom.

CHAPTER VIII.—How, departing from Rome, he approached Charles, duke of the Franks, and what he accomplished by preaching among the Hessians and afterward in Thuringia; concerning tyrants and corrupted religion in that province; concerning messengers sent again to Rome and two small monasteries built.

[Col. 0619B]

22. As he traveled through the long bends of the roads and reached the borders of immense peoples, he came at last to the aforesaid prince of the Franks. Received reverently by him, he delivered to Duke Charles the letters of the aforementioned Roman pontiff and apostolic see. Placed under Charles’s authority and protection [Note: [Col. 0619D] Othlonus reports the letter of Pope Gregory to Duke Charles in Book I, chapter 16. Charles’s letter, by which he accepts Boniface into his protection and defense, may be read as Letter 32 among the Bonifacian letters.], he returned, with the duke’s consent, to the borders of the Hessians, which had previously been under siege.

Then many of the Hessians, already subject to the Catholic faith and strengthened by the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, received the laying on of hands. Others, not yet strengthened in mind, refused to receive the teachings of the undefiled faith in their entirety. Some secretly sacrificed to trees and springs [Note: [Col. 0619D] Tacitus refers to this in his work On the Germans: “They consecrate groves and forests and call them by the names of gods. They observe omens and lots more than anyone.” Agathias likewise writes in Book I of his Gothic War: “They worship certain trees, and likewise the waters of rivers,” and so forth.]; others did so openly.

Some secretly practiced divination, augury, magic, and incantations [Col. 0619C]; others openly. Some attended to omens and auspices and maintained various rites of sacrifice. Others, whose minds were sounder, rejected every profanation of paganism and committed none of these things.

At their counsel and instigation he attempted to cut down a certain tree of extraordinary size, called in the ancient pagan language the Oak of Jupiter, in the place called Gicesmere [Note: [Col. 0619D] This is Geismar in Lower Hesse, formerly a village and now a town cleansed of recent impure opinions. Servatus Lupus calls it the village of Geismar in chapter 20 of the Life of Wigbert; today it belongs to the lordship of Schönberg. Nicolaus Serarius says much the same in Book III of his History of Mainz.], while the servants of God who accompanied him stood nearby.

When, strengthened by steadfastness of mind, he had cut down the tree, a great crowd of pagans was present. They were zealously cursing within themselves the enemy of their gods [that is, they were devoting him to curses]. But when the tree had been cut only a little, immediately the immense mass of the oak was shaken from above by a divine breath, its crown was shattered, and it fell. As if by the assistance of a heavenly command, it split into four parts, and four trunks of immense size and equal length appeared, without any labor on the part of the brothers who stood there [Col. 0620A]. At this sight, the pagans who had previously cursed him now, with their position reversed, gave praise to the Lord, abandoning their former curse and believing.

23. Then the bishop of supreme holiness, after deliberating with the brothers, constructed a wooden oratory from the material of the aforesaid tree [Note: [Col. 0619D] In the course of time this sacred structure grew into a very spacious and notable building, as may still be seen today, says Serarius; but it is occupied by heretics.]. He dedicated it in honor of the holy Apostle Peter.

After all that we have mentioned had been completed and accomplished with the assistance of heavenly providence, he set out for Thuringia [Note: [Col. 0620D] Before Boniface entered Thuringia, he is said to have overthrown other idols: namely, in Eichsfeld—which is a region between Hesse and Thuringia—the idol Stuf at Mount Stuffon, where a church dedicated to Saint Martin, still frequented by the faithful as a place of pilgrimage, now stands; Retton in the territory of Hildesheim; Biele in the Thuringian Biel Mountains; and others, which the Lutheran Letzner discusses at length in chapter 19 of his Charlemagne.]. He addressed the elders and leaders of the people and, calling upon them to abandon the blindness of ignorance, urged them to return to the Christian religion they had once received [Note: [Col. 0620D] Thuringia, conquered by Theodoric, son of Clovis the Great, had also accepted Christian laws, according to Gregory, bishop of Tours, in Book III, chapters 4, 7, and 9.], because, as the authority of their kings was growing weak [read: withdrawing], a large multitude of their counts had either been overtaken by bodily death through the dangerous rule of Theobald and Heden [Al., Beden], who exercised over them the grievous tyranny of a ducal office and a hostile power of devastation rather than devotion, or had been carried off into captivity by the enemy.

They were bound by various evils to such an extent that the remaining multitude of the people submitted itself to the rule of the Saxons. When the dominion of religious dukes ceased, zeal for Christianity and religion also ceased among them. False brothers who led the people astray were introduced, and under the name of religion they brought in a very extensive sect of heretical depravity. Among these were Torchtwine, Berchthere, Eanbercht, and Hunred—men guilty of fornication and adultery, whom the Lord condemned according to the Apostle.

They stirred up a very powerful conflict against the man of God; but, refuted by the true opposition of his words, they received a sentence worthy of condemnation. When the brightness of faith had been renewed among the people and the populace had been rescued from the immense snare of error, the friends of the profane enemy and the hostile seducers mentioned above having been expelled, he cultivated a great harvest with very few reapers and initially endured great poverty and frugality in this world. Hemmed in by severe afflictions and tribulations, he propagated the seeds of God’s word. But as the multitude of believers gradually grew strong, the number of preachers also increased.
