[Col. 0621A] **24.** At that time the churches were suddenly restored, and his teaching of preaching spread abroad in many forms. A monastery too was built at a place called Ordorp [Note: [Col. 0621D] The Ordorp or Ordorff monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in Thuringia, at the River Oraham or Oram, not far from the town of Erfurt. From Othlo’s Book I, chapter 23, we learn on what occasion it was dedicated by Saint Boniface in honor of Saint Michael. For some time Saint Wigbert, abbot of Fritislaria, presided over this monastery by Boniface’s command, as appears from chapter 6 of his Life.], after a community of servants of God and the holiness of monks had been gathered there; they acquired their food and clothing for themselves by laboring diligently with their own hands, in apostolic fashion. Thus the report of his holy preaching was spread abroad and grew to such an extent that his fame resounded through a very large part of Europe. From the regions of Britain a great multitude of servants of God came to him, both readers and scribes and men learned in other arts. Very many of them submitted themselves to his regular discipline and called the people away from the profanation of wandering paganism in many places. Some were dispersed through the province of the Hessians, others through Thuringia, and they preached the word of God widely throughout the people’s villages and settlements.

**25.** And when a great multitude of both peoples received the sacraments of the faith, with many thousands of men baptized, Pope Gregory II of blessed memory having by then died and Gregory the Younger, of the aforesaid apostolic see, presiding over the chair of the apostolic dignity, his messengers again came to Rome. They addressed the holy pontiff of the apostolic see and made known to him the bonds of their former friendship, mercifully granted by his predecessor to Saint Boniface and his household. They also recounted his devoted future submission to the apostolic see, and begged that henceforth he might continue in devoted submission to the familiarity and communion of the holy pontiff and of the whole apostolic see, as they had been instructed. Immediately, therefore, the holy pope of the apostolic see gave a peaceful reply and granted the familiarity and friendship of himself and of the apostolic see both to Saint Boniface and to those subject to him. Having taken up the archiepiscopal pallium [Note: [Col. 0621D] On the archiepiscopal dignity conferred on Boniface, read the notes to Othlo’s Book I, chapters 35 and 37.], together with gifts and various relics of the saints, he honorably sent the envoys back to their homeland.

**26.** When the messengers arrived and reported the apostolic see’s voluntary responses, Boniface, now rejoicing and greatly strengthened by the support of his devotion to the apostolic see, and inspired by the aid of divine mercy, built two churches for the Lord. One was at Fridislar [Note: [Col. 0621D] The monastery of Fritislaria was discussed above in the Acts of Saint Wigbert the abbot, under the year 747 [Col. 0622D]. Concerning Hamanaburg—whether it stood at the place where Homburg now is, not far from Fritislaria, or at Amelburg near Marburg—there is nothing further to say.], which he consecrated in honor of Saints Peter and Paul, the princes of the apostles; the other was at Hamanaburch, and this too he dedicated in honor of Saint Michael the archangel. He also attached two little monasteries to the two churches and installed in them a considerable number of people serving God, so that even to this day glory, blessing, and thanksgiving are devoutly offered to the Lord God.

When all these things had been properly completed, he went to the lands of the Bavarians during the time of Duke Hucpert [Note: [Col. 0622D] Read the Acts of Saint Rupert under the year 717.], and diligently carried on the work of preaching among them, visiting and inspecting many churches. He was armed with such zeal for divine strength that he condemned and rejected a certain schismatic deceived by heretical depravity, named Eremwlfus [Variant: Heremwlfus], in accordance with the decrees of the canons; he corrected the people’s idolatry of that perverse sect, and then returned again to the brothers of his diocese in order to establish its government, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Having the desire to come to the brothers” (Romans 15).

**CHAPTER IX.—His third journey to Rome; how, on his return, he turned aside in response to an invitation from Odilo, duke of the Bavarians; how he established four bishoprics in Bavaria; and how, under the dukes Caroloman and Pippin, he held synods in Francia and restored orthodox religion.**

[Col. 0622B]

**27.** Having thus briefly excerpted some evidence of this man’s merits, let us now recount in a few words how consistently he governed himself by religious discipline throughout all the stages of his life. It has long been the custom of the saints that each day, through the examples of others, they should advance themselves toward better things; and as the count of their days diminishes, the power of their innermost love should also increase.

When only a very small number of churches had been built in Hesse and Thuringia, and individual guardians had been appointed for each, he came to Rome for the third time, accompanied by a company of disciples, because of his close fellowship with the holy apostolic pontiff and with the entire clergy. He wished to enjoy the saving conversation of the apostolic Father and, now advanced in age, to commend himself to the prayers of the saints. After the immense hardship of the journey, when he was presented to the apostolic lord Gregory the Younger, the Second [Note: [Col. 0622D] This is Gregory III, called here “the Younger Second” and likewise in chapter 10. This third journey of Boniface to Rome took place in the year 738, according to the notes to Othlo’s Book I, chapter 28.], he was kindly received by him. He was held in such honor by all, both Romans and visitors, that many flocked to his salutary teaching. A great multitude of Franks and Bavarians, as well as Saxons arriving from Britain and people from other provinces, diligently adhered to his admonition.

**28.** When he had remained in these regions for a considerable part of a year, traveling around and praying at the relics of the saints, he then took leave of the venerable man, the pontiff of the apostolic see, and returned honorably enriched with gifts and relics of the saints. Reaching Italy and entering the walls of the city of Ticena [Pavia], he rested with the venerable Liodbrand, king of the Lombards, whose limbs were already wearied by old age. On departing, he not only had been invited by Odilo, duke of the Bavarians [Col. 0623A], but also willingly visited the inhabitants. He remained among them for many days, preaching and evangelizing the word of God, restoring the sacraments of true faith and religion, and driving away the destroyers of churches and corrupters of the people. Some of these had previously put themselves forward under the false rank of bishop; others claimed the office of presbyter; still others, inventing these and countless other things, had led the people astray to a great extent.

But the holy man, devoted to God from childhood, could not endure an injury to his Lord. He restrained the aforesaid duke and the whole populace from the unjust sect of heretical falsehood and from the fornication of priestly deception; and, with Duke Odilo consenting, he divided the province of the Bavarians into four parishes and appointed four bishops to preside over these districts, raising them to the episcopal rank through ordination. The first, named John, received the episcopal chair of the church in the town called Salzburg. The second was Erembercht, who held the primacy as overseer of the Church of Freising [Note: [Col. 0623C] This signifies the Greek word ἐπισκοπός, “overseer,” as is well known.]. The third was Goibaldus [Note: [Col. 0623C] Others write Gaibaldus. His see, once called Reginum, is now called Radasbona or Ratisbon. John, bishop of Salzburg, is honored among the Benedictine saints; concerning him, see the eulogy of Saint Rupert [Col. 0623D] the bishop, under the year 717.], who undertook the pastoral office of watchman over the Church of the city of Regina. The fourth was Vivillo, who obtained the dignity of sacred oversight over the Church of Patavium [Passau].

When everything was being rightly conducted with the order of Christianity confirmed, and the rights of the canons had been restored in Bavaria, he returned to his own churches. Caring for the people entrusted to him, looking after the folds of the flocks, and providing watchfulness for the congregation, he rescued the sheep from the impious bites of wolves.

**29.** When the temporal reign of the glorious Duke Charles had ended, and the authority of his sons Caroloman and Pippin had been strengthened, then, with the Lord God’s help and through the prompting of Saint Boniface the archbishop, the constitution of the Christian religion was confirmed. The synodal decrees of the orthodox Fathers were corrected among the Franks, and everything was amended and cleansed by the authority of the canons. The unjust union of laymen with concubines was partly dissolved through the exhortation of the holy man, and the wicked union of clerics with their wives was likewise separated and abolished.

So great a fervor of divine charity was kindled in the aforesaid dukes through the teaching of Saint Boniface that they freed the people to a considerable extent from the judgment of a perverse, long-established custom. The people, entangled in their own will and deceived by the suggestions of heretics, had forfeited the rights of the eternal inheritance. Indeed, the sect of heretics had so suffocated the light of spiritual teaching among the people that the darkness of heretical deception covered a large part of the populace. Among these were Elberchtus [Note: [Col. 0623D] Variant: Aldebertus. Compare Othlo.] and Clemens, who, seduced by a profane greed for money, persistently turned the people away from the path of truth.

But Saint Boniface the archbishop, with the glorious dukes Caroloman and Pippin consenting, expelled them from the unity of the Church. In accordance with the Apostle (1 Corinthians 3), they were handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord.

**CHAPTER X.—How, by repeatedly holding synodal assemblies in Francia, he went to Frisia to preach.**

**30.** When bishops and presbyters, deacons and clerics, and every ecclesiastical rank had assembled together—those whom Caroloman, duke of illustrious memory, had summoned under the authority of his rule—the fifth synodal council was held [Note: [Col. 0623D] He means the Council of Soissons, held in the eleventh year of King Childeric, in the year of Christ 744. In it the Nicene faith and the canonical judgments of other synods were confirmed (canon 1); Adalbert was condemned with his heresy (canon 2); Clement’s little crosses were consigned to the fire (canon 7); Abel was appointed over the Church of Rheims and Ardobert over that of Sens (canon 3); and the letters obtained from Pope Zachary were used to confirm the whole proceeding. They are found in Othlo, Book II, chapter 10, and fit this passage well. Willibald further implies that Boniface was then archbishop of the city of Mainz; yet from another letter of Zachary, reported in Othlo, Book II, chapter 7, it is clearly inferred that the matter stood otherwise.

But if Willibald here indicates the Council of Soissons, a difficulty arises: why is it said to have been summoned by Caroloman’s command, when the commonly circulated Acts of that council mention only Pippin [Col. 0624C]? In any event, for it to be called the fifth, four earlier councils under Caroloman must have preceded it, although no memory survives except of two, namely the Germanic and the Liptinense. Nevertheless, Willibald himself took part in both the Germanic and the Liptinense synods and deserves trust, if anyone does.

It seems, indeed, that two Germanic synods must be distinguished. One was held under Pope Gregory III, at which Boniface ordained four bishops for the Bavarians; Gregory’s letter to Boniface concerning the convocation of this synod on the Danube is preserved in Othlo, Book I, chapter 30. The other was held during the pontificate of Pope Zachary in the year 742, at which seven chapters were established and confirmed in the following year at Liptina, Othlo, Book I, chapter 34.], at which Boniface, archbishop of the city of Mainz, presiding in the pontificate with Caroloman’s consent and support, as legate of the Roman Church and apostolic see, first sent by the holy and venerable pontiff of the apostolic see, Gregory the Younger [Note: [Col. 0624D] This should be read in this way, not as in Serarius, where one Gregory is mentioned as follows: “Gregory the Younger with the First Third, an honorable man.” For Boniface had first received the dignity of legate in Germany from Gregory II, called the Younger, and afterward from his successor Gregory III. We have demonstrated under the year 731 that the title “Younger” was attributed by the ancients to Gregory II, not Gregory III. Read Walafrid, On Ecclesiastical Affairs, chapter 8.], and afterward by Gregory III, an honorable man, urged that the numerous canonical enactments of the first four principal synods be observed for the salutary increase of heavenly doctrine.

And just as at Nicaea, while Constantine Augustus governed the world’s empire, the treacherous blasphemy of Arius was overthrown; and as the assembly of one hundred and fifty Fathers, while the elder Theodosius ruled at Constantinople, condemned Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit was God; and as the unity of two hundred bishops, assembled under the younger Theodosius at the city of Ephesus, separated Nestorius, who professed two persons in Christ, from the catholic Church by a just anathema; and as the gathering of six hundred and thirty priests at the Council of Chalcedon anathematized Eutyches, abbot of the city of Constantinople, and Dioscorus, his defender, who rebelled against the catholic faith, in accordance with the previously defined judgment of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0625D] It is remarkable that no mention is made of the sixth council against the Monothelites.]:

so, likewise, in Francia, after the perfidy of the heretics had been completely eradicated and the conspiracy of the wicked uprooted, the growth of divine law was increased, and the canons of the synodal general councils were received. The assembly of bishops of the spiritual synodal council also met according to the definition of the authentic constitution. Yet because of the daily expectation of wars and the hostile uprising of the barbarian peoples surrounding the region—for foreign plunderers of other peoples were savagely attempting to destroy Francia—it was either scarcely held at all or was given over to such great forgetfulness that, its memory entirely erased from the present age, it could no longer be known by any means. For the world, by a natural process, suffers each day either some loss through decline or at least some recovery; nor, though renewed in every respect, does it entirely escape its own deterioration, but, hastening toward its predetermined end, it presses forward.

Therefore, if in this mortal life of our pilgrimage anything has been discovered by spiritual authors for the common benefit of those weakened in this world, it must be preserved by Catholics with the strength of a great defense and held fast with the mind’s immovable resolve, even if it has sometimes been implanted in human minds, lest either human forgetfulness creep in or the alluring pleasure of worldly delight, at the devil’s instigation, obstruct it.

For this reason, this holy bishop of the Lord, inspired by the care of the most diligent solicitude, took pains to rescue the people from the deadly persuasion of the crooked serpent and repeatedly urged Duke Caroloman to convene the aforesaid assembly of synods, so that the wisdom of spiritual knowledge might be revealed both to those then living and to posterity, and that the knowledge of Christianity might become known after the deception surrounding souls had been turned away.

**31.** When he set before all ranks a kind of mirror of canonical rectitude as an example of right living, and an evident trace of truth began to appear to everyone, he, now decrepit through the long old age of his life and conscious of his own weakness, offered salutary counsel. In accordance with the rule of ecclesiastical order, he provided the peoples with pastoral leadership, so that whether he lived or died, the people would not lack the healing service of pastors. He promoted two men of good ability to the episcopal order, Willibald and Burchard, and distributed among them the churches entrusted to him in the innermost parts of eastern Francia and along the borders of the Bavarians [Col. 0626A].

He entrusted to Willibald the parish of his administration at a place called Eichstat [Note: [Col. 0625D] In their letters, cited by Othlo, Book II, chapters 1 and 2, Boniface and Pope Zachary do not mention the city of Eichstat. In its place they write Erpesfurt [Col. 0626D]. Read the notes in Book II, chapter 1, and the Life of Saint Willibald below.]. To Burchard he assigned the office of its dignity at the place called Wirtzaburg, and entrusted to his office the churches on the borders of the Franks, Saxons, and Slavs. Until the glorious day of his departure, he unceasingly opened to the peoples the narrow way of the heavenly kingdom.

**32.** When Pippin, by the Lord’s gift, the fortunate successor of his aforesaid brother, received the Frankish kingdom and, with the people’s disturbance somewhat calmed, had been raised to kingship, he began anxiously to offer devout vows to the Lord, immediately to recover the synodal ordinances, and to restore the canonical ministries [Variant: mysteries] faithfully begun by his brother at the exhortation of Saint Boniface [Col. 0626B], archbishop. He also held Boniface in preeminence both in manner and honor and obeyed his commands in the Lord.

But because the holy man, weighed down by bodily weakness, could not attend all the assemblies of the councils, he now, with the counsel and advice of the glorious king, determined to provide a suitable minister for the aforesaid flock. He appointed Lullus (see the Acts below), his disciple of ingenious character, to instruct so great a multitude of people; he raised and ordained him to the episcopal rank and bound him to the inheritance which he had acquired in Christ through strenuous labor. Lullus had been his faithful companion in the Lord during his pilgrimage and a witness of both his suffering and his consolation.

**CHAPTER XI.—The Passion of Saint Boniface.**

[Col. 0626C]

**33.** When the Lord wished to rescue his servant Saint Boniface from the temptation of this world and relieve him from the tribulations of temporal life, it was then also determined, by the Lord’s dispensation, that he should reach Frisia, which he had once abandoned in body though not in mind, accompanied by servants of God traveling with him. Thus, where he had first begun the increase of his rewards by entering upon the work of preaching, he might also, on returning from the world, receive the wages of his recompense.

By a remarkable prophetic foreknowledge, he foretold to the aforesaid bishop Lullus the day of his approaching death and indicated the end by which he would at last leave the world. He explained to him in order the construction of the churches and the instruction of the people, saying:

“I wish to complete the journey I have resolved to undertake; I shall not be able to call myself back from the journey I desire to make. For the day of my release is already near, and the time of my death approaches. Having laid aside the prison of the body, I shall return to the prize of eternal recompense. But you, my dearest son, bring to completion the construction of the churches in Thuringia which I began, according to the measure of perfection. Recall the people most earnestly from the pathless way of error, and complete at Fulda the building of the basilica already begun; there bring my body, aged through the course of many years.”

When he had finished these words, he added still more extensive words of this kind, saying:

“My son, provide all things with your most prudent counsel, whatever must be joined to the needs of our journey here; and place in the case of my books the linen in which my decrepit body is to be wrapped.”

**34.** When the aforesaid bishop of such great religious devotion could no longer restrain his sighs and immediately burst into tears, Saint Boniface, after the conversation had ended, turned to other matters. After not many days had passed, he did not withdraw from the journey he had undertaken. Instead, taking companions with him, he boarded a ship and, penetrating along the channel of the River Rhine, sought out the places of the ports by night navigation. At last, entering the watery fields of the Frisians, he safely crossed the lake called in their language Elmere (see below, no. 38), and traveled around inspecting the unfruitful shores that lacked the divine seed.

When he had escaped the danger of rivers, the sea, and immense waters, he then fell into a danger that was not dangerous: he visited the pagan nation of the Frisians [Note: [Col. 0627D] Eigil the abbot relates that Boniface did this once and again during the final two years of his life, in the Acts of Saint Sturm, no. 15, under the year 779.]. Separated by intervening waters, it is divided into the districts of many fields, so that, although they are called by different names, they nevertheless lay claim to the identity of a single people. But since it would be lengthy to recount them in order, we shall endeavor to strip of anonymity only those whose names can truthfully be brought into the sequence of our narrative, so that both the place and the language may equally reveal the holiness of the blessed man reported by us and disclose by what kind of end he would leave this world.

[Col. 0627C] **35.** Traveling through the whole of Frisia, he diligently preached the word of the Lord, rejecting the pagan rite and destroying the erroneous custom of paganism. He built churches with great zeal, after breaking the renown of the shrines. Together with his fellow soldier and fellow bishop Coebaneus, he baptized many thousands of men and women and also children [Note: [Col. 0627D] Others call him Eobanus, concerning whom we spoke in the preceding observations, no. 9. Concerning others, see the appendix after Othlo below. Canisius reads “chorepiscopus Doban.”].

To assist the weakness of his old age, he installed Coebaneus among the Frisians as bishop in the city called Trecht [Variant: Trehet, Trehit, now Utrecht], together with presbyters and deacons whose names are these: Wintrung, Walteri, and Ethelheri, endowed with the priestly office; Hamunt, Scirbald, and Bosa, assigned to the service of the Levites; and Waccar, Gundwaccar [Variant: Gundecar], Illesehere, and Bathowlf [Col. 0627D], raised to the monastic order of monks.

By spreading the seed of eternal life so widely among the people with Saint Boniface, they proclaimed it abroad, with the Lord God’s protection, to such an extent that, since according to the rule of apostolic instruction they had one heart and one soul, they also had the same palm of martyrdom and reward of triumph.

**36.** After the splendor of the faith had shone throughout Frisia, as we have said, and the happy end of this holy life was drawing near, he set up his tents beside the bank of the river called Bordne [Note: [Col. 0627D] The River Burdo or Bordne (Burde), once dividing the Westrachians from the Ostrachians—that is, the Western Frisians from the Eastern Frisians. They are now separated by the River Ems, as we noted in observation 7 preceding the Life of Saint Willibrord. The Continuator of Fredegar agrees with Willibald on this point; in chapter 19 he says that the Frankish duke Charles penetrated the Westrachia and Ostrachia (for this is how it should be read), called islands of the Frisians, and established a camp on the River Burdo.

The place where Saint Boniface suffered martyrdom is called in the letter of the pseudo-Liudger to Rixfrid the village of Dokem or Dockum, and by the anonymous author Dockinga. It is now a city of the diocese of Leeuwarden, formerly belonging to the district of Ostrachia, that is, to the Eastern Frisians. Concerning the church built there in honor of Saint Paul and Saint Boniface, read our appendix after Book II of Othlo.], which lies on the borders of those whom the rustic language calls Ostar and Westher [the anonymous author has Astroche and Westroche]. He was accompanied only by a number of his own attendants.

Because he had announced to the people the feast day of the Confirmation of the neophytes and the laying on of hands and confirmation by the bishop of those recently baptized, everyone who had been dispersed far and wide had now returned to his own home, so that, in accordance with the holy bishop’s appointed decision, all might present themselves on the day predetermined for their confirmation.

When the appointed day had dawned and the sun, rising with the light of dawn, was already breaking forth, then, in the reverse order, enemies arrived in place of friends, and new executioners in place of newly instructed worshipers of the faith. A great multitude of the enemy, bristling with weapons, carrying spears and shields, burst into the camp. At once the boys sprang out from the camp and attacked them with weapons. These boys, afterward Martyrs, attempted to defend the saints against the senseless army of the raging people.

But as soon as the man of God heard the attack of the turbulent crowd, he summoned the choir of clerics to him, took the relics of the saints which he was accustomed always to carry with him, and went out from the tent. Immediately rebuking them, he forbade the boys to engage in battle, saying:

“Stop, boys, from the conflict, and lay aside the warfare of battle, because we are truly taught by the testimony of Scripture not to return evil for evil, but even good for evil. The long-desired day has now come, and the appointed time of our release is near. Therefore be strengthened in the Lord and gratefully endure the grace of his permission; hope in him, and he will deliver your souls.”

Then, addressing the priests, deacons, and men of the lower orders who stood by, servants subject to God’s service, he admonished them in a father’s voice, saying:

“Brothers and men, be strong in spirit, and do not fear those who kill the body, since they cannot kill the soul that endures without end. Rather, rejoice in the Lord and fasten the anchor of your hope upon him. He will immediately repay you with the reward of recompense and grant you a seat in the heavenly court among the citizens of the angels above. Do not subject yourselves to the empty pleasure of this world; do not delight in the fleeting flatteries of the pagans. Instead, steadfastly undergo here the sudden crisis of death, so that you may reign with Christ forever.”

**37.** As he gently urged his disciples toward the crown of martyrdom with such teaching and encouragement, the furious tumult of the pagans immediately rushed upon them with swords and every kind of military armor and stained the bodies of the saints with the blessed slaughter. After the mortal flesh of the righteous had been slain, the rejoicing crowd of pagans seized the victorious spoil of their own condemnation; they plundered the camp and distributed the booty by carrying it away.

They also took the cases containing many volumes of books and the chests of relics. Believing that a great quantity of gold and silver was stored there, they carried the cases and chests to the ships in which the daily provisions of the clerics and boys were kept, together with a little wine that still remained as part of the same allowance [Col. 0629B]. The vessels were still closed with their covers. When they discovered the drink of the precious liquid, they immediately began to satisfy their greedy bellies and intoxicate their wine-soaked stomachs.

At last, after deliberating over the spoils they had received, by the marvelous disposition of almighty God they began to discuss and consider how the gold and silver they had not seen might be divided among them. As they spoke at length about the value of so much money, an argument arose, and finally such discord began to produce hostility that the maddened crowd, driven insane by the fury of its madness, divided into two factions. In the end they cruelly turned against one another the weapons with which they had earlier slaughtered the holy martyrs.

When a very large part of the raging crowd had been struck down, those who had survived ran joyfully to the gain acquired at the cost of souls and lives, while their adversaries lay dead—those who had opposed them over the treasure of greed they had desired for themselves. Breaking open the book repositories, they discovered volumes in place of gold and sheets of divine knowledge in place of silver. Thus deprived of the precious price of gold and silver, they scattered the books they had found across the open plain; some they threw into the reeds of the marshes, and others they hid and abandoned in various places.

Yet by the grace of the Almighty and by the prayers of Saint Boniface, supreme pontiff and martyr, they were later found unharmed and undefiled, after a great interval of time had passed, and were returned by their individual discoverers to the house [Note: [Col. 0629D] Namely, the monastery of Fulda, where three books of Saint Boniface are still preserved among the sacred treasures (κειμήλια): the first contains the canons of the New Testament; the second, reddened by the blood of the martyr, contains the letter of Saint Leo to Bishop Theodore, Saint Ambrose’s sermon on the Holy Spirit and his little book On the Good of Death, the little book of Saint Faustus the Confessor, the letter of Agnellus to Arminius on the rule of faith, a list of the regions and cities in which the bodies of the apostles rest, and other things of this kind; the third contains the Gospel written, as they say, by the hand of Saint Boniface himself.], where even to this day they benefit the salvation of souls.

But the executioners, saddened by the loss of the money they had valued, returned home and, after a three-day truce, suffered a greater loss of their household possessions and also the loss of life through death, receiving retaliation. For the almighty Creator and Restorer of the world wished to take vengeance on his enemies, to punish with the customary zeal of mercy the blood shed by the saints, and, moved by the fresh fury of their recent wickedness, to display publicly the wrath that had long been prolonged against the worshipers of idols.

**CHAPTER XII.—The translation of the sacred body to the monastery of Fulda.**
38. When the unexpected temporal slaughter of the holy martyrs thereafter flew through the villages, hamlets, and the whole province, the Christians suddenly learned of the martyrs’ bodily death. Gathering a very large expeditionary army, they then advanced eagerly to the borders of the neighboring territory as warriors ready for future vengeance; [Col. 0630B] and, when the reckoning of the aforesaid days had come round, they attacked the land of the unbelievers, who were safe from danger but inhospitable in their lack of devotion, and struck down the pagans who came to meet them from the opposite direction in a great slaughter.

[Note: [Col. 0629D] John of Beka attributes the deed to Widekind, prince of farther Frisia, who, crossing the Lavica, reduced the counties of Oostergo and Westergo to a vast wilderness, the native inhabitants having been destroyed. Yet, as Arnold Buchelius observes, no prince named Widekind is celebrated among the Frisians at that time, unless one has regard to Widekind, prince of the Saxons, who, after a long war with Charlemagne, believed in Christ only later. Emmius, in *On Frisian Matters*, book IV, more reasonably attributes it to Pippin’s prefect. Or was Abbo, Pippin’s prefect, mentioned below in no. 40, the author of this deed?]

But since the pagan people were unable to withstand the first assault of the Christian army, they turned in flight and fell in a great slaughter as well; and, turning their backs, they lost their lives together with all their household goods and heirs. Thus the Christians, having plundered the wives and children of the superstitious, as well as their male and female slaves, returned to their own land. And in a wondrous way it came about that the surviving inhabitants of the pagan territory, broken by the evils that had befallen them, avoided eternal torments instead, being illumined by the radiance of faith; and they accepted the instruction of the aforesaid bishop, which they had rejected while he lived, but which, now that he was dying [Al.: dead], [Col. 0630C] they received, terrified by the restraint of divine rebuke.

The body of the blessed bishop, carried across the strait called Elmere by favorable sails and blasts of wind,

[Note: [Col. 0630D] John of Beka calls it the Flevi channel—that is, the inlet of the German Sea between the present-day Dutch and Frisian territories, into which the eastern channel of the Rhine flows with the Isala near the city of Kampen. The inhabitants call this lake the Southern Sea.]

together with the bodies of the other martyrs, was brought after not many days to the aforesaid city called Trecht. There it was placed and buried until religious and faithful brothers in the Lord from Mainz, sent by Bishop Lull—indeed the successor of this holy bishop and martyr of Christ—sailed there to bring the body of the blessed man to the monastery that he had built during his lifetime and that lies beside the river called the Fulda. One of them, named Hadda, who had been the leader of the journey and the escort of the others and who led a life of singular holiness and private chastity and continence, had been personally entrusted by the aforesaid prelate with this embassy and with transporting the holy body, together with the brothers traveling with him, so that greater honor might be offered to the man through devotion worthy of sacred reverence, and so that the testimony of the many concerning what they would learn by hearing or seeing might carry greater authority.

When these honorable brothers of such holy fellowship reached the aforesaid city, a small gathering of the people had come out to meet them. Then the prefects of that city, in the hearing of the travelers, loudly proclaimed the prohibition issued by the glorious King Pippin: it was decreed that the body of the aforesaid bishop was not to be removed from there. But because the power of the Almighty is stronger than that of human beings, a wondrous and memorable miracle was immediately heard by all who were present to have been performed through angelic rather than human agency. The church bell,

[Note: [Col. 0631D] This story is reported quite differently by Eigil in the *Acts of Saint Sturm*, no. 15, where there is no mention at all of a bell. Rather, it is said that when the people of Trecht wished to carry the body of Saint Boniface to the greater basilica, it remained immovably fixed in place; and that, frightened by this miracle, the people of Trecht allowed it to be transferred to Fulda.]

as a sign of warning concerning the holy body, was set in motion without any human hand touching it, [Col. 0631B] so that everyone, struck by sudden fear and panic, stood in utter terror and cried out that the body of this righteous man ought to be returned. And so it was immediately returned. The brothers of holy memory carried it away honorably with psalms and hymns and, without the labor of rowers, brought it on the thirtieth day after his death to the aforementioned city of Mainz.

By the wondrous providence of Almighty God it also happened that on one and the same day, not on a day fixed in advance by human determination but as though on the appointed day of predestination, both the envoys bearing the holy body and many faithful men and women from distant regions far and wide gathered for the funeral rites of the holy man. The aforementioned lord bishop, successor to that bishop of such venerable rank, who at that time was present at the royal palace, entirely unaware of this matter and ignorant of the arrival of the holy body, reached the city we have mentioned as though at one and the same moment. Such grief had fallen upon all who had come from elsewhere, and upon the citizens of that city as well, and such joy surpassed it, that they both mourned the temporal death of the body of so great a bishop and, though he had been lost bodily, believed that he would thereafter be a perpetual patron to themselves and to their descendants.

39. Therefore, since these two reasons had arisen, they were moved in heart and, together with the priests and deacons and every ecclesiastical order, brought him to the place that he had predestined during his lifetime.

[Note: [Col. 0631D] Before the holy body was carried to Fulda, the townspeople of Mainz had attempted to claim it for themselves, as Othlo testifies in the *Life of Saint Sturm*. [Col. 0632D] We shall discuss the tomb of Saint Boniface in the appendix.]

There they placed him, having buried him according to custom in a new sarcophagus made in the church; [Col. 0631D] and, when everything had been duly completed, they returned and reached their own homes strengthened by the power of faith.

At the place where they had deposited the holy body, divine blessings thereafter overflowed. Through the prayers of the holy man, those who come to that same place oppressed by various illnesses obtain a healing remedy for body and mind alike. Some, already dead throughout their bodies and almost entirely lifeless, though meanwhile breathing out their final breath, were restored to their former health. Others, whose eyes were weighed down by blindness, recovered their sight. Others, bound by the snares of the devil and even afflicted in mind and driven mad, afterward retained the integrity of their understanding. Restored to their former health, they praised and glorified God, who deemed it worthy to enrich and honor his servant, adorned with so great a gift, and to glorify him in present and future ages by the radiant manifestation of miracles, when the fortieth year of his pilgrimage had come to an end. This was the seven hundred and fifty-fifth year of the Lord’s Incarnation (the year will be discussed below), with the eighth indiction.

He had served as bishop for thirty-six years, six months, and six days; and thus, in the order stated above, on the Nones of June, rewarded with the triumph of martyrdom, he departed to the Lord, to whom be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

[The following material was taken by Canisius from the Ingolstadt Codex.]

40. Having recounted the deeds of the blessed man, through which he flourished in infancy and childhood, in adolescence and youth, and even in old age, let us return to those things that, after he had completed the course of this world and the happy journey of this life, were wondrously accomplished, with the Lord cooperating, to attest to mortals the holiness of the blessed man’s life. Let us recall to memory a certain memorable miracle, worthy of imitation by the people, which, as was learned from the glorious King Pippin himself by those who had been present at the miracle, was transmitted to us through the venerable Bishop Lull and communicated in this way through his report: at the place where the precious blood of the holy martyr had once been shed, with the counsel of the people and of a great part of the Frisian population, they began to construct a certain mound, because of the immense incursions of the *ledon*,

[Note: [Col. 0632D] The *ledon* is the greater tide; the *malina*, the lesser tide of the sea, says Simeon Dunelmensis, or rather Turgot, in the book *On the Deeds of the Kings of England*, under the year 793, in volume I of the *History of Britain*. In the *Life of Saint Condedus*, chapter 6, in the second century, one reads *marina malinae et lidonis*. Theodoricus writes in the *Life of Saint Rumold*, apud Surius, that the city of Mechelen in Belgium was so called because of the *malina* and the *ledon*. Read Glaber, book III, chapter 3.]

and the *malina*, which are set in motion by the sea’s changing tide and the ocean’s ebb, and also by the lowering and swelling of the waters, constructing it from the bottom upward to a considerable height. Upon it, as was later done, they intended to build a church and establish a habitation of servants of God in the same place.

But while they were already building the work of the mound in its entirety [Col. 0632D] and completing the whole structure of the building, they also returned to themselves [F.: having returned], while the inhabitants and residents of that place were disputing among themselves about the scarcity of fresh [Al.: non-salty] water that causes great hardship throughout all Frisia to human beings and animals alike. Then at last, by the mercy of the Lord, the man who held the office of prefect over that district and place according to the proclamation of the glorious King Pippin, and who was the director of the work itself, named Abba [F.: Abbo], mounted a horse with his companions. After riding around the mound and inspecting it, suddenly a certain boy’s horse, with its feet unexpectedly pressing so deeply into the ground, was threatened with total collapse and fell headlong, its forelegs embedded in the earth. The more agile and alert men quickly dismounted from their horses and pulled out the horse that was stuck in the ground.

Immediately a miracle worthy of astonishment and spectacle was shown to those who were present: a crystal-clear spring, sweetened with an extraordinarily pleasant taste, burst forth contrary to the custom of that land [Note: [Col. 0633A] John Gerbrandus mentions this spring in book III, chapter 16, of the *Belgian Chronicle*], and flowed through previously unknown channels, so that it already seemed to be a very large stream. Astonished by this miracle, they returned home exultant and joyful and proclaimed among the people what they had seen.

## AUTHOR’S CONCLUSION

Published by Georg Wicelius in the *Hagialogy* from a manuscript of the Fulda Codex.

I, Willibald, bishop, and so forth. I first wrote the life and passion of Boniface on wax tablets for the examination of Lull and Megengaud; after their review, I transcribed it onto parchment, and here, in the place called Saint Victor’s outside the walls of Mainz, where Lull and Rabanus [Note: [Col. 0633A] This was not Rabanus Maurus, the monk and abbot of Fulda, later archbishop of Mainz, who was not yet born when Lull’s term was ending; rather, it was another man of the same name, and perhaps the very one whom Lull, bishop of Mainz, commends in letter 62 among the Bonifacian letters in these words: “Likewise, let each of you sing Masses for the two laymen Megenfrith and Hrabanx.” The partly ruined walls of Saint Victor’s church still survive; within them was the parish of Weisenau, as Serarius testifies in book I, chapter 31, of the *History of Mainz.] were occupied in prayer, and so forth.

[Col. 0633]

# ANOTHER LIFE OF SAINT BONIFACE

By Othlo, a Benedictine monk who lived after the middle of the eleventh century.

## PREFACE TO THE MONKS OF FULDA

[Col. 0633B]

### 1

Brothers of Fulda, I have endeavored to comply with your requests as far as the smallness of my knowledge permitted. You asked me to disclose in clearer language the Life of our holy father Boniface, a work that had long ago been published in an especially polished and elegant style—namely, that of Saint Willibald—but which in certain places is so obscure to a feeble understanding that it is difficult to see where its meaning is heading.

At first I dismissed this request as nothing, wondering why, when so many learned fathers live among you and in the surrounding regions, you should ever have thought of entrusting so difficult a task to me, an unskilled man almost entirely ignorant of liberal learning. Then one of you told me that work on the same project had previously been undertaken before Pope Saint Leo,

[Note: [Col. 0633D] Understand Pope Leo IX, from whom Egbert—also called Eppo, abbot of Fulda from 1058 to 1038 [the dates are evidently corrupt]—requested ancient monuments with which he might illuminate the deeds of his patron. From this it is possible to determine Othlo’s period.]

and that, so that he might be more fully equipped for the work, Abbot Egbert had sent several books and a writer to Rome with him; but that after Egbert’s death, the books had remained there and the requested work had not been completed. Then, taking pity on such circumstances, I eventually applied my mind to the matter, wishing to fulfill your request if any learning were to support me.

Although I had long possessed the will, I could not find in myself the ability to carry it out. I told you what I wanted to do and what I was unable to do. But you, as you know, repeated the same thing again and again, saying that if only I possessed a firm will, the Lord would provide everything else. Often stirred by such exhortation, I finally attempted to fulfill your prayers, [Col. 0633D] placing my greatest confidence in him who said, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm LXXX); and who, just as he often grants victory through the few, so also, by granting skill to the unskilled, displays the power of his grace. [Col. 0634B]

I have prefaced this explanation so that no one, supposing that I had undertaken so great a work of my own accord through arrogance, might say that it is a cause of great presumption to transfer into another form anything that has been uttered in any manner by a holy man, as though by some later corrector. It is not as though the very holy words of the prophets and the Gospel, enveloped in many obscurities, have not been translated by certain writers into another language or into a clearer meaning.

### 2

Having first offered these remarks against all detractors, who find nothing sweeter than tearing others apart and setting snares in the path along which they themselves do not wish to walk, I now wish to make clear to the reader that my principal aim in this work was to express the same meaning in clearer words, except for those passages whose difficulty and obscurity I was entirely unable to investigate.

I pursued what was easier to such an extent that, as can be demonstrated, I sometimes set down the very same words. For what need have we lowly people, who have become a spectacle to the world, of knotty and convoluted speech? Let lovers of secular wisdom have Cicero; we, the unskilled and obscure, the despised and contemptible, should follow Christ, who chose fishermen, not philosophers, as his disciples.

### 3

Among these matters I wish to make known to your affection that, when I examined the very book which you asked me to explain, I found that it did not contain many notable accounts of miracles and letters that I had found in other books. I therefore undertook to gather material from those books and insert it in places that seemed appropriate. Perhaps that venerable man who first wrote the Life of Saint Boniface unknowingly omitted many of his miracles and letters. Yet, when I consider all the letters that you possess concerning him, nowhere does the authority of so great a prelate seem greater than in the letters sent by him or to him.

There one sees most clearly how great was the reverence with which he was first received by the Roman pontiff; how the pope ordained him and sent him to preach to all the peoples of Germany; with what labor he converted that same Germany to the faith of Christ; and how he rescued it not only from pagans and heretics but also from pseudo-Christians and corrupt priests, as though from the bites of wolves.

There one also sees how much favor he obtained from the Frankish princes, namely Carloman and Pippin; and how, after he had appointed him prelate of the Church of Mainz, he made that church—which had previously been subject to another church—the metropolitan church of all Germany, with the consent of the apostolic pontiff, out of love and honor for him; how many episcopal sees he established; and what privileges he obtained for certain churches.

Finally, one observes there what is especially necessary for you now: how he enriched the place of his body—namely, your monastery—with possessions and special tithes.

### 4

Although such great authority is nullified by certain priests of the present day,

[Note: [Col. 0635D] Nicolaus Serarius refers this to the time of Abbot Widerad of Fulda, when the Fulda monastery was stripped of nearly all its possessions through the faction of Hecelo, bishop of Hildesheim, as Lambert of Hersfeld testifies under the year 1063. Yet this complaint fits more properly the pseudo-synod held at Erfurt in 1073, to exact the tithes of the Thuringians; this matter inflamed the Thuringians and Saxons against the king, as is recorded in the manuscript *Magdeburg Chronicle*.]

this will nevertheless fall upon them as a testimony to their condemnation: although they know that the ancient boundaries and decrees of the holy Fathers ought not to be transgressed, they transgress them to the utmost, forgetting those words that the Lord speaks in the Gospel to the chosen shepherds and teachers: “Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X).

For these words were not spoken only about the rulers of preceding times, but also about those who would govern his Church until the consummation of the age—not destroy it. Concerning destroyers and perverse shepherds the Lord says elsewhere: “Woe to you, lawyers, who have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves have not entered, and you have prevented those who wished to enter” (Luke XI). And again: “Woe to you, hypocrites, who tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have abandoned the weightier matters of the law—that is, judgment, mercy, and faith. These you ought to have done, without omitting the others” (Matthew XXIII). Many similar things are also said in the prophet Ezekiel about such shepherds.

[Col. 0635D] But, if it pleases us, let us ask these same shepherds how they wish to strengthen their own position if they have judged the statutes of the fathers who came before them worthy of destruction; or how a building placed upon a foundation can stand if they must cast away its foundations. The first Fathers were the foundations of the Church, as it is written: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Psalm LXXXVI, 1). Therefore, whoever disdains to follow such foundations of the stones placed above them is expelled from the heavenly building.

Let us also present an argument that is familiar to everyone. If someone undertakes to clear a forest belonging to his jurisdiction for cultivation, he measures out for himself fields of whatever length and breadth he wishes; to others, however, he distributes not what they themselves choose, but whatever measure he wishes, since he has the power to divide it among each according to his will.

Since everyone knows that this is so, why, I ask, is it unknown that the first princes of the churches—the apostles, namely, and all those who, following in their footsteps, first handed on the sacred faith to each people after clearing away the forests of various errors—had power in certain peoples and provinces to grant the possessions or tithes that fell to them to this or that church? For, in accordance with the decrees of the holy canons, they divided the tithes into four portions,

[Note: [Col. 0636D] Pope Gregory II also commands this below, in book I, chapter 18; it was still in force in the time of Hincmar, as is clear from his *Capitulary*, chapter 16. Read the First Council of Orléans, canon 5.]

giving one to themselves, another to the clergy, a third to the poor, and a fourth for the restoration of churches. Did they, consulting only their own greed in the distribution of tithes, forget the poor and the restoration of churches, as, alas, we see happening now?

The holy canons, by whose authority tithes are exacted, command not merely that tithes be given but also that they be distributed among various recipients, so that hostels for strangers may exist in every city and village and so that the poor and pilgrims may be fed. Yet this holy and necessary precept is not merely neglected in many places; it is almost unknown. For only this is read: that tithes are to be given to bishops. But what is to be done with them afterward, or whether anything else must be cared for concerning monasteries destroyed by clerics—miserable thing to say—and laypeople, and overturned without regard for the judgments of Christian religion, is consigned to oblivion or ignorance.

Hence I fear that the Psalmist, prophesying, said of the rulers of the present time, corrupted by insatiable greed: “They are corrupt and have become abominable in their pursuits” (Psalm XIII). Since nothing can be called corrupt unless it was previously whole, those rulers or shepherds may indeed be said to have once been whole because they had been equipped by God with complete wisdom for rendering true judgment. But they are corrupt because they judge not according to the wisdom given to them, but according to the amount of profit they can obtain.

And would that these shepherds merely disdained to divide tithes among the poor and did not forbid certain others—by which I mean monks, among whom some such care is still practiced—from doing so, endeavoring to remove from their right the tithes of ancient tradition.

Why, then, could Saint Boniface, to whom God granted such power throughout all Germany that he could establish churches and monasteries wherever he wished, erect episcopal sees, and divide their parishes, not give some possessions and tithes to any place that he had specially chosen for himself? By the same authority by which modern bishops customarily give tithes to soldiers and other secular men, could not Saint Boniface distribute those same tithes to monks or the poor?

If his other statutes seem holy, if everything that he distributed to the canons is praiseworthy, why, I ask, is this one act alone—that which he gave to monks and the poor—declared unjust? Alas, alas, that the man who was permitted to give so much to the rich is said to have had no permission to distribute even a little to the poor.

At this, heavens, be astonished, and let the world and all who dwell in it mourn, because the world has now been placed in wickedness, to such an extent that it envies the lives and dares to destroy those who were specially chosen and set apart from the world so that they might intercede for it with greater devotion.

### 5

But let this interruption of complaint now come to an end, so that the pen may return to the point from which it departed. I said before, and say again, that among all the letters concerning Saint Boniface that you possess, his letters seemed to me the most important. Therefore I endeavored to gather into one collection whatever letters I could find that were necessary for this work, hoping that from them some rival and some reader ignorant of so great an authority might be built up.

Accordingly, I earnestly ask and admonish you also, brothers of Fulda, to read these same letters with the utmost attention, beseeching God that, through the prayers of the man by whom or through whom they were written, and who—as is stated in them—once rescued the holy Church established in Germany from corrupt priests through the greatest labor, he may now also deign to defend you and your place from the power of men like them.

With the Lord’s help, I intend to write two little books, one concerning the life of the holy man and the other concerning the letters mentioned above. In the first I shall relate who he was and what labor he undertook in the holy Church before receiving the see of Mainz; in the second, what glorious deeds he performed afterward until the end of his life.

Who I am that I bring you such a gift of labor,

You know, and so, I beg you, do not tell it to many,

Lest the lowliness of my person cause my work to be despised.

Rather, let this be your concern: to seek Christ,

So that what is written here may remain pleasing to him.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0637D]

## I. Boniface as a boy yearns for the monastic life

When the English people had been subjected to the yoke of the sacred faith through the apostolate of Pope Saint Gregory, and, aided by his merits, had begun to shine among many nations in the generation of holy men, bringing forth many lights of the holy Church by which the various blindnesses of hearts might be illumined, it was granted to this world to produce among its lights Saint Boniface as well, like a certain morning star brighter than the other stars.

He, carefully raised by his parents, also became, as time passed, a lover of great virtues. For while he was still a little boy, if it happened that he heard some cleric or layman conveying knowledge of the divine word, he immediately began, as far as the tenderness of his age permitted, to consider what benefit might come from it to himself and to his character.

As he thus raised himself toward heavenly things through prolonged meditation, he revealed to his father what he was carrying in his heart and asked him to take account of his wishes. His father, hearing this, was first astonished; then, rebuking him and using now threats, now entreaties, he tried to drive him toward the concerns of secular life. Moreover, so that he might more easily turn the boy’s still tender mind away from the completion of the purpose he had conceived, he promised that after his own death he would make him heir to his estates and all his possessions.

He further protested that active life was more bearable for slippery human age and frail humanity than contemplative life, and that it was better for someone to seek companionship among the middling or lowest citizens of the heavenly kingdom through easier pursuits than to begin the greatest and almost impossible struggles for perfection and then, unable to complete them, fail along the way.

## II. At last his father consents, and he professes the monastic life

But the holy boy, already filled with divine virtue, the more his father tried to call him back to secular concerns, the more steadfastly continued in his undertaking and yearned to attain knowledge of the sacred writings.

Thus, by a marvelous dispensation, it came about that his father—the only obstacle—was seized by a sudden illness and laid aside his former stubbornness of mind. Through suitable messengers he sent the boy to the monastery that is now called by its ancient English name Adescancastre, commending him to Wolfhard, the venerable abbot of that monastery. Wolfhard immediately received him kindly, as the monastic order required, commended him to the brothers, and the boy began well all the duties of religion that his age permitted, completing them better from day to day.

## III. Carefully instructed, he moves to another monastery for the sake of study

When he had passed beyond the years of childhood, he devoted himself so completely to the institutions of the venerable brothers and to the exercise of sacred reading that the marks of many virtues continually increased in him. In him was fulfilled what the Psalmist testifies concerning the progress of certain people, saying: “They go from strength to strength” (Psalm VIII).

Finally, since he was devoted to unceasing meditation on the sacred Scriptures and for many years observed the whole discipline of the rule under the direction of the aforesaid abbot, but was unable there to satisfy his desire for learning divine letters because of the scarcity of teachers, he came, with the consent of his abbot and brothers, to the monastery that is still called Nuiscelle. There he chose as his teacher Winbert, of blessed memory, who at that time honorably presided over the monastery.

At last, having obtained the instruction he desired both in the subtleties of grammar and metrics and in spiritual understanding, he began to excel in these subjects to such an extent that the fame of his learning spread everywhere and others also flocked to him for the sake of study.

Nevertheless, he did not exalt himself in the least because of so great a gift of knowledge, nor did he despise anyone of lesser intelligence. Rather, the more God advanced him above others in literary understanding and in the excellence of other virtues, the more humble and devoted he was seen to be in the practice of compassion and submission, continually recalling the saying of the Wise One: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclesiasticus III).

## IV. Ordained priest at the age of thirty

Since, with the zeal we have described, he surpassed others in humility and submission, while others, stirred by the report of his wisdom or instructed by his most salutary teaching, in turn honored him as a father, everyone praising him and advancing him through the several degrees of the ecclesiastical order, he was finally chosen for the dignity of the priestly office when he was thirty years old or somewhat older.

What sort of man he showed himself to be in the contrition [perhaps: condition] of the twofold human being, so that he might become worthy to share in the heavenly sacrament, is better gathered from the testimony of his deeds than from any indication in words.

## V. He brings the decrees of a synod to the archbishop

At that same time, while In, king of the West Saxons, was reigning, a new disturbance arose in those regions. To suppress it, a synodal council of servants of God was immediately established at the command of the aforesaid king and on the advice of his leading men.

When everyone had assembled and they had determined the cause of the disagreement that had arisen, it pleased certain wise men that everything decided there should be reported to the venerable archbishop of the city of Canterbury, named Berthwald. The king, together with the multitude of all the clergy and laity, agreed and asked who would be most suitable to carry this embassy.

Then the leading archimandrite among them, Winberth, whom we mentioned above; Wintra, who presided over the monastery called Wessexbury; Beorwart, who governed the monastery called Glastonbury; and many other venerable men summoned Saint Boniface and brought him before the king, saying that he was suitable for so important an embassy.

The king soon entrusted the matter of the embassy to him and assigned companions to accompany him. He set out for Kent—that is, Canterbury—and wisely reported everything in order to the aforementioned archbishop, as he had been instructed. After not many days he returned and diligently fulfilled the embassy entrusted to him, bringing the response to the aforesaid king and the servants of God already mentioned. He thereby brought great joy to everyone.

For this reason his name became celebrated among both secular and ecclesiastical men, so much so that afterward he was very often requested to take part in their synodal assemblies.

## VI. Although the abbot consents reluctantly, he crosses to Frisia

But because his mind, already devoted to God, had been separated from every form of human approval, he began in every way to consider how he might leave the company of his parents and relatives and migrate, for Christ’s name, to some distant place.

After he had pondered and carefully deliberated on this for a very long time, he finally brought the matter to the attention of the aforesaid abbot and tried, through persistent entreaty, to incline him toward agreement with his will. Although the abbot, astonished at such a proposal, resisted the petitioner for a long time and denied him permission, at last, by divine providence and predestination, the petitioner’s words prevailed.

The abbot and his brothers showed such devotion and care for the journey he had chosen that they supplied him with everything necessary for the road and offered various prayers for him with tears, asking that the good angel of the Lord might everywhere be his companion and direct him toward every success. They also permitted two brothers to go with him, so that he might be supported by their bodily and spiritual assistance.

Thus strengthened by the support of both kinds, he set out on a favorable journey. He reached the place called Lundenwic in the ancient language of the English and Saxons; and, after a short interval, he crossed over to Dorstet, where he remained for some time and rendered due praises to God day and night.

But since during that period a hostile conflict arising between the glorious prince Charles, duke of the Franks, and Ratbod, king of the Frisians, was disturbing the peoples on both sides, and since most of the churches of Christ that had previously been subject to Frankish rule in Frisia were being grievously returned to the worship of idols under Ratbod’s persecution, the man of God, perceiving the magnitude of such perversity, departed from those regions and reached Trecht. There too he remained for several days and addressed the arriving King Ratbod, entreating him to desist from such great wickedness.

## VII. Returning to his homeland, he refuses the place of the dead abbot and seeks Rome
After this, having traversed the regions of that land, he diligently investigated whether any opportunity for preaching was open somewhere in that province. When, after a prolonged inquiry, he realized that he would labor in vain by preaching there, he left the fields barren of spiritual fertility and returned to his native soil.

Meanwhile it happened that the Father of his monastery, having laid aside the prison of the flesh, ended his present life. At his death the brothers were deeply saddened, but the blessed man gladdened them through spiritual conversations, [Col. 0640D] and instructed them in every way that, while preserving the rule of the regular life, they should choose a spiritual Father. They all therefore earnestly entreated the holy man—then called Winfrid—to undertake pastoral care over them. But he, cherishing higher aims in his heart, did not disdain their prayers with any proud disdain. Rather, humbly revealing what his purpose was—namely, that, having rejected all the resources and honors of his homeland, he wished to travel abroad for the love of Christ and the salvation of others—he obtained the brothers’ consent and permission for his wishes.

And so that those wishes might possess greater authority, he also approached the venerable bishop of that place, named Daniel, asking that he might deserve to depart for Rome with the bishop’s blessing and letters of recommendation. The bishop, moved by divine prompting, kindly received this request and effectively fulfilled it. For, acting with the foresight of a shepherd, he appointed a man of good character named Stephen to preside over the congregation that had been deprived of its head, and he sent this servant of God, who desired to undertake the long roads of pilgrimage, toward the places he desired, supplied with letters.

### VIII.—He is sent into Germany by Pope Gregory.

Having received this blessing, he immediately bade farewell to the brothers and set out across long stretches of land and along unknown sea-routes, until a considerable company of servants of God, burning with the same spirit, gathered to him from every direction. All these men, therefore, visited many holy churches each day with one accord, beseeching that, with God’s help, they might cross the Alpine heights more safely and deserve to experience the Lombards’ ferocity toward them softened. When they had passed unharmed through all the dangers posed by that most savage people and had successfully reached the threshold of the blessed apostle Peter, they immediately offered Christ the thanks that were due. There, praying for the remission of their sins and a fortunate conclusion to their journey, they found the aid they had hoped for.

For after the holy man had addressed the venerable prelate of the apostolic see, named Gregory, who was then regarded as the Second of that name, and had disclosed to him the reason for his arrival and the desire with which he had labored for so long, the prelate at once looked upon him with a cheerful face and asked whether he had brought letters of recommendation from his bishop. He promptly produced a sheet, folded according to custom, [Col. 0641C] and handed it to the apostolic prelate. The latter, having received and read the letter and having learned of the holy man’s desire, thereafter held frequent conversations with him. Reverently keeping him there for some time, he gave him whatever relics of the saints he requested. He also entrusted him with the responsibility of preaching among all the peoples of Germany and gave him a letter, of which the following copy is preserved.

### IX.—Gregory’s letter.

“Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to Boniface, a religious presbyter. The religious purpose of your undertaking, made known to us, demands, etc.” (See below, Letter 2.)

### X.—He visits Frisia and announces the word of God.

Having received this letter from the venerable pope, he departed from there [Col. 0641D] for Liutprand, king of the Lombards, who received him honorably, and with whom he stayed for some time as a guest. Setting out from there, he crossed the steep and precipitous Alpine heights. Traversing the unknown borders of the Bavarians and Germany, he reached Thuringia, observing and investigating everything like a most prudent bee, seeking where he might later gather the nectar-like sweetness of the holy faith.

When he remained in Thuringia for several days, he addressed all the leaders of that province with spiritual words and recalled them to recognition of the sacred faith and to the path of the whole religion. He also found certain priests devoted to various crimes; admonishing them with evangelical discourses, he corrected them according to the standard of canonical discipline.

Meanwhile, having heard of the death of Ratbod, king of the Frisians, who during that period had inflicted great persecution upon Christians, he was filled with great joy and reached Frisia by sea. There, scattering the seeds of the divine word, he drew many back from the error of idolatry.

### XI.—He collaborates with Willibrord but refuses to become a bishop.

At the same time, through the venerable Willibrord, bishop of the Church of Utrecht, the trumpet of heavenly doctrine resounded in Frisia. The holy servant of God Boniface rejoiced in and wholly attached himself to Willibrord’s work, laboring with him for three continuous years both in destroying shrines and in building churches, as well as in all divine affairs.

It therefore happened that, because the aforesaid bishop, weighed down by already advanced old age, wished—at the urging of his disciples—to provide support for his declining years, he earnestly entreated this servant of God to accept the rank of episcopal rule and govern the people entrusted to him. But Boniface humbly rejected such a proposal, declaring that he was not at all worthy of the episcopal rank. He repeatedly begged that such a height of dignity not be imposed upon him while he was still in the years of youth, affirming also that, in accordance with the precepts of canonical discipline, he had not yet fully reached the age of fifty, which was appropriate to the summit of this rank.

When the aforementioned bishop reproved him in gentle words and urged him to accept the episcopal office, and when various arguments had been exchanged in this spiritual dispute, the holy man, placed in so great a struggle, finally offered a suitable speech of excuse, [Col. 0642C] saying:

“Holy bishop, I do not dare accept the burden of governance that you wish to impose upon me, unworthy though I am, because I was sent into Germany by Pope Gregory for the purpose of evangelizing. Since I came into these barbarian nations in fulfillment of that mission, I voluntarily subjected myself to its governing authority. Therefore I do not presume in any way to disregard so great a commission and undertake some other task. Hence, venerable Father, I beg that, with your favor and permission, I may be permitted to go to those regions to which I was sent by the apostolic prelate.”

When the holy Willibrord heard this, he gave him his blessing and allowed him to depart.

### XII.—He converts the Hessians and others to Christ. He sends Binna to Rome.

[Col. 0642D] Departing from there, he reached a place called Amanaburg, having God everywhere as his companion. Supported by God’s power and protection, wherever he went he spread knowledge of sacred doctrine.

As he won an immense people for the Lord by preaching in Frisia, and as many, instructed by his spiritual teaching, reached recognition of the truth, he obtained the aforementioned place, which was governed by two brothers, namely Dietih and Dierorolf. With the help of the Lord God, he gathered there a considerable congregation of brothers and built a monastery.

At that time he also visited other parts of Germany for the purpose of preaching, namely the Hessians, who lived on the border of Saxony. When he had likewise converted a large part of them from the worship of pagan superstition [Col. 0643A] and had washed many thousands of people in the sacrament of baptism, he sent one of his own faithful men, named Binna, to Rome with letters. He announced to the venerable apostolic prelate all that divine mercy had accomplished through him, and how great a multitude of people, enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, had received from him the bath of regeneration.

He also wrote, in the form of prudent questions, about various matters pertaining to the daily needs of ecclesiastical discipline and the care of the people newly converted. The aforementioned envoy faithfully carrying out everything entrusted to him, delivered the letters to the apostolic prelate, received from him answers to all the questions submitted, and returned as quickly as possible, bringing them to his master.

### XIII.—Called to Rome by Gregory, he gives an account of his faith.

[Col. 0643B]

When the holy man had read the letters delivered to him and understood that, among other things, he had been invited to Rome, he immediately strove to fulfill the highest degree of obedience. Accompanied by a company of dependents and brothers, he reached the borders of Italy. When he saw the walls of the city of Rome, he offered fitting praises of thanks to almighty God and commended himself to the protection of the blessed apostles.

As soon as the venerable Pope Gregory learned of the holy man’s arrival, he invited him to himself, greeted him with familiar words, and assigned him to an honorable guesthouse. When the appointed day for their conversation arrived, this servant of God was invited to the church of the blessed apostle Peter. After they had satisfied themselves with mutual and peaceful conversation, [Col. 0643C] the apostolic prelate questioned him about the Creed and the tradition of the Catholic faith.

The man of God replied:

“Because, apostolic lord, I am not competent to answer such an inquiry in ordinary speech, I ask that you grant me time to write down the faith that you demand from me, so that you may recognize it laid bare in written letters alone.”

When the pope kindly received and granted this request, a short time afterward the man of God presented to the aforesaid ruler, in writing, a statement of the holy and catholic faith expressed with complete coherence and eloquence.

After reading it, the pope made him sit beside him and carefully admonished him to retain this faith steadfastly. He also discussed with him many matters concerning religious and spiritual life, so that at times they spent nearly an entire day in conversation. Finally, he asked how many peoples, previously wandering astray through idolatry or crimes, were receiving the teachings of the faith through his preaching.

### XIV.—He is ordained bishop by the same pope.

When he had satisfied the apostolic prelate by answering all these questions, the pope then informed the holy man that he wished to impose upon him the episcopal rank, so that he might correct those who were wandering astray with greater firmness and convert them to the way of truth, supported by the greater authority of his apostolic dignity. He would also be more acceptable to all in the office of preaching insofar as it became more widely known that he had been ordained for this purpose by the apostolic prelate. [Col. 0644A]

The man of God carefully considered all these matters. At the same time, he took heed of what is written: “He who did not desire blessing, it shall be far from him” (Psalm 108). He therefore did not reject the grace of so great a blessing.

When the day of his ordination arrived—namely, the day before the Kalends of December, that is, on the feast of the birth of the holy apostle Andrew—the venerable pope conferred upon him the episcopal order and the dignity of another name, Boniface, for previously he had been called Winfrid.

Then, so as to bind him more strictly to show obedience to the pope and his successors and to observe the whole tradition of the sacred faith, the pope demanded and received from him an oath, which is found written in the ancient copies as follows:

“In the name of the Lord God, our Savior Jesus [Col. 0644B] Christ, etc.” (See below, the Oath.)

### XV.—He is commended by letters from the pope.

After he had fulfilled this promise by swearing before Pope Gregory, the pope for his part endeavored to assist, honor, and revere him in all things. He gave him a book containing the most sacred laws of ecclesiastical discipline, arranged in pontifical councils, and instructed him to educate both the clergy and the other peoples subject to his rule according to those regulations.

He also confirmed by privilege the perpetual preservation of the familiarity of the apostolic see with Boniface and with all those subject to him. Thus, in letters that he sent, he commended Boniface not only to the illustrious Duke Charles, who at that time governed the kingdom of the Franks, but also to all the ecclesiastical men and princes established in Germany. [Col. 0644C]

Since the present place requires that the copies of those letters then sent be inserted, we now wish to insert them: first, the letter addressed to Duke Charles, and then those addressed to the other princes.

### XVI.—First, to Charles, duke of the Franks.

“To the illustrious lord and son Charles, duke, Pope Gregory. We have learned that you, most beloved in Christ, etc.” (See below, Letter 5.)

### XVII.—Then to the bishops, etc.
