“Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the most reverend and holy brothers who are fellow bishops, to religious presbyters and deacons, to illustrious dukes, magnificent castaldi, and also to counts and all Christians who fear God. Since we are greatly concerned for the sake of vigilance, etc.”

[Note: [Col. 0643] Others call them *guastaldi*; they administered villas or royal estates and were called *domestici* by the Gauls.]

(See below, Letter 6.)

### XVIII.—To the clergy and the people.

“Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, greetings in the Lord to the most beloved sons, the clergy and the people. Nothing should be withheld from commendable desires, etc.” (See below, Letter 10.)

### XIX.—To the Thuringian princes.

“To the magnificent men Asolf, Godolau, Wilarius, Guntharius, Albordus, and to all the beloved Christian faithful of Thuringia, Pope Gregory. The steadfastness of your magnificent faith, made known to us, etc.” (See below, Letter 8.)

### XX.—And to the people of Thuringia.

“Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to the entire people of Thuringia. The Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, true God, etc.” (See below, Letter 7.)

### XXI.—To the Old Saxons.

“Pope Gregory to the entire people of the province of the Old Saxons. I am debtor to the wise and to the foolish, dearest brothers, etc.” (See below, Letter 9.)

### XXII.—With Duke Charles’ approval, he undertakes the mission to the Hessians.

Supported by the authority of so many letters, the holy bishop Boniface set out for Germany. Coming to the aforementioned prince Charles, he delivered to him the letters of the Roman pontiff. Submitting himself to Charles’ authority and protection, and with his consent, he proceeded into the territory of the Hessians, among whom he had previously begun to preach.

When he arrived there, he found that many of them, having abandoned the practice of the Christian religion, were entangled in various errors. Some secretly or openly sacrificed to trees and springs; others practiced augury and divination, magic and incantations; still others pursued various abominable sacrileges. Only a few remained on the way of truth that they had once received.

With their counsel and with the servants of God standing beside him, he attempted to cut down a certain tree of extraordinary size which, in the ancient language of the pagans, was called Jupiter’s tree, at a place called Geismar. A great multitude of pagans gathered for the cutting of this tree, wishing to rush upon the holy [Col. 0645C] man as an enemy of their gods and kill him during the work of felling it.

But when the tree had been cut into only a little, it was suddenly split into four parts, as though moved by divine command. When the pagans who had gathered there with perverse intent saw this, they cast aside all their malice, blessed God, and believed.

Then the holy bishop, having taken counsel with the brothers, built an oratory from the mass of that immense tree and dedicated it in honor of the holy apostle Peter.

### XXIII.—In Thuringia he refutes false Christians. He founds the monastery at Ordorf in honor of Michael, and the reason for this.

After these events he also went to Thuringia and endeavored to correct the leaders of that people, who had in large part fallen away from the Christian religion. For after the rule of religious leaders over them had ceased, zeal for the Christian religion also began to cease. Certain false Christians—whose names were Drothwin and Bertheri, Canbereth and Hunred—came among them as guests and introduced a very extensive sect of heretical depravity.

These men, being fornicators and adulterers, stirred up a very serious conflict against the man of God. Refuted by truthful arguments, they received a sentence worthy of recompense. For they were excommunicated and expelled from the Church.

When the fame of Boniface’s preaching spread everywhere and the multitude of believers had increased, [Col. 0646A] churches were restored and monasteries built. At that time, after a multitude of servants of God had been gathered, a monastery was constructed at a place called Ordorf, under the patronage of the holy archangel Michael. All of them, living according to the apostolic way, acquired food and clothing by their own labor.

Why that monastery was built in honor of Saint Michael must be briefly explained. When Saint Boniface was passing through Thuringia preaching and baptizing, he fixed his tents and spent the night near a river called the Oraha. Then, throughout the entire night, a great light extending from heaven surrounded the place where the bishop was staying. In that light the holy archangel Michael appeared to the bishop, addressed him, and strengthened him in the Lord.

When morning came, Boniface praised and blessed God and celebrated the solemnity of Mass there. Then he ordered a meal to be prepared for himself at the same place. When he heard from his servant that the servant had no food with which he could eat, he replied:

“Could the one who was able to feed a multitude of people in the desert for forty years with manna sent from heaven not be able to provide food for me, his unworthy servant, for a single day’s meal?”

After saying this, he ordered that the table be set. Meanwhile, a bird flew up, brought a fish sufficient for a single day’s meal, and threw it down before the table. When the holy bishop saw this, he gave thanks to God and ordered the fish that had been brought to be prepared quickly. After it had been prepared and eaten, he ordered the remains to be thrown into the river.

### XXIV.—From where the author obtained this account.

[Col. 0646C] Setting out from there and traversing Thuringia, he diligently investigated whose property the place was where so great a vision had appeared to him. When he learned that the possessor of that place was Hugo, called the Elder, he asked him to be willing to give it to him.

Hugo agreed to the request and was the first of all the Thuringians to hand over his inheritance to the venerable bishop. Then Albot and several others handed over estates adjoining the aforementioned place.

Having acquired these properties, Saint Boniface returned and ordered the undergrowth to be cleared and the land cultivated. After laying the foundation, he had a church constructed.

I found these things written in an old book and therefore decided to insert them, so that, once the reason why the aforementioned monastery was built had been recognized, both the place itself and its founder—worthy of an angelic visitation—might be held in greater veneration.

### XXV.—He recruits fellow workers from Britain.

While Saint Bishop Boniface was preaching and baptizing in the regions of Thuringia and Hesse, he recognized that the harvest there was indeed great, but that there were few laborers to instruct the vast multitude of believers. Therefore, sending to his native province and homeland, he caused many religious women and men, trained in various kinds of knowledge, to come from there, and he divided among them the burden of his labor.

Among them were the distinguished men Burchard and Lull, Willibald and his brother Wunnibald, Witta and Gregory.

[Note: [Col. 0645D] The anonymous author differs somewhat. He chose some from his own people, others from the region of the Franks, and some also from the borders of Ireland [Col. 0646D] so that they might be his fellow workers in the Lord’s vineyard. They were as follows: Wigbert from the English; the blessed Gregory from a noble Frankish family; the venerable Sturm and Lul; Megingot; Willibald and his brother Wunnibald; and many others. Read below the Acts of Saints Lioba and Walpurgis.]

The religious women were Chunihilt, the maternal aunt of Saint Lull, and her daughter Berathgit, as well as Chunidrut, Thecla, Lioba, and Walpurgis, the sister of Willibald and Wunnibald.

Chunihilt and her daughter Berathgit, both highly educated in the liberal arts, were appointed teachers in the region of Thuringia. Chunitrud was sent to Bavaria to scatter the seeds of the divine word there. Thecla he placed beside the river Main, in the places called Kitzingen [Note: [Col. 0647D] It is called *Chitzzinga* in the Life of Saint Sturm, no. 14. It is now a town situated on the river Main in Franconia, [Col. 0648D] under the authority of the Lutheran margrave of Ansbach.] and Ochsenfurt. He also appointed Lioba at Bischofsheim to preside over the multitude of virgins gathered there.

### XXVI.—He sends envoys to Gregory III. He receives the pallium and a letter from him.

After he had baptized thousands of people, brought to the sacred faith both by himself and through his own countrymen, cleansing them with the water of baptism [perhaps: “having led them forth”], and after Gregory II of blessed memory, bishop of the apostolic see, had died and Gregory III had occupied the same see, the blessed Boniface again sent envoys to Rome. They were to renew with the aforementioned prelate the bonds of their former friendship, seek all the favor of fellowship that he had received from his predecessor, promise on his behalf every submission due to the apostolic see, and announce the conversion of the many who lived in Germany.

When the aforementioned envoys arrived in Rome and made such announcements to the venerable pope, he immediately gave thanks to God. Then he promised not only all the rights of fellowship and friendship requested by Saint Boniface, but also things that he had not requested. He sent him the archiepiscopal pallium and also returned to the holy bishop a letter containing answers to the various matters about which he had been questioned. A copy of it will be inserted below.

“To the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop, sent from this apostolic see to illuminate the German people and the nations dwelling round about in the shadow of death and established in error, Gregory, servant of the servants of God. We were greatly delighted when we read, etc.” (See below, Letter 25.)

### XXVII.—He builds two monasteries.

The envoys returned, bringing the gracious gifts and writings of the apostolic prelate, and made Saint Boniface exceedingly joyful. Therefore, offering God the thanks and praises that were due, he immediately built two churches for the Lord: one at Frideslar, which he consecrated in honor of the prince of the apostles, Saint Peter; the other at Hamanaburg, which he dedicated in honor of the holy archangel Michael.

He also attached two small monasteries to the two churches and placed in them a considerable congregation of those serving God, where the offices of divine praise and service are performed to this day.

After these things had been accomplished, Saint Boniface [Col. 0648A] visited the lands of the Bavarians, over whom Duke Hugbert ruled at that time. Exercising the work of preaching among them with the greatest diligence, he was armed with such zeal for divine devotion that he condemned, according to the decrees of the canons, a certain schismatic named Ermwolf, full of heretical depravity, and expelled him from the Church [perhaps: “had condemned”].

After these matters had been completed, he returned once more to those who lived within the diocese under his governance, traveling everywhere and restoring whatever the needs of the churches required.

### XXVIII.—He goes to Rome for the third time and brings back gifts and letters for the bishops.

At that time he also decided to go to Rome, both so that he might enjoy the salutary recognition and conversation of the apostolic Father, whose face he had not yet seen, and so that he might commend himself to the prayers of the holy apostles and of the other saints resting in the city of Rome.

He therefore set out for Rome [Note: [Col. 0648D] This third journey of Boniface to Rome undoubtedly took place around the autumn of A.D. 738. His return occurred the following year; after he had established bishops in the province of Bavaria, he received approval of his action from Pope Gregory on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, in the thirty-third year of the reign of Leo and the eighth indiction—that is, in A.D. 740; see below, chapter 32.] accompanied by a large crowd of Franks and Bavarians, as well as people who had come from Britain. Presented to the apostolic prelate, he was kindly received by him. He was held in such veneration by all the Romans that many flocked to his salutary teaching and kept him with them for a long time.

Afterward, when he decided to return, the apostolic prelate honorably enriched him with gifts and relics of the saints, whatever he had requested. He also gave him certain letters to transmit to all the bishops, abbots, and princes established in Germany. Copies of these will be inserted below.

[Col. 0648C] “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all our most beloved bishops, venerable presbyters, and religious abbots of all the provinces. With the Lord cooperating and confirming the word, the most holy man who is present, etc.” (See below, Letter 43.)

### XXIX.—To the nobles and people of Germany.

“Pope Gregory to all the nobles and peoples of the provinces of Germany: to the Thuringians and Hessians, the Bortharians and Nistresians, the Wedrevians and Lognaians, the Sudwodians and Graveldians, and to all those established in the eastern region. Since our predecessor, Gregory of holy memory, etc.” (See below, Letter 44.)

### XXX.—And to the bishops of Bavaria.

“To our most beloved bishops established in the province of Bavaria and Alamannia, Wiggo, Luidon, [Col. 0648D] Rudolf, and Wivilo, as well as Adda, Pope Gregory. The catholic authority of the holy Fathers commands that, etc.” (See below, Letter 45.)

### XXXI.—He establishes three bishops in Bavaria.

Having received such letters, Saint Boniface departed from Rome. Reaching Italy, he entered the walls of the city of Ticinum and stayed for some time with Liutprand, king of the Lombards.

Departing from there, he visited the lands of the Bavarians at the invitation of Duke Otilo. He remained among them for many days, preaching the word of God and renewing there the sacraments of the true faith. Among other things, he drove away certain destroyers of churches and seducers of the people. Some of these falsely claimed the episcopal rank; others assumed the office of presbyter; still others, following countless fabrications of perversity, led a large part of the people astray.

But when the holy bishop saw that so great a fraud and wickedness among the priests could not otherwise be prevented, with the consent of Duke Otilo he divided the province of Bavaria into four dioceses. He appointed three men of great virtue over them and, after ordaining them, elevated them to the episcopal rank.

The first, named John, received the episcopal see in the town called Salzburg. The second, Erimbert, undertook episcopal governance in the Church of Freising.

[Note: [Col. 0649D] He was the nephew and successor of Saint Corbinian, concerning whom see above, under the year 730. Concerning John, see the Life of Saint Rupert, under the year 717.]

The third, Gowibolt, was appointed bishop in the city of Regensburg, which is the metropolis of Bavaria.

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Arnulf, a monk formerly a count, calls him Gaubaldus in Book I, chapter 1, of the Life of Saint Emmeram, in Canisius, vol. II, *Antiquae Lectiones*, where Gaubaldus opened the tomb of the blessed Emmeram. Arnulf adds in Book II: “From the time when bishops were first ordained in Bavaria by the blessed Boniface, monks and canons succeeded one another in this episcopate in turn, so that if the predecessor was a canon, the successor became a monk.” This custom [Col. 0650D] continued down to his own time. As a result, the monks of Saint Emmeram had no other abbot than the bishop.]

Vivilus, who had already been ordained by the apostolic prelate, was also placed over the Church of Passau; but his diocese, which was the fourth, was divided by Saint Boniface like the others.

After these bishops had been appointed and all that required correction in Bavaria had been corrected, Boniface returned to his own churches. Not long afterward, he reported to the apostolic prelate by letter all that he had accomplished in correcting matters in Bavaria. The prelate, praising his deeds, sent back the following letter.

### XXXII.—He receives approval of his action from Gregory.

“To the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop, Gregory, servant of the servants of God. Concerning the distinguished teacher of the nations and blessed apostle Paul, etc.” (See below, Letter 46.)

### XXXIII.—With Carolomannus’ approval, he celebrates the synod of Liptina.

At that time, Duke Charles the Illustrious completed the course of his temporal life, and his sons, Carolomannus and Pippin, succeeded to their father’s power.

But because all the rights of their father’s kingdom were administered according to the will of Carolomannus [Note: [Col. 0650D] Two councils were held under Carolomannus: one in Germany, at an uncertain place, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May in A.D. 742; the other on the Kalends of March of the following year at Liptina in the district of Cambrai, where the canons of the earlier synod were reread and approved, with four canons added, of which Othlonus reports only one, at the end. Read the complete Acts of both synods in Sirmond.]—who was the elder—Saint Boniface approached him and, carrying letters from the apostolic prelate, earnestly urged him to cultivate the practice of the Christian religion, which his father had begun and fostered with the greatest zeal, with the same zeal, for the love of God, the stability of his kingdom, and the common salvation of all subject to him.

Stung by these petitions as though by a divine utterance, [Col. 0650A] he endeavored, by both royal and canonical authority, to recall to the way of justice all those living under his rule, both lay and clerical, who were straying from the Christian religion.

For he ordered that, once a synodal assembly had been held, everything should be corrected there according to the decrees of the canons. Since the statutes of that synodal assembly seem capable of providing great instruction not only to secular but also to ecclesiastical rulers, we wish to set them down here just as we found them written in ancient copies. They are found written as follows.

### XXXIV.—The German synod confirmed at Liptina.

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, I, Carolomannus, etc.” (See below, German Council.)

### XXXV.—The author inveighs against those who hate monks.

[Col. 0650B]

When the statutes of so great a religion, enacted at that time by newly converted princes, are compared with the laws now issued by certain of our rulers, men instructed from childhood to old age in every Christian discipline, it can easily be recognized how much more perfect those neophytes were than these most learned Fathers. For these men not only neglect to intercede with kings and princes for the benefit of holy places, but themselves utterly destroy the holy places entrusted to them.

O wicked customs, deserving of universal grief! O most pitiable change in morals! Children are found more religious than old men, the blind than those who see, the inexperienced than the learned, laymen than clerics.

Formerly, in many provinces where the vineyard of the holy Church had recently been planted and even knowledge of spiritual fruits had not yet reached everyone, many secular men used to say:

“Because, in our weakness, we are unable to restrain ourselves completely from the accustomed pleasures of the world, let us at least gather others who practice restraint into the service of God and feed them with our bodily resources, so that they may feed us with their prayers and other spiritual assistance, lest we perish.”

But now, when some knowledge and experience of all the virtues, set forth also in books, has reached nearly everyone’s awareness, and no Christian can say, “No one hired us” (Matthew 20), many clerics and laymen alike are accustomed to say:

“What benefit do so many monasteries or such great crowds of monks provide? It would be much better if the estates by which those monks are uselessly fattened were made available for our service.”

Many indeed confess this in words, but far more acknowledge it by the testimony of their deeds, as though their wickedness and irreligion would be punished less severely by the Lord if no monk or religious person were found in this world.

### XXXVI.—He praises Carolomannus and Charles the Great for their love of monks.

[Col. 0651A]

But the aforesaid Carolomannus had a very different mind. Although before the preaching of Saint Boniface he had known little about the Christian religion, nevertheless, when admonished and exhorted by him, he soon began to become so perfected in the fear and love of God that he prudently ordered both human and divine affairs, and understood that secular rights could accomplish nothing without the administration of divine service, to which the monastic and cenobitic community is dedicated.

Likewise Charles the Great, namely the son of his brother Pippin mentioned above, who subjected all the kingdoms from Rome to Frisia and from Hungary to Britain to his rule, while contending against those same peoples, did not believe that he could obtain victory in any other way unless, in the meantime, he assisted all the monasteries already established in those kingdoms with some provision. If anyone doubts this, let him first read his deeds, then go around the monasteries which he had founded during his reign in Italy, Gaul, or Germany, and he will find some elevated by Charles’s generosity—some by a privilege of liberty, others by gifts of estates—unless, perhaps, they were later taken away by succeeding kings or bishops.

For many kings who succeeded that same Charles, although they shone forth in illustrious character and in many good pursuits, nevertheless committed a very serious fault in this: they either themselves destroyed certain monasteries, both by imposing an immense burden of service upon them and by taking away their estates, or handed them over to bishops or even to certain laymen who cared nothing for monastic religion, so that they might be destroyed. But our Charles is reported not only never to have done these things; on the contrary, he once freed certain properties belonging to a bishopric from episcopal jurisdiction, after restoring them with estates twice their former value, acting upon common counsel, and elevated them by royal liberty. As I think, he foresaw through the spirit of prophecy what we ourselves perceive and what our predecessors long ago saw fulfilled: that holy places which had been sufficiently endowed with all necessities by their founders, but had been handed over to bishops, would come into the greatest poverty and into the destruction of the entire regular discipline.

Yet I do not say this because I know that all monasteries subject to bishops have been destroyed, but because the greater part have. Nevertheless, this seems all the more grievous and pitiable in proportion as it is done not by those ignorant of the precepts of divine law, but by the most learned—men who, while destroying the monasteries entrusted to them, not only sin themselves but also make laymen sin in the same destruction. For what layman does not think that he may now do whatever he sees clerics doing?

Therefore, in all these matters we may set Charles before us as an example. Just as among his successors, that is, among the kings, no one like him was found who would keep the law of the Most High, so none of them after him possessed such glory and such power in this world. Rightly, therefore, it is said of him: “His memory shall not depart, and his name shall be sought from generation to generation.” Since, then, the occasion presented itself for us, by recalling how great religion had been under the ancient rulers and how great had been the destruction of that same religion under the modern ones, to encourage some people toward better things through such contrasts, by which what is better is made clear, let no one judge these matters unworthy of reading or hearing. Rather, let him consider whether he is guilty amid so great a destruction, and strive to repent and amend while, by the Lord’s favor, we possess time for forgiveness, lest, overtaken by the day of death, we seek a period for repentance and be unable to find one.

But enough has been said about these matters; let us now return to the beginning of the discourse we undertook.

### XXXVII.—Gewilieb, deposed for homicide, is succeeded in the see of Mainz.

When, therefore, a synodal assembly was being held at the command of Carolomannus and by the counsel of Saint Boniface, many clerics who had been deceived by heretical depravity were expelled from communion with the Church; bishops also who had been accused of some stain of a capital crime were deposed. The chief authors of the entire error that had then grown up in Germany were two heretics, one called Clemens and the other Aldebertus [also Eldebertus]. When later we begin to produce the letters sent to Pope Zacharias concerning them, they will be discussed more appropriately, for in those letters their entire deadly heresy is recounted.

[Note: Willibald omitted this history—namely, Gewilieb’s deposition and Boniface’s succession; both are inferred to have occurred in 745 from Book II, chapters 7 and 9. Compare the notes on chapter 10 of Willibald.] 

At that time a certain bishop named Gewilieb [also Gewiliob; Sur., Gervilius], who presided over the city of Mainz, was deposed. Why he was deposed I shall relate below. In those days the Saxons were devastating the region of Thuringia. Therefore the inhabitants of that region, fleeing for refuge to the aforementioned prince Carolomannus, sought assistance from him. He immediately sent an army for their rescue, and Gerold, then bishop of Mainz—namely, the father of the aforementioned Gewilieb—was ordered to go with it.

When a battle had taken place, with the combatants striking one another, Bishop Gerold was killed there among the others. Then his son Gewilieb, still a layman serving at the palace, was advanced to the clerical office in order to assuage his grief over his father, and after his father’s death was appointed to govern the Church of Mainz.

Not long afterward Carolomannus again assembled an army and marched against the Saxons, taking the same Gewilieb with him. When the armies of both peoples were stationed on opposite banks of the river Wisaraha, Gewilieb ordered his servant to go among the enemy and diligently inquire the name of the man who had killed his father. When the servant, carrying out his orders, was told by someone that the man he sought was nearby, he said: “Ask him to come here as quickly as possible, for my lord wishes to speak with him.”

When he came and each side had been informed of the other’s arrival, both mounted their horses and rode out. Meeting and speaking with one another in the middle of the river, Bishop Gewilieb said:

> “Receive now the steel with which I avenge my dear father.”

Having said this, he immediately pierced him with his sword.

The man at once fell from his horse and breathed his last in the river. When his people recognized what had happened, cries arose everywhere, and both sides fought fiercely after forming their battle lines. The Saxons were defeated, and Carolomannus returned with his men to their own territory, no one imputing to Gewilieb the deed as a crime of homicide. Thus, after his return, Gewilieb continued to claim his customary episcopal privileges.

But Saint Boniface, among other discussions concerning correction, also brought this matter before the synodal assembly, asserting that no one polluted by the guilt of homicide ought to exercise the episcopal priesthood. He also charged Gewilieb with having seen him with his own eyes playing with birds and dogs, which was in no way permissible for a bishop.

When Gewilieb heard this, and perceived that he could in no way kick against the goad either of secular power or of canonical authority—which, through Saint Boniface, was being brought to bear upon everyone present—he consented to the common judgment and was deposed from the episcopal order. After his deposition, Saint Boniface was immediately placed over the Church of Mainz by the aforementioned princes, namely Carolomannus and his brother Pippin. And, in order that his dignity might be greater, those same princes decreed that the Church of Mainz, which had previously been subject to another, should become the metropolitan church of all the churches situated in Germany. They then sent a delegation and obtained this from the apostolic bishop.

[Note: Othlonus reports Zacharias’s letters concerning this matter below, Book II, chapter 9.]

### XXXVIII.—He appoints three bishops. Boniface is to be venerated by the Germans as a father.

Supported, then, by such authority, Saint Boniface began, like a new archimandrite, to plant everywhere what belonged to God and to uproot what belonged to the devil; he built monasteries and churches and appointed the most vigilant shepherds over those churches.

For, besides the many bishops whom he had previously appointed—including the venerable men Willibaldus and Burchardus—he appointed the former bishop in the place called Eichstätt and the latter bishop in the city called Würzburg. At that time he sent Gregory, consecrated to the episcopal order, to Trech [Note: Correct this, since the printed editions read Attriech. Nevertheless, Gregory was not appointed to Lower Utrecht before Boniface’s passion. In the French language it was then called Trech or Trecht, as we learn from Othlonus himself above, Book I, chapter 6. Compare Willibaldus, chapter 10, no. 31, where he makes no mention of Gregory. Read the Life of Saint Gregory below.]. While he was still alive, he also appointed Lullus as his successor and bishop at Mainz.

Many other things were done by him in Germany at that time, but they are found written only in letters. Therefore I wish to insert those letters, whether sent by him to Pope Zacharias, who at that time governed the apostolic see, or by Zacharias to him, or on his behalf to various princes of Germany—those letters, that is, which we can gather from wherever possible.

For we wish to omit the letters he sent to the peoples of his own nation, namely the English, lest we seem to impose some weariness upon our readers, especially since what is ours is sufficient for us. By “ours” I mean what he wrote for the salvation of our fathers, that is, the Germans, or what he received in writing from others. In these letters it can especially be recognized how great a care and discipline, how great a fatherly affection and piety, he possessed toward all the sons of his Church whom he had begotten through the Gospel, and how, in accordance with the Apostle, he became all things to all people in order to win them all.

Therefore I say confidently that whoever among his sons—namely, the Germans—after recognizing the labor of so great a Father, whether from his writings or from common speech, does not embrace him with as much veneration as he is able, is found negligent in the honor which we are commanded to show to parents. If negligence is a sin, and every sin is punished, then negligence too must be punished.

Furthermore, if, in accordance with the Apostle, we revere the fathers who instructed us in the flesh, shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits? For not only is almighty God called the spiritual Father, but so also are all those whose teaching and examples instruct us in the knowledge of truth and urge us toward steadfastness in religion.

Thus Abraham, on account of the merit of his faith and obedience, was called the father of all who believe in Christ, as an example for all to imitate. In the same way Saint Boniface may be called the father of all the inhabitants of Germany, because he first begot them for Christ by the word of holy preaching, strengthened them by his example, and finally gave his own life for them—a love greater than which no one can show.

Since this love is the origin and end of every good thing, let us also bring this little book to an end here, so that, while our labor pauses for a time, the reader and hearer may recover their strength for reading.

## BOOK TWO

In the preceding little book, insofar as the smallness of our talent permitted and as the testimony of ancient writers taught us, we spoke of the conduct, journeying, and preaching of our holy Father Boniface. Now, with God’s help, I wish in the following book to reveal how much he labored for the holy Church after receiving the episcopate of the Church of Mainz: how he fought against heretics and false Christians, and by what outcome he completed the blessed crown of his passion.

But the earlier part must be explained only through the letters, because in them it is found written sufficiently and clearly. It is not fitting that, while passing over matters set forth plainly to a prudent mind, we should compose others as though they were better, since such a fault is unsuitable even in secular writings, much less in sacred ones.

Having thus given this preliminary account, let us now proceed to write the letters we promised, placing first the letter which he sent to Pope Zacharias at the beginning. Although it was sent before the synod mentioned below [read: mentioned above], nevertheless, because it partly concerns the sequence of the following letters, and because all these letters were written during the time of the same bishop, we too have decided to present them together.

### I.—Boniface writes to Zacharias.

“Boniface, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved lord Zacharias, a man of apostolic dignity, adorned with the insignia of the supreme pontificate. We confess, lord Father, that after we learned, etc.” (See below, Letter 49.)

### II.—Zacharias’s reply.

“Zacharias, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy brother Bishop Boniface. Having received the letters of your most holy fraternity, etc.” (See below, Letter 50.)

### III.—Whether a defective baptism must be repeated, and in what form.

“Zacharias, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop. Virgilius and Sidonius, devout men among the Bavarians, etc.” (See below, Letter 56.)

### IV.—The Roman synod under Zacharias against Aldebertus and Clemens.

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, during the reign of our most pious lord Augustus, etc.” (See below, Roman Council.)

#### Boniface’s letter read at the synod.

“To the most excellent Father and apostolic pontiff, Pope Zacharias: Boniface, servant of the servants of God, wishes salvation in Christ. Nearly thirty years ago, after I had, etc.” (See below, Letter 57.)

### V.—Zacharias’s encyclical letter to the bishops.

“To our most beloved Reginfridus, etc. I give thanks to almighty God the Father and to the Lord, etc.” (See below, Letter 68.)

### VI.—Another encyclical letter concerning confirmation of the synod held by Boniface.

“Pope Zacharias to all, etc. The most reverend, etc., having reported to us, etc.” (See below, Letter 48.)

### VII.—Another concerning the same matter and various questions.

“To the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop: Zacharias, etc. When the letters of your most holy fraternity, etc., came to us.” (See below, Letter 60.)

### VIII.—Zacharias’s letter concerning the articles sent to Pippin and concerning the heretics.

“To the most reverend fellow bishop Boniface: Zacharias, etc. The Apostle Paul admirably admonishes us, etc.” (See below, Letter 64.)

### IX.—He replies to various questions.

“To the reverend brother Boniface, fellow bishop: Zacharias, etc. At the sacred thresholds of the blessed apostles, etc.” (See below, Letter 71.)

### X.—Zacharias’s confirmation concerning the archbishops who had been ordained.

“To the most reverend brother Boniface: Zacharias. We read in the book of the Acts of the Apostles, etc.” (See below, Letter 54.)

### XI.—Zacharias complains that Boniface asks for a pallium only for Grimo.

“To the reverend brother Boniface: Zacharias, etc. Having received the letters of your holy fraternity, etc.” (See below, Letter 55.)

### XII.—Boniface, through Lullus, consults Zacharias concerning conduct with evil priests.

“To the most reverend Father . . . Zacharias: Boniface, etc. The holiness of your fatherly piety, etc.” (See below, Letter 75.)

### XIII.—Zacharias’s reply.

“To the most reverend brother and fellow bishop Boniface: Zacharias, etc. Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord, etc.” (See below, Letter 76.)

### XIV.—Zacharias congratulates Boniface and confirms Mainz as a metropolitan see for him.

“Pope Zacharias to Boniface, etc. How our Lord God, etc.” (See below, Letter 72.)

### XV.—He grants a privilege to the monastery of Fulda.

“Pope Zacharias to Bishop Boniface, etc. Since things should always be granted, etc.” (See below, Letter 77.)

### XVI.—The author was unable to find all of Boniface’s letters.

Thus far, by indicating the series of letters, it is sufficient to show what labor and how great a care holy Boniface had for all those whom he converted to the practice of Christianity. If anyone is troubled that many letters mentioned in the letters written above are not also found written here, let him know that this happened because I was unable to find them anywhere.

I wish first, then, to relate how great was the devotion of the prince Carolomannus toward the monastery of Fulda. It seems reasonable to make this devotion known not only to declare the benefits conferred by so great a man, but also for the benefit of those who deserve to be built up by good examples, and likewise for the confusion of those who, although they know, see, and hear everything that is best, nevertheless persist in their customary wickedness—confessing God only with their mouths but denying him by their deeds, opening the ears of their hearts to the love of secular life but hardening them against the divine commandments.

The aforementioned prince, although he was pressed by war on every side from the neighboring provinces, was not for that reason withdrawn from caring for holy places and the servants of God. He firmly believed that spiritual weapons—that is, the virtues of the soul—were much stronger than bodily ones, and placed no hope in numbers without spiritual strength, in accordance with the saying: “The king is not saved by great might, and the giant shall not be saved by the abundance of his strength” (Psalm 32).

After, as can be learned from the preceding writings of this book, he had corrected the affairs of Christian religion by expelling both false Christians and heretics, in accordance with the counsel of Saint Boniface, he also fulfilled Boniface’s wishes in the newly constructed monastery of Fulda.

For when Abbot Sturm had begun to inhabit with certain brothers the place where that monastery now stands, and had sufficiently praised the quality of the place while reporting it to Saint Boniface, he then went to Carolomannus and humbly begged him, saying:

“I beseech almighty God for your perpetual reward: if you are willing to help me, allow me to build a monastery and establish monastic life in your eastern kingdom. For we have found in the wilderness called Bochonia, beside the river called Fulda, a place quite suitable for serving God. It belongs to your dominion, and we ask that this place be granted to us by your piety, so that we may be able to serve Christ there.”

When he heard this, Carolomannus rejoiced by God’s providence. He summoned all the soldiers of his palace, announced the bishop’s petition to them, and in their presence handed over the requested place to the bishop, saying:

“I therefore surrender to the jurisdiction of the Lord, from this day forward, the place that you request and that you say is situated beside the bank of the river Fulda—everything within it that lies under my authority—so that from that place the boundary extends for three miles in every direction: east and west, north and south.”

[Note: That is, a boundary; hence the term “margraves,” because they guarded the boundaries of a kingdom or province. Boniface expressed the boundaries of this donation more distinctly in a document prepared by him in the year 747 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the sixth year of the principate of the noble men Carolomannus and his brother Pippin, on March 22, in Brower, *Antiquities of Fulda*, Book I, chapter 4. Compare the Life of Saint Sturm, under the year 779.]

After this transfer had been made, he also sent messengers to gather all the nobles living in the region of Grabfeld and humbly ask them that all who possessed any property within the aforementioned boundary should do what the prince had done, namely, hand it over for the service of the Lord and of the monastery to be built by Saint Boniface.

When all those mentioned had been assembled by the messengers and had learned of the prince’s request, they immediately handed over, with complete devotion, whatever property they possessed there to God, to Saint Boniface, and also to the venerable abbot Sturm, to possess. In order that this transfer might remain permanently confirmed, Carolomannus, at whose prompting all these things were being done, ordered a charter of his transfer to be written, and took care to authenticate it with his own seal.

### XVII.—Carolomannus, desiring the monastic life, yields the kingdom to Pippin.

As Carolomannus did these and similar things, and progressed more and more in love of God and neighbor, he was unable, while remaining in secular clothing, to fulfill that same love with the integrity he desired. He therefore chose the better part, which would not be taken away from him.

For he abandoned the broad kingdoms of earthly power and, going to Monte Cassino, where at that time the discipline of monastic life was exceedingly strict, became a monk there, entrusting the duties of the kingdom to his brother Pippin.

Pippin, having received the sole rule of the paternal and fraternal power, which was then called the office of mayor of the palace [*Majordomatus*, “mayor of the palace”], cultivated the same devotion and the same concern as his brother, in both divine and secular affairs, following the counsel of Saint Boniface in everything.

It happened, therefore, that although he constantly strove to submit himself to God, who casts down the mighty from their seats and exalts the humble, he obtained the excellence of royal power.

[Note: He was indeed anointed king by Boniface, as will be demonstrated below in the appendix.]

Raised to such dignity, he continued, in the same way as before, to love and venerate Saint Boniface. He therefore also took care to confirm his brother’s transfer by his own letter. I wish to insert a copy of that letter here, so that all the faithful may be instructed by it, while wicked plunderers may see and be confounded.

### XVIII.—Pippin’s privilege likewise.

“Pippin, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to Boniface, archbishop and German legate sent from the apostolic see. Since your venerable fatherhood has petitioned our excellence, etc.” (See below, Letter 95.)

### XIX.—Adalger’s donation vindicated from heaven. Vengeance upon those who opposed it.

At the same time it happened that a certain cleric named Adalger, a man of good conduct, adhered to Saint Boniface and faithfully served him. After a short time, when he was seized by a serious illness and felt himself to be at the point of death, with the counsel of the man of God he transferred to Saint Martin whatever estates he possessed from his paternal inheritance.

After his death, however, his brothers Asperth and Truttmunt brought under their own control everything he had transferred in the places named below: at Amanaburg, at Brettenbrunum, and at Seleheim.

[Note: This place was near Amanaburg and the monastery of Fritzlar, on the border of Hesse and Thuringia.]

When the bishop’s agents admonished them concerning this matter, they replied that they wished to affirm under oath that they were rightfully claiming their brother’s estates. The bishop promised that he would be present for the oath.

When the appointed day arrived and a large crowd of their relatives had gathered so that they might fulfill the oath they had promised, the man of God also arrived. When the aforesaid men had brought with them to the altar those who were to assist them in making the oath, the bishop said:

“You alone swear, if you wish; I do not want you to bring perdition upon all these who have gathered.”

But they delayed no longer and took the oath. When this had been done, the bishop said to them:

“You have sworn?”

They replied: “We have sworn.”

Then the bishop said to Asperth: “May a great bear kill you.”

Afterward he said to Truttmund: “May you never see a son or daughter born from your seed.”

The outcome of events proved that both things happened just as the holy bishop had foretold. For, after a short time, while Asperth was sitting at table, men came saying that a large bear was roaming through the field. He quickly mounted a horse and seized a hunting spear, then began to pursue the bear before his companions could prepare themselves. On that journey he fell from his horse, and, his entire body being shattered at the joints of his limbs, he died.

When his servants hurried to him and arrived, they found him already dead. But when Truttmunt heard that the holy man’s prophecy had been fulfilled in his brother, he was greatly terrified and immediately restored to the altar of Saint Martin the estates that he had unjustly taken.

### XX.—Boniface returns to Frisia, with Lullus appointed in his place at Mainz.

After these things, when Saint Boniface saw that the seeds of the divine word which he had cast within the borders of Germany and Gaul had already sprouted and were bearing fruit in the hearts of believers, and, foreseeing the approaching dissolution of his body, longed with all his heart to come and appear before the face of God, he resolved to visit the peoples of the Frisians. They had once been converted to the practice of the Christian religion by his teaching, but, through the devil’s deception, some of them had again fallen back into their former error of paganism.

He wished either to reconcile them to God and end his present life there in fruitful peace, or, if this should be more pleasing to God, to endure until death whatever adversity and torment might confront him there for God’s name.

Before undertaking so perilous a journey, however, he knew that it was not fitting for him, while laboring to save the sheep of others, to allow his own sheep entrusted to him to perish. Therefore, with the consent of the revered King Pippin, as well as of the bishops, abbots, canons, and all the nobles belonging to his diocese, he chose and ordained Saint Lullus as bishop in his place. He had already obtained from the apostolic bishop that Lullus should be ordained for him.

After this was done, he took Lullus by the hand and commended him to all the princes gathered there, so that they might obey him as a father and assist him in all his necessities.

### XXI.—His instructions to Lullus and his departure.

Then he went to those who lived in Thuringia and to those who lived around the Rhine, and did the same things. Finally, admonishing Lullus himself, he said:

“Since the time of my dissolution is approaching, it is my will to depart wherever divine grace may wish to direct me. But you, dearest son, care for the souls entrusted to you; recall the people from error; complete the basilica of my monastery near Fulda, which has already been begun; and there commit my body to burial, wherever I may die.

“Also provide what is now necessary for our journey, and place in the book chest my linen cloth, in which this decrepit body is to be wrapped after my death.”

When Saint Boniface had finished speaking, blessed Lullus, although he drew many sighs from the depths of his heart and had wept from excessive grief, nevertheless did not dare to suggest anything other than what so great a Father had proposed.

After a few days had passed, Boniface boarded a ship with the companions chosen for such a journey and was carried along the channel of the Rhine until, entering the watery fields of the Frisians, he safely reached a lake called Almeri in their language.

Going about through the surrounding regions, he preached the word of the Lord with confidence and built churches with immense zeal. The Lord bestowed such grace upon his servant that after a few days he baptized many thousands of men and women together with his fellow soldier, the chorepiscopus [Note: It seems that *coepiscopus* should be read. Eoban was in fact a bishop, as was observed at the beginning of the Life. Certainly Willibaldus in the preceding Life, no. 25, Usuardus, and other martyrologists call Eoban Boniface’s fellow bishop.], Eoban.

For, to lighten his old age, Boniface appointed Eoban as his substitute, entrusting him with the episcopate in the city called Trecht. He also had as his helpers three presbyters and the same number of deacons, whose names were Wintrung, Walther, and Adalher, Hamunt, Skirbalt, and Derso. Vaccar and Kundekar, Williher and Hadolf belonged to the monastic order and followed him.

All of these, laboring unanimously with Saint Boniface in preaching the Gospel, deserved to become his companions in the crown of martyrdom.

### XXII.—Boniface, surrounded by the Frisians, addresses his companions.

For when they had traveled through the broad regions of the Frisians for the sake of preaching and had come to a certain river called Borthne, which lies in the territory of those who in the rustic language are called Auster and Westeriche, Saint Boniface, accompanied only by a retinue of his servants, ordered tents to be pitched there. He wished to await in that place the arrival of those who had recently been baptized, for the sake of their confirmation. The day appointed for that confirmation was approaching.

When the appointed day arrived and the rising sun had already occupied the higher degrees of its course, all those who were being awaited like sons by their father—though unworthy to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit, which was to be offered to them on that day through sacred confirmation—turned around and, instead of friends, became enemies; instead of newly initiated worshipers of the faith, new executioners. With great uproar and a dreadful display of weapons, they burst into the camp of the saints.

[Note: Othlonus is mistaken, as we shall prove in the appendix, no. 9.]

When the boys saw this, they rushed out of the camp, armed themselves, and eagerly desired to defend the saints against the multitude of the raging people. But Saint Boniface, hearing the attack of the tumultuous crowd, first fled to the refuge of the spiritual fortification, taking up the relics of the saints which he was accustomed to carry with him continually.

Then he summoned the clerics to him, went out from the tent, and restrained his boys, who were prepared to resist, saying:

“Do not, I beg you, my boys, fight; do not wage war against our adversaries. For we are taught by the words of sacred Scripture not only not to return evil for evil, but also to offer good in return for good.

“Already the long-desired day has arrived; already that time has come when we are invited from the laborious misery of this world to the joys of eternal blessedness. Why, then, do you wish to separate and take away from us so great a grace and so great a glory? Rather, be strong in the Lord, and allow us gratefully to receive the gifts of divine grace that have been offered.

“Hope only in the Lord, and he will deliver us from every danger.”

By saying these and similar things, he restrained the spirits of his men from every disturbance of battle. Then, admonishing the clerics of every order in his native and free voice, he said:

“O dearest brothers, if any care for divine love or any memory of my admonition remains in you, show it at this present hour, recalling those words of the Lord: ‘Do not be afraid of those who kill the body, because they cannot kill the soul.’

“Therefore fasten the anchor of your hope in God, because after the brief span of this life he will make you companions of the heavenly citizens in the reward of eternal recompense.

“Do not, I beg you, lose in this very brief hour the long and unconquerable battles of your minds; do not become entangled in the perverse flatteries of the pagans. Rather, for the love of him who suffered for us, endure steadfastly and courageously the sudden danger of death that now threatens us, so that you may be able to rejoice with him forever.”

### XXIII.—He suffers martyrdom with his companions. After robbing their possessions, the assassins kill one another in mutual slaughter; the survivors scatter the books, later recover them, and themselves are killed three days afterward.

Yet the words of this salutary exhortation by Saint Boniface, urging his disciples toward the crown of martyrdom, had scarcely been completed when, behold, a raging multitude of pagans, armed with swords and every kind of weapon, rushed upon them and stained their bodies with a glorious slaughter. When they had done this, immediately increasing the cause of their own condemnation, they first entered the camp and carried away everything stored there, both the books and the small reliquary chests, supposing that they would find in them many treasures of gold and silver. Then, running to the ships, they also carried away whatever remained there from the daily provisions of the clerics and boys. When they had found some wine among the other things, they began to taste it and to intoxicate their raging minds.

After this they set about discussing and considering how they might divide among themselves the treasure of gold and silver they supposed they had found. But when, as they talked at length about the division of so much money, they could not settle the matter by peaceful agreement, such discord and dispute suddenly arose among them that, in the same fury and madness, and with the same weapons with which they had earlier slaughtered the holy martyrs, they killed one another in a fitting mutual massacre. The just judgment of God overtook them and permitted them to fall into so corrupt a mind that the very sword which they had drawn to kill the ministers of their salvation they drove into their own hearts.

When this slaughter had ended, those who remained, rejoicing again in the prospect of money, rushed about and, having broken open the repositories of the books, found volumes instead of gold and sheets of divine teaching instead of silver. Seized, therefore, by their customary madness, they scattered the books they had found—some across the level plain, others through marshy places—and threw and concealed some in whatever unsuitable locations they could find. Nevertheless, by the grace of almighty God, so that it might become clear how great was the merit of the man whose books they had been, after a long period of time they were found unharmed and carried back by their individual discoverers to the churches where they can still be found today.

Among those books was found a Gospel book which the blessed man, because of his holiness, was accustomed always to carry with him. Although it had been cut through the middle with a sharp sword—as can still be verified by those who inspect it—no letter lost its integrity through that incision. [Note: This codex, together with certain others mentioned above, is still preserved in the sacristy at Fulda, according to Serrarius and Browerus.] It is said that Saint Boniface held it in his hands at the moment when the sword was being swung to sever his head, either as protection for his head, as many people do, or even as the spiritual shield which he believed such a book to be, and held it out against the executioner. In this sign both the wondrous power of God and the venerable holiness of blessed Boniface may plainly be recognized. For it seems more marvelous that not one letter of the cut book was erased than it would have been if no mark of the blow of the sword had been found in the book.

After the executioners who remained had found no indication of the money they had imagined, they returned home in great sorrow, intending, after a three-day interval, to suffer punishments fitting their crime. For when all the Christians living in the vicinity of that region heard of the unforeseen killing of the holy men, they assembled and invaded the land of those who had slaughtered the saints with armed force. When the pagans gathered to resist them but were entirely unable to prevail, they turned to flight and fell, struck down by the great valor of the pursuing Christians. The Christians, having gained victory over the pagans, carried away all their property and returned to their own homes. Thus it came about that those who had not hesitated to slaughter the ministers of their salvation were crushed by a double destruction: they began to be crushed in the present life and were afterward assigned to eternal condemnation.

### XXIV. The body of Saint Boniface, first buried at Utrecht, is transferred to Fulda

The body of the blessed bishop was taken by the clerics of the Utrecht church and, after a few days, carried to Utrecht, where it was buried with great veneration. When Saint Lullus learned this, he assembled a multitude of venerable men, both laymen and clerics, and informed them both of the glorious passion of Saint Boniface and of how he had been buried at the Utrecht church. At the same time, disclosing to everyone the place where the holy bishop, while still alive, had instructed him that his body should be buried, he asked them to provide assistance for the love of God, so that he might fulfill the holy man’s command.

When very many showed themselves ready to provide such assistance, he chose from among them those who seemed most suitable and sent both sailors and horsemen to the aforesaid city to take away the body of Saint Boniface. When these envoys hurried there with all speed and arrived at Utrecht, the citizens of that place, learning why they had come, themselves assembled the elders of the people and the judges to resist them. Since they saw that they could not engage the arriving multitude, they asserted, as witnesses, that King Pippin had ordered that the body of Saint Boniface not be removed from there. [Note: Eigil, abbot, reports in the Life of Saint Sturm, no. 16, that Pippin’s order was communicated in favor of the people of Mainz.]

The envoys, however, believing this to have been fabricated rather than true, persisted with all their strength in the cause for which they had come, divine power strengthening and assisting them so that they might obtain their wish. The outcome of the matter also proved that this was so. For while a dispute was being carried on on both sides over the holy body, meanwhile the church signal, commonly called a *glocca* [Al.: *clocca*; al.: *clogga*], began to sound without human movement. When they heard it, all the inhabitants who were there, gathered for battle, were terrified by the divine sign, stood amazed, and decreed that the holy man’s body should be returned. It was immediately returned and received with due honor by the venerable envoys mentioned above.

Without labor on the part of the rowers, on the thirtieth day after his death—as though that day had been appointed for this purpose—many men and women living far away had gathered there. Unaware of the arrival of the holy body, they had decided to come there solely to await or meet the envoys. The venerable Bishop Lullus also, who had hastened to the royal court immediately after sending the envoys, arrived that very day, although unaware of the return of his men and the arrival of the holy body. God alone arranged this fitting coincidence, so that when those who had come together arrived, those who had been overcome with great sorrow at the loss of their father and teacher might also experience a common joy, having learned that they could have him as an everlasting patron before God.

### XXV. The people of Mainz resist in vain

Having received so great a treasure as a pledge, many in the city of Mainz held that the holy man’s body should be buried there, where he had been bishop. They asserted that this was the right of all churches: wherever someone had possessed an episcopal see, there he should also be buried. The dispute of some who made this assertion gained such force [Note: Because of that dispute, the internal organs of Saint Boniface were conceded to the people of Mainz; they are still venerated among them today, according to Serrarius, *History of Mainz*, book III, note 47. Compare the *Life of Saint Sturm*, no. 16.] that Saint Lullus almost consented to their counsel, unless Saint Boniface had appeared in a vision to a venerable deacon named Otpertus and said:

“Tell Bishop Lullus to transfer my body without any hesitation to the site of my monastery.”

When many who heard this command did not at all believe it, Bishop Lullus, having brought out the relics of the saints, ordered Otpertus to establish by oath whether his vision was true. Without any hesitation, he fulfilled the command and confirmed the vision by oath. When this had been done, everyone not only consented to the transfer of the holy body, which they had previously opposed, but also began to assist in whatever the undertaking required.

Some hurried to bring ships, so that they might quickly proceed across the Rhine; others, following the holy funeral, recited the litany, psalmody, and other songs of divine praise. When one crowd, proceeding farther and unable to continue, turned back, another crowd nevertheless came from the neighboring region, rejoicing to walk beside the holy body of the man whom it believed and hoped would intercede for it before the Lord. The joy and compunction that arose in very many people there from the patronage of so great a man cannot adequately be expressed in our writings. For this reason, in certain places where they spent the night or rested at midday with the holy body, they later built churches in his honor.

Thus, accompanied by such joy, he was brought to the site of the monastery at Fulda, where he had often desired to be buried and had repeatedly entrusted this task to the blessed Bishop Lullus. Lullus, striving with the utmost diligence to fulfill his petition, restored to the earth with due veneration what belonged to it, while he took every care to commend his soul, through all manner of prayers, to be joined to the joys of heaven.

### XXVI

At the place of his venerable tomb, through his merits, innumerable benefits occur for those whom fitting faith urges to obtain what they ask, benefits both for the inner and for the outer person. Benefits for the inner person arise when they obtain forgiveness for their sins; benefits for the outer person when they escape some bodily illness or weakness. Whenever neither of these benefits is obtained there, this must not be attributed either to divine severity or to any ineffectiveness of Saint Boniface’s patronage before God, but rather to those who, held captive by unbelief, do not deserve to be heard. The Evangelist bears witness to this when he says of our Lord: “Because of the unbelief of some, he could perform no mighty works” (Matthew 13).

Miracles sometimes also cease because of negligence toward divine worship and because of the incorrigible wickedness of the inhabitants. They cease also because, when such miracles occasionally occur through the intercession of the saints, neither the praises nor the thanks due to God and his saints are rendered, and the events are not even committed to memory.

Saint Boniface held the episcopate for thirty-six years, six months, and six days. He suffered together with his companions on the Nones of June, in the fortieth year of his pilgrimage, that is, in the year 750 of the Lord’s Incarnation. [Note: Add five [years], from Willibaldus. More will be said about this matter below.] The same Lord was reigning, to whom be praise and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# APPENDIX TO THE PRECEDING TWO LIVES OF SAINT BONIFACE

## On the remaining deeds of Saint Boniface, his age, the year of his martyrdom, his companions and authors; and on his cult, churches, translation, and writings

### 1

Since certain deeds of Saint Boniface and other matters relating to him have been omitted by the writers of his Life, it is useful to append them here by way of a conclusion.

### 2

First of all, worthy of mention is the letter of Daniel, bishop of the city of Winchester among the western Saxons, in which he prescribes certain salutary counsels to Saint Boniface for the easy propagation of the Gospel. The substance of the letter is that Boniface should not labor to assert propositions contrary to what the Germans believe concerning the genealogy of false gods. Rather, he should allow them to maintain this, so that he may at least prove that gods and goddesses, born in the manner of human beings, were human beings rather than gods, and that they did not previously exist. Once they have been compelled to acknowledge that the gods had a beginning, he should ask whether they think this world had a beginning or has always existed without a beginning. If it had a beginning, who created it? If they say the opposite, they are to be refuted.

Daniel develops these and many other points not unreasonably in his letter, which is found as number 67 among the Boniface letters.

### 3

Boniface’s zeal and truly apostolic freedom are demonstrated not only by the letter reported by Othlonus, book II, chapter 11, from which it is understood that Boniface lodged complaints with Pope Zacharias about the simony and other vices of the Romans—as is also clear from chapter 1—but also by another letter of Boniface, number 19 in Serrarius’s edition, in which he rebukes Ethelbald, king of the Mercians, for thefts, adulteries, fornications and incest, and for violations of ecclesiastical property. In another letter, number 105, he warns Cuthbert, archbishop of Canterbury, to chastise the nuns for the luxury and pomp of their clothing.

“And lest anyone wonder,” says William, monk of Malmesbury, book I of *The Kings of England*, chapter 4, “that he was conducting another man’s business, since it did not concern him how and by what morals the English people lived, he knew himself to be bound by an oath imposed by Pope Gregory III [read: II], not to conceal the conduct of neighboring peoples from apostolic knowledge. Therefore, if admonitions did not succeed, he would act so that such vices might not remain hidden from the pope.”

Nor, William adds, could the letters of so great a man have been fruitless, since he sent them with vigilant minds, out of regard for his mission and his love for his fellow countrymen. For both Archbishop Cuthbert and King Ethelbald convened a council to correct the excesses that Boniface had rebuked—namely, the Council of Clovesho, whose thirty-one chapters the same author summarizes in book I of *The Deeds of the Bishops of Canterbury*.

In the passage cited shortly before, he also reports a writing of Ethelbald, an indication of his devotion, produced at the same council, by which he restored liberty to churches and monasteries and granted them immunity from public taxes, for the love of the heavenly homeland and the remedy of his soul. These measures should rightly be attributed to Boniface’s admonitions and zeal.

### 4

Those who say that Charlemagne was baptized by Boniface at the royal estate of Ingelheim, two miles from Mainz, are asserting something altogether uncertain. But that Pippin received royal anointing from Boniface is an established fact, although the writers of the Life omitted it. This is attested by the Frankish Annals, in their account of the deeds of Pippin and Charles the Great under the year 750, as well as by the Annals of Einhard; the Fulda Annals place it under 752, and Aimoinus under 751. The Frankish Annals and those of Einhard are to be preferred; Abbot Regino of Prüm, Marianus Scotus, Sigebert the monk, and others agree with them.

Nor should you oppose to this the commonly circulated Anastasius, in the Life of Pope Stephen III, or the letter of Emperor Louis the Pious to Hilduin, in which—as also in Anastasius—the anointing of Pippin by Pope Stephen is said in these words: “At the altar before the tomb of Saint Denis, together with his two sons Carloman and Charles, he is said to have been anointed king of the Franks.”

Do not, I say, oppose these statements. For Pippin is expressly recorded as having been anointed twice, first by Boniface and afterward by Pope Stephen, in the Annals of Einhard, whose words are these:

“In the year 750. In this year, according to the decree of the Roman pontiff, Pippin was called king of the Franks, and, consecrated by sacred anointing by the hand of Boniface, archbishop and martyr of blessed memory, and raised according to Frankish custom to the throne of the kingdom in the city of Soissons, he was invested with the dignity of this honor.

“And in the year 754, after Pope Stephen had received from King Pippin a guarantee of the protection of the Roman Church, he consecrated him by sacred anointing to the honor of royal dignity, together with his two sons Charles and Carloman.”

### 5

John Gerbrandus, a Carmelite, reports in book III, chapters 12 and 13 of his *Chronicle of the Low Countries*, two charters of King Pippin by which he confirms to the Utrecht Church, in honor of Archbishop Boniface, the properties granted by his predecessors. The same author, in chapter 14, recalls the dispute of Saint Boniface with Hilger, bishop of Cologne, and Boniface’s letter on that matter to Pope Stephen, which we have already examined in the Life of Saint Willibrord.

### 6

Here would be the place to set Saint Boniface’s virtues before our eyes. We have already shown his zeal above. His humility is attested by letter 25 in these words:

“And because I am the last and worst of all the legates whom the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church has sent to preach the Gospel, pray to the Lord’s mercy that I may not die altogether without the fruit of the Gospel, but that he may confirm my heart with a principal spirit. He willed that I, an unworthy shepherd, should be called among the people, so that, when the wolf comes, I may not flee like a hireling, but, following the example of the Good Shepherd, may strive faithfully and confidently to defend the lambs together with their mothers—that is, the Catholic Church together with her sons and daughters—against heretics, schismatics, and hypocrites.”

His concern for his own people and for peoples recently converted to the faith is demonstrated by letter 92. But, leaving these matters aside, we must proceed to the time of his death and to the authors.

### 7

Willibaldus dates the martyrdom of Saint Boniface to the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 755, indiction 8, after thirty-six years, six months, and six days of episcopacy. In place of “episcopacy,” one should read “apostolate,” for that many years elapsed from Saint Boniface’s mission until his death; his mission preceded his episcopal ordination by four years.

Othlonus’s reading does not differ from Willibaldus’s, except that, through what is probably the carelessness of scribes, “fifty-five” is found written as “fifty” in the manuscript codices. To these authorities are added Adam, canon of Bremen, in chapter 8 of his history, and Lambert of Hersfeld, in his Chronicle—both weighty authorities, though later in time.

Yet most authorities of comparable standing assign the martyrdom of Saint Boniface to the year 754: Einhard; the continuator of the epitome of the venerable Bede; Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, in chapter 30 of his little work or letter 44; the Fulda Annals and writers, the first of whom is Eigil, in the Life of Saint Sturm, abbot; the Annals of Metz and of Saint-Bertin; and also Marianus Scotus and Sigebert. They appear to deserve our adherence, as being very weighty authorities of comparable rank, most of them native to the events.

### 8

Boniface’s chronology may therefore be arranged as follows.

Around the year 680 he was born at Crediton in Devon and was called Winfred. At approximately seven years of age he was entrusted to the monks of the monastery of Adescancaster. As a young man he studied letters among the monks of Nursling, became a priest in the thirtieth year of his age, around 710 in the Christian era, and shortly afterward was sent by the Fathers assembled in a council among the West Saxons to Canterbury to present to Archbishop Berhtwald the decrees enacted in the synod.

Around the year 716 he first crossed into Frisia, as is clear from the conflict then raging between Charles, duke of the Franks, and Radbod, which began to be stirred up in that year. Considering the time of war unsuitable for evangelical preaching, Boniface returned to his homeland after scarcely half a year had elapsed.

In the year 718, having either renounced or declined the dignity of abbot, he again planned to go to Frisia. Furnished with letters from Bishop Daniel, at the beginning of autumn he set out for Rome to receive a blessing from Pope Gregory II. Having received it, he was sent to Germany when spring returned, with letters from Gregory dated on the Ides of May, in the third year of Emperor Leo, indiction 2—that is, in the year 719.

He entered Frisia with Willibrord and spent three years there. Afterward he persuaded very many Thuringians and Hessians to accept the Christian religion. When Gregory received news of this, he rejoiced and summoned Boniface to himself, granting him episcopal ordination in the seventh year of Emperor Leo, indiction 6, on the day before the Kalends of December. Gregory III also bestowed upon him archiepiscopal dignity and the pallium in the year 732.

After Boniface had been elevated by this dignity, he traveled to Rome for the third time. In 742 he held a synod in Germany and confirmed its acts in the synod of Liptina the following year. Then, in 744, he convened a council at Soissons. In the following year he was formally assigned to the see of Mainz, having until then been archbishop without a defined see.

He anointed Pippin king in the aforesaid city of Soissons in the year 750. Finally, in Frisia, he met his death for the religion which during his life he had preached with such devotion, an old man of approximately seventy-five years. All these matters are evident from his Acts and the notes appended to them.

### 9

Othlonus, misunderstanding Willibaldus’s narrative, wrote in book II, chapter 21, that Boniface was martyred by newly converted believers who were to receive the sacrament of confirmation that very day. Willibaldus certainly did not mean this; instead, he says that enemies or pagans attacked Boniface on the appointed day on which the laying on of hands was to be performed for the neophytes.

An anonymous author explains Willibaldus’s meaning in these words:

“The herald of the Gospel’s message sounded throughout Frisia with the whole trumpet of salvation. But the ancient serpent, jealous of every good thing and from the beginning of the world always hostile to the human race, stirred up certain men from a cruel people who had not yet been emancipated from diabolical superstitions—his own agents, that is, against the servant of God and his fellow soldiers. For they said that they would rather die than abandon the rites of their fathers.

“As soon as the athletes of God heard this, they went joyfully with their own shepherd as quickly as possible to the village called Dokkum, where they knew that executioners, with a bloodthirsty multitude, had gathered to slaughter the servants of God.”

Although other authors say that the holy martyrs did not thrust themselves into the hands of the executioners, but rather generously submitted themselves to them, there are those who say that the descendants of these assassins still exist, divinely marked by a white mass of hair on the crown of the head as a sign of their dreadful sacrilege.

### 10

The anonymous author identifies the martyr companions as follows:

“Therefore, when the day of the glorious contest dawned, Saint Eobanus, his fellow worker and fellow bishop, together with the other companions—namely, priests, monks, and deacons, whose names are these: Wintrung and Walthere, as well as Adelhere, elevated to the priestly rank; Hamund, Scirbald, and Bosa, assigned to the office of the levitical order; Waccar and Gundecar, Illehere and Batthewlf, devoted to the monastic life; and so forth.”

Willibaldus and Othlonus, as well as Rabanus Maurus and the monk Notkerus in their martyrologies, give almost the same names, except that Othlonus reads *Bderso* for Bosa, *Williheri* for Illehere, and *Hadolt* for Batthewlf or Batowlf, while Rabanus and Notkerus have *Hadowlfe*.

The anonymous author adds:

“The number of the holy martyrs who suffered for Christ together with the blessed bishop Boniface was fifty-two. But the bodies of the martyrs named above and thirteen others were placed by the faithful in a sarcophagus, loaded onto a ship with the blessed Bishop Boniface, and brought to Utrecht with joyful gladness and a prosperous voyage. There they were received with hymns and psalms of God and buried with all fear and veneration in the church consecrated in honor of the most holy Trinity.

“Not many days afterward the body of Saint Boniface was brought to the monastery at Fulda. The bodies of other holy martyrs, whose names have been handed over to oblivion through sloth and negligence but are undoubtedly written in the book of life, were received by the faithful people in the same place where they received the palm of martyrdom. Later, by the favor of Christ and by royal command, a church was built there in honor of the holy martyrs.

“In these places—Utrecht, Fulda, and Dokkum—God grants benefits to the faithful people through signs and miracles on account of the merits of the holy martyrs.”

Thus far the anonymous author, whose work we read in a manuscript codex at Compiègne. In Bede’s epitome it is said that Boniface was crowned with martyrdom together with fifty-three others. The number fifty-two is given by Hucbaldus, monk of Elnon, in the Life of Saint Lebwin; by John of Beka and William Heda in the *Chronicle of Utrecht*; and also by John Gerbrandus in the *Chronicle of the Low Countries*, chapter 16.

### 11

Not long after his martyrdom, Saint Boniface was honored among the English with solemn worship. The letter of Cuthbert, archbishop of Canterbury, number 70 among the Boniface letters, bears witness to this in these words:

“We both lovingly hold him and laudably venerate him among the outstanding and excellent teachers of orthodox faith. Therefore, in our general synod, where we also discussed more fully among ourselves the other matters which we now briefly set before your holiness, we announced his natal day and that of his company who suffered martyrdom with him and decreed that it should be solemnly celebrated each year with regular observance,” and so forth.
