Read also letters 74 and 78.

Nor did the peoples of Germany and Gaul neglect his cult. Shortly after the death of Saint Boniface, they celebrated the day of his passion with festive rites, as is clear both from letter 5 of Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, and from the poem which Walahfrid Strabo sang on his feast:

“May the joys of this present day, holy Boniface,

By the Lord’s gift, save us through your merits.”

At the beginning of the eleventh century, Saint Meinwerk, bishop of Paderborn, instituted the annual celebration of the day of Saint Boniface and his companions throughout the entire bishopric of Paderborn. Moreover, various chapels and churches were built for the same holy martyr immediately after his death, and the faithful frequented them with religious vows.

### 12

The first church may be that of Saints Paul and Boniface, built at the place of the martyrdom called Dokkum. Wion reports these verses, attributed to Alcuin, although they do not occur among Alcuin’s epigrams:

“Here the illustrious Father Boniface, rich in gracious merits,

Together with his companions poured out a flood of blood,

Receiving the renowned crowns of sacred martyrdom.

O most blessed earth, exceedingly rich in the blood of saints!

Here the victorious soldier flies across to the rewards of heaven.

Therefore, whoever you are who read this, I urge you,

Bowing your knee in supplication, press kisses to these lands,

And let it become your hope, through tears, to ascend to heaven.

Here there could have been [lacuna]

Here lies that blood, more precious than all gold,

And these limbs, drenched in heavenly dew, rest. [Perhaps: ‘here’]

Paul assists from one side, and the teacher Boniface from the other,

For this hall is established as dedicated to them both.”

Dokkum, or Dockum—commonly Dockem and Dockum—on the river Burdon, with a monastery attached to the church, as we learn from the conclusion of the Life written by Saint Willibaldus, became a town of the diocese of Leeuwarden. It is said that the Gospel codex written by the hand of Saint Boniface is preserved there.

### 13

Nor should we omit what Einhard in his Annals (*Ancient Frankish Annals* in Chesnius, volume II, page 14) and the Fulda writers record under the year 774 concerning the church at Fritzlar.

While Charlemagne was occupied in the Italian expedition against Desiderius, king of the Lombards, the Saxons, as the Frankish Annals report, came out with a great army against the borders of the Franks as far as Büraburg. The border inhabitants entered the fortress, and the Saxons themselves came to a certain basilica called Fritzlar, which Saint Boniface had consecrated and had foretold by the spirit of prophecy would never be consumed by fire.

The Saxons began with great determination to attack the basilica, seeking by every device [French: *engin*] to burn it. While they were doing this, two young men in white garments appeared to certain Christians who were in the fortress, and likewise to certain pagans who were present at the place. They protected the basilica, and it was not burned.

The Fulda writers add:

“Nevertheless, one of the enemy was found dead beside the basilica, kneeling, having piled up wood and leaning over the fire, apparently in the act of blowing upon it.”

Regino records the same event. Compare the Acts of Saint Wigbert, abbot, under the year 747, chapter 19.

### 14

The church of Parthenon, called “in the Cells,” situated about eighteen miles from Fulda toward the summer sunrise, near the boundary between eastern Francia and the region of Henneberg, was dedicated in the year 815 by Heistulf, archbishop of Mainz, at the request of Raitger, abbot of the Church of Fulda. It was dedicated in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ; Saint Boniface the martyr; Saint John the Baptist; Saints Peter and Paul; Martin; Benedict; and Cecilia, as recorded by Browerus in book II of the *Antiquities of Fulda*, chapter 12.

### 15

I pass over the other churches and chapels dedicated to Saint Boniface, both in that early period and later, in order to come to the celebrated dedication of the Fulda basilica.

When the body of the holy martyr was first transferred to Fulda, Browerus says, book II of the *Antiquities*, chapter 1, it rested in an apse toward the east, enclosed by a portico or arched structure in the middle of the church, near the altar which the holy man had built while alive and beside which he had wished to be buried after death. At separate intervals, on the northern side, it had Lioba, a woman of outstanding religious devotion and proven holiness who had presided over the monastery of the virgins at Bischofsheim; and on the southern side, Abbot Sturm, likewise of equal sanctity, each buried in his own apse.

Candidus, in the Life of Saint Sturm, abbot, and Ruodolfus, in the Acts of Saint Lioba, which will be reported in their proper places, likewise relate this. Relevant here are the verses of Rabanus Maurus, inscription 82, placed in the church of Saint Mary beside the tomb of Saint Boniface:

“After the gracious Boniface had completed his martyrdom,

The martyr and bishop, seeking the heights of heaven,

Was brought here from Frisia and duly placed in this shrine;

As he departed, he left here a portion of his blood.

Over this tomb Rabanus, a lowly servant,

An unworthy bishop, yet still his native servant,

Ordered a structure to be built in praise of the saint.

For his sake, reader, pour forth prayers to the Lord.”

In the year 778, as is recorded in the Fulda Annals, the monks of the Fulda monastery, because of fear of the Saxons, took with them the bones of Saint Boniface the martyr and fled from the monastery for nearly fourteen miles. Read the Life of Saint Sturm, no. 23, under the year 779.

After the sacred relics had been returned to the tomb, they were placed in the eastern crypt of the new basilica built by Saint Eigil. Above the vaulted structure an altar was placed and dedicated in honor of Saint Boniface, as was also the principal church. This is established by an ancient document reported by Browerus, book II, chapter 3, in the following form:

“In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 818, indiction 12, in the month of November, on the first day of the month, this temple was dedicated by Heistulf, archbishop of the Church of Mainz, in honor of the holy Savior, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, and in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, and Saint Peter the apostle, and the other apostles of the Lord, and Saint John the Baptist, and Saint Boniface, martyr of Christ, and many other saints.

“On that same day, by the same archbishop and the other bishops and priests, the body of Saint Boniface, martyr of Christ, was transferred—sixty-five years, four months, and twenty-six days having elapsed after his martyrdom—to the place which the venerable Abbot Eigil, together with the brothers of the same monastery, had prepared for it with great zeal and pious devotion.”

His relics are still preserved in the same basilica: his head in a separate reliquary, and his other bones in a precious shrine. Some of his books are also preserved, those which we noted under Willibaldus, chapter 12, together with his pastoral staff, belt, and ring.

Let this suffice concerning Saint Boniface.

# VERSES ONCE INSCRIBED IN THE TEMPLE OF THE CITADEL OF MAINZ

“Born from royal stock, Boniface,

Voluntarily leaving Britain,

By the authority of the supreme pontiff,

Became the apostle of Germany.”

# THE FIRST PART OF ALL THE EXTANT WORKS OF SAINT BONIFACE, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

## LETTERS OF BONIFACE OF MAINZ

# NOTICE OF THE EDITOR OF THE *PATROLOGIA*

Since it is necessary to preface the following collection of the Letters of Saint Boniface, we shall say a few incidental things about the general arrangement we have assigned to his works. The writings of the holy Father are here divided into three parts. The first contains the Letters, the Oath, and the Councils; the second, Sermons; the third, Miscellaneous Opuscula.

### I

Everything that we present in the first part was formerly included and mixed together under the single title “Letters.” The Oath and the Councils, however, seemed to us worthy of distinct classification, and we have followed Dr. J. A. Giles, whom we shall mention several times below, who had already published them separately.

As for the Letters themselves, the care we have devoted to them will become clear from the few remarks that follow.

Thus far three principal editions of these letters are counted: one published at Mainz by Serrarius in 1605; another, also at Mainz, by Wurdtwein in 1766; and the latest, very recently published in London by Dr. J. A. Giles. In each case the editors maintained a particular order according to a particular method. We shall do the same in our edition, and with good reason.

In the earlier recensions, many letters had been inserted that did not belong to Saint Boniface, but related only either to him, to his successors, or to the Church. Since in our *Library* each Father who wrote them has his own place, we have returned each person’s letters to his proper location: those of Aldhelm and of Popes Gregory II and III to the earlier section, where their works are to be consulted; those of Pope Zacharias, Lullus, and others to the present or following volumes below.

Under the title of an appendix, however, we retain some twenty letters whose proper authors or dates are unknown, because they would have had no better place anywhere else.

Our arrangement of the Letters of Saint Boniface is therefore entirely new. The prefaces and tables that follow will nevertheless assist the reader in understanding the other editions.

## II. Sermons

The sermons contained in the second part we have reviewed after the aforementioned Doctor Giles, who appended the following note:

> “Concerning the sermons or homilies that have been circulated under Boniface’s name, there is no reason for us to say much. Martenius first published them in volume V of his very extensive collection of *Ancient Writers* [Col. 0671B], p. 186. What the editor had to say about them, in the preliminary notice [Col. 0672A] that we have repeated in our edition (below, before the sermons themselves), the reader may consult. In the Paris manuscript (Supp. 205), which I collated word for word with Martenius’s edition, only fourteen homilies are extant. The manuscript is sufficiently ancient; nevertheless, I cannot rid my mind of a certain suspicion that these sermons, in their wording and style, may bear the flavor of a later age, one more suited both to reading and to understanding. One or another of these sermons also exists in Paris Manuscript 340, but interspersed with others. I inspected all of them, but judged it superfluous to distinguish them by numbers.”

## III. Miscellaneous Works

Finally, concerning the miscellaneous short works contained in the third part, there seems to be nothing that needs to be said, except that they were first collected by the English editor, whom we follow.

[Col. 0671]

# SERRARIUS’S PREFACE TO HIS EDITION OF THE LETTERS OF SAINT BONIFACE

## I. On the usefulness of these letters

[Col. 0671B]

The letters of the ancients, and especially of the saints and of our fathers in Christ, are useful for many purposes, but chiefly for four.

1. **For the faith.** For in them many things that modern innovators attack and slander are presented admirably, as certain, holy, and salutary—for example, the most holy sacrifice of the Mass, prayer for the faithful departed, invocation of the saints, veneration of relics [Col. 0671C], the authority of the Roman pontiff, and similar matters.

2. **For morals.** For in them there is frequent rebuke of vices, praise of virtues, explanation of eternal rewards and punishments, and other matters of the same kind.

3. **For preserving the memory of those by whom, to whom, and about whom the letters were written.** “The one thing,” says Saint Jerome, *Letter* 42, “that makes absent persons present is a letter.” Cicero writes to his brother Quintus: “When I read what you have written, I seem to hear you.”

4. **For history.** When Vopiscus of Syracuse was required to write the deeds of the emperor Aurelian, he took particular pains to collect letters from diaries, linen books, Sibylline books, and finally from various libraries. “For,” he says, “it is important for us to know the letters written to Aurelian.” And afterward: “There exists a letter which I thought ought to be inserted, as I usually do, for the sake of credibility—or rather, as I see other writers of annals doing.” Again [Col. 0671D]: “There is a letter of Aurelian concerning the Sibylline Books.” For I too inserted it as evidence of the facts; and for this reason he so frequently and diligently drew such letter-sheets from every corner of all the libraries—he who in our age was the first Caesar in Roman history.

Otholon likewise testifies that he searched for these Boniface letters with great zeal, in the prologue to the *Life of Saint Boniface* and in Book II, chapter 17. Then, as though affected by a kind of grief or anxiety, he adds:

> “If anyone is troubled that very many letters mentioned in the letters written above are not likewise found here in writing, let him know that this happened because I was nowhere able to find them.”

By these words he also indicates that, if he had obtained as many letters of Saint Boniface as are now published, he would have rejoiced with immense joy and, together with that Gospel woman, Luke 15:19, summoned his friends and neighbors and said to them: “Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma that I had lost.”

## II. On the manuscript copies of these letters

[Col. 0672B]

The most reverend and illustrious Baronius saw two manuscript copies of these letters of Saint Boniface, and one of them is cited in the correction of the Gregorian canon law. But when I learned that copies had been requested and solicited from others in Italy for publication, and that they nevertheless could not be persuaded to send them, I abandoned all hope of ever seeing them. At the same time, I immediately reflected that, if—as Plato is said once to have advised—we dug into the soil of our Germany down to the chalk, perhaps some copies might be found.

With God favorably directing our fortunes, and holy Boniface assisting by his prayers, one was discovered by a member of our Society, the Reverend Father Jacob Gretser, in the celebrated and richly endowed library of the University of Ingolstadt. Another was found by the most reverend and most distinguished Doctor Pistorius, renowned for his writings, disputations, and labors on behalf of the Catholic Church, in the extensive and illustrious imperial library at Vienna.

There was also once a third copy in the splendid storehouse of books at the monastery of Fulda. But this was carried off by that filthiest harpy—I mean Illyricus—and afterward torn and mutilated in various ways. Thus a Lutheran preacher who had seen its remains in the Helmstedt library said that even from this it was sufficiently apparent what practice that dreadful Celaeno had been accustomed to follow in handling, defacing, and mutilating ancient works.

From the first two German copies, then, which the learned men I have praised most courteously sent us [Col. 0672D], this edition has now been transcribed—first by hand, and afterward by the printer’s compositor.

## III. On the principal exemplar of this work

I chiefly followed the imperial manuscript copy, first because it was written in a much older hand, as the antiquity of its characters and parchment pages demonstrates. The Ingolstadt copy, by contrast, was transcribed in 1497 at the monastery of Sponheim, by order of Abbot Trithemius, by a novice monk, as the end of the Codex testifies in Greek and Latin.

Second, the same imperial copy contains many more letters: it has 117, whereas the Ingolstadt copy has only 78.

Third, those same 117 letters had never previously been published in their entirety, apart from certain ones selected by the most reverend and illustrious Baronius, mentioned above, and included in volume IX of his *Annals*. After him, and largely from him, the same letters were reproduced, though almost entirely in German, by that J. Letzner [Col. 0673A], about whom see the note before the *Life of Saint Boniface*, Book III, Mainz, p. 321.

Of the 78 Ingolstadt letters, however, almost all of the first twenty-nine had long ago appeared both in the *Letters of the Pontiffs* and in Othlon’s *Life of Saint Boniface*, which I also included in Book III of the Mainz collection.

It also appeared that most of the later Ingolstadt letters had been copied either from the imperial manuscript or from another copy agreeing with it. Thus, after Ingolstadt letter 71, the following was written:

> “This letter, already placed above, has been omitted here because, as appears, in the Codex from which this copy was made it had already been placed earlier, just as in the imperial manuscript this letter is number 50.”

## IV. On the transcription of the imperial exemplar

In transcribing ancient Codices, it seems worthwhile to alter nothing. This was entirely my settled decision and determination. Yet it was not possible to follow it in every respect.

First, some errors of the copyists occasionally intervened; these will be indicated in their proper place [Col. 0673B], especially in the first letter and in a few others.

Next, I did not wish to be excessively fussy about the old spelling of certain words, partly because such spellings are today troublesome and ridiculous to most people, and partly because in some cases what is evident is not so much an orthography as a scribal blunder and incompetence. Nevertheless, so that those who are more devoted to antiquity may suffer no loss, I shall indicate somewhat below which forms appear to belong to the former category.

Third, the following was repeated continually: “Letter of Saint Boniface.” Likewise: “Letter of Saint Boniface.” But why should we serve up this same cabbage so many times? It is sufficiently clear from the title and salutation, which introduce almost every individual letter.

In all other matters and words I took care not knowingly or deliberately to deviate even a finger’s breadth from the proposed exemplar. Thus, although some rough, disjointed, and almost *agrammata*—“unwritten” or “unlettered” [Greek: ἀγράμματα]—passages occurred, I left them as they stood; someone else may perhaps correct or explain them more successfully from another source.

Nevertheless, I noted in the margin the various readings of various copies, and sometimes certain conjectures, together with the addition of certain letters [Col. 0673C], about which I shall speak shortly.

## V. On certain unknown characters in the same imperial Codex, and on some of my sigla

Certain unknown characters occasionally occur in the imperial copy, which I thought were ancient English or Saxon characters. Yet a large number of them are unlike those that the editor places before Asser the Englishman.

Nevertheless, by comparing them in various ways, I constructed almost an entire alphabet of them. If the types had been available, I would have given it here to the readers, together with the signs by which letters were designated in that more ancient age.

In place of these, and of similar signs, whenever something could not be represented or seemed to be missing, I added a series of dots as follows: . . . . . .

My other sigla are these—for Justinian calls such abbreviated signs of words *compendious marks*, as will be said in connection with Letter 99:

- **C.** Imperial copy.
- **I.** Ingolstadt copy.
- **C. I.** Both.
- **B.** Baronian copy.
- **L.** Letznerian copy.
- **S.** Surius, in the *Life of Saint Boniface*.
- **V.** The Latin translator of the Vulgate Bible.
- **F.** It can perhaps be read.

Since I had returned the Ingolstadt Codex because the opportunity for transporting it was offered before I was able to receive the imperial copy, I made haste to transcribe it from a copy that had been collated only with the imperial manuscript.

## VI. On the style of these letters

“And yet,” says Saint Jerome in his letter to Marcella, “for some people these are not agreeable feasts, since they do not smell of more than a hundred [the reading is uncertain] and Apicius does not season them; in them nothing is redolent of the sauce of the teachers of this age.” Not every land bears everything.

Those who always desire a highly Latin, polished, and elegant style have Cicero, Manutius, Muretus, Lipsius, and several others. In these letters of Saint Boniface the language is simple and familiar: in that age, not inelegant; in ours, tolerable—except in a few passages, verses, or letters with which students or female students rejoiced in addressing their teachers in whatever manner they could.

A candid simplicity of heart and conduct shines everywhere; virtue, Christian charity, and modesty gleam throughout. But in the imperial volume the later letters had been written with far more errors by the copyists than the earlier ones.

## VII. On the old spelling and language in these letters

I now present what I noted in Note 4 and promised to provide. In the imperial Codex, then, the following forms are written:

- *Abunculus* for *avunculus* — uncle.
- *Adolari* for *adulari* — to flatter.
- *Amminiculum* for *adminiculum* — support, aid.
- *Auxilio* for *auxilior* — I assist.
- *Anbacum*, as in Greek Ἀμβακούμ, for *Habacuc* — Habakkuk.
- *Bernacula* for *vernacula* — native, vernacular.
- *Bonevolentia* for *benevolentia* — goodwill.
- In Letter 45, *boenivola voluntas* — “goodwill”; but is this not an error?
- In Letter 100, *bovibus* for *bobus* — oxen.
- *Caraxo*, from Greek χαράττω — I engrave, inscribe.
- *Carulus* and *Carlus* for *Carolus* — Charles.
- *Coacerbo* for *coacervo* — I heap up.
- *Commonio* for *communio* — communion.
- *Conloco* for *colloco* — I place.
- *Compatesco* for *compatior* — I suffer with.
- *Consolo* for *consolor* — I console.
- *Cotidie* for *quotidie* — daily.
- *Curbare* for *curvare* — to bend.
- *Danielus* for *Daniel* — Daniel.
- *Dirego* for *dirigo* — I direct.
- *Diphhongae* for *diphthongi* — diphthongs.
- *Epistula* for *epistola* — letter.
- *Epistiuncula* for *epistolium* — little letter.
- *Fantasma* for *phantasma* — apparition.
- *Fatesco* for *fatisco* — I split, gape.
- *Floriet* for *florebit* — it will flourish.
- *Forasticus* for *externus* — foreign, external.
- *Have* for *ave* — hail.
- *Honerosus* for *onerosus* — burdensome.
- *Idolatria* for *idololatria* — idolatry.
- *Ihesus* for *Jesus* — Jesus.

But the Venerable Bede, at the beginning of his book *On Music*, p. 35, teaches that the character written between *i* and *e* is the Greek eta, η, and that Latin writers insert it because of the authority of the name. Perhaps it was also done for this reason: to indicate that the *e* is not short but long, and that in this sweetest and most honeyed name it should not be pronounced hastily, but slowly and with a kind of pause and a reverent sense of devotion.

- *Inlaesus* for *illaesus* — unharmed.
- *Inluster* for *illuster* — illustrious.
- *Inluminatus* for *illuminatus* — illuminated.
- *Inormitas* for *innormitas* or *enormitas* — irregularity, enormity.
- *Inrogare* for *irrogare* — to impose.
- *Interduciae* for *induciae* — truces.
- *Ipsud* for *ipsum* — itself.
- *Juvar* for *jubar* — radiance.
- *Noberunt* for *noverunt* — they have known.
- *Oboedientia* for *obedientia* — obedience.
- *Obtunsus* for *obtusus* — blunt, dull.
- *Oloserica* for *holoserica* — silk.
- *Psalmigraphus* for *psalmographus* — psalm-writer.
- *Repperio* for *reperio* — I find.
- *Reverentissimus* for *reverendissimus* — most reverend, as *amantissimus* occurs in Capitolinus, in the *Life of Albinus*, and in Spartianus, in the *Life of Geta*.
- *Subfragium* for *suffragium* — support, vote.
- *Sobrius*, used where *sobrie* would be expected — soberly.
- *Veteresco* for *veterasco* — I grow old.
- *Volbere* for *volvere* — to roll.
- *Vocifero* for *vociferor* — I shout.

In all these forms you can see, among other features, that *o* is often placed for *u* and conversely, and likewise *b* for *u*, as in the Florentine *Pandects* and very frequently elsewhere, as Brissonius teaches in his single-volume *Parergon*. Some of these matters will be noted again in their proper places, as well as other similar matters.

[Col. 0675]

# WURDTWEIN’S PREFACE

[Col. 0675A]

## GREETINGS TO THE READER

Among the principal monuments of sacred Germany, the letters of Saint Boniface, archbishop and martyr of the See of Mainz, rightly deserve to be counted. For they abundantly testify how dreadful was the condition of the churches of Germany in the seventh and eighth centuries [Note: [Col. 0675A] In Letter 2, Gregory II writes to the ancient Saxons: “I announce to you that the kingdom of God is near, so that no one may deceive you any longer or mislead you through lofty words, or so that you may seek your salvation in any kind of metal, worshiping idols made by human hands—of gold, silver, bronze, stone, or any material whatever—which were fashioned by the pagans of old as false gods and in which demons are known to dwell,” etc. And in Letter 51 of Boniface to Pope Zacharias: “The Franks,” the elders say, “have held no synod for more than eighty years, nor had they an archbishop; nor did they establish or restore the canonical rights of churches for anyone. But now, for the most part, episcopal sees in the cities have been handed over to greedy laymen for possession, or to adulterous clerics, fornicators, and publicans for secular enjoyment,” etc. In the same place: “The ecclesiastical religion has for a long time—that is, for no less than sixty or seventy years—been trampled upon and dispersed.”] and how necessary it was that a man full of zeal for religion should be raised up, strong in battle, who would overthrow the worship of idols [Note: [Col. 0675B] See the Council of Liptina under number 57 and the list of superstitions and pagan practices placed there, as well as Letter 59], uproot the thorns and thickets of superstition [Note: [Col. 0675B] Pope Gregory III to the nobles and people of Germany, Letter 44: “You who have been baptized in the name of Christ have put on Christ. Abstain from every form of pagan worship, correcting not only yourselves but also your subjects, wholly rejecting and casting away diviners, soothsayers, sacrifices for the dead, omens from groves or springs, amulets, enchanters, magicians, and various observances that used to be practiced in your territories,” etc.], and form workers [Note: [Col. 0675C] See the year 725 and the instructions for converting pagans proposed to Boniface by Daniel the bishop, numbers 13 and 14. Add the year 722, etc.] who would bring back those who had gone astray and keep those who had been restored on the path of salvation.

For this great task God appointed Winfrid, afterward called Boniface, from England [Note: [Col. 0675C] Compare the notes before the first letter, especially Note b]. Bound by oath [Col. 0676A] to the primate of the whole Church [Note: [Col. 0675C] This was Pope Gregory II, from the year 715 to 731. In 723 Boniface promised, by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the inseparable Trinity, that he would show all faithfulness and purity toward the holy Catholic faith and, by God’s working, persevere in the unity of that faith, in which the salvation of all Christians is unquestionably found; that he would in no way, under anyone’s persuasion, consent to act against the unity of the common and universal Church, etc. The complete oath will be found below, [Col. 0675D] before Letter 5.] he was sent to preach the Gospel to the nations, to teach sound doctrine, to cut down Jupiter’s trees [Note: [Col. 0676B] See Schiminck’s dissertation on the Tree of Jupiter], and to plant and water the seed of the true faith, while God gave the growth [Note: [Col. 0676B] 1 Corinthians 3:6].

These present letters, arranged in chronological order, as far as possible and only with the greatest difficulty, not only indicate the apostolic labors of Boniface undertaken with the utmost constancy from the year 716 to the year 755 [Note: [Col. 0676B] By spreading the word of God through Hesse, Eichsfeld, Saxony, Thuringia, Frisia and Gaul, as well as Bavaria, etc., and Swabia, etc.—Letters 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 60, etc.; by founding bishoprics and establishing churches—Letters 15 and 52, etc.; by dividing Bavaria into four parishes or bishoprics—Letter 46; by celebrating two synods each year—Letters 45 and 56, etc. God blessed these labors so abundantly that, according to Pope Gregory III, Boniface liberated as many as one hundred thousand souls in Germany from pagan power, etc. (Letter 46).], but also contain many doctrines of the Christian religion, as well as the customary ecclesiastical discipline of this age.

To avoid becoming too lengthy in this preface, we shall cite only a few examples [Note: [Col. 0676B] The oath of Boniface and Letters 73 and 163 speak generally of the Catholic faith; Letters 2 and 92 of the triune and one God; Letter 7 of the incarnate Word of God. The sacrament of baptism is discussed in Letters 2, 6, 7, 24, 72, and 82; and Letter 10 says: “The sacrament of holy baptism should be administered only at the feast of Easter and at Pentecost, except to those who, when danger of death presses, must be aided by such remedies lest they perish eternally.” The sacrament of confirmation is mentioned in Letter 46; its non-repetition in Letter 24; the Eucharist and the sacrifice of the Mass in Letters 26 and 28; the sacred mysteries are to be celebrated in a consecrated place in Letter 58; the holiness of the priesthood in Letter 145; Masses for the dead and communal suffrages are indicated in Letters 130, 144, 127, 3, 21, 25, 29, 93, 108, and 109. The power of the keys is repeatedly invoked in Boniface’s oath, and penances for crimes are listed in Letters 56 and 58. In this same letter it is said: “Let all priests request from the bishop the oil of the sick, keep it with them, and admonish the sick faithful to seek it, so that, after being anointed with that same oil by the priests, they may be healed, because the prayer of faith will save the sick.” Letter 10 teaches what the conferral of orders should be like. Letter 58 indicates ordinations in the four Ember seasons; Letter 75 concerns priests; Letter 168 concerns one promoted to the diaconate. [Col. 0676D] In Letters 50 and 56 Pope Zacharias complains that there was no distinction between laymen and priests, who are not permitted to fight. For what kind of victory is there when priests, who for one hour handle the Lord’s mysteries and offer Christ’s own body for the redemption of their souls, afterward kill Christians whom they ought to serve, or pagans to whom they ought to preach Christ, with their own sacrilegious hands? The tonsure on the heads of clerics is also mentioned in Letter 163. They plainly state in Letters 58, 72, 75, and 109 that legitimate marriage is indissoluble, except in the case of fornication or by the consent of both parties. [Col. 0677B] Letter 24 discusses the degrees of relationship within which marriage is forbidden. “While they acknowledge themselves to be related by affinity, they ought not to enter into such a marital union; but because moderation, especially among so barbarous a people, is more pleasing than strict severity, they may be permitted to marry after the fourth generation.” On the Lord’s Supper, Letter 56 states that the priest should always receive new chrism from the bishop of the parish; Letters 56 and 58 prescribe chrism and holy oil. Letter 75 concerns metropolitans; Letters 59 and 25 the use of the pallium; and Pope Zacharias says in Letter 60 that pallia should be given freely. Letter 73 explains the office of a bishop, and Letters 51 and 52 mention a coadjutor in the episcopate; Letter 58 concerns the obligation of priests to reside at their own churches. Letter 58 provides a list of feasts throughout the year. Letter 163 states that Easter is to be celebrated according to the standard of the Council of Nicaea. The cult of relics is mentioned in Letter 33 and in many others. The intercession of the saints in heaven occurs in Letter 117. The Mother of God, blessed Mary ever-virgin, appears in Letter 113. The sign of the cross occurs in Letter 82. Prayers to avert rain occur in Letter 107. Thanksgiving for the fertility of the year occurs in Letter 109. Prayers for one another occur in Letters 3, 12, and 16, and throughout the letters. The study of Sacred Scripture is strongly commended in Letters 4 and 156, as is the tradition of the holy Fathers in Letter 163, etc. [Col. 0678B] We omit many further matters that may be read in the letters themselves.] 

This brief survey recommends the present work of letters sufficiently and more than sufficiently, both for its usefulness and for its excellence. [Col. 0677A] Although their style is neither Ciceronian nor Plinian, and is even less suited to the polished flowers of this age, the language is nevertheless simple and familiar, in that age not inelegant, and in ours tolerable—except in a few verses or letters with which students or female students rejoiced in addressing their teachers in whatever way they could. A candid simplicity of heart and conduct shines everywhere; Christian virtue, charity, and modesty gleam throughout.

When Othlon undertook to write the *Life of Saint Boniface* at the request of the monks of Fulda, he judged Boniface’s letters extremely suitable for completing this work [Note: [Col. 0678B] Othlon, in the prologue: “Brothers of Fulda, I have endeavored to comply with your requests as far as the smallness of my knowledge permitted. You asked me to open up, with a clearer interpretation, the *Life of our holy Father Boniface*, which had long ago been published in a particularly elegant style, namely that of Saint Willibald, but which in certain places is so obscure to a weak understanding that it is difficult to see where the argument is leading . . . . . In the same place: ‘Perhaps that venerable man who first wrote the *Life of Saint Boniface*—he means Willibald—omitted many of his virtues and letters because he did not know them. But when I consider all the letters that you possess concerning him, nowhere does the authority of so great a prelate seem greater than in the letters written by him or addressed to him. There it is most plainly seen with what reverence he was first received by the Roman pontiff, how the pontiff ordained and sent him to preach to all the peoples of Germany, and with what labor he converted that same Germany to the faith of Christ,’ [Col. 0678C] etc. In the same place: ‘I said before, and say again, that among all the letters that you possess concerning Saint Boniface, his own letters seem to me the most important. Therefore, whatever I could find that was necessary for this work, I endeavored to gather together in one place . . . For this reason, brothers of Fulda, I earnestly ask and admonish you to read these letters with the greatest attention.’]

Othlon inserted approximately thirty letters into the *Life of Boniface*. Only in the previous century did Jacob Gretser find, in the library of the University of Ingolstadt, a copy of seventy-eight letters transcribed in the monastery of Sponheim by a novice monk, by order of Abbot Trithemius, in the year 1497.

Pistorius found another copy of 117 letters in the imperial library at Vienna. He was exceptionally renowned for his writings, disputations, and other literary labors. From both copies Nicolaus Serarius produced one, and in 1605 caused 151 letters to be printed at Mainz by the press of Balthasar Lippius. The same letters, together with Serarius’s notes, were included in volume XIII of the *Greatest Library of the Fathers*, from p. 70 to p. 160.

We have been more fortunate, since we obtained a parchment Codex preserved in the library of the metropolitan church of Mainz and venerable for its antiquity. Its characters, set at the front of this book, refer it to the ninth century. From it we have increased the number of letters, and have added historical-critical notes and variant readings of considerable importance. From another parchment manuscript Codex from Karlsruhe, we have also added several previously unpublished letters near the end of the work.

Friendly reader, use diligently this new labor, undertaken for the glory and benefit of sacred Germany, and remain perpetually well. Written from my study among the Vangiones, on the sixth day before the Ides of September, in the year 1787.

[Col. 0677]

# ANOTHER PREFACE OF WURDTWEIN

## THE LETTERS OF SAINT BONIFACE [Note: [Col. 0677D] Arranged, for the most part at least, in a more reliable chronological order. Serarius designated the letter that is first in our edition as number 33; he considered our second letter to be his number 118, and so on.]

[Note: [Col. 0677D] Formerly called Wynfrith. See Letter 1, which Bishop Daniel addressed to all Christians in order to commend Wynfrith to their charity. His homeland was the English town of Kirton, called Cridiadunum by Camden and Nicolaus Harpesfeldus, in the county of Devon. Mabillon, in his preliminary observations, § VI, p. 2, writes: “Boniface was born in western Saxony, specifically in the present county of Devon, in the town of Crediant, Crediton, or Kirton, once an episcopal see, about six miles from Exeter.” William Camden and John Speed assert this, on the basis of local tradition and living memory, in their description of Devon. Boniface himself, in Letter 1 to Zacharias, which begins, “We confess, Lord,” etc. (Letter 132 in Serarius), identifies his homeland when he says: “The synod and church in which I was born and raised—that is, in transmarine Saxony, the London synod,” etc.

In the Cologne Carthusian manuscript: “Blessed Boniface had his native soil on the island called Britain, which is now inhabited by the English people, who are thought to have derived their origin from the Saxons.”

Egilward, Book I *On Saint Burchard*, chapter 2: “Winfrid, a native of England.”

Wandelbert, June 5:

> On the Nones, Boniface shines as bishop,  
> Born among the English, who brought the children  
> Of Ocean to Christ,  
> Submitting the necks of the Frisians  
> To the pure washing.

Trithemius is therefore wrong to assert that Winfrid was Scottish by nationality, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 249 [Col. 0679B], and in Book II of *On the Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapter 34, as well as Book III, chapter 161. Nor was Marianus Scotus, before Trithemius, correct in Book II of his *Chronicle* under the years 715 and 741, and likewise in Book III under the year 743; nor was Thomas Dempster afterward correct in Book II of his *Scottish History*, chapter 130.]

## ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ AND MARTYR

[Col. 0677C]

Some say that Saint Boniface descended from a royal family [Col. 0677D], because in a certain document he is called a relative [Col. 0678C] of Saint Walburga, daughter of King Richard of England. Concerning that king, the following epitaph is read in the city of Lucca in Italy:

[Col. 0679A]

> Here lies King Richard, gracious bearer of the scepter.  
> He was king of the English; now he possesses the kingdom of heaven.  
> He abandoned his kingdom and relinquished all things for Christ.  
> Thus England gave us holy Richard.  
> He was the father of holy Walburga, the gracious virgin,  
> And likewise of Saint Willibald and Saint Winibald.  
> May the support of these grant us the kingdoms of heaven.  
> Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0679B] But the claim that Richard was the king and father of Willibald and Winibald has not yet been established as historical fact. See Gretser, Book I of the *Observations on the Commentary of Philip, Bishop of Eichstätt*, chapter 1; Sagittarius, chapter 1, § V, p. 121.

Nor is this proved by the verses once read in the church of the citadel of Mainz:

> Boniface, born of royal stock,  
> Voluntarily leaving Britain,  
> By the authority of the supreme pontiff, became  
> The apostle of Germany.

These verses require proof that they belong to a later age. Mabillon concludes briefly in his preliminary observations, § VII, p. 2:

> “There is no point in investigating through vain conjectures the parents of Boniface, whom the silence of the ancients has left unknown to us; indeed, it is neither proper nor appropriate. Those who attribute royal lineage to him and call him a relative of Saints Willibald and Wunibald rely on no legitimate evidence. The established fact is what the anonymous author of the *Life* reports: Boniface was born of noble ancestry and was related by kinship to the nun Leobgytha.”]

Our Winfrid, while not yet beyond his childhood years, entered a monastery [Note: [Col. 0679C] Othlon, *Life of Saint Boniface*, Book I, chapter 3: “The holy boy, already filled with divine virtue, the more earnestly his father tried to call him back to worldly affairs, the more steadfastly he persisted in his undertaking and longed to attain knowledge of the sacred writings. Thus, by a wonderful dispensation, it came about that his father, who alone was an obstacle, was seized by a sudden illness, laid aside his former stubbornness of mind, and sent the boy through suitable messengers to the monastery then known by the ancient name Adescancastre. He commended him to Wolfhard, the venerable abbot of that monastery. Wolfhard immediately received him kindly, as the monastic order required, entrusted him to the brothers, and the boy began well to undertake all the duties of religion that his age permitted, and fulfilled them better from day to day.”

Concerning the monastery of Adescancastre, Mabillon notes in the cited work, p. 6: “Adescancastre, or ‘at Esca fortress,’ which Edward Maihew, in his *Anglo-Benedictine Martyrology*, not wrongly interprets as Exeter, commonly called Excester, the principal city of Devon on the River Exe. It was called Adescancastrum, as though ‘the fortress on the Exe,’ although no monument reports that a monastery then existed at Exeter.”]

When Winfrid, devoted to unceasing meditation on Sacred Scripture, had for many years observed the whole discipline of regular life under the governance of the abbot mentioned above, and could not there be satisfied in sacred reading, both because of the magnitude of his desire and because of the scarcity of teachers, he arrived, with the consent of his abbot and brothers, at the monastery that is still called Nuiscelle, and chose as his teacher the abbot Winbert, of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0679D] The name of this abbot is written in various forms: Wynbrecht, Winbercht, Winbertus, Wimbertus, Wiribertus, and Wigbertus. But he is not the same man whose *Life* [Col. 0680B] was written by Lupus Servatus and who was abbot of Fritzlar.]

There, at last, having obtained the learning he desired in the grammatical arts, metrical subtlety, and spiritual understanding [Col. 0679B], he began to excel in these fields to such a degree that, when the fame of his knowledge spread everywhere, others too came to him to learn.

The greater his progress in the sciences, the more he considered himself lesser than others, and he anticipated everyone in humility and submission. Others, in turn, stirred by reports of his wisdom or instructed by his most salutary teaching, anticipated him in mutual honor. Thus, while everyone acclaimed him as a father and advanced him through the several degrees of ecclesiastical order, he was finally chosen for the dignity of the priestly office when he was thirty years old [Note: [Col. 0680B] This canonical regulation seems to have been in force in the monasteries of England at that time: no one was to be raised to the priesthood before his thirtieth year. The Venerable Bede writes in his *Epitome* about himself: “In the nineteenth year of my life I received the diaconate, and in the thirtieth year the rank of presbyter, both through the ministry of the most reverend Bishop John, by order of Abbot Ceolfrid.”] or somewhat older.

After receiving the dignity of the priesthood, the manner in which he conducted himself in the contrition [possibly: condition] of both kinds of man, so that he might become worthy to partake of the heavenly sacrament, is better gathered from the testimony of his works than from any judgment expressed in words.

Winfrid’s reputation for learning, piety, and wisdom grew day by day. Accordingly, he was chosen above others by the synod to be sent to the archbishop of Canterbury on an important matter of public business. Having successfully completed the mission, he returned and brought immense joy to everyone.

Burning meanwhile with an intense desire to preach the Gospel in foreign regions, he obtained only with great difficulty from his abbot permission to travel abroad. With some companions of like zeal he came from there to Lundenwic [Note: London. In the Willibaldine Life of St. Boniface it is read: “After traversing immense regions of the earth, rejoicing in the prosperous company of the brethren, he came to the place where there was a market for goods, and which to this day, in the ancient language of the English [and] Saxons, is called Lundenwich”; Scriverius calls it Ludenwick. He came to London, which Bede calls “the emporium of many arriving by land and sea.” Mabillon.] and from there to Dorstet [Note: Torstat in Ptolemy and Tacitus; Batavodurum. “This,” says Bertius, “is Wyckte Duerste in our language.” Concerning it Marcellinus writes in chapter 13: “The holy bishops Willebrord and Swibert, together with priests and clerics, traversing Holland and Frisia everywhere, instructed the unformed people in evangelical teachings, teaching them to abandon the profane worship of idolatry by abolishing it; they baptized catechumens, confirmed neophytes, celebrated the sacred orders, and preached the Gospel of peace constantly and devoutly in every village; and in each place they ordained priests and deacons to assist them in the word of faith and in the ministry of baptism, especially in the great settlement of Duerstat, where, preaching for two years, they brought the entire people to the faith of Christ. Changing the temples of idols into churches of Christ, they dedicated fifty-two parish churches there, with the assistance of Gunther the soldier and other friends.” Wicduerstede is a city of Frisia on the river Laca, commonly called the Locke. Mabillon. Dorstes, Scriverius.].

But since at that same time hostile discord had arisen between Charles, the illustrious prince and duke of the Franks [Note: He was called Martel by surname. He was the son of Pippin; and, so that he might be distinguished from the earlier Pippin called of Laon—of whose daughter Begga and Ansegisus, a prince and later bishop of Metz, he was born—he was called the younger and the second, as well as Crassus and Heristallus. He was the father of Carloman and Pippin.], and Ratbod, king of the Frisians [Note: Ratbod is called duke of the Frisians by Jonas in the Life of St. Wulfrannus; in Willibald, Othlonus, Alcuin, the Annals of Pithou, and elsewhere, he is called king. He waged many serious wars with the kings, dukes, or mayors of the palace of the Franks. For when Charles’s father, Pippin, had taken Lower Frisia from him and expelled him from Wiltaburg, now called Utrecht, and when Pippin himself had died in the year 714, Ratbod came as far as Cologne with a great and powerful army against his son Charles, inflicting heavy losses on him in a battle begun in March of the year 715, as the cited Annals testify.], peoples on both sides were thrown into confusion, and the greater part of the churches of Christ [Col. 0681A], which had previously been subject to Frankish rule in Frisia, under the pressure of Ratbod’s persecution was sorrowfully restored to the worship of idols [Note: These facts correct those who assign Boniface’s first journey into Frisia to the year 704: first, because Berwald, mentioned in chapter 4 of Othlonus’s Life of Boniface, was not yet abbot of Glastonbury in that year; and second, because Charles Martel had scarcely then passed beyond infancy [Col. 0681C], whereas he began war with Ratbod only in the year 716. Mabillon, on Willibald, chapter 4, page 8.]. Therefore the man of God Winfrid, having perceived the great mass of this perversity, departed from those regions for Treth [Note: Trecht, Trectis, formerly Trajectum and now Utrecht. Concerning it Bede writes in book V, chapter 12: “St. Willibrord was given by Pippin the site of an episcopal see in his renowned castle, which in the ancient language of those peoples is called Wiltaburg, that is, the town of the Wiltans, while in the Frankish language it is called Trajectum, or Trechtum.” Bertius says that among the ancient Batavians it means “market”; hence Halstrechtum, Moerendrechtum, Papendrechtum, Barendrechtum, and similar names.] and there addressed King Ratbod, urging him to desist from such great wickedness; but in vain. When, after prolonged investigation, he understood that he was laboring there fruitlessly by preaching, he left the fields barren of spiritual fertility and migrated back to his native land [Note: This was that grave and sorrowful period which, hostile to the peace of the Gospel, caused Winfrid to return to England with almost no fruit from his preaching, just as earlier St. Willfrid had returned to the same England from that sterile field without sheaves, having been unable to bend the mind of the same King Ratbod, around the year 677. Marcellinus says in the Swibertine Life, chapter 5: “The distinctive gift of the sanctity of the saints is this: when they see that, for a time, their labor is accomplishing nothing, without the spiritual greenness of growth, they migrate to other, more favorable places where labor bears fruit; for a place is inhabited in vain if the fruit of holiness is absent.” [Col. 0682C] Alcuin likewise writes of St. Willibrord: “When the man of God perceived that he could not bear fruit among Ratbod’s people, he turned his evangelizing journey toward the fiercest peoples of the Danes. At that time, it is said, Ongendus ruled there, a man more savage than every wild beast and harder than every stone; nevertheless, at God’s command, he treated the herald of truth honorably. When Willibrord encountered him hardened in character, devoted to idolatry, and without any hope of a better life, he took thirty boys from that country, to instruct them in the Christian faith, and hastened to return to the chosen people of the Frankish kingdom.” Since, therefore, permission to preach the word of God was denied our Winfrid, and he could accomplish nothing good in Frisia, he returned to England before autumn had ended and withdrew into his monastery at Nutschall.].

Thus the year 716 is the first year of Winfrid’s mission, as the author of the Würzburg Chronicle correctly noted, published by Baluzius in book I of the *Miscellanea*; but there the first journey to Frisia is confused with the mission later entrusted to him by Gregory II. The same must be said of Peter the Librarian in Duchesne, volume III, page 540.

Boniface himself, in letter number 135 according to Serarius’s arrangement, addressed to Pope Zachary in the year 745 and quoted there by Baronius as number 24, says: “After I had bound myself, nearly thirty years ago, by a vow, with the consent and command of Gregory, the apostolic bishop of venerable memory, the earlier Gregory [that is, Gregory II], to the familiarity and service of the Apostolic See, I was accustomed to report to the apostolic pontiff whatever joy or sorrow befell me.” From that year to 745, however, thirty incomplete years had elapsed. Moreover, the cited Willibald testifies that this holy apostle of Germany was crowned with martyrdom in the year 755 [Col. 0682A], after the fortieth year of his pilgrimage had been completed. Othlonus says: “He suffered in the fortieth year of his pilgrimage.” Therefore this date is certain and beyond doubt, and that pilgrimage consequently began in this year. Serarius, who accurately connected Boniface’s return to England with this year, and who inferred from Willibald’s words that Boniface spent two winters in England after returning from Frisia, from which he had set out in autumn, and that at the beginning of the third he proceeded to Rome—that is, in the year 718—also observed that he then remained a full two years in his native land.

Meanwhile it happened that the father of his monastery, having laid aside the prison of the flesh, ended his present life. The brethren were exceedingly saddened by his death; but the blessed man, by spiritual conversations, comforted them and thoroughly instructed them to preserve the rule of regular life and to choose some spiritual father. They all earnestly begged that holy man, who at that time was called Winfrid, to deign to undertake pastoral care over them [Col. 0682B]. But he cherished higher purposes in his heart; he did not accept their pleas, and disclosed to the brethren his intention of travelling for the love of Christ and for the salvation of his neighbor. At last, having received permission, he went to Bishop Daniel and asked him to grant him the benefit of his blessing and letters of recommendation as he prepared to travel to Rome. The bishop gladly consented and dismissed the servant of God, who was about to undertake a long journey abroad, to his desired destination with letters from himself.

[Col. 0681]

## PREFATORY NOTE BY DR. J. A. GILES

[Col. 0681D] Because of the rarity of the manuscripts of the letters of St. Boniface, I confess that at first I entirely despaired of correcting the text. At last I obtained a single book, indeed of a later period, preserved in the Royal Library at Paris under number 3859 A; by using it to correct the text of the sixty letters contained in that codex, I achieved at least something. What those letters are, the reader will easily see by consulting the table of letters that follows. We have retained almost all of Würdtwein’s notes, as well as the observations he repeatedly inserted concerning the life and deeds of St. Boniface among the letters.

We have also included the letter of Cuthbert the abbot, which he sent to Cuthwin concerning Bede’s death: this was done so that all the letters circulated under the name of that abbot might be gathered together. In all of them the glorious Bede is equally discussed. Likewise, the letters written by the blessed Aldhelm or to Aldhelm by others, which we recently published among the works of Aldhelm [Oxford, octavo, 1844], do not appear here.

## ALPHABETICAL ORDER OF THE LETTERS OF ST. BONIFACE

A indicates the order of this edition. B indicates the order of Würdtwein’s edition. C indicates the order of Serrarius’s edition. D indicates the order of the Paris manuscript.

Those letters marked with an asterisk under the letter A we have not thought it necessary to repeat here, since they have been published above among the works of Aldhelm.

[Col. 0685]

## NEW ORDER OF THE LETTERS OF ST. BONIFACE, COMPARED WITH THE ORDERS PREVIOUSLY PUBLISHED

[Col. 0687]

## I. LETTERS

[Note: This seems to be the letter that Boniface, setting out from England for Rome, received from his bishop, in order to secure the favor of those to whom he was going. It therefore appears rightly assignable to the year 718. Würdtwein.]

### LETTER I. DANIEL TO ALL THE KINGS, ETC. [A.D. 718]

To the most devout and merciful kings, to all the most reverend and beloved dukes and bishops, to the religious, and also to abbots, priests, and spiritual sons marked with the name of Christ: Daniel, servant of the servants of God.

Although all the faithful are bound to observe God’s commandments with the utmost sincere devotion, the sacred Scriptures demonstrate how great is the duty of hospitality and how acceptable to God is the service of humanity shown to travellers. Blessed Abraham, because of his merciful hospitality, was permitted to receive the presence of the holy angels and to enjoy their revered conversation. Lot likewise was rescued from the flames of Sodom through this mystery of piety. The grace of hospitality saved him from destruction by fire while he obeyed the heavenly commands. So too it will bring salvation to your affection, when, receiving this religious priest and servant of almighty God, Winfrid, who bears these letters, you show him the charity that God both loves and commands.

Therefore, when you receive the servants of God, you receive the One whose majesty all things serve, since he promises: “Whoever receives you receives me.” By doing these things with devotion of heart, you both fulfill God’s commandments and, trusting in the oracle of the divine promise, will possess an eternal reward with him. May heavenly grace preserve your illustrious dignity unharmed.

[Note: By this letter Gregory II appointed Boniface apostle of the Germans. The year in which he did this is indicated by the second indiction, which corresponds to the year of Christ 719. Giles.]

### LETTER II. GREGORY TO BONIFACE [A.D. 719]

[Note: Gregory. In these letters of St. Boniface there are chiefly five pontiffs to or from whom the letters are addressed. The first is Gregory II, and the letters concerning him run from this letter 118 through 127. The second is Gregory III, from letter 127 through 131. The third is Zachary, from 131 through 145. The fourth is Stephen III, concerning whom see above, letters 91 and 97. The fifth is Leo III, above, letter 75.

Gregory II began to hold the Apostolic See, as Baronius reports in volume II, in the year of our Lord 714. His immediate successor was Gregory III, in 731; his immediate successor was Zachary, in 742; Zachary’s almost immediate successor was Stephen III, in 752—for Stephen II, who was absolutely immediate, was pope for only four days. Paul I succeeded him in 757; Stephen IV succeeded Paul in 768; Adrian succeeded Stephen in 772; and finally Leo III succeeded Adrian in 796.

This chronological notation will be useful to anyone examining the dates of the letters themselves, and sometimes even their authors, as will be evident below concerning Gregory II and Gregory III. Baronius attributes letter 122 to Gregory III, while others attribute it to Gregory II. The order of these letters in the pontifical letters in volume II of the Councils is also different from the order here: letter 119 is there number 4; 120 is 5; 121 is 8; 122 is 2; 124 is 3; and 125 is 7. Serrarius.]

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to Boniface, religious priest.

The intention of your religious purpose, which has been revealed to us and burns piously in Christ, and the report brought forward concerning your most sincere faith, which has been approved, require us to employ you as a fellow minister in the administration of the word of God, whose care we bear by God’s grace.

Having learned, therefore, that from childhood you have studied the sacred Scriptures, and that you have extended the natural gifts of your progress toward the increase of the talent entrusted to you from heaven, under the guidance of divine fear [Paris: love], namely, that you have devoted the grace of your knowledge of the heavenly oracle to the labor of saving preaching, applying yourself earnestly to making the mystery of faith known to unbelieving nations [Col. 0690A], we rejoice in your faith and desire to become helpers of the grace bestowed upon you.

Since, therefore, by the modest provision of the Apostolic See you have brought these efforts and this pious intention to their proper conclusion—like a member of its own body seeking the head, proving the movement of your mind and humbly submitting yourself to the judgment of the head, hastening by its direction along the right path so that you may be strengthened and become the fullness of the bodily structure—we therefore, in the name of the indivisible Trinity, by the unshaken authority of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, whose teaching office we exercise and whose sacred see we administer, establish the modesty of your religious vocation.

We command that, wherever, with God’s assent, you are able to go among whatever peoples are held in the error of unbelief, you strive in the word of God with that saving fire which the Lord came to cast upon the earth. By making known the ministry of the kingdom of God, through the proclamation of the name of Christ our Lord and God and through persuasion of the truth, and by preaching in the spirit of power, love, and self-control, you are to pour the teaching of both Testaments into unlearned minds with harmonious reasoning.

Finally, we wish you to attend to the discipline of the sacrament that you should endeavor to maintain for those who are about to be initiated and who will beforehand believe in God, according to the formula of the offices of your holy [read: our] Apostolic See, which has been set forth in advance for your instruction. Whatever you perceive to be lacking for the work you have undertaken, you shall take care to report to us as soon as you are able.

Farewell. Given on the Ides of May, in the third year of the reign of our most devout Lord Augustus Leo, crowned by God, great emperor, in the second indiction.

[Note: With these letters and a large collection of relics, Boniface, returning with his servants from among the Lombards, approached King Liutprand. He was honorably received by him; after recovering his strength there, he set out, crossed the lofty and precipitous ridges of the Alps, traversed the unknown regions of the Bavarians and the neighboring boundaries of Germany, and arrived in Thuringia according to the command given him by the apostolic pontiff. Addressing senators and the leading men of the people in spiritual words, he recalled them to the true path of knowledge and the light of understanding. He also admonished priests devoted to various crimes with evangelical speeches and corrected them according to the norm of canonical discipline.

Meanwhile, hearing of the death of Ratbod, king of the Frisians, he sailed to Frisia, sowed the seeds of heavenly doctrine, and, once the famine of the word of God had been dispelled, nourished a people infected with pagan superstition with the food of eternal preaching, withdrawing a very large part of them from the error of idolatry. At that same time Willibrord, bishop of the Church of Trajectum, exercised the office of preaching in Frisia. Boniface rejoiced in and adhered to his efforts in every way, laboring with him for three continuous years both in destroying temples and in building churches of the true God and in all divine affairs. Würdtwein.]

[Note: By this letter Bugga, who is Eadburga, follows Boniface to the Frisians, whose king Rathbod died in the year of our Lord 719.]

### LETTER III. BUGGA TO BONIFACE [CIRCA A.D. 720]

[Note: The annalists Nazarius, Petavianus, and Tilianus report that Radbod died in this year, 719, in which the Franks fought at Soissons. St. Ermin, abbot and bishop of Laubach, foretold his death. For in the Life written by Anso, abbot of the same monastery, we read:

“When the wickedness of the aforesaid man Radbod had reached its fullness, he began to gather crowds of pagans and a very large army, desiring to invade the territory of the Franks and take vengeance upon them. When the Franks heard this, they feared him greatly, remembering that formerly they had been severely wounded by him and had turned their backs. Then the Lord took pity on his servants and did not permit him to enter the kingdom of the Franks, but struck him, and he died.

It happened that on that very day St. Ermin was riding from his monastery to a village called Fleon. At about the ninth hour of the day, he checked his horse’s pace slightly and said to the companions around him: ‘Truly I tell you that just now an earthly and lofty greatness has fallen.’”

Anso adds that Radbod died at the very moment when this had been revealed to St. Ermin. Othlonus, together with Willibald, asserts in book I, chapter 11, that St. Boniface remained in Frisia for three years. This is confirmed by the pontificate of Pope Gregory II, by whom Boniface was ordained bishop in the year 723—that is, after four years from the time when he had been sent into Germany. These facts correct those who have stated that Boniface remained in Frisia for thirteen years. Würdtwein.]

To Boniface, venerable servant of God and endowed with the adornment of many spiritual gifts, or Winfrid, most worthy priest of God: Bugga, a vine of native stock, sends perpetual charity and health.

Let your holiness know that I never cease to give thanks to almighty God because, as I learned from the inscription of your blessedness, he has granted you his mercy in many ways and has guided you most piously as you passed through unknown districts.

First, he inclined the pontiff of the glorious see to favor the desire of your mind; afterward he struck down before you Rathbod, the enemy of the Catholic Church; then, through a dream, he revealed himself to you, showing that you were clearly destined to reap God’s harvest and gather sheaves of holy souls into the granary of the heavenly King.

For this reason I confess all the more that no change in temporal circumstances can bend the condition of my mind away from the guardianship of the charity I have pledged you. Rather, the force of love grows hotter within me as I know for certain that, through the support of your prayers, you have reached some harbor of rest.

Therefore I humbly urge you again to deign to offer to the Lord the earnestness of your intercessions for my smallness, so that by his grace he may keep me safe under your protection.

Let your charity also know that I have not yet been able to obtain the passions of the martyrs which you asked me to send you. But whenever I am able, I shall do so. And you, dearest to me, send to my lowliness, for my consolation, what you promised in your sweetest letters—that is, some collections of the sacred Scriptures.

Likewise I ask you to deign to offer the oblations of the holy Masses for the soul of a relative of mine, who was dearer to me than all others and whose name was N. Through the same bearer I now send you fifty solidi and an altar-cloth, since I was entirely unable to obtain larger gifts. Yet these have been sent with the greatest charity, although they are small in appearance.

Farewell in this world, holy one, and in unfeigned charity.

### LETTER IV

[Note: I now come to a second kind of brief annotation, those belonging specifically to individual letters of various sorts. In the first of these, the first thing to note is that scarcely anywhere has the typographer erred so often, or deviated so frequently from the Imperial manuscript, as here. The reason is that, since this letter is manuscript Ingolstadt 39, he had a copy of it before his eyes.

Everything should therefore be corrected according to the Imperial exemplar as follows: first, the words “Winfredus to Nithard” should be removed, since they are sufficiently expressed in the words that follow; second, one should write: *quem mihi non temp.*; third, *adulantium* should be written instead of *adolantium*; fourth, *immarcessibilis*; fifth, *the chain of charity, V., to Nithard*; sixth, *Wynfrethus*, and this last form should also be observed thereafter.

A second point should be noted. In this letter and in several others, especially the first four, a certain very recent copyist—whom I sometimes call in the margin “the Anonymous”—has supplied either little strokes or dots under certain words, while in some places he has added a conjecture. Thus, in this title, he seems to have found written *facetiae urbanitas*; he himself corrected it to *facetae*, while the Ingolstadt manuscript has *faceta*.

This latter reading is not bad, whether *blandimenta faceta* (“witty flatteries”), *mellita faceta* (“honeyed wit”), or *urbanitas per mellitatem faceta* (“courtesy made witty by sweetness”) is understood. Nevertheless, the first reading seems preferable, so that the phrase may mean “honeyed wit of courtesy,” or at least “courtesy made honeyed and witty through the blandishments of flattering words.”

Just as, for *feriae*, which is plural only in Latin, the Church says *feria prima*, *feria secunda*, and so forth, as Venerable Bede notes in the book *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 6, so here *facētia* is used in place of *facētiae*. And just as the ancients derived from honey the words *mellillum* and *mellina*, and likewise the verb *mellare*, from which Pliny, book XI, chapters 15 and 16, gives *mellatio*, so St. Boniface here uses either *mellitas* or the verb *mellitare*, from which come *mellitatus*, *mellitata*, and *mellitatum*.

But a third matter deserves still greater attention: the reason that true friendship arose between St. Boniface and Nithard; and fourth, how the same saint was formerly called Wynfrethus or Winfridus and later Boniface. This change is discussed at length in book III of the Mainz edition, note 16, page 466. There was another Winfrid, of whom Bede speaks in book IV of the *History*, chapters 3 and 5. Henceforth something will be noted whenever the wording requires it. Serrarius.]

Winfrid. In the year 722 Clement, bishop of Trajectum, already weighed down by extreme old age, begged Boniface to undertake the rank of episcopal governance and rule the people entrusted to him. But Boniface replied that he was in no way worthy of the episcopal office, and insisted with every prayer that so great a dignity should not be imposed upon him while he was still in the years of youth. He added that he had been sent into Germany by Pope Gregory to preach the Gospel to unbelievers.

Therefore he departed from Frisia and arrived—after staying in a small palace below Trier, from which he took Gregory with him—at a place called Amöneburg. There he gathered a considerable community of brethren and built a monastery. He then entered the lands of the Chatti, who border upon the Saxons, turned them away from the worship of idols, and immersed them in sacred baptism.

He reported these most salutary advances of the Catholic faith to Pope Gregory by letter, sending to him a certain faithful man named Binna, who brought back letters from the apostolic prelate summoning Boniface to Rome. Boniface, striving toward the highest degree of obedience, soon set out for Italy surrounded by a band of brethren. When he caught sight of the walls of the city of Rome, he gave thanks to God and commended himself to the patronage of the blessed apostles.

The Roman pontiff immediately invited him to his presence and, after greeting him with familiar words, assigned him an honorable hospice. On the appointed day they met in the church of St. Peter and held discussions concerning the Creed and the tradition of the Catholic faith [Col. 0693A], which were afterward committed to writing.

When Boniface had satisfied the pontiff in everything, it was announced to him that he was to be honored with the episcopal rank, so that he might correct any who were wandering and convert them to the way of truth with greater firmness, being supported by the greater authority of episcopal dignity, and so that he might be more acceptable to all in the office of preaching, insofar as it would be more evident that he had been ordained for this purpose by an apostolic prelate.

The man of God carefully weighed all these matters and did not refuse the grace of so great a blessing. When the day of his ordination arrived, which was the day before the Kalends of December, on the feast of St. Andrew the apostle, Gregory required and received from him an oath—so that he might bind him more strictly to show obedience to himself and his successors and to observe the whole tradition of the sacred faith—which is found written in the ancient copies as follows [Col. 0693B]: “See below.”

After he had given this oath to Pope Gregory in the prescribed form, Gregory in turn labored in every way to assist, advance, and honor him. He gave him as a gift a little book containing the most sacred laws of ecclesiastical discipline, arranged in pontifical assemblies, and commanded that both clergy and people subject to his rule should be instructed in those regulations. By granting a privilege, he confirmed perpetually the familiarity of the Apostolic See both to Boniface and to all those subject to him.

He also gave him letters, commending him for protection not only to Charles, the illustrious duke who at that time governed the kingdom of the Franks, but also to all the ecclesiastical men and princes of Germany.

All these matters were completed with astonishing speed on the day after his ordination—a rare occurrence in a city where, from every church, rains of business continually drip, or rather, descending in dense torrents, carry a flood with them. Yet because these matters concerning the conversion of the nations were to be preferred to all others, Pope Gregory wished everything to be settled first. Würdtwein.]

[Col. 0693B]

### WINFRID TO NITHARD [CIRCA A.D. 720]

To my dearest companion and most beloved friend, whom neither the fleeting gift of temporal gold nor the witty courtesy of honeyed flatteries won over to me, but whom the celebrated kinship of spiritual necessity has recently joined to me with an unfading chain of charity: Winfrid, your suppliant in Christ Jesus, sends perpetual health.

[Col. 0693A] With the humble writings of my mediocrity, I pray, dearest brother, that you may not be reluctant to recall the sayings of the most wise [Col. 0694A] Solomon.

[Note: [Col. 0693C] Solomon. There is a dissertation concerning the author and authority of the book from which these words are drawn. For among the Latins this book is sometimes called, without an author’s name, Ecclesiasticus; among the Greeks, πανάρετος (*panaretos*, “all-virtuous”); by Origen, in his *Treatise 24 on Matthew*; by Pope Zachary below, in Letter 140; and in the Ritual books of the Mass simply Wisdom—as when one reads “Behold the great priest,” or at the beginning of Saturday, or on certain virgins’ feasts, “I confess,” and at the feast of Saint John the Evangelist. At other times an author is cited, and indeed:

1. Jesus. Thus explicitly in the prologue of the book, as found in the Greek and corrected Roman Latin versions.

2. Sirach. Thus in the Greek title of the same book, σοφία Σειράχ (“the Wisdom of Sirach”); and in Procopius of Gaza, preface to Genesis; Hilary, on Psalm 144.

3. Jesus son of Sirach. Thus in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book VIII, chapter 2; Antiochus, Homily 84; Damascene, *On the Faith*, book IV, chapter 18; Saint Jerome, on Daniel IX and in Letter 115, where he says that he saw this Hebrew book entitled “The Proverbs of Jesus son of Sirach.” The same is also handed down in chapter 50, verse 29, of that book.

4. Jesus, grandfather of Sirach, and his son Sirach, and this man’s son and that man’s grandson, another Jesus. Thus a certain Greek prologue in the Complutensian Edition.

5. Solomon. Thus our Saint Boniface in this passage and again below, in Letter 105. The same author was also named by Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book V, chapter 5; Origen, Homily 8 on Numbers and Homily 1 on Ezekiel; Saint Athanasius, in his *Apology for His Flight*; Saint Basil, in the *Longer Rules*, response 17; Saint Chrysostom, Homily 51 on Matthew; Pope Fabian, Letter 2; Saint Cyprian, Letter 65, *Exhortation to Martyrs*, chapter 9, and *To Quirinus*, book III, chapter 20; Marcellinus, Letter to Bishop Solomon; Saint Hilary, on Psalm 144; Saint Ambrose, *On Duties*, book I, final chapter, and *To a Consecrated Virgin*, chapter 2; Optatus of Milevis, book III; Saint Damasus, Letter 6; Saint Jerome, on Ecclesiastes IX and Psalm 73; [Col. 0694A] Innocent I, Letter to Exuperius; Saint Paulinus, *Birthday Poem 10 of Saint Felix*; Maximus of Turin, Homily 2 on Easter; Saint Leo, Sermon 5 on Lent, chapter 3; Sedulius, on Romans XII; Saint Gregory, Homily 1 on Ezekiel, *Books of Kings*, chapter II, book IV, Letter 82; Chromatius, on Matthew V and VI; Cassiodorus, on Psalm 55; Pelagius I, Letter to Vigilius; Laurence of Novara, Homily on Almsgiving; John, Letter 2 to Valerius; Eligius, Homily 8; Haymo, on Romans I; Paschasius, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, chapter 2; Saint Bernard, Letters 5 and 190.

But in truth:

1. The true author is Jesus son of Sirach—not Sirach, and not Solomon—because all Scripture asserts this, as was cited earlier from chapter 50 of his book.

2. This Jesus wrote the book in Hebrew, and afterward his grandson translated it into Greek. The cited Greek and Latin preface asserts this, and Saint Jerome, in Letter 115, testifies that he saw a Hebrew copy. Münster, drawing from the Innovators, reports that it still exists among the Jews of Constantinople.

3. That Jesus had a son named Sirach, and that this man’s son and interpreter was also named Jesus, is stated by the cited Complutensian prologue, Saint Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*, Saint Damascene in the cited passage, and most others.

4. Jesus the grandfather is also said to have had a father named Sirach, and for that reason the Innovator Cornelius Bertram, in the book entitled *Franckenthal Lucubrations*, says that he was the Ben-Sira whose Proverbs, with scholia, exist among the Hebrews, since Ben-Sira is virtually “son of Sirach.”

The first part is true, from the same cited passage, chapter 50, and from all those who call the author Jesus son of Sirach, since his grandson was not the author but merely the translator, as has been said.

The second part, however, appears false: first, because *Ben-Sira* in Hebrew has a different ending; second, because the common opinion of the Hebrews is that Ben-Sira lived in the generation after Jeremiah. But Jesus, the author of Ecclesiasticus, lived after Onias the high priest, in the time of his son Simeon the Just, about whom chapter 50 speaks. Third, the same Hebrews say that Ben-Sira had a son named Uzziel and a grandson named Joseph—not Sirach and Jesus. Since both were renowned for wisdom, both are cited by the Hebrew scholar of Ben-Sira’s Proverbs. Fourth, that book of Ben-Sira’s Proverbs was either the same as our Ecclesiasticus or a different book. If it was the same, then either our Ecclesiasticus is incomplete, because certain things are missing from it, or it contains additions, since it has many things that are not there. If it was different, how is it credible that the same author wrote different books about nearly the same subjects, in nearly the same manner and style, without ever indicating elsewhere that he had said one and the same thing? Fifth, this Innovator is opposed by another Innovator, Drusius, in his preface to Ben-Sira.

5. When the Greeks call it “the Wisdom of Sirach,” this is said for the sake of brevity, instead of “the Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach.” Brevity is likewise intended when it is called simply “Wisdom.”

6. When authors designate Solomon as the author, Bellarmine thinks, in *On the Word of God*, chapter 14, that this should be understood as meaning that he collected Solomon’s sayings and reduced them to a single volume—or, more briefly and more correctly, that this attribution was made because of the similarity of wisdom, teaching, and proverbial style.
