Saint Augustine says this explicitly, *City of God*, book XVII, chapter 20:

> “Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus, because of a certain similarity of expression, have acquired the custom of being called Solomon’s, although the more learned do not doubt that they are not his.”

And in *On Christian Doctrine*, book II, chapter 8:

> “Those two books, one entitled Wisdom and the other Ecclesiasticus, are said, because of a certain similarity, to be Solomon’s. For it is most consistently reported that Jesus son of Sirach wrote them.”

Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book V, chapter 3:

> “Ecclesiasticus, because of the great similarity of its meaning and equality of expression, is prefaced with Solomon’s name.”

The Athanasian Synopsis likewise signifies this, as does the cited Complutensian prologue when it says:

> Ὀπαδὸς τοῦ Σολομῶντος οὗτος ὁ Ἰησοῦς γέγονεν, καὶ οὐδὲν ἧττον ἐκείνου περὶ τὴν σοφίαν, παιδείαν εὐδοκιμήσας, πολυμαθὴς ἀληθῶς καὶ ὢν καὶ καλούμενος.

> “This Jesus became a follower of Solomon and, having excelled no less than he in wisdom and education, was truly both learned in many things and so called.”

Enough concerning the author. As for its authority, which is canonical, Saint Augustine treats it in the cited book *On Christian Doctrine*; Bellarmine does so in the same cited passage; and more fully Jodocus Coccius, *Catholic Treasury*, book VI, article 17. SER.]

who says: [Note: [Col. 0694D] “May he be ashamed.” This is found in the same I manuscript. For C reads with the dative, “may it shame you to remember,” and in the same way below, Letter 142, p. 220. It means “may it not be burdensome to you,” just as *tibi liquet* means “it is clear to you,” literally “it is liquid for you.” Otherwise grammarians reject this construction, and Saint Augustine says of the grammatical forms *taedet* and *piget*: “*Taedet* signifies weariness, just as *piget* signifies, as it were, reluctance. For when we say *piget me fecisse*, that is, ‘I am reluctant to have done it,’ we mean, ‘My spirit does not arise to approve what I did.’ These verbs are all declined in this way: *pudet me*, *piget me*, and so forth, except *libet* and *licet*, *patet* and *liquet*. For with these we join the dative case.” SER.] of him who says: [Note: [Col. 0694D] “In all things.” The same saying is cited again later, Letter 45. SER.]

> “In all your works remember your last end, and you will never sin.”

And elsewhere:

> “Walk while you have the light of life, lest the darkness of death overtake you.”

For all things that are now present will quickly pass away, and those that will remain forever will soon arrive. All the precious things of this world—whether the beauty of gold and silver, the varied brilliance of gems, the rich variety of luxurious foods, or the acquired diversity of elegant clothing, a most similar collection [P.: “comparison”] of things—pass away like a shadow, collapse like smoke, and wither like foam, according to the truthful saying of the Psalmist:

> “Man is like grass; his days are like the flower of the field; so he will flourish.” [Note: [Col. 0695D] *Floriet*, “he will flourish.” Just as formerly there were many verbs of different declensions, so also *florere* and *florire* were used. The latter has been retained, with slight alteration, in Italian and French, which are, as it were, shoots and branches of Latin. Thus one finds *fervit, lavit, sonit, fulgit, obedibo, operibo, parilit, pervenibunt, dicebo*, instead of *fervet, lavat, sonat, fulget, obediam, operiam, pariet, pervenient, dicam* (see Nonius); and *exiet* and *transiet* are very common instead of *exibit* and *transibit*. Tibullus: “But if you are slow, age will pass away.” SER.]

And elsewhere:

> “My days have declined like a shadow, and I have withered like grass.”

For this reason all the gold-seekers [Note: [Col. 0695D] *Ambrones.* Festus says that the Ambrones were a Gallic people who, after losing their settlements through a sudden inundation of the sea, began to support themselves and their families by robbery and plunder. Gaius Marius destroyed them together with the Cimbri and Teutons. From this it came about that men of disgraceful life were called “Ambrones.” Scaliger appears to deny the first part of the story, following Strabo, book I and especially book VII. But Strabo denies only that they departed because of the daily and regular tides of the sea, not because of some sudden and unusual inundation, as Festus says. Isidore, on the contrary, writes in *Etymologies*, book X, chapter 2: “Historians relate of the Umbri that they survived a time of watery disaster and rains, and for this reason were called in Greek *ombrios*.” The remainder of the history is followed by Plutarch, *Marius*; Livy, books LXVII–LXVIII; and Florus, book III, chapter 3. In Isidore’s glossary, *ambro* means “devourer, squanderer of inheritances, bankrupt, luxurious, extravagant,” and this precisely explains the present passage and the one occurring below, Letter 65: “with Ambronian jaws.” See also *Adages*, “Ambrones.” SER.—On the Ambrones, see the note to Letter 9. EDIT.]

—the Ambrones [Note: [Col. 0696C] *Apolo.* This is how these words are written in Caesar’s Latin manuscripts; but what are they meant to signify? Perhaps, by allusion to the preceding account of the inundation, one should read ἀπὸ τῶν κυμάτων, “deprived of or afflicted by the waves,” with *agris*—“fields,” not *agiis*, as it was corruptly printed. SER.] *apoto grammaton agiis frustratis afflicti* [corrupt and uncertain; the note proposes “afflicted by the waves, their fields ruined”]—are known to serve on watch, and to have stretched out, in vain, the fragile webs of spiders, catching only a light breath or dust; because, according to the Psalmist, [Note: [Col. 0696C] *κατά.* This too is written in Latin in C; but at that time they liked to speak half in Greek, using it for “according to the Psalmist,” and likewise elsewhere. SER.]

> “They hoard up, and do not know for whom they gather it.”

And while the exactor whom no one can escape, namely death, snarls cruelly with bloodstained teeth at the threshold, then, trembling and deprived of every divine support, they suddenly lose and perish together with their precious soul and their deceptive wealth, which the avaricious had diligently served day and night. Thereafter, seized by diabolical hands, they enter the most dreadful gates [Col. 0696A] of Erebia, where they will suffer eternal punishments. [Note: [Col. 0696C] *Herebia.* C has *erebia*. Among the Hebrews this word occurs in Genesis I, 5; Exodus XVIII, 13; Psalm 59, 7; and Psalm 104, 9. Elsewhere it signifies evening and may be written either *hereb* or *ereb*, as I recently said in *Trihaeresy*, book III, chapter 3, and *Minerval*, book III. For this reason one may write *herebus* or *erebus*, since the latter derives from the former, as Scaliger teaches in his note on Festus, p. LIX. SER.]

Since all these things are so, without any risk of falsehood, I strive to implore you, earnestly entreating you with prayers interwoven with charity, that, having truthfully considered all these matters, you hasten to revive the grace of your natural talent which is in you, together with your knowledge of the liberal arts; and that you do not spiritually extinguish the burning fire of divine understanding with the watery mud and damp dust of earthly desire. Rather, remembering the Psalmist, who speaks concerning the blessed man:

> “His delight is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he meditates day and night.”

And elsewhere:

> “How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all the day.”

And Moses in Deuteronomy: [Note: [Col. 0696D] “In Deuteronomy.” The sense is indeed found in Deuteronomy, chapter VI, but the wording is more closely found in Joshua, chapter 1. Hence it appears that Saint Boniface was accustomed to cite Holy Scripture from memory. SER.]

> “Let not the book of the law depart from your mouth; and you shall meditate on it all days and nights.”

[Col. 0696B] [Note: [Col. 0696D] In many places, even where the meaning is sufficiently clear, the grammatical construction is entirely defective. To correct it without newly produced manuscript codices would be exceedingly rash. GILES.]

After removing all further obstacles arising from matters that will be of no benefit, strive to pursue the study of the sacred writings with concentrated attention, and thereby acquire the loveliness of glorious and true beauty—that is, divine wisdom, which is more splendid than gold, more beautiful than silver, more fiery than the carbuncle, whiter than crystal, and more precious than topaz. According to the declaration of the eloquent preacher, [Note: [Col. 0696D] “Preacher.” He is called *Ecclesiastes* by the usual Greek name. SER.] no precious thing is worthy of it.

For what is more fittingly sought from the young, Christian brother, or what at last is possessed more soberly by the old [Note: [Col. 0696D] “More soberly.” Instead of *more soberly*. Venerable Bede, *On Orthography*, p. 94: “*Sobrius* accepts neither a comparative nor a superlative; instead of these we say *magis sobrius* and *maxime sobrius*.” But this usage occurs, as in Lucretius, book IV, with *egregius* meaning “more excellent”:

> “Nothing is more excellent than to distinguish clear things from doubtful.”

And in Ulpian, *exiguius*; in Peter Damian, Letter to Gislerius, *idoneior*; and in volume XI of Baronius, Briss. *l. sing.* SER.] than the knowledge of the sacred Scriptures? For, guiding the ship of our soul without any shipwreck amid the dangers of the storm, it brings it to the shore of the most delightful paradise and to the everlasting joys of the angels above. Concerning these the wise man mentioned above said:

> “Wisdom prevails over wickedness. She reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly. I loved her and sought her from my youth, and I became a seeker of her beauty.” [Note: [Col. 0697D] “Seeker.” Our Vulgate version has *lover*, but read *contubernium*, not *contuberniam*. SER.]

She glorifies nobility by possessing fellowship with God; indeed, the Lord of all loved her. For she is the teacher of God’s discipline.

Therefore, if the almighty Lord wills that I should at some time return to these regions, as I intend, I promise that along the way I shall prove to you a faithful friend in all these matters, [Col. 0697B] and [Note: [Col. 0697D] “In the study of the divine Scriptures.” See how devoted Saint Boniface was to this study, and how ardently he desired both to learn the sacred Scriptures more and more and to teach others what he had learned in them. Compare this letter with Saint Augustine’s Letter 41 to Licentius; Gregory the Great’s Letter 40, book IV; Letter 26, book VI; and Letter 25, book XII, where he writes: “I sought those who would join you in the fellowship of sacred reading, and I found no one, and I deeply lamented the poverty of goodness. And although I am a very secret sinner, nevertheless, if you wish to come to the threshold of blessed Peter the Apostle, you will be able to have me as a close companion in sacred eloquence.” SER.]

in the study of the divine Scriptures, insofar as my strength permits, your most devoted assistant.

[Note: [Col. 0697D] These verses are absent from the Paris manuscript. GILES.]

Farewell, brother, with the powers

Of your flourishing youth,

That you may flourish with the Lord

Upon the eternal throne,

Where the martyrs in their ranks

Sing to the King in the heavenly realm,

And the prophets with apostolic

Praises shall resound.

Nidhard, now spurn

The blackest contagions

Of the lowest world,

And favorably reject

These punishments of Tartarus,

Seeking to examine

The high hosts above the heavens

Which the Lord forever adorns

Among the heavenly angelic ones.

Where the King of kings perpetually

Enriches his citizens throughout the age,

The image of the Cherubim, so [Note: [Col. 0697D] “Cherubin.” The Hebrew ending is *cherubim*, *seraphim*; the Chaldean is *cherubin*, *seraphin*. SER.]

that you too may bear it with the seraphim,

Sprung from the apostles,

Son of the prophets,

So that in the highest seat you may rejoice,

And shine together with them,

Seizing the golden rewards

Of the exalted kingdom,

And on the heavenly throne

Praise Christ with proclamation.

**LETTER V. GREGORY TO CHARLES. [A.D. 723.]**

To the glorious lord and son in Christ, Charles, duke, Pope Gregory.

Having learned that you, most beloved in Christ, are of religious mind, etc. (See above, Letter 2 of Pope Gregory II.)

**LETTER VI. GREGORY TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF GERMANY. [A.D. 723.]**

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to all the most reverend and holy brothers, fellow bishops, devout priests or deacons, glorious dukes, magnificent [Note: [Col. 0697D] *Castaldis.* Others write *guastaldus*, and Amerbach, in Charlemagne’s Constitutions, thinks it means “host” or “innkeeper,” as though derived from *gasthalter*. But the pontiff in this passage calls them magnificent *gastalds* and places them before the counts; this interpretation is also contradicted in the same Pontifical of Zachary, where he says that Liutprand, king of the Lombards, sent to the pope in his service Duke Aldeprand, Tacipert the *castald*, and Raming the Tuscan *castald*. Charlemagne likewise writes to dukes, counts, and *gastalds*. Amerbach adds that he would not object to interpreting *gastalds* as “appointed men,” as though from *gestellte* or *bestellte*. But appointed for what purpose? This is explained in Lombard Book II, title 17, and elsewhere, where it is said that royal estates and houses were entrusted to them, so that they were like those called *castellani* in Poland, Gaul, and elsewhere. They were said to derive either from the Latin *casa* or *castrum*, or from the German *gast*, because they held estates and fortresses in which kings generally lodged; and even in military matters they were close to the dukes. See Lombard Book I, title 15; Paul the Deacon, book V, chapter 11; Peter of Vinea, Letter 6, chapter 25, where, discussing the fiefs of the *castaldiae*, Emperor Frederick says that a castle comes from us, apparently indicating that the name derives from *castrum*, while even today *ein castel* remains in common use. HOTOMANN, *On Feudal Terms*. SER.]

castles, counts also, and all Christians who fear God.

Being exceedingly concerned, etc. (See above, Letter 3 of Pope Gregory II.)

**LETTER VII. GREGORY TO THE PEOPLE OF THURINGIA. [A.D. 723.]**

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to the entire people of Thuringia.

The Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, true God, who descended from heaven, etc. (See above, Letter 6 of Pope Gregory II.)

**LETTER VIII. GREGORY TO THE NOBLES OF THURINGIA. [A.D. 723.]**

To the magnificent men Asolf, Godola, Wilarius, Cuntarius, [Col. 0698C] Albord, and all the Thuringian faithful Christians beloved by God, Pope Gregory.

The magnificent faith reported to us, etc. (See above, Letter 5 of Pope Gregory II.)

**LETTER IX. GREGORY TO THE PEOPLE OF OLD SAXONY. [A.D. 723.]**

Pope Gregory to the entire people of the province of [Note: [Col. 0698D] Leibniz, volume I of the *Brunswick Historical Writers*, p. 37, cites among excerpts from ancient authors a passage from Nennius’s *History of the Britons*, edited by Thomas Gale, taken from the account of the Anglo-Saxons’ arrival in Britain: “Twelve thousand men were baptized with him [Edwin] in one day; Saint Paulinus, archbishop of York, baptized them, and for forty days did not cease baptizing every kind of Ambrones, that is, Old Saxons.” It is noteworthy that the Saxons are here called by the name “Ambrones,” perhaps a designation borrowed from ancient Roman history, where the Cimbri, Teutons, and Ambrones were associated. In this sense Leibniz thinks that the word here signifies nothing other than Teutons, or Germans. Perhaps some trace of that name remained among the Saxons when they crossed into Britain; and at a later time the Westphalians were often designated by the old authors as Old Saxons. The Angarians were part of them, if the term is taken more broadly to include everything between the Rhine and the Weser. WURDT.]

Old Saxony.

[Col. 0699A] I am a debtor to the wise and to the foolish, brothers, etc. (See above, Letter 7 of Pope Gregory II.)

**LETTER X. GREGORY TO THE PEOPLE AND CLERGY OF GERMANY. [A.D. 723.]**

[Note: [Col. 0699C] Equipped with so many and such great apostolic letters, Boniface returned to Germany. Coming to the prince Charles, he delivered to him the letters of the Roman pontiff and humbly commended himself to Charles’s protection. With Charles’s consent he then went to the region of the Chatti, whom they call Hessians, among whom he had already begun to preach. There he found many of them, having abandoned the practice of the Christian religion and become entangled in various errors. Some secretly or openly sacrificed to trees and springs; others practiced augury and divination, magic arts and incantations; only a few persevered in the way of truth which they had once received. With their aid and counsel he attempted to cut down, at a place called Geismar, a tree of extraordinary size which the pagans called the Oak of Jupiter, while servants of God stood with him. A great multitude of pagans then gathered, intending to attack the holy man as an enemy of their gods. But when they saw that the tree, after being cut only a little, was immediately split into four parts, they abandoned all their hostility and believed in the true God. From the great mass of the tree they constructed an oratory dedicated in honor of Saint Peter. WURDT.]

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to the clergy, the ecclesiastical order, and the people dwelling there, his most beloved sons in the Lord, greetings.

Delaying nothing in response to commendable desires, etc. (See above, Letter 4 of Pope Gregory II.)

**LETTER XI. CHARLES TO BISHOPS, DUKES, ETC. [A.D. 724.]**

To the holy and apostolic lords, the fathers in Christ, bishops, dukes, counts, vicars, household officials, or all our agents, our young men, or the messengers traveling about, and our friends, the illustrious man Charles, mayor of the palace, wishing you well.

Know how the apostolic man and father in Christ, Boniface the bishop, came to us and informed us that we ought to receive him under our *mundeburdium* [Note: [Col. 0699D] *Mundeburgium.* Thus in C, but in this same letter *mundeburdium* is written twice. Both forms are acceptable, as Hotomann says in *On Feudal Terms*. It is nothing other than guardianship or protection; and *mamburgus* means protector or advocate. In the formula of the kingdom received by Boso, in William Paradinus, *Burgundian History*, book I: “To all, as you have instructed me, I shall preserve law, justice, and right guardianship, with God’s help.” In the Imperial Codex, after various books and treatises, there is a donation made by a certain Wilibert to the Cologne Church of Saint Peter in the year 871, in which it reads: “That you may be under the defense and guardianship of that church, and under the wing of the pontiff who at that time appears to preside there.” SER.] or protection. Know that we have gladly done this. Accordingly, we caused our firm hand to be given him, so that wherever he may appear to travel, he shall be secure and protected by our favor, or under our guardianship and protection, on the condition that he render justice and likewise receive justice. And if any accusation or necessity should arise for him that cannot be settled according to law, he shall remain secure and protected, both he himself and those who appear to depend upon him, until he comes before us; no one shall be permitted to inflict any opposition or injury upon him, but he shall at all times remain secure and protected under our guardianship and defense. And so that this may be believed with greater certainty, I have undersigned it with my own hand and sealed it below with our ring.

[Note: [Col. 0700C] The apostolic man, oppressed by every kind of poverty among fierce, harsh, and uncivilized peoples, carried out the work of salvation trusting in God alone. Meanwhile, by the providence of God, the minds of the faithful were moved: some brought him clothing, others alms for food, others books, and still others sent him consolation and encouragement by letter. Among these was that Daniel, bishop in England, who had given him letters of recommendation when he first traveled to Rome to Pope Gregory. When he learned that Boniface had undertaken the difficult task of preaching the Gospel to the nations, he sent him a catechetical instruction by which those pagans could be taught the articles of the faith. WURDT.]

**LETTER XII. BONIFACE TO DANIEL.**

[Note: [Col. 0700D] To Daniel. In C the characters mentioned in Letter 1 are unfamiliar, and mean “To Daniel the bishop, from Boniface.” The same characters precede this: “Letter of the blessed Boniface, bishop.” This Daniel was bishop of the city of Winchester among the West Saxons, renowned for holiness and learning. See the Venerable Bede, *History*, book V, chapters 19 and 24; Othlonus, *Life of Boniface*, book I, chapter 10; and below, Letters 66 and 67, in which mention is made near the end of the blindness referred to here. SER.]

To the most beloved lord Daniel, bishop, Boniface, servant of the servants of God, sends the desired greeting of charity in Christ.

It is recognized as customary among human beings, when something sad and burdensome [Note: [Col. 0700D] “Onerous.” C. has *honerosum*. The former is more usual today; nevertheless, if we consult Varro, book IV of *On the Latin Language*, the latter is better. “*Honos*,” he says, “comes from *honestus* through *honere*. Thus *honestas* is so called because it is honored; and it is said: ‘Honor is a burden that sustains the republic.’” SER.] has happened to others, to seek comfort or advice for an anxious mind from those whose friendship or wisdom, and whose alliance, they especially [W. in margin: “maxima,” “greatest”] trust. In the same way, I too, trusting in the approved wisdom and friendship of your fatherhood, lay before you the distresses of my weary mind and seek the counsel and comfort of your piety. [Col. 0700B]

For, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement [W. in margin: “dictum,” “saying”], we have not only battles outside and fears within, but also battles within together with fear—especially because of false priests and hypocrites, who oppose God, ruin themselves, and lead the people astray through very many scandals and various errors. They say to the people, in accordance with the Prophet’s saying, “Peace, peace!” when there is no peace; and the seed of the word, which we take from the bosom of the catholic and apostolic Church and have been entrusted to sow, they try to sow over with weeds, choke it, or turn it into grass of a poisonous kind. [Col. 0701A]

What we plant they do not water so that it may grow, but seek to uproot it so that it may wither. They offer and teach the people [Note: [Col. 0701C] “New sects.” See Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitorium*, chapters 26–27. SER.] new sects and errors of various kinds. Some abstain from foods that God created to be received; some feed themselves exclusively on honey and milk, rejecting bread and other foods. Others assert—a claim extremely harmful to the people—that murderers or adulterers, even while persisting in those crimes, can nevertheless become priests of God.

But the people, according to the Apostle’s saying, “will not endure sound doctrine, but will heap up teachers for themselves according to their own desires, having itching ears.” [Col. 0701B]

We, while seeking the assistance of the Frankish court as our protection, cannot, in accordance with the command of the canons, abstain from and separate ourselves from the bodily communion of such men, except for this one matter: during the solemn celebrations of Mass, in the sacred mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood, we do not communicate with them, and we avoid their counsel [Note: [Col. 0701C] The Paris manuscript has in the margin: “I think *concilium* and *consessum* should be read.” GILES.] and consent.

For when we labor and struggle with such men, with pagans, and with a mixed [W. in margin: omits “with”] and plebeian multitude, they seem to be external [Note: [Col. 0701D] “External”—those things that are outside, as opposed to internal things. Hence what follows: “But internal things are when …” Note also the twofold kind of temptation by which the minds of the saints and of those who earnestly devote themselves to the salvation of others are afflicted and tormented. There are external troubles, such as labor, hunger, thirst, weariness, and sleeplessness. There are also internal troubles, which wound the mind much more severely, such as scandals and the apostasy of certain people. So also below, letters 13 and 85. SER.] battles. Internal battles arise when a priest, deacon, ecclesiastic [W. in the margin: “cleric”], or monk departs from the faith and truth from the bosom of Mother Church, then breaks out with pagans into insults against the children of the Church, and becomes a dreadful obstacle to the Gospel of Christ’s glory. [Col. 0701C]

Regarding all these matters, so that we may fulfill the course of our ministry without harm to our souls, we first seek before God the intercession of your fatherhood. And with heartfelt prayers, by God, we earnestly beseech you to intercede for us, so that God, the merciful consoler of those who labor, may deign amid such storms of differing circumstances to preserve our souls unharmed and sound, free from sins.

Concerning the communion of the priests mentioned above, I eagerly desire to hear and heed your wholesome counsel. [Col. 0702A] For [Note: [Col. 0701D] “Without the protection.” Just as a hammer and axe must serve the smith, and other tools other craftsmen, and the body must serve the mind, helping it attain its proper end, so temporal power must serve spiritual power. See Saint Augustine, letter 50; Bellarmine, *On the Laity*, book III, chapter 18. SER.] without the protection of the Frankish ruler I can neither govern the people nor defend [W. in margin: omits “defend”] the priests and deacons, monks, or handmaids of God; nor can I prohibit the rites of the pagans and the sacrileges of idols in Germany without his command and the fear inspired by him.

When I come to him seeking assistance in these matters, I cannot in any canonical manner abstain bodily from the communion of such men, except only from their consent. For I fear guilt from that communion [Note: [Col. 0701D] “From that communion.” So also below, letter 141 (letter 75). SER.], because I remember that, at the time of my ordination, in accordance with the command of Pope Gregory, I swore at the body of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 0701D] “At the body.” The oath of Saint Boniface is given below, p. 163. I have explained in book III of *Mainz*, note 15, how it was made at the body of Saint Peter. See Saint Gregory, letter 3, book X. SER.] that I would avoid the communion of such men if I were unable to convert them to the canonical way.

Yet again I fear greater harm to the preaching that I owe to the people if I do not come to the Frankish ruler. If your fatherhood wishes to decide, judge, and direct what should be done in this matter for your sorrowful and doubtful [Note: [Col. 0702C] “Son.” The reason is given by Othlonus, cited above, book I, chapter 10. SER.] son, please inform me.

For I seem to be separated from them to a very great extent if, in matters of will, counsel, and consent, and in ecclesiastical ministry where they are not canonical, I abstain from them.

Furthermore, if I may presume to do so, I wish earnestly to ask your fatherhood’s clemency for one consolation during my pilgrimage: namely, that you send me the book of the Prophets which the abbot Winbertus [Note: [Col. 0702D] Winbertus. Othlonus, book I, chapter 4. SER.], of venerable memory and formerly my teacher, left behind when he departed this life for the Lord. In it six prophets are found written in one volume in clear and complete letters [Note: [Col. 0702D] “Six.” Either these words through “are found” should be read parenthetically, or, as in the Caesarean manuscript, one should read: “where six …” and so forth. SER.]. [Col. 0702C]

And if God inspires your heart to do this, you cannot send a greater consolation for the old age of my life, nor a greater advance of reward for yourself. For I cannot obtain in this land such a book of the Prophets as I desire, and, with my eyes growing dim, I cannot clearly distinguish small, connected letters [Note: [Col. 0702D] Wurdtwein has “learn the letters,” and in the margin “learn the letters clearly.” GILES.]. That is why I ask for the book mentioned above: it is written in such clearly distinguished and complete letters.

Meanwhile, through the priest Forthereus, I send you letters and small gifts [Note: [Col. 0702D] “Gifts.” In former times it was customary among holy people to send such things as a sign, nourishment, and increase of charity, as is clear from the letters of Saint Augustine, Paulinus, and others. Examples occur frequently below, in letters 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, and 20. It would be tedious to enumerate them all. See Saint Gregory, letter 37, book VI; letter 57, book VII; letter 47, book XI; letter 16, book XII. SER.], as a sign of pure charity: namely, [Note: [Col. 0702D] “A *casula*.” Today this is understood in sacred usage as the outer sacred vestment with which the priest is clothed when about to perform sacred rites, as also in the miracle of Saint Althelmus emerging from a *casula*, mentioned in the following letter 4. Among the ancients it meant a rustic little house, from *casa*, below, letter 83; hence Festus’s *casaria*, “she who guards the house,” Greek *οἰκουρίς* (“housekeeper”). It can also mean an ordinary garment, as in Saint Augustine, book XXII, chapter 8, concerning the tailor who had lost a *casula* and was splendidly clothed again through the prayers of the holy martyrs. A garment is, as it were, a kind of nearer house of a human being, while a house is a more distant and larger garment. Rabanus, *Institutions of the Clergy*, book I, chapter 21: “*Casula* is so called from *casa*, because it covers the whole person, like a small house.” Perhaps it also comes from the Hebrew verb *casah*, “to cover” or “conceal,” from which, in Exodus 22:25, Job 24:7 and 31:19, comes *cesuth*, that is, “a garment of covering.” Perhaps also from *casaque* among certain Gauls and Germans. But see Stephen Durandus, *On Ecclesiastical Rites*, book II, chapter 9, no. 17. Here it is taken for a certain shaggy cloth, and perhaps it may be read as “for wiping the feet,” as below, letter 89, although below, letter 8, this is not possible because “when you have washed” is added there. Yet this reading occurs everywhere, including below, letter 11. Since it is said to be “not silk,” it appears to mean that it is not a sacred *casula*, which is generally made of silk. In C. it is written *oloserica*. SER.—I do not know whether in this passage we can interpret *villosa* substantivally, for one would scarcely grant that our fathers used a *casula* to wipe the feet. GILES.] a *casula*, not of silk, but mixed with goats’ down and shaggy, for wiping the feet of your affection. [Col. 0703A]

Recently, through a priest who came to Germany from your presence, I learned that bodily blindness had befallen you. But, as you, Lord, know better, it is he—or the one through whom he spoke—who said: “Whom the Lord loves, he chastises,” and so forth. The Apostle Paul also said: “When I am weak, then I am strong,” and “Power is made perfect in weakness.” And the Psalmist: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous,” and so forth.

You have, my Father, as Anthony is said to have said to Didymus [Note: [Col. 0703D] “About Didymus.” Saint Jerome records that he was his student in divine Scripture in the letter to Pammachius and Oceanus beginning *Schedulae*. In his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* he says of him: “Didymus of Alexandria, blind from early childhood and therefore ignorant even of the elements, nevertheless furnished everyone with so great a marvel of himself that he learned dialectic and geometry, subjects especially dependent on sight, to perfection.” After listing his many distinguished works, Jerome says that Didymus was still alive and eighty-four years old. When Saint Jerome was an infant—that is, easily sixty years earlier, since he wrote that book in the fourteenth year of Theodosius, as he says at the end—the event concerning the eyes of the blind Didymus related here occurred, as Saint Jerome himself recounts in his letter to the blind Castrutius, beginning “A holy son.” Concerning a man of our own age, Genebrardus writes in his *Chronicle*: “Robert Mancop, a Scot blind from childhood, advanced so far in learning at Paris that he was created doctor of theology at Rome and archbishop of Armagh; afterward he became papal legate in Ireland.” In another letter to a blind man named Abigaus, Saint Jerome says: “Do not grieve, if you do not possess what ants, flies, and serpents possess—that is, eyes of flesh—but rejoice that you possess that eye of which it is said in the Song of Songs: ‘You have wounded me, my sister, my bride, with one of your eyes,’ by which God is seen.” The same Saint Jerome calls that blind Didymus “my seer” in the preface to his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians. Likewise, among the Hebrews, Joseph, the blind Chaldaean paraphrast of the Hagiographa, is customarily called *Sagginehor*, that is, “rich in light,” or “all-eyed.” SER.] said that he possessed eyes by which God and his angels, and the glorious joys of the heavenly Jerusalem, can be seen and contemplated [Note: [Col. 0704D] “To contemplate.” Passive, as in Saint Augustine, *Against Maximinus*, book II, chapter 11, “to contemplate”; book XVIII, chapter 54, “to begin”; and in the Psalms, “to venerate.” On the eyes by which God is seen, see Augustine, letters 6, 111, and 112. SER.].

For this reason, trusting in your wisdom and patience, I believe that God has given you this for the perfection of your virtues and the increase of your merits, and so that with spiritual eyes you may more clearly see and desire those things which the Lord commands and loves, and may look upon or desire less those things which the Lord does not love but has forbidden. [Col. 0703B]

For what are bodily eyes, at this dangerous time, except, so to speak, for the most part truly [Note: [Col. 0704D] “Windows.” Saint Jerome uses the same argument in the letter to Abigaus already cited. SER.] windows of sins? Through them we either look upon sins and sinners, or, what is worse, by contemplating and desiring crimes we contract them within ourselves.

I earnestly desire that your holiness may be well and pray for me in Christ.

## LETTER XIII. DANIEL TO BONIFACE [A.D. 724]

To Boniface, archbishop, most reverend and deservedly embraced by all the orthodox, distinguished by manifold knowledge and adorned with the grace of various virtues: Daniel, servant of God’s people, sends the most sincere greeting in the Lord, who surpasses all the heights of heaven.

When we read the letter sent by your brotherhood, we were greatly moved by grief, because it seemed intolerable to those who love you if any misfortune had befallen the one they love. Yet, as we repeatedly turned it over, we found some consolation in the fact that the inextricable cunning of the crafty enemy would never have attempted to assault the practices of our religion with such violence and such varied opposition of wars or errors through the persons of exalted priests or any other reprobates, unless he recognized in them an excellence of greater merit. [Col. 0704A]

Therefore, you must first take care that the glorious undertaking—which, as I think, is comparable to apostolic struggles—not be abandoned on account of the snares of those who, equipped with deceits, are accustomed to resist saving doctrine. Rather, the difficulties imposed must be borne all the more willingly, the more certainly we know that the pressures of the saints and martyrs belong to this world, while in heaven there is, by the Lord’s promise, an exceedingly abundant reward. May we deserve to have him as our helper here, if only we are not wearied by endurance in tribulations, and there as our rewarder, rejoicing with the righteous. [Col. 0704B]

Therefore, since your excellence has deigned to seek counsel from our lowliness, we think it will be beneficial for you to strive with unconquered patience to endure what you know cannot occur without God’s providence.

Although the destruction caused by external battles is savage, and the ferocity of internal strife itself is even more brutally to be feared—for I am certainly not surprised, since Christ Jesus once testified that brother would be handed over to death by brother, and son by father, and parents by their descendants for his name’s sake—there are those who attack by their most superstitious observance of foods, seeking to destroy the Lord’s work—foods which will almost perish with equal loss in human use. Others, pursuing shameful profit, proclaim severity to the people either out of a desire to flatter or even to gain the praise of those men, and out of zeal for your condemnation [W. in the margin: “falsely, security”]; they repeat the name of peace with feigned charm, and, according to Isaiah’s prophetic prediction, call evil good and good evil, and so forth. Or they may try to choke the crop entrusted to your reverence by sowing barren weeds among it, although the Lord warns [W. in margin: “in a certain clause”] that before the harvest is ripe no one should presume to uproot it. We shall speak more fully of this below. [Col. 0704C–0705A]

Even if, I say, they bring forth doctrines unheard of until now in order to deceive the hearts of the less discerning—doctrines which you, being well instructed in the divine will, have neither failed to recognize when introduced nor lack what may suitably be opposed to them—still, so as not to delay you by taking everything one by one, I shall speak briefly. [Col. 0705B]

Although all the arguments of the impious faction are employed to assail and afflict you, nevertheless, following the example of the saints who went before, bear patiently what cannot be healed by correction.

Regarding the priesthood of murderers and adulterers who presume, without any repentance, to persist in their sins, the most sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs sufficiently persuade you. If, then, to murderers who continually practice repentance, perfection—that is, the grace of Christ’s communion—is granted near the end of life, by what reasoning is the care of governing Christian conduct entrusted to those who remain uncorrected? And how will an adulterer, who has not repented of his disgraceful conduct even late in life, usurp the priestly office, since, according to the statutes of Pope Innocent and the others, anyone who marries a widow or takes a second wife is restrained not only from the ministry of ecclesiastical dignity but even from the clergy? Even these concessions have been made indulgently on account of the frailty of the flesh, whereas adulteries are prohibited by all who are most learned. [Col. 0705C]

What counsel could be so appropriate concerning separation from the communion of sons [W. in the margin: “false brothers”], brothers, or priests that it would separate you from them in bodily matters, lest you perhaps begin to depart from this world? For they everywhere and always seek to intrude themselves, among the very dangers in which the Apostle Paul declared himself entangled. The other founders of the Christian religion likewise acknowledge either that they themselves suffered these things or that their successors would have to suffer them. [Col. 0705D]

You say that you are kept very far from them in the sacred offerings of sacrifices, lest you seem to give what is holy to dogs. What Saint Augustine thought about this we shall indicate subtly [W. in margin: “subtus,” “below”], among other matters. Moreover, you sometimes live among them not willingly, not by consent, nor by your own choice, but compelled by necessity alone. Indeed, Jerome says: “In the Gospel the will is sought; even if it has not achieved its effect, it nevertheless does not lose its reward.”

Therefore, if you are associated with them, for example in sharing food or dwelling in the same place, did not he who came not to call the righteous but sinners go to the banquets of sinners, so that he might have an opportunity to teach? This applies also to the fact that you must sometimes approach the ruler and pray with him for ecclesiastical peace. For they often pretend, as true shepherds, to intervene on behalf of the sheep. [Col. 0706A]

First, let us know that what is written must be fulfilled: “Be subject to every human institution,” and so forth, and “to every authority that is higher,” and so forth. Then [W. in margin: “Deinde,” “then/next”] we must consider that the likeness of wheat and weeds has been proposed concerning the mingling of evil and good.

“Clean and unclean animals,” says Augustine, “are read to have entered the ark. The unclean animals did not enter in whatever way they pleased, with the structure of the ark broken, but entered with it intact through the one and same door which the builder had made. For,” he says, “through these likenesses and declarations no counsel of indolence was given to the good, by which they might neglect what they ought to prohibit, but a counsel of patience, by which they might endure, while preserving the doctrine of truth, what they are unable to correct.” [Col. 0706B]

It is also said: “When, therefore, we find in the Church evil people whom ecclesiastical discipline cannot correct or restrain, then let not an impious and destructive presumption rise in our heart, by which we imagine that we must separate ourselves from them so as not to be defiled by their sins, and thus first [W. in margin: “post,” “afterward”] try to draw ourselves away, as though we were pure and holy disciples, from the structure of unity, as though segregated from the company of the wicked.

“The scriptural likenesses come to mind by which it has been demonstrated that the wicked will remain mingled with the good in the Church until the end of the age and the time of judgment, and that nothing from the unity of the good will harm their participation [Paris manuscript: “and participation”] in the sacraments, provided they have not consented to the wicked persons’ deeds.

“But when the power to exercise discipline against the reprobate or wicked is present with those through whom the Church is governed, while peace is preserved, then again, lest we sleep through carelessness and sloth, we must be roused by other goads of instruction that pertain to the severity of restraint. Thus there is also a proper way of overlooking and tolerating the wicked in the Church, and there is again a proper way of chastising and correcting them—not of forfeiting [Paris manuscript: “admitting”] or removing them from communion—so that we neither grow sluggish under the name of patience nor become cruel under the pretext of diligence.” [Col. 0706C]

I shall state what I have excerpted from the works of the ancient teachers and what ought usefully to be recalled amid such pernicious barbarism: perhaps, in the aforesaid accommodation, we may be charged by someone with some kind of dissimulation or even feigning [Paris manuscript: “you accuse”], if we read [Paris manuscript: “we read”] that a useful dissimulation is to be adopted at the proper time. [Col. 0706D]

Thus Cephas withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision; and the Chosen Vessel shaved his head and circumcised Timothy. The Son of God himself pretended that he was going farther, and pretended not to know what he knew, as in the Gospel: “Who touched me?” and “Where have you laid him?” The Psalmist also changed his countenance before Abimelech; and Joseph, pretending to play with his brothers, spoke to them; and Israel covered his limbs with goatskins. He did this so that he might be thought to be what he was not. And if it is considered carefully and faithfully, it is not a lie but a mystery.

For through the goatskins sins are signified; and through the one who covered himself with them is signified the one who bears the sins of others. [Col. 0707A]

We have written these things to your charity—not as though you were ignorant of the authority of antiquity or in need of admonition from our rusticity, but lest we should seem to have detracted anything from your requests—with hesitation, because we have learned that you have undertaken business with those greater than yourself. We have spoken out of love and obedience, moved more by these than relying on skill or boldness, revealing rather than commanding, lest we seem in any respect to oppose those who are greatly superior.

We gladly receive the exhortatory admonitions of your suggestion concerning the need to endure the present bodily affliction, and, insofar as our strength permits, with the Lord himself assisting us—who in his mercy has admonished us—we shall obey your salutary words.

Let your benevolent affection also know that, although we are separated by a vast interval of land, divided by the immense expanse of the sea and by the unequal climate of the sky, we are nevertheless weighed down by an equal burden of tribulations. For Satan’s activity is the same here and there. [Col. 0707B]

Therefore I earnestly beg [W. in margin: “you, that we”] that we continually fortify one another through a mutual exchange of prayers, remembering the saying: “If two or three of you agree,” and so forth.

Farewell. Farewell a hundredfold, dearest to me, and, in another hand, and so forth.

## LETTER XIV. DANIEL TO BONIFACE [A.D. 724]

[Note: [Col. 0707D] This is a catechetical letter. SER.]

To the venerable and beloved bishop Boniface: Daniel, servant of God’s people. [Col. 0707C]

Although, my dearest brother and fellow priest, I rejoice that you deserve the first palm of virtue, because, trusting in the greatness of faith, you go forth confidently [Paris manuscript: “attack/set upon,” *aggrediendo*] and tirelessly subdue the rocky and barren hearts of the gentiles, hitherto sterile, with the plowshare of evangelical preaching, turning them through daily labor into fertile clods, so that the prophetic and evangelical saying may truly be applied to you: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness,” and so forth, nevertheless a share of the second palm will not inappropriately also be granted to those who, rejoicing in so pious and salutary a work, support it with whatever assistance they can and supply its needs with suitable helps, so that they may strive more eagerly to advance the work of preaching already begun and to beget spiritual children for Christ. [Col. 0707D]

Therefore, out of devoted goodwill, I have taken care to offer a few suggestions to your prudence, so that you may better understand, according to my judgment, by what method you can most readily overcome the stubbornness of the uncultivated. You should not advance contrary arguments against them concerning the genealogy of their gods, however false. [Col. 0708A] According to their own opinion, in which they assert that any beings were generated by others through the union of male and female, concede that they say this, so that you may at least demonstrate that the gods and goddesses, having been born in the manner of human beings, were human beings rather than gods, and began to exist when previously they did not.

When they have been compelled to learn that the gods had a beginning, since some were generated by others, ask them in turn whether they believe that this world also had a beginning or that it has always existed without a beginning. If it had a beginning, who created it? For, plainly, before the constitution of the world, they find no place in which gods, who had not yet been generated, could subsist or dwell.

By “world” I mean not only this visible world, heaven and earth, but also all the extended spaces of places that even the pagans themselves can imagine in their thoughts. Therefore, if they contend that the world has always existed without a beginning, strive to refute and convict them of this by many proofs and arguments. [Col. 0708B]

Again, in their disputation, ask who ruled the world before the gods were born, and who governed it. How could they subject to their dominion or make their own a world that had always existed before them? From where, or from whom, or when was the first god or goddess substituted or generated? Do they suppose that they still generate other gods and goddesses, or, if they no longer generate them, when and why did they cease from intercourse and childbirth? But if they still generate them, the number of gods produced has by now become infinite. Yet who is more powerful among so many and such great beings is unknown to mortals. One must be extremely careful not to offend the more powerful one.

Do they think that the gods should be worshiped for temporal and present blessedness, or rather for eternal and future blessedness? [Col. 0708C] If for temporal blessedness, let them say in what respect the pagans are already happier than Christians. What benefit, moreover, do the pagans suppose that they confer upon gods who have all things in their power through their sacrifices? Or why do the gods permit those subject to their power to do what they offer to them? If they need such things, why do they not choose better things for themselves? But if they do not need them, let them consider that they imagine in vain that they can appease the gods with such offerings of victims.

You should present these and many other similar arguments, which it would now be tedious to enumerate, not by insulting or provoking them, but calmly and with great moderation. At intervals, these superstitions should be compared with our Christian doctrines, and should be touched, as it were, from the side, so that the pagans may be more ashamed than angered by their absurd opinions, and may not think that we are unaware of their wicked rites and fables. [Col. 0708D]

This too should be added: if the gods are almighty, benevolent, and just, they not only reward their worshipers but also punish those who despise them. And if they do both these things in time, why then do they submit to Christians, who turn almost the whole world away from their worship and overthrow their idols? And yet Christians possess fertile lands, provinces rich in wine and oil and abundant in other resources, while the pagans, together with their gods, have been left lands always stiff with cold, in which the gods, driven out from the whole world, are now falsely thought to reign. [Col. 0709A]

The authority of the Christian world should also be frequently brought before them. In comparison with it, they are very few, yet still persist in their ancient vanity. And lest they boast that the gods have always exercised a legitimate princely dominion over those nations, it should be made clear to them that the whole world was once devoted to the worship of idols, until, enlightened, made alive, and reconciled to God through the grace of Christ, the true almighty Creator, Ruler, and one God became known. [Col. 0709B]

For when, among Christians, the children of the faithful are baptized daily, what else are they doing except cleansing each one of them from the stain and guilt of paganism, in which the whole world was once established?

I have wished briefly to recall these matters to your affection out of charity, my brother, while I am weighed down and afflicted by bodily [Note: [Col. 0709C] “Illness.” Above, letter 3 (letter 12). SER.] sickness, so that I can appropriately say with the Psalmist: “I have known, O Lord, that your judgment is just, and truly you have afflicted me.”

Therefore I earnestly ask your reverence to deign, together with those who serve Christ with you in spirit, to pour out prayers of supplication for me, so that the Lord, who has given me to drink of the wine of compunction, may soon anticipate me with his mercy; so that he who has justly corrected may mercifully forgive, and by his goodness may enable me also, rejoicing, to sing the prophetic words: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations, O Lord, have gladdened my soul.” [Col. 0710A]

I wish that you may be well in Christ and remember me, my dearest fellow priest.

## LETTER XV. GREGORY TO BONIFACE [A.D. 724]

[Note: [Col. 0709C] Baronius, who advanced Leo’s reign by one year, wrote in the margin of these letters “Leo’s ninth year” instead of the eighth, but incorrectly. Since Leo and his son Constantine are said to have become emperors in the same month, namely March—Leo in 717 and Constantine in 720—all subscriptions assign three more years to Leo than to Constantine, never four. Serarius, in his notes on the same letter, read: “With Augustus Leo reigning, in his eighth year, in the eighth year of his patriciate.” But the designation of the consulship must be retained throughout, and, with Sirmondus, one should read: “in the eighth year, after his consulship, in the eighth year.” Since the editor of the decretal edition did not know that, from the time of Constantine Pogonatus, emperors mentioned as many consulships as years of their reign, he deliberately omitted the consulship; indeed, Sirmondus himself had not penetrated this secret when, in his notes on the text of the Oath issued by Boniface at Rome, he wrote concerning Leo’s reign and consulship: “Leo the Isaurian began his reign on the eighth day before the Kalends of April and soon, as is conjectured, assumed the consulship on the nearest Kalends, in the year of Christ 717.” Cointius likewise remained with this consulship in the cited passage, book [unclear], no. 20, and moreover thought that the year of the patriciate should be retained with Serarius. But from Constantine Pogonatus onward the emperors assumed both imperial power and the consulship on the same day, precisely as the emperors of ancient Rome assumed tribunician power together with the empire. Pagi, under the year 724, no. 4.

“While preaching and baptizing [A.D. 725] in the regions of the Thuringians and Hessians, Boniface saw that the harvest was indeed abundant but that there were few laborers to instruct the people in the faith. He sent to his homeland and caused several religious women and men, distinguished both for virtue and learning, to come from there, and divided among them the burden of his sacred labor.

“According to Othlonus, book I, chapter 25, the chief men among them were Burchardus and Lullus, Willibald and his brother Wunnibald, Witta, and Gregory. The religious women were Lullus’s maternal aunt, Chunihilt, and her daughter Berathgit, Chunitrut, Thecla, Lioba, and Waltpurgis, the sister of Willibald and Wunibald. Chunihilt and her daughter Berathgit, highly learned in the liberal arts, were appointed teachers in the region of the Thuringians. Chunitrud was sent to Bavaria to scatter the seeds of the divine word there. Thecla he established beside the river Main, in places called Kitzingen and Ochsenfurt. He also appointed Lioba to Bischofsheim on the Tauber, so that she might preside there over a multitude of gathered virgins.

“Pagi, under this year, no. 11, notes concerning Lioba that she was also called Leobgytha. But the arrival of these religious women in Germany should not be assigned to the time of Gregory II, since it is clear from the Life of Saint Lioba written by Rudolphus, a monk of Fulda, that Boniface sent the abbot Sturm to summon nuns and handmaids of God from England to Germany; yet Sturm was not made abbot of Fulda until the year 744. Eccardus, in the cited passage, p. 358, objects to this and maintains his opinion that this summons occurred in 725.

“Every church in England also supported Boniface as he labored in the Gospel: some offered themselves for the work of the ministry, others—as we saw above—helped him with books and other gifts, others bestowed prayers, and others wrote letters to him, and so forth. Among those who, in that same year, succeeded to the paternal kingdom of Kent, Aethilbert sent the following letter to him, according to Bede, book V, chapter 24.” WURDT.] [Col. 0710C–D]

To the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop: Gregory, servant of the servants of God.

“Believe that we have been moved by the concern of pastoral vigilance,” and so forth. (See above, letter 9, of Gregory II.)

## LETTER XVI. N. . . . DEACON TO EADBURGA [A.D. 725]

To the most reverend and dearly beloved in Christ, Eadburga, abbess: N., an unworthy and insignificant deacon, sends perpetual greetings in the Lord. [Col. 0710B]

I earnestly beseech your gracious kindness, with prayers from the depths of my heart, that you deign to remember me in the support of your holy prayers, just as your benevolent charity promised me through our brother N., who was returning. I also urgently beg this of you: may the ship of my frailty, which is shaken daily by the storms of the present world, be strengthened by the support of your steadfastness, so that, through the frequent assistance of your prayers, you may protect me against the poisoned darts of the ancient enemy.

I have sent small gifts to your revered affection: namely, one silver stylus, and a quantity of storax and cinnamon, so that from these trifles you may recognize how welcome to me are the gifts brought by your greeting. And if you wish to command anything of me through the bearer of these lines, who is called Ceola, or through anyone else, that charity which has joined us in spiritual kinship knows that I wish to fulfill it with all my strength. Meanwhile, I beg you not to refuse to send me a letter of your sweetness. I desire that you may be well, and we pray that you may advance in Christ through holy successes.

> **Note:** *Graphium* means a stylus, pointed on one side, with which letters were written in wax, and flat on the other, with which what had been incorrectly written was smoothed over and erased. Symposius, in his riddle, whose title is *Grafio*:
>
> “Flat at the top, but I am not flat at the bottom.”
>
> —WURDT.

> **Note:** *Ceola.* Below, Epistle 12 (Epistle 52), Baronius has *Ceda*. In the Venetian Annals, Bede, Book I, chapter 8, concerning him? —SER.

## EPISTLE XVII. BONIFACE TO EADBURGA. [A.D. 725]

To the sister Eadburga, abbess, whom we must embrace with the golden bond of spiritual love and bind with the kiss of divine and virginal charity, Boniface, bishop and legate of the Roman Church, sends greeting in the Lord.

We implore your kindness with prayers from the depths of our hearts, that you may deign to intercede for us with the author of all things. And so that you may not be unaware of the reason for this prayer, know that, because our sins demand it, the conduct of our pilgrimage is battered by various storms. Everywhere there is labor, everywhere sorrow; battles without, fears within. Most grievous of all is that the treachery of false brothers prevails over the malice of the unbelieving pagans.

Therefore pray to the merciful defender of our life and the sole saving refuge of those who labor, the Lamb of God who took away the sins of the world, that, while we move among the lairs of such wolves, he may keep us unharmed under the protection of his right hand. May the beautiful feet of those who carry the lamp of evangelical peace not be found there as the dark footprints of wandering apostates; rather, may the most merciful Father, with our loins girded, make our lamps burn in our hands and illuminate the hearts of the gentiles so that they may contemplate the Gospel of the glory of Christ.

Meanwhile I beg that your piety may deign to intercede for these pagans who have been entrusted to us by the Apostolic See, so that the Savior of the world may deign to rescue them from the worship of idols and gather them among the children of the one mother, the Catholic Church, to the praise and glory of his name—he who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

Farewell.

## EPISTLE XVIII. BONIFACE TO EADBURGA. [A.D. 725]

> **Note:** *Eadburga.* Baronius, under the year 719, number 15, thinks that Egburga or Bugga is none other than Eadburga the abbess, to whom Boniface’s letters 17, 18, 19, and others are extant. Yet it is probable that Bugga and Eadburga were different women, as Mabillon says: first, because when Boniface writes to the former he always calls her Bugga, whereas he calls this woman Eadburga; and second, because this appears to have been the Eadburga whom Leobgytha states in Epistle 36 among the Bonifacian letters to have instructed her, and thus she must have been abbess of the monastery of Winburn, where Leobgytha was educated, whereas Eadburga was abbess of the monastery of Thanet. Pagi, under the year 724, number 2. —WURDT.

To his most beloved sister Eadburga, abbess, long ago joined to him by the closeness of spiritual kinship, Boniface, servant of the servants of God, sends perpetual salvation in Christ.

May the eternal rewarder of the just gladden in the heavenly court of the angels the most beloved sister who, by sending gifts of holy books, has consoled the exiled German with spiritual light. For he who must traverse the dark corners of the German peoples will fall into the snare of death unless he has the word of the Lord as a lamp for his feet and a light for his paths.

Moreover, trusting carefully in your charity, I beg you to deign to pray for me, because, as my sins demand, I am shaken by the storms of a dangerous sea. Pray that he who dwells on high and regards the humble, forgiving sins, may grant me a word in the opening of my mouth, so that the Gospel of the glory of Christ may run and be glorified among the nations.

## EPISTLE XIX. BONIFACE TO EADBURGA. [A.D. 725]

To the most reverend and beloved sister Eadburga, abbess, Boniface, servant of the servants of God, sends the desired greeting of charity in Christ.

I beseech the almighty Lord, the retributor and rewarder of all good works, that in the heavenly dwellings and eternal tabernacles he may restore to you an eternal reward for all the benefits that you have bestowed upon me, in the heavenly court of the blessed angels. For often your piety has consoled my sadness, either by the comfort of books or by the assistance of clothing.

Thus I continue to beg you to increase what you have begun: namely, that you write for me in gold the Epistles of my lord, the holy apostle Peter, for the honor and reverence of the sacred Scriptures in the sight of carnal people when they are preached. I have always particularly desired to have with me the words of him who sent me on this journey, and I am sending the priest Eoban to write what I request.

Therefore, dearest sister, act on this request of ours as your kindness has always done with all my petitions, so that here too your work may shine in golden letters, to the glory of the heavenly Father. I desire that you may be well in Christ and advance toward better things through holy virtues.

> **Note:** “With gold.” Eadburga was skilled in calligraphy and not ignorant of the liberal arts. For Leobgytha, a nun of Winburn, testifies in Epistle 36 that she learned the poetic art from Eadburga. The cited epistle is numbered 21 in our reckoning. It had already become customary to write books on purple parchment in gold and silver and to decorate them with variegated colors. Saint Jerome, in the preface to Job, says:
>
> “Let those who wish have ancient books written on purple parchment in gold and silver, or in uncial letters, as they commonly say—burdens rather written than books—provided that they allow me and my poor people to have little sheets, and books corrected rather than beautiful.”
>
> Likewise, in his letter to Eustochium, he says: “The parchments are dyed purple, and gold melts into the letters.” Two such books of Epistles and Gospels, written in the age of the Frankish emperors, are preserved in the church at Worms. —WURDT.

## EPISTLE XX. BONIFACE TO EADBURGA. [A.D. 725]

> **Note:** Serrarius has: “A notable letter of Boniface to Eadburga the abbess,” and in a note: “‘Notable’—not in C.; nevertheless the letter is worthy of notice on account of its subject.” —EDITOR.

### [Col. 0713A]

To the most blessed virgin—indeed, most beloved lady—Eadburga, accomplished in the little rule of monastic life, Winfred, the least servant in Christ Jesus, sends the greeting of profound charity.

You asked me, dearest sister, to write down and send you an account of the remarkable visions shown to that man who recently died in the monastery of Abbess Milburga and came back to life, just as I learned of them from the account of the venerable abbess Hildetida, W., and S. Hebelida. Now indeed I give thanks to almighty God that, with God’s protection granted, I am able to fulfill the wish of your affection all the more fully and clearly, because

> **Note:** “He himself, together with the aforementioned brother who had returned from the dead.” Tertullian, intending to relate a certain vision, says in *On Idolatry*, chapter 15:
>
> “I call God’s authority to witness that it is not safe to conceal anything whatsoever that has been shown to a man, certainly for the benefit of all.”
>
> The account related here has a double testimony: first, the outstanding faith of the narrator himself, holy Boniface; then the confirmation—not by hearsay but by the eyes—of the man who related it to him. That most wretched rich banqueter in hell said to Abraham, Luke 16:30: “If someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent,” and many, as Saint Chrysostom says in Homily 66, are accustomed to say: “If only someone would come from the dead and report what was happening, everyone would believe him,” and so forth. Yet this certainly does not happen.
>
> Lazarus returned from the dead, and many believed in Jesus, John 11:45; but did everyone believe? That young man, the son of the widow at Nain, also returned, and all who were present were indeed seized with fear and glorified God; but were all who afterward saw and heard him thereby brought to repentance? The same is true of the others whom the Lord himself, the apostles, or the prophets restored to life.
>
> When Joram, king of Israel and son of Ahab, heard from Gehazi a certain eyewitness account of the son of the Shunammite woman who had returned to life—indeed, when he himself saw that man with his own eyes and heard him relate the matter with his own ears—did he reform? Did he abandon his impiety and evil ways? What happens to unbelievers also happens to thieves and robbers, who see gallows and wheels everywhere and yet do not cease stealing and committing robbery. Those people perhaps hope that they may escape and that their crimes will always remain concealed; but can we in any way escape eternal punishments unless we repent?
>
> Before the eyes of all of us, the deaths and funerals of people known and familiar to us every day—young and old, rich and poor—are taking place. It is certain that we too must follow them, and yet are we moved? Therefore, if someone had gone from the dead to the brothers of that banqueter, they would not on that account have immediately reproached themselves, repented, and abandoned the license of their lives.
>
> As Saint Chrysostom says in Homily 4 on Lazarus: “If God had known that the dead would benefit the living, he would never have omitted it, nor would he have passed over so great a gain, since he provides everything useful for us.”
>
> This applies to the ordinary and common course of the world. But with regard to an extraordinary and private law, as Saint Gregory says in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 36, heavenly mercy sometimes disposes, from the abundance of its great compassion, that certain people should suddenly return to their bodies even after death, so that they may fear the torments of hell, which they had not believed when they heard of them, at least when they have seen them—and not they alone, but also others who receive this knowledge from them.
>
> This happens in two ways. Either they are truly dead, or they only appear to be dead and are not. For the soul may be separated from the body in two ways: one separation is complete, when all the bonds and connections of nature have been dissolved; the other is incomplete, through ecstasy, retaining either only one or at least a minimal form of consciousness and life, however obscure and almost nonexistent.
>
> Lazarus, the man of Nain, and the man of Shunem mentioned above belong to the higher category. To the latter belong Saint Fursey in the Venerable Bede, Book III of the *History*, chapter 19, and those whom Saint Gregory, in the title of the cited chapter, says seem to have been brought out of the body as if through an error. He begins that chapter as follows:
>
> “When this happens, if it is carefully considered, it is not an error but a warning, because, certainly, this experience—whether an ecstasy and incomplete death or a true and complete death—is divinely granted as a warning and benefit to those to whom it happens and to others, if both are willing.”
>
> What the souls of those who depart from their bodies, whether completely or incompletely, see may also be of two kinds: either realities as they exist in themselves, or likenesses of realities, insofar as it is useful that those realities should then be signified and revealed. Thus Saint Gregory explains the matter in the cited passage: the magnificent structures of great houses seen in the other world; the sweetest fragrances; profound and dreadful rivers; slippery bridges; and the most terrible stenches. The things related here to holy Boniface, as well as those related to the Venerable Bede in Book V of his *History*, chapters 13 and 15, may be understood in this way.
>
> Here everything is related as though the narrator had been truly and completely dead—and this could have happened. Yet everything could also be understood as resembling ecstatic death, according to Saint Gregory’s opinion in the cited passage, where he uses similar expressions concerning two or three deceased persons. This may also be inferred from what is said near the end of this very letter: the man who reported these things to Saint Boniface had been absent from his body only a few hours, from the first crowing of the cock at night until first light.
>
> Bede, in *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 5, says: “The divisions of the night are seven: twilight, evening, the time of silence, the dead of night, cockcrow, morning, and dawn”; and Macrobius says nearly the same in Book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 4.
>
> But the things concerning the affairs of the future age that were displayed before his eyes were merely images and painted representations of those realities. They pertain to the fire of hell and eternal condemnation; to purgatory and punishment brought to an end; to everlasting joy and blessedness; to the condition of good and evil spirits—whether those spirits were dead human beings or still living people serving virtue or vice—and to the operation of human conscience, with its accusation or defense, and to the severity of divine judgment. This is virtually the whole meaning.
>
> Romans 2:16 speaks of “thoughts accusing and also defending one another.” Fourth Esdras, final chapter, verse 96: “Iniquities stand as accusers.”
>
> On such returns of the dead or of those already blessed or condemned, one may read Alfonso Tostado, Book IV on Kings, chapter 4, question 56; our Gregory; Valentianus, volume IV, distinction 11, question 1, part 2; likewise our Raderus, notes on his *Viridarium*, pages 175 and following, where similar histories occur on pages 173 and 179; Saint Augustine, Epistles 100 and 101, and *On the Care to Be Had for the Dead*, chapter 12; and the *Life of Saint Anno* in Surius.

I myself spoke with the aforementioned brother who had returned from the dead when he recently arrived in these regions from overseas, and he explained to me in his own words the astonishing visions that he had seen when, in spirit, he was carried outside his body.

For he said that, through the pain of a violent illness, he had suddenly been stripped of the body’s heaviness. The experience was very much like this: suppose that the eyes of a seeing and waking person are covered with an exceedingly dense covering, and that the covering is suddenly removed; then everything that previously had been unseen, covered, and unknown becomes clear. So, when the earthly covering of flesh had been cast aside, the whole world had been gathered before his sight, so that he could behold all the regions of the earth, its peoples, and its seas under a single view.

Angels of such immense brightness and splendor had received him as he came out of his body that, because of their excessive radiance, he could not look at them at all. They were singing in harmonious and joyful voices:

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger,  
nor chastise me in your wrath.”

“And they lifted me,” he said, “upward into the air. I saw, surrounding the whole world, a burning fire and a flame of immense size, breathing forth and rising terribly toward the heights. It almost seemed as though, within a single sphere, it encompassed the structure of the entire world, unless a holy angel had restrained it by impressing upon it the sign of the holy cross of Christ. For whenever he impressed the sign of Christ’s cross against the threatening flame, the great flame diminished on that side and subsided.

“I was tormented unbearably by the terrible heat of this flame, especially in my burning eyes, which were struck by the radiance of the shining spirits, until the angel of the splendid vision touched my head by placing his hand upon it, as though protecting it, and made me safe from the injury of the flames.”

Moreover, he reported that during the time in which he was outside his body such a great multitude of souls departing from their bodies had gathered there, where he was, that he thought there had never previously been so many of the entire human race on earth.

He also said that an innumerable crowd of evil spirits and a most radiant choir of heavenly angels were present. He reported that the wretched spirits and holy angels had held a great dispute among themselves concerning the souls departing from the body: the demons accusing them and weighing down the burden of their sins, while the angels relieved and defended them.

He himself had heard everything: his own sins, the actual offenses he had committed from his youth, which he had either neglected or consigned to oblivion when he should have confessed them, or which he had not known at all to be sins, had cried out against him in their own voices, accused him most harshly, and each particular vice had presented itself as if in its own person, saying one thing or another:

“I am your greed, by which you repeatedly desired unlawful things and things contrary to God’s commandments.”

“I am your vainglory, by which you boastfully exalted yourself before people.”

“I am the lie in which you sinned by lying.”

“I am the idle word that you spoke vainly.”

“I am the gaze by which you sinned in looking at unlawful things.”

“I am obstinacy and disobedience, through which you were disobedient to your spiritual elders.”

“I am torpor and laziness in neglecting holy studies.”

“I am wandering thought and useless anxiety, by which you occupied yourself beyond measure, whether in church or outside the church.”

“I am sleepiness, by which, overcome, you rose late to confess to God.”

“I am the idle journey.”

“I am negligence and carelessness, through which you became inattentive to the study of sacred reading.”

And so forth: all the other vices of this kind that he had committed while living in the flesh and had neglected to confess.

Many things that he had entirely failed to understand as sins also cried out against him with terrible voices. Likewise, the evil spirits, agreeing in all the vices, accused him and testified harshly against him. They recalled the places and times of his wicked deeds and confirmed their charges by loudly proclaiming the same things as sins.

He also saw there a certain man whom he had wounded while still living in secular dress, and whom he reported to be still alive in this world, brought forward as a witness to his evil deeds. The man’s bloody and open wound, and the blood itself, crying out in its own voice, reproached him and charged him with the crime of cruelly shedding blood. Thus, when his crimes had been heaped up and counted, they affirmed that he had unquestionably been a guilty sinner, subject to their jurisdiction and condition.

> **Note:** “Each particular vice.” Whether vice is conceived as a habit or as an act. Observe here that the accusation is instituted only from those sins that had not been explicitly expiated through sacramental confession—not through deceitful and sacrilegious silence, but through some negligence, forgetfulness, or ignorance. At times other sins that confession had erased are also read as being reproached, but in such a way that no guilt or disgrace is thereby inflicted.
>
> Something similar can be observed among the possessed, who sometimes reveal hidden and secret matters. Of these, Silvester Giraldus records one that occurred in his own time in Book I of *Cambria*, chapter 12, in these words:
>
> “When those whose secrets the demon had reproached had confessed these matters and returned after the penance that followed, he reproached them with nothing—indeed, as I knew, he said: ‘But now I do not know.’ To others, however, he uttered this as an insult: ‘I remain silent. What I know, I do not know.’”
>
> From this it appears that after confession and penance demons either know nothing of human sins at all, or know them only for the harm and disgrace of those people. For, as Augustine says, “If a human being covers, God uncovers; and if a human being uncovers, God covers.” Read Augustine’s entire exposition of Psalm 22. —SER.

On the other hand, he said, the small virtues of my soul cried out in my defense—virtues that I, wretchedly, unworthily, and imperfectly, had practiced. One said:

“I am obedience, which you displayed toward your spiritual elders.”

Another said:

“I am fasting, by which you disciplined your body as it fought against the desire of the flesh.”

Another:

“I am pure prayer, which you poured out in the presence of the Lord.”

Another:

“I am service to the sick, which you kindly rendered to those who were ill.”

Another:

“I am the psalm that you sang in satisfaction to God, in place of idle speech.”

Thus each virtue, defending me, cried out against its rival sin. Those angelic spirits of immense brightness magnified these virtues and defended me, affirming their testimony. And all these virtues appeared to me greatly increased and much greater and more excellent than they had ever been worthily accomplished through my own strength.

Meanwhile he reported that, as though in the lower regions beneath this world, he had seen many fiery pits belching forth dreadful flames.
