From the earth, fires of terrifying flame burst forth and flew about, while the spirits of wretched human beings, resembling black birds, wept and howled through the flames, shrieking in human words and voices and mourning their own merits and their present punishment. They rested for a little while, clinging to the rims of the pits, and then, howling again, fell into the pits.

> **Note:** The Paris manuscript has: “with a foul and terrible flame of fire bursting forth.” Should one read *erumpentes* (“bursting forth”) or *erumpentem* (“bursting forth”)? —GILES.

And one of the angels said:

“This very brief rest indicates that, on the day of the future judgment, almighty God will grant these souls relief from punishment and perpetual rest.”

But beneath those pits, still farther below, in the deepest abyss, as though in the lower hell, I heard a dreadful and terrifying groan and a cry of mourning souls, difficult to describe in words.

And the angel said to him:

“The murmuring and weeping that you hear below belong to those souls to whom the merciful compassion of the Lord will never come; eternal fire will torment them without end.”

He also saw a place of extraordinary beauty, in which a glorious multitude of the most beautiful human beings rejoiced with wondrous happiness. They invited him to come, if it were permitted him, to rejoice with them in their joys. From that place came a fragrance of extraordinary sweetness, which was the breath of the blessed spirits rejoicing there. The holy angels affirmed that this place was the renowned paradise of God.

He also saw a fiery, pitch-black river, boiling and burning, a vision of extraordinary terror and the most dreadful appearance. A piece of wood had been laid across it in place of a bridge. Holy and glorious souls, leaving that assembly, hastened toward it, desiring to cross to the farther bank. Some crossed steadily without stumbling; others, weakened, fell from the wood into the Tartarean river; and others were immersed in it as though submerged with their whole bodies.

Still others were immersed only in part:

> **Note:** Vurtdwein has: “some as far as the knees, some to the middle of the knee, and others as far as the armpits.” —GILES.

Yet each of those who fell emerged from the river onto the opposite bank much brighter and more beautiful than before falling into the pitch-black, boiling river.

And one of the blessed angels said of those souls who fell:

“These are souls that, after leaving mortal life, still needed some merciful correction from God because certain slight vices had not been entirely cleansed away, so that they might be offered worthily to God.”

On this side of that river he also gazed upon shining walls of the most brilliant splendor, of astonishing length and immeasurable height. The holy angels said:

“For this is that holy and renowned heavenly city, Jerusalem, in which these holy souls will rejoice forever.”

He said that those souls and the walls of that glorious city, toward which they hurried after crossing the river, shone with such an immense brilliance of light and radiance that, because the pupils of his eyes were dazzled, he could not look at them at all because of the excessive brightness.

> **Note:** “Beautiful.” Here consider the statements of two apostles. First, Saint Peter, 1 Peter 4:18: “If the righteous will scarcely be saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?” Second, Saint James 5:20: “Whoever brings a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins.” Add also Daniel 12:3: “Those who instruct many in righteousness will shine like stars for everlasting eternities,” as Rabbi Abraham Zacuth also explains this passage from the Hebrew in the preface to his *Book of Genealogies*. —WURDT.

He also related that among others the soul of a certain man had come to that assembly, a man who had died while holding the office of abbot. That soul appeared exceedingly beautiful and handsome. The evil spirits seized it and contended that it belonged to their lot and jurisdiction.

Then one of the choir of angels replied:

“I shall quickly show you, most wretched spirits, that this soul is proved not to belong to your power.”

After he had said this, a great company of radiant souls suddenly appeared. They said:

“This man was our elder and teacher, and through his instruction he won us all for God. By this price he was redeemed, and he is recognized as not belonging to your jurisdiction.”

As though they were entering battle with the demons alongside the angels, they rescued that soul from the power of the evil spirits by the angels’ assistance and set it free.

Then the angel rebuked the demons and said:

“Know now and understand that you have seized this soul without legal right. Depart, most wretched spirits, into eternal fire.”

When the angel had said this, the evil spirits immediately raised a great wail and howl. In an instant, as if in the blink of an eye, they hurled themselves with swift flight into the aforementioned pits of burning fire. After a short interval they emerged and again disputed in that assembly concerning the merits of souls.

He said that at that time he was able to observe the merits of various people living in this life. Those who were not subject to crimes and who, relying upon holy virtues, were known to have almighty God as their protector were always kept safe and defended by the angels and were joined to them by charity and kinship.

But those who had been polluted by wicked crimes and the filth of a stained life always had an opposing spirit accompanying them, continually urging them toward crimes. Whenever they sinned in word or deed, that spirit constantly brought the matter forward, as though for joy and celebration, and displayed it among the other most wicked spirits.

When a person sinned, the evil spirit did not delay, waiting until he sinned again. Rather, it presented each vice separately to the notice of the other spirits; then, as soon as it had urged the person to sin, it immediately displayed to the demons what had been perpetrated.

Meanwhile he related that he had seen a girl who, in this earthly life, was grinding at a mill. She saw beside her a new spindle lying there, decorated with carved designs. It appeared beautiful to her, and she stole it.

Then, as though filled with immense joy, five most loathsome spirits reported this theft to the others in that assembly, bearing witness that she was guilty of theft and a sinner.

He also added:

“I saw there the sorrowful soul of a certain brother who had died shortly before. I myself had previously cared for him during the illness that preceded his death and had arranged his funeral. As he was dying, he instructed me to tell his brother, speaking as his witness, that he should manumit, for the sake of his soul, a certain female slave whom the two brothers had jointly held in their power.

“But his brother, hindered by greed, did not fulfill his request. Therefore the soul mentioned above accused the faithless brother with deep sighs, and complained bitterly while rebuking him.”

He likewise testified concerning Ceolred, king of the Mercians, who, without doubt, was still in the body at the time when these things were seen. As I said, he saw him protected against the assault of the demons by a kind of angelic covering, as though by the extension and placing over him of a large book.

The demons, panting, begged the angels that, once that protection had been removed, they might be permitted to exercise their will of cruelty against him. They charged him with a horrible and unspeakable multitude of crimes, threatening that he would be shut up under the harshest prison-bars of hell and would there be tormented with eternal pains, as his sins deserved.

Then the angels, becoming sadder than usual, said:

“Alas that this sinful man is not permitted to defend himself more! Because of his own merits, we can offer him no assistance.”

And they removed the protection of the covering placed over him.

Then the demons, rejoicing and exulting, gathered from all parts of the world in greater numbers than he thought all the living creatures in the world could constitute. They tore him apart and wearied him immeasurably with various torments.

At last the blessed angels commanded the man who, carried outside his body in spiritual contemplation, had seen and heard all these things to return without delay to his own body. They commanded him not to hesitate to make known everything that had been shown to him to those who believed and who inquired with divine purpose, but to refuse to recount it to those who mocked.

> **Note:** “He should refuse.” So that a greater judgment might not thereby come upon them. For many even ridicule such things and are not led by them to salutary fear; see above. —SER.

They also commanded him to explain in due order to a certain woman who lived in a distant region the sins she had committed, and to tell her that she could reconcile almighty God to herself through satisfaction if she wished.

They further commanded him to explain all these spiritual visions to a certain priest, Bugga, and afterward to proclaim them to people according to the instruction he received from him. He was also to confess the sins attributed to him by the unclean spirits and amend them according to the judgment of the aforementioned priest. As evidence of the angelic command, he was to testify to the priest that for many years he had worn an iron belt around his waist, without any human being knowing it, compelled by love of the Lord.

As for his own body, he said that while he was outside it he had abhorred it so intensely that, throughout all the visions, he had seen nothing so hateful, nothing so contemptible, nothing emitting such a dreadful stench—apart from the demons and the blazing fire—as his own body. He had abhorred it because he saw his brothers and fellow servants kindly carrying out the funeral rites for his body, and they had tended what he hated.

Nevertheless, commanded by the angels, he returned at first light to the body from which he had departed at the first cockcrow.

When he had returned to his body, he could see absolutely nothing with his bodily eyes for a full week; instead, his eyes, filled with blisters, frequently shed blood. Later, concerning the devout priest and the sinful woman, he proved that what the angels had revealed to him was true, as those people themselves confessed it. The subsequent events concerning the death of the wicked king likewise proved beyond doubt that the things he had seen about him were true.

> **Note:** “Other things.” Some of them seem to occur below, in Epistle 71, which may, if desired, be compared with this one. —SER.

He reported that many other things of this kind had been shown to him, but that, because his memory had been weakened, he could not recall them in order. He said that after these astonishing visions his memory had not remained as tenacious as it had been before.

These matters, which I have written down because you earnestly requested them, he related in the hearing of three religious and highly venerable brothers who were in communion with me. They are recognized as faithful witnesses and guarantors of what I have written.

Farewell, true virgin of life. May you live angelically in uprightness and holiness, and may you always reign in the heavens with Christ.

## EPISTLE XXI. LEOBGITHA TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 725]

> **Note:** *Leobgitha.* She was first called Truthgeba, then by the name Leobgyta, and in contracted form Lioba or Lieba, as her Life testifies. It was written in the ninth century by Rudolph, a monk of Fulda, from the faithful account of four of her disciples—namely Agatha, Thecla the Younger, Nana, and Eoliba. Her father was Diemo, or Tinne, and her mother Ebba. Since she was her parents’ only daughter, she was consecrated to God from childhood and placed under the discipline of Tetta, abbess of Winburn. Boniface wrote several letters to her. She herself appears to have written this letter to Boniface first, commending to him her father Tinne, who had died eight years earlier, and her mother Ebba, who was still alive and who, she says, was joined to him by ties of kinship. —WURDT.

### [Col. 0720C]

To the most reverend lord Boniface, adorned with the insignia of the highest dignity, most beloved in Christ and joined to me by the closeness of kinship, Leobgitha, the least handmaid among those who bear the light yoke of Christ, sends perpetual health.

I ask your clemency to remember the former friendship which you long ago formed with my father, whose name in the western regions is Tinne. He was taken from this life eight years ago, so that you might not refuse to offer prayers to God for his soul. I also commend to you the memory of my mother, whose name is Ebbe; she is, as you know better, joined to you by the bonds of kinship, and still lives laboriously, having long been severely afflicted by illness. I am the only daughter of both my parents. Would that, although I am unworthy, I might deserve to accept you in the place of a brother, since in no one of my own family has so great a confidence of hope been placed as in you.

I have taken care to send this little gift—not because it was worthy of the sight of your graciousness, but so that you might retain the memory of my smallness and not consign it to oblivion because of the great distance between our places; rather, may the bond of true affection tie the remaining knot forever. This, beloved brother, I earnestly entreat: may I be protected by the shield of your prayers against the poisoned arrows of the hidden enemy. I also ask that you deign to correct the rusticity of this letter and not refuse to send me some words of your graciousness, for example, which I long eagerly to hear.

I have endeavored to compose the verses written below according to the discipline of poetic tradition—not trusting in boldness, but wishing to exercise the rudiments of my slender little talent and needing your assistance. I learned this art from the instruction of Eadburga, who never ceases diligently to search out the divine law. Farewell, living through a longer age and a happier life, and interceding for me.

Almighty Judge, alone who created all things,

who ever shines with light in the Father’s kingdom,

where Christ’s glory, continually aflame, may thus reign;

may it always preserve you unharmed by everlasting law.

## EPISTLE XXII. BONIFACE TO CERTAIN NUNS. [A.D. 725]

To the venerable and beloved, dearest sisters Leobgitha and Thecla, and also Cynehilda, and to all the sisters dwelling with you who are to be loved in Christ: the greeting of eternal charity.

I beseech and command you, as dearest daughters—and we trust that you already do this continually, have done it, and will do it—that in your frequent prayers you entreat the Lord to deliver us, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, from unreasonable and wicked men. For not all possess faith.

And know that we praise God, and that the tribulations of our heart have been enlarged, so that the Lord God, who is the refuge of the poor and the hope of the humble, may rescue us from our necessities and from the temptations of this wicked age, so that the word of the Lord may run and the glorious Gospel of Christ be glorified, and so that the grace of the Lord may not prove fruitless in me.

And because I am the last and worst of all the messengers whom the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church has sent to preach the Gospel, I ask that I may not die wholly barren of the fruit of the Gospel, nor return empty of sons and daughters in number, lest, when the Lord comes, I be judged guilty concerning the talent that was hidden, and lest, because my sins demand it, I receive from him who sent me, in place of the reward of labor, punishment for fruitless labor.

For many—what is worse—whom I had judged would be sheep destined to be placed at Christ’s right hand at the future judgment are, conversely, recognized as foul and wanton goats to be stationed at the left. Pray also to the Lord’s mercy that God may strengthen my heart with a governing spirit, since he has willed that I, an unworthy man, be called shepherd among the people, so that, when the wolf comes, I may not flee like a hired servant, but, following the example of the good shepherd, may strive faithfully and confidently to defend the lambs together with their mothers—that is, the Catholic Church together with her sons and daughters—against heretics, schismatics, and hypocrites.

Moreover, because the days are evil, do not be foolish, but understand what the will of God is. Therefore keep watch, stand firm in the faith, act courageously, and be strengthened. Let all your actions be done in charity; and, according to the Gospel, “In your patience you will possess your souls.” And remember the holy apostles and prophets, because they labored greatly in the Lord; therefore they obtained eternal rewards. And, according to the Psalmist, “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them from them all”; and, according to the Gospel, “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.”

## EPISTLE XXIII. BONIFACE TO LEOBGITHA. [A.D. 725]

To Leobgitha, venerable servant of Christ and to be held forever in the most sincere charity, Boniface, servant of the servants of God: the desired greeting in Christ.

Let it be known to your holy affection that our brother and fellow priest named Forhthat reported to us that he was obtaining from you, through his prayers, a certain period of time for a learned girl’s work, if our consent granted permission. Therefore, according as your affection has judged it advisable in this matter for the increase of her merit, know without doubt that our will consents and favors it. Farewell in Christ.

## EPISTLE XXIV. [Note: According to the opinion of the Ingolstadt Codex, it ought to be said that both Epistle 122 [Serrarius’s order, that is, our edition’s Epistle 10] and this one, 126 [our edition’s 24], belong to Gregory II. Nevertheless, Baronius attributes that one to Gregory III, although in volume II of the Councils it is expressly attributed to Gregory II; indeed, it is cited there as the very last one, and it is cited in the same manner and order by Gratian, *C.* “Those who [turn away] from the pagans,” *On Consecration*, distinction 4. Baronius, however, seems preferable. First, because Othlonus likewise relates this, book I of the *Life of Saint Boniface*, chapter 32. Second, because the pontiff who wrote this letter also sent Saint Boniface the archiepiscopal pallium, as the letter itself reports; but Gregory III is the one who made him archbishop, in book I of the *Life*, chapter 31. Third, because it is well known to everyone that Gratian often errs in such titles and numbers.

As for the latter letter, volume II of the Councils supports it against Baronius: it numbers this letter of Gregory III as the fourth, as does Gratian repeatedly, *C.* “What you proposed,” 32, question 7; *C.* “Little ones,” *On Consecration*, distinction 4; *C.* “Concerning man,” distinction 5, in the same work; Bellarmine, book IV *On the Roman Pontiff*, chapter 12, and book I *On Marriage*, chapter 17; and even the Centuriators cited by him.

Yet all these considerations are outweighed by the date given at the end of the letter itself: namely, the tenth year of Leo the Isaurian, the seventh of his son Copronymus, and the tenth indiction. For Gregory II had not yet died before the fourteenth indiction and the sixteenth year of the same Leo, as Anastasius the Librarian testifies, nor had Gregory III yet been elected to the pontificate. Therefore, in the margin of this letter, 126, read as follows: Baronius, in the year 726, Gregory II. For these are his words: “This is a letter of Gregory II, but it has been wrongly placed under Gregory III, since from the indiction contained in it I find that it was written in the year 726.” —Ser.]

## EPISTLE XXIV. GREGORY TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 726]

To the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop, Gregory, servant of the servants of God.

“Your messenger Denval, sent by you, was desirable to me,” etc. (See above, Epistle 14 of Pope Gregory II.)

## EPISTLE XXV. GREGORY TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 732]

To the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop, sent from this apostolic see for the illumination of the German people, or of the nations dwelling round about in the shadow of death and established in error, Gregory, servant of the servants of God.

“We were greatly rejoiced when we read the letters of your most holy fraternity,” etc. (See above, Epistle 1 of Pope Gregory III.)

## EPISTLE XXVI. [Note: Sigebaldus. He was king of the West Saxons, among whom was Bishop Daniel, mentioned above. These people were called the West Gewisse. Bede, book III of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 7. He converted them to the Christian faith, and their first bishop was Byrinus, succeeded by Agilbert the Gaul, then Wini, and then Eleutherius, as Bede says in the same work, book IV, chapter 12. The fifth bishop was Heddi; in the same place. The sixth were Daniel and Aldhelmus. For his parish, or diocese, was divided into two bishoprics; book V, chapter 19. But after four years he died and had Forthere as his successor; in the same place, in the final chapter, and in the *Epitome*. Whether Erenwald succeeded him, of whom this letter speaks, or whether he was the same man as Erenwald, is uncertain. Concerning Forthere, see Epistles 58 and 66.

Mabillon, third Benedictine century, part II, in the preliminary observations to the *Life of Saint Boniface*, no. 8, infers from this letter that King Sigebald asked Boniface, who was already established in the regions beyond the sea, to be his bishop, but that Boniface refused the dignity so as not to neglect the conversion of the pagans. In fact, however, the letter was written not by King Sigebald but by the monk Sigebald, as the humble style of the writing suggests, together with the request for mutual remembrance in the sacrifices; he does not ask Boniface to come to England, as Alford observed for this year, no. 17.

Nor, while Boniface was alive, was there any king named Sigebald in West Saxony. Conversely, when Saint Boniface’s successor Lullus governed the Church of Mainz, a letter was written by him among the Bonifacian letters, number 107, bearing this inscription: “To the dearest son Denebald … Sigewald ….” This Sigewald does not seem different from Sigebald, from whom the present letter comes; and Sigebald therefore obtained from Lullus what he had been unable to obtain from Boniface: permission to live with him. For that letter was written to monks residing in Thuringia. —Pagi.]

## EPISTLE XXVI. SIGEBALD TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 732]

To Boniface, most reverend prelate and archbishop, whose prerogative of pious fatherhood is proclaimed, Sigebald, although unworthy and the last of God’s servants, servant of God’s servants: the desired greeting in the Lord.

First, with prayers supported by earnest entreaty—as though kneeling on bended knees—I beg you to grant my request, which I asked you through your priest named Eobo, namely, that he should make my petition and desire known to you. This is that you should be my bishop together with my bishop Daniel. In your clemency you granted this to me, if he had done what I asked him.

I expected from you, my lord, that some word of consolation would come to me. Let it be known to you that from that time onward I have had your name inscribed when I celebrated the solemnities of the Mass, together with the names of our bishops; nor do I now cease, so long as I remain alive. And if I outlive you, I shall inscribe your name together with the name of our father, Bishop Erenwald.

I shall also make this clear to you: I write this not because I have confidence in the merit of my sinful self, but because of the mercy of God and the hope that you have in God.

Therefore I beseech you that my remembrance, according to my smallness, may remain with you both in the present and in the future. Farewell in Christ.

## EPISTLE XXVII. BONIFACE TO A CERTAIN WOMAN [Note: It appears that this woman is Eadburga, because, concerning the prayers she requests and their causes, Saint Boniface says: “I have already prayed about this.” This had been done above, in Epistles 17 and 18. —Ser.] [A.D. 732]

To the most reverend and beloved handmaid of Christ, N., Boniface, suppliant servant of the servants of God, sends in Christ a sincere greeting of charity.

With heartfelt prayers we earnestly implore the clemency of your charity to intercede with the Lord for us sinners, because we have been shaken and battered by many and varied storms, whether from pagans, false Christians, fornicating clerics, or pseudo-priests—and especially, as we fear, because our own merits demand it.

But that we may be consoled and delivered by your prayers, we beseech you and trust in the Lord Jesus that through the prayers of your affection we may deserve to find both forgiveness of sins and calm after the storms. For the faithful-promising Apostle James said: “Confess your sins to one another, so that you may be saved.” For “the constant prayer of a righteous person is very powerful.”

And the evangelist John says in his First Epistle: “We know that he hears us, whatever we ask; we know that we have the requests that we ask of him.”

And because I have already prayed about this very matter, I ask that you not be displeased that I ought not to ask rarely for what I desire always to be done without interruption, since daily tribulation urges me to seek the divine consolations of brothers and sisters.

Moreover, because we fear that the same temptations of Satan exist there as here, heed the Apostle’s saying: “Stand firm and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not vain in the Lord.” And elsewhere: “Keep watch, stand firm in the faith, act courageously, and be strengthened. Let all your actions be done in charity.”

And if poverty touches you, do not forget the Gospel saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” If tribulation comes, remember the truth that says: “In your patience you will possess our souls.” And in the Psalm: “The patience of the poor will not perish forever.” If bodily illness comes, let the saying of the Apostle Paul be brought forth: “When I am weak, then I am strong,” and “power is perfected in weakness.”

## EPISTLE XXVIII. TORTHELMUS TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 733]

To my sweetest lord, governing always in Christ the leadership of pastoral care, endowed with the most sincere devotion of charity and especially rich in God’s grace, Boniface—also called Winfridus—archbishop: Torthelmus, bishop and servant of the servants of God, sends greetings in the Lord.

We have received the desirable letters of your excellence. On rereading them, we recognized your most pious devotion and your most fervent love, by which [Paris edition: *ut*, “that”], under the protection of the Lord’s right hand, you meditate day and night on converting to the Catholic and apostolic faith, for the redemption of your soul, the hearts of the pagan Saxons. Who, hearing these gracious things, would not rejoice? Who would not exult and be glad at these works—that our people should believe in Christ, almighty God?

Through the bearer of your written messages I send you a small gift, but a pledge of great affection, and at the same time I inform you that we have most gladly accepted everything which you deigned to request from our smallness: namely, that in the sacred celebrations of the Mass and in our daily prayers, remembrance of your holiness is observed. We desire and earnestly pray—conscious of our weakness—that the same practice may be observed on your part, all the more perfectly toward us because you are far superior to us in merit.

Let your exaltedness therefore hasten to gather and dedicate a new people to Christ. Indeed, you have as protector the Redeemer of the human race, our Lord Jesus. Greeting your excellence with brotherly affection, we continually beseech the divine clemency to deign to assist you and all who belong to you in all your works, so that you may reign with Christ in the age to come.

## EPISTLE XXIX. EWBALDUS TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 733]

To the most glorious and most reverend, with every sentiment of honor, Archbishop Boniface, Ebwaldus of the East Angles, supported by royal power through God’s gift, together with the whole abbey and the entire congregation of God’s servants in our province, who day and night knock in prayer at the throne of the Most High for the safety of the Churches: greetings in God, the rewarder of all.

First of all, dearest one, we want you to know that we gratefully accept the fact that our smallness has been commended to your holy prayers. Just as your goodness, prompted by God, has prescribed concerning the solemnities of Masses and the constancy of prayers, so also may our mediocrity strive to fulfill this with devoted mind. The memory of your name ought to be perpetually counted in the seven synaxes of our monasteries [Note: “In the sevenfold [services]”: he means the canonical prayers of the seven hours, on which see above, Epistle 17 (now 69). Bede, book III, chapter 127, calls this “the solemn psalmody of canonical time.” See Stephen Durandus, almost all of book III. —Ser.], since perfection is often signified by the number seven.

With these matters properly arranged, and with God’s help the rules for souls duly established and the disposition of the inner person appropriately ordered, we wish the external supports and earthly possessions which, by God’s generosity, have been brought under our authority to remain under the direction of your will. Yet we ask that, through the benevolence of your graciousness, you cause the assistance of your prayers to be frequent in the Churches of God; and just as God’s predestination willed you to become a shepherd among his people, so we strive to regard you as our patron.

The names also of the dead and of those entering upon the universal way will be brought from both sides as the occasion of the year requires, so that God, the God of gods and Lord of lords, who willed to place you in the governance of the episcopate, may deign through you to lead his people to recognition of the undivided Trinity and to the substance of unity. Live, and bring your life to its end with happy strides.

S. [lacuna] us.

Moreover, most pious Father, we wish to inform you that you should know that the bearer of this letter has been sent by us with a devoted mind. Just as we have found him to be faithful to you, so you will find him truthful in all matters concerning us.

## EPISTLE XXX. [Note: Cangitha. Cangyth is also read as Eangyth. —Wurdt.] CANGITHA TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 733]

To Winfridus, blessed in the Lord, venerable in faith and affection, called Boniface, endowed with the privilege of the priesthood and crowned with the flowers of virginal chastity as with garlands of lilies, and also instructed in the knowledge of doctrine: Cangitha, an unworthy handmaid of the handmaids of God and, without merit, bearing the name of abbess, together with her only daughter Eadburga, called Bugge, sends eternal greetings in the Holy Trinity.

No word of our mouths is sufficient to return thanks for the greatness and affection which you sent across the sea in your letter, through the bearer of your pious written message. We ought to rejoice if the praise with which we have been praised is true; yet we must greatly fear lest undeserved praise be more a reproach than a commendation.

Most beloved brother, magnified more by spiritual than by bodily affection and by the generosity of spiritual gifts, we wished these things to be disclosed to you alone; and God alone is our witness to the tears with which you see us drenched. We have been weighed down by many immense burdens of misery, like an exceedingly heavy load or an oppressive pressure. The commotions of worldly affairs sweep us along like whirlpools of foaming sea and like heaps of waves dashed against rocks, when the violence of winds and the storms of tempests drive the vast Euripus with extreme fury, the keels of boats being tossed upward and the ship’s mast thrown downward.

In the same way, the little boats of our souls are shaken by great mechanisms of misery and by the manifold magnitude of calamities. As the voice of truth is said in the Gospel concerning the house: “The rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house,” and so forth.

First of all, and above all the other things that kindle external troubles, stands the remembered, innumerable chain of sins, together with the complete absence of any perfect confidence in good. It is not merely the recollection of our own souls, but—what is more difficult and much heavier—the recollection of all the souls entrusted to us, of every sex and age. We shall have to serve people of many minds and differing ways, and afterward render an account before the sublime tribunal of Christ—not only for manifest sins of deeds or words, but also for hidden thoughts concealed from human beings, with God alone as witness; and we shall have to wage battle with a single rank against a double one, and with ten thousand against twenty thousand.

Meanwhile, a steep difficulty and contention in domestic affairs is added to our souls [Wurdtwein: “with additions”], together with the various discords sown by the hater of all good, who infects the rancid hearts of men with malice and spreads it among all people, especially through monasteries and the associations of monks. And he knows that the powerful suffer powerful torments.

Poverty and lack of temporal goods also distress us, as does the narrowness of our rural plot and royal hostility, because we are accused before him by those who envy us, as a certain wise man says: “Witchcraft and envy obscure many good things.”

Likewise there are the obligations to the king and queen, the bishop and prefect, the authorities and counts—things which would take too long to enumerate and which can more easily be considered in the mind than expressed in speech.

To all these miseries are added the loss of friends, a multitude of fellow sufferers, and a crowd of relatives and kinsmen. We have no son, brother, father, or uncle, except for one only daughter, entirely deprived of every dear person in this world, apart from only one sister of hers, a very aged mother, and the son of their brother—he too most unfortunate because of his own mental derangement [Note: Wurdtwein has: “because of us, without his deserving it.” —Editor.] and because our king greatly hates his people.

There is no other person who is related to us; God has carried them away by various circumstances. Some of them died in their native land, and their bodies rest in the squalid dust of the earth, destined to rise again on the day of necessity, when the master’s trumpet will resound and the human race will emerge from dark tombs to render an account; their spirits, borne aloft in angelic arms, will reign with Christ, where all pain will cease, envy will waste away, and sorrow and groaning will flee from the face of the saints.

Others, however, left the shores of their homeland, entrusted themselves to the watery plains, and sought the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of many martyrs, virgins, and confessors, whose number and names God knows.

Because of all these things and causes of this kind, which can scarcely be enumerated in a single day—even though, as the saying goes, the seasons of July or August prolong the summer—we are weary of our life, and have almost grown utterly weary of living.

Every person, failing in his own cause and distrustful of his own counsels, seeks a faithful friend in whose advice he may trust, one who distrusts himself in his own counsels; and he should have such confidence in that friend that he may disclose and open every secret of his heart. As the saying goes, what is sweeter than to have someone with whom you can speak about everything as with yourself?

Therefore, solely because of all these necessities of misery, which we have enumerated in lengthy speech, it was necessary for us to seek a faithful friend—one in whom we could trust more than in ourselves, who would count our pains, miseries, and poverty as his own, sympathize with us, console us, support us with his words, and lift us up with most wholesome speech.

We sought such a friend for a long time, and we trust that in you we have found the friend whom we desired, wished for, and hoped for. If only God had granted us that, through his angel—as he sent the prophet Habakkuk with food to Daniel the seer in the lions’ den, and Philip, one of the seven deacons, to the eunuch—we might reach those lands and that distant place where you live; and if it had been permitted us to hear living words from your mouth, how sweet your words would be to my throat, Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!

But because we have not deserved this by our merits, and are divided by a long interval of land and sea and by the boundaries of many provinces, we nevertheless wish to make known to you, brother Boniface, in view of the confidence mentioned above, that much time has passed since we, like many others—whether relatives, kinsmen, or strangers—desired to seek the mistress of the world, Rome, and there obtain forgiveness for our sins, as many others have done and still do. I especially desire this, since I am advanced in age and have committed and perpetrated far more in my life.

Wale, formerly my abbess and spiritual mother, was aware of this will and purpose of mine, as was my only daughter, who was still in the years of youth and did not know how to pursue this desire.

But we know that there are many who criticize this intention and disparage this love. They support their opinion with the claim that the synodal canons prescribe that each person should remain in the place where he has been established and where he has made his vow, and there fulfill his vows to God.

Yet because we all live with differing wills, and because our circumstances and the hidden judgments of God are uncertain to us, as the Prophet says, “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God, and your judgments are a great abyss,” his secret will and dispensation in this matter are deeply hidden from us.

Therefore, concerning these uncertain and hidden matters, we both, with suppliant and prostrate faces, implore you to be our Aaron—that is, our mountain of strength—to support and guide us by the aid of your prayers; and direct the censer of your supplications like incense in the presence of the Divinity, so that the lifting up of your hands may be compared with the evening sacrifice.

For we truly trust in God and implore his clemency, that through the supplication of your mouth and your heartfelt prayers he may show us through you what he judges will be beneficial and useful to us—whether to live in our native land or to be exiled in pilgrimage.

Likewise, we ask your piety to deign to send your reply across the sea and answer what we have written in these pages in rustic style and unpolished speech, because we have no confidence in those who glory in appearance and not in heart.

We also ask you, by your faith and charity toward God and your love toward your neighbor, to receive with charity and affection that brother mentioned above without a name, our necessary friend Denewald, if God should arrange or decree that he direct his journey to those parts of the earth and that pilgrimage where you live. If his will or desire requires it, deign with your blessing, grace, and *eulogia* to direct him to the venerable brother named Berther, adorned with the dignity of the priesthood and marked with the title of confessor [Note: “It concerns a confessor.” Concerning the name and distinguished title of confessor, see Saint Cyprian and Baronius in the *Martyrology*, on 2 January. It is possible that this confessor possessed such a status. Yet since the proclamation of the Gospel is called the confession of faith, he may be called a distinguished confessor in the sense that he rendered distinguished service by announcing the Gospel to the nations. —Ser.], who long inhabited that pilgrimage.

Farewell, most faithful and beloved spiritual brother, beloved with sincere and pure affection, and prosper in the Lord who is beloved. A friend is long sought, scarcely found, and difficult to preserve. Pray for us, so that the bitter crimes of our offenses may not harm us.

[Note: This excellent and most learned woman to whom this letter is written is called Buggan, Bugge, and Bugga, as Bedan calls her below in Epistle 9, Beda in Epistle 8, and Bedas [does]. Baronius, p. 53, also notes that she is sometimes called Eadburga. She was born of royal stock and was related to Ethelbert, king of Kent; she was the daughter of Cangith, concerning whom there is frequent mention later in Epistles 13, 14, 20, 21, 28, 35, 40, and elsewhere. There the matters I have mentioned are confirmed, and the occasion of the chaste love that existed between her and Saint Boniface, along with many other things, is shown.

Yet the heading of the Caesarean Epistle 38 causes me some doubt: there she is carefully written not as Edelburg but as Heaburg, and not as Cangyth but as Eangyth, although the alteration of one letter or another could very easily have crept in. Epistle 103 below also testifies that she survived Saint Boniface. Another Edelburga was a queen, book II of Bede’s *History*, chapters 9 and 14, and book IV, chapter 10. Below, however, in Epistle 21, Bugga is the name of a priest.]

## EPISTLE XXXI. BONIFACE TO BUGGA. [A.D. 733]

To the venerable and most beloved sister Buggan, Boniface, who is also Winfridus [Note: “Servant of the servants of God.” Today the supreme pontiffs alone generally retain this title, but formerly others also readily adopted it, since it is both an indication of humility and a kind of reminder of duty. For those who preside over others, since they ought to serve their welfare and advantage—for otherwise their power would be tyrannical—rightly understand themselves to be their servants. “In appearance we surpass the rest in splendor,” says Agamemnon in the poet, “but in truth we are ministers of the multitude.” Plutarch praises Nicias because he considered himself such and actually proved himself to be so. How much more fitting, then, is such a thought and expression for ecclesiastical bishops, whose greatest and first bishop after our Savior Jesus, holy Peter, says in the First Epistle, chapter 5: “Feed the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion but willingly according to God; not for shameful gain but eagerly; not as domineering over the clergy, but becoming examples to the flock from the heart.” And Saint Jerome, on Ephesians 5: “Let bishops hear, let presbyters hear, let every order of teachers hear that they are subject to those under them, and let them imitate the Apostle who says: ‘Although I was free from all, I made myself a servant to all, that I might win all,’” and so forth.

The occasion of this title is said to have arisen with Saint Gregory, in opposition to the pride of John, patriarch of Constantinople, who arrogantly and falsely dared to style himself Ecumenical, or universal, bishop. Concerning him and to him the same Saint Gregory writes in book IV, letters 34, 36, 38, and 39. In the gloss on *C.* “Whenever,” 1, question 7, the following couplet of this kind is reported:

“Rome, once the servants of the Lord of lords were your masters;

the servants of servants are now your masters.”]

the servant of the servants of God: the desired greeting of charity in Christ.

Dearest sister,

[Note: [Col. 0730D] The Paris manuscript reads *priusquam* (“before”), but *prius* and *post* are very frequently confused with one another in the manuscripts. GILES.]

After the fear of Christ and the love of pilgrimage had separated us by a long and broad expanse of land and sea, I heard from the reports of many about the storms of affliction that, with God permitting, have overtaken you in your old age. Stricken with grief, I groaned, reflecting that after you had sought the repose of the contemplative life and had laid aside the greater cares of monasteries, more frequent and more powerful tribulations had confronted you.

Now, venerable sister, sharing in your tribulations, I send you these fraternal, exhortatory, and consolatory letters, mindful of your kindnesses [Col. 0729C] and of our longstanding friendship. I ask that this saying of Truth not slip from your mind, the saying: “By your patience you will possess your souls.” And the word of the wisest Solomon: “Whom God loves, he rebukes,”

[Note: [Col. 0730D] “and chastises.” This is lacking in Manuscript C. I.]

“and he chastises every son whom he receives.” And the Psalmist’s saying: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them from them all.” And elsewhere: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise.”

And remember the apostolic saying in which he declared: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.” And elsewhere: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that [Note: [Col. 0730D] “tribulation.” In C. is added: “And so forth, up to ‘who loved us.’ I have here written out the words in full, and occasionally elsewhere; at other times I have retained this abbreviation, or another, and so forth, such as are customarily used in citing passages from Scripture and other familiar sayings among the Hebrews. So also in Letter 3 and thereafter.] tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing, and testing produces hope; but hope does not disappoint.”

Always rejoice and be glad in this hope, dearest sister, because you will not be disappointed. Despise the tribulations of the world with all the exertion of your mind, [Col. 0730B] because all the soldiers of Christ, of either sex, have despised and regarded as nothing the storms, tribulations, and infirmities of this age. Saint Paul bears witness to this when he says: “When I am weak, then I am strong.” And elsewhere: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Shall anguish, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or persecution, or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we conquer through him who loved us.”

He is the father and lover of your chaste virginity; he who, at the earliest time of your youth, invited you to himself with the voice of paternal love and called you his daughter, saying through the Prophet: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, because the king has desired your beauty.” He is the one who now, in your old age, desires to adorn and embellish the beauty and loveliness [Note: [Col. 0732D] [ [Col. 0731A] This note appears at the foot of column 732, but the callout letter (c) has not been printed in the text.] Wietberga. B. has *Wictburga*, concerning whom see below, Letter 111 (now 123). For further relevant material see Bar., p. 53. SER.] [Col. 0731A] of your soul through labors and tribulations.

But you, dearest, rejoicing in hope of the future inheritance of the heavenly homeland, oppose the shield of faith and patience against every adversity, whether of heart or body. With Christ the Bridegroom cooperating, may you complete in old age, for the glory of God, the building of the Gospel tower that you began in the vigor of youth, so that when Christ comes you may deserve, together with the wise virgins, to carry out to meet him a shining lamp with oil.

[Note: [Col. 0731D] “With the wise.” Matthew XXV.]

Meanwhile, I beg you with the deepest prayers: mindful of our ancient promise, deign to pray for me, so that the Lord, who is our Redeemer and the salvation of all, may rescue my soul from these manifold dangers in spiritual fruitfulness. Farewell in Christ.

## LETTER XXXII. BONIFACE TO BUGGA. [A.D. 733]

[Col. 0731B]

To the most beloved lady and sister in Christ, Buggа, abbess, preferred above all other women in the love of Christ, Boniface, the insignificant and unworthy bishop, sends greetings in Christ.

Dearest sister, let it be known to you concerning that matter about which you questioned me by letter, that I neither dare personally forbid you the journey of pilgrimage nor confidently advise you to undertake it. But I shall say what seems right to me.

If you abandoned the care that you had shown toward the servants and handmaids of God and toward the monastic life in order to obtain repose and contemplation of God, how ought you now, with labor and wearisome anxiety, to serve the words and wishes of secular people? For it seems better to me that, if because of secular people you cannot in your own country possess the freedom of a tranquil mind, you should acquire, through pilgrimage, the freedom of contemplation, if you wish and are able—just as our sister Wetberga did. She informed me by letter that she had found, beside the threshold of Saint Peter, the quiet life that she had long desired and sought.

Regarding your desire, she sent me this message—for I had written to her about you—that you should wait until the rebellions, temptations, and threats of the Saracens that have recently arisen among the Romans have subsided, and until, God willing, she sends you her letter of invitation. This also seems best to me: prepare the necessities for your journey, wait for her message, and afterward do what the Lord’s mercy commands.

As for the compilation of sayings about which you asked, you must pardon my shortcomings, because, owing to pressing labors and continual journeys, I do not yet have what you requested completely written out. But when I have finished it, I shall take care to send it to your presence.

Regarding the gifts—that is, the garments—which you sent, we give thanks and pray to almighty God that he may place for you the reward of eternal recompense with the angels and archangels on the heights of heaven.

I therefore beg you before God, dearest sister—indeed, sweetest mother and lady—to deign to pray for me continually, because for my sins I am wearied by many tribulations and am troubled by a far greater tribulation and anxiety of mind than by bodily labor. Know that the ancient faith between us will never fail. Farewell in Christ.

## LETTER XXXIII. EGBURGA TO WINFRID. [A.D. 733]

To the holy abbot and true friend, rightly and deservedly to be honored, filled with divine knowledge and religious devotion, Winfrid, Egburga, the least of your disciples, male and female, sends eternal health in the Lord.

[Col. 0732B]

I confess that, when through the inner person I tasted the bond of your charity, it was like a kind of honeyed sweetness; this flavor remains within my very entrails. And although, as soon as I obtained it, I was deprived of the sight of you by bodily distance, nevertheless I shall always clasp your neck in the embraces of a sister.

Therefore, my beloved brother of long ago, now you are called both abbot and brother, together with us, in the Lord of lords. For after bitter death and cruel separation took from me my own brother Osher, whom I had been accustomed to love above all others, I preferred you, through the love of charity, to almost everyone else of the male sex.

And, not to prolong my words in various ways, no day turns and no night passes without remembrance of your instruction. Therefore, believe me, with God as my witness, that I embrace you with the highest love, and I trust concerning you that you are never forgetful of the friendship that it was certain you had with my brother.

Although I am slower in knowledge and inferior to him in merit, I am nevertheless not unequal to him in devotion toward your charity. And although the succession of time, running swiftly, has separated us, the dark cloud of grief has never left me; rather, longer periods of time have added greater gains of injury to me, as it is written: “Love of a human being brings grief, but the love of Christ illuminates the heart.”

And after my dearest sister Wetburga suddenly vanished from my eyes—as though from an inflicted wound and renewed grief—she with whom I grew up, with whom I shared the same nurse’s breast, one mother for us both in the Lord, and who abandoned me, I call Jesus to witness: everywhere pain, everywhere fear, everywhere the image of death.

I would have preferred to die, if that had pleased the Lord, under whose auspices nothing hidden remains unknown, or if lingering death had not delayed. But what shall I say now? Before we could foresee it, bitter death did not separate us from one another [W. omits “not”], but a more bitter division: her, as I believe, fortunate; me, unfortunate, whom it permitted, as if some kind of deposit, to serve this age.

Knowing how greatly I loved her and how dearly I cherished her—her whom, as I hear, a prison now confines in the city of Rome—but the love of Christ, which blossomed and flourished in her breast, is stronger and more powerful than every chain, and perfect love casts out fear. Behold, I say, that supreme Ruler of Olympus rejoices with ineffable delight, because he adorns you so with divine teaching and you meditate day and night upon his law, as it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!”

She now walks the steep and narrow path; but I still lie in the lowest places, hindered by the law of the flesh as by a kind of fetter. She, rejoicing, will sing together with the Lord at the future judgment and say: “I was in prison, and you visited me.” But you, at the regeneration, when the twelve apostles sit on twelve thrones, will sit there also, rejoicing before the tribunal of the eternal King as a gilded leader of all whom you have acquired through your own labor.

But I still mourn in the valley of tears, as is deserved, for my own sins, because God had made me unworthy to cling to such companions. Therefore, believe me: no sailor tossed by a storm longs for harbor so greatly, no thirsty fields long for rain so greatly, no anxious mother on the curving shore awaits her son so greatly, as I long to enjoy the sight of you.

But because, on account of my sins and weighed down by countless offenses, I have been driven into despair, so that this might come to pass and I might be released from the dangers threatening me, I, a sinner, prostrate at the feet of your exaltedness, imploring from the innermost recesses of my heart, have cried out to you from the ends of the earth, O most blessed lord. My anxious heart asks you to raise me upon the rock of your prayers, because you have become my hope, a tower of strength against the face of the visible and invisible enemy.

And for the consolation of my immense grief and the calming of the wave of sorrow, I beg that through your intercession my weakness may be supported, as by certain props, so that it may not collapse altogether. Likewise, as a suppliant, I earnestly ask that you deign to send me some consolation, either in holy relics or at least in a few words written by your blessedness, so that in them I may always have your presence. Farewell, living continually in prosperous success before God, and interceding for me three and four times over.

I likewise, Ealdbertus, a poor little servant of Christ, greet you in the Lord with every affection. I beg you to remember in your godly prayers the friendship that you once promised. Although we are separated in body, let us nevertheless be joined in remembrance.

## LETTER XXXIV. CENA TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 733]

[Col. 0733D]

To the venerable bishop Boniface, lover of Christ, Cena, unworthy, sends greetings.

I confess to you now, dearest one, that although I rarely behold you with bodily eyes, I nevertheless do not cease continually to see you with the spiritual lights of my heart. These small gifts are more signs of charity than worthy of your holiness.

I also make this known to you: until the end of my life I shall always remember you in my prayers. And I ask you, by the friendship entrusted between us, to remain faithful to my insignificance, as I trust you; and to assist me in your prayers, so that almighty God may order my life according to his will.

And I ask that, if any of your people should ever come to this province, he may visit my poverty. If in any matter—whether of bodily benefit or spiritual assistance—I can help either you or any of your people, let him inform me, and I shall, for the great salvation of my soul, strive to fulfill your command and instruction according to my strength. Farewell always in the Lord.

## LETTER XXXV. DEN., L., AND B. TO KANEBADA. [A.D. 733]

[Note: [Col. 0733D] *Kanebadae.* This name is written in an unknown script, so that I am uncertain about the final syllable. It was written thus: DAII, except that the lower part of the D was not closed. SER.]

[Col. 0734B]

To the most beloved lady and most religious abbess in Christ, Kanebada, endowed with the nobility of royal lineage, Den., L., and B., your sons and dependents, send greetings of everlasting health.

We wish you to recognize the clemency of your graciousness, because we enclose you above all women within the chamber of our hearts in love: after the death of our father and mother and of our other relatives, we crossed over to the Germanic peoples, and, having been received under the rule of monastic life of the venerable archbishop Boniface, we assist him in his labor insofar as the poverty and lowliness of our nature permit.

Now, therefore, from the innermost recesses of our hearts, we humbly entreat you to deign to include us in the fellowship of your sacred congregation, and not to refuse to lead our little boat, wearied by the stormy waves of this world, to the harbor of salvation under the protection of your prayers.

[Note: [Col. 0734D] “Our little boat.” He also used it as feminine in Book VII; so did Caesar and Tibullus.] Do not refuse to protect us against the black arrows of our offenses with the shield of your prayer, just as we also pray continually, through divine assistance, for the well-being of your exaltedness.

If we were bodily present, we would hope to obtain this by diligent petition, kneeling on bent knees and entreating you amid salty showers of tears; now, though absent, we request the same with urgent prayers.

We also wish your discerning diligence to know that, if it should happen that any one of us visits the scepters of this British land, we shall seek no human obedience or instruction beforehand, but first the submission of ourselves to your benevolence, since we have placed the firmest hope of our minds in you.

Likewise, we beg you to send us, through the bearers of this letter, our two boys, Beiloe and Man, whom I, Lul, and our father [Note: [Col. 0734D] “Our father.” Did Saint Boniface perhaps manumit these boys, that is, these servants?] released as free persons and sent to Rome, entrusting them to our uncle—if they are free by their own will, if it is their desire, and if they are in your power. And if anyone should wish to prevent them from undertaking the journey without justification, we beg you to deign to defend them.

A small transmission of gifts also accompanies this little note: three very modest presents, namely incense, pepper, and cinnamon, but sent with every affection of mind. We ask you not to consider the size of this gift, but to attend to the love of spiritual charity.

We also ask you to correct the rusticity of this little letter and not to refuse to send us some words of your sweetness, which we eagerly and joyfully strive to hear. Farewell, living for the Lord through a longer age and a happier life, and interceding for us.

## LETTER XXXVI. BONIFACE TO ALL CATHOLICS. [A.D. 733]

To all most reverend fellow bishops, venerable priests, candidates for grace, deacons, canons, clerics, abbots and abbesses set over the true flock of Christ, humble monks subject for God’s sake, consecrated and devoted virgins, and all consecrated handmaids of Christ—indeed, generally, to all Catholics fearing God, born from the stock and lineage of the English—Boniface, a native of that same people, legate of the universal Church in Germany, servant of the apostolic see, called archbishop without any claim of merit, sends the greeting of the humblest communion and the most sincere charity in Christ.

[Col. 0735B]

With the deepest prayers we beg your fraternal clemency to deign to remember our insignificance in your prayers, so that we may be delivered from the snare of Satan the hunter and from troublesome and evil men; so that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified; and so that through your devout prayers you may strive to obtain that God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who desires all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of God, may turn the hearts of the pagan Saxons to the Catholic faith, that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by which they are held captive, and be gathered among the children of Mother Church.

Have mercy on them, because they too are accustomed to say:

[Note: [Col. 0735D] “To be of one.” This should be punctuated in this way. For the Saxons said to Saint Boniface and the English preaching Jesus Christ: “We are of one blood and one bone,” because the Saxons who went to England became the English, as I have said in the Mainz material and below, in the note to Letter 19.]

“We are of one blood and one bone.” Remembering that the way of all the earth is drawing near, and that no one in hell will confess the Lord, nor will death praise him—and remembering that the way of all the earth is drawing near—know that in this request I have received the support, agreement, and blessing of two pontiffs of the Roman Church.

[Note: [Col. 0736D] “Two,” namely Gregory II and III.]

Act now on this appeal of ours, so that the rewards of your merit may shine and increase in the heavenly court of the angels. May almighty God and Creator eternally preserve the unity and fellowship of your love, strong and flourishing in Christ.

## LETTER XXXVII. BONIFACE TO CUTHBERT AND OTHERS. [A.D. 735]

To the most beloved and reverend Cuthbert, abbot, and to all the brothers of his holy congregation, Boniface, servant of the servants of God, sends the greeting of fraternal charity in Christ.

With the deepest prayers we beg your fraternal piety to assist us, laboring among the savage and ignorant peoples of Germany and planting the seeds of the Gospel, through your most holy prayers. By the prayers of your holiness, may the fierce heat of the Babylonian flame be extinguished in us, and may what has been scattered in the furrows rise multiplied to full fruit, because, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth.” May it be granted to us “to proclaim the word with the opening of our mouth,” and may the word of the Lord run and be glorified.

Meanwhile, we ask you to deign to send us some [W.: “the remainder”] of the little works of Bede the monk, that most discerning investigator of Scripture, whom we have recently heard shone among you in the house of God like an ecclesiastical candle through his knowledge of Scripture.

And, if it is not burdensome for you, send us one gift [P.: “a bell”], a great consolation to us in our pilgrimage. As a token also of our innermost charity, we have sent you goatskins for bedding, as they are called here. Although they are not worthy, we ask you to accept them in remembrance.

May the gracious Trinity and the one Divinity increase and preserve your fraternity, flourishing and advancing here in holy virtues, and in future blessedness glorify you by rewarding you with joy among the shining ranks of the angels.

## LETTER XXXVIII. BONIFACE TO EGBERT. [A.D. 736]

To Egbert, an archbishop endowed with the insignia of the highest pontificate, a friend embraced in the arms of charity—indeed, a brother joined to us by spiritual kinship—Boniface, an insignificant bishop, legate in Germany of the Catholic and apostolic Church, sends the greeting of unfading charity flourishing in Christ.

We received with grateful and joyful hearts the gifts and little books of your sweetest blessedness that you sent us. Raising our hands toward heaven, we entreated the heavenly King to repay you with the flourishing rewards of your merit in the heavenly court of the angels.

Now, however, we earnestly ask the clemency of your holiness to deign to pray for us who are laboring and in danger, because great necessity presses upon us to seek the assistance of the righteous. For it is written: “The persistent prayer of the righteous is very powerful.”

The brevity of a letter prevents us from recounting all the evils that we suffer outwardly and inwardly. Now, therefore, earnestly desiring and begging, we ask you to send us, for the joy of our sorrow, as you have already done, some small portion or spark from the candle of the Church that the Holy Spirit has kindled in the regions of your province—that is, some portion of the treatises that Bede, that spiritual priest and investigator of the holy Scriptures, composed by opening them up.

Above all, if possible, send what seems to us useful, manageable, and most suitable for our preaching: something on the annual lectionary and on the Proverbs of Solomon, since we have heard that he composed commentaries on them.

[Col. 0737A]

Meanwhile, the greatest necessity compels us to seek your counsel and judgment. I have found a priest who, many years ago, fell into fornication and, after penance, was restored by the Franks to the office of his rank. He now lives in a very extensive district of faithful but erring peoples, and ministers there alone, without other priests, baptizing and celebrating the solemn rites of the Mass.

Now, if I remove such a man according to the strictest canons, infants will die without the holy font of regeneration because of the scarcity of priests, if I have no better man with whom to replace the one who fell. Judge, therefore, between me and the erring people whether it is better—or at least the lesser evil—for such a man to fulfill the ministry of the holy altar, or for a multitude of pagans to die because they cannot acquire a more upright minister.

Or suppose that, among a multitude of priests, I find one who has fallen into the same sin and, after penance, has again been restored to his former rank, and in whom the whole multitude of priests and people has confidence because of his good reputation. If he is now degraded, the hidden sin revealed, the multitude of the common people is scandalized, and through that scandal very many souls perish, there will be the greatest hatred of priests and distrust of the ministers of the Church, so that all will regard them as faithless, trusting no one and despising everyone.

For this reason we have boldly presumed to allow him, with patience and consent, to continue in the divine ministry, judging that the doubtful danger and temerity of one man is lighter than the ruin and destruction of the souls of almost the entire people.

Concerning all these matters, I earnestly desire to learn and hear through your written counsel what I ought to endure, necessity compelling me to avoid scandals, and what I ought to reject.

Furthermore, as a substitute for a kiss, we have sent your exaltedness two little cups of wine through this bearer of the letter, asking that, through our prayers and the charity between us, you make a joyful day of it with your brothers.

We therefore beg you to act concerning these requests of ours so that the rewards of your merit may shine in the heights of heaven.

## LETTER XXXIX. BONIFACE TO PECHTHELM. [A.D. 736]

[Note: [Col. 0737C] *To Pechthelm.* The Venerable Bede writes and describes him in this way in Book V of his *History*, at the final chapter: “Pecthelmus was bishop in that [English] Church which is called Candida Casa; recently, as the populations of the faithful multiplied, it was raised to the rank of a bishopric, and he became its first bishop.” Earlier, in chapter 19, Bede also reported the miracle that is related here concerning the blessed Heddi. And earlier still, in chapter 14, he recounted the story of a dying soldier who rejected confession and despaired.]

To the most beloved and reverend brother, dear to me, Pechthelm, fellow bishop, Boniface, an insignificant servant of the servants of God, sends the desirable greeting of charity in Christ.

With the deepest and most urgent prayers we implore the paternal clemency of your holiness, because, being in danger, we need to be assisted by your prayers worthy of God. Since the German Sea is dangerous for those who sail upon it, may we, with your prayers and under God’s governance, reach the shore of eternal tranquility without stain or damage to our souls.

And while we strive to offer the light of evangelical truth to the blind, who do not know their own darkness and refuse to see, may we not be enveloped in the darkness of our own sins, nor run—or have run—in vain; but, supported by your intercessions, may we proceed unstained and enlightened toward the light of eternity.

Furthermore, we have sent you small gifts as a token of charity: a corporal cloth variegated with white markings and a shaggy cloth for wiping the feet of God’s servants. We ask you not to disdain accepting them in remembrance.

We also desire to hear your counsel and response concerning one matter. Priests throughout France and Gaul, as well as the Romans, assert that a man who takes in marriage the widow whose son he had previously received as an adopted son in baptism is guilty of a very serious crime.

[Note: [Col. 0737C] “He received him as an adopted son.” To adopt a son is one thing; to adopt someone in baptism, or to receive him as an adopted son, is another. [Col. 0737D] This is what was formerly meant by the chapter *In catechismo*, in *De consecratione*, distinction 47, and what today we call being a godfather—or, as Saint Boniface later puts it, in Letter 15, raising someone from the sacred baptismal font.

Some more recent writers call the person who does this the sponsor, the guardian of the sacred initiation. Tertullian, in *On Baptism*, calls him the sponsor of faith; Saint Augustine, in Book I of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 34, and in Letter 25, calls him the one who presents the candidate; the *Life of Saint Epiphanius* in Lipomanus, volume VI, folio 36, calls him the father; the Council of Mainz under Charlemagne, chapter 47, calls him the co-father; Dionysius the Areopagite, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 2, calls him ἀνάδοχον, ἡγεμόνα, and καθηγεμόνα—that is, the sponsor, leader, and spiritual guide.

The Council of Mainz briefly indicates the duty of such a spiritual parent when it says: “We command that the co-fathers or relatives instruct their spiritual children in the Catholic faith.” Saint Augustine treats this and several other matters seriously and elegantly in Sermon 163 *On the Season*, which is the seventh sermon for the octave of Easter; so also does Saint Chrysostom on 1 Corinthians, Homily 12, and the canon *Vos autem*, in *De consecratione*, distinction 4.

Through this notable action, a spiritual kinship usually arises between the sponsor, the baptized person, and both of the baptized person’s parents. Ecclesiastical law prevents marriage among all those whom I have mentioned, and dissolves marriages already contracted, as many canons and chapters teach in canon law, in Gratian, 30, questions 1 and 3, and in the Decretals, and Book VI, concerning spiritual kinship.

God is witness that the importance once assigned to this bond by the Roman pontiffs Julius and Celestine and by various councils is also attested by Pope Deusdedit in his letter to Gordian, bishop of Spain.

If the volumes of canons, and the order and sequence that exist now, had existed in the time of Saint Boniface, he would never have been so greatly uncertain about this question. His diligence in investigating and asking questions, which is praiseworthy here and also in Letters 15 and 22, and his humility of spirit, which deserves to be imitated, are nevertheless commendable: he questioned not only bishops and others, but also his former disciples, now wishing as an elder to be taught by them, as in Letter 22. Moreover, he preferred obediently to submit to the decrees of the Fathers and the Church rather than cling stubbornly to the argument and reasoning behind his doubt, as in Letter 15.

Yet the same reasoning explains why Luther today, in *The Babylonian Captivity*, and Beza, in his book *On Marriage*, boldly and arrogantly oppose all those authorities, scorn all the honor of spiritual kinship, and regard it as nothing. Such, indeed, is the distance between one human being and another: the arrogant person from the modest, the heretic from the Catholic.

See the Council of Trent, Session 24, chapter [Col. 0739C] 2; Bellarmine, *On Marriage*, chapter 30; Zonaras, volume [Col. 0739D] III, on Nicephorus Phocas; the Venerable Bede, Book IV of the *History*, chapter 13; and Aimon, Book IV, chapter 57.]

He had received as an adopted son the son of another man from the sacred baptismal font, and afterward married the boy’s widowed mother. They assert that this is a sin, indeed a capital sin, and command that in such cases the marriage be dissolved. They even maintain that, under Christian emperors, the crime of such a marriage ought to be punished by a capital sentence or removed through perpetual pilgrimage.

If you find that this has been counted as so great a sin in the decrees or canons of the Catholic Fathers, or even in sacred Scripture [W. in the margin: “sacred discourse”], take care to inform me, so that I may understand and know what authority lies behind that judgment.

For I cannot understand at all why spiritual kinship should be such a great sin in the joining of bodily intercourse in one place, when we are all shown to be sons and daughters, brothers and sisters, of Christ and the Church in holy baptism.

I wish you to prosper in holy virtues in Christ and to enjoy long life in Christ.

## LETTER XL. BONIFACE TO NOTHELM. [A.D. 736]

[Note: [Col. 0739D] “In the year 736.” Around the year 736 Boniface went to the lands of the Bavarians, over which Duke Hugbert ruled at that time. Applying himself diligently to preaching among them, he was armed with such zeal for divine devotion that he condemned and expelled from the Church a certain schismatic, Ermwolf by name, full of heretical perversity, in accordance with the decrees of the canons.

After these things had been completed, he returned again to those who lived within the diocese under his governance, visiting every place and restoring whatever the care of the churches required. (Othlo and Willibald.)

Boniface then set out for Rome [A.D. 738], accompanied by a large crowd of Franks and Bavarians, as well as people arriving from Britain. He was presented to the apostolic ruler and kindly received by him. He was held in such great veneration by all the Romans that many flocked to his saving instruction and kept him among them for a long time.

[Col. 0740C] At last he returned from Rome to Germany with relics of the saints and papal letters to various recipients. [Col. 0740D] On his return from Rome, when he was in Bavaria, Boniface received into his care Sturm, who later became the first abbot of Fulda, after his parents had offered him to Boniface. This is clearly indicated by Eigil in his *Life of Sturm*, chapter 2.

He took him with him and entrusted him to Abbot Wigbert at Fritzlar to be educated. There Sturm committed the Book of Psalms to memory, applied himself to sacred Scripture by night and by day, and advanced so far that not long afterward he was ordained priest by common consent. WURDT.]

To Nothelm.

To Nothelm, our most beloved archbishop, endowed with the insignia of the highest pontificate, Boniface, an insignificant servant of the servants of God, sends the desirable greeting of eternal charity in Christ.

[Col. 0739B]

With the deepest prayers I beg the clemency of your graciousness to deign to remember me in your holy prayers and to strive, through your prayers, to establish in the harbor of the firm rock the vessel of my mind, battered by the waves of various storms among the Germanic peoples.

And when I have been joined to you in fraternal fellowship—not otherwise than as your predecessor, Archbishop Berthwald of venerable memory, granted me when I was departing from my homeland—may I deserve, bound to you by a spiritual bond and joined by the glue of charity, likewise [W., in the margin: “together”] to remain associated with you, together with the fraternal companions of my pilgrimage, in the unity of the Catholic faith and the sweetness of spiritual love.

I also earnestly and diligently ask you to take care to send me a copy of that letter which, as they say, contains the questions of Augustine, bishop and first preacher of the English, and the responses of Saint Gregory the pope. Among other chapters it contains the statement that in the third degree of kinship the faithful are permitted to contract marriages.

Take care also, with scrupulous caution, to investigate whether the aforesaid writing can be proved to be the work of our father, Saint Gregory, or not. For, as the officials of the Roman Church affirm, it was sought in the archive of the Roman Church but was not found there among the other copies of the aforesaid pontiff.

Furthermore, I desire to hear your counsel concerning a sin committed, which I unknowingly committed in permitting a certain man to marry. It happened in this way.

[Col. 0740A]

A certain man, as many are accustomed to do, raised the son of another from the sacred baptismal font and adopted him as his own son. Later, he took the boy’s widowed mother as his wife. The Romans assert that this is a sin, and a capital sin, so that they command that marriages of this kind be dissolved. They maintain that, while Christian emperors were reigning, the crime of such a marriage ought to be punished by a capital sentence or removed through perpetual pilgrimage.

If you find that this is counted as so great a sin in the decrees or canons of the Catholic Fathers, or even in sacred discourse [W. in the margin: “sacred eloquence”], take care to inform me, so that I may understand and know what authority lies behind that judgment.

For I cannot understand at all why spiritual kinship should be such a great sin in the joining of bodily intercourse in one place, when we are all shown in holy baptism to be sons and daughters, brothers and sisters, of Christ and the Church.

Likewise, I ask you to take care to inform me in what year from the Incarnation of Christ the first preachers sent by Saint Gregory came to the English people. Farewell.

## LETTER XLI. BONIFACE TO DUDDO. [A.D. 736]

To his beloved son Duddo, abbot, Boniface, also called Winfrid, servant of the servants of God, sends the desirable greeting of charity in Christ.
