I desire you to remember, dearest son, the saying of a certain wise man who said: “Keep your old friend,” so that you may not forget in old age the ancient friendship which we began and maintained long ago in our boyhood, but may remember your father, now decrepit and with all his limbs inclining toward the way of all the earth.

Although I had been a teacher of little learning, nevertheless I strove to be, as you yourself are witness, wholly devoted to you. Remembering that devotion, have pity now on an old man, worn out by the storms of the German sea that buffet him from every side. That is, strive to raise me up by prayers poured out to God and to assist me in the sacred Scriptures, especially in the spiritual treatises of the holy Fathers, because [Note: A spiritual treatise is recognized as a teacher of those who read sacred eloquence. A beautiful thought. For, as he says, the books of laymen are images, as Saint Gregory attests, book VII, letters 53 and 109. Likewise, the books, or treatises, of the holy Fathers are mute teachers of those who read the sacred writings. See, therefore, how Saint Boniface seeks and requests books from every quarter: above, letters 8 and 9; below, 28, 35, 40, 85, 104, and 150; and his disciple and successor, Saint Lull, letters 89, 95, 99, 109, and 111. SER.] a spiritual treatise is recognized as a teacher of those who read sacred eloquence.

I ask you to be so kind as to send me, for assistance in divine knowledge, the part of the treatise on the Apostle Paul which I lack. For I possess treatises on two Epistles, namely, on Romans and on the First to the Corinthians. Likewise, whatever you discover in your sacred study and judge to be useful to me, and think that I either do not know or do not possess in writing, kindly disclose to me, as a faithful son to a rustic father, and deign to direct to me written replies from your blessedness. And, if it pleases you, let us always both do this in our dealings with one another.

Whatever my son, the priest Eoba, the bearer of my letters, tells you verbally [Note: On marriage. Above, letter 11 (now 39).] concerning the marriage of the women whose children we received in baptism, seek in the Scriptures the grounds on which it is judged to be a capital sin among the Romans. And if anywhere in ecclesiastical writings you find anything discussed concerning this sin, do not hesitate to make it known to me. We wish your beloved blessedness to remain well and to prosper in Christ through favorable success.

## LETTER XLII. BONIFACE TO GEPPAN AND OTHERS. [A.D. 738.]

To our dearest sons Geppan and Eoban, Tatwino and Wigbert, and to all our brothers and sisters, Boniface, servant of the servants of God: salvation in Christ through pure charity.

[Note: Geppan and Eoban, Tatwino, etc. Serarius writes in the margin that, instead of Tatwino, Tacuino should be read, and that Wixi is the same as Wygb. Hence, in the Imperial Codex which he used, Wixi is written, which he interprets as Wygbert. But another reading is suggested by letter 17, in which both in the heading and throughout the letter Tatuvinus and Abbot Tatuvinus are mentioned; the former was a monk, the latter abbot of Fritzlar. The Roman copy obtained by Baronius is also corrupt in the name Tatuvinus; and since its heading reads, “To Eoban, Tacuino, Wyz, and all the brothers,” it appears that both Wyz and Wixi are corrupt names and should not be understood as referring to Wigbert. In this letter Boniface says: “The apostolic pontiff gladly and joyfully received us,” etc. But now, while we await here the council of priests or the synod’s decision, we still do not know when the apostolic pontiff will cause this to take place. Baronius explains these words as referring to some synod to be convened at Augsburg, and from them concludes that the letter was sent from there. Yet the words of Gregory’s letter to the bishops established in the province of Bavaria and Alemannia—the forty-fifth in order, brought from Rome by Boniface—show that this letter was written at Rome and that Boniface was speaking of a synod to be held there. In it Pope Gregory says: “According as you have been instructed by our aforesaid fellow priest”—namely, Boniface—“so, holding to Catholic and apostolic doctrine, may you please the Lord our God and Savior. Wherever he commands you to assemble for the celebration of councils, whether beside the Danube, or in the city of Augsburg, or wherever he shall judge, may you be found ready for the name of Christ.” Therefore, when Boniface writes in letter 27 that he is waiting to see when the Roman pontiff will cause a synod to be held, this cannot be understood as referring to a synod to be convened in Germany, since the place and time of its proclamation would depend on Boniface’s decision. Whether that Roman synod was later held, none of the ancients reports. WURDT.]

Let it be known to your charity, and give thanks to God, [Col. 0742A] because, having come safely to the threshold of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the apostolic pontiff received us gladly and joyfully, gave us favorable answers concerning our mission, and issued counsel and instructions that we should return to you and persevere in the work we have begun.

But now, while we await here the counsel of the priests, or the decision of the synod, we still do not know when the apostolic pontiff will cause this to take place. Once it has been completed, however, God willing and life permitting, we shall hasten into your presence.

Knowing this, await us with fraternal charity and unity of faith, bearing one another’s burdens; thus you will fulfill the law of Christ and renew our joy. Farewell in Christ, and pray for us.

## LETTER XLIII. GREGORY TO ALL THE BISHOPS. [A.D. 739.]

[Col. 0742B]

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops dear to us, the venerable priests, and the religious abbots of all the provinces.

“With the Lord working together and confirming the word . . . the most holy man,” etc. (See above, letter 2 of Pope Gregory III.)

## LETTER XLIV. GREGORY TO ALL THE NOBLES OF GERMANY. [A.D. 739.]

Pope Gregory to all the nobles and the people of the provinces of Germany: the Thuringians and Hessians, the Borthari, [Col. 0743A] the Nistresi, Wedrevi and Lognai, the Suduosi and the inhabitants of Grabfeld, and all those established in the eastern region.

[Note: Thuringians. Thuringians. Here, and in letters 119 and 129 (now 8 and 45), various names are read incorrectly in volume II of the Councils. Here, indeed, the familiar Thuringians and Hessians occur, whereas earlier, in letter 62, they were written Tyringi, and in letter 98, Tiringi.

But Borthari—whether Bojani or Bojoarii?—are perhaps rather those neighboring the Hessians who are called Boraburg or Varburg and inhabit the boundaries of Fritzlar and Paderborn.

The Nistresi are westerners; for some writers call Neustria and Neustresia the western kingdom, which others call Westerreichia, just as Austria, or Oesterreichia, is the eastern kingdom. Aimoinus shows this in book IV, chapter 57; Beatus, book I, folios 62 and 75. Even today the French say Austrice or Austrio for Österreich, and Italians still readily end ethnic names in -esi, as in Francesi, Portugalesi, and Anglesi.

The Wedrecii—or, as they are written in Othlonus, book I, chapter 37, Wedrevi—are the Wederavi. Their Wederavia, being near Mainz, is also well known, taking its name from the river Wedera.

There are still some monasteries in that region which retain the Catholic faith, but the two principal men's monasteries are Elfestattense, mentioned in the Life of Count Godfrey, and Arnesburg, through which the river Wedera, mentioned shortly before, flows.

The Lognai are inhabitants of the same Wederavia, beside the river called Lan or Logana, as are the Lichenses. At Zosimus, the emperor Probus defeated the German nation of the Logiones.

The Sudvodi are southerners, as though Sudwohni, that is, “southern inhabitants.” Thus, in Tacitus, in his book On Germany, the Ingevones are thought to be the inland and inner Germans, as in Bede, book III of the History, chapter 21, the Middelengi.

Unless the foregoing is intended, four regions of peoples seem to be indicated here: Nistresi, westerners; Westdrevi, easterners; Nordai, northerners; and Sudvodi, southerners. From these names came Nordmanni, Northumbri, and Venti, names used today among the Belgians and Saxons and formerly also among the Franks, as Einhard writes in his Life of Charlemagne.

Finally, the Graffeldi are called Grabfeldi in Othlonus, and sometimes Grapfeldi, as also in the Frankish annals of Pithoeus, under the year 850 [Col. 0743C] in Baronius, volume IX. In the Frankfurt edition they appear as Grabfelden. They seem to have been people who, after cutting down the forests that stood there, laid out new fields and made gardens, meadows, and newly cleared lands.

In the territory of Fulda and in Eisfeld, because roderen and raderen mean “to cut out roots” or “to uproot completely,” many villages are found whose names end in -rod and -rad. There is also Könighofen im Grabfeldt in Franconia. WURDT.]

Since our predecessor Gregory, bishop of blessed memory, etc. (See above, letter 3 of Pope Gregory III.)

[Note: Equipped with these letters, Boniface departed from Rome after having spent nearly a year there. On reaching the city of Pavia, he stayed for some time with Liutprand, king of the Lombards. From there, invited by Duke Otilo, he visited the lands of the Bavarians and remained there many days, preaching the word of God and renewing the sacraments of the true faith. Among other things, he drove away certain destroyers of churches and seducers of the people. Some of these falsely claimed the rank of bishop; others had assigned themselves to the office of priest; still others, following countless fabrications of perversity, had led a large part of the people astray.

Then, with Duke Otilo’s agreement, he divided the province of Bavaria into four dioceses and placed over them three men of great virtue, whom he elevated to the episcopal rank by ordination. The first, named John, received the episcopal see in the town called Salzburg. The second, Erinbert, assumed episcopal government in the church of Freising. The third, Gowibolt, was appointed bishop in the city of Regensburg, which is the metropolis of Bavaria. Vivalus, already ordained by the apostolic bishop, was also placed over the church of Passau; but his diocese, which was the fourth, was divided by Saint Boniface like the others.

Boniface reported all these events in the Bavarian lands to the pontiff, who praised and approved everything. WURDT.]

## LETTER XLV. GREGORY TO THE BISHOPS OF BAVARIA AND ALEMANNIA. [A.D. 739.]

To our dearest bishops established in the province of Bavaria and Alemannia: Wigo, Luid, Rudolt, and Vivilo.

The authority of the Catholic faith and of the holy Fathers commands, etc. (See above, letter 4 of Pope Gregory III.)

## LETTER XLVI. GREGORY TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 739.]

[Col. 0743B]

To the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop, Gregory, servant of the servants of God.

It is the voice of the outstanding teacher of the nations and blessed apostle Paul, etc. (See above, letter 7 of Pope Gregory III.)

## LETTER XLVII. BONIFACE TO REGENBERTH. [A.D. 742.]

To the most illustrious son Regenberth, prefect, Boniface, servant of the servants of God: everlasting salvation in the Lord.

We beseech the clemency of your dignity through our prayers: permit this bearer of my letters, who is traveling to Rome for ecclesiastical replies and for the sake of prayer, to pass safely through your territories, and deign to assist him in his personal needs, as you did for my previous messengers, as they reported to me on their return.

[Note: “Messenger.” In that age this was a very common name for a messenger or letter-carrier, as above and below, letters 75, 91, 104, and 107. He is also often called a bearer or carrier, letters 33, 35, 39, 40, and 72. In the Constitutions of Charlemagne and the gloss, chapter 1, On the Immunity of the Church, it is said that missus is the common Italian word, 102 and 110; and see Cassiodorus, book I of the Variorum, final letter; book VIII, chapter 8; book VIII, letter 10; Isidore, book VI of the Etymologies, chapter 8; and the Theodosian Code, “If a certain thing is requested,” On Documents: bearers and carriers of money. Among the ancients, portitores otherwise means tax collectors who, sitting at the harbor, questioned everyone in order to collect a tax from them. NONIUS.]

Act, therefore, concerning this request, so that your reward before God may increase and multiply. Farewell in Christ.

## LETTER XLVIII. ZACHARIAS TO THE BISHOPS AND OTHERS THROUGHOUT GAUL. [A.D. 742.]

Pope Zacharias to all the bishops, priests, deacons, abbots, and also all the dukes, counts, and all who fear God established throughout Gaul and the Frankish provinces.

Our most reverend and holy brother reported to us, etc. (See below, letter 4 of Pope Zacharias.)

## LETTER XLIX. BONIFACE TO ZACHARIAS. [A.D. 742.]

To the most beloved lord Zacharias, an apostolic man adorned with the insignia of the highest pontificate, Boniface, servant of the servants of God.

We confess, Lord Father, that after we heard from messengers who brought the report that Gregory, pontiff of the apostolic See and your predecessor of venerable memory, had been released from the bodily prison and had departed to the Lord, we never heard anything that gave us greater happiness and joy, nor did we give thanks to God with palms raised toward heaven, than that the Most High Judge had granted your merciful fatherhood to govern the canonical laws and direct the helm of the apostolic See.

Therefore, kneeling before your feet, we earnestly beseech you with the deepest prayers that, just as, by the authority of Saint Peter, we were devoted servants and obedient subject-disciples of your predecessors, so we may also deserve to become obedient servants and subjects of your piety under canonical authority. We desire to preserve the Catholic faith and the unity of the Roman Church, and I do not cease inviting and inclining to obedience to the apostolic See as many hearers or disciples as God grants me in this mission.

We must also inform your fatherhood that, by God’s grace, after traveling through and somewhat correcting the peoples of Germany, we ordained three bishops and divided the province into three dioceses. We earnestly ask that the three towns or cities in which they have been established and ordained be confirmed and secured by letters of your authority.

We have decreed that one episcopal see shall be in the fortress called [Note: Würzburg. Everything concerning these matters is clear from the notes on Saint Kilian and from book III of the Mainz history.] Würzburg; another in the town called Buraburg; and the third in the place called Erfurt, which was formerly a city of pagan rustics. We earnestly request that these three places be strengthened and confirmed by a charter and authority proper to your Apostolate, [Col. 0745A] so that, if the Lord wills, through the authority and command of Saint Peter and by apostolic orders, three episcopal sees in Germany may be founded and established, and so that present or future generations may not presume either to corrupt the dioceses or to violate the command of the apostolic See.

Let it likewise be known to your fatherhood that Carloman, duke of the Franks, summoned me and asked me to convene a synod in that part of the Frankish kingdom which lies under his power. He promised that he wished to correct and reform something concerning ecclesiastical religion, which had been trampled upon and thrown into disorder for a long time—namely, for no fewer than sixty or seventy years.

Therefore, if, inspired by God, he truly wishes to fulfill this plan, he must have and understand the instruction and command of your authority, that is, of the apostolic See. For, as the elders say, the Franks have held no synod for more than eighty years, have had no archbishop, and have neither founded nor renewed the canonical rights of the churches for anyone.

Now, for the most part, episcopal sees in the cities have been handed over for possession to greedy laymen, or to adulterous clerics, fornicators, and publicans, for secular enjoyment. If, then, at the request of the duke mentioned above, I am to remove and correct this situation through your word, I desire to have at hand the command and judgment of the apostolic See together with the ecclesiastical canons.

If I find among them deacons who, from their childhood, have always lived in fornication, always in adultery, and always in every kind of uncleanness; who have come to the diaconate under such a reputation; and who now, while serving as deacons, have four or five or more concubines at night in their beds, yet neither blush nor fear to read the Gospel and call themselves deacons; and if, advancing in such incestuous conduct to the order of priesthood, they persist in the same sins and add sin to sin, perform the priestly office, and claim that they can intercede for the people and offer sacred oblations; and, finally, what is worse, if, ascending step by step under such reputations, they are ordained and called bishops—if, I say, I find such men among them, I ask that I may have a command, written by your authority, in which you define the status of such men, so that by an apostolic reply they may be convicted and condemned as sinners.

Some bishops are also found among them who, although they say that they are not fornicators or adulterers, are drunkards and violent men, or hunters, and men who fight armed in the army and shed human blood with their own hands, whether that of pagans or Christians. And since I am recognized as a servant and legate of the apostolic See, let there be one word—mine here and yours there—so that, if necessary, we may jointly send messengers for judgment by your authority.

Furthermore, I must ask your counsel and permission concerning one matter. Your predecessor of venerable memory, as you have heard, commanded me in your presence to appoint, after my death, if God willed, a priest as my heir and successor in ecclesiastical service. If this is God’s will, it pleases me. But now I am uncertain and do not know whether it can be done, because afterward that man’s brother killed the uncle of the duke of the Franks, and we still do not know how this disagreement can be reconciled and brought to an end.

I ask, therefore, that I may have permission from your authority, so that, with the counsel of the servants of God, I may make concerning this election whatever may seem best to us jointly, for God, for the usefulness or spiritual fruit of the Church, and for the defense of religion. Thus may I have your consent to do what God may inspire me to judge best, since this seems unable to be done if the prince is opposed.

Furthermore, I must seek and ask your fatherly counsel concerning a certain confusion and scandal in preaching which recently came to us and troubled our mind, while bringing shame upon the priests of the churches. A certain layman of high rank came to us and said that he had received permission from Gregory, the pontiff of the apostolic See, of holy memory, to take as his wife the widow of his uncle. She herself had also been the wife of his cousin, and while the latter was alive she had left him. The man who now desires to take her as his wife claims that permission was granted to him, although he is recognized as being related to her in the third degree. She had also vowed a vow of chastity and had been veiled, but afterward cast off the veil and married.

The man mentioned above claims that such a marriage was permitted to him by the apostolic pontiff. We do not consider this true, because the synod and Church in which I was born and raised—that is, in transmarine Saxony—the synod of London, which was first established and organized by the disciples of Saint Gregory, namely, the archbishops Augustine, Laurence, Justus, and Mellitus, judged such a union and marriage, on the authority of sacred Scripture, to be a very great crime, incest, a horrible outrage, and a damnable sacrilege.

Therefore, may your fatherhood not disdain to reveal the truth of this matter, so that scandals, schisms, or new errors may not arise and grow from it among the priests of the Church or the Christian people. For carnal people—the ignorant Alemanni, Bavarians, or Franks—[Note: “If near the city of Rome.” As the whole world is shaped according to the example of its king, so also according to the customs of that city which, as Horace says in book IV of the Odes, is “the foremost of cities”; and as Saint Jerome says at the end of his commentary on Ephesians, “mistress of cities, citadel of the Roman empire”; in the preface to Ezekiel, “the clearest light of all lands”; as Rutilius says, “the most beautiful queen of this world”; and as Saint Chrysostom says, Homily 2 on Romans: “The summit of cities, toward which all the inhabited world looked.”

But just as, again, those who wish to detract from the glory of great men and princes, or at least to excuse or dignify their own wickedness through them, repeatedly recount all their faults—magnifying the small ones and enlarging the great ones beyond measure—so it also happens with the sins of the city of Rome. Very false reports are often brought from there; minor things are exaggerated, and great things are made enormous and immense, as you see once and again in this very letter. It is as though any royal city in this world were so beautiful that it had no sewers; any house so clean that it contained no cheap or dirty vessels; any flame so bright that it produced no smoke or smoky residue.

It generally happens that wherever many people gather, many vices also gather, as Josephus indicates in book I Against Apion. And although these vices are sometimes drained away or blocked up—for the vigilant eye of pastoral care ought to provide for this—they nevertheless flow back and grow again little by little, as Zacharias rightly indicates here.

It is the part of the prudent to direct their eyes and minds to the many good things that are in Rome and turn them away from its evils. Each person will bear his own burden.

It happened in recent years that two distinguished noblemen from Germany went to Rome: one a Catholic, the other a heretic. The first visited churches, hospitals, religious associations, libraries, and the homes of learned men; the other lingered in inns and taverns or inspected everything else. When they returned, one praised Rome at a gathering of friends, while the other condemned it. Some of the simpler guests were astonished at so great a difference between the eyes of the two witnesses. Then one of the wiser men said: “Does not the bee and the spider often approach the same garden and the same flower? But the bee draws honey from it, while the spider draws poison. There is one odor at altars, another at pigsties.”

See Baronius, p. 145, and book XII, “Sed licet,” in the Digest, On the Duties of the Governor, where Proculus wisely says: “One should consider not so much what has been done at Rome as what ought to be done.” SER.] if they see anyone near the city of Rome doing any of the sins that we forbid, think that it is lawful and permitted by the priests, and count it as a reproach against us; they take it as a scandal to their own lives.

They claim that each year they have seen, in the city of Rome and near a church, by day or night, when [Note: The Kalends of January. Letter 128, p. 177; penitential canon 88, On Those Who Observe the Kalends of January; Burchard of Worms, book I, chapter 94; book X, chapters 16 and 17; book XIX, chapter 5; Saint Ambrose, sermon 11; Saint Augustine, on Psalm 98, and volume X, in the fragment On the Kalends of January; Saint Chrysostom, homily On the Kalends; Chrysologus, folio [Col. 0748C] 55; the Council of Tours, chapter 23; the Council of Auxerre, chapter 1. SER.] the Kalends of January arrive, people lead dances through the streets according to pagan custom, celebrate acclamations in the manner of the Gentiles and sacrilegious songs, load tables with food on that day or night, and refuse to lend anyone from their household fire, an iron tool, or any useful object to a neighbor.

They also say that they have seen women there, in pagan fashion, wearing amulets and bindings tied around their arms and legs, and publicly offering them for sale so that others may purchase them. Because these things are seen there among carnal and foolish people, they produce for us here both reproach [Col. 0747B] and an impediment to preaching and teaching.

Of such things the Apostle says in rebuke: “You observe days and seasons; I fear that I have labored among you in vain.” And [Note: Saint Augustine. Lipsius of Leuven thinks that this sermon, 241, On Time, bears the phraseology of Severianus. Yet this pontiff transcribes it precisely as Saint Augustine’s. Concerning amulets, I spoke in book II of Trithemius, chapter 3. SER.] Saint Augustine said: “For whoever has believed in the evils mentioned above—that is, [Note: Caragi. Perhaps the word was Phoenician, since Saint Augustine uses it once and again in that vernacular expression. Among the Greeks, at least, κάραγος, according to Hesychius, is a great and shrill sound, such as a saw makes. Or perhaps caragi are those who, through certain incantations, inflict κάρος—that is, heavy sleep and drowsiness—on people? For certain herbs and some incantations have a soporific power. SER.

Caragus means the same as a sorcerer or deceiver who uses magical characters. The Council of Auxerre, chapter 4: ‘It is not permitted to consult sorcerers, omens, or caragi.’ The canons of the old Council of Narbonne, A.D. 598, canon 14: ‘If any men or women diviners, whom they call charagi and sorticularii,’ etc. The Life of Saint Eligius, written by Saint Audoenus, book II, chapter 15: ‘You shall observe none of the customs of the pagans; do not presume to consult caraji, diviners, or enchanters . . .’ And shortly afterward: ‘Let no enchanters, diviners, sorcerers, or caragi be sought.’ WURDT.] caragi, diviners, haruspices, amulets, or any other kinds of omens—and even if he fasts, prays, runs constantly to church, gives abundant alms, and torments his body with every affliction, none of this will benefit him so long as he has not abandoned those sacrileges.”

For if your fatherhood prohibits these pagan practices there in the city of Rome, you will acquire both a reward for yourself and the greatest benefit for us in ecclesiastical instruction.

The bishops and priests of the Frankish people who were adulterers or most persistent fornicators—whose sons born of fornication convict them [Col. 0747C] of this—returning from the apostolic See, say that the Roman pontiff gave them permission to exercise the episcopal ministry in the Church. We dispute this, because we have never heard that the apostolic See judged contrary to the decrees of the canons.

We make all these matters known to you, dearest lord, so that we may give such men a reply based on your authority, so that through the caution of your teaching the sheep of the Church may not be led astray, but the ravening wolves, convicted and overcome, may perish.

Meanwhile we have sent you small gifts—not because they are worthy of your fatherhood, but as tokens of charity, obedience, and devotion: one [Note: “Villosam.” Villosa were called rough towels, or shaggy linen cloths used for wiping the feet or hands. The term occurs several times in the letters of Boniface. In the Chronicle of Fontanelle: “shaggy linens for wiping the hands.” WURDT.

Rather, it occurs only once or twice in Boniface’s letters; for example, on page 40, where see what I noted. GILES.] rough towel, and a little silver and gold.

With the right hand of the Lord protecting you, we wish your blessedness to remain safe and prosper in Christ through length of days.

May God, enthroned on high, preserve you in the holy sanctuary,

And may he make long the years of the ruler of the apostolic See [Note: “Long.” B has “for a long time,” and the most reverend Baronius thinks that one verse is missing here; but the sense is sound even if none is missing: “May he perfect you with honey-flowing doctrine and pious grace.” SER.

Therefore, in the text, *pious grace* should be restored in place of *pre-grace*. EDIT.]

May honey-flowing doctrine throughout the world

Make you pleasing to the peoples, and may the pious grace of Christ make you worthy of God.

May the flourishing mother receive her splendid joys,

And may the house of the Lord rejoice in a second offspring.

## LETTER L. ZACHARIAS TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 742.]

To the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, bishop, Zacharias, servant of the servants of God.

Having received the letters of your most holy brotherhood through Denehard, your religious priest, etc. (See below, letter 1 of Pope Zacharias.)

[Note: This letter is placed as number 131 in the Serrarian edition; letter 133 is of the same tenor and is headed: “To our beloved Burchard, of the holy church of Würzburg, Zacharias, pope. With the Lord working,” etc.

Concerning the same letter Serrarius notes: “If a proper chronological order of the letters were established, this letter 131 would be placed before 132 and 142. In the heading of this letter, first, instead of *to our dearest ones*, one should read *to our dearest one*, as it appears in volume II of the Councils and in Baronius. The error seems to have arisen because this letter was common to three bishops mentioned in it. But was it common in such a way that only one copy was sent from Rome, or were three copies sent, one to each? Baronius seems to think the former, in the year 742, and the plural heading supports him. But in that case not merely one bishop’s location should have been named, but the other two as well. Moreover, in letter 133 the same letter appears with the bishop’s name changed, so that it is evident that a third copy was likewise addressed to the third bishop.

Second, instead of Wittanae, as it is read in Baronius and volume II of the Councils, one finds Witta; this is the man elsewhere called Albuinus, Albinus, and Alboinus. Third, Barbarana is the name of the church over which Witta, or Albinus, presided. For if, according to the old orthography, b is changed into u, we shall have either Varvar or Varbar, which today is Varburg, formerly Buriburg or Buraburg, letter 132. Hence in another codex it is written “church of Birburg.” WURDT.]

## LETTER LI. ZACHARIAS TO WITTA. [A.D. 742.]

[Col. 0749A]

To our dearest Witta, of the holy church of Barbarana, Pope Zacharias.

With the Lord working together and confirming the word, for the extension of the law of Christianity, etc. (See below, letter 3 of Pope Zacharias.)

## LETTER LII. BONIFACE TO EGBERT. [A.D. 742.]

[Note: Ecberht. In the Epitome of Bede, under the year 732: “Egbert was made bishop of York in place of Wilfrid.” Later, under the year 735: “Bishop Egbert, having received the pallium from the apostolic See, was confirmed as archbishop, the first after Paulinus”; his death is recorded there under the year 766, and he is said to have been endowed with royal lineage and imbued with divine knowledge.

Another man, however, is the one who brought the Scots of Iona over to the Catholic Easter, in book V of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 23; he died joyfully on the very day of Catholic Easter in the year 728, or, in the Epitome, 729.]

To the most beloved and reverend brother Egbert, archbishop, Boniface, servant of the servants of God, Germanic legate of the apostolic See: sincere greeting in Christ, in spiritual brotherhood.

Having received the gifts and books from your Charity, I raised my hands on high and gave great thanks to almighty God, who granted me, journeying so far from home, to find such a friend—one who sent me assistance in earthly matters and, in spiritual matters, divine consolation through prayer and the unity of communion.

Now, with the innermost prayers of my heart, I beg the clemency of your Holiness that I may be counted as united with the synod of your brotherhood, together with the servants of God laboring with me; and that you may be my counselor and helper in seeking out and investigating the ecclesiastical regulations concerning the judgments of God. Know that I am not addressing you with the playful voice of idle words, but in a deliberate and orderly manner; and do not judge me arrogant, proud, or excessively pleased with my own judgment.

For when the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church sent an unworthy and insignificant preacher to preach to the erroneous or pagan peoples of Germany, it commanded me, by the authority of the Roman pontiff, that if anywhere, while traveling among Christians, I should see erroneous peoples, ecclesiastical regulations corrupted by evil custom, or people led astray from the Catholic faith by a devious path, I should strive with all my strength to invite and restore them to the way of salvation.

Desiring to observe this command, I sent an admonitory or petitionary letter to King Ethel­bald of the Mercians, with the counsel and consent of the bishops who are with us.

[Note: Ethel­bald. Venerable Bede, Book V, final chapter: “Edilbald, king of the Mercians”; and in the *Epitome*, under the year 740: “Edilwald.” In Baronius, *Athebaldus*; and under 757 again *Edilbaldus*, where his wretched murder is discussed. More on him below, Letters 10, 12, and 19.] I ordered it to be presented to your brotherhood’s sight, so that, if anything in it has been wrongly set down, you might correct it; that you might season what is right with the salt of your wisdom and confirm it by your authority; and that, if you should see any root of the crimes discussed in that letter against the Mercian king beginning to grow among your people, you, like a prudent and wise cultivator, might cut it off in time with the sickle of the Lord’s authority and uproot it completely—lest, when it has blossomed, their vine become a vine of Sodom, their stock a shoot of Gomorrah, and their wine the gall of dragons and the incurable poison of asps.

For it is an unheard-of evil in past ages and, as the servants of God who know the Scriptures say, surpasses Sodomite lust threefold or fourfold: that a Christian people should, contrary to the custom of the whole earth—indeed, contrary to God’s command—despise lawful marriages, cling to incestuous and lustful adulteries, and pursue the unspeakable fornications of consecrated and veiled women.

Moreover, may you kindly write and send me some treatises from the works of Bede the reader, whom, as we recently heard, divine grace has enriched with spiritual understanding and permitted to shine in your province, so that we too may enjoy the candle which the Lord has granted you.

Meanwhile, as a token of affection, I have sent your brotherhood copies of the letters of Saint Gregory, which I took from the archive of the Roman Church and did not think had reached Britain. I shall send more again if you command it, for I took many copies from there; also a corporal cloth (*pallium corporale*) and one shaggy cloth for wiping the feet of the servants of God after they have washed.

We wish your Blessedness health and progress in sacred virtues through Christ.

## LETTER LIII. BONIFACE TO ETHELBALD [A.D. 742]

To the most reverend and beloved lord Ethel­bald, king of the Mercians, Boniface, servant of the servants of God, sends the greeting of profound charity.

We beseech the clemency of your Highness to deign to offer assistance and help to this messenger of mine, named Ceola, the bearer of these letters, in our need, on his journey, and in whatever necessity may befall him; and may you receive a reward from God [P. reads: “for God”] on his behalf and for our messengers who came to you last year, since, as they reported, you gave them assistance in everything.

Meanwhile, as a sign of true love and devoted friendship, we have sent you one goshawk, two falcons, two shields, and two spears. Although these little gifts are not worthy, we ask that, for the sake of charity, you deign to accept them as a blessing.

Let us all hear the conclusion of the matter: Fear God and observe his commandments.

We also ask that, if our words written to your presence reach you through another messenger, you deign to lend them your hearing and take care to listen attentively.

Farewell in Christ.

## LETTER LIV. ZACHARIAS TO BONIFACE [A.D. 743]

To the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, Zacharias.

We have read in the Book of the Acts of the Apostles, etc. (See below, Letter 5 of Pope Zacharias.)

## LETTER LV. ZACHARIAS TO BONIFACE [A.D. 743]

To the reverend brother Boniface, Zacharias, servant of the servants of God.

Having received the letters of your holy brotherhood through the bearer of this letter, etc. (See below, Letter 6 of Pope Zacharias.)

## LETTER LVI. ZACHARIAS TO BONIFACE [A.D. 744]

To the reverend and most holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop, Zacharias, servant of the servants of God.

Virgil and Sedonius, devout men, etc. (See below, Letter 7 of Pope Zacharias.)

[Note: The first letters of Pope Gregory II to Boniface, granting permission to preach the Gospel to the peoples, were issued on the Ides of May, in the third year of the emperor Leo’s reign, the second indiction—that is, in the year 719. But Boniface, having gone to Rome from the year 717 onward, had dedicated himself to the apostolic ministry; from 717 to 745 there are nearly thirty years. See Letter 118 among those edited by Serarius. WURDT.]

## LETTER LVII. BONIFACE TO ZACHARIAS [A.D. 744]

To the most excellent Father and apostolic pontiff, Pope Zacharias, relying on the authority and teaching of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, Boniface, the insignificant servant of the servants of God, sends the desirable greeting of charity in Christ.

After I had bound myself by an earlier vow, nearly thirty years ago, to the familiarity and service of the Apostolic See, with the assent and command of the apostolic bishop Gregory, of venerable memory, I was accustomed to report to the apostolic pontiff whatever joy or sorrow befell me, so that we might praise God together in times of joy and so that I might be strengthened by his counsel in times of sorrow. As then, so now I beseech your Piety that I may do so, as it is written: “Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you.”

Let it therefore be known to your Fatherhood that, after you entrusted me, unworthy as I am, with presiding over a priestly council and synodal assembly in the province of the Franks, as they themselves had requested, I endured many injuries and persecutions, especially from false priests, adulterous deacons, and fornicator clerics.

My greatest labor, however, was against two utterly wicked and notorious heretics who blaspheme against God and the Catholic faith. One of them, called Aldebert, is a Gaul by nation and descent; the other, called Clement, is a Scot by descent. They differ in the form of their error but are equal in the weight of their sins.

Against these men I beseech your apostolic authority to defend and assist my insignificance and, by your letters, to correct the Frankish and Gallic people, so that they do not follow the fables of heretics, empty wonders, and signs of the Antichrist’s forerunner, but return to canonical law and the way of true teaching.

I also ask that, by your word, these two heretics be committed to prison, if this seems just to you, once I have made their life and teaching known to you; and that no one speak with them or share communion with them, lest someone, leavened by the ferment of their teaching, perish. Let them live separated, and, in accordance with the apostle’s dictum concerning such men, let them be “handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.” In accordance with the Gospel command, until they listen to the Church, let them be to us “as the heathen and the tax collectors,” until they learn not to blaspheme or tear Christ’s tunic.

Because of these men I suffer persecutions, hostility, and the curses of many peoples, and the Church of Christ endures an impediment to faith and holy teaching. For they say of Aldebert that I have taken away from them a most holy apostle, their patron and intercessor, and a worker and demonstrator of miracles.

But let your Piety, after hearing of his life, judge from the fruit of his works whether he is a wolf in sheep’s clothing, or not. From his earliest age he was a hypocrite, saying that an angel of the Lord in human form had brought him relics of marvelous yet uncertain sanctity from the ends of the earth, and that by means of them he could obtain from God whatever he asked.

Then, through that deception, as the apostle Paul foretold, he entered the houses of many and led captive little women burdened with sins and driven by various desires. He deceived a multitude of country people, who said that he was a man of apostolic holiness and performed signs and wonders.

Afterward he brought together unlearned bishops, who, contrary to the commands of the canons, irregularly ordained him as bishop without a canonical title. [Note: *Ordinarunt*: that is, [they ordained] him bishop. SER.] Finally, he was so lifted up in pride that he made himself equal to the apostles of Christ. He disdained consecrating a church in honor of any apostle or martyr, reproaching people even for taking such great pains to visit the thresholds of the holy apostles.

Later—in an absurd act—he dedicated chapels in honor of his own name, or, more truly, polluted them. He also made little crosses [Note: *Cruciculae*: little crosses; Letter 144, SER.] and small oratories in the fields, near springs, or wherever it seemed good to him, and ordered public prayers to be celebrated there. Eventually crowds of people, rejecting the other bishops and abandoning the ancient churches, began to hold assemblies in such places, saying: “The merits of Saint Aldebert will help us.”

He even gave his fingernails and hair to be honored and carried together with the relics of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. Finally, he did what seemed the greatest crime and blasphemy against God. When people came and prostrated themselves at his feet, wishing to confess their sins, he said: “I know all your sins, because all your secrets are known to me. There is no need to confess; your former sins have been forgiven. Return safely and absolved to your homes in peace.”

He imitated in his dress, gait, and conduct everything that the holy Gospel testifies hypocrites to have done.

The other heretic, called Clement, contends against the Catholic Church and denies and rejects the canons of the Churches of Christ. He refuses the treatises and sermons of the holy Fathers Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory. He despises synodal law and, relying on his own judgment, asserts that, even after two sons were born to him in adultery, he can be a bishop of Christian law under the title of bishop.

Introducing Judaism, he judges it lawful for a Christian, if he wishes, to take his deceased brother’s widow as his wife. He also contends against the faith of the holy Fathers, saying that Christ, the Son of God, descended to hell and released from there all whom the prison of hell held—believers and unbelievers alike, worshipers of God together with worshipers of idols. He asserts many other horrible doctrines concerning God’s predestination that contradict the Catholic faith.

Therefore, concerning this heretic also, I beg you to take care, by your letters, to order Duke Carloman to have him placed in custody, so that he may not sow the seeds of Satan more widely and so that one diseased sheep may not perhaps infect the whole flock.

We wish your Holiness health and joy in prosperous progress throughout a long life.

## LETTER LVIII. GEMMULUS TO BONIFACE [A.D. 744]

[Note: The name Gemmulus is absent from Baronius both in this letter and in the following one. He assigns this letter to the year 745 and the next to 742. Both mention *cozumbri*, but the spelling varies. Here the form is *corzumber*, in the following letter *coczumber*, while Baronius has *cotzumber* in both. What it properly is I have not yet discovered, although I have asked many people. It nevertheless appears to have been a costly kind of incense, of extraordinary odor and fragrance, which, as the Saint says in the following letter, was customarily burned in the temple in honor of God and for the pious magnificence of sacred rites while the solemnities of Mass and the other morning and evening prayers were being celebrated. In Letter 148 it is distinguished from cinnamon and costus; could it be storax? For here above, in Letter 147, it was joined with those two. Or is it perhaps something like *cocha zumbri*? Among Arab physicians, *cocha* is an incense and *zumbri* an aromatic bark, mentioned by Isaac Abenamaran. From that incense, apothecaries prepare *cochiae*, or pills, which, as though by their own smoke, disperse catarrhs. SED.]

To the most holy lord, adorned by the merits of the apostles, the archbishop Boniface, Gemmulus, an unworthy deacon of the Holy See.

Having received your lofty and God-beloved letter, I reread it with great honor and every fitting reverence. Because after so much time I was deemed worthy to be visited through your words, I gave thanks to our almighty God, who also gladdened me, his unworthy servant, with news of your safety.

Therefore, everything that you commanded us through the letters recently sent, insofar as the Lord has deigned to grant us strength, and also what you brought before the apostolic lord, has been received, announced, and reread by us. Know that all the writings sent to you by him were dictated by us, in accordance with your wish.

We also reported what you would not have expected to occur, and a synod of priests was held with the apostolic lord presiding. The sacrilegious life of that most wicked Aldebert and all his writings were reread before the synod, together with the letter of your most holy Fatherhood in which you brought charges concerning him and Clement’s madness. When these proceedings had been completed, a sentence of anathema was promulgated against them and against all who had followed their wicked sect; a copy of it has been sent to you by the apostolic lord.

These acts took place in the presence of our present Father, Deneard, the venerable priest. He himself will be able to tell you in person that all these matters were carried out by us.

Know for certain, most holy Father, that I offer myself ready in everything to obey your commands. For I know that, aided by your prayers, I have been rescued from the temptations of the enemy, and that the Lord has had mercy on his servant and granted him healing. Although surrounded by various illnesses and unworthy as I am, I follow that gift of the apostle’s consolation in which he says: “When I am weak, then I am strong.”

I shall gladly glory in my weaknesses, so that, through your holy prayers, the power of Christ may dwell in me. As for our venerable sisters and handmaids of God who have hastened to the thresholds of the holy princes of the apostles, and whom your holy Fatherhood instructed us to commend to our care, we care for them, insofar as the Lord has deigned to grant us strength, because of your holy command.

We have received the blessing you sent us: namely, a silver cup and one linen cloth, which we received as a double blessing, since we were deemed worthy to be visited by so great a Father. Although we are unable to repay you, nevertheless, in return for your charity, we have sent with great reverence four ounces of cinnamon, two pounds of pepper, and one pound of *cozumbri*.

I ask that you order these to be received without offense, and I earnestly beg you to deign to pray for us.

May the divine Majesty preserve your most holy Fatherhood unharmed, praying for us, O Father, adorned by the merits of the apostles.

[Note: In the Ingolstadt codex, letters of Saint Boniface to Pope Stephen followed this letter, but they have already been placed earlier from the Imperial Codex, as have several others. I append a few more from volume 9 of Baronius’s *Annals*, which he transcribed from the libraries of Saint Mary and Antonius Augustinus. WURDT.]

## LETTER LIX. GEMMULUS TO BONIFACE [A.D. 744]

To the most holy and greatly desired Father, to be remembered with every affection of charity, Boniface, archbishop of the province of Germany, Gemmulus, an unworthy deacon of the Holy See.

I declare that, having received the venerable words of your most holy Fatherhood, sent through the present bearer, Deneard, a venerable man, I accepted them with all the reverence and affection of charity that was fitting. I likewise received the blessing you sent me, which my lowliness values above gold and silver, because I learned that your graciousness remembers me in its holy prayers. May the divine Majesty grant that you remain unharmed as long as heavenly clemency wills me to survive, so that, aided by your sacred intercessions, I may be found, by God’s favor, increasingly able to fight against the snares of the ancient enemy.

Meanwhile, you informed me that you wished us to send you those letters of Saint Gregory. [Note: On Saint Gregory: see what Saint Boniface was accustomed most diligently to request and seek out from every quarter—namely books, and especially those of the Fathers and Saints, such as here the letters of Saint Gregory. SER.] But for the present we have been entirely unable to obey the commands of your holy Fatherhood, because your aforementioned priest found me suffering for a time from excessive exhaustion and gouty pain, so that he left me afflicted by that pain; he will also report this to you in person.

But if life remains with me and your prayer does not fail me, once I have been fully restored to health I shall obey the commands of your most holy Fatherhood. Thus, when you send your messenger here on another occasion, you will find that what you commanded has been fulfilled, and what you desire will be completed without delay.

For through the priest mentioned above we have sent you a small amount of *cozumbri*, which you may offer to the Lord as incense in the morning and evening, or while you celebrate the solemnities of Mass; it has extraordinary odor and fragrance. But I ask that you receive it without offense, since it is sent in pure charity.

I greet your most holy Fatherhood in the Lord and earnestly beg you to order prayers to be offered for us. Through you I also greet the entire Church that is with you, and ask that its members pray for me. For “the prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working.”

Although I am a sinner, I too, remembering you before the sacred shrines of the apostles, devote myself to prayer.

Having said this, we wish your Fatherhood health in the Lord. May he grant that, in the work to which you have been appointed, the fruit of good works may flourish ever more abundantly and may be brought to increase. May the divine Majesty, the undivided Trinity, preserve your Holiness while you pray for us.

## LETTER LX. ZACHARIAS TO BONIFACE [A.D. 745]

To the reverend and most holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop, Zacharias, servant of the servants of God.

When the words of your most holy brotherhood had been brought to us, etc. (See below, Letter 10 of Pope Zacharias.)

## LETTER LXI. BONIFACE TO HEREFRID [A.D. 745]

[Note: Heref. C.: *Herefritho*. In the epitome of the Venerable Bede: “In the year 747, Herefridus, a man of God, died.” Since he was a man of God, the otherwise pleasure-loving king sometimes listened to his admonitions. See Book IV of the *History*, chapter 29, and the *Life of Saint Cuthbert*.]

To the most beloved and reverend brother Herefrid, priest, Boniface, servant of the servants of God, sends eternal charity in Christ.

With heartfelt prayers I beg the clemency of your Holiness to deign to remember me in your sacred prayers. Since your brotherhood has already done so, and I do not doubt that you will continue to do so—as those who report it and come from you tell us—may the saying of the holy apostle James be fulfilled in us, for he said: “Pray for one another, so that you may be saved.” For “the prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working.”

Moreover, we eight bishops who have assembled for one synod, whose names we have written below [Note: In all the copies I have seen, those names are absent.], jointly beseech you, dearest brother, to interpret and recite to King Ethel­bald of the Mercians the words of our admonition, and to announce them to him carefully, enumerating and proclaiming them in the same manner and order in which we send them to you in writing.

For we have heard that, out of fear of God, you do not fear the person of any man, and that the aforementioned king is sometimes willing to listen, at least to some extent, to your admonitions.

Let it be known to your Charity that we directed these words of our admonition to that king for no other reason than pure charitable friendship, and because we, born and raised among that same English people, are living here as exiles by command of the Apostolic See. We rejoice and give thanks for the good qualities and praises of our people, but we are distressed and saddened by its sins and reproaches.

For we endure the disgrace of our people, whether from Christians or pagans, when they say that the English nation, rejecting the custom of other peoples and disregarding apostolic command—or rather, God’s ordinance—disdains to have lawful wives and, indulging in fornication and adultery like neighing horses or braying asses, fouls and confounds everything shamefully.

Therefore, if this greatest crime is true, dearest brother, let us all together entreat the aforementioned king to correct himself along with his people, lest the whole nation perish with its prince, both here and in the future. Rather, by amending and correcting his own life, let him direct his entire people toward the way of salvation by his example, and let him merit eternal reward from the very source from which he previously contracted sin.

Moreover, we have sent you a portion of incense and a *sabanum* as a blessing and sign of pure charity.

[Note: *Sabanum*. It is understood from the following account of Victor of Utica, Book III *On the Vandal Persecution*, that this was a kind of garment or linen cloth: “When Muritta, a Catholic deacon, was about to be tortured by Elpidophorus, an Arian apostate, on account of the faith, before he was stripped, says Victor, he secretly and stealthily, without anyone knowing, carried the *sabana* with which, when he received Elpidophorus from the font, he had formerly covered him. When these were shaken out and displayed before everyone, he is said to have moved the whole city to weeping and tears with these words: ‘These are the linen cloths, Elpidophorus, minister of error, which will accuse you when the majesty of the Judge comes.’ The same expression occurs again below in Letter 145, in Serarius’s edition. See the canon *Post Baptismum*, *On Consecration*, distinction 4; Saint Gregory, Book VII, Letter 5. For Uguccio and John of Genoa, *sabanum* means a napkin or cloth for wiping the face. The ancient glosses say: ‘A *manutergium* is so called because it wipes the hands, while *sabanus* is Greek.’ The glosses to Book I of Alexander the Latrosophist, *On Diseases*, say: ‘A *sabanum* is a fine cloth.’ Elsewhere: ‘A *sabanum* is a cloth made of cotton.’ Matthaeus Silvaticus: Greek *sabanon*; *sabanum* is a garment, a rough wiping cloth, namely one used by people in baths, or any linen cloth assigned for this purpose. WURDT.]

May the Holy Trinity preserve your fraternal love, flourishing in holy works and advancing in approved conduct, and keep you eternally in good health.

## LETTER LXII. BONIFACE AND THE BISHOPS TO ETHELBALD [A.D. 745]

To the most beloved lord Ethel­bald, preferable in the love of Christ to other kings, ruler of the illustrious scepters of the English kingdom: Boniface, archbishop and Germanic legate of the Roman Church, together with his fellow bishops Wera, Burgard, Warbert, Abel, and Willibald, sends perpetual charity in Christ.

We confess before God and the holy angels that whenever, through faithful messengers, we have heard of your prosperity and faith in the Lord and of your good works before God and men, we have rejoiced and given thanks to God among those who rejoice and pray for you. We ask and beseech the Savior of the world to preserve you safe, steadfast in faith, and upright in works before God, for a long time in the rule of a Christian people.

But whenever some injury to your affection—whether concerning the condition of your kingdom or the outcome of wars—or, what is more serious, some dangerous damage to the salvation of your soul has reached us by report, grief and sorrow torment us, because we rejoice with your joy in God’s will and are saddened by your adversity.

For we have heard that you give very many alms, and we rejoice with you in this, because those who give alms to the least of their needy brothers will, according to the truth of the Gospel, hear a merciful judgment from the Lord on the day of judgment. He says: “As long as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me. Come, you blessed; come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

We have also heard that you firmly prohibit thefts and iniquities, perjuries and robberies, and that you are recognized as a defender of widows and the poor, and that you possess established peace in your kingdom.

In this too we have praised God and rejoiced, because the very truth and peace that is ours, namely Christ, said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.”

But meanwhile a report of ill repute concerning the conduct of Your Piety has reached our ears. When we heard it, we were saddened, and we wish that it were not true. For, after hearing it from many informants, we have learned that you have never taken a lawful wife in marriage—an institution established by the Lord God from the very beginning of the world and commanded and enjoined through the Lord’s apostle Paul [Note: “A commandment. Our modern innovators in marriage would abuse this passage, were it not that the Saint immediately adds that refraining from taking a wife out of fear and love of God is not blameworthy, but rather praiseworthy. Observe also how gravely the Saint speaks against those same innovators when he calls nuns, or religious women, brides of God, and teaches that to touch them lustfully is a most grievous crime.”]—who teaches: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband.”

For if you wished to do this for the sake of chastity and abstinence, so that you refrained from union with a wife out of fear and love of God, and if you have proved before God that this is true and has been fulfilled, then we too rejoice in this, since it is not blameworthy but rather praiseworthy.

But if, God forbid, as many say, you have taken neither a lawful wife nor observed abstinence for the sake of chastity and God, but, with lust ruling you, have sullied the reputation of your glory before God and human beings through the crime of sexual immorality and adultery, then we are deeply saddened, because this is recognized both as an outrage in the sight of God and as a disgrace to your reputation before human beings.

And, what is worse, those who report these things to us add that this infamous crime was committed especially with nuns and virgins consecrated to God in monasteries. There is no doubt that this sin is therefore doubled. To give an example: what punishment would a boy incur from his master if he violated his master’s wife by adultery? How much greater, then, is the guilt of one who has defiled the bride of Christ, the creator of heaven and earth, with the corruption of his lust and desire?

As blessed Paul the Apostle says: “Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit?” [Col. 0758C] And elsewhere: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him. God’s temple is holy, and that is what you are.”

Again, in his discourse and in the enumeration of sins, he joins adulterers and fornicators to those enslaved to idolatry, saying: “Do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God.”

Among the Greeks and Romans, one who was guilty of this was treated almost as though he had brought blasphemy upon the Lord [Note: “Guilty of this. Perhaps, ‘guilty in this,’ or ‘let him be guilty of this,’ namely, of having done it.”]: if, when specifically questioned about this sin before ordination, he was found guilty of having slept with a veiled woman consecrated to the Lord [Note: “Nun. Also in this letter below, and in the two councils to be cited below, pp. 112–113. In the Constitutions of Charlemagne, however, pp. 238 and 263, the form is *nunnanes*. Amerbach does indeed give their Germanic derivation there, but it is neither sufficiently appropriate nor plausible. Rhodiginus says that among the Egyptians monks are called *nonnos* and nuns *nonnas*, book V, chapter 12. Saint Jerome, *To Eustochium, On the Preservation of Virginity*: ‘They are called chaste women and nuns.’ In attempting to prove from the proper name in Suidas that *nonna* means a virgin, Erasmus offers an insufficient argument. The Venerable Bede, in his *Book on Numbers*, p. 113, says that among the Hebrews the number is called *nonna*, but one should read *mona*, since the verb *manah* means ‘to count,’ although that noun, *mona*, or even *manah*, more often signifies a portion or part in Scripture: 1 Kings 1:5; 9:23, 26; and elsewhere.”] the man is barred from every rank of God’s priesthood.

For this reason, dearest son, you must carefully consider how weighty this sin is judged to be before the eyes of the eternal Judge: it places the perpetrator among the servants of idolatry and casts him out of the divine ministry of the altar, even if he was previously reconciled to God after completing penance.

For bodies consecrated to God by a vow of personal dedication and by the words of a priest are called temples of God in sacred Scripture. Therefore those who violate them are recognized, according to the Apostle, as sons of perdition. But the chief of the apostles, Peter, forbidding the lustful to indulge their desires, said: “The past time is sufficient,” and the remainder of the passage as far as “the dead.” And: “The price of a prostitute is scarcely one loaf of bread, but a woman captures a man’s precious soul.”

Elsewhere he says: “The guilt is not great when someone has stolen. For he steals to fill a hungry soul; and, when caught, he will repay sevenfold. But the adulterer, because of the poverty of his heart, destroys his own soul.” [Col. 0759B]

It would take too long to enumerate how many spiritual physicians have condemned the poison and horror of this sin and forbidden it with fearful warnings, because fornication is more serious and worse than almost every other sin. It can truly be called the snare of death, the pit of hell, and the abyss of destruction.

Therefore we beseech and entreat you, dearest son, by Christ the Son of God, by his coming, and by his kingdom, that if this is true—if you are involved in this crime—you correct your life through repentance and amend it by purification.

And remember that it is proved indecent for you to turn, through lust, the image of God created in you [Col. 0759C] into the image and likeness of the evil devil. You, whom not your own merits but God’s abundant mercy made king and ruler over many, must not make yourself, through lust, a servant of the evil spirit. For, according to the Apostle’s saying, “Whatever sin a person commits, he is its slave.”

This is regarded as a reproach and disgrace not only by Christians but even by pagans themselves. For the pagans, although they do not know the true God, naturally observe what belongs to the law and what God established from the beginning in this matter: while preserving the bonds of marriage with their own wives, they punish fornicators and adulterers.

For in ancient Saxony [Note: “Ancient Saxony. This is the name given to that part of Germany from which the later Saxony in England arose. For around the year of our Lord 409, when the Saxons were summoned to provide assistance against enemies, they were also given a place among the Britons in which to live; by force they gradually retained and enlarged it. Hence the new Saxons, or Anglo-Saxons, in England; while the Saxons simply, or perhaps the Old Saxons, as in Letter 121, are in Germany. See Bede, *History*, book I, chapters 10, 11, and 15, and book V, chapters 10–12. I have discussed that land and its peoples in book III of the *Moguntina*, note 1. Here beautiful examples of Germanic pagan severity toward adulterers are added, which Saint Boniface praises, just as the Lord praised the unjust steward for those things in his conduct that were good, not for everything he did, Luke 16. For no one should praise the fact that someone either inflicted death upon himself or was compelled to inflict it.”] if a virgin has polluted her father’s house through adultery, or if a married woman, having broken the marriage bond, has committed adultery, they sometimes compel her to end her life by hanging herself with a rope, and they hang her seducer above her funeral pyre after she has been burned and consumed.

At other times, after assembling an army of women, they have the women lead her, after flogging her, through the surrounding villages. They beat her with rods, cut away her clothing up to the belt, and with their knives cut and prick her entire body, leaving her bloody and torn by countless wounds. They send her from village to village, and new floggers continually take their turn, driven by zeal for chastity, until they leave her either dead or barely alive, so that the others may fear to commit adultery and fornication.

And the Wends—who are the most foul and degraded kind of people—preserve their mutual marital love with such great zeal that, when a woman’s own husband dies, she refuses to go on living. A woman among them is judged praiseworthy if she has taken her own life so that she may burn together with her husband on a single funeral pyre.

Thus the pagans, who do not know God and do not possess the law, “naturally do what belongs to the law,” according to the Apostle’s saying, “and show that the work of the law is written in their hearts.”

Moreover, dearest son, since you are known as a Christian and a true worshiper of God, if in the corruption of your youthful adolescence you have been defiled by lust, wrapped in the stench of adultery, and plunged into the abyss of desire as into a pit of hell, now is the time for you, remembering your Lord, to recover from the devil’s snares and wash the soul soiled by the stench of lust.

Now is the time for you, out of fear of your Creator, not to presume ever again to repeat or defile yourself with such an abomination. It is time to spare the multitude of the perishing people, which, by following the example of a sinful ruler, was falling into the pit of death. For as many as we draw toward the life of the heavenly homeland through good examples, so many will without doubt follow us toward destruction through bad examples; and for all these, we shall receive either punishments or rewards from the eternal Judge.

For if the English people, as has been reported throughout these provinces and is reproached to us in France and Italy—and is even a reproach among the pagans—have rejected lawful marriages and, living in lust and adultery after the manner of the people of Sodom, led a foul life, then from such intercourse with prostitutes degenerate, base, and lust-maddened peoples must be expected to be born.

In the end, the whole population will decline toward what is worse and baser, and finally will become neither strong in secular warfare nor steadfast in the faith, neither honorable among human beings nor beloved by God. The same thing happened to other peoples of Spain, Provence, and Burgundy: they withdrew from God in this way and committed fornication until the almighty Judge permitted the avenging punishments for such crimes to come upon them and rage against them through ignorance of God’s law and through the Saracens.

It must also be noted that another monstrous crime lies hidden beneath that offense: namely, murder. For when those prostitutes, whether they are women of monasteries or of the world, give birth in sin to offspring conceived wrongly, they often kill the greater part of them. They do not fill the churches of Christ with adopted children, but fill tombs with bodies and hell with miserable souls.

Moreover, it has been reported to us that you have broken many privileges of churches and monasteries and taken away certain properties from them. If this is true, it is recognized as a great sin, as sacred Scripture testifies, saying: “Whoever takes anything from father or mother and says, ‘This is not a sin,’ is a participant in murder.”

Our father is undoubtedly God, who created us; our mother is the Church, which spiritually gave birth to us in baptism. Therefore whoever defrauds or seizes the money of Christ and the Church will be judged a murderer before the sight of the righteous Judge.

Regarding this, one of the wise said: “Whoever seizes his neighbor’s money commits iniquity; but whoever takes the Church’s money commits sacrilege.”

It is also said that your prefects and counts inflict greater violence and servitude upon monks and priests than any of the Christian kings before them had done. Therefore, after the apostolic pontiff Saint Gregory converted the English people to the true God and the Catholic faith by sending preachers from the apostolic see, the privileges of the churches in the kingdom of the English remained intact and inviolate until the time of King Ceolred of the Mercians [Note: “Ceolred. In Bede, *History*, book V, chapter 14, he is called Coenredus, and in the *Epitome*, Ceolredus. But in book V, chapter 20, there are two Coenreds, both kings of the Mercians. The first, says Bede, more nobly relinquished the scepter of the kingdom and became a monk at Rome. The second was the son of King Æthelred, who later became a monk and abbot, book V, chapter 20. This passage concerns the later Ceolred, whose condemnation is discussed below in Letters 21 and 71. He was succeeded by Æthelbald, to whom Bede’s *Epitome* already refers in the year 740. Æthelbald was finally killed in 754—three years after Saint Boniface’s martyrdom—by his own guardians, as Bede says, being miserably slain by treachery at night. Beornred began to reign.] and of Osred, king of the Deirans and Bernicians [Note: “Osred. King of the Northumbrians, a boy of about eight years, he reigned for eleven years, according to Bede, book V, chapter 19; and in the *Epitome*: ‘In the year 716, Osred, king of the Northumbrians, was killed, and Ceolred, king of the Mercians, died.’ In chapter 23, after the death of the former, Coenred is said to have been king of the Northumbrians; Osric succeeded him, chapter 24; and Osric was succeeded by Ceolwulf, Coenred’s brother, who had reigned earlier, in the same place; Eadberht succeeded him in the *Epitome*, in the year 737. Saint Boniface therefore says that this young and lustful Osred lost his life. Note here the sad ends of kings who despised God’s laws, violated sacred things, and were excessively devoted to youthful pleasures.”]

These two kings, through the devil’s prompting and by their criminal examples, publicly demonstrated that two great sins might be committed in the provinces of the English against the evangelical and apostolic commands of our Savior: namely, the superstition and adultery of nuns, and the destruction of monasteries. Remaining in these sins, they were condemned by God’s just judgment, cast down from the royal height of this life, overtaken by premature and terrible deaths, excluded from perpetual light, and plunged into the depths of hell and the abyss of Tartarus.

For Ceolred, the predecessor of Your Reverence, while splendidly feasting among his counts, as those who were present testified, was suddenly driven into madness of mind by the evil spirit. That spirit had persuaded him to trust in the law condemned by God; and, without repentance or confession, raging and deranged, conversing with the devil and abhorring God’s priests, he undoubtedly passed from this light to the torments of hell.

Osred, too, was driven on by the spirit of lust as he fornicated, violated consecrated virgins in the monasteries of nuns, and raged madly, until he lost his glorious kingdom, his youthful life, and his very lustful soul through a contemptible and shameful death.

[Note: “After the word ‘lost,’ the following is read in Baronius, volume IX, p. 175: ‘Charles also, prince of the Franks, destroyer of many monasteries and one who converted ecclesiastical funds to his own uses, was consumed by a long and shameful disease of the groin.’ Then it continues: ‘Therefore, dearest son, …’ WURDT.”]

Therefore, dearest son, beware of the pit into which you have seen others fall before your eyes. Beware of the darts of the ancient enemy, by which you have seen your own relatives wounded and fall before you. Guard yourself against the snare of the ambusher, in which you have seen your acquaintances and fellow soldiers strangled, losing both the present life and the future one.

Do not follow such examples toward destruction. For such people, according to the prophecy of sacred Scripture, are those who oppressed the righteous and took away the fruits of their labors. On the day of judgment they will say:

“We have wandered from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine upon us. The sun did not rise for us. We did not know the way of the Lord. What did pride profit us? Or what did the boasting of riches contribute to us? All those things passed away like a shadow, and like a messenger running ahead, and like a ship crossing the sea whose track cannot be found, or like a bird flying through the air.”

And shortly afterward:

“So we too, once born, immediately ceased to exist. For we were consumed in wickedness.”

Those who sinned spoke such words in hell, because “the hope of the ungodly is like down carried off by the wind, like thin foam scattered by a storm, like smoke dispersed by the wind, and like the memory of a guest who passes by for a single day.”

And elsewhere:

“The number of a human being’s days, even if it is great, is a hundred years—reckoned as a tiny drop from the great sea.”

All these things, according to the authority of sacred Scripture, are made closely comparable through the comparison of things.

Thus James, the brother of the Lord and apostle, speaking about the impious rich man, said: “He will pass away like a flower of grass. For the sun rose with its heat, dried up the grass, its flower fell, and the beauty of its appearance perished; so also will the rich man wither in his ways.”

And Truth itself, speaking in the Gospel, declared: “For what will it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?”

## LETTER LXIII. BONIFACE TO CUTHBERT [A.D. 745]

[Note: “To Cuthbert. See above, Letter 70. This letter deserves to be read very frequently by all pastors of souls, especially bishops and archbishops. SER.”]

To his brother joined to him by the bond of spiritual kinship, raised to the dignity of the archbishop’s office, his fellow bishop Cuthbert, Boniface, Germanic legate of the Catholic, Apostolic, Roman Church, sends the desired greeting of charity in Christ.

For it is written in the Book of Solomon: “Blessed is the person who finds a friend with whom he can speak as with himself.” When your most sweet letters, interwoven with brotherly affection, were brought to us by your son, the deacon Cyneberht, together with gifts expressive of your generosity, we received them while giving great thanks to God and to you.

Through him your charity also sent us the honey-sweet conversations of your living voice concerning brotherly counsel. We desire that these spiritual conversations of counsel may, God willing, continually pass between us for as long as we live in this mortal life, by the aid of him from whom alone come holy desires, right counsels, and just works [Note: “Holy desires. From a familiar prayer: ‘God, from whom come holy …,’ which, as is evident here, is of very ancient origin. SER.”]—things that you know better and more fully, since God has granted you many gifts, and that you are able to do more wisely and more completely.

We, as your faithful and devoted servants in small matters, should strive to be instructed, mutually chained by the golden bond of heavenly love that cannot be broken [Note: “To be instructed. It should be separated by a comma from the following noun, ‘golden.’”].

For the labor of our ministry is recognized as belonging to one and the same cause, and an equal watchfulness over the churches and peoples entrusted to us is required of us: whether in teaching, correcting and admonishing, or defending the canonical and lay orders.

Therefore, since you have indicated this most humbly, let us do likewise. A greater solicitude for the churches and care for the peoples rests upon us because of the pallia entrusted and given to us than rests upon other bishops, who care only for their own dioceses.

Therefore, dearest brother—not because your wisdom needs to hear or read the regulations of our rusticity, but because of your good, humble, and holy will—we think you would rather know than not know what the priests here have decreed must be observed. We send these decrees to you for correction and amendment.

In our synodal assembly we decreed and confessed the Catholic faith [Note: “The Catholic faith. The excellent beginning of the decrees, which was recently, as recorded in book III of the *Moguntina*, note 47, renewed in Saint Boniface’s chapel and deservedly painted there in uncial letters. The remaining statutes, eight or nine in number, are exceedingly useful. After them Saint Boniface discusses whether the care of souls once undertaken can be abandoned. See cause 7, question 1, especially chapter *Sicut vir*; concerning the pallium, Letter 122, book III of the *Moguntina*, note 26; Gratian, distinction 100; and the *Decretals*, title ‘On the Authority and Use of the Pallium.’ Paul Scaliger, *Oration to the Pontiff*.
