SER.”], and our desire to preserve, to the end of our lives, the unity and submission of the Roman Church; to submit to Saint Peter and his vicar; to convene a synod every year; to seek metropolitan pallia from that see; and in every respect to desire to follow canonically the commands of Saint Peter, so that we may be numbered among the sheep entrusted to him.

We all agreed to this confession, signed it, and sent it to the body of Saint Peter, the chief of the apostles. The Roman clergy and pontiff received it with joy.

We decreed that every year the decrees of the canons, the rights of the Church, and the rule of regular life should be read and reaffirmed in a synod.

We decreed that the metropolitan who has been raised by the pallium should exhort, admonish, and investigate the others, determining who among them is diligent concerning the salvation of the people and who is a negligent servant of God.

We prohibited hunting and wandering through the woods with dogs, and also prohibited the keeping of hawks and falcons.

We decreed that each year, during Lent, every priest should give his bishop an account of his ministry: concerning the Catholic faith, baptism, and every order of his ministry.

We decreed that every year each bishop should carefully travel throughout his diocese to confirm the people, teach the population, investigate, and prohibit pagan observances, diviners or sorcerers, omens, amulets, incantations, and every impurity of the pagans.

We forbade God’s servants to use pompous clothing, cloaks, or weapons.

We decreed that it belongs to the metropolitan, according to the statutes of the canons, to investigate the conduct of the bishops subject to him and the nature of their diligence concerning the peoples. He must admonish them so that bishops returning from the synod, holding an assembly in their own dioceses with priests and abbots, may instruct them to observe the synod’s commands.

If any bishop is unable to correct or amend something in his own diocese, he must likewise bring it forward for correction at the synod before the archbishop and openly before everyone, just as the Roman Church, when it ordained us, bound us by an oath to report faithfully to the apostolic see and to the vicar of Saint Peter for correction anything in which we saw priests or peoples deviating from the law of God and were unable to correct it.

For in this way, unless I am mistaken, all bishops must inform the metropolitan, and the metropolitan the Roman pontiff, of anything concerning the correction of peoples that is impossible for them to remedy; and thus they will become free from the blood of lost souls.

Moreover, dearest brother, since an equal labor and a greater danger threaten us than other priests, because the ancient canons command that all metropolitans should know how to bear responsibility for the whole province, let me give an example of what I fear: we have once undertaken to steer a ship amid the waves of a violent sea, and we can neither govern it safely nor abandon it without sin.

For, as one of the wise says, if it is dangerous not to steer a ship cautiously among the waves, how much more dangerous is it to abandon it, tossing amid swelling waves in a storm?

Therefore the Church, which sails like a great ship across the sea of this world and is battered in this life by various waves of temptation, must not be abandoned but governed.

As examples of this we have the earlier Fathers: Clement, Cornelius, and many others in the city of Rome; Cyprian in Carthage; and Athanasius in Alexandria. Under pagan emperors they governed Christ’s ship—indeed, his most beloved bride, the Church—by teaching, defending, laboring, and suffering even to the shedding of blood.

I can certainly say of myself, in accordance with the voice of the Song of Songs: “The sons of my mother fought against me; they appointed me guardian of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I did not guard.”

For the vineyard, according to the prophet Nahum, is “the house of Israel belonging to the Lord of hosts”; now, evidently, it is recognized as the Catholic Church. By order of the Roman pontiff and at the request of the princes of the Franks and Gauls, I undertook to convene and exhort its synod [Note: “By order of the pontiff. Here you see how Saint Boniface did not seek the episcopate or archiepiscopate, but took it up at the pontiff’s command and at the request of the princes of the Franks and Gauls; and, once he had assumed it, how vigilantly and diligently he carried it out, and how willingly he would have relinquished it if permitted. SER.”], hoping to restore Christ’s law. I dug around it and brought a basket of manure, but I did not guard it. When I expected it to produce grapes, it produced wild grapes.

And, according to another prophet: “The work of the olive will lie, and the fields will not produce food.”

But alas! The work of my labor appears, by comparison, to resemble a dog barking and seeing thieves and robbers break into, undermine, and ravage its master’s house, while, having no defenders to assist it, it whimpers, groans, and mourns.

Now, because I am placed in such danger, I set forth what seems to me right and prudent, seeking your wholesome counsel and desiring to know your judgment. I speak of the freedom to preach, as the Apostle Paul declared to the priests in the Acts of the Apostles:

“I testify to you this day that I am innocent of everyone’s blood. For I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood. I preached the kingdom of God as I walked among you, so that I might keep myself free from everyone’s destruction.”

The Apostle calls him a bishop, the prophet a watchman, and the Savior of the world a shepherd and priest of the Church; and they all establish that anyone who, while silent, leaves the people’s sins unrebuked is guilty of the blood of lost souls.

For this reason a terrible and immense necessity compels us, according to the Apostle’s saying, to present ourselves as an example to the faithful. That is, unless my judgment deceives me, a teacher must live so justly that his words are not nullified by deeds that contradict them, and so that, while he lives cautiously concerning his own conduct, he is not condemned through silence for another’s sin.

For the overseer of God’s Church is appointed for this purpose: not only to train others by the example of a good life, but also, by preaching boldly, to set each person’s sins before his eyes [Col. 0766A] and to show what punishment awaits the stubborn and what glory awaits the obedient.

For according to the Lord’s word to Ezekiel, to whom the administration of the word was entrusted, even if a man lives holy but is ashamed or afraid to rebuke those living destructively, he will perish with all those who were lost while he remained silent.

And what will it profit him not to be punished for his own sin, when he must be punished for another’s?

The Lord, speaking to Ezekiel, severely forbids the priest’s silence and calls the priest a watchman. Just as it is the watchman’s task to see more than everyone else from a higher place, so the priest must be higher in the excellence of his merits and possess a greater grace of knowledge, by which he can instruct others.

“Having heard,” says the divine word, “you shall announce the message to them from me.”

This indicates that the priest must say what he has learned from divine reading and what God has inspired in him: “You shall announce it to them from me,” he says, not from yourself; you will speak my words, and there is no reason for you to boast of them as though they were your own. “From me,” he says, “you shall announce it to them.”

“If, when I say to the wicked, ‘Wicked one, you shall surely die,’ you do not speak, so that the wicked person may guard himself in his way, that wicked person will die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand.”

It is as though he were saying plainly: “If you do not announce his sins to him, and if you do not rebuke him so that he may turn and live, then I will hand over to everlasting flames both you, who did not admonish him, and the one who sinned while you remained silent.”

Therefore, let us not have hearts so stony or so made of iron that these words of the Lord do not terrify us. Let us not be so alienated from the faith that we do not believe these words of the Lord.

Rather, let us rouse and exhort our brothers with the venerable words of the holy apostle Peter: “Be sober and vigilant, and awaken, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about seeking someone to devour. Resist him, strong in faith, knowing that the same suffering is being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.”

And let us admonish the bishops of our synod, who are subject to us, with the adjuration of the holy apostle Paul, who says to Timothy:

“I testify before God and Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead, by his coming and his kingdom: preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; rebuke, entreat, reproach, with all patience and teaching.”

For the time foretold by the apostles has already come, when people will not endure sound doctrine but will heap up teachers for themselves according to their own desires, and so forth.

Let us cry out with strength, according to the prophet’s saying, because we announce peace on earth to people of good will. For he cries out with strength whom neither fear nor shame prevents from preaching the word of life.

With the Lord’s help, let us strive not to be among those false shepherds of the sheep whom the prophet accuses, saying:

“Thus says the Lord God: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves! Are not flocks fed by shepherds? You ate the milk and clothed yourselves with the wool; you slaughtered what was fat, but you did not feed my flock. You did not strengthen what was weak, heal what was sick, bind up what was broken, bring back what had been cast away, or seek what had perished. Instead, you ruled them harshly and with power. My sheep were scattered because there was no shepherd, and they became food for every beast of the field.”

The “woe” that the prophet speaks places a curse upon them. By shepherds he signifies bishops; by the Lord’s flocks, the faithful peoples who are to be fed.

They feed themselves when they attend not to the salvation of the people but to their own desires. They receive the milk and wool of Christ’s sheep through the daily offerings and tithes of the faithful, and they lay aside the care of the Lord’s flock.

They do not heal with spiritual counsel the person weakened by sins. They do not strengthen with priestly assistance the one broken by various tribulations. They do not recall the wanderer to the way of salvation. They do not seek with pastoral diligence the person already lost through despair of forgiveness. Nor do they defend the afflicted against the violence of the powerful, who rage against them like wild beasts. They do not merely fail to rebuke rich or powerful sinners; they even honor them.

Therefore the divine word strikes the pride of such men with threats, saying: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel!” And again: “Therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: Behold, I myself will require my flock from their hand, and I will cause them to cease, so that they may no longer feed the flock or feed themselves any longer.”

What else does this mean but: “Shepherds who feed themselves and not the flocks I will cast down from the height of honor among the rejected and the accursed”?

But who would not tremble at all these things, except one who does not believe in what is to come?

God has set forth everything he wished to be observed so openly and confirmed it by the authority of his own name that we would more easily—though it is impious even to say so—despise these things than pretend, by lying, that we do not understand what is so clear and divine.

How have we heard the words, “Thus says God”? Who could fail to believe that what God says will come to pass, except one who does not believe in God?

Terrified by consideration of these things and others like them, I have been overcome by fear and trembling. The darkness of my sins has almost covered me, and I would have wished and desired entirely to lay down the helm of the Church, once I had undertaken it, if I could find either examples of the Fathers or passages of sacred Scripture agreeing with such a course.

Therefore, dearest brother, since all these things are so, and truth can be wearied but cannot be conquered or deceived, let our weary mind take refuge in him who says through Solomon: “Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not rely on your own prudence in all your ways. Acknowledge him, and he himself will direct your steps.” And elsewhere: “The name of the Lord is a most strong tower. The righteous man takes refuge in it and will be saved.”

Let us stand firm in justice and prepare our souls for temptation, so that we may endure God’s support, and say to him: “Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation.” [Col. 0768A] Let us trust in him who has imposed this burden upon us. What we cannot carry by ourselves, let us carry through him who is almighty, who says: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

Let us stand in battle on the day of the Lord, since days of distress and tribulation have come upon us. Let us die, if God wills, for the holy laws of our fathers, so that we may deserve to obtain an eternal inheritance with them. Let us not be mute dogs; let us not be silent watchmen; let us not be hirelings who flee from the wolf. Rather, let us be vigilant shepherds, watching over Christ’s flock, preaching to great and small, rich and poor, the whole counsel of God, to people of every rank and age, insofar as God grants us the ability, in season and out of season, in the manner that Saint Gregory set down in his *Pastoral Book*.

[Note: [Col. 0767D] Moreover, do not remain silent. A useful admonition concerning the prohibition of women from making long journeys, especially when the journey appears to bear the outward appearance of piety. There are considerations of persons and other circumstances, and sometimes there are “superfluous and foolish visits” (*περιτταὶ καὶ ἀνόητοι ἐπιδημίαι*), as Saint Chrysostom says in his second homily on Romans. SER.]

Moreover, I do not conceal from your charity that all the servants of God who here appear to be most approved, whether in learning or in the fear of God, are displeased that the goodness, honor, and chastity of your Church are being mocked. It would be some relief from this disgrace if the synod and your princes prohibited women and veiled females from making that journey and undertaking the repeated travel to the city of Rome, both on their way there and on their return, since many of them perish and only a few return unharmed.

For there are very few cities in Lombardy, or in Francia, or in Gaul, in which there is not an adulterous woman or prostitute of the English race. This is a scandal and disgrace to your entire Church.

But when a layman—whether emperor, king, or one of the prefects or counts—supported by secular power, violently seizes a monastery from the authority of a bishop, abbot, or abbess, and begins to govern it in the place of the abbot, keeping monks under his authority and possessing money that was purchased by Christ’s blood, the ancient Fathers called such a man a robber and sacrilegious person, a murderer of the poor, and a wolf of the devil entering Christ’s fold; they judged him deserving of condemnation by the greatest bond of anathema before the tribunal of Christ.

Concerning such men, remember the words of the holy Apostle Paul to Timothy: “Command those who are rich in this world not to be high-minded, nor to put their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things.”

If such men do not accept the Church’s correction, they are to be treated as Gentiles and publicans, and the Church of God has no communion with them, whether living or dead. Since such men are found both here and there, let us sound the trumpet of God against them, lest we be condemned for keeping silent.

Strive with every effort to prohibit the superfluous and hateful-to-God superstition concerning clothing. For those ornaments of garments—which, as they themselves think, are called by others a disgrace—those broad bands, [Note: [Col. 0768D] *Vermium*. Witnesses that contain certain inserted multicolored designs, as though they were inlaid work, and images of worms. *Vermiculatum* is used by Nonius for something minute and painted with vermilion. In Cicero, *On the Orator* III, and Pliny, book XXXVI, chapter 25, a *vermiculated* pavement or inlaid work means a mosaic—or, as it is not incorrectly called today, a *musaic*. For just as *Achaicus* comes from *Achaeus*, so *μουσαϊκός* comes from *μουσαῖον*. SER.]

—those garments studded with broad bands and images of worms—anticipate the coming of Antichrist, sent on ahead by him, since through his ministers he seeks by cunning to introduce fornication and luxury within the cloisters of monasteries.

## LETTER LXIV. ZACHARIAS TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 747]

[Col. 0769A]

To the most reverend and holy Boniface, fellow bishop, Zacharias, servant of the servants of God.

“The blessed Apostle Paul admirably admonishes us,” etc. (See below, Letter 9 of Pope Zacharias.)

## LETTER LXV. ZACHARIAS TO PIPPIN AND OTHERS. [A.D. 747]

To the most excellent and most Christian lord Pippin, mayor of the palace, etc., Zacharias, bishop, etc.

“We rejoice with great joy in the Lord,” etc. (See below, Letter 8 of Pope Zacharias.)

[Note: [Col. 0769C] Joannes Philippus Vorburgius, in volume IX of his *Histories*, p. 425, and Cointius, under the year 747, also present this charter from Brower. Toward the end of the preceding century, the monks of Fulda likewise presented it before the tribunal of the Sacred Rota at Rome, but in a somewhat different form. I shall select a few variant readings from the many.

Where Brower’s closing formula reads, “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation,” the Fulda copy reads, “in the year of the divine Incarnation.” Brower has “on the twelfth day of March,” whereas the Fulda copy has “on the twenty-second day of March.” Brower calls the last three witnesses prefects; the Fulda copy calls them priests.

Brower reads: “The sign of Boniface, archbishop, who ordered this charter to be written for the information of all.” The Fulda copy instead reads: “Who ordered this charter to be written for the information of all.” In the Fulda copy, where Brower reads “by transfer and investiture,” it reads “by transfer and retention.” There are, moreover, countless differences in the proper names.

After these editions of the charter from the Fulda archive, a third edition has recently appeared, in which the part of the closing formula that is last in Brower and the Fulda copy is inverted so that it comes first, while the first part becomes last. There too, instead of the reading “first by Megenhelmus,” one finds “edited by Megenhelmus.” In addition, this new edition omits the following words found in Brower and the Fulda copy: “by Pippin, with these boundaries circumscribed, to our Lord and Savior, and by the aforesaid”—not to mention other alterations.

We ought not to have failed to mention even these few matters, since the celebrated charter leads the collection of the Fulda documents. Yet I do not wish anyone to suppose that by doing so I intend to call it suspect of forgery. For although both at its beginning and at its end there are some features that may not satisfy every sharp-nosed critic, nevertheless, as regards the boundary of the monastery of Fulda, I believe it to be correct, since it does not include more than the four thousand paces that, as we learn from the historians, were assigned to this place.

As for the witnesses, they too appear to be correct. For who would have subscribed with greater right than Boniface the founder; Bishop Burchard, the diocesan; Sturmius, destined to be the first rector of the place; and the clerics and priests of the persons mentioned before?

Perhaps the year will trouble someone. For it seems unusual that Boniface should first have taken care in the year 747 to record the boundaries of the Fulda site, when he had arranged for them to be described only three years earlier. But we suppose that when the holy archbishop learned that Carolomannus, from whom he had received the estate, was about to withdraw from government, he immediately thought of obtaining confirmation of that place from Pippin.

To secure it more certainly, the best plan was to summon the witnesses who had been present at the description of the boundaries two years earlier and ask them to subscribe the charter that was to be presented to Pippin.

This is offered in defense of the body of the charter itself; we do not vouch for its beginning and closing formula to anyone. Nor would I readily vouch to anyone that these witnesses, whom Boniface could easily gather at Fulda in the years 744 and 747, could just as easily have been gathered by King Pippin at Attigny in Champagne in the year 755. WURDT.]

## LETTER LXVI. BONIFACE TO RELIGIOUS MEN IN GAUL. [A.D. 747]

[Col. 0769B]

Boniface, the German legate of the holy Roman Church, to the religious men who fear the Lord and are established in the kingdom of the Franks.

I believe that it is known to many how Carolomannus, an illustrious man who rules in the Frankish kingdom together with his brother Pippin, granted us a place in the Buchonian Forest suitable for the construction of a monastery and permanently donated it to the servants of God.

Therefore, it pleased us to record how that place is established within fixed boundaries and to confirm the record below with suitable witnesses who were present at the aforesaid prince’s transfer and investiture of the place.

He continues:

The boundary of the church and monastery of the holy Savior, which is situated on the bank of the river Fulda, begins first on the eastern side at the spring of the stream called [Col. 0769C] Crumbenbach. From there it proceeds along that stream until it enters the southern Huna; then it crosses the hill Leohunhuog, which some call Kuffiso, and proceeds to the place where Uhtinabahes enters the other Huna.

From there it crosses to the source of the stream called [Col. 0770A] Rodenbach, then to the source of Wolfesbahes, and follows that stream until it enters the Biberaha. It then follows its bank downstream as far as the mouth of Larbrunnen.

From there it proceeds to the place where the other Crumbenbach enters the Treisbach, and then upstream along the Crumbenbach to its source. From there it crosses to the summit of Rosberg and proceeds again by a dry torrent into the Huna, then downstream along its bank as far as the mouth of Martbach.

From there it goes to the place where the river Lutire enters the Fulda, and then upstream along the bank of the Lutire to the mouth of Biunbach, and upstream along that stream to its source.

From there it crosses the road called Antsanvia to the road called Ortheswehe. From there it proceeds to the wallow that lies on the mountain called Himelesberg. Then it crosses to the source of the stream called [Col. 0770B] Scalkesbach and follows its bank until it enters the Fliedena.

From there it goes downstream to the mouth of Scammunfulda, and from its mouth upstream to the point where that river divides into channels. It then crosses between the middle channels that arise from the river Fulda and proceeds to the source of the stream called Sudromilbach. From there it goes to the source of the aforesaid Crumbenbach.

Thus the place was transferred by Pippin, with these boundaries marked out, to our Lord and Savior, and by the aforesaid prince Carolomannus, so that the same place might be entrusted and useful to God and our Savior until the end of the age, for gathering and nourishing his servants without any hindrance or seizure by others.

The signs or crosses of Boniface the archbishop, Burchard the bishop, Sturmius the abbot, [Col. 0770C] Megenhelmus the priest, Folcherannus the priest, Megingozus the priest, Traundis the prefect, Luitfridus the prefect, and Rumolfus the prefect are then appended.

The closing formula is:

“In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 747, and in the sixth year of the rule of the noble men Carolomannus and his brother Pippin, on the twenty-second day of the month of March. This charter of record was first written in the monastery of Fulda by Megenhelmus the priest, by divine command and permission.”

## LETTER LXVII. BONIFACE TO ANDHUNUS. [A.D. 747]

To the most beloved Father Andhunus, bound to me by the bond of charity, heartfelt greetings.

Why did you not send the garments that you ought to have sent from the province of the [Note: [Col. 0771B] *Fresians*. Those who are now called Frisians and Frisians were called *Fresae*, *Fresi*, and *Fresones* in Bede, book V, chapters 10 and 12; in the *Life of Cuthbert*, chapter 44; and in book VI *On the Ages*; and likewise throughout the Frankish Annals. Here, see Letter 97, now numbered 94. I have discussed the origin of the name in book II of the *Mainz History*, chapter 19, and in the notes to the chapter on the Franks in the *Life of Saint Kilian*. SER.]

Frisians? Now, by almighty God, see to it at once that they come.

Tell us something about our bishop: whether he had gone to the synod of the duke of the western provinces, or to Carolomannus’s son. [Note: [Col. 0771B] Carolomannus does not seem to have resigned his kingdom outright to Pippin, but rather to have appointed him guardian of his son until the boy reached a suitable age. This is revealed by this letter to Andhunus, abbot in the province of Frisia, for it says: “Tell me something about our bishop, whether he had gone to the synod of the duke of the western provinces, or to Carolomannus’s son.” The bishop about whom he asks is Boniface, and Carolomannus’s son is Drogo, whom Pippin left in Austrasia to be educated. It therefore appears that this letter was written at precisely the time when it was not yet known to everyone that Pippin had appropriated the whole Frankish kingdom to himself. Later this became very well known. (Eccardus, cited work, p. 478.) WURDT.]

Write back to us by letter, and quickly send back again this messenger who is going there, named Hartleih. I ask you, lord, to arrange this both for the one remaining there without difficulty and for the one coming here.

Farewell, O flowers of the Church, and pray for us, and we for you, so that the peace of Christ may remain in us. Amen.

## LETTER LXVIII. ZACHARIAS TO VARIOUS BISHOPS. [A.D. 747]

[Col. 0772A]

To our most beloved Reginfridus, bishop of Rouen, etc., Zacharias, etc.

“I give thanks to almighty God the Father, and to the Lord Jesus Christ, his only Son, and to the Holy Spirit,” etc. (See below, Letter 12 of Pope Zacharias.)

## LETTER LXIX. BONIFACE TO CERTAIN MONKS. [A.D. 747]

To his dearest sons Tatwinus and Wigbertus, priests; Bernardus and Hedde; Hunfridus and Stirme, Boniface, servant of the servants of God, sends perpetual greetings in the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0771C] Concerning the persons to whom this letter was sent, see Pagi’s *Critical Commentary*, under the year 719, no. 5 and following. It was sent in the year 747, shortly after the death of Saint Wigbert, abbot of Fritzlar, who departed to God in that same Christian year.

In it Boniface entreats the monks to take greater care to preserve the monastic rule of life, precisely because their father Wigbert had died: Wigbert the priest and Megingord the deacon were to explain the rule to them and be teachers of the boys; Stirme was to be in the kitchen, and so forth.

Boniface adds: “Ask Abbot Tatwinus, and whatever he tells you, do it; and let each one strive, according to his strength [Col. 0771D] and his own character, to preserve chastity,” and so on, up to “until the time of our return, according to God’s will.”

Thus, in the monastery of Fritzlar, situated in lower Hesse, just as at that time there were two Wiberts—one the abbot, the other a monk of the same monastery—so there were also two Tatwinuses. One of them succeeded Saint Wigbert in governing the monastery of Fritzlar, as the Magdeburg centuriators correctly observed in century 8, p. 834.

The monk Stirme was different from Saint Sturmius, the first abbot of Fulda, who was administering that monastery at the time when this letter was sent. Brower, in his *Fuldensian Antiquities*, and others who confused the two were therefore seriously mistaken.

Finally, Megingord the deacon—or, as he is called elsewhere, Megingus or Megingozus—was a great friend of Saint Boniface, as is stated in chapter 5 of the *Life of Saint Wigbert*. He was later raised to the bishopric of Würzburg, or, as we now say, Herbipolis.

Several men named Wigbert flourished at this time, and learned men have not infrequently taken one for another. It is therefore useful to present the more distinguished of them here, so that confusion may be avoided and the various errors more easily corrected.

The first is Wigbert, of whom Bede speaks in book V, chapter 10 and following. Bede says that he preached the Gospel in Frisia for two continuous years; when he found no audience among the barbarians, he returned to England.

The second is Wigbert, abbot of Nutscell in England and teacher of Saint Boniface, as Boniface himself calls him in Letter 3 to Daniel, bishop of Winchester. This Wigbert died in the year 718, as is clear both from Willibald and from Othlonus in the *Life of Saint Boniface*.

Cointius, under the year 833, no. 18 and following, where he cites our letter of Boniface as no. 17, maintains that it was sent by Boniface to England after the death of his teacher, and that Boniface wrote it there when he had not yet spent a long time in Germany and was still considering a return to his homeland.

Yet neither Willibald nor Othlonus in his *Life* of Boniface, nor Boniface himself in any of his letters, indicates in a single word that, after returning to Gaul or Germany, Boniface intended to return to England. Therefore, this letter was sent from some monastery in Germany near Fritzlar, from which he was about to return to Fritzlar while distributing duties among the monks of that monastery.

But Willibald, in chapter 5 of the *Life of Saint Boniface*, and Othlonus, book I, chapter 7, settle the dispute completely. They write that, after Wigbert, abbot of Nutscell, had died, the monks wanted Boniface to be placed over them, but could not obtain this from him; and that after he had stayed with the brothers for some time, he committed himself to the sea.

Indeed, Willibald testifies that he did not set sail from England until the winter season had already passed. Compare what is read above before Letter 1.

The third is Wigbert, the holy and celebrated abbot of Fritzlar, on whose account the discussion of the other Wiberts now arises.

The fourth is Wigbert, a monk of Fritzlar, who was the teacher of Saint Sturmius, the first abbot of Fulda, as is recorded in that saint’s Life.

The fifth is Wigbert, a monk of the monastery of Glentingaburg, or Glastonbury, situated in the county of Somerset. Letter 53 among the letters of Boniface is addressed to its fathers and brothers: “To the fathers and brothers established in the monastery of Glestingaburg.” In it Wigbert the priest says:

“I want you to know, dearest ones, that when our archbishop Boniface heard of our arrival, he himself deigned to come a long way to meet us and receive us with great kindness.”

All writers up to the present have wrongly confused this Wigbert with Saint Wigbert, abbot of Fritzlar. Hence, because Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, writes in the *Life of Saint Wigbert* that Saint Wigbert was appointed abbot of Fritzlar by Boniface after Boniface had assumed the bishopric of Mainz, they concluded that Saint Wigbert could not have been called abbot before the year 745.

Yet Lupus expressly says that Wigbert came to Germany before Boniface assumed the episcopate. This Wigbert, therefore, was a different man from Saint Wigbert, abbot of Fritzlar. On this matter Pagius gives a fuller account under the year 747, nos. 9 and 10, etc.

The sixth is Wigbert, abbot of an uncertain place situated not far from the diocese of Mainz, as is clear from Letter 83 among the letters of Boniface. Its title is: “To the most holy Lord Lullus, ever preserved by God, bishop, Wigbert, servant of the servants of God, although unworthy, your abbot in all things,” etc. In that letter he asks Lullus to visit the monastery over which he presides.

The seventh is Wigbert, parish priest or rural priest in the diocese of Mainz. Letters 102 and 110 among the letters of Boniface are addressed to Lullus, bishop of Mainz, concerning him. Cointius explains them under the year 754, no. 105 and following, where he makes the serious error of confusing Saint Wigbert with this seventh Wigbert the abbot and postpones the former’s death to that Christian year. See Pagius, at the place cited.

The letters cited above will be found in Serarius’s arrangement. WURDT.]

I entreat your affection with paternal love to take still greater care to preserve the monastic rule of life, since your father Wigbert has died.

Let Wigbert the priest and Megingord the deacon explain your rule to you, [Col. 0773A] and let them observe the appointed hours [Note: [Col. 0774D] *Appointed hours*. The ecclesiastical prayers seem to be meant here, which are sometimes called the canonical hours and the course of the divine office. Bellarmine discusses them against the heretics in book I, *On Good Works*, chapters 12 and 13, and below, here in Letter 76. SER.], and the course of the Church, and admonish the others; let them be teachers of the boys and preach the word of God to the brothers.

Let Hedde be provost and admonish your servants, and let Hunfridus assist him wherever there is need. Let Stirme be in the kitchen. Let Bernardus be the workman and build your small houses wherever necessary, and let him explain everything to you wherever you have need.

Ask Abbot Tatwinus, and whatever he tells you, do it. Let each person strive, according to his strength and his own character, to preserve chastity, to help one another in your common life, and to remain in brotherly love until the time of our return, according to God’s will.

Then, praising the Lord together in all things, let us give thanks to him. Farewell in Christ.

## LETTER LXX. WETBERTUS TO THE MONKS OF GLESTINGABURG. [A.D. 747]

To the holy lords and fathers and brothers, beloved in Christ, established in the monastery of Glestingaburg, Wetbertus the priest, certainly your servant and a suppliant of the servants of God, sends greetings in the Lord.

Blessed is God, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. By his will he has also directed our journey prosperously into these provinces—namely, to the borderland of the pagan Hessians and Saxons—across the sea and through the dangers of this world, not through our merit but through your permission, your prayers, and his mercy.

You know, brothers, that distances of land do not divide us, since the charity of Christ binds us together. Therefore your brotherhood and reverence, and likewise prayers to God for you, always remain in me.

I want you to know, dearest ones, that when our archbishop Boniface heard of our arrival, he himself deigned to come a long way to meet us and receive us with great kindness.

Now, beloved ones, believe that our labor is not fruitless for us in the Lord, but is your reward. For almighty God, through his mercy and your merits, brings the good sufficiency of our work to completion, although it is exceedingly dangerous and laborious to live amid almost every kind of hardship: hunger and thirst, cold, and the attacks of pagans among whom we dwell.

Therefore, I ask you, pray diligently [Col. 0773D] that we may have speech when our mouths are opened [Col. 0774A], perseverance in the work, and fruit.

Farewell in the Lord. Greet the brothers all around, first Abbot Ingeldus and our community, and inform my mother Tetta and her community of the success of our journey.

With united and earnest prayers I beg you all to devote yourselves in return to the urgency of our prayer. I desire that the divine clemency guard your blessedness as you pray for us.

## LETTER LXXI. ZACHARIAS TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 748]

To the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop, Zacharias, servant of the servants of God.

“To the sacred thresholds of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles,” etc. (See below, Letter 11 of Pope Zacharias.)

## LETTER LXXII. ZACHARIAS TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 748]

[Col. 0774B]

Pope Zacharias sends perpetual greetings to Boniface, bishop of the holy church of Mainz.

“How our Lord God has shown himself propitious toward his Church,” etc. (See below, Letter 14 of Pope Zacharias.)

## LETTER LXXIII. AETHILBERTUS TO BONIFACE. [CIRCA A.D. 749]

[Note: [Col. 0774D] *Aethilbertus*. Thus it is always written in C.; elsewhere it appears without the diphthong, as *Edilbertus*, as in the Venerable Bede, who, in book V of his *History*, the final chapter, says that he was made king of the Kentish people in the year 725. SER.]

To the most blessed lord, the archbishop Winfrid, deservedly adorned with the episcopal fillet, also called Boniface, Ethilbert, king of Kent, sends greetings in the Lord of lords.

A few years ago, the venerable abbess named Bugge, after she had visited the most sacred sites of the city of Rome for the sake of prayer, and from there had returned again and reached her native land, came to the monastery of nuns that she had previously governed well under ecclesiastical authority.

When I came to meet her at her request, among the many desirable things she undertook to impress upon my hearing this above all: that you had given her permission to speak familiarly with your approachable and gracious holiness about matters necessary to her while you were both in Rome, and that you had not ceased frequently to visit and wear down the thresholds of the blessed apostles.

Then she immediately added that she would diligently address your fatherhood on my behalf with humble and earnest prayers, prompted as she was by the awareness of our close kinship, so that, just as she had deserved to be imbued in person [W.: more deeply] with saving instructions and strengthened by the blessing of your prayers, so I too, although absent and unknown in bodily presence, yet present in spirit, might be enriched by your customary benevolence with this same gift, which I greatly need.

When they said with unquestioning confidence that you had promised to do this, I confess that I cannot easily express in words how much joy and consolation I received from it. I was all the more delighted, as is customary, because, from an unexpected hope, it had suddenly brought forth so many and such precious gifts.

Therefore it seems entirely useful and fitting for me to address your radiant blessedness far and wide by reading friendly letters or through the representation of faithful envoys. I do not think I could fulfill this at any other time better or more effectively than now, when there are with your excellence religious men who have been sent by you here to Britain as prudent and faithful envoys, and who now, with God’s help, desire to reach your gracious presence as quickly as possible in obedience to your command.

Thus it pleased me greatly to send to you the present bearer of this letter, named Ethelhun, a monk in religious habit, together with your aforementioned men, as though by a more cautious and safer route, and through him to offer these words of greeting and petition to your charity.

By these words we first declare that all of us together offer abundant thanks to almighty God, who has bestowed upon you such grace of his mercy that through the word and labor of your preaching he has converted to the rule of the Christian faith an innumerable multitude of pagans miserably deceived by the ancient error of idolatry.

Therefore, with God’s help, we still hope and desire many more things, confident that he who has begun to work through you will not cease to accomplish greater things day by day.

Through this bearer of these letters my devotion has also sent to your reverence, with great affection, certain small gifts: namely, a silver cup gilded inside, weighing three and a half pounds, and two [Note: [Col. 0775D] *Repta*. This word will also occur below, in Letter 77, p. 108. But what if it has some connection with Reptacestir—that is, the town or fortress of Repta, of which Bede speaks in book I, chapter 1? For Bede’s *cestir* means a fortress, just as in British *caer*, as in Giraldus, chapter 5 of book I and book X of the *Itinerary through Wales*. SER.] repta.

We have sent you these gifts neither with the intention nor on the occasion of receiving any earthly profit or temporal repayment for them. Rather, kneeling—which is much more necessary—I beseech you with all the depths of my heart that, since the days are evil and various unforeseen disturbances multiply daily in this world filled with scandals, you may deign to assist us with the many and frequent support of your prayers.

May your venerable affection, always filled with living memory, also be able to provoke others to do the same, whether by commanding or by suggesting it—both while you hear that I still exist in this mortal flesh and even after my death, if I should deserve to have you survive me. [Note: [Col. 0776D] *Survive me*. It appears from the *Epitome* of the Venerable Bede that Saint Boniface himself was the survivor. SER.]

Having briefly and summarily set these matters forth, I desire one further thing from you, which, according to what has been reported to me, I do not at all think would be very difficult for you to obtain: namely, two [Note: [Col. 0776D] *Falcons*. Otherwise, the best falcons are found in Cambria or Wales, according to Silvester Giraldus, book I of the *Itinerary through Wales*, chapter 12. Hence the falconers in the Constitutions of Charlemagne. SER.] falcons whose skill and boldness in the art would be such that they would willingly seize cranes while capturing them and, having seized them, strike them down upon the ground.

For this reason we ask you to acquire and send these birds to us, since very few hawks of this kind are found in our regions—that is, in Kent—that produce such good offspring and are raised, trained, and taught to be spirited and warlike in the aforesaid art.

Finally, at the end of the letter I ask you to write back to the person writing to you and kindly inform me by your letter whether the things I sent you have been safely delivered.

May divine mercy grant your blessedness, as you pray for us, a long life.

## LETTER LXXIV. BENEDICTUS TO BONIFACE. [CIRCA A.D. 750]

To the most holy and most beloved Father Boniface, archbishop, Benedict, bishop and vicedominus of the holy apostolic see, sends greetings.

The present Lullus, a venerable priest sent by your fatherly holiness, brought us your honorable words. Their text stated that you were distressed by many necessities and storms caused by men who do not fear God, false bishops, pseudopriests, [Col. 0776C] and fornicating clerics [W.: clerics of the Lord], by their wicked actions and evil intrusions, and also by the anger of hostile and persecuting peoples, whose unjust persecution will end in everlasting destruction.

For, most holy Father, how many torments all the saints endured so that they might securely possess the palm of eternal life! We have an outstanding comforter in the Apostle Paul, who teaches: “We must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations.”

Great is your reward, most holy Father, and your crown of glory before almighty God, since you endure all things patiently for the sake of the divine command and the preaching of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Lord our God and Savior.

Although I am a sinner, I beseech his power, so that, with my lord Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, interceding—for you exercise his office among fierce and untamed peoples—he may in his mercy guard you; and so that, after the course of your ministry, on the day of his coming, you may be able to bring forth abundant fruit and receive from God, the creator of all things, the reward of a hundredfold recompense and possess eternal life.

Indeed, commending myself to your holy prayers, I have appeared as an assistant to your aforementioned envoy, insofar as I have been able in word and deed.

Finally, I received the blessing sent by your blessedness as from my father, and I gave thanks to almighty God and to your most holy fatherhood.

For, most blessed Father, I have sent a small gift to your holiness: one sabanum (a linen cloth), one facitergium (a hand-towel), and a little incense. I ask that your honorable fatherhood not disdain to accept it without offense.

Farewell always in Christ, most beloved Father!

[Note: [Col. 0777D] The following letter is a response to this one, and the matters treated in them are clear from what is said on p. 163. The matters not written here but explained in the following letter had been entrusted by Saint Boniface to his legate, the blessed Lullus, for presentation to the pontiff, as Boniface himself indicates at the beginning, and the pontiff later while replying. This letter was not extant when the *Mainz Materials* were published, as is stated in book III, p. 414, in chapter 14 of book II of the *Life of Saint Boniface*, under its title. SER.]

## LETTER LXXV. BONIFACE TO ZACHARIAS. [A.D. 751]

To the most reverend Father and beloved lord, a master to be revered with fear and honor, endowed with the privilege of apostolic dignity and exalted by the apostolic see’s pontifical fillet, Zacharias: Boniface, your insignificant servant, although unworthy and least of all, yet your most devoted German legate, sends the desirable greeting of unfading charity in Christ.

I earnestly beseech Your Paternal Holiness, with suppliant prayers, graciously to receive this priest of mine, bearer of my letters, named Lull, with a kindly disposition. For he has certain private matters of mine which he ought to disclose only to Your Piety: some he must tell you face to face, some show you written in letters, and concerning certain necessities of mine inquire and ask, so that he may bring back to me, for the consolation of my old age, Your Paternity’s reply and counsel, by the authority of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. After hearing and considering all these things, if there are matters which please you and which have been done well, I shall strive, God willing, to increase them; but if anything—as I fear—displeases you, then, at the command of Your Apostolate, may I either deserve indulgence or undergo fitting penance.

For the predecessor of Your predecessor, Gregory, of venerable memory, when he ordained me, unworthy as I was, and sent me to preach the word of faith to the German peoples, bound me by an oath to become a supporter and helper, in word, deed, and agreement, of canonical and just bishops and priests. By God’s grace I have endeavored to fulfill this. But false priests, hypocrites, and deceivers of peoples I was either to correct onto the way of salvation or to avoid, abstaining from communion with them. This I observed in part, but in part I was unable to guard and fulfill.

Spiritually I fulfilled the oath, because my soul did not enter into their agreement or counsel. Bodily, however, I could not abstain from them altogether, when I came to the prince of the Franks, compelled by the needs of the Churches, and found there men such as I did not wish to find; nevertheless, I did not share communion with them in the holy communion of the body of Christ.

The aforesaid apostolic pontiff also commanded me that, wherever I visited peoples, I should report their conduct and customs to the pontiff of the apostolic see. In the Lord I trust that I have done so.

As for what I previously made known to Your Holiness concerning archbishops and the pallia to be requested from the Roman Church, in accordance with the promises of the Franks, I beg the indulgence of the Apostolic See. For those who made the promise delayed and did not fulfill it; the matter is still being deferred and debated, and it is not known who among them wishes to bring it to completion. Yet, as far as my will was concerned, the promise would have been fulfilled.

There is also a wooded place in a wilderness of immense solitude, situated amid the nations of our preaching. There, having built a monastery, we established monks living under the rule of the holy Father Benedict—men of strict abstinence, without meat and wine, without beer and servants, content with the labor of their own hands.

I acquired this aforesaid place through the just labor of religious and God-fearing men, especially the former prince of the Franks, Carloman, and dedicated it in honor of the holy Savior. In that place, with Your Piety’s consent, I have proposed to recover, by resting for a little while or for a few days, my body wearied by old age, and after death to lie there.

For four peoples to whom, by God’s grace, we have preached the word of Christ are known to dwell around this place. With Your intercession, I can be useful to them for as long as I live and retain understanding. For I desire, accompanied by God’s grace and supported by your prayers, to persevere among the German peoples to whom I was sent, in the fellowship of the Roman Church and in your service, and to obey your command, as it is written: “Hear the judgment of the Father, beloved children, and act accordingly, so that you may be saved.” And elsewhere: “He who honors his father shall live a longer life.” And again: “Honor your father, so that a blessing from the Lord may come upon you, and a father’s blessing establishes the houses of his children.”

## LETTER LXXVI. ZACHARIAS TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 751]

To the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop, Zacharias, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

“Blessed be God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” etc. (See below, Letter 13 of Pope Zacharias.)

## LETTER LXXVII. ZACHARIAS TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 751]

Pope Zacharias to Bishop Boniface, and through him to the brothers in the monastery built by him, and to the abbots who shall succeed them forever.

“Since whatever accords with reasonable desires ought always to be granted,” etc. (See below, Letter 15 of Pope Zacharias.)

## LETTER LXXVIII. BONIFACE TO STEPHEN. [A.D. 752]

To the most excellent lord Stephen, preferred to and loved above the other pontiffs, endowed with the privilege of the Apostolate,

[Note: Stephen III.]

Pope, Boniface, an insignificant bishop, a disciple of the Roman Church, sends the desired greeting of charity in Christ.

I earnestly and insistently beg Your Holiness’s clemency, from the depths of my heart, that I may deserve to obtain and possess from Your Benevolence fellowship and unity with the Apostolic See, and that, as a disciple of Your Piety, serving the Apostolic See, I may remain your faithful and devoted servant, in the same manner in which I previously served the Apostolic See under your three predecessors: the two Gregories, of venerable memory,

[Note: Gregory II and Gregory III.]

and Zacharias, who always strengthened and assisted me by the encouragement and authority of their letters.

I beg Your Piety to do the same, so that I may more effectively perform and fulfill the command of Your Paternity. For if, during this Roman mission, which I have carried out for thirty-six years, I have accomplished anything useful for the aforesaid Church, I desire still to fulfill and increase it.

But if anything is found to have been done or said by me with insufficient skill or unjustly, I promise that I am ready and willing to correct it according to Roman judgment, with humility.

Meanwhile, I beg that my lord’s Piety not be displeased because I sent my messenger and letters to Your Presence so late. This happened because I was preoccupied with restoring the churches which the pagans had burned. Through their *tituli* and cells they devastated and burned more than thirty churches.

[Note: In the Roman synod, after Letter 135 (now 67), the name of these *tituli* frequently occurs here and elsewhere. On this subject see the second volume of the *Annals* and Baronius in the *Martyrology*; our de Roa, *On the Nativity*, chapter 22; Graetser, Book II, *On the Cross*, chapter 7. SER.]

This was the reason for the delay of my letters and of my appeal to Your Paternity, and not any negligence or carelessness.

## LETTER LXXIX. BONIFACE TO FULFRED. [A.D. 752]

Boniface, servant of the servants of God, bishop by the grace of Christ, sends perpetual charity in Christ to his dearest fellow priest Fulfred

[Alternative: Fulfrad.]

I cannot repay with worthy thanks, as much as you deserve, the spiritual friendship of your brotherly love, which you have often shown me for God’s sake in my necessities.

[W. in the margin: “which you have shown me.”]

But I beseech almighty God to repay you eternally, in joy among the angels, with the rewards of your recompense on the highest summit of heaven.

Now, in the name of Christ, I beg you to bring to a good end what you began with a good beginning: namely, to greet in my name our glorious and beloved King Pippin

[Note: Our king. Below, Letters 96, 100, and 104 (now 93, 101, and 80). The king whom Saint Boniface himself crowned: Book III of the Mainz materials, notes 38–40. SER.]

and to give him great thanks for all the works of kindness which he has done for me. Tell him also what seems likewise to me and to my friends: that, through these illnesses, I must soon bring this temporal life and the course of my days to an end.

Therefore I beg our king’s majesty, for the name of Christ, the Son of God, to deign, while I am still alive, to inform and instruct me concerning what reward he wishes afterward to grant my disciples.

For almost all of them are foreigners. Some are priests, established in many places for the service of the Church

and of the peoples. Some are monks in our cells, and some have been assigned to teach children to read. There are also certain elders who, having lived and labored with me for a long time, have helped me.

I am anxious about all of them, lest after my death they be scattered, but rather that they may have the counsel of your reward and the protection of your majesty, and not be dispersed like sheep without a shepherd, and that the peoples near the frontier of the pagans may not lose the law of Christ.

Therefore I earnestly beg Your Benevolent Clemency, in God’s name, that you cause my spiritual son and fellow bishop Lull—if God wills, and if it is pleasing to Your Clemency—to be appointed and established in this ministry of the peoples and churches as preacher and teacher of priests and peoples.

I hope that, if God wills, through him the priests may have a teacher, the monks a regular instructor, and the Christian peoples a faithful preacher and shepherd.

I especially ask that this be done because my priests near the frontier of the pagans live a very poor life.

[Note: *Marca*: a boundary. Hence *marchiones* among Hottomannus, *On Old Feudal Law*. SER.]

They can obtain bread to eat, but they cannot find clothing there unless they have counsel and a helper from elsewhere, so that they may be able to endure and

[Note: *Indurare*: for *durare*, *perdurare*, or *perseverare*, “to endure” or “persevere.” SER.]

remain in those places for the ministry of the people, just as I have helped them.

And if the kindness of Christ should inspire this in you, and if you are willing to consent to and do what I ask, deign to communicate and make it known to me through these messengers of mine who are present, or by a letter expressing Your Piety’s will, so that, whether I live or die, I may be happier through your benefaction.

## LETTER LXXX. BONIFACE TO PIPPIN. [A.D. 752]

To the most excellent lord Pippin, king of the Franks, Boniface, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord.

We give great thanks for Your Majesty’s graciousness, praying the Lord Jesus Christ to repay you with an eternal reward in the kingdom of heaven, because you have graciously deigned to hear our petitions and to console my old age and infirmity.

Now, glorious son, know that through God’s mercy I believe that I may once again be in your service. Therefore we ask you to inform us whether we ought to come to your assembly,

so that we may fulfill your will.

A certain servant of our Church, himself a most deceitful man, who was craftily fleeing from us, named Ansfrid, came to us with your written note, asking us to render him justice. We have sent him to you with these same letters and with our messenger, so that you may recognize that he lied to you. We ask you to defend us, for the sake of your reward, against such falsifiers, and not to believe their lies.

Farewell always in God.

## LETTER LXXXI. BONIFACE TO GRIPO. [A.D. 752]

Boniface, servant of the servants of God, sends the desired greeting in Christ to Gripo, son of Charles.

I beseech and adjure Your Piety, by God the almighty Father, by Jesus Christ his Son, and by the Holy Spirit, by the holy Trinity and unity of God, that if God grants you authority, you strive to help the servants of God—priests and presbyters who are in Thuringia—and to defend the monks and maidservants of Christ against the malice of the pagans. Help the Christian people also, so that the pagans may not destroy them, and so that you may have an everlasting reward before the tribunal of Christ.

Know that we remember you before God, just as your father while alive and your mother long ago commended you to me.

We beseech God, the Savior of the world, to direct your way and your life toward the salvation of your soul, so that you may remain always in God’s grace, both here and in the age to come.

Meanwhile, remember, dearest son, that according to the voice of the psalmist: “Every human being is like grass; his days are like a flower of the field, and so he shall blossom.” And the Apostle says: “The whole world lies in the evil one.” Again, in the Gospel, the Truth said: “For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” And again, in the Gospel, concerning the glory of the righteous: “Behold, the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.” And the Apostle Paul, concerning the blessedness of eternal life: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him.”

Therefore, sons, act so that the rewards of your recompense may shine and increase on the highest summit of heaven. We desire that you may prosper in Christ through length of days.

## LETTER LXXXII. BONIFACE TO OPTATUS. [A.D. 752]

To the most reverend brother, indeed most beloved fellow priest, Optatus,

[Note: “Abbot.” Indeclinable, and correctly so according to its Hebrew or Syriac origin; it is found in one form, and sometimes in Bede, in all cases, as in the title of Letter 88 (now 112). SER.]

abbot, and to the entire holy congregation under his care, observing the norm of regular life, Boniface, a bishop named without any privilege of merit, sends the desired greeting of charity in Christ.

With heartfelt prayers we earnestly beseech Your Holiness’s venerable Clemency to deign to receive and hold us, unworthy though we are, in the unity of brotherly love and spiritual fellowship, so that among us there may be one faith of mind and one piety of action.

As Peter, prince of the apostles, exhorts us, saying: “Above all, have mutual charity toward one another, because charity covers a multitude of sins.” And the Truth himself said: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” Likewise the Apostle Paul admonishes us, saying: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.” And elsewhere: “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith.”

May Your Fraternity, living a regular spiritual life in peaceful tranquility and brotherly concord, deign to pray for our frailty, so that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified; so that, according to the Apostle’s saying, we may be delivered from troublesome and evil men, from the temptations of wicked spirits, and from the tribulations of adversaries; and so that the light of the Gospel, the glory of Christ, and the way of life—which we ought both to show to peoples and nations and to walk in ourselves—may not be darkened or hidden from us.

We also earnestly beseech you that there be among us the fellowship of brotherly charity, common prayer for the living, and prayers and the solemn celebrations of Masses for those who have departed from this world, when the names of the dead are sent among us in turn.

Meanwhile, if Your Fraternity deigns to entrust anything to us for completion or communication, we shall fulfill your desire in all things.

Therefore act upon this petition of ours, so that the rewards of your recompense may shine and increase on the highest summit of heaven, in the heavenly court of the angels.

May the Savior of the world eternally preserve your blessedness—long-lived, vigorous, advancing in noble strength, and fragrant with the sweetest blossoms of deeds and words.

## LETTER LXXXIII. THEOPHYLACIAS TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 752]

To the distinguished father and lord, adorned with heavenly insignia, Boniface, archbishop, Theophylacias, an unworthy archdeacon of the holy Apostolic See.

Among his riddles, a certain highly learned man long ago proclaimed as follows: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deep, because they do not know how to caress the faults of sinners, but prick them.”

Therefore, up to this time, not without deep sorrow, compelled by that Davidic song from the grief of my inmost heart, I have been forced to sing: “I announced and spoke: they have been multiplied beyond number.” And that many come to the faith, while few are brought to the number of the elect, is proclaimed by the Lord himself: “Many are called, but few are chosen.”

You, indeed, distinguished and resplendent summit of the priesthood, make known in an illustrious manner through written pages what must be recorded and brought to notice.

[The following passage is textually obscure and corrupt in the supplied text.]

Distinctly, with greater vigilance, concerning what we have individually set before the ears of my angelic and blessed lord, and in accordance with that rosy and angelic desired longing—the text then has an uncertain “desideratus ann. latus,” while P. reads “ante latus”—the thrice-blessed lord, now in the Apostolic See, deigns at present to strengthen you by instruction, so that you may judge appropriately not only concerning those schismatics and heretics, or excommunicated persons, who wickedly deviate from the rule of orthodox faith, but also so that the peoples of the Franks and Gauls, embracing the path of faith with customary

[W.: “firm”]

steadfastness, may flourish, striving that, under your holy governance, not only the western peoples but nations everywhere may blossom.

For it is written: “The persistent prayer of a righteous man is very powerful.” And David says similarly: “If Moses had not stood before God to turn away his anger, he would have destroyed them.”

For we, retaining our former love of fellowship, although various circumstances now divide the two peoples and the seas, nevertheless have this written word: “Many waters could not extinguish love, nor will rivers overwhelm it.”

As a small gift of blessing, in remembrance of us, we have sent cinnamon, costus, pepper, and incense, all sealed together. We earnestly ask that, although it is very little, you receive it as something great.

For it is written: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within,” and: “To everyone who has, more will be given.” For whoever possesses perfect charity also deserves to receive every gift, with the Holy Spirit ministering them.

May the almighty maker and judge of all things, who in your holy time has called the western peoples and those dwelling everywhere around them to the faith of the catholic and apostolic holy See through the eloquence of your blessed preaching, cause them to flourish forever, as we desire.

## LETTER LXXXIV. THEOPHYLACIAS TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 752]

To the distinguished father and lord, adorned with heavenly insignia, Boniface, revered archbishop, Theophylacias, an unworthy deacon of the holy Apostolic See.

Among pleasant meadows fragrant with scents, the rose is often surrounded by thorns. Thus, when the Holy Spirit shines upon him, the resplendent judge frequently glows like a rose-colored flower, and the honey-sweet teachings of eternal salvation abound

[W.: “abounds”; P.: “it pours forth … praiseworthy.”]

and pour forth, indeed, in the fields.

O most blessed one in the heavenly realms! May the talents entrusted to your distinguished blessedness be returned by you to Christ among the stars not only doubled but even increased by half again, and may that hidden voice be fulfilled through the song of Christ, who says: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your Lord.”

Finally, for the increase of your labor, together with your holy co-angelic father, the apostolic lord, and with all the priests and people of our holy Church, we diligently implore the clemency of our Lord Jesus Christ: may he graciously command that those enlightened by the teachings of Your Most Holy Paternity and drinking from the living fountain, together with their sower, be confirmed and preserved in the path of holy and orthodox faith; and may he open the hearts of those who are to believe,

[Note: The following words differ in P., which has: “and uncover them from the foul veil, while inflaming them.”]

and uncover their veil, so that, with the Holy Spirit inflaming them, they may hasten joyfully and fearlessly to arrive at the faith of Christ, just as the Lord’s clemency decreed: “And I have other sheep which are not of this fold,” and so forth.

Therefore, lord and most holy Father, we ask your ambrosial Goodness, sanctified by God,

[W. omits “sanctified.”] to deign in every way, for God’s sake and because of our humble friendship, to cherish and hold in your care Lull, your most holy and greatly beloved blessed archdeacon, our dearest and sweetest companion and brother.

Our love for him is certainly [P. omits *et* (“and”)] sincere, because he renders faithful and agreeable service to Your gracious Paternity, adorned with its great insignia. For this reason, repeatedly bending the knee,

[W.: “likewise.”]

we beseech your dignified wisdom not to disdain to grant him a much greater reciprocal favor promptly,

[W.: “her,” apparently referring to “favor.”]

on account of our smallness; and, when you frequently pour forth prayers to the Lord God, do not fail to remember us, because it is written: “The persistent prayer of a righteous man is very powerful.”

Having first offered these words, we greet Your Most Holy Paternity, invested by God and nectarous in sweetness, and we wish that, with God’s favor, you may receive rewards throughout eternal ages and experience the desired result in response to our prayers for your well-being.

Finally, we have sent you a small blessing from the generosity of the blessed apostle Peter. For God’s sake, deign to receive with a grateful heart costus, cinnamon, and *xerosyrace*.

[Note: Serrarius has *serastyracem*, with the note: “Or is this an invented name, *cerastirax*, a kind of storax resembling wax?” See Pliny, Book XII, chapters 18 and 26; Book XXIV, chapters 6 and 7.]

## LETTER LXXXV. N. TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 752]

To my most desired lord and most devoted teacher in the study of letters, Boniface, endowed with the insignia of the highest pontificate, N., one of the many beneficiaries of Your Piety, sends the beloved greeting of devoted charity in Christ.

Sacred Scripture admonishes us not to do anything rashly without counsel, as it is written: “Do everything with counsel,” and so forth.

Therefore, judging it appropriate to send the writings of my rusticity to Your Sagacity’s majesty, and by them to make known the occasion and desire of my petition,

[Note: Serrarius and Wurdt have “however carefully considered”; P. has “inasmuch as both have been examined.”]

so that, after due consideration, my prudent teacher may decide what seems best to him and calmly make known to his servant the inclination of his will, to which I may willingly submit, I confess to you, dearest of teachers, that after, with Your Holiness’s permission, I went to Thuringia for the purpose of reading and investigation—if the small spark of my little intellect is capable of understanding or investigating anything at all—I attribute it, after God, first to the reward due to Your Goodness.

I have been unable to devote myself to reading as diligently as I knew I needed to, for two reasons that oppose me: dimness of the eyes and pain in the head, and, thirdly and especially, an illness in my inward parts, namely, sluggishness of mind.

Therefore may Your Paternity grant me permission to remain here a little longer, so that you may give milk, according to the Apostle, to your thirsty son, who is not yet accustomed to his usual food of bread, and may receive him back stronger, at a suitable time for your service, with Christ’s abundant clemency going before and your prayers interceding.

But if Your Discretion should prefer something else, if He grants me strength, then, since endless ages can neither add nor take anything away, I shall return promptly at the very time you command.

Meanwhile, by God’s mercy, whose fullness is the whole earth, I beseech you, like a suppliant kneeling and bending my knee, embracing the feet of Your Majesty, to deign to intercede for my countless crimes before the merciful and just Judge.

Yet I do not thereby disturb Your serenity, since our Jesus, the glory of heaven and salvation of the world, to whom all things are open and from whom nothing hidden is concealed, commands, saying: “Ask, and it will be given to you,” and so forth.

For I do not think that this should be regarded as some form of inflated presumption creeping into me; rather, I believe that a remedy for salvation may be found, since I acknowledge myself sick and seek a physician. Therefore, beloved Father, I have sent you the verses written below for correction, desiring to merit writings from Your diligence, so that from them I may certainly recognize the winding paths of my error.

May the divinity of the holy and undivided Trinity preserve Your Excellence, who continually presides far and wide over the catholic peoples of the Churches, until the final course of life, advancing against all adversities.

May almighty God cause you to grow in the work of mercy,

In everlasting gain of many souls;

May you, rich in the wealth of heaven, deserve to hear

At last the joyful voice: “Good and faithful servant,

Ascend now to the highest joys of your Lord and God.

Because you were faithful over a few things, I shall set you

Over many; may this be your sure rest and salvation,

And hope, by God’s favor, who likewise created all things

And reigns, alive through the ages, before all others,

Without beginning or end, whose clemency

Urged wretched me generously to approach you as teacher.

Pressed down by the heavy burden of sin, without light in my heart,

I loved wandering leisure, believing it sweet,

Although it is always harmful to every soul.

But grace removed the darkness of my dull heart,

The grace of Christ the Savior, generously increasing

Its holy gifts within my foolish senses. To him be praise and honor without end.

And may the reward and crown of your heavenly labor grow for you in the high citadel,

You guide of the straight path,

I who am the final part of your great intellect.”

## LETTER LXXXVI. BONIFACE TO GEMMULUS. [A.D. 752]

To the most reverend and beloved son Gemmulus, archdeacon, Boniface, an insignificant servant of the servants of God, sends the beloved greeting of eternal charity in Christ.

Spiritual charity often joins those whom a long distance separates bodily. And this is recognized as no small hardship of pilgrimage: a friend sadly and sorrowfully remembers a friend whom he ardently loves when that friend is far away, while he finds it difficult to endure an opposing enemy who is near and troubling.

Would that I had you, brother, near me as a comforter in this pilgrimage, that I might use your holy counsel, rejoice in your consolation, delight in seeing your beloved face, and be refreshed by your holy exhortation.

But because the condition of mortal life and the nature of things do not permit this to happen, let true charity accomplish the one great thing which God grants and commands when he says: “This is my commandment: that you love one another,” and so forth.

Let him truly love in God the one whom he cannot hold bodily present. And, as Saint Augustine said, although one may be in the East and the other in the West, those joined together by charity are never separated from one another.

[Note: Saint Augustine, *Sermon 42 on Time*: “Charity itself is truly that which habitually unites and joins together spiritually those separated bodily. For two who love one another with holy love, even if one is in the East and the other in the West, are so joined by the bond of charity that they are never separated from one another. Therefore here one may also read *ab* rather than *ad*.”]

And the Savior of the world said: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

Therefore, according to James, who said: “The prayer of faith will save the sick person,” and shortly afterward: “Pray for one another, so that you may be saved,” let us pray for one another, so that we may be saved; and may the Lord’s Piety, which has separated us on earth, gather us joyfully on the heights of heaven.

## LETTER LXXXVII. BONIFACE TO ANONYMOUS. [A.D. 752]

To the most reverend brother, joined to us by the closeness of spiritual kinship, Boniface, an insignificant servant of the servants of God, sends perpetual charity in Christ.

With heartfelt prayers we earnestly ask Your Fraternity’s Clemency to deign to remember our lowliness and intercede for us, because, as our sins demand, we are shaken on every side by the storms of a dangerous sea.

We ask that he who dwells on high and looks upon the lowly, forgiving our offenses, may grant us a word in the opening of our mouth, so that the Gospel of Christ’s glory may run and be glorified among the nations.

## LETTER LXXXVIII. BONIFACE TO DENEHARD. [A.D. 752]

Boniface, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings in Christ to Denehard, presbyter.

I command you, dearest brother, concerning the boy Athaler now present: if necessity should arise for him in his case, strive to help him as a free man, and make promises on his behalf to his friends as though for a free man, not as though for a slave.

I have approved this arrangement because he intends to take a wife for himself, so that he need not fear that he is a slave.

Farewell in Christ.

## LETTER LXXXIX. BONIFACE TO ALDHER. [A.D. 752]

To the venerable brother Aldher, abbot, Boniface, an insignificant servant of the servants of God, sends greetings in Christ.

With prayers from the marrow and depths of our hearts we beseech Your Charity’s Clemency to deign to remember us by interceding for us in your most holy prayers.

By your gracious prayers, implore the merciful Lord—who is the reason for our pilgrimage—to protect and guide with his right hand the ship of our frailty, lest it be submerged by the waves of the German storms, and, preserving it unharmed, bring it to the tranquil shore of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Greet all the brothers of your holy congregation, our dearest in God, with the kiss of our love and devotion.

We also commend ourselves to your prayers, so that, whether living or dying, we may be joined to your communion in charity. We wish to deserve this from you, strengthened by the devotion of brotherly charity according to Your Clemency’s will, insofar as power grants the means for its fulfillment.

We also ask you to take care to intercede for the German peoples devoted to the worship of idols. Entreat the Lord, who poured out his own blood for the salvation of the whole world and wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, to convert them to the knowledge of the Creator and to the embrace of Mother Church.

Likewise, we ask that you arrange for prayers and the solemn celebration of Masses to be offered for the souls of the brothers who labored with us in the Lord and now sleep; the bearer of these letters has supplied their names.

We earnestly desire that Your Blessedness may prosper in Christ through holy success.

[Note: Letter of Saint Boniface, archbishop, to Pope Stephen II, in which he asks that the Church of Utrecht, donated by Dagobert I to the bishop of Cologne, be made immediately subject to the Roman pontiff. The beginning of this letter is missing among the Bonifacian letters edited by Serrarius, as is its conclusion. The letter begins thus in the Mainz manuscript. WURDT.]

## LETTER XC. BONIFACE TO STEPHEN. [A.D. 753]

To the venerable and beloved lord Stephen, pope, endowed with the privilege of the Apostolate, Boniface, an insignificant German legate or envoy of the catholic and apostolic Roman Church, sends the desired greeting of charity in Christ.

At the time of Sergius, pontiff of the apostolic see, a certain presbyter of the Saxon race, named Willibrord and also called Clement, came to the thresholds of the holy apostles. He was a man of extraordinary abstinence and holiness. The aforesaid pope ordained him bishop and sent him to preach to the pagan people of the Frisians along the shores of the western Ocean.

After preaching for fifty years, he converted most of the Frisian people to the faith of Christ, destroyed their temples and shrines, built churches, and established an episcopal see and a church in honor of the holy Savior at the place and fortress called Trajectum. He remained in that see and in the church of the holy Savior, which he had built, preaching until debilitated by old age. He appointed a fellow bishop to fulfill the ministry in his place, and, when the days of his long life had ended, he departed in peace to the Lord.

The Frankish prince Carolomannus ordered that a bishop be appointed and ordained to that see, and I did so. But now the bishop of Cologne [Note: The bishop of Cologne. Hildegarius occupied the see of Cologne from 750 to 760. In the latter year he was killed by the Saxons not far from the Weser during Pippin’s expedition against the Saxons. See the Newenarian and Pithoean Annals.
