Wurdt.] usurps the see of the aforesaid bishop Clement, who was ordained by Pope Sergius, and claims that it belongs to him, on account of the foundations of a certain church destroyed by the pagans.

Willibrord found that church utterly demolished down to its foundations in the fortress of Trajectum, rebuilt it from its foundations through his own labor, and consecrated it in honor of Saint Martin. He further asserts that, in ancient times, King Dagobert of the Franks [Note: Dagobert. King Dagobert I appears to have given the fortress of Trajectum on the Rhine to Saint Cunibert around the year 631. See Moerckens, *Conatus Chronologicus Archiepiscopatus Coloniensis*, p. 43. Wurdt.] had granted the fortress of Trajectum, together with the destroyed church, to the jurisdiction of Cologne on the condition that the bishop of Cologne should convert the Frisian people to the faith of Christ and be their preacher—which he himself did not do.

He neither preached nor converted the Frisians to the faith of Christ; rather, the Frisian people remained pagan until the venerable pontiff Sergius of the Roman see sent the aforementioned servant of God, the bishop Willibrord, to preach to that people. As I have said, Willibrord converted that people to the faith of Christ.

Now the bishop of Cologne wishes to reduce the see of the aforesaid preacher Willibrord to his own authority, so that it may not be an episcopal see subject to the Roman pontiff and preaching to the Frisian people. I replied to him, as I believed, that the command of the apostolic see, the ordination of Pope Sergius, and the commission of the venerable preacher Willibrord ought to prevail and have greater authority, so that the see might be an episcopal see subject to the Roman pontiff and preaching to the Frisian people, since a large part of them is still pagan. The foundations of the little church had been demolished, trampled down by pagans, and abandoned through the negligence of bishops.

But he does not consent. [Note: He does not consent. Hildegarius, relying on the ancient possession, opposed Saint Boniface; and in fact the church of Trajectum remained subject to the metropolitan of Cologne until 1549. Wurdt.] Now may you deign to inform me of this matter through the judgment of your fatherly authority; and, if the reply which I gave to that bishop of Cologne is just and pleasing to you, may you confirm it by your authority, so that the command of Pope Sergius and that see may remain secure.

For in this way you can help us, if it pleases you, by ordering that a copy be made from the archives of your church and sent to me—whatever Saint Sergius commanded concerning the aforesaid bishop Willibrord after ordaining him—so that by the authority of your holiness I may be able to refute and overcome those who oppose us. But if the matter appears otherwise to your holiness, and another course seems more just, may you deign to make your fatherly counsel known to me, so that I may follow it.

## LETTER XCI. [Note: “The preceding letter of King Pippin was published from the original in the Fulda Archive by Schannat, engraved on copper, and is notable for several variant readings, in *Vindiciae Archivii Fuldensis*, p. 42, plate III. See also Schlaegel, *De Nummis Hersfeldensibus*, p. 57.” These words were written in the margin of the Paris manuscript by a later hand. Giles.—Aubertus Miraeus, dean of the cathedral church of Antwerp, reports in his diplomatic and historical works, vol. I, fol. 494, a charter by which Pippin, king of the Franks, in the year 755, confirmed to the cathedral church of Saint Martin at Trajectum the gifts bestowed by Pippin, Charles Martel, and Carolomannus, at the request of Saint Boniface, archbishop of Trajectum and Mainz. Its wording is as follows:

“Pippin, illustrious king of the Franks. If we do not refuse the requests of priests in all matters, we trust that the Lord will reward us for it. Therefore the venerable man Boniface, archbishop, requested of us that we should renew the confirmation concerning the property of his church of Saint Martin, which has been built in the village called Trajectum on the river Rhine—namely, the things which Pippin, or Charles or Carolomannus, gave to Saint Martin.

Therefore, whatever Pippin, king of the Franks, granted to the house of God or to that bishopric, such as the whole tithe from lands, slaves, tolls, commercial transactions, or whatever taxes appeared to belong to the treasury, as we have said, the whole tenth part we have gladly and justly granted and confirmed to that house of God, Saint Martin’s, in which we have granted and confirmed that Lord Boniface, archbishop, should preside as guardian: for lights and for the support of the monks or canons who there convert pagans to Christianity and, by the mercy of God, teach those whom they have converted to preserve their Christianity, according to what the other Christians preserve of their Christianity and according to what is contained in their decrees—namely, what our aforementioned predecessors Pippin, Charles, and Carolomannus granted to that house of God in their charters.

Know this; and so that the authority of our confirmation may be held more firmly and preserved more securely through the ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the seal of our hand.

‘The sign of Pippin, glorious king of the Franks. I, Widmarus, having been ordered, have examined and subscribed. Given, as issued, in the month of May, on the twenty-third day, in the second year of the reign of that glorious king. Enacted at the public palace of Virmeria, happily, in the name of God.’” Wurdt.] PIPPIN TO BONIFACE. [A.D. 755]

Pippin, illustrious king of the Franks, to Boniface, archbishop and Germanic legate sent by the apostolic see.

Since your venerable fatherhood has petitioned our Excellence on behalf of the monastery which you have recently built in the wilderness of Buchonia beside the river Fulda, at the place which our brother Carolomannus of blessed memory granted to you by a lawful donation, so that, just as it is known to have been exalted by the privilege of the apostolic see through the authority of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, whose legation you exercise, it might likewise be strengthened by a decree of our authority, we have been pleased to grant your petitions.

Therefore, for the honor of God and the veneration of Saint Peter, we have ordered this series of our decree to be written. Through it, with the consent of the bishops and our other faithful subjects, we fully strengthen the privilege of the apostolic see conferred upon you by blessed Zacharias. We decree that none of the priests in the kingdom divinely entrusted to us claim any authority for himself in the aforesaid monastery, except the apostolic see; and that, unless invited by the abbot, no one presume to celebrate the solemnities of Mass there. Rather, let the monastery remain securely and unshakably confirmed in the condition in which it is known to be subject to the apostolic see.

Let it also enjoy perpetual security, without contradiction from any person, with regard both to the places and possessions which it now holds or owns and to whatever divine piety may in future add to the rights of that monastery from the gifts and offerings and tithes of the faithful.

But if anyone should wish to oppose the decree of our authority, let him experience the sentence of apostolic severity expressed in the privilege. Nevertheless, let this which we have confirmed by our authority for the love of God and the veneration of Saint Peter remain established, strengthened by our hand and supported both by the impression of our ring and by the attestation of our faithful subjects.

## LETTER XCII. ATTOTAM . . . [DATE UNCERTAIN]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: Hlodovurgus, otherwise Ludovicus, son of Charles the Great and emperor, as below in Letter 117. Something concerning the spelling of this name is noted in Hincmar’s Letter 1 and in the book *On German Names*.]

Ludovicus Magnus, emperor.

To your Lordship, my lord—though I do not dare to speak thus—but because of my great need I beseech your holiness: I, Attotam, an unworthy presbyter, have been your servant from my birth. Now I ask your holiness to deign to extend your consolation to me, a sinner, because I have no refuge except with you, where the whole people has its refuge.

The cleric Fortwinus has a church in the county of Erkengario [Note: Erkengario. In the manuscript C it might be read *Erkengano*]. Fortwinus then [Note: “Exhorted.” In manuscript C, *ortavit*. It therefore appears to be *artavit* or *oravit*, or, as above, *consolo* and similar forms.] exhorted me to sing in that church, and I ought to have had half of that tithe above all else. In this way I served that church for a year and a half, yet received nothing from it.

Therefore we entered into an agreement. Afterwards I asked him for my share of that tithe, and he burned with excessive anger against me. He came upon me by night with his relatives Albricus, Kebahardus, and Wolframmus, and they scourged me until they had almost beaten the life from my body.

I, most wretched of the wretched, sought God’s mercy and holy remedy, and called upon your name. But they said that neither a saint nor any human being should be able to free me from their hands.

Afterwards they dragged me to the altar of Saint Remedius [Note: Saint Remedius. Saint Remedius the bishop is mentioned by Usuard and in the Roman Martyrology, on the third day, fol. 2], and made me swear stability toward that church. They also made me swear another oath, that throughout my life I should not appeal to your piety or to your messenger, so that they might do me justice.

Then I sought my justice from them, but found none. Now I fear my unconsecration; I fear what they did not fear. Therefore I beseech your holiness that I may obtain my justice, since I can find neither justice nor mercy among them except through your mercy, and for the redemption of the soul of your father, whose servant I formerly was.

## LETTER XCIII. [Note: In Serrarius this letter bears the title “A Petition of Appeal,” with the note: “To Ludovicus, son of Charles the Great, mentioned above in Letter 107. For the letter says, ‘in the service of your father.’” Ser.] . . . TO LUDOVICUS. [DATE UNCERTAIN]

To your most devout ears, most merciful and glorious emperor, I shall try to report—not with the boldness of presumption, but because of my great need—how our paternal inheritance was first taken away from me, a sinner, and from my paternal sister, and still remains withheld.

Therefore, most devout emperor and most merciful helper of all who are in need, we greatly require your protection, so that through your mercy and almsgiving I may be able to reach that inheritance, since in no other way can it be restored to us except through your most devoted and always benevolent clemency in doing justice.

Thus far, my lord, however imperfectly stated, may your Excellence deign to hear the appeal of our misery.

We had a father, most serene emperor, named Richart, and a paternal uncle named Richolf; both were Saxons, and their inheritance lay in Saxony itself. While they were in the service of your father, the lord Emperor Charles of blessed memory, their relatives and fellow countrymen [Note: *Pagenses*. Those belonging to the same district. Although *pagus* is said to derive from Greek πήγη, that is, “spring,” it does not signify only one small village, but sometimes a collection of several villages bound and held together by a certain authority, law, and right. Today it is called a satrapy or prefecture. Ser.]—being enraged against them on account of Christianity—plundered everything which they had in their houses as the product of their own labor, because they perceived that they wished to persist in the Christian faith and were in no way willing to deny it.

Afterwards it happened that the lord Emperor sent my paternal uncle Richolf on a royal mission [Note: *In missaticum*. On a legation, so that they were sent as envoys or legates. Hence a little later it says: “Those who killed the aforesaid envoys.” Here, however, it may be taken for a village, since below the district of Marscheim is mentioned. Ser.] across the Elbe with the men written below, namely Count Gotessedo, Count . . . , Count . . . , and . . .; all of them were killed there together for the establishment of Christianity.

When my father Richart heard this, he went to report it to the lord Emperor Charles. While he was on the road, my mother was seized by the same men who had previously killed those aforesaid envoys. They handed her over into the custody of sureties, and divided among themselves by robbery everything else which they found there, whether provisions or any other possessions.

When my father learned of this, he crossed over secretly, seized her almost as though in a theft, and fled with her to the district called Marstheim, to his maternal inheritance. He remained there until, by order of the lord Emperor, the Saxons were led out of Saxony and transported elsewhere [Note: “They were led out.” The transportation of the Saxons into foreign regions and settlements is clearly described in Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne*. Ser.]. At that time my father and mother were also led away with them.

After they had been led away and had dwelt for whatever periods of time in that migration, alienated from their own land, my father was taken from this life by the final day. My mother, my sister, and I remained; and, by God’s mercy, the three of us still survive. Yet we have not reached our paternal inheritance.

Therefore, most devout emperor, who never cease mercifully to provide all the poor, and all who are in need, with a secure refuge for the love of God, may you also, in response to this appeal, deign to assist us, who have been stripped of our paternal inheritance, through your almsgiving. Through your faithful servants, deign to investigate whether it ought justly to belong to us or not, if this is decreed by your most holy Excellence.

For many witnesses from those districts can be produced concerning this matter; they know it well and will truly be able to disclose it, O most merciful and most serene emperor.

## LETTER XCIV. ANONYMOUS TO ANONYMOUS. [DATE UNCERTAIN]

To my most reverend lord, venerable with every effort of virtue and, after God, my special patron, your suppliant and humble servant in the Lord sends greetings.

I confess, O most blessed bishop, that I had long resolved, if the state of affairs and the fleeting changes of time permitted it, to celebrate the approaching solemnity of the Nativity of the Lord there, rejoicing in the company of the brothers, and afterwards, with life as my companion, to enjoy the accessible presence of your charity.

But because we have been restrained by various obstacles and impediments, as the bearer of this letter will declare more fully in person, we have been unable to accomplish this. I therefore ask you to grant pardon for the difficulty.

For considerable periods of time must be extended in this study, at least by one who, kindled by the diligent acuity of reading, will probe to the marrow the laws of Roman jurisprudence, examine from the innermost heart all the decrees of the jurists, and—what is much more difficult and intricate than these—distinguish, by a pedestrian rule, a hundred kinds of meter, and examine, along a proper succession of syllables, the melodies intermingled with song. For students of this subject an obscurity all the more impenetrable is presented because the number of learned teachers is so rare.

But the narrow limits of a letter do not allow us to reason at length about these matters: namely, how the hidden instruments of the metrical art are combined in letters, *logoi* (terms or words), poetic feet, figures, verses, tones, and durations; how the pathic discipline of the sevenfold division treats acephalous, lagarous, poecilic, and other varieties; which verses are called monosemic, pentasemic, or quidecasemic; and how catalectic, brachycatalectic, or hypercatalectic verses are recognized.

These matters, as I think, and others like them, cannot possibly be grasped within a brief interval or in a momentary stroke.

What need is there to mention the method of calculation, when the impending discussion of computation has pressed so heavily upon my mind that I began to regard as insignificant all my former labor in reading, whose secret chambers I had previously believed I knew? To use the words of blessed Jerome, I who had seemed to myself a little scholar have again begun to be a disciple.

Moreover, concerning the zodiacal circle of twelve signs, which revolve in the turning of heaven, I think it best to remain silent, lest a dark and profound subject, if proclaimed in a cheap form of explanation, be disgraced and diminished—especially since mastery of the art of astrology and the exceedingly difficult calculation of the horoscope require the painstaking investigation of a learned teacher.

For this reason, dearest father, we have touched upon these matters briefly and step by step, not enticed by the noisy verbosity of loquacity, but so that you may know that such profound secrets of things cannot be understood exactly unless frequent and extended meditation is applied.

Greet in Christ all the company of my associates, from the least to the greatest. I beseech and adjure them, through the clemency of Christ, to pour out prayers to the Lord for me, oppressed by the weight of sins and the burden of crimes.

## LETTER XCV. ANONYMOUS TO ANONYMOUS. [DATE UNCERTAIN]

To the holy and venerable brothers, the distinguished provost and all the brothers subject to him in Christ, from the monastery of the distinguished [monastery], greetings in Christ.

[Note: A formula formerly used for sending the names of recently deceased brothers, so that prayers and Masses might be offered for them. The individual names were explicitly added, as is indicated in the following Letter 109 and Letter 111; hence the words here, “and the rest.” The same duty of mutual charity flourishes among others as well, including in the present confraternities of the Blessed Virgin, and especially in our Society of Jesus, so much so that names are sent here even from India and the New World, and from here to there. Would that I, though unworthy, may deserve to enjoy after death this great assistance—which, as we have seen, so many people, and Saint Boniface himself so often and so earnestly, desired. Amen. Ser.]

Accordingly, we have sent the names of our brothers who recently died, so that you may remember them in your holy prayers according to the customary practice, and so that you may send the same written names in turn to the other monasteries, just as we do whenever the names of deceased brothers come to us from you or from the other monasteries. This is it, and the rest.

[Note: Although in manuscript C there is neither a title nor a number for this letter, it nevertheless appears to be different from the preceding one, since at the end of that letter it says, “Finally.” Moreover, this is a different question, although it is adjacent to the preceding one: whether someone who has bound himself by a mortal sin after baptism can become a priest. The answer is no. This should surely be understood first, so that one who has sinned in this way may humbly recognize himself as unworthy of the priesthood; and secondly, so that no mention of this matter may continue here. This applies if the sin is a cause of scandal, or penance has not yet expiated it, or it has indeed been expiated but by solemn penance; see canon *Canones*, distinction 50. Ser.]

## LETTER XCVI. ANONYMOUS TO ANONYMOUS. [DATE UNCERTAIN]

[The beginning is missing.]

For sometimes, and in accordance with the merit of the peoples, the persons of those who are chosen are themselves chosen; thus peoples know that they have received bishops as rulers corresponding to their own merit.

But the law itself testifies that one who, after baptism, has been defiled by some mortal sin is not to be promoted to the priesthood. For Moses commanded in the law that priests should not offer any blemished animal upon the altar of God. Later, through Malachi, God reproached the priests of Israel who despised this command, saying:

“You are priests who have polluted my name, and you have said: ‘In what way have we polluted it?’ By offering polluted bread upon my altar, and you offered the blind and the lame.”

Therefore, in Numbers, the red heifer, whose ashes are the purification of the people, is likewise commanded to be offered upon the altar of the Lord only if it has performed no earthly work, has not drawn the yoke of sin, and has not been bound by the fetters of sins.

But why should we add more? If one who is already placed in the episcopate or presbyterate and has committed some mortal sin ought not to offer bread to the Lord, how much more should anyone, knowing that “the mighty shall suffer mighty torments,” withdraw from this position—which is not so much an honor as a burden—and not seek to occupy the place of others who are worthy!

For one who presides over the instruction and formation of peoples in virtue must necessarily be holy in all things and held blameworthy in nothing. Whoever reproves another for sin must himself be free from sin.

### Prayer for Oneself

Lord Jesus Christ, be merciful to me, a sinner, because you alone are immortal and without sin.

Lord our God, you are blessed, who bless all things; you are holy, who sanctify. Lord our God, forgive me, your servant, because I am a sinner and unworthy, since I have presumed to invoke you at your holy altar, because I have sinned before you and before your angels. But grant us forgiveness of sins, and strengthen your holy Church in the true faith, and teach us to do your will all the days of our life. Through the Lord.

### Secret

Receive, most merciful Father, with kindness the sacrifice of reconciliation and praise which I, your unworthy servant, offer to you for your male and female servants, because you know my formation; you know everything that I have done in your sight and in the sight of your saints. You do not desire the death of a sinner, but that he should turn and live. Look upon me and have mercy on me, because you are a gracious and merciful God, who live and reign forever and ever. Amen.

Lord, grant me peace and health, faith and chastity, food and clothing. You, Lord, made me from the clay of the earth, bones and sinews; you strengthened me by the Holy Spirit; you entrusted me to yourself. I am yours, Lord; guard me.

Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, whom I presume to adore with all my heart, with all my soul, and with all my strength, you created me. Whatever I have done after holy baptism against your will, in word, thought, or deed, forgive my sins; and those who have sinned against me I forgive before the sight of God and all the angelic virtues.

Lord God Almighty, I confess my sins to you, the sins I have committed and carried out; grant me true repentance.

Most high Lord, I have sinned. Lord, I have sinned in sleep and laziness. I have sinned, Lord, wretched as I am; and, alas, wretched as I am, I have polluted the sacraments by my own will. Alas, wretched as I am, my sins are so many within me. God, have mercy; you desire no one to perish. Grant me true repentance, and deem me worthy to be heard.

## LETTER XCVII. ANONYMOUS TO ANONYMOUS. [DATE UNCERTAIN]

[The beginning is missing.]

For some, the tormenting fire rose as high as their armpits, some as high as their necks, and for others it boiled above their heads, mixed with fire and ink. There she saw abbots, abbesses, counts, and a multitude of every sex being tortured in various ways. She also saw places prepared according to the merits of their sins for many who were still alive, of every rank and condition, and that all souls would at some time be released from the pits, either on the day of judgment or before it.

She said that she had seen one woman redeemed from a certain pit through the solemn celebration of Masses, and declared that this is the greatest benefit for souls departing from the body. She said that the whole human race and the entire world had been gathered before her sight, so that she could discern what each person had done, whether good or evil, naming what each had done while living in the body at that hour; and she could have recounted the merits of almost all living people.

Afterwards she saw the land of the living and rejoicing, full of fragrant flowers, and many souls of people known and unknown to us, just as she testified that she had seen them in all the places.

Then, from that land, she saw a path extending to the first heaven in the form of a rainbow, and from there another path to the second, and from the second to the third. She saw assemblies of the living and the dead clothed in white, and above them a heaven always more beautiful than the one below.

She reported that in the monastery itself the judge had commanded Ingedraga to reveal to everyone who remained there all their sins and offenses; no command or prohibition had been given to the other people, and so forth.

There are many more things which she indicated to us individually and by name, but it would take too long for me to explain them. I especially remember this: she saw demons divided into three exceedingly large companies. One was in the air, another on land and in the sea, and the third was preparing torments in the places of punishment.

She saw the first company striving to deceive human beings in this ordinary life; the second continually and eagerly pursuing in the air the souls departing from the prison of the body and handing them over to torments. In those punitive pits she saw Cuthburg and Wialan, once enjoying royal power, sunk down. One, Cuthburg, was immersed as far as the armpits; her head and shoulder were conspicuous, while the rest of her limbs were covered with spots. The other, Wialan, had a flame extending above her head, and her entire soul was being burned at once.

She saw the ministers of punishment throw into their faces their own carnal desires, like boiling mud, and heard from their voices a horrible howling, which seemed miserably to resound throughout almost the whole world.

There she also saw the former exile and count called Ceola Snoding, with his back bent and his head and feet fixed in hooks. She saw your abbot in that same place, amid a double smoke; Aethilbald, once a royal tyrant; and also a great multitude of infants who had died, especially without baptism, under Bishop Daniel, all sorrowful and grieving.

She perceived the soul of each one according to its particular appearance, corresponding to its former limbs but differing in form: some shone with the brilliance of the sun, others with that of the moon, and others with the rays of the stars, each in its own way and together.

As for those living contemptuaries who still remain and who despise so beneficial a revelation—Daniel the soldier, Bregwulf, and their companions in shared fornications, and the punishments they had deserved, which she testified that she had seen—I think we ought to remain silent.

At the end of this vision she heard an indescribable sound resounding through those three regions of heavenly lights and among all the multitudes of souls dwelling there. Above, it descended into the lower regions like the voice of many trumpets, wonderfully overcoming them.

Immediately afterwards, when the music had withdrawn and the angelic guides and her sister were admonishing her, she retained in her faithful mind the love of the Creator; then she was restored to her body.

Nevertheless, amid the anguish of the flesh, for some time she saw an innumerable multitude of unclean spirits lamenting mournfully, because they had learned that, by God’s gift, their wickednesses, which they had practiced, had been disclosed to human beings.

As confirmation of this vision, she foretold the recovery from her illness, which had previously continued for two years while almost her entire body was bound together at once. We now recognize this broadly as having occurred through the mercy of God.

Nor was this all: she clearly made known to her close associates, one by one, particular matters unknown to the others—not only to them, but also to the king, the queen, the bishops, and many others whose names it would take too long to include in writing.

By the command of that Judge she also imposed a fast lasting forty days for the common offenses of the entire household mentioned above. She foretold the vengeance that would come upon human beings in their own bodies because of their common negligence toward the external admonitions of God through creation, and many other things like these.

Before this, while she had returned from the contemplation above, she mournfully declared that she had seen this miserable life covered, as though with the blackest veil, by the vices of pride, envy, greed, detraction, and others, and left without the light of eternal brightness.

Farewell in Christ, and remember me without ceasing in your prayers with brotherly love.

## LETTER XCVIII. DANIEL TO FORTHERIUS. [DATE UNCERTAIN]

To Forthere, father of God’s household and worthy fellow priest, Daniel, servant of the holy people.

Having read the supplicatory letters brought to us concerning the diaconate of my elected brother Merwalth, although he had come later than the duly appointed time to those who had obtained the orders of presbyter and deacon, we did not defer him.

Although the request appeared unfamiliar and untimely, the pious petition of the brothers nevertheless prevailed, since, together with you, we saw that he lacked nothing in merit for promotion to the order of deacon.

After our hesitation had been set aside and his stubbornness abandoned, he finally became willing, even though late, and was received into the office of honor.

Therefore, since you perceive that enough has been done for you in this matter and that you have honorably attained the object of your desire, regard him as already established among the Levites, and join him in perfect devotion in the work of teaching, so that you may be able to acquire confidence in Christ Jesus.

May the glory of almighty God cause you to flourish long in the Catholic faith and in prosperous success.

## LETTER XCIX. . . . TO BALDHARDUS. [DATE UNCERTAIN]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the holy Trinity, to my beloved and only brother Baldhardus, perpetual greetings in Christ.

Know that the words of your embassy came to me through a faithful messenger named Aldred, as did the gifts, which I embraced with deepest affection.

And now I confess to you that, with the Lord’s help, I desire to fulfill everything you commanded me, if your will deigns to come to me. For I can in no way quiet the fountain of my tears when I see and hear that others are going to their friends.

Then I remember that I was abandoned by my parents in my youth and remained here alone. Yet I was not abandoned by the Lord; rather, I give thanks to God for his immense goodness, which he often customarily bestows, through the entrails of his mercy, upon those who do not deserve it. Thus he has preserved us unharmed.

And now, my brother, I adjure and beseech you to remove the sadness from my soul, because it harms me greatly.

For I say that even if it is only for the space of one day and you then depart again, at the Lord’s command and according to your will, nevertheless sadness will withdraw from my soul and grief from my heart.

But if it displeases you to fulfill my request, then I call God as witness that our love will never have been abandoned in me.

And now I truly tell you that I know nothing better than for you to come there, if you wish, rather than for me to remain here.

But if some other course seems better to you, I can then tell you that my mind desires to come there where the bodies of our parents rest, to end my temporal life there, and to reach the place where the perfect dwelling is seen, the land of the living, and the joys of angels rejoicing without end.

Farewell in Christ.

You will receive the little gift, small though it is and laden with the greatest affection, which we sent you through the faithful messenger named Aldred: namely, one ribbon.

I seek prayers for myself,

Your fair woman (*formosa famina*),

That Christ may abolish

Both new and old sins;

That I may be armed by angelic powers

At my right and left side.

[Note: “Hail.” So also in Poem 3 after Letter 69, and in Saint Augustine, Letter 43. It appears to derive from the Hebrew verb *chaueh*, meaning “live” or “be safe.” Cujacius collects many examples in Book I of his *Observations*, chapter 15. Yet *habe* is written for *have* according to the orthography noted in many places, in general note 7. Ser.]

Hail, dear bearer of the cross,

Happily unto the end

Of prayers; may the chief matters be disclosed

Of your *sophae entiae* [sic; perhaps “wisdom”],

That dread perils,

With immeasurable clemency,

Surrounded by legions

And divine majesty—

A greeting from your sister—

Preserve your reputation simply.

## LETTER C. BERTGITHA TO BALDHARDUS. [DATE UNCERTAIN]

To Balthard, his most beloved brother in the Lord and dearest in the flesh, Berthgyth sends greetings in Christ’s name.

My soul is weary of my life because of the love of our brotherhood. For I have been left alone and deprived of the help of my relatives. My father and my mother have abandoned me, but the Lord has received me. Many gatherings of waters lie between you and me; nevertheless, let us be joined by charity, because true charity is never broken by the limits of place. Yet I say that sadness has never departed from my soul, nor does my mind find rest even in sleep, because love is strong as death. Therefore I ask you now, my dearest brother, to come to me, or to have me come to you, so that I may see you before I die, because your love never departs from my soul. Your only sister greets you in Christ, brother. I pray for you as I do for myself, by day and by night, at hours and moments, that you may always possess health with Christ.

[Col. 0798C]

Fare well, living happily;

May salvation be yours through the ages;

Let us live for the Lord alone,

That you may be simply holy,

May life forever in the world be granted you from on high.

Indeed, in prayers, with abundant tears poured down to the ground, I very often ask him to provide help, so that we may be worthy of the glory where the exceedingly joyful songs of the angels resound, where the bright joy of Christ’s heavenly clemency and lofty praise endures through the ages. May we be strong; join us, victorious, to the angelic hosts, enduring forever in the joys of paradise: Elon and El (“God”), and Michael, Acaddai, Adonai (“Lord”), Allevatia [uncertain], Alleluia (“Praise the Lord”).

## LETTER CI. LATITO TO N. [DATE UNCERTAIN]

[Col. 0798D]

To the most reverend and most holy N., I, Latito, least of all, send unending greetings in the Lord.

I hear concerning you that you are about to begin a journey, and I urge you not to falter. Come, do what you have begun. Remember the Saxon saying: “Ost daed lata domae foreldit sigi sit hagahuem suurltit thiana.” [The supplied Saxon wording is opaque, and no reliable English translation can be given without conjecture.]

Yet I do not know that such a thing is in you. You should not work here, but go where the harvest is, with God’s help, as the Savior says: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few,” and so forth. What should I say of myself, the least of all, who live under another’s rule, possessing no profit, as is the custom here of all who dwell here, possessing nothing except daily allowances? Yet I do not grieve on account of excessive poverty, since the Lord consoled us by saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

## LETTER CII. ANONYMOUS TO ANONYMOUS [DATE UNCERTAIN]

To the most reverend and dearest brother in Christ, N., unending greetings.

I therefore entreat you to deign to provide consolation for me, the least of all, and with a most compassionate mind to assist my needs with the little books of which mention had been made—that is, with what I need.

## LETTER CIII. ANONYMOUS TO ANONYMOUS [DATE UNCERTAIN]

[Col. 0799B]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, I most willingly grant to this brother, named N., permission to return to the monastery of the venerable abbot, in which the aforesaid brother first vowed to God the service owed to him, with the peace of our community; and there let him strive faithfully to serve Christ.

## LETTER CIV. BERTHWALD TO FORTHERIUS [DATE UNCERTAIN] (C)

To the most reverend and most holy fellow bishop Forthere, Berthwald, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings in the Lord.

Since my petition, in which I entreated you in person concerning the venerable abbot Beorwald’s granting the redemption of a captive girl who is shown to have relatives among us, turned out contrary to what I believed to no avail, Harassed anew by their entreaties, I have thought it most useful to send these letters to you through the girl’s own brother, named Eppa. Through them I beg you to obtain without fail from the aforesaid abbot that he accept three hundred solidi for the girl from the hand of the bearer of this letter and hand her over to him, to be brought here, so that she may spend the remainder of her life with her kinsmen, not in the sorrow of servitude but in the joy of freedom. When your goodwill has brought this matter to completion, you will receive a reward from God and thanks from me. Our brother Beorwald, moreover, loses nothing, as I judge, of what he justly possessed in her.

What I ought to have done earlier, I beg you—when you remember me in frequent prayers—to deign nonetheless to remember me. May Jesus Christ our Lord preserve your reverence safe for a long age.

## LETTER CV. H. TO N. [DATE UNCERTAIN]

To my only and most beloved brother N., H., the least of God’s handmaids, sends greetings in Christ.

What is this, my brother, that you have allowed so long a time to pass? Why have you delayed coming? Why do you not consider that I am alone in this land, and that no other brother visits me, nor does any of my relatives come to me? And if you do this because I have so far been unable to offer some benefit according to what your mind would have diligently wished, nevertheless you ought, without anyone else persuading you or changing your mind, to forget the rights of charity and kinship.

O brother, my brother, how can you afflict the mind of my little self, day and night, with constant mourning, tears, and sadness, through the absence of your charity? Do you not know for certain that among all the living I prefer no one else to your love? Behold, I cannot tell you everything by letter. I now hold it as certain that you have no concern for my insignificance.

## LETTER CVI. ANONYMOUS TO ANONYMOUS [DATE UNCERTAIN]

To a revered and beloved brother in Christ, I wish the desirable salvation of eternal well-being.

I confess to your charity that I have never wished to place faith in false tales of words, nor did I believe that any bitter shoots of malicious disparagement should grow concerning the fidelity of your devoted charity. Rather, I judge that the goodwill of your love is mindful of Solomon’s saying: “Do not contrive evil against your friend, when he himself has trusted in you.”

And now I bear a trusting heart concerning the perseverance of your devotion. I give you thanks for the aid of sacred Scripture which you kindly took care to send me; and I beg that, whenever you are able to help me in writing on parchment, you send it. Whatever you entrust to me, necessary for your bodily support, I shall willingly and faithfully do for you. Although we are separated by a great distance of place, may we nevertheless be united by spiritual charity. Fare always in the Lord, and deign to be mindful of my insignificance in your holy prayers.

## LETTER CVII. WETBERT TO ANONYMOUS [DATE UNCERTAIN]

[Col. 0800C]

To my most beloved brother and fellow presbyter N., Wethbert, insignificant in Christ, sends the greeting of eternal charity.

With urgent prayers of intimate charity I earnestly beg you to deign to remember me in your sacred prayers, because I am struck by the hammer of worldly temptation, while vain things trouble me.

## LETTER CVIII. THE COMMUNITY OF THREE MONASTERIES TO COENGILSO AND OTHERS [DATE UNCERTAIN]

To the brothers most beloved in Christ, the abbots Coengilso and Ingeld, and especially to our kinsman Wiehtbert the presbyter, the entire community of the three monasteries—that is, of the most reverend father Aldhun, of Cneuburga, handmaid of Christ, and likewise of Coenburga, the abbesses—sends perpetual and indissoluble greetings in the Lord.

For we gladly and gratefully received the little gifts of your greeting, and, with God’s help, we desire to repay them with things worthy of them. We also agree to maintain continually, with good spirit and pure faith toward you, the communion in prayer which you wrote that you wished to have with us, at the hours which you specified.

I, Cneuburg, also beg you, Wiethbert, faithful presbyter, to keep memorially the names of our deceased sisters and to transmit them to all our friends round about. The first of them was Quoengyth, my own sister, and Edlu, who, while she was still living, was the mother of Etan and a kinswoman of Aldhun, formerly your abbot. The burial of both of them took place on the same day, namely, on the Ides of September.

May the almighty Lord deign to preserve your blessedness, which prays for us, safe forever, most beloved brothers and lords. Emmanuel. Greet all Christ’s servants round about with our truest words, most beloved brothers.

## LETTER CIX. ANONYMOUS TO ANONYMOUS [DATE UNCERTAIN]

Having received your letter, dearest brother N., brought to us concerning your present condition, we received it with joy, giving thanks to God because we heard that, while you were far away on pilgrimage, the Lord showed his kindness toward you. All the kin and blood-relatives of your family greet you in Christ and beseech you to strive diligently to advance in good works in God, with our prayers added, so that he who is the giver of all consolation, who has separated us bodily on the journey of this miserable life, may join us forever in his kingdom, which endures without end. Fare always, greeted by the supplicating voices of your friends. May the Lord protect your life from now and forever.

## LETTER CX. ANONYMOUS TO ANONYMOUS [DATE UNCERTAIN]

To the most reverend brother and proven soldier of Christ, N. [Note: In C there is a single letter that appears to be R, but it could be read as N. SER.], a king in the glorious heavenly Lord, greetings of divine well-being.

From the report of certain venerable servants of God I have learned that you have been gravely afflicted by the bitter illness of disease, long tormented and laboriously wearied, yet not mournfully overcome. When this became known to me, I gave thanks to the spiritual Father and understood that you had been visited by heavenly grace, enriched by a divine gift, and adorned with a spiritual mark.

This visitation by the chastening Lord, I say, invites you to be joined to him with eager desire and unfading charity. Therefore what has been said must never be erased from memory: “The king desired your beauty.” Through attentive meditation, do not fail to understand that, although for a time you have been weakened by the hand of the Lord who chastens and loves you, you have nevertheless been prepared eternally for the salvation of your soul, because God chastises every son whom he receives.

And, rejoicing and glad, say with the apostle Paul: “When I am weak, then I am strong,” and “power is made perfect in weakness,” so that bodily weakness may be spiritual strength, and so that you may deserve to be a son of the Most High, who invites you to the bridal chamber of the eternal king. I desire that you may continually prosper in Christ with favorable success, and so forth.

## LETTER CXI. ANONYMOUS TO ANONYMOUS [DATE UNCERTAIN]

N., unworthy through the love of intimate affection, sends greetings of well-being in the Lord to N., who with great governance directs the fourfold kingdoms of the three-part world.

[Note: “Triquadri”: because the world is divided into three parts—Europe, Asia, and Africa. Jordanes likewise calls Britain “triquadra” in Book I, *On the Affairs of the Goths*, whereas others call it “triquetra.” The fourfold kingdoms are those four from Daniel, chapter II, concerning which the letter itself speaks. SER.]

For I think, most loving sister, that you will recognize what is often read as having been foretold in divine oracles: that, as the end of the world now approaches and the statue once fashioned from four kinds of metals is about to fall, the hydra too is always threatening with new hisses, and Scylla, with her inherited brood, does not cease barking. The kite also flies downward, and the dove to her windows.

Therefore, dearest, although I am somewhat far removed from you in equality of merits, I nevertheless strive daily to be near you by frequent remembrance. I beg you to remember our words, which we pledged together when I had departed. Fare well, living through a longer age, and, with a happier life, intercede for me. I have written these few things to you, not arrogantly commending myself, but humbly asking for your prayers, as for a sister whom I have recently found. Fare well.

In heaven, life everlasting already burns for the just,

By which the saints will always shine with beautiful light

In the Father’s kingdom, like the bright Titan in the world,

And through august Jerusalem, resounding with a thundering voice.

Thus they always praise the Lord, singing without end,

And together they compose holy strains through the air with their voices;

Here they continually celebrate songs to Christ on high,

[Col. 0802C]

[Note: “Whom the choir”: The verse is simply defective. Yet formerly writers allowed themselves many liberties in Greek words, even those of good reputation. Joseph Scaliger says in Book II of his work on Ausonius, chapter 21, that Latin poets had this peculiar practice: not only did they disregard Greek declensions in Greek words and bring them under Latin rules, but they also overturned quantity, measuring it only by accent. He proves this with several examples from Plautus, by whom the second syllable is shortened in *Phaedromus* (“bright-running,” φαίδρομος) and in *Philippus* (“horse-loving,” φίλιππος). Ausonius likewise pronounced *trigonon* (“triangle”) and *tetragonon* (“quadrangle”) in this way:

“Through an equal number of parts the rule of triangles proceeds.”

“Lightning flashes with life-giving appearance in the four-sided figure.”

Others did the same; and even the Christian Prudentius, shortening the second syllable, said *eidōla* (“images,” εἴδωλα), and likewise *ekklēsia* (“assembly” or “church,” ἐκκλησία), with the second syllable shortened. In this manner, therefore, the second syllable in *martyrōn* (“of martyrs,” μαρτύρων) is lengthened here. The first syllable in *choros* (“chorus”) is lengthened not because of the accent, since it is written χορό, but because of the following *r*. The same could also be said of *martyrum*. “B and r commonly make syllables common,” says the venerable Bede in his *On the Art of Meter*, p. 39. These matters are therefore noted once for verses of this kind. SER.]

Whom the entire choir of martyrs likewise adores,

Rejoicing greatly in the Lord, pouring forth many praises

From the heart, giving thanks to man and to God,

Lifting its happier face in gentle, wondrous melodies.

Believe me, for I embrace you with the greatest love.

Fare well, little virgin in Christ,

You are a great concern to me;

I weave praises for you,

And I ask you with trembling:

Return with fervor the vows

Which we pledged together,

You, Christ’s young disciple,

And knowledgeable in the work;

And I repeat my thanks,

Lamb, for Christ’s love,

In the highest heaven;

Remember them steadfastly.

## LETTER CXII. ELFLEDA TO ADOLANA [DATE UNCERTAIN]

[Col. 0803A]

To the holy lady Adolana, honored by God, abbess, Elfleda, handmaid of the ecclesiastical household, sends the greeting of eternal well-being in the Lord.

Ever since, through the widely reported testimony of those arriving from those regions, we came to know the form of your holiness, we first began to love you inwardly, from the depths of our heart, in accordance with the Lord’s command, the Lord saying: “This is my commandment, that you love one another.” Therefore, supported by prayers, we humbly ask that in your most holy and fiery oracles you deign to defend us before the almighty Lord, since our humility will not at all be reluctant to repay you in kind. The apostle James commands and says this very thing: “Pray for one another, that you may be saved.”

Moreover, to your supreme holiness and customary piety we earnestly commend N., a devoted handmaid of God and religious abbess, our dearest and most faithful daughter from the years of her adolescence. For the love of Christ and in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, she desires to go to their holy thresholds, but until now we have detained her because of the necessity and usefulness of the souls entrusted to her. We beg that she and those accompanying her be received by you with the affection of true charity into the bosom of your compassionate kindness, so that, with God’s help and aided by your piety, she may at last complete the journey long desired and often begun.

For this reason, asking again and again, we request that she be sent with your little letters and messages to the most holy city of Rome, with a favorable journey aided by the holy standard-bearing prince of the apostles, Peter. And if, God willing, she should ever be present, whatever she may suggest in person, on any occasion requiring it, concerning the needs of her journey, she will find ready with you.

May divine grace deign to protect your holiness, who prays for us.

[Col. 0803]

## II. THE OATH BY WHICH SAINT BONIFACE BOUND HIMSELF TO POPE GREGORY II

[Col. 0803B]

In the name of the Lord God, our Savior Jesus Christ, while the lord Leo the Great was emperor, in the seventh year [Note: After his consulship. Mabillon, on this passage, p. 36; Sirmond and the Rheims and Pithoean manuscripts restore “the sixth year,” and prove it from the fact that Leo the Isaurian entered upon the empire on the eighth day before the Kalends of April and, as is conjectured, obtained the consulship on the following Kalends, in the year of Christ 717, in the fifteenth indiction. Boniface, however, was consecrated on the day before the Kalends of December, in the sixth indiction; hence the sixth year of Leo’s empire and consulship, A.D. 722. Marianus Scotus in his *Chronicle* favors Sirmond. Nevertheless, Leo’s seventh year and the sixth indiction seem to be retained here, the indiction being reckoned not from 25 September but from the Kalends of January. For Boniface returned to Germany from his first Roman journey near the end of 719; then he remained with Willibrord for three years; thereafter he converted the Saxons and Hessians to the faith, a task completed in less than one year; and then, summoned to Rome, he received episcopal consecration from Gregory II in A.D. 723, in the seventh indiction, as Pagius observed. WURDT.] after his consulship, and also in the fourth year of the emperor Constantine the Great, his son, in the sixth indiction.

I, Boniface, bishop by the grace of God, promise to you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to your vicar, blessed Pope Gregory, and to his successors, by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, the inseparable Trinity, and by this most sacred body of yours, that I will show every faithfulness and purity of the holy Catholic faith and, with God working, will persevere in the unity of that same faith, in which the salvation of all Christians is undoubtedly shown to consist. In no way will I consent, at anyone’s persuasion, against the unity of the common and universal Church. Rather, as I have said, I will show in every respect my faithfulness, purity, and cooperation to you and to the interests of your Church, to which the power of binding and loosing has been given by the Lord God, and to your aforesaid vicar and his successors.

And if I should learn that bishops are behaving contrary to the ancient institutions of the holy Fathers, I will have no communion or association with them; rather, if I am able to prevent it, I will prevent it; if I am unable, I will immediately report this faithfully to my apostolic lord.

But if—which God forbid—I should attempt in any way, by any device or opportunity, to do anything contrary to the terms of this profession of mine, may I be found guilty in the eternal judgment and incur the vengeance of Ananias and Sapphira, who presumed to defraud you even of their own possessions.

[Note: “Presumed”: Just as the title “pope,” which at first was common to all bishops, is later read as having been assigned only to the supreme pontiff, so too with “apostolic.” Gregory the Great, Book V, Letter 37: “Although there are many apostles, nevertheless, because of that primacy, only the see of the prince of the apostles has grown strong in authority.” Rupert of Deutz, Book I, *On the Divine Office*, chapter 27: “The successors of the other apostles are called patriarchs; but Peter’s successor, because of the excellence of the prince of the apostles, is called apostolic.” WURDT.]

I, Boniface, the insignificant bishop, wrote this little document of the oath with my own hand and, placing it upon the most sacred body of Saint Peter, made the oath as prescribed, with God as witness and judge; and I promise to preserve it.

[Note: “I promise”: There are those who loudly proclaim that the Roman Church is the center of unity, although the rays continually extend from the center toward the circumference of the circle. These people disparage the foregoing sworn profession of faith as though it had first been deposited by Boniface, although they ought to know from ecclesiastical history that it was already customary under Pope Gelasius, toward the end of the fifth century. Moreover, Pope Gregory II acted most prudently in requiring this profession, since Boniface, although commended by Daniel, bishop of England, was entirely unknown at Rome, a stranger arriving from a distant kingdom who was to be sent to preach the Gospel of Christ in Germany, which had long lacked an archbishop, as we shall see below. That bishop would deserve to be called imprudent who entrusted the care of souls to an untested and completely unknown priest. Moreover, Boniface conducted the sacred mission in Germany with the consent of princes and bishops. WURDT.]

## III. COUNCILS HELD UNDER SAINT BONIFACE (C, S)

### I. THE COUNCIL OF BAVARIA, HELD IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 740

[Col. 0805A]

Baronius, father of ecclesiastical history, and Spondanus, under this year; Mabillon, in the third century of the *Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict*, part II, in the notes on chapter 10 of the *Life of Saint Willibald*; Eckart, Book XXII of the *History of the Franks*, no. 11; Marcus Hansizius, volume I of *Sacred Germany*, p. 124; and the editor of Meichelbeck’s *Chronicle of Benediktbeuern*, no. 31 and following, assert that a synod was celebrated this year, 740, by Saint Boniface in Bavaria.

We shall examine the contrary opinion of the distinguished men Pagius, in his *Criticism* under the year 742, and Mansi, in the supplement to the *Councils*, volume I, who defer Saint Boniface’s first synod to the year 742, in a special digression after this century.

The location of this council is uncertain. This seems certain: it was held in Bavaria, either at Augsburg, as the pope had advised, or beside the bank of the Danube. Eckart thinks that it was held at Freising; the editor of Meichelbeck, at Regensburg. Nor are the persons who took part in the council known with sufficient certainty. In Eckart’s view, besides the clergy and fellow bishops, Saint Boniface’s ordinary companions—Lull, Eoban, Sturm, and the others—were present, as were Viggo of Augsburg, Luido of Speyer, Rudolt of Constance, and Adda, or Hetto, or Philippus, bishops of the churches of Strasbourg, because Gregory III, in letters written in 739, among the *Serariana*, no. 129, invited them to hasten to celebrate the councils announced by Saint Boniface.

For this year they assign the establishment by Saint Boniface of a new episcopal see at Neuburg on the Danube, later united with the diocese of Augsburg about the year 801. See *The Treatise on the Former Bishopric at Neuburg on the Danube*, whose author is Michael Stein, canon and librarian of Rebdorf. It appears in *The New Historical Treatises of the Bavarian Academy of Sciences*, first volume, 1779, pp. 383–424. WURDT.

### II. THE COUNCIL OF SALZBURG ON THE FRANCONIAN SAALE, HELD IN A.D. 741

[Col. 0805D]

The year 741 was still running when Saint Boniface convened a second synod at Salzburg on the Franconian Saale. No one has informed us which bishops were present at it. Meanwhile, one might believe that among others Edda, or Etto, of Strasbourg, and Regenfrid of Cologne were there; they also took part in another synod or council in the following year. I would not affirm that the bishops of Bavaria were present as well, for they did not yet acknowledge the Franks as their lords.

The bishoprics in the new Francia, or Franconia, which had recently been cut off from Thuringia, and in Hesse, were then to be founded. Boniface therefore divided the entire province into three dioceses and established as episcopal sees Würzburg, famous for the martyrdom of Saint Kilian; Büraburg in Hesse; and Eichstätt on the borders of Bavaria. [Eckart, *Frankish Affairs*, Book XXIII, who supplies these details, places Eichstätt where Erfurt should be.]

The first two bishops consecrated were Burchard of Würzburg, to whose care, as Willibald testifies, the churches on the borders of the Franks, Saxons, and Slavs were also entrusted, and Witta—Wizo or Wettanus—or, as Lupus of Ferrières calls him in Latin, Albuin of Büraburg, since Willibald, who was to be placed over Eichstätt, had not yet arrived. Willibald reports in the *Life of Boniface*, chapter 10, that Boniface promoted Burchard to be bishop in the innermost parts of the eastern Franks, in the place called Würzburg, and he is the first to have counted the region formerly called Thuringia as part of eastern Francia.

No one mentions Witta’s consecration; but that it happened at this time is shown by what we shall soon hear and by the letters of Pope Zachary. Willibald, summoned by Boniface, also arrived shortly afterward. The words of the Heidenheim nun concerning Saint Willibald, chapter 20, are noteworthy; from them we learn the time and place of the synod. After reporting that Willibald had been ordained priest by Boniface—which happened in 740—she continues:

“And after the cycle of one year had passed”—that is, in the year 741—“Saint Boniface ordered him to come to him in Thuringia; and immediately that venerable man of God, Saint Willibald, came into Thuringia according to Saint Boniface’s command.”

She then relates that Willibald visited his brother Wunebald at Heidenheim on the way, and continues:

“It was the autumn season when Saint Willibald came into Thuringia, and immediately afterward Saint Boniface the archbishop, together with Saint Burchard and Wizo, ordained and consecrated him to the sacred authority of the episcopate.”

A little later she adds:

“When Saint Willibald had been consecrated bishop, he was forty-one years old; and it was then autumn. At about that time, three weeks before the feast of Saint Martin, he was consecrated bishop in the place called Sallpurg.”

The anonymous author of the *Life of Willibald* calls this place the city of Salzburg, although he ought to have called it a fortress. The district called Salagewe or Salzgau and the forest called Salzforst belonged to this fortress; the latter was called the forest of the Frankish kings because of their autumn hunting, delight, and recreation.

Those who seek this Salzburg at Salzburg on the Thuringian Saale, near the town of Hoff, or elsewhere, miss the truth by many parasangs. For in the time of Duke Charles that region was inhabited by Slavic Sorbs, who were finally subdued under the Saxon emperors and firmly and steadily subjected to the kingdom of Germany. Previously, although they had been conquered several times, they always bit the reins and threw them off at every opportunity.

Einhard, in the *Life of Charlemagne*, says that the Franks ruled the Germans from the Rhine to the Saale, which divides the Thuringians and the Sorbs. But how could Boniface have convened a synod there, where pagans and ill-disposed neighbors of the Franks lived? Such councils were held in cities, villages, and royal palaces, among which Salzburg was one, so that all who gathered might be safe and secure from every attack.

Since the region in which Salzburg lies, or the district of Salagewe, was still counted as part of Thuringia, it is clear that this former name had not yet fallen into disuse but was still commonly used. Eckart, in the cited work. WURDT.

### III. THE FIRST GERMAN COUNCIL, CELEBRATED BY THE AUTHORITY OF SAINT BONIFACE ON THE ELEVENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF MAY, A.D. 742, UNDER CARLOMANN, MAYOR OF THE PALACE

[Col. 0807A]

In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. I, Carlomann, duke and prince of the Franks, in the year 742 from the Incarnation of the Lord, namely, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, with the counsel of the servants of God and of my nobles, gathered the bishops who are in my kingdom, together with their presbyters, for a council and synod out of fear of Christ: namely, Boniface the archbishop, Burchard, Regenfrid, Wintan, Witbald, Dadan, Eddan, and the remaining bishops with their presbyters, so that they might give me counsel concerning how the law of God and ecclesiastical religion might be restored, since they had collapsed in ruin after being dissipated in the days of former rulers, and how the Christian people might attain the salvation of their souls and not perish after being deceived by false priests.

Therefore, by the counsel of my priests, religious men, and nobles, we appointed bishops throughout the cities and established over them Boniface as archbishop, who is the envoy of Saint Peter. We also decreed that a synod should be gathered every year, so that, in our presence, the decrees of the canons and the rights of the Church might be restored and the Christian religion corrected. We restored to the churches the monies that had been fraudulently taken from them; but we removed false presbyters and fornicating deacons and clerics from the revenues of the churches, degraded them, and compelled them to do penance.

We entirely prohibited the servants of God from carrying weapons, fighting, or going on campaign or to war, except only those who have been selected for the sake of the divine mystery [W.: manuscript, “ministry”], namely, for fulfilling the solemn rites of the Mass and carrying the protection of the saints. The prince may take with him one or two bishops, with their chaplains and presbyters; and each prefect may have one presbyter who is able to judge people confessing their sins and assign penance.

We also prohibited all servants of God from hunting and wandering through the forests with dogs, and from keeping hawks and falcons.

[Col. 0807D]

We also decreed, in accordance with the canons of the saints, that every presbyter living in a parish must be subject to the bishop in whose parish he lives, and must always, during Lent, give and show that bishop an account of the order and practice of his ministry, whether concerning baptism, the Catholic faith, prayers, or the order of the Mass. Whenever a bishop, by canonical right, travels through the parish to confirm the people, the presbyter must always be ready to receive the bishop with a contribution and assistance from the people who are to be confirmed there. At the Lord’s Supper he must always receive new chrism from the bishop, so that the bishop may be witness to his chastity, life, faith, and teaching.

We also decreed that, in accordance with canonical precaution, we should not admit into ecclesiastical ministry any unknown bishops or presbyters coming from elsewhere before synodal examination.

We further decreed that, according to the canons, every bishop should exercise care in his parish, with the assistance of the *gravio*, who is its defender, so that the people of God do not practice pagan rites but cast away and reject every impurity: whether profane sacrifices for the dead; sorcerers or diviners; phylacteries and auguries; incantations; or sacrificial offerings which foolish people make beside churches according to pagan custom under the name of holy martyrs or confessors, provoking God and his saints to anger.

They should also diligently prohibit those sacrilegious fires which the brothers call “Ned fires” [W.: manuscript, “Niedseor”], as well as every pagan observance of whatever kind.

We likewise decreed that after this synod, which was held on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, any servant of God or handmaid of Christ who should fall into the crime of fornication must do penance in prison on bread and water. If the person is an ordained presbyter, he must remain in prison for two years; he must first be seen to have been flogged and wounded [Mansi: flayed], and afterward the bishop must increase the punishment. If a cleric or monk falls into this sin, after the third beating he is to be sent to prison and do penance there for the course of a year. Veiled nuns are likewise to be held to the same penance, and all the hair of their heads is to be shaved.

We further decreed that presbyters and deacons should not wear cloaks, in the manner of laymen, but chasubles, according to the custom of the servants of God; and that no one should permit women to live in his house. Monks and monastic handmaids of God should strive, according to the rule of Saint Benedict, to order, govern, and live in their monasteries or hospices, and should not neglect to lead their own lives according to the ordinance of the aforesaid Father.

[Note: “Neglect”: Othlonus continues: “We also decreed, with the counsel of the servants of God and the Christian people, on account of the wars and persecutions of the many peoples who are around us, that, under a lease and fixed payment, we retain for a certain time some portion of the Church’s property for the assistance of our army, with God’s permission, on the condition that every year a solidus—that is, twelve denarii—from each household be paid back to the church or monastery. This arrangement is to be made so that, if the person to whom the property was entrusted dies, the church may be restored to possession of its own property. Again, if necessity compels the prince to order it, the lease is to be renewed and a new document written, and provision is to be made in every way that the churches or monasteries whose property has been granted on lease do not suffer want and poverty; but, if poverty compels it, the possession is to be returned intact to the church, the house of God.

“Likewise, we command that, in accordance with the decrees of the canons, adulteries and incestuous marriages be prohibited and corrected by the judgment of the bishops, and that Christian slaves not be handed over to pagans.” W.]

## IV. THE COUNCIL OF LIPTINES, IN WHICH THE DECREES OF THE PRECEDING GERMAN COUNCIL WERE APPROVED AND NEW ONES ENACTED, CELEBRATED UNDER CARLOMANN, MAYOR OF THE PALACE, ON THE KALENDS OF MARCH IN THE YEAR 743

[Col. 0809A]

Now, at this synodal assembly, which was convened on the Kalends of March at the place called Liptinas, all the venerable priests of God, counts, and prefects, agreeing with the decrees of the preceding synod, confirmed them and promised that they wished to fulfill and observe them. The entire clergy of the ecclesiastical order—bishops, priests, deacons, and the remaining clerics—accepting the canons of the ancient Fathers, promised that they wished to restore ecclesiastical rights in conduct, doctrine, and ministry. The abbots and monks, for their part, accepted the rule of the holy Father Benedict, in order to restore the standard of regular life.

As for fornicating and adulterous clerics who, while previously holding holy places or monasteries, had polluted them, we ordered that they be removed from there and brought to penance. If, after this decree, they should fall into the crime of fornication or adultery, let them undergo the judgment of the preceding synod. The same applies to monks and nuns.

We also decree, with the counsel of the servants of God and of the Christian people, on account of the wars threatening us and the persecutions of the other peoples who surround us, that we may retain for some time, under a precarious tenure and annual rent, a portion of the Church’s money for the assistance of our army, with God’s indulgence; on this condition: that every year one solidus—that is, twelve denarii—from each *casada* be returned to the church or monastery. This is to be done in such a way that, if the person to whom the money was lent should die, the church shall be restored to possession of its own property; and, again, if necessity should compel it, or the prince should order it, the precarious tenure shall be renewed, a new document shall be written, and it shall be entirely ensured that the churches or monasteries whose property has been granted under precarious tenure do not suffer want or poverty. But if poverty should compel it, the possession shall be returned intact to the church or house of God.

Likewise, we order that, in accordance with the decrees of the canons, adulteries and incestuous marriages that are not lawful be prohibited and corrected by the judgment of the bishops, and that Christian slaves not be handed over to pagans.

We also decreed—as my father had previously ordered—that anyone who performs pagan observances in any matter shall be fined and condemned to fifteen solidi.

[Note: In the most ancient collection of canons, manuscript Codex Palatinus 542, more than nine hundred years old, as reported in the *Monumenta Paderbornensia*, p. 336, following the council held at Liptinas by Duke Carlomannus there is appended, in the old Theotisc language, a renunciation of the devil and his works, together with a list of pagan superstitions from which the council ordered that the people be recalled through the diligence of the bishops, Part I, canon 5. According to Luke Holstenius, the list is immediately followed by two addresses to the people concerning the avoidance of incestuous marriages, which the same council, Part II, canon 3, commanded the bishops to prohibit. These materials therefore appear altogether to belong to the acts of that council.

For a better understanding of the pagan practices, it is useful to add a few notes.

I. Concerning sacrilege at the tombs of the dead. Funerals were magnificent and costly; and everything that the surviving neighbors imagined to have been dear to the living was carried into the fire. Even animals were burned together with the corpse of the deceased, and sometimes also slaves and dependents. Charles the Great ordered in the *Capitularies*: “If anyone causes the body of a dead man to be consumed by fire according to the pagan rite and reduces his bones to ashes, he shall be punished by death.”

II. Concerning sacrilege committed over the dead, that is, *Dadsisas*. Funeral banquets and feasts were arranged, not without extravagance. They were called *parentalia*, because sons performed them in honor of their pagan parents, as Jerome says in his commentary on Jeremiah. Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, records: “For the sake of their appetite, people first began preparing meals for the dead, which they themselves would eat,” and so forth. Charles the Great prohibited this superstitious rite in the *Capitularies*: “Let the faithful be warned not to perform for their dead those things that have remained from the pagan rite ... and not to presume to eat or drink upon their tombs.”

III. Concerning the *Spurcalia* in February. By this pagan practice I understand the extremely impure festivals of Bacchus. When Boniface prohibited them, the pagan people replied—as is reported in Letter 132 to Pope Zacharias—in these words:

“Carnal men, ignorant Alemanni ... or Franks, if they see something being done near the city of Rome from among those sins that we prohibit, think that it is permitted and approved by the priests, and they reproach us and take scandal at our way of life, just as they claim to have seen every year in the city of Rome and near the church of Saint Peter, on the day or night when the Kalends of January begin, people leading dances through the streets according to pagan custom, celebrating acclamations in the manner of the heathen and sacrilegious songs, and loading their tables with food on that day or night, while refusing to lend anyone from their household—even to a neighbor—fire, an iron tool, or anything useful.

“They also say that they saw women there, according to pagan custom, wearing phylacteries and bindings tied around their arms and legs, and publicly offering them for sale so that others might purchase them. Because all these things are seen there among carnal and foolish people, they become for us both a reproach and an obstacle to preaching and teaching ... If your Holiness prohibits these pagan practices there in the city of Rome, you will gain both a reward for yourself and the greatest benefit for us in ecclesiastical instruction.”

To this the pontiff replies in Letter 142:

“Concerning the Kalends of January and other omens, phylacteries, incantations, and various other observances that, as you have said, are practiced in the pagan manner at Saint Peter’s or in the city of Rome, we judge this to be detestable and destructive both to us and to all Christians. For the Lord says: ‘You shall not practice augury,’ or rather, ‘You shall not observe dreams.’ Scripture likewise says: ‘Let there be no omens in Israel, nor observation in the house of Jacob.’

“Thus we judge that we too must beware, so that we pay attention to no omens or observances, because we have been taught by the Fathers that all these things have been cut off; and because, through the instigation of the devil, they were again sprouting up, from the day on which divine Clemency commanded us—although we are unworthy—to act in the place of the apostles, we immediately cut all these things away. In the same way we wish your Holiness to preach to the peoples subject to you and lead them to the way of eternal life.

“For by the constitution of our predecessor and fosterer of holy memory, Pope Gregory, all these things were also piously and faithfully cut away, along with many other various things that, at the devil’s prompting, were sprouting up in Christ’s fold; following its example, we hastened to issue a like directive for the salvation of that people.

IV. Concerning *casulae*, that is, shrines. *Casulae* were small temples consecrated to gods, made not of stone but of wood, constructed with little labor and at small expense. Saint Ambrose, Letter 29: ‘For what is it except a shrine, in which there is an assembly of heathens?’ Commodianus, *Instructions* 24:

‘Go out from there, outside; again you seek your shrines.’

Charles the Great, in the *Capitularies*: ‘First, concerning the major capitularies, this was pleasing to all: that the churches of Christ now being built in Saxony and set apart for God should receive no less honor, but greater and more excellent honor, than the shrines of idols had received.’

V. Concerning sacrilege in churches. Charles the Great, *Capitulary* 2: ‘If anyone enters a church violently and by force or stealth removes anything from it, or burns the church itself with fire, let him suffer death.’

On the fierce and barbarous character and cruelty of the ancient Germans and Saxons, Einhard says in the *Life of Charlemagne*: ‘The Saxons, like almost all the peoples inhabiting Germany, are naturally fierce, devoted to the worship of demons, and opposed to our religion; they do not consider it shameful either to violate or to transgress divine or human laws.’ Such fierceness and cruelty therefore had to be suppressed and restrained by capital punishment.

VI. Concerning the sacred groves called *Nimidae*. Tacitus says in *The Customs of the Germans*: ‘They consecrate groves and woodland places and call them by the names of gods; they behold that secret place with reverence alone.’ *Nimidae* means, as it were, sacred rites of the nymphs. The pagan rites that they performed for forests and trees in their groves were abominable and monstrous, since they sometimes sacrificed human beings there together with animals. We know that Saint Boniface cut down the tree of Jupiter in Hesse, and so forth. Compare the stone inscriptions to the Nymphs of Triputi, to Augusta Diana, and others, in Hanselmann, *Proof of How Far the Power of the Romans Extended*, vol. I, pp. 73 and 225; vol. II, pp. 77 and 244.

Charles the Great, *Capitulary* 20: ‘If anyone makes a vow at springs, trees, or groves, or offers anything in the manner of the heathen, and eats in honor of demons, then, if he is noble, he shall pay sixty solidi; if freeborn, thirty; if a dependent, fifteen. But if they do not have the means to pay immediately, they shall be assigned to the service of the church until the solidi themselves have been paid.’

VII. Concerning what they do upon stones. To fulfill vows at stones was a form of pagan superstition. Saint Eligius, in Saint Ouen’s *Life of Eligius*, Book II, chapter 15: ‘Let no Christian presume to fulfill vows at shrines, stones, springs, or trees ...’ The Council of Nantes, canon 20: ‘The stones, too, which, deceived by the mockeries of demons in ruined and wooded places, they venerate, and where they make and present vows, shall be dug up completely,’ and so forth. Add the Second Council of Arles, canon 23; the Second Council of Tours, canon 22; and the Council of Aachen of 789, canon 63.

VIII. Concerning the sacred rites of Mercury or Jupiter. Tacitus, in his book *On Germany*: ‘Of the gods they chiefly worship Mercury, to whom on appointed days they deem it lawful to offer even human victims, and by publicly slaying a man they celebrate the horrific beginnings of barbarian ritual.’ On the superstition relating to Mercury, the learned Lamey has written eloquently; see the *Proceedings of the Electoral Palatine Academy*, vol. I, p. 205 and following. Very many altars dedicated to Jupiter Optimus Maximus can be found in Germany.

IX. Concerning sacrifice offered to one of the saints. Under Carlomannus it was ordered:

‘Let the bishop in his parish take care that the people of God do not perform pagan practices or sacrifice victims, as foolish men do in pagan fashion under the name of holy martyrs or confessors, provoking God and the saints to anger.’
