Saint Augustine therefore correctly says in *The City of God*, Book VIII, chapter 27:

‘Yet we do not establish for those same martyrs temples, priesthoods, sacred rites, or sacrifices, because their God—not they themselves—is our God. Certainly we honor their memorials as those of holy men of God, who fought for the truth even unto the death of their bodies, so that the true religion might become known when false religions and fictions had been refuted. But who has ever heard a priest standing at an altar—even one built for the honor and worship of God over the holy body of a martyr—say in his prayers: “I offer sacrifice to you, Peter, or Paul, or Cyprian”? At their memorials sacrifice is offered to God, who made them both human beings and martyrs and joined them to his holy angels in heavenly honor. Thus, by that celebration, we give thanks to the true God for their victories, and, calling upon the same God, we are encouraged by the renewal of their memory to imitate such crowns and palms.

“Whatever acts of religious service are therefore performed at the places of martyrs are adornments of their memorials, not sacred rites or sacrifices offered to the dead as gods. Moreover, those who carry their meals there—which, indeed, better Christians do not do, and in most parts of the world no such custom exists—when they have set them down, pray and then carry them away to eat, or distribute some of them to the needy.”

X. Concerning phylacteries and bindings. The ancients called *phylacteria* amulets for warding off or driving away diseases. The Church has always proscribed these as diabolical inventions. In the Council of Regensburg of 742:

‘Let the people of God not practice pagan rites, but reject all the impurities of heathenism, whether sacrifices for the dead, sorcerers, diviners, phylacteries and omens, or incantations.’

And in *Capitularies*, Book VI, chapter 72:

‘Let phylacteries, false inscriptions, or bindings made by clerics or laymen never be produced, which the foolish think help against fevers and other diseases, because they are marks of magical art.’

In Gratian’s *Decree* 26, question 5, chapter *Si quis*: ‘If anyone consults soothsayers, haruspices, or enchanters, or uses phylacteries, let him be anathema.’ The gloss explains: ‘Here phylacteries means sheets on which incantations are written.’

Bindings were also superstitiously used to drive away diseases. Uncertain characters and other signs were worn around the neck or tied around other parts of the body. Isidore, Book VIII, chapter 9:

‘To all these things belong the bindings of accursed remedies, which the medical art condemns, whether in incantations, characters, or any objects that are hung up and tied. In all these things lies the art of demons, arising from a baneful association of human beings and evil angels. Therefore Christians must avoid all such things and reject and condemn them utterly with every form of abhorrence.’

Saint Ouen, Book II of the *Life of Saint Eligius*, chapter 15:

‘Let no one presume to hang bindings around the neck of a human being or any animal, even if they are made by clerics and even if it is said that the object is holy and contains sacred readings, because there is not Christ’s remedy in them but the devil’s poison.’

Gregory of Tours, Book II of the *Miracles*, chapter 45: ‘He mutters incantations, casts lots, and hangs bindings around his neck.’ And Book IV of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 36: ‘When she came and visited the sick woman, she removed the bindings that fools had sold, and poured oil from the blessed tomb into her mouth.’

Saint Boniface, in his letter to Pope Zacharias: ‘They also say that they saw women there who, in pagan fashion, wore phylacteries and bindings tied around their arms and legs,’ and so forth. See above.

XI. Concerning sacrificial springs. The worship of springs and sacrifices offered to them is repeatedly prohibited in the Councils of Auxerre, canon 3; Nantes, canon 23; the Second Council of Arles, canon 23; and the Twelfth Council of Toledo, canon 11. Add Cluverus, Book I of *Germanic Antiquities*, chapter 34, and the *Capitulary of Charles the Great* cited above.

Adam of Bremen says in his ancient scholia:

‘Near that temple is a very large tree extending its branches widely, always green in summer and winter; no one knows what kind it is. There is also a spring where pagan sacrifices are customarily performed and a living man is submerged. When he has been submerged, the vow of the people is considered fulfilled.’

XII. Concerning incantations. Magical illusions and deceptions. The *Saxon Mirror*, Book II, article 13, section 6: ‘If any Christian ... should apostatize, or administer poison to anyone, or enchant him,’ and so forth. The *Life of Saint Praejectus*: ‘Since he had been entirely unable to obtain healing from physicians or enchanters.’ Fredegar, *Epitome*, chapter 9: ‘The king ordered Mummolus to be branded, through Fredegund’s agency, because they believed that he had killed her son by enchantment.’ Volume III of the *Spanish Councils*, p. 7: ‘Concerning the prohibition against priests or clerics making incantations or even harmful bindings.’

XIII. Concerning omens from birds, horses, ox dung, or sneezing. Tacitus says of the omens of the Germans that they observe auspices and lots as much as anyone. He also records: ‘To question the voices and flight of birds is characteristic of the nation; they also test the omens and warnings of horses.’

Procopius, Book IV of the *Gothic War*, speaking of Hermegisclus, king of the Varni in Westphalia, says:

‘Once, while Hermegisclus was riding through the countryside with the leaders of the Varni, he saw a bird loudly croaking. Whether he understood the bird’s sound or learned of it from another source, he pretended to understand the omen and publicly announced to everyone present that death was threatening his life after forty days, and that the bird foretold this to him.’

Among some people there still remains the superstitious belief that their impending death is foretold if they hear an owl crying near their homes.

Concerning omens from horses, Tacitus says:

‘It is characteristic of the nation also to test the omens and warnings of horses. They are publicly kept in the same groves and sacred woods, white and untouched by any mortal labor. The priest, king, or leader of the state accompanies them when they are yoked to the sacred chariot, observing their neighing and snorting. No omen is trusted more, not only by the common people but also by the nobles and priests; for they believe themselves to be the gods’ ministers and the horses to be aware of the gods.’

The Germans also divined from fresh ox dung that favorable things would follow, and from old dung that unfavorable things would follow, as we gather from a surviving proverb. A trace of divination from sneezing appears in the formulas with which we call out to someone who sneezes: ‘May it prosper,’ ‘May it advance,’ ‘God help,’ ‘May God further what has begun,’ ‘May he bless it’—from which people commonly infer: ‘Therefore the matter is true; therefore the affair will turn out well.’

XIV. Concerning diviners and sorcerers. Diviners are those who pretend to be filled with divine power and, by a certain fraudulent cunning, impose upon people by conjecturing the future. Pope Gregory III, in the penitential judgments, chapter 16:

‘Soothsayers are those who sacrifice around the altars of idols ... If anyone observes omens, auspices, or divinations, or makes a vow outside the church, or performs divinations in his incantations—which is altogether diabolical—let him do penance for three years.’

Concerning sorcerers, the Council of Auxerre of 578, chapter 3:

‘It is not permitted to consult sorcerers or omens, nor to inspect the lots that they call “of the saints,” or those which they make from wood or bread.’

The “lots of the saints” means inspecting the Gospel or another sacred book: when the book was opened, whatever first met the eyes was taken as a lot or oracle. Hence Charles the Great’s *Capitulary*, chapter 22:

‘We decree that diviners and sorcerers be handed over to churches and priests,’ that is, for punishment and correction.

XV. Concerning fire produced by friction from wood, that is, *Nodfyr*. Pliny, *Natural History*, Book XVI, chapter 40, records:

‘Wood is rubbed against wood and catches fire through friction, the dry tinder, fungus, or leaves readily receiving the fire.’

*Nodfyr* is therefore suitably derived from *Nöthen*, “to compel,” and *fyr*, *feuer*, “fire,” that is, fire compelled from wood. Just as most ancient customs passed into superstition, so fire kindled by friction was believed to be sacred and useful for averting evils. In former times it was used for purification and for burning victims, for the Easter fires in honor of the goddess Eostre, and also for the fires called those of Saint John, which perhaps had once customarily been kindled for Jupiter.

In many places in Germany these fires are still customary. Those who pass through them or run through their smoke, whether human beings or animals, are believed to remain free for an entire year from fever and other diseases.

XVI. Concerning the brains of animals. It is sufficiently clear that divinations from the brains of animals—whether *haruspicia* or *extispicia*—were customary. Since the heads of sacrificed animals were specially offered to the gods, and since the ancients believed that, as the principal parts of animals, they contained many mysteries in the brain, perhaps they consulted the gods by inspecting the brain and sought the future from it.

XVII. Concerning pagan observation at the hearth or at the beginning of any undertaking. Omens were inferred from the smoke’s rising straight into the ether, or from its being pressed down or scattered in various directions by the wind. Painters wishing to represent the sacrifices of Abel and Cain depict the flame on Abel’s altar as bright and the smoke rising straight toward heaven, but the fire and smoke of Cain’s altar as disturbed and forced downward by the wind.

The Germans believed, according to Tacitus, that the most auspicious beginning for undertakings occurred on certain days, either when the moon was beginning or when it was full. Who does not know how firmly observations of the moon still remain among farmers and gardeners? They believe and insist that these grains and vegetables must be sown or transplanted during the waxing or waning moon, and that otherwise they will not thrive—a belief deriving from pagan superstition.

XVIII. Concerning uncertain places that they venerate as saints. The common people call uncertain places *Unsteten*—places whose location is unknown. If someone walking here or there is suddenly seized by illness, or if a limb of his body begins to hurt, people ignorant of the cause say that he has “gone over an *Unstete*,” or that he has trodden upon a place whose location is unknown. Because that place is thought to be sacred, they imagine that the spirit of the place has punished him as its violator and despiser.

XIX. Concerning what they call “asking for the good of Saint Mary.” Meinders, in the *Treasury of Frankish and Saxon Antiquities*, wrongly asserts that here Charles the Great prohibited the worship and invocation of the blessed Virgin Mary and the saints, as well as images. The conjecture of Eckard, in Book XXIII of *Frankish Affairs*, comes closer to the truth. He says that *petendo* has been corruptly written for *petensiro*, that is, *serpillum* or *gallium*, a herb.

These herbs may have been collected and used superstitiously to drive away serpents and poisonous animals, or to secure affection; they may have been worn around the neck, especially hung near the bed, or mixed with bedding. The fuller discussion that Eckard gives in the cited work, p. 426, deserves to be read in support of this opinion.

XX. Concerning the festivals that they hold for Jupiter and Mercury. *Thor* was the German name of Jupiter; hence Thursday is called by the northern peoples *Thorstag*, and among us, with the inserted *n*, *Donrstag*.

Adam of Bremen writes about the Swedes:

‘That noble people possesses a very famous temple called Upsala, not far from the city of Sigtuna or Birka. In this temple, which is entirely furnished with gold, the people venerate statues of three gods, so that the most powerful of them, Thor, has a couch in the middle; on either side Wodan and Fricco occupy their places. Their meanings are as follows: Thor, they say, presides in the air and governs thunder and lightning, winds and rains, fair weather and crops.’

He further says:

‘Thor, with his scepter, appears to represent Jupiter ... If plague or famine threatens, they sacrifice to the idol Thor.’

The same Adam of Bremen says:

‘The other god is Wodan, that is, the stronger; he governs wars and grants human beings strength against their enemies.’ He adds that, when war threatens, they sacrifice to Wodan.

Paul the Deacon, Book I of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 9, reports:

‘Wodan, whom, with a prefixed letter, they called Godan, is the same as the one whom the Romans call Mercury, and he is worshiped as a god by all the peoples of Germany.’

A day of the week was sacred to him, which the Belgians and northern peoples called *Woensdag* or *Wodansdag*. The Germans, however, together with his worship, abolished his name and called Wednesday *Mittwochen*, or “the middle of the week.”

XXI. Concerning a lunar eclipse, which they call *vinceluna*. Many peoples of Germany were persuaded that, when the moon was eclipsed—that is, when it was darkened by the earth’s shadow coming between the sun and the moon—it was harmed by sorcerers and witches through some magical spell and suffered a kind of fainting. They called out to the suffering moon, “Conquer, moon!” as though it were being attacked by the sun.

Hence Juvenal says:

> No one now wearies the trumpets, no one the bronze;
>
> Only one thing can come to the aid of the laboring moon.

Pope Gregory III, in the *Penitential*, chapter 23, and Bede [Egbert], in the *Book on Remedies for Sins*, chapter 21:

‘When the moon is darkened, they trust that they can defend it by their shouts or by their magical practices, in sacrilegious fashion.’

And the *Penitential of Thérouanne*:

‘If you have observed the traditions of the pagans, which, as though by hereditary right and through the devil’s agency, fathers have handed down to their sons even to the present day—that is, so that you might be able, by your shouts or assistance, to restore the brightness of the elements, the colors, the moon, the sun, or the course of the stars, or of the new moon or lunar eclipse ...’

XXII. Concerning storms, horns, and shells. Against storm-makers, the *Visigothic Law*, Book VI, title II, law 2, pronounces as follows:

‘Sorcerers and those who are said by certain incantations to send hail upon vineyards and crops, and those who by invoking demons disturb the minds of human beings, or who celebrate nocturnal sacrifices to demons and wickedly invoke them through abominable invocations, wherever they are found or discovered by a judge, official, or administrator of the place, shall be publicly beaten with two hundred lashes and, disgracefully shorn, shall be compelled against their will to go around ten neighboring estates, so that others may be corrected by their example.’

Emperor Louis, in the second supplement to the *Capitularies*, title 18, recalls those who foolishly imagined that they had storms, thunder, and hail under their control, in these words:

‘For they claim that by their magic they can disturb the air, send hail, foretell the future, take milk away and give it to others, and perform countless other things of this sort.’

Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Book IV, therefore says:

‘Antiquity, still uncivilized, believed that rains could both be drawn down by songs and driven away.’

The reason that horns are discussed among superstitions comes from the fact that horns were used in place of cups. Caesar, *Gallic War*, Book VI, describes the aurochs and adds:

‘The size, shape, and appearance of their horns differ greatly from those of our cattle. They carefully collect them, encase them with silver around the rims, and use them as cups at the most lavish banquets.’

That better wine was served in horns is shown by a charter of Arnold, provost of the Blessed Virgin Mary at the Steps in Mainz, from the year 1222, in which, among other provisions, it is ordered:

‘Likewise, from the beginning of Advent until the day of the Innocents, wine called “horn wine” shall be served or distributed.’

See Johannes, *Writers on the Affairs of Mainz*, Book II, p. 668.

At the festivals of pagan gods, people once drank from consecrated horns and made libations to the gods. Our ancestors, after being converted to the Christian faith, could not immediately abstain from their customary drinking parties; therefore they emptied horns and cups in honor of God, his saints, kings, and great men. When superstition concerning horns is noted here, it therefore means horns consecrated to idols and emptied in their honor.

Shells are mentioned in connection with superstitious uses—namely, vessels, spoons, and bowls consecrated to demons in pagan sacrifices, for tasting the broths of victims cooked in a sacred cauldron. Sorcerers also possessed shells or bowls consecrated to a demon, in which they supplied others with drinks prepared by magical arts, making them inflamed either with love or with hatred.

XXIII. Concerning furrows around settlements. The Germans did not have contiguous and connected buildings, but houses scattered here and there with adjoining fields, meadows, and thickets. Around these settlements they drew furrows, using certain superstitious rites and ceremonies to ward off fire, enemies, and every other adversity.

Lucretius, Book I of *On the Nature of Things*, records this superstitious custom of drawing furrows around a city:

> Then he orders the entire city
>
> To be encircled by its frightened citizens,
>
> And, purifying the walls with a solemn rite,
>
> To draw a long boundary around the outer limits.

XXIV. Concerning the pagan running that they call *Yrias*, with torn garments or shoes. Eckard, cited above, restores the word *Yrias* as *Scyrias*, which is the same as *Scy*, *Scu*, *rias*, or *riss*, referring to torn shoes.

This pagan running, performed with torn shoes, was customary on the Kalends of January. When Saint Boniface wished to abolish it in New Francia, the newly converted Franks declared that they had seen it every year in the city of Rome and near the church of Saint Peter, on the day or night when the Kalends of January began: people led dances through the streets according to pagan custom, celebrated acclamations in the manner of the heathen and sacrilegious songs, loaded their tables with food on that day or night, and refused to lend anyone from their household—fire, an iron tool, or anything useful—to a neighbor. Thus in Boniface’s letter to Pope Zacharias.

Bishop Faustinus, in his sermon on the Kalends of January, explains this pagan rite in detail:

‘On these days, miserable men—and, what is worse, some baptized people—assume adulterated forms and monstrous appearances; I do not know whether the first thing to be felt is laughter or rather grief. For what wise person could believe that there are any sane people who, making themselves into a little stag, wish to transform themselves into the appearance of wild beasts?

‘Some dress in the skins of animals; others put on the heads of beasts, rejoicing and exulting if they have transformed themselves into animal forms so completely that they do not appear to be human beings. By this they show and prove that they have not merely the appearance or outward form, but the understanding, of animals. Although they wish to represent the likenesses of various animals in themselves, it is nevertheless certain that in them the heart of beasts is more evident than the outward shapes.

‘And what sort of thing, or how shameful, is it that men born as men dress in women’s tunics and, through the most disgraceful transformation, weaken manly strength into the figures of girls, not blushing to insert military arms into women’s clothing? They display bearded faces and wish to appear as women; they therefore rightly no longer possess manly strength, having passed into women’s attire. It must be believed that by a just judgment they came to lose military courage because they had disfigured themselves in the appearance of women ...

‘Reject those observances also as the poisons of the devil, since—what is worse—many among the Christian people are still not ashamed to observe them. For there are people who on the Kalends of January observe omens so carefully that they give neither fire from their house nor any other benefit to anyone who asks.

‘They also receive diabolical New Year’s gifts from others and themselves give them to others. Others, even peasants, on the night that has passed, arrange on their little tables many things necessary for eating and wish them to remain set out throughout the entire night, believing that the Kalends of January can provide them with this assistance, so that their banquets may continue throughout the whole year in such abundance.’

XXV. Concerning the practice of inventing saints out of any dead persons. Through this superstition, once the one true God had been forgotten, many thousands of gods and spirits arose. They even carefully composed their genealogies, as is clear from the letter of Daniel, bishop of Winchester, to Boniface, tracing their origins back to more celebrated and distinguished men.

Remigius indicates that Clovis I, king of the Franks, while still a pagan, believed in a thousand little gods, when he sings in his epitaph:

> He despised believing in a thousand
>
> Divinities, monsters terrifying in varied forms.

XXVI. Concerning an image made of sprinkled flour. Pagans made loaves of various shapes in honor of their gods and offered them to those gods; they imagined that these loaves possessed special powers. Hence arose the custom of making various images out of sweetened bread around the Christmas season and using them to amuse children. Hence the particular wheat-flour bread called *Heidewegge*, as well as *Christ-Wecke*, *Bretzel*, and *Martens-Hörner*.

The word *consparsa*—“sprinkled”—seems to indicate that flour sprinkled with water drawn from a sacred spring, or blessed through certain ceremonies, was regarded as consecrated. Later, among Christians, the sprinkling of blessed water was likewise called *consparsus*.

XXVII. Concerning images made from cloths. Our ancestors made various images and offered them worship as household gods. In the same way, they superstitiously preserved figures made from cloth, such as those of the *alrunae*, or prophetic women, believing that these figures uttered oracles and brought happiness to their worshipers.

Eventually they shaped the root of the mandrake, dug up amid various ceremonies, so that it displayed the form of a human body, inserting grains of barley or millet at the places where they wanted hairs to grow. They dressed this root in clean clothing, arranged it carefully, venerated it in the household shrine, and called it an *alruna*; that name still clings to the herb.

XXVIII. Concerning the image that they carry through the fields. Under this superstitious rite are understood the *Ambarvalia* of the pagans, which were also practiced by the Romans. Tibullus, Book I, elegy 2:

> We purify the crops and the fields,
The rite survives as handed down from ancient times. Meinders, cited above, here and elsewhere, rashly asserts, out of a preconceived hatred of the Roman Catholic Church, that this superstition still remains within it, and he misunderstands the passage found in the *Life of Saint Maresvidis* [Col. 0818B]:

> We have decreed, it says, that every year, on the second day of Pentecost, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, you should carry the same patron saint around your parishes in a long circuit, purifying your houses; and, in place of the pagan *Ambarvalia*—that is, in place of the *Ambarvalia* customary among the pagans—you should sacrifice yourselves in tears and varied devotion, bring alms for the refreshment of the poor, and, spending the night in this courtyard, celebrate vigils and songs over the relics, so that on the following morning, completing the circuit you have determined upon with pious purification, you may return to the monastery with due honor. I trust, however, in the mercy of this patron, that through him the seeds of the land of Gyrade will spring forth more abundantly, and that the various inclemencies of the air will cease.

Whoever understands the genuine doctrine concerning the veneration and invocation of the saints will interpret the aforesaid passage more mildly than Hermann Adolphus Meinders.

### XXIX. On wooden feet and hands according to pagan custom

When the pagans were lying ill, they made vows to obtain health [Col. 0818C]; and, once restored to their former health, they customarily consecrated, as a token of gratitude to the deity whom they had invoked, an image of the limb that had been afflicted by the illness. Our ancestors likewise imitated this custom according to pagan usage, since they had worshiped deities who had eyes but did not see, ears but did not hear, and so forth.

### XXX. On the belief that women command the moon and can take away people’s hearts, according to the pagans

Our ancestors falsely believed that there were women to whom the moon was obedient, and that the influence of the moon produced various harmful effects in human beings; they attributed to these women illnesses that returned at particular intervals. Hence they also called a person suffering from a wasting illness or epilepsy “lunatic.”

Audoenus recalls this superstition in *The Life of Saint Eligius*, book II, chapter 15, where we read:

> God made the moon for this purpose: to mark the seasons and moderate the darkness of the nights—not to obstruct anyone’s work or make a person insane, as fools think, because they suppose that those possessed by demons suffer from the moon.

It was once also believed that, when the moon had been bound by magical incantations [Col. 0818D], witches received the power, merely by looking at or beholding people, to consume their hearts and thus kill them. Tibullus speaks of fascination as follows:

> I saw her drawing the stars down from heaven;  
> by her song she turns the course of the swift river.  
> By song she splits the earth and draws forth the spirits of the dead  
> from their tombs, and devours their bones from the warm funeral pyre.  
> When she wishes, she drives the clouds from the gloomy sky;  
> when she wishes, she summons snow across the summer world.

All these superstitions and pagan practices, which were in use in the time of Saint Boniface, were condemned by him at the synod held in the year 742. And although the bishops of the Church are vigilant and especially concerned to eradicate abuses of this kind, many traces of them nevertheless remain in wicked hearts. Wheat and weeds will remain until the time of harvest. [WURDT.]

## Renunciation of the devil, his works, and superstitions

“Do you renounce the devil?”  
Response: “I renounce the devil.”

“Do you renounce all the devil’s worship?”  
Response: “I renounce all the devil’s worship.”

“Do you renounce all the devil’s works?”  
Response: “I renounce all the devil’s works, and the worship of Thunor, Woden, and Saxnot, and of all the evil spirits who are their companions.”

“Do you believe in God the almighty Father?”  
Response: “I believe in God the almighty Father.”

“Do you believe in Christ, God’s Son?”  
Response: “I believe in Christ, God’s Son.”

“Do you believe in the Holy Spirit?”  
Response: “I believe in the Holy Spirit.”

## Index of superstitions and pagan practices

[Col. 0810C] On sacrilege at the graves of the dead. On sacrilege concerning the dead, that is, *Dadsisas*. On the Februarian purifications. [Col. 0811A] On little shrines, that is, temples. On sacrileges committed through churches. On the sacred groves, which they call *Nimidas*. On the practices they perform upon stones. [Col. 0812A] On the sacred rites of Mercury or Jupiter. On the sacrifice made to one of the saints. On phylacteries and amulets. [Col. 0813A] On sacrificial springs. On incantations. On auguries—whether from birds, horses, or cattle dung, or from sneezing. On diviners and sorcerers. On rubbed fire, that is, *Nodfyr*. [Col. 0814A] On the brains of animals. On pagan observance at the hearth, or at the beginning of any undertaking. On obscure places that they venerate as saints. On asking for what they call good things from Saint Mary. [Col. 0815A] On the festivals they hold for Jupiter or Mercury. On the eclipse of the moon, which they call *vinceluna*. On storms, horns, and shells. [Col. 0816A] On furrows around estates. On the pagan procession called *Yrias*, with torn garments or shoes. [Col. 0817A] On making saints for themselves out of any dead persons. On the image made from sprinkled flour. On images made from cloth. On the image that they carry through the fields. On wooden feet and hands according to pagan custom. On the belief that women command the moon and can take away people’s hearts, according to the pagans. [Col. 0818A]

## Address of priests to the people concerning illicit marriages

“Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman over my people. Therefore, when you hear a word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them from me, not from yourself. If, when I say to the wicked man, ‘Wicked man, you shall surely die,’ you do not speak so that the wicked man may guard himself from his way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, [Col. 0819A] but I shall require his blood from your hand. But if you announce it to the wicked man, and he does not turn back from his wickedness and his wicked way, he himself shall die in his iniquity, but you shall have saved your own life.

“Moreover, if a righteous man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, I shall place a stumbling block before him, and he shall die. Because you did not announce it to him, he shall die in his sin, and the righteous deeds he performed shall not be remembered; but I shall require his blood from your hand. But if you announce to the righteous man that the righteous man should not sin, and he does not sin, he shall surely live, because you announced it to him, and you have saved your own life.”

See, dearest sons, what danger rests upon us if we remain silent. Far be it, far be it from us that our silence should become your destruction. If we love you, we must expose [Col. 0819B] what harms you, lest what kills you come upon you.

Therefore listen carefully to the words of our God, by which he forbids you criminal unions, so that you may live by his eternal gifts. Behold, our God cries out and, foreseeing the unlawful frenzy of human lust, bears witness that no one should be defiled with his mother, nor with his stepmother, nor with his sister born of his father, nor with his sister born of his mother—whether she was born within or outside the marriage. Not with the daughter of his son or daughter, not with a granddaughter born of his daughter, not with the daughter of his stepmother, not with his father’s sister, not with his mother’s sister, not with his uncle’s wife, not with his daughter-in-law, not with his brother’s wife, not with his wife’s daughter, not with the daughter of your wife’s son, not with her daughter’s daughter, not with your wife’s sister, not with a menstruating woman, not with your neighbor’s wife, not with two women at the same time—whether they are enslaved or free, or one free and one enslaved. [Col. 0819C]

Not with a male in a female manner, not with any animal, not with your mother-in-law. A woman must not lie beneath an animal. A man must not lie with his daughter and mother, nor with your uncle’s wife.

He also speaks concerning the future priest: not with a woman divorced by her husband, not with a prostitute, not with a widow, but with a virgin.

Behold, dearest ones, what kind of embassy we bring to you—not from just anyone who could be bought with money, but from the one whose blood, poured out for you, has made you his debtors. We admonish your holiness: live with lawful spouses; live chastely. Let no one further defile himself with unlawful unions. Let no one joined to such persons approach the body of so great a Lord before completing a worthy period of penance, lest he receive not a remedy but a wound. For what is taken unworthily [Col. 0819D] is punishment, not healing.

Dearest ones, we are human beings full of filth, yet we do not wish our limbs to be touched by the unclean; and do we believe that the only-begotten Son of God willingly receives the filth of our crimes into his body? Brothers, behold, our King, who deemed us worthy of this embassy, follows immediately behind us. Let us prepare our houses clean for him, if we wish him to dwell in our very bodies.

We beg you, dearest sons—we beg you, entrails of holy Mother Church—that you who are accustomed to fear the laws of the world may deign patiently to hear the law of our God. He is the one who speaks to you through the service of our tongue, he whose paschal benefits you celebrated shortly before [Col. 0820A]: the one who did not spare his only-begotten Son from the hands of his persecutors, so that he might enroll us as heirs among his children.

If you have recognized how great a gift was granted to us through his Passion, hear his command more promptly, lest, while we remain disobedient to his orders, we be judged ungrateful for his benefits.

There is no doubt, dearest sons, that there are some—and would that they were few—who complain about our negligence, asking why we preach the remedies of your salvation so late. Their complaint is just, however, if they are now willing easily to receive the medicine. For if someone does not allow himself to be healed even late, what complaint does he have against the physician’s delay? Rather, the longer the illness has lasted, the greater the humility that should follow.

Who could tolerate a proud sick person who both complains that he has fallen into illness and refuses to receive health? [Col. 0820B] How many do we find, dearest sons, who live shamefully and yet bring accusations, saying: Why did Christ come so late? Why did he permit so many thousands of people to perish before his Incarnation?

If we accept their complaint, then even after receiving the gift of so great a physician we must remain sick. Why do you accuse the Sun of Justice because it rose late, when even after its rising you walk in darkness? Or because clouds often occupy the sky for a long time, must we not rejoice when calm has returned? Why do you waver, brother? Why do you waver pointlessly? Behold, it is now permitted to return to the quiet of clear weather. Why do you again desire the rocks? No one wished to keep you from perishing in the storm merely because the harbor appeared late.

## On the Sabbath

[Col. 0820C] Our most magnificent fathers, assembled at Laodicea in Phrygia and mindful of our salvation, enacted many provisions that it is fitting for us to observe. Among other matters, dearest sons, they dealt with Christians who are known to keep the Sabbath, or in some manner to Judaize. For they decreed under anathema against those known to imitate them.

We too wish to instruct you concerning this matter, you who have been baptized and regenerated in Christ. Behold, you have become members of Christ. We admonish you, we fear for you—not only because of pagans, not only because of heretics, but also because of faithless Jews who desire you to Judaize and rest on the Sabbath, so that the name of Christ which you have received may be defiled in you.

But one must act according to the definition of the Fathers, who command us to work on the Sabbath, in accordance with the Lord’s saying, who says in the Gospel: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.” Therefore the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.

When the Jews watched him in the synagogue to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him, he said to the man who had a withered hand: “Rise and stand in the midst.” And he said to them: “Is it lawful on the Sabbaths to do good or to do evil, to save a life or to destroy it?” But they were silent. And looking around at them with anger, grieved at the blindness of their hearts, he said to the man: “Stretch out your hand.” And he stretched it out, and his hand was restored.

Likewise, according to the evangelist Luke, Jesus was teaching in their synagogue on the Sabbaths, and there he healed a woman who had had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years. When the Jews were indignant about this, he said to them: “Hypocrites, does not each one of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or donkey from the manger and lead it to water? And ought not this daughter of Abraham to be released from this bond on the Sabbath day?”

For this also let the Jews be ashamed. You see, dearest ones, that the Lord worked on the Sabbaths for this reason: because we who are Christians must not observe the Sabbath according to the letter.

For Christians ought to observe the Sabbath in this way: we must abstain from robbery, fraud, perjury, blasphemy, unlawful things, accepting gifts against the innocent, and quarrels. Let us fear fornications as we fear death; for fornication does not release the soul from the body, but causes the soul always to burn together with the body.

I beseech you by the name that has been invoked over you, and by the sacraments that you have received, to imitate those whom you see doing good among the people of God, so that the sacrament of the one who did not wish to descend from the wood and deigned to rise from the tomb may remain in you.

He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever.

## Certain statutes of Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz and martyr, promulgated, it seems, at the same Council of Leptines

We are also compelled to observe the statute of the canons in this matter:

I. No priest shall abandon the church entrusted to him without the consent of the bishop and transfer to another at the persuasion of laymen.

II. No priest shall presume to celebrate the sacred mysteries anywhere except in consecrated places, out of contempt for the Church.

[Col. 0821C] III. No priest shall erect another altar in a consecrated church except one sanctified by the bishop, so that there may be a distinction between what is consecrated and what is not consecrated.

IV. Priests must not travel anywhere without sacred chrism, blessed oil, and the saving Eucharist. But wherever they are summoned, even by chance, they must immediately be found ready for their office and for rendering what is owed.

V. Priests must keep the chrism under seal and must not presume to give it to anyone under the pretext of medicine or any other purpose; for it is a kind of sacrament and must be touched by no one except priests. If they do so, they shall be deprived of their honor.

VI. Laymen must not expel priests from churches, [Col. 0821D] nor presume to install them, without the consent of their bishops.

VII. Laymen must not dare to demand gifts from priests on account of recommending a church to any priest.

VIII. Priests must strive to live well and must teach the people accordingly.

IX. Each bishop must diligently inquire in his diocese where his priests come from; and if he finds a fugitive, he must cause him to return to his own bishop.

X. Whoever abandons his own bishop and flees to another shall be degraded.

XI. Abbots and abbesses must live chastely, so that among their male or female subjects [Col. 0822A] they may display an example of holy conduct. If they do not do so, they shall be corrected by the bishop. But if they do not listen to the bishop at all, the bishop shall have the emperor informed.

XII. Each bishop must carefully provide in his diocese that wherever there is a monastery of monks, they live according to the rule and as monks; and wherever there is canonical life, they live well and canonically.

XIII. Bishops must investigate the monasteries of girls with the greatest diligence: first, how the abbess herself conducts herself and whether she lives chastely; then the nuns [the printed text reads *nonanes*] must be carefully examined, lest they commit adultery and fornication. The superiors of the monasteries must make the strictest inquiry into this.

XIV. Concerning monasteries of girls: priests [Col. 0822B] are to be permitted to come there at the proper time for the solemn celebration of Mass and then return to their own churches.

XV. More persons must not be sent into a monastery of canons, monks, or girls than it is able to support.

XVI. Each bishop must carefully examine his priests in his diocese and ensure that they properly perform their signings and baptisms; and they must teach the priests what each word or sentence in that baptism signifies by itself.

XVII. Each priest must be carefully examined by his bishop concerning his life and conduct, so that he does not have women living with him in his house at all.

XVIII. If anyone is departing from the body, he must not be deprived of the final and [Col. 0822C] necessary viaticum.

XIX. It is not permitted to place one dead person upon another dead person.

XX. It is not permitted to give the Eucharist or the kiss to the dead, nor to wrap their bodies in veils or cloaks.

XXI. It is not permitted to conduct secular dances or girls’ songs in the church, nor to prepare banquets in the church, because it is written: “My house shall be called a house of prayer.”

XXII. Men must not bathe together with women.

XXIII. In the altar at which the bishop has celebrated Mass, it is not permitted for a priest to celebrate Mass later on that same day.

XXIV. On the vigil of Easter, the vigils must not be completed before the second hour of the night, because on that [Col. 0822D] night it is not permitted to drink after midnight; nor is this permitted at Christmas or at the other solemnities.

XXV. Priests must also announce to all the faithful subject to them that they are to commit the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer to memory, so that they may be saved through faith and prayer, with the Holy Spirit giving light.

XXVI. Priests must announce that neither men nor women may receive boys or girls from the sacred font as godchildren unless they know the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer by heart.

XXVII. No priest should fail to make a point of openly questioning those who are to be baptized, in the very language in which they were born, concerning their renunciations or confessions, so that they may understand what they renounce or what they confess. [Col. 0823A] Whoever disdains to act in this way must withdraw from the diocese.

XXVIII. If there is doubt concerning whether certain persons have been baptized, they shall be baptized without any scruple, but with these words spoken beforehand: not “I baptize you,” but “If you have not yet been baptized, I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

XXIX. All priests must request from the bishop the oil for the sick, keep it with them, and admonish sick believers to seek it, so that, anointed with the same oil, they may be healed by the priests; for “the prayer of faith will save the sick.”

XXX. Priests must also teach the people to observe the four prescribed seasonal fasts, namely, in March, June, September, and December, when sacred orders are conferred according to the statutes of the canons.

[Col. 0823B] XXXI. And since we are hindered by various necessities from fully observing the statutes of the canons concerning the reconciliation of penitents, this must by no means be neglected. Each priest must see to it that, immediately after receiving the confession of penitents, he reconciles each one after offering a prayer. To the dying, communion and reconciliation must be given without delay.

XXXII. If someone requests penance while ill and, when the priest who has been summoned to him arrives, he has become speechless because of the illness or has fallen into delirium, those who heard him shall bear witness, and he shall receive penance. If he is immediately believed to be dying, he shall be reconciled by the laying on of hands, and the Eucharist shall be poured into his mouth. If he survives, [Col. 0823C] the aforementioned witnesses shall inform him that his request has been fulfilled, and he shall be subjected to the prescribed penance for as long as the priest who imposed the penance judges appropriate.

XXXIII. If any priest or cleric observes auguries, divinations, dreams, lots, or phylacteries—that is, written formulas—he must know that he is subject to the penalties of the canons.

XXXIV. Priests must make this known to all the people: on the Saturday of Pentecost, just as on Holy Saturday of Easter, everyone must fast and assemble at the church at the ninth hour, when the celebration takes place, just as on Holy Saturday at evening. They must likewise keep Pentecost Day itself as a most solemn feast, like Easter.

XXXV. Each priest [Col. 0823D] must publicly admonish the people to abstain from illicit unions and, according to the Lord’s command, that a lawful marriage may in no way be separated for any reason except on account of fornication, unless both parties consent—and this for the sake of the service of God.

[Col. 0824A] XXXVI. Priests must announce that throughout the year Sundays are to be observed as Sabbaths.

### First arrangement

At Christmas, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, four days.

At the Circumcision of the Lord, on the Kalends of January, one day.

At the Epiphany, on the eighth day before the Ides of January, one day.

At the Purification of Saint Mary, on the fourth day before the Nones of February, one day.

At the Lord’s Easter, after Sunday, three days.

At the Ascension of the Lord, one day.

At the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, one day.

At the Passion of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, on the third day before the Kalends of July, one day.

At the Assumption of Saint Mary, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September, one day.

At the Nativity of Saint Mary, on the sixth day before the Ides of September, one day.

At the Passion of Saint Andrew the Apostle, on the day before the Kalends of December, one day.

### VI. [Note]

[Col. 0823D] In this council, the first canon defines that the faith of the Council of Nicaea and the canonical judgments of the other synods, established by the saints, are to be proclaimed to the people. It is called by all writers of synods—Binius, Sirmond, Labbe, and Hardouin—the council held at Soissons under Pippin.

Nevertheless, Willibald, a contemporary biographer of Saint Boniface, calls it the fifth synodal council under Duke Carloman, at which Saint Boniface presided, and at which he admonished that the decrees of the four principal councils should be observed, with bishops, priests, deacons, and clerics assembled together.

It follows that we must say either that this was the synod held in Austrasia under Carloman, corresponding to the one held in Neustria under Pippin; or that, by order of both dukes, the bishops of both Neustria and Austrasia assembled at Soissons under the presidency of Boniface, legate of the Apostolic See; or that the bishops of Austrasia accepted what had been established at Soissons under Pippin. In one of these three ways the fifth synodal council mentioned by Willibald—at which the four first general councils were discussed—can be verified.

See the *Acts of the Saints* under the day of June, p. 468, second column.

## THE COUNCIL OF SOISSONS

Celebrated under Pippin, mayor of the palace, by twenty-three bishops, on the sixth day before the Nones of March, in the year of Christ 744, in the third year of Pope Zacharias and the second year of King Childeric.

## TITLES OF THE CHAPTERS

I. On the Nicene faith and the ancient canons to be promulgated throughout the whole kingdom.

II. On a synod to be assembled every year, and on the heretic Adalbert condemned at the synod.

III. On bishops appointed in the cities under the archbishops Abel and Ardobert. On monks; on abbots not going themselves to war but sending others; and on clerics abstaining from fornication, lay dress, and hunting.

IV. That laymen avoid all fornication, perjury, and false testimony, protect the Church, and that the priests of the parishes be subject to their bishop.

V. That unknown bishops or priests not be admitted to ministry without examination.

VI. That bishops provide that the people do not practice paganism, and that lawful measures exist throughout the cities.

VII. That Adalbert’s little crosses be committed to the fire.

VIII. That clerics not keep foreign women in their homes.

IX. That no one marry a consecrated woman or a near relation, nor should a wife take another husband while her husband survives.

X. On transgressors of these canons.

## PREFACE

In the name of God and of the Trinity. In the year 744 from the Incarnation of Christ, on the sixth day before the Nones of March, and on the fourteenth day of the moon, in the second year of Childeric, king of the Franks.

I, Pippin, duke and prince of the Franks: Since it is not unknown to many how we, in the name of God and with the consent of the bishops, priests, and servants of God, after consultation and discussion with the counts and nobles of the Franks, resolved to hold a synod or council at the city of Soissons, we have indeed done so in the name of God.

## CANONS

[Col. 0825B] I. First, we decree that the Catholic faith established by the 318 bishops at the Council of Nicaea is to be proclaimed throughout our entire region, together with the canonical judgments of the other holy men, which they established in their synods, so that the law of God and ecclesiastical order may be restored—an order that, dissipated in the days of earlier rulers, has collapsed.

II. Therefore, together with the consent of the bishops, priests, servants of God, and nobles, and after their counsel, we decree that every year we must renew the synod, so that the Christian people may attain the salvation of souls and so that heresy may not rise again among the people. Thus we found the heresy of Adalbert: twenty-three bishops and many other priests publicly condemned him with one voice, with the consent of the prince and the people. They condemned Adalbert so that the people, deceived by false priests, might not perish any longer.

III. Therefore, after consultation with the priests and nobles, we established and appointed legitimate bishops throughout the cities. For this reason we appointed over them the archbishops Abel and Ardobert, so that both the bishops and the rest of the people might have recourse to their judgments in every ecclesiastical necessity.

We decree that the order of monks and of handmaids of God remain stable according to the holy rule, and that the monks or handmaids of God be supported from ecclesiastical property that has been taken away from them, until their needs have been satisfied. Any surplus is to be assessed as revenue. Legitimate abbots must not go to war themselves, but must send only their men; and all clerics must abstain from fornication, must not wear lay dress, must not keep dogs for hunting, and must not carry hawks.

IV. Likewise we decree that laymen live lawfully, commit no varieties of fornication, consent to no perjuries in the Church, give no false testimony, and preserve the Church of God in every necessity.

Each priest who is in a parish must obey and be subject to the bishop; he must always render an account of the order and administration of his ministry to his bishop on the Lord’s Supper, and must request chrism and oil. When the bishop makes his canonical visitation of the parish to confirm the people, the abbots and priests must be ready to receive the bishop in aid of his duty.

V. We decree that visiting bishops or priests from other regions are not to be received into the ministry of the Church unless they have first been examined by the bishop whose diocese it is.

VI. We decree absolutely that each bishop must be concerned in his diocese that the Christian people do not practice paganism, and that throughout all the cities there be lawful measures and standards, according to the requirements of the time.

VII. Likewise we decree that all those little crosses which Adalbert had planted throughout the parishes be consumed by fire.

[Col. 0826B] VIII. Likewise we decree that no cleric may have a woman living with him in his house, except his mother, sister, or niece.

IX. Likewise we decree that no layman may have a woman consecrated to God as his wife, nor his own relative; that no other man may take a woman while her husband is alive; and that no woman may take another man while her husband is alive, because a husband must not dismiss his wife except on account of proven fornication.

X. If anyone wishes to transgress this decree, which the twenty-three bishops, together with the other priests and servants of God and with the consent of Prince Pippin and the counsel of the Frankish nobles, have established; or wishes to violate the law; or despises it, he shall be judged by the prince himself, or by the bishops, or by the counts. Each person shall pay the composition prescribed in the law, according to his rank.

And if we observe all these things written above, we shall be able to find the mercy of Christ forever and ever. Amen.

Sign of the illustrious Pippin, mayor of the palace. Sign of Radbod. Sign of Aribert. Sign of Helmigaud.

### VII. [Note]

[Col. 0825D] First published by Baluze, volume I of the *Capitularies*, from an old manuscript codex of the Thuane Library, with the following title: “From the council of kings, at which Boniface, legate of the Roman See, was present,” p. 151 and following. [WURDT.]

## UNCERTAIN COUNCIL [c. A.D. 745]

A capitulary of uncertain date issued at a synod attended by Boniface, legate of the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0826D] [Around the year of Christ 744, in the third year of Pope Zacharias and the second year of King Childeric III.]

## THE CHAPTERS BEGIN

I. On an exposed infant.

II. On the thirtieth-day observances for the dead.

III. On a woman who has given birth.

IV. On clerics who grow their hair long.

V. On priests who depart.

VI. On the place of laymen in the church.

VII. On the servants of clerics.

VIII. On invaders of ecclesiastical property.

IX. On the rule concerning prayers.

X. On the profession of priests.

[Col. 0827A] XI. On the wills of priests.

XII. On archdeacons.

XIII. On composers of songs.

XIV. On the form of an oath.

XV. On freedmen, that they are not to be witnesses.

XVI. On exchange.

XVII. On sureties.

XVIII. On the parties in legal proceedings.

XIX. On agnates and cognates.

XX. On counterfeit money.

XXI. On homicides fleeing to the church.

XXII. On robbers.

XXIII. On the Lord’s Day.

XXIV. On property bought from a thief.

XXV. On killing another person’s animal.

[Col. 0827B] XXVI. On compensation for a burned house.

XXVII. On a neighborhood road.

XXVIII. On entrusted property that has been burned.

## THE AFORESAID CHAPTERS AND THEIR TEXT BEGIN

### On an exposed infant

I. If an exposed child is found and taken in through compassion before anyone’s church, the person who takes it in shall place a written declaration with it. If the child who has been taken in is not sought out and recognized within ten days, the person who collected it shall possess it securely. But whoever thereafter brings a claim against him shall be condemned as a homicide, as the authority of the Fathers has decreed.

### On the thirtieth-day observances for the dead

II. Let the faithful arrange for fasts and offerings to be completed for thirty days on behalf of deceased friends; and let them not place one dead person upon another, nor leave the bones of the dead upon the ground. If they do so, they shall be subject to canonical judgment.

### On a woman who has given birth

III. When a woman has given birth, if she immediately enters the church to give thanks, she is burdened by no weight of sin on this account. For it is the pleasure of the flesh, not the pain, that is at fault; but in the bringing forth of offspring there is groaning. Therefore, if we forbid a woman who has given birth to enter the church, we would be assigning her own punishment to her as guilt.

### On clerics who grow their hair long

IV. It has been decreed that clerics who grow their hair long are to be shorn by the archdeacon, even against their will. They are not permitted to have clothing or footwear unless these are suitable for religion.

### On priests who depart

V. Concerning priests who leave or have left their own titular churches without the bishop’s permission, it has been decreed that they are to be held excluded from communion until they return to their titular churches.

### On the place of laymen in the church

VI. Laymen must not presume at all to stand beside the altar within the railings, whether during vigils or during Masses.

### On the servants of clerics

VII. By divine authority we prohibit the servants of churches, bishops, or clerics from being worn out by judges or public officials through various compulsory services. If any judge or official wishes to occupy a cleric or an ecclesiastical servant in public or private business, he shall be made an outsider by the Church to which he causes the impediment.

### On invaders of ecclesiastical property

VIII. Whoever petitions kings for ecclesiastical property and, driven by dreadful greed, seizes the substance of the needy: whatever he obtains shall be considered void, and he himself shall be excluded from the church that he desires to despoil.

### On the rule concerning prayers

IX. In prayers no one should direct his prayer except to the Father, according to the saying: “If you ask the Father for anything in my name.” And he should first treat these matters together with instruction.

### On the professions of priests

X. When priests or deacons are appointed throughout the parishes, they ought to make a profession to their bishop.

### On the wills of priests

XI. Priests who, after ordination, acquire estates from their poverty must confirm them by wills in favor of the churches. Otherwise, they are to be regarded as defrauders.

### On archdeacons

XII. Bishops must ensure that the greed of their archdeacons does not nourish wrongdoing, because in many ways iniquity lies to itself.

### On composers of songs

XIII. Whoever composes songs as a blasphemy against another, or whoever sings them, shall be judged outside the ordinary procedure. For the law commands that such a person be exiled.

### On the form of an oath

[Col. 0828C] XIV. Every oath must be sworn in the church and over relics: “So may God help him, and those saints whose relics these are!”

### On freedmen, that they are not to be witnesses

XV. A freedman or freedwoman may not give testimony against anyone in any legal matter, except in those cases in which free birth is lacking, as was stated above concerning enslaved persons. For our clemency considers it unworthy that the testimony of freedmen should inflict harm upon the freeborn.

Those born from freedmen or freedwomen are admitted as witnesses beginning with the third generation.

### On exchange

XVI. An exchange, if it has not been extorted by force or fear, shall have the same validity as a sale.

### On a surety

XVII. If anyone, disregarding the surety, prefers to hold his debtor, the surety and his heir shall be released from the bond of suretyship.

### On the parties in legal proceedings

XVIII. There ought to be four parties in legal proceedings: an accuser, a defender, witnesses, and a judge. The accuser should use assertion to enlarge the case; the defender, mitigation to diminish it; the witnesses, truth; and the judge, equity.

### On agnates and cognates

XIX. Agnates are those who descend through the male line; cognates are those who descend through the female line. Therefore, paternal uncles and the sons of paternal uncles are both agnates and cognates. Maternal uncles, however, and the sons of maternal uncles are cognates, not agnates.

## On Counterfeit Coinage

**XX.** Concerning counterfeit coinage, we decree that whoever is proved to have struck it shall have his hand cut off; and whoever consented to this, if he is free, shall pay sixty solidi; if he is a slave, he shall receive sixty blows.

## On Murderers Fleeing to a Church

**XXI.** Murderers and other defendants who ought to die under the laws, if they flee to a church, shall be given no food.

## On Robbers

**XXII.** Concerning robbers, we order that the following be observed: for the first offense, let him lose one eye; for the second, let his nose be cut off; for the third offense, if he has not reformed, [Col. 0829B] let him die.

## On Sunday

**XXIII.** If anyone performs servile work on Sunday, a free man who yokes oxen shall lose the right-hand ox. And if he does any of the other things that are prohibited, let him make satisfaction for them to the priests, just as satisfaction is customarily made before judges for other negligences, and let him also receive penance. The same shall apply to the principal feast days.

## On a Purchase from a Thief

**XXIV.** If anyone, unknowingly, buys something from a thief, let him search for the thief after being granted a period of time. If he cannot find him, let him prove by oath that he is innocent, restore the object, and not cease searching for the thief. But if he conceals the thief and is afterward discovered to have committed perjury, let him himself also be condemned as a thief.

[Col. 0829C]

## On an Animal Belonging to Another, Killed by Accident

**XXV.** If anyone, through an accident, kills another person’s animal, and does not deny it, let him not delay in giving an animal of the same kind, and let him receive the carcass of the dead animal.

## On Compensation for a Burned House

**XXVI.** If anyone burns another person’s house, let him first restore all the buildings, compensate for whatever burned there, and, in addition, pay sixty solidi and be punished by public penance. And for however many people escape from that fire, let him pay compensation to each according to his law, and restore whatever they lost.

## On a Common Road

**XXVII.** If anyone blocks a common or pastoral road, let him pay compensation according to his law and open the road itself.

[Col. 0829D]

## On Goods Entrusted to Someone That Are Burned

**XXVIII.** If goods have been entrusted to anyone, or handed over to him for sale, and in his house, together with his own goods, they . . . . .

*[The remainder is missing in the manuscript.]*

# VIII. COUNCIL AT AN UNCERTAIN LOCATION, HELD IN THE FRANKISH PROVINCE IN THE YEAR 745

The sixth synod celebrated by Saint Boniface was held in the year 745, at an uncertain location, in the Frankish province. Serarius thinks that it was convened at Mainz, but Eckartus, *Rerum Francicarum*, book XXIII, p. 466, says that this opinion lacks foundation. Boniface himself testifies in his letter to the presbyter Herefrid, among the *Bonifaciana* [Col. 0830A], no. 10, that eight bishops were present at the synod, all of them Englishmen.

The letter numbered 19 has preserved the names of six bishops for us. It was written to King Æthelbald of Mercia by Boniface, archbishop and Germanic legate of the Roman Church, together with Wevera, Burchard, Warbeth, Abel, and Wilibald, fellow bishops. The name Wevera appears to be corrupt, derived from that of Wettena, or Wittani, bishop of Bureburg. Burchard presided over the Church of Würzburg. Warbeth is the same person as Hartbert, archbishop of Sens; and Abel was archbishop of Reims. Since they were not received in their own sees, they were at that time staying with Boniface. It is known that Wilibald was bishop of Eichstätt. The names of the remaining two bishops are unknown to us.

Aldebert and Clement were condemned at this synod, as is clear from the acts of the Roman council. Gewiliebus, bishop of Mainz, had already been deprived of the episcopal rank; later writers improperly call him Gervilio. For after committing murder in the preceding year, he had nevertheless continued to perform sacred functions. Therefore [Col. 0830B] Saint Boniface exposed his crime at the synod and declared that no one polluted by the guilt of murder ought to exercise episcopal office. He also charged him with having seen with his own eyes that he played with birds and dogs, something wholly unbecoming to a bishop.

Gewiliebus, having confessed his guilt, submitted himself to the judgment of the synod, as Othlonus reports in book I, chapter 37, and acknowledged that he was justly to be deposed from the episcopal order. Nevertheless, from Zacharias’s letter, no. 138, one may conclude that he appealed from the synod’s sentence to the pope.

Saint Boniface sent the acts concerning Aldebert and Clement to Rome by the presbyter Deneardus. It should be noted there that the two heretics who had just been rebuked in the year 742 had not repented and were therefore condemned with greater solemnity. The further acts of the synod may be discerned from the letters mentioned above. W.

# IX. THIRD GERMANIC COUNCIL, CONVENED BY THE AUTHORITY OF SAINT BONIFACE, LEGATE OF THE ROMAN SEE, IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 745, AT WHICH THE HERETICS ALDEBERT AND CLEMENT WERE CONDEMNED, AND AFTER GERVILIO, BISHOP OF MAINZ, WAS DEPOSED FOR THE CRIME OF MURDER, SAINT BONIFACE WAS MADE ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

[Col. 0830C]

When the synod was being held by order of Carloman and on the advice of Boniface, not only were many clerics of every kind infected with heretical depravity expelled from communion with the Church, but bishops also, disgraced by the stains of capital crimes, were deposed. The two principal authors of the whole error then spreading through Germany were the heretics Clement and Aldebert; more will be said about them at the proper point, when we have produced the letters sent to Pope Zacharias. For those letters record their destructive heresy.

At that time Gervilio, bishop of the see of Mainz, was also deposed. The cause of his deposition was as follows.

[Col. 0830D]

At that time, when the Saxons were laying waste Thuringia, the people of that province implored Carloman’s aid. He immediately sent an army, together with Gerold, bishop of Mainz and father of Gervilio. In the actual conflict Gerold was killed, along with many others.

His son Gervilio, who was then still a layman serving at the palace, was admitted into the clergy in order to alleviate the grief he had conceived from his father’s death, and was installed in his place in the bishopric of Mainz. Not long afterward Carloman again gathered an army and set out against the Saxons, taking Gervilio with him.

When both armies were encamped on opposite banks of the River Weser—the author calls it the Wisarah—Gervilio ordered his servant to go to the enemy camp and carefully inquire the name of the man who had killed his father. The servant went and learned from someone that the man he sought was not far away. He asked him to come quickly to a meeting with his master.

The man came, and when his arrival had been announced, horses were prepared. Bishop Gervilio went out to meet him, and while they were speaking in midstream, Gervilio, secretly carrying a sword, stabbed the man, saying:

> Receive now the iron with which I avenge my beloved father.

He immediately fell from his horse and breathed out his life in the river. When his killing was suddenly discovered, a shout arose and both sides rushed to arms. A savage battle followed. After the Saxons were defeated, Carloman withdrew to his own territory, and at that time no one imputed to Gervilio as murder what he had done. Thus, having returned home, he continued to perform the duties of a bishop as usual.

But Saint Boniface, the prelate, also pronounced the following at the synod: no one who had been polluted by the killing of a man could exercise the priesthood. He also charged him with having seen with his own eyes that he played with birds and dogs, which was not lawful for a bishop.

When Gervilio heard this, he realized that he could in no way kick against the goad of either secular power or canonical authority, which Saint Boniface was bringing forward before everyone present. He therefore subscribed to the judgment of all and was deprived of office.

After his deposition, Saint Boniface was placed over the see of Mainz by Carloman and his brother Pippin. And, so that his dignity might be more eminent, the same princes decided to elevate the Church of Mainz, which at that time was subject to another, into the metropolitan church of all Germany; and, having immediately sent an embassy to the Roman pontiff, they obtained this.

WURDT.

# X. [Note: [Col. 0831D] Roman Synod. It occurs as nos. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, in the Paris Codex. Concerning the year [745], Sirmondus notes: The indiction 14, in the month of October, agrees with this year. Two eras for the years of Constantine are mentioned. The first begins from the time when he had begun to reign with his father Leo the Isaurian, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, in the year 720; the second counts the years during which he ruled alone after his father’s death, beginning on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, in indiction 9—that is, in the year of Christ 741. Although in this passage he does not count the years of the reign, but rather those after the consulship, the result is the same, since Constantine appears to have given the consulship a few days after the anniversary of his accession to the empire, as was said concerning his father. Therefore the subscriptions of the remaining letters should also be tested according to this standard. SIRMOND.] ROMAN SYNOD. SENT TO SAINT BONIFACE AND OTHERS IN GERMANY CONCERNING THE HERETICS CONDEMNED BY SAINT BONIFACE. [A.D. 745.]

In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, while the most pious Lord Augustus Constantine the emperor was reigning, in the twenty-sixth year, in the fifth year after his consulship, on the twenty-fifth day of October, in the fourteenth indiction, with the most holy and blessed [Col. 0831C] Lord Zacharias the pope presiding in the Lateran patriarchate, in the basilica called that of Theodore; with the most holy bishops sitting together with him—Epiphanius of Silva Candida, Benedict of Nomentum, Venantius of Praeneste, Gregory of Porto, Nicetas of Gabii, Theodore of Orte, Gratiosus of Velletri—and the venerable presbyters, namely John the archpresbyter, Gregory, Stephen, another Stephen, Dominic, Theodore, Anastasius, George, Sergius, Jordan, Leo, another Leo, Gregory, Stephen, Eustochius, Procopius, and Theophanius; with the holy Gospels placed in the midst; and with the deacons and the entire clergy also standing by, Gregory, the regional notary and *nomenclator*, said:

“Deneardus, the religious presbyter, legate of Boniface [Col. 0831D], the most holy archbishop of the province of Germany, sent to your holy apostolate, is before the veil and asks to enter. What do you command?”

It was said: “Let him enter.”

When he had entered, Zacharias, the most holy and blessed pope of the holy catholic and apostolic city of Rome, said:

“A few days ago you brought us the written statements of our most reverend and most holy brother Boniface, archbishop [Col. 0832A], through which he indicated to us what seemed appropriate to them. Why, then, have you again requested to enter our secretariat?”

Deneardus, the religious presbyter, said:

“My lord, when, in accordance with the command of your holy apostolate, my lord Bishop Boniface, servant of your piety, had convened a synod in the province of the Franks and found there false priests, heretics, and schismatics—namely Aldebert and Clement—he deprived them of the priesthood and, together with the princes of the Franks, had them confined in custody.

“But they are not living in repentance, as had been judged; on the contrary, they continue to lead the people astray. For this reason I, sent by my aforesaid lord, offer to your holy apostolate this letter, which I carry in my hands, so that you may have it read aloud before the most holy [Col. 0832B] council.”

It was said: “Let the letter be received and reread in our presence.”

The regional notary and *sacellarius* Theophanius received it and reread it in these words:

*(The letter reread by Theophanius, the regional notary, is the fifty-seventh in this edition. [Note: [Col. 0832D] See above, col. 751. EDIT.])*

When it had been reread, Zacharias, the most holy and blessed pope, said:

“You have heard, dearest brothers, what has been reread in this letter concerning those sacrilegious men who proclaimed themselves apostles to their own condemnation.”

The most holy bishops and venerable presbyters answered:

“We have certainly heard everything: they are not apostles, but ministers of Satan and forerunners of Antichrist. For when did any of the apostles, or [Col. 0832C] any of the saints, exhibit shrines to the people from their own hair or fingernails, as this sacrilegious and pernicious man Aldebert has attempted to do? But this crime must be cut away by your holy apostolate, both in his case and also in the case of that transgressor Clement, who despises the sacred canons, the expositions of the holy Fathers, and the sayings of the saints, so that they may receive a sentence worthy of their transgressions.”

Zacharias, the most holy and blessed pope, said:

“Because the hour is already late today, at the next session their life and deeds shall be reread, and, with God’s help, what ought to be done shall be considered by common agreement.”

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, while the most pious Lord Augustus Constantine, [Col. 0832D] the great emperor, was reigning, in the twenty-sixth year, in the fifth year after his consulship, on the twenty-fifth day of October, in the fourteenth indiction, with the most holy and blessed Lord Zacharias the pope presiding in the Lateran patriarchate, in the basilica called that of Theodore; with the most holy bishops also sitting together with him—Epiphanius of Silva Candida, Benedict of Nomentum, Venantius of Praeneste, Gregory of Porto, Nicetas of Gabii, Theodore of Ostia, Gratiosus [Col. 0833A] of Velletri—and the venerable presbyters, namely John the archpresbyter, Gregory, Stephen, another Stephen, Dominic, Theodore, Anastasius, George, Sergius, Jordan, Leo, another Leo, Gregory, Stephen, Eustachius, Procopius, and Theophanius; with the holy Gospels placed in the midst; and with the deacons and the entire clergy also standing by, Gregory, the regional notary and *nomenclator*, said:

“In accordance with the command of your holy apostolate, which you gave at the previous session, Deneardus, the religious presbyter, is present before the veil. What do you command?”

It was said: “Let him enter.”

When he had entered, Zacharias, the most holy and blessed pope, said:

“Present to the council now assembled the deeds of that most infamous Aldebert, and whatever else has been written concerning him, which you held in your hands at the previous [Col. 0833B] session, so that they may be read.”

The regional notary and *sacellarius* Theophanius received them and reread his Life, whose beginning was as follows:

> In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Here begins the Life of the holy and blessed servant of God, illustrious and altogether beautiful, born by God’s election, Saint Aldebert the bishop.

He was born of humble parents and crowned by the grace of God, because, while he was still in his mother’s womb, he received there the grace of God. And before his most blessed birth had taken place, his mother saw, as if in a vision, a little calf emerging from her right side. That calf signified the grace which he had received from the angel before he came out of the womb.

[Col. 0833C]

When this little book had been read aloud to the end, Zacharias, the most holy and blessed pope, said:

“What answer do you give to these blasphemies, most holy brothers?”

Epiphanius, the most holy bishop of Silva Candida, said:

“Certainly, apostolic lord, by divine inspiration the heart of your holy apostolate was moved to admonish the aforesaid Boniface, our most holy brother and bishop, and the princes of the Franks, so that after a long time a council of priests might be convened in those regions and these schisms and blasphemies might not remain altogether concealed from your holy apostolate.”

Zacharias, the most holy and blessed pope, said:

“If the religious presbyter Deneardus has anything further to present to us for rereading, let him present it.”

Deneardus, the religious presbyter [Col. 0833D], replied:

“Here, lord, is the letter which he used and circulated as being from Jesus and as having fallen from heaven.”

The regional notary and *sacellarius* Theophanius received it and reread it, whose beginning was as follows:

> In the name of God begins the letter of our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, which fell in Jerusalem and was found by the archangel Michael at the gate of Ephraim. Through the hands of a priest named Leora this letter was read and copied, and he sent it to the city of Jeremiah, to another priest named Talasius. Talasius himself sent it to the city of Arabia, to another priest named Leobanius. Leobanius himself sent this letter to the city of Wetfavia, where Macharius, the priest of God, received it and sent it to the mountain of Saint Michael the archangel.

[Col. 0834A]

> This letter itself, through the hands of the angel of the Lord, reached the city of Rome, to the place of the tomb of Saint Peter, where the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been established. The twelve popes who are in the city of Rome kept three-day vigils and remained in fasting and prayers day and night, and so forth, until the end, which was read aloud.

Zacharias, the most holy and blessed pope, said:

“Certainly, dearest brothers, this Aldebert has been turned to madness. And all who use this wicked letter are, like little children, without soundness of mind and are mad with womanish understanding. But so that the more impressionable may not be deceived any further, we cannot leave this case against him unexamined and without a sentence.”

The most holy bishops and venerable presbyters [Col. 0834B] answered:

“By divine illumination we recognize that the heart of your holy apostolate has been enlightened, and that what you have said has proceeded through the administration of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, as you have foreseen, let sentence be pronounced against both of them.”

Zacharias, the most holy and blessed pope, said:

“Not merely as it has been foreseen by us alone, but it must be considered together with your holiness. If it pleases the Lord, at the next session whatever appears right and whatever the Lord administers to his servants, a sentence shall be promulgated from all his deeds.”
