In the name of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, while the most pious Lord Augustus Constantine [Col. 0834C], the great emperor, was reigning, in the twenty-sixth year, in the fifth year after his consulship, on the twenty-fifth day of October, in the fourteenth indiction, with the most holy and blessed Lord Zacharias the pope presiding in the Lateran patriarchate, in the basilica called that of Theodore; with the most holy bishops also sitting together with him—Epiphanius of Silva Candida, Benedict of Nomentum, Venantius of Praeneste, Gregory of Porto, Nicetas of Gabii, Theodore of Ostia, Gratiosus of Velletri—and the venerable presbyters John the archpresbyter, Gregory, Stephen, another Stephen, Dominic, Theodore, Anastasius, George, Sergius, Jordan, Leo, another Leo, Gregory, Stephen, Eustachius, Procopius, and Theophanius; with the holy Gospels placed in the midst; and with the deacons and the entire clergy also standing by, Gregory, the regional notary and *nomenclator* [Col. 0834D], said:

“According to what was commanded by your holy apostolate at the previous session, that the religious presbyter Deneardus should present himself before you today, he is here before the doors. What do you command?”

It was said: “Let him enter.”

When he had entered, Zacharias, the most holy and blessed pope, said:

“Do you have anything further from the writings of those sacrilegious men to present before this holy council for rereading?”

Deneardus, the religious presbyter, replied:

“Yes, my lord. I have the prayer which Aldebert attempted to compose for himself. Here I carry it in my hands. Command that it be received.”

The regional notary Theophanius received it and reread it before everyone. Its beginning was as follows:

> Lord God almighty, Father of Christ, the Son of God, our [Col. 0835A] Lord Jesus Christ, Alpha and Omega, who sit upon the seventh throne and upon the cherubim and seraphim, you are great mercy, and for you sweetness is sufficient. Father of the holy angels, who made heaven and earth, the sea and everything that is in them, I invoke and call upon you, and I invite you over me, most wretched, because you deigned to say: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, I will do.” Therefore I ask you, because my soul trusts in you.

As it was read in order, they came to the passage where it said:

> I beg you, and adjure you, and entreat you, O angel Uriel, angel Ragull, angel Tubuel, angel Michael, angel Inias, angel Tubuas, angel Sabaoc, angel Simiel.

When this sacrilegious prayer had been read aloud to the end, Zacharias, the most holy and blessed [Col. 0835B] pope, said:

“What answer do you give to this, most holy brothers?”

The most holy bishops and venerable presbyters answered:

“What is to be done except that everything reread to us should be burned in the fire, while its authors should be struck by the bond of anathema? For these are not the names of angels, except for the name of Michael, but the names of demons, which he invoked in his prayers to obtain help for himself. We, instructed by your holy apostolate and taught by divine authority, know the names of no more than three angels: Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael. This man, under the pretext of angels, has introduced the names of demons.”

The most holy and blessed pope Zacharias said:

“It has been wisely proposed by your Holiness that all his writings be burned in the fire; [Col. 0835C] but it is appropriate that they be preserved in our archive, for his refutation and perpetual confusion. Now, since everything has been completed, the sentence concerning both men mentioned above must be considered.”

The entire council said:

“Aldebert, whose deeds and wicked inventions have been reread to us, and who presumed to call himself an apostle, exhibiting his hair and fingernails to the people as sacred objects, while leading the people astray through various errors, and who, under the pretext of angels, invoked demons to aid him: let him be deposed from every priestly office, doing penance for his offenses, and let him no longer lead the people astray.

“But if he persists in these errors and leads the people astray further, let him be anathema and condemned by the eternal judgment of God; [Col. 0835D] and so also let everyone be condemned who consents to him, follows his teaching, or associates himself with him.

“Likewise, let Clement, who through his folly rejects the writings of the holy Fathers and thinks lightly of all synodal acts, and who moreover introduces Judaism among Christians by preaching that the wife of a deceased brother may be joined in marriage to his surviving brother, and who further teaches that our Lord Jesus Christ, descending to the underworld, brought out from there all the pious and impious together, be deposed from every priestly office and bound by the bond of anathema. Unless he repents, let him be condemned by the eternal judgment of God, and likewise all who consent to his sacrilegious preaching.”

Zacharias, bishop of the holy catholic and apostolic city of Rome [Col. 0836A], subscribed to these acts and to the sentence promulgated by us.

Epiphanius, bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida, subscribed to these acts and to the sentence promulgated by us.

# XI. COUNCIL OF MAINZ UNDER POPE STEPHEN II, 1; KING PIPPIN, 1. [AROUND A.D. 752.] AT IT LULLUS WAS ORDAINED BISHOP BY SAINT BONIFACE, AND THE OTHER BISHOPS AND ABBOTS PREVIOUSLY APPOINTED WERE CONFIRMED

[Col. 0838A]

Finally . . . having set out for his own diocese by command of the Roman pontiff, with the consent of the venerable prince Pippin, by permission of synodal authority, and with the approval of all the bishops and abbots, as well as the canons, monks, and all the Christians belonging to it.

But he first bound Lullus by an oath, saying:

“Indeed, I am setting out courageously wherever divine grace wishes to direct me. But now give me your word that, wherever I die, you will transfer my body to the place appointed.”

And he promised that he would faithfully observe everything to the best of his ability.

[Col. 0837]

# MANSI’S DISSERTATION

## On the Synods Held in Germany, Gaul, and Italy by Saint Boniface and Pope Zacharias, and on the Correspondence between Pope Zacharias and Saint Boniface

[Col. 0837B]

The chronology of the synods held by Saint Boniface, or held on his account, as well as of the letters of Pope Zacharias to Saint Boniface and of Saint Boniface to him, is so obscure that it occupied the most learned writers of our age for a long time; yet their labors have not advanced the matter so far that it has been brought fully into the clear light. I have likewise attempted to dispel these shadows in my annotations on Baronius. Although I trust that I have succeeded well in some matters, I now realize, and candidly confess, that in others I have not reached the truth.

The matter must therefore be treated anew in its entirety. To make this succeed, I think that the era of the emperors marked in those documents should be abandoned, since it varies in the various manuscript codices and is not indicated with sufficient accuracy by Theophanes, as Pagius testifies in his *Critique of Baronius*. I shall therefore arrange that chronology according to what the letters and synods themselves reveal when compared with one another, with the additional assistance of the indictions by which each of these documents is dated.

First of all, therefore, I establish the council called Germanic, since we know absolutely nothing about the precise place where the bishops assembled. In its preface we read that those bishops came together in the year of Christ 742, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. But since that era of the Incarnation was rarely used in that period, I think nothing should be based on it, as it may have been added later.

[Col. 0837D]

It is certain that a certain Bishop Burchard sat among the fathers of that council. He was plainly none other than Burchard of Würzburg, whom Pope Zacharias, already appointed bishop by Saint Boniface, confirms in the episcopal see in his second letter in Labbe, volume XII. That letter is dated the Kalends of April, in the eleventh indiction, namely in the year 743. From this one may correctly conclude that Burchard had obtained the episcopate shortly before April of that year. How, then, could he have sat among the bishops in April of the year 742?

Let the council therefore be placed one year later than it has hitherto been placed, namely in the year 743. In that year the eleventh day before the Kalends of May—the day dated in the acts of that council—fell on a Sunday. I have often observed that councils in ancient practice began on Sunday.

Three letters preceded this council: the first was from Saint Boniface to Saint Zacharias, informing him about the three bishops established in Germany, among whom was the bishop of Würzburg; the other two were from Saint Zacharias, one to Saint Boniface, ordering him to celebrate a council in Francia, and the other to Burchard, which we mentioned above. Both were dated on the Kalends of April, in the eleventh indiction—that is, in the year 743—shortly before the Germanic Council.

[Col. 0838C]

In the following year, 744, the Council of Soissons assembled. Since its preface says that it was held on the sixth day, or, as the most carefully corrected codices have it, on the sixth day before the Nones of March, with the moon at fourteen days, these chronological indications assign it to 2 March in the year 744.

At it, the heresy of Adalbertus was condemned; Abel and Adalbertus were announced as archbishops over the bishops ordained throughout the cities—Abel as archbishop of Reims and the other as archbishop of Sens. The year of this council, which we have assigned, is indicated by Zacharias’s letter to Saint Boniface, the fourth among the Labbe letters. In it the pontiff says that he is sending the pallia to Abel and Adalbert, whom, he says, “you established through every metropolitan see in the provinces”—namely, at the Council of Soissons, as I have already observed. The letter was dated on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the twelfth indiction—that is, in the year 744.

Not long after Soissons, in the same year, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, Zacharias held a council at Rome, as may be read in Labbe, volume XII. I discussed the date of this council in my annotations on Pagius, under the year 743, section 15.

[Col. 0838D]

I am completely certain that this Roman Council was held in the year 744, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. The year is indicated by the chronological markers prefixed to the acts of the council. The thirty-second year of Liutprand extended from June of the year 743 to the same month of the following year. The second year of Artabasdus indicates the era of his reign that we assigned in the note under the year 741, beginning in June of the year 742. [Col. 0839A] The twelfth indiction ran from September of the year 743 to September of the year 744.

The day and month remain, but the letter of Saint Pope Zacharias to Austrobertus also indicates these. I demonstrated in the note under the year 742, section 13, that the letter is genuine. Since the year assigned to that letter is corrupt, I must demonstrate that the Roman council expressed in it is this council. I infer this from the fact that the letter reports that the council was held on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April under Pope Zacharias. Moreover, in the year 744 that day fell on a Sunday, on which day, as we have often said, councils were accustomed to be convened in that period.

Since the year 744, the council’s heading, and the day and month all agree, no other location for the council need be sought.

The Acts of that council Zacharias sent the following year to Austrobert, archbishop of Vienne, together with a letter dated the Nones of March, numbered 16 among Labbe’s collection. Pagius, in his *Critique of Baronius*, doubts the authenticity of this document; I defended its genuineness in my note to the year 742, no. 13. The authenticity of Zacharias’s letter to Austrobert is perfectly clear to me, although I do not deny that its chronological indications ought to be corrected, on the basis of what Pagius has admirably established. But it is wholly unjust to derive an argument against the authenticity of the letter from an erroneous dating, especially since Pagius has marked so many otherwise genuine letters of Zacharias with this same defect.

Besides this argument, Pagius brings forward another, based on the fact that in the same letter the pope writes that he had learned from a certain Clement, sent by Austrobert, archbishop of Vienne, [Col. 0839B] that the churches of the province had been disturbed by the violence of invading peoples. Pagius rightly thinks that this refers to the Saracen incursions into Gaul. Although that incursion occurred in the year 739, we can easily understand that the harm it inflicted upon the churches could not have been repaired so quickly. Thus Austrobert could have complained to Zacharias of those afflictions, which perhaps were still continuing in his Church in the year 743. The pope, in turn, shared with him the misfortunes that the Lombards were inflicting upon Roman territory.

For although their king Luitprand showed himself more equitable toward the pope, he nevertheless did not entirely cease to harass him. In the year 743, after peace had been granted to the Romans at the pope’s request, he again attacked with hostile arms the city of Ravenna, which had been entrusted to the protection of the Roman Church. See Pagius under the year 743, no. 14. Indeed, the use of arms ceased not long afterward, but fear did not cease. For, according to Anastasius, Saint Zacharias, having obtained peace and returned to the City, [Col. 0839C] devoted himself to prayer, asking almighty God to bring consolation to the people of Ravenna and to the Roman people, oppressed by that ambusher and assailant, King Luitprand. Hence, quite appropriately, in that letter written at this period the holy pontiff complains that the Roman frontiers were being harassed by the Lombards.

There remains Pagius’s argument, drawn from the fact that Wilicarius, who succeeded Austrobert, had abandoned his bishopric and assumed the monastic habit before the year 742. “How, then,” he says, “is Austrobert acting as bishop in the year 745, which we believe to be the date of that letter?” I admit that Austrobert preceded Wilicarius; but neither Addo of Vienne nor any other ancient writer indicated the year in which Wilicarius assumed the episcopate. Addo does indeed mark the succession of the bishops of Vienne at intervals in his history, but he does not assign the definite year in which each bishop began his tenure.

From this letter we learn that Austrobert prolonged his episcopate until the year 745. I therefore regard this letter as free from every suspicion of [Col. 0839D] forgery, but I believe that it should be transferred from the year 742 to the year 745, since I think that the Roman council mentioned in it is the very Roman council whose Acts survive, and which I demonstrated in my note to the year 743, no. 15, must be assigned from the year 743 to the year 744.

I believe that a letter of Saint Zacharias to Saint Boniface, numbered 5 among Labbe’s collection, was written in November of that same year, 744, since in it the pontiff recalls that Saint Boniface had appointed Abel and Adalbert as metropolitans, as was determined above in the Council of Soissons. The letter is dated the Nones of November, in the thirteenth indiction—that is, in the year 744.

Next comes the year 745, in which the Council of Liptina first presents itself. I believe that it is designated by these words from letter 9 of Saint Zacharias to Saint Boniface, written on the day before the Kalends of November, in the fourteenth indiction, that is, in the year 745: “Concerning the synod assembled in [Col. 0840A] the province of the Franks through Pippin and Carloman, etc.” That this synod is the Council of Liptina itself is unambiguously demonstrated by these words from the same letter: “As for the tribute which you sought, since you were unable to obtain anything else from the Franks except that, as the year comes around, twelve denarii should be paid by each household of slaves—that is, one solidus—etc.”

Who would not recognize here the express wording of canon 2 of Liptina: “That every year one solidus, that is, twelve denarii, be paid to the church from each household”? This council therefore met in that very year, on the day stated in the Acts: the Kalends of March, which then fell on Monday, the day on which councils customarily began according to ancient practice.

Since this council was composed of Gauls and Germans, as can be inferred from the words of Saint Zacharias’s letter, we might reasonably suppose that letter 11 of Saint Zacharias to the bishops of Gaul and Germany— in which he praises them for their union with the Roman Church and for their agreement with Saint Boniface [Col. 0840B]—was written immediately after that council.

The Roman council begun by Saint Zacharias on 25 October, at which Adalbert and Clement were removed from the priestly office after being convicted of heretical superstition from their own deeds; and the Fathers declared that, unless they subsequently repented, they were to be condemned by anathema. You will find the Acts of this council in Labbe, volume XII, Venetian edition. Saint Zacharias informed Saint Boniface that he had held this council in letter 9, written on the day before the Kalends of November of the same year.

The year 746, on the Kalends of July, in the fourteenth indiction, provides letter 6 of Saint Zacharias to Saint Boniface concerning the non-repetition of baptism, which a priest had administered with words barbarously inflected. Perhaps toward the end of the same year, letter 7 was sent to Pippin, mayor of the palace, replying to the matters about which Pippin had questioned him. That letter lacks chronological indications.

Immediately at the beginning of the following year, 747, Saint [Col. 0840C] Zacharias, in letter 8, instructed Saint Boniface by letter that the answers he had written to Pippin’s questions should be read aloud in the priestly assembly. The letter was dated the Nones of January, in the fifteenth indiction—that is, at the beginning of the year 747. It likewise ordered that, when a council had been assembled for this matter, the case of Adalbert, Clement, and Godolsatius should again be examined; and, if they were found to have returned to the path of righteousness, that they should be dealt with according to the rule of the canons.

According to this letter, the council which Labbe published under the name of the Second German Council was easily convened, and its place can likewise readily be assigned to this year. Besides these two German councils held under Saint Boniface, I by no means recognize a third, although Labbe distinguishes one in volume XII. For the council which Labbe calls the third—at which Adelbert and Clement were condemned—is either identical with the Council of Soissons, if the first condemnation of Adelbert is meant, or with the second [Col. 0840D] German Council, if the reference is to the renewed judgment of the case of the heretics.

There is another matter in the Venetian edition of Labbe that I consider worthy of notice. After having listed in volume XII a certain Third German Council under Saint Boniface in the year 745, the editor then introduces, also in volume XII, another Third German Council of the year 747 under Saint Boniface, noting from Willibald, the author of Saint Boniface’s Life, that it was the fifth of the councils held by Saint Boniface. These statements are taken from Pagius, in his *Critique*, under the year 747, nos. 2 and 3. But they do not fit together.

First, if three other German councils preceded this German council, and if the Councils of Soissons and Liptina, in which Saint Boniface took part, are added as well, this German council of the year 747 would have to be counted not as the third but as the fourth German council; and, apart from that, it would be the sixth rather than the fifth among the councils celebrated by Saint Boniface. How can this agree with Willibald, who [Col. 0841A] records five councils held by Saint Boniface?

Therefore, so that all these matters may be consistent and Willibald, a contemporary writer, may retain his credibility, I judge this synod to be the German council which I call the second, following the method of counting preserved by Labbe. It was held after the Nones of January in the year 747, while Carloman was still in power, in obedience to the pope’s instructions. These required Boniface to assemble a council, publicly read the pope’s replies to Pippin’s questions, and reconsider the case of Adelbert and the others. Willibald records in the *Life of Saint Boniface*, chapter 10, that the confirmation of the preceding four synods, which Saint Boniface had already held, was also dealt with there.

But how could this last council be called the fifth, when, from what we have established so far, no more than four councils result—namely, the Council of Soissons, the Council of Liptina, one German council, and then this other German council?

I admit that another council remains to be sought, [Col. 0841B] and that perhaps it preceded all the councils we have discussed. We might reasonably suppose that Saint Boniface convened it when he established three episcopal sees in Germany, about which he informed Saint Zacharias in his letter to him. The same pontiff replied in a letter dated the Kalends of April, in the eleventh indiction—that is, in the year 743. The establishment of episcopal sees was usually determined in councils at that time.

Accordingly, there is no impropriety in assigning a council held by Saint Boniface in Germany to about the year 742. It must have preceded that German council of the year 743, mentioned above at the beginning of this dissertation, which consequently ought to be called not the first but the second.

At the end of the year 747, or in the following year, 748, Saint Boniface sent Saint Zacharias a letter that is no longer extant. The pontiff replied in letter 10, dated the Kalends of May, in the first indiction—that is, in the year 748. Since in it the pontiff writes that he had learned [Col. 0841C] of Boniface’s episcopal see being transferred from Cologne (Agrippina) to Mainz, we might reasonably infer that letter 13 of Saint Zacharias to Saint Boniface, concerning the establishment of the see of Mainz, belongs to the same year, and perhaps to the same day and month as the earlier letter, although the year 751 may have been incorrectly attached to that letter.

The years 749 and 750 offer nothing requiring investigation. The following year, 751, on the day before the Nones of November, in the fifth indiction, presents letter 12 of Zacharias to Saint Boniface, in which he replies to several questions submitted through a letter delivered by Lullus. You should therefore place before this letter of Saint Zacharias the letter which Labbe incorrectly placed after it. Another letter, no. 14, concerning the monastery of Fulda, should be attached to the same preceding letter of Saint Zacharias; in it Saint Boniface states that he had built the monastery in his own letter on the subject.

It has been useful to discuss these matters in order to establish the correct chronological arrangement of the councils [Col. 0841D] convened on the occasion and during the time of Saint Boniface, and of the letters exchanged between Saint Zacharias the pontiff and Saint Boniface. It remains to display what has been set out at greater length in a single overview, in the form of a chronological table.

## Chronological Table of the Councils and Letters of Saint Zacharias and Saint Boniface

**A.D. 742.** The German Council, mentioned by no ancient or more recent writer, at which three episcopal sees in Germany were established by Saint Boniface. Saint Boniface informed Saint Zacharias of them in a letter to be read in Labbe, volume XII, p. 311.

**743.** Saint Zacharias replies to Saint Boniface in letter 1.

2. A letter of the same pontiff to Burchard, bishop of Würzburg, recently elected.

[Col. 0842A] The German Council which Labbe and the others call the first.

**744.** The Council of Sens is held, at which Adalbert is condemned, and Abel and Adalbert—the former of Rheims, the latter of Sens—are appointed metropolitans.

The First Roman Council of Saint Zacharias.

Letter 4 of Saint Zacharias to Saint Boniface.

Letter 5 of Saint Zacharias to Saint Boniface.

**745.** The Council of Liptina.

Letters 3, 16, and 11 of Saint Zacharias to the Franks and Gauls.

Letter 17 of Saint Zacharias to Austrobert, to whom he sends the Acts of the Roman Council of the preceding year.

Saint Boniface writes to the pontiff concerning Adelbert’s errors; the letter is read at the following Roman council.

[Col. 0842B] The Second Roman Council.

Letter 9 of Saint Zacharias to Saint Boniface.

**746.** Letter 6 of Saint Zacharias to Saint Boniface concerning the non-repetition of baptism.

Letter 7 of the same holy pontiff, in which he replies to several questions of Pippin.

**747.** Letter 8 of Saint Zacharias to Saint Boniface, in which Boniface is instructed to read aloud at the council soon to be held the answers given to Pippin’s questions.

The German Council, which is the third according to Labbe and the fifth among the councils held by Saint Boniface up to that time.

Saint Boniface consults the Roman pontiff about many matters in a letter sent through Burchard. The letter itself is no longer extant.

**748.** Saint Zacharias replies to Saint Boniface’s preceding questions in letter 10.

**749.**

[Col. 0842C] **750.**

**751.** Saint Boniface again consults Saint Zacharias in a letter sent through Lullus, to be read in Labbe, volume XII.

Saint Zacharias replies to him in three letters, 12, 13, and 14.

This is the chronological arrangement of the councils of Saint Boniface and Saint Zacharias the pontiff, together with the letters exchanged between them. I have not discovered where the letter of Saint Boniface to Grifo should be placed, since it lacks a date. I omitted letter 15 of Saint Zacharias to the bishops of the Franks as doubtful, since it touches upon the controversy concerning the removal of Saint Benedict’s body.

Of the statutes of Saint Boniface, various portions of which Labbe published, I accept all the remainder. One collection of canons remains, however, which Dacherius published under the name of Saint Boniface in the *Spicilegium*, volume IX, old edition, and from which Labbe likewise drew material in volume XII. [Col. 0842D] Canon 15 demonstrates that this collection is the work of a writer from a period foreign to Saint Boniface: it clearly expresses and distinguishes monasteries of canons and monks.

You will find no such distinction anywhere in the writings of the ancients, except after the time when, through the measures of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, the canons of churches were ordered to live under a common rule and in community. Moreover, some of these canons are themselves word-for-word the canons of the Councils of Mainz and Arles V, which were held toward the end of Charlemagne’s life, namely in the year 813.

Compare canon 14 of Saint Boniface, which is chapter 26 of the Council of Mainz. Chapter 19 of Mainz is Saint Boniface’s canon 15. Arles 6 corresponds to Boniface’s canon 12, just as canon 5 of this collection reproduces canon 27 of Mainz in almost the same words. Finally, the capitulary of Charlemagne’s thirteenth year of rule reproduces several of these canons of Boniface. I therefore believe that these constitutions were issued either during the decline of Charlemagne’s reign or under Louis the Pious.

# The Second Part of the Complete Extant Works of Saint Boniface, Archbishop of Mainz

[Col. 0843]

## Preliminary Notice Concerning the Following Sermons of Saint Boniface, Prefixed to the Martenian Edition

[Col. 0843A] Boniface, whose sermons we publish here, is that great Boniface who was called Winfrid by his native name, the apostle of the Germans, born among distinguished parents in Wessex, England. He had scarcely completed his fifth year when he conceived the plan of abandoning the world, and no entreaties of his parents could keep him from taking refuge in a neighboring monastery.

As a young man he moved for the sake of study to the monastery of Nursling, where, under Abbot Winbert, he made such rapid progress in learning that shortly afterward he also undertook the task of teaching others. Ordained to the priesthood at the age of thirty, he exercised the office of preaching first in his homeland and then in Germany, with universal acclaim.

When he returned to his monastery, he refused the dignity of abbot. Armed with letters from his own bishop Daniel, he went to Rome, and Gregory II again sent him to Germany for the purpose of preaching. He first undertook the conversion of Thuringia, and then of Frisia, where he was joined by Bishop Willibrord of Utrecht. He converted many people to the faith of Christ.

Returning to Rome to report to Gregory III the successful results of his labors, the pontiff had him ordained bishop, honored with the pallium, and sent back to Germany with the authority of an apostolic legate. Relying upon this authority, and aided by the favor of the Frankish kings, Boniface promoted the Christian faith in those regions so successfully that he baptized at least one hundred thousand unbelievers in the sacred waters.

He established various bishoprics in Germany and fixed his own see at Mainz. Finally, after enduring many labors, he was crowned with martyrdom in the year 754, on the Nones of June.

[Col. 0844A] He wrote an excellent book of letters, which the learned Jesuit priest Serrarius published at Mainz. He also wrote several Lives of the saints, if we are to believe Trithemius. Mabillon denies that the *Life of Saint Livinus the Martyr*, commonly attributed to him, was written by Boniface. Pope Zacharias praises his book *On the True and Catholic Faith* in a letter written to him and preserved by Othlonus, book II, chapter 9.

Furthermore, we transcribed the following fifteen sermons from a manuscript belonging to the most illustrious chancellor of France, Monsieur Daguesseau, written eight hundred years ago. Mabillon had recovered the first ten from two manuscripts of Queen Christina of Sweden, nos. 1302 and 1335; we collated them with those manuscripts. We obtained the fifteenth from our own Bernard Pez.

All of them breathe the spirit of a truly apostolic man who instructed his converts in the rudiments of the faith and in good morals through familiar conversation. Although they are written in a simple style and occasionally disregard the rules of grammar, they should not for that reason be despised; rather, they should be valued most highly. For whatever proceeds from apostolic men ought to be preserved as more precious than all gold.

Saint Boniface was instructing barbarous peoples, and he was sometimes compelled to address them in a barbarous manner. In other respects, these sermons can contribute considerably not only to the formation of morals but also to the elucidation of ecclesiastical discipline. An example is his teaching in sermon 13 concerning the continence of married people throughout the whole season of Lent, and in the preceding sermon concerning the beginning of Lent only on Sunday.

[Col. 0843]

# Sermons

## Sermon I: Concerning Right Faith

[Col. 0843C]

1. Dearest brothers, it is necessary for everyone who desires to reach the kingdom of heaven, which has been promised and prepared for us by almighty God, to hold firmly and without hesitation the right and catholic faith. For no one can attain eternal blessedness unless he pleases God, and no one can please God except through the right faith.

Faith is indeed the foundation of all good things; faith is the beginning of human salvation. Without it no one can attain the dignity of the children of God, because without it no one in this world receives the grace of justification, nor in the future possesses eternal life.

Therefore it is extremely necessary for every person to learn the catholic and apostolic faith carefully, especially the preachers of the Christian people and the teachers of God’s churches. How can anyone teach what he has not learned? Or how can anyone be a shepherd if he does not know how to feed the flock entrusted to him with the bread of life? Let the one who does not know not be ashamed to learn what he lacks; nor let the one who knows be slow to teach what he knows.

2. This is the catholic faith: that we believe in one God the Father almighty, and in his only Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit: the Father, because he has a Son; the Son, because he has a Father; the Holy Spirit, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

The Father, then, is the beginning of divinity, because just as he was never not God, so he was never not Father. From him the Son was born; from him the Holy Spirit proceeds, not being born, because he is not the Son; nor is he unbegotten, since he is not the Father; nor was he made, but proceeds as God from God the Father.

The Father is eternal because he has an eternal Son, whose eternal Father he is. The Son is eternal because he is coeternal with the Father. The Holy Spirit is eternal because he is coeternal with the Father and the Son. This one God is the holy Trinity.

The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit created heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them; and according to his will he governs all things. All Christians who desire to possess eternal life ought to believe in this one God.

We must firmly believe in the forgiveness of all sins in holy baptism. No Catholic can doubt that judgment will come for the good and the wicked immediately after the end of this life. Pagans, the impious, and sinners who have refused to confess their crimes or to correct them through repentance will suffer everlasting punishment. Eternal glory will remain for the repentant and the just.

No Christian ought to doubt the resurrection of the dead at the last day, at the end of this world. Rather, just as Christ rose from the dead on the third day, so all human beings, good and wicked alike, must rise on the last day with their own bodies: the wicked for their shame and punishment, but the just for everlasting glory.

## Sermon II: Concerning the Origin of the Human Condition

[Col. 0845C]

1. Beloved brothers, we must know the origin of the human condition, so that from it we may recognize the immense mercy of our Creator. He created our first parents, namely Adam and Eve his wife, from the clay of the earth, and breathed into them a rational and intellectual spirit, by which they might know and praise their Creator. He established them in the sweetest happiness of paradise, so that they might live there without labor, pain, or the danger of death until they were transferred to the perpetual blessedness of the heavenly kingdom.

He commanded them not to eat the fruit of one tree, so that through obedience to one commandment they might merit eternal glory. But through the devil’s deceit and envy they were led to eat of the fruit forbidden to them.

Because of this fault they were also cast into the misery of this earthly condition and placed under the power of the devil. Because of the disobedience involved in the first commandment, all human beings were born with sins, living in labor and losing human life amid the pains of death.

No one could reach the happiness of paradise or the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom after the end of this life until almighty God sent his only-begotten Son, born of a Virgin, into the world, as he had promised long beforehand through his prophets to the holy fathers.

As blessed Paul, the preacher of the world, said: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son into this world, so that he might wash away the sin of the whole world.”

When this fullness of time came according to God’s predestination, the angel Gabriel was sent by God, as we read in the holy Gospel, to a city of Galilee called Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man named Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary.

The angel entered to her and said: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.” When she heard this, she was troubled at his word and considered what sort of greeting this might be. And the angel said to her: “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. Behold, you will conceive and bear a son in your womb, and you will call his name Jesus. He will be great before the Lord, and he will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever; and his kingdom will have no end.”

Mary said to the angel: “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” And the angel answered her: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.”

At that time there was such peace in the world that the dominion of the whole earth belonged to one city, which is called Rome; and that city, as well as the whole world, had one emperor and ruler, named Augustus. He also established such an edict throughout the world that every person should go to his own homeland and pay the emperor a census tax for himself; every fugitive slave should return to his master, and if his master could not be found, he should be killed, lest he disturb the peace which Augustus had established throughout the entire world.

This happened by God’s providence, so that there might be peace throughout the world when the one who would preach true peace to humanity was born—he who would reconcile all things in heaven and on earth and establish harmony between the angelic orders and human nature.

At this time of such peace and such serene joy among all peoples everywhere, as the Gospel history relates, he was born in the Jewish nation and in Bethlehem, the city of David: born of the Virgin Mary, not through human union but through the inspiration and fruitfulness of the Holy Spirit, so that virginity might remain intact both in childbirth and after childbirth.

2. On that same night, as we read in the Gospel, when God the Son was born into the world, “there were shepherds in that region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock.” And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them, and the brightness of God shone around them, and they were terrified with great fear.

The angel of God answered and said to the shepherds: “Do not be afraid. For behold, I bring you good news of great joy, which will be for all the people: today a Savior has been born for us, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. And this will be a sign for you: you will find an infant lying in a manger.”

And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

The shepherds came and found the infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger, and Mary his mother, just as the angels had foretold to them.

This is the beginning of our salvation and the renewal of the human race. In it God, through the mercy of the Lord, descended to humanity, so that human beings through obedience might be able to ascend to God. For through disobedience they had been expelled from the happiness of paradise.

God, who was born of a Virgin, not only restored that happiness to us, but also opened the gates of the heavenly kingdom to believers who keep his commandments. He granted that those who had been children of wrath in sins and misery should be children of God in faith and love, and he shattered and crushed every yoke of diabolical servitude, so that the devil might no longer be able to exercise dominion over anyone who wished to keep God’s commandments and guard himself from sins.

3. Therefore those who are not afraid to sin and do not care to confess their sins or correct them through repentance are slaves of the devil. But those who take care to guard themselves from sins, or to wash away their sins through confession and repentance, and who rejoice to live according to God’s commandments, are children of God’s love and heirs of eternal blessedness.

This is the great nobility: that an earthly human being should become a child of God. This glorious nobility and great freedom must be carefully preserved through good morals. The most high Father, who is God of all, wishes to have as his children only those who are good, chaste, faithful, and obedient to his commandments.

It is right that we love him with perfect love, since he loved us so greatly. Although he is the eternal God, he wished to be born as a human being for our salvation, and to do and suffer everything that is recorded in the holy Gospel.

He shone so wondrously before the people that it could truly be recognized that the very one who appeared to be human in the weakness of the flesh was God in the power of divinity.

At his birth the angels, as we have heard, sang in praise of God: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.” Let us also sing glory to God with the angels, praising his ineffable mercy, by which he humbled himself in order to exalt us.

He became the Son of Man so that he might make us children of God. He came into the region of our mortality so that he might raise us into the region of his glory.

The angels also added in a hymnic voice: “And on earth peace to people of good will.” For true peace consists in being subject to almighty God with good will, always doing his will rather than our own, because his will is our salvation.

Let us cleanse ourselves from every iniquity of body and soul. Let us live in chastity and in love of God and of human beings. Let us serve God joyfully in every good work—in mercy and devotion, in justice and patience, and in hope of God’s goodness.

Knowing with complete certainty that whatever good we do in almsgiving, humility, and obedience to his commandments, our Lord will restore all of it to us in eternal blessedness.

## Sermon III: Concerning the Twofold Practice of Justice

1. The first justice, then, is not to do the evil things which the devil suggests. The second is to do the good things which almighty God urges us to do, because God desires the salvation of our souls, as it is said: “He desires all people to be saved.”

Let us therefore hear, beloved, what are the evils which the devil suggests, and afterward what are the good things which the Lord our God wishes us to do, so that we may be children of his love and not children of eternal destruction.

The first and worst of sins is pride, through which the devil, although he had been a most glorious angel in heaven, fell and became guilty of eternal destruction together with all his followers.

The second was disobedience, through which the first human being fell from paradise when he did not keep the commandment of almighty God. He was sent into this mortality and became liable, throughout the posterity of his children, to eternal condemnation. As we have said, almighty God came into the world to turn that condemnation away from us and to free us from every misery.

Furthermore, the Lord God forbids us to obey the devil, because he desires to have many companions in his destruction. Those who do the devil’s will through fornication, murder, adultery, drunkenness, false testimony, perjury, injustice, robbery, and iniquity; those who harbor envy and hatred and practice slander against their brothers—these are condemned with the devil and his angels to eternal misery in everlasting fire.

But those who do the will of almighty God and obey his commandments will reign in eternal glory with Christ and his holy angels.

2. These are the divine commandments through which almighty God will grant us eternal blessedness.

First is love of God and love of human beings: we must love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind—that is, with all our understanding and all our will—and must always keep his will and commandments in mind.

We must love other people as ourselves, doing nothing to anyone that we do not wish another to do to us; rather, we must act toward others as we wish them to act toward us.

We must be merciful toward the poor and afflicted, and do good to them according to our ability and their need. If anyone sins against us, we must forgive him, so that God may forgive our sins, because we read in the Gospel that Truth itself says: “If you forgive people their sins which they have committed against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins.”

Let us practice humility in the sight of the Lord, because, as it is written: “Humble yourselves under the hand of almighty God, so that he may exalt you in the time of tribulation.” For, as we said earlier, the angels fell from heaven through pride. But God’s mercy has granted us, through humility, to ascend to the angelic seats.

Let us also have patience, as the Lord himself said: “By your patience you will possess your souls.” Let us return evil to no one for evil, and let us carefully preserve the chastity of our bodies, because the Holy Spirit, as it is written, does not dwell in a body subject to sins.

Let us not commit theft, but from our own honest labor let us give alms to the poor, so that they may pray for us and God may forgive our sins, because, as it is read in the Book of Wisdom, “the wealth of a man is the redemption of his soul.”

Let us be obedient to ecclesiastical teachers with a pure heart and a good conscience. Let us honor the churches of Christ and come more frequently to prayers. Let us honor our parents, as the Lord commanded in the Law: “Honor your father and your mother.”

Parents, for their part, should instruct their children in every form of chastity and fear of God, not permitting them to steal, commit fornication, become drunk, or do anything unjust.

Wives should fear and honor their husbands and preserve chastity for them. Likewise, husbands should love their wives and should first practice toward them the chastity they demand from their wives, so that they may see their husbands’ good example.

Let the poor and afflicted rejoice in their poverty and hope in God’s mercy, who says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

Let them live in chastity, in right faith, and in hope of eternal recompense, and let them patiently endure their hardships, so that almighty God may grant them eternal blessedness.

The priests and the entire clergy of the holy Church, who ought to stand in the service of God day and night, should live in every respect blamelessly before secular people and in every place, so that many may be instructed by their good example. Let their meditation be on the law of God and on ecclesiastical service, day and night. Let them not be drunkards, nor greedy, nor talkative at banquets, nor seekers of riches in this world; rather, let them prepare for themselves an eternal treasure in the heavenly kingdom. Let them therefore show all people examples of good conduct, and teach Christ’s people in truth and faith, so that they may appear before the presence of the Lord our God with the gain of many [Col. 0849C] holy souls, and be made worthy of a manifold reward.

### 4.

Let adolescents and younger men be obedient to their elders in all spiritual instruction, doing nothing without the counsel of their elders. Let them be subject in humility and obedience, so that, at the proper time according to their age, they may be found worthy to minister to Christ God. Whoever has not learned what is good in youth, how will he be able to possess or teach it in old age?

For everyone everywhere—whether rich or poor, old or young, masters or servants, superiors or subjects—must love God and diligently keep his commandments. Let them be truthful in speech, just in judgment, [Col. 0849D] merciful in compassion, diligent in service, humble in conduct, patient amid every adversity, and let them carefully learn the true and catholic faith, living in faith, hope, and charity. Let them keep the public fasts in chastity, and adorn their fasting with almsgiving, giving to the poor what they deny themselves. Let them also faithfully render their tithes to the Lord God almighty, so that the Lord God may send his blessing upon their labors.

Let them come frequently to the churches, especially on feast days. Let them not engage in empty talk in the churches, but be attentive to prayer and compunction of heart, as is fitting in the house of God and in the presence of the Most High King. And if anyone should fall through some sin, let him rise again quickly through confession and cleanse himself by penance, because God’s mercy is rich [Col. 0850A] in forgiving the sinner, if he wishes to turn back to the way of righteousness, as the prophet says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.”

Again, elsewhere, concerning the final will and deed: “On whatever day a person turns back, he shall surely live and shall not die.” The envy of the Devil therefore persuades us to sin; but the mercy of the Lord, who desires our salvation, urges us to turn from sin to the way of righteousness, so that we may be made worthy of eternal glory with his saints.

We must know and believe with complete certainty that all our deeds and thoughts will be judged on the last day. But for sinners who do not wish to abandon their sins and obey God’s commandments, there will be eternal torments in everlasting fire with the Devil and his angels. For those, however, who turn with their whole heart to almighty God, [Col. 0850B] living in charity and obeying God’s commandments, there will be eternal glory, blessedness, and joy with Christ and his saints, forever and ever.

## SERMON IV. On the Eight Evangelical Beatitudes

### 1.

When the Lord Jesus was preaching in a certain place and healing many sick people, great crowds gathered to him. He went up to a higher place and began to teach them, saying:

“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. [Col. 0850C] Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God. Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

The Lord promised the blessedness of the kingdom of heaven to those who keep his commandments. First he speaks of humility, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” and so forth. For he says “poor in spirit” so that we should not think blessed those whom necessity and want make poor. Rather, those are truly blessed who humble themselves in spirit and, even if they possess riches, are not lifted up in pride, but in humility glorify God, who always does good to those who hope in him.

Humility is the foundation of all good things: “For theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Through pride and disobedience, humanity lost the kingdom of heaven; therefore, [Col. 0850D] through humility and obedience, we must acquire the kingdom of God.

### 2.

“Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.” God is meek toward us, and grants us all that is necessary; he does this so that we may be meek and kind toward our neighbors, and always willingly do the good that we can, just as the Lord himself admonishes elsewhere, saying: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls.”

The meek shall possess the earth—not this corruptible earth, which is full of the bodies of the dead, often oppressed through pride and polluted by bloody wars, but that earth which the meek shall have, of which a certain holy man says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord [Col. 0851A] in the land of the living.” That is the land where angels and the souls of the saints dwell, where joy is eternal and happiness without end.

### 3.

“Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted.” Blessed are those who weep for their sins in this world, lest they mourn with the Devil in eternal punishments. It is better to repent here for a short time for one’s offenses and rejoice forever with the saints than to indulge immoderately in the brief joys of this age and afterward be punished with eternal torments.

Let us, then, be like those to whom the Lord says: “You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy.”

### 4.

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.” Not all who hunger and thirst are blessed, but only those who always hunger for righteousness. We must hunger [Col. 0851B] for righteousness in such a way that we never think ourselves sufficiently righteous, but always entreat God to increase our merits in goodness. For whoever thinks he has enough righteousness does not hunger for righteousness, but is lifted up in pride and immediately falls. The humble person, however, will always go from virtue to virtue and will always delight in making progress toward what is better.

### 5.

“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” We greatly desire that God forgive our offenses when we repent. Therefore we too must forgive the debts of our neighbors when they ask, just as the Lord himself said: “Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful.” For the merciful shall obtain mercy, because if we forgive people their sins, our heavenly [Col. 0851C] Father will also forgive us our offenses.

### 6.

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Those will be pure in heart who drive from their hearts every malice, deceit, envy, and desire, and cleanse their consciences through charity, chastity, justice, and the other holy virtues, so that they may see God in the heavenly kingdom.

For God does not wish to dwell in a body polluted by sins. Therefore let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and mind, so that God may dwell in our hearts and direct us toward every good work. If we confess our sins, amend our ways, and do not return to the same sins, God will cleanse us from our offenses, fill us with heavenly virtues, and make us worthy [Col. 0851D] of heavenly blessedness with all the saints.

But if we hide them, God will reveal them, whether we wish it or not. It is better to confess one’s sins to a single person than to have them made public and be confounded for them at that dreadful judgment before the three realms of heaven, earth, and the underworld—not for correction, but for everlasting punishment.

### 7.

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” We must pursue peace in such a way that first we establish peace between God and ourselves, following what he has commanded and fleeing the evils that are hateful to God. Then we must make peace among our neighbors whenever we see them in disagreement with one another.

Through peace we shall be called sons of God. Great is the goodness of God and ineffable the clemency of the Creator: we are not worthy even to be [Col. 0852A] servants of God, yet we are called his sons. Let us therefore strive, through good works, to become worthy of so great an inheritance, and let us not separate ourselves from so loving a Father, who has deigned to number us among his children.

### 8.

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Christ, the Son of God, endured scourging and insults for us, and finally accepted death itself for us. Therefore we too must patiently endure every adversity for his name, because through many tribulations we shall enter the kingdom of God, if we endure them for righteousness’ sake.

A blessedness is therefore prepared for us in heaven. Let us prepare ourselves for it by good works; let us hasten toward it with all our desire. All the holy angels await us in heaven [Col. 0852B] and rejoice that we may wish to come to them. Let us therefore praise God’s mercy and give him thanks in all things. Let us continually beseech him that he who has deigned to redeem us may himself cleanse us from all sins and make us sharers in his kingdom with all the saints.

To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON V. On Faith and Works of Love

### 1.

I admonish you to remember what you promised to almighty God in baptism: first, to believe in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ his Son, and in the Holy Spirit, one almighty God in perfect Trinity.

But since it is written, “Faith without works is dead,” and whoever [Col. 0852C] knows God ought to keep his commandments, these are the commandments of God that we proclaim for you to do and observe: that you love the God whom you have confessed with your whole heart, your whole mind, and your whole strength; and then your neighbors as yourselves. On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend.

“The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord,” but its perfection is charity. Therefore, so that you may attain this charity, which is God, have peace with everyone, as the Apostle commands and the Lord says: “Love peace and truth.” Have patience, because the Lord says: “In your patience you shall possess your souls.” Have mercy, because the Lord commanded: “Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful.” And again: [Col. 0852D] “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.”

Be kind, as the Apostle commands: “Be kind and compassionate toward one another, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you.” Be chaste, as the Apostle says: “Pursue peace and chastity, without which no one shall see God.” Be undefiled in heart and body, because God says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

Keep faith with your spouses, because the Lord says: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate.” Let husbands love their wives chastely, as the Apostle commands: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the Church.” Let wives fear their husbands, because God says to the woman: “You shall be under your husband’s authority, and he shall rule over you all your days.”

Teach your children to fear God, and your household likewise, lest through [Col. 0853A] your negligence anything belonging to God perish. Also exhort all your neighbors to do good, because it is written: “Whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins.”

Restore those who are at odds to harmony, because blessed are the feet that carry peace. Whoever hears cases should judge justly, because God says: “Judge justly for your neighbor.” And again: “By the judgment with which you judge, you shall be judged.” Do not accept gifts, because God’s word says that they “blind the eyes of the wise and overturn the words of the just.” And the Lord says that in his tabernacle—that is, in his kingdom—there dwells the one who does not accept gifts against the innocent.

### 2.

Observe the Lord’s Day and hasten to church, because on that day Christ rose from the dead, to give [Col. 0853B] us also an example of resurrection. Pray there, and carefully avoid idle stories and excessive talk, because it is written: “My house is a house of prayer.” Therefore you ought to pray there and not engage in useless chatter.

Give alms according to your means, for just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sins. Be hospitable to one another, because the Lord will say at the judgment: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me.” Some people also pleased angels by receiving them as guests. Welcome travelers, and remember that you yourselves are travelers in this world.

Visit the sick, because the Lord will also say: “I was sick, and you visited me.” Serve widows and orphans, because the Lord will say: “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me.”

Render tithes to the churches, because the Lord commanded, saying: [Col. 0853C] “Give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s”—that is, taxes and tribute—“and to God what is God’s”—that is, tithes, firstfruits, and all the vows that you have vowed. As the Lord commanded: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them”; and, “What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another.” For this is the Law and the Prophets.

If you fulfill this charity toward one another, you will fulfill all the commandments. Fear God alone everywhere and honor the king, because, as it is written, “There is no authority except from God, and whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance.” Therefore obey godly commands.

Do not withhold the rightful tax, as the Apostle commands: “To whom tribute is due, tribute; to whom tax is due, tax.” You who are bodily servants, obey your masters, as the Apostle commands, [Col. 0853D] not serving merely for show, as though pleasing human beings, but with good faith and a simple heart. And you masters, do the same toward your servants, preserving justice and mercy for them, knowing that their Lord and yours is in heaven.

### 3.

Learn the Lord’s Prayer by heart, because in it every need of the present and future life is comprehensively contained in brief form. Christ taught it, and therefore it is called the Lord’s Prayer, since he commanded us to pray in this way.

Learn the Creed also by heart, because it is written: “Without faith it is impossible to please God.” Therefore believe yourselves, as it says there, and hand on this same faith to your children and also to those whom you received at baptism, because you became their sponsors for this reason: so that they ought to believe in this way under your instruction.

[Col. 0854A] Know also that you must not be baptized more than once, nor approach confirmation more than once, because the apostles also laid hands upon believers only once, so that they might receive the Holy Spirit.

### 4.

Love lawful and public fasts, especially, because through abstinence and almsgiving God is appeased by the people, just as he spared the Ninevites when they fasted for three days. Love justice, as it is written: “Love justice, you who judge the earth.” Do not consent to the Devil’s persuasions, but, as the Apostle commands, “resist the Devil, and he will flee from you.” Receive communion of the Lord’s body and blood at the appointed times.

### 5.

These, my dearly beloved brothers, are works of faith, which all Christians together ought to preserve. Whoever does not wish to become a participant [Col. 0854B] in them in this world will not be able to be a participant in the kingdom of God in the future.

We, although humble and lowly, have nevertheless been stirred by your love and concern; therefore we have listed these things for you, so that no one may excuse himself by saying: “I do not know how to distinguish good from evil, or justice from injustice; I do not know what I should abandon or what I should do.”

Now, therefore, “turn away from evil,” as it is written, “and do good. Seek peace and pursue it.” If you do this, the Lord will increase your understanding and strength, so that you may also be able to learn and fulfill the more excellent and greater divine commandments. And if you persevere continually in these works to the end, he will not only forgive your sins, but will also grant you the eternal and heavenly kingdom as his own children, so that you may be, as the Apostle says, “heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ.”

[Col. 0854C] ### 6.

Believe also that Christ, the Son of God, will come on the day of judgment to judge the living and the dead, just as, when he ascended into heaven, he commanded the apostles through the angels, who said: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.”

Then every human being will see him, as the prophet says: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God.” The wicked will see him, so that they may fear the one whom they despised, but they will not rejoice, because they had no joy in him, as it is written: “Let the wicked be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God.”

Then the righteous will be separated from the wicked, by whom they were oppressed in this world. The wicked will be punished with the Devil in the prison of his torment; the righteous will be glorified with him in the kingdom of God. The wicked will receive bodies so that, with those with whom [Col. 0854D] they sinned, they may be tormented forever. The upright and righteous will receive bodies so that, in those bodies in which they faithfully served God, they may mercifully receive their reward from God.

Then all will rise again, as the Apostle says: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed,” because only the righteous will be changed for glory. Then, as the Truth says, the wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.

Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. There will be life with God without fear of death; there will be unfailing light and never darkness; there will be salvation disturbed by no sickness; there will be unfailing satisfaction for those who now hunger and thirst for righteousness; there will be happiness corrupted by no fear; there will be joy consumed by no sorrow; there will be eternal glory with angels and archangels, with patriarchs and prophets, with [Col. 0855A] apostles and martyrs, with confessors and holy virgins who follow Christ wherever he goes.

There greater, better, more pleasing, sweeter, more delightful, and more lovable gifts have been given to the saints than can be spoken or imagined, because, as the Apostle says, “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him”—joys to which may he bring you who created you.

These things, little children; these things, dearest brothers, which I, a sinner, have humbly suggested to you with my mouth—may the almighty Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, speak them more beneficially to your understanding and heart by its power. He lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON VI. On Capital Sins and the Principal Commandments of God

[Col. 0855B] ### 1.

Hear and understand, dearest ones: this is the word of faith that we preach—that we should believe in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, and believe in the Holy Spirit, one almighty God in unity and Trinity, threefold in persons and names, and one in the deity of majesty and power.

This is the word of faith that we preach: that we should distinguish between good and evil, between the godly and the ungodly, between righteousness and iniquity—that is, between capital sins and the capital and principal precepts and commandments of God.

These, then, are the capital sins: sacrilege, which is called the worship of idols. All pagan sacrifices and divinations are sacrileges, as are sacrifices to the dead—whether sacrifices made at the bodies of the deceased or over their graves [reading uncertain]—as well as divinations, amulets, and offerings made upon rocks, at springs, or beside trees, to Jupiter, Mercury, or other pagan gods. All these are demons, along with many other things that it would take too long to enumerate. According to the judgment of the holy Fathers, all of them are recognized as sacrileges and capital sins, [Col. 0855C] to be avoided and detested by Christians.

Murder, adultery, fornication—whether with human beings, with animals and cattle, between males, or between females, burning with desire for one another—all these are capital sins. Theft and robbery, false testimony, perjury, slander, greed, pride, envy, hatred, vainglory, and drunkenness are all without doubt proved to be capital sins.

[Col. 0855D] These are the things that plunge people into ruin and destruction. This is the wickedness that holy Peter commanded us to cast away when he says: “This is the word that was proclaimed to you: Therefore, laying aside all wickedness and all deceit.” Of such people the Apostle Paul says: “Those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them.”

These are the works of Satan, which Christians renounce in baptism. Satan will seek these works in us on the day of our departure. If he finds them, he claims us as guilty for himself and drags us with him, naked, weeping, and mourning, to the gates of hell and to eternal punishments. There death is always suffered, and the wicked life will never end through death; there burning heat boils up in sulfurous [Col. 0856A] flames, and cold among trembling and mourning souls is intolerable and never-ending.

There the eyes of those who here refused to see with the eyes of their hearts the lamp of the Lord—that is, the holy Gospel—will suffer darkness without light. There the ears of those who here refused to hear the commandments of life in Christ’s Gospel will hear nothing but lamentation and groaning. There those who here refused to give food and drink to the wretched who hungered and thirsted will hunger and thirst forever. There death will always be desired but never granted by those who here refused to think about their own death. There every evil is found in general, and no good will be seen.

### 2.

The commandments of God are true faith and an unstained life. True faith is the catholic faith, which we explained above. The love of God means loving the Lord God [Col. 0856B] with all one’s heart, all one’s soul, and all one’s strength; and then loving one’s neighbor as oneself.

The fear of the Lord is as it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” Peace, kindness, patience, humility, self-restraint, moderation, justice, and mercy.

The works of mercy are to give food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked; to visit and serve the sick and those confined in prison; to receive guests; to bury the dead; to judge justly; to praise justice; to detest and not practice iniquity; to help widows and orphans; to receive travelers; to distribute alms among the poor; to aid those suffering tribulation; to render tithes every year; to pray always in every place under his dominion; to preserve chastity; [Col. 0856C] to love fasting; to love peace always; and to give thanks to God for everything.

For those who do and fulfill these things, eternal kingdoms are prepared. On the day of judgment the Savior of the world will say to them: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father, where there is light without darkness and life without death, eternal joy and gladness without end, and spiritual goods greater and better than the human tongue can express, as it is written: “Neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him.”

## SERMON VII. On Faith and Charity

[Col. 0856D] ### 1.

Above all, a person must seek what true knowledge and true wisdom are, because the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. True knowledge is to withdraw from the service of the Devil, which consists in sins; and perfect wisdom is to worship God according to the truth of his commandments. For in these two things blessed life is acquired, as the Psalmist says: “Turn away from evil and do good.” Nor is it enough for anyone merely not to do evil unless he also does good; nor is it enough to do good unless he also abandons evil.

Therefore everyone who is wise in this way will unquestionably be blessed forever. There is no wisdom better than that by which God is understood and feared according to the measure of the human mind, and his future judgment is believed. For what is more just than to love God and keep his commandments—[Col. 0857A] the God through whom we were created when we did not exist, and freed from the service of the Devil; God bestowed on us all the good things we possess?

Therefore let each person strive with the greatest urgency to complete the good he has begun, so that he may deserve to receive an everlasting reward from the Lord. Let God be loved with all our strength, he who protects all who willingly and with sincere charity subject their body and soul to him. For every creature, whether it wishes to or not, is subject to the one God and Lord. But we are admonished to serve the Lord our God with our whole will.

### 2.

Faith is the first thing that subjects the soul to God, because knowledge of divinity and understanding of truth must be learned through catholic faith, since without faith it is impossible to please God. Truly blessed is the one who both lives well by believing rightly [Col. 0857B] and preserves the true faith by living well.

Therefore, just as faith without good works is useless, so good works accomplish nothing without true faith. This is the catholic faith: that we believe in one God, the almighty Father, and in his only Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit—that is, one God, an eternal Trinity of one substance: God, from whom all things are, through whom all things are, and in whom all things are.

### 3.

Among the commandments of God, charity holds the chief place. Therefore it must be loved and preserved, without whose perfection, the Apostle Paul testifies, nothing can please God. Accordingly, when the Lord himself was asked by a certain scribe what the greatest commandment was, he replied: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart [Col. 0857C] and with all your soul and with all your mind.” He added: “The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend.

When he says “with all your heart, soul, and mind,” this means that God is to be loved with the whole understanding, the whole will, and the entire memory. The love of God consists entirely in keeping his commandments, as he says elsewhere: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words.” Therefore the Truth himself also says elsewhere: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” The Apostle likewise says: “Love is the fullness of the law.” And the evangelist John says: “We have this commandment from God: that whoever loves God must also love his neighbor.”

### 4.

If anyone should ask who one’s neighbor is, [Col. 0857D] let him know that every Christian is rightly called a neighbor, because in baptism we are all sanctified as sons of God, so that spiritually we may be brothers in perfect charity. Spiritual generation is nobler than physical generation. Concerning it the Truth himself says in the Gospel: “Unless someone is born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.”

Let a person learn what the commandments of God are and keep them as far as he is able; in this way he may know that he possesses the charity of God. Therefore no one, however heavily burdened by an immense weight of sins, ought to despair of the goodness of divine compassion. Rather, in every distress of tribulations, one should run in hope to the consolation of heavenly mercy, because in God alone all hope and salvation unquestionably consist.

Whoever faithfully [Col. 0858A] loves and continually worships God and Lord, and perseveringly fulfills his commandments, will be made worthy to possess everlasting glory with the angels; the heavenly kingdom lies open according to merits. Therefore, just as the blessedness of God’s kingdom is proclaimed equally to all, so the entry into God’s kingdom is open equally to every sex, age, and person according to the dignity of their merits. There it does not matter who someone was in this world—a layperson or cleric, rich or poor, younger or older, servant or master—but each person will be crowned with everlasting glory according to the merit of his good work.

## SERMON VIII. How One Should Live Here, and How One Should Live in the Future
Let us consider, beloved brothers, continually how we should live in this present life, and how we shall live after the end of this life [Col. 0858B]. Human beings can by no means perish like animals without reason; rather, every human being possesses an immortal soul, which will be judged according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil. The salvation of each person consists in obeying God’s commands and always doing his will with complete devotion—he who wills all people to be saved and no one to perish. Therefore, after the sacrament of baptism he established a second purification, penance, so that the evils we commit after the washing of baptism may be healed by the remedies of penance; so that we who were previously engaged in evil deeds may afterward, once converted, live in good works. For it is not enough merely to abandon evil unless we immediately also do the good works commanded to us, as the prophet says: “Turn away from [Col. 0858C] evil and do good.”

The evil of pride must indeed be exchanged for the good of humility, so that we who through pride were followers of the devil may through humility be imitators of Christ. Thus, through pride the angelic powers fell from heavenly glory, but through the humility of Christ the human race is called to heavenly glory. Pride is the beginning of every sin, by which human beings refused to obey the commands of their God. From this came the downfall of the first human being, because he disdained obeying the command of his Creator. And if that first human being was expelled from the joys of paradise through disobedience, may we, through obedience to God’s commands, be able to attain everlasting life, as the Lord says in the Gospel to someone asking him how he could possess eternal life [Col. 0858D]: “If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments.” Among these commandments of the Lord, the greatest and most just is this: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength.” The second is like it: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” This means: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another”—something human nature itself teaches, since no one wishes another person to harm him. Therefore no one ought to harm another; and just as we desire others to help us in our needs, so we ought also to help others in their needs, according to the measure of our abilities. We should be kind and merciful toward all people, just as God the Father is kind and merciful toward us. He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and gives rain to our earth so that seeds may bear fruit, so that the earth may produce and yield the fruit by which the life of our mortality is sustained [Col. 0859A].

For this reason it is necessary to love him and obey his commands, so that through his mercy we may be protected from every adversity and through him may abound in eternal blessings.
