His goodness never abandons us, provided that we do not abandon his will; and his will is our salvation, prosperity, and eternal blessedness. Therefore, with all our strength, let us flee the vices and crimes that the devil urges upon us, doing the good works that God himself has commanded us to do—that is, love of God and neighbor, as we have said, and compassion and mercy toward the afflicted.

Let us not be greedy in gathering or hoarding, but generous in giving, because “a man’s own riches are his redemption” [Col. 0859B], and Christ will reward the gifts given to the poor. Just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving erases sin. Likewise, through fasting, prayers, abstinence from carnal desires, confession, and penance, all sins can be erased.

But let no one lie secure in his sins, because no one can know the final day. Rather, let him rise through confession and penance and return to the Lord his God, because he is merciful in forgiving, if we are not sluggish in repenting. Let us be chaste and sober in our bodies, fleeing fornication and other bodily impurities, and let us drive every unlawful pleasure away from us. Let us cleanse our hearts and bodies in the sight of the Lord our God, so that we may be worthy to be a dwelling place for the Holy Spirit [Col. 0859C].

Let none of you commit thefts, robberies, false testimony, perjury, murder, or similar crimes. Let no one harbor envy or hatred or secret dissension against another, but let him live peacefully with everyone [Col. 0859C], as the Lord says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” Guard yourselves in every way against feasting, drunkenness, empty talk, and shameful speech, because drunkards, as the Apostle says, will not possess the kingdom of God.

Do not practice augury, incantations, or magical bindings, nor put your trust in them, because these are devices of the devil, not the commands of the Lord. Rather, hasten to the church of Christ; there seek the health of your bodies and the salvation of your souls. For in the power of almighty God lie the salvation and life of us all [Col. 0859D]; his mercy never abandons those who hope in him. Therefore let us hope and believe, through his goodness, that every good thing comes to us.

Let us be patient and repay no one evil for evil, but let us forgive those who sin against us, so that divine mercy may deign to forgive us our offenses, as we customarily say in the Lord’s Prayer. Let us always have God present everywhere. And if we fear sinning in the presence of a human being, how much more should we fear sinning before the eyes of God, who sees with complete clarity everything we think, say, or do? We have him as a witness throughout our life, and after this life we have him as judge. Let us always fulfill his will with complete love and strength, so that he may deign to grant us eternal glory [Col. 0860A] with his saints; so that, while the impious are handed over with the devil to everlasting flames for their sins and crimes, we may, for our good works, deserve by divine grace to enter with Christ and the angelic choirs into the joys of eternal blessedness.

## SERMON IX. Which actions must be avoided with every effort, and which must be pursued with the full exertion of our strength

1. Beloved, we ought to consider the condition of the present life, and which actions we must avoid with every effort and which we must pursue with the full exertion of our strength. In everything that can be done here, we must always observe how we may resist the devil, our deceiver, and how we may please God Jesus, our redeemer [Col. 0860B]. We please him when we do what he commanded and reject what he forbade. He forbids us to commit sins and iniquities, and commands us to heal those committed quickly with the medicine of penance. He has commanded us to live rightly and devoutly, to seek eternal things, and to attend carefully to each person’s place and condition, lest anyone appear empty or less useful in his proper place.

There is one soul in our body, in which life consists, but there are many members distinguished by different functions. So in the Church there is one faith, which ought to work everywhere through love, but there are different dignities, each having its own ministries. For one order consists of those set over others, another of those subject to them; one of the rich, another of the poor; one of the old, another of the young. Each person has his own commands, just as each member has its own function in the body [Col. 0860C].

The duty of bishops is to forbid what is wrong, console the fainthearted, and rebuke the insolent. The royal dignity, moreover, ought to be an object of fear and veneration to the peoples, because “there is no authority except from God.” Likewise, all the powerful and judges who adhere to the king ought to be faithful, humble, and merciful; they must judge with equity and not for gifts, defend widows, orphans, and the poor, be subject to their bishops, oppress no one by force, not covet unjust wealth, and give their own possessions to the needy rather than seize what belongs to others.

2. Likewise, among the people of God there are some wise and others foolish. It is the duty of the wise to complete in action the good things they know and to preach them to others [Col. 0860D]. What does it profit a traveler to know the road if he does not wish to enter it? But the person who knows the way of God, enters it, and leads others in is like the firmament, which shines with many stars. Whoever builds up many people will glory in the reward of many.

The powerful, therefore, ought always to have God present to them. Even if they do not fear human beings, they should nevertheless fear God, and use the authority granted to them for God’s honor and the salvation of their souls. Those who are foolish and uneducated should learn humbly from the wise, because “the one who is ignorant will be ignored”; they should not think that ignorance can excuse them before the strict Judge, who examines each person’s secrets.

3. There are three classes among the human race. Some know what is good and do what they know; these are the best of human beings and are close to God [Col. 0861A]. The second class consists of those who do not know good things by themselves but nevertheless wish to learn from those who know well and to fulfill what they have learned; their life is useful in the Church. But the life of the person who despises learning the good he does not know is useless to everyone and harmful to many.

Therefore, let the one who knows what is good do it, and let the one who does not know learn, so that the former may rejoice in his knowledge and the latter may make progress through his diligence.

Some in the Church are rich and others poor. The poor are commanded to be humble and to hope in God, who said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit”; and they should love the better riches all the more eagerly because they are empty of earthly ones.

The rich are commanded to give what is their own, not to seize what belongs to others, and to clothe and dress people, because the rich, through the abundance of their wealth, make many unnecessary expenditures, whether in food or clothing [Col. 0861B]. Therefore let the feeding of the poor wash away the sins produced by excess, because just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin. A rich person who spares his wealth does not spare his soul; or to whom is he generous if he is miserly toward himself? Let each person consider at what price he would wish to redeem himself from the present fire if he were compelled to burn for even one day; how much more severe is the fire of judgment? The fire of Gehenna is moreover eternal.

Therefore, whoever possesses riches should go before the face of the Judge and show mercy to the wretched, so that God may show mercy to him, since, as has been said, he shows mercy to the poor. “Lend to the Lord, and he himself will repay you.”

It is fitting for old men to be devout, orderly in conduct, and to adorn their gray hair with sobriety, always thinking about entering the next life. Young men ought to devote themselves to the obedience and submission of their elders [Col. 0861C], so that they may continually advance in the house of God and become better and better. They should not allow themselves to be enslaved to evil spirits through empty amusements and harmful desires, but should strive to bring themselves, chaste and undefiled, to mature age.

4. Parents are also commanded to educate their children in the fear of God. For what benefit is it to a parent to have a son assigned to everlasting torments? Therefore fathers should educate their children more diligently in the discipline of piety, so that through the blessing of their inheritance they may possess them both in this age and in the age to come.

Children also should obey their parents, for Christ himself is read to have been subject to his parents. Husbands should love their wives in chastity and with a pure conscience, and, as though they were the more fragile vessel, should show them the honor due to them in the fear of God [Col. 0861D]. Wives should be subject to their husbands in fear and faith, knowing that the subjection of a wife to her husband was established by God.

There are also other commandments common in the Church to every dignity, age, and sex: to love the Lord God with all one’s heart, with all one’s mind, and with all one’s strength, and one’s neighbor as oneself; and no one should do to another what he would not wish done to himself. Patience is also necessary for everyone, as are compassion, generosity in mercy, equity in justice, purity of faith, firmness of hope, perseverance in prayer, and gentleness of character.

By these and similar sacrifices divine clemency is won. These commandments of salvation are fitting for everyone and are known to be necessary for all [Col. 0862A]. By these steps the heavenly journey is made, and by these keys the gate of the heavenly homeland is opened. By these footprints all the saints completed the course of the present life, and those who now reign with Christ reached him by these paths. This way is not burdensome but exceedingly glorious: it is completed in a brief span, yet crowned with perpetual joy and glory.

Whoever does not cease to travel this road becomes a sharer in angelic blessedness and enjoys forever the sight of the Lord God almighty himself, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON X. On the Incarnation of the Son of God and the restoration of the human race

1. In the beginning almighty God created human beings in his image and likeness in paradise and willed them to be eternal. But after the first parent of the human race was expelled from the joys of paradise because of sin and entered the misery of this exile and blindness that we endure, he could no longer see those joys of the heavenly homeland that he had previously contemplated [Col. 0862B].

In paradise, human beings had become accustomed to enjoying the words of God and, with purity of heart and exalted vision, to sharing in the spirits of the blessed angels. But humanity lost these delights when it sinned in paradise.

After the first human being fell to this place, he withdrew from the light of the mind by which he had contemplated that reality. From his flesh, then, we were born into the blindness of this exile. We have indeed heard that there is a heavenly homeland; we have heard that its citizens are God’s angels; we have heard that the spirits of the perfected righteous are companions of those same angels. But carnal people, because they cannot know invisible things through experience [Col. 0862C], doubt whether things they do not see with bodily eyes truly exist.

When they hear of supreme and invisible realities, they doubt whether they are true, because they know as visible only the lowest things into which they were born. Therefore the only-begotten Son of the Father, creator of invisible and visible things, came for the redemption of the human race. The only-begotten Son of the Father was incarnate for this reason: to lead us into faith.

O how great is the goodness of our God, who created and liberated us! He endured many reproaches and insults in words from the faithless Jews so that, by his example, we might preserve true patience. He received the slaps of those who insulted him so that he might free the souls of believers from the devil’s snares. He did not hide his face from the spittle of the faithless [Col. 0862D], so that he might wash us with the water of salvation. Silently he endured scourging so that he might save us from everlasting punishments. He endured blows so that he might grant us everlasting honors among the choirs of angels. In his thirst he accepted the bitterness of gall so that he might intoxicate us with eternal sweetness. In order to prepare life for the dead, Life itself proceeded even to death.

Why, then, is it considered harsh for a human being to endure scourging from God for evil deeds, if God endured such great evils from human beings for the sake of good? Or how can anyone of sound understanding be ungrateful for being struck, if he himself did not leave this life without scourging—he who lived here without sin?

Our redeemer endured all these things and many others for our salvation, and for love of him we ought to abandon every vice and evil desire, because he loved us so greatly that he poured out his holy blood for us [Col. 0863A]. Let us therefore follow, beloved brothers, the strict and difficult path of our redeemer. Let no love of earthly things overcome us; let no pride inflate us; let no anger tear us apart; let no lust defile us; let no envy consume us.

Our redeemer died because of his love for us, beloved brothers, and through love of him let us learn to conquer ourselves. If we do this perfectly, we shall not only escape the punishments that threaten us, but also receive a common reward of glory with the martyrs.

2. Therefore, beloved brothers, possessing this hope, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit. Whatever is evil and sordid, let us neither do with the body nor contemplate in the mind, as befits saints, so that in the future resurrection we may deserve to go to glory, not to punishment [Col. 0863B].

Some will rise so as to receive heavenly rewards from God; others so as to suffer everlasting torments with the devil. For the Lord says in the Gospel concerning the wicked and unjust: “Then the impious will go into everlasting fire, but the righteous into eternal life.”

Therefore, beloved brothers, hold most firmly to this resurrection, which has been confirmed by apostolic and divine voices. Know that our Lord Jesus Christ rose from the dead and, made immortal, sits at the right hand of the Father; he deigns to call us to similar rewards of resurrection.

Show yourselves worthy to receive that heavenly and eternal glory, which you can attain if you preserve yourselves holy in all things. Abstain from every evil work: hatred, enmity, drunkenness, fornication, theft, and perjury. For God hates all these things and those who do them, and he will punish them in the future [Col. 0863C].

Therefore be kind, merciful, humble, chaste, and always do the things that God loves in his saints, so that you may reach eternal life with his saints, through Jesus Christ our Lord, who deigns to protect us in all things and assist us by his grace. To him be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever.

## SERMON XI. On the two kingdoms established by God

God established two kingdoms: that of the present age, I mean, and that of the future. He appointed periods for each and decreed that the day of his judgment should be awaited—the day he himself has fixed, on which the separation of all things and of souls will take place [Col. 0863D]. Then the impious will indeed be handed over to eternal fire for their sins, while those who have lived according to the will of God the Creator, having received blessing for their good works, will shine with brilliant light, be brought into the eternal age, and receive eternal gifts of ineffable blessings.

Now, brothers, these are holy days of purification, spiritual days for souls, in which there is some bodily weariness but gain for the soul. Therefore, as the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” Let us therefore devote ourselves to God alone, abandon the beloved things that pass away in this world, and cling to God the merciful Father, as the psalmist admonishes and says: “Be still and know that I am the Lord.”

To be still for the Lord, then, is to persist in his praises, cast off the burdens of sins through penance, and turn to God the Creator [Col. 0864A]. Do not imitate wicked Christians. For there are some—what is worse—who commit many crimes and sins after baptism and do not seek the remedy of penance, but, loosening the reins of sin, are carried through every field of wickedness down the precipices of lust to the underworld; and without any remorse or correction of life they presume to approach the altar and receive communion.

But you who have been baptized, do not imitate such people, lest, if you wish to imitate them, you perish with them in eternal punishment. Preserve the sacrament of baptism within you. Flee drunkenness as though it were a pit of hell; fear pride, envy, and vanity as the devil’s sword.

Do not slander, because it is written: “The one who slanders his brother will be uprooted from the land of the living.” Do not curse, because it is written: “Those who curse will not possess the kingdom of God” [Col. 0864B]. Do not give false testimony, because it is written: “A false witness will not go unpunished.” Do not lie, because it is written: “The mouth that lies kills the soul.” Do not hate one another, because it is written: “The one who hates his brother is a murderer”; for whoever does this loses the sacrament of baptism.

Do not commit theft by any means. Do not practice fraud. Avoid dishonest scales and double measures as deadly poisons. Gather frequently at church; show both honor and love to your priests. From your own substance also pay tithes, and give alms according to your means. Do not accept gifts against the innocent, but whenever you hear cases, heed God and judge with justice, lest, while you wish unjustly to acquire money, you be unable to escape eternal punishment [Col. 0864C].

Whoever thinks carefully about the salvation of his soul should flee as far as he can whatever harms it. For the person who thinks only about this life is like the animals and beasts. What do animals seek except to eat, drink, and sleep? Such is the person who thinks more about his flesh than his soul, who loves the appetite or lust more than chastity and justice.

You ought to know, beloved, that we became Christians so that we might always think about the future age and eternal blessedness, and labor more for the soul than for the body, because our flesh will be in this world for only a few years [Col. 0864D]. But our soul, if we act well, will reign in heaven without end.

Let us therefore do penance, brothers, so that we may deserve to have God as the propitiator of our sins. Let us entreat him, because we have provoked him; let us humble ourselves, so that he may exalt us; let us lament, so that he may gladden us; let us mourn, so that he may console us. Let us cast away from us evil habit and, as though with a garment, clothe ourselves in strength of spirit—especially we who have already merited an angelic way of life, so that we may deserve to reach the fellowship of the angels.

There, freed from every evil report, may we deserve to hear that blessed and desirable voice: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord.” May this be granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XII. Exhortation concerning the fasts of Lent

[Col. 0865A]

1. Beloved brothers, we have been appointed to show you the way of your salvation, insofar as divine clemency deigns to grant us understanding. Therefore we ask you to strive at every hour to fulfill the Lord’s commands carefully, with attentive minds and devout dedication, so that, strengthened in divine love, you may not be separated from it by any temptations. Rather, by always doing what is good, may you abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit, so that by his grace you may preserve the faith and baptism you have received before the sight of the supreme God and our Savior Jesus Christ.

For we were created for the praise of his holy name. He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood [Col. 0865B], because he endured death for us in order by his death to destroy him who held the power of death—that is, the devil. By rescuing the human race from his power, he opened the kingdoms of heaven to believers, where the faithful enjoy eternal life and possess the greatest fruit of eternal life.

The greatest fruit is God alone, the rewarder of eternal life. Therefore let us worship the one God and Lord, and serve him alone, so that he may deign to reward us with the fullest fruit. Let us flee everything subject to the devil’s power, so that, strengthened by divine power, we may prevail against his ancient wickedness.

2. Beloved brothers, we ought always to praise with complete devotion [Col. 0865C] the mercy of our redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, and with devout intention submit ourselves to his command, with good will and sincere love—especially during these holy days that are now beginning. By fasting, praying, and giving alms, let us entrust our soul and body to the divine majesty.

For our salvation, the Lord Jesus Christ came among human beings and fasted for forty days and forty nights, taking no food at all. We too, as far as we can, strive during the annual season of Lent to afflict our flesh through abstinence, because we need to fast from unlawful thoughts, words, and deeds, living according to heavenly and spiritual commands.

In the Mosaic Law [Col. 0865D] the whole people were commanded to offer tithes and first fruits to the Lord God. Thus we ought to offer the beginnings of our intentions and the completion of our works to God’s grace, and pay tithes of the days of the year in our bodies during this most sacred season, because these are the days appointed for us to give the tithes of our flesh to God.

From the present day, as you know, beloved brothers, until Easter there are forty-two days. Of these, we fast for thirty-six days, while we spend the six Sundays with joy, using our food. Since the year consists of 360 days, the entire period of the year is tithed in the number of thirty-six days.

During these days we ought to come to church and, through the practice of our deeds, humbly offer ourselves before the divine majesty with pure hearts and chaste bodies [Col. 0866A], asking almighty God to deign to forgive us because we have lived throughout the year more negligently than we ought.

Thinking wisely and faithfully about these things, beloved brothers, let us hasten to take refuge in the remedies of penance. Through chastity and works of justice and mercy, let us obtain eternal rewards for ourselves with God. We ought to spend these days doing good all the more diligently, because fasts earn great forgiveness for our sins before God when they are undertaken for the love of God and not for empty glory.

3. This is the perfect and reasonable fast: when our body fasts, the soul prays. Through fasting, prayer more easily penetrates heaven. Then the spiritual person is joined to the angels. Through this, vices are overthrown, the flesh is humbled, and the devil’s temptations are conquered [Col. 0866B].

Do not neglect your soul. Just as you provide food daily for your flesh so that it may not fail, so let good works be the daily nourishment of your mind. Let the body be fed with food and the spirit nourished by devout action. Do not deny to the soul, which will live forever, what you give to the flesh, which will die.

The life of the body is the soul; the life of the soul is God. And just as a dead body is without a soul, so a soul is dead without God. Therefore let us have Jesus Christ our Savior in our hearts through good works, so that he may deign to preserve our soul and body.

It is right for each person to love the Lord God with all his heart, with all his mind, and with all his strength, and his neighbor [Col. 0866C] as himself; and no one should do to another what he does not wish done to himself.

Therefore, beloved, see to it that you cleanse your hearts and discipline your bodies, so that you may be considered worthy to receive the Holy Spirit, whose dwelling and house you are, believing rightly and acting well—not as mortal beings, but as eternal spiritual ones.

4. Watch, brothers, in every good work. Keep in memory what you have heard in the preaching of your salvation, and do what has been commanded. Have Christ in your heart and the sign of the holy cross on your forehead.

We have many invisible enemies who strive to impede our course and place the snares of their overthrow along our paths, so that, once we are entangled in harmful desires, they may block the road of life for us. Arm yourselves against them with the sign of Christ’s cross, because this is what the evil spirits, our enemies, flee and fear. By this sign they were condemned, and by this sign we were freed [Col. 0866D].

Let us place this sign first in every work; let it protect us while we sleep and arm us while we are awake, so that the enemy lying in wait may be unable to harm us in any affair, whether we sleep or remain awake. For our king, Jesus Christ, if he sees us flee to his standard because of any tribulation or fear, will immediately rescue and protect us by the right hand of his power from every adversity, for the praise and glory of his holy name.

He is the true God who must be praised and worshiped, who guards those who hope in him. Let us ask him, beloved brothers, to protect us here and lead us to eternal life.

## SERMON XIII. Why the fasts of Lent should be honored more than other fasts

[Col. 0867A]

Beloved brothers, we ought always, at every time, to humble ourselves and serve the Lord our God, but especially during these holy days of Lent. We explain to you, brothers, why we ought to honor these holy fasts more than other fasts: because our redeemer, coming among human beings, fasted for forty days and forty nights and took no food at all.

We too, as far as we can, with God’s help, should cleanse ourselves from our sins through abstinence. You know that from the present day until the joys of the Easter solemnity there are six weeks, making forty-two days [Col. 0867B]. When the six Sundays are subtracted from the days of abstinence, no more than thirty-six days remain in abstinence. Since the year consists of 360 days, we are afflicted for thirty-six days, as though giving the tithes of our year to God, so that we who have lived for ourselves during the year we have received may submit ourselves to our Creator through abstinence in his tithes.

Therefore, beloved brothers, just as you are commanded in the Law to offer tithes of your possessions, so strive to offer tithes of your days. Let each person, as far as his strength permits, mortify his flesh and afflict its desires, because the flesh, when pleased, drew us into sin; when afflicted, let it lead us back to forgiveness. Thus we who fell through sin may rise through forgiveness, and may always do what is good, because the Apostle [Col. 0867C] says: “Everyone will receive from the Lord whatever good he has done.”

Therefore, brothers, whatever good you can do, do it without sadness, because it is written: “God loves a cheerful giver.” Let each person strive to abstain from every evil deed, not only from fornication—which is never lawful—but also from lawful marriage during these forty days.

Similarly, let him cast away idle jokes and empty and shameful words, and meditate day and night on turning every deed to the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ, with holy prayers, vigils, and almsgiving, and with gatherings in church. When he comes to church, let him ask almighty God to direct his way according to God’s will [Col. 0867D], to deign to forgive his sins, and to listen willingly to the word of God without hindering another, because the Lord admonishes us, saying: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.”

Let us complete these holy fasts according to the will of God, because fasting is a holy thing, a heavenly work. Whoever practices it in holiness is joined to God and becomes spiritual. Through it vices are overthrown, the flesh is humbled, and the devil’s temptations are conquered.

Therefore let us flee every vice: fornication, impurity, enmity, contention, rivalry, anger, quarrels, dissension, murder, envy, drunkenness, and revelry. Let us possess love and joy, peace and patience, endurance and goodness, moderation and self-control, so that, instructed in good works, we may prevail over the devil’s temptations and grow in the fear of God, now and always doing his will [Col. 0868A].

For at every hour we ought to be adorned and radiant, especially during these forty days, because during them, as we said above, we ought to give the tithes of our year to God.

Beloved brothers, let us always cleanse body and soul, so that at the hour of our departure we may be found worthy before God, and on the day of judgment, when our Lord Jesus Christ comes in his majesty with his angels, may deserve to enter eternal life and live there in blessedness forever.

There is certain security there, secure tranquility, tranquil joy, happy eternity, eternal happiness; there perfect love exists, no fear, eternal salvation overflows, and truth reigns. There no one deceives or is deceived; there are all good things [Col. 0868B]. Our Lord Jesus Christ is there, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. May he grant us to reach that life and happiness. Amen.

## SERMON XIV. On the day of the Easter solemnity

1. Thanks be to our God and Savior, who has allowed us to arrive safely at the celebration of the Lord’s day of the Easter solemnity. Today, throughout the whole world, the resurrection of our Savior Jesus Christ our Lord is celebrated in the holy churches of Christ.

Therefore, beloved brothers, it is fitting that we speak somewhat about so great a solemnity. Jesus Christ appeared in the flesh, deigned to die by his will, rose by his power, and showed by example what he promised us as a reward [Col. 0868C]. He alone died in time, yet he was by no means the only one to rise. For it is written: “Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose.”

Behold, we know that human beings rose with God, and we do not doubt that these were pure human beings. Therefore, if we are members of our Redeemer, let us confidently expect in ourselves what is known to have occurred in the head, who is Christ Jesus. For, as the Apostle Paul says: “He died for our sins and rose for our justification.”

O great mercy of our Redeemer, the only-begotten Son of God, and of our Savior Jesus Christ our Lord, who came into this world to save sinners, because before the coming of the Savior all human beings were guilty through the fault of the first transgression of Adam and Eve his wife [Col. 0868D]!

## 2

You have often heard, dearly beloved brothers, how our first parents transgressed God’s commandment; let us now speak of it briefly. They had been placed in a paradise of such great happiness that, if they had wished to preserve that paradisal blessedness by abstaining from the fruit of the forbidden tree, they would always have remained without death and misery. For the Lord God commanded them not to eat the fruit of one tree, lest they should think that everything was permitted to them and believe themselves like God if they were subject to no law. That paradise was situated on earth, and yet, as we said above, it was of such great blessedness that, if they kept God’s commandment, they would always have remained without death and misery until they were transferred into the heavenly kingdoms.

But the ancient enemy, envying man because he did not want man to possess such happiness—the happiness from which he himself had been cast down through his pride, since he had been created good by God but had fallen from heaven through his pride—therefore envied man’s glory because he had lost his own. Through the serpent he tempted the woman and persuaded her to eat from the fruit of that tree concerning which the Lord had commanded them not to eat, saying: “If you taste from the tree, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.” The woman consented to the persuasion, ate, and gave some to her husband, and he ate. Then, after the sin, both were cast from paradise into this wretched life, and every human being was held under the power of death because of that transgression. All descended into the prison of hell; the righteous, however, did not burn there, although they were in hell, sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. No human being could shake that condemnation from himself; all were detained in hell until Jesus Christ our Lord deigned to be born into the world through the womb of Mary, ever-virgin, so that the one who had been Creator might become the liberator of humanity.

In the same flesh which he assumed for our salvation and that of all, he endured many injuries from the treacherous Jewish people—not because he was unable to avenge himself, but because he offered us an example of patience, so that we might endure tribulations and injuries with forbearance. He endured the devil’s temptations and overcame him by his power. By his divinity he could have plunged him into the abyss, yet he answered nothing except with words of gentleness. He tolerated from the treacherous Jews much blasphemy in words and, moreover, scourges, spitting, blows, a crown of thorns, and many wounds. After all these things, and many others, when placed upon the cross he did not refuse to have his body pierced by nails. By laying down his soul, he endured death; not from necessity, but by his own will, he placed his flesh in the tomb. He descended to the lower regions and bound the prince of death—that is, the devil. He broke the iron bars of the gates of hell and, rescuing all the righteous from there, restored them to their former freedom. Rising from death, he displayed in himself the light of eternal salvation to us who believe in him.

## 3

Venerating the glory of his resurrection with annual devotion, we celebrate it today. Let us therefore rejoice, beloved, and exult in the Lord, because in this holy solemnity our Redeemer, by rising again, has shown us immortal life, which he will give us through his grace if we are willing to pass from vices to virtues.

Therefore let us cleanse ourselves from every iniquity and serve the Lord our God, Jesus Christ, because he poured out his holy blood for us in order to redeem us from every iniquity. For this reason we ought to live holily, justly, and devoutly in this world, and place nothing before the love of God, who loved us so greatly that, as we have said, he himself died for us.

Now, dearly beloved brothers, let us joyfully celebrate his resurrection and prepare ourselves for him with a pure heart and a chaste body, so that through these Paschal festivals which we are observing here we may deserve to reach the heavenly realms and there live forever in blessedness with the holy angels and all the righteous, as the Lord himself said: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.”

May Jesus Christ our Lord, who created us and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, deign to lead us to that eternal joy, for ever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XV. On Renunciation in Baptism

## 1

Listen, brothers, and consider more attentively what you renounced in baptism. You renounced the devil, all his works, and all his pomps.

What, then, are the works of the devil? They are pride, idolatry, envy, murder, detraction, lying, perjury, hatred, fornication, adultery, every kind of pollution, thefts, false testimony, robbery, gluttony, drunkenness, obscene speech, quarrels, anger, poisonings, incantations, seeking out diviners, believing in witches and fabricated werewolves, causing abortion, being disobedient to masters, and possessing amulets. These and similar evil works are the works of the devil, and you renounced all of them in baptism. As the Apostle says: “Those who do such things are worthy of death and will not inherit the kingdom of God.”

But because we trust in God’s mercy that you will renounce all the things mentioned above in heart and deed, so that you may deserve to obtain forgiveness, I admonish you, dearly beloved brothers, to remember what you promised to almighty God.

## 2

First, you promised to believe in almighty God, in Jesus Christ his Son, and in the Holy Spirit: one almighty God in perfect Trinity.

## 3

These are the commandments of God which you must do and preserve, so that you may love the God whom you have confessed with all your heart, with all your mind, and with all your strength. Then love your neighbors as yourselves. On all these commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend.

Be patient; be merciful, kind, chaste, and undefiled. Teach your children to fear God, and likewise your household. Reconcile those who are at odds. Whoever hears cases should judge justly and accept no gifts, because gifts blind even the wise.

## 4

Observe the Lord’s Day; assemble at church, praying there and not engaging in idle talk. Give alms according to your means, because just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin.

Receive strangers hospitably; visit the sick; minister to widows and orphans; pay tithes to the churches; and whatever you do not wish done to you, do not do to another. Fear God alone everywhere.

Servants, be subject to your masters; and masters, preserve justice toward your servants. Hold fast to the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed, and hand them on to your children and your godchildren, for whom you became sponsors in baptism.

Love fasting; love justice; resist the devil; receive the Eucharist at the appointed times. These are the works which God commanded you to do and preserve, and others like them.

## 5

Believe in the Christ who will come, in the resurrection of the flesh, and in the judgment of all human beings. There the impious will be distinguished for eternal fire, but the righteous for eternal life.

There is life with God without death, light without darkness, salvation without sickness, fullness without hunger, happiness without fear, and joy without sadness. There is eternal glory; there the righteous will shine like the sun, because “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart how much God has prepared for those who love him.”

## 6

I also admonish you about this, dearly beloved brothers: since the Lord’s Nativity is approaching, abstain from every kind of luxury, from every kind of fornication, from every impurity, and from all evil works. Reject anger, hatred, and envy from your hearts like poison.

Preserve chastity even with your own wives. Adorn yourselves with good works. Distribute alms to Christ’s poor. Frequently invite the poor to more lavish banquets. Preserve peace with everyone; reconcile those who are at odds.

If, with Christ’s help, you faithfully wish to fulfill this, then in this world you will be able to approach the Lord’s altar without fear, and in the future you will happily attain eternal blessedness.

# The Third Part of the Complete Extant Works of Saint Boniface, Archbishop of Mainz. Miscellaneous Short Works

[Col. 0871]

## I.

[Note: Serrarius published this work together with the letters of Boniface, p. 232, prefacing it with the following note: “To the letters of Saint Boniface I append the Life and Martyrdom of Saint Livinus, who is also sometimes called Libvinus, although Arnoldus Wion, whom I cite in book III of my *Moguntina*, note 48, p. 559, seems to distinguish them. This history was very kindly supplied to me from Antwerp, toward the end of the preceding Frankfurt Fair, by the Reverend and highly learned man D. Aubert Miraeus, canon of Antwerp, a man most devoted to and knowledgeable in Christian history, with the following inscription.” I have considered it a matter of conscience not to alter Serrarius’s text, for I have never seen any manuscript copies. GILES.]

# LIFE AND MARTYRDOM OF SAINT LIVINUS, BISHOP AND MARTYR

[Attributed to Boniface.]

## Prologue

[Col. 0871B]

Boniface, a sinful man, servant of the servants of our Lord Jesus Christ, to all the churches founded upon the firm rock under the authority of the holy and undivided Trinity: the highest happiness and the glory of eternal happiness.

The venerable triumph of the glorious passion of the most blessed Father Livinus, bishop beloved by God, has established that the solemnity of our joy today should be ceremonially celebrated by us, in an honor of the greatest veneration, and accompanied by votive observances. The renown of so great a Father’s merits has been made known to the world. We earnestly exhort you to rejoice with him, as that solemn season of the year which pours forth its dew awakens us to the joys of this devotion—the season in which that most victorious combatant, an athlete and wondrous martyr, passed joyfully from the conflict of the present age, fighting invincibly for the confession of the holy Trinity and triumphing over his persecutors, as well as over the assaults of cruel punishments. He went to the King of heaven, to be enthroned in the laurels of merited dignity in the confession of the martyrs, to be glorified with equal honor, and to enjoy their companionship in the blessedness of eternal peace.

We learned the distinguished signs of the great virtues of this most excellent holy athlete of Christ, which we unfold to your love, from three of his disciples, namely Foillanus, Elias, and Kilianus. They confessed that, out of a devoted affection of holy charity, they had each renounced his own possessions for the hope of eternal life and had earnestly clung to his footsteps, been instructed by his admonitions, and conformed themselves to his examples. Kissing our hands and falling on their knees to the ground, they entreated us, amid sorrowful sighs and streams of tears, to write these things and entrust them to posterity for preservation.

We resisted their wish at length, because we feared the smallness and inadequacy of our own ability. Yet the right of due love, by the tenderness of its weakness, and also by the gem-bearing wings of a twofold affection, surpassed the hidden chambers of our devoted heart. At last the aspiration of fraternal union, by the power of the Holy Spirit and with grace cooperating, flowed back into our soul, which distrusted its own strength and was timid before the difficulty it was about to undertake. We therefore endeavored to satisfy their love and judged it worthy that these matters should be set forth word for word to the praise and glory of the pious Father.

# The Passion of Saint Livinus, Bishop and Martyr Begins

[Col. 0873A]

At the time when Calomagnus, the illustrious king of the Scots, was distinguished by the virtues of a man eminent in the Christian religion and, by divine Providence, auspiciously governed both the royal scepter and the central power of imperial monarchy, there was a certain Scottish senator named Theagnius. He was exceedingly distinguished by the noble lineage of his birth, chief among that king’s nobles, and, above all his courtiers, held the highest office. He was an energetic man, a skilled keeper of royal secrets, and widely celebrated in eloquent report for the arrangements of his supreme wisdom.

He also had a wife named Agalunia, distinguished in ancestry and merits, specifically a daughter of Ephigenius, the most renowned king of the Irish. By the inspiration of the Lord, united in equal spiritual accord and girded with divine laws, they shone with remarkable signs of virtue. The Lord, who had visited them with his grace, deigned to console them with the following glory.

One Sunday night, while they were resting together on their bed, richly adorned according to royal taste, neither fully awake nor completely asleep, a dove of milky color seemed to descend from heaven, flashing with the inestimable brightness of heavenly glory. It rested upon the pillow of their bed and looked serenely upon them. Spreading its wings, it overshadowed them and, with honey-sweet mouth, let fall three little milky drops, like the purest milk, upon the blessed woman’s lips, then flew back through the air toward heaven.

Immediately a vaporous radiance, filled with an extraordinary fragrance of aromatic sweetness, passed throughout the entire royal palace and extended until morning in unbroken rays. The infant whom the blessed mother then happened to be carrying in her womb, already illuminated by the life-giving breath, began to move its limbs, and—believe it with certainty—rejoiced at the regard of the heavenly visitation.

Then the high-minded duke Theagnius and the venerable matron Agalunia, astonished by the rarity of such fragrance, as dawn was already shining, summoned to them Menalchius, the duke’s brother, who at that time governed the rights of the chief bishopric. He was an esteemed man, outstanding in the elevation of his holiness, and they carefully related to him the details of so great a matter.

Inspired by the grace of the Holy Spirit, he replied in turn: “This vision, clearly manifested by God, is not only a cause of our rejoicing; it will also be a source of joy to the peoples of many nations. For, by God’s gift, a child will be born to you who has already been sanctified in his mother’s womb and nourished with spiritual milk. He will be a supreme bishop, a lamp for his homeland, and an unwavering defender of divine law for God’s peoples on the way to eternal salvation.”

When the venerable day arrived on which the illustrious mother, the worthy Agalunia, visited by heaven, brought forth this blessed child into the world, all the inhabitants of that region were seized by such joys of wondrous delight, and such immense serenity shone forth in brilliant sunlight—and continued to shine for an entire month—that everyone marveled. They confessed that they had never read of such an abundance of great joys and such vast serenity even in the most ancient records—or, what shall we say, that they had never heard of it in the sayings of the ancient Fathers.

At that same time blessed Augustine, a Father of outstanding holiness, sent by blessed Gregory, apostolic bishop of the Roman See, as the first bishop of the English and as the most splendid and supreme lamp of truth, had come to the aforementioned king Calomagnus on his own mission, divine Providence evidently supplying the occasion. He too marveled at the joy of such an extraordinary event.

For all the king’s chief men and the entire majesty of the royal court, together with the citizens of the country, were transformed into an astonishing joy of exultation. Moved by the prophetic Spirit of truth and by mutual conversations, they rejoiced together and declared in the adjoining halls that this child, beloved by God, would become the light of the peoples and the supreme patron of the entire region.

The pious king and the most devout queen, together with the venerable bishops Augustine, bishop of the English, and Menalchius, the chief bishop, received him from the sacred font of blessed regeneration. They gave him the name Livinus, after the brother of his glorious mother Agalunia, an archbishop of the Irish Church who had won the martyr’s palm at Verbanus for the name of Christ.

As soon as they lifted the child from the water, all who were present clearly saw a column-like radiance descend, brighter than the rays of the shining sun, hover over the head of the blessed child, and a right hand brighter than gleaming gold flash forth from above and mark the infant three times with the sign of the holy cross. At the same time a heavenly voice thundered: “Beloved by God and by human beings, whose memory is in blessing.” With this verse the divine vision returned to the heavenly palaces.

Surrounded by such manifestations of heavenly miracles and mysteries, the king and queen, the venerable Fathers and ministers of the divine mystery—namely, the supreme bishops Augustine and Menalchius—and the others, with equal devotion, praised Christ the Lord on high.

The child, God’s chosen one, surpassed his infant years by rational self-restraint. Day by day, though his bodily strength was still so slight, he displayed outwardly the image of virtue and, through mature conduct, was already preparing himself to be summoned by the citizens of heaven, eagerly longing to become their companion and beloved friend. He yearned to attain blessedness and, contemplating the future, renounced temporal things. Whenever he feared that the weakness of the flesh might cause him to fall while doing good, strengthened by spiritual assistance he advanced splendidly through the striving for perfection.

Behold, the youth already worthy of remembrance—most blessed Livinus, the conspicuous athlete of Christ—was helmeted with the chastity of divine fervor, armored with constancy of faith, and inflamed on every side with the exaltation of the heavenly army. When he had passed the age of nine years, destined to be praised for the enduring virtues of his merits, he began to be glorified in the world by such wondrous signs. He would fight triumphantly against the fiercest tyrant of this world and his deadly snares as the warlike standard-bearer of the supreme King.

On the holy day of Pentecost, when the aforementioned duke Theagnius, accompanied by the venerable boy and surrounded by the retinue of his nobles, was proceeding to a monastery built for God in honor of holy Mary, the Virgin and Mother of God, desiring to be refreshed by divine praises and fortified by the Sacraments, the inhabitants of that place brought forward two men bound with iron chains, whom the ancient serpent had most pitiably driven mad and deprived of human society.

One of them had killed a man and two women; the other, in his madness, had struck down his own wife and two sons in death. When the venerable boy Livinus saw them, he said to his father and his retinue:

“Beloved, I ask you to implore the mercy of almighty God with me, so that, in keeping with the nature of this matter, he may open the regard of his glory through your prayers.”

With hands outstretched and eyes likewise raised toward heaven, he prayed:

“Eternal God the Father, merciful hearer and refuge of those who faithfully entreat you, be present to your servants. In your loving heart heed our prayers, and let the grace of your blessing blossom over the work of your own creation, which is disfigured by the burden of such dreadful weakness, so that your name may be glorified in it and the favor of your great mercy be proclaimed throughout the ages.”

When all had cried out “Amen,” the venerable boy Livinus, standard-bearer of heavenly compassion, came forward fearlessly, placed his hands upon the heads of both men, and said:

“In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, may every deception of the devil’s phantom be uprooted from you. May you be cleansed into a most pure vessel of holy faith and become a dwelling of the Holy Spirit.”

Then, as everyone watched, an extremely dreadful smoke mixed with dark blood boiled forth from their mouths and nostrils. At the same time a black mass of filthy flies poured out and, flying into the air with a shrill and confused sound, disappeared.

The heavenly physician cleansed them, fortified them with the sign of the holy cross, and confirmed them in holy confession. Made more confident and perceptive, they renounced all their possessions, began to follow the footsteps of the blessed boy Livinus, and spent the rest of their lives with him in holy conduct.

One of them was called Herimus, the other Simphronius. In the faith of the holy Trinity and following the example of their pious teacher, they are known among us as worthy and outstanding confessors of God and co-heirs of the kingdom of Jesus Christ.

Thus almighty God wished to make his beloved servant, blessed Livinus, known to the world through these and other signs worthy of divine praise and through the great works of his divine power. By the evident reasoning of his discerning arrangement, he mercifully decreed that Livinus should be honorably enrolled among the sacred company of his chosen ones—those whom he ordained before the foundation of the world for eternal glory and through whom he would display the light of his truth—through the virtues of their merits.

The boy of remarkable character, adorned with divine gifts and radiant with the spirit of humility, incomparably absorbed in contemplation of the future life, sought with all his effort to possess the summit of complete perfection, heavenly grace going before him and his gracious will following after.

He had chosen the rule of ecclesiastical discipline as the pattern by which to regulate his life contemplatively, under the guidance of the blessed presbyter Benignus, a man of high Scottish birth and noble blood, but elevated still higher by the radiance of holy virtues. Desiring to be conformed to him through spiritual discipline joined to tender devotion of mind, Livinus sought to be perfectly instructed by the melodies of David’s psalms, the honey-sweet readings of the holy Gospels, and the other divine exercises.

Refreshed, as it were, by a banquet of heavenly regard, he was already setting foot upon the beautiful field of paradisal delight and, day by day, most effectively driving out vices through the steps of virtue, passing onward into glory.

Who could fully describe the subtle intelligence and effectiveness of his mind? With the grace of the Holy Spirit cooperating, no difficulty in understanding anything hindered his capacity—not in the study of divine readings, nor in the examples of good conduct. The distinguished preacher speaks of such matters when he says: “There is no delay in learning where the Holy Spirit is present as teacher.”

While the youth Livinus, beloved by God, was flourishing most diligently in these studies, it happened that his teacher Benignus, a man worthy of remembrance, departed this life and obtained the heavenly reward. The disciple commended his death to the Lord daily with vigils and prayers, devoted with extraordinary piety.

A certain housewife named Salvia, nurse of the venerable boy Livinus, had been languishing for many days from a continual illness and was already hastening toward her final hour, weighed down by the burden of death. Her face had become almost unrecognizable; her cheeks were sunken and overwhelmed by extreme pallor. Beneath rigid eyelids she feebly looked at those standing around her, recognizing no one, because the clouding of her outward sight prevented it.

Therefore not only the familiar gathering of the citizens and the devoted companionship of her household were saddened by inescapable grief, but the glorious duke and the venerable dignity of his palace likewise sympathized most tenderly with such sorrow, in heartfelt contrition.

When she appeared to be falling into the ruin of death and was wholly despaired of, the holy boy Livinus, destined to be glorified for his glorious virtues, was summoned and quickly arrived. Trusting in the light of heavenly illumination, he hastened through the midst of the grieving crowd to the bed of his beloved nurse, who was already beginning to die. When he understood that human assistance had fallen silent, he earnestly sought to provide heavenly help.

The youth Livinus, beloved by God and skilled in the art of heavenly medicine, stood near the lifeless limbs, his eyes and hands raised toward heaven, his face drenched with tears. What his heartfelt devotion could not express because of repeated sobs of grief, he proclaimed through the evident merits of his prayer.

The prayer had just ended when the body of the deceased woman, having received back its spirit, recovered. She sat up, raised her hands, gave thanks to God, and said:

“When I was being led through unknown and winding places of the roads, through darkness, by black spirits, and was being plunged into a dark pit boiling with sulfur and fire, the holy archangel Michael appeared with the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and with the holy apostle Peter, flashing with heavenly brightness. With a threatening countenance he said to those gloomy spirits: ‘Do not harm this soul; let her go, because Christ commands, through the merits of his beloved Livinus, that she return to her body.’

“They, confounded, disappeared. Then the holy archangel Michael, the holy patriarchs, and the holy apostle Peter took my soul and placed it back in my body.

“Let us rejoice now, because we have for our sake a pious patron crowned by God with the splendor of chastity and piety, equal to the angels, a citizen of the patriarchs, companion of the apostles, co-heir with the martyrs, and equal to the whole company of the saints.”

After uttering these and many other similar things with a simple heart and receiving the blessing of the blessed Father, she lived unharmed for many years thereafter.

When this outstanding recruit of the heavenly army was being magnified among the people by such signs, he feared that, lifted up by human favor, he might be deprived of the summit of his perfection and that the mirror of his splendid brightness might be mixed with certain incitements of seductive praise. He therefore frequently sought solitude and, with his three disciples Foillanus, Helias, and Kilianus, whom we mentioned earlier, hid among groves and thickets where birds nested. As was his custom, he was content with herbs, wild fruits, and scant draughts of muddy water.

Whatever he had or could have had, he cheerfully distributed with generous hand to those in need. For he was a skilled scribe and devoted himself diligently to this work, chiefly concerned to acquire something with which he might refresh the needy and the poor. To show in his sincere simplicity that he regarded the world and everything in it as crucified to him, he worked with his own hands and, from whatever he earned, frequently gave away some portion, fearing to become entangled in the guilt of greed.

The fame of his virtues, like the sweetest fragrance of spices, wafted abroad with the scent of unfading, honeyed sweetness. It filled the palace of the aforementioned king Calomagnus with indescribable joy, made the region famous throughout the Scottish lands, and gladly flooded the hearts of everyone.

The pious king admired the worthy praises of so great a man and rejoiced with devoted favor in the things gloriously accomplished through him. It happened that he ordered Livinus to be brought before him with honor and urged him through humble entreaty, saying:

“O most blessed Father, we know that you flourish according to the rule of every virtue, as the examples of your good deeds testify. Therefore, with all the affection of our heart, we ask you to deign to remain with us, to make use of our royal resources, and to allow us to enjoy your salutary admonitions and the evangelical teachings you impart.”

Through entreaties of this kind, the glorious king, his nobles, and all the members of his court troubled the friend of God day after day.

But the man of God Livinus did not turn his mind away from the heavenly covenant. Thinking more about the things of God than about the things of the world, he feared that, if he satisfied their wishes, the holy purpose of his mind might, on some occasion, be stained by the prompting of the malicious tempter and that he might be cast down from his state of sobriety.

As he struggled anxiously with these concerns, an angel of the Lord stood beside him and offered him these words of consolation, addressing him by his own name:

“Hail, brother Livinus. Do not be anxious. It is time for you to receive consolation. Leave this place and go to blessed Bishop Augustine; through his teachings and pious instruction, with the Lord cooperating, you will be wonderfully exalted.”

After these words, the angelic vision withdrew.

Blessed Livinus, knowing that all things were being carried out divinely concerning him, obtained the king’s permission and departed from the palace as quickly as possible, striving to fulfill the angelic commands.

While he was traveling and hastening toward the great sea across which he had to sail, a young man of radiant appearance, graceful in his bearing, met him. With sweet speech he addressed the holy man of God as follows:

“Do not hesitate, brother. I am the one whom almighty God has appointed as guardian of your life. My care will never be absent from you; I shall be your defender and guide in all your ways and deeds. I know the reason for your journey. Let us hasten where you are going, because God will grant us a prosperous journey.”

As he spoke and went before them, while holy Livinus and his three disciples followed together, they crossed that great sea on dry feet, heavenly mercy accompanying them.

As long as blessed Livinus and his aforementioned disciples—Foillanus, Helias, and Kilianus—walked on foot across the waters of the sea, it seemed to them that they were traveling across a field green with the most luxuriant grass, whitening with roses and lilies, and blooming with every kind of beautiful plant.

When they reached the shore and stood with secure steps upon the land, their guide departed from them. As they watched, he ascended into heaven, surrounded by great splendor of snowy brightness.

The man of God, recognizing that he had thus been gloriously illuminated by divine power through the efficacy of his merits, was struck with humble awe and at the same time strengthened by hope of heavenly consolation. Together with his disciples he offered due praises to heavenly grace.

When these things had been properly accomplished, he hastened by a swift and favorable journey to holy Bishop Augustine. The blessed bishop clearly recognized his arrival through a revelation of the Holy Spirit and, realizing that the beloved minister of God had been divinely entrusted to his care, received him kindly.

With extraordinary devotion of charity he nourished him for five years and three months, instructed him in letters, and, in accordance with the angelic promise, visibly conformed him through his examples worthy of God to the summit of supreme perfection. He consecrated and exalted him through sacred ordination to the honor of the holy priesthood.

On the very day of his ordination, as a pledge of eternal charity, the pious teacher gave his beloved and devoted disciple a purple chasuble richly adorned with gold and jewels, and a stole with an orarium, woven with precious gems and shining gold.

When all these things had been worthily completed through the cooperation of the grace of the nourishing Spirit, the venerable priest of God Livinus, having received the blessing of his pious teacher, the distinguished bishop Augustine, returned to his homeland with heavenly mercy accompanying him.

At his arrival, the prince of the kingdom and the citizens of the country rejoiced with great delight. Meanwhile it happened that Menalchius, chief bishop and brother of the glorious duke Theagnius, the father of the blessed priest of Christ Livinus, happily departed from this world. Everyone mourned his passing, and all were overwhelmed by indescribable sorrow.

After his death, the aforementioned king Calomagnus, his circle of palatines, their courtiers, and the gathering of the whole region, with equal affection of heart, proclaimed that the holy priest Livinus ought to be most worthily elevated to this office.

The king, agreeing to all this with still greater devotion, placed the blessed man three and four times—in due honor and at the Lord’s command—in the chair of the archbishopric.

At the very hour when he received the episcopal blessing, according to the custom by which the shepherds of the holy Church of God are consecrated, while the other bishops and clergy and the devout people were present to make the merits of the blessed bishop Livinus known to the world and to confirm these divine ministries, a voice from above resounded openly before everyone, saying:

“Behold the great priest, who in his days pleased God and was found righteous.”

The holy voice had not yet finished these divine words when suddenly a crown appeared above the head of the venerable bishop Livinus. It was fashioned of glowing gold and flashing gems, woven with flourishing flowers, and brightly suffused within and without by purple colors like roses. Its fragrance of sweetness filled those standing nearby.

This also prefigured that the most blessed bishop would become a worthy martyr of Christ, flowing in the rosy blood of his martyrdom, crowned with the diadem of the heavenly kingdom, and enjoying blessed immortality in the confession of the martyrs for ever.

The glorious bishop Livinus therefore humbly and devoutly received the authority of governance, with the Lord granting it. Kindled by spiritual love, he watched over the flock entrusted to his care and admonished, taught, corrected, and abundantly refreshed it with the food of perpetual verdure—faith, hope, charity, and the other teachings of the Lord’s command, without which one cannot reach the homeland of eternal glory.

For the heavenly physician, just as he was accustomed to heal the souls of his people, so also, with heavenly mercy present, restored the diseased bodies of many to human health.

Among the other virtues of his merits worthy of praise, after he had been elevated to episcopal honor, with the grace of the Lord cooperating, he performed the following remarkable miracles.

[Col. 0880A] A certain head of a household, a Scot named Abdias, was at once paralyzed and leprous, deprived of all use of his limbs. He had existed in this nearly lifeless condition for nine years, unable to move his tongue for speaking, raise his hands to his mouth, or draw up his feet beneath him. He lay wholly rigid on a bed and had nothing vital or mobile in him except his mouth and eyes, by whose signs he could scarcely indicate that what he needed should be provided.

When the distinguished bishop, glorified for this very reason, was making his rounds among the sheepfolds, administering to his sheep the nourishment of eternal life, he happened by chance to enter the house of that sick man. At his entrance the invalid immediately raised his head, gained the power of speech, and, feeling health returning to him, cried out:

“Good for me, good for me! Who is entering? Either the Lord our God himself, or his angel, is visiting us.”

The holy bishop stood amazed, perhaps unaware of what the Lord had determined to accomplish there through his preceding merits. He said to the sick man:

“Why do you cry out so, brother? Peace be with you. Rise and bring me a little water to drink, for I am very tired.”

Then the man rose, now healthy, dutifully fulfilled the command of the man of God, and joyfully gave thanks to God with him for his health. Thereafter he passed through the course of his life in sound condition. After this remarkable and wondrous miracle had gloriously been performed, an even greater marvel followed.

One day, as he was walking along the seashore, certain sailors, overtaken by an extremely violent storm, began to be in grave danger and to perish together with all their merchandise. When the man of God saw that the final extremity was already threatening them, relying on his customary fervor in the Holy Spirit, he hastened to them by a safe path, walking across the sea. He displayed to them the sign of the holy cross and said:

“Have confidence in the Lord, brothers, for he does not despise those who trust in him.”

At these words the storm ceased and a great calm arose. The helmsman, who had fallen from the prow and had been carried far out to sea—about the distance an arrow can be shot—was seen by the venerable father beginning to sink. He ran over the waves to him, seized his right hand with his own right hand, pulled him out, and brought him with him to dry land. The others followed in a prosperous voyage, singing joyful praises to the almighty Lord God, perhaps because he had deigned to save them through his holy pontiff Livinus.

Who would remain silent about this man’s praises, unless he were mute? Who would disdain to draw from the virtues of his merits, unless he neglected to love Christ? For we know that he did nothing other than what we read that Christ taught.

He was also a flower of truth and humility, a lamp of justice, a jewel of chastity, and a model of sobriety. In all his pursuits he labored earnestly and acted diligently so that he might become a leader and example of every virtue. He was constant in prayers, content with vigils and fasts. He generously relieved the poor in their necessities. In receiving guests, especially travelers and monks, he watched over them with the greatest devotion. With his own hands he washed their feet; with profound devotion he offered them water for their hands; with the greatest liberality he supplied food and drink; and to the needy he gave clothing with abundant generosity.

Even beneath his purple pontifical garments, adorned with gold and gems, he was always clothed in sackcloth. He lived each day on ash-baked bread mixed with ashes and on an exceedingly small taste of water. Through continual meditation he most diligently frequented monasteries and holy places, attending prayers, psalmody, and the celebration of Masses.

[Col. 0881A] Who could recount how many sick and infirm people were restored to health by the shadow of his blessed body, by the touch of his garments, or merely by hearing the voice of his devout admonition? Clearly, we should believe him equal to the blessed apostles, since he possessed equal dignity through purity of mind and sobriety of a clean body.

He was humble toward the poor, gentle toward those subject to him, and approachable toward the powerful, so that by the moderation of his conduct and the pleasantness of his speech he might draw everyone onto the path of heavenly joys. He knew that those set over others through worldly powers, with their swollen necks, could in no way be bent toward the perfection of Christian religion unless they were imbued with apostolic teaching through the gentlest admonitions of true piety—being made all things to all people in order to win them all.

He anticipated those higher than himself in rank and cherished his subordinates with paternal love, so that through the familiarity of his manner of life he might more readily pour the words of life into the hearts of all.

He was indeed a man of God, harmoniously proportioned in bearing, action, dress, and every bodily manner: elongated in his limbs and slender, of moderate height, with a large head, blond hair, and gray, very sparse hair mingled at the temples and forehead. He had broad, extended ears; very wakeful and cheerful eyes; bristling gray eyebrows; and an exceedingly white forehead around the brow and temples. His cheeks, thin from frequent fasting, were nevertheless very red and remarkably pleasant; he had a gray beard, supple and slender fingers, and absolutely no superfluity in his limbs.

[Col. 0881B] The more beautifully he shone outwardly in bodily form, the more brilliantly he sparkled inwardly through the Holy Spirit dwelling within him. As he surpassed others as a mirror of every holiness through the growing virtues of his merits, he seemed to have deserved a heavenly eminence, so that not only the Scottish and British peoples, but also the Irish and the neighboring peoples of the surrounding regions, together with their princes, admired the praises of his renown. From every direction they flocked to him in extraordinary numbers to hear the words of life from his mouth.

Like a loving father, he fed all these people with spiritual nourishment and strengthened them with his blessing. All the sick and weak in body, and all who were hindered by various ailments and came to him, returned joyfully to their homes, refreshed by his kindness and invigorated with the strength they desired.

Yet his spirit was not lifted into boastful pride because of these things. Rather, beyond what can be admired, it was founded upon the vigilance of true humility, upon the pledge of gentleness, patience, chastity, temperance, justice, love of God and neighbor, and the foundation of eternal charity. Accordingly, he shunned the favorable, rumor-bearing chatter of the crowd as though it were the mouth of a fire-breathing dragon.

Always concerned with the things of God, not with those of the world, he knew that the Lord had magnified his glory in him. Through the seriousness of his holy meditation he tempered amusement, and he reproached himself for guilt if, by remaining in one region, he were to gain profit from the talent entrusted to him. Since he knew that many peoples were entangled in the blindness of their error and ought to be illumined by the radiance of the Lord’s brightness, it seemed to him that the lamp of Christ, kindled within him by the stone of the Holy Spirit, ought more worthily to be placed upon a lampstand, so that it might shine more abundantly for the salvation of many and lead them to the most radiant dwellings of heavenly life.

[Col. 0882A] While he was therefore troubled by such concerns, by the Lord’s providence he impressed upon an archdeacon of holy memory named Sylvanus the duties of governance, lest Christ’s sheep be without a shepherd while he himself, preaching in foreign regions among various nations, watched over the feeding of the flocks.

When he had traversed many places, scattering the seeds of the divine seed, driving demons from possessed bodies, and healing the bodies of many sick people, he came with his disciples to a certain monastery called by the name of the village Gandavum. Blessed Bishop Amandus had founded it after uprooting the shrines of the Gentiles. He himself dedicated it to the honor of the holy apostle Peter and all the apostles. Having gathered worshipers there, he set over them as abbot a man named Florbert, a leader of holy religion, distinguished in character and filled with examples of every uprightness.

He was received by him and by the other brothers with the service of monastic charity. There he also found a man of remarkable holiness and an outstanding confessor of Christ, Bavo, recently fallen asleep in the Lord. He had been buried in the monastery of Saint Peter and the holy apostles by the blessed Bishop Amandus, Abbot Florbert, and the devoted brothers, with fitting honor, and was shining with glorious miracles.

Livinus remained in that place for thirty days and kept unceasing vigil before the tomb of Saint Bavo, offering his prayers and the celebrations of Mass to the Lord God. When these days had been completed, he blessed the brothers of the monastery and the devout people of the district with pontifical authority and confirmed them in the way of truth. Receiving from the monastery’s administration the provisions necessary for the journey, he departed and, by God’s arrangement, hastened into the land of Brabant.

[Col. 0882D] As the venerable bishop entered it with saving footsteps, he admired the exceedingly pleasant land, beautiful and most delightful, abounding through the Lord’s kindness in milk and honey, overflowing with the fertility of various crops and trees, and rich in an abundance of every good thing.

He also observed that its inhabitants shone in the natural form of their bodies, were well ordered in their clothing, honorable in speech and seriousness of conduct, great-hearted men, outstanding warriors, fit for royal service, and formed by every exercise of their pursuits.

But, according to the psalmic expression, like a horse and a mule that have no understanding, they were restrained by bit and bridle under Satan. Transgressing God’s law, they were polluted by adulteries, robberies, thefts, perjuries, and murders. Like savage dogs, biting one another in pestilential frenzy, they alternately defrauded one another by deceit and struck one another down in mutual slaughter.

Finally, when the evangelical man saw them becoming worse from day to day in their conduct, he labored for them with vigils, tears, and prayers, lest insatiable Tartarus swallow such venerable persons in its greedy jaws and drag them with it into perdition. He did not cease to travel daily through their towns, villages, and fortresses, letting the words of life fall into their ears.

With divine grace following, very many of them escaped the snares of the evil persecutor through his instruction and gained eternal life.

As he went about correcting, exhorting, and calling the peoples of that region back to the way of life, it happened that he entered an estate called by its old name Holthem. There a man possessed by a demon met him, crying out:

“O servant of God, Livinus, what have we to do with you? Behold, you have invaded my kingdom and deprived me of my army. Why do you continue to persecute me? For know that if you drive me out of here, I will cause you to suffer many injuries in this place.”

The minister of truth, relying on the Holy Spirit, stretched out his hand and opposed to him the sign of the holy cross, saying:

“Be silent, persecutor of every good thing, and depart from this creature of God. From now on, harm neither him nor any human being.”

Immediately the demon departed. In the sight of everyone, he came out of the man’s body like smoke mixed with the foulest blood. The man, greatly exhausted, lay as though dead. After an hour he rose, gave thanks to God with the blessed man, and returned home in good health. In an unwearied voice he proclaimed to the people the power of the holy Father, by whose merits he had been deemed worthy of deliverance.

[Col. 0883C] When two noble women heard of the fame of the illustrious bishop—women of the highest rank and most distinguished noble birth—they devoutly received him into their hospitality so that they might enjoy his most sacred conversations and be comforted by his visitation through the grace of God, which they saw shining in him. One was named Berta and the other Erapahildis.

Lady Erapahildis had a son named Pugelbert, who had lost his sight for thirteen years and five months because of a swelling of the vesicles (*tuberatio vesicarum*) and could not see the light of heaven. But when Saint Livinus of God made the sign of the holy cross over his eyes, he was illumined through the cooperation of divine grace.

Meanwhile, as the report of this deed spread, an innumerable crowd of illustrious men and women came to him, bringing with them whatever sick people they had. They obtained heavenly medicine for their souls and bodies.
