[Col. 0884A] Yet it is most wretched to say that nearly all the citizens of the surrounding provinces were, like beasts, untamable in heart, exasperated, rebellious against God. They said that the virtues they saw being performed in the world through God’s servants were worthless, arrogantly rejected the law of Christ, killed his priests, and either expelled those who labored to bring them into the way of salvation or, raging without restraint, put them to a cruel death.

Therefore the most steadfast athlete of Christ, girded with divine laws, attacked them. As a preacher of evangelical disputation, he persisted in eloquent instruction, becoming an imitator of our Savior. He showed favoritism toward no one, but carefully examined and reproved all according to the quality of their works, striving, as a faithful laborer, to gather the fruit of the divine seed into the Lord’s granary in a wheat harvest.

He admonished those who believed to persevere in good works. Strengthened by the Holy Spirit, he rebuked more sharply those who were perverse in heart and unbelieving. Finally, as he devoted himself daily to holy divine instruction, announcing eternal joys to the blessed and everlasting punishments to the wretched, the faithful received his saving admonitions with eager hearts and understanding.

But the unbelievers, obstinately resisting, said that this evangelical disputant was deceitful and a seducer; that he had not watched over the salvation of souls, but had traveled through the regions of foreign peoples out of love of earthly gain; and that he deserved to be treated with insults, exiled, or cruelly killed rather than obeyed in his teachings.

Persisting stubbornly in this malicious error, some of them struck the holy martyr of God with lead-weighted boxing-gloves (*plumbatis cestibus*), while others, raging with staffs and many injuries, tormented him. Among them was one named Walbertus, burning at the devil’s instigation. He thrust an iron forceps into the saint’s mouth, cut out his tongue, and threw it before the people, saying:

“Behold the tongue of this seducer, which by speaking falsely turned our people away. It deserves nothing else than to be thrown to dogs for them to devour.”

[Col. 0884D] When the perverse man dared to do such things, a flame went out from the wrath of God and consumed that criminal and sixteen men with him who had advised this crime, so that not even their ashes could be found.

The most steadfast herald of Christ was not abandoned by God. His tongue was restored, and with greater confidence he expounded the divine laws to the people. Yet the malignant crowd, untouched by this blow, did not cease to riot against the holy martyr of Christ. They shouted that he was a sorcerer and enchanter, and declared that the things they had seen divinely happen around him were false and meaningless.

While these things were occurring, one of them named Geraldus, more cruel than the others, stretched out his arm to crush and strike the holy martyr of Christ with his fist. But, prevented by the just judgment of God, he remained for three days with his arm extended, rigid and confounded. Coming to his senses, he threw himself at the feet of the holy martyr and was restored to health.

The blessed bishop continually sang unwearied praises to God for the divine virtues by which he was daily glorified. With his whole heart he strove to become himself an offering with the palm of martyrdom, for whose love he had resolved to suffer death.

[Col. 0885A] When the hour of his reward was approaching, on Sunday night, while he was keeping vigil in prayer according to his usual custom, the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him with his disciples, surrounded by a great light, and said:

“Rejoice, my beloved. Work steadfastly. Today, about the sixth hour, I will receive you into my kingdom, and you will rejoice with me forever with your brothers.”

Strengthened by this vision, the soldier of Christ, knowing that the day of his reward was near, summoned at daybreak the people of the faithful who had been saved through his teaching. He admonished them to persist in the way of truth and taught them the things that belong to the kingdom of God.

[Col. 0885B] When his speech was finished, he blessed them and, bending his knees before them, gave thanks for the service of kindness by which they had most devoutly received him. He kissed each one and wept, moving them all to devout tears. After piously greeting them all in Christ, he departed against their wishes and began to set out with his disciples toward a village called Escha, intending to announce the kingdom of God to those citizens, in case he might there also attain the promise of Christ.

When two brothers, Walbertus and Menizo, ministers of the devil, learned that the beloved friend of God was departing, they thought he was fleeing. Gathering their fellow soldiers, men like themselves in savagery, they spewed forth from their feline hearts these deadly words:

“That blasphemer has profaned our law and led the people astray. But, knowing that he can no longer advance his cause among us by his sorceries, he has decided to leave secretly. He will not depart after having insulted us in this way. Let us follow him more quickly, so that we may avenge our disgrace.”

Their accomplices, hateful to God—children of darkness, driven on by the angels of their father Satan—raged with still greater cruelty, speaking even worse insults unjustly against the holy man of God. In a common conspiracy they rushed together to shed innocent blood. Of them it is plainly written:

“Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they dealt deceitfully; the venom of asps is beneath their lips.”

It continues:

“Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood.”

[Col. 0885D] The unconquered martyr of Christ Livinus stood in prayer, with eyes and hands raised toward heaven. Suddenly, when he had entered the contest, the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a snow-white dove. With its most gentle mouth it let three drops of rose-colored blood fall upon his head and said:

“Do not be afraid, dearest one. The door of life is open to you; the hour has come for you to enter into the joy of your Lord.”

After saying this, it circled around him three times and rose into heaven.

The holy bishop of God continued more diligently in prayer. Then one of his disciples, named Foillanus, said to him:

“Father, I hear the clatter of weapons and the approach of a crowd of foot soldiers.”

He had not yet finished speaking when the sons of iniquity, Walbertus and his brother Menizo, arrived with their companions. They were mad dogs, and with threatening eyes they raged against the holy martyr of God.

But the strongest athlete of Christ came forward and said steadfastly to them:

“Why have you come, brothers? If you regret having wandered this far and seek pardon, God is ready to open the door of his mercy to those who piously knock, just as he himself says: ‘Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.’

Seeing that they had received the heavenly admonitions with blinded minds, the blessed martyr of Christ Livinus said:

“Brothers, I know that you seek to kill me, but I am secure in the mercy of God, who says: ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.’

“Now you will inflict temporal death upon me, but I shall begin to be born into heavenly light, so that I may live with Christ forever.”

[Col. 0886B] “And now wait a little while until I pray.”

After allowing some time, he stretched out his hands toward heaven, was lifted high above the earth, and, bathed in heavenly brightness in the air, prayed:

“God, who sanctified me in my mother’s womb, who illumined my birth with the splendor of your grace, and who were my guide upon the sea, hear me, your servant, Lord. May those who unjustly persecute me for your name not be erased from the book of life. When they have been sated with my blood and, inspired by the grace of your mercies, have repented, receive them into the number of your elect.

“Grant, Lord, that in the place where the presence of my relics or the memory of my name shall be found, there may always be safety and an abundance of peace, and that the fullness of every good thing may flourish.

“And those who are distressed on the sea, or in the waters, or on land, or in prison, or in sickness, or in any affliction, and who remember my name—hear them, Lord, so that they may truly know that you are faithful in your elect and holy in all your works.

“And if they fall into sins and call upon you through me, may they be absolved by your clemency and praise your blessed name forever.

“And above all, Lord, let those who commemorate this day of my assumption with devotion have the whole year made secure for them by the presence of your grace. Let neither sickness nor troublesome distress rule over them, but let them have the tranquility of peace, health, and sobriety, which may lead them joyfully to the kingdom of your glory.

“Grant this, you who live and reign with your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and with the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages.”

[Col. 0886D] His disciples and the faithful standing by answered:

“Amen.”

Then a voice sent forth by God was heard:

“My beloved,” it said, “know that concerning all these things for which you have kindly prayed, you have unquestionably been heard.”

After this, the most steadfast martyr of Christ and glorious triumphant victor, Livinus, strengthened by divine aid, descended to them and said:

“My dearest brothers, I stand as the sacrifice of my King, who is calling me. I await the glory he has prepared for me in heaven; his angels are present, awaiting me. Be strong, and if anything is lacking in your strength, let your cruelty supply it in my passion.

“These companions of mine are Christ’s sheep. I ask peace for them. They have never harmed anyone; they are innocent.”

He kissed them and said:

“May almighty God guard you, my dearest ones, in eternal life.”

[Col. 0887A] Then, looking up to heaven, he said:

“Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit. You have redeemed me, Lord God of truth.”

Meanwhile the aforementioned brothers, Walbertus and Menizo, ministers of the devil, rushed upon him. After inflicting many wounds, they finally beheaded the teacher of their salvation. In the sight of everyone, his soul was received by angels and was deemed worthy to ascend into the secrets of heaven with the great brightness of heavenly glory.

The most blessed bishop and martyr of Christ, Livinus, suffered on the day before the Ides of November, under the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, and who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages.

When the illustrious men and women who had been illumined through his teaching learned of this deed, they came groaning and weeping to the blessed body. Among them was the aforementioned matron Erapahildis, who had housed the venerable man and supported him most devotedly with her resources. She carried in her arms a child whom the holy martyr Livinus had very recently lifted from the sacred font, giving him the name Bricius; he was still dressed in the white baptismal garment.

Before all the others she burst into a lamenting cry, declaring that the blessed man, the illuminator of his homeland, was innocent and that he was unjustly suffering so cruel a death. Then Walbertus, Satan’s henchman, inflamed by the devil, sprang upon her and split her head in two with his small double axe. She died immediately. He cut the infant into three parts and threw them beside the body of the blessed martyr Livinus.

It is firmly believed that they possess the glory of martyrdom in the company of the venerable bishop and martyr Livinus.

The disciples took the body of their pious teacher and the parts of the infant’s little body and placed them together in a tomb prepared for him by angelic hands. They buried the blessed Erapahildis, martyr of Christ, separately near the tomb of the blessed martyr Livinus.

[Col. 0887]

## II. On Penance

[Col. 0887B] **Note:** This fragment, which perhaps survives only from a larger work, was first published by Labbius (*Concil. Paris.*, fol., vol. VII, p. 1478), with this prefatory note:

[Col. 0887C] “In the same Fécamp manuscript codex are found the following items pertaining to penitential booklets, which, so far as I know, have not been published elsewhere. They also exist in Paris codex 1535.” **GILES.**

How can we perform in one year the penance of seven years? A three-day penance in place of thirty days and nights: the chanting of psalms. One hundred and twenty Psalters for twelve months; for one day, fifty psalms and the Lord’s Prayer five times.

Likewise, for one day: *Blessed are the undefiled* four times, *Have mercy on me, O God* six times, and the Lord’s Prayer five times; and, prostrating oneself on the ground, saying the Lord’s Prayer with a genuflection seventy times. Let him do this for one day.

If he wishes to chant fewer psalms but still wishes to endure the penance, let him frequently prostrate himself in prayer one hundred times and say: “Have mercy on me, O God, and forgive my sins.” Let him do this for one day.

Whoever wishes to confess his sins ought to confess them with tears, because tears do not merely ask for pardon but earn it. Let him ask a priest to sing Masses for him, unless they are capital crimes, which he ought first to wash away with tears.

The chanting of one Mass can redeem twelve days; ten Masses, four months; twenty Masses, eight months; thirty Masses can redeem twelve months.

If he wishes to confess, let it be with tears.

Thanks be to God.

[Col. 0887]

## III. Riddles on the Virtues, Which Saint Boniface Sent to His Sister

[Col. 0887C]

For I have sent my sister ten golden apples,

which grew with kindly flowers upon the tree of life.

Sweetly they hung from its sacred branches,

while the tree of life hung upon the tree of death.

Playing with them, may you grasp the joys of life,

and, filling yourself with the sweetness of the life to come,

may you be inspired as you eat great draughts of nectar.

The fragrance of nard fills the nostrils as it breathes;

with these apples you may compare the kingdoms that are to come,

and thus one day celebrate the sweet joys of heaven.

There are other apples, exceedingly bitter, of another tree,

which flourish pestilentially upon the tree of bitter death.

Adam ate them and was slain by dreadful death.

Infected by the breath and gall of the ancient dragon,

viperous and malignantly poisonous as of old,

let the virgin strive never to touch them with her hands.

It is impious to chew and profane to taste them,

lest her teeth grind, darkened by malignant pestilence,

or the holy covenants be broken by such apples,

or the rewards of the heavenly kingdom be lost in vain.

[Col. 0888C]

Who could behold or what reckoning equal

the splendid gifts of the abode that I have bestowed upon fools,

from which the ordinances of the present life are governed

and the rewards of the kingdom to come are newly granted?

May the heavenly commands be fulfilled through my rites;

with such things I shall always pity the human race.

I help mortal kind with kindly virtues

to serve the Lord, the lofty ruler, through heavenly commands.

May they trample the grim amusements of worldly luxury—

kingdoms and clamour; [I am] the daughter of the king of heaven.

I shall knock upon the Thunderer, so that souls may strive toward rest;

may he loosen the bonds of deed, word, or thought.

[Col. 0889A]

Indeed, the offspring of the bow-bearing one from the heavenly seats—

the Redeemer restores all ages through my prayers.

The ethereal Judge creates me without a heel,

in whom he enclosed neither the limits nor the periods of age

in time, but wondrously created me far beyond time.

### Catholic Faith

Fertile and strong, flourishing in lofty virtues,

I am called the guide and messenger of the Most High enthroned.

While through the world I carry back the people of Christ from their stain,

those who live according to my strength and equal laws

are consecrated to Christ, and their ancient sins are removed.

A proclamation: all things will be seen beforehand under God’s law.

From earthly dwellers I send many illustrious ones

to the joys of heaven, and I am fitted to the heavenly seats.

Here, without me, no one shares in holy Peter;

and he who seeks Paul throughout all the regions of the world,

my light-bearing rays emerge for the dark ages.

No one ascends through me to the chosen rewards of the kingdom,

nor does the grace of Christ shine upon the wretched.

Yet, alas, miserable as I am, I do not ascend into the kingdoms of heaven.

### Hope Speaks

As a holy companion I exhort all people, accompanying them with good fortune,

to grasp eternal life in heaven through their merits.

No one ascends through the heights of heaven without me,

but thereafter they are separated, sorrowful and wretched.

Too fortunate would I be if I had not lied,

promising golden things while the world’s amusements remained standing.

I continually lead earthborn people toward the heavenly kingdoms,

so that, relying upon their strength, they may consign punishments to their bodies,

while seeking the golden realms of the age to come.

### Justice Said

Behold, fiery Jupiter is said to be my father;

and in speech I am called a virgin by the utterance of fools.

But because of various crimes I have left the wicked lands;

my face is rarely seen anywhere by earthborn people.

I would have been renowned as the daughter of the king of heaven,

so that, while my father governed the world with such laws,

I might rejoice in his embrace and fashion kisses for my father,

and the golden race of human beings might always rejoice through the ages,

if they observed the rule given by the kindly virgin.

A crowd of evils has pressed upon the peoples, despising me,

while they continually trample the commands of Christ the Thunderer.

Therefore, lamenting, they enter the grim blackness of Erebus,

the fiery Tartarus of King Pluto.

### Truth Says

No one can conquer me, though many can destroy me.

Yet it is also wondrous that I stand in the seats of Christ,

reigning and rejoicing there together with the citizens of the clergy,

an inhabitant among the heavenly ones.

But, seeking my sister, I travel through the countryside,

through lands that many old men say have been abandoned.

I no longer wish to dwell in the world’s scepters,

having failed to find my holy sister through sorrowful merit.

The ancient prophet David sang this in verse:

that on earth human beings are vain.

With me, the virgin, removed,

I shall cross beyond the place where I was always fleeing;

now I shall climb to the stars.

### Mercy Says

Behold, as twin sisters differing in character and law,

we both persist together upon all the paths of the Lord.

But my sister alone would plunge mortals into dark shadows

and make them wander through the punishments of Erebus,

through the byways of Dis,

if she alone held the kingdoms of the age throughout the world.

I strive to break her hostile powers,

crying out and saying, “Sister, dearest one, spare them.”

O happy race of heaven that has found me, the virgin!

Through my rule I forgive the sins of earthly people.

I give the heavenly ones a time of life;

I give the light of Olympus;

I give the immense field of the world, adorned with various flowers,

so that the golden race of human beings may climb to the summit of heaven.

Yet I am not absent from the sacred boundaries of the Most High enthroned,

obtaining forgiveness for wretched mortals of this age,

continually serving Christ through the ages.

### Patience Says

Through me true and false prophets are tested,

and the wicked are expelled far from the boundary of the saints.

The pious deeds performed for my sake are not lost.

I turn the afflictions of my people into their own merit,

and, by the example of their merit,

Through extraordinary efforts I turn dreadful sins into holy rewards.

Through me the grim anger of many is restrained,

and the fiery fury of strife that burns with terrifying force.

I shall be called the nurse and guardian of virtues.

Through my skill the heavenly commands are continually fulfilled,

because I stand in the heavenly ranks among Christ’s seats.

I shall accompany the tranquil eternal King forever.

### True Christian Peace

The age would everywhere become peaceful for mortals,

and I would govern an eternal empire alone throughout the world.

Once sent to Christ’s people from heaven in a song,

while the true offspring of God blessed the ages by his birth,

behold, I am enriched in the name of the ruler of the ages.

I reign perpetually among Christ’s three native realms,

and, dwelling as queen in the lands of the just,

I shall be called their queen.

The heavenly inhabitants continually hold me at heaven’s summit;

whatever kingdoms I illumine, they bear my joys.

…[lacuna] citizens, and now I am entreated to be present in prayers.

If I deign to serve spirit and body for them,

the grim, savage wars of battle do not torment them.

I always flee infamous discord everywhere.

The ethereal Judge ordered that I should always possess these things.

I am broken by the efforts and malicious mind of the savage,

but for me there is a wondrous golden gate, the hall of heaven.

Alas! How far am I from miserable, sick mortals,

who disdain to have me in their own house?

For them the kingdom of heaven is closed beneath the vault of the heavens.

Therefore do not despise such a bride, peoples:

without this virgin the temple of heaven cannot be entered.

### Christian Humility Confesses

Here, among you, I alone scarcely number the sacred sisters.

Because I appear darker in despised garments,

fools scorn me; behold, I am despised by all.

No other is anywhere found so lowly on earth.

But the Lord will grant the aid of freedom from heaven;

as far as I am lowest upon the ground,

so near am I to heaven.

Clothed in my blood, Christ saves the lands.

No one will climb the lofty summits of heaven

if he lacks me personally—lest, perhaps, my sisters—

for one most beloved bride belongs together with the Lord Christ:

peasants and kings, and unmarried girls,

countless heroes born in better ages,

the beautiful, outstanding crown of the holy martyrs,

and men terrible in their merits together with kindly mothers.

Amid such a great number, no one, except through me,

will receive the holy joys of the Most High King.

I am continually present as nurse and guardian to all,

pleasing the eternal King and soothing his heart.

The monk is called tearful and empty in mind

if, swollen with a perverse heart, he rejects my deeds.

Among the few earthborn I am approved as a lovable guest,

and nevertheless, as the most excellent virgin born of the Most High,

I accompany the throne, leading many ranks through the air.

Relying upon the strength of my bridegroom, I am a holy warrior-maiden;

I keep my simple covenant with the King of kings.

### Virginity Says

Flourishing with kindly flowers of perpetual life,

renowned, I bear the crown of virtues together with the saints.

I accompany Mary, mother of the King of the ages,

rejoicing that she bore the one who was destined to become her own parent,

he who saved the wicked ages by his own blood.

# In the Year of the Lord 752. Saint Zacharias, Roman Pontiff

[Col. 0891]

## Historical Notice on Pope Saint Zacharias

*(Liber Pontificalis, from various editions)*

[Col. 0891B] **[Note 1.]** The patrimonies of the Apostolic See ought to be reclaimed by the supreme pontiffs, both by the right of patrimony—as that prelate who deserved so well of the same See rightly maintained (Blanchin, *Anastasius*, vol. II, p. 299)—and by another, higher right arising from divine laws, according to which things sacred to God are to be administered, possessed, retained, vindicated, and recovered by the high priest from sacrilegious usurpers whenever they are occupied. Hence these two great pontiffs—Gregory III, whose interregnum still remains to be considered, and Zacharias, whose beginnings, tenure, and death remain to be examined—both celebrated for the innocence of their conduct and the holiness of their lives, attempted to recover by different means the cities of Ameria, Horta, Polimartium, and Blera, which King Luitprand of the Lombards had taken from the Holy See. Gregory sought to recover them by force of arms; Zacharias by diplomatic action.

Gregory had lost them because he had protected Trasamund, duke of Spoleto, within the walls of Rome from the fury of Luitprand. When his forces had been increased by Roman troops, so that he might more easily recover his duchy and the cities of the Church, he discovered that the treaty-breaker had betrayed him. He therefore sent an embassy twice to Charles Martel, whom he calls the sub-king of France, and asked for assistance so that the rights of the Church might be asserted by their combined arms. Meanwhile Charles died, and a few days later Saint Gregory also died.

But what was most desirable from the all-good and all-great God did occur: Zacharias immediately succeeded Gregory, and Pepin succeeded Charles—the latter distinguished in the glory of arms, the former outstanding in practical action. For after several years Pepin greatly extended the patrimonies of the Holy See in every direction. Zacharias, scarcely raised to the See of Peter, negotiated through envoys with the king of the Lombards for the restoration of the cities, and assisted him with Roman troops against the treaty-breaking Trasamund. When the king failed to keep his promises, Zacharias promptly and fearlessly approached his camp in the territory of Spoleto. He did not return to Rome until the patrimonies that had long before been seized had been restored, together with the four cities taken two years earlier, which he himself personally took possession of; then he entered Rome, where, while attending to sacred things, he rendered thanks to Christ, the vindicator of the Church.

These events were accomplished by both pontiffs within three years, as may be seen in my arrangement of them in the *Caesarean Pontifical Chronology* [Col. 0892C]—unless someone prefers to enter the labyrinths of the Deacon and of the Frankish writers, from which not even Pagi, a man of such great learning, managed to emerge. But, lest I seem to wander too far from my purpose, I return to the reckoning of time.

After the death of Saint Gregory III, as was stated in the notes on him, on 28 November, the day on which he is commemorated in the Martyrologies, the pontificate remained vacant for four days, as is correctly stated by the commonly received text and by two Freherian manuscripts, the Cavensis, and the fourth Ambrosian manuscript—not eight days, as is read in certain manuscripts and catalogues—while all the others, especially the Colbertine manuscripts, except the seventh, are silent about the interregnum. Thus, counting four days from 28 November, the day of death belonging to Gregory’s pontificate, one reaches 3 December. Since the letter A of the Sunday cycle shows that this day fell on a Sunday in the year 741, it must be assigned to the ordination of Zacharias.

Zacharias held the See for ten years, three months, and thirteen days, as is correctly stated by the Lucensis Catalogue and the second Freherian manuscript—one day more than the others and one month more than the two Colbertine catalogues, which reckon incorrectly [Col. 0892D]. For from the day of his death, 15 March 752, on which Anastasius attests that Zacharias was buried, and to which the Martyrologies bear witness, it is evident that this pontiff held office for ten years, three months, and thirteen days, with the days both of his ordination and of his death included.

Since these things are so, Pagi cannot at all be followed when, on his own authority, he wishes Saint Zacharias to have been ordained on 30 November, the feast of Saint Andrew. To omit what I have often discussed elsewhere—perhaps to the point of weariness—about the Sundays proper for ordinations, and what I shall have to recall in the following note, by what reasoning can four days be inserted between the 28th and the 30th? I cannot embrace this even in thought, much less in imagination.

Although Regino, whom alone one ought to have followed in establishing the date of Gregory’s death, has included the day of burial in his total—a point that seems novel to Pagi, although it is customary in all the manuscripts and catalogues—from this it will indeed be possible, given the constraints that hem us in, to calculate the interregnum. But how will the greater difficulty that arises elsewhere be overcome? Roman pontiffs were not elected until the third day after the burial, both according to the constitution of Boniface III, already praised elsewhere, and according to the praiseworthy custom of the Roman Church. Therefore, unless one wishes to destroy the monuments of antiquity, the Roman Ordines, and the *Diurnus* of the pontiffs, one must say that the election took place on 30 November [Col. 0893B].

If anyone were to combine this election with the ordination, as though the elected man were sent to the Lateran patriarchium—as was customary—and then rushed with all speed to the Vatican, with all the other ceremonies performed that the *Ordo* and the *Diurnus* describe, he would seem not to know the ancient rites sufficiently. For during this period the *enthronement* (*enthronismos*, ἐνθρονισμός) preceded the consecration and took place immediately after the election.

I do not assert this without evidence. Anastasius, speaking of the successor of Saint Zacharias (section 227), says that he was elected in the Basilica of Saint Mary at the Crib:

> “All of them, with acclamations of praise, carried him without delay into the Basilica of the Savior, which is called the Constantinian Basilica; then they entered within and, according to custom, introduced him into the patriarchium.”

More clearly, in the case of Valentinus (section 455), likewise elected in the Basilica of Saint Mary, he says:

> “Then, with fitting praises of glory and the fullness of honor, he was led by them to the Lateran patriarchium and placed upon the pontifical throne.”

The consecration took place on another day—namely, Sunday—whose arrival was awaited after the enthronement. Anastasius bears witness to this in the same place:

> “When the day of his consecration had dawned in clear light, all the Romans, leading the aforesaid bishop from the palace to the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, consecrated him, with divine majesty assisting, as supreme pontiff upon the high throne.”

Thus the enthronement took place on the very day of the election in the Lateran patriarchium; then, on another day—undoubtedly Sunday—the consecration took place in the Basilica of Saint Peter. From this point the tenure of the consecrated man began to be reckoned; for the time during which he was merely elected and, in whatever manner, enthroned belonged to the interregnum. Consequently Pagi, who correctly taught this in the year A.D. 67, now destroys his earlier position by adopting the opposite doctrine.

Thus the ordination of Saint Zacharias has been vindicated and restored to its proper day [Col. 0893D], as was right. For since, when ordaining the bishop of Interamna on a Sunday, he gave the greatest defender of pontifical antiquity the occasion to assert that bishops were not ordained except on Sundays (Blanchin, vol. II, *Anastasius*, p. 25), it is not even to be imagined that he himself was not consecrated on a Sunday.

Having, I say, vindicated the ordination of Zacharias, one must not pass over in culpable silence the final year of his pontificate, marked by two memorable events. The year of the holy pontiff’s death is made notable by the end of the Exarchate of Ravenna and the beginning of the Carolingian kings, who rendered such great service to the Apostolic See.

The period of the Exarchate, which lasted approximately 184 years—from the year 567, when the patrician Longinus came to Italy, to 751, when the patrician Eutychius departed for Constantinople—came to an end around July of the year 751, when Ahistulf, king of the Lombards, captured Ravenna. Bachmius learnedly observes this in his commentary on Agnellus, part 2, under “The Schism of Maurus,” where he produces a charter dated in the palace of Ravenna on the fourth day of July, in the third year of our most fortunate reign, in the fourth indiction [Col. 0894A]. Therefore the exarchs were expelled from Italy approximately nine months before the death of Saint Zacharias.

Pagi connects the beginning of the Carolingians with the very month of the pontiff’s death, March. In his discussion of the year 752, numbers 1–11, he establishes this connection with great learning. No argument is needed regarding the date, for we have the Frankish annals as witnesses. Here are the very words from the Fulda manuscripts of Pithou:

> **752.** Pope Zacharias, on the authority of the holy apostle Peter, commands the people of the Franks that Pepin, who exercised royal power, should also enjoy the dignity of the name. Thus King Childeric, the last of the Merovingians to rule the Franks, was deposed and sent to a monastery. Pepin, however, was anointed king in the city of Soissons by Saint Boniface, archbishop, and elevated to the honor of the kingdom.

The Bertinian annals, which are silent for this year, say under the year 754:

> “Stephen confirmed Pepin with holy anointing, and with him anointed his two sons, Charles and Carloman.”

Therefore, if he confirmed him, Pepin had previously been inaugurated. On this matter Pagi should be consulted at the cited place, where, against Cointius and Mabillon, he most eloquently establishes Pepin’s accession and the deposition of Childeric III, the last of the Merovingians.

**CENNUS.**

**2. Zacharias.** After an interregnum of only four days following the death of Gregory III, Zacharias was elected pontiff—namely, on the first day on which the nobles gathered in the Lateran patriarchium to deliberate jointly concerning the election [Col. 0894C]. During the preceding three days, the proper rites had been performed for the deceased pontiff, and no deliberations concerning the election could be undertaken. This hurried and peaceful election appears to have been secured both by Zacharias’ merits and by the fact that the tyranny of the exarchs had been weakened: the Italian army had not obeyed the heretical emperor Leo and had openly revolted from Copronymus.

**BENCINUS.**

**3. Zacharias.** In the year 741, on 5 December, which was the eighth day after Gregory’s death, Zacharias was created pontiff with the unanimous consent of all.

“He held office for ten years, etc.” The number of years, months, and ten days previously assigned to his tenure is correctly inferred from the beginning and end of his pontificate.

**BIN. and LABB.**

**4. Zacharias**, son of Polychronius of Siberena in Magna Graecia, now called Calabria; first a regular canon, then a monk of Saint Benedict; soon made cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church by Pope Gregory III. Under the heretical and most impious iconoclast emperor Constantine Copronymus Augustus, he was the fifteenth pope native to the realm and held office for ten years, three months, and fourteen days. He was created on the Kalends of December and consecrated on the third day before the Nones of the same month in the year 741. He is numbered among the best and holiest pontiffs.

**CIACONIUS.**

**5. By nationality a Greek.** Although the writers agree that Zacharias came from Magna Graecia, which is now Calabria, they disagree about the place. Some do not identify his homeland; others assign it to Sybaris, as do Ciaconius and Ferracius. Nevertheless, this pontiff came from the city of Siberena, commonly called Santa Severina, as constant tradition teaches and as appears from the Breviary of the Lateran Canons, where it reads:

> “Zacharias, born in the Calabrian city of Siberena.”

See Baronius with his notes.

**THOMAS ACETUS.**

Zacharias, a Greek by nationality and the son of Polychronius, held office for ten years, three months, and [Note: [Col. 0891B] The Lucensis manuscript reads “ten”; another source reads “fifteen.”] fourteen days. He was a most gentle and gracious man, adorned with every virtue, a lover of the clergy and of all the Roman people, slow to anger and quick to pity, returning evil to no one and not exacting vengeance according to merit. Rather, pious and merciful from the time of his ordination, he returned good for evil even to those who had previously been his persecutors, advancing them to honors and at the same time enriching them with means.

[Note: [Col. 0894D] He found all Italy in turmoil. The holy pontiff found all Italy disturbed by the arms of the Lombards, and their king Luitprand preparing for war against the Roman duchy, from which he had already taken four cities, namely Horta, Polimartium, Ameria, and Blera. Therefore, having sent an embassy to the aforesaid king of the Lombards—as Anastasius relates—he proclaimed salutary admonitions to him. Moved by the warnings of the holy man, Luitprand promised to return the four aforementioned cities, which he had taken from the Roman duchy. But when King Luitprand nevertheless failed to restore them, Zacharias decided to meet him at Interamna, in the territory of Spoleto, in the year 742. Thus, accompanied by the entire Roman clergy, he left the city and set out for that place.

When the king learned of this, unwilling to be surpassed in courtesy, he sent an envoy to meet him and escort him as far as Narni, where many dukes and soldiers received him. As Zacharias approached Interamna, the king met him with the rest of the nobles and soldiers. He traveled with him for some distance in the most agreeable conversation and then dismissed him to a palace prepared for him.

The following day, when they had again come together for a meeting, the holy pontiff so soothed the king’s spirit that he granted him everything he requested and restored to the holy man the four cities that he himself, two years earlier, had taken by siege on behalf of the aforementioned Trasamund, duke of Spoleto—that is, on his account—together with their inhabitants. “He also confirmed them by a grant,” says the same Anastasius, who adds that the king voluntarily restored to the pontiff the Sabine patrimony, seized from the Roman Church thirty years earlier, and furthermore reconceded to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the patrimonies of Narni, Ancona, and Auximum, as well as the valley of the Sutrian territory called Magna, by a deed of gift. He also confirmed peace with the Roman duchy for twenty years and restored to the pontiff all the captives whom he held. Finally, the four cities were restored and the pontiff returned to Rome.

**PAGIUS.**]

He found all Italy [Note: [Col. 0893A] The Lucensis manuscript reads “the province of Italy.”] in great turmoil, as well as the Roman duchy, which Luitprand, king of the Lombards, was attacking on account of Trasamund, duke of Spoleto [Note: [Col. 0895C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “Trasamundus.”], who had taken refuge in this Roman city while the same king was pursuing him. Since the aforesaid Trasamund had not been handed over by his predecessor, Pope Gregory of blessed memory, nor by Stephen, formerly patrician and duke, nor by the whole Roman army, the same king laid siege on his behalf, and four cities were taken from the Roman duchy [Note: [Col. 0895C] Another source reads “were taken away”]: Ameria, [Note: [Col. 0895C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “Hortas.”] Horta, Polimartium, and Blera.

Thus the same king returned to his palace around the month of August, in the seventh indiction. Trasamund, however, the duke, after consulting with the Romans and gathering the general army of the Roman duchy, entered the territory of the duchy of Spoleto in two divisions. The Marsicans and Forconians, and [Note: [Col. 0895C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “the Valvenses and Pennenses”; another source reads “the Balvenses or Ginnenses.”] the Balvenses or Prinenses, immediately submitted to Trasamund, driven by fear because of the size of the Roman army. Then, entering [Note: [Col. 0895C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “the Persian or Ravennate territory”; another source reads “through Ravennate territory.”] through Sabine territory, they came to the city of Reate. The people of Reate immediately submitted as well.

From there, advancing, he entered Spoleto in the month of December [Note: [Col. 0896C] Another source reads “in the fifteenth indiction”], in the aforesaid indiction. There was great turmoil between the Romans and the Lombards, since the people of Benevento and Spoleto were also campaigning together with the Romans [Note: [Col. 0896C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “were joined together.”].

But when Trasamund, duke of Spoleto, refused to fulfill what he had promised to the aforesaid pontiff, the patrician, and the Romans concerning the recovery of the four cities that had been lost on his account, together with the other articles that he had pledged, and when the aforementioned king [Note: [Col. 0896C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “after the army had been moved.”] was preparing to move against the Roman duchy. [Note: [Col. 0896C] Against the Roman duchy. Rome and its duchy readily passed from the Greeks to the Roman pontiff because of Leo’s heretical edicts, the peoples refusing obedience to the heretical emperor. Moreover, the Roman duchy, frequently mentioned in the preceding narrative and whose governors were chosen by the emperors, consisted of the city of Rome together with castles, towns, and villages, including those in parts of Tuscany. These were Portus, Centumcellae, Caere, Bleda, Maturana, Surium, Nepet, the Castle of Gallesium, Horta, Polimartium, Ameria, Tuder, Perusia, Narni, and Otricoli. In Latium were Signia, Anagnia, Ferentinum, Alatrium, Patricum, Frusino, and Tibur. That under Gregory II this duchy was subject to the direction of the Roman See is evident even from the fact that the Roman army, with the pontiff himself commanding, suppressed the rebels and the tyrant Tiberius and compelled Luitprand to restore the places he had seized in this duchy. Thus, from the time of Gregory II and his successors, clearer indications of supreme temporal dominion appear. **BENCINUS.**] Pope Gregory of blessed memory was taken from this life by divine summons. By divine will, the most holy Zacharias was elected to the pontificate.

Almighty God bestowed such grace upon him that he did not hesitate to place his own life at risk for the salvation of the Roman people. He therefore sent an embassy to the aforementioned king of the Lombards and proclaimed salutary admonitions to him. Moved by the warnings of the holy man, the king promised to return the four aforementioned cities, which he had taken from the Roman duchy [Note: [Col. 0896C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “from the duke.”].

When, after the army had been mobilized to seize Trasamund, duke of Spoleto, the Roman army, at the exhortation of the holy man, joined the aforesaid king in assistance [Note: [Col. 0896C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “went out”], Trasamund himself, realizing his deception, left the city of Spoleto and surrendered to the aforesaid king.

When the same [Note: [Col. 0896C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “Luitprand.”] king delayed in restoring, according to his promise, the four cities that he had already promised [Note: [Col. 0896C] Another source reads “already mentioned”], the aforesaid pontiff, as a true shepherd, placing his hope in God, left this Roman city with the priests and clergy and confidently and courageously set out for Interamna, where the king himself was residing in the territory of Spoleto. When he had reached the city of Horta and the king had learned of his arrival, the king sent his envoy Grimoald to meet him and escort him as far as the city of Narni.

At the arrival of this holy man, the aforementioned king sent his dukes, his nobles, and most of his army [Note: [Col. 0897C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “and a large army.”] to meet him. The king received him about eight miles from the city of Narni. On Friday they escorted him to the Basilica of blessed Valentine, bishop and martyr, situated in the aforesaid city of Interamna in the duchy [Note: [Col. 0897C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “duchy of Spoleto.”] of Spoleto. Before the doors of that basilica the same king, with the rest of his nobles and army, received the holy man [Note: [Col. 0897C] Another source reads “the king, with the rest of his army, received the holy man.”].

After prayer and mutual greeting [Note: [Col. 0897C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “mutual greeting”; another source reads “mutual greetings being exchanged there”], when he had been instructed by divine conversations and had shown him charity, the king left the same church and went nearly half a mile in his service. Thus both men remained in their tents on that Friday.

On Saturday they met again. Filled with divine grace, the pontiff addressed him with admonitions pleasing to God, urging him to desist from hostile action and the shedding of blood and always to pursue the things that make for peace. Moved by his pious words and admiring both the constancy and the admonition of the holy man [Note: [Col. 0897C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “his constancy”], he obtained through the grace of the Holy Spirit everything he asked of him and [Note: [Col. 0897D] The four aforementioned cities, etc. The historian explicitly notes that the cities were returned to the pontiff together with their inhabitants. This plainly indicates something other than merely beneficial ownership, whatever more recent writers may assert when they contend that during that period the Roman pontiff exercised no royal right or supreme authority, which supposedly remained entirely with the emperor. They ought nevertheless to have observed that the Lombard king restored the cities and the territories belonging to them, as well as the captives taken in wartime, not to the emperor or to any of his officials, but solely to the pontiff and the Apostolic See; and that the restoration was ratified and confirmed by a solemn donation signed before the altar by the king, who took it from the altar and, after signing, placed it back upon the altar. The same applies to the possession which one pontiff acquired, without being dependent in any way upon the emperor.] restored to the same holy man the four aforementioned cities, which he himself had taken two years before by siege on behalf of the aforesaid Trasamund, duke of Spoleto, together with their inhabitants [Col. 0897C].

He also confirmed them by a grant in the oratory of the Savior located within the church of blessed Peter the apostle, built in his name. He likewise reconceded to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, by a deed of gift, the Sabine patrimony, which had been taken away for nearly thirty years, as well as the patrimonies of Narni and Auximum [Col. 0898A], and also Ancona [Note: [Col. 0897C] In another source, “and Ancona” is absent], Namanata [Note: [Col. 0897C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “Polimartian”; another source reads “Humanata”], and the valley called Magna, situated in the territory of Sutri. The same king confirmed peace with the Roman duchy for twenty years [Note: [Col. 0897C] Another source reads “confirmed it in the tenth year”].

He also restored to the most blessed pontiff all the captives whom he held from various Roman provinces, sending letters both into his own Tuscany and across the Po, together with the Ravennate captives—consuls Leo, Sergius, Victor, and Agnellus [Note: [Col. 0898C] Another source reads “together with the Ravennate captives”; the Lucensis manuscript reads “Agnellus” and “consuls.”].

In the aforesaid Basilica of blessed Valentine, at the request of the same king, he ordained another bishop in place of the bishop of Consentia [Note: [Col. 0898C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “Consentia”; other sources read “Constantia” or “Cosentia”], who had died. While the king himself and his judges were present at the consecration, through the inspiration of divine compunction, he uttered words of such great sweetness that, when they saw the holy man pouring forth many prayers, some of the Lombards were moved to tears.

[Note: [Col. 0898D] On that same Sunday, after the solemn celebration of Mass had been completed, the pontiff invited the same king to lunch, so that he might receive the apostolic blessing. Here “blessing” means a meal or refreshment, either because it begins with the blessing of the table or because it is given in the manner of a *eulogia*, that is, a blessing. *Life of Louis the Pious*: “When he was first sent away from his father in the spring, his father asked him why, although he was a king, he was so poor in household resources that he could not even offer himself a blessing unless it was requested.” And below: “After sharing together in the blessing of bread and wine, the emperor returned to the city.” Council of Melfi, under Urban II: “Let bishops and abbots retain for themselves tithes from vineyards, fields, and crops that they cultivate for their own use or for the use of the brethren, for a blessing or for receiving guests.” Canon, *Questions* 16, question 1.

**ALTASERRA.**]

On that same Sunday, after the solemn celebration of Mass, the most blessed pontiff invited the same king to lunch, so that he might receive the apostolic blessing. There he took food with such great enjoyment and cheerfulness of heart that the king himself said he did not remember ever having feasted so lavishly [Note: [Col. 0898C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “having eaten”; another source reads “having eaten by himself.”].

On the following day, which was Monday, when he took leave of him, the king sent to serve him his nephew Agiprand, duke of Clusium [Note: [Col. 0898C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “Aldeprandus”; another source reads “Aprandus”], or Tacipertus, the castellan, together with Ramingus, castellan of Tuscany [Note: [Col. 0898C] The Lucensis manuscript reads “Raningus”], and Grimoald, so that they might serve the holy man as far as the aforementioned cities and hand those cities over to him with their inhabitants. And this was done.

First they delivered the city of Ameria, then Horta. When they had met at the fortress of Polimartium and had received him, the route, because of the circuit required around the boundaries of the territory, would have been long if they had traveled to the city of Blera through the parts of Sutri and across the territory of the Lombards in Tuscany. Since Blera was nearby, however, namely by way of the fortress [Note: [Col. 0899B] The Lucensis manuscript reads “Laterium.”] of Viterbo, Grimoald, the king’s envoy, escorted the most blessed pontiff as far as the city of Blera. There Ramingus, the aforementioned castellan, and the aforesaid Grimoald, the envoy, handed the city over to the holy man.

Thus, by God’s favor, he returned to this city of Rome with the palm of victory. Gathering the entire people, he addressed them and instructed them all to leave the church of the Mother of God, called *ad Martyres* (the Pantheon), and proceed together in a general litany to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in order to render thanks to almighty God. And so it was done.

When these matters had been completed in the tenth indiction, in the following, eleventh indiction [Note: [Col. 0899C] While the aforesaid king was oppressing the province of Ravenna excessively. In the year 743, King Luitprand again attempted to subject the exarchate of Ravenna to himself and prepared to besiege Ravenna. Therefore the pontiff, at the request of Eutychius the exarch and John, archbishop of Ravenna, went to that city, leaving the Roman city in the charge of Stephen, patrician and duke. Before departing Rome he sent envoys with gifts to Luitprand, begging him to abandon his plan and return the fortress of Cesena to the Ravennates. But when he could obtain nothing, he came to Ravenna, where the Ravennates received him with abundant tears, crying out and saying: “He has come, he has come, our Father, who left his sheep and has hastened to free us who were lost.”

From that city he sent the priest Stephen and Ambrosius, the primicerius, to the king to announce his arrival. He himself entered Lombard territory and became a foot-soldier with his envoys, whom the said king refused to receive. But when the pontiff had reached the Po on 28 June, the king sent his nobles to receive him, and with them he arrived at Ticinum, where the king was residing. The king came outside the walls of the city to meet him. Then, in order to celebrate the solemn Masses for the vigil of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he went to his basilica, which is called the Golden Heaven; afterward, when the offering had been completed, he entered the same city.

On the following day, Zacharias the pontiff was invited to celebrate the birthday feast of that prince of the apostles. He celebrated the solemn Masses, and there they received food together. On the next day the king invited him to his palace. Having been honorably received there, the pontiff begged him no longer to oppress the province of Ravenna, but to restore the cities he had taken, together with their territories, and also the fortress of Cesena. Although reluctantly, the king replied that he would do so. As the pontiff departed, the king escorted him as far as the Po and gave him men from among his nobles to restore the Ravennate territories, especially Cesena. After these places had been recovered, the pontiff returned to the city and, having given thanks to God, celebrated again the feast of the birthdays of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul.

All these matters are established by Anastasius. From them Marca, *On Concord*, book III, chapter 11, number 5, concludes that it cannot be demonstrated more clearly that “during this period the supreme pontiffs retained the administration of the empire, and that imperial officials presided over affairs at Ravenna and Rome, so that every hope of preserving Italy was placed in the supreme dignity of the pontiff.” “From these facts,” says Baronius, “see, under the year 743, how unjust are the complaints of the Easterners against the Roman pontiff, namely, that he stripped the Eastern emperors of the Western Empire.”

**PAGIUS.**]

while the aforesaid king was excessively oppressing the province of Ravenna and was preparing to launch an attack and besiege the city of Ravenna, the most excellent patrician and exarch Eutychius, together with John, archbishop of the Church of Ravenna, the entire people of the aforesaid city, and the cities of the Pentapolis and Emilia, sent a written petition to the holy man, asking him to hasten to their liberation [Note: [Col. 0899B] The Lucensis manuscript reads “to come to their aid.”].

The holy man therefore sent an embassy and gifts to the same king through Benedict, bishop and vice-lord, and Ambrosius, primicerius of the notaries [Col. 0900A], asking him to cease his attack [Note: [Col. 0900B] The Lucensis manuscript reads “fortification”] and return the fortress of Cesena to the Ravennates. But the king would not yield.

When the most holy man saw his stubborn persistence, fortified by the trophy of faith, he left the Roman city, entrusting it to the governance of Stephen, patrician and duke, and, not like a hireling but like a true shepherd who leaves the sheep only to rescue those about to perish, hastened to them. As he set out, he and his priests and clergy commended themselves in prayer to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, together with the travelers. By the will of almighty God, so that they would not be scorched by the heat during the day until they reached the place where they were to pitch their tents, a cloud covered them; toward evening it settled [Note: [Col. 0900B] The Lucensis manuscript reads “withdrew.”].

On the following day it was divinely appointed for their protection. The most excellent exarch mentioned above came to meet it as far as the Basilica of blessed Christopher, situated at a place called Aquila, approximately fifty miles from the city of Ravenna.

[Note: [Col. 0900D] The cloud itself accompanied them, covering them, as far as the Basilica of Saint Apollinaris in the city of Ravenna. *Conviare* means “to travel along a road together with another.” Anastasius below, in the same section: “Afterward the same king, going from place to place, accompanied the same holy man as far as the Po and escorted him.” **ALTASERRA.**]

The cloud itself accompanied them, covering them, as far as the Basilica of Saint Apollinaris in the city of Ravenna. Then a sign occurred: fiery hosts in the clouds went before the holy pontiff on the road he was to take toward the city of Ticinum.

When he left the city of Ravenna, men and women of every sex and age, giving thanks to almighty God with abundant tears, received the same holy pontiff, crying out and saying:

[Note: [Col. 0900B] The Lucensis manuscript reads “He has come, he has come.”]

> “Well has our Shepherd come, who left his sheep and hastened to us, who were about to perish, in order to set us free.”

From the city of Ravenna the pope also sent to the aforementioned king the priest Stephen and Ambrosius, the primicerius, to announce his arrival.

[Note: [Col. 0901D] “These men entered the territory of the Lombards, into a city called Imola.” Imola is a city of Emilia, formerly the Forum of Cornelius, later called Imola, from the fortress of the city whose name was Imola. Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book II, chapter 18: “And the Forum of Cornelius, whose fortress is called Imola.” The Forum of Cornelius was a city of Gallia Cisalpina, later called Lombardy, concerning which Martial, book III, epigram 4:

> “If anyone inquires in what lands, in what city we are—”

You may, if you wish, report that I am at Forum Cornelii. Forum Cornelii was an episcopal city, formerly a suffragan of the metropolitan see of Milan. Hence Ambrose, bishop of Milan, when the church was vacant, appointed one of its suffragans as visitor. He himself bears witness to this in Letter 44, to Constantius, his fellow bishop:

“I commend to you, my son, the church at Forum Cornelii, so that you may visit it frequently in the immediate future, until a bishop is appointed for it.”

Today it is subject to the metropolitan see of Ravenna. Gregory, Book VI, Letter 39, where I discussed this. ALTASERRA.]

These men, having entered the territory of the Lombards and the city called Imola [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “the borders”], learned that those who were trying to obstruct the aforementioned holy man’s journey had sent word of this by a letter written during the silence of the night [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “who were attempting treachery”; another copy: “because they were hindering him”]. When the already mentioned pontiff learned of it, at daybreak on Saturday, he was not terrified by fear of death, but relying on Christ’s help, boldly left the city of Ravenna and entered the territory of the Lombards [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “the borders”]. [The reading is uncertain: *sesquipes factus est suis missis*.] The aforementioned king, struck with grief, refused to receive the men who were preceding him [Col. 0901B].

The supreme pontiff himself reached the Po on the twenty-eighth day of June [Note: Another copy: “he joined him,” and so throughout]. There the king sent his nobles to receive him.

[Note: Having arrived with them at Pavia, where the king himself was staying, and passing outside the walls of that city, at the ninth hour of prayer he went to its basilica, called “At the Golden Heaven,” in order to celebrate the solemn masses of the vigil of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. The ninth hour of prayer is specified because the sacred office is distributed among fixed hours: matins, the first, third, sixth, ninth, vespers, and compline. Rule of Benedict, chapter 16. ALTASERRA.]

Having arrived with them at Pavia, where the king himself was staying, and passing outside the walls of that city, he went at the ninth hour of prayer to its basilica, called “At the Golden Heaven,” to celebrate the solemn masses of the vigil of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “After the libation had been completed”; another copy: “And after the libation had been supplied.”] After completing the offering, he entered the same city and remained there.

On another day, having been invited by the aforementioned king to celebrate the birthday feast of that prince of the apostles in the aforesaid church, he celebrated the solemn mass. There, after mutually greeting one another, they received food together [Col. 0901C; another copy: “the citizens”], and thus returned to the aforementioned city.

On another day the same king invited the holy man, through his nobles, to proceed to his palace. [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “And by that king …”] After he had been received by the king with great honor, he addressed the king with salutary admonitions, entreating him no longer to oppress the province of Ravenna by making an incursion [Note: another copy: “by the aforesaid movement”], but rather to return to him the cities of Ravenna that had been taken [Note: another copy: “And, after taking away the borders of the city of Ravenna, he would restore it …”], together with the fortress of Cesena.

[Col. 0902A] After much resistance, the aforesaid king was induced to extend the borders of the city of Ravenna as they had previously been held [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “which he had initially retained”]. He restored two parts of the territory of the fortress of Cesena to the public interest. But he retained the third part of the same fortress under a pretext, with an agreement established that, by the Kalends of June, when his envoys had returned from the royal city, he would restore both that fortress and the third part that he was holding as security to the public interest.

This same king, going from place to place as far as the Po [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “meeting the same holy man”], entertained the holy man and escorted him [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “Another copy: ‘having accompanied him to …’; another: ‘having entertained him, he escorted him. In which place …’”]. At that place he bade him farewell and, with suitable arrangements, released him to return, assigning to his service his dukes and chief men, as well as other men who were to restore the aforesaid territories of Ravenna and the fortress of Cesena. And so it was done [Col. 0902B].

God worked marvelously, liberating the peoples of Ravenna and the Pentapolis from the oppression and calamity by which they had been held; and they were supplied with grain, oil, and wine. Returning to the city of Rome with all who were with him, they gave thanks to God [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “giving thanks”], and once again celebrated the birthday feast of the blessed princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, with all the people. He devoted himself to prayer, asking almighty God to grant mercy and consolation to the people of Ravenna and Rome against that ambusher and persecutor, King Liutprand.

Divine clemency did not disregard his prayers, but removed that same king from this life before the previously appointed day [Note: another copy: “before the appointed time concerning this …”], and all persecution ceased. Joy arose not only among the Romans and Ravennates, but also among the Lombard people, because they drove Aldibra[n]d, his nephew, whom he had left as king, a hostile man, from the kingdom [Note: another copy: “they drove the malicious one from the kingdom”], and the Lombards chose Ratchis, who had been duke, as their king.

When a report was sent to him [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “after an embassy had been sent”], Ratchis, immediately moved by reverence for the prince of the apostles and by the prayers of the most blessed pontiff, made peace; and the whole people of Italy rested in peace for twenty years [Note: “Having made peace.” Zacharias, following the custom of supreme rulers, made peace with Ratchis, who had taken up the Lombard government after the death of King Liutprand. BENCINUS.]

[Note: During his pontificate, in the Lateran patriarchate, before the basilica of the blessed Theodore, he built a new dining hall, which he adorned with various marbles, glass, metals, mosaic work, and painting; and he also decorated both the oratory of blessed Sylvester and the portico with sacred images. The passage is corrupt: in place of *vitio*, read *vitreis*—“with glass.” The ancients coated the walls of buildings with glass joined by bitumen instead of plaster. Vopiscus, in *Firmus*: “For it is said that he covered the house with square pieces of glass set with bitumen and other substances.” Seneca, Letter 86: “But now who can endure bathing in that way? He seems poor and filthy to himself unless the walls shine with great and costly circles, unless the chamber is hidden by glass.” ALTASERRA.]

During his pontificate, in the Lateran patriarchate, before the basilica of the blessed Theodore the pope, he built anew a dining hall, which he adorned with various marbles, glass, metals, mosaic work, and painting; and he also decorated the oratory of blessed Sylvester and the portico with sacred images. There also he ordered his entire property to be brought in through the hands of Ambrosius, first of the notaries.

He built from the foundations, before the Lateran treasury, a portico and a tower. There he installed bronze doors and grilles, and decorated the front with an image of the Savior [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “a pergola”]. By the ascending stairs he constructed, above the same tower, an upper dining hall and bronze grilles. There he painted a description of the world and adorned it with various verses, and restored almost the entire patriarchate anew. For he had found that place in great poverty.

[Note: During his pontificate, in the church of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, he made hanging curtains between the columns from silk cloths. Curtains were used between columns to adorn churches, made of silk cloth or pallia. Anastasius, in the Life of Hadrian: “And through various arches, fifty-seven silk curtains.” Further: “Curtains of silk pallia, twenty in number, and twenty linen ones.” The same author, in the Life of Leo III: “And larger silk curtains, stamped, having a border and a cross of *bathin* or *fundatus*.” Read *blathin*. The same author below in the same passage: “He also made, through silver arches, Paschal curtains with a border of *stauraci*.” Among the ancients, images were also placed between columns. Marcus Tullius, *Against Verres* 3: “Where are those statues now, Verres? I mean those which we recently saw at your house, arranged beside every column, in every intercolumniation, indeed in the grove, under the open sky.” There were even groves between the columns of larger buildings—that is, rows of trees planted for ornament. Horace, Book I, Letter 10:

“Indeed a grove is cultivated among varied columns.”]

During his pontificate, in the church of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, he made hanging curtains between the columns from silk cloths [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “silken”].

[Note: During his pontificate, in the church of the aforesaid prince of the apostles, he arranged in the bookcase all the books belonging to his household that are read at matins throughout the annual cycle. Zacharias placed his own books in the bookcase of the Roman church. A bookcase is a library of books. “But if a library,” *On the Embassy* 3. Pliny, Book II, Letter 17: “A bookcase was inserted into its wall in the form of a library.” Sidonius, Book II, Letter 9: “You might think you were looking at either grammatical reading desks, the benches of an Athenaeum, or bookcases piled up by booksellers.” By analogy, Lupus of Ferrières called Saint Martin’s bookcase a bookcase, Letter 16: “We earnestly beg you to send the commentaries of Boethius on Cicero’s *Topics*, which Amalricus has in a parchment manuscript in Saint Martin’s bookcase.” Ekkehard the Younger, *On the Affairs of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, chapter 10: “They go to the bookcase, or rather to the narrow treasury of Saint Gall.” Elsewhere, *armarium* means a place where objects are deposited for safekeeping. Jerome, on Ezekiel, Book IV, chapter 15: “They contain them in cupboards, chests, and little boxes.” ALTASERRA.]

During his pontificate, in the church of the aforesaid prince of the apostles, he arranged in the bookcase all the books belonging to his household that are read at matins throughout the annual cycle [Note: another copy: “he arranged them in the bookcase for matins”].

[Note: During his pontificate, he newly established an endowed estate at Laurentum, adding the estate of Fonteianum. An endowed estate is a *massa* or property equipped with buildings, tenants, and agricultural implements. Anastasius, below in the same passage: “And he assigned that endowed estate to blessed Peter as a perpetual possession; this endowed estate of Saint Cecilia is still called so today.” He described that endowed estate for his own use, that is, for the use of the church’s patrimony. “During his pontificate he established another endowed estate at the fourteenth mile from this city of Rome, in the patrimony of Tuscany, and bound it by statutes to remain for the use of the church. He acquired by his own efforts, under the right of blessed Peter, the estates called Antrus and Formias, and established them as endowed estates. Concerning all the endowed estates, under anathema and prohibition, he decreed that none of his successors in the pontificate, nor any other person, should in any way be permitted to alienate those estates from the church’s use.” The same author, in the Life of Hadrian: “This most blessed prelate newly made and established four endowed estates.” Leo III established private estates as endowed estates. The Life of Louis the Pious: “At that same time, when Leo the apostolic see was suffering from an adverse misfortune, they attempted, without awaiting any judge, to seize and restore to themselves all the estates which the Romans call endowed estates, which had recently been established by that same apostolic see, as well as those which they claimed had been taken from them contrary to law.” ALTASERRA.]

During his pontificate, he newly established the endowed estate of Laurentum [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “the hidden estate of Laurentum”], adding the estate of Fonteianum [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “Fontinian”; another copy: “Fontian”], which is called Paunaria [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “Paunasia”; another copy: “Pannaria”].

During his pontificate, he established twenty pounds of gold annually for the purchase of oil, so that the proceeds from it might be used for the apostolic lamps. He bound this arrangement under the bond of anathema.

He made for the altar of blessed Peter a vestment woven of gold, bearing the Nativity of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, and adorned it with precious gems. He likewise made four curtains of genuine silk [Note: another copy: “and adorned with gems, and also four genuine silk curtains. He made a crown, etc.”], which he adorned with wheels and various ornaments woven in gold [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “in red”; another copy: “in votive designs”]. He also made, from his own resources, a crown of pure silver with dolphins, weighing 120 pounds.

This most blessed man, according to ecclesiastical custom—

[Note: This most blessed Zacharias, called pontiff, according to ecclesiastical custom, sent to the church of Constantinople a synodical letter concerning his orthodox profession of faith in the year 742; and he also sent another petition through his representatives to the emperor Constantine. But when these men entered the palace of the royal city, they found Artabasdus, an usurper and rebel. After the eyes of both Artabasdus and his sons had been put out, Constantine Copronymus, although a heretic, sought the envoy of the apostolic see, dismissed him to Rome, and, in accordance with what the most blessed pontiff Zacharias had requested, sent him a written grant of the two estates called Nymphas and Normias, which belonged to the public treasury, to be possessed in perpetuity by that most holy pope and the holy Roman Church, says Anastasius. This grant occurred in the year 743, as the deposition of Artabasdus shows. Moreover, *massa* is the same as *mansus* or *mansa*, and designates a specific portion of land, as Du Cange explains in his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, under the words *Mansus* and *Massa*. From this Baron’s annotator observes that it is clearly evident that Gregory II had not shaken off the yoke of the empire, nor consequently struck Leo the Isaurian with anathema; for Zacharias would not have had any dealings with Constantine, a worse man than his father Leo, if Constantine had been excommunicated by his predecessor and punished by the payment of tribute. PAGIUS.]

According to ecclesiastical custom and the orthodox profession of his faith, he sent a synodical letter to the church of Constantinople, while also directing another petition to the serene Emperor Constantine. When the representatives of the apostolic see proceeded to the royal city, they found within the imperial palace a certain usurper and rebel named Artaustus [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “Artavastus”; another copy: “Artavasdus”; another: “Ajtaustus”]. For while that same emperor had departed to fight against the people of the Agarenes, the aforesaid Artaustus immediately, after distributing rewards to the people who had remained in the royal city, seized the imperial throne. Afterwards, having gathered a multitude from the eastern armies, the aforementioned Emperor Constantine proceeded to Constantinople, attacked it vigorously, and surrounded it with a circumvallation from outside. He captured the city and recovered the height of his former rule.

[Col. 0905B] Immediately he put out the eyes of the aforesaid Artaustus and his sons, and exiled many of his fellow rebels from their own homes [Col. 0906A]. Afterwards, seeking the envoy of the apostolic see [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “the envoys”], who had happened to arrive there during the time of the disturbance, and finding him, he released him to return to the apostolic see. In accordance with what the most blessed pontiff had requested, he sent a written grant of the two estates called Nymphas and Normias [Note: Codex Lucullanus and another copy: “estates”], which belonged to the public treasury, to that most holy and blessed pope and the holy Roman Church, to be possessed in perpetuity.

[Note: During his pontificate, in the year 747, Charles Martel’s son Carloman, for the sake of devotion, entrusted the kingdom, together with his son Drogo, into the hands of his brother Pippin, and came to Rome to the thresholds of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, intending to persevere in the monastic order. This is attested by the continuator of Fredegar, supported by the annalists of Metz, Lorsch, Petau, and Moissac, as well as by the author of the Chronicle of Saint-Denis. Anastasius reports the same, understanding the word “clerical” to mean the monastic state, in which sense this word is commonly used elsewhere. Hence those writers must be corrected who assert that Carloman first went to Cassino and became a monk there; for Herkempert writes that he went to Rome and was made a monk by Pope Zacharias, and afterward, after some time, proceeded to Cassino. In the intervening period he built a monastery on Mount Soracte in honor of Saint Sylvester, where he is said once to have hidden during the persecution under Constantine, as Einhard writes in the Annals under the year 746. The same account appears here in the Life of Charlemagne, chapter 2, and from it in Adrevald, *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chapter 14. Adrevald adds that many nobles from Francia, traveling to Rome to fulfill their vows and interrupting the leisure in which Carloman took the greatest delight at the monastery on Mount Soracte, compelled him to change his residence. From these facts it follows that Carloman was clothed in the monastic habit by Pope Zacharias himself at Rome. PAGIUS.]

During his pontificate [Note: 1. Carloman. He was Pippin’s brother; both were sons of Charles Martel. The pontiffs Gregory II and Gregory III had long before entered into treaties with the Franks, and Zacharias renewed them. In 746, when Pippin consulted him about which brother seemed more worthy of the royal dignity—whether the one languishing in idleness and contributing nothing to the common welfare of the peoples, or the one thinking day and night about the safety and protection of the kingdom—he replied that the king who served the welfare of the kingdom and the security of the people should unquestionably be chosen. When asked, he issued a decree that Pippin should be made king. Thus the Bertinian Annals, under the year 749, report that Burchard and Fulrad were sent to act concerning the transfer of the kingdom to Pippin: “Burchard, bishop of Würzburg, and Fulrad, chaplain, were sent to Pope Zacharias to ask about the kings in Francia who in those days, not possessing royal power, were—if it was right—kings or not. Pope Zacharias ordered Pippin that it would be better for the one who possessed power to be called king than for the one who remained without royal power, so that the order might not be disturbed. Therefore, by apostolic authority, he ordered Pippin to become king.” Under the year 750: “Pippin was elected king according to Frankish custom, anointed by the hand of Saint Boniface, archbishop of blessed memory, and raised by the Franks to the kingship in the city of Soissons. Childeric, who was falsely called king, was tonsured and sent to the monastery of Sithiu.” The continuator of Fredegar likewise wrote under the year 751: “And the land rested from battles. At that time, after a report had been sent and authority had been received from the apostolic see, the illustrious Pippin, by the election of all Francia, was elevated to the royal throne with the consecration of bishops and the submission of the nobles, together with Queen Bertrada, as the ancient order requires.” The Annals edited by Pithoeus state: “In the year 752 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Pope Zacharias, by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter, ordered the Frankish people that Pippin, who exercised royal power, should also enjoy the dignity of the name. Thus King Childeric, the last of the Merovingians to rule the Franks, was deposed and sent to a monastery. Pippin, however, was anointed in the city of Soissons by Saint Boniface, archbishop, and elevated to the honor of the kingdom.” The epoch of the royal line of the Carolingians should begin in the year 752, as Antonius Pagi proves at length under that year in his *Critique* of Cardinal Baronius. BENCINUS.

2. Carloman, son of Charles, king of the Franks.
