It was already long since the mayors of the palace of Francia had arrogated supreme power to themselves, and nothing remained to the descendants of the great Clovis except the royal name. But Pippin, surnamed the Short, the last of the mayors of the palace, eventually undertook the great task of claiming for himself royal dignity, title, and right. To carry out this plan and make its outcome firm and valid, he understood that, besides the consent of the nobles of the kingdom, he needed the authority of the apostolic see to support him, lest subject peoples should imagine that they could change their kings at will. Einhard says in the Annals, as Marca reports (*History of Spain*, Book III, chapter 4), that he adds the authority of the apostolic see “so that the peoples may not think that changes of kings are permitted to their own discretion”; to this he adds the consent of the nobles and the continuous succession of the two lines of kings, whose apathy and inertia had been fatal to the Christian commonwealth.

A highly opportune occasion presented itself for winning the favor of the holy see for Pippin’s affairs, since he alone could crush the Lombards and support the religion that was everywhere in danger. A very recent author observes that Pippin used the services of Saint Boniface, the archbishop, to carry out the matter and test Zacharias’s disposition—what his future position in the matter would be (P. Daniel, *History of France*, under Pippin). For this reason he sent the same Boniface to the pontiff, together with one of his priests, to consult him about various matters pertaining to his ministry. Among other things he wrote:

“By earnest prayers I beseech the holiness of your fatherly piety graciously to receive this priest of mine; for he has certain secrets of mine which he must disclose only to your piety, some of them orally … He must bring back to me the response and counsel of your fatherhood by the authority of Saint Peter the apostle, so that, after hearing and considering all these matters, if there are any that please you, I may strive, with God’s help, to carry them out” (*Life of Boniface*, Book II, chapter 9).

The pontiff responded orally to Boniface’s priest concerning these secret matters, but made it clear from the outcome that his answer favored Pippin’s plan. Meanwhile, Zacharias says in Letter 12 to Boniface:

“In the meantime, your aforementioned messenger Lul, with his other companions, clearly reported everything that had been entrusted to them by your holy fraternity, both orally and in writing; concerning these matters we have sent our response back to your fraternity, both orally and in writing.”

And indeed, as we learn from the Chronicle edited by Pithoeus, the Annals of Fulda, and the Annals of Loisel, the matter occurred as follows:

“Burchard, bishop of Würzburg, and Fulrad, chaplain, were sent by Pippin to Rome to Pope Zacharias, to consult the pontiff about the case of the kings who were in Francia at that time. They had only the name of king and no royal power, which was all held by the mayor of the palace. He therefore asked that it be decided which of them ought justly to be called and be king: the one who sat safely at home, or the one who bore responsibility for the entire kingdom and all the burdens of its affairs. Through these men the pontiff ordered that it was better for the one in whom supreme power resided to be called king; and, granting his authority, he ordered Pippin to be established as king.”

According to the sanction of the Roman pontiff, Pippin was called king of the Franks and, for this dignity of honor, was anointed with sacred chrism by the hand of Boniface, archbishop of blessed memory, and, according to Frankish custom, was raised to the throne of the kingdom in the city of Soissons. Childeric, however, who bore the false name of king, was tonsured and sent to a monastery; he was the last Merovingian to rule the Franks.

Besides the three authors mentioned above, who speak of the transfer of the Frankish kingdom from the first dynasty to the second, and besides Einhard, secretary to Charlemagne, who says that Pippin “was made king from prefect of the palace by the authority of the Roman pontiff” (*Life of Charlemagne*), the same account can also be found in the epigraph of a little work composed by a contemporary of Pippin, a copy of which Mabillon saw in Papebroch’s possession. He quotes the very words in his *Diplomatic Work*, taken from the end of Gregory of Tours’ book *On the Glory of the Confessors*. They read:

“If you wish to know, reader, in what period this little book appears to have been written and published for the glorious praise of the holy martyrs, you will find that it was in the year 767 from the Incarnation of the Lord, during the reign of the most fortunate, tranquil, and Catholic Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, son of blessed memory of the former prince Charles, in the sixteenth year of his most fortunate reign in the name of God … The aforesaid most flourishing lord, Pippin the pious king, was elevated to the throne of the kingdom three years earlier by the authority and command of the lord Zacharias, pope of blessed memory, by the anointing of holy chrism at the hands of the blessed priests of Gaul, and by the election of all the Franks” (*At the end of Saint Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Confessors*, and in Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, Book V, plate 22).

To tell the truth, I cannot sufficiently marvel at the fact that several recent writers, both Protestants and some of our own authors [Natalis Alexander, section 8, dissertation 2], accuse the testimonies of the ancients concerning the truth of this matter of being false, although no suspicion can exist concerning it.

Pippin was also granted by the same pontiff Zacharias the power to appoint bishops of the kingdom of the Franks, so that he might apply a healing hand to the abuses and excesses of those times whenever elections were held. This occurred while he was still mayor of the palace, for he received such a grant at the Council of Soissons, held in the year 744, eight years before he ascended the royal throne. After Pippin had explained the needs of the kingdom to Zacharias, the Roman pope, at a synod attended by the martyr Boniface, he received his consent so that, through the diligence of men whom he had proven most trustworthy, he might remedy the severity of the times whenever bishops died (Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, Letter 81 to Amulo, archbishop of Lyon). SOMMIER.]

Carloman, son of Charles, king of the Franks [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “duke or under-king,”], abandoning the glory and power of the present life, came in devotion with some of his faithful men to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. He entrusted himself to that apostle of God and, promising that he would remain in a special habit [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “spiritual”], received from that most holy pontiff the yoke of the clerical state.

Among many other gifts, he offered to the blessed apostle Peter, before the Confession, a large silver arch weighing seventy pounds. After some time he proceeded to the monastery of blessed Benedict, situated in the territory of the people of Aquino [Col. 0908A], in which he swore and professed that he would spend the rest of his life.

[Note: At that same time it happened that several Venetian merchants came to this city of Rome and, extending the market for their merchandise, appeared to purchase a multitude of slaves, both male and female, whom they were attempting to transport to Africa for a pagan people. This notes the shameful commerce of the Venetians in buying slaves of both sexes in order to sell them to pagans in Africa, a practice which the pontiff prohibited. This kind of commerce was common. Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book I, chapter 1: “From this populous Germania innumerable bands of captives were often carried away and sold for a price to southern peoples.” An even more shameful kind of commerce was practiced by merchants from Verdun, who used to castrate slaves—called *carsamantia*—so that they could be sold to the Saracens in Spain. Liutprand of Cremona, Book VI, chapter 3: “I offered the emperor four *carsamantia*, more valuable than all those named; the Greeks call a boy whose male organs and penis have been removed a *carsamantius*, a eunuch. Merchants from Verdun customarily make such slaves for enormous profit and take them to Spain.” ALTASERRA.]

At that same time it happened that several Venetian merchants came to this city of Rome and, extending the market for their merchandise, appeared to purchase a multitude of slaves, both male and female, whom they were attempting to transport to Africa for a pagan people. When the most holy father learned of this, he prohibited it, judging that it was not right for those washed clean by the baptism of Christ to serve pagan peoples. He paid the same Venetians the price that they were proved to have paid for their purchase, redeemed them all from the yoke of slavery, and released them to live as free people.

[Note: At that time Ratchis, after King Liutprand had died, was chosen as king of the Lombards after the brief reign of his nephew Hildeprand, who was thrown from the throne in the seventh month. Ratchis, duke of Friuli, was appointed with the favor of all the Lombards, a man highly commended for his bodily strength, a quality greatly valued among that people; but he was far more commendable for his extraordinary piety. After renouncing the royal dignity, he embraced monastic life in the monastery of Cassino and observed it until the end of his life, as Leo, cardinal bishop of Ostia, relates (*Chronicle of Cassino*, Book I, chapter 8). I do not hesitate to append the words of this historian, although he is later than our Anastasius, since what he relates places the events narrated here in a favorable light.

“In those days,” says the cardinal of Ostia, “Ratchis, king of the Lombards, proceeded with a powerful army to capture the city of Perugia and was vigorously attacking it from every side. Pope Zacharias went to him and, through many prayers and admonitions and by granting him many gifts, compelled him to return. The king carefully remembered his admonition, and not long afterward, moved by divine inspiration, abandoned royal dignity and glory. After he had reigned for five years and six months, he came devoutly to Rome with his wife and daughter, to the threshold of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. There the aforesaid bishop of the apostolic see, Zacharias, cut his hair and made him a cleric; he also clothed him in the monastic habit together with his wife and daughter. Soon, when the same apostolic prelate sent him there, he arrived at this monastery of blessed Benedict, committed himself to be instructed under the regular discipline, and, after a sufficiently religious and God-pleasing life, met his end there.

“To this day there remains a vineyard quite near the monastery, commonly called Ratchis’s vineyard, which some of our people believe that Ratchis himself both planted and inhabited. His wife, named Tasia, and his daughter Rattruda, with the permission and assistance of the aforesaid abbot, built at their own expense a monastery for girls not far from Cassino, at a place called Pallumbariola. Endowed with many resources, they lived there under strict supervision and rigorous discipline and ended their final day there.” MAFEUS.]

At that time [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “Ratchis”; another copy: “Rachis”], Ratchis, king of the Lombards, proceeded with great indignation to capture the city of Perugia [Note: Like the other towns of the Pentapolis. Flaminia is a province of Italy in which Ravenna and the five cities called the Pentapolis are situated, according to Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book II, chapter 19. Hence Anastasius said earlier: “Ravenna, and the cities of the Pentapolis and Emilia.” ALTASERRA.], like the other towns of the Pentapolis; after surrounding it, he attacked it vigorously.

When the most holy pope heard this, relying immediately on divine hope, he took with him some of his clergy [Col. 0909B] and nobles and, with as many as were needed, reached the same city. After presenting the king with very many gifts and earnestly entreating him concerning the city, with the Lord’s help he removed him from its siege [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “from the blockade”]. By preaching what was salutary to him, he also succeeded, with God’s help, in inclining his mind toward a particular resolve.

After some days, the same King Ratchis, abandoning royal dignity [Col. 0910A]—

[Note: King Ratchis, abandoning his royal dignity. Without regard for the twenty-year peace which he had established with the Roman pontiff, Ratchis, king of the Lombards, invaded the province of the Pentapolis, laying everything waste with fire and sword and surrounding Perugia with a siege. Hearing this, Pope Zacharias, taking certain members of his clergy and relying on divine hope, reached the same city and, having appeased him with gifts and prayers, induced him to lift the siege. Indeed, through sacred exhortations he instilled such disgust for secular life in him that, after renouncing the kingdom, he professed a religious life under the rule of Saint Benedict with his wife Thesia and daughter Rattruda: he in the monastery of Cassino, and they in a monastery for women which they built and endowed not far from Cassino, as is clear from Anastasius, in the Life of Zacharias; Leo of Ostia, in the *Chronicle of Cassino*, chapter 8; and Sigebert, in his *Chronicle*, where he records that Ratchis sent his renunciation to the world in the year 749. The same year is also given by the anonymous monk of Nonantula in the Life of Saint Anselm, the first abbot of Nonantula in Italy, preserved by Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, century IV, part I. PAGIUS.]

After some days, King Ratchis, abandoning his royal [Col. 0910A] dignity, proceeded honorably with his wife and children to the threshold of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Having received a prayer from the aforesaid most holy pope, he became a cleric and was clothed in the monastic habit, together with his wife and children.

In the time of this man, finally, our Lord God deigned to disclose a great treasure in this Roman city through the same life-giving pontiff. In the venerable patriarchate, therefore, that most holy pope found the head of the blessed martyr George preserved in a chest; in it he also found a label, likewise written in Greek letters, identifying it as his. [Note: [Col. 0909B] The Lucan Codex has *pittacium*.]

[Note: [Col. 0910D] A *pittacium*, that is, a slip or brief inscription indicating whose relics they are, is attached to chests—that is, reliquaries—containing saints’ relics. Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, ch. 36: “There is there a tomb adjoining this one on the left; on its upper front is written: ‘Of holy memory, Galla.’” A *pittacium* is a slip. Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 23: “He publicly displayed a label of the Law.” Its diminutive is *pittaciolum*. Flodoard, *History of Rheims*, bk. III, ch. 23: “A slip irrationally drawn up and subscribed by your hand.” Jerome, *On Matthew*, bk. IV, ch. 23: “They called those little labels of the Decalogue phylacteries.” John the Deacon, bk. II, ch. 45: “And, writing a prayer on a label, he gave it to one of his deacons.” Elsewhere *pittacium* means a strip for binding wounds. Cornelius Celsus, bk. III, ch. 10: “Two strips, equal to the breadth and length of the forehead.” Vegetius, *Veterinary Art*, bk. I, ch. 22: “Place a strip upon the wound, so that it may close more carefully.” ALTASERRA.]

The most holy pope, exceedingly joyful and satisfied, immediately assembled the people of the city of Rome and, with hymns and spiritual songs, had it carried to the venerable deaconry of that name, situated in the second region of this Roman city, at the Golden Veil. There the almighty God deigns to perform immeasurable miracles and benefits, to the praise of his name, through that most sacred martyr. [Note: [Col. 0910B] The Lucan Codex has “deigned.”]

During his time, Theodore the Elder, son of Megistus Cataxanti, died. For the forgiveness of his sins, he left to blessed Peter the estate which he had enjoyed by paternal inheritance. It was situated five miles from this Roman city, on the Tiburtine Way, and contained an oratory of Saint Cecilia. [Note: [Col. 0910B] The Lucan Codex has “of the magnificent king Cataxanti.”] The most blessed pope adorned it with buildings of extensive construction and paintings, and enlarged its boundaries on every side. He made a fitting recompense to those who appeared to possess lands in the neighborhood of that place; he used no force against anyone, but, as befitted a father, purchased all the estates adjoining the place at a friendly price by mutual agreement. He established the cultivated estate and house as belonging to blessed Peter by perpetual right and as remaining permanently in his possession. This cultivated estate is called Saint Cecilia’s House down to the present day.

He also built in it an oratory of Saint Abbacyrus, where he deposited many relics of the saints. He entered this cultivated estate in the register for his own use, namely for the papal household. [Note: [Col. 0911B] The Lucan Codex has “of Abbot Cyrus.”]

He established another cultivated estate in the fourteenth mile from this Roman city, in the patrimony of Tuscia, and by formal enactments bound it to remain for the use of the Church. [Note: [Col. 0911B] The Lucan Codex has “in the patrimony.”] This included lands which are seen to have once been left by Anna, the former wife of Agatho the primicerius, and granted to blessed Peter. [Note: [Col. 0911B] The Lucan Codex adds: “so that certain lands as well as annual legacies…”] By his own efforts he acquired for blessed Peter, by lawful title, the estates called Antro and Formias, and likewise established them as cultivated estates.

And, having drawn up formal records of all the cultivated estates mentioned above, [Note: [Col. 0912B] The Lucan Codex has “cultivated houses.”] [Note: [Col. 0912B] The Lucan Codex has “of administration.”] and having assembled the priestly college, he decreed under the penalties of anathema:

“No successor of his among the pontiffs, nor any other person whatsoever, shall in any way be permitted to alienate these cultivated estates from the use of the Church.”

He made for the altar of the blessed apostle Andrew, at blessed Peter’s, an exceedingly fine vestment.

[Note: [Col. 0911C] 1. This most blessed pope decreed that on frequent days the expense of food—also called almsgiving down to the present time—should be carried from the venerable patriarchate by the *paracellarii* and distributed to the poor and pilgrims who reside at blessed Peter’s, etc. The *paracellarii* are the superintendents of the storeroom of the Lateran patriarchate, from which daily allowances were distributed to the poor and pilgrims. Anastasius, in his Life of Hadrian: “And fifty loaves, together with two measures of wine and a cauldron full of stew, shall be distributed every day by the hands of one most faithful *paracellarius* to those same poor.” Hence the storeroom of the Lateran patriarchate is called the *paracellarium*. Anastasius, in his Life of Hadrian I: “The wine, moreover, and the various legumes which annually grow on the estates and lands of that cultivated estate shall likewise be carefully brought into the *paracellarium* of your holy church and stored separately; and the pigs which each year have been fattened on acorns in the farmsteads of the aforesaid cultivated estate shall likewise be slaughtered, one hundred head from them, and stored in the same *paracellarium*.” ALTASERRA.

2. “This most blessed pope, by his exceedingly prudent care.” It is an old complaint of John the Deacon, Book IV of the Life of Saint Gregory the Great, chapter 75, and after him of all Catholics, that the translation of the blessed Gregory’s *Dialogues*, which holy Pope Zacharias rendered into Greek, was corrupted. John the Deacon says in the passage just cited:

“These books Zacharias, bishop of the holy Roman Church, most learned in both Greek and Latin, translated into Greek in the time of the emperor Constantine—namely, Copronymus—after approximately 175 years [more accurately, 158], and circulated among the Eastern Churches, although the Greeks’ cunning perversity scraped away and removed the name of the Son from the reference to the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father.”

The Greek translation was indeed corrupted, as can still be recognized from the final chapter of Book II. Where the Latin text of the *Dialogues* reads:

“Since it is certain that the Paraclete Spirit always proceeds from the Father and the Son,”

the Greek has:

**Φανερὸν οὖν ὑπάρχει, ὅτι τὸ παράκλητον πνεῦμα ἐκ τοῦ πατρὸς προέρχεται, καὶ ἐν τῷ υἱῷ διαμένει.**

The meaning is: “It is therefore plainly evident that the Paraclete Spirit proceeds from the Father and remains in the Son.”

Some suspect that Photius, a highly skilled craftsman of corruptions, was the author of this corrupted reading, because in his *Bibliotheca* he praises Saint Gregory’s *Dialogues* with extraordinary commendation, as though, when passing judgment on books he had read, he were at that time forging weapons with which he would one day attack the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son.

But while Photius was praising Gregory, it seems to me much more probable that he was not then preparing such stratagems: first, because, as I said in my account of the Life of Saint Gregory the Great, Photius wrote his *Bibliotheca* when he was serving as Basil’s legate in Assyria—that is, before he seized the see of Constantinople; and also because Photius praises not merely the writing of the *Dialogues*, but all Gregory’s works, exalting them as highly as he can, and rightly so.

Moreover, if Photius had secured for himself and his schism a defense from Gregory’s corrupted *Dialogues*, while Gregory openly says in so many other places that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, what advantage would that have been? In the Creed which he promulgated at the beginning of his pontificate he says: “The Holy Spirit, neither begotten nor unbegotten, but coeternal, proceeding from the Father and the Son.” In the *Moralia*, Book I, number 30, he says: “While [speaking of] the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from himself—that is, from the Son”; and in Book V, number 65: “Who, proceeding from the Father and receiving from that which belongs to the Son,” and so forth. Still more plainly, Homily 26 on the Gospels, near the beginning: “He proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

The final chapter of Book II, therefore, was not corrupted by Photius, but by some other Greek-speaking man of the Greek faith. Otherwise, by praising all the writings of blessed Gregory, and especially his homilies on the Gospels, he would have supplied weapons rather than removed them from the Latins, who could easily have used Gregory’s own confession both to assert the supreme authority of his teaching and to demonstrate from his writings the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. MAFEUS.]

This most blessed pope decreed that on frequent days the cost of food—also called almsgiving down to the present time—should be carried from the venerable patriarchate by the *paracellarii* and distributed to the poor and pilgrims who reside at blessed Peter’s. He likewise decreed that the same food-alms should be distributed to all the needy and sick throughout every district of this Roman city. [Note: [Col. 0912B] The Lucan Codex has “by the storeroom keepers.”]

During his time, the covering of the titular church of the blessed martyr of Christ, Eusebius, suddenly fell. [Note: [Col. 0912B] The Lucan Codex has “covering.”] That most holy man, exerting all his strength and working prudently, repaired what had fallen, restoring it as it had been in ancient times and renovating it excellently. [Note: [Col. 0913A] The Lucan Codex has “his.”]

This eminent pontiff brought many holy places into a better condition and made excellent vestments for the altars of those churches of God. He loved his clergy greatly and annually granted them twice, and more than twice, the customary presbyterial allowances. Embracing everyone as a father and good shepherd, and nourishing them usefully, he allowed no one at all to be troubled. Thus, during his time, the people entrusted to him by God lived in great security and joy.

[Note: [Col. 0913B] This most blessed pope is said to have translated the four books of the *Dialogues* which Pope Gregory of blessed memory composed from Latin into Greek. Anastasius the Librarian, in his Life of Zacharias; Photius, Codex 252; and John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 75 of the Life of that same Saint Gregory, transmit this account. John writes:

“These books”—namely, the *Dialogues*—“Zacharias, bishop of the holy Roman Church, most learned in Greek and Latin, translated into Greek in the time of the emperor Constantine, after approximately 175 years” (John the Deacon counts at least fifteen years too many), “and circulated among the Eastern Churches, although the Greeks’ cunning perversity scraped away and removed the name of the Son from the reference to the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father.”

For although Gregory had left written in Book II of the *Dialogues*, final chapter:

“For it is certain that the Paraclete Spirit proceeds always from the Father and the Son,”

the commonly circulated Greek text of Zacharias reads:

“It is therefore plainly evident that the Paraclete Spirit proceeds from the Father and remains in the Son.” PAGIUS.]

This most blessed pope, by his exceedingly prudent care, translated into Greek the four books of the *Dialogues* which Pope Gregory of blessed memory had composed in Latin, and through the history contained in that translation enlightened many who did not understand Latin reading.

He held three ordinations during the month of March: he created thirty priests, five deacons, and eighty-five bishops for various places.

He was buried at blessed Peter the apostle’s on the Ides of March, in the fifth indiction, and his episcopal see was vacant for twelve days.

[Note: [Col. 0913C] “He was buried at blessed Peter the apostle’s on the Ides of March, in the fifth indiction.” Once again I must deal with Natalis Alexander, who, in the *Ecclesiastical History of the Eighth Century*, volume V, stubbornly denies, in the face of a cloud of witnesses unanimously affirming that the transfer of the Frankish kingdom from Childeric, the last of the Merovingian kings, to Pippin, the first of the Carolingians, was carried out by apostolic authority. He says, in article 5, chapter 7 of that century, that Childeric was deposed and Pippin made king at the persuasion or by the agency of Pope Zacharias, and calls the matter a fable.

I shall briefly summarize the arguments on which he relies and the means by which he attempts to evade the clearest testimony of the ancient writers.

Natalis first makes this his foundation: that the ancient annalists do not agree whether Childeric’s deposition and Pippin’s elevation to the kingship took place on the authority of Stephen or of Zacharias. He shows that it could not be attributed to Stephen because, after Zacharias died on 15 March, as Anastasius reports, in the fifth indiction—which indicates the year of Christ 752—Pope Stephen III was inaugurated toward the end of that same month. Stephen did not travel to Francia until November of the seventh indiction, which began on the Kalends of September, namely, in the year 753, when Pippin had already been reigning for a year and a half.

But neither, he says, could it be attributed to Zacharias, whom Anastasius calls a very gentle and gracious man, adorned with every virtue, and so devoted to justice and piety that he could not, without the greatest injustice, have violently removed from his ancestral throne and thrust into a monastery an innocent youth who, because of his age, had not yet had the opportunity to prove what sort of man he was—Childeric, who was scarcely eighteen years old.

Add to this that Anastasius’s silence in the Life of Zacharias is more decisive: the papal author would certainly not have silently passed over a matter famous throughout the world and highly favorable to the dignity and authority of the apostolic see.

But Zacharias did not know who the true king of the Franks was. Indeed, he indicates in his letter to Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, that he regarded Charles Martel, Pippin’s father, as king; and in Letter 5 to the same man he calls Charles’s sons “princes of Gaul.” Almost all writers, moreover, make Stephen the author of Childeric’s deposition and of Pippin’s release from his oath and elevation to the kingship, not Zacharias.

To the large company of writers who committed the same event to posterity, Natalis replies that the number of writers is of no weight for establishing authority when they are shown by the surest documents to be false, and when the source from which they drew their fictions is identified. He says that the source was Einhard, from whom all the others received the same fable and enlarged it with new inventions.

He says that Einhard himself confesses in the Life of Charlemagne that he did not know what concerned Charles’s birth and infancy, because there were no trustworthy authors who had written about them, and that he knew even less about what preceded his birth; that what he published about the idleness of the Merovingian kings was false; that much may have been invented by him to flatter the Carolingian kings; that they did not grow long beards, since almost all of them died beardless; that their splendid generosity toward churches and monasteries sufficiently refutes the exaggerated claims that they possessed nothing except a village yielding a very small income and a precarious livelihood supplied to them by the palace mayor; that the ancient Frankish annalists do not agree about the date: some say Pippin ascended the throne in 750, others in 753; some say he was anointed king by Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, others by the Roman pontiff Stephen; that they also err about the place, saying that the event occurred at Soissons, whereas Pippin was anointed king by Stephen in the monastery of Saint-Denis in the territory of Paris, after Childeric had died, as Anastasius writes in the Life of Stephen; and finally, that Pippin was elevated to the kingdom by the authority of the pontiff in accordance with Frankish custom, although it was not the custom of the Franks to request and receive kings from the Roman pontiff, but to raise them upon a shield and acclaim them in the assembly of the kingdom.

What certainty, he asks, can be promised from such contradictions? Thus does Natalis, mixing everything together, unsuccessfully defend a bad cause against pontifical authority.

I, however, reply that scarcely in all history does there occur an event whose establishment is supported by the faith and authority of so many writers, conspiring with such agreement. I mean an event so widely known that almost at the same time it was recorded in writing by Franks, Germans, Lombards, Italians, and Greeks.

There is no time here to burden the reader hastening to Anastasius’s text with a lengthy mass of citations, which he can obtain, if he wishes, from the collectors of Frankish and German historical writers. I shall cite only two authors whose undeniable reliability it would be shameless—or rather deranged—to diminish. One of them, Cointius, whom Alexander praises, wrongly considers interpolated; the other both men deceitfully conceal and pass over in malicious silence.

Leaving aside Einhard, the annalists of Lorsch, Fulda, Loisel, and Metz, Paul the Deacon, Theophanes, Anastasius, the Monk of Engolism, Ado of Vienne, Egilward, and Regino of Prüm—authors either contemporary or nearly so, since all wrote before the year 1000—I first present the author of the continuation of the history composed at Childebrand’s command. The following subscription, read in the manuscript Codex D of Petavius, reveals that he was Nibelung:

“Up to this point the illustrious man Childebrand, count and uncle of the aforesaid King Pippin, arranged for the writing. From this point authority passes to the illustrious man Nibelung, his son, likewise a count.”

Nibelung therefore writes:

“For two years the land rested from wars. During that time, by common counsel and consent of all the Franks, a report having been sent and authority received from the apostolic see, the exalted Pippin was raised to the throne of the kingdom by the election of all Francia, with the consecration of the bishops and the submission of the nobles, together with Bertrada, as the ancient order requires.”

A second most lucid document is produced for us by the learned Mabillon, Book V of *De re diplomatica*, page 384: namely, the subscription of an anonymous writer to the book on the *Glory of the Confessors* of Saint Gregory of Tours. Mabillon says that he had a copy from the Reverend Fathers Henschenius and Papebrochius, in whose possession the autograph was preserved.

If you wish to know, reader, at what time this little book appears to have been written and published for the precious praise of the holy martyrs, you will find the following:

“In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 767, in the time of the most fortunate, peaceful, and Catholic Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, son of the late Charles the prince of blessed memory, in the sixteenth year of his most fortunate reign, in the fifth indiction; and in the thirteenth year of his sons, Charles and Carloman, likewise kings of the Franks—who, through the hands of Stephen, a man of holy memory, the most blessed lord pope, together with the aforesaid father, the most glorious lord Pippin, king, were consecrated with sacred Chrism by divine providence and through the intercession of the most holy Peter and Paul.

“For the aforesaid lord Pippin, the most illustrious, pious king, had been elevated to the throne of the kingdom three years earlier, by the authority and command of the lord Pope Zacharias, of holy memory, by the anointing of sacred Chrism through the hands of the most blessed priests of Gaul and by the election of all the Franks.

“Afterward, through the hands of that same pontiff Stephen, on one day, in the church of the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius—where the venerable man Folrad is known to be archpriest and abbot—he was anointed and blessed as king and patrician, together with the aforesaid sons Charles and Carloman, in the name of the Holy Trinity.

“On that same day, in the church of the blessed martyrs, the aforesaid venerable pontiff also blessed Bertrada, the noble and most devout wife of the aforementioned most illustrious king, who was clothed in royal robes, with the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. At the same time he confirmed the princes of the Franks with the blessing and grace of the Holy Spirit, and bound them all by such a prohibition and law of excommunication that they should never presume to choose a king from another family, but only from among those whom divine mercy had deigned to exalt and whom it had determined to confirm and consecrate through the hands of their vicar, the most blessed pontiff, by the intercession of the holy apostles.

“We have inserted these matters briefly for your charity on the final little page of this booklet so that, through the succession of times and the report of the common people, posterity may forever be able to know the lineage of later generations.”

This illustrious testimony contains so exact a designation of every circumstance—place, time, and persons—that it seems to have been composed, as it were, by divine providence in order to refute the quibbles of crafty men.

The deposition of Childeric and the elevation of Pippin to the throne must therefore be attributed to Zacharias and Stephen. Pope Zacharias gave his assent to the envoys sent to him by the Frankish people—Burchard, bishop of Würzburg, and Fulrad the Chaplain—who asked him to declare which man he judged worthy of the kingdom: whether the one who bore the name of king but did nothing else, like Childeric, or the one who performed all the affairs of the kingdom, like Pippin. He declared, by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter, that Pippin was king, and ordered him to be anointed king by Boniface, archbishop of Mainz. This was done in the city of Soissons.

Again, three years later, Pippin was anointed with Chrism and crowned by Pope Stephen in the monastery of Saint-Denis, together with his wife Bertrada and his sons Charles and Carloman. Thus the writers are reconciled: some attribute Pippin’s elevation to the throne to Zacharias, others to Stephen.

If some chronological disagreement occurs among the annals of writers from different peoples, while all agree completely about the event itself, it should either be disregarded or reconciled by carefully assigning to their proper years the different events that preceded and followed it.

Pippin’s elevation to the throne must certainly be placed in the year of Christ 751, in the fourth indiction. The events which occurred in the different years of Pippin’s reign agree most exactly with this date. The council of Verneuil was held by the authority of King Pippin at the Palace of Verneuil on the fifth day before the Ides of July, in the year of Christ 755 and the fourth year of King Pippin. The anonymous writer mentioned above dates the composition of his booklet from the Incarnation of the Lord 767 and the sixteenth year of Pippin’s reign. Sirmond, in his notes on the said Council of Verneuil, aligns Pippin’s third regnal year with the year of Christ 754, his sixth with 757, and his tenth with 761. Pippin died in the year of the Lord 768, after seventeen years of reign. Those who assign him fifteen years of reign appear to begin the count from his anointing as king by Pope Stephen.

I set these matters before the eyes of the reader, arranged by years and indictions:

- In the year 749, indiction 2, envoys were sent to Pope Zacharias at Rome.
- In the year 750, indiction 3, the envoys returned to Francia with the holy responses of Pope Zacharias.
- In the year 751, indiction 4, Pippin was anointed king in the city of Soissons by Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz.
- In the year 752, indiction 5, on 15 March, Pope Zacharias died.
- In the year 752, indiction 5, on 27 March, Stephen III was elected pope.
- In the year 753, indiction 7, on 15 November, Pope Stephen set out for Francia.
- In the year 754, indiction 7, on 28 July, Pope Stephen anointed Pippin and his sons Charles and Carloman as kings, together with Bertrada his wife.
- In the year 757, indiction 10, on 24 April, Pope Stephen died.
- In the year 768, indiction 7, on 24 September, King Pippin died after seventeen years of reign.

I shall answer one by one the points which Natalis advanced against this account.

It is false, first, that Zacharias called Charles Martel king of the Franks in any of the letters addressed to Boniface. On the contrary, he openly recognized Pippin as mayor of the palace, addressing him by that title in Letter 7: “To the most excellent and most Christian lord Pippin, mayor of the palace,” although in Letter 3 he had called Carloman and Pippin “princes of the Franks,” evidently as a mark of honor, since they were the sons of Charles Martel, the mayor of the palace, whom Gregory III called “sub-king” in Letters 5 and 6 addressed to him.

Natalis throws a customary cloud over Zacharias’s well-established piety and justice by bringing forward Childeric’s deposition and Pippin’s substitution as king—an action requested by a solemn embassy from all the orders of the Franks because of Pippin’s outstanding virtues and, by contrast, the idleness of the Merovingians, especially Childeric, who is called “the Stupid” by the authorities.

Anastasius is silent about this in the Life of Pope Zacharias, which was chiefly concerned with matters relating to the administration, adornment, titles, and gifts of the churches and evidently thought it right to pass over an event famous throughout the world. But he relates the matter fully in the *Ecclesiastical History*, which he wrote after Nicephorus, George Syncellus, and Theophanes.

Einhard professes that he did not know the matters relating to Charlemagne’s birth and infancy and therefore passes them over in silence. But he recounts Pippin’s elevation to the throne, which occurred before everyone’s eyes and was celebrated by every tongue, and narrates its causes according to the rules of history.

What he reports about the Merovingians’ appearance—that they went about with their hair flowing freely and their beards hanging down—sufficiently confirms the seals of the Merovingians, which represent their faces as wild in appearance. These may be seen both in Mabillon, Book V of *De re diplomatica*, and in Johann Heineccius, *On the Seals of the Ancient Germans*. Natalis has corrupted *submissa* (“hanging down”) into *promissa* (“grown long”). The latter means to nourish a long beard, which would scarcely suit men who died at twenty or twenty-four years of age; the former means not to shave the beard, but to wear the hair growing on the chin uncut.

The fact that these Merovingians were content with the possession and revenues of a single estate is not disproved by the magnificent donations made to churches and monasteries. Such donations were made in their name but by the authority of the mayors of the palace, who managed the kingdom and its royal revenues.

Childeric’s tonsure, his being sent away to a monastery, and Pippin’s release from his oath are attributed by the writers to Pope Stephen, who was present in Gaul and could carry out in person what Zacharias, being absent, could not adequately direct.

It is false, however, that in the Life of Stephen III Anastasius wrote that Childeric died upon Stephen’s arrival in Gaul, as Natalis claims.

Finally, no author says that it was the custom of the Franks to request their kings from the Roman pontiff. Rather, at this particular stage of affairs, when the transfer of the kingdom from one royal family to another was under discussion, the Franks considered it appropriate to seek the advice of the Roman pontiff, so that, with his authority obtained, they might carry out what they had planned. Once this had been secured, in accordance with the custom of the nation, they placed Pippin upon a shield and established him as king. BALDINUS.]

[Col. 0917]

## LETTERS AND DECREES OF SAINT ZACHARIAS, ROMAN PONTIFF

*(Mansi, Collection of Councils, volume XII.)*

### FIRST LETTER. BONIFACE, ARCHBISHOP, TO POPE ZACHARIAS

[Col. 0917B]

“We confess, lord father, that after…” (See above, Letter 49 of Saint Boniface.)

[Note: [Col. 0917C] This letter was undoubtedly sent before the German synod: since the synod had not yet been held, Boniface consulted Zacharias, and Zacharias not only permitted but also ordered the convocation of the aforesaid synod.

Yet that synod, held at an uncertain place in Germany, begins in all editions with these words:

“I, Carloman, duke and prince of the Franks, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 742, namely on the Kalends of May…”

It is therefore necessary that an error has entered either the dates expressed in the letter or those mentioned in the synod.

I am certain, however, that the synod was convened on the day stated in it and that Zacharias’s letter was written at Rome approximately two months earlier. The error therefore entered both in the years of Constantine and in the indiction and month in which the letter is said to have been issued.

Since Artabasdus was hailed as emperor in the year 741, after 27 June, if Zacharias had sent that letter to Boniface in the year 743, he would have appended not the years of Constantine but those of Artabasdus, as he later made customary.

Therefore, in the subscription of the same letter of Zacharias, the second year of the emperor’s reign, wrongly introduced into the Roman and Labbean editions, must be deleted, and the text restored as follows:

“Given on the Kalends of February, while our lord Constantine, the most pious Augustus, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning in the twenty-second year, in the tenth indiction.”]

### SECOND LETTER. POPE ZACHARIAS TO BONIFACE, ARCHBISHOP

He responds to the individual points of the preceding letter:

I. That he approves the bishoprics established in Germany.  
II. Likewise, that a synod should be held in the kingdom of Francia.  
III. Meanwhile, that he should not permit fornicators and bloodstained men to exercise the priesthood.  
IV. That he should not designate his successor unless death is imminent.  
V. That no credence should be given to the man who claimed that incestuous marriages had been permitted to him.  
VI. That the pagan rites which existed at Rome were henceforth prohibited.  
VII. That no faith should be placed in those priests who boasted that they had received permission from the apostolic see.

Zacharias, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, bishop.

After receiving the letters of your most holy fraternity through Deneard, your devout priest, and learning that you are safe and well—as we always desire—we have rendered great thanks to our almighty and most merciful God, who deigns to grant you prosperity in every good work. You pour great joy into our hearts whenever letters from your holiness are sent to us, when we find in them matters pertaining to the salvation of souls, while new peoples are daily added through your preaching to the bosom of holy Mother Church.

### I

We have learned that you have ordained three bishops in the several places according to the sequence of your letters. They are to preside over that people which our Lord God has deigned to gather to himself through your holiness, and you have asked that episcopal sees there be confirmed by the authority of our see.

But let your holy fraternity consider the matter carefully and distinguish by subtle examination whether this is expedient, and whether the places or the populations are shown to be such that they deserve to have bishops. You remember, dearest brother, what the sacred canons command us to observe: that we should by no means ordain bishops in little villages or small towns, lest the name of bishop be cheapened.

Nevertheless, moved by your most sincere letters, which we love, we allow what you have requested to be granted without delay, and by apostolic authority we decree that episcopal sees shall exist there, deserving to have bishops in succession and to preside over the peoples, and in which the word of preaching may be made known to those subject to them.

These are: the castle called Würzburg; another in the town called Buraburg; and a third in the place called Erphesfurt. Henceforth no one shall be permitted in any way to violate what we have sanctioned; we have decreed that it shall remain firm by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter.

### II

You informed us that our son Carloman had asked you to come to him so that you might hold a synod in a city of the kingdom of the Franks, established under his jurisdiction or authority, because the entire ecclesiastical rule and discipline had been utterly abolished in that province. This is a matter greatly to be mourned, since for so long a period no synod of priests has been held there.

We gladly grant this request and command that it be done. For neither what the priesthood is nor what is done by those who call themselves priests is known.

### III

But when, with God’s help, what was promised by the aforesaid son of ours has been brought to completion, and your fraternity has taken your seat with that most excellent man at the council mentioned, if you find any bishops, priests, or deacons to have transgressed the canons or the statutes of the Fathers—that is, if they are found in adultery or fornication, or if they have had several wives, or if they have shed the blood of Christians or pagans, [Note: [Col. 0919D] Baronius reads: “or even in other capital vices which your holiness finds to have violated the canons.” HARD.] or if your holiness finds them to have violated any other chapter of the canons—let your apostolic authority by no means permit them to exercise the priesthood, because such men are called false priests by their own mouth and are known to be worse and more depraved than secular men, since they abstain neither from fornication nor from unlawful marriages, nor keep their hands innocent of shedding human blood.

What sort of priests can they suppose themselves to be, or what can they think of themselves, when God says: “My priests shall marry only once” (Leviticus XXI)? And the Apostle says: “The husband of one wife” (I Timothy III), and so forth. This is permitted before the priesthood has been received. From the day on which they receive the priesthood, however, they must be forbidden even marriage itself.

How do those desire to exercise the priesthood who are shown to be entangled in such crimes, so that we would not wish even secular Christians to be involved in these offenses? How do they not fear touching the divine mysteries? Or how do they dare approach to pray for sins, when the sacred canons do not even permit a pure cleric who is not a priest to marry a second time? These men, by contrast, not only refuse to abstain from one wife after receiving the priesthood, but, enveloped in lust, commit crimes worse than those of secular people, so that they dare to have several wives, although they are not permitted to touch even one after receiving the ministry.

Disregarding these matters and provoking God to anger, they commit greater crimes by killing Christians and pagans with their own hands. Thus those to whom they ought to have administered the bath of regeneration for the remission of sins and bestowed the sacraments of Christ, lest they perish forever, are themselves destroyed by the sacrilegious hands of those very men.

What wise person with understanding would regard as priests those who neither abstain from fornication nor keep their hands innocent of shedding blood? And who would believe that God is appeased by their sacrifices, when the Prophet says: “The Lord abhors the bloodthirsty and deceitful man” (Psalm V)? These men, as I have said, we admonish not to exercise the priesthood or touch the divine mysteries. Whatever else you find them to have transgressed against ecclesiastical discipline, as stated above, keep the canons and the institutions of the Fathers before you, and judge according to what you have been taught in them.

[Col. 0920B] ### IV

As for what you said concerning your desire to appoint a successor, so that a bishop might be chosen in your place while you are still alive, we allow this on no account, because it is shown to be contrary to every ecclesiastical rule and to the institutions of the Fathers.

But we wish him to assist you and to be your helper in the Gospel of Christ, as the Apostle says: “If anyone has served well, he acquires for himself a good standing” (I Timothy III). For it is clearly most reprehensible that, while you are alive, we should substitute another for you.

Rather, we admonish you that, for as long as divine clemency commands you to remain here, you should pray without ceasing that God grant you as successor one who can be pleasing to Him, and who may govern irreproachably the people whom He has willed to call to His grace through the diligence of your holiness, and labor to lead them to the way of life.

For how can we grant what you have requested, [Note: [Col. 0920D] Baron: “Even if we should wish to.” HARD.] even if we should wish to do so, when we are frail human beings subject to the condition of death, ignorant of what the coming day may bring, and unable to discover which of us will depart this present age first?

But if divine clemency should will that he survive the day of your departure, and if you recognize him as suitable and it has been determined according to your will, at the hour when you know that you are about to depart this present age, designate your successor in the presence of everyone, so that he may come here to be ordained.

We allow no one else what, compelled by charity, we have judged it right to grant you.

[Col. 0920D] ### V

As for the man who is said to have taken as wife his maternal uncle’s widow—who herself had been the wife of his cousin—and who was shown to wear the sacred veil, and who publicized that permission had been granted him by our predecessor of blessed memory to take her in a pernicious marriage: far be it from us to believe that our predecessor ordered this.

For matters that are found to be contrary to the institutions of the Fathers or the canons are not directed from this apostolic see. Therefore, brother, do not cease warning, exhorting, and rebuking them, so that they may withdraw from such a criminal marriage and not perish forever.

Let them remember that they have been redeemed by the blood of Christ, and that they must not voluntarily surrender themselves—unless they have withdrawn from that incestuous marriage—to the power of the devil. Rather, let them belong to God Himself, to Christ His Son, and to the Holy Spirit, in whose name they were rescued from the power of that ancient enemy.

Labor among them, most holy brother, for you know what is written: “Whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (James III). We too have sent written admonitions concerning this matter.

### VI

As for the Kalends of January, and the other forms of augury, amulets, incantations, and various other observances which you said are practiced according to pagan custom among the blessed Apostle Peter or in the city of Rome, we judge this to be detestable and harmful both to us and to all Christians, since God says: “You shall not practice augury or observe dreams” (Leviticus XIX). And again: “There is no augury in Israel, nor divination in the house of Jacob” (Numbers XXIII).

We therefore judge that we too must beware, so that we pay attention to no auguries or observances, since we have been taught by the Fathers that all these things have been cut off. And because they were again sprouting up through the instigation of the devil, from the day on which divine clemency commanded us—although we are unworthy—to act in the place of the apostle, we immediately cut them all off.

In the same way we wish your holiness to preach to the peoples subject to you and lead them to the way of eternal life. For by the constitution of our predecessor and fosterer, Pope Gregory, of holy memory, all these things, and many other diverse practices that were sprouting up at the devil’s prompting in Christ’s fold, were piously and faithfully cut off. In imitation of him, we have hastened to direct these instructions for the salvation of that people.

### VII

As for those priests who hold false opinions, who are also proved to be adulterers and fornicators, and who assert that an indulgence has been granted them by the apostolic see, claiming in turn that permission to preach has been conceded to them: let your holy fraternity believe this on no account. Rather, exercise canonical punishment against them in the same way as against those about whom you have been instructed above by us.

For we wish you to do nothing other than what the sacred canons command, or what you are recognized as having been instructed to do by this apostolic see.

In accordance with the petition of your holiness, we have also sent letters of confirmation to each of your three bishops, which we wish you to bestow upon them by the hands of your holiness. We have sent other writings to our son Carloman, so that he may hasten to fulfill what he promised you and provide assistance.

But these matters, dearest brother, concerning all the chapters set out above, we have answered, as the Lord has granted, in order to cut away all the scandals of diabolical fraud.

As for your holy fraternity, if anything else should occur hereafter, let it strive to correct it in the parishes entrusted to it by God, as the sacred canons teach. For it is not fitting for us to preach anything other than what we have been taught by the holy Fathers.

But if, through the cunning of the enemy, something new should occur which your holy fraternity cannot discern by the institutions of the canons, do not hesitate to make it known to us, so that, with God’s help, we may hasten to reply to you without delay concerning whatever may serve to correct the new people.

For your holy fraternity should know, dearest brother, that we hold your love in the depths of our hearts, so that we desire to see you bodily every day, and regard you as a member of our fellowship—as truly a minister of God and steward of the churches of Christ.

For the rest, take courage in the Lord, dearest brother, be strong, and labor at the work to which divine clemency has willed to call you. A great hope of reward awaits you, which God has promised to those who love Him.

And although we are sinners, we nevertheless do not cease to implore without interruption the immense clemency of our God, that He who began the good work in you may bring it to completion. And may blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, cooperate with you in all the good things that you desire to accomplish for Him.

May God keep you safe, most reverend brother.

Given on the Kalends of April, while our most pious lord Augustus Constantine, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, the second year of his imperial rule, indiction 11.

## LETTER III. OF POPE ZACHARY

[Note: [Col. 0921C] On the same day on which Zachary wrote to Boniface, he also wrote to the bishops of the new sees instituted by him, namely, to Burchard, bishop of Würzburg; to Witta, bishop of Buraburg; and to Adalarius, bishop of Erfurt. Among the Bonifacian letters, letters 131 and 133 are addressed to the bishops Witta and Burchard. In Serarius’s edition the former bears this title: “Pope Zachary to our most beloved Witta of the holy Church of Barbarena.” Among Zachary’s letters this occupies the second place, and was published by Binius with the following title: “Pope Zachary to our most beloved Witta of the holy Church of Barbarena.” Sirmond, knowing that the bishop of the Church of Würzburg was not Witta but the provost Burchard, gave this same second letter the following inscription, followed by Labbe in his edition of the Councils: “Pope Zachary to our most beloved Burchard, bishop of the holy Church of Würzburg.” Yet, as Cointius says, year 742, no. 19, among the letters inserted among the Bonifacian letters, one is addressed to Witta and another to Burchard: the letter to Witta is letter 133, with these words: “Pope Zachary to our most beloved Burchard of the holy Church of Würzburg.” Serarius, in note 29 to the Life of Saint Boniface, p. 501, says that Zachary’s second letter bears this inscription: “Pope Zachary to our most beloved Witta of the holy Church of Birbug.” In his notes on the same letter he observes that the first word of the inscription is read not as dilectissimo, “most beloved,” but as dilectissimis, “most beloved,” in the Imperial Codex, since the letter seems to have been common to three bishops—namely Burchard, Witta, and Adalarius. This opinion is most probable, and there are three copies of this letter, with the same title, each directed to one of the three bishops, as its wording indicates. The letter is said to have been given on the Kalends of April, while the great emperor Constantine was reigning, in the twenty-fourth year, the second year of his imperial rule, indiction 11. Yet these chronological notes must be corrected in the same way as in the letter of Pope Zachary to Boniface reported immediately below, since both were given at nearly the same time. PAGIUS.]

### To Burchard, Bishop of Würzburg

He confirms his episcopal see, instituted by the archbishop Boniface.

[Note: [Col. 0922D] In the Collection of Letters of the Supreme Pontiffs it reads: “Pope Zachary to our most beloved Witta of the holy Church of Barbarena.” HARD.]

Pope Zachary to our most beloved Burchard, bishop of the holy Church of Würzburg.

With the Lord cooperating and confirming the word, for the extension of the law of Christianity and of the path of orthodox faith, in order to teach according to what this holy Roman Church—which, by God’s authority, we preside over—preaches, it has become known to us through our most holy and reverend brother and fellow bishop Boniface that he recently separated and established episcopal sees in the regions of Germany, where your beloved self presides, and divided the province into three parishes.

When we learned this, with great rejoicing and with palms extended toward the stars, we gave thanks to the Lord God, the illuminator and giver of all good things, and to our Savior Jesus Christ, who makes the two one.

The aforesaid most holy man requested through his letter that your sees be confirmed by apostolic authority. Therefore, with ardent spirit, with divine assistance, and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom God and our Savior Jesus Christ gave the power of binding and loosing human sins in heaven and on earth, we confirm them and decree that your episcopal sees shall remain firm.

By the authority of that prince of the apostles, we forbid all present and future generations to dare act against this arrangement of yours, which by God’s favor has been made among you at our command.

We further forbid anyone, in accordance with the tradition of the holy canons, to be transferred there from another bishopric or to ordain a bishop after your summons from this world, unless it is one who has exercised the office of our apostolic see in those regions.

Nor may anyone presume to invade another’s parishes or take away churches. For, although we do not believe it will happen, if anyone should attempt with rash presumption to act against this command of ours, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema under God’s eternal judgment.

But if anyone observes the apostolic commands and attains the rule of right and orthodox faith, may he receive the grace of blessing.

For the rest, we ask divine clemency to confirm and strengthen what the Lord has accomplished in you. May the love of God, peace, and grace be with your spirit, most holy and beloved ones.

Labor with all your strength for the faith of Christ, and strive to fulfill His ministry, so that you may be worthy to say with the distinguished Apostle: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. For the rest, the crown of righteousness has been laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will render to me on that day” (I Timothy IV).

Greeting you in the Lord, we desire that you be well. Farewell.

Given on the Kalends of April, while the lord Constantine, the great emperor, was reigning, in the twenty-fourth year, the second year of his imperial rule, indiction 11.

## LETTER IV. LETTER OF POPE ZACHARY TO THE FRANKS AND GAULS

He praises them for what had rightly been established at the synod and urges them to continue obeying the admonitions of Boniface.

Pope Zachary to all the bishops, priests, deacons, abbots, and also all dukes, counts, and all who fear God, established throughout the Gallic and Frankish provinces.

When our most reverend and holy brother Boniface, bishop, reported to us that, while a synod had been assembled in your province in accordance with our admonition, through the agency of our sons, your princes Pippin and Carloman, and while the aforesaid Boniface was acting in our place, the Lord had inclined your hearts, together with those of your princes, toward his preaching, so that you obeyed all his admonitions and expelled from among you false, schismatic, murderous, and fornicating priests, we gave thanks to our almighty God and have prayed for you without ceasing, that He who began the good work in you may bring it to completion.

For I beseech you all before God to obey his admonitions firmly. We have appointed him in those regions in our place to preach, so that, with God’s favor, he may lead you to the way of righteousness and you may be preserved from every crime.

Until now, because of your sins, you have had false and erring priests. Hence all the pagan peoples prevailed over you in battle, because there was no distinction between laymen and priests, although priests are not permitted to fight.

For what victory can be granted where priests, at one hour, handle the Lord’s mysteries and offer the Lord’s body to Christians for the redemption of their souls, and afterward kill with their own sacrilegious hands the Christians to whom they ought to have ministered these things, or the pagans to whom they ought to have preached Christ?

And it comes to pass according to the Lord’s word: “You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt has lost its savor, with what will it be seasoned? It is thereafter good for nothing except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by men” (Matthew V).

Since these things are so, and since such priests have been among you, how will you be able to conquer your enemies? But if you have priests who are pure and chaste, free from every act of fornication and homicide, as the sacred canons command, and as our aforesaid brother Boniface preaches in our place, and if you obey him in everything, no nation will be able to stand before you. All the pagan peoples will fall before your face, and you will be victorious; moreover, by doing good, you will possess eternal life.

But you, dearest brothers, who are true priests or are subject to regular discipline, present yourselves in such a way that you may truly be ministers of God and stewards of God’s mysteries, so that our ministry may not be reviled, lest what is written come to pass among you: “As the people are, so is the priest” (Isaiah XXIV). And if this should happen, what praise will you receive from men, or what reward may you expect from God?

Therefore correct yourselves as true priests, and conduct your priesthood in such a way that a good testimony may remain for both you and them from those who are outside; so that you may obtain praise from men and may be worthy to receive from God the reward of recompense in eternal blessedness, because through you many have been led to the right faith of Christ while having blameless priests.

Come together at the synod every year to discuss the unity of the Church, so that, if anything adverse should occur, it may be cut out by the roots and God’s Church may remain unshaken.

Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0925C] By this letter Zachary confirms what had been done at the synod of Liptina. The Roman pontiff testifies that two matters in particular had been reported to him by Boniface. First, that not merely Carloman but both brothers together, Carloman and Pippin, had proved to be his partners and assistants in preaching. Secondly, he speaks of the three metropolitans commended to him in Boniface’s letters. He distinguishes Grimo from the other two and declares that Grimo was already known to him, while Abel and Artbert had most recently been instituted as archbishops. Grimo had been raised to the archbishopric of Rouen several years earlier; concerning him, see the Anonymous Life in the Acts of the Archbishops of Rouen, published by Mabillon in volume II of the Analecta, who lived under Gregory VII, Roman pontiff. Abel was instituted archbishop of Rheims, a church which Milo, archbishop of Trier, was ruining, while also dissipating both archbishoprics. Ardebert, or Artbert, was constituted bishop of Sens.

The subscription of this letter presents great difficulty and is reported in various forms by different authors. All agree on the day, although it has been incorrectly transcribed, as we shall soon demonstrate. They also agree on the third year of the emperors Artabasdus and Nicephorus; but since both were overthrown in November of the Christian year 743, and Nicephorus was crowned by his father around the Kalends of May in the Christian year 743, there is no doubt that, where it reads “in the third year of the great emperor Nicephorus,” it should read “in the first year of the great emperor Nicephorus.” Thus the subscription of this letter should be restored as follows: “Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, while the lord Artabasdus, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the third year, after his consulship in the third year, but also while Nicephorus, the great emperor, was reigning, in the first year, indiction 12.” After Pope Zachary had written this letter, he received another letter from Boniface, which has not reached us, but which Zachary mentions and to which Letter 5 replies, given on the Nones of November.

In it the pontiff says: “Having received the letter of your fraternity, and so forth, we fell into a kind of ecstasy . . . because it was found to differ greatly from the words which your fraternity had sent during the preceding month of August, in which you informed us that a council, and so forth.” Since Boniface’s letter to Zachary, in which he requested three pallia, was given in August, as Zachary himself testifies, while Letter IV of the same pontiff is said by the error of copyists to have been given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, and since Boniface’s letter was written in August and Zachary replies to it by sending the three pallia requested, the reply must necessarily have been given after August; otherwise it would have preceded rather than followed the request for the three pallia, although Zachary writes the contrary and expressly asserts that those pallia had been requested from him.

Moreover, both letters of Zachary, Letter 4 and Letter 5, are shown to have been written during indiction 12 and the Christian year 745, after the celebration of the council held at Liptina on the Kalends of March, by the words of Zachary cited above: “The council was held with God’s help and with Carloman giving his consent.” For Liptina, as everyone agrees, was in Carloman’s dominion. Therefore Sirmond and Cointius were mistaken in maintaining that both letters were given after the council of Soissons, since Soissons belonged not to Carloman but to Pippin.

Furthermore, since both subscriptions mention the emperor Artabasdus, who certainly was deposed in November of the Christian year 743, how could these letters have been given in 744, when the council at Soissons was held, as Sirmond wishes, or in 745, as Cointius believes? PAGIUS.]

## LETTER V. OF POPE ZACHARY TO BONIFACE, ARCHBISHOP

He sends pallia for three metropolitans and speaks about two false prophets discovered in Francia.

Zachary, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop.

We read in the Book of the Acts of the Apostles that the Holy Spirit commanded the apostles: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have called them” (Acts XIII)—that is, so that by preaching the Christian religion and the grace of that same Holy Spirit they might illuminate the whole world.

Through the illumination of their preaching and teaching, with the protection of Christ, the Catholic Church of God has remained and remains resplendent, illuminated also by the teachings of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. By divine inspiration, we believe that your most holy fraternity has been sent to those regions as one who follows in their footsteps, so that likewise the same Holy Spirit has taken you up for the same work, for the illumination of those peoples.

Therefore we rejoice greatly in the Lord and offer immense praise to His omnipotence. But when the series of your words was unfolded to us one by one, we rejoiced in the Lord much more, who has deigned to bestow His grace upon you in such a way that you softened the hearts of that harsh people, so that they willingly inclined themselves to obey the faith and submit to the divine commands.

For you informed us how and in what manner God had touched the hearts of our most excellent sons Pippin and Carloman, so that through divine inspiration they might strive to be your partners and assistants in preaching. Their reward remains abundant in heaven, because blessed is the man through whom God is blessed.

Concerning the metropolitan bishops—namely, Grimo, whom we already know, and Abel and Artbert, [Note: [Col. 0926D] Baronius reads “Abel or Albert.” HARD.] whom you established in the several metropolitan provinces—we confirm this through your testimony and send pallia for their firm establishment and for the growth of God’s Church, so that they may advance in a better condition.

We have sent them instructions concerning the nature of the pallium and how those who are permitted to use it must profess their faith. We inform them so that they may know the use of the pallium: that they should preach the way of salvation to those subject to them; that ecclesiastical discipline should be preserved in their churches and remain unshaken; and that the priesthood entrusted to them should be, as far as human condition permits, not polluted as it was before, but pure and acceptable to God.

Thus none of them should be found to depart from the sacred canons, and their sacrifice should be offered pure to God, so that the Lord may be appeased by their gifts and the people of God, with minds purified from every filth of vice, may be able to offer sincere service to God.

You also reported to us, dearest brother, that you had found two false prophets in that same province of the Franks, whom we should call not false prophets but rather false Christians.

Of these, according to the tenor of your letter, we find one to be a new Simon. [Note: [Col. 0926D] He means Adelbert. MANSI.] He claimed the priesthood for himself and did not at all restrain himself from lust. He led the people astray and preached empty things, surrendering not only his own soul to the devil’s power but also plunging the hearts of the people into destruction, [Note: [Col. 0927D] The Roman edition reads the following words in this manner: “and leading the people astray through falsehoods, so that he removed them from the Church of God and caused them to dissent from the Christian law; and, setting up crosses in the fields and little oratories there, he led the people astray, abandoning the public churches and running to those signs which he falsely made. He caused himself to be called by the name of Holiness and consecrated churches in his own name, asserting that he also knew the names of angels, which names he sent written in your letter. We affirm that these names belong not to angels but rather to demons. But as for the other one, etc.” MANSI.] and through his deceits withdrawing them from the Church of God, setting up crosses in the fields, establishing little oratories to lead the people astray, abandoning the public and ancient churches, having himself called by the name of Holiness, consecrating churches in his own name, and asserting that he knew the names of angels—indeed, rather, of demons.

[Note: [Col. 0928D] He is speaking of Clement. MANSI.]

The other was so devoted to lust that he kept a concubine and fathered two sons by her, yet claimed the priesthood for himself, asserting that it was just according to the tradition of the Old Testament for a surviving brother to take the wife of his deceased brother, and because Christ, rising from the dead, had left no one there but had brought them all out. We judge all these things to be detestable and criminal.

Your fraternal holiness rightly condemned them according to ecclesiastical rule, confined them in custody, and most appropriately called them ministers and forerunners of Antichrist.

For the rest, strive, dearest brother, act manfully, and remain ever-watchful in the ministry of Christ, so that Christ’s flock may increase still more, that an abundant reward of eternal recompense may remain for you, and that, as we believe, you may share fellowship with the saints and elect of God.

May God keep you safe, most reverend brother.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, while the lord Artabasdus, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the third year, [Col. 0927C] after his consulship in the third year, and also while Nicephorus, the great emperor, was reigning, in the third year, indiction 12 [another reading: 10].

## LETTER VI. OF POPE ZACHARY TO BONIFACE, ARCHBISHOP

I. He wonders why he now requests a pallium for one man, Grimo, when he formerly requested them for three. II. He refutes the accusation of the simoniacal stain with which he was charged. III. He delegates to him his authority not only in Bavaria but throughout all Gaul.

### I

Having received the letters of your most holy fraternity through the bearer of this letter and reread what they contained, we fell into a kind of ecstasy and great amazement, because they were found to differ greatly from the words that your fraternity had sent during the past month of August, [Col. 0927D] in which you informed us that, with God’s help and with Carloman giving and affirming his consent, a council had been held; that you had suspended from sacred office false priests who were not worthy to touch the divine ministry; and that you had established three archbishops, one in each metropolitan city.

You disclosed that Grimo had been established in the city called [Note: [Col. 0928D] It should read Rodomus or Rodomum, whence Remigius is called bishop of Rodomus by Sigebert in the year 751—that is, of Rouen. MANSI.] Rouen; secondly, Abel in the city called Rheims; and thirdly, Artbert in the city called Sens. He had also been with us and had brought us letters from you, Carloman, and Pippin, in which you requested that we send three pallia to the three metropolitan bishops named above. We granted them for the union and restoration of the churches of Christ.

But now, receiving your letter again, we are, as we said, greatly astonished, because previously you had petitioned us, together with the aforesaid princes of Gaul, for three pallia, and afterward for Grimo alone.

We wish your fraternity to inform us why you first sent to us concerning three and afterward concerning one, so that, being made certain about this, we may retain no ambiguity.

### II

We have also found in your aforesaid letter matters that greatly disturb our minds: you report such things to us as though we were corruptors of the canons and were seeking to abolish the traditions of the Fathers, and as though, God forbid, we had fallen with our clerics into the simoniacal heresy, accepting and compelling those to whom we give pallia to offer us gifts, and demanding money from them.

But, dearest brother, we exhort your charity that your fraternity not write anything of this kind to us in the future. It is offensive and injurious to us when what we utterly detest is brought before us.
