Far be it from us and from our clerics to sell for a price the gift that we have received through the grace of the Holy Spirit. When, as we said above, we were asked at your suggestion for those three pallia, no one sought any advantage from them.

Moreover, the documents which, according to custom, are issued from our archives for your confirmation and instruction, we granted from our own resources, taking nothing from them. Far be it that any such simoniacal crime should be charged against us by your fraternity.

For we anathematize all who have dared to sell the gift of the Holy Spirit for a price.

### III

You also informed us through other letters that in Bavaria you had found a false priest who asserted that he had been ordained bishop by us. Your fraternity acted very well in not believing him, since the false man made every false claim. Finding him false, suspend him from the priesthood.

For by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we command you to tolerate no one whom you find deviating from the sacred canons in the exercise of the sacred ministry.

And since you asked whether you ought to have the right of preaching in the province of Bavaria, which our predecessor had granted you, with God’s help we do not diminish what our predecessor and forefather granted you, but increase it.

Not only in Bavaria but throughout the entire province of Gaul, for as long as divine majesty commands you to remain, we entrust preaching to you in our place. If you find anyone holding opinions contrary to the Christian religion or to the institutions of the canons, strive spiritually to reform him according to the rule of righteousness.

May the Lord keep you safe, most reverend and holy brother.

Given [Note: [Col. 0929D] Since everyone agrees that this letter was written in the same year as the preceding one, there is no doubt that it should read: “Given on the Nones of November, while the lord most pious Augustus Artabasdus, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the third year, after his consulship in the third year, and also while Nicephorus, the great emperor, his son, was reigning, in the first year, indiction 12,” which prevailed in November of the year 743, when Artabasdus and Nicephorus were captured and blinded by the emperor Constantine. PAGIUS on the year 743, no. 11.] on the Nones of November, while the lord most pious Augustus Artabasdus, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the third year, after his consulship in the third year, and also while Nicephorus, the great emperor and his son, was reigning, in the third year, indiction 13.

## LETTER VII. OF POPE ZACHARY TO BONIFACE, BISHOP

That the baptism administered by an unlearned priest with malformed words must not be repeated.

Zachary, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and holy brother Boniface, bishop.

Virgilius and Sidonius, devout men residing in the province of the Bavarians, used letters addressed to us in which they informed us that your revered fraternity had ordered them to baptize Christians anew. When we heard this, we were greatly disturbed and fell into a certain astonishment, if the matter is as reported. For they related that there had been in that same province [Col. 0929C] a priest who completely lacked knowledge of the Latin language; and while baptizing, being ignorant of Latin speech and mangling the language, he said: “I baptize you in the name of the Fatherland, and of the Daughter, and of the Holy Spirit.” For this reason, your revered fraternity considered rebaptizing them.

But, most holy brother, if the one who baptized did not introduce an error or heresy, but merely, through ignorance of Roman speech, mangling the language as we have said above, pronounced the words while baptizing, we cannot consent that they be baptized again. For—as your holy fraternity has rightly learned—whoever has been baptized by heretics in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit must in no way be rebaptized, but must be cleansed solely through the laying on of hands.

For, most holy brother, if the matter is as it was reported to us, do not preach such things to them any longer; rather, as the holy Fathers teach and proclaim, let your holiness strive to preserve them. May God keep you safe, most revered brother.

Given on the Kalends of July, while our lord, the most devout Augustus Constantine, crowned by God as great emperor, was reigning, in the twenty-sixth year [Note: [Col. 0930D] There is an error in the twenty-sixth year; it should be read as the twenty-fifth year, while the twelfth indiction should be retained. The letter was written in the year of Christ 744. See Pagius under that year, no. 2.], in the fourth year of his reign, in the fourteenth indiction.

## LETTER VIII. POPE ZACHARIAS TO PIPPIN, MAYOR OF THE PALACE, AND ALSO TO THE BISHOPS, ABBOTS, AND NOBLES OF THE FRANKS

[Col. 0930A]

He responds concerning various chapters sent by Pippin through Ardobanius:

I. On the honor due to metropolitans. II. On condemned bishops, priests, and deacons. III. On priests who are arrogant. IV. On rural priests. V. On monks, the handmaids of God. VI. On widows who are not to be veiled. VII. On a layman who drives away his wife. VIII. On priests and deacons who hold separate assemblies. IX. On clerics and monks who do not remain in their profession. X. On clerics who are in poorhouses, monasteries, and martyria. XI. Which clerics must abstain from their wives. [Col. 0930B] XII. On those who leave their wives or husbands. XIII. On monks who become clerics. XIV. On priests and deacons who fall into crime. XV. On churches that laymen build on their own property. XVI. On clerics who leave their own churches. XVII. On bishops who receive the clerics of others. XVIII. Which clerics may marry wives. XIX. That priests and deacons should not be received without letters of recommendation. XX. On veiled virgins who go astray. XXI. On un veiled virgins who go astray. XXII. On women who marry two brothers, or men who take two sisters as wives. XXIII. On those who deliberately commit homicide. XXIV. On those who commit homicide unintentionally. XXV. On those who have adulterous wives, or are themselves adulterers. XXVI. On monks and virgins who do not keep their profession. [Col. 0930C] XXVII. On those who marry after undertaking a profession of virginity.

To the most excellent and most Christian lord Pippin, mayor of the palace, and to all the bishops of the Churches who are most dear to us, and to the devout abbots, and to all the God-fearing princes established in the region of the Franks, Zacharias, bishop of the holy catholic and apostolic Church of God at Rome, sends greetings in the Lord. May grace and peace be granted to you by God the almighty Father, and by the Lord Jesus Christ, his only Son, and by the Holy Spirit.

We rejoice with great joy in the Lord, having learned through the report of our most discerning and God-preserved beloved son Pippin of your good manner of life; and that, just as you are united and cooperative in good arrangements pleasing to God, so you preserve, as is fitting, the venerable places of God’s Church situated throughout your entire province, together with their prelates, priests, and devout abbots, in holy habit and priestly conduct, devoting yourselves to prayers and persisting in supplications to implore divine power and victory granted from heaven against pagan and unbelieving [Col. 0931A] peoples for your defenders.

For when you approach God in true confession and with a simple heart, just as that friend of God Moses fought by praying (Exodus XVII), and Joshua son of Nun conquered by waging the Lord’s wars with the people of Israel, so you too, my dearest ones, must act, so that you may assist your people by praying and clinging to good works, turning away from secular cares and business. For it is written: “Be still and see, for the Lord is sweet” (Psalm XLV). And again: “Draw near to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Psalm XXXIII).

Princes and secular men, as well as warriors, ought to undertake the care and concern required against the cunning of enemies and for the defense of the province. But it belongs to prelates, priests, and servants of God to devote themselves to salutary [Col. 0931B] counsels and prayers, so that while you pray and they fight, the province may, with God’s help, remain safe, and this may become for you salvation, praise, and an everlasting reward.

By this, indeed, your prelacy will appear in holiness, and the principate of our beloved son Pippin will be approved through the power and good ordering of his subjects. Therefore, as our aforementioned son Pippin requested of us, with your counsel, that we give an answer concerning all the chapters of which he informed us, insofar as we are able in the Lord, we have ordered that what we possess from the teaching of the holy Fathers and what the authority of the sacred canons has sanctioned be written below concerning each chapter; and we have also included in our replies what, with God’s inspiration, we have been able to decree by apostolic authority.

[Col. 0931C] **I. How the metropolitan bishop ought to be honored**

In chapter 35 of the canons of the holy apostles it is written: [Note: [Col. 0931D] Here and in all places where chapters of the Canons are cited, see the *Code of the Canons of the Roman Church*, edited by François Pithaeus and printed at the royal press in 1687, p. 3.]

“It is fitting that the bishops of each people know who among them is first, whom they should regard as their head, and that they do nothing further without his knowledge, except only those things which each one separately has to do with his own parish and the villages subject to it; nor should he do anything without the knowledge of all. For thus there will be unanimity, and God will be glorified through Christ in the Holy Spirit.”

Likewise, in chapter 9 of the canon of the Council of Antioch, it is contained as follows:

“It is fitting that the bishops of each region know that the metropolitan bishop bears responsibility for the whole province; for this reason all those everywhere who appear to have business to conduct should come together at the metropolis. Therefore it has seemed good that he excel in honor, and that the other bishops do nothing beyond him, according to the ancient rule established by the Fathers, except only those things that concern their own diocese and the possessions subject to them.

“For each bishop must have authority over his own parish, so that he may govern it according to the reverence due to each person, and exercise care over every possession under his authority. Thus he may ordain priests and deacons, and determine each matter by his own judgment. But let him attempt nothing further beyond the metropolitan bishop; nor should the metropolitan undertake anything without the counsel of the other priests.”

Likewise, chapter 32 of the book of the decrees of blessed Leo contains the following:

“Therefore, according to the canons of the holy Fathers, composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, we decree that the metropolitan bishops of the individual provinces, whose care has been entrusted to your fraternity by delegation from us, retain unimpaired the right of the dignity entrusted to them from ancient times, so that they depart from the rules laid down neither through negligence nor presumption, whether in holiness of dress or of conduct.

“For we also add, by apostolic authority, that a bishop should use garments according to his dignity. Likewise, cardinal priests, and those who wish to live in the monastic life, should, clothed in more distinguished attire before the people subject to them, discharge the duty of preaching, while preserving their profession in the secrecy of their hearts, so that God, who sees in secret, may repay them openly. For it is written: ‘What you say in your hearts, and be pricked in your beds’ (Psalm IV). It is not the honor of garments that commends us, but the splendor of souls.

“But monks must continually use woolen garments, according to the norm and rule of monastic discipline and the tradition of the holy and approved Fathers. For if, having renounced the things of the world, they have devoted themselves wholly to God, they ought to abstain from all illicit things, so that, insofar as they have endured labor in their bodies, they may deserve to receive from God an equal reward of recompense.

“For Christ gave the apostles the divine command not to possess two tunics (Matthew X). He said ‘tunics,’ namely woolen ones, not linen ones. Therefore, whoever obeys the Lord’s command and clings to good works will possess eternal life.”

Likewise, chapter 10 of the canon of the Council of Antioch decreed concerning those called chorepiscopi:

“Those who are called chorepiscopi in villages or estates, although they have received the laying on of hands from bishops and have been consecrated as bishops, nevertheless the holy synod has decided that they should recognize their proper status and govern the Churches subject to them, being content with their administration and care. They may also ordain readers, subdeacons, and exorcists, and these promotions should suffice for them. But they may not dare to ordain either a priest or a deacon apart from the bishop of the city to whom they themselves, together with the estate, are subject.

“If anyone attempts to transgress these statutes, he shall be deposed and deprived of the honor he held. The bishop of the city to whom the chorepiscopus is subject shall ordain the chorepiscopus.”

**II. On condemned bishops, priests, and deacons, who must not usurp their former office**

Chapter 29 of the book of the canons of the holy apostles states:

“If any bishop, priest, or deacon, having been justly deposed for specified crimes, dares to take up again the ministry formerly entrusted to him, let him be completely cut off from the Church.”

**III. On arrogant priests**

From the Council of Carthage, chapter 9:

“If any priest, puffed up against his bishop, creates a schism, let him be anathema.”

All the bishops said:

“If any priest has been corrected by his superior, he ought certainly to bring his complaint before neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard by them and through them he may be reconciled to his own bishop. But if he does not do this and—God forbid—puffed up with pride, withdraws by separating himself from communion with his bishop, and offers sacrifice to God separately with certain others, let him be held anathema and lose his position. If he does not have a just complaint against the bishop, an inquiry must be made.”

**IV. On rural priests and the obedience they owe to bishops and cardinal priests**

Chapter 13 of the Council of Neocaesarea contains the following:

“Rural priests may not offer in the church of the city in the presence of the bishop or of the priests of that city, nor give the consecrated bread or present the chalice. But if these men are absent and the rural priests are summoned to give the prayer, they alone may give it. Chorepiscopi, too, appear to exist as an example and likeness of the seventy, so that when they have ministered, they may be honored because of the zeal they show toward the poor.”

**V. On monks, that is, the handmaids of God**

It was asked whether they may attend the solemn celebration of Mass, publicly read lessons on Holy Saturday, or sing at Masses, whether the Alleluia or the responsory. Concerning this, chapter 26 of the book of the decrees of blessed Pope Gelasius states:

“It is unlawful for women to minister at the sacred altars or to presume to undertake any of those duties assigned to the service of men. Nevertheless, we have heard with indignation that such contempt has fallen upon sacred things that women are said to minister at the sacred altars and to have a sex to which such things do not belong perform everything assigned exclusively to the service of men. Yet the guilt and crime of all the offenses that we have individually touched upon fall upon those priests who either commit these things or, by failing to make public those who commit them, show that they favor their wicked excesses.”

**VI. On widows, whether they can save their souls in their own dwellings**

The same book, chapter 21, contains the following:

“Let widows not be veiled by pontiffs; and if, after having professed continence, they trample upon it after changing their intention, let them themselves give an account to God for their deeds.”

For we have discussed above at greater length the matter of widows who are not to be veiled under any blessing. If, by their own will and with a changeable mind, they trample upon the chastity of marriage that they professed, it will be their concern what satisfaction they ought to offer God in order to appease him. For just as, if they perhaps could not remain continent, they were in no way forbidden to marry, according to the Apostle (1 Timothy V), so, after deliberating with themselves, they ought to have guarded the promise of chastity that they made to God. We must not impose any snare upon such women, but only set before them the exhortation of an eternal reward and the punishments of divine judgment, so that our conscience may be clear and their own intention may give an account to God for itself.

[Col. 0934A] **VII. On a layman who drives away his wife**

Chapter 48 of the canons of the holy apostles states:

“If any layman, driving away his own wife, takes another, or takes a woman dismissed by another man, let him be deprived of communion.”

**VIII. On priests and deacons who withdraw from ecclesiastical ministry and hold separate assemblies**

Chapter 5 of the canon of the Council of Antioch has promulgated the following:

“If any priest or deacon, despising his own bishop, separates himself from the Church, gathers people separately, and sets up an altar, and does not heed the bishop who admonishes him, nor consent or obey when summoned once and again, let him be condemned altogether and receive no further remedy, because he cannot recover his dignity.

“But if he persists in disturbing and troubling the Church, let him, as a seditious person, be suppressed by external authorities.”

**IX. On clerics and monks who do not remain in their profession**

What was asked is decreed in chapter 7 of the Council of Chalcedon:

“Those who have once been assigned to the clergy, or have chosen the life of monks, we decree must not enter military service or any worldly dignity. But those who attempt this and do not repent, so as to return to what they first chose for God’s sake, are to be anathematized.”

**X. On clerics who are in poorhouses, monasteries, and martyria**

Chapter 9 of the canon of the Council of Chalcedon decrees as follows:

“Clerics who are placed in charge of poorhouses, or who are ordained in monasteries and basilicas [Col. 0934C] of martyrs, must remain under the authority of the bishops who are in each city, according to the traditions of the holy Fathers, and must not rebelliously withdraw from their bishop. Those who dare to overturn this arrangement in any way and do not submit to their own bishop shall, if they are clerics, be subject to canonical correction; but if they are laymen or monks, they shall be deprived of communion.”

**XI. Which clerics must abstain from their wives**

Chapter 37 of the Council of Africa contains the following:

“Moreover, since the incontinence of certain clerics, even with regard to their own wives, was reported, it was decided that bishops, priests, and deacons should, according to their own statutes, also abstain from their wives; and if they do not do so, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office. Other clerics, however, are not to be compelled to this, but the practice should be observed according to the custom of each Church.”

**XII. On those who leave their wives or husbands, so that they remain in that state**

Chapter 69 of the aforementioned Council of Africa contains the following:

“It has been decided that, according to evangelical and apostolic discipline, neither a man dismissed by his wife nor a woman dismissed by her husband may be joined to another; rather, let them remain as they are or be reconciled to one another. If they despise this, let them be brought to penance.”

**XIII. What should be done if a monk becomes a cleric**

Chapter 17 of the decree of blessed Pope Innocent contains the following:

“Concerning monks who remain for a long time in monasteries and afterward attain the clerical order: they must not deviate from their own profession. For either, just as he was in the monastery and what he observed for a long time, he ought not to lose after being placed in a better rank; or, if he was corrupted, then baptized, and, while remaining in the monastery, wished to enter the clerical order, he cannot have a wife at all, since one who had previously been corrupted cannot be blessed with a bride.

“This rule is observed among clerics, especially since the ancient rule holds that anyone who, after being corrupted and baptized, wishes to become a cleric must promise that he will never take a wife.”

**XIV. That priests or deacons who fall into any crime cannot obtain the remedy of penance through the laying on of hands**

Chapter 16 of the decree of blessed Pope Leo decrees as follows:

“It is foreign to ecclesiastical custom that those who have been consecrated to the priestly honor or the rank of deacon should receive, for any crime of theirs, the remedy of penance through the laying on of hands. This undoubtedly derives from apostolic tradition, according to what is written: ‘If a priest sins, who will pray for him?’ (1 Samuel II).

“Therefore, for those who have fallen in this way, a secluded retreat must be sought in order to merit God’s mercy, where their satisfaction may be worthy and also fruitful.”

**XV. On laymen who build churches on their own property**

With regard to the question of laymen who build churches on their own property—who ought to govern or administer them—the holy Fathers have established the following, and it is contained in the apostolic precepts, according to the petitioner’s request:

“If on any estate, of whatever legal ownership, an oratory or basilica has been built out of devotion, in honor of any saint, the oratory having been founded in the parish of whichever bishop it belongs to, then, after a lawful donation has first been received—that is, one providing the stated amount [the text is incomplete: praestante tot] and secured by municipal records—the said oratory shall be solemnly consecrated without public Masses.

“Thus, neither at that place nor in future times shall baptisteries be constructed, nor shall a cardinal priest be appointed. But if they wish to celebrate Masses there, they must request a priest anew from the bishop, so that nothing whatsoever may be presumed by any other priest unless he has been appointed by the bishop.”

**XVI. On clerics who leave their own churches**

Chapter 15 of the canons of the holy apostles contains the following:

“If any priest, deacon, or anyone from the number of clerics, leaving his own parish, goes to another and, departing entirely without the knowledge of his bishop, dwells in another parish, we shall not permit him to minister any longer, especially if, summoned by his bishop, he refuses to return and persists in his disorder. Nevertheless, let him communicate there as a layman.”

**XVII. On bishops who receive the clerics of another bishop, and are therefore to be excommunicated**

The same canon, chapter 16, contains the following:

“If the bishop with whom it is established that the aforementioned clerics are staying, disregarding as nothing the suspension decreed against them, should perhaps receive them as clerics, let him, as a teacher of disorder, be deprived of communion.”

**XVIII. Which clerics may take wives**

Chapter 17 of the canons of the holy apostles decrees:

“As for the unmarried men who have been advanced to the clergy, we command that, if they wish, they may take wives—but only if they are readers or singers.”

**XIX. That no priest or deacon be received without letters of recommendation**

The same canon of the holy apostles contains the following:

“No bishop from abroad, nor priest or deacon, shall be received without letters of recommendation. When they bring written documents, let them be examined carefully, and let them be received if they have proved to be preachers of piety. Otherwise, let neither necessary assistance be supplied to them nor let them be admitted to communion in any way, because much arises from surreptitious entry.”

**XX. On veiled virgins who go astray**

What should be done with them is asserted in chapter 19 of the book of the decrees of blessed Pope Innocent:

“Those who are spiritually married to Christ and veiled by a priest, if afterward they either marry publicly or secretly corrupt themselves, are not to be admitted to perform penance unless the one to whom they had joined themselves has departed from the world.

“For if this rule is observed among human beings, so that any woman who marries another while her husband is alive is regarded as an adulteress and is not granted permission to perform penance unless one of the two has died, how much more must it be observed with regard to the woman who had joined herself to an immortal bridegroom and afterward passed over to human marriage?”

[Col. 0936C] **XXI. On un veiled virgins who go astray**

The same book, chapter 20, contains the following:

“Those who have not yet been covered by the sacred veil but have always pretended to remain in the profession of virginity—even if they have not been veiled, should they perhaps marry—must perform penance for a considerable period, because their pledge was held by the Lord.

“For if among human beings a contract made in good faith is ordinarily dissolved in no way, how much more will this promise, which she made with God, be unable to be dissolved without punishment? For if the Apostle Paul said that those who departed from the profession of widowhood had condemnation because they had made their first faith void, how much more those virgins who have attempted to break faith with their earlier promise?”

[Col. 0936D] **XXII. On women who marry two brothers, or men who take two sisters as wives**

Chapter 11 of the Council of Neocaesarea contains the following:

“If a woman marries two brothers, let her be cast out until death. Nevertheless, at the end of her life, out of mercy, if she promises that, once restored to health, she will dissolve the bonds of this union, let her obtain the fruit of penance. But if the woman or the man dies in such a marriage, penance will be difficult during the life that remains.”

But we, with divine grace assisting us, in accordance with the decrees of our predecessors and former pontiffs, say with much greater firmness that, as far as a line of kinship can be recognized, no one is to be joined in marriage, according to the rite and norm of Christianity and Roman religion. [Col. 0937A] Nor should anyone, God forbid, take a spiritual relation—that is, a godmother—or a daughter as a wife in rash presumption. For this is a wickedness and a destructive sin before God and his angels. It is so grave that none of the holy Fathers, nor any of the holy synods, nor even the imperial laws, has judged anyone in this matter; rather, fearing the terrible judgment of God, they have remained silent and refrained from pronouncing a sentence.

**XXIII. On those who deliberately commit homicide**

Chapter 21 of the Council of Ancyra contains the following:

“Those who have voluntarily committed homicide must continually submit themselves to penance, but they shall attain perfection toward the end of their life.”

**XXIV. On those who commit homicide unintentionally**

The same canon, chapter 22, contains the following:

“Concerning homicides committed unintentionally, the earlier decision ordered that perfection be attained after seven years of penance, while the second required the completion of a period of five years.”

**XXV. On those who have adulterous wives or are themselves found to be adulterers**

Chapter 19 of the Council of Ancyra contains the following:

“If anyone’s wife has committed adultery, or if he himself has committed adultery, he ought to attain perfection through seven years of penance, according to the former degrees.”

**XXVI. On monks and virgins who do not keep their profession**

Chapter 6 of the book of the decrees of blessed Pope Siricius contains the following:

“Moreover, certain monks and nuns, having cast aside their profession of holiness, have sunk into such great wantonness that at first, secretly or under the pretext of monasteries, they joined themselves in illicit and sacrilegious contamination; afterward, driven into an abyss by despair of conscience, they freely fathered children from illicit embraces—something condemned both by public laws and by ecclesiastical rights.

“These shameless and detestable persons must therefore be expelled from the company of monasteries and the assemblies of clerics, so that, shut away in their own prisons and lamenting such a great crime in continual mourning, they may be able to burn away their impurity in the purifying fire of penitence, and so that, at least at death, forgiveness may be able to come to their aid through the grace of communion, solely in view of mercy.”

**XXVII. On those who, not under compulsion but by their own will, undertake a profession of virginity, and sin by marrying even though they have not yet been consecrated**

Chapter 27 of the book of the decrees of blessed Pope Leo contains the following:

“Girls who, not compelled by the command of their parents but by their own voluntary judgment, have undertaken the profession and habit of virginity, if afterward they choose marriage, transgress, even if the grace of consecration has not yet come to them; and certainly they would not have been deprived of that gift if they had remained in their profession.”

[Col. 0938A] Therefore, dearest and most beloved ones, we have ordered that the matters appended above be delivered and carried out for the knowledge and preaching of your prelacy and for the edification of the people entrusted to you by God. Insofar as, through God’s mercy, we have been able, we have drawn out from among the other chapters the sanctions of the holy apostles and of the blessed Fathers, as well as the decrees of approved and most blessed pontiffs, briefly touching upon the meaning contained in each chapter.

We exhort your most prudent holiness and the affection of the nobles that, in every respect, turning neither to the right nor to the left, but walking along the royal way, you observe the apostolic commands with the greatest steadfastness.

Moreover, most beloved ones, we have given these matters to you as instructions, so that neither we may be judged before God for silence, nor you be compelled to render an account before him for neglect, as it is written in the Lord’s command: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John XV).

Therefore, offering no excuse, care for the salvation of all rational souls, running in the contest in such a way that your ministry may not be disgraced, but that you may rather receive the prize of victory’s palm, according to the saying of the distinguished Apostle, having the crown of righteousness stored up through adherence to good works in the heavenly dwelling. May the just judge, the Lord our God and Savior Jesus Christ, grant it to you on that day—he who lives in unity with God the almighty Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. [Col. 0938C] Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0937D] **Letter.** This letter is found without a year or indiction in the *Life of Saint Boniface* in Serarius’s *History of Mainz*. In the Roman edition—which we have followed here—it is assigned to the twenty-eighth year of Constantine, counting from the time when he began to reign with his father, and to the sixth year from the time when he reigned alone after his father’s death. Nevertheless, Baronius says that an error must have crept into the numbers, since they do not agree with one another: the twenty-eighth year of the reign would likewise be the eighth year, not the sixth, from the time when he began to reign alone; yet both numbers are found to be corrupt. See below, the acts of the Second Roman Council. Binius.]

## LETTER IX. POPE ZACHARIAS TO BONIFACE, ARCHBISHOP

That the matters he wrote in reply concerning Pippin’s chapters should be read in council, and that Aldebert, Godolsacius, and Clement should be examined again.

To the most revered and most holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop, Zacharias, servant of the servants of God.

Blessed Paul aptly admonishes us when he says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians XI). For this reason, through the special [Roman Edition: spiritual] bond of charity, although absent in body, we are always present in spirit to your holy fraternity, so that, holding you in our inmost heart as a most beloved brother and fellow priest, although sinners, yet trusting in divine hope, we do not cease continually to remember you in our prayers. We ask the immense divinity of Christ our God to strengthen you in carrying out his ministry, so that on the day of his coming you may deserve to utter that gracious word: “Behold, I and the children whom you have given me; I have not lost any of them” (Isaiah VIII).

Then, amid those who have pleased him from the beginning of the world, a high-sounding and desirable voice may harmoniously bring you, at their invitation, to the place where he will say: “Come, you blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV).

With these matters thus proceeding, know, dearest brother, that Pippin, the most excellent mayor of the palace of the Frankish people, requested from us through his agent, a devout priest named Ardobanius [Roman Edition: Ardochamus], certain chapters concerning the priestly order and matters pertaining to the salvation of souls, as well as the manner in which they ought to guard themselves against illicit union according to the practice of the Christian religion and the ordinances of the sacred canons.

Although your fraternal holiness has already learned through experience what has been decreed by us concerning this matter, nevertheless, granting an attentive ear to his requests, we have sent apostolic instructions written in brief form. We have also instructed that they be made public by being read before the priestly college, and that your fraternal holiness be summoned there.

When the council has been assembled for this purpose, let those sacrilegious and contumacious men, the former bishops Aldebert, Godolsacius, and Clement, be brought forward, so that their case may once more be sifted by careful investigation. If you find that they have altogether deviated from the path of righteousness, and if, once convicted, they are found inclined to turn back to the way of righteousness, so that what is good and pleasing appears in your eyes, arrange their case with the ruler of the province according to the sanctions of the sacred canons.

But if they persist in arrogance and obstinately proclaim that they are not guilty, then, together with two or three of the most proven and prudent priests, send these men to us, so that their case may be investigated by a thorough inquiry before the apostolic see, and so that they may receive the end they deserve according to their merits.

Act, then, most beloved brother, in the ministry entrusted to you, and may you deserve to obtain eternal life, receiving from almighty God the reward of recompense. May God keep you safe, most revered brother.

Given on the Nones of January, while our lord, the most devout Augustus Constantine, crowned by God as great emperor, was reigning [Note: [Col. 0939D] Labbeus says in his *Chronology* that the twenty-seventh year should be written, and that this was the year of Christ 747. Harduinus. See Pagius, who proves the same at greater length under the year of Christ 744, nos. 4 and following.], in the twenty-eighth year, in the sixth year of his reign, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER X. POPE ZACHARIAS TO BONIFACE, ARCHBISHOP

He replies to three of his letters, among other matters concerning the annual payment of twelve denarii to the churches by each married pair of servants; the proceedings of the Roman synod against Aldebert and Clement; and the establishment of the metropolitan see of Cologne Agrippina.

[Col. 0939D] To the most revered and most holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop, Zacharias, servant of the servants of God.

When the words of your most holy fraternity had been delivered to us, and we had had them read through one by one, we found in the sequence of your letter that, because of our sins, while you were laboring to sow the seeds of the Lord’s wheat in order to increase the spiritual harvest, suddenly the enemy sowed weeds over them, so as to hinder your holiness in your good work. We grieved over this. But let your holy fraternity not cease its labor, and let it apply itself continually to prayer together with the brothers who are with you. Constructing spiritual hoes and uprooting the weeds, let it carry them away to be burned, as blessed Pope Gregory says [Note: See above, Letter 1 of Pope Gregory II to Boniface.]:

> “For, he says, let the good work be in your will [Roman Edition: our will]; for by divine help it will be brought to perfection.”

Since matters stand thus, dearest brother, take courage in the Lord, and he himself will be your helper. We must grieve over the incursion of the peoples that has occurred among your flocks. But let this adversity in no way disturb your fraternity, since the city of Rome too has often been devastated by disasters that have occurred; nevertheless, the Lord in his omnipotence has deigned to console it from above. Thus we believe that he will also console you.

Therefore, most reverend brother, preach fasting and litanies of supplication to God to the people entrusted to you, and his surpassing clemency will assist you. As we have already said, let no adversity disturb you; rather, do not in any way fail in the good work you have begun. We, although unworthy and sinners, will assist you with our prayers—and, insofar as we can, with those of our fellow priests.

Concerning the synod assembled in the province of the Franks through the agency of Pippin and Carloman, our most excellent sons, and held by your holiness as our representative in accordance with the instruction of our letter, we have learned how you acted and have given thanks to our almighty God, who strengthened their hearts so that they might be your helpers in this pious work. You carried out everything excellently and canonically, both concerning false bishops, fornicators, and schismatics, and also concerning the other men bearing the name of priests who were acting against the statutes of the canons or against the catholic Church of God and the apostolic Church. Concerning these matters we reply point by point according to your report.

You reported that all the princes of the Franks had chosen a city reaching as far as the borders of the pagans and the territories of the Germanic peoples, where you had previously preached, so that you might possess a metropolitan see there perpetually, instructing from that place the other bishops in the way of righteousness, and so that your successors might possess it thereafter by perpetual right. We gladly accept what they decreed, since it is evident that it was done by God’s will. But as for the fact that certain false priests and schismatics tried to obstruct this, the Lord will disperse their vain struggle and will establish those things that accord with and conform to the statutes of the holy Fathers. And because the princes of the Franks themselves also proved to be your helpers in this matter, may almighty God repay them with the reward of recompense and lavish upon them innumerable blessings.

[Note: A passage from this letter is cited by Ivo of Chartres, Part I, chapter 150: “Likewise concerning that false bishop,” but under a false title, as though it were from a letter of Gregory III, whereas it belongs to Zacharias. Sirmond.]

Likewise, concerning that false bishop whom you said was the son of an adulterous cleric and a murderer, born of adultery and raised without discipline, together with the other dreadful evils that you recounted individually, and who consequently consecrated priests like himself: your reverend fraternity remembers how many times we have written to you [Roman Edition: that we have written to you three times already] that no murderer, no adulterer, and no fornicator ought to touch the sacred ministry; nor should a penitent, or anyone whom the sacred canons prohibit from being a priest, do so.

Regarding those baptized by him, or the churches he consecrated, let your fraternity inquire whether he consecrated the churches in the name of the holy Trinity, or similarly baptized children while he was exercising the priesthood. If so, both the consecration of the churches and the baptism of the children are to be confirmed.

You also reported that those who were expelled by you as priests publicly claim in the province of the Franks that they were absolved by us. Let your holiness in no way believe this. For—although it is impossible—if we had done such a thing, we would have indicated it to your charity by our letters. But, since this is impossible, do not believe it in any way: we do not preach one thing and do another, nor do we send instructions of the sort they chatter about. Rather, with God’s help, we judge that what we preach must be observed to the very end.

We strongly urge your holiness to hold firmly to this: you must obey altogether the institutions of the holy Fathers and the rulings of the sacred canons, because we in no way preach one thing and do another. As for your entreaty that we write to the princes of the Franks and to the other Franks, as you requested, we have written to them point by point, asking that they be your friends and helpers in the Lord’s work.

Concerning the tribute you sought, since you were unable to obtain anything else from the Franks for payment to churches or monasteries except that, when the year turns, twelve denarii should be paid by each married couple of servants: give thanks to God that you were able to obtain even this. When the Lord grants peace, the lights of the saints will increase [Roman Edition: will be increased], because tribulation is now occurring from the Saracens, Saxons, and Frisians, as you yourself informed us.

You also asked about those who, because of capital sins, have been deposed from the priestly rank after you found them adulterers or murderers, so that they may be neither priests nor clerics, and who do not wish to live as monks under penance. Instead, they go to the palace of the king of the Franks and ask him to assign them places belonging to churches or monasteries, so that they may live a lay life and scatter the holy places. Concerning this also we have sent instructions to the princes of the Franks, explaining how it ought to be done.

In another letter of yours we found contained everything that the false and schismatic bishops Aldebert and Clement had done against you, through which you indicated all their acts and their most impious error [Roman Edition adds: individually]. We assembled our brothers and fellow priests and had the most wicked acts of those evil men read aloud in their presence. When they had been read before the entire council, everyone, moved by pious zeal, condemned their schismatic doctrines, their most wicked traditions, and the most criminal life that Aldebert had had written for himself, and they cried out with one voice that these things should be burned in the fire.

But we judged that this was not right. Instead, for the purpose of preserving them—or condemning them eternally—we ordered that they be kept in the archive of the holy Church, and we ourselves wrote an appropriate sentence against them. We have sent to your holiness, brother, a copy of the proceedings, so that, when it has been read in the province of the Franks, every schismatic who hears that such a judgment has been pronounced by the holy catholic and apostolic Church of God may recover from the perversity of his thinking.

In your third letter, moreover, you informed us about another seducer named Geolebo, who formerly exercised the name and honor of a false bishop. But since he is hastening to us without anyone’s permission or consultation, when he arrives, if it pleases the Lord, matters will be dealt with accordingly.

As for your reverence, we wish that, with the Lord’s assistance, as you have begun, you should celebrate a council every year at a suitable time in the province of the Franks in our place. Thus, through the gathering of priests and through the authority of the sacred canons, no adversary should dare to sprout there in any way; rather, as the unity of God’s Church and ecclesiastical and apostolic discipline are extended everywhere in those regions, all the peoples, even in the western districts, may become true Catholics and no longer be overwhelmed by errors through false priests and perish.

When you assemble the council, let your fraternity deal with the metropolitans whom we have confirmed concerning what you said: that no one should be received without letters of recommendation. Nevertheless, on this matter itself, and on all the interests of the holy Church, we have sent letters of admonition to the princes of the Franks, as we stated above.

As for that city which was recently called Agrippina but is now called Cologne, at the request of the Franks we have confirmed by a command of our authority that it is to be a metropolitan see under your name, and we have sent to your holiness, for future times, the establishment of that same metropolitan Church.

May God keep you safe, most reverend and dearest brother.

Given on the day before the Kalends of November, while our most pious lord Augustus Constantine, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in year twenty-seven, in the fifth year of his reign, in the fourteenth indiction.

[Note: Constantine’s twenty-seventh year. The circumstances require that it be read “twenty-sixth year,” as in the Roman synod; for it was written immediately after the synod, as the note of the inscription and the following letter of the deacon Gemmulus also indicate. Sirmond.]

[Note: Sirmond corrects it to “twenty-sixth”; Labbe, in his Chronology, similarly corrects it to “year twenty-six, the fifth year of his reign, indiction thirteen,” and says that this was the year of Christ 745. Hardouin. But the fourteenth indiction must be retained, since it coincided with November of the year 745. Mansi.]

## Letter XI. Pope Zacharias to Boniface, Archbishop

He replies to the letters brought by Bishop Burchard, especially concerning the form and minister of baptism; certain wandering bishops and presbyters; the heresy of Samson, a Scottish presbyter, concerning baptism; the presbyter Virgilius and another error of his; the metropolitan see, established not at Cologne but at Mainz; and finally he permits Boniface to choose a successor for himself.

[Col. 0943A]

To the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop, Zacharias, servant of the servants of God.

Burchard, the bishop dear to us, was presented at the sacred threshold of the blessed prince of the apostles Peter and before our sight. He brought us the greetings of your fraternal holiness, through whose letter we learned that your fraternity is engaged in a great struggle and is laboring zealously in preaching the gospel of Christ our God and exhorting people to the holy catholic and orthodox true faith, which we received from our Redeemer, God and Lord Jesus Christ, through the blessed prince of the apostles Peter, established by him, and through Paul, the vessel of election, and all the apostles.

Having learned this, although we are sinners, we raised our hands toward heaven and gave immense thanks to almighty God, asking his ineffable divinity to confirm and strengthen the heart of your fraternity even more, and to grant that you remain sound and strong in body for as long as he decrees that you survive in this life, so that you may complete the ministry imposed upon you and carry the profit of souls to the day of Christ Jesus, and may deserve to hear that desirable voice which the Lord will address to those who love him:

> “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25).

Various chapters were inserted in these same greetings of yours, concerning which you earnestly requested that the judgment, counsel, and consolation of the apostolic see be sent to you.

The first chapter concerned the synod of the province in which you were born and raised, and which the first preachers sent from the apostolic see—Augustine, Laurence, Justus, and Honorius—judged and governed among the English and Saxon peoples in the island of Britain. In your own times Theodore, most recently—a Greek who had become Latin (*Latinus*), formerly a philosopher, educated at Athens, ordained at Rome, raised to the dignity of the pallium, and sent to the aforesaid Britain—also governed it.

In that synod a decree and judgment was most firmly prescribed and carefully demonstrated: whoever had been washed without invocation of the Trinity did not possess the sacrament of regeneration. This is entirely true. For if someone was immersed in the baptismal font without invocation of the Trinity, he is not complete unless he has been baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

You wrote that some people affirm the following: if someone, with the Trinity invoked and according to the rule established by the Lord, has been immersed in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, he unquestionably possesses the sacrament; and that baptism has been so firmly consecrated by the evangelical words that, even if the person administering it were the most wicked heretic, schismatic, robber, thief, or adulterer, it would nevertheless be Christ’s baptism, consecrated by the evangelical words. Conversely, even if the minister were righteous, if he did not name the Trinity in the washing according to the rule established by the Lord, what he gave would not be true baptism.

Concerning those unclean and uncertain heretical and schismatic men who baptize those requesting it in the name of the Trinity, and also concerning those who immerse people in the baptismal font without invocation of the Trinity, your fraternity knows what the sequence of the sacred canons contains about them; we urge you to hold firmly to it. For it is written, as the Lord says:

> “Be holy, for I also am holy” (Leviticus 21).

What you received, brother, from our predecessor, Pope Gregory of holy memory, pontiff of this apostolic see—remain steadfast in it, and in no way depart from the evangelical and apostolic teaching handed down by the holy Fathers. Clothed in the breastplate of faith and the helmet of salvation, resist manfully against the wickedness of diabolical fraud by representing the apostolic office.

For it is written:

> “Behold, I have made your face strong against their face, and I will strengthen your steadfastness against their contentions, and your steadfastness will be stronger than rock” (Ezekiel 3, according to the Septuagint).

Concerning the sacrilegious presbyters whom you mentioned, who used to sacrifice bulls and goats to pagan gods, eating the sacrifices of the dead, and whose ministry was polluted, and who themselves were found to be adulterers and died in that state; since it is now unknown whether they said the Trinity while baptizing or not, those who are still alive fear that they were not baptized in the course of such a ministry. In response to them, you ordered everyone to be baptized.

You also observed in the said synod that the priests decreed that if anyone failed to name even one Person of the Trinity in baptism, that baptism could not be true. This is certainly true, because whoever has not confessed one of the Holy Trinity cannot be a complete Christian. Whoever confesses the Father and the Son but does not confess the Holy Spirit possesses neither the Father nor the Son. Whoever confesses the Father and the Holy Spirit but does not confess the Son possesses neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit, but is empty of divine grace.

Your fraternity reported that you had found false priests—erroneous impostors under the name of bishops or presbyters—far more numerous than the Catholics. They had never been ordained by Catholic bishops, deceived the people, and confused and disturbed the ministries of the Church. They included deceivers [Roman Edition: or deceivers], *gyrovagi*—wandering clerics—adulterers, murderers, effeminate men, men who sleep with males, sacrilegious men, hypocrites, and many tonsured slaves who had fled from their masters, transforming themselves from slaves of the devil into ministers of Christ.

They lived without bishops, according to their own will, and had popular defenders against the bishops, so that their wicked ways would not be restrained. They gathered around themselves a consenting populace and carried out their erroneous ministry not in the catholic Church but in rural places and the cells of peasants, where their ignorant folly could be concealed from the bishops. They neither preached the catholic faith to pagans nor themselves possessed the right faith. Nor did they call [Roman Edition: teach] or ask those whom they were to baptize—if they were of an age already capable of understanding—to receive in the sense of their hearts and understand the solemn words that every catechumen ought to profess, namely: “I renounce Satan,” and so forth.

Nor did they mark them with the sign of Christ, which ought to precede baptism. Nor did they teach any belief in the one God and the Holy Trinity, nor ask them to believe in their hearts for righteousness, so that confession with their mouths might result in salvation.

Whenever you find these ministers of Satan and not of Christ, dearest to us, assemble the provincial and priestly college, avoid them entirely, deprive them of priestly honor, and order them to end their lives under the monastic rule and the discipline of penance. Thus, afflicted in the flesh, they may eventually return to the way of righteousness; and if they believe in their hearts, the true confession of their mouths may result in their salvation.

But if they are not converted, your justice as a preacher will not perish. You will have, comforting you against the wickedness of the malicious, the canonical sanction of the holy apostles and the other approved Fathers.

Take courage, therefore, most reverend brother dear to me, and prevail in the Law, in the Gospel of Christ, and in the preaching of the catholic and orthodox faith, for it will itself glorify you. The tribulation of our body is temporary and has an end; testing produces hope. “Hope does not disappoint,” as the Apostle says, “because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress?” (Romans 5), and so forth.

Even if we are cast down, brother, we do not perish. We carry the death of Jesus in our body, so that the life of Jesus may be made manifest in our body on the day of his coming, as we have been taught by his divine voice:

> “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5).

Strengthen, therefore, all the orthodox bishops, priests, deacons, clerics, religious abbots and monks most dear to us, as well as the most glorious leaders and all nobles who observe Christian law, so that they may be our helpers against the adversaries of the orthodox faith, and against all heretics and schismatics. Thus they too may deserve to rejoice over the fruit of their good work in the heavenly kingdoms, as it is written:

> “The one who conquers I will make a pillar in the temple of my God, and I will write my name upon him” (Revelation 3).

Meanwhile your reverend fraternity wrote that you had found a certain presbyter named Samson, a Scot by birth, wandering from the way of truth. He said and affirmed that, without the mystical invocation or the washing of regeneration, a catholic Christian could be made through the laying on of an episcopal hand.

The man who says this is empty of the Holy Spirit, alien from the grace of Christ, and must be cast out from the fellowship of the priesthood. For who can be a Catholic unless he is baptized, according to the Lord’s command, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and is thus consecrated through the laying on of hands? Expel this wicked man, who preaches such things, condemned by the holy Church of God.

As for those men who were baptized by heretics and are held by doubt as to whether they were baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit: after investigating the truth of the matter, if they were baptized by erroneous priests, do not fail to fulfill without hesitation what has been entrusted to you by the good-memory predecessor of ours, Pope Gregory, and by the sacred canons, so that they may not perish forever but rather be saved through evangelical consecration.

We have also examined the volume that you sent to all the bishops, presbyters, deacons, and others living a religious life, written concerning the unity of the catholic faith and apostolic teaching. Know that it is very acceptable to us, since, through the grace of the Holy Spirit poured into you, dearest brother, you have earnestly labored to produce it.

Meanwhile, in other writings of your fraternity, you requested that a priest be sent by us to the regions of France and Gaul to celebrate councils. But while, by God’s favor, your holiness remains alive, representing there the apostolic see and our office, it is not necessary to send another there.

As for those whom you find possessing knowledge of sacred doctrine, holding the holy law, and undoubtedly defending the orthodox faith, endeavor to send them to the places where you foresee that they are needed, to preach the word of salvation. Assemble councils with the provincial bishops, and arrange that they be celebrated wherever and whenever seems right to you. Those whom you find deviating, cause their faces to be covered with disgrace, so that they may be without honor before men. For the Lord our God will be with you.

We have also received the document setting forth a true and orthodox profession and catholic unity, which your reverend fraternity sent with the bishops of the Frankish region who are most dear to us. When we opened it, we were filled with immense joy, giving innumerable thanks to almighty God because he had deigned to restore their unanimity to fellowship with us, so that the holy Church, their spiritual mother, might rejoice.

In our place, dearest brother, greet them all with the kiss of Christ’s peace. We too, giving thanks for their affection, have sent them apostolic letters.

Your fraternal holiness also informed us that the man Virgilius—and we do not know whether he should be called a presbyter—acts maliciously against you because you convicted him of being erroneous in relation to catholic doctrine. He made insinuations to Otilo, duke of the Bavarians, in order to sow hatred between you and him, saying that he had also been absolved by us so that he might obtain the diocese of one deceased bishop among the four whom your fraternity ordained there.

This is entirely untrue, for wickedness has lied to itself.

Concerning his perverse and wicked doctrine, by which he has spoken against God and his own soul: if it is established that he professes that there is another world and other human beings beneath the earth, or that there are another sun and another moon, expel him from the Church after consultation, depriving him of priestly honor.

Nevertheless, in writing to the aforesaid duke, we are also sending letters summoning the aforementioned Virgilius, so that, when he has been presented to us and examined through careful investigation, if he is found to be erroneous, he may be condemned by canonical sanctions. For those who sow sorrows reap them.

Thus it is written:

> “Perverse thoughts separate from God, but tested virtue rebukes the foolish” (Wisdom 1).

Concerning the aforesaid Sidonius and the presbyter Virgilius, we have learned what your holiness wrote. We wrote to them as was fitting, threatening them; but your fraternity is accorded greater credibility than they are. If it pleases the Lord and life permits, we summon them to the apostolic see by apostolic letters, as stated above.

You have taught them, but they have not accepted it; and what is written has happened in them:

> “Whoever teaches wisdom to a fool is like one who glues pottery together.”

> “It is easier to carry sand, salt, and a mass of iron than an imprudent, foolish, and impious man” (Ecclesiasticus 22; 16),

because one who is fainthearted thinks vain thoughts, and an imprudent and erring man thinks foolish things.

Therefore, brother, do not let your heart be provoked to anger. In your patience, wherever you find such men, admonish them, entreat them, reprove them, rebuke them, so that they may turn from error to the way of truth. If they are converted, you have saved their souls; but if they persist in hardness, you will not lose the reward of your ministry.

As for them, avoid them in accordance with the Apostle’s command (2 Timothy 2).

Finally, another letter of your fraternity contained what you had written long ago about the city of Agrippina: that the Franks had not persevered in the promise they had made, and that your fraternity was now residing in the city of Mainz. You requested that, with our counsel, as old age and a full span of days came upon you, together with bodily weakness, you might, if you could find another man, place him in the same see over which you preside, in your own stead.

You, dearest brother, were sent as a legate and envoy of the apostolic see, as you have been. With God as our helper, we therefore offer this counsel to your reverend holiness: for the salvation of rational souls, through Christ the Creator, do not in any way abandon the see of the holy Church of Mainz that you hold, so that the Lord’s command may be fulfilled in you:

> “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10).

But if the Lord grants, in accordance with your request, a perfect man who can undertake the concern and care of the salvation of souls, appoint him bishop in your place. And he will, in the Gospel entrusted to you and in bearing Christ’s ministry, seek out and strengthen the Church of God in every place.

We therefore pray our Lord and Redeemer that, through the sacred intercessions of his holy mother, the ever-virgin Mary our Lady, and of the blessed princes of the apostles Peter and Paul, he may deign to preserve your fraternal holiness, which prays for us, safe and unharmed.

May God keep you safe, most reverend and holy brother.

Given on the Kalends of May, while our most pious lord Augustus Constantine, crowned by God, the great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in year twenty-nine, after his consulship in year seven, in the first indiction.

## Letter XII. Pope Zacharias to Various Bishops of Gaul and Germany

[Note: This letter has no subscription indicating its year. But since it is placed after the Roman synod in the manuscripts, and since it is clear from the name of Ragenfrid, bishop of Rouen, that it was written somewhat after the death of Grimo, who was discussed in the preceding letters, I readily agree with Baronius, who thinks it was written in the year of Christ 748, together with the other letter of Zacharias to Boniface sent through Burchard. It should therefore be moved to that place. Sirmond.]

He praises their union among themselves and with the Roman Church, and urges them to remain steadfast in their ministries together with Boniface, archbishop and vicar of the apostolic see.

To our dearest Reginfrid [Alternative: to our dearest ones: Reginfrid], bishop of Rouen; Raimbert, bishop of Amiens; Deodatus, bishop of Beauvais; Eliseus, bishop of Noyon; Fulcarius, bishop of Tongeren; David, bishop of Speyer; Aetherius, bishop of Thérouanne; Treward, bishop of Cambrai; Burchard, bishop of Würzburg; Genebaud, bishop of Laon; Romanus, bishop of Meaux; Agilulf, bishop of Cologne; Heddo, bishop of Strasbourg; and the other most beloved fellow bishops, and also to the presbyters and deacons, and to all the orthodox clergy of the Churches of God who hold apostolic doctrine: Zacharias, endowed with divine grace, pontiff of the apostolic see and servant of the servants of God, sends greetings in the Lord.

[Note: David of Speyer. From Spira Nemetum, which Zacharias himself calls Spiracia in Letter 13. It was incorrectly read as “of Quimper,” and shortly thereafter “Aetherius of Le Mans” instead of “of Thérouanne,” or “of the Morini.” Sirmond.]

I give thanks to almighty God the Father, and to the Lord Jesus Christ, his only Son, and to the Holy Spirit, who has deigned to inflame all your hearts through the grace poured into you by him, so that you may walk in the unity of faith and the bond of peace. May the splendor of the Lord our God be upon you, dearest to me, together with abundant grace, peace, and charity, so that you may be one body of your spiritual mother, the holy catholic and apostolic Church of God.

By God’s authority, although we are far inferior in strength to so great a dignity, we preside over that Church, fulfilling the prophetic saying:

> “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell together as one” (Psalm 133).

Even if, because of the distance of the journey, we are absent in body, we are always present to you in the spirit of love, holding you in our inmost heart and praying continually that God and our Lord Jesus Christ may confirm your hearts still more and strengthen you in the preaching of the Gospel and in the ministry that you perform. Thus the people entrusted to you, freed by God’s help from diabolical fraud through your admonitions, may remain safe, and you may deserve to carry the profit of their souls to the day of Christ.

For it is written:

> “The children of wisdom are the Church of the righteous, and their nation is obedience and love” (Ecclesiasticus 3).

I therefore entreat you, dearest to me, to walk worthily of the calling to which you have been called, as is fitting for saints, with great patience, bearing with one another in love and eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace and charity. For “the end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unhypocritical faith” (1 Timothy 1).

I rejoice in you, dearest ones, because your faith and unity toward us are precious and manifest, not only before God but also before all human beings, since with the greatest goodwill you have turned toward your patron [Roman Edition: supporter] and teacher, established by God, the blessed prince of the apostles Peter.

Your faith and good reputation are praiseworthy, because you think the very thing that ought to be thought. Now, with God cooperating, your holiness has been joined to our fellowship in one pastoral fold. We have one shepherd, appointed by the Shepherd of shepherds, the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ: the prince of the apostles and our teacher.

You therefore have, in our place, to confirm your love and labor with you in the Gospel of Christ, the most holy and reverend Boniface, our brother and archbishop, the legate of the apostolic see and representative of our office.

Let your steadfastness stand against the contentions of those who think contrary things and not the things of God. Your steadfastness will be stronger than rock, as it is written:

> “Do not fear them, nor be terrified before them who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. What you hear in the ear, preach in the light, fearing him who can kill both soul and body and cast them into Gehenna” (Matthew 10).

My brothers, although we walk in the flesh, let us not wage war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but powerful through God for the destruction of the enemy’s strongholds, offering saving counsels [Roman Edition: destroying counsels], destroying every impiety that raises itself against the knowledge of God, and taking every understanding captive and bringing every thought into obedience to Christ (2 Corinthians 10).

For the rest, brothers, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might (Ephesians 6). May abundant peace and grace be bestowed upon you by God and our Lord Jesus Christ. We embrace and kiss your charity, as though present, in the unity of the Spirit and in the bond of the peace and charity of Christ.

May God keep you safe, dearest to us.

## Letter XIII. Pope Zacharias to Boniface, Archbishop

He replies to Boniface’s letter and to his various questions, which he had presented through Lullus.

To the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop, Zacharias, servant of the servants of God.

Benedictus be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who gathers what has been scattered, preserves what has been gathered, and increases faith and trust in his servants for preaching the word of the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, with the same Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. To him be glory and praise, for he is the helper and protector of those who believe in him. For he himself said: “Whoever believes in me will live and will not die” [Col. 0950A] (John XI), “because I am the way, the truth, and the life” (ibid., XIV).

We praise and exalt his holy name, rejoicing and glad through these messengers and through the letters of your holy brotherhood, having learned that you survive in this life and are prospering in the Lord. We ask the immeasurable divinity of our God to preserve you long-lived for preaching the Gospel and the sacrament of his holy faith ever more abundantly, to fortify you by his protection, and in merciful kindness to guard you from the snares of your adversaries.

Your holy brotherhood therefore reported in its letters that our predecessor, Gregory of blessed memory, bishop of this holy apostolic see, when he had sent your brotherhood to preach the word of the Gospel in the regions of Germany, had instructed you that, whenever you were able to find orthodox bishops, priests, or anyone else perfected in the word of exhortation, you should strengthen them further and share fellowship with them—and this was done. But if you found deceptive bishops, false priests, or anyone deviating from the straight path of the faith, you were to have no fellowship with them. You confessed that, with God’s spiritual consolation, you have preserved this instruction to the present day. Or, if you were altogether unable to abstain from them when you physically approached them, because of the principal and human favor of the Frankish people and under the pressure of necessity for the Churches of God, nevertheless your soul was not defiled by their council or by agreement in communion with them.

Therefore, because you associated with them without consenting to their wickedness, you have suffered no loss before God [Col. 0950C]. For if they obeyed while you preached, they would be saved; but if they remained in their wickedness, they themselves would perish. You, however, in accordance with the prophet’s saying, “saved your soul” (Ezekiel XXXV).

Concerning the bishops and pallia of the Franks, you wrote that, in accordance with their promise, they have not yet fulfilled what they said they would do. If they fulfill it according to their word, they will receive praise for it; but if they act otherwise, they will see to it themselves. For we, by the generosity of divine grace, freely give what we have freely received. Your good will in this matter has indeed been accepted by us.

You also asked that the monastery situated in the vastest solitude and amid the peoples to whom you preach, founded by you and dedicated in honor of our God and Savior, where you also ordered monks to live under the rule of blessed Benedict—in short, you asked that this venerable monastery be fortified by a privilege of the apostolic see. We have granted this, acceding to your wishes and ordering it according to your petition and desire.

For it is fitting that an excellent preacher and minister of the divine office should attain what he desires and bring the good work he has begun to its completion, as it is written in the Lord’s command: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew X). And: “Blessed is that servant whom, when his lord comes, he finds doing so; for he will set him over all his possessions” (Matthew XXIV).

Meanwhile, your aforementioned messenger Lul, together with his other companions, made known and clearly reported everything that had been entrusted to them by your holy brotherhood, both orally and in writing [Col. 0951A]. We have sent a reply to your brotherhood concerning these matters, both orally and in writing. The written document they presented contained the following chapters, appended below, about which you asked us to indicate what should be accepted and what rejected.

First, concerning birds—that is, jackdaws, crows, and storks—which must altogether be avoided as food by Christians; and beavers, hares, and wild horses are to be avoided even more. Yet, most holy brother, you are thoroughly well versed in all the sacred Scriptures.

Concerning the paschal fire, about which you inquired: from the time when, through the grace of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ and through his precious blood, the Church was dedicated, on the Thursday of Easter, while the sacred chrism is consecrated, three large lamps, filled with oil collected from the various lamps of the church, shall burn continually with great care in a more secluded place of the church, representing the inner tabernacle, so that the oil itself may suffice until the third day. From these candles the priest shall renew the fire taken on Holy Saturday for the baptism of the sacred font.

Concerning crystals, as you stated, we have no tradition.

You asked what should be done with those afflicted by the royal disease, whether they are human beings or horses. If people have this disease from birth or by descent, they must live outside the city, but they are not to be excluded from receiving alms from the people. If, however, someone—great or small—is afflicted not from birth but by an illness that has come upon him, he must not be cast out; rather, if possible, he should be treated. Nevertheless, when he comes into the church for communion, he shall enter to receive the sacrament after everything has been completed [perhaps, “after the filling/replenishment”].

Horses contaminated by the aforesaid disease, if they cannot be cured, are to be thrown into wells and pits, lest the others be contaminated by infection with the same disease.

As for animals that have been torn by raging—that is, rabid—wolves or dogs, they must be separated from the others, lest the others be contaminated by the raging and biting animals. If there are only a few, they are to be thrown into pits, as we said above.

Your brotherhood also asked whether consecrated women may, like men, wash one another’s feet, both on the Lord’s Supper and on other days. This is the Lord’s command, and whoever fulfills it through faith will receive praise for it. For men and women have one Lord, who is in heaven.

Concerning the blessings performed by the Gauls, as you know, brother, they vary through many abuses. They do not perform them according to apostolic tradition, but out of vainglory, bringing condemnation upon themselves, since it is written: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than what was preached, let him be anathema” (Galatians I).

You have received the rule of Catholic tradition, dearest brother. Thus preach to all and teach everyone, just as you received it from the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve.

You also asked whether it is permitted to ordain a priest before his thirtieth year. It is good and appropriate, dearest brother, if it can be done and suitable men can be found, that men of mature age and good reputation be ordained priests, according to the ordinances of the sacred canons. But if such men cannot be found and necessity requires it, let levites and priests be ordained from the age of twenty-five upward, as is contained in the law of the Lord.

Concerning Milo [Note: [Col. 0951D] Milo is the man to whom Marcellus granted the bishopric of Reims after the expulsion of Saint Rigobert. Flodoard, book XI, chapter 2: “Charles drove Rigobert from the bishopric and gave it to a certain Milo, a cleric with only the tonsure, who had accompanied him to war.” When he discusses the same Milo again below, he also records these very words of Zacharias. Sirmond.] and men like him, who greatly harm the Churches of God, preach to them opportunely and importunately, in accordance with the Apostle’s words, that they should withdraw from such wicked conduct (II Timothy III) [Col. 0952B]. If they heed your admonitions, they will save their souls; but if not, they themselves will perish, wrapped in their sins. You, however, who preach rightly, will not lose your reward.

You also asked after how much time bacon ought to be eaten. The Fathers have established no rule for us concerning this. But to you, asking for advice, we reply that it ought not to be eaten before it has been dried by smoke or cooked by fire. If, however, one wishes to eat it uncooked, it should be eaten after the Paschal feast.

As for the condemned bishop about whom you inquired—one who is a warrior and fornicator and who attempts, after his degradation, to claim the Church’s property for himself—he must be rejected altogether and with abhorrence. “For what share does a believer have with an unbeliever? Or what communion does Christ have with Belial?” (II Corinthians XV). The traditions of the holy Fathers and the ordinances of the sacred canons have condemned him.

You also indicated that, because of necessity and the poverty of those petitioning to be ordained, you had incurred offense by promoting priests and deacons outside the lawful times and days. We say to you, brother, as you well know, that the sacred canons teach that priests are to be ordained at suitable times. Nevertheless, for what you did out of zeal for the faith, we ask pardon from the Lord our God.

Concerning the tribute of the Churches—that is, the solidus from each household—accept it and have no hesitation, so long as you can distribute alms from it, share it among Christ’s poor, and complete the work of the holy Churches [Col. 0952D] according to the ordinances of the canons.
