If there are priests who were promoted from among the laity and who, previously entangled in criminal cases, were ordained while concealing their sin, but whose wicked action was later revealed, deprive them of priestly vesture and submit them to penance. For God does not hate the sinner who confesses, but the sinner who denies.

You also asked whether it is permissible to flee persecution by the pagans. On this matter, brother, we offer salutary advice. If it is possible and you find a place, persist in preaching to them. But if you cannot endure their persecution, you have the Lord’s commandment (Matthew XX) to enter another city.

You also asked what should be done with an excommunicated bishop who disregards apostolic authority. He is detestable before God and human beings, and one who has not been condemned must not communicate with him while he remains condemned. They themselves will be condemned on the day of wrath and of the revelation of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, when he sits to judge the human race, as it is written: “I will resist the proud, says the Lord” (James IV).

You asked whether tribute ought to be collected from the Slavs inhabiting the land of Christians. This requires no advice, since the matter is clear. If they live there without tribute, they will eventually claim the land itself as their own. But if they pay tribute, they acknowledge that the ruler possesses the land.

You also asked us, most holy brother, in how many places crosses should be made during the celebration of the sacred canon, so that we might inform your holiness. Mercifully inclined to your wishes, we marked in the scroll given to your religious priest Lul how many signs of the holy cross should be inserted in each place.

With matters thus arranged, we beseech the Lord’s mercy—although we are sinners—that he fortify you and strengthen you with his aid, and grant that we may always receive joyful reports of your prosperity. May God preserve you unharmed, most reverend brother.

Given on the eleventh day before the Nones of November, while our most pious lord Augustus Constantine, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the thirty-second year, in the eleventh year after his consulship, indiction 5.

## LETTER XIV. POPE ZACHARIAS TO BONIFACE, ARCHBISHOP

**The elevation of the see of Mainz into a metropolitan see**

To the most reverend and holy brother Boniface, fellow bishop, Zacharias, servant of the servants of God.

It would take too long to recount one by one how the Lord our God has shown favor to the holy Church and has cooperated with the labors of your most holy brotherhood. Nevertheless, to confirm what we set forth, we relate what we have learned in part from your own account.

When your brotherly holiness had been sent into the province of Germany to preach by our predecessor, Lord Pope Gregory, of holy memory, after beginning the work and spiritually building it up in some measure [Col. 0953D], you returned to Rome, were ordained bishop by him, and were sent back by him to preach again. With God going before you, you have labored in that preaching for twenty-five years to this day, counting from the time when you received the bishopric.

You also held a council in the province of the Franks in our place, and, with God granting their agreement, they all submitted in obedience according to the ordinances of the canons. While your brotherhood was occupied in these pious works, you did not claim a cathedral see for yourself until now.

But when God increased your preaching, you wished us to confirm a cathedral church to you and to your successors, in accordance with the petition of those same Frankish sons. Therefore, by the authority of blessed Peter the apostle, we decree that the aforesaid Church of Mainz is confirmed as a metropolitan see for you and your successors in perpetuity. It shall have under it these five cities: Tongeren, Cologne, Worms, Speyer, and Utrecht, together with all the peoples of Germany whom your brotherhood has caused, through its preaching, to acknowledge the light of Christ.

Having determined these matters, we order, by this document of confirmation, that it be preserved in your church in perpetuity for the confirmation of its status.

Farewell in good health.

Given on the day before the Nones of November, while our most pious lord Augustus Constantine, the great emperor, was reigning, in the thirty-second year, in the eleventh year after his consulship, indiction 5.

## LETTER XV. POPE ZACHARIAS TO BONIFACE, ARCHBISHOP

**The privilege of the monastery of Fulda**

Pope Zacharias to Bishop Boniface, and through him to the abbots who shall succeed him in the monastery he built, forever.

Since whatever accords with reasonable desires should always be granted, the pious devotion of a founder ought not to be denied, through the proclamation of a pious foundation, in the granting of privileges.

Therefore, since you asked us that the monastery of the Savior which you built, situated in a place called Buchonia [Roman edition: Bothonia], beside the bank of the River Fulda, be adorned with the insignia of a privilege of the apostolic see [Col. 0954C], so that, established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, it may be subject to the authority of no other Church—in this matter, favoring your pious desires, by this authority of ours we commit to execution what has been requested.

Accordingly, by this authority we prohibit every priest of any Church from exercising any jurisdiction whatsoever in the aforesaid monastery, except the apostolic see. No one is to presume to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there unless he has been invited by the abbot of the monastery, so that, in accordance with the condition of places subject to apostolic privileges, the endowed place may remain undisturbed.

By this document of our decree we establish this, and under threat of anathema forbid every prelate of any Church, or any person invested with whatever dignity [Col. 0954D], to presume in any way to violate this present constitution granted by us to the aforesaid monastery.

Farewell in good health.

[Note: [Col. 0953D] **Letter to Griphon.** It appears among the letters of Boniface as number 16. The annals of Pithou and others published after Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne* without the author’s name mention Griphon and his dispute with his brother Pippin. In reality, however, they are also by Einhard, as the preface to the manuscript booklet on the miracles of Saint Sebastian, composed during the reign of Louis the Pious, demonstrates. Sirmond.]

## LETTER XVI. BONIFACE TO GRIPHON, BROTHER OF PIPPIN, MAYOR OF THE PALACE

He commends to him the clerics and monks who are in Thuringia, asking him to defend them from the injuries of the pagans.

Boniface, servant of the servants of God, to Griphon, son of Charles: desirable salvation in Christ.

I beseech and adjure your piety, etc. (See above, Boniface’s letter 81.)

[Note: [Col. 0955D] We transcribed this from the papers of Pithou, although the same letter is also read in Androvaldus, book I of *The Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chapter 15. But he cites it in the wrong place, confusing the times of Zacharias and Stephen. Moreover, he omitted the name of Optatus, abbot of Cassino, whom Pope Stephen mentions near the end of letter 8 to Pippin in the *Codex Carolinus*. Boniface’s letter number 106 to him also exists: “To the most reverend brother—or rather, most beloved fellow priest—Optatus the abbot, and to the entire holy congregation under his care, preserving the norm of regular life.” Boniface.]

## LETTER XVII. POPE ZACHARIAS TO THE BISHOPS OF THE FRANKS

**On reconciling Pippin and Griphon in concord and peace, and on restoring the body of Saint Benedict to the monks of Cassino**

Zacharias, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to all the priests and presbyters of the Franks.

The distinguished Apostle teaches: “For those who love God, all things work together for good” (Romans VIII). And again, he himself says: “While we have the opportunity, let us do good to everyone” (Galatians VI). Elsewhere Scripture testifies: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” (Romans X).

Therefore, since the religious abbot Optatus, priest of the monastery of Saint Benedict, and Carolomanus, the God-beloved monk and brother of our son Pippin, the most excellent mayor of the palace, have sent through these religious servants of God, the monks, words of concord and peace between Pippin and his brother Griphon, so that we too might direct his excellence by admonition and bring them back to the harmony of peace, with you mediating peacefully for God’s sake—and likewise concerning the body of blessed Benedict, which was secretly taken from its tomb and should be restored—we gladly lend our ear to this work of justice and mercy.

We exhort your love and holiness first of all to bring the brother and his brother back to the unity of peace, so that wickedness may be put to shame in their midst. May the love of God, as you preach and minister it, abound among them.

Then, in accordance with the petition of the monk-servants of God, may his highness and your holiness unquestionably send the body of the aforesaid blessed Benedict back to its proper place, so that they may rejoice at the return of their father, while you may receive everlasting reward and praise for having acted justly in bringing him back to his tomb, from which he was secretly removed.

Your holiness need fear no offense before God from this good work of restoration, since it is believed that, to obtain this result, they have been moved by the prayers of that same saint and by the will of the aforesaid religious servant of God.

Farewell in good health.

## LETTER XVIII. BONIFACE, ARCHBISHOP, TO POPE ZACHARIAS, SENT THROUGH THE PRIEST LUL

He explains how he conducted himself in the matters that Pope Gregory II had commanded him, and concerning the monastery of Fulda that he had built.

[Col. 0956A]

“To the most reverend father and most beloved lord, etc., Zacharias, Boniface, your insignificant servant, etc.

The holiness of your fatherly piety, etc.” (See above, Boniface’s letter 75.)

[Note: [Col. 0955D] This letter appears to be spurious. The first year of Constantine Augustus corresponds indeed to the year of Christ 742; but the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, on which day the council is said to have been held, belongs to the preceding year of Christ, when Zacharias was not yet Roman pontiff and Leo the Isaurian was still alive.

Moreover, the pontiff says that he received from Clement, sent by the same archbishop, a report that the Churches of the province of Vienne had been disturbed by the devastation of peoples [Col. 0956D]. This can refer only to the invasion of the Saracens into Gaul in the year 739, since after that year the Church of Vienne was not devastated.

Third, the pontiff says: “The Lombards, whose savagery has everywhere increased, devastate our borders so that, as the prophet says of the king of Babylon, ‘They have stripped us of our bones’” (Jeremiah L). This conflicts with what Anastasius records in his *Life of Pope Zacharias*, where he carefully relates what took place in the preceding years between that pontiff and King Liutprand of the Lombards.

Finally, Wilicarius succeeded Austrobert, as Ado of Vienne testifies in his sixth age; he adds that both the Viennese and Lyonnais provinces remained for several years without bishops. Since Wilicarius had become a monk before the year 742, Pope Zacharias could not in 742 have written to Austrobert, his predecessor, who had died before Wilicarius’s episcopate. In that year and for several subsequent years, the Church of Vienne was without a bishop.]

## LETTER XIX. POPE ZACHARIAS TO AUSTROBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF VIENNE

He sends a copy of the synod held at Rome on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April and replies concerning what should be done with bishops ordained for money.

[Col. 0956B]

Zacharias, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend brother Austrobert, archbishop of the holy Church of Vienne.

The priest Clement, sent by your holiness, came to us reporting that the Churches of your province had been disturbed by the devastation of peoples. We were therefore made very sad. But why should your holiness be surprised by such things, when you know from the Gospel that all these events were foretold by the Lord? “Wickedness will abound,” he says, “and the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew XIV).

The Lombards also, whose savagery has everywhere increased, devastate our borders, just as the prophet says of the king of Babylon: “They have stripped us of our bones” (Jeremiah L). Let us consider God’s just judgments and waste away because of our iniquities.

Furthermore, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April we held a synod at Rome, a copy of which our beloved priest will bring to your holiness.

Concerning bishops ordained for money, we write this to you: if they are useful, they are to be corrected most severely for this offense, but they are not to be completely removed from their order. Let them grieve over what they unlawfully committed while in so high an order. Henceforth, however, let your prudence see to it that such heresy has no place in your province.

We have sent you a dalmatic, so that, since your Church received the teaching of the faith from this see, it may also receive from it the distinction of honor in sacerdotal dress.

Given on the Nones of March, in the first year of the reign of Constantine Augustus.

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LETTER

[Col. 0957A]

The letter of Zacharias, Roman pontiff, which I append here has indeed been published by all collectors of councils, but no one has published it in full. Before Labbe, only one fragment of it had appeared, taken from canon 30, question 4 of the *Pytacium*. Labbe added another from a manuscript codex. I present a third fragment, together with variants that should not be despised.

All these materials were supplied by that old codex of the Burchardian decree, which I have often used profitably in this work. They were not, however, taken from Burchard himself, but from the person who added certain additions of his own to our codex.

Nor do I think I have performed a useless service for the Church by presenting a fuller version of Zacharias’s letter to Theodore of Turin, since it is famous among the ancients. Nicholas I appeals to it in his *Responses to the Bulgarians*, chapter 39, as does the same Nicholas in his letter to Charles of Mainz. That letter may be seen in Labbe’s Venetian edition, volume IX, page 1269.

## LETTER XX. POPE ZACHARIAS TO THEODORE, BISHOP OF TURIN

**A son may not marry the woman whom his father received from the sacred baptismal font**

[Col. 0957B]

Zacharias, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and holy brother Theodore, bishop of the Church of Pavia.

Your reverend [Note: [Col. 0957C] Edition: “venerable.”] brotherhood presented us with a *pytacium* [Note: [Col. 0957C] Canon: *Pytacium* 30, question 3], by which you wished to ask us whether it is permissible for a son whose father received another man’s daughter from the sacred baptismal font [Note: Edition: “has received”]—that is, the daughter of the spiritual father of that same father [Note: Edition: “the son of that same father”]—to take her in marriage. It is cruel to say this, but you asserted that such a thing had occurred in your case [Note: Edition: “stated”].

Your brotherhood, however, knows well what the Lord commands through Moses, saying: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father” (Leviticus XVIII, 7). For your father’s daughter is your nakedness [Note: Edition: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister. She is first your father’s daughter. For the nakedness of your father and the nakedness of your sister is your nakedness. You shall not uncover…”].

“Nakedness is not uncovered” is said when abstention from one’s own blood relationship is commanded [Note: [Col. 0958C] The edition omits the text up to “on every occasion,” etc.]. Much more, therefore, we must altogether beware of the daughter of our spiritual father, with the greatest abhorrence and with every occasion or pretext set aside, lest someone who has become involved in such a crime and has not restrained the reins of lust incur the anger of the divine judgment [Note: Edition: “human judgment”] [Note: [Col. 0958C] Edition: “the vein” instead of “the reins” of lust. Hitherto in Gratian.].

Accordingly, all unions in such a crime must be avoided, lest the unwary perish forever. But if anyone [sic], despising the salvation of his soul, has rashly entered into such a pernicious marriage [Note: [Col. 0958C] The edition adds “author”], your brotherhood must strive in every way to separate them and subject them to worthy penance, so that, with the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ granting it, you may win their souls back from eternal damnation.

You also asked whether the children who are proven to have been born from them may be joined in marriage. Why should these children be forbidden marriage or compelled to do penance on this account? They are shown to be free from condemnation in this matter, because the father will not bear torment for the son, nor the son for the father. The Lord says through the prophet: “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine” [Note: The editions read: “The soul of the father is mine; the soul of the son is mine”]; “the soul that sins shall itself be punished” (Ezekiel XVIII, 4).

[Col. 0958B]

But, dearest brother, let what has been said suffice. Be careful not to permit your subjects to act otherwise, lest you be found to have deviated from the straight path [Note: [Col. 0958D] Here the editions end; the remainder is supplied from a manuscript]. Rather, strive altogether to carry out the commands of our apostolic see, so that you may deserve to stand blameless before the Creator, the Lord our God, when he comes to judge, and say: “Behold, I am here, and the children whom you gave me; I have not lost any of them” (John XII). May you hear from him: “Well done, good servant” (Matthew XXV), and what follows.

Concerning that chapter about which you informed us—namely, within what degree of generation relatives may be joined in marriage—some wish to claim that what Saint Gregory sent to the people of the English is to be observed up to the fourth generation.

But that pious Father imposed certain lighter requirements upon the inexperienced and those newly coming to Christ, lest, if he imposed more burdensome ones, they should bear them harshly and that hard people should altogether cast aside everything they had accepted.

We, however, do not wish the people entrusted to you to observe this as though they were people who have only recently accepted Christ. Rather, they should observe it as people nourished from infancy in the holy Catholic Church. Once they have recognized their relationship by blood, they must abstain in every way, just as the holy Catholic and apostolic Roman Church of God holds and teaches.

# DECREES OF POPE ZACHARIAS

From Gratian and others.

[Col. 0957]

## NOTICE

[Col. 0957D]

I do not know by what fate it happened that, although Gratian transferred several decrees of Pope Zacharias into his collection, Labbe omitted all of them. Since I could find no adequate reason for this omission, I have judged that they were passed over by chance and should be supplied here. I considered it preferable to provide some things that might be superfluous rather than appear to omit what is necessary, especially since I possess the complete decree of this pontiff and can produce it from the manuscript Codex Pistoriensis.

Although, through the injustice of the person who assembled the book, the text has been so erased in the codex that several letters are sometimes missing, the diligence of the learned Joseph Borelli, a priest of Pistoia and my friend, who was highly practiced in reading ancient writings, overcame all the difficulties, so that the text could be presented almost complete.

Mansi.

## I

[Col. 0959A]

You have had intercourse with your wife’s sister. If you did so, keep neither of them; and if the woman who was your wife was not aware of the crime, let her marry in the Lord, whomever she wishes [Note: [Col. 0959] An ancient hand in my Lucchese codex adds above the line these words: “after your death.” Mansi.]. But you and the adulteress must remain without hope of marriage, and as long as you live, perform penance according to the priest’s command.

## II

It is not proper ever to give in marriage to a man the daughter whom one has received from the sacred font, because by divine judgment they are found to be siblings. If anyone involved in such a crime does not restrain the reins of lust, he shall be abominated by the Catholic Church.

But if he converts, after the separation he shall do penance for seven years. Let this condition apply equally to those who were accomplices with the perpetrator; that is, let him do penance together with those who cooperated and consented.

## III

Concerning the degrees of relationship, about which you were pleased to consult my insignificance, I have decided to state briefly what I think together with all cultivators of orthodox faith.

I altogether dissent from those who perversely calculate the succession of relationships and thereby distort the degree. They establish two anew and consequently make the first degree the second; then they make the second the third. In this way they corrupt part of the sequence of generations, so that, when we see the tree constructed from the relationship cut off by them, the body, so to speak, appears truncated in its limbs [Col. 0960A].

Accordingly, we calculate the degrees of relationship as follows. I and my brother are one generation and constitute the first degree; we are separated by no degree. Again, my son and my brother’s son are a second generation and constitute the second degree; they are not separated from one another by any further degree. The remaining successions are to be counted in the same way.

As for affinity, which you say is a relationship—that which extends to a man through his wife’s family, or to a wife through her husband’s family—the reasoning is perfectly clear. If, according to divine judgment, my wife and I are one flesh, then her relationship and mine become one relationship for me and for her.

Therefore, my wife’s sister and I will be in one and the nearest degree; her daughter in the second degree; her granddaughter in the third. The same procedure is to be followed on both sides in the remaining successions.

As for the wife of one of my relatives, whatever her degree, I must regard her in the same way as the corresponding degree of that relative would be regarded in a woman of my own kin. The same rule must plainly be observed by my wife concerning the husbands of her female relatives and concerning all the degrees of generation.

Those who think otherwise are antichrists.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 752: STEPHEN II, ROMAN PONTIFF

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON POPE STEPHEN II

(*Book of the Pontiffs, from various editions*)

[Col. 0959C] **1. Stephen.** On the twelfth day after the death of Zacharias, on 27 March in the year of Our Lord 752, Stephen II was elected. BIN. and LABBE. — **2. Stephen.** After Pope Zacharias had been buried in the Vatican basilica on the Ides of March, 752, the see remained vacant for twelve days, as all the manuscripts and catalogues unanimously attest (except the Colbertine manuscripts, six of which say nothing about the interval between pontificates, while the seventh extends it by one day). Indeed, exactly that number of days elapses up to the 26th of the aforesaid month, on which it is certain that Stephen was ordained as successor. This is shown both by the length of his pontificate—five years and twenty-nine days, as stated by the catalogue of Lucca and three Colbertine manuscripts, while the Freherian first manuscript, the Royal, Mazarin, Thuane, and three Ambrosian manuscripts count one day fewer than the other manuscripts—and by the date of his burial, generally recorded as 26 April, the sixth day before the Kalends of May, indiction 10, which indicates the year [Col. 0960C] 757, although in the common text, and in some manuscripts, a difference of one day, or even two, occurs. If these calculations are correctly made, as Pagius also maintains in the year 757, section 1, it is necessary for me to explain somewhat more fully the two remaining points that I had reserved for discussion concerning this pope against Pagius: namely, that the ordinations of the Roman pontiffs could not be separated from Sundays, and that the epoch of the restored freedom of ordinations must be placed in the year 684.

As to the first point, the analysis of the twelve-day interval between pontificates plainly shows that Sundays were preferred to all the more solemn festivals, as I said concerning John VI. To avoid lingering needlessly over words, Anastasius says that on the third day after Zacharias’s burial the clergy and people customarily chose for themselves a certain Stephen; and on the day of the election itself, 17 March, a Friday, they sent him to the Lateran patriarchate, or enthroned him there. I have already shown that these were the same thing in the case of Zacharias. He remained there for two days, that is, on the same Friday and on Saturday. On the third day, Sunday—undoubtedly appointed for the ordination—while he had scarcely awakened and, sitting, was arranging his household affairs, he suddenly became mentally deranged and fell silent; on the following day, Monday, he died.

Anastasius does not list this man among the pontiffs, since he was not consecrated, as is clear from the Life of Adrian I, section 292, where he calls the next one the second, whereas we call him the third. Nevertheless, because Panvinus and Cardinal Baronius number this man and call him the second, when the election of the other Stephen is reached it remains uncertain whether the election was held, according to custom, on the third day after the burial, or immediately—as Anastasius seems to suggest when he relates that everyone assembled at Saint Mary at the Crib and with one voice elected Stephen, whom, on the basis of the foregoing, I call the second, or alternatively the third. In any event, lest I seem to be deceiving Pagius, I shall pursue the calculation as though the electors had waited for the third day.

Accordingly, on Wednesday, 22 March, Stephen [Col. 0961B] was elected pope and enthroned in the Lateran patriarchate. What followed? Was he consecrated four days later, on the day sacred to the Annunciation of the Lord’s Incarnation, in accordance with Pagius’s oft-repeated axiom that the ordinations of pontiffs were customarily performed on Sundays or on more solemn days? Certainly not. Rather, the following Sunday, which was due for the pontiff’s ordination, was awaited; and what must especially be observed is that it was awaited at a time when there can no longer be any doubt that the Church enjoyed full freedom to ordain, without the confirmation of the exarchs, who had been driven out the preceding year.

What arguments do I use to prove that the ordinations of pontiffs were performed only on Sundays, when Anastasius himself openly confirms precisely what I am investigating? In discussing the consecrations of Constantine the intruder, after Saint Paul, and of Stephen III, or IV, he plainly makes clear that they were not performed except on Sundays. Although these two cases belong to the fifth volume, I nevertheless wish to touch on them here [Col. 0961C], so that what I have hitherto argued concerning ordinations may be attached to a new support.

In the year 767, on 28 June, Saint Paul I died in the basilica of Saint Paul, where he was staying at the time. “And the episcopate remained vacant,” says Anastasius, “for one year and one month,” during which—as it is read in the second Freherian manuscript—Constantine, the transgressor and invader of the apostolic see, held power. For on 28 July of the following year, 768, the presbyters Sergius and Waldipert, together with the Lombards, entered Rome. They killed Toto, duke of Nepi, who had installed his brother Constantine; and after several hours, Anastasius continues, “the judges of the Roman militia … under guard secured Constantine with his surviving brother Passivus and with Bishop Theodore.” Thus the invasion ceased, an interval which Anastasius rightly calls the period between pontificates. Nor should he be challenged on the ground that, although very careful in recording the time of the invasion, he appears to have made the interval shorter by ten days, since, when he enumerates the remaining days individually, he leaves no doubt about any of them, as we shall see in its proper place.

Thus, in the aforesaid year 767, on 28 June, with a Sunday occurring, Toto, the duke of Nepi, seized by the desire to make his lay brother Constantine pope, entered Rome surrounded by a band of partisans. He arranged that his brother should be elected in his own house, then hurried with him to the Lateran patriarchate, had him made a cleric by the greatest sacrilege, and enthroned him, while Paul was still alive; shortly afterward, on that same day, Paul died. The following day, Monday, was sacred to the feast of the apostles. What could have been more opportune for Toto, who trampled upon the sacred canons and supported his intruded brother with armed force, than to have the man whom he had enthroned on the preceding day consecrated as quickly as possible on the following day in the basilica of Saint Peter, so that he might appear to be the legitimate pontiff? Yet, because there was no memory of a pontiff having been consecrated outside Sunday, six days had to be awaited under arms.

“When Sunday arrived,” says Anastasius, “the pontiff again hastened with a multitude of armed troops to the basilica of blessed Peter, and there he was consecrated by George, bishop of Praeneste, and two other bishops, Eustathius of Albano and Citonatus of Porto.” This example of an intruded pseudo-pontiff, who—as in other matters the canons had been violated—would have been ordained not only on a less solemn day but on any day whatsoever, had not pontifical consecration been joined to Sunday, confirms my position more strongly than anything else that could be produced.

Moreover, the same Anastasius, when discussing the ordination of Stephen III, or IV, although this does not work against Pagius, since no feast occurred between the election and Sunday, nevertheless speaks so absolutely of an ordination performed on Sunday that he plainly reveals the custom of those times. “At daybreak on Saturday,” he says, “one day before the ordination of the aforesaid most blessed Pope Stephen.” And below: “Thus, on the following Sunday, the aforesaid most blessed Stephen received the consecration of the pontificate.” Perhaps more evidence will be available if anyone rises to defend Pagius against this opinion.

The second matter that remains for me to prove is the epoch of the restored freedom of the ordination of Roman pontiffs. I said that it could be dated from the year 684, when Pogonatus, with the liberality and reverence that he showed toward the apostolic see, granted Pope Benedict by an imperial decree that thereafter the clergy and people should not await any command of the emperor, but should consecrate the elected pontiff without delay. Yet, against Mabillon’s opinion, which carries this epoch down to Charlemagne, I preferred, with the very learned Pagius and Blanchinus, to extend it by approximately seventy years, namely to the beginning of the reign of Pippin, king of the Franks. Following Pagius, I place this at the Kalends of March in the year 752, while Zacharias was still alive.

Nevertheless, this must be held firmly and certainly: after Constantine Pogonatus, when the Romans sent their envoys to Ravenna after the election of a pontiff had been made, they did so more as an act of obedience than in order to request confirmation. The ordination of Zacharias himself will serve as an example: it was performed after a four-day interval between pontificates, before Pippin was king and without consulting the exarch. Hence Pagius says that the custom of requesting confirmation continued until Gregory III, Zacharias’s predecessor (Annals, 731, section 20). But he establishes this only by private authority, without producing any evidence except a conjecture drawn from the Westerners’ hostility to the Isaurian Iconoclast; and although these considerations may be highly probable, they do not prove that the certain epoch from which confirmation of pontiffs was no longer requested should be established in the age of Gregory III.

For this reason I have embraced the opinion of the very learned prelate Blanchinus. When the choice between Mabillon’s and Pagius’s opinions was offered to him, he preferred the former, although he followed it with a difference of several years, saying that the matter should be examined down to the reign of Pippin, whereas Pagius refers it to the time of Charles Martel. Thus, interpreting his view, I affirm that the freedom of pontifical ordination began in the very year of Saint Zacharias’s death, when Pippin was inaugurated as king, namely 752. For the exarchs had been expelled in July of the preceding year, and the emperors of the East had no remaining authority in Italy. This cannot be asserted on the basis of the brief interval between pontificates after Gregory III, both because the exarchate had not yet been expelled and because, owing to the wars that were breaking out, the ordination may have been hurried.

In any event, during those sixty-eight years that elapsed from the imperial decree of Pogonatus—that is, from the year 684—the Roman clergy and people sent their legates to the exarch, I say, more out of courtesy and obedience than in order to request confirmation, since no law compelled them to do so. And if no schisms had occurred, as I have noted elsewhere, which taught that legitimate elections needed to be more firmly established, they would not even have gone for the sake of obedience. Once that servitude, which the Church had accepted for the sake of peace under the auspices of the most pious Pogonatus, had been cast off, we nowhere read that it was again endured. Those who think otherwise, in order to accommodate themselves to the emperors, are prophesying.

A time will come when we shall see the pontiffs themselves grant the emperors of the West the power, as a favor of gratitude, to participate in the elections of pontiffs. Since these matters belong, according to Mabillon, to the fourth period of pontifical creation, I shall discuss them in volume V. CENNUS.]

Stephen II, a Roman by nationality, the son of Constantine, sat for five years and twenty-eight days. After his father’s death he was left as a child in the venerable Lateran palace, [Col. 0960C] where he remained under the pontiffs of blessed memory for instruction in the apostolic [Col. 0961A] tradition. Advancing him individually through the ecclesiastical [Col. 0962A] orders, they ordained him to the order of deacon. When Pope Zacharias, the lord of blessed memory [Col. 0963A], died,

[Note: [Col. 0963D] **A certain Stephen.** This man was Italian by nationality and Roman on his father’s side, a cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church. Under the emperor Constantine Copronymus he sat in the chair of Peter for four days. He was created on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, and on the fourth day after his election he was overcome by profound sleep. On the following day, when he had awakened and had begun to arrange his household affairs, he suddenly became mentally deranged and lost his voice; on the day after that he died, struck by apoplexy. Before he received consecration, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, the see remained vacant for one day. The writers of pontifical history do not include him among the pontiffs, either because he was not consecrated or because he lived for such a very short time. This was not rightly done, since he was lawfully elected and was considered a man of immense spirit and courage; therefore he should not be removed from the number of pontiffs, even if he had lived for only one hour. CIACONIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 0964C] **A certain Stephen, etc.** After Pope Zacharias died, a certain priest named Stephen, a Roman by nationality, was immediately created Roman pontiff by the people and admitted to the Lateran patriarchate. He remained there for two days; on the third day, after rising from sleep and arranging his household affairs, he suddenly became mentally deranged while sitting and fell silent, and on the following day he died, says Anastasius, who does not number him among the Roman pontiffs. Onuphrius, in his Ecclesiastical Chronicle and in his notes on Platina, and after him Baronius, count this Stephen among the Roman pontiffs. But this opinion is opposed by all the ancient writers and by all the catalogues of the Roman pontiffs, in none of which the name of this priest Stephen is found, because he was merely elected pope and was never ordained. For although it was customary for the elected man immediately after his election to be brought into possession of the patriarchate, he was not simply called, nor was he truly, a pontiff before he had been ordained. Thus Anastasius and Frodoardus, in the Fragment concerning the Roman pontiffs—whom we have often cited and who died in the sixty-second year of the tenth century—call the next Stephen the second of that name, and thereafter the other pontiffs of this name, preserving the numerical designation. They certainly would not have done so if this elected Stephen had then been counted among the Roman pontiffs. Therefore, to avoid confusion, we shall indeed call the Stephen who followed this man Stephen II, but with the addition “by others, III,” and so with the others down to Stephen X. PAGIUS.]

The entire people elected a certain priest Stephen to the office of the pontificate and sent him into the Lateran patriarchate. He remained there for two days; on the third day, after rising from sleep and, while seated, arranging his household affairs, he suddenly became mentally deranged and fell silent; on the following day he died.

After this, the entire people of God assembled within the venerable basilica of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God, at the Crib. There, asking the mercy of the Lord our God and of that same lady, our holy and ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, they chose the aforesaid most blessed man as pontiff with good will and unanimous voice. With sincere hearts and acclamations of praise they all carried him to the basilica of the Savior called Constantiniana [Col. 0963B], and from there entered within and, according to custom, brought him into the patriarchate.

For this most blessed pope was a lover of the churches of God, preserving ecclesiastical tradition with firm constancy [Note: [Col. 0963C] Codex of Lucca: “he preserved”; another reading: “preserving it firmly and steadfastly”]. He was a swift helper of Christ’s poor and a preacher of the word of God with great steadfastness. He cared for widows and orphans [Note: Codex of Lucca: “namely, by almsgiving rather than bodily presence”] much more effectively and was a most courageous defender, by God’s power, of his flock.

He immediately restored the four hostels for pilgrims and the poor that had been established in ancient times in this Roman city and had remained abandoned for a long period. In them he arranged every provision, distributing resources in their various places, both within and outside, and he contributed many gifts to them. He also confirmed them by a charter of privilege under the prohibition of anathema. [Note: Another reading: “of his native land.”]

Likewise, he is recognized as having founded anew a hostel in the plantana [Note: Codex of Lucca: “plantaria”], arranging there for one hundred of Christ’s poor and decreeing that their daily sustenance should be provided.

Outside the walls of this Roman city, beside the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, he also built two hostels, to which he contributed many goods. He joined them to the venerable deaconries existing outside there, so that they might remain perpetually [Note: Codex of Lucca: “so that they might remain perpetually”]: namely, the deaconry of the holy Mother of God and the two deaconries of blessed Sylvester; and he fortified them with apostolic privileges so that they might endure forever.

Meanwhile, when a great persecution had arisen in this Roman city and in the cities subject to it from Aistulf, king of the Lombards [Note: Codex of Lucca: “Aistulf”], and the violent cruelty of that king was pressing hard, the same most blessed pope, in the third month after his ordination to the apostolate, appointed his brother, the most holy Paul the Deacon, and Ambrosius the primicerius, and sent them with very many gifts to the same Lombard king Aistulf, in order to arrange and confirm a treaty of peace. These men, having come to him and having distributed the gifts so that they might more easily obtain their request from him, arranged and confirmed with him a treaty of peace for forty years.

But that insolent Lombard king, seized by the cunning of the ancient enemy, broke the very treaty of peace after scarcely four months, falling into the guilt of perjury. He inflicted many insults upon the aforesaid most holy man and the entire Roman people and directed various threats against him [Note: Codex of Lucca: “he directed them”]. For, wishing—since God was opposed to him—to invade this entire province, he tried to impose a burdensome tribute upon the inhabitants of this Roman city [Note: Codex of Lucca: “to add”]. He eagerly sought to exact a single gold solidus annually from every head [Note: Codex of Lucca: “to take away”]. He also arrogantly declared that he would subject this Roman city and the forts dependent upon it to his jurisdiction.

When the same most holy pope saw that the destructive cruelty of the aforesaid king was threatening with great force, he summoned to himself the religious abbots of the venerable monasteries of Saints Vincent and Benedict and sent them in his place to that most cruel king. Through them he urgently asked that a treaty of peace [Note: Codex of Lucca: “together with tranquility”] be obtained and confirmed, together with tranquility for the people of God on both sides [Note: Codex of Lucca: “to be confirmed”]. But when the king received them and held them in utter contempt, he spurned their counsels [Note: Codex of Lucca: “their gifts”] and, to the detriment of his own soul, dismissed them confused and unsuccessful to their monasteries, warning them not to return to the most holy pope.

When the chief father himself heard this, he immediately—as he frequently used to do—commended to almighty God his own cause and that of the people entrusted to him, and made known to the divine majesty this mournful lament.

While these things were taking place [Note: Codex of Lucca: “he arrived”], John the imperial Silentiary came to Rome, bringing to the same most holy pontiff an imperial command, and at the same time he carried to the aforesaid impious king another command, accompanied by an exhortation [Note: Codex of Lucca: “the accompanying words”], that he restore to their rightful master the territories of the empire that he had usurped by diabolical cunning [Note: another reading: “to his dominion”].

The aforesaid imperial envoy the most holy pope immediately sent with his aforementioned brother, the most holy Paul the Deacon, to that wicked Aistulf at Ravenna. After receiving them, Aistulf dismissed them with an empty response, attaching to the imperial envoy a certain villain of his own people, steeped in diabolical counsels, who was preparing to hasten to the royal [Note: Codex of Lucca: “who was about to depart”] city [Note: “that is, Constantinople”]. The envoys returned to Rome and, presented to the same most holy pope, reported to him that they had accomplished nothing.

Then, having learned the evil king’s plan, the aforesaid most holy man sent his envoys to the imperial city [Note: [Col. 0965C] “He sent his envoys to the imperial city.” Stephen II was created pontiff in the most difficult circumstances. At the very beginning of his pontificate, Aistulf, king of the Lombards, broke the treaty that he had made with the Roman Church and resolved to attack Rome. At that time the Romans had not yet abandoned their allegiance to the emperor. For after their great estates had been invaded, the Roman pontiffs continued to honor the rule of the emperor Leo and of his son Constantine Copronymus, did not abandon the interests of the empire, and the Roman city, although afflicted by the calamities of war inflicted by King Aistulf, acknowledged the authority of Constantine. Constantine sent John the Silentiary to Rome with letters for the pope and for Aistulf. John went to Ravenna with Paul, the brother of Pope Stephen, but could not obtain from Aistulf the restoration of the provinces that he had taken from the Roman Empire. Therefore Pope Stephen asked the emperor through envoys to come in every possible way with an army to defend these parts of Italy, as he had often written to him, and to free this city of Rome and the whole Italian province from the attacks of the son of iniquity, as Anastasius says. PAGIUS.]

and apostolic envoys, begging the imperial clemency to come, as he had often written, with an army to defend these regions of Italy by every means and to free this Roman city and the whole Italian province from the attacks of the son of iniquity.

[Col. 0966B] Meanwhile, persisting in his wickedness [Note: Codex of Lucca: “in his ruin”], the aforesaid most atrocious king of the Lombards blazed with furious anger and, roaring like a lion, did not cease to direct deadly threats against the Romans. He asserted that all would be slaughtered with one sword unless, as has been stated, they submitted themselves to his dominion. [Note: Codex of Lucca: “Again.”]

Again the aforesaid most holy Father, having assembled the entire Roman community, admonished them in the following words with paternal affection:

“I beg you, dearest sons, let us implore the Lord’s mercy for the burden of our sins; and he will be our helper and, in his most provident mercy, will deliver us from the hands of our persecutors.”

The entire people obeyed these saving admonitions, and all assembled together, shedding tears, prayed to our almighty Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0965D] “On one of these days, proceeding carefully with great humility in a litany with the most sacred image of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, which is called Anteropsita.” In the litanies the image of Christ the Savior was customarily carried about with the cross. It was called *anteropsita*, perhaps a compound of the Latin *ante*, “before,” and the Greek ὄψις, “sight” or “spectacle,” because it seemed to be carried before the litany. Bede, *History*, book I, chapter 26, concerning Augustine, the first bishop of the English, and his companions, says: “But they, endowed not with demonic but with divine power, came bearing a silver cross as their standard and an image of the Lord Savior painted on a panel, and singing litanies they supplicated the Lord for eternal salvation, both their own and that of those for whom and to whom they had come.” And below: “It is reported that, as they approached the city according to their custom with the holy cross and the image of the great King, our Lord Jesus Christ, they sang this litany with one voice.” The image of the Savior was held in the greatest veneration among the faithful. On 9 November the commemoration is celebrated of the image of the Savior which, after being crucified by the Jews, poured forth abundant blood, as is stated in the Roman Martyrology. Hence many churches throughout the world have been dedicated to the Savior, in Rome and elsewhere. Augustine, *Against Julian*, book I: “Thus mothers throughout the whole world run daily with their little ones not only to Christ—that is, to the child—but to Christ himself, that is, also to the Savior.” ALTASERRA.]

On one of these days, proceeding with great humility and care in a litany with the most sacred image of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, which is called *antheropsita* [Note: another reading: *acheroposita*; perhaps *acheropoeta*], and receiving along with it various other sacred mysteries [Note: Codex of Lucca: “ministries”], the same most holy pope carried the holy image on his own shoulder together with the other priests. Both he and the entire people walked barefoot and, with ashes placed on the heads of all the people, proceeded amid the greatest wailing [Note: Codex of Lucca: “lamentation”] to the church of the holy Mother of God called at the Crib. There they prayed to our most merciful Lord, binding and fastening to the adorable cross of our God the covenant which the wicked king of the Lombards had broken.

[Note: [Col. 0967C] “At the same time, receiving with it various other sacred mysteries, and the same most holy pope carrying the holy image on his own shoulder together with the other priests, while both he and the entire people walked barefoot, they proceeded to the church of the holy Mother of God called at the Crib, ashes being placed on the heads of all the people, with the greatest wailing.” In the litany the pontiff proceeded with the clergy and people barefoot, and both he and the presbyters carried on their shoulders the image of Christ and various relics of the saints. It was the duty of deacons on the feast days of martyrs to carry the relics of the saints on their shoulders. Council of Braga III, canon 5. ALTASERRA.]

This most blessed pope diligently assembled all his priests and clergy in the Lateran patriarchate. He urged them with all their strength to search the divine Scripture [Note: another reading: “to follow”] and to devote themselves to spiritual reading, so that they might be found effective in every reply to and refutation of the adversaries of the Church of God. He did not cease continually, by admonishing and refuting, to teach the entire people of God to be sober, to act piously, and to guard themselves from every wickedness.

For the salvation of the province and of all Christians, this most blessed man decreed that a litany should be performed every Saturday, with no neglect or postponement. One Saturday was to be at Saint Mary, the Mother of God, at the Crib; another at the blessed apostle Peter; and another at the blessed apostle Paul.

This most blessed pope restored the basilica of Saint Lawrence situated above Saint Clement in the third region. It had long remained in ruins. He also restored the covering of the cemetery of Saint Soter, which had collapsed.

Thus, while the same most holy man repeatedly entreated the aforesaid pestilential king of the Lombards, giving him innumerable gifts for the flocks entrusted to him by God and for the lost sheep—that is, for the entire army of Ravenna [Note: Codex of Lucca and others: “exarchate”] and the whole population of this province of Italy, whom the impious king had deceived by diabolical fraud and held in his possession—and while he obtained nothing from him in this matter, [Note: [Col. 0967C] “Seeing that no assistance could be expected from the imperial power, etc.” Since no hope of aid remained from the East and King Aistulf was besieging Rome in order to subject it to his authority and invading the cities of the Roman Church, Stephen offered public prayers for the safety of the city and judged that the only aid for its salvation was to implore the arms of Gallic piety. “Secretly,” says Anastasius, “through a certain pilgrim he sent his letters to Pippin, king of the Franks,” urging him by those letters to send assistance. After receiving these letters, Pippin sent the abbot Droctegangus to Rome. Just as the aforesaid pilgrim was followed by other apostolic messengers, so the abbot Droctegangus was followed by other royal envoys, Chrodegang, bishop, and Autcharius, duke; Droctegangus meanwhile departed toward Francia carrying letters to the king and the nobles. PAGIUS.]

seeing in particular that no help could be obtained from the imperial power [Note: Codex of Lucca: “moreover”], then, just as his predecessors of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0967D] “Lord Gregory.” From Anastasius it is clear that both Gregorys, II and III, as well as Zacharias, made treaties with the kings of the Franks. No historical evidence survives concerning Gregory II, since many records have been obliterated by the injury of time. But concerning Gregory III, Fredegar’s Continuator, a nearly contemporary writer, reports the following in chapter 110: “At that time blessed Pope Gregory twice sent from Rome to Charles Martel a legation such as had never before been sent to any previous age, bearing the keys of the venerable tomb, together with the chains of Saint Peter and great and countless gifts; and after a pact had been made that he should withdraw from the emperor’s party, he confirmed the Roman consulship for the aforesaid prince Charles.” Concerning the legation received and its deeds he adds: “He received that embassy with extraordinary and magnificent honor, bestowed precious gifts, and with great rewards sent with their companions to Rome, to the thresholds of Saints Peter and Paul, Grimo, abbot of the monastery of Corbie, and Sygobert, recluse of the basilica of the martyr Saint Denis.” The annalist of Metz gives the same account: “In the year 741, when Charles the prince had subdued the peoples situated all around and was arranging within the boundaries of his rule what pertained to peace, he received twice in that same year an embassy sent from the apostolic see by the most blessed Pope Gregory. They presented him with the keys of the venerable tomb of the prince of the apostles Peter, and with his precious chains, together with great gifts—something that no prelate of the Roman city had previously sent to any Frankish prince.” The aforesaid prelate Gregory had also sent him a letter by decree of the Roman princes, stating that the Roman people, having abandoned the emperor’s rule, wished to turn to Charles’s defense and unconquerable clemency. I think that the decree of the Roman princes was nothing other than the decree by which they had elected Charles Martel consul. For, as we have seen above, decrees of elections were customarily used in this age with subscriptions. BENCINUS.]

Lord Gregory, and another Gregory, and Lord Zacharias, most blessed pontiffs, sent to Charles, king of the Franks, of most excellent memory, asking him for assistance because of the oppressions and invasions that they themselves had suffered in this Roman province at the hands of the wicked Lombard people.

So now this venerable Father too, inspired by divine grace [Note: Codex of Lucca: “inspiring”], secretly sent through a certain pilgrim his letters to Pippin, king of the Franks, written in the midst of the great sorrow that afflicted this province.

[Note: [Col. 0968D] “Secretly through a certain pilgrim.” King Aistulf was then harassing and constraining the pontifical territory with invasions and oppressions to such a degree that every recourse to the kings of Francia was obstructed. Therefore Pippin sent Bishop Rodingus and Duke Autcharius into Italy to accompany Stephen, the pontiff, when he was about to depart for Francia.]

[Note: [Col. 0969B] Codex of Lucca: “Even now he did not cease sending, so that the Frankish king himself might send his envoys here to Rome, by which means he would have caused him to be summoned to himself.]”

When the cities and this Roman province were being severely oppressed [Note: [Col. 0969B] Codex of Lucca: “severely.”] by that same king of the Lombards, suddenly there arrived [Note: [Col. 0969C] “The abbot Rodigangus, already sent by the aforesaid king in the name of the Franks. Rodigangus the abbot, whom Pippin sent to Rome to reply by letter to the letters which the pontiff had sent him through a foreigner, so that he might pass more safely through the Lombard territory, which was hostile to the Roman pontiff. In the two letters preserved in the *Codex Carolinus* he is called Droctegangus. The tenth letter contains these words: ‘The present abbot Droctegangus has been presented at the sacred threshold of your protector, the blessed prince of the apostles Peter, and before our eyes.’ And the eleventh letter says: ‘Just as we sent through the present Droctegangus, the religious abbot, and his companions.’ Of what monastery Droctegangus was abbot, I am entirely uncertain. In the *Life of Saint John, Abbot of Gorze*, in Bollandus under 27 February, it is suggested that Droctegangus governed the abbey of Gorze, situated in the diocese of Metz.—But the illustrious deeds and holiness of life of Rodigangus, or Chrodegangus, bishop of Metz, have made the matter much clearer. The same Pippin later sent him to Stephen, as is read in the following section of Anastasius. Of this bishop Chrodegangus Paul the Deacon relates, in his book on the bishops of the city of Metz, that he was born in the Hasbaniensis district, his father being Sigrammus and his mother Landrada, of the foremost Frankish nobility (for King Pippin was Rodigangus’s maternal uncle, as is read in the charter of donation produced by the distinguished Father Calmet, in volume one of his French-written *History of Lorraine*, p. 281, as evidence); that he was brought up in the palace of Charles the Mayor and became his *referendarius*, that is, keeper of the royal ring; and that finally, in Pippin’s time, he attained the episcopal dignity of the city of Metz. Indeed, in the manuscript of Anastasius, both the Thuane and Ambrosian copies, he is said to have been honored with the Pallium by Stephen, in these words, enclosed in parentheses in that manuscript: ‘And while he was staying in Francia, he granted the pallium to Rodigangus, the most holy bishop, and ordained him archbishop.’ Lambecius bears witness to this in book II, chapter 8, of his *Imperial Library*.—As for his embassy to Stephen III, which Anastasius reports here, the celebrated Warnefridus gives the following account: ‘Since he was wealthy in every respect, he was specially chosen by King Pippin and the whole Frankish assembly, and sent to Rome; and, as the wishes of all ardently desired, he summoned the venerable Pope Stephen to Gaul.’ In the *Chronicle of Lorsch*, not only is Rodigangus’s embassy mentioned, but his zeal is also praised, by which he obtained from Pippin that the exarchate of Ravenna and the other patrimonies which the Lombards had seized by force should be restored to blessed Peter. Among other highly memorable deeds [the *Chronicle* says], ‘summoning Pope Stephen to Gaul and arming Pippin with all the forces of the Franks against the tyranny of the Lombards, he devoted constant zeal and effort to having the exarchate of Ravenna and many of blessed Peter’s patrimonies restored to the Roman see.’ MAFEUS.] [Note: [Col. 0969B] Codex of Lucca: “Rodigandus.”] the abbot Rodigangus, already sent by the aforesaid king in the name of the Franks, through whom he sent word that he would fulfill the entire will and request of the aforesaid most holy pope. Afterwards another envoy, one of his intimates, arrived, announcing the very same things.

And when, as has been said, the ancient Roman city and all the fortresses were being held in check by the Lombards, so that they had even seized the fortress of Ciaccanum [Note: [Col. 0969B] Mansi: “Ciccanense”; another copy: “and also the fortress of Ciccaves.”], which belonged to the tenants of the holy Church of God [Note: [Col. 0970D] “Immediately John, the imperial *silentiarius*, came from the royal city. In the palace there was a corps of *silentiarii*, who kept watch in the imperial court. Anastasius is said to have been raised from the corps of *silentiarii* to the imperial office. Evagrius, book III, chapter 31. Ambrose, in the funeral oration for Valentinian: ‘In the evening the *silentiarius* departed.’ ALTASERRA.], immediately [Note: [Col. 0969B] Codex of Lucca: “came from the royal city.”] the aforesaid John, the imperial *silentiarius*, came to the royal city with the envoys of the same most holy pontiff, bringing with him both what the envoy of the wicked king of the Lombards had carried away and an imperial command, in which it was inserted [Note: [Col. 0969B] Codex of Lucca: “to the king.”] that the same most holy pope had hastened to the king of the Lombards in order to recover the city of Ravenna and the cities [Note: [Col. 0969B] Codex of Lucca: “to it.”] belonging to it. For this reason Pope Stephen also sent to that blasphemous king an envoy of his own, for his safety and for that of those who were to travel with him [Note: [Col. 0969B] In another copy, “blasphemous” is absent.]. When he had immediately returned, the envoys of the aforesaid Pippin, king of the Franks, also arrived, namely [Note: [Col. 0970B] Codex of Lucca: “Bishop Rothingandus to Francia.”] the bishop Rodigangus and [Note: [Col. 0970B] Another copy: “Autcharius.”] the duke Autecharius, so that they might escort the aforesaid most holy pope to his king of Francia, as he had requested in sending for him. They found him already prepared to proceed against the aforesaid king of the Lombards, in order to gather together all the Lord’s lost sheepfolds [Note: [Col. 0970B] Codex of Lucca: “sheep”; in another copy, “in the sheepfolds” is absent.].

Then that most blessed pope, having recourse to the mercy of our almighty God, went out from this Roman city to the blessed apostle Peter, on the fourteenth day of the month of October, in the seventh indiction [Note: [Col. 0970B] Codex of Lucca reads incorrectly: “XIV, indiction VIII, month I, indiction VII.”]. Many Romans and inhabitants of the other cities followed him, weeping and wailing, and would by no means allow him to proceed alone. That most holy man, placing his confidence [Note: [Col. 0970B] Another copy: “commending himself.”] in the power of God and in the protection of the holy Mother of God and of the blessed princes of the apostles, steadfastly proceeded for the salvation of all, although held back by bodily weakness [Note: [Col. 0970B] Another copy: “weakened.”]. He undertook the arduous journey, encouraging and commending the whole flock of the Lord to the good shepherd, our Lord, and to the prince of the blessed apostles, Peter. Taking with him certain priests from [Note: [Col. 0971C] Codex of Lucca: “from the clergy of this holy Church.”] this holy Church, as well as nobles and others of clerical rank, together with leading men from the army, and with Christ going before him, he continued the journey he had begun; and during the journey the Lord granted him great serenity of weather.

[Note: [Col. 0971C] Codex of Lucca: “When he had arrived within the Lombard borders.”]

When he had come almost to the fortieth milestone of the Lombard frontier, a great sign appeared in the sky one night, like [Note: [Col. 0971C] Another copy: “a sword.”] a fiery globe inclining toward the southern quarter, from the regions of Gaul toward the territories of the Lombards. Accordingly, one of the same Frankish envoys, namely [Note: [Col. 0971C] Another copy: “the duke Autcharius.”] the duke Autecharius, went ahead as quickly as possible to Ticinum and waited there for him.

[Note: [Col. 0971C] “But when he had drawn near, and so forth. Pope Stephen, encouraged by the arrival of the royal envoys, the bishop Chrodegangus of Metz and the duke Autecharius, left the Roman city on the fourteenth day of October, in the seventh indiction, according to Anastasius; consequently this was in the year 753. He then proceeded with them into Lombardy and from there into Francia, as he had requested. Passing through Pavia, he was entirely unable to obtain from King Aistulf the restoration of what had been taken away. Therefore, on the fifteenth day of November of the aforesaid seventh indiction, setting out from the city of Pavia, he began his journey to Francia. Continuing the journey he had begun, he reached the monastery of Agaunum, or Saint Maurice, where he stayed for several days. That celebrated monastery of Agaunum, now called Tornatense from the small town founded there, was situated in the kingdom of Burgundy not far from Octodurum; on this matter the second volume of the *Baronian Criticism* should be consulted. To that monastery came Fulradus, priest and chaplain—or archchaplain—of the palace, and the duke Rotardus, sent by King Pippin, asking the same pontiff to proceed to his king. They escorted him to him with great honor, together with all who were with him. PAGIUS.]”

But when the aforesaid most blessed pope had already drawn near to the city of Pavia, the aforementioned Aistulf, that most wicked king [Note: [Col. 0971C] In another copy, “most wicked” is absent.], sent his envoys to him, adjuring him on no account to dare to say anything to him about requesting the city of Ravenna and the exarchate belonging to it [Note: [Col. 0971D] “Requesting the city of Ravenna. Aistulf held Ravenna. Hence, when Stephen continued his journey toward Pavia, the king ordered that he should not pass through Ravenna or through the exarchate. For this reason Agnellus’s slanderous falsehood in the *Life of Sergius of Ravenna* is exposed, where he relates certain old women’s tales about Stephen’s entering Ravenna to plunder the treasury of that church. On this matter see his *Life of Sergius*, chapter 4, p. 172, and Bacchinius in his observations on the same. BENCINUS.], or the remaining places of the commonwealth which he himself or his predecessors, the kings of the Lombards, had invaded. He replied by sending word that he would not, through fear of any terror whatsoever, remain silent about making such a request [Note: [Col. 0971C] Codex of Lucca: “that through fear of no terror he would be silent about seeking such a thing.”].

When he had reached the city of Pavia and been presented to the aforesaid wicked king, he gave him many gifts, earnestly entreated him, and, bursting into tears, begged him to return the Lord’s sheep which he had taken away and to restore what belonged to its rightful owners. But he was entirely unable to obtain this from him. The imperial envoy likewise made the request, presented him with imperial letters, and could obtain nothing. The aforesaid Frankish envoys, however, pressed Aistulf strongly to allow the most holy pope to proceed to Francia. Thereupon he summoned the aforementioned blessed man and asked whether it was his wish to hasten to Francia. The pope did not conceal this, but openly declared his intention to him. Whereupon he, like a lion, gnashed his teeth; and for this reason he repeatedly sent his attendants to him secretly, in order somehow to turn him aside from such a purpose.

[Note: [Col. 0972C] Another copy: “On another day, in the presence of Bishop Rodigangus, he asked.”]

On another occasion, in the presence of the most holy bishop Rodigangus, the aforementioned king of the Lombards [Note: [Col. 0972C] Codex of Lucca: “whether he wished to go to Francia.”] asked the same blessed pope whether he wished to go to Francia, and [Note: [Col. 0972C] Codex of Lucca: “replied.”] addressed him as follows: “If it is your will to release me, it is certainly my will to depart.” Then he was released by him. Taking with him priests of this holy Church of God and members of the clergy, namely George, bishop of Ostia; [Note: [Col. 0972C] Codex of Lucca: “Willarius”; another copy: “Quilcharius.”] Wilearius, bishop of Nomentum; Leo, Philip, George, and Stephen, priests; Theophylact, archdeacon; Pardus and Gemmulus, deacons; Ambrose, *primicerius*; Boniface, [Note: [Col. 0972C] Another copy: “the *secundicerius* Leo, etc.”] the second; Leo and Christopher, *regionarii*, and others, on the fifteenth day of November of the aforesaid [Note: [Col. 0972C] Mansi omits “seventh.”] seventh indiction, he set out from the city of Pavia and began his journey to Francia.

After his release, the aforementioned king of the Lombards still attempted to turn him aside from the journey described above, but this did not escape the notice of the most holy man.

[Note: [Col. 0972D] “Thus, with great speed and with God going before him, he reached the Frankish passes. *Clusae* are the defiles of the Alps through which passage is open. *Frankish Annals*: ‘To those very narrow mountain passages which they call *clusae*.’ Anastasius below, in the same work: ‘To guard the Frankish passes.’ And below: ‘And completely overthrew the Lombard passes.’ The Lombard *clusae* are said to have been overthrown because the *clusae*, in order to be safer, had been fortified with defenses. The same author below, in the account of Adrian: ‘But the aforementioned Desiderius and the whole multitude of the Lombard army stood firmly in those very passes to resist, which they had carefully fortified with structures and various walls.’ Liutprand, *History*, book I, chapter 2: ‘For it was separated from us by certain exceedingly difficult barriers, which they call *clusae*.’ The same author, book V, chapter 18, calls them *clausurae*. Regino, *Chronicle* I: ‘He sought the Thermopylae, that is, the Lombard barriers.’ Radevicus, *On the Deeds of Frederick*, book I, chapter 3: ‘He penetrated their barriers, which they had made in narrow places by cutting through the dense forests.’ Cassiodorus, *Variae* II.19: ‘We command that provisions be supplied without hesitation to all Goths and Romans and to those who preside over the harbors and barriers, with sixty soldiers stationed continually in the Augustan barriers, just as provisions have also been decreed for others.’ Cujacius, *Observations* III.24. ALTASERRA.]”

Thus, with great speed and with God going before him, he reached the Frankish [Note: [Col. 0972C] Codex of Lucca: “reached the passes.”] passes. After entering them with those who were with him, he immediately gave praises to almighty God.

[Note: [Col. 0973B] “And continuing the journey he had begun, he reached the venerable monastery of Saint Maurice, martyr of Christ. Around the year 600, Sigismund, king of Burgundy, founded at Agaunum in the Allobroges a monastery consecrated to blessed Maurice. Almoine, book II, chapter 4: ‘Saint-Maurice in Chablais on the Rhône.’ ALTASERRA.]”

Continuing the journey he had begun, he reached the venerable monastery of Saint Maurice, the holy martyr of Christ. It had also been arranged that the king of the Franks would meet him there. By the Lord’s favor, the same most blessed pontiff arrived safely, together with all who were with him. After they had stayed there for several days [Note: [Col. 0973A] Codex of Lucca: “They met … Rothaldus”; another copy: “Fulradus the abbot and Rottardus, sent by,” etc.], Fulradus the abbot and the duke Rothardus, sent by the aforementioned Pippin, the most excellent king of the Franks, arrived at the aforesaid venerable monastery [Note: [Col. 0973B] “Fulradus the abbot, etc. Sommier, *Dogmatic History*, book VIII, chapter 34. During his journey toward Francia, Stephen answered various questions concerning discipline. With regard to marriage, he declared that, after a concubine had been dismissed, taking a lawful wife did not constitute a second marriage. A marriage could not be dissolved because impotence arose after its celebration, or because another illness intervened, except in the case of leprosy or demonic possession. A man who changed his place of residence (*caelum mutans*, literally “changing his sky”) could not likewise change his wife, so long as the woman whom he had lawfully married remained alive. It was not permitted to marry the godmother of one’s baptism or confirmation. A man who had repudiated one woman could not be joined to another wife. Penance ought to be imposed on those who, after vowing virginity but before entering a monastery, marry. Religious men and women who marry ought to be separated from communion. A widow who marries after having professed religious life ought to be confined in a monastery for the rest of her life. Spouses ought to be separated if either suffers from leprosy, lest they produce leprous offspring. A man who, uncertain whether he had been ordained a priest, had celebrated the sacrifice of the Mass and administered baptism, but afterward renounced the ministry and married, ought to be cast into a monastery to do penance for as long as he lived; and the same should be done with the woman whom he married, provided that she had not been unaware that the man had exercised the priestly office. Finally, a woman who, believing her absent husband to be dead, married another, must return to the first husband, if he survives, under penalty of excommunication.—II. Concerning baptism he decreed that anyone who, having water available, baptizes with wine is to be excommunicated; but if he has no water and the child is in danger, he will be free from punishment. Baptism by immersion is valid. A priest who, uncertain whether he has been validly ordained, administers baptism in the meantime is to be punished with penance until the end of his life.—III. Finally, he established the following for the clergy: that a bishop condemned for certain offenses by the unanimous consent of the bishops of his province could not be judged again by others. In clerical cases, the diocesan bishop should associate with himself six colleagues from neighboring dioceses, to be chosen by the accused if he is a priest, or three if he is a deacon; but the bishop himself should hear and decide the cases of the other clergy. A priest who has been convicted and has confessed by his own mouth that he committed the crime of incontinence before ordination is to be barred from the sacred celebration of Mass, but not from the other functions of the priesthood. Clerics and monks are not to wear their hair long. The same pontiff granted Abbot Fulradus authority to build monasteries wherever he could in Francia. His privilege runs as follows: ‘By this apostolic authority we grant and bestow upon you, our beloved son Fulradus, and upon all your successors who are abbots, the license and power to build monasteries wherever you wish in the province of Francia. And by this authority we prohibit any bishop of any church or any other priest from exercising any jurisdiction whatever in the aforesaid monasteries, except the apostolic see.’ (*Privilege of Stephen II granted to Abbot Fulradus.*) SOMMIER.] Fulradus the abbot and Rothardus the duke, sent by the aforementioned Pippin, the most excellent king of the Franks, asking the same most holy pontiff to proceed to his king. They escorted him to him with great honor, together with all [Note: [Col. 0973A] Mansi does not contain “who were with him.”] who were with him.

[Note: [Col. 0974B] “When that king heard, and so forth. After Christmas Day, King Pippin immediately went to the royal estate of Pontigon, in the district of Pertensis, situated not far from Victoriacus-Incensus, to meet the pope, together with his wife, his sons, and his leading men. He had sent his eldest son Charles ahead for many miles to meet him, with his own nobles; he himself, with his wife Bertrada and his other son Carloman, presented himself at the third milestone. At the pope’s sight he dismounted from his horse, bowed to the ground, and received him together with his wife, sons, and nobles, even performing for some distance the service of a groom, as Anastasius testifies. The pontiff proceeded to the aforesaid palace on the sixth day of January, on the most sacred solemnity of the Epiphany of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and therefore in the year 754. As for the year, Anastasius is supported by the later author of the appendix to the continuation of Fredegar and by the annalist of Metz. While the pontiff was at the Pontigon palace, on the following day he begged King Pippin to defend the cause of blessed Peter and the Roman commonwealth. King Pippin promised the pontiff that he would take every measure to restore the exarchate of Ravenna and the rights of the commonwealth, as the annals of Metz testify. PAGIUS.]”

When that same king heard of the arrival of the same most blessed pontiff, he hastened greatly to meet him, together with his wife, his sons, and his leading men. For this purpose, accompanied by one hundred thousand [reading uncertain], he sent his son named Charles to meet the coangelic pope [Note: [Col. 0974A] In another copy, “coangelic” is absent.] with some of his nobles.

[Note: [Col. 0974D] “And in his palace, at a place called Pontigone. Pippin received Pope Stephen, who had come into Gaul to seek assistance against the Lombards, in his palace, which was called Ponticone or Pontigone. Ponticone or Pontigone was a royal estate in the district of Catalaunensis, famous for the synod of Pontigone, which Aimoinus mentions in book V, chapter 33, and which is reported among the Capitularies of Charles the Bald, edited by Jacques Sirmond. Gregory of Tours calls it Ponticon in book IV, chapter 23, and book VI, chapter 37. In *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, book IV, chapter 40, he likewise calls it the royal estate of Pontigone; Frodoard, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 952, calls it a fiscal estate, that is, a royal estate. ALTASERRA.]”

And in his palace, at a place called [Note: [Col. 0974A] Another copy: “Pontianae.”] Ponticone, after descending from his horse at a distance of almost three miles [Col. 0975A], he prostrated himself on the ground with great humility, together with his wife, sons, and nobles, and received the same most holy pope.

[Note: [Col. 0975B] “He also proceeded for some distance beside the pope’s saddle in place of a groom. Pippin performed the office of groom for the pontiff, riding beside his saddle. A *strator* is one who spreads a saddle on his lord’s horse and assists him as he mounts. In the emperor’s court there were *stratores* among the palace offices. Spartianus, in *Antoninus Caracalla*: ‘When his groom was lifting him onto his horse, he stabbed him in the side with a dagger.’ Pontius the Deacon, in the *Life of Cyprian*, in Surius under 14 September: ‘Two officials came to him, one a groom of the office of Galerius Maximus, the *proconsul*, and the other an equestrian groom and guardian of that office.’ The office of the grooms was to inspect the military horses supplied by the provincials. *Codex*, single law, “On Grooms.” Ammianus, book XXIX: ‘Constantine, the groom, dared to exchange a few military horses from among those which he had been sent to Sardinia to inspect.’ Louis the Younger also, taking Nicholas I’s horse by the bridle, led the mounted man on foot in the manner of a groom.]”

He also proceeded for some distance beside his saddle in place of a groom. Then the aforesaid gracious man [Note: [Col. 0975A] In another copy, “gracious” is absent.], together with all his people, raised his voice and gave glory and unceasing praises to almighty God.
