With hymns and spiritual songs, they all proceeded with the king to the aforesaid palace, on the sixth day of the month of January, on the most sacred solemnity of the Epiphany of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. There, sitting together inside the oratory, the same most blessed pope tearfully entreated the aforementioned [Note: [Col. 0975A] In another copy, “most Christian” is absent.] most Christian king to arrange, through a treaty of peace, the cause of blessed Peter and of the Roman commonwealth. The king immediately satisfied the most blessed pope with an oath, promising that he would obey all his commands and admonitions with all his strength and, whenever the pope should wish it, would restore the exarchate of Ravenna and the rights or territories of the commonwealth [Note: [Col. 0975A] Codex of Lucca: “or the other territories belonging to the commonwealth.”] in every way [Note: [Col. 0975A] Codex of Lucca: “restore in every way.”].

[Note: [Col. 0975C] “But since winter was approaching. From the Pontigon palace Pope Stephen went to the monastery of Saint Denis near Paris. ‘But since winter was approaching,’ Anastasius adds, ‘he caused the same most holy pope, with all his companions, to go to Paris to spend the winter at the venerable monastery of blessed Denis.’ King Pippin then sent an embassy to Aistulf, king of the Lombards, asking him, out of reverence for the most blessed Peter and Paul, not to make a hostile incursion into the region of Rome and, because of Pippin’s request, not to do the superstitious and impious things contrary to the law which he had never before done in Rome, says the anonymous author who added the second appendix to the continuation of Fredegar. Beginning the year with the Kalends of March, he adds that when King Pippin had failed to obtain through his envoys what he had requested, and Aistulf had scorned to do it, after the year 753 had elapsed, Pippin ordered all the Franks to come to him on the Kalends of March at Brennacum, a royal estate in the district and kingdom of Soissons, situated on the river Vidula, which is commonly called Braine. PAGIUS.]”

But since winter was approaching, he arranged for the same most holy pope, together with all his companions [Note: [Col. 0976A] Codex of Lucca: “to Paris.”], to go to Paris to reside [Note: [Col. 0976A] Codex of Lucca and another copy: “to spend the winter.”] at the venerable monastery of blessed Denis.

When this had been done, and he had arrived at the same venerable monastery with the aforementioned [Note: [Col. 0976A] In another copy, “most Christian” is absent, and so throughout.] most Christian Pippin [Note: [Col. 0976A] Codex of Lucca: “with Pippin accompanying him.”], by the Lord’s favor, after several days [Note: [Col. 0975D] “The same most Christian King Pippin, by the grace of Christ, was anointed king of the Franks by the same most holy pope, together with his two sons. In that same year, namely 754, or rather on the same day, 28 July, on which Pope Stephen anointed Pippin and his sons Charles and Carloman as kings, he declared them also patricians of the Romans. One and the same celebration confirmed the kingship and conferred the patriciate. I infer this first from the letters of Pope Stephen. The first letter written to Pippin, before he went to Gaul, bears this title: ‘To the most excellent lord, his son Pippin, king, Pope Stephen.’ For Pippin had been declared king by Zacharias, his predecessor, and consecrated by Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, but had not yet been made a patrician. The third letter written by that same Stephen, after his return from Gaul, bears this other title: ‘To the most excellent lords, his sons, King Pippin, our spiritual co-father, and likewise Kings Charles and Carloman, both patricians of the Romans, Pope Stephen.’ But the Anonymous whom I have cited from Mabillon, in his notes on Zacharias, states this most clearly: ‘Afterward, on one day, in the church of the blessed martyrs Denis, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, by the hands of the same pontiff Stephen, Pippin, together with his aforesaid sons Charles and Carloman, was anointed and blessed as king and patrician in the name of the Holy Trinity.’—What Stephen conferred on Pippin by conferring the patriciate upon him, insofar as the obscurity of the matter permits—and the preoccupations and partisan interests of later writers have made it still more obscure—I shall try to explain briefly. The dignity of the patriciate, after the Roman commonwealth had been disturbed, its ancestral institutions overthrown, and imperial power established in the hands of the emperors of Constantinople, was bestowed on those whom the favor of the prince raised to the chief offices of the empire. The most eminent Norisius observes, in dissertation 4 of his *Pisan Cenotaphs*, that access to the dignity of the patriciate was especially open to those who had served well as commanders of the army in war. Idacius, in his *Chronicle*, at the beginning of the reign of Valentinian III, says: ‘Felix is appointed patrician from the office of commander of the army’; and under the ninth year of the same emperor: ‘Aetius, commander of both armies, is appointed patrician.’ In imperial rescripts sent to illustrious men, those who were also called commanders of the army are designated by the title of patrician. Theodosius’s Novel 24 is sent to Aetius, count and commander of both armies, and patrician; Majorian’s Novel 2 to Ricimer, illustrious man, count and commander of both armies, and patrician. In Gruter’s great collection of inscriptions, p. 10, no. 6, the following is read:

> FL. FELIX. V. C. MAGISTER. UTRIUSQ. MILITIAE. PATRICIUS. ET. EXCONS. OR. ET. PANDUSA. EJUS. INL. FEMINA. VOTI. COMPOTES. DE. PROPRIO. FECERUNT.

‘Flavius Felix, illustrious man, commander of both armies, patrician and former consul, and Pandusa, his illustrious wife, fulfilled their vow and erected this at their own expense.’

But that Asterius who corrected, with consular authority, the Virgil manuscript preserved in the Medicean Library [Col. 0977A] counts the patriciate among the more honorable titles, although he had not been commander of the army. At the end of the *Bucolics* [Col. 0978A] the following is read:

> TURCIUS RUFIUS APRONIANUS ASTERIUS [Col. 0979A] V. C. ET INL. EX COMITE DOMEST. PROTECT. EX. COM. PRIV. LARGIT. EX PRAEF. URBI PATRICIUS ET CONSUL ORDIN. LEGI ET DISTINXSI CODICEM FRATRIS MACARII V. C.

‘Turcius Rufius Apronianus Asterius, a most distinguished and illustrious man, former count of the household protectors, former count of the private largesses, former prefect of the city, patrician and ordinary consul, read and punctuated the codex of his brother Macarius, a most distinguished man.’”]

The consulship of Asterius fell in the year of Christ 494, [Col. 0979B] from which it is permissible to infer the antiquity and value of that singular Codex. Corrected by Asterius in that year, yet written long before, it seems to have preceded that Tiburtine Cornutian document bearing the signatures of the consuls Leo Augustus IV and Probienus, men of consular rank, namely in the year of Christ 471, which the eminent Suaresius, Mabillon, and Blanchinus regarded as the most ancient of all.

Anastasius calls Belisarius a patrician, and likewise calls several exarchs of Ravenna patricians: John, Eleutherius, Isaac, Paul, Romanus, Theodore, and Eutychius.

The dignity of the patriciate was one degree lower than the dignity of the consulship. I learn this from Cassiodorus, who, in book VI, chapter 2, while reciting the formula of the patriciate, says:

> “It precedes men of the praetorian prefecture and of the other dignities, yielding only to one splendor, which we know is sometimes also assumed by us.”

He means the consulship.

That the emperors thereafter joined to the dignity of the patriciate the obligation of protecting and defending churches and the poor against the violence of the powerful is taught us by the formula [Col. 0979C] with which the emperor created a patrician. This formula is reported by Paul the Deacon, in the *History of the Lombards*, in the Vatican Manuscript, and was transcribed by Pagius in the *Life of Gregory III*:

> “We grant you this honor, that you may administer justice to the churches of God and to the poor, and that thereafter you may render an account before the Most High Judge.”

Then the emperor should put a mantle upon him, place a ring on his right index finger, and give him a piece of cotton written in his own hand:

> “Be a merciful and just patrician.”

Then he should place a golden circlet upon his head and dismiss him.

From this Peter de Marca, book I of *On Concord*, chapter 12, concludes that patricians enjoyed, by a certain extraordinary right, the care and defense of churches not subject to them. For since it belongs to a ruler, by ordinary right, to protect the churches situated within his dominion against the violence of the powerful, through the conferral of the patriciate he granted the leading citizens an extraordinary right of protection. For this reason they were called defenders and advocates whenever they provided defense and guardianship to particular churches.

I pass over that matter, [Col. 0979D] but I deny what he adds: that the Roman patriciate embraced two things—both the jurisdiction by which kings exercised power in the city with the consent of the pope and the Roman people, and the protection or defense which they promised to the Roman Church. Hence he wrongly concludes:

> “Thus the patriciate of the Romans, besides sovereignty over the City and the Roman duchy, included that defense which had been established by agreements entered into with the Roman pontiffs.”

Certainly, agreements were made and confirmed by solemn oath between Pope Stephen and King Pippin concerning the defense and protection of the Roman Church. But I consistently deny that Stephen granted Pippin jurisdiction over the city of Rome and the Roman duchy. De Marca, whom Pagius rashly followed, invented this by his own imagination and without any foundation.

For he himself had not seen the document of the agreements in which he could have read of such a grant, nor is any trace of it found either in the letters sent by Stephen to Pippin [Col. 0980A] or in the *Life of Stephen* written by Anastasius, who had seen the document kept in his own time in the archive of the holy Roman Church.

Two things were agreed between Stephen and Pippin. The first was that Stephen would confer upon Pippin the singular and distinguished honor of the Roman patriciate, an honor previously granted to no one, by virtue of which Pippin would assume the protection, defense, and advocacy of the Roman Church, of the patrimonies of blessed Peter, and of all the rights and full claims of the apostolic see. The second was that Pippin, in virtue of this protection, would strive with all his strength to restore the Church’s rights, to rescue the exarchate of Ravenna from the hands of the Lombards, and to deliver it to the Roman pontiff.

The first point is clearly demonstrated by Stephen’s letters to Pippin. In Letter 3:

> “What none of your parents deserved to receive, you have received; and the prince of the apostles, making you his special possession above all other kings and peoples, has entrusted all his causes to you. You will render an account to God of how you have contended for the justice of that doorkeeper of the kingdom of heaven.”

A little earlier he had said:

> “For this reason the Lord, through my humility and by the mediation of blessed Peter, anointed you as kings, so that through you his holy Church might be exalted and the prince of the apostles might receive his justice.”

And in Letter 4:

> “Since, as has been stated above, by God’s command we have entrusted no one else but only your most beloved Excellence, or your dearest sons, and the entire Frankish people, with the protection of the holy Church of God of blessed Peter and of our Roman commonwealth.” [Col. 0980C]

The second point is likewise established by the same letters. In Letter 3:

> “For when we were brought before your honey-sweet presence, we entrusted all the causes of the prince of the apostles to your hands, since, inspired by God, you were pleased to lend an ear to our petitions, and you promised blessed Peter that you would exact his justice and provide for the defense of the holy Church of God.”

A little later:

> “Therefore I ask you, most excellent sons protected by God, and I earnestly implore you: let the cause of the holy Church of God and of blessed Peter grieve you; and what you promised would be offered to blessed Peter by donation, you must hand over to him for possession.”

And further:

> “Quickly and without impediment, return to blessed Peter, by your donation, the cities, places, all the hostages, and the captives which you promised him, or everything contained in that donation.”

And in Letter 6:

> “May you deign to grant full justice [Col. 0980D] to that same Church of God . . . so that you may order the remaining cities, which had been joined under one dominion, together with the established boundaries, territories, places, and even the forests [*saltora*], to be restored in their entirety to your spiritual mother, the holy Church. I ask you, my son, I ask you before the living God . . . to order that everything which you promised to blessed Peter under oath be fulfilled, and, as you have begun, to grant him full justice.”

These alone were the agreements established between Stephen and Pippin, and no others. Nowhere in those letters is there any word about jurisdiction over the City or the Roman duchy being granted to Pippin—although there had been frequent opportunity to speak of such a matter, especially in the hardships in which Rome found itself, besieged by the Lombards. The pontiff could have implored Pippin’s help for that city by calling the king to share in its dominion.

Anastasius, too, accurately recounts the oath and the promise made by Pippin to Stephen: to fight for the Church of God and to restore, or donate, the exarchate of Ravenna [Col. 0981A] to the Roman Church. But he says not a word about that imagined grant of jurisdiction.

Anastasius says in the *Life of Stephen III*, no. 243:

> “Pippin, who by the present oath satisfied that most blessed pope, promised to obey with all his strength all his commands and admonitions, and, whenever it should please him, to restore in every possible way the exarchate of Ravenna and the rights or territories of the Roman commonwealth.”

And no. 245:

> “The most excellent Pippin, king of the Franks, professed with all his strength that he would fight for the cause of the holy Church of God, just as he had formerly promised the aforesaid most blessed pontiff.” [Col. 0981B]

And no. 253:

> “For all these cities which had been recovered, he sent a written donation, in the name of blessed Peter, the holy Roman Church, and all the pontiffs of the apostolic see in perpetuity, for possession. This document is still preserved to the present day in the archive of our holy Church . . . The aforesaid venerable abbot Fulrad, priest of the Ravennates, joining his forces with the envoys of the aforesaid King Aistulf, entered each of the cities of the Pentapolis and Emilia, receiving them and taking hostages from each one, while also bringing with him the leading men and the keys of the city gates, and came to Rome.”

And the keys themselves, no. 254:

> “He placed in the confession of blessed Peter both the keys of the city of Ravenna and those of the various cities of the exarchate of Ravenna, together with the above-mentioned donation sent concerning them by their king, and delivered them to that apostle, to his most holy vicar the pope, and to all his successors, the pontiffs, to possess and administer forever.”

He then lists individually the cities which, in the king’s name, the abbot Fulrad, the king’s envoy, delivered to Pope Stephen for the Roman pontiffs to possess and administer perpetually, handing over their keys. He reserved for the king no dominion over them, nor any appearance of dominion or of any right whatsoever, but donated—or rather restored—all rights and claims to Peter and Peter’s successors.

What more is needed? If, by conferring the patriciate, Stephen had granted Pippin any right over the city of Rome, he could no longer, in the letters sent to Pippin, have used those expressions and terms by which he made his complete dominion over the city and over the Roman citizens evident. Yet he speaks of “his Roman commonwealth,” “his people,” and “his Roman city.”

In Letter 3:

> “For our entire people of the Roman commonwealth suffers with us in great sorrow and bitterest tears.” [Col. 0981D]

In Letter 4:

> “We have entrusted the holy Church of God and our Roman people to protection.”

In Letter 5:

> “Therefore provide for me my Roman people, entrusted to me by God . . . provided only that you protect my special people and my Roman city . . .”

This manner of speaking is clear evidence not of an alienated or divided jurisdiction, but of jurisdiction always fully retained and preserved by the pope.

The first Frankish emperors themselves likewise spoke in their acts of the protection and defense of the holy Roman Church, but never of jurisdiction over the City or the Roman duchy granted to them by the popes.

Charles the Great, in the division of his kingdom among his sons made in the year 806, says:

> “Above all, we command that the three brothers together assume the care and defense of the Church of Saint Peter, just as formerly our grandfather Charles, King Pippin of blessed memory, and later we ourselves assumed it; and that with God’s help they strive to defend it from its enemies and ensure that it receives its justice, insofar as this pertains to them [Col. 0982A] and reason demands.”

Louis the Pious, likewise in the division of his kingdom, which Baluzius reports in volume I of the *Capitularies*, in the year 837, says:

> “Above all, we command and order that the three brothers together assume the care and defense of the Church of Saint Peter, just as formerly our great-grandfather Charles, our grandfather Pippin, our father Charles, emperor of blessed memory, and later we ourselves assumed it.” [Col. 0982B]

I have thought it appropriate to discuss these matters concerning the Roman patriciate briefly in my notes to the *Life of Stephen*. Whoever desires fuller knowledge should consult the excellent treatise entitled *Defense of the Rights of the Church over Comacchio*, where its most learned author—who has deserved extremely well not only of the Roman Church but also of the entire republic of letters—formerly elucidated this same subject with appropriate distinction.

**BALDINUS.**

The same [Col. 0977A] most Christian [Note: [Col. 0977A] 1. King Pippin, etc. Besides Anastasius, this is asserted here by Thesphorus, book XXII; Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapter 5; Egilwaldus, book II, chapter 1; and the emperor Louis himself, in a letter written to Hilduin, which is found in the ancient version of the *Areopagitic* works. BIN. and LABB. — King Pippin and his two sons were anointed kings. War was being prepared on every side against King Aistulf, but because of the grave and dangerous illness of Pope Stephen the expedition was delayed for a time. Stephen was ill around the end of July in the monastery of Saint-Denis, as is established both by Anastasius and by Stephen himself in his letter preserved by Hilduin in the *Areopagitics*. After this comes the account of the anointing of Pippin, his sons, and his wife by Stephen:

> “In this year,” says Hilduin, [Col. 0977B] “which is the 754th from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August.”

Stephen, therefore, was healed by a remarkable miracle through the intercession of that same martyr Saint Denis, as both Anastasius and the pontiff himself report in the aforementioned letter, anointed Pippin and his sons Charles and Carloman, and his wife Bertrada, as kings of the Franks, on the twenty-eighth day of July. That date fell on a Sunday in the year 754; for ceremonies of this kind were customarily performed on Sundays or on more solemn feast days.

Thus Pippin was anointed king twice: first by Saint Boniface, legate of the apostolic see, as was shown under Pope Zacharias; and second by Pope Stephen, as testified by the Bertinian, Loiselian, and Metz annalists and others, as well as by Anastasius. — PAGIUS.]

While anointing Pippin, Charles, and Carloman as kings, Stephen called them Roman patricians, as is inferred from the letter written to them that survives in the *Codex Carolinus*, no. 9, whose inscription reads:

> “To our most excellent sons, Pippin the king and our spiritual co-father, and likewise to Charles and Carloman, kings and both patricians of the Romans: Stephen, pope.”

The matter, however, is placed beyond doubt by the Metz annalist, who writes under the year 754:

> “He”—namely Stephen—“according to the custom of the ancestors, by sacred anointing ordained Pippin, the most devout prince, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans; and he crowned his two sons, Charles and Carloman, with the same honor, in a fortunate succession.”

Since in this letter, and quite frequently in the inscription and text of other letters, Stephen calls Pippin his spiritual co-father, and even calls Charles and Carloman his spiritual sons, while in Letter 8 of the *Codex Carolinus* he also calls their mother Bertrada his spiritual co-mother, no other explanation of this matter can be offered than that Stephen II had lifted Charles and Carloman from the sacred font—that is, had baptized them—before anointing them kings.

Therefore, says Cointius in the *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, under the year 754, no. 58, those are mistaken who maintain that Charles was baptized at Mainz by Boniface, bishop of that city.

— PAGIUS.

King Pippin was anointed by the same most holy pontiff, etc. While arms were being prepared on both sides, and the same was being done in Francia, the pontiff anointed the king, his sons, and his wife. Hilduin clearly recounts the event in the *Areopagitics*:

> “In the year which is 754 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, blessed Pope Stephen anointed the flourishing King Pippin as king of the Franks, together with his two sons Charles and Carloman; and he also consecrated Bertrada, the wife of the illustrious King Pippin, clothed in royal robes, in the name of God by the grace of the sevenfold Spirit of the Holy Spirit. He sanctified the nobles of the Franks with apostolic blessing and bound them by the authority of blessed Peter, given to him by the Lord Jesus Christ, true God. He adjured them never, throughout the course of succeeding ages, to presume in any way to establish as king over themselves anyone from another stock, unless he came from the lineage of those whom divine providence had chosen to protect the most holy apostolic see and whom, through that vicar—namely, the vicar of Saint Peter, indeed of our Lord Jesus Christ—it had deigned to exalt to royal power and consecrate with the most sacred anointing.” [Col. 0978A]

Nor did he merely, as the Metz annalist says, “according to the custom of the ancestors, by sacred anointing ordain Pippin, the most devout prince, king of the Franks.” Rather, so that he might commend the patronage of the apostolic see to them ever more strongly, he also declared him a Roman patrician, and crowned his two sons, Charles and Carloman, with the same honor in a fortunate succession.

— SOMMIER.]

King Pippin, by the grace of Christ, was anointed by the same most holy [Col. 0978A] pope together with his two sons [Note: [Col. 0978A] They were anointed kings. For establishing the royal era of the Carolingians, which ancient and modern chronologists attach to the year 752, it is useful to transcribe the note found in an old manuscript Codex of Saint Gregory of Tours’ book *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, in Mabillon, book V of *On Diplomatics*, p. 354, plate 22:

> “If you wish to know, reader, at what time this little book appears to have been written and issued for the precious praise of the holy martyrs, you will find the year 767 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the time of Pippin, the most fortunate, tranquil, and Catholic king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, son of Charles the prince of blessed memory, in the sixteenth year of his most fortunate reign in the name of God, indiction 5; and also in the thirteenth year of his sons, the same kings of the Franks, Charles and Carloman, who by the hands of the man of holy memory, the most blessed Lord Pope Stephen, together with the aforesaid father and glorious lord King Pippin, were consecrated with sacred chrism by divine providence and through the intercession of Saints Peter and Paul. For the aforesaid most flourishing and devout lord King Pippin had been elevated to the royal throne three years earlier by the authority and command of the lord Pope Zacharias, of holy memory, through the anointing of sacred chrism by the hands of the priests of Gaul and by the election of all the Franks. Afterwards, by the hands of that same pontiff Stephen, on one day, in the church of the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius—where the venerable man Folrad is also known to be archpresbyter and abbot—he was anointed and blessed as king and patrician, together with his aforementioned sons Charles and Carloman, in the name of the holy Trinity. In that same church of the blessed martyrs, on one and the same day, the aforesaid venerable pontiff blessed Bertrada, the most noble and devout wife of the aforementioned flourishing king, who was most devotedly attached to the holy martyrs, after she had been clothed in royal robes, by the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. At the same time he confirmed the princes of the Franks with blessing and the grace of the Holy Spirit, and bound them all by such a prohibition and law of excommunication that they should never presume to choose a king from another’s loins, but only from among those whom divine mercy had deigned to exalt and whom it had resolved, through the intercession of the holy apostles and by the hands of their most blessed vicar the pontiff, to confirm and consecrate. We have therefore inserted this briefly for your charity on the final little page of this book, so that through the succession of time and the reports of the people, posterity may forever be able to know the lineage.”

The Bertinian Annals also say under the year 753:

> “Pope Stephen came to Francia, seeking assistance and support for the rights of Saint Peter. Likewise Carloman, a monk and brother of the aforesaid King Pippin, came to Francia at the command of his abbot, as though to disturb the apostolic petition.”

And under the year 754:

> “Stephen confirmed Pippin as king by holy anointing, and with him anointed his two sons, Lord Charles and Carloman, as kings, in the year of the Lord 754, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August.”

— BENC.]

They were anointed kings [Col. 0979A] of the Franks. Afterwards, however, the most blessed pope was severely weakened by the excessive hardship of the journey and by the unfavorable season, so that all, both his own people and [Note: [Col. 0979A] Codex Luc., “the Franks who were present there,”] all the Franks present there, despaired of his life. But the ineffable mercy of the Lord our God, who does not abandon those who hope in him and who desires every human being to be saved [Note: [Col. 0980A] Codex Luc., “while he desired him to be saved,”], preserved the most Christian lord: when they expected to find him dead in the morning, they suddenly found him well on the following day.

King Pippin, however, having been released by the admonition, grace, and prayer of that venerable pontiff [Note: [Col. 0981A] Codex Luc., “to the place . . . Paris”; another reading, “at Paris.”] [Note: [Col. 0982B] 1. “At the place called Carisiacus.” Carisiacus was a royal estate, famous for the Synod of Carisiacus, which is preserved in the *Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, and for the death of Charles Martel. Fredegarius, *Chronicle*, chapter 110: “Coming to the palace estate of Carisiacus on the River Oise, he was seized by a violent fever and died in peace” (Crécy-sur-Oise).

ALTASERRA.

2. “At the place called Carisiacus.” Pippin later went to Carisiacus at the request of Pope Stephen and celebrated Easter there, as Regino writes in his *Chronicle*: “In the year 754, Easter was celebrated on the fourteenth day of April.” As I have said, Regino writes that Pippin celebrated it at Carisiacus in the year when Stephen II was in Francia, although he wrongly says that this was 751. Carisiacus is now commonly called Quirsi or Chirsi in French; it is a place on the River Oise, then a palatine estate, a few leagues from the city of Noviomagus. Mabillon has published a discussion of it in book IV of *On Diplomatics*, p. 258. Pope Stephen was brought there, and there the promise was made to him by Pippin and his sons Charles and Carloman that the things seized from the Lombards would be restored to the Roman pontiff, as the same Anastasius testifies under Hadrian I.] proceeded to the place called Carisiacus, and there gathered all the nobles of his royal power. Instructing them with the admonition of so great a father, [Col. 0982A] he resolved with them to carry out what, with Christ’s favor, he had once decreed together with that most blessed pope.

Meanwhile the impious Aistulf [Note: [Col. 0982C] 1. “Meanwhile the impious Aistulf [sent for] Carloman.” Aistulf resolved upon this embassy to Gaul in order to undermine the cause of the Roman Church. Carloman, Pippin’s brother, who at that time was living as a monk in the monastery of Cassino, accepted it reluctantly, since he had been compelled by the virtue of obedience to undertake it by his abbot Gratianus, who feared that, as had happened before, the monastery, restored with so much labor, might again be destroyed by the Lombards. Eginhard, Aimoinus, Leo of Ostia, and other ancient writers testify to this. One or two testimonies will not be useless here.

Eginhard, in the *Annals* under the year 753, gives this explanation for Carloman’s journey:

> “Because neither he dared resist the commands of his abbot, nor his abbot the orders of the king of the Lombards, who had commanded him to do this.”

Leo of Ostia, also recounting the events at Cassino, says the same in book I, chapter 7:

> “Afterwards, when Aistulf, king of the Lombards, asked him to go to his brother Pippin, king of the Franks, on certain affairs of his kingdom, and when his abbot also requested that he do so, he consented reluctantly and eventually set out. After he had stayed there for some time, prevented from returning by the business for which he had come, he died. His brother Pippin afterwards placed his body in a golden coffin and, together with many other gifts, sent it back here, namely to his monastery.”

I have thought it worthwhile to append these authorities here because, contrary to the testimony of the ancients, shameless men in our own time have dared to write that Carloman undertook his journey to Gaul on behalf of Aistulf because he himself disapproved of the pontiff’s cause, ambition, and desire to rule. Yet in the most holy pontiff Stephen there was certainly no ambition and no desire for domination; he cared solely that the cause of blessed Peter’s justice, which the perjured Aistulf was ruining by force and wickedness, should be defended by Pippin.

Certainly, concerning Carloman’s stay in Gaul, our author reports the following:

> “When he had arrived there, he strove with all his might and contended most vigorously to undermine the cause of the holy Church of God, in accordance with what he had been sent by the aforesaid Aistulf, the tyrant whose name should not be spoken.”

But, through the Lord’s favor, he was entirely unable to incline the firm heart of his brother, the most Christian Pippin, king of the Franks, to this course.

If, however, we have the ancient writers as witnesses that Carloman reluctantly undertook the embassy on behalf of Aistulf, how can anyone maintain that he approved Aistulf’s cause and disapproved the pontiff’s? If he vigorously defended Aistulf’s side before his brother Pippin, it should rather be thought that he did so lest he once again expose the Cassinese monastery, to which he had devoted himself, to the savagery of the Lombards. Who does not see that this would have happened if Carloman, as envoy, had handled their affairs perfunctorily before Pippin?

MAFEUS.

2. “Meanwhile the impious Aistulf.” While Pippin was at Carisiacus with Pope Stephen, Carloman, his brother and then a monk of Cassino, came there from Italy as well. He strove with all his might and contended vehemently to undermine the cause of the holy Church of God, in accordance with the instructions with which he had been sent by King Aistulf, says Anastasius. But what Eginhard writes in the *Annals* under the year 753 is more plausible: namely, that Carloman undertook that embassy unwillingly, since he dared neither disregard the orders of his abbot nor resist the commands of the king of the Lombards, who had ordered him to do this. The Lauresham annalist and many others likewise write that Carloman undertook the embassy at the command of his abbot.

But Pippin, as he had already promised the pontiff, undertook the patronage of the pontiff and of the Roman Church.

PAGIUS.]

sent Carloman, the brother of the most gracious King Pippin, from the monastery of blessed [Col. 0983A] Benedict, where he had devoutly lived a monastic life for a long period [Note: [Col. 0983C] Codex Luc., “as a monk,”], persuading him by diabolical suggestions to go into the province of Francia [Note: [Col. 0983C] Codex Luc., “to obey him in the province of Francia”] in order to oppose and resist the cause of the redemption of the holy Church of God and of the Roman commonwealth.

When he had arrived there [Note: [Col. 0983C] Codex Luc., “had reached there,”] he strove with all his might and contended most vehemently to overthrow the cause of the holy Church of God, in accordance with the instructions with which the aforesaid [Note: [Col. 0983C] In another copy, “the tyrant, whose name should not be spoken,”] Aistulf, the tyrant whose name should not be spoken, had sent him.

But, through the Lord’s favor, he was entirely unable to incline the firm heart of his brother, the most Christian Pippin, king of the Franks, to this course. Rather, having discovered the cunning of the most wicked Aistulf, that same excellent Pippin, king of the Franks, declared with all his strength that he would contend for the cause of the holy Church of God, as he had previously promised the aforesaid most blessed pontiff.

[Col. 0983B] Then, by common agreement, that same most holy pope and the aforementioned king of the Franks, after taking counsel together, placed Carloman in a monastery there in Francia, in accordance with the fact that the aforesaid Carloman had devoted himself to living a monastic life. [Note: [Col. 0983C] Codex Luc., “at Vienna.”] There, after some days, he departed this life by divine calling, in the year of the Lord 755.

The most Christian Pippin, king of the Franks, as a faithful servant of blessed Peter and obedient to the salutary admonitions of the aforesaid most holy pontiff [Note: [Col. 0983C] Codex Luc., “commands”; another reading, “requests,”] sent his envoys to the most wicked Lombard king Aistulf concerning a peace treaty and the restoration of the rights of the holy Church of God and of the Roman commonwealth [Note: [Col. 0983C] In another copy, “the aforesaid holy” is absent]. Twice and a third time, in accordance with the admonition of the aforesaid most blessed pope, he entreated him and promised him many gifts, asking only that he peacefully restore their property to its rightful owners [Col. 0984A]. But he delayed obeying, sin standing in the way [Note: [Col. 0984C] Another reading, “he was unwilling”; “For this purpose”].

When that distinguished king of the Franks saw that in no way could he soften the stony heart of the most savage Aistulf, he resolved to make a general expedition against him. And while the columns of the Frankish army were already marching over nearly half the distance, the same holy man again entreated the aforesaid most gracious King Pippin [Note: [Col. 0984C] Another reading, “that the same pope entreated”;] [Note: [Col. 0984C] Codex Luc., “that he should again . . . send”] to send once more to the most savage Aistulf, king of the Lombards, if somehow he might finally, even at that late hour, calm his ferocity and salutarily persuade him to restore what belonged to the rightful owners, without the shedding of human blood.

And so it happened: that most gracious king of the Franks again sent his envoys to Aistulf.

[Col. 0984B] But that same most blessed pope, like a true father and good shepherd, lest Christian blood should be shed, sent him apostolic letters of admonition and entreaty. In them he adjured and solemnly charged him by all the divine mysteries and by the day of the future judgment to restore peacefully, without any shedding of blood, the rights of the holy Church of God and of the Roman commonwealth. But because of his iniquity he was unwilling to comply.

Instead, he sent threats and expressions of anger to the aforesaid pontiff, to the most excellent King Pippin, and to all the Franks. [Note: [Col. 0984C] Another copy: “Then Pippin set out, promising,” etc.]

Then, fixed in the mercy of almighty God, the aforesaid Pippin, king of the Franks, set out on his journey [Note: [Col. 0984C] Codex Luc., “continued his journey,”], sending ahead of his arrival certain of his nobles [Note: [Col. 0984C] In another copy, “of his nobles” is absent], together with military men, to guard the Frankish [Col. 0984C] passes [Note: [Col. 0984C] Codex Luc., “fortifications.”].

[Note: [Col. 0984D] “The Frankish passes.” The *clusae* or *clausae* were the narrow passages of the Alps through which, as through gates, the enemy’s approach was barred.

The Bertinian Annals say of these:

> “King Pippin, proceeding into Italy at the apostolic invitation and seeking the justice of the blessed apostle Peter, was opposed by Aistulf, king of the Lombards, who denied the aforesaid justice. He went to the Lombard passes to meet King Pippin and the Franks. They engaged in battle, and, with the Lord’s help and through the intercession of the blessed apostle Peter, King Pippin and the Franks emerged victorious. In that same year, 755, Pope Stephen was brought to the holy see by envoys of Lord King Pippin, together with Fulrad and the others who were with them.”

The remaining events which the cited annalist recounts correspond exactly to those found in the *Pontifical Acts.

BENCINUS.]

There, having assembled, they remained at a distance, awaiting the arrival of their own king.

Hearing, therefore, that those Franks who had come to guard the passes were few [Note: [Col. 0985B] Another copy: “that King Aistulf learned that only a small number of those Franks were present to guard their possessions, etc.”], that arrogant Aistulf [Note: [Col. 0985B] Codex Luc., “a few”] trusted in his own ferocity [Note: [Col. 0985B] Codex Luc., “strength”], suddenly opened the passes and at dawn fell upon them with numerous armies.

But the just Judge, the Lord our God and Savior Jesus Christ, granted victory to those very few Franks. They defeated and slaughtered that multitude of Lombards, so that Aistulf himself, seized by flight, could scarcely have escaped from their hands had he not fled without weapons as far as the city of Pavia [Note: [Col. 0985B] Another copy: “in which he settled with his men. But they . . .”], where, out of fear of the Franks, he withdrew with some of his men.

The Franks, however, entering the passes, seized the entire Lombard encampment [Note: [Col. 0985B] Mansi has *cunctorum* and in the margin: “ditch,” that is, “camp”] after the slaughter had been completed, carrying away abundant spoils.

[Col. 0985B] Then the most Christian Pippin, king of the Franks, together with his followers, and the aforementioned most blessed pope, having been made [the source's reading is uncertain], reached the walls of the city of Pavia. After besieging it for several days, the army of the Franks courageously pressed it hard. [Note: Codex Luc., “constricted it.”]

Then the aforementioned most blessed and angelic fellow-pope entreated the most benevolent king Pippin that this evil might no longer continue and that Christian blood might not be shed, urging with saving admonition that the matter should be brought to an end peacefully. [Note: Codex Luc., “might come to pass.”] [Note: “In response, King Pippin, hearing that they longed for peace and were promising in writing a treaty that had been agreed upon, said to the supreme pontiff: ‘Let it be done according to your command, most blessed father.’”]

In response, the most Christian Pippin, king of the Franks, hearing and fulfilling the admonition of that same most blessed Father and good shepherd, entered upon a peace pleasing to God and confirmed by written treaties the agreements of the parties between the Romans, the Franks, and the Lombards. That same king of the Franks took hostages from the Lombards; Aistulf himself promised, under a terrible and most solemn oath, and confirmed in the written document of the treaty [Col. 0985C] that he would immediately restore the city of Ravenna together with various other cities.

[Note: “He would immediately restore the city of Ravenna. Meanwhile, when Pippin had sent envoys to King Aistulf and had obtained nothing from him that he had requested, he marched against him with an army,” as the author cited in the second Appendix to the Continuation of Fredegar and Anastasius relate. Anastasius says that this expedition occurred in September, when the eighth indiction had already begun, and therefore in September of the same year, 754. King Pippin accordingly sent some of his nobles ahead of his own arrival, together with part of the army, to guard the Franks’ own passes, or the Alpine defiles. Then, crossing the Alps with his entire army, he defeated Aistulf, king of the Lombards, in battle in the very jaws of the mountains; pursuing him in flight, he besieged him at Pavia. Meanwhile, the pontiff, fearing a new shedding of Christian blood, negotiated with him; and after receiving from Aistulf an oath and hostages for the restoration of Ravenna and the other cities, he himself returned to Gaul. PAGIUS.]

[Note: Alternative reading: “And after this, having separated from one another in perjury, Aistulf,” etc.]

[Note: “And after this peace had been made,” etc. After these events had been most happily accomplished, King Pippin, victorious, returned with his men to Gaul, while Pope Stephen returned to Rome. There he was received by his people with the greatest joy and publicly rendered, according to custom, worthy praises to God in the Basilica of Saint Peter for so many and such great benefits. Jerome, brother of King Pippin, accompanied Stephen to Rome, as the annalist of Fulda records; but the annalists of Loisel, Lorsch, Saint-Bertin, and Regino add to Jerome Fulrad, one of Pippin’s envoys. “Pippin himself,” says the annalist of Lorsch, “returned to his kingdom and sent Pope Stephen back to Rome with Fulrad, priest and chaplain, and a considerable force of Franks.” Stephen reached Rome before the end of the year 754, as will become clear from what follows. Paul Aemilius adds that Pippin brought home glory, since he, the first of all mortals, had undertaken a foreign war against a people renowned for its achievements, for the sake of religion and without any personal advantage, and had brought it to completion without personal gain. PAGIUS.]

And afterward, peace having been made between the Romans, the Franks, [Col. 0986B] and the Lombards, King Pippin returned to his own territories, taking the Lombard hostages with him. When they had separated from one another, that faithless Aistulf, king of the Lombards, falling into the usual guilt of perjury, delayed restoring what he had promised on oath.

While the aforementioned most holy pope was returning to Rome, after some time had passed, [Note: “Filled with intense fury,” etc. As that year was drawing to a close, Jerome, brother of King Pippin, and Fulrad, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Denis, returned from Rome to Francia with the letters cited in the *Codex Carolinus*, no. 7. In those letters Pope Stephen complained to Pippin, Charles, and Carloman, kings of the Franks, and to the Roman patricians, that King Aistulf was in no way keeping his promises and had restored nothing either to the Roman Church or to the Roman commonwealth. In those letters the pontiff says of Aistulf: “He did not permit even a space of one palm’s breadth of land to be restored to blessed Peter, to the holy Church of God, or to the Roman commonwealth, although they—namely Pippin and his sons—had freely confirmed by a deed of donation that cities and territories were to be restored to blessed Peter, to the holy Church of God, and to the Roman commonwealth.” From these words it may also be inferred that, when peace was reached between Stephen and Aistulf, Pippin imposed this condition upon Aistulf: that he should restore what had been taken from both the Roman Church and the Roman commonwealth, but not from the Roman Empire, as some writers incorrectly state. Aistulf not only failed to restore what had been taken from the Roman Church; after Fulrad and Jerome had returned to Gaul, he immediately began to trouble Pope Stephen through *scamarae*, or scouts, and through plundering and devastation. Moved by this, Stephen arranged for letters, found as no. 9 in the *Codex Carolinus*, to be delivered without delay by Willharius, or Wilearius, bishop of Nomentum, to the aforementioned kings. In them he urged them to compel Aistulf to restore to the Church and commonwealth of Rome what he had taken and what Pippin had decided to give to the Roman See: “For,” he says, “as we first announced to your Christianity, the wicked King Aistulf, after the devil entered his treacherous heart, made void everything that he had promised through an oath to restore to blessed Peter through our envoys, and he was unwilling to return even a space of one palm’s breadth of land to blessed Peter . . . For not only was he unwilling to restore the property of blessed Peter, as he had determined, but he also did not cease, and does not cease, by his command, to carry out *scamarae*, plundering, and devastation in the cities and territories of blessed Peter . . . Therefore I ask you, most excellent sons protected by God, and earnestly entreat you: let the cause of the holy Church of God and of blessed Peter grieve you, and what you promised would be offered to blessed Peter by donation, you must hand over to him. PAGIUS.]

filled with intense fury, Aistulf, the adversary and enemy of his own soul, with God opposed to him, not only failed to fulfill what he had promised but also raised a general uprising. With the entire Lombard people of his kingdom he came against this Roman city, which he besieged for a period of three months. [Note: “Besieging it for three months.” At the beginning of the year 755, King Aistulf gathered a huge army, surrounded the city of Rome with a siege, devastated and burned all the surrounding places, both sacred and secular, threw holy images into the fire, polluted the most sacred body of the Lord, tore monks with blows, violated nuns, slaughtered the other clergy and laypeople of both sexes, killed little children pulled from their mothers’ breasts, and finally committed every kind of impiety and cruelty. In these desperate circumstances Stephen suddenly sent envoys to King Aistulf concerning the observance of the treaties. But when they brought back no peaceful response, he placed all his hope, after God, in the kings and people of the Franks. He ordered Warner, an abbot sent to him by Pippin, who had performed the military duty of defending the city with distinction, to travel by sea to Francia, so that he might arrive more safely and quickly, together with his envoys, Bishop George and Count Thomeric, and to report all these matters to Pippin, earnestly adjuring him by everything sacred to fulfill at last what he had once promised. Through those envoys he sent two letters to Francia: one in his own name to King Pippin; the other in his own name and in the name of all the Romans placed in affliction, to the same Pippin and his sons, and also to the bishops, abbots, priests, monks, dukes, counts, and all the other Franks. From these letters it is clear that Rome was already under siege on the Kalends of January. PAGIUS.]

and, surrounding it on every side, attacked it vigorously each day, destroying and utterly laying waste with sword and fire everything outside the city. That same pestilential Aistulf pressed on ever more fiercely, hoping that he might capture this Roman city; for he also dug up many bodies of saints and carried away their sacred mysteries, to the great destruction of souls. [Note: Codex Luc., “their cemeteries”; another reading, “their burial grounds.” “Accordingly, he offered that fortress of Narni, which he had earlier restored through the envoys of the Franks, to the rights of blessed Peter the apostle. Thus were the deeds of Aistulf,” etc.]

When these impious deeds of the same Aistulf had been reported as quickly as possible to the ears of the aforementioned king of the Franks, [Note: Codex Luc., “came to his ears.”] the most blessed pontiff also [Col. 0988C] arranged his envoys and sent them to Francia by sea, together with a certain religious man named Warner, who had previously been sent to Rome by that same king of the Franks. [Note: “By the sea route,” etc. When the Lombards pressed the siege more fiercely, Stephen, in a new and extraordinary example—one adopted neither by his predecessors nor afterward by his successors—wrote in the name of Saint Peter the apostle himself to the same kings, Pippin, Charles, and Carloman, and to the entire Frankish nation. He earnestly and eloquently entreated all of them, employing every possible means to arouse compassion, to hasten to the aid of the afflicted Church and city of Rome. Just as all nations that had taken refuge with the powerful Frankish people had been saved, so they should hasten to free the holy Church of God and its people from the oppression of their enemies. From the letter to King Pippin it is clear that the Church and the Roman people had placed all their hope in the most Christian king and in the Franks as their liberators: “Help us,” he says, “and assist us with the greatest speed, most Christian one . . . I beg you, let us not perish, lest the nations throughout the whole world say: ‘Where is the confidence of the Romans [Col. 0988D] which, after the Lord, they had in the kings of the Franks?’ . . . Save us before we perish, most Christian king . . . Consider, son, consider, and reflect on this completely. I adjure you by the living God, because the souls both of us and of the entire Roman people, after God and his prince of the apostles, depend upon your excellence protected by God and upon the Frankish people entrusted to you by God . . . For we have entrusted the holy Church of God and the people of the Roman commonwealth to no one else but your most beloved Excellence, your sweetest sons, and the entire Frankish people, by the command of God and of blessed Peter. PAGIUS.]

He reported everything that had happened, and everything that the cruel tyrant Aistulf had perpetrated, to the aforementioned most Christian and God-fearing Pippin, king of the Franks, in a detailed account in his apostolic reports, [Note: Codex Luc., “with cunning”;] [Note: Another reading, “with a report.”] adjuring him most earnestly and firmly, under the threat of the divine day of judgment, to fulfill everything that he had promised to blessed Peter. [Note: Codex Luc., “adjuring him under the day of divine judgment to fulfill everything that he had promised to blessed Peter.”]

In response, the most Christian Pippin, king of the Franks, moved by the fervor of faith, again raised a general expedition with God’s power and advanced into Lombard territory. [Note: Codex Luc., “he came, and likewise those below came,” for “joined.”] He utterly overthrew the Lombards’ passes. For when the aforementioned most Christian Pippin, king of the Franks, was approaching the aforementioned Lombard passes, imperial envoys arrived in this Roman city—namely Gregory, the *protosecretis*, [Note: Codex Luc., “*proto a secretis*,” and likewise below;] and John, the *silentiarius*, sent to the aforementioned king of the Franks. [Note: “The most blessed pope received them and announced to them the expedition of the aforementioned king of the Franks. The movement, or expedition, of an army was sometimes proclaimed by a military token. Ammianus, Book XXI: ‘By the token of the announced march he ordered them to proceed into Pannonia.’ The same author, Book XXIII: ‘Before spring had fully matured, having sent the expeditionary token through the military units, he ordered all to cross the Euphrates.’ More often the signal for marching was given by a trumpet. Curtius, Book III: ‘It was handed down by ancestral custom among the Persians that they should proceed only after sunrise, when the day was already bright. The signal was given from the king’s tent by a trumpet.’ The same author, Book V: ‘When he wished to move the camp, the trumpet gave the signal.’ And below: ‘During the third watch he proceeded in silence, without even the trumpet’s signal, along the route that had been indicated.’ ALTASERRA.]

The most blessed pope received them and announced to them the expedition of the aforementioned king of the Franks. They, however, considered it doubtful and did not believe it. The envoy of the apostolic see joined them, and he dismissed them to go to Francia. [Note: Mansi writes in the margin: “He released them, that is, dismissed them.”] Traveling by sea, they arrived as quickly as possible at Massilia. When they entered it, they learned that the aforementioned king of the Franks had already entered Lombard territory, in accordance with the exhortation of the aforementioned most blessed pope and the promise that he had made to blessed Peter under oath.

When the imperial envoys learned this, they became sad and tried deceitfully to detain the envoy of the apostolic see at Massilia, so that he would not hurry to the aforementioned king, afflicting him severely. [Note: Codex Luc., “very greatly.”]

But, through the intervention of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, their cunning trickery was brought to nothing. Accordingly, one of them, namely Gregory the *protosecretis*, went ahead of the envoy of the apostolic see and quickly caught up with the aforementioned king of the Franks. He found him in Lombard territory, not far from the city of Pavia. Entreating him earnestly and promising many things, he offered imperial gifts so that Pippin might grant Ravenna, or the other cities and fortresses of the same exarchate, to imperial rule. But he was utterly unable to incline the heart of the very firm aforementioned most Christian and benevolent faithful servant of God and lover of the apostle Peter, namely the aforementioned Pippin, king of the Franks, so that he would assign those cities and territories to imperial rule. [Note: Another reading: “The heart of the aforementioned Pippin, king of the Franks, was indeed unable to be inclined,” etc.]

That worshiper of God, the most gentle king, asserted that in no way could those cities be alienated from the power of blessed Peter, from the rights of the Roman Church, or from the pontiff of the apostolic see. He also affirmed under oath that he would never have undertaken this struggle at the urging of any human being, except for love of blessed Peter and remission of sins. He further declared that no abundance of treasure could persuade him to take away what he had once offered to blessed Peter. Having given this answer to the imperial envoy, he immediately dismissed him to return to his own people by another route; and the envoy reached Rome without accomplishing anything.

While the aforementioned benevolent Pippin, king of the Franks, was besieging and pressing the city of Pavia, Aistulf, the most savage king of the Lombards, declared that, if Pippin would grant him pardon and withdraw from the siege, he would in every way restore the cities, set down in the treaty, whose restoration he had previously scorned. After confirming again the earlier treaty that had been agreed between the parties during the preceding eighth indiction, [Note: “He restored the aforesaid cities. When Pippin learned of King Aistulf’s deceit, he burned with anger and grief and, by a new decree of war, ordered new levies among the peoples. Then he marched with his army against the Lombards, drove Aistulf into the Alpine defiles, and besieged him at Pavia. He refused ever to grant pardon to Aistulf, who begged it for the broken treaty, until Aistulf had handed over to the Roman pontiff Ravenna with the entire exarchate, the Pentapolis, and twenty cities included in those provinces. ‘He compelled Aistulf,’ says Anastasius, ‘to confirm the treaty that had been made between the parties during the preceding eighth indiction, and he sent the written donation to Rome, to Pope Stephen.’ This therefore occurred after August of the same year 755, when the ninth indiction began in September. When Pippin returned to Francia, he left in Italy Fulrad, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Denis, to receive from Aistulf the cities contained in the treaty and immediately transfer those received into the power of the Roman pontiff, as Anastasius relates. PAGIUS.]

he restored the aforesaid cities, adding also the fortress called Comiaclum. [Note: Codex Luc., “Comacium.”]

Of all these cities that he had recovered, he sent a written deed of donation to be possessed perpetually by blessed Peter, by the holy Roman Church, and by all the pontiffs of the apostolic see; it is still kept to this day in the archive of our holy Church. To receive these cities, that most Christian king of the Franks sent his counselor, namely the venerable abbot and priest Fulrad. Immediately [Note: In another manuscript, “his excellence” is absent. Instead of these words, Codex Luc. has “the king himself.”] his excellence returned happily with his armies to Francia.

The aforementioned venerable abbot and priest Fulrad, joining the territories of Ravenna with the envoys of the aforementioned King Aistulf, entered each of the cities of both the Pentapolis and Emilia, received them, took hostages from each one, and brought back with him the leading men together with the keys of the city gates. Thus he reached Rome.

[Note: 1. “He placed the keys both of the city of Ravenna and of the various cities of the exarchate of Ravenna, together with the donation concerning them issued by their king, in the confession of blessed Peter, and handed them over to that apostle, to his vicar the most holy pope, and to all his successor-pontiffs, to possess and administer perpetually. King Pippin of the Franks granted to Peter and his successors the exarchate of Ravenna, taken by arms from Aistulf, king of the Lombards, as a sign of donation, after depositing the keys over the confession—that is, the tomb—of blessed Peter. The handing over of the keys is a symbol of submission or donation. The Frankish Annals, under the year 800: ‘Aran the Saracen, prefect of Huesca, sent the keys of the city, together with other gifts, to the king, promising that he would surrender it.’ The prince of the city granted Capua to the emperor Basil through the presentation of golden keys. Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book I, chapter 39: ‘Since the prince of Capua, secretly favoring the emperor Basil of Constantinople, sent him golden keys, by these he handed over to the empire both himself and the city of Capua, indeed his entire principality.’ Charles the Great received the keys of the Jerusalem sepulcher from the patriarch as a token of blessing. Frankish Annals, under the year 801: ‘On the same day Zacharias the priest, whom the king had sent to Jerusalem, came to Rome with two monks whom the patriarch had sent with him to the king; for the sake of blessing they brought the keys of the Lord’s sepulcher and of the place of Calvary, together with a banner.’ ALTASERRA.

“2. ‘And the keys both of the city of Ravenna and of the various [cities],’ etc. Fulrad proceeded with Aistulf’s representatives into the exarchate and the Pentapolis. He received all the cities except Ferrara, Faenza, and certain others; taking hostages from each and bringing their leading men with him, he went to Rome and deposited the keys of each city, together with the tablets of the donation made by King Pippin, in the confession of Saint Peter. At Ravenna there can still be read on an ancient tablet the following inscription, reported by Papirius Masson, Book II:

PIPPIN THE PIOUS, THE FIRST, OPENED THE WAY FOR THE ENLARGEMENT OF THE CHURCH AND [THE EXARCHATE] OF RAVENNA, WITH ITS MOST EXTENSIVE . . . . . . . the remaining words are worn away.

But that inscription was placed long after Pippin’s death and after he had imitators, since it calls him the first to enlarge the Church. Nor do writers agree about what Pippin’s donation contained or which cities it included. For, besides the cities listed by Anastasius, Leo of Ostia, in *History of Monte Cassino*, Book I, chapter 7, extends the same donation within broader boundaries. Whatever the case may be, it seems certain—as Baronius’s annotator says—that from this time the Roman pontiffs exercised full administration in civil affairs, both at Rome and in the exarchate of Ravenna, except when they were occasionally hindered by rebellions. ‘For,’ he says, ‘from the time when Pippin granted the exarchate of Ravenna to the prince of the apostles and his successors, the Romans completely shook off the rule of the heretical emperor Constantine Copronymus, who was unable to defend them against the Lombards, and established a commonwealth whose head was called the Roman pontiff and whose defender and protector was called Pippin, king of the Franks.’ Hence, when Stephen II speaks in his letters of Aistulf and of the distress of the city of Rome, he nowhere mentions the emperor and calls the Romans his people, as may be seen in his letters 3, 4, and 6 to King Pippin. The same forms of speech are used by Pope Paul, Stephen’s successor, in letters 2 and 7 to Pippin, and by Hadrian I in letter 4 to Charles the Great, written in the year 775. Nor does it matter that in the subscriptions of those letters the pontiffs mention the years of the emperor Constantine. They are said to have been issued ‘in the reign of the most pious Lord Augustus Constantine, crowned by God, great emperor,’ in his thirty-second year or another year of that same emperor. Likewise, the Roman council of 743 is said to have been held in the second year of the emperor Artabasdus and the thirty-second year of King Liutprand; it does not follow from this that Rome was subject to Liutprand, king of the Lombards. The aforementioned Roman pontiffs therefore used those formulas at that time as chronological designations, which implied no subjection. PAGIUS.”]

He placed the keys both of the city of Ravenna and of the various cities of the exarchate of Ravenna, together with the aforementioned donation concerning them issued by their king, in the confession of blessed Peter, and handed them over to that apostle, to his vicar the most holy pope, and to all his successor-pontiffs, to possess and administer perpetually. [Note: “To possess and administer perpetually.” Before Stephen departed from King Pippin, he warned him that no trust should be placed either in the words or in the writings of the Lombard king and his people, since they would not have kept their promises if the Frankish army had returned across the Alps, unless the peace agreement were carried out. King Aistulf, writing from Rome, says: “With flattering words, persuasion, and oaths, he and his judges mocked your prudence, and you believed those who spoke falsely rather than us who asserted the truth” (Stephen II, Letter 3, to Pippin and his sons). And indeed, as the pontiff had predicted, so it happened. Once Aistulf was freed from fear and from the danger of losing his dominion, he deceived the commissioners whom Pippin had left in Italy to prevent him from seizing what belonged to others. As Stephen continues there, “he made void everything that he had promised through an oath to restore to blessed Peter through your envoys, and he was unwilling to return even a space of one palm’s breadth of land to blessed Peter.” Moreover, Aistulf, having led out a powerful army, besieged Rome and left undone no cruelty or impiety that he did not order to be perpetrated in the neighboring places. Therefore, in such desperate circumstances, the pontiff, lacking counsel, again turned to Pippin and the Frankish people and implored them to complete what they had promised: “What you promised would be offered to blessed Peter by donation, you must hand over to him for his possession” (the same author, Letters 3 and 4). Indeed, so that he might penetrate their hearts more deeply and obtain aid more quickly, he sent the Franks a letter written in the name of Saint Peter, in these words: ‘Through the word of evangelical preaching that we have received, your hope of future reward is surely joined to this apostolic Roman Church of God entrusted to us. Therefore I, Peter, apostle of God, who regard you as adopted sons, exhort and urge your love, calling upon all of you to rescue from the hands of adversaries this Roman city and the people entrusted to me by God, and also the house where I rest according to the flesh, and to deliver them from the contamination of the nations. I solemnly admonish you to free the Church of God entrusted to me by divine power, because they are suffering the greatest afflictions and oppressions from the most wicked people of the Lombards’ (the same author, Letter 5, to the Franks). Having heard this, Pippin crossed the Alps with great speed and besieged Ticinum a second time, so that he might recall Aistulf from the siege of the city and defend the royal seat. He did not return to Francia until he had seen everything fully accomplished. The rest is set out clearly enough by Anastasius. SOMMIER.”]

namely Ravenna, Ariminum, [Note: Another reading, “Pisaurum, Conca, Fanum,” etc.] Pisaurum, Fanum, Cesena, Senigallia, Jesi, [Note: Another reading, “Forum Populi, Forum Livii,” etc.] Forum Pompilii, Forum Livii, together with the fortress of Sussubium, [Note: Another reading, “Feletri, Mount Acerreagius, Mount Eucatus, Serra Castellum, Saint Marinus, Babium, Urbinum, Callis,” etc.] Mount Feretrus, Acerragius, Mount Lucarus, Serra, the fortress of Saint Marianus, Bobium, Urbinum, Callium, Luculi, [Note: “Eugubium or Comiaclum. Eugubium, today Comacchio, an episcopal city of Umbria, came to the apostolic see through Pippin’s donation together with the exarchate of Ravenna. Anastasius, in his account of Hadrian: ‘Or Comaclium of the exarchate of Ravenna.’ ALTASERRA.] Eugubium, or Comiaclum. He also handed over the city of Narni, which for many years had been seized from the duchy of Spoleto by the Roman side. [Note: Codex Luc., “by the duke of Spoleto.”]

While these things were taking place, that wretched Aistulf, going to a certain place for veneration, was struck by a divine blow and died. Then a certain Lombard duke named Desiderius, who had been sent by that most wicked Aistulf into the region of Tuscany, heard that Aistulf had died. He immediately gathered the entire multitude of the armies of Tuscany and tried to seize the throne of the Lombard kingdom.

Radechisus, formerly king and afterward a monk, the brother of the aforementioned Aistulf, despised his person; [Note: Codex Luc., “Rachia”; another reading, “Ratchis.”] and many other Lombard nobles joined him. Despising Desiderius, they gathered a great force from across the Alps, as well as the remaining multitude of the Lombard armies, and set out to fight against him.

[Note: “In response, the aforementioned Desiderius,” etc. After Aistulf, king of the Lombards, died in the year 756, Pope Stephen suppressed the disturbances that had arisen among the Lombards over the succession. He helped Desiderius, duke of Tuscany, obtain the kingdom, concluding a treaty with him and securing Frankish assistance for him on the condition that he restore to the Roman Church the cities that Aistulf had retained in violation of the treaty until his death and that were included in Pippin’s donation, as Anastasius the Librarian testifies. These cities were Faenza, [Col. 0994C] Imola, and Ferrara with their territories; Auximum, Ancona, and Humana with their territories; and Bologna, as is clear from Stephen’s letters to King Pippin on this matter, sent through Abbot Fulrad, Bishop George, and John the *sacellarius*. In them he asked Pippin to enter into friendship and a peace treaty with Desiderius once Desiderius had fulfilled his promises. Stephen, however, recovered only the duchy of Ferrara, while King Desiderius retained the other cities contrary to his promises. PAGIUS.]

In response, the aforementioned Desiderius earnestly entreated the aforementioned most blessed pontiff to bring him aid, so that he might be able to assume the royal dignity, promising under oath to fulfill the entire will of the aforementioned most blessed pontiff. He also declared that he would restore to the commonwealth the cities that remained, and indeed would give abundant gifts.

Then that distinguished Father and good shepherd, after consulting with the often-mentioned venerable priest and abbot Fulrad, counselor of the most Christian Pippin, king of the Franks, sent his own brother, namely the deacon Paul, and his counselor Christopher, together with the aforementioned Fulrad, into the territory of Tuscany to the aforementioned Desiderius. Speaking with him, Desiderius immediately declared in writing, under a terrible oath, that he would fulfill the entire promise set out above.

After this had been accomplished, he immediately sent his envoy, namely the venerable priest Stephen, with apostolic letters of exhortation, to the aforementioned Radechisus and to the entire Lombard people. The aforementioned venerable Fulrad also hurried to the aid of Desiderius with some Franks. He arranged that, if necessity required it, many Roman forces would come to his assistance. [Note: Codex Luc., “to meet him.”] Through the support of the acceptable prayers of the aforementioned most holy pontiff, God so disposed all things that, without any loss of life, the aforementioned Desiderius, through the intervention of the aforementioned angelic fellow-pope, assumed the royal dignity that he desired. [Note: Codex Luc., “through his consent; Rachis, however, returned to the monastery.”]

While these things were taking place, the most holy pontiff sent his envoy and recovered from those cities that the aforementioned King Desiderius had promised to restore to the same blessed pope, namely Faenza with the fortress of Tiberiacum, or Gabellum, and the entire duchy of Ferrara.

With God’s approval, he enlarged the commonwealth and, like a good shepherd laying down his life, rescued the entire people of the Lord—namely the rational sheep entrusted to him—from all the snares of their enemies. Completing his course and accomplishing everything beneficially, he ended his life at God’s summons and departed to eternal rest.

He performed one ordination in the month of March: eleven priests, two deacons, and twenty bishops in various places. [Note: Another reading: “two priests, two deacons, and four bishops in various places.”] The see was vacant for thirty-five days. [Note: Another reading: “twenty-two days.”] He was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, in the tenth indiction. [Note: This repetition is absent in another manuscript.] The see was vacant for thirty-two days.

[Col. 0993]

## Letters and Decrees of Stephen II, Roman Pontiff

*(Mansi, Conciliar Collection, volume XII.)*

### First Letter of Stephen II to Pippin, King of the Franks

He gives thanks for the promises conveyed by Abbot Droctegang, whom Pippin had sent to Pope Stephen after Stephen had indicated that he wished to come to Francia.

[Col. 0993D]

To the most excellent lord, his son King Pippin: Pope Stephen.

The present Abbot Droctegang, having been presented before the sacred thresholds of your protector, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and before our eyes, conveyed the words of greeting and well-being imposed upon him from your excellence, preserved by God and most dearly loved. Therefore, having become joyful, we have given countless thanks to almighty God, asking his divine mercy—although we are sinners and unworthy—that in his goodness he protect you, most excellent son, and confirm your kingdom ever more fully and perfectly in his fear and in apostolic love, so that you may enjoy the present life in lasting happiness and may deserve to become a sharer in eternal blessedness through the fruit of apostolic love.

For the present Droctegang, your faithful envoy, according to what he said to us, we have sent back through him an appropriate response, orally entrusting to him what was fitting for your most exalted goodness. Command, son, that he be believed in all things, because in everything that you commanded, with Christ’s cooperation, we gave him salutary instructions for you.

But fulfill the Lord’s saying, as it is written: “For whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10). For from this you will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.

We ask this of you, son: when you order your envoys to be sent back to us with their responses, command that this John, a religious man, be sent with them. He is your faithful servant and reports responses prudently.

Farewell.

### Letter II of Pope Stephen II to the Nobles of the Franks

That they should support his petition before King Pippin and offer him their assistance in undertaking the cause of the Church.

Stephen, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to all the glorious men, our sons, the dukes of the Frankish people.

Joyfully the holy mother Church rejoices in the advancement of her faithful sons. Therefore, although absent in body but present in spirit, we greet your glorious prudence and affection, most exalted sons, embracing you as though present in person with the kiss of peace, saying: “Do good, O Lord, to those who are good and upright in heart” (Psalm 124). For we have confidence that you fear God, love your protector, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and will be cooperators and helpers with the whole devotion of your hearts in accomplishing his interests through our supplication. Be assured that, for the struggle you undertake on behalf of his holy Church, your spiritual mother, your sins will be forgiven by that same prince of the apostles; and in return for the course of your labor you will receive a hundredfold from the hand of God and possess eternal life.

For this reason we beseech and adjure your most wise charity, by God and by our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the future day of judgment, on which we shall all render an account before the tribunal of the eternal Judge for our deeds, that no pretext intervene to prevent you from helping our son Pippin, the most excellent king preserved by God, to accomplish the interests of your patron, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, as we have communicated through the present Droctegangus, a religious abbot, and his companions. Thus, when you join your efforts to ours and our supplication has been fulfilled, may your sins be blotted out by the generosity of that prince of the apostles, whose cause this is; and may he, possessing the authority granted him by God, as bearer of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, open the door for you and lead you into eternal life.

But attend, sons, and labor with the greatest diligence to share in what we have desired, knowing that if anyone turns aside in another direction, he will be excluded from the inheritance of eternal blessedness. For it is written: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10). “For those who love God, all things work together for good” (Romans 8).

Farewell.

## LETTER III. POPE STEPHEN II TO PIPPIN AND HIS SONS, THE KINGS

While Aistulf delays restoring the cities and harasses the Church with fresh attacks, he implores the king to bring aid and earnestly seeks that he fulfill in reality the donation promised to blessed Peter.

To our most excellent lords and sons, Pippin the king and our spiritual co-father, and likewise Charles and Carloman, also kings and both patricians of the Romans, Pope Stephen.

The prophetic assertion of the prudent and most wise Solomon is reported as follows: “A good name is better than mercy” (Ecclesiasticus 7). A good name, indeed, consists in guarding with an unstained heart and a pure conscience the faith that one has promised, and fulfilling it by one’s deeds. A good name consists in striving with all one’s strength for the exaltation of the holy Church of God, through which the salvation of Christians exists. A good name concerning you had gone forth among all nations, if it had been fulfilled by deeds.

For our merciful and greatly compassionate Redeemer, the Lord, is propitious toward those whom he recognizes as entirely faithful to and defenders of his holy Church with complete integrity of mind. What reward or payment under heaven can be considered or compared with that which must be rendered for the defense of God’s Church and the house of blessed Peter?

For this reason the same King of kings and Lord of lords established your most excellent goodness, protected by God, as rulers over crowds of peoples and many nations, so that through you the holy Church of God might be exalted. He could have vindicated his holy Church and demanded justice for his prince of the apostles in another way, as it pleased him; but because he wished to test your mind and conscience, spiritual co-father protected by God, and most beloved sons, he therefore commanded our wretchedness to come to you.

We entrusted our body and soul to great labors upon a broad road and into a distant province, placing great confidence in your faith. At God’s command we set out, afflicted by snow and cold, heat and floods, powerful rivers and most savage mountains, as well as by various dangers. Indeed, when we were presented before your honey-sweet eyes, we commended all the affairs of the prince of the apostles into your hands, since, inspired by God, you deigned to lend an ear to our petitions. You promised blessed Peter that you would exact his justice and provide for the defense of the holy Church of God; and, as truly faithful men of God, you hastened to fight with pure mind for the defense of God’s Church.
