But the almighty Lord, who “puts an end to wars from the beginning,” who humbles the proud and exalts the humble, immediately demonstrated the justice of blessed Peter to your goodness and to all Christians, and displayed such a resplendent miracle that it is altogether glorious to recount. Those enemies of God and of the holy Church who trusted in their ferocity, whose feet were swift to shed blood, attacked your small number of troops; and the almighty Lord, through the hand of blessed Peter, deigned to grant you victory, so that those who had been innumerable were slain by a few men.

Those enemies of blessed Peter were humbled to the ground, and through the intercessions of blessed Peter the Lord cast such fear and trembling into them that they were reduced to nothing. For it is not a human sword but the sword of God that fights.

When the wicked King Aistulf saw his own deception, his judges—destroyed by God along with him—mocked your prudence with flattering speeches, persuasions, and oaths; and you believed them more when they spoke falsehoods than us when we asserted the truth. Our heart, most excellent sons, was filled with great sorrow and sadness because your goodness was unwilling to listen to us.

Everything that we told you at God’s command we declared truthfully, and it has now been exposed, as the deeds themselves show. For, just as we first told your Christian selves, the wicked King Aistulf, after the treacherous devil entered his heart, rendered void everything that he had promised through an oath to restore to blessed Peter by means of your envoys, and he was unwilling to return to blessed Peter even a span of land.

From the day on which we departed from your honey-sweet goodness, he seemed to afflict and trouble us so greatly that no human mouth can recount it. He appeared to hold the holy Church of God, our humility, and your envoys in the greatest contempt; indeed, evil commands and orders were issued even to take our own life.

Why say more? He troubled us so greatly that, if it may be said, the very stones themselves would weep for us. Yet your counselor Fulrad, priest and abbot, together with his companions, if they have God before their eyes, can relate everything to you. For not only was he unwilling to return the property of blessed Peter as he had determined; by his command he also neither ceased nor ceases to commit plunder, raids, and devastation in the cities and places belonging to blessed Peter.

He has forgotten the God who made him and has transgressed the Christian faith. How can he—or those who agreed with him—be trusted any longer, when they made so many solemn promises concerning the mysteries of God and refused to keep them? Truly, we foretold to you everything concerning the falsehood and deceit of that impious king; and, just as we said, these things are now manifest to you, and his perjury has been revealed.

Therefore I ask you, most excellent sons protected by God, and I earnestly beseech you: let the holy Church of God and the cause of blessed Peter grieve you; and what you promised would be offered to blessed Peter by donation, you must hand over to him for his possession. Remember, and hold firmly always in your hearts what you promised to that same doorkeeper of the kingdom of heaven.

Let no persuasion or acquittance deceive you now. Consider how powerful an exactor that same prince of the apostles, blessed Peter, is. Look upon everything that you promised him and pledged to offer by donation, and hasten to hand it over, lest you mourn forever and remain condemned in the life to come.

The life of this world is short; it declines like a shadow and grows old like a garment. Seek with your whole mind and an undivided heart that eternal life which blessed Peter promised you on account of his cause and justice. Strive to complete the good work that you began, and hasten to return to your protector, blessed Peter, what you confirmed by your own hand in the donation, for it is written: “It is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill the vow” (Ecclesiastes 5).

Know that, just as a legal deed, the prince of the apostles holds your donation firmly, and it is necessary for you to fulfill that deed. Otherwise, when the just Judge comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire, at the future judgment that same prince of the apostles may display that deed and, finding it to have no force, compel you to render a strict account with him.

Rather, fulfill quickly what you promised, so that you may again possess the eternal life that you have received as a promise from that prince of the apostles.

I adjure you, most excellent sons protected by God, by almighty God, who contains all things by his power; by his holy mother, the glorious ever-virgin Mary, our Lady; by the powers of heaven; by the blessed princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul; and by the dreadful day of judgment, when we shall all be compelled to stand and render an account of our deeds, where no clever excuse exists: quickly and without any impediment return to blessed Peter, through your donation, the cities and places, and all the hostages and captives—or everything contained in that donation. For this reason the Lord, through my humility and through blessed Peter, anointed you as kings: so that through you his holy Church might be exalted and the prince of the apostles might receive his justice.

We had a great desire in our heart to behold your honey-sweet faces and rejoice in the joy of your happiness, according to what the most wise Solomon says: “Through the streets and squares I sought the one whom my soul loves” (Song of Songs 3). And certainly, those whom we loved we found by God’s command, and those whom we desired we embraced. For this reason the blessing and grace of blessed Peter have been poured out upon you, as the Lord had ordained.

What none of your parents deserved to receive, you have received; and the prince of the apostles, making you his special possessions above other kings and nations, has entrusted all his affairs to you. You will render an account to God of how you have fought for the justice of that doorkeeper of the kingdom of heaven.

All our people of the Roman commonwealth are afflicted with us by great sorrow and bitterest tears, because, while we hastened to so long and distant a province, our flesh was diminished by the exertion of the arduous journey; and thus we returned empty and fruitless, without the outcome of justice. Nevertheless, in accordance with the Lord’s command, we wretched men acted and commended all the affairs of blessed Peter to you. The matter belongs to you, whether for sin or for reward.

All nations had firmly held that blessed Peter would now obtain his justice through your powerful arm, but it did not happen, and everyone was struck with great astonishment of heart at this. Yet I ask your most excellent goodness to remove this reproach from the nations and demonstrate your faith to all by your deeds, since, as it is written, faith without works is useless.

With what confidence or strength can you go forth to overcome your enemies if you do not complete the justice of blessed Peter, as you promised and began? For if you fulfill by deeds what you began, you will always be victorious and most powerful over your enemies; you will possess the present kingdom for many years with a good reputation, and you will receive eternal life.

For so great a task we have sent to you Willarius, a most reverend and holy brother, our fellow bishop and faithful servant, who will relate to you with his own mouth everything concerning our tribulation and the cause of blessed Peter. Command that you believe him in all things and bring the cause of blessed Peter to a good conclusion.

May heavenly grace preserve your excellent person in safety.

## LETTER IV. POPE STEPHEN II TO KING PIPPIN

With the city of Rome besieged by Aistulf and the Lombards, he writes tearful letters in which he again implores Pippin for aid with every possible entreaty.

To our most excellent lord and son, and our spiritual co-father, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Stephen.

We believe that even the forms of all the elements themselves could recount how much we are surrounded by grievous and most bitter sorrow, how greatly we are constrained by anxiety and distress, and how many tears our streaming eyes pour out as evils continually multiply. For who, witnessing these tribulations, would not mourn? Who, hearing of these calamities that cling to us, would not howl?

Therefore we speak the words of the chaste Susanna, a good woman: “Distress surrounds us on every side, and we do not know what to do” (Daniel 13–14). O most excellent and most Christian son, would that the almighty Lord, creator of all things, just as in former times he sent the prophet Habakkuk, carried by an angel in sudden flight, to refresh and console Daniel, the pre-eminent prophet, hidden in the lions’ den, had likewise now, if it may be said, made your excellence, preserved by God, present for even one hour, so that you might behold the grievous and mournful distress and tribulations that we are suffering most cruelly from the Lombard people and their wicked king!

Behold, days of distress have come upon us; the days of weeping and bitterness, days of anxiety, groaning, and sorrow are at hand. For what we feared has happened, and what we dreaded has occurred. Therefore, distressed, afflicted, oppressed, and surrounded on every side by the most wicked King Aistulf and the Lombard people, with tears poured out and our breasts beaten, we beseech the Lord with the prophet and say: “Help us, O God our Savior, and for the honor of your name deliver us” (Psalm 78). And again: “Take hold of arms and shield and rise to our assistance. Lord, judge those who harm us and fight against those who fight against us” (Psalm 34).

Although we seem to have often made our tribulations known to your goodness, now also, compelled by great danger, we have resolved to report with mourning and groaning the perils and evils that we have suffered from that arrogant king and his Lombard people.

We believe that everything is already known to your nobility, most Christian and excellent son and spiritual co-father: how the treaties of peace were broken by the impious King Aistulf and his people, and how we were unable to obtain anything according to what he had determined and confirmed by the bond of an oath. Since no improvement has been made for us—in fact, after the desolation of our entire province and the many murders committed by that people—we ask you also to recognize what we say with great tears and sorrow of heart, most excellent son and spiritual co-father.

On the very Kalends of January, the entire army of Aistulf, king of the Lombards, came together from the regions of Tuscany against this city of Rome and encamped beside the gates of blessed Peter, blessed Pancratius, and the Portuensian Gate. Aistulf himself, with other armies, joined them from another side and pitched his tents beside the Salarian Gate and the other gates. He sent word to us, saying:

“Open the Salarian Gate for me and I will enter the city. Hand over your bishop to me, and I will have compassion on you. Otherwise, I will overthrow the walls, kill you all with one sword, and see who can rescue you from my hands.”

All the Beneventans as well assembled against this city of Rome and encamped beside the gate of blessed Paul the apostle and the other gates of this Roman city. They consumed all the estates outside the city, far and wide, with sword and fire; burning every house, they destroyed them almost to their foundations.

They set fire to the churches of God and, casting the most sacred images of the saints into the flames, destroyed them with their swords. They put the holy gifts—that is, the body of our Lord Jesus Christ—into their polluted vessels, which they call bellows, and, having stuffed themselves with an abundance of meat, ate those same gifts.

They removed the altar cloths and all the ornaments of the churches of God—an act too cruel to describe—and used them for their own purposes. They beat the servants of God, the monks who lived in monasteries for the divine office, with terrible blows and tore many of them to pieces. They dragged away and violated holy women and recluses who, from childhood and the time of puberty, had devoted themselves to enclosure for the love of God; indeed, even in the very act of violation they appear to have killed others [reading uncertain].

They burned with fire all the cultivated houses belonging to blessed Peter, and, as has been said, burning the houses of all the Romans, they utterly destroyed those outside the city. They carried away all the livestock, cut down the vineyards almost to their roots, and, trampling the crops, completely devoured them.

No hope of living remained either for the house of our holy Church or for anyone residing in this Roman city, because, as has been said, they consumed everything with sword and fire and killed many people. They slaughtered the numerous household of blessed Peter and of all the Romans, men and women alike, and led many others away captive.

The impious Lombards even separated innocent infants from their mothers’ breasts, violated them by force, and killed them. They committed such evils in this Roman city as pagan peoples certainly never perpetrated; indeed, if it may be said, the very stones themselves, seeing our desolation, howl with us.

For fifty-five days they besieged and surrounded this afflicted Roman city on every side and, day and night, with the worst fury, incessantly waged fierce battles against us at the walls of this Roman city. They did not cease attacking us, so that, if God should avert it, the wicked Aistulf might subject us all to his power and kill us with one sword.

They tauntingly declared to us: “Behold, you are surrounded by us, and you will not escape our hands. Let the Franks come now and rescue you from our hands!”

They also took the city of Narni, which your Christianity had granted to blessed Peter, and seized some of our cities. Therefore, constrained by necessity and with the greatest ingenuity, we were scarcely able to send these present letters and our envoys to your most excellent Christian self by sea. We wrote them with great tears.

Indeed, with truth as our witness, we say that each letter expressed tears mixed with blood. Would that the Lord might grant that, at the hour when you read our mournful appeal, tears filled with blood might flow before your presence from every letter!

Therefore, most excellent son and spiritual co-father, I ask you—and as though personally present I throw myself upon the ground and prostrate myself at your feet, adjuring you in the presence of the divine mysteries—before the living and true God and his prince of the apostles, blessed Peter, to come to our aid with utmost haste and the greatest speed, lest we perish. For, after the Lord, we have entrusted the souls of all of us Romans into your hands.

Do not abandon us; then may the Lord not abandon you in all your actions and works. Do not despise us; then may the Lord not despise you when you call upon his power. Do not withdraw your help from us, most Christian son and spiritual co-father; then may the Lord not withdraw his help and protection from you and your people when you enter battle against your enemies.

Help us and assist us with great speed, most Christian one; then may you receive help from almighty God, who through the institution of blessed Peter anointed you king over the crowds of peoples.

Come, come, son, and help us before the sword of our enemies reaches our heart. I ask you: do not let us perish, lest the nations throughout the whole world say: “Where is the confidence that the Romans had, after the Lord, in the kings of the Franks?”

Do not allow us to perish, and do not delay or postpone bringing us comfort; do not separate us from your help. Then may you not be alienated from the kingdom of God or separated from your most beloved wife, the most excellent queen and our spiritual co-mother.

Do not allow us any longer to be anxious, endangered, and to persevere in mourning and weeping, good and most excellent son and spiritual co-father; then may mourning not come upon you because of your and my most beloved sons, the lords Charles and Carloman, most excellent kings and patricians.

Do not harden your ear against hearing us, and do not turn your face away from us, lest we be put to shame in our petitions and perish to the end. Then may the Lord not harden his ear against hearing your prayers or turn his face away from you on that future day of judgment, when, together with blessed Peter and his other apostles, he will sit to judge every rank, every sex, every human power, and the world by fire. And may it not be said to you—may the Godhead avert it—“I do not know you, because you did not help the Church of God or take care to defend his special people in danger.”

Hear me, son, hear me, and help us. Behold, the time to save us is here. Save us before we perish, most Christian king. For what is better or more honorable than to save those who are in danger and distress? For it is written: “The one who saves is like one who builds” (Isaiah 1).

Therefore the pre-eminent prophet Isaiah says: “Assist the oppressed.” All the nations situated around you, which through God’s power have taken refuge in your most powerful Frankish people, have been saved. Although you do not hesitate to grant assistance to all nations and they are saved through you, you ought much more to free the holy Church of God and its people from the attack of their enemies.

O how great was the confidence in our heart when we were privileged to behold your honey-sweet face and were bound and joined to you in the bond of charity, expecting to remain in great peace and security! But when we were separated from you and ceased to see the light, darkness broke forth, and our final state became worse than the first.

Consider, son, consider, and reflect most carefully—I adjure you by the living God—for the souls of us and of all the Roman people, after God and his prince of the apostles, depend upon your excellence, protected by God, and upon the Frankish people entrusted to you by God. For, as has been said, we have placed our souls in your bosom. And if it should happen—God forbid, and may divine mercy avert it—that we perish, weigh, I beseech you, and consider in every way to whose soul this will be reckoned as sin.

Believe this completely, most Christian one: if any calamity should befall us—God forbid that we perish—you, protected by God and most beloved by us, will render an account for everything before the tribunal of God, together with all your judges. For, as has been said, we have entrusted the holy Church of God and the people of our Roman commonwealth to no one else but your most loving excellence, your most beloved sons, and the entire Frankish people, by God’s command and that of blessed Peter, for their protection.

Behold, we have made all our griefs, anxieties, and distresses known to your goodness, protected by God. You, most excellent son and spiritual co-father, act and, after the Lord, free those who have taken refuge in you, so that, bearing good fruit, you may deserve on the day of future judgment to say:

“My lord, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, behold, I am your humble servant. Having completed my course and kept faith with you, I have defended and liberated the Church entrusted to you by heavenly mercy from the hands of its persecutors. Standing undefiled before you, I offer you the children whom you entrusted to me to rescue from the hands of the enemies, now safe and unharmed.”

Then, while holding the government of the kingdom in the present life and reigning with Christ in the world to come, may you deserve to obtain the joys of heavenly rewards, hearing that desirable paternal voice which says: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25).

May heavenly grace preserve your excellence in safety.

## EMBOLUM

We have sent with the greatest urgency to your most Christian excellence our present envoy, George, our most reverend and holy brother and fellow bishop, together with Warneharius, a religious abbot and your envoy, as well as Thomaricus and the count, likewise our distinguished envoys. They will relate to you by word of mouth, with a precise account, all our sufferings and the entire desolation that we have suffered and continually suffer from the Lombard people and their arrogant king, just as they saw them with their own eyes.

Command that your most Christian excellence believe them in all things as you would believe ourselves, and hasten greatly to secure our liberation. And I adjure you, son protected by God and spiritual co-father, by the living and true God, never again to disbelieve our sufferings or in any way neglect to free us. Otherwise, if—God forbid—you delay believing us further and neglect to rescue us, calamity and destruction may fall upon us, and this may bring you great loss, sin, and condemnation in the present and eternal life, because we have entrusted you with the souls of all of us Romans.

Rather, as has been said, we adjure you again and again, most excellent son and spiritual co-father preserved by God, by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the undivided Trinity, to command that our tribulations, distresses, sufferings, and desolations be believed without any doubt, to help us for God’s sake, and to hasten with the greatest speed to free us from the hands of our enemies, the Lombards.

Thus, bearing abundant fruit, may you become victorious over all barbarian nations through the intercession of blessed Peter and possess eternal life.

The aforementioned abbot Warneharius, out of love for blessed Peter, put on a coat of mail and kept watch day and night upon the walls of this afflicted Roman city; and for the defense and liberation of all of us Romans he fought with all his strength as a good athlete of Christ.

## LETTER V. POPE STEPHEN II TO THE FRANKS

It was sent under the name of the apostle Peter and Stephen to the same people for aid against the Lombards.

Peter, called an apostle by Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, who, reigning with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit before all ages, in the last times was incarnate and became human for the salvation of us all, redeemed us with his precious blood according to the will of the Father’s glory, just as he appointed through his holy prophets in the sacred Scriptures—and, through me, the whole catholic and apostolic Roman Church of God, head of all the Churches of God, founded upon the firm rock through the blood of that same Redeemer of ours—and Stephen, bishop of that same nourishing Church: may grace, peace, and power be more fully bestowed by the Lord your God for the rescue of that same holy Church of God and its Roman people entrusted to me from the hands of their persecutors, upon you, the most excellent men Pippin, Charles, and Carloman, the three kings, and upon the most holy bishops, abbots, priests, and all religious monks, as well as the dukes, counts, all the assembled armies, and the people residing in Francia.

I, Peter the apostle, when I was called by Christ, the Son of the living God, at the decree of heavenly mercy, was appointed by him as the illuminator of the whole world through his power, while our Lord God himself confirmed it: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 2, as printed); and again: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven” (John 20). And, commending his sheep to me, his lowly servant and called apostle, individually, he said: “Feed my sheep; feed my lambs” (John 21). And again: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16).

Therefore, let all who, hearing my preaching, have fulfilled it believe with certainty that by God’s command their sins are released in this world, and that they will proceed cleansed and without blemish into that life.

For [because] the illumination of the Holy Spirit has shone forth in your resplendent hearts, and through receiving the word of evangelical preaching you have become lovers of the holy and unique Trinity, surely in this apostolic Roman Church of God entrusted to us the hope of your future reward is joined with us.

Therefore I, Peter the apostle of God, who regard you as adopted sons, exhort you all and earnestly admonish you to defend from the hands of adversaries this Roman city and the people entrusted to me by God, and also to rescue from the pollution of the nations the house where I rest according to the flesh. I urge you to liberate the Church of God entrusted to me by divine power, and I solemnly admonish you because they are suffering the greatest afflictions and oppressions from the worst people, the Lombards.

Do not understand this otherwise, beloved ones; but confidently believe that I myself stand alive before you as though in the flesh, and through this exhortation bind and compel you with powerful adjurations. For, according to the promise that we received from that same Lord God and our Redeemer, we regard all you peoples of the Franks as special among all nations.

Therefore I solemnly admonish and warn you, as though in a symbolic charge, and with a firm obligation I adjure you, most Christian kings Pippin, Charles, and Carloman, and all priests, bishops, abbots, presbyters, and all religious monks, as well as all judges; likewise the dukes, counts, the entire people of the Frankish kingdom, and, as though alive in the flesh and standing bodily before you, I, Peter the apostle of God, address you. Believe firmly that this word of exhortation addresses you: although I am absent in the flesh, I am not absent from you in spirit. For it is written: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet receives a prophet’s reward” (Matthew 10).

Moreover, our Lady, Mary, the mother of God, ever-virgin, solemnly adjures, warns, and commands you together with us by great obligations. So too do the thrones, dominions, and the entire army of the heavenly host, as well as the martyrs and confessors of Christ and all who are pleasing to God. All these, joining us in exhorting and adjuring you, solemnly charge you to grieve for this Roman city entrusted to us by the Lord God and for the Lord’s sheep dwelling in it, and also for the holy Church of God entrusted to me by the Lord.

Defend and liberate it with the greatest haste from the hands of the Lombard persecutors. Do not—God forbid—allow my body, which suffered torments for the Lord Jesus Christ, or my house, where by God’s command it rests, to be polluted by them; and do not allow my special people to be further torn apart or slaughtered by that Lombard people, who are guilty of such great wickedness in their perjury and are proved to be transgressors of the divine Scriptures.

Therefore provide my Roman people, entrusted to me by God—your brothers in this life—with support through the Lord’s cooperation and with all your strength. Thus I, Peter, called the apostle of God, will provide you with reciprocal patronage in this life and on the day of future judgment; I will prepare for you in the kingdom of God bright and splendid tabernacles and, promising you the joys of the infinite paradise and the rewards of eternal recompense, will grant them to you in return—provided that you swiftly defend my special people and my Roman city, your Roman brothers, from the hands of the wicked Lombards.

Run, I exhort and adjure you by the living and true God. Run and come to the aid of the cause before the living fountain from which you were consecrated and reborn dries up; before that small ember remaining from the most blazing flame, from which you came to know your light, is extinguished; before your spiritual mother, the holy Church of God, in which you hope to receive eternal life, is humbled, invaded, violated, and polluted by the impious.

I adjure you, my dearest adopted sons—I adjure you by the grace of the Holy Spirit—and, in the presence of the exceedingly terrible God, creator of all, I, Peter the apostle of God, [Col. 1006B] exhort and admonish you, together with the holy Catholic and apostolic Church of God, which the Lord entrusted to me: do not allow this Roman city, in which the Lord established my body, which he also entrusted to me and appointed as the foundation of faith, to perish. Liberate it and its Roman people, your brothers, and by no means allow them to be invaded by the Lombard nation. For in this way your provinces and possessions have been invaded by peoples whom you do not know. Do not separate yourselves from my Roman people, lest you likewise be strangers to or separated from the kingdom of God and eternal life. Whatever you ask of me, I will come to your aid and offer you protection. Come to the aid of my Roman people, your brothers, and fight with greater resolve; bring your struggle to an end [Col. 1006C] [devote yourselves] to their liberation. For no one receives a crown except the one who has fought lawfully; fight bravely for the liberation of the holy Church of God, lest you perish forever.

I adjure you, as has been said, dearest sons, by the living God, and I solemnly charge you: do not permit this Roman city of mine, and the people dwelling in it, to be further torn apart by the Lombard nation, lest your bodies and souls also be torn and tortured in the eternal and unquenchable Tartarean fire with the devil and his pestilential angels; and lest the sheep of the Lord’s flock, entrusted by God—namely, the Roman people—be scattered any further, lest the Lord scatter and cast you away as the Israelite people was scattered [Col. 1006D].

For it has been declared that, among all the peoples beneath heaven, your Frankish nation has been and is first in relation to the apostle of God, Peter; therefore I entrusted to you, through the hands of my vicar, the Church which the Lord committed to me, so that you might rescue it from the hands of its enemies. Hold firmly to this: I, the servant of God called the apostle, have assisted all your needs when you recently prayed, and by God’s power I granted you victory over your enemies; and I will grant it hereafter as well—believe this—if you hasten with the utmost speed to liberate this Roman city of mine. Remember also how, when the enemies of the holy Church of God began battle against you, I caused them to be overthrown by you, who were few in number compared with them [Col. 1007A]. Therefore fight to fulfill this admonition of mine swiftly, so that you may more fully deserve to obtain my assistance through the grace given to me by Christ our Lord.

Behold, dearest sons, I have admonished you by preaching. If you obey quickly, it will bring you great reward, and you will be aided by my intercessions; in the present life you will overcome all your enemies, and, living long, you will eat the good things of the earth and without doubt enjoy eternal life. But if, which we do not believe, you cause any delay or devise any pretext and do not hasten to fulfill this exhortation of ours—to liberate this Roman city of mine and the people dwelling in it, the holy apostolic Church of God entrusted to me by the Lord [Col. 1007B]—know that, by the authority of the holy and unique Trinity and through the grace of the apostolate given to me by Christ our Lord, you will be alienated from the kingdom of God and eternal life for transgressing our admonition.

But may God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who redeemed us with his precious blood and led us to the light of truth, and who made us preachers and illuminators of the whole world, grant you to think, understand, and arrange these matters with the greatest speed, so that you may come more quickly to rescue this Roman city and its people, as well as the holy Church of God entrusted to me by God. May he mercifully command that, as faithful servants of his power, with my intercessions on your behalf, he preserve you in the present life long-lived, safe, and victorious [Col. 1007C], and in the age to come make you more abundantly worthy to receive the gifts of his recompense with his saints and elect. Farewell.

## LETTER VI. OF POPE STEPHEN II TO KING PIPPIN

He gives thanks for the liberation of the city and for the benefit conferred upon the Roman Church. Concerning the death of King Aistulf and his successor Desiderius. He asks that he order Desiderius to restore, in accordance with the faith he had given, the remaining cities of the exarchate and the Pentapolis that had not yet been returned. Sent through the envoys Bishop George and John the sacellarius.

To the most excellent lord, our spiritual fellow-father, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans: Stephen, pope.

We cannot express with our tongue, most excellent son, how much we rejoice in your deed and in your life [Col. 1007D]. In our own days we have indeed seen miracles accomplished by divine power: through your excellence, the holy Roman Church, mother and head of all the Churches of God and foundation of the Christian faith, which had been lamenting under the attacks and dangers of the enemy, has now been transferred and firmly established in a great solidity of joy, and the sorrowing souls of Christians have been raised to the greatest gladness by your most powerful protection.

For this, in view of your deed and our exultation, we gladly cry out with the angels: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II). And because last year, at this very season, we were grievously wounded by the enemy’s devastating assault and surrounded on every side [Col. 1008A], whereas now, rescued by your most powerful aid from the dangers threatening us, we rejoice with immeasurable joy, blessing the name of the Lord and saying with the Psalmist in harmonious voice: “This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm LXXVI). And again: “In the evening weeping will remain, but in the morning there will be joy” (Psalm XXIX).

What breast, even one of stone, would not immediately melt into praise of almighty God and love for your excellence upon learning of such a benevolent deed accomplished by your renowned goodness? I confess, most excellent son and spiritual fellow-father, that I often delight in recounting to peoples gathered from every region of the world the wondrous things accomplished through you, often marveling together with them and unceasingly proclaiming, with extended and honeyed voice, the praises of your excellence [Col. 1008B]. These things often awaken me even at the very moments of the hours, and with an unwavering gaze I pour out prayers to almighty God for the immense goodness of yourself and the safety of the entire Frankish people.

Finally, most beloved and God-inspired king, victorious, fortunate, and exceedingly strong through divine providence, your life itself plainly testifies to all how blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, received the devotion you showed by fighting on his behalf. For it is written: “The vows of the righteous are pleasing” (Proverbs XV). It is altogether fitting, most excellent son, to offer great praises of thanksgiving to your goodness and, glorifying the name of the Lord for such immense benevolence, to sing with joyful voice: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, for in visiting his people and desiring to bring redemption to his people, he has raised up for us, in our days, a most powerful liberator, most Christian victor” [Col. 1008C].

What else should I call you but a new Moses, and what else should I declare you to be but a radiant King David? For just as they liberated the people of God from the oppressions of the Philistines, so you also, victor blessed by God and most powerful king, have striven through your struggle to rescue the Church of God and its afflicted people from the assaults of the enemy.

Blessed are you, excellent son, by God Most High, who made heaven and earth; and blessed is the God whose protection has placed your enemies in your hands. May the Lord bless you with the beauty of righteousness, and may he watch over and protect in all things your most beloved sons and my spiritual children, the lords Charles and Carloman, appointed by God as kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans [Col. 1008D], together with their most Christian mother, the most excellent queen, your sweetest wife and our faithful spiritual fellow-mother. May God enlarge your offspring, bless them forever, grant you perpetual enjoyment of the royal throne, and preserve unharmed the entire Frankish people remaining under your rule.

Farewell in the Lord, most gracious king, because through you the enemies of the holy Church of God have been humbled, the holy Church of God itself has been raised to great joy, its own people rejoice, and through you God is blessed; therefore his blessing has been poured out upon you more fully, for you have brought the greatest joy to the whole world. These are great things and must be attributed to the praises of almighty God, but amid them we constantly ask the clemency of our most merciful God to grant you in return the joys of his heavenly kingdom [Col. 1009A].

Therefore, with great confidence, as though standing visibly before your honeyed presence, I ask you on bended knees, and earnestly implore you before the living God, to command that you remain firmly in this good work, as we confidently trust, until the end—for the perfect exaltation of the holy Church of God, the liberation of its people, and its complete security. Deign to grant that same Church of God full justice, and command that an excellent and speedy conclusion be brought to the cause of your patron, blessed Peter, so that the remaining cities, which were joined under a single dominion, together with their established boundaries, territories, localities, and woodland estates [Col. 1009B], may be ordered to be restored in their entirety to your spiritual mother, the holy Church. Thus the people of God, whom you redeemed from the hands of their enemies, may be able, assisted by your aid, to live in great security and joy.

For our son, beloved of God, Fulrad, your faithful servant, having observed everything, was satisfied that this people could in no way live outside their boundaries, territories, possessions, and those cities which had always been joined with them under a single dominion. I ask you, son—I ask you before the living God—and I firmly adjure you, spiritual fellow-father, to remain steadfast in this good work. Do not, God forbid, favor human flatteries, persuasions, or promises and turn aside to another course; but, fearing God truly, command that everything you promised under oath to blessed Peter be fulfilled, and, just as you began, grant him full justice [Col. 1009C].

For that tyrant, Aistulf, the devil’s follower, devourer of Christian blood and destroyer of the Churches of God, has been struck by a divine blow and plunged into the abyss of hell. On those very days when, after the cycle of a year, he set out to devastate this Roman city, he was struck by a divine sword, so that at the very time when, testing his faith, he committed various sacrilegious crimes, he also ended his impious life.

Now, by God’s providence, through the hands of his prince, blessed Peter the apostle, and also through your most powerful arm, with the energetic leadership of the man beloved of God, Fulrad, your faithful servant and our beloved son [Col. 1009D], Desiderius, a most gentle man, has been appointed king over the Lombard people. In the presence of Fulrad himself he promised under oath to restore to blessed Peter the remaining cities—Faenza, Imola, and Ferrara—with their boundaries, as well as the woodland estates and all the territories, and also the cities of Osimo, Ancona, and Numana with their territories.

Afterward, through Duke Garinodus and Grimoaldus, he promised to return to us the city of Bologna with its boundaries. He declared that he would always remain in peaceful tranquility with the same Church of God and our people, and testified that he would be faithful toward your kingdom, protected by God. He asked us to plead with your goodness that you command a great peace and concord to be confirmed with him and the entire Lombard people [Col. 1010A].

For the whole duchy of Spoleto, through the hands of blessed Peter and your most powerful arm, has appointed a duke for itself. Both the people of Spoleto and those of Benevento desire to commend themselves through us to your excellence, preserved by God, and they press upon your goodness with still greater urgency in making this request.

Therefore we ask you, most excellent son and spiritual fellow-father, that if the aforesaid Desiderius, as he promised, fully restores to the holy Church of God and to the Roman commonwealth the justice belonging to them and to blessed Peter, your protector, and remains in peaceful tranquility with the Church of God and our people together with his entire nation, as is contained in the agreements confirmed by your goodness, you command that your God-inspired ears incline to what he has requested [Col. 1010B].

Meanwhile we ask this with the greatest urgency: command that a message be sent to King Desiderius very swiftly, adjuring, admonishing, and even commanding him to restore in full to the holy Church the remaining cities, localities, territories, patrimonies, and woodland estates. Command that such a foundation and such an excellent settlement be established in his case that, with the Lord’s assistance, the holy Church of God may remain secure until the end of the age, that full justice may remain from the just judge, the Lord our God, and that a memorial name may remain for you through the ages, likewise for all your Frankish people protected by Christ.

Inspired by God, complete the cause of the holy Church with the greatest haste, for there are other canonical matters which we must complete, pertaining to the great praise of your kingdom and to the immense reward of your soul and of the entire Frankish people [Col. 1010C]. We earnestly ask your exalted goodness, inspired by God and by his prince of the apostles, blessed Peter, to command such arrangements concerning the Greek party that the holy Catholic and apostolic faith may through you remain whole and unshaken forever, and that the holy Church of God may be freed and made secure from them and from their pernicious malice, as it has been from others, and may receive all that belongs to it.

Thus, for the salvation of your souls, the unceasing provision of lamps may continue in the Churches of God, and the hunger of the poor, needy, and pilgrims may likewise be cut off, so that they may attain true satiety. As for how you spoke with the Silentiarius and how your goodness released him, inform us, together with a copy of the letter you gave him [Col. 1010D], so that we may know how to act in common concord, as has been established between us and the beloved Fulrad.

Our beloved son Fulrad himself has carried out all matters according to your command, and we have given him the greatest thanks for his struggle. As he returns to you, he will report to your goodness everything that has been done.

We ask you to receive our present most faithful men, namely George, our most reverend and holy brother and fellow-bishop, and John, our regional official and sacellarius, with a more cheerful countenance, and to command that they be accepted in all things. Deign to believe everything they say to your goodness on our behalf, and command that they be released to return to us with the matters accomplished and joyful messages [Col. 1011A].

We also beseech your goodness to command that our most reverend brother and fellow-bishop Wileharius be released so that he may join us with the utmost speed [printed variant: “so that he may migrate”]. May almighty God protect you in all your actions, most excellent victorious king, by the extension of his right hand; may he grant you prosperity in the present life and, after the course of many years, eternal joys; may he cause you to rejoice with your sweetest wife, the most excellent queen and our spiritual fellow-mother, and with your and my sweetest sons; and may he grant you to enjoy the governance of your kingdom bestowed upon you by God [Col. 1011B].

May you who hold the power of kingship in the present life also reign forever with Christ in the age to come, deserving to hear that lordly promise: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew XXV), because you have fought the good fight, completed the course, and kept the faith. Receive the crowns laid up for you, and accept the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.

We also make known to your exalted excellence, guarded by God, that Optatus, the devout abbot of your monastery of Saint Benedict, has petitioned us on behalf of his monks who departed with your brother, asking that you command them to be released. But command us to state concerning them whatever your will may be. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

## LETTER VII. OF POPE STEPHEN II TO KING PIPPIN, AND TO CHARLES AND CARLOMAN

That they compel Aistulf, king of the Lombards, who violated his oath to restore the cities and localities granted to him, to fulfill the justice promised.

[Col. 1011C]

To the most excellent lords, Pippin, king and our spiritual fellow-father, and Charles and Carloman, likewise kings and both patricians of the Romans: Stephen, pope.

Since the name of your kingdom has shone most brilliantly among the other peoples in sincere faith toward blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, you must strive earnestly that, in the very matter by which all Christians declare you more glorious than other peoples in the service of blessed Peter, you may please almighty God more perfectly—he who grants salvation to kings for the defense of his holy Church—so that you may have the faith you cherish toward that same prince of the apostles as your helper in all things [Col. 1011D].

We had wished, most excellent sons, to prolong our discourse further, but because our heart is utterly crushed by grief over the many tribulations inflicted upon us by the wicked Lombard king Aistulf, and our spirit is weary, we have avoided a lengthy speech and have endeavored to make known to your most Christian excellences the one thing that is necessary.

Protected by God, our spiritual fellow-father, and you, sweetest sons, for the reward of your souls, just as our merciful God has deigned to grant you victories from heaven, you have striven to exact the justice of blessed Peter as far as you could [Col. 1012A], and your goodness confirmed by a deed of donation that it was to be restored.

But now, just as we previously declared to your Christianity concerning the wickedness of that impious king, behold, his lie, wicked perversity, and perjury have already been revealed. For the ancient enemy of the human race, the devil, invaded his treacherous heart, and he dared to invalidate what had been affirmed under the bond of an oath. He did not allow even a span of land to be returned to blessed Peter, the holy Church of God, or the Roman commonwealth. From the day on which we were separated from one another, he has tried to afflict us and hold the holy Church of God in great disgrace to such an extent that human tongues cannot recount it; even the stones themselves, if such a thing may be said, would weep over our tribulation with great howling [Col. 1012B]. He appeared to afflict us so greatly that our infirmity seemed to have been renewed in us once again.

I grieve exceedingly, most excellent sons, because, not listening to our words of misfortune, you chose to believe the lie rather than the truth, mocking and deriding us. Thus we returned without the effecting of blessed Peter’s justice to our own fold and the people entrusted to us.

All Christians firmly believed that blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, had now received his justice through your most powerful arm, since the Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, through the intercessions of his prince of the apostles, had deigned to grant you such an immense victory in your most fortunate times for the defense of his holy Church [Col. 1012C]. Yet, trusting that wicked king, you confirmed by your own will, through a deed of donation, that the cities and localities which he had promised under oath were to be restored to blessed Peter, the holy Church of God, and the commonwealth. But he, forgetting the Christian faith and God, who ordained that he should be born, dared to invalidate what had been secured by oath.

Therefore, “iniquity has descended upon his crown” (Psalm VII). The snare he dug has been exposed, and he has fallen into it because of his command and perjury.

I adjure you, most excellent sons protected by God, by the Lord our God, his holy, glorious, and ever-virgin mother Mary, our lady, all the powers of heaven, and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, who anointed you as kings: let the holy Church of God grieve you, and, in accordance with the donation which you were ordered to offer to that same protector of yours, our Lord blessed Peter, strive to restore and surrender everything to the holy Church of God [Col. 1012D]. Do not now believe the deceptive words or delusive commands of that most wicked king or of his judges.

For his lie has been exposed, so that he can no longer possess any power to be believed. Rather, having recognized his wicked character and wicked will, frustrate his snares, and hasten to restore and surrender to blessed Peter, for the reward of your souls, what you once promised him and confirmed by a donation sealed with your own hand.

The blessed apostle Paul says: “It is better not to vow than, after vowing, not to fulfill” (Ecclesiasticus V). For we have entrusted all the causes of the holy Church of God to your care, and on the day of the fearful judgment you will render an account to God and to blessed Peter of how you have fought for the cause of that same prince of the apostles and for the restoration of his cities and localities.

This good work has been reserved for you through the passage of many years, so that through you the Church may be exalted and the prince of the apostles may receive his justice. None of your parents merited such a radiant gift, but God chose and foreknew you before eternal times, as it is written: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified” (Romans VIII).

You have been called; strive with the utmost speed to render justice to that prince of the apostles, for it is written: “Faith is justified by works” (James II). Your son Fulrad, your counselor, together with his companions, will recount to you all our tribulations, those we have endured and those we are again suffering with God’s help. Act in the cause of blessed Peter so that, with the Lord’s favor, you may be victorious in this matter and, through the intercession of that prince of the apostles, blessed Peter, possess eternal joys in the future. Farewell, most excellent sons.

## LETTER VIII, OR DECREE, OF POPE STEPHEN II

Concerning the hospice and house in Rome granted to Abbot Fulrad.

Stephen, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Fulrad, beloved priest and abbot.

[Col. 1013C]

It is fitting for us to grant the desires of petitioners our assent in such a way that ecclesiastical utility may not thereby suffer loss in succeeding times. For a petition seems then to achieve an appropriate result when ecclesiastical estates, properly ordered, have undoubtedly been brought to a better condition.

Therefore, since you asked us to grant you for a time, by a written decree, the hospice situated within the basilica of blessed Peter beside the tomb of blessed Pope Leo, which the monk Ratchis held and which belonged to the jurisdiction of that basilica of blessed Peter; and likewise the house situated beside the monastery of blessed Martin, with its lower and upper parts, its building plot and little garden, which the monk Nazarius held and which belonged to the venerable monastery of Saint Stephen at the house of the patrician Galla [Col. 1013D], yielding to your prayers, by the tenor of this decree we grant you possession, from the present tenth indiction, throughout the days of your life, of the aforesaid hospice and house, with their lower and upper parts and everything belonging to them in full.

After your death, however, both the hospice and the house, as described above, shall likewise return in full to the jurisdiction of the aforesaid pious places, whose property they are. Farewell.

## LETTER IX. OF POPE STEPHEN II TO ABBOT FULRAD

The letter or bull of Pope Stephen II to Fulrad, abbot of Saint-Denis, by which he grants the monks of Saint-Denis several provisions plainly new and unusual, is too well known for Labbeus to have overlooked it [Col. 1014A]. He published it from the edition of Sirmondus, and appropriately so, since it is more authentic than the version which Mabillonius printed in the third century of the Order of Saint Benedict from Benedictine manuscript codices. Since, however, learned men vigorously dispute its authenticity, and those who accept it as genuine disagree among themselves as to which version is more reliable, it is useful to present it from both the edition of Mabillonius and that of Labbeus, or Sirmondus.

[Note: [Col. 1013] The text of the edition of Sirmondus and Labbeus and the text of the edition of Mabillonius are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### Edition of Sirmondus and Labbeus

Stephen, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Fulrad, beloved of God, archpresbyter and abbot of the venerable monasteries founded under God’s guidance, and perpetually to all his successors, abbots in succession [Col. 1014B].

Since things that accord with reasonable desires must always be granted, the devotion of the founder of a pious foundation must not be denied when privileges are to be bestowed. Therefore, since you asked us, our dearest son, to grant you permission to build monasteries in the province of France, wherever you might wish, in various places—whether on those belonging to your property, or on those that have come to you through a deed of purchase, or even from the possessions of your parents, or from wherever they may come to you—and that the monasteries founded by you might be fortified with the privileges of the apostolic see, so that, established under the jurisdiction of the holy Church which, by God’s authority, we serve, they might not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other Church [Col. 1014D]:

Favoring your pious desires, therefore, and committing to effect by our authority what is requested, through this apostolic authority we grant to you, the aforesaid beloved son of ours Fulrad, and to your other successors who are abbots, permission and power to build monasteries wherever you wish in the province of France—whether in places belonging to your property, or in those which have come or will come to you, our aforesaid son, through a deed of purchase, or which have come or will come to you from any source whatsoever [Col. 1015A].

[Col. 1015D] By this authority we prohibit any bishop of any Church, or any other priest, from exercising any jurisdiction whatsoever in the aforesaid monasteries, except the apostolic see. Thus no bishop, other priest, or layman shall presume to inflict any opposition whatsoever upon those monasteries [Col. 1016A], unless you, man beloved of God, or your successor abbots, should perhaps permit some priest to perform a particular service when you have built those venerable places.

We also entirely forbid any bishop to presume to ordain a presbyter or deacon, or members of the other ecclesiastical orders, in the aforesaid monasteries, or to celebrate Mass there, unless he has been invited by the abbot holding office at that time [Col. 1016B]. No bishop of any other Church shall dare to condemn the bishop who has performed such an ordination of sacred orders in those monasteries for that reason. We likewise grant you permission to consecrate the altar tables and chrism. And, promulgating and decreeing this by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we sanction that no council of bishops and laymen shall in any way dare to consecrate you as bishop without the consent of our most excellent son, King Pippin, or of your affection, man beloved of God [Col. 1016C].

You shall also have permission to bring all your causes and those of your monastery before the most holy apostolic see [Col. 1016D], and to enjoy your property in all respects, whenever you wish to present your claims, together with a Frankish envoy, to the apostolic see. Meanwhile, let no one condemn you; rather, as the true personal familiar of the most holy apostolic see, may you receive from all the honor of the highest distinction. We further promulgate that the venerable monasteries built by you, confirmed under the authority of the most holy see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, shall be protected in all respects by apostolic protection [Col. 1017A], so that, in accordance with what has been established by apostolic privileges, they may remain permanently endowed without disturbance.

By this text of our decree we establish and forbid, under threat of anathema, that any prelate of any Church, or anyone endowed with power of whatever rank, presume in any way to become a violator of this present constitution, granted by us to the aforesaid monasteries [Col. 1017B].

[Col. 1017C]

Farewell. IV Kalends of March, while the most devout lord Constantine, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning: in the thirty-eighth year, in the eighteenth year after his consulship; and with Leo the elder, his son, reigning as emperor, in the fourth year, indiction ten.

### Edition of Mabillonius

[Col. 1014A]

Stephen, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Fulrad, beloved of God, priest and founder [printed: “abbari,” probably for *abbati*, “abbot”] of venerable and various monasteries, under God’s guidance, and perpetually to all his successors, abbots in succession [Col. 1014B].

Since things that are desired for appropriate reasons must always be granted, the devotion of the founder of a holy sanctuary ought to be increased by us in the granting of privileges. Therefore, since you asked us, our dearest son, to grant you permission to build monasteries in the kingdom of France, wherever you might wish, in the fields and settlements of various places [Col. 1014C], whether on those that are your property, or on those that have come to you through a deed of purchase, or on the possessions of your parents, or on whatever may come to you from any source, and that those monasteries, just as they have been built by you without opposition from any judge or claimant, might remain in the future free under the law of the holy Roman Church [Col. 1014D], which by God’s authority we serve, firmly established by us through privileges:

Favoring these pious desires, therefore, and committing what you ask to effect by our blessing, through this apostolic authority we grant to you and to your other successors, the abbots of the monastery of the holy martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, permission [Col. 1015A] and power to build monasteries wherever you wish in the kingdom of France—whether in places belonging to your property, or in those which have come to you through a deed of purchase, through a royal grant, through a gift from your parents, or from whatever source or wherever they may have come to you by any lawful means.

And since, at the petition [Col. 1015B] of Chludovius, son of King Dagobert, the lord Landericus, bishop of the city of Paris, with the counsel of his canons and of his fellow-bishops of that region, released your monastery and all the clerics of whatever orders serving it within the precinct of your monastery from his authority and that of all his successors, we likewise grant you, by a singular privilege, a bishop [Col. 1015C], who, chosen from among you by the abbot or by the brothers in your monastery and consecrated by our brother bishops of that region, shall oversee those monasteries built by you, govern them everywhere in our name, and serve the preaching ministry both in your monastery itself and in those subject to it [Col. 1015D].

To prevent the bishop or priest of any Church from invading those monasteries built by you, deceived by some bond of greed, and from bringing, through envy or any other pretext, some opposition against the bishop whom you or your successors have chosen and caused to be ordained, we prohibit this. Rather, let your remaining monasteries be under apostolic authority [Col. 1016A], just as the holy place itself is established, to which all the aforesaid monasteries appear to belong.

Promulgating and decreeing these provisions by the authority of Christ our God and Lord, of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of ourselves, we sanction that what we have laid down shall remain confirmed in this manner. No bishop of any Church shall dare, in the aforesaid monasteries, to ordain a presbyter or deacon, celebrate any ecclesiastical ministry, or convene a council, except the person whom the abbot then in office has invited to perform these duties [Col. 1016B].

[Col. 1016C] But as for matters concerning you and your monasteries, you and your successors in times to come shall have permission, by our command, to bring them and lodge an appeal concerning them before our apostolic hearing; and when you come to us, or send your representatives, meanwhile no one shall be able to condemn you or them—namely, your successors—or presume in any way to invade your possessions.

[Col. 1017A] But if any king, bishop, or any of the powers of this age should wish to act against this our authority, and should attempt to defraud anything from our apostolic authority, let him be regarded as sacrilegious, and let him have neither part nor fellowship in the kingdom of Christ and God; rather, let him be anathema, Maranatha, forever.

But whoever preserves this authority of ours and of the apostolic see, let him be filled by the Lord Jesus [Col. 1017C] Christ with heavenly blessing forever and ever.

Farewell. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, while our most devout lord Augustus Constantine, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the eighteenth year of his reign, and while Leo, his son and fellow-emperor, was also reigning, in the fourth year, in the tenth indiction.

## LETTER X. POPE STEPHEN II TO ABBOT FULRAD.

[Col. 1017D] Stephen, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Fulrad, our beloved, religious presbyter and abbot.

We have the greatest care and concern that men who come in a religious spirit, fervent in their hearts with the love of Christ, should worthily be granted the adornment of apostolic vesture; this certainly pertains to the praise of the holy Church of God, so that, if any who are worthily clothed in it are invited, they may be able to pour out prayers for us to Christ our God. Considering your conduct, which is earnest in good works, and moved by the greatest love for our most excellent son, King Pippin, we have determined to adorn your beloved religious office with an udon, a sandal, and, when riding on horseback, a mappula. All these aforesaid things are to be used by you alone until your death; they are by no means to be handed over to a presbyter who succeeds you. Rather, when it happens that you die, we decree that these same vestments be buried with you, so that, by this blessing and honor, you may pray to Christ the Lord without ceasing, day and night, for the life and safety of our son King Pippin and for our salvation.

## LETTER XI. POPE STEPHEN II TO ABBOT FULRAD.

Stephen, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Fulrad, religious presbyter and abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Denis, martyr of Christ, and through him to that venerable monastery forever.

We have an excessive care and concern to confer priestly honor upon those who know how to live religiously and chastely in all things and to please God, so that those upon whom dignity is bestowed may be found blameless on that terrible day when they stand before the divine Judge, and so that, if they should prove worthy, we may not incur the guilt of sin through the sacred honor conferred upon them. Therefore, moved by the great love of the protector and patron of the aforesaid honorable monastery, Saint Denis, martyr of Christ, situated within the province of Gaul, we have deemed it fitting, by our apostolic authority, to appoint six deacons worthy of the honor of the sacred altar and approved by good testimony. They are to be clothed in the stole and the ornament of the dalmatic, so that, if they perform the sacred ministry at all times, our reward may increase in our days through the honored order of the diaconate in the aforesaid venerable [Col. 1018C] monastery; and so that, in return for such a benefit, they may unquestionably not cease in future times to commemorate our name continually at the sacred Masses, and also, in return for the benefit bestowed, may not cease to offer hospitality in the aforesaid venerable monastery to the envoys of our holy Church as they come and go, insofar as humanly possible. Thus the religious monks dwelling there may thereby acquire a good reputation for themselves before this holy apostolic see and, before the almighty Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ and our own lord and founder, the blessed chief apostle Peter, may possess eternal blessedness.

Farewell.

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS ON THE TWO FOLLOWING LETTERS.

[Col. 1018D]

It is inferred from letters of Pope Stephen himself that he held a synod in the first year of his pontificate, on the second day before the Ides of January, and therefore in the year of Christ 753. These letters are read in the monk of Nonantola’s *Life of Saint Anselm, Abbot of Nonantola*, and in Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. II, in the section on the bishops of Modena, no. 10. There the following words of Stephen occur:

“While many bishops were residing with us at the thresholds of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and a synodal council was being held, Flavius Aistulf, the most excellent king of the Italian kingdom, came to the feet of the aforesaid apostles,” and so forth.

Of those who took part in this synod, no one is named except Sergius, archbishop of Ravenna. Here are the letters issued in this council, from the supplement to Mansi, vol. I, p. 601.

## GIOVANNI DOMENICO MANSI’S CENSURE OF THESE LETTERS OF POPE STEPHEN II.

[Col. 1019A]

The unusual heading of these letters, wholly contrary to the customs of that age, makes both these letters of Stephen and the entire council held under him suspect to me. For who has ever heard, from genuine documents of his age, the expression: “Serving in the Italian kingdom and the Roman patriarchate”? Nor are the years of his pontificate ever written in Stephen’s genuine letters; rather, it was customary to date letters by the years of the Greek emperors, or sometimes by those of the Lombard kings. It would scarcely be credible that Aistulf, who during these years hated the pope and the Romans, was so devout toward Saint Peter that he visited Rome and showed himself so obedient toward the pope—especially since the author of the *Liber Pontificalis*, who follows Stephen’s deeds with the greatest care, is silent about it.

## LETTER XII. POPE STEPHEN II TO ALL THE BISHOPS.

[Col. 1019B]

Stephen, servant of the servants of God, to all venerable brothers and fellow bishops, and to all religious Christians serving God in the Italian kingdom and the Roman patriarchate.

While many bishops were residing with us at the thresholds of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul, and a synodal council was being held, Flavius Aistulf, the most excellent king of the Italian kingdom, came to the feet of the aforesaid apostles. Among the other gifts that he brought to the church of the blessed apostle Peter, he presented one charter, in which it was contained that, out of reverence for the Lord Savior, the blessed ever-virgin Mary, and all the holy apostles, he had built a monastery in the territory of Modena, at a place called Nonantola. He had granted the charter to a venerable man named Anselm, the abbot. Having Anselm with him, he likewise presented both the man and the charter before the most sacred body of the holy apostle Peter, and thus endowed [gave] the aforesaid monastery to the holy Roman see, which by God’s authority we are seen to govern.

The aforesaid king requested our munificence that we permit the body of the most holy Pope Sylvester, together with other relics of the saints, to be carried with the same Abbot Anselm to the aforesaid venerable monastery; that we immediately consecrate the abbot with our own hands by a blessing; that we clothe him in the cowl according to the rule of Saint Benedict; and that we place in his hands [Col. 1019D] both the pastoral staff and the sandals [Note: [Col. 1019D] Read *pedules*. The use of these, granted to abbots together with the staff a thousand years ago, is attested to us by Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, in his collection of canons, where he discusses the ordination of an abbot by a bishop, who gives him the staff and sandals. MURATOR.] according to the rite. We granted his most holy request with a joyful countenance.

And because our most holy brother Sergius, bishop of the holy Church of Ravenna, was present with us, we commended the venerable abbot and his monastery to be governed under his rule, in our stead, forever—but only if he were invited by the abbot of the monastery. If any adversity should befall him or his successors from any prelate, especially from the bishop of the Church of Modena, in whose diocese it is known to have been built, it should have refuge under the holy Church of Ravenna because of the great distance of the lands separating it from the Roman see.

We also ordered him to carry the aforesaid holy body of Saint Sylvester [Note: [Col. 1020D] Nevertheless, the Romans claim that the body of Saint Sylvester—or perhaps part of it—is preserved among them in the church of the blessed Sylvester and Martin of the Mountains. MURATOR.], together with the other relics of the saints, to the aforesaid monastery himself and there deposit them, and to consecrate the altars and the church by our apostolic authority. We also conferred upon that holy place, by an apostolic privilege, the protection of our holy Roman Church, just as the most holy Pope Gregory granted it to many Churches. And we ordered this document to be subscribed.

## LETTER XIII. POPE STEPHEN II TO THE RELIGIOUS ANSELM.

Stephen, servant of the servants of God, apostolic bishop of the Holy Roman Church, to Anselm, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Sylvester situated at Nonantola in the territory of Modena, and through you to that venerable monastery forever.

Whatever is known to pertain to the praise of our Lord God and Savior, the Redeemer, and whatever concerns the stability of venerable places, it is fitting for us to secure with the greatest diligent care, by apostolic and rational judgment, so that perpetual praises—perhaps [read: *songs*]—may thereby be more effectively offered to the same Lord God, our propitiator, and so that rewards of the best recompense in the heavenly courts may be assigned to us, who, although unworthy, nevertheless by divine grace exercise the care of pastoral governance.

[Col. 1020C] Therefore, since it is evident that your religious office has brought us the charter of the most devout king Aistulf concerning the aforesaid monastery and all places and possessions belonging to it, and since you have requested that we reconfirm it by the document of our apostolic privilege, we, inclined by your prayers, at this present time, in the fourteenth indiction [read: sixth], confirm forever the aforesaid monastery under the control and authority of you and your successors as abbots, together with everything belonging to it, and by irrevocable right decree that the following shall remain: namely, the monastery of Saint Sylvester, also called Nonantola, in the territory of Modena.

Therefore, by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter, to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the power of binding and loosing have been granted by the Lord our God in heaven and on earth, we proclaim and decree, and by a judgment of firm stability establish, that the same venerable monastery, with all its places, manses, estates, and farms, houses and families, hereditary servants, as well as its goods, possessions, crops, tithes, waters, mills, olive groves, and whatever it appears to have or hold in any places whatsoever, or whatever may have been legally donated or granted into its possession, or may have come to it justly in any manner, shall be able to hold and possess these without any dispute forever.

And let no king, bishop, duke, official, or person of small or great status be permitted in any way to encroach upon the aforesaid venerable monastery or upon anything known to belong to it, or to make an invasion; nor let any priest presume to enter there or celebrate the solemn rites of Mass. Nor let any bishop, abbot, count, or any person, great or small, make a residence or demand expenses in the aforesaid monastery or in its cells or churches, or exact any compulsory service—except [what is due] for pilgrims and guests. Nor let anyone dare to hold any kind of conference or court in the monastery itself or in its aforesaid cells, unless invited by the abbot.

Thus what we establish for the praise of God and the stability [Col. 1021B] of the aforesaid monastery may remain firm and stable. We entirely prohibit the bishop in whose diocese the aforesaid monastery is situated from attempting anything contrary to the terms of this decree granted by our pious petition, or from claiming its baptismal churches for himself in any way. Neither he nor his successors shall presume to touch what has been prohibited. Nor shall he presume to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass there unless invited by the abbot of the aforesaid monastery. Nor shall any bishop dare to ordain priests in the aforesaid monastery, or in anything subject to its jurisdiction, or for its clergy, unless, as has been stated, he has been invited by the abbot. And if chrism or anything pertaining to the sacred mysteries is requested by the monastery, we grant that it may be obtained from whichever prelates the monastery prefers.

Nor do we ever permit tithes to be paid except to the churches of the aforesaid venerable monastery belonging to our diocese.

We also establish and confirm by inviolable apostolic sanction that no one shall ever presume to become abbot in the aforesaid monastery from another monastery, or from any church or place whatsoever, nor shall anyone be installed by any authority. Rather, when the abbot of the aforesaid monastery has been called by God and the time of his release has arrived, an abbot shall always be chosen from the monastery’s own congregation and installed there with the consent of all the monks, for the advancement and most diligent governance of those who remain there for the love of God and serve in the monastic order.

Nevertheless, by the prohibition of our pontificate, we forbid anyone to seek by any device any document or confirmation concerning the possessions of the aforesaid monastery or the aforesaid abbacy contrary to this our command. If any document or petition has been obtained, or should hereafter appear, we order that it be null and void, deprived of all force.

Moreover, if anyone—which we do not believe—should presume to violate or despise this apostolic privilege established by us in any respect, let him know that, by the authority of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul, he is bound by the chains of anathema of the 308 [read: 318] Fathers, and is appointed to be burned with the devil and his most dreadful pomp in the punishment of eternal fire, and to be utterly excluded from the kingdom of God.

But whoever proves to be its observer and guardian shall receive the grace of blessing and eternal life from our most merciful Lord God.

Written by the hand of Sergius, scriniary of the Holy Roman Church, in the sixth indiction, in the month of January. Given on the Ides of January, by the hand of Anastasius, bishop of the diocesan clergy of the holy apostolic see, in the first year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of the lord Stephen, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter. [Col. 1022B] Farewell.

## REVELATION OF POPE STEPHEN II.

When he was afflicted by a deadly illness in the monastery of Saint Denis, he testified that he had been divinely delivered through the favor of that holy martyr.

Stephen, bishop and servant of the servants of God.

Just as no one ought to boast about his own merits, so he ought not to pass over in silence the works of God that are performed in him through His saints without his own merits; rather, he should proclaim them, because this is how the angel admonishes Tobias (Tob. XII).

Therefore, because of the oppression of the holy Church by the most savage and blasphemous king—I will not say Aistulf—I came to the most excellent and faithful Christian lord, King Pippin, in Gaul, where I fell sick unto death and remained for some time in the region of Paris [Col. 1022C] in the venerable monastery of the blessed martyr of Christ, Denis.

When the physicians had already despaired of me, I was praying in the church of that blessed martyr beneath the bells. I saw before the altar the good shepherd, Lord Peter, and the teacher of the nations, Lord Paul, and I recognized them clearly in my mind [Note: [Col. 1021D] Concerning their *surcaria*. We have restored this reading from two very ancient manuscripts in place of *surtaria*; likewise, shortly before, we restored *with their whole mind* in place of *with a clear mind*, both of which readings appeared in the edition of the Councils. The word *surcarium*, according to the Glossaries, signifies both a kind of undergarment worn, as it were, over the flesh, and another kind of outer and upper garment, singular and distinguished, now called in French *cotte d’armes*, or formerly *surcot*, which is today used by heralds. PETRUS DE LANDE.] in their *surcaria*. Three times blessed Lord Denis stood to the right of Lord Peter, slender and tall, with a handsome face, white hair, clothed in a most dazzling white *colobium* with a purple stripe, and a wholly purple cloak patterned with gold; and they were speaking joyfully among themselves.

The good shepherd, Lord Peter, said: “This brother of ours is asking for health.”

And blessed Lord Paul said: “He will be healed at once.”
