He approached, placed his hand amicably upon Lord Denis’s breast, and looked toward Lord Peter. Lord Peter said joyfully to Lord Denis: “His healing is by your grace.”

Immediately blessed Denis, holding a censer of incense and a palm in his hand, came to me with a presbyter and a deacon who were standing nearby, and said to me: “Peace be with you, brother. Do not be afraid; you will not die before you return safely to your own see. Rise up healed, and dedicate this altar in honor of God and His apostles Peter [Col. 1023A] and Paul, whom you see, offering Masses of thanksgiving.”

For there was an immeasurable brightness and sweetness there.

Soon, by the grace of God, I became well, and I wanted to fulfill what had been commanded to me. Those who were present said that I was becoming demented. Therefore I related to them [in due order], and to the king and his nobles, what I had seen and how I had been healed, and I fulfilled what had been commanded to me [all of it]. Blessed be God.

## ADDITION TO THE REVELATION OF POPE STEPHEN II.

In an old manuscript from Fleury concerning the deeds of the pontiffs, the following is read:

To this most holy Pope Stephen, a revelation and a remembrance were shown concerning the consecration of the altar of the apostles Peter and Paul, which is situated before the tomb of [Col. 1023B] the saints Denis, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August. He had gone to King Pippin because of the oppression of the most savage and unmentionable Aistulf, and lay ill in the monastery of Saints Denis and his companions; but, restored to health by the prayers of the saints, he consecrated the altar. Not long afterward, at Ferrières, he blessed Pippin and his two sons, Charles and Carloman, as kings of the Franks, and declared that no one except someone from their lineage should ever be made king in the kingdom of Gaul throughout succeeding ages. These things were done in the year 754 from the Lord’s Incarnation.

## ANOTHER ADDITION TO THE REVELATION OF POPE STEPHEN II.

From manuscripts of the Church of Sens and of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

[Col. 1023C] These things were accomplished by blessed Pope Stephen, through divine clemency, with the assistance of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, through the most blessed martyr Denis, in this year, which is 754 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August.

The same manuscripts then continue:

Because he was strengthened by the power of Christ during the celebration of the consecration of the aforesaid altar and the offering of the most sacred sacrifice, he anointed as kings of the Franks the most flourishing King Pippin and his two sons, Charles and Carloman. He also, in the name of God, marked Bertrada, wife of the illustrious King Pippin, clothed in royal garments, with the grace of the sevenfold Holy Spirit; and, sanctifying the nobles of the Franks with apostolic blessing, he bound them by the authority of the blessed Peter entrusted to him by the Lord Jesus Christ. He adjured them never, throughout the succession of ages, to presume in any way to establish over themselves as king anyone of another stock, either they themselves or any born from their lineage, but only from their offspring, whom divine providence deigned to choose to safeguard the most holy apostolic see [Note: [Col. 1023C] for divine providence to protect the apostolic see. Pope Anastasius II first wrote this to Clovis, who had recently been converted to the faith; Pope Pelagius II foretold and desired the same concerning the king’s descendants, writing to Aunacharius, bishop of Auxerre, in these words:

“We do not believe that it is purposeless, or arranged without the administration of divine providence, that your kings resemble the Roman Empire in the confession of orthodox faith, except so that they might provide this city, from which they had sprung, and all Italy with neighboring helpers, and so that the power to assist us”—that is, the pope and the apostolic see—“might have been divinely given to your kings.”

Stephen II likewise declared this in honor of the second dynasty of our kings. He himself also experienced it in the protection and donation of King Pippin, so that the other Roman pontiffs and the kings of the Franks followed one another together and in turn, both the prophecies of Anastasius and Pelagius and Stephen’s example: the former by seeking refuge and accepting aid, the latter by protecting and making gifts. Much later, something similar was done by Pope Innocent II among the kings of our third dynasty against the schism of Peter of León. The abbot Suger relates this in the *Life of Louis, King of the Franks, called the Fat*:

“When the faction of Peter of León prevailed both through the support of his relatives and through the protection of the Roman nobility, Lord Pope Innocent decided to leave the City with his followers. Therefore, proceeding under naval protection to the parts of Balliae, he chose as a safe and approved asylum for the defense of his person and the Church, after God, the most noble kingdom of the Franks; and, sending his messengers to King Louis, he earnestly requested assistance for both his person and the Church.” PETRUS DE LANDE.]

and to exalt and consecrate him with the most sacred anointing to royal power through him—namely, the vicar of Saint Peter, indeed of our Lord Jesus Christ.

## RESPONSES OF POPE STEPHEN II.

[Note: [Col. 1024D] First published by P. Jacobus Sirmond, of the Society of Jesus, from the Laud manuscript. HARD.]

While he was in France, at the estate of Carisiacum, [Note: [Col. 1024D] A Breton monastery. At the end, the Laud manuscript reads: “Here end the responses that Lord Pope Stephen gave at the estate of Carisiacum, in the Breton monastery, to the questions put to him.” We understand, therefore, that the responses were given privately to the monks of Britanniacum at Carisiacum. The estate of Carisiacum, where there was a royal palace on the River Oise, is mentioned in Anastasius’s account of Pope Stephen’s arrival in France. Hincmarus indicates the location of the Breton monastery in his examination of Willebert, bishop of Châlons: “The place of his ordination was announced to all, in the monastery called Britennacus, in the diocese of Noyon.” JAC. SIRM.] he gave the following responses in the year of Christ 754 to various questions concerning which he had been consulted.

### I. Concerning one who dismisses a slave woman and marries a freeborn woman.

In a letter of Pope Leo to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, chapter 5, it is contained as follows:

“To dismiss a slave woman from one’s bed (31, q. 2) and to take a wife of certain free birth is not a duplication of marriage but an advancement in honor.”

### II. If one of the spouses is unable to render the marital debt.

If someone has entered into marriage and it happens that one of the spouses is unable to render the marital debt, they may not be separated, nor on account of any other illness, except if the illness of demonic possession or the stain of leprosy should supervene. But if they are free from these two illnesses and remain joined to one another, let one render service to the other.

### III. Concerning one who has a wife in his homeland but lives in another region.

If someone, in a foreign country, takes a slave woman into partnership, and afterward, having returned to his own country, takes a freeborn woman, and it should again happen that he returns to the country where he previously lived, while the slave woman whom he formerly had has been joined to another man, such a person may take another wife—but not while the freeborn woman whom he had in his own country is alive.

### IV. If someone marries his spiritual co-mother from baptism or confirmation.

Let no one have his spiritual co-mother, whether from the sacred font or from confirmation, joined to him in marriage, secretly on either side. If they have been joined, let them be separated.

### V. Whether a man who has repudiated his wife may take another wife.

If a wife has been repudiated by her husband, whether it is lawful for the husband, while she is alive, to take another wife is addressed in the letter of Lord Pope Innocent to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse:

“Those who, after a divorce, have joined themselves to another marriage are plainly adulterers on both sides. Those who, while their wife is alive, although they appear to have been separated from the marriage, have hastened to another union cannot fail to be regarded as adulterers, to such an extent that even the persons to whom such men are joined appear themselves to have committed adultery, according to what we read in the Gospel: ‘Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery’ (Matthew XIX). Therefore all such persons are to be excluded from communion.”

### VI. Concerning virgins who are not veiled, if they marry.

Concerning those who, transgressing their promised virginity, entered into marriage, the letter of blessed Pope Innocent to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, chapter 15, contains the following:

“Those women, however, (27, q. 1) who have not yet been covered with the sacred veil but have nevertheless promised that they would always live in the purpose of virginity—although they are not veiled—if they should happen to marry, must perform penance for some time, because their vow was held by the Lord. For if, among human beings, a contract made in good faith is ordinarily dissolved in no way, how much more should this promise, which she made with God, not be dissolved without punishment? For if the apostle Paul said that those who departed from their purpose of widowhood have condemnation, because they made their first faith void (1 Timothy V), how much more do virgins who have not at all kept faith with their covenant?”

### VII. Concerning monks and nuns if they enter into marriage.

Concerning monks and nuns fleeing from the monastery, the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 16, contains the following:

“It is not permitted for a virgin who has consecrated herself to God (27, q. 1, ‘If any virgin’), and likewise for a monk, to contract marital rights. If they are found to have perpetrated this, let them be excommunicated. But for those who confess, we decree that the bishop of the same place has authority to grant kindness and mercy.”

### VIII. Concerning a widow who, after receiving the veil, later marries.

Concerning a woman who, after her husband’s death, had been veiled for some time and afterward takes a husband, the letter of Pope Siricius to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, chapter 5, contains the following:

“But concerning those who, after having performed penance, like dogs and pigs returning to their former vomit and wallowing place, have again sought the belt of military service, theatrical pleasures, new marriages, and illicit sexual relations, and whose professed lack of restraint has been revealed by children begotten after absolution: concerning these, since they now have no further refuge for doing penance, we have decreed that they are to be joined to the faithful in the Church only in prayer, and that they may attend the celebration of the sacred mysteries, although they do not deserve it; but let them be excluded from the banquet of the Lord’s table, so that, corrected at least by this severity, they may discipline themselves and others may be deterred from such things. Nevertheless, because they have fallen through bodily weakness, when they begin to depart to God, we have wished them to be strengthened by the grace of communion through the provision for the journey.

“We judge that the same arrangement is to be observed concerning women who, after penance, have bound themselves by such pollutions. Therefore, according to the judgment of this venerable man, we decree that the same woman, who, after abandoning such a wicked marriage, has been joined to monastic dress but did not persevere in what she had promised to God, is to be sent without delay to a monastery, so that there she may end her life in her penance.”

### IX. If a healthy man takes a leprous woman as wife.

If a healthy man takes a leprous woman as wife, or if leprosy should afterward come upon her, then, setting negligence aside, they are to be separated, lest children conceived be polluted by the stain of leprosy. For it is proper that a clean person be joined to a clean person.

### X. Concerning one who, not knowing by whom he was ordained, celebrated Masses and baptized, and afterward abandoned his office and married.

Concerning that presbyter who says that he does not know who blessed him, yet for some time celebrated Masses and baptized, and afterward abandoned that office and took a wife: who could doubt that this presbyter is wholly guilty? By sacrilegious audacity he should not at all have used what he did not know had been conferred upon him. Therefore he must be entirely removed and sent to a monastery, so that there, under worthy penance, he may end his life in mourning.

The infants whom he baptized, however, if they were baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, are unquestionably proven to have been baptized, because even laypeople, when necessity presses, have been granted permission to provide this assistance, lest those who are to be baptized perish forever.

But if the woman whom that sacrilegious pseudo-presbyter took as his wife knew that he was exercising the office of a presbyter and was joined to him knowingly, she too is to be subjected to penance in a monastery. If she did this in ignorance, no guilt is attributed to her.

### XI. Concerning a presbyter who, because there was no water, baptized a child in danger with wine.

If someone baptized a child in extreme danger with wine because he could not find water, no guilt is attributed to him on that account [Note: [Col. 1025D] We think that what is enclosed in parentheses is a gloss, either rashly brought by a scribe from the margin into the text, or transferred carelessly from the neighboring canons; or, certainly, with the number changed, it should be read as follows: [Col. 1026D] “But let the infant remain in that baptism.” In chapters XIII and XIV, however, the plural number is wholly appropriate, as the matter itself shows.] (let infants thus remain in that baptism). But if water was available, let that presbyter be excommunicated and subjected to penance, because he presumed to act contrary to the judgment of the canons.

### XII. Whether it is lawful to baptize by pouring water from a vessel or with the hands.

[Col. 1027A]

Whether, in case of necessity, it is lawful to pour water over the head of an infant lying ill with a vessel or with the hands, and thus to baptize him. If this baptism has been performed in the name of the Holy Trinity, it will remain fully valid, especially since necessity demands that the person detained by illness be reborn in this way and become a participant in the kingdom of God.

### XIII. Concerning a presbyter who baptized without knowing the Creed, the Lord’s Prayer, or the psalms, and whether he himself had been ordained.

Concerning that presbyter who baptized but knows neither the Creed, nor the Lord’s Prayer, nor the psalms, and does not know whether a bishop blessed him: first of all, let him lose the dignity which he presumed unlawfully to exercise; let him be sent to a monastery under strict penance, and, mourning throughout all the days of his life over what he did improperly, let him live a monastic life.

The infants whom he baptized, however, if they were baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, are to remain in that baptism.

### XIV. Concerning a presbyter who added certain words to the baptismal formula and does not know whether the bishop ordained him.

Concerning that presbyter who baptized in this rustic manner—“In the name of the Father I immerse, and of the Son I immerse, and of the Holy Spirit I immerse”—and the presbyter himself does not know whether it was a bishop who blessed him: since he is ignorant of his own ordination, he must be entirely removed and sent to a monastery under strict penance, so that throughout all the days of his life he may live in mourning and weeping under the monastic habit.

The infants whom he baptized, although in a rustic manner, are to remain in that baptism, because they were baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity.

### XV. Concerning bishops who have been accused and condemned.

Concerning an accused bishop, the Council of Antioch, chapter 15, contains the following:

“If any bishop (6, q. 4), accused of definite crimes, is condemned by all the bishops of the same province, and all, with one accord, have issued the same form of decree against him, he is not to be judged in any way before other bishops; rather, the judgment of the bishops of the province who agreed together is to remain firm.”

### XVI. Concerning accused presbyters and deacons.

Concerning accused presbyters or deacons, the Council of Carthage, chapter 20, contains the following:

“But if presbyters [Col. 1027D] or deacons are accused, they are to join with their own bishop a lawful number of colleagues from neighboring places, whom the accused themselves shall request from him—namely, six in the case of a presbyter, and three in the case of a deacon—and together they shall investigate their case, observing the same procedure regarding days, postponements, and examination of persons between the accusers and those accused. But the cases of the other clerics may be heard and concluded by the bishop of the place alone.”

### XVII. Concerning a presbyter whose crime, committed before ordination, became known.

## XVII. On a Presbyter Who Fell into a Criminal Offense, and Whose Sin Was Made Public

Concerning a presbyter who fell into a criminal offense, and whose sin was made public, the following is contained in the Council of Neocaesarea, canon 9:

“If a presbyter, having been overtaken by a bodily sin, is advanced [to ordination] (15, q. 1, ‘who committed it’), and confesses that he sinned before his ordination, he shall not consecrate the offerings, but shall remain in his other functions on account of his good zeal. For many have said that other sins can be forgiven through the laying on of hands. But if he has not confessed regarding himself, and cannot be clearly accused, he shall be left to the judgment of his own authority.”

## XVIII. On Clerics’ or Monks’ Hair Not Being Allowed to Grow Long

Let no cleric or monk presume to let his hair grow long; otherwise, let him be anathema.

## XIX. On a Woman Who Married Another Man When Her Husband Was Falsely Believed to Have Died in a Foreign Province

Concerning a woman separated from her husband, when her husband was believed to be living in a foreign province, the following is contained in a letter of blessed Pope Leo addressed to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia:

“Since, therefore, you say that certain marriages have been so divided by the devastation of war and the gravest attacks of hostility that, after the men had been led away into captivity, their wives remained abandoned—wives who either believed their husbands to have been killed or thought that they would never be freed from their captors—and, compelled by solitude [or, according to the variant, anxiety], entered into marriage with other men; and since, now that circumstances have been turned toward better things with the Lord’s help, some of those who were thought to have perished have returned, your Charity rightly appears uncertain about what ought to be ordained by us concerning the women who have been joined to other husbands.

“But because we know that it is written that a woman is joined by God to God [or: that a wife is joined by God] (Prov. XIX), and because we have again recognized the command that what God has joined together, a human being must not separate (Matt. XIX), we must necessarily believe that the bonds of legitimate marriages are to be restored. Once the evils brought about by hostility have been removed, what each person legitimately possessed must be restored to that person, and every effort must be made so that each person receives what is his or her own.

“Nevertheless, the man who assumed the person of a husband who was already thought not to exist must not be judged culpable or regarded as an invader of another’s right. For in this way many things belonging to those who had been led into captivity could have passed into the possession of others; yet it is entirely just that, when those persons return, their own property should be restored to them. If this rule is rightly observed with slaves, fields, houses, possessions, and even estates, how much more must it be observed in the restoration of marriages, so that what was disturbed by the necessity of war may be restored through the remedy of peace?

“And therefore, if the husbands, after a long captivity, continue to love their wives so that they desire them to return to their marital union, what necessity brought about must be set aside and judged blameless, and what fidelity demands must be restored. But if some women have been so captivated by love for their later husbands that they prefer to remain with them rather than return to their legitimate marital union, they must rightly be censured, even to the extent of being deprived of ecclesiastical communion. They have chosen the defilement of sin over a matter that could be excused, showing that, because of their incontinence, they preferred what a just pardon could have expiated.

“Therefore, let the marriages return voluntarily to their proper state, and let them in no way turn into a reproach of ill will what the condition of necessity extorted. For just as those women who refuse to return to their husbands must be regarded as impious, so those who return to the affection established by God must rightly be judged praiseworthy.”

**In the year of the Lord 758. Saint Pirminius, abbot.**

[Col. 1029]

## Notice Concerning Saint Pirminius, Abbot

*(Galland, Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. XIII.)*

[Col. 1029B] That Pirminius was an abbot is sufficiently clear from the title of his little work; learned men also conjecture that he was a chorepiscopus. He died in the year 758, as Mabillon teaches, and as is stated in the *Literary History of France* (vol. IV, p. 125). Therefore, a typographical error appears to have entered Fabricius, where his death is recorded ten years later.

Pirminius’s little work, *On Each of the Canonical Books*, first appeared among Mabillon’s *Analecta*, from which we too have taken it. Although it is written in barbarous Latin, it contains many passages by which Catholic doctrines and ecclesiastical customs can be confirmed or illustrated. Nothing more certain is known about him.

Nevertheless, he appears to have been one of those who held that one ought to abstain from eating blood or carrion. For this reason, Evantius seems to have directed his pen against him and his followers when he says:

“In certain districts of Zaragoza, you assert that you have found Christians not yet instructed in the sacred Scriptures . . . who say that a person becomes unclean by eating the blood of some animal.”

Certainly, Pirminius strives especially to confirm his teaching from the Acts of the Apostles, a testimony which Evantius attempts particularly to weaken. In any case, they conjecture that he was at least a chorepiscopus from the very wording of his discourse; no one, so far as I know, has yet identified the place.

If someone locates him in the diocese of Zaragoza on the authority of Evantius, he will perhaps affirm a matter that is not implausible. He will also find support in the words *Karagios* and *Karakares*, which Philesacus shows were still in use among the Spaniards in his own time. It must nevertheless be admitted that those superstitions of which Pirminius complains prevailed both in Gaul and in Spain. In the appropriate place we have noted that Bernard in Gratian’s *Canons* should be consulted concerning this matter (can. 16, c. 26, q. 7).

[Col. 1029]

# Saint Pirminius the Abbot: *Scarapsus on Each of the Canonical Books*

*[Note: [Col. 1029] That is, “collection.” For *scaro* in barbarous Latin means “to compel soldiers” or “to muster soldiers.”]*

*(Galland, Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. XIII.)*

[Col. 1029D] Most beloved brothers, the Holy Spirit admonishes us through the prophets, priests, Levites, and all the teachers of the Catholic Church, saying:

“Cry out; do not cease. Raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their sins.”

And again:

“If you do not announce his wickedness to the wicked man, he will die in his sins, and I will require his blood from your hand.”

And the Lord says in the Gospel:

“Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel.”

And to you, brothers, who gather in the church, the Lord says through the prophet:

“Come, children; listen to me. I will teach you the fear of the Lord.”

And again:

“Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”

And the Lord says in the Gospel:

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.”

Therefore, most beloved, we ask your Charity to listen attentively to what is said for your salvation. A lengthy arrangement is being made from the divine Scriptures, but so that you may retain at least a little of it in your memory, we commend to you a few things from among many.

When the Lord had made heaven and earth in the beginning, and had made spiritual creatures—namely, angels—in that heavenly dwelling, one of them, who had first been made an archangel above all others, saw himself shining with such great glory. He did not give honor to God his Creator, but said that he was like Him. Because of this pride, he was cast down with many other angels who had agreed with him from that heavenly seat into this air, which is beneath heaven. Having lost the light of his glory, he became the devil.

Likewise, those angels who had agreed with him were cast out of heaven with him; having lost the splendor of their glory, they became demons. The others, however, who remained subject to God persevered in the glory of their brightness in the Lord’s presence, and these are called holy angels.

After this fall of the angels, God formed the human being from the clay of the earth, so that, if he kept the Lord’s commandment, he might succeed without death to that heavenly place from which those fallen angels had fallen; but, if he transgressed God’s commandment, he would surely die.

When the devil saw that the human being had been made for the purpose of succeeding in the kingdom of God to the place from which he himself had fallen, he was moved by envy and persuaded the human being to transgress God’s commands. God had commanded the human being, saying:

“Eat from every tree of paradise, but do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for on whatever day you eat from it, you shall surely die.”

Against God’s command, at the devil’s persuasion, the human being took and ate fruit from that tree. Because of this offense, he was cast from paradise into the exile of this world, where he would suffer many labors and sorrows.

The first human being was called Adam, and his wife was called Eve; the following words, *quod creavit* (“because [she] created”), are uncertain. From these two the entire human race was propagated. Having forgotten their Creator God, they committed many crimes and provoked Him to anger.

Because of this, God sent the flood and destroyed everyone except one just man named Noah, together with his three sons and their wives, whom He preserved for the restoration of the human race. From the first man, Adam, until the flood, 2,242 years passed.

After the flood, the human race was again restored through the sons of Noah. When the growing multitude began to fill the world, human beings once more forgot God, the Creator of the world, and began to worship created things and to commit many other evil deeds, which would take too long to enumerate.

When God saw such great wickedness among human beings, He gave the law through His servant Moses, written by the finger of God on two stone tablets.

On the first tablet:

“Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God. You shall not take the name of your God in vain. Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day. For six days you shall labor and do all your work; but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. You shall do no work on it.”

On the second tablet:

“Honor your father and your mother. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not kill. You shall not steal. You shall not give false testimony. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.”

And again:

“You shall not covet anything belonging to your neighbor.”

Even after receiving the law, human beings transgressed it. Later they returned to idols and the worship of demons, and, held fast in many crimes and sins, they went astray.

Again, when God saw such great human folly and hardness—for He did not wish to destroy the human being whom He had created—He sent His prophets, admonishing them through the Holy Spirit to return from the worship of idols and the transgression of the law to divine worship and the commandments of God.

But neither the law given through Moses nor the prophets themselves could free them from the original sins that they had inherited from Adam, because every soul, whether of sinners or of the righteous, when it departed from the body, descended into hell because of those original sins inherited from Adam, since the first human being had transgressed God’s command in paradise.

*[Note: [Col. 1031D] This must be understood with an appropriate distinction—namely, in the sense in which we say that before Christ the gates of heaven were closed because of Adam’s sin. See below, section “After This.”]*

But when God saw that the whole world was perishing, He had mercy on the human race:

“He sent His Son, born of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law.”

The Son of God deigned to descend from the bosom of the Father—that is, the Word entered the womb of holy Mary, ever-virgin. He came in such humility that, through humility, He might conquer the devil, the author of death, and free the human race through the cross of His Passion.

While He shone with the Father in heaven, on earth He lay wrapped in swaddling clothes in a manger. He was driven into Egypt; in the flesh He was circumcised; He was baptized by John in the Jordan River when He was about thirty years old. He preached to Jews and Gentiles that they should abandon all evil deeds and demonic practices, do penance, and receive baptism; and that they should keep His commandments, which are the four Gospels and the rest of sacred Scripture.

He chose twelve disciples, so that whatever they preached throughout the whole world, all might believe in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and might be baptized for the remission of all sins.

These are the apostles: Peter, Andrew, James, John, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, Simon the Zealot, Judas of James, and James of Alphaeus.

Thus the Lord taught them to pray:

“Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth. Give us today our supersubstantial bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors; and do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. IV, 9 ff.).

Christ Himself, the Son of God, changed water into wine; with five loaves and two fish He fed five thousand people; He walked upon the sea; He cleansed lepers; He cast out demons; He made the deaf hear and the mute speak; He healed the paralytics; He gave sight to the blind; and He healed every sickness and disease among the people.

[Col. 1033A] The Lord Himself fasted for forty days and forty nights, and afterward He was hungry. The devil approached Him and said:

“If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread.”

Christ answered him:

“Human beings do not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.”

The devil said to Him:

“If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.”

Jesus said to him:

“You shall not tempt the Lord your God.”

Then the devil showed Him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and said to Him:

“All these I will give you if you fall down and worship me.”

Then He said to him:

“Get behind me, Satan; for it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God and serve Him alone.’”

Then the devil left Him, and behold, angels approached and ministered to Him.

Here it is shown that one devil tempted both Adam and Christ, and tempted them for the same reason. He tempted Adam through gluttony when he said:

“Why did God command you not to eat from this tree?” (Gen. III, 1).

He suggested vainglory when he said:

“Knowing good and evil.”

Thus he tempts every person, if he can conquer him, through gluttony, fornication, luxury, uncleanness, and immodesty. If a person falls into these, he suggests vainglory to him, from which boasting, exaltation, and pride arise. If a person does not sin in these matters, he suggests greed; from this arise enmities, quarrels, anger, discord, thefts, murders, and jealousies.

Therefore, let us take up the weapons of Christ and conquer the enemy, just as our teacher Christ taught, and let us laugh at him.

*[Note: [Col. 1033] Perhaps the word *cadit* should be deleted here, and the following clause should instead be read with a comma: “and if a person does not fall into these.” EDITOR.]*

## After This

After this, He came with His twelve disciples to supper on the fifth day of the week, which is called Thursday and the Lord’s Supper. The devil, through envy, put it into the heart of one [variant: *uni*, “one”] of those twelve disciples, named Judas Iscariot, as also into that of the Jews, that, with the Jews’ cooperation, he might hand Christ the Son of God over that very night to be crucified for thirty pieces of silver.

He came willingly, not unwillingly, to His Passion for our salvation. For us He endured reproaches, mockery, spitting, blows, scourging, and a crown of thorns.

And [perhaps *et*, “and”] on the day called Friday, the day after the supper, at the sixth hour, He was suspended on the cross by the Jews. On that day darkness came over the whole earth from the seventh hour until the ninth hour; the earth was shaken; the rocks were split; the tombs were opened; and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose. After His resurrection they came out of the tombs, entered the holy city, and appeared to many (Matt. XXVII, 45, 52–53).

The Lord Himself was nailed to the cross with nails for us, given vinegar to drink, and pierced with a spear. At the ninth hour He gave up His spirit, and blood and water flowed from His side.

What was signified by the blood, if not redemption? What by the water, if not the sacrament of baptism?

Then Christ’s body lay in the tomb. While that sacred body lay in the tomb, Christ’s soul descended into hell. From there He rescued Adam, the first human being, and all the patriarchs, prophets, and righteous persons who were being held there because of original sins.

Hence the Lord says:

“I will be your death, O Death; I will be your bite, O Hell” (Hos. XIII, 14).

For our Lord Jesus Christ was the bite of hell: He took some away and left some there. He took away the righteous and left the sinners.

For that divinity of God which is impassible—that is, the Word—was with the Father in heaven, with the body in the tomb, and with Christ’s soul in hell, because humanity without divinity could not redeem the world.

Then He bound the devil and stripped hell.

On the third day—the day that all Christians celebrate as Easter, the Lord’s Day—He rose from the tomb. After His resurrection He appeared to human beings, and for forty days, until His ascension into heaven, He walked among human beings in this world with the apostles. He showed them the wound of the spear in His side and the marks of the nails in His hands.

Speaking to them about the kingdom of God, He raised His hands over them, blessed them, and said:

“Go into the world, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you.”

He commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the Father’s promise. And He said to them:

“You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses.”

When He had said this, while they were watching, He was lifted up, and a cloud received Him from their sight.

As they were gazing into heaven while He went away, behold, two men stood beside them in white garments and said:

“Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw Him going into heaven.”

This took place on the fifth day of the week, which is called Thursday, the day of the Lord’s Ascension.

Then the Lord’s disciples returned to Jerusalem and persevered unanimously in prayer until the tenth day, which is Pentecost. It is called the fiftieth day and falls on the Lord’s Day.

On that day, at the third hour, suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the whole house where the apostles were sitting. Divided tongues appeared to them as though of fire, and one rested upon each of them. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance.

And they composed the Creed:

Peter: “I believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth.”

John: “And in Jesus Christ, His only Son, our Lord.”

James said: “Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.”

Andrew said: “Who suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried.”

Philip said: “He descended into hell.”

Thomas said: “On the third day He rose from the dead.”

Bartholomew said: “He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the almighty Father.”

Matthew said: “From there He will come to judge the living and the dead.”

James of Alphaeus said: “I believe in the Holy Spirit.”

Simon the Zealot said: “The holy Catholic Church.”

Judas of James said: “The communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins.”

Thomas again said: “The resurrection of the flesh, eternal life.”

[Col. 1035A] Then, as Christ had foretold, they were dispersed throughout the whole world to preach to all nations and baptize them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

The apostles blessed bishops and ordained deacons, presbyters, and the remaining orders of the Catholic Church. After the apostles’ departure, these were to act in the Catholic people, according to the apostolic order written above, vigilantly and prudently through the succession of bishops until the end of the world.

And now the good are established, through God’s grace, for the salvation of the righteous; the wicked, however, are established not according to apostolic constitution but through greed, like Simon Magus, or through many other evil inventions of their own, for the ruin of the people. They wish rather to rule than to benefit in the churches of God.

But one must consider what is written:

“Do the good things that they tell you; but, God forbid, if they do evil things, do not do them.”

And elsewhere it is written:

“Whoever strives to make progress should not consider what evil others do, but what good he himself ought to do.”

For those good men who preside over Catholic churches, who preach to you what is right and fulfill it in their works, show the peoples a twofold goodness, fulfilling the Gospel command:

“Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

Therefore, most beloved, as the Holy Spirit says through the prophet:

“I will pour clean water over you, and you shall be cleansed from all your impurities and from all your idols. I will cleanse you and give you a new heart, and I will place a new spirit within you.”

And in the Gospel:

“No one enters the kingdom of God unless he has been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit”—that is, unless he has believed and been baptized.

Therefore, brothers, we bring back to your memory what covenant we made with God in the baptismal font. For example, when each of us was asked his name by the priest, and we were asked what we were called, you responded—if you were already able to respond—or certainly the person who made the profession of faith on your behalf, who received you from the font, said: “He is called John,” or another name.

The priest asked:

“John, do you renounce the devil, all his works, and all his pomps?”

You responded:

“I renounce”—that is, “I despise and abandon all evil and demonic works.”

After this renunciation of the devil and all his works, the priest asked you:

“Do you believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth?”

And you responded:

“I believe.”

And again:

“Do you also believe in Jesus Christ, His only Son, our Lord, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried, descended into hell, rose from the dead on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the almighty Father, and will come from there to judge the living and the dead?”

And you responded:

“I believe.”

For the third time the priest asked:

“Do you believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy Catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life?”

You responded—or your sponsor responded for you:

“I believe.”

Behold the nature of the covenant, promise, and confession that is held before the Lord. Having believed, you were baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, for the remission of all sins. You were anointed by the priest with the chrism of salvation unto eternal life. Your body was clothed in a white garment, and Christ clothed your soul in heavenly grace. A holy angel was assigned to you to guard you, and, having received the Christian name, you were enrolled in the Catholic Church and made a member of Christ, as the Apostle says:

“You are Christ’s body, and members of His member.”

For Christians are numbered from Christ.

Let no Christian who has the name but does not have the deeds boast. A Christian is one who imitates and follows Christ in all things, as the Apostle says:

“Whoever says that he believes in Christ ought to walk as He walked.”

And whoever says that he believes in God but does not keep His commandments is a liar.

The Lord Himself says in the Gospel:

“If you love me, keep my commandments.”

Therefore, brothers, we who have been baptized and have received God’s commandments ought to keep them, as the Holy Spirit admonishes us through sacred Scripture: namely, to turn away from evil and do good.

What is it to turn away from evil, if not to abandon the devil together with all his works?

There are therefore eight principal vices that plunge people into destruction and ruin: greed, gluttony, fornication, anger, sadness, acedia, vainglory, and pride. From these eight vices arise many other evil vices and sins, which it would take too long to enumerate. Nevertheless, with Christ’s favor, we shall say something briefly about them below.

Therefore, most beloved, we ask your Charity to listen with the inner ear of your hearts to what the Lord Himself, or sacred Scripture, prohibits concerning the vices mentioned above, so that you may never commit them, and so that anyone who has committed them may know how he ought to amend his life.

Concerning greed, He says not to covet your neighbor’s property. And Solomon says:

“Nothing is more wicked than to love money.”

And the Apostle says:

“Greed is the root of all evils.”

Concerning gluttony, He said:

“Beware of gluttony, through which the first man, Adam, was expelled from paradise, for it is written: Do not be led astray into the satisfaction of the belly.”

And through the prophet:

“This was the iniquity of Sodom: pride, fullness of bread, and abundance.”

And the Apostle:

“Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires.”

And the Lord says in the Gospel:

“Woe to you who are full, for you shall hunger.”

Let no one commit fornication, for the Lord says in the law:

“Whoever lies with a male as with a woman, or whoever commits an abomination, shall die the death.”

And the Apostle says:

“God will judge fornicators and adulterers.” [Editorial correction: *adulteratores*, “adulterers,” is perhaps intended.]

Every impure pollution is called fornication.

And again the Apostle says:

“Neither fornicators, nor those who lie with males, nor the effeminate will possess the kingdom of God.”

Let no one hold anger in his heart against his neighbor, for the Lord says in the Gospel:

“Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment.”

And the Apostle:

“The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God.”

And:

“Let not the sun go down upon your anger.”

Do not grieve over transitory things, for it is written:

“Worldly sorrow produces death.”

Let no one be idle, for it is written:

“The soul of one who does nothing will hunger.”

And again:

“Idleness is the enemy of the soul.”

And the Apostle says:

“Anyone unwilling to work should not eat.”

Despise vainglory. Whatever we do for the sake of adornment or human praise is called vainglory. Hence it is written:

“God scatters the bones of those who please human beings.”

And the Apostle says:

“Do not become desirous of empty glory.”

And again the Apostle:

“If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be Christ’s servant.”

And the Lord says in the Gospel:

“Take care not to perform your righteousness before human beings, in order to be seen by them; otherwise you have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.”

Flee pride, because everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before God.

And again:

“God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.”

And again:

“Whoever exalts himself will be humbled.”

Let no one commit murder, for it is written:

“Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed.”

And the Lord says:

“You shall not kill; whoever kills will be liable to judgment.”

And the Apostle says:

“No murderer has a share in eternal life.”

Let no one commit adultery, for the Lord says in the law:

“You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.”

And the Apostle says:

“Neither will adulterers possess the kingdom of God.”

And the Lord says:

“Everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

Let no one presume to separate a legitimate marriage except by mutual consent, for the love of Christ, who says:

“Whoever leaves his wife, and so forth, will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life.”

And concerning fornication: when the Pharisees were testing the Lord Jesus Christ, they asked Him:

“Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?”

Jesus answered:

“Have you not read that He who made them from the beginning made them male and female? And He said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.’ Therefore they are no longer two but one flesh. What God has joined together, let no human being separate.”

They said to Him:

“Why, then, did Moses command that a certificate of divorce be given to her and that she be dismissed from the house?”

He said to them:

“Because of the hardness of your hearts Moses permitted you to divorce your wives; but from the beginning it was not so. I say to you that whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another commits adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.”

Hence the Apostle says:

“I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband.”

And again:

“Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife.”

And elsewhere it is written:

“Whoever keeps an adulterous woman is foolish and impious.”

Therefore, wherever there is fornication or suspicion of fornication, let the wife be freely dismissed.

But if she is barren, ugly, advanced in years, foul-smelling, drunk, of bad character, lustful, foolish, gluttonous, wandering, quarrelsome, or abusive, she must be kept nevertheless, whether you wish it or not, and must be regarded as she was accepted. While you were free, you voluntarily subjected yourself.

Let no one defile himself through incestuous unions, for the Lord said in the book of Leviticus, when He gave the law to the people:

“I am the Lord. No man shall approach a close blood-relative. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father, your mother, or your father’s wife; nor that of your sister, your son’s daughter, or a granddaughter; nor of the daughter of the daughter of your father’s wife; nor of your father’s sister, your mother’s sister, and your father’s [the text is uncertain]. Nor shall you approach the wife of one joined to you by affinity. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your son’s wife, your brother’s wife, or of your wife and her daughter. You shall not take her daughter’s daughter, or her daughter, to uncover her shame, because they are her flesh, and such intercourse is incest.”

And again the Lord Himself says:

“Whoever lies with his stepmother or with his daughter-in-law, let both die.”

And whoever takes a woman’s mother in addition to the woman herself shall be burned alive with them. Those who have intercourse with the wife of their paternal uncle or maternal uncle shall die.

And elsewhere it is written that consanguinity is established up to the sixth degree of kinship, so that, just as the generation and condition of the human race are completed in six ages of the world, so kinship should end at the same number of degrees.

*[Note: [Col. 1037] Compare Bernard, on canons 7, 12, 13, and 21, c. 35, q. 2.]*

Let no one approach a menstruating woman, for the Lord says:

“You shall not approach a woman who is suffering her menstrual period.”

Again, in the same place:

“A woman who has a flow of blood when her month returns shall be separated for seven days. Everyone who touches her will be unclean.”

And again:

“If a man has intercourse with her during the time of her menstrual blood, he will be unclean.”

And through the prophet Ezekiel the Lord says:

“You shall not approach a menstruating woman.”

Let no one be greedy, for the Apostle says:

“Come now, you rich; weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted, and your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be a testimony against you and will eat your flesh like fire.”

And again the Apostle says:

“Neither will the greedy possess the kingdom of God.”

And the Lord says in the Gospel:

“Whoever has two tunics should give to the one who has none, and likewise with food.”

Let no one presume to take interest, for the Lord says:

“You shall not lend money to your brother at interest, nor grain, nor anything else.”

And again:

“If your brother has become poor, do not take interest from him, more than you gave.”

And the Lord says in the Gospel:

“Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you.”

Let no one possess double measures or unjust scales, for the Lord says:

“You shall not have among your possessions different weights, greater and smaller; nor shall you have in your house a larger and a smaller measure. You shall have a just and true weight; your measure shall be equal and just” (Deut. XXV, 15).

And the Lord says in the Gospel:

“What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but loses himself?”

And again the Lord Himself:

“Whatever you wish that human beings should do good to you, you also do to them.”

Likewise, do not presume to enslave a person, for the Lord says in the law:

“Whoever steals a person and sells him, and is convicted of the crime, shall die.”

And again:

“You shall not defraud your neighbor or oppress him.”

And:

“What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another.”

Let no one steal, for the Lord says in the law:

“You shall not steal.”

And the Apostle says:

“Neither will thieves possess the kingdom of God.”

And the Lord says:

“You shall not covet anything belonging to your neighbor.”

Let no one take anything from another by force or through evil cunning, for the Lord says through the prophet:

“You shall seize nothing by force.”

And the Lord says in the Gospel:

“Do not bring charges against anyone, do not practice extortion, and be content with your wages.”

And the Apostle says:

“Neither will the rapacious possess the kingdom of God.”

No one shall judge his neighbor’s case unjustly, nor, out of love for relatives and friends or for anyone else, nor because of gifts or hatred, shall anyone pervert his judgment, because in Deuteronomy the Lord says: “You shall not pervert judgment.” And through the prophet the Lord says: “Woe to those who justify the wicked for gifts and take away the justice of the righteous from him.” And the Lord in the Gospel says: “With whatever judgment you judge, you shall be judged, and with whatever measure you measure, it shall be measured back to you.”

[Col. 1039B]

Do not unjustly injure anyone, nor repay evil with evil, because the Lord says through the prophet: “You shall not grieve a human being.” And the Apostle says: “Do not repay anyone evil for evil.” And the Lord in the Gospel says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who slander you. And to the one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also. And from the one who takes away your garment, do not withhold your tunic. Give to everyone who asks of you. And: From the one who takes away what is yours, do not demand it back.”

[Col. 1039C]

Do not unjustly oppress the stranger, nor the widow, nor the orphan, nor the poor, because in Exodus the Lord says: “You shall not grieve the stranger; you shall not harm the widow and the orphan.” And again: “You shall not withhold the wage of the needy.” And in the prophet he says: “Turn your hand away from the injury of the poor.”

No one shall swear falsely, because the Lord says: “You shall not swear falsely, but you shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord.” And the Apostle says: “Do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath.” And in Solomon: “A man who swears frequently will be filled with iniquity, and sin will not depart from his house.” And the Lord in the Gospel says: “Do not swear at all, either by heaven or by earth or by your head. Let your speech be ‘yes, yes,’ ‘no, no.’ Whatever is more than these is from evil.”

[Col. 1039D]

No one shall presume to give false testimony or to consent to it, because it is written: “A false witness shall not go unpunished.” And elsewhere: “Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul.” Whoever gives false testimony is a participant with those who crucified Christ.

Do not blaspheme, because the Lord said to Moses: “Whoever blasphemes the name of the Lord shall die.” And the Lord in the Gospel says: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, either in this age or in the future.” And the Apostle says: “Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, and blasphemy be taken away from you.” Do not speak any falsehood together with every kind of malice. Everything that is a lie is sin. “The mouth that lies kills the soul.”

[Col. 1040A]

And again: “You shall destroy those who speak lies.” Flee shameful words. A single utterance quickly pollutes the mind. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. The good person brings forth good things from the good treasure; the evil person brings forth evil things from the evil treasure.”

Do not love excessive talk, because it is written in the prophet: “A talkative man shall not prosper upon the earth.” And again: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue.” And in the Gospel: “For every idle word that people speak, they shall give an account of it on the day of judgment. By your words you shall be condemned.”

No one should be quick and ready to laugh, because it is written: “Laughter shall be mingled with sorrow, and grief overtakes the end of joy.” “I counted laughter as error, and concerning joy I said: ‘It is deceived in vain.’” And again: “A fool raises his voice in laughter.”

[Col. 1040B]

And in the Gospel: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep.”

Let no one slander his neighbor. Slander is a grave sin; hence it is written: “Whoever slanders shall be uprooted from the land of the living.” And the Apostle says: “Do not slander one another, brothers.” When you slander another, examine yourself. No one would ever slander another who had rightly examined himself. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Why do you see the splinter in your brother’s eye and do not see the beam in your own eye?”

Let no one curse, because in Leviticus the Lord says: “Whoever curses his father and mother shall die.” And the Apostle says: “Do not curse.” And again he himself says: “Revilers shall not possess the kingdom of God.”

[Col. 1040C]

Let no one harbor envy against his neighbor, because it is written: “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world.” And because Christ was crucified through envy, whoever envies his neighbor crucifies Christ.

Let no one hate a human being, but rather vices and sins. Hatred excludes a person from the kingdom of God. Hence the Apostle says: “Whoever does not love remains in death. Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that every murderer does not have eternal life abiding in him.”

And the Lord in the Gospel says: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins.”

Do not stir up quarrels and scandals; flee all enmities, contentions, rivalries, disputes, dissensions, sects, and everything else of this kind, as the Apostle says: “Those who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God.”

[Col. 1040D]

Do not eat carrion [Note: [Col. 1039] Compare the Letter of Evantius on these matters], nor blood, nor animals or bees that beasts, dogs, or hawks have consumed, if they are found dead, because in Leviticus the Lord says: “You shall not eat the blood of any flesh, because the life of the flesh is in the blood. Whoever eats it, his life shall perish.” And again: “They shall not eat carrion or anything seized by a beast.” And the four decrees of the Acts of the Apostles commanded abstention from fornication, from what has been strangled, from blood, and from idolatry.

Let no one get drunk, because the Apostle says: “Drunkards shall not possess the kingdom of God.” And elsewhere: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery.” And the Lord in the Gospel says: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony, drunkenness, and worldly cares.”

[Col. 1041A]

Let no one force or importunately urge another to drink more than is proper, because the Lord says through the prophet: “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening, so that they may burn with wine.” And again: “Woe to those who are powerful at drinking wine and strong men at mixing drunkenness.” And through the prophet Joel the Lord says: “Awake, drunkards, and weep; howl, all you who drink wine to sweetness.”

People become drunk not only on wine, but also on other kinds of drink, which are prepared in various ways. Hence the Nazirite were commanded not to drink wine or *sicera*—that is, strong drink—at all, for both make people drunk and produce fleshly lust equally.

[Col. 1041B]

No woman shall take a potion to cause an abortion, lest she kill either a conceived or a newborn child; nor should women take any diabolical potions by which they may become unable to conceive. A woman who does this shall recognize herself as guilty of as many murders as she could have borne children.

[Note: [Col. 1041] Here and in what follows, compare Berardus, chapter 26, question 7.]

Do not worship idols—not stones, nor trees, nor corners, nor springs. Do not worship at crossroads, nor fulfill vows there. Do not practice or believe in enchanters, diviners, *karagii*, haruspices, fortune-tellers, seers, magicians, sorcerers, sneezers, auguries made through the ears, or any other evil and diabolical devices.

For what else is it but the worship of the devil to observe the Vulcanalia and the Kalends, to cover laurel branches, to observe one’s step, to scatter grain over a tree trunk, to throw wine and bread into a spring, for women at their looms to invoke Minerva, to observe the day of Venus or another day for weddings, or to take note of the day on which one sets out on a journey?

Do not wear *karachares*—bundled herbs—hung around yourselves or your belongings. Do not believe in storm-makers, nor give them anything on that account. Do not believe those who say that they cast impurities over roofs so that they may announce some future event to people, whether good or evil, because only God knows the future.

Do not parade about as little servants or little wagons during Lent or at any other time. Men must not wear women’s clothing, nor women men’s clothing, either at the Kalends or at any other of the many revels. Do not make or place limbs made of wood at crossroads, on trees, or elsewhere, because they can provide you with no healing.

[Col. 1041C]

When the moon is obscured, do not utter cries. Do not believe diabolical incantations, nor let anyone presume to place them upon himself. No Christian shall presume to perform dance-spectacles, songs, dancing, games, or diabolical revels—whether in a church, in houses, at a crossroads, or anywhere else.

Let no one utter from his mouth *mimaritiae* [an uncertain term], or shameful, amorous, or lustful words. Do not believe or worship any diabolical amulets or any of the things mentioned above; do not fulfill their vows or render them any honor, because in Exodus the Lord says: “You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness of what is in heaven above, or on earth below, or of what is in the waters under the earth. You shall not worship them or serve them.”

[Col. 1042A]

And again: “Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be killed, except to the Lord alone.” And in Leviticus the Lord says: “You shall not practice divination or observe dreams.” And again in Deuteronomy: “Let there not be found among you one who raises up diviners, or observes dreams or omens; nor a sorcerer, enchanter, consulter of *python* spirits, or seer, nor one who seeks truth from the dead. For the Lord abhors all these things.”

And again the Lord says: “A woman shall not wear men’s clothing, nor a man use women’s clothing; for whoever does these things is abominable before God.” And again: “Cursed is the person who makes a carved image.”

And the Prophet says: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let not your prophets who are among you and your diviners deceive you. Do not pay attention to your dreams which you dream, for they prophesy falsehood to you.” But worship and honor the triune and one God.

Bring to the holy Church offerings, little candles, oil, incense, firstfruits, tithes, alms, and all your goods. Keep the splendid solemnities and the Lord’s days, and the feasts of the holy martyrs and confessors. Come to keep vigil, to worship God, to hear Mass, and to receive the sacrifice, according to what sacred Scripture says.

[Col. 1042B]

Let no one presume to chatter in the Church itself or wherever the divine reading is being recited; instead, gladly hear the sacred readings, as the Lord says through Moses: “Hear, O Israel, and be silent.”

Do not despise the Lord’s Day, but observe it with reverence. Do not perform servile work on it—that is, work in a field, meadow, or vineyard, or any other heavy labor. Do not bring lawsuits or speak accusations against one another on the Lord’s Day, except only what is necessary for preparing food to restore the body, because this Lord’s Day was created first; on it darkness was removed and light appeared, the elements of the world were formed, and the angels were created.

[Col. 1042C]

On this day the people were freed from the land of Egypt, as from the darkness of sins, as though through the baptismal font and the Red Sea. On this day heavenly food, that is, manna, was first given to human beings. Concerning it Moses commanded the people: “You shall observe the first and the last day.” Concerning it the Prophet says: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.”

On this day Christ also rose from the dead; on this day the Holy Spirit descended from heaven upon the apostles. It is therefore called the Lord’s Day, so that on it, abstaining from earthly works and the allurements of the world, we may serve only the divine worship.

[Col. 1042D]

Therefore we ask you: since so many and such great sacred testimonies are spoken concerning this day, keep that day, as is fitting for Christians and as it is written, with great honor and diligence, in the love of Christ, in return for eternal life.

Let no one withhold tithes from all his fruits, because in Exodus the Lord says: “You shall not delay offering your tithes and your firstfruits.” And in Leviticus: “All the tithes of the land, whether of the fruits or of the produce of trees, belong to the Lord; the oxen, sheep, and goats that pass under the shepherd’s rod—whatever comes tenth shall be sanctified to the Lord. It shall not be selected, whether good or bad, nor shall one exchange it for another. If anyone changes it, both the thing exchanged and its replacement shall be sanctified to the Lord, and it shall not be redeemed.”

[Col. 1043A]

And in Exodus: “You shall bring the firstfruits of your land into the house of the Lord your God.”

Let no one delay fulfilling what he has vowed to the Lord, because in Numbers the Lord says: “When you make a vow to the Lord your God, you shall not delay fulfilling it, because the Lord your God will require it of you, and if you delay, it will be counted as sin against you. But if you do not wish to promise, you will be without sin. You shall observe and do what you have promised to the Lord your God by your own will and with your mouth.”

No one, after committing capital sins, shall presume to communicate in the body and blood of the Lord before making his confession and practicing true penance through the counsel of a priest, according to ecclesiastical order, because in Leviticus the Lord says: “Every person from your offspring who approaches the consecrated things which the children of Israel have offered to the Lord, while uncleanness is in him, shall perish before the Lord, because I am the Lord.”

[Col. 1043B]

And the Apostle says: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood. Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink from the cup; for whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body. For this reason many among you are weak and sick, and many have fallen asleep.”

Let no Christian allow himself to withdraw or remain away for long from the body and blood of Christ, because the Lord says in the Gospel: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever; and the bread which I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.” And again: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.” And again: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.”

[Col. 1043C]

Therefore I admonish you: any Christian who has committed a serious offense after baptism must make a pure confession to a priest and practice true penance; after performing his penance, at the time appointed for him by the priest, he must offer his offering to the priest and receive communion in the body and blood of Christ.

[Col. 1043D]

Therefore, dearest ones, let us consider what is written: “Contraries are healed by contraries.” And what the Lord says through the Prophet: “Cease to act perversely and learn to do good.” And again: “Turn away from evil and do good.” And the Apostle says: “Strip off the old person and put on the new.” And again: “Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good.” And again: “Take up the breastplate of righteousness and the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” And this: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near.”

Let us therefore lay aside the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light; let us walk honorably as in the day. Behold how the merciful Lord admonishes us to turn from evil to good.

I therefore beseech you, brothers, that whoever has done any of the things mentioned above, or similar things, against the Lord’s command, never despair of mercy, because the Lord says through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.”

[Col. 1044A]

But each person should, with right faith, give a pure confession to the priest, as has already been said, and perform true penance; he should perfectly mourn what he has done wrongly and amend himself through righteous labor, alms, and good works. Let him take care not to sin again, because it is written: “Wash yourselves; be clean.” And: “Whoever hides his crimes shall not prosper. But whoever confesses and abandons them shall obtain mercy.” And this: “When you have turned and groaned, then you shall be saved.”

And in the Gospel: “Repent; the kingdom of heaven has drawn near to you.” And the Apostle says: “Confess your sins to one another.”

[Col. 1044B]

And therefore, dearest ones, since the Lord admonishes us through so many testimonies and commandments written above to cease from every evil work and turn to every good work, why are we so slow to turn or amend ourselves, when, by the Lord’s help, remedies are within our power, since the merciful Lord promises us forgiveness in the present time and eternal glory in the future?

Let us therefore consider, brothers, what the Lord says through the prophet: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day; you do not know what the coming day will bring; from morning until evening the time will change.” And elsewhere: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” And the Lord in the Gospel: “See that your flight does not take place in winter or on the Sabbath.”

[Col. 1044C]

And again: “Watch and pray, for you do not know the day or the hour.” And the Apostle says: “For what is your life? It is a vapor appearing for a little while and then vanishing.”

Therefore, as the days pass, our end will draw near. We admonish and beseech you, dearest brothers, that whoever was greedy or avaricious, and had harmed someone by evil means or unjustly retained his possessions, should become generous in almsgiving, because the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow.”

And the same Lord says: “Fool, this night your soul is demanded of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” And the Apostle said: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these.” And elsewhere: “Whoever possesses the goods of the world and sees his brother in need but closes his heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him?”

[Col. 1044D]

And again the Lord in the Gospel: “Give alms from what remains, and behold, everything will be clean for you.” And again the Lord: “Sell what you possess and give alms, and make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven.”

Whoever was drunk and gluttonous should become sober and abstinent, frugal and sparing in food and drink, as it is written: “Has cheerful flesh drawn us to guilt? Let afflicted flesh lead us back to forgiveness.” It is better to take little daily than to consume a great amount rarely. And the Apostle fasted frequently, and Christ fasted, who committed no sin, and he himself said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst.” And again: “Blessed are you who hunger, for you shall be satisfied.”

Whoever was a fornicator, lustful, or adulterous should become pure and chaste or continent, because the Apostle says: “Your bodies are members of Christ.” And again: “Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit.” Flee fornication. And again: “Therefore glorify God in your body.”

[Col. 1045A]

And again he himself says: “Brothers, you are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you. If anyone destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him; for the temple of God is holy, and that is what you are.”

Whoever was angry should become patient, as the Lord said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” And again: “By your patience you will possess your souls.” And the Apostle says: “Be patient toward all.”

Whoever was sad because of temporal losses or worldly cares should become cheerful and rejoice because of eternal goods and promises, because the Lord says in the Gospel:

[Col. 1045B]

“When people hate you, and when they separate you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil because of the Son of Man, rejoice on that day and exult. For behold, your reward is great in heaven.”

And again: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world”—where there is unfailing light and everlasting joy. And the Apostle says: “Rejoice in the Lord always.” And again he himself says: “Rejoice always in all things.”

Whoever was *acedia*-ridden—that is, idle—should work with his own hands or labor at some useful craft, so that he may have something for himself and give to others for eternal glory, as it is written: “Honor the Lord your God from your righteous labors, and offer him from the fruits of righteousness.” And the Prophet says: “You shall eat the labor of your hands; you are blessed, and it shall be well with you.”

[Col. 1045C]

And the Apostle says: “These hands served my needs and those who were with me.” And the Lord says: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”

Whoever did something for empty glory or human praise should begin to please God alone through good works, for the sake of eternal recompense and heavenly glory, as the Apostle says: “Whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.” And again: “Let no one glory in human beings.” And again: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?”

And the Lord says: “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing, so that your almsgiving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you openly.”

[Col. 1045D]

And elsewhere it is written: “Nothing for temporal reputation, but everything for God; not for fame, but for eternal life,” as the Apostle says: “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

Whoever was proud should become humble, as it is written: “Humility never suffers ruin and never incurs downfall.” Be despised in your own eyes. Whoever displeases himself pleases God. The more despised you are before human eyes, the more precious you will be before the eyes of God.

Recognize that the Lord came in humility, because he humbled himself in the form of a servant. Hence the Apostle says: “In humility consider others superior to yourselves,” and the rest: “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and becoming in the likeness of human beings” [lacuna] “as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death.” And the rest.

[Col. 1046A]

And the Lord himself says: “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted.” And elsewhere: “The more humble you are, the more the height of glory will follow you.” And again the Lord himself: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart.”

Whoever was a thief should become useful; whoever was sleepy should become watchful; whoever was double-tongued should become good-speaking; whoever was a slanderer or envious should become pure and kind; whoever was occupied in idle words and evil works should persevere in good speech and holy works.

Whoever once entangled himself in just causes and came late to church should now return to it more frequently and devote himself to sacred prayers. Whoever was unbelieving should become faithful, as it is written: “It was counted to him as righteousness.” And elsewhere: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace, and sin no more.”

But against each vice or sin—which would take too long to enumerate here—we must fight with contrary virtues and good works, with God’s help, because one must first abandon evil and then do good.

And so that the things we have mentioned above may remain firmly fixed in your hearts and minds, we briefly recall them to your memory. For we believe that whoever faithfully hears and believes and fulfills these things in good works can be saved through God’s power and mercy, as has already been said.

Brothers, believe in God the almighty Father, creator of heaven and earth; believe also in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, and so forth.

[Col. 1046B]

See, brothers: just as our Lord Jesus Christ, having suffered at the age of thirty, rose from the dead on the third day, so all of us, the entire human race, whatever age we died at—whether as a child, an old person, or having been made alive and then died in the mother’s womb—shall all rise at the age of thirty. We shall all come to judgment, sinners and righteous alike.

The righteous, and those who were sinners but performed true penance and persevered in good works, shall receive the kingdom of God in the flesh, because God’s judgment is just: that soul and flesh which in the present life performed true penance, endured suffering for Christ, and persevered in good works—those same flesh and soul shall rejoice with Christ and all the saints in paradise, with the holy angels.

[Col. 1046C]

As the Lord says in the Gospel: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world, because I was hungry and you gave me food,” and the rest of the good works.

[Col. 1046D]

“Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of God.”

But to the sinners he will say: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels, because I was hungry and you did not give me food,” and the rest of the good works which they did not perform.

For this too is God’s just judgment: that the flesh and soul which sinned here in the present life, did not perform true penance, and persevered in evil works—those same flesh and soul shall be tormented in hell, because the Lord says in the Gospel: “Gather the weeds into bundles to burn them.”

[Col. 1047A]

The weeds are sinful human beings.
