Hell must burn sinful human beings: “Bind the bundles to burn them”—that is, murderers with murderers, adulterers with adulterers, the rapacious with the rapacious—so that whoever here were alike in guilt will likewise be alike there in torments. The greater the sins people have committed, the more fiercely the eternal fire will burn against them.

Believe, therefore, dearest ones, in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God in Trinity. Love him with all your heart and all your mind, and love your neighbors as yourselves.

Let no one among you commit murder, adultery, fornication, or lust. Flee uncleanness and immodesty. You shall not steal; you shall not covet your neighbor’s property; you shall not give false testimony. Do not carry anger through to completion; do not keep wrath until evening, but return to peace before sunset.

[Col. 1047B]

Do not retain deceit or malice in your hearts. Do not make a false peace among yourselves. Do not lie to one another. Do not swear or swear falsely. Do not repay evil with evil. Do not act unjustly, injuriously, or wrongly toward anyone; but if someone injures you, endure it patiently for God’s sake.

Love your enemies and pray for them. Do not curse; and if someone curses you, do not curse in return, but bless all the more. Endure persecution for the sake of righteousness.

Do not hate anyone, but hate vices and sins. Do not be proud or drunk; do not pursue the appetite of concupiscence. Do not be sleepy, lazy, or devoted to idleness.

[Col. 1047C]

Do not slander one another. Do not be murmurers. Do not love excessive talk or varied words. Do not love excessive laughter, but mourn your sins and negligences with tears and groaning [lacuna] day and night, imploring God’s mercy in prayer, so that he may forgive your past and present evils and command you to guard yourselves from future sin.

Do not practice idolatry, sorcery, enmities, contentions, rivalries, disputes, hostilities, provocations, heresies, envy, jealousy, banquets, or other such things, because the Apostle testifies that you must not do these things.

Whatever God commanded through sacred Scripture that a person must not do, no Christian shall presume to do. And whoever has acted against God’s command must quickly amend himself through pure confession and true penance, with good works and righteous alms, before death suddenly snatches him away.

[Col. 1047D]

Observe in every respect everything that God commanded through sacred Scripture. Love your friends in the love of God, and love your enemies for God’s sake.

Wherever you are, pray without ceasing, as the Apostle says, and give thanks to God in all things. Come frequently to the Church with devoted spirit and right faith, especially on all the Lord’s days, and attend all the splendid feasts, both the evening vigils and the morning services, as well as the celebration of Mass.

Let no one dare bring cases for judgment there, conduct business, or utter idle stories from his mouth. Flee dances, dancing, and shameful or lustful songs like a diabolical arrow. Do not presume to perform them in the churches, in your houses, in the streets, or anywhere else, because this has remained from pagan custom.

[Col. 1048A]

Do not believe or worship any diabolical amulets, enchanters, diviners, *karagii*, haruspices, seers, fortune-tellers, magicians, sorcerers, omen-readers, storm-makers, or any other evil practices together with the diabolical devices mentioned above. Do not fulfill vows to them or render them any honor.

Instead, come together in the holy Church. In the Church, pray and sing psalms silently in your hearts, and attend carefully to the word of God and sacred Scripture, so that you may be as Scripture says: meditate on the law of God day and night. Fulfill your good vows to God in the churches.

[Col. 1048B]

Bring the firstfruits of all your crops to the priests for blessing, and afterward eat from them. Give tithes from all your fruits and livestock to the churches every year. From the nine parts that remain to you, give alms; by these redeem your sins, as it is written: “Almsgiving delivers from death, and it itself purifies sins” (Tobit 12:9).

Whoever is rich and possesses much should give much, as it is written: “From the one to whom more has been entrusted, more will be required.” And the Apostle says: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these”—that is, rational food and clothing, as much as is necessary, not as much as wicked desire seeks. Whatever remains must be given as alms for the sake of eternal life.

[Col. 1048C]

Whoever is poorer should give a little according to his ability, because the poor widow was praised by the Lord more than the rich for two coins, and the Lord promised that the reward for a cup of cold water would not be lost. Whoever has no possessions from which to give alms should have a good will; that good will itself will be counted as the deed.

When you come together at church, give the poor, according to your means, either money or something else. Give incense, little candles, and oil for the church lamps, as much as you are able, because the Lord says: “You shall not appear before me empty-handed.”

Offer the offerings consecrated on the altars, and after performing penance and being reconciled according to the priest’s counsel, communicate from them. And abstain from your own wives for several days beforehand, so that you may receive the holy sacrifice with a pure heart.

[Col. 1048D]

Honor your priests and obey them according to God, as the Lord says: “Whoever hears you hears me.”

Let a son and daughter honor their father and mother. Likewise, all Christians, honor one another, as it is written: “Anticipate one another in showing honor.”

Give food to the hungry and drink to the thirsty. Receive guests, especially the poor and strangers, into your houses; show them kindness and wash their feet. Clothe the naked, assist those in tribulation, comfort the sorrowful, visit the sick, bury the dead, visit those in prison, and minister to them from your goods.

[Col. 1049A]

Help widows and orphans in their tribulations. Give assistance, as far as you can, to the poor and to all who are oppressed by wicked people or by an unjust judgment.

Always preserve right judgment and justice. Show mercy in all things. Have and preserve peace with everyone, and recall those who are at odds to harmony.

Hold the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer yourselves, and teach them to your sons and daughters, so that they too may hold them.

Know that you have become sponsors before God for the children whom you received from the font in baptism. Therefore always teach and admonish them, and frequently warn and correct all your dependents, so that they may live soberly, chastely, and justly; correct them immediately.

[Col. 1049B]

Speak truth from your heart and mouth. Maintain chastity and continence. Practice sobriety and moderation in drink and food. Love fasting. Honor your elders. Love your young people spiritually in the love of Christ, and be patient toward all.

Do good to those who hate you. Let charity and joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, hope, faith, modesty, gentleness, continence, chastity, and love be in you, and preserve these qualities in good thoughts, words, and holy works.

Hold to humility. Observe everything. Place all your hope in the Lord. When you see something good in yourselves, attribute it to God’s glory, for he gave it to you, not to your own praise. And when you see evil in yourselves, know that it has been done by you through your own fault and negligence.

Fear the day of judgment and dread Gehenna. Desire eternal life. Guard your thoughts, words, and works always toward the good, day and night.

[Col. 1049C]

Always expect your passage from this world, which draws nearer every day. Fulfill God’s commandments daily in your deeds, and never despair of God’s mercy. What one does not want done to oneself, let one not do to another; and as you want people to do good to you, you also do likewise to them.

Preserve charity in all things, which is love of God and neighbor.

No one should deceive himself, brothers: every person who, after baptism, commits mortal crimes—murder and adultery, fornication, theft, false testimony, perjury, drunkenness, or other similar mortal crimes—if he does not perform penance, give proper alms, and persevere in good works, will never enter the kingdom of God nor possess eternal glory. He will descend with the devil into hell, because the Apostle says: “Those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God.” Accordingly, it is written: “God by no means spares those who offend,” because he either strikes the sinner with a temporal scourge for purification, leaves him to be punished by eternal judgment, or the person himself purges by punishment what he has wrongly committed. Thus, then, it is true that God does not spare the offender. And elsewhere it is written: “God leaves no sins unpunished,” that is, without vengeance, because certainly either we punish our sins here through penance, or God punishes them through the severity of his judgment.

And believe this most certainly: every person, however sinful or criminal he may have been, however many evils he may have committed, if he performs true penance, gives proper alms, and death finds him in good devotion with righteous works, will never go to hell. Rather, he is lifted by angels into heaven and will possess eternal glory. Hence the Lord said: “He will not be judged twice for the same thing.” And the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged by the Lord”; that is, the one who here, in the present life, judges himself through penance for the judgment will not again be judged when he reaches the end of this present life. Hence it is written: “If we perform perfect penance, God not only forgives our faults but, after our faults, promises rewards.”

Therefore, brothers, let us now hasten to amend our lives, so that whatever we have done wrongly against God’s commandment, we may mourn and correct, and no longer sin. Let us preserve ourselves in good will and right thought, with holy words and works, with the help and guidance of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## A.D. 760. Cyprian, monk of Cassino.

[Col. 1049]

## Historical Notice.

*(Peter the Deacon, Book on Illustrious Men, chapter 7.)*

[Col. 1049C] Cyprian, a priest, became a monk under Abbot Petronax in the same monastery of Cassino. He composed a hymn about the miracles of Saint Benedict, to be sung on Benedict’s feast. He flourished in the time of the emperors Leo, Constantine, and Irene.

[Col. 1051]

## Hymn on Saint Benedict.

*(From Prospero Martinengo and Sacred Italy, volume II.)*

[Col. 1051A]

With the golden ray of the sun everlasting  
the whole world is adorned on this day,  
so that, blessed Benedict, at your festivals  
it may appear more radiant.

Rich in wondrous deeds,  
the signs of virtues, the special gift  
of your Rule, offer you praises  
through everlasting time.

He shines forth from tender years  
in the character by which you ordered your life,  
when you gave your inmost heart  
to no pleasure.

A broken vessel is restored first  
in triumph, a woman’s loss;  
as a boy, by your tearful prayer  
you restored it sound.

Quickly displaying a holy way of life,  
you abandon your studies and your father’s possessions,  
flee, and are blessed  
with a wholesome garment.

You had cherished your limbs in a small cave  
for nine times four months,  
remaining there known to no human being,  
but to One alone.

Festivals pleasing to you by the divine will  
bring you food; though hidden, you are seen.  
Fame spreads, every wound of the mind  
perishes through the wound of the flesh.

Hence the sign of the cross breaks  
a glass vessel of poison; the wandering mind is driven away  
at the touch of a little rod; from hollowed marble  
water flows.

The iron leaps back onto its handle;  
soft water guides human steps,  
where Placidus, swept away [probably *raptus* for printed *ruptus*], is said  
to have seen your sheepskin cloak (*melotes*).

A beloved bird carried the dreadful food;  
you weep greatly, moved by the death of the guilty enemy.  
Leaving your customary place, you sought  
the pleasant Liris.

*[Note: Liris, also called Carnellus, is a river of Campania that flows along the Cassino territory on the southern side. Consult the notes of Angelo de Nuce on chapter 5 of Book I of the Cassino Chronicle.]*

The slippery serpent rages upon the spread altar;  
it increases the burden and rattles with false fire,  
but is powerless to oppose  
the work begun.

Limbs torn apart by the collapsed wall  
are restored to health; the wrong secretly done  
is shown to the brothers, and the king’s  
craft is revealed [F., “cunning”].

Poison kills the one who tasted it, and the ruin  
of the chosen seat is exposed; spirits are seized,  
and a serpent is seen hiding, snatched away  
with the wine.

You reproach the brother for the vain thing he did;  
you inspect the utterly rebellious table [probably *mensam* for printed *mensem*].  
You disclose the abundance, and, heavy with sleep,  
you advise the informer.

The earth drove the treacherous bodies far away;  
the dragon stopped the wanderer; the royal ulcer withdrew;  
coins took their place, and the dreadful  
plague fled.

What falls as glass proves to be safe;  
vessels produce oil; the water-serpent  
is driven away by the right hand, and the vision  
releases the bonds of the hands.

When the boy was restored to life,  
you saw the soul of your sister enter  
the heavenly dwelling, and, as though beneath  
a single ray of the sun, you saw everything.

The holy bishop climbs through the burning sphere;  
you are the way, heaven, flashing with torches,  
when April approaches on the ninth day  
after the Kalends.

The joyful choir of angels sings you,  
as do patriarchs, apostles,  
and prophets, blessed by merits  
on every side.

So that this people may remember this praise,  
here you are gladly called father.  
Teach them fittingly, refresh them generously,  
and grant them access to heaven.

Christ, reward of devoted labor,  
grant that we may be helped by the prayer  
of this man, whose example made us abandon  
the doomed filth of the world.

May this hymn of ours, Benedict our prince,  
always be pleasing to you,  
you who are the salvation, light, honor,  
and everlasting praise of your monks.

The precious goal of the heavenly King  
makes you famous through true trophies.  
Therefore we continually seek you,  
in great numbers, night and day.

May glory remain with the exalted Father,  
and a sacred diadem with his Son,  
and with you, equal power of both,  
gracious Spirit. Amen.

## A.D. 766. Saint Chrodegang, Bishop of Metz.

[Col. 1053]

## Historical Notice on Saint Chrodegang.

*(Fabricius, Library of the Middle and Later Ages.)*

[Col. 1053A] Chrodegang—also called Chrotgangus, Grodegangus, Crodogandus, and Crodogangus [Note: See Charles le Cointe, volume V of the Annals of the Franks, p. 74], Ruggandus by Trithemius in chapter 255 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and Rotgangus in the epitaph preserved by Mabillon, volume I, p. 425 (new edition, p. 377)—was named as follows:

“Rotgangus was his name; Christ was his glory.”

He was the nephew of King Pepin through his sister and was bishop of Metz from 743 to 766. Concerning him, besides the works of the Sammarthani in volume III of *Christian Gaul*, p. 711; the *Acts of the Saints* for 6 March; the *Benedictine Acts of the Saints*, section III, part II, p. 204; and the *Life of Chrodegang* published from a thirteenth-century manuscript of Wolfenbüttel by Johann Georg Eccard in volume I of the *Würzburg Writers*, p. 912, see also Martin Meurisse, Bishop of Madaura, in his *History of the Bishops of Metz*, published in French at Metz in 1634, folio.

He wrote a Rule for the clergy of Metz to observe, following in many respects the traces of the Rule of Saint Benedict. Lucas d’Achery published it divided into eighty-six chapters at Paris in 1654, in quarto, volume I of the *Spicilegium*, p. 205 (new edition, volume I, p. 565). But Labbe, in volume VII of the Councils, p. 1444, published another version of thirty-four chapters, less interpolated and more consistent, from the Sirmond manuscript; Hardouin published it from Labbe in volume IV, p. 1181; and most recently Colet published it in the Venetian edition of the Councils, volume IX, following the Council of Aachen of 816, together with that interpolated Rule of the Canons, assembled from Chrodegang, that Council of Aachen, and other sources.

Charles le Cointe likewise published an authentic version in volume V of the *Annals of the Church of the Franks*, under the year 737, pp. 567–587, from a manuscript collated with the editions of d’Achery and Labbe. [Col. 1053C] Paul Warnefrid says more about this Chrodegang in his fragment on the bishops of Metz, preserved by André du Chesne in volume I of the *Frankish Affairs*, p. 204 and following, where mention is also made of the rule established for the clergy, as likewise in Sigebert, chapter 78.

John Morin had published several excerpts from that Rule before d’Achery, in his collection of penitential booklets, appended to his work *On the Discipline of the Ancient Church in the Administration of Penance*. That work, after the Paris edition of 1651, was reprinted at Brussels in 1685 and at Venice in 1702, folio.

Finally, besides the editors of the Councils—Labbe, Hardouin, and Colet—the praised le Cointe offers, under the year 756, Chrodegang’s Privilege for the Abbey of Gorze in volume V, p. 562. On the Roman chant of the Psalms, introduced by Chrodegang first into Metz and then into other churches of Gaul, see Henry Warton’s supplement to Usher’s *On Sacred Vernacular Languages*, p. 358.

## Epitaph of Chrodegang, Bishop of Metz.

*(Mabillon, New Analecta, p. 377.)*

[Col. 1054B]

Whoever comes here from the west, or whoever comes from the east,  
know that here lie the ashes of a devout bishop.

This urn holds an outstanding man,  
adorned in character and upright on the path of virtues.

His deeds were holy, his meditation the law, his doctrine faithful;  
Rotgangus was his name; Christ was his glory.

From the Roman see he received the sacred pallium,  
and that Father raised him among the Fathers.

Here he established the clergy in the duties of holy life;  
in the Church he was its light and honor.

By example and by words he sent minds toward the heavenly kingdom,  
and he flourished greatly in so noble an art.

Retaining the virtues and avoiding the monsters of vice,  
the pinnacle of episcopal dignity flourished fully in him.

He was a comforter to widows and a protector to the wretched;  
the orphaned crowd also recognized him as a father.

Welcomed by kings and revered by all the people,  
his life was a model of salvation for everyone.

After completing the course of his life,  
when old age had come, he gave earth to earth  
and sent his soul to the stars.

[Col. 1053]

## Testimonies of the Ancients Concerning Saint Chrodegang.

[Col. 1053C] Sigebert of Gembloux, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 78:

“Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, the nephew of King Pepin through his sister, ennobling the nobility of his lineage by the fervor of holy religion, wrote a Rule, which he specifically gave to the clergy of the Church of Metz to observe.” [Col. 1055A] It is therefore different from the one that has been printed—that is, from our version—which displays the clearest traces of the city of Metz in many places.

Paul the Deacon, in his book on the bishops of the Church of Metz, volume II of the *Frankish Histories*:

“From this point the outstanding bishop Chrodegang, deserving of every praise, was chosen. He was born in the district of Hasbania, to his father Sigramnus and his mother Landrada, both descended from the first nobility of the Frankish race. He was brought up by Charles the Mayor of the Palace himself and became his referendary; finally, in the time of King Pepin, he earned episcopal dignity.

“He was altogether illustrious and radiant with every nobility, handsome in appearance, most eloquent in speech, and trained both in his native language and in Latin. He nourished the servants of God and was not only a provider for orphans and widows but also their most merciful protector. Since he was wealthy in every respect and had been singled out by King Pepin and the entire assembly of the Franks, he was sent to Rome, and, as everyone earnestly desired, summoned the venerable Pope Stephen to Gaul.

“He gathered the clergy together and made them live within the enclosure of the cloister in the manner of a monastery. He established a rule for them concerning how they ought to serve in the Church, and generously supplied them with food and the necessities of life, so that, having no need to occupy themselves with perishable business, they might devote themselves solely to the divine offices. He also ordered that this clergy, abundantly instructed in divine law and imbued with Roman chant, should observe the custom and order of the Roman Church—something that had by no means been done until that time in the Church of Metz.”

Then, omitting many other matters concerning the churches founded by him:

“He governed the Church of Metz for twenty-three years, five months, and five days. He died on the day before the Nones of March, in the time of King Pepin. He rests in the monastery of Gorze, which he built from its foundations.”

Anastasius, librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the life of Pope Stephen III:

“When the cities and provinces of the Romans were being grievously oppressed by the king of the Lombards, suddenly Chrodegang, abbot, arrived as envoy of Pepin, king of the Franks, through whom he sent word that he would fulfill every wish and request of the most holy pope mentioned above.” And shortly afterward:

“Immediately the aforesaid envoys of Pepin, king of the Franks, arrived together—namely, Chrodegang the bishop and Autchar the duke—so that they might bring the aforesaid most holy pope to his king in Francia, as he had requested through his message.”

And near the end:

“While he was in Francia, he bestowed the pallium upon Chrodegang, the most holy bishop, and ordained him archbishop.”

## Rule of the Canons According to d’Achery’s Recension

[Col. 1055]

## Lucas d’Achery’s Prefatory Notice to His Following Rule of Saint Chrodegang.

*(d’Achery’s* Spicilegium, *volume I.)*

[Col. 1055C] The Fathers of the Council of Aachen, celebrated in the year of salvation 816, valued this Rule of Chrodegang—or Codegrand—so highly that whatever could contribute to the canonical formation of clerical conduct they transferred into their own decrees, although suppressing his name. I have not failed to indicate this in the notes.

The Rule of Saint Benedict, the strictest—indeed, evangelical—master of life (I use the words of Gregory the Great [Book IV of the *Register*, chapter 9]), disciple of the supreme Truth, had become so deeply fixed in Codegrand’s mind and memory that, in composing laws for the canons, he repeatedly made its words, sentences, periods, and even chapters his own. He merely substituted the name “canon” for “monk,” being more indulgent toward clerics in order not to hinder them.

Nor is this surprising, since that Rule, once inspired by divine power but afterward treated with utter contempt through human folly, was cultivated with greater zeal in its author’s age and spread far and wide. The venerable bishop seems to suggest that Benedict was filled with the spirit of all the righteous (the same is said in *Dialogues*, Book II, chapter 8), so that his Rule, like that little spring which grew into a river (Esther 10:6), sprinkled and watered the whole Western Church in many ways (Baronius, under the year 529). Thus those devoted to divine contemplation, ecclesiastical duties, and secular affairs could draw abundantly from the water of saving wisdom (Ecclesiasticus 15:3), springing up into eternal life (John 4:14).

I offer the learned reader things already better known: the councils resound with them, the Fathers resound with them, and almost countless historians resound with them.

[Col. 1056C] From the fact that Codegrand possessed the holy Rule so readily, one may infer either that he had very frequently handled it and committed it to memory, or even that he had entered the Benedictine fellowship, as certain writers affirm. Although this argument might perhaps not persuade those unfamiliar with the Rule, it carries great weight among us who are steeped in it. A Frenchman or Spaniard easily recognizes an idiom of his own language that a foreigner neither notices nor penetrates; likewise, the style and words of Saint Benedict cannot deceive us.

Whatever the truth may be, let us hear Paul Warnefrid, an author of the highest quality and Chrodegang’s equal, who raises him to the highest praise in summary and speaks of the Rule of the Canons:

“From this point the outstanding bishop Chrodegang, deserving of every praise, was chosen. He was born in the district of Hasbania, to his father Sigramnus and his mother Landrada, descended from the first nobility of the Franks. He was brought up by Charles the Mayor of the Palace himself and became his referendary; finally, in the time of King Pepin, he earned episcopal dignity.

“He was altogether illustrious and radiant with every nobility; handsome in appearance, most eloquent in speech, and trained both in his native language and in Latin. He nourished the servants of God and was not only a provider for orphans and widows but also their most merciful protector. Since he was wealthy in every respect and had been singled out by King Pepin and the entire assembly of the Franks, he was sent to Rome and, as everyone earnestly desired, summoned the venerable Pope Stephen to Gaul.

“He gathered the clergy together and made them live within the enclosure of the cloister in the manner of a monastery, and established a rule for them concerning how they ought to serve in the Church. He generously supplied them with food and the necessities of life, so that, having no need to occupy themselves with perishable business, they might devote themselves solely to the divine offices. He also ordered that the clergy, abundantly instructed in divine law and imbued with Roman chant, should observe the custom and order of the Roman Church—a practice that had by no means existed until then in the Church of Metz.

“Together with the assistance of King Pepin, he ordered the seat of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr to be built, with its altar, screens, presbytery, and surrounding arches. Likewise, he ordered a presbytery to be made in the great church of blessed Peter. He also constructed an ambo decorated with gold and silver, and arches surrounding the throne before the altar.

“Moreover, he built a monastery in the parish of Saint Stephen, in the district of the Moselle, in honor of the most blessed Apostle Peter. He endowed it with great wealth, established monks there, and united them in one charity under the Rule of the holy Father Benedict. He also built another monastery called Gorze, where he likewise gathered a considerable number of monks.

“Finally, he requested from Paul, the Roman pontiff, the bodies of three holy martyrs: that of blessed Gorgonius, which rests at Gorze; that of blessed Nabor, which was buried in the monastery of Hilary; and that of blessed Nazarius, which he placed beyond the Rhine River in the monastery called Lorsch, where a basilica of wondrous beauty had been built in honor of that martyr.

“This estate had formerly been given to the same Bishop Chrodegang, for the benefit of Saint Stephen, by Chilliswindis, a once-devout woman, and her son Cancro. This blessed man was generous in almsgiving, pure in charity, and a receiver of guests and pilgrims.

“But since it would be lengthy to recount in order all the good works he performed, let it suffice to have touched on these few among the many. He consecrated very many bishops in different cities, as well as priests, deacons, and the other ecclesiastical orders, according to the custom of the Roman Church, on the Saturdays of the four seasons of the year.

“He governed the Church of Metz for twenty-three years, five months, and five days. He died on the day before the Nones of March, in the time of King Pepin. He rests in the monastery of Gorze, which he built from its foundations.”

[Col. 1058B] Thus far Paul the Deacon, in the fragment on the bishops of the Church of Metz, in André du Chesne’s *Writers of Frankish History*, volume II, p. 204.

[Col. 1057]

## Rule of the Canons of Saint Chrodegang, Bishop of Metz, According to d’Achery’s Recension (C)

## Preface

[Col. 1057C] In the time of the most devout and serene Pepin, Chrodegang, servant of the servants of God and bishop of the city of Metz:

If the authority of the canons of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, and of the other holy Fathers, had remained inviolate, and if bishop and clergy lived according to the standard of their rectitude, it would seem superfluous for us, insignificant and least of all, to reconsider or say anything new about a matter so orderly established. But since the negligence of pastors and subjects has grown excessively in these times, what else can we do, having come into so grave a danger, except, insofar as we can—if not insofar as we ought—with God’s inspiration, bring our clergy back to the line of rectitude?

[Col. 1057D] After I had obtained the episcopal chair of this see and begun to keep watch over the care of my pastoral office, and had seen that the clergy and people had fallen into such great negligence, I began sorrowfully to ask myself what I ought to do. But supported by divine assistance, helped by the consolation of spiritual brothers, and encouraged by the prospect of restoration, I wished—compelled by necessity—to make a small decree by which the clergy might restrain themselves from unlawful practices, abandon their vices, and leave behind evils long and widely usurped, so that, when the mind had been emptied of its accustomed vices, good and excellent things might more easily be implanted.

For, intent upon the sacred Scriptures, we decree that all should be united in the divine offices, constant in sacred readings, ready for obedience to their bishop and provost as the canonical order demands, joined together in charity, united by good zeal and the most fervent love, and removed from quarrels, scandals, and hatred. Whoever is their pastor should care not only for their bodily needs but also for their spiritual needs, and should exercise the most vigilant concern in both respects, insofar as he has the ability, so that he may repress vices and hasten to cut them out at the root as soon as they begin to arise, insofar as he can. He should also strive to provide them with whatever is necessary for human use according to the form set out below.

Thus, when Christ—the Shepherd of shepherds and Judge of the living and the dead—on the last and dreadful day sits upon the seat of his majesty to judge all nations, and all the clergy behold him with unveiled face, we may perhaps not deserve to hear, together with the chief shepherds and the flocks entrusted to them, the words spoken for talents entrusted and spiritual profits multiplied: “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21). At least let this be granted: that full forgiveness of sins may be bestowed, because it is clear to whom the forgiveness of sins is granted in full. No unhappy person can be judged who has received whatever portion in paradise; but the lot there is given to those who, insofar as they can, hasten toward it through the merit of their life during the course of this age, while it is still possible to run.

[Col. 1059A] Let us therefore direct our minds toward this, insofar as we can, since we cannot do so insofar as we ought, and let our life grow bitter in penance, lest divine vengeance—which is now gentle and waits—afterward rage in punishment.

## Here Begins the Rule.

[Col. 1059]

## Chapter I — On Humility

[Col. 1059A]

*[Note: Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 7.]*

Divine Scripture cries out to us, saying: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). “The more humble you are, the more the height of glory follows you” (Proverbs 29:23). And because “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6), and “everyone who is arrogant is unclean before the Lord” (Proverbs 16:5), whenever you see a proud person, do not doubt that he is a son of the devil; and whenever you see a humble person, you ought to believe that he is a son of God.

We touch briefly on many things in order to urge all people to love humility and draw them away from pride, that detestable enemy of God. Since it is fitting for the whole human race to possess humility, it is exceedingly unjust, evil, and detestable for those who have especially joined themselves to the service of God to abandon humility and ally themselves with diabolical pride. Christ dwells in humility; the devil in pride.

Therefore, whoever, persuaded by the devil, has until now lived proud and exalted, with a rigid expression, must, with God’s help, rise again through humility, charity, obedience, and the other good commandments of God. For it is far better to reign with Christ in the heavenly kingdoms through humility than to sink with the devil into hell through pride.

## Chapter II — On the Order of the Congregation of Canons

*[Note: From chapter 63 of the Rule of Saint Benedict.]*

Let the canons preserve their orders as they have been arranged in their ranks, according to the legitimate institution of the Roman Church, in every place—whether in church or wherever they have gathered together and circumstances require it—except for those whom the bishop has placed in a higher rank or degraded for specific reasons. All the rest, as we have said, must preserve their orders just as they have been arranged.

Let the younger honor their elders, and let the elders love their juniors in God. In addressing one another by name, no one may call another by his bare name; rather, according to the constitution of the holy apostolic see, he should call him by his name with the rank of his ministry added first, whatever that rank may be.

Whenever clergy meet one another, the younger should bow and ask the elder’s blessing. If he finds the elder seated, the junior should rise when the senior passes, give him his seat, and not presume to sit down with him unless his elder commands him to do so, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “Outdoing one another in showing honor” (Romans 12).

Let small boys and adolescents preserve their ranks with discipline in the oratory or at Mass; wherever they are, let them have supervision and discipline.

## Chapter III — On Maintaining Discretion in Gathering Canons

*[Note: This chapter is included in the Council of Aachen of 816, chapter 118.]*

The provosts and prelates of the Church must take the greatest care not to admit more clerics into the churches entrusted to them than reason allows and the resources of the church can support. Otherwise, if they indiscreetly gather too many, they will be unable either to govern them or to assist them as they ought.

There are some who seek empty glory from human beings and wish to have an innumerable congregation of clergy, while taking no care to provide them with support for either soul or body. Since such men, when gathered together, do not receive the necessary stipends from their prelates and observe neither canonical order nor the divine offices, they abandon the cloister and the fellowship of the others and become wandering and wanton, devoted to gluttony, drunkenness, and their other pleasures. Whatever has been forbidden to them, they make lawful for themselves.

Therefore, the provosts must prudently ensure that they observe discretion in this matter: they should admit into the congregation neither more than is proper and the resources of the church can support, nor cast out those whom they can reasonably govern out of greed.

## Chapter IV — That Clerics Established in a Canonical Congregation Should Not Receive or Demand Excessive Stipends, but Only What Is Necessary

*[Note: The Council cited above, chapter 120.]*

The judgments of the holy Fathers teach that clerics should not be seekers of riches and should not take the goods of the Church without due regard. Hence Prosper says:

*[Note: Prosper,* On the Contempt of the World, *Book II, chapter 10.]*

“Those who serve the Church and either willingly accept or demand things they do not need think too carnally; for it is unworthy if the faithful and diligent devotion of clerics should despise eternal rewards for the sake of a worldly stipend.”

Why does he accept something for which he will have to render an account? Why does he multiply his own sins by those of others? Hence it is necessary—indeed beneficial—for clerics to avoid endangering themselves when receiving ecclesiastical provisions. Therefore, from their own resources as well as from those of the Church, they should neither accept nor demand more than is proper. They should receive food, drink, and clothing, and be content with these, lest, by receiving more, they appear to burden the poor.

*[Note: Prosper, same work, chapter 11.]*

“They do not accept without grave sin what the poor person was going to live on.”

Those who neither possess abundant personal resources nor have property of the Church, and who render great service to the Church, should receive in the canonical congregation food, clothing, and portions of alms, because Prosper’s book says of such people:

“Clerics whom either free choice or birth has made poor, living in a congregation, should receive the necessities of life, because they are led to receive them not by the desire to possess but by the necessity of living.”

Moreover, if there are people who do not wish to possess either their own property or that of the Church, the prelates ought, with the most provident administration, to provide for their needs from the resources of the Church, bearing in mind what Prosper says:

*[Note: Same work, chapter 9; but the text varies.]*

“Let him,” he says, “share with all who have nothing whatever he possesses from the resources of the Church.”

They must also care for those burdened by illness or old age, who are known to have formerly labored in the service of the Church.

## Chapter V — On Those Who Gather into the Congregation Entrusted to Them Only Clerics from the Church’s Household

*[Note: Council of Aachen, chapter 119.]*

There are some who gather into the churches entrusted to them clerics only from the ecclesiastical household. They seem to do this so that, if they ever inflict any injury upon them or withdraw their appropriate stipends, those clerics may not dare to bring any complaint against them, fearing that they might either be subjected to the harshest beatings or cruelly reduced once more to human servitude.

This is not said to mean that people of proven conduct from the Church’s household should not be admitted into the congregation, especially since with God there is no partiality. Rather, it is said so that, for the reason we have stated, none of the prelates, excluding the noble, should admit only base persons into his congregation.

## Chapter VI — Which Clerics Established in a Canonical Congregation Should Receive Ecclesiastical Stipends

*[Note: Same council, chapter 120.]*

Since the judgments of the holy Fathers cited above teach that clerics should not be seekers of riches and should not take the goods of the Church without due regard, we have thought it useful to bring forward, by way of example, several chapters from Prosper’s book, in which we read:

*[Note: Prosper, Book II, chapter 10.]*

“Those who serve the Church and either willingly accept or demand things they do not need think too carnally.”

Likewise:

“It is sufficiently unworthy if the faithful and diligent devotion of clerics despises eternal rewards for the sake of a worldly stipend.”

Likewise:

“If someone does not wish to leave his own possessions for the sake of having enough to live on, why does he accept something for which he will have to render an account?”

## Chapter VII — That Food and Drink Should Be Received Equally in a Canonical Congregation

*[Note: Council of Aachen, chapter 121.]*

In many congregations of canons it is customary for an unreasonable and indiscriminate practice to occur: certain clerics who abound in wealth and contribute little or nothing useful to the Church receive a larger allowance than the others who diligently perform the divine office. Yet this practice can in no way be found to have been sanctioned either by the authority of Scripture or by the traditions of the holy Fathers.

It is reasonable and just before God and human beings that in every canonical congregation, from the least to the greatest, all should receive food and drink equally—namely, those who have been admitted among the number of the canons for some useful purpose. Although many subjects are rightly honored by their prelates with other things more than the rest, in this fellowship, with personal distinctions set aside, there ought to be one equality of food and drink.

## Chapter VIII — On the Measure of Food and Drink

*[Note: Some material from this chapter appears in the council mentioned above, chapter 122.]*

When the clergy eat once or twice a day, each person, from the least to the greatest, should receive four pounds of bread. When they eat twice a day, they should receive porridge at the sixth hour and one serving of meat between two persons. If they receive one other dish and have no food provisions, then they should have two servings of meat. At supper they should either have one serving between two persons or receive other food.

During the time when they must live in the manner of Lent, at the sixth hour two clerics should receive a portion of cheese and other food; if they have fish, legumes, or something else, a third item should be added. At supper they should receive other food between two persons and a portion of cheese; and if God gives more, they should receive it with thanksgiving.

When there is only one meal in the day, two persons should receive one portion of other food, a portion of cheese, and a serving of legumes or some other dish. If it happens that in that year there are no acorns or beechnuts, and they have no means of making up this measure with meat, the bishop, or his subordinate, should provide, according to the ability God has granted, either Lenten food or something else by which they may have comfort.

If the region is wine-producing, they shall receive five pounds of wine per day (provided that the season’s sterility does not prevent this); but if it is not abundantly wine-producing, three pounds of wine and three of beer. They shall beware of drunkenness. If it should happen that there is less wine, and the bishop or his subordinate cannot make up this measure, he shall make up as much as possible with beer, according to what is available, and provide them with consolation; and for those who abstain from wine, the bishop or his subordinate shall ensure that they have as much beer as they ought to have had wine. But when the resources of the Church are insufficient, or the land has been barren—as often happens, impeded by our sins—and the prelates cannot provide the canons with as much wine, fermented drink, or beer as they ought, they shall provide them with a drink made from various materials. They shall not murmur, but rather accept with thanksgiving whatever can be given them, remembering John the Baptist, who drank neither wine, nor fermented drink, nor anything else capable of causing drunkenness; for wherever drunkenness occurs, there are disgrace and sin. And we admonish this also: that the clergy should always lead a sober life.

[Note: From chapter 40 of the Rule of Saint Benedict.]

And because we cannot persuade them not to drink wine, let us at least consent to this: that drunkenness should not dominate them, since the Apostle declares that all drunkards are excluded from the kingdom of God unless they amend through worthy repentance. Therefore, let the canons have vegetable gardens, from which, together with other additions, they may daily prepare some kind of dish, serving one another in turn.

## CHAPTER IX—The weekly kitchen servers

[Note: From chapter 35 of the same Rule.]

The clerical canons shall serve one another in such a way that no one is excused from kitchen duty unless illness or some serious and necessary business has preoccupied him, because through this greater reward and charity are acquired. For the weak, however, assistance shall be arranged, so that they do not perform this task with sadness; rather, everyone shall have assistance according to the size of the community or the circumstances of the place.

The archdeacon, provost, cellarer, and those occupied with more important duties shall be excused from kitchen service. The rest shall serve one another in charity. The person completing his week’s service shall clean the vessels on Saturday and return intact and clean to the cellarer the utensils of his ministry that he received for serving. If anything has been diminished from them, he shall ask pardon in chapter on Saturday and restore the vessels, or whatever has been diminished, to its place.

## CHAPTER X—The archdeacon or provost

[Note: From chapter 2 of the Rule of Saint Benedict.]

They ought to be prudent as serpents and simple as doves—that is, wise for what is good and simple with regard to evil—and instructed in the evangelical precepts and the regulations of the holy Fathers and the canons, so that they may teach the clergy the divine law. They should so conform themselves to the clergy that they demonstrate the divine precepts not only through persuasive words but also through more straightforward examples, because they must always preserve the form given by the Apostle, where he says: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke” (1 Timothy 4), mingling times with times, and terrors with encouragements.

They ought to rebuke the undisciplined and restless more severely, but watch over the obedient, gentle, and patient so that they may advance toward better things. They should rebuke and correct the negligent, contemptuous, and proud. They must not overlook the sins of offenders; rather, as soon as they begin to arise, they must cut them off at the root as soon as they are able, remembering the danger of Eli the priest on account of his sons (1 Samuel 2). They should correct the more honorable and intelligent after a first and second admonition; but they should restrain the wicked, hard-hearted, proud, or disobedient at the very beginning of their sin by blows and punishment, knowing that it is written: “A fool is not corrected by words” (Proverbs 18:2). And again: “Strike your son with a rod, and you will deliver his soul from death.”

Whatever they cannot decide for themselves justly and reasonably according to canonical discipline, they shall disclose to the bishop; and he shall, according to God’s will, punish what must be punished and correct what must be corrected. The archdeacon or principal officer must be faithful and obedient to God and the bishop in all his actions and works; he must not be proud, rebellious, or contemptuous, but chaste, sober, patient, kind, and merciful. He must love the clergy and hate vices, not allow them to be nourished, but hasten prudently to cut them off. Let them beware lest, while preaching to others, they themselves become disqualified.

[Note: Saint Benedict’s chapter 65, approximately halfway through.]

If the archdeacon or provost should be found—God forbid—to be proud, lifted up, contradictory, or contemptuous of canonical discipline, he shall, according to the Lord’s command, be admonished once and again. If he does not amend, he shall be judged by the bishop according to the measure of his fault. If he is not corrected even then, he shall be expelled from his orders, and others who are worthy and who fulfill the will of God or of their bishop according to the divine command shall be appointed in their places.

## CHAPTER XI—The cellarer

[Note: The same Rule, chapter 31.]

The cellarer must fear God, be sober, not a winebibber, contentious, or irascible, but moderate, cautious in conduct, and faithful; not proud, slow, wasteful, or an excessive and disorderly squanderer, nor negligent. Whatever he receives into his care for the use of the clergy, he shall guard, lest the servants appointed there dissipate the brothers’ provisions either by secretly taking them or by living negligently in any other way. These servants shall be chosen from the Church’s most faithful household and carefully trained for these duties, so that they may most appropriately assist the brothers’ needs both through the art of baking and through purity of faith. The same procedure is to be observed for the cooks.

## CHAPTER XII—The porter

[Note: Saint Benedict’s chapter 3.]

One porter, together with his junior assistant, shall guard the doors of the enclosure or the entrances for a year or longer, if this pleases the bishop or his subordinate.

[Note: From this chapter of the Council of Aachen, chapter 143.]

The porter should be a brother of approved conduct, sober, patient, and wise, who knows how to receive and give a reply. It shall be his duty, with complete obedience and appropriate humility, to close and unlock the canons’ gate at the proper times, so that through it no one may be allowed to enter or leave without permission. He must also ensure that he does not provide those who are more inclined to idleness than to divine service with an opportunity to wander outside, nor become—God forbid—a participant in their frivolities.

Moreover, he must receive those who arrive with charity and announce their arrival and the reason for it to the superior. After the evening and compline offices have been completed and the gates locked, the same porter shall bring their keys to the person who holds the superior’s place, so that no opportunity to enter or leave at unsuitable hours remains. If that porter is found to be disobedient or insolent, he shall be judged like the other negligent ministers.

## CHAPTER XIII—That the canons’ enclosure, in which the canons sleep, must be carefully fortified

[Col. 1065A]

[Note: Chapter 117 of the same council.]

It shall be the concern of the superiors to fortify the minds of their subjects continually with readings from the Holy Scriptures, lest the invisible wolf find an entrance through which it can enter the Lord’s sheepfold and seize one of the sheep. Furthermore, it is necessary that they surround on every side with strong defenses the enclosure in which the clergy entrusted to them are to live canonically, so that absolutely no one has access to enter or leave except through the gate.

Within it there shall also be dormitories, refectories, storerooms, and the other dwellings necessary for the use of the brothers living together in one community. All shall sleep in one dormitory, except those to whom the bishop has granted permission, according to what seems reasonable to him.

[Col. 1065B] [Note: Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 22.]

Within the enclosure they shall sleep separately in assigned places, each in his own bed, mixed with the elders for the sake of good oversight, so that the elders may observe what the younger men are doing according to God. No woman shall enter the enclosure, nor any layman, except only if the bishop, archdeacon, or provost orders them to come to the refectory for the purpose of eating, leaving their weapons outside the refectory. If it should be necessary for laymen to carry out work there, [lacuna] once they have completed their work, they shall go outside with the greatest haste. If the clergy lack cooks and it is necessary for lay cooks to enter solely for cooking, then, once their service is completed, they shall leave immediately.

## CHAPTER XIV—What the clergy, rising from bed at night, must first say and do

[Col. 1065C]

When the clergy rise from bed during the night hours for the divine office, they shall first impress upon themselves the sign of the holy cross by invoking the holy Trinity. Then they shall say the verse: “Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise” (Psalm 50:16). Then the psalm: “O God, come to my assistance” (Psalm 69), in full, with the Gloria. They shall then attend to their bodily natural need, and afterward hasten to the oratory, singing the psalm: “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul” (Psalm 24), entering with the utmost reverence and care so as not to disturb those who are praying. Then, prostrate in a suitable place, they shall pour out prayers in the sight of the Lord, more with the heart than with the mouth, so that their voice may be nearer to God than to themselves, saying:

[Col. 1065D] “I give you thanks, almighty Father, who have deigned to guard me during this night, and I beseech your mercy, merciful Lord, to grant me to pass the coming day in your holy service, with such humility and discretion that our service may please you. Amen.”

Then all shall be prepared, standing in their places in the choir in order, so that when the final signal has ceased they may, with the greatest humility and decorum, offer praise to God in the presence of his angels. If anyone has a frequent cough or phlegm rises from his chest or nostrils, he shall cast it behind his back or beside him, carefully and discreetly, so that it does not become nauseating to those of weaker constitution. Whatever is expelled shall always be trodden underfoot, so that when they bend for prayer their garments are not soiled. This is to be observed inside the church, in every assembly, and in the portico: whatever is spat out must always be trodden underfoot.

## CHAPTER XV—The divine offices at night

[Note: Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 8.]

In winter, that is, from the Kalends of November until Easter, they shall rise at the eighth hour of the night, with due regard for reason, so that they may rest a little longer after midnight and rise for the vigils already digested. After the nocturns have ended, they shall say the verse: “The saints shall exult in glory” (Psalm 149:5), or: “Let the righteous exult in the sight of God” (Psalm 67:4). Then the Kyrie eleison and the Lord’s Prayer. They shall make an interval, except on Sundays and the feasts of the saints, according to the judgment of the bishop or his subordinate—that is, they may sing forty or fifty psalms, according to what seems appropriate and what the hour permits; and those who require something from the Psalter or the readings shall devote themselves to meditation.

No one shall presume to sleep during this interval, unless illness compels him, and even then only by permission; whoever acts otherwise shall be excommunicated. All the rest shall maintain the order of the vigils until the appointed matins. During this interval there shall be profound silence, both in speech and in action, walking, or the sound of anything, so that each person may, without disturbing another, confess his sins to the Lord with groaning, sighing, and tears, and pray and petition the almighty Lord for pardon and remission of them.

## CHAPTER XVI—The antiquity of the vigils

[Note: Isidore, *On the Offices*, book 1, chapter 22, and the Council of Aachen, chapter 129.]

The devotion of the vigils is ancient, a familiar blessing to all the saints. Isaiah says: “During the night my spirit watches for you, O God” (Isaiah 26). David likewise says: “At midnight I rose to confess to you because of the judgments of your righteousness” (Psalm 118). At this time the destroying angel passed through and struck the firstborn of the Egyptians; therefore we too must keep vigil, lest we be mixed in with the dangers of Egypt. The Savior also asserts in the Gospel that he will come during these same hours. Thus, arousing his hearers to keep watch, he says: “Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching” (Matthew 24). “And if he comes in the evening,” he says, “and if at midnight, and if at cockcrow, and finds them watching, blessed indeed are those servants. Therefore you also must be ready, because you do not know at what hour the Son of Man will come” (Luke 12). He taught vigils not only in words but also confirmed them by example. For the Gospel bears witness that Jesus spent the night in prayer to God (Luke 6). Paul and Silas likewise, while held in public custody, are remembered as praying around midnight and, though bound, singing a hymn with all listening to them (Acts 16). Suddenly an earthquake occurred, the foundations of the prison were shaken, the doors opened of their own accord, and everyone’s chains were released.

Therefore, during these hours we ought to practice frequent psalmody and prayer in the holy offices and await our end—even if it should come—with confidence while engaged in such an activity. There is, however, a certain group of heretics who consider sacred vigils excessive, saying that night was made for rest, just as day was made for work. In Greek they are called *Nyctages*, that is, “sleepy ones.”

## CHAPTER XVII—Matins

[Note: Isidore, *On the Offices*, book 1, chapter 23; and the Council of Aachen, chapter 130.]

Concerning the antiquity and authority of matins, David says: “At matins I will meditate on you, because you have been my helper” (Psalm 62). And elsewhere: “My eyes have gone before you at dawn, so that I might meditate on your words” (Psalm 118). In the New Testament, from the time when our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to be born in Bethlehem, the office of the matins celebration has become customary throughout the world. At the radiance of the morning light our Lord and Savior rose from the underworld; indeed, at that same time the hope of the future resurrection is believed by all, when the righteous, rising as if from the sleep of slumber, will keep watch.

## CHAPTER XVIII—Prime

When the clergy assemble in the church to sing prime, after the office itself has been completed, before the fiftieth psalm they shall confess their faults to one another in turn, saying: “I confess to the Lord and to you, brother, that I have sinned in thought, word, and deed; therefore I ask you, pray for me.” The other shall reply: “May almighty God have mercy on you and forgive you all your sins; may he free you from every evil, preserve you in every good, and lead you to eternal life.” The first shall say: “Amen.” With humble hearts, praying earnestly for one another, they shall perform this for each other.

When this has been completed, they shall assemble daily in chapter. According to this institution, which with God’s help we have established for their benefit, each day they shall read some chapter, except on Sunday, Wednesday, Friday, and the feasts of the saints, when they shall read treatises, other homilies, or something else that edifies the hearers. We have therefore decreed that all the clergy shall come daily to chapter, so that the soul may hear the word of God; and the bishop, archdeacon, or whoever appears to preside in their place shall there command what must be commanded, correct what must be corrected, and diligently arrange what must be done.

After the reading, the date of the month and the phase of the moon are recited, along with the names of the saints whose feasts the following day will celebrate. Then all say together the verse: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115:15). The superior follows with this prayer: “May they and all the saints of God intercede for us sinners with the Lord, so that we may be worthy to possess eternal life. Amen.” Then the verse “O God, come to my assistance” is said three times, begun by the superior and answered by the others; they add “Glory be to the Father,” and so forth. Then the Kyrie eleison and the Lord’s Prayer. Then: “And lead us not into temptation,” and so forth; “And let there come upon us…”; “Look upon your servants” (Psalm 89), together to the end of the psalm, adding the Gloria.

Then the superior says: “May you deign, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, to direct, sanctify, and guard our hearts, bodies, and senses today, in your way, in your law, and in the works of your commandments. Direct our feet into the way of peace, the way of salvation, and the way of your righteousness, so that here and forever, with your help, we may be worthy to be saved—you who live and reign as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for endless ages of ages. Amen.”

Then: “Our help…” The others respond: “In the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

After this, whoever is guilty shall ask pardon and receive judgment according to the measure of his fault. Whoever asks pardon for a fault shall be judged by the superior with greater mercy and more leniently in proportion as he humbles himself more and acknowledges himself guilty. For it is necessary that all our negligence—of thought, tongue, or deed—be judged in the present life through true confession and humility, and not make us guilty after death.

## CHAPTER XIX—Daily manual labor

[Note: Rule of Blessed Benedict, chapters 35 and 48.]

Rising from chapter, they shall go, either together or separately, to the work assigned to them, as reason requires. Maintaining silence, they shall sing their psalms, either in pairs or singly, as appropriate, speaking of nothing else unless it is necessary to speak cautiously about the work itself. When they begin their work, they shall say: “Blessed are you, Lord God, who have helped me and comforted me. Amen. May almighty God have mercy on us. Amen.” When there is no need to perform communal work, each person shall do whatever work he has, because idleness is the enemy of the soul.

## CHAPTER XX—The hours of the day

[Note: Council of Aachen, chapter 126, from Isidore, book 1, chapter 19, *On the Offices*.]

Daniel and the three youths devoted the third, sixth, and ninth hours to supplications to the Lord. Thus, since three hours extend from sunrise to the time of supplication, they declare to us the reverence due to the Trinity. At the third hour the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles. At the sixth hour Christ suffered. At the ninth hour he gave up his spirit.

## CHAPTER XXI—The evening hour

[Col. 1068D]

[Note: The same, chapter 127, from the same work, chapter 20.]

The office at the end of the day follows the close of the daylight and the setting of the day’s light; its solemn celebration comes from the Old Testament. David is witness, saying: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice” (Psalm 140). In the New Testament, at the same time, while the apostles were eating, our Lord and Savior handed on the mystery of his body and blood. At these times it is fitting for us to be present before the sight of God in honor and remembrance of such great sacraments and to resound in his worship and praises.

## CHAPTER XXII—Compline

[Col. 1069A]

[Note: Council of Aachen, chapters 128 and following, from the same work, chapter 21.]

The celebration of compline is found in the examples of the Fathers. David says: “If I climb into the bed of my couch, if I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob” (Psalm 131). But if we wish to be the Lord’s place and desire to be regarded as his dwelling and temple, let us imitate the examples of the saints, lest it be said of us what is written: “They slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands” (Psalm 75).

## CHAPTER XXIII—The silence observed after compline

After compline has been completed, there shall be profound silence, and prayers shall be said privately with remembrance of sins. Then they shall give thanks to God, saying: “I give you thanks, Lord, holy Father, almighty and eternal God, who have deigned to guard me on this day. Through your holy mercy, grant me to pass through this night with a pure heart and body, so that, rising in the morning, I may be able to offer you acceptable service, through Christ our Lord. Amen.”

They shall walk in the church and dormitory with great caution. When they have come to their own beds, as the clergy settle themselves, each shall say the psalm: “O God, come to my assistance” (Psalm 69), in full, with the Gloria. Then he shall say the verse: “Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door of protection around my lips” (Psalm 140:3). Just as, rising in the morning, he asked the Lord to open his lips, so, when resting, he should ask the Lord to set a guard over his mouth.

## CHAPTER XXIV—That the canons must religiously observe the canonical hours

[Note: The same, chapter 131.]

The canons should take the greatest care to guard the aforesaid hours with vigilant attention and to perform the divine office during them humbly and devoutly. As soon as the signal is heard, they shall hasten to the church, leaving behind whatever may be in their hands, provided that it does not perish. If someone is far from the church and cannot attend the work of God at the canonical hours, he shall perform the work of God with reverent fear wherever he then is. The church custodian shall ensure that the signals are sounded at the proper hours.

[Note: As in the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 50.]

The canons must beware of entering, standing, or sitting in the church pompously, dishonorably, disorderly, or proudly.

## CHAPTER XXV—Diligence in psalmody

[Note: Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 19.]

We believe that the divine presence is everywhere and that the eyes of the Lord observe the good and the wicked. Above all, however, let us believe this without any doubt when we attend the divine office. Therefore let us always remember what the Prophet says: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Psalm 2). And again: “Sing psalms wisely” (Psalm 46). And: “In the sight of the angels I will sing to you” (Psalm 137).

Let us therefore consider how we ought to stand and pray in the presence of the divinity and his angels, and let us stand for psalmody in such a way that our mind agrees with our voice.

[Note: Saint Benedict, in the same place, chapter 20.]

For if we wish to make a request of good or powerful human beings, we do not presume to do so except with humility and reverence; how much more, then, must the Lord of all be entreated by us with humility and purity?

## CHAPTER XXVI—That one must not stand pompously in church

[Note: Council of Aachen, chapter 131.]

As soon as the signal is heard, all the canons shall hasten to the church. They shall enter it not pompously, dishonorably, or disorderly, but with fear of God. Except for the weak, they shall not use staffs, crutches, or clubs in the choir; rather, they must stand and sing psalms there religiously.

For there are some among the clergy who spend almost the whole day tirelessly in secular business and disputes. As soon as they enter the church to perform the divine office, they appear so exhausted that they can neither devote themselves to prayer nor stand for psalmody. Instead, seated, they habitually engage not in divine but in frivolous conversation, uttering secular words to one another and—something forbidden even to say—shameful and obscene ones.

This execrable practice must be torn out by the roots from those who do these things and from those who perhaps wish to imitate them, in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matthew 21).

## CHAPTER XXVII—Those traveling on a journey

[Note: Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 50.]

Whoever from the clergy travels on a journey with the bishop or with someone else must not neglect his order, insofar as the journey and circumstances permit. The appointed hours must not pass them by, whether those of the divine offices or of anything else.

## CHAPTER XXVIII—Those who commit certain lesser faults

[Note: From chapter 46 of the same Rule.]

If anyone from the clergy arrives late for the work of God or for the table, or if his superior has ordered him for some reason to sing the psalmody or Masses and he has failed to fulfill this, or if he has broken or lost something, or committed some excess, and, instead of coming immediately before the bishop or those under him, he has voluntarily made satisfaction or concealed his offense, then, when it becomes known through another person, he shall undergo a more severe correction. If he has confessed voluntarily, however, he shall undergo a lighter correction, according to the measure of his fault. The form of correction shall depend upon the judgment of the bishop or of his subordinate.

[Note: From chapter 21 of the same Rule.]

Whoever is found guilty of lesser faults shall, on that day, be deprived of participation at the table and shall not appoint a psalm or antiphon in the oratory, nor recite a reading. He shall receive his food after the clergy have eaten: for example, if the clergy eat at the sixth hour, he shall eat at the ninth; if the clergy eat at the ninth, he shall eat in the evening.

## CHAPTER XXIX—Serious faults

If a cleric belonging to the canonical order commits the crime of a serious fault—that is, homicide, fornication, adultery, theft, or anything similar among the principal vices—he shall first be subjected to corporal punishment. Then, for as long as the bishop or his subordinates determine, he shall be punished by imprisonment or exile, knowing that terrible sentence of the Lord’s Apostle: “To deliver such a man to the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 5).

While he is in prison, no one from the clergy shall associate with him in any fellowship or conversation, except the person whom the superior orders to do so. He alone shall remain in mourning penitence for as long as the superior considers appropriate.

After leaving prison, if it seems right to the bishop or his subordinates, he shall continue to perform public penance: that is, he shall be suspended both from the oratory and from the table. At all the canonical hours he shall come before the church door, wherever the superior has ordered, and lie prostrate with his entire body before the threshold of the church until everyone has entered. Then he shall rise, stand outside the church before that same door, and perform his office there as far as he is able, lying or standing before the threshold and associating with no one. As those leaving the church depart, he shall likewise lie prostrate until everyone has gone outside.

He shall abstain for as long and in the manner that the bishop or his subordinates determine, according to the measure or time they judge suitable for him. No one shall bless him until he has been reconciled.

## CHAPTER XXX—The reconciliation of a penitent for a capital crime

[Col. 1071C]

This is the order for one performing public penance: receive him on Wednesday morning at the beginning of Lent, that is, at the beginning of the fasts; cover him with a hair shirt and pray for him; and enclose him until the Lord’s Supper. On that same day he shall be presented in the midst of the church. When he comes, having been summoned for reconciliation before the bishop or clergy, he shall lie prostrate with his entire body upon the ground before the apse in complete humility and ask pardon from everyone. The bishop or his subordinate shall say prayers over him for reconciliation on the Thursday of the Lord’s Supper.

## CHAPTER XXXI—Confessions

Scripture exhorts us, saying: “Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him” (Psalm 36:5). It also says: “Confess to the Lord, for his mercy is everlasting” (Psalm 105:1). Again: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not hide my iniquities” (Psalm 31:5). Again: “I will confess my iniquities against myself to the Lord; and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (ibid. 6). And again: “Confess your sins to one another” (James 5:16), and let them be blotted out. Elsewhere: “Whoever conceals his crimes will not be set aright, but whoever confesses them will save his soul from death” (Proverbs 28:13). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3:2).

Since, at the devil’s prompting, we have now committed many things against the will and commandment of God, it is necessary that we amend them through true humility and confession, doing penance as the holy Fathers established. Thereafter, whenever an evil thought comes into the heart at the devil’s prompting, let him confess it promptly to the bishop or superior, so that through true confession and penance we may be worthy to possess the kingdom of God. For one who sins before the eyes of God but is ashamed to confess to a human being is exceedingly wicked.

## CHAPTER XXXII—The order for receiving penance and making confession

This is the prayer of our penance and confession, which we must likewise perform before God and his priests: each year, three times—that is, during the three Lents—the faithful people shall make their confession to their own priest; and whoever does more does better. Monks shall make confession every Saturday, willingly, to their bishop or superior.

When you wish to confess your sins, act manfully and do not be ashamed, because forgiveness comes from this; without confession there is no forgiveness.

First, humbly prostrate yourself upon the ground in prayer before God, and ask blessed Mary, together with the holy apostles, martyrs, and confessors, to intercede for you with the Lord. Pray that almighty God may deign to give you perfect wisdom, knowledge, and true understanding for confessing your sins. Then rise with confidence and true faith and say to him:

“Servant of God, do you believe in God the almighty Father, creator of heaven and earth?”

**Answer:** “I believe.”

[Col. 1072C]

**Question:** “Do you believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?”

**Answer:** “I believe.”

**Question:** “Do you believe that these three persons, as we have said—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are three persons and one God?”

**Answer:** “I believe.”

**Question:** “Do you believe that in the very flesh in which you now are, you will receive what you have done and what you will do, whether good or evil?”

**Answer:** “I believe.”

**Question:** “Do you believe that resurrection and eternal life await you after death?”

**Answer:** “I believe.”

[Col. 1072D]

**Question:** “Are you willing to forgive all those who have sinned against you, so that God may forgive you all your sins? For the same Lord says in the Gospel: ‘If you forgive people their sins, your sins will be forgiven you’” (Matthew 18:35).

**Answer:** “I am willing.”

Afterward, inquire carefully whether he has with him evil deeds that separate a person—as the Apostle says—from the kingdom of God. These are: evil thought; evil and idle speech; hatred; envy; detraction; cursing; abuse; shameful speech; buffoonery; dissimulation; flattery; grumbling; carnal desire; arrogance; negligence; laziness; dishonoring others; dishonoring the good; dishonoring relatives; ignorance of Sundays and the solemn feasts of the saints; anger; greed; false testimony; sleepiness; lack of moderation in food; robbery; gluttony; drunkenness; feasting; fornication; adultery; sacrilege; pride; perjury; theft; homicide; and things similar to these.

After he has confessed his sins, if he is willing to renounce them, assign him penance; if he is unwilling, do not assign him penance, because you cannot. If he is willing to renounce those sins, make him confess them and finally say: “Many are my sins in deeds, words, and thoughts.” Then assign him penance measured according to the canons, and afterward pour prayers and supplications over him.

In all things it must be guarded against that those who fall into serious sins and those who commit certain lesser offenses should be judged equally; rather, the remedy must be applied according to the illness.

## CHAPTER XXXIII—Excommunication for offenses

If any cleric is obstinate, disobedient, proud, drunken, a detractor, rebellious, double-tongued, fornicator, contradictory, contentious, a robber, thief, grumbler, rebuker, transgressor of an imposed fast, despiser of standing and worshiping beside the cross, one who persists in something contrary, or contemptuous of the commands of the bishop or of those under him, and does not ask pardon of his own accord, he shall, according to the Lord’s command, be admonished once, twice, and three times in private by his superiors. If he does not amend, he shall be rebuked publicly before everyone. If he does not correct himself even then, he shall be subjected to excommunication.

[Col. 1073C] But if he is wicked, of limited understanding, or incorrigible, he shall be subjected to corporal punishment.

## CHAPTER XXXIV—Observances of Lent
Although at all times the life of Christians ought to be simple and sober, it is especially fitting for religious minds to live more continently during these days and to strive to cling to God with diligent devotion. Therefore we decree that during those forty days before Easter, with complete purity of mind and body, our clergy, by God’s command, shall keep watch over themselves as far as they are able.

As for the consumption of food and drink, insofar as God grants assistance, they shall practice moderation: that is, every day except Sundays, from the beginning of Lent [Col. 1073D] until holy Easter, they shall take their meal in the refectory after the prescribed Vespers, and shall abstain from those foods or drinks which the bishop, or those under him, shall reasonably determine. During those forty days they shall take no meal elsewhere—not in the city itself, nor in monasteries, nor in any other places, nor in their own houses—unless they have been far away for a useful purpose at the proper hour for taking their food and cannot be present with the brothers.

During these forty days the clerics shall devote themselves to reading, except on their Sundays, from the first appointed hour until the full third hour; and, unless necessity requires it, they shall not go outside the cloister, unless the bishop, or his subordinate, has judged that what must be done should be done. [Col. 1074A] After the third hour they shall hold chapter at that time, and afterward do whatever is appropriate, whether reading or working.

### CHAPTER XXXV—The times when clerics are to take food once or twice a day

From Easter until Pentecost, the canons shall eat twice a day and shall have permission to eat meat—except penitents—apart from Wednesdays and Fridays only. From Pentecost until the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, they shall likewise eat twice a day and abstain from meat. From the Nativity of Saint John until the passing of Saint Martin, they shall again eat twice a day and abstain from meat on Wednesdays and Fridays.
