From the feast of Saint Martin until the Nativity [Col. 1074B] of the Lord, all shall abstain from meat and fast until the ninth hour, and on all these days they shall eat in the refectory. From the Nativity of the Lord until the beginning of Lent, on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays they shall eat in the refectory at the ninth hour. On the remaining days of this period they shall eat twice in the refectory. During these times they shall abstain from meat on Wednesdays and Fridays. If a feast day falls on one of these weekdays, then, if the prior permits it, they may eat meat on account of illness.

### CHAPTER XXXVI—The feasts of the saints

It has pleased us to make this known: every year, insofar as God grants the ability, we and our clergy shall celebrate the feasts of the Lord, of holy Mary, of the twelve apostles, and of the remaining saints whose observance exists in this province, diligently performing the divine office by day and by night. The bishop, or his subordinate, shall provide a meal in his own house for the clergy on the Nativity and Epiphany of the Lord, Easter, the closing day of Easter, the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, and the feasts of the saints of his province, if he is present. If he is absent, then on these days they shall have a sufficient meal in the refectory, as written above. After they have left the refectory, they may drink in the warming room two or three times, in such a way that there may be refreshment and drunkenness may not prevail.

On the other feast days, as is customary in the Church, let the prelates provide their clerics with food and drink according to what they can best arrange. Meanwhile, let the prelates beware [Col. 1074D] lest they withhold from their subjects, through any form of concealment or stinginess, what they ought to give or are able to give. Otherwise, compelled by poverty, they may be forced to wander about in different places and involve themselves in disgraceful occupations; and, abandoning ecclesiastical service, they may begin to live without discipline and serve their own pleasures. The prelates who could have been rewarded by the Lord for generously supplying them with what was necessary must then be judged strictly and severely.

### CHAPTER XXXVII—That no one should presume to strike or excommunicate another

[Note: [Col. 1073D] From the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 70.]

Every occasion for presumption must be avoided in this canonical order: no one is to be permitted to excommunicate or strike his equal, even if someone, by his own presumption, provokes him to do so. He is not to seek revenge, either in word or deed; rather, he should come to the prior, and the prior should determine the matter according to due order. Anyone who presumes to do this shall be judged by the bishop or by his subordinate.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII—That in the congregation of canons no one may defend another

[Note: [Col. 1075D] From the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 69.]

Every possible precaution must be taken so that, on no occasion, one person presumes to defend another. Nor should the canons presume to do this under the pretext of kinship, friendship, or intimacy, because serious opportunities for scandal commonly arise in the congregation from this cause. If anyone transgresses in this matter, let him be restrained more severely by the prior, so that the others may be afraid.

### CHAPTER XXXIX—The good zeal which the servants of God ought to have for one another

[Note: [Col. 1075D] The same, chapter 72.]

Just as there is an evil zeal of bitterness, which separates one from God and leads to hell, so there is a good zeal, which separates one from vices and leads to God and eternal life. Let the servants of God exercise this zeal with the most fervent love: they should anticipate one another in showing honor and endure with the greatest patience one another’s weaknesses, whether of body or of character. If any vices are reported, they must be restrained and correction applied, together with those by whom the matter has been committed, so that—as the Apostle says—[lacuna] they may be able to destroy vices if they arise and call each person to a better condition. For it is written: “You who love the Lord, hate evil” (Psalm 95:10). Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul. He truly loves his soul who guards himself and draws others, both by words and deeds, toward the example of good conduct.

### CHAPTER XL—Sick canons

[Note: [Col. 1076D] Saint Benedict, Rule, chapter 36.]

If anyone from the clergy falls ill, the bishop or his subordinate shall take the greatest care of him and see that the sick man is not neglected; rather, he is to be served as truly as Christ himself. Quarters should be assigned to the sick, reasonably arranged, suitable, and fit for their habitation. One member of the clergy, fearing God, shall be appointed to care for the sick man and attend with the utmost diligence to all his needs [Col. 1075D]. If necessary, he shall have assistance, according to what the prior determines. He should know that, if he has ministered well, he acquires from God a worthy rank.

The sick man himself, however, should recognize that he is being served for the honor of God and should not distress his attendant through his excesses. It must also be stipulated that a sick person may take food and drink at any hour, whenever he desires or is able, if he cannot do so at the proper time.

### CHAPTER XLI—The clothing and footwear of clerics

That half of the clergy who are seniors shall receive new cloaks and new woolen garments each year; and whenever they receive new ones, they shall always return those they received the previous year. The other half of the clergy shall receive those old cloaks and garments which their seniors return to them each year. The seniors shall not exchange those cloaks and garments which they are obliged to return.

Each senior cleric shall receive three *campsiles* annually, and each junior cleric shall receive two *campsiles* annually. The entire clergy shall receive each year four pairs of footwear, consisting of *pelles buccinas* and soles. They shall receive the garments at the feast of Saint Martin, the *campsiles* at Easter, and the footwear on the Kalends of September.

### CHAPTER XLII—Alms to be received

If anyone wishes to give an offering to a priest for his Mass, or for confession, or to a cleric for psalms and hymns, or for himself, or for any dear one of his, whether living or dead, the priest or cleric shall accept this offering from the giver and do with it whatever he wishes. If an offering is given by the donor for all the priests, they shall hold it in common and perform psalmody or Masses for him in mercy.

### CHAPTER XLIII—The measure of alms which priests are to receive and distribute

We consider it exceedingly burdensome if the priests alone should be required to carry such immense burdens of sinners, since several more easily obtain God’s mercy than one alone. Each person ought to fear for his own conscience; how much more, then, should he not heap upon himself, beyond his strength, the burden of the sins of others.

### CHAPTER XLIV—The care which clerics ought to have for the people entrusted to them

We must beware lest, through our negligence, our people fall into danger, as it were placed in a state of security without baptism, confirmation, confession, and preaching. Therefore we decree that throughout the entire year the word of salvation shall be preached to them twice each month, from the fifteenth day to the fifteenth day, so that, with God’s help, they may attain eternal life. If preaching is constant on all feast days and Sundays, it is more beneficial; and preaching should be adapted to what the common people are able to understand.

### CHAPTER XLV—To whom the support of the poor should be entrusted

[Note: [Col. 1076D] Council of Aachen, chapter 141.]

We are instructed by evangelical and apostolic teachings concerning the gathering in of strangers; therefore, above all, we ought to take care that the Lord may rightly say of us: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25:35). Accordingly, the prelates of the Church, following the examples of the Fathers who came before them, ought to prepare some place of reception where the poor may be gathered, and assign there from the property of the Church only so much as will enable them, according to the resources available, to have the necessary expenses, except for the tithes which are contributed there from the Church’s estates.

The canons, too, should most willingly contribute to this hospital, for the use of the poor, tithes both from the crops and from all offerings of alms. A brother of good reputation should be appointed to receive guests and beggars who are pilgrims, recognizing Christ in them, and gladly provide them with what is necessary according to his ability. He must in no way divert to his own use what ought to be devoted to the poor, lest, together with Judas who stole the Lord’s moneybox, he receive the sentence of condemnation.

The prelates must also beware lest they regard the care of the poor as insignificant. And if the clerics cannot do so at other times, at least during Lent they ought to wash the feet of the poor at the appropriate hospital, according to the Gospel passage: “If I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, how much more ought you to wash one another’s feet?” (John 13:14), and so forth. Therefore it is appropriate that the hospital for the poor be located in a suitable place, where the brothers can come to it with the greatest ease.

If the person to whom the hospital has been entrusted neglects the care of the poor and turns their property to his own use, although he is worthy of divine vengeance, he must nevertheless be judged more severely than other offenders by the superiors and removed from his ministry. And rightly so, since he has appropriated to his own uses the price of sins, the food of the poor, and the treasure to be stored up in heaven.

### CHAPTER XLVI—The superiors

[Note: [Col. 1077D] Council of Aachen, chapter 139.]

Although all who preside may properly be called superiors, custom has established that those are called superiors who exercise a certain responsibility of prior within the authority of other prelates. Those who, according to this custom, are called superiors must be appointed as men of such character and diligence that they possess a reputable way of life and faithfully and humbly fulfill what has been entrusted to them. Because they are placed over others, they must by no means regard the canonical institutions as insignificant; rather, the more deeply they are occupied with the care of the brothers, the more diligently they must strive to obey heavenly commands.

They ought therefore to be useful to the entire congregation and faithfully serve in the ministry entrusted to them. Whatever they ought to give to the brothers, let them provide readily and charitably at the proper time, so that through faithful administration they may acquire from the Lord a worthy rank [Col. 1077D].

### CHAPTER XLVII—What sort of men should serve in place of the prelates in the congregation

[Note: [Col. 1077D] The same, chapter 138. From the Rule of Blessed Benedict, chapters 21, 64, 65.]

The prelates of the Church ought to choose from the congregation entrusted to them brothers of good reputation, among whom they can safely distribute the burdens of governance. They should also confer upon them such dignity that, acting in their place, they may correct the disobedient by canonical discipline and encourage the obedient toward better things.

They are not to be appointed according to personal standing or according to the order in which they were admitted into the college of brothers, but according to the merit of their lives and the precedence of their spiritual gifts [Col. 1078A]. They should be constant in the congregation and care for the brothers with vigilant diligence. Just as they surpass others in authority, so they must instruct them by the example of an innocent life, so that, according to the Apostle, they may be examples to the others “in word, in conduct, in charity, in faith, and in chastity,” and so forth (1 Timothy 4).

If they begin to become puffed up because of their priorate, show no concern for the care of the brothers, and repeatedly prove incorrigible, they shall be removed from their ministry, and others who can perform it diligently shall be appointed in their place.

### CHAPTER XLVIII—The rearing and safeguarding of boys

[Note: [Col. 1078D] Council of Aachen, chapter 135.]

The rulers of the Churches ought to watch diligently so that the boys and adolescents who are reared or educated in the congregation entrusted to them may be bound by continual ecclesiastical disciplines in such a way that their wanton age, which is greatly inclined to sin, can find no opportunity to rush into sinful acts. Therefore, for guarding and spiritually educating such persons, the prelates should appoint a brother of reputable life who will care for them with the greatest diligence and bind them very strictly, so that, instructed in ecclesiastical teachings and clothed in spiritual armor, they may both fittingly serve the needs of the Church and eventually be worthy of promotion to ecclesiastical orders.

Moreover, for suitable edification and instruction concerning the matter at hand, we have wished to insert into this work a certain saying of the holy Fathers, which runs as follows: “[Note: [Col. 1078D] Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 23.] For every age, from adolescence onward, is inclined toward evil. Whoever among the clergy is mature or adolescent should dwell together in a single chamber of the courtyard, so that they may spend the years of slippery youth not in luxury but in ecclesiastical disciplines, assigned to a most approved senior whom they may have both as a teacher of doctrine and as a witness to their life,” and so forth.

With these matters thus set forth, the boys ought to be assigned for safekeeping to a most approved senior, even if they are educated by another. If the brother to whom this care is entrusted neglects them, teaches them something other than what is proper, or inflicts upon them any stain of harm, he shall be corrected with the utmost severity and removed from office. They shall then be entrusted to another brother who will instruct them by examples of an innocent life and encourage them to perform good works.

### CHAPTER XLIX—That all the canons should assemble for Compline

When the appointed daytime hours of the offices have been completed by all the canons with the most devout service, they must come, at the signal, to Compline with the greatest devotion, at the beginning of night. When it has been completed, they ought not to devote themselves to meals, drinking, or idle conversation; rather, putting all these things aside, they should humbly and decently go to the dormitory. Under no circumstances should two sleep in one bed, but each should rest in a separate bed. [Note: [Col. 1078D] Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 22.]

A lamp [Col. 1079A] should also burn continually in the dormitory throughout the night. Finally, no one is to do anything shameful or indecent in the dormitory; no one should presume to disturb another or compel him to break into useless and idle talk. Anyone who despises this chapter shall be corrected with the utmost severity by the prelates and masters.

### CHAPTER L—The singers

[Note: [Col. 1079D] Council of Aachen, chapter 137.]

Singers must take the greatest care not to defile the gift divinely bestowed upon them with vices, but rather to adorn it with humility, sobriety, chastity, and the other ornaments of holy virtues. Their melody should raise the minds of the people standing around to the remembrance and love of heavenly things, not only through the sublimity of the words being sung but also through the sweetness of the sounds.

As the holy Fathers have handed down, a singer ought to be distinguished and eminent both in voice and in skill, so that by the delight of sweetness he may stir the minds of those listening, and so forth. Therefore singers should not proudly set themselves above the others because of the gift bestowed upon them, but should show themselves humble companions. It must also be arranged for them when the divine office is to be performed in a measured manner and when more quietly: specifically, they should extend the singing and moderate the voices of the others according to the number of clerics, the character of the office, and the length of the time. They should also pronounce the sound of the vowel letters well and beautifully.

Those who are less capable in this art should remain silent until they have been better instructed, rather than, by wishing to sing what they do not know, forcing the voices of others to become discordant [Col. 1079C]. The psalms in church should not be recited hurriedly, nor with loud, disorderly, or excessive voices, but clearly and distinctly, with compunction of heart, so that the minds of those reciting may be nourished by their sweetness and the ears of those listening may be soothed by their pronunciation. For although the sound of song in other offices is usually produced in a loud voice, such a voice must nevertheless be avoided in reciting the psalms.

Meanwhile, senior brothers of especially reputable life should be appointed to take turns being with the singers’ school at the appointed time, lest those who ought to be learning either devote themselves to idleness or persist in empty and superfluous stories. If the singers become proud and refuse to teach others the art they have learned with divine assistance, they must be judged severely and strictly, so that, corrected and reformed, they may endeavor to distribute to others the talent certainly bestowed upon them by God.

### CHAPTER LI—What sort of men should be appointed to read and sing in church

[Note: [Col. 1079D] The same, chapter 133.]

Those should be appointed to read, sing, and chant in church who render the praises owed to the Lord not proudly but humbly; who delight the learned through the sweetness of reading and melody and instruct the less learned; and who desire the edification of the people in reading or song more than the vainest popular applause. Those who cannot perform these duties skillfully should first be instructed by teachers and, once trained, strive to fulfill them, so that they may edify those who listen.

### CHAPTER LII—The manner of correction

[Note: [Col. 1080D] The same, chapter 134.]

Although those who despise the canonical institutions must be punished chiefly by episcopal judgment, the measure of correction must be extended according to the measure of the faults, as we have stated above. All these matters properly depend upon the judgment of the prelates, by whom they must be tempered with the greatest discretion. For the same prelates must imitate the conduct of the most skilled physicians in dealing with offenders: with great care for discernment, they must apply what is suitable and appropriate to each person, carefully weighing the need to provide remedies in proportion to the size of the wounds, so that they neither give one person what harms him nor withhold from another what helps [Col. 1080B].

Having omitted those whose delinquent age is not to be spared, but whose sides must rather be struck continually with rods so that they do not grow hard, we shall briefly and concisely show how the other offenders ought to be treated, according to divine authority, the example of the holy Fathers, and their traditions.

If any brother established in the canonical congregation neglects to attend the canonical hours; enters the church not reverently but pompously or disorderly; performs the work of God negligently; delays coming to the conference; refuses to carry out the obedience imposed upon him by his masters; fails, according to his ability, to apply himself to reading, singing, or the other ecclesiastical disciplines; comes late to the table not out of necessity but through fault; leaves the cloister without permission; after being permitted to leave, lingers beyond the time assigned to him; attempts to walk about in the streets or sit at crossroads; commits anything indecent or shameful in the dormitory, whether in words or deeds; presumes, without unavoidable cause, to sleep anywhere except in the dormitory with the others; neglects to serve the brothers obediently in the duty of charity; sows among the brothers the discord detested by the Scripture of God; proves contumacious, proud, or murmuring toward this institution; or attempts to do anything else of this kind—he is first to be admonished according to the Lord’s command, not only once, twice, or three times, but even more frequently. If he does not yield to these admonitions, he shall be corrected by public rebuke [Col. 1080D].

If he resists even this, he shall be forbidden all food except bread and shall use bread and water alone until he gives worthy satisfaction. If he still does not reform, he shall be separated from the table and from the fellowship of the brothers, removed from the choir of those singing psalms, and compelled to stand apart in a place appointed by the prelates for those negligent in this way, so that he may at least be corrected by the shame of separation.

Then, if he proves incorrigible by these methods and his age permits it, the appropriate chastisement of blows shall be applied, as Solomon says: “A fool is not corrected by words” (Proverbs 18:2), according to the judgment of blessed Gregory: [Col. 1081A] “He who does not heed the words of one commanding should be admonished with blows, so that punishments may draw him toward good desires whom rewards do not invite.”

But if he is the sort of person whom either age or personal condition does not permit to be beaten, he shall be corrected by public rebuke, continual affliction through fasts, and the shame of separation, until he obtains pardon through worthy satisfaction in penance. If both—the one who is beaten and the one whom age or personal condition forbids to be beaten—still prove incorrigible, there should be a place within the canons’ cloister, as is known to exist in many places, where they may be confined for a time and punished according to the measure of their fault, according to the Apostle: “Delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 5:5). [Note: [Col. 1081D] Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 28.]

If they still do not obey after so many most salutary admonitions and corrections, a common prayer shall be offered for them by the entire congregation, so that they may finally be healed by the Lord. If they appear wholly beyond correction and incorrigible, then, lest their deadly contagion spread among many, they must be separated from the fellowship of the others, like diseased sheep, and brought before the bishop.

If anyone in the college of canons commits a criminal offense, he is to be granted no delay: either he must voluntarily perform penance for the crime committed, or, if he resists doing so, he must be brought before the bishop, so that the bishop may impose public penance upon him.

The rulers must remember that the Church is called a dove in the divine Scriptures. A dove does not tear with its claws, but strikes gently with its wings [Col. 1081C]. Therefore they must also observe most carefully that, as stated above, correction itself be thoroughly tempered according to the measure of the faults, the persons, and the ages, so that neither the vice of negligence may grow nor correction exceed the measure of gentleness. Otherwise, as blessed Maximus says, either excessive leniency may grant the sinner permission to restrain those who would correct him, or immoderate severity may fail to recall the offender from his fall.

They must likewise beware lest they strike the errors of offenders out of resentment for some matter. Rather, as blessed Augustine says, they should be persecutors of crimes and liberators of human beings. Let them hate vices and love people. Let them hate what has been introduced by the devil’s prompting and love what has been created by God’s goodness. Let them hold a staff and a rod in their hand: the staff, by which they spiritually support the weaknesses of other men [Col. 1081D]; the rod, by which they strike the vices of offenders with zeal for righteousness.

Meanwhile, when brothers have been excommunicated for offenses, the other brothers must not favor them, deceive them with their flatteries, or defend their errors. Rather, they should assist them so that they may be corrected strictly by the judgment of equity.

### CHAPTER LIII—That canons should not wear monks’ cowls

[Note: [Col. 1081D] Council of Aachen, chapter 125.]

We have discovered that among many canons a reprehensible practice has grown up: contrary to ecclesiastical custom, they wear cowls, which are intended for monks alone. Yet they ought not at all to appropriate the habit of those whose way of life they in some measure do not share. For just as it is indecent for them, following the custom of laymen, to carry military weapons, so it is surely dishonorable and highly improper for them to put on the garments of another way of life.

The habits of the various orders have therefore been distinguished from one another in the Church so that, when they are seen, it may be clearly recognized what way of life the wearer follows, or in what service he fights for the Lord. For the Law of the Lord also prohibits a man from wearing a woman’s garment and a woman from wearing a man’s garment, so that each sex may walk clothed in the garment suitable to it. Just as it is shameful for a man to wear a woman’s garment and for a woman to wear a man’s garment, so it is highly improper for a canon to wear a monastic garment—unless, together with the garment, he also wishes to assume the monastic way of life.

Since this practice is approved by no authority but is rightly reproved and rejected by those who think soundly, it ought henceforth to be completely prohibited.

### CHAPTER LIV—That they should maintain moderation in the care of clothing

[Note: [Col. 1081D] Council of Aachen, chapter 124.]

That God should be sought by care of the heart rather than of the body is evident from the clear testimonies of Holy Scripture. Therefore the canons must beware lest, through immoderate attention to clothing, they dishonor the dignity of religion.

Jerome says: “[Note: [Col. 1082D] Letter to Eustochium.] There are some whose entire concern is with clothing: whether they smell good, whether their foot slips out of loose leather. Their hair is curled by the marks of the curling iron; their fingers gleam with rings; and, lest a wetter road splash their soles, they scarcely press down the tips of their feet. When you see such men, consider them bridegrooms rather than clerics.”

Gregory says: “[Note: [Col. 1082D] Homily 6 on the Gospels.] Let no one think that there is no sin in the flowing and elaborate care of clothing. For if this were not a fault, the Lord would in no way have praised John for the roughness of his garment. If care of clothing were not a fault, the Apostle Paul would certainly not have restrained women by his Letter from seeking costly garments, saying: ‘Not in costly clothing’” (1 Timothy 2:9).

Therefore the canons ought to obey holy authority and display humility with the greatest devotion—in heart, mind, conduct, dress, manner of walking, and fairness. They should desire to shine more through holy conduct and outstanding character than through the adornment of clothing.

[Col. 1082D] Moreover, their clothing should be such that it is free from any occasion of vanity. No one should specially presume anything that is not generally maintained by all. The clothing, footwear, and bedding of clerics should be moderate and suitable in style, neither excessively fine nor excessively shabby. For just as a path must be kept between fire and water, so that a person is neither burned nor drowned, so we must regulate our way between the height of pride and the abyss of negligence.

### CHAPTER LV—That the prelates should provide their subjects with a twofold nourishment

[Col. 1083A]

[Note: [Col. 1083D] Council of Aachen, chapter 123.]

The prelates must labor diligently to instruct those over whom they preside in right living by words and examples. They must keep firmly in mind that they are to treat them not as their own but as the flock of their Lord, according to what is said to Peter: “If you love me, feed my sheep,” he says, “not yours.”

We say this because there are some who feed Christ’s sheep not for the love of Christ but for the sake of their own glory, domination, or profit. They ought carefully to provide them with earthly support and at the same time diligently offer them examples of virtue through the word of preaching. Therefore each prelate should strive to supply Christ’s household with both spiritual and bodily sustenance, so that he may deserve to become that evangelical servant of whom it is said: “The faithful and wise servant, whom the Lord has appointed over his household, to give them food at the proper time” (Matthew 24:45; Luke 12:42).

Thus, just as they provide their subjects with what is necessary for the body, so they must likewise strive to ensure that those subjects observe their order with the greatest devotion and similarly render due honor to their prelates and masters. They must fulfill the divine office at the canonical hours; they must not devote themselves to idleness, serve idle talk, engage in detraction or the other enticements of vice, but rather devote themselves to prayer, reading, any of the Church’s tasks, or their own useful occupations, or be instructed in sacred teachings and the disciplines of various arts [Col. 1083C]. In this way, no one in the congregation, existing uselessly or idly, will receive the Church’s support without service.

Therefore let the prelates earnestly provide this twofold nourishment to the sheep entrusted to them, since they will render an account to the Lord for their souls.

### CHAPTER LVI—The avoidance by clerics of intimacy with unrelated women

[Note: [Col. 1083D] Council of Aachen, chapter 98.]

The frequent visits of women are indeed the first temptations, and they make clerics blameworthy. What have you truly to do with women, you who converse with the Lord at the altar? Everyone in public—peasants, plowmen, and vine-growers in the fields—will daily tear you apart with severe reproaches if you insist on living with women contrary to the deposit of faith [Col. 1083D]. Were women present in the choir of the apostles? Prevent virgins who are not of your family from dwelling with you. No one walks securely among serpents and scorpions. He cannot dwell with the Lord with his whole heart who is joined to frequent visits from women. When straw approaches, it kindles fire; when a woman approaches, she corrupts the mind. If women live with men, the devil’s larder will not be lacking. It is the devil’s door, the way of iniquity, the scorpion’s blow [Col. 1084A], and a harmful kind of thing. No soldier goes to war with his wife.

Therefore I command and command again that women rarely, or never, wear out the threshold of the canons’ guesthouse. When a man or woman has turned to the Lord after the sin they committed against one another, they must never do penance in the same village; there must be no greeting or service between them, no sight of one another, no conversation—unless some emergency intervenes—and, as the common saying goes, they must not drink from the same fountain. No fosterling is to pass between the two; no little gift, no conversation, as we have said, and no remembrance of the other should rest in either person’s mind. Whenever such a thought occurs, the person should quickly ask forgiveness from God.

The canons must remember that they cannot be more holy than David or wiser than Solomon [Col. 1084B]. [Note: [Col. 1083D] From Jerome’s letter to Nepotian.] They must remember that a woman expelled the cultivator of paradise from his possession.

### CHAPTER LVII—Clerics who do not remain in their calling

We decree that those who have once been assigned to the clergy, or who have sought the life of monks, shall enter neither military service nor any worldly dignity. Those who attempt this and do not do penance, so that they may return to what they first undertook for God, shall be anathematized.

### CHAPTER LVIII—Humiliation of the flesh for God’s sake

[Note: [Col. 1083D] From Jerome’s Letter 13 to Paulinus.]

Crowds of people, public offices, entertainments, banquets, and the greetings of people are to be avoided as if they were certain chains of pleasure. Let food be cheap and taken in the evening. Bread with vegetables and legumes, and occasionally a little fish, should be regarded as the height of luxury. Whoever desires to reign with Christ will not be overly concerned about what he may turn into dung and urine from expensive foods and drinks. One should often sleep with an empty stomach; frequent vigils afflict the flesh and the senses. With the body bent, the mind should be raised to God. Holy reading should always be in the hand, and prayer frequently in the mouth. Relief from their expenses should be distributed to the poor by one’s own hand. A humility of clothing should not be sought by a puffed-up mind. The company of worldly people, especially the powerful, should be avoided.

Something must always be done, so that the devil may find a person occupied in work. The ears and tongue must be disciplined away from idle talk. [Note: [Col. 1084D] From Jerome’s letter to Nepotianus, in part.] And in church one must stand with fear and reverence; and one must always either pray, sing, read, or listen. Alms should be given to the just God from honest labor. It is better not to have anything to give than shamelessly to ask for something to be given. A cleric who is a merchant, who becomes rich from poverty, and who becomes renowned from obscurity, must be avoided as a kind of plague.

## CHAPTER LIX — On irascible teachers

[Note: [Col. 1084D] Isidore, *Sentences*, book III, chapter 40; and the Council of Aachen, chapter 33.] Irascible teachers, through the rage of their fury, turn the discipline of correction into savage cruelty; and from the very source by which they could have corrected their subjects, they instead wound them. Therefore an angry teacher punishes faults without measure, because his heart, scattered among worldly concerns, is not gathered into the love of the one Godhead.

## CHAPTER LX — On the teaching and examples of teachers

[Note: [Col. 1085D] Isidore, cited above, chapter 36; and the council, chapter 20.] An ecclesiastical teacher must shine both in teaching and in life; for teaching without life makes a person arrogant, while life without teaching renders him useless. A teacher’s preaching must be confirmed by good works, so that what he teaches in words he may inculcate by example. That is true teaching which is followed by a pattern of good living; for nothing is more shameful than for someone to neglect fulfilling in deed the good that he preaches. Preaching is then delivered usefully when it is effectively fulfilled by the one who delivers it. Every teacher must devote himself both to good action and to good preaching; for one without the other does not make a perfect person. Rather, the teacher should first act well, so that afterward he may be able to teach well. In that clear teaching, the likeness of the fathers and humility for God’s sake must also be maintained.

## CHAPTER LXI — On silence

At all times the greatest silence must be kept in church, both by the people and by the clergy, except for what pertains to the praise of God. Let us consider what the Prophet says: “I said, I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue.” Likewise: “I set a guard over my mouth; I was silent and humbled, and I kept silence from good things” (Psalm 38). [Note: [Col. 1085D] From chapter 6 of Saint Benedict’s Rule.] Here the Prophet shows that, if one must sometimes keep silent even from good words for the sake of silence, how much more must one abstain from evil words on account of the punishment of sin? Hence Holy Scripture says: “[Note: [Col. 1085D] Saint Augustine, sermon 214, *On the Season*.] For whoever causes people to chatter in church will have to render an evil account both for himself and for others on the day of judgment.” [Note: [Col. 1085D] Saint Benedict, cited above.] Therefore, although permission to speak rarely in church is granted, and only concerning good and holy words, for the sake of silence, since it is written, “In much speaking sin will not be absent,” and elsewhere, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs 10; 14), it is fitting for a teacher to speak and teach, but it is proper for a disciple to be silent and listen.

Whoever has not carefully observed this silence in church but has broken it shall do penance that same day on bread and water. If he repeats the offense, let him do penance for three days on bread and water. If he repeats it a third time, let him do penance for seven [Col. 1085D] days in the manner stated above. If he dares to do this still more often, let him be subjected to corporal discipline, so that the others may be afraid.

## CHAPTER LXII — On drunkenness, which the clergy must avoid and detest

The Lord says in the Gospel: “Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts perhaps be weighed down with carousing” (Luke 21:34). And the Apostle says: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Ephesians 5:18). Solomon says: “Wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness is tumultuous; whoever delights in these things will not be wise. There is no secrecy where drunkenness reigns” (Proverbs 20:1). Elsewhere it is said: “A drunken laborer will not become rich. Wine and women cause the wise to apostatize” (Ecclesiasticus 19:1–2). And elsewhere: “Do not invite into your assembly those who always love to become drunk with wine” (Ecclesiasticus 31:30). The Apostle condemns wine-loving priests, and the ancient Law forbids it (Leviticus 10:9): those who serve at the altar shall not drink wine or strong drink. [Note: [Col. 1086D] Jerome, letter 2.] In Hebrew usage, *sicera* denotes every drink that can cause drunkenness: flee whatever intoxicates and changes the state of the mind, just as you flee wine.

> If you desire to be good and wish to discern the truth,  
> Flee biting wine as the companion of death.  
> No fever of mankind is greater than the glassy liquid;  
> Because of it the ears grow deaf, and at last the tongue stammers.  
> Tell me, drunkard—do you live, or are you burdened with death?  
> Behold, you lie pale and rest without understanding;  
> You sense neither good nor evil, neither hard nor soft.

[Col. 1086B] Beware of drunkenness in everything, brothers, because it is a great overthrow of the soul. For just as fire easily ignites tow and lighter straw, so drunkenness corrupts the soul and casts it down into great sin. The Lord says through the Prophet: “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and continue drinking wine until evening” (Isaiah 5:11). And elsewhere it is said: “Woe to those who are powerful in drinking wine and strong men at mixing drunkenness” (ibid., 22).

Basil says: “For very many people have contracted the greatest bodily weakness through wine and have not been able to recover their former strength. A drunkard thinks that he is doing something excellent when he has been hurled headlong into ruin. Dearest brothers, do not become drunk; [Col. 1086C] do not erase your names from heaven by drinking immoderately. There are many—what is worse—who not only make themselves drunk but also urge others to drink more than is proper. O unhappy one who does this! Is it not enough that you yourself perish, unless you also destroy others? Is it not enough that you yourself fall into that drunkenness, unless you drag others along with you? It is not enough for the wretched drunkard to drown himself in drunkenness unless he also tries to entangle others with him. Do not do this evil, brothers, do not; hear the Apostle saying: ‘Nor will drunkards possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Corinthians 6:10). For a drunk person recognizes neither father, mother, friend, nor enemy; he does not distinguish between good and evil, and fears neither fire nor sword. Thus false brothers and persecutors are those who despise God and [Col. 1086D] the Church; they distinguish neither good nor evil, and fear neither the sword of the present life nor the fire of the Gehenna to come. When a person is drunk, he cannot free his heart or his limbs.”

## CHAPTER LXIII — On clerics

[Note: [Col. 1086D] Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 1. He cites the Council of Aachen, chapter 99.] Therefore all who have been ordained in the degrees of ecclesiastical ministry are generally called clerics. Our teachers say that *clerus* or *clerici* takes its name from this: Matthias was chosen by lot, and we read that he was the first ordained by the apostles (Acts 1:26). [Col. 1087A] Likewise, in those times all whom the leaders of the churches ordained were chosen by lot. *Clerus* is interpreted as “lot”; hence inheritance is called in Greek *cleronomia*, and an heir *cleronomus*. Therefore, they say, they are called clerics because they are given as the Lord’s inheritance by lot, or because the Lord himself is their lot, as it is written concerning them, with the Lord speaking: “I am their inheritance” (Deuteronomy 18:2). Hence those who possess God as their inheritance ought to strive to serve God without any impediment from the world, and to seek to be poor in spirit, so that they may fittingly say with the Psalmist: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Psalm 15:5).

## CHAPTER LXIV — On the rules of clerics

[Note: [Col. 1087D] Isidore, at the cited place, chapter 2; and the council, chapter 100.] The law of the Fathers therefore provides that, withdrawn from ordinary life, clerics abstain from the pleasures of the world; that they attend neither spectacles nor public celebrations; that they avoid public banquets, while observing private ones that are not only modest but also sober. They must by no means engage in usury or in disgraceful profit-making occupations, nor pursue any practice of fraud. They must flee love of money as the source of all crimes, and cast aside secular offices and business. They must not ascend the steps of honor through ambition. They must not accept gifts for the healing benefits of God. They must beware of deceit and conspiracies; flee hatred, rivalry, detraction, and envy; and walk neither with wandering eyes, nor with an unbridled tongue, nor with insolent and haughty gestures. Rather, they must display modesty and reverence of mind through a simple manner and walk. They must utterly detest obscenity both in words [Col. 1087C] and in deeds.

They must avoid excessively frequent visits to widows and virgins; they must in no way seek the companionship of unrelated women; and they must strive continually to preserve the chastity of an inviolate body, or at least bind themselves by the bond of a single marriage. They must also show due obedience to their elders and must not exalt themselves through any desire for vainglory. Finally, they must devote themselves continually to instruction, reading, psalms, hymns, and songs. For those who seek to offer themselves wholly to divine worship ought to be such that, while applying themselves to knowledge, they administer the grace of teaching to the people.

## CHAPTER LXV — On the kinds of clerics

[Note: [Col. 1087D] Isidore, in the same place, chapter 3; and the council, chapter 101.] There are two kinds of clerics. One consists of ecclesiastics living under episcopal governance; the other consists of the Acephali—“headless,” that is, those who do not know whom they should follow. Neither among the laity does the pursuit of secular offices retain them, nor among the clergy does divine religion retain them; but, released and wandering, they are embraced only by a shameful and unsettled life. Fearing no one, they pursue the freedom to carry out their will; like brute animals, they enjoy their liberty and desire, possessing the sign of religion but not its duty. They are like Hippocentaurs, who are neither horses [Col. 1088A] nor human beings, “a mixed race,” as the Poet says, “and a two-formed offspring.” [Note: [Col. 1087D] *Aeneid* VI.] Our western region is sufficiently and more than sufficiently polluted by their sordid and infamous multitude.

## CHAPTER LXVI — On priests who sin

[Note: [Col. 1087D] Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 1; Council of Nicaea, chapter 78.] A presbyter or deacon who has been caught in fornication, perjury, theft, or homicide shall be deposed; nevertheless, he shall not be deprived of communion, for Scripture says: “The Lord will not judge twice for the same thing.”

## CHAPTER LXVII — That a presbyter should have one church

[Note: [Col. 1087D] Council of Nantes, chapter 8.] A presbyter shall have no more than one church, just as a man has one wife.

## CHAPTER LXVIII — That clerics should avoid wedding banquets

[Note: [Col. 1088D] Council of Vannes, chapter 11, and Council of Agde, chapter 39.] Presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and those of the lower orders, who are not permitted to take wives, must avoid the banquets of other people’s weddings. Nor should they mingle in gatherings where amorous and shameful songs are sung, or where obscene movements of the body are displayed in dances and performances, lest hearing and sight, dedicated to sacred mysteries, be polluted by the contagion of shameful spectacles and words.

## CHAPTER LXIX — That the priesthood must not be sought through ambition

[Note: [Col. 1088D] Gregory, book VI, letter 169, beginning.] Just as one who, when invited, refuses, and when sought, withdraws, is to be offered at the sacred altars, so one who voluntarily seeks the office or intrudes himself importunately must undoubtedly be rejected. For what does one who strives to climb to higher places do except diminish himself by increasing? Why does he not consider that the blessing is being turned into a curse for him?

## CHAPTER LXX — On presbyters being removed from their office

[Col. 1088C]

[Note: [Col. 1088D] Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 1.] Those presbyters who have begotten children within their presbyterate must be removed from their office.

## CHAPTER LXXI — It is prescribed that one pray for the sick and anoint them

The Apostle James wrote: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring the presbyters into his house, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (James 5:14). [Note: [Col. 1088D] Innocent, book I, letter 1. Bede, on the Epistle of James, chapter 5, middle.] There is no doubt that this must be understood of faithful people who are ill, who may be anointed with holy oil. This oil, once prepared by the bishop, may be used not only by priests but by all Christians, for anointing themselves or their own people in necessity. For this reason it was said to the presbyters: bishops, occupied with other duties, cannot go to all the sick. Moreover, if a bishop is able, or considers someone worthy of being visited by him, he may without hesitation visit, bless, and touch him with chrism, since he is the one whose office it is to prepare the chrism. But this may not be poured out upon penitents, because it is a kind of sacrament; for those who are denied the other sacraments, how can it be thought that one kind may be granted?

## CHAPTER LXXII — That offerings ought not to be made in houses

[Col. 1089A]

[Note: [Col. 1089D] Council of Laodicea, chapter 58.] Offerings ought not to be celebrated in houses by bishops or presbyters.

## CHAPTER LXXIII — How the bridegroom and bride are to be blessed

[Note: [Col. 1089D] Council of Carthage IV, chapter 13.] The bridegroom and bride shall be blessed by the priest with prayers and offerings; the bride shall be endowed according to the laws and guarded by bridesmen; and she shall be received publicly and solemnly. They shall also abstain for two or three days, and they shall be instructed to preserve chastity between them and to have marital relations at the appointed times, so that they may produce for God and the world children who are not illegitimate but heirs.

## CHAPTER LXXIV — On observing the principal solemnities

[Col. 1089B] On the principal solemnities—that is, at the Nativity, the Octave, the Epiphany of the Lord, Easter, the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, and the feasts of the saints, namely Saint Stephen, Saint John the Evangelist, the feast of the Innocents, and the Purification, as well as the Assumption of Saint Mary; likewise on the feasts of the blessed apostles, Saint John the Baptist, Saint Lawrence, and Saint Martin, and on the feast of any saint whose honor is specially celebrated in any parish—a full office shall be celebrated, and food shall be taken twice.

## CHAPTER LXXV — On the distribution of tithes

[Note: [Col. 1089D] Ecbert, archbishop of York, excerpt 5.] The priests shall receive the tithes of the people and shall have the names of all who have given them written upon the altar. They shall divide those tithes according to canonical authority [Col. 1089C] in the presence of witnesses. They shall first select a portion for the adornment of the church; they shall mercifully distribute the second portion, through the hands of the faithful, for the use of the poor and pilgrims, with all humility; and the priests alone shall reserve the third portion for themselves.

## CHAPTER LXXVI — That presbyters should not be sent indiscriminately by bishops or laypeople to different places

It has been decreed that presbyters, as has hitherto been done, must not be sent indiscriminately to different places, either by bishops, other prelates, or laypeople, lest, because of their absence, the services of the churches in which they have been appointed be neglected and the souls entrusted to them be endangered.

## CHAPTER LXXVII — On those who dare to celebrate Mass alone, contrary to canonical authority

[Col. 1089D]

[Note: [Col. 1089D] *On Consecration*, distinction 1.] It has been decreed that no presbyter shall dare to celebrate Mass alone, because neither the words of the Lord and Savior, by which he entrusted to his disciples the celebration of the mysteries of his body and blood, nor the teaching of the Apostle Paul, nor, if the Acts of the Apostles are read carefully, anything found there declares that this ought in any way to be done. [Note: [Col. 1090D] Theodulf, *Capitularies*, chapter 7.] For even if a solitary consecrator of the Lord’s body and blood should be questioned or despised, what could he answer? To whom does he say, “The Lord be with you,” or from whom does he receive the response, [Col. 1090A] “And with your spirit”? For whom does he supplicate God when he says, “Remember, Lord, your male and female servants, and all who are present,” when no one is present? This custom, contrary to apostolic and ecclesiastical authority, must be eradicated and utterly uprooted by the priests of the Lord. If anyone henceforth dares to do this, he shall be subject to the danger of losing his rank.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII — That presbyters may not be appointed to churches, or expelled from them, without consulting the bishop

[Note: [Col. 1090D] Council of Chalon II, chapter 42.] It has been decreed that presbyters may neither be appointed to any churches nor expelled from them without the authority or consent of the bishops. If anyone thereafter attempts to do this, let him be strictly punished by synodal judgment.

## CHAPTER LXXIX — On the books that each person ought to have with him in church

[Col. 1090B]

These are the books that every priest ought to have in his church, through which the Masses, epistles, Gospel, baptismal rite, penance, cycles of years, and nocturnal readings may be understood. If anyone does not have such books, let him be degraded from the Church, because in him is fulfilled what is written in the books: “Mute dogs cannot bark” (Isaiah 56:10). These are bad presbyters who desire to receive the pastoral ministry of the Church, yet cannot preach to the people.

## CHAPTER LXXX — On not receiving clerics from another church, and on those who receive them without letters of recommendation or witnesses from clerics serving in that same church

[Col. 1090C]

[Note: [Col. 1090D] Council of Antioch, chapter 3; Council of Arles II, chapter 13; Council of Epaon, chapters 5 and 6.] It has already been established that clerics may not serve in the Church of another city or under the power of laypeople, but must remain there where from the beginning they were judged worthy to minister. Strangers who have come from their homeland to some church out of necessity [are not to be received without sealed documents]. Whoever, after this decree, receives a cleric of another church—unless for a reasonable excuse—shall be suspended from communion, both the one who receives him and the one who is received, until he causes the cleric to return to his own church.

## CHAPTER LXXXI — A letter of a certain servant of God, sent in the name of Christ to priests and clerics, addressed to them for the purpose of preaching and instruction

[Col. 1090D] To the most beloved priests, the bishops of the churches of Christ, and to all the clergy everywhere serving in those churches, and to all servants of God dwelling throughout the whole world: eternal salvation in the Lord our Savior.

Let your affection know that I am always solicitous and greatly desire to know about your salvation, health, and life. May the God of us all fulfill our pious desire and yours in glory and in the discipline of holy living. Therefore, since by the heavenly mercy of the Lord we are rulers of the people belonging to him, it is fitting that we think with the greatest care of God’s aid for the salvation of those who seem to have been entrusted to us, lest—God forbid—we be compelled to render a strict account before the Shepherd of all concerning souls entrusted to us and thwarted by the snares of the ancient enemy, unless correction of offenses intervenes in advance. Hence we ask you to live justly, piously, and holily, to be an example to the other faithful, and to live with chaste heart and body under the canonical rule.

Moreover, I ask you to consider and always keep before the eyes of your mind and body what we and you are. Are we not human beings? And from what are human beings made, except from earth? And what is earth except dust and ashes? And what shall we be, except what has been said: “When Christ appears, if we have acted well, we shall be like him” (Colossians 3:4)—that is, in immortality and eternity? Let us deny what we are, so that we may begin to be what we are not. Therefore every good thing must be hoped for from the supreme God, because “unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 126). And, “Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain” (ibid.). Let us therefore ask, seek, and knock: “The one who asks receives, the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Luke 11:10). Let us always consider the final day of our departure. Let us adorn our end and carefully order our life. And to the extent that we are uncertain about the day of our death, let us be equally prepared in our good actions, so that whenever it comes, it may always find us ready. Let us consider and weigh the fact that the Judge will come in strictness, and will appear as an examiner not only of deeds but also of thoughts. Let us labor in God’s work as much as we can, if not as much as we ought; for, as the Apostle says, “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us.” Therefore we and all the faithful must earnestly strive to run faithfully toward that glory.

I also exhort your diligence, O priests and dearest brothers, to remember how great are the burdens of souls that you have undertaken. Since you have accepted their care, lay aside a life of security, which is useless to soul and body, because those who have accepted souls to govern must prepare themselves to render an account in the sight of God. Therefore, insofar as you are able, by word and example, as we said above, do not cease to admonish the sheep entrusted to you, so that at the judgment, acquitted together with the Prophet, you may be able to say: “Lord, I have not hidden your justice in my heart.” And: “I have declared your truth and your salvation” (Psalm 39:11). Think upon the final day and preserve your rule; reckon your stewardship, because you will have to render an account on the day of judgment for all who have perished through your negligence. And, if you are to obtain profit and reward from your work, you ought to benefit more than to rule.

O spiritual priests, love your clergy and your people, and do not consider any parents closer to you than those who dwell with you in the house and work of God. For where spiritual love and affection are, there God the mediator dwells, who said: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). Humbly consider your own frailty and patiently bear the care of the weak. [Note: [Col. 1091D] Saint Benedict, chapters 64 and 48, and elsewhere.] Be moderate in your authority, as the rule teaches. Likewise, I advise you to distinguish and temper the tasks that you impose. Always consider your discretion, so that whatever your subjects do, they may do without murmuring, so that souls may be saved and bodies may not be burdened beyond measure. I also admonish all the clerics subject to you to obey you humbly, strive with all their strength to fulfill the canonical rule, submit to your authority without murmuring, and serve the Lord sweetly. For every person ought to be subject to the higher powers [Col. 1092B] and to his superiors (Romans 13:1; Titus 3:1); how much more ought the servants of God humbly to obey their superiors?

I also advise them to remember the canonical rule and always keep its precepts before their eyes. For who knows what may happen to him or to another in this life? Or who has ever reached a good end while disobedient? We are struck with no small fear when we read that the end of many saints was perilous, and that after so many labors had been accomplished, some were even hurled from the heights to the depths. Their fall ought to become our progress, since we read that the first human being also fell through disobedience. Many and innumerable examples could indeed be gathered concerning these matters, but these are sufficient for us now, so that in these things you may take care not to commit disobedience in any matter against Christ.

Do not delight in excessive luxuries, except insofar as they seem to sustain the body, and not insofar as human desire is tempted to seek them. Do not be adorned with elaborate clothing, but be content with the body’s necessities in a simple manner. Maintain discipline in such a way that you do not lose your soul. Do not give yourselves over to forgetfulness or adopt any false security; rather, prepare nourishment for both body and soul for yourselves [and] for the clerics subject to you, so that they may always serve joyfully with you under the service to which they have devoted themselves. Then in the future you may receive your reward and hear the Lord’s voice, where it says: “Because you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord” [Col. 1092D] (Matthew 25:21). May our Lord and Savior, through the prayers of all his saints, deem it worthy to lead me, a sinner, and all of you, together with all those entrusted to us, unharmed into eternal life, he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER LXXXII — Another letter to a bishop

To my sweetest lord, the bishop: perpetual greetings in Christ. Dearest father, may you fare well in Christ and always please him. I greet you, and through you all your clerics. Console and strengthen them, insofar as you are able, in the service of our Lord Jesus Christ. [Note: [Col. 1092D] Saint Benedict, chapter 2, section 70.] I advise your prudence to rebuke sinners before everyone, so that the others may have fear. For whoever sees the evils of his neighbors and nevertheless restrains his tongue in silence becomes the cause of their death, because he has refused to heal those whom he could have healed. Let us therefore, who have been placed in a dangerous order, take care that we not be useless servants. Let us always remember the command of him who said: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John 15:12). For the salvation of all consists in this commandment; it is plainly necessary for everyone, and especially for those who receive the flock of Christ to govern.

Therefore, dearest shepherd, diligently strive to instruct the flock that you have received to govern, and labor to lead it through the pastures of life by holy admonitions. In every good work you have Christ as your helper, and the saint whom you serve as your intercessor. Just as you appear to have the governance and administration of the house of the Lord, so strive to adorn your subjects with good morals and make them stand most devoutly in divine praise. Let your clerics continually do in the churches what the angels always do in heaven. It is yours to command; theirs to obey. It is yours to go before; theirs to follow. Therefore there should be one will among all in the service of God, so that there may be one reward in the kingdom of God.

Let no one withdraw from divine praises at the canonical hours, lest through anyone’s negligence a place be found empty in the sight of God. Let the words of God be spoken in the churches with the innermost affection of the heart, and let the services of almighty God be celebrated with great reverence. [Col. 1093C] Let every ministry of Christ be fulfilled humbly and devoutly. Let every obedience in the necessities of the world be carried out faithfully and energetically. Let there be among all the most harmonious peace, most holy charity, and devotion to the regular life. Let the elders instruct the younger by good example and diligent admonition, and love them as sons; and let the younger honor them as fathers and obey their commands with every readiness.

Your way of life, venerable shepherd, must be an example of salvation to everyone. Take care that no one be scandalized by your life, but rather built up and strengthened on the way of truth, because an eternal reward is determined for you from their salvation. Gray hairs announce that the final day is hastening; therefore be ready at every hour to meet the Lord your God. Brotherly love, alms for the poor, and chastity of life will prepare a step for you in heaven.

On feast days, when the people come to church, have the words of God preached to them. Wherever you go, let clerics who fully perform the service of God go with you, adorned with sobriety and unaccustomed to drunkenness; let the uprightness of their lives be instruction in salvation to others. Have care everywhere, and especially for the poor, widows, and orphans, so that on the fearful day you may hear from the Lord, together with the others who give alms: “As long as you did it to one of these least ones, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40). [Col. 1094A] Be a father to the afflicted; carefully examine the case of those who cry out to you; and forgive those who sin against you, so that God may forgive your sins. Be just in judgments and merciful in debts; a teacher of virtues, honorable in conduct, pleasant in speech, praiseworthy in life, and devout in every work of God.

Also exhort the clerics to read the Holy Scriptures most diligently. Let them not rely on knowledge of the tongue alone, so that they may be able to resist those who contradict the truth. For the times are dangerous, as the Apostle foretold, because many false teachers will arise, introducing sects, who will strive to stain the Catholic faith with impious assertions. Therefore the Church needs more defenders who are able to defend the camp of God manfully, not only by holiness of life but also by the teaching of truth.

I have directed these little letters of pious admonition to you not as though you were ignorant, but to show the faith of the true charity that is in my breast. May almighty God cause you and your dearest clerics to progress in every good thing and grant you to reach the blessedness of eternal glory, he who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII — On discernment in teaching

[Note: [Col. 1093D] Isidore, *Sentences*, book III, chapter 43; Council of Aachen, chapter 23.] The same teaching is not to be applied to everyone; rather, the teachers’ exhortation must vary according to the character of their conduct. For some are corrected by a harsh rebuke, while others are corrected by a gentle exhortation. Just as skilled physicians treat various bodily diseases with different medicines, so that the remedy may vary according to the variety of wounds [Col. 1094C], so the teacher of the Church must apply to each person the appropriate remedy of teaching and announce what is suitable to each according to age, sex, and vocation.

Not everything that is closed is to be opened to everyone. For there are many who cannot grasp such things, and if they are disclosed to them indiscriminately, they immediately either disparage them or neglect them. To uneducated or carnal peoples, plain and common matters—not the highest and most difficult—must be preached, lest they be overwhelmed by the vastness of the teaching rather than instructed. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3:2). To carnal minds it is fitting to preach neither matters too lofty concerning heavenly things nor earthly things, but to teach them moderately, as their beginnings and character require. When the raven sees its chicks to be white in color, it feeds them no food, but simply waits until they darken to their father’s color; then it restores them with frequent feeding. Thus the diligent teacher of the Church does not open the deeper mysteries of spiritual understanding unless he sees those whom he teaches becoming dark through confession of repentance in his likeness and, having laid aside worldly brightness, putting on the garment of lamentation in remembrance of sin.

[Note: [Col. 1093] Isidore; and the council, in the same place, shortly afterward. Gregory, in the prologue to book III of the *Pastoral Rule*.] The elders of the people should first be taught, so that those below them may more easily be taught through them.

[Col. 1095A] The same exhortation does not suit everyone, because not everyone is bound by the same character. Often what harms some benefits others, since even herbs that nourish certain animals kill others; a gentle whistle calms horses but incites puppies; a medicine that reduces one illness adds strength to another; and bread that strengthens the life of the strong kills the little ones. Therefore the speech of teachers must be shaped according to the character of their hearers. “[Note: [Col. 1095D] From Gregory, book II of the *Pastoral Rule*, chapter 4, middle.] A teacher must always have the voice of preaching, lest by silence he offend the judgment of the heavenly Observer. When a teacher enters the tabernacle or leaves it, he dies if no sound is heard from him, because he provokes God’s anger against himself if he proceeds without the sound of preaching.”

Frogs seem to be in water and yet without water [Col. 1095B], yet they remain in the rottenness of the marsh and utter bold, impatient, and importunate cries. So hypocritical teachers seem to be in the water of wisdom, yet remain entangled in the mud of heresy; they emit voices opposed to the truth and harm the good at inopportune times, driven by the spirit of the devil. They go out to kings of the earth to gather them—that is, the impious—and inspire them to fight against the saints, who are kings of righteousness. Although every falsehood assumes the likeness of truth, the dignity of true wisdom nevertheless differs from the semblance of teaching.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV — On a cleric abandoning the clerical state

[Note: [Col. 1095D] Second Council of Hispania, chapter 3.] If any cleric, abandoning the order of his office, wishes to live a lay life or gives himself over to secular military service, let him be punished with excommunication.

## CHAPTER LXXXV — On the fact that one person from the canonical order is not easily overcome

[Col. 1095C]

[Note: [Col. 1096D] Second Council of Rome, canon 3.] Silvester says: “Let no acolyte bring any accusation against a subdeacon, no exorcist against an acolyte, no lector against an exorcist, and no doorkeeper against a lector. And a subdeacon, exorcist, doorkeeper, lector, or acolyte who has children and a wife, and who in every respect preaches Christ, shall not be condemned; thus the mystical truth is given, except on the testimony of seven witnesses. A deacon shall not be condemned except on the testimony of thirty-six, and a presbyter shall not be condemned except on the testimony of forty-four.”

## CHAPTER LXXXVI—That the Canons Must Guard Against the Transformations of Demons

[Col. 1095D] Canonical clerics must be admonished to be cautious, [Col. 1096A] lest they be deceived by demons through subtle thoughts. Therefore the form of the devil must also be watched for among the clerics, so that if anyone comes to them—whether man or woman, old or young, known or unknown—prayer may be offered before all else, so that the name of the Lord may first be invoked; for if it is some transformation of a demon, it will immediately flee once the prayer has been made. And if demons arise in their thoughts and suggest something by which they ought to be praised or exalted, they must not consent to them; rather, they should then humble themselves all the more in the sight of God and regard as nothing whatever they suggest to them that is unlawful.

Demons came to a certain monk named Or in the form of a heavenly army and in angelic dress, driving fiery chariots with great display, [Col. 1096B] as though escorting some great king. The one who seemed to be regarded by the others as king said to him: “You have fulfilled everything, O man; only this remains for you: that you worship me. But if you worship me, I shall transport you as I did Elijah.” Hearing this, the monk Or said in his heart: “What is this? Every day I worship my Savior, who is my king. If this were the one whom I worship, how could he ask me to do what he would know I perform unceasingly?” After this he answered him: “I have my own King, whom I worship every day without interruption; but you are not my king.” Immediately that enemy disappeared at these words.

Likewise, Bishop Fortunatus drove an unclean spirit out of a certain man. When the evil spirit saw that evening had already come and that there was a private hour away from human company, it pretended to be a stranger, began to go around the streets of the city, and cried out: “O holy man, Bishop Fortunatus! Look what he has done: he has driven a stranger from the lodging-house. I am looking for somewhere to rest, but I cannot find it in his city.” At that time a certain man was sitting by the embers in a lodging-house with his wife and little son. Hearing the voice and asking what the bishop had done to him, he invited him into the lodging-house and made him sit beside him near the embers. While they were conversing with one another, that same evil spirit attacked his little son, threw him into the same embers, and immediately snatched away his life there. The wretched, bereaved man recognized both the one whom he himself had received and the one whom the bishop had expelled.

# [RULE OF THE CANONS ACCORDING TO LABBE’S RECENSION]

[Col. 1095]

## PHILIPPE LABBE’S OBSERVATION ON HIS SUBSEQUENT EDITION OF THE RULE OF SAINT CHRODEGANG

[Col. 1095D] We obtained a copy transcribed from a very ancient manuscript of the Palatine Library at Heidelberg, transferred to the Vatican, and sent from Rome through the efforts of the most eminent prince, Cardinal Francesco Barberini. We present it to you, reader, after collating it not only with our own copy, produced long ago through the assistance of the Reverend Father Jacques Sirmond from the manuscripts of Angers and Fécamp, but also with the printed edition of Dom Luc d’Achery, O.S.B., in volume I of the *Spicilegium*. From that careful and diligent collation we have learned, and are prepared to demonstrate by very powerful arguments, that this canonical rule of regular canons—which we are the first to bring to public light—is precisely the one that Chrodegang [Col. 1097A] prescribed specifically for his canons at Metz. I judge that the commonly circulated rule, however, was first stripped by some anonymous author so that it might be common to all canons spread throughout the Christian world, rather than attached to one city alone; then it was enriched with prescriptions gathered from various sources and, in many places, awkwardly stitched into the earlier order, prescriptions suitable to the regular institution of canons, especially from the Council of Aachen celebrated in the year 816. Nor, I think, will you judge otherwise if you wish to compare the two little works with each other.

[Col. 1097]

# THE RULE OF THE CANONS OF SAINT CHRODEGANG, BISHOP OF METZ, ACCORDING TO LABBE’S EDITION (C)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1097B] In the time of the most devout and serene King Pippin, Chrodegang, servant of the servants of God, bishop of the city of Metz.

If the authority of the three hundred and eighteen and the other holy Fathers’ canons had endured, and if the clergy and bishop lived according to the standard of their rectitude, it would seem superfluous for us, insignificant and least of all, to reconsider anything concerning a matter so orderly arranged, or to appear to say something new [Note: [Col. 1097D] Another reading: “to reconsider or to say.”]. But since negligence among shepherds and their subjects has greatly increased in these times, what else is there for us to do, who have come into so grave a crisis, except, insofar as we can, if not insofar as we ought, to bring our clergy back to the line of rectitude, with God inspiring us? [Note: [Col. 1097D] He had Metz alone in mind.]

[Col. 1097C] Therefore, although unworthy, having obtained the pontifical chair of this see, and having begun to keep watch over the care of my pastoral office, when I saw that both clergy and people had fallen into such great negligence, I began sorrowfully to complain, asking what I ought to do [Note: [Col. 1097D] Another reading: “to seek.”]. But, supported by divine help and aided by the consolation of spiritual brothers [Note: [Col. 1097D] Another reading adds: “and encouraged by recovery,”] I wished, compelled by necessity, to make a small decree by which the clergy might restrain themselves from unlawful things, lay aside what was vicious, and abandon evils long and widely practiced; so that, while the mind is emptied of its accustomed vices, it may more easily receive whatever things are good and excellent. [Note: [Col. 1098D] Another reading: “all good and excellent things.”]

Relying on the sacred Scriptures [Note: [Col. 1098D] Another reading: “being attentive,”] we decree that all be of one mind, diligent in divine offices and sacred readings, ready for obedience to their bishop and superior, as the canonical order requires, [Col. 1097D] bound together in charity, most fervent in good zeal [Note: [Col. 1098D] Another reading: “and in most fervent love,”] united in love, and removed from quarrels, scandals, and hatred. Whoever is their pastor must care not only for bodily matters but also for spiritual ones, and must exercise the keenest possible diligence in both respects, insofar as he has the ability, so that he may restrain vices and, as soon as they begin to arise, hasten to cut them out at the root, insofar as he is able; and he must dare to provide them with whatever is necessary for human use according to the form set out below.

Thus, when Christ, the Shepherd of shepherds and Judge of the living and the dead, sits on the last and fearsome day upon the seat of his majesty to judge all nations, and all the clergy behold him with unveiled face, if we do not deserve, together with the highest shepherds and the flocks entrusted to them, to hear for the talents administered and the spiritual gains multiplied, “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matt. 25), may at least full forgiveness of sins be granted to us. For it is clear that entry into the kingdom is not denied to those whose sins are wholly forgiven; nor can one be called unhappy who has been granted any share whatever in paradise. But there the lot is given to those who, insofar as they can, hasten during the course of this present age, while it is permitted, to run toward that goal through the merit of their life.

Let us therefore direct our minds toward this, insofar as we can, since we cannot do so insofar as we ought; and let our life grow bitter for a time in penance, lest the divine vengeance, which is now gentle and waits, later rage in punishment.

# HERE BEGINS THE RULE

[Col. 1097]

## CHAPTER I—On Humility

[Col. 1097D]

Divine Scripture cries out to us: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14). And, “The more humble you are, the greater the height of glory follows you” (James 4). And because “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Prov. 16), everyone who is arrogant is unclean before the Lord. Whenever you see a proud person, do not doubt that he is a son of the devil [Note: [Col. 1099D] Another reading: “whomever.”]; and whenever you perceive someone humble, you must certainly believe that he is a son of God. We have touched briefly on many things in order to encourage your minds to love humility and [Note: [Col. 1099D] Another reading: “to withdraw from them pride, hateful and hostile to God,”] to draw them away from pride, which is hateful and hostile to God. For although humility is fitting for the whole human race of Christians and for the entire common people, it is exceedingly unjust, wicked, and detestable that those who have joined themselves more particularly to God’s service should abandon humility and ally themselves with pride or the tyranny of the devil.
