Therefore it is necessary that whoever, persuaded by the devil, has until now lived proud and arrogant in appearance [Note: [Col. 1099D] Another reading: “and stern of face,”] should henceforth, with God’s help, rise again through humility, charity, obedience, and the other good commandments of God, because it is far better to reign with Christ in the heavenly places through humility than to be plunged with the devil and the other despisers into hell through pride.

## CHAPTER II—On the Order of the Congregation of Canons

Let the canons preserve their ranks as they have been arranged in their degrees according to the legitimate institution of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 1099D] D’Achery noted that this and certain other matters are drawn from the Rule of Saint Benedict.], in every place whatsoever—that is, in church and wherever they may gather together when circumstances require it—except those whom the bishop has placed in a higher rank or degraded for definite reasons. Let all the rest, as we have said, preserve their ranks as they have been arranged. Thus the younger shall honor their elders, and the elders shall love their juniors in God.

[Note: [Col. 1100D] Another reading: “of the persons themselves.”] In addressing another by name, no one may call him by his bare name; rather, according to the constitution of the holy Church and the apostolic see, he must call him by his name with the degree of his ministry, whatever it may be, added first. Whenever the younger clergy encounter one another [Note: [Col. 1100D] Another reading: “the younger clergy should bow and receive a blessing from the elder,”] the younger, having bowed, shall ask the elder for his blessing. If he finds the elder seated, the younger shall rise when the elder passes and give him his place to sit; nor may the younger presume to sit down with him unless his elder orders him to do so, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “In honor, outdo one another” (Rom. 12).

Little boys and adolescents shall preserve their ranks with discipline in the oratory and at table [Note: [Col. 1100D] Another reading: “at Masses,”] and outside, [Note: [Col. 1100D] Another reading: “and wherever they may be,”] wherever they are, they shall maintain discipline.

## CHAPTER III—That All Shall Sleep Together in the Cloister

[Col. 1099D]

We establish that the canonical clergy who, under this order, ought with God’s help to live together shall all sleep in one dormitory, except those to whom the bishop has granted permission, according to what he reasonably considers appropriate, to sleep separately in the same cloister in designated quarters. They shall sleep one to each bed, and in the dormitory likewise they shall sleep separately, mixed in with the elders for the sake of good supervision, so that the elders may see to it that the younger act according to God’s will.

No woman shall enter the cloister, nor any layman, except when the bishop, archdeacon, or chief cantor orders it. When laymen come into the refectory for the sake of eating, they shall leave their weapons outside the refectory, and as soon as they have come out of the refectory they shall be led outside the cloister. If it is necessary for work to be done, laymen may enter there; but once they have completed their work, they shall leave immediately and with the greatest haste. Apart from a necessity—if the clerical cooks are absent and there is need—lay cooks may enter only for cooking; once their service is completed, they shall quickly go out.

In those quarters the canonical clerics shall not keep any of their own clergy without the permission of their bishop. If he permits them to do so, their conduct must be marked by such humility and fear of God that they displease neither God nor the bishop nor those who govern the congregation under their authority. If they act otherwise, the one in charge shall either excommunicate them or have them undergo corporal discipline.

Within those quarters in the cloister, neither cleric nor layman may presume to drink, eat, or sleep, except the clerics who belong to that congregation, or those clerics who, by order of their bishop, serve their elders there in that cloister. Whoever keeps one of the clergy in the cloister, as we have said, must see to it that he has a chasuble with the other vestments, and that on Sundays and other [Col. 1100C] festivals they stand clothed in their ranks in the church of God.

## CHAPTER IV—On Compline and Silence

Let all the clergy belonging to that congregation come to Compline. At the beginning of night, let the first signal for Compline always sound. When the one appointed for this has caused that first signal to be heard, let them immediately come to their cloister from wherever they may be. When they hear the same signal again, let them all be in the church [Note: [Col. 1100D] This is the principal basilica of the city of Metz.] of Saint Stephen, and there let them sing Compline in the name of God.

After they have sung Compline, they shall neither drink nor eat until the proper hour of the following day. All shall keep silence, and no one shall speak with another until morning, after Prime has been sung, unless necessity requires it; and then they shall speak in a subdued voice and with great caution, so that their voice cannot be heard from the neighboring quarters. Whoever has not been present at Compline shall thereafter presume neither to knock at that door during the night nor to enter the cloister by any route before coming to Matins.

Neither the archdeacon, nor the chief cantor, nor the doorkeeper may grant anyone permission to enter there after Compline, except for Matins, unless some circumstance occurs such that it is necessary for the archdeacon, chief cantor, or whoever is then responsible for the matter to explain to the bishop why it was done. If it is indeed necessary, then they may have permission to enter and leave.

If it happens that some matter must be announced in the cloister after Compline, let the messenger come to the guardian of Saint Stephen, explain it to him, and let him announce it in the cloister. If—which God forbid—it happens that one of that clergy who has come into the city before Compline, or who was already there, is so bold, presumptuous, or negligent, at the devil’s prompting, as to spend a night somewhere in the city rather than in his own cloister, then, if he does this once and it was not done through fault, let him be corrected in words. If that cleric repeats it, let him remain that day on bread and water. If he does it a third time, let him remain three days on bread and water. If he presumes to do it thereafter, let him be subjected to corporal discipline, so that the others may fear.

If, at the devil’s prompting, he has delayed in some way so that he did not come into the city before Compline, in order to have permission to remain outside the cloister, and the bishop, archdeacon, or chief cantor is able to discover this, let the cleric who committed this fault either be excommunicated or undergo corporal discipline.

## CHAPTER V—On the Divine Offices at Night

During the winter season, that is, from the Kalends of November until Easter, let there be a longer rest after midnight, according to reasonable consideration, and, once they have digested their food, let them rise for the vigils. When the nocturns are finished, let them say a verse, [Note: [Col. 1101D] Another reading: “The saints shall exult in glory,” or “Let the righteous exult in the sight of God,”] the *Kyrie eleison*, and the Lord’s Prayer, and let them make an interval.

On Sundays and the festivals of the saints, however, according to the judgment of the bishop or of those who are under him [Note: [Col. 1101D] Another reading: “who are subsequently under him,”] the one who directs this may have forty or fifty psalms sung, [Note: [Col. 1101D] Another reading: “they may change this according to what seems appropriate and what the hour permits,”] as seems appropriate to him and as the hour permits. Those who need the Psalter or a reading [Note: [Col. 1101D] Another reading: “of the Psalter or of readings,”] shall devote themselves to meditation, and those who are able to comprehend shall meditate during that interval. Those who cannot do so shall all sing or read in the church. No one may presume to sleep during that interval except under the compulsion of illness, and then only with permission. Whoever acts otherwise shall be excommunicated. Let all the rest maintain the order of the vigils until Matins has been sung. [Note: [Col. 1102D] The interpolator removed this, adding other material from chapter 131 of the Council of Aachen.] At Prime, let all sing Prime in the church of Saint Stephen.

## CHAPTER VI—That All Shall Come to All the Canonical Hours for the Divine Office

At the hour of the divine office, as soon as the signal has been heard, everyone shall leave whatever may be in his hands and come with the greatest haste, provided he is near enough to that house to be able to reach it there. If someone is far from that church and cannot arrive for the work of God at the canonical hours, the archdeacon, judging that this is the case, shall perform the work of God with reverent fear wherever he then is. The archdeacon, chief cantor, or church custodian shall see to it that the signals sound at the proper hours.

## CHAPTER VII—On Discipline in Psalmody [Note: [Col. 1102D] Another reading: “diligence.”]

We believe that the divine presence is everywhere and that the eyes of the Lord watch the good and the wicked. Let us believe this especially, without any doubt, when we attend the divine work. Therefore let us always remember what the prophet said: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Ps. 2). And again: “Sing praise wisely” (Ps. 46). And: “In the sight of the angels I will sing praise to you” (Ps. 137).

For if, when we wish to present something to powerful men [Note: [Col. 1102D] Another reading: “to good or powerful men,”] we do not presume to do so except with humility and reverence, how much more must we entreat the Lord God of all things with complete humility and pure devotion? [Note: [Col. 1102D] The interpolator deleted what follows, together with almost the whole next chapter.] We have taken care to establish this in fear, according to what the Roman Church observes and what our synod has judged: when our clergy attend the divine work in church, no one may hold a staff in his hands in church unless compelled by illness.

## CHAPTER VIII—That They Shall Come Daily to the Chapter Meeting

It is necessary that all the canonical clergy come daily to the chapter meeting, hear the words of God there, and each day reread some chapter from this little rule of ours, which we have composed with God’s help for their benefit and the salvation of their souls. Only on Sunday, Wednesday, and Friday shall they read at the chapter meeting treatises and other homilies, or whatever may edify those who hear it.

We have ordered everyone to come daily to the chapter meeting so that the soul may hear the word of God, and so that the bishop, archdeacon, or whoever at that time appears to be in charge may there issue whatever orders he has to give, correct whatever must be corrected, and diligently arrange whatever ought to be done.

When the clerics go from Prime to their quarters, they shall immediately hasten to prepare themselves, so that when they hear the signal for the chapter meeting they may come ready and quickly. All the clergy who appear to be outside the cloister and remain in the city shall come to the chapter meeting every Sunday prepared in chasubles or official vestments, as the Roman Order prescribes.

On those Sundays and on the distinguished festivals of the saints, all the clergy who, as we have said, are outside the cloister shall come to the nocturns and Matins, and on those days they shall keep their stations prepared, so that each may remain at his office until Mass has been completed. If they act otherwise, they shall be excommunicated by the archdeacon or chief cantor, [Col. 1103A] or, if necessary, they shall also undergo corporal discipline. On those Sundays and distinguished festivals of the saints, as we have said, everyone shall eat in the refectory with the other clergy, at the tables assigned to them.

## CHAPTER IX—On Daily Manual Labor [Note: [Col. 1103D] Another reading: “daily work.”]

[Note: [Col. 1103D] The interpolator turned everything completely upside down.] Idleness is hostile to the soul. Therefore we decree that, at the command of the bishop, archdeacon, chief cantor, or those appointed by them, the clergy shall leave the chapter meeting for whatever work is assigned to them and fulfill their obedience with good will and without murmuring. When common work is not necessary, each person shall afterward do whatever work he has to do.

## CHAPTER X—On Those Departing on a Journey

[Col. 1103B]

Whoever from the clergy travels with the bishop or departs elsewhere shall not neglect his order insofar as the journey or circumstances permit. Nor should the appointed hours pass them by, whether those concerning the divine offices or any others.

## CHAPTER XI—On the Good Zeal That the Servants of God Ought to Have

[Note: [Col. 1103D] Another reading adds: “for one another.”]

Just as there is an evil zeal of bitterness that separates one from God and leads to hell, so there is a good zeal that separates one from vice and leads to the Lord and eternal life. Let the servants of God exercise this zeal with the most fervent love: let them anticipate one another in honor, and let them bear with the weaknesses of one another—whether of body or of conduct—with the greatest patience.

If any vices must be restrained or correction applied, let them agree in goodness with those entrusted with this responsibility, and let them become, as the Apostle says, God’s fellow workers [Note: [Col. 1103D] The following is supplied from the Vulgate edition.] so that, if vices arise, they may destroy them and urge each person toward a better state. For it is written: “You who love the Lord, hate evil” (Ps. 95); and “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul.” He loves his own soul well who guards himself and draws others, by word and deed, toward an example of good conduct. [Note: [Col. 1103D] The printed editions transmit this corruptly.]

## CHAPTER XII—That No One Presume to Strike or Excommunicate Another

[Note: [Col. 1103D] Perhaps: “so that every occasion for presumption may be avoided.”] We forbid every occasion of presumption in this canonical order and command and establish that no one may excommunicate or strike his equal. Even if someone by his own presumption provokes him to this [Note: [Col. 1103D] Another reading: “incites him,”] by words or deeds, it is not his place to adjudicate the matter [Note: [Col. 1104D] Another reading: “to claim jurisdiction over it,”] but he must come to his superior. The superior shall decide the matter according to the order, and whoever presumes to do this shall be judged by the bishop or by the one who is under him.

## CHAPTER XIII—That in the Congregation of Clerics No One May Defend Another

[Col. 1104A]

Every precaution must be taken so that no one presumes, for any reason, to defend another; nor may the canons presume to do this under the pretext of kinship, friendship, or familiarity, because serious occasions for scandal commonly arise in the congregation from this cause. If anyone transgresses these provisions, let him be restrained more severely, so that the others may be afraid.

## CHAPTER XIV—On Confessions

Scripture exhorts us, saying: “Reveal your way to the Lord and hope in him” (Ps. 36). And again it says: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever” (Ps. 105). Again the prophet says: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not hide my iniquities” (Ps. 31). And again: “I said, ‘I will declare my iniquities against myself to the Lord’; and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (ibid.). And likewise: “Confess your sins to one another, so that they may be blotted out” (James 5). And elsewhere: “He who hides his crimes will not prosper, but he who confesses them saves his soul from death” (Prov. 28).

The Lord also says in the Gospel: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 3). Therefore, since at the devil’s urging we have now committed many things against the will of God or against God’s commandment, it is necessary that we correct them through true confession and true [Note: [Col. 1104D] Another reading: “humility,”] amendment, as Scripture teaches.

The holy Fathers, who were perfect, established that from the present time onward [Note: [Col. 1104D] Another reading: “henceforth.”], whenever an evil thought arose in the heart of God’s servants at the devil’s urging, they should immediately confess it in humble confession to their superior. [Note: [Col. 1104D] Another reading: “quickly to the bishop or superior.”]

[Note: [Col. 1104D] The following material is absent from the printed editions.] We are now lazy and fragile, and although we do not follow their footsteps in everything, it is necessary that we imitate their footsteps at least in part, according to the ability God has granted us, so that through true confession we may deserve to possess the kingdom of God.

We therefore establish that twice a year our clergy shall make their confessions purely to their bishop: once at the beginning of Lent before Easter, and the other time from the middle of August until the Kalends of November. Between these dates [Note: [Col. 1104D] Read: “between these dates.”], with the bishop’s permission, anyone who needs to make his confession to the bishop or to another priest whom the bishop designates may do so at another time, whenever he wishes and has need.

Those whose sins do not prevent it ought, from among the clergy, to receive the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ every Sunday and on the distinguished festivals, because the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6). For if anyone receives the sacred mysteries unworthily, he eats and drinks judgment upon himself (1 Cor.).

If any member of the clergy—which God forbid—when making his confession to his bishop, is so filled with a diabolical spirit that he dares to conceal some of his sins from his bishop, and goes about giving his confessions to other priests, wishing to hide his crimes from his bishop because he fears that the bishop will remove him from his rank, or, if he has not yet attained a rank, that he will not advance to a rank, or that the bishop will advance him to the Lord’s body, or that he ought to pursue those vices [Note: [Col. 1105D] Perhaps: “remove him from the Lord’s body.”]—if the bishop is able to investigate this by any means and it is proven to him, let the offender undergo corporal discipline or imprisonment, or whatever else the bishop deems appropriate according to the measure of the fault, so that the others may fear and not fall into such a crime.

For [Note: [Col. 1105D] The interpolator did not omit to append this saying, but it is mutilated in the other part.] he is exceedingly wicked who sins before God’s eyes and is ashamed to confess to a human being, when, through God’s mercy, he ought to receive from that sin the counsel of healing.

## CHAPTER XV—On More Serious Faults

If any cleric of the canonical order [Note: [Col. 1105D] Another reading: “the crime of a more serious fault,”] commits serious faults—that is, homicide, fornication, adultery, theft, or one of these principal vices or something similar—let him first be subjected to corporal punishment. Then, for as long as the bishop or those under him decide, let him undergo imprisonment or exile, mindful of that terrible sentence of the Apostle: “To hand such a man over for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (1 Cor. 5).

While he is in prison, no one from the clergy may associate with him in any way or converse with him, except the person whom the superior orders to do so. He shall remain alone in the mourning of penance [Note: [Col. 1105D] Another reading: “in the grief of penance,”] for as long as seems appropriate to the superior.

After he has left prison, if the bishop or those under him deem it appropriate, let him continue to perform public penance. That is, let him be suspended from the oratory and from [Note: [Col. 1105D] Another reading: “the table,”] Mass. At every canonical hour he shall come before the church door, where the superior has ordered, and lie prostrate with his whole body before the very threshold [Note: [Col. 1105D] The printed editions have *limitem*, “threshold,” less correctly.] of the church until everyone has entered. Then let him rise, stand outside the church before that same door, and perform his office there as far as he can. When the people leave the church, he shall likewise lie prostrate until everyone has gone out. Whether lying or standing before that threshold, he shall speak with no one.

[Col. 1105D] As for abstinence, let it last as long and be conducted in the manner the bishop or those under him deem appropriate, with the measure and hour they consider suitable. No one may bless him until he has been reconciled. [Note: [Col. 1106D] The interpolator omitted what follows, together with chapter 16.] When he is summoned to be reconciled before the bishop or clergy, let him come and, with complete humility, lie prostrate with his whole body on the ground and ask forgiveness from everyone. Then let the bishop reconcile him according to the canonical order.

## CHAPTER XVI—On Those Who Associate Without Permission with the Excommunicated

[Col. 1106A]

If any brother [Note: [Col. 1106D] Perhaps: “with anyone,”] presumes, without the permission of the bishop or those under him, to associate in any way with an excommunicated cleric, to speak with him, to send him a message, or to send him letters, let him be subjected to the punishment of excommunication.

## CHAPTER XVII—On Bodily Excommunication

If any cleric is stubborn, disobedient, proud, drunken, a slanderer, a contradiction-maker, rebellious, quarrelsome, murmuring, violates an imposed fast, contemptuously refuses to stand at the cross when ordered, or, after being rebuked, fails to ask forgiveness, or is found in any respect to be opposed to this little rule and to the commands of the bishop [Col. 1106B] or those under him, let him, according to the command of our Lord, be admonished once [Note: [Col. 1106D] Another reading: “twice and three times,”] and a second time in private by his elders. If he does not amend, let him be rebuked publicly before everyone. If even then he does not correct himself, and if he understands what sort of punishment it is, let him be subjected to excommunication. But if he is wicked, or of limited understanding, or incorrigible, let him be subjected to corporal punishment.

## CHAPTER XVIII—On Those Who Offend in Certain Lesser Matters

If any member of the clergy comes late to the work of God or to the table, or if for some reason his superior orders him to sing the psalmody or Masses and he does not fulfill it at all, or if he breaks or loses something, or commits some other excess, and, instead of coming immediately before the bishop or those under him, he does not voluntarily make satisfaction and disclose his offense, but it becomes known through another, let him undergo a more severe correction according to the measure of the fault, as the bishop or those under him deem appropriate.

But if he confesses voluntarily, let him undergo the lighter correction, as we have said, according to the measure of the fault. [Note: [Col. 1106D] The interpolator appended certain other matters.]

## CHAPTER XIX—What the Measure of Excommunication Should Be

The measure of excommunication or discipline must extend according to the measure of the fault; the measure of faults depends upon the judgment of the bishop or those under him. For those who walk in serious sins and those who offend in certain minor matters are not to be judged equally. Rather, medicine must be applied according to the disease, [Note: [Col. 1106D] Perhaps: “because otherwise the merciful physician does not heal,”] since neither does a merciful physician heal wounds, nor can one who refuses to receive spiritual medicine attain the health that spiritual medicine provides.

## CHAPTER XX—On the Observances of Lent
Although the life of Christians ought to be simple and sober at all times, it is especially fitting for religious minds to live more continently during these days and to strive to cling to God with diligent service. Therefore, during those forty days before Easter, we decree that our clergy, with complete purity of mind and body, shall, by God’s command, keep themselves in due measure as far as they are able. As for the taking of food and drink, insofar as God grants assistance, let them practice moderation; that is, every day except Sundays, from the beginning of Lent until holy Easter, let them always eat their meal after the appointed Vespers; and let them abstain from such foods and drink as the bishop, with due consideration, shall determine. In no place—neither in the city itself, nor in monasteries, nor in any other places or their own houses—shall they eat during these forty days, unless perhaps they are far away and cannot be present with the brothers at the proper hour to receive their meal. In that case, because of this necessity, they shall have permission to take such food as the rest of the clergy, but they shall ensure that it does not precede the proper hours.

[Col. 1107A]  
[Note: [Col. 1107D] Perhaps, “with God’s help.”]

During this Lent the brothers shall devote themselves to reading from the appointed first hour until the full third hour. They shall not go outside the cloister except to those churches that are within the house, unless necessity arises and the bishop, or his subordinate, judges that what must be done should be done.

[Note: [Col. 1107D] Alternatively: “and afterward let them do what is appropriate, whether in reading or in working.” In the printed editions, chapter 35 adds here the title: “Concerning the times at which the clergy are to eat once or twice a day.”]

After the third hour they shall then hold chapter.

From Easter until Pentecost they shall eat twice a day and shall have permission to eat meat, except penitents, and except on Friday alone.

[Note: [Col. 1108D] The Vulgate adds “Thursday.”]

From Pentecost until the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist they shall likewise eat twice a day and abstain from meat until the Mass itself. From the Nativity of Saint John until the passing of Saint Martin they shall likewise eat twice a day and abstain from meat on Wednesday and Friday. From the passing of Saint Martin until Christmas, everyone shall abstain from meat, fast until the ninth hour on all these days, and eat in the refectory. From Christmas until the beginning of Lent, on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday they shall eat in the refectory at the ninth hour; on the other days of this period they shall eat twice in the same refectory. During these times they shall abstain from meat on Wednesday and Friday. If a feast day falls on either of these two days, they may eat meat if the prior permits it.

[Note: [Col. 1108D] The interpolator omitted this, as well as material apparently added later by Angelram, Chrodogang’s successor, which clearly proves that this is a particular rule for the people of Metz, even if all the other evidence were lacking.]

For the infirmity of our clergy, however, we have provided that if, on Wednesday or Friday, or during any of the other periods in which we have decreed that they abstain from meat, necessity requires it, the bishop, or his subordinates, may make an exception on account of their infirmities, needs, or festivals, according to what he foresees to be appropriate.

[Col. 1107D]

I, Angilram, archbishop and chaplain of the most excellent King Charles, have thought it right to add that, while we and our clergy appear to celebrate with devoted minds from Pentecost until the octave of that second Easter, or the coming of the Holy Spirit, during these most sacred eight days the clergy of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, as well as our own, shall have permission to eat meat, except those who, for the benefit of their souls and because of an imposed penance, wish to abstain.

## CHAPTER XXI — Concerning the arrangement of the tables

[Note: [Col. 1108D] This entire chapter is absent from the printed editions.]

The first table shall be that of the bishop with guests and travelers; the archdeacon, or those whom the bishop appoints, shall sit there. The second table shall be with the priests, the third with the deacons, the fourth with the subdeacons, the fifth with the remaining orders, and the sixth with the abbots or those whom the prior appoints. At the seventh table the canonical clergy who live outside the cloister in the city shall eat on Sundays and on the principal feast days.

When the hour for eating has arrived and the signal for the refectory has sounded, the brothers shall come there quickly, enter the refectory together, pray together, and recite the verse. When the bishop or another priest has pronounced the blessing over the tables, they shall all answer, “Amen”; and, according to the order that has been arranged, each shall go to his own table.

The clergy shall maintain complete silence in the refectory while they are there and until they go out, so that they may hear that reading from Scripture and meditate upon it in their hearts. For it is necessary that when they receive bodily food, the soul too should then be nourished by spiritual food.

[Col. 1108C]

The reader, cellarer, doorkeeper, weekly server, and those who serve when the bishop eats in the refectory with the clergy shall, before the brothers come into the refectory, receive a mixture of bread and drink, so that it may not be burdensome for them to endure fasting while the clergy eat. The reader shall continue reading until the prior orders him to stop, so that he may complete the reading.

This must be guarded against above all: no priest, deacon, subdeacon, or anyone else from the clergy may carry food or anything else intended for eating or drinking out of the refectory without the bishop’s permission.

It must also be guarded against that, before the legitimate hour, no one except those responsible for making preparations may enter the refectory to eat or drink without the permission of the bishop or of the person presiding at that time; nor may anyone disturb the cellarer contrary to due order. They shall ask for what is to be asked for at the proper hours, and what is to be given shall be given.

In the refectory itself, neither layman nor cleric, except those who belong to the congregation itself, may eat or drink without the permission of the bishop or his subordinates. In the cloister where the clergy come to chapter, or in the refectory, none of the clerical servants who are subject there to their senior may enter unless necessity requires it or the bishop, or his subordinates, commands it.

## CHAPTER XXII — Concerning the measure of food

[Note: [Col. 1109D] The interpolator inserted “once or twice” and some other matter.]

When our clergy eat twice a day at the times appointed, as written above, they shall receive as much bread as is sufficient. They shall receive stew at the sixth hour. Two persons shall receive one serving of meat and one portion of food; if they have no other food, they shall receive two servings of meat or bacon. At supper, two persons shall receive either one serving of meat or one portion of food.

When they are to lead the Lenten life, two brothers shall receive at the sixth hour a portion of cheese and one portion of food; and if they have fish, legumes, or anything else, a third item shall be added. At supper, two shall receive one portion of food or a portion of cheese; and if God grants more, they shall receive it with thanksgiving.

When there is only one meal in the day, two shall receive one portion of food, a portion of cheese, and one serving of legumes or another stew. If it happens that in that year there are no acorns or beechnuts and they have no means by which they may later complete the measure with meat, the bishop shall make provision according to the ability that God has granted, whether from the Lenten provisions or from elsewhere, so that they may have some consolation.

## CHAPTER XXIII — Concerning the measure of drink

[Col. 1109C]  
[Note: [Col. 1109D] Everything else appears in the common editions as chapter 8.]

When food is to be taken twice a day, the priests shall receive three cups at the sixth hour and two at supper. The deacons who are in that order shall receive three at the sixth hour and two at supper. The subdeacons shall receive two at the sixth hour and two at supper. The remaining orders shall receive two at the sixth hour and one at supper.

When there is only one meal in the day, they shall receive at the sixth hour as many cups as they formerly received when they ate twice; whatever drink they formerly received at supper shall remain with the cellarer. They must guard against drunkenness in every way.

If it happens that there is little wine and the bishop cannot fulfill this measure, let him provide according to what he can manage. The brothers must not grumble, but give thanks to God and endure it with equanimity. For if it is possible for them to have even that much, it must not be withheld for any reason. For those who abstain from wine, the bishop or his subordinate shall provide as much beer as they ought to have had wine. If the bishop wishes to add some drink to the measure written above, that shall remain within his authority, and he shall provide them with beer as a consolation.

When some meal is required by circumstances, we permit no more than one meal, at which they shall receive three cups according to the measure written above. Even this seems excessive to us, because wine makes even the wise apostatize (Ecclesiasticus 19), and where drunkenness is, there are disgrace and sin. We admonish this also: our clergy must lead an entirely sober life. Since we cannot persuade them not to drink wine, let us at least agree to this—that drunkenness should not rule over them. For the Apostle declares that all drunkards are excluded from the kingdom of God unless they amend through worthy repentance.

[Note: [Col. 1109D] The canons should have vegetable gardens, from which, with other additions, they may prepare some stew for themselves each day in turn. The Vulgate has this from the Council of Aachen.]

## CHAPTER XXIV — Concerning the weekly kitchen servers

The canonical clergy shall serve one another in such a way that no one is excused from kitchen duty unless illness or some pressing matter of serious utility has prevented him, because from this greater reward and charity are acquired.

[Note: [Col. 1110D] Alternatively, “illness or some cause.”] Let provision be made for the weak, so that they do not perform this with sadness, but so that everyone may have assistance according to the size of the congregation or the circumstances of the place.

The archdeacon, the primicerius, the cellarer, and those three guardians of the churches—one of Saint Stephen, another of Saint Peter, and the third of Saint Mary—who are occupied with more important duties, shall be excused from the kitchen.

[Note: [Col. 1110D] The interpolator deleted these, as less necessary to his institution.] The others, however, shall serve one another in charity.

The person leaving the weekly duty shall clean everything on Saturday. He shall return to the cellarer the service vessels that he received for serving, sound and clean. If any of them has been diminished or damaged, he shall ask pardon in chapter on Saturday, restore the vessel or whatever has been diminished to its proper place, and perform penance according to the judgment of the bishop or his subordinate.

## CHAPTER XXV — Concerning the archdeacon or primicerius

[Note: [Col. 1110D] Alternatively, “provost.”]

They ought to be wise as serpents and innocent as doves; that is, wise in what is good and simple in what is evil. They should be learned in the Gospels and in the canonical institutions of the holy Fathers, so that they may teach the clergy the divine law and this small rule.

[Note: [Col. 1110D] Alternatively, “the evangelical precepts.”] They should conform themselves to the clergy, so that they may demonstrate the divine precepts to the simpler members not only through effective words but also through example.

They must always preserve the apostolic pattern expressed in the words: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke” (1 Timothy 4); that is, mingling different times with different times and gentleness with threats. They should reprove the undisciplined and restless more harshly; they should entreat the obedient, gentle, and patient so that they may advance toward what is better; and they should rebuke and correct the negligent, contemptuous, and proud. They must not conceal the sins of offenders, but as soon as they begin to arise, cut them off at the root as far as they are able, mindful of the danger of Eli the priest of Shiloh.

[Note: [Col. 1110D] Alternatively, “of his sons.”]

They should correct the more honorable and intelligent with words at the first and second admonition. But they should restrain the wicked, hardhearted, proud, or disobedient at the very beginning of their sin with blows and bodily punishment, knowing what is written: “A fool is not corrected by words” (Proverbs 18); and again: “Strike your son with a rod, and you will deliver his soul from death” (ibid.).

Whatever they are unable to determine by themselves justly and reasonably according to the canonical rule or this small rule, they must disclose entirely to the bishop. He himself shall correct what must be chastised and amend what must be corrected according to God’s will.

The archdeacon and primicerius must be faithful and obedient to God and the bishop in all their actions and works.

[Note: [Col. 1111D] Alternatively, “primitiarius.”] They must not be proud, rebellious, or contemptuous, but chaste and sober, patient, kind, and merciful. “Mercy must always triumph over judgment,” so that they too may obtain mercy. Let them love the clergy and hate vices. In correction itself let them act prudently, observing the rule “nothing in excess,” lest, while they desire to scrape away the rust, the vessel be broken. Let them remember that a bruised reed must not be crushed.

We do not mean by this that they should allow vices to be nourished, but that they should hasten to cut them off prudently and charitably. Let them beware lest, while preaching to others, they themselves become reprobate, keeping in mind the Lord’s command: “You saw the speck in your brother’s eye, but did not see the beam in your own; remove the beam from your eye first, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye” (Matthew 7).

[Note: [Col. 1111D] Alternatively, “provost.”]

If the archdeacon or primicerius should be found—God forbid—to be proud, arrogant, contradictory, or contemptuous of the canonical rule or of this small rule, they shall be admonished once and again according to the Lord’s command. If they do not amend, they shall be judged by the bishop according to the measure of their fault. If they do not correct themselves even then, they shall be expelled from their orders, and others who are worthy and who fulfill the will of God and of their bishop according to the divine command shall be appointed in their places.

## CHAPTER XXVI — Concerning the cellarer

The cellarer must fear God, be sober, not given to wine, not quarrelsome, and not hot-tempered, but moderate, careful in conduct, and faithful.

[Note: [Col. 1111D] Another version adds: “not proud, not slow, not wasteful, not an excessive and disorderly squanderer, not negligent.”]

Whatever he receives into his care for the use of the clergy, he must guard faithfully. Without the permission of his bishop or of his subordinate he must do nothing.

[Note: [Col. 1111D] Several other provisions are added in the printed editions, chapter 11.]

He must not be wasteful or destroyer of the clergy’s resources, because if he is, he will undoubtedly have to render an account to God on the day of judgment. If he administers well, he will acquire for himself a good standing.

## CHAPTER XXVII — Concerning the doorkeeper

One doorkeeper, together with his junior assistant, shall guard the doors, cloisters, and entrances for a year or longer, if the bishop wishes.

[Note: [Col. 1111D] Alternatively, “the doors of the cloister or cloister entrance.”]

The doorkeeper must be sober and patient, knowing how to receive and give a response,

[Note: [Col. 1111D] Alternatively, “a brother of proven life.”]

[Note: [Col. 1111D] The doorkeeper’s office and what follows appear in the printed editions as chapter 12; much of what is read here, as well as several other things, is absent there.]

and he must faithfully guard the doors or entrances of the cloister. He must not presume to act contrary to this rule. If he does, he shall be excommunicated. At Compline he shall return the keys of the doors to the archdeacon. If the archdeacon is elsewhere, his subordinate shall receive the keys.

The guardians of the churches who sleep there or in nearby dwellings shall maintain silence, as the other clergy do, insofar as they can. After Compline they shall neither eat nor drink. They shall not allow those who have remained outside the cloister after Compline to enter, nor those who are inside the cloister to go out through the entrances entrusted to them. If they do so, they shall be judged by the bishop or his subordinates.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — Concerning sick canonical clergy who have joined this order as their special way of life and have no means of meeting their needs during illness

[Col. 1112B]

If any member of the clergy who has joined this order as his special way of life falls ill and has no means of meeting his needs during his illness, then, after the bishop, the archdeacon and primicerius shall take the greatest care of him.

[Note: [Col. 1112D] These names are omitted in the printed editions, chapter 40, and in many other places.]

They must beware lest the sick be neglected; they must be served as truly as Christ himself. For he said: “I was sick, and you visited me”; and, “Whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for me.” Therefore, whatever necessities may be useful or required by the sick must be provided for them completely and without any delay, because in them he regards whatever they themselves have lacked or in which they have been neglected.

[Col. 1112C]

Without doubt, on the dreadful day of judgment, when the King of the living and the dead sits upon his throne of majesty, they will have to render an account of all this—of how they ministered to them. If the archdeacon or primicerius does not have sufficient means to provide fully for their needs, they must make this known entirely to the bishop. He, in the fear and love of God, shall make provision so that what is necessary for these sick persons may be supplied and they may have the means to meet their needs.

Suitable and fitting dwellings shall be assigned to these sick persons, properly arranged above them, where they may stay while recovering from their illnesses. One member of the clergy, fearing God, shall be appointed to take the greatest care of all their needs. He shall have assistance, if necessary, according to what the prior determines, so that the sick may be served without grumbling or negligence. Let him know that if he ministers well, he will acquire a good standing for himself.

[Note: [Col. 1112D] Alternatively, “will acquire it from God.”]

The sick themselves should also recognize that service is being rendered to them for the honor of God, and should not distress those serving them through their excessive demands. Only as long as they are sick are they to be carried and cared for in this way; once they have improved, they shall return to their orders.

[Note: [Col. 1112D] The interpolator adds: “And this too must be stated: a sick person may take food and drink at any hour, whenever he desires or is able, if he cannot do so at the proper time.”]

## CHAPTER XXIX — Concerning the clothing, footwear, and firewood of the clergy

[Col. 1113A]

That half of the clergy who are senior shall receive new capes each year, and shall always return the old ones that they received in the preceding year when they receive the new ones.

[Note: [Col. 1113D] Alternatively: “Each of the senior clergy shall receive three *campsiles* annually, and each of the junior clergy two *campsiles* annually.”]

The other half of the clergy shall receive those old capes that the seniors return each year, and the seniors shall not exchange the capes that they are required to return.

[Note: [Col. 1113D] In the Angers manuscript they are called *cansiles*.]

The priests who serve continually in the house there shall receive *sarciles*, as shall the seven deacons who hold that rank; alternatively, they may receive wool from which they can have two *sarciles* a year. The other clergy shall each receive one. The priests and deacons shall receive two *camisiles* each year; the subdeacons, one and a half *camisiles*; and those in the remaining orders, one each.

For footwear, the entire clergy shall each year receive cowhide leather and four pairs of soles.

[Note: [Col. 1113D] Alternatively, “ox-hide.”]

[Note: [Col. 1113D] Alternatively, “sandals.”]

[Note: [Col. 1113D] The common version adds: “And they shall have clothing at the passing of Saint Martin, *campsiles* at Easter, and footwear on the Kalends of September.” It omits what concerns firewood.]

Concerning firewood, we have determined that they should be able to purchase enough for the year from four pounds of denarii. The firewood should be purchased from the tolls that belong to them in the city or in the villages—that is, four pounds should be allocated for this purpose. On the Kalends of May they shall receive this toll and then purchase the firewood.

The capes, *sarciles*, and footwear shall be purchased from the surplus of the tolls mentioned above and from the footwear allowance that the bishop customarily gives to the clergy each year, as well as from the alms that God specifically grants to that clergy. If anything remains from these resources, they shall purchase whatever else they need or store it in their treasury.

If they do not have enough there to make these purchases, the bishop shall provide for it and send what is necessary for the whole requirement to be fulfilled, according to what is written above.

They shall receive the clothing—the capes and *sarciles*—at the passing of Saint Martin; they shall receive the *camisiles* twenty days after Easter; and they shall have the footwear on the Kalends of September. If anyone from that clergy has received from the bishop such a benefit from the church that he can use it to provide his own necessities, namely capes and footwear—

## CHAPTER XXX — Concerning the feasts of the saints

We have thought it right to make this known: on the feasts of the Lord, of holy Mary, of the twelve apostles, and of the other saints that it is customary to celebrate each year in this province, we and our clergy shall, insofar as God grants the ability, ensure that the divine office is performed day and night.

The bishop shall provide a meal for the clergy in the house on the Nativity of the Lord and on Easter,

[Note: [Col. 1114D] Alternatively: “or his subordinate.”]

[Note: [Col. 1114D] Alternatively: “and on Epiphany, Easter, the close of Easter, the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, and the feasts of the saints of his province.”]

if he is present at the time. If he is absent on those days, they shall have a sufficient meal in their refectory, as written above. After they leave the refectory, they shall drink twice or three times in the warming-house,

[Note: [Col. 1114D] Alternatively, “in the fireplace room.”]

as may provide consolation without drunkenness taking control.

On Epiphany, mid-Easter, the close of Easter, the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, and the bishop’s birthday, the bishop shall provide them with a meal in the refectory at the sixth hour. As for those abbeys that we have in this city or nearby outside it, the custom has been that they provide a meal for the clergy. This must not cease, insofar as circumstances permit.

[Col. 1114B]

The archdeacon, or whoever at that time appears to preside under the bishop’s authority, shall receive this, provide a meal for the clergy from it in the refectory, and reserve whatever remains with the cellarer for their use.

[Note: [Col. 1114D] The interpolator substituted another provision in its place.]

The archdeacon shall also provide them with a meal at the sixth hour in the refectory on the Purification of holy Mary, on the feast of all the apostles, on the feast of Saint John the Baptist, and on the feast of Saint Remigius, from what he himself has provided for their use.

## CHAPTER XXXI — Concerning the person who wishes to join himself to this special canonical order of the congregation and make a formal donation to the church of blessed Paul the apostle from the possessions he owns, while retaining usufruct for his lifetime

[Note: [Col. 1114D] The interpolator omitted the entire chapter, along with certain others.]

Although we read that the ancient Church in the time of the apostles existed in such unanimous concord and had abandoned everything, so that individuals sold their estates and laid the proceeds at the apostles’ feet, and none of them dared to call anything his own, but everything was common to them; hence they were said to have “one heart and one soul” (Acts 4). For every day, breaking bread around the houses, men and women, children and the entire populace, inflamed by the ardor of faith and stirred by the love of religion, shared in common what they received and supplied everyone with sufficiency in thanksgiving.

But because this cannot be persuaded in our own times, let us at least agree to draw our minds toward some small likeness of their way of life. For it is exceedingly sluggish, lukewarm, and lax devotion if we, who ought to serve the canonical orders in a special way, refuse to consent even in the smallest degree to that perfection to which, as we have said, the whole populace consented for the sake of God.

If we cannot leave everything, let us retain only what is necessary for our use, so that whatever we leave—willingly or unwillingly—may be left not to our carnal heirs and relatives, but to the Church in which, by God’s authority, we serve together and from whose resources we receive our support. Let us leave it in place of an inheritance, so that, if we are not granted a crown with those perfect ones because of perfect renunciation and contempt for this world, at least the divine mercy may grant us forgiveness of sins, as to the least of them.

Saint Prosper,

[Note: [Col. 1115D] Or rather Julianus Pomerius, *On the Contemplative Life*.]

or other holy Fathers, have decreed according to divine authority that those clergy who wish to live from the resources of the Church should donate, by written instruments, the private property they possess to God and to the Church which they serve. In this way they may use the Church’s resources more freely and without grave guilt. Just as those clergy rejoice in the Church’s resources, so the Church should rejoice that their resources have been increased and improved for the benefit of its poor.

Nevertheless, while they live, if they so wish, the clergy shall retain their property by usufruct, through the benefit of the Church, so that everything may be held in common.

[Note: [Col. 1115D] Read: “and after their death.”]

After their death, the property shall return to the Church or to the canonical order to which it had previously been given.

Similarly, we declare that those clergy who have sufficient means from their own resources ought to live from those resources, provided, however, that if they are infirm and unwilling to give everything wholly to the Church of God which they serve, they may devote themselves to that Church in the love of Christ by free and diligent service. They should know that for this they will receive special mercy from God, since they serve him from their own resources while using the Church’s resources like the other canons.

For if they leave to the almoner for distribution what they would otherwise have received on account of their orders, to be given without sin to those who possess nothing, they possess their own resources without sin; in a certain sense they too leave their own when, content with their private resources, they judge that they have no right to receive anything.

[Note: [Col. 1115D] This is very involved.]

If they think that they ought therefore to receive a portion of what is contributed to the Church, and do not appear to reject it because they cannot leave their own possessions, while considering it disgraceful to have it returned among their own poor, let them know that it is more disgraceful to possess the alms of the poor and to live on them.

For this must be provided for: the mother Church, which is known to be bound by the command of the canons to be continually attentive to the relief of the poor, widows, orphans, and needy alike, must not be burdened.

Therefore, whoever wishes to join this canonical order, which we now desire, however imperfectly, to restore, as we stated in the little decree that we composed, and who wishes formally to donate by this present instrument the property he possesses to the church of blessed Paul, for the work of God or for the clergy serving there, shall make the donation solemnly.

He may also receive from the bishop, if he wishes, a *precaria* concerning it, on the condition that, while he lives, he shall hold those possessions by usufruct. After his death,

[Note: [Col. 1115D] Read: “after his death,” as above.]

all those possessions, together with every addition and improvement, shall return in their entirety to the church to which they were given or to the congregation itself, without any assignment to another person or any awaited transfer.

He shall be permitted, while he lives and remains in that order, to give alms from all movable property belonging to those possessions, whether to the poor, to the congregation itself, or wherever else he wishes, and to meet his own needs.

If anything from that movable property remains after his death, half shall be distributed as alms to the poor, to his promised beneficiaries,

[Text uncertain: *promissas* may refer to persons to whom he had made promises.]

or wherever he wishes, with the archdeacon, primicerius, or the person whom he requested while alive acting as distributor. The other half shall return as alms to the clergy or to the congregation itself.

The clergy shall have no power to diminish, sell, or transfer any of the possessions they hold by *precaria*—neither lands, vineyards, woods, meadows, houses, buildings, slaves, tenants, nor any other immovable property—except, as we have said, the produce or whatever they may have been able to cultivate there. While they live, they may do with these as they wish.

If it happens, through the devil’s prompting, that one of these brothers who holds such possessions by *precaria* falls into a serious or minor crime, he shall perform penance according to the bishop’s judgment. Nevertheless, he must not be stripped of the possessions that he holds by *precaria* on account of this.

If anyone else wishes to join this congregation in the same manner as we established above, whether one of our abbots or any outsider from the clergy, he shall do so under the same terms as the other brothers.

If there is another person who wishes to join them and leave everything entirely for the sake of perfection, the bishop shall provide them with what is necessary, so that he may complete the good work which, inspired by God, he has begun.

## CHAPTER XXXII — Concerning alms

We establish the following concerning the receipt of alms. If someone wishes to give something as alms to one priest for his Mass, confession,

[Note: [Col. 1116D] Alternatively: “or to a cleric for psalms and hymns, or for himself.”]

illness, or any dear one, whether living or dead, the priest

[Note: [Col. 1116D] Alternatively: “or cleric.”]

shall receive it from the donor and do with it what he wishes.

If someone wishes to give something as alms to all the priests under such a condition, or for any purpose whatsoever, it must go entirely both to all the priests and to all the canons, and they shall all hold this alms in common.

Likewise, the alms that come in common for the entire clergy shall be held by all in common, and they shall perform psalmody or Masses for those alms, as the bishop has established.

We have set a measure for the alms that priests may receive for their own use because we have judged it an exceedingly heavy burden if such enormous loads of sinners’ offenses were to fall upon those priests alone.

[Note: [Col. 1116D] Alternatively: “sins.”]

For many more easily obtain God’s mercy for sinners than one person, however diligent; and each person ought to fear for his own conscience. How much more should he not heap upon himself, beyond his strength, a burden of sins belonging to others?

The archdeacon or primicerius shall receive these alms and spend them on the needs of the brothers, as their needs require and as the bishop judges. If anything remains from them, they shall store it in the brothers’ wardrobe.

## CHAPTER XXXIII — How they are to come to chapter or Mass on Sundays and the feasts of the saints

On Sundays, on the feasts of the saints,

[Col. 1117B]

or whenever the bishop or his subordinates commands it, all shall put on their vestments in the morning after Prime has been sung. The officials shall wear chasubles, as the ecclesiastical order requires. They shall be ready and hasten without delay to the office.

As soon as the first signal is heard, all shall come to chapter. After hearing the reading, they shall proceed together to the church. When the second signal has been given, they shall sing Terce, then sit in their ranks and await the bishop, as is the custom of the Roman Church. After that, no one shall leave his place in the order until everything has been completed, except those who accompany the bishop in service or those who are occupied with some task that cannot in any way be postponed; and they must make this known to the bishop or his subordinates.

If anyone from the clergy of any order—whether priests, deacons, subdeacons, or acolytes—is not present and ready at that time to perform his office, and any negligence or delay occurs through him, unless it is because of serious illness, he shall be deprived of wine or drink on the following day.

[Col. 1117C]

If he repeats this through laziness or contempt, he shall be restrained more severely by the bishop or his subordinates, so that the others may be afraid. On the remaining days they shall come to chapter as prescribed above in this rule.

If there is a public station at those suburban churches and the brothers have kept vigil there, after completing the vigil they shall return decorously to the cloisters in the morning, so that they may come without fail to the chapter. If anyone is negligent and delays, and is not present at chapter, he shall be punished for this on the first and second occasion. If he does not amend his conduct, on the day when he has failed to come to chapter he shall abstain from wine until the following day.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

[Note: This chapter and the preceding one are absent from the Vulgate editions.]

### Concerning the matricularians, that they are to come to hear the divine reading at the appointed church in the house

Having written, as far as seemed appropriate to us, given our modest abilities and understanding, about the matters most necessary for correcting the life of clerical canons, we now come to the matricularians, both those living at home and those in the suburban districts. Their way of life was not in accordance with the institution of the ancient Church; rather, under great danger and negligence—or, so to speak, without preaching and confession—they had been placed in a certain security. They did not come to the church in the house for the public station to hear the word of God, nor to the other stations; instead, they all remained seated, each in his own place.

Therefore, with the agreement of our spiritual brothers, we have decreed that twice each month throughout the year, every fourteen days, on Saturday, all the matricularians—both those who are in the house and those who hold matricularies at the other churches within the city or in the villages—shall all come to the appointed gathering in the church in the house. In the morning they shall wait in their places until the bell rings at the hour of Terce. Then the bishop, if he is not occupied with other duties, shall come and order a reading from the treatises or homilies of the holy Fathers, appropriate readings that edify those who hear them and teach them the way of salvation, so that, with God’s help, they may reach eternal life.

When Terce has been said, if the bishop has not come, the priest who is custodian of the church of Saint Stephen shall, in his place, according to his ability, read to them and teach them the way of salvation. The priest must take the utmost care that, at the appointed hour, if the bishop has not come, he does not fail to fulfill what is written here. The matricularians shall make their confessions to that priest twice a year: once in Lent, and a second time from the Mass of Saint Remigius until the passing of Saint Martin.

If, at the devil’s prompting, any vices or scandals arise among them, so that the one who has committed such an act must make confession, he shall do so at the next gathering where they hear the reading. When the reading has ended, he shall make his confession purely to that priest. If he does not wish to confess his sin and conceals it, and if it is discovered by another, the one who concealed the offense shall, by the priest who announces the word of God to them, either be excommunicated or subjected to corporal punishment, according to the nature of his fault.

For each matricular register there shall be a chief matricularian chosen from among them, who shall diligently supervise them. If any of them wishes to conceal his crimes, and their chief is able to investigate the matter, he must not conceal it from the priest who reads the lesson to them. If he does so, the person who committed the offense shall likewise be judged by that priest. If the priest himself is unable to correct the matter, it shall be reported to the archdeacon or the chief matricularian, so that they may correct it reasonably according to the nature of the fault. If necessary, it shall be brought to the bishop’s attention, so that he himself may correct it.

As we have said, all the matricularians without exception shall come to the reading on the appointed days, and they shall disclose their needs, both spiritual and bodily, to the priest. He shall either correct the matter himself or report it to their superiors. [lacuna] If any of the matricularians remains away and does not come to the reading, unless compelled by illness, he shall be admonished once and again. If he does not amend his conduct, he shall be excommunicated. If he does this again out of contempt, he shall be expelled from the matricula, and another who wishes to hear the word of God shall be sent in his place.

We have also decreed that, from our alms or those of our successors, whenever they come to hear that reading, they shall always receive from the house, each one, one loaf of bread and, on one occasion, a portion of bacon, and on the other occasion a portion of cheese. They shall do this throughout the whole year, as we have said, whenever any of these matricularians come there. During Lent they shall receive wine with bread on two occasions, one sextarius among four persons. On Maundy Thursday they shall receive wine with bread in the aforesaid measure, together with a portion of bacon and cheese.

We have determined that eight modii of baked bread are to be provided for each such occasion. On the occasion when they are to receive bacon, they shall receive six bacons; and when they receive cheese, they shall receive one weight on each occasion. In grain this amounts to 200 modii per year, from the grain that comes from Warmacinse; they shall receive it whenever it arrives.

Of bacon they shall receive sixty bacons on the Kalends of January; of cheese, twelve weights at the Mass of Saint Martin; and of wine, twenty-four modii at the Mass of Saint Martin. The archdeacon or the chief matricularian shall receive all this, and they shall see that it is distributed in this manner, as may please God and as we have decreed. May our reward, or that of our successors, or of those who carry this out, thereby decrease. [Note: [Col. 0119B] Perhaps, “increase thereby.”]

For the purchase of wood with which they are to make the bread, the bishop shall give two and a half ounces of money on the Kalends of May. If anything remains from what we have mentioned above, the archbishop or the chief matricularian, or whomever they appoint, shall give it to other poor people who need it.

## [Col. 1119] Diploma of Saint Chrodegang, Bishop of Metz, for the Foundation of the Monastery of Gorze

*(Brequigny, Diplomatarium, vol. II, new edition.)*

[Col. 1119C] In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

I, Chrodegangus, although unworthy, if not in deed or in name, bishop by the grace of God, with the authorization and will of the illustrious man Pippin, our lord and mayor of the palace, and with the consent of all our peers, the abbots, priests, deacons, subdeacons, and people of the church of Saint Stephen of Metz, as well as of those good laymen who are seen to be engaged there in the service of Saint Stephen, have reflected, in view of the uncertainty of human frailty, on how, with the Lord’s gift, we might wash away our sins and reach eternal joys.

Therefore, from the possessions of Saint Stephen we give to that basilica of Saint Peter and Saint Stephen and of the other saints, which we have newly built at the end of Haldiniaca, in the county of Scarponne, where Gorze rises, and to the cell that we have constructed there, and for the work of the servants of God dwelling there, by this testament—that the monks or poor people there may have food, clothing, and other support—everything that we acquired or that came to us by sale, donation, or exchange in the territory of Haldianica, where we built that basilica of Saint Peter; everything that in any part of that territory we acquired, two *leugae* at a time, or that was handed over or exchanged to us, or that is subsequently acquired there, or that by any lawful means comes to us.

Let all this, by this testament, benefit the aforesaid cell for the increase of our reward. Whatever the house of Saint Stephen possessed in that territory of Haldiniac shall likewise benefit that basilica or that cell of Saint Peter and increase its resources.

We also give, in the county of Scarponne, at the place called Siurone, whatever Rigoaldus transferred to Saint Stephen’s portion by his written instruments, together with the basilica constructed in honor of Saint Paul, and whatever pertains to it in Godolinovilla and Bodelocurte, in the territory of Haldiniaca and in the territory of Baudiciaca, in the territory of Aconiaca, and whatever Rigoaldus and his brother Gontrannus transferred to Saint Stephen’s portion in those territories by their written instruments. We also give whatever Bavo transferred by his written instrument to the house of Saint Stephen in Tantalino villa.

We also give, in the county of Scarponne, in the village of Buesarias, whatever the house of Saint Stephen is lawfully seen to possess there or in those territories, as has already been said, whatever good men transferred to the house of Saint Stephen by their written instruments.

We also give, in the same county of Scarponne, the village of Saint Stephen called Puina, with its manses, courtyards, gardens, houses, buildings, lands, fields, meadows, vineyards, woods, cultivated and uncultivated land, waters and watercourses, slaves, *liti*, *alcolabi* and *epistolarii*, livestock of both kinds and sexes, movable and immovable property, and whatever has come there by sale, donation, or exchange to that house of Saint Peter or to that cell, so that, with God’s help, it may increase their resources.

We give to Novum Sartum half of the woodland where the brothers or their men may obtain timber for that house of Saint Peter.

We also give the possessions of Saint Remigius, together with the basilica constructed at Sigeium, and whatever pertains to it, including whatever Adventius has until now held as a benefice of Saint Stephen.

We also give at Sigeium four vineyards with their winegrowers, their wives, their manses, and their allotments. Their names are these: Harduinus, winegrower; his wife, an *epistolaria*; Erlofridus, winegrower; his wife, Raganlindis; Erlulfus, winegrower; his wife, an *epistolaria*; Wandelbertus, winegrower; his wife, an *epistolaria*.

In the same village we give female slaves named Amelbergane, Rigobertane, and Eminane, together with the tithe from those demesne vineyards, both of wine and of grain, and from anything else.

We also give at Castellum three vineyards with their winegrowers, their wives, their manses, and their allotments. Their names are these: Adelfridus, winegrower, whose wife is a female slave named Gaucia; Anglifridus, winegrower, with his wife; likewise Adelfridus with his wife Wandelbergane, a female slave, and his sister, a female slave.

We also give at Gaudiacum the oratory constructed in honor of Saint Andrew, and whatever pertains to it, including whatever Teudonius has held there as a benefice of Saint Stephen.

We also give at Cuberacum the basilica constructed in honor of Saint Martin, which Candidianus the chancellor has held as a benefice, and whatever pertains to that basilica, so that it may increase the resources of that house of Saint Peter and of the brothers or monks there. The tithe from Prunidum—of grain, hay, cows, pigs, rams, beasts of burden, and anything else—shall likewise increase the resources of that aforesaid house.

We also give the tithe from Miliriacum of the wine collected there each year.

We also give, above the Moselle, the village of Cluseradum with the little village called Riviniacus, with its manses, small courtyards, gardens, houses, buildings, lands, fields, meadows, vineyards, woods, cultivated and uncultivated land, waters and watercourses, slaves, *liti*, *accolabi*, *epistolarii*, livestock of both kinds and sexes, movable and immovable property, and whatever the house of Saint Stephen is seen to possess in that territory. Let it all benefit that house of Saint Peter or that cell, as was said above, and the monks or brothers there, increasing their resources.

We also give every year the entire tithe of the wine from Bredraculum.

Let all the things stated above perpetually increase the resources of Gorze and of the monks and poor people there who hope for alms.

If, however, any of my successors or brothers of the aforesaid clergy of Metz, or any other person, should attempt to act against this little page of my testament, or wish to do anything concerning it, or attempt to diminish it without my consent, or refuse to fulfill my devotion in every respect, or disdain to observe the agreements stated above, let him know—although I do not wish to curse anyone—that nevertheless he will have to answer with me for this before the tribunal of Christ on the dreadful day of judgment.

And so that this little page of our testament may remain undisturbed for all time, I have strengthened it with my own hand and asked our brothers and the other good men who gave their consent to confirm it.

Executed publicly at Andernach, in the royal palace, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 745, indiction 13, epact 14, concurrent 4, in the sixth year of King Childeric, on the twentieth day of May. Seal of the illustrious man Pippin, mayor of the palace.

## [Col. 1121] Confirmation of the Preceding Privilege

[Note: [Col. 1121C] Our Sirmond could with equal right have assigned that document of Compiegne—whether one calls it a decree or a council—to the immediately preceding year, 756, or to the present year, 757, since it is established by judgments that are certain and beyond all controversy that a synod was held at the palace of Compiegne in the year 756.

[Col. 1121D] The diploma of Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, gives testimony of greater authority than any exception could weaken: it was confirmed at that place by the subscriptions of the bishops, in confirmation of the privilege of the abbey of Gorze, which he had founded. You will owe this, reader, to the courtesy of the Reverend Father Alexander Wilthemius, a most learned member of our society, who several years ago sent it to me from Luxembourg, together with the foundation charter of the distinguished abbey of Saint Salvator at Prüm, granted on August 13 in the eleventh year of the reign of that same most glorious King Pippin, and with many other documents.

Ph. Labbe.]

In the name of God.

I, Chrodegangus, although a sinner, bishop of the city of Metz, while examining in the volumes of the divine Scriptures, as far as my limited understanding allowed, with attentive ears and diligent consideration, what the Son of God said—hearing, “Give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6), and elsewhere, “Give alms, and behold, everything will be clean for you” (Luke 11)—therefore began, sorrowfully, to inquire what I should do for the remedy of my soul, for washing away the burdens of my sins, or in what respects I might imitate the examples of the ancient Fathers, my predecessors in the episcopate, in works that we believe pleased God.

Accordingly, with God’s help, with the authorization and will of our lord, the most pious and most glorious King Pippin of the Franks, and with the consent of our brothers, the canons, and of the spiritual and God-fearing faithful laymen of Saint Stephen, I built a monastery at the place called Gorze, in the county of Scarponne, in honor of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, as well as Saint Stephen and the other saints.

I founded and endowed that monastery with possessions and lands that had lawfully come to me through sales [Note: [Col. 1121D] Perhaps, “and exchanges.” Hardouin.] and exchanges, on the condition that in the monastery the monks should henceforth and forever, throughout perpetual ages, live according to the order and rule of our holy father Benedict the abbot. As it is written there, they are to possess absolutely nothing as their own, but everything is to be held in common among them, so that they may be able to pray both for themselves and for others.

Therefore, the affection of charity and love for those brothers compelled us, for the sake of their peace and order, to ensure that, with God’s help, they might fulfill their rule and order, and that this might remain as a reward for us and our successors, and that what we had established might be brought to its proper conclusion along an unshaken path, so that, by God’s favor, it might thereafter possess lasting stability. No one should therefore accuse us of making new decrees, when from ancient times, according to the judgment of bishops, they have seen other monasteries subject to them preserved and secure in every respect.

Therefore, for the sake of divine regard and for the remedy of our soul and of our successors, the bishops, with the authorization and will of the most pious and most glorious King Pippin and the consent of our brothers, it was fitting that we preserve them for their peace and tranquility [Note: [Col. 1123D] Perhaps, “for us and them.” Hardouin.], and that neither we, nor our archdeacon, nor the other administrators of Saint Stephen, should permit them to be disturbed, condemned, or stripped of their possessions by any person whatsoever, contrary to the order of justice [Note: [Col. 1123D] Perhaps, “that neither.” Hardouin.]. Rather, after examining their instruments, they shall hold and possess those possessions in tranquil order, according to the constitution that we established for them.

Nor shall we take away anything that we have given and established for that monastery, or that has been donated and confirmed by God-fearing people [Note: [Col. 1123D] Perhaps, “or by God.” Hardouin.], or anything transmitted as a gift or offered upon the altar, or anything from sacred books or from whatever objects pertain to the adornment of divine worship, whether these things have been granted at present or are to be granted in the future.

I humbly implore and ask my lords and successors, the bishops, and the other administrators of Saint Stephen, for the sake of the name of the Holy Trinity, to preserve forever, for the reward that is to accrue to them from what has been stated above, those brothers who are seen to belong to that monastery.

Let that monastery be subject to the *mundeburd* and protection of the church of Saint Stephen of Metz, as is contained in the document that we drew up concerning that monastery for the church of Saint Stephen [Note: [Col. 1123D] See Ducange, *Glossary*, under the word *Mundibardus*. Hardouin.], so that they may pray to the Lord’s mercy for the life and safety of the king, the stability of the Frankish kingdom, and their bishops and their subjects.

According to divine providence, when the abbot of that monastery departs to the Lord, the entire congregation of monks shall unanimously elect as their abbot the man whom they have found to be of the best rule and worthy in the merits of his life. They shall do so with the consent and will of the bishop of the city. They shall have him as their abbot.

If, God forbid, they cannot find such a man within their congregation who can govern them according to the rule, then the bishop himself, with their consent and will, shall choose an abbot from another monastery, as we have said, who will preside over them regularly and according to the order. The aforesaid bishop shall not, by any means, pretext, or desire, place any abbot in that monastery except one who will govern them according to the rule.

If that bishop or any other authority acts otherwise, he will have to render an account for it before the divine tribunal, in the sight of God, together with the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and Saint Stephen, the first martyr.
