If the aforesaid bishop comes to that monastery, whenever he wishes, to gain the reward of prayer or to visit the brothers [Note: [Col. 1124D] Perhaps, “to gain,” as is read immediately afterward, “to gain the souls.” Hardouin.], or if he spends some time there to gain souls, when he wishes thereafter to return in God’s name, he shall depart without demanding any earthly gift.

Thus may the monks who are called solitaries, in perfect peace and security, rejoice for long ages under the protection of the Lord, living under the holy rule, and may they pray more fully and attentively for the progress of the Church, the welfare of the king, and the safety of the country.

If, God forbid, those monks should be found lukewarm or negligent in their rule or religious observance, they shall be corrected by their abbot according to their rule. But if the abbot himself is unable to prevail, then the aforesaid bishop must discipline them, since nothing of canonical authority is overthrown by whatever is bestowed by bishops in trust for the sake of peaceful tranquility [Note: [Col. 1124D] Perhaps, “by the bishops.” Hardouin.].

[Note: [Col. 1124D] Perhaps, “so that this may.” Hardouin.] So that this may stand more firmly in strength, we and our fathers, the lord bishops, have decreed that it be confirmed by our signatures at the synod, and our faithful brothers of the congregation of Saint Stephen, who consented, have also subscribed.

Chrodegangus, a sinner and bishop, reread and subscribed this confirmation made by me.

Adalfridus, a sinner and bishop, subscribed.

Lupus, a sinner and bishop, having heard this, subscribed.

I, Fulcharius, called an unworthy bishop, subscribed through Rothingus the advocate.

Vulfrannus, called bishop, subscribed in the name of Christ.

Herineus, bishop, subscribed through Segimondus.

I, Mangaudus, bishop, subscribed.

Memorianus Chorchidianus subscribed.

Deotmarus, although a sinner and bishop, subscribed.

Rabigandus, abbot, subscribed.

Jacob, a sinner and bishop, subscribed.

Mensebius, a sinner and bishop, subscribed.

Audo, a sinner and bishop, subscribed.

Chardobachius, although a sinner and bishop, subscribed.

Lendenaus, bishop, subscribed.

I, Lupus, although an unworthy bishop, subscribed in the name of Christ.

Tedecharius, a sinner and bishop, subscribed.

Fortunus, a sinner and bishop, subscribed.

Sedonius, although a sinner and bishop, subscribed.

Deofridus, bishop, subscribed.

Sadrius, bishop, subscribed.

I, Angilrannus, subscribed.

Sadebertus, although an unworthy bishop, subscribed.

Rotelinus subscribed; Gontelmus; Brandomus; Sigibertus; Zacharias; Rachinnatus; I, Gonterius; Abbo; Adelelinus; Angelelinus; Sadrius.

I, Richerus, or Wasco, although an unworthy deacon, having been ordered to do so, reread and subscribed this confirmation.

Executed publicly at the palace of Compiegne, in the synod assembled there, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 756, indiction 9, epact 15, concurrent 4, in the sixth year—or, as others prefer, the fourth year—of the reign of Pippin, the glorious king, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June.

## In the Year of the Lord 700: Saint Paul I, Roman Pontiff

## [Col. 1125] Historical Notice on Saint Pope Paul I

*(The Book of the Pontiffs, from various editions.)*
[Col. 1125C] **Note 1.** Paul. In the year 757, on 28 May, Paul, brother of his predecessor Stephen, obtained the pontificate by the greater number of votes against Theophylact. BIN. and LABB.

**Note 2.** Paul, son of Constantine, a Roman, full brother of Pope Stephen the Younger, was made cardinal of the Holy Roman Church by Pope Zachary. Under the emperors Constantine and Leo Augustus, he was elected and consecrated on 29 May 757 in the Lateran patriarchate. He learned morals and ecclesiastical doctrine under the pontiffs Gregory III and Zachary, by whom he was admitted, together with his brother, to the order of deacons. After his brother’s death, however, Paul was appointed in his place on account of the integrity of his life and his learning, although there was no precedent in the supreme priesthood for the succession of two brothers, nor has such a thing ever been seen afterward. CIACONIUS.

**Note 3.** Since the exarchs had already been expelled, and the kings of the Lombards were not merely failing to enter upon whatever rights they possessed, but were being extraordinarily harassed by Pippin, king of the Franks, whose obedience and reverence toward the supreme pontiffs were complete, there was no reason for the Apostolic See to remain vacant again for any considerable time or not to receive a newly elected pontiff immediately after his election and consecration. But internal disagreement—which we learn from Anastasius himself—was the cause of the longer interregnum.

It is worthwhile to reproduce his account here in his own words, both to confirm what I have taught elsewhere concerning the *enthronism*, with consecration preceding it, and to make clear that it was customary in those times to think about choosing a successor only after the deposition at Saint Peter’s—a point Pagius did not sufficiently notice when he found occasion to place consecrations outside Sunday.

Speaking, therefore, of the election and consecration of Saint Paul, who was the full brother of the recently deceased pontiff, Anastasius reports that the causes of the interregnum were the dissensions among the electors: the greater part adhered to Paul, who had never left the Lateran patriarchate, while another part adhered to the archdeacon Theophylact in his own house. And when Stephen, he says, had been buried with great honor in the basilica of blessed Peter, immediately the same assembly of the people that was attached to the aforementioned blessed Paul, then a deacon, elected him to the summit of the pontificate, because it was larger and stronger. After this, those who had joined the aforementioned archdeacon dispersed. And thus, with God’s favor, that same most holy man was consecrated pontiff in the most sacred Apostolic See of blessed Peter.

All these events took place after Stephen’s death, in the year 757. Concerning the length of the interregnum, there are two opinions in the manuscripts and catalogues. Most authorities report that the see was vacant for one month and five days, or thirty-five days, as do the catalogues of Lucca, Farfa, and six Colbertine manuscripts (the fifth Colbertine manuscript, erroneously, has twenty-two days), as well as two Freherian manuscripts and the other Thuanus manuscript, together with two Ambrosian manuscripts—the first, very ancient one, which ends here, and the fourth.

Others, however, count an interregnum of thirty-two days, as do the common edition, the Regius manuscript, the Mazarin manuscript, the first Thuanus manuscript, the second and third Ambrosian manuscripts, and the Farnesian manuscript, although none of the catalogues supports them.

In either case, both opinions lead us to the date of Saint Paul’s ordination, 29 May, which in the year 757 fell on a Sunday. The only difference between them is that the first opinion, namely the thirty-five-day calculation, which the *AA.* follow in Pagius, reckons the interregnum from the day of Stephen II—or, alternatively, III—’s death, which the duration of his pontificate shows to have occurred on 24 April, and includes that day in the total. The second, the thirty-two-day calculation, reckons the interregnum, according to custom, from the day of burial and excludes the day of death from the total.

I have therefore thought that this twofold opinion concerning the interregnum may be reconciled for the benefit of learned readers who favor the first view, by having the two-day interval between Stephen’s death and burial fill out the difference.

Thus Saint Paul the Deacon, brother of his predecessor, once the people’s dissension had subsided, was consecrated on 29 May 757 and sat as pope, by the unanimous testimony of all the manuscripts and catalogues, for ten years and one month—that is, until 28 June 767.

The biographer, whoever he may have been, does not mention the burial of this pontiff, but carefully recounts everything that concerns his piety, with no chronological indication. From another source, however, the year of his death is certain. For the *Bertinian Annals* (*Script. Italic.*, vol. II), speaking of Pippin’s return from the Aquitanian expedition under the year 767, say: “And he returned to Bourges, and there he was informed of the death of Pope Paul.”

Indeed, Anastasius himself gives the actual day of his death in the *Life of Stephen III*, alternatively IV, his consecrated successor. It must be inferred from the deposition of the usurper Constantine, about whom I have spoken sufficiently in the preceding note, where I also touched upon some of the days that elapsed between the overthrow of the usurper and Stephen’s ordination—days which Anastasius omitted. Anastasius’s words are:

“On the twenty-eighth day of the month of July” (which fell on a Thursday), “in the sixth indiction” (the year 768), “in the evening, at the very twilight of night, on the vigil of the blessed martyrs Abdon and Sennen, they occupied the Salarian Bridge” (the Lombards, and so forth). “On the following day” (Friday), “crossing the Milvian Bridge, they came to Rome and did what I have said above: they cast down Constantine the usurper and deserter from the Lateran patriarchate” and threw him into prison.

Marianus Scotus agrees remarkably with this in his *Chronicle*, despite Pagius’s futile objection: “Constantine was deposed on Friday, in the month of July”—not, indeed, from the rank of the pontificate, which happened later, but from the eminence that he had usurped.

Therefore, if attention is paid to what Anastasius says concerning the interregnum after Saint Paul—“And the episcopate ceased for one year and one month”—to which the second Freherian manuscript appropriately adds, “during which Constantine, the transgressor and usurper of the Apostolic See, came into being,” and likewise to what the same Anastasius says in the *Life of Stephen III*, or IV, concerning Constantine: “And he held the Apostolic See under usurpation for the space of one year and one month”—if, I say, attention is paid to these statements, there can be absolutely no doubt that Saint Paul died on 28 June 767. For from that date to 29 July of the following year, 768, one year and one month are counted, just as the ten years and one month during which the holy pontiff governed the Church run from 29 May 757 to the aforementioned day of his death.

These notes on the chronology of Saint Paul I, who brings this fourth volume to a close, had not yet been committed to the press when the frequently praised Father Joseph Blanchinus, ever vigilant in illustrating pontifical history, gave me an outstanding document taken from a manuscript of the celebrated chapter library of Verona. It splendidly confirms the death of that same Saint Paul, the deposition of the pseudo-pope Constantine, and the election of Stephen III, alternatively IV.

And since he does not allow anyone to be deprived of his proper praise, he testified to me that he owed the document to the most learned archpriest and chancellor of the distinguished chapter of Verona, Bartholomeo Campagnola. His highly conspicuous skill in reading and examining ancient manuscripts and charters for the public benefit is admired by V. C. Ludovicus Muratorius (*Script. Ital.*, vol. II, part 2, p. 685) and Bishop Blanchinus (*Anast.*, vol. III, prolegomena, p. 35), excellent judges in such matters.

Blanchinus says that, at the request of the latter and in company with the very learned Count Otholino Otholinius, Campagnola copied this document with the greatest fidelity and sent it to him on 28 May of the present year, 1735.

The document in question is nearly the complete first session of the Roman council under Stephen III, alternatively IV. From its third and fourth sessions Lucas Holstenius extracted a venerable fragment (*Collect. Rom.*, p. 259), and another is found in Acheri’s *Spicilegium*. From these sources the same material has been transferred into later collections of councils; previously, everyone obtained only a bare memory of this council from Anastasius.

From this newly discovered document, at last, those twelve Frankish bishops emerge whom Sirmond did not transcribe in full from the Panvinian papers, and who consequently deceived the Sammarthani, Antonio Pagius, and other writers, even the most keen-sighted. There also emerge all those bishops whom Anastasius says were assembled from Campania, Tuscany, and the province of Italy—forty in number—of whom Ughellus and everyone who wrote before this day recognized scarcely three or four as having been named elsewhere by Anastasius.

I would give the whole document here, were I not more appropriately going to publish it in the following volume, in order to illustrate the life of Stephen III, alternatively IV. Meanwhile, so that learned men may not take this amiss, and so that the prefects of the most distinguished libraries of Europe, celebrated both by name and by their writings, may be encouraged to bring forth something similar, I shall publish this outstanding document separately from Anastasius, together with several notes, for the greatest benefit of ecclesiastical history. CENNUS.]

Paul, a Roman by nation, son of Constantine, sat for ten years and one month. From early childhood he was entrusted, together with his own elder brother Stephen, his predecessor in the pontificate, to the Lateran patriarchate for instruction in ecclesiastical discipline, during the time of Lord Gregory II the Younger, pontiff. Later he was consecrated by Lord Zachary, the most blessed pope, in the order of deacons together with the aforesaid brother.

For when that same brother and predecessor of his, the pontiff, was approaching the end of his life, immediately [Note: Alternatively, “the people of this Roman city.”] the people of this Roman city were divided with him: some, holding with the archdeacon Theophylact, gathered and remained in his house. Others, however, agreed with the same blessed Paul the deacon; the greater part of the judges and people held with him, rather than with the aforementioned archdeacon Theophylact. The most holy man himself did not at all withdraw from the Lateran patriarchate, but continued faithfully to serve his sick brother and predecessor, the pontiff, together with the other faithful.

When the aforementioned brother and predecessor of his, the pontiff, had departed this life and had been buried with great honor in the basilica of blessed Peter, immediately the same assembly of the people that adhered to the often-mentioned blessed Paul, then a deacon, because it was larger and stronger,

**Note.** [Col. 1128C] They elected him to the summit of the pontificate. When Paul had been created pontiff, he sent a letter to Pippin, king of the Franks, informing him of the death of his brother Stephen and of his own election, and indicating that he would remain in the friendship with the Franks begun by that same Stephen, asking Pippin to do likewise.

This was the first letter he himself sent, since it was written before his ordination. Its superscription is: “To the most excellent lord, son Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans: Paul the Deacon, and by the name of God elect of the holy Apostolic See.” This letter is correctly placed first in order in Labbe’s collection of councils; in the *Codex Carolinus*, however, it is number 13.

This is an appropriate place to remind the reader about the author of the *Codex Carolinus*. In 1613 Jacob Gretzer published at Ingolstadt letters sent by the Roman pontiffs Gregory III, Zachary, Stephen II, Paul, Stephen III, Hadrian, and the pseudo-pope Constantine to Charles Martel, mayor of the palace; to Pippin; to Charlemagne; and to his brother Carloman.

These letters had formerly been collected into a single volume through the industry and care of Charlemagne himself, and there are ninety-nine of them in all. In the year 791 Charlemagne had them copied out again, because they had already been partly erased by excessive age, as is clear from an ancient inscription written in capital letters, which was prefixed to the collection by the very person who, at his command, copied them into a single corpus.

This collection is called the *Codex Carolinus* after its author, Charles the Great. Lambecius, moreover, in book II of the *Bibliotheca Caesarea*, chapter 5, testifies that it was extracted from an ancient manuscript of that same library. But he says that the person who copied the *Codex* and sent it to Gretzer arrogated to himself excessive freedom in correcting and changing certain passages; it would therefore be worthwhile to collate that first edition in full with the aforementioned authentic exemplar.

Finally, all those letters are earlier than the year 791, since their collection was made in that year. They are also found in Duchesne, volume III. PAGIUS.]

They elected him to the summit of the pontificate. After this, those who had joined the aforementioned archdeacon dispersed. And thus, with God’s favor, that same most holy man was consecrated pontiff in the most sacred Apostolic See of blessed Peter.

He lived during the reigns of the emperors Constantine and Leo. For he was gentle and exceedingly merciful, never returning evil for evil to anyone. And if he heard that someone nearby was being harassed by unjust agents for some slight cause,

**Note.** [Col. 1129A] The Lucan manuscript reads: “was troubled.”

nevertheless, moved by compassion, he brought him consolation and showed him mercy.

He himself, as many have testified, went by night in person through the cells of poor and sick people who were bedridden and unable to rise from their own little beds,

**Note.** [Col. 1129B] Cells of poor sick people. A *cella* is a dwelling or little house of the lower classes. Martial, book III, epigram 30:

“From where have you got your little toga and the rent of a dark cell?”

The cell of a prostitute, where she stands for sale in a brothel. Petronius, in the *Satyricon*:

“By then the prostitute had demanded an as for the cell.”

Cells of slaves. Columella, *On Agriculture*, book I, chapter 6: “For the best health of slaves, cells facing the equinoctial midday will be built.” Petronius, in the *Satyricon*: “Not far from the doorkeeper’s cell.” ALTASERRA.]

and also visited, in the silence of the night, other needy people with their families, supplying them with abundant nourishment and bringing them assistance and aid.

He also visited prisons and other places of confinement during those same secret hours of the night. If he found any people shut up there, he bought them back from the danger of death and released them to go free. He also redeemed from the yoke of servitude many who were bound by debts and oppressed by their moneylenders, paying the debts themselves. He brought aid to widows, orphans, and all the needy.

For he was a most courageous defender of the orthodox faith.

**Note 1.** Therefore he often sent his agents to the aforementioned emperors Constantine and Leo Augustus with apostolic letters of entreaty and admonition. The most holy pontiff Paul labored greatly over the grave matter of the worship of sacred images, against which the Constantinopolitan emperors Constantine Copronymus and his son Leo had declared an impious war. To recall those impious emperors from their evil judgment, he repeatedly sent agents to them and composed several letters full both of entreaties and admonitions. The ravages of time, together with human indolence and negligence, have deprived us of copies of those letters. Besides Anastasius, Pope Hadrian mentions them in the second session of the Second Council of Nicaea.

Our Librarian, however, says nothing about the letters that Paul sent to Pippin in Gaul. He ought at least to have indicated them, if he did not wish to recite them, in order to weave the history of this pontiff, who was no less concerned to defend ecclesiastical doctrines against the heresy of the Iconoclasts than to protect and vindicate the rights of the Apostolic See—both its patrimonies and its provinces, namely the Pentapolis and the Exarchate of Ravenna, which had been added to the rights of that see by the recent donation of King Pippin—from the injuries and plots of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and from the threatened attacks of Constantine and Leo.

These letters exist in the *Codex Carolinus*, thirty-one in number. If anyone, relying on Anastasius’s silence, were to deny that these letters belonged to Paul, he would make a disgraceful error and openly reveal his ignorance. Their unquestionable existence is established by the fact that each bears Paul’s name in authentic manuscripts, both in the imperial library, from which Gretzer copied, and in the Vatican Library, from which Onuphrius Panvinius extracted the arguments of each letter—arguments which Baronius recites in order under the year 767. His order, however, arranged according to the sequence of the years, differs from the order in which the letters occur in the *Codex Carolinus*.

How wrongly, therefore, Natalis Alexander, on the basis of Anastasius’s similar silence in the *Life of Pope Zachary*, charges as false Childeric’s deposition and Pippin’s elevation to the Frankish kingship, effected by the authority of that same Zachary, when by the same reasoning he could have declared Paul’s letters to Pippin—otherwise undeniable—incredible and unworthy of credence. Let the prudent reader judge from this Natalis’s intellect and zeal toward the Holy See, and likewise the force of a negative argument in cases of this kind. BALDINUS.

**Note 2.** “He often sent his agents with apostolic letters of entreaty and admonition, etc.” The letters that the holy pontiff wrote to the emperor concerning this matter, explicitly mentioned by Pope Hadrian I in his letter to Constantine and Irene, the Augusti, certainly do not survive. The letters that he sent on the same occasion to King Pippin are likewise missing; in them he asked Pippin to use his authority to intercede with the Iconoclast emperor in order to turn him away from persecuting the Church.

This much is established by Paul’s seventh letter to Pippin: he knew well that the persecution of the Greek emperor and his unjust designs against the Apostolic See arose from the fact that the pontiff was defending the orthodox faith and the tradition of venerable antiquity, which the impious emperor was attempting to overthrow:

“For, as your Excellency has been fully informed, those most wicked Greeks persecute us for no other reason than the holy and orthodox faith and the pious tradition of the venerable Fathers, which they desire to destroy and trample underfoot.” (*Paul, Letter 7 to King Pippin, Codex Carolinus* 34.)

Constantine had formed the plan, directed against the Apostolic See, of recovering the Exarchate of Ravenna, which Pippin, after defeating the Lombards, had legitimately brought under his own power and had granted to the Roman pontiff to possess with full authority and useful dominion.

The emperor understood perfectly that he could never attain his desired end so long as the Franks supplied the pontiff with resources and assistance. Unless he could draw the king of the Lombards over to his side by enticing him with the hope of advantage, he left nothing unattempted. For this reason he sent envoys to Francia, who moved every stone in order to damage the pontiff’s reputation and withdraw King Pippin from the alliance he had made with him.

At the same time he had agents in Ravenna and throughout the entire exarchate, stirring up the peoples to revolt against the pontiff. He also ordered that a marriage be proposed between his son Leo, whom he had associated with himself in the empire, and Pippin’s daughter Giselida. And so that the difference of religion—which, as the emperor said, the pontiff was putting forward as a reason for declining—would not be an obstacle, he requested that a religious conference be held in Francia. At it, his envoys, whom he intended to send for that purpose, would give an account of the orthodoxy that he wished to be maintained throughout the empire.

Yet neither the conference held near Paris nor all the schemes that Copronymus devised and employed against Pippin accomplished anything toward drawing that excellent prince away from the Catholic faith and the defense of the Holy See. (*Paul, Letter 20 and others to Pippin, in the Codex Carolinus; Ado in his Chronicle; Einhard under the year 767.*)

Therefore Constantine turned elsewhere and lent his ears to the king of the Lombards, who promised to join him in an alliance against the pope. They concluded a pact on these terms: both would fight with their combined forces to bring Ravenna and Otranto under their control; the Lombards would possess the former, while the Greeks would possess the latter together with the neighboring region; and the emperor would immediately dispatch a very powerful fleet to Italy for the stated purpose.

Copronymus did not, however, carry this out. He persuaded himself that the troops he had in Sicily and the neighboring regions would be sufficient to recover Ravenna without the Lombards’ assistance, at a time when King Pippin could not aid the pontiff, since he was occupied in war with the dukes subject to him in Bavaria and Aquitaine.

But the pontiff, having timely discovered his plans, immediately disclosed them to King Pippin, so that he might compel the king of the Lombards, as well as the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento and the other neighboring rulers, to protect the Holy See if the Greeks should take up arms against it.

“Be so good as to send your agent at once to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, so that, if necessity is reported, he may grant us assistance against the invasion of those same enemies; and command the Beneventans, Spoletans, and Tuscans who dwell near us to come to our aid.” (*Paul, Letter 7 to King Pippin, Codex Carolinus* 34.)

When the emperor learned this, he undertook none of the measures he had planned. On the contrary, the king of the Lombards harassed Paul throughout the whole period of his pontificate.

First, he refused to return to the Holy See the cities of Bologna, Imola, Ancona, and others, which he had promised to return so that he might receive its support against Ratchis, who was contending with him for the Lombard kingdom. Then he brought war into the Pentapolis and ravaged it. Finally, he expelled the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento, who depended upon the Holy See, and installed others who were subject to himself.

When the pontiff rightly complained of these matters, Desiderius prolonged the dispute in words, promising that he would fully execute the agreement made at Pavia between Stephen and Aistulf, provided that Pippin returned the hostages whom he had taken to Francia.

But Paul, whom Desiderius believed he was mocking, outwitted him. Under the pretext of sending envoys to request the hostages, he instructed them to disclose the Lombards’ treachery to the king and implore his assistance, since among all princes he alone could recall the treaty-breaking Lombard to his duty and support those subject to the Church.

“It is clear that, above all kings and powerful men, you excel in pious works . . . . Therefore, so that the contest of your pious activity may be brought to effect, it is fitting that we frequently send apostolic letters to you, as the liberator of the Holy Church of God itself and of its special people.” (*The same author, Letter 2 to Pippin, Codex Carolinus* 15.)

Accordingly, Pippin, becoming ever more devoted to the Holy See, sent two of the chief commanders of his court to Desiderius. They informed him that the king himself would come to Italy with a powerful army unless he satisfied the pontiff.

Terrified by this unexpected threat, the Lombard returned to Paul part of what he was retaining as belonging to the pontifical jurisdiction and promised that he would restore everything else that remained in his possession.

“When your Remedius Germanus and Autcharius, the most glorious duke, had joined us, he established between them and Desiderius, king of the Lombards, that throughout the entire coming month of April he would fully restore to us all the rights of our patron, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—that is, all patrimonies, rights, places, boundaries, and territories of our various cities belonging to the Roman commonwealth. Accordingly, the same king of the Lombards is known to have restored some of these rights to us; and he professes and solemnly promises that he will restore all the remaining rights to us.” (*The same author, Letter 3 to Pippin, Codex Carolinus* 17 and 19.)

But Desiderius did not keep his promises. Secretly, as we have said, he dealt with the emperor so that, after forming an alliance with him, he might take up arms against the pontiff’s rights. When this scheme came to nothing, instead of restoring to Saint Peter and his successor the cities and territories that he had unlawfully seized, as he had promised King Pippin whenever Pippin pressed him to do so, he planned new invasions.

For this reason he remained a source of trouble to the holy pontiff for as long as he lived, as his final letter plainly shows:

“Let your most excellent Christian Majesty know for certain that, unless the boundaries of our cities and the patrimonies invaded by those same Lombards are returned to us, they will plot to invade even those possessions that they previously restored.” (*The same author, Letters 17 and 19, Codex Carolinus.*) SOMMIER.]

Therefore he often sent his agents to the aforementioned emperors Constantine and Leo with apostolic letters of entreaty and admonition, seeking the restoration and confirmation to their former state of veneration of the most sacred images of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, of his holy Mother, and of all the blessed apostles, prophets, martyrs, and confessors.

**Note.** [Col. 1132D] “With letters of admonition.” These and the preceding letters of Paul to the emperor Constantine and King Pippin are missing. The former are mentioned in Pope Hadrian’s letter to Constantine and Irene Augustus. BIN. and LABB.]

For this most blessed pontiff, with all his spiritual efforts, continually exercised great and anxious care for the cemeteries of the saints.

**Note.** [Col. 1131B] Alternatively: “with common [or communal] spiritual efforts.”

Therefore, seeing that many places in those same cemeteries of the saints had been neglected, had suffered extensive destruction through the decay of antiquity, and had already been brought close to ruin, he immediately removed the bodies of the saints from those ruined cemeteries. Bringing them into this Roman city with hymns and spiritual songs, he took care to have some of them reburied with fitting honor in the titular churches and deaconries, or in monasteries and other churches.

[Note: [Col. 1132D] This most holy prelate built a monastery in his own house. Concerning the church and monastery founded by Paul I, there is preserved in Cardinal Baronius, under the year of Christ 761, a constitution or privilege issued by the same pontiff in the Roman synod, which clearly confirms what Anastasius relates here. For, after Paul had spoken in that constitution about certain cemeteries of the holy martyrs, some collapsed through age and others destroyed by the sacrilegious violence of the Lombards, he adds the following: “Accordingly, having observed the slothful neglect of those same holy places, and greatly lamenting it, worn down by the deepest grief, I judged it fitting, with God’s approval, to remove those same holy martyrs, confessors of Christ, and virgins from those ruined places. We brought them with hymns and spiritual songs into this Roman city, and, placing and entombing their most holy bodies in the church which I had newly built from its foundations in their honor—within the walls, namely, in the house that had come to me by inheritance from my parents, in which I am known to have been born and raised—we established them there. In that place I founded a congregation of monks under a special rule, in honor and in the name of the blessed Stephen, pope and martyr, and Silvester, pope and confessor of Christ; their venerable bodies rest there. I judged that the monastery should belong to male monks; that is, I decreed that psalmody should be performed there perpetually.” Since Anastasius states that this perpetual psalmody was performed in Greek chant, it can easily be inferred that Paul entrusted this monastery to Greek monks who, when persecution raged in the East under the rule of the Iconoclast emperors, were driven from their homes and withdrew to Rome. For the impious emperor Copronymus, burning with the greatest hatred against monks, whom he recognized as vigorous opponents of his heresy and powerful defenders of the sacred images, issued about this time an edict by which, imposing every kind of punishment, he forbade monks to live within his dominion. Therefore, as they migrated to various places, all who came to Rome were kindly received by Pope Paul and given this most fully equipped monastery, where they might perform the Church’s offices according to their rite and honor as they ought the relics of Christ’s martyrs and confessors resting there. But how magnificent the foundation of this monastery was, beyond what our author reports about it, can also be understood from the words of the constitution promulgated by Paul, in the presence and, as I said above, with the confirmation of the council: “And behold,” Paul says, “the monastery founded by us in their honor, with the Lord’s favor, we have enriched exceedingly with various estates and properties, urban and rural possessions, and all necessary equipment; and we have granted everything sufficient for the furnishing of the lamps, the diligent offering of sacrifices, and the needs of the monks residing there: estates, farms, farmsteads, tenant holdings, vineyards, gardens as well, olive groves, houses and guesthouses, saltworks and watermills, fisheries, and the remaining landed properties situated in various places and cities, together with the property of the serving slaves. We have also added and confirmed under the jurisdiction and authority of our monastery certain monasteries and venerable places, with all their possessions and everything generally and wholly belonging to them.” Nor can Paul’s constitution for that reason be branded as false because the chronological dates do not properly agree in the copy published by Baronius under the year mentioned, at the end of which appears this subscription: “Given on the fourth day before the Nones of June, while the lord Constantine Augustus, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the forty-first year from the time when he began to reign with his father, and in the twenty-first year after his consulship, in the fourteenth indiction.” Since Constantine Copronymus was declared co-emperor with his father on the last day of March in the year 720, and on the eighteenth day of June in the year 741 assumed the consulship according to custom and succeeded his father Leo and his impiety, his forty-first imperial year cannot coincide with the twentieth year of his consulship; for the consulship exceeds the imperial reign by one year. Yet Paul’s constitution, called by Baronius a worthy monument of the holy pontiff, should not for that reason be criticized as a forgery.

1. Because the chronological dates incorrectly recorded in Baronius’s copy may perhaps agree correctly in the original preserved at Rome by the nuns of Saint Silvester, who had been substituted for the monks because of the changes of the times; I was not granted permission to see it, especially since the printed diploma of Paul suffers from a slight error, one easily made by the hands of copyists.

2. Because the sequence of the constitution agrees both with our historian and with the account attached to the letter that Stephen III wrote concerning the recovery of his health, divinely restored to him through the blessed martyr Dionysius; there this monastery is called “at the Holy Martyrs in the School of the Greeks,” and is said to have been nobly built by Paul, his brother. It is extant among Hilduin’s Areopagitic writings in volume V of Surius.

3. Finally, because many ancient diplomas, which everyone accepts with consistent confidence, would have to be rejected, since, as scholars know, copyists have very often made mistakes in transcribing chronological dates. MAFEUS.]

This most holy prelate built from its foundations, in his own house, a monastery in honor of Saint Stephen, namely the martyr and pontiff, and also of the blessed Silvester, likewise pontiff and confessor of Christ. There he also built a shrine in the upper parts of the same monastery and buried their bodies with great veneration. Within the enclosure of the monastery he newly built from its foundations a church of astonishing beauty. He adorned it with mosaic and marble, lavishing all its decoration in gold, silver, and various materials; and he also made there a silver ciborium [Note: [Col. 1132B] Codex of Lucca: “ciborium”] weighing pounds. There too he buried with the greatest devotion the bodies of countless saints, which he had removed from the aforementioned ruined cemeteries. In that same monastery he bestowed many estates, possessions, and urban and rural properties, enriching it excessively and abundantly with gold and silver, other kinds of goods, and every necessity. There he also established a congregation of monks, decreeing that it should be a cenobium for psalmody in the Greek manner [Note: [Col. 1134D] “Greek chant.” Pope Paul had received monks who had fled after the persecution of Constantine Copronymus had spread throughout Greece, and he built the monastery of Saint Stephen at Rome as their dwelling. Theophanes speaks in the following manner of that persecution, stirred up by Copronymus chiefly against monks, p. 373: “He also declared that monasteries—those sacred dwellings built for the glory of God and as refuges for the saved—should, by the decision of soldiers corrupted by his depravity, become common and profane houses. He assigned the monastery of the Dalmatians, the most famous cenobium in Byzantium, as quarters for soldiers; and he overturned from their foundations other sacred buildings, such as those known by the names of Callistratus, Dius, and Maximinus, which are praised, as well as other religious houses of monks and dwellings of virgins. But those whom he discovered to be either distinguished in military skill or conspicuous in rank, previously most necessary to him and aware of his secret lusts and shameful acts, and devoted to the monastic life, he condemned to certain death, conjecturing that he would be put to shame by their confessions. The monk Stephen the Younger was responsible for their migration to the West, as we read in his Life, volume I of Loppin’s Greek Analecta, p. 456. ‘Since,’ the holy man said to the monks, ‘three regions remain among those who do not share communion with this impious heresy, I advise you to hasten to them. For there is no other place subject to the Dragon that does not comply with his empty talk.’ That monks also came to Rome among the other places was likewise reported by Stephen the deacon in the Life cited above: ‘Then one could see Byzantium deprived of its monastic order and Nazarene garb, as though carried away into captivity. One went to the Euxine Pontus, another to Cyprus; another planned to depart for Rome.’ For the rest, consult Theophanes if you wish. BENCINUS. — ‘Greek chant.’ When the impious emperor Copronymus had forbidden monks by an edict to remain in the East, a great multitude of Greek monks had withdrawn to Rome. Since the Greek language was peculiar to them, he wished them, once settled in the monastery, to perform what they had been accustomed to perform in their Eastern monasteries—namely, to chant the psalms and perform the other ecclesiastical offices in their own language. BIN and LABB.]. He decreed that it should be a cenobium of psalmody in the Greek manner, and established that solemn praises should be offered assiduously and without interruption to our almighty God and to all the saints resting there, under severe prohibitions.

He newly built a church within this Roman city, on the Sacred Way, beside the temple of Romulus [Note: [Col. 1133A] Another reading: “at Rome”], in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. At that place those most blessed princes of the apostles, when they were crowned with martyrdom for Christ’s name, were seen to bend their own knees while offering prayers to our Redeemer [Note: [Col. 1133A] Mansi omits “while”]. At that spot, their knees are known still to be marked as a testimony for every generation that will come at the end, on a certain very hard stone. He also newly built, outside the walls of this Roman city, within the church of the blessed apostle Peter, a shrine in honor of the holy Mother of God, beside the oratory of Saint Leo the pope, near the entrance doors of Saint Petronilla and of the blessed apostle Andrew. He adorned it with mosaic and various metals. There he also installed an image of the holy Mother of God in a statue of gilded silver weighing one hundred pounds [Note: [Col. 1134A] In another copy the number is absent]. In that shrine he also built a burial place for himself.

[Note: [Col. 1136A] “Here, while in the church of the blessed Paul.” In the same year, 767, Pope Paul, while staying in the church of the blessed apostle Paul during the summer because of the intensity of the heat, was seized by bodily illness and there was called to heaven, to receive from God the reward of his labors, on the twenty-eighth day of June. He had sat for ten years and one month, as Anastasius writes, together with Martin of Poland and Liutprand. Because of the honor that he had continually and zealously shown the apostle Paul, he wished to be buried first in that same basilica of Saint Paul. After several months had passed, however, he was transferred to the Vatican and buried in the oratory that he himself had erected near the high altar. Baronius entered his name in the Roman Martyrology under June 28, the day on which he completed his mortal life; previously his name had been recorded under January 27 by Peter de Natalibus, book III, chapter 30, by the Carthusians of Cologne in their Additions to Usuard, and by Canisius, Maurolycus, Felicius, and Galesinius. PAGIUS.]

Here, while staying in the church of the blessed apostle Paul during the summer because of the severe heat, he was overtaken by bodily illness and ended his life there, where he was also buried. His corpse remained unburied there for nearly three months [Note: [Col. 1135A] Codex of Lucca and others: “buried”]. Afterwards all the Roman citizens and people of other nations gathered, crossed the river Tiber by boat with his body, and carried it to the blessed Peter with the honor of psalmody. They buried him in the aforementioned shrine that he had built. He held one ordination in the month of December: twelve priests, two deacons, and three bishops in various places [Note: [Col. 1136A] In another copy “three and the rest” are absent]. The episcopate was vacant for one year and one month.

[Col. 1135]

# Letters of Saint Paul I, Roman Pontiff

## Complete Letters of the Codex Carolinus

Of which Labbe had given only a summary from Baronius.

### Letter I

Copy of the letter sent to Lord Pippin the king, in which Paul, deacon and elect of the holy Roman Church, announces through Immo the death of Pope Stephen.

[Col. 1135C]

[Note: [Col. 1135C] Grets.: Summary in Baronius and the Centuriators.]

To the most excellent lord, his son Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans: Paul, deacon and, in the name of God, elect of the holy apostolic see, with profound groaning and immense sorrow of heart.

We inform your excellence, most powerful victorious king, protected by God, that the lord Stephen, pope of holy memory and my brother, has been taken from this light by God’s calling to eternal rest [Col. 1136C]. At his passing, even the stones, if one may say so, wept for us and shed tears. My wretchedness was chosen by the entire multitude of peoples for the succession to his apostolate. While these things were taking place, Immo, sent by your most Christian excellence, arrived in Rome [Note: [Col. 1136C] Lambecus: “Immo joined Rome”]. After speaking with him, together with our nobles, we judged it appropriate to retain him here [Note: [Col. 1136C] The same: “to keep him here”] until, by God’s providence, we had been enlightened by the sacred apostolic blessing [Col. 1137A; Note: [Col. 1137D] Lambecus: “we had been instructed”]. Then, once he had been more fully satisfied concerning our purity—or that of all the people [Note: [Col. 1137D] Grets.: perhaps “or of the whole people”; Lambecus: “or of all the people”—] and the affection that we bear toward your most benign excellence and the entire Frankish nation, we released him to return to you with our apostolic envoys [Note: [Col. 1137D] The same: “we dismissed him”].

For you should know for certain, most excellent one, protected by God, our king, after God, our helper and defender, that we remain firm and steadfast, even to the point of soul and the shedding of our blood, in that faith, affection, concord of charity, and covenant of peace which the aforesaid lord of blessed memory, my brother and most holy pontiff, confirmed with you; and we shall remain so with our people to the end [Note: [Col. 1137D] The same: “We remain with our people”]. Therefore, with outstretched palms to heaven, we continually beseech the mercy of our Lord God for the safety of your excellence, of your sweetest sons, and of the most excellent queen, so that your aid and firmest protection may always be extended over us [Note: [Col. 1137D] The same omits “your”]. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

### Letter II

Likewise, a copy of the letter of Paul, bishop of holy memory of Rome, sent through Andrew and Gundricus, containing thanksgivings and petitions in the desire to obtain aid against the Lombards.

To the most excellent lord, his son and our spiritual kinsman, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans: Pope Paul, with the greatest effort of honor and affection of love.

[Col. 1137C]

We gladly accepted and received the letters sent by your illustrious excellence, brought by Andrew and Gunderic, most diligent envoys of your Christian realm [Note: [Col. 1137D] The same: “we received them, namely the letters”; Grets.: the word “letters” appears to be redundant]. Reading them again with our customary rejoicing, in mind and heart, we were exceedingly delighted, since through them we learned of the desires, affection, and joy that we had long wished for concerning your prosperity, giving immense thanks to almighty God, who has granted that we should rejoice, as we so often desire, in your complete safety [Note: [Col. 1137D] Lambecus: “We have learned of your abundant prosperity, giving immense thanks to almighty God”]. For nothing in this life has ever been sweeter or more pleasing to us than continually learning through favorable reports of the joys of your safety. Indeed, the joy of your prosperity has become the exultation of the holy Church of God [Note: [Col. 1138D] Grets.: “the exaltation”] and the richest defense of all the orthodox. Finally, through the letters that you sent us, you have made us certain in every respect that you are prepared to come to the aid and defense of the holy Church of God wherever necessity should arise, and that you will remain firmly in that faith and affection with the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and with the most holy pope of blessed memory, my lord and brother Stephen. You are concerned that everything be fulfilled and inviolably preserved, affirming that you will uphold everything that you promised to that same apostle of God and confessed for the forgiveness of your sins.

Since the heart of your excellence is in God’s hand, and since, by divine blessing and the grace of holy anointing, you are recognized as anointed king by his apostle and the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, the blessed Peter, most excellent and pre-eminent king, this gives us great grounds for confidence that you will remain steadfast in that same charity, affection, and promise which you sought to make to the gatekeeper of the heavenly kingdom. Without doubt, through both letters and the envoys whom you diligently send to us, you will provide us with material for confidence [Note: [Col. 1138D] Muratori’s reading: “a basis”].

Accordingly, we too shall remain firmly in your charity and affection throughout all the days of our life, and no interruption of time will be able to separate us from your love, charity, and affection, which is joined between us [Note: [Col. 1138D] Grets.: “which is in our midst”; Lambecus: “which is in our midst”]. Therefore, with earnest prayers, and adjuring your excellence before the fearful future judgment, I beseech and implore you to command that what has been uttered from your honey-sweet mouth and promised to blessed Peter remain firm and constant [Note: [Col. 1138D] The same: “that you order”]. Reject the impious suggestions and empty promises of the enemies of the holy Church of God and the orthodox faith, and strive always to please God and blessed Peter, who has granted you the government of the present kingdom [Col. 1138C; Note: [Col. 1138D] The same: “so that he may grant you the height or summit of temporal royal power”]. Since he has deigned to bestow upon you the height of temporal royal power, may he also grant you the everlasting possession of the heavenly kingdoms and deign to grant you immense victories over your enemies through the intercession of the prince of the apostles.

Concerning what your excellence informed us—that King Desiderius of the Lombards had told you that no harm or invasion had been inflicted by the Lombards in our territories—let your benevolent excellence believe us: you were not told the truth in this matter [Note: [Col. 1138D] The same: “had inflicted”; the wording is corrupt]. For, most gracious son and our spiritual kinsman, most Christian king, after such great devastations had been committed by those same Lombards in our boundaries and cities, and after he had been admonished by us concerning this, he sent us letters threatening us. Compelled by necessity, we sent those letters to your excellence within our apostolic letters during the past year, for you to examine.

They attacked the city of Senigallia [Note: [Col. 1138D] The same and Grets.: “Senigallia”] in a hostile manner, laying waste with sword and fire the peoples who lived outside that same city [Col. 1139A], carrying away a very large amount of plunder [Note: [Col. 1139D] Lambecus: “taking away”], and killing several men there. Likewise, invading the region of Campania—namely our fortress called Valentis—they acted in the same way as pagan peoples. We have been unable to obtain justice from them for these acts to this very day. Therefore we sent to your excellence asking you to agree to send your envoy, so that by his presence justice might be achieved between the parties and there might be no delay in obtaining that justice from either our side or the Lombard side.

Accordingly, for your fullest satisfaction, we arranged an inquiry in the presence of your aforementioned faithful envoys together with the royal envoys of the Lombard king. Your envoys were satisfied concerning such great iniquities and learned that the truth was ours and the falsehood theirs [Note: [Col. 1139D] Grets.: “our truth”]. For this reason we cannot remain silent about the many acts of malice inflicted upon us by them [Note: [Col. 1139D] The same: “the malicious acts continually inflicted upon us by them”]. Rather, it is necessary that everything be made known to your royal eminence, since, after God, you are the liberator of this province, so that all the people of this province, redeemed by you, may attain their justice through you.

Meanwhile, most excellent and gracious king, most Christian son and spiritual kinsman, we have received the table which long ago you offered to the lord and our brother, Stephen, pope of blessed memory, and through him to the blessed apostle Peter. With hymns and spiritual songs, solemnly offering litanic praises to God, we brought it into the hall of that prince of the apostles [Col. 1139C]. Your envoys offered it on your behalf in the sacred confession, namely over the body of that same gatekeeper of the kingdom of heaven. We sanctified it with the chrism of anointing, placed the sacred offering upon it, and offered a sacrifice of praise to almighty God for the recompense of your father’s soul [Note: [Col. 1139D] The same: “for the eternal remuneration”; and Lambecus: “for the eternal”] and the stability of your kingdom [Note: [Col. 1139D] The same: “we offered”]. By apostolic authority, under the threat of anathema, we decreed that no one ever be permitted to alienate it from the church of blessed Peter. And behold, may your memorial remain forever shining in that apostolic hall; believe that you will receive its reward in the heavenly kingdoms from the just retributor, the Lord God, and from blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

[Col. 1139D] Concerning Regio and Peter, about whom you informed us, we have understood everything; but we leave this to your will, so that you may deal with them as you please—whether by retaining them there with you [Note: [Col. 1140D] Lambecus: “or there”] or by releasing them to us—for whatever pleases you seems entirely fitting and favorable to us. Finally, your aforementioned envoys reported to us in full detail everything that you had entrusted to them. We answered each matter individually and, having instructed them concerning everything, dismissed them to report it to you [Col. 1140A]. We also settled the case of the aforementioned Andrew according to his wish and your command.

May almighty God, who is rich in mercies, protect you continually with the arm of his outstretched power, subject all adversaries and rebels beneath your royal feet, and grant that you may possess the scepter of the kingdom for a long and prosperous life, together with your most excellent daughter and our spiritual godmother, the most gracious queen, and your beloved sons Charles and Carloman, most excellent kings and patricians of the Romans, and the most noble Gisela; and may he grant that you enjoy eternal rewards with the saints and elect. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

### Letter III

Likewise, a copy of the letter of the same pope addressed to Lord Pippin the king concerning the defense of the holy Church of God and the monastery situated near Mount Soracte that he granted to him, giving great thanks.

[Col. 1140B]

[Note: [Col. 1140D] Summary 25 in Baronius and the Centuriators.]

To the most excellent lord, his son and our spiritual kinsman, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans: Pope Paul.

When we turn over in our memory the histories of the divine Scriptures and consider the merits of God’s various elect, and when we bring before the eyes of our mind the zeal inspired in you by God, we find that in these days you, most excellent son and spiritual kinsman, have shone forth among the nations as a new Moses [Note: [Col. 1140D] Grets.: “among the nations”]. Moses received commands from the divine majesty so that he might rescue the Israelite people from the oppression of their afflicters [Col. 1140C]. You too, most excellent and distinguished king, have been divinely inspired to liberate the holy universal catholic and apostolic Church of God.

Through Moses, finally, the Lord delivered on Mount Sinai the commandments of the law to that Hebrew people for observance and illuminated them with the light of his splendor. Through you also our Redeemer, mediator of God and humanity, has granted peace to his Church and to the entire Christian people, redeemed by his precious blood, and has bestowed complete defense of the orthodox faith.

And just as Moses the lawgiver destroyed the abominations of the nations and the worship of demons, so you, most Christian of kings, have rejected the schism of heretics and the authors of impious doctrine. For this reason, by the light of divine grace and the oil of sanctification, you have rightly been recognized as anointed and numbered among the faithful kings who formerly pleased God. Therefore it is fitting to sing the Psalmist’s voice and praise of your excellence: “The Lord found you, most gracious king, faithful to him and keeping his commandments; therefore he anointed you with holy oil. And behold, his hand shall aid you, and his arm shall strengthen you” [Note: [Col. 1140D] The same: Psalm 88].

It is no wonder that so gracious a king has been adorned with so great a divine gift, for: “The Spirit, where he wills and in whom he wills, inspires” (John 3) those who shine with devout works, as your excellence is known to shine [Col. 1141A]. For although your most excellent Christian piety has often proclaimed how the love of your affection toward the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and toward our charity burns through your customary letters and messengers, nevertheless, through the words that you have now sent by the bearers of this letter, you have most fully revealed to us the affection of your fatherhood. You have signified, good and most excellent son, spiritual kinsman, and, after God, our defender and liberator, that you will remain with firm perseverance in love for that prince of the apostles and in charity toward us.

We are therefore confident in the promise of your unchanging word [Note: [Col. 1141D] Lambecus: “we exist”; Grets.: “we shall exist”]. For we know whom we have believed, and we are certain that everything will be accomplished according to your words, just as you affirm [Col. 1141B]. What, then, shall we be able to offer in return to your excellence? What reciprocity could we render for such great benefits, which your exalted and distinguished excellence has deigned to bestow upon the holy Church of God and the Christian faith, when our mind is urged day and night to offer praises of thanksgiving?

Rather, I marvel and am greatly astonished at how the loquacity of my mouth can express such great supports of benefits. Nevertheless, “I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm 115:13). With my eyes and outstretched palms often raised to heaven, I shall continually implore divine mercy for you, that he himself may look upon you from the throne of his majesty, cherish the height of your kingdom, grant you immense victories from heaven, deign to subject all barbarian peoples beneath your feet, and enlarge the boundaries of your royal power.

For we, most excellent son and spiritual kinsman, call upon God, the witness of truth, in whose hand is the heart of your excellence [Note: [Col. 1141D] Grets.: “is ruled”; Lambecus: “is corrected.” This should be emended, since, as we have often made known the purity of our heart, we remain in your love and charity just as we did between you and the lord and our brother, Stephen, of holy memory, etc.], that, just as it was often confirmed by our lord and brother, Stephen, the most holy pope of blessed memory, and through him with the holy Church of God, so we shall remain and shall continue to remain obedient to your wishes. Far be it from us ever to be separated from your love [Note: [Col. 1142D] Lambecus: “how”]. No gift of rewards, no kind of promise, and no persuasive flattery will be able, as we have often said, to tear us away from your charity [Col. 1141D].

But I ask, and as though present I beseech your honey-sweet excellence, most gracious of kings, to complete the exaltation already begun of your spiritual mother, the Church, and to command that you remain the firmest defender of the Christian faith [Note: [Col. 1142D] The same: “that you command”], so that from this time the memory of your name may be celebrated in the house of the Lord to the end of the world, and that through the intercession of the apostles you may receive both the prosperities of the present life and the joys of eternal blessedness.

Meanwhile, most excellent son and spiritual kinsman, since, inspired by God, you have deigned to grant us that monastery situated beside Mount Soracte [Note: [Col. 1142D] Grets.: “Soracte”], we offer immense and innumerable thanks to your exalted excellence. May the Lord be your retributor for this and grant you a worthy recompense of heavenly rewards in eternal blessedness.

We recognize that we have subjected that monastery to our own monastery for the praise of God, for the memory of you, and for eternal reward, because the blessed Silvester, illuminator of the Christian faith, whose holy body lies buried by us in our monastery, once dwelt there while fleeing the persecution of the pagans [Note: [Col. 1142D] Lambecus: “formerly”]. We therefore judged it fitting that it should be under his authority, since his revered body rests there.

Nevertheless, we absolutely do not wish to do anything concerning either this monastery or any other matter apart from your will; rather, we strive to act in every matter according to your wishes. Thus our spirit was made joyful, and we returned immense thanks to almighty God and to your excellence because, inspired by God, you deigned to hear our petition, most gracious king, and announced that the command of your royal eminence should be sent to our monastery, securing that holy dwelling firmly, now and in all past and future times.

Therefore we ask divine mercy that, just as you strive to confirm our monastery, established for the praise of God, so he may deign to confirm your kingdom over all nations. Let your most excellent Christian piety know for certain [Note: [Col. 1142D] The same: “let it believe”] that all those martyrs who shed their blood in confession of Christ’s name and rest in that holy monastery will be your most steadfast intercessors before divine mercy.

Concerning what you informed us—that you had been assured of our safety—we, good and most Christian king, confess ourselves safe in this respect: when the safety of your body and the health of your soul increase, with God’s help, your safety becomes our prosperity.

Having said this, may God, almighty creator and judge of all things, sustain you by his grace and grant that, with great victory, you may enjoy for a long and prosperous old age the scepters of royal power, together with your sweetest wife, your exalted daughter and our spiritual godmother, the lady Bertrada, most excellent queen, and your beloved sons and ours, the distinguished kings and patricians of the Romans, Lords Charles and Carloman, and also the most noble Lady Gisela; and may he grant you the joys of the heavenly kingdom to possess with the saints and elect throughout endless ages. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

### Letter IV

Likewise, a copy of the letter sent to Lord Pippin the king by the abbots Witmarus and Gerbertus and by Hugbaldus, containing praises of thanksgiving for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and asking that he should always strive toward this end.

[Col. 1143A]

[Note: [Col. 1143D] Grets.: Summary 24 in Baronius and the Centuriators.]

To the most excellent lord, his son and our spiritual kinsman, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans: Pope Paul.

While such an exceedingly great affection of love toward your excellence, inspired by God [Lambecius: “instituted by God”], persists within us, for this reason, just as thirsty earth longs for a rain-bearing inundation, so also we desire to learn tidings of your prosperity and to rejoice in your advancement. For herein lies the devotion of our heart to rejoice, [Col. 1143B] since, plainly, your safety is our security.

Meanwhile, we received with great affection the text of the two letters which your excellence sent: one, indeed, first conveyed by Peter, your first defensor, and the other by your present most faithful envoys, namely the abbots Widmar and Gerbert, and the illustrious man Hugbald. As we examined their pages, we immediately learned clearly everything written in them, at once rendering immense praises to our God, who has granted us to rejoice in your well-being.

Finally, in your own reports, the steadfastness of your mind, enlightened by God [Idem: “customary”], brought us the confident hope that you would do more earnestly what you have made known [Col. 1143C] and diligently demonstrated by your deeds: that you would contend with all your strength for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and the defense of the orthodox faith, and that you would remain in that pledge of faith which you made to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to our predecessor, lord and most blessed brother, Pope Stephen. Thus we have been firmly bound together in the connection of love.

Therefore, in accordance with what we sent while making our request [Idem: “the aforesaid”], you appear to have sent to us the aforesaid envoys, who were to stand before the king of the Lombards on behalf of the various causes and rights of the holy Church of God, and to assist us with their support. For this we return innumerable thanks to you, because, truly, as a kind king and lover of your spiritual mother, the holy Church of God, you always strive to act, most Christian son and spiritual co-father; and assuredly the Lord will be for you, both in the present and in the future, a worthy recompensor.

Therefore, most excellent son protected by God, and spiritual co-father, may we remain steadfast in the love of your charity; nor is there any circumstance of affairs or times that could separate us from your charity, because you truly stand, after God, as our defender and helper. The aforesaid envoys of yours [Idem: “the aforesaid”], finally, standing in our presence together with the envoys of the Lombards, as well as those of Gentapolus and the men of each of our cities, had proof established before them concerning certain rights existing between the two parties—namely, concerning property restored between the parties.

For concerning the boundaries of our cities and the patrimonies of blessed Peter, retained and invaded by those same Lombards, nothing has yet been done; indeed, they have again invaded even those things which they had first restored. Accordingly, it was decided that our envoys and the envoys of each of our cities should proceed with your envoys to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, so that, in the presence of those men and of the aforesaid king, proof might be established concerning those same boundaries and patrimonies, and everything might be restored to us according to the agreement [Idem: “according to the terms of the pact”]. We do not know what will result from this; nevertheless, through your aforesaid envoys [Lambecius: “the aforementioned envoys”], you can recognize the merit of the matter.

Therefore, we ask your excellence, protected by God, to order matters in such a way that we may be able to receive complete justice in everything, so that the same blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, for the restoration of whose lights you are contending, may be your most steadfast helper and best remunerator. For let your most excellent Christian character know with certainty that, if the boundaries of our cities invaded by those same Lombards and the patrimonies are not restored to us, they will also plot to invade those things which they first restored.

Therefore, we earnestly ask your Christian character to arrange, according to your customary policy, that the exaltation of the holy Church of God and the safety of this province, redeemed by you through God’s power, may advance [Col. 1144C], and that, after your envoys reported to us more clearly everything which they had been charged by your pre-eminent excellence to undertake [Idem: “indeed, that you should order arrangements to be made, as is customary, for those very things to be restored to us at our requests, so that your customary …”], we gave them an answer point by point and instructed them concerning everything which they ought to report to your excellence, and which they should strive to make known to your ears as our requests.

With these matters thus set forth, we beseech the mercy of our almighty God to grant that he may cherish you with his grace and allow you, in the present temporal kingdom, to enjoy a long old age [Note: “And the present temporal kingdom in a long old age”], with bodily prosperity and health of soul, together with your sweetest wife, your most excellent queen, daughter and our spiritual co-mother, and your most pre-eminent offspring; and may he grant you also, throughout endless ages, the joys of heavenly rewards to possess. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

## LETTER V

Likewise, a copy of the letter to the lord King Pippin, sent through Abbot Haribert and Count Dodo, containing the richest blessings and praises of thanksgiving for the firm and unchangeable word of his promise and his great perseverance in bringing the apostolic causes to completion.

[Note: Grets., Summary 23, in Baronius and the Centuriators.]

To the most excellent son and our spiritual co-father, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

I cannot express in words, nor can the abundance of speech wholly encompass, most excellent and truly, above all kings, most Christian and orthodox of kings, how deeply the affection of our heart rejoices in your merits and in your pious zeal for good works. For, plainly, through the protection of your struggle and your laborious endeavor, your holy catholic and apostolic universal spiritual mother, the Church of God, and the orthodox faith of Christians stand rescued from the attacks of their rivals; and for this reason praises are continually rendered to our Redeemer, the Lord God, by all Christian people, because of the assistance of such a great benefit which you have supplied.

Therefore, most Christian son and spiritual co-father, the minds of all the faithful rightly consider you a sharer in all things with that illustrious and pre-eminent king David and distinguished prophet in the heavenly kingdoms, because your Christianity is recognized to equal him not only in the insignia of honor but also in deeds, as the action itself demonstrates. For when the ark of the Lord had been recovered from the Philistines, he rejoiced and delighted in hymns and spiritual songs, with the playing of the psaltery. You too, in joyful gladness, strive to offer to our almighty Lord God the foundation and head of all Christians, the holy Roman Church, which you are redeeming, together with the entire people subject to it. Your goodness yearns to bring to completion such a pious work, and you may believe that, for it, you will obtain the reward of recompense already stored up for you in the heavenly citadels [Col. 1145C].

For the most diligent men who have hastened to you—namely, Abbot Haribert and Count Dodo, your most faithful envoys to your excellence—have brought us honey-sweet and most desirable words sent by your illustrious Christianity. In them you carefully endeavored to assure us of your firm and unchangeable word of promise and of the steadfastness of your great perseverance, which you appear to be displaying in bringing the apostolic causes to completion. We are firmly and wholly confident in your benign purpose that you will remain steadfast to the end and act with still greater perfection, just as you promised to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to our predecessor, lord and most blessed brother, Pope Stephen.

Meanwhile, it was also conveyed in those same letters of yours that, although you had wished us to learn through your present envoys what you desired from your side, you did not wish that this should be disclosed in writing. Instead, after informing your aforesaid envoys about the merits of each matter, which ought to be made known to our ears [Lambecius: “the aforesaid … which ought to be made known to our ears, etc.”], they acted exactly as you had instructed them. We, for our part, gave them a clearer account of each matter concerning which they had spoken to us, and explained how they should report our life, instituted by God, to your royal power [Col. 1146A].

Moreover, we have sent our present envoys—namely, John the subdeacon and abbot, and Peter, our first defensor—together with them to your royal presence [Note: “summits”]. We ask that you kindly receive them in your customary manner and order them to believe everything in all respects that they report to you from our instruction [Lambecius: “order them to believe; and likewise order them to arrange the affairs of the holy Church of God, as we have great confidence in you after God, so that…”], so that the complete liberation and exaltation of the holy Church of God and the advancement of the orthodox faith may be achieved, and so that you may deservedly attain in heaven the crown of the reward stored up for you.

Now may almighty God, who dwells on high and looks upon the lowly, who encloses the whole world within the span of his hand, in whose hand lies all the authority of kingdoms, protect you with his grace and grant you victories from heaven, subjecting to your royal eminence all nations that oppose you [Col. 1146B]. May he cause you to possess the government of the kingdom through enduring and prosperous times, together with your most excellent daughter and our spiritual co-mother, the most gracious queen, your sweetest wife, and your beloved children Charles and Carloman, most excellent kings, and the most noble and excellent Gisla, our spiritual daughter; and may he grant you eternal life to possess throughout endless ages. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

## LETTER VI

Likewise, a copy of the letter of the same pope to the lord King Pippin, sent through Bishop Wilharius, Dodo, and Wichard, containing thanksgiving, the steadfastness of that pope’s faith, and the declaration that no favor or terror could in any way separate him from his love or charity.

[Note: Grets., Summary 21, in Baronius and the Centuriators.]

To the most excellent son and our spiritual co-father, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

No human speech, as I think, will suffice to render thanks to your illustrious and most gracious excellence for the great protection of benefit which you have bestowed upon the holy Church of God and the Roman people. Nor can the rewards of this world worthily be repaid to you for these things. Nevertheless, there is one, sole, and true God, existing in three substances [Idem: “persons”], who can grant and repay your excellence the rightful joys of the kingdom [Lambecius: “of the heavenly kingdom”] and the triumph of victory.

Meanwhile, when the most reverend brother and fellow bishop Wilharius, together with Dodo and Wichard [Grets.: Wulchard], your most faithful envoys, hastened to us, they presented us with honey-sweet and most desirable letters sent by your most Christian excellence. As we looked upon them, immediately, having learned of the prosperity of your excellence, the inward organs of our heart overflowed with the customary joyful delight of exultation, while we continually implored our Creator and Redeemer, the Lord God, to grant that we might long and diligently rejoice in your ever-greater happiness and in the victories over your enemies granted to you from heaven.

But, most excellent son and spiritual co-father, through those same honey-sweet and honorable words of yours [Editor: “perhaps ‘honey-sweet and …,’ etc.”] you gave us the most certain confidence of your customary promise: that you would contend with firm perseverance for the defense of the holy Church of God, of the entire Roman people, and of the whole province, in accordance with what you promised to blessed Peter and to his vicar, our predecessor, my lord and brother of holy memory, Pope Stephen, and that you would remain in that faith of your pledge. And indeed, good and most Christian king instituted by God, this gives us great confidence in the matter of believing [Grets.: “gives confidence to us”]. For the minds of the faithful cannot judge otherwise than according to what we repeatedly see you carrying out with pious intent and have learned through the experience of events.

But now, most powerful of kings, behold the opportunity; behold, the days of necessity and the advancing time compel your Christianity to act as quickly as possible [Col. 1147B]. For we have no confidence elsewhere, after God, his holy and glorious Mother, and his most sacred apostles, except in your illustrious excellence. You, most Christian one, are our refuge after God; you, with God’s arm, are our firm assistance; and the security of your kingdom, strengthened by God, is our immense joy. Thus both we and our entire people of this province—may the divine majesty satisfy you—shall remain firm and immovable in your charity and affection, and constant in our love for your kingdom of the Franks, protected by God. No human favor or terror [Idem: “favor or terror”] will be able to separate us from the sweetness of your love [Col. 1147C] and the affection of charity; rather, life and death alike shall be ours in your love [Idem: “our life in your love”].

Since you made known that you had sent your present envoys for this purpose, wishing to learn through them whether full justice had been done to us by the Lombard side or not, they themselves have learned the entire substance of the matter. They have recognized the crafty cunning and customary deceitful statement of those same rivals of yours and ours; and, when they return to you, God willing, they will disclose these things to your ears.

When they reported to us one by one everything which they had been charged by you to undertake, we gave a response to each matter and placed in their mouths the things which they should bring before your excellence, desiring by this means to obtain the desired outcome from your excellence.

May almighty God deign to look from the throne of his majesty upon you, your kingdom, your beloved wife, the exalted queen who is also our spiritual co-mother, and your sweetest natural children, who are our spiritual sons, as well as upon the entire people of the Franks. May he extend over you the right hand of his arm, grant you victories from heaven, cast all your adversaries down before your face, and grant you the present life in a long old age and future blessedness to possess eternally. May God keep you unharmed, most excellent son.

## LETTER VII

Likewise, a copy of the letter of the same pope to the lord King Pippin, sent through Flavinus the chaplain, John the subdeacon and abbot, and Pamphilus, regional defensor of the holy Church [Lambecius: “sent”], containing thanksgiving for those envoys and describing how they, together with the imperial envoys, were honorably received, and so forth.

[Note: Grets., Summary in Baronius and the Centuriators.]
