Through them, most excellent and most eminent sons, you made known that you would always remain in love toward the blessed Peter, your spiritual mother, the holy Church of God, and us, and that you would contend courageously for the defense of that holy Church of God and of the orthodox faith.

Indeed, good and most excellent kings, we have complete confidence in such steadfastness of yours, placing great hope in you after God. But may the almighty Lord, who is rich in mercies, bring you to full maturity, granting you long and happy times; may he strengthen in you the power of his arm; may he make you victorious over all barbarian nations; may he enlarge the boundaries of your kingdom; and may he permit the offspring of your illustrious seed to sit upon the royal throne of your power to the end of the age, for the eternal exaltation of his universal holy Church and the defense of the orthodox faith.

But I ask, most excellent sons, that you become imitators of your most Christian father and, following his footsteps that are pleasing to God, strive to complete the good work that you have begun and to contend manfully with him, so that the most ample exaltation of the holy Church of God may be secured; and, once blessed Peter has recovered his rights through your aid, may you receive from this, before God and his angels, through the intervention of blessed Peter, that same prince of the apostles, the reward of heavenly prizes, and may the memory of your name remain praiseworthy, proclaimed throughout all ages. [Col. 1175B] [Note: [Col. 1175C] In Lamb.: “may your praiseworthy fame remain.”]

Now may almighty God, who by the word of his power established all things from nothing, make you adhere to his divine commandments, direct your endeavors according to his good pleasure, grant you the skill of prudence by which you may be able to govern the height of your kingdom, subject the nations of hostile peoples beneath your feet, and, just as in the present life he has granted you royal dignity, so also bestow upon you the joys of heavenly rewards.

## EPISTLE XXIII

Likewise, a copy of a letter of the same pope addressed to the lords Charles and Carloman, kings, containing thanksgivings and very abundant blessings.

To the most excellent lords, Charles and Carloman, sons, kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, Pope Paul.

Having received the report sent by Your Excellence, brought by the bearers of this letter—namely Droctegand and the religious abbots—we have been refreshed by the welcome news of your safety. We pray that the Lord, in his mercy, may both protect and direct your life and deeds, and bring you to full maturity.

Through those same words you made known that you felt the greatest embarrassment because meanwhile you had been unable to send us the benefit of gifts through the bearers of this letter. But what is it, sweetest and most beloved sons, most victorious kings, that makes you long to gladden us with your gifts? For we desire no other gifts than diligently to learn of the prosperity of your safety and to rejoice in your progress. This is our enrichment: your joyful exultation, which we eagerly embrace. [Note: [Col. 1175C] Grets. and Lamb.: “the joy of your exultation, which we eagerly embrace. This is.”] This is the exaltation of the holy Church of God, and the integrity of your protection is the defense of the orthodox faith. For the Lord has chosen you above all kings, established you as liberators of his holy catholic and apostolic Church, and deigned to anoint you kings through the hands of blessed Peter.

But may almighty God, through whom kings reign, bring you to full maturity, and grant that the throne of the kingdom be possessed by you and your illustrious offspring through prosperous ages, for the exaltation of his holy Church and the most ample defense of the orthodox faith of Christians. May he grant you victories from heaven, subjecting all barbarian nations beneath your God-imitating feet, and may he deign to bestow the joys of eternal life, so that, just as you reign in the present life, you may also deserve to reign with Christ in the age to come. And may all the people say: [Col. 1176C] [Note: [Col. 1176C] Grets.: “in Psalm 105.”] Amen, let it be, let it be. Farewell in good health.

# COLLECTION OF THE LETTERS OF PAUL FROM LABBE

## EPISTLE I

Of Paul, elected Pope I, to King Pippin. [Note: [Col. 1175D] These letters, like the preceding ones, were first transferred in their entirety by me into this collection; they were taken by Labbe from the Codex Carolinus and ought to have been given in their order. But, for the printers’ convenience, so that they would not be compelled so often to lay aside Labbe and take him up again, at the risk of error (for I am far from the place of publication), I decided to give them here in one continuous series with the others added by Labbe. MANSI.] Written concerning his election to the pontificate, before his consecration. He promises that he and his people will remain in the faith and concord that his predecessor Stephen had pledged to King Pippin.

[Col. 1175D]

To the most excellent lord, Pippin, son, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Paul the deacon, and, in God’s name, elected to the holy apostolic see.

With heavy sighing and immense sorrow of heart, we make known to Your Excellence, most powerful victorious king protected by God, that the lord and my brother Stephen, a pope of holy memory, has been taken from this light by God’s summons to eternal rest. At his departure even the stones themselves, if one may say so, wept tears along with us. In the order of his apostolate my misery has been chosen by the whole multitude of the peoples.

While these things were taking place, Immo, the envoy of Your Most Christian Excellence, came to Rome. After speaking with him, together with our nobles, we judged it appropriate to detain him here until, by God’s providence, we had been enlightened by the sacred apostolic blessing. Then, once he had been fully satisfied concerning the purity and affection of myself and the entire people that we bear toward Your most gracious Excellence and the whole Frankish nation, we would release him to return to you with our apostolic envoys.

For you should know with certainty, most excellent and God-protected king, our helper and defender after God, that we, remaining firm and steadfast unto our soul and the shedding of our blood in that faith, affection, concord of charity, and covenant of peace which the aforesaid lord of most blessed memory, my brother and most holy pontiff, confirmed with you, shall remain with our people to the end.

Therefore, with hands continually extended toward heaven, we beseech the clemency of our Lord God for the safety of Your Excellence, for the health of your sweetest sons and of the most excellent queen, asking that your aid and firmest protection may always be extended over us. May heavenly grace preserve Your Excellence unharmed.

## EPISTLE II

To King Pippin. Among other matters, he accuses King Desiderius of not restoring the cities promised to the Roman Church, and asks Pippin to compel him to return them. He also asks Pippin not to put faith in another letter that he had written, at Desiderius’s urging, concerning the release of his hostages.

[Col. 1177B]

To the most excellent lord, Pippin, son and our spiritual kinsman, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

Whenever, contemplating the evident merits of Your Excellency with mystical reflection and considering them with the eyes of my heart, I bring them together, I am compelled to marvel greatly at the unblemished and extraordinary steadfastness of your mind, and at the most fervent affection that you continually display toward the love of God and toward his prince of the apostles, since you strive to favor God more than human beings.

Hence it is clear that, through pious actions, you surpass all kings and powerful men, because, having assumed a heavenly triumph, you voluntarily devoted yourself, most excellent son and spiritual kinsman, to liberating the Church of God. Therefore, so that the contest of your pious undertaking may be brought to fulfillment, it is fitting that we frequently send apostolic letters to you, as the liberator of this holy Church of God and of its peculiar people.

First of all, nothing is more nectar-sweet and desirable to us than to learn of the joys of Your Prosperity. Then, as quickly as possible, we must make known whatever things are necessary for the holy Church of God and for us, so that you may recognize, most excellent son and our spiritual kinsman, that not long ago the apostolic letters informed Your Excellence of what has been impiously done and cruelly perpetrated in these regions by Desiderius, king of the Lombards.

Accordingly, when we saw how pernicious his conduct was, we judged it appropriate to detain here your most faithful envoy, Rodbert, so that, seeing and learning firsthand what the malice of the aforesaid King Desiderius and of the Lombard people had already begun to produce, he might make Your Exalted Excellence more fully informed.

For, just as before, so now we make known to Your Excellence, preserved by God, that the aforesaid king of the Lombards, passing through the cities of the Pentapolis which you bestowed upon blessed Peter as a great ransom for your soul, consumed with sword and fire all the crops and everything pertaining to human sustenance. In the same way he laid waste, to the great contempt of your kingdom, Spoleto and Benevento, which had placed themselves under the power preserved for you by God, and devastated the places and cities of those duchies with sword and fire.

He has seized Albinus, duke of Spoleto, and with him the nobles who had given an oath of allegiance to blessed Peter and to you; after inflicting dreadful wounds upon them, he keeps them in chains.

When he was approaching Benevento, the Beneventan duke immediately fled to the city of Otranto. When Desiderius was pressing him to leave that city, he in no way accomplished his purpose; instead, he appointed another duke in that same duchy of Benevento, named Arigis.

Immediately afterward, King Desiderius sent to Naples and summoned George, the imperial envoy who had been sent to you in Francia. He spoke secretly with him, entered into a plan with him, and sent letters to the emperor, urging him to dispatch his imperial armies into this province of Italy.

Desiderius himself, together with the entire Lombard people, declared that, although God was opposed to him, he would lend assistance to the aforesaid imperial armies, so that, with one army attacking on one side and Desiderius himself with the whole Lombard people fighting on the other, they might seize the city of Ravenna, and the emperor might accomplish—may the Lord prevent it—whatever he wished.

He also arranged with the same imperial envoy George that the Sicilian fleet of dromons should be sent to the city of Otranto, so that Greeks and Lombards, besieging it together, might seize that city and grant it to the emperor with the people and resources contained in it, while returning only that duke and his tutor John to the aforesaid king.

After the dissolution of those duchies, the same king of the Lombards came here to us at Rome. In conversation with him, we earnestly exhorted him and adjured him forcefully, by the most sacred body of blessed Peter and also by Your Excellence, protected by God, to restore the cities—namely Imola, Bologna, Osimo, and Ancona—which he had promised in our presence, through your envoys, the abbot Folrad, beloved of God, and Rodbert, to Your Most Christian Excellence and, through you, to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

He was by no means inclined to agree. Instead, pretending—as a true trickster would—to comply, he produced various excuses, saying that if he received the hostages whom Francia appears to hold there, he would then maintain peaceful concord with us.

Therefore we ask you, most excellent son and spiritual kinsman, and earnestly beseech your Excellence, inspired by God, to order the complete liberation of the holy Church of God and of its peculiar people, and to remain firm in what you promised to blessed Peter as a great ransom for your soul. Deign to constrain Desiderius, king of the Lombards, so that he may restore and fulfill in every respect for blessed Peter, your protector, the promise solemnly made before God.

Let it be your concern, good and most powerful king, to rescue this holy Church of God and its peculiar people from the attacks of their enemies more completely, just as you have begun, so that, with God’s approval, the contest of your gracious undertaking may bear abundant fruit. Thus, on the day of the coming of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, may you shine like the most radiant sun among all kings and powerful men, and may you deserve to offer to the divine Majesty that holy Church of God and its people, rescued through your aid, without any violence of injury; then may you receive a hundredfold reward from that same Lord God, our judge, and possess eternal life.

I adjure you, most excellent son, by almighty God and by his prince of the apostles, blessed Peter, to order that our prayers be heard with a gracious regard and a most willing heart, so that almighty God may incline the ears of his divinity to you in the matters for which you implore his power, and make you victorious over all barbarian nations.

For absolutely all the peoples who dwell upon the face of the whole earth know of the struggle that you have undertaken for the defense of the holy Church of God, and they laudably proclaim you a great and foremost king.

We also do not cease to extend and spread your good reputation far and wide, since, after God, we place your most steadfast faith in our breast like an impregnable wall, possessing great confidence of hope in you after the protection of God. Indeed, on account of the merit of your spotless promise and faith, we expect frequently to obtain this.

Accordingly, we have urgently sent our envoys—namely our most reverend and most holy brother and fellow bishop George, and our beloved son Stephen the priest—to Your Excellence, protected by God. When they have been presented to your God-pleasing footsteps together with Rodbert, your most faithful envoy, they will report orally to Your Most Christian Excellence everything that has been done and whatever the merit of the matter requires, as well as what is necessary for us.

Our spirit was breathing with the greatest desire to send apostolic letters of greeting and visitation to Your Excellence, to report the course of events; but we were entirely unable to do so because of the Lombard king’s plots, which threaten us on every side.

Nevertheless, behold, we have already secretly sent Your Excellence two declarations in apostolic letters, with the greatest care, and we do not know whether those letters have reached you. Hence we fear that they may be intercepted by the Lombards.

For this reason we have now sent you, through our aforementioned envoys, another letter, as though complying with the will of the aforesaid King Desiderius, for the release of his hostages and the confirmation of peace.

But, good and most excellent son and spiritual kinsman, we wrote this letter in such a form so that our envoys might be able to travel across to you in Francia. For if we had not done this, they would have been entirely unable to cross the Lombard territories.

Therefore, once you have received the letter, do not in any way carry out its contents, nor permit the aforesaid hostages to be returned to the Lombard side. Rather, we adjure you, most excellent son and spiritual kinsman, by the living God and the body of blessed Peter, to order that Desiderius himself, or his Lombard people, be strongly constrained, so that he may return to Your Honey-sweet Excellence, and through you to blessed Peter, your patron, the cities that he promised.

For, as stated above, we have been unable to establish any firm agreement with him concerning the things that he first promised.

We pray almighty God that, with a gracious regard, he may look down from the throne of his Majesty upon you and your kingdom, surround Your Excellence with his right hand, fortify you in all things, and permit you to complete the course of this present life healthfully and to govern the power of your kingdom for many years, together with your most excellent daughter, protected by God, our spiritual kinswoman, and your and my most beloved sons.

May you rejoice in their flowering offspring. May almighty God grant that your most splendid seed enjoy the same height of royal power to the end of the world, and may he grant you infinite joys in the age to come with his saints and elect, so that, having obtained in the present life and in future blessedness the crown of the reward promised to you, you may deserve to reign with Christ. May heavenly grace preserve Your Excellence unharmed.

## EMBOLUM

As a token of true blessing, we have sent you one *appallatea* [uncertain reading: perhaps a type of cloak], a sword set with gems, with its belt; one ring containing a hyacinth; and one purple cloak bearing peacocks. We ask that you order this small blessing to be received without taking offense. To the lords Charles and Carloman, in token of the great apostolic blessing, individual rings containing hyacinths.

## EPISTLE III

To King Pippin. He praises Pippin and gives thanks because, when the envoys—his brother Remigius and the duke Autharius—were approaching, King Desiderius restored part of the cities and patrimonies of the Church, and declared that he would return the remaining part at a fixed time.

[Col. 1180D]

To the most excellent lord, Pippin, son and our spiritual kinsman, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

Since Your Excellence has been approved before the heavenly tribunal by the merit of good works, this has now been demonstrated openly by the actual results of the deeds that have been performed.

## EPISTLE IV

To King Pippin. He again complains about King Desiderius, because he did not provide the complete restoration promised to the envoys, and about the threatening letters that he had written. He asks Pippin to send three envoys for the sake of the Church.

To the most excellent lord, Pippin, son and our spiritual kinsman, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

[Col. 1181A]

Through these apostolic words, good and most powerful king, most excellent son and spiritual kinsman, we strive to make known to Your Excellence, instituted by God, as our liberator after God, whatever comes to our knowledge from the various regions.

Let Your Excellence know that certain most sincere faithful men of your spiritual mother, our holy Church, have informed us that six patricians, bringing with them three hundred ships and likewise the Sicilian fleet, have been released from the royal city and are hastening toward us in this Roman city.

What they intend to do, or for what purpose they have been sent, we do not know the truth. We have been told only that they are resolved to proceed to us and to enter Francia to reach Your Highly Praiseworthy Excellence. We have sent to Your Excellence, below this writing, the letters addressed to us, so that you may examine them.

We also make this known to Your Excellence for its preservation: when, in the presence of your envoys, it had been agreed with Desiderius, king of the Lombards, that we should first receive in full our Roman rights from all the Lombard cities and afterward, in return, should grant the Lombards their full rights from all our cities, we relied upon this promise that he made in the presence of your aforesaid envoys and sent our own envoys to receive and grant these rights.

But he, employing various crafty excuses, was in no way willing first to grant us in full, as had been agreed, the rights that we demand from all his cities, and then to receive his own in full from all our cities. Instead, he preferred to grant them piecemeal—something from one city and then receive something from another—wishing by this means to cause delay, so that our Roman side might not obtain its rightful due.

And behold, our envoys, having obtained nothing, returned to us without result. From that time onward he has inflicted numerous depredations and many unheard-of evils upon our territories.

Therefore, behold, he immediately sent his letters, in which, trusting in his ferocity, having no fear of God before his eyes and not fearing blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he sent us threats and uttered empty words of slander.

We have now sent these letters, below the text of this writing, to your splendid and God-established eminence, so that, when Your Exalted Excellence recognizes their contents, you may consider how great are his wickedness and the proud arrogance of his heart, since he rises up against blessed Peter and your royal power and threatens to inflict evils upon us.

But after God, we place our hope, like an impregnable wall, most firmly in Your Excellence, strengthened by God. Therefore, with bent knee, we ask—and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, also appeals through us to Your Exalted Excellence—that, inspired by almighty God, who has established you as defender and liberator of his holy Church, you order that our safety be most fully secured and that you continue to be our accustomed helper and protector against the ferocity and arrogance of all our enemies.

Thus, through the intercession of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, may you deserve to obtain a most profitable reward from our Redeemer, the Lord God; and, just as you may obtain an earthly kingdom, so may you also deserve to obtain a heavenly kingdom with the saints and elect of God throughout endless ages.

We have instructed your most faithful vassal Conibert to report everything to your royal power in a detailed account, more clearly.

We also earnestly ask Your Gracious Excellence to send us suitable envoys, such as you may choose, who will be found here to assist us. One of them, however, should hasten to Ticinum, so that, after speaking with King Desiderius, he may report to Your Excellence whatever reply he gives.

The other two should hasten to join us according to your arrangement and direction, so that, as stated, they may remain here to assist us. May heavenly grace preserve Your Excellence unharmed.

## EPISTLE V

To King Pippin. Concerning the sacred table donated by King Pippin to Pope Stephen: by what rite it was offered at Rome by Pippin’s envoys at the confession of blessed Peter, and how it was received and consecrated by Pope Paul.

To the most excellent lord, Pippin, son and our spiritual kinsman, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

We received with the greatest effort of honor and affection the letters sent by Your Illustrious Excellence, brought by Andrew and Gunderic, most diligent men and envoys of Your Christian Majesty.

And afterward: In the meantime, most excellent, gracious, and most Christian king, son and spiritual kinsman, we received that table which you formerly offered to the lord of holy memory, our most blessed brother, Pope Stephen, and through him to the apostle blessed Peter.

With hymns and spiritual songs, solemnly offering praises to God in the litany, we brought it inside the hall of that same prince of the apostles. Your envoys offered it in your name at the sacred confessio, namely over the body of that same gatekeeper of heaven.

After sanctifying it with the chrism of anointing and placing the sacred oblation upon it, we offered a sacrifice of praise to almighty God for the eternal reward of your soul and the stability of your kingdom. By apostolic judgment, with the imposition of an anathema, we decreed that no one should ever be permitted to alienate it from the Church of blessed Peter.

And behold, your memorial remains shining forever in that apostolic hall. Believe that you will obtain its reward from the just-rewarding Lord God and from blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in the heavenly kingdoms.

Regarding George and Peter, we have understood everything that you made known. But we leave it to your will to deal with them as you please, whether by keeping them with you or by releasing them to us, since whatever pleases you appears entirely suitable and favorable to us.

Finally, your aforesaid envoys reported to us in detail everything that you had instructed them to convey. We gave them answers concerning each matter and released them, fully instructed, to report everything to you.

May almighty God, who is rich in mercy, protect you continually with the arm of his power extended in defense, subject all adversaries and rebels beneath your royal feet, and grant you to possess the government of the kingdom for a long and healthy time, together with your most excellent daughter and our spiritual kinswoman, the most gracious queen, and your and my most beloved sons, Charles and Carloman, most excellent kings and patricians of the Romans, and Gisila, most noble, and to enjoy eternal joys with the saints and elect. May heavenly grace preserve Your Excellence unharmed.

## EPISTLE VI

To King Pippin. He gives thanks for the *sabanum* sent to him, in which Pippin’s daughter had been received after being washed in the sacred waters, and explains how he received it.

To the most excellent lord, Pippin, son and our spiritual kinsman, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

The bearer of this letter, the most diligent Vulfardus, Your Excellence’s most faithful servant, brought us a letter full of joy. We received it with immense happiness, opened it for reading, and were restored with great exultation, recognizing through it the splendid affection of Your Excellence toward the holy apostolic Roman Church and toward your patron, the gatekeeper of the kingdom of heaven, the blessed prince of the apostles Peter.

For this reason we render more effective and continual thanks to almighty God, since in these days he has bestowed upon his holy Church so eminent and mighty a protector.

Meanwhile, most Christian victorious king, by God’s providence, we have celebrated with a twofold joy of festivity, in that we have attained the desires longed for by our heart and have likewise been joined together in the bond of spiritual alliance.

The aforesaid illustrious envoy of your fellowship brought us the most precious gift of heavenly grace, namely the *sabanum* [Note: [Col. 1183D] That is, the *sabanum*. In the same matter, Victor of Utica, Book III, concerning the deacon Mirita and the apostate Epidophorus: “Secretly, perhaps, unknown to everyone, he was carrying that cloth with which, when he received him from the font, he had earlier covered him. ‘These,’ he said, ‘are the linens, Epidophorus, that will accuse you when the Majesty of the Judge comes.’ Sirmond.] in which our sweetest and most beloved spiritual daughter was washed and received in the most sacred bath.

With great joy, having gathered a company of the people, we received it while celebrating the solemn rites of Mass inside the hall of the sacred body of your helper, the blessed Petronilla, which is now known to have been dedicated for the eternal praise of your name. Through the *sabanum* that was brought, we rejoice as though we had received her in person.

Therefore, because the love of faith has kindled your gracious heart to be joined to us through the bond of spiritual alliance, according to what you promised to the lord and my brother, Pope Stephen of blessed memory and most holy, we render great acts of thanksgiving to Your Excellence, protected by God. We frequently implore divine mercy that, preserving and protecting you upon the throne of your kingdom through prosperous ages, it may permit you to rejoice with great happiness in the full maturity of this spiritual daughter of ours, for the exaltation of his holy Church.

And because the abundant authority of that grace of the Holy Spirit—namely, spiritual kinship, which by God’s help stands confirmed between us—has given us confidence, I ask and beseech you, most gracious spiritual kinsman and excellent king, to order that the good work of the redemption of God’s Church and of the full restoration of blessed Peter’s rights be completed.

Your distinguished goodness has made known to us through your words that you wished to learn the outcome of the causes brought against us. Therefore we make Your Excellence, protected by God, certain that up to now we have received nothing of what we instructed your Excellence to request through our envoys.

For those faithless and malicious men, persisting in great arrogance of heart, are by no means inclined to restore the rights of blessed Peter. Yet your envoys can learn how everything has been conducted by reporting it to you; and we have sent our subsequent envoy to you, bearing worthy thanks to Your Excellence for everything, and through him we send you answers concerning all that may happen hereafter.

As for Archbishop Sergius, we continually press the matter, according to what Your Excellence has been informed, so that he may be restored to his Church.

We ask Your Excellent Goodness to order that our most reverend and holy brother and fellow bishop Vulcharius be held commended in all things, just as the aforesaid lord and my brother, the most holy Pope Stephen of blessed memory, commended him to Your Gracious Excellence.

With these matters set forth, may our three-in-one God protect you with his extended right hand, together with your sweetest wife, the most excellent queen and our spiritual kinswoman, and your and my most beloved sons, preserving you safely upon the throne of the kingdom; and in the present life and in eternal blessedness may he grant you to prosper abundantly. May heavenly grace preserve Your Excellence unharmed.

## EPISTLE VII

To King Pippin. He asks for aid against the Greeks, who were reported to be preparing to attack Ravenna, and asks him also to stir up King Desiderius and others to provide assistance.

[Col. 1184D]

To the most excellent lord, Pippin, son and our spiritual kinsman, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

Through these apostolic words we make known to Your Exalted Christian Majesty, preserved by God, that, after your envoys who had recently joined us had been released—namely Vulcharius, our most holy brother and fellow bishop, Felix the religious man, and Ratbert, an illustrious man—an envoy from the faithful of the holy Church of God, your spiritual mother, joined us. These faithful are accustomed always to report the truth to us, and he informed us that the wicked Greeks, enemies of the holy Church of God and attackers of the orthodox faith, with God opposed to them, desire to invade us and the territory of Ravenna and are making preparations.

Since, after God and blessed Peter, our hope lies nowhere else than with Your Most Noble Excellence, we therefore ask you with earnest supplications, most excellent son and spiritual kinsman, to order, for God’s sake and out of reverence for blessed Peter, that the safety of this province, redeemed by you, be secured. Deign immediately to send your envoy to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, so that, if the need is reported, he may provide us assistance against the attack of those same enemies.

Command the Beneventans, the Spoletans, and the Tuscans who dwell nearby to come to our aid.

We also beseech Your Excellence, instituted by God, to order that your envoy be sent to us when the coming month of March arrives. He should remain here at Rome with us, so that, if necessity demands, he may press King Desiderius to send us the same assistance.

For, as Your Excellence has been fully informed, those most wicked Greeks persecute us for no other reason than the holy and orthodox faith and the pious, venerable tradition of the Fathers, which they desire to destroy and trample underfoot.

Therefore, may Your Accustomed Goodness order that the madness of those same enemies be reduced to nothing, and that this province, more completely redeemed through your struggle and granted by you to blessed Peter for the remedy of your soul, remain secure from the plots of its adversaries through your customary protection.

May abundant reward be recorded for you in heaven, and may the praise of your name and the exaltation of the whole nation—just as has already happened—be proclaimed now much more widely throughout the entire world. May the Lord, through the intercession of blessed Peter, grant you from heaven the triumph of victory over all nations, while, through your aid, the attackers of the holy orthodox faith are confounded, and peace, joy, and observance of the Christian faith are proclaimed in all the Churches. On account of this, may heavenly joys rightly be bestowed upon you by God. May heavenly grace preserve Your Excellence unharmed.

## EPISTLE VIII

To Charles and Carloman, sons of King Pippin. He praises them and exhorts them to follow in the footsteps of their parents in guarding the defense of the Church.

To the most noble and excellent lords, Charles and Carloman, sons, kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, Pope Paul.

Once, almighty God, seeing the lamentation of his Israelite people and the impious oppression inflicted by the Egyptians, took pity on them and sent his servant Moses, through whom he performed signs and wonders, rescued that same people, and, instructing them through him in the law, led them to the rest they desired. Joshua too was joined to him, to wage the Lord’s wars; and he granted them other helpers, worshipers of his divine name. Yet in all these men his divine majesty was not so well pleased as in King David, of whom he says: “I have anointed my servant, according to my heart, with holy oil” (Psalm 88); and to him and to his offspring he gloriously granted a kingdom to possess forever.

Thus, most excellent and most noble sons, kings instituted by God, our same Lord God has been pleased with your most Christian excellence; sanctifying you in your mother’s womb, he raised you to so great a royal summit, sending his apostle, blessed Peter, through his vicar, and anointing you and your most excellent father with holy oil. He filled you with heavenly blessings and entrusted to you his holy catholic and apostolic Church, and the orthodox faith of Christians, to exalt and defend manfully.

This, most excellent sons, you have resolved to accomplish with all your strength, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit and aided by heavenly protection. Through your assistance and struggle, that same holy Church of God, your spiritual mother, liberated from the snares of her enemies, rejoices in the Lord Jesus Christ; your pious works shine forth in the sight of the divine majesty; and, together with Kings David and Solomon and the other worshipers of God, your names have been enrolled in the heavenly kingdoms. [Col. 1186B]

Meanwhile, while we recognize that we have been relieved by so great a benefit of yours, love urges us, most Christian and most beloved sons, diligently to learn of your prosperity and rejoice in the Lord. Therefore, with fatherly affection, we discharge the bond of visitation and greeting through these apostolic letters, sending to your excellence our present Peter, chief among the defenders of our holy Church and our faithful messenger, so that in our place he may convey our desired greeting. We ask that you receive him kindly and through him make us certain and joyful regarding your well-being.

We earnestly ask your excellence, most beloved sons, that, following the pious footsteps of your Christian parents, you become their imitators—namely, of your grandfather and great-grandfather, and of your most excellent and God-appointed father, the great king, and of your most excellent mother, the queen whom God preserve. They are proved, above all kings, faithful to God and blessed Peter, and their merits shine in the heavenly kingdoms. Therefore we ask the most merciful patience of our God that, protecting you by his grace, he grant you the enjoyment of royal scepters through ages of prosperity, enlarge the boundaries of your kingdom, grant you victories from heaven, cast all your adversaries beneath your feet, and grant you to possess not only an earthly kingdom but also a heavenly one through endless ages. Farewell.

## LETTER IX. TO KING PEPIN

He states that the monks sent to Rome by Remedius, Pepin’s brother, to learn the modulation of psalmody have been entrusted to the instruction of Simeon, prior of the singers’ school, as requested.

[Col. 1187A]

To the most excellent lord, son, and our spiritual kinsman, Pepin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

Since the love of charity that we bear toward your distinguished excellence, illumined by God, grows all the more vigorously in our heart, it is therefore our concern, most excellent of kings, to obey your will energetically and splendidly with all our efforts—especially since we appear to have been relieved by the very great protection of your excellence and, after God, rescued from the fury of those who lay snares.

Therefore, whenever the texts of your communications are brought to us, we receive them with a grateful spirit and immediately strive to put into effect what their wording expresses. Accordingly, having received and reread the words now sent by your excellence, protected by God, we promptly and willingly fulfilled everything contained in them. For we found written in them that we ought to entrust to Simeon, prior of the singers’ school, the monks of your brother Remedius, dear to God, who are present here, so that he might instruct them in the modulation of psalmody, which they had been unable to learn from him when he was in your regions. For this reason, you say that your brother was greatly saddened, because he had not instructed his monks perfectly. [Col. 1187C]

Indeed, most kindly king, we assure your Christian devotion that, unless George, who presided over that school, had departed this life, we would in no way have attempted to withdraw Simeon from the service of your brother. But after the aforesaid George died and Simeon, as his successor, took his place, we summoned him to us for the instruction of the school. Far be it from us to do in any way anything that might be burdensome to you or to your faithful. Rather, as stated above, remaining steadfast in the love of your charity, we strive with the greatest willingness, insofar as our strength permits, to obey your will.

For this reason we have entrusted the aforesaid monks of your brother to the aforementioned Simeon. Having placed them suitably, we ordered them to be instructed in that same modulation of psalmody with diligent care; and, out of our great love for your excellence and your most noble brother, we arranged with effective attention that they remain constantly in the same ecclesiastical school of song until they are perfectly instructed.

For the rest, we wish your excellence to prosper in the Lord through ages of prosperity and to enjoy the royal scepter, and, through the intercession of blessed Peter, to obtain triumphal victories over your enemies. May heavenly grace keep your excellence safe.

## LETTER X. TO ALL THE FRANKS

He gives thanks for the faithful service rendered to the Roman Church. He praises the Frankish people and its kings and bestows abundant blessings.

[Col. 1188A]

Paul, servant of the servants of God, to all our beloved bishops, venerable priests and abbots, religious monks, illustrious dukes and counts, and to the entire community beloved by Christ of the army established in the God-protected kingdom of the Franks.

As we consider—and as though we saw glowing before our eyes—the splendid faith of your strength, beloved by Christ, and the laborious struggle that you undertake, striving with all your efforts to liberate the holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church, which, through the word of preaching, has begotten you as her sincere and special sons, we are seized by great wonder. Nor do we cease to proclaim throughout the world these praises of your name and of your blessed race.

O most beloved and most cherished by us, what return shall we make to your army? What abundance of treasures could be worthy of the many benefits and protections that you have conferred upon the holy Church? Although our reflection and ability are constrained when considering how to repay you suitably, nevertheless our Lord God is a just judge in heaven, and he will repay the worthy merits of your works.

Indeed, the name of your people has been raised above many generations of nations, and the kingdom of the Franks shines forth, flashing in the sight of the Lord, adorned with kings who are such kind liberators of the holy catholic and apostolic Church of God. For a new Moses and a new David in all his works has become the most Christian son and spiritual kinsman beloved by God, the lord Pepin, the most victorious king by God’s will. Through him the Church of God, exalted, triumphs, and the catholic faith remains undefiled by the weapon of heretics.

And you, dearest ones—a holy nation, a royal priesthood, a people of acquisition, whom the Lord God of Israel has blessed—rejoice and exult, because your names and those of your kings have been written in heaven, and your reward is great before God and his angels. [Col. 1188D]

You have acquired as your protector the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom our Redeemer granted the power of binding and loosing sins in heaven and on earth. May almighty God, through the intercessions of that same apostle, bless, protect, strengthen, and fortify your community beloved by God, and order your actions according to his good pleasure. May he grant you victory from heaven, enlarge your borders, subject all barbarian nations to your most excellent kings, and bring about the complete liberation and exaltation of the holy universal Church of God and the integrity of the orthodox faith.

May he grant you to understand what pleases him, and illuminate your hearts far more abundantly with love for blessed Peter and his apostolic see. May you, obeying his apostolic commands with faithful zeal, deserve to complete the course of this present life with victory and a good reputation, and to enjoy eternal joys with the citizens of heaven.

## LETTER XI, OR CHARTER OF IMMUNITY FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT HILARY OF GALIATA, SITUATED UNDER THE CHURCH OF RAVENNA

Accordingly, by divine will, some … years ago, our brother in office and in blessed memory, the most blessed Stephen, prelate of this apostolic see, had hastened to the region of France in order to redeem the province of Italy, and at the same time the exarchate of Ravenna, from the hands of foreign peoples. As he was returning, it happened that his journey passed through the monastery of blessed Hilary, situated in the territory of Populonia. When the fury of his rivals had ceased, he was received with the greatest gratitude and humility of honor by Anscausus, formerly bishop of Populonia and abbot of that venerable monastery; and … the same most blessed pontiff … the aforesaid Anscausus, formerly a bishop, generously supplied him with provisions for that journey.

When our same most blessed predecessor, the bishop of this apostolic see, had by his laborious struggle and through God’s providence redeemed that province—namely, the exarchate of Ravenna—from the yoke of the domination of foreign peoples, he then, in return for the favor he had received, granted the aforesaid monastery to Bishop Anscausus for the enjoyment of his lifetime. We therefore confirmed the generosity of this grant under the document of apostolic command and subjected it to the jurisdiction of our holy Church. [Col. 1189C]

But now, when Anscausus has departed this life by divine calling, having ascertained the truth of the matter, we recognize that the aforesaid venerable monastery has existed for a long time under the legal authority of the holy Church of Ravenna. Therefore, considering it wholly contrary to reason that this venerable place should be withdrawn from the holy Church of Ravenna … and declaring that everything previously promulgated improperly and irrationally for its removal is null and invalid, we so decree.

Therefore, through this document of our apostolic command, we again decree that the venerable monastery of blessed Hilary, with everything belonging to it, remain under the jurisdiction of the Church of Ravenna and of your reverend fraternity and your successors, permanently and for all time. Let that venerable place be perpetually administered as seems good to you … and to your successors.

We decree by apostolic censure, under the prohibition of anathema and by the solemn appeal to the divine Judge, that no person whatsoever, small or great, may in any way remove that venerable monastery from the jurisdiction of the holy Church of Ravenna or from that of your fraternal reverence and your successors. And if any document contrary to your Church of Ravenna should be found concerning that monastery, we decree it null and void.

Given on the Nones of February, while our most devout lord Augustus, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in his fortieth year, and in the twentieth [read: nineteenth] year after his consulship, and in the seventh year of Emperor Leo, his son, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XII. TO ABBOT JOHN

Concerning the church and monasteries that he established in his paternal house under the title of Saints Stephen, pope and martyr, and Sylvester, pope and confessor.

Paul, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Icontius [Leontius], a religious priest and abbot of the venerable monastery of Saints Stephen, martyr, and Sylvester, confessor of Christ, and of the countless other martyrs and confessors of God resting in that same holy monastery, founded by us with God’s consent, and to that venerable monastery with him, in perpetuity.

Amid the various pursuits and the diverse activities of human instability that are undertaken in this temporal life, those things must especially be accomplished with every effort of the mind that concern the praise of our Lord God and the most celebrated honor of his saints. Indeed, all things prosperous follow if we first take care to accomplish what is glorious to God and resplendent for his saints.

For this reason, while the grace of the ineffable power of our divine Redeemer has deigned to look upon my lowliness, I earnestly strive, with great care and with an almost breathless affection of love, to procure praises for him through his enduring kindness and mercy and to offer the desires of my vows to his majesty. Moved by the inspiration of divine illumination, I have therefore zealously sought, although unworthy, to provide what pertains to the worship of God and the worthy veneration of the saints, and to confirm it with the greatest force of authority.

For I confess that I have been greatly aided before the divine mercy by the most excellent intercessions of those same saints; for, weighed down by the heavy burden of sins, I am worthy through no progress in virtues to discharge so great and terrible an office of the apostolic see, unless divine favor has gone before me through their protection. Nevertheless, in this the Lord our God, the all-knowing Creator and Redeemer of his own omnipotence, gives evidence: through the grace of his power, he brings to the hope of advancement those things that are despised by those very saints. This is plainly seen to have happened in my case. [Col. 1190D]

Therefore, restored by immense joy of thanksgiving, my mouth speaks the praise of the Lord, my heart and tongue bless his holy name, and, in keeping with his great compassion, I offer my vows.

Accordingly, after many years had passed, the ancient cemeteries of various holy martyrs and confessors of Christ situated outside the walls of this city of Rome remained largely neglected and ruined. Later it happened that they were utterly destroyed by the impious attack of the Lombard peoples. They also dug up some of the tombs of those martyrs, devastated them impiously, and plundered certain saints, carrying away and transporting their bodies. From that time onward, the honor of veneration owed to them was altogether negligently and carelessly rendered.

Indeed—and it is sacrilegious to say it—even various animals had access to some of those same cemeteries of the saints. Their animal enclosures stood there, in which they discharged filthy stench.

When I saw the negligent neglect of those holy places, and deeply lamented it, worn down by the greatest sorrow, I judged it fitting, with God’s consent, to remove those holy martyrs and confessors of Christ, and the virgins among them, from those ruined places. With hymns and spiritual songs we brought them into this city of Rome and placed and buried their most holy bodies in a church that I had newly built from its foundations in their honor—inside the walls, in a house that had come to me by parental succession, where I am known to have been born and raised.

There I established a congregation of monks under a special rule in honor and in the name of blessed Stephen, pope and martyr, and Sylvester, pope and confessor of Christ. Since their venerable bodies rest there, I decreed that it should be a monastery of male monks, specifically for the practice of chanting psalmody, and determined that praises should continually be offered there to the Lord God our Redeemer. I also ordained that the eternal memory of the veneration of those saints resting there should be celebrated to the glory of divine power, and that daily prayers should be poured out for the prolongation and stability of the state, for the salvation of all faithful Christians, and for the forgiveness of my sins; and that due and fitting honor should be rendered to all these saints of God.

Since those martyrs of Christ, rejecting the flatteries of human glory and enduring various punishments of torture, were beheaded for the name of Christ and became friends of God, it is entirely fitting that, just as their souls triumph with the angels in the heavenly kingdoms, so also on earth their most sacred bodies, placed in radiant dwellings, should be properly venerated by all Christians, since they do not cease to implore the divine omnipotence more earnestly on behalf of their worshipers. I commend myself to the protection of those holy ones, trusting that through their intercessions I may be freed from the burden of sins by which I am oppressed.

And behold, with the Lord’s favor, we have richly endowed the monastery founded by us in their honor with various estates, resources, and urban and rural possessions, and with all necessary equipment. We have granted everything sufficient for the arrangement of the lamps, the continual offering of sacrifices, and the uses of the monks residing there: estates, farms, small holdings, tenant settlements, vineyards and gardens, olive groves, houses and guesthouses, saltworks, water mills, fisheries, and the remaining landed possessions situated in various places and cities, together with the personal property of the servants serving there.

We have also added and confirmed under the law and authority of our monastery certain monasteries and venerable places, with all their possessions and everything generally and wholly belonging to them.

All these places, possessions, and urban or rural estates, with everything generally and wholly belonging to them, wherever and in whatever city they are situated, which have already been granted by us to the aforesaid monastery or may hereafter be bestowed, and which are or may be confirmed there by pontifical commands and other directives, we, with the priestly council presiding, decree and sanction by apostolic censure, with the solemn appeal to divine judgment, and decree that our successors in the episcopate must preserve them.

They are to remain perpetually in that venerable monastery and, by perpetual right, to serve its use for the daily offering of sacrifice, the arrangement of the lamps, and the support of the monks residing there. [Col. 1192B]

Therefore, under the terrible and fearful future day of the coming of our great Lord Jesus Christ, on which he will judge the living and the dead and the world by fire, and also under the greatest prohibitions of anathema by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we decree that none of our episcopal successors, nor any person, great or small, whatever honor or dignity he possesses, may in any way, by any more elaborate device of ingenuity, dissolve what we have established for the sake of the praise of our Redeemer and the honor of his saints.

Nor may anyone remove from those places, possessions, resources, families, or personal property anything that is recognized as belonging to the same venerable monastery, or alienate it in any way. Rather, as stated above, everything must remain permanently and intact in that holy place.

Nor may the abbot who at any time governs that monastery presume in any way to lease or sell to anyone any place that is in the monastery’s possession, or to appropriate or defraud it of anything belonging to it.

We further establish and decree that the entire congregation of monks residing in that holy monastery shall offer praises to our Lord God each day and render due honor there to the martyrs and confessors of Christ who rest there. They shall also strive to offer the fullest praises to our Redeemer, who has come to their aid with strength [read: has subjected powers]. For it is written: “And I will add to all your praise” (Psalm 70).

In promulgating this as well, we sanction and, by the power of our almighty God, under the terrible obligation of anathema, solemnly decree that no one may ever presume to inflict any opposition or malice upon our monastery or upon the matters belonging to it. Rather, out of fear of God and the greatest honor for his saints, let everyone bring assistance and aid to it and to the matters and interests belonging to it, so that they too may become participants in this good work and obtain from almighty God the rewards of recompense for such a benefit.

[Col. 1193A]

All these things, promulgated by us for the praise of our Redeemer, confirmed by the entire episcopal council, and strengthened by the greatest obligations, we decree before the living and true God must be preserved forever.

But if any of our episcopal successors, or any other person, powerful or inferior, great or small, whatever honor or dignity he possesses, should presume by any argument or contrived pretext to destroy, dissolve, violate, or break what we have established for the worship of God—or should attempt to remove or alienate from that holy place any place, possession, or anything recognized as belonging to the aforesaid venerable monastery—let him know that, by the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he is bound by an unbreakable bond of anathema and excluded from the kingdom of God.

Let him regard all those same holy martyrs, confessors, and virgins of Christ as his adversaries, and on the fearful day of examination and judgment let him be required, together with those saints, to render an account before the tribunal of almighty God.

For I appeal to that Judge who is the recompensor of all, for whose praise we are known to have established these things, that he inflict the anger of his power upon all transgressors of this apostolic constitution and strike with an incurable wound of vengeance all who attempt to injure our aforesaid monastery, display a hostile intention toward matters belonging to it, or presume to take away anything belonging to it.

Let their life be laborious, wretched, and exceedingly mournful; let them waste away in weakness and, unless they repent, obtain no forgiveness of their sins, receiving the sentence of Ananias and Sapphira, who, [reading uncertain; F.: *infecti*, “infected”] by the guilt of lying, expired at the feet of the apostles.

May it happen to them as to Dathan and Abiram, whom, when the earth opened its mouth, it swallowed alive. And, assigned with the devil and his most atrocious and detestable pageantry, with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and with all the impious, may they burn forever in Tartarean fire and unquenchable flame, plunged into the abyss of chaos.

[Col. 1193D]

But those who are found defending our monastery, which we established for the praise of God and the honor of his saints, and who faithfully observe everything established and contained in this apostolic document, preserving all its provisions intact with sincere minds, may be found at God’s right hand, established in the place of light. May they have as steadfast protectors all the holy martyrs, confessors, and virgins of God who rest in that venerable monastery; and through their intercessions may they be helped in the present life and, in the blessedness of the future heavenly kingdom, obtain joy with the angels of God and all the saints and elect throughout endless ages.

[Col. 1196B]

On the nineteenth day of July we brought into this sanctuary the body of blessed Sylvester, bishop and confessor of Christ.

## LETTER OF POPE PAUL I

Which neither the Carolinus nor the Labbeanus manuscripts had supplied.

[Wilkins, *Concilia Magnae Britanniae*, vol. I.]

## TO ECGBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK, AND EADBERHT, SON OF THE KING OF THE ENGLISH

That he restore to Forthred the monasteries taken from him by the king’s son.

[Col. 1195]

[Col. 1195C]

To our most beloved brother Ecgbert, archbishop, and also to Eadberht, most excellent son and king, Pope Paul sends greeting.

The arbiter and maker of all things, our triune and one Lord God, who, forming all things from nothing by a single word, created human nature from [*de*] clay, and to whom the structure of heaven and the material of the earth serve according to an eternal law, appointed your most prudent nobility to carry out the care of his own people, so that you might strive with vigilant care and eager devotion to accomplish whatever pertains to the worship of his divine majesty. Thus, through the protection afforded by your diligence, the salvation of those who are not free from the hidden snares of this world may be guarded.

For, most beloved, we have learned abundantly through the reports of many that you possess effective diligence. And because you yearn with devoted mind to ponder more attentively that life blossoming with flowers, whose end is cut off by no boundary, we have therefore gladly judged it fitting, through our apostolic admonition and affection, to request from your excellence what concerns the salvation of your soul.

Accordingly, when the religious abbot Forthred came in person to the thresholds of your protectors, the blessed princes of the apostles Peter and Paul, he reported to us, saying that three monasteries had been granted to him by a certain abbess—namely, the monasteries called Staningagrave, Cuchawalda, and Donaemuthe.

Your excellence forcibly took these monasteries away from him and gave them to a certain Patricius, his brother, called Moll. We have been made exceedingly sad by this matter, most excellent son, because you have acted entirely contrary to God’s command. It is plainly evident that this concerns the destruction of your soul, since you took those monasteries away from one who perseveres in the service of divine worship and strove to grant them to one who labors amid the cares of this world.

For it is not lawful, most excellent son, for you to place human favor before your eyes rather than the fear of God. Your most excellent prudence ought to have bestowed assistance and support upon those venerable places from your own resources, lands, and pleasant properties. For it is written: “Honor the Lord from your own substance” (Proverbs 3:9).

Therefore we exhort your diligence and admonish you through the apostolic see that, truly obedient to him as you ought to be, and for love of your protector, you restore those three monasteries to the aforesaid abbot Forthred. Thus, in accordance with the way they were granted to him by the aforesaid abbess, he may deserve to enjoy them without any ambiguity or hostile harassment.

And, according to the prudence bestowed and implanted in you, hasten to cherish all venerable places for God’s sake and protect them in every respect. Let it also be your concern in every way to restore to those holy places whatever has been taken from them, so that, with the wicked usurpation of vices cut away, no layman or any other person may again be permitted to invade what belongs to pious places. Rather, through your zeal, let those things that pertain to the purpose of religion be promoted more abundantly.

From this, most excellent son, you will receive divine assistance as your reward, prevail against the cunning of the savage enemy, and unquestionably deserve to attain eternal life.

## In the Year of Our Lord 770. Alanus, Abbot.

[Col. 1197]

## [NOTE.]

This manuscript of the *Homiliary* is mentioned among the other codices of the Burana Library by Bernard Pez, volume III of the *Anecdota*, part III, in these words:

> “The *Homiliary* of Alan, abbot of St. Mary. In a parchment manuscript in quarto, of the eighth or ninth century, the work is divided into two parts. The first contains homilies of the Fathers from Advent of the Lord until Easter; the second, the remainder up to the end of the ecclesiastical year. This appears to be the *Sermonary* listed in the description of the money and books offered by Queen Kisyla to the church of Cochalon. Moreover, this same work is preserved in an equally ancient codex in folio in the Tegernsee Library, where the author is called Alan. From this Tegernsee copy we transcribed the complete preface, which begins as follows: ‘With the grace of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ shining forth, the darkness of obscurity having been driven from the field of the Law, and the deadly poison of the letter of the Law having been excluded’—so the manuscript reads—‘the apostles arose like certain evangelical cultivators,’ and so forth. The conclusion of the preface is this: ‘For these things, and others contained or following below, I, Alan, the last of all God’s servants, called abbot in name but not in deed, in the monastery of the undefiled Holy Mother of the Lord, the blessed Virgin Mary, have taken care to gather together in this volume for the benefit of many.’”

**In the year of the Lord 770. St. Ambrose, Bishop of Cahors.**

[Col. 1197]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(From the continued Acts of the Saints of the Bollandists, prepared by the Reverend Fathers Joseph Vendemoere and Joseph Vanhecke, priests of the Society of Jesus.—Brussels, 1845.)*

## § I. The Saint’s memory in the sacred calendars and his cult

[Col. 1197B]

1. Usuard, and various copies of Ado, commemorate Saint Ambrose on this day; but they do not agree concerning the various details surrounding the present announcement. For in the copies of Ado, brought forward by Monsieur George outside the pure text of Ado, under 17 October, we read [Note: *Martyrologium of Ado*, Rome, 1745, p. 531]:

> “At the city of Bourges, the feast of Saint Ambrose, priest and confessor.”

The anonymous Fulda Martyrology, which, according to the testimony of the same George [Note: *Ibid.*, Preface, XV], was written in the tenth century, likewise announces the saint in these words [Note: *Ibid.*, p. 671]:

> “The feast of Saint Ambrose, priest and confessor.”

Usuard, moreover, as edited by our Sollerius, has:

> “In the territory of Bourges, Saint Ambrose the confessor.”

But because in Usuard of Molanus the words “bishop of Cahors” are added in a different type [Col. 1197C], Molanus himself, and our Sollerius who follows him, regard them as an addition. All these hagiologists therefore speak as though the episcopal insignia of Cahors ought not to be attributed to Saint Ambrose. Nevertheless, this silence ought not to prejudice our saint’s episcopate, since it is expressly asserted in his *Life*, which will be published below. Although that *Life* does not appear to be contemporary, it is nevertheless sufficiently ancient to establish its reliability concerning the principal circumstance of his life.

Furthermore, the Usuardine reading presented to us by Sollerius is not altogether certain. For the genuine Martyrology of Usuard, published at Paris in 1718 by D. Bouillard, a monk of the Benedictine congregation of Saint-Maur, as though it were the author’s autograph, reads differently:

> “In the district of Bourges, Saint Ambrose, bishop of Cahors.”

Sollerius indeed declares this reading to be genuine [Col. 1198C], “but I consider the other, which is ours, to be truly Usuardine.” We have no opportunity to investigate the merits of the other reading more thoroughly, especially since the Benedictine just mentioned admits that the announcement of Saint Ambrose was written over an erasure. On the other hand, as we have already said, and as we shall demonstrate more clearly below, it is certain to us that our saint occupied the see of Cahors.

The Roman Martyrology, therefore, compiled by Baronius, rightly announces him today:

> “In the territory of Bourges, Saint Ambrose, bishop of Cahors.”

The Paris Martyrology, published by order of Cardinal de Noailles, and the Auxerre Martyrology, published by order of Charles de Caylus, likewise attribute the episcopate of Cahors to Saint Ambrose, saying:

> “At Bourges, the deposition of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Cahors.”

Thus the copies of Ado that call the saint simply a priest must be interpreted in such a way that his episcopal dignity remains intact—unless, indeed, we assign this error of title to the ignorance of interpolators. Otherwise it will be necessary to say that he is called simply a priest because, having laid aside his episcopal dignity, he voluntarily returned to this lower order.

2. What we have so far said about the Martyrologies abundantly demonstrates that the cult of Saint Ambrose, although not very widespread, rests nevertheless upon the firmest foundations. The Church of Cahors celebrates his memory with the rite commonly called semidouble, according to the present Breviary of Cahors. Formerly, however, Saint Ambrose was celebrated with a double rite, as we learn from the Proper of the Saints of the same diocese. The Reverend Father Layrac, secretary of the diocese of Cahors, kindly shared with us a copy of both legends. The antiquity of his cult is proved by the *Life* inserted in the Cahors Sanctorale, which Guillaume de la Croix presents in his book *Series and Acts of the Bishops of Cahors*.

Because of the saint’s burial there, and of a monastery or chapter founded under his invocation, the diocese of Bourges also celebrates his feast, probably with a semidouble rite. For the Bourges liturgical calendar before me belongs to the year 1831; and therefore, because Sunday coincides with 16 October, it prescribes only a commemoration of the saint.

In the Bourges Breviary published in 1625 by order of Roland Habert, archbishop, a copy of which we possess in a partly manuscript and partly printed codex containing various Proper Offices of the dioceses of France, Saint Ambrose’s feast is celebrated with a double rite, and the following prayer is recited:

> “Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, that your faithful may worthily celebrate the solemnity of Saint Ambrose, your confessor and pontiff, so that, by your aid, they may experience here what they faithfully perform and attain it with eternal affections. Through Christ.”

The Regular Canons of the Gallican Congregation, however, whose church was dedicated to Saint Ambrose, celebrated the feast of their patron on 18 October, as the Reverend Father Figier, canon and secretary of the archbishopric of Bourges, wrote to us in a letter dated 22 November 1840. From him we also received other excellent information concerning Saint Ambrose.

The monastery, together with the church attached to it, founded—or rather restored—under his invocation by Gaufrid, called the Noble, viscount of Bourges, also provides us with very strong evidence of his cult. A charter concerning this matter is preserved among the instruments of the Church of Bourges in the *Gallia Christiana* [Note: vol. II, Instruments, col. 49]. From it it is clear that the said Gaufrid did not so much found the church of Saint Peter and Saint Ambrose as restore to it what it had lost. For he speaks as follows:

> “A thousand and twelve years have passed from the institution of the Lord’s Incarnation until the time when this charter was executed . . . Therefore I, Gaufrid, viscount of the city of Bourges, give thanks to almighty God, who causes me to foresee and behold the salvation of my soul and the honor of my body, since I have wished to restore to honor and stability the place of Saint Peter and Saint Ambrose, who rests in that church. Of my own good will, therefore, I, Gaufrid, together with my wife Eldeburgis, and my sons Gaufrid and Madalbert, and Odo and Ebbo, my wife’s brothers, for the salvation of the soul of Radulf, my wife’s father, and for the salvation of our souls and those of all our relatives, with King Robert’s consent and Bishop Dagbert’s confirmation, RETURN to that place of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the lands belonging to it, namely these . . . I ALSO GIVE from my own property two fairs, one on the feast of Saint Peter in the month of June, and the other on the nativity of Saint Ambrose, each lasting seven days and as many nights, and so forth.”

The property Gaufrid restored seems to have come to that church through the inheritance or dowry of Eldeburgis, since he restored it at the wish of his said wife and her brothers, and chiefly for the salvation of the soul of Radulf, her father. When he indicates that some things were restored by him to the church of his own good will, while others were given from his own property, he sufficiently demonstrates that the church had formerly been endowed with its own possessions, and therefore that he was not so much its founder as its restorer.

Indeed, a temple must already have existed there before Saint Ambrose’s death, as is proved by the burial of Sigini, bishop of Bourges, who died shortly after the middle of the eighth century. A fragment of his epitaph is quoted in the *Gallia Christiana*:

> Here lies the faithful shepherd and husband of the Church;  
> A hard stone conceals his beloved remains.

3. The church of Saint Ambrose that Gaufrid founded or restored was, however, more a secular chapter of canons than a monastery of regulars. For the charter mentioned above allows each canon to dispose of his prebend as he wishes, so that he may give it to another canon or leave it to him; and such freedom is very far removed from the rigor of religious life.

Here are Gaufrid’s words:

> “I also restore to them [the canons] whatever shall come to the altar of that holy Peter and to the whole of that church, whether gold or silver, lands, lamps, or any other things whatsoever that shall come or be given. We grant those canons the right to add to or remove from their own community as many as they wish; this shall remain in their own right and power. We also grant the prebends of that place to the same canons on the condition that no bishop, no abbot, and no man ever presume to sell, give away, or remove them. But each canon shall have the power to give or leave his prebend to another canon, with the counsel of the other canons who actually serve in the same place . . . This gift was made on 3 August, in the tenth year of the reign of King Robert, while Dagbert presided in the chair of the Church of Bourges, in the eighth year of his episcopate.”

These chronological indications, however, agree neither with one another nor with the year 1012. For Dagbert probably obtained the bishopric of Bourges nine full years before Robert, after the death of his father Hugh Capet in 996, assumed the kingdom of France. Consequently, Robert’s tenth year would rather coincide with the eighteenth year of Dagbert’s episcopate.

Neither of these years agrees with the common era 1012, but rather with 1005 or 1006. This is the chronology adopted by Guillaume de la Croix in his book on the succession and acts of the bishops of Cahors [Note: p. 34]. Since neither time, resources, nor even the importance of the matter permit us to untangle these complications, it will suffice here to indicate Gaufrid’s charter, and therefore to establish that the restoration of the church of Saint Ambrose must be placed within the first twelve years of the eleventh century.

In the course of time the chapter of Saint Ambrose at Bourges was transferred from a secular condition to the regular order of the Canons of Saint Augustine under Peter of Castra, archbishop, in 1151 [Note: Labbe, *Bibliotheca Manuscriptorum*, vol. II, p. 58], as we shall demonstrate more fully below.

[Col. 1201C]

4. The acts of Saint Ambrose are contained chiefly in four monuments. Two of these are readings from the ancient Breviary of Bourges and the Cahors Sanctorale; they agree sufficiently with each other to suggest that they derived their historical narrative from one another. The third monument is a rhythmic hymn presented to us by Guillaume de la Croix [Note: *Series of the Bishops of Cahors*, p. 36]. It contains nothing that is not reported in the other writings. Indeed, in its narrative it includes only what the saint did at Cahors, with no mention of his journey to Rome or Tours, or of his death or burial at Bourges. After relating how the blessed bishop, having been discovered in a cave, came out of it when the people begged him to resume the governance of his Church, the hymn concludes with a brief prayer to Saint Ambrose [Col. 1201D]:

> Ambrose, pious confessor,  
> Be our intercessor;  
> Be our advocate,  
> When the Judge is angry with us.

The fourth monument is the *Life of Saint Ambrose*, written in a rather fuller, but nevertheless simple, style. We publish it below from the Library of the manuscripts of Philippe Labbe [Note: vol. II, p. 347]. To Labbe’s edition we shall add variant readings, chiefly from the codex of Queen Christina of Sweden, which our John Bollandus testifies that he carefully extracted, and which we found in the cabinets of the Royal Library of Brussels.

Because this codex is more recent than Labbe’s, it contains various additions, some of which illuminate the events narrated and agree with them very closely. We shall therefore place these after Labbe’s copy among the annotations, or append them to the text in the explanatory notes. Shorter variants, consisting merely in the addition, omission, or transposition of a word or two, we shall, according to our custom, place in the margin of the primary text, with the siglum RS, by which we shall designate the codex of the Queen of Sweden.

The *Life of Saint Allogiosus*, published in the *Gallia Christiana* [Note: vol. I, Instruments of the Church of Cahors, col. 28], might also be counted among these monuments; Edmund Martene extracted it from an eight-hundred-year-old codex [Note: *Ibid.*, col. 118].

> “The collectors say that no mention of this saint is found elsewhere; from this *Life*, however, we could not learn when he lived. Therefore we have relegated his acts among the instruments.”

No Allogiosus ever existed at Cahors. It is simply a corruption of the name Ambrose. For, apart from a few minor details, the text is word for word like the *Acts of Saint Ambrose*, as is evident even to a casual reader.

5. The *Acts* that we shall publish below have an anonymous author who does not indicate his own period except in these words, with which he concludes his narrative:

> “His disciple, Agrippinus by name, followed him wherever he went and taught everything that has been written.”

The text of the Queen of Sweden reads somewhat differently:

> “His disciple, Agrippinus by name, who followed him wherever he went, taught us everything that has been written about him.”

From both texts it may be inferred that the anonymous author drew his narrative from an eyewitness, namely Agrippinus, archdeacon of the Church of Cahors, a close companion of our saint and the only person who knew of his secret withdrawal.

There is another detail that has the character of something native and contemporary, in section 10: when Saint Ambrose came out of the cave, “his beard descended to his breast,” and “he was like a layman, because during those three years a razor had not passed over his head.” Such an image, which depicts a very minor matter vividly to the eye and agrees perfectly with contemporary customs, would scarcely, in my judgment, have occurred to a writer who had not either seen the event himself or heard it from an eyewitness.

For that clerics in the Western Church formerly customarily shaved their beards is attested above all by Saint Gregory VII, book VIII, letter 10, to Orzoccu, judge of Cagliari [Note: Labbe, vol. X of the Councils, col. 258 and following]:

> “From the very beginnings of the Christian faith, the clergy of the entire Western Church have maintained the custom of shaving the beard.”

The testimony of Ratramnus, monk of Corbie and a ninth-century writer, agrees with this. In book IV, chapter 5, of his *Objections to the Greeks* [Note: In d’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. I, p. 102, Paris edition, 1723], he says that the Greeks do not hesitate “to blame clerics for cutting the beard, not only those of the Romans but of all the Western Churches.” He appropriately replies:

> “This clerical appearance—whether with the beard shorn or grown—is not uniform in all Churches, but varies and differs according to the custom of one’s ancestors. Nor has contention ever arisen on this account between the Churches, whether Western or Eastern; rather, each has retained what it received from its forebears or what the practice of the provinces has approved.”

A little further on, however, he says:

> “Following this custom, the clerics of the Romans and of nearly all the Churches throughout the West shave their beards.”

This suggests that a few exceptions existed in the West. For that reason, the reading of canon 44 of the Fourth Council of Carthage, held in 398, as given by Molanus [Note: *On the History of Sacred Images*, p. 302, note y], should not be retained:

> “A cleric shall neither grow his hair nor shave his beard,”

as though African clerics had been forbidden to cut their beards. For manuscripts of the best authority omit the word “shave” [Note: Labbe, vol. II of the Councils, col. 1203]; and in that form the canon supports our argument. Anyone wishing to know more about this discipline should consult Cardinal Baronius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, year 58, §137 and following.

Moreover, the antiquity of the celebrated *Life of Saint Ambrose* is made more certain by its silence concerning a second translation to Bourges. It simply says that he is now resting in the village of Ernotrum; yet it is clear from section 3, as it is read in the codex of the Queen of Sweden, that by the tenth century Saint Ambrose’s body had already been translated to Bourges and was being venerated there.
