Indeed, it is quite probable that in the preceding century the relics of the sacred body had been brought within the city because of the fury of the Normans, as we shall see below.

From this it may be concluded that the codex of the Queen of Sweden is by a somewhat later hand, since it adds the translation of the body near the end. The Labbe text, speaking of the village of Ernotrum, says:

> “There his body rests in peace, where the Lord has deigned to display many miracles through him.”

The codex of the Queen of Sweden, however, reads:

> “Where his body rested . . . afterward, by the Lord’s command, his body was translated near the city of Bourges, and he was placed in a place called Bissiacus, while Our Lord Jesus Christ reigned,” and so forth.

From all this it is sufficiently clear that the *Life* published below was composed by an anonymous author roughly contemporary with the saint.

## § II. Saint Ambrose’s episcopate and his activities during it

6. Saint Ambrose’s biographers report nothing about his birth, youth, or actions before his episcopate. For the statement suggested by the *Life* improperly entitled *The Life of Saint Allogiosus*, mentioned above in section 4—that Saint Ambrose had been married before becoming bishop and had been tempted by his wife—is of no significance. It is found in that one codex alone, enclosed in brackets, and connected by no link with what precedes or follows; it therefore appears to be wholly an addition.

It is regrettable that no ancient writings reveal the period in which the saint lived. Consequently, the date at which he assumed the bishopric of Cahors and the date of his death necessarily remain uncertain. The Cahors Sanctorale asserts that he “was bishop of the city of Cahors in the time of Pippin, king of the Franks.” The catalogues of the bishops of Cahors agree with this.

It is not equally clear, however, that Saint Ambrose first occupied the see after Pippin, king of the Franks, was acclaimed in 752, as Guillaume de la Croix seems to imply in the text quoted above. He says that the saint lived after 751, when Pippin was anointed king in March; for many years began with the paschal solemnity.

The condition of Gaul at that time makes it necessary to offer some preliminary observations concerning churches that had been left vacant. It is certain from a letter of Saint Boniface of Mainz to Pope Zachary, written in 742, letter 51 [Note: Wurdtwein, *Letters of Saint Boniface*, p. 106; Serarius, *Letters*, 132], that the condition of the Church in Gaul was extremely wretched, especially under Charles Martel:

> “For the Franks,” he says, “have held no synod for more than eighty years, nor had they an archbishop, nor anywhere established or renewed the canonical rights of the Churches. Now, for the most part, episcopal sees throughout the cities have been handed over to greedy laymen for possession, or to adulterous clerics, fornicators, and publicans for secular enjoyment.”

To avert these evils from the Churches of Gaul, Saint Boniface wrote that Carloman, duke of the Franks, to whom the government of Austrasia had fallen, wished to convene a synod in which the things that had “long been trampled underfoot and scattered” might be corrected and restored.

This was accomplished to some extent by the second canon of the Council of Liptina [Note: Labbe, vol. VI of the Councils, col. 1537]. With the bishops and Carloman agreeing, it was decreed that the things formerly taken from the Churches should indeed remain in the possession of their holders, but “under precarious tenure and a census,” so that twelve denarii should be paid each year for “each household,” or, as Pope Zachary says in letter 70 to Boniface [Note: Wurdtwein, p. 184; Serarius, 138], “for each marriage-pair of servants.” In addition, when the lay possessor died, the property itself was to be restored to the Church.

I think it worthwhile to explain something here about *precarium*, since such agreements, customary under ancient law but long since abolished, have scarcely left any trace of themselves. The doctors correctly define *precarium* from the very words of canon law, chapter 3, *De precariis* (III, 14):

> “That which is granted for use at the request of the petitioner, for as long as the one who granted it permits.”

It is therefore a grant of use that is always revocable. From this it is already evident that what the Council of Liptina is said to have granted “under precarious tenure,” since it was subject to another’s use until the death of the lay possessor, cannot strictly be called a *precarium*. Rather, it approaches a *precaria*, which is defined as:

> “That which is granted for use until the death of the one to whom the use is granted.”

This kind of agreement must not be confused with *precariae*. For *precariae* are:

> “A contract by which a thing is given for use for a fixed period; and if the period of the grant is longer, then, lest its memory perish through the passage of time, it must be renewed every five years.”

Ostiensis explains the nature and difference of these agreements rather neatly in four verses: [That is: *preca*—]

> *Riae, Ria, Rium*—three things with one beginning:  
> *Riae* are customarily renewed every five years;  
> *Ria* lasts for life and does not wish to be revoked before then;  
> *Rium* ends whenever its grantor wishes.

7. But this restoration of the Churches seems, as the aforementioned letter of Saint Boniface indicates, to have concerned Austrasia, which Carloman governed, though it ought to have extended to the other parts of Gaul, in which Cahors was situated.

Nevertheless, Pope Zachary’s letter 9 [Note: Wurdtwein, p. 184; Serarius, 138], “given on the day before the Kalends of November, while the most pious lord Constantine, crowned by God, Augustus and great emperor, was reigning, in the twenty-seventh year of his reign, the fifth year of his imperial rule, indiction fourteen,” plainly says that a synod had been convened “through the intervention of Pippin and Carloman.” It also says that the synod dealt with the payment to the Church of an annual census of twelve denarii.

No record survives, however, of a council at which Pippin and Carloman met with the bishops of all Gaul. It is therefore probable that the synod was divided into two parts: Liptina for Austrasia, in 743 according to Philip Labbe [Note: vol. VI of the Councils, col. 1537], or, as Mansi holds [Note: vol. I Supplement, col. 551], in 745; and Soissons for the rest of Gaul, in 744. From the third canon of this council [Note: Labbe, vol. VI of the Councils, col. 1553] it is clear that “legitimate bishops were then appointed throughout the cities, and an annual census was likewise to be paid from the things that had been taken away.” Thus the Synod of Soissons appears to correspond very closely with that of Liptina.

The question may therefore be asked whether Saint Ambrose was placed over the Church of Cahors in that year, 744. The answer would not be doubtful if the condition of Aquitaine had been peaceful. But since at precisely that time all affairs in that province were greatly disturbed, I would readily allow that one or two years passed between the synodal decree and the restoration of the see of Cahors.

We are not, however, compelled to extend Saint Ambrose’s episcopate until the time of King Pippin, that is, until 752. Since Carloman went into Aquitaine in 744 and the following year, it is probable that he then settled ecclesiastical affairs. Saint Ambrose’s episcopate should therefore be dated from approximately this period.

It consequently seems necessary to depart from the opinion of Guillaume de la Croix [Note: *Series and Acts of the Bishops of Cahors*, p. 32] and Adrien Baillet, who thought that the beginning of our saint’s episcopate should be placed after the year 752, when Pippin was acclaimed king. The Cahors historian Cathala-Cothure [Note: *Ibid.*, p. 82]—of whom we shall also speak below—should likewise be corrected, since he says that Saint Ambrose assumed the governance of the Church of Cahors in the year 742. At that time, certainly, conditions in Gaul were not yet sufficiently mature for the reform of the ecclesiastical order to begin.

8. The anonymous author reports very little about Saint Ambrose’s activities during his episcopate. In section 1 he says:

> “Every day and night he was always devoted to vigils and prayers. For he did not trust in the riches of the world or in the treasures of the Church, but in the mercy of the Lord, because he was full of the grace of God. He did not love the world, nor the possessions and goods that are in the world. The resources of the Church and his own wealth, whatever he possessed, he distributed to the poor. He covered the naked, fed the hungry, gave drink to the thirsty, redeemed captives, and prepared a treasure for himself in heaven.
>
> “All the senators in the city spoke wicked words against him. When the holy man of God, Ambrose, saw that all of them were raging against him, he turned to prayer and said to the Lord: ‘Lord, my God, who blessed Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, bless my soul and all my inward parts in your holy name. Lead me out of this city and from this wicked people, who oppose me and blaspheme the works that I perform in your name.’
>
> “When he had said this, full of the grace of God, he shut himself up in a little cell that was beside the church . . . After this he remained there for many days.”

From this manner of life we readily believe what is read in the Breviary of Cahors:

> “Ambrose, desiring to restore the splendor of his Church, afflicted by long-standing calamities, undertook to correct the discipline of the clergy and the morals of the people by salutary admonitions and examples.”

Thus, if we read in the anonymous author that our saint “shut himself up beside his church,” this should be understood to mean that he cultivated the solitude of his cell without allowing pastoral care to suffer any harm.

The Breviary of Cahors therefore rightly follows the anonymous author closely when it adds that his miracles carried the sounder portion of the people away in admiration. This certainly would not have happened had he neglected his episcopal office and devoted himself exclusively to contemplation. Moreover, how could they have said in section 8:

> “Woe to us sinners, who opposed his works and did not see the many miracles that God performed through him,”

if the saint had not governed the people entrusted to him by his words and examples?

9. It is uncertain how long Saint Ambrose presided over his Church before laying aside the burden of the episcopate and withdrawing into a solitude unknown to everyone. The Breviaries of Cahors assign seven years to his administration, but apparently without the support of any suitable authority.

The Cahors historian Cathala-Cothure [Note: *Ibid.*, p. 87] conjectures that Saint Ambrose began to inhabit the wilderness in the year when the Basilica of Figeac was consecrated, in the presence of Pope Stephen II [Note: Sometimes also called Stephen III, as may be seen in the chronologists] and King Pippin, because his name does not occur among the bishops who attended that consecration.

I have not yet found an ancient author, however, who lists the names of the bishops present at the consecration of Figeac. Guillaume de la Croix, who in section 67 [Note: *Series of the Bishops of Cahors*, p. 59] gives a detailed account of this extraordinary consecration, does say, on the basis of the Acts preserved in the Figeac archive:

> “Many bishops were present, among them the most blessed Vivianus, of celebrated memory, who at that time flourished as bishop and count of the see of Saintes.”

But our authors place Saint Vivianus of Saintes around 28 August [Note: Vol. VI of the August *Acts of the Saints*, p. 461], and say that he died around the middle of the fifth century. It is certain that Saint Gregory of Tours, who died in 595, says in his book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 57 [Note: *Bibliotheca maxima Patrum*, vol. XI, p. 883], that Saint Vivianus, or Bibianus, rests in the suburb of the city of Saintes. It is therefore certain that he died at least sixty years before the consecration of Figeac.

The Acts of the Figeac archive are consequently suspect in this matter and do not deserve credence. Indeed, the very extraordinary consecration of the church of Figeac, at least insofar as it would need to be supported by contemporary charters, is wholly unstable.

Cointius proves carefully [Note: *For the Year 754*, § LXIV, vol. V, p. 449] that Pope Stephen II, who is said to have issued a bull [Note: *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, Instruments, col. 43] at that same monastery of Figeac on 7 November, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 755, indiction 7, and the fourth year of the pontificate of Pope Stephen II, was not in Gaul in that same year, 755.

If the consecration is moved back to the preceding year, when Stephen actually stayed in Gaul, the difficulty is not removed. For it is established that Pope Stephen, leaving Paris, proceeded directly through the Alps into Italy and was at Rome in January of the year 755.

Moreover, the bull of Pope Stephen itself, supposedly given at Cahors, contains certain features that do not accord with the style of the eighth century [Col. 1207C]. For the cited bull says:

> “Furthermore, no archbishop, bishop, or cardinal shall have the power to excommunicate him [the abbot of Figeac], except the Roman Pontiff alone.”

Although the dignity and pre-eminence of the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church are very ancient, it nevertheless seems to belong to later centuries for cardinals to be mentioned by this special designation. From this, too, the Figeac bull appears certainly to have undergone some interpolation.

10. The diploma of King Pippin is also cited [Note: [Col. 1207D] D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 319]: “given in the same place”—that is, in the monastery of Figeac—“on the sixth day before the Ides of November, in the year 755 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the ninth indiction.” But since in this charter the king says that, “in the presence of the lord Pope Stephen, he had beheld the monastery of Figeac miraculously consecrated by God,” the same objections seem applicable against King Pippin’s charter as were brought against Pope Stephen’s bull: namely, that there is no trace of Pope Stephen’s journey toward Aquitaine, and that no suitable time can be found, whether we consider the year 754 or the following year. Nevertheless, the subsequent bulls of various Roman [Col. 1208A] pontiffs seem to remove such blemishes, since they base the new privileges granted to the monks of Figeac upon Stephen’s original bull. Hence the authors of *Gallia Christiana* say [Note: [Col. 1207D] Vol. I, *Instruments*, col. 43] that “nothing should be taken away from the authority of Stephen’s letters.”

Yet the bulls cited are themselves rightly considered suspect. First, a bull of Pope Paschal I from the year 822 is cited [Note: [Col. 1207D] Ibid.], in which it is said that “the monastery called Conques” should be under the governance of Aymar “as it formerly was,” and that he should restore it “to its prioral dignity, since it has been destroyed.” But this is wholly contrary to what is found in the *Life of Louis the Pious*, written by a contemporary known as the Astronomer. For in that work [Note: [Col. 1208D] D. Bouquet, vol. VI, p. 95] the monastery of Conques is counted among the many monasteries repaired by Louis the Pious, indeed among those built from their foundations.

The contemporary account is corroborated by a diploma of the same Louis [Note: [Col. 1208D] *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, col. 236], “given on the sixth day before the Ides of April, in the sixth year, by the favor of Christ, of the empire of our lord Louis, most excellent Augustus, in the twelfth indiction. Issued at the royal palace of Aachen.” Now, in this sixth year of Louis, that is, in the year of Christ 820, it is said that a church was built there in honor of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ; Medrald is named as abbot; and a congregation continually increasing in number is mentioned, which eventually began to serve under the Rule of Saint Benedict. None of this at all agrees with what is said to have been written two years later by Paschal I.

Nor can the rescript of Urban II, cited by Guillaume de la Croix [Note: [Col. 1208D] *Series of the Bishops of Cahors*, p. 56], come to the aid of the aforementioned bulls. After an opening very similar to that of Paschal’s bull, the pope grants a plenary indulgence [Col. 1208C] to the church of Figeac. For it is addressed to Stephen, bishop of Cahors, although it is established that in the year of Christ 1093, when the bull is said to have been issued, not some Stephen but Gerald II occupied the see of Cahors, as the authors of *Gallia Christiana* prove [Note: [Col. 1208D] Vol. I, cols. 127–128].

I therefore believe that all these bulls are forged, and forged for this reason: a dispute had arisen between the monks of Figeac and Conques concerning the primacy of one monastery over the other. In their defense the monks of Figeac cited, besides the aforesaid letters of Pope Stephen and King Pippin, a diploma of the same prince, in which [Note: [Col. 1208D] Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, book XXVII, § III, vol. II, p. 395] “the hermits of Conques were commended to the abbot of Figeac, so that from his abundance he might supply their want; and because they lived in exceedingly rough, difficult, and very confined places, they were to have their head in a spacious and pleasant place, where their bodies might both be relieved from labor and refreshed after hardship.”

Then the following is added concerning the election of the abbot:

“When the abbot of these men—that is, of the monks of Figeac—dies, for as long as they are able to find one among themselves, let them elect from their own number someone who can govern them according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. But if someone among the hermits of Conques should appear better suited to them, let them not disdain to take a father for themselves from there; yet in such a way that the reverence due to the abbacy be reserved to the earlier monastery, namely Figeac, while the dignity of the priory remain at Conques.”

Thus far the Figeac monks. But the monks of Conques sing an entirely different song. They produce a diploma issued by Pippin, king of Aquitaine and son of Louis the Pious [Note: [Col. 1209D] Bosc, *Memoirs Concerning the History of Rouergue*, vol. III, p. 153], on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, in the first indiction, in the twenty-fifth year of the empire of Louis Caesar Augustus and the twenty-second year of our reign”—that is, in the year 838.

In this charter it is said:

“Meanwhile it pleased our serenity that, since the same monastery of Conques is situated in difficult and exceedingly rough places, so that, because of its confinement, it obstructs the habitation of many, and because of the roughness of the site prevents provisions from being brought there, a monastery should be built in a place called Figeac, which we have nevertheless decided henceforth to call New Conques, so that, once that place has been relieved [sic] of the hardship and scarcity involved in transporting provisions, those dwelling there may serve God more freely and pleasantly . . .; yet in such a way that the dignity of the priory and the reverence due to antiquity be reserved to the earlier monastery, Conques.”

These statements certainly cannot stand together with the assertions of the monks of Figeac, since they plainly contradict one another. In the meantime, it is not my task to settle this tangled dispute. It is enough to observe that some forger lies behind it. In my judgment, the diploma of Conques flows with sufficient clarity, and it employs a wording that does not seem suited to deciding the controversy—for example, the expression “dignity of the priory,” which the monks of Figeac cleverly twisted to serve their own cause.

Urban II finally settled this unpleasant dispute at the Council of Nemausus in the year 1097, when he left both monasteries [Col. 1209C] to their own rights [Note: [Col. 1209D] Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, third century, part II, p. 448; and *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, *Instruments*, p. 44]. But enough of this. We must return to our Saint Ambrose.

11. As we have seen, nothing can be deduced from the records of Figeac for determining the time when Saint Ambrose withdrew into a solitude unknown to everyone. Indeed, the date seems to have to be postponed until the year of Christ 760, when Waifarius, duke of Aquitaine, began to rebel against King Pippin because, as Ademar says in his *Chronicle* [Note: [Col. 1209D] Labbe, *Library of Manuscripts*, vol. II, p. 137], he was unwilling to submit to the rights of the churches.

It was probably around that time that our saint, weary of fruitless labor among an unteachable people and of the continual seizure of the goods of his Church, sought solitude. It must also be considered that the Saint ought previously to have cultivated his flock for several years before he could lawfully lay down the episcopal burden on account of the people’s stubbornness. Hence it is altogether likely that the Saint withdrew around the year 759, as more recent writers maintain, among them Baillet.

Taking advantage of this occasion, the lawyer Cathala-Cothure, in his *History of the Region of Cahors* [Note: [Col. 1210D] *History of Quercy*, vol. I, p. 82], condemns from his tripod the conduct of Saint Ambrose as though it were abnormal and contrary to right reason. Here are his words, rendered into Latin:

“Even in that century examples of this kind of imprudent fervor were still to be seen. Men abandoned essential duties without remorse in order to pursue chosen austerities which, the more unusual they were, the more they both harmed and attracted people, while they carried the ignorant populace away in admiration. This conduct of Saint Ambrose, although praiseworthy in itself, is remote from our customs and would provoke laughter. Yet how many there are even today who, because of the talents with which they are endowed and the offices they hold, could administer the commonwealth excellently, but frustrate the hopes of nature and indeed of humanity when they devote themselves to pursuits that they prefer to the public good? So true is it that human beings of every age are, with scarcely any exception, perfectly like one another!”

Such are the words of the lawyer Cathala-Cothure.

[Col. 1210B] 12. If we cite these words and append a brief refutation, it is not because we consider the book of our lawyer so celebrated that it could be dangerous. But since the same things repeatedly appear here that, in the manner of the eighteenth century, were sung everywhere by all who affected novelty, and since they are still treated in ordinary conversation and in published books, it will be worthwhile briefly to refute what has been said here, so that truth may have its proper place.

First, the lawyer Cathala reproaches Saint Ambrose for hiding himself in solitude after laying down his episcopal office. He calls such conduct imprudent; that is, he says that the Saint ought to have been troubled in conscience because he preferred voluntary austerities to his official duty. Yet the lawyer ought to have known from canon law—for it is not permissible for a jurist to be ignorant of the law—that the stubbornness or wickedness of the people entrusted to a pastor is numbered among the legitimate causes of resignation.

For these words are read in chapter 10, “On Resignation” (1, 9):

“Because of the wickedness of the people, a prelate is sometimes compelled to withdraw from governing them, when the people are so stiff-necked that he can make no progress among them; rather, because of their stubbornness, the more earnestly he strives, the more they are permitted, by a just judgment, to fail, as the Lord says through the Prophet [Note: [Col. 1210D] Ezekiel 3:26]: ‘I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth . . . because they are a rebellious house.’ And the Apostles are read to have said to the Jews [Note: [Col. 1210D] Acts 13:46; the Vulgate is slightly different: ‘Since you reject it—that is, the word—and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn,’ etc.]: ‘Behold, we turn to the Gentiles, because you have made yourselves unworthy of the word of God.’

“Nevertheless, a pastor ought not to abandon his flock for every fault, lest he be compared with the hireling who sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees. But with the permission of his superior, he may then, not so much flee timidly as prudently withdraw, when the sheep are transformed into wolves; and when those who ought humbly to obey begin to contradict irrevocably. Although such people must be severely punished for their crime, they must nevertheless for a time be tolerated for the sake of utility; for he draws blood who squeezes too hard.”

The canon cited appears to portray Saint Ambrose in his true colors, amid a people unwilling to hear their pastor. The blessed man therefore rightly withdrew from the wickedness [Col. 1211A] of an unteachable people.

Around the same time Saint Ado presents a similar abandonment of a see in his *Chronicle* [Note: [Col. 1211D] Pertz, *Monuments of German History*, vol. II, p. 319]:

“When the Franks, with a sufficiently furious and insane policy, were turning the sacred possessions of the churches to their own uses, Wilicarius, seeing his Church of Vienne being dishonorably humiliated, abandoned the episcopate and entered the monastery of the holy martyrs of Agaunum, where he led a venerable life. After the province of Vienne and Lyon had been devastated and laid waste, both Churches remained without bishops for several years, while laymen sacrilegiously and barbarously retained the sacred possessions of the Churches.”

Wilicarius left his Church because it had been devastated. In addition to this circumstance, the stubbornness of the people and the certain hope of obtaining a successor in the episcopate encouraged our Saint to flee into solitude. Therefore, if in similar circumstances today some bishop, having laid aside his episcopal insignia, were to seek solitude, that action would be entirely consistent with good conduct and would not merely provoke laughter; it would also provide the people of our own time with the greatest edification.

13. But when the lawyer Cathala, in astonishment, further declares that this kind of weakness of mind still persists, it seems at first sight that one must conclude that the matter cannot arouse such admiration merely by its frequency. For since, as he himself admits, that error has always existed and everywhere, it must be attributed to the very character of Christianity.

How, then, does our lawyer dare, with such peremptory authority as a private individual, to condemn what has been approved by the judgment of every age? The lawyer must therefore be accused of feigning admiration so that he might at least indirectly attack those institutions of the Church that were especially devoted to prayer and contemplation, and that were most violently assailed at the time—namely, in 1785—when the author composed his *History of the Region of Cahors.

Hence he says that nature, and indeed humanity, is frustrated in its hopes whenever someone applies himself to chosen pursuits that are less useful to the commonwealth. By these words he points to those devoted to the monastic life, whom he portrays as occupied with frivolous matters—as though spending one’s life in continual prayer and wearing down one’s body with austerities were frivolous.

But those who have even touched the primary principles of the Christian religion with their fingertips know that human affairs depend upon prayer to God. It is therefore useful both to individuals and to the whole commonwealth that there should always be people who pray everywhere, “lifting up holy hands” [Note: [Col. 1211D] 1 Timothy 2:8], so that the scourges of divine wrath may be averted, perseverance may be granted to the just, and amendment of life to sinners.

Saint Augustine certainly recognized this usefulness of the anchorites in book I, chapter 31, of *The Morals of the Catholic Church* [Note: [Col. 1212D] Vol. I of the works, p. 710, Paris edition, 1779]:

“I will say nothing about those who, completely withdrawn from the sight of all human beings, live in the most deserted lands, content with bread alone, which is brought to them at fixed intervals, and with water; who enjoy converse with God, to whom they have clung with pure minds, and who are most blessed in contemplating that beauty which cannot be perceived except by the understanding of the saints.

“I will say nothing, I repeat, about these people. For to some they seem to have abandoned human affairs more than they ought, because those people do not understand how greatly their spirit benefits us through prayers, and how greatly their life benefits us as an example, although we are not permitted to see their bodies. But I consider it lengthy and superfluous to discuss this matter. For how can that exceptionally lofty summit of holiness, which anyone who sees it does not spontaneously regard with wonder and honor, be made visible by our speech?

“They need only be admonished who vainly boast that the temperance and continence of the most holy Christians of the Catholic faith have advanced so far that they seem to some people to require restriction and to be recalled, as it were, within human limits—so far have their minds risen above humanity, in the judgment even of those who dislike this.”

Thus speaks Saint Augustine, very appropriately refuting our lawyer.

[Col. 1212B] 14. But if Cathala the lawyer rejects these arguments because they are drawn from the inmost principles of the Catholic religion, let him, I beg, attend to the fact that monasticism is useful not only because it preserves the evangelical precepts and counsels intact and encourages others to a holier life, but also because it greatly benefits civil society.

To say nothing here of how much assistance monks once contributed to the spread of agriculture and the preservation of the sciences and arts, no one who looks attentively at the present condition of affairs will deny that even in our own age it would be desirable for more people to pursue solitude.

Such is the condition of our times that nearly everyone who has learned even a little literature readily believes himself born for everything. Nothing seems so lofty or difficult that he does not hope to attain it with a light touch. One thing often prevents him from reaching the goal he desires with the most ardent wishes: namely, a limited household income or one burdened with debt, which closes every path to honors and pleasures.

Hence such people devise everything and undertake everything so that they may finally possess wealth. No path to acquiring it is easier than that by which, once the commonwealth has been thrown into disorder, they can seize the fortunes of others without difficulty. They covet the wealth of others, which they want to make their own without labor, and they attempt in every way to scrape it together.

Who does not clearly see that, in these troubled times, the peace and tranquility of the state would be best served if there were monasteries to which the young could run—young people burdensome to themselves, a disgrace to their families, and hostile to society as a whole?

There they might mortify their bodies with hunger, vigils, and even astonishing austerities; or, if they preferred, devoted to idleness, they might play with anagrams, chronograms, or other literary toys of that kind. Certainly they themselves would then rest to the greatest benefit of both commonwealths, and would allow their fellow citizens to enjoy tranquility. In a word, it would be immensely useful simply that they should not do harm.

Today we see so many leaders of impiety threatening their fellow citizens with ruin and destruction—men who harass, disturb, and attempt to overthrow the commonwealth—who, if they were monks, would lead a harmless, even if perhaps useless, life [Note: [Col. 1212D] De Maistre, *On the Pope*, book III, chapter XI].

So true is it—if I may set our own epiphonema against Cathala’s—that otherwise energetic men, from minute and fabricated circumstances, forge principles which, if put into practice, produce the gravest evils, to be suffered not merely by one person but sometimes by an entire kingdom. Enough has been said concerning the opinions of the lawyer Cathala.

§ III. The opinion of Casimir Oudinus is examined: he makes Saint Ambrose of Cahors the author of the books *On the Mysteries* and *On the Sacraments*, commonly attributed to Saint Ambrose of Milan.

Casimir Oudinus held the singular opinion [Note: [Col. 1213D] *On Ancient Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, col. 1827 ff.] that the treatises *On the Mysteries* and *On the Sacraments*, formerly commonly published under the name of Saint Ambrose of Milan and Doctor of the Church, should be attributed to our Saint Ambrose.

Although we do not wish to detract in any way from the glory of the saints whose lives we are composing, we would nevertheless fail in our duty and in the reverence owed to the saints if we tried to adorn them with the spoils of others.

Nor did Oudinus advance his opinion with the aim of increasing the praise of Saint Ambrose of Cahors through these treatises. Rather, as a crafty man, he wished to tear down these most powerful monuments of Catholic tradition. For he knew that they would lose much of their authority if they were shown to be not only four centuries more recent but also published by some obscure bishop, who is even called a rhapsodist.

It will therefore be worthwhile to examine the singular opinion of this apostate writer and to refute it insofar as the purpose of this work requires. Oudinus supports his view principally with the following arguments. First, he asserts that one and the same author composed both the treatise *On the Mysteries* and the six treatises *On the Sacraments*. Upon this assertion, as upon a firm foundation, he then builds another conjecture: that this writer was not the bishop of Milan, Saint Ambrose, but must altogether have been some Gallic bishop who should be placed between the years 774 and 800. From this, according to Oudinus, it follows almost automatically that no other author can be assigned to these treatises than Saint Ambrose, bishop of Cahors.

Oudinus gathers various arguments to prove these opinions, and they must now be carefully examined, lest the same labor have to be repeated on 7 December, when Saint Ambrose of Milan will be discussed.

16. The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, in the new edition of Saint Ambrose’s works that they prepared in 1688, affirm without qualification that the holy bishop of Milan is the author of the book *On the Mysteries* [Note: [Col. 1213D] Vol. V of the works, pp. 177 ff., Venetian edition]. But they subsequently write that, in their view, the author of the treatises *On the Sacraments* is different from Saint Ambrose, who is the author of the book *On the Sacraments* [Note: [Col. 1213D] Ibid., p. 199]. The Venetian editors of 1781 adopted the same opinion and confirmed it by their judgment; it is their edition that we are using in the present dissertation.

Oudinus says that they borrowed this opinion [Col. 1214A] from Albertinus, a heterodox theologian, while suppressing his name. Albertinus, in book II, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, chapter 1, had concluded with these words, which we transcribe from Oudinus himself [Note: [Col. 1214D] In the cited passage]:

“Let readers therefore judge whether it is foolish to doubt the author of these books *On the Sacraments*, as Bellarmine rashly declares, or whether, on the contrary, it is unjust to wish to attribute them to him. Among the opponents themselves—that is, among Catholics—Arnoldus, citing them in part I, chapter 13, *On Frequent Communion*, says: ‘If they are indeed by Ambrose.’ I believe that they are by a seventh-century author, pieced together from Ambrose’s treatise *On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries*, and attributed to Ambrose because of their similarity, since the name of the rhapsodist was unknown.”

Whether the Benedictine editors discerned by their own acumen that the two works did not have one and the same author, or borrowed that opinion from the aforementioned Albertinus or from Godefridus Hermant, author of the *Life of Saint Ambrose of Milan*, makes little difference. The only matter to be examined here is by what force of reasoning Oudinus was led to this opinion and defended it with such zeal.

He confirms his view with four arguments, which must be considered in turn. The first is that “in many manuscripts the books *On the Mysteries* and *On the Sacraments* are found joined together under Ambrose’s name;” the second is based on the similarity of style in both works; the third on the uniformity of a certain distinctive doctrine; and the fourth, finally, on the connection that exists among these various treatises. Thus, just as the second book *On the Sacraments* calls for the first, so also the treatise *On the Sacraments* necessarily presupposes that the book *On the Mysteries* had already been delivered.

The Benedictine editors already confronted the first difficulty in their learned preface, which they placed before the books *On the Sacraments* [Note: [Col. 1214D] Vol. V of the works, p. 204]. Since many ancient writers were cited who attributed these books to Ambrose, the editors replied:

“Those writers did not themselves examine the matter—that is, who the author of the books was—independently and deliberately. Rather, they either followed one another, or trusted their manuscripts, in which they found the same little work inscribed in one place with the name of Ambrose and in another joined to a treatise bearing the same title. For since the oldest manuscripts generally display no author’s name, those who undertook to copy them, knowing that Ambrose had written on this very subject, did not hesitate to assign them to him. Others, although they did not think the books were Ambrosian, nevertheless judged that they should be appended to the book *On the Mysteries* because of the similarity of their subject.”

The aforementioned Albertinus accepts this final explanation as correct: the two treatises are found almost everywhere joined together because the books *On the Sacraments* were pieced together from the book *On the Mysteries* and therefore closely resemble it.

This same argument easily explains why Ratramnus called the book *On the Mysteries* the first book *On the Sacraments*. See Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, fourth century, part I, chapter 6, article 26 [Note: [Col. 1215D] Vol. IV, p. 313, Venetian edition, 1778].

17. The difficulty drawn from the similarity of style is resolved in the same way. Some have admitted this similarity, as can be seen in Oudinus, chapter 1, no. 3. Others have denied it, including the Benedictine editors [Note: [Col. 1215D] Vol. V of Saint Ambrose’s works, p. 207], Tillemont [Note: [Col. 1215D] *Memoirs for Use in Ecclesiastical History*, vol. X, p. 765, note LXII, on Saint Ambrose] in the *Ecclesiastical Monuments*, who also cites Cardinal Bona, *Liturgical Matters*, book I, chapter 7; D. Ceillier, *Ecclesiastical Authors* [Note: [Col. 1215D] *Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. XVII, chapter 4, § 14, p. 487]; and even heterodox writers.

For Albertinus, when he says that the books *On the Sacraments* [Note: [Col. 1215D] Ambrose’s works, vol. V, p. 200] “teem with barbarisms, contain many things—some of them ridiculous and utterly unworthy of Ambrosian dignity, and some even mutually inconsistent and contradictory,” did not, I say, acknowledge any similarity of style between the two works.

There is nevertheless some similarity between them, namely whenever the author of the books *On the Sacraments* takes something from the book *On the Mysteries*, except where he occasionally corrupts it excessively. But whenever he attempts to fly, as the saying goes, on his own wings, he is entirely unlike the true Ambrose. Those cold and childish questions that occur in the books *On the Sacraments* are nowhere sprinkled through the genuine works of Ambrose of Milan.

As for what the adversary says about the similarity of a distinctive doctrine concerning the washing of feet, this has long since been refuted. What, indeed, is so distinctive about it? That the feet are washed after baptism? Yet it is noted that this was done both at Milan and elsewhere, by Basnage himself [Note: [Col. 1216D] Preface to Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, chapter 5, § 35, vol. I, p. 57] in his edition of Canisius’s *Readings*, and by Cornelius a Lapide in his commentary on John, chapter XIII, verse 1, where he cites Gabriel Vásquez. The same is also attested by C. Chardon [Note: [Col. 1216D] *History of the Sacraments*, vol. V, p. 351] in his *History of the Sacraments*, and by many others.

But, they say, the author of the book *On the Mysteries*, chapter 6, “asserts that hereditary sins are removed by the washing of the feet, while personal sins are remitted through baptism.” To this corresponds what is said in book III, chapter 1, *On the Sacraments* [Note: [Col. 1216D] Ambrose’s works, vol. V, p. 222]:

“Yet there are some who say and attempt to excuse the matter by arguing that this should not be done as a mystery, nor in baptism, nor in regeneration; rather, the feet should be washed as those of a guest”—an explanation that is nevertheless suggested in the Gothic Missal and in the ancient Gallican Missal [Note: [Col. 1216D] Joseph Maria Thomasius, *Sacramental Code*, pp. 335 and 475]. “One thing concerns humility; another concerns sanctification. Finally, hear that sanctification is a mystery: ‘Unless I wash your feet, you will have no part with me’ (John XIII) . . . Because Adam was tripped up by the devil and poison was poured over his feet, you wash the feet so that, in the part where the serpent lay in wait, a greater aid of sanctification may be added, so that afterward it cannot trip you up.”

The author of the book *On the Mysteries* has been more than sufficiently vindicated from every error in the note that the Benedictine editors appended to the passage cited. In a similar manner, the author of the books *On the Sacraments* is freed from blame. His own words sufficiently indicate in what sense he said that the washing of the feet is a mystery established for sanctification.

For, first, if he had believed that sin was removed through the washing of the feet, then, when he objected that “the Roman Church does not have this custom,” he would certainly have accused that Church of a serious and extremely damnable error. Why, then, does he immediately add: “whose type and form we follow in everything”? Why does he offer as the reason for this omission: “Perhaps it has departed from it because of the multitude”? Certainly he would not have offered such a reason if he had believed that the washing of the feet was a sacrament instituted for the remission of original sin. Finally, he would not have added: “I say this not because I blame others”—which he ought to have done if the matter concerned the neglect of a sacrament of the greatest necessity—“but that I may commend my own duties.”

[Col. 1216B] 18. The author’s own words most clearly vindicate him from every serious error. For shortly afterward, explaining the words, “The one who has bathed does not need to wash again, except to wash his feet,” he says:

“Why is this? Because in baptism every fault is washed away. The fault therefore departs. But because Adam was tripped up by the devil and poison was poured over his feet, you wash the feet so that, in the part where the serpent lay in wait, a greater aid of sanctification may be added, so that afterward it cannot trip you up. You wash the feet, therefore, so that you may wash away the serpent’s poisons. It also contributes to humility, so that in the mystery we are not ashamed of what we disdain in service.”

In precise words the author says that every fault is washed away in baptism—or, in the language of the Council of Trent, session V, canon 5, “everything that possesses the true and proper character of sin is removed.” “But that concupiscence, or the tinder of sin, remains in those who have been baptized, this holy synod confesses and maintains . . . . This concupiscence, which the Apostle sometimes calls sin, the holy synod declares that the Catholic Church has never understood to be truly and properly sin, but rather so called because it is from sin and inclines toward sin.”

Therefore, once every fault has been washed away, aid for sanctification is supplied against this evil—that is, heavenly grace. Through its help, as the Council of Trent says in the same place, concupiscence “cannot harm those who do not consent to it but resist it manfully; indeed, whoever fights lawfully will be crowned.”

From this, then, the supposed distinctiveness of the doctrine that some have attributed to both works disappears entirely. The third argument with which Oudinus attempted to support his opinion therefore collapses.

19. But now Oudinus brings openly into the arena his Achilles, which, as he himself says, no one can break [Note: [Col. 1216D] *On Ancient Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, col. 1835], and which was therefore probably “concealed by the Benedictine editors” so that they could make their distinction between the treatise *On the Mysteries* and the six books *On the Sacraments* more plausible.

Oudinus calls the treatise *On the Mysteries* one of the books written *On the Sacraments*, and he does so for two reasons: first, so that the number of sermons may be seven; and second, so that certain words in the first book *On the Sacraments* may receive a convenient interpretation.

The answer to both points is easy. For there seems to be no necessity for admitting seven books or sermons. Even if it is granted that an entire week was spent instructing the newly baptized, it by no means follows that Easter Sunday was not too busy a day for a sermon to be delivered.

But even if that necessity were admitted, it still would not follow that the book *On the Mysteries* should be attached to the treatises *On the Sacraments*. For it is reasonable to suspect that there were formerly seven sermons, as can be seen in the Benedictine editors’ preface toward its end [Note: [Col. 1217D] Ambrose, vol. V, p. 208] and in note B to book VI, chapter 5, [Col. 1217B] no. 25 [Note: [Col. 1217D] Ibid., p. 246]. But on this hypothesis, because the sermon that would have to be called the seventh is shorter, it would seem somewhat truncated.

Whatever may be thought of this conjecture, the author of the books *On the Sacraments* begins the first book in such a way as plainly to show that he is then beginning to discuss the sacraments for the first time. Here are his words:

“I begin a discourse on the sacraments that you have received. It was not appropriate to offer an explanation of this matter beforehand.”

And although elsewhere he always connects the following sermon with the preceding one, either in explicit words or by repetition, in the first sermon *On the Sacraments* he says absolutely nothing that even slightly suggests that he had delivered an entire treatise on the mysteries the day before.

“But,” says Oudinus [Note: [Col. 1217D] *On Ancient Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, col. 1834], “let us see whether the first book—that is, the book *On the Mysteries*—is recalled by the second—that is, by the first book *On the Sacraments*—for there is no doubt about the others.”

These are the words of the second sermon, otherwise known as the book *On the Sacraments*:

“And behold, as a dove, the Holy Spirit descended. It was not a dove that descended, but something like a dove. Remember what I said: Christ assumed flesh, not something like flesh, but the truth of this flesh; he truly assumed flesh. The Holy Spirit, however, descended in the form of a dove, not in the reality of a dove, but in the form of a dove.”

Oudinus says that the author is alluding to the sermon which he calls the first, *On the Mysteries*. But we interpret the words “Remember what I said” as having been spoken to sharpen the attention of those present—namely, so that they might correctly understand the difference between “a dove” and “something like a dove,” which he develops through a certain analogy drawn from the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1217D], as is clear to the reader.

### 20

Oudinus assigns these words an entirely different meaning. He asserts that the words “remember what I said” must be referred to the book *On the Mysteries*, specifically chapter 4, which he quotes at length. Yet I judge that the hearers would be all the less likely to find there what Oudinus says is concealed in that passage, and I assert that this would be still more difficult even for sharp-eyed readers equipped with a commentary. And lest I seem to be practicing deception here, these are the words of Saint Ambrose to which the author of the books *On the Sacraments* is said to have alluded while commenting on John 1:32 [Note: [Col. 1218D] Ambrose, vol. V, p. 188]: [Col. 1218A]

> “Because I saw the Spirit descending like a dove.”

He says:

> “And here, why did the Spirit descend like a dove, unless so that you might see, unless so that you might recognize that even that dove which righteous Noah sent out from the ark was a likeness of this dove, so that you might recognize the type of the sacrament? Perhaps you will say: Since that was a true dove which was sent out, whereas here he descended as if a dove, how do we say that there he was a likeness and here the reality, when according to the Greeks it is written that the Spirit descended in the form of a dove? (The Greek text of Luke 7:22 has: Καταβῆναι τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον σωματικῷ εἴδει, ὡσεὶ περιστερὰν, ἐπ’ αὐτόν, ‘the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form, like a dove, upon him.’) But what is as true as the Divinity, which always remains? A creature, however, cannot be the reality, but only a form, which is easily dissolved [Col. 1218B] and changed. Likewise, because in those who are baptized there ought not to be a mere form but true simplicity . . . . . Yet we read that the form is also to be taken for the reality, both concerning Christ: ‘And being found in form as a man’; and concerning God the Father: ‘Nor have you seen his form.’”

When the two passages cited are compared, it becomes evident that the author of the books *On the Sacraments*, when he says “remember what I said,” could not have been pointing to the passage cited from the book *On the Mysteries*. Consequently, the treatise *On the Sacraments* in no way contradicts the book *On the Mysteries*.

### 21

Having refuted the arguments of our critic, it is fitting to show that various considerations indicate that the two works have different authors. First of all, the baptismal ceremonies employed by the two bishops differ from one another. For the author of the books *On the Sacraments*, book [lacuna], [Col. 1218C] chapter 1 [Note: [Col. 1218D] Ibid., p. 209], asks at length why the nostrils of the person being baptized are touched, whereas Saint Ambrose says nothing of the sort in his book *On the Mysteries*, chapter 1; he merely says that the touching of the mouth is omitted in the case of women.

Saint Ambrose then has in his book *On the Mysteries*, chapter 4:

> “After this, of course, you ascended to the priest. Consider what followed: was it not what David says, ‘Like ointment on the head, which ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron’? (Psalm 132:2.)”

By these words the saint indicates that the sacrament of confirmation had been conferred. After the sacred seal of confirmation comes the washing of the feet:

> “We are all anointed for the kingdom of God and for the priesthood with spiritual grace. You ascended from the font; remember the Gospel reading. For our Lord Jesus washed the feet of his disciples, etc.”

Then [Col. 1218D] he concludes the entire passage with these words:

> “After this you received white garments, etc.”

But the author who composed the books *On the Sacraments* completes the ceremonies of baptism in an entirely different order. For in book III, chapter 1 [Note: [Col. 1218D] Ibid., p. 222], after baptism, without any intervening rite, comes the washing of the feet:

> “You ascended from the font; what followed? . . . . . The high priest, girded, washed your feet, etc.”

In the following chapter, after explaining the washing of the feet:

> “The spiritual seal follows, which you heard read today, etc.”

Everyone can see how different this order of ceremonies is from the Ambrosian order.

Oudinus does indeed contend [Col. 1219A] [Note: [Col. 1219D] *Script.*, vol. I, col. 1854 and following] that this passage either does or could concern the presbyteral anointing administered to the newly baptized by a priest of the second order, anointing which, having been introduced after Saint Gregory the Great, would indicate an author later than the seventh century. But even granting Oudinus’s argument—which I in no way approve—the essential point remains: the two treatises differ in the order and sequence of their rites.

Other considerations could be added in confirmation of our argument, such as the differing versions of Sacred Scripture, anointing before the renunciation, the beginning of the sacrifice of the Holy Mass, and so forth. All these things show that the two treatises do not have one and the same author.

### 22

With these matters prefaced, we have now covered the middle ground. It remains to show that, although the books *On the Sacraments* do not seem to be attributed to Saint Ambrose of Milan, they ought certainly not to be attributed to Saint Ambrose of Cahors. Once this has been established, it will become clear that he is not the author of the treatise *On the Mysteries* either—unless one wishes to say that the copy is older than the original.

The arguments by which Oudinus attempts to support his singular opinion are of two kinds: first, because the names were identical, Ambrose of Milan could easily have been confused with Ambrose of Cahors, chapter 6, no. 2 [Note: [Col. 1219D] *Script.*, vol. I, col. 1858]; second, all the characteristics found in these little works can be applied especially well to Saint Ambrose of Cahors, ibid., no. 3 [Note: [Col. 1219D] Ibid., col. 1860].

But, I ask, at what time did this confusion of names arise? Oudinus suggests that it could have arisen between the eighth and twelfth centuries, since he says at the cited place [Col. 1219C]:

> “The manuscript codices found in great numbers in libraries are either anonymous or bear simply the name Ambrose or Saint Ambrose, and none add or specify that he was bishop or archbishop of Milan. Nor, so far as I know, did anyone before Alger and Hugh of Saint Victor, writing in the middle of the twelfth century, expressly cite anything under the name of Ambrose, archbishop of Milan.”

I could readily concede that these works were not expressly attributed to the holy bishop of Milan. But what follows from that? Shall we therefore attribute them to the bishop of Cahors? And especially when it is already clear that in the ninth century the bishop of Milan was intended, as is sufficiently established from Saint Paschasius Radbertus’s treatise *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, in the preface [Note: [Col. 1219D] *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XIX, p. 730].

No sensible person will doubt that Paschasius is speaking of Ambrose of Milan in the following words:

> “But in order that your youthful understanding may read these things more securely, dearest son, I have thought it fitting to note at the beginning the Catholic teachers of the Church. From among the many, we have, as it were, strained out a little milk of tenderness: namely Cyprian, Ambrose, Hilary, Augustine, John, Jerome, Isidore, Hesychius, and Bede.”

Anyone who doubted that Paschasius here meant Cyprian of Carthage, Hilary of Poitiers, and Augustine of Hippo would be said to be looking for a knot in a rush. Who, then, will deny that Ambrose of Milan is also meant here—especially since he is placed among the cited teachers of the Church in something like chronological order? [Col. 1220A]

This argument is strengthened by the fact that Paschasius Radbertus, when writing his treatise around the year 831—as is clear from the exile of Abbot Wala—and therefore, according to Oudinus’s chronology, scarcely thirty years after the death of Saint Ambrose of Cahors [Note: [Col. 1220D] See *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. IV, p. 138], would not have placed his name among the teachers mentioned above if Ambrose of Cahors, then scarcely known, could have been understood.

### 23

The same consideration applies to Ratramnus, who calls his Ambrose “the holy Doctor,” a designation that does not simply fit our recently deceased Ambrose of Cahors. But since Ratramnus appears to have cited only the book *On the Mysteries*, there is no need to dwell on the matter.

Indeed, Oudinus himself seems to surrender to the victorious truth when, near the end of the cited no. 2 [Note: [Col. 1220D] *Script.*, vol. I, col. 1839], he says:

> “Thus Paschasius and Ratramnus, when they read, together with those who followed them, the name of Ambrose the bishop or Saint Ambrose, and did not know Ambrose, bishop of Cahors, either by reputation or by name, carelessly and inattentively supposed these treatises to be by Ambrose of Milan.”

He repeats the same point near the end of the cited no. 3, lest it escape memory:

> “Already in the ninth century, in the time of Ratramnus and Paschasius, these little works were believed to belong to the archbishop of Milan and were cited by both as his genuine works.”

Oudinus therefore admits that when Paschasius and Ratramnus name Ambrose, they are to be understood as referring to the bishop of Milan. Why, then, does he say that no one expressly cited these treatises under the name of the archbishop of Milan, if they wrote in such a way that they could refer to no other bishop?

All danger of confusion is therefore absent when the name Ambrose or Saint Ambrose, without any further title, is placed before these treatises. For, according to Oudinus himself, it is established that the bishop of Milan is intended.

The matter is finally settled by what John Mabillon reports in his *Museum Italicum*, vol. I, part II [Note: [Col. 1220D] pp. 4 and 7]: that in the monastery of Saint Gall there is a codex written in large letters a thousand years ago. Since Mabillon published his book in 1687, it follows that the treatise *On the Sacraments* already existed before the time of Saint Ambrose of Cahors.

Oudinus presses his argument at the cited place [Col. 1220D] on the ground that a work *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues* was attributed to Saint Ambrose of Milan, although it actually belongs to Ambrose Autpert, abbot of Saint Vincent at the Volturno, a writer of the eighth century. Thus, he argues, the treatise of Saint Ambrose of Cahors could likewise have been attributed to the bishop of Milan.

Although an argument drawn from such a similarity is not logically compelling, we reply first that this did not result so much from the ease of confusion as from ignorance of the true author. For the treatise *On the Conflict of Vices* was attributed not only to Saint Ambrose but also to Saints Augustine, Leo, and Isidore, as the editors of the works of Saint Augustine report [Note: [Col. 1221D] vol. VI, *Opera Appendix*, p. 219]. Second, this error became prevalent only after the eleventh century, for the chronicler of Saint Vincent expressly asserts that Autpert composed the book *On the Conflict* [Note: [Col. 1221D] *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis sancti Benedicti*, century III, part II, p. 263, no. 7]. It is therefore not surprising that some error gained currency in later centuries.

But concerning Saint Ambrose of Cahors, if we accept Oudinus’s account, his own contemporaries would have attributed the work of another author to him. Let this suffice concerning the alleged ease of confusion.

### 24

Nor is our critic any more successful in judging the similarity of the characteristics, which is the second part of his proof. Oudinus first attempts to show, in chapters 4 and 5 [Note: [Col. 1221D] *Script.*, vol. I, col. 1845] of his dissertation, that “some Gaul was the author of both treatises” [Col. 1221B]:

> “There are three things,” he says, “from which we clearly infer that a Gallic bishop was the author of these treatises or sermons: first, from the washing of the feet of neophytes, which he admits was customary in baptism in the Church; second, from the conformity of the liturgy and of the other rites of the Roman Church in the sacraments, which he likewise embraced; third, from the barbarous Latin Gallicisms with which all these sermons are sprinkled.”

Let us follow the footsteps of our critic, but in a somewhat reversed order.

What he objects concerning barbarous Latin Gallicisms proves too much and therefore proves nothing. It would show that the treatises belong not so much to the eighth or ninth century as to the beginning of the eighteenth, since most of the Gallic expressions that he contrasts with Latin are so characteristic of that age that they were not in use before then and became obsolete afterward.

Moreover, let the reader consult chapter 4, no. 3, where he will sometimes find, in place of the alleged agreement, an obvious difference between the two idioms. He will admit that the phrases cited are no more Gallic idioms than Italian, Spanish, or even German ones.

Finally, Oudinus clings to what is commonly called a false supposition, as though the use of the French language flourished in the eighth century in the form in which it flourishes today. In that century the language used by the inhabitants of Gaul was corrupted Latin mixed with various idioms, especially Germanic [Note: [Col. 1221D] Compare *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. IV, p. 132].

Indeed, even if we granted that the French language in its present form flourished in the Merovingian kingdom, the inference would still not hold for Aquitaine, which until the time of King Pippin—the period in which Saint Ambrose of Cahors lived—was more subject to the Visigoths and Saracens. Oudinus would surely have been more successful if he had identified Arabic or Gothic idioms in the sermons of Saint Ambrose.

### 25

Oudinus further presents the washing of the feet in baptism as a distinctive and peculiar ceremony of the Gallican Church, and from this concludes that both treatises belong to some Gallican bishop. But this has already been refuted above, in no. 17, so it need not be repeated here.

What our critic says about the conformity of the liturgy and of the other sacramental rites of the Roman Church deserves fuller examination. Anyone who runs quickly through the treatises *On the Mysteries* and *On the Sacraments* will easily convince himself that these books belong rather to the fourth or fifth century than to the eighth.

For who, on seeing the strict observance of the discipline of secrecy, the large number of adults to be baptized, the imminent danger of persecution, the discussions concerning language, the refuted heresies of the Arians, Priscillianists, and Macedonians of the fourth and fifth centuries, and other matters of this kind, could persuade himself that these books were written in the middle of the eighth century?

These considerations would be more than sufficient to overthrow Oudinus’s system. But Oudinus reasons from the following words in book III of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 1:

> “We are not unaware that the Roman Church does not have this custom; in everything we follow its type and form.”

In chapter 5, no. 3 [Note: [Col. 1222D] *Script.*, vol. I, col. 1854], he argues:

> “This anonymous Gaul follows the Roman order in all the rites of baptism, except for the washing of the feet, as he expressly states. Since this little work concerning the Roman order was written after the Roman pontiffs had been freed from the yoke of the Lombards through the kings of Gaul, Pippin and Charlemagne, it is clear that the anonymous author who follows and imitates it flourished no earlier than the end of the eighth century.”

This is Oudinus’s conclusion. But the critic abuses the words in which the writer says that he follows the type and form of the Roman Church in everything, as though by these words he were indicating the Roman Order as it existed in the eighth century. For if the writer were to be understood in this sense, he would not have added shortly afterward, as though he possessed authority concerning rites:

> “In everything I desire to follow the Roman Church; nevertheless, we too are human beings and have understanding. Therefore, what is observed more correctly elsewhere, we also preserve more correctly.”

If the Roman Order had already been received with the consent of both authorities, what bishop would have dared to call its rites into question and subject them to his own sole judgment?

### 26

But if we compare the rites of the Roman Order [Note: [Col. 1222D] *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XIII, p. 639] with those described in the books *On the Sacraments*, we shall see that there is a great difference between them. Only a few points need be noted here, lest the discussion become too long.

In the books *On the Sacraments* there is no mention of the litanies, the blessing of the paschal candle, or its immersion in the water—all of which are found in the Roman Order [Note: [Col. 1222D] Ibid., p. 693 and following]. The questions taken from the Creed are different, as is the form of confirmation. These points are sufficient to show that the author did not have the Roman Order before his eyes.

Oudinus is pressed still more closely, because in the books cited not even the Gallican Order is presented. From this it follows that the author did not belong to Gaul. For in book I of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 11 [Note: [Col. 1222D] Ambrose, vol. V of the works, p. 210], there is a twofold renunciation by those being baptized, [Col. 1223A] whereas in the ancient Gallican Missal [Note: [Col. 1223D] Thomasi, *Codex Sacramentorum*, p. 475], edited by the Blessed Cardinal Joseph Maria Thomasius, a man distinguished no less for learning than for holiness, there is only one renunciation. The same is true of the Gallican Sacramentary of the seventh century cited by Martène [Note: [Col. 1223D] *De Antiquis Ecclesiae Ritibus*, vol. I, p. 65, Venetian edition, 1783].

In most of the other ritual books of Gaul, however, three renunciations are prescribed, as the cited Martène states. In the eighth century, the custom of a threefold renunciation appears to have prevailed everywhere in Gaul, as is clear from the Council of Leptines in 743 [Note: [Col. 1223D] Harzheim, *Concilia Germaniae*, vol. I, p. 51] and from other documents cited by the distinguished Antonius Binterim, a man worthy of praise for so many reasons, in his learned German work on the antiquities of the Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 1223D] *Denkwürdigkeiten der christlich-katholischen Kirche*, vol. I, part I, p. 94].

### 27

It is useful here to compare another rite customarily observed in the Gallican Church, of which, however, nothing is said in the book *On the Sacraments*.

Saint Gregory of Tours, book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 24 [Note: [Col. 1223D] *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XI, p. 837], says:

> “Then, after sanctifying the water with an exorcism and sprinkling chrism over it, all the people draw water with devotion.”

This sprinkling was customary not only in Spain, about which Gregory is speaking; it can also be seen both in the Gothic [Note: [Col. 1223D] *Codex Sacramentorum*, p. 334] and in the ancient Gallican Missal [Note: [Col. 1223D] Ibid., p. 475], edited by the Blessed Joseph Thomasius mentioned above.

Nevertheless, our author—who, according to Oudinus’s conjecture, was a Gaul—entirely omits this rite in book I of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 1223D] Ambrose, vol. V of the works, p. 213]. For when describing the consecration of the baptismal water, he says nothing about chrism. These are his words:

> “For as soon as the priest enters, he performs an exorcism over the substance of the water; afterward he offers an invocation and prayer, so that the font may be sanctified and the presence of the eternal Trinity may be present.”

The author examines this rite and the others with complete precision. His silence therefore creates a presumption that cannot easily be dismissed: namely, that this Gallican custom did not prevail in his Church.

This is also confirmed by the fact that in the cited passage he is entirely occupied with explaining why Christ descended first and the Holy Spirit came afterward. If the rite involving chrism had been observed, I have no doubt that the author would have alluded to it, since among the holy Fathers the metaphor of chrism in relation to Christ is common.

When the rites described in the books *On the Sacraments* are compared with those found in the ritual books of the Gallican Church, various other differences will appear. From them it will become clear that these sermons cannot be attributed to a Gaul who lived in the eighth century, and therefore must be denied to Saint Ambrose of Cahors.

If, then, the books *On the Sacraments* do not have our Cahorsian saint as their author, how much less can the treatise *On the Mysteries* have him as its author? For, on account of the reasons set out at length by the Benedictine editors in the prologue prefixed to this book [Col. 1224A], and by several others, including some heterodox writers, it is rightly counted among the genuine works of Saint Ambrose of Milan.

This judgment is confirmed by the work itself. Some of the liturgical practices found in it still partly prevail at Milan, and the baptismal rites described in the acts of the synods held at Milan under Saint Charles Borromeo [Note: [Col. 1224D] *Acta Ecclesiae Mediolanensis*, p. 410] are based upon this treatise.

### 28

Since the books *On the Sacraments* certainly do not have the bishop of Cahors as their author and do not appear to have the bishop of Milan as their author, certain investigators have gone further and attempted to determine who should be regarded as the writer of the books *On the Sacraments*.

Different scholars have followed different opinions. In their prologue to the book *On the Sacraments* [Note: [Col. 1224D] Ambrose, works, vol. V, p. 206], the Benedictines appear inclined toward the opinion of Godefroy Hermant in his *Life of Saint Ambrose* [Note: [Col. 1224D] Hermant, *Life of Saint Ambrose: Clarifications*, p. 30. Compare Lebrun, *Explanation of the Mass*, vol. III, p. 25 (Paris edition, 1777, octavo), who judges the author to belong to the sixth century], who held that these books belonged to one of this saint’s disciples, who governed the Church of Milan not long after him.

What chiefly prevents us from giving our vote to this view is that the author, in book III, chapter 11, declares that he wishes to follow the example of the Roman Church in the sacred rites [Note: [Col. 1224D] Ambrose, works, vol. V, p. 222]:

> “We are not unaware,” he says, “that the Roman Church does not have this custom, whose type and form we follow in everything. Yet it does not have the custom of washing the feet . . . . . In everything I desire to follow the Roman Church; nevertheless, we too are human beings and have understanding. Therefore, what is observed more correctly elsewhere, we also preserve more correctly.”

From these words it is clear [Col. 1224C] that the author follows the Roman rites then in use, with one addition, namely the washing of the feet. Since the well-known maxim is “An exception confirms the rule,” it must be concluded that all the remaining ceremonies agree especially closely with the type and form of the Roman Church.

But such conformity cannot apply to the Ambrosian rite, which existed in its entirety at all times, even before Saint Ambrose. We lack ritual books with which to investigate this matter more fully.

I shall mention one point here, which some have thought might reveal the Milanese rite. In book IV of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 1224D] Ibid., p. 232], the author gives the following form for the consecration of the bread:

> “Take and eat from this, all of you; for this is my body, which will be broken for many.”

Pamelius says that this form is Ambrosian in volume I of his *Latin Liturgy*. But Muratori utterly denies this in the work of Augustin Krazer [Note: [Col. 1224D] *On the Antiquity of the Liturgies*, p. 631]:

> “He [Muratori] asked the distinguished Joseph Anthony Sassi, prefect of the Ambrosian Library, to send him the canon of the Mass from the most ancient of all Ambrosian Missals. He examined a very ancient parchment codex, whose antiquity he judged to belong to the ninth or tenth century, and found the words of consecration to be the same as those of the Romans and the entire canon similar to the Roman one. Hence it is probable that Pamelius was misled by the author of the book *On the Sacraments*, who was formerly attributed to Saint Ambrose but is now, by sharp-sighted critics, more correctly denied to the bishop of Milan.”

This is of great importance, for we are dealing with the most sacred formula, which hardly ever changes once it has been adopted. This single argument therefore makes probable the judgment of those who deny that these books belong to any bishop of Milan.

It would be futile to seek another author amid the scarcity of liturgical books from which we suffer. Unless a ritual book were found whose ceremonies accurately agreed with the rites expressed by Ambrosiaster, I do not see how anything certain could be pronounced either about the writer of these books or about the time in which he lived.

As a final note, I shall add that Robert Sala, a Cistercian, in his edition of the works of Cardinal Bona, suspected that the author of the books *On the Sacraments* was Saint Maximus of Turin [Note: [Col. 1225D] *Literary History of Italy*, vol. IV, p. 76. Compare Le Brun, *Explanation of the Mass*, vol. III, p. 210]. But apart from a bare conjecture, Sala offers nothing to give his opinion any strength. Nor did the new edition of the works of Saint Maximus, prepared at Rome in 1784, provide me with any illumination.

## § IV. Saint Ambrose, revealed by a heavenly sign, sets out for Rome and dies on his return

### 29

We saw in § II that Saint Ambrose of Cahors left the episcopal dignity in such a way that he afterward refused to resume it. The wickedness of the people whom he had to govern was the canonical reason for resigning the episcopate.

Although the Saint wished the place of his solitude to remain secret, there is nevertheless no doubt that his intention to lay down the episcopal burden became known to the people of Cahors, so that they could proceed lawfully to the election of his successor.

For another bishop was substituted while Saint Ambrose was still alive, as is evident from Life, no. 9, where, after finding a key in a fish, Saint Ambrose says to his disciple: “Go into the city to the bishop.” There was therefore another bishop appointed in place of Saint Ambrose.

This too is shown not to conflict with the ancient discipline of the Church by Saint Gregory the Great, whose Life, written by John the Deacon [Note: [Col. 1225D] *Acta Sanctorum*, 12 March, p. 194, no. 39], says:

> “When bishops voluntarily resign their sees, Gregory in no way denied them successors; he judged that afterward they should be adequately supported from the revenues of the Church they had left.”

Saint Augustine also mentions voluntary resignation in book II against Cresconius, chapter 11 [Note: [Col. 1225D] vol. IX of the works, col. 415], when he says:

> “We are not bishops for our own sake, but for the sake of those to whom we administer the word and sacrament of the Lord. Accordingly, when necessity concerning their governance without scandal requires it, we ought either to be or not to be, because we exist not for ourselves but for others. Finally, some men endowed with holy humility, because of certain circumstances in themselves that moved them piously and religiously, laid down the office of bishop not only without blame but even with praise.”

To these considerations must be added the fact that Waifarius occupied Aquitaine while Saint Ambrose was still seated as bishop. Eginhard writes the following about this in *On the Deeds of King Pippin* [Note: [Col. 1226D] In D. Bouquet, vol. V, p. 199]:

> “When Waifarius, duke of Aquitaine, refused to restore to the rectors of the venerable places the properties under his control that belonged to the churches established under the authority of King Pippin, and scorned to listen to the king when he admonished him about these matters through his envoys, by his obstinacy he provoked war against himself. For the king, having gathered forces from every direction, entered Aquitaine and declared that he would recover the property of the churches by war.”

The devastations of churches of this kind had formerly provided a reason for resigning the episcopate, as Saint Ado has already testified for us in his *Chronicle* [Note: [Col. 1226D] Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae*, vol. II, p. 319]. There is therefore nothing surprising in Saint Ambrose’s likewise leaving the episcopal chair to another for a similar reason.

For the entire question presently under discussion, Louis Thomasius may usefully be consulted in his work *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, part II, book II, chapter 52, where he presents numerous examples of bishops of Gaul who left their sees at approximately this period.

### 30

Gulielmus de la Croix [Note: [Col. 1226D] *Series of the Bishops of Cahors*, p. 43] places Aymatus as the successor of Saint Ambrose. He proves Aymatus’s episcopate from a charter concerning the consecration of the altar of the monastery of Aniane, in the diocese of Maguelonne, said to have been celebrated in the tenth year of King Charlemagne by Pope Leo III, in the presence of 366 bishops. Among these bishops appears Aymatus, bishop of Cahors.

But learned scholars rightly reject that document, which is the sole support for Aymatus’s episcopate. For the fourteenth year of King Charles corresponds to the year of Christ 781 or the following year, at which time it was certainly not Leo III but Hadrian I who occupied the Roman see. Therefore the aforementioned Gulielmus substitutes the thirty-fourth year for the fourteenth year of Charles, saying that the first numerical sign was somewhat altered—or, more accurately, restored.

Yet even by this calculation he would not reach the year of Christ 804, when Pope Leo came to Gaul, unless he assigns the beginning of Charles’s reign to the year of Christ 769. But Gulielmus strikes a reef here, for Charles had succeeded his father Pippin in the preceding year.
