Leaving aside these chronological tangles, it is established from another source that when Pope Leo was in Gaul he did not enter Aquitaine. The *Annals of Metz* [Note: [Col. 1226D] In D. Bouquet, vol. V, p. 352] contain the following:

> “In the middle of November it was announced to him—Charlemagne, in the year 804—that Pope Leo wished to celebrate Christmas with him wherever he might choose. The king received this gladly, and immediately sent his son Charles to Saint Maurice, ordering him to receive the pope honorably. He himself went to meet him at the city of Reims, in the basilica of Saint Remigius, bishop and confessor. Having received him there, he escorted him as far as Quierzy and celebrated Christmas with him there. Departing together from that place, they arrived at the city of Soissons. There, leaving the pope, he went to the monastery of Chelles to visit his sister Gisela, who was ill during those days. After enjoying her company, he had Pope Leo, whom he had left at Saint-Médard, come to meet him at the royal villa of Quierzy. He then took him to Aachen and, after honoring him with great gifts, had his men escort him—since he wished to travel through Bavaria—as far as Ravenna. He remained with him, the Emperor, for eight days and, as stated, returned to Rome.”

From this account it appears that the Aniane document is fictitious and that Aymatus’s episcopate, of which Gulielmus de la Croix writes, rests on no testimony [Note: [Col. 1227D] Compare Cointius, *Annals of France*, year 805, § XI, vol. VII, p. 35].

### 31

The bishop of Cahors who succeeded Saint Ambrose when he withdrew into solitude must therefore be regarded as unknown, unless he was Angarius, also called Agarnus or Awarnus.

He was certainly already seated as bishop in the second year of the reign of Louis, son of Charlemagne, in Aquitaine—that is, in the year of Christ 783—as may be seen in Mabillon’s *Annals*, book XXV, § XXXIX [Note: [Col. 1227D] *Benedictine Annals*, vol. II, p. 249].

This is established by a charter of Angarius, dated in the year 773 of the Lord, the second year of King Louis of the Franks. John Mabillon correctly notes at the cited place that 783 should be read instead of 772, which properly corresponds to the second year of the reign of Louis the Pious in Aquitaine, since he was anointed king of Aquitaine at Rome by Pope Hadrian in 781, as the *Annals of Metz* report [Note: [Col. 1227D] In D. Bouquet, vol. V, p. 343].

Angarius, therefore, already bishop of Cahors in 783, lived at least until the nineteenth year of the ninth century, as is established by a parchment of the abbey of Figeac concerning the exchange of the cell of Jonante between Bishop Angarius and Pippin, king of Aquitaine. The subscription of this charter is as follows:

> “Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, in the sixth year of the empire of Louis and the sixth year of our reign.” [Note: [Col. 1227D] Gulielmus de la Croix, *Series of the Bishops of Cahors*, p. 43.]

Since no scholar denies the authority of this charter, only one difficulty remains: namely, how the sixth year of Louis the Pious as emperor could coincide with the seventh year of the reign of his son Pippin in Aquitaine. For Pippin appears to have begun his reign after the Kalends of November [Col. 1227D] in the year of Christ 814, as Mansi proves in his note on Pagi’s *Critica* under the year 838, § I. On the other hand, we know that the empire of Louis the Pious began at least from the Kalends of May of that same year.

Thus, in the month of May, Louis preceded Pippin by one year. Cointius [Note: [Col. 1228D] *Annals of France*, year 820, § XXVII, vol. VII, p. 533] therefore reasonably suspects “that the chronological numerals were transposed, and that Louis’s seventh year and King Pippin’s sixth year should be read.” In that case, Angarius would have occupied the see of Cahors in the common year 820.

If, however, anyone prefers to read Pippin’s fifth year, there is nothing that prevents it.

Let this suffice concerning the successor of Saint Ambrose, without our being able to assert whether some intermediate bishop stood between our Saint and Angarius.

32. Saint Ambrose, having resigned the episcopate, either secretly, as the shorter Life of him extracted from the Cahors lectionary suggests [Note: [Col. 1228D] Royal Library of Brussels, MS II. 8014, fol. 22], or—as is more probable—in accordance with his provident care for his Church, after warning the clergy so that they might be able to elect another bishop in his place, set out for Rome to visit the thresholds of the holy Apostles. The author of the shorter Life cited a little earlier says that our Saint was invited by clergy and people to undertake the pastoral office again, but that he “alleged that a prior vow first had to be fulfilled,” namely, the visitation of the thresholds of the holy Apostles, and that on his return he died in his homeland. The Life printed below says nothing of such a vow: it simply states that Saint Ambrose, after refusing the episcopate that was offered to him, went to Rome. Nevertheless, the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden [Note: [Col. 1228D] Notes on the Life] adds that he replied to his successor in the episcopate:

“You, dearest brother, will sit in your place. But I shall go to Rome in the name of my Lord Jesus Christ; and if it pleases my Lord, I shall return here; otherwise, possess everything. Do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry, and be sober.”

It therefore seems that the Saint, released from his voluntary imprisonment, went to Rome not only for prayer but also for consultation: namely, whether he ought to undertake the pastoral burden again, or whether he should seek another solitude. If faith may be placed both in the Cahors Sanctorale, in William de la Croix [Note: [Col. 1228D] Series of the Bishops of Cahors, p. 36], and in the shorter Life of the Cahors Lectionary, Saint Ambrose set out for Rome intending afterward to return to Cahors. The Sanctorale says:

“But I shall go to Rome and visit the thresholds of the Apostles Peter and Paul; and if God permits me to return here, I am ready to fulfill whatever he wills.”

The Lectionary states the matter more clearly [Note: [Col. 1228D] Moysiac Lectionary, MS under no. 8014, Royal Library of Brussels]:

“He went to Rome to the apostolic thresholds, then to the basilica of blessed Martin of Tours; but on his return to his homeland he died.”

From this it is clear that the Saint really did wish to return to Cahors, so that, following the counsel of the Roman Pontiff, he might either assume again the government of his people or spend the remainder of his life in solitude, prayer, and penance.

33. It was customary for all Christians, but especially for priests, bishops, and even those who were moved by a desire for a holier life, to visit the sacred thresholds of the Apostles, both so that they might be aided by the patronage of the saints and also so that they might be guided by the counsels of the Roman Pontiff. Antiquity supplies us with many examples. It is uncertain, moreover, how much time our Saint Ambrose spent on his Roman pilgrimage. Since, however, he does not seem to have wished to remain in Rome, and on his return visited the tomb of Saint Martin of Tours, nothing compels us to assign more than two years to this pilgrimage. If, then, we knew with certainty approximately when the Saint had left his solitude at Cahors, it would not be very difficult to establish the date of his death with greater precision.

For the present, however, until we can follow firmer evidence, nothing prevents us from placing the Saint’s withdrawal around the year 765, when Waifarius was raging most fiercely against the churches of Aquitaine. Since the Saint does not object to such persecutions as a reason why he could not return to his see, it may rightly be inferred that his departure from the cave occurred after Waifarius’s death, that is, after the year 768 [Col. 1229B]. Counting three years of solitude backward from that date, we arrive at the year 765.

Saint Ambrose, having gone to Rome to visit the thresholds of the holy Apostles, seems afterward to have wished to return to Cahors. For he refused the episcopal insignia that were offered to him in such a way that he nevertheless wished to consult the Apostolic See, as the Cahors Sanctorale in William de la Croix plainly indicates [Note: [Col. 1229D] Series of the Bishops of Cahors, p. 36]. When the bishop appointed in his place had said to him:

“Lord and good shepherd, although unworthy, I have been appointed in your place. Therefore I beg you: return to your home, take up your see, govern your people, and remain in the place prepared for you as long as you live; I, however, shall depart elsewhere,”

Ambrose then said to him:

“Meanwhile, may God govern his Church and your people” (or “his people”?). “But I shall go to Rome and visit the thresholds of the Apostles Peter and Paul; and if God permits me to return here, I am ready to fulfill whatever he wills; otherwise, govern all these things rightly.”

The Cahors Lectionary, MS under no. 8014, Royal Library of Brussels, says:

“He went to Rome to the apostolic thresholds, then to the basilica of blessed Martin of Tours; but on his return to his homeland he died on the sixteenth of October at Arbot, a town in Berry.”

We have already indicated above, no. 31, that the Lectionary cited does not agree in certain respects with the other writers who dealt with Saint Ambrose and therefore does not deserve complete confidence. Consequently, it cannot be concluded with certainty that the Saint really was returning to his own city when he died. There are, nevertheless, other considerations that support this view: first, his own words quoted above, in which he clearly declares that he would return; and then the fact that all his biographers say that he died on the road.

34. It therefore cannot be proved that what Adrien Baillet says in the Life of Saint Ambrose is correct. I give his words in Latin:

“From there [Tours] he withdrew into the region of Berry, and built himself a cell in the village of Serisio, above the river Arnon, about four Berry leagues distant.”

The lessons of the Berry Breviary of 1783, kindly communicated to us by the Reverend Mr. Figier, canon and secretary of the archbishopric of Bourges, contain something similar. They are supported by the Cahors Proper of the Saints, edited by Henri de Briqueville [Note: [Col. 1229D] Gallia Christiana, vol. I, col. 154], by the authors of the History of the Gallican Church [Note: [Col. 1230D] History of the Gallican Church, vol. VI, p. 105], and by Butler under 16 October.

There are certainly many authorities that would support this account, if they rested on a suitable foundation. Yet the older records say nothing about Saint Ambrose’s stay in the region of Berry, except perhaps the Berry Breviary, which Philippe Labbe calls very ancient in his Bibliotheca Manuscriptorum [Note: [Col. 1230D] Vol. II, p. 346]. It says:

“After some time, on returning from Rome and staying in the region of Berry, in the village of Arnot, having been purified through many tribulations, he gave back his glorious spirit to God.”

This stay, however, may be explained as referring to his final illness, which forced him to remain in the aforementioned region. Moreover, this Breviary is less ancient than the Life printed below, which, in my judgment, sufficiently suggests that the Saint did not wish to linger in the village of Serisio:

“He went to Rome, and returned to the city of Bourges; and when he had arrived at the village of Ernotrum, it happened that he fell asleep in the Lord.”

Since no other document of equal antiquity has come to light, and since the authors mentioned above seem to follow rather closely the traces of this older Life, it appears that the supposed residence in Berry is more a conjecture than a historical fact. This is well demonstrated by the Cahors Breviary, edited by order of Bertrand Du Guesclin, bishop, around the middle of the eighteenth century. The Cahors Proper of Henri de Briqueville de la Luzerne had said in the Lessons of Saint Ambrose:

“Afterward he went to the people of Berry, settled his dwelling in a region then obscure [Col. 1230C], and there ended his glorious life.”

Omitting the mention of a Berry residence, the Cahors Breviary says:

“At last he died among the people of Berry, at Serisio, by the river Arnon.”

Nor is this without reason. For if, after Waifarius’s death, Saint Ambrose emerged from his cave at Cahors—as we stated above in the preceding number was probable—it is not apparent how the Saint could have established a residence among the people of Berry, when everyone says that he died around the year 770. The two years between Waifarius’s death and that date are scarcely sufficient for him to complete properly the Roman and Tours pilgrimages. Finally, as I said above, the Saint does not seem to have intended to leave his homeland in such a way that he would never return. His only uncertainty was whether he would someday resume the episcopal insignia that he had laid down.

Certainly everyone will agree with me that the words of the Berry Breviary of 1783—that the Saint lived for a long time in obscurity in the village of Sericiacum in the territory of Bourges—have no historical weight.

35. We have already said that all the more recent writers place the year of Saint Ambrose’s death around 770. None of the ancient writers, however, supports this opinion. Hence the modern writers proceed here by conjecture. I readily accept the conjecture, provided that they are willing to embrace, however tentatively, the opinion established in the preceding number; unless they follow that view, I do not see from what records they can prove their position [Col. 1231A].

On the other hand, once our opinion is admitted, the Saint’s chronology proceeds correctly, and anyone can easily see that the date of Saint Ambrose’s death can scarcely be far removed from the year 770.

The place of the Saint’s death is more precisely indicated in the ancient Life:

“When he had arrived at the village of Ernotrum, it happened that he fell asleep in the Lord.”

Ernotrum—also called Ernodurum or the village of Arnot—is a village four leagues southwest of the city of Bourges, and today, because of Saint Ambrose, is called Saint-Ambroix-sur-Arnon, in the district of Carophin (the canton of Charost, department of Cher). A road once paved by the Romans led to this village, sufficiently demonstrating the ancient prominence of the place.

Near Ernotrum lies the little village of Sericiacum (Seris), now Marats, where Saint Ambrose actually died. He was not, however, buried at Sericiacum, as the Reverend Mr. Figier, a canon of Bourges, writes to me on 12 November 1840. Rather, he was buried at Ernotrum, in the church where, as miracles became famous, a great concourse of people gathered. We need not, therefore, accept the words of the Cahors Sanctorale, which says:

“After not many days, the inhabitants of that place built a church in his honor, which exists to this very day.”

We know that Ernotrum took its name from Saint Ambrose, but the earlier authorities are silent on whether the Saint, buried in the open country, later acquired a church. Indeed, it is far more probable that, rather than the inhabitants building a sacred edifice in the Saint’s honor, they deposited his holy body in a church that had already been built.

The Sanctorale cited above plainly confuses the burial at Ernotrum with the one at Bourges, since immediately after the words just quoted it adds:

“There is also a monastery there, which is called the Abbey of Saint Ambrose.”

This is true of the city of Bourges, but not at all of the village of Ernotrum. Albert Butler makes the same error, although Adrien Baillet properly distinguishes the two places.

36. After the body of Saint Ambrose had lain for some time at Ernotrum, it was translated to Bourges, at least in the tenth century, as is sufficiently established by the charter of Geoffrey, viscount of Bourges, which we discussed above in no. 2. For when, in 1012, Geoffrey restored to the monastery of Saint Peter and Saint Ambrose whatever it had lost, the body of the holy bishop was already resting in that church [Col. 1231D], and the monastery was already bearing the name of our Ambrose. Both facts show that the translation of the relics had taken place before Geoffrey’s donation and that, as devotion to the Saint spread among the people of Berry, the monastery had received the new designation of Saint Ambrose.

Such developments do not ordinarily take place within a brief period of twelve years. Therefore the authors are right to assign the translation at least to the tenth century. It is especially probable that the holy bishop’s relics were brought to Bourges as early as the ninth century, when the Normans were ravaging Gaul with terrible violence, forcing monks to abandon their monasteries and flee with the relics of the saints to the most strongly fortified cities.

Many ancient records show that the Normans were a serious threat to Aquitaine and therefore to the region of Bourges. In the Annals of Saint-Vaast under the year 889 [Note: [Col. 1231D] In D. Bouquet, vol. VIII, p. 88], we read:

“The Danes or Normans, according to their custom, devastated Burgundy, Neustria, and part of Aquitaine with fire and sword, no one resisting.”

The same Annals report a similar calamity under the year 898 [Note: [Col. 1231D] Ibid., p. 92]. Under the twenty-third year of the tenth century, Flodoard’s Chronicle states [Note: [Col. 1231D] Ibid., p. 179] that the Normans had plundered Aquitaine and Auvergne. Hence King Rudolf, in the thirtieth year of that same century, says, as Flodoard, quoted above, reports [Note: [Col. 1232D] Ibid., p. 186]:

“He almost destroyed in a single battle the Northmen who were troubling Aquitaine with their raids.”

The same source tells us that this devastation in Aquitaine continued for seven years, as does a Historical Fragment first published by Chesne [Note: [Col. 1232D] Ibid., p. 298].

We could cite many other records showing that the Normans were disastrous to the region of Bourges. It is therefore probable that the body of Saint Ambrose was translated into the city of Bourges toward the end of the ninth century or at the beginning of the tenth. This is also supported to some extent by the fact that, if the translation had occurred not through flight but from piety, some trace of a solemn celebration would at least have survived.

37. After the body of Saint Ambrose had been translated from Ernotrum to Bourges, it was buried in the church of Saint Peter. That this church already existed before the Saint’s death is proved by the burial there of Siginus, who died around the middle of the eighth century, as we said above in no. 2.

As the faithful’s devotion toward Saint Ambrose increased, the church took its name from him. Philippe Labbe describes it, together with the cloister attached to it, from the archives as follows [Note: [Col. 1232D] Bibliotheca Manuscriptorum, vol. II, p. 57]:

“There is a certain place near the walls of the city of Bourges, situated toward the north, called Brisiacum. In ancient times it was constructed in great honor, consecrated in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, and of Saint Ambrose the bishop, and honorably adorned with a very large company of canons. But when the persecution of the infidels broke in, it was reduced almost to nothing. Although they destroyed the buildings, they did not take away the sanctity.

“After many years had passed, Geoffrey, viscount of the city of Bourges, with the counsel and assistance of all the nobles of the duchy of Berry, magnificently rebuilt it in the year 1012 from the Incarnation of the Lord. He restored the estates and other rights of Saint Peter and Saint Ambrose, which he unjustly held, by order of King Robert and of Lord Dagbert, archbishop of Bourges (see above, no. 3) . . . .

“When the devotion of the secular canons gradually grew cold, and they were no longer devoted to the offices of the altar, but through their madness had become a disgrace to the clerical order, the reverend Father in Christ, the Lord Peter de Castra, archbishop of Bourges, a man richly endowed with every quality of true wisdom, expelled them and introduced regular canons—men distinguished for the integrity of their conduct and, so to speak, even more excellent by their very uprightness—in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1151. The same bishop recorded this in the following words:

“‘The care of the pastoral office reminds us that we must always foster and love the good of holy religion, and, with God’s help, propagate it for the better during the time of our priesthood in the churches entrusted to us by God. Therefore I, Peter, by the grace of God archbishop of the Church of Bourges, wishing to establish in the city of Bourges some refuge for the salvation of souls, where many might correct their conduct and offer worthy fruits of penance to God, have taken care to bring the church of Saint Ambrose of Brisiacum from its many abuses to the standard and rule of the canonical order. In that church we have now established the order of regular canons, to be observed according to the rule of Saint Augustine.

“‘What has therefore been beneficially done by us out of pious devotion must likewise be pursued with religious diligence. Accordingly, by the authority of the Church of Bourges and of ourselves, we decree that the canonical order according to the rule of blessed Augustine shall henceforth be permanently held and observed in the aforesaid church of Saint Ambrose of Brisiacum. We earnestly and devoutly beseech our successors to foster that church and the institution of this religion continually and to labor to promote them for the better; and in the name of almighty God and blessed Stephen the Protomartyr we admonish them, etc.’”

“To prevent the work from becoming excessively long, we have cut it short.” Thus far Philippe Labbe.

38. The abbey established under the canonical rule by Peter de Castra was first governed by regular abbots. The first was Godefredus, who, according to the authors of *Gallia Christiana*, governed it from at least 1150 to 1163 [Note: [Col. 1233D] Vol. II, col. 181].

In the course of time the abbey was converted into a commendam, as may be seen in the place cited. In the sixteenth century, when the Calvinists were disturbing France, Gabriel de Montgommery, lieutenant of the Prince of Condé, entered Bourges through the gate of Saint Ambrose on 27 May 1562 and, following the custom of the sectarians, overturned the altars, broke the sacred images, and burned the relics of the saints [Note: [Col. 1233D] De Thou, *Universal History*, book XXX, vol. III, p. 190].

Among the churches destroyed by the fury of the Calvinists must be counted the monastery and church of Saint Ambrose, and even his sacred body. It had already been thrown from its coffin and was probably about to be committed to the flames when, through the efforts of Catholics, it was rescued from the hands of the impious [Note: [Col. 1233D] La Croix, *Series of the Bishops of Cahors*, p. 34] and placed in a new chest.

Afterward, in 1571, Louis de la Mer de Matha, an Auvergnat and commendatory abbot, restored the ruined buildings from their foundations. They later acquired new splendor when, in 1634, under James Maugis, commendatory abbot, the monastery became the sole house of the French congregation of regular canons [Note: [Col. 1233D] *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 182].

The abbey thereafter seems to have remained peaceful until, toward the end of the preceding century, sacred and secular affairs alike were thrown into confusion in France. The abbey of Saint Ambrose also experienced the common calamity and passed into the treasury of the state. After the buildings had been sold, the church nevertheless remained until the twenty-eighth year of the present century, when it too was leveled to the ground, except for the apse. That apse could still serve Catholic worship today if the owner of the property were willing to restore it; but it is said that there is no prospect of this.

As for the relics of the Saint, they perished, like most others, in the upheaval, and no trace of them has been found to this day. Before that time, at least part of the relics had been enclosed in a silver bust, which was carried about in processions.

39. The cult of Saint Ambrose seems to have been introduced into the bishopric of Cahors at a later time. For no earlier record of it has been found than a charter issued by Raymond III [Note: [Col. 1234D] Not II, as La Croix has it, p. 158; compare *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, col. 137], called Panchellus, in which he orders a chapel to be erected in honor of Saint Ambrose, his patron—a word that indicates a somewhat earlier devotion.

Here are his words from William de la Croix [Note: [Col. 1234D] *Series of the Bishops of Cahors*, p. 171]:

“To all, etc. Raymond, by the grace of God bishop of Cahors. You should know that we, together with the venerable chapter of Cahors, wishing and intending, as far as we can and ought, to avoid the losses and dangers of the Church of Cahors, in head and members, and to promote virtue with all our strength, wish, order, and decree that half the revenues of churches that are vacant or shall become vacant in our city and diocese of Cahors, for the year in which they become vacant, when their rectors and chaplains or perpetual vicars resign or die, shall be assigned to this purpose. They shall be collected by certain canons, to be chosen each year by us and our aforesaid chapter, who shall be obliged to render to us and to the said chapter a definite and lawful account of receipts and expenditures.

“Thus, first and before all else, in honor of God and of blessed Ambrose, our patron and formerly bishop of Cahors, a suitable and honorable oratory shall be built from the aforesaid revenues and goods, in the place, cave, or grotto in which or in one of which, near the old bridge of Cahors beside the river Lot, the said Saint is said to have led a strict life for a long time and to have performed voluntary penance, as is undoubtedly attested by very many miracles revealed there and elsewhere through divine grace on account of his merits . . . .

“In witness of these things, we, the aforesaid bishop, have caused these letters to be authenticated by our seal together with the seal of the said chapter. We, the chapter of Cahors, have attached our common seal together with the seal of the said lord bishop. Given at Cahors on the Thursday before the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, in the year of the Lord 1308.”

The Roman Church now celebrates two feasts of the Chair of Saint Peter: on 18 January and on 22 February, because of the Roman and Antiochene sees. It would therefore be difficult to assign the exact day to the charter cited unless it were first established which feast is meant here.

Both feasts of the Chair are indeed celebrated in the most ancient martyrologies, as our Soller demonstrated in his edition of Usuard. Yet the earlier feast, on 18 January, had become obsolete among many, as is clear from the ancient Sacramentary of Saint Gregory the Great, the Gothic Missal, and others, whereas the other feast was always retained by all the churches.

This is further confirmed by the fact that the council of Cognac, held in the diocese of Bordeaux around the year 1255 [Note: [Col. 1235B] Labbe, vol. XI, part I of the Councils, col. 749], lists the Chair of Saint Peter among the holidays, but after the Conversion of Saint Paul and therefore in February.

Since Raymond of Cahors simply says that the charter was given on the Thursday before the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, I have no doubt that he means the Chair of Saint Peter in February. Since, moreover, in the leap year 1308 the Sunday letter for that month was F, it follows that the Thursday before the feast of the Chair was 15 February.

Pope Paul IV, by a bull dated 8 January 1558, restored the feast of the Roman Chair on 18 January, which had become obsolete in several churches [Note: [Col. 1235B] The bull appears in *Acts of the Saints*, 18 January, p. 182. Bollandus says it was dated on the Ides of January, whereas the *Roman Bullary* gives 8 January, vol. I, p. 833, Luxembourg edition, 1727. Compare Bianchini, *Anastasius*, vol. IV, pp. 150 ff.].

To return to Saint Ambrose: his chapel, built by Raymond, still exists, although in later times it was partly or wholly restored. Toward the end of the preceding century, this chapel and the adjoining land were assigned to and sold by the public treasury. Nevertheless, though profaned, it remains, and there is some hope that it may someday be restored to the worship of Saint Ambrose, as the Reverend Mr. Layrac, secretary to the most illustrious bishop of Cahors, writes to me [Col. 1236B].

[Col. 1235]

[NOTE.]

Since certain people had attributed two writings, namely, *On the Sacraments* and *On the Mysteries*, to Saint Ambrose, bishop of Cahors, we thought it appropriate to assign them a place in our Library. There is no need, however, to print the works in question here, both because the preceding notice has shown that they do not belong to Saint Ambrose of Cahors and because these same writings are already included among the works of Saint Ambrose of Milan, in volume XVI of *Patrologia*. EDITOR.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 771. STEPHEN III, ROMAN PONTIFF.

[Col. 1235]

HISTORICAL NOTICE ON POPE STEPHEN III

(*From the Book of the Pontiffs, in Mansi’s Collection of Councils, vol. XII.*)

[Col. 1235C] [Note: Stephen. After the expulsion of the false popes Constantine and Philip, Pope Stephen, fourth of that name, was canonically and legitimately created pontiff on 5 August in the year of the Redemption 768, according to the prescriptions of the sacred canons. Anastasius incorrectly calls him the third, as is clear from what was said above. After the election had taken place, and after punishment and death had overtaken all who had invaded the Apostolic See, he sent a delegation to King Pepin to arrange a synod. But since Pepin died before their arrival, his sons and heirs of the kingdom, Charles and Carloman, granted that twelve of the most learned bishops of Gaul should be sent to Rome for the council. When this had been completed, as we shall relate below, a schism arose in the Church of Ravenna after the death of Sergius, archbishop of that city. The entire clergy had elected Leo to replace the deceased; the king of the Lombards had forcibly intruded a certain Michael, a keeper of the church archives. Stephen repeatedly warned him to yield the episcopate to the one legitimately elected, but in vain, until Charles, king of the Franks, compelled the people of Ravenna to depose the intruder Michael from the episcopate and send him bound to Rome.

“Desiderius, king of the Lombards, had Christopher the primicerius and Sergius the secundicerius, who warned him to restore the rights of the Church, blinded contrary to the oath of fidelity he had given to the pontiff, and afterward killed Christopher. When the pontiff reproached the perjured king, the latter is said to have replied: ‘Let the apostolic Stephen be satisfied that I have removed Christopher and Sergius, who dominated him, from the scene, so that there is no need to demand rights.’ These events are related by Anastasius in the Lives of Stephen III and Hadrian.]

Stephen III, a Sicilian by nation, son of Olivus [Note: [Col. 1235C] In another copy, Olibrius], sat for three years, five months, and twenty-eight days [Note: [Col. 1235C] In another copy, “twenty-eight days” is absent, as are the words “and a vigorous man”]. He was a vigorous man, learned in the divine Scriptures, imbued with ecclesiastical traditions, and steadfastly persevering in their observance.

When he came from the island of Sicily to this Roman city, Lord Gregory, of holy memory, the third pope, entrusted him to the monastery of Saint Chrysogonus, which he was then newly founding. There he became both a cleric and a monk. Later Lord Pope Zachary removed him from that monastery [Note: [Col. 1236C] The Lucca codex reads, “taking him away”] and ordered him to be placed in the chamber of the Lateran patriarchate [Note: [Col. 1236C] The Lucca codex reads, “appointed him to his own chamber”]. He afterward ordained him priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. Yet, because of his modesty and chastity, he kept him in his office at the Lateran.

The other blessed pontiffs, namely Lords Stephen and Paul, likewise kept this most holy Stephen in their service because of his pious observances [Note: [Col. 1237D] In another copy, “pious” is absent]. When his predecessor, Lord Pope Paul, was staying in the church of blessed Paul during the summer because of the oppressive heat, and was overtaken there by a severe illness from which he also died, this most blessed Stephen remained day and night in the service of that same predecessor and pontiff. He did not withdraw from his bedside in any way until the pope gave up his spirit.

While Pope Paul lay ill and had not yet breathed his last, a certain Toto, duke of the city of Nepi and formerly its inhabitant, gathered with his brothers Constantine, Passivus, and Paschal an army and a band of country people from Nepi itself and from other cities of Tuscia. Entering this Roman city through the gate of blessed Pancratius, they stood armed in the house of the aforesaid Toto and there suddenly elected Constantine, Toto’s brother, who was still a layman.

They introduced him into the Lateran patriarchate by force and like robbers, many of them wearing breastplates [Note: [Col. 1237D] The Lucca codex reads, “as marauders”]. They ascended with him into the vicedominium and immediately summoned Bishop George [Note: [Col. 1237D] The Lucca codex reads, “Gregory”], compelling him to give Constantine the clerical prayer. The bishop absolutely refused to do this. Falling to the ground, he prostrated himself at Constantine’s feet and earnestly adjured him, by all the divine mysteries, to give way and withdraw from his impious act of presumption, lest through him such an unheard-of novelty should arise in the Church of God.

While he was uttering these words of adjuration, many of those wicked men who had made the same impious election became enraged, rose against him, and threatened him violently. Seized with fear, he gave Constantine the clerical prayer. Constantine thereby became a cleric and seized the Lateran patriarchate.

When the next day dawned, on the second day of the week, Constantine was ordained subdeacon and deacon by the same bishop in the oratory of Saint Lawrence within the patriarchate, contrary to the regulations of the sacred canons [Note: [Col. 1237D] The Lucca codex reads, “in the same patriarchate”]. He then compelled the entire people to swear allegiance to him. When Sunday arrived, he again hastened with a multitude of armed troops to the basilica of blessed Peter, where he was consecrated pontiff by the same George, bishop of Praeneste, and by two other bishops, Eustratius of Alba and Citonatus of Porto [Note: [Col. 1237D] The Lucca codex reads, “Citonatus”]. He held the Apostolic See by force for one year and one month.

When Christopher the primicerius and counsellor saw this, he and his son Sergius, then serving as saccellarius [Note: [Col. 1238D] The Lucca codex reads, “sacellarius”], moved by zeal for the faith, preferred to die rather than witness such an impious novelty and wicked presumption perpetrated against the Apostolic See. Continuing each day in weeping and tears, they pretended that they wished to become monks. They asked Constantine to release them and to allow them to go to the monastery of the Savior of our Lord Jesus Christ, claiming that they would there assume the monastic habit.

Christopher the primicerius gave an oath, and Constantine, believing them, released them [Note: [Col. 1238D] Mansi: “That is, he dismissed them”]. As they hastened away and entered Lombard territory, the abbot of the aforesaid monastery wished to bring them into it. But Christopher the primicerius and his son Sergius, formerly saccellarius and afterward secundicerius, turned aside from the road. They earnestly adjured Theodicius, duke of Spoleto, to conduct them across the Po to Desiderius, their king of the Lombards [Note: [Col. 1238D] The Lucca codex reads, “to escort them”], since they were striving thereby to accomplish the redemption of the holy Church of God.

The duke of Spoleto transported them to his king. When they had been brought into his presence, they earnestly begged the king to grant his assistance, so that the error of such a novelty might be cut off from the Church of God.

While the aforesaid Christopher the primicerius and his son Sergius were staying with that king, the aforesaid Constantine, invader of the Apostolic See, ordained priests and deacons. Within the course of that year and one month he ordained eight priests, four deacons, and also eight bishops in various places [Note: [Col. 1238D] In another copy: “He ordained eight bishops in that same month,” and so forth].

[Col. 1238C] The aforesaid George of Praeneste, who had ordained Constantine first as deacon and then as pontiff, was seized not many days after Constantine’s consecration by a severe and dreadful illness. He became immobile and afterward was entirely unable to celebrate the solemnities of Mass. For his right hand withered and became contracted. He could not even bring it to his mouth, and thus, trembling and wasting away, he ended his life.

While these things were taking place, the aforementioned Christopher and Sergius, having been released by the king of the Lombards, made their way to the city of Reate. Sergius and the priest Waldipertus, together with the people of Reate and Forconium and other Lombards of the duchy of Spoleto, advanced suddenly and unexpectedly into this Roman city on the twenty-eighth day of July, at the sixth indiction, in the evening, at the very twilight of night, on the vigil of the blessed martyrs Abdon and Sennen, and seized the Salarian Bridge.

On the following day, crossing the Milvian Bridge, they came to the Gate of Saint Peter; proceeding from there, they approached the Gate of Saint Pancratius. Certain kinsmen of the aforementioned Christopher and Sergius were watching and guarding that gate. When they saw Sergius approaching it, they signaled to him and immediately opened the gate. [Col. 1239A] Thus the aforementioned Sergius and Waldipert, together with the Lombards, entered the city of Rome. They climbed along the city walls bearing a small banner, fearing the Roman people; and the Lombards did not dare descend from the Janiculum, but remained there in great trembling.

When Toto and Passivus, brothers by birth, heard this, they did not know what scheme and treachery the traitors had devised against him. They ran with several others to the aforementioned gate. Demetrius, the secundicerius, and Gratiosus, then a chartularius and later a duke, also hurried there with them; they too were part of the plot with the aforementioned most wicked traitors. As they approached those same Lombards, one of them, Racipert by name, a warrior who appeared superior to all the others, confronted Duke Toto. [Col. 1239B] He attacked Toto; Toto rushed upon him, struck him forcefully, and killed him. Seeing this, the Lombards turned and attempted to flee. But Demetrius the secundicerius and Gratiosus, standing behind the aforementioned Toto, struck him in the back with their spears. Thus they overcame him and killed him.

Passivus fled into the Lateran patriarchate and announced to his brother Constantine what had happened. When Constantine heard this, he fled with the aforementioned Passivus, Bishop Theodore, and his vicedominus into the Basilica of the Savior. Descending to the fountain, they remained for a short time in the church of Saint Venantius. Considering where they might find greater safety, they went up into the vestry. From there they entered the oratory of Saint Caesarius, closed the doors behind them, and remained there. After several hours, the judges of the Roman militia assembled, expelled them from the oratory, and placed them under guard.

On the following Sunday, the presbyter Waldipert, without the knowledge of the aforementioned Sergius, gathered several Romans. They went to the monastery of Saint Vitus and brought out from there the presbyter Philip. They chose him and, acclaiming him joyfully with loud voices—“Philip pope! Saint Peter has chosen him!”—they led him, as customary, into the Basilica of the Savior. [Note: Another reading: “laudum” (“of praises”).] There, after the bishop had said the prayer, and as he granted peace to everyone according to ancient custom, they brought him into the Lateran patriarchate. There likewise, seated on the pontifical throne and again granting peace as was customary, he went up and took possession of the table, as pontiffs were accustomed to do, while several of the leading clergy and military nobles sat with him.

A short time later, on that same day, the aforementioned Christopher the primicerius arrived. After learning the circumstances of Philip’s election, he immediately went up in great anger and declared under oath before all the Romans that he would not leave Rome until the presbyter Philip had been expelled from the Lateran patriarchate. Then the aforementioned Gratiosus, hastening with several Romans, expelled the aforesaid presbyter Philip [Col. 1240A] from that patriarchate. Philip descended by the staircase leading to the bathhouse and, with great reverence, returned to his monastery.

On the following day, the aforementioned Christopher the primicerius gathered in the Tribus [Note: [Col. 1239D] Another version: “he causes everyone to do so.”] enough priests and leading clergy, military nobles, the entire army, honorable citizens, and the whole assembly of the Roman people, from the greatest to the least. After deliberating together, they all agreed with one mind and one consent upon the person of the aforementioned blessed Stephen.

They went to the title-church of Blessed Cecilia, where that presbyter [Note: [Col. 1239D] Another version: “while living there, he was leading a spiritual life with …”] was residing, and elected him pope. With acclamations and praises they carried him into the Lateran patriarchate, and after everything required for his election had properly been completed, by God’s authority he assumed the summit of the pontificate.

While that most holy man was still the elected pope, certain wicked men assembled—men who did not have God before their eyes and did not fear the terrible judgment to come. They had been sent by certain poisonous instigators of evil, to whom the Lord rendered a fitting recompense for their deeds. Seizing Bishop Theodore and his vicedominus, they did what it is impious to say: they tore out their eyes and cruelly cut out Theodore’s tongue. [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “Constantini quod” (“of Constantine, which …”); the printed variant is fragmentary.] They also attempted to tear out Passivus’s eyes, and displayed such great impiety toward them that they did not even permit them to be carried to their own homes, where their people could have cared for them. Instead, after taking away all their possessions, households, and estates [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “ablatis” (“having taken away”)], they had one of them—namely Bishop Theodore—confined in the monastery of the Clivus Scauri, [Col. 1240C] where, burning with hunger and thirst and crying out for water, he gave up his spirit.

They sent Passivus to the monastery of Saint Sylvester. As for Constantine, the invader of the Apostolic See, when he had been brought into the midst of the assembly, they attached great weights to his feet, made him sit upon a woman’s saddle on a horse, and carried him before everyone to the monastery at Cellas Novas.

At dawn on Saturday, one day before the ordination of the aforementioned most blessed Pope Stephen, several bishops, presbyters, and members of the clergy assembled in the Basilica of the Savior. The aforementioned Constantine was again brought into their midst, and, after the sacred canons had been read, he was deposed. For the subdeacon Maurianus removed the orarium from his neck and threw it at his feet; then he cut off his [Note: [Col. 1240D] Perhaps: “his clasp” or “his fastening.”] clasp. Thus, on the following Sunday, the aforementioned most blessed Stephen received the consecration of the pontificate.

The entire Roman people then made a penitential confession and supplication before the divine mercy. All confessed that they had sinned in the impious ordination of the aforementioned Constantine, invader of the Apostolic See, because they had not resisted him. This confession was read aloud from the ambo of the Basilica of Saint Peter by Leontius the scriniarius.

After this, the entire armies of the city of Rome, Tuscany, and Campania assembled and went to Alatri in Campania, where Gracilis the tribune was residing. He was an associate of the aforementioned Constantine, invader of the Apostolic See, and through him many evils had been perpetrated in the regions of Campania. They vigorously besieged that city, seized Gracilis from it, and brought him here to Rome. They confined him in strict custody, where he remained imprisoned for several days.

Later, certain Campanians who had come here to Rome, urged on by other men still more wicked and impious, seized Gracilis from that prison [Note: [Col. 1241D] Codex Lucullanus: “taking him away.”] and, pretending to transport him to a monastery, reached the Colosseum. There they tore out his eyes and cut out his tongue. Some days after this, when Tuscan and Campanian forces had gathered here at Rome, they conferred with the aforementioned Gratiosus and his more powerful associates, through whose authority such evils were being committed. These men, fearing neither God [Note: [Col. 1241D] Codex Lucullanus: “they proceeded.”], went at dawn with a military contingent from Tuscany and Campania to the monastery at Cellas Novas, where the aforementioned Constantine, invader of the Apostolic See, had been confined. They expelled him from the monastery, tore out his eyes, and left him blind, lying in the street.

After these events had been completed, certain men rose up, alleging that the aforementioned presbyter Waldipert, born of Lombard stock, had entered into a plot with Theodicius, duke of Spoleto, and certain Romans to kill the aforementioned Christopher the primicerius and other Roman nobles, and to hand the city of Rome over to the Lombard nation. Therefore a certain Christopher the vicedominus was sent with a multitude of people to arrest him.

When Waldipert learned of this, he fled into the church of the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, called “at the Martyrs.” The same vicedominus dragged him out from there. Waldipert was carrying an image of that Mother of God. They had him confined in a most dreadful prison called Ferrata, in the Great Cellar. After a few days they expelled the presbyter Waldipert from that prison, threw him to the ground, and beside the boundary-marker [sic] of the Lateran field tore out his eyes and cruelly and impiously cut out his tongue. They sent him to the hospice of Valerius, where he later ended his life as a result of having had his eyes torn out. [Col. 1241D]

At the beginning of his ordination, when that most holy bishop had assumed the height of the pontificate, he sent to the regions of Francia, to the illustrious men Pippin, Charles, and Carloman, kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, the aforementioned Sergius, the secundicerius and at that time nomenclator. Through his apostolic letters he begged and urged their excellences to send several bishops who were knowledgeable and thoroughly learned in all the divine Scriptures and in the institutions of the holy canons, in order to hold a council in this city of Rome concerning the impious prescription of the new error and rashness [Note: [Col. 1241D] Codex Lucullanus: “presumption”], which the aforementioned Constantine, invader of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 1241D] Codex Lucullanus: “usurper”], had dared to perpetrate.

When the aforementioned Sergius hurried to the regions of the Franks, he learned that the most Christian King Pippin had departed this life. [Note: [Col. 1241D] “He had departed this life. Those who refer the death of the most Christian King Pippin either to the preceding or to the following year are therefore mistaken. In this same year, 768, around the eighth or ninth day before the Kalends of October, Charlemagne was crowned at Noyon and his brother Carloman at Soissons. To Charles, to whom another woman’s pledge of marriage had been given either by himself or by his father, the pontiff, in the third letter that follows, dissuades marriage with Bertha, daughter of Desiderius, king of the Lombards. After living with her in marriage for one year, he dismissed her, perhaps as cold and impotent, and took Hildegard of Swabia as his wife. Aimoinus, Book IV, chapters 68 and following.”]

Continuing his journey, he reached Pippin’s sons, the brothers Charles and Carloman, kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans. [Col. 1242B] Having delivered the apostolic letters to them, he was kindly received by them. They showed him fitting hospitality, and nevertheless he obtained from their excellences everything for which he had been sent. Those most Christian kings sent twelve bishops from the regions of the Franks, highly learned in the divine Scriptures and in the ceremonies of the holy canons—namely, men of proven excellence. [Note: [Col. 1242D] In another version, “namely” is absent; two lines are also erased.]

When these men reached the city of Rome in April, in the seventh indiction, the aforementioned most holy Pope Stephen immediately gathered various bishops of Tuscany and Campania, along with several from this province of Italy. [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “congregans” (“gathering”).] After they had all assembled, a council was held in the Basilica of Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, beside the Lateran palace. With that most blessed pope presiding, and all the bishops sitting together with him, Constantine, the invader of the Apostolic See, now blinded in his eyes [Note: [Col. 1242D] Another version: “without his eyes”], was brought into their midst.

After a careful inquiry into why, while still a layman, he had presumed to invade the Apostolic See and perpetrate such an error of impious innovation in the Church of God, he confessed before everyone that he had suffered violence from the people and had been elected and compelled by the people’s force [Note: [Col. 1242D] Another version: “by the people’s arm”] to be led into the Lateran patriarchate, because of the burdens and wrongs that Lord Pope Paul had inflicted upon the Roman people. Falling to the ground with his hands extended on the pavement, he lamented that he was guilty and had sinned beyond the number of the sands of the sea, asking that he might obtain mercy and forgiveness from that priestly council. They had him lifted from the ground, but on that day pronounced no sentence concerning him.

On the following day they brought him again and questioned him about the same impious innovation. He replied that he had done nothing new, saying:

“For Sergius, archbishop of Ravenna, while still a layman, was made archbishop; and Stephen of the city of Naples, also a layman, was suddenly consecrated bishop.”

While the aforementioned Constantine continued making such arguments, all the priests, angered with zeal for ecclesiastical tradition, had his neck struck with slaps and expelled him from the church.

Then, after all the records of his case had been exposed, together with the council that had been issued in writing as though confirming him, they burned them in the middle of the presbytery of that church. [Note: Another reading: “desertis simul e concilio illo quod, etc.” (“… having simultaneously abandoned from that council which, etc.”); fragmentary as printed.] Having done this, the most holy Pope Stephen threw himself to the ground with all the priests and the Roman people. Crying out “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”), they all confessed with great weeping that they had sinned because they had received communion from the hands of Constantine himself. For this reason penance was imposed upon everyone [Note: [Col. 1243D] Another version: “was assigned to them.”]

Then the sacred canons were brought forward and carefully examined. The same priestly council issued a sentence under the prohibition of anathema: no layman, nor anyone from another order, might ever presume to be promoted to the honor of the sacred pontificate unless he had first advanced through the distinct grades and had become a cardinal deacon or presbyter.

They also decreed that several other matters requiring canonical correction [Note: [Col. 1243D] Codex Lucullanus: “amendment”] in Constantine’s case should be remedied in the same council.

Concerning the bishops, presbyters, and deacons whom Constantine had consecrated, the council promulgated the following decree. If any of those bishops had previously been a presbyter or deacon, he was to return to his former rank of honor. If he had become acceptable before the people of his city [Note: [Col. 1243D] Another version: “if they had been acceptable”], he was to come again to the Apostolic See after a decree of election had been made in the customary manner by the clergy and people, and was to receive consecration and blessing from the same most holy Pope Stephen [Note: [Col. 1243D] Codex Lucullanus: “they would receive.”]

Those presbyters and deacons whom Constantine had consecrated were likewise to return to the status in which they had previously existed. Later, if any of them became acceptable to the aforementioned most blessed pontiff [Note: [Col. 1243D] Another version: “had become acceptable before the aforementioned most blessed pontiff”], he would consecrate them as presbyters or deacons [Note: [Col. 1243D] Codex Lucullanus: “would reconcile them”]. They decreed that those among them who were to be reconciled [Note: [Col. 1243D] Codex Lucullanus: “consecranat” (“were consecrated”)], might in no way rise to a higher honor [Note: [Col. 1244D] Codex Lucullanus: “a more distinguished honor”], nor be advanced to the summit of the pontificate [Note: [Col. 1243D] Another version: “might rise to the summit of the pontificate”], lest such an impious error of innovation should sprout up in the Church of God.

The aforementioned most blessed Pope Stephen himself then declared in a clear voice before the entire priestly college that he would in no way become involved in, or undertake at all, the consecration of those presbyters or [Col. 1244A] deacons.

Concerning the laymen whom Constantine had consecrated as presbyters or deacons, it was promulgated that they were to remain in religious dress for all the days of their lives, whether in their own homes or wherever they might be [Note: [Col. 1244D] Another version: “wherever they wished”].

After these judgments had been promulgated, the bishops who had been ordained by Constantine returned and, in accordance with the judgment of the council, were again elected by the clergy and people in their former rank of honor. After the customary decree had been made and they had hastened to the Apostolic See, they were reconciled and consecrated by the same most holy pope [Note: [Col. 1244D] Codex Lucullanus: “reconciled, and thus …”]. The presbyters and deacons, however, remained in that condition until the death of the pontiff and were never consecrated by him.

For the council also decreed that everything which Constantine had done in the ecclesiastical sacraments and divine worship should be repeated [Note: [Col. 1244D] Codex Lucullanus: “ought to have been repeated”], except for holy baptism and sacred chrism.

After all these decrees had been promulgated, various testimonies of the holy Fathers concerning the sacred images of Our Lord Jesus Christ, of his holy and glorious Mother, the ever-virgin Mary, our Lady, and of the blessed apostles, all the saints, prophets, martyrs, and confessors were immediately brought before the same council. After carefully investigating many matters, they decreed that all Christians should venerate those sacred images with great devotion, just as all the predecessors who had been pontiffs of this Apostolic See, and all the venerable Fathers, had until that time observed their honor and handed it down to everyone as a remembrance of pious compunction. They condemned and anathematized that detestable synod which had recently been held in the regions of Greece for the destruction [Note: [Col. 1244D] Codex Lucullanus: “removal”] of those sacred images.

When everything that had to be promulgated in the council had been completed, the same most blessed pontiff gathered all the priests, the clergy, and the entire people. They proceeded to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, with hymns and spiritual songs, walking barefoot. There Leontius the scriniarius went up into the ambo and read aloud to the people everything that had been done in that council.

Three bishops also—Gregory of Silva Candida, Eustratius of Albano, and Theodosius of Tibur—went up into the ambo of that church and pronounced an obligation under anathema, should anyone at any time presume to transgress any part of everything established in that council [Note: [Col. 1244D] Another version: “lest anyone …”].

After these synodal proceedings had been completed, it happened, some time later, that Sergius, archbishop of the city of Ravenna, departed this life. Immediately Michael, a scriniarius of that church who held no priestly office [Note: [Col. 1244D] Codex Lucullanus: “Michael”], rose up and went to Ariminum to Maurice, duke of Ariminum. That most wicked Maurice gathered an army [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “inde” (“thence”)], together with the counsel of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and hurried to Ravenna and entered it. By force of arms he chose the aforementioned Michael [Note: [Col. 1245D] Codex Lucullanus: “Michael”] and installed him in the episcopal see of the Church of Ravenna.

They carried Leo the archdeacon, who had been elected to the archiepiscopal office, to Ariminum, where Maurice had him held in strict custody. Then the aforementioned Michael [Note: [Col. 1245D] Codex Lucullanus: “Michael”], Maurice, and the judges of Ravenna promptly sent to the aforementioned most blessed Pope Stephen, promising him abundant gifts so that he would consecrate Michael as archbishop.

But the most blessed bishop [Col. 1245B] was not swayed by any promise of gifts to consecrate that Michael. He asserted that this could in no way be done, since the aforementioned Michael did not at all possess priestly rank.

He sent him letters and messengers repeatedly, with admonitions and exhortations, urging him to abandon that unjust undertaking. But Michael refused in any way to heed the apostolic admonitions. He gave many gifts to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, as well as treasures, ornaments of that church, and various other goods. By force of arms, for a full year and longer, he occupied the episcopal see of that church [Note: [Col. 1245D] Codex Lucullanus: “invaded it”], stripping it bare and reducing it to great poverty.

But when the most powerful associates of Michael could in no way bend the firm resolve of that most holy pontiff, and when the messengers of the illustrious Charles, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, were present, the most blessed bishop sent both his own messengers and the aforementioned Frankish envoys to admonish all the Ravennans. Immediately they rose up against Michael and threw him out of the episcopal residence with disgrace. They sent him here to Rome in chains and elected the aforesaid Leo, archdeacon of that church. Leo hastened to the Apostolic See with the priests and clergy of the Church of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 1245D] Another version adds: “of that church, and its judges and people”], and was ordained and consecrated to the archiepiscopal office by the same most holy Pope Stephen.

That aforementioned most blessed bishop was an observer of ecclesiastical tradition. Accordingly, he restored the Church’s ancient rite in its various clerical offices. He decreed that every Sunday the solemn celebration of Mass should be performed on the altar of Saint Peter by the seven cardinal bishops serving weekly in rotation, who minister in the Church of the Savior, and that the “Glory to God in the highest” should be sung. [Note: [Col. 1245D] Another version: “and should be sung over the steps by which they enter the altar.”]

He also made three silver railings over the steps by which they enter the altar, where the images are displayed on the façade: one in the Basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, another in the Basilica of the blessed Paul, and another at the church of the blessed apostle Andrew.

That most blessed pontiff continually endeavored to send his messengers and letters of admonition to the aforementioned illustrious Charles, king of the Franks, and likewise to his brother Carloman, also king. For the aforementioned Christopher the primicerius and Sergius the secundicerius were repeatedly pressing for the rights of Saint Peter, which Desiderius, king of the Lombards, stubbornly refused to return to the holy Church of God. [Note: [Col. 1246D] Mansi, in the margin: “justices,” that is, “rights.”]

For this reason Desiderius himself, inflamed with excessive fury and indignation against the aforementioned Christopher and Sergius, sought to destroy and eliminate them. To achieve this wicked design, he pretended that he would come here to Rome to Saint Peter for the sake of prayer, so that he might capture them. He secretly sent gifts to Paul the chamberlain, surnamed Afiarta, and to his other impious followers, and persuaded them to bring Christopher and Sergius under apostolic displeasure. Paul agreed with him and secretly plotted their betrayal [Note: [Col. 1246D] Another version: “their destruction”].

When the aforementioned Christopher and Sergius learned of this, and learned that the arrogant King Desiderius was going to Rome, they immediately gathered a multitude from the people of Tuscany and Campania, as well as from the duchy of Perugia, and courageously prepared, with that assembly of people, to resist King Desiderius. They also closed the gates of this city of Rome, constructed others in their place, and all remained armed for the defense of their own [Col. 1246C] city.

While this was happening, the aforementioned King Desiderius suddenly arrived at Saint Peter with his Lombard army [Note: [Col. 1246D] Mansi, in the margin: “he joined,” that is, “he arrived”]. Immediately he sent his messengers to the aforementioned pontiff, begging him to come to him [Note: [Col. 1246D] Another version: “to go out”]; and this was done. When the pontiff had been brought into his presence and had likewise spoken about the rights of Saint Peter, the most blessed pontiff returned and reentered the city.

The aforementioned Paul the chamberlain and his most wicked associates, however, having conferred with the aforesaid Lombard king, sought to incite the Roman people against Christopher and Sergius so that they would kill them. When this was reported to Christopher and Sergius, they gathered the people and went armed into the Lateran to seize those who were plotting against them. [Note: [Col. 1246D] Codex Lucullanus: “When this had been announced, they were immediately saved.”]

After the customary announcement had been made, the entire multitude of people who had come with them attacked and entered with weapons into the Basilica of Lord Pope Theodore, where the aforementioned pontiff was sitting. He rebuked them sharply for presuming to enter that holy patriarchate while armed, and, speaking with them, ordered them to withdraw.

On the following day the aforementioned pontiff again went out to Saint Peter to speak with the same king. When they were together, Desiderius set aside the matters concerning the rights of Saint Peter and insisted only upon deceiving [Note: [Col. 1247D] Perhaps read: “the seizure of”] the aforementioned Christopher and Sergius. He therefore closed all the gates of Saint Peter and permitted none of the Romans who had gone out with the most holy pontiff to leave that church.

Then that gracious pontiff [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “Almus” (“gracious”)] sent Andrew, bishop of Praeneste, and Jordan, bishop of Segni, to the city gate leading out toward Saint Peter, where the aforementioned Christopher and Sergius were staying with a multitude of people. They were to urge them either to enter a monastery for the salvation of their souls or to make haste to him at Saint Peter.

But the aforementioned men, fearing the wicked cruelty of the Lombard king, did not dare go out to him. They declared that they ought first to be handed over to the hands of their own Roman brothers and fellow citizens rather than to a foreign people. When the people who were with them heard these words delivered by the aforementioned pontiff through the mouths of the bishops, they were immediately thrown into confusion; their hearts were broken, and each began to withdraw from Christopher and Sergius.

A certain duke, Gratiosus, a kinsman of the aforementioned Sergius, pretended that he was going to his own house. Gathering several Romans, they proceeded together to the Porta Portuensis. Finding the gate closed, they dared to remove it from its hinge, and thus, during the night, went out to the aforementioned pontiff.

When Christopher and Sergius saw that they had been placed in a position of great deception, Sergius first, during that same night, when the bell sounded, descended by the wall and hurried to Saint Peter. The Lombard guards seized him at the steps of Saint Peter’s church and led him to their king. Christopher followed him, and both were brought before the eyes of the aforementioned pontiff. Wishing to preserve them safely, he ordered them to become monks.

After taking his leave of the aforementioned king [Note: [Col. 1247D] Codex Lucullanus: “making his departure”], the same most blessed pontiff entered Rome. He left the aforementioned Christopher and Sergius in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, wishing to bring them safely into Rome under cover of night and in silence because of the plots of their enemies.

But when the sun seemed to be declining toward sunset, the aforementioned Paul the chamberlain and his other most wicked associates immediately gathered a multitude of people. They hurried to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, entered into an impious plot with him, and removed those same Christopher and Sergius from the church of the blessed apostle Peter. With many Lombards they hastened as far as the city gate, where they tore out their eyes.

Thus the aforementioned Christopher was taken to the monastery of Saint Agatha, where he died three days later from the pain caused by the tearing out of his eyes [Note: [Col. 1248D] Codex Lucullanus: “the extraction.”] Sergius was carried to the monastery of the Clivus Scauri and afterward taken to the Lateran cellar [Col. 1248A], where he remained until the death of the aforementioned pontiff.

All these evils came about through the wicked interventions of Desiderius, king of the Lombards. That most holy pontiff held one ordination in the month of December: five presbyters, four deacons, and bishops in various places, numbering . . . . . He was buried at Saint Peter the apostle, and the episcopate was vacant for eight days. [Note: [Col. 1248D] Another version: “nine.”]

[Col. 1248A]

## LETTERS OF STEPHEN III

### FIRST LETTER. STEPHEN III, POPE, TO BERTRADA, QUEEN, CONSECRATED TO GOD

Concerning Itherius, the royal envoy, whom he relates to have labored energetically in the interests of the Church in the duchy of Benevento. For this reason he gives thanks and asks that Itherius’s fidelity be rewarded.

[Col. 1248B] To the religious lady Bertrada, daughter consecrated to God, and to the lord Charles, son and king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans: Stephen, pope.

While your holy spiritual mother, the universal Church of God, relieved and rejoicing with an immeasurable delight because of the accumulated assistance you have furnished in so many apostolic causes and interests, no declaration of speech, as I think, will be sufficient to express the praises of thanksgiving owed to your most holy religiosity and to your most Christian excellence.

Yet although no recompense worthy of you can be rendered by human beings for such a pious work of yours, nevertheless our merciful God, who is powerful and knows how to repay good with good, will himself bestow upon you an abundant recompense of heavenly rewards for your labors. Our sincere affection of heart toward you also continually offers prayers on your behalf to the divine majesty.

Accordingly, the present Itherius, a religious and most prudent man, truly a sincere and faithful servant both of ours and of yours, whom you sent with his companions and your other envoys to execute and secure the rights of your patron, the blessed Peter, arrived among us and immediately departed for the regions of the duchy of Benevento to recover in those parts the patrimony of that protector of yours, the prince of the apostles.

That most diligent man strove in every respect according to your will and ours, and, in accordance with what you had commanded him, displayed the steadfastness of his labor in those apostolic interests. Thus our heart rejoiced greatly in the struggle of his defense and in his firm perseverance in action. For indeed, just as the grace of heavenly favor illuminates his prudence with great knowledge, so it adorns him with the merits of piety and the integrity of unaltered faith. We found in him such fidelity in your service and ours as our mind had long wished to discover in him.

Therefore we offer the greatest and countless thanks to your most religious sobriety and to your most Christian excellence. And so, as though we were present, we earnestly ask your kindness to command that the widest grace of your favor, the generosity of your munificence, and worthy consolation be bestowed upon that religious man for his laborious struggle, which, as has been said, he has displayed in your apostolic service and ours. Thus, just as it is said that, through the intercession of blessed Peter, a worthy reward for his work has been inscribed for him in the heavenly kingdoms by almighty God, so may he receive from you the assistance of consolation.

May our almighty God, through the intercession of the sacred princes of the apostles, surround you with his grace and grant you in abundance the joys of swift happiness in the present life and of eternal happiness. May heavenly grace preserve your religiosity and your excellence unharmed. [Col. 1249B]

### SECOND LETTER. STEPHEN III, POPE, TO BERTRADA, QUEEN, AND CHARLES, KING

Likewise, a copy of the letter of the same pope addressed to the lord Charles, king, and to his exalted mother, concerning Christopher and his son Sergius, who, together with Dodo and the other Franks, attempted to kill Pope Stephen.

[Note: [Col. 1249D] Grets: Baronius and the Centuriators provide a summary of this letter.]

To the religious lady Bertrada, daughter consecrated to God, and to the most illustrious lord Charles, son and king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans: Stephen, pope.

With great sorrow and groaning of heart, we are striving to make known to the ears of your God-consecrated religiousness and of your most excellent Christianity, through these our apostolic words, the danger of tribulation and death that had already befallen us through the followers of the devil. For the most wicked Christopher and his utterly wicked son Sergius, taking counsel with Dodo, the envoy of your brother, King Carloman, were plotting to kill us.

Therefore, having gathered an army with that same Dodo, his Franks, and certain other utterly wicked accomplices of theirs, they entered armed into the holy patriarchate of the Lateran. They smashed the doors and pierced all the curtains of that venerable patriarchate with their lances; then they entered inside, into the basilica of Lord Pope Theodore, where no one had ever been accustomed even to enter with a knife, wearing cuirasses and carrying lances, into the place where we were seated. Thus those wicked men were plotting to kill us. [Col. 1249C]

But almighty God, seeing the uprightness of our heart—that we had never at any time conceived evil against anyone—snatched us from their hands. And only with great ingenuity, while here with us was our most excellent son Desiderius, king of the Lombards, to administer various restitutions owed to us and to blessed Peter, were we able on that occasion, together with our clergy, to take refuge with your protector. Immediately we sent our priests to those same wicked men, Christopher and Sergius, so that they might repent of the evil which they had undertaken to inflict upon us [Note: [Col. 1249D] Lamb. reads: “which they had undertaken to inflict upon us”], and hasten to us, to blessed Peter. [Col. 1250A]

As soon as they heard this, they at once formed companies with Dodo and his Franks, closed the city gates, resisted vigorously, threatened us, and absolutely refused to permit us to enter the city. But while they persisted in that perfidy, and our entire people learned of their wicked plan, they immediately abandoned them; indeed, many of them descended over the wall and hastened to us. Others, opening the city gate, came forward into our presence. Thus those wicked men, compelled and unwilling, were led to us in the church of Saint Peter. The entire people tried to kill them, and only with difficulty were we able to rescue them from their hands. [Col. 1250B]

And while we were planning to bring them safely inside the city under the silence of night, so that no one who saw them might kill them, suddenly those who had always been plotting against them attacked them and tore out their eyes—so we say, with God as our witness—without our will or counsel.

Therefore our heart is crushed by great sorrow; and believe us, daughter consecrated to God, and most excellent son: had the protection of God, and of the Apostle Saint Peter, and the assistance of our most excellent son King Desiderius not been present [Note: [Col. 1250D] The same source reads: “had not been present”], both we and our clergy, as well as all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own community, would already have fallen into mortal danger [Note: [Col. 1250D] The same source reads: “would have fallen”].

Behold how many wicked deeds and diabolical instigations the aforesaid Dodo sowed and carried out here, although he ought to have remained faithfully in the service of blessed Peter and ours. On the contrary, he plotted against our life, not acting according to what his king had commanded him: that he should remain faithfully in the service of blessed Peter and in obedience to us. And we firmly believe that, when such great wickedness of his reaches the ears of our most excellent son Carloman, it will in no way please him, since this Dodo, together with his aforesaid most wicked followers, desired to bring the holy Church of God into such humiliation and devastation. [Col. 1250C]

For this reason we have made known our tribulations, anxieties, and dangers to your religious and most devout Christianity, established by God, and to your excellence, because almighty God has certainly not abandoned those who believe in him and trust in his mercy.

[Col. 1250D] Let your God-loving religiousness and your most Christian excellence know that, in the name of the Lord, by good will we reached an agreement with the aforesaid most excellent and God-preserved son of ours, King Desiderius, and received from him all the restitutions owed to blessed Peter, fully and in their entirety. Nevertheless, through your envoys you will also be completely satisfied concerning this matter. May almighty God surround you with the right hand of his protection, grant that you may enjoy the government of your present kingdom through lasting [Note: [Col. 1250D] Grets. reads: “long-lasting”] and prosperous times, and make you attain in many ways the eternal joys of rewards. [Col. 1251A] May heavenly grace preserve your religiousness and your excellence unharmed.

## Letter III. Pope Stephen III to Kings Charles and Carloman

He congratulates them because they have been reconciled to fraternal concord. He asks that they compel the Lombards to return what they have seized from the patrimony of the Church.

To the most excellent lords, Charles and Carloman, kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, Stephen, pope.

Blessed is the Lord our God, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who exists as the consoler and propitiator of all who call upon him in truth. For he, our Redeemer, hearing the prayers of those who cry out to him, turns the tribulations of the sorrowful into joy. This we now see poured out upon us and upon the entire special people of his holy Church through the clemency of divine piety and the kindness of his mercy: hearing the vows of our prayer, he has now, by God’s favor, turned into great joy the lamentation of our sorrow that until now we have endured because of the division of discord which the ancient enemy, the foe of peace, had introduced among your brothership—having confounded that pestilential rival and causing you, who are truly uterine and full brothers, to be joined in mutual affection and concord.

Accordingly, most excellent sons, great and most victorious kings, your most faithful and diligent envoys who came to us—namely, the most reverend and most holy brother of ours Gauzibertus, bishop, together with the religious Fuchbertus and Ansfredus, as well as your most glorious Helmagarius—brought us honorable and exceedingly welcome words sent by your royal power, established by God. Through them you informed us that disputes and lawsuits had arisen between you, but that, with the Lord’s approval, you now appear to have been converted to true affection, unity of concord, and brotherly love. [Col. 1251C]

When we heard this, we were filled with great joy and gladness, together with all our people of this province redeemed by you. We celebrated a double festival of rejoicing, offering immense thanksgiving to our almighty God and praising his victorious clemency, singing and saying with one voice, in the words of the prophet: “Blessed are you, Lord our God, and blessed are all your works.”

Behold, now our God rejoices in heaven; the entire choir of angels rejoices; and on earth also the whole Christian people exults, while the devil alone, the enemy of peace and sower of discord, mourns, seeing that he has been defeated and overcome. The minds of the faithful could not have expected anything else to happen except what we now rejoice has come to pass. May almighty God multiply in you that peace and fraternal affection which he granted to his holy apostles, and strengthen it once multiplied. [Col. 1251D]
