Therefore, concerning your unity, your holy spiritual mother, the Church of God, and all her people rejoice. For it was also reported in these very letters of yours that, with all your strength, you would strive to exact the restitutions owed to your protector, blessed Peter, and to the holy Church of God; and that you had promised to remain faithful to the pledge of love made by your father of holy memory, Lord Pippin, to that prince of the apostles and to his vicars. You promised to carry out in full the restitutions owed to the holy Church of God and to promote her exaltation. [Col. 1252A]

Indeed, most excellent sons, most Christian and great kings, we are entirely confident and satisfied about this: no human persuasion or lavish gift of treasures will be able to turn you aside or in any way alter you from the promise that you made to blessed Peter. Yet we have now proved your steadfastness, since you have taken care to please not a corruptible and fragile man, but almighty God and the prince of his apostles.

Therefore we earnestly ask you, as though we were present before you, and we adjure your excellence before the living God who commanded you to reign, that you order the full restitutions owed to blessed Peter to be exacted with the utmost speed, according to the capitulary that we have sent you through these your most faithful envoys, and returned to blessed Peter, just as your promise contains. May you also deign to fulfill everything that you promised to blessed Peter and to his vicars together with your father of holy memory, so that, through the intercession of that same prince of the apostles, you may receive from almighty God perfect blessedness in the present and future life. [Col. 1252B]

After God, we place our confidence in you; and in your love and affection of charity we shall remain firm, together with all our people, even unto our soul and the shedding of our blood. Nevertheless, concerning this matter and all the restitutions owed to blessed Peter, we have spoken more fully with your aforesaid envoys, who are to recount everything to your royal majesty. And now, just as thirsty earth awaits rain, so we request your assistance and the fitting fulfillment of our petitions.

And see, most excellent sons, for we adjure you by the dreadful day of judgment: blessed Peter also, through us, exhorts and adjures you to order the restitutions owed to that same prince of the apostles to be exacted from the Lombards with the utmost speed, firmly constraining them by the power of God so that that prince of the apostles and the holy Roman Church may receive what is their own. [Col. 1252C]

For if—which we do not believe—you neglect or delay exacting those restitutions, know that you will have to render a strict account of these matters before the tribunal of Christ to that same prince of the apostles. But if anyone tells you that we have received the restitutions owed to blessed Peter, do not believe him in any way.

May almighty God protect you with his right hand, grant you victory from heaven, and send his angel before your face to go ahead of you and cast your enemies down before your feet. May he extend the boundaries of your kingdom established by God, grant that you may enjoy the government of your present kingdom for a long and prosperous time, and, after the length of this life, grant you the heavenly kingdoms to possess throughout infinite ages. [Col. 1253A]

[Note: [Col. 1253D] The Frankish annals record that in the year 570 of our Redeemer a marriage took place between Charles and Bertrada, daughter of Desiderius, king of the Lombards. For in Aimoinus we read the following: “Bertrada, mother of kings, having spoken with Carloman, her younger son, at Saluces, set out for Italy for the sake of peace. Having completed the business for which she had gone there—for she had gone to seek in marriage for her son, King Charles, the daughter of Desiderius, king of the Lombards—and having also worshiped at Rome at the thresholds of the holy apostles, she returned to her sons in Gaul.” This is Aimoinus. The same account is given by Einhard (or by his continuator, drawing on the brief versions of the Frankish annals) in the Life of Charles. It is indicated that, by the will of their deceased father, they had been designated and joined in marriage to women from other families; the pontiff says shortly afterward, near the beginning, in these words: “For, most gentle and benign kings established by God, by God’s will and counsel you have already been joined in a legitimate marriage at the command of your father,” etc. He therefore dissuades the husbands from a marriage with women who had already been designated for them. See Baronius, under the year 770, nos. 8 and 11. Binius.]

## Letter IV. Pope Stephen III to Kings Charles and Carloman

He earnestly strives to dissuade them from having either of them marry the daughter of Desiderius, or from giving their sister Gisila in marriage to the son of Desiderius.

To the most excellent sons, Charles and Carloman, kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, Stephen, pope.

As we recall to mind the outstanding lives and worthy merits of the works of all God’s elect, we discover that none of them could be removed by any difference of circumstance from the state of their heart or the steadfastness of their original pledge. Thus, although surrounded by the various persuasions and flatteries of the ancient enemy, they are known to have remained unchanging in the firmness of their mind, and for this reason they deserved to reach their desired joys in triumph and victory.

It must certainly be considered that, if anyone is overcome after being enticed by certain persuasions, he will immediately strive to turn aside from the straight path that leads to eternal life, descending by precipitous ways, so that he may fall from this into ever-increasing guilt. For it is generally certain that the ancient enemy strives to steal into the minds of the faithful through the weakness of human nature. Thus, long ago, while the first man was established in paradise, he was able through the weakness of the woman’s nature, by his poisonous flatteries, to persuade him to transgress the divine command; and for this reason the destruction of dreadful death entered the human race. [Col. 1253B]

Therefore, most excellent sons and great kings, the more clearly we see that he repeatedly persists in ambushing the hearts of the faithful in order to deceive them, the more diligently we must resist his efforts, lest he be able to entangle anyone in his arguments.

Accordingly, information has reached us—which we state with great sorrow of heart—that Desiderius, king of the Lombards, is known to be persuading your excellence to join his daughter in marriage to one of your number. If this is indeed so, it is a specifically diabolical instigation, and it appears to be not so much a marital union as an alliance in a most wicked contrivance. For we have discovered, as we are instructed by the history of Holy Scripture, that many have turned aside from God’s commandments through an unjust union with another nation and have fallen into great crimes. [Col. 1253C]

What kind of folly is this, most excellent sons and great kings—indeed, can it even be spoken—that your illustrious Frankish people, which shines above all nations, and the splendid and most noble offspring of your royal power, should be polluted, God forbid, by the faithless and most foul people of the Lombards, a people scarcely to be counted among the nations, from whose nation it is well known that a race of lepers has arisen? No one who possesses a sound mind can even suspect that such renowned kings would be entangled in so detestable and abominable a contagion.

“For what fellowship has light with darkness, or what portion has the faithful with the unbeliever?” For, most gentle and benign kings established by God, by God’s will and counsel you have already been joined in a lawful marriage, at the command of your father, receiving, as illustrious and noble kings, from your own country—namely, from that most noble Frankish people—beautiful wives, and you ought to be devoted to their love. Certainly, it is not lawful for you, after dismissing them, to take other wives or to mingle yourselves with the kinship of a foreign nation. [Col. 1254A]

For none of your ancestors—neither your grandfather nor your great-grandfather, nor even your father—took a wife from another kingdom or a foreign nation. Who among your most noble family ever deigned to defile or mingle himself with the savage people of the Lombards, so that now you are being persuaded—may the Lord avert it—to be polluted by that same horrible people?

Thus no one who took a wife from a foreign nation remained free from harm. Consider, I ask, how many and how powerful men, turning aside from God’s commandments through marriages with foreigners and following the will of their wives of another nation, became entangled in grave offenses and suffered immense dangers. For it is impious even to allow the thought to rise in your hearts that you should take other wives in addition to those whom it is certain you first received. [Col. 1254B]

It is not fitting for you to commit such a wicked deed, since you keep the law of God and rebuke others so that they may not do such things. Pagan nations do this. Far be this from you, who are perfect Christians, a holy nation, and a royal priesthood.

Remember and consider that you were anointed by the hands of the vicar of blessed Peter and sanctified by heavenly blessing; therefore you must beware lest you become entangled in such great crimes. Remember, most excellent sons, that our predecessor of holy memory, Lord Pope Stephen, adjured your father, of most excellent memory, never to presume to dismiss your lady mother; and he, as a truly most Christian king, obeyed her salutary admonitions. [Col. 1254C]

Your excellence must also remember that you pledged to blessed Peter and to the aforesaid vicar of his, or to his successors, that our friends would be your friends and our enemies your enemies, just as we too are known to remain firmly bound by that same pledge.

How, then, do you now strive to act against your own souls and wish to form an alliance with our enemies, when that perjured Lombard people, continually attacking the Church of God and invading this Roman province of ours, are demonstrably our enemies? Therefore, I ask you, make a point of recalling this also: when the Emperor Constantine was striving to persuade your father of holy memory, that most gentle man, to accept your most noble sister Gisila as the wife of his son, he also declared that you might not be joined to another nation, nor in any way dare to act contrary to the will of the pontiffs of the apostolic see. [Col. 1255A]

For what reason, then, are you now trying to act contrary to the apostolic commands and the will of the vicar of the prince of the apostles—something your father never did? Do you not know that you are not spurning our unworthiness, but blessed Peter, whose representatives we are, though unworthy? For it is written: “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever spurns you spurns me” (Luke 10).

Remember, I ask, most excellent sons, how your aforesaid lord and father appeared to speak faithfully to you, promising in your presence to blessed Peter and to his aforementioned vicar, Lord Pope Stephen, that you should firmly remain faithful to the holy Church, obedient to all the pontiffs of the apostolic see, and steadfast in unimpaired charity. [Col. 1255B]

Afterward, it is certain that you repeatedly made the same promise to our predecessor, Lord Pope Paul, together with that same father of yours, through envoys and letters. And after the death of that aforementioned father of holy memory, you yourselves repeatedly promised us, both through your envoys and by letters, and also through our most faithful nomenclator Sergius and through other envoys of ours, that you would remain faithful to the holy Church of God and to us, just as your father had done.

But I ask you also to recall how the aforesaid Lord Pope Stephen, at his departure, strove through his letters, under a terrible adjuration, to exhort you to remain firm and steadfast in your devotion to the holy Church of God and in your unimpaired charity toward the pontiffs of the apostolic see, and to fulfill everything according to the pledge that you made to that apostle of God. [Col. 1255C]

And now, is this your promise? Oh, how great a labor that same supreme and most blessed pontiff endured! Though so weak, he exposed himself to the danger of so long a journey. Unless the Lord comes to his aid, his labor will have been brought to nothing; and that journey which our predecessor undertook there, hastening to Francia, has become for us a great disaster, since our enemies have now been lifted into a greater frenzy of arrogance than before. Behold, we see coming to pass what we feared: our joy has been turned into mourning, the last evils have become worse than the first, and from the place where we expected light to arise, darkness has burst forth. [Col. 1255D]

Therefore blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom the keys of the heavenly kingdom were given by the Lord God, and to whom the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth was granted, earnestly adjures your excellence through our misery. We also, together with all the bishops, presbyters, and other priests, all the nobles and clergy of our holy Church, the abbots and all those devoted to divine worship, as well as the officials and judges and the entire Roman people of this province of ours, adjure you under the oath of divine judgment, by the living and true God, who is the judge of the living and the dead, by the ineffable power of his divine majesty, and by the dreadful day of the future judgment, when all princes and powers and the entire human race will have to stand in trembling; and also by all the divine mysteries and the most sacred body of blessed Peter: let no one of your brothers presume in any way to take the daughter of the aforesaid Desiderius, king of the Lombards, in marriage. [Col. 1256A]

Nor again let your most noble sister, the God-beloved Gisila, be given to the son of the aforesaid Desiderius; nor dare you in any way dismiss your wives. Rather, remembering what you promised to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, resist those same Lombard enemies like men, firmly constraining them so that they must return what belongs to the holy Church and the Roman commonwealth. For, transgressing everything they promised you, they do not cease daily to afflict and oppress us; and now, since they are not at all inclined to return anything to us, they are even known to be invading our borders. Only through a stratagem, in the presence of your envoys, do they pretend to render us our restitutions. Nothing is accomplished in fact, and we have been able to receive nothing whatever from them of what is ours. [Col. 1256B]

Therefore, so that all our sufferings might be carefully brought to your ears, we have sent our envoys, namely our beloved son Peter and Pamphilus, regional defensor of our holy Church. We have carefully instructed them concerning the tribulation threatening us and concerning each of the matters that must be reported to your royal majesty. We ask you to receive them with your customary kindness, to deign to lend your God-inspired ears to our petition, and to order the complete liberation and exaltation of the holy Church of God, your spiritual mother, and the defense of this province redeemed by you, so that you may receive perfect recompense from God our just judge, through the intercession of his prince of the apostles, blessed Peter. [Col. 1256C]

We have therefore placed this exhortation and adjuration of ours at the confession of blessed Peter, offered sacrifice and offerings upon it to our God, and sent it to you with tears from that sacred confession.

And if anyone—which we do not wish—should presume to act against the terms of this our adjuration and exhortation, let him know that, by the authority of my lord blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he is bound by the bond of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and appointed to be burned in eternal fires with the devil, his most savage pomp, and the other impious. [Col. 1256D]

But may whoever proves to be an observer and guardian of this our exhortation be enlightened by heavenly blessings from our Lord and become a participant in the eternal joys of rewards with all God’s saints and elect. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

## Letter V. Pope Stephen III to King Carloman

He asks that he become his spiritual co-parent.

To the most excellent lord, his son Carloman, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Stephen, pope.

Since our almighty Creator and Lord has deigned to pour such grace of pious concern and such effective diligence into your honey-sweet royal heart for the defense and exaltation of his holy Church, most excellent son and most kindly king, the illustrious memory of your celebrated name and the wisdom bestowed upon you from heaven remain renowned throughout the whole world; and in the heavenly kingdoms the worthy merits of your works shine forth.

Blessed, therefore, are you, good and most Christian king. In view of the steadfastness of your faith, which you are known to possess in apostolic affairs and in the fervor of your love for us, we remain firm in our affection for you and never cease diligently to pour out prayers to our Creator for your immense joy and for the stability of your kingdom established by God.

Meanwhile, the religious abbot Beraldus and the illustrious man Audbertus, coming to us, brought honorable and exceedingly welcome words from your excellence, protected by God. We received and reread them with great respect and recognized fully what they contained. Your most faithful envoys themselves also reported to us more fully what your excellence, protected by God, had entrusted to them; concerning these matters, we have answered your faithful men point by point, and they are to recount everything clearly to your majesty, inspired by God. [Col. 1257C–1258A]

But because the fervor of your love burns firmly in our inmost heart, a great longing presses upon us, most excellent of kings: that, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, the affection of spiritual co-parenthood might arise between us. Therefore we earnestly ask your Christianity, good and most excellent king, son established by God, that from the splendid and royal offspring which the Lord has deigned to grant you for the exaltation of his holy Church, we may receive a spiritual son into our arms from the font of sacred baptism, or even through the anointing of the venerated chrism. Thus, with this grace of spiritual co-parenthood strengthened among us by God’s favor, both we and all our people may be lifted into joy and rejoice together in the Lord. [Col. 1258B]

May almighty God, through whom kings reign and princes govern, protect you with his grace, grant you victory from heaven for the defense of his holy Church, and deign to preserve you, long-lived and in good health, upon the throne of the kingdom together with our most excellent and Christian daughter, the queen, your sweetest wife, and your beloved children; and may he grant you the eternal joys of the heavenly kingdom to possess. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed. [Col. 1258C]

## In the Year of the Lord 776. Saint Sturm, Abbot of Fulda

[Col. 1257]

## Historical Notice on Saint Sturm

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca mediae et infimae aetatis.)*

[Col. 1257D] Sturm, also called Sturmius by others, was born in Noricum. At the beginning of the eighth century he was a companion and follower of Boniface, educated in the monastery of Fritzlar, and later the first abbot of Fulda. He died in the year 776 or 779. Historians speak of him in various places, especially Eccard, volume I of *Frankish Affairs*. Two writings of his were published anonymously by Mabillon, volume IV of the *Analecta*, pages 454–457. The first is entitled *Order of the Office in the House or Church of Freising before Easter*; the other, *Ancient Customs of the Monasteries of the Order of Saint Benedict*. Mabillon himself later acknowledged that these little works were by Sturm, who had collected them during his Italian journey, especially in the monastery of Cassino. They were subsequently published again under his name in the book *Ancient Monastic Discipline*, Paris, 1726, quarto, page 4. See *Literary History of France*, volume IV, page 161.

[Col. 1257]

## Life of Saint Sturm by Eigil

*(See this Life below, under the year 722, among Eigil’s works.)*

## Extant Writings of Saint Sturm, Abbot of Fulda

[Col. 1259]

## Order of the Office [Note: [Col. 1259] In French, “the Dome”] in the House of Saint Benedict before Easter

*(Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 151, new edition.)*

[Col. 1259A] First, on the Sunday before Palm Sunday—that is, fifteen days before Easter—they do not sing the short responsory with the *Gloria*, and on Monday they veil the images.

Likewise, on the Sunday on which the olive branches are blessed, they sing Terce while seated at Saint Peter’s. All read the lesson according to custom. After the lesson follows the Introit, the reading from the Apostle, and the gradual proper to that day, together with the Gospel of Palm Sunday. The olive branches are blessed, and they begin the antiphon, “Hosanna to the Son of David.” After this comes “Behold, how good,” and they enter Saint Benedict’s; after the prayer has been said, they begin another antiphon, “A great multitude.” The Litany follows, and with it they enter for the principal Mass.

At that Mass they read the lesson from the Apostle, the gradual and tract, the Gospel, and the Passion of the Lord according to Matthew. When the Mass is completed, they go with psalmody to the refectory. [Col. 1259B]

Likewise, after Palm Sunday they hold a nocturn only for three nights. On Wednesday, however—that is, on the vigil of the Lord’s Supper—after None has been completed, they enter for Mass. They read two lessons and sing two graduals, each with five verses. The Passion of the Lord according to Luke follows. After Compline, at those vigils they do not sound the signal again until the Mass on Holy Saturday; nor do the readers ask for a blessing, nor say the customary words at the end. The same procedure is followed at table.

When all have assembled in the oratory, they do not say the verse, nor the invitatory, nor does the priest complete it; nor do they say a prayer, except that they simply begin the antiphon. The nine psalms are divided into three groups—three, three, and three—with nine great responsories, nine lessons from the Lamentations of Jeremiah, and a tract on the Passion of the Lord. This is done until Holy Saturday. [Col. 1259C]

Likewise, on the Lord’s Supper, Mass is celebrated at Vespers. On entering the refectory, they receive individual drinks and bread, and whatever has been set before them. When they leave, the abbot washes everyone’s feet; afterward they dine.

And on the night of the Lord’s Supper—which is Good Friday—when they begin Matins, they extinguish one candle at each antiphon. Likewise, on Friday at Terce they read the Passion of the Lord according to Matthew; at Sext, according to Mark. At the ninth hour they read a lesson from the prophet Hosea, followed by the gradual with five verses, “Lord, I have heard.” Then comes a reading from Exodus and the tract, “He who dwells in the shelter.” After this, the Passion of the Lord according to John follows. Then the priest pours forth twelve prayers with an equal number of litanies. When all this has been completed, they venerate the holy cross. After Vespers has been celebrated, they go to refresh themselves. [Col. 1259D–1260A]

On Saturday, after the ninth hour, when the signal has been sounded, they enter the oratory. After the prayer has been said, they begin the twelve lessons with nine prayers and an equal number of graduals; the blessings follow, together with the blessing of the candle and of the water.

When they leave, they proceed with the litany to Saint Peter. When the litany has been completed there, after the prayer has been said, they proceed from there to Saint Benedict with another litany. When that too has been completed there, after the prayer has likewise been said, they begin another; with it they proceed to the principal Mass. After Mass, when Vespers has been celebrated, they go with psalmody to the refectory. [Col. 1260B]

Likewise, on Sunday they go with an antiphon and holy water through each dwelling. When everything has been finished and completed, they proceed with psalmody to the refectory. On Monday they go with the cross, the relics, and holy water through each workplace; on returning, they celebrate Mass at Saint Peter’s.

On Tuesday they proceed downward [that is, lower or below], joining themselves to one another and greeting one another at Saint Peter’s in the city. Beginning the litany, they enter the church; they read a lesson from the Acts of the Apostles, the gradual, and the Alleluia; the Gospel follows. After the prayer has been said, they begin an antiphon and proceed to the cell of the holy Savior. After the solemnities of the Mass have been completed, they begin an antiphon and go to the refectory. [Col. 1260C]

When all these things have been completed, on Monday and Tuesday they have eight lessons; on the remaining days, until the sixth day of the octave and until Pentecost, three lessons every night; and at Matins [Lauds], “The Lord reigns,” and “Shout joyfully to God.”

[Col. 1260D] On these feasts there are twelve readings, and “The Lord reigns” is said: Easter, the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, Saint John the Baptist, Saint Peter, Saint Lawrence, Saint Mary, Saint Martin, the Nativity of the Lord, the Epiphany [Col. 1261A] of the Lord, the Octave of the Lord, the Octave of the Epiphany, the Purification of Saint Mary, the Nativity of Saints Faustinus and Jovita, and the deposition of Saint Benedict the abbot, Saint Gregory the pope, and Saint Germanus the bishop. On these feasts, however, there is neither procession nor fasting until evening on the vigil—namely, the Octave of the Lord, the Octave of the Epiphany, and the Purification of Saint Mary. On the remaining feasts of the saints there are eight readings.

[Note: [Col. 1261A] NOTE.—The Order given above is found in a codex of the library of Saint Ulrich at Augsburg, written about nine hundred years ago. We conjecture that it is the ancient Order of the Church of Freising, which was also dedicated to Saint Benedict and initially entrusted to monks by Saint Corbinian, bishop, as we have shown elsewhere. The following deserves notice: on Good Friday the Passion of the Lord is prescribed to be read in three forms. [Col. 1262A] In that codex an old Calendar, or brief Martyrology, written in another hand, precedes it; then follows the Rule of Saint Benedict, at whose end one reads, “For the one who does these things, life will be eternal.” Then follow the verses, “Who [bears] the gentle yoke,” etc. Next comes the order for reading the sacred books in the Roman Church; afterward, the Order that we have just published, together with ecclesiastical hymns. There is also a brief treatise on weights, without the author’s name, in which occur these words: “Twelve ounces make a pound. . . . One and a half pounds make a hemina; two heminae make a sextarius. Twenty-four sextarii make a modius; fifteen modii, a gomor; two gomor, a corus.” Because of the similarity of subject, we append to this Order the ancient Customs once observed in our monasteries, from a very old codex of Saint Gall. Finally, there follows a letter, or rescript, of the Cassinese monks in reply to a letter from German monks concerning the Cluniac rites; we found this letter on the cover of a codex in the public library of Basel.]

[Col. 1261]

# ANCIENT CUSTOMS OF THE MONASTERIES OF THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT

(Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 152, new edition.)

[Col. 1261B] The fathers of monasteries earnestly strive, with the greatest care, to observe the holy Rule, so that they may provide their brothers with what is necessary in food and clothing according to the statutes of the holy Rule; so that they may remove from them every occasion for worldly anxiety, exclude the deadly poison of any private property and of murmuring, and make them suitable for their profession. For they spend the generosity of alms, or any offering whatsoever, and especially the revenues of their possessions, on this above all: that they provide their brothers with necessities, not superfluities, so that they may more freely require from them the observance of their holy calling. They set aside the cares and anxieties of earthly matters, and according to the precepts of the Rule diligently devote themselves to the winning of souls.

[Col. 1261C] 1. In the oratory: the strictest silence, the utmost reverence in psalmody, a measured, more elevated manner of singing, and the most orderly manner of standing in choir; measured modulation in all activities, with all confused haste removed; and the swiftest assembly at every signal.

2. In the sacristy: profound silence, the most immaculate administration, a very proper and orderly distribution of priestly vestments, and a highly distinct sounding of the bells.

3. In the guesthouse: the most honorable reception of monastic guests, with a separate house for receiving other guests.

4. In the refectory: the strictest silence, and the most orderly and clean administration of food and drink; [Col. 1261D] and, according to the Rule, equal distribution in all things as necessity requires, taking care in everything that they nowhere exceed the measure of the Rule.

5. In the cloisters during the hour of reading: the strictest silence and the greatest devotion to reading by everyone; [Col. 1262B] nevertheless, silence and humility were always carefully observed in their dwelling places.

6. In the dormitory: the most orderly arrangement of the beds, and an equal and uniform division of the bedding. We saw nothing there painted, variegated, or made of linen, nor did we see such things in the guest dormitory.

7. No kind of oath was either heard among them or presumed by anyone; and they always maintained nocturnal silence, whether inside or outside, until they recited the verse in the chapter house.

We remember this regular order among those who are eminent in the regular stronghold.

1. First of all, from Vespers until the chapter meeting, which takes place after Prime, the strictest silence is to be maintained. After the hours of Matins, no one is to return to his bed, [Col. 1262C] except when the full office is celebrated, or when someone happens to have risen before the hour—apart from the sick and those unable to do so because of extreme weariness, whose weakness is to be considered by the prior.

2. After the reading of the chapter, everyone is to go out to the work assigned by the prior, taking the greatest care in the modulation of the Psalms and in conversations about spiritual matters, lest idle words creep in; thus, according to the authority of the Rule, they are not to speak until the interrogation. This interrogation is to be considered by the wise, so that they may grasp it in a few words.

3. After the work, Terce, and Mass, all are to assemble fully for reading in the place assigned, except those appointed to various duties. Of the latter, those who are able should attend, their conscience being their witness [Col. 1262D] as to whether they can do so, while maintaining the strictest silence during the reading. Unless the prior orders some more learned brother to give a reading to the less learned brothers or to those needing instruction, provided he is confident in that brother’s conduct.

[Col. 1263A] 4. When these arrangements have been made, the brother in charge of the hourly signals is to go to the kitchen to see whether what is being prepared for the brothers’ use is already ready. When it is ready, he is to sound the signal at greater length, so that all the brothers can assemble in the church. Once they have gathered together, he is to strike a second, shorter signal. When the office is finished, the abbot—or, if he is not present with the brothers, the one next to him—should stand; and the senior dean should hasten to sound the signal of the refectory. When it is heard, the abbot should go first, and the other brothers should follow most decorously, so that no voice or murmur of anyone may be heard there.

5. After the meal they return quickly to their beds, especially the young or negligent, whose conduct is observed. If there are some who are well regarded and wish to do so, they may spend a little time, but only briefly, [Col. 1263B] in prayer in the church. No one, however, is to be found in the cloister or in a forbidden place, lest—God forbid—someone devote himself to storytelling or idleness. Indeed, the aforementioned fathers do not even grant this concession.

6. Likewise, when the prior has struck the signal for None at greater length, it is to be sustained by the second in the manner described above; and everything else that we have said above concerning the hour of Sext is to be completed. There are some who wish to recite the verse after the drink at None, as earlier in the chapter house, in order to release the silence, which they carefully maintain until that hour. But let the abbot see whether he wishes this to be observed. After None, as we have already stated, all things are to be observed in the work.

7. We also saw that the greatest care was taken of the younger brothers, and that two men were appointed to this care, whose life in the monastery was regarded as thoroughly proven. The young men never dared to withdraw from their sight, whether by day or by night.

8. There were also two inspectors who, at every hour while the brothers were awake, went around the monastery so that no brother might be absent from his proper place. If someone was absent, it was immediately recorded on tablets, presented before the abbot in the assembly of the brothers, and corrected according to the Rule’s discipline in proportion to his own [Col. 1264A] presumption. They also observed many other practices, which the brevity of this little document prevents us from recording and which are better learned from the spoken account of those fathers.

9. Concerning the forms of penance, they decide with the greatest caution. They say that there are seven regular forms. The first is admonition once, again, and a third time. The second is public correction before everyone, without excommunication. The third is excommunication for lighter faults. The fourth is excommunication for more serious faults. The fifth is punishment by blows, or bodily chastisement. The sixth is common prayer by everyone. The seventh is expulsion from the monastery, if I remember correctly. Other forms of penance are also found in regular discipline, but these are the more excellent ones.

[Col. 1264B] 10. We also saw another practice worthy of observation. If anyone desired to attain perfection in silence, no brother presumed to speak anywhere, except the two appointed for this purpose. In the church no one spoke apart from what concerned the divine office and words of prayer. If anyone had to speak to someone, he touched the abbot’s garment or that of another brother and indicated the designated place. After stating a very few words, or words of reason, they immediately withdrew, fearing that because of necessary words they might fall into harmful and useless ones.

11. The aforementioned inspectors observed the following: if they saw anyone laughing or whispering something, it was immediately recorded on tablets, and he was corrected most gently at the proper time.

[Col. 1264C] 12. They burned with such great charity toward one another that if it happened that any one of them had to be away for a longer time for the common good, all desired his return with such affection that no mother could have desired her only son more intensely, until he came back. When he had been restored to his own, they immediately rushed upon his neck to kiss him with brotherly affection, fulfilling what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Then you will truly be my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

# APPENDIX

[Col. 1263]

# FRAGMENT OF A ROYAL JUDGMENT AGAINST SINLEI, WHO HAD USURPED PROPERTY BELONGING TO THE CHURCH OF FULDA

[Col. 1263D] Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man. When, in the name of God, we were sitting at the villa of Longlario together with the nobles, bishops, illustrious dukes, and counts, to hear the cases of all and to settle them by lawful judgment, there came the venerable man Sturmio, abbot of the monastery of Fulda, where the lord and holy Boniface rests bodily. He brought a complaint and made a claim against a certain man named Sinlei, because of those properties at the place called Autmondistat, which the lord King Pippin granted by his decree for the cause of Saint Boniface, together with its dependencies [lacuna], houses, buildings, meadows, woods, waters, and watercourses, and everything entirely that appears to belong to that villa of Autmondistat [lacuna].

Enacted on the third day of November, in the fourth year of our reign.

Thiotgandus recognized and subscribed.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 778. SAINT AMBROSE AUTPERTUS, BENEVENTAN ABBOT

[Col. 1265]

# NOTICE CONCERNING SAINT AMBROSE AUTPERTUS

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae aetatis*.)

[Col. 1265A] Ambrose Autpertus, incorrectly called Ansbertus by some, a Gaul and Benedictine monk, and thereafter abbot of Saint Vincent at the sources of the river Vulturnus in Samnium, in the years 777 and 778, in which he died. See the *Acta Sanctorum*, 19 July, vol. IV, p. 646 ff., and Mabillon, *Sanctorum Benedictinorum saeculum* III, part II, p. 256. As he himself attests at the end of his work [Note: [Col. 1265C] Compare Alberic, monk of the Three Fountains, under the year 767, p. 102 ff.], he wrote ten books of commentaries on the Apocalypse under Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and Pope Paul I, and dedicated them in the year of Christ 767 to Paul’s successor Stephen. They were published at Cologne in 1536, and in the Cologne *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. IX, and the Lyon edition, vol. XIII, p. 403. He also wrote the Life of Saints Paldon, Tato, and Taso, brothers and abbots of the monastery of Saint Vincent of Vulturnus, and a historical account of his monastery, [Col. 1265B] which appears in Ughelli, vol. VI, p. 458 (new edition, p. 369), in Mabillon, *Sanctorum Benedictinorum saeculum* III, p. 423, and in the *Acta Sanctorum* on 11 January. But I do not believe that the commentaries on the Psalms and on the Song of Songs, which Labbe writes were published at Cologne and elsewhere, were actually published. Others know nothing of them, except that Oudinus testifies that a manuscript on the Song of Songs exists in the library of Fleury; nor is there any mention of them in Alberic, where he discusses this Ambrose’s lengthy exposition of the Apocalypse.

[Col. 1265C] Trithemius mentions him in chapter 287 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and in book II, chapter 106, of *Illustrious Benedictines*. There he attributes to the same Ambrose [Col. 1266A] Autpertus, whom he says flourished in the year 890, ten books on the Apocalypse, as well as works on the Psalter, the Song of Songs, and a book *On Desire*—whose information he seems to have taken from Sigebert, chapter 91—and a book of Letters to Various Persons. There is, however, strong suspicion that Sigebert, Trithemius, Sixtus of Siena, and others who follow in their footsteps confuse this Ambrose with Autpertus, abbot of Monte Cassino from 834 to 837, concerning whom Peter the Deacon writes in chapter 13 and John Baptist Marus on p. 172 ff.; or perhaps with another, later man of the same name.

To Autpertus of Monte Cassino they attribute a sermon on the Assumption of Mary among the Augustinian sermons on the saints, and, in Combefis’s *Bibliotheca Concionatoria*, a sermon on the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary, or on the reading of Luke 2:22 ff. [Col. 1266B] at the end of the works of Saint Ambrose, Paris editions of 1642, 1665, etc.; and in the Old Homiliary published by Baluzius under Alcuin’s name, vol. I of the *Miscellany*, p. 382, sermons in praise of Saint Matthias the apostle and other saints; also a sermon on the Nativity of Mary, one for the feast of All Saints, a sermon *On Desire* containing eighty testimonies from Scripture, beginning “The Church of the saints”; a sermon for the dedication of a church; a prayer against the seven-times-seven vices; a homily on Mark 9:2 ff.; and so forth. Finally, a book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, often published among the works of Saint Ambrose and Augustine [Note: [Col. 1266C] Vol. VI of the Amsterdam edition, p. 699.]

[Col. 1265]

# LIFE OF SAINT AMBROSE AUTPERTUS, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT VINCENT AT VULTURNUS IN BENEVENTO

(From the Chronicle of the same monastery, written in the eleventh century, in Mabillon, *Acta Benedictina*, third century.)

# PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Col. 1265D] 1. Autpertus, or Autbertus, is the same person as Ambrose Autpertus, called Ansbertus by some, whose ten books on the Apocalypse survive. Before demonstrating this, it is useful to set forth certain preliminary matters concerning his Life, which is supplied to us by the chronicler of the monastery of Saint Vincent on the river Vulturnus in Benevento. This monastery was mentioned above, under the year 720, in the Life of Saint Paldon written by Autpertus himself. This chronicler lived in the eleventh century, as is clear from his Chronicle published by Chesne in volume III of the *History of the Franks*.

2. The name of Autpertus does not appear in the Benedictine calendars, or in the Roman calendar, or in Ferrari’s catalogue. Nevertheless, this chronicler, who examined his deeds more closely, calls him most holy. Ferdinand Ughelli agrees in volume VI of *Sacred Italy*, where he calls Autpertus a saint. Certainly his piety and holiness [Col. 1267A] are demonstrated by the works he left behind, which must be discussed here.

3. Paul the Deacon, in book VI, chapter 40, of *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, speaking of the origins of the monastery of Saint Vincent near the Vulturnus, praises the writings of the highly learned man Autbertus, abbot of that monastery, which he composed concerning the first founders of the place. The chronicler published here also lists several of his works in section 7, among them a book *On the Conflict of Vices*, perhaps the work wrongly attributed to Augustine but attributed to Ambrose in several manuscript copies—perhaps because of an error in the name, since it is established that our Autpertus was also called Ambrose. Indeed, this name appears in the title of his Exposition on the Apocalypse.

4. This exposition was first published at Cologne in 1536, and then in volume IX of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* under the name of Ambrose Ansbertus, a Gaulish priest and most eloquent man. Trithemius calls him a monk and priest of the Order of Saint Benedict, and, together with Bellarmine [Col. 1267B] and others, asserts that he flourished in the year of the Lord 890. Yet they are wrong by an entire century in their calculation, as very pious and equally learned men observed—those who composed the Office of the Most Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist from readings of the Fathers.

They rightly prove this from the conclusion of the Exposition on the Apocalypse, which in the printed books reads as follows:

“Ambrose, also called Ansbertus (more correctly Autpertus or Autbertus), born in the province of Gaul, but for the greater part instructed in divine matters in the region of Samnium, at the monastery of the martyr of Christ, Vincent; and not only that, but also devoted to the sacred altars for offering the gifts of Christ, through the work of the blessed and inseparable Trinity, with the merits of the blessed Virgin Mary also assisting, in the time of Paul, Roman pontiff, and likewise of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and of Arechis, duke of the same province in which I dwell, I composed and completed this work. For ease of understanding I have called it the *Mirror of the Little Ones*.”

Paul I, as they rightly observe, presided over the Roman See from 757 to 767, precisely the period when Desiderius held power in Italy. Autpertus’s commentary is represented by two excellent and very old copies in the library of Corbie. The inscription of the first is this: “Here begins the letter of Ambrose Autpertus to Stephen, bishop of the city of Rome, concerning his books.” The letter begins: “To the most blessed Stephen, Ambrose Autpertus, priest,” etc. This was Stephen III, successor of Paul, whose authority Autpertus invoked against the detractors of his already published work.

The title of the second part is: “In the name of the holy Trinity, here begins the second part of the exposition of Autpertus the priest on the Apocalypse.” It begins with the fifth book. At the end, the conclusion quoted above from the printed codices is lacking.

We have also read a homily by the same author in two equally ancient parchment books, composed on the Gospel of the Transfiguration, preceded by this title: “Here begins the homily of Autpertus the priest on the reading from the Gospel according to Matthew, in which the Lord is said to have been transfigured on the mountain before three [Col. 1267D] disciples.” After the words of the Gospel have been introduced, it continues: “Here begins the homily on the same reading, delivered to the monks in the monastery of Saint Vincent.”

“It often happens, indeed it happens almost always, that in the houses of kings and princes some base and despised person cleans gold or silver vessels. But what are the hearts of the elect in the holy Church, which are, so to speak, royal vessels?” etc.

This homily has nowhere been published in print, nor have two others that we possess in manuscript, one on the Purification and the other on the Assumption of the Blessed Mary. The title and opening of the first are as follows: “A sermon on the reading of the holy Gospel, delivered by Lord Aubertus, priest and abbot, on the Purification of Saint Mary. If the faithful carefully consider what the feast of this day is,” etc. The other begins: “A sermon of Autbertus the priest on the Assumption of Saint Mary. Beloved brothers, here is present the venerable day surpassing the solemnities of all the saints,” etc.

From the fragment that we shall report at the end of this Life, you will understand what Autpertus’s view was in that sermon concerning the Assumption of the Mother of God. It is indeed said below, in section 7, that Autpertus composed certain homilies on the Gospels with a beautiful exposition of his sermons.

In these works he is generally called priest, only once abbot; he is always called Autpertus or Autbertus, and sometimes Ambrose Autpertus, in the manuscript books. Moreover, he was not yet abbot when he commented on the Apocalypse, since he composed that exposition during the pontificate of Pope Paul, whereas he became abbot under Pope Hadrian, as will be shown below.

5. Having prefaced these matters concerning Autpertus’s works, it is useful to extract certain passages from his commentaries on the Apocalypse that contribute greatly to clarifying the events of his life. What studies he devoted himself to he declares at the beginning of book VIII in the following manner:

“We find very few faithful interpreters whom secular learning did not first imbue before they passed on to explaining the divine Scriptures; and who, when they came out of Egypt, were not enriched by the wealth of the Egyptians—such as Jerome, Augustine, Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, and many others. Yet I know that this has by no means happened to me, least of all. For I did not come out of Egypt laden with riches, since it never happened that I was educated in the school of worldly wisdom. Plato contributed nothing to me, Cicero nothing, Homer nothing, Virgil nothing, Donatus nothing, Pompeius nothing, Servius nothing, Sergius nothing, Priscian nothing. But if I seem perhaps to possess anything, I confess that I received it from Christ in the storehouse of the Lord’s preaching—not that knowledge of those men was denied me, but that I took greater delight in the words of the humblest fisherman than in those of the most arrogant orator, and devoted myself more to divine than to human discourse.”

From this we understand that Autpertus devoted himself entirely to the reading, meditation, and preaching of the sacred Scriptures. By “the sacred Scriptures” he also understands the holy Fathers, whom he cites repeatedly, especially Augustine and Gregory the Great.

6. He likewise mentions his devotion to preaching at the beginning of book IX. To John—and indeed to the Church in John—it is said: “Take the book and eat it.” By these words, he says, I strike myself when I speak, for although I have received a small ability to understand, I often dissipate myself in empty matters without any compelling necessity; and often, under the pretext of divine preaching, I associate with worldly men more familiarly than is proper.

Opposed to this is the saying: “Write wisdom in the time of leisure; and he who is less occupied with activity will perceive it.” Yet in one of the matters I have mentioned, great consolation comes to us, because when, compelled by charity for the benefit of many, we descend to lower things, we rise all the more vigorously to understand higher things. [lacuna]

Meanwhile, when we go out from familiar meditation on Scripture to the office of preaching, and return from the office of preaching to familiar meditation on Scripture, we must examine ourselves by careful inquiry and weigh with keen attention what and how great are the things in which we are making progress or have suffered loss, so that, with fear and hope striking the soul from both sides, neither pride may hurl it headlong nor despair plunge it again into the abyss.

7. He himself reveals what moved him to write, at the very beginning of book I:

“If it is asked of me why, after all the ecclesiastical writers have fallen silent, I presume to undertake this task, I quickly answer with humble submission: because I recognize that divine grace has impelled me to this very thing. If anyone complains that the life of an interpreter is unworthy, I reproach myself in this matter rather than others. Yet it is not unworthy of God to bring forth his words through a man who, though a sinner, is nevertheless in some measure a Christian; for long ago he prophesied through sacrilegious and impious men.”

And at the end of book X:

“But I beseech you, my Lord, teacher of angels and human beings, do not count among such men the one who seeks to undertake a more corrected life together with salutary doctrine. And since he cannot do this unless he receives it from you—you who have granted the gift of knowledge—I ask that you grant also the will, zeal, and strength to do good. If the will, zeal, and strength to do good do not follow the gift of knowledge, it is enough for me, Lord, to be foolish and dull. For I did not leave my homeland and parents so that you might bestow on me the gifts of knowledge, but so that you might lead me to eternal life through perfection in the virtues. I certainly do not want this exchange. But if I do not deserve both—namely, teaching and action—then, I beg you, take away teaching, provided only that you grant the practice of the virtues. Would that all who devote themselves to sacred studies were moved by a similar impulse! This is what I especially wish those of our people who apply themselves to letters to attend to.”

8. How devoted Autpertus was to the holy Fathers is attested in many places, especially at the end of book X, in these words:

“As far, therefore, as the correctness of the faith is concerned, the exposition is guarded in each individual statement, so that if he should perhaps wish to rebuke me in these matters, let him rebuke also—as I mention a few out of many—Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, and our Gregory.”

Here observe that he calls Gregory “our” Gregory, that is, a Benedictine, as the distinguished man Emericus Bigotius had previously noticed and communicated to me in writing.

9. Although Autpertus was such a man, he was not free from envy. When he published his books on the Apocalypse, he immediately suffered detractors, against whom he invoked the authority of Pope Stephen, by which he attempted to fortify himself. His letter to Stephen on this matter survives. In it he defends the freedom of the entire Church, namely, that each person may compose books according to what he has received from above, without another’s opposition; and he declares that whoever tries to abolish this freedom of the spirit ought to be condemned.

Further on he says:

“Recently I published ten books on the Apocalypse of John. Although it would have been sufficient for me that they were strengthened by testimonies of the sacred Scriptures corresponding to the true faith and that they were supported by the understanding of earlier interpreters, nevertheless, looking to my humility, I ask that they also remain firm and useful by your decree, since I find that there has been no other interpreter besides myself.”

It is worthy of observation in these words that Autpertus was the first to seek a decree of the Roman pontiff for the confirmation of his books.

10. Finally, he was so far from shrinking from the vigils required by study that he even undertook the labor of a copyist. Thus he says in a prayer to God:

“And because in this work, so full of labor, the assistance of copyists seems to be lacking, I beseech you, Lord, that neither the hand forming the characters of the words nor the outward sight observing the words formed in letters may impede the heart searching inwardly into the hidden mysteries; and so may the intention of the heart remain watchful within, so that the hand’s task may in no way grow sluggish outwardly.”

He repeats the same at the beginning of book V. It is remarkable that so great a man—as we read also happened to the venerable Bede and Paul the Deacon—lacked even one companion to offer pen and hand for recording his thoughts and words.

11. We have prefaced these matters at such length because Ambrose Autpertus has until now been insufficiently known, and the account of his deeds supplied by the chronicler below is not enough to commend his achievements.

12. At the time when Autpertus flourished in the Vincentian monastery, Magnus also lived there, a learned man of remarkable conduct, as is read in the Acts of Saint Walfrid, abbot of Palatiolum, above under the year 765. Magnus assisted Walfrid in establishing his monastery.

# HERE BEGINS THE LIFE

[Col. 1269]

[Col. 1269C] 1. I think it worthwhile to recount at somewhat greater length what follows concerning the most holy abbot Autpertus. Indeed, I do not doubt that I can be helped before God by his merits. His origin, deeds, and arrival in this holy monastery of Christ’s Levite Vincent have been handed down partly by an old written account; partly, having learned them from the trustworthy reports of venerable fathers, I have gathered them together and, writing them to the praise of our almighty God, offer to posterity the perfection of true religion and an example of perseverance to those who strive for the love of God in the institutions of the sacred monastery.

Thus whoever looks upon him may contemplate his nobility and turn as quickly as possible from the vanity of the world; whoever attends to his prudence and charity may pursue the humility of Christ with greater eagerness; and if he zealously strove to trample upon the riches of the world, he may rejoice all the more in the happiness promised him by the Lord in heaven. If, being poor, he renounced his own will and professed under the yoke of the holy Rule to serve God as a soldier, let him know that he ought no longer to worry about tomorrow; but let him remember that the Lord will also deem those humble in spirit worthy of salvation.

2. This most holy Father, born in the provinces of Gaul to parents exceptionally distinguished both in the religion of Christ and in worldly rank, shone conspicuous in Christianity like a ray of the sun. When he was still in his youthful years, he was committed to the study of letters. Guarding Christ’s commandments innocently with all his strength, he acquired the effectiveness of a true philosopher of Christ in both divine and worldly philosophy.

Afterward he was received into the royal court of the emperor Charles, of blessed memory. Since he was loved by everyone, and especially by that same emperor Charles and his pious father Pippin, he began to be regarded as the emperor’s most prudent teacher and instructor, and as the most energetic archchancellor of the imperial court [Note: [Col. 1269D] Autpertus was certainly Charles’s teacher, but he was not archchancellor. He was already a monk before Charles assumed the rule of the Franks, as is clear from the conclusion of the Exposition on the Apocalypse cited above.] above all others.

Although he was revered and exalted by everyone with the special honors and services that were rightly his, he nevertheless guarded even more attentively the simplicity of his pious heart and the sincerity of pure charity.

3. At that time, the monastery of the blessed martyr Vincent at the source of the river Vulturnus had been built by the holy fathers Paldon, Tato, and Taso, and there remained a great congregation of saints serving God, which at that time was nearly preferred to the principal monasteries of Italy. It happened that the reputation of their holy religious life, spreading far and wide, reached the ears of the most merciful emperor Charles.

Moved by divine love, and especially persuaded by his venerable teacher and archchancellor Autpertus, he first wished to investigate the truth of this reputation. He sent his *apocrisiarius* to that monastery; then, coming to Rome with a great company of powerful men to pray at the threshold of the first prince, Peter, and to avenge the destruction of the churches and people of the homeland, he completed the necessary affairs and deigned to approach the same monastery with a very large multitude of both devout bishops and abbots, as well as accompanying counts and marquises.

How honorably he was received there by the holy fathers and how humbly he himself entered is more fully contained in the book [Note: [Col. 1271D] This book, as we think, still lies hidden in darkness. Would that someone might either publish it in print or send it to us.] of their Life. It was written with considerable clarity at the command of Lord Taso, the abbot, by the venerable Peter, priest and monk of the sacred monastery.

4. When the same most serene emperor, after the magnificent gifts he had bestowed there and after confirming by royal decree the possessions they held far and wide, had prostrated himself before the footsteps of the holy fathers, commending himself for a long time to their prayers, and, having received their blessings, wished to return in haste, the man of God Autpertus observed the examples of pious conduct in the holy fathers and admired them greatly. His mind already delighted in becoming like them.

After some time had passed [Note: [Col. 1271D] Here the author confuses the order of events. According to Einhard, Charles attacked Arechis in the year 786, and, if we believe Leo Marsicanus in book I, chapter 12, of the *Cassinese Chronicle*, he went to Monte Cassino in 774. I am inclined, however, to follow Paul Warnefridus, or any other author whose supplement to the *History of the Lombards* appears in Marquard Freher’s *Corpus of Frankish Historians*. It says: “In the year 787 King Charles, coming to Rome, proceeded into the land of Benevento and visited the monastery of Saint Benedict.” Lambert of Hersfeld agrees. Yet Autpertus had already embraced the monastic life several years earlier, as follows from the evidence.] the emperor Charles attacked Benevento and harassed its citizens with a prolonged siege, but the city was altogether difficult for him to capture. Meanwhile Arechis, prince of that city, taking pious thought for the safety of his citizens, made a pact with him by giving two of his children as hostages.

Then the emperor, returning from there, went to the monastery of Saint Benedict, commending himself to the prayers of the servants of God. He bestowed many gifts there and confirmed by imperial decree whatever they possessed, adding many other things as well. To the monastery of the martyr of Christ, Vincent, he likewise sent great gifts on his behalf, and reverently dispatched both the venerable man Autpertus and the distinguished Aetherius, master of the imperial court [Note: [Col. 1272D] In the copy transmitted to us, “Alcuin” was read; but this reading of Chesne is preferable. In Pope Paul’s letter to Charles the Great, which appears as no. 44 in volume III of Chesne’s *History of the Franks*, it is said: “Itherius, with his companions and the other envoys of Charles, went into the parts of the duchy of Benevento to carry out and administer justice.”], who faithfully conveyed his pious wishes to the servants of God.

### 5

Then the venerable servant of God Autpertus, moved by love of holy religion, prostrating himself at the emperor’s feet, begged that he might now serve God, abandoning worldly tumult, and remain most willingly until the end of his life in the monastery of Saint Vincent; he proposed to give himself to God for the emperor’s welfare. When the emperor heard this, he shed many tears out of devotion to the man. Although he seemed to be deprived of great assistance by his departure, nevertheless, after being petitioned by many, he granted what was requested. Following his example, many from the royal court laid aside the military belt and joined him in the holy purpose of religious life; everything they appeared to possess they completely abandoned for the love of God, as though they had never seen it.

### 6

When the man of God had put on the habit of holy religion, he considered himself inferior to everyone with such inward feeling of heart that he wished to know nothing at all [Al., “to possess nothing”] except the necessities of daily sustenance supplied by the abbot. Even these, in fact, he seemed to take on equal terms with the others. Although he had been extremely luxurious in the royal court, he devoted himself so entirely to divine service that no hour passed empty for him: either he applied himself to prayer, or his mind was occupied with sacred reading.

### 7

Finally, as we have learned, he expounded very many books of the Holy Scriptures. In his exposition of Moses’ Leviticus, Solomon’s Song of Songs, and the Psalter, he disclosed through a document of words, with honeyed sweetness, what divine mysteries of the sacraments lie hidden in them and what constitutes the moral discipline of each believer or the observance of Christ’s commandments. He also produced a book *On the Conflict of the Vices* [Note: Is this the work that exists among the spurious works of Augustine under this title in volume IX, and that is also attributed to Saint Ambrose in several manuscript codices? We gave his book *On the Deeds of Paldon*, etc., above under the year 720; that book is praised by Paul Warnefrid in book VI of *The History of the Lombards*, chapter 40, where he calls Autpertus a most learned man. His commentary on the Apocalypse and his homily preached on the Transfiguration were mentioned above. The rest still lie concealed.], and he published several homilies on the Gospels in the beautiful exposition of his discourses. He also wrote a full account of the life of the blessed Fathers Paldon, Tato, and Taso, together with the history of their monastery, and presented them to all monks as an example in such a way that, by the gift of the divine Trinity, he showed those three brothers to be both a mirror and a rule of life, especially in charity and in love of poverty for Christ’s sake. The venerable Paul the Deacon also bears witness to this in the history that he wrote at that time concerning the Lombards’ arrival in Italy, where he commends this same man, the most learned Autpertus, and says that he was abbot of that monastery.

### 8

It is further reported that one day, while that most faithful Father Autpertus was pouring out lengthy prayers to the Lord in the church of the blessed Mother of God, Mary, and earnestly entreating that same Mother of God in prayer to grant him fluency of speech—for he had been somewhat impeded in his speech—he suddenly fell asleep before the sacred altar. In a vision he saw the most blessed and glorious Lady of the world, the perpetual virgin Mary, standing before him, her face joyful and radiant beyond the brightness of the sun. As though assenting to his prayer, she touched his lips. She ordered him to rise from the pavement and henceforth to offer the vows of her praise and raise songs of proclamation, as she had now desired; and she promised that she would always be present with him. Rising joyfully from the vision, he began with eloquent speech to offer the praises he had been commanded to offer, and with an eager heart he rendered worthy hymns.

### 9

When this holy Father had served the Lord for many years in the same venerable monastery of Christ’s precious martyr Vincent, and had already become an example to all of upright living, the venerable abbot of that holy community, John, died. Although unwilling and resisting, Autpertus himself assumed the office of sacred governance as the seventh abbot after Saint Paldon [Note: Paldon’s successors were Tato, Taso, Atto, Herempertus, and John; Autpertus was appointed after them in 776, after he had served the Lord there for many years]. From that time onward he strove to administer the care of the flock entrusted to him so worthily that, by opening to all the treasure of the heavenly King, he taught his subjects through the devotion of his faith to grasp more eagerly the true riches that must be preferred to worldly wealth—not only by his words but also by his conduct—and he became a model for the flock, as the blessed Apostle teaches.

From the illustrious Emperor Charles he obtained the following charter for his monastery [Note: This diploma is mentioned in the aforementioned history of the martyrs, which will be presented in the next century under the year 882]:

> In the name of our Lord God Jesus Christ, Charles, by the divinely ordained clemency of God, king of the Franks. When the petitions of priests and servants of God that have been brought to our ears receive our assent, we bring them to fulfillment with God’s help. By this we not only exercise royal custom, but also add a benefit of no small importance both for the prosperity of the present life and for the blessedness of the life to come.
>
> Therefore let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, both those now present and those to come, that the venerable man Autpertus, our intercessor, abbot of Saint Vincent, deacon and martyr of Christ—which is situated in the territory of Beneventum above the river Vulturnus—having been sent there by us, implored our clemency that we should confirm, by a charter of our confirmation, the charters of the Lombard kings and dukes Aistulf, Desiderius, and Gisulf, adding to them whatever might seem suitable and appropriate to us.
>
> Because of our love for our Lord Jesus Christ and for the remedy of our souls, we grant and confirm, according to his request, the aforementioned charters, written instruments, and offerings, declaring the estates themselves by name within these boundaries: from Zitula [Al., Zetula], as it ascends along the Sangro to Mount Malus; from there, as it joins Mount Acze; then, following that same Mount Acze, to the river Melfa; and as the Melfa runs down to the point where it joins the small river called Mellarinus; from there to the summit of the mountain above the city, which mountain is called Barbola; then along the ridge of that same mountain to Mount Arcanus, Mount Martha, and Mount Casale; and beyond these mountains, encircling them externally, to the garden of the stream called Bavennola [Al., Ravennola]; then as that Bavennola runs down to the river Vulturnus; and where the Vulturnus joins the river Vantra; and where the Vantra joins the river Forulus; and as the Forulus runs as far as the old road; and from there joins the Biurius [Al., Bivio] called Gizzoli; and from there goes to a stream in which water does not always run; and thus proceeds to the Sangro.
>
> All the castles, villages, and woods situated within these boundaries are included, together with the church of the blessed Apostle Peter situated at the place called Trite [Note: Chesnius has the erroneous reading “Iritae.” In the previously mentioned history of the martyrs, the Lombard king Desiderius is said to have built, at the command of the prince of the apostles Peter, a monastery in honor of his name in the valley of Tritana beside the river Siler, etc.]; the church of Saint Mary at Apianice; the church of Saint Mary at the Two Basilicas; the church of Saint Mary at Canneto [Al., Cameto]; the church of Saint Mary at Palene; and the church of Saint Mary at Quinque Millia, with all their appurtenances.
>
> This is granted on the condition that the aforesaid abbot and his successors have authority over everything just mentioned, both in this charter and in the other written instruments: to hold, lawfully exchange, administer, instruct, or do whatever is just. From now on, no one shall have permission to inflict any opposition or annoyance upon the parties of the aforesaid monastery within the aforementioned boundaries, whether through the illustrious boundaries [Possibly: “marked boundaries”], through the possessions of relatives, or by any other means, except by means of wholly authentic documents with which litigants may legally defend themselves and properly recorded just conveyances.
>
> We further order that the aforesaid monastery, with all the monasteries and cells mentioned above, together with the property and households belonging to them and with the brothers and monks serving God there, shall remain forever under the protection and guardianship of our authority.
>
> If anyone should rise against this grant or confirmation of ours, or should attempt to inflict any annoyance, let him know that he shall pay two thousand pounds of pure gold, half to our sacred palace and half to the same venerable monastery.
>
> And so that this gift of ours may obtain firmer force, retain inviolate and unchangeable permanence through the course of the years, and be believed and carefully preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.
>
> Sign of the lord Charles, most serene king.
>
> Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 775 from the Lord’s incarnation [Note: At that time neither the indiction nor the year of the incarnation was customarily appended, but the year of the reign was. We have omitted here, following Chesnius, other diplomas of altogether doubtful authenticity. One was that of Charlemagne, if it please God, in which the discovery of the body of Saint Peregrinus, made by him through heavenly instruction, is recounted; this is attributed to King Charles III in volume VI of *Italia Sacra*, columns 139–140].

### 10

After the venerable abbot Autpertus had completed one year, two months, and twenty-five days in holy governance, receiving the palm of a just work, he happily departed to Christ in the year 778 of the Lord’s incarnation, in the second indiction [Al., first], on the nineteenth day of July. He was buried in a worthy tomb in the church of Saint Peter.

## Appendix

[Col. 1275]

### Concerning Autpertus’s death, translation, and sermon on the feast of the Assumption

#### 1

Pope Hadrian I, in his letter to Charlemagne—letter 72 among the papal letters in volume III of Chesnius—mentions the death of Saint Autpertus, or Autbertus, in these words:

> Your lofty royal excellence directed that the disputes between the monks of the venerable monastery of Saint Vincent and the abbots of that same monastery, namely Autbertus and Potho, should be discussed and examined according to both canon and rule before our judgment. For the aforesaid abbot Autbertus, while traveling along the road, was overtaken by sudden death and was unable to present himself before our apostolic presence.

Another letter of Hadrian, numbered 79, had preceded this one. From it we learn that Potho was falsely accused before Charles of lèse-majesté. Hadrian pleaded on his behalf; then, having been made arbitrator of the case by Charles, he summoned the accusers and Potho himself to Rome.

One is compelled to wonder why there were two abbots in the monastery of Saint Vincent at that time, Autpertus and Potho. Had Autpertus, already advanced in age, yielded his dignity to Potho? Or rather, was Potho deposed because of the unjust accusations of the abbots, and was Autpertus appointed in his place? In the catalogue reported by Ferdinand Ughelli, Hainardus is listed as Autpertus’s successor, and Potho as Hainardus’s successor after three years and ten months.

#### 2

“After the Church’s final desolation,” says the chronicler, “when, concerning the death of Abbot Joshua, we had learned through widespread report that some people had often experienced divine benefits at Joshua’s body, we brought his bones, together with those of the venerable Autpertus and other ancient Fathers, to this place and placed them in a great sarcophagus, along with the body of our lord Abbot Hilary.”

Hilary died in 1044; more about him elsewhere.

#### 3

It is useful to insert here a fragment of Saint Autpertus’s sermon on the Assumption of blessed Mary. In a Cluniac manuscript the sermon bears this title:

> Here begins the sermon of the presbyter Autbertus on the Assumption of holy Mary.

“Beloved brothers, the venerable day surpassing all the solemnities of the saints is here; yes, I say, the splendid day is here, the illustrious day, the day on which the virgin Mary is believed to have departed from the world. Therefore let the whole earth resound with praises in great exultation, illumined by the departure of so great a virgin; for it is utterly unfitting that the solemnity of the memory of her through whom we were worthy to receive the Author of life should not be held in the greatest honor. It must also be judged most perverse that, when we celebrate the victories of the holy martyrs, we should not prefer her solemnity to theirs, since she brought forth the Prince of martyrs for this world.

“On this day, appropriately, the virgin Mary proclaims to that heavenly Bridegroom: ‘You have held my right hand, and in your will you have led me, and with glory you have received me.’ Today, I say, she appropriately hears from the Bridegroom, Son, and Lord: ‘Winter has now passed, the rain has gone away and departed. Rise, my beloved, my bride, my dove, and come.’

“We say this, brothers, because, as the Church of Christ has now accepted as customary, it is handed down that on this day the virgin Mary was assumed into heaven. But no catholic history relates in what manner she passed from here to the heavenly realms. The Church of God is accustomed not only to reject apocryphal accounts but even to remain ignorant of these matters [Supplement: ‘as is customary’]. Some writings concerning her Assumption have indeed been composed without an author’s name; as I have said, they are avoided so carefully that they are not permitted to be read as confirmation of the truth of the event.

“Thus certain people are troubled because her body is not found on earth, nor is her Assumption with the flesh, as it is read in apocryphal writings, found in catholic history. They should be told that, if the body of Moses—who spoke with God face to face—is not found on earth by human beings, it is madness to seek the body of her through whom that same God of majesty shone forth incarnate on earth. It is not fitting for anyone to be anxious about knowledge of her body when he does not doubt that she has been raised above the angels and reigns with Christ.

“It should be enough for human knowledge truly to confess her to be the queen of angels, because she bore the King of angels. Nor is any Latin commentator found to have openly said anything about her death. When Ambrose of blessed memory was treating that verse of the Gospel in which Simeon says to the Lord’s mother, ‘And a sword will pierce your own soul,’ he said: ‘Neither history nor the text teaches that Mary ended her life by the sword.’ Isidore likewise says: ‘It is uncertain whether by this saying he meant the sword of the spirit or the sword of persecution.’

“But why should I speak of these matters about which I am talking, when even the evangelist John himself, who received her into his own keeping before the cross of the Lord, did not commit anything concerning this for posterity to retain in writing? No one could have committed this more faithfully, if God had wished to reveal it, than the man who undertook to care for her; nor, contrary to custom, did a son abandon his mother. It therefore remains that a human being must not deceitfully invent as openly revealed what God wished to remain hidden.

“The true judgment concerning her Assumption, however, is shown to be this: following the Apostle, whether in the body or outside the body, we believe that she was assumed above the heavens, though we do not know which. Thus let us say something in praise of the most sacred Virgin.

“But what can we, so insignificant, what can we, so small in our action, say in her praise, when, even if all our limbs were changed into tongues, no one would be sufficient to praise her? She of whom we speak is higher than heaven; she whom we attempt to praise is deeper than the abyss. For she carried enclosed in her immaculate womb the God whom no creature can contain.

“She alone was worthy to be called both Mother and Bride. She undid the losses of the first death; she brought redemption to the lost human race. The mother of our race, Eve, brought punishment into the world; the Mother of our Lord brought joy into the world. Eve, the author of sin; Mary, the author of merit …” [and almost everything that follows from Augustine’s Sermon 18, *On the Saints*].

From this homily we gather, first, that the term “Assumption” was already in use in the Church in Autpertus’s time. Second, that the author so moderates his judgment that he defines nothing concerning the bodily Assumption of the Mother of God, but says that we should believe her assumed above the heavens, whether in the body or outside the body. This was also the view of Adamnan in book I of *On the Holy Places*, and of the Anonymous author who committed the *Itinerary of Saint Willibald* to writing below, although the nun who wrote that same *Itinerary* held a different opinion.
