## All the Extant Writings of Saint Ambrose Autpertus, Abbot of Beneventum

[Note: Several writings attributed to Saint Ambrose Autpertus never appeared so evidently genuine that they were not assigned to other authors and published with their works. Such was the fate of the commentaries on the Song of Songs and on the Apocalypse, as well as the treatise *On the Conflict of the Vices and Virtues*. We ourselves have already published all of these in various places: the first in volume III of Saint Augustine, in the Appendix (*Patrologia*, XXXV); the second in volume IV of Saint Ambrose of Milan (*Patrologia*, XVII); and the third in volume VI of the aforementioned Saint Augustine, in the Appendix (*Patrologia*, XL). It is therefore enough to refer the reader back to those places.]

## Sermon on Avarice

*(From the manuscript of the illustrious lord Chauvelin, written approximately 800 years ago, in Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, volume IX.)*

### Preliminary Observation

Ambrose Autbertus, whom some incorrectly make the teacher and archchancellor of Charlemagne, was born in the province of Gaul and assumed the monastic habit in the region of Samnium, at the monastery of Saint Vincent on the Vulturnus. Since he had been impeded in his speech, he is said to have received a ready facility of speaking through the merits of the most blessed virgin Mary; and he achieved this so successfully that Paul Warnefrid honored him with the title “most learned man.” He lived in the monastery in such a way that he deserved to be numbered among the holiest monks and finally to be promoted to the abbatial dignity. He died in the year 779.

As the Chronicle of Saint Vincent records, he left behind numerous monuments of his intellect: works on Leviticus, the Song of Songs, and the Psalter; a book also on the Conflict of the Vices; and homilies, besides a commentary on the Apocalypse, which is his principal work, composed with uncommon learning and piety. In chapter 91, Sigebertus and Trithemius add a book *On Avarice*, which Philip Labbeus believes to have been lost in his *Historical Dissertation on Ecclesiastical Writers*. But this work, which long lay hidden in darkness, has at last come to light through the aid of the very ancient manuscript of the most illustrious lord Chauvelin, approximately 800 years old; there it bears the title not of a book but of a sermon. I shall append to it a sermon on the Purification of Blessed Mary and a homily on the Transfiguration of the Lord. We present the former here from manuscripts of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and Fleury collated with one another, and the latter from two manuscripts of the library of the monastery of Corbie.

## Here Begins the Sermon

### 1

Who could doubt, dearest brothers, that the Church of the saints is God’s field, when the Apostle cries out, “You are God’s cultivation” (1 Corinthians 3:9), and the Lord bears witness in the Gospel concerning the seed that was sown: “Some fell on good soil and produced fruit a hundredfold” (Luke 8:8)?

If, then, it is a field, as the Apostle teaches, it needs cultivation. It would not need cultivation unless it produced the thorns of vices. Indeed, an apt comparison is drawn between a field and human hearts, because just as the former produces bodily thorns and thistles, so the latter produces spiritual ones. Hence, too, it was expressed figuratively in the first curse: “It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Genesis 3:18).

But there is this difference between them: in the fields of the earth, many thorn-prickles grow from many roots, whereas in earthly hearts the stings of all the vices proceed from the single root of avarice. For one vice is that of gluttony (*gastrimargia*), another of fornication, another of envy, another of anger, another of sadness, another of vain glory, another of *cenodoxia* (vainglorious display), another of pride; and although these produce many and innumerable shoots from themselves, they nevertheless all sprout, as has been said, from the one root of avarice. The Apostle bears witness to this when he says: “The root of all evils is avarice” (1 Timothy 6:10).

The preachers of God’s holy Church, whether in the Old or the New Testament, have tried, like strong farmers, to uproot it completely from earthly hearts—sometimes by rebukes, sometimes by exhortations, sometimes by terrors, sometimes by persuasions, as though with ploughs, mattocks, rakes, and hoes—but they have not been able to do so, even though they have labored greatly in this work. For it is an inextricable and, so to speak, ineradicable evil. The more you try to cut off its branches, the more numerous shoots it produces for you to cut away. Therefore, since it cannot be uprooted completely, its abundance of branches must always be cut back. And because in our own times it is seen to have occupied almost the whole world, let us too, according to the strength given us from above, strive by whatever means we can toward its eradication.

### 2

But meanwhile a question arises: how can pride be believed to arise from avarice, to say nothing of the other vices, when another Scripture plainly testifies, “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclesiasticus 10:13)? If pride is the beginning of every sin, how is avarice the root of all evils? Only because the two are one and each proceeds from the other: avarice produces pride, and pride produces avarice. We recognize that this occurred in our first parent. If the avarice had not come first by which he wished to become like God, he would never have raised himself in pride against his Creator; yet if pride had not swollen within him, he would never have dared to desire such things.

The Apostle John joins and describes these two chief vices in such a way that, setting the others aside, he seems to admit that these alone exist in the world, and that all the rest demonstrably derive their origin from them. For he says: “Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2:16).

### 3

Although, wherever desire is mentioned, pride is consequently understood, we must now discuss one of them and dispute against avarice alone. When it has fully possessed someone’s mind, it immediately makes that person a worshiper of idols. I ought to be killed for teaching such things, stoned for proclaiming them, unless the Apostle to the Gentiles himself bears witness to them. For he says: “And avarice, which is the worship of idols” (Ephesians 5:5).

Who, I ask, among Christians would listen to anyone who called him an unbeliever and devoted to idols? And yet he desires to be precisely what, because he is that, he does not wish to hear. Perhaps one of them will say: How does someone serve idols when he burns with earthly desires?

Listen, whoever you are, to the brief explanation. God is to be worshiped by faith; faith consists in knowledge of God; and knowledge of God is understood in obedience to his commandments. Thus Paul also says of certain people: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16). John likewise attests the same thing in his Epistle: “Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4).

God therefore commands abstinence, while the ancient enemy persuades us to gluttony; God commands sobriety, the enemy drunkenness; God commands chastity, the enemy fornication; God humility, the enemy pride; God concord, the enemy discord; God peace, the enemy strife; God gentleness, the enemy anger; God love, the enemy hatred; God generosity, the enemy stinginess; God almsgiving, the enemy robbery; God truth, the enemy falsehood; God that we should not swear, the enemy that we should persist in perjuries; God commands us to abstain from fraud, the enemy to cling to false testimonies.

God commands concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, “You shall not eat from it” (Genesis 2:17); the enemy, on the contrary, says: “On whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.” God commands: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his house, nor his field, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that belongs to him” (Deuteronomy 5:21); the enemy, however, urges: “I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me.”

Now let us see whose worshiper a person is and whose word he obeys. Is it not the one whose command he appears to fulfill? Who does not see that a person’s service makes him a worshiper of the one whom he serves? These words plainly indicate that those who devote themselves to avarice become worshipers of demons, even if blessed Paul had not affirmed this.

### 4

The evil of this avarice, which surpasses and exceeds everything else and from which all evils spring, is elsewhere exposed and condemned by sacred Scripture in these words: “There is nothing more wicked than a miser”; and again: “There is nothing more unjust than to love money” (Ecclesiasticus 10:9–10).

Why should it be surprising if the Apostle calls this same avarice the worship of idols? The many-sided evil of avarice devastates the hearts of the rich more wickedly than those of the poor. Although the poor desire to possess many things in this world, they cannot obtain many things; consequently, since the effect of their covetousness is diminished, their capacity for harm is also restrained.

The rich, however, because they can obtain more, seek more numerous opportunities for sin in order to find more things to acquire. Avarice is like a kind of fire: it burns more intensely in some and less intensely in others, but once it begins to burn, it never says, “It is enough.” It is like ordinary fire, which multiplies its flames more violently the more abundant the quantity of wood it receives. Hence it is written: “The miser is not filled with money” (Ecclesiasticus 5:9).

### 5

This root of all evils certainly produces envy as its first shoot, as James bears witness when he says: “Do you think that Scripture speaks in vain: ‘The spirit that dwells in you desires to envy’?” (James 4:5). Hence Solomon says: “I considered all the labors and industry of human beings, and I observed that they lie open to a neighbor’s envy” (Ecclesiastes 4:4).

It is clear and true that we envy others in those matters in which we wish to equal them, whether in temporal possessions or in worldly honors. Therefore, whoever seeks to extinguish the deadly poison of envy must take care to desire nothing transitory in this world. Let him hear whose member is the person who neglects to avoid this vice. For it is written: “Through the envy of the devil, death entered the world” (Wisdom 2:24). Those who belong to his party imitate him.

Meanwhile, we must know that some people wish to surpass others in wealth or honors, but do not pursue those whom they cannot outstrip. Others, however, are kindled against them by such a flame of envy that they cannot look upon them with an even temper or with eyes of goodwill.

From this also arises the planning of murder. Unless divine providence removes the opportunity for carrying it out, life is destroyed either secretly by the suffocation of poison or by some other device, or openly by a material sword. Some do this so that, after those people have been killed, they may unjustly seize their goods or honors by whatever means; others do not seek to obtain another’s profits or offices, but only that those whom they envy should lose them. Even if they are unable to extinguish their victims’ lives, they are nevertheless already held guilty of murder because of the very planning of hatred.

Thus John also says in his Epistle: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that every murderer does not have an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God” (John 3:15).

Wherever persistent planning of hatred has taken root, the malice of harming will not be absent. The unhappy person is always seeking how he might injure the one whom he wished to destroy but could not kill completely. He attaches himself in friendship to the enemy or advocate of that person, with whom previously he perhaps would not even have been willing to speak. Although he knows for certain that the other person is being tortured by an accusation without cause, he nevertheless does not hesitate, while raging against one person, to commit perjury or bear false witness on behalf of another. Nor does he remember the sentence that says: “The perjured will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 15:5). And this one: “A false witness will not go unpunished” (Proverbs 19:9).

### 6

How the poor are oppressed by the rich, and by what methods and devices they are defrauded of the fruits of their labors, is known more fully to those who inflict and to those who suffer these things than to us, who seek to learn about them partly from the divine books and partly from the wicked signs of the schemes that burst forth from the oppressors themselves.

Some people, especially the rulers of this world, overturn the justice of certain persons by an evil judgment merely to win human favor, lest judgment offend the minds of their own people. They also fear losing temporal honor through the cause of sedition unless they act according to the will of their ministers. By the skill of their cleverness, they divert laws that either they themselves or others have promulgated to a meaning other than that which the laws themselves express. They persist in arguments of cunning until they pervert what is just as though they were acting rightly.

Thus, by a devilish art, they scrutinize the aforementioned law of the edict in such a way that they bend even manifest justice, though it resists them, toward whatever error of iniquity they desire. To such people the Lord rightly says through Isaiah: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter” (Isaiah 5:20).

Again, the Lord speaks about them through the same prophet, saying: “Woe to those who make unjust laws, writing injustice. They wrote them to oppress the poor in judgment and to do violence to the cause of the humble of my people, so that widows might become their prey and they might plunder orphans” (Isaiah 10:1).

They make unjust laws and, in writing injustice, write it down because, with the style of their speech, they perversely argue before human eyes what they rightly know within their hearts. To them the same prophet directs his speech in a lamentable voice when he adds: “What will you do on the day of visitation and of calamity coming from afar? To whose help will you flee, and where will you leave your glory?” (Isaiah 10:3).

The divine word also speaks to them in warning through a certain wise man, saying: “Hear, O kings, and understand; learn, you judges of the ends of the earth. Give ear, you who rule the multitudes and take pride in the crowds of nations. For power has been given to you by the Lord, and strength by the Most High, who will examine your works and scrutinize your thoughts. For although you were ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly, nor did you keep the law of justice, nor did you walk according to God’s will. He will appear terribly and swiftly to you, because a most severe judgment will fall upon those who rule; the powerful will suffer powerful torments, and a stronger torture awaits those who are stronger” (Wisdom 6:2ff.).

### 7

Others, however, pervert or preserve right judgment solely out of desire for temporal possessions, because they both withhold justice from one person and sell it to another.

[The text reads, “For that day”; read, “Of those.”] Of those who pervert right judgment by accepting a payment, the prophet Isaiah says to the princes of Judah: “Your princes are faithless, companions of thieves; they all love gifts and pursue rewards. They do not judge for the orphan, and the widow’s case does not come before them” (Isaiah 1:23). Of any one of them the Holy Spirit says through Solomon: “Whoever shows partiality in judgment does not act well; for a person will abandon truth for a piece of bread” (Proverbs 28:21). And again: “It is not good to accept the person of the wicked, so as to turn aside from the truth of judgment” (Proverbs 18:5).

The word of God warns us in the same book that such people must be avoided when it says: “Do not envy the wicked, nor desire to be with them, because their minds meditate robbery, and their lips speak deceit” (Proverbs 24:1). What recompense follows them is revealed there when it says: “The robbery of the wicked will drag them away, because they refused to do judgment” (Proverbs 21:7).

By the oppression of such people the Lord is provoked to judicial vengeance, as he himself bears witness through the Psalmist, saying: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord” (Psalm 11:6).

O rich man! O man blinded by avarice! O perverse judge! If you despise the poor man lying beneath your feet, why do you not tremble before his Lord—and your own Lord—rising in anger against you?

Vengeance often comes suddenly upon you. It is even reported that your bones and flesh, as recently happened to a certain person, are consumed by fire in your tombs. But when one person is taken away for condemnation, and, his spirit enslaved to the fires of Gehenna, his body is burned even in the tomb, another is inflamed still more wickedly toward oppression.

Hear, rich in earthly happiness but poor in heavenly goods; hear what the God who judges all says to you: “You shall not do violence to the poor because he is poor, nor crush the needy at the gate, because the Lord will judge his case and will pierce those who pierced his soul” (Proverbs 22:22).

8. But, on the other hand, those who do not alter the cause of a just judgment for a reward, but sell it, consider that they have committed no fault in such an action. For they propose to themselves certain tales worthy of ridicule and say: “To conduct anyone’s case and not accept a payment is angelic; to conduct it and accept one is human; not to conduct it and accept one is diabolical.” I make it my aim to ask them whether this which they call human is a sin or not. Tell me, please: is violating God’s commandments a sin or is it not? And certainly, in the words of God, in the divine law, this is generally commanded to all under one rule: “You shall not accept [Col. 1283B] gifts, because gifts blind the eyes of the wise and alter the words of the just” (Deut. XVI, 19). And again: “You shall execute exactly what is just” (Ibid. 20). For how does one execute exactly what is just who appears to pronounce a just sentence in judgment not for the sake of justice but for the sake of money?

Why do you not see, wretched men, how greatly your speech is foolish, when, while verbally detesting the deeds of evil angels and praising the words of good ones, you blaspheme them by your actions? Why do you not imitate what you praise, just as you detest what you condemn? Or perhaps you believe that you belong to neither the number of the good angels nor that of the evil, since you strive to imitate neither the one nor the other? But do not deceive yourselves: whatever appears to deviate from the commandments of God is altogether diabolical.

In contrast, this is rightly said elsewhere of a just [Col. 1283C] judge: “He who shakes his hands free of every gift, he shall dwell on high” (Isa. XXXV, 15). Here we must understand that if the one who shakes his hands free of every gift will dwell on high, the one who does not do this will remain not in the heights of heaven but in the lower regions of the earth, by which the underworld is signified.

Samuel showed himself free from accepting gifts when, having been removed from the leadership of the Israelite people, he said: “Thus I have conducted myself before you from my youth until this day. Behold, I am here; speak concerning me before the Lord and before his anointed, whether I have taken a gift from anyone’s hand; and behold, I will restore it to you today” (I Sam. XII, 2).

And lest someone who rightly defends the justice of the laws without the reward of a gift be thought to be destitute of spiritual [Col. 1283D] gifts without divine recompense, the Lord intervenes and, through the prophet’s admonition [variant: “the prophet admonishing”], promises, saying: “Seek judgment, assist the oppressed, judge for the orphan, defend the widow, and so forth; and if your sins are like scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and if they are red like vermilion, they shall become white like wool” (Isa. I, 17). Hence through Solomon he speaks with an immeasurable feeling of compassion and says: “In judging, be merciful to orphans as a father, and be like a husband to their mother; and you will be like an obedient son of the Most High, and he will have mercy on you more than a mother” (Eccli. IV, 10).

But you, O furnace kindled by the heat of avarice, mind inflamed by its fires, seek rather the straw that will set you ablaze than the abolition of sins that would protect you from the fire. What is it, I ask, that [Col. 1284A] you acquire, and what is it that you lose? The thing you acquire is plainly perishable; the thing you lose is everlasting. Tell me, I say, what greater reward could he promise you than to take you as a son, for the sake of his love alone, while you pronounce just judgments, and to cherish you not merely as a mother but to have compassion on you with inward affections greater than a mother’s?

“But,” many say, “we do not accept from those who suffer the poverty of want, but from those who abound in riches.” To this we reply that it makes no difference whether someone sells God’s justice to a rich person or to a poor one. He will be punished by a similar penalty in either case if he has not administered what belongs to God freely, but has applied it to his own uses, profits, and business affairs.

Such men also customarily alter the name of the gift itself and say that they have not accepted a gift but a [Col. 1284B] greeting. I do not know whether I should call them more foolish or more cunning. To them it must surely be said that they should pay attention to what they have received and not applaud themselves because they have given it a new name.

“But,” they say, “we do not seek a payment; they themselves freely give it to us. What does it matter to us if they voluntarily offer a gift?” To this we reply: What you say is entirely true—they give it freely. But they give it freely for this reason: because otherwise they cannot find justice. They certainly would not give if they could reach justice by another means; and therefore, in a certain sense, willingly and unwillingly, they pay you the gift.

[Col. 1284C]

9. When by these and very many other testimonies of Scripture we convict such men that they ought not by any art or ingenuity to seek gifts or “greetings,” they cast aside the blush of modesty and burst into complaint, saying: “If these things are so, how will the palaces stand? How will judges please their lords?”

To this we truthfully reply that palaces fall all the more from the very point at which, according to your opinion, they seem to stand. For from this come nation rising against nation, kingdom rising against kingdom, one people falling before another, disasters, famine, destruction, and dangers; and from the place where the earthly lord is placated, the heavenly Lord is provoked to anger.

For this reason the blessed Apostle says: “Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil, and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into destruction [Col. 1284D] and perdition” (I Tim. VI, 9). And through Solomon it is said: “He who hastens to become rich will not be innocent” (Prov. XXVIII, 20). And again: “If you become rich, you will not be free from sin” (Eccli. XI, 10).

For this reason the Lord sets before such people the difficulty of entering the kingdom of heaven, saying: “Those who have money will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty” (Matt. XIX, 23). And again: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Luke XVIII, 25).

When yesterday I was setting these testimonies of Scripture before a certain exceedingly wealthy prince of this world, he replied to me that they ought to be understood not of actual money but of riches. But spare yourself, I beg you, excellent friend; remove your empty security. Consider [Col. 1285A] what Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, and blessed Gregory have written on these matters. Believe those who, following the Apostle, said that the root of all evils is the desire for money—not accusing the rich, but condemning the appetite for riches.

For true is the sentence of Scripture, spoken by the Spirit of God, in which it is said: “Nothing is more wicked than to love money” (Eccli. X, 10). In contrast, the blessed Apostle admonishes his beloved disciple, saying: “Command the rich of this world not to be proud, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment” (I Tim. VI, 17); and to do good, to become rich in good works, to give readily, to share, and to lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life.

[Col. 1285B]

10. But, so that I may not shrink from the labor of uprooting the avarice I have begun to attack, behold, O avaricious men: you have acquired much by every sort of art and amassed much by every kind of ingenuity. But could you equal Solomon? What does he now possess of those things in which he labored? Is not everything for which he labored, as he himself said, vanity?

For he says: “I magnified my works; I built houses for myself, planted vineyards, made gardens and orchards, and enclosed them with trees of every kind. I constructed pools of water for myself, to irrigate a forest of budding trees. I possessed male and female slaves and had a large household. I also had herds of cattle and great flocks of sheep, beyond all who were before me in Jerusalem. I heaped up for myself silver and gold, and [Col. 1285C] the wealth of kings and provinces. I made for myself male and female singers, and the delights of the sons of men: cups and jugs for the service of pouring out wines. I surpassed in wealth all who were before me in Jerusalem, and I did not deny my eyes anything that they desired, nor did I restrain my heart from enjoying every pleasure and delighting in the things I had prepared. And I considered this my portion, if I made use of my labor.

“And when I turned to all the works that my hands had done, and to the labors in which I had toiled in vain, I saw vanity and affliction of spirit in everything, and that nothing endures under the sun” (Eccl. II, 4).

What, then, is fuller of vanity than for a person to desire with all his mind to gather riches in a place where he is not permitted to dwell forever? In contrast, the Lord [Col. 1285D] admonishes us, saying: “Do not lay up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves dig through and steal. But lay up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not dig through or steal” (Matt. VI, 19).

What is also more wretched than to acquire almost all the happiness of the world and in a moment descend to the underworld? The blessed Job reproves the madness of such people by lamenting and saying: “Why do the wicked prosper? It is well with those who do evil; they are lifted up and strengthened by riches. Their offspring remain before them, a multitude of relatives and descendants in their sight. Their houses are safe and peaceful, and the rod of God is not upon them. Their ox conceives and does not miscarry; their cow gives birth and is not deprived of its offspring. Their little ones go out like flocks; [Col. 1286A] they rejoice in play, hold the tambourine and lyre, and delight at the sound of the organ. They spend their days in prosperity and in a moment descend to the underworld” (Job XXI, 7).

Hence, in the Gospel, the Lord said to two brothers who wished to divide an inheritance, warning them to beware of all avarice: “The field of a certain rich man produced abundant crops, and he considered within himself, saying: ‘What shall I do, since I have nowhere to gather my crops?’ And he said: ‘This I will do: I will demolish my barns and build larger ones, and there I will gather everything that has been born for me, and my goods. And I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many good things laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, and feast.’ But God said to him: ‘Fool, this night they are demanding your soul from you; and whose will those things be that you have prepared?’” (Luke XII, 19).

What is more senseless than to rejoice in acquiring even the whole world [Col. 1286B] and to incur the loss of one’s soul? Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world and suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. XVI, 26). And again: “What exchange will a person give for his soul?” (Ibid.)

But you, O fire of Babylon, selling your soul for earthly advantages, say to the poor person: “Give, give this or that, because if you do not wish to give now, you will later rejoice if you are able to give.” You fasten a crime upon the one who resists, bind the opponent with chains, beat and strike him, and thus, by whatever means, reach the object of your desire.

Woe to you, insatiable plague! Behold how much you desired; perhaps you acquired it all. Do you think you have seen a dream? What you possessed is not [Col. 1286C] yours, because just as, when coming into this world, you bring nothing with you, so when departing from the world you take nothing away. The word of Paul applies to you: “We brought nothing into this world, and neither can we take anything away” (I Tim. VI, 7). Job likewise says: “Naked I came forth from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there” (Job I, 12).

Hence the same man speaks of any wealthy person who does not look ahead to the future: “When the rich person sleeps, he will take nothing away; he will open his eyes and find nothing. Want will seize him like water; at night a storm will overwhelm him; a scorching wind will carry him away, and like a whirlwind it will snatch him from his place” (Job XXVII, 19).

Hence through the Psalmist it is said: “They slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. LXXV, 6). And again: “Do not fear when a person becomes rich [Col. 1286D] and when the glory of his house is multiplied, because when he dies he will take none of these things, nor will the glory of his house descend with him” (Ps. XLVIII, 17). Therefore he had said earlier: “They will leave their riches to others; their graves are their houses forever” (Ibid. XI).

11. Why, then, O wretched people, do you not consider what you possess, what you are, and what you will shortly become? Certainly, what you possess temporally is not yours, because the voice of Truth says: “If you were not faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke XVI, 12).

But what are you, if you attend carefully? You will find yourselves vapor, wind, and shadow. For James also said: “What is your life? It is vapor [Col. 1287A] appearing for a little while” (James IV, 14). Job likewise continues: “Remember that my life is wind” (Job VII, 7). Bildad also responds and speaks a true statement: “We do not know, because our days upon the earth are like a shadow” (Job VIII, 9). Hence through the Psalmist it is said: “My days have declined like a shadow” (Ps. CI, 12). And, pronouncing judgment concerning every wicked person, the same Psalmist says: “I saw the wicked exalted and raised up above the cedars of Lebanon. I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. XXXVI, 35).

Hence the aforementioned Job [lacuna] speaks in amazement, saying: “When a person has died and has been stripped bare, where, I ask, is he?” (Job XIV, 10).

But what you will shortly become is shown by the bones of the dead and the ashes in the tombs. Go, then, O rich person, to the monuments [Col. 1287B] of kings and wealthy men, and there look at yourself. There inquire into the temporal glory that they loved and that you anxiously pursue.

Does a dead person not seem to speak to you from the tomb—not indeed in words but by examples: “What you are, I was; and what I am, you too will shortly be”?

For I was once wealthy and fat. After the wanton and countless pleasures of this life, I came to the death of the flesh; after the death of the flesh, I became worms; after the worms, I was reduced to dust.

Where now is the pride of life? Where are the allurements and pleasures of carnal vices? Where is the affection that flattered me from my wife? Where is the growing progress of my children? Where is the obedient retinue of servants? Where is the income from fields, vineyards, and woods that filled my mind? Where is the exceedingly heavy weight of [Col. 1287C] treasures? Where is the splendor of clothing, shining with diverse designs, gold, gems, and pearls? Where, I say, are all these things?

You surely perceive, unless you are blind, that they are no longer with me. Would that the only condemnation were this: both of the one whose example cries out such things in a certain way and of you, to whom such things cry out. But rather, an eternal torment follows.

Hear, then, what the dwelling of the wicked is, and what the condemnation of the reprobate is after they have departed from this life. For concerning their eternal habitation it is written: “Its streams shall be turned into pitch, and its soil into burning pitch; by night and by day it shall not be extinguished forever; its smoke shall rise from generation to generation” (Isa. XXXIV, 9).

[Col. 1287D]

12. Before the coming of our Mediator, even those who lived piously in this life descended to this land of the wicked and this condemnation of the reprobate, although they were not punished with their suffering. Hence blessed Job, entreating, says: “Leave me, so that I may mourn a little before I go to the land of darkness and covered with the gloom of death, a land of misery and darkness, where the shadow of death and no order dwell, but everlasting horror” (Job X, 20).

Concerning this habitation of the wicked it is said through Isaiah: “Hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without any limit; and its strong men, its people, and its lofty and glorious ones shall descend to it” (Isa. V, 14).

Concerning this the angel says in the Apocalypse: “Hell and death were cast into the lake of fire; this is the second death, the lake of fire” [Col. 1288A] (Apoc. XX, 14).

Concerning this also the Lord says in the Gospel: “Cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XXII, 13).

This habitation will be inherited not only by the souls of the wicked, but also by immortal worms that tear their bodies apart, as Holy Scripture bears witness, saying: “The almighty Lord will take vengeance on them; on the day of judgment he will visit them. For he will give fire and worms in their flesh, so that they may burn and feel forever” (Judith XVI, 20). And again: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished, and they shall be for the satisfaction of sight to all flesh” (Mark IX, 44).

13. Fear, wretched people, the streams turned into pitch, because it will suddenly seize those whom it has seized and will not permit them to have free [Col. 1288B] steps for walking. Fear the soil of the tombs, because it exhales an intolerable stench. Dread the earth burning with pitch, because it burns those whom it receives and at the same time renders them bound. Fear the land of misery, because there all indulgence will be absent.

Dread the mouth of hell opened without any limit, because, devouring all cruelly and insatiably, it knows neither how to be satisfied nor how to say, “Enough.” Flee the lake of fire, because it plunges, kills, and burns those whom it receives. Beware the outer darkness, because no light approaches it. Strive to escape the weeping and gnashing of teeth, which will never have an end. Fear the immortal worms, because in eating your flesh they will have no satiety.

And when so many and such great torments have clung to you forever, the singularly harsher torture of avarice will never be [Col. 1288C] absent. Hence through James it is said to you: “Come now, you rich; weep, howling over the miseries that will come upon you. Your riches have rotted, your garments have been eaten by moths, your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will consume your flesh like fire” (James V, 1).

Therefore, taking thought for yourselves, remember such things, we beg you; and remembering, fear lest you fall into such things. You who refuse not only to hold one finger in fire for a little while, but also to endure hunger and thirst, cold, or nakedness, fear and dread with the greatest intensity the many and great torments we have described, which you will endure forever.

Nor should the expectation of the day of judgment [Col. 1288D] depart from your memory, if somehow, by the gift of the Lord Jesus Christ, your attention may once be separated from love of the present world. For concerning that day we read written in the prophet: “The day of the Lord is near, near and very swift. The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; there the strong man shall be troubled” (Zeph. I, 14). “That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and blast.”

Concerning that day Peter says: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief; on it the heavens will pass away with great force, and the elements will be dissolved by heat” (II Pet. III, 10). Hence the Psalmist says: “Fire shall burn in his sight, and around him a mighty storm” (Ps. XLIX, 2).

Hence the prophet speaks in the person of our Judge, saying: “Wait for me, says the Lord, for the day of my resurrection in the future, because my judgment is to gather the nations and assemble kingdoms, to pour out upon them my indignation and all the anger of my fury; for in the fire of my zeal the whole earth shall be devoured” (Zeph. III, 8).

Behold: wrath, tribulation and distress, [Col. 1289A] calamity and misery, darkness and gloom, cloud and whirlwind, trumpet and blast, fire consuming the elements, and a mighty storm devastating everything. The wrath of the Judge is intolerable, his fury unbearable. And what sinner would not fear such things?

If Paul, surpassing the labors and virtues of the saints, feared such things—for trembling, he himself cries out: “There remains a fearful expectation of judgment and the fury of fire that will consume the adversaries. It is fearful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. X, 27, 31)—who would not tremble?

There, certainly, an innumerable multitude of angels will appear [Col. 1289B] for the vengeance of the wicked. While the heavens and earth burn, and the Lord and the apostles also sit in judgment, they will separate the wicked from among the just. As though separating weeds from wheat, they will bind bundles for burning, arranging and joining like with like: the avaricious with the avaricious, adulterers with adulterers, murderers with murderers, fornicators with fornicators, thieves with thieves, robbers with robbers, liars with liars, perjurers with perjurers, gluttons with gluttons, drunkards with drunkards, the arrogant with the arrogant, the proud with the proud.

Thus the punishment remaining there will correspond to the company whose conduct in this life was alike. But there will be no return to forgiveness thereafter, because they will go into eternal punishment, nor will anyone bend the Judge’s anger toward mercy by prayers. [Col. 1289C] For he will repay everyone according to his works.

Indeed, they will multiply their prayers, and the wretched, lamenting, will cry out: “Lord, Lord, open to us!” (Luke XIII, 25). Yet from within they will be answered: “Amen I say to you, I do not know who you are. Depart from me, workers of iniquity. There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Ibid., 27).

14. Perhaps those for whom we bring forward such things from the divine utterances will say: “Behold, you have terrified us, and we have now almost succumbed to despair. If these things are so, who among us will be saved? What must we do?”

I answer not with my own words but with the Lord’s: “Enter by the narrow way, because the gate is wide and [Col. 1289D] the way spacious that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter by it; for the gate is narrow and the way constricted that leads to life, and there are few who find it” (Luke XIII, 24).

But they say: “The constricted way and narrow gate are set before those who abandon the world, who despise houses, fields, wives, children, male and female servants, and all the things in which worldly people are entangled by earthly affection, so that they may please the one to whom they have commended themselves.”

What you say is true, but for you too, according to the measure of your station and the strength of your capacity, the constricted way and narrow gate are set before you. For the Lord proposed only two gates and two ways. He said that through the wide gate and spacious way many hasten to destruction, and that through the narrow gate and constricted way few enter into life. He showed neither a third gate nor a third [Col. 1290A] way.

Seek a third one, if anywhere you can find it, and walk and enter through it. But do not deceive yourselves: there is no more; no other way to life remains. Enter through it.

For the constricted way and narrow gate for secular men consist in not coveting what belongs to another; not seizing it by theft, fraud, lying, perjury, false testimony, a reward, or any sort of “greeting”; being content with one’s own labors and just income; not amassing more than the need of one soul requires; joining oneself sexually to no one except one’s own wife; abstaining even from one’s own wife at unlawful times; observing intact the appointed fast of the days of Lent; setting aside the spectacles of the world and attending the thresholds of the church; receiving food expenses not for pleasure but for the [Col. 1290B] body’s necessity; and, beyond all these things, devoting oneself to the generosity of almsgiving for daily and minor offenses or even for more serious sins.

For those who possess earthly goods, this is without doubt the higher virtue and a special abolition of sins—provided that each person ceases to sin while administering this mercy to the needy. Hence it is written: “Just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sins.”

Hence also the Lord admonishes in the Gospel, saying: “Nevertheless, give alms from what remains, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke XI, 41). Hence through a certain righteous man it is said: “Almsgiving delivers from every sin and from death, and does not permit the soul to go into darkness” (Tob. IV, 11).

[Col. 1290C]

15. Great confidence before the supreme God will belong to almsgiving for all who practice it. To them also, as the Gospel bears witness, it will be said at the end: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was a guest, and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me; ill, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me” (Matt. XXV, 34).

The distribution of mercy itself must proceed from willingness and cheerfulness, not from sadness, because “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX, 7). It should be bestowed more generously to the extent that each person recognizes that he has received more. Hence again a certain man of God admonishes his only child, saying: “As you are able, so be [Col. 1290D] merciful. If you have much, give abundantly; but if you have little, be eager to impart even the little willingly. For you are storing up a good reward for yourself on the day of necessity” (Tob. IV, 8).

But since it profits no one to devote himself to almsgiving unless he strives to turn away from evil deeds, a certain wise man testifies, saying: “What does it profit one who washes after contact with a dead person and again touches the dead? What benefit is there in his washing?” (I Cor. XV, 29). Hence through Isaiah the Lord also admonishes, saying: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. I, 16). Hence the Psalmist says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI, 27).

But what is more deserving of mourning than praise is that some people seize more so that they may have something from which to give a little to the giver of all things. How detestable the offering of such people is, Holy Scripture [Col. 1291A] indicates when it says: “He who offers a sacrifice from the plunder of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son before his father” (Eccli. XXXIII, 24). For just as the killing of a son and the shedding of his blood cannot please the eyes of the father who begot him, so an offering acquired through evil cannot please almighty God.

Hence through Isaiah it is said concerning such people: “He who offers an offering from the poor man’s substance is like one who offers swine’s blood; he who remembers incense is like one who blesses an idol” (Isa. LXVI, 3). Certainly, nothing in the Old Testament is as hateful as an offering of swine’s blood. Yet nothing in the New and Old Testaments is more execrable than blessing an idol; and an offering of mercy made from the plunder of the poor is rightly compared with these things.

In contrast, Holy Scripture commands, saying: “From your substance give [Col. 1291B] alms, and do not turn your face away from any poor person” (Tob. IV, 7). “From your substance,” it says, not from another’s, because just as from what is yours you find God’s clemency, so from what is another’s you incur his anger.

16. At this point that also appropriately comes to mind which I recognize was omitted from memory. Some people prepare offerings for almighty God from just labors and revenues, yet take for their own uses things acquired wickedly. To them it must be said that, although such offerings may be thought just, the gifts of those who have not striven to preserve an immaculate life cannot please the supreme Good.

For what is more precious to our Creator than our soul? Or are our gifts more precious? If the soul is inwardly defiled, will any other outward gift please him?

It remains, therefore, that you offer your giver nothing from [Col. 1291C] iniquity and appropriate nothing for your own evil use; but from just labors and just revenues both offer to him and live yourselves.

It also remains that temporal property should be for use, while the one who created you and prepared temporal goods should alone be the object of desire, so that when the things he has given pass away, you may come to the one who gave them, with whom you may rejoice without end and reign without end; in whose kingdom you may shine like the sun, give off the fragrance of blooming lilies and roses, and abound forever in every richness.

There a city has been prepared for the saints and those [Col. 1292A] who fear God. Its foundations consist of the adornment of every precious stone; it has gates made each from a single pearl; its street is of the purest gold. Through its midst flows the river of the water of life, and on both sides of the river stands the tree of life, bearing twelve fruits through the twelve months.

There the hidden manna and the bread of angels are given to those who eat them. They bring such satiety that they never cause weariness; they remove hunger in such a way that they never take away desire from the one who eats. There no one will need the sun, the moon, or a lamp, because night will not exist there, and the Lord God almighty will be the light of all.

From that light, which the saints will then [Col. 1292B] see, the light that we now see has received its light. That light is far more exalted and far more excellent than this, because the former is creative and the latter created; the former is the light of minds, the latter the light of bodies.

Therefore that light will not be such as we are accustomed to see with the eyes of the flesh. Nor will those good things mentioned above be such as anyone can see, hear, or conceive in this life; rather, they will be much more excellent and much more blessed, because, as Scripture says: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II, 9).

Seek that light, then; desire it; strive toward it with the desire of your mind. I, certainly, who dare not deceive anyone with flatteries and seek to withhold from no one what is useful, have brought forward these promises not against the avaricious but against avarice, not against nature but against vice.

I cannot find better [Col. 1292C] counsel to give. And although, in uprooting avarice, I have displayed all the labor I could, nevertheless, striking at its shoots and cutting them down as though with blows from more than eighty testimonies of Scripture, I shall not be without reward, retaining as my faithful guarantor the mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1291]

SERMON ON THE GOSPEL READING, EDITED BY LORD AUBERT, PRIEST AND ABBOT, ON THE PURIFICATION OF SAINT MARY

(From two manuscripts, one of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and the other of Fleury, in Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. IX.) (C)

[Col. 1291D]

1. The faithful should carefully consider what the feast of this day is; they should undertake to celebrate it with the same devotional affection with which they have observed the solemnities of the Lord’s birth, circumcision, and manifestation. For this solemnity belongs to the same one to whom those belong; nor is this one less than those—a point that we shall plainly demonstrate with proofs in this sermon.

The solemnity of this day is, just as it is unknown to some, so honored by many above the other solemnities of the year—especially in that place where the Catholic Church received primacy in its first pastor. For they hold it in such great reverence that on that [Col. 1292D] day the entire crowd of the city, gathered together, celebrating the solemn rites of Mass and glittering with immense lights of candles, and no one enters the public station without holding a light in his hands, as though they were offering the Lord to the temple—or rather, receiving him—and demonstrating outwardly, through the religious observance of their offering, the light of faith with which they shine inwardly.

2. Today, in accordance with the Law and the Gospel, after forty days had been completed from Christ’s birth, the same Lord was presented in the temple by his parents. Today he was received by holy Simeon and offered to the Father together with sacred gifts. Today he was publicly proclaimed by that same Simeon and Anna [Col. 1293A] to those awaiting the redemption of Israel.

O how devout a spectacle, one in which only the devout are shown to delight! Here stands a virgin and mother—not of just anyone, but of God. Here a little infant is received, the small son of a virgin, whose divinity the world cannot contain. Prophets come from every side, and both sexes prophesy concerning the child. An offering is presented for the child—not one that cleanses sins, but one that reveals mysteries.

And because I wish to raise up the proclamation of this day, I shall gladly pass through the Gospel reading itself in conversation, in which I recognize these things being narrated, so that it may respond to what I say—or rather, so that the voice of my exhortation may respond to what it narrates.

Finally, Luke the evangelist, treating more fully and more orderly than [Col. 1293B] the other evangelists the true history of Christ’s incarnation, after his annunciation by the angel, after his birth declared by the voices of angels, and after his circumcision on the eighth day in his parents’ house, follows these events in order, saying:

### 3

After the days of her purification had been completed according to the law of Moses, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord: “Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Luke 2:21).

[Col. 1293C] It is clear to all the faithful that the mother of the Redeemer did not in any way contract, from his birth, a stain from which she needed purification during those days by abstaining from the holy places. She conceived as a virgin without human desire and without human intercourse; she gave birth as a virgin without any corruption of the flesh, and remained a virgin forever. Moreover, the male born from her did not open her womb.

But the evangelist, weaving this together according to the account of the law, conceals the mystery of the divine incarnation from the impious and presents the mother as observing the law. Nor is it surprising that the mother observed the law which her Son had not come to abolish but to fulfill. She knew in what manner she had conceived, by what process she had given birth, and who he was whom she had borne. Yet, observing the common law, she awaited the day of purification and concealed the majesty of her Son.

This is why, when she found him in the Temple at twelve years of age among the teachers of the law, she called him Joseph’s son, saying: “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I, grieving, have been searching for you” (Luke 2:48). Yet she undoubtedly knew that she had conceived him without intercourse with Joseph and brought him forth without violation of her virginity.

[Col. 1293D] But why did she conceal the mystery of his conception and birth, when she knew him to be the immeasurable God? Was it because she begrudged him to others, when, carrying him to the Temple, she placed him in the hands of the holy old man? Far from it. She did so so that, filled with the spirit of prophecy, she would not reveal the Redeemer of the world to the impious. For, already full of grace and inspired by the Spirit of divinity, she knew that, if the rulers of this age had known him, they would never have crucified him for our salvation.

Offer, therefore, most blessed Virgin, as one observing the law, in the Temple the one whom you brought forth, so that he may be revealed not to all but to a few. Who is he whom you have borne? For the present let him appear humble, “a stone cut from the mountain without hands,” so that he may be rejected by the builders, [Col. 1294A] until, striking the statue upon its feet, he grows into a great mountain and fills the whole world.

O how small! O how great is he whom you have borne! Small in humanity, great in divinity; small in the kingdom of the Jews, great in the kingdom of the nations.

Yet he was not judged small by everyone in the kingdom of the Jews. For you yourself, who bore him, grew from that very people of Israel into a shoot. You arose as a shoot from the root of Jesse; you blossomed as Aaron’s rod, you put forth leaves and bore a nut.

And because you recognized his immensity more than anyone else, although you saw him born from you as such a tiny one, undoubtedly, trembling, you adored as almighty God the infant whom you had borne; and, adoring, you trembled. Yet, recognizing the Son according to his humanity, you nursed him, embraced him, and nourished him.

[Col. 1294B] Who, I ask, can disclose to us such services performed by you, and the disposition of your heart, O most blessed Virgin, when on one side you saw born from you such a tiny infant, while on the other you contemplated the immeasurable God? On one side, the created; on the other, the Creator. On one side, the weak; on the other, the strongest. On one side, the one needing nourishment; on the other, the one who nourishes. On one side, the one who did not speak; on the other, the one who taught the angels.

Who, I say, could unlock for us the secrets of your heart—how you inclined your thoughts toward both realities—when, holding in your hands the one and the same God and Son of Man, you adored him on one side as Lord and kissed him on the other as a little child?

Who would not be struck dumb with astonishment at so ineffable a miracle? Who would not become almost speechless? A girl gives birth to her own Creator and the Creator of all; she carries her own Ruler and the Ruler of all.

O wondrous spectacle, [Col. 1294C] before which not only human nature but even angelic nature stands astonished!

### 4

To this, dearest brothers, lift the eyes of your faith; turn toward this the affection of your devotion. There receive Christ, humbled for your sake in the flesh; but adore in his divinity the exalted God. Embrace the little one, but contemplate the immeasurable one.

Now, beloved, if we ask what was mystically signified by the fact that our Redeemer wished to be carried by his mother and parents from his own city to Jerusalem, to the Temple of the Lord, we find that the glorious mother and virgin, together with her relatives, represented that Church which believed from the Jews through the apostles.

For when is the Church not a virgin, whose members the Apostle [Col. 1294D] addresses, saying: “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2)? When is she not a mother, of whom it is said through the Psalmist, “A man shall say: Mother Zion”; and of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matthew 21:10)? When are the elect not relatives, since they are called brothers and sisters?

The mother, therefore, and the relatives carry our Redeemer from Nazareth to Jerusalem, to the Temple of the Lord, because that primitive Church, present among the first disciples, rejected by the Jews, brought the dispensation of the same Redeemer to the knowledge of the nations.

That Church, consisting not only of the nations but also of the Jews, is rightly called Jerusalem, that is, “Vision of peace.” [Col. 1295A] Of it the Psalmist says: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in unity with itself” (Psalm 122:3).

She is also the Temple. Now Paul says to the faithful: “The Temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17). And when the apostles come from the Jews to the nations announcing Christ, Jerusalem comes together with Jerusalem and Temple meets Temple, since all these are one city, Jerusalem, and one Temple.

In this city and Temple, therefore, Christ, offered by the apostles, is received. Hence the Church herself speaks to God the Father in the words of the Psalmist, saying: “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your Temple” (Psalm 48:10)—that is understood, “in the midst of the Church, which is your Temple.”

Whether, then, according to the historical account or according to the mystical understanding, the reason why Christ is brought by his parents to the holy [Col. 1295B] city and Temple is made clear when it is added:

### 5

“To offer sacrifices, according to what was said in the law of the Lord: a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons” (Luke 2:24).

The law had indeed commanded that, if someone happened to lack a lamb but found one of these alternatives—that is, either a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons—he should offer it to God as an offering for his son; and no one who offered either of these was disadvantaged by the other alternative.

But because both signify the mysteries of Christ and of the Church, we must believe that the mother found and offered both for the sacrifice. In this offering of birds, then, was prefigured that offering which was made for the salvation of the world at evening—the passion of the Lord, through which we have been reconciled to God.

[Col. 1295C] Concerning this sacrifice Paul says to the faithful: “Walk in love, as Christ also loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, as a fragrant odor” (Ephesians 5:2). And again: “He loved me,” he says, “and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Since all the elect are members of Christ, the turtledoves are signified in the turtledove, and the pigeons in the pigeon. This offering of birds also signifies the mortification of the elect, to whom the same apostle says: “I appeal to you, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Romans 12:1).

[Col. 1295D] But there can be no sacrifice of mortification acceptable to God in those who do not possess the purity of true faith and the harmony of true charity. Therefore it is not without reason that the sacrifice which is said to have been mystically offered for the Lord is narrated as having been made from turtledoves and pigeons.

In the turtledove, chastity is found; in the pigeon, charity is commended. The turtledove preserves unstained fidelity to one mate; the pigeon does not abandon the unity of its fellow inhabitants.

A Catholic Christian, therefore, becomes truly a spiritual turtledove if he preserves the true faith of the Trinity with firm belief and rejects the mind of heretical depravity as the defilement of fornication. He becomes a pigeon if he remains patiently until the end in the Catholic fellowship and stands firm with immovable steadfastness against the stumbling-blocks of temptations, so that neither heretical fornication corrupts the chastity of faith in his heart nor [Col. 1296A] bitter dissension destroys the unity of ecclesiastical charity.

For this is the Catholic Church: she preserves faith in the one Lord as in her lawful husband and multiplies the congregation of many in faith.

It follows:

### 6

“And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon. This man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was in him. He had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ. And he came in the Spirit into the Temple” (Luke 2:25).

Nothing less than holiness is specially attributed to this man, who is described as dwelling in Jerusalem, that is, in the Vision of peace; as righteous through the practice of faith; devout through reverence; astonished by the consolation of Israel; filled with the Holy Spirit; [Col. 1296B] and strengthened by the Spirit’s answer concerning the vision of the incarnate Word.

O with what ardent desire this man awaited, according to the promise of the Holy Spirit, seeing the Redeemer in the flesh! What, we may ask, was the persistence of his prayer, by which he deserved to be strengthened through a divine response concerning what he requested? What words, uttered amid groans, continued in his holy supplication? For he did not cease asking until he received an answer concerning what he sought.

In earlier times there were indeed many people kindled by a similar desire, as the Lord testifies when he says to the disciples: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke 10:24). But this was granted only to this one among them, who appeared last in the fullness of time. [Col. 1296C]

Yet if we attentively consider the desire of the holy men who came afterward, for whom Christ was life and death gain, we find that they wished to behold the divinity of the same Savior with no less burning anxiety than Simeon desired to see his flesh.

Hence Paul says: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23). Hence the Psalmist speaks in the person of the Church: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 42:3).

[Col. 1296D] Who, then, would not now see that all the elect are signified in the one righteous Simeon? They are now found righteous through faith and action, devout through expectation of what is to come, and astonished by the consolation that will come. The Holy Spirit is also recognized as dwelling in them, since it is said through the Apostle: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). And again he says to the faithful: “Your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God.”

They too receive an answer from the Holy Spirit that they will not see death before they have seen the Lord’s Christ. For, while still in this corruptible life, through the grace of that same Holy Spirit revealing him, they behold with the open eyes of faith the one who promised to remain with them until the end of the age—not now as a little one in the flesh, but as immeasurable in divinity.

They too say with Paul: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way.”

These people also dwell in Jerusalem and come in the spirit into the Temple into which Christ is brought. They [Col. 1297A] are Jerusalem, who dwell in Jerusalem.

Brothers, we have passed over these matters briefly, so that, while striving to indicate the mysteries of this day and its holy proclamation concerning the little child, we might not become burdensome to anyone.

It follows:

“And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law, he took him into his arms, blessed him, and said: ‘Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation’” (Luke 2:27).

Here the expectation both of one person and of many—indeed, of all the righteous—is fulfilled. But let us speak first of the one, and then let us speak of all. For we wish to direct our effort toward this end: that what is said about one may truly be understood of all.

[Col. 1297B] Behold, while we specifically wish to speak about one venerable old man, the Virgin’s praiseworthy wisdom presents itself—not supported by human skill but inspired by the Spirit of divinity. Coming to offer her Son, and preserving the humility appropriate to her nature, she handed him over to the prophet’s hands to be offered, certainly not unaware of who he was, since she was entrusting to his hands the one who was both God and man, to be dedicated as a sacrifice.

She offers the Lord of the prophets to a prophet; she offers the only-begotten one to one man—indeed, to all in one, she who bore him as Savior for all.

She does not cease even now to offer the one whom she bore, when by her holy intercessions she causes the same Redeemer to be united to the elect. And, to speak truly, she does this with the most devout maternal affection. For she counts as her children all whom divine grace joins to Christ.

[Col. 1297C] When is she not herself the mother of the elect, since she bore their brother? If Christ is the brother of believers, why should she who bore Christ not be the mother of believers?

Therefore, I beg you, most blessed Virgin, offer Christ to us by your devout intercessions. You do not know how to begrudge your children, nor do you take account of the injuries of your children, by whom you are not honored as you ought to be. She who is overcome by the love of giving birth endures the irreverence of her children.

Foster, therefore, even by your devout prayers, those who are unworthy of such great merits, whom you brought forth in the One. Plead with your only Son for the offenses of the many.

### 8

### 8

[Col. 1297D] But now, dearest brothers, let us hear what Simeon says in particular as he receives Christ into his arms. For he says: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29), as though he were saying:

“You have wearied me with a long expectation; you have detained me for a long time. But now, at last, having seen the one whom I awaited, you dismiss me in peace from the dangers of human life. You dismiss me in peace because, according to your promise, through the mystery of the incarnate Word, my enmity having been removed, I have deserved to be reconciled to you. You dismiss me in peace because I see peace. For he is our peace, who made both one.”

All the elect say this, too: those who receive Christ into their arms and behold God’s salvation with the eyes of faith.

For what does it mean to receive Christ into one’s arms except to embrace him through devout works in his members? Through arms, that is, through the limbs, the power of action is expressed.

When they satisfy Christ who is hungry in one person, [Col. 1298A] give drink to him who is thirsty in another, receive him as a stranger in another, clothe him when naked in another, and visit him when sick or imprisoned in another, they undoubtedly embrace that same little child every day through these devoted actions as through arms.

And because, when they do these things, they know with complete faith that they receive him in these people, they do not doubt that they see him in them—the one who said: “As long as you did it for one of the least of these who are mine, you did it for me.” They rightly believe that, through these same works, they return to the peace of God and are absolved from the stumbling-block of sin.

Rightly, then, the same Simeon exclaims, saying: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation.”

[Col. 1298B] It is as though the elect were saying:

“Therefore, by your promise absolving us from the stumbling-block of sin, you now make us, reconciled in peace, approach heavenly things through the steps of love, because with the eyes of faith we have deserved to behold your salvation—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ—in his members, and to embrace him through devout works.”

Concerning this salvation, whether he or they, they still say to God the Father: “Which you have prepared before the face of all peoples.”

Unless “all peoples” is understood as meaning a part of all peoples—the part that saw the Savior in the flesh—the literal interpretation will not stand, because not all peoples saw him with bodily or even with the eyes of faith.

This salvation, therefore, is said to have been prepared before the face of all peoples because people from all nations believed in him and, believing in him, looked upon him with the eyes of faith.

For when the Lord says to Thomas, “Because you have seen me, [Col. 1298C] you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:29), he was speaking of bodily vision.

“A light for revelation to the nations and the glory of your people Israel” (Luke 2:32).

By this light the nations were revealed from darkness, found, and illumined, as it is written: “The people of the nations, who walked in darkness, have seen a great light. Light has arisen for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death” (Isaiah 9:2).

Concerning this light the evangelist John testifies, saying: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9). Concerning it he says in his Epistle: “God is light, and there is no darkness in him at all” (1 John 1:5). Concerning this same light he says in the Gospel: “The light came into the world, and people loved darkness more than light” (John 3: [Col. 1298D] 19) (John 3:19). And again: “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world” (John 9:5).

Although this light is also the glory of the nations, it is said to have been prepared for the glory of Israel because, whether in the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles—or even in Christ himself, the head of all—or in the utterances of God, that people is shown to be more glorious than the nations.

The Apostle bears witness to this when he says: “What advantage, then, has the Jew? Or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way. First, indeed, because the utterances of God were entrusted to them” (Romans 3:1).

And again: “To them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenant, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises; to them belong the patriarchs, and from them, according to the flesh, comes Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen” (Luke 2:35).

It follows:

### 9

[Col. 1299A] “And Joseph and Mary, his mother, were amazed at the things that were spoken about him.”

While they were amazed, we too are amazed: why were they amazed at the things that the holy prophet said about him?

Had Joseph not already heard in a dream from the angel: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife; for that which has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:20–21)?

And had not the most holy Virgin herself, who knew that she had borne a son while preserving her virginity, heard from the angel, before she conceived or gave birth: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you. Blessed are you among women. The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:28, 35)?

[Col. 1299B] Why, then, were they amazed at the things that were spoken about him? Was it not because, while others were amazed, they concealed the mystery from the impious?

What is the meaning of such things being said about such a tiny infant, and of their own amazement? But let them hear still greater things about him. It follows:

### 10

“Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother: ‘Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be opposed’” (Luke 2:34).

In the one person of our Redeemer, God and man, we confess that there is a perfect nature of God and a perfect nature of man.

From one nature he is Lord, from the other a servant; from one strong, from the other weak; from one great, from the other small; [Col. 1299C] from one creating, from the other created; from one feeding, from the other hungry; from one restoring, from the other thirsty; from one shining forth through miracles, from the other succumbing to insults; from one giving life, from the other dying; from one raising up, from the other raised.

And although one thing in him is Lord and another servant; one thing strong and another weak; one thing great and another small; one thing creating and another created; one thing feeding and another hungry; one thing restoring and another thirsty; one thing shining through miracles and another succumbing to insults; one thing giving life and another dying; one thing raising up and another raised—

[Col. 1299D] yet it is not one Lord and another servant; one strong and another weak; one great and another small; one creating and another created; one feeding and another hungry; one restoring and another thirsty; one shining through miracles and another succumbing to insults; one giving life and another dying; one raising up and another raised.

Rather, he is one and the same Son of God and of man: from one nature, as has been said, Lord; from the other, servant; from one, strong; from the other, weak; from one, great; from the other, small; from one, creating; from the other, created; from one, feeding; from the other, hungry; from one, restoring; from the other, thirsty; from one, shining through miracles; from the other, succumbing to insults; from one, giving life; from the other, dying; from one, raising up; from the other, raised.

Placed before mortal eyes, he was revered as God according to one nature and despised as man according to the other.

[Col. 1300A] Indeed, when the Jewish people saw him feeding so many thousands of people with five loaves, healing the sick, cleansing lepers, and raising the dead, they thought he was God. Again, when they saw the same man hungry, thirsty, weary, sleeping, and succumbing to insults, they supposed that he was merely human.

These things occurred among the uncertain crowds, but not among the disciples. For the hearts of those who enjoyed his constant private teachings did not fluctuate in this way. To them he himself said: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of God, but to the others in parables, so that, seeing, they may not see, and hearing, they may not understand” (Luke 8:10).

But when he was about to come to the passion of death, faith perished. All, abandoning him, fled (Matthew 26:56). [Col. 1300B] One of them, following the bound man from a distance, reached the courtyard and denied that he knew him.

And who would not have fallen when he fell in the passion of death, when his chief lover, frightened by the voice of a single servant girl, denied him not once but three times?

But when he rose in the flesh from the dead, the disciple’s soul also rose.

Both events—the disciples’ fall into the sleep of faithlessness on the night when he was handed over, and their restoration through the rising of the same Redeemer—were signified before his passion.

His death, therefore, became the fall of many. Let it be said:

### 11

“Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel,” as though it were said:

“When he dies, many of those who are standing will fall; when he rises, many of those who have fallen will rise.”

But because many fell when he died and many rose when he rose, yet not all believed in him who rose from the dead, [Col. 1300C] it is rightly added: “And for a sign that will be opposed.”

What we mark, we conceal from the knowledge of others. What, then, was the flesh of the Redeemer before the eyes of unbelievers except a kind of seal concealing his divinity?

Our Redeemer, therefore, was appointed as a sign—but a sign to which contradiction was made. What cause made this contradiction? What did it assert in opposition? To whom did it make contradiction?

To answer briefly, as though someone were asking: What cause made contradiction, if not the death of the flesh? What did it assert in opposition, if not that he was not God because he could die as a man? To whom did it make contradiction, if not to every unbeliever?

This opposition became a stumbling-block to some and foolishness to others, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “We preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling-block and to the nations foolishness” (1 Corinthians 1:23).

### 12

[Col. 1300D] The venerable righteous old man and prophet of God then continues and says to the mother of Jesus:

“And your own soul a sword will pierce, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke 2:35).

In sacred Scripture, temporal tribulation is sometimes represented by the name of a sword, as the Psalmist testifies. Wishing the sufferings inflicted by persecutors to fall back upon them, he says: “Let their sword enter their own hearts” (Psalm 37:15).

The same Psalmist speaks of Joseph, saying: [Col. 1301A] “Iron passed through his soul until his word came” (Psalm 105:18), as though he were saying: “He remained in that tribulation of servitude or imprisonment until what he had foretold would happen came to pass.”
