Nor do we understand anything else to be represented by the sword in this passage. Although many tribulations pierced the soul of the most blessed Virgin, the passage specifically designates that tribulation which, when the Lord was dying on the cross, pierced her maternal heart.

Let the holy prophet therefore say to her: “And your own soul a sword will pierce, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”

It is as though he were saying:

“When the sword of tribulation strikes your maternal heart, you will see hanging on the cross the one whom, when announced by the angel, you conceived as a virgin and, while preserving your virginity, brought forth as a son. Through this event, both the wickedness of the Jews rejoicing and the weakness of the fleeing disciples will be exposed.”

Indeed, while he hung on the cross, the Jews who were present mocked him, telling him to come down; [Col. 1301B] the apostles, fleeing from the cross, did not believe that he could come down from it. While these things were happening, it was necessary that the devout maternal heart be pierced by the sword of tribulation through the passion of the same Redeemer.

### 13

But now, as we began, let us briefly demonstrate what these things signify mystically.

Who, established within the holy Church, does not see falling at the death of our Redeemer those who assert either that he was merely a mortal human being or that he did not possess true flesh in his passion or resurrection?

And who does not see rising in his resurrection those who affirm that, by divine grace, they have been restored from the faithlessness of an evil belief, [Col. 1301C] and that he truly suffered in true flesh, while the impassibility of his divinity remained intact, and was truly raised in true flesh by his majesty?

Was Christ not made a fall for some and a resurrection for others, when Paul said of himself and his companions: “We are the good odor of Christ to God, both among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing; to some an odor of death unto death, and to others an odor of life unto life” (2 Corinthians 2:15)?

Concerning those for whom the humanity of his flesh concealed the Savior’s divinity, he says: “If our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing” (2 Corinthians 4:3).

Now, if we attend devoutly, as is fitting, we find that the blessed Virgin, whose soul is said to have been pierced by a sword, represented a type of the Church, whose soul was pierced by the sword—that is, by the word of preaching.

[Col. 1301D] That holy preaching is represented by a sword is testified by the Apostle Paul, who says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:17).

The sword pierces Mary’s soul because the word of God penetrates the hearts of the elect; penetrating them, it puts error to death, and having put error to death, it changes them into the truth of life.

“So that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed,” he says (Luke 2:35), as though he were saying:

“For this reason the sword of the divine word, utterly putting error to death in the hearts of the holy and transforming them into the doctrine of truth, causes each person, while examining the vices and virtues of some by speaking about them, to reveal what lies within.”

Hence Paul says: “If all prophesy, and an unbeliever or an unlearned person enters, he is convicted by all; the secrets of his heart are also made manifest, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you” (1 Corinthians 14:24–25).

[Col. 1302A] Who these prophets are, Paul himself explains later, saying: “Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge” (1 Corinthians 14:29).

We must pray, then, that this same sword may pierce our hearts, so that, as we preach and set forth the virtues and vices of individuals, the inner realities of each may be disclosed.

It follows:

### 14

“And there was Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in age and had lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity. She was a widow until the age of eighty-four. She did not depart from the Temple, serving with fasts and observances night and day. And coming at that very hour, she gave thanks to the Lord and spoke about him to all who were awaiting the redemption of Jerusalem” (Luke 2:36–38).

[Col. 1302B] These matters are clear according to the historical account and contain nothing obscure. They commend the chastity of the blessed woman, her persistence in fasting and prayer, and her attachment night and day to the Temple of God. Yet certain mysteries of the Church lie hidden in them.

For what is signified by Anna, whose name is interpreted as “grace of God,” except the Church of the elect? To her members the Apostle says: “You have been saved by grace through faith” (Ephesians 2:8).

She is also rightly described as the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. Phanuel is interpreted as “the face of God,” while Asher is called “blessed.”

Who else are represented by the face of God except those who, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, first brought human hearts to the knowledge of God?

[Col. 1302C] Because anyone is recognized by the face, those through whom knowledge of divinity is revealed are rightly called the face of God. They are also rightly called Asher, that is, blessed, because they deserved to be instructed toward eternal fatherhood, either through the natural understanding inspired within them or through the law given externally.

Hence it is written: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, Lord, and whom you teach from your law” (Psalm 94:12).

These words plainly show that the Church of the elect is the daughter of the patriarchs and prophets. She is rightly called a prophetess, whether in spirit or in word. Concerning her it is further said that she had lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity.

[Col. 1302D] And who else is her husband except the one of whom the prophet Isaiah says: “In that day seven women will take hold of one man, saying: ‘We will eat our own bread and wear our own garments; only let your name be invoked over us. Take away our disgrace’” (Isaiah 4:1)?

Who else is her husband except the one of whom the Apocalypse of John says: “I saw the holy city, Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Revelation 21:2)?

Before she was joined to Christ, she was called a virgin either because at that time she did not worship idols or because, though not corrupted, she was barren.

Christ united her to himself when, assuming human nature, he began the Gospel.

[Col. 1303A] The fact that she is described as having lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity figurally encompasses the period of that preaching in the number seven. During this period she received from him the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit and deserved mystically to be united in the seven women, or the seven churches.

And because, when he ascended into heaven, his human presence was taken away, she is rightly also said to have remained a widow.

Is she not rightly called a widow, of whom blessed Job, mentioning heretics, says: “He fed the barren woman who does not bear, and he did not do good to the widow” (Job 24:21)?

The time of joy, then, during which she enjoyed the presence of her husband in the flesh, and the time of sorrow during which the Church would be deprived of his presence, are indicated by her husband when he says: “The children of the bridegroom cannot fast as long as the bridegroom is with them. The time will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast” (Matthew 9:15).

[Col. 1303B] In the number eighty-four, the years during which she is described as a widow, the whole period of the present life is expressed.

We read that the children of Israel had forty-two stopping places on their journey before they entered the promised land. What else is signified by these except the pilgrimage of the present life, in which we are exercised by the tribulations of the wilderness until we come to the land of the living?

But because of the two Testaments—the Old and the New—the same number, forty-two, is doubled, producing eighty-four.

Just as, because of the two Testaments, the number twelve is doubled in the twenty-four elders and signifies the Church, so, because of the same Testaments, the number forty-two is doubled in eighty-four and represents the present time of the Church. What is explained there through stopping places is explained here through years.

[Col. 1303C] Both numbers harmoniously signify the pilgrimage of the same Church, concerning which it is rightly added:

### 15

“She did not depart from the Temple, serving with fasts and prayers night and day.”

For she herself is the Temple. As a widow, serving with fasts and prayers in the Temple, and deprived of the bodily appearance of her bridegroom—for she is not yet able to behold him with bodily eyes—she devotes herself to nothing more than fasting and prayer.

[Col. 1303D] Hence the Psalmist says: “My tears have been my bread day and night, while it is said to me every day, ‘Where is your God?’” (Psalm 42:3–4).

She rightly places fasting first and then joins prayers to it. What kind of supplication can there be where feasting reigns? What kind of prayer can there be where continual drinking dominates?

But in saying this, he also intends the fasting of the heart to be understood. Unless someone strives to fast from impure thoughts, he cannot be joined to God through prayer.

Whether by this fasting or by that fasting, supported at the same time by prayers, she is described as serving night and day—that is understood, in prosperity and adversity—and as not ceasing from good works.

It follows:

[Col. 1304A] **16.** And when they had completed everything according to the law of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, to their own city, Nazareth (Luke 2:39). Here, figuratively, the final conversion of the Jews is signified: when Enoch and Elijah are preaching, Christ returns to them, after everything has been accomplished in Jerusalem—that is, in the Church of the Gentiles—according to the law of the Lord, namely, the New Testament. For just as after the sacrifice has been completed Christ returns with his parents from Jerusalem to his own city, so, when the fullness of the Gentiles has been brought in, he finally returns with the holy preachers to gather those from whom he assumed his flesh. It follows:

**17.** “The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was with him” (Luke 2:40). [Col. 1304B] These things are said of him according to his humanity, not according to his divinity. He does not grow in his own nature, in which he is full, but in ours, in which he was made a little lower than the angels. [Col. 1305C] Nor is he strengthened in his own nature, in which he is the strength of all and in which is the fullness of wisdom, but in ours, in which he emptied himself for us. Nor does he need the grace of God in his own nature, in which he grants grace to all, but in ours, in which he received those things that he possesses with the Father. All these things, moreover, can more properly be referred to his body, which is the Church, than to the head himself. For how long will that be consumed of which the Apostle says: “Until we all attain to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be children” (Ephesians 4:13)? [Col. 1304C] Daily the child Jesus grows in faith; daily the child Jesus is strengthened in virtues; daily the child Jesus is filled with the word of wisdom; daily the child Jesus is justified by the grace of salvation. We have spoken briefly of the solemnity of this great day; we have passed swiftly over the mysteries of such profound sacraments, both because we have taken account of the length of the Gospel reading and because we had only a short time for reading these things.

**18.** For the rest, dearest brothers, I admonish your charity—if indeed this discourse has made your minds attentive—to consider with what devotion you ought henceforth to celebrate the solemnity of this day. May that spectacle not be regarded as something insignificant: in it the Son of the Virgin is embraced as God and man; [Col. 1304D] in it the virgin is shown to be a mother; in it the prophet, indeed the expectation of all the prophets, is fulfilled; in it many mysteries of the Church are disclosed. May he himself deign to impress this upon your hearts—he who on this day, by the illumination of the Holy Spirit, inwardly stirred holy and righteous Simeon and taught, indeed certainly compelled, him to go to the temple where he himself was being offered by his parents. He lives and reigns as God with God the Father and the same Holy Spirit, with equal power, equal strength, equal majesty, and equal eternity, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1305]

# HOMILY ON THE TRANSFIGURATION OF THE LORD

(From a Corbie manuscript of approximately the year 800, in Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. IX.)

[Col. 1305A] In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Here begins the homily of the presbyter Autbert on the Gospel reading according to Matthew, in which the Lord is reported to have been transfigured on a mountain before three disciples.

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.’ And after six days Jesus took Peter and James and John, etc.” (Matthew 16:28). The entire Gospel of the Transfiguration is given.

The Gospel reading according to Matthew ends.

Here begins the homily on the same reading, delivered to the monks in the monastery of Saint Vincent.

**1.** It sometimes happens—indeed, it happens almost always—that in the houses of kings and princes some ordinary and despised person cleans golden [Col. 1305B] or silver vessels. What, then, are the hearts of the elect in the holy Church except certain royal vessels, so to speak? Paul bears witness to this when he says: “In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay; some for honor, some for dishonor” (Romans 9:21). Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel sanctified for honor and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work.

You, therefore, dearest brothers—you are vessels of the eternal King, shining like precious metal through the practice of sacred religion. But remember that, as long as you live here, you cannot possibly be without the stains of vices. Hence John, whom the Lord especially loved, says in his Epistle: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). Therefore, lest the rust of sins consume God’s vessels, it is necessary that this hand of holy preaching wipe them daily; and none of you is unaware that this work of cleansing has been entrusted to me, the least worthy of all God’s servants. But I ask you not to be offended by the ugliness of this little man, provided that by whatever means he may, he removes the filth of sins from your hearts.

I therefore undertake to expound the reading of the holy Gospel in which our Lord is reported to have been transfigured on a mountain before three disciples, and, insofar as I can, to examine the secrets of its mysteries—not because it has not already been explained before me, but because something in it that has not yet been said may have been reserved for me to say.

As your fraternity has now heard, before [Col. 1305D] our Redeemer ascended the mountain to be transfigured, he said to the apostles: “There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom” (Matthew 16:28). One of the interpreters understood this to have been said of the state of the Church that would soon come. But the subsequent course of the reading makes clear that the Lord spoke of his own transformation, when the Evangelist added:

[Col. 1306A]

**2.** “And after six days Jesus took Peter and James and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain privately, and he was transfigured before them” (Matthew 17:1). These are certainly the three apostles whom he said would not taste death until they saw him transformed in glory; yet in this transformation of his it was demonstrated what the Church of the saints will be like in the heavenly homeland.

But first we must ask why Matthew reported that the Savior’s transfiguration took place after six days, while Luke said it took place after eight. Did either of them depart from the truth, since each seems not to agree with the other? We must understand that Matthew, in mentioning the days, expressed the whole from the whole, while Luke expressed a part from the whole. [Col. 1306B] It was evening when the Lord spoke these words, and Matthew did not touch upon that fact at all. Luke, however, counted it as the whole day. It was morning when the same Lord was transfigured on the mountain; just as Matthew left this out entirely, so Luke took it as representing the whole day.

Thus Matthew, signifying the whole from the whole, inserted only the six complete days in between. Luke, however, showing the whole by reference to its parts, counted both the evening of the first day and the morning of the eighth day. Here a figure of speech is understood which in Greek is called *synecdoche*; in Latin it may be called either “the whole from a part” or, conversely, “a part from the whole.” Through frequent application in the sacred pages, this figure resolves many questions, including especially that question concerning the Lord’s being declared to have lain in the tomb for three days and three nights, [Col. 1306C] although it is evident that he gave up his spirit on Friday, when the day was already declining—at the ninth hour—and rose before dawn on Sunday.

**3.** We must also ask why, when he went up the mountain to pray with only three disciples, he revealed the glory of his majesty at that time to only three. Could it be thought that he did this without cause, concealing the mysteries of his revelation from the other apostles, to whom holy authority testifies that he said: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” (Luke 8:10)? And again: “Everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15)?

[Col. 1306D] Let us therefore grant that Peter, James, and John were leaders and pillars among the other apostles, as Paul says, “Peter and James and John, who seemed to be pillars”;” and for this reason the Lord revealed his secrets to them more than to the others. To them alone, moreover, he privately disclosed the sorrow of his heart concerning the betrayal by Judas—or by the Jews—which was soon to occur as his passion approached.

Yet would anyone on that account suppose that this deed lacked a hidden mystery? Certainly not. It was not without the sacrament of a prefiguration that Peter, James, and John alone were taken up to behold the great glory of the Redeemer.

[Col. 1307A] Peter took his name, as it were, from *petra*, “rock”; and the Rock was Christ, as the Apostle Paul taught. To this Rock Peter says: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16). In these words the faith of the whole Church is expressed. And how appropriately the Rock answered Peter: “And I say to you, You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (ibid. 18). He plainly said: “I will build you upon myself, since you bear the figure of that Church which is built upon me through you.”

Hence, when the blessed Peter, using prophetic testimony, said: “Behold, I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone, most precious, founded upon the foundation,” he immediately added: “And you, as living stones, are built up into spiritual houses” (1 Peter 2:6). [Col. 1307B] Likewise Paul, when he said: “No one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus,” immediately added: “But let each one see how he builds upon it” (1 Corinthians 3:11). Therefore, when it is said that Peter is placed upon this foundation as one being built up, the whole Church is clearly situated to be built upon Christ.

James is translated into our language as “supplanter.” Supplanter of whom, except of vices? And certainly, in the person of James, we supplant vices when, through the holy discipline of prayer, we claim the firstborn things of virtues. The Psalmist speaks of this supplanting of vices, saying: “Blessed is he who will seize and dash his little ones against the rock” (Psalm 136:9).

[Col. 1307C] John, however, is interpreted as “dove.” Through him, without doubt, are signified those who within the holy Church of God burn with love of God and neighbor. For the Holy Spirit is represented by the dove, and he is shown to be the love of the Father and the Son. It is written: “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

Thus faith is shown in the apostle Peter, the practice of virtues in James, and love in John. Therefore, it was not unfitting that only these three ascended the mountain with the Lord, since in their persons they bear the figure of all the saints.

But now, setting forth the words of the reading itself, let us discuss them one by one.

**4.** “Jesus took Peter and James and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain privately; and he was transfigured before them” (Matthew 17:1). [Col. 1307D] Everyone who is transfigured is changed into another form. Hence Luke, expressing this same point, says: “As he was praying, the appearance of his face became different” (Luke 9:29).

Here the madness of heretics must be avoided entirely: they think that after the day of judgment human bodies can be changed into another nature. Yet the same mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who, according to the Apostle, “will transform our lowly body to be conformed to his glorious body,” appeared after his resurrection to the disciples in a locked room and said: “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39).

[Col. 1308A] What else was meant by these words except that his body possessed another glory, but not another nature—a body which he offered to be touched and brought through closed doors in true flesh and with true bones? Therefore, when it is said, “He was transfigured” (Matthew 17:2), that is, “he was changed into another form,” this refers not to nature but to glory. Hence it is immediately added:

**5.** “And his face shone like the sun” (ibid.). This certainly is the other form, this is the other appearance of his face: he who was visible in the flesh suddenly appeared radiant in majesty.

What is surprising if such great majesty is said to have suddenly flashed forth in the body, when we commonly say the same thing every day about someone whom we see either washed after being dirty or joyful after sorrow: “He is not the one he was; he is different from what he was”?

It should also be noted that prayer preceded the glorification of the Redeemer. As Luke says, he ascended [Col. 1308B] the mountain for this reason: to pray. By this action he showed that all who belong to the contemplation of his majesty must pray without ceasing, and must always pray not in the depths but on the mountain.

Those who do not yield to any earthly desires through the allurements of vices can do this continually; fixed in the love of heavenly things, they look toward what is above. Hence Paul, bound by the chains of afflictions, said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

The Lord also admonishes us by his example in other places. Though he had no rest during the day even for eating, he spent the night in prayer on the mountain, exhausted as he was. If permission is granted to interpret this action, it teaches us to seek outward solitude itself for prayer, so that one may appeal to God more intimately when no human tumult has driven him elsewhere.

[Col. 1308C] But what shall we wretched people say about these things, burdened as we are by countless weights of sins, who at the very outset anticipate the time for evening study with sleep? If our God and Lord, conceived without sin and born without sin, carried through to an undeserved death, allowed himself a little sleep on some nights and scarcely any on others—thus presenting himself as an example to sinners—and, bending his knees repeatedly with frequent sighs and groans, kept night watches filled with tears, as though he himself were subject to the sins of mortals, it is nevertheless not surprising that he did this for us, since he had come to die for us.

He bore our sins, and therefore he appealed to the Father as though he were a sinner. [Col. 1308D] Yet he also offered himself as an example for imitation, so that we too might learn to appeal to the Father with him on our behalf and not cease from prayers, since even now he appears before the face of God and intercedes for us.

Let us therefore shake off the sluggishness of our torpor. To imitate so great an example of the Redeemer, let at least this move us: although, as we have said, no personal sins were pleading against him, as his blessed passion approached he prayed more frequently and at greater length, struggling so intensely that, instead of sweat from his body, drops of blood flowed. “He was in agony,” says the Evangelist, “and he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground” (Luke 22:44).

Therefore, lest we become negligent through laziness toward sacred vigils and prayers, let us always recall these things, dearest [Col. 1309A] brothers. Certainly, such a powerful labor must be undertaken, for by it the entrance of temptation is closed and every assault of evils is avoided. “Pray,” says the Lord, “that you may not enter into temptation” (ibid. 46). And again: “Watch at all times, praying that you may be considered worthy to escape all these things that are about to happen and to stand before the Son of Man” (Luke 21:36). And again: “It is necessary always to pray and not to lose heart” (Luke 18:1).

**6.** Since we know that it is written concerning the saints: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Wisdom 3:7), how is Christ’s face compared here with the brightness of the sun? Or will the righteous have in the kingdom of the Father, which it is impious to say, as much glory as the one who justified them? [Col. 1309B] Who except a heretic would say this?

It seems to me that this happened for four reasons: either because he was still mortal, and the mortality of his flesh did not allow the glory of his divinity to be displayed as it truly was; or because, before the eyes of those who saw him, he moderated the magnitude of his radiance so that they could look upon it; or because he was displaying only that form which he knew he would show to both the elect and the reprobate on the day of judgment; or, certainly, because he was showing more truly and more profitably, in his own glory, what the form of his members would be like when they shine in the future, as has been said.

It follows:

**7.** “And his garments became white as snow” (Matthew 17:2). This brightness, brothers, which flowed outward through Christ’s [Col. 1309C] garments, proceeded from that inner light of his which no bodily eye of the human race can behold, as it is written: “No one has ever seen God” (1 John 4:12); and again: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exodus 33:20). Indeed, even the angels do not see it as it sees itself, although they behold it daily insofar as it has been granted to them.

For sacred Scripture testifies to both points: they see the face of the Father daily, and they desire to behold it so that they may be able to do so. Great indeed is the force and power of that inner light, which poured forth so much light outwardly that it granted even his garments the glory of flashing majesty.

From that light, beloved, all things that shine are illuminated: the sun outwardly, the moon and stars; but the angels and human souls inwardly. Therefore, we marvel that the Lord shone outwardly on the mountain with the brightness of the sun; let us rather marvel that he shines inwardly with divinity.

Let us venerate him as he appeared on the mountain before the three disciples; let us desire him as he will appear in heaven to all who are pure in heart. [Col. 1309D] In truth, the impious too will see him in the future as he appeared outwardly on the mountain; but only the blessed will see him as he remained inwardly.

**8.** The Church of the righteous may be represented by the garments of our Redeemer, shining with the whiteness of snow—not as it is now, since here it is not without sin, but as it will be in the future, when it will no longer be able to sin.

Thus, through the brightness of snow, both the brightness of purity may be signified and the heat of vices, which will be utterly [Col. 1310A] abolished, may be shown. Snow possesses whiteness, but admits no heat at all. So it will one day happen to God’s elect, to those who reach the glory of God: they will possess the whiteness of purity and will never again feel any heat arising from the corruption of the flesh.

It follows.

**9.** “And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him” (Matthew 17:3). Some think that Moses will come with Elijah to precede Christ’s final advent, because both appeared in this transfiguration of his. But others have understood the matter better: they say that Enoch will come with Elijah, so that they may then arrive to die for Christ, since they have not yet paid the debt of death in the flesh.

[Col. 1310B] Enoch, as the Apostle teaches, “was taken up so that he should not see death”; and Elijah was raised to heaven so that, having been sent down from there to some region of the earth, he might remain alive until that time.

Moses did not appear with Elijah in that glorification because he is to come with him to suffer, but so that the Gospel might have testimony from the Law and the Prophets.

Behold: Moses fasted for forty days, Elijah for forty, and the Lord for forty. But since it is not surprising that in the Lord there should occur what had previously occurred in any servant, let us see whether a great mystery lies hidden in this number of forty days.

[Col. 1310C] Was it difficult for the Lord to extend his fast to a hundred or a thousand days, when he had enabled his servants to pass forty days without the sustenance of bodily food? Who, then, would not take offense at the fact that he was able to fast more than a servant, unless the same number of days expressed not so much a miracle of virtue as the mystery of virtue?

Who, then, does not know that the Mosaic Law is twofold, distinguished both in the spiritual Decalogue and in the service of sacrifices? That the legal command is twofold is especially clear from the fact that it seems to be fulfilled by one part, while by the other it is in no way fulfilled.

For David says to the Lord: “I have run in the way of your commandments” (Psalm 118:32). And again: “I have not turned aside from your commandments” (ibid. 157). Behold the fulfillment of the Law—but clearly of the spiritual commandments of the Decalogue, just as the Apostle says: “The Law is holy, and its commandment is holy and righteous and good,” and, according to this, “the one who does them will live by them” (Romans 7:12).

[Col. 1310D] Peter, on the other hand, says: “Why are you testing God by placing a yoke upon the necks of the disciples which neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear?” (Acts 15:10). Behold the diminution of the Law—but plainly of its carnal service, in accordance with what is also said: “I gave them commandments that were not good, by which they would not live.” And likewise the Apostle says: “The Law brought nothing to perfection” (Hebrews 7:19).

It must also be understood that, insofar as the Law is spiritual and can be observed—that is, in the ten commandments—it passed over into the New Testament to be kept when the fullness of time arrived. But insofar as it is carnal and cannot be borne—that is, in the service of sacrifices—it lost its observance when the Lord died on the cross.

Therefore, if the Law is spiritual in the commandments of the Decalogue but carnal in the service of sacrifices, [Col. 1311A] on the one side it displayed a sacred fast, and on the other a banquet burdened with excess. Since we now utterly reject the greed of carnal sacrifices, it remains for us to say something about the fast of the spiritual Law.

**10.** What else does it mean to say, “You shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet your neighbor’s property, nor desire his wife, his male servant, his female servant, his ox, his sheep, his donkey, nor anything that belongs to him,” except to impose a certain fast upon the soul? Does the one who turns away from evil in order to cling to good not truly fast?

But for this fast of the Decalogue to rise to forty, it must await from afar the commands of the New Testament and eventually run toward the Gospel. [Col. 1311B] Let Moses and Elijah, therefore, come to the Lord as the Law and prophecy come to the Gospel. Let the Decalogue become fourfold; let it encompass within the scope of its preaching, through the four corners of heaven, the whole world among the elect; and let the fast of forty days appear consecrated in both Testaments, from beginning to end.

For that person mystically fasts for forty days who observes the Law spiritually through the four books of the holy Gospel and preserves the laws of charity in loving God and neighbor. Hence it is written: “Love is the fullness of the Law” (Romans 13:10).

When the Lord said in the Gospel: “Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength”—and added, “This is the first and greatest commandment in the Law; the second [Col. 1311C] is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself”—he immediately continued: “On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 22:37).

Whoever rejects everything that draws the soul toward the desires of the flesh keeps these two highest and chief commandments, because, as John says: “If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2:15).

Therefore the Lord rightly displayed Moses and Elijah in his transformation. To signify the grace of a future reality, he made them like himself in fasting, so that, by showing the agreement of both Testaments according to the rule of interpretation stated above, he might demonstrate that all those predestined for life must always observe, amid the hardship of this [Col. 1311D] pilgrimage, a fast of forty days through the brief summary of the Law, by which the twofold and evangelical love would be displayed. This love continually causes them both to cling to what is good and to turn away from what is evil at all times.

**11.** Nor do I think that this should be passed over in silence: Moses fasts in the wilderness, Elijah in the wilderness, and the Lord fasts in the wilderness. By this, surely, the pilgrimage of this life is signified, in which, as blessed Job indicates, human life is shown to be a time of testing.

Hence there are bitter waters and fiery serpents in the wilderness. Hence the children of Israel, after a period of forty years—as though after the completion of a forty-day fast in solitude—reach the [Col. 1312A] land flowing with milk and honey. Hence we too, after observing abstinence for forty days before the resurrection, attain to the jubilee, which is a year of remission and full of joy.

**12.** But let us consider what the bitter waters in the desert signify, and what the fiery serpents signify. First, we may reasonably judge that, just as the manna on which the Jewish people fed, as holy authority testifies, did not provide the same taste to all who ate it—being for some an increase of salvation and for others a loss of salvation—so those waters were sweet to some and bitter to others.

Those who were able to understand the remedies of the saving wood did not feel their bitterness at all; those who drew only the water without faith did feel it.

[Col. 1312B] Likewise, only those who looked upon the bronze serpent and attended more faithfully to the mystery could be healed from the serpents’ bites. Holy Scripture declares that not everyone who looked upon it was healed by that act alone—as though it openly said: not by what was outwardly disclosed according to the letter, but by what was hidden inwardly in the mystery.

What, then, do the bitter waters signify except the adversities of this world? From them the one who tasted undeservedly drank: he who, in order to reign seated at the right hand of the Father, drank from the stream along the way. Hence he was fed with gall; hence he was given vinegar to drink; hence the merciful Creator both thirsts for what is bitter and, tasting bitterness, says: “It is finished” (John 19:30).

[Col. 1312C] But from what source were the bitter waters changed into sweetness, except through the admixture of the saving wood? When the people of Israel murmured because of the bitterness of the water, Moses cried out to the Lord, who showed him a piece of wood. When he had thrown it into the water, the waters were changed into sweetness.

This is truly the tree of life in the paradise of God; this is the tree planted beside streams of water—namely, the Lord Jesus Christ, perfect God and man. Solomon also speaks of him: “Blessed is the person who finds wisdom; she is a tree of life to those who grasp her, and blessed is the one who holds fast to her” (Proverbs 3:18).

When the wood was cast into the bitter waters, whatever bitterness they seemed to possess was immediately changed into sweetness. For when the passion of the blessed Mediator is mingled with our tribulations, the weight of their burden is lightened.

But it must be understood that, according to the interpretation of our smallness stated above, [Col. 1312D] the waters remain bitter for some, while for others they provide sweetness. Hence some desire the one and the same cup of suffering, while others flee from it. Those desire it for whom its bitterness is sweet; those flee from it to whom bitter things are displeasing. Those desire it who take the narrow way; those flee from it who travel voluptuously along the broad and spacious roads of the world.

Only the one who draws the sweetness of the wood from within into the turning of the water does not feel the water’s bitterness; because, in comparison with the sweetness that is introduced, he does not feel the bitterness that was already present. For whoever fully tastes what sweetness lies hidden within the mystery of the cross considers everything associated with the cross, even bitter things, to be sweet.

[Col. 1313A] Hence holy Scripture declares: “To a hungry soul even bitter things seem sweet” (Proverbs 27:7). Who is so ungrateful that, even if not through open martyrdom, at least through hidden martyrdom, he would not willingly follow the teacher of the cross, remembering what is written: “If we do not suffer with him, we shall not reign with him” (2 Timothy 2:12), and what Peter urges: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps” (1 Peter 2:21)?

Paul had found such people among the Hebrews, to whom he said: “Looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising its shame” (Hebrews 12:2). He also wanted those to whom he spoke to become like them, so that he might turn the bitterness of suffering into sweetness: “Knowing,” he said, “that just as you are partners in suffering, so also you will be partners in consolation” (2 Corinthians 1:7).

[Col. 1313B] But in saying these things, we must distinguish between the two Testaments and see how the waters were bitter there but have become sweet here.

The waters were bitter for those of whom Moses said: “The Egyptians hated the children of Israel and afflicted them, mocking them and making their lives bitter with hard labor in clay and brick, and with every kind of service by which they oppressed them in their work in the land” (Exodus 1:12).

They were also bitter for those whose person Jeremiah represented under the figure of a woman, saying: “My belly is troubled; my heart is overturned within me, because I am full of bitterness” (Lamentations 1:20). And above: “He surrounded me with gall and labor” (Lamentations 3:15). And again: “He filled me with bitterness and saturated me with wormwood” (ibid. 15).

[Col. 1313C] But through the admixture of the saving wood they were changed into sweetness for those of whom Luke bore witness, saying: “The apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name” (Acts 5:41).

The waters were also bitter for Moses himself when, in sorrow, he complained: “Why, Lord, have you afflicted your servant? Why have I not found favor before you? Why have you placed the burden of this entire people upon me? I cannot bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me. If it seems otherwise to you, I ask that you kill me, so that I may find favor in your sight and not be afflicted by such evils” (Exodus 17:4). And again: “A little more and they will stone me.”

They were bitter also for Elijah when, fleeing through the wilderness from Jezebel’s persecutions and suffering violence, he cried out: “It is enough, Lord; take my life, I ask, for I am no better than my fathers” (1 Kings 19:4).

[Col. 1313D] But through the admixture of the remedial wood they were changed into sweetness for Paul, when he said to the faithful: “I now rejoice in my sufferings for you” (Romans 5:3). And again: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). And again: “I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus” (Acts 21:13).

**13.** There is also another interpretation of the bitter waters, frequently impressed upon us by our predecessors: their bitterness is rightly referred to the pain of circumcision in the flesh and to the retribution of punishment for guilt.

But the healing power of the wood turns the bitterness of the waters into sweetness, because our Redeemer, taking upon himself the severity of the Law that was not due to him, fulfilling the Law and at the same time abolishing its decrees, changed everything harsh in its commandments into the grace of the gentleness of the New Testament.

[Col. 1314A] What else do the fiery serpents signify except the deadly suggestions of the ancient enemy? To this judgment Paul agrees when he says: “Take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one” (Ephesians 6:16).

For this purpose, nothing—or rather, this alone—is especially effective: those who have been bitten and are not to die are commanded to look upon the bronze serpent. In this action it is not our interpretation that falters; rather, the Lord’s own exposition of the passage confirms it. For he says: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (Luke 19:14).

[Col. 1314B] Behold: the hidden adversary has suggested some crime in your mind; you consented, and the serpent has bitten you. But, lest you be utterly destroyed, look upon the bronze serpent—that is, upon the Lord hanging on the cross. When his passion is properly considered, it is found to extinguish within us all the evils of vices.

It is properly considered when we endeavor, according to our strength, to imitate it. Begin, then, to desire to imitate Christ’s passion, and there will be no mortal crime that can destroy you. Since Paul says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Galatians 5:24), what sinful pleasures, I ask, will be able to steal upon such people?

For whoever has been crucified surely does not feel the bite of the poisonous serpent amid the pain of his own impending death. [Col. 1314C] Give me any dead person who is able to feel a snake’s bite. And certainly the same distinguished preacher says to the faithful: “You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3).

## 14

Behold, as briefly as we have been able to indicate, why the Lord displayed Moses and Elijah at the Transfiguration: He had them as companions and harmonious servants in the mystery of fasting. How fitting, too, that he brought Moses and Elijah before the eyes of Peter and John, so that, with the deeds of the Old and New Testaments agreeing, the two persons on either side might be regarded as corresponding either in deed or in mystery.

Moses, in order to pass over to eat manna, divided the sea; Peter, in order to reach Christ, who is the true and heavenly manna, walked upon the sea. Elijah, in order to seek the heights, ascended in a fiery chariot; John, in order to penetrate the secrets of the Word, reclined upon Christ’s flaming breast.

But what are we to do with James? Are we to separate him from this harmony and judge him inferior to Peter or John in the prefiguration, although we find that he corresponds to the persons of Moses and Elijah for another reason? For Jacob, as we have said, is interpreted as “supplanter,” and this is plainly shown to suit Moses and Elijah very well. One of them secretly killed the Egyptian who was lying in wait for a Hebrew and hid him in the sand; the other, mocking Baal, slaughtered the prophets at the torrent. The authority of the Fathers has shown that all these things pertain to the extinction of vices.

But let us see, if we can, what were the words of the lawgiver and the prophet to the Lord of both of them—something I would perhaps rashly, indeed certainly as a vain presumer, assert, had I not learned from another evangelist what those words were.

## 15

“Behold,” he says, “two men were speaking with him. They were Moses and Elijah, and they were speaking of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke IX, 31).

What departure was this, except the undeserved torment of his passion undertaken for the life of the world? He had indeed already begun it, but had not yet completed it, because he had begun to suffer our miseries, yet had not entered into the punishment of the cross.

Their words to him may therefore be understood as follows: “You have come, the one who was to be sent, born of a Virgin; you have grown, hungered, thirsted, and sat down weary. But you have not yet, amid torments, handed over your spirit. You have begun, therefore, but have not yet completed what you will then perfectly complete when, as a merciful Creator, you hang upon the cross.”

This may also be understood in such a way that the same departure began in the prophets, but was by no means completed in them; it was to be completed in the Lord of the prophets. Hence the Lord himself says to the Jews: “And you, fill up the measure of your fathers” (Matthew XXIII, 32), as though he were saying plainly: “They killed the prophets, but the measure was not yet full. You kill the Lord of the prophets, and the measure of your fathers will be full.”

For all the sufferings of the righteous are brought to completion in the passion of their Lord. And where was he to complete this departure, except in Jerusalem? For he himself says: “It cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke XIII, 33).

O wretched, O condemnable Jerusalem, which alone reached so great a summit of condemnation that none of the prophets shed blood outside you, and no innocent blood was shed upon the earth that did not come upon you—from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you, bloodstained beast, trampled between the temple and the altar (Matthew XXIII, 35), because of the one whom, before Pilate, you demanded should come upon you and your offspring, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew XXVII, 25).

Yet how much good you procured for the world by this your greatest and most unspeakable crime, one of your own people, unknowingly prophesying, cries out: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people, lest the whole nation perish” [Col. 1315D] (John XVIII, 14).

The text continues:

## 16

“Then Peter answered and said to Jesus: Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, let us make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” (Matthew XVII, 4).

I beg you, blessed apostle Peter, not to be displeased by the authority of a most humble servant who reproves you, provided that no servile rashness be found in the one who reproves. With the freedom of humility, I ask of you what I find that others have already asked.

Tell me, I beg you: were you taken up onto the mountain so that, with tents fixed, you might possess the Lord alone with a few companions? Or were you taken up for this reason: that, having seen the glory of his body, when a little later you came to bonds, scourges, spitting, blows, the torments of the cross, and burial, you might not deny that he is God—or the complete God-man—and your teacher?

It is well that the suddenly glorified face of Christ now pleases you so greatly that you do not wish to descend from the mountain. But wait a little. Certainly, having forgotten such things, you will deny that you know this man before the servant girl, when that hour draws near, so that what is said of him through the prophet may be fulfilled: “There is no beauty in him, nor comeliness; and we saw him, and there was no appearance in him; and his face was as though hidden and despised, and we did not esteem him” (Isaiah LIII, 2).

Rather, should you not have said: “Lord, hasten the time when all that has been written about you may be fulfilled. And, as you pass into your glory, show me not the face you now have, but present yourself as you truly are”?

But you must be granted indulgence: you were suffering sleep when you said such things. For the evangelist speaks of you and your companions in this way: “But Peter and those who were with him were weighed down with sleep” (Luke IX, 32)—sleep, that is, not of the flesh but of the mind.

Hence, forgetting yourself and your companions, you were concerned with the Lord, Moses, and Elijah: “Let us make,” you said, “three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” Behold, the Lord shines with the brightness of the sun, while a luminous cloud overshadows Moses and Elijah. For whom, then, are tents needed: for you, upon whom none of these things has come, or for those to whom such a gift has been granted?

What, then, do you think about yourself and your fellow companions? Or perhaps you wish to join two of them to each tent, so that they may be the lords and you, in each tent, the servants of its lord? Who, then, among you will be the servant of the Lord? Who of Moses? Who of Elijah?

It would have been more tolerable to say: “Lord, let us make one tent here, so that Moses and Elijah, I, James, and John may serve you together in one tent.”

## 17

But we, dearest brothers, just as we do not follow Peter’s ignorance in this saying, so let us venerate his outstanding love for the Lord. The same most vigorous executor of his affection, unable to conceal it within, displayed it outwardly on many occasions through clear signs.

That is why, when the Lord himself asked the twelve, “Whom do you say that I am?” he was the first to answer: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew XVI, 15).

That is why he would not allow the teacher to suffer, but rebuked him when he foretold his passion, saying: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen” (ibid. XVI, 22).

That is why, when the hour of the same Lord’s passion was approaching and he said, “All of you will suffer scandal because of me on this night” (Matthew XXVI, 31), while the others were troubled, this fearless man answered: “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I will never be scandalized” (ibid. XXVI, 33). And again: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (ibid. XXVI, 35).

That is why, after he had been seized, Peter drew his sword and, directing an uncertain blow at the persecutor’s ear, cut it off.

That is why, when he was in the little boat and saw Christ on the shore, he plunged himself a second time into the waves, so that he might come to him before all the others.

The Lord confirmed this after he had risen from the dead. Knowing what he was asking, he said: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” And he replied: “Lord, you know that I love you” (John XXI, 15).

In this love, although—as the evangelist says—he did not know what he was saying, when he saw the brightness of the Lord’s face he wished to remain on the mountain and not descend even for a moment. He rejected the glory of the world and despised everything that charms in the world; only the face of Christ, shining with the brightness of the sun, pleased him.

What do we suppose? How would it have pleased him if he had then been able to behold through mortal flesh the one whom he now sees stripped of mortality? Certainly, he would have despised not only the earth lying beneath him but even the heaven above him, provided only that he might remain forever on the mountain with the Lord.

But Peter must descend from the mountain. For the time being, the poor Lord must be followed, and Peter must imitate the one who said: “Foxes have holes, and the birds of the air nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew VIII, 20).

He must be imitated in the torment of the cross, with the form of the cross inverted and turned upward; and thus the face of Christ must be gazed upon eternally, without any temporal failing. Nor did blessed Peter himself then reject this, for although he wished to remain with the Lord on the mountain, he nevertheless asked his will concerning the fixing of the tents.

For he said: “Lord, if you wish, let us make three tents here.” The consequent meaning is: “If you do not wish it, let us not make them. If you wish it, let us remain; if you do not wish to remain, let us descend.”

The text continues:

## 18

“While he was still speaking, behold, a luminous cloud overshadowed them. And behold, a voice from the cloud saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew XVII, 5).

Come now, blessed Peter: your concern with fixing the tents has been removed. Moses has departed; Elijah has departed—the men for whom you wished to make tents. They were servants, not lords. They had come not to give orders, but to fulfill what was right by listening.

The one who remains is the Lord; the one whom you have followed is the beloved Son. In him alone the Father was well pleased.

Certainly Moses could be called a son of God, and Elijah could be called one also. Moses was beloved by God, and Elijah was beloved by him; God was pleased with Moses, and he was pleased with Elijah. Yet in comparison with this one who was born from the substance of the Father, neither Moses nor Elijah is a son; neither Moses nor Elijah is beloved by God; neither Moses nor Elijah is accepted.

Rather, as the paternal voice taught: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Therefore, listen not to Moses, not to Elijah, but to him.

Moses had commanded that tents be made, but Christ commands that the Church be built. Listen, therefore, to him, venerable Peter, who appointed you not a maker of tents but a shepherd of his sheep.

What, brothers, do we think is signified by the luminous cloud, except the grace of the New Testament? Even before the Mediator’s coming, as it is written, “dark water was in the clouds of the air”—that is, obscure knowledge of words in the law and the prophets. But now the doctrine of the New Testament is not in a dark cloud; through a luminous cloud, the paternal voice thunders with clarity.

And it should be noted that the luminous cloud holds and overshadows Moses and Elijah; it removes them and conceals them. Yet although it holds and conceals Moses and Elijah, Moses and Elijah no longer sound forth from the cloud in which they lie hidden. The Father alone speaks through the cloud. The luminous cloud alone expresses the paternal voice.

Thus the grace of the New Testament overshadows and preserves the law and prophecy; it conceals and holds them. It overshadows them in the letter and preserves them in the spirit. It conceals them in figures and holds them in mysteries. In this way, whatever the law and prophecy say, although it must be observed spiritually, is received.

O how many things the law and prophecy spoke concerning the future grace of the New Testament before the Redeemer’s coming in the flesh, when the water was dark in the clouds of the air!

But when the time came for the luminous cloud, when the luminous cloud overshadowed Moses and Elijah, Moses was silent and Elijah was silent. Through the luminous cloud alone the paternal voice resounded: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.”

## 19

“And when the disciples heard this, they fell upon their faces on the ground and were very much afraid. But when they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one except Jesus alone” (Matthew XVII, 6).

That voice, which struck the disciples’ ears—whether the Lord himself moved the substance of the cloud, or did so through an angelic creature—nevertheless sounded through the cloud.

Because it came from the cloud which cast the disciples down upon the ground, it was made like thunder, just as on that occasion when, as his passion approached, the same Son said to the Father: “Now my soul is troubled, and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But for this reason I have come to this hour. Father, glorify your name.”

Then a voice came from heaven: “I have both glorified it and I will glorify it again.” The crowd standing there and hearing it said that thunder had occurred (John XII, 27).

But why is it that, when the crowd heard thunder there, it did not fall down, whereas here the disciples fell upon their faces? Is it not because there pride was afraid, while here humility trembled? Nor does humility tremble without reason, since it received the reward of so great a fear.

Therefore the Lord immediately approaches, touches the disciples, commands them to rise, and orders them not to be afraid. Yet these gifts also suggest something of spiritual grace to us.

It is as though the Lord were saying openly to the disciples:

“It would have been right to fear if the voice had commanded you to listen to Moses, or had urged you to imitate Elijah. One of them killed twenty-three thousand sinners in a single day and showed no mercy; the other slaughtered the prophets of Baal without any compassion and burned two captains of fifty men, together with their fifty soldiers—one hundred men in all—with heavenly fire.

“But because I am proclaimed as the one to whom you must listen—I who justify the publican confessing in the temple, receive the apostle who denied me, release the adulterous woman sentenced to stoning, and sanctify the repentant thief upon the cross—why are you afraid in an unfamiliar manner?

“Let there be fear in the law, but love in the Gospel. For there is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John IV, 18).

The text continues:

## 20

“And as they were descending from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying: Tell no one of the vision until the Son of Man has risen from the dead” (Luke XVII, 8).

They did not descend from the mountain immediately after Moses and Elijah had been taken away from the sight of the Lord and the apostles. Rather, as another evangelist relates, they remained there that same night and came down onto the plain on the following day, while the crowds were waiting for them.

But I do not know, brothers, whether they experienced the night who had been permitted to see such light. Although that light, being bodily, was removed from the eyes of the flesh, it nevertheless remained in their hearts, where, being incorporeal, it suffered no setting.

Thus blessed Moses also, contemplating the inner light within, felt neither hunger nor thirst nor darkness for forty days and nights. So greatly did the light that had shone upon him expand the sight of the inner man that he could even see those things which God had made in the beginning, before man existed.

That is the very light which shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. Why was this? Because “men loved darkness more than light” (John III, 19).

The persecutors of Christ could not see this light, and therefore they reached the point of putting him to death, blind. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians II, 8).

They could have known it if they had been able to reach the vision that occurred on the mountain. But if that had happened, Christ’s birth among us would have profited us nothing.

That is why he sternly warns the disciples not to make this vision known to anyone before his resurrection.

Finally, when the passion of the merciful Redeemer was at hand, Pilate heard him say: “My kingdom is not from here” (John XVIII, 36), and also: “Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice” (ibid. 37). From these indications, he supposed that this man was the Son of God and repeatedly sought to rescue and release him.

That is why he ordered him to be scourged, clothed in purple, and crowned with thorns, so that by this very vision, full of mockery, he might satisfy the rage of the Jews and turn them away from killing him.

If, then, Pilate, troubled about his power by such slight indications in his words, wished to release him on the basis of so many and such great arguments, what would he have done if he had been able to know how Christ had appeared on the mountain before the three disciples? I believe he would have regarded as nothing the very power of Caesar that he feared.

Therefore the merciful Redeemer forbade the disciples to reveal to anyone the one whom they recognized, so that he might be despised as unknown, seized, bound, scourged, spat upon, struck with blows, crowned with thorns, crucified, killed, and buried.

Thus the lost sheep might be sought, found, and, once found, placed upon the shoulders of the merciful shepherd, so that when the shepherd rose from the dead, the found sheep might be carried with the shepherd to heaven—he who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

---

## The Life of Saints Paldo, Taso, and Tato by Saint Ambrose Autpert, the Beneventan Abbot

*(From volume VI of Ferdinando Ughelli’s Sacred Italy, in Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order, century III.)*

### Preliminary Observations

[Col. 1319C] **1.** Paulus Warnefridus, deacon and monk of Cassino, writes as follows about these Acts and their author in Book VI, chapter 40, of *The Deeds of the Lombards*:

“The monastery of the blessed martyr Vincent, situated near the source of the river Volturnus and now resplendent with a great community, had already been built by three noble brothers—Tato, Taso, and Paldo—as the writings of the most learned Autpert, abbot of that same monastery, indicate in the volume he composed on this subject.”

More about Saint Autpert, or Autpertus, may be found under the year 778, when he is said to have died.

**2.** In his diploma, Charlemagne calls the holy men Paldo, Tuton, and Taso. Some likewise depict him as Tuton, and the author of the *Life of Saint Thomas, Abbot of Farfa*, calls him Baldon.

**3.** The monastery of Saint Vincent was once extremely celebrated. It was situated in the province of Samnium, or Benevento, at the source of the river Volturnus, about twelve miles from Cassino.

In the *Chronicle of the Vincentian Monastery*, various fragments of which were published by Andreas Chesnius in volume II of the *History of France*, many matters worthy of praise are related.

Autpertus and Josue, most holy abbots, flourished there after the holy founders of the monastery. Josue flourished in the ninth century, when nine hundred monks of the same monastery were also martyred by the Saracens.

In the eleventh century the venerable abbot Hilary also flourished; he is said to have performed miracles after his death.

The same monastery was governed by Nicholas of Fractura, a doctor of canon law and formerly a monk of Cassino, who illuminated the rule of Saint Father Benedict with commentaries in the year 1298.

According to the testimony of the distinguished man Angelo de Nuce, abbot of Cassino, in his notes on the *Chronicle of Cassino*, Book I, chapter 4, this monastery now breathes solitude and dread on every side, deprived of all monastic observance and entrusted only to a commendatory abbot.

**4.** It is clear that the rule of Saint Father Benedict was imposed upon the monastery from its foundation. At that time no monasteries were founded except according to its prescription.

Below, in section 18, Autpert praises the rule of Saint Father Benedict. In the diploma of Charlemagne reported in the *Life of Saint Autpert*, the king grants the Vincentian monks permission to elect an abbot according to the rule of Saint Benedict.

## Prologue of the Author

[Col. 1319D] **1.** The first parent of the human race, made in the image of God and placed in the paradise of delight, was admonished by Life itself, which is God, to keep the commandments of life; and, lest he should regard this lightly, he was threatened with death.

But he despised these commands, willingly abandoned the Creator, and followed the destroyer.

God, however, who, being truth, does not know how to lie, subjected him to the death with which he had threatened him. For he had said to him and to his wife: “On whatever day you eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall die by death” (Genesis II, 17).

This sentence clearly indicates not only the death of the body but also the death of the soul.

But because the most merciful God saw that man had been miserably deceived by the serpent’s persuasion and that he was a creature made from fragile material, he did not wish him to remain condemned forever.

Thus it came about that the only-begotten Son of God took flesh and died for us, so that the death of the soul would no longer reign in us, and so that what we had lost in Adam we might receive again in Christ.

Hence it is written: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Galatians IV, 4).

But none of us can express in words the ardor of love with which he did this for us. For the Son of God himself says: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John III, 16).

Paul again says: “He loved me and gave himself for me.” Concerning him he says further:

“Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized; rather, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and being found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross” (Philippians II, 6).

Living among men in this human form, in every respect as a man except sin, he showed them the way by which they could return to the joys they had abandoned.

But if we ask what this way is, let us attend to the Lord speaking in the Gospel. He says: “I am the way, and no one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV, 6).

Behold, we have heard the way by which we may return to our homeland. Let us now see how we should direct our steps so as to walk upon it.

“Whoever,” says John, “claims to remain in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (1 John II, 6).

It is pleasing to contemplate these footprints of Christ: the steps by which he walked in the flesh for us.

To say nothing of the other things fully narrated in the Gospel, he proceeded from baptism to temptation and fasting, from fasting to preaching, from preaching to insults, from insults to scourging, from scourging to spitting, from spitting to the cross, and from the cross to burial.

These are the steps of God upon the earth, concerning which the Psalmist says: “The steps of my God and King were seen as he entered” (Psalm LXVII, 25).

Declaring that these steps must be imitated, Peter says to the faithful: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps” (1 Peter II, 21).

The Way itself indicates that he must be followed through these sufferings, saying: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke IX, 23).

And Paul says: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians VI, 14).

These steps enter the narrow way that leads to life. They walk upon the asp and basilisk and trample the lion and the dragon. The apostles walked in these steps, and the martyrs and confessors followed them.

The perfect monks walked in these steps, to whom the Lord says particularly: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew XI, 29).

**2.** But because we have come into the time of which the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel, “Iniquity will abound, and the charity of many will grow cold” (Matthew XXIV, 12), and because, according to the judgment of the Apocalypse, we see monks who are not at all fervent but—what must be mourned—lukewarm, we place before the minds of our hearers three men recently converted to Christ and tested according to evangelical perfection: Paldo, Taso, and Tato, worthy to be compared with the sweat and labors of the holy Fathers.

Thus those who, being lazy and languid, complain that they cannot imitate our ancient Fathers may blush when they recall the life of these recent converts.

I undertake to write about them not out of a rash impulse, but following the instructions of my abbot. I set down in writing only those things for which witnesses still exist who affirm that they heard them from these men.

## Here Begins the Life

[Col. 1321D] **3.** Three men of noble birth, closely related by blood—Paldo, Taso, and Tato—were Beneventan. Paldo, the elder, was born of one brother, while Taso and Tato were born of the other.

Stirred by the evangelical voice and inflamed by divine love, they formed one judgment, one plan, and one vow: to leave their homeland, wealth, and parents; to follow the naked Christ naked; to fight naked against the naked adversary; and, as they desired, to seek the province of Gaul.

There, led by the body but not by the mind, they intended to seek different monasteries and submit the necks of their minds to Christ’s gentle yoke.

They foresaw that they should do this diligently so that, for Christ’s sake, they might not enjoy bodily even a single remaining sight.

What more is there to say? Just as they had conceived it in heart and mind, they prepare their journey. They make no delay and offer no postponement.

But fearing the bonds of their fleshly parents, which always become an impediment to those converted to Christ, they deceive their eyes by a pious pretense, yet in such a way that they do not incur the crime of lying.

For they say that they wish to go to Rome, commend themselves to the intercessions of the chief of the apostles, Peter, and kiss his desired threshold. And this they did.

As befits noblemen, they load animals with provisions, prepare horses for riding, and strengthen themselves with the services of attendants. Knowing what they intended to do—known to themselves and to God alone—they set their feet upon the road.

A venerable stock, from a most exalted parent,

Shone first, like the light of day, from the world’s beginning.

From purple birth Benevento received this honor;

By right it drew from the city men who would bring salvation.

With serene hearts they seek to climb the realms above;

Worthily they bear the sacred signs on behalf of God’s law.

They trample all earthly things, scorning treasures as dung.

Rejoice to offer magnificent praises to God,

To whom belong salvation and power,

The good and unconquered King.

**4.** But when they had crossed their own boundaries and entered the province of the Marsi—

[Note: [Col. 1323D] A province of Latium beside Lake Fucinus, called Valeria, in which Saint Equitius the abbot flourished. Paul the Deacon writes in *The Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 20: “The province of Valeria, to which Nursia is joined, lies between Umbria, Campania, and Picenum, and on the east touches the region of the Samnites . . . I therefore think that the region of the Marsi should also be counted within the province of Valeria, because it is not described by the ancients in the catalogue of the provinces of Italy. But if anyone proves by sound reasoning that this was a province in its own right, his reasonable judgment must in every respect be retained.”]

—they dismounted from their horses and told the boys to return home with the horses and the things that had been brought.

They said that this was because they had made a vow that the three of them alone should go to Rome on foot.

As the attendants wept and mourned, the three commanded them with the authority of masters to depart.

After they had gone away, while the aforesaid servants of Christ continued along the road, poor men covered in cheap and torn garments met them.

Already inflamed with love of poverty, they said among themselves:

“Let there be nothing in us that the world honors, nothing that a robber can seize. Let us remove these garments, give them to the poor, and clothe ourselves in their cheapest and dirtiest clothing.”

From this, let those who claim the name of monk understand how great a crime it is to live under the poor Christ while walking in elegant clothing but not in elegant conduct.

For behold: the men through whom this monastery began its existence, clothed in such garments, gave the beginning of their conversion.

The world falls toward the depths and leads the wretched to Tartarus.

Let us change our garments; God, instruct our minds.

Let there be nothing that the strong man, thief, or robber can take away.

**5.** To return to the subject: they continued the journey they had begun and arrived at the monastery of the glorious Mother of God Mary, which is in the Sabine region. There the venerable man Thomas was abbot.

[Note: [Col. 1324D] The account of Thomas, the restorer of the monastery of Farfa, is given under the year 715, where this pilgrimage of the saints is described at length.]

I have heard from many people that, once established in the regions of the East, he devoted himself to prayer at the Redeemer’s tomb for so long—as he himself related—that he obtained what he had asked for in his prayers.

Finally, they say, one night, when he was exhausted by prayer and overcome by sleep, someone appeared to him carrying in his hand a bread of extraordinary beauty. He said to him: “Take this bread and depart. But know that you will never have less of it.”

From then on, as those who had seen him say, he was a man of such great contrition that he could scarcely speak about God without tears.

When he had received the aforesaid servants of God as guests, as is the custom of monks and good Christians, he proceeded with the brothers to wash their feet according to the Lord’s command, as was his custom.

But those who had arrived covered their delicate and fair limbs with cheap and dirty garments, while presenting an elegant and carefully arranged appearance of face.

For this reason, their secret could not remain hidden from the eyes of the man of God.

**6.** When the duty of charity had been completed and the course of the night had passed, as dawn was beginning the day, he privately questioned them in gentle speech: who they were, where they came from, and why they had arrived.

He asked whether they might perhaps be suffering some disadvantage or had fled after committing a crime, promising that he would provide whatever assistance he could—provided only that they confess why they had chosen to undertake so great a deception.

At this they were astonished. Seeing that their plan could not be concealed from the elder, they accepted his counsel and related everything in order: who they were, where they came from, why they had arrived, what they had done, whose sons they were, what their names were, how they wished to go to Rome and then seek the regions of Gaul.

They bound him with many entreaties not to become an impediment to their purpose.

At this the venerable old man sighed and said:

“By no means, sons, do I wish to hinder you in this most praiseworthy purpose; rather, I wish to help you. Nor will I leave you for the time being. I shall travel with you for a while, and you will have me as your companion on your journey as far as the threshold of the apostles.”

The man full of God desired to become a participant in their journey for this reason: so that, as he in fact did, he might recall them from the length of that journey by his salutary counsels.

No one who sees this monastery is unaware that this happened by God’s providence.

By their appearance, form, and gift he recognizes their doctrine;

The kindly Father revives them with counsel and lightens their burden by service,

So that they may not fear, may find favor, and may discover that the difficult labor is made easy.

**7.** In the meantime they traveled together, as the elder wished, and, shedding many tears, entrusted their devotion to the intercessions of the apostles.

When their prayer was completed, the aforesaid Father, whose memory is revered, began to admonish them in persuasive words to return with him to the monastery.

They should remain with him for a while and learn their intended discipline by seeing and practicing it; then, at last, they should hasten wherever the Lord wished to call them.

To use his own words:

“Listen, sons, to my counsel. Return with me to the monastery which I serve. Because of the ardor of your desire, although this is outside the monastery’s custom, I shall receive you within, so that you may eat together with the brothers, sleep together, devote yourselves together to prayer, and go out together to manual labor.

“Tested by these exercises, you will learn in what ways you can fulfill the purpose of a monk.”

As he said these and similar things, they gave their assent and returned with him to the monastery, where they remained for a few days and were fully instructed.

Behold, blessed Rome, they seek you together while seeking Peter’s threshold:

The brothers and the faithful old man,

Whom the very ship of faith bears along the shores.
