**8.** It happened that, while the father of the two brothers—namely Tato and Taso—was searching for them here and there with their other relatives, they came to Rome at a very rapid pace.

When they diligently searched for them and could not find them there at all, they heard from people who spoke that the brothers were in the monastery of the glorious Mother of God Mary.

Then, driven by the goads of even greater love, they almost flew across the intervening distance and reached the aforesaid monastery.

They asked the aforesaid Father of the monastery to present the brothers before their eyes.

But the venerable old man, persuasive as he was in speech, urged the brothers to come out. When they resisted, he compelled them to obey his command.

As soon as they had gone out and their parents saw them, they began to weep bitterly. Raising their voices, they said to them:

“Why have you left us sinners as though we were dead? Why have you abandoned care for our souls? Is there no feeling of affection in you, no compassion for your relatives?

“We beg you,” they said, “we beg you, and by God, the Creator of heaven and earth, we entreat you not to abandon us. We are ready to convert to Christ and to leave the world completely.

“If you refuse, we call heaven and earth to witness that God will demand our blood from your hands.”

But although the brothers were not at all moved by these words, tears, and sobs, and said that they intended to seek Gaul as they had promised God, the old man is reported—so that we now clearly understand the reason—to have addressed them as follows:

“Take confidence, sons, take confidence, and rely upon the mercy of God. For if you now lend an obedient ear to my counsels, many will enter the heavenly kingdom through the example of your deeds.

“Listen, sons of men; listen to your father’s counsel, and do not reject the entreaties of these people. If you wish, I shall show you a place prepared for you by God.

“For I hope in the Lord that there God will fulfill your desire, and that there he will make you bear fruit acceptable to God. Learn the sign of the place and hasten to it as quickly as possible.”

Neither their father, by his admonitions, nor their parents, by their lamentation, moved them.

Rather, they rightly declared that they despised their homeland and nation,

Rejecting soft things and enduring hard things for Christ.

9. Now, beloved, there is a place to which I desire you to go, in the region of Samnium, on the bank of the river Volturnus, where it takes its rise at a distance of about a thousand paces. At that place there stands an oratory dedicated in the name of Christ’s martyr Vincent; on both sides of the river, however, is an extremely dense forest, which provides habitation only for wild beasts and hiding places for robbers. But the almighty Lord, whom you desire to serve, will preserve you unharmed in that same place and will make it peaceful and secure for all travelers, free from fear of robbers. He will also make it abound in cherry trees, bushes, thorns, and fruit-bearing trees. “Go,” he said, “my sons, and remain in that place without fear of anyone.”

The father urges them to go and shows them paths accessible to none,

Among many trees, where the rivers are adorned with beautiful foliage,

And mountains cold with mournful winds and snows.

10. Softened, then, by these and similar words from the rigidity of their obstinacy, and attending as though Christ were speaking through the elder, they recalled the Apostle’s saying, “Let no one seek his own interests, but those of another” (1 Cor. 10:24). They withdrew their minds from what they had begun, received a blessing from him, and set out on their journey. They arrived at this place where we live, carrying with them no provisions for the body except food for the journey in a small basket, already mindful of that command which says, “Do not be anxious about what you shall eat or what you shall drink” (Matt. 6:31), and, “Do not be anxious about tomorrow” (ibid., 34). But he who rises like a compassionate father on behalf of the poverty of the needy and the groaning of the poor, and who promises such things to those who act in this way, saying, “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (ibid.), seeing their faith, quickly came to their aid by giving them provisions.

Three undertake the journey; they bring nothing here but their bodies.

Christ is their provision, food, shelter, and mercy.

The sacred law of God is their light by night and day.

11. When they reached, as has been said, this place in which we dwell, they lacked everything necessary for the body’s use. They immediately lifted their minds to him in whom and through whom all things live. At last they entered the oratory, performed the office of divine praise, and, when night came, laid down their limbs for rest. But why do I say “for rest,” when they merely placed their bodies upon the ground, putting stones beneath their heads after the custom of the patriarch Jacob? Yet I do call it rest: although the flesh wastes away, the spirit grows fat.

And behold, after a short interval, a certain unknown man came to them in the silence of night. Knocking at the royal door—that is, the door of the oratory—he said, “Who is resting in this place?” At the voice, the venerable Taso sprang up and silently came to him. The man said to him: “I have heard from those who told me that pilgrims are staying here. Therefore, coming from my shepherds, I have brought a bushel of flour and wine. If you have somewhere to store what I have brought, take it.”

Then Taso, finding some small vessels, received what was offered as though it had been given him by God. After the man departed, no one ever discovered who he was who had so gratefully offered this gift. From these signs it is clear how great was the perfection with which those men began, through whom almighty God was pleased to raise this place to such excellence and magnitude.

An angel approached and said, “Who is resting here?”

Taso sprang forth silently, with grateful heart;

Giving him gifts—wine and fine flour—the angel went back outside.

12. Persisting earnestly, then, in this poverty of Christ, their life—which God had determined to display as an example to many—resounded far and wide. It could no longer remain hidden, like a lamp placed upon a lampstand. When many desired to imitate their life, a multitude of brothers began to flock to them.

Sacred accounts report that, far and wide, he governed his charge among three hundred companions and won the palm of warfare;

And they receive many drawn from the mighty whirlpool.

13. The first to preside over the sacred flock was Paldo, a servant of God. He was altogether most gentle, and in all his actions showed what he preached aloud to his subjects. He was so much a lover of Christ’s poverty that he did not burn, like worldly men, with desire for earthly riches.

It is reported that, to strengthen the brothers’ souls so that they might persevere in the poverty they had begun, he said: “Believe me, brothers: that monk who remains in this monastery and perseveres until the end will in no way suffer eternal punishments, but will possess eternal life. Moreover, this monastery of the holy congregation will remain until the end of the world for the preservation of souls.”

Some, not understanding the intention with which he said these things, deceive themselves with a false security [Note: Many peddle privileges of this kind; this distinguished place should correct them. Read Angelus de Nuce, chapter 17 of the Life of Saint Father Benedict.], believing that, even while living wickedly and acting contrary to the Rule of the Fathers [Note: In the Rule of Saint Benedict it is indeed called the Rule of the Fathers; the Roman Order also gives it this name where it discusses the appointment of an abbot. Read the Preface prefixed to this volume.], they can remain in this monastery and thereby be saved in the future.

Yet it is clear to everyone that whoever remains in this place while persisting in crime, and does not correct himself before the day of his final death, cannot pass into life. It must therefore be said to such people that the man of God did not pronounce a judgment contrary to the divine words; rather, he said that this judgment would remain applicable to those who wished to imitate the sober and chaste life and praiseworthy poverty of the members of that congregation.

Resplendent with a glorious crown and sacred diadem,

The venerable Paldo is first appointed abbot,

And sends countless souls above the heavens to Christ.

14. Meanwhile, as the crowd of brothers increased, they began to possess resources by which they could assist those whom they governed, contrary to their vow. Forgetting the saying of the aforesaid venerable Father Thomas—that many would be saved through them in this place—and earnestly seeking their beloved poverty [F. seek it], they attempted to cast away what they appeared to possess.

But when the multitude of brothers resisted them by divine judgment, they strove instead, in accordance with the Apostle, to seek not what was individually their own but what belonged to another, and to fulfill the saying, “I have become all things to all, that I might save all” (1 Cor. 9:22). It is reported that at that time there was great charity among them, great harmony of unity, and great compassion of brotherhood.

Certain things are indeed related about them that are worthy of miracles. But our purpose here has been directed solely toward recounting in writing the ways in which they conquered the world and the devil. For no miracle can be greater than that they abandoned the world with their whole minds.

Since many appear to share in miracles but by no means have their names written in heaven, at this time we seek not marvels in the Church but a perfect life. Therefore the Lord discourages the disciples when they rejoice in the subjection of demons, saying, “Do not rejoice in this, that the demons are subject to you” (Luke 10:20). What they ought to rejoice in, he makes clear by adding: “But rejoice that your names are written in heaven.”

It was a great virtue and a great and admirable sign to have raised so many from earth to heaven, from darkness to light, from death to life, and from exile back to their homeland, by the example of their way of life.

To continue my account: the often-mentioned venerable Paldo, a man fully perfected in evangelical perfection, having passed beyond human affairs, ended the course of his present life on the fifth day before the Ides of October, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 720, while Gregory II, of venerable memory, occupied the apostolic see. He had undertaken the governance of the sacred monastery in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 707, under the holy pope Sisinnius.

Behold, paradise, gather your blossoming flowers;

Paldo, who governed your reins for seventeen years,

Is blessed when he received your joys.

15. Taso succeeded him in the holy governance. He was younger in years but more ardent than all of them in his holy purpose.

Since it sometimes happens that a superior, if he neglects to consider and observe the weaknesses of the infirm, and wishes to constrain them more harshly—not according to what they are able to bear, but according to what the rigor of his discipline dictates—cannot lead them where he desires, something similar is known to have happened to him, for excessive zeal was able to dominate him.

When the brothers were altogether unable to follow him on a difficult journey, they abandoned and rejected him and appointed his elder brother in his place. Consequently, a report was sent to the Roman pontiff by both parties. When Pope Gregory II heard this, he condemned the action, noted that they had acted contrary to the canons, and declared that they had stretched out their hands against the Lord’s anointed.

He imposed penance upon them and deprived the action of its force. They were scarcely able to complete the penance imposed upon them, and only with great difficulty, because of the oppressive heat of the atmosphere.

After him Taso follows, retaining the governance of his companion [Note: Nevertheless, the list of abbots edited by Ughelli gives Tato rather than Taso. But Taso, who was named above in the third place, was indeed younger in age, although he preceded the other in governance.],

Younger in years, yet strong in wisdom.

This man was eager, strong, and ardent in the power of his heart.

16. But to show how grave was the crime committed by those who had rejected the shepherd chosen by God, almighty God, not appeased by this penance, immediately and without delay exercised judgment in retribution.

For they began one by one to depart from human affairs, so that one burial-place became the memorial repository of two or three bodies [Note: That is, one tomb; for “memorial” is often used to designate the tomb of a saint.]. This sentence spread in such a way until scarcely anyone remained alive who had been stained by the counsel of that offense. Nor did he himself remain long; he followed them in death.

We attach the adversity of this event to this work so that thereafter both shepherd and flock may remain strangers to such sedition. Although we do not dare to assert that they were condemned by this action, since they had begun to repent—the shepherd having erred through the fervor of zeal, and the flock through faintheartedness—it remains uncertain whether this judgment completely cleansed them from the guilt of the offense, or whether they were also released after death by the punishment of purgatorial fire [Note: Here is an explicit passage concerning Purgatory, of which Gregory the Great speaks in Book IV, chapter 39 of the *Dialogues*, and elsewhere.].

The aforesaid Father Taso died on the third day before the Ides of January, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 729, in the eleventh indiction [L., 12].

Placed over his brother, Taso bore the punishment of the offense,

Departing after eight years, to whom the office had yielded;

After him came the number of brothers slain by the plague.

17. After the plague of this disaster, as usually happens, some joyful and pleasant things followed, when the surviving Tato succeeded to the paternal office.

He was filled with charity, the mother of all virtues; most diligent in gathering souls; exceedingly fervent in zeal for God; abundant in piety; and most cautious in discernment. Like a mother over her children, he was always solicitous for his subjects, exercising himself most severely in labors while sparing the flock like a father. He was gentler than the gentle and exercised the zeal of discipline among the proud.

It is reported that, from the time he adopted the monastic habit, he never used baths, never washed his head, and never applied a razor to his head or beard. More difficult still, while laboring at manual work by day and devoting himself to continual vigils by night, he did not remove the burden of a breastplate worn against his flesh for as long as bodily strength permitted.

When, however, his exhausted and wearied limbs could no longer bear it, he secretly ordered a ring to be made for himself from the same material, and wore it until the day of his death. They assert that he refused bedding. It is also reported that he spent an entire week in fasting.

Filled with these and other virtues, and persevering to the end, he died perfected and in peace on the third day before the Ides of December, in the sixth indiction [L., 7], rejoicing with happy gladness, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 739 [Note: Ato succeeded Tato; Pope Stephen II is said to have sent him, together with Abbot Optatus of Cassino, to pacify Aistulf. Read Anastasius the Librarian.].

He who had first been rejected later became a worthy shepherd,

After eleven years had passed since Taso presided.

Persevering to the end, he completed a long span of time—

A man great in devotion and generous also in possessions.

18. Let this suffice concerning those whose examples and glorious deeds led us from the turmoil of the world to this place of rest.

But when we observe their fervor, we are compelled to say something about the lukewarmness of our own way of life. Although I fear to strike myself first by speaking, I shall nevertheless recount without shame the faults in which I lie and in which I recognize that those like me lie [Note: A pious shamelessness indeed. For posterity is scarcely less concerned to recognize the faults of its ancestors than their virtues; and shame at the crimes of others is a warning and an initial correction for their followers. The chronicler Trudo was moved by the same spirit. For this reason he set down both the virtues and the faults of the founders of his monastery in its history, so that, when the uprightness or wickedness of each was read, the upright might be inflamed by the example of their predecessors to advance ever further toward better things, while the wicked, shamed by the life held up before them, might at least turn back from their evil deeds.] Perhaps through this confession of humility God will grant me forgiveness, and salutary correction will be provided for them.

But where shall I begin? From what point shall I take up my speech? In every respect the holy purpose we have undertaken is violated by us, and scarcely anything remains to us except what the holy Father Benedict foretold (Rule, chapter 1): that by our tonsure and habit we lie to God.

Almost all of us appear ready for pride, contention, scandal, detraction, lying, cursing, injurious accusation, insolence, anger, bitterness and contempt, whispering, grumbling, gluttony, and the adornment of clothing. In short, to touch upon everything briefly, we hate the tribulations, persecutions, adversities, afflictions, sufferings, insults, humility, submission, and poverty through which the saints obtained the heavenly kingdom.

We seek what is ours, not what belongs to another; we desire false honors and consequently envy and bite one another. Whatever presently delights us, whatever sweetness there is, we seek with our whole minds. I do not know by what other path, our inner vision deceiving us, we can trust that we shall reach life while straying from the road of the saints.

For the Lord says: “Narrow and strait is the way that leads to life, and few are those who enter by it” (Matt. 7:14; Acts 14:21). The Apostle, however, said: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Rom. 8:17). And again: “If we do not suffer with him, neither shall we reign with him” (2 Tim. 2:12); and, “No one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (ibid., 5).

Come, our monks: what shall we say to these things? Shall we truly call either Scripture a liar—or ourselves liars? For to those who travel without a road, the labor of the journey is toil, not progress.

Or perhaps, deceived, we might say—speaking according to our misery—that the Lord said, “Blessed are those who are clothed in a cowl,” or “those who fast until the ninth hour”? By no means. He spoke instead of those who pretend to a false religion: “They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves” (Matt. 5:3). Of those who will be blessed he said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” and so forth.

Let us who recoil from these things consider the ways in which Scripture condemns what we now seem to pursue. For it is written: “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6); and, “Whoever slanders his brother shall be rooted out” (ibid., 11); and, “The revilers shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10); and, “You will destroy those who speak lies” (Ps. 5:7); and, “The accuser of our brothers has fallen” (Rev. 12:10); and, “Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. 5:22); and, “Woe to the one who causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble” (ibid., 18:6).

We are worthy of as many deaths as the evil examples by which we cause scandal. But let us, beloved brothers, attend to the examples of the poor of former times whom I have mentioned, lest we appear to run in vain. Let us labor with every effort, exertion, and strength, so that, drawn out from the precipices I have described, we may be able to walk along the road of the saints.

For if one good were perfectly present in us, all the evils enumerated would by no means be present. And what is this good, if not the new commandment? “I give you a new commandment,” says the Lord, “that you love one another” (John 13:34); and, “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

“For whoever loves,” says the Apostle, “has fulfilled the law” (Rom. 13:8); and, “Love is the fullness of the law” (ibid., 10). I say, however, that whoever loves his brother does not slander him but corrects him; whoever slanders does not love; and whoever does not love, as John teaches, remains in death (1 John 3:14).

If the root of this love were in us, all the fruits of virtue would ripen. But because it is lacking, they wither in the flower.

19. But since we have received from the compassionate Redeemer a period of reprieve in which to correct ourselves, let us act so that we may advance toward better things.

For it is not enough to have abandoned our homeland, wealth, and parents unless we also mortify ourselves. Let us therefore consider the day of death daily, and we shall not sin eternally. Let us contemplate the Lord’s sufferings, and we shall not grieve over present injuries.

Let us proceed along the path of this exile in such a way that, when we leave the body, we may find the angel of light, through whom, defended from the accuser, we may arrive there where all of us shall praise God with the angels without end; where there will be no fear of death, no sorrow, no pain, no bitterness, no darkness of gloom, but an eternal day, a blessed day.

Those who are found there will have no need of the light of the sun; illumined by the Lamb himself, they will shine like the sun in the kingdom of the Father. There they will be forever blessed, forever joyful, forever rejoicing, and forever reigning with Christ without end. There love will reign in each person, and God will be all in all—he who lives and reigns in perfect Trinity throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## Gregory III

Historical notice. 557  
Letters. 575  

**First letter** (Gregory’s letter to Boniface, archbishop).—He sends him the archiepiscopal pallium and instructs him how he is to use it. He grants authority to establish new bishoprics. He replies concerning a certain presbyter and his various questions. Same page.  

**Letter II** (Gregory’s letter to all bishops, presbyters, and abbots).—He commends Boniface, returning to Germany, to their care, so that they may assist him and, if anyone wishes to join him, not hinder him. 578  

**Letter III** (Gregory’s letter to the nobles and people of the provinces of Germany).—Since Boniface is returning to them, he urges them to obey him and to cast all pagan rites far away. 579  

**Letter IV** (Gregory’s letter to the bishops of Bavaria and Alamannia).—They are to receive Boniface appropriately, as acting in the place of the Apostolic See, and to assemble at the councils he has summoned. 580  

**Letter V** (Gregory’s letter to Charles Martel).—Concerning the defense of the holy Roman Church against the kings of the Lombards, who were harassing her with their arms. 581  

**Letter VI** (the same author’s letter to the same person).—On the same matter. 583  

**Letter VII** (the same author’s letter to Boniface, archbishop).—He approves the division of Bavaria into four bishoprics. He answers several of Boniface’s questions. He orders that a council be held beside the bank of the Danube. Same page.

## Saint Zacharias

### Letters of Saint Zacharias

917  

**First letter** (Boniface’s letter to Pope Zacharias). Same page.  

**Letter II** (Pope Zacharias’s letter to Boniface).—He replies point by point to the preceding letter. Same page.  

**Letter III** (the same author’s letter to Burchard, bishop of Würzburg).—He confirms the episcopal see established by Archbishop Boniface. 922  

**Letter IV** (the same author’s letter to the Franks and Gauls).—He praises them for what had been rightly established in the synod and urges them to continue obeying Boniface’s instructions. 923  

**Letter V** (the same author’s letter to Boniface, archbishop).—He sends pallia for three metropolitans and writes concerning two false prophets discovered in Francia. 925  

**Letter VI** (the same author’s letter to the same person).—He is surprised that Boniface now requests a pallium for one Grimo, although previously he had requested one for three. He refutes the accusation of simoniacal defilement with which he was charged. He delegates his authority to Boniface not only in Bavaria but throughout all Gaul. 927  

**Letter VII** (the same author’s letter to the same person).—Baptism administered by an unskilled priest with broken wording is not to be repeated. 929  

**Letter VIII** (the same author’s letter to Pippin, mayor of the palace, and likewise to the bishops, abbots, and nobles of the Franks).—He replies concerning various articles sent by Pippin through Ardoban. 930  

**Letter IX** (the same author’s letter to Boniface).—He orders that what he wrote in reply to Pippin’s articles be read aloud in the council, and that Aldebert, Godolsacius, and Clement be examined again. 938  

**Letter X** (the same author’s letter to Boniface).—He replies to three letters from Boniface, among other matters concerning the annual census of twelve denarii to be paid to the churches by each marriage of slaves; the proceedings of the Roman synod against Aldebert and Clement; and the establishment of a metropolitan see at Cologne. 939  

**Letter XI** (the same author’s letter to the same person).—He replies to the letters brought by Bishop Burchard, chiefly concerning the form and minister of baptism; certain wandering bishops and presbyters; the heresy of the Scottish presbyter Samson concerning baptism; the error of the presbyter Virgilius as well; and the metropolitan see being fixed not at Cologne but at Mainz. [Col. 1340] Finally, he permits Boniface to choose his successor. 943  

**Letter XII** (the same author’s letter to the various bishops of Gaul and Germany).—He praises their union with one another and with the Roman Church and urges them to persevere in their ministries with Archbishop Boniface, vicar of the Apostolic See. 948  

**Letter XIII** (the same author’s letter to Boniface).—He replies to Boniface’s letter and to his various questions, which he had posed through Lullus. 949  

**Letter XIV** (the same author’s letter to the same person).—The elevation of the see of Mainz to metropolitan status. 953  

**Letter XV** (the same author’s letter to the same person).—The privilege of the monastery of Fulda. 954  

**Letter XVI** (Boniface’s letter to Grippo, brother of Pippin, mayor of the palace). Same page.  

**Letter XVII** (Zacharias’s letter to the bishops of the Franks).—Concerning the establishment of harmony and peace between Pippin and Grippo, and the return of the body of Saint Benedict to the monks of Monte Cassino. 955  

**Letter XVIII** (the letter of Boniface, archbishop, to Pope Zacharias, sent through the presbyter Lullus).—He explains how he conducted himself in the matters Pope Gregory II had commanded him, and concerning the monastery of Fulda that he had built. 956  

**Letter XIX** (Zacharias’s letter to Austrobert, archbishop of Vienne).—He sends a copy of the synod held at Rome on 22 March and replies concerning what should be done with bishops ordained for money. Same page.  

**Letter XX** (the same author’s letter to Theodore, bishop of Turin).—It is not permitted for a son to marry a woman whom his father had received from the sacred baptismal font. 957  

Decrees. Same page.

### Letters of Pope Stephen

993  

**First letter** (Stephen’s letter to King Pippin).—He gives thanks for the promises made through Abbot Droctegang, who had been sent by Pippin to Stephen when Pippin had indicated that he wished to come to Francia. Same page.  

**Letter II** (the same author’s letter to the nobles of the Franks).—They are to support his petition before King Pippin and contribute their assistance to him in undertaking the cause of the Church. 995  

**Letter III** (the same author’s letter to King Pippin and his sons).—Since Aistulf delays restoring the cities and continues to harass the Church with new attacks, he begs the king to provide aid and earnestly to fulfill in reality the donation promised to Saint Peter. 996  

**Letter IV** (the same author’s letter to Pippin).—With Rome besieged by Aistulf and the Lombards, he writes a tearful letter in which he again implores Pippin’s aid with all his prayers. 999  

**Letter V** (the same author’s letter to the Franks).—It was sent in the name of the apostle Peter and of Stephen to the same people, seeking assistance against the Lombards. 1004  

**Letter VI** (the same author’s letter to Pippin).—He gives thanks for the liberation of the city and for the benefit conferred upon the Roman Church. Concerning the death of King Aistulf and his successor Desiderius. He asks Pippin to order Desiderius to restore the remaining cities of the Exarchate and the Pentapolis that had not yet been returned, in accordance with the pledge he had given. 1007  

**Letter VII** (the same author’s letter to the same person and to Charles and Carloman).—They are to compel Aistulf, king of the Lombards, who violated his oath to restore the cities and places granted to him, to fulfill his promises in justice. 1011  

**Letter VIII.**—Stephen’s grant concerning the hospice and house in Rome granted to Abbot Fulrad. 1013

## Paul I

Historical notice concerning Pope Paul. 1125  

Letters. 1135  

**First letter.**—Paul, deacon of the Roman Church, reports the death of Pope Stephen. Same page.  

**Letter II.**—Paul, pope, gives thanks to King Pippin and requests aid against the Lombards. 1137  

**Letter III.**—To King Pippin, concerning the defense of the holy Church of God and the monastery that he granted to Paul near Mount Serapte. 1140  

**Letter IV.**—Also addressed to Pippin, containing praises of thanksgiving for the rejoicing of the holy Church of God and requesting that he always strive for this. 1143  

**Letter V.**—Also addressed to Pippin, containing abundant blessings and praises of thanksgiving for the firm and unchangeable word of his promise and for his great perseverance in accomplishing apostolic causes. 1144  

**Letter VI.**—Also addressed to Pippin, containing thanksgiving and the steadfastness of the same pope’s faith: that no favor or fear might in any way separate him from his love or charity. 1146  

**Letter VII.**—Thanksgiving is rendered to Pippin for the envoys themselves and for how they were received together with the imperial envoys. 1148  

**Letter VIII.**—Also to Pippin, concerning the embassy of Bishop Remedius and Count Audecarius, and how he recovered part of the rights of Saint Peter from Desiderius, formerly king. [Col. 1343] 1151  

**Letter IX.**—Paul gives thanks to Pippin for the liberation of the Church and asks that he might be deemed worthy to receive from the sacred baptismal font his son, who had then been born. 1153  

**Letter X.**—To Pippin, containing thanksgiving and abundant blessings for his life and safety, as well as for those of Charles and Carloman; also a directive that he sent to the presbyter Marinus concerning the title of Chrysogonus and the books he sent him. 1155  

**Letter XI.**—Containing abundant praises and concerning the apostolic envoys and the Greeks staying in Francia, namely George and Peter. 1157  

**Letter XII.**—He gives thanks to Pippin for the defense of the Church, begging him to return his hostages to King Desiderius and confirm the treaties of peace with him. 1160  

**Letter XIII.**—To Pippin, concerning the defense of the holy Church of God, containing thanksgiving and abundant blessings for the preservation of the integrity of orthodox faith. 1162  

**Letter XIV.**—Pope Paul asks that King Pippin send his envoys to the region of Rome and inform him of his health and safety, how he had fared on the journey, and how the Lord had delivered his enemies into his hands. 1163  

**Letter XV.**—The pontiff gives thanks to King Pippin; concerning his health and that of Charles; concerning the presbyter Marinus; and concerning Ravenna, how wicked plots were being devised against it. 1164  

**Letter XVI.**—To the king, concerning the defense of the Church and the conference with King Desiderius in the city of Ravenna. 1166  

**Letter XVII.**—To the king, concerning a certain monk, Acosma, sent by the patriarch of Alexandria. 1168  

**Letter XVIII.**—Of the people and senate of Rome in general to Pippin, containing thanksgiving and treating of the letter that the king had sent to the same people concerning the preservation of faith toward the Roman Church and the lord Paul the pope. Same page.  

**Letter XIX.**—After prefacing thanksgiving for the exaltation of the holy Roman Church, Paul asks Pippin to send his envoy to Rome. 1170  

**Letter XX.**—Paul inquires about Pippin’s health and at the same time about his envoys who had been sent to the royal city. 1172  

**Letter XXI.**—Paul writes to Pippin concerning the presbyter Marinus and his wicked counsel, and concerning his consecration. 1173  

**Letter XXII.**—To Kings Charles and Carloman, concerning the letters sent by them and urging them always to strive with their lord father for the defense of the holy Church of God. 1174  

**Letter XXIII.**—To the same persons, whom Saint Paul thanks and for whom he prays for good fortune. 1175  

### Labbé’s Collection of Paul’s Letters

Same page.  

**First letter** (Paul’s letter to King Pippin).—Concerning his election to the pontificate, he promises that he will remain with his own people in the faith and concord that Stephen, his predecessor, had shown toward King Pippin. Same page.  

**Letter II** (to the same person).—Among other matters, he accuses King Desiderius of not restoring the cities promised to the Roman Church, and asks Pippin to compel him to return them; he also asks him not to trust the other letters that Paul had written at Desiderius’s urging concerning the release of his hostages. 1177  

**Letter III** (to the same person).—He praises Pippin and gives thanks that, when the legates themselves—his brother Remigius and Duke Autharius—arrived, King Desiderius restored some of the cities and properties of the Church and agreed to return the remainder at a fixed time. 1180  

**Letter IV** (to the same person).—He again complains about King Desiderius, because he did not provide the complete restoration promised to the legates, and concerning the threatening letter he had written. He asks Pippin to send three legates on the Church’s behalf. Same page.  

**Letter V** (to the same person).—Concerning the sacred table donated by King Pippin to Pope Stephen: by what rite it was offered in Rome by Pippin’s envoys [Col. 1344] at the confession of blessed Peter, and how it was received and consecrated by Pope Paul. 1182  

**Letter VI** (to the same person).—He gives thanks for the sabanum sent to him, in which Pippin’s daughter had been received after being washed in the sacred waters, and explains in what manner he received it. 1183  

**Letter VII** (to the same person).—He requests aid against the Greeks, who were reported to be preparing to attack Ravenna; he also asks Pippin to stir up King Desiderius and others to provide assistance. 1184  

**Letter VIII** (to Charles and Carloman).—He praises them and urges them to follow the example of their parents in protecting the Church. 1185  

**Letter IX** (to King Pippin).—The monks sent to Rome by Remedius, Pippin’s brother, to learn the art of psalmody have been entrusted to Simeon, head of the school of singers, as requested. 1187  

**Letter X** (to the same person).—He gives thanks for the faithful service rendered to the Roman Church. He praises the Frankish people and its kings and bestows abundant blessings. 1188  

**Letter XI**, or Diploma concerning the immunity of the monastery of Saint Hilary of Galeata, situated under the Church of Ravenna. 1189  

**Letter XII** (to John, abbot).—Concerning the church and monasteries that he established in his ancestral home under the title of Saint Stephen, pope and martyr, and Saint Sylvester, pope and confessor. 1190  

Letter of Paul, absent both from the Carolingian and from Labbé’s codices, to Egbert, archbishop of York, and Eadbert, son of the king of the English. 1195

### Letters of Stephen III

1248  

**First letter** (to Bertrada, queen consecrated to God).—He reports that Itherius, the royal envoy, had worked vigorously for the interests of the Church in the duchy of Benevento; for this reason he gives thanks and asks that Itherius’s loyalty be rewarded. Same page.  

**Letter II** (to the same woman and to King Charles).—Concerning Christopher and his son Sergius, who, together with Dodo and the other Franks, attempted to kill Pope Stephen. 1249  

**Letter III** (to Kings Charles and Carloman).—He congratulates them on being reconciled to fraternal harmony. He asks them to compel the Lombards to return what they had seized from the patrimony of the Church. 1251  

**Letter IV** (to the same persons).—He earnestly strives to dissuade either of them from marrying Desiderius’s daughter or from giving their sister Gisila in marriage to Desiderius’s son. 1253  

**Letter V** (to Carloman).—He asks him to become his spiritual co-father. 1257
